## 1:1 Introduction: J. N. J. D. Abraham Calovius's Illustrated Bible of the Old Testament: in Which I. The Emp
J. N. J. D. ABRAHAM CALOVIUS'S ILLUSTRATED BIBLE OF THE OLD TESTAMENT: IN WHICH I. The emphases of the words and the genuine meaning of the sayings are elicited from the sources, the context, and the analogy of Scripture: II. The principal versions are compared with the Hebrew text, the sincerity of which is vindicated everywhere: III. The expositions of both ancient and more recent interpreters are weighed, and the truer ones of the Fathers themselves, of Blessed Luther, and of other theologians are established in their own words: IV. The more difficult passages and textual, historical, genealogical, and other doubts are resolved: V. Apparent contradictions are discussed: VI. Various theoretical and practical questions are solved: VII. Prophetic oracles concerning CHRIST and his kingdom, and whatever else pertains entirely to the confirmation of the Evangelical faith, are asserted by design: VIII. The corruptions of the Jews and heretics, especially modern ones, are clearly refuted: IX. Grotian depravations and ψευδερμηνείαι (false interpretations) are submitted to a just examination and exploded; AND SO THIS IS ESPECIALLY AND DILIGENTLY PURSUED, THAT THE SINGLE LITERAL SENSE OF SCRIPTURE MAY BE ASSERTED AND CONFIRMED FROM EVERY SIDE, VOLUME II CONTAINING THE MAJOR AND MINOR PROPHETS, To which is subjoined VOLUME THREE exhibiting the Apocryphal books; With all the GROTIAN NOTES also inserted according to the wish of the learned.

AT DRESDEN AND LEIPZIG, At the expense of Johann Christoph Zimmermann, AT HILDBURGHAUSEN, BALTHASAR PENTZOLD PRINTED IT, IN THE YEAR 1719.

VOLUME II. CONTAINING THE MAJOR AND MINOR PROPHETS, To which is appended VOLUME III, exhibiting the Apocryphal Books; Also with the GROTIAN NOTES of scholars inserted throughout at their request.

TO THE MOST SERENE AND MOST HIGH PRINCE AND LORD, LORD JOHANN GEORG III, HEIR TO THE ELECTORATE OF SAXONY, DUKE OF SAXONY, JULICH, CLEVES, AND BERG, LANDGRAVE OF THURINGIA, MARGRAVE OF MEISSEN, AS ALSO OF UPPER AND LOWER LUSATIA, COUNT OF THE MARK AND RAVENSBERG, LORD IN RAVENSTEIN, &c. &c., MY MOST CLEMENT LORD.

THE GRACE OF GOD THE FATHER AND EVERY KIND OF BLESSING, JESUS CHRIST, THE WISDOM THROUGH WHOM PRINCES RULE, THE PEACE OF THE PRINCE, THE SALVATION OF GOD, THE PERPETUAL TREASURE OF THE HEART, THE INCREASES OF THE PRINCELY SPIRIT, AND THE MOST AMPLE WEALTH, AND WHATEVER AT ALL ORNAMENT A CHRISTIAN PRINCE AND RENDER HIM HAPPY, AUGUST, AND GLORIOUS, I PRAY AGAIN AND AGAIN FROM THE HEART TO THE MOST HOLY AND ALWAYS GLORIOUS TRINITY.

MOST SERENE PRINCE, MOST CLEMENT LORD.

Sacred literature is the unique delight, the greatest wealth, and the chief crown of glory for all the faithful, even for Great Princes and Kings. Let DAVID, the ideal of the best Kings and Princes, a man after God's own heart, be a lesson to us; to whom the word of the Lord was sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, more desirable than gold and much precious stone.

How sweet, he says, are your words to my throat, more than honey to my mouth: My soul has coveted, I have desired your justifications at all times: I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches. The law of your mouth is good to me, above thousands of gold and silver. Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz. Your testimonies are my eternal inheritance, because they are the exultation of my heart. I will rejoice over your words, as one who finds many spoils. Blessed are they who search your testimonies. Blessed is he whose pleasure is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates on his law day and night.

Nor did DAVID instruct his son and Most Serene Successor, SOLOMON, in any other way, whether by word or by his own example: which Solomon himself proclaims, and sets forth as an example to all parents; for concerning the wisdom of the divine word, which alone provides true wisdom, he testifies that he was thus admonished by his most wise Parent: Take hold of it, and it will exalt you, you will be glorified by it, when you have embraced it; it will give to your head an increase of graces, and a renowned CROWN will protect you. Therefore, the MOST WISE one likewise commends this Wisdom of the divine word to other mortals. The acquisition of it, he says, is better than the trade of silver, and of the first and purest gold; its fruit is more precious than all riches; and all things that are desired cannot be compared to it. Length of days is in its right hand, and in its left are riches and glory.

Wherefore David, about to die, as if in a Testament, enjoined this to Solomon above all 1 Kings II, 2. 3. 4. I am entering the way of all the earth, take courage, and be a man. And observe the charges of the Lord your God, that you may walk in his ways, that you may keep his Ceremonies, and his precepts, and judgments, and testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses: that you may understand all that you do, and whithersoever you turn yourself: that the Lord may confirm his words, which he spoke concerning me, saying: If your sons keep their ways, and walk before me in truth, with all their heart, and with all their soul, there shall not be taken away from you a man from the throne of Israel.

Concerning the delights of the Holy Scriptures, which those who are devoted to them experience in abundance, those most sweet similitudes by which the Holy Spirit renders them pleasing to us bear witness; for Scripture is compared to honey and the honeycomb, than which nothing is sweeter to our palate; to the tree of life, than which nothing is more pleasant; to manna, than which gift there was nothing more welcome to the Israelites when they were destitute of food in the horrid desert; to wine, than whose color, odor, and flavor nothing is more delightful; to water, than which nothing is more desirable to those who, like Samson, are extremely thirsty; to milk, than which nothing is sweeter in early infancy; to a garden, than which nothing is more agreeable. Therefore, the Bridegroom rhetorizes with most sweet words concerning the spiritual garden of our soul, inviting us into the same: Come into my garden, my sister, my spouse.

I have gathered my myrrh with my spices: I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk; Eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, O most beloved. By its rivers, as David testifies, we are inebriated from the abundance of the house of the Lord, and we are watered as with a torrent of pleasure. She herself, as Sirach is the author, feeds us with the bread of life and understanding, and waters us with the water of saving Wisdom.

If it pleases you to hear the Fathers, Irenaeus likes the comparison of Paradise to a garden of pleasure. It is necessary, he says, to take refuge in the Church, and to be educated in her bosom, and to be nourished by the Lord's Scriptures. The Paradise of the Church is planted in this world. Of every tree of Paradise you shall eat food, says the Spirit of God, that is, eat of every Scripture of the Lord. It pleased Chrysostom in a special homily concerning Paradise, or the garden, or the sacred Scriptures, in which many things are contained that delight with their own sweetness; which could not displease even the μισογράφοις (haters of writing) Papists themselves, as Jodocus Coccius is an example in his Thesaurus: It is indeed sweet, he says, the meadow and the garden; yet the divine reading of Scripture breathes much sweeter than either. For there it is possible to find flowers, but they wither in time: Here, however, occur sentences remaining in their native vigor. There the West Wind blows, here the breeze of the Holy Spirit breathes. There thorns hedge in the garden as a wall, here the providence of God renders the reader safe: There cicadas make noise with their shrillness, here the Prophets resound with sweet joy: There some delight is conceived from the very sight: Here, however, much utility is gathered from the very reading itself. A garden is circumscribed by some one place, but the divine Scriptures are carried about in every place of the habitable earth. A garden indeed serves needs according to the quality of the seasons: But the Scriptures in the winter time just as in the summer endure with leaves flourishing on all sides, and are weighed down by the burden of fruits. Let us therefore be attentive to the reading of the Scriptures. For if you are attentive to this, it will drive anxiety from you, it will bring incredible pleasure to your heart, having removed malice it will fix the roots of virtue in your soul, and among those turmoils of business, which fluctuate like the manner of waves agitating themselves, it will not allow you to be troubled by any disturbance. Although the sea may be agitated by storms, you sail in tranquility. For you have the reading of the Scriptures, which may moderate and govern you.

Cyril of Alexandria, praised by the same Coccius in his Commentary on the Right Faith in God, harmonizes with Chrysostom in the Greek Church: Just as farmers gather the most fragrant flowers at the opportune time from the fields, and having gathered them and skillfully arranged them in baskets, offer them to their masters; whom they soon embrace benevolently and with a grateful mind: So we, who have undertaken the duty of teaching, from the divine Scripture, as if from some field, do not exhibit for viewing the beauty of flowers that quickly wither, but [we exhibit] the fragrance of speech and doctrine which, through the Holy Spirit of piety toward Christ, contains an unfading charm, and with great sweetness and abundance redolent of its mystery; for it is written: We are the good odor of Christ to God.

We add a third from the choir of Greek Fathers, Olympiodorus: The Divine Scripture itself, he says, is like a certain fertile and fragrant field, and as it were a Paradise planted with the best trees, and having a hidden treasure. What forbids us to add a fourth, about two hundred and more years later than Olympiodorus, three centuries later than Chrysostom, and nearly six centuries later than Irenaeus, yet an excellent Doctor among the Greeks, and one in agreement with them, Damascenus, who thus excites us to the reading of the Holy Scriptures: Let us knock, he says, at that most beautiful garden of the Scriptures: that garden, I say, wondrously fragrant and sweet, endowed with the highest elegance, and resounding in our ears with the chirping of birds of every kind, both spiritual and divinely inspired, which touches our heart, soothes and mitigates it when affected by sorrow, and calms it when stirred by anger, and bestows eternal joy, etc. From the fountain of this garden let us draw perennial and most pure waters leaping up into eternal life. Here let us dwell with a certain insatiable pleasure and delight. For such is the grace of the Scriptures that it cannot be exhausted or consumed.

Nor was the mind of the Doctors of the Latin Church once any different. Let Ambrose be a witness, discussing the sweetness of Scripture in Ep. XLIV: "Divine Scripture is a sea having within itself profound meanings, the depth of prophetic enigmas, into which sea many rivers have entered. There are, therefore, also sweet and clear rivers, there are also snowy fountains, which leap into eternal life: there are also good discourses, like a honeycomb, and pleasing sentiments, which irrigate the minds of the hearers with a certain spiritual drink, and soothe them with the sweetness of moral precepts."

"Jerome to Celantia, Vol. I, p. 110. The broad and immense field of divine law extends. Which, blooming with diverse testimonies of truth, like certain heavenly flowers, feeds and refreshes the mind of the reader with wonderful delight. To know all these things always, and to revolve them with oneself, is a huge benefit for preserving justice. And again: The divine word is most rich, having all delights within itself. Whatever you wish is born from the divine word. As the Jews hand down, since manna, when they ate it, tasted according to the will

"of each one in the mouth. Gregory the Great writes thus concerning the Holy Scriptures: Holy Scripture generates the water of Wisdom in such a way that it both always refreshes those who drink, and yet does not cease to flow. The knowledge of Holy Scripture flows with such force that, while it touches the elect, it removes them from the love of this life and, by the force of its impetus, carries them over

"to those who are clinging to it. The Venerable Bede says: Divine Scripture is called bitter water, because it does not spare those who sin, but is sweet to the just, to whom it promises eternal

"rewards: And thus to some it is blessed water, to others cursed. Alcuin advises thus: We ought to rejoice in the reading of the Holy Scriptures, where we are fed and drink from the tree of life, which is planted by the streams of waters.

Theodulphus of Orleans sang thus concerning the books of Holy Scripture: This food satisfies the heart with eternal nourishment, and feeds the hunger for justice, the more it is possessed. This drink coming from the Paradise-born spring, which the more one nourishes, the more every good thing thirsts for it. The precious law of God it is, for what is more precious than that, which the fountain of life, the light and origin of good, gives?

If we listen to Radulphus Flaviacensis, who flourished in the tenth century; Holy Scripture is a table for us, and a spiritual refreshment, given to us for consolation against our enemies. With whom Berno of Reichenau in the eleventh century agrees: This is that table, filled with dishes of heavenly food: which confers rest to the weary, health to the infirm, recovery to the fallen, and strength to those standing in the faith. Ludolphus the Carthusian of Saxony in the fourteenth century also agrees: Holy Scripture is our food, and the bread of life and understanding, by which we are daily refreshed, lest we fail in the desert of this pilgrimage: Whence it is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

But not even the Jesuits themselves could deny this sweetness of the Holy Scriptures, although it is notorious that the Roman Pontiff is less than fair to the Holy Scriptures. It is pleasing to bring forward only one or two in confirmation of the matter. Hieremias Drexelius thus praises Basil the Great: He, having been enticed from the beginning by the studies of philosophy, when he truly tasted the sweetness of holier knowledge, spurned human arts and disciplines, and began to admire divine studies alone, and to embrace them with such affection that, having forbidden himself all use of bread and wine (so they say), he clung to sacred reading day and night, until he became master of more wholesome wisdom. He seeks his cook and kitchen in books, about to feast for whole days and whole nights without loathing. Concerning the Holy

“Regarding the praises of the reading of Holy Scripture, Bernard pronounces thus: Hence it is no wonder that sacred reading is so highly commended to all by Bernard. Reading, he says, seeks the sweetness of the blessed life, meditation finds it, prayer asks for it, contemplation tastes it. Reading places, as it were, solid food into the mouth, meditation chews and breaks it, prayer acquires the flavor; contemplation is the sweetness itself, which judges and refreshes. From these we can gather that reading without meditation is dry, meditation without reading is erroneous. Affection must often be drawn from the series of reading, and prayer must be formed, which interrupts the reading, and does not so much hinder it by interrupting, as it continually restores a purer mind to the understanding of the reading.

Cornelius à Lapide on Holy Scripture in the Song of Songs has it thus: Just as the honeycomb contains honey, and wine contains warm spirits, which it breathes into the one drinking: So Holy Scripture contains divine doctrine sweeter than honey, and warmer than wine.

And in the preface to the Commentary on the Pentateuch: The Royal Psalmist calls him blessed, not who pours forth God's utterances to others, but who meditates on His law day and night; this one, therefore, is like a tree planted by the streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season. For this purpose, indeed, God most especially willed that the sacred books be written for us, and proposed His word, that it might be a lamp to our feet, and give light to our paths, that walking among these most lucid gardens of pleasure and more than Alcinous's, we might be fed by the most delightful sight of heavenly fruits, and enjoy their taste. And truly, just as in Paradise, among the flourishing shoots of trees and flowers, or the glowing faces of apples, it is necessary for one passing by to be refreshed at least by the scent and color; and just as we see that one who walks in the sun, even for the sake of his mind, nevertheless becomes warm and is imbued with a redness; so the minds, senses, counsels, vows, and morals of those who religiously and assiduously read, hear, and learn the divine Scriptures must needs be tinged with a certain color of divinity and kindled with holy affections. And Jod. praises. Coccius, among other things, [cites] a writing which appeared in the year of Christ 900 under the title: Altercation of the Synagogue and the Church, in which these things are read: Just as a draught of wine liquor not only healthfully and sweetly refreshes the body, but also adds no small joy to the minds of those drinking: So the words of heavenly eloquence soothe the hearing of the listener or reader: So from the sweetness of spiritual grace they work the hope of eternal joys.

To these sentences of the Holy Fathers we append the praises of Holy Scripture by our B. LUTHER, analogous to these, which are read in Tom. I. Jenens. Germ. fol. 80: The holy Word of God has many names in Scripture, for the sake of its countless virtues and works, for it is truly everything, and almighty. It is called a spiritual sword, so that one may resist the devil and all spiritual enemies with it. It is called a light, a morning rain, an evening rain, a heavenly dew, gold, silver, medicine, clothing, ornament, and many such things. Thus it is also called bread, because the soul is fed, strengthened, grown, and satisfied by it, and one should not understand here only bare bread; for in the same way as Scripture expresses through bodily bread all kinds of food of the body, however precious they are: So also through spiritual Bread, all the foods of the soul, which are quite countless; for there are many kinds of souls on earth, and each one in particular does not always have the same need and aptitude, and yet the Word of God gives to all, who have any need, an overflowing satisfaction; for if all the food of kings that ever existed and could exist were in a heap, they could not be compared in the least to the smallest word of God. Therefore the Lord Christ calls it in the Gospel a Royal Feast, etc. And through Isaiah, a precious, choice, and magnificent meal. Thus far Megalander.

And for that reason, Basil the Emperor of Constantinople, with the same Coccius praising him, around the year of Christ 860, exhorted his son Leo in this manner: O son, just as tender plants irrigated by fountains grow green, and bear flowers and fruits: So your mind, irrigated by the studies of sacred letters, will grow more and more, and for fruits will produce excellent virtues. For the body is indeed fattened by foods, because they are crammed one upon another: but the soul is nourished and invigorated by holy discourses. But this is the difference, that the food of the body, sweet only to the palate and the tongue, both increases corruption, and is increased by corruption, and finally passes into corruption: but the nourishment of the soul brings everlasting joy to the mind, and produces incorruption, and leads to immortality. Meditate therefore throughout your whole life on these so fruitful discourses, that you may enjoy their great fruits, and wisely administer your kingdom.

Nor indeed do the sacred scriptures bring only delights and pleasures that are not worldly, but heavenly; but they also provide riches and inestimable treasures. In these are found those abundant riches of the grace of God, who is rich in mercy because of his excessive charity, with which he loved us: in them is that hidden treasure, for which all things must be sold, namely Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge: there we have gold ignited and proven, by which we are made wealthy: The words of the Lord, which are silver, examined by fire, proven and purified sevenfold. From them we have faith, which is much more precious than gold, which is proven by fire. Therefore they are deservedly desirable to us above gold. Concerning the treasures of Scripture, the golden mouth of Eloquence: Deservedly, he says, is the reading of the divine Scriptures compared to some treasure. For just as whoever wishes to take even a small fruit from it, produces for himself many riches; so also in Holy Scripture, even in a brief expression, it is permitted to find a varied force of meanings and ineffable riches. For neither is there a syllable, says the same Chrysostom, or a tittle in the sacred scriptures, in the depth of which there is not some great treasure. For indeed those who dig for metals do not remain on the surface, but when they have descended very deeply, and have been able to obtain fragments of gold, they separate them from the earth with great labor and diligence, and after that much labor they find some brief consolation for their labors. But if they show so much zeal for corruptible, uncertain, and harmful things: it is much more fitting that we, where riches cannot be taken away, and the treasure cannot be consumed, and one does not go astray in hope, should apply equal or greater zeal. Which St. Chrysostom inculcates again and again: Just as in gold mines, he says in homily XXXV on John, no one who understands the matter allows even the smallest vein to be omitted, as it contributes greatly to increasing riches: So in the divine Scriptures not one iota, or one apex, but not even half is to be passed over, but all things are to be investigated most diligently. This is our salvation, says St. Chrysostom again, homily X on Genesis. These are spiritual riches, this is security, if we thus fortify ourselves daily both through reading, and through hearing, and through spiritual dissertation. Augustine, a contemporary of Chrysostom, book 2 de doctrina Christiana, chapter 42, has it thus: As much less as is the abundance of gold, silver, and clothing which that people took with them from Egypt, in comparison to the riches which they later obtained in Jerusalem, which are shown especially in King Solomon: so much should be all knowledge, which is indeed useful, collected from the books of the gentiles, if it is compared to the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Gregory the Great, book 2 in Ezechiel, homily 18. Wisdom, he says, and the knowledge of spiritual doctrine are true riches, in comparison to which those things that can pass away are called false: Concerning these riches it is said through Solomon: A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise. But except for the fact that spiritual riches lead to the eternal fatherland, there is a great distance between them and earthly riches. Because spiritual riches, when spent, increase, but earthly riches are either spent and fail, or are kept and are not life-giving. Those who contain these true riches within themselves are rightly called treasuries. Our German Chrysostom, B. Luther, must also be heard, who, explaining Psalm CXLVII at verse 8, celebrated this treasure of the divine word thus: Hitherto he has given thanks to GOD for the benefits of temporal goods and worldly station: Here he gives thanks for spiritual benefits, which is without any measure greater and higher than temporal goods, although it does not have as glorious an appearance as temporal goods, but is of low esteem, namely GOD's Word, or preaching, that is the precious treasure which brings all salvation with it, both in this and in the other life, and so abundantly that whoever has it is joyful in it even in the highest poverty and misery, and would not give it for all the world's goods, but would much rather lose everything, even life itself, and would rather be in death with it than live in revelry without it; but there are few who truly have it. Therefore David has placed this benefit last, at the end, where a song should sound best of all. But who can express how great this benefit is? For who can recount all the virtue and power of the Divine Word? Since all Holy Scripture and preaching, and all Christian books, do nothing else but praise GOD's Word, as we indeed do daily by writing, reading, preaching, singing, composing, and painting. For this benefit remains, and keeps us ourselves too, when those other benefits pass away, and when we leave them behind through death, and part from one another; but this one does not leave us, nor does it part from us, but presses through death with us, and tears us out, and brings us into an eternal life, where there will be no dying, nor care of death.

Since these things are so, it is entirely worthy of cedar that which Francis Petrarch reported about ROBERT, King of Sicily, nearly three hundred years ago, that he was so delighted by sacred letters that he said to him under oath: I swear to you, Petrarch, that letters are much dearer to me than the kingdom, and if I must lack one or the other, I would more equably lack the diadem than sacred letters.

Finally, Holy Scripture brings not only delights and riches, but if, beyond pleasantness and utility, honesty, or rather honor and glory, be desired, no greater glory, no more eminent dignity, no more august crown can be expected than from Holy Scripture. For the King of Kings, CHRIST JESUS, who had the law of GOD in the bowels of his heart, the Hieropsalmist celebrates the GOD of glory: You anticipated him with blessings of sweetness; you placed upon his head a CROWN of precious stone. Great is his glory in your salvation: you will place glory and great beauty upon him. Nor indeed did DAVID value his royal crown as much as that which he commended to his August Son SOLOMON, celebrated by that very same King of all whom the sun ever saw—as the wisest and most opulent, so also the most glorious—above all worldly wisdom, above all temporal opulence, above all secular glory, and commended to all the faithful, even kings and other supreme heads. That indeed shines uniquely in sacred letters, is obtained uniquely through the study of sacred letters, and the wisdom of sacred letters sparkles more splendidly than all the gold and all the gems of the whole world. Those who are gloriously adorned in this age, and are truly blessed and august, are those whom God crowns with grace and mercies: but they will be adorned infinitely more gloriously, having attained the supreme degree of blessedness and the most august majesty, upon whom will be placed the crown of life, the crown of justice, the crown of glory: that incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading crown, which is reserved for us in heaven.

Hugo de S. Victore, interpreted by the Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide, celebrates the Blessed Virgin, because she crowned Christ with a crown of justice, situated in the ordering and balancing of the four passions of the soul, namely love and fear, joy and sadness, as if they were four precious stones; because he who has these four ordered is just, that is, composed, and he who has them unordered is unjust; but Christ assumed them most ordered from the most pure flesh of the Blessed Virgin, in whom they were supremely ordered and composed, because she lacked all concupiscence and perturbation. Since children for the most part take after their mother, and assume the disposition and character of the mother rather than the father. But these things are contrary to Holy Scripture, which does not make the Blessed Virgin free from all concupiscence and perturbation; nay, they are impious and blasphemous: in that they assert that Christ was adorned by his mother with these four affections, that he was crowned by his mother with a crown of justice, and for that reason they claim that the Son of the Virgin takes after his mother. For it was not from Mary that Christ received the crown of justice, but Mary received the crown of justice from Christ, her Redeemer, Savior, and Lord, and she was adorned with those precious gems of the principal affections of the soul, not in such a way that she was devoid of all vicious passion or concupiscence, but in such a way as human infirmity in this life allows; which not only the Dominicans—therefore called 'Maculists' by the Franciscans—acknowledge, proclaiming the opinion concerning the immaculate conception of the Virgin to be heretical and blasphemous, but neither did the Roman Pontiffs (to whom, however, the Parisian Jesuits, condemned for this reason for heresy by the Parisian parish priests, did not hesitate to ascribe THE SAME infallibility of judgment even outside a general Council, both in questions of law and of fact, which Christ himself had) Sixtus IV, Alexander VI. Leo X, Pius V, Paul V, Gregory XV could judge that dispute in no other way than by imposing silence on both parties, the Franciscans and the Dominicans alike, with most severe Bulls, yet considered as lighter bulls. But the Word of God, or Holy Scripture, procures for not only the Virgin Mary, but for all the faithful, the crown of the manifold grace with which the Holy Trinity adorns them in the kingdom of grace, and of the glory with which it will crown the elect in the kingdom of eternal glory: because it is the word of grace, the word of life and salvation, Spirit and life, and the power of God unto salvation: through which Jerusalem, that is, the Church,

With Jerome saying, after the manifold adornment, after the crown, after the abundance of gold and silver, after the garments and most beautiful cloaks, after the incredible beauty, she progresses into a Queen, who in the Apocalypse is described as a bride adorned and composed for her husband, of whom it is said in the Psalms: 'The Queen stood at thy right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety.' For there can be no other life, as St. Jerome again says in the Proemium to the Lamentations of Jeremiah, without the knowledge of the Scriptures, through which even Christ himself is known, who is the life of believers! He who wishes to be wise and blessed, as Lactantius warns, let him hear the voice of God, let him learn justice, let him know the sacrament of his own birth, let him despise human things, let him look up to divine things, so that he may be able

to attain. If you say to me, says Chrysostom, that [verse] from the Psalms: 'Blessed is he who fears God,' and you are able to know what it is that you are saying: you do not call the rich man, nor the prince, nor the handsome man, nor him who is strong in power, nor him who possesses magnificent houses, nor him who holds magistracies, nor him who obtains a kingdom, in short, no one else, except him who is pious and religious, who is held by the study of Wisdom, who fears GOD, blessed, not only because of future things, but also because of present things: for even in this life this man is more powerful than that one. Cornelius à Lapide himself celebrates a certain man, who described the life of Henry Suso, the author of the 'Horologium Sapientiae Aeternae' [Clock of Eternal Wisdom], breaking out into these words: 'If she were betrothed to me, Lord JESUS, a powerful Queen, that would be a joy to me.' Now therefore, eternal Wisdom you are the empress of my heart, and the parent of all grace. In you, I have an abundance of riches, honor, and power. I desire nothing else that this world possesses. He celebrates again and again the opinion of R. Simeon in Pircke Aboth: that there are three crowns, the crown of the law, the crown of the priesthood, and the crown of empire. But that the crown of a good name (from wisdom and an honest life) is far more illustrious and precious than all these. But he omits the chief crown: namely, the crown of glory: nor does he rightly prefer the crown of a good name to the crown of the law. For if a good name arises from the Wisdom of the divine word or the law, the crown of Wisdom and the divine word, the mother of that most precious crown, is to be preferred above all. Which crown of Wisdom furthermore also procures for us the crown of glory, as much more splendid than the crown of a good name as heaven excels earth, and divine things excel human.

Who, therefore, among the faithful devoted to God, will not love, will not pursue, and will not prefer far above all pleasures, all treasures, all crowns, and honors of the whole world, this Wisdom of the divine word, the procurer of such great delights, such great riches, such great crowns, dignities, and beatitudes? And for this reason, Most Serene Prince, I trust that the humble offering of the SECOND VOLUME OF THE ILLUSTRATED BIBLES OF THE OLD TESTAMENT will not be unwelcome, in which I have primarily endeavored to manifest and bring into the light Christ Jesus, who is the unique pleasure of our Spirit, the treasure of the soul, and the most precious crown of the heart, hidden as if in a golden urn within the Prophetic Scriptures. Whom, as the unique savior, Your Serene Highness is accustomed to express with your own hand from the Pandects of the Old Testament, and from that very ancient sacred writer, the ocean of all Prophets no less than Historians, the chosen Moses, so that it may be inscribed by the finger of the Spirit of GOD upon the altar of your heart: THE LORD IS MY BANNER. For this is that Jehovah the Lord, who appeared to Moses in the burning bush, Exod. 3. Who through Moses delivered the people from the hand of Pharaoh, c. XIV. who professed himself the Physician of Israel, c. XV. by whom the glory of the Lord was seen by the people. Manna given from heaven c. XVI. who was tempted by the people in the desert c. XVII. That Lord, whose exaltation on the wood of the cross Moses foreshadowed through the raising of the banner in the desert, on which the bronze serpent hung, Num. XXI. That Lord, who was given as a banner, to which those who fear GOD may run, because of the truth (promised to Abraham) so that they may be saved by the right hand of the Lord, Psal. LX. That Lord, who stands as a banner for the peoples, whom the nations seek, Isa. XI. and in whom the nations hope, Rom. XV. That Lord, in whom and through whom Joshua obtained victory against the Amalekites; that King of glory, the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle, Psal. XXIV. of whom Moses sang in his final Canticle, Deut. XXXIII. Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, O people, who are saved in the LORD, and the shield of your help, and the sword of your glory! Finally, THAT LORD, who was revealed to CONSTANTINE THE GREAT by a not dissimilar symbol, IN THIS YOU SHALL CONQUER, granted him a glorious victory.

MAY THIS BANNER OF YOURS, MOST SERENE PRINCE, be for Your Serene Highness a symbol of your trust in confession, a trophy of victories in battle and struggle, and a perpetual and proper sign of glorious exaltation in your rule. That this LORD may ever be for Your Serene Highness the Author and Finisher of faith, the bestower of victory, and the giver of glory, as I have prayed from the bottom of my pious heart, I present to Your Serene Highness the Holy Prophets, who prefer that august symbol, THE LORD MY BANNER, to all princes and all the faithful. For in this SECOND volume of the ILLUSTRATED BIBLES, I have, with the Lord’s permission, devoted my greatest efforts to ensuring that that LORD, whom the faithful Israelites have professed by their symbols, IN THE LORD IS OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS AND STRENGTH, likewise JEHOVAH ZIDKENU, OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS, then against others, and especially against the Judaizing Grotius, I might in turn vindicate the Prophets, so that in that firmament of HOLY LIGHTS (I understand the divine Prophets, and their most sacred volumes) that bright and morning star, that day-star, nay the Sun of righteousness, might shine and flash in the Church with its own splendor and native brightness, having driven away the deceits. I add, moreover, as companion lesser stars, the writers of the Apocrypha, and the books usually added to the O.T., in which, along with admonitions making for true Wisdom, also examples of heroes illustrious in faith sparkle, to which it is believed that the similar symbol WHO IS LIKE UNTO THEE AMONG THE GODS O LORD? inscribed on banners according to the initial letters, and commonly read as MACCABEE, gave its name; which are contained in the THIRD VOLUME of this Biblical work. And all these things I most humbly now present to the most gracious view of Your Serene Highness.

Illumine, MOST SERENE PRINCE, with the splendor of your grace and clemency this work, whatever it is, of sacred labor, which I acknowledge to be of itself very opaque and less worthy of the sight of so great a Prince: yet I will not rashly say (such is my confidence in the Lord) that it receives some light from the native light of the Prophetic Scripture shining in a dark place, with the Apostolic illustration added, and that it will shine, most illustrious, with the rays of Your splendor, together with the author, your most humble servant, I trust. May that great Light, in whom we have the light of life, and in whose light we see light, look upon you with the countenance of His grace, and enrich and gladden with all gifts and increases of Princely happiness, perpetually, with You, Most Serene Prince, your AUGUST Consort, and your twin most illustrious offspring, JOHN GEORGE THE FOURTH, and FREDERICK AUGUSTUS, for the hope, fruit, and singular joy of the most afflicted church! Which I shall not cease to implore with pious prayers

Of Your Serene Highness.

An indefatigable intercessor before God

ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, D.

Latin:

J. N. J. D. ABRAHAMI CALOVII BIBLIA TESTAM. VETERIS ILLUSTRATA: IN QUIBUS Emphases vocum ac mens dicto rum genuina e fontibus, contextu & analogia Scripturæ eruuntur: II. Versiones præcipuæ cum Ebræo textu, vindicatâ ubique hujus sinceritate, conferuntur: III. Expositiones cùm veterum, tùm recentiorum interpretum expendun- tur, veriores Patrum ipsorummet, B. Lutheri, & aliorum Theologorum propriis verbis stabiliuntur: IV. Loci difficiliora & dubia textualia, Historica, Genealogica, & alia expediuntur: V. Contradictiones apparentes di- scutiuntur: VI. Quæstiones variæ, Theoreticæ & Practicæ, solvuntur: VII. Oracula Prophetica de CHRISTO, ejusque regno, & quæcunque omninò ad fidei Evangelicæ confirmationem faciunt, ex instituto adse- runtur: VIII. Corruptelæ Judæorum & Hæreticorum, maximè modernorum, luculenter re- tunduntur: IX. Grotianæ depravationes & ψευδερμηνείαι justo examini sistun- tur & exploduntur; ADEOQUE ID IMPRIMIS SEDULO AGITUR, UT UNICUS LITERALIS SCRIPTURÆ SENSUS UNDIQUAQUE ADSERATUR, ET CONFIRMETUR, TOMUS II. CONTINENS PROPHETAS MAJORES ET MINORES, Cui subjungitur TOMUS TERTIUS Libros Apocryphos exhibens; Insertis etiam ex voto eruditorum GROTIANIS NOTIS universis.

DRESDAE ET LIPSIAE, Sumptibus Johannis Christophori Zimmermanni, HILDBURGHUSÆ, IMPRIMEBAT BALTHASAR PENTZOLD, ANNO M DCC XIX.

DRESDÆ ET LIPSIÆ, Sumptibus Johannis Christophori Zimmermanni, HILDBURGHUSÆ, IMPRIMEBAT BALTHASAR PENTZOLD, ANNO MDCCXIX.

SERENISSIMO ET CELSISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO JOHANNI GEORGIO III ELECTORATUS SAXONICI HÆREDI, DUCI SAXONIÆ, JULIÆ, CLIVIÆ, ET MONTIUM, LANDGRAVIO THURINGIÆ MARCHIONI MISNIÆ, UT ET SUPERIORIS, ET INFERIORIS LUSATIÆ, COMITI MARCÆ ET RAVENSPERGI, DOMINO IN RAVENSTEIN, &c. &c. DOMINO MEO CLEMENTISSIMO

GRATIAM DEI PATRIS ET BENEDICTIONEM OMNIGENAM, JESUM CHRISTUM, SAPIENTIAM, PER QUAM PRINCIPES IMPERANT, PACEM PRINCIPIS, SALUTARE DEI, THESAURUM CORDIS PERPETUUM, SPIRITUS PRINCIPALIS INCREMENTA, ATQUE OPULENTIAM LARGISSIMAM, ET QVÆCUNQVE OMNINO PRINCIPEM CHRISTIANUM ORNANT, FELICEM, AUGUSTUM, ET GLORIOSUM REDDUNT, A. S. S. ET SEMPER GLORIOSA TRINITATE ITERUM ITERUMQUE ANIMITUS PRECOR.

SERENISSIME PRINCEPS, DOMINE CLEMENTISSIME.

LItera sacra fidelium quorumvis, etiam Magnorum Principum & Regum unice sunt delitia, maxima divitiæ, & præcipua corona gloria. DAVID Regum & Principum optimorum idea, vir secundum cor Dei, documento nobis sit; cui verbum Domini dulcius erat super mel & favum, desiderabilius super aurum, & lapidem pretiosum multum.

Quam dulcia, inquit, faucibus meis eloquia tua super mel ori meo: Concupivit anima mea, desideravi justificationes tuas in omni tempore: In via testimoniorum tuorum delectatus sum, sicut in omnibus divitiis. Bonum mihi lex oris tui, super millia auri & argenti. Ideo dilexi mandata tua super aurum & topazion. Testimonia tua hereditas mea æterna, quia cordis mei exultatio sunt. Lætabor ego super eloquia tua, sicut qui invenit spolia multa. Beati, qui scrutantur testimonia. Beatus, cui in lege Domini voluptas, & qui in lege ejus meditatur die ac nocte.

Nec aliter sive verbo, sive exemplo suo informavit DAVID filium & Successorem Serenissimum, SALOMONEM: quod Salomo ipse deprædicat, omnibusque parentibus in exemplum sistit; De sapientia enim verbi divini, quod unice veram præstat sapientiam, ita sese a Parente sapientissimo commonitum, testatur: Accipe illam, & exaltabit te, glorificaberis ab ea, cum eam fueris amplexatus; dabit capiti tuo augmenta gratiarum, & CORONA inclyta proteget te. Idcirco hanc verbi divini Sapientiam aliis pariter commendat mortalium SAPIENTISSIMUS. Melior, inquit, est acquisitio ejus negotiatione argenti, & auri primi, & purissimi; fructus ejus pretiosior est cunctis opibus; & omnia quæ desiderantur, huic non valent comparari. Longitudo dierum in dextera ejus, & in sinistra illius divitiæ & gloria.

Quapropter moriturus David, velut in Testamento, Salomoni hoc injunxit imprimis 1. Reg. II, 2. 3. 4. Ego ingredior viam universæ terræ, confortare, & esto vir. Et observa custodias Domini Dei tui, ut ambules in viis ejus, ut custodias Ceremonias ejus, & præcepta ejus, & judicia, & testimonia, sicut scriptum est in lege Moysi: ut intelligas universa quæ facis, & quocumque te verteris: ut confirmet Dominus sermones suos, & quos locutus est de me, dicens: Si custodierint filii tui vias suas, & ambulaverint coram me in veritate, in omni corde suo, & in omni anima sua, non auferetur tibi vir de solio Israel.

De delitiis S literarum, quas affatim experiuntur, qui dediti sunt iisdem, suavissimæ illæ similitudines, quibus easdem gratas nobis reddit Spiritus S. testantur; Comparatur enim Scriptura melli, & favo mellis, quo nihil gutturi nostro dulcius, ligno vitæ, quo nihil jucundius, mannæ, quo dono Israelitis in horrido deserto cibo destitutis nihil erat gratius, vino, cujus colore, odore, sapore nihil delectabilius, aquæ, qua extreme cum Simsone sitientibus nihil desiderabilius, lacti, quo in prima infantia nihil svavius, horto, quo nihil amœnius. Ideo suavissimis verbis rhetoricatur de horto Spirituali animæ nostræ Sponsus in eundem nos invitans: Veni in hortum meum Soror mea Sponsa.

Messui myrrham meam cum aromatibus meis: Comedi favum cum melle meo, bibi vinum cum lacte meo; Comedite amici, & bibite, & inebriamini charissimi. Ejus fluminibus, Davide teste, inebriamur ab ubertate domus Domini, & ceu torrente voluptatis potamur. Ipsa, Syracide autore, cibat nos pane vitæ, & intellectus, & aqua Sapientiæ salutaris potat nos.

Si Patres audire juvat, placet Irenæo Paradisi ceu horti voluptatis similitu- do. Oportet, inquit, confugere ad Ecclesiam, & ejus sinu educari, & Domini- cis Scripturis enutriri. Plantatus est Ecclesiæ Paradisus in hoc mundo. De omni ligno Paradisi escas manducabis, inquit Spiritus Dei, hoc est, de omni Scriptura Dominica manducate. Chrysostomo peculiari homilia de Para- diso, sive horto, vel Scripturis sacris agere libuit, in qua multa habentur sua- vitate sua oblectantia; quæ nec ipsis μισογράφοις Papistis displicere potuere, uti exemplo est Jod. Coccius in Thesauro suo, Suave quidem, inquit, est pra- tum & hortus; utroq; tamen suavius multo spirat divina Scripturæ lectio. Illic siquidem flores invenire est, sed qui tempore marcescunt: Hic autem oc- currunt sententiæ in nativo vigore permanentes. Illic adspirat Favonius, hic afflat aura Spiritus S. Illic spina pro muro obsepiunt hortum, hic Dei provi- dentia tutum reddit lectorem: Illic cicadæ stridore suo obstrepentes, hic Pro- phetæ suavi jubilo personantes: Illic ex ipso aspectu quiddam oblectationis concipitur: Hic autem ex ipsa mox lectione plurimum decerpitur utilitatis. Hortus uno quopiam circumscribitur loco, divinæ autem Scripturæ nullo non loco terræ habitabilis circumferuntur. Hortus utiq; pro temporum qua- litate servit necessitatibus: Scripturæ autem tempore hyberno perinde atque æstivo perennant comantibus undiq; foliis, & fructuum pondere degravan- tur. Attenti itaq; simus lectioni Scripturarum. Ad hanc etenim attentus si fueris, anxietatem à te depellet, cordi tuo inferet incredibilem voluptatem, sublata malitia radices virtutis affiget animæ, interq; turbellas istas nego- tiorum, quæ ritu undarum sese agitantium fluctuant, non te sinet ulla confli- ctari perturbatione. Insanis licet agitetur mare procellis, tu in tranquillo navigas. Habes enim, quæ te moderetur atq; gubernet, Scripturarum lectio- nem.

Chrysostomo in Ecclesia Græca concinit Cyrillus Alexandrinus Com- mentario de recta in Deum fide eidem Coccio laudatus: Quemadmodum agricolæ fragrantissimos quosq; flores opportuno tempore ex agris decerpunt, decerptosq; ac scite in calathis compositos dominis suis offerunt; quos illi mox benevole gratoque animo complectuntur: Ita nos, qui docendi munus suscepimus, ex divina Scriptura, veluti ex agro quopiam non florum cito marcescentium decorem spectandum exhibemus, sed sermone doctrinæq; qua per Spiritum S.pietatis in Christum immarcessibilem venustatem continet, magnaq; suavitate & ubertate illius mysterium redolet, fragrantium: scri- ptum est enim: Christi bonus odor sumus Deo.

Addimus & tertium è Græco- rum Patrum choro Olympiodorum: Divina ipsa, inquit ille, Scriptura est ve- lut ager quidam ferax & odoratus, quasique Paradisus optimis arboribus consitus, habensq; Thesaurum occultum. Quid vetat addere & quartum ducentis circiter, & quod excurrit, annis Olympiodoro, Chrysostomo tribus, Ireneo sex propemodum seculis ætate inferiorem, at eximium inter Græcos Doctorem, illisque hic σύμφωνον, Damascenum, qui ita ad lectionem S. lite- rarum nos excitat: Pulsemus, inquit, ad pulcherrimum illum hortum Scri- pturarum: illum, inquam, mire fragrantem & suavem, summaq; elegantia præditum, ac spiritualium & divinitus afflatarum cujusvis generis avium garritibus aures nostras circumsonantem, quiq; cor nostrum attingit, illudq; mœrore affectum lenit ac mitigat, & ira percitum sedat, sempiternaq; læ- tia diffuudit, &c. Ex hujs horti fonte perennes, & purissimos latices in vitam æternam salientes hauriamus. Hic cum inexplebili quadam voluptate & amœnitate versemur. Ejusmodi est enim Scripturarum gratia, ut exhau- riri atque consumi nequeat.

Nec alia mens quondam fuit Latinæ Ecclesiæ Doctoribus. Testis sit Am- „brosius, de dulcedine Scripturæ differens Epist. XLIV. Mare est Scriptura divi- „na habens in se sensus profundos, altitudinem Propheticorum ænigmatum, „in quod mare plurima introierunt flumina. Sunt ergo & fluvii dulces atque „perspicui, sunt & fontes nivei, qui saliant in vitam æternam: Sunt & sermones „boni, sicut favum mellis, & gratæ sententiæ, quæ animos audientium spiri- „tuali quodam potu irrigent, & præceptorum moralium suavitate mulceant.

„Hieronymus ad Celant. T. I. p. 110. Latus & immensus divinæ legis campus „extenditur. Qui diversis testimoniis veritatis, velut cœlestibus quibusdam „floribus vernans, mira oblectatione legentis animum pascit ac refovet. Quæ „omnia semper cognoscere, secumque revolvere ingens ad conservandam ju- „stitiam beneficium est. Et rursus: Pinguissimus est sermo divinus, omnes in se „habens delitias. Quicquid volueris ex sermone divino nascitur. Sicut tra- „dunt Judæi, quoniam manna, quando comedebant, secundum voluntatem

„uniuscujusque sic sapiebat in ore. Gregorius M. ita de S. literis scribit: S. Scri- „ptura sic aquam Sapientiæ generat, ut & potantes semper reficiat, & tamen „manare non desistat. Scripturæ S. scientia tanto fluit impetu, ut electos dum „tangit, ab hujus vitæ amore submoveat & ad æterna gaudia, vi impetus sui

„quosque adhærentes trajiciat. Venerabilis Beda, Aqua amara, inquit, Scriptu- „ra divina dicitur, quia peccantibus non parcit, at justis dulcis, quibus æterna

„præmia repromittit: Et ita aliis aqua benedicta est, aliis maledicta Alcuinus „ita monet: Lætari debemus in lectione sanctarum Scripturarum, ubi pasca- „mur & potemus de ligno vitæ, quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum.

Theodulphus Aurelianensis sic cecinit de Script. S. libris: Hic cibus æterno satiat præcordia pastu, Justitiæque famem, quo mage habetur, alit. Hic Paradisigeno veniens de gurgite potus, Quem quo plus quis alit, plus sitit omne bonum. Lex pretiosa Dei est, quid enim pretiosius illa, Quam dat fons vitæ, lux & origo boni?

Si Radulphum Flaviacensem, qui seculo decimo floruit, audiamus; S. Scri- ptura mensa nobis est, & spiritualis refectio, ad consolationem nobis data con- tra inimicos. Cui consonat Berno Augiensis seculo undecimo: Hæc est illa mensa, cælestium dapum ferculis referta: Quæ lassis requiem, infirmis sani- tatem, lapsis recuperationem, stantibus in fide confert fortitudinem. Con- sonat & Ludolphus Saxo Carthufianus decimo quarto seculo: Sacra Scriptu- ra est cibus noster, ac panis vitæ & intellectus, quo quotidie reficimur, ne defi- ciamus in hujus peregrinationis deserto: Unde scriptum est: Non in solo pane vivit homo, sed in omni verbo, quod procedit ex ore Dei.

Sed nec Jesuitæ ipsimet diffiteri hanc S. literarum dulcedinem potuerunt etsi min9 æquum S. Scripturis Pontificem Romanum esse, notorium sit. Unum tantum atq; alterum in rei fidem adducere placet. Basilium M. Hierimias „Drexelius hisce deprædicat: Hic à principio Philosophiæ studiis inescatus, „ubi vero sanctioris scientiæ dulcedinem gustavit, humanas artes & disciplinas „aspernatus, divina solum studia mirari, eaq; tanto affectu complecti cœpit, ut „panis vinique usu omni sibimet interdicto (sic ajunt) perdius & pernox lecti- „oni sacræ inhæserit, dum salubrioris sapientiæ compos fieret. Hic cocum & „culinam in libris repetit, totos dies, noctes totas sine fastidio epulaturus. De S.

„Bernhardi vero elogiis lectionis Scripturæ S.ita pronunciat: Hinc nihil mi- „ri, Lectionem sacram à Bernhardotantopere omnibus esse commendatam. „Beatæ vitæ dulcedinem, inquit, lectio inquirit, meditatio invenit, oratio po- „stulat,contemplatio degustat. Lectio quasi solidum cibum ori apponit,medi- „tatio masticat & frangit,oratio saporem acquirit; Contemplatio est ipsa dul- „cedo,quæ judicat & reficit. Ex his possumus colligere, quod Lectio fine me- „ditatione arida est,meditatio sine lectione erronea. Hauriendus est sæpe de „Lectionis serie affectus,& formanda oratio,quæ Lectionem interrumpat,& „non tam impediat interrumpendo, quam puriorem continuo animum ad „intelligentiam lectionis restituat.

Cornelius à Lapide de Scriptura S. in Can- „ticum Canticorum ita habet: Sicut favus continet mel, & vinum continet „Spiritus calidos,quos bibenti adspirat: Sic Sacra Scriptura continet divinam „doctrinam melle dulciorem, & vino calidiorem.

Et in præf. Comment. in Pentat. Regius Psaltes beatum vocat,non qui in alios Dei eloquia profundit, sed qui in lege ejus meditatur die ac nocte,hunc proinde esse ut lignum plan- tatum secus decursus aquarum, quod fructum suum dabit in tempore suo. Hoc utique fine vel maxime sacros codices nobis conscribi voluit Deus, ver- bumq; suum proposuit,ut lucerna esset pedibus,daretq; lumen semitis nostris, ut inter hosce lucidissima voluptatis & plusquam Alcinoi hortos inambu- lantes,jucundissimo cælestium fructuum pasceremur aspectu, & gustu frue- remur Et sane uti in Paradiso, inter vernantes arborum florumq; surculos, aut rutilantes malorum facies,necesse est prætereuntem,vel odore saltem & colore refici; Utq; qui in sole,licet animi causa, deambulat,calescere tamen, & rubedine imbui videmus ; Ita divinas Literas religiose affidueq; legenti- um,audientium,discentium mentes,sensus,consilia,vota,moresq; veluti quo- dam divinitatis colore tingi sanctisq; affectibus accendi necesse est. Et laudat Jod. Coccius inter alia scriptum,quod A. Christi 900.sub titulo: Altercatio Sy- nagogæ & Ecclesiæ,prodiit,in quo hæc leguntur: Sicut haustus vinei liquoris corpus non solum salubriter,suaviterq; profundit, verum etiam potantium animis jucunditatem non parvam adjicit: Sic verba cælestis eloquii, sicut auditum audientis,vel legentis demulcent: Sic ex spiritualis gratiæ dulcore gaudiorum æternorum spem operantur.

Quibus S. Patrum sententiis subjungimus B. LUTHERI nostri elo- gia Scripturæ S. his analoga, quæ Tom. I. Jenens. Germ. fol. 80. leguntur: Das heilige Wort GOttes hat viel Namen in der Schrifft/ um seiner unzehlichen Tugend und Werck willen,deß es ist fürwar alle Ding,und allmächtig. Es heißt ein geistl. Schwerdt/ daß man dem Teuffel und allen geistl. Feinden damit widersteht. Es heißt ein Licht/ein Mor- genregen/ ein Abendregen/ ein himmlischer Thau/ Gold/ Silber/ Ertzney/ Kleider/ Ge- schmuck/ und viel dergleichen. Also heißt es auch ein Brodt/ darum/ daß die Seel davon gespeiset/gestärcket/groß und satt wird/ und man soll nicht allein das blosse Brod hierüben verstehen/ denn zu gleicher weise/ als die Schrifft durch das leibliche Brod ausdruckt aller- ley Speise des Leibes/wie köstlich sie sind: Also auch durch das geistl. Brod / alle die Spei- sen der Seelen/die gar unzehlich sind; denn mancherley Seelen sind auf Erden/und eine ieg- liche besonder / nicht allezeit einerley Nothdurfft und Geschicklichkeit hat/ und doch das Wort GOttes allen/die einer ieglichen Nothdurfft überschwenglich satt gibt/ denn wenn aller Könige Speise/die ie gewest und seyn mögen,über einen Hauffen wären/so möchten sie nicht dem geringsten Wort GOttes wenig vergleicht werden. Darum nennet es der HErr Christus im Evangelio eine Königliche Wirthschafft 2c. Und durch Jesaiam/ ein köstlich/ erlesen und prächtig Mahl. Hactenus Megalander.

Atque ea ratione Basilius Imperator Constantinopolitanus laudante eo- dem Coccio circa A.Christi 860. Leonem filium suum hunc in modum exhor- „tatus est: o fili, quemadmodum teneræ plantæ fontibus irrigatæ virescunt, „floresq; & fructus ferunt: Ita mens tua sacrarum literarū studiis irrigata, ma- „gis ac magis augescet,ac pro fructibus egregias virtutes producet. Nam cor- pus quidem saginatur cibis, quia alius super alium infarciuntur: Animus vero ,,sanctis sermonibus alitur ac vegetatur. Sed hoc interest, quod cibus ille cor- ,,poris, palato solum ac linguæ suauis, & corruptionem auget, & à corruptione ,,augetur, & in corruptionem tandem abit: animi vero alimentum sempiter- ,,nam menti adfert lætitiam, & incorruptionem parit, & ad immortalitatem ,,deducit. Meditare ergo per omnem vitam istos ita frugiferos sermones, ut ,,tantis eorum fructibus perfruaris, ac regnum tuum sapienter administres.

Nec vero delitias tantum & voluptates non mundanas, sed cœlestes adfe- runt sacræ literæ; sed etiam divitias & thesauros inæstimabiles sufficiunt. In ,,his abundantes illæ divitiæ gratiæ Dei inveniuntur, qui dives in misericordia ,,est ob nimiam charitatem suam, qua dilexit nos: in illis thesaurus iste abscon- ditus est, ob quem vendenda sunt omnia, Christus nempe, in quo reconditi sunt omnes thesauri Sapientiæ & cognitionis: illic aurum habemus ignitum & probatum, quo locupletes reddimur: Eloquia Domini, quæ argentum, igne examinatum probatum & purgatum septuplum. Ex illis fidem habemus, quæ multum pretiosior est auro, quod per ignem probatur. Ideo merito ipsæ nobis desiderabiles super aurum. De thesauris Scripturæ aureum Eloquentiæ os: Me- ,,rito, inquit, thesauro cuipiam confertur divinarum Scripturarum lectio. ,,Nam sicut ex illo quisquis vel parvum fructum capere velit, multas sibi parit ,,divitias; Ita & in S. Scriptura etiam in brevi dictione variam sententiarum ,,vim & ineffabiles divitias invenire licet. Neque enim vel Syllaba, inquit idem ,,Chrysostomus, vel apiculus est in sacris literis, in cujus profundo non sit gran- ,,dis quispiam thesaurus. Enim vero qui metalla effodiunt, non in superficie ,,manent, sed cum valde profunde descenderint, & auri ramenta habere potue- ,,rint, magno labore & sedulitate ea à terra separant, postque multum illum ,,laborem brevem aliquam laborum inveniunt consolationem. Quod si illi ,,tantum præ se ferunt studium in corruptibilibus, incertis, & noxiis: Multo ,,magis addecet, ut nos, ubi divitiæ aufferri nequeunt, & thesaurus absumi non ,,potest, & spe non aberratur, par vel majus studium adhibeamus. Quod sæpe ,,sæpius inculcat S. Chrysostomus: Quemadmodum in auri metallis, ait hom. XXXV. in Joh. ne minimam quidem venam quispiam, qui rem intelligat, omittere patitur, utpote quæ ad augendas divitias plurimum faciat: Ita in divinis Scripturis ne unum jota, aut unus apex, sed ne dimidium quidem prætermittendum est, sed omnia diligentius investiganda. Hæc nostra salus est, inquit iterum S. Chrysost. hom. X. in Gen. Hæ spirituales divitiæ, hæc secu- ritas, si sic nos ipsos quotidie muniamus & per lectionem, & per auditionem & per dissertationem spiritualem. Augustinus σύγχρονος Chrysost. l. 2. de ,,doctr. Christ. c. 42. ita habet: Quantum minor est auri, argenti, vestisque co- ,,pia, quam de Ægypto secum abstulit ille populus, in comparatione divitia- ,,rum, quas postea Hierosolymæ consecutus est, quæ maxime in Salomo- ,,ne Rege ostenduntur: tanta sit cuncta scientia, quæ quidem est utilis ,,collecta de libris gentilium, si divinarum Scripturarum scientiæ compa- ,,retur. Gregorius Magnus l. 2. in Ezech. homil. 18. Sapientia, inquit, ,,atque Scientia doctrinæ spiritualis veræ sunt divitiæ, in quarum com- ,,paratione, quæ transire possunt, falsæ nominantur: De his divitiis per ,,Salomonem dicitur : Thesaurus desiderabilis requiescit in ore sa- ,,pientis. Excepto autem eo, quod ad æternam patriam divitiæ spi- ,,rituales ducunt, est eis à terrenis divitiis magna distantia. Quia ,,spirituales divitiæ erogatæ proficiunt, terrenæ autem divitiæ aut ero- ,,gantur & deficiunt, aut retinentur, & vitales non sunt. Qui erga ,,has in se veras divitias continent, recte gazophylacia nominantur. Audiendus etiam Chrysostomus noster Germanicus, B. Lutherus, qui Psal- mum CXLVII. explicans ad v. 8. ita hunc verbi divini thesaurum celebravit: Bißher hat er GOTT gedanckt für die Wohlthaten zeitlicher Güter/ und weltli- chen Stand: Hie danckt er für die geistlichen Wohlthaten/welches ohn alle Maß grösser und höher ist/ denn das zeitliche Gut / wiewohl es nicht so herrlichen Schein hat/ als das zeitliche / sondern geringen Ansehens ist / nemlich GOttes Wort / oder Predigt/ das ist der theure Schatz/ der alle Seligkeit mit sich brin= get/beyde in diesem und in jenem Leben/ auch so reichlich/daß wer es hat/auch in höchster Armuth und Elend frölich davon ist/ und um aller Welt Gut nicht gä= be/ sondern viel lieber alles Dinges/ auch des Lebens empöre/ und lieber im Tod damit seyn wollt/dann ohne das im Sause leben/ aber wenig sind/ die es recht haben. Darum hat David diese Wohlthat zuletzt am Ende gesetzt/ da ein Lied soll am allerbesten klingen. Wer will aber diese Wohlthat ausreden/wie groß sie sey? Denn wer kan alle Tugend und Krafft des Göttlichen Worts erzehlen? So alle heilige Schrifft und Predigt / und alle Christliche Bücher nichts an= ders thun / denn GOttes Wort preisen / wie wir denn auch täglich thun mit schreiben/ lesen/ predigen/singen/ tichten und mahlen. Denn diese Wohlthat bleibt / und behält uns selber auch/ wenn jene Wohlthaten vergehen/ und wenn wir durch den Tod dieselbigen lassen/und uns von einander scheiden/ diese aber läst uns nicht/ scheidet sich auch nicht von uns/sondern dringet mit uns durch den Tod/ und reißt uns heraus/ und bringt uns in ein ewiges Leben/da kein Ster= ben/ noch Sorge des Todes seyn wird.

Hæc cum ita sese habeant, cedro dignum omnino est, quod de ROBERTO Siciliæ Rege Franciscus Petrarcha ante trecentos fere annos perhibuit, Eun- dem ita literis sacris delectatum fuisse, ut juratus ei dixerit : Juro tibi Petrarcha, multo chariores mihi esse literas quàm regnum, & si alterutro mihi carendum sit, æquanimius me diademate, quam literis sacris cari- turum.

Denique non delitias ac divitias tantum adferunt S. literæ, sed si præter jucunditatem,& utilitatem,honestas,vel potius honor & gloria desideretur, nulla major gloria, nulla eminentior dignitas, nulla augustior corona, quam à S. literis expectari potest. Ob Regem Regum, CHRISTUM JESUM, qui le- gem DEI habebat in visceribus cordis sui, celebrat Hiero-Psaltes DEUM gloriæ: prævenisti eum in benedictionibus dulcedinis; posuisti in capite ejus CORONAM de lapide pretioso. Magna est gloria ejus in salutari tuo: gloriam & magnum decorem impones super eum. Nec vero coronam suam Regiam tanti fecit DAVID, quam illam, quam Augusto Filio SALOMO- NI commendavit, ab eodem ipso Regum omnium, quos Sol unquam vidit, ut sapientissimo atque opulentissimo, ita gloriosissimo præ omni mundana sapientia, præ omni temporali opulentia, præ omni seculari gloria ma- xime celebratam, omnibusque fidelibus, etiam Regibus aliisque summis capitibus commendatam. Ea vero in sacris literis effulget unice, per S. li- terarum studium obtinetur unice, & sapientia literarum sacrarum coru- scat, omni auro, omnibusque gemmis totius orbis splendidius. Qua in hoc seculo gloriosè ornantur, vereque beati sunt & augusti, quos coronat Deus gratia & miserationibus : sed infinities gloriosius ornabuntur, su- premum beatitudinis gradum, & augustissimam majestatem adepti, qui- bus imponetur corona vitæ, corona justitiæ, corona gloriæ: incorrupti- bilis illa, incontaminata & immarcescibilis corona, qua asservatur nobis in cœlis.

Hugo de S. Victore interprete Cornelio à Lapide Jesuita B. Virginem cele- „brat, quod coronarit Christum corona justitiæ, sita in ordinatione & adæqua- „tione quatuor animi passionum, puta amoris, & timoris, gaudii & tristitiæ, „ceu quatuor lapidibus pretiosis, quod qui has quatuor habet ordinatas, hic ju- „stus, id est, compositus sit, qui inordinatas, injustus, Christus autem eas ordi- „natissimas assumserit ex carne purissima B. Virginis,in qua summe fuerint or- „dinatæ, & compositæ, eò quod ipsa omni caruerit concupiscentia, & pertur- „batione. Siquidem pueri ut plurimum matrizent, ac matris potius, quam „patris indolem & morem induant. Sed hæc Scripturæ S. adversa sunt, quæ ab omni concupiscentia & perturbatione liberam non facit B. Virginem; imo impia sunt, & blasphema: qua Christum à matre ornatum esse quatuor istis affectionibus, à matre coronatum esse corona justitiæ, eaq; ratione ut filium Virginis matrizare afferunt. Non enim à Maria Christus, sed à Christo Redemptore Salvatore ac Domino suo, Maria coronam justitiæ accepit, gem- misq; illis pretiosis affectionum animi principalium ornata est, non ut omnis expers fuerit vitiosæ passionis, aut concupiscentiæ, sed ita, ut fert humana in hac vita infirmitas; quod non Dominicani tantum, ideo Maculistæ Franci- scanis dicti, agnoscunt, hæreticam etiam ac blasphemam proclamantes sen- tentiam de immaculata Virginis conceptione, sed nec Pontifices Romani (quibus tamen EANDEM judicii infallibilitatem etiam extra Concilium ge- nerale,tum in quæstionibus juris, tum facti quam Christus ipse habuit, Jesui- tæ Parisienses, à Parochis Parisinis ob id hærefeos damnati, adscribere non du- bitarunt) Sixtus IV. Alexander VI. Leo X. Pius V. Paulus V. Gregorius XV. aliter dijudicare eam litem potuere, quam utrisque, Franciscanis pariter & Dominicanis Bullis severissimis, sed bullis levioribus habitis, imponendo si- lentium. Verbum autem Dei, vel Scriptura S. non Mariæ tantum Virgini, sed fidelibus omnibus coronam & gratiæ multiplicis, qua eos ornat S. S. Trinita, in regno gratiæ, & gloriæ, qua coronabit electos in regno æternæ gloriæ, conciliat: quia verbum est gratiæ, verbum vitæ & salutis, Spiritus & vita, & potentia Dei ad salutem: per quod Hierusalem, id est, Ecclesia,

„Hieronymo dicente, post ornatum multiplicem, post coronam, post auri & „argenti abundantiam, post indumenta, palliaq; pulcherrima, post decorem „incredibilem proficit in Reginam, quæ in Apocalypsi quasi sponsa ornata, „atque composita describitur viro suo, de qua in Psalmis: Astitit Regina à „dexteris tuis in vestitu deaurato circumdata varietate. Non enim alia, ut iterum S. Hieronymus Proœm. in lament. Jerem. potest esse vita sine scientia Scripturarum, per quam etiam ipse Christus cognoscitur, qui est vita cre- dentium! Qui vult sapiens & beatus esse, Lactantio monente, audiat Dei vocem, discat justitiam, sacramentum nativitatis suæ norit, humana con- temnat, divina suspiciat, ut summum illud bonum, ad quod natus est, possit

„adipisci. Si dixeris mihi, inquit Chrysostomus, ex Psalmis illud: Beatus „qui timet Deum, & potueris scire, quidnam sit id quod dicis: non divitem, „non principem, non formosum, non eum qui valet viribus, non eum, „qui ædes possidet magnificas, non eum, qui gerit magistratus, non eum, qui regnum obtinet, nullum denique alium, nisi eum, qui pius „est & religiosus, qui studio Sapientiæ tenetur, qui DEUM timet, bea- „tum dicis, non solum propter futura, sed etiam propter præsentia: nam „etiam in hac vita hic quoque est illo potentior. Celebrat ipse Cornelius à Lapide quendam, qui Henrici Satonis autoris horarum de æterna sapien- tia vitam descripsit, in hæc verba prorumpentem: Si mihi desponsata foret, Do- mine JESU, Regina potens, esset id mihi gaudio. Nunc igitur, æterna Sapi- entia, tu mei cordis imperatrix, & totius gratiæ parens es. In te divitiarum, honoris, potentiæ affatim mihi suppetit. Nihil prætereà appeto, quicquid hic mundus habet. Celebrat iterum iterumq; R. Simeonis, in Pircke Aboth sententiam: Tres esse coronas, coronam legis, coronam Sacerdotii, & coronam imperii. Verum coronam bonæ famæ (ex sapientia & vita honesta) illustriorem longe & pretiosiorem his omnibus esse. Sed omittit præcipuam coronam: coronam nempe gloriæ: nec recte præfert coronam bonæ famæ coronæ legis. Nam si bona fama ex Sapientia verbi divini vel legis oritur, præferenda omnino est corona Sapientiæ & verbi divini, genitrix pretiosissimæ illius coronæ. Quæ Sapientiæ corona præterea etiam coronam gloriæ nobis conciliat, coronâ famæ tantò splendidiorem, quantum præstant cœlum terra, divina humanis.

Hanc ergò tantarum delitiarum, tantarum divitiarum, tantarum coronarum, dignitatum & beatitudinum conciliatricem Sapientiam verbi divini, ecquis fidelium Deo deditorum non amabit, non sectabitur, non omnibus voluptatibus, omnibus thesauris, omnibus coronis, & honoribus totius orbis longissime præferet? Atque hoc nomine S. T. C. Princeps Serenissime, non ingratam fore humilimam oblationem TOMI SECUNDI BIBLIORUM ILLUSTRATORUM VET. TEST. confido, in quo id imprimis egi, ut Christum Jesum, qui unica Spiritus nostri voluptas, animæ thesaurus, pretiosissima corona cordis est, in Scripturis Propheticis veluti urna aurea reconditum manifestarem & in apricum producerem. Quem unicum sospitatorem SYMBOLO è Veteris Testamenti Pandectis, & ex ipso antiquissimo Scriptore sacro, Prophetarum non minus quam Historicorum omnium oceano, Mose delecto, manu sua exprimere solet S. T. C. ut altari cordis sui digito DEI Spiritus S. inscribatur: DOMINUS VEXILLUM MEUM. Hic enim est Jehovah Dominus ille, qui Mosi in rubo ardente visus est, Exod. 3. Qui per Mosen populum è manu Pharaonis liberavit c. XIV. qui se Israelis Medicum professus est, c. XV. à quo cum gloriâ Domini populo conspiceretur. Manna de cœlo datum c. XVI. qui à populo tentatus est in deserto c. XVII. Dominus ille, cujus exaltationem in ligno crucis Moses adumbravit per erectionem vexilli in deserto, in quo pendebat serpens æneus, Num. XXI. Dominus ille, qui datus est in vexillum, ad quod concurrant timentes DEUM, propter veritatem (Abrahæ promissam) ut salventur dextera Domini, Psal. LX. Dominus ille, qui in vexillum populorum stat, quem gentes requirunt, Esa. XI. & in quo sperant gentes Rom. XV. Dominus ille, in quo & per quem contra Amalekitas Josua victoriam obtinuit; Rex ille gloriæ, Dominus fortis & potens, Dominus potens in prælio Psal. XXIV. de quo Moses in novissimo Cantico suo cecinit, Deut. XXXIII. Beatus es tu Israel! Quis similis tui popule, qui salvaris in DOMINO, & scutum auxilii tui, & gladius gloriæ tuæ! denique DOMINUS ILLE, qui CONSTANTINO MAGNO Symbolo non absimili, IN HOC VINCES, patefactus, gloriosam ei victoriam concessit.

HOC VEXILLUM TUUM PRINCEPS SERENISSIME, ut fiducia tua Symbolum in confessione, victoriarum trophæum in prælio & agone, exaltationis gloriosæ signum in regimine perpetuum & proprium sit S. T. C. Hic DOMINUS ut S. T. C. Autor & Consummator fidei, victoria largitor, gloriæ dator, ex animi pii voto nunquam non sit, animitus precatus, Symbolum illud augustum, DOMINUM VEXILLUM MEUM omnibus Principibus, omnibus fidelibus præferentes, Sanctos Prophetas S. T. C. sisto. In hoc enim SECUNDO BIBLIORUM ILLUSTRATORUM volumine operam, concedente Domino, cum maxime dedi, ut DOMINUM illum, quem Symbolis bolis suis professi fideles Israëlitae sunt, IN DOMINO JUSTITIA ET FORTITUDO NOSTRA, item JEHOVAH ZIDKENU, JUSTITIA NOSTRA, tùm adversus alios, tùm imprimis adversus Judaizantem Grotium, Prophetis vicissim vindicarem, ut in firmamento illo LUMINUM SANCTORUM (Prophetas divinos intelligo, eorumque Sacrosancta volumina) stella illa splendida, & matutina, phosphorus ille, imò Sol justitiae, in Ecclesia, splendore suo, & claritate nativa, depulsis offuciis rutilet atque fulgeat. Addo autem comites stellas minores Apocryphorum Scriptores, & libros V. T. addi solitos, in quibus cum Monita ad veram Sapientiam, etiam facientia, tùm Exempla Heroum fide illustrium scintillant, quibus simile Symbolum QUIS EST SICUT TU INTER DEOS DOMINE? vexillis secundùm literas initiales inscriptum, vulgoque MACABI lectum, nomen dedisse creditur; Quae continentur TOMO TERTIO Operis hujus Biblici. Atque haec omnia S. T. C. gratiosissimo obtutui humilime nunc exhibeo.

Illustra, PRINCEPS SERENISSIME, splendore gratiae tuae atque clementiae hoc quidquid est operae sacrae, quod ex sese valdè opacum, & tanti Principis conspectu minùs dignum agnosco: lucem tamen aliquam à luce nativa Scripturae Propheticae in tenebricoso loco lucente, accedente illustratione Apostolica accipere, non temerè (quae mea est in Domino fiducia) dixero, & radiis splendoris Tui illustrissimus, juxta cum Autore servo humilimo, coruscaturum confido. Ita gratiae suae vultu respiciat, omnibusque felicitatis Principalis donis & incrementis locupletet, & exhilaret perpetuo, Tecum Princeps Serenissime, AUGUSTAM Conjugem, geminamque prolem Illustrissimam, JOHANNEM GEORGIUM QUARTUM, & FRIDERICUM AUGUSTUM, in spem, fructum, & laetitiam ecclesiae afflictissimae singularem, Lux illa magna, in qua lucem vitae habemus, & in cujus lumine videmus lumen! Quod piis precibus exorare nullus intermittam

S. T. C.

Indefessus apud Deum intercessor

ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, D.

## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus, Amen. Abraham Calovius's Illustrated Bible of the Old Testament. Vol
In the Name of Jesus, Amen. Abraham Calovius's Illustrated Bible of the Old Testament. Volume II.

Part I.

Latin:

I. N. J. D. ABRAHAMI CALOVII BIBLIA ILLUSTRATA VET. TESTAMENTI. TOMUS II.

PARS I.

## 1:1 Introduction: Presenting Annotations on the Major Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel
Presenting annotations on the Major Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel.

Latin:

EXHIBENS ANNOTATA AD PROPHETAS MAJORES ESAIAM. JEREMIAM. EZECHIELEM. DANIELEM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Dedicatory Preface to the Four Major Prophets. To the Most Illustrious Lord, Lord Henry, B
DEDICATORY PREFACE TO THE FOUR MAJOR PROPHETS. TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LORD, LORD HENRY, BARON OF FRIESEN, Lord in Schönfeld, Jessen, & Puskaw, Chamberlain to the Most Serene Elector of Saxony, and Most Excellent Councillor in the Privy Council, and Most Eminent Director of the same Sacred Council, my Most Gracious Lord. MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LORD.

Those things which are eminent and preeminent in the Prophets of the Old Testament, we see shining forth most especially in the four Major ones, as they are called. The leader of the Apostles recalls them to three main heads: to the investigation of salvation, which is through faith in Christ; to the προμαρτυρίαν, or fore-testification, if I may so render it, of the passion of Christ and the glory that would follow the same; and to the scrutiny of the principal character, what and what kind of time that is, which the Spirit of Christ, who was in them, had defined for the fulfillment of these things. For we must not believe, with the Pelagians, Francesco Pucci, the Scholastics, and the Innovators, that the Prophets were devoid of the knowledge of salvation, which the Apostolic Council concluded the ancients, just as we, had obtained through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: Even though we understand those things which were diligently searched out by the Prophets, placed in clear light without labor, through the Son manifested in the flesh: For all the Prophets bear witness to Christ, that through his name we obtain remission of sins through faith in him. But since the economy of the Son of God is contained especially in this knowledge and faith of salvation—who for us men, and for our salvation, as we profess in the Nicene Creed, descended from heaven, and was incarnate, and in that economy the passion and death of the Son of God is especially set forth to be believed, namely that he was delivered up for our sins, as well as his resurrection and glory, that he was raised and taken up into glory, for our justification—it was incumbent upon the Prophets in the Old Testament, when they were about to deliver the way of salvation to the people, primarily to search out the sufferings that were to be in Christ, and the glory that would follow them, how it behooved him to occupy the heavenly kingdom, and having sent the Spirit from heaven, to gather to himself a Church throughout the whole world, in which he might rule in the kingdom of grace, and by which he might be eternally glorified in the kingdom of glory. But in order that our faith might be placed in safety, and that no one might have need to hesitate concerning that person, without whom salvation can come to none of mortals, certain and infallible characters have been designated by the Prophets, from which the same can be recognized beyond doubt: among which the Chronological characters easily hold the principal place, as to what and what kind of time of arrival, or πλήρωμα χρόνου, was defined for the redemption of the world. Whence St. Irenaeus, Bishop of the people of Lyons, very close to the age of the Apostles, teaches that this was included in the RULE OF FAITH, which he testifies the Church, scattered throughout the whole world even to the ends of the earth, received from the Apostles and their disciples and diligently guards: that the Church believed that the Holy Spirit preached through the PROPHETS THE DISPOSITIONS OF GOD AND THE ADVENT, and that birth which is from a virgin, and the passion, and the resurrection from the dead, and the ascension in the flesh. The same Holy Father says it is MANIFEST that the PATRIARCHS & PROPHETS prefigured OUR FAITH, and sowed in the earth the ADVENT OF THE SON OF GOD, who and what kind he was to be, so that those who were to be later men, having the fear of GOD, might easily receive the ADVENT OF CHRIST, INSTRUCTED by the PROPHETS. Which he elegantly illustrates and confirms by the example of the Eunuch of Queen Candace: For this reason Philip, when he had found the Eunuch of the Queen of the Ethiopians reading those things which are written, 'As a sheep he was led to the slaughter,' etc., easily persuaded him to believe that He is Christ Jesus, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and suffered whatever the Prophet foretold, and that He is the Son of God, who gives eternal life to men. And immediately as he baptized him, he departed from Him. For NOTHING else was lacking to him who had been PRE-CATECHIZED by the PROPHETS; he was ignorant not of GOD the Father, not of the (economy or) disposition of HIS CONVERSATION, but only of the advent of the SON OF GOD (namely, that he had already come into the world), which when he had briefly learned, he went on his way rejoicing, to be a herald in Ethiopia of the advent of Christ. Wherefore Philip did not labor much concerning him, because he had been PRE-PREPARED by the PROPHETS in the fear of GOD. These things concerning the Prophets says St. Irenaeus. In this PRE-CATECHIZATION or PRE-PREPARATION, if we may so speak, without doubt the Major Prophets excel. St. Jerome certainly attributes this praise to ISAIAH, that he contains all the mysteries of the Lord; and elsewhere, he says, Isaiah seems to me not to weave a prophecy, but a Gospel. In which, to pass over many others, he has the Great Bishop of Hippo agreeing, whose words are these: Isaiah, among those things which he argued as wicked, and commanded as just, and foretold as future evils to a sinful people, also prophesied much more than the others concerning CHRIST and the CHURCH, that is, concerning the King and the city which he founded, so that by CERTAIN

He might be called an Evangelist rather than a Prophet. St. Augustine says this truly. For St. ISAIAH did not only set forth clearly enough the true salvation, and the way and method of attaining it through faith in the Messiah, but he also executed, as an Evangelist of the Old Testament, those things which are to be believed concerning Christ as Sacraments or mysteries, regarding his Person, his twofold State, and his threefold office, speaking perspicuously of the eternal Deity of Christ, whom he describes as JEHOVAH the true God, besides whom there is no GOD, and whom he describes by attributes and works that are truly and merely Divine, and presents as one to be followed with divine honor and worship; and likewise of his temporal conception and birth from a virgin, his passion, death, resurrection, and glory: also of the offering for our sins, and his intercession, and finally of the kingdom and the Church, and the subjects of the Messiah. All of which things Isaiah illustrated with the characters of works, signs, places, and times in such a way that he easily makes the palm of victory in this regard doubtful for other Prophets.
