Although indeed such great light does not shine forth from the other major Prophets, nevertheless very significant oracles concerning the mysteries of faith are found among them: indeed, to touch upon only a few, JEREMIAH exhibited a very illustrious Symbol and confession of the catholic Faith on two occasions, concerning the righteous branch of DAVID, which is Jehovah our righteousness, in whom alone salvation and true tranquility come to us, and concerning the King and the Kingdom, outside the boundaries of which neither judgment nor justice has any place anywhere on earth: EZEKIEL indeed described that unique Shepherd, the true DAVID, the servant of the Lord, in and under whom the covenant of eternal peace flourishes, and who alone feeds us for eternal life: DANIEL finally graphically delineated his Kingdom, which crushes all others, and to which all things must yield, as it will have no end, with eternal power and glory granted to it, and subjects from all peoples, nations, and languages serving him with true faith; furthermore, he illustrated the anointing of the Messiah, and his death and excision, and the expiatory sacrifice with as if living colors, and he designated the character of the time more accurately than all others, so that, as St. Jerome truly warns, no Prophet spoke so openly about Christ (as far as chronological calculation is concerned). For he says, he does not only write that he is to come, which is common to the others, but he also teaches at what time he is to come, and arranges the Kings in order, and enumerates the years, and announces the most manifest signs. This is St. Jerome.

For the closer the Prophets became to the fullness of time, the more evident the characters of the times and other circumstances they received and recorded, at the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, so that they might strengthen the faith of the saints, which could easily be shaken by the calamities of the last times, and sharpen the desire for the advent of the Messiah. Although indeed those two intermediate men, JEREMIAH and EZEKIEL, do not seem to contribute anything to the scrutiny of the time of the advent of the Messiah, nevertheless, in my Biblical Chronicle, I have demonstrated that the sacred CHRONOLOGY, which in its entirety in the Scriptures of the O.T. according to all its Epochs looks toward that acceptable time which all the saints longed for, would not have its consistent rationale unless the term from which and to which the Babylonian servitude was designated were defined by Jeremiah (whose calculation Daniel followed), and this most celebrated Epoch were accurately defined by its limits. And it was entirely important that Ezekiel should count the years from the voluntary migration of Jeconiah, not indeed as the common run of Chronologists rashly decide with Scaliger, because of the Epoch of the Babylonian Captivity, but because of the years of the reign of Zedekiah, the last King of the Jews, which began with the deportation of Jeconiah, and for other reasons in Sacred History, concerning which [I speak] in the Biblical Chronicle.

Since these things are so, the work is placed, without any doubt, most excellently into the Quadriga of these highly excellent Prophets, when both the primary Scope of the Holy Scriptures, which St. Paul assigns to this, that they instruct us for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, is held in account, and the Prophetic Oracles concerning the person of Christ, his States, offices, benefits, and the Church, as his Kingdom, and the privileges, success, and lot of that spiritual kingdom on this earth are recalled for more accurate consideration, and are brought to their integrity, where they suffer violence, by a just refutation, lest the Chronological characters, which the Spirit of Christ himself defined, be neglected. I have primarily prefixed this triple goal to these annotations of whatever sort they may be; but how I have attained it, I leave to be judged by the pious and learned Reader. I certainly believed that nothing more useful could be proposed by me in this Chair of B. Luther entrusted to me, in the Scrutiny of the Prophetic writings, both so that the very nucleus and marrow of the Prophetic predictions, in which there is Spirit and life, might be exhibited to the cultivators of the Holy Scriptures, and so that the Harmony of the Old and New Testament, of predictions and events, might be placed in the open, and it might be clearly evident how truly St. Augustine said that the New Testament is veiled in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New.

Indeed, all of this already seemed necessary, when I saw—not so much with these eyes of mine, but felt with my very hands—that the kernel was being taken from the Prophetic writings, leaving only the shell; that the marrow was being drained, while the empty bones remained; that the way of salvation of the faithful of the Old Testament, who are one Church with us and have one faith and one hope, was being subverted; that Christ, with his sufferings and glory, his offices and benefits, who is the Sun of the entire Scripture, was being obscured and suffering an eclipse as great as he ever suffered; that the characters of the times and other similar things were being called into doubt; and that the true sense of the letters, intended solely by the Holy Spirit, was being depraved: and all this by a MAN OF UNUSUAL ERUDITION, most skilled in Oriental languages, and most versed in Antiquity, both sacred and exotic. That this INCOMPARABLE writer, in the Christian religion, has been a blind disciple of the Rabbis—who are teachers of NO sects and ALL sects, and blind themselves—and has finally indulged his own genius, however capacious, too much, his commentaries on the entire Scripture proclaim with a loud voice. Concerning the other writings of this GREAT MAN, I do not rashly take it upon myself to pass judgment.

May it be permitted to bring forward only a few things, and as it were in a medley, to the present matter, so that one may know the lion by his claw. For those prophecies concerning Christ, which the very evidence of the words and the infallible interpretation of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament ought to have placed beyond all question and doubt, are snatched away to entirely different persons and into a sense plainly alien, so that instead of Christian annotations we read Rabbinic, and more than Rabbinic, commentaries. Whatever holy ISAIAH predicts in a disconnected manner concerning the conception and birth of Christ IMMANUEL from a VIRGIN, concerning the child born to us, concerning the Son given to us, that mighty GOD, the Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace, concerning the Shoot from the root of Jesse, in whom the Spirit of the Lord rests, and who slays the wicked with the spirit of his lips, concerning the banner of the peoples in whom the nations trust, concerning the King who shall reign in righteousness, under whom the Spirit shall be poured out from on high, and concerning the eyes of the blind and the tongues of the mute to be opened at the coming of our GOD, CHRIST the Redeemer—all those things the Grotian commentaries twist toward King HEZEKIAH. A hymn

A Eucharistic song to be sung by the faithful in praise of Christ triumphant over death, which he devours in victory, is drawn out to the rescue from the hand of Sennacherib and the liberation of Jerusalem from the siege. The oracle concerning John the Proto-baptist, the forerunner of Christ, concerning the Prophets at the time of the destruction of the city by the Chaldeans, the prophecies concerning Christ the just servant of God who does not break the bruised reed and does not extinguish the smoking flax, concerning the name of the nations and the salvation of the Lord even to the end of the earth, is expounded concerning the Prophet Isaiah himself; whom Grotius, along with the teachers of the Jews, says is the one who did not deny his body to those striking him and his cheeks to those plucking them, to whom a learned tongue was given by GOD to sustain him who is weary, and that Witness, and Leader and Teacher of the Gentiles, to whom Isaiah invites all who are thirsty to draw living waters, the Evangelists of Peace, whose feet are beautiful upon the mountains of Judea, the Holy Spirit has interpreted as the Apostles, Grotius [interprets as] JEREMIAH, the Prophet of the Old Testament. The whole of chapter 53 of Isaiah, than which no clearer passage exists in the entire Code of Hebrew Scripture concerning the passion and satisfaction of Christ and the glory that followed him, he twists likewise to JEREMIAH with a boldness unheard of in the Christian world, even though he himself in his book On the Truth of the Christian Religion expounded the whole chapter paraphrastically, with this clause added: Who can be named, either of kings or prophets, to whom these things correspond? What the Prophet prophesied concerning the fruitfulness of the Gentiles, with the Apostle as interpreter, even though, as Augustine says, they are so clear that even enemies are forced to understand them against their will, Grotius drags off to the restoration of the earthly Jerusalem: he contends that the Redeemer of Zion, whose name those from the west and whose glory those from the rising of the sun acknowledge, is not Christ but Cyrus: concerning whom he also asserts that this command resounds: Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold your Savior comes, Behold his reward is with him, and his work before him. That prophetic exhortation, Arise, shine, O Jerusalem, for your light has come, he draws to the earthly happiness of Jerusalem, and by that light, in which the nations are said to walk, he understands not CHRIST, but Isaiah himself; nor does he interpret as concerning CHRIST, but as concerning Isaiah himself, what CHRIST in the School of Nazareth (Irenaeus says this was done in Capernaum by a mnemonic error) most clearly testified were predicted concerning himself: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me: nor is that champion for salvation, who trod the winepress alone, the Messiah to Grotius, but Judas Maccabeus, to whose times the remaining prophecies in this Prophet, which deal with the calling of the Gentiles and the spiritual and heavenly joy of the faithful, are also twisted by the same man.

Now, what JEREMIAH handed down concerning the abrogation of the Levitical worship, the conversation of the nations, and the preaching of the Gospel under the New Testament, Grotius explains in a sense clearly contrary, not concerning the abrogation of the Levitical worship, nor the time of the New Testament, but concerning the tranquil state of the Jewish polity under the Old Testament. The righteous Branch of David, which is called, and is, Jehovah our righteousness, according to the author himself is not Christ, but Zerubbabel: nor does he wish the Shepherd of David, predicted by EZEKIEL, to be any other than Zerubbabel, to whom he also drew the oracle of Zechariah concerning the King about to enter Jerusalem upon an ass and a colt the foal of asses.

In order to cast darkness upon the lights of DANIEL, he contends that by the Fourth kingdom is meant not the fourth Monarchy, but the kingdom of the Seleucids and Lagids: and that the Son of man brought to the Ancient of days is not Christ, but the Roman people: he is also less than fair to the chronological calculation of the Prophet, as if the Prophet, as is commonly said of a Praetor, cares little for trifles: but in the oracle concerning the LXX Weeks, which is the only one concerning the Messiah in the Major

Prophets that he leaves, he wishes to designate not the benefit of Christ, but the punishment of the Jews, namely the destruction of their own polity, so that iniquity may be atoned for, and he determines that it does not define the time of the coming of the Messiah, but the end of the Jewish polity; nay, with the Jews he makes the Messiah a worldly Prince, who ought to have liberated Jerusalem and the Jews, as his own people, from impending evils, if, that is, they had obeyed him: Finally, what Daniel predicted toward the end of his prophecy concerning the chief enemy of the kingdom of Christ, the great Anti-Christ, and concerning the eternal glory of the faithful, he drags—with Porphyry the Apostate, whose footsteps he follows closely, even though already refuted by Jerome—to Antiochus and the return of the Jews into the city, who, having been ejected from there on account of religion, were brought back, as the saying goes, by the scruff of the neck. Thus Grotius preferred to sail with apostates, Jews, and heretics everywhere, rather than to join the crown of the Doctors of the Church. Which we show πρὸς ὄμμα in these commentaries of ours.

For such things are not to be endured in the Christian world, nor were they to be passed over without just censure, which commend themselves remarkably by the authority and omnigenous erudition of GREAT MEN, and which can easily fascinate even the most learned men on account of their refined style of speaking and the analysis of entire contexts often very ingeniously agitated: especially because truths are mixed with falsehoods, fitting things with distorted and unfitting ones, and, as Irenaeus speaks, dross with silver; poisons coated with honey are here offered, not without great danger. Therefore, the glory of CHRIST the Redeemer, the salvation of the Church purchased by his blood, and the instruction of the youth committed to our faith, and also the excitement of Great Men, moved me at last to apply my mind to a work truly great, and (I do not deny) very unequal to my shoulders, and to set my hand to it. The complaint and vow of Andreas Rivetus, an octogenarian man, a theologian easily the Prince among the Reformed in this century, who recalled the Grotian syncretism with the Papists under censure, was twenty-three years ago: others perhaps will refute that audacity with which Grotius deformed the Prophetic Books in their chief oracles concerning Christ, as if he had been hired for that purpose by the enemies of the Christian name. And since he was not ignorant that, among others, ISAIAH had poured forth the most express oracles concerning the coming Messiah, he labored especially in corrupting that one. But after Rivetus had brought forward some things by way of example, which, as he says, a Christian soul does not read without horror, he added this: Someone will arise, if he has not already arisen, and girded for that sacred war, who will recall to examination all those corruptions by which that man perverts Holy Scripture in many ways, and will repel that poison with NECESSARY antidotes.

But since no one, whether from the Reformed or from our Church, has arisen who would undertake this, having invoked the help of the Holy Spirit, in the name of Jesus, I have set about the matter. For after I had, by divine grace, exhibited in a compendium the Papistic Matæologia, which has been sufficiently exposed to the Christian world ever since the beginning of the Reformation of the blessed LUTHER, according to the Roman Catholic propositions set forth in the Colloquy of Thorn, of which I was a participant in some capacity, and had confuted the Socinian heresy in very many writings and, ὡς ἐν ἐπιτομῇ, in the Syntagma of the routed Socinianism, and had recalled the new sect of the Arminians to the anvil of disputations, and had instituted an examination into the dogmas of the Calvinists and their Syncretism, and had likewise weighed the Calixtine, Nicolaitan, and Rinteln Syncretism, along with the harmony which the innovators foster with various heresies, in the balance of truth, lest those biblical commentaries, as dangerous as they are subtle and specious, should deceive our hearers (which happened to many in England, even to the most learned Walton and his συνέργοις in the Biblical Work) and inflict further damage upon the Church,

With the help of God, it seemed necessary to take precautions with no ordinary effort. I therefore ordered the continuation of the System of Commonplaces to rest for a while, even though it was already completed in four volumes and advanced to some extent, so that I might devote my efforts to defending the Holy Scriptures. And in the case of Moses and the shorter historical writings, it could be dealt with in brief lines, but in the book of Psalms and the Song of Songs, there was need for greater care: because Grotius did not leave the Prophetic Hymns untouched, but rather perverted almost all of them entirely, and treated that most holy Song, like a profane epithalamium, concerning the love of Solomon for his Egyptian Bride, with very indecent things even mixed in, which were not free from scandal. However, the Prophets required the greatest effort, so that they might be restored to their true meaning and defended against various corruptions, especially regarding the prophecies about the Messiah and the sacred chronological calculation, in which Grotius for the most part followed the novelties and errors of Scaliger. Indeed, I do not deny that Grotius, in history and in the interpretation of words and phrases, owing to his excellent equipment of doctrine in sacred and profane philology, often contributed his own share to the understanding of the Holy Scriptures; whose observations, therefore, I also deservedly embrace and approve in some places; but in the Prophets, the great man preferred to side with the Rabbis and others who diverge from the meaning of Scripture, or to pursue his own private interpretation, rather than to acquiesce to the genuine meaning of the Holy Spirit, even though it is pointed out by antiquity or shines forth clearly from the letter. These Meditations, therefore, consecrated solely to heavenly truth, born in this Electoral Academy from pious and diligent investigation of the Sacred texts, inquiry into the Divine sources, collation of similar passages, explanation of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament, and the opinions and meditations of the best interpreters, both ancient and modern (whose chain we have sometimes woven), and publicly proposed, I have not hesitated to offer to YOU, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS HERO, with the devotion that is due, because I am certain that you are a diligent searcher of the Sacred Scriptures and of Hebrew truth itself, a rare example at that pinnacle of honors: and because my public Academic studies ought to approve themselves primarily to the PRESIDENT of the Holier Senate, for which purpose I have also previously woven together a syllabus of my works: furthermore, divine grace willed that YOU alone should remain in that highest College throughout these nineteen years, which I complete in this renowned Electoral [Academy] on this, its birthday; whose unusual kindness, bound up with the manifold erudition of SO GREAT A HERO, exhibited to me as a stranger upon my first arrival at the Electoral seat, I have always humbly venerated, and have now deemed worthy of being celebrated publicly as well. Finally, since the sad fates hanging over the Church of GOD from every side, alas!—which that most unhappy itch for reconciling the twice-over dissenting religions in faith has produced—seem to demand some remedy, with divine grace favoring, primarily from the MOST SERENE ELECTOR OF SAXONY, OUR LORD, of whom, YOU, ILLUSTRIOUS HERO, are believed to be as it were the HEART and SOUL in the Holier Council, I have decided to piously commend the cause of the most afflicted Church to you, as our Stator and Eliakim, even though I do not doubt that the most holy studies of the INTIMATE SENATE are already watching over the same of their own accord, and I have recognized this by my own example, when more than once it took me under its protection for the sake of religion, and by other public documents, which I venerate and proclaim with a devout heart.

For which reason, since these Meditations of mine also desire the patronage and favor of the MOST SERENE [ELECTOR], so that under the shadow of his wings they may be advanced for the more brilliant uses of the Church into the public sphere, with more refined care, together with other sacred commentaries adorned on the Books of the Old and New Testament, they do not despair of YOU, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LORD, as an intermediary, which, because of their own worthlessness, they would never dare to hope for. May divine kindness preserve YOU, LORD, for the MOST SERENE House, may it preserve you for the whole Church, and may it never cease to direct you with Its Spirit, and may it fill you and your most illustrious family with every kind of happiness on every side! May you thus thrive, flourish, and endure, the IMMORTAL ORNAMENT OF OUR AGE: At Wittenberg, on the day of St. Luke, the birthday of the Academy, in the Year of the Restored World 1669.

CONCERNING THE PROPHETIC BOOKS OF THE MAJOR AND MINOR PROPHETS.

We spoke about the Prophets in general before the book of Joshua; now we shall speak about the Prophets who are so called, the later ones, who are distributed into Major and Minor. The Major, as is most well known, are Isaiah, Jeremiah with the Lamentations, Ezekiel, and Daniel; the Minor are Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Zephaniah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. They are designated as Major, however, not because of their authority or the gravity of their sentiments, or even the majesty of their words, in which all the Prophets are equal, just as the Spirit gave each one to speak, but from the larger writings, or because the four Prophets composed lengthy volumes, as Augustine says in Book XVIII of The City of God, ch. 19. For although Hosea and Zechariah exceed Daniel in the number of chapters, yet because the chapters of Hosea and Zechariah are rather short, while those of Daniel are more lengthy, the volume of Hosea and Zechariah itself is smaller than the book of Daniel.

However, the order is not the same among the LXX as it is in the Hebrew codex of the Minor Prophets, about which Jerome writes in Joel. For they place Amos second after Hosea, Micah third, 4. Joel, 5. Obadiah, 6. Jonah, 7. Nahum, 8. Habakkuk, 9. Zephaniah, 10. Haggai, 11. Zechariah, 12. Malachi. The Hebrews, however, observe the order placed above.

As for the chronology, three classes are usually established; for some prophesied before the Babylonian captivity, others in captivity, and others finally after the captivity, concerning which order, however, chronologists vary, especially regarding Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk, as noted by Augustine, book XVIII, De Civitate Dei, chapter 31. We also add Joel, because their time is not expressed, nor sufficiently certain. The Rabbis, Clement of Alexandria, book 1, Stromata, Jerome in his Epitaph of Paula and preface to Obadiah, Lyranus, and others place Obadiah first of all, because they think he was the steward of Ahab, but although he had the same name, it is not certain that he was the prophet, nor does the argument of the prophet Obadiah fit that time; indeed, if it is compared with Jeremiah, it is gathered that Obadiah lived rather after the capture of Jeconiah under Zedekiah around the time of the desolation of Jerusalem. Jerome makes Habakkuk a contemporary of Daniel, and attributes to him the apocryphal writing about Habakkuk bringing food from Judea to Daniel in the lions' den; but the chronology does not agree: because Judea was not yet occupied in the time of Habakkuk. For he threatens in ch. 1 that God is about to raise up the Chaldeans against it. Cf. B. Luth. in the preface to Habakkuk.

Now the first of all the Prophets was JONAH, who nevertheless did not live under Ahab, nor was he a σύγχρονος (contemporary) of Elisha, which is what must be said by the Hebrews, who make him the son of the widow of Zarephath, raised from the dead by Elijah, with the agreement of Epiphanius in his book on the Prophets & Athanasius to Antioch. q. 64. But Jonah was the son of Amittai, and his homeland was Gath-hepher, not Zarephath, which is situated in the region of the Sidonians, Luke 4:26. Some gather that he flourished finally under Amaziah, King of Judah, and Jeroboam II, King of Israel, from 2 Kings 14: others refer him to the times of Uzziah and of Joash, King of Israel, under whom, with Israel being greatly oppressed by the Syrians, he predicted their liberation through Jeroboam, 2 Kings 14:25. That at any rate is certain, that Jonah must be considered the first of all among the Prophets.

Most make Hosea the second, who flourished in the time of Uzziah, King of Judah, and Jeroboam II, King of Israel, and prophesied concerning the abduction of the Israelites, which happened about 70 years later.

The third is Amos, who lived at the same time as Uzziah and Jeroboam. The fourth is Isaiah, who began to prophesy under Uzziah. The fifth is Joel, whom the ancients make a σύγχρονος (contemporary) of Hosea and Amos, to whom the argument of the book seems to favor. And it is difficult, among those contemporaries, to indicate who indeed prophesied in the first, who in the second, and who in the third place. Therefore authors vary: most, however, assign the place next to Hosea after Jonah, and perhaps he will not have erred who, just as Isaiah is first among the major Prophets not only by the size of his volume but also by the time of his prophecy, whom the other major Prophets correctly follow in order of time: so similarly among those who prophesied in the holy land, he will have established as earlier in time among the minor Prophets those who are placed earlier in order, as they are presented in our codices, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, all of whom seem to some to have prophesied under Uzziah; to whom is joined Jonah, who prophesied outside the holy land at that time, or a little before. B. Luther, however, in his Commentary on Joel, observes that Joel lived in the time of Hezekiah or Manasseh: see what we said on Joel 1:6, almost toward the end.

There follows in our Codices, by reason of age, Micah, as one who began to prophesy under Jotham, son of Uzziah, in the Kingdom of Judah, and Nahum, who prophesied in the kingdom of Israel, as also Habakkuk, whom they refer to the times of Manasseh, with the prophecy not denying it. Finally, Zephaniah prophesied under Josiah, c. 1:1, to whom Jeremiah was a σύγχρονος (contemporary). And these prophesied before the captivity. But under the captivity, Ezekiel prophesied in the fifth year after the abduction of Jeconiah, c. 1:2. Obadiah, who prophesied against the Idumeans after they had insulted the Jews because of the destruction of Jerusalem (which was also done by Jeremiah and Ezekiel, so that they can appear as σύγχρονοι (contemporaries), which B. Luther also judged in his Preface to Obadiah, Vol. III, Jena, Latin), and Daniel under the final times of Nebuchadnezzar and thereafter. After the captivity, Haggai began to prophesy in the 2nd year of Darius on the 1st day of the 6th month; Zechariah arose in the same year, 8th month: Finally, Malachi prophesied when the temple had already been rebuilt; after whom no Prophet existed any longer; just as in the time of the Maccabees it is denied that there was a Prophet, 1 Macc. c. 4:43, c. 9:3, c. 14:41. Cf. Joseph. against Apion, August. book 17, City of God, c. 24.

Cornelius à Lapide makes Hosea the first, but on a slippery argument, or rather none at all, because, namely, at Hos. 1:2 it is called the beginning of the Lord's speaking in Hosea. By which the beginning of all Prophecy is not noted, because many prophets had already preceded, but the beginning of the Hoseanic revelation. He places Jonah, however, under Jotham, son of Uzziah, against the most open text of 2 Kings 14:26, by which it is taught that in the time of Jeroboam the prophecies of Jonah had already been fulfilled. But it is evident from Chronology that Jotham, son of Uzziah, began to reign only 37 years after the death of Jeroboam II. Therefore, Cornelius stumbled openly here in Chronology. Nor does the order of Grotius deserve approval, who assigned the first place to Hosea, and only the fifth to the Prophet Jonah.

ISAGOGICAL CANONS ON THE PROPHETS.

Interpreters are accustomed to present certain Canons, both concerning the form and manner of speaking or the Style of the Prophets, and concerning the method and order, which may be of use in the reading of the Prophets. It is helpful to have sampled some of them here. We omit, however, partly those which deal with tropes and figures: for these pertain to sacred Rhetoric, and are not peculiar to the Prophets; and partly those which they invent concerning the various sense of Scripture, since we acknowledge no sense of Scripture but a single one.

Canon I. The Prophets, concerning future things, often use the words of their own time; for example, concerning the Christian Church, they designate the Church of the Old Testament and the people of the O.T., and thence by Zion and Jerusalem they designate the Church of the N.T.; by Jewish feasts, the Sabbath, the feast of tabernacles, and other festive joys, they designate the spiritual happiness of the Christians; by words of temporal happiness, they designate the happiness of the pious in the time of the N.T., of which those were the type and shadow; and by the names of the enemies of the Jewish people, the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, etc., they denote the enemies of the Christian Church.

II. The Prophets delight in tropes and figures, especially Metaphors, allegories, parabolic phrases, and prosopopoeias, not for the sake of obscurity, but for elegance and the power of moving.

III. Sometimes they pass from one metaphor to another, and occasionally return to the former.

IV. They are accustomed to attribute the name of the figure to the thing figured, e.g., when they call Christ David.

V. They sometimes change the proper names of nations according to the change of morals, as when they call faithful men the true Israel, the impious Canaanites, Amorites, Sodomites, and call the world now Egypt, now Edom.

VI. They sometimes use proper names in such a way that they simultaneously allude to their etymon; yet they do not take them in the same place both as proper and as appellative.

VII. When they distinguish the ten tribes from the two, they call the two the kingdom of Judah, the house of David, Jerusalem, or Zion; but they express the ten by Israel or Jacob, or by Samaria, which was the head of the kingdom, or by Joseph or Ephraim, from whom Jeroboam, the first author of the division, arose.

VIII. The Prophets occasionally take mental or vocal words for real ones, such as 'to be called' for 'to be', 'to speak judgments' for 'to inflict them': sometimes they use active real words for mental or vocal ones, as for instance 'I do' for 'I think, I foresee, I destine to do'. To this may be referred the fact that all providence of God is called an evocation, a stirring up, or a command, because God does not give corruption to evil wills, but order, as Hugh of St. Victor says, lib. 1. de Sacram. P. 5. c. 29. Thus God is said to have stirred up the Chaldeans against the Jews, even though He only ordered their evil will, and did not instill it into them, and had predicted it through the Prophets, and thus seemed to have sounded the trumpet for them.

IX. The prophets speak of Christ and the salvation obtained through him as if of a battle and victory, so that they may demonstrate that the battle announced in the proto-Gospel is unfolding.

X. They speak of provinces and cities as if they were men, or rather women, both on account of their beauty and their luxury.

XI. The prophets not infrequently treat their subjects through dialogue, in which they introduce now one person, now another, as speaking.

XII. Sometimes they omit the subject of a verb, to be understood from the circumstances of the text, from the verb itself, or from elsewhere, as in Lam. 3:1, Cant. 1:3.

XIII. Often they also omit signs of comparison, as in Hos. 14:8, cf. Prov. 4:3, Ps. 11:2, Ps. 12:7.

XIV. Sometimes they place a specific species for the genus; as in Isa. 1:15, by the name of blood and homicide, any grave sin is understood.

XV. The prophets do not precisely preserve the order of times, as histories do: and they not infrequently pass to another history. Because their sermons, inspired now on this matter, now on that, were afterwards affixed to doors and stored in chambers, and from these the volumes of the Prophets are believed to have been subsequently woven together.

XVI. The prophets not infrequently pass from the type to the antitype, from the things of their own time to the things of the New Testament, from history or legal discourse to oracles concerning the Messiah and his kingdom, and to evangelical discourse: yet they do not speak in the same words both of the type and of the antitype, and of Old and New Testament things: even though in the words of the literal sense concerning the Messiah and future things under the New Testament, phrases, allusions, and similitudes from Old Testament things are frequent.

XVII. The prophets are accustomed to append joyful things to adverse ones, and to console those whom they first terrified, and thus to temper their message so that both the unbelieving may be struck and smitten, and the faithful may be uplifted and confirmed.

XVIII. By Sion and Jerusalem, the prophets understand now the Jews remaining in Judaism, who are not converted to Christ, now the Jews converted to Christ, and sometimes they fly immediately from the latter to the former.

XIX. Spiritual promises pertain to the faithful, the genuine children of the Church, and sometimes begin only in the present Church, to be perfectly fulfilled in the heavenly Church.

XX. The prophets sometimes promise things which are not to be fulfilled in those to whom they seem to be promised, but in their descendants.

Many things have been predicted, which have undoubtedly been fulfilled, even if neither sacred nor secular history records how and when they were fulfilled.

Prophets are accustomed, when they have prophesied against the Jews, to turn their threats toward the nations hostile to the Jews, for the sake of the consolation of the Jews and the conversion of the nations to the Messiah and the people of the Lord.

Prophets delight in number or rhythms, or quasi-rhythms, and not infrequently they say in the latter hemistich and verse what they had said in other words in the former, for the sake of elegance and emphasis.

ON THE INTERPRETERS OF THE PROPHETS.

The commentators on the Prophets must also be touched upon, among whom Origen, Apollinaris, Didymus, Pierius, Eusebius, and Polychronius are celebrated in antiquity, but whose writings on the Prophets have perished. These were then succeeded among the Greeks by Cyril, Theodoret, and Chrysostom; among the Latins by Jerome and Gregory

the Great, from among those whose writings still survive. From later centuries there are a certain Thomas, Lyranus, Hugo, Dionysius, Arias Montanus, Vatablus, Forerus, Em. Saa, Corn. à Lapide, Sanchez, and Christopher à Castro, who have commented on the Prophets, as well as from our own side after B. Luther, Ioh. Brentius, Selneccerus, and Pappus. From the Reformed: Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bullinger, Calvin, Pellicanus, Marloratus, Piscator, Musculus: who, however, did not all expound all the Prophets. On Isaiah specifically, there exists from our side B. Luther, Tom. III. Jen. Lat., Snepfius, Tilemannus Heshusius, Arcularius, Forsterus, and on some chapters of Isaiah B. Sam. Bohlius, as well as Dn. D. Augustus Varenius. From the Reformed: Hyperius, Mollerus, Scultetus. From the Papists: Adam Sasbouth, Hector Pintus, Didacus Alvarez, Paulus à Palatio, Leo à Castro. These were preceded by Gifelbertus the Englishman in the year 1140, and Henry Winchingan in the year 1447. Matthæus Ebroicensis, Michaël Messanus (in the year 1350). Thomas Hasselbachius, in the year 1410, a lecturer at the Viennese Gymnasium for 21 years, expounding Isaiah, did not reach the end of chapter 1, having prepared 24 books. Among the ancients, Procopius Gazæus is praised. On Jeremiah: D. Pomeranus, Herbrandus, Heilbrunnerus, B. Hülsemannus. From the Reformed: Polanus, Tossanus, Broughtonus, Lavaterus; from the Papists: Rupertus, Maldonatus, Andreas Capilla, Mich. Gislerius. On the Lamentations of Jeremiah: B. Hunnius, B. Hülsemannus, Ioh. Tarnovius, and Quistorpius. From the Reformed: Tossanus, Lavaterus; from the Papists: Rabanus, Hugo de S. Victore, Capilla, Pintus, Maldonatus. On Ezekiel: B. Hülsemannus, and on the temple of Ezekiel B. Hafenrefferus; from the Papists: Capilla, Pintus, Petrus Serranus, Hieron. Prado, and Ioh. Vilalpandus, who spent sixteen years at the expense of the King of Spain to elucidate the first 28 chapters and the last three chapters of Ezekiel. There also wrote from the ancients Alexander Necham the Englishman in the year 1210, Jerome Savonarola, Simon Asligeniensis, etc. On Daniel wrote Ægid. Hunnius, Polycarp. Lyserus, Salomon Gesnerus, Mich. Waltherus, L. Rhau, and Dn. D. Martinus Gejerus, as well as D. Svaningius; from the Reformed: Polanus, Junius, Iodocus Nahum, Rollocus, Broughtonus, Constant. L'Empereur in notes to R. Iachiades. From the Papists: Pererius, Pintus, and Maldonatus. From the ancients, Apollinarius wrote on Daniel (against Porphyry), Joachim Abbas, and Mich. Picardus. On the Minor Prophets: Wigandus, Winckelmannus, Ioh. Tarnovius, Iohan. Himmelins; and from the Reformed: Danæus and Ioh. Coccejus; from the Papists: Maldonatus, Fr. Ribera, and Christoph. à Castro, following Guido the Carthusian, Guilhelm. Melitonensis, and Stephen the Englishman. All of these were preceded by the ancients Theodoret and Remigius. On Hosea, after Cyril, Didymus, and Pierius, [came] Rufinus, Theophilus, Meisnerus and Gesnerus; as well as from the Reformed: Zanchius, Mollerus, Pareus, and Rivetus, as well as Mercerus. On Joel and Amos: Rufinus, Beda, Theophylactus, Selneccerus, Gesnerus, D. Hoë, Mercerus, and Pareus. On Obadiah: Urb. Regius, Gesnerus and Mercerus, Rainoldus, and Drusius. On Jonah, after Guilh. Pepin, Ioh. Catard, Theophyl., Bugenhag. jun., Snepfius, Krakevitz, August. Pfeiffer from our side; Mercerus, Junius, and Drusius, Ioh. Leusden from the Reformed, and Gabriel à Costa, a Papist. On Micah: Savonarola, David Chytreus, and B. Höpfnerus. On Nahum: Cyprianus Monachus, Theophyl., Chytreus, Ludov. Crocius, and Drusius. On Habakkuk: Theophyl., Victorin. Petav., Chytreus, and Drusius; on Zephaniah: Bucerus, Urbanus Regius, and Drusius. On the last three Minor Prophets: Urban. Regius, Zacharias Schilterus, Balduinus, as well as Jodocus Willich and Balth. Willius. On Haggai: Callistus

Placentinus, Georg. Vicelius, Ioh. Eckius, & Pareus; on Zechariah Didym. Savanorol. & Ioh. de Rairoles. Finally, on Malachi, Polanus & Gabriel à Costa.

But of these interpreters, some, and especially our own, have investigated the literal sense most thoroughly; others are occupied at the same time, or even chiefly, with the mystical sense, which is for the most part to be observed in the Papal interpreters. Cornelius à Lapide himself prefers those who have devoted effort to the literal sense, and among them he awards the palm to Jerome, whom he honors with these eulogies: 'This one man is to us a Lucifer,' our St. Jerome prefers the same. That phoenix of his age, a man most skilled in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin, and by the reckoning of the Church the greatest doctor in expounding the Holy Scriptures: for he grew old in these until extreme gray hairs, and, as St. Augustine testifies, read all the ancient Greek and Latin commentators, who indeed, had this man not first broken the ice, the way of the Prophets would have been impassable for all posterity; but by the beneficent providence of God, the labor and doctrine of Jerome stood so firm in this whole work that this doctoral laurel and gem of his writings shines forth above all others; I say the most excellent work of his works, in which he conquered himself. These Meletemata of ours on the Prophets will also show that Jerome is cited with well-deserved praises: in which we have devoted much effort so that the Hieronymian views might be heard, as we judged them to contribute much to illustrating and confirming the true mind of the Prophets.

Nor is that distinction of interpreters to be neglected: that one kind of them is Jewish, who interpret everything said about Judah, Jerusalem, Babylon, Moab, and Edom as being about the Jews, to whom Cornelius à Lapide adds Hugo, Lyranus, and the commentary ascribed to Thomas, but we add besides

Latin:

PRÆFATIO DEDICATORIA QUATUOR MAJORUM PROPHETARUM. ILLUSTRISSIMO DOMINO, DOMINO HENRICO, LIBERO BARONI A FRIESEN, DOMINO IN Schönfeld/ Jessen/ & Puskaw/ Serenissimi Saxoniæ Electoris Comiti Cubiculario, & in Senatu Intimiori Confi- liario Excellentissimo, Ejusdemque Sanctioris Senatus Directori Eminentissimo, Domino meo Gratiosissimo. ILLUSTRISSIME DOMINE.

QUæ in Prophetis V. T. eminent ac præcellunt, ea in quatuor Majoribus quos vocant, cum maxime effulgere videmus. Revocat illa ad tria potissimum capita Coryphæus Apostolorum: ad indagationem salutis, quæ est per fidem in Christum, ad προμαρτυρίαν, seu prætestificationem, ut ita reddam, passionis Christi, & gloriæ eandem consequuturæ, & ad scrutinium characteris præcipui, quod & quale illud tempus sit, quod Spiritus Christi, qui in ipsis erat, iisdem adimplendis definiverat. Non enim cum Pelagianis, Francisco Puccio, Scholasticis, ac Novatoribus credendum est, expertes fuisse Prophetas cognitionis salutis, quam per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi veteres, æque ac nos, adeptos esse, Concilium Apostolicum conclusit: Etsi quæ à Prophetis scrutinio sedulo eruta sunt, nos fine labore, in clara luce, per filium in carne manifestatum, posita intelligamus: Omnes enim Prophetæ testimonium perhibent Christo, quod in nomine ejus remissionem peccatorum consequamur per fidem in ipsum. Quum vero in hac salutis cognitione ac fide præcipue contineatur Filii DEI œconomia, qui propter nos homines, & propter salutem nostram, ut in Symbolo Niceno profitemur, de cælis descendit, & incarnatus est, & in œconomia illa præprimis passio & mors Filii DEI credenda exhibeatur, quod nempe traditus sit propter peccata nostra, nec non resurrectio, & gloria, quod resuscitatus sit, & ingloria assumptus, propter justificationem nostram: Prophetis sane in V. T. viam salutis populo tradituris id imprimis incumbebat, scrutari passiones, quæ in Christo futuræ erant, & gloriam easdem sequuturam, quomodo oportuerit ipsum regnum cæleste occupare, missoque de cœlo Spiritu Ecclesiam per universum orbem sibi congregare, in qua dominetur in regno gratiæ, & à qua æternum glorificetur in regno gloriæ. Ut autem fides nostra in tuto collocaretur, nec de persona illa, citra quam nulli mortalium salus contingere potest, hærere quispiam opus haberet, characteres certi, ac infallibiles designati à Prophetis sunt, è quibus eadem indubitato dignosci queat: inter quos principem facile locum obtinent characteres Chronologici, quodnam & quale illud tempus adventus, vel πλήρωμα χρόνου sit, quod redemptioni orbis definitum fuit. Unde S. Irenæus Lugdunensium Episcopus Apostolorum ætati valde vicinus REGULÆ FIDEI, quam Ecclesiam per universum orbem usq́; ad fines terræ disseminatam ab Apostolis, & discipulis eorum accepisse, ac diligenter custodire testatur, hoc inclusum fuisse docet, quod Ecclesia crediderit, Spiritum S. per PROPHETAS prædicasse DISPOSITIONES DEI ET ADVENTUM, & eam, quæ est ex virgine generationem, & passionem, & resurrectionem à mortuis, & in carne ascensionem, Idem Sanctus Pater MANIFESTUM esse, ait, quod PATRIARCHÆ & PROPHETÆ præfigurarint NOSTRAM FIDEM, & disseminarint in terram ADVENTUM FILII DEI, quis & qualis futurus erat, ut qui posteriores erant futuri homines, habentes timorem DEI, facile susciperent ADVENTUM CHRISTI, INSTRUCTI à PROPHETIS. Quod eleganter illustrat, & confirmat Evnuchi Reginæ Candacès exemplo: Propter hoc Philippus, cum invenisset Evnuchum Reginæ Æthiopum legentem ea, quæ scripta sunt, quemadmodum ovis ad victimam ductus est &c. facile suasit ei credere Eum esse Christum Jesum, qui sub Pontio Pilato crucifixus est, & passus est, quæcunque prædixit Propheta, eumq́; esse Filium Dei, qui æternam vitam hominibus dat. Et statim ut baptizavit eum, discessit ab Eo. NIHIL enim aliud deerat ei, qui à PROPHETIS fuerat PRÆCATECHIZATUS, non DEUM Patrem, non CONVERSATIONIS (œconomiam vel) dispositionem, sed solum adventum ignorabat FILII DEI (quod nempe jam in mundum venerit) quem cum breviter cognovisset, agebat iter gaudens, præco futurus in Æthiopia Christi adventus. Quapropter non multum laboravit circa eum Philippus, quia erat timore DEI PRÆAPTATUS à PPOPHETIS. Hæc de Prophetis S. Irenæus. In hac PRÆCATECHIZATIONE vel PRÆAPTATIONE, ut ita loquamur, sine dubio, præcellunt Majores Prophetæ, ESAIAE certe hoc Elogii tribuit S. Hieronymus, quod universa Domini Sacramenta contineat; & alibi, Esaias, inquit, non Prophetiam mihi videtur texere, sed Evangelium. In quo, ut alios plures taceam, Magnum Hipponensium Episcopum consentientem habet, cujus hæc sunt: Esaias inter illa, quæ iniqua arguit, & justa præcepit, & peccatori populo mala futura prædixit, etiam de CHRISTO, & ECCLESIA, hoc est, de Rege, & ea, quam condidit, civitate multo plura, quam cæteri prophetavit, ita ut à QUIBUSDAM

Evangelista potius quam Propheta dictus fuerit. Hæc ex vero S. Augustinus. Non enim veram tantum salutem, & viam ac rationem perveniendi ad eam, per fidem in Messiam, luculenter satis pro- posuit S. ESAIAS, sed sigillatim ea quæ de Christo sunt credenda Sacramenta, vel mysteria, quantum ad Personam, Statum geminum, & triplex offi- cium ejusdem, exequutus est Veteris Testamenti Evangelista, perspicue differens de æterna Christi Deitate, quem ut JEHOVAM verum Deum, extra quem non est DEUS, & ab attributis atque operi- bus vere, ac mere Divinis describit, & honore, cul- tuque divino prosequendum fistit; nec non de temporali conceptione ac nativitate è virgine, passione, morte, resurrectione, ac gloria: De oblatione item pro peccatis nostris, ac intercessione ejus, de regno denique & Ecclesia, ac subditis Messiæ. Quæ omnia characteribus operum, signorum, locorum & tem- porum ita illustravit Esaias, ut palmam etiam in eo aliis Prophetis facile ambiguam reddat.

Quamvis vero cætera tanta lux non affulgeat a- liis Prophetis majoribus, valde tamen insignia de mysteriis fidei penes eos reperiuntur oracula: si- quidem, ut aliqua tantum attingam, JEREMIAS Symbolum, & confessionem Fidei catholicam ad- modum illustrem binis vicibus exhibuerit, de ger- mine DAVIDIS justo, quod Jehovab justitia nostra, in quo uno salus, & tranquillitas vera nobis obtingit, deque Rege, & Regno, extra cujus pomœria nec ju- dicium, nec justitia uspiam in terra locum habet: E- ZECHIEL vero unicum illum Pastorem, DAVIDEM verum servum Domini descripserit, in & sub quo fœdus pacis æternæ viget, quique nos unice ad æter- nam vitam pascit: DANIEL denique Regnum ejus, quod cætera comminuit, & cui nullum habituro finem cedere omnia debent, cum æterna potestate ac gloria ei concessa, & subditis ex omnibus populis, nationi- bus & linguis vera fide ipsi servientibus graphice de- lineârit, adhæc unctionem Messiæ, ejusque mortem & excisionem, ac sacrificium expiatorium vivis quasi coloribus illustrârit, temporis etiam characterem præ omnibus aliis accuratissime designârit, ut ex vero S. Hieronymus commoneat, nullum Prophe- tam tam aperte de Christo, (quantum ad computum chronologicum) dixisse. Non enim, inquit, solum scribit eum esse venturum, quod est commune cum cæ- teris, sed etiam quo tempore venturus sit, docet, & Re- ges per ordinem digerit, & annos enumerat, ac mani- festissima signa prænunciat. Hæc S. Hieronymus.

Quo enim temporum plenitudini propiores facti sunt Prophetæ, eo evidentiores temporum, & aliarum circumstantiarum characteres, sugge- rente Spiritu Sancto, acceperunt, & consignarunt, ut fidem Sanctorum, quæ calamitatibus novissimo- rum temporum facile concuti poterat, roborarent, ac desiderium adventus Messiæ acuerent. Quan- quam vero duum-viri illi intermedii, JEREMIAS & EZECHIEL, non videantur quicquam ad scrutinium temporis adventus Messiæ conferre, CHRONOLO- GIAE tamen sacræ, quam totam in Scripturis V. T. juxta omnes Epochas suas, tempus illud accepta- bile, quod omnes sancti anhelabant, respicere, in Chronico Biblico demonstravi, sua haud constaret ratio, nisi à Jeremia, (cujus calculum sequutus est Daniel) terminus à quo & ad quem Babylonicæ servi- tutis designaretur, & hæc tam celebris Epocha accu- rate suis definiretur limitibus. Et intererat o- mnino, ut numeraret Ezechiel annos à spontanea Jechoniæ transmigratione, non quidem ut vulgus Chronologorum cum Scaligero temere statuit, pro- pter Epocham Captivitatis Babylonicæ, sed propter annos regiminis Zedekiæ, ultimi Judæorum Regis, qui cum Jechoniæ deportatione cœperunt, & ob alia in Historia Sacra, de quib. in Chronico Biblico.

Haec quum ita habeant, optime, procul ambi- guo, in Quadrigam horum perquam excellentium Prophetarum collocatur opera, cum & praecipuus S. literarum Scopus, quem S. Paulus hunc assignat, quod instruant nos ad salutem per fidem in Christum Jesum, pensi habetur, & Oracula Prophetica de Christi persona, Statibus, officiis, beneficiis, & Eccle- sia, ceu Regno ejus, ac privilegiis, successu, & sorte re- gni illius spiritualis in his terris sub accuratiorem considerationem revocantur, suaeque integritati, ubi vim patiuntur, justo Elencho adferuntur, ne e characteres Chronologici, quos ipse Spiritus Christi definivit, negliguntur. Quam triplicem metam hisce qualibuscunque Annotationibus potissimum praefixi, quomodo autem assequutus sim, pio, & E- rudito Lectori dijudicandum permitto. Nihil certe utilius in hac mihi credita B. Lutheri Cathe- dra, in Scrutinio Propheticorum scriptorum, abs me proponi potuisse, credidi, tum ut nucleus ipse, ac medulla vaticiniorum Propheticorum, in quo Spi- ritus est, & vita, S. Literarum cultoribus exhibere- tur, tum ut Harmonia Veteris & Novi Testamenti, praedictionum & eventuum in aprico poneretur, & quam vere S. Augustinus Novum Testamentum in Veteri velari, Vetus in Novo revelari, dixerit, pa- lam constaret.

Id vero omne jam necessarium etiam videba- tur, ubi nucleum e Propheticis scriptis, solo relicto putamine, tolli, medullam, ossibus inanibus rema- nentibus, exhauriri, viam Salutis fidelium Vet. Test. qui nobiscum una sunt Ecclesia, unam fidem, unam spem habent, interverti, Christum, cum passionibus & gloria, officiis, & beneficiis ejus, qui Sol est univer- sae Scripturae, obscurari, & eclipsin pati, quantum unquam passus est, maximam, characteres tempo- rum, aliosque similes in dubium vocari, sensum ve- rum & literarum a S. S. unice intentum depravari non tam oculis hisce meis videbam, quam manibus ipsis palpabam: idque omne a VIRO INUSITA- TAE ERUDITIONIS, Linguarum Orientalium callentissimo, in Antiquitate tam sacra, quam Exo- tica versatissimo. Quem INCOMPARABILEM Scriptorem in Religione Christiana & NULLA- RUM, & OMNIUM Partium, adhuc Caecorum Doctorum Rabbinorum caecum discipulum, suo denique, etsi capacissimo, ingenio nimium in- dulsisse, commentationes ejus in universam Scri- pturam sonora voce clamant. De caeteris VIRI MAGNI scriptis haud temere mihi sumo judi- cium.

Liceat pauca tantum, & veluti per Saturam in rem praesentem adducere, ut ex ungue Leonem. Nimirum Vaticinia illa de Christo, quae & ipsa ver- borum evidentia & infallibilis Spiritus Sancti in Novo Testamento interpretatio extra omnem quaestionem, & dubietatem constituere debebat, ad personas prorsus alias, & in sensum plane alie- num abripiuntur, ut vice Christianarum Annota- tionum Rabbinica, & plusquam Rabbinica com- menta legamus. Quae S. ESAIAS de conceptio- ne ac nativitate Christi IMMANUEL e VIR- GINE, quae de puero nobis nato, de Filio nobis dato, DEO illo forti, Patre aeternitatis, ac Principe Pa- cis, quae de Surculo e radice Jesse, in quo requiescit Spiritus Domini, quique Spiritu labiorum suorum impium interfecit, de vexillo populorum, in quo con- fidunt gentes, de Rege in justitia regnaturo, sub quo Spiritus de excelsis effundendus, quaeque de oculis caecorum, & linguis mutorum, sub adventum DEI nostri CHRISTI Redemtoris aperiendis, asynd- di foni praedicit, ea omnia ad EZECHIAM Re- gem detorquent Grotiana commentaria. Hymnus

Eucharisticus fidelib. in laudem Christi triumphantis ris mortis, quam in victoriam devorat, decantandus ad ereptionem è manu Sennacheribi, & Hierosolymæ a obsidione liberationem pertrahitur. Oraculum de Johanne Proto-baptista Christi prodromo de Prophetis tempore exitii urbis Chaldaici, vaticinia de Christo servo Dei justo calamum quaffatum non conterente, linumque fumigans non extinguente, de nomine gentium, ac salutari Domini usque ad extremum terræ de Propheta ipso Esaia exponitur; quem etiam cum Judæorum Magistris Grotius Eum esse dicit qui corpus suum percutientibus & genas suas vellentibus non denegavit, cui à DEO lingua erudita data ad sustentandum eum qui lassus est, & Testem illum, ac Ducem & Præceptorem Gentium, ad quem omnes sitientes Esaias ad hauriendum aquas vivas invitat, Evangelistas Pacis, quorum pedes pulcri sunt super montes Iude, Spiritus S. de Apostolis interpretatus est, Grotius de JEREMIA V. T. Propheta. Totum caput Esaiæ 53. quo nullum disertius in universo Ebrææ Scripturæ Codice de passione & satisfactione Christi, eumque consequuta gloria extat, ad JEREMIAM itidem πρεβλότητι in Christiano orbe inaudita detorquet, tametsi Ipse in libr. de Verit. Relig. Christ. totum caput Paraphrastice exposuerit, addita tali clausula: Quis potest nominari aut Regum aut Prophetarum, in quem hæc congruant? Quæ de gentilitatis fœcunditate, Apostolo interprete, vaticinatus est Propheta, etsi Augustino dicente ita aperta sint, ut etiam inimici intelligere cogantur inviti, ad restaurationem Hierosolymæ terrenæ abripit Grotius: Redemtorem Sion, cujus nomen ab occidenti, & gloriam, qui ab ortu Solis sunt, agnoscunt, non Christum, sed Cyrum esse contendit: quo de etiam κέλευσμα illud resonare asserit: Dicite filiæ Sion, Ecce Salvator tuus venit, Ecce merces ejus cum eo, & opus ejus coram illo. Excitationem illam Propheticam, Surge, illuminare Ierusalem, quia lux tua venit, ad felicitatem terrenam Hierosolymæ trahit, & per lumen illud, in quo gentes ambulare dicuntur, non CHRISTUM, sed Esaiam ipsum intelligit; nec de CHRISTO, sed Esaia ipso interpretatur, quæ CHRISTUS in Schola Nazarethana (Ireneus per ἁμάρτημα μνημονικὸν in Capernaitica id factum dicit) disertissime de se prædicta esse testatus est, Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me Dominus: neque propugnator ille ad Salvandum, qui torcular calcavit solus, Messias Grotio est, sed Iudas Maccabeus, ad cujus tempora etiam reliqua in hoc Propheta vaticinia, quæ de vocatione gentium, deque gaudio spirituali & cœlesti fidelium agunt, ab eodem detorquentur.

Jam quæ JEREMIAS de abrogatione cultus Levitici, conversatione gentium, prædicatione Evangelii sub N. Testam. tradidit, ea sensu plane contrario Grotius non de abrogatione cultus Levitici, nec de tempore N. Test. sed de tranquillo Statu Politiæ Judaicæ sub V. T. explicat Grotius. Germen Davidis justum, quod vocatur, & est Iehovah justitia nostra, ipso autore non Christus est, sed Zorobabel: nec alium esse vult Pastorem David, ab EZECHIELE prædictum, quam Zorobabelem, ad quem etiam oraculum Zachariæ de Rege Hierosolymam super asino & pullo filio asinarum ingressuro pertraxit.

Luci DANIELIS ut offundat tenebras, per regnum Quartum non quartam Monarchiam, sed Seleucidarum, & Lagidarum regnum: Filiumque hominis ad antiquum dierum adductum non Christum, sed Romanum populum esse contendit: in calculum etiam Prophetæ Chronologicum minus æquus est, ac si Propheta, quod de Prætore vulgo dicitur, modicum parum curet: in oraculo vero de LXX. Septimanis, quod unicum de Messia in Majoribus

Prophetis relinquit, non beneficium Christi, sed pœnam Judæorum, Politiæ nempè ipsorum destructio- nem, ut luatur iniquitas, designari vult, neque adven- tus Messiæ tempus, sed terminum Politiæ Iudaicæ de- finiri statuit, imo cum Judæis Messiam Principem terrenum facit, qui Hierosolymam & Iudæos, ceu populum suum à malis impendentibus liberare debue- rit, si sc. ei paruissent: Deniq; quæ sub finem Pro- phetiæ suæ Daniel de hoste regni Christi præcipuo Anti-Christo magno, & de gloria æterna fidelium præ- dixit, cum Porphyrio Apostata, cujus, etsi ab Hiero- nymo jam refutati, pressè legit vestigia, ad Antio- chum, & reditum Iudæorum in urbem, qui ob religio- nem inde ejecti, obtorto, quod dicitur, collo, ab- ripit. Sic velificari Apostatis, Iudæis & Hæreticis passim maluit Grotius, quam accedere coronæ Do- ctorum Ecclesiæ. Quod πρὸς ὄμμα in hisce com- mentationibus nostris ostendimus.

Non enim ferenda talia in Orbe Christiano, nec quæ VIRI MAGNI autoritate, ac eruditione o- mnigena insigniter se commendant, & doctissimos etiam quosq; ob exasciatum genus dicendi, & ana- lysin integrorum contextuum sæpe admodum in- geniosè exagitatam, facile fascinare possunt, sine justa censura transmittenda erant: imprimis quia vera falsis, congrua detortis, & incongruis, & ut I- ræneus loquitur, aramentum argento commixta sunt, venena melle circumlita hic propinantur, non sine ingenti periculo. Gloria itaq; CHRISTI Redem- toris, Salus Ecclesiæ sanguine ejus partæ, & infor- matio juventutis fidei nostræ commissæ, excitatio etiam Magnorum Virorum me commovebant tan- dem, ut operi sane grandi, humerisy; meis (non diffiteor) valde impari animum applicarem, ma- numq; admoverem. Andreæ Riveti, Viri Octuagena- rii, Theologi inter Reform. hoc seculo facile Prin- cipis, qui SyncretismumGrotianum cumPontificiis sub censuram revocavit, querela, & votum ante i- psos viginti tres annos fuit: Audaciam illam alii for- tasse redarguent, qua Grotius Propheticos Libros in præcipuis eorum de Christo oraculis ita deformavit, quasi ab hostibus Christiani nominis ad id fuisset con- ductus. Cumque non ignoraret, inter alios ESAIAM expressissima de venturo Messia oracula fudisse, in eo præsertim corrumpendo laboravit. Postquam vero Rivetus nonnulla exempli loco in medium addu- xiffet, quæ, uti ait, anima Christiana sine horrore non legit, hæc subjecit: Exorietur aliquis si jam non ortus fuerit, & ad sacrum illud bellum accinctus, qui cor- ruptelas omnes illas, quibus Sacram Scripturam mul- tis modis pervertit vir ille, ad examen revocabit, & NECESSARIIS antidotis venenum istud propellet.

Quum vero nemo sive è Reformatis, sive innostra Ecclesia sit exortus, qui hoc susciperet, invocato Spiritus S. auxilio, in nomine Iesu, rem aggressus sum. Postquam enim, divina gratia, Matæologiam Papisticam Orbi Christiano inde à Reformationis B. LUTHERI auspicio satis detectam, compen- dio, juxta propositiones Romano-Catholicas in Collo- quio Thoruniensi, cujus pars qualiscunque fui, pro- positas, exhibueram, Socinianam hæresin Scriptis bene multis, & ὡς ἐν ἐπιτομῇ Syntagmate Socinismi profligati confutâram, Novellam Arminianorum sectam sub Disputationum incudem revoraram, in Calvinianorum dogmata, & Syncretismum Exa- men institueram, Calixtinum item, Nicolaitanum, & Rintelensiu Syncretismum, cum Harmonia, quamNo- vatores alunt cum variis hærefibus, ad lancê verita- tis exegeram, ne commentationes istæ Biblicæ, tam periculofæ, quam argutæ, ac speciosæ auditoribus nostris imponerent, (quod in Anglia multis, Erudi- tissimo etiam Waltono, & συνέργοις in Opere Biblico accidit) damnumque amplius inferrent Ecclesiæ,

Ξὺν θεῶ παλάμῃ, studio non vulgari præcavendum videbatur. Jussi itaque tantisper quiescere conti- nuationem Systematis Locorum Communium, etsi quatuor jam Tomis expediti, & aliquousque pro- večti, ut S. literis vindicandis operam navarem. Et in Mose quidem, scriptisque Historicis brevioribus agi poterat lineis, sed in Psalmorum libro, & Can- tico Canticorum majori cura opus erat: quod ne- que Hymnos Propheticos intemeratos reliquerit Grotius, quin plerosque omnes prorsus perverte- ret, & Canticum illud Sanctissimum, instar propha- ni Epithalamii, de amore Salomonis adversus Sponsam Ægyptiam, admixtis etiam valde inde- centibus, nec scandalo vacantibus, tractàrit. Ma- ximam tamen operam requirebant Prophetæ, ut ve- ro sensui restituerentur, & à corruptelis variis, im- primis quoad vaticinia de Messia, & computum sa- crum Chronologicum, in quo Scaligerianis novita- tes & exerrationes plerumque sequutus est Gro- tius, adsereretur. Enim vero non raro Grotium in Historia, & vocum, ac phrasium interpretatione, pro excellenti in Philologia Sacra & prophana Doctrinæ apparatu, ad intelligentiam S. literarum suum quoddam ἐπι- βάλλον μέρος attulisse, haud diffiteor; cujus proinde observationes alicubi etiam merito am- plector, & approbo; in Prophetis vero plerumque cum Rabbinis, aliisque à sensu Scripturæ divarican- tibus facere, aut ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν sectari, quam sensui Spiritus S. genuino, etsi ab antiquitate monstrato, vel è litera luculenter effulgenti acquiescere Vir summus maluit. Hæc ergo Meletemata soli veritati cœlesti con- secranea, pia, & sedula textuum Sacrorum ἐρευνήσει, fontium Divinorum indagatione, locorum similium collatione, Spiritus Sancti in Novo Testamento expli- catione, Interpp. optimorum quà Veterum, quà recen- tiorum (quorum veluti Catenam quandam non- nunquam teximus) sententiis, & meditationibus adhibitis in hac Electorali Academia enata, pu- bliceq; proposita TIBI, HEROS ILLUSTRISSI- ME, jam ea, qua par est, Devotione offerre non dubitavi, quod Te Sacrarum literarum, ipsiusque veritatis Ebraicæ, raro in isto Honorum apice exem- plo,scrutatorem sedulum esse, certus sim: quodque Sanctioris Senatus PRÆSIDI studia mea publica Academica se imprimis, qua possunt, probare de- beant, qua fini etiam antea syllabum aliquem ope- rarum mearum pertexui: adhæc TE unum super- esse divina gratia voluit in summo illo Collegio, per annos hosce undeviginti, quos in hac incluta Electorali, hodierno Ejusdem Natali, compleo; cujus inusitatam humanitatem, cum multivaria TANTI HEROIS eruditione devinctissimam, sub primum in sedem Electoralem adventum mihi peregrino exhibitam summisse veneratus semper sum, & nunc publice quoque celebrandam duxi. Denique quum tristia undiquaque Ecclesiæ DEI, eheu! incumbentia fata, quæ maxime infelix il- lud conciliandarum δὶς διὰ πασῶν dissidentium in fide religionum Cacoëthes procreavit, remedium aliquod, divina secundante gratia, à SERENISSI- MO SAXONIÆ ELECTORE DOMINO NO- STRO potissimum exposcere videantur, cujus, TU HEROS INCLUTE, veluti COR esse crederis, atque ANIMA in Sanctiori Consilio, causam Ecclesiæ afflictissimæ Tibi, ceu Statori & Eliakimo Nostro pie commendandam statui, etsi pro eadem ultro excubare studia INTIMIORIS SENATUS sanctissima, nullus ambigam, meoque ipsius exemplo, cum plus vice simplici in tutelam, religionis causa, me suscepit, & aliis documentiş

publicis, quæ devoto pectore veneror ac deprædi- co, agno verim. Quo nomine quum & hæc Mea Patrocinium, ac Gratiam SERENISSIMI, ut sub umbra alarum ejus, ad usus luculentiores Ecclesiæ, in publicum, limatiori cura, juxta cum aliis com- mentationibus sacris in Libros Veteris & Novi Te- stamenti adornatis provehantur, desiderent, TE, ILLUSTRISSIME DOMINE, proxeneta non desperant, quod ob sui vilitatem nunquam spe- rare auderent. Servet TE, DOMINE, divi- na benignitas SERENISSIMÆ Domui, servet universæ Ecclesiæ, Spirituque Suo nunquam non dirigat, & cum familia illustrissima omnigena feli- citate undiquaq; repleat! Ita vigeas, floreas, peren- nes SECULI NOSTRI ORNAMENTUM IM- MORTALE: Witebergae die S. Lucæ Acade- miæ Natali Anno O. R. cIɔ Iɔc LXIX.

DE PROPHETICIS LIBRIS MAJORUM ET MINORUM PROPHETARUM.

DE Prophetis in genere diximus ante librum Josuæ, nunc de Prophetis, quos ita vocant, posterioribus, qui in Majores & Minores distribuuntur, dicemus. Majores, uti no- tissimum est, sunt Esaias, Jeremias cum Threnis, E- zechiel & Daniel, Minores Oseas, Joël, Amos, Obadias, Jonas, Micheas, Sophonias, Nahum, Habacuc, Hag- gæus, Zacharias, Malachias. Indigitantur autem Ma- jores non ob auctoritatem, aut sententiarum gravita- tem, vel verborum etiam majestatem, qua omnes Prophetæ pares sunt, quemadmodum unicuique Spiritus dedit eloqui, sed à Scriptis majoribus, seu quia quatuor Prophetæ prolixa volumina condide- runt, dicente Augustino l. XVIII. de Civitate Dei c. 19. Quamvis enim Hoseas, & Zacharias, nume- ro capitum excedant Danielem, tamen quia capi- ta Oseæ & Zachariæ sunt breviuscula, Danielis au- tem prolixiora, ipsum etiam Oseæ & Zachariæ volumen libro Danielis minus est.

Non autem idem ordo est apud LXX. qui in Ebræo codice Minorum Prophetarum, de quo Hieronym. in Joël. Illi enim post Hoseam Amos secundum, tertium Micheam ponunt, 4. Joëlem, 5. Obadiam, 6. Jonam, 7. Nahumum, 8. Habacu- cum, 9. Sophoniam, 10. Aggæum, 11. Zachariam, 12. Malachiam. Ebræi autem ordinem supra po- situm observant.

Quod ad Chronotaxin, tres solent constitui classes; Siquidem aliqui ante captivitatem Babylo- nicam vaticinati sint, alii in captivitate, alii denique post captivitatem, de quo ordine tamen variant Chronologi, imprimis in Obadia, Nahum, & Ha- bacuc, notante August. l, XVIII. de Civ. Dei c. 31. addimus etiam de Joële, quia illorum tempus non est expressum, nec satis certum. Primum omnium faciunt Rabbini, Clem. Alex. l. 1. Strom. Hier. in E- pit. Paul. & præfat Obad. Lyranus & alii Obadiam, quia putant ipsum fuisse oeconomum Ahabi, sed licet hic idem nomen habuerit, non tamen con- stat eum Prophetam fuisse, neque argumentum Obadiæ Prophetæ isti tempori congruit, imo si cum Jeremia conferatur, Obadias potius post ca- ptum Jechoniam sub Zedekia circa tempus desola- tionis Hierosolymæ vixisse colligitur. Habacu- cum Hieronymus Danieli σύγχρονον facit, eiq; scri- ptum apocryphum de Habacuco ex Judæa Danieli cibum in foveam leonum afferenti tribuit; sed non convenit Chronologia: quia nondum erat Judæa occupata Habacuci tempore. Minatur enim illi c. 1. Deum suscitaturo adversus eum Chaldæos. Conf. B. Luth. in præfat. in Habacuc.

Primus autem omnium Prophetarum fuit JONAS, qui tamen non sub Achabo vixit, aut σύγχρονος Elisæi fuit, quod Ebræis dicendum, qui illum filium viduæ Sareptanæ faciunt, ab Elia resuscitatum, annuente Epiphanio l. de Prophetis & Athanas. ad Antioch. q. 64. Sed Jonas filius A- mithai fuit, ac patria ejus Gad Hepher non Sarepta in Sidoniorum regione sita Luc. 4, 26. Sub Ama- zia demum Rege Juda, & Ieroboamo II. Rege Is- raël, ex 2. Reg. 14. eum floruisse nonnulli colligunt: alii ad Uziæ tempora referunt, & Joasi Regis Israël, sub quo Israele à Syris valde oppresso liberationem eorum per Jeroboamum prædixerit 2. Reg. 14, 25. Illud utique certum est, Ionam primum omnium inter Prophetas habendum esse.

Alterum faciunt plerique Hoseam, qui tem- pore Usiæ Regis Judæ & Jeroboami II. Regis Is- raël floruit & de Israëlitis abductione, quæ 70. circi- ter annis postea evenit, vaticinatus est.

Tertius est Amos, qui eodem tempore Usiæ & Jeroboami vixit. Quartus Esaias, qui vaticinari cœpit sub Usia. Quintus Joël, quem Hoseæ & Amoso σύγχρονον faciunt veteres, quibus argu- mentum libri favere videtur. Et difficile est, inter illos coætaneos indicare, quisnam primus, quis se- cundo, quisve tertio loco vaticinatus sit. Ideo au- tores variant: pleriq; tamen post Jonam Hoseæ pro- ximum assignant locum, nec fortassis erraverit, qui uti Esaias inter majores Prophetas non tantum vo- luminis magnitudine, sed etiam prophetiæ tempore primus est, quem cæteri majores Prophetæ ordine temporis recte sequuntur: ita similiter inter eos, qui in terra sancta vaticinati sunt, è minoribus Prophe- tis tempore priores statuerit, qui priores ordine col- locantur, uti in nostris codicibus exhibentur, Ho- seam, Joël, Amos, Obadiam, qui omnes quibus- dam sub Usia vaticinati videntur; quibus subjun- gitur Jonas, qui extra terram sanctam, isto tempore, vel paulo ante vaticinatus est. Joelem tamen Eze- chiæ vel Manassis tempore vixisse, B. Lutherus in Comment. ad Joël. observat: vide, quæ ad Joel. 1. v. 6. fere sub finem diximus.

Subsequitur in Codicibus nostris ratione æ- tatis, Micheas, utpote, qui sub Iotham Usiæ filio prophetare cœpit in Regno Judæ, & Nahum, qui in regno Israelis vaticinatus est, ut & Habacuc, quem ad Manassis tempora, non abnuente prophetia, re- ferunt. Denique Sophonias sub Josia vaticinatus est c. 1. v. 1. cui σύγχρονος Jeremias fuit. Atque hi ante captivitatem prophetarunt. Sub captivitate vero vaticinati sunt Ezechiel anno quinto post abductum Jechoniam c. 1, 2. Oba- dias, qui contra Idumæos prophetavit, postquam Judæis ob excidium Hierosolymitanum insulta- rant, (quod & à Jeremia, & Ezechiele factum, ut σύγ- χρονοι videri possint, quod etiam B. Lutherus Præ- fat. in Obad. T. III. Jenens. Lat. censuit,) & Daniel sub extrema Nebucadn. tempora & deinceps. Post captivitatem Haggæus anno II. Darii die 1. mensis VI. vaticinari cœpit, Zacharias anno eodem M. VIII. exortus est: Denique Malachias templo jam reædificato vaticinatus est; post quem nullus amplius Propheta extitit; uti tempore Maccabæo- rum negatur Propheta fuisse 1. Macc. c. 4, 43. c. 9, 3. c. 14, 41. Conf. Joseph. contr. Appion. August. l. 17. de Civ. Dei c. 24.

Cornel. à Lapide Hoseam primum facit, sed argumento lubrico, imo nullo, quia sc. Hos. 1, 2. dicitur principium loquendi Domini in Osee. Quo non notatur initium omnis Prophetiæ, quia multi jam præcesserant vates, sed initium revelationis Ho- seanæ. Ionam vero locat sub Iothamo filio Uziæ contra textum apertiffimum 2. Reg. 14, 26. quo docetur, Ieroboami tempore jam impleta fuisse va- ticinia Jonæ. At è Chronologia constat Iothamum Uziæ filium 37. annis demum post fata Jeroboami II. regnare cœpisse. Impegit ergo hic aperte Cor- nelius in Chronologiam. Nec meretur calculum ordo Grotii, qui primum locum Hoseæ, quintum demum Ionæ Prophetæ assignavit.

CANONES ISAGOGICI AD PROPHETAS.

SOlent interpp. Canones quosdam tum de for- ma & genere dicendi; vel Stylo Propheta- rum, tum de methodo, & ordine exhibere, qui usui esse queant in lectione Prophetica. Eorum nonnullos delibasse hic juvat. Mittimus autem partim illos, qui de tropis & figuris agunt: hi enim pertinent ad Rhetoricam sacram, nec Pro- phetarum sunt proprii: partim, quas de vario Scripturæ sensu fingunt, quum non nisi unicum Scripturæ sensum agnoscamus.

Canon I. Prophetæ de rebus futuris utun- tur sæpe verbis sui temporis; ut puta de Ecclesia Christiana veteris Ecclesiæ & populi V. T. inde per Sionem, & Ierusalem Ecclesiam N.T. per festa Iudai- ca, Sabbatum, tabernaculorum festum & alia gaudia festiva Christianorum, per verba felicitatis tempora- lis piorum temporum felicitatem spiritualem tem- pore N. T. cujus illa typus & umbra erant, desi- gnant, & per nomina hostium populi Judaici Phi- listinos, Moabitas, Ammonitas &c. hostes Eccle- siæ Christianæ denotant.

II. Prophetæ gaudent tropis & figuris, impri- mis Metaphoris, allegoriis, parabolicis phrasibus, prosopopœiis, non ob obscuritatem, sed ob elegan- tiam, & vim movendi.

III. Nonnunquam transeunt ab unâ metaphorâ ad aliam, ac subinde ad priorem redeunt.

IV. Nomen figuræ solent tribuere rei figuratæ v. g. cum Christum Davidem vocant.

V. Nomina propria gentium pro morum mutatio- ne quandoq́; commutant, uti cum homines fideles verum Israel, impios Cananæos, Amorrhæos, Sodo- mitas, mundum modo Ægyptum, modo Edom vocitant.

VI. Nomina propria aliquando ita adhibent, ut simul ad eorum etymon alludant; non tamen eodem loco & ut propria, & ut appellativa eadem acci- piunt.

VII. Cum decem tribus à duabus distinguunt, duas vocant regnum Iuda, domum David, Ierusa- lem, vel Sion, decem vero per Israel vel Iacob, vel per Samariam, quæ caput regni erat, vel per Io- seph aut Ephraim, ex quo ortus est Jeroboam pri- mus divisionis autor, exprimunt.

VIII. Prophetæ subinde verba mentalia vel voca- lia pro realibus accipiunt, ut vocari pro esse, judicia loqui, pro infligere: nonnunquam verba activa realia pro mentalibus aut vocalibus usurpant, ut po- te facio, pro cogito, prævideo, destino facere. Quo referri potest, quod omnis providentia Dei voce- tur evocatio, suscitatio, aut præceptum, quia Deus malis voluntatibus non dat corruptionem, sed ordi- nem, dicente Hugone Victor. l. 1. de Sacram. P. 5. c. 29. Sic excitasse dicitur Deus Chaldæos contra Judæos, etsi tantum ordinarii malam eorum volun- tatem, non autem eam ipsis indiderit, & per Pro- phetas prædixerit, adeoque veluti classicum ceci- nisse ipsis visus fuerit.

IX. Prophetæ de Christo & salute per eum parta loquuntur quasi de pugna & victoria, ut nempe prælium prot-Evangelio denunciatum se explica- re demonstrent.

X. De provinciis & civitatibus loquuntur quasi viri essent, vel potius fæminæ, tum ob pulcritudinem tum ob luxum earum.

XI. Prophetæ non raro res suas tractant per Dia- logismum, in quo modo unam modo aliam perso- nam introducunt loquentem.

XII. Nonnunquam reticent suppositum verbi è circumstantiis textus, verbo ipso, vel aliunde in- telligendum, ut Thren. 3, 1. Cant. 1, 3.

XIII. Sæpe etiam omittunt notas similitudinis ut Hos. 14, 8. conf. Prov. 4, 3. Pf. 11, 2. Pf. 12, 7.

XIV. Pro genere quandoque ponunt certam spe- ciem; uti Esa. 1, 15. sanguinis, & homicidii nomine quodvis grave peccatum intelligitur.

XV. Prophetæ non servant præcise ordinem tem- porum, ut historiæ: & ad aliam historiam non raro transeunt. Quia conciones ipsorum modo de hac, modo de alia materia inspiratæ, postea valvis affi- xæ, & in exedris repositæ, & ex illis volumina Pro- phetarum deinceps contexta creduntur.

XVI. Prophetæ non raro transeunt à typo ad an- titypum, à rebus sui temporis ad res N. T. ab histo- ria vel concione legali ad oracula de Messia & regno e- jus, ac concionem Evangelicam: non tamen iisdem verbis & de typo, & de antitypo, & de V. & N. T. rebus loquuntur: utut in verbis literali sensu de Messia, & rebus futuris sub N. T. agentibus, phra- ses, allusiones, & similitudines frequentes sint à re- bus V. T.

XVII. Solent Prophetæ adversis læta subjungere, & quos primum terruerunt, deinde consolari, atq; ita sua temperare, ut & increduli feriantur, ac per- cellantur, & fideles erigantur, ac confirmentur.

XVIII. Prophetæ per Sion & Jerusalem nunc Judæos in Judaismo manentes, qui ad Christum non convertuntur, nunc Judæos ad Christum conversos intelligunt, & quandoque statim ab his ad illos avo- lant.

XIX. Promissiones spirituales pertinent ad fide- les, genuinos Ecclesiæ filios, & incipiunt quando- que solum in Ecclesia præsenti, perfecte implendæ in cœlesti Ecclesia.

XX. Prophetæ nonnunquam promittunt, quæ non in illis, quibus promitti videntur, sed in posteris ipso- rum implenda sunt.

XXI. Multa prædicta sunt, quæ indubie com- pleta, etsi quomodo & quando impleta sint, nec sacra nec exotica historia referat.

XXII. Solent Prophetæ, cum vaticinati sunt contra Judæos, ad inimicas Judæis nationes mi- nas convertere, ob Judæorum consolationem, & gentium ad Messiam & populum Domini conver- sionem.

XXIII. Prophetæ numero vel rhythmis dele- ctantur, aut q. rhythmis, idemque non raro dicunt posteriori hemistichio & versu, quod aliis verbis in priori dixerant, elegantiæ & emphaseos gratia.

DE INTERPRETIBUS PRO- PHETARUM.

Attingendi etiam sunt Commentatores Pro- phetarum, è quibus in antiquitate cele- brantur Origenes, Apollinaris, Didymus, Pierius, Eusebius, Polychronius, sed quo- rum scripta in Prophetas interierunt. Quos exce- perunt deinde inter Græcos Cyrillus, Theodoretus, Chrysostomus: inter Latinos Hieronymus, Gregorius

M. ex iis, quorum scripta adhuc supersunt. E se- quioribus seculis sunt Thomas quidam, Lyranus, Hugo, Dionysius, Arias Montanus, Vatablus, Forerus, Em. Saa, Corn. à Lapide, Sanchez & Christophorus à Castro, qui in Prophetas commentati sunt, nec non è nostris post B. Lutherum Ioh. Brentius, Selneccerus, & Pappus. E Reformatis Zvinglius, Oecolampadius, Bullinger, Calvinus, Pellicanus, Marloratus, Piscator, Musculus: qui tamen non omnes Prophetas uni- versos exposuere. In Esaiam peculiariter extat è Nostris B. Lutherus Tom. III. Jen. Lat. Snepfius, Ti- lemannus Heshusius, Arcularius, Forsterus, & in ali- quot capita Esaia B. Sam. Bohlius, nec non Dn. D. Augustus Varenius. E Reformatis Hyperius, Mollerus, Scultetus. E Pontificiis Adamus Sas- bouth, Hector Pintus, Didacus Alvarez, Paulus à Palatio, Leo à Castro. Quibus præivere Gifelbertus Anglus Anno 1140. Henricus Winchingan Anno 1447. Matthæus Ebroicensis, Michaël Messanus (Anno 1350.) Thomas Hasselbachius Anno 1410. in Gymnasio Viennensi lector 21. annis Esaiam enar- rans non pervenit ad finem cap. 1. libris 24. concin- natis. E veteribus laudatur Procopius Gazæus. In Jeremiam D. Pomeranus, Herbrandus, Heilbrunne- rus, B. Hülsemannus. E Reformatis Polanus, Tos- sanus, Brugtonus, Lavaterus: è Pontificiis Rupertus, Maldonatus, Andreas Capilla, Mich. Gislerius. In Threnos Jeremiæ B. Hunnius, B. Hülsemannus, Ioh. Tarnovius, & Quistorpius. E Reformatis Tos- sanus, Lavaterus, è Pontificiis Rabanus, Hugo de S. Victore, Capilla, Pintus, Maldonatus. In Ezechi- lem B. Hülsemannus, & in templum Ezechielis B. Hafenrefferus, è Pontificiis Capilla, Pintus, Petrus Serranus, Hieron. Prado, & Ioh. Vilalpandus, quoad 28. prima, & tria ultima capita in Ezechiele diluci- danda, sumtu Regis Hispan. sedecim annos con- sumserunt. Scripsere & è veteribus Alexand. Ne- chan Anglus Anno 1210. Hieronymus Savanorola, Simon Asligeniensis, &c. In Danielem scripsit Æ- gid. Hunnius, Polycarp. Lyserus, Salomon Gesnerus, Mich. Waltherus, L. Rhau, & Dn. D. Martinus Ge- jerus, ut & D. Svaningius: è Reformatis Polanus, Iunius, Iodocus Nahum, Rollocus, Brughtonus, Con- stant. L'Empereur in notis ad R. Iachiad. E Pontifi- ciis Pererius, Pintus & Maldonatus. E veteribus in Danielem scripsit Apollinarius (contra Porphy- rium) Ioachim Abbas, & Mich. Picardus. In Pro- phetas minores Wigandus, Winckelmannus, Ioh. Tarnovius, Iohan. Himmelins; & è Reformatis Da- næus & Ioh. Coccejus; è Pontificiis Maldonatus, Fr. Riebera & Christoph. à Castro post Guidonem Car- thus. Guilhelm. Melitonens. & Stephan. Anglum. Quibus omnibus è veteribus præivêre Theodoretus & Remigius. In Hoseam post Cyrillum, Didym. & Pierium, Ruffin. Theophil. Meisnerus & Gesnerus; nec non è Reformatis Zanchius, Mollerus, Pareus, & Rivetus, ut & Mercerus. In Joëlem & Amos Ruffinus, Beda, Theophylactus, Selneccerus, Gesne- rus, D. Hoë, Mercerus ac Pareus. In Obadiam llrb. Regius, Gesnerus & Mercerus, Rainoldus, ac Drusius. In Jonam post Guilh. Pepin. Ioh. Catard. Theophyl. Bugenhag. jun. Snepfius, Krakevviz, August. Illos, qui sensui literali operam dederunt, præfert ipse Cornel. à Lap. & inter eos palmam de- fert Hieronymo, quem hisce elogiis mactat: Unus hic nobis Lucifer eadam præfert noster S. Hieronym. Phænix ille sui ævi, vir græce, hebraice, latine peritis- simus, & Ecclesiæ calculo in exponendis sacris scri- pturis doctor maximus: quippe qui in hisce ad extre- mam canitiem consenuerit, & teste S. Augustino vete- res omnes Græcos & Latinos commentatores legerit, qui sane nisi hic primus glaciem perfregisset, posteris o- mnibus Prophetarum invia fuisset via; sed Dei be- nefica providentia in hoc toto opere ita labor & do- ctrina Hieronymi constitit, ut hæc laurea ejus docto- ralis & scriptorum gemma præ omnibus emicet; opus dico operum ejus præstantissimum, in quo ipse seipsum vicit. Non immeritis laudibus afferri Hieronymum hæc etiam nostra in Prophetas Meletemata doce- bunt: in quibus magnam partem operam navavi- mus, ut Hieronymiana audirentur, utpote quæ ad illustrandam & confirmandam veram Propheta- rum mentem multum conducere judicavimus.

## 1:1 Introduction: I. N. On Isaiah in the Press
I. N. ON ISAIAH IN THE PRESS
