Concerning the Prophets in the Old Testament, there exists a remarkable opinion of Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria, easily the chief among them, in the preface to book 1 of his Commentary on Isaiah: 'The Blessed Prophet Isaiah seems to me not only to have been greatly adorned by the grace of prophecy, but also by the decorations (ἀυχήμασιν) of the Apostle. For this Prophet is at once a Prophet and an Apostle, and in this writing of his he will have discourses not lacking the splendor of Evangelical preaching.' To which is akin the judgment of Eusebius in the fragments on the life of the Prophets, in Procopius: 'Τὸ πλεῖσον τῆς προφητείας ἀυτ̃́ ἐςὶν ἐυαγγέλια περὶ τῆς ἐν σαρκὶ παρεσίας τ̃́ Λόγε ̥̃̄ ̊͛ ̃͛̄ Θε̥̃ ̊͛, κ̓ ̊͛ ὧν ἀνεδέ- ξατο δι' ἡμᾶς παθῶν': The greatest part of his prophecy embraces the Gospels concerning the incarnation and advent of the Word of God, and those things which He endured when He suffered for us. All who piously search and investigate the oracles of Isaiah acknowledge with one voice that this is a most true judgment, and one that proceeded not from the tripod of Apollo, but from the dictation of the Holy Spirit. The most learned D. Jerome, easily the most erudite among the Latin interpreters and Doctors, agrees entirely with the most eminent of the Greek interpreters, St. Cyril, and the Greek-speaking polymath Eusebius: and therefore he takes upon himself the task of explaining Isaiah not as a Prophet only, but as an Evangelist and Apostle, writing thus in the preface to the first of his Commentaries on Isaiah to the virgin Eustochium: 'Supported by the help of your prayers, which you meditate upon day and night in the law of God, and being a temple of the Holy Spirit, I will imitate the householder who brings forth from his treasure'—we add some Reformed [interpreters] along with Calvin himself, and Hugo Grotius, some of whom, even if they refer these things to Christ and the times of the New Testament in the mystical sense, as they call it, nevertheless weaken the true sense of the Prophet, as Cornelius admits. For, he says, even if they themselves admit that these prophecies pertain allegorically at least to Christ and the Church, they nevertheless snatch away the letter and the literal sense, which is the basis and foundation of Holy Scripture, and once that is snatched away, how easily will the Jews evade the allegorical? For they will deny that that sense is of Holy Scripture, and will say that it is a figment of the human brain, and fabricated by Christians.

The other kind is allegorical, and of those who interpret almost everything about Christ, about the Church of the New Testament, about the calling of the Gentiles, and about spiritual men, and who take what is said about Nebuchadnezzar, Sennacherib, etc., as being about the Devil; in which manner Leocastrius twists the whole of Isaiah toward Christ, certainly with no bad intention, namely to wrest him away from the Jews. Coccejus draws most things toward the times of later centuries in the New Testament, closer to the most recent ones, and seeks I know not what mysteries in the Prophetic oracles, clearly apocalyptic, all but making the Prophets commentators on the Johannine Apocalypse, or heralds similar to the Apocalypse, akin to John the Apostle.

The third is the middle way, of those who, when the text demands it, explain some things as concerning the affairs of the Old Testament, and others, by a prior interpretation of Holy Scripture, as concerning Christ and the affairs of the New Testament, and who press strictly for the single literal sense which it appears the Holy Spirit intended; that this is the best and safest method of interpreting, it is not right to doubt, since the Holy Spirit intends something certain, and it is necessary that there be one sense for one statement, just as the form of a thing is but one.

N. I. PROPHETAM QUIUM.

new and old, and the Bridegroom saying in the Song of Songs, new and old, my kinsman, I have kept for thee: and thus I shall expound Isaiah, so that I may show him to be not only a Prophet, but an Evangelist and an Apostle. For he himself says of himself and with the other Evangelists: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace! And to him, as if to an Apostle, God speaks: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And he answers, Behold me, send me. And let no one think that I desire to comprehend the argument of this volume in a brief discourse; since the present writing contains all the sacraments of the Lord, and both the Emmanuel born of a virgin, and the performer of illustrious works and miracles, is preached as dead and buried and rising from the dead, and the Savior of all nations. To the leaders of the Greeks and Latins we add the A and Ω of the German Fathers, our great man Luther in the German preface to Isaiah. He prepares and readies his people to wait for the future kingdom of Christ, of which he prophesies so clearly and manifoldly as no other prophet does, so that he even describes the mother of Christ, the Virgin Mary, how she should conceive and bear him with intact virginity, Chap. 7, 14, and his suffering in the 53rd chapter, together with his resurrection from the dead, and proclaims his kingdom powerfully and plainly, as if it had happened at that time. That he must have been a truly excellent, highly enlightened prophet. For all prophets do this, that they teach and rebuke the present people, and besides that, proclaim Christ's future and kingdom, and direct and point the people toward it, as as to the common Savior, both of the former and the future, yet one more than the other, one more abundantly than the other, but Isaiah above them all, most and most abundantly. Hæc B. Lutherus.…

is: We believed Jeremiah was deservedly cast into prison and worn down, God holding him in hatred as an enemy of the city and the temple and a Pseudo-Prophet: But in truth he was wounded (that is, badly treated) by our crime; the fault was in us, not in him. He was worn down by our fault; we thought most wickedly of him and therefore treated him cruelly. Who of the Jews has more horribly depraved the Evangelical text of the Prophet? I shudder, indeed, to transcribe all the annotations which the Jewish spirit suggested to him on this chapter. Now, the voice of one crying in the desert, Chap. 40, John, the forerunner of Christ, openly professed himself to be, John 1, to which indeed Grotius contradicts to his face, pretending this to be the sense of the Prophet's words, that in the times of the Babylonian destruction the Prophets ought to cry out to the Jews, so that they might remove the bad morals which were delaying their restoration. Christ himself, when he was teaching publicly in the synagogue at Nazareth, testified with a sonorous voice that he was the one who is introduced in Chap. 61 speaking thus: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to announce to the meek: For when the Prophetic text had been read and he had closed the book, and the eyes of all were intent upon him, Today, he said, this Scripture is fulfilled in your ears, Luke 4. But what of the Judaizing Grotius? Isaiah speaks here of himself, as the Chaldean notes. Forsooth, the Chaldean is of greater authority to him, nay, the recent Rabbis were most wicked, than Christ, the hypostatic Wisdom of God! But if we wished to review all the corruptions of Grotius, all the oracles of the Prophet would have to be traversed: For since he has not spared these so evident ones, everyone easily understands what the Grotian claws have attempted in others!

Nor indeed was there any doubt among Christians concerning this evidence and clarity of Isaiah in the prophecies about Christ, if you except Theodore of Mopsuestia, who is read to have deprived all the Prophets of their core and marrow, that is, of the prophecies about Christ, struck by anathema at the 5th Council of Constantinople. What then shall we say of Hugo Grotius, who is so far from leaving intact that praise to this most vocal Prophet, as Chrysostom called him in Hom. 8 on Genesis, that he distorts all his most luminous prophecies about the Messiah, written by the rays of the Sun himself, to anyone else rather than understanding them of Christ, with a truly profane daring and effort, and one entirely unheard of in the Church of Christ. Whence I am most persuaded that if anyone by chance happens upon his annotations on Isaiah, and they do not bear the name of the author prefixed on the front, he would believe that he is reading a certain Jew, not a Christian. So much does Grotius Judaize in this Prophet, perverting with the Jews even those oracles which have been plainly explained of Christ by the Holy Spirit himself in the New Testament, and dragging them, as they say, by the neck to any other things whatsoever. What is clearer, what is more certain in the Church of Christ, than that the virginal birth was predicted by Isaiah, and designated by the name Immanuel in Chap. 7? Since both the most evident prophecy and the interpretation of the Holy Spirit in Matt. 1 is superior to any exception: Grotius, however, with the Jews, understands it of a son, I know not whose, of Isaiah, whom he had begotten from a virgin and young woman taken as a wife, and to whom he had given the name Immanuel. Most luminous is the prediction of this grandiloquent Prophet concerning the child given to us, and the son born to us, Chap. 9, to whom the name MIGHTY GOD, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, which St. Matthew Chap. 4 and the Angel Gabriel Luke 1 do not allow us to doubt sounds of Christ. But here Grotius preferred to lend his ears to the Jews, and to explain it of Hezekiah, as far as the letter is concerned, since, insisting on the Jewish Gloss, he did not hesitate to pervert the source text, as if the Prophet does not indicate that he whose names are recited here should be called the mighty God, but the counselor of the mighty God, nor does he name him Father of the age otherwise than that he is to leave behind many descendants for a long time, or prince of peace, whose peace is to have no end, than that he is to enjoy peace at the end of his days. The rod from the root of Jesse upon whom the Spirit of the Lord rests, Chap. 11, is by the confession of all who have given their name to Christ the Messiah; Grotius, however, here again intrudes Hezekiah, even though the whole of this chapter, as Jerome observes, not only Christians, but the whole circumcision admit speaks of the Messiah, with this only difference, that the Jews take all the writings literally concerning the one to come and his temporal kingdom: most Christians understand them metaphorically concerning the spiritual kingdom of him who has already come, Christ GOD. Concerning the passion of Christ and his resurrection, there is not easily a clearer prophecy in the whole Scripture of the Old Testament than Chap. 53 of our Prophet: which therefore Augustine in lib. 1 de Consens. Evangel. c. 1 judged to need no explanation, and Corn. à Lapide, a Jesuit, that is, of the order of those whom Grotius acknowledged as his masters while he lived, might not undeservedly say that this chapter ought to be inscribed, The Passion of JESUS CHRIST according to Isaiah, just as the passion of Jesus Christ according to Matthew or Mark is inscribed. Nor yet did Grotius fear to cast shadows upon such great light, and to interpret the whole prophecy of Jeremiah with the Jews. The sense, he says,

Nor indeed is it permitted to excuse or cover up the collusion with the Jews by those things which he asserts, that Christ is indicated somewhere in a more sublime sense. For since in the literal sense, i.e., in the very letter of the text intended by the Holy Spirit, he takes it not of Christ, but of any others whatsoever, in most things he is worse than the Jews themselves, who acknowledged that these things treat of the Messiah according to the mind of the Holy Spirit. Which is the reason why, for the sake of vindicating the genuine meaning of such a great Prophet against Grotius, we judge that these prophecies must be treated a little more fully, nor shall we spare labor here, which is nowhere better placed than in the scrutiny of the Prophetic oracles, when the Messiah is sought in them, John 5:39. Nor is there any investigation more holy, or more worthy, or more healthful, or finally more vital, than when Christ, the light, shield, protection, glory, joy, and highest treasure of our soul, is unearthed from those gold mines of the Prophets—in whose very pregnant and far-richest veins he is hidden—by religious ἐξεύρεσις (discovery), and is openly set forth for the refreshment and strengthening of pious minds and the holy Church.

Moreover, so that we may also offer some advice at the very threshold regarding the time in which this standard-bearer of the Prophets flourished, Isaiah is called the son of Amoz; by which name is not understood the Prophet so named, Amos of Tekoa, as Clement of Alexandria and Cedrenus thought, despite the different spelling of the names; but rather some other man, who is believed by the Hebrews to be the brother of Amaziah, King of Judah, and according to some in Jerome’s Commentary on chapter 20 of Isaiah, the father-in-law or grandfather-in-law, or the father of the father-in-law of Manasseh. He began to prophesy about 800 years before Christ under Uzziah. It is not known with certainty in which year precisely he began. Eusebius assigns the 17th year of Uzziah. Thus he would have prophesied for 36 years under Uzziah, 16 under Jotham, the same number under Ahaz, and 29 under Hezekiah, if he had reached the reign of Manasseh, and would have completed 96 years of prophesying, or even more, if, as is believed by some, he was killed by Manasseh when he was already quite old. Under Manasseh, certainly They report that he was sawn asunder: Justin, Contra Tryphonem; Origen, Homily 1 on Isaiah; Dorotheus; Epiphanius in The Life of Isaiah; Chrysostom, Epistle to Cyril; Augustine, Book 18 of The City of God, ch. 24; and thus it is believed in the Roman Church according to the Roman Martyrology, ch. 6, book 1. With this agrees the Alexandrian Chronicle, which says: The prophet Isaiah died, divided by a saw by Manasseh; he prophesied for ninety years, and was buried above the oak of Rogel. Which tradition, however, hardly deserves to be believed. For neither is the age of the Prophet, who would have had to live over 120 years to have finished his life in this way, likely—being unusual in those centuries—nor does the title or inscription fit, by which it is said that Isaiah prophesied only under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, but not under Manasseh; of whom he would certainly not have neglected to make mention if he had reached his times; and had he lived while he was already older and more wicked; whence Abulensis himself did not hesitate to contradict that tradition in 4 Kings, ch. 21, q. 17. Which also, not being drawn from anywhere else than from Jewish pools and the Babylonian Talmud, renders itself entirely suspect to Jerome himself, even though he calls it most certain in book 15 at the end of Isaiah, and even by those fables with which it is stuffed; not to mention that the reasons they give for the killing of the Prophet are of no likelihood, such as that he bitterly rebuked King Manasseh and the princes and the people, ch. 1, calling them princes of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah, and that against the protestation of the Lord in Exodus 33:20, 'No man shall see me and live,' he wrote that he had seen GOD sitting upon the Cherubim, ch. 6; because those rebukes and the testimony of that vision were made many years before Manasseh was raised to the kingdom: for Manasseh killed him when he had already become older and more wicked, says Cornelius. Compare Robert Baillie in Historical and Chronological Works, part 1, p. 87.

Some attribute to Isaiah, besides this book of prophecies, a historical one which no longer survives: which Cornelius à Lapide thinks is evident from 2 Chronicles 26:22. But what is said there to have been described by Isaiah concerning the deeds of King Uzziah is contained in the books of Kings, to which it can be said that Isaiah contributed his own share, so that there is no need to posit a separate book that has perished. The book concerning the 'Ascension,' which the Archontics used under the name of Isaiah, according to Jerome and Epiphanius, is not worthy of mention, being manifestly fictitious, nay, heretical, by which it is taught that Melchizedek was the Holy Spirit. Nor will that admirable vision of the Prophet Isaiah in a trance of the mind, which contains the mysteries of the divine Trinity and the redemption of the fallen human race, published at Venice and mentioned by Sixtus of Siena in the Bibliotheca Sancta under the entry for Isaiah, detain us, being spurious and entirely fabulous. Wherefore, directly to

We proceed to the genuine prophecies of our Prophet in the name of the Lord, which can be distributed partly according to chronology and partly according to the underlying subject matter. In the former way, he presents his discourses: (I.) Under Uzziah in the first five chapters; (II.) Under Jotham, ch. 6; (III.) Under Ahaz, from ch. 7 up to ch. 14 inclusive; (IV.) Under Hezekiah from ch. 15 to the end of the book. In the latter way, some discourses are more legal, others more evangelical. We say the former are contained in the first chapters up to 40 exclusive; the latter in the subsequent ones from ch. 40 up to the last. The former, however, are both simple and mixed. These again can be distinguished by taking into account the Kings of Judah under whom they were instituted, namely, first before Hezekiah, then under Hezekiah. Before Hezekiah, under Uzziah, Jotham, and Ahaz; the rest under Hezekiah: because they are (1.) Domestic, directed to the people of Judah from ch. 1

up to 13: and these are two. The first indicates to the Jews, who were educated and exalted by God, desolation for their apostasy, down to a small remnant, with an exhortation to repentance, ch. 1, illustrated by a double vision: the former concerning the gathering of the Gentiles to Zion and the rejection of the Jews, and other very grave punishments preceding, ch. 2, and their causes, ch. 3, so that the kingdom of Christ is to be preserved in the remnant of Israel, ch. 4, the fault of which is not in God, who planted and cared for this vineyard, but in the people, who brought upon themselves its devastation by the nations, to be summoned by the Lord on account of various sins and unbelief, ch. 5; the latter concerning the glory of Christ, which will fill the whole earth, and the hardening of the people, and their rejection down to a certain holy Seed, ch. 6. To the second discourse is prefixed the occasion of the danger to Judea in the time of Ahaz, and the sign of the virgin birth being erected for the faithful, on account of the impending Assyrian affliction in particular, ch. 7; he predicts that in extreme ingratitude and blindness, some disciples of the Lord will still be preserved, ch. 8; and that a light will arise upon the Gentiles sitting in darkness, with the birth of the Messiah, the Prince of Peace, who will adorn the kingdom of David in judgment and justice: so that although the Israelites may have perished, ch. 10, not only is the Assyrian enemy to be humbled, but also some remnant from Israel ought one day to be saved: and although he is to subjugate some cities of the Jews, he himself is nevertheless to be cut off at last, with them being liberated, ch. 10. Moreover, that a shoot must one day arise from the root of Jesse, under whom the enemies themselves are to be gathered to the people of the Lord and subjected to him, ch. 11; which thanks and salvation the Church is to celebrate with Eucharistic Canticles, ch. 12. (2.) Exotic sermons denounced against the enemies of the people for the sake of the Church, up to chapter 24. The remaining sermons of the first order, which we have called mixed, because they pertain mostly to the Israelite people, yet have a reflection upon others brought in for the sake of the execution of divine judgment, and because they consist partly of prophecy, partly of history bringing light to prophecy. First, they are proposed for the edification of the faithful after divine judgments, both concerning the conversion of the nations and the glorification of the elect, chapter 24, whence also the Prophet celebrates God, chapter 25, and exhibits the Song of the faithful, chapters 26 and 27, so that the Jews may have comfort on account of the future devastation. Then they denounce woe to Israel, chapter 28, and the total destruction of Jerusalem, chapter 29. Furthermore, the confidence placed in the Egyptians is noted, chapters 30 and 31, protection is promised to the penitent, with the destruction of the Assyrians, and chapter 32, the Messiah is presented with the benefits of the New Testament. Moreover, to the Assyrians, chapter 33, woe is denounced, as also to all the unfaithful, chapter 34, eternal destruction: and chapter 35, for the sake of the faithful, comfort concerning the advent of Christ is subjoined, and his characteristics are hinted at. Thus, therefore, those sermons prophetically intimate punishment to the people: but they temper the same excellently and clearly with Evangelical consolations. To which finally is admixed the History of chapters 36, 37, 38, and 39, inasmuch as it serves not a little both the preceding and the following prophecies.

The latter of the order, namely the more Evangelical sermons, both look back to ancient times, especially on account of the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, chapter 39, predicted, even though they also prophesy concerning Christ and his Church under the New Testament up to chapter 49, and they pertain properly to the times of the New Testament, and treat of Christ and his kingdom, especially after the Jews have been rejected: which last part Bullinger, in his preface to Isaiah, distributes into six sermons, so that the first pertains to chapters 49, 50, 51, commonly to Christ and the Church; the second, chapters 52 and 53, treats particularly of the liberation of the human race and the liberator Christ; the third, chapters 54 and 55, explains how widely the benefit of redemptio nis extends; the fourth concerns the offices of the Redeemer and sound doctrine, chapters 56, 57, 58, 59; the fifth treats of the kingdom of Christ and his ministers, chapters 60 up to 64. The last teaches concerning the rejection of the Jews, the calling of the Gentiles, the happiness of the faithful, and the unhappiness of the unfaithful, and with the final judgment of the Lord let it conclude the whole treatment.

Blessed Luther in his preface assigns the parts of this Prophet differently, but he understands the principal contents, not the sections of the book following one another in order: and he leaves it in the middle whether the order of the chapters and sermons, as it now stands, proceeded from the Prophet himself or from someone else: he says that in the first part Isaiah teaches his people, partly by reproving various sins, partly by instructing and preparing his own [people] to await the future kingdom of Christ: that the second part of the prophecy pertains properly to the Monarchy of the Assyrians, and to Sennacherib, who is about to devastate the neighboring regions, and also the kingdom of Israel, and then will also grievously afflict Judah, with promises concerning the liberation of Jerusalem: he says that the third [part] looks to the Monarchy of the Chaldeans, as far as the Babylonian captivity and the devastation of Jerusalem, with the consolation of the people, so that they may not despair of the restoration and of the kingdom of Christ, and with magnificent promises of the future kingdom of Christ. But since the order of the prophecy is preserved according to the former distribution, which we do not doubt is θεόπνευςον [divinely inspired], the same seems not undeservedly to be preferred.

We subjoin, however, still the division of Mr. Dr. Varenius, which in his commentary on the 12 chapters

of Isaiah, p. 30, he proposed thus: We posit three greatest sections in Isaiah. One, which ends in ch. 12; the second, which ends in 39; the third, which [is] one with the Prophet. The foundation of the division [is] in disparate materials and clauses. Thus in part 1, it is treated most principally of the incarnation of the Messiah, namely his birth from a virgin, his natures, his Person: of the other mysteries of the economy and of the kingdom of Christ itself, [it is treated] only in the most general way. In the second part, it is treated of the desolation of bodily kingdoms, especially those which often brought great calamities upon the Davidic Church, so that in this way mortals may be lifted up to the kingdom of Christ alone. In the 3rd part, there now begins expressly a special treatment of the Evangelical kingdom of Christ and its formation, from John the Baptist onwards, from whom therefore Isaiah the Evangelist, clear even if under a shadow, begins. Here whatever there is of Evangelical mystery is revealed most specially, both on the part of the King (and his person, status, office) and on the part of the kingdom. The clause of the first part is the Evangelical jubilation in ch. 12. The clause of the second part is the Angelic history, teaching by an admirable example that which he had hitherto intimated to the nations through a sad symbol, namely the Mass. The clause of the third part is the final judgment rigorously described; which is the reason why the Jews do not read the last verse in the last [chapter] of Isaiah: but stop at the penultimate [verse] repeated after the last. Among the Jews, another division obtains, according to the special prophecies or great Parashot, which they place at 36 in Isaiah, and variously subdivide again. This is what he said. We acquiesce in the distinction previously handed down, about to illustrate our same Prophet, by the grace of God, now.

Latin:

I. N AD ESAIAM PRÆLO

DE Prophetarum in V. T. facile præcipuo Esaia præclara extat sententia Cyrilli Archi-Episcopi Alexandrini, in proœm. lib. 1. Comment. in Esa. Videtur mihi Beatus Propheta Esaias non sola prophetiæ gratia plurimum exornatus; sed & de- coribus (ἀυχήμασιν) Apostoli. Est enim hic Prophe- ta simul & Apostolus, & in hac scriptione sua habebit sermones, Evangelicæ prædicationis splendore non ca- rentes: Cui gemina est Eusebii in fragmentis de vi- ta Prophetarum, apud Procopium Ἐπίκρισις: Τὸ πλεῖσον τῆς προφητείας ἀυτ̃́ ἐςὶν ἐυαγγέλια περὶ τῆς ἐν σαρκὶ παρεσίας τ̃́ Λόγε ̥̃̄ ̊͛ ̃͛̄ Θε̥̃ ̊͛, κ̓ ̊͛ ὧν ἀνεδέ- ξατο δι' ἡμᾶς παθῶν: Maxima Prophetiæ ipsius pars complectitur Evangelia de incarnatione & adventu Verbi Dei, iisq́; quæ sustinuit, cum pro nobis pateretur. Verissimum hoc, & non quidem ex Apollinis tri- pode, sed è Spiritus S. dictamine profectum judi- cium uno ore omnes agnoscunt, qui Esaiæ oracula pie scrutantur, & indagant. Græcorum interpre- tum eminentissimo S. Cyrillo, Polyhistori Græcani- co Eusebio ex asse consonat inter Latinos Interpre- tes & Doctores facile eruditissimus D. Hierony- mus: ideoque non ut Prophetam solum explican- dum sibi sumit Esaiam, sed ut Evangelistam & Apo- stolum, ad Eustochium virginem proœmio in pri- mum Commentariorum Esaiæ sic scribens: Ora- tionum tuarum fultus auxilio, quæ diebus ac noctibus in lege Dei meditaris, & templum es Spiritus Sancti, imitabor patremfamiliâs, qui de thesauro suo profert addimus Reformatos nonnullos cum Calvino ipso, & Hugonem Grotium, quorum nonnulli, etsi sensu mystico,quem vocant,ea etiam ad Christum,& tem- pora N. T. referant, verum tamen sensum Prophetæ, fatente Cornelio enervant. Esto enim, inquit ille, fateantur ipsi allegorice saltem hæc vaticinia ad Chri- stum & Ecclesiam pertinere, tamen literam & litera- lem sensum,qui sacræ scripturæ basis est & fundamen- tum, Christianis eripiunt,quo erepto,quam facile elu- dent Judæi allegoricum? Illum enim sensum esse S. Scripturæ pernegabunt,dicentque eum humani cerebri esse commentum, & a Christianis confictum.

Alterum genus est allegoricum, & eorum, qui omnia pene de Christo, de Ecclesia N.T.de gentium vocatione, & viris spiritualibus interpretantur, & quæ de Nabuchodon. Sennacherib &c. dicuntur, de Diabolo accipiunt, quo pacto Leocastrius totum E- saiam ad Christum torquet animo sane non malo, ut nempe eum Judæis extorqueat. Coccejus plera- que ad tempora posteriorum seculorum in Novo Test. novissimis propiora trahit,& nescio quæ my- steria in oraculis Propheticis quærit, plane apoca- lyptica, tantum non Prophetas faciens Commen- tatores Apocalypseos Johanneæ, aut Apocalypseos similis denunciatores, Johanni Apostolo geminos.

Tertium est medium, eorum,qui nonnulla, cum textus postulat, de rebus Vet. Test. alia prævia in- terpretatione S. Script. de Christo & rebus N. T. explicant, ac sensum unicum literalem, quem inten- disse Spiritum S. apparet,presse urgent; quam esse optimam ac tutissimam interpretandi rationem, dubitare fas non est, quum Spiritus S. certi quid intendat, & unius sententiæ unum esse oporteat sensum, uti forma rei non est nisi unica.

N. I. PROPHETAM QUIUM.

nova & vetera, & Sponsum dicentem in Cantico Canticorum, nova & vetera, fratruelis meus servare tibi: sicque exponam Esaiam, ut illum non solum Prophetam, sed Evangelistam & Apostolum doceam. Ipse enim de se & cum cæteris Evangelistis ait: Quam speciosi pedesEvangelizantium pacem! Et ad ipsum, quasi ad Apostolum, loquitur Deus: Quem mittam, & quis ibit ad populum istum? Et ille respondet,Ec- ce ego, mitte me. Nullusque putet, me voluminis istius argumentum brevi cupere sermone comprehen- dere; quum universa Domini sacramenta præsens scriptura contineat, & tam natus de virgine Ema- nuel, quam illustrium patrator operum atque signo- rum, mortuus ac sepultus & resurgens ab inferis, & Salvator universarum gentium prædicetur. Græco- rum & Latinorum antefignanis addimus Germani- corum Patrum A & Ω, Megalandrum nostrum Lu- therum in præfat. Germ. in Esa. Er schicket und be- reitet sein Volck, auf das zukünfftige Reich Christi zu warten/von welchem er so klärlich und mannich- faltiglich weissaget,als sonst kein Prophet thut,daß er auch die Mutter Christi,die Jungfraw Maria be- schreibet,wie sie ihn empfangen und gebären solt mit unversehrter Jungfrauschafft, Cap.7, 14. und sein Leiden im 53.Cap. sammt seiner Aufferstehung von den Todten,und sein Reich gewaltiglich und dürre herauß verkündiget,als wäre es dazumal geschehe. Daß gar ein trefflicher hocherleuchteter Prophet muß gewesen seyn.Denn also thun alle Propheten, daß sie das gegenwärtige Volck lehren und straf- fen,daneben Christus Zukunfft und Reich verkün- digen,und das Volck drauf richten und weisen,als auf den gemeinen Heyland, beyde der vorigen und zukünfftigen, doch einer mehr denn der ander, einer reichlicher denn der ander, Jesaias aber über sie al- le am meisten und reichesten. Hæc B. Lutherus.

eft: Nos credidimus Ieremiam merito conjectum in carcerem, & tritum, Deo illum exofum habente, ut hostem urbis, & templi, ac Pseudo-Prophetam: At vero ipse vulneratus (id est, male tractatus est) no- stro crimine, in nobis culpa fuit, non in ipso fuit. At- tritus est per nostram culpam; iniquissima de eo senst- mus & propterea crudeliter eum tractavimus. Quis Judæorum horribilius depravavit textum Pro- phetæ Evangelicum? Horreo, profecto, ad- scribere omnia, quæ Judaicus ipsi spiritus in hoc caput suggessit annotata. Jam vocem clamantis in deserto, Cap. 40. Johannes Christi prodromus se es- se palam Judæis professus est Joh. 1. cui vero in os contradicit Grotius, hunc verborum Prophetæ sensum esse prætendens, quod temporibus exitii Ba- bylonici Iudæis clamare debeant Prophetæ, ut malos mores auferant, qui restitutionem eorum moraban- tur. Christus ipse, cum in synagoga Nazarethana publice doceret, sonora voce testatus est, se illum esse, qui cap. 61. ita loquens introducitur: Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit Dominus me ad an- nunciandum mansuetis: Prælecto enim textu Pro- phetico cum librum clausisset, omniumq; oculi in eum intenti essent, Hodie, dixit, impleta est hæc Scri- ptura in auribus vestris, Luc. 4. Quid vero Judaizans Grotius? Loquitur hic Esaias de se, ut notat Chal- dæus. Scilicet majoris autoritatis ipsi Chaldæus, imo Rabbini recentes nequissimi fuêre, quam Christus Sapientia Dei hypostatica! Sed si omnes corruptelas Grotii recensere vellemus, oracula o- mnia Prophetæ percurrenda essent: Quum enim istis tam evidentibus non pepercerit, facile quisque intelligit, quid in aliis tentarint ungues Grotiani!

Neque vero de hac evidentia & deenóteti Esaix in vaticiniis de Christo inter Christianos dubium ullum fuit, si Theodoretum Mopsvestanum excipias, qui Prophetas omnes nucleo, & medulla sua, hoc est, vaticiniis de Christo privasse legitur, anathema- te percussus in Synodo V. Constantinopolitana. Quid ergo de Hugone Grotio dicemus, qui tantum abest, ut Prophetæ huic vocalissimo, quem ita vocavit Chry- sostomus hom. 8. in Genes. laudem istam integram relinquat, ut omnia ejus vaticinia de Messia lucu- lentissima, Solisque ipsius radiis scripta, in quemvis alium potius detorqueat, quam de Christo intelli- gat, ausu & molimine vere prophano, & in Ecclesia Christi penitus inaudito. Unde persuasissimus sum, si quis forte fortuna in annotata ejus ad Esaiam in- cidat, eaque præfixum in fronte autoris nomen non gerunt, Eundem crediturum se Iudæum quendam, non Christianum legere. Adeo judaizat in hoc Propheta Grotius, ea etiam oracula, quæ ab ipso Spiritu S. in Novo Test. planadi stoon de Christo exposita sunt, cum Judæis pervertens, & obtorto, quod ajunt, collo ad quævis alia abripiens. Quid clarius, quid in Ecclesia Christi certius, quam quod partus virgineus prædictus ab Esaia sit, ac nomine Immanuel designatus Cap. 7.? Siquidem & vatici- nium evidentissimum, & interpretatio Spiritus S. Matth. 1. omni exceptione superior fit: Grotius ta- men cum Judæis id de filio, nescio quo, Esaia intel- ligit, quem è virgine & juvencula in uxorem ducta, procreârit, & cui nomen Immanuel imposuerit. Perquam luculenta est prædictio grandiloqui hu- jus Prophetæ de puero nobis dato, & filio nobis nato, Cap. 9. cui nomen DEUS fortis, Pater æternus, Princeps pacis, quam de Christo sonare non per- mittit nos ambigere S. Matthæus Cap. 4. Angelus- que Gabriel Luc. 1. At maluit hic Grotius aures præbere Iudæis, & de Ezechia explicare, quoad li- teram, cum insistens Judaicæ Glossæ, fontium tex- tum ita pervertere non dubitârit, quasi non Deum fortem; sed Dei fortis consultatorem appellandum esse eum, cujus nomina hic recensentur, indigitet Propheta, nec aliter Patrem seculi nuncupet, quam quod multos post se relicturus sit posteros, in longum tempus, aut pacis principem, cujus pacis finis nullus fu- turus, quam quod ad finem dierum suorum pace fruiturus sit. Virga de radice Ieffe super quam Spiri- tus Domini requiescit, Cap. 11. omnium, qui Christo nomen dedêre, confessione Messias est; Gro- tius vero Ezechiam hic iterum intrudit, utut to- tum hoc caput, observante Hieronymo, non Chri- stiani tantum, sed tota circumcisio ne de Messia loqui fa- teantur, hoc tantum discrimine, quod Iudæi de ventu- ro, & de regno ejus temporali omnia scripta ad literam accipiant: Christiani plerique metaphorice de spiri- tuali regno ejus, qui jam venit, Christi DEI intelli- gant. De passione Christi ejusque resurrectione lu- culentior prophetia non habetur facile in universa Scriptura Vet. Test. quam Cap. 53. Prophetæ No- stri: quam proinde explicatione non egere censuit Augustinus lib. 1. de Consens. Evangel. c. 1. ac Corn. à Lapide, Iesuita, hoc est, ex eorum ordine, quos pro Magistris suis, dum viveret, agnovit Grotius, non immerito dixerit, hoc caput inscribi debere, Paf- sio JESU CHRISTI secundum Esaiam, æque uti passio Iesu Christi secundum Matthæum aut Marcum inscribitur. Neque tamen veritus est Grotius tantæ luci tenebras inducere, totumque vaticinium de Ieremia cum Judæis interpretari. Sensus, inquit,

Neque vero collusionem cum Idæis excusare, aut tegere illa segata licet, quod alicubi sensu sub- limiori Christum indigitari asserat. Nam cum sensu literali h.e. in ipsa textus litera à Spiritu S. intento non de Christo, sed quibusvis aliis potius accipiat, in plerisque Judæis ipsis deterior est, qui ea de Mes- sia ex mente Spiritus S. agere agnoverunt. Quæ causa est, cur ad vindicandum genuinam senten- tiam, tanti Prophetæ adversus Grotium hæc vati- cinia paulo plenius tractanda censeamus, nec ope- ræ hic parcamus, quæ nuspiam rectius collocatur, quam in scrutinio oraculorum Propheticorum, cum quæritur in illis Messias Joh. 5,39. Neque vel sanctior, vel dignior, vel salubrior, vel denique sua vior ulla est indagatio, quam ubiChristus animæ no- stræ lux, scutum, præsidium, decus, gaudium, & thesau- rus summus ex aurifodinis illis Prophetarum, in quarum venis admodum prægnantibus, longeque ditissimis reconditus est, religiosa égevres erui- tur, & ad piarum mentium, sanctæque Ecclesiæ re- fectionem,ac confortationem palam exponitur.

Cæterum, ut de tempore, quo floruit hic Pro. phetarum Antesignanus, nonnihil in ipso limine etiam moneamus, vocatur Esaias filius Amofi; quo nomine non Propheta ita nuncupatus intelligitur, Amos Thekoënsis, uti, repugnante diversa nominum scriptione, Clemens Alexandrin. & Cedrenus puta- runt; sed alius quidam, qui Ebræis frater Amasiæ, Regis Judæ, creditur, & juxta nonnullos apud Hie- ronymum Comm. in cap. 20. Ef. socer vel profocer, seu pater soceri Manassis. Prophetare autem cœpit annis circiter 800. ante Christum sub Uffia. De anno, quo præcise cœperit, non constat certo. An- num Ufiæ 17. affignat Eusebius. Ita 36. annis sub Usia, 16.sub Jotham, totidem subAchaz vaticinatus fuiffet, & 29. sub Ezechia, si Manasfis regnum atti- gisset, & prophetando 96. annos confecisset, imo adhuc plures, si,quod à nonnullis creditur, à Ma- nasse jam grandiore occisus fuit. Sub Manaffe certe eum serra dissectum esse tradunt Justin. contr. Tryph. Origenes hom. 1. in Esa. Dorotheus, Epi- phan. in Vit. Es. Chrysostom. Epist. ad Cyr. Augu- stin. l. 18. de Civ. DEI c. 24. atque ita creditur in Ecclesia Romana secundum Martyrologium Rom. c. 6. l. 1. Cui consonat Chronicon Alexandr. ita habens: Esaias vates à Manasse serra divisus oc- cubuit, vaticinatus est annis nonaginta, tumulatus super quercum Rogel. Quæ vero traditio fidem vix meretur. Nam nec ætas Prophetæ, quem oportuisset ita ultra 120. annos vivendo confecisse, verisimilis est, istis seculis inusitata, neque titulus congruit, vel inscriptio, qua dicitur, tantum pro- phetasse Esaias sub Usia, Jotham, Achaz & Ezechia, non vero sub Manasse; Cujus mentionem utique non neglexisset, si tempora ejusdem attigisset; & quum ille jam grandior & nequior esset, vixisset; unde Abulensis ipse non dubitavit traditioni illi contradicere in 4. Libr. Regum C. 21. q. 17. Quæ etiam aliunde non hausta, quam è lacunis Judaicis, & Talmude Babylonico, Hieronymo ipso, etsi eam certissimam vocet lib. 15. in finem Esaiæ, & vel fa- bellis istis, quibus stipata est, prorsus suspectam se reddit; ut taceam, quod causæ, quas reddunt, oc- cisionis Prophetæ, nullius sint verisimilitudinis, ut- pote quod acerbe Regem Manassem & Principes, & populum reprehenderit, c. 1. vocando eos princi- pes Sodomorum, & populum Gomorrhæ, quodque adversus protestationem Domini Exod. 33, 20. non videbit me homo, & vivet, scripserit se DEUM su- per Cherubim sedentem vidisse, c. 6. quia illæ incre- pationes, & visionis istius testificatio jam multis annis factæ, antequam Manasses ad regnum evehe- retur: occidisse enim eum Manassen, cum jam gran- dior esset effectus, & nequior, ait Cornelius. Conf. Robert. Bailius in Oper. Histor. & Chronol. part. 1. p. 87.

Adscribunt nonnulli Esaiæ præter hunc Pro- phetiarum librum, Historicum, qui amplius non supersit: quod Cornel. à Lapide è 2. Paral. 26, 22. patere arbitratur. Sed quæ ibi de Regis Usiæ gestis descripta ab Esaia dicuntur, in libris Regum conti- nentur, ad quos suum ἐπιβάλλον μέρος contulis- se Esaiam dici potest, ut opus non sit Librum pecu- liarem statuere, qui interierit. Liber de ἀναβάσει seu ascensione, quo sub nomine Esaiæ usi Archonti- ci sunt, referente Hieron. & Epiphanio, non dignus est, qui commemoretur, utpote manifeste fictitius, imo hæreticus, quo docetur, Melchisedechum fuis- se Spiritum sanctum. Neque visio illa admirabilis Esaiæ Prophetæ in raptu mentis, quæ divinæ Trinita- tis arcana, & lapsi generis humani redemtionem con- tinet, Venetiis edita, & à Sixto Senensi in Bibl. S. in voce Esaiæ commemorata, nos detinebit, spuria quippe, ac fabulosa prorsus. Quocirca recta ad

Germana vaticinia Prophetæ nostri, in nomine Do- mini, procedimus, quæ distribui possunt partim se- cundum Chronologiam, partim secundum substra- tam materiam. Priori modo conciones exhibet (I.) Sub Usia quinque capp. prioribus: (II.) Sub Jotham c. 6. (III.) Sub Achaz. c. 7. usque ad c. 14. inclusive. (IV.) Sub Ezechia à c. 15. ad finem li- bri. Posteriori modo conciones aliæ sunt magis le- gales, aliæ magis Evangelicæ. Illas dicimus priori- bus capp. usque ad 40. exclusive: has posteriori- bus à c. 40. usque ad ultimum contineri. Priores vero tum simplices sunt, tum mixtæ. Illæ iterum sic distingui possunt habita simul Regum Judæ, sub quibus institutæ sunt, ratione, utpote primum ante Ezechiam, deinde sub Ezechia. Ante Ezechiam sub Usia, Iotham, & Achaz: cæteræ sub Ezechia: quod sint (1.) Domesticæ ad populum Judæ à cap. 1.

usque ad 13. directæ: eæque duæ. Prima Judæis à Deo educatis & exaltatis ob apostasiam, desola- tionem ad exiguas reliquias indicit cum exhorta- tione ad pœnitentiam c. 1. illustrata gemina visione: priori de gentium ad Zionem aggregatione, ac Ju- dæorum reprobatione, præviisque aliis gravissimis pœnis c. 2. & earum causis c. 3. ita ut regnum Chri- sti in reliquiis Israelis conservandum sit c. 4. cujus culpa non in Deo, qui hanc vineam plantavit, & cu- ravit, sed in populo, qui devastationem ejus, per gentes, ob peccata varia, & incredulitatem à Do- mino advocandas, sibi conciliavit c. 5. posteriori de gloria Christi, repletura universam terram, & in- duratione populi, & usque ad sanctum quoddam Se- men rejectione c. 6. Alteri Concioni præmittitur occasio periculum Judææ, tempore Achaz, & erectis signo partus virginei fidelibus, ob imminentem im- primis Assyriacam afflictionem c. 7. in extrema in- gratitudine, & cæcitate quosdam adhuc Domini di- scipulos conservatum iri prædicit c. 8. lucemque ex- orituram super gentes in tenebris sedentes, nato Messia, Pacis principe, regnum Davidis adornaturo in judicio & justitia: ut quanquam Israëlita inter- ierint c. 10. non hostis tantum Assyrius humilian- dus sit, sed & reliquiæ nonnullæ ex Israële salvari olim debeant: & quanquam Judæorum civitates nonnullas subjugaturus sit, excindendus tamen ipse tandem sit, iis liberatis c. 10. Quin exoriri aliquando debeat è radice Isai germen, sub quo ad popu- lum Domini hostes ipsi aggregandi sint, eique sub- jiciendi c. 11. quam gratiam & salutem celebratura sit Ecclesia Canticis Eucharisticis c. 12. (2.) Con- ciones exoticæ hostibus populi in gratiam Ecclesiæ denunciatæ, usque ad cap. 24. Reliquæ conciones prioris ordinis, quas mixtas diximus, quod ad po- pulum quidem Israëlitioum spectent maxime, re- flexionem tamen ad alios exequutionis judicii divini causa adhibitos, habeant, & quod partim prophe- tia, partim Historia prophetiæ lucem inferente, constent. Primum erigendis fidelibus propositæ sunt post judicia divina, tum de conversione gen- tium, tum de glorificatione electorum cap. 24. unde & Propheta Deum celebrat, c. 25. & Canticum fide- lium exhibet c. 26. & 27. ut Judæi ob vastationem futuram solatium habeant. Deinde Israëli væ de- nunciant, c. 28. Et totale excidium Hierosolymo- rum c. 29. Porro fiducia notata in Ægyptios locata c. 30. & 31. pœnitentibus præsidium, cum Assyrio- rum exitio promittitur, & c. 32. Messias cum bene- ficiis N. T. sistitur. Assyriis autem c. 33. væ denun- ciatur, ut & infidelibus universis c. 34. æternum exi- tium: ac cap. 35. fidelium causa solatium de adven- tu Christi subjungitur, ejusque characteres innu- untur. Sic ergo conciones illæ propheticè quidem pœnam populo intimant: Sed eandem Evangelicis consolationibus egregie & præclare temperant. Quibus tandem admixta est Historia cap. 36. 37. 38. & 39. utpote quæ & præcedentibus, & sequentibus vaticiniis non parum inservit.

Posterior ordinis, magis nempe Evangelicæ conciones tum vetera simul tempora, maxime ob liberationem è captivitate Babylonica, c. 39. prædi- ctam, respiciunt, etsi de Christo, ejusq; Ecclesia sub N. Test. etiam vaticinentur usque ad cap. 49. tum proprie ad N. Test. tempora spectant, ac de Christo ejusque regno agunt, imprimis post rejectos Judæos: quam partem postremam Bullingerus præfat. in Es. in sex sermones distribuit, ita ut primus c. 49. 50. 51. pertineat communiter ad Christum & Ecclesiam; Se- cundus c. 52. & 53. peculiariter de liberatione generis humani & liberatore Christo agat; Tertius c. 54. & 55. explicet, quam late pateat beneficium redemtio- nis; Quartus de officiis Redemtorum, & doctrina sana c. 56. 57. 58. 59. differat; Quintus de regno Christi, & ministris ejus tractet c. 60. usque ad 64. Postre- mus de repudio Judæorum, vocatione gentium, fe- licitate fidelium, & infidelium infelicitate doceat, ac ultimo judicio Domini totam tractationem con- cludat.

B. Lutherus in præfat. aliter partes assignat hu- jus Prophetæ, sed intelligit contenta præcipua, non sectiones libri, ordine sese consequentes: & in medio relinquit, num ordo capitum, & concionum pro- uti nunc habet, ab ipso Propheta, num vero ab alio quopiam profectus sit: in prima parte docere Esaiam, ait, populum suum, partim reprehendendo varia peccata, partim instruendo & præparando suos, ut expectent futurum regnum Christi: Se- cundam Prophetiæ partem pertinere proprie ad Monarchiam Assyriorum, & ad Sennacheribum, qui finitimas regiones vastaturus sit, etiam Israelis re- gnum, tum Judam quoque graviter afflicturus, cum promissionibus de liberatione Hierosolymæ: Tertiam ad Monarchiam Chaldæorum spectare ait, quantum ad captivitatem Babylonicam & vastatio- nem Hierosolymæ cum consolatione populi, ne desperent de reductione & de regno Christi, ac ma- gnificis promissionibus futuri regni Christi. Sed quum juxta priorem distributionem ordo Prophe- tiæ servetur, quem non dubitamus θεόπνευςον, ea- dem non immerito præferenda videtur.

Subjungimus tamen adhuc Dn. D. Varenii divisionem, quam in commentario ad 12. capita

Es. p. 30. ita proposuit: Ponimus tres in Isaiah sectio- nes maxumas. Unam, quæ definit in cap. 12. se- cundam, quæ definit in 39. tertiam, quæ una cum Propheta. Fundamentum divisionis in materiis dispa- ratis, & clausulis. Sic in parte 1. principalissime agi- tur de Messiæ incarnatione, nativitate sc. ex virgine, naturis, Persona: de cæteris mysteriis τῆς οἰκονομίας & ipso Christi regno non nisi generalissime. In secun- da parte agitur de regnorum corporalium, illorum imprimis, quæ Ecclesiæ Davidicæ magnas sæpe cala- mitates intulerunt, desolatione, ut ita ad solum Chri- sti regnum attollantur mortales. In 3. parte jam incipit ex professo specialis tractatio de regno Christi Evangelico ejusque formatione jam inde à Joh. Ba- ptista, à quo proinde orditur Isaiah Evangelista clarus etsi sub umbra. Hic quicquid est mysterii Evangelici specialissime revelatur, tum à parte Re- gis (ejusque personæ, status, officii) tum à parte regni. Clausula partis primæ est jubilus Evangeli- cus in cap. 12. Clausula partis secundæ est historia Angelica, admirabili exemplo id docens, quod ha- ctenus per symbolum triste nationibus, Massa sc. intimaverat. Clausula partis tertiæ est judicium no- vissimum rigorose descriptum; quæ causa est, quod Judæi non legant in Isaia ultimo versum ultimum: sed desinant in iterato post ultimum penultimo. Apud Judæos obtinet alia divisio, juxta Prophetias speciales vel Pharaschas magnas, quas 36. in Isaia po- nunt, & varie iterum fnbdividunt. Hæc ille. Nos acquiescimus prius traditæ distinctione, juxta ean- dem Prophetam nostrum B. C. D. jam illustraturi.

## 1:1 Introduction: In the Name of Jesus. Annotations on Isaiah. Part I. More Legal
In the Name of Jesus. ANNOTATIONS ON ISAIAH. PART I. MORE LEGAL.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD ESAIAM. PARS I. MAGIS LEGALIS.

## 1:1 Argument
SECTION I. DOMESTIC SERMONS, OR THOSE HELD TO THE JEWS (i.e.) UNDER UZZIAH from Chapter I to VI.

SERMON I. CHAPTER I.

After the designation of the time, the final desolation is announced to the Jews, who had been educated by God, on account of their apostasy, concerning which there is a pathetic complaint, up to a small remnant, with the rejection of their sacrifices and feasts themselves, with a grave exhortation to repentance, and a promise of grace made to the faithful.

Latin:

SECTIO I. CONCIONES DOMESTICÆ, SEU AD JUDÆOS HABITÆ (l.) SUB USIA à Cap. I. ad VI.

CONCIO I. CAPUT I.

Post designationem temporis, Iudæis à Deo educatis, ob apostasiam, de qua pa- thetica querela, indicitur novissima desolatio usq; ad exiguas reliquias, cum victimarum & feriarum ipsarum rejectione, gravig exhortatione ad pænitentiam, & promissione gratiæ fidelibus facta.

## 1:2
Vers. 2. HEAR O HEAVENS AND GIVE EAR O EARTH] He repeats the words of Moses from Deut. 32, so that he may signify that those times have now come which Moses had foreseen, with piety and justice overturned, and the law remaining only in rituals. Thus also verse 10 is from v. 32 of the said chapter of Deuteronomy,

Although the same words are employed by Isaiah to excite attention as Moses prefixed to his Song, yet the same subject matter or the same time cannot be concluded from it with certainty. But the whole body of the prophecy must be considered, and its scope: Meanwhile, we have shown in our explanation of the Song of Moses that some things also pertain to the New Testament: to which we shall teach later that certain things in this Isaianic prophecy or first prophetic discourse also look, not so much from the conformity of the introduction, as from the ἐχονήσῃ of the prophecy itself.

Latin:

Vers. 2. AUDITE COELI ET AURIBUS PERCIPE TERRA] Verba Mosis repetit ex Deut. 32. ut significet jam illa venisse tempora, quæ Moses præviderat, eversa pie- tate, ac justitia, lege in solis ritibus remanente. Sic & versus 10. est ex v. 32. dicti capitis Deuteronomii,

QUamvis eadem adhibeantur ver- ba ab Esaia ad excitandam at- tentionem, quæ Moses Cantico suo præmisit, non eadem tamen materia, aut idem tempus inde concludi certo potest. Sed respiciendum est totum vaticinii corpus, & scopus ejusdem: Interim ad N. Test. pertinere quoque nonnulla è Mosis Cantico, in explicatione ejus o- stendimus: quo etiam quædam in hoc vaticinio Esaiano seu concione prima Prophetica spectare non tam ex ingressus conformitate, quam ex i- psius vaticinii ἐχονήσῃ postea docebimus.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. YOUR LAND IS DESOLATE] Supply, shall be. Take the following in the same way, for a siege by Rezin and Pekah is predicted.

Others wish the Prophet to speak of the present calamity; not of a future one. I prefer, says Calvin, to resolve all these sentences into the past tense, because the Prophet is rather narrating how great the disasters are that have already occurred, than denouncing the vengeance of God. For he reproaches their madness and stupor, because they lie astonished at their own evils. But the secure state of affairs in the kingdom of Judah under Uzziah, in whose time Isaiah began to prophesy, stands in the way of this explanation; a difficulty which Calvin touches upon, but does not solve, except by saying that the opinion of the Jews is not without probable reason, because these things pertain to the reign of Jotham, not Uzziah. However, he thinks this discourse was placed in the first position because it contains the sum of the doctrine which is related afterwards. But it is evident from 2 Chron. 27 that the state of the kingdom of Judah was not so miserable even in the time of Jotham, who was a pious King and reigned happily. Therefore Junius refers these to the earlier times under King Amaziah, concerning which 2 Kings 12 and 14, 2 Chronicles 25, to the times of Joash and Amaziah, our blessed Gesner says: Although indeed the kingdom of Judah underwent some crisis and slaughter in the time of Amaziah, both by Hazael, King of Syria, in the time of Joash, and by Joash, King of Israel, 2 Chron. 24:23-24, ch. 25:22, yet the calamity in Judah at that time was not such as the Prophet here outlines, so that from the sole of the foot even to the head there was no soundness, so that the whole region was desolate and the cities were burned with fire; much less was the daughter of Zion left at that time as a booth in a vineyard, and as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers. Therefore, the prophecy is more correctly referred to the reign of Ahaz by Brentius and others, not to the sole siege made by Rezin and Pekah, as Grotius wishes, but to all the calamities which occurred under his reign through the Syrians, Israelites, Edomites, and Philistines, because God humbled Judah for the sins of Ahaz, as may be read in 2 Chron. 28. But those interpret it even more fittingly who refer it to the devastation of Judea made by Sennacherib, along with Oecolampadius, where, after all the fortified cities of Judea were conquered, Jerusalem alone remained, and not even that as it was once frequented, but despised: Or, as they say with Basil the Great, the desolation of the Chaldeans in the time of the Babylonian captivity is predicted. For then the daughter of Zion was utterly forsaken, then the whole land was deserted, then things were reduced to a small seed, of which v. 9 says: Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and we would have been like Gomorrah. Others, however, among the Fathers understand it of the final devastation made by the Romans, or at least combine both those desolations; to whom Cornelius à Lapide and Tirinus accede. Your land (shall be) desolate, your cities (shall be) burned with fire, strangers (shall be) devouring your region, or with the present tense used for the future, devours, that is, they shall certainly devour, namely the Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar, and much more the Romans under Titus and Vespasian. For these did not leave a stone upon a stone in Jerusalem. Although we readily concede that the sins of the people, to whom the Prophet was preaching under King Uzziah, are noted here by him, such as the defection from the true worship of GOD and piety, stubborn obstinacy, and impenitence, and the abominable hypocrisy which even in those times deserved rebuke: since it is certain that the Prophets instituted their invectives and corrections primarily for the causes of the present: yet because he foresaw by the Spirit that in subsequent times the posterity would not be better, but worse, and that those crimes would be brought to their peak in the final times, he therefore places the final destruction of this people before their eyes, so that they might fear the wrath of God and avert the most grievous judgments of God in their own age. For the fact that the punishments and calamities here are designated not of past times, but of future ones, and especially under the final times, is gathered first from the universal languor: From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it. Which, whether they are understood concerning the languor of guilt with Basil, or more correctly concerning the languor of punishment and penalty with others, the irreparable corruption of the whole Judean kingdom fits most especially the final times: which argument Jerome uses. After the Babylonian captivity under Zerubbabel, and Ezra and Nehemiah, Israel returned to Judea and received its ancient state. Also under various princes and kings, the temple was built more narrowly, to such an extent that they even merited the friendships of foreign nations, the Lacedaemonians, Athenians, and Romans. Therefore, refer this which he says, 'there is no soundness in it,' to the final captivity, when after Titus and Vespasian and the final destruction of Jerusalem under Aelius Hadrian, up to the present time there is no remedy. Israel lies pierced and covered with wounds, because it killed the physician who had come to heal the house of Israel. Then from the total desolation of the land. Your land is desolate, says the Prophet; your cities are burned with fire, strangers devour your region in your presence, and it shall be desolate as in a hostile devastation. To which Jerome says: These things were in part fulfilled under the Babylonians, with the temple burned and Jerusalem overturned, when the Samaritans possessed the region of the ten tribes, and the land of promise was reduced to such a solitude that it was ravaged by lions. But what is to come is described more fully and perfectly under the Roman captivity, when the Roman army devastated the whole of Judea, and the cities were burned, and strangers are currently devouring their region, and the desolation of the Jews will persist until the end of the world. Cyril of Alexandria, book 1, Orations on Isaiah. The chapter seems to speak of him who is adorned with the prerogatives of the Kingdom: the heart, of the sacred and select Levitical tribe, the care of the whole body of the nation: the feet, of those who hold the original station among the people. Therefore, when the Jewish land had endured unbearable calamities, being depopulated now by the Babylonians, now by neighboring nations, and because of its impiety toward Christ was to be burned by the hands of the Romans, when their kingdom was also to be overturned (for foreigners subdued them) and when the duties of the Priesthood ceased among them, with sacrifices subverted and the temple removed, according to the voice of the Prophet; hence he says: Why should you be struck down any more, adding to your iniquity? Blessed Gesner acknowledges that Jerusalem, with its neighboring cities, towns, and the whole region, was devastated as mentioned in verses 8 and 9, so that hardly a hut, such as a shelter in a vineyard, remains of such a splendid, opulent, and populous city. These things certainly do not fit the times of Joash and Amaziah. Thirdly, from the small remnants of seed: Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and we would have been like Gomorrah. This prophecy was fulfilled most especially in the destruction and rejection of the Jewish people in the New Testament, so that hardly a small seed remained, which the Lord saved for Himself by grace. Cyril interprets this, therefore, as referring to the Apostles and those who believed through them. This is also confirmed by Apostolic authority: since the Apostle interprets these words concerning the Jewish remnants of his own time in Romans 9:30. But it is helpful here to hear Jerome again: The Apostle Paul discusses this passage more fully to the Romans, writing: I say then, has God rejected His people? Far from it. For I also am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected His people whom He foreknew. And a little later: Even so then, at this present time, a remnant according to the election of grace has been saved (c. 11:5.) From which it is shown that the previous things, which the Prophetic discourse threatened against Jerusalem and Judah, are not to be referred to the time of the Babylonian captivity, but to the final one of the Romans, when the remnants of the people were saved in the Apostles. To this point, Josephus, in book 6 of the Jewish War, chapter 16, compares the impiety of the people of his own time with the impiety of Sodom. I think, he says, that if the Romans had delayed in coming against the guilty, either the city would have been swallowed by a chasm in the earth, or would have perished by a flood, or would have suffered the fires of lightning and Sodom. For it bore a much more impious progeny than that one had borne. Therefore, by the Princes of the Jews and the people of Gomorrah, Jerome understands the Scribes and Pharisees and the people who shouted: Crucify, crucify such a one; and what the Prophet marvels at, How has the faithful city become a harlot? he refers to the passion of Christ, when all turned aside, and the city, which was previously full of judgment, is now full of homicide, who killed the Prophets and the Lord Savior Himself: because tavern-keepers are said to mix water with wine from the law

of God is received by the traditions of the Pharisees. Again, when it is predicted that the judges of the people are to be restored, such as they were before, this refers either to the restoration of similar judges after the Babylonian captivity, as the Jews wish, of Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and others; or certainly more truly and correctly to the Apostles, and those who through the Apostles believed and were constituted as leaders of the churches. Concerning whom Cyril also explains this from Psalm 45: Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children. Furthermore, when it is promised in v. 26, After this thou shalt be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city: This, says Jerome, clearly refers to the Church, which is about to believe in the Lord, and the prophetic discourse embraces both Jews and Gentiles. And so also Hugo, Haymo, Dionysius, Forerius, Cornel. à Lapide, Tirinus, Mercerus: and no less do almost all of our own refer this latter promise in v. 26 to the times of the New Testament. Brentius himself at v. 21, how has the faithful city become a harlot, etc. Now in the third part, in which he persists until the end of the chapter, he prophesies that God, having destroyed all the impious, will restore and reform the Jerusalemite kingdom. This is a prophecy concerning the kingdom of Christ, in which alone true righteousness reigns and is preserved, in which alone also there is true and perpetual happiness. And at v. 24, Alas, I will be comforted concerning my enemies. What the Prophet prophesies here concerning the Jewish kingdom was indeed fulfilled somewhat in the incursion of King Sennacherib into the borders of the Jerusalemite kingdom, and later in the Babylonian devastation; but it was most fulfilled at the time when the Israelite nation was cast off, so that it would no longer be the people of God. At v. 26, similar judges and counselors are now promised, whom God is to raise up at the coming of Christ. These are the Apostles; who propagated the Gospel of Christ into the whole world, who were constituted judges over the twelve tribes of Israel, nay, over the whole human race. When, therefore, these things shall come to pass, then thou shalt be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city. These are the surnames of the heavenly Jerusalem, or of the kingdom of Christ and the Church. Nor was there any kingdom on earth, nor any city, which has obtained these epithets.

This explanation also seems most convenient for the reason that, according to the same, this first chapter of Isaiah exhibits the entrance and summary of the whole prophecy, which is completed then by the reproof of the sins of the people—of ignorance and neglect of God, of pride, of trust in their own strength and works, and of contempt and defrauding of their neighbor, and especially of idolatry from the first time, from which He adopted them as His sons and people, up to the latest times, which He foresaw in spirit would not be better, but worse: and thus He predicted the judgment of God, in various punishments, and in the very destruction and reprobation of the Jews: then by the Evangelical promise of divine grace, especially in the gathering of the Church of the New Testament from the Jewish remnants and the Gentiles, and other mysteries of the New Testament. All of which Isaiah executes more fully throughout the whole prophecy: so that the earlier chapters are almost entirely devoted to reproof up to the 40th, but the rest, which pertain to the promises and especially to the New Testament, are explained in the later chapters. Add to these now the collation of the second chapter, by which the calling of the Gentiles and the reprobation of the Jews is more abundantly explained, and thus that interpretation is not obscurely confirmed. Whence Jerome observes that in the first chapter the Prophet, threatening the Jews, comes to the salvation of the Gentiles; in the second, beginning from the salvation of the Gentiles, having punished Israel, he gathers the Church from both callings of those believing in Christ. Which Blessed Gesner also acknowledges in the argument of Chapter 2. The reformation of the Church, he says, promised in the previous chapter, Isaiah describes most excellently in this one in three parts: I. The amplitude and dignity of the Church itself in the New Testament: II. The impiety of the cast-off Jewish nation:

III. The divine majesty of Christ the King. Calvin at Ch. 2, verse 1. This prophecy is a confirmation of that doctrine which we had a little before (chapter 1) concerning the restoring of the Church. But that this prophecy in chapter 2 deals with the kingdom of Christ under the New Testament, he openly confesses at v. 2. When he names the end or extremity of days, let us remember that he is speaking of the kingdom of Christ, etc. Finally, if this prophecy meant that the remaining cities of Judea were to be devastated, and Jerusalem was to remain surviving, and that this had been predicted by the Prophet at the time of Ahaz or Hezekiah, when Jerusalem was being besieged, the Prophet, together with the King, if not also the people, could certainly have known even then, when either Rezin with Pekah or Sennacherib wanted to besiege Jerusalem, that they would be in vain, that the city would be liberated, and would remain surviving, and therefore the enemies would depart with their business unfinished. For they would have understood that from this prophecy long ago. But the contrary appears from history and the subsequent chapters of this Prophet, from the fear and anxiety especially of both Ahaz and Hezekiah, both of whom had to be specifically encouraged by the Prophet with the prediction of future liberation and confirmed by a sign in chapters 7 and 37. To which may now be added also the authority of the interpreters, especially the ancients, Jerome, Cyril, and in part also Basil, as well as our own Brentius, and others, which is not to be rejected here, especially when it is fortified by the explanation of the Apostle himself.

Latin:

Vers. 7. TERRA VESTRA DESERTA] Supple, erit. Sic sume & sequentia, Prædicitur enim obsidio per Rasinem ac Phaceen.

Alii Prophetam loqui volunt de præsente cala- mitate; non de futura. Omnes istas sententias, in- quit Calvinus, in tempus præteritum malo resolvere, quia potius narrat Propheta, quanta jam cades acci- derint, quam Dei vindictam denunciet. Exprobrat enim vecordiam & stuporem, quod ad sua mala ja- ceant attoniti. Sed huic explicationi obstat status incolumis rerum in regno Juda sub Usia, cujus tempore prophetizandi initium fecit Esaias; quam difficultatem tangit, non solvit Calvinus, nisi quod Judæorum opinionem probabili ratione non carere dicat, quod hæc ad regnum Jotham, non Usiæ per- tineant. Primo autem loco positam censet hanc con- cionem ideo, quod summam doctrinæ, quæ postea refertur, contineat. Sed ne Jothami quidem tem- pore regni Judæ statum tam miserabilem fuisse, qui Rex pius erat, & feliciter fatis regnavit, è 2. Chron. 27. constat. Proinde ad priora tempora sub Rege Amazia hæc refert Junius, de quibus 2. Reg. 12. & 14. 2. Chronic. 25. ad tempora Joasi, & Amaziæ B. Gesnerus noster: Quanquam vero ab Hasaële Rege Syriæ tempore Joas, tum à Joaso Re- ge Israëlis, tempore Amaziæ regnum Judæ discri- men & cladem aliquam subierit, 2. Paral. 24, 23. 24. c. 25, 22. non tamen ea tum fuit in Juda calamitas, quam hic adumbrat Propheta, ut à planta pedis usq; ad caput non fuerit sanitas, ut tota Regio desolata, & civitates igne exustæ fuerint: multo minus filia Sion, ut umbraculum in vinea, & sicut tugurium in cucumerario relicta isto tempore. Ideo rectius ad regnum Ahas refertur vaticinium à Brencio & aliis, non ad solam obsidionem per Rasinem ac Phaceen factam, uti vult Grotius; sed ad universas calami- tates, quæ sub regno ejus evenêre per Syros, Israë- litas, Edomitas, Philistæos, quia Deus humiliavit Ju- da ob peccata Ahas, uti legere est 2. Par. 28. Sed convenientius adhuc interpretantur, qui ad deva- stationem Judææ per Sennacheribum factam referunt cum Oecolampadio, ubi expugnatis omnibus Judææ civitatibus munitis unica Hierosolyma residua fuit, neque illa ita, ut olim frequentata, sed contemta: Vel cum Basilio Magno prædici ajunt desolationem Chaldæorum tempore captivitatis Babylonicæ. Tum enim prorsus derelicta fuit filia Sion, tum tota ter- ra deserta, tum res ad exiguum semen rediit, de quo v. 9. Nisi Dominus Exercituum reliquisset nobis semen, quasi Sodoma fuissemus & quasi Gomorrha si- miles essemus. Alii tamen è Patribus de novissima devastatione à Romanis facta intelligunt, aut certe conjungunt utramque illam desolationem; quibus accedit Cornel. à Lapide & Tirinus. Terra vestra de- serta (erit) civitates vestræ succensæ (erunt) regionem vestram alieni devorantes (erunt,) vel præsentibus positis pro futuris, devorat, id est, certo devora- bunt sc. Babylonii sub Nabuchodonosore, & mul- to magis Romani sub Tito & Vespasiano. Hi enim in Jerusalem non reliquerunt lapidem super lapi- dem. Quanquam vero facile concedamus, peccata populi, cui tam concionabatur sub Usia Rege Pro- pheta, hic ab ipso notata esse, utpote defectionem à vero DEI cultu, & pietate, obstinatam pervicaciam, & impœnitentiam, & abominandam hypocrisin, quæ istis etiam temporibus reprehensionem mereban- tur: siquidem certum sit, quod præsentium po- tissimum causas invectivas & ἐπανορθώσεως insti- tuerint Prophetæ: quia tamen Spiritu prævide- bat, subsequentibus temporibus non meliorem, sed deteriorem fore posteritatem, & scelera illa ad ἀκ- μὴν perductum iri novissimis temporibus, ideo fi- nalem πανωλεθρίαν hujus populi sub oculos po- nit, ut iram Dei vereantur, ac judicia Dei gravissi- ma sua ætate avertant. Quod enim hic supplicia & calamitates non præteritorum temporum, sed futuro- rum, ac imprimis sub extrema tempora designentur, colligitur primum ex universali languore: A planta pedis usq; ad verticem non est in eo sanitas. Quæ sive de languore culpæ intelligantur cum Basilio, seu rectius de pœnæ, & supplicii languore cum aliis, totius Ju- daici regni corruptio irreparabilis novissimis tem- poribus maxime congruit: Quo argumento utitur Hieronymus. Post Babylonicam captivitatem sub Zorobabel, & Esdra ac Nehemia Israël reversus est in Judæam, & antiquum recepit statum. Sub diver- sis quoque Principibus ac Regibus templum angustius fabricatum est, in tantum, ut etiam exterarum gen- tium Lacedæmoniorum & Atheniensium ac Romano- rum mererentur amicitias. Ergo hoc quod dicit, non est in eo sanitas, ad extremam refer captivitatem, quando post Titum & Vespasianum & ultimam ever- sionem Hierusalem sub Ælio Hadriano usque ad præsens tempus nullum remedium est. Jacet confos- sus & contumulatus Israël, quia interfecit medicum, qui ad curandum venerat domum Israël. Deinde è terræ omnimoda desolatione. Terra vestra deserta, inquit Propheta; civitates vestræ igne succensæ, re- gionem vestram in conspectu vestro alieni devorant, & desolabitur sicut in vastitate hostili. Ad quæ Hie- ronymus: Hæc sub Babyloniis ex parte completa sunt, incenso templo,subversa Hierusalem, quando Regio- nem decem tribuum Samaritani possederunt, & in tantam redacta est terra promissionis solitudinem, ut leonibus vastaretur. Plenius autem atq; perfectius quod futurum sit, sub Romana captivitate describi- tur, quando universam Judæam Romanus vastavit exercitus, civitatesque succensæ sunt, & regionem eo- rum impræsentiarum alieni devorant, & usque ad finem mundi perseverabit vastitas Judæorum. Cyril- lus Alexandrinus lib. 1. Orat. in Esa. Caput videtur dicere eum, qui Regni prærogativis ornatus est: Cor vero sacram & selectam tribum Leviticam totius cor- poris curam gentem: Pedes eos, qui pristinam sta- tionem in populo obtinent. Proinde cum terra Ju- daica calamitates non ferendas sustinuisset, depopu- lantibus eam nunc Babyloniis, nunc finitimis genti- bus, & propter impietatem in Christum Romanorum manibus esset concremanda,cum eorum etiam regnum esset evertendum (alienigenæ enim eos subegerunt) cumq; Sacerdotii munera apud eos cessarent, sacrifi- ciis subversis, templo sublato, juxta Prophetæ vocem; hinc dicit: Quid percutiamini ultra addentes ini- quitatem? Agnofcit B. Gesnerus, Hierosolymam cum vicinis urbibus, oppidis & tota regione v. 8. 9. di- ctita vastatam,ut vix casa,qualis est umbraculum in vinea,de tam splendida, opulenta, populosaq; urbe re- liqua sit. Quæ certe Joasi, & Amaziæ temporibus non conveniunt. Tertio è seminis exiguis reliquiis: Nisi Dominus exercituum nobis reliquisset semen,qua- si Sodoma fuissemus & quasi Gomorrha similes esse- mus. Quod vaticinium impletum maxime in N. T. populi Judaici clade & reprobatione facta, ut vix semen exiguum reliquum fuerit, quod ex gratia sibi servavit Dominus. Id ergo de Apostolis, & qui per eos crediderunt, interpretatur Cyrillus. Quod Apostolica etiam autoritate confirmatur: Siquidem hæc verba interpretetur Apostolus de reliquiis Ju- daicis sui temporis Rom. 9,30. Sed juvat hic ite- rum audire Hieronymum: Hunc locum Paulus A- postolus ad Romanos plenius differit, scribens: Dico ergo,nunquid repulit Deus populum suum? absit. Nam & ego Israelita sum ex semine Abraham de tribu Benjamin. Non repulit Deus plebem suam, quam præscivit. Et post paululum: Sic ergo & in isto tempore reliquiæ secundum electionem gra- tiæ salvæ factæ sunt (c. 11, 5.) Ex quo ostenditur, su- perior a,quæ contra Hierusalem & Judam sermo Pro- pheticus comminatus est, non ad Babylonica captivi- tatis referenda tempus, sed ad ultimam Romanorum, quando in Apostolis salvæ factæ sunt reliquiæ populo- rum. Huc facit, quod cum Sodomæ impietate comparet Joseph. lib. 6. Bell. Jud. c. 16. impietatem populi sui temporis. Puto,inquit, si Romani contra noxios venire tardassent,aut hiatu terræ devorandam fuisse civitatem, aut diluvio perituram, aut fulmi- num ac Sodomæ incendia passuram. Multo enim ma- gis impiam progeniem tulit, quam illa tulerat. Ideo Hieronymus per Principes Iudæorum & populum Comorrhæ intelligit Scribas & Pharisæos & popu- lum subclamatem: Crucifige, crucifige talem; & quod miratur Propheta, Quomodo civitas fidelis meretrix facta sit? ad passionem Christi refert, quando omnes declinaverunt, & civitas, quæ prius fuit plena judicii,nunc plena est homicidii, qui inter- fecerunt Prophetas & ipsum Dominum Salvatorem: quod caupones miscere dicuntur vino aquam de lege

Dei accipit traditionibus Pharisæorum violata. Rursus cum prædicuntur restituendi Judices po- puli, quales fuerunt prius, id vel de restitutione Ju- dicium similium post captivitatem Babylonicam, ut Judæi volunt, Zorobabelis, Esdræ, Nehemiæ & a- liorum; vel certe verius & rectius de Apostolis, & qui per Apostolos crediderunt & Ecclesiarum princi- pes constituti sunt. De quibus etiam hæc explicat Cyrillus e Psal. 45. Loco patrum erunt tibi filii. Por- ro cum promittitur v. 26. Posthac vocaberis civitas justa, urbs fidelis: Hæc perspicue, inquit Hieronymus, de Ecclesia, quæ in Dominum creditura est, tam de Judæis quam de Gentibus Propheticus sermo comple- Etitur. Atq; ita etiam Hugo, Haymo, Dionysius, Fore- rius, Cornel. à Lapide, Tirinus, Mercerus: nec minus è nostris plerique omnes promissionem hanc postre- mam v. 26. ad tempora N. T. referentes. Brentius ipse ad v. 21. quomodo facta est meretrix civitas fi- delis, &c. Nunc in tertia parte, in qua perseverat usq; ad finem capitis, vaticinatur, Deum perditis omnibus impiis, restauraturum & reformaturum regnum Hie- rosolymitanum. Hoc est vaticinium de regno Christi, in quo solo vera justitia dominatur & conservatur, in quo solo etiam vera est & perpetua felicitas. Et ad v. 24. Heu ego consolabor (me) ab hostibus meis. Quod Propheta h. l. vaticinatur de regno Judaico, nonnihil quidem factum est in incursione Regis San- herib, in fines regni Hierosolymitani, & postea in de- vastatione Babylonica; sed maxime impletum est eo tempore, quo abjecta est Gens Israëlita, ne esset populus Dei. Ad v. 26. Promittuntur nunc similes Judices, & Consiliarii, quos Deus in adventu Chri- sti sit excitaturus. Hi sunt Apostoli; qui Evangelium Christi propagarunt in totum orbem terrarum, qui constituti sunt Judices super XII. tribus Israël, imo super totum genus humanum. Cum ergo hæc fient, tunc vocaberis civitas justa, urbs fidelis. Hæ sunt cognomina cælestis Hierusalem, seu regni Christi & Ec- clesiæ. Nec fuit ullum regnum in terris, nec ulla civi- tas, quæ hæc Epitheta reportaverit.

Hæc explicatio etiam ideo convenientissima vi- detur, quod secundum eandem primum hocce caput Esaiæ ingressum & summam exhibeat totius Prophe- tiæ, quæ absolvitur tum reprehensione peccatorum populi ignorantiæ & neglectus Dei, superbiæ, fiduciæ, suarum virium, & operum, & contemtus & defrau- dationis proximi, ac cumprimis idololatriæ inde à primo tempore, ex quo eos in filios & populum suum adoptavit, usq; ad novissima tempora, quæ non me- liora, sed deteriora fore in spiritu prævidit: adeoq; judicium Dei prædixit, in variis suppliciis, inque ipso etiam excidio & reprobatione Judæorum: tum promissione Evangelica gratiæ divinæ, maxime in collectione Ecclesiæ N. Test. è reliquiis Judaicis & gentibus, aliisque N. T. mysteriis. Quæ omnia plenius exequitur Esaias per totam Prophetiam: ita ut reprehensioni fere priora capita impendantur usq; ad 40. cætera vero, quæ ad promissiones & ad Nov. imprimis Testamentum pertinent, posteriori- bus Capp. expediantur. Adde his jam capitis secun- di collationem, quo uberius vocatio gentium & re- probatio Judæorum explicatur, adeoq; interpreta- tio ista haud obscure comprobatur. Unde Hierony- mus observat, in primo capite Prophetam Judæis com- minantem ad gentium venire salutem; in secundo à gentium salute incipientem, punito Israële, ex utraque vocatione credentes in Christum Ecclesiam congrega- re. Quod agnoscit etiam B. Gesnerus in argumento Cap. 2. Reformationem, inquit, Ecclesiæ superiori ca- pite promissam in isto Esaias excellentissime describit tribus partibus: I. Ipsius Ecclesiæ in N. T. amplitudi- ne & dignitate: II. Abjectæ gentis Judaicæ impietate:

III. Christi Regis divina majestate. Calvin. ad C. 2. vers. 1. Haec Prophetia confirmatio est ejus doctrinae, quam paulo ante (cap. 1.) habuimus de restituenda Ec- clesia. Hac autem Prophetia cap. 2. de regno Christi sub N. Test. agi, aperte fatetur ad v. 2. Cum finem vel extremitatem dierum nominat, memineri- mus eum de regno Christi loqui, &c. Denique si hoc sibi vellet vaticinium, reliquas civitates Judaeae deva- standas, Hierosolymam superstitem futuram, idque tempore Abasi, vel Hiskiae, cum obsideretur Hiero- solyma, praedictum fuisset à Propheta, certus uti- que Propheta cum Rege, si non etiam populus esse potuisset, jam tum, ubi obsidere vellet sive Razin cum Peka, sive Senacheribus Hierosolyma, frustra il- los fore, liberatum iri urbem, ac superstitem re- mansuram, ideoque re infecta hostes discessuros. Id enim ex hoc vaticinio jampridem intellexis- sent.
