Contrarium autem apparet ex historia & capi- tibus subsequentibus hujus Prophetae, è pavore & an- xietate cumprimis tum Ahazi, tum Ezechiae, qui u- terque peculiariter erigendus erat à Propheta prae- dictione futurae liberationis, ac signo confirman- dus cap. 7. & 37. Quibus accedat nunc etiam autho- ritas Interpretum, cumprimis Veterum, Hierony- mi, Cyrilli, ex parte etiam Basilii, ut & Brentii no- stri, ac aliorum, quae hic respuenda non est, maxi- me quum ipsius Apostoli explicatione munita sit.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. AND THE DAUGHTER OF ZION SHALL BE LEFT AS A COTTAGE IN A VINEYARD.] The affairs of the city of Jerusalem will be greatly cut down, with the fields taken away on all sides.

This threatening imports not only that, but a far more grievous punishment, not merely the seizure of fields, but the abandonment of the Daughter of Sion herself and her devastation. Far more correctly, therefore, did the Ancients weigh the emphasis of the simile and the prediction. St. Jerome: That all Israel was called a vine, the Prophet himself testifies in the following (ch. 5). As long as this vine brought forth most abundant fruits, it had God as its guardian: but after all who passed by the way vintaged it, and the boar out of the wood wasted it, the Lord left His temple, and rising up in anger said, Arise, let us go hence: and your house shall be left to you desolate (Matt. 23) and through Jeremiah (ch. 12) I have forsaken my house. The simile of the devastation of the temple and Jerusalem is taken from farmers, who, as long as the vine is full of grapes, place guards in booths. In a cucumber patch also, which the LXX call the keeping of apples, small huts are made for the sake of the heat of the Sun and to ward off its rays, and from there they drive away either men or small beasts that are accustomed to lie in wait for the growing crops. But when such produce has been taken away, the drying booths and huts of the shrubs remain with the guardian departing, because he has nothing further to guard. Therefore, the omnipotent God also abandoned the temple and made the city desolate; which it is not necessary to prove with words, especially for us, who see Sion desolate and Jerusalem overturned, and the temple razed to the ground. Similarly, Cyril of Alexandria understands the abandonment of the daughter of Sion, that is, Jerusalem. For while it still had the fruits of righteousness, the Lord deemed it worthy of secure fortification and guardianship and all mercy: As long as Israel was the vine of the Lord of Hosts, it was hedged about and judged worthy of a fence. But it brought forth thorns and was delivered by God to oppressors. For He says (Isa. 5) I will take away its hedge and it shall be for plundering, and I will leave my vineyard, and it shall not be pruned nor dug: The Savior also teaches that the vineyard had been deserted and abandoned by GOD (Matt. 23) Behold your house shall be left to you desolate. Others explain it thus: As in fields it appea- small huts are scattered here and there, which have the appearance of neither cities nor villages: thus in the whole kingdom of Judah no city, no entire village is seen; the whole is like a devastated city, in which only one or another small house has remained safe from the burning of fire. Thus Brentius, whom Osiander followed; nor does Calvin think otherwise: I think this is the Prophet's meaning, that the evils of which he discourses reach even to the city itself, so that, diminished and worn away, it bears the appearance of an ignoble hut. Certainly, both that simile and the very words imply the devastation of a city, not the plundering of fields. AND AS A CITY, WHICH IS DEVASTATED; the Hebrew word is observed to be taken and devastated by siege through metalepsis, as Vatablus notes: which R. David Kimchi also explains as devastation. For נצר is also 'he devastated', and מצורים are desert places, and shrines of the dead, as Oecolampadius observed. The same Jerome rendered it: A city, which is devastated. Although the word נותר denotes not abandonment, but remaining, when something survives and a remnant stays, yet the description added, that the daughter of Zion is to remain as a booth and a hut, teaches entirely that it will be deserted and abandoned: whence both explanations which we have brought forward come back to almost the same thing as far as the sense is concerned. If the city itself survives like a hut, as Junius, the English, Italian, Tigurine, and Genevan interpreters, as well as Piscator, render the Hebrew ונותרה בת ציון, it must be that little of the city remains, and that it is devastated and deserted in the highest degree. Which sense verse 9 also confirms: that they are not far from being like Sodom and Gomorrah, which does not fit the times of Sennacherib, and rather looks to a total devastation of the city, with a small seed of the people preserved.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET DERELINQUETUR FILIA SION UT UMBRACULUM IN VINEA.] Res urbis Hierosoly- morum valde erunt accisae, agris undique ereptis.

Non id tantum haec comminatio, sed longe graviorem poenam importat, non agrorum solum ereptionem, sed ipsius Filiae Sion derelictionem ejus- demque devastationem. Longe ergo rectius em- phasin similitudinis & praedictionis expenderunt Veteres. S. Hieronymus: Quod vinea appellatus sit omnis Israël, idem in consequentibus Propheta te- statur (cap. 5.) Haec vinea quamdiu uberrimos attulit fructus, habuit custodem Deum: postquam vero vin- demiaverunt eum omnes transeuntes viam, & vasta- vit eam aper de sylva, reliquit templum suum Do- minus, iratusque consurgens ait, Surgite, abeamus hinc: & relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta (Matth. 23.) & per Hieremiam (c. 12.) Reliqui do- mum meam. Similitudo autem vastationis templi & Hierusalem sumta est ab agricolis, qui quamdiu vinea uvarum plena est, ponunt custodes in umbracu- lis. In Cucumerario quoque, quod LXX. po- morum custodiam vocant, parvulae fiunt casulae pro- pter ardorem Solis ac radios declinandos, & inde vel homines, vel bestiolas, quae insidiari solent natis fru- gibus, abigunt. Quum autem ablata fuerint istius- modi genimina, remanent arentia fruticum umbracu- la casulaeque recedente custode, quia non habet ul- tra, quod servet. Ergo & omnipotens Deus dere- liquit templum, & urbem fecit esse desertam; quod non necesse est sermonibus approbare, nobis praesertim, qui videmus desertam Sion & eversam Hierusalem, templumque usque ad solum dirutum. Similiter Cyrillus Alexand. derelictionem filiae Sion, hoc est, Hierosolymae, intelligit. Dum enim adhuc fructus justitiae haberet, secura munitione & custo- dia & omni misericordia eam dignatus est Dominus: Quamdiu erat Israël vinea Domini Sabaoth, ob- vallabatur & sepimento digna judicabatur. Pepe- rit autem spinas & tradita est à Deo opprimentibus. Inquit enim (Esa. 5.) auferam sepem ejus & erit direptioni, & relinquam vineam meam, & non putabitur neque fodietur: Desertam etiam ac de- relictam fuisse à DEO vineam, Servator docet (Matth. 23.) Ecce relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta. Alii sic exponunt: Sicut in agris appa- rent hinc inde parva quædam tuguriola, quæ nec ur bium nec vicorum speciem habent: ita in toto regno Iu dæ nulla civitas, nullus viculus integer videtur; totum est veluti devastata civitas, in qua tantum una aut altera domuncula ab incendio ignis tuta permansit. Sic Brentius, quem secutus est Osiander; nec aliter Calvinus: Prophetæ mentem hanc esse puto, quod mala, de quibus disserit, ad civitatem usque ipsam pertingant, ut imminuta & attrita ignobilis tugurii speciem referat. Vastationem certe urbis, non agrorum ereptionem cum similitudo ista, tum et- iam verba ipsa inferunt. ET SICUT CIVI- TAS, QUÆ VASTATUR; Ebræum verbum obseffa per metalepsin est obsidendo capta & vastata notante Vatablo: quod R. David Kimchi etiam exponit per devastationem. Nam נצר est etiam va- stavit, & מצורים loca sunt deserta, & mortuorum delubra, ut obfervavit Oecolampadius. Idem Hie- ronymus reddidit: Civitas, quæ vastatur. Quamvis verbum נותר non derelictionem notet, sed relictio- nem, cum aliquid superat, & reliquum manet, de- scriptio tamen adjecta, quod remansura sit filia Sion, ut umbraculum & tuguriolum, omnino eandem de- sertam ab derelictam fore docet: Unde utraque ex- plicatio, quam adduximus, eodem, quantum ad sensum, pene recidit. Si civitas ipsa tanquam tu- guriolum superat, uti Ebræa ונותרה בת ציון Iu- nius, Anglus, Italus, Tigurinus & Genevensis Inter- pretes, nec non Piscator reddunt, oportet parum de civitate residuum esse, eamque vastatam & deser- tam esse maxime. Quem sensum v. 9. etiam con- firmat: parum abesse, quin similes Sodomæ sint, & Gomorrhæ, quod temporibus Sennacheribi non con- gruit, & vastationem totalem civitatis, exiguo po- puli servato semine, potius spectat.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. FIRST VISION. Concerning the confluence of the nations to the mountain of the Lord, because of the going forth of the Word from Zion, and the extreme casting away of the Jewish people because of idolatry and various crimes.

Latin:

CAPUT II. VISIO PRIMA. De gentium ad montem Domini confluxu, ob Verbi exitum è Zione, & populi Iudaici ob idololatriam; & varia scelera extrema projectione.

## 2:2
Ver. 2. AND IT SHALL BE IN THE LAST DAYS THE MOUNTAIN OF THE HOUSE OF THE LORD SHALL BE PREPARED ON THE TOP OF THE MOUNTAINS.] For 'last days' you may correctly put 'hereafter' from the Hebrew. It looks to that time when the city was freed from the siege of Rezin and Pekah.

corrupts both the words and the scope of the Prophet. For the words themselves do not sound of the time immediately impending, or what is to happen hereafter; but they properly sound of the 'last days' and are to be taken according to the usage of Scripture: nor is there any question here of the liberation of the city from a siege, but a peculiar prophecy is exhibited concerning the exaltation of the mountain or the Church through the calling and confluence of the nations to it. Therefore, a new inscription first adorns it, so that it may be understood that something peculiar is proposed here; and that not concerning the city only, but also the Jewish people. The word, which Isaiah, the son of Amoz, saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. Then indeed he promises an exaltation not common, but most eminent; not, I say, a liberation only from the power of enemies, but an elevation above all mountains and hills, above all the kingdoms and powers of the world. And it shall be in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be elevated above the hills. Which is not to be understood with the Jews concerning an external Mount Zion and its bodily exaltation, which they believe is to be placed upon Mount Carmel and Tabor; but concerning the sublimity of the Church in the time of the New Testament, which is denominated from the Sionean mount, because the temple of the Lord was there, a figure of the Church, and because from that mountain and temple the proclamation of the Gospel had to be propagated through the world. For this is the most high house of the Lord, just as if it were situated on a mountain, Matt. 5:14, and it is designated everywhere by Mount Zion, Cf. Gal. 4:26. The house of the Lord is the Church, 1 Tim. 3:15. Cf. 2 Chron. 33:15, and it is called the Mountain of the Lord, or the Holy Mountain, Psalm 15:1, 24:3, 48:2, Isa. 30:17, both because of its firmness, Psalm 46:3, 125:1, and because of the sublimity of its preservation: since its inhabitants aspire from earthly things to sublime things, and have their citizenship in heaven, Col. 3:2, Phil. 3:20. The word נכון signifies founded, stabilized, straight, disposed and ordered, whole and perfect, all of which suit the Church, so firmly established and prepared that not even the gates of hell can prevail against it, Matt. 16:18. Therefore, Athanasius (Epist. ad Epictet. near the beginning), Eusebius (lib. 2 demonstr. Evang. c. 32), and Cyril of Alexandria (in this place) understand the Church by the mountain. It is read, he says, that that Zion of the Jews was situated and built on a mountain, yet it is understood here not sensibly, but spiritually as the Church, which is also compared to a mountain. For it is truly exalted, and illustrious, and known to all everywhere. It is also exalted in another way, since it savors of nothing earthly, and is above earthly things, and beholds the glory of God, as far as is permitted, with the eyes of the mind, and glories in very sublime dogmas about God.

Furthermore, what need is there for the explanation of others? For the Prophet himself declares what kind of exaltation he understands: All nations shall flow unto it, and many peoples shall go, and shall say: Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths. That these things were said concerning the calling of the nations to the Church of Christ is so clear that one must marvel that Grotius is still blind to such great light. But to what times does that universal calling of ALL Nations look, if not to the times of the New Testament? Therefore, fourthly, the emphasis of the word אחרית must be pressed here, not lightly passed over: because these things are to happen באחרית הימים in the last, or in the novelty τῶν ἡμερῶν of those days, concerning which he prophesied, or absolutely in the last days, which indeed bring an end to the Old Testament, and in respect of it are called the last, but not in respect of the end of the world, as the Jews wish; Wherefore the LXX Interpreters rightly explain it, ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις, the Vulgate, in the last days; rightly also do the Doctors of the Church, both ancient and more recent, interpret these by common consent as the time of the New Testament, which is called the fullness of time Gal. 4, 4, and the last time, 1 John 2, 18, Heb. 1, 1. From which not even Calvin thought one should depart here, however much he otherwise willingly Judaizes. When he names the end or extremity of days, let us remember that he is speaking of the kingdom of Christ: and at the same time the reason must be held, why he so calls the kingdom of Christ. For until that time all things were as it were suspended, so that the people might not fix their eyes on the present state of things, which was only a shadow: but on the Redeemer, through whom the truth was to be exhibited. Therefore, after Christ arrived, if that time is compared with ours, the end of the ages truly falls upon us. But the Fathers who lived then, it behooved them to strive toward Christ as if with outstretched arms. And since the restoration of all things depended on his arrival, not undeservedly are they commanded to defer their hope until this point. It was indeed always useful for them to know that the state of the Church would be more perfect under Christ: especially because they were kept under figures, and meanwhile were subject to various inclinations: because the Lord, deliberately so that he might keep them in suspense, wished to awaken them in various ways. But there was a peculiar circumstance of this prophecy: because for four hundred years or thereabouts they could have been destroyed a thousand times over, had not the fullness of time come to mind, in which the integrity of the Church was to be restored. Therefore, just as the Church was almost overturned by various storms, each of the faithful seized upon this voice in their shipwreck like a plank, until they could swim into port. It is to be noted meanwhile that the perfection of the days began from the coming of Christ in such a way that they flow in a continuous series, until he appears again for our salvation. The Jews themselves explain it concerning the last days, of which this is the Rule in Michlal Jophi: every place in which it is said 'in the end of days' treats of the days of the Messiah: Conf. Gen. 49, 1. 10. Num. 24, 15. 17. Jer. 23, 6. But they cavil that it is not to be accepted concerning our Messiah: because he did not come in the last days: to which a response was given by the blessed Tarnovius on Micah 4, 2.

Fifth, let a comparison be instituted of those things which were predicted concerning the devastation of the city and the temple, then it will appear that neither Grotius's gloss about the city being freed from siege, nor any other, whatever it may be, has a place here, other than a spiritual exaltation on the mystical MOUNT ZION, which took place in the time of the New Testament. Jerusalem was indeed to be exalted, both through the proclamation of the Gospel and through the miracles performed by Christ; but this mountain of the house of the Lord embraces not only Jerusalem and Mount Zion or the Jewish Church, but all the Churches throughout the whole world, namely the entire Catholic Church, which especially after the devastation of Jerusalem and Mount Zion raised its head, and ought to have raised it according to this prophecy; and therefore R. Solomon interprets the present passage with us concerning the spiritual Church to be exalted in the manner of the Rabbis themselves, nor did Calvin understand it otherwise: whose words it is pleasing to transcribe: 'But who could have risen so suddenly after Zion had fallen with the greatest disgrace once the temple was destroyed? Yet Isaiah did not prophesy in vain.' For this hill was at last truly lifted up above all mountains: since from there the voice of the Lord was heard, and it thundered through the whole world, which would lift us up even to heaven; from here the heavenly majesty of GOD shone forth: Finally, since it was the sanctuary of God, it surpassed the whole world in outstanding height. Moreover, the use of the prophecy is to be noted: namely, that Isaiah wished to bring consolation, which would support the spirits of the people in captivity: so that although no temple existed, no sacrifices were being made, and everything lay in ruins, this hope might nevertheless flourish in the souls of the pious: and in such great desolation, and such unsightly ruins, they might conceive these things in their mind. The mountain of the Lord is indeed deserted, but he will still have his seat in it, and the glory of this mountain will be greater than that of all others. Therefore, so that they would not doubt that this would happen, the Prophet painted a picture for them here, as it were, in which they might behold the glory of GOD. For although the mountain existed, it was nevertheless almost detestable in its foul solitude, after it had lost its beauty, having been deserted by God. But it behooved the pious to look not at those ruins, but at this vision. Furthermore, why he speaks so magnificently about the exaltation of Mount Zion appears sufficiently from what follows: because from there flowed the Gospel, in which the image of God shines forth. For other mountains could surpass it in height: but because the glory of God is preeminent, the mountain in which it is revealed must also be eminent. Therefore, he does not proclaim Mount Zion by itself, but with its adornment: by which the whole world was also to be enlightened.

Accordingly, sixth, the exegesis of the Prophet is to be carefully noted, by which he explains that sublime height of Mount Zion, not only through the confluence of the nations to the Church, but also through the going forth of the Evangelical doctrine from Zion into the world: because the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. Which do not fit the time of the city being freed from the siege of Rhesen; but look to the times of the New Testament. For the highest glory of Mount Zion is that the doctrine of the Gospel had to be preached first by Christ himself and his Apostles in Jerusalem, and from there be propagated and diffused into the whole world, Luke 24. For the Law goes forth from Zion, not that which teaches the offering of external victims, or the performing of other ceremonies; but תורה, doctrine so called κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν, the doctrine of the Gospel, Ps. 19, 8. Rom. 8, 2. and the Word of the Lord goes forth from Jerusalem, from where the Apostles were sent into the world, so that the oracles of the Lord were no longer entrusted to the Jews alone; but were propagated through the whole world, Psalm 147, 19. Rom. 3, 2. chap. 10, 18. Therefore Jerome on this passage explains the Word going forth from Jerusalem: 'Why is it said that the Word went forth from Jerusalem? Both because the Lord often taught in the temple, and because the Church, founded first in Jerusalem, sowed the Churches of the whole world.' And he observes the emphasis of the word 'will go forth': 'And he did not say beautifully: the Word and the Law of the Lord will be and will remain in Zion and in Jerusalem: but it will go forth, so that he might signify that all nations are to be irrigated by that fountain of the doctrine of God.' Whence it is manifest that, whether you understand the whole Church with Cyril through the mountain of the house of the Lord, or, with Jerome leading the way here, concerning Mount Zion, in which Jerusalem was built; the sense remains consistent, and the times of the New Testament are designated. Which later explanation is also approved by Brentius, because the Messiah himself taught in it, because he performed many miracles there, and because the Holy Spirit was sent to the Apostles there at the Feast of Pentecost, and from there the Apostles began to divulge the Gospel. What of the fact that the gloss of Grotius in no way agrees with the words of the Prophet: For to be exalted above all mountains and hills, and to be freed from a siege, differ as much as heaven and earth: Nor can it be fitted to the parallel passage, Micah 4, 2, where the same prophecy is repeated in exactly the same words, nor can it by any reason be accepted concerning the liberation from the siege made by Rasi: because there is no mention of that siege or time there. Although neither in this place is there anything concerning the same, but the threat and prediction of the preceding chapter is wrongly dragged into it. Grotius himself acknowledges on Micah 4, 2 that Micah is prophesying about another time: whose prophecy he refers to the times after the return from the Babylonian captivity. And on Luke 24, 47, he admits that there is a prophecy here about the beginning of the Evangelical proclamation being made in the time of the New Testament in Jerusalem.

Verse of the same. AND ALL NATIONS SHALL FLOW UNTO HIM] That is, many from the enemy peoples of the Syrians will betake themselves to Jerusalem, as to the safest place, and there in the court of the nations will worship God. Moreover, in a more sublime sense, the Hebrews also understand this passage concerning the times of the Messiah. Compare Dan. 2, 35.

Grotius Judaizes again in a very illustrious passage. For if this so distinguished and clear oracle is not to be accepted concerning the calling of the Gentiles, what then will be so clear, concerning which you could be indubitably certain, that the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of the Messiah is predicted? It is a question here of a UNIVERSAL, and not indeed of some particular calling, or of the confluence of a few: And all nations shall flow unto him. But when was that done after Jerusalem was freed from the siege of Rasi? When did, I will not say all nations, but many only, in a distinguished number of various peoples, flow together there? Let him designate the time, let him produce histories, and let not Grotius invent these things solely from his own ingenuity. And who were those peoples, which nations? Wherefore, the Doctors of the Church by common consent explain it concerning the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of the Messiah, which the Holy Spirit also predicted elsewhere would be universal: All nations shall flow unto him. For all nations, says Jerome, shall serve him, it was said: Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance and for thy possession the ends of the earth (Ps. 2) that they may serve him (according to Zephaniah ch. 3) under one yoke, of whom the same Prophet testifies: From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia they shall bring you offerings: and in the 71st Psalm we read, before him the Ethiopians shall fall down. All the others agree with Jerome. They shall flow to that mountain, that is, they will not come moved by fear or danger to actions with a small band, but willingly, mutually encouraging and exciting one another, with pleasure and dancing they shall flow, like an overflowing river, in a greatest and innumerable multitude. Furthermore, at what time did the Law go forth from Zion and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem? Was it done at the time of Rezin, or of the liberation of Jerusalem itself? But at that time the nations set out to Mount Zion according to Isaiah, when the word of the Lord goes forth from Zion, of which our Brentius says beautifully: Let the thing itself interpret how the nations are said to set out to Mount Zion. For from that death the Gospel was spread into the whole world among all nations. In whatever place, therefore, nations receive the Gospel of Christ, they are said to have set out to Mount Zion. Thus Cornelius and others in Caesarea approached Mount Zion, when they believed in Christ and received the Holy Spirit, even though they had not then set out to Jerusalem. Away, therefore, with the Jewish gloss about the external journey of the nations to the city of Jerusalem. And that journey is to be instituted not only for the sake of worshipping God in the court of the Gentiles, but for the sake of learning the ways of the Lord.

For they say, He will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths. Which is to be understood concerning the doctrine of the Gospel that is to go forth from Zion. For that doctrine, which will go forth from Zion, will be a different doctrine than that which previously went forth from Mount Sinai: which antithesis the Prophet insinuates here. The Law reached a few men; this doctrine will penetrate to all nations. The Law terrified, so that they fled and trembled when it was promulgated: this will be welcome, and to it they will hasten with remarkable eagerness. The Law shows, it does not take away sins; it kills, it does not give life; it condemns, it does not save men. This doctrine, however, takes away sins, gives life to men, and saves those who believe in Christ. Furthermore, at what time did the Lord judge the nations and reprove many peoples, so that swords were beaten into plowshares, nor did nation lift up sword against nation? That universal tranquility never happened to the world, nor will it ever happen. It is not, therefore, to be understood of external tranquility: for the sense of the words implies this: Every zeal for warring will be turned to peace, and instead of discord there will be concord in the whole world. Although Jerome thinks this was fulfilled in the time of Augustus, when all wars ceased, he nevertheless admits that the soldiers and legions of the Romans were sent against barbarian nations: nor does he reject the spiritual understanding, when the hardness of the heart is broken by the plowshare of Christ, and the thorns of vices are spiritually eradicated. And the Doctors of the Church explain this unanimity concerning the spiritual peace and concord which flourishes among the true believers of Christ, with Irenaeus lib. 4. cap. 67, Tertullian lib. 3. against Marcion cap. 21, Athanasius in his Oration on the Incarnation of the Word, and Origen against Celsus lib. 5, of which that peace of the whole world under the empire of Augustus, at the time of the Lord's birth, was a certain symbol. When, therefore, the Prophet said that Christ would judge the nations and peoples, that is, would rule from sea to sea in the whole world by his Gospel, he explains the manner by which he is to receive and preserve the kingdom: that he is not going to do this in the manner of worldly Monarchs, who are accustomed to occupy, preserve, and extend a kingdom by war, but by peaceful and tranquil means; that the Apostles were not to spread the Gospel of Christ on earth with an armed army and a powerful hand, but by preaching that is tranquil, as far as in them lies. For no better method, which is the opinion of Blessed Luther, can be initiated for removing discord than that which Christ uses, who in one sentence equally reproves and condemns all of sin. Those who hear and believe this, for what will they litigate? Since they see that they are no more righteous, holy, and wise than others. It is therefore easy to agree among Christians, who feel that all are to be saved by the same grace, and that no one's merit or demerit is said to be greater than another's. Which explanation is confirmed by a similar prophecy concerning spiritual peace and the city in the kingdom of Christ, Isa. 11:6. The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, etc. Indeed, from all the prophecies that deal with the peace of the kingdom of Christ, they predict that it will be devoid of all discord, all fear, and war. Grotius himself, in his book on the Truth of the Christian Religion 5. §. 18, grants that these things are to be accepted concerning the times of the Messiah, as far as the first sense is concerned, and that they are to be explained figuratively: which one may also observe in lib. 1. de jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 2. §. 8. where he notes that this prophecy must be accepted either under a certain condition, if, namely, all peoples receive and fulfill the law of Christ, for if all were Christians and lived like Christians, there would be no wars, or it must be understood purely, as its fulfillment, as also the general conversion of the Jews, is still to be expected. But such a golden age with the general conversion of the Jews is rashly expected in this dregs of the world, and at that time when it is predicted that faith will fail and will scarcely be found. Nor is there need for that hypothetical, or Hackspan's hyperbolic manner of speaking, because neither is a hypothesis to be invented where none occurs in the text, and hyperbole is not to be admitted rashly in Scripture. And therefore it is better to understand it with the ancients concerning spiritual peace. But to the Jews, who in the time of the Messiah invent a universal earthly peace from this and similar passages, the opinion of the Talmud in Massecheth Berachoth cap. 5 is deservedly opposed. and in Massech. Sanhedr. cap. ult., praised by a certain Samuel: There is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah, except the subjection of kingdoms: whence Maimonides accepts these things parabolically, and thinks they are to be referred to eternal life: which we grant by reason of a perfect and consummated completion. But that such concord has a place spiritually in the kingdom of the Messiah, although not in that degree of perfection which will be in the other life, we are clearly taught and confirmed in this prophetic passage.

Now that apostrophe to the Jews: Come, O house of Jacob, and let us walk in the light of God, whether it be of the nations, as Rupertus wishes, or of the Prophet, what else does it mean, but that the Jews should not neglect to receive the Messiah, seeing that they are the House of Jacob, to whom his promise was primarily made; that they should not yield to the nations in this, but rather strive with them toward the Messiah, so that they may be illuminated by that light of grace, faith, and salvation! I think, says Cyril, that the Prophet in this hortatory speech, which he employs, urges the Israelites to listen to Christ saying; while you have the light, walk in the light, lest darkness overtake you. For he himself is the light, etc. Since the Jews neglected this, Isaiah hence predicts the rejection of the house of Israel, and has set forth its causes, as we shall teach in v. 6. Therefore, this prophecy does not only pertain to the Messiah according to a more sublime sense, but it treats literally of his kingdom and the calling of the Gentiles, which some Jews, Rabbi Solomon and others (who are sounder in this part than Grotius), also explain literally concerning the Messiah.

Which was also for that reason repeated by Micah in the same words in chapter 4, 2, although on a different occasion, so that we might not doubt that, according to the letter and the proper and direct intention of the Holy Spirit, it was treated by Isaiah not concerning the deliverance from the siege of the city, or an external departure to Mount Zion, but concerning the spiritual exaltation of Mount Zion, and the gathering of the nations to the kingdom of the Messiah; which the Prophets did not cease to inculcate on every given occasion. For the same words of Isaiah and Micah cannot be applied to different times, affairs, and conditions without significant distortion, since it is too manifest that both, moved by the same Spirit, are predicting the same thing in the same words, and that the New Testament looks to those times. That passage also, which Grotius compares, Dan. II. 35, what else does it imply but the kingdom of Christ? That stone, which is said to have become a great mountain and filled the whole earth, is without doubt to be understood of Christ and his kingdom filling the whole earth. If, therefore, this mountain in Isaiah ought to be taken in the same sense, what is more certain than that the kingdom of Christ to be diffused through the whole world is designated, according to the proper and literal meaning of the prophecy!

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET ERIT IN NOVISSIMIS DIEBUS PRÆ- PARATUS MONS DOMUS DOMINI IN VERTI- CE MONTIVM.] Pro novissimis diebus recte ex He- bræo ponas posthac. Spectat id tempus, quo urbs ab ob- sidione Rasinis & Phaceæ liberata est.

Depravat & verba & scopum Prophetæ. Non enim de tempore proxime imminente, seu quid post hinc futurum sit; sed de diebus novissimis verba ipsa proprie sonant & ex usu Scripturæ accipienda sunt: neq; de liberatione urbis ab obsidione hic agitur, sed peculiaris Prophetia de exaltatione montis vel Ec- clesiæ per vocationem & confluxum gentium ad ean- dem exhibetur. Ideo primum nova επιγραφή eam ornat, ut aliquid peculiare hic proponi intel- ligatur; idq; non urbem tantum concernens, sed et- iam populum Iuda. Verbum, quod vidit Esaias, filius Amos super Juda & Jerusalem. Tum vero exalta- tionem non vulgarem, sed eminentissimam promit- tit; non, inquam, liberationem tantum ab hostium potentia, sed elevationem supra omnes montes & colles, super omnia regna & potestates mundi. Et erit in novissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Do- mini in vertice montium, & elevabitur super colles. Quæ non cum Iudæis de externo monte Sion, ejusq; corporali exaltatione, quem credunt monti Carmelo & Tabori imponendum; sed de sublimitate Ecclesiæ tempore N. Test. quæ à Sioneo monte, quia ibi tem- plum Domini erat figura Ecclesiæ, & quia è monte illo, & templo præconium Evangelii per orbem propagari debuit, denominatur, intelligenda. Hæc enim est domus Domini altissima, perinde ac si in monte sita esset, Matth. 5, 14. & passim per montem Sion designatur, Conf. Gal. 4, 26. Domus Domini Ecclesia est, 1. Tim. 3, 15. Conf. 2. Chron. 33, 15. & vo- catur Mons Domini, vel Mons sanctus, Psalm. 15, 1. 24, 3. 48, 2. Esa. 30, 17. tum ob firmitatem Psal. 46, 3. 125, 1. tum ob conservationis sublimitatem: quum incolæ ejus à terrenis ad sublimia adspirent, ac πολίτευμα suum in cœlis habeant, Col. 3, 2. Phil. 3, 20. Verbum נכון significat fundatum, stabili- tum, rectum, dispositum & ordinatum, integrum ac perfectum, quæ omnia Ecclesiæ conveniunt, ita fir- matæ ac præparatæ, ut ne portæ inferorum adver- sus eam prævalere possint, Matth. 16, 18. Ideo per montem Ecclesiam intelligunt Athanasius Epist. ad Epictet. sub init. Eusebius lib. 2. demonstr. Evang. c. 32. Cyrillus Alexandrinus in h. l. Legitur quidem, inquit, Sion illa Judæorum in monte sita & ædifica- ta, intelligitur tamen hic ὀυκ ἀισθητῶς, ἀλλὰ πνευ- ματικῶς, non sensibiliter, sed spiritualiter Ecclesia, quæ etiam monti comparatur. Etenim vere est ex- celsa, & illustris & omnibus ubique notissima. Ali- ter etiam excelsa est, quoniam terreni nihil sapit, & supra res terrenas est, & gloriam Dei, quatenus li- cet, animi oculis intuetur, & sublimibus admodum de Deo dogmatibus gloriatur.

Porro quid opus aliorum explicatione ? De- clarat enim ipse Propheta, qualem intelligat ex- altationem: Fluent ad eum omnes gentes, & ibunt po- puli multi, & dicent: Venite, & adscendamus ad montem Domini, & ad domum Dei Jacob, & docebit nos vias suas, & ambulabimus in semitis ejus. Quæ de vocatione gentium ad Ecclesiam Christi dicta esse, tam luculentum est, ut mirari oporteat ad tan- tam lucem adhuc cæcutire Grotium. Illa vero uni- versalis Gentium OMNIUM vocatio ad quænam tempora spectat, nisi ad N. Test. tempora? Pro- inde quarto vocis אחרית emphasis usitata hic premenda, non leviter transmittenda est: quod hæc eventura sint באחרית הימים in novissimo, vel in novitate τῶν ἡμερῶν illorum dierum, de quibus va- ticinatus est, vel absolute in novissimis diebus, qui sci- licet finem adferunt Veteri Testamento, ejusque re- spectu novissimi nuncupantur, non autem respectu finis mundi, ut Judæi volunt; Quare recte LXX. In- terpretes exponunt, ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις, Vul- gatus, in novissimis diebus; recte etiam hæc Docto- res Ecclesiæ cum veteres, tum recentiores de tempore Novi Testamenti, quod plenitudo temporis Gal. 4, 4. & tempus novissimum, 1. Joh. 2, 18. Ebr. 1, 1. vocatur, communi consensu interpretantur. A quo ne Cal- vinus quidem hic abeundum censuit, utut alias li- benter Judaizet. Cum finem vel extremitatem die- rum nominat, meminerimus eum de regno Christi lo- qui: atque simul tenenda ratio, cur ita regnum Chri- sti vocet. Nam usque ad illud tempus omnia veluti sus- pensa erant, ne populus oculos defigeret in præsentem rerum statum, qui umbra tantum fuit: sed in Re- demtorem, per quem exhibenda erat veritas. Post- quam ergo advenit Christus, si tempus illud conferatur cum nostro, finis ætatum vere in nos incidit. Qui vero tunc vixerunt Patres, eos oportuit velut proten- sis brachiis ad Christum contendere. Et cum rerum omnium instauratio ab ejus adventu penderet, non immerito huc usq; jubentur spem suam differre. Sem- per quidem illis utile fuit cognoscere perfectiorem sub Christo fore Ecclesiæ statum: præsertim quia sub figuris detinebantur, & interea variis inclinationibus obnoxii erant: quia Dominus consulto ut suspen- sos teneret, variis modis expergefacere eos voluit. Sed hujus vaticinii peculiaris fuit circumstantia: quia per annos quadringentos vel circiter millies exanima- ri poterant, nisi in mentem venisset dierum plenitudo, in qua Ecclesiæ restituenda erat integritas. Ergo pro- ut variis tempestatibus fere subversa fuit Ecclesia, quisque fidelium in suo naufragio vocem hanc instar tabulæ arripuit, quousque in portum enataret. No- tandum interea est, perfectionem dierum ita cœpis- se à Christi adventu, ut continua tamen serie fluant, usque dum rursus appareat in salutem nostram. Ju- dæi ipsi exponunt de novissimis diebus, quorum hæc est Regula in Michlal Jophi: omnis locus in quo dicitur in fine dierum, agit de diebus Messiæ: Conf. Gen. 49, 1. 10. Num. 24, 15. 17. Jer. 23, 6. sed cavillantur, de Messia nostro accipienda non esse: quia ille non venerit in diebus novissimis: quibus respon- sum à B. Tarnovio ad Mich. 4, 2.

Quinto Collatio instituatur eorum, quæ prædi- cta sunt de civitatis & templi devastatione, tum ne- que Glossam Grotii de urbe ab obsidione liberan- da, neque aliam, quæcunque illa sit, exaltationem hic locum habere, apparebit, quam spiritualem in MONTE SION mystico, Novi Testamenti tem- pore factam. Exaltanda quidem etiam Hieroso- lyma tum per præconium Evangelii, tum per mi- racula à Christo patrata; Sed hic mons domus Do- mini non tantum Hierosolyma & montem Sion aut Ecclesiam Judaicam, sed universas Ecclesias per totum orbem complectitur, totam nempe Ca- tholicam Ecclesiam, quæ maxime post devastationem Hierosolymorum, & montis Sion, caput erexit, atque erigere secundum hoc vaticinium debuit; ideóq; de Ecclesia spirituali modo extollenda è Rabbinis ipsis nobiscum locum præsentem interpretatur R. Salomo, nec aliter intellexit Calvinus: cujus ver- ba adscribere placet: Qui vero Sion postquam exci- so templo cum summo dedecore conciderat, tam repen- te surgere potuit? Non est tamen frustra vaticinatus Isaias. Hic enim collis tandem supra omnes montes vere evectus est: quoniam inde audita est vox Domi- ni, ac per totum orbem detonuit, quæ nos in cœlum usq; erigeret, hinc refulsit cœlestis DEI majestas: De- nique quum esset Dei sacrarium, præstanti altitudine totum mundum superavit. Est autem notandus Pro- phetiæ usus: quod scilicet consolationem afferre voluit Isaias, quæ in captivitate populi animos fulciret: ut quamvis nullum extaret templum, nulla sacrificia fierent, diruta jacerent omnia, vigeret tamen spes ista in animis piorum: atque in tanta vastitate, tamque deformibus ruinis hæc animo conciperent. Mons qui- dem Domini desertus est, sed adhuc in ea sedem habe- bit, majorque erit hujus montis gloria, quam cætero- rum omnium. Ne ergo id futurum dubitarent, Pro- pheta ipsis velut tabulam hic depinxit, in qua DEI gloriam intuerentur. Nam etsi mons extabat, fuit ta- men fœda solitudine fere detestabilis, postquam à Deo desertus decorem suum perdiderat. Pios autem non ruinas illas, sed visionem hanc spectare oportebat. Porro cur tam magnifice loquatur de exaltatione montis Sion, satis apparet ex sequentibus: quoniam illinc manavit Evangelium, in quo refulget imago Dei. Montes enim alii poterant altitudine superare: sed quia gloria Dei præeminet, montem etiam in quo patefit eminere necesse est. Montem ergo Sion per se non prædicat, sed cum suo ornatu: quo etiam univer- sus orbis illustrandus erat.

Proinde sexto notanda probe ἐξήγησις Prophe- tæ, qua sublimem illam altitudinem montis Sion explicat, non modo per confluxum gentium ad Eccle- siam, sed etiam per egressum doctrinæ Evangelicæ è Sione in orbem terrarum: quia de Sion exibit lex, & verbum Domini de Jerusalem. Quæ non conve- niunt tempori liberatæ urbis ab obsidione Rasen; sed ad N. Test. tempora spectant. Summa enim gloria montis Sion est, quod doctrina Evangelii ab ipso Christo & Apostolis ejus Hierosolymis pri- mum prædicari debuerit, atque inde propagari & diffundi in totum terrarum orbem, Luc. 24. Nam Sione prodit Lex, non quæ docet offerre externas victimas, aut alias præstare ceremonias; sed תורה תורה doctrina κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν ita dicta, doctrina Evangelii, Ps. 19, 8. Rom. 8, 2. & Verbum Domini prodit Hierosoly- mis, unde emissi sunt in orbem Apostoli, ut non amplius solis Judæis concredita eloquia Domini; sed per totum mundum propagata fuerint, Psal. 147, 19. Rom. 3, 2. cap. 10, 18. Ideo Hieronymus ad h. l. de Jerusalem exiturum verbum explicat, Cur de Ierusalem exiisse dicatur Verbum? tum quod Dominus sæpe in templo docuerit, tum quod fundata primum in Hierusalem Ecclesia totius orbis Ecclesias seminârit. Et observat emphasin vo- cis exibit: Et pulcre non dixit: in Sion, & in Hieru- salem erit, & manebit Verbum, & Lex Domini: sed egredietur, ut de illo fonte omnes nationes doctrina Dei significet irrigandas. Unde manifestum est, sive cum Cyrillo per montem domus Domini intelligas totam Ecclesiam, sive Hieronymo hic præeunte, de monte Sion, in quo ædificata Hierusalem; sensum sibi constare, ac tempora Nov. Testam. designari. Quæ posterior explicatio Brentio etiam probatur, quod Messias ipse in eo docuerit, quod multa ibi ediderit miracula, & quod Apostolis ibi missus in Festo Pentecostes Spiritus S. atque inde Apostoli inceperint ibi divulgare Evangelium. Quid quod glossa Grotii verbis Prophetæ nullatenus conve- niat: Nam exaltari supra omnes montes & colles, & liberari ab obsidione toto cælo differunt: Neque aptari possit parallelo loco, Mich. 4 2. ubi iisdem plane verbis eadem Prophetia repetitur, nec ulla ratione de liberatione ab obsidione per Rasi facta accipi potest: quia nulla ejus obsidionis aut tem- poris ibi mentio. Quanquam neque hoc in loco quicquam de eadem habeatur, sed comminatio & prædictio capitis præcedentis perperam eo traha- tur. Agnoscit ipse Grotius ad Mich. 4, 2. de alio tempore Micheam vaticinari: cujus Prophetiam refert ad tempora post reditum è captivitate Babylo- nica. Et ad Luc. 24, 47. fatetur hic vaticinium haberi de initio præconii Evangelici faciendo tem- pore N. T. in Jerusalein.

Vers. eod. ET FLUENT AD EUM OMNES GEN- TES] Id est, multi ex populis hostibus Syrorum Hieroso- lyma se, ut ad locum tutissimum, conferent, & ibi in atro gentium Deum adorabunt. Cæterum sublimiore sensu hunc locum de Messiæ temporibus etiam Hebræi intelli- gunt. Confer. Dan. 2, 35.

Judaizat iterum Grotius in loco perquam il- lustri. Si enim hoc tam insigne & luculentum ora- culum de vocatione gentium accipiendum non sit, quodnam denique tam clarum erit, de quo indu- bitato certus esse queas, prædici gentium vocatio- nem ad regnum Messiæ? Agitur hic de UNIVER- SALI, non vero de particulari quadam vocatione, aut paucorum quorundam confluxu: Et fluent ad eum OMNES gentes. Quando autem id factum post liberatam ab obsidione Rasi Hierosolymam? Quando non dicam omnes gentes, sed multæ tan- tum, insigni populorum variorum numero, eo confluxêre? Designet tempus, producat historias, nec ex ingenio suo solum ea confingat Grotius. Et quinam illi populi fuêre, quænam gentes? Qua- propter de vocatione gentium ad regnum Messiæ, quam universalem fore etiam alias prædixit Spiri- tus Sanctus, id explicant communi consensu Do- ctores Ecclesiæ: Fluent ad eum omnes gentes. Omnes enim gentes, inquit Hieronymus, servient ei, dictum est: Postula à me, & dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terræ (Psal. 2 ut serviant ei(juxta Sophoniam cap. 3.) sub jugo uno de quibus idem Propheta testatur: Ex finibus fluvio- rum Æthiopiæ afferent tibi hostias: & in 71. Psalm legimus, in conspectu ejus procident Æthiopes. Hiero- nymo consentiunt cæteri omnes. Fluent ad eum montem, hoc est, non venient commoti seu metu aut periculo ad actiones parva manu, sed ultro, mutuo se animantes, & excitantes,cum voluptate ac tripudio fluent, quasi flumen inundans, maxima & innume- rabili multitudine. Porro quonam tempore de Sion exivit Lex & Verbum Domini de Hierusalem? num factum id tempore Rezin, vel liberatæ ac eodem Hierosolymæ? Eo autem tempore ad montem Sion proficiscuntur gentes secundum Esaiam, quo de Zion egreditur verbum Domini, de quo pul- chre Brentius noster: Res ipsa interpretetur, quo- modo gentes dicantur proficisci ad montem Zion. Nam ab eo morte divulgatum est Evangelium in totum or- bem terræ inter omnes gentes. In quocunque igitur loco gentes accipiunt Evangelium Christi, dicuntur profectæ esse ad montem Zion. Sic Cornelius & alii in Cæsarea accesserunt ad montem Zion, cum crede- rent in Christum & acciperent Spiritum Sanctum, etiamsi non fuerunt tunc profecti in Hierusalem. Apage ergo Judaicam glossam de profectione gentium externa ad urbem Hierusalem. Neque tantum adorandi Deum ergo in atrio gentium, sed discendi vias Domini causa profectio illa instituenda.

Dicunt enim, Docebit nos vias suas, & ambulabi- mus in semitis ejus. Quæ de doctrina Evangelii exitura è Sion intelligenda. Ea enim doctrina, quæ de Zion exibit, erit alia doctrina, quam quæ antea exivit de monte Sinai: quam antithesin hic insinuat Propheta. Lex ad paucos pervenit homi- nes; hæc doctrina ad omnes gentes penetrabit. Lex terrebat, ut fugerent ac tremerent, cum eadem promulgaretur: hæc grata erit, & ad quam cum in- signi προθυμίᾳ properabunt. Lex ostendit, non aufert peccata, occidit, non vivificat, damnat, non salvat homines. Hæc autem doctrina aufert pec- cata, vivificat homines, & salvat credentes in Chri- stum. Ulterius, quonam tempore judicavit Dominus gentes & arguit populos multos, ut gladii conflaren- tur in vomeres, nec levaret gens contra gentem gla- dium? Universalis illa tranquillitas nunquam obtigit mundo, nec obtinget unquam. Non ergo de tranquillitate externa intelligenda: sensus enim verborum hoc importat: Omne bellandi studium vertetur ad pacem, & pro discordia erit in toto orbe terrarum concordia. Quod quanquam Hieronymus tempore Augusti impletum censeat, cum omnia bel- la cessarunt, fatetur tamen, milites & legiones Ro- manorum contra barbaras gentes delegatas fuisse: ne- que spiritualem intelligentiam reprobat, quando duritia cordis Christi vomere frangitur, & spiritua- liter eradicantur spinæ vitiorum. Et de spirituali pace ac concordia, quæ apud veros Christi fideles viget, cum Irenæo lib. 4. cap. 67. Tertull. lib. 3. contraMar- cion. cap. 21. Athanasio Orat. de incarnat. Verbi, & Origene contra Cels. lib. 5. explicant ὁμοθυμαδὸν Doctores Ecclesiæ, cujus Symbolum quoddam fuit pax illa totius orbis, sub imperio Augusti, tempore nativitatis Dominicæ. Quum ergo dixerit Pro- pheta, Christum judicaturum gentes & populos, hoc est, dominaturum à mari usque ad mare in toto or- be, Evangelio suo, modum exponit, quo acceptu- rus & conservaturus sit regnum: quod id non fit facturus more mundanorum Monarcharum, qui solent bello occupare, conservare, & proferre re- gnum, sed pacatis & tranquillis; quod Apostoli non sint vulgaturi Evangelium Christi in terris ar- p mato exercitu & potenti manu, sed tranquilla, quantum in ipsis est, prædicatione. Neq; enim melior ratio, quæ B. Lutheri est sententia, tollendæ discordiæ iniri poterit, quam ea est, qua Christus utitur, qui una sententia pariter omnes peccati arguit & damnat. Hoc qui audiunt & credunt, pro quare litigabunt? cum videant se nihilo aliis justiores, sanctiores & sapientiores esse. Facile igitur inter Christianos convenit, qui sentiunt, eadem gratia salvandos omnes, nullum cujusquam præ aliis meritum aut demeritum esse dicitur. Quæ explicatio è simili Prophetia de spirituali pace & civitate in regno Christi, Esa. 11, 6. confirmatur. Habitabit lupus cum agno, &c. Imo ex omnibus vaticiniis, quæ de pace regni Christi agunt, idque omnis discordiæ, omnis metus & belli expers fore prædicant. Grotius ipse lib. de Verit. Relig. Christ. 5. §. 18. hæc de Messiæ temporibus accipienda esse largitur, quoad primum sensum, eaque figurate explicanda: quod etiam observare licet in lib. 1. de jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 2. §. 8. ubi notat, vaticinium hoc aut sub conditione quadam accipiendum esse, si scilicet omnes populi Christi legem suscipiant, atq; impleant, nam si omnes Christiani sint, & Christiane vivant, nulla fore bella, aut intelligendum esse pure, ut implementum ejus, ut & conversio generalis Judæorum, adhuc sit expectandum. Sed aureum ejusmodi seculum cum generali conversione Judæorum temere expectatur in hac fece mundi, eoque tempore, quo fidem defituram & vix inventum iri prædictum est. Neque opus est illa hypothetica, aut Hackspanii hyperbolica locutione, quia nec hypothesis fingenda est, ubi nulla in textu occurrit, & hyperbole non admittenda temere in Scriptura est. Ideoque præstat cum veteribus de spirituali pace intelligere. Judæis autem, qui tempore Messiæ ex hoc & similibus locis fingunt universalem terrenam pacem, merito opponitur Talmudis sententia in Massecheth Berachoth cap. 5. & in Massech. Sanhedr. cap. ult. à Samuele quodam laudata: Non est inter mundum hunc & dies Messiæ differentia, nisi subjectio regnorum: unde Maimonid. ea parabolice accipit, & ad vitam æternam referri putat: quod ratione perfecti & consummati complementi largimur. Sed in regno Messiæ etiam locum habere spiritualiter ejusmodi concordiam, quamvis non eo perfectionis gradu, qui in altera vita erit, hoc loco prophetico luculenter edocemur, & confirmamur.

Jam apostrophe illa ad Judæos: Venite domus Iacob, & ambulemus in lumine Dei, seu gentium sit, uti Rupertus vult, seu Prophetæ, quid aliud sibi vult, quam ne Judæi negligant suscipere Messiam, utpote Domus Iacob, cui promissio ejus imprimis facta; ne in eo gentibus cedant, quin potius cum illis ad Messiam contendant, ut ab eo lumine gratiæ, fidei & salutis illuminentur! Arbitror, inquit Cyrillus, Prophetam in hac exhortatoria oratione, quam adhibet, hortari Israelitas, ut dicenti Christo auscultent; quamdiu lucem habetis, ambulate in luce, ne tenebræ vos comprehendant. Ipse siquidem est lux, &c. Quod quum neglexerint Judæi, hinc prædicit Esaias abjectionem domus Israël, ejusque causas exposuit, uti id v. 6. docebimus. Non ergo tantum secundum sensum sublimiorem ad Messiam pertinet hæc prophetia, sed ad literam de ejusdem regno & gentium vocatione agit, quam secundum literam etiam de Messia explicant (saniores hac in parte Grotio) Judæi nonnulli Rabbi Salomo & alii.

Quæ etiam ideò à Michæa repetita iisdem verbis fuit cap. 4, 2. ut ut occasione diversa, ne dubitaremus, secundum literam & ex intentione Spiritus S. propria ac directa ab Esaia actum esse non de libe- ratione ab obfidione civitatis, aut externa profe- ctione ad montem Sion, sed de exaltatione montis Sion spirituali, & aggregatione gentium ad regnum Messiæ; quam quavis data occasione inculcare haud intermisêre Prophetæ. Verba enim eadem Esaiæ & Michæ absque ςρεβλότητι insigni non pos- sunt diversis temporibus, rebus ac conditionibus applicari, quum nimis manifestum sit, utrumque eodem Spiritu agitatum, rem eandem, verbis iis- dem prædicere ac N. T. est. tempora respicere. Lo- cus etiam ille, quem confert Grotius, Dan. II. 35. quid aliud, quam regnum Christi infert? Lapis il- le, qui factus dicitur mons magnus, & implevit uni- versam terram, de Christo regno suo universam ter- ram implente, sine dubio intelligendus est. Si ergo hic mons apud Esaiam eodem sensu accipi debeat, quid certius, quam quod regnum Christi per to- tum orbem diffundendum designetur, secundum propriam & literalem vaticinii sententiam!

## 2:6
Vers. 6. FOR THOU HAST CAST AWAY THY PEOPLE]

That is, thou hadst cast away, thou hadst permitted him to be pressed by a hard siege. A gloss too jejune, and alien to the text! The discourse is not about a past event, much less about the siege of Rezin, which is by no means to be considered as the casting away of the people; because the city was delivered from that siege: but the Prophet is prophesying about the future casting away, or rejection, of the Jewish people. For the words are clear, FOR THOU HAST CAST AWAY thy people, the House of Jacob. The verb נטש means he left, he repelled by casting away. Therefore Cyril connects these things to the preceding thus: If therefore, he says, you do not desire to walk with him in the light of the Lord, that is, if you reject the preaching of Christ and utterly and entirely turn away from his illumination, he himself also will dismiss his people. And the most grave causes of the rejected people are added; namely, that they have been filled more than the Orientals with Magical arts, the Chaldeans for instance: מקדם From the east, or with oriental things. Thus also Pagninus and Arias Montanus: (Or FROM THE EAST, as the Genevan, Piscator, and the English, as if they had been taught by the Orientals,) and they practice magic, like the impious nations of the Philistines, and abound in strange children (Christ being neglected and rejected, and they, as degenerate children, adhering to seducers, impious and blasphemous Teachers, instead of the Patriarchs) and his (the people's) land is filled with horses and his chariots are innumerable, that is, as Osiander again rightly says: the Jewish nation is not devoted to true piety, nor does it study the saving knowledge of God, but they have minds inflamed with the desire of warring and obtaining glory by arms, such as Josephus the Historian clearly testifies the Jews were around the times of the incarnation of the Son of God. And his land is filled with idols: they have worshipped the work of their own hands. These, therefore, are the causes of the rejected Jewish people, the study of Magical arts, the acceptance of false doctrines, avarice, ambition, and pride, as well as idolatry: concerning which see more at length B. Brentius on this passage. Whence the Prophet concludes: And thou wilt not forgive them these sins: thou wilt leave them in their infidelity and impiety, and wilt utterly cast them away: which things certainly look to the final rejection.

Vers. same. AND THEY HAVE ADHERED TO STRANGE CHILDREN]

Because the Assyrian customs pleased them, they shall be delivered to the Assyrians. But some Hebrews understand by strange children the doctrines and institutions of the nations.

The Hebrews rightly understand those imbued with the doctrines of the nations: for they are not genuine children of the Church who adhere to or applaud strange Teachers. Therefore, not only the Assyrians and their customs are designated, but any strangers to whom they themselves, having abandoned the Messiah, the true and only Teacher, have adhered, and also the institutions of the nations.

that gloss does not fit, that they are to be delivered to the Assyrians, with the prior comment about the siege of Rezin, King of Syria, from which the people were being delivered. B. Luther beautifully: they make many strange children: And in the marginal gloss: These are children of false doctrine and idolatry, who have more unbelief than the nations of the East. The Genevan, Italian, English, Piscator, and Liosveld. The Hebrew: וּבְיַלְדֵי נָכְרִים יַשְׂפִּיקוּ they render, and he is delighted with the children of strangers: Because they are delighted with them, therefore they cause their number to be increased. Which some also think was done by marriages entered into with strangers against the law of God, Deut. 7, 1. 2. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 6. PROJECISTI ENIM POPVLVM TVVM]

Id est, projeceras, permiseras dura obsidione eum premi. Glossa nimis jejuna, & à textu aliena! Non de re præterita, nedum de obsidione Rezin sermo est, quæ nequaquam pro populi projectione ha- benda; quia ab illa obsidione liberata est civitas: sed de futura projectione, vel reprobatione popu- li Judaici vaticinatur Propheta. Verba enim lucu- lenta sunt, PROJECISTI enim populum tuum, Do- mum Jacob. Verbum נטש reliquit, abjiciendo repulit. Ideo hæc ita præcedentibus nectit Cyrillus: Si non igitur, inquit, una vobiscum desideratis in luce Domini ambulare, id est, si Christi prædicationem rejicitis & illustrationem ejus aversamini prorsus penitusque, & ipse populum suum dimittet. Et adduntur causæ reprobati populi gravissimæ; utpote quod repleti sint magis, quam Orientales artibus Magicis, Chaldæos puta: מקדם Præ oriente, vel orientalibus. Sic etiam Pagninus, & Ariamonta- nus: (Vel EX ORIENTE, uti Genevens. Piscator, Anglus, quasi ab Orientalibus edocti fuerint, ) & magiam exerceant, ut impiæ gentes Philistium, & abundent alienis filiis (Christo neglecto, & abje- cto, ac Patriarchis tanquam degeneres filii adhæ- reant seductoribus, impiis & blasphemis Doctori- bus) & repleta sit terra ejus (populi) equis & innume- rabiles quadrigæ ejus, id est, ut recte iterum Osian- der: gens Judaica non dedita est veræ pietati, nec studet salutari Dei agnitioni, sed habent animos accensos cupiditate bellandi & gloriam armis pa- randi, quales Judæos fuisse circa tempora incarna- tionis Filii Dei, Josephus Historicus luculenter te- statur. Et repleta est terra ejus idolis: opus manuum suarum adoraverunt. Hæc ergo causæ sunt re- probati Judaici populi, studium artium Magica- rum, falsarum doctrinarum susceptio, avaritia, am- bitio & superbia, nec non idololatria: de quibus videatur prolixius B. Brentius in hunc locum. Un- de concludit Propheta: Et non dimittes eis hæc sce- lera: relinques eos in sua infidelitate & impieta- te, ac penitus projicies eosdem: quæ utique fina- lem reprobationem spectant.

Vers. eod. ET PVERIS ALIENIS ADHÆSERVNT]

Quia placuerunt illis mores Assyrii, tradentur Assyriis. At Hebræi quidam per natos alienos intelligunt doctrinas & instituta gentium.

Recte Ebræi doctrinis gentium imbutos intelli- gunt: illi enim non sunt genuini Ecclesiæ filii, qui alienis adhærent vel applaudunt Doctoribus. Non ergo tantum Assyrii, eorumque mores, sed quivis alieni, quibus ipsi, relicto Messia, vero & unico Doctore, adhæserunt, designantur, neque & instituta gentium.

convenit glossa illa, quod tradendi sint Assyriis, priori commento de obsidione Resinis Regis Sy- riæ, à qua liberabatur populus. B. Lutherus pul- chre; machen der frembden Kinder viel: Et in glof- sa marginali: Das sind Kinder der falschen Lehre und Abgötterey, die mehr Mißglaubens haben denn die Heyden gegen Morgen. Genevens. Ital. An- glicus, Piscator & Liosveld. Ebræa: וּבְיַלְדֵי נָכְרִים יַשְׂפִּיקוּ reddunt, & delectatus liberis alienorum: Quia illis delectantur, ideo faciunt ut numerus eo- rum augeatur. Quod nonnulli etiam factum pu- tant connubiis initis cum alienis adversus legem Dei, Deut. 7, 1. 2. 3.

## 2:7
Ver. 7. THEIR LAND IS FILLED WITH SILVER AND GOLD, AND THERE IS NO END TO THEIR TREASURES: AND THEIR LAND IS FILLED WITH HORSES, AND THEIR CHARIOTS ARE INNUMERABLE: AND THEIR LAND IS FILLED WITH IDOLS] From riches comes luxury: from luxury, contempt of the law. Compare Deut. 32:15, 16. And the law had expressly forbidden the King to have treasures and hosts of horses, as a matter of foresight.

Nowhere did this law forbid these things: nor are riches condemned here, but the pursuit and excessive desire for money, neglecting the care of the kingdom of God. Not the multitude of horses and chariots, but the desire for war, and the pride and confidence in horses and chariots. Compare Brentius on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 7. REPLETA EST TERRA ARGENTO ET AURO, ET NON EST FINIS THESAVRORUM E- JUS: ET REPLETA EST TERRA EJUS EQUIS, ET INNUMERABILES QUADRIGÆ EJUS: ET RE- PLETA EST TERRA EJUS IDOLIS] Ex divitiis luxus: ex luxu comtemtus legis. Confer Deut. 32, 15. 16. Et thesauros habere, & equorum agmina, lex provida disferte Regi interdixerat.

Nuspiam hæc lex interdixit: neque hic impro- bantur divitiæ, sed aucupia & nimia studia pecu- niæ relicta cura regni Dei. Non equorum & qua- drigarum multitudo, sed studium belli, & fastus ac confidentia in equis & quadrigis. Confer. Bren- tius in h. l.

## 2:11
Ver. 11. BUT THE LORD ALONE SHALL BE EXALTED IN THAT DAY: FOR THE DAY OF THE LORD OF HOSTS IS UPON EVERY ONE THAT IS PROUD AND LOFTY] He returns to the times of the liberated city: at which time many Jews, having been most grievously vexed by idolaters, but liberated by God, were weary of the worship rendered to idols.

This is not about the time of the liberated city, nor does history testify that the people became better at that time. And what is predicted here is far greater and more illustrious than that many, having been most grievously afflicted by idolatry, should desist from it. For the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day: indeed, it is even added: And the idols shall be utterly destroyed. Which speak of the total abolition of idols. Therefore, these things pertain to the Church, or the communion of the faithful; in which the Lord Messiah Jehovah alone, our righteousness, is exalted, and all idols have been abolished. And this refers to the times of the New Testament, so that the prophecy may be continued, which Lucas Osiander, along with Brentius, has rightly observed. For from that time, when the city of Jerusalem was finally laid waste, the Jews have offered no more sacrifice; and thus their impious religion, full of hypocrisy, which was truly idolatrous worship, was abolished along with the gross idolatry of the Gentiles.

Latin:

Vers. 11. EXALTABITUR AUTEM DOMINUS SOLIUS IN DIE ILLA: QUIA DIES DOMINI EX- ERCITUVM SVPER OMNEM SVPERBVM ET EX- CELSVM] Redit ad tempora liberatæ urbis: quo tempo- re multos Judæos ab idololatris pessime vexatos, à Deo autem liberatos tæderet cultus præstiti idolis.

Non hic de tempore urbis liberatæ, neque tum meliorem evasisse populum historia testatur. Et longe amplius atque illustrius est, quod hic prædicitur, quam quod multi ab idololatria pessi- me afflicti destiterint. Solus enim Dominus exal- tabitur in die illa: imo additur etiam: Et idola penitus comburentur. Quæ de totali idolorum a- bolitione loquuntur. Proinde ad Ecclesiam hæc pertinent, vel fidelium communionem; in qua so- lus Dominus Messias Iehovah justitia nostra exalta- tus,& idola omnia abolita sunt. Et respicitur hic ad tempora Novi Testamenti, ut continuetur vatici- nium, quod probe observavit cum Brentio Lucas Osiander. Ab eo enim tempore, quo urbs Hie- rusalem postremo est vastata, nullum amplius sa- crificium Judæi obtulerunt; adeoque impia ipso- rum religio plena hypocriseos, quæ vere cultus i- dololatricus erat, una cum gentium crassa idolo- latria abolita est.

## 2:13
Ver. 13. UPON ALL THE CEDARS OF LEBANON.] The King and Princes of Syria. UPON ALL THE OAKS OF BASHAN.] That is, upon the King and Princes of Israel. Ver. 16. UPON ALL THE SHIPS OF TARSHISH.] Upon Tyre, which was allied with the Syrians at that time.

The day of vengeance is not described here as being upon the Syrians, the Israelites, or Tyre, but upon the Jews. For he had threatened the casting away of these, and had described their impiety and sins; whence he subjoins: Enter therefore (O perverse and hardened nation of the Jews) into the rock, and hide in the dust from the face of the fear of the Lord, and from the glory of his Majesty, that is, as Osiander rightly paraphrases: The Jews, out of desperation in the greatest straits, will desire to hide themselves in the caverns of the earth and rocks, because of the tremendous Majesty of God, avenging their impiety. The Jews felt this trembling when God, in the times of Titus Vespasian, revealed His wrath toward them. Concerning which anxiety Christ predicted to the Jews: Then, he says, they will begin to say to the mountains, fall upon us, and the hills, cover us, Luke 23. But all the ungodly will perfectly feel incredible anguish and despair when on the last day they will see the Son of Man coming in His majesty to judge the living and the dead. Whence these things of the συνεχείας Propheticæ are to be understood not of the Syrians or Israelites or Tyre, but of the Jews themselves. The lofty eyes, says the Prophet, of man shall be humbled and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day. Then CHRIST sitting at the right hand of GOD will humble the pride of the Jewish people (for these He calls men) and will depress the haughtiness of the nobles (these He calls men) among the Jewish people; so that the whole nation is to fall into extreme destruction; but the majesty of CHRIST will be celebrated through the preaching of the Gospel, and will stand out alone, the hypocritical religion of the Jews being prostrated. For the day of the vengeance of the Lord of hosts shall come upon EVERY proud and lofty one, and upon every arrogant one, and he shall be humbled and confounded, whoever had previously borne a lofty spirit in that nation, and had been proud in the opinion of wisdom, justice, or power and strength. For the time of divine vengeance shall come upon all the lofty and erect cedar trees of Mount Lebanon, and upon all the most powerful oaks of the region of Bashan, that is, whatever is eminent and proud in this people, and seems powerful, that the Lord will prostrate and cast down. And upon all the high mountains, and upon all the lifted-up hills: that is, even those places in which they had the exercises of their religion (especially indeed the Jerusalem temple, placed upon Mount Zion) will be utterly laid waste (for the Prophet uses the words and phrases of his own age: because then the Jews were accustomed to sacrifice upon mountains and hills against the express word.) He signifies therefore that the religion of the Jews is about to collapse. And upon every high tower, and upon every fortified wall: that is, their fortified citadels and towns will be cast down. (For no fortifications can resist the divine wrath.) And upon all the ships of Tarshish, more correctly, of the sea (that is, the Lord will overturn their entire trade, and will take away and scatter their profits.) And upon everything that is beautiful to behold: that is, whatever they have even adorned for themselves, and prepared for pleasures, all will be laid waste, corrupted, and plundered. Whoever has read the historian Josephus concerning the destruction of the region of Judea and the city of Jerusalem will confess that the Prophet has vividly depicted the matter in a few words. Osiander explained these things best of all others. B. Brentius agrees with him: he judges that by the cedars of Lebanon the temple built from cedars is meant; and because the Jews sacrificed under oaks and on mountains, he thinks that by cedars, oaks, and mountains are understood the Sacred rites, which were either divinely established in the temple, or humanly devised in other places. The Gospel of Christ therefore abolished all the illustrious Sacred rites of the Jews; because it is openly revealed through the Gospel that no sacred rites, however excellent, justify a man by the merit of his action; but that one only attains justice on account of Christ through faith. For the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. The justice of Christ alone will be illustrated through the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SVPER OMNES CEDROS LIBANI.] Re- gem & Principes Syriæ. SVPER OMNES QVERCVS BASAN.] Id est, su- per Regem & Principes Israelis. Vers. 16. SVPER OMNES NAVES THARSIS.] Su- per Tyrum, quæ Syris fœderata eo tempore.

Dies vindictæ non super Syros Israëlitas, aut Tyrum, sed super Judæos hic describitur. Nam ho- rum projectionem comminatus erat, horum im- pietatem ac peccata descripserat; unde subjungit; Ingredere igitur (o perversa & indurata Judæorum gens) in petram, & abscondere fossa à facie timoris Domini, & à gloria Majestatis ejus, id est, uti recte παραφράζει Osiander: Judæi præ desperatione in summis angustiis cupient se abscondere in caver- nis terræ & petrarum, propter tremendam Maje- statem Dei, ulciscentis ipsorum impietatem. Hanc trepidationem senserunt Judæi, cum Deus tem- poribus Titi Vespasiani iram suam erga eos reve- laret. De qua anxietate prædixit Christus Judæis: Tunc incipient, inquit, dicere montibus, cadite su- per nos, & collibus, operite nos, Luc. 23. Sentient autem perfecte omnes impii incredibilem angu- stiam, & desperationem, cum in novissimo die videbunt filium hominis venientem in sua maje- state ad judicandum vivos ac mortuos. Unde non de Syris aut Israëlitis aut Tyro, sed de Judæis ipsis hæc vi συνεχείας Propheticæ accipienda. O- culi sublimes, inquit Propheta, hominis humilia- buntur & incurvabitur altitudo virorum: exaltabi- tur autem DOMINUS solus in die illa. Tunc CHRISTUS sedens ad dexteram DEI humiliabit superbiam Judaicæ plebis (hos enim homines vo- cat) & deprimet fastum optimatum (hos viros ap- pellat) in populo Judaico; ita ut in extremum ex- itium tota gens sit ruitura; CHRISTI vero ma- jestas celebrabitur per Evangelii prædicationem, & eminebit sola, prostrata religione Judæorum hypocritica. Quia dies vindictæ Domini Deiex- ercituum super OMNEM superbum & excelsum, & super omnem arrogantem veniet & humilia- bitur atque confundetur, quicunque gesserat sub- limes spiritus in ea gente, & opinione sapientiæ, justitiæ aut potentiæ ac fortitudinis antea super- bierat. Etenim veniet tempus vindictæ divinæ super omnes arbores cedros montis Libani sublimes & ere- ctas, & super omnes validissimas quercus regionis Basan, id est, quicquid in hoc populo eminet & superbit, validumque videtur, id prosternet atque dejiciet Dominus. Et super omnes montes excelsos, & super omnes colles elevatos: id est, loca etiam illa, in quibus habuerunt suæ religionis exercitia (præsertim vero templum Hierosoly- mitanum, monti Sion impositum) penitus vasta- buntur (Propheta enim utitur sui seculi vocabulis & phrasibus: quia tunc solebant Judæi super mon- tes & colles contra expressum verbum sacrificare.) Significat igitur religionem Judæorum corruitu- ram. Et super omnem turrim excelsam, & super omnem murum munitum: id est, dejicientur eo- rum munitæ arces & oppida. (Nullæ enim mu- nitiones iræ divinæ resistere queunt.) Et super o- mnes naves Tharsis, rectius, maris (id est, totam i- psorum negotiationem Dominus evertet, & pro- ventus eorum auferet atque disperget.) Et super o- mne, quod visu pulchrum est: id est, quicquid et- iam sibi adornarunt, & ad voluptates parârunt, to- tum vastabitur, corrumpetur, diripietur. Qui Jo- sephum historicum legerit de regionis Judææ & urbis Hierosolymorum excidio, fatebitur, Pro- phetam rem luculenter paucis verbis depinxisse. Hæc omnia optime Osiander præ aliis exposuit. Cui consonat B. Brentius: Cedris Libani templum è Cedris extructum respici; & quia sub quercubus & in montibus sacrificarunt Judæi, ideo per cedros, quer- cus & montes Sacra intelligi censet, quæ vel in tem- emplo fuerunt divinitus constituta, vel in aliis locis humanitus excogitata. Evangelium igitur Christi abolevit omnia illustria Judæorum Sacra; quia per Evangelium palam revelatur, nulla sacra, quan- tumvis præclara, justificare hominem merito suæ actionis; sed justitiam tantum contingere propter Christum per fidem. Dominus enim solus exal- tabitur in die illa. Sola justitia Christi illustrabitur per Evangelium.

## 2:21
Vers. 21. MOLES] The interpreter here reads as one word, חפרפרות, as does also Aben Ezra, who himself also understands moles. There is almost no kind of living creature that has not been worshipped as a Deity in some part of Egypt.

Not a various reading here, but a different interpretation. For some understand pits by פריורי, others, explaining two words joined together concerning one thing, think that by לחפור פירורי is understood a (bird) piercing fruits or a mole digging up the earth. See Buxtorff in Vindic. ver. Ebr. p. 841.

Latin:

Vers. 21. TALPAS] Legit hic interpres una voce, חפרפרות, ut & Aben Ezra, qui & ipse talpas intelli- git. Nullum ferme est animantis genus, quod non in a- liqua parte Ægypti sit cultum pro Numine.

Non hic varia lectio, sed diversa interpretatio. Nam nonnulli per פריורי foveas intelligunt, alii voces duas conjunctim de una re explicantes per לחפור פירורי fructus perforantem (avem) vel terram suffodientem talpam intelligi putant. Vid. Buxtorff. in Vindic. ver. Ebr. p. 841.

## 2:22
Vers. 22. CEASE YE THEREFORE FROM MAN.] Do not place trust in any of men.

WHOSE BREATH IS IN HIS NOSTRILS.] His life depends on the air, which being cut off, he will perish.

FOR HE IS ACCOUNTED AS HIGH.] In the Hebrew: for how little is he to be esteemed?

This is the explanation of Calvin, and his followers, Tremellius, Junius, the Genevan Interpreter, and others. But they depart without cause from the interpretation of the pious Ancients, who accept these things concerning Christ. Origen, in the presence of Jerome at this passage, explained it thus: Because it is said singularly of one man, it can be referred to the Lord Savior, the Prophet commanding that they cease from Him, who is accounted as something great, although for the present He appears as a man, and has breath in His nostrils, just as other men also breathe. Which sense Jerome also defends against the Jews, explaining it in almost the same way as Calvin. For what, he says, is the sequence of words, and what is the order of the discourse in relation to the senses, that we should say: Since these things are so and the day of the Lord is to come, in which the entire state of Judea is to be overturned, and all things are to be crushed; I warn and command you to cease from man, who so breathes and lives as we men do, because he is to be reckoned as nothing. Would any man praise someone in such a way as to say: beware, lest you offend him, who is absolutely nothing! These things he says against the Jews, who are thus far sounder than Calvin and Grotius, in that they understood, as Jerome notes, that the prophecy is about CHRIST, even though they confessed to corrupting the same. B. Luther, and most of our own people, explain it with the ancient Doctors concerning the Messiah, even though they understand the words: Whose breath is in his nostrils: not of fragility, but of his anger against the impious: Cease, he has breath in his nostrils, that is, says B. Luther, he is powerful in anger. Thus Luke says of Paul, αναπνέων την οργήν, breathing out anger. This is a periphrasis for grave anger, says Brentius: For when men are angry, they exhale a heavier breath through their nostrils than when they are of a tranquil mind. It is written of Paul still raging against the Church: Paul breathing out threats; and of a horse provoked to anger Job says (Chap. 39, 19.) The glory of his nostrils is terror. And so to have breath in his nostrils in this place is to be severe and angry. Compare Jud. 8, 3. Psal. 2, 12.

That I prefer this explanation to that of Calvin and Grotius, these things persuade, because the Prophet had predicted that they would enter into (1) the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones from the face of the fear of the LORD, and from the glory of his majesty, when he shall have arisen to strike the earth. Which is to be understood of CHRIST, to whom all judgment is given, who alone is to be exalted in that day or time, from whose face and anger the impious will also wish to be hidden in the day of universal judgment, Apocalyp. 6. verse 17. From him, therefore, he warns that we must now cease and desist, since his anger is most vehement and intolerable; whom the Jews will indeed consider merely a naked man, but they ought to have known how exalted he himself is reckoned. Therefore, by the man whose breath is in his nostrils, and who is reckoned so exalted, the same is to be understood, whose face will be so formidable, and whose judgment in striking the earth will be so terrible. (2.) Because that admonition, appended in the place of an epiphonema, does not cohere with the preceding prophecy, if it is accepted in the sense of Calvin or Grotius. Whence Calvin and his followers find it necessary to tear apart the text, and to transfer this last verse to the following Chapter, by which they might introduce some connection, as in Calvi nium and Junium can be seen. But it is to do violence to the sacred text, and not to draw out the meaning, but to bring it in. For it is manifest from the Hebrew Codices and ancient translations that these words are the conclusion of the second, not the beginning of the third chapter.

(3.) Because this exhortation coheres and agrees perfectly with the whole prophecy of the second chapter, and its immediate words. Which Jerome already shows: Therefore, on the contrary, it is to be understood here: since all these things are about to come to you, and are predicted by a prophetic spirit; I warn and command that you desist from him who is indeed a man according to the flesh, and has a soul, and thus breathes, and draws breath through his nostrils, as we men breathe and live, but according to the divine majesty he is, and is reputed, and is believed to be exalted.

(4.) Nor should it be neglected that Origen observes that the discourse here is singularly about one man, whom the Prophet demonstrates δεικτικῶς (demonstratively) with the prefixed He Hajediah, to indicate that it is about a certain subject, and indeed about him concerning whom it has been treated thus far.

(5.) Jerome urges the word בַּמֶּה, which among the Hebrews is not 'exalted,' but 'in what,' that is, or the height and sublimity itself. But because that word has other points placed under it, it is more correctly rendered by Aquila, 'in whom he is reputed': for בַּמֶּה is 'in what.'
