Yet the meaning results in the same thing: because that interrogation is not to be understood in a diminishing sense, but in an eminent one. For that man (הָאָדָם) is exalted, from whom the Jews are ordered to abstain, and the fear of his wrath is proposed. And the verb נֶחְשָׁב brings in an estimation, but not a deprecation of the thing. Therefore Osiander rightly: 'For how much is he to be estimated?' that is, truly that man JESUS CHRIST is inestimable, to whom no one in this world is to be compared. And as to the sense, Blessed Luther is excellent: 'For you do not know how highly He is esteemed.' Concerning the excellence of this man, see the parallel passage 2 Sam. 7:19, 1 Chron. 17:13.

(6.) The verb חִדְלוּ is 'cease,' 'desist'; nor is it found anywhere in the sense of Grotius for 'placing trust in him,' much less in this construction חִדְלוּ לָכֶם 'cease for yourselves from man,' which does not bring in a cessation from the placing of trust in man, about which nothing is held in the whole chapter; but from the provocation of that man, in whose nostrils is breath. Where, I ask, is 'to desist from man' [the same as] 'not to depend on man,' 'not to place trust in man'? Therefore, this sense, newly invented by Calvin without example from Scripture, is in vain. The Hebrews themselves understood the sense to be, 'I warn you to cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils.' Mr. D. Varenius in Commentary on 12 Chapters of Isaiah, p. 81. The verb, he says, חָדַל, constructed personally with the intervention of a pronominal idiom and the particle מֵ or מִן, always signifies the abstention of an inferior from an inferior by provoking, by provoking to vengeance, never by trusting, or fearing, or harassing an inferior. Cf. 2 Chron. 25:6, and more so 35:21. For here there is clearly a parallelism. These are the words of him who discusses this passage at length in the same place, and refutes the interpretations of others.

(7.) We can also urge the connection (συνέχειαν) of the following chapter with Basil, Cyril, and Jerome, which he proposes here thus: And the order is: because you did not want to cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils, who is reputed exalted, but on the contrary you shed the blood of the just, and thought an evil counsel, saying, 'Let us bind the just, because he is useless to us.' Therefore you shall eat the fruit of your inventions. Nothing is strong among the Jews after the passion of the Lord, nothing is valid, but all things are weak and languid, etc. For after the killing of him, as Jerome had said before, all graces and gifts were taken away from the Jews. Which order Blessed Luther also insinuates: In the previous chapter he describes the power of the kingdom of Christ, now he threatens desolation to the Jews, who were not going to receive Christ. (8.) B. Gesnerus observes that that same man is the Lord of hosts himself, because it is immediately subjoined in Chapter 3:1. 'For behold, the Lord, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem,' etc. From him, therefore, they are ordered to cease, whose most grave judgment the following chapter describes. That Isaiah (says our interpreter) does not speak about any mortal man, the coherence of the text argues; since he wishes to exhort the hearers to repentance and the recognition of Christ with four arguments, because, namely, Christ is about to utterly destroy his contemners, to subject the proud to himself, to devastate idols, and finally to afflict the unfaithful with eternal punishments. To these reasons follows the conclusion, that they should not contemn, but embrace and venerate the Messiah, even though he is a man, since that same man is the Lord, the Lord of hosts, as the unbroken connection of the first verse of the following chapter shows. Add to these the authority and consensus of the Interpreters, along with the ancients Origen and Jerome, who calls this a clear prophecy about Christ; then from the more recent Orthodox, and also most of the Papists, Sanctius, Delrio, Cornelius à Lapide, Luisius, Menochius, Tirinus, and others, who likewise interpret it concerning Christ. To Calvin and his associates we oppose Oecolampadius, who sides with us here, and rejects the opinion of Calvin and Grotius regarding the Jews. We shall transcribe his words, because they illustrate the passage and the coherence with the following chapter. Before he narrates their punishment to the Jews, he warns them again, lest they stumble on the stone of offense, contemning the humility, and thus also the death of Christ, than whom no one humbled himself more, who says: 'I am a worm and not a man.' To whom there is breath in his nostrils: that is, who is humble, and fragile, and such a one as seems about to expire at any moment, and thus of no reputation, so that you say: 'In what is he reputed?' For truly he is a hidden God. And they are rightly warned about this also. For after the return from Babylon there were no idols among the Jews, as was said before. Therefore they are warned, lest they be offended in Christ, who seemed humble to them: for because of this sin judgment hung over them, and the blood was required of them. But what if you explain, breath in his nostrils? Just as אף signifies wrath, and nostrils, as in the Psalms: And smoke went up in his wrath. And let the sense be. See that while you offend a man, who seems despised to you, you do not exasperate the judge of the world, in whose hands is the winnowing fan. The Jews explain, that hope should not be had in any man, because he is fragile, just as Jer. also says: Cursed is he who puts flesh as his arm. And the Psalmist: Do not trust in princes, in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. Which sentiment is indeed pious, but it passes over the mystery. This is Oecolampadius.

Latin:

Vers. 22. QVIESCITE ERGO AB HOMINE.] No- lite fiduciam in ullo hominum ponere.

CVJVS SPIRITVS IN NARIBVS EJVS EST.] Vi- ta ejus ab aëre pendet, quo intercluso peribit.

QVIA EXCELSVS REPVTATVS EST IPSE.] In Hebreo: quantilli enim ipse faciendus est?

Explicatio Calvini est, & asseclarum, Tremellii, Junii, Interpret. Genevensis, & aliorum. Sed dif- cedunt illi sine causa a piorum Veterum interpre- tatione, qui haec de Christo accipiunt. Origenes apud Hieronymum ad h. l. ita exposuit: Quia singulari- ter de uno homine dicitur, referri potest ad Dominum Salvatorem jubente Propheta, ut quiescant ab eo, qui in magno aliquo reputatus, licet impreesentiarum vi- deatur ut homo, & spiramen habere in naribus, sicut & caeteri spirant homines. Quem sensum propugnat etiam Hieronymus adversus Judaeos, eodem fere modo, cum Calvino explicantes. Quae est enim, in- quit, verborum consequentia, & qui ordo orationis ad sensus, ut dicamus: Cum haec ita se habeant & dies ventura sit Domini, in qua universus Judaea sta- tus subvertendus est, & omnia conterenda; moneo vos atque praecipio, ut quiescatis ab homine, qui ita spirat & vivit, ut nos homines, quia in nihili compu- tandus est. Quisquamne hominum ita quempiam laudet, ut dicat: cavete, ne offendatis eum, quio- mnino nihil est! Haec ille contra Judaeos, qui ha- ctenus Calvino & Grotio saniores sunt, quod in- tellexerint, notante Hieronymo, Prophetiam esse de CHRISTO, etsi eandem corrumpere fatege- rint. B. Lutherus, & Nostrates plerique omnes. cum antiquis Doctoribus de Messia explicant, etsi verba: Cujus spiritus in naribus ejus: non de fragi- litate, sed de ira ejus adversus impios intelligant: Quiescite, habet spiritum in naribus, id est, inquit B. Lutherus, est potens in ira. Sic Lucas de Paulo in- quit, αναπνέων την οργήν, spirans iram. Haec est pe- riphrasis gravis irae, ait Brentius: Homines enim cum irascuntur, efflant per nares graviorem spiri- tum, quam cum sunt tranquillo animo. De Paulo adhuc grassante in Ecclesiam scriptum est: Paulus spirans minas; & de equo ad iracundiam provocato dicit Job (Cap. 39, 19.) Gloria narium ejus terror. I- taque Spiritum in naribus habere hoc loco est, seve- rum & iratum esse. Confer. Jud. 8, 3. Psal. 2, 12.

Ut praeferam hanc explicationem Calvinianae & Grotii, haec suadent, quia praedixerat Prophe- ta fore, ut vel in (1) fissuras petrarum & cavernas saxorum a facie formidinis DOMINI, & a glo- ria majestatis ejus ingrederentur, cum surrexe- rit percutere terram. Quod de CHRISTO, cui omne datum judicium, qui solus exaltandus in die vel tempore illo, accipiendum, a cujus etiam facie atque ira abscondi optabunt impii in die pantocritico, Apocalyp. 6. vers. 17. Ab illo ergo quiescendum esse ac desistendum nunc monet, quum ira ejus vehementissima sit, & intolera bi- lis; quem nudum tantum hominem habituri qui- dem sunt Judaei, sed scire debebant, quam ex- celsus ipse reputatus sit. Per hominem ergo, cu- jus spiritus in naribus ejus, & qui tam ex- celsus reputatus est, idem intelligendus, cujus facies tam formidabilis, & judicium in terra per- cutienda tam terribile erit. (2.) Quia admoni- tio illa, Epiphonematis loco subjuncta, non co- haeret cum praecedente vaticinio, si Calvini aut Grotii sensu accipiatur. Unde Calvinus & asse- clae necessum habent discerpere textum, & ver- sum hunc ultimum transferre ad sequens Caput, quo aliquam συνέχειαν inducant, ut apud Calvi- nium & Junium videre est. Quod vero est vim inferre textui sacro, & sensum non educere, sed inducere. Manifestum enim est ex Ebræis Codici- bus & translationibus antiquis, hæc verba esse conclusionem secundi, non initium tertii capi- tis.

(3.) Quia cohæret & optime congruit hæc parænesis cum toto vaticinio secundi capitis, & proximis ejus verbis. Quod ostendit jam Hie- ronymus: Ergo è contrario hic intelligendum: cum hæc universa ventura sint vobis, & prophetali spi- ritu prædicantur; moneo atque præcipio, ut quie- scatis ab eo, qui secundum carnem quidem homo est, & habet animam, & ita spirat, & naribus halitum trahit, ut nos homines spiramus & vivi- mus, sed secundum divinam majestatem excelsus & est, & reputatur, & creditur.

(4.) Neque negligendum, quòd Origenes observat, singula- riter de uno homine hic sermonem esse, quem Propheta δεικτικῶς demonstrat præfixo He Haje- diah, ut de certo subjecto agi, & de eo qui- dem, quo de hactenus actum, indicaret.

(5.) Hieronymus urget vocem בַּמֶּה quæ apud E- bræos non excelsus, sed excelsum, hoc est, vel ipsa altitudo atque sublimitas. Sed quia vox illa alia puncta substrata habet, rectius redditur ab Aquila, in quo reputatus est ipse: nam בַּמֶּה est in quo. Sententia tamen eadem redundat: quia non intelligenda interrogatio illa sensu imminuen- te, sed eminenti. Nam extollitur הָאָדָם homo ille, à quo abstinere jubentur Judæi, ac metuen- da ira ejus proponitur. Et verbum נֶחְשָׁב æ- stimationem, non vero deprecationem rei in- fert. Ideo recte Osiander: Quanti enim æsti- mandus est? id est, profecto inæstimabilis est ho- mo ille JESUS CHRISTUS, cui nemo in hoc mundo est comparandus. Et ad sensum optime Beatus Lutherus: Denn ihr wisset nicht, wie hoch Er geachtet ist. De excellentia hujus ho- minis vid. locus parallelus 2. Sam. 7, 19. 1. Chron. 17, 13.

(6.) Verbum חִדְלוּ est quiescite, de- sinite; neque sensu Grotii pro fiduciam in illo po- nere uspiam reperitur, nedum in hac constructio- ne חִדְלוּ לָכֶם cessate vobis ab homine, quæ non cessationem à collocatione fiduciæ in homine, de qua in toto capite nihil habetur; sed ab irritatio- ne hominis istius, in cujus naribus spiritus est, in- fert. Ubi obsecro desinere ab homine est, non pendere ab homine, non collocare in homine fidu- ciam? Frustra ergo hic sensus noviter confictus à Calvino sine Scripturæ exemplo. Ebræi ipsi in- tellexêre, sensum esse, moneo ut quiescatis ab ho- mine, cujus spiritus in naribus ejus. Dn. D. Va- renius in Commentar. ad 12. Capp. Esa. p. 81. Ver- bum, inquit, חָדַל constructum personaliter inter- cedente idiotismo pronominali & particula מֵvel מִן semper dicit absistentiam inferioris à superiori irri- tando, ad vindictam provocando, nunquam à con- fidendo, vel timendo, vel inferiorem lacessendo. Conf. 2. Chron. 25, 6. & magis 35, 21. Hic enim pla- ne parallelismus est. Hæc ille, qui de hoc lo- co ibidem fuse disserit, & alienas interpretationes profligat.

(7.) Sequentis capitis συνέχειαν etiam urgere possumus cum Basilio, Cyrillo, Hie- ronymo, quam hic ita proponit: Et est ordo: quo- niam noluistis cessare ab homine, cujus spiritus in na- ribus ejus, qui excelsus reputatus est, sed è contrario fudistis sanguinem justi, & cogitastis consilium pessi- mum, dicentes, alligemus justum, quia inutilis est no- bis. Ideo fructum ad inventionum vestrarum come- detis. Nihil apud Judæos post passionem Domini forte, nihil validum est, sed omnia infirma & lan- guida &c. Post interfectionem quippe illius, ut antea dixerat Hieronymus, omnes gratiæ & donationes sublatæ sunt à Judæis. Quem ordinem insinuat quoque B. Lutherus: Superiore cap. describit poten- tiam regni Christi, jam minatur vastitatem Judæis, qui Christum non erant recepturi. (8.) B. Gesnerus nester observat, quod idem ille homo sit ipse Do- minus exercituum, quia immediate subjungitur Cap. 3, 1. Ecce enim Dominator Dominus exercituum auferet de Jerusalem &c. Ab illo ergo quiescere jubentur, cujus judicium gravissimum Caput se- quens describit. Quod Esaias (inquit ἑρμηνεύ- της noster) non loquatur de quovis mortali homine, cohærentia textus arguit; siquidem auditores ad pœ- nitentiam & agnitionem Christi adhortari vult qua- tuor argumentis, quia nimirum Christus contemto- res sui funditus sit deleturus, superbos sibi subje- cturus, idola devastaturus, & denique æternis pœnis infideles affecturus. Ad hasce rationes sequitur conclu- sio, ut Messiam, licet hominem, non contemnant, sed amplectantur & venerentur, cum idem ille homo sit Do- minator Dominus exercituum, ut indivulsa connexio primi versiculi sequentis capitis ostendit. Adde his autoritatem & consensum Interpretum cum vete- rum Origenis & Hieronymi, qui hanc perspicuam de Christo Prophetiam dicit; tum è recentioribus Or- thodoxorum, nec non Pontificiorum plerorumq; Sanctii, Delrio, Cornelii à Lapide, Luisii, Menochii, Tirini, & aliorum, qui pariter de Christo interpre- tantur. Calvino & Sociis opponimus Oecolampa- dium, qui hic nobiscum facit, & Calvini ac Grotii sententiam in Judæis reprobat. Adscribemus ver- ba ejus, quia locum & cohærentiam cum Cap. sequ. illustrant. Antequam Judæis suam pœnam nar- raret, monet iterum, ne impingant in lapidem offen- sionis, contemnentes humilitatem, atque adeo & mor- tem Christi, quò nemo se magis humiliavit, qui dicit: Ego sum vermis & non homo. Cui flatus in naribus est: hoc est, qui humilis est, & fragilis, atq; talis, qui propediem expiraturus videatur, & ita nullius repu- tationis, ut dicatis: In quo enim reputatus est? Vere enim absconditus Deus est. Et recte etiam de hoc monentur. Post reditum enim à Babylone non fue- runt idola apud Judæos, sicut antea dictum. Igi- tur monentur, ne in Christo, qui illis humilis videbatur, offenderentur: propter hoc enim peccatum judicium eis impendebat, & requisitus est sanguis ab eis. Quid autem si exponas, flatus in naribus ejus? Sicut אף iram, & nares significat, ut in Psalmis: Et ascendit fumus in ira ejus. Et sit sensus. Videte ne dum ho- minem, qui vobis despectus videtur, offenditis, judicem mundi, in cujus manibus est ventilabrum, exasperetis. Judæi exponunt, ne in ullo homine spes habeatur, quia fragilis sit, sicut & Hier. dicit: Maledictus, qui po- nit carnem brachium suum. Et Psaltes: Nolite confidere in principibus, in filiis hominum, in quibus non est salus. Quæ sententia pia quidem est, sed my- sterium præterit. Hæc Oecolampadius.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

Concerning the various punishments that will precede the reprobation of the people, the lack of provisions and suitable men, and their causes, in all estates, the seduction of the people, oppression, and the pride of the sex, especially the maidenly. Vers. 1. HE WILL TAKE AWAY FROM JERUSALEM AND FROM JUDAH THE MIGHTY AND THE STRONG.] He describes those times, which are treated in 2 Kings 24 and 25, etc. Vers. 2. THE PRUDENT] Here it is taken in a good sense for sagacious. Vers. 4. AND EFFEMINATE SHALL RULE OVER THEM.] For the Hebrew Parfuli. But they seem to be boys and little ones are to be understood kings of no counsel, such as Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah. Thus also below, by the name of women, men of womanish spirit seem to be understood.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

De variis pœnis reprobationem populi ante- gressuris, defectu annonæ & virorum ido- neorum, earumque causis, in omnibus sta- tibus, populi seductione, oppressione, & superbia sexus imprimis virginei. Vers. 1. AUFERET A JERUSALEM ET A JVDA VALIDVM ET FORTEM.] Describit tempora illa, de quibus agitur 2. Reg. 24. & 25. seqq. Vers. 2. ALIOLVM] Bonam in partem hic sumitur pro sagace. Vers. 4. ET EFFOEMINATI DOMINABVNTVR EIS.] Pro Hebræo Parfuli. Videntur autem puerorum & parvulorum nomine intelligi reges nullius consilii, qualis Joakin, Joachim, Sedecias. Sic & infra mulierum nomine intelligendi videntur viri muliebris animi.

## 3:5
Ver. 5. THE CHILD SHALL BEHAVE HIMSELF PROUDLY AGAINST THE ANCIENT] An excellent description of disorder.

Latin:

Vers. 5. TVMVLTVABITVR PVER CONTRA SE- NEM] Egregia ἀταξίας descriptio.

## 3:7
Ver. 7. I AM NO HEALER] I have not wherewith to relieve your poverty.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NON SVM MEDICVS] Non habeo unde inopiæ vestræ subveniam.

## 3:9
Ver. 9. THEY DECLARE THEIR SIN AS SODOM] It denotes a brazen forehead.

Latin:

Vers. 9. PECCATVM SVVM QVASI SODOMA PRÆDICAVERVNT] Perfrictum frontem designat.

## 3:17
Ver. 17. THE LORD WILL SMITE WITH A SCAB THE CROWN OF THE HEAD OF THE DAUGHTERS OF ZION] Which was accustomed to be done to slaves.

AND THE LORD WILL DISCOVER THEIR SECRET PARTS] More correctly, their buttocks. For the word פות is translated as pudenda, and by similitude the fundament is so called. This was accustomed to be done to women for the sake of ignominy. See below 20, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 17. DECALVABIT DOMINVS VERTICEM FILIARVM SION] Quod servis fieri solebat.

ET DOMINVS CRINEM EARVM NVDABIT] Rectius nates. Nam vox פות ὕφαιμα vertitur, & per si- militudinem sic appellatur podex. Solebat id feminis i- gnominiæ causa fieri. Vide infra 20, 4.

## 3:18
Ver. 18. THE BRAVERY OF THEIR TINKLING ORNAMENTS] The Greeks: τὴν δόξαν τῶν ἱματισκῶν αὐτῶν. But עכס, as the Hebrews teach us, were rattles on the feet of women, which they used while dancing. There follows in the Hebrew, השביסים, which are eyelet-bands: ἐμπλόκια to the Greeks: for which our version put little moons. They are necklaces hanging from the neck, in the manner of little moons.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ORNAMENTVM CALCEAMENTO- RVM] Græci: τὴν δόξαν τῶν ἱματισκῶν αὐτῶν. Sed עכס, ut nos docent Hebræi, erant crepitacula in pedibus mu- lierum, quibus inter saltandum utebantur. Sequitur in Hebræo, השביסים, quæ sunt vittæ ocellatæ: ἐμ- πλόκια Græcis: pro quibus lunulas noster posuit. Sunt monilia de collo pendentia, lunulæ in modum.

## 3:19
Ver. 19. AND THE CHAINS] So also the Targum. They understand, however, a string of pearls, with which the neck was encircled.

AND THE BRACELETS] Here in the Hebrew there is also 'and armlets'.

AND THE MUFFLERS] What is here in the Hebrew signifies rather veils, by which the faces of women, except for the eyes, are covered.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ET TORQVES] Sic & Thargum. Intelli- gunt autem lineam ex unionibus, qua collum cingebatur.

ET MONILIA] Hic in Hebræo est & armillas.

ET ARMILLAS] Quod hic in Hebræo est, magis si- gnificat velamina, quibus mulierum facies, præter ocu- los obtegitur.

## 3:20
Ver. 20. AND THE BONNETS] In the Hebrew it is rather headbands.

AND THE ORNAMENTS OF THE LEGS] Which are 'genualia' (garters/knee-bands) in Ovid.

AND LITTLE WALLS (MURENULAS)] Chains woven from gold into little rods, in a winding order. Thus Jerome interprets this word to Marcella.

AND SCENT-BOXES] That is, odoriferous boxes. In Hebrew: בתי הנפש, little houses of breath.

AND EARRINGS] The Hebrew name is from enchanting. You will see the reason at Genesis 35:4.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ET DISCRIMINALIA] In Hebræo potius est mitellas.

ET PERISCELIDAS] Quæ genualia Ovidio.

ET MVRENVLAS] Catenas contextas ex auro in vir- gulas sentescente, flexuoso ordine. Ita hanc vocem inter- pretatur Hieronymus ad Marcellam.

ET OLFACTORIOLA] Id est, pyxides odoriferas. In Hebræo: בתי הנפש domunculas halitus.

ET INAVRES] Nomen Hebræum ab incantando est. Causam videbis ad Genes. XXXV. 4.

## 3:21
AND RINGS] On the fingers.

AND GEMS HANGING ON THE FOREHEAD.] In Hebrew: circles of the nostrils. It is also accustomed to be called by the one word נזם, as in Proverbs 11:22, Ezekiel 16:12.

Verse 21. AND CHANGEABLE GARMENTS] εἵματά τ' ἐξημοιβὰ in Homer. See what [is said] at Matthew 10:10.

Latin:

ET ANNVLOS] In digitis.

ET GEMMAS IN FRONTE PENDENTES.] In Hebræo: circulos narium. Id una voce etiam נזם dici solet, ut Prov. XI. 22. Ezech. XVI. 12.

Vers. 21. ET MVTATORIA] εἵματά τ' ἐξημοιβὰ Ho- mero. Vide quæ ad Matth. X. 10.

## 3:22
AND LITTLE CLOAKS] The Hebrew word המעטפות signifies coverings. They seem to be understood as bed-spreads. We gather from the Greek interpretation here that they were περιπόρφυρα & μεσοπόρφυρα, that is, accustomed to be woven around or woven between with purple.

AND LINENS] המטפחות: from the passage in Ruth 3:15, it appears to be περιζώματα, those girdles under the breast which women are accustomed to use at home. Therefore the LXX do not translate badly here τὰ ἐπιβλήματα τὰ κατὰ τὴν οἰκίαν (the coverings for the house).

AND NEEDLES] It appears that חריטים are purses or bags, 2 Kings 5:23, where the Greeks translated it ἐν θυλακίοις (in little bags). Women are accustomed to have certain little purses hanging from their bosom.

Verse 22. AND MIRRORS] Counsel of form. Τὰ διαφανῆ λακωνικὰ (the transparent Laconian [mirrors]) among the LXX.

Latin:

ET PALLIOLA] Vox Hebræa המעטפות operimen- ta significat. Videntur intelligi peristromata lectorum. περιπόρφυρα & μεσοπόρφυρα ea fuisse, id est, purpura cir- cumtexi aut intertexi solita, colligimus ex Græca hic in- terpretatione.

ET LINTEAMINA] המטפחות : ex loco Ruth. 3, 15. apparet esse περιζώματα, succinctus illos subter pectus, quibus mulieres domi folent uti. Itaque LXX. non male hic vertunt τὰ ἐπιβλήματα τὰ κατὰ τὴν οἰκίαν.

ET ACVS] חריטים esse crumenas sive folles ap- paret 2. Reg. V. 23. ubi Græci ἐν θυλακίοις verterunt. So- lent feminæ habere crumenulas quasdam de sinu penden- tes.

Vers. 22. ET SPECVLA] Consilium formæ. Τὰ διαφα- νῆ λακωνικὰ apud LXX.

## 3:23
AND FINE LINENS] See what [is said] at Matthew 27:59.

AND HEADBANDS] The Hebrew word signifies wrappers, around the forehead, as it seems. I am surprised that the Greeks express this with so many words: τὰ ὑακίνθινα καὶ κόκκινα καὶ τὴν βύσον σὺν χρυσῷ καὶ ὑακίνθῳ συγκαθυφασμένα (the hyacinthine and scarlet and the fine linen woven together with gold and hyacinth).

AND THERISTRA] Namely θέριστρα κατάλιπα, that is, summer wraps, as the Greeks have it here. When I read this list of the world and of women's finery among the Jews, there comes to mind a passage pertaining to Roman women, and indeed in times not yet corrupt, namely the second Punic War, in Plautus's Aulularia:

There stands the fuller, the embroiderer, the goldsmith, the wool-worker, the tavern-keepers, the makers of borders, the makers of undergarments, etc. And in the Epidicus: What was she wearing, a regilla, an inducula, or a mendicula? Or an impluviata? As those women make names for garments. Then: What of those women who find new names for clothing every year: a thin tunic, a thick tunic, a linen cloth, etc.

Latin:

ET SINDONES] Vide quæ ad Matth. 27, 59.

ET VITTAS] Vox Hebræa involucra significat, cir- cum frontem, ut videtur. Miror Græcos hoc tot verbis exprimere: τὰ ὑακίνθινα καὶ κόκκινα καὶ τὴν βύσον σὺν χρυσῷ καὶ ὑακίνθῳ συγκαθυφασμένα.

ET THERISTRA] Nempe θέριστρα κατάλιπα, id est, stragulas æstivas, ut hic habent Græci. Cum hunc cen- sum mundi & ornatus muliebris apud Judæos lego, in mentem venit loci ad feminas Romanas pertinentis, & qui- dem temporibus non corruptis ideo, belli scilicet Punici secundi in Plauti Aulularia:

Stat fullo, phrygio, aurifex, lanarius, Caupones, patagiarii, indusiarii, &c. Et in Epidico: Quid erat induta, an regillam induculam, aut mendi- culam. An impluviatam: Vt istæ faciunt vestimentis nomi- na. Deinde: Quid istæ quæ vesti quotannis nomina inveniunt nova: Tunicam rallam, tunicam spissam, linteolum cæ- ficium: &c.

## 3:24
Vers. 24. AND INSTEAD OF SWEET SMELL THERE SHALL BE STENCH] In the Hebrew: Instead of spice, a dissolution: that is, putrefaction and filth.

AND INSTEAD OF A GIRDLE A ROPE] Instead of a belt, a breaking: that is, torn clothes.

AND INSTEAD OF WELL-SET HAIR BALDNESS] In the Hebrew: instead of work (and) equality: that is, instead of beautifully combed and arranged hair.

AND INSTEAD OF A STOMACHER SACKCLOTH] פתיגיל is a foreign word, signifying, as many Hebrews think, a magnificent kind of girdle, to which is opposed the belt of sackcloth: that is, a rope; with which sackcloths are accustomed to be bound.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET ERIT PRO SVAVI ODORE FOE- TOR] In Hebræo: Loco aromatis, dissolutio: id est, pu- stredo & illuvies.

ET PRO ZONA FVNICVLVS] Loco cinguli con- fractio: id est, vestes lacerae.

ET PRO CRISPANTI CRINE CALVITIVM] In Hebraeo: pro opere (&) aequalitate: id est, pro pulchre pexis ac dispositis comis.

ET PRO FASCIA PECTORALI CILICIVM] פתיגיל est vox barbara, significans, ut multi Hebraei cen- sent, zonae genus magnificum, cui opponitur tingulum sac- ci: id est, funis; quo cilicia constringi solent.

## 3:25
THY MOST BEAUTIFUL MEN ALSO] For this in the Hebrew is, burning instead of beauty: and it coheres with the preceding, not, as in the Latin, with the following: for כי is not here a preposition, but a noun, as רוי from רוה, for because of the cultivation of their form, women will be scorched by the suns.

Vers. 25. AND HER GATES SHALL LAMENT AND MOURN] A transition from the second person to the third, which is frequent for the Hebrews.

Latin:

PVLCHERRIMI QVOQVE VIRI TVI] Pro hoc in Hebraeo est, adustio pro pulchritudine: & cohaeret cum praecedentibus, non, ut in Latino, cum consequentibus: nam כי non est hic praepositio, sed nomen, ut רוי a רוה pro formae cultu feminae solibus urentur.

Vers. 25. ET MOEREBVNT, ATQVE LVGEBVNT PORTAE EJVS] Transitio a secunda persona ad tertiam, quae Hebraeis frequens.

## 3:26
Vers. 26. AND BEING DESOLATE SHE SHALL SIT ON THE GROUND] Cleansed: it is in the Hebrew: that is, deprived of all things, just as the cleanness of teeth is put for famine, Amos 4:6. Judea shall sit on the ground, not on a throne.

Grotius therefore refers these things to the times of the abduction of the Jews under King Jehoiakim and the subsequent Babylonian captivity under King Zedekiah. But since he explained the preceding things concerning the time of Ahaz and the siege of Rezin; and since these things cohere with the preceding, and look to the same times, the reason for the continuity and context will not easily stand for itself. But much less will Grotius's hypothesis have a place, that all these prophecies, from Chapter 1 to 40 of Isaiah, look to the times of Hezekiah, which he handed down at the beginning of Chapter 30. To which he has also attempted to twist prophetic oracles here and there. Let Grotius therefore return here to favor with his own, and his chief (though most false) hypothesis. Although indeed some interpreters, especially the Jews, which Jerome [mentions] at chapter 3.

& 4. observes, that some have referred these to the Babylonians, yet others have acknowledged that they rather look toward the Romans, namely Jerome, Basil the Great, Cyril of Alexandria, Rupert, Brentius, Gesner & others, Cornelius a Lapide, Menochius, Tirinus; or at least they believed them to pertain to that former devastation and calamity in such a way that the punishments of the following times, even up to the total ruin of the people, are designated. To which the explanation of Blessed Luther seems to incline: and likewise Osiander on this passage. Furthermore, this Prophet prophesies not only of those times in which the Jewish nation was entirely cast off, when Jerusalem was finally devastated: but also of that calamity which occurred under Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian king: for that destruction of the city was a certain prelude, and as it were a type, of the final destruction. And just as Christ joins in Matthew XXIV the devastation of Jerusalem and the end of the world: so this Prophet embraces the penultimate and the final devastation of the city in one prophecy. So also the Weimar Paraphrasts; and from the Reformed, Tremellius and Junius: who not inappropriately [say] on this passage; The Prophet teaches that the judgment of God will pervade all of Judea far and wide, [affecting] the highest, the lowest, men and women, goods

& bodies: men indeed up to verse 17, women from there up to the end, after the matter of goods and the possession of all things has been dealt with in verse 2. These judgments, however, were not effected at only one certain time, since the Prophet taught above in chapter 5 and following that they had already begun from his own times. But they pertain to all subsequent times, in which the Jews suffered all these evils and changes up to the full time of rejection. These things which are predicted here certainly agree especially with these latest times, as Jerome, Brentius, and Osiander have taught. God threatens that He will take away the Prophet, which did not happen at the time of the Babylonian destruction, but the Roman. Oecolampadius acknowledges the evidence of the prophecy: You have here that prophecy MANIFESTLY pertaining to the times of Christ. For Jacob had said, Gen. 49: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until he comes who is to be sent. And you see here that neither a fifty-year-old nor a counsellor nor an elder is left. In the Babylonian captivity it was still possible to find prophets, and elders and leaders, who also brought back the tribe of Judah. Isaiah predicts here in verse 5 a notable seduction. And the people shall rush, man against man, and every one against his neighbour, the fulfilment of which is especially detected in the final destruction, concerning which Jerome says: Josephus writes that these things happened to the people of the Jews under Titus the son of Vespasian, and that, when they were being besieged by the Romans, the sedition was divided into three parts, and some held the citadel and the temple, and others the lower, and others the upper part of the city. Grotius acknowledges that in those words of verse 5, the children shall behave themselves proudly against the elder, an excellent description of anarchy is exhibited. But that [anarchy] flourished not so much at the time of the Babylonian as of the Roman destruction. He threatens total ruin, and designates its cause as blasphemy against the Lord, which especially fits the most recent age and ruin of the Jewish Synagogue. Let us hear St. Jerome again on verse 8: For Jerusalem is ruined, and Judah is fallen, because their tongue and their doings are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty. The Prophet speaks these things; not, as most think, he who had been chosen as prince. And he says that for this reason no one wants to rule over a sinful people, because both Judah and Jerusalem and the city and the province of Judea or the tribe of Judah have fallen equally, and he gives the causes of their impiety, because they blasphemed against the Lord and said: away with him, away with him, crucify such a one, we have no king but Caesar: and they provoked the most merciful Lord to bitterness by the fury of their tongue. Blessed Luther: This is the sin of the denied and rejected Christ; the tongue is the doctrine of the Pharisees, the doings are hypocrisy and the sin of obstinacy, because they would not believe in so many miracles performed, etc.

Then there can be no doubt that the things which are predicted in verse 25 and following are more rightly applied to the final destruction, and have their full fulfilment in it. And her gates shall mourn and lament, and she shall sit desolate on the ground or cleansed, that is, deprived of all things, just as the cleanness of teeth is used for famine in Amos 4:6, just as Grotius explains here: she shall sit on the ground, not on a throne, and seven women shall take hold of one man: the slaughter will be so great that seven women will be content with one common husband for the sake of protection and defence, and indeed will live at their own expense, contrary to what was the custom, as Grotius says here again. Which vengeance, just as it was most illustrious at the time of the last devastation, with so many hundreds of thousands of men extinguished: so it still lasts even today among the Jews, as our blessed Luther observes. Finally, that notable prophecy concerning Christ, which is immediately added in Chapter 4:2, In that day shall the branch of the Lord be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent, etc., clearly convinces that the preceding things also pertain to the times of the New Testament: which Grotius strives in vain to pervert with the Jews into a foreign sense, as we shall now teach.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ET DESOLATA IN TERRA SEDEBIT] Mundata: est in Hebraeo: id est, privata rebus omnibus, sicut mundities dentium pro fame ponitur, Amos 4, 6. Judaea humi sedebit, non in solio.

REfert ergo haec Grotius ad tempora abductio- nis Judaeorum sub rege Joackim & subsequuta sub rege Sedecia captivitatis Babylonicae. Sed quum superiora exposuerit de tempore Ahasi & obsidio- ne Resinis; haec autem superioribus cohaereant, eademque tempora respiciant, non facile συνε- χείας & contextus ratio ita sibi constabit. Multo ve- ro minus locum habitura est hypothesis Grotii, quod omnia haec vaticinia, a Cap. 1. ad 40. Esaiae, tempora Ezechiae spectent, quam sub Cap. 30. initium tradidit. Ad quam etiam passim vaticinia Prophetica detor- quere conatus est. Redeat ergo hic Grotius in gratiam cum propria, & palmaria sua (etsi falsissi- ma) hypothesi. Quanquam vero Interpp. nonnul- li, Judaei cumprimis, quod Hieronymus ad cap. 3.

& 4. observat, ad Babylonios haec retulerint, alii ta- men ad Romanos ea potius spectare agnoverunt, Hieronymus nempe, Basilius M. Cyrillus Alexan- drinus, Rupertus, Brentius, Gesn. & alii, Cornelius a Lapide, Menochius, Tirinus; vel certe ita ad prio- rem illam devastationem & calamitatem pertine- re credidere, ut sequentium etiam temporum sup- plicia usque ad totalem ruinam populi designen- tur. Quo videtur abire B. Lutheri explicatio: at- que ita Osiander in h. l. Caeterum Propheta hic non tantum de iis temporibus vaticinatur, quibus Judaea gens omnino fuit abjecta, cum ultimo vastaretur Je- rufalem: sed ea etiam calamitate, quae contigit sub Nebucadnezare Babylonico rege: id enim urbis ex- cidium ultimi excidii praeludium quoddam, & quasi ty- pus fuit. Et sicut Christus conjungit Matth. XXIV. devastationem Hierosolymae & finem mundi: ita hic Propheta penultimam & postremam devastationem urbis una Prophetia complectitur. Sic etiam Para- phrasta Vinarienses; & e Reformatis Tremellius, ac Junius: qui non incommode ad h. locum; Docet Propheta, judicium Dei longe lateque Judaeam totam pervasurum, summos, infimos, viros & mulieres, bona

& corpora: viros quidem usque ad v. 17. mulieres v. inde ad finem usq;, postquam de bonis & rerum omni- um possessione actum est v. 2. Haec autem judicia non uno tantum certo tempore effecta sunt, cum ea jam in- de a suis temporibus coepisse Propheta docuerit supra cap. 5. & seq. Sed ad tempora omnia consequentia pertinent, quibus omnia haec mala mutationesque Judaei perpessi sunt usque ad plenum rejectionis tempus. His certe temporibus novissimis con- veniunt apprime, quae hic praedicuntur, ut Hie- ronymus, Brentius & Osiander docuere. Minatur Deus, se ablaturum Prophetam, quod factum non est tempore Babylonici excidii, sed Romani. A- gnoscit Oecolampadius evidentiam vaticinii: Ha- bes hic prophetiam illam MANIFESTE pertinere ad tempora Christi. Dixerat enim Jacob Gen. 49. Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, neque dux de femo- re, donec veniat, qui mittendus est. Et vides hic ne- que quinquagenarium neque consiliarium neque Senem relinqui. In captivitate Babylonica erat adhuc inveni- re Prophetas, & Senes ac Duces, qui & reduxerunt tribum Juda. Prædicit Esaias hic vers. 5. insignem seductionem. Et irruet populus, vir in virum, & unusquisq; ad proximum suum, cujus complemen- tum in novissimo excidio præcipue deprehendi- tur, de quo Hieronymus: Hæc sub Tito filio Vespafia- ni accidisse populo Judæorum scribit Josephus, & quod, cum expugnarentur à Romanis, fuerit in tres partes divisa seditio, & alii arcem & templum, & alii infe- riorem, alii superiorem partem urbis tenuerint. Ver- bis illis v. 5. tumultuabuntur pueri contra senem, egregiam ἀναρχίας descriptionem exhiberi agno- scit Grotius. Ea autem non tam Babylonici, quam Romani excidii tempore vigebat. Ruinam mina- tur totalem, & causam ejus designat blasphemiam contra Dominum, quæ maxime novissimæ Judaicæ Synagogæ ætati, & ruinæ conveniunt. Audiamus iterum S. Hieronymum ad v. 8. Ruit enim Hiequ- salem, & Juda concidit, quia lingua eorum & adin- ventiones eorum contra Dominum, ut provocarent oculos majestatis ejus. Hæc Propheta loquitur; non ut plerique arbitrantur, ille, qui princeps fuerat ele- ctus. Et dicit ideo nullum velle præesse populo peccatori, quia & Juda & Hierusalem & urbs & Judæa pro- vincia sive tribus Juda pariter conciderint, causasq; reddit impietatis eorum, quia contra Dominum blas- phemaverunt & dixerunt: tolle, tolle, crucifige talem, non habemus Regem, nisi Cæsarem: & clementissi- mum Dominum furore linguæ suæ ad amaritudinem provocaverunt. B. Lutherus: Hoc est peccatum ne- gati & repudiati Christi; lingua est doctrina Phari- sæorum, studia sunt hypocrisis & peccatum pertina- ciæ, quod nolebant credere tot editis miraculis &c.

Tum quæ v. 25. seq. prædicuntur, rectius novissimo excidio aptari, & in eo plenum suum complemen- tum habere, dubitari non potest. Et mærebunt, & lugebunt portæ ejus, & desolata in terra sedebit vel mundata, id est, privata rebus omnibus, sicut mun- dities dentium pro fame ponitur Amos 4, 6. quem- admodum exponit hic Grotius: humi sedebit, non in solio, & apprehendent septem mulieres virum u- num: tanta erit clades, ut septenæ fæminæ tutelæ præsidiique causa contentæ futuræ sint uno communi marito, & quidem suis impensis victuræ, contra, quam mos habebat, uti hic iterum Grotius. Quæ vindicta uti tempore postremæ vastationis, tot centenis millibus ex viris extinctis, maxime illu- stris fuit: sic etiamnum hodie apud Judæos durat, observante hoc B. Luthero nostro. Denique in- signis illa de Christo Prophetia, quæ immediate subjungitur Cap. 4, 2. in die illa germen Domini in magnificentia, & in gloria, & fructus terræ sublimis, &c. præcedentia etiam ad tempora N. T. pertine- re luculenter convincit: quam frustra cum Judæis in alienum sensum pervertere satagit Grotius, uti jam docebimus.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

Concerning the Kingdom of Christ the branch of the Lord being preserved in the remnant, and their cleansing and protection.

Verse 1. AND SEVEN WOMEN SHALL TAKE HOLD OF ONE MAN] The slaughter will be so great that seven women, for the sake of protection and defence, will be content with one common husband, and indeed will live at their own expense; contrary to what was the custom.

LET THY NAME BE CALLED UPON US] Lucan: - - - Let it be permitted to have written on the tomb, Marcia of Cato.

TAKE AWAY OUR REPROACH] Celibacy in an over-ripe age.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

De Regno Christi germinis Domini in reliquiis conservando, earumque mundatione ac protectione.

Vers. 1. ET APPREHENDENT SEPTEM MVLIE- RES VIRVM VNVM] Tanta erit clades, ut septenæ fœ- minæ, tutelæ præsidique causa, contentæ futuræ sint uno communi marito, & quidem suis impensis victuræ; con- tra quam mos habebat.

INVOCETVR NOMEN TVVM SVPER NOS] Lucanus: - - - Liceat tumulo scripsisse, Catonis Marcia.

AUFER OPPROBRIUM NOSTRUM] Cæliba- tum in ætate ὑπεράκμῳ.

## 4:2
Ver. 2.

IN THAT DAY THE BRANCH OF THE LORD SHALL BE IN MAGNIFICENCE AND GLORY] Here a new section ought to have begun. For the discourse is about the reality. The branch of the Lord is in the first sense the remnant of the exiles, who having returned home in the times of Ezra and Nehemiah led a praiseworthy life: mystically, however, Christ, and Christians.

There is no reason why the division of the Hebrew text should be argued with. For although the Evangelical prophecy begins here, yet because it coheres with the preceding prediction and pertains to the same times, he who divided the chapters wished to refer some part of the former prophecy to the present chapter, so that it might be understood more correctly. The Holy Spirit also indicated this coherence by the designation of time, IN THAT DAY shall be the branch. Whence it ought not to be doubted that both prophecies look to the same times. But while Grotius understands the remnant of the people by the branch of the Lord, he Judaizes in a manner peculiar and perpetual to himself: but he does violence to the text. For in that day, in which seven women shall take hold of one man, i.e., the Babylonian slaughter, according to Grotius, was there such magnificence of the remnant of the people? Or were those who returned already there on that day, when such a great slaughter happened? Thus the times of the Babylonian calamity are confounded with those more serene times of the liberation of the people, which are separated by 70 years. But then how is it proven that the branch of the Lord and the fruit of the earth are the remnant of the returning people? And how shall we understand the magnificence and glory of the branch as referring to a praiseworthy life, when these are greatly distinct, magnificence and glory, as well as beauty and sublimity and a praiseworthy life? Furthermore, if the discourse is about those remnants, how can the branch be explained as referring to Christ, or, what is more absurd, to Christ and Christians at the same time? Were those remnants types of Christ, or even of Christians? And in what does the nature of the type consist? Or how do such disparate senses agree with the same passage? If the discourse is about the day of the return from the Babylonian captivity, how can that day be understood as referring to the day or time of the N. Testament? There is, therefore, only one sense of this prophecy, as of all others, which from the Sp. intended by the Holy Spirit, and is commonly called literal; according to which almost all Christian interpreters, and also some from the Jews, understand these things of the days of the Messiah, although they do not agree in explaining the word branch, which some explain of the Messiah himself, others of the faithful and the Church of Christ in the time of the N. T. Which opinions Grotius mixes together along with the Jewish commentary, so that, forsooth, he may please everyone, but wrongly and absurdly.

The better part of interpreters maintains that the Messiah is understood here by the branch of Jehovah according to the letter; to which we subscribe: (1.) because this name is peculiarly proper in the prophecies to the Messiah, who is pointed out as the branch by the Prophets Jer. 23, 6. 33, 16. Zech. 3, 8. 6, 12. of whom also the root itself צמח germinated, is used more often Ps. 24, 12. 132, 17. Isa. 43, 19. c. 61, 11. 12. Zech. 6, 12. By which similar word נצר a shoot is also designated by Isaiah Chap. 11, 1. (2.) The name צמח יהוה is explained by apposition as Branch of Jehovah or Lord, or by regimen as branch of Jehovah or of the Lord. In the former sense it cannot be taken of any other than Christ, who is both the branch and Jehovah. In the latter sense it again fits Christ most excellently. For he is the branch of Jehovah GOD the Father by reason of his divine nature with respect to eternal generation, and furthermore he can be called the branch of God the Father with respect to his human nature, because he is given to the world by the Father and is supremely acceptable to him. Another appellation is also added פרי הארץ fruit of the earth. Whence the former to the divine nature, this latter, however, some interpreters refer to the human nature. The Prophet, says Osiander, calls Christ the branch of the Lord, to signify that he is the Son of God eternally begotten, consubstantial with the Father. Shortly after, he calls him the fruit of the earth to assert his true humanity. For man is earth, Gen. 3, which is also the explanation of Brentius and Gesner. The Vinarians, however, refer both names to the origin of Christ's humanity.

(3.) To whom does that magnificence and sublimity belong more than to Christ? Indeed, what branch is there to whom that could belong, if not the righteous branch of David, Jehovah the Messiah, our righteousness, Jer. 23, 6. Who is the exultation or ornament to the faithful, if not Christ, in whom alone one ought to glory, 1 Cor. 1, 31. For thus the Prophet says of that branch: In that day the branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth shall be sublime, and an exultation to those who have been saved from Israel. Or as it is in the Hebrew, an ornament to the escape of Israel. Therefore blessed Luther: The branch of the Lord and the fruit of the earth is Christ. He, he says, shall be in majesty and glory, he shall be extolled above all adversaries, he shall live and abundantly give us all things. And Bernard, sermon 2 on Pentecost. That branch, which sprouted from the rod of Jesse by the greenness of a virgin, was in magnificence when he had risen from the dead, because then, O Lord my God, you were magnified exceedingly, putting on confession and ornament, clothed with light as with a garment. But how great is the glory of the ascending one, when you are led to the Father in the midst of angels and holy souls, and with a triumphal palm you bring the assumed man into the very identity of divinity and praise? Who could conceive, let alone how sublime the fruit of Jesse is in the session at the right hand of the Father, which certainly dazzles the eyes of celestial natures, which the angelic gaze trembles at, and does not reach. Let therefore the exultation come, Lord Jesus, to those who have been saved from Israel. While I compare Oecolampadius on this passage, I see him gravely urging this argument of ours: Therefore I shall transcribe his passage from his commentaries on Isaiah, book 2, fol. 43. The sense is: He who is the branch of the Lord and the fruit of the earth, shall be the joy and glory of those who shall then have been liberated, that is, of all the faithful. For they shall not reject Christ, but shall follow him with their whole heart, exhilarated by the Holy Spirit, and all their joy and exultation shall be, not in riches, not in honors, not in the luxury of clothes, feasts, magnificent houses, or pageants: nor as the Pharisees in their fasts, prayers, and works, but in that branch. Zeph. 3: Praise, daughter of Zion, jubilate, Israel, rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem, the Lord has taken away your judgment, he has turned away your enemies. The King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst. Whence also the blessed virgin: My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has exulted in God my Savior. 1 Cor. 1: Christ is made unto us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. That as it is written, he who glories, let him glory in the Lord. Jer. 9: In this let him who glories glory, to know and to know me, because I am the Lord, who does mercy and judgment and righteousness. But how much joy Christ brought to his own, John says: We saw his glory, as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of thanks and truth. Was not Christ seen as joy and glory, sublimity and magnificence to those who for his sake were leaving all things, to whom nothing pleased except Christ, who also did not refuse to die for Christ with joy. And thus that is true happiness.

(4.) Here are described the benefits which we obtain through the Messiah, and which are to be attributed solely to the righteous branch, the Messiah: namely, sanctification, election or inscription in the book of life, the washing away of the filth of sin, the gift of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of judgment and of burning, and gracious protection. For thus our Prophet: And the Lord shall create over every place of Mount Zion, and

where he is called upon, a cloud by day and smoke and the splendor of a flaming fire by night. The LXX render: And he shall come, and every place of Mount Zion and all things that are in its circuit shall be: a cloud shall protect by day, and the light of a flaming fire by night. To which words Jerome on this passage: But who shall come except he of whom it is written: He shall come from Zion, who may deliver. And of whom another Prophet commemorates: Yet a little while, he who is to come shall come, and shall not delay. When he shall have come, the pristine happiness shall be restored to the people, which they once had in the desert: the Lord preceding them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire: so that they may never be troubled in prosperity or in adversity. Cyril on this passage: so that those who inhabit the intelligible Zion, that is, the Church, may flee the heat and trials of this life, which proceed from temptations, and the burnings, he will hang over them almost like a cloud, and Christ himself will be a protector, he will dispel the darkness of ignorance and Diabolical wickedness, shining upon the mind like light in the gloom and like the flashing of fire.

Which the Prophet explains when he adds: For there shall be a protection over all the glory; that is, over the Church, which above other kingdoms of this world is alone especially glorious in the sight of God, and over all who believe in Christ, who themselves also are glorious before God above all the monarchs of this earth, as Brentius beautifully says here: with blessed Luther preceding in the marginal gloss, who in his Commentary on this passage excellently illustrates this whole place. Thus far, he says on verse 5, Tom. 3, Oper. Lat. Jenens. p. 295, he has described the opulence of the kingdom of Christ, likewise the distribution of spiritual gifts, and the power and efficacy of cleansing. But because Satan cannot bear this knowledge, and our King is hidden, and no weapons have been handed to us for avenging ourselves, but a command for obeying and enduring. Therefore he now touches upon the cross also. The Lord, he says, will protect and defend Sion, that is, His Church, which is in danger on account of that branch. Christ will be the true cloud, that is, He will refresh and console His own. And He will be a fire, which will shine in temptations. In Him will be the strength and power of believers, etc. And afterwards: Learn this diligently, however, which the Prophet warns here, that Christ alone is appointed to be a protection and a shade for those laboring from heat and rain. Fix your eyes on Him, cling to Him, just as you are also warned by the divine voice, Hear Him. He who hears another, who looks to something other than this flesh, it is all over for him. For He alone protects us from the heat which arises from the contemplation of majesty. He alone defends us from the rain and violence of Satan. This shade gives us refreshment, so that those thoughts of wrath may depart. For wrath cannot be present there, where you see the Son of God delivered to death for you, so that you might live. Wherefore I commend to you those titles of Christ with which the Prophet adorns Him, that He is a tabernacle for a shade from the heat. A refuge and a hiding place from the rain and the storm. Thus B. Luther.

5. The interpretation of Grotius and those who understand the Church by the branch does not agree with the text, in which the Church and believers are distinguished from this branch, and this branch is openly separated from the Church or believers, namely those who have been saved from Israel, or who have been left in Sion, and the remnant in Jerusalem, and thus the saints who are written in life, and its beauty and exaltation are spoken of. By this argument Junius seems to be convinced, so that he might abandon the opinion of his teacher Calvin, whose words it is pleasing to add: At that time the branch of Jehovah will be for glory and honor, that is, Christ Jehovah below v. 4, who, when the kingdom of God was almost dead, was raised up by God the Father and sent forth, like a branch sprouting from a root; others, however, for the Church take it as sprouting from the remnant of Israel, in this sense: The Church collected from the remnant of Israel will be most adorned, others [take it] for spiritual gifts, which Jehovah pours into the Church: But since the proper name of the Church in the Prophet is Israel, or the remnant of Israel in this verse and the following, and furthermore the grace evident words: then this is a proper attribute of Christ, which the same Prophet later explained more copiously as time went on, infra 2, the sum of which this chapter contains, we have preferred this interpretation to others, finally the very sequence of the words is also constructed more simply in this way, than if you were to say: will the sprout of Jehovah be for the remnant of Israel? that is, will they sprout from Jehovah? but gifts are never called by this name, but Christ himself obtains this appellation, and related ones, infra 2. Jerem. 23. & 33. Zach. 3. & 6. Thus far Junius. From which I think it is manifest how unjust a censure Calvin passes upon the explanation of Bernhard, Lyranus, B. Luther, and Brentius, which is both strengthened by the common calculation of our Doctors, and has even been received by most Papists. This passage is indeed commonly wont to be explained of Christ, and although the opinion is plausible in itself, it receives more color from the saying of Zechariah: Behold him, whose name is the Sprout. This same thing is also confirmed by the fact that the Prophet speaks of this sprout not simply, but with an honorific addition, as if it were proposed to commend the divinity of Christ. For afterwards he adds, the fruit of the earth, this they refer to the human nature. But having weighed everything more closely, I do not doubt that he takes the sprout of God and the fruit of the earth for a copious and unusual produce of glory, with which he will refresh the famished. For he speaks just as if the earth, after devastation, were sterile and covered in squalor, promising no Sprout in the future, so that he might make the grace of God more desirable by an unusual fertility, as if barren and sterile fields were producing unexpected herbs. The Prophet's purpose indeed looks to this, that the glory of God will be illustrious when the new Church arises, and as if it were creating a people for itself from nothing, and enriching them with every kind of good. Those who restrict it to the person of Christ make themselves ridiculous to the Jews, as if they were TWISTING the places of Scripture to their own advantage. But how rash this judgment is, and how jejune and incongruous the gloss, Calvin's teacher Oecolampadius and his disciple Franc. Junius have already taught. But it is so far from being ridiculous to the Jews that this passage is explained of Christ, that Calvin could have learned from Oecolampadius [about] the Targum and the LXX Interpreters. that the Jews are with us here: whose opinion I add here, so that the modern disciples of both may correct their Calvin from it. Therefore, he says, in this paragraph he teaches the happiness of the Church from joy and boasting in Christ, from holiness and security. But here Christ is called the sprout of the Lord, and the fruit of the earth. For he has a Father in heaven as God, as true God, for which reason he is called the sprout of the Lord: and a mother on earth as true man, for which reason he is called the fruit of the earth. Behold, you have the mystery of the incarnation. Jerome explains the sprout as the primitive Church: But Lyranus and others more correctly [explain it as] Christ, who is also in Jerem. 23: Behold the days come, and I will raise up to David a righteous sprout, and a King shall reign, and shall be wise. And the Targum of R. Jonathan says here manifestly: In that time the Messiah of the Lord shall be for joy and beauty. The Greek most clearly says ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἐκλάμψει θεὸς. In that day God shall shine forth. The sense therefore is: He who is the sprout of the Lord and the fruit of the earth, will be the joy and glory of those who shall then have been liberated, that is: of all the faithful. The rest which he subjoins have been brought forward before, which we judge to be certainly more solid than the inventions of Calvin.

Ver. 2. EVERYONE WHO IS WRITTEN IN LIFE IN JERUSALEM.] Whoever shall be written in the register of those returning,

A sufficiently cold gloss. The discourse is not about the inscription in the register of those returning, but in the book of life, which Scripture calls [it]. For it has already been shown that it is not a matter of the Babylonian reduction of exiles, but of the remnant of the Jews who will be saved from the Roman destruction. But those were inserted into no register. Furthermore, when mention is made in the Holy Scriptures of inscription in life or in a book or the book of life, or in heaven, the elect and the faithful are designated, and their predestination and election to eternal life. For Holy Scripture sometimes names the inscription in a book Exod. 32, 32. Dan. 12, 1. sometimes makes mention of the book of the living and the writing with the just Psalm 69, 29. sometimes of the book of life, in which are the names of the faithful, Phil. 4, 2. Apoc. 3, 5. ch. 13, 8. ch. 17, 8. ch. 20, 15. ch. 21, 26. sometimes simply the book of life Apoc. 20, 12. Ch. 22, 19. sometimes names are said to be written in heaven Luke 10, 20. Thirdly, the discourse is about the advent of the Messiah, who is called the sprout of Jehovah, who is said to be about to be a magnificence and beauty to those who shall have been saved: and thus to the faithful in the time of the N.T., the remnant of the Jews: whose phrase this is: who are written in life. Therefore, without doubt, the elect to eternal life are designated by this phrase. Fourthly, those are said to be written in life who shall have been left holy in Jerusalem: whose filth shall be washed away. But were all the returning exiles holy? Fifthly, to those written in life, gracious protection, and defense, and other spiritual benefits are promised. Therefore, this is not to be understood of a bodily return, or a register of those returning. Therefore the Chaldean Paraphrase renders it, to eternal life. Our theologians interpret it concerning the book of life and the elect from the Jewish people; as also Zwingli, Junius, and others of the Reformed; Jerome understands it particularly of the Apostles and those who believed through them.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

IN ILLA DIE ERIT GERMEN DOMINI IN MAGNIFICENTIA ET GLORIA] Hic debuerat in- choari nova sectio. Est enim sermo de realia. Germen Domini sunt primo sensu reliquiæ exulum, quæ Esdræ ac Nehemiæ temporibus domum reversæ laudabilem vitam duxerunt: μυστικῶς autem Christus, & Christiani.

Non est, quod arguatur textus Ebræi distin- ctio. Quamvis enim Prophetia Evangelica hic inchoetur, eam tamen cohærere cum prædi- ctione antecedenti, atque ad eadem pertinere tem- pora, ut rectius intelligeretur, partem aliquam pri- oris vaticinii ad præsens caput referre voluit, qui capita distinxit. Quam cohærentiam etiam indica- vit temporis designatione Sp. Sanctus, IN DIE IL- LA erit germen. Unde dubitari non debet, utram- que prophetiam ad eadem tempora spectare. Dum autem reliquias populi intelligit Grotius per germen Domini, Judaizat more sibi proprio & perpetuo: sed vim textui facit. Num enim in illa die, qua se- ptem mulieres virum unum apprehendent, h. e. cladis Babylonica, secundum Grotium, tanta fuit magni- ficentia reliquiarum populi? aut num illa die rever- sæ illæ jam erant, qua clades tanta accidit? Confun- duntur ita tempora cladis Babylonicæ cum sere- nioribus illis temporibus liberationis populi, quæ 70. annis separata sunt. Tum vero quomodo pro- bitur, germen Domini & fructum terræ esse reli- quias populi reduces? Et quomodo magnificentiam & gloriam germinis de vita laudabili intelligemus, quum hæc maximopere distincta sunt, magnifi- centia & gloria, nec non decor & sublimitas & vita laudabilis? Porro si de reliquiis istis sermo, quo- modo germen de Christo explicari potest, aut quod absurdius, de Christo simul & Christianis? Num reliquiæ illæ typi Christi, aut etiam Christianorum fuêre? & in quonam ratio typi consistit? aut quo- modo tam disparati sensus eidem loco congruunt? Si de die reditus è captivitate Babylonica sermo, quo- modo dies illa de die vel tempore N. Test. intelligi potest? Unus ergo tantum sensus vaticinii hujus, uti aliorum omnium, est, qui à Sp. Sancto intendi- tur, ac communiter literalis dicitur; juxta quem plerique omnes Christiani Interpp. etiam è Judeis nonnulli hæc de diebus Messiæ intelligunt, quamvis in voce germinis explicanda non conveniant, quam alii de Messia ipso, alii de fidelibus & Ecclesia Christi tempore N. T. explicant. Quas sententias una cum Judaico commento commiscet Grotius, ut scil. omnibus placeat, sed perperam & absurde.

Messiam autem per germen Jehovah secundum literam hic intelligi potior Interpp. pars statuit; cui nos suffragamur: (1.) quia nomen hoc peculia- riter proprium in vaticiniis est Messiæ, qui germen à Prophetis indigitatur Ier. 23, 6. 33, 16. Zach. 3, 8. 6, 12. de quo etiam radix ipsa צמח germinavit, sæpius usurpatur Psal. 24, 12. 132, 17. Esa. 43, 19. c. 61, 11. 12. Zachar. 6, 12. Qua voce simili נצר surculus ab E- saia quoque designatus est Cap. 11, 1. (2.) Nomen צמח יהוה per appositionem explicatur Germen Iehovah vel Dominus, vel per regimen germen Iehovæ seu Domini. Priori sensu de alio, quam Christo accipi non potest, qui & germen est, & Iehovah. Posteriori sensu Christo iterum opti- me convenit. Nam is germen Jehovæ DEI Patris est ratione divinæ naturæ respectu æternæ regenerationis, & præterea germen Dei Patris dici potest respectu humanæ naturæ, quod à Patre mun- do detur ipsique summe acceptabile sit. Additur & alia appellatio פרי הארץ fructus terræ. Unde pri- orem ad divinam naturam, hanc v. posteriorem vo- cem ad humanam referunt Interpp. nonnulli. Vo- cat Propheta, inquit Osiander, Christum germen Domini, ut significet, eum esse filium Dei ab æterno ge- nitum Patri consubstantialem. Paulo post appellat fructum terræ ad asserendam ejus veram humanita- tem. Homo enim terra est Gen. 3. quæ etiam Brentii est & Gesn. explicatio. Vinarienses tamen utrum- que nomen ad ortum humanitatis Christi referunt.

(3.) Magnificentia illa & sublimitas cui magis con- venit, quam Christo? imo quodnam germen est, cui illa convenire queat, nisi germen justum Davidis, Jehovah Messias, justitia nostra Jer. 23, 6. Quis ex- ultatio vel decor fidelibus, nisi Christus, in quo uno gloriari oportet 1. Cor. 1, 31. Sic enim de germine illo Propheta: In die illa erit germen Domini in ma- gnificentia & in gloria, & fructus terræ sublimis, & exultatio his, qui salvati fuerint de Israel. Vel ut in Ebræo est, decor evasioni Israel. Ideo B. Luthe- rus: Germen Domini & fructus terræ Christus est. Is, inquit, erit in majestate & gloria, extolletur su- per omnes adversarios, vivet & abunde nobis dabit omnia. Et Bernhard. ferm. 2. de Pentec. Istud ger- men, quod de virga Jesse virore virginis pullulavit, in magnificentia fuit, cum resurrexisset à mortuis, quia tunc, Domine Deus meus, magnificatus es vehemen- ter, confessionem & decorem induens, amictus lumine sicut vestimento. Quanta autem adscendentis gloria, cum medius angelorum & animarum sanctarum ad Patrem deduceris, & triumphali palma cælis inve- ctas susceptum hominem in ipsa divinitatis & laudis identitate? Quis cogitet, nedum quam sit fructus Jes- sæ sublimis in consessu ad dextram Patris, quod utique cælestium oculos reverberat naturarum, quod angeli- cus intuitus contremit, non attingit. Veniat ergo ex- altatio Domine Jesu his, qui salvati sunt de Israel. Dum Oecolampadium in h. l. confero, video eun- dum hoc argumentum nostrum graviter urgere: Ideo locum ejus adscribam ex hypomnemat. in Es. l. 2. f. 43. Sensus est: Ille qui est germen Domini & fructus terræ, erit gaudium & gloria eorum, qui tunc liberati fuerint, hoc est, omnium fidelium. Illi enim non rejicient Christum, sed sequentur toto corde, Spi- ritu Sancto exhilarati, eritq́; omne gaudium, & exul- tatio eorum, non in divitiis, non in honoribus, non in luxu vestium, epularum, ædium magnificarum, pom- parum: nec sicut Pharisæi in suis jejuniis, orationi- bus & operibus, sed in germine illo. Sopho. 3. Lauda filia Zion, jubila Israel, lætare & exulta in omni cor- de, filia Hierusalem, abstulit Dominus judicium tuum, avertit inimicos tuos. Rex Israel Dominus in medio tui. Unde & beata virgo: Magnificat anima mea in Domino, & exultavit Spiritus meus in Deo salu- tari meo. 1. Cor. 1. Christus factus nobis à Deo sa- pientia, justitiaque & sanctificatio ac redemtio. Ut quemadmodum scriptum est, qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Hier. 9. In hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, scire & nosse me, quia ego sum Dominus, qui facio mi- sericordiam & judicium & justitiam. Quantum autem gaudium Christus attulerit suis, dicit Joannes: Vidi- mus gloriam ejus, quasi unigeniti à Patre, plenum gra- tia & veritate. Annon gaudium & gloria, sublimitas & magnificentia visus est Christus illis, qui propter eum relinquebant omnia, quibus præter Christum ni- hil placebat, qui & pro Christo cum gaudio mori non detrectabant. Atque adeo illa vera felicitas est.

(4.) Describuntur hic beneficia, quæ per Messiam nobis obtingunt, uniceque germini justo Messiæ accepto ferenda sunt: utpote sanctificatio, electio vel inscriptio in librum vitæ, ablutio sordium peccati, Spiritus Sancti, Spiritus judicii & ardoris donatio, ac gratiosa protectio. Sic enim Propheta noster: Et creabit Dominus supra omnem locum montis Sion, &

ubi invocatus est, nubem per diem & fumum & splen- dorem ignis flammantis in nocte. LXX. reddunt: Et veniet, & erit omnis locus montis Sion & omnia, quæ in circuitu ejus sunt: proteget nubes per diem, & lumen ignis flammantis in nocte. Ad quæ verba Hie- ronymus in h. l. Quis autem veniet nisi ille, de quo scriptum est; Veniet ex Sion, qui liberet. Et de quo alius Propheta commemorat: Adhuc paululum mo- dicum, qui venturus est, veniet, & non tardabit. Cum ille venerit, reddetur populo felicitas pristina, quam aliquando habuere in eremo: præcedente Domino eos per diem in columna nubis, & per noctem in colu- mna ignis: ut nec in prosperis, nec in adversis ali- quando turbentur. Cyrillus ad h. l. ut vitæ hujus æstum & probationes, quæ ex tentationibus profici- scuntur, atque ustiones fugiant hi, qui Sion intelligi- bilem habitant: id est, Ecclesiam, nubis instar pro- pemodum impendebit, & protector erit Christus ipse, ignorationis & Diabolicæ nequitiæ dispellet tenebras, illucescens menti tanquam lux in caligine & tanquam ignis coruscatio.

Quod exponit Propheta, cum addit: Erit enim protectio super omnem gloriam; h. e. super Eccle- siam, quæ præ aliis regnis hujus mundi sola est præ- cipue gloriosa in conspectu Dei, & super omnes credentes in Christum, quæ & ipsi præ omnibus hu- jus terræ Monarchis sunt coram Deo gloriosi, ut pulchre hic Brentius: præeunte in glossa margina- li B. Luthero, qui in Comment. ad h. l. egregie to- tum hunc locum illustrat. Hactenus, inquit ad vers. 5. Tom. 3. Oper. Lat. Jenens. p. 295. descripsit opu- lentiam regni Christi, item distributionem donorum spiritualium, & vim efficaciam purgandi. Quia autem Satan hanc cognitionem ferre non potest, & noster Rex est absconditus, neque arma nobis tradita sunt ad vindicandum nos, sed mandatum ad paren- dum & sustinendum. Ideo jam crucem quoque attin- git. Dominus, inquit, Sion, id est, Ecclesiam suam, quæ propter illud germen in periculo est, tuebitur ac defendet. Christus erit vera nubes, id est, refrigera- bit, & consolabitur suos. Et erit ignis, qui lucebit in tentationibus. In eo erit robur & virtus creden- tium &c. Et postmodum: Hoc autem diligenter discite, quod Propheta hic monet, solum Christum esse constitutum, ut sit protectio & umbraculum laboran- tium æstu & pluvia. In hunc figite oculos, in hoc hæ- rete, sicut etiam divina voce monemini, Hunc audite. Qui alium audit, qui præter hanc carnem aliud spe- ctat, de illo actum est. Hic enim solus nos protegit ab æstu, qui oritur ex majestatis contemplatione. Solus nos defendit à pluvia & violentia Satanæ. Hæc um- bra nobis dat refrigerium, ut abeant illæ cogitationes iræ. Neque enim potest ira ibi adesse, ubi pro te vides traditum Filium Dei in mortem, ut tu viveres. Qua- re commendo vobis appellationes illas Christi, quibus eum Propheta ornat, quod sit tabernaculum in um- bram ab æstu. Refugium & absconsio à pluvia & tur- bine. Hæc B. Lutherus.

5. Grotii & eorum interpretatio, qui per germen Ecclesiam intelligunt, non congruit textui, in quo Ecclesia & credentes distinguuntur ab hoc germi- ne, ac germen hoc ab Ecclesia vel credentibus, illis nempe, qui salvati fuerint de Israel, vel qui relicti fuerint in Sion, & residui in Jerusalem, adeoque san- ctis, qui scripti sunt in vita, aperte separatur, ac illius decor & exaltatio dicitur. Quo argumento convi- ctus Junius videtur, ut Calvini Præceptoris senten- tiam relinqueret, cujus verba adjicere placet: Tem- pore illo erit germen Jehovæ gloriæ & honori, id est, Ch. Jehovah infra v. 4. qui intermortuo regno Dei prope- modum excitatus est à Deo Patre & submissus, velut germen è radice epullulans; alii vero pro Ecclesia repullulante accipiunt ex reliquiis Israëlis, hoc sensu: Ec- clesia ex reliquiis Israëlis collecta erit ornatissima, alii pro donis spiritualibus, quæ Jehova in Eccle- siam profundit: Sed cum proprium apud Prophetam nomen Ecclesiæ sit Israel, aut reliquiæ Israelis hoc ver- su & seqq. præterea gratia sive dona Dei evidentissimis verbis exprimantur: deinde hoc proprium sit attri- butum Christi, quod deinceps procedente tempore copiosius exposuit idem Propheta infr. 2. cujus sum- mam hoc caput continet, interpretationem hanc aliis prætulimus, denique ipsa quoque verborum consequu- tio simplicius ita construitur, quam si dixeris: erit germen Jehovæ reliquiis Israelis? id est, germinabunt à Jehovah: dona vero nusquam sic appellantur, sed Christus ipse hanc appellationem, & cognatas obtinet, infr. 2. Jerem. 23. & 33. Zach. 3. & 6. Hactenus Ju- nius. Equibus manifestum esse arbitror, quam iniqua censura notarir Calvinus Bernhardi, Lyrani, B. Lutheri, Brentii explicationem, quæ & nostro- rum Doctorum communi calculo roborata, & pe- nes Papisticos plerosque recepta etiam est. Locus hic quidem vulgo de Christo exponi solet, & cum per se plausibilis sit opinio, plus coloris accipit ex dicto Za- chariæ: Ecce eum, cujus nomen est Germen. Hoc idem etiam confirmat, quod Propheta non simpliciter, sed cum adjectione honorifica loquatur de hoc germi- ne, ac si Christi divinitatem commendare propositum esset. Postea enim addit, fructus terræ, hoc ad huma- nam naturam referunt. Sed omnibus propius expen- sis non dubito, germen Dei & fructum terræ accipere pro copioso & insolito gloriæ proventu, quo famelicos recreabit. Perinde enim loquitur, ac si terra post va- stationem sterilis & squalore obsita, nullum Germen in futurum promitteret, quo magis insolitâ fœcundi- tate optabilem reddat Dei gratiam, ac si agri jejuni & steriles inexpectatam herbam producerent. Huc qui- dem spectat Prophetæ consilium, gloriam Dei fore il- lustrem, cum exorietur nova Ecclesia, ac se è nihilo crearet sibi populum, ac bonis omne genus locupletaret. Qui restringunt ad Christi personam, ridiculos se fa- ciunt Judæis, ac si proprie Scripturæ locos in suum commodum TORQUERENT. Sed quam teme- rarium hoc sit judicium, & glossa quam jejuna atq; inconcinna, jam Calvini Præceptor Oecolampadius, & Discipulus Franc. Junius docuêre. Judæis vero tantum abest, ut ridiculum sit, hunc locum de Chri- sto explicari, ut ab Oecolampadio discere potuerit Calvinus Targum & LXX. Interpp. Judæos hic no- biscum facere: cujus sententiam hic adjicio, ut inde Calvinum suum corrigant moderni utriusque Discipuli. Igitur hoc paragrapho, inquit, docet feli- citatem Ecclesiæ ex gaudio &SDK gloriatione in Christo, ex sanctitate & securitate. Dicitur autem hic Christus germen Domini, & fructus terræ. Nam & Patrem ha- bet in cœlis Deum, ut verus Deus, propter quod ger- men Domini dicitur: & matrem in terris ut verus homo, propter quod fructus terræ vocatur. Ecce ha- bes incarnationis mysterium. Hieronymus exponit germen, primitivam Ecclesiam: Sed rectius Lyranus & alii Christum, qui & Jerem. 23. Ecce dies veniunt, & suscitabo David germen justitiæ, & regnabit Rex, & sapiens erit. Et Thargum R. Jonathan hic mani- festè inquit: In tempore illo erit Messias Domini in gaudium & decorem. Græcus clarissime dicit ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἐκλάμψει θεὸς. In die illo effulge- bit Deus. Sensus ergo est: Ille qui est germen Do- mini & fructus terræ, erit gaudium & gloria eorum, qui tunc liberati fuerint, hoc est: omnium fidelium. Cætera quæ subjungit, antea adducta sunt, quæ utique commentis Calvini solidiora judicamus.

Vers. 2. OMNIS QVI SCRIPTVS EST IN VITA IN JERVSALEM.] Quicunque scribetur in matricula reducum,

Glossa satis frigida. Non de inscriptione in reducum matricula, sed in libro vitae, quem vocat Scriptura, sermo est. Nam non agi de exulum re- ductione Babylonica, sed de reliquiis Judaeorum, qui servabuntur e Romano exitio, jam ostensum. Illi vero nulli matriculae inserti sunt. Adhaec cum in- scriptionis in vita vel in libro aut libro vitae, vel in cae- lis in S. literis mentio fit, electi ac fideles designan- tur, eorundemque praedestinatio & electio ad vi- tam aeternam. Nam Scriptura Sacra modo inscri- ptionem in libro nominat Exod. 32, 32. Dan. 12, 1. modo libri viventium & scriptionis cum justis men- tionem facit Psalm. 69, 29. modo libri vitae, in quo sunt nomina fidelium, Phil. 4, 2. Apoc. 3, 5. cap. 13, 8. cap. 17, 8. c. 20, 15. c. 21, 26. modo libri vitae simplici- ter Apoc. 20, 12. Cap. 22, 19. modo nomina in caelis scripta dicuntur Luc. 10, 20. Tertio de adventu Messiae, qui germen Jehovah dicitur, sermo est, qui dicitur futurus magnificentia & decor his, qui sal- vati fuerint: adeoque fidelibus tempore N. T. reli- quiis Judaeorum: quorum haec phraseis est: qui sunt scripti in vita. Proinde sine dubio electi ad vi- tam aeternam hac phrasi designantur. Quarto illi inscripti in vita dicuntur, qui relicti fuerint sancti in Jerusalem: quorum sordes abluentur. At num omnes exules reduces sancti fuere? Quinto scri- ptis in vita gratiosa protectio, ac defensio, & alia beneficia spiritualia promittuntur. Non ergo de corporali reditu, aut redeuntium matricula haec intelligenda. Ideo Chaldaica Paraphrasis reddit, ad vitam aeternam. Theologi nostri de libro vitae ac electis e populo Iudaico interpretantur; ut & Zuin- glius, Iunius, aliique e Reformatis; Hieronymus pe- culiariter de Apostolis & qui per eos crediderunt, intelligit.

## 4:4
Ver. 4. IF THE LORD SHALL HAVE WASHED AWAY THE FILTH OF THE DAUGHTERS OF SION.) For if, put after. The sense is: these things will happen, when God shall have purged the people by a long calamity, and shall have shown them of what character are the people addicted to idols.

This is Grotius according to his preconceived gloss of the prophecy. But the Prophet says nothing about a return from Babylon, nor about a purging through long calamity: which certainly was not so much of those who returned, as of their parents: who, having met their fate within the 70 years of captivity in Babylon, did not return. That washing away of filth is to be understood as the cleansing from sins; which are called filth in Scripture. Therefore, the washing of the blood of Jerusalem is added, which the Prophet urged in ch. 1, 16. Your hands are full of blood; wash yourselves, be clean. Such is the washing which is proper to the saints and the faithful, written in life, or in the book of life. The washing is said to be done in the spirit of judgment, and of burning; concerning which Cyril says in this place. By the spirit of judgment he contends in judgment with this world, and with Satan: and the latter he casts out, as one inflicting injury: but those who were afflicted with injury he justified from the world through faith. The Spirit of burning, he says, we call the grace in Holy Baptism, generated in us not without the Spirit; since we are baptized with the Holy Spirit and with divine and intelligible fire, which wears away and consumes the filth of vice in us, and melts and smelts the defilement of sin. Cf. Mal. 3. B. Luther in this place. The Prophet attributes two offices to the Holy Spirit: it is the Spirit of judgment, by which Christ exercises judgment, so that He may condemn, purge, and mortify the old man. Moreover, the Spirit of judgment pertains to the filth, just as John calls Him the Spirit who convicts. He is called the Spirit of burning because He does not grow weary, but vehemently insists that we grow and be confirmed from day to day. Moreover, the Spirit of burning pertains to the blood, that is, to the guilt of blood. For our heart is unclean, and we are all murderers before GOD. Osiander's Paraphrase tends in the same direction: God will purge His Church from defilements of sins and crimes, which are signified by foul excrements and the uncleanness of menstrual blood. He will purge them, however, in the spirit of judgment and of burning, that is, the Son of God will cleanse His Church from sins, when with most ardent Zeal He will invade Satan, that He may overcome him and consign him by His just judgment to eternal torments (through His passion).

Latin:

Vers. 4. SI ABLVERIT DOMINVS SORDES FI- LIARVM SION.) Pro si, pone postquam. Sensus est: fient ista, ubi Deus longa calamitate populum expurgave- rit, & ostenderit illis quali ingenio sint populi idolis addicti.

Haec Grotius juxta praeconceptam Glossam vaticinii. At Propheta nec de reditu e Babylonia, nec de expurgatione per longam calamitatem, quic- quam habet: quae certe non tam fuit reducum, quam parentum eorundem: qui intra 70. annos captivitatis in Babylonia fatis functi, non reversi funt. Ablutio illa sordium de mundatione a pecca- tis intelligenda; quae sordes dicuntur in Scriptura. Ideo additur lotio sanguinis Jerusalem, quam sua- debat Propheta c. 1, 16. Manus vestrae sanguine ple- nae sunt; lavamini, mundi estote. Talis est ablutio, quae propria est sanctorum ac fidelium, scriptorum in vita, vel libro vitae. Dicitur ablutio fieri in spi- ritu judicii, & ardoris; de quo Cyrillus in h. l. Iu- dicii spiritus judicio contendit cum mundo hoc, & cum Satana: & hunc quidem ejicit, ut injuria afficien- tem: illos vero justificavit e mundo per fidem injuria affectos. Ardoris vero Spiritum, inquit, dicimus gra- tiam in S. Baptismo, non absque Spiritu nobis ingenera- tam; cum baptisati Sp. Sancto & igne divino, ac intel- ligibili, qui sordes vitiositatis in nobis deterit, ac absu- mit, & peccati inquinationem liquat, & excoquit. Conf. Mal. 3. B. Lutherus in h. l.
