Tribuit Propheta Spiritui Sancto duo officia: Spiritus judicii est, quo Christus judicium exercet, ut damnet, purget ac mor- tificet veterem hominem. Pertinet autem Spiritus ju- dicii ad sordes, sicut Iohannes vocat Spiritum arguen- tem. Spiritus ardoris dicitur, quod non defatige- tur, sed vehementer instet, ut de die in diem cresca- mus & confirmemur. Pertinet autem spiritus ardoris ad sanguinem h. e. ad reatum sanguinis. Immundum enim est cor nostrum, & omnes sumus homicidae co- ram DEO. Eodem tendit Osiandri Paraphrasis: Deus purgabit Ecclesiam suam ab inquinamentis peccatorum & scelerum: quæ per fœtida excremen- ta & immunditiem sanguinis menstrui significantur. Expurgabit autem ea in spiritu judicii & ardoris, id est, mundabit Filius Dei Ecclesiam suam à peccatis, cum ardentissimo Zelo invadet Satanam, ut eum de- vincat & justo suo judicio æternis cruciatibus addicat; Ecclesiam v. suam ex ipsius tyrannide (per passionem suam) liberet.

## 4:5
Ver. 5. AND THE LORD WILL CREATE UPON EVERY PLACE OF MOUNT ZION, AND WHERE HE HATH BEEN CALLED UPON, A CLOUD BY DAY, AND SMOKE, AND THE SPLENDOR OF A FLAMING FIRE BY NIGHT.] In the Hebrew it is: Upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon every assembly thereof. But often among the Hebrews, by similar things other similar things are understood, as here by the cloud by day, and the fire by night, the protection of God, no less present than it was of old to the Israelites who had gone out from Egypt. And the Hebrews experienced this almost up to the times of Antiochus.

Ver. same. UPON ALL THE GLORY A PROTECTION] That is, they will be protected even more than at that time of the exodus. For in that cloud was the glory of the Lord, that is, the conspicuous majesty. Exod. 16, 10. 24, 16. Num. 14, 10.

Thus Grotius understands glory as the majesty of the protecting God: but neither the words nor the context allow it. For the protection of God is distinguished from glory, and protection is said to be over the glory. So that the object of protection, to whom this glory will accrue, i.e., the Church, which is the glory of God, and glorious in the sight of God, may be established; just as UPON EVERY PLACE of Zion [there is] a cloud and the splendor of fire: so UPON ALL THE GLORY [there is] a protection. And these mutually declare each other. Therefore nothing is more certain than that it is implied that over the faithful or the Churches of Christ, which are glorious and lovely in the eyes of the Lord, and in which the glory of God shines, there will be a covering of protection, because God will protect them with His grace.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET CREABIT DOMINUS SUPER O- MNEM LOCUM MONTIS SION, ET UBI INVO- CATUS EST, NUBEM PER DIEM, ET FUMUM, ET SPLENDOREM IGNIS FLAMMANTIS IN NO- CTE.] In Hebræo est: Super omne habitaculum montis Sion, & super omnem cætum ejus. Sæpe autem apud He- bræos per res similes aliæ res similes intelliguntur, ut hic per nubem de die, & ignem de nocte, præsidium Dei, non minus præsens, quam olim Israëlitus ex Ægy- pto egressis adfuit. Et experti id sunt Hebræi ferme ad tempora usque Antiochi.

Vers. eod. SUPER OMNEM ENIM GLORIAM PROTECTIO] Id est, magis etiam protegentur, quam illo tempore exitus. Nam in illa nube erat gloria Domini, id est, conspicua majestas. Exod. 16, 10. 24, 16. Num. 14, 10.

Sic Grotius gloriam intelligit protegentis Dei ma- jestatem: sed neque verba neque contextus pati- tur. Nam protectio Dei à gloria distinguitur, & super gloriam protectio esse dicitur. Ut objectum protectionis, cui hæc obtinget gloria, h. e. Eccle- sia, quæ Dei gloria est, & gloriosa in conspectu Dei, constituatur; uti SUPER OMNEM LO- CUM Sion nubes & splendor ignis: ita SUPER OMNEM GLORIAM protectio. Atque hæc mutuo se declarant. Ideo nihil certius, quam quod innuatur, super fideles vel Ecclesias Christi, quæ in oculis Domini gloriosæ sunt & amabiles, & in qui- bus gloria Dei refulget, protectionum operimen- tum fore, quia Deus proteget easdem gratia sua.

## 4:6
AND THE TABERNACLE SHALL BE FOR A SHADOW IN THE DAY FROM THE HEAT, AND FOR A SECURITY AND A HIDING PLACE FROM THE WHIRLWIND AND FROM THE RAIN] That is, just as the covering of a tent defended the Israelites of old from the Sun, wind, and rain, so now God will render these safe from all evils. See the History of Ezra 4. 5. 6. Nehem. 4.

Latin:

ET TABERNACULUM ERIT IN UMBRACVLVM DIEI AB ÆSTV, ET IN SECVRITATEM ET AB- SCONSIONEM A TVRBINE ET A PLVVIA] Id est, sicut tentorii regmen defendebat olim Israëlitus à Sole, vento & pluvia, sic nunc hos Deus ab omnibus malis tu- tos præstabit. Vide Historiam Esdræ 4. 5. 6. Nehem. 4.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

The cause of the devastated vineyard lies not with God, who planted it, but with the people, in [their] avarice, drunkenness, iniquity, [and] contempt of the word of God, whence a sign is to be raised up among the nations against the Jews.

I WILL SING TO MY BELOVED] In honor of God, whom I love most, I will sing. That this is the sense is evident below [in verse] 7. A SONG OF MY KINSMAN.] For דוֹדִי also here the LXX read דוֹדַי, altogether more correctly; he says that he will speak those things which God could say by the best of rights. OF HIS VINEYARD] That is, about his vineyard. Namely, of the people of the 12 tribes, as the word itself explains. IN A HORN THE SON OF OIL] That is, on a very fertile mountain. Thus also the Chaldean understood it here.

By both names, therefore, he understands God the Father; but although some admit that God the Father is designated by 'beloved,' they say that the Son of God is indicated by the other word. Others, however, understand the Messiah by both. That is certainly certain, that the Father cannot be understood, but that the Messiah is designated in the latter place. As one whom the Prophet calls his kinsman because of the kinship which exists between him and the same [person], by reason of the flesh. Since, therefore, Grotius sees that the word דוֹדִי 'my kinsman' does not suit God the Father, he accuses the authentic text of corruption, and pretends that it previously had דוֹדַי 'my beloved'; and he invents this sense of the words, which in the Hebrew, Latin, and other texts have, A SONG OF MY KINSMAN, that he says he will speak those things which God could say by the best of rights. But under what pretext? Because the LXX read it so. But we deny that they read it so. For it has been frequently warned that from the words of their version it cannot be concluded beyond doubt what the reading of the words of the authentic text is: since they have not always followed the letter of the word, but have not rarely expressed the sense which they themselves had conceived in their mind. Therefore, one must adhere more to the Hebrew Codices. And it is known that Jerome also in Canticles rendered this word as 'beloved'; because he believed it made no difference to the sense in which way it is explained. Here, however, both Aquila explained it as 'kinsman' and Jerome as 'kinsman,' which the genuine meaning of the word brings about. Cyril, although he reads with the LXX 'to the beloved,' nevertheless explains it concerning Christ, who is so called by the Father in Matt. 3, 17. Jerome explains it in two ways: First thus: This beloved (Christ) made a mournful song for his vineyard: which I will sing to my beloved and miserable people. Then, however, in this way: I will sing to the omnipotent God the Father a Song of Christ, who is my kinsman, that is, generated from the same nation as I.

He calls Christ his cousin; because he is a kinsman to him, and it is handed down that Amos, the father of Amaziah, King of Judah, who is reckoned among the ancestors of Christ according to the flesh in Matthew 1, was the brother of Isaiah. He calls it the Song of the Cousin, which, to wit, Christ could have used at that time concerning the Israelites, and was to use concerning the same in the fullness of time, Matthew 21:33, regarding the divine beneficence toward the people, and the detestable ingratitude and malice of the people toward God.

Verse of the same. ON A HORN, THE SON OF OIL. For the word 'in cornu' [on a horn], which Pagninus rendered 'in colle' [on a hill], the Chaldean has 'in monte excelso' [on a high mountain]. A horn, says Musculus, is called a little hill curved in the manner of a horn and exposed to the morning, midday, and afternoon sun. 'The son of oil,' that is, fat, as if it were born of oil. The Chaldean and the LXX have 'in a fat land or place.' Doubtless, mountain vineyards are preferred to those which are in the plain. The Prophet understands, however, the land of Judah, concerning which both are known, that it is both high and fat, flowing with milk and honey. Such it was when Israel lived in the grace of God, as Scripture testifies; what it became afterward, because of the malice of its inhabitants, one may still see.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

Causa vastatæ vineæ non penes Deum, qui eam plantavit, sed populum, in avaritia, ebrie- tate, iniquitate, comtemtu verbi Dei sita, unde signum in nationibus elevandum con- tra Iudæos.

CANTABO DILECTO MEO] In honorem Dei, quem maxime diligo, cantabo. Hunc sensum esse patet infra 7. CANTICVM PATRVELIS MEI.] Pro דוֹדִי etiam hic דוֹדַי legerunt LXX. rectius omnino; dicit se ea di- cturum, quæ Deus jure optimo dicere posset. VINEÆ SVÆ] Id est, de vinea sua. Populo sc. 12. tribuum, ut ipsa vox explicat. IN CORNV FILIO OLEI] Id est, in monte pin- guissimo. Ita & Chaldæus hic accepit.

PEr utrumque ergo nomen intelligit Deum Pa- trem; sed quamvis per dilectum nonnulli Deum Patrem designari admittant, altera tamen voce Fi- lium Dei indigitari ajunt. Alii v. per utrumq; Messi- am intelligunt. Id sane certum est, Patrem intelli- gi non posse, sed Messiam designari posteriori loco. Utpote quem Propheta vocat patruelem suum ob cognationem, quæ ipsi cum eodem intercedit, ra- tione carnis. Quum ergo vocem דּוֹדִי Patruelis mei videat Grotius Deo Patri non convenire, corru- ptionis reum peragit textum authenticum, eun- demque prius habuisse דוֹדַי dilecti mei fingit; atq; hunc sensum comminiscitur verborum, quæ in E- bræo Latino, & aliis textibus habent, CANTICUM PATRUELIS MEI, quod dicat, se ea dicturum, quæ Deus jure optimo dicere posset. Sed quo prætex- tu? Quia LXX. ita legerunt. At negamus ita eos legisse. Sæpius n. monitum, è versionis ipsorum verbis non posse concludi indubitato lectionem verborum textus authentici: quum non semper verbi literam sequuti sint, sed sensum non raro, quem ipsi animo conceperant, expresserint. Magis ergo inhærendum Ebræis Codicibus. Et notum est, quod Hieronymus etiam in Cant. vocem hanc dilectus reddiderit; quod ad sensum interesse nihil crediderit, utro modo exponatur. Hic autem tum Aquila πατράδελφον, tum Hieronymus Patruelem exposuit, quod infert vocis genuina significatio. Cyrillus quamvis cum LXX. legat τῷ ἀγαπητῷ, exponit tamen de Christo, qui à Patre ita vocatur Matth. 3, 17. Hieronymus bifariam exponit: Pri- mo ita: Hic dilectus (Christus) carmen lugubre fecit vineæ suæ: quod ego cantabo dilecto atque miserabili populo meo. Deinde v. hoc modo: Cantabo o- mnipotenti Deo Patri Canticum Christi, qui est Pa- truelis meus, hoc est, ex eadem gente mecum generatus.

Patruelem autem vocat Christum; quia cogna- tus ei est, traditurque, quod Amos Esaiæ Pater Ama- siæ, Regis Judæ, qui inter Majores Christi secun- dum carnem recensetur Matth. 1. frater fuerit. Canticum Patruelis nominat, quo sc. Christus & isto tempore uti potuerit de Israë̈litis, & in plenitu- dine temporis de iisdem usurus erat Matth. 21, 33. de divina erga populum beneficentia, & detestanda populi adversus Deum ingratitudine, ac malitia.

Vers. eod. IN CORNU FILIO OLEI. Pro voce in cornu, quam Pagninus reddidit in colle, Chald. habet, in monte excelso. Cornu, ait Mu- sculus, vocatur colliculus in modum cornu incurvus ac soli antemeridiano, meridiano & pomeridiano exposi- tus. Filio olei, id est, pingui, adeo ac si natus esset ex oleo. Chald. & LXX. in terra vel loco pingui. Nimirum præferuntur vineæ montanæ iis, quæ sunt in planitie. Intelligit autem Propheta terram Judaicam, de qua utrumque notum, quod sit & al- ta, & pinguis, fluens lacte, ac melle. Tum talis erat cum Israël in gratia Dei viveret, teste Scriptura; Qualis postea facta sit, propter malitiam inhabi- tantium, etiamnum videre licet.

## 5:2
Verse 2. AND HE HEDGED IT ABOUT] Lest travelers should easily run into it. Thus God rendered the people obedient to Him safe from the violence of their neighbors.

It is therefore often the divine providence by which the Lord's vineyard was guarded, lest it be laid waste by wild beasts, the neighboring nations being sufficiently wild.

AND HE GATHERED OUT THE STONES THEREOF] He cleared it of stones, as Pliny speaks. Thus God cast out of the Israelite land the stony gods and their worshippers.

The Vulgate, ELEGIT [chose], is not sufficiently convenient: Saa indeed tries to assist it thus, that is, he cast out of it, as if he were to say, he purged it of stones. Some render the Hebrew, 'and he built with stones,' or 'he fortified it,' as Saa himself interpreted from the LXX interpreters, 'he surrounded it with the material of stones.' But Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Avenarius, and others are pleased with what pleased Grotius; and that meaning of the removal or ejection of stones from a place is confirmed by Isaiah 62:10, where the same word occurs concerning removing stones from the way: and such an ejection of stones contributes to the purging of the vineyard. The hedge, the winepress, the tower, and the clearing of stones signify in general that God has cultivated the Church in all things, says Corn. a Lap. But he understands more correctly that the stones which God took away from the vineyard are not only idols, but also sins and all impediments to divine worship and religion.

AND HE PLANTED IT WITH THE CHOICEST VINE] Better: He planted it with a noble vine. He gave to it the land of Joshua and the Judges, excellent men.

Saa also amends the Vulgate for this reason: that the Lord planted the vineyard with most noble vines; and so also Corn. à Lapid. understands the Patriarchs: But it is better rather to extend those generous vines, from which also the Prophets and pious Kings, and others of the faithful of ancient time were.

AND HE BUILT A TOWER IN THE MIDST THEREOF] Namely, for the protection of the vineyard. Thus the city of Jerusalem in a most fortified place, in the midst of Judea.

AND HE DUG A WINEPRESS IN IT] An altar flowing with the blood of victims.

The Chaldean interprets the tower as the Sanctuary. Origen, Jerome, Bede, Euthymius, and Theophylact understand it as the Temple. Some explain the tower as Holy Scripture, as in Cant. 4:4. Cornelius à Lapide wishes for the Doctors and Pastors themselves, and the watchmen of the people, to be designated by the tower. But they rather look out from the temple as if from a tower and fortress, as from their watchtower, and there they keep watch for the vineyard, Isa. 62:6, Ezek. 3:17, Hab. 2:1. Musculus on this passage says: The tower, he says, in the midst of the Lord's vineyard was Zion, a watchtower assigned for the guarding of the whole vineyard, to which were appointed guards, namely, the priests, elders, judges, and princes of the people. What is added concerning the WINEPRESS is not to be referred to the altar, but is subjoined by way of similarity, because the Ministers of the word and the Prophets labor not only to warn of imminent dangers of soul and body that are to be avoided, but also to express the sweet juice of piety by their doctrine and exhortations, just as must is wont to be expressed from ripe grapes in a winepress. A certain winepress, says Musculus, was the ministry of the Prophets, for extracting the fruit of true piety. Some apply it to the winepress of the cross, just as is held concerning the winepress of wrath in Isa. 63:3; but the explanation concerning the Ministry is simpler.

AND IT BROUGHT FORTH WILD GRAPES] The Greeks [say] Ἀκάνθας. The Hebrew word באש or באשה signifies every vice of the field, and is translated both as σαπρὶα and βάτ␄. Thus the Israelites brought forth idolatry, murders, and adulteries.

The Chaldean explained grapes as good works, and wild grapes as wicked works, rendering the sense, not the words. But what those are, the subsequent ἐξήγησις, or explanation of the parable, in v. 7 and following, teaches, namely: injustice, v. 7; avarice, v. 8; drunkenness and security, v. 11 and following; conspiracy in iniquity, v. 18, 19; total perversity, by which they knowingly and willingly make good out of evil and evil out of good, v. 20; the persuasion of one's own wisdom with contempt for true wisdom, v. 21 (Compare Prov. 3:7, Rom. 12:3); drunkenness, v. 22; bribery, v. 23; the rejection and blaspheming of the divine word, v. 24. On account of which a final destruction is at last announced to them by the Romans, v. 26. Therefore the Son of GOD grieves and complains that the outcome did not correspond to His gracious will, and expectation, and the cultivation of so diligent a vineyard; and that instead of good and sweet fruits, the Jews brought forth the worst and utterly useless ones, and that not only in those times of Isaiah, but also in the most recent ones, which He indulged them with by His kindness. For this complaint does not only look to those times, but since He foresees no amendment, nay rather greater increases of impiety, on account of which the final πανολεθρία (total destruction) is at last to follow, it is to be believed that they are excited to repentance by this most grave legal discourse, so that because the matter is concluded and utterly desperate, a final destruction is simultaneously indicated: which is manifest from the preceding [chapters], concerning which [we spoke] around chapter 1, and those things which follow in chapter 6. For it is the same people, not by reason of time and the numerical unity of individuals, but by reason of succession, and the same political and ecclesiastical society and communion, until the same is abolished: And therefore it is dealt with as one people and one vineyard, once planted, and to be preserved until it is utterly devastated by its own fault, the rain of grace having been often removed, and it having been utterly left in its desolation forever, so that it brings forth nothing but thorns and thistles. That this indicates the ultimate and final destruction is clear, v. 5, 6. Compare Matt. 21:41, 43. Therefore, [the phrase] I WILL COMMAND THE CLOUDS THAT THEY RAIN NOT, Cornel. a Lapid. explains thus from Jerome, Cyril, and Basil: The sense is, as if it were said: I, God, will forbid the Apostles and their followers (whom he understands by the clouds from Isa. 60:8, Joel 2:23, following Jerome) to water the Jews with the rain of holy Doctrine and the Gospel, but [I will command them] to pour it out upon the Gentiles. To this point tend those WOES, which are likewise repeated by Christ on account of the sins and impenitence of the Jews at length in Matt. 23, on account of which a final extermination is announced to them there in v. 38, which are to be compared entirely with these complaints and threats. For they explain each other.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET SEPIVIT EAM] Ne viatores facile in eam incurrerent. Sic Deus populum sibi parentem à vi finitimorum tutum præstitit.

Sæpe ergo est divina providentia, qua custodita est Domini vinea, ne à feris, gentibus vicinis satis feris, vastaretur.

ET LAPIDES ELEGIT EX EA] Elapidavit eam, ut Plinius loquitur. Sic Deus è terra Israelitica ejecit lapi- deos Deos, & illorum cultores.

Non satis commode Vulgata, ELEGIT: quam ita quidem juvare conatur Saa, id est, ejecit ex ea, quasi dicat, purgavit eam à lapidibus: Nonnulli Ebræa reddunt, & lapidibus construxit, vel muni- vit eam, uti ex LXX. Interpp. ipse Saa interpretatus est, lapidum materia cinxit. Sed Pagnino, Aria- montano, Avenario, aliisque placet, quod Grotio placuit; & confirmatur illa significatio remotionis vel ejectionis lapidum è loco Esa. 62, 10. ubi ea- dem vox occurrit de removendis è via lapidibus: Facitque talis ejectio lapidum ad vineæ purgatio- nem. Sepes, torcular, turris, elapidatio significant in genere, Deum Ecclesiam per omnia excoluisse, ait Corn. à Lap. Rectius autem non de solis idolis, sed etiam de peccatis, omnibusque divini cultus ac re- ligionis impedimentis lapides, quos Deus è vinea abstulit, intelligit.

ET PLANTAVIT EAM ELECTAM] Melius: Conse- vit eam generosa vite. Dedit ei terræ Josuam & Judices vi- ros egregios.

Emendat & Saa ea ratione Vulgatam: quod vi- tibus nobissimis conseverit vineam Dominus; atque ita etiam Corn. à Lapid. Patriarchas intelligens: Sed præstat potius extendere vites illas generosas, è quibus etiam Prophetæ & Reges pii, aliique fide- les fuère antiqui temporis.

ET ÆDIFICAVIT TURRIM IN MEDIO EJUS] Nempe ad custodiam vineæ. Sic urbs Hierosolyma in lo- co munitissimo, in medio Judææ.

ET TORCVLAR EXSTRVXIT IN EA] Altare manans sanguine victimarum.

Turrim Sanctuarium exponit Chald. Templum Origenes, Hieronym. Beda, Euthym. Theophylact. intelligunt. Nonnulli turrim de Scriptura S. ex- plicant, ut Cant. 4,4. Cornelius à Lap. per turrim etiam ipsos Doctores & Pastores, speculatores- que populi designari vult. Sed illi potius ex templo quasi turri & arce ceu specula sua prospi- ciunt, ibique vigilant pro vinea Esa. 62, 6. Ezech. 3, 17. Hab. 2, 1. Musculus in h. l. Turris, inquit, in medio vineæ Domini Zion erat, specula custodiæ totius vineæ deputata, cui erant impositi custodes, sacer- dotes videlicet, seniores, judices ac principes populi. Quod de TORCULARI additur, non ad altare referendum, sed vi similitudinis subjungitur, quod Ministri verbi & Prophetæ non modo de im- minentibus, & effugiendis periculis animæ & cor- poris monere, sed etiam doctrina & exhortationi- bus suis suavem pietatis succum exprimere labo- rent, veluti à maturis uvis in torculari mustum ex- primi solet. Torcular quoddam, inquit Musculus, erat ministerium Prophetarum, ad extorquendum veræ pie- tatis fructum. Nonnulli ad torcular crucis, quemad- modum de torculari iræ Ef. 63, 3. habetur, appli- cant; sed simplicior est explicatio de Ministerio.

ET FECIT LABRVSCAS] Græci Ἀκάνθας. Vox Hebræa באש vel באשה omne agri vitium significat, vertiturque & σαπρὶα, & βάτ␄. Sic Israëlitæ idolola- triam, cædes, adulteria protulerunt.

Chald. uvas exposuit per bona opera, labruscas per opera iniqua, sensum non verba reddendo. Quænam vero illa sint, subjuncta ἐξήγησις, vel ex- plicatio parabolæ, v. 7. seqq. docet, nimirum inju- stitia, v. 7. avaritia, v. 8. temulentia & securitas, v. 11. seqq. Conspiratio in iniquitate, v. 18. 19. summa per- versitas, qua ex malo bonum, ex bono malum scien- tes volentes faciunt, v. 20. propriæ sapientiæ persuasio cum comtemtu veræ sapientiæ, v. 21. (Conf. Prov. 3, 7. Rom. 12, 3,) ebriositas, v. 22. δωροφαγία v. 23. verbi divini rejectio & blasphematio, v. 24. Ob quæ finalis tandem interitus per Romanos ipsis indicitur v. 26. Id ergo dolet, & queritur Filius DEI, quod non re- sponderit eventus voluntati suæ gratiosæ, & ex- pectationi, ac culturæ tam sedulæ vineæ; quodque pro bonis & suavibus fructibus Judæi pessimos, & plane inutiles protulerint, idque non istis tantum Esaiæ temporibus, sed novissimis etiam, quæ ipsis benignitate sua indulsit. Hæc enim querela non modo illa respicit tempora, sed quum nullam e- mendationem, imo majora incrementa impietatis prævideat, ob quæ novissima πανολεθρία tandem subseqvutura fit, ita ad pœnitentiam hac concione legali gravissima eosdem excitari credendum est, ut ob rem conclamatam & desperatam penitus in- dicetur simul finalis interitus: quod ex antecedenti- bus, de quibus circa cap. 1. & iis, quæ c. 6. sequuntur, manifestum est. Idem enim est populus, non ra- tione temporis & numericæ individuorum unitatis, sed ratione successionis, & ejusdem politicæ, atque Ecclesia- stîœ societatis & communionis, donec eadem abo- leatur: Ideoque cum ipso agitur, ut uno populo & vinea una, semel plantata, & conservanda, donec culpa sua prorsus devastetur, sæpe protectionis di- vinæ ablata, pluvia gratiæ denegata, e aque penitus in desolatione sua in perpetuum relicta, ut non nisi spinas, & tribulos proferat. Quæ ultimum, & fina- le excidium indicare, in aprico est, v. 5. 6. Conf. Matth. 21, 41. 43. Ideo nulla, NUBIBUS MAN- DABO NE PLUANT Cornel. a Lapid. ex Hieron. Cyrillo, & Bafilio ita explicat: Sensus est, quasi dica- tur: Ego Deus vetabo Apostolis eorumque asseclis (quos per nubes intelligit ex Es. 60, 8. Ioel. 2, 23. præeunte Hieron.) ne Judæos rigent imbre sanctæ Doctrinæ, & Evangelii, sed eo gentes perfundant. Huc faciunt illa VÆ, quæ ingeminantur itidem a Christo ob peccata & impœnitentiam Judæorum prolixe Matth. 23. ob quæ ipsis exterminium fina- le ibidem indicitur v. 38. quæ cum his omnino con- ferenda sunt & querelis & comminationibus. Mu- tuo enim sese explicant.

## 5:3
Vers. 3. JUDGE BETWEEN ME AND MY VINEYARD] The great goodness of God, who permits men to judge concerning His actions, Compare Gen. 18:25 and following.

Thus Christ in Matt. 21, the planter of the vineyard, defers judgment to the hearers, and the Pharisees themselves pronounce the sentence: He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard to others.

Latin:

Vers. 3. JVDICATE INTER ME ET VINEAM MEAM] Magna Dei bonitas, qui de actionibus suis ju- dicium hominibus permittit, Conf. Gen. 18, 25. & seqq.

Sic Christus Matth. 21. plantator vineæ judicium defert auditoribus, & pronunciant ipsimet Pha- risæi sententiam, malos male perdet, illis & aliis co- lonis vineam elocabit.

## 5:4
Ver. 4. WHAT IS IT THAT I OUGHT TO HAVE DONE MORE TO MY VINEYARD, AND I HAVE NOT DONE TO IT.

The Son of GOD protests that He omitted nothing of those things which could be required for the cultivation of His vineyard among the Israelites, and therefore that He expended upon those who bear only wild grapes all that was to be expended so that they might bear grapes. Cf. Jer. 2, 21. Matt. 23, 37.

Ver. same. WHY DID I EXPECT THAT IT WOULD BRING FORTH GRAPES, AND IT BROUGHT FORTH WILD GRAPES] You might translate better: Why, when I expected it to produce grapes, did it produce tares?

He therefore objects to the Israelites their extreme impiety, ingratitude, and contumacy in return for the highest benefits, because they were strangers to the pursuits of piety and justice, and because they contaminated themselves with various crimes. For wild grapes, Aquila translated σαπρίας, rotten grapes, the worst fruits: the LXX, thorns: Symmachus ἀτελεῖς, imperfect, that is, unripe grapes. The Hebrew בְּאֻשִׁים means stinking: since they bring forth wild grapes that are not only not pleasing to God, but most adverse, as things that are stinking are wont to be unpleasant on account of their odor. This is a very illustrious passage concerning the efficacious grace of God, which He exhibits even to the reprobate themselves, so that they may be converted, and concerning the manner of divine operation in the conversion of men according to our Orthodoxy, against the absolute decrees and irresistible grace of the Calvinists. Because all the means necessary for bearing grapes were applied to the vineyard of the Lord by God the vinedresser, and indeed to that end, that it itself might bear fruit: and they were applied with such measure and fullness that the Lord protests: What is it that I ought to have done more to my vineyard, and I have not done to it? And so that He may publicly appeal to the judgment of the reprobate themselves, and convince them by their own judgment of the sufficiency of the means applied: and openly complain of the frustrated expectation of grapes. The Calvinists twist themselves greatly in trying to elide this classic passage, but in vain. For as to what they object, 1., those words, what is it that I ought to have done? that they do not treat of benefits, but of the punishments which the vineyard by its sterility has deserved, that is extremely inept, and contrary both to the words themselves, 'what is to be done' עוֹד ADHUC or AMPLIUS, which speak openly of further benefits, a heap of which he had just recounted, and to the whole context: in which first the benefits of God are celebrated, then the malice of the Jews is designated, and finally divine punishments are announced. And the Reformed themselves, Calvin, Musculus, Franz, Junius, acknowledge that this complaint is instituted concerning benefits exhibited in vain, and the desired fruits not produced by the Israelites. Calvin has it thus: He asks first, what could be desired from the best farmer or head of a household, which he himself did not provide for his vineyard. Hence he concludes, there is no excu sation, that he has been unworthily cheated of his labor. Although in the second member he seems to expostulate with himself, because he expected some pleasing or desirable fruit from so wicked a people, so that when the outcome does not respond to our expectation, we complain to ourselves, and are indignant that we have devoted effort in vain among the ungrateful, whose depravity ought to have restrained us: the SIMPLER sense here, however, will be that when I have performed ALL parts of my duty, and have surpassed the vows of all in the cultivation of my vineyard, how does it happen that he pays me back such an unjust reward, and for the hoped-for fruit brings forth mere bitterness. Musculus says, two things are to be observed here: one is, that God is not lacking in his duty. His duty, however, is to provide ALL things to his people which are NECESSARY for them. He protests that he has provided those things. The other is, that our condemnation will be in this, that we either do not embrace this grace of divine providence, or we misapply it, so that no excuse is left to us.

Franc. Junius explains the words of the Lord thus, as if he were saying, I appeal to your conscience, you yourselves recognize, and in good faith determine, through whom it stood that it did not bear fruit worthy of its condition: if even the slightest thing is desired from me by merit, I will provide it: but since I have FULLY performed my parts, what remains, unless the vineyard be said to be at fault? These things are those convinced by the force of truth. Calvin indeed tries subsequently to inject his heterodoxy, that God does not penetrate effectively by the power of his Spirit into the hearts of men, to render them obedient to himself, and adds that they complain in vain that this was lacking to them, since external calling removes the pretext of ignorance more than enough: but if the grace of God is not in itself and its nature effective, which is exhibited to the reprobate, do they not have an excuse, not indeed of ignorance, but of non-conversion, because, to wit, that grace was denied to them which is necessary for conversion: and how then would God have provided to the reprobate all things which he owed, or all things which were NECESSARY for them for conversion! how could they be condemned for grace either not received or misapplied, to whom that grace by which they could be converted was absolutely denied, and who, because of this absolute denial, could in no way receive or well apply the grace exhibited by external calling.

And therefore others 2. betake themselves to this with the Embdeners in the Dordrecht judgments, that parables do not make dogmas: But who does not know, I pray, that parables, when they are not extended beyond their scope, but one insists on the intention of the one proposing them, prove things effectively? The scope of the Lord, however, is to teach by this parabolic complaint, not that he, but the reprobate themselves are at fault, because they are not converted, not his grace, inasmuch as he denies it to no one, and had sufficiently exhibited it to the Israelites, or a defect, or inefficacy, but the malice of the reprobate, because they reject the grace of God, and place an obstacle in its way.

But as to what 3. Perkins and Molinæus in Anatomy c. 37, 41, 49 except, that only external means are considered here as sufficiently applied, but not the internal aid of grace, which is simply sufficient: since only mention is made of external things, namely the fertile replanting of the place, the placing of the hedge around, the clearing of stones, the building of the winepress, but not the secret vegetation, the mildness of the sky, the timely rain: To that I reply: That those external things are only commemorated because of the nature of the parable. For he who performs the duty of a vinedresser can provide nothing but external things. But that God, who is compared to the vinedresser, can and wills more, there is no doubt: indeed he protests that he has omitted nothing, and therefore expostulates with the vineyard. But if he had not applied the internal aid of grace, or had denied it by an absolute good pleasure, with what appearance of truth could he have thus protested and expostulated? And how could he expect a yield, who absolutely denies the necessary and sufficient means of the same, which he alone has in his hand? Would not the excuse of the Israelites have been ready, however various the benefits you have bestowed upon us, because nevertheless you have not bestowed upon us so much grace, indeed you have denied it out of mere good pleasure, as is necessary for us for this, that we may be converted, and bear fruit pleasing to you, we are not at fault, from whom is demanded that which we cannot provide, and for which the grace, which we need in order to provide it, is not offered, but [it is the fault of] him who demands from us what we cannot do, nor yet grants, or wishes to grant, that we may be able; see Defens. Remonstr. concerning article IV. in their Synodical Writings p. 89 seqq. Rightly therefore Augustine Epist. CV. Those to whom God does not impart mercy, so that he does not impart it, they deserve it.

Whence Henr. Bulling. in expos. Matth. Year 1542. C. 23, 37. Both the benefit of God and the ingratitude of the people is amplified by that, that he tried to save them not once, but many times; HOW OFTEN, he says, I wanted. But hear, how badly they responded to the beneficent Father! The most impious people did not want, I say, did not want to be gathered and saved in the friendship and covenant of God. They preferred to be scattered and destroyed. Whence they perished by their own fault, malice, and rebellion, not by any moroseness of God. For God wanted to save, and he attested this will of his not once, indeed HE MOVED EVERY STONE TO SAVE. But they did not want to be saved, where then are those who preach a certain most rigid FATE AND NECESSITY of sinning and perishing? Jerusalem COULD HAVE BEEN SAVED, if only it had wanted, that is, unless it had REPELLED the mercy and sound counsel of God. Therefore we cannot approve that Stoic necessity in the matter of salvation. The same Bullinger in Decad. sermon. Year 1562. Zurich edition, decade 5, sermon 7, p. 342. From this GRACE OF GOD (by which the sons of God are made from the sons of the Devil) no one is excluded, except he who excludes himself by his own vice and fault through disobedience. Which is certainly the grace of conversion. Let the other Reformed acknowledge this, and give glory to divine grace, nor let them accuse it as if it were ineffective for the reprobate, or restrict it to the elect alone out of the mere good pleasure of God, against the most clear testimonies of Scripture: Isa. 65:2, 12; Prov. 1:24; Ezek. 18:23, 32; ch. 33:11; 1 Tim. 2:4; 2 Pet. 3:9.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVID EST QVOD DEBVI VLTRA FA- CERE VINEÆ MEÆ, ET NON FECI EI.

Protestatur Filius DEI, nihil se intermisisse eo- rum, quæ ad culturam vineæ suæ penes Israëlitas requiri poterant, adeoq; omne illud impendisse iis, qui labruscas solum ferunt, quod impendendum erat, ut uvas ferrent, Conf. Jer. 2, 21. Matth. 23, 37.

Vers. eod. AN QVOD EXPECTAVI VT FACE- RET UVAS, ET FECIT LABRVSCAS] Melius ver- tas: Cur me expectante, ut produceret uvas, produxit lolium?

Objicit ergo Israëlitis extremam impietatem, ingratitudinem & contumaciam pro summis bene- ficiis, quod alieni fuerint a studiis pietatis & justi- tiæ, quodque variis se contaminaverint sceleribus. Pro labruscis transtulit Aquila σαπρίας putres u- vas, fructus pessimos: LXX. Spinas: Symmachus ἀτελεῖς imperfectas, id est, immaturas uvas. Ebr. בְּאֻשִׁים est fœtentes: quum non modo non gratas Deo, sed maxime adversas, ut fœtida ob odorem in- gratumesse solent, proferant labruscas. Est autem lo- cus hic valde illustris de gratia Dei efficace, quam ex- hibet ipsis etiam reprobis, ut convertantur, & de mo- do operationis divinæ in conversione hominum pro Orthodoxia nostra, adversus absoluta decreta, & gratiam irresistibilem Calvinianorum. Quia vineæ domini omnia media uvis ferendis necessaria a Deo vinitore adhibita fuêre, & eo quidem fine, ut ipsa fructus ferret: & ea adhibita mensura, ac ple- nitudine, ut protestetur Dominus: Quid est, quod debui ultra facere vineæ meæ, & non feci ei? utq; pu- blice ad ipsorummet reproborum judicium pro- vocet, eosq; de sufficientia mediorum adhibitorum proprio judicio convincat: ac de frustranea uva- rum expectatione palam conqueratur. Torquent se valde Calviniani in elidendo loco hocce classi- co, sed frustra. Nam quod 1. obvertunt, verba illa, quid est, quod facere debui? non de beneficiis, sed de suppliciis, quæ vinea sterilitate sua promerita sit, age- re, id perquam ineptum est, & tum verbis ipsis, quid faciendum עוֹד ADHUC velAMPLIUS, quæ aperte de beneficiis ulterioribus, qualium cumulum recensuerat, loquuntur, & contextui toti contra- rium: in quo celebrantur primum Dei beneficia, tum designatur Judæorum malitia, demum indi- cuntur divina supplicia. Et querelam hanc de frustra exhibitis beneficiis, & non editis ab Israëli- tis fructibus desideratis institui, agnoscunt Refor- mati ipsi Calvinus, Musculus, Franz. Junius. Cal- vinus ita habet: Quærit primo, quid desiderari possit ab optimo agricola aut patrefamilias, quod non ipse praestiterit vineæ suæ. Hinc colligit, nihil esse excu- sationis, quod indigne fraudatus sit suo labore. Quan- quam secundo membro videtur secum ipse expostulare, quod fructum aliquem gratum vel optabilem à tam sce- lerato populo expectaverit, ut quum expectationi no- stræ eventus non respondet, conquerimur ipsi nobis- cum, atque indignamur, nos male operam locasse apud ingratos, quorum pravitas nos cohibere debue- rat: SIMPLICIOR tamen hic erit sensus, quum OMNIBUS officii partibus defunctus fuerim, ac su- peraverim omnium vota in vineæ meæ cultu, qui fit, ut tam iniquam mihi mercedem rependat, & pro fructu sperato meram proferat amaritudinem. Mu- sculus duo, inquit, sunt hic observanda: unum est, non deesse Deum officio suo. Officium autem illius est OMNIA præstare populo suo, quæ illi sunt NE- CESSARIA. Præstitisse se illa protestatur. Alte- rum est, condemnationem nostri fore in eo, quod gra- tiam hanc div. providentiæ vel non amplectimur, vel male collocamus, ut nulla nobis relinquatur excusatio.

Franc. Junius sic explicat verba Domini, quasi di- cat, appello conscientiam vestram, vos ipsi cognoscite, & bona fide statuite, per utrum steterit, quo minus fructum dignum conditione sua tulerit: si vel tan- tillum merito à me desiderabitur, ego præstabo: sed cum partibus meis PLANE perfunctus sim, quid superest, nisi ut vinea in culpa esse dicatur? Hæc illi vi verita- tis convicti. Conatur quidem Calvinus deinceps ingerere suam heterodoxiam, quod non penetret Deus efficaciter Spiritus sui virtute in corda hominum, ut eos sibi morigeros reddat, additque frustra eos ob- strepere, hoc sibi defuisse, quando ignorantiæ prætex- tum satis superque tollit externa vocatio: sed si gra- tia Dei in se & natura sua efficax non sit, quæ repro- bis exhibetur, annon excusationem habent non quidem ignorantiæ, sed non-conversionis, quia sc. denegata sibi fuit ea gratia, qua ad conversionem opus est: & quomodo ita præstitisset Deus penes reprobos omnia, quæ debuit, aut omnia, quæ illis NECESSARIA ad conversionem erant! quomo- do ob gratiam vel non susceptam, vel male collo- catam isti condemnari possent, quibus ea gratia, qua converti poterant, absolute denegata, quique ob hanc absolutam denegationem gratiam externa vocatione exhibitam suscipere, aut bene collocare minime potuerunt.

Ideoque alii 2. eo se recipiunt cum Embdsensibus in judic. Dordracensib. quod parabolæ non faciant dogmata: Sed quis nescit, obsecro, parabolas quando non extenduntur ultra scopum, sed in- tentione proferentis insistitur, efficaciter proba- re? Scopus autem Domini est ista querela para- bolica docere, non se sed reprobos ipsos in culpa esse, quod non convertantur, non gratiæ suæ, ut- pote quam nemini denegat, quamque sufficienter Israëlitis exhibuerat, seu defectum, seu ineffica- ciam, sed reproborum malitiam, quod gratiam Dei rejiciant, eique obicem ponant.

Quod vero 3. Perkinsus & Molinæus in Ana- tom. c. 37. 41. 49. excipiunt, respici hic tantum exter- na media ceu sufficienter adhibita, non vero internum gratiæ auxilium, simpliciter sufficiens: siquidem tantum externorum mentio fiat, loci nimirum ferti- lis repastinationis, circumpositionis sepis, exossatio- nis, ædificationis torcularis, non vero arcanæ vegeta- tionis, clementiæ cæli, pluviæ tempestivæ: Ad id resp. Quod externa tantum illa commemorentur, ob parabolæ rationem fit. Nam qui vinitoris officio fungitur, præstare nil nisi externa potest. Deum au- tem, qui vinitori comparatur, plura & posse, & vel- le, nullum est dubium: imo nihil se prætermisisse protestatur, atque ideo cum vinea expostulat. Si autem internum gratiæ auxilium non adhibuisset, vel absoluto beneplacito denegasset, qua veritatis spe- cie ita protestari & expostulare potuisset? Et quo- modo proventum expectare potuit, qui media e- jusdem necessaria, & sufficientia, quæ solus in ma- nu habet, absolute denegat? Annon parata fuis- set IsraëBackgroundlitarum excusatio, utcunque varia in nos contuleris beneficia, quia tamen nobis tantum gra- tiæ haud contulisti, imo ex mero beneplacito dene- gasti, quantum ad id nobis opus est, ut converta- mur, & fructus feramus tibi gratos, non nos in cul- pa sumus, à quibus postulatur id, quod præstare non possumus, & ad quod gratia, qua opus nobis est ut præstemus, non præbetur, sed qui id quod non possumus à nobis postulat, nec tamen largitur, aut largiri vult, ut possimus; vid. Defens. Remonstr. cir- ca artic. IV. in Scriptis eorum Synod. p. 89. seqq. Re- cte itaque August. Epist. CV. Quibus Deus misericor- diam non impertitur, ut non impertiatur, merentur.

Unde Henr. Bulling. in expos. Matth. Anno 1542. C. 23, 37. Amplificatur & illo Dei beneficium, & populi in- gratitudo quod non semel, sed multoties servare cona- tus est; QVOTIES, inquit, volui. Verum audi, quam male responderint benefico Patri! Noluit, noluit, inquam, impiissimus populus colligi atque servari in amicitia & fœdere Dei. Dispergi & perdi maluit. Unde propria culpa, malitia, & rebellione, nulla Dei morositate periit. Nam Deus servare voluit, & hanc voluntatem suam non semel attestatus est, imo O- MNEM MOVIT LAPIDEM UT SERVARET. At isti servari noluerunt, ubi ergo sunt, qui FATUM ET NECESSITATEM quandam rigidissimam peccandi & pereundi prædicant? POTUISSET SER- VARI Jerusalem, si modo voluisset, hoc est, nisi REPULISSET Dei misericordiam & sanum consi- lium. Non ergo possumus probare Stoicam illam in negotio salutis necessitatem. Idem Bullingerus in Decad. sermon. Anno 1562. Tiguri edit. dec. 5. serm. 7. p. 342. Hæc GRATIA DEI (qua filii DEI ex filiis Diaboli fiunt) nemo exclusus est, nisi qui se suo vitio, & culpa per inobedientiam excludit. Quæ utique est conversionis gratia. Id agnoscant & cæteri Reformati, ac divinæ gratiæ dent glo- riam, nec eam criminentur ceu inefficacem qua re- probos, aut restringant ad solos electos ex mero Dei beneplacito contra luculentissima Scripturæ testimonia Esa. 65, 2. 12. Prov. 1, 24. Ezech. 18, 23. 32. cap. 33, 11. 1. Tim. 2, 4. 2. Pet. 3, 9.

## 5:5
Verse 5. I WILL TAKE AWAY ITS HEDGE] I will expose it to the nations.

Latin:

Vers. 5. AUFERAM SEPEM EJUS] Exponam eam gentibus.

## 5:6
Verse 6. IT SHALL NOT BE PRUNED AND IT SHALL NOT BE DIGGED] No one will take care of it.

AND I WILL COMMAND THE CLOUDS THAT THEY RAIN NO RAIN UPON IT] I will withdraw my benevolence from it.

The clouds are the Prophets and Apostles, according to Hector Pinto. The Apostles and their followers, according to Cornel. Is doctrine signified by the name of water? Thus Moses, like a certain cloud (as Pinto speaks), Deut. 32, said, 'Let my doctrine grow as the rain,' whence he renders this sense: I will command the Prophets and Apostles not to irrigate the people of the Jews with their doctrine, which he says was fulfilled after the death of Christ, and thus he infers from this: Since it is certain that in the Babylonian captivity the Jews did not lack Prophets, but were irrigated by doctrine, it is openly concluded that this prophecy of Isaiah is to be understood concerning the captivity by the Romans. Others take it more simply concerning the withdrawal of divine grace, which is granted through the word and ministry, by which, no differently than is accustomed to happen when God commands the clouds not to rain, the Jews will be deprived of the rain of spiritual doctrine and grace: since it has already been indicated before that they would be deprived of the work of the ministry: 'It shall not be pruned, nor shall it be digged': for this is done through the ministers of the word. Cf. Ps. 68:10; Hos. 6:4.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NON PVTABITVR ET NON FODITVR] Nemo ejus curam geret.

ET NUBIBVS MANDABO NE PLVANT SVPER EAM IMBREM] Benevolentiam meam ei subducam.

Nubes sunt Prophetæ, & Apostoli, juxta Hector Pintum. Apostoli eorumque asseclæ, juxta Cornel. nomine aquæ doctrina significatur? Ita Moses vel- uti quædam nubes (ut Pintus loquitur) Deut. 32. di- cebat, crescat, ut pluvia doctrina mea, unde hunc sensum reddit, Prophetis & Apostolis præcipiam, ne Judæorum populum irrigent doctrina sua, quod post Christi mortem impletum ait, adeoque hinc in- fert: Cum constet in Babylonica captivitate Judæos non caruisse Prophetis, sed fuisse doctrina irrigatos, aperte concluditur, esse hanc Esaiæ vaticinationem de captivitate per Romanos intelligendam. Alii sim- plicius de gratiæ divinæ, quæ per verbum & mi- nisterium conceditur, subtractione accipiunt, qua non secus atque fieri solet, cum Deus nubibus mandat, ne pluant, Spirituali doctrinæ, & gratiæ pluvia carituri sint Judæi: quum ministerii opera eos privatum iri antea jam indicatum sit: Non pu- tabitur, neque fodietur: hoc enim per verbi mini- stros fit. Conf. Psal. 68, 10. Hos. 6, 4.

## 5:8
Vers. 8. WOE TO YOU WHO JOIN HOUSE TO HOUSE &c.] You who remove neighbors on all sides, and say without end: - - - oh if that next corner would approach, which now disfigures the little field. As Horace says: to whom also belongs that: Now a few plows will leave a few acres for royal piles. And what follows in Carm. 2, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 8. VÆ QUI CONJUNGITIS DOMUM AD DOMUM &c.] Qui undique vicinos submovetis, & fi- ne fine dicitis: - - - ô si angulus ille Proximus accedat, qui nunc denormat agellum. Ut ait Horatius: cujus est & illud: Iam pauca aratra jugera regiæ Moles relinquent. Et quæ sequuntur Carm. 2, 15.

## 5:10
Vers. 10. THEY SHALL MAKE ONE SMALL FLASK] A bath, which is the smallest measure for liquids.

Latin:

Vers. 10. FACIENT LAGUNCULAM UNAM] Ba- tum, quæ minima mensura in liquidis.

## 5:12
Vers. 12. AND YOU DO NOT REGARD THE WORK OF THE LORD &c.] You do not consider the evils which God is preparing for you. Cf. Amos 6, 6.

Not only the punishments imminent to them, but other judgments of GOD as well, for happy is he whom the dangers of others make cautious, and not only punishments, but also the benefits which God has shown them, and still shows even now through the denunciation of penalties and the exhortation to repentance, are comprehended under the name of the WORK and DEEDS of the Lord, although we do not deny that the imminent evils are particularly regarded. See v. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ET OPUS DOMINI NON RESPICITIS &c.) Non consideratis mala quæ vobis Deus præparat. Conf. Amosi 6, 6.

Non tantum supplicia ipsis imminentia, sed alia etiam DEI judicia, nam felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum, nec solum supplicia, sed etiam beneficia, quæ ipsis exhibuit Deus, & ex mera μα- κροθυμίᾳ adhuc etiam per denunciationem pœ- narum, & exhortationem ad pœnitentiam exhi- bet, sub nomine OPERIS & FACTORUM Do- mini comprehenduntur, etsi peculiariter mala im- minentia respici non negemus. Vide v. 19.

## 5:14
Vers. 14. THEREFORE HELL HAS ENLARGED ITS SOUL] Soul for itself, by personification. The graves were to be enlarged on account of the huge crowd of the dying.

So also Heshusius on this passage, but by hell, Gehenna is more correctly understood; for it had already been spoken of before concerning punishment and temporal destruction, that they were to be led captive because they have no knowledge, or, as it is in the Hebrew, unexpectedly, that their nobles or honorable men were to perish by famine, and the multitude, or the common people, ought to wither away with thirst. (God thus punishing gluttony and drunkenness, and the contempt of His word with exile, famine, and thirst, so that the punishments correspond to the sins.) Now, therefore, eternal punishment is also implied: that hell gapes most greedily to devour such impious men, as Osiander rightly says. Cf. Prov. 30, 16. 1 Cor. 6, 10. Acts 6, 8. The meaning of the word שְׁאוֹל as hell is more famous than as grave. The avaricious, the rapacious, the drunkards open their mouths without end or limit to devour the goods of the poor and to consume wine, as if it were hell; therefore hell, that insatiable beast, will in turn swallow them up; so Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, Cornelius à Lapide, Hector Pintus, and others.

Latin:

Vers. 14. PROPTEREA DILATAVIT INFERNUS ANIMAM SUAM] Animam pro semet, κατὰ προσωπο- ποιΐαν. Sepulchra dilatanda erant ob ingentem turbam morientium.

Ita etiam Heshusius in hunc loc. sed per infer- num rectius gehenna intelligitur; nam de pœna & interitu temporali jam ante dictum erat, quod ca- ptivi ducendi, quia non habent scientiam, vel, ut in Ebr. est, ex improviso, quod nobiles vel honorati eo- rum interituri sint fame, & multitudo, vel plebs siti exarescere debeat. (Deo ita crapulam & ebrieta- tem, ac contemtum verbi sui exilio, fame ac siti pu- niente, ut supplicia respondeant peccatis.) Jam er- go etiam æterna subjicitur pœna: quod inhiet in- fernus avidissime devorandis tam impiis hominibus, ut recte Osiand. Conf. Prov. 30, 16. 1. Cor. 6, 10. Act. 6, 8. Famosior est inferni, quam sepulcri significatio vo- cis שְׁאוֹל. Avari, rapaces, ebriosi aperiunt ora sine fine, ac termino, ad devorandum bona pauperum, & absumendum vinum, ac si esset infernus; ideo infernus bestia illa insatiabilis deglutiet vicissim eosdem; Ita Hieronymus, Cyrillus Alexandr. Cor- nel. à Lap. Hector Pintus & alii.

## 5:15
Vers. 15. MAN SHALL BE BOWED DOWN, AND MAN SHALL BE HUMBLED.

By 'man' any commoner, by 'man' [vir] the nobles and the principal men are designated according to the custom of Scripture, as Haymo notes. They are said to be bowed down and humbled so that they may be absorbed by hell according to Pintus, or rather generally, that they are to be bowed down both in this age and in the next: since not only are secure and impenitent gluttons exposed to the greatest miseries in this life, but they are also eternally humbled, Luke 16. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 15. INCURVABITUR HOMO, ET HUMILIABITUR VIR.

Per hominem plebejus quisque, per virum nobiles & primarii more Scripturæ, notante Haymone designantur. Incurvari autem & humilia- ri dicuntur, ut absorbeantur ab inferno juxta Pintum, vel potius generatim, quod tum in hoc tum in altero seculo incurvandi sint: quum non modo in hac vita summis miseriis exponantur e- pulones securi, & impœnitentes, sed etiam æter- num humilientur, Luc. 16. 24.

## 5:17
Vers. 17. AND THE LAMBS SHALL FEED ACCORDING TO THEIR ORDER.

Heb. כְּדָבְרָם Mich. 2, 12. is rendered according to their folds. By lambs according to their folds, and strangers eating the deserts turned into fertility (in the Hebrew it is, and the foreigners shall feed in the fat deserts) are understood the nations which had been alien to Christ, and become His sheep, about to find the most sufficient food for their souls in those very deserts, which shall be turned into fat soil and joyful pastures. John 10, 11. 16. Cf. Jerome and especially Cyril of Alexandria on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET PASCENTUR AGNI JUX- TA ORDINEM SUUM.

Ebr. כְּדָבְרָם Mich. 2, 12. redditur juxta caulas suas. Per agnos juxta caulas suas, & adve- nas deserta in ubertatem versa comedentes (in Ebr. est, & in desertis pinguibus pascentur alienigenæ) intelli- guntur gentes, quæ alienæ fuerant à Christo, & o- ves ejus fiunt, inventuræ animæ pabulum sufficien- tissimum in ipsis desertis, quæ vertentur in pingue solum, & læta pascua. Joh. 10, 11. 16. Conf. Hiero- nym. & imprimis Cyrill. Alex. in h. l.

## 5:20
Vers. 20. WOE TO YOU WHO CALL EVIL GOOD, AND GOOD EVIL] You who confuse the limits and names of the honest and the dishonest.

B. Luther explains this wild grape as the vices of doctrine, because the rest sound of the vices of morals; but v. 20, 21 seems to deal especially with the vices of the intellect, attempting to persuade the Israelites not to distrust true and false religion so much: S. Jerome joins the vices of doctrine and morals, and refers them to the scribes and Pharisees receiving the traditions of men. So also S. Basil in this place. Because the nature of truth is sweet, it is certain that a lie is bitter. Conf. 2 Cor. 6, 16 and Basil. Interrog. CCVII.

Latin:

Vers. 20. VÆ QUI DICITIS MALUM BO- NUM, ET BONUM MALUM] Qui honesti, & inhonesti limites ac nomina confunditis.

B. Lutherus hanc labruscam de vitiis doctrinæ exponit, quia de vitiis morum reliqua sonant; at v. 20. 21. præcipue agi videtur de vitiis intellectus, Israëlitis persuadere conantis, non diffidere adeo veram & falsam religionem: S. Hieronym. vitia do- ctrinæ & morum conjungit, & ad scribas & Phari- sæos traditiones hominum recipientes refert. Ita & S. Basilius in h. l. Quia dulcis est veritatis natura, constat mendacium esse amarum. Conf. 2. Cor. 6, 16. & Basil. Interrog. CCVII.

## 5:25
Vers. 25. AS THE TONGUE OF FIRE DEVOURS THE STUBBLE.

That is, the flame of fire, which has the appearance of a tongue, because it is red and tends to a point, whence it is said to lick the wood. Corn. à Lap. and Pintus, along with the Holy Fathers, understand it of the Romans, as if he were saying that the Romans will so burn this vineyard, luxuriating in vices and growing wild like dry stubble, that hardly a trace of it will remain.

SO THEIR ROOT SHALL BE AS DUST, &c.

Thus the whole plant or tree with its root, and sprout, and shoots, and indeed the whole people of the Jews with their stocks, will perish by slaughter, will vanish, and will go up in smoke.

Vers. 25. THE MOUNTAINS ARE TROUBLED.

The destruction of the Jews will be so horrible that even the mountains seem to be amazed and troubled, as Cornelius explains. Hector Pintus understands the mountains as powerful men: that the punishment will be so great that even they will tremble: he admits, however, that the mountains can be understood simply: as in Psalm 18, 8, which sense, as the simpler one, should be retained. Now, the Jews, Lyranus, and Sanctius explain these things, and those which follow, concerning the destruction of the Jews by the Chaldeans: Heshusius concerning the devastation of the kingdom of Israel by Shalmaneser: Corn. à Lapid. and Pintus, following Jerome and Cyril of Alexandria, concerning the final destruction of the Jews by the Romans: which the context teaches is entirely looked to, and the weight of the words compels. We do not, however, deny the explanation of the Blessed Pappus, that these things sound of both destructions, Chaldean and Roman, and the Osiandrian Paraphrase, that these things thus look to the final destruction, on account of the ingratitude and hardening of the Jewish people foreseen after their liberation from the Babylonian captivity, and its extreme malice, security, and impenitence, so that the desolation of the Chaldeans and the Babylonian captivity is not excluded, but included. And those words in v. 25 indicate this: HIS HAND IS STRETCHED OUT STILL: because the devastation of the Romans, although most grave, was not enough, but God still punishes the Jews with exile and blindness, and the desolation will persevere until the end, Dan. 9, 27. Whence also to v. 13, Therefore he is led captive, &c. S. Jerome says these things happened according to the letter to the Jewish people under Vespasian and Titus, the Roman Princes, as both Greek and Latin history narrates. And to v. 24. It is to be noted in all these things that he does not reproach them for idolatry, nor other sins for which they offended God, but because they rejected the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the word of the Lord. Add also what we shall observe that he has already handed down to v. 26.

Latin:

Vers. 25. SICUT DEVORAT STIPULAM LINGUA IGNIS.

Id est flamma ignis, quæ linguæ habet speciem, quia rubet, & in acutiem tendit, unde dicitur lam- bere ligna. De Romanis intelligit Corn. à Lap. & Pintus cum S. Patribus, quasi dicat, Romani hanc vineam vitiis luxuriantem, & sylvescentem, quasi sti- pulam aridam ita comburent, ut vix ejus vestigium re- maneat.

SIC RADIX EORUM QUASI FAVILLA ERIT, &c.

Sic tota planta vel arbor cum radice, & germi- ne, ac surculis, adeoque totus Judæorum populus cum suis stirpibus internecione peribit, evanescet, & in fumum ibit.

Vers. 25. CONTURBATI SUNT MONTES.

Tam horridum erit excidium Judæorum, ut etiam montes admirari & turbari videantur, ut ex- plicat Cornelius. Hector Pintus Viros potentes per montes intelligit: Tantum fore supplicium, ut etiam illi tremant: fatetur tamen posse montes simpliciter intelligi: uti Psal. 18, 8. qui sensus ceu simplicior reti- nendus. Explicant autem hæc, & quæ sequuntur, Iu- dei, Lyranus, & Sanctius de excidio Judæorum per Chaldæos facto: Heshusius de vastatione regni Israë- lis per Salmanassarem: Cornel. à Lapid. & Pintus præeunte Hieronymo & Cyrillo Alex. de ultimo Ju- dæorum exitio per Romanos: quod omnino respici contextus docet, ac verborum pondera cogunt. Non abnuimus tamen B. Pappi explicationi, quod de utroque excidio, Chaldaico, & Romano hæc so- nent, & Osiandrinæ Paraphrasi, quod ita hæc exitium finale respiciant, ob prævisam post liberationem è Babylonica captivitate ingratitudinem & indura- tionem populi Judaici, ejusq; extremam malitiam, securitatem, & impœnitentiam, ut desolatio Chal- dæorum, & captivitas Babylonica non excludatur, sed includatur. Atque hoc indicant verba illa v. 25. ADHUC MANUS EJUS EXTENTA: quia de- vastatio Romanorum, etsi gravissima, non sufficie- bat, quin punit adhuc Deus Judæos exilio, & cæci- tate, & usq; ad finem perseverabit desolatio, Dan. 9, 27. unde etiam ad v. 13. Propterea ductus est capti- vus, &c. S. Hieron. hæc, inquit, juxta literam accidisse populo Judæorum sub Vespasiano, & Tito, Romanis Principibus, tam Græca, quam Latina narrat historia. Et ad v. 24. Notandum in his omnibus, quod non eis exprobret idololatriam, non alia peccata, propter quæ offenderint Deum, sed quia objecerunt legem Evange- lii & sermonem Domini blasphemarunt. Adde etiam, quæ jam ad v. 26. ab eo tradita observabimus.

## 5:26
Vers. 26. AND HE WILL LIFT UP A SIGN.

The Hebrews, says Jerome, understand this passage concerning the Babylonians and Nebuchadnezzar: but we, joining the following to the preceding, say that the sign lifted up among the nations from afar is so because they rejected the law of the Gospel, &c. For if the discourse were about the Babylonians, according to prophetic custom he would have said: I will call him who is from the North; but now he signifies nations placed far away, and those who dwell in the ends of the earth, without doubt the Romans and all the peoples of Italy, Gaul, and Spain, who were subject under the Roman Emperors Vespasian and Hadrian. Which argument Cyril of Alexandria also uses, book 1, Orat. IV on Isaiah. But that sense which Jerome says he read in the commentaries of a certain person, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, is foreign, as it does not agree either with this threatening or with those things which follow. Our explanation, however, is especially confirmed by what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ET ELEVABIT SIGNUM.

Hebræi, ait Hieronymus, hunc locum de Baby- loniis, & de Nabuchodonosor intelligunt: nos autem sequentia superioribus copulantes, ideo signum in na- tionibus procul elevatum dicimus esse, quoniam ab- jecerunt legem Evangelii, &c. Si enim de Babyloniis esset sermo, juxta consuetudinem propheticam dixisset: vocabo eum, qui ab Aquilone est; nunc vero gentes longe positas significat, & quæ in finibus terræ commo- rantur, haud dubium quin Romanos & omnes Italiæ, Galliarumque & Hispaniæ populos, qui sub Vaspas. & Hadr. Rom. Imp. subjacebant. Quo argumento uti- tur & Cyrill. Alex. l. 1. Orat. IV. Esai. Alienus au- tem est ille sensus, quem in cujusdam commenta- riis se legisse Hieron. ait, de vocatione gentium, utpo- te qui non congruit vel huic comminationi, vel iis quæ sequuntur. Nostra autem hæc explicatio per sequentia apprime confirmatur.

## 6:1 Argument
II. AFTER THE DEATH OF UZZIAH UNDER JOTHAM. CHAP. VI. SECOND VISION.

Concerning the glory of Christ about to fill the whole earth, and the hardening of the people, and its rejection, down to a certain holy seed.

Vers. 1. I SAW THE LORD SITTING UPON A THRONE HIGH AND LIFTED UP] I saw, in a trance, of course, as Peter did in Acts 10:10, 11:11. By the Lord, understand an excellent brightness. It signifies a tribunal erected for God, wishing to institute judgment itself concerning the King, and the nobles, and the people. But this tribunal seemed to him to be erected in the temple as if in the palace of God, as will appear from what follows.

A perverse depravity. He makes it from Jehovah, a brightness: just as the Socinians grumble that the Prophet saw not Christ, but the brightness of His Prophet, at John 12:41. For the Prophet is said to have seen the Lord Himself, not merely some brightness: even if he saw the brightness and glory of the Lord, or the Lord in brightness and glory, and at the same time in the spirit foresaw the glory of the Messiah to be established on the throne of divine majesty, as St. John testifies in Chapter 12:41. These things said Isaiah, when he saw His glory: and spoke of Him. Nevertheless, even of the rulers many believed in Him. Truly St. Cyril of Alexandria, Vol. II of his Works, Commentary on Isaiah, p. 102: 'But that the Prophet saw the Son in the glory of God and the Father, no one will be able to doubt, since John writes openly concerning Him: These things said Isaiah, when he saw His glory, etc.' Therefore, too far from the declaration of the Holy Spirit... Grotius departs, when he believes that not the Lord, but the excellent brightness of the Lord was seen, and thinks that nothing else was signified than the tribunal and judgment to be instituted concerning the King and the nobles and the people. For the glory of the Son of GOD was seen and exhibited here to the Prophet. 'Observe for me,' says Cyril, 'the excellence of the divine dignity, and the dominion over every creature. For He is on a high and lifted up throne, excellently crowned with the most beautiful insignia of the kingdom. Likewise, the supreme powers, than which no created things are read to be higher, stand around on every side, taking the place of household servants, and adorning Him with praises.' 'The whole earth,' he says, 'is full of His glory.' But in my judgment, we ought not to think that the throne of God is placed in a limitation of place: for that is truly foolish and frivolous: but the throne of God is placed on high, insofar as the glory of the divine kingdom is understood to surpass every nature falling under understanding. Then the sitting, which is spoken of Him, seems to denote, as it were, firmness and stability and constancy in the same tenor of honors. For blessed David sings thus: 'God sits on His holy throne,' and the Prophet Jeremiah says to Him: 'You sit forever, and we shall be forever.' For the nature of things is always and entirely subject to corruption, and there is a certain measure and limit to those things which have a beginning. But the architect and maker of all things, Wisdom, sits, as I have said, that is, is unmoved, and remains in the same way.

Latin:

II. POST MORTEM USIÆ SUB IOTHAMO. CAP. VI. VISIO ALTERA.

De gloria Christi universam terram repletu- ra, & induratione populi & ejus, usque ad sanctum quoddam semen rejectione.

Vers. 1. VIDI DOMINUM SEDENTEM SUPER SO- LIUM EXCELSUM ET ELEVATUM] Vidi ἐν ἐκςάσει scilicet, ut Petrus Act. 10, 10. 11, II. Dominum intellige, fulgorem eximium. Tribunal Deo erectum significat, i- psum judicium velle instituere de Rege, & primoribus, & populo. Visum autem est ei hoc tribunal erectum in templo tanquam in Dei regia, ut ex sequentibus apparebit.

PErversa depravatio. E Jehova facit fulgorem: uti Sociniani Prophetam non Christum, sed gloriam ejus Prophetam vidisse ad Joh. 12, 41. og- ganniunt. Dominum enim ipsum, non tantum fulgo- rem aliquem vidisse Propheta dicitur: etsi viderit fulgorem & gloriam Domini, vel Dominum in fulgore & gloria, ac simul in spiritu præviderit Mes- siæ gloriam in throno majestatis divinæ constituen- di, teste S. Johanne Cap. 12, 41. Hæc dixit Esaias, quando vidit gloriam Ejus: & locutus est de Eo. Ve- runtamen & ex principibus multi crediderunt in eum. Vere S. Cyrillus Alexandr. Tom. II. Oper. Com. in E- sa. p. 102. Prophetam autem vidisse filium in gloria Dei & Patris, nemo dubitare poterit, cum Johan- nes de eo aperte scribat: Hæc dixit Esaias, cum vi- dit gloriam ejus &c. Nimis ergo à Sp. Sancti decla- ratione abit Grotius, cum non Dominum, sed ful- gorem Domini eximium visum credit, neque aliud significatum putat, quam tribunal & judicium de Rege & primoribus & populo instituendum. Visa enim & exhibita hic est Prophetæ gloria Filii DEI. Specta vero mihi, inquit Cyrillus, divinæ dignitatis præstantiam, & in omnem creaturam dominatum. Ille enim est in excelso & elevato throno, pulcherrimis regni insignibus egregie coronatus. Suprema item potestates, quibus nullæ res genitæ superiores leguntur, undiquaque circumstant, domesticorum locum tenen- tes, eumque ornantes laudibus. Plena est, inquit, terra universa gloria ejus; Dei autem thronum non in sub- limitate loci terminata positum, meo judicio, existi- mare debemus: id enim profecto stultum est & frivo- lum: at in sublimi thronus Dei positus est, quatenus divini regni gloria omnem naturam sub intelligentiam cadentem, superare intelligitur. Deinde sessio, quæ de eo dicitur, veluti firmitatem & stabilitatem in eo- dem honorum tenore constantiamque videtur subno- tare. Psallit enim sic & beatus David: Deus se- det in throno sancto suo, & Propheta Hieremias ad eum dicit: Tu sedes in sempiternum, & nos erimus in sempiternum. Semper enim & omnino corruptioni obnoxia est rerum natura, & eorum, quæ ortum habent, mensura quædam est & terminus. Sedet autem uti dixi, omnium rerum architectrix & opifex sa- pientia, id est, immota est, & eodem modo permanet.

## 6:2
Vers. 2. SERAPHIM STOOD ABOVE IT] Better, according to that: i.e., the throne. Seraphim are Angels of a fiery form, ministers of divine wrath, which is compared to a flame.

WITH TWO THEY COVERED HIS FACE] Better, their own. Namely, just as men do not dare to look directly at the sun, so the Angels do not dare to look at God.

WITH TWO THEY COVERED HIS FEET] And here understand their own, and by feet, in the Hebrew manner, those things which modesty commands to be covered in men, to which correspond in the Angels themselves certain weaknesses, if they are compared to God. See Job 4:18.

AND WITH TWO THEY FLEW] This signifies the very swift ministries of the Angels.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SERAPHIM STABANT SUPER ILLUD] Melius, juxta illud: sc. solium. Seraphim Angeli forma ignea, ministri divinæ iræ, quæ flammæ comparatur.

DUABUS VELABANT FACIEM EJUS] Me- lius, suam. Nempe sicut homines solem contra tueri non audent, ita Angeli Deum.

DUABUS VELABANT PEDES EJUS] Et hic in- tellige suos, & per pedes more Hebræo ea, quæ in homini- bus velari jubet pudor, quibus respondent in ipsis etiam An- gelis imbecillitates quædam, si Deo comparentur. vide Job. 4, 18.

ET DUABUS VOLABANT] Hoc significat celer- rima Angelorum ministeria.

## 6:3
Vers. 3. AND THEY WERE SAYING, HOLY, HOLY, HOLY] That is, the judgments of God are just against the king, the nobles, and the people. But the triple repetition of one word affirms vehemently, see Ezek. 21:27, Jer. 22:29. From this passage is taken the Trisagion, the name of a hymn in the Greek Church.

Again the Jewish and Socinian chord goes astray. He is not ignorant that, by the common calculation and suffrage of the Catholic Church, Greek and Latin, or Eastern and Western, this Trisagion is explained concerning the Most Holy Trinity, because the Seraphim cried out in honor of the same with triple words, HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, and he himself praises the Trisagion of the Greek Church, and yet he fights against the Church with the Jews and Photinians, that that triple repetition does not contain any mystery, or at least does not affirm it vehemently, or insinuate triple judgments against the King, the Nobles, and the people. What, therefore, is to be thought of Grotius, who preferred to Judaize and Arianize again rather than follow the Church, and knowingly and prudently set aside its faith here, is clear of its own accord. For that this Trisagion was not said to the Son alone, are the words of Damascenus, Book III, On the Orthodox Faith. Fid. c. 10. But as to the Trinity, the divine and holy Athanasius, Basil and Gregory, and the whole chorus of the other Fathers are witnesses, that by the threefold Holiness the holy Seraphim insinuate the three supersubstantial hypostases of the Deity; but by the one dominion they signify the one substance and kingdom of the divine ruling Trinity. Cyril in h. l. 'When they say Holy three times, they conclude the hymn in this, Lord of Sabaoth, establishing the holy triad in one nature of the Deity, for we clearly say that the Son and the Holy Spirit subsist afterwards here. Nor does any reason divide those whom we speak of into any natural diversity, but in the Triple hypostasis one Deity is understood.' Nor indeed do the holy Seraphim make it testified to us by this, that they declare the whole earth full of his majesty, foretelling future things and announcing the mystery of the dispensation administered through Christ. I pass over the fact that the Jews themselves acknowledged the mystery in this repetition: since in the Targum of Jonathan Ben Uziel this paraphrase is found: קדיש אבא Holy Father, קדיש ברא קדיש רוחא קדישא Holy Son, Holy Spirit Holy; and R. Simeon Ben Iobai thus explained the τρισάγιον in Comment. ad h. l. קדש זה אב. קדש זה בן קדש זה רוח הקדש. Holy this is the Father, Holy this is the Son, Holy this is the Holy Spirit: See Galatinus, book 11, on the secrets of Catholic truth, chapter 1. Weidnerus in the principal places of the Christian Faith, tract 1. D. Helvicus Tom. IV. Disp. Giessenf. X. Which explanation is founded in the very propriety of the threefold word SANCTUS, SANCTUS, SANCTUS, repetition. For 'Holy Jehovah' is not the same as 'just are the judgments of God,' as Grotius foolishly says, since the Lord is holy in himself, even if there were none upon whom he might exercise judgments, and holiness is an absolute, essential, and eternal attribute of God, which who would say of the judgments of God? Thus, therefore, the Seraphim acknowledge three, to whom this essential and eternal attribute of God belongs in the Deity. For we have shown that there are more אלהים קדשים, that is, holy divine persons of the same divine essence, from Jos. 24:19, in the 'Invincible plurality of divine persons,' c. 7, p. 38, seqq. 'You will not be able to serve Jehovah, because he is holy Elohim.' These most holy divine persons, therefore, the Seraphim define by the number three, when they designate the Elohim Kedoschim by their τρισάγιον. Then indeed Scripture acknowledges neither more nor fewer to whom the essential name Jehovah and the attribute Holy belong than these three, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, whose one essence, one glory, and one throne of majesty it establishes, whom it wills to be celebrated in the whole earth, Matt. 28:19, whom it teaches to be worshipped and adored by the Seraphim themselves, and whom it is certain also sent the Prophet as their Legate: who, as they are that one true God, so they are acknowledged by the whole Catholic Church as the King and Lord Zebaoth, whom Isaiah saw. Therefore they themselves also say in the plural in v. 9: 'Who will go לנו for Us,' to indicate the plurality of the divine persons and when that trisagion is repeated in the New Testament, Apoc. 4:8, it certainly does not there imply God's judgment against a triple order; King, nobles, and people; therefore, there must be some other reason for this threefold proclamation, HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, than that which is invented here by Grotius. But what need have we Christians of many words? Since the Holy Spirit in the New Testament has clearly expounded it; He testifies openly not only that the glory and holiness of God the Father were celebrated (concerning which there is clearly no doubt), but also that of the Son of God, John ch. 12:40, 41, teaching that the Prophet saw the glory of the Son of God there, and spoke of Him: and that the holiness and glory of the Holy Spirit are also celebrated there, the Apostle is a witness, Acts 28:26, when he says that the Holy Spirit spoke there with the Prophet, and that He said: Go, and you shall say to this people. Wherefore Grotius ought to have lent his ears here to the Holy Spirit, To the holy, not to the unbelieving Jews, to the holy Fathers, and to the whole Catholic Church, not to an Arian handful, or even to a Judaizing and Arianizing Calvin, whom he himself otherwise holds to be impious and blasphemous: whom our blessed Hunnius deservedly restrained in his Calvin. Judaiz. & Anti-Pareo. Oecolampadius certainly, in the same School, not to mention other more recent disciples of Calvin himself, who almost all ὁμοθυμαδὸν acknowledge with us that the mystery of the H. Trinity is insinuated by this threefold repetition, makes this our explanation, or rather the opinion of the whole Catholic Church, superior to all doubt: and he defends it against all Jewish glosses in book II of his Hypomnemat. on Isaiah 6. That angelic hymn, which the Greeks call the trisagion, without doubt indicates the trinity of persons and the unity of the divine nature, which the angels behold and praise, and by beholding are blessed, in which we also are baptized: the Hebrews, our perpetual adversaries, lest they say nothing, say that 'holy' is said three times because of the parity of creatures, which He created, and because of which He becomes praiseworthy: and they posit three worlds, the super-celestial, the celestial, and the sub-celestial. Holy, therefore, in the creation of the angels, Holy in the creation of the heavens, and Holy in the creation of those things which are under heaven. But the Angels, because of their eminence, praise the Spirit more for His own sake than for the sake of the creatures, offering in this what they call a morning sacrifice. Others explain it somewhat more tolerably, that 'holy' is said three times because of the three times, past, present, and future. To which John seems to have looked in the Apocalypse, chapter 1. Grace to you, and peace from Him who is, and who was, and who is to come. Certainly, it is fitting that God be praised at all times. But we, with the Catholic Church, sing: Holy Father, Holy Son, Holy Spirit. One Holy Lord Zebaoth, that is, of the heavenly hosts. We have satisfied Calixtus and the other Innovators, especially Christian Drejer, who have recently opposed themselves here to the Church and denied that the faith of the Holy Trinity is taught there, in the Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica: to whom also an abundant answer has been given by our Dr. Weller in his most learned Anti-Calixtine writings. Hackspan, certainly, however otherwise not sufficiently fair to the testimonies of the Holy Trinity in the Old Testament, acknowledges that this saying, against the Photinians who accept the New Testament, is in truth convincing. The Calvinists, he says, indeed deny that anything can be derived from there either against the Jews or against the Photinians: But wrongly: For let the passages John 12:41, where the discourse is about Christ, and Acts 28:25, where it is about the Holy Spirit, be compared, and in turn Apoc. 4:8, where Christ is likewise hinted at, and it will easily appear that the Trinity is involved in this threefold repetition. Socinus himself, in his Defensio Animadversionum Posnaniensium, ch. 12, p. 309, confesses that if the Trinity were proved from elsewhere, this passage would have some strength. But that the same Hackspan thinks this argument against the Jews only insinuates, not convinces, in that he wished to serve the hypothesis of Calixtus. But since the Jews themselves have been convicted from this concerning the Holy Trinity, which from blessed Gerhard, Vol. II, Dispp. p. 1210, and Helvicus acknowledges, and the threefold repetition, according to his own explanation of the Old Testament, cannot be understood otherwise than of three persons (for this same Hackspan refutes other glosses and causes of the threefold repetition) and it is taught by Isaiah himself that the Holy Jehovah of hosts is the Father, Son, and Spirit, ch. 48:16, ch. 63:7, seqq., and here indeed it is openly indicated that there are several persons, by whom Isaiah was sent, v. 8, who are that one Jehovah: ought this not to be considered a sufficiently clear testimony even for convincing the Jews themselves? Which indeed was also opposed by the Jewish Fathers. Compare what we have said about it in Vol. III of our Systema Theologicum. P. Weidner, in his Conversio Judæorum in locis fidei, p. 38, teaches that the Jews recognized the mystery in it: who recite this passage, and Deut. 6:4, morning and evening every day with great veneration and worship.

Verse of the same.

THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL OF HIS GLORY] In the Hebrew: All this earth. Judea, namely; God will reveal Himself wondrously in these very places.

It is rashly restricted to the land of Judea, what is said of all the earth. For account must be taken of the little word of universality, since it is very well known that the prefix ה does not always have the force of demonstrating a certain thing, even from the very beginning of the Bible, Gen. 1:1, where הארץ also denotes earth simply, not some region. Furthermore, John taught that the glory of the Messiah was seen here, which spread itself through the whole earth, not through Judea alone; nay, it filled the remaining parts of the earth more, when, with the Jews rejected, the Gentiles were assumed, in whom He Himself was glorified through the Holy Spirit.
