Indeed, what is truly a sign, and was to be credible to the human race, is this: that the Firstborn of all creatures, having been made flesh from a virginal womb, should truly become a little boy: occupying that through the Prophetic Spirit, in one way and another, as I have recounted to you, he pronounced it: so that when it was done, it might be recognized as having been done by the power and counsel of the Creator of all things: no otherwise than as from the rib of Adam's side one Eve came into existence, and all other living things took their origin and beginning from the word of God. But you also dare to adulterate the translations of your elders, who were with King Ptolemy of Egypt: alleging that the Scripture does not have what they translated: But behold a young woman shall conceive in the womb. As if indeed anything of great importance were being designated, if a woman were to give birth from sexual intercourse, which indeed most young women do, all except the sterile: Whom, however, God can also cause to bear offspring when He wills. For the mother of Samuel, being barren, gave birth through the counsel and will of God: And the wife of the holy Patriarch Abraham; And Elizabeth, who bore John the Baptist, and certain others similarly. Wherefore it ought not to be considered impossible by you that God can do all things that He wills: especially when it has been announced by prophecies what is to come. It does not befit you to either adulterate the prophecies themselves with a rash daring, or to interpret them wrongly, for you will only do injury to yourselves: but you will harm God not at all. Socinus himself recognized the force and evidence of this argument; therefore in his sacred lectures, as he calls them, p. 44. Since it is written thus;

Behold, God gives you a sign, behold, a young woman conceiving etc. it seems sufficiently clear; that this sign given by the Lord consists chiefly in this, that that young woman was to conceive and give birth, which in NO WAY can be reconciled to the sense of those times, whoever we might wish that young woman to have been. Whence he concludes p. 48. that this must be referred to Jesus himself; especially indeed for the reason that it is sufficiently clear, (I recite his words) that God gave the conception and birth of that girl as a miraculous sign. For the very words of God MANIFESTLY teach that, when He says to Ahaz: Ask for yourself a sign, either below in the earth, or above in Heaven. For these words indicate entirely that by the name of a sign, some miraculous thing ought to be understood.

Thirdly, the words of the prophecy are manifest: BEHOLD, A VIRGIN SHALL CONCEIVE. The particle Behold, which is accustomed to be used when something singular and admirable is proposed, is not prefixed here without cause, so that, namely, that admirable sign which God was about to give them might be carefully observed. Behold, he says, says Oecolampadius, so that it may signify not a common miracle, but a sign worthy of God and excellent. But then there is talk of a virgin, whose virginity is undefiled and untouched. For this is what the word עלמה imports, which denotes not a young woman, as Socinus renders it, but a virgin, nor does it occur anywhere in the Scriptures otherwise than of an undefiled virgin. For it is a name of status, not of age, which by the force of its origin from עלם hides, signifies a hidden virgin, just as Jerome interprets in quaest. Hebr. in Genes. Tom. 3, a virgin guarded with excessive diligence, so that the intensity of virginity is hinted at, so that, namely, she is both a virgin and hidden. It cannot, therefore, be understood of her who has been brought out publicly for marriage, who is by no means עלמה hidden, or ἀπόκρυφος, secluded and unknown; much less of a woman known by a man, and whose ערוה αἰσχημοσύνη has been uncovered, for these things are opposites. It was the custom among the Orientals that virgins should be brought up in secret and remain hidden at home. Whence they have the name עלמה, and conversely, the name for a harlot among the Chaldeans is נפקת ברא, one going out of doors, Gen. 34, 31. And thus also among the Greeks, virgins were called ἀγναὶ ἀκλειστοι, 2 Macc. 3, which refers to those who did not go out of their parents' houses by reason of modesty and virginal shame, as the Gloss has it in that place: who had their own παρθενῶνας, in which they were brought up apart from the sight of men, as Casaubon notes in Exerc. ad Appar. Annal. n. 53. They were also called θαλαμευόμεναι, as if brought up in chambers. And in this sense the word עלמה is always used in the Scriptures for an unknown and untouched virgin, Gen. 24, 43. Exod. 2, 8. Psalm 68, 26. Cant. 1, 3. chap. 6, 8. I add also Proverbs 30, 19. For the way of a man with a virgin is altogether hidden, who insinuates himself through various ways to the untouched virgin whom he loves, whether by secretly lying in wait for her virginity, so that not even the wisest Solomon could trace those ways, or even while he wishes to win her honestly for himself into a partnership of life and as a helper. And indeed, it is a most inscrutable thing how men insinuate themselves to virgins and win them, and how not rarely persons, neither seen nor known to each other before, by the secret providence of God, unite and are joined together. The matter is otherwise with harlots: who often prostitute themselves openly, so that the way of a man to a harlot is by no means so hidden. The more secretly an Alma is enclosed, the more wonderful is the way of a man to her, by which he desires to insinuate himself to her, since desire is thus the more sharpened. The thoughts, counsels, and affections of the mind in the love of such an Alma, who can search them out, when he is inflamed with desire for her!

mature! And he teaches that by the opposition of the fates in the following verse 19, by the word עלמה, an undefiled virgin is designated. For here Alma is openly opposed to an adulterous woman. Note here what Episcopius himself, even though he conspires with Grotius, argues for asserting the proper meaning of the word Alma regarding this passage on page 177. First, he says, no necessity compels one to believe that that word signifies any other girl than a virgin. For nothing prevents the sense of those words from being this: that it cannot be known more certainly whether one is marrying her who is truly a virgin and of undefiled modesty, than the track of an eagle in the sky can be known and detected, etc. not only as some explain these words, from the outward appearance, because it often happens that she who is believed to be a virgin is nevertheless not a virgin; but also because there are no undoubted signs, neither a priori nor a posteriori, which can convict a woman of prostitution or defiled virginity, unless it is discovered that she is pregnant and already carrying a womb: For what is read in Deut. XXII concerning בּתוּלים or the signs of virginity; that, according to the authors of the Jews themselves, should not be understood according to the letter, and reason as well as experience prove it to be uncertain and fallacious, as has been demonstrated by us at length in the examination of that passage. But I also add secondly; that the reason is manifest in the text why עלמה should be taken there for a virgin. For it is immediately added in the following verse 20, כן דרך thus is the way of an adulterous woman. The particle כן signifies similarity, not identity. But if the preceding word עלמה signified a girl or an adulterous woman, there would be an identity of speech here, and this example would not differ at all from the prior example. Therefore the wise man would not have said, thus is the way of an adulterous woman, but this, or this which I have said, is the way of a deflowered girl and a harlot. But because he said, thus is the way of an adulterous woman, he signifies not obscurely that he intended this: that the traces and signs of virginity, whether undefiled or defiled, are so uncertain that she who is believed to be a virgin, and who sells herself as a virgin, cannot be convicted of prostituted modesty by a spouse marrying her, any more than an adulterous woman, who has spread her body to many, and yet wishes to seem chaste and modest, can be convicted of adultery: or if anyone prefers it thus: No trace or outward sign appears in a virgin, from which it can be certainly detected that she is not a virgin after she has admitted a man, any more than any outward trace appears in an adulteress from which it can be certainly detected that she is an adulteress: not that perhaps it cannot be known or recognized by a husband or spouse or adulterer, but that it cannot be observed by others, or appear outwardly to anyone, no more than the trace of a ship appears in the sea to those looking from afar, although it appears sufficiently to those seeing it from close by. These are the words of Episcopius. We are not now going to say anything about the interpretation of those who understand the way of the man in the virgin (Mary Theotokos) incarnate, with Burgers on Isaiah 7, addition 5, folio 21, Weidner, Tract 2 on the mysteries of faith, page 256, Salmeron, Cornelius à Lapide, and others. Which opinion can be read in those authors. Nor is there any reason why you should object with Grotius that the virgin is pointed out whom Isaiah later married. For it is not established that the prophet joined a virgin to a former spouse, or married one after her death. And what would be new or miraculous in the fact that a virgin, when taken as a wife, cohabits with her husband, conceives and gives birth, unless Grotius wishes to play the fool with the Jews, who dream of this as a singular thing here, that he predicted the birth would be not of the female, but of the stronger sex? Regarding which Oecolampadius rightly says: What kind of miracle is this, if a girl conceives by a man? For this happens daily. Now if they wish to save the miracle in this, that the Prophet predicted she would bring forth a son: and in a future and uncertain matter affirmed a certainty: for she could also have brought forth a female, what could be more foolish than this? For in future contingent events, no one would rightly call it a sign if someone guesses happily. For who would call it a miracle if someone says that a union is thrown in all the dice by a gambler on the first throw, since this can also happen otherwise. Therefore, either they must confess a virgin incorrupt or deny that a miracle is indicated. Nor would the miracle then be in Alma, but, for a miracle, if you believe Apella, the Prophet must be held to be one who could predict a male. But away with those follies. St. Jerome diligently treated this argument concerning the word העלמה from the ancients: whose words are worthy to be read here. He has it thus on verse 14: When, however, it is said; the Lord himself will give us a sign; it ought to be new and wonderful. But if a young woman or a girl, as the Jews wish, and not a virgin gives birth, what kind of sign can it be called, since here it is a name of age, not of integrity? --- Furthermore, Alma among us is an ambiguous word; for it is called both an adolescent girl, and hidden, that is, ἀπόκρυφος. ---- Therefore Alma is not only called a girl or a virgin, but with emphasis, a hidden and secret virgin, who has never been exposed to the sights of men, but has been guarded by the great diligence of her parents. The Punic language also, which is said to flow from the fountains of the Hebrews, properly calls a virgin alma. ----- And as far as my memory serves me, I do not think I have ever read Alma used for a married woman, but for her who is a virgin, so that she is not only a virgin, but a virgin of younger age, and in the years of adolescence: For it can happen that a virgin is an old woman, but that one was a virgin in girlish years: or certainly a virgin, not a girl, and who could not yet know a man, but was already marriageable. Which seems to be established from the places Gen. XXIV. 43, Exod. II. 8, Ps. LXVIII. 26, Cant. I. 3.

What of the fact that the Prophet speaks expressly in the fourth place about a VIRGIN, not one who is about to conceive after she has been joined to a husband, of which nothing is held here, but one who is both a VIRGIN and already pregnant. BEHOLD A VIRGIN CONCEIVES, or is pregnant. For the word הרה is of the past tense, not the future: or certainly it is a participle, as is the following ילדת, so that a pregnant and bearing virgin may be designated: because all things are present to God. Therefore, it is not regarded that the Prophet is about to approach a virgin and is about to beget a son from her; but he points out a pregnant virgin: who is both a virgin, and pregnant or with child. Which Blessed Luther urges against the Jews in his book on Schem-Hamphorasch, fol. 130. Secondly, Isaiah says that such an Alma is pregnant, and that this shall be a miracle and a sign. He does not say, She will become pregnant, as some Rabbis would gladly have interpreted. They must be ashamed of their own grammar, for הרה means concepit, is pregnant. She is pregnant, she has conceived. But yet they want to twist their way out of it, saying that the Prophet in his old age took a young maiden and made her pregnant; upon that he looked, and says: Behold, the Alma is pregnant, and will bear a son. So that the meaning is, that is not the sign, that the Alma is pregnant, that the Prophet has already accomplished, he is her husband, but that she bears a son and not a maiden. Whom shall we now believe? God says, that shall be a sign, that the Alma is pregnant. The Jew says, oh no, God lies, that is no sign, because the Prophet has made the Alma pregnant. Thus we have here two texts. The text of Isaiah stands bright and clear there, God will give you a sign, behold, the Alma is pregnant, etc. But the Jews' text is this: Behold, the Alma has a husband, and is pregnant by the Prophet, then God will give you a sign, that she

A son will give birth, and not a daughter. Hæc Megalanders adversus Judæos. Which also constrain Grotius, inasmuch as he would prefer that it be read in the text with the Jews, 'She shall conceive'; indeed, he rendered the past verb here against the laws of grammar in the future, so that he might snatch it away for the future impregnation of the Prophetess. Which the Jews have rightly understood, that it must be rendered in the past; therefore they explain it concerning the Prophet's wife who was already pregnant; nor can a sign be placed in that, that the Alma had been impregnated by the Prophet; for what is new in that, or worthy of such magnificent prophetic speech concerning an admirable sign? But when the words are accepted as they sound, they openly exhibit a huge miracle, as was warned before, concerning A PREGNANT VIRGIN. Fifth, it is also to be observed regarding the He Hajediah, which demonstrates by the word העלמה not some certain virgin, because none could be designated at that time; but a certain singular one, such as was Mary, the mother of Immanuel. Socinus acknowledged this likewise in lect. Sacr. p. 54. From which it follows that there is nothing absurd if in this place that letter does not signify some certain girl, but a certain singular one, as Mary, the mother of Jesus, was certainly singular. Indeed, it seems to be said that that signification of that letter, so that it might indicate some known and certain thing, hardly has a place in that prophecy, and in that word Alma, to which it is prefixed. For neither had any mention been made of any young woman before, nor, to whomever that name is finally referred, for that time in which that prophecy was issued; whether she is the one with whom the Prophet had intercourse, or whoever else, it does not appear by any reason how she was known and certain, so that that sense, if I may say so, relative and indicative of that letter, could be accommodated to her.

Sixth, he, concerning whose conception and birth it is treated here, was to be called, i.e., was in reality to be Immanuel. For thus Grotius himself interprets: 'Certainly,' he says, 'he who does not read the Prophets sluggishly, cannot be ignorant that he is also said by them to be called by some name, who is not to be addressed by that sound of voice, but whose deeds that word is suitable to celebrate.' Places occur everywhere: Is. 1:26, 9:6, 56:7, 60:14, 62:4, Jer. 3:17 & 23:6, Ezech. 48:35, Zach. 8:3. Therefore where in Is. 14:20 there is יקרא, the Chaldean has יתקים, 'he shall remain': & Luke, citing the said place, Is. 56:7, translates יקרא as ἕξιν 19:46. Such is below Ναζαραῖος κληθήσε & υἱοὶ θεῦ κληθήσονται; where we shall also cite a similar expression of Philo. But neither the son of Isaiah, nor any other ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος is in reality עמנואל, that is, God with us. For by this name the union of the divine and human nature is introduced; which Grotius acknowledges, if not a restricted and limited, but a more perfect signification of the word is attended to. But that it is to be accepted in the latter sense the Angel taught in Matt. 1, nor does Grotius deny it. But from where will it be proven that it is also to be understood in a restricted and limited way? That is repugnant to the laws of τῆς ἑρμηνείας, which teach that one word does not have more than one signification in the same place. Nor does that restricted signification have any foundation in the Holy Scriptures. Furthermore, if that word were to note that God himself wishes to be present and to benignly regard and help them, as Grotius explains, that name will not be proper to that son whom Grotius imagines for himself, the Prophet's, but it will be suitable to all whom God has wished to be present with graciously; indeed, it will have to be claimed by a better reason for not a few others, to whom God has proven his aid more, such as Moses, Joshua, David, Hezekiah, and others. Whence, not even with that jejune interpretation admitted, which he drew from Socinus, that Immanuel denotes the present favor of God, could that name be peculiarly claimed for Isaiah's son: since to him, or even to the Jewish people

Judaic, such a singular and such a notable grace did not happen, that before any other times the name Immanuel should then have been imposed and appropriated to someone for the singular favor and help of God. Which Socinus also confesses on p. 44. Since that peace and quiet, which was in the land of Judah after those devastations of the Kings of Syria and Israel, of which it is treated there by name, and not even afterwards of the King of Assyria, was very brief and doubtful, it hardly seems that for a thing of such a kind, unless something else lay beneath it, that name Immanuel, which signifies openly and simply the present favor and help of God, ought to be given to that boy. The συνέχεια is also to be noted here, concerning which Cyril says excellently: 'He will therefore bring forth a son, and you, O house of David, who now,' he says, 'refuse to believe in God and to ask a sign from him for the confirmation of those things which have been promised, because you are more addicted to idols, you shall call his name Emmanuel, i.e., you shall confess that God has appeared in human form. For when the only-begotten Word of God appeared according to us, then he also became with us. For he who was above every creature became like us.' Worthy of observation also are those things which Jerome has here, who likewise refers the word קראת to the house of David, and explains it concerning the invocation of the name Immanuel. Therefore that boy, who will be born from the virgin, O House of David, let him now be called by you Emmanuel, that is, God with us, because you will prove by the things themselves, having been liberated from two enemy kings, that you have God present: and he who will afterwards be called Jesus, that is, Savior, for the reason that he is about to save the whole human race, let him now be called by you by the name of Emmanuel. And afterwards: 'And the sense is, O house of David, to whom it is commanded by the word of God, that you call, that is, invoke, being established in danger, the name of Emmanuel, that is, of God with us: do not marvel at the novelty of the thing, if a virgin brings forth God, who has such power, that he who is to be born much later might liberate you now, having been invoked: for he himself is the one who was seen by Abraham, and spoke to Moses.'

To this Immanuel, seventhly, the land of Judea is attributed as his own, Is. 8, 8. And the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of THY LAND O Immanuel. This, however, can by no means be said of the son of Isaiah. For was the kingdom and land of Judah the possession of the Prophet's son? Clearly, Immanuel is established by the Prophet as the legitimate Lord of Judea, over which the Prophet's son obtained no dominion; nor did any other person exist at that time whose land Judea was, under the devastation of Judea made by Sennacherib, except Hezekiah, whom indeed both Grotius and Socinus, whom he followed, readily grant cannot be understood by the boy promised here, nay, they prove it with an invincible argument: because Hezekiah was already born at that time, and was even nine years old when this promise was made. I shall transcribe the words of Socinus, since the book is not easily accessible: That some, just as Justin affirms in his dialogue with Trypho the Jew concerning the Jews of his own time, say that that boy, who was to be called Immanuel, is Hezekiah, the son of Ahaz who was then reigning, from which it would follow that it was deservedly and properly said that the land of Judah was his, since he was the King of that land, that can in no way be admitted. Since when Hezekiah began to reign, he was already 25 years old. But Ahaz, in whose time that prediction was made, held the kingdom for only sixteen years, so that even if we wish that these things were predicted at the very beginning of the reign of Ahaz, as indeed is likely, it would be necessary that Hezekiah, who became King immediately after his father's death, was already nine years old when the prediction itself was made. How therefore could Hezekiah be that boy, who was born after this prediction? who else, therefore, can be understood, whose own the land of Judea becomes besides Christ, of whom it is said in Isa. IX, that of his government there shall be no end? Indeed, the very standard-bearer of the heretics, F. Socinus, admits that this ἀξίωμα (title) applies to the son of Isaiah only improperly. He does not deny, however, that it applies properly to Christ. Now can it be said, unless quite improperly, that the land of Judah belonged to that boy born of the Prophetess? Or what was the point of making that apostrophe to him who was to be called Immanuel, if that boy were to be the son of the Prophet? But not even improperly was the land of Judah the son of the Prophet's, to whom no dominion at all over Judea, whether proper, improper, direct, or indirect, belongs. Whence some of the Jews, with R. David Kimchi, gather from these words: Thy land, O Immanuel; that this boy is the son of King Ahaz. To this point, says Kimchi, is what is said in chapter 8, 8: 'He shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel,' namely, because he was the King's son. But Hezekiah his son, to whom the dominion of the land belonged, had already been born to him long before, and therefore his birth cannot be said to be promised here, nor was he ever called Immanuel. It remains, therefore, that we understand the prophecy of the Messiah, whose land, and all its breadth, and fullness it was. To whom the Prophet, as supreme Lord and Judge, complains that the Army of the Assyrians extends its wings over his land.

Eighth, the dissipation of the counsels and confederacies of various peoples is attributed to Immanuel, so that the people of God might act and glory confidently against such powerful enemies without dread and fear, because of this protector of theirs, Immanuel. 'Gather yourselves, O ye people, and be broken in pieces; and give ear, all ye of far countries. Gird yourselves, and be broken in pieces; take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for IMMANUEL,' Is. 8, 9. 10. To whom can this of mortals be attributed? And who was there then, by whose strength they could rely with such boldness against any machinations and counsels whatsoever, even clandestine and hidden, of the most powerful enemies? Whence we conclude: He is designated by this name Immanuel, in whom the Jews could trust against any machinations, who could most easily dissipate the counsels and leagues of any enemies. But this not Isaiah, not the King's son, not any other of mortals, but only the Messiah, the son of the virgin, as he who is the same Son of God, the great and mighty God, Jehovah Zebaoth, could perform. In him alone was one to trust; he alone was to be their dread and fear and Sanctification.

Whence ninth, the opposition is to be well noted, which is instituted between the enemies, whom the people could fear, and this protector of theirs, who alone ought to have been their dread, who is called Jehovah of Hosts, so that it is thus manifest that that Immanuel is not a mere man, but is Jehovah of Hosts himself. 'Say ye not, A confederacy; for all that this people shall say, a confederacy is; and fear ye not their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.' Who does not see here, as before Immanuel was opposed to the enemies, as the dissipator of their counsels and machinations, and the savior of the people: So the same is now opposed to the same as Jehovah of Hosts, who alone ought to be the people's dread and terror, under whose protection the people themselves have no need at all to dread and fear the enemies, but can be secure from them: provided they fear and sanctify this Lord Immanuel.

Which the explanation of the New Testament also confirms in the tenth place. For that that Messiah is he who is proposed here as the Lord of Hosts to be feared and sanctified, is not obscurely clear from Luke 2. 34, Rom. 9. 32, 1. Pet. 2. 6. We argue thus: He who is to the unbelieving a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, for a gin and for ruin, but to the faithful for a sanctification, is Jehovah of Hosts, who alone ought to have been the dread and terror to the Jews, by whom they could and ought to rely against enemies, so as not to fear their counsels and machinations. But Christ is he who is to the unbelieving a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, for a gin and for ruin; but to the faithful for a sanctification, as Simeon testifies in Luke 2: 'Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many'; and Paul in Rom. 9: 'Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness. Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law.' For they stumbled at that stumbling-stone and rock of offence; and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed; (Is. 28, 16, which place is parallel to ours) and Peter in 1. Epist. 2: 'To whom coming (he designates Christ) as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious.--- Wherefore also it is contained in the Scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence.' We conclude therefore: Therefore Christ is Jehovah of Hosts, who alone ought to have been the dread and terror to the Jews, by whom they could and ought to rely against their enemies and their counsels and machinations.

Eleventh, nor is that at all to be neglected, which is said, that that Virgin shall call her son Immanuel. For since otherwise the naming of children belongs to the father among the Hebrews, Gen. 16:15, ch. 21:3, what reason is there why the naming of her son is here attributed to the mother, unless it be that he himself is to be ἀπάτωρ [fatherless], and is to be born from a virgin mother. For if Haalmah were understood to be joined to a husband, the husband would certainly impose the name upon the son, not Haalmah herself. And thus the Angel attributes the naming of the son to the Virgin Mary, Luke 1:31. You shall bring forth a son, and shall call his name Jesus. Strength is added to the argument if it is observed that no mention of a man is made here at all, which Oecolampadius noted in this place: Observe that there is no mention of a man here, and it is the custom of Scripture that generation is ascribed to the man. For if it had been Isaiah's wife, he would have said: Behold, your wife shall bear you a son; just as we read concerning Abraham: Sarah your wife shall bear you a son. Here, however, all things are attributed to the virgin, that she is pregnant, that she shall bring forth, that she shall call his name.

Twelfth, therefore, the angelic annunciation, if it be compared with the present prophecy, points out with a finger as it were extended the Haalmah, this virgin, whom the Prophet had designated: Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God. Behold, you shall conceive in your womb, and shall bring forth a son, and shall call his name Jesus. What the Prophet said, BEHOLD, A VIRGIN SHALL CONCEIVE; that the angel interpreted: BEHOLD, YOU A VIRGIN SHALL CONCEIVE. What the Prophet: BEHOLD, A VIRGIN SHALL BRING FORTH A SON; that the Angel, BEHOLD, YOU A VIRGIN SHALL BRING FORTH A SON. What the Prophet: THE VIRGIN SHALL CALL THE NAME OF THAT SON OF HERS IMMANUEL; that the Angel, YOU VIRGIN MARY SHALL CALL THE NAME OF YOUR SON JESUS. What is more evident than that the Angel taught in this way that the Prophet spoke not of a married virgin, but of a pure virgin, of an Alma, who did not know a man, as Mary speaks of herself: and that he testified, that no other virgin than Mary, no other son of a virgin than Jesus, is indicated by the Prophet?

Thirteenth, if anyone in such great light still doubts, the Holy Spirit wished to remove every doubt when He described the revelation made to Joseph concerning the birth of Jesus, the son of the virgin. For He referred to this Prophetic prediction, by which He openly testifies that the same had been predicted by Him, Matt. 1:22. Now all this was done that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the Prophet saying: Behold, a virgin shall have in the womb and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel, which is interpreted, God with us. What place is there now for the Socinian-Grotian gloss, that the Prophet did not speak of a pure virgin, according to the literal and first obvious sense, not of Mary the Christ-bearer, but of the wife of Isaiah: not of Jesus, the son of the virgin, but of I know not what son of Isaiah begotten from marriage; since the Angel himself quite clearly designates the Prophetic prediction, just as was done in the annunciation of Gabriel, sent to Mary, Luke 1, and thus by the Prophetic prediction informs Joseph, who was anxious about the pregnancy of his spouse Mary, in such a way that no scruple could remain for him, no doubts about a virgin bearing in the womb with her virginity intact: or at least the Evangelist informs us in such a way, if anyone does not admit these things brought forward by the angel. But if the Prophet had dealt in any way (not to say in a proper and literal sense) with a virgin to be taken by him, and to conceive from his συνουσία, the scruple would not have been removed from Joseph at all, but rather his doubt and anxiety would have been increased in many ways. What? That it seems to be clear from this, that at that time among the people of God the oracle concerning the wife of Isaiah was by no means understood: nor could the virgin herself, or Joseph her spouse, have been made more certain or confirmed in faith by a reference to the Prophetic oracle in the angelic annunciation, nor would the Evangelist have simply testified that the Prophetic prediction had been fulfilled in Him. This certainly is manifest, that according to the intention and mind of the Holy Spirit, who is the only infallible interpreter of Himself both through the Prophet and through the Evangelist, the prediction ought to be understood not of the wife or son of Isaiah, but of Mary the undefiled virgin, and her son Jesus. But that the oracle concerning a virgin bearing in the womb and her son, with the Holy Spirit as witness, was fulfilled in an unmarried virgin, bearing in the womb from the Holy Spirit, without the union of a man, in Mary the θεοτόκος, and her son Jesus, the Savior of His people, that can in NO, IN NO WAY be understood or explained, according to the judgment and mind of the Holy Spirit, of such a virgin who, having been given only to marriage, was impregnated through marital συνουσία, or of the son of a Prophet, or of some other person. Nor should it be passed over lightly here that the Angel in Luke 1 and the Evangelist in Matthew 1 take those names as ἰσοδυναμοῦντα, not because they are simply equivalent, but κατὰ. Because the name Immanuel implies that God will be with us, not by a bare παράστασις and gracious assistance, but in such a way that God is to be a partaker of our nature and is to save us; and thus it is a name both of person and of office. That God will be with us by the assumption or communion of our nature, and by our liberation and Salvation. For just as God, when He is said to be present to someone, is not only at hand to him, but also helps him, so that not even then is a bare παρουσία, but also a divine ἐνέργεια and operation implied: so when it is hinted here that He is to join Himself to our nature by a personal union, the grace, help, and salvation which He is to bring by that hypostatic presence and conjunction is designated at the same time. Therefore, as the name Jesus first designates the office, but yet presupposes and connotes the θεάνθρωπος person, to whom this whole office belongs: so the name Immanuel first designates the θεάνθρωπος person, but at the same time inserts the end of the personal union of the divine and human nature, the reconciliation of God and man, and the reduction of man to God, and thus the salvation of the human race. Whence by the very fact that Christ is Jesus, i.e. Savior, He is also Immanuel by reason of His person, because no one could save from sins except God and man, Immanuel. He is the same by reason of His office, because He reconciles God to us, and us to God. Therefore Christ is Jesus, i.e., Savior and Immanuel at the same time, because He is Savior through the reunion and reconciliation of us with God. Since the Prophet did not wish to signify precisely how Christ was to be named, but who He really was and what He would be, which Grotius acknowledged above. Since therefore Immanuel is the same as Jesus, as far as the truth of the thing signified is concerned, regarding person and office, it is manifest that this oracle cannot in any way be understood of the son of Isaiah, who was neither ever called Immanuel, nor was or could be Immanuel regarding the truth of the thing, or Jesus: but that the name Immanuel belongs to Christ alone, just as the name Jesus. Whence that opinion, concerning the son of Isaiah as a type of Christ, was long ago marked with a black coal by the holy Fathers, and rejected. He who maintains this Judaizes, St. Jerome pronounced on this passage p. 34. Some of ours, Judaizing, contends that the Prophet Isaiah had two sons, Jasub and Emmanuel: And that Emmanuel was generated from his wife the Prophetess, as a type of the Lord Savior: so that the former son Jasub, which is interpreted 'left' or 'converting', signifies the Jewish people, who were left, and afterwards returned. But the second, that is, Emmanuel and 'God with us', the calling of the Gentiles: after the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. And on chapter 8:18, whence I wonder that some of ours understand those boys to be the two sons of Isaiah, whom he generated from the conception of the Prophetess woman: Jasub namely and Emmanuel, of whom the former preceded in the rejection of the former people, the following in the assumption of the Gentiles. Whoever accepts this will consequently also affirm that the Prophet Hosea truly had a harlot for a wife. These things Jerome.

Let there now be added to these arguments, in the final place, the testimonies which can be sought from the Jews themselves and others ἐξ ἐναντίας (from the opposite side). For among the Jews, not only did the 72 Elders understand the word Alma as a pure virgin, when they rendered it—not as Symmachus and Theodotion did, in favor of the Jews, as νεανις (young woman), but as ἡ παρθένος (the virgin), which word denotes a pure virgin. Whence Irenaeus, in book 3, chapter 24, urges that version. But Aquila also rendered it ἀπόκρυφον (hidden), and both Chaldean translators, Onkelos and Jonathan, interpret עלמתא as a virgin: not to mention the fact that R. Hakkadosh attempts to extract the name מרים (Mary) from the word עלמת by means of the Kabbalah. R. David Kimchi denies that the word is to be understood as the Prophet's wife; for if it had been the Prophet's wife, he would have said 'the Prophetess,' just as it is said, 'and he approached the Prophetess.' To this point pertains what is said in chapter 8, verse 8: 'Immanuel shall fill the breadth of your land.' Thus, therefore, the Jews themselves disagree in their opinions, nor do they find one in which they might agree. Some explain it as referring to Hezekiah, whom R. Solomon refutes by chronology; others as referring to the son of Isaiah, with R. Solomon and Aben-Ezra, whom, as I have said, R. David Kimchi refutes; Kimchi interprets it as referring to a certain girl or wife of Ahaz and her son, concerning whom, however, not a word is read anywhere in Scripture. In a certain hidden book of the Jews, this opinion is found, that a certain girl not yet mature for a man conceived and gave birth, and that this was proposed as a peculiar sign, Helvicus disp. 14. t. 9. Giess. p. 32. testifies: whom R. Solomon also cites. Furthermore, others say the sign was in this, that the Prophet could predict with certainty immediately after conception concerning the fetus of the young woman, that it would be a male. R. Aben-Ezra and R. David Kimchi [say the sign was] in this, that the infant, scarcely born, immediately ate butter and honey, and knew to reject evil (food), and choose good, or sweet. Thus, those who abandon the certain meaning of the Holy Spirit must fluctuate in their opinions and take refuge in various absurdities. Socinus confesses that the miracle which is predicted here does not in any way fit the time of the Prophet, or the wife of the Prophet, which he proves thus: It is enough, he says in lect. sacr. f. 44. to exclude every miraculous thing in the conception and birth of the wife of the Prophet, that which is there (chap. 8.) is explicitly narrated, namely that the Prophet approached her, which words without doubt honestly signify that he had relations with her. He also confesses that the land of Judah was only improperly the land of that boy born of the Prophetess: and he could not save that double sense of his concerning the son of the Prophet and concerning Christ, without taking refuge in the profane asylum of a desperate cause, that God was accustomed to speak obscurely in His predictions, just as the Devil was accustomed to speak obscurely in the responses which he gave among the Gentiles, who therefore, by that obscurity, easily persuaded men who were not unskilled nor entirely ignorant of divine matters that those responses were divine, so that from the fact that his predictions were obscure and could be accommodated to many senses, just as the divine predictions themselves are, he was called Loxias. To this finally returns that accusation of ambiguities and equivocations concerning the Holy Scriptures!

In the School of Calvin, Fr. Spanheim refutes Musculus, who likewise establishes his own type in this oracle, since some boy is promised by God to be born at that time from a young girl, but from the union of a man: and the antitype, insofar as the MESSIAH is simultaneously figured here, part 1. Dubior. Evangel. Dub. 34. p. 296. What, he says, could be proposed to the people as miraculous or extraordinary in a girl conceiving and giving birth by a man? This also is added, that the impiety of Ahaz was so great that, if the Prophet had indeed designated some girl in particular, he would have taken pains in every way to ensure she did not unite with anyone, much less that she conceive from him, or at least that her fetus would not be nurtured softly, so that the truth of the Prophetic oracle would not be established by him. Indeed, no remedy at all for the incredulity of the Jews, or of Ahaz, would have been provided here. For this promise could be just as uncertain as the previous one concerning their liberation, until it was proven by the event itself: I. The birth after some months. II. His education after the passage of some years; and before this happened, their minds were left suspended and anxious concerning their own preservation. But the promise concerning the Messiah was certain, about which it was a sin to doubt, and which not even Ahaz himself dared to call into doubt openly, as it was that in which the Jews constituted the beginning and the end of their boasting and hope. Add that by this means that excellent privilege of the Messiah is not a little obscured, namely that he alone was to be born of an עַלְמָה virgin. Moreover, the application of Matthew could be called into doubt in this way: for it will be easy for the Jews to object that, at least in the principal points, there must be a conformity between the type and the antitype. But this is one of the principal points, to be conceived from an עַלְמָה. If therefore the type was not born of an עַלְמָה virgin, no solid proof could be given that the Messiah must be born of a virgin. And thus both the scope and the application of Matthew, and the singular prerogative of the Messiah would collapse. Indeed, since countless boys could have been brought into the light in Judea at that time, be nurtured peacefully, and survive the destruction of those Kings, what peculiar thing could be sought for the conviction of Ahaz and the incredulous Jews from such a birth, where there was nothing singular or excellent above others? These and many other things are in the same place by Spanheim. Musculus himself, although he does not profess to reject that opinion rashly—that this oracle does not treat of the Messiah in a literal sense, but only typically—nevertheless says that he approaches that interpretation hesitantly. Others among the Papists refute Salmeron, who likewise invents a double sense here. Tirinus notes that Haalmah is nowhere in the Scriptures taken for any other girl than a virgin and one untouched by a man: and that the prophecy of Isaiah here concerning the conception of Christ in the virginal womb of Mary IS A MATTER OF FAITH, from Matt. 1, 22, so that it is not permitted for Christians to doubt this. Compare also Isaiah on this passage.

Nor indeed is there any reason for you to say that the birth of the Messiah could not be established by the Prophet as a sign of liberation for Ahaz, inasmuch as it followed only some centuries after him; and therefore, so that the reason for the sign given might stand for him, and the scruples of the Jews might be more rightly satisfied, a type of that kind must be established. For it must be noted that the sign is not established here for Ahaz alone; but when he refused through infidelity to ask for a sign, it was given, as the words of the text have it, to the whole house of David: which is not to be restricted to the times of Isaiah: since not only in that age, but for seven centuries, up to the birth of Christ, the house of David, from which the Messiah was to be born, and the rest of the Jews, and especially the faithful and holy among them, were to be raised up and confirmed concerning the certainty and fulfillment of the divine promises. The Lord was therefore about to give that sign of divine grace in the house of David, by which the faithful in every age have always raised themselves up and taken comfort: and which is promised here to the house of David; which was the blessed fruit of the womb of the Virgin Mary, through whom all grace and blessing is obtained, in whom and through whom all promises are also amen, 2 Cor. 1. Therefore Cyril of Alexandria, Comment. in Es. 1, 1. orat. 5. But with Ahaz refusing and saying most perversely, I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord, (for he attended more to the impostures of vain prophets) God Himself, of His own accord, in a way, exhibited the sign to the house of David. For it was necessary, it was necessary that the announcement of salvation through Christ be made to those who were of the Davidic family, i.e., from the tribe of Judah, from which Christ Himself was born according to the flesh. From this sign, therefore, the house of David could conclude that it would by no means be destroyed by its enemies, but was to be preserved until the fullness of time; by this sign they were also made more certain, because by a new promise it was given to them, and by a new name the Messiah was distinguished, concerning the gracious assistance and aid of God in the present necessity: that the Son of God, who would be willing to assume human nature from this family, would deign even then to succor it particularly and to snatch it from the dangers of its enemies. That was a sign of the power of God, since Ahaz had not at all believed that God could deliver the Jews from the hand of those enemies, Rezin and Pekah. For it is a far greater argument of divine power, which God was about to give to his descendants and grandchildren, by raising up the Messiah from a virgin, and through him delivering the whole human race from more powerful enemies—sin, death, hell, and the Devil; it was a sign of God's enriching grace, which could not be confirmed by a more significant and more admirable argument than by the exhibition of the Messiah, to be provided in his own time, whom therefore, as a son of a virgin born from the house of David, and Immanuel, God with us, by the fellowship of nature and the aid of grace, He promises by a new and illustrious promise.

It is therefore not obscure how this promise could give assurance to Ahaz of deliverance from those two Kings; for it not only presented a proof of greater power, but was also the foundation of the Davidic preservation, which then seemed to be in peril if Jerusalem were handed over into the hands of those two most hostile Kings, and indeed the foundation of all other promises; as if the Prophet were saying: If God is at some time going to give you what is greater, what is more difficult, what is utterly stupendous and unheard of, that a virgin should conceive and bear Immanuel, how much more will He give you this, which is less? If God is not only to be truthful in the exhibition of the Messiah, but also sufficiently powerful in the preservation of the Davidic house until the times of the Messiah, He ought certainly to seem to you also truthful and sufficiently powerful in fulfilling the promise promulgated by me concerning your preservation and deliverance from the hand of those two Kings; thus Spanheim explains it. Which is also the interpretation of Maldonatus, Eman. Saa, Gabr. Vasquez, and others. If God will at some time deliver the oppressed people from that greater force and destruction, He will surely perform it much more easily from the two tails of smoking firebrands. And if such was the power of love in God that He gave His only-begotten Son, how would He deny other things, which are infinitely lighter. To this point belongs the distinction of Hornbeck, lib. 3. against the Jews, cap. 1, p. 227. Not the exhibition of the sign, but indeed its certain promise could be a sign of the thing then to be performed. Since whatever God predicts, on account of His infallibility, is held—and deservedly ought to be held—as fulfilled, not only here but also elsewhere throughout. And therefore the Prophet also speaks here in the past tense: Behold, a virgin HAS CONCEIVED. Add that some think a twofold sign is proposed here, with Franc. Junius in Parall. lib. 1. part. 4. The one common, pertaining to the refutation of the infidelity of Ahaz and the Jews, namely the promise concerning Christ, which God gave from the beginning of the Church concerning the seed of the woman, in whom all promises are Yes and Amen; the other more special, pertaining particularly to the promised deliverance from those kings: which Junius wishes to be derived from verses 15 and 16; others restrict it to verse 16 alone: namely, the pledging of the little boy: that before he knows to refuse the evil and choose the good, those Kings are to be exterminated from their own land and kingdom. The former sign was to be derived from the first principles of the Jewish religion. The latter struck the eyes, so that Ahaz would be inexcusable from every side. As the blessed Sam. Bohl, Rostock theologian, my once very beloved friend, says in Comment. moral. 3. Es. c. 10. p. 106. Which can therefore be seen as joined, so that they might mutually confirm one another, and the Jews might be made more certain of the truth of the deliverance from the Kings and the extermination of the same through the repeated promise concerning the seed of the woman: and conversely, when they saw the promise of that deliverance fulfilled shortly, they would be established in the faith concerning the advent of the Messiah by this promise at the same time. Nor indeed is there need that confirmatory signs should precede in time; since they sometimes follow, as is manifest in Exod. 3:12, in the sign of the mission of Moses for the leading out of the people, the offering on the mountain after the leading out: such as are also read in 1 Sam. 2:34, c. 10:2, 1 Kings 22:25, 28, Es. 37:30, Jer. 44:29, which signs are proposed for this reason, that by the promise of future signs the faith of the pious may be both confirmed and exercised at the same time, lest they distrust His word when it has not been confirmed by a present sign, Jos. 4:48, in which sense Grotius interpreted verse 9 of this 7th Chapter. Do you not believe, therefore, because you are not confirmed? By some conspicuous sign, that is. Although if we weigh the matter rightly, the virginal birth should not be looked upon as a subsequent sign, but indefinitely, which my Bohlius well observed on p. 52. This is that sign which God, unasked, gave to King Ahaz or the house of David, or rather recalled to memory. This is that sign which God made conspicuous both from heaven and from the underworld; and when Ahaz would not choose even one part of it, the Creator exhibited both. This is that sign which ought to have worked toward Hascheket, and true faith in them, when all things visible to the eyes seem to be snatched away. This is that sign which testified that it was not a labor for God, which is for men. This is that sign which designates Christ Jesus not simply and absolutely as future, nor as past; but as indefinite, the Savior who is yesterday, today, and forever. For although future things are predicted, we see them happen in a certain respect: This is that sign, at the memory of which you tremble, O Satan, the gates of the underworld totter, and the true Jerusalem rejoices indefinitely. For it is a sign which the Lord Himself gave, strengthened the incredulous Ahaz, and comforted the faithful Hezekiah. What? That it does not even appear necessary that the word אות, when God promises that He will give it, should be understood as a sign; after Ahaz, through infidelity, refused to ask for a sign at the command of God. For although God employs the same name, nothing seems to stand in the way of it being taken generally now concerning a new and stupendous thing, as if to say: You indeed persist in your infidelity, O King, but know that you, with the whole house of David, because of His truth and the faithful whom He keeps for Himself in His people, and that deliverance which you call into doubt, having been announced from the mouth of God, He will fulfill and will give a miracle far more eminent and much more incredible to human reason, namely, that a virgin among you shall conceive and bear God Himself. See Blasius Viegas on Ap. 12 and Barrad. T. 1, l. 8, c. 6. From which it is manifest that the oracle is perfectly consistent, nor is there need that we, with the Jews and Judaizers, should invent a literal sense about some boy then born as a sign of deliverance. But who will allow himself to be persuaded that the Jews can be satisfied when one goes over to the opinion of the Jews? Will not the Apellas thus boast, that Christians are offering them the herb: and will they not be confirmed in their reprobate opinion? And how will they be convinced concerning a typical sense of this kind, namely that this boy must have been a figure of the Messiah, when there is deep silence about him in Isaiah: nay, it is inappropriate that a boy born in wedlock should be established as a type of a son to be born of a pure virgin: and Musculus himself confesses that the Jews are blinded all the more by those types and shadows, since they do not receive the light of truth exhibited in the New Testament. Deservedly, therefore, Bohlius in Comment. ad h. l. p. 75. We are commanded, therefore, we are driven, we are compelled and we are impelled to refer all these things ONLY simply, purely and absolutely to Jesus of Nazareth, the son of the immaculate virgin, so that its weight may be left to the sign.

Latin:

Vers. 14. DABIT DOMINVS IPSE VOBIS SIGNVM] Non petentibus.

VOCABITVR NOMEN EJVS IMMANVEL] Præter alterum nomen Maher-Schalal Hasbaz VIII. 1. Si- gnificat nomen Emmanuel certum Dei auxilium contra Syros & Israëlitas, & in urbe conservanda contra Senna- cheribum. Alterum nomen vastitatem agri & oppidorum excidia.

sperta de nativitate communi & ordinaria, non singu- lari & miraculosa, de homine simplice & mero, non θεανθρώπῳ, quo ergo jure adversus Judæos urge- bitur amplius, aut quo jure saltem inter Christianos explicabitur illud de virgine illibata, partu miraculo- so & supposito divino, de Christo θεανθρώπῳ? A- gnoscit Grotius adversus Judæos id urgeri non posse, ideo saltem mysterium id subesse Christia- nis liquido apparere ait. Sed ne his quidem appa- ret liquido! Quis enim sub virgine virum experta, mystico sensu subesse virginem illibatam, virum non expertam; quis sub partu ordinario è conjugio vi- ri & fœminæ prodeunte, partum virginalem; quis sub homine ψιλῷ θεάνθρωπον subintelligit aut subintelligendum esse sibi persuaderi patietur! Au- diamus tamen, quomodo mysticum suum sensum colligat Grotius? Primo ita concludit: Si omnes liberationes populi Judaici præsagia fuêre ejus libera- tionis, quam Deus per Christum erat effecturus; sane & illa insignis liberatio ab obsidione hostili, quam Propheta promittebat, eo pertinuit. Sed quid hoc ad mysticum sensum! Non enim quæritur de fa- cto aliquo typico, de liberatione præfigurativa, sed de sensu verborum Propheticorum à Spiritu S. intento, neque si factum, quod prædicitur, figuram fuisse liberationis Christi nobis constet, ideo verbis Pro- pheticis præter sensum literalem mysticus subest. Multæ sunt historiæ V. T. quæ typum aliquem præbent, & instar typi applicari possunt: de qui- bus tamen non, ubicunque in Vet. Testam. legun- tur, dicere ideo convenit, quod in relatione histo- rica sensus illius subsit, mysterium exhibens. Non ergo è factis præfigurantibus & typicis sensus mysti- cus dictionum statim colligendus. Adhæc, quid ad verba illa; Ecce, virgo concipiet, & filium pa- riet, liberatio! num si promissa sub signo nascitu- ri filii Prophetæ liberatio typus agnoscatur libera- tionis Christi, oraculum, quod filium Prophetæ nasciturum prædicit, quantum ad literalem sen- sum, mysticum etiam ideo sensum continet, de virginis filio sine viri opera eidem nascituro? Quæ hic cohærentia; quæ evidentia, ut liquido myste- rium hoc appareat? Denique annon ea ratione in omnibus liberationibus, quæ prædictæ leguntur, prædictam sensu mystico etiam liberationem per Christum futuram, prædictam etiam Christi nati- vitatem è matre virgine concludendum?

Porro secundo id adhibet Grotius, quod Ga- briel Mariam Luc. 1, 32. docuerit, stabilitatem regni Davidici à Propheta promissam verum πλήρωμα in æterno regno Christi habuisse. Sed Gabriel non hoc oraculum, quantum ad regni Christi æter- nitatem, respicit, neque eam è stabilitate Regni Da- vidici colligit, (hæc enim ἀπαίδευτος, & infirma plane foret collectio, è regni Davidici stabilitate æternitatem regni Christi demonstrare) sed digi- tum intendit ad cap. 9. Es. in quo non de Davidis regno agitur, aut sub Davidis regno Messiæ re- gnum adumbratur, sed ipsum Messiæ regnum se- cundum proprium & nativum oraculi prophetici sensum describitur. Tum vero etiamsi hic pro- missa fuerit regni Davidici stabilitas, in præsenti oraculo, neutiquam inde probari posset æternum Christi regnum, aut quo documento ostendetur, stabilitatem Davidici regni πλήρωμα in regno æ- terno Christi habuisse? Denique si hoc etiam ad- mitteretur, nondum tamen sensus mysticus de vir- ginis filio subesset sensui literali, de filio Esaiæ com- muni connubii lege procreato.

Quapropter tertio ad nomen virginis se reci- pit Grotius. Illud autem, virgo concipiet, quanto, inquit, excellentiorem habet sensum, si referatur ad eam, quæ ita concepit, ut virgo post conceptum ma- neret, quod soli Mariæ convenit. Verum huic sensui nullus locus erit, si per virginem hic uxor Esaiæ aut juvencula, quam debebat Esaias ducere, intelliga- tur sensu literali; quia una eademque vox in eo- dem loco semel posita, non potest tam contraria significata simul obtinere. Vox העלמה, si hoc in loco, virgo concipiet, notat virginem in matrimo- nium ductam, vel virum expertam, non potest in eodem loco significare virginem innuptam, quæ salva virginitate conceperit. Non ergo tantum eminentior hoc loco sensus est de Maria virgine il- libata, sed unice verus & genuinus; siquidem ver- ba hæc VIRGO CONCIPIET, VIRGO PA- RIET, uti sonant, sensu simplici primumque obvio conceptum, & partum virginalem illæsa vir- ginitate inferant, neque aliter in hoc oraculo acci- pi possint aut debeant.

Addit Grotius quarto mystici sensus sui hanc etiam rationem à nomine Immanuel desumtam. Nomen enim Immanuel, sicut & Jesu, habere qui- dem & in aliis suam potest significationem restrictam atque limitatam; at in Christo aliam habet infinitis partibus perfectiorem. Nam is est, in quo illa præcla- ra Dei promissa omnia sunt ναι και ἀμὴν 1. Cor. 1, 20. is est verbum, quod caro factum inter nos habitavit, Joh. 1, 14. in ipso deniq; habitat τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότη- τος σωματικῶς, Col. 2, 8. In hunc, qui non credunt, eos manet Φοβερὰ ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως, Ebr. 10, 27. Sed hic iterum constringi potest Grotius è propria ὑποθέ- σει. Si enim vox עמנואל ita intelligenda hoc in lo- co est, ut notet θεάνθρωπον, verbum, quod caro factum est, eum in quo habitat plenitudo Deitatis corpo- raliter, non potest utique ea hoc loco de ψιλῷ ἀν- θρώπῳ intelligi, & vice versa: si filius hic promissus est merus homo Esaiæ vel cujuscunque alterius fi- lius, qui dicatur solum Immanuel ad designandam gratiosam Dei adsistentiam, quomodo per filium hic promissum intelligi potest Jesus θεάνθρωπος, Dei & Mariæ virginis filius, & per nomen Imma- nuel designari divinæ & humanæ naturæ unio in persona Christi hypostatica! Si dicas, Esaiæ fi- lium typum Christi fuisse, ponamus sane hæc, (etsi nullo indicio id constet, neque de Esaiæ filio ullo verbo hic mentio fiat) quid tum certius erit, quam quod oraculum hoc, juxta illam hypothesin, de filio Esaiæ sensu literali agens, nihil omnino faciat ad nativitatem Filii Dei è Maria virgine; multo minus eminentiorem quendam sensum simul exhi- beat, juxta quem partum virginis θεανθρώπου in- ferat! Nam si dicere velis: mysticum sensum sub- esse huic literali de filio Esaiæ, eo quod hic typus Messsiæ esse debuerit, non modo gratis assumes hunc typum, quem è Propheta demonstrare debe- bas, in quo nihil de eo invenire est, quod Esaiæ fi- lius Messiæ typus extiterit, (nemo ergo Judæorum id tibi largietur:) sed ineptum etiam fuerit infan- tem è congressu maritali natum, constituere ty- pum partus virginei, qua talis, vel conceptionem & partum uxoris typum facere conceptionis, & partus illibatæ virginis; nec minus ineptum, no- men Immanuel, quod notet solum παράστασιν, & assistentiam præstandam filio Esaiæ, eique ideo im- ponendum sit, hac notione typum esse unionis hy- postaticæ divinæ & humanæ naturæ in Christo: quo pacto omnes, quibus unquam auxilio suo Deus præsto fuit, hoc nomine notari potuissent, simul- que mysterium unionis hypostaticæ typice adum- brassent; quod quam inconveniens sit, nemo non videt. At ineptius longe, sub sensu literali de na- tivitate meri hominis à parentibus suis procreandi mysterium, vel sensum alium mysticum latere de nativitate θεανθρώπου è virgine matre, voces virgo concipiet, de virgine nuptui data è συνουσία viri con- cipiente intelligendas esse, nomen Immanuel nihil aliud secundum literalem sensum hic inferre, quam auxilium Dei, & sub istis tamen verbis my- sterium subesse de illibatæ virginis conceptione, salva virginitate futura, & de persona θεανθρώπῳ, quæ Immanuel, hoc est, nobiscum Deus, ideo vocan- da sit, quod Deus nostræ naturæ consors futurus, vel nostram naturam assumpturus sit in unitatem divinæ suæ hypostaseos. Nemo Christianorum sub tali literali sensu tantum mysterium somnia- vit unquam, tantum abest, ut veritatem hujus mysterii, stante isto sensu literali, Judæorum ulli ex hoc oraculo demonstraturus sit: qui redarguent potius inde Evangelistas, quod ex verbis Pro- pheticis sensum plane alium & contrarium infe- rentibus (juxta Grotianam hypothesin,) tantum mysterium exsculpere nequicquam conati fuerint. Quomodo itaque concludere jam potest Grotius; verissime ergo à Mattheo scriptum esse, in nativitate Christi verba Esaiæ πληρωθῆναι, id est, consumma- ta esse; siquidem in verbis Esaiæ secundum sensum proprium & germanum, juxta Grotium, nihil de nativitate Christi habeatur, nec sub illis verbis, si eo sensu accipi debeant, ex intentione Spiritus Sancti contrarius sensus, quem mysticum vocat, subesse possit, uti jam πρὸς ὄμμα demonstra- tum. Recte itaque Rivetus Animadversion. ad annot. Grotii in Cassandr. pag. 238. Si is est sen- sus simplex, & primo obvius verborum Esaiæ, quem vult Grotius, quicquid postea dicatur de mystico, de ea, quæ virgo peperit, quæ per illam mulierculam, quæ ex mariti congressu peperit, fuerit significata, id totum erit incertum, imo & ἀπροσδιόνυσον. Quid enim commune mulieri post concubitum cum viro pa- rienti cum virgine, quæ virgo concepit & peperit? Justinus certe Martyr non obscure, sed apertis verbis αὐτολεξεὶ Esaiam partum virginis prædi- xisse censuit; nec est quisquam ex antiquis, qui hic typum somniârit. Jam vero, inquit Justinus A- pol. 2. pro Christian. p. 58. quemadmodum ex vir- gine oriundum disertis verbis Esaias prædixerit, au- dite. Prædixit autem ad hunc modum: Ecce virgo uterum gestabit, & pariet filium, & dicent super nomi- ne ejus Emanuel, hoc est Nobiscum Deus. Nam quæ incredibilia & impossibilia habita apud homines e- rant, ea Deus per Spiritum propheticum futura præ- monstravit: ut cum facta essent, in dubium per in- credulitatem non vocarentur, sed propter prædictio- nem certa per fidem haberentur. Ne autem aliqui prophetiam, quam produximus, non intelligentes (per cavillationem) nobis ea objiciant, quæ Poëtis nos re- cte objecimus, Jovem rei Venereæ gratia ad mulieres ventitasse dicentibus, declarare verba ista visum est. Itaque quod dictum est: Ecce, virgo uterum gestabit, significat virginem absque consuetudine venerea con- cepturam fuisse. Si enim cum quocunque consue- visset, non jam virgo fuisset. Seductus autem hic Grotius tum à Judæis, quod antea observavimus: siquidem de Esaiæ filio R. Salomo Jarchi, R. Lipo- manus & R. Menasse Ben Israël in Conciliat. Hi- span. in Es. explicent: quibus R. Isaac Ben Abra- ham lib. contr. Nov. T. cap. 21. adstipulatur: Tum à Socino hac in parte Judaizante, cujus vestigiis hic pressè inhæret, uti videre est in Lectionibus sacr. locor. p. 37. seqq. Prolixe enim Socinus contendit, verba Esaiæ in eum sensum accipienda esse, ut quic- quid hic prædicitur, pertineat manifeste ad tempora illa ipsius Achazi Regis, & quisnam iste puer sit, in- quit, ex juvencula nasciturus, & quænam illa ju- vencula, omnino constare videre est e cap. 8. Esaiae, quod nempe puer ille, cujus nomen vocandum, festina spolium, accelera predam, sit ille quidem, de quo cap. 7. agitur, Esaiae nempe filius. Porro ob Evan- gelistae Matthaei explicationem, perinde uti Grotius, observat Socinus, unam eandemque praedictionem plures, quam unum sensum habere. In eo tamen magis sanus fuit Socinus, quam Noster: quod, etsi asseruerit, ALIQUO MODO accommodari posse & accommodandam esse illam praedictionem ad alium quempiam, praeter Jesum Nazarenum, ad puerum nempe illum ex prophetissa & Esaia natum, cogno- verit tamen, si proprietas verborum spectetur, & totius loci atque sententiae, ad ipsum Jesum praecipue ac potissimum referendam eandem esse. Quod etiam argumentis aliquot confirmavit: Sed talibus, quae omnino probant, non praecipue, sed unice ad Je- sum eandem pertinere, secundum verborum & lo- ci ac sententiae totius proprietatem. Grotius vero simplicem primoque obvium sensum, h. e. proprium fa- cit de Esaiae filio: non autem admittit secundum proprietatem verborum ac loci totius sermonem esse de Jesu Nazareno. Deterior ergo sine dubio sententia Grotii, magisque adversa cum Propheti- co vaticinio, tum interpretationi Evangelistarum. Grotium sequutus est Simon Episcopius Instit. Theol. lib. 3. cap. 14. prolixe ejusdem sententiam, eademque cum ipso ratione adstruere satagens. Unde, ne fucum ea ulli faciat, & imprimis ad vin- dicandam divinam veritatem, expendenda eadem paulo uberius erit.

Primum autem observandum, quod mere pre- caria sint hypotheses ac rationes, quibus hic nititur Grotius, omni fundamento solido destitutae; imo nonnullae etiam Scripturae S. adversae. Unde enim docebitur, eundem esse puerum, cui nomen Im- manuel imponendum, & qui Maher-Schalal-Has- baz vocandus erat. Unde ostendetur, Prophetis- sam illam tum fuisse virginem, aut quod ei nupserit Esaias, eaque fine testes adhibuerit? Unde evince- tur, quod illa de filiis in portentum datis intelligen- da sint de duobus filiis Esaiae, Schear-Jasub & Im- manuel? Quae omnia temere sine probatione as- sumit Grotius.

Tum vero signum hic datur po- pulo Judaico non vulgare, sed prorsus singulare & admirandum. Quum enim Deus jusserit per Pro- phetam, ut Rex ipse postularet signum aliquod, sive in Caelo, sive in terra, eoque renuente, signum ipse dederit, manifestum est de admirando quo- dam signo hic agi: de signo ingenti, quod vox אות importat, quae cum verbo מופת ostentum, conjungi solet Exod. 4, 9. 17. 25. Deut. 6, 21. Ef. 20, 3. de signo, quod cum quovis alio, sive in Caelo, sive in terra da- to, contendere possit. Tale enim postulare Rex jussus erat. De signo, quod Deus ipse daturus erat, quod non levius esse potest, quam quod Achas pe- tere dubitabat: de signo, quod non Regi infideli Deum hypocritice illudenti, sed domui David, non in praesens tantum, sed in perpetuam gratiae obsignationem daturus erat Deus. Audite ergo do- mus David, nunquid parum vobis est molestos esse hominibus, quia molesti estis & Deo meo? Propter hoc dabit Dominus ipse vobis signum. Non ergo vul- gare, sed prorsus insigne atque eximium est, quod hic promittitur. Agnovit hoc Musculus: Non dicit, pete tibi signum a me, sed a Domino. Tale signum, inquit, pete, quod nec ego, nec quisquam alius, sed Dominus solus praestare poterit, ut scias, me ab illo ad te esse missum. Grotius ipse signum plane mi- raculosum postulandum fuisse, fatetur, ita expli- cans: Pete tibi signum a Domino Deo tuo in pro- fundum inferni. Puta, ut terra statim moveatur aut dehiscat. SIVE IN EXCELSVM SUPRA, puta ut Sol subito deficiat. Quid autem admirandi est in eo, quod virgo juvencula, dum nuptui datur, è συνοικίᾳ maritali concipiat, ac pariat? At virginem illibatam concipere ac parere, id prorsus mirabile est; DEUM hominem fieri tale tantumq; signum est, quo nihil magis admirandum auditum est un- quam, quod signum tum de cælo desuper, tum in- ferius in terra evenit: quia Deus in cœlis est ho- mo in terra factus, & per admirandam Spiritus è Cœlis ἐπίλευσιν, in utero virginis matris conce- ptus est in terris, quod est ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυ- στήριον 1. Tim. 3, 15. & novum illud, quod solum est sub sole novum, Jer. 31, 22. ob quod Cyprianus, vel quisquis autor est ille perantiquus, Serm. 3. de Nat. Domini merito exclamat: O Domine, quam admira- bile est nomen tuum! Vere tu es Deus, qui facis mira- bilia. Non modo mundi hujus staturam admiror, non terræ stabilitatem &c. miror Deum in utero virginis, miror omnipotentem in cunabulis, miror, quomodo Verbo Dei caro adhæserit, quomodo incorporeus Deus tegumentum corporis nostri induerit! Præclare hic Cyrillus lib. 1. Orat. 4. in Es. p. 122. Valedicamus igitur errorum præstigiis, & quod rectum verumque est, amplectamur, sanctam virginem hac prophetia nobis à Deo denotari credamus. Sic enim erit para- doxum vere, atque incredibile & signum maximum in profundum simul & excelsum, juxta divinam pro- missionem. E supernis enim, & ex Deo Patre secun- dum naturam genitus filius unigenitus, exinanivit seipsum, & ex utero virginali editus est secundum carnem, non humana seminis emissione, unde genera- tio sequuta sit, sed vi & efficientia Sancti Spiritus: & ante eum Justinus Martyr Dial. cum Tryph. pag. 242. Si non è virgine iste, de quo Esaias dicebat, nasciturus erat, in quem Spiritus Sanctus exclama- bat; Ecce dominus dabit signum: Ecce virgo in utero concipiet, & pariet filium? Si perinde atque alii o- mnes primogeniti, ille quoque ex concubitu gignen- dus erat, quodnam signum non cunctis primogenitis commune se facere dixit? Enimvero quod vere si- gnum est, & humani generi credibile futurum erat, hoc est, ut ex virginali utero Primogenitus creatu- rarum omnium caro factus, vere puellus fieret: oc- cupans id per Propheticum Spiritum, alio atque alio modo, sicut vobis recensui, pronunciavit: ut cum factum esset, virtute & consilio rerum universarum conditoris factum esse agnosceretur: haud aliter, quam ex costa lateris Adæ una Eva exstitit, atque a- lia animantia omnia verbo Dei ortum principiumque suum cæpere. Vos autem in his quoq́; adulterare trans- lationes seniorum vestrorum, qui apud regem Ægy- ptii Ptolemæum fuere, audetis: allegantes, non habere Scripturam sicut illi verterunt: Sed ecce juvencula in utero concipiet. Quasi vero magnæ quidquam rei designaretur, si mulier ex concubitu paritura esset, quod quidem juvenculæ mulieres pleræque faciunt o- mnes exceptis sterilibus: Quas tamen & ipsas, cum vult, efficere potest, ut prolem gignant, Deus. Nam Samuelis mater infœcunda per consilium & volunta- tem Dei peperit: Et Uxor sancti Patriarchæ A- braæ; Et Elisabeth, quæ Johannem Baptistam ge- nuit, & aliæ quædam similiter. Quocirca non pro im- possibili vos habere illud oportet, facere Deum posse quæ vult omnia: præcipue vero cum quid futurum es- se vaticiniis est prænunciatum. Non decet vos vatici- nia ipsa ausu temerario vel adulterare, vel perperam exponere, nam vobis ipsis tantum injuriam facietis: Deo autem nihil nocebitis. Argumenti hujus vim & evidentiam agnovit ipse Socinus; ideo in lectio- nib. sacris, quas vocat, p. 44. Cum ita scriptum sit;

Ecce, Deus dat vobis signum, ecce, juvencula con- cipiens &c. satis constare videtur; signum hoc à Do- mino datum, in eo præcipue consistere, quod juvencula illa conceptura & paritura esset, id quod NULLO PACTO ad sensum illis temporibus accommodatum convenire potest, quamcunque tandem fuisse velimus juvenculam istam. Unde concludit p. 48. ad ipsum Jesum hoc referendum esse; præsertim vero ob id, quod satis aperte constat, (verba ejus recito) Deum de- disse conceptum & partum illius puellæ pro signo mi- rifico. Id enim docent MANIFESTE ipsius Dei verba, cum ait Achazo: Pete tibi signum, sive in- ferius in terra, sive superius in Cœlo. Hæc enim verba omnino indicant, nomine signi intelligi debere rem aliquam mirificam.

Tertio verba vaticinii manifesta sunt: ECCE, VIRGO CONCIPIET. Particula Ecce, quæ adhiberi consuevit, quum ali- quid singulare & admirandum proponitur, non præter causam hic præmittitur, ut nempe observe- tur probe signum illud admirandum, quod Deus ipsis daturus erat. Ecce dicit, ait Oecolampadius, ut non vulgare significet miraculum, sed signum Deo dignum & excellens. Tum vero de virgine sermo est, cujus virginitas intemerata est, & illibata. Hoc enim vox עלמה importat, quæ non juvenculam, uti reddit Socinus, sed virginem notat, neque aliter, quam de virgine illibata uspiam in Sacris occurrit. Est enim status, non ætatis nomen, quod vi origi- nis ab עלם abscondit, virginem absconditam signi- ficat, velut Hieronymus quæst. Hebr. in Genes. Tom. 3. interpretatur, virginem nimia diligentia custoditam, ut ἐπίτασις virginitatis innuatur, ut nem- pe & virgo sit, & abscondita. Non ergo accipi po- test de ea, quæ nuptum palam educta est, quæ mini- me עלמה abscondita est, vel ἀπόκρυφος, reclusa & incognita; nedum de muliere à viro cognita, & cu- jus ערוה αἰσχημοσύνη retecta, hæc enim opposita sunt. Receptum erat apud Orientales, ut virgi- nes secreto educarentur, ac domi latitarent. Unde ipsis nomen עלמה, & ex adverso Scorto nomen a- pud Chaldæos נפקת ברא prodiens foras, Gen. 34, 31. Atque ita etiam Græcis virgines dictæ ἀγναὶ ἀ- κλειστοι, 2. Macc. 2. quæ de domibus parentum non exi- bant ratione pudicitiæ & verecundiæ virginalis, uti Glossa ibidem habet: quæ suas habuere παρθενῶ- νας, in quibus educabantur seorsim à virorum con- spectu, notante Casaubono Exerc. ad Appar. Annal. n. 53. θαλαμευόμεναι etiam dictæ, quasi in thalamis educatæ. Atque hoc sensu vox עלמה de incognitâ, & illibatâ virgine semper adhibetur in Sacris, Gen. 24, 43. Exod. 2, 8. Psalm. 68, 20. Cant. 1, 3. cap. 6, 7. addo & Proverb. 30, 14. 19. Via enim viri in virgi- ne abscondita omnino est, qui per varias vias virgi- ni illibatæ, quam deperit, sese insinuat, sive occul- te ejus virginitati insidiando, ut ne sapientissimus quidem Salomo vias illas indagare norit, sive et- iam dum honeste eam sibi conciliare vult in vitæ societatem, & adjutorium. Et profecto res ma- xime imperscrutabilis est, quomodo sese viri vir- ginibus insinuent easque concilient, quodque non raro personæ antea neque visæ, neque no- tæ invicem, arcana Dei providentia coalescunt & copulantur. Secus se res cum scortis habet: quæ sæpe palam se prostituunt, ut via viri ad scortum nequaquam tam occulta sit. Quo oc- cultius conclusa est Alma, eo magis mirabilis via viri est ad eandem, qua se insinuare eidem cupit, si- quidem magis ita desiderium acuatur. Cogitatio- nes, consilia, affectus animi in amore talis Almæ quis perscrutari potest, cum desiderio ejus inflam- matur!

matur! Et docet fatis oppositio in vers. seq. 19. per vocem עלמה virginem illibatam designari. Siqui- dem hic Alma aperte opponatur mulieri adulteræ. Notanda hic, quæ Episcopius ipse, etiamsi cum Gro- tio conspiret, pro asserendo vocis Alma significa- tu proprio de hoc loco disputat pag. 177. Primum, inquit, nulla necessitas cogit, ut vox illa aliam puel- lam, quam virginem significare credatur. Nihil enim vetat, sensum verborum istorum hunc esse, non posse magis certo sciri, an quis eam ducat, quæ revera virgo est, & illibatæ pudicitiæ, quam sciri ac deprehendi potest vestigium aquilæ in cœlo &c. non modo uti qui- dam verba hæc exponunt, ex aspectu exteriore, quia sæpe evenit, ut quæ virgo esse creditur, virgo tamen non sit; sed etiam quia nulla indubitata indicia sunt, nec à priori, nec à posteriori, quæ aliquam prostitutæ aut delibatæ virginitatis convincere possunt, nisi com- periatur gravida esse, & uterum jam ferre: Quod enim Deut. XXII. legitur de בּתוּלים sive signis vir- ginitatis; id ipsis Judæis autoribus secundum literam intelligi non debet, & ratio etiam atque experientia incertum ac fallax esse evincunt, uti in examine loci istius à nobis prolixe demonstratum est. Sed & secun- do addo; Rationem in textu manifestam esse, cur עלמה isthic pro virgine accipi debeat. Subjicitur e- nim statim vers. seq. 20. כן דרך sic via (est) mulie- ris adulterantis. Particula כן similitudinem signifi- cat, non identitatem. At si vox præcedens עלמה signi- ficaret puellam sive mulierem adulteram, identitas o- rationis hic esset, & exemplum hoc nihil differret à priori exemplo. Itaque non dixisset sapiens, sic est via mulieris adulteræ, sed hæc, sive hoc, quod dixi, est via puellæ defloratæ & meretricis. Quia vero di- xit, sic est via mulieris adulterantis, eo non obscure significat, se id voluisse: Tam incerta esse virginitatis seu illibatæ, seu delibatæ vestigia atque indicia, ut ea, quæ virgo esse creditur, & quæ pro virgine se venditat, non magis convinci possit à conjuge eam ducente, pro- stitutæ pudicitiæ, quam fœmina adultera, quæ cor- pus suum pluribus vulgavit, & casta tamen & pudi- ca videri vult, adulterii convinci potest: vel si quis ita malit: Nullum vestigium atque indicium exterius apparere in virgine, unde certo deprehendi possit, eam virginem non esse, postquam virum admisit, non ma- gis, quam vestigium exterius ullum apparet in adulte- ra, unde certo deprehendi possit, eam adulteram es- se: non quod forte à viro aut conjuge aut adultero id sciri non possit aut cognosci, sed quod ab aliis id observa- ri nequeat, aut forinsecus id nemini appareat, non ma- gis quam eminus, aut ex specula prospectantibus ap- paret vestigium navis in mari, quanquam cominus videntibus id satis appareat. Hæc Episcopius. Non jam dicturi quicquam sumus de illorum interpre- tatione, qui viam virorum maximi in virgine (Ma- ria Θεοτόκῳ) incarnati, intelligunt cum Burgersi ad Es. 7. addit. 5. fol. 21. Weidnero Tract. 2. de myst. fid. p. 256. Salmerone, Cornel. à Lapide & aliis. Quæ sen- tentia apud authores illos legi poterit. Nec est, quod cum Grotio excipias, virginem indigitari, quam deinde duxerit Esaias. Nam neque constat, virginem priori conjugi adjunxisse, aut post ejus fata duxisse Prophetam. Et quidnam novi, aut mi- randi in eo foret, quod virgo, cum in uxorem du- cta, cohabitat marito, concipiat atque pariat, nisi cum Iudæis ineptire velit Grotius, qui hoc singu- lare hic somniant, quod prædixerit partum fore non fœminei, sed potioris sexus. Quo de recte Oecolam- padius: Quale hoc miraculum, si puella ex viro con- cipiat? nam hoc quotidie contingit. Jam si miracu- lum in hoc salvare volunt, quod Propheta prædixit progenituram filium: & in re futura ac incerta cer- tum affirmavit: poterat enim & fœmellam parere, quid hoc ineptius esse queat? In futuris enim contin- gentibus nemo signum jure dixerit, si quis feliciter conjectet.
