This is to be understood partly of the remarkable majesty of the Apostles, which they attained among pious men by performing miracles in the name of Christ, and by which they were an object of the greatest admiration to all: partly of the extreme hatred with which the impious pursued and cursed them. You will be, he says, hated by all for my name's sake. And again: The time will come that whoever kills you will think that he is offering service to GOD. And Paul: We have been made a spectacle to the world and to Angels and to men. And soon after: We are as the offscouring of the world, the refuse of all things even to this day. This is certainly an astonishing wonder and miracle, that those who are ministers of true and perpetual salvation are held to be the authors of every curse on earth. It is also to be understood partly of the fewness of those who believe in Christ. For it is a wonderful portent that, although Christ was so diligently announced by the Prophets, and after he had come, testified to his majesty with such great miracles, yet so few believed in him. Therefore, the Prophet in another place exclaims in the name of the Apostles: Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? This prophecy also heals the stumbling block, lest we think that JESUS is not the CHRIST because few Jews believed in him. For if the greatest multitude of the Jews had acknowledged him, they would not have been a sign and a wonder. But this is a wonder, that so few believed in him. All these things are Brentius's, which it pleased me to bring forward to illustrate this remarkable passage. For they clearly present the meaning of the Prophet according to the Apostolic explanation, and they are far more certain than those which either Grotius or other interpreters bring forward here. Whence most of our own people interpret it in the same way.

Verse of the same. FROM THE LORD OF HOSTS] Instead of, from himself, by his own will.

Moreover, the repetition of the word Lord in such expressions is not idle, nor is there any reason why we should depart from the letter. Holy Scripture is accustomed to indicate the mystery of the Trinity in this way; which Brentius, Osiander, and others have also rightly observed here. In this place, says Brentius, three persons are clearly proclaimed in one divine nature. For the text holds it thus: Behold (here I am) I and the children, whom the LORD has given me for signs and wonders in Israel, from the Lord of Hosts, who dwells in Mount Zion. For the Son of GOD speaks these words, just as the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches, concerning whom it was said before, as Peter explains: Sanctify the Lord of Hosts himself, and he shall be to you for a sanctification, etc. You have, therefore, one person in the divine nature. But the Son of GOD says that the Lord has given him children. This is another person in the divine nature, namely, the Father. For God the Father gives men to his Son. Everything, he says, that the Father gives me will come to me. And again: Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me. At the end he adds: From the Lord, or with the Lord, or through the Lord of Hosts. This is the third person in the divine nature, namely, the Holy Spirit. For those whom God the Father gives to his Son, he gives them with the Holy Spirit. This is a clear sermon concerning the Trinity, so that you may know that not only the Apostles, but also the Prophets clearly preached concerning three persons in one divine nature. For what is added: Who dwells in Zion, signifies the unity of the divine nature in three persons. For the Father dwelt in Zion, because he veiled Himself by His word in the mercy seat, which was in Zion, and He instituted His sacred rites there. The Son dwelt in Zion, because He was foreshadowed by the sacred rites in Zion, and was preached there by promises. Furthermore, when He had assumed man, He Himself preached His Gospel in Zion, and performed many miracles in that place. The Holy Spirit dwelt in Zion, because since the promises concerning Christ were announced in Zion, and sacred rites foreshadowing Christ were performed, the Holy Spirit was effective through these in the pious. Added to this is the fact that the Holy Spirit was also poured out upon believers in Zion on the day of Pentecost. Wherefore it is rightly said that He dwelt in Zion.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ET PUERI MEI QUOS DEDIT MIHI DOMINUS IN SIGNUM, ET IN PORTENTUM ISRAEL] Nempe per nomina ipsis divinitus imposita, si- gnificationem habentia rerum futurarum.

Non hæc verba Esaiæ sunt ceu loquentis de sese, uti vult Grotius, neque ut gerentis typum Christi, & sanctorum omnium, quod placuit Oecolampadio & aliis: sed verba sunt ipsius Domini. Habe- mus enim interpretem indubitatum Spiritum Sanctum, Ebr. 2. v. 11. seqq. Qui enim sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur, ex uno omnes; propter hanc causam non confunditur fratres eos vocare dicens: Annun- ciabo nomen tuum fratribus: in nomine Ecclesiæ lau- dabo te (Psal. 22, 23.) Et iterum, ecce ego fidens in eum; & iterum: Ecce ego & pueri mei, quos dedit mi- hi Deus. Quæ verba ex eo loco desumta sunt. Si ergo Propheta hic de sese loqueretur, non vero Dominus, Apostolus non posset inde probare, quod Dominus nos sibi jungat, ac fratres suos faciat. Unde Cyrillus Alexandr. in h. l. Personam ipsius Emmanuelis introducit, qui in ipso spem collocantibus conjunctionem spiritualem videlicet indulget. Effu- dit enim Filius suum Spiritum in nos, & quasi dome- stici ac intimi facti sumus, in ipsoque clamamus, Ab- ba Pater. Quare pueros Dei & Patris nos vocat, utpote regenerationem per Spiritum habentes, ut & fratres ejus, qui natura vere est Filius, nuncupemur. Quod etiam Belgici Interpretes deserto Calvino suo agnoscunt, verba nempe hæc esse ipsiusmet Christi. Postquam ergo Dominus per Esaiam mo- nuit, ut populus Messiam Dominum Zebaoth sancti- ficet, Immanuel ipse jam Prophetam jubet ligare testimonium, signare legem in discipulis suis. Non Prophetæ discipuli, sed Domini sunt. Prophe- ta jubetur à Domino, qui hic loquitur, ligare le- gem, uti fatentur hic Belgici interpretes. Proin- de vi συνεχείας, quum cohæreant verba, Do- minus orationem pertexit. Cujus ergo sunt disci- puli, ejus etiam sunt pueri. At discipuli sunt Domini. Unde recte B. Bohlius: Versum צוֹר E- saiæ sanus adscribere non potest. Hinc enim Rabbi Salomo repetendum vel reassumendum putat כּה אָמַר יְהוָה ad vocem וְחִכִּיתִי . Nam præstolabor adscribunt Esaiæ, at repugnat causale, rationem enim ille dare tenetur, qui loquitur, cur in לִמּוּדַי obsignanda sit תּוֹרָה nempe quia ipse, qui loquitur cum Esaia, cum discipulis sit præstolaturus, nec ad exemplum Esaiæ auditorum irritaturus Dominum; hinc dico pueri cu- jus sunt לִמּוּדִים, ejus sunt etiam יְלָדִים. Sensum ita exprimit Osiandrina Paraphrasis: Nunc Chri- stus ipse loquitur de cæcitate gentis Judaicæ. Liga testimonium, obsigna legem in discipulis meis, id est, video futurum esse, ut testimonium seu verbum DEI auditoribus meis sit instar voluminis compli- cati, & colligati, & quasi Epistola annulo obsigna- ta, ut nemo legere queat, quid in voluntate aut Epi- stola contineatur. Et tamen expectabo Dominum, ut aliquorum saltem Judæorum misereatur eosque convertat, qui nunc abscondit faciem suam à do- mo Jacob, & perinde se gerit, ac si totum hunc populum omnino abjecisset: & præstolabor eum: quosdam enim Judæos salvabit, ne tota gens in æternum pereat. Refert autem CHRI- STUS salutem Judæorum ad Patrem cœlestem quia loquitur in statu exinanitionis suæ (etsi autem pauci admodum Judæi serio ad Christum conver- tantur: tamen non dubium est, eam gentem di- vinitus, inter tot hostes à Deo conservari, quod in ea sint adhuc aliquot electi, qui Evangelio Christi sunt credituri & salvandi.) Interim vero (inquit Christus) habeo aliquos, qui in me cre- dunt. Ecce ego (inquit Filius Dei) & pueri seu fi- lii (mei) quos dedit mihi Dominus Deus Pater, quos illuminavit Pater cœlestis salutari mea agnitione: quos ego non modo fraterno, sed paterno etiam affectu complector. (Hoc dictum de Christo & fidelibus ejus interpretatur Apostolus ad He- bræos 2. cap.) Sumus autem in signum & por- tentum; rectius: in signa & portenta, populo Israël, id est, obstupescent homines (imprimis Judæi) ad miracula, quæ ego & discipuli mei edi- turi sumus: & ad afflictiones, quas propter ver- bum Evangelii constanter sustinebimus (Specta- culum enim, inquit Paulus, facti sumus mundo, & angelis, & hominibus, 1. Corinth. 4.) Hoc sic disponetur à Domino exercituum (id est, per Spi- ritum Sanctum, DEUM æternum,) qui habitat in monte Sion, qui adest suæ Ecclesiæ admiran- dis donis: eaque effundet in Apostolos in urbe Hierusalem (Vide, quanto amore nos Christus complectatur: quippe quos filios suos vocat.) Observa etiam Trinitatis testimonium. Hæc O- siander. Alii ligandam esse quidem hanc doctri- nam plerisque, quibus clausa ea est propria culpa, quales erant Pharisæi & Sacerdotes in diebus car- nis Christi cum maxima populi parte: aliis autem obsignandam esse, qui per fidem susceperunt ean- dem: & à Spiritu Sancto obsignantur, utpote qui vere sunt Messiæ discipuli, quo abit Belgarum inter- pretatio: vel liganda plerisque testimonia Veteris Testamenti, donec tradantur discipulis Messiæ sub Novo Testamento, ut palam promulgentur, vel liganda ut integra, & probe colligata discipu- lis Domini tradantur. Discipulis non minus li- ganda, quam obsignanda docet S. Hieronymus: Liga testimonium, &c. vox Domini loquentis ad Prophetam; quia, inquit, factus est Dominus in lapidem offensionis & in petram scandali duabus domibus Israël, & missum ad se Emmanuel suscipe- re noluerunt: Liga testimonia Veteris Testamenti, & trade illa discipulis meis, qui Evangelium susci- piant, Apostolis videlicet sive Apostolicis viris. Vel certe lex & Prophetia usque ad Johannem ligetur apud eos & clausa sit atque signata, ut, quod le- gunt, non intelligant. At aliis liganda, aliis vero obsignanda intelligit Franciscus Junius: Liga te- stimonium, id est, Prophetiam hunc & volumen tuum, de quo v. 1. involve, ne amplius sit in oculis i- storum, quandoquidem ut infideles ludificantur eam. Configua legem inter discipulos meos: id est, eam annuncia, committe & erudi illos, quos nosti tactos à Deo esse.

Accipi autem omnino possunt verba illa sen- su exegetico & copulativo: neque necessum est, ut explicentur sensu disjunctivo & antithetico, si scil. monere dicatur Filius Dei, ut testimonium vel Ev- angelium ligetur in cordibus discipulorum, quo fide Christo devinciantur & adhæreant, & lex signetur vel inscribatur in iisdem, quo vera obedientia ejus- dem figuram in vita & actionibus suis referant. Quo fere abit Brentii expositio: Etsi plurimi Is- raëlitæ & cives Hierosolymitani offendantur in me & cadant, tamen reliqui erunt inter ipsos nonnulli pii, qui mei erunt discipuli, & in quibus testimonium & lex ligabitur & obsignabitur, hoc est, à quibus meum Evangelium recipietur, & in quibus sigillo Spiritus Sancti ita confirmabitur, ut magna fide i- psum amplectantur & toto corde ei adhæreant. Non ergo calculum meretur Grotii glossa: Testificatio- nem hanc obliga, & ei signa impone & da custodien- dam discipulis post te, ut omnino apud posteros cer- tum sit, hæc abs te Regi ac populo esse denunciata. Ni- mis hæc jejuna sunt. Non enim tantum hanc prophetiam respicere Dominum, sed sententias istas latius se porrigere ac doctrinam cœlestem universam concernere, cujus discipuli sunt cre- dentes, & antecedentia & consequentia evincunt. His ergo omnibus se jam in exemplum sistit Do- minus Messias veræ & constantis fiduciæ, Ego ex- pectabo Dominum, qui abscondit faciem suam à Ja- cob & præstolabor eum. Ecce ego & pueri, quos mi- hi dedit Dominus in signum & in portentum Is- raël. Si enim Messias ipse expectavit Dominum, quidni expectare eum deberet Achaz? Quam συν- έχειαν reddit Bohlius: Si Messias præstolatus Do- minum, ut misereretur Jacobi, cum prorfus faciem suam ab eodem abscondit, neque vana ejus fuit expe- ctatio & fiducia, exemplo utique ejus expectare Do- minum & fiduciam in eum collocare debebant Judæi, à quibus tum nondum ita omnino faciem suam ab- sconderat Dominus. Omnibus enim in meritum & exemplum datur Messias, cujus discipuli atque imitatores cumprimis Judæi esse debebant, ut lex & testimonium Domini in iisdem obsignaretur. Quum Messias è Jacobi posteritate, stirpe Juda & domo Davidis oriturus in plenitudine temporis, expectaturus sit Dominum, ubi prorsus Dominus avertisse faciem suam à Jacob videbitur, certa esse poterat domus David, Achab cum suis & universo populo Judaico, nunc non prævalituros hostes nec ad incitas redactum iri familiam Davidicam, aut populum Judaicum ejusdemque politiam, prout hostes minitabantur. Quod si de tempore Novi Testamenti explicentur cum Brentio, quæ præcedunt de offensione ad lapidem scandali, casu & contritione populi, qua abjiciendi erant Israë- litæ propter incredulitatem, & obsignandi, quot- quot recepturi erant Evangelium, præstolaturus dicetur Messias Dominum, qui faciem suam ab- scondit à Jacob, & minatur, se posteros Jacobi abjecturum, & expectaturus, quos ille sibi datu- rus sit sive è Judæis sive è gentibus, ut recipiat eos- dem ac tueatur servetque ad æternam vitam. Jam itaque sistit sese Christus, ac sibi non deesse pueros atque discipulos, quos dedit Dominus, etsi sint in signum & portentum in Israële, testatur. Ecce ego & pueri, quos dedit mihi Dominus. Quem lo- cum tanto Spiritus Sancti acumine, uti Brentius noster loquitur, inspexit Epistola ad Ebræos, ut per- spicue doceat, Christum his verbis concionari se humanæ carnis participem fore. Sic enim scribit cap. 2. Ecce ego & pueri mei, quos dedit mihi Deus. Posteaquam igitur pueri commercium habent cum carne & sanguine, & ipse similiter particeps factus est eorundem, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, Diabolum, & liberos redderet eos, quicunque metu mortis per o- mnem vitam obnoxii erant servituti. Hoc autem non est otiose cogitandum, sed in usum transfe- rendum, ut non solum sciamus à Prophetis prædi- ctum esse, Filium Dei suscepturum humanam car- nem, verum etiam collaturum eum cœlestia sua beneficia in omnes illos, qui credunt in ipsum, ut sicut ipse particeps est humanæ carnis & sanguinis, ita qui humanam habent carnem & sanguinem, & credunt in ipsum, participes fiant victoriæ ejus, quam ex morte & Diabolo reportavit. Deinde di- cit discipulos suos fore inter homines signa & por- tenta. Hoc intelligendum est partim de insigni majestate Apostolorum, quam edendis miraculis in nomine Christi inter homines pios consecuti sunt, & qua omnibus fuerunt summæ admiratio- ni: partim de summo odio, quo eos impii prosecuti & execrati sunt. Eritis, inquit, odio habiti ab o- mnibus propter nomen meum. Et iterum: Veniet tempus, ut quisquis interficiat vos, videatur cul- tum præstare DEO. Et Paulus: Spectaculum facti sumus mundo & Angelis & hominibus. Ac mox: Veluti piacula mundi sumus, omnium rejectamentum ad hunc usque diem. Hoc certe stupendum est portentum ac miraculum, quod qui sunt veræ & perpetuæ salutis ministri, habe- antur Authores omnis maledictionis in terra. Partim etiam intelligendum est de paucitate cre- dentium in Christum. Mirandum enim portentum est, quod cum Christus tam diligenter fuerit à Prophetis adnunciatus, & postquam venisset, tan- tis miraculis testatus sit suam majestatem, tam pauci tamen in ipsum crediderunt. Itaque Pro- pheta in alio loco nomine Apostolorum excla- mat: Quis credidit auditui nostro, & cui brachium DOMINI revelatum est? Medetur & hoc vatici- nium offendiculo, ne existimemus JESUM ideo non esse CHRISTUM, quòd pauci Judæi in eum crediderint. Nam si maxima Judæorum multitu- do agnovisset eum, non fuissent signum & porten- tum. Hoc autem portentum est, quod tam pau- ci crediderunt in eum. Hæc omnia Brentius, quæ ad locum insignem illustrandum adducere placuit. Sistunt enim perspicue sententiam Prophetæ jux- ta explicationem Apostolicam, ac longe certiora sunt, quàm quæ vel Grotius vel alii interpretes hic adferunt. Unde nostrates plerique omnes eo- dem modo interpretantur.

Vers. eod. A DOMINO EXERCITUUM] Pro, à sese, pro sua voluntate.

Non otiosa autem est in talibus locutioni- bus repetitio vocis Domini, neque est, cur disce- damus à litera. Solet Scriptura sacra ita innuere mysterium Trinitatis; quod hic etiam recte ob- servavit Brentius, Osiander, & alii. Prædicantur hoc loco, inquit Brentius, perspicue tres personæ in una divina natura. Sic enim habet textus: Ecce (hic sum) ego & pueri, quos dedit mihi DO- MINUS ad signa & portenta in Israël, à Domino Zebaoth, qui habitat in monte Zion. Hæc enim verba loquitur Filius DEI, quemadmodum do- cet Epistola ad Hebræos, de quo ante dictum est, ut Petrus exponit: Dominum Zebaoth ipsum sanctificate, & erit vobis in sanctificationem, &c. habes igitur unam personam in divina natu- ra. Dicit autem Filius DEI, quod dederit sibi pueros Dominus. Hæc est alia persona in divi- na natura, videlicet, Pater. Deus enim Pater dat filio suo homines. Omne, inquit, quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet. Et iterum: Pater quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego & illi sint me- cum. Ad extremum addit: A Domino, vel cum Domino, vel per Dominum Zebaoth. Hæc est tertia persona in divina natura, videlicet Spi- ritus Sanctus. Quos enim Deus Pater dat Filio suo, eos dat cum Spiritu Sancto. Hæc est per- spicua concio de Trinitate, ut cognoscas, quod non solum Apostoli, verum etiam Prophetæ cla- re de tribus personis in una divina natura prædi- caverint. Nam quod adjicitur: Qui habitat in Sion, significat unitatem divinæ naturæ, in tribus personis. Pater enim habitavit in Zion, quia re- velavit se verbo suo in propitiatorio, quod erat in Zion, & instituit illic sacra sua. Filius habita- vit in Zion, quia adumbratus fuit sacris in Zion, & prædicatus fuit ibi promissionibus. Præterea cum assumsisset hominem, prædicavit ipse in Zion Evangelium suum, & edidit in eo loco multa mi- racula. Spiritus Sanctus habitavit in Zion, quia cum in Zion adnunciatæ sint promissiones de Christo, & facta sint sacra adumbrantia Christum, fuit Spiritus S. per hæc efficax in piis. Accedit huc, quod & in Zion effusus sit Spiritus S. super credentes in die Pentecostes. Quare recte dicitur in Zion habitasse.

## 8:19
Vers. 19. AND WHEN THEY SHALL SAY TO YOU: SEEK OF THE PYTHONIC SPIRITS AND OF THE DIVINERS, WHO CHIRP IN THEIR INCANTATIONS: SHALL NOT A PEOPLE REQUIRE OF THEIR GOD] Up to here are the words of the idolaters: Is it not fair that every people should consult its own God.

FOR THE LIVING FROM THE DEAD?] In the Hebrew: for the living to the dead? This is now what God wishes to be answered to those idolaters: Shall one go to the dead for the living? This is indeed because most of the gods of the nations were kings long dead, whom some worshipped simply, others as having been translated to the stars.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ET CUM DIXERINT AD VOS: QUÆ- RITE A PYTHONIBUS ET A DIVINIS, QUI STRI- DENT IN INCANTATIONIBUS SUIS: NUMQUID NON POPULUS A DEO SUO REQUIRET] Hucus- que sunt verba Idololatrarum: An non æquum est quisque populus suum Deum consulat.

PRO VIVIS A MORTUIS?] In Hebræo: pro vi- bis ad mortuos? Hoc jam est quod illis idololatris respon- deri vult Deus: An pro vivis ibitur ad mortuos? Id vero id- eo, quia plerique Dii gentium erant reges pridem mortui, quos alii simpliciter, alii ut in astra relatos, veneraban- tur.

## 8:20
Vers. 20. TO THE LAW RATHER AND TO THE TESTIMONY] Let them hold themselves to my testimony and doctrine. The word וְאֶל־ is taken here again, as just now.

BUT IF THEY SHALL NOT SPEAK ACCORDING TO THIS WORD, THERE SHALL BE NO MORNING LIGHT FOR THEM] If they speak otherwise, all prosperity (this the Hebrews signify by the name of light, just as darkness will presently be put for adverse things) will be far from them.

Whence will Grotius prove that this special testimony is being referred to? If it were being designated, the He Hajediah would have been used in the customary manner. And by what proof is it established that the present prophecy is noted by the word of the law here? Grotius assumes it precariously, with no proof added. Wherefore we accept the law here rather in its proper and more famous sense. Nor is it permitted to doubt that it is a general dissuasion from Pythonic spirits and from diviners, and that the people are recalled by them to the law and to the testimony; it is to be believed that they are recalled to the word of God generally, and not solely and uniquely to this prophecy of the πα- ρανέος and the present one. Furthermore, where the testimony is distinguished from the law, which was done in verse 16, the Gospel is not undeservedly understood by the testimony (unless the text suggests otherwise): for what else are those Evangelical oracles than the testimonies of the Prophets concerning the Messiah, as Peter interprets in Acts 10:43. To the law therefore and to the testimony the Jews are recalled, that is, to the law and the Gospel, and thus to the unique word of God, which is completed in these parts, law and Gospel, and was accustomed to be divided into the law of Moses and the Prophets or prophecies concerning Christ under the Old Testament, as in Luke 16:29. Abraham said: They have Moses and the Prophets, let them hear them. Which passage is parallel to ours: since indeed, even though they are now dead, the brothers of the glutton are recalled to hear Moses and the Prophets. Genebrardus on Psalm 119 teaches that the law and the testimony are synonyms, and denote the word of God: and therefore there is no place for Becanus's gloss, that the prediction of future events is denoted by that word; nor for that of Marcus Marinus, who understands an oath by the law and the testimony. For the sentence of Scripture is opposed to the Pythonesses, and not an oath. Finally, the threat subjoined of the deprivation of morning light is likewise general, and concerns all who refuse to hear the word of God and go away to Pythonic spirits. But if they shall not speak according to this word, namely the laws and testimonies, or if they refuse to obey this counsel, and to hear the law and the Gospel, Moses and the Prophets, there shall be no morning light for them. Just as, on the contrary, in general, to all who attend to the prophetic discourse, the Holy Spirit promises the rising of the morning light, or the day-star, 2 Pet. 1:19. By the morning light Grotius understands all prosperity, but, as it appears, Grotius is concerned with temporal prosperity. But God threatens such persons most of all with the deprivation of spiritual and eternal happiness, under which is comprehended the deprivation of spiritual light, grace, and salvation, which Immanuel was to bring; indeed, the deprivation of Immanuel Himself; just as conversely, when the morning light is said to be about to rise for those who observe the prophetic discourse, φωσφόρος ἀνατεί- λη ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, 2 Pet. 1:19, it is indicated that Christ Himself will illuminate their hearts with His light, grace, and salvation, who is ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς καὶ ὀρθρινὸς, Rev. 22:16. Some refer those words to doctrine, to whom there is no dawn, because, namely, לו is said in the singular, not להם in the plural. But it is more consistent with the text and the accentuation that it be referred to the person, and thus that an Enallage of number, most common in Scripture, be established.

Latin:

Vers. 20. AD LEGEM MAGIS ET AD TESTI- MONIUM] Teneant se isti meæ testificationi ac doctrinæ. Vox וְאֶל־ hic iterum sumitur, ut modo.

QUOD SI NON DIXERINT JUXTA VERBUM HOC, NON ERIT EIS MATUTINA LUX] Si ali- ter loquentur, omnis prosperitas (hanc lucis nomine si- gnificant Hebræi, ut jamjam caligo ponetur pro rebus adversis) ab ipsis longe aberit.

Unde probabit Grotius, hanc specialem testifi- cationem respici? Quæ si designaretur, more con- sueto He Hajediah adhibitum fuisset. Et quo do- cumento constat; voce legis hic præsens vaticinium notari? Assumit eam Grotius precario, nulla addi- ta probatione. Quapropter legem potius proprie ac famosiori sensu hic accipimus. Neque ambigere licet, quin generalis dehortatio sit à Pythonibus & à divinis, populusque ab illis revocetur ad legem & ad testimonium; ad verbum Dei generatim, non autem solum atque unice ad hanc Prophetiam πα- ρανέος & præsenti eundem revocari, credendum est. Porro ubi testimonium à lege distinguitur, quod vers. 16. est factum, per testimonium Evangelium (nisi aliud suadeat textus) non immerito intelligi- tur: quid enim illa Evangelica oracula aliud sunt, quam testimonia Prophetarum de Messia, interpre- te Petro Act. 10,43. Ad legem ergo & ad testimo- nium revocantur Judæi, hoc est, ad legem & Evan- gelium, adeoque ad unicum Dei verbum, quod his partibus, lege atque Evangelio absolvitur, & in le- gem Mosis, ac Prophetas vel Prophetias de Christo dividi consuevit sub V. Test. uti Luc. 16, 29. Abra- ham dixit: Habent Mosen & Prophetas, illos au- diant. Qui locus nostro parallelus est: siquidem etiam, illis jam mortuis, revocentur fratres epulo- nis ad audiendum Mosen & Prophetas. Genebrar- dus ad Psal. 119. legem & testimonium docet esse Sy- nonyma, & notare verbum Dei: ideoque Becani glossæ locus non est, futurorum prædictionem ea voce notari; neque Marc. Marini, qui per legem & testimonium juramentum intelligit. Opponi- tur enim Pythonissis sententia Scripturæ, non au- tem juramentum. Denique comminatio subjun- cta privationis lucis matutinæ generalis itidem est, & omnes, qui verbum Dei audire detrectant & ad Pythones abeunt, concernit. Quod si non dixerint juxta verbum hoc, leges nempe ac testimonia, aut si consilio huic parere, & legem & Evangelium, Mosen & Prophetas audire detrectarint, non erit eis matutina lux. Quemadmodum ex adverso in genere omnibus, qui attendunt sermoni Prophe- tico Spiritus S. promittit exortum lucis matutinæ, vel phosphori, 2. Pet. 1, 19. Per matutinam lucem o- mnem prosperitatem intelligit Grotius, sed, uti ap- paret, de prosperitate temporali Grotio res est. At felicitatis spiritualis ac æternæ privationem maxi- me talibus minatur Deus, sub qua comprehendi- tur privatio spiritualis lucis, gratiæ ac salutis, quam Immanuel afferre debebat; imo privatio ipsiusmet Immanuelis; quemadmodum vice versa cum oritura dicitur illis, qui observant Propheti- cum sermonem, lux matutina, φωσφόρος ἀνατεί- λη ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, 2. Petr. 1, 19. Christum ipsum luce, gratia & salute sua collustraturum cor- da ipsorum, indigitatur, qui est ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς καὶ ὀρθρινὸς, Apoc. 22, 16. Nonnulli ad doctrinam referunt illa verba, cui non est ei aurora, quia scili- cet לו in singulari dicitur, non להם in plurali. Sed magis textui, & accentuationi convenit, ut ad personam referatur, adeoque Enallage numeri Scri- pturæ maxime usitata statuatur.

## 8:21
Vers. 21. AND HE SHALL PASS THROUGH IT] Through this: The Prophet said this, pointing to the land with his finger.

AND SHALL CURSE HIS KING] He will plot defections, about which we have just treated.

AND SHALL LOOK UPWARD] From God, whom they have despised, no help will come to them.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ET TRANSIBIT PER EAM] Per hanc: Hoc dixit Propheta, digito terram monstrans.

ET MALEDICET REGI SUO] Defectiones mo- lietur, de quibus actum est modo.

ET SUSPICIET SURSUM] A Deo, quem spre- verunt, nullum ipsis auxilium veniet.

## 8:22
AND TO THE EARTH] Nor by men.

Verse 22. AND HE SHALL NOT BE ABLE TO FLY AWAY FROM HIS DISTRESS] In the Hebrew: he who shall have been constrained at this time shall not fly away. However, the Greeks and the Latin [version] have attached these words to this chapter better than the Hebrews to the chapter which follows. But in the Greek texts, ἀπορηθήσεται seems to be written instead of ἀποπτήσεται.

That the Hebrew punctuation is correct will appear in the following chapter: to which Grotius rashly prefers the Greeks and the Latin. However, it is clear from this gloss of his that he establishes merely temporal punishments here, having followed his Jews. But most Christian interpreters accept these primarily as spiritual punishments, which the emphatic descriptions altogether imply. The word בה is indeed commonly accepted as 'through this land,' namely as Grotius wishes: But I do not know whether Bohlius's explanation is more convenient: FOR THIS REASON, (because feminine forms are accustomed to be used for neuters) the people or everyone among the people shall wander, because they have not spoken according to this word, but have consulted pythons and diviners, and shall fall or rather shall be hardened and shall hunger, shall sustain a famine of the word of God: and when they shall hunger, they shall be angry, shall rage and shall curse their King the Messiah and their God, and shall look upward and shall gaze at the earth, and behold there shall be (everywhere mere) tribulation and darkness and dissolution and distress and gloom pursuing. Brentius correctly notes here the degrees and orders of spiritual punishments into which false doctrine precipitates men. The first punishment is blindness: there shall be no morning light for them. The second is a fall and ruin from blindness into all kinds of outrages. The third is hunger or spiritual famine, because they are in need of true righteousness. The fourth is indignation: because they are destitute of peace of conscience, and therefore they are excited to anger and indignation and become blasphemous, as are found among the Jews, nothing but virulent insults against God and their King, that is, Christ our Lord. The fifth is despair: They shall look, he says, upward and downward, but they shall never find help. Wherefore there follow at last mere darkness, distresses, and perpetual destruction. Brentius refers this prediction to the Jews at the time of the New Testament, whom Osiander followed in his paraphrase: Now the Prophet exhorts them to beware of the Pseudo-Teachers (whom he figuratively denotes under the name of Magi, because they are to be considered no better than Magi and Enchanters and Necromancers, and, as Brentius says, are thus distinguished by words of Isaiah used in that time) and to flee to the law and to the testimony; but to the Jews, who prefer to hear the Pharisees and Scribes, or even the Sadducees, the saving light of the knowledge of Christ will not arise, &c. which explanation he does not disapprove of it. Moreover, the Nazarenes explain that passage thus; when the Scribes & Pharisees have said to you, that you should hear them, who do all things for the sake of their belly & build in the manner of Magi in their incantations, so that they may deceive you, you ought to answer them: It is no wonder if you follow your traditions, since every nation consults its own idols. Therefore we also ought not to consult the dead for the living; rather God has given us the law & the testimonies of the Scriptures, which if you are unwilling to follow, you will not have light, but darkness will always oppress you. And thus also Cyril of Alexandria explains it in book 1 of his Orations on Isaiah.

Latin:

ET AD TERRAM] Nec ab hominibus.

Vers. 22. ET NON POTERIT AVOLARE DE ANGUSTIA SUA] In Hebræo: non avolabit, qui con- strictus fuerit isto tempore. Melius autem hæc verba Græ- ci & Latinus capiti huic attexuere, quam Hebræi capiti quod sequetur. Sed in Græcis ἀπορηθήσεται scriptum vi- detur pro ἀποπτήσεται.

Recte se habere Ebræam distinctionem, se- quenti capite apparebit: cui temere præfert Græ- cos, & Latinum Grotius. Liquet autem ex hac ejus glossa, quod mere temporales pœnas hic con- stituat, Judæos suos sequutus. Christiani vero Inter- pretes plerique de spiritualibus pœnis hæc imprimis accipiunt, quas Emphaticæ descriptiones omnino important. Vox בה solet quidem communiter ita accipi per hanc terram, scilicet uti vult Grotius: Sed nescio, annon commodior sit Bohlii explica- tio: PROPTER HOC, (quia fœminina solent pro neutris poni) vagabitur populus vel quisq; in po- pulo, quod scilicet non dixerit secundum verbum hoc, sed Pythones & divinos consuluerit, & cor- ruet vel potius condurabitur & esuriet, famem ver- bi Dei sustinebit: & cum esurierit, irascetur, fre- met & maledicet Regi suo Messiæ & Deo suo, & suspiciet sursum & ad terram intuebitur, & ecce erit (ubique mera) tribulatio & tenebræ & dissolu- tio & angustia & caligo persequens. Recte Bren- tius hic gradus & ordines pœnarum spiritualium notat, in quas falsa doctrina homines præcipitant. Prima pœna est cæcitas: non erit eis matutina lux. Secunda casus & ruina ex cæcitate in omnia gene- ra flagitiorum. Tertia esuries seu fames spiritualis, quia indigent veræ justitiæ. Quarta indignatio: quia destituuntur pace conscientiæ, ideoque exci- tantur ad iram & indignationem ac blasphemi fiunt, uti penes Judæos non inveniuntur, nisi viru- lenta convitia adversus Deum & Regem ipsorum, hoc est, Christum Dominum nostrum. Quinta est desperatio: Suspicient, inquit, sursum & deorsum, sed nunquam invenient auxilium. Quare sequun- tur postremo meræ tenebræ, angustiæ & perpetuus interitus. Refert hanc prædictionem Brentius ad Judæos tempore N. Test. quem sequutus est Osian- der in paraphrasi: Nunc hortatur Propheta, ut à Pseudo-Doctoribus (quos sub Magorum nomine figurate notat, quia non meliores illi habendi, quam Magi & Incantatores & Necromantici, &, ut Brentius, verbis Esaiæ tempore usitatis ita insi- gniuntur) caveamus, & ad legem & ad testimonium confugiamus; Judæis autem, qui maluerint Phari- sæos & Scribas, aut etiam Sadducæos audire, non orietur lux salvifica cognitionis Christi, &c. quam explicationem Nazarenorum veterum fuisse, ob- servat Hieronymus, neque improbat eandem. Cæ- terum Nazareni locum istum ita edisserunt; cum dixerint ad vos Scribæ & Pharisæi, ut eos audiatis, qui omnia ventris causa faciunt & in morem Ma- gorum struunt in incantationibus suis, ut vos deci- piant, hoc eis respondere debetis: Non mirum, si vos vestras traditiones sequamini, cum unaquæque gens sua consulat idola. Ergo & nos a vobis mor- tuis de viventibus consulere non debemus; magis nobis Deus legem dedit & testimonia Scriptura- rum, quam si sequi nolueritis, non habebitis lu- cem, sed semper caligo vos opprimet. Atque i- ta etiam explicat Cyrillus Alexandr. lib. 1. Orat. in Esaiam.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

Concerning the light about to arise upon those sitting in darkness, with the eternal Messiah, Prince of Peace, born to adorn the kingdom of David in judgment & justice, even though the Israelites are to perish through the Syrians & Philistines, & through internal dissensions, because of injustice & hypocrisy.

Vers. 1. AT THE FIRST TIME THE LAND OF ZEBULUN WAS LIGHTENED, AND THE LAND OF NAPHTALI] That is, At first the land of Zebulun & the land of Naphtali will be lightly afflicted. Namely, by Tiglath-Pileser, who carried away a few from those places, and left many, 2 Kings 15:29.

AND AFTERWARD THE WAY OF THE SEA BEYOND JORDAN, GALILEE OF THE GENTILES WAS MADE HEAVY] That is: But afterward the way of the sea beyond Jordan (namely, to those who come from the Euphrates) & Galilee of the Gentiles, or of the newcomers, as we have interpreted this word at Matt. 4:15, will be more heavily afflicted. This heavier affliction is that deportation made by Shalmaneser, 2 Kings 17 & 18; for we noted there that the same history is repeated twice. That way from Syria coming to the sea, to which Galilee of the Gentiles is joined, comprises a great part of the land of the ten tribes, which Shalmaneser made completely empty of its inhabitants.

These things cohere in the sources of truth with the preceding words: כִּי for (or rather although, or even BUT, as this particle is sometimes accustomed to be taken; see Ps. 25:11, 2 Sam. 24:10, Josh. 17:18) there will not be for it obscurity according to the distress which was for it at the first time by him who caused the land of Zebulun to be lightened. That obscurity will not remain, but this people in darkness will see a great light. And to almost that sense the Dutch Paraphrasts: For the land which had been distressed will not (entirely) be obscured. As (God) made it despised at the first time near the land of Zebulun, &c. And Fr. Junius with Tremellius: for it will not be obscured: which had been affected by distress. (Hebr. there will not be obscurity; to whom there had been distress. To which also the translation of Ludovicus de Dieu in his Animadversions on this passage tends: But obscurity is not brought (or will not be brought) to that land to which distress was brought: As also that of Piscator: Yet the (land) which will have been distressed (both) at the first time will not (entirely) be darkened, &c. These, therefore, with others who were able to examine the Hebrew text, and have followed it (not adhering to the Latin or Greek), do not hold these as a continuation of threats, as for Grotius all those things are mere threats, but from there they took the beginning of a most eminent promise concerning a great light. Although indeed according to the translation of B. Luther and the Weimar Paraphrase a continuation of threats is also held here, yet they refer those preceding words already spoken not with Grotius to the eighth chapter, but with the sources to this ninth chapter: and they understand that threat spiritually, by which they exaggerate the spiritual darkness and miseries, which were far more grievous and foul than those corporal afflictions to which the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were subject: so that the light and joy promised by the advent of the Messiah in this chapter might be rendered so much the more pleasing and illustrious. Which things, however, Grotius completely inverts. For there will indeed be another trouble that causes them distress, than was at the former time, when it went lightly, &c. Those things, therefore, because 'not obscurity to him who is distressed, according to the first time' are taken in a comparative sense in the translation of B. Luther, that the distress and obscurity to come will be even greater, which are understood by others in a negative sense, that those lands are not to be entirely obscured. Both, however, leave the prophecy concerning Christ intact, just as it is expounded in the New Testament.

It is clear, however, in both ways, that Grotius had no cause to abandon the Hebrew text and prefer the versions, as far as the distinction in this first clause of the ninth chapter is concerned. Furthermore, since in the sources that particle כ (as) coheres with the word עת (time), it is wrongly separated, nay, entirely neglected in the Latin, which Grotius defends, כעת AS THE TIME before, which teaches here that some comparison is made of the first and most recent time with yet another time. Which Grotius entirely neglects. Thirdly, in the Hebrew text it is not THE LAND HAS BEEN ALLEVIATED, but HE ALLEVIATED or HE CAUSED TO ALLEVIATE the land, namely GOD, which emphasis is not to be passed over. Junius refers it to time: As this former time affected more lightly the land of Zebulun. Boblius renders it thus: When the King of Assyria was pressing the whole land with a burden. Fourthly, those things which are joined here, namely the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, others distinguish, especially Ludovicus de Dieu, who translates it thus: But there is not brought (or shall not be brought) darkness to it (the land) to which anguish has been brought: as in the former time He (GOD) acted more lightly toward the land of Zebulun and toward the land of Naphtali: but in the latter time He acted more heavily by the way of the sea beyond the Jordan in the border of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. He renders this sense, however: Although the land of Israel may have been reduced to great anguish, as is evident from the fact that first He afflicted the land of Zebulun and Naphtali more lightly through Tiglath-Pileser, then He afflicted the whole land more heavily, both the maritime region and that which is beyond the Jordan, and also Galilee, which is in the border of the nations, through Shalmaneser, nevertheless it shall not be reduced to full darkness, but the people seeing in darkness, etc. Fr. Junius, however, joins them, and in our judgment not badly: so that Galilee may be more clearly designated by those circumstances, of which we shall now speak. Fifthly, Grotius renders Galilee of the nations as Galilee of the neighbors. He explains the cause of the appellation at the same time at Matthew 4, verse 15. For that tract of land was inhabited not by men of one nation, but by those gathered from everywhere on account of the advantages of the adjacent sea, and had this name, not from Solomon's pact with Hiram, as some think, but from the most ancient times. For in Genesis 14:1, Tidal is named מלך גוים βασιλεὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν (King of the nations), and in Joshua 12:23, after many Kings of Syria of Palestine, there is likewise listed ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐθνῶν (the King of the nations) with the addition of לגלגל, where Gilgal seems to be the same as in this place in the Prophet, and in 1 Kings 9:11 גליל, elsewhere גלילה or גלילות, the proper name of Galilee, to be sure, but coming from the common notion of a border. And Strabo notes that Galilee was inhabited by Egyptians, Arabs, Phoeni- cians: Josephus says that many Σύγκλυδας (mixed multitudes) were in Tiberias. Some wish for Galilee of the Gentiles to be indicated, because it is adjacent to the Gentiles. Others, with Osiander, because it was once to be defended by a garrison of Gentiles. Junius, however, prefers that Galilee of the Gentiles be rendered as populous Galilee, and he observes that by these words, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, populous Galilee, lower Galilee is defined (not upper, as most think), which extends along the Jordan, is adjacent to the sea of Tiberias or the lake of Gennesaret, and is a most fertile region, as Moses testifies, Deut. 33:24, and most populous. That most people attribute this appellation to upper Galilee, because it is adjacent to the Gentiles, has indeed a semblance of truth, he says, but the expression lacks an example; furthermore, it is absent from the circumstances which have just been posited. Since these circumstances pertain not to upper, but to lower Galilee. Finally, it departs from the interpretation of Matthew. Isaac Casaubon in his Notes on the New Testament on Matt. 4:15 agrees with Junius. I assent to the most learned interpreters of the Old Testament, who interpret Galilee of the Gentiles (τῶν ἐϑνῶν) from the perpetual custom of speaking of the Hebrews as populous Galilee. The same men seem to me most correctly to understand these things concerning lower, not upper Galilee; for Capernaum was there. Nevertheless, Walther, with Chemnitz in his Harmony on Isa. 9:2, thinks that both Galilees are indicated, both upper through Zebulun and lower through Naphtali, and that the former is called Galilee of the Gentiles because it is on the border of the Gentiles near Tyre and Sidon, and was inhabited by both Jews and Gentiles; and he wishes that Matthew looked to this, when in chapter 4:23 he commemorates that Jesus went about all Galilee; to which Cornelius à Lapide on Isa. 9:1 agrees. He who brings these things concerning the way of the sea from Adrichomius, and approves them with his own vote: The way of the sea, of which there is mention in the Prophecy of Isaiah, the book of Tobit, and the Gospel, and from which it has its name, because it leads from Syria into the West to the Red or Mediterranean Sea, is a certain public road, which, taking its beginning in Syria, passes through the mountainous region of Trachonitis, and the cities of Cadar and Carozam, and the Jordan river, and finally the city of Capernaum; and from there, proceeding along the shore of the sea of Galilee; it passed by the cities of Bethsaida, Naphtali, Sephet, and Naason, and running down through Galilee of the Gentiles, and the valley of Asher, which is now called St. George, to Ptolemais, it unloads its merchandise to be distributed throughout the entire West at the great sea.

Sixth, I do not know whether those opposite words הקל and הכביד are not explained here by Brentius and Osiander in a more convenient sense, it was held as vile, and it shall be glorified. This is Osiander's paraphrase: That land or region of Galilee, which the two tribes Zebulun and Naphtali held, which region the sea or lake of Gennesaret also washes, was once indeed in great contempt, because those tribes were not famous (Brentius alleges several causes, such as that it was exposed to the incursions of the Gentiles, and that the men of that region imitated the customs of the Gentiles because of their proximity, and that no excellent Prophet ever arose from that region, John 7). But in the last time, when the Messiah will dwell on earth, it will become very famous; but that will then be held by the garrison of the Gentiles or the Romans, whence he also calls it Galilee of the Gentiles. For there was a royal or Caesarean Roman Captain in Capernaum, John 4. Ludov. de Dieu agrees with this explanation. We only add that perhaps it can also be explained in this way: But there shall not be brought darkness to it (the land) to which anguish has been brought, just as at the first time he gave ignominy toward the land of Zebulun and toward the land of Naphtali, so at the last (time) he will give glory, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, in the border of the Gentiles, but what will that glory be? the people sitting in darkness will see, etc. nothing forced. For כי is customary for 'but' (see 2 Sam. 16:17, Gen. 45:8), כ to have the force of similarity, for the apodotic particle (ἀποδοτικῇ) the conjunction vau, and this is most customary. Such is that 'as in heaven and on earth'; הקל for to despise, 2 Sam. 19:43, Ezek. 22:7. הכביד for to honor, Jer. 30:19. והכבדתים ולא יצערו 'I will honor them, and they shall not be held as small,' for צער is to be small, to be held as of little account. The sense is: Although God is about to afflict his land gravely, he will not, however, suffer it to lie hidden completely in darkness. But just as he once exposed it to contempt, so he will finally honor it, when the light of the Gospel is about to shine upon the people sitting in darkness. Everyone sees how this agrees with the mind and scope of the Evangelist. Which interpretation the Dutch translators and Paraphrasts have also followed. And D. Varenius is not alien to it, thus illustrating the Dutch Paraphrase in his Commentary on this place, p. 357. That land, although entirely pressed by anguish, will not be completely obscured, will not be reduced to full obscurity; but the same God, just as in the former time he made the land of Zebulun and Naphtali contemptible and completely despised, by sending in the hostile forces of Tiglath-Pileser the Assyrian, through which the land of the Israelites was treated ignominiously: so in the last times he will gloriously illuminate it, and most splendidly adorn it, through the first evangelical preaching of the Messiah, through the first doctoral manifestation of the same Messiah in this tunic of the Israelites, so that that people sitting in darkness will first see that great light.

However, the translation of B. Luther, Junius, Tremellius, and Piscator favors the Vulgate and Grotius: and we do not think that one should contend about these, provided that the scope and sense of the Prophet, illustrated by the explanation of the New Testament, that the Holy Spirit instituted the commemoration of these lands in order to designate the place which was to be illuminated by the light of the Gospel at the beginning of the New Testament, is not neglected. Which Grotius completely disregarded: and therefore he separated the calamities of these lands from the darkness, of which verse 2 speaks, and the light promised to the people; drawing these to any other things, and he understood neither the obscuration and darkness, nor the light, as concerning spiritual gloom and illumination, but only as concerning bodily calamity and liberation.

To make the matter clear, it must be shown that a place is defined here in which the light of the Evangelical proclamation ought first to have arisen. Which indeed ought to have been undoubted among Christians, since St. Matthew taught it most openly in chapter 4, 12 et seqq. 'When however Jesus had heard that John had been delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee: and leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zabulon and Naphthali, THAT IT MIGHT BE FULFILLED, which was spoken by Esaias the Prophet: The land of Zabulon and the land of Naphthalim, by the way of the sea beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles; the people which sat in darkness saw great light: and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.' What could have been said more clearly to teach that Esaias had designated the land of Zabulon and the land of Naphthalim, the way of the sea beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles, as the place in which the people sat in darkness, whom Christ ought to have illuminated with the light of the Gospel above others? Was it right here for Grotius to lend his ears to the Jews rather than to the holy Evangelist, who teaches in most clear words that the Prophet had prophesied here in what region Christ was to begin the preaching of the Gospel? Nor is there any reason to say with Grotius on Matt. 4, 14 that Matthew had cited the κᾀπ᾿ ἄν of verse 2, chapter 9 of Esaias, but because it could not be sufficiently understood of what people the Prophet was speaking, from the preceding clause he had added only those things which pertained to the designation of that people: for that was the Evangelist's chief purpose, to designate that people. Therefore he wished to cite not only verse 2, but also the preceding words, which openly teach which people saw the light, namely, in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali by the way of the sea beyond or at the Jordan (as Grotius prefers, because the word πέραν is so taken in John 1:28, Num. 32:19) dwelling in Galilee of the Gentiles. For he explains the reason why Christ withdrew into Galilee, and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, and illuminated those lands with the light of his word and miracles at the beginning of his ministry! because, forsooth, it had been so predicted long ago. Whence also Matthew subjoins and reports that Christ taught the Apostles by the sea of Galilee and preached the Gospel of the kingdom, and healed every sickness, and that great crowds from Galilee and Decapolis and from Jerusalem followed him beyond the Jordan. But although Grotius confesses that the people who are said to be illuminated in verse 2 are designated by the words of the preceding clause, which have been repeated by Matthew, and which the context teaches were brought forward by the Evangelist for the sake of proof, Isaiah is certainly prophesying specifically and διακριτικῶς [distinctively] about those lands being illuminated by a great light ἐπ' ἀγώνιον [for a contest]. Nor will those words, the way of the sea beyond Jordan Galilee of the Gentiles, designate the whole kingdom of Israel, which has the Mediterranean Sea to the west, the crossing of the Jordan to the east, and the border of the Gentiles to the north, as Oecolampadius explains and Abraham Scultetus executes more prolixly in book 2 of his Exercitationes Evangelicae. c. 10, nor does Ludovicus de Dieu deny it, l. c. For thus the peculiar places which Matthew wished to point out would not have been defined by them.

If you say with Grotius: Although the words of Isaiah deal directly with some liberation which happened closer to those times, there nevertheless underlies an ὑπόνοια [hidden meaning] of the times of Christ: to which Calvin's opinion also tends: or with Zwingli, that Matthew uses the Prophet allegorikῶς [allegorically] in this place, so that just as Zebulun and Naphtali formerly felt the extermination first, so it is fair that the light should now arise for the former: or with Scultetus, that an allusion is made by Matthew and an analogy of the moderns with the ancients is instituted: or with Spanheim, part 3, Dub. Evangel. 21, p. 326, that the words of the Prophet are brought forward by the Evangelist in a mystical or accommodative and even transumptive sense: or with Cornelius à Lapide, as well as Tirinus, that a spiritual depredation is figured here, by which those lands of Zebulun and Naphtali were first to be lightly despoiled through Immanuel, with the Apostles being gathered from there, then a more brilliant prey, with innumerable miracles being performed there and more being converted. I reply. (1) It is falsely supposed that a double sense of the same saying is given, that it is literal and mystical, proper and transumptive, a true διάνοια [meaning], and I know not what latent analogical ὑπόνοια [hidden meaning]. For double senses of the same Scripture passage are never to be admitted. (2) The words of the Prophet have been brought forward by the Evangelist for the sake of proof: But from a bare mystical, accommodative, transumptive sense, from a bare ὑπόνοια and analogical allusion, no proof or demonstration can be instituted. (3) The Evangelist with care and study selects from the Prophet those things which made for designating the place of the auspicious beginnings of the preaching and miracles of Christ, and he urges and presses the very words; the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali: then also those, the way of the sea beyond Jordan of Galilee of the Gentiles: so that it may be established that that region has been designated and defined διακριτικῶς [distinctively], to be ennobled by the illumination of the great light of Christ above others. Why else would he bring these forward peculiarly and indeed with this formula? unless that had been predicted by the Prophet, in the proving of which he is occupied in that same place.

(4) Nor does he only bring forward those Prophetic things by design, but by a connected narrative he also explains them in such a way that it can be obscure to no one that the Holy Spirit has here demonstrated the genuine complement of the Prophetic prophecy and indicated its true meaning. (5) The συνέχεια [continuity] in Isaiah is correct if it is accepted concerning the times of the New Testament. For if you say with Calvin, Piscator, Junius and Tremellius, Scultetus, Spanheim, de Dieu, Thomas, likewise Hugo, Vatablus, Adam, Cornelius, and Grotius himself, that mention of a lighter affliction under Tiglath-Pileser, and a heavier one under Shalmaneser, had preceded: the sense of the oracle will thus be established: that those lands will not be obscured perpetually: but are to be illuminated at length through the advent of Christ, as Junius and Piscator teach in their notes, and Ludovicus de Dieu, l. c. If with the Vinarie Paraphrasts you believe that a greater calamity is still designated than there was at either of those times, but a spiritual one, which however is to be exchanged with spiritual light and joy, the scope and allegation of the Evangelist will still have its full force. Which is most in the open if, in verse 1 of the chapter, with Brentius, Osiander, Hieronymus Prado, Ludovicus de Dieu, and the Belgian Interpreters, you acknowledge that a mention of the calamity of that land, which had been despised and afflicted formerly, was indeed premised; but at the same time the glorification of the same was indicated, which the second clause of this chapter explains as being about to happen through the shining of a great light. (6) These cohere so conveniently with the preceding chapter, as Brentius noted. For since it was said before that only the doctrine of Christ is to be followed, the Prophet now explains in what region Christ is to teach his Gospel at the beginning, and what fruit his doctrine is to bring. (7) Those things which follow in this chapter agree excellently here concerning Christ, if it is said that the subject here is also Christ in the literal sense: not so if these are to be understood properly and according to the letter concerning the times closer to Isaiah. (8) The darkness and shadow of death, in which the people are said to sit, designate not a corporal calamity, but a spiritual one. (9) That great light brought not a liberation from a temporal calamity, but an illumination, which is done through the word of the Gospel, with the Apostle as interpreter. It is certainly nowhere explained as concerning a temporal liberation. But who will admit that the accommodative sense of so distinguished a prophecy was indeed handed down by the Holy Spirit, but the genuine and literal one was never explained by the same: Whence (10) those who invent a different literal sense than the one the Evangelist handed down have nothing certain. Grotius explains with Thomas, Hugo, and Jansenius, concerning the light of the deliverance from the army of Sennacherib: Scultetus concerning the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity: others in Spanheim concerning both: some concerning the calamity and deliverance in the time of the Maccabees. Calvin concerning the Babylonian redemption, but as a prelude to the restoration of the Church up to the coming of the Messiah, upon whom all liberty, all bestowal of benefits depends. What certainty is here? (11) One may compare with this oracle the prophecy of David, Ps. 68. Their leaders the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali, who were also described by their homeland as the first heralds of the Gospel; concerning which see our annotations on Psalm 68. (12) Jerome understands according to the literal sense the illumination which the coming of Christ brought to those places designated by the Prophet: because the Savior first preached the Gospel in the regions of the two tribes, which is understood by the sea of the lake of Gennesaret; which is formed by the flowing Jordan, on whose shore Capernaum and Tiberias and Bethsaida and Chorazin are situated: in which region the Lord dwelt most of all: and he brings forward to that opinion the ancient converted Hebrews and the Nazarenes themselves. In the first time these two tribes, Zabulon and Naphthalim, were captured by the Assyrians and led into a hostile land, and Galilee was deserted, which the Prophet now says has been lightened, in that it sustained the sins of the people: Afterwards, however, not only the two tribes, but also the rest, who dwelt beyond the Jordan and in Samaria, were led into captivity. And this, they say, Scripture now says: that the region whose people were first led into captivity and began to serve the Babylonians, and which was previously involved in the darkness of error, it itself first saw the light of the preaching Christ, and from it the Gospel was sown among all nations: The Nazarenes attempt to explain this passage thus: With the coming of Christ, and the shining of his preaching, first the land of Zabulon and the land of Naphthalim were freed from the errors of the Scribes and Pharisees, and shook off the most heavy yoke of Jewish traditions from their necks. Afterwards, however, through the Gospel of Paul, who was the last of all the Apostles, the preaching was made heavy, i.e., multiplied, and the Gospel of Christ shone into the ends of the nations and the way of the whole sea. Finally, the whole world, which before walked or sat in darkness and was held in the bonds of idolatry and death, beheld the clear light of the Gospel. Cyril of Alexandria explained it similarly. He begins to demonstrate (the Prophet) who are the first who believed and who were the first-fruits of those who were called to the knowledge of Emmanuel, saying: Behold I and the children whom God has given; for they relate that the borders of Zabulon and Naphthalim lie near the sea of Tiberias and are in the extreme parts of the Jewish region, so that they are conterminous with the Galilee of the nations. They say that most of the Holy Apostles were from these tribes especially. Which Cyril demonstrates at length from Matt. 4 and John 1 in the same place. Brentius follows this explanation of the Fathers, or rather of Matthew; I am not ignorant of what Hebrew interpreters write concerning the meaning of these words. But although it will be permissible sometimes to seek the meaning of words from Hebrew interpreters, although they are also accustomed to hallucinate greatly in this matter: yet the Holy Spirit did not propose to us Hebrew writers as certain interpreters of the true meaning of Holy Scripture, but proposed those Apostolic Writings: These are the Commentaries from which the true meaning of the Prophets is to be sought. Therefore, Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist, about to describe the beginning of the sermons and miracles of Jesus Christ, says thus: Jesus withdrew into Galilee, etc. Here you see clearly that, with Matthew or rather the Holy Spirit as interpreter, Isaiah prophesied in this place in which region Christ was to begin the preaching of his Gospel. What is therefore said here is to be read thus: At the first time the land of Zabulon and the land of Naphthalim was held in contempt. But at the last time the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee or the border of the nations, was glorified, i.e., although the maritime region, which is beyond the Jordan, in which the city of Capernaum is situated, was at the beginning reputed for many times to be the most vile and contemptible; yet in the last times when the Messiah has arrived, this Region will be illustrated with the greatest glory, and will become by far the most famous of all. How therefore will this happen? It follows: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light, to those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death light has risen for them; i.e., the inhabitants of this region have hitherto been overwhelmed by great darkness. They did not see where one must go toward justice and life. But after Christ came, they were the first of all who saw the light of the Gospel and his miracles. For Christ began the preaching of his Gospel in that region, published his first miracles in it, and chose his Apostles there. He went about (says Matthew) all Galilee, teaching in their Synagogues, and preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and curing every disease and every infirmity among the people. By these things again you see how much the Spirit of Isaiah was enlightened, that he not only knew that Christ was about to come and preach his Gospel, but also in what region, and even in what part of the region he was about to begin the preaching of his Gospel. Whence do you think he drew this, if not from the Holy Spirit himself? Perhaps he was helped somewhat by that passage which is in Ps. 67: The princes of Judah, their leaders, the princes of Zabulon and the princes of Naphthalim. And Ps. 88: Thabor and Hermon shall exult in thy name. But to indicate about seven hundred years before such a certain region in which Christ was to begin the sermon of his Gospel and his miracles, this finally comes from a singular and notable revelation of the Holy Spirit. But this was revealed to the Prophet not only for the sake of his contemporary hearers, so that they might confirm their faith, lest in the incursion of the two enemies, the king of Israel and the king of Syria, they should despair of their safety and of the Advent of Christ: For these Kings were threatening that they would destroy the family of David, from which Christ was to come: but it was also revealed to him for our sake and for the whole Church of Christ, so that when we see that it has been fulfilled even in this part in Jesus the son of the virgin Mary, which Isaiah predicted, we may certainly know that this one alone is the true Messiah. Whence I think it was done not without divine dispensation that the Jews themselves testified before Pilate that Jesus had begun his preaching in Galilee. He stirs up, they say, the people, teaching throughout all Judea, having begun from Galilee even to this place. For GOD wished by this outcry of the Jews to admonish the pious of this Prophetic saying, so that they might know that even by the testimony of the impious this prophecy concerning Christ was fulfilled in Jesus. Thus far Brentius. In whose footsteps Luc. Osiander follows in his paraphrase, as in most other things. Nor do others of our people deny that the lands designated here are those of the first Evangelical proclamation. Not a few even from the Reformed themselves agree: Oecolampadius in this place confesses that the truth of Matthew compels this passage to be referred to the times of Christ, and he follows almost the explanation of the Nazarenes brought forward above. Even from among the disciples of Calvin, Junius and Tremellius acknowledge that these times refer literally to Christ, here departing from the footsteps of their teacher; at v. 1 follows a most certain definition of the liberation through Christ: by which the Prophet explains that the rise and, as it were, the first light of the Gospel would begin precisely where the calamity had begun, and he circumscribes the place in the most explicit words. The opinion of Johannes Piscator is the same: to the strengthening of which also contribute the things which Spanheim has in the place cited, even though he agrees with Scultetus: nor would he wish to reject the explanation of Calvin here. The sum, he says, p. 327, of the consolation is that that land is not to be obscured (perpetually, that is to say), which had either experienced or was about to experience a double disaster; one lighter from Tiglath-Pileser, another heavier from Shalmaneser, but that God would at length liberate His people walking in darkness and would bring it about that they see a great light and that the light should shine upon those also who were to dwell in the land of the shadow of death. Among the Papists, Lyranus is especially to be brought forward, who openly refutes the opinion approved by Grotius: because in the first place it implies contradictions, at least in the manner of speaking: because he calls the first captivity (by Tiglath-Pileser, which is the first for Grotius according to this saying) an alleviation, and the second (by Shalmaneser) an aggravation, when nevertheless it was of the same nature. Then because mention of Galilee would not be made here, when it is said to be most recently aggravated, inasmuch as it was captivated in the first captivity at least in great part: But rather Samaria, which was the metropolis of the kingdom, and captured by Shalmaneser.

Thirdly, because in Matt. 4 it is said that this prophecy is fulfilled to the letter concerning Christ: and since all expositions say that chapter 7, which is had concerning the son of the virgin, is to be understood of Christ, Lyranus thinks that every Catholic is compelled by the same necessity to understand this prophecy also of Christ, because it is said that this was done by Matthew just as much, that it might be fulfilled which the Prophet said in Matt. 4, as that which was said concerning the birth of the virgin in Matt. 1. The same Lyranus explains these words of Isaiah concerning the proclamation of Christ in this manner: that in the first time the land of Zabulon and the land of Naphthalim was lightened, because there Christ, around the beginning of his preaching, taught publicly and frequently and performed miracles: and thus that land was lightened from the yoke of the Devil through the power of Christ: nevertheless, because many of them returned to their vomit, therefore he adds and says: And in the last time, that is, around the end of his preaching, the way of the sea was made heavy: concerning which aggravation see Matt. 11:20 et seqq. Then he began to upbraid the cities in which his mighty works were done, woe to thee Chorazin, woe to thee Bethsaida, which were upon the sea of Galilee, in the borders of Zabulon and Naphthalim: and afterwards it is added concerning Capharnaum, where Christ dwelt around the beginning of his preaching, because through the preaching of Christ it was disposed toward the attainment of blessedness by believing: but afterwards it was depressed through the demerit of damnation by returning to the vomit. The Jesuit Menochius, whom Grotius is accustomed to value highly, confesses that according to the evangelical letter, truth and Christ himself are understood by the great light. Cornelius à Lapide, although he labors to prove that opinion concerning spiritual depredation, which Tirinus and Menochius made their own, could not however disapprove of the explanation of Brentius and Hieronymus Prado brought up above: Otherwise, he says, AND NOT BADLY does Hieronymus Prado take these things in Ezech. p. 275. To be lightened, he says, is to be held in low esteem: to be aggravated is to be honored: for this also is signified by the Hebrew הִכְבִּיד and הֵקַל hecal and hicbid, as if to say: formerly Galilee was held of no account by the Jews, both because it was further away from Jerusalem, and because it had defected from Judah and the temple, and because it had abject towns, such as those twenty which Solomon gave to Hiram King of Tyre, which were therefore called the land of Chabul, that is, vile and ignoble: Whence also Christ was called a Galilean by the Jews and by Julian the Apostate as a reproach: but in the last days this Galilee, with the Messiah visiting, dwelling, and preaching in it, will be most honorable. For in a similar way Haggai said in ch. 2:10 that the temple built by Zerubbabel would be more august than Solomon's, on account of the presence and preaching of Christ in it. And Micah in ch. 5:2 extols Bethlehem from the fact that Christ will be born in it.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

De luce super sedentes in tenebris oritura nato Messia æterno Pacis Principe regnum Da- vidis adornaturo in judicio, & justitia, ut- ut per Syros & Philistæos, & per intestina dissidia interituri sint Israëlitæ ob injusti- tiam, & hypocrisin.

Vers. 1. PRIMO TEMPORE ALLEVIATA EST TERRA ZABULON, ET TERRA NAPHTHALI] Id est, Prius leviter affligetur terra Zabulon & terra Naphtha- li. Nempe per Theglath Phalasarem, qui paucos trans- tulit ex illis locis, multos reliquit, 2. Reg. 15, 29.

ET NOVISSIMO AGGRAVATA EST VIA MARIS TRANS JORDANEM GALILÆA GEN- TIUM] Id est: Post vero gravius affligetur via maris trans Jordanem (nempe iis, qui ab Euphrate veniunt) & Galilæa gentium, sive convenarum, ut hanc vocem interpretati sumus ad Matth. 4, 15. Hæc afflictio gravior, est illa depor- tatio facta per Salmanassarem, 2. Reg. 17. & 18. nam bis eandem historiam repeti, ibi notavimus. Via illa a Syria venientibus ad mare, cui cohæret Galilæa gentium, magnam partem comprehendit terræ decem tribuum, quam plane vacuam indigenis fecit Salmanassar.

COhærent hæc in fontibus veritatis cum verbis præcedentibus: כִּי quia (vel potius quamvis, vel etiam SED, uti solet hæc particula nonnun- quam accipi. vide Ps. 25, 11. 2. Sam. 24, 10. Jos. 17, 18.) non erit ei obscuratio secundum angustiam, quæ fuit ei tempore primo ab eo, qui alleviare fecit terram Zabulon. Non manebit illa obscuratio, sed popu- lus iste in tenebris lucem magnam videbit. Atque ad eum fere sensum Belgæ Paraphrastæ. Nam non (omnino) obscurabitur terra, quæ coangustata erat. Sicut (Deus) eam primo tempore contemptam fecit juxta terram Zabulon, &c. Et Fr. Junius cum Tre- mellio: nam non obscurabitur: quæ affecta fuerat an- gustia. (Hebr. non erit obscuratum; cui fuerit an- gustatum. Quo etiam Ludovici de Dieu translatio in Animadv. ad h. l. abit: Sed non est allata (vel non adferetur) obscuratio ei terræ, cui allata est angustia: Ut & Piscatoris: Doch wird nicht (gar) verfinstert werden das (Land) welches wird geängstiget seyn worden (beyde) zu der ersten Zeit, 2c. Hi ergo cum aliis, qui Ebræum textum scrutari potuêre, eun- demque sequuti sunt, (non Latino aut Græcis ad- hæsere,) hæc non pro minarum continuatione ha- bent, uti Grotio universa ista meræ sunt commina- tiones, sed inde auspicium promissionis eminen- tissimæ de luce magna sumsere. Quanquam vero juxta B. Lutheri translationem & Vinariensem Para- phrasin etiam continuatio hic comminationum habeatur, referunt tamen hi verba illa præcedentia jam dicta non cum Grotio ad caput octavum, sed cum fontibus ad hoc nonum caput: & comminatio- nem illam spiritualiter intelligunt, qua tenebras & miserias spirituales, quæ illis corporalibus afflictio- nibus, quibus terra Zabulon & terra Naphthali ob- noxia fuit, longe graviores & tetriores: easque ex- aggerant, ut lux & lætitia à Messiæ adventu promif- sa hoc capite, tanto gratior & illustrior reddatur. Quæ vero Grotius plane invertit. Denn es wird wol eine andere Mühe seyn, die ihnen angst thut, denn zur vorigen Zeit war, da es leicht zugieng, &c. Illa ergo, quia non obtenebratio ei, qui coarctatur, secundum tempus primum sensu Comparativo acci- piuntur in translatione B. Lutheri, quod major ad- huc futura sit angustia & obtenebratio, quæ ab aliis sensu negativo, quod non omnino obscurandæ sint illæ terræ, intelliguntur. Utrique autem integrum relinquunt vaticinium de Christo, sicut id in N. T. expositum.

Liquet autem utroque modo, non habuisse Grotium causam Hebræum textum relinquendi, & versiones præferendi, quantum ad distinctionem in hoc primo capitis noni commate. Porro quum in fontibus illud SECUNDUM particula כ cohæreat cum voce עת, perperam istud divellitur, imo pror- sus negligitur in Latino, cui patrocinatur Grotius, כעת SECUNDUM TEMPUS prius, quod hic collationem aliquam fieri docet primi & novissimi temporis cum alio adhuc tempore. Quam pror- sus negligit Grotius. Tertio in Ebræo textu non est ALLEVIATA EST terra, sed alleviavit vel alleviare fecit terram DEUS scil. quæ emphasis non prætermittenda. Junius ad tempus refert: Sicut tempus hoc prius levius affecit in terra Zabulon. Boblius ita reddit: Cum Rex Assur terram totam o- nere premebat. Quarto illa, quæ hic conjungun- tur, nimirum via maris, trans Jordanem, Galilæa gentium, alii distinguunt, imprimis Ludovicus de Dieu, qui sic transfert: Sed non est allata (vel non adferetur) obscuratio ei (terræ) cui allata est angu- stia: sicut tempore priori levius egit (DEUS) versus terram Zabulon & versus terram Naphthali: poste- riori autem gravius egit via maris trans Jordanem in confinio gentium. Populus, qui ambulavit in tenebris viderunt lucem magnam. Sensum autem hunc red- dit: Etsi in magnam angustiam redacta sit terra Is- raël, sicut inde patet, quod primum levius terram Za- bulon & Naphthali per Tiglath Pelezer, deinde gra- vius universam terram, tum maritimam, tum quæ ultra Jordanem est, etiam Galilæam, quæ in confi- nio gentium est, per Salmanassarem afflixerit Deus, tamen ad plenam obscuritatem non redigetur, sed po- pulus videns in tenebris, &c. Conjungit tamen illa Fr. Junius, idque nostro judicio non male: ut Ga- lilæa ab istis circumstantiis apertius designetur, de quo jam dicemus. Quinto Galilæam gentium Gro- tius reddit Galilæam convenarum. Causam appel- lationis simul exponit ad Matth. 4. v. 15. Nam tra- ctus iste non unius nationis hominibus, sed undiq; col- lectis ob adjacentis maris commoda habitatus, nomen hoc habuit, non ex Salomonis cum Hieronymo pactio- ne, ut quidam existimant, sed ab antiquissimis usque temporibus. Nam Gen. 14, 1. nominatur Tidbal מלך גוים βασιλεὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν, & Jos. 12, 23. post multos Reges Syriæ Palestinæ itidem recensetur ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐθνῶν addito לגלגל, ubi Gilgal idem videtur, quod a- pud Prophetam hoc loco, & 1. Reg. 9, 11. גליל alibi גלילה aut גלילות proprium nimirum Galilææ nomen, sed ex communi limitis notione veniens. Et Strabo notat Galilæam habitatam ab Ægyptiis, Arabibus, Phœni- cibus: Σύγκλυδας multos fuisfe Tiberiade ait Jose- phus. Alii Galilæam gentium indigitari volunt, quod gentibus contermina sit. Alii, quod præsidio gentium olim defendenda sit, cum Osiandro. Junius autem mavult reddi Galilæam populosam, & observat his verbis, via maris, secundum Jordanem, Galilæa po- pulosa, definiri inferiorem Galilæam (non superio- rem, ut plerique existimant) quæ secundum Jorda- nem protenditur, ad mare Tiberiades sive lacum Gene- zareth adjacet & feracissima regio est teste Mose, Deut. 33, 24. ac populosissima. Quod pleriq; appellationem hanc tribuunt superiori Galilææ, quia gentibus con- termina est, habere quidem speciem, ait, sed loquutio- nem exemplo carere; præterea à circumstantiis ab- esse, quæ modo positæ sunt. Siquidem hæ circumstan- tiæ non ad superiorem, sed ad inferiorem Galilæam pertineant. Postremo discadere ab interpretatione Matthæi. Adstipulatur Junio Isaac. Casaubonus in Notis ad Nov. Testam. ad Matth. 4, 15. Assentior doctissimis V. T. Interpretibus, qui Galilæam τῶν ἐϑ- νῶν interpretantur ex perpetua loquendi consuetudi- ne Hebræorum Galilæa populosa. Iidem rectissime videntur mihi de inferiori, non superiori Galilæa hæc accipere; nam ibi fuit Capernaum. Utramque ta- men Galilæam indigitari, tum superiorem per Za- bulon, tum inferiorem per Naphthalim, illamque vocari Galilæam gentium, quia in confinio gentium juxta Tyrum & Sidonem, & tum à Judæis & gen- tibus habitata, cum Chemnitio Waltherus in Har- monia ad Esa. 9, 2. putat; eoque respexisse vult Matthæum; cum cap. 4, 23. commemorat Jesum circumivisse totam Galilæam; quibus adstipulatur Cornelius à Lapide ad Esa. 9, 1. Qui de via maris ex Adrichomio, hæc adducit, & suffragio suo compro- bat: Via maris, cujus in Prophetia Esaiæ, libro To- biæ, & Evangelio sit mentio, indeq; nomen habet, quod è Syria in Occidentem ad mare rubrum seu Mediter- raneum ducat, publica quædam via est, quæ initium in Syria sumens, per montana Trachonitidis regionis, & civitates Cadar & Carozam, atq; Iordanem fluvium, tandemq; urbem Capharnaum transit; illincq; per lit- tus maris Galilææ procedens; juxta civitates Betsai- dam, Nephthali, Sephet & Naason præteriit, & per Galilæam gentium, ac vallem Aser, quæ nunc S. Geor- gius appellatur, Ptolemaidem decurrens, merces suas in universam occidentem distrahendas, ad mare ma- gnum exonerat.

Sexto nescio, annon verba illa opposita הקל & הכביד commodiori sensu hic à Brentio & Osiandro exponantur, vilis habita est, & glorificabitur. Osi- andri hæc est paraphrasis: Terra seu regio illa Ga- lilææ, quam tenuerunt duæ tribus Zabulon & Naphthali, quam etiam regionem alluit mare seu la- cus Genezareth, olim quidem in magno fuit contemtu, propterea quod hæ tribus non essent celebres (plures causas allegat Brentius, utpote quod patuerit in- cursionibus gentium, quodque homines illius re- gionis gentium mores propter vicinitatem imitati sint, & quod nullus unquam excellens Propheta ex ea regione exortus sit, Johan. 7.) Sed po- stremo tempore, quum Messias in terris versabitur, ad- modum inclarescet; ea autem tum tenebitur præsidio gentium seu Romanorum, unde & Galilæam gentium eam vocat. Fuit enim regius seu Cæsareus Capita- neus Romanus in Capernaum Joh. 4. Cui expli- cationi accedit Ludov. de Dieu. Addimus solum- modo, etiam hoc modo exponi fortassis posse: Sed non adferetur obscuratio ei (terræ) cui allata est angu- stia, sicut tempore primo ignominiam dedit versus terram Zabulon & versus terram Naphthali, sic po- stremo (tempore) gloriam dabit, via maris, trans Ior- danem, in confinio gentium, quæ autem ista gloria erit? populus sedens in tenebris videbit, &c. nihil co- actum. Nam כי pro sed usitatum (vid. 2. Sam. 16, 17, Gen. 45, 8.) כ similitudinis habere, pro particula ἀ- ποδοτικῇ copulam vau, & hoc usitatissimum. Tale est illud ὡς ἐν ὀυρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς; הקל pro vilipen- dere 2. Sam. 19, 43.
