If, however, a sense of opposition is admitted, it will be indicated simply: that the Lord is not going to use the work of many, but is going to conquer by his own hand, which has a place in the business of redemption rather than in the slaughter of Sennacherib. For here he used the work of an angel. But the Lord alone accomplished that, the sole author of our life and salvation. But because one should not depart from the letter of the text without cause, everything must be explained in one context. Which was done by Jerome: whose ἐξήγησις was recently adduced. Cornelius à Lapide proposes it thus, that it is a catachresis and a metaphor from soldiers and a battle, in which the bodies and clothes of the enemies are bloodied and burned: for thus will Christ burn the enemies, namely the Demons themselves and their followers. For he speaks of the Demons, as if they were soldiers, anthropopathōs: whence he attributes to them clothes and blood. Similar is Is. 72, 3. And just as the violent plunder of Gideon was done with the tumult of the camps of Midian, as is wont to happen in such matters: so the violent plunder of Christ moves a tumult both in hell and in the camps of the world. Which are also approved by Stephanus Menochius. The explanation of our Brentius is simpler: Every violent plunder, which is done with tumult, and a garment mixed with blood shall be for burning and food for fire: i.e., every war will be finished and consumed at the advent of Christ. For what he says, violent plunder with tumult and a garment mixed with blood, is a paraphrase of war, in which tumultuous plunderings and bloody battles are wont to occur. These will be for the burning of food for fire, i.e., they will be reduced to ashes, or will receive an end. The Prophet therefore signifies that there will be no more war, no plunder, no bloody battle. Similarly, Osiander, rendering this παράφρασιν: that is, the Lord will abolish weapons and garments soaked in blood and will restore peace. Blessed Luther preceded him, rendering it thus: There will be peace and charity among Christians. War itself with all things that pertain to war will be consumed by fire and will vanish into smoke: and thus it will cease to be. And from there Christ is immediately introduced as the prince of peace. Ludov. de Dieu does not depart much from this, animadv. p. 474. I refer the whole third verse, just as those which precede and those which follow, to the times of the Messiah, in which both the nation of the Church was multi-

CHAP. IX. v. 5.

plied and joy was amplified. One cause is given in verse 4, because the yoke of the Church imposed by enemies has been broken. Another in verse 5, because every attempt of the enemies is vain, which is expressed by these words כִּי כָל־סְאוֹן סֹאֵן בְּרַעַשׁ וְשִׂמְלָה מְגוֹלָלָה בִדָמִים וְהָיְתָה לִשְׂרֵפָה מַאֲכֹלֶת אֵשׁ for every conflict of the one conflicting was indeed with noise, and a garment polluted with slaughters, and yet it was for burning as food for fire. The sense is: Although the enemy conflictor acted with great effort, so that all his conflict was with great noise, and he seemed to have already obtained victory, because he had already polluted his garment with the blood of the Church, he nevertheless fell from his victory, and this very garment polluted with the blood of the Church was delivered to the fire. The author of this victory is the child born to us, who is clearly described in v. 6 seqq.

We shall now subjoin the program which we proposed on the feast of the Nativity of the Lord in the year 1671 concerning this prophecy, which will serve for its illustration:

We recall the Nativity not of some earthly Prince or King, but of the King of Kings, and the Lord of glory, the prince of life: Not of a man, but of GOD: nor of GOD only, but of GOD-Man, the Man-Lord, the Davidic sprout, which is Jehovah, Immanuel, God with us, (Gen. 4,1. Jer. 23,1. Is. 7, 14.) On account of which the Prophets danced nine centuries before, and with holy Isaiah as interpreter, sang with a common voice: A child is born to us, a Son is given to us. On account of which all the Angels were exhilarated on the very night of the Nativity, and with a primary interpreter from their own heavenly choir, they preached to the Bethlehemite Shepherds, Today a Savior is born to you, who is CHRIST the Lord, in the city of David. The whole assembly of the faithful resonated there with the Evangelical Prophet. The whole Angelic host sang in harmony with the Angelic Evangelist. On both sides it was sung, GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST! In both places it was vowed, PEACE ON EARTH, GOOD WILL TOWARD MEN. Nor is there any doubt that on this very festival Angels and Prophets, and indeed the blessed souls of any of the faithful, the Spirits of just men made perfect, constitute one choir; and with a fuller voice, with more perfect joy, they now resound in heaven those things which are sung in our assemblies of the faithful on earth: so that they may testify to the blessed ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν (recapitulation) under one head, CHRIST, and demonstrate the unity of the glorious society of the Church triumphant and militant, angelic, and of those who are now ἰσάγγελοι (equal to the angels). What! The Most Holy Trinity Itself now exults, because GLORY IN THE HIGHEST can now be rendered to GOD THE FATHER by the human race, for whom joy arises even over one sinner who repents. Now our PEACE is the SON OF GOD ON EARTH, whose delights are to be with the sons of men. Now εὐδοκία (good will), and GOOD WILL is restored through the HOLY SPIRIT IN MEN, who rejoices to dwell in us and to fill us with solid joy. Would that! Ah, would that these mortal ears might perceive, even for a single moment, those ἄῤῥητα (unspeakable things) with the Apostle, with how great and how immense a joy we would be filled! However, until we are joined to that most blessed choir in that Holy of Holies, let us sing together in the courts of the tabernacle of the Lord with the saints inhabiting the earth everywhere; nor let us doubt that the Holy Angels are also mingled with our assemblies, although they are not seen, and that they produce most sweet harmonies with us, although they are not heard. Indeed, let us not hesitate to provoke them to harmonic concert with the lyre and Davidic melodies: Bless the Lord, all his Angels, Bless the Lord, all his virtues: Bless the Lord, O my soul. Furthermore, let us believe with certain confidence that He is present to us in the midst of sacred assemblies, that the author of jubilation, the supreme Director of the choir, the Triune, and over all things forever Blessed GOD, dwells in the hearts of those who jubilate; and therefore, that we have heaven on earth, because we have the Lord of heaven in our hearts, so that our joy may be perfect in Him. We shall rejoice before You, the Prophet sings, as those who rejoice in the harvest, as victors exult when they have captured booty, when they divide the spoils. In time of peace, the chief joy is in the harvest: (Ps. 126:6.) in time of war, the chief joy is in the distribution of spoils (2 Kings 7:9). He who is our PEACE has reconciled peace to us: so that we may enjoy a most fertile harvest of spiritual goods. Yet the most bitter war had first to be waged by Him; the head over much land had to be crushed (Psalm 110:6), so that the prey might be snatched away and the spoils divided. By this victory, peace was established, that true peace, not as the world gives, but as the life and light of the world gives: (John 14:27; 1:4.) For He overcame the yoke of the burden, and the staff of the shoulder, and the rod of the oppressor, as in the day of Midian: Every violent plundering with tumult, and garment rolled in blood, was for burning, and food for fire (Isa. 9:4, 5). Now peace flourishes, and charity, as the blessed Luther’s paraphrase excellently has it: The war itself, with all that pertained to war, was consumed by fire and vanished into smoke. What the Prophet says, 'violent plundering with tumult, and garment mixed in blood,' according to our interpreter Brentius, is a paraphrase of war, in which tumultuous rapine and bloody battles are wont to occur. These were for the burning of food for fire, were reduced to ashes, and received their end. Therefore, no more war is to be feared: true and eternal peace has been restored. Under this PRINCE OF PEACE the government is multiplied, and of His peace there is no end. He Himself sits upon the throne of David, and upon His kingdom, because the Successor of David is the true Solomon. To confirm it and strengthen it in judgment and in justice, from now and even forever. In judgment for His subjects against the prince of the world, who is already judged and has no power against this kingdom: In justice, with which He endows all His faithful subjects, having Himself been made for us by GOD justice (1 Cor. 1:30), whom we all profess, JEHOVAH OUR JUSTICE (Jer. 23:6), and in whom we all individually glory, IN THE LORD IS MY JUSTICE (Isa. 45:25). The zeal of the Lord of Hosts has done this: Zeal for vindicating the human race miserably subjugated, zeal for restoring the honor of God, vehemently shaken by sin introduced into the world. Therefore the armies of the Lord of the universe, the angelic in heaven and the Evangelical on earth, now dance for joy in the Lord and celebrate the Lord with one voice, in most sweet harmony. Indeed, it seems to interfere with this spiritual joy that the Prophet predicted, 'You have multiplied the nation, and not magnified the joy,' as the Vulgate Latin has it: But these things either do not concern us, to whom sitting in darkness that great light has arisen, but those who love darkness more than light, and especially the Jews, of whom St. John says: He came into His own, and His own received Him not: who therefore mourn by their own fault, by spurning and rejecting the joy that was prepared and announced for all people; to which the blessed Luther’s interpretation, conforming to Jerome’s, almost leads: The nations receive the Gospel and thus the Church is increased by the accession of the nations, but the Jews envy the nations this happiness of the nations, as He says, 'I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation:' or the words of the Prophetic text must be rendered otherwise from the fountains of truth: namely, under a negative interrogation, which is wont to affirm strongly, 'You have multiplied the nation, would you not have magnified the joy?' They rejoiced before You according to the joy in the harvest. For the Prophet wished to mix nothing sad into this so joyful Evangelical assembly, and strove to magnify the birth-joy as much as possible. Yet he seems to have used that manner of speaking by design, as being highly appropriate to the matter, namely, to express it by a negative interrogation rather than a categorical affirmation, because the mourning of the Jews was to produce the joy of the nations, or as the Apostle speaks (Rom. 11:15), their ruin was the reconciliation of the others. But what mourning, what ruin of the Jews, or even of other unbelievers, will be able to intercept the joy that we have in the Lord for any of the believers? For it is not to be imputed to the Savior who was to be born, who ought to have brought joy to all, but to the people who were not going to receive Him, that they mourn and are mourned, and that thus, as a result, the joy was not multiplied as it could have been by the power of the nativity and the saving grace which has shone upon all men, and the holy nation could have been multiplied and joy could have spread everywhere. For He who is the Rock of salvation to all by divine destination, and by His own merit, may be a rock of scandal and a stone of offense by the fault of those who stumble and the demerit of the unbelievers. Meanwhile, the birth-announcement remains valid and intact: 'Behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people: for unto you is born this day a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.' (Luke 2:10.) The firm and Catholic testimony of Saint Simeon remains (v. 30, 31): 'You have prepared Your SALVATION before the face of ALL peoples, a light for the revelation of the nations, and the glory of Your people Israel.' And that Zacharian EXULT, 'Behold, your King comes to you,' (Chap. 9:9), concerns all; and that Davidic word (Psalm 118:24) is intimated to all: 'This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it:' it is commanded to all by the Apostle (Phil. 4:4): 'Rejoice in the Lord always: again I say, rejoice:' Christ the Savior is announced to all, to the whole (human) creation, I say, which is under heaven (Coloss. 1:24, 28). 'It is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners' (1 Tim. 1:15), 'to seek and to save that which was lost' (Luke 19:10). Wherefore, 'Jubilate to GOD, all the earth.' For 'all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our GOD' (Psalm 98:4, 3). 'Praise the Lord, all nations; praise Him, all peoples' (Psalm 117:1, 2). 'For His mercy is confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever.' But in order that this joy may arise and be amplified in our heart, there is need for meditation on the newborn LITTLE JESUS; wherefore the Evangelist of the Old Testament sets before us His most sweet names, to be pondered with a devout mind. He says to us that a LITTLE CHILD is born, that we may meditate upon His human generation, brought about for the sake of our regeneration: for the Son of GOD was made man, that we men might be made sons of GOD, as S. Irenæus admonishes. He points out that a SON is given to us, that we may venerate His eternal generation from the essence of the Father: concerning which the eternal Father said to Him, Thou art my Son, I this day (which is GOD’s eternal day, for in GOD there is nothing but eternity) have begotten Thee. (Psalm 2, 7.) For we could not be led back to the eternal Father except by the eternal Word, the eternal Son of GOD, Iohan. 1, 14. 18. cap. 14, 6. nor was there need of any other to restore the exemplar of the divine image for men except for him who was the image of the Father, as S. Athanasius says, (de incarnat. Verbi DEI T. I. p. m. 72.) Nor is this common little child to be thought of, or the Son: But he whose government is upon his shoulders. Who also bore the government from the beginning of his birth, truly πορφυρογέννητος, born Lord, and King of the Jews, and he alone bore the same upon his own shoulders, which can be said of none of the earthly Princes, for these divide the burden of government with their counselors and ministers: and he voluntarily took upon himself the government upon his shoulders, which is very burdensome, ἀβάςακτον to every creature, and while other princes impose burdens upon the shoulders of their subjects, he himself took upon his own shoulders from all men the burden which was unbearable for all, namely the burden of fulfilling the law for all, the burden of carrying the guilt of the sin and the punishment of all, in which is his Government; For Christ is not carried, which are the words of B. Luther, by his government and his subjects, but he himself carries his government, i.e., he is our servant, so that we may be free, and Kings. Who at all (asks Tertull. l. contr. Judæos c. 10. & l. 3. contr. Marc. c. 19.) who at all of the Kings bears the insignia of his power on his shoulder, and not either a diadem on his head, or a scepter in his hand, or some mark of his own clothing! But CHRIST JESUS, the only King of the new ages, carried his glory, and power, and sublimity on his shoulder, namely the cross: and this oracle shows the virtue of this cross (as Justin teaches Apol. 2. pro Christ.) which he applied to his shoulders, having been driven onto the same. TO US therefore (as S. Cyril suggests in h. l.) he says that the Son has been given to us. For the only-begotten Word of GOD was made man, not for his own sake, but rather that he might restore our condition, just as it was from the beginning, and that he might offer his own body to GOD and the Father as a sweet-smelling savor (on the cross) as the price and redemption of the life of all. Therefore he is truly called WONDERFUL; wonderful on account of the person consisting of a twofold nature (1. Tim. 3, 16. Roman. 9, 5.) of a twofold birth, namely the temporal process from Bethlehem, and the process from the days of eternity thence (Mich. 5, 2. Matth. 2, 6.) wonderful on account of his office, in which wonderful power shines forth, wonderful wisdom, wonderful charity and Φιλανθρωπία: wonderful on account of his state, both of emptying and of exaltation, in which both, and in all the acts and degrees of both, the stupendous mighty works of GOD, and mere miracles are beheld, so that he may rightly answer the one asking, Why do you ask my name, which is WONDERFUL? (Jud. 13, 18.) For no one knows his name, except himself: (Apocal. 19, 12. Proverb. 30, 4.) He was truly a COUNSELOR in the eternal council of the H. Trinity, where no creature is of the Councils (Esa. 40, 13. Roman. 11, 34.) But the only-begotten Son of GOD, who is in the bosom of the Father (Johan. 1, 18.) the eternal Wisdom of GOD, who testifies, mine is counsel (Proverb. 8, 14. 22.) he gave counsel concerning our salvation: who alone also manifests to us the counsel of GOD, (Matth. 11, 27. Luc. 7, 30. Actor. 20, 27.) & while Princes have many counselors, to whom however none can give counsel by which subjects may attain true happiness, the Little Child born to us, the Son given to us, HE HIMSELF is our counselor, and he alone gives counsel for attaining heavenly goods. Yet he is a counselor in such a way that he is GOD HIMSELF. Worldly counselors are not THEMSELVES princes, and they are only mortal and weak men, both the counselors and the Princes themselves.

But the MESSIAH is not only man, but EL, GOD omnipotent: truly GIBBOR or Hero, for overcoming not only bodily enemies, but primarily spiritual ones, sin, death, the Devil, and hell, as a Giant of twofold substance: And therefore also called FATHER OF THE COMING AGE: or as it is in the source, Eternal Father, or of eternity: Father not of the fatherland, such as princes are, but of the whole creature by reason of creation, of all men by reason of redemption, of all the faithful by reason of regeneration: whose Fatherhood as it is from eternity, so it extends into eternity, and thus into the future age. Father not by person, but by affection, which is truly paternal, truly eternal. Finally PRINCE OF PEACE, because he is so a Father that he is also a Prince, so that he may have us as sons and heirs, and subjects: to whom he acquired PEACE with his own blood, gives PEACE through the Gospel the Word of peace, and seals PEACE through the Holy Spirit the Spirit of peace.

Therefore let us meditate on these things at these solemn birthday celebrations, let us admire these, let us venerate these: which even the angels themselves desire to look into (1. Petr. 1, 12.) so that here, and eternally, with them, we may rejoice over them. But let this be done not only with an attentive ear, a grateful tongue, a devout mind, but also with a sober, chaste, and religious life. Let gluttony and impurity be avoided, because our JESULUS is most Holy: Let contention and Cyclopean shouting be banished, because our JESULUS is most meek: Let scurrility and any impiety whatsoever be excluded with perpetual infamy, because our JESULUS is a most just avenger: Glory be to GOD in the highest, let Peace flourish on earth, let good will be fostered among men, so that our good will may be uniquely in GOD, and likewise let there be grateful good will from GOD in us on account of our JESULUS. Finally, in honor of JESULUS, show gratitude also to the ministers assigned to his manger, by depositing Eucharistic gifts at the altar. For to CHRIST himself, ah what a generous rewarder? is given what is given to the Ministers of Christ! P. P. Wittenberg, on the eve of the Birthday, in the year 1670.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QUIA OMNIS VIOLENTA PRÆDATIO CUM TUMULTU, ET VESTIMENTUM MISTUM SANGUINE ERIT IN COMBUSTIONEM, ET CI- BUS IGNIS] In Hebræo sic est: Omnis pugna bellantium (solet esse) cum strepitu & vestimentis obvolutis sanguine, (Hæc vero erit ut) pabulum ignis ad combustionem. Aliæ clades ho- stium solent parari multo labore, multoque sanguine, hæc vero similis erit incendio subito consumenti. Plane e- nim subito, sine tumultu, sine vulnere, sine Hebræorum labore, aut periculo. Ab Angelo extincti sunt Assyrii. Nul- la flamma tam celeriter eos occidere potuisset. Vid. 10, 16.

Hæc iterum Rabbinis debet Grotius. Sed il- la parenthesis in textu non habetur, de suo illa inse- rit Grotius (Hæc vero erit ut) vel potius de com- mentis Rabbinicis. In fontibus vero occurrit vau copulativum. Si tamen admittatur sensus opposi- tionis, simpliciter id indicabitur: quod Dominus non sit usurus multorum opera, sed sua manu vi- cturus sit, quod in redemtionis negotio potius lo- cum habet, quam in cæde Sennacheribi. Hic enim opera angeli usus est. Illam vero solus Dominus perfecit, vitæ & salutis nostræ autor unicus. Quia vero non est absque causa discedendum à textus li- tera, uno contextu exponenda omnia sunt. Quod factum ab Hieronymo est: cujus proxime adducta ἐξήγησις. Eam sic proponit Cornelius à Lapide, quod catachresis sit & metaphora à militibus & prælio, in quo corpora & vestes hostium cruentæ comburuntur: Sic enim Christus hostes, ipsos sc. Dæ- mones eorumq́; asseclas, comburet. Loquitur enim de Dæmonibus, quasi militibus anthropopathōs: unde iis attribuit vestes & sanguinem. Simile est Es. 72, 3. Et sicut Gedeonis violenta prædatio facta est cum tu- multu castrorum Midian, ut in ejusmodi rebus fieri solet: ita Christi prædatio violenta tumultum movet tum in tartaro, tum in castris mundi. Quæ proban- tur etiam Stephano Menochio. Simplicior est Bren- tii nostri explicatio: Omnis violenta prædatio, quæ fit tumultu, & vestimentum mixtum sanguine erit in combustionem & cibum ignis: h. e. omne bellum fi- nietur & absumetur in adventu Christi. Quod enim dicit, violenta prædatio cum tumultu & vestimentum mixtum sanguine, paraphrasis est belli, in quo so- lent fieri tumultuosæ rapinæ & cruenta prælia. Hæc erunt in combustionem cibi ignis, h. e. redigentur in cinereum, seu accipient finem. Significat ergo Prophe- ta, nullum amplius bellum, nullam rapinam, nullum cruentum prælium fore. Similiter Osiander hanc reddens παράφρασιν: id est, Dominus arma & vestimenta sanguine madentia abolebit & pacem resti- tuet. Præivit B. Lutherus sic reddens: Erit pax & charitas inter Christianos. Bellum ipsum cum omni- bus, quæ ad bellum spectant igne absumetur & in fu- mum abibit: adeòq́; esse desinet. Atq́; inde introducitur Christus statim ut pacis princeps. Non multum abit Ludov. de Dieu animadv. p. 474. Totum versum tertium, sicut & quæ antecedunt & quæ sequuntur, ad tempora Messiæ refero, quibus & gens Ecclesiæ multi-

CAP. IX. v. 5.

plicata & gaudium amplificatum fuit. Causa una datur vers. 4. quia jugum Ecclesiæ ab hostibus impo- situm diruptum est. Altera versu 5. quia omnis conatus hostium irritus est, quod his verbis exprimitur כִּי כָל־סְאוֹן סֹאֵן בְּרַעַשׁ וְשִׂמְלָה מְגוֹלָלָה בִדָמִים וְהָיְתָה לִשְׂרֵפָה מַאֲכֹלֶת אֵשׁ quia omnis quidem conflictus confligentis fuit cum strepitu, & vestimen- tum inquinatum cædibus, & tamen fuit in combustio- nem in cibum ignis. Sensus est: Etsi hostis conflictor magno conatu rem egerit, adeo ut omnis ejus conflictus fuerit cum ingenti strepitu, & jam victoria potitus vi- deretur, quia vestimentum suum jam sanguine Ecclesiæ polluerat, excidit tamen sua victoria, & hoc ipsum vestimentum sanguine Ecclesiæ inquinatum igni tradi- tum est. Author hujus victoriæ est puer nobis natus, qui v. 6. seqq. præclare describitur.

Subjungemus nunc programma, quod in festo Nativitatis Dominicæ Anno 1671. de hoc vaticinio proposuimus, quod illustrationi ejusdem inser- viet:

Nativitatem recolimus non Principis, aut Re- gis alicujus terreni, sed Regum Regis, & Domini glo- riæ,vitæ principis: Non hominis, sed DEI: nec DEI tantum,sed DEI-Hominis, Viri-Domini, ger- minis Davidici,quod Jehovah est, Immanuel, Deus nobiscum, (Gen. 4,1. Jer. 23,1. Es. 7, 14.) Ob quam novem ante seculis tripudiarunt Prophetæ, & san- cto Esaia interprete, communi voce cantarunt: Parvulus natus est nobis, Filius datus est nobis. Ob quam exhilarati in ipsa Nativitatis nocte sunt uni- versi Angeli, & interprete primario ex ipsorum cœlesti choro prædicarunt Pastoribus Bethlehe- miticis, Hodie natus est vobis Salvator, qui est CHRISTUS Dominus, in civitate David. Con- sonabat illic Prophetæ Evangelico totus fide- lium cœtus. Concinebat Angelo Evangelistæ to- tus Angelicus exercitus. Utrobique cantabatur, GLORIA IN EXCELSIS DEO! Utrobique vovebatur, PAX IN TERRA, BONA VO- LUNTAS IN HOMINIBUS. Neque dubium est, hac ipsa festivitate unum constituere chorum Angelos & Prophetas, imo & fidelium quorumvis a- nimas beatas, Spiritus justorum perfectorum; & ple- niori voce, perfectiori gaudio hæc resonare jam in cœlis, quæ in nostris fidelium cœtibus cantan- tur in terris: ut beatam ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν testentur sub uno capite CHRISTO, & Ecclesiæ triumpham- tis, ac militantis, Angelicæ, & eorum, qui jam ἰσ- άγγελοι sunt, gloriosæ societatis unitatem demon- strent. Quid! exultat jam ipsa Sacratissima Trinitas, quia jam GLORIA IN EXCELSIS DEO PATRI reddi potest ab humano genere, cui gaudium exo- ritur etiam super uno peccatore, pœnitentiam agente. Jam PAX nostra DEI FILIUS IN TERRA, cu- jus deliciæ sunt esse cum filiis hominum. Jam εὐδο- κία, & VOLUNTAS BONA per SPIRITUM SANCTUM redintegratur IN HOMINIBUS, qui gaudet in nobis habitare,nosque solido reple- re gaudio. Utinam! ah utinam mortales hæ au- res cum Apostolo ἄῤῥητα illa vel ad unicum mo- mentum perciperent, quanta & quam immensa perfinderemur lætitia? Donec autem choro bea- tissimo in isto Sancto Sanctorum adjungamur, con- cinamus in atriis tabernaculi Domini cum sanctis quaquaversum terras incolentibus; neq; ambiga- mus, nostris quoque cœtibus immisceri Sanctos Angelos, licet non videantur, & concentus nobis- cum suavissimos edere, licet non audiantur. Quin provocare eos ad harmonicum concentum ne du- bitemus lyra modulisque Davidicis: Benedicite Domino omnes Angeli ejus, Benedicite Domino o- mnes virtutes ejus: Benedic anima mea Domino. Certa insuper fiducia credamus, adesse nobis in medio cœtuum sacrorum, habitare in cordis ju- bilantium jubilorum autorem, chori Directorem supremum, Triunum, & super omnia in secula Bene- dictum DEUM: adeoǵ, cœlum nos habere in ter- ris, quia habemus Dominum cæli in cordibus, ut gaudium nostrum in ipso perfectum sit. Lætabimur coram te, canit Propheta, sicut qui lætantur in messe, sicut exultant victores capta præda, quando dividunt spolia. Tempore pacis præcipua lætitia in messe est: (Pf. 126, 6.) tempore belli præcipua lætitia in distri- butione spoliorum est (2. Reg. 7, 9.) Pacem conci- liavit nobis, qui PAX nostra est: ut messe frua- mur bonorum spiritualium fertilissima. Bellum ta- men prius debellandum ipsi fuit acerrimum; con- quassandum erat caput super terram multam, (Psal. 110, 6.) ut præda eriperetur, & spolia dividerentur. Qua victoria pax constituta est, pax illa vera, non quam mundus dat, sed quam dat vita, & lux mundi: (Joh. 14, 27. c. 1, 4.) Jugum enim oneris, & virgam humeri & sceptrum exactoris superavit, sicut in die Madian: Omnis violenta prædatio cum tumultu, & vestimentum mistum cum sanguine fuit in combustio- nem, & cibus ignis (Ef. 9, 4. 5.) Jam pax viget, & charitas, ut præclare B. Lutheri habet paraphra- sis: Bellum ipsum cum omnibus, quæ ad bellum spe- ctabant, igne absumtum est, & in fumum abiit. Quod Propheta dicit, Violenta prædatio cum tu- multu, & vestimentum mixtum in sanguine, Brentio nostro interprete, belli est paraphrasis, in quo solent fieri tumultuosæ rapinæ, & cruenta prælia. Hæc fue- runt in combustionem cibi ignis, redacta sunt in ci- nerem, finemq́, acceperunt. Nullum ergo amplius bellum metuendum: pax reddita est vera, atque æterna. Sub hoc PACIS PRINCIPE multipli- catur imperium, & pacis ejus non est finis. Sedet ipse super solium David, & super regnum ejus, quia Successor Davidis verus Salomo est. Ut confirmet illud & corroboret in judicio, & in justitia, à modo, & usq́, in sempiternum. In judicio pro subditis suis adversus principem mundi, qui jam judicatus est, nec quicquam contra regnum hoc valet: In justi- tia, qua subditos suos fideles universos donat, fa- ctus ipse nobis à DEO justitia (1. Cor. 1, 30.) quem profitemur omnes, JEHOVA JUSTITIA NOSTRA, (Jer. 23, 6.) & in quo gloriamur sin- guli, IN DOMINO MEA JUSTITIA (Esa. 45, 25.) Zelus Domini Exercituum fecit hoc: Zelus pro vindicando genere humano misere subjuga- to, Zelus pro restituendo Dei honore, vehementer per peccatum in mundum introductum labefacta- to. Ideo exercitus Domini universi, angelici in cœ- lis, & Evangelici in terris tripudiant jam in Domi- no, & concelebrant Dominum, una voce, harmo- nia suavissima. Intercedere quidem spirituali huic lætitiæ videtur, quod Propheta prædixit, Multi- plicasti gentem, & non magnificasti lætitiam, ut Vulga- ta Latina habet: Sed hæc aut non concernunt nos, quibus in tenebris sedentibus lux illa magna orta est, sed eos, qui tenebras magis diligunt, quam lucem, & imprimis Judæos, de quibus S. Johannes: in sua ve- nit, & sui eum non receperunt: qui proinde culpa propria lugent, gaudium, quod omni populo para- tum, & annunciatum, spernendo & respuendo; quo fere abit B. Lutheri Hieronymianæ conformis interpretatio; Recipiunt gentes Evangelium atque sic augetur Ecclesia accesfione gentium, sed eam felici- tatem gentium Judæi gentibus invident, sicut dicit, in gente stulta irritabo eos: aut è fontibus verita- tis aliter reddenda verba textus Prophetici sunt: nimirum sub interrogatione negante, quæ for- titer affirmare solet, multiplicasti gentem, annon ne- amplificasses gaudium? Gavisi sunt coram te secun- dum gaudium in messe. Nihil enim triste immi- scere in hac tam læta concione Evangelica Pro- pheta voluit, & gaudium Genethliacum quam maxime amplificare studuit. Ea tamen loquen- di ratione ex instituto usus videtur, utpote rei apprime congrua, ut nempe interrogatione ne- gante potius, quam affirmatione Categorica eam exprimeret, quia lætitiam gentium luctus paritu- rus erat Judæorum, vel ut Apostolus loquitur (Rom. 11, 15.) horum ruina, illorum fuit propitia- tio. Qui vero luctus, quæ ruina seu Judæorum, seu aliorum etiam incredulorum, gaudium, quod in Domino habemus, nulli intervertere poterit credentium. Non enim Servatori nasci- turo, qui lætitiam adferre debuit omnibus, sed populo eundem non suscepturo imputandum, quod lugeat, & lugeatur, quodque ita ex even- tu non sit multiplicata lætitia, uti vi nativitatis & gratiæ salutiferæ, quæ illuxit omnibus hominibus, & multiplicari gens Sancta, & diffundere sese undiquaque potuit lætitia. Nam qui Petra salu- tis est omnibus ex destinatione divina, merito- que proprio, petra sit Scandali & lapis offensionis, ex culpa impingentium, & incredulorum de- merito. Manet interim ratum, & illibatum nuncium Genethliacum: Ecce Evangelizo vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit omni populo: quia natus est vobis hodie Salvator, qui est Christus Domi- nus. (Luc. 2, 10.) Manet firmum & Catholicum Sancti Simeonis testimonium (vers. 30. 31.) Para- sti SALUTARE tuum ante faciem OMNIUM populorum, lumen ad revelationem gentium, & gloriam plebis tuæ Israël. Et EXULTA il- lud Zacharianum, Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi, (Cap. 9, 9.) omnes concernit; omnibusque in- timatur illud Davidicum (Psalm. 118, 24.) Hæc est dies, quam fecit Dominus, exultemus, & lætemur in ea: omnibus præcipitur per Aposto- lum, (Phil. 4, 4.) Gaudete in Domino semper: iterum dico gaudete: omnibus annunciatur Chri- stus Salvator, universæ, inquam, creaturæ (humanæ) quæ sub cælo est, (Coloss. 1, 24. 28.) Fidelis sermo, & omni acceptione dignus quod Christus Jesus venit in hunc mundum peccatores salvos facere (1. Timoth. 1, 15.) quærere & salvum facere, quod perierat (Luc. 19, 10.) Quapropter jubilate DEO omnis terra. Viderunt enim omnes termini terræ salutare DEI nostri (Psalm. 98. 4. 3.) Laudate Dominum omnes gentes, lau- date eum omnes populi (Psalm. 117, 1. 2.) Quo- niam confirmata est super nos misericordia ejus, & veritas Domini manet in æternum. Ut vero gaudium illud in corde nostro exoriatur, & amplificetur, Meditatione opus est JESULI recens nati; Quocirca nomina ejusdem dulcis- sima sistit nobis Evangelista Veteris Testamen- ti, devota mente expendenda. PARVU- LUM dicit nobis natum, ut generationem ejus humanam, Nostræ regenerationis causa factam, meditemur: Filius enim DEI factus est ho- mo, ut nos homines efficeremur filii DEI, mo- nente S. Irenæo. FILIUM nobis datum indigitat, ut generationem ejus æternam ex es- sentia Patris factam veneremur: de qua æternus Pater ei dixit, Filius meus es tu, Ego hodie, (quod DEI hodie æternum hodie est, in DEO enim nil est nisi æternitas) genui Te. (Psalm. 2, 7.) Non enim nisi ab æterno Verbo, æterno DEI Filio, ad æternum Patrem reduci poteramus Iohan. 1, 14. 18. cap. 14, 6. neque ullius alterius opus fuit, exemplar imaginis divinæ hominibus restituere, nisi ejus, qui erat imago Patris, di- cente S. Athanasio, (de incarnat. Verbi DEI T. I. p. m. 72.) Neque v. vulgaris hic cogitandus parvulus, aut Filius: Sed cujus principatus super humeros ejus. Qui & principatum gessit ab ini- tio nativitatis, vere πορφυρογέννητος, natus Dominus, & Rex Judæorum, & unus solus super humeris propriis eundem gessit, quod de nullo Principum terrenorum dici potest, hi enim di- vidunt onus principatus cum consiliariis, & mi- nistris suis: & principatum super humeros valde onerosum, omni creaturæ ἀβάςακτον, sponte suscepit, ac quum principes alii subditorum hu- meris imponant onera, ipse ab universis homini- bus onus, quod omnibus importabile erat, onus nempe implendæ legis pro omnibus, onus portan- di reatus culpæ, & pœnæ omnium, in quo est Principatus ejus, in suos suscepit humeros; Neq; enim portatur Christus, quæ B. Lutheri verba sunt, à principatu, & subditis suis, sed ipse por- tat principatum suum, h. e. noster servus est, ut nos simus liberi, & Reges. Quis omnino (quæ- rit Tertull. l. contr. Judæos c. 10. & l. 3. contr. Marc. c. 19.) quis omnino Regum insigne potestatis suæ humero præfert, & non aut in capite diadema, aut in manu sceptrum, aut aliquam propriæ vestis notam! Sed solus Rex novus novorum seculorum CHRISTUS JESUS gloriam, & potestatem & sublimitatem suam in humero extulit, crucem sci- licet: atque hujus crucis virtutem ostendit hoc oraculum (docente Justino Apol. 2. pro Christ.) quam humeris applicuit, in eandem actus. NO- BIS ergo (quod S. Cyrillus suggerit in h. l.) no- bis datum esse Filium dicit. Factus est enim homo unigenitum DEI Verbum, non propter se ipsum, sed potius ut nostram conditionem, sicuti fuit à principio, restauraret, & ut omnium vitæ pretium ac redemtionem suum corpus DEO, & Patri in odorem suavitatis (in cruce) offerret. Ideo vere ADMIRABILIS dicitur; admirabi- lis ob suppositum gemina constans natura (1. Tim. 3, 16. Roman. 9, 5.) geminæ nativitatis, processus nempe è Bethlehem temporalis, & processus inde à diebus seculi, æterni Mich. 5, 2. Matth. 2, 6.) admirabilis ob officium, in quo admiranda elu- cescit potentia, admiranda sapientia, admiranda charitas & Φιλανθρωπία: admirabilis ob statum cum exinanitionis, tum exaltationis, in quo u- troque & omnibus utriusque actibus, & gradi- bus stupenda DEI magnalia, meraque mira- cula spectantur, ut merito sciscitanti respon- deat, Quid quæris nomen meum, quod est MI- RABILE? (Jud. 13, 18.) Nomen enim ejus ne- mo novit, nisi ipse: (Apocal. 19, 12. Proverb. 30, 4.) Vere CONSILIARIUS fuit in æterno con- cilio S. S. Trinitatis, ubi nulla creatura est à Con- siliis (Esa. 40, 13. Roman. 11, 34.) Filius vero DEI unigenitus, qui est in sinu Patris (Johan. 1, 18.) æterna DEI Sapientia, quæ testatur, meum est consilium (Proverb. 8, 14. 22.) consilium de salute nostra dedit: qui solus etiam nobis consi- lium DEI manifestat, (Matth. 11, 27. Luc. 7, 30. Actor. 20, 27.) & quum Principes habeant mul- tos consiliarios, quorum tamen nulli consilia da- re possunt, quibus subditi veram consequantur felicitatem, Parvulus nobis natus, Filius nobis da- tus, IPSE consiliarius noster est, solusque dat consilia ad consequenda bona cœlestia. Sic ta- men consiliarius est, ut DEUS IPSE sit. Mundani consiliarii non sunt IPSI principes, & homines tantum mortales & imbecilles sunt cum consiliarii, tum etiam ipsimet Principes.

MESSIAS autem non homo tantum est, sed EL, DEUS omnipotens : vere GIBBOR vel Heros, ad debellandum non hostes corporales tantum, sed imprimis spirituales, peccatum, mortem, Diabolum, & infernum, utpote Gigas geminæ substantiæ: Ideoque PATER VENTURI SECULI etiam dictus: vel ut in fonte est, Pater æternus, aut æternitatis: Pater non patriæ, quales principes sunt, sed creaturæ universæ ratione creationis, hominum omnium ratione redemtionis, fidelium omnium ratione regenerationis: cujus Paternitas uti ab æterno est, ita in æternum, adeoque in futurum se porrigit seculum. Pater non persona, sed affectu, qui vere paternus, vere æternus est. Denique PRINCEPS PACIS, quia ita Pater, ut Princeps etiam sit, ut nos & filios atque hæredes habeat, & subditos: quibus PACEM proprio sanguine acquisivit, PACEM per Evangelium Verbum pacis donat, PACEM per Spiritum S. Spiritum pacis obsignat.

Hæc ergo solemnibus hisce genethliacis meditemur, hæc miremur, hæc veneremur: quæ & angeli ipsi desiderant παρακύψαι (1. Petr. 1, 12.) ut hic, & æternum, cum iisdem, de illis lætemur. Id autem fiat non aure modo attenta, lingua grata, mente devota, sed vita etiam sobria, casta, & religiosa. Vitetur crapula, & impuritas, quia JESULUS noster est Sanctissimus: Relegetur contentio,, & boatus cyclopicus, quia JESULUS noster est mitissimus: Excludatur cum perpetua infamia Scurrilitas, & impietas quævis, quia JESULUS noster vindex est justissimus: Gloria sit DEO in excelsis, Pax vigeat in terris, beneplacitum foveatur in hominibus, ut nostrum in DEO unice sit beneplacitum, & DEO in nobis propter JESULUM nostrum itidem gratum sit beneplacitum. Denique in honorem JESULI ministris ad præsepe ejus destinatis gratitudinem etiam testemini, depositis ad aram muneribus Eucharisticis. CHRISTO enim ipsi, ah quam largo remuneratori? datur, quod Ministris Christi datur! P. P. Witebergæ profesto Genethliaco Anni cIƆ IƆc LXX.

## 9:6
Vers. 6.

FOR A LITTLE CHILD IS BORN TO US] That is, will be born. For Hebrew past tenses are taken for futures.

AND A SON IS GIVEN TO US] Will be given. Hezekiah, very unlike his father Ahaz. Concerning the same below XI. Yet so that not only Christians acknowledge that these things pertain much more excellently to the Messiah, but also the Chaldean in this place.

Grotius Judaizes very badly again, while he understands the prophecy concerning Hezekiah according to the literal sense. Although he does indeed add that these things pertain to the Messiah in a more excellent way, and that both Christians and the Chaldean [paraphrase] acknowledge this, he has not, however, indicated whether he approves of that explanation with his own vote. Nor, if he wishes it to be understood of Christ in a mystical sense, which he believed was said according to the letter concerning Hezekiah, does he have the support of any Christians or of the Chaldean interpreter: who certainly interpret it not of Hezekiah at the same time, but SOLELY of Christ. But he performs a welcome service for the blind Jews, by whose Rabbis he is seduced here also to make Hezekiah the object of the native sense: For if they obtain this, they will easily be able to concede that those things can be transferred mystically to the Messiah in their own way. However, that double sense cannot stand. For if the child born is Hezekiah, according to

The Messiah cannot be the same: If those epithets are here attributed to Hezekiah, they cannot be explained as referring to the Messiah. For one must not look at whom they COULD be accepted as referring to, or to whom they MIGHT be suitable, but rather of whom they are here enunciated by the intention of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be twofold, since the Holy Spirit willed a certain sense to be in His prophecies, and did not bring forth the same things with a different mind in ambiguous words that introduce a clearly disparate sense, nor did He will them to be understood in a disparate sense. Nor can those things be understood of Hezekiah. For no word has been brought forth concerning him up to this point, nor is any trace of that matter detected, which the Prophet has prophesied here concerning Hezekiah. But then he dealt with liberation and the spiritual yoke: which cannot be ascribed to Hezekiah. He dealt with joy before the Lord and in the Lord, which is the spiritual joy of the faithful. And he established the birth of the child as the cause of this joy and liberation. But did the birth of Hezekiah bring that spiritual joy and liberation? Jerome on this passage: Therefore the Devil and all his violent predation, by which he had suppressed the human race and had mingled blood with blood, will be for burning and food for eternal fire, because a child is born to us of a virgin, of whom it was said above: before the child knows, etc. Furthermore, it deals with the birth of him who was to bring light to those walking in darkness, the Galileans and the Jews. Which we have taught up to this point must be understood solely of Christ; indeed, the Holy Spirit teaches it with a resounding voice in Matthew 4, but no one would say it of Hezekiah. Nor is it permitted to doubt that the Prophet wished to confirm the faithful again with this most magnificent and illustrious promise concerning the most august sign, which he had promised them before, Chapter 7, and to teach more fully what they ought to hold and believe concerning the virgin's son, Immanuel; since this was the chief care of the Prophets, to excite and confirm faith in the Messiah, in which duty Isaiah, the leader of the Prophets, was occupied above others. And these arguments, drawn from the context of the preceding verses, shine with their own light. Now if we attend to the very words of the present prophecy, The child, says the Prophet, is born to us, the Son is given to us: calling him a child and at the same time a Son, certainly not through empty tautology: But as the pious ancients observed, so that by the word child he designates the human nature, and by the word Son the divine. Because this child is truly the Son of God, as the Angel testifies. The holy thing (or that holy child) which (or who) shall be born of thee, shall be called the Son of the Highest. And the parallel passage concerning the only-begotten Son of God given to us, John 3:16, illustrates this excellently. Calvin has it thus here: Son without addition cannot be understood as other than the Son of GOD. And now it is attributed to Christ by way of excellence, so that we may know that by this distinguished mark he is discerned from the rest of the human race. Nor is there any doubt that Isaiah looked toward that solemn oracle; which was flying about through the mouths of all: I will be to him a Father and he shall be to me a Son: just as it is repeated in Psalm 2: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. For unless the matter had been commonly known and celebrated, that the Messiah would be the Son of God, Isaiah would have called him Son simply, ineptly and without sense. Wherefore this eulogy depends upon the previous prophecy: from which the Apostle in Hebrews 1 gathers the excellence of Christ, that he is exalted above all Angels. Moreover, although Christ was contemptible in the guise of a child: yet his dignity is adorned by the title of Son. Nor should that US be rashly passed over. For the Prophet includes himself and any of the faithful with this word: to whom the Messiah (and not indeed Hezekiah) was peculiarly born and given, just as he also called the same Immanuel, God with us, above. To us, he says, that child is born; to us that son is given, who is Immanuel, God with us. Concerning which word Us, Cyril on this passage says: he says that the Son is given to us. For the only-begotten Word of GOD was made man, not for his own sake, but rather so that he might restore our condition, as it was from the beginning, and so that he might offer his own body to GOD and the Father as a price and redemption for the life of all, in an odor of sweetness. But above all, the names and epithets must be weighed, as well as the duties and mighty works, which are attributed to this child, which are so great that they by no means suit any of the mortal Kings, nor could they be transferred to Hezekiah, except through a remarkable perversity. Grotius indeed attempts to explain everything concerning Hezekiah; but just as he clearly judaizes in this, so it is too manifest how greatly the most illustrious words are perverted and the whole prophecy is enervated. Whence from this collusion with the Jews he deserved nothing other than the detestation of all men of heart. For who would bear with an equal mind, when this child is said to be called Wonderful, that it be adapted to Hezekiah because of the highest virtues that were in him; when neither David, nor Moses, nor Abraham himself, or any of the faithful obtained that name: much less does it suit Hezekiah as his own: but no one should doubt that it suits the Messiah. Who also calls himself so in Judges 13:18. Who will admit that those most diverse titles, Counselor, Mighty God, which every interpreter of the Christians and Jews has held to be distinct, are to be explained in a new and unheard-of manner in the construct state as CONSULTANT OF THE MIGHTY GOD! Who will not detest that depravation of the most eminent title, Father of the future age or Eternal Father, that is, one who is going to leave many descendants after him and for a long time: by which pact that august epithet, Father of eternity, would suit Abraham rather, and with even better right Noah, and most powerfully Adam, but by no means should it be claimed for Hezekiah as his own peculiarly. Who will suffer that title to be appropriated to Hezekiah, that he is to be called Prince of peace! For that name would suit others with better right, especially Solomon, if one must speak of a mere man. And how jejune is that gloss, his empire shall be multiplied, that is, it will last for 29 years. Thus it would much more fittingly apply to the reign of Azariah, who reigned for 52 years; or Joash, who reigned 40 years; and Asa, who presided for 41 years, and others. How frivolous, nay, perverse is the interpretation of the words, OF THE INCREASE OF HIS GOVERNMENT AND PEACE THERE SHALL BE NO END, i.e., he will enjoy peace until the end of his days. The tenor of the words themselves proves that it promises an eternal peace that will lack an end. How base is that depravation FROM HENCEFORTH EVEN FOR EVER, that is, from the beginning to the end of life? For what is new here in Hezekiah, when it is agreed concerning most other pious and faithful Kings that they established their kingdoms in judgment and justice until the end of their lives, in the sense in which Grotius explains this; although it can be said ἁπλῶς of none of the Kings, nor of Hezekiah, that he confirmed his kingdom and established it in judgment and in justice. For no one has ever been found who has not at some time departed from judgment and justice, whether through ignorance and infirmity, or through voluntary declination. And that these things are said of Christ in a peculiar sense, and are appropriated to him, is confirmed by other parallel passages it stands; to whom also all these titles undoubtedly belong. We have here Grotius confessing. In Christ, he says, both these things, and those which precede, have a meaning that is as much more august as it is also clearer. Why then does he not allow that meaning, which is not only much more august but also clearer, to be the native, proper, and literal meaning? I argue thus: The meaning which is much more august and much clearer in a very significant prophecy is without doubt to be held more as the literal and proper one than a meaning that is less august, less clear, nay, altogether doubtful, obscure, insufficient, foreign, unusual, and joined with a significant twisting of the words. But the meaning concerning the Messiah is much more august and clearer in this most significant prophecy: and therefore it is to be held more as the literal one than the Grotian one.

What of the fact that the Angel Gabriel explained this prophecy concerning Christ, and indeed in such a sense that it is clear that it cannot apply to Hezekiah: for that Christ is the one who, by the power of this prophecy, ought to sit upon the throne of David and be an eternal King, whose kingdom shall have no end, is testified in Luke 1:33. Therefore he openly teaches that the prophecy is to be understood concerning that King whose kingdom has no end: nor are the prophetic words, 'Of his peace there shall be no end,' and 'from henceforth and even forever,' to be understood otherwise than of eternal peace and of an eternal empire having no end. Grotius does not deny this angelic interpretation of the prophetic saying at Matthew 22:42. But if you further compare with this oracle the prophecy of Isaiah 11:1 concerning the rod from the root of Jesse, because Grotius acknowledges that the same subject is being dealt with in both places, the Jewish gloss concerning Hezekiah can be further refuted from it: since it is clear that the prophet was prophesying there not of Hezekiah, but of Christ, as we shall prove at chapter 11. Add to these now the judgment of the whole Christian Church. For hitherto no one among Christians has doubted that the prophet is here prophesying literally concerning the Messiah. Concerning which unanimous consent the Doctors of the ancient Church understood this oracle. Justin against Trypho, Tertullian against Marcion, Novatian on the Trinity, ch. 26, Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, and Basil the Great in this place. Athanasius, Ambrose, and other Fathers everywhere assume this as undoubted, that it is a question here of the Son of God: which also the Fathers are read to have used everywhere in their disputations against the Arians and other heretics. Nor was any doubt moved concerning it by the heretics themselves: certainly Hezekiah came into no one's mind. Nay, our ancestors valued this saying so much that they commended it to the Church in a public hymn: and the Church uses it at the Feast of the Nativity of the Lord, when it sings: 'A child is born,' etc. Nor has any of the recent Jews conceded that it is a question here of Hezekiah according to the letter. Calvin himself, who otherwise willingly judaizes in such matters, censured the impudence of the Jews in this place: 'The Jews distort this passage more impudently; for they interpret it concerning Hezekiah.' The Socinians, who are accustomed to attempt everything in the oracles concerning the Deity of Christ, confess that it is a question here of Christ: 'Christ is to be called the mighty God in Isaiah,' says Crellius, book 1, On the True Religion, ch. 8. Similarly Volckelius, book 5, ch. 10: 'Isaiah long ago predicted that Christ would be called the Father of eternity or of the future age.' Schlichting, Disputation on the Trinity against Meisner, pp. 244, 260: 'By the name of Father, a certain person, namely Christ, is designated here.' Nor does Episcopius the Arminian, whom Grotius is accustomed to follow, think otherwise. Why many words? Grotius himself confessed that this prophecy is to be understood in no other way than of Christ. Since at Matthew 22:42 he says that Christ would be acknowledged by the Jews as the son of David from the prophecy of Isaiah 9:7, and that Gabriel finally used it as a MOST CLEAR prophecy to Mary in Luke 1. But how would that be a most clear prophecy concerning the Messiah, if in its native sense it dealt with Hezekiah?

AND HIS GOVERNMENT HAS BEEN MADE UPON HIS SHOULDER] That is, he will be born in the purple: from the very cradle he will bear the royal purple: as one born to the kingdom. Compare Ezekiel 28:13.

What is peculiar in this concerning Hezekiah? Were not all the Kings of Judah from David onwards born in the purple, just as Hezekiah was? Since they were likewise hereditary kings. Certainly Hezekiah has nothing in this matter that is proper and singular above others. But if by that phrase it is designated, not that this child was merely born into the kingdom, but that he exercised government from his very birth, this would certainly fit no one except the Messiah: who, born King of the Jews, wore the purple from his very cradle, and was celebrated by the angels in the cradle as Lord, and was adored by the Magi of the East as King of the Jews. The ancients explain this in the sense that this little child exercised government from the beginning of his conception, and that by the power of his origin because of the hypostatic union of the human nature with the divine. He is said, however, to bear the government upon his shoulders, because the signs of rule are carried on the shoulders. Whence a Prince is called 'nasi', a bearer of his people and of the Republic. and a chariot and a charioteer, because he not only directs like a charioteer, but also carries the burdens like a chariot. Furthermore, he is also said to carry the government upon his shoulders to the distinction of other emperors and princes: who impose a great part of their government and rule upon the shoulders of their counselors and officials. Therefore, it can be said of no worldly monarch that he carries the entire government upon his own shoulders; because kingdoms can neither be administered nor defended by one man alone; nay, the government and administration of a worldly kingdom is imposed more upon the shoulders of others than upon the own shoulders of the king. But Christ is such a King whose government is upon his own shoulders alone; he alone is the one who rules, governs, and preserves his people throughout the whole world. He alone is the one who defends and protects it against Satan, death, and hell. Thirdly, the obedience of Christ is also noted, when it is said that the government is upon his shoulders, that is, the dominion imposed upon him; certainly not light, but very burdensome. For just as burdens are wont to be imposed upon shoulders by others, namely by princes upon subjects: so upon this prince was imposed the burden of the government and administration of rule, to which pertains above all the rescue of subjects from the power of spiritual enemies. This burden Christ took upon his shoulders and endured, becoming obedient to God the Father even unto death, even the death of the cross, Phil. 2. And in this he differs again greatly from any worldly monarch whatsoever. For these do not carry burdens themselves, but impose them upon their subjects; nor is it their place to obey, but to command. But the government of this King entails submission and obedience. And therefore he suffered the government to be imposed upon his shoulders, that he himself might undergo the burdens which had to be endured: as obedience, submission, and patience are wont to be noted in the Scriptures when something is said to be imposed upon the shoulders. To some it seems that there is an allusion here to the rod of the shoulder, of which in verse 4, as if to say: the Devil and tyrants impose the rod and scepter, along with the burdens of their empire, upon the shoulders of their subjects: but Christ will sustain upon his own shoulders the rod and burden of his government. Hence, therefore, Fourthly, this is also applied to the cross of Christ, which was imposed upon his shoulders. Because his government is in the cross: through the cross he both destroyed his enemies and liberated his subjects.

The same, through the power of his cross, rules and governs his people. That cross, too, which he carried on his shoulders, what else is it but the standard and scepter of the empire of this our King, clearly proper and peculiar to him? Concerning which Tertullian, book against the Jews, chapter 10: "What king at all carries the standard of his power on his shoulder, and not either a diadem on his head, or a scepter in his hand, or some mark of his own garment? But the new King of the new ages alone, Christ Jesus, has lifted up his new glory and power and sublimity on his shoulder, namely the cross, so that according to David's prophecy, the Lord has reigned from the tree." Just as in Psalm 95:10, the ancient interpreters in the Greek version of the Seventy read: "God has reigned from the tree." Which Tertullian repeats in the same words, book 3 against Marcion, chapter 19. Cyril notes and approves the same sense handed down by others: since our Lord Jesus Christ, carrying the cross on his shoulders, came to his saving passion and was exalted and obtained the world through himself, hence it is said that his government is upon his shoulder. Thus Basil: "Whose government is upon his shoulder, that is, the kingdom and power in his cross." For exalted onto the cross, he drew all things to himself. And so also Jerome, Augustine, and before them all, Justin, Apology 2 for the Christians, shows that this oracle is the power of the cross, which he applied to his shoulders when he was led to the same.

Fifthly, his fortitude is also designated in this way. For since fortitude is denoted by the shoulder, the government is said to be made upon his shoulders, because by his own power and fortitude he carries the same on his shoulders and by his arm. Cyril renders this sense: and this Prophetic speech seems to be joined with the former, namely, to call the shoulder fortitude. For all our strength is situated in the arms and shoulders. And indeed the Son is called the arm of God and the Father (Isaiah 53:1). Christ therefore ruled the world by his own power, for he is the fortitude of God and the Father. Jerome also explains it similarly in this place.

Sixthly, Blessed Luther observes another thing still proper to this King: namely, that he carries his subjects on his shoulder. It seems to me it can be explained most simply: that we, who are his government, are carried on his shoulder, contrary to what is accustomed to happen in the kingdoms of the world. For in the world, subjects carry and tolerate their Kings, by whom both the property and the bodies of the subjects are reduced to servitude: but the condition of the Kingdom of Christ is different, for Christ is not carried by his government and his subjects, but he himself carries his government, that is, he is our servant, so that we may be free and Kings. Thus he still carries us today. But just as he himself carries us, so he wishes in turn that his stones should carry one another, so that nevertheless the carrying of all of us, by which we carry others after the example of Christ, may be carried by that very cornerstone, Christ. This opinion pleases me more, because it contains the form of the kingdom of Christ both in himself and in his members. These are the words of Blessed Luther. However, those opinions can be joined, because they are subordinate and all contribute to the kingdom of Christ.

Verse of the same. AND HIS NAME SHALL BE CALLED] In the Hebrew it is, "he shall call": supply "everyone." The Chaldean also translated it as "he shall be called." It is known, however, to the Hebrews that it is said that someone is called thus or so, to whom such titles or epithets are appropriate.

Verse of the same. ADMIRABLE] Because of the supreme mighty works that will be in him.

Too thinly. If this child is called admirable only because of his mighty works, this name is not proper to him: which, however, the Prophet indicates, because others also have been famous for mighty works. More correctly, therefore, other interpreters, who explain this unanimously concerning Christ as truly admirable, both by reason of the person, in whom we can never sufficiently wonder at the admittedly great mystery of the hypostatic union of the two natures 1. Timothy 3:16, and by reason of the office, in which admirable power, wisdom, and goodness shine forth: in the Prophetic office, by which the doctrine and the power of that doctrine are admirable, and the stupendous miracles by which he sealed it: in the Priestly, by which the wonderful sacrifice and the effect of the same are truly admirable: In the Kingly, finally, by which the wonderful defeat of enemies and the government of the Church, and then finally by reason of his state and his emptying and exaltation, in which both and in all their acts the stupendous great works of God and mere miracles occur. In sum, there is nothing that is not admirable in this child, whom the Prophet describes: Who also called himself admirable, Judges 13:18. "Why do you ask my name, which is פלא admirable!" Brentius observes that this surname is attributed to the Messiah by antithesis to worldly Princes. For these cannot wonderfully help their own and free them from dangers. They help them sometimes, but according to the custom of this age, either with external arms or the aid of allies. But the Messiah helps and frees his own wonderfully and with no other helper. There are, however, twofold miracles of the Messiah by which he helped his people: Some are bodily: For he restored sight to the blind; cleanliness to the lepers, health to the lame, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, life to the dead. Thus no worldly Monarch could help his own. Others are spiritual. For the Messiah wonderfully preserves his own; in sins, so that they may be reckoned righteous: in death, so that they may have life; in errors, so that they may be firm, so that they may receive the heavenly fief. For he is such an admirable helper and liberator that when all things seem lost and desperate by human standards, he himself is present with his aid.

COUNSELOR, MIGHTY GOD] Rather, consultant of the mighty God: that is, he who in all business will seek counsel from God, namely through the Prophets, as will now follow.

A remarkable and detestable corruption of the names of the Messiah, so that they might be twisted toward Hezekiah. Such a thing did not even come to the mind of the Jewish teachers themselves, who are most ingenious at devising anything. For they acknowledged that those names are distinct, because the matter is clear: and therefore, so as not to bestow such august names upon the Messiah, they invented the fiction that GOD the Father is described by them, inasmuch as He was about to name Hezekiah the prince of peace, in this manner: And he shall call him wonderful, counselor, God, strong, Father everlasting, prince of peace. This is an open corruption. Since the matter here is not about the names of God, but about the appellations of the child. These six are indeed numbered by Jerome and other interpreters: WONDERFUL, COUNSELOR, GOD, STRONG, FATHER EVERLASTING, PRINCE OF PEACE. All the rest are simple, and are placed as separate names; the Makkaph dash teaches that the last two are compound names: just as the name פלא is uttered simply concerning the child; so also the name יעץ: and similarly also the name אל and גבור, as they are rightly rendered by the Vulgate: wonderful, counselor, God, strong. Furthermore, what is this peculiar thing, to seek counsel from God? Did not other faithful and holy kings also do this? Nor is it simply true of Hezekiah that he consulted God through the Prophet in all things. He certainly did not consult Him when he showed his treasures to the Babylonian envoys, being met on that account with a severe rebuke by the Prophet, and visited with a most heavy punishment upon his sons, Isa. 39, 5. 6. 7. But because it has been proven that this passage treats of the Messiah: nor does Grotius dissent, to whom those names, he claims, apply in a more august and much plainer sense; how will that explanation be consistent with itself? Did the Messiah also have to seek counsel from God through the Prophets in all things? How much more correctly, therefore, do the Interpreters affirm the divine majesty of these names: by which, the LXX Interpreters, as Jerome believes, were terrified, since they did not dare to say of this boy that he should be openly called God, and instead of these six names they placed 'Angel of the great counsel' etc. Indeed, even the very enemies of the Deity of Christ, the Arians and Photinians, who have dared to deny or call into question everything in such august oracles, acknowledge that the name of God אל is here attributed to the Messiah: as is evident concerning the ancient Arians from Athanasius and other champions of antiquity, and also concerning Socinus, Crellius, Volckelius, Schlichtingius, and other more recent ones, throughout their writings. Jerome indeed observed that some of the ancient Interpreters had joined two names here, but he does not approve of that explanation. However, it has not been permitted for anyone to explain it in the way that Grotius has. Whence that new discovery is to be attributed to the author himself, along with many others. For, says Jerome, not as most think, are two names to be joined, so that we read 'Wonderful Counselor' and again 'Mighty God', but 'Wonderful' is to be read separately, which in Hebrew is called פֶּלֶא, and 'Counselor' separately, which in their language is called יֹעֵץ, and 'GOD' separately, which in Hebrew is called אֵל, etc. What of the fact that the Grotian explanation does not at all agree with the Hebrew word יֹעֵץ: for it is established by the constant use of the word יָעַץ in the Qal and by the induction of examples that it denotes him who gives counsel and advises someone, not him who seeks the counsel of another; nor is there any doubt about this among the Hebrews. But how was Hezekiah a Counselor of God, when God denies that He has anyone for a counselor (Isa. 40:13; Rom. 11:34)? Whence it is most manifest that he is called a counselor here not with respect to God, but with respect to men. How this name is proper to the Messiah, our Brentius rightly teaches. This is also an epithet of antithesis toward worldly princes. For these cannot give counsel to all their peoples in their affairs, but the work of Counselors is necessary for them. They have many Consultants who help them in the administration of the kingdom: And yet neither the princes nor their counselors can give those counsels to the peoples by which they might attain true happiness. But the Messiah himself is the counselor; he does not need the counsel of others, but he alone suffices for the giving of Counsel, and that for the attainment of heavenly goods.

Furthermore, the name אל most evidently convinces that the Oracle cannot be understood of Hezekiah or any mere man. For this name is proper to God alone, nor does it befit any creature, as we have demonstrated from the induction of all the passages when we treated of the Hebrew divine names in Vol. II on the Augustinian Confessions. I only add the Brentian collation: The third title is God. Worldly Princes are only men. But the Messiah is not only man, but also God omnipotent, which is the sum of all majesty.

The fourth title is Strong or Hero or Giant. Worldly princes, although they are sometimes endowed with excellent fortitude, nevertheless are either not spiritual Heroes who dare and are able to undertake single combat with the adversary, such as

a Hero David was against Goliath, or if they are bodily Heroes, they are not, however, spiritual Heroes who dare and are able to undertake single combat with death and carry off the victory. The Messiah alone is that Hero who entered into singular combat with Death and Hell, and also carried off the victory, which not only he himself enjoys, but also as many as believe in him.

FATHER OF THE FUTURE AGE] In the Hebrew, 'future' is not there. He is the Father of the age who is to leave many descendants after him, and for a long time.

Although 'FUTURE' is not contained in the Hebrew, eternity is nevertheless noted by the Hebrew word עד. And therefore he is called the eternal Father or Father of eternity, and consequently this Fatherhood also extends into the future age. It is manifest, therefore, that this cannot be adapted to Hezekiah. For how does his fatherhood extend itself into eternity? And the gloss is unheard of, that he is the Father of the age who is to leave many descendants after him, and for a long time. It is certain that the name עד denotes eternity, not a long time. But then, it is a far different thing to be the Father of an age than to leave descendants for a long time. Finally, this is not proper to Hezekiah; it is common to him with many, nay, it befits countless others more than it does him. The Hebrews themselves acknowledged that the Hebrew name אבי עד is proper to GOD alone: and therefore they understood it of God the Father. But because he is openly named Son in the same place, it is manifest that the fatherhood is to be understood, not such as it is κατ' ἔσω (inwardly) within the complex of the Deity, with respect to the only-begotten Son, which is proper to the first divine person; but such as it is κατ' ἔξω (outwardly) with respect to us. Brentius has this concerning this: The fifth (title) is ETERNAL FATHER. Other princes are called Fathers of the Fatherland, because they either defend the Fatherland from hostile incursion, or import a great quantity of grain in time of famine. Which benefits, although they are to be acknowledged with a grateful mind, are nevertheless not perpetual: and Princes are easily changed. But Christ is not called Father of the Fatherland: but, which is far greater, ETERNAL FATHER. First, therefore, he is called FATHER, not by his person in the divine nature: for thus he is the Son, not the Father, but he is called Father by affection. For he always has a fatherly affection toward his people, and he does not change this affection into eternity, Isa. 49. Then he is also called the eternal Father, because he preserves his people not only in this life, but also in the future and perpetual life. Other princes can preserve their people only in this life, and that only with bodily benefits, and for a very short time; but Christ is the eternal Father, he preserves in the midst of death, and raises to eternal life. Similarly, B. Luther in this place: Eternal Father. This name does not signify the person, but the work of the person. So that he is the eternal Father, who always begets, always increases his kingdom and his Church; he always remains Father, he is not and will not ever become a judge, but there is in him a fatherly affection without end. However, what Zwingli has here is not sound. But for the Son to be called the eternal Father is not harsh to pious ears, which have learned that persons are also put for the essence by alloeosis. For in truth the Son is not the Father, but that which the Father is. Thus everywhere Zwingli injects his alloeosis, called by B. Luther the mask of the Devil. But nowhere does Scripture confuse essence and persons. The Son is not called Father because he is that which the Father is; but because he is Father with respect to us: therefore the divine essence is not directly inferred by that name: but in which that Paternal affection towards us, and the external work of regeneration, is appropriate only to the divine nature. That this name אבי־עד might be explained more fully, it will be worth the effort to repeat what we have said about it elsewhere. It can, however, be understood either neutrally and ἁπλῶς (simply), as ὁ λόγος (the Word) is considered καθ’ ἑυτὸ (in itself), insofar as he himself is eternal: in which way the Chaldean seems to have understood it, who rendered it גברא קים לעלמא, a man remaining forever. Thus it will be permissible to explain the Hebrew עַד & עָלְמוֹא (Targum) concerning absolute eternity, which is from the part before and after, although neither this nor that (which is even more emphatic) infers an all-encompassing eternity by itself and formally. But just as the matter of the subject truly imports the same in Isaiah 57:15, so also in this place, since he is called here אבי עד, who is אל גבור (the mighty God), whom it is established is altogether eternal: both are also joined in this way 1. John 5:20. Or actively and σχετικῶς (relatively), the Word is the Father of eternity, that is, the author and origin, in which way it is established that the word 'Father' sometimes denotes the first author and origin; see Genesis 4:20, John 8:44. To this the LXX seem to have looked, translating it πατὴρ ᾃ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος, Father of the future age, that is, of eternal life. For this is a paraphrase of it, Hebrews 6:5. And Vatablus, who translates it, author of life. But without doubt more things are involved in this name, which we unfold according to the Scriptures as follows. Namely, that by this title there is attributed to Christ (1) The foundation of the ages. For the Apostle teaches that the ages were made through him, Hebrews 1:2. Just as all things are said to have been made through him, which indeed were made, John 1:2. (2) The preparation of eternity, because in him eternal glory and a glorious eternity were prepared for the elect before the foundations of the world were laid, Ephesians 1:4, Colossians 1:5. (3) The acquisition of eternal life, because he himself is the author of life, Acts 3:15, and he gave eternal life to the world meritoriously and by reason of acquisition, John 6:33, when he gave his flesh, the bread of life, for the life of the world, ibid. v. 51. (4) Eternal redemption, which Christ is said to have found, Hebrews 9:12, truly eternal: and that both intensively by the immensity of his vigor, to which nothing is lacking for the highest perfection of efficacy; and extensively by the immensity of duration, because it is not merely temporary, as were the typical δικαιώματα (ordinances) of the Old Testament, but perpetual, which extends itself from the beginning of the world even to the end: whence Jesus Christ is called χθὲς καὶ σήμερον ὁ αὐτὸς, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας (yesterday and today the same, and forever), Hebrews 13:8, so that no mortal has been redeemed from sin and death, or is being redeemed yet, or can ever be redeemed hereafter, except through this redemption of Jesus Christ. Compare Acts 15:11 and chapter 4:12. And that it is not momentary, as are the fleeting and transitory redemptions of this life, but eternal, to be perpetuated and consummated in the other life through infinite myriads of ages. (5) The government of the Church of the New Testament. For God subjected to Christ τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλεσαν (the world to come), Hebrews 2:5, that is, that happy age which the Prophets had predicted would be begun by the first coming of Christ, the completion of which we still await, whose Father is Christ, 1 Corinthians 15:15. He calls the Church of the New Testament μέλλεσαν (to come), not in respect to himself, but in respect to the Fathers: in which way he also calls those goods μέλλοντα (to come) which, under the Old Testament, were not yet present as regards the ἀντίτυπον (antitype) and εἰκόνα (image), but only as regards the τύπον (type) and σκιὰν (shadow), Hebrews 10:1, of which Christ is the λειτυργὸς (minister), Hebrews 9:11. (6) Regeneration to eternal life; because in Christ Jesus we are regenerated through the Gospel to eternal life, 1 Corinthians 4:25. and through faith in him we are children of God, John 1:12, Galatians 3:26, and heirs of eternal life, Romans 8:16. (7) The donation of eternal life; because he gives eternal life to those who believe, John 3:36, chapter 5:24, chapter 6:46, chapter 10:28, he gives his life-giving flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk, John

6:54, he grants the Gospel, which is the word of eternal life, chapter 6:68, add chapter 5:39, Acts 5:20, Philippians 2:16, and he bestows the Holy Spirit, who is the life of the spirit, so that in this life also we may have eternal life, but as regards a foretaste or a preliminary drinking through faith and inchoatively, Romans 8:24, 2 Corinthians 5:7, which we shall obtain from Christ, as regards plenary enjoyment, through sight and consummatively in regeneration, or as the Syrian translates חדתא בעלמא (in the new world) or the world to come, Matthew 19:18, chapter 25:46, Luke 22:29, John 6:40, 2 Timothy 4:8, Revelation 2:10. Thus therefore Christ is אבי עד both by reason of his divine nature (1) ὀυσιωδῶς κῃ κυρίως (essentially and principally), seeing that he is life itself, John 11:25, chapter 14:6, ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς κῃ ζωὴ αἰώνιος (the true God and eternal life), 1 John 5:20, (2) ἐνεργητικῶς καὶ δευτέρως (efficiently and less principally), insofar as he is the author of eternity and the ages, Hebrews 1:2, John 1:3, and by reason of his human nature ὑποστατικῶς καὶ ὀργανικῶς (personally and instrumentally), because human flesh, raised into the ὑπόστασιν (hypostasis) of the Son of God, became an ἐνυπόστατον (subsistent) and ἐνεργητικὸν ὄργανον τῆς θεότητος (effective instrument of the divinity), through which the Word repaired eternal life and imparts the same to us, John 6:33, 51, 54, and by reason of both; partly ἱλασικῶς (propitiatorily) and as regards merit, because ὁ ἀρχηγὸς τῆς ζωῆς καὶ σωτηρίας (the author of life and salvation) merited eternal life for us, Acts 3:15, Hebrews 2:10, 2 Timothy 1:10, partly κοινωνικῶς (communally) and as regards the gift, because he gives eternal life to those who believe in him, John 3:16, partly δεσποτικῶς (despotically) and as regards the dominion which he himself obtains, as Lord of the future world and age, Hebrews 2:5, chapter 6:5, that is, of the more perfect state of the Church, which indeed begins to be established in the present, but will be consummated in the future age.

PRINCEPS PACIS (Prince of Peace)] A peaceful prince and one who will live in peace.

A very jejune interpretation; nor does it appear how that is proper to Hezekiah. That august eulogy שׂר שׁלום, Prince of Peace, is not immediately deserved by him who lives in peace and is studious of peace. There is no doubt, however, but that it is proper to Christ in a peculiar way: who, as he is called Prince of Life because he is the author of life, Acts 3:15, so he is called Prince of Peace because he himself is the author of the peace which we have with God and among ourselves. Whence he is also called our peace in the abstract, Ephesians 2. Other princes, says Brentius, are usually for the most part the authors of wars and many calamities. And even if you should find a worldly prince most studious of peace, yet he cannot bring it about that private individuals should maintain peace among themselves, even if there were no public war. But Christ is truly the Prince of Peace, and is deservedly named Friedenrichus, which in Latin signifies rich and full of peace. First, because he pacifies God and men. For there was a great dissension between God and men: because since man is a sinner, he could not be in agreement with God. But Christ reconciled them, so that men, justified by faith, might have peace. Next, Christ is also the author of mutual peace among those who believe in him. For he who believes in Christ keeps peace, as far as in him lies, with all men. It is indeed impossible that a pious person should always enjoy external tranquility in this age.
