And here we have an interpretation beyond all exception, which the Holy Spirit Himself delivered in Romans 9:27, who from this prophecy demonstrates not only the salvation of the remnants from the Israelites, but also the conversion of the Gentiles to CHRIST. But Isaiah cries out for Israel: If the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved. For the Lord will make a consummating and abbreviating word in righteousness, because the Lord will make an abbreviated word upon the earth. The Lord consummates and abbreviates the word, while He fulfills the word concerning consummation and abbreviation, and that ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ (in righteousness), so that, namely, the earth may be inundated with righteousness according to the Prophetic oracle. Therefore, those things which are predicted concerning the conversion of the remnants to the mighty God, even if they also look to the times of Hezekiah, according to the interpretation of Jerome and Cyril, will nevertheless especially have their fulfillment in the time of the New Testament, according to the Apostolic interpretation. The promise is general, that remnants will always be preserved, which were to be fulfilled both at the time of the devastation made by Sennacherib, and especially under the New Testament, where a total consummation and destruction of the Israelites seemed about to follow. But which abbreviated consummation of the Jews will make for the propagation of righteousness through the orb of the lands. Brentius and Osiander also refer verse 20 here: At that time, when CHRIST shall come into this world, the Israelites will no longer trust in the external defenses of men, but will trust in the holy Lord of Israel, who is CHRIST our Lord, and they will truly be converted to the mighty GOD, they will acknowledge CHRIST, who is the mighty GOD, preserving all believers to eternal life. In the Hebrew words a difficulty seems to occur, which the translation of the LXX Interpreters, not being understood, seems to have increased. כִּלָּיוֹן חָרוּץ שׁוֹטֵף צְדָקָה Which Ludovicus de Dieu thinks can be rendered thus clearly: He makes a precise consummation overflow in righteousness. Not bad. But it involves the sense in His own precise or absolute decree of predestination. But B. Luther explained it most clearly and very appositely: For when the destruction is checked (for then the consummation is cut off or abbreviated), then righteousness comes overflowing. The immense mercy of God provides this, that the consummation may be cut off and checked, lest the whole of Israel be utterly consumed and destroyed; and that then, when a barrier and limit is placed to the destruction, righteousness may overflow and diffuse itself like a river. For the LORD God of Hosts will let a destruction go (He will make a consummation) and yet check the same (He will make an abbreviation, He will cut off the consummation, and stop its impetus) in the whole land. So that from there also righteousness may diffuse itself more abundantly through the whole earth; which sense the Apostolic explanation excellently confirms in Romans 11, where B. Luther has it thus: For a destruction and a checking will happen unto righteousness, and the LORD will do that same checking upon the earth. A clear gloss is added: Although the greater part falls away and remains unbelieving, He will not, however, let them all fall thus, but will preserve the rest and through them spread His Word and grace the more richly, whereby they become righteous and glorious. Nothing could be said more excellently to explain the mind of the Prophet, as the Holy Spirit declares it through the Apostle. Nor do the LXX, whose version the Apostle brought forward, differ thus, as far as the sense goes: λόγον γὰρ

συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ (consummating and cutting off in righteousness), God consummates the word, that word, namely, which He predicted concerning the consummation to be performed, but in such a way that He cuts it off in righteousness or mercy, so that He may set a limit to the consummation and to the decree and word of the consummation through His immense mercy, ὅτι λόγον συντετμημένον κύριος, κύριος δυνάμεων ποιήσει ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ ὅλῃ (because the Lord, the Lord of hosts, will perform an abbreviated word in the whole inhabited world), because that abbreviated word or decree (not absolute, but restricted and tempered by mercy, for it is called abbreviated for this reason, because it as it were cuts off the consummation which God had threatened, and sets a limit to it) the Lord, the Lord of hosts, is about to do or execute through the whole earth. These things do not favor an absolute decree, but are entirely repugnant to it, and confirm the gracious election of the remnants, of which the Apostle speaks. Grotius does not fear to claim that the Apostolic discourse is absurd, in his annotation on Romans 9, verse 27. In the right order, he says, ὅτι (that) ought to have preceded λόγον συντελῶν (a consummating word). But in the Pauline text, such as we now have, it is quite absurd that γὰρ (for) is placed first, then ὅτι (that). This reading is entirely interpolated from the LXX. But the old reading exists in that manuscript which I so often praise, and it has it thus: λόγον γὰρ συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων ποιήσει κύριος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (for the Lord will perform a consummating and cutting off word upon the earth), which suffice, and sufficiently express that which Isaiah wills. But there is no absurdity of discourse, according to the explanation already delivered by us. Nor is one Codex to be preferred to all the rest. Furthermore, the others agree with the Hebrew text. Therefore, without doubt, they are to be preferred to this manuscript. And since Grotius confesses that Paul did not omit that ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ (in righteousness), how will the manuscript of Grotius, which omitted it, deserve trust?

Latin:

Vers. 23. IN MEDIO OMNIS TERRÆ] Judææ. Exiguus erit populus pro eo, qui fuit. Vide supra 7, 21.

Non de reditu in agros & oppida, sed de con- versione ad Deum hæc loquuntur. Quod do- cent tum antecedentia; non adjiciet residuum Israel inniti super eo, qui percutit eos, id est, super Assyrio, sed innitetur super Dominum sanctum Israel in veri- tate, hoc est, vere in uno Deo, non in hominibus spem & fiduciam suam collocabit: tum nomen ipsum Sear-Jasub, quod impositum est conver- sionis significandæ ergo, & explicatio ejusdem evi- dentissima, quæ hic habetur: Reliquiæ converten- tur; quorsum? in agrosne & oppida? minime. Ad Deum, inquam, fortem convertentur reliquiæ Jacob. Quis hic locus glossæ Grotianæ de reditu ad agros. Tum consequentia v. 22. Si enim fuerit populus tuus Israel quasi arena maris, reliquiæ con- vertentur ex eo, consummatio abbreviata inundabit justitiam. Consummationem enim & abbreviatio- nem Dominus DEUS exercituum faciet in medio o- mnis terræ. Hæc iterum de spirituali conversione reliquiarum loquuntur; de reliquiis signanter lo- quor. Quanquam enim futurus sit populus Israe- liticus innumerabilis, instar arenæ maris, pauci tamen ex illa multitudine, & quidem coram mun- do ut plurimum conspectabiles amplectentur Ev- angelium. Consummatio abbreviata inundabit ju- stitiam, id est, imo quum abjicientur Israelitæ Deo, consummationem tamen illam & productionem il- lam abbreviabit Dominus, ut nonnulli etiam ex ea- dem salventur & tum ipsi justitia repleantur, quia Christi justitia longe perfectissima est instar abun- dantissimi fontis justitiæ, tum alios quoque inundent justitia, ac ad veram justitiam perducant, veram justitiam instar fluminis in gentes dispergant. Fa- ciet enim Deus non tantum consummationem & per- ditionem illam, sed & abbreviationem, hoc est, præ- stabit, ut ex ea perditione per detractionem reli- quiæ nonnullæ adhuc serventur. Eodem sensu consummatio abbreviata est parvus ille numerus fide- lium è Judæis, qui redigentur pene ad consummatio- nem: quem efficiet Dominus inundare vera ju- stitia: gentes passim in medio omnis terræ, quia reliquiæ illæ superstites Judæorum diffuderunt ju- stitiam per universam terram: quod cumprimis factum est tempore Novi Testamenti. Unde non malo sensu reddit Oecolampadius, consummata & abbreviatæ illæ reliquiæ, Apostoli, scilicet, inun- dabunt alios justitia, utpote Doctores totius mundi. Atque hic habemus interpretationem omni exce- ptione majorem, quam ipse Spiritus Sanctus tra- didit Roman. 9, 27. qui ex hoc vaticinio non modo reliquiarum ex Israelitis salutem, sed etiam gentium conversionem ad CHRISTUM demonstrat. E- saias autem clamat pro Israel: Si fuerit numerus filiorum Israel tanquam arena maris, reliquiæ salvæ fient. Verbum enim consummans & abbrevians in æquitate, quia verbum breviatum faciet Dominus super terram. Verbum consummat & abbreviat Dominus, dum verbum de consummatione & abbreviatione implet, idque ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ut nem- pe inundetur terra secundum oraculum Propheti- cum justitia. Ideo quæ de reliquiarum con- versione ad Deum fortem prædicuntur, etsi ad E- zechiæ tempora etiam spectent, interprete Hierony- mo & Cyrillo, præcipue tamen complementum habitura erunt tempore Novi Testamenti, juxta in- terpretationem Apostolicam. Generalis est pro- missio, servatum iri semper reliquias, quæ & tem- pore vastationis à Sennacheribo factæ, & maxi- me sub Novo Testamento, ubi consummatio & perditio Israëlitartum totalis sequutura videbatur implenda. Quæ vero consummatio abbreviata Judæorum faciet ad justitiæ propagationem per or- bem terrarum. Brentius & Osiander versum etiam 20. huc referunt: Eo tempore, quo CHRISTUS in hunc mundum veniet, Israëlitæ non amplius confident externis hominum præsidiis, sed con- fident Domino sancto Israëlis, qui est CHRISTUS Dominus noster, & convertentur vere ad DEUM fortem, agnoscent CHRISTUM, qui est DEUS fortis, conservans omnes credentes ad æternam vitam. In verbis Ebræis difficultas videtur occur- rere, quam LXX. Interpp. translatio non intelle- cta auxisse videtur. כִּלָּיוֹן חָרוּץ שׁוֹטֵף צְדָקָה Quæ Ludovicus de Dieu ita perspicue reddi posse censet: Consummationem præcisam exundare facit in justitia. Non male. Sed sensum involvit ipse decreto suo præciso, vel absoluto prædestinationis. B. Lutherus autem luculentissime & perquam appo- site exposuit: Denn wenn dem Verderben ge= steuret wird, (tum enim consummatio præscindi- tur vel abbreviatur) so kömmt die Gerechtigkeit überschwenglich. Præstat id immensa Dei mise- ricordia, ut præscindatur consummatio ac suffla- minetur, ne penitus totus Israël consummetur & perdatur; & ut tum, quando perditioni obex & meta ponitur, justitia sese exundet & diffundatur instar fluminis. Denn der HERR HErr Ze= baoth wird ein Verderben gehen lassen (consum- mationem faciet) und demselbigen doch steuren (abbreviationem faciet, præscindet consumma- tionem, ac impetum ejus sistit) im ganzen Lande. Ut inde etiam justitia per universam terram se abundantius diffundat; quem sensum explicatio Apostolica egregie confirmat Roman. 11. ubi B. Lutherus ita habet: Denn es wird ein Verderben und Steuren geschehen zur Gerechtigkeit, und der HERR wird dasselbige Steuren thun auff Er= den. Addita luculenta glossa: Obwol das grös= sere Theil dahin fällt und ungläubig bleibet, wird er sie doch nicht alle lassen also fallen, sondern die übrigen erhalten und durch sie sein Wort und Gnade desto reichlicher außbreiten, dadurch sie ge= recht und herrlich werden. Nihil poterat præcla- rius dici ad explicandam mentem Prophetæ, pro- ut eam declarat Spiritus Sanctus per Apostolum. Neque discrepant ita LXX. quorum versionem adduxit Apostolus, quantum ad sensum: λόγον γὰρ

συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, Deus ver- bum consummat, illud nempe verbum, quod præ- dixit de consummatione perficienda, sed ita ut præscindat in justitia vel misericordia, ut consumma- tioni & consummationis decreto & verbo modum sta- tuat per immensam suam misericordiam, ὅτι λόγον συντετμημένον κύριος, κύριος δυνάμεων ποιήσει ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ ὅλῃ, quia verbum illud præcisum vel decretum (non absolutum, sed per misericordiam restrictum & temperatum, ideo enim præcisum di- citur, quod consummationem, quam minatus erat Deus, veluti præscindat, éique modum statuat) facturus vel executurus est Dominus, Dominus ex- ercituum per universam terram. Non hæc abso- luto decreto favent, sed repugnant prorsus eidem, atque electionem reliquiarum gratiosam, de qua Apostolus, confirmant. Grotius non veretur, sermonem Apostolicum absurditatis postulare, annotatione ad Romanos 9. vers. 27. Recto ordi- ne, inquit, ὅτι debuit præcedere λόγον συντελῶν. In Paulino autem textu, qualem nunc habemus, sa- tis absurdum est poni primum γὰρ, deinde ὅτι. Omnino hæc lectio interpolata ex LXX. Vetus au- tem lectio extat in manuscripto illo, quem toties lau- do, & sic habet: λόγον γὰρ συντελῶν καὶ συντέ- μνων ποιήσει κύριος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, quæ sufficiunt, satisq́; exprimunt id, quod vult Esaias. At nulla est sermonis absurditas, juxta explicationem à no- bis jam traditam. Neque præferendus est unus Codex reliquis omnibus. Adhæc consentiunt cæteri Ebræo textui. Proinde sine dubio huic manuscripto præferendi sunt. Et quum fateatur Grotius, Paulum non omisisse illud ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, quomodo fidem merebitur manuscriptus Grotii, qui illud omisit?

## 10:25
Vers. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

## 10:26
IN THE WAY OF EGYPT] That is, after the manner of Egypt. Just as He once treated the Egyptians, so He will treat the Assyrians.

Vers. 26.

BY THE SLAUGHTER OF MIDIAN AT THE ROCK OF OREB] Jud. 7:25.

AND HIS ROD OVER THE SEA] That is, in the Red Sea.

Latin:

IN VIA ÆGYPTI] Id est, ad modum Ægypti. Sic- ut Ægyptios olim tractavit, sic tractabit Assyrios.

Vers. 26.

JUXTA PLAGAM MADIAN IN PETRA O- REB] Jud. 7, 25.

ET VIRGAM SUAM SUPER MARE] Id est, in mari rubro.

## 10:27
Ver. 27.

AND THE YOKE SHALL ROT FROM THE FACE OF THE OIL] That yoke, which the Assyrians had imposed upon Judea, shall utterly perish, on account of Hezekiah, anointed with holy oil. There is an allusion to the power of oil, which easily loosens any knots.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

ET COMPUTRESCET JUGUM A FACIE O- LEI] Jugum illud, quod Assyrii Judææ imposuerant, pla- ne interibit, propter Ezechiam unctum sacro oleo. Al- luditur ad vim olei, quod nodos quosvis facile laxat.

## 10:28
Ver. 28.

HE SHALL COME TO AIATH] This is an ἐπάνοδος (recapitulation), which describes the whole journey of Sennacherib. The Hebrews say, however, that the Assyrians completed a ten-day journey in one day: which you should understand regarding those vanguard troops sent ahead under Rabshakeh. Ajath or Hajath is the region where the town of Hai had been.

HE SHALL PASS TO MAGRON] 1 Sam. 14, 2.

AT MICHMASH HE SHALL DEPOSIT HIS BAGGAGE] He will store his packs there, so that he may be more unencumbered. See 2 Sam. 13, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

VENIET IN AIATH] Est ἐπάνοδος, quæ totum iter Sennacheribi describit. Ajunt autem Hebræi Assyrios decem dierum iter uno die confecisse: quod intellige de antesignanis illis præmissis sub Rabsace. Ajath sive Ha- jath est regio, ubi Hai oppidum fuerat.

TRANSIBIT IN MAGRON] 1. Sam. 14, 2.

APUD MACHMAS COMMENDABIT VASA SUA] Sarcinas ibi reponet, quo sit expeditior. Vide 2.Sam. 13, 2.

## 10:29
Ver. 29.

THEY HAVE PASSED IN HASTE: GEBA IS OUR LODGING] In the Hebrew: They have crossed the ford, namely of the Jordan: they spent the night at Geba in an inn: that is, there they will first rest under a roof.

RAMAH IS ASTONISHED] Ramah has trembled. Understand the Ramah of Benjamin, of which Joshua 18, 25 and Matthew 2, 18 speak.

GIBEAH OF SAUL HAS FLED] 1 Kings 14, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

TRANSIERUNT CURSIM: GABA SEDES NOSTRA] In Hebræo: Transierunt vadum, nempe Jor- danis: Gabæ in diversorio pernoctarunt: id est, ibi pri- mum sub tecto quiescent.

OBSTUPUIT RAMA] Trepidavit Rama. Ramam Benjaminis intellige, de qua Josue 18, 25. & Matth. 2, 18.

GABAATH SAULIS FUGIT] 1. Reg. 14, 2.

## 10:30
Ver. 30.

WAIL WITH THY VOICE, O DAUGHTER OF GALLIM] Wail, O Daughter, that is, the town of Gallim. Anathoth (whence Jeremiah 1, 1), Madmenah, and Gebim belong to Benjamin.

ATTENDE LAISA] Better: Make Laisa hear; raise such a loud wail that it may be heard to the furthest borders, where Laisa is. Jud. 18, 7.

PAUPERCULA ANATHOT] That is, you will be miserable.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

HINNI VOCE TUA FILIA GALLIM] Ejula, Filia, id est, oppidum Gallim. Anathoth, (unde Jere- mias 1, 1.) Medemena, Gabim ad Benjaminem pertinent.

ATTENDE LAISA] Melius: Fac audire Laisam; ita altum ejulatum tolle, ut ad ultimos fines exaudiatur, ubi Laisa. Jud. 18, 7.

PAUPERCULA ANATHOT] Id est, misera eris.

## 10:31
Ver. 31.

HABITATORES JABIM CONFORTAMINI] Better: they gathered themselves, namely for flight.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

HABITATORES JABIM CONFORTAMINI] Melius: congregarunt se, nempe ad fugam.

## 10:32
Ver. 32. YET THERE IS A DAY, THAT IN NOBE

STETUR] After so many places captured, there will still remain enough of the day to reach Nob: from where Jerusalem could be seen. See 1 Sam. 21, 1. Nehem. 11, 32. HE WILL WAVE HIS HAND OVER THE MOUNTAIN OF THE DAUGHTER OF ZION, THE HILL OF JERUSALEM] He has threatened dire things to the city, 2 Kings 18, 19 & seqq. 19, 21 & seqq. Verse 33. HE WILL BREAK THE LITTLE JAR IN TERROR] In the Hebrew: He will break that branch terribly. But by the branch, Rabshakeh seems to be understood, who had despised both the city and God. AND THE STATURE OF THE LOFTY SHALL BE CUT DOWN] The lofty, supply trees: by which princes are signified. AND THE SUBLIME SHALL BE HUMBLED] He says the same thing twice, as he often does. Verse 34. AND THE THICKETS OF THE FOREST SHALL BE OVERTHROWN WITH IRON] Thickets, that is, soldiers. AND LEBANON SHALL FALL WITH THE LOFTY] Lebanon shall fall through a strong one. Mount Lebanon supports very many trees. Thus the king had supported the army. But he shall fall through a powerful one, that is, through the very heir destined for the kingdom, 2 Kings 19, 37.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ADHUC DIES EST, UT IN NOBE

STETUR] Post tot loca capta restabit adhuc satis diei, ut Nobam perveniatur: unde Hierosolyma cerni poterat. Vi- de 1. Sam. 21, 1. Nehem. 11, 32. AGITABIT MANUM SUAM SUPER MON- TEM FILIÆ SION, COLLEM JERUSALEM] Mina- tus dira est urbi, 2. Reg. 18,19. & seqq. 19,21. & seqq. Vers. 33. CONFRINGET LAGUNCULAM IN TER- RORE] In Hebræo: Abrumpet ramum istum terribiliter. Per ramum autem intelligendus videtur Rabsaces, qui & urbem & Deum contemserat. ET EXCELSI STATURA SUCCIDENTUR] Ex- celsæ, supple arbores: per quas principes significantur. ET SUBLIMES HUMILIABUNTUR ] Idem bis dicit, ut sæpe. Vers. 34. ET SUBVERTENTUR CONDENSA SAL- TUS FERRO] Virgulta, id est, milites. ET LIBANUS CUM EXCELSIS CADET] Li- banus per fortem cadet. Libanus mons arbores plurimas sustinet. Sic rex sustinuerat exercitum. Is autem cadet per potentem, id est, per ipsum hæredem regni destina- tum, 2. Reg. 19, 37.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. Concerning the shoot from the root of Jesse, under whom the Gentile enemies themselves are to be gathered to the people of the Lord by an erected sign, and are to be subjected to the Lord.

Verse 1. AND A ROD SHALL COME FORTH FROM THE ROOT OF JESSE] He returns to the praises of Hezekiah, under which, in a more sublime sense, the praises of the Messiah lie hidden. For Root, in the Hebrew here it is trunk, rightly: Because by the loss of the ten tribes, and by the incursions of so many enemies, the affairs of the house of David had been greatly cut down. AND A FLOWER] A tender shoot born from that trunk, see 53, 2. Verse 2. AND THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD SHALL REST UPON HIM] He will be perpetually present with him: which spirit is distributed into its six parts. But it grew in Christianity: therefore it is distributed into seven, Rev. 1, 4. THE SPIRIT OF WISDOM] Wisdom חכמה is the knowledge of divine things, to the Hebrews מרכבה. AND OF UNDERSTANDING] The knowledge of natural things, בראשית to the Hebrews. THE SPIRIT OF COUNSEL] Prudence, especially in political matters. AND OF FORTITUDE] Constancy in adversity, which Hezekiah showed remarkably in the time of Sennacherib. THE SPIRIT OF KNOWLEDGE] Concerning the interpretation of the law. AND OF PIETY] In the Hebrew: and of the fear of the Lord: which signifies piety. This gift surpasses all the others. Verse 3. AND THE SPIRIT OF THE FEAR OF THE LORD SHALL FILL HIM] In the Hebrew: and his consolation (that is, solace) in the fear of the Lord, or piety. Because of his piety, he will trust in God in the greatest dangers. HE SHALL NOT JUDGE ACCORDING TO THE SIGHT OF THE EYES] He will not despair, even if he sees a very great hostile army against him. NOR SHALL HE ARGUE ACCORDING TO THE HEARING OF THE EARS] He will dispute. He will not make a conjecture about the future from rumors. For he will believe the Prophets. BUT HE SHALL JUDGE THE POOR IN JUSTICE] In the Hebrew: for But it is And: for a new sense is begun. He says he will provide fair justice for the poor and the rich. AND HE SHALL ARGUE IN EQUITY FOR THE MEEK OF THE EARTH] That is, he will be their defender, as kings ought to be. Verse 4. AND HE SHALL STRIKE THE EARTH WITH THE ROD OF HIS MOUTH] He calls impious men the earth, as appears from the following member containing the same sense in other words: namely, that they think nothing of God, but fix the particle of divine breath to the ground: The rod of his mouth, and what follows, the Spirit of his lips, that is, his prayers: for through these he finished the Assyrians. Verse 5. AND JUSTICE SHALL BE THE GIRDLE OF HIS LOINS, AND FAITH THE BELT OF HIS REINS] That is, he will always have pious and just men around him. Thus the Chaldean here, very well. Verse 6. THE WOLF SHALL DWELL WITH THE LAMB] All these figurative expressions signify a deep and unshaken peace, which was to be after the times of Sennacherib under Hezekiah, through which even the very weakest were to obtain their own, without fear of plunder. These are the effects of the justice of kings.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. De germine è radice Isai, sub quo ad populum Domini hostes ipsi gentiles erecto signo ag- gregandi, Dominoœ subjiciendi sint.

Vers. 1. ET EGREDIETUR VIRGA DE RADICE JESSE] Redit ad laudes Ezechiæ, sub quibus sensu sub- limiore latent Messiæ laudes. Pro Radice in Hebræo hic est trunco, recte: Quia amissione decem tribuum, & tot hostium incursionibus, valde accisæ erant res domus Davidis. ET FLOS] Surculus tener ex illo trunco enatus, vi- de 53, 2. Vers. 2. ET REQUIESCET SUPER EUM SPIRI- TUS DOMINI] Perpetuo ipsi aderit: qui spiritus in sex suas partes distribuitur. Crevit autem in Christianismo: ideo distribuitur in septem, Apoc. 1, 4. SPIRITUS SAPIENTIÆ] Sapientia חכמה est cognitio rerum divinarum, Hebræis מרכבה. ET INTELLECTUS] Cognitio rerum naturalium, בראשית Hebræis. SPIRITUS CONSILII] Prudentia in rebus Politi- cis maxime. ET FORTITUDINIS ] Constantia in adversis, quam tempore Sennacheribi egregie ostendit Ezechias. SPIRITUS SCIENTIÆ] Circa interpretationem legis. ET PIETATIS] In Hebræo: & timoris Domini: quod pietatem significat. Hoc donum cætera omnia su- perat. Vers. 3. ET REPLEBIT EUM SPIRITUS TIMO- RIS DOMINI] In Hebræo: & consolari ipsius (id est, so- latium) in timore Domini, sive pietate. Pro pietate sua in maximis periculis Deo confidet. NON SECUNDUM VISIONEM OCULORUM JUDICABIT] Non desperabit, etiamsi maximum con- tra se exercitum hostilem videat. NEQUE SECUNDUM AURIUM AUDITUM ARGUET] Disputabit. Non ex rumoribus de futuro con- jecturam faciet. Credet enim Prophetis. SED JUDICABIT IN JUSTITIA PAUPERES] In Hebræo: pro Sed est Et: novus enim sensus inchoatur. Æquum ait jus præstabit pauperi & diviti. ET ARGUET IN ÆQUITATE PRO MAN- SUETIS TERRÆ ] Id est, erit eorum defensor, ut re- ges esse debent. Vers. 4. ET PERCUTIET TERRAM VIRGA O- RIS SUI] Terram vocat homines impios, ut ex sequenti membro eundem sensum verbis aliis continente apparet: quod scilicet nihil de Deo cogitent, sed humi affigant di- vinæ particulam auræ: Virga oris sui, & quod sequitur, Spiritu labiorum suorum, id est, precibus suis: per has e- nim confecit Assyrios. Vers. 5. ET ERIT JUSTITIA CINGULUM LUMBORUM EJUS, ET FIDES CINCTORIUM RE- NUM EJUS] Id est, pios viros ac justos semper circum se habebit. Ita hic Chaldæus, optime. Vers. 6. HABITABIT LUPUS CUM AGNO ] O- mnes hæ locutiones figuratæ significant altam & incon- cussam pacem, quæ post Sennacheribi tempora futura e- rat sub Ezechia, per quam etiam infirmissimi quique suum erant obtenturi, sine metu rapinæ. Hi sunt effectus ju- stitiæ regum.

## 11:8
Verse 8. OVER THE HOLES OF THE ASP] Asps love hiding places. AND IN THE CAVERN OF THE BASILISK] צפע The Greeks translate it sometimes as κεράςην, sometimes as ἀσπίδα, that is, a certain kind of asp distinct from others. Verse 10. IN THAT DAY THE ROOT OF JESSE, WHO STANDS AS A SIGN FOR THE PEOPLES, THE GENTILES SHALL SEEK HIM] In the Hebrew: they shall seek: that is, many from the Gentiles will run to Hezekiah to be converted to the true God. AND HIS SEPULCHER SHALL BE GLORIOUS] And his rest shall be glory: that is, full of glory. Rest signifies dwelling.

It was not dealt with in the preceding parts concerning Hezekiah, nor were his praises celebrated, so that the Prophet could have returned to them here. For in chapter 9, he did not deal with Hezekiah, but with CHRIST. Nor is the discourse here about Hezekiah: but a prophecy about Christ. If his praises are continued here, who was proclaimed in chapter 9, 6, it must be established that not Hezekiah, but Christ is celebrated here, because those eulogies in chapter 9, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, in no way befit Hezekiah, but Christ alone. Furthermore, the prophecy here is held concerning him who was yet to come forth one day from the root of Jesse: but Hezekiah was already born when Isaiah was predicting this. The Prophet prophesies about a rod to come forth from a trunk, when, namely, the family of David had been almost truncated and reduced to extremities: But that did not happen in the time of Isaiah. But when the Messiah appeared, it seemed that the family of David was almost finished. Furthermore, although those eulogies may in some way apply to a pious King endowed with illustrious virtues, because the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, etc., rests upon him, this is nevertheless certain, that they are uttered not in a common, but in a more eminent manner: for nothing common is predicted here, nor can those encomiums about the judgment of this King, which occur here, be claimed for any worldly Prince. He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor shall he argue according to the hearing of the ears. For these imply καρδιογνωσίαν and divine omniscience, because he will institute judgment by looking even at the counsels of the heart, not according to external appearance, or the report of others, which can often deceive. He shall judge the poor in justice, and shall argue in equity for the meek of the earth. To always administer justice is not the lot of any Prince. For often through ignorance, not rarely through infirmity, most frequently through the fault of ministers, they neglect the course of justice. Nor do they judge all things themselves, but exercise judgments through others. This one, however, will never deflect from justice, nor will he need the work of others. Justice will be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the belt of his reins. Which, while it is to be wished for in earthly Kings, can by no means be affirmed: because neither the girdle of justice, nor the belt of faithfulness always adheres to them, or is proper and perpetual to them. And how can those things be applied to Hezekiah; he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and he shall slay the wicked with the breath of his lips. Which we are certain, from the Apostolic interpretation in 2 Thessalonians 2, were said of Christ, and of the Antichrist, whom he himself is to slay by the spirit of his mouth. Now if those things, which follow concerning the dwelling of the wolf with the lamb, etc. follow, you weigh them, they do not suit the time of Hezekiah, to whom Sennacherib was hostile, nor the age of any of the kings, because, even if public peace flourishes, private treacheries, rapines, and discords nevertheless never cease. They are therefore to be understood solely of the spiritual peace in the kingdom of the Messiah. Moreover, the things which are predicted concerning the root of Jesse, that it is to be lifted up as a sign for the peoples, and that the nations themselves shall pray to it, and that that rest shall be glorious, in no way suit Hezekiah, whom the nations did not pray to, nor does history testify that he was erected as a sign for the nations. These things are proper to the Messiah alone: to whom the gathering of the nations was due, Gen. 49:10, and to whom the nations were to be converted: whose knowledge the earth is to be filled with, just as the waters cover the sea. How those things are also explained by him, the Holy Spirit, Rom. 15:12, so that the conversion of the nations to the faith of Christ is demonstrated from it. pass over the fact that the other things which are submitted in this chapter seem to be understood of Christ as well, and of the times of the New Testament, that the Apostles are to preach to the Philistines, Idumeans, Moabites, Egyptians, etc., concerning which see especially Brentius in his Commentary and Osiander in his Paraphrase. Thus far, certainly, in the Christian Church it has been undoubted that the prophecy at the beginning of this chapter is held to be not of Hezekiah, but of Christ alone: but Grotius preferred to lend an ear to the Jews, R. Aben Ezra and R. Mose Hatcohen, than to follow the interpretation of the Christian Church. Although other Jews are also sounder, and understand the prophecy concerning the Messiah as to the literal sense; Jerome himself is the authority that in Jerome's time all accepted it concerning the Messiah: The whole of this chapter and the following, he says, both Christians and the whole circumcision confess to speak of the Messiah, with this difference only, that the Jews accept everything simply and literally concerning the one who is to come and his temporal kingdom; Christians understand most things metaphorically concerning the spiritual kingdom of him who has already come, Christ God.

Therefore, the designation of the birth and lineage of Christ is held here first. A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower from his root. That a King should be born to the Jews from the lineage of David was nothing new. For all had come forth from his family since the time of David. Nor was Hezekiah to be born at last, but he had already been born, which argument Abarbenel himself urges: Because Hezekiah was born ten years when this prophecy was brought forth: How therefore could he have said וְיָצָא AND SHALL GO FORTH? Which words teach that he was to be born many days after him. And it is clearly a matter of a peculiar King here. Because the prophecy is absolutely unique. The Jews confess this, interpreting the rod and the flower from the root of Jesse as the Messiah, because, namely, royal power is demonstrated in the rod, and beauty in the flower, as Jerome observes, who indeed understands the Messiah by the flower, but his mother by the rod. But let us understand the rod from the root of Jesse as the holy virgin Mary, who had no shoot coherent with herself, of whom we also read above: Behold a virgin shall conceive and bear a son. And the flower as the Lord Savior, who says in the Song of Songs (ch. 2): I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. Other ancients, however, understand both the rod and the flower as Christ. Cyril of Alexandria named Christ the rod from the root of Jesse according to the flesh, and furthermore also the flower. By the rod, he says, it seems to be obliquely indicated that he possesses royal dignity: But the flower, again, is so called because the nature of man in him reflourished unto incorruption and unto the newness of evangelical conversation, or also because of the sweet fragrance falling under understanding. So also Basil in this place, Hilary in Ps. 2, as also Origen in homily IX. Jerome also observes here the condition of the Davidic family at the time the Messiah was to be born. For the root, which only the LXX translated, in the Hebrew it is written גֶּזַע which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated as trunk. And for the flower, which in Hebrew is called נֵצֶר they translated as sprout, so as to show that long after, at the time of the Babylonian captivity, with no one possessing the glory of the ancient kingdom from the stock, the Messiah arose as if from a trunk, and Christ from Mary. Concerning David it was once said with contempt, 1 Kings 12: What portion have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse? The Prophet therefore makes mention of Jesse here, to signify that Christ would arise then, when the posterity of David was to be completely despised and rejected.

Then the peculiar appellation of Christ is also to be noted. Who was to be called a Nazarene according to the Prophets, as Matthew ch. 2 testifies. For the learned ancients derived this appellation from the present passage in Hebrew. Concerning which Jerome again says: That which all ecclesiastics seek in the Gospel of Matthew, and do not find where it is written: That he shall be called a Nazarene, the learned among the Hebrews think it is taken from this passage. Elsewhere Jerome notes in his Epistle to Pammachius on the best kind of translating that these words can be rendered thus: And a Nazirite shall grow from his root.

Thirdly, Brentius observes the order here. For since the Prophet said in ch. 10:20 that the remnant of Israel would place their trust not in the Assyrians, but in the holy Lord of Israel: he now explains who that holy Lord of Israel is, in whom alone one must trust, namely the Messiah, who is to arise from the root of David: that the Assyrian trees would be overturned, ch. 10:18, but a shoot would come forth from the almost dead trunk of David.

Fourthly, the description of the King here is that by which Christ is clearly distinguished from worldly Kings. The Spirit of the Lord rests perpetually upon him, so that it cannot be taken away from him, which can be said of no worldly King. The Spirit of wisdom and understanding rests upon him: these are by nature dull, and not rarely err in the administration of their kingdoms. The Spirit of counsel and fortitude rests upon him, so that he may suffice for ruling his subjects: these, however, are in need of the counsel of others and of foreign help: they are not able to rule and defend their subjects alone. The Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord rests upon him: these, however, fail both in the knowledge and in the fear of the Lord, so that they neither perfectly know him, nor worship him as is fitting. In a word: to him the Spirit is given οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου John 3:34, therefore the Spirit of the Lord is said to rest upon him, and this is indicated to be proper to this King. These, however, although they are instructed by the Spirit of the Lord, κατὰ τὸ μέτρον, according to a certain measure of the gift of Christ, receive the same, Eph. 4, 7. Since, therefore, the Spirit is said to rest upon Him, others who receive the Spirit obtain the same only from Him, because He rests upon Him. Without Christ, therefore (which Jerome rightly infers), no one can be wise, nor understanding, nor a counselor, nor strong, nor learned, nor pious, nor full of the fear of God. Moreover, those things which Grotius has here concerning the wisdom of divine things, the knowledge of natural things, prudence in political affairs, and constancy in adversity, and the spirit of knowledge regarding the interpretation of the law and the word of the Lord in Hezekiah, are too jejune. Furthermore, that he excelled in these gifts above all others, so that this is proper to him, that the Spirit of the Lord thus rested upon him, and that this was perpetual for him, is asserted only rashly. The things which Grotius sprinkled here about the spirit being distributed into six parts, but in Revelation 1:4 into seven, are trifles: because, forsooth, the Spirit grew in Christianity. For there the Holy Spirit is introduced as sevenfold in function, i.e., manifesting Himself in the Church through various gifts, which was also done by Him under the Old Testament. But who will gather from this passage that only six gifts of the Holy Spirit had a place in the Old Testament, or will admit from the apocalyptic description of the Spirit that the seventh gift of the Holy Spirit began in the New Testament?

Fifthly, the administration of the office of this King is to be observed: which occurs (1.) in the fear of the Lord. His smelling (as it is held in the Hebrew) shall be in the fear of the Lord; i.e., He shall judge keenly, but always with the true fear of God; He shall burden no one with a rash judgment, as Osiander explains: which sense is not inconvenient and is approved by the Rabbis themselves, R. David Kimchi, R. Aben Ezra: because pious and impious men with easy effort the Messiah is to discern, and will have no need of the vision of the eyes, or the hearing of the ears: because the sense of smell seems more certain, since the sense of hearing and sight sometimes deceive. See Sixt. Amama Anti-Barb. l. 4. p. 653. Others understand by his smell his sacrifice, which is a sweet-smelling savor to God, see Luther's marginal gloss, to which Glassius agrees, Phil. S. l. 5. tr. 1. c. 7. Grotius translates it thus: And his consolation (i. e. comfort) in the fear of the Lord or piety. For his piety in the greatest dangers he will trust in God. But that is a new commentary, and sufficiently alien to the phrase and the text. For he is now engaged in explaining the office of the Prophet, how it is administered by this King. Nor does he have anything in these words about confidence in God. Not to mention that in his own piety no one could place solid comfort in adversity, which is rather to be placed in the mercy of the Lord.

(2) He will administer the kingdom in justice and equity. He will never deviate from the path of justice. He will not judge according to the vision of the eyes, i. e. not according to external appearance, by which other worldly judges are very often deceived: nor will he argue according to the hearing of the ears, i. e. from rumors, which are not rarely mendacious. He will not pass judgment from acts and proofs alone, as they are exposed to eyes and ears, as worldly judges do, because he himself sees all things before him, even all hidden things, and furthermore the hearts and reins of men, and has the innermost counsels of hearts thoroughly perceived. These things also are said, says Brentius, by way of antithesis to worldly Kings. For these by their nature are not so just and so fearing of God, that if a great hope of gain has been proposed, or some great danger presented, they would not decline from the rectitude of judgment, and would not respect persons: nor are they so perspicacious in judging controversies that they can look into the hearts of men: but they must needs judge according to those things which are alleged and proven. For to judge according to the vision of the eyes is to respect persons, i. e. to condemn him who has a just cause, because he is either poor or an enemy: but to absolve him who has an unjust cause, because he is either rich or a friend. These things are wont to happen frequently in human judgments. But to argue according to the hearing of the ears is either to pronounce sentence when only one side has been heard, or to judge according to public fame alone, the matter not being diligently examined, which although it is most iniquitous, yet it is also wont to happen often and much in civil judgments. Furthermore, to judge according to the vision of the eyes and the hearing of the ears is also to judge according to things alleged and proven, as the jurists speak. These things judges, since they are men who cannot look into the hearts of litigants, nor know hidden things, must needs follow in discerning controversies: but CHRIST is a far different Judge. But Grotius's glosses are most alien. He will not judge according to the vision of the eyes, i. e. he will not despair, even if he sees a great hostile army against him. Nor will he argue according to the hearing of the ears, i. e. he will dispute. He will not make a conjecture about the future from rumors. For he believes the Prophets. Who would draw either these things or those from the words of the Prophet! To no one, I think, before Grotius did such a sense come into mind: which is an indication of a sense brought in, not drawn out from the words of Scripture. The words themselves cry out that the discourse is about judgment. And what follows also openly expresses this. But HE SHALL JUDGE THE POOR IN JUSTICE, AND ARGUE IN EQUITY FOR THE MEEK OF THE EARTH. These things teach that he is not to be a respecter of persons: not to cast away the poor and the miserable because of misery, but to defend them with supreme justice; and not to condemn the afflicted, but to pronounce sentence in equity for them against those who afflict and oppress. Which praises are proper and perpetual to Christ. B. Luther translates it thus: He will judge the poor with justice and punish the miserable in the land with judgment, He will make them just through grace, and yet let the remaining old Adam in the flesh be punished through the cross, and that is called to punish with judgment, that is, not in fury nor in wrath, but with reason, and for their benefit. Grotius himself at John 5:30 explained these things about Christ: Therefore my judgment is just because I do not depart from the rule of the Father. See the prophecy of Isaiah 11:4.

Sixthly occurs the destruction of any impious ones whatsoever who oppose themselves to this King and kingdom. And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth: and with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the impious. Worldly Kings fight with swords and lances, and subdue enemies to themselves with a violent hand. But this King will not subdue the earth to himself with swords, but with the rod of his mouth: he will not slay the impious with lances, but with the Spirit of his lips. That this is to be understood specifically, and primarily of the great Anti-Christ, by being slain by the spirit of the mouth of the Lord, we know from the Apostolic explanation in 2 Thessalonians 2:8. Grotius wrongly explains the rod of the mouth and the spirit of the lips as prayers, through which Hezekiah finished off the Assyrians: because prayers are nowhere designated by the spirit of the lips and the rod of the mouth, nor are the Assyrians alone to be understood by the earth being struck, but, as Grotius admits, the impious also, who, namely, think nothing of God, but fix the particle of divine breath to the ground. And that Anti-Christ is included here, or peculiarly designated, is certain from the aforementioned parallel passage. Whence it is also gathered that by the spirit of the lips or of the mouth of the Lord, the Holy Spirit, who is so called in Psalm 33:6, is to be understood, and by the rod, the word of the Gospel, through which the Holy Spirit strikes the impious and destroys the kingdom of Anti-Christ: which is called a scepter in Psalm 110:2 and Psalm 45:7, and is the sword of the Holy Spirit in Ephesians 6:17, the sword proceeding from the mouth of the Lord of Lords and King of Kings Christ Jesus, sharp on both sides, with which the nations are struck in Revelation 19:15, who is also said there to rule the same with a rod of iron from Psalm 2:9. Therefore these things are to be understood solely of Christ; and by no means of Hezekiah.

Seventh, the virtues, justice, and faithfulness of this King are celebrated. And justice shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the belt of his reins. In the kingdoms of this world, one often departs from justice, and even the best Princes are not rarely carried away by their passions, or are bewitched by others, so that through ignorance and infirmity they sometimes deflect from the path of rectitude; nor do they always keep faith and agreed-upon covenants with their subjects, even if they have been confirmed by letters, seals, and indeed oaths. This King, however, will never allow himself to be led away from justice, he will never violate his faithfulness: which again are proper to Christ alone. That Jewish gloss, which Grotius brings forward from the Chaldean, that by the girdle and belt pious and just men are understood, whom he is always to have with him, does not sufficiently agree with the words, which speak of the justice and faithfulness of the King himself, not of pious counselors: nor can it be affirmed of Hezekiah, or any King, that they always have pious and just men with them, and that they always prevail among them: since wicked and unjust men often force themselves into courts, and sometimes even find a place with the most pious princes, and indeed, under the guise of rectitude, not rarely prevail with their counsels.

Eighth, the happiness and tranquility of the kingdom is described in verse 6 and following. Such will be the tranquility in this kingdom, that wild and forest beasts shall be tamed and shall dwell familiarly with domestic ones; and there shall be one flock of sheep and of lions, calves, and bears. Such is the tameness of fierce beasts, that a little boy can drive them to pasture, and that the nature of serpents also becomes tame, and young children will play with asps and serpents. Finally, in the whole holy mountain—which what else is it but the Church?—there will be no beast that brings harm or injury to anyone. Everyone sees that this cannot be understood of an earthly kingdom, but must be accepted solely of the kingdom of Christ. What is held in verse 7 about a boy leading a wolf with a lamb, interpreters explain as referring to the despised ministers of the word. By infants barely weaned from their mother's breast, the Weimar theologians understand the newly converted. The underage and infants, Ps. 8, 3. Matt. 11, 25. That is, the holy apostles together with their faithful successors will not be afraid to preach the name of the Lord Christ among the worst and most poisonous peoples, and also to stand before kings and the powerful. Acts 9, 15. 2 Tim. 4, 17. Grotius's interpretation concerning a high and unshaken peace under Hezekiah after the times of Sennacherib is too thin. For even if public wars ceased, who will say that there were no private murders, robberies, discords, and contentions under his reign? There was no lack of wolves, leopards, lions, bears, serpents, and asps for the pious. It is therefore necessary that we understand this of the kingdom of Christ and the communion of saints. Therefore, the explanation is also added: They shall not hurt and they shall not kill in all my holy mountain. Brentius interprets these things concerning the change of a curse into a blessing, that not even beasts, which were ordained for the punishment of sin, can be a harm to the faithful, Hos. 2, Ezek. 34. But Osiander and other interpreters interpret it more correctly as a change of minds, that those who were previously often cruel and violent, like lions, leopards, bears, asps, and basilisks, ought to be so changed and tamed that they will not only grant peace but also exhibit the duties of Christian charity with tireless zeal. Jerome here excellently refutes the Jews who understand these things carnally, whom we shall cite for the sake of illustrating the text: 'These things also, the Jews and our Judaizers contend will happen according to the letter, so that in the charity of Christ, whom they think will come at the end of the world, all beasts will be reduced to tameness, and having laid aside their former ferocity, the wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the rest with the rest, which we now see are contrary to one another.' We ought to ask them, if all things of the present passage are accepted as they are written, and nothing is referred to spiritual understanding, according to that of the Apostle, who says, 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with all spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ': therefore, let not the root and the rod and the flower be referred to a sense; let the earth struck by the word of God, and the wicked one killed by the spirit of his lips, be understood as they are written, and let them be forced to teach how justice and truth are girded about the loins of the Lord with incorporeal things. But let us also ask them this, what is worthy of the Lord's Majesty, that the wolf and the lamb should feed together, and the leopard lie down with the kid, and the lion eat straw, and a little boy put his hand into the hole of asps? unless perhaps, according to the fables of the poets, they will restore to us the golden age of Saturn, in which wolves and lambs will feed together, and rivers will run full of honeyed wine, and the sweetest honey will drip from the leaves of trees, and all things will be filled with milky fountains. But if they should answer that these things will happen for the blessedness of the times, so that without any harm to anyone, men may enjoy all good things, let them hear from us that nothing is good except virtue, and nothing is evil except vice, as the Psalmist says: 'Who is the man who desires life, and loves to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking guile. Depart from evil and do good.' Moreover, riches and health of body, and an abundance of all things—and their opposites, poverty, infirmity, and need—are not even reckoned among goods or evils by the philosophers of the world: but are called indifferent. Whence also the Stoics, who agree with our dogma in most things, call nothing good except honesty and virtue alone: nothing evil except baseness. We have said these things briefly so that we may convince our Judaizers that they are snoring in a very deep sleep. Otherwise, according to the life-giving spirit, the understanding is easy. For the wolf is Paul, who was previously persecuting and tearing the Church: of whom it was said, 'Benjamin is a ravenous wolf,' he dwelt with the Lamb, or Ananias, by whom he was baptized: or the Apostle Peter, to whom it was said, 'Feed my lambs,' etc. Furthermore, the cause of such great happiness and tranquility is also subjoined, which befits the Kingdom of Christ alone, because the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the water of the sea covering it. For this tameness is from the knowledge of God and the Savior, and the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the grace and mercy of God fills the minds of men with love. For faith is effective through charity, Gal. 5, v. 6. Let us hear St. Jerome again: 'Lest we think this (about the holy mountain) is said of Mount Zion according to the error of the Hebrews, in the following verse the sacraments of evangelical preaching are shown, because the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, i.e., that which was said more obscurely above, the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid. And according to his custom, the prophetic words are unfolded at the end: As the water (he says) of the sea covering it. Just as the waters of the sea cover the depths of the sea—that is, the earth which is covered by the waves—so the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord.' The blessed Apostle Peter also testifies that he saw this conjunction of previously diverse characters in a linen sheet, which was let down from heaven, having four principles, by which we may understand the four corners of the world, so that we may know that the earth is filled with the knowledge of God: In which vessel there were quadrupeds and serpents, and beasts of the sky, so that what the ark provided in the flood, the Church provides in the world.

Ninth, the expansion of this kingdom is predicted: that it is to be carried to the nations. Which was not fulfilled in Hezekiah, but in Christ. In that day the root of Jesse shall be famous, i.e., a shoot born from the root of Jesse, which stands as a sign for the peoples, erected like a banner, so that various peoples may flow unto him. The nations shall beseech him: nor will this lack success: The nations throughout the whole world shall worship and are to venerate the same. And his sepulchre shall be glorious. In the Hebrew, his rest shall be glorious; the Church is the rest of Christ, who wishes to dwell and rest in the hearts of the faithful, in the Church: which is glorious, not indeed with worldly and external, but with spiritual and internal glory, shining in the eyes of the Lord, and also emitting its rays throughout the world. Matt. 5, 16. Phil. 2, 15. Ps. 45, 10. Which is the interpretation of the Reformers and of B. Glassius on John ch. 17, to which, however, others object that the Church is nowhere called the rest of God. Jerome explained it concerning his death and sepulchre. Concerning which he has this: For his rest, in the Hebrew is placed מְנֻחָתוֹ which all have translated similarly. For honor also, in the Hebrew is read כָּבוֹד which clearly signifies glory. And the sense is: his death shall be glorious: so that that which the Savior prays for in the Gospel may be fulfilled: Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with thee before the world was. It has been spoken of his birth, it has been spoken of the other sacraments in between, he comes to death, which is not called by the customary name of mortals, but because there was perpetual life in Christ, it is called rest. For we, in order to make the sense manifest to the reader, have translated sepulchre instead of sleep and rest, with another word, but the same sense. Whence many Doctors comment here concerning the glorious burial of Christ. Cyril provides both meanings p. 202. If anyone would prefer to signify here by the rest the death of Christ in the flesh, which he sustained for our sake willingly, not as sustaining death (for he was life by nature) but as making the flesh rest for a time: this was to him nothing other than honor. For the Savior of all, and our Lord Jesus Christ, was glorified when he had undergone slaughter for the world, and had suffered voluntary death for the life of all. And afterwards: For the mind of the Saints is a guest-house pleasing to him, and he dwells with the worthy, and rests with the holy souls of those who worship him. Those who have attained this, to them it is an honor and glory. For what is to be compared with this nobility and glory, to have God dwelling and living in the heart? Therefore, provided we wish it, his rest will be honor in us also in this respect. B. Luther in Comm. Psalm. 3. T. 2. Lat. p. 23. hints that Psalm 16 should be compared. and my flesh shall rest in hope: and he explains it thus: And his rest shall be glory, as if he were to say, since the glory of other Kings ends in death, and their glory (as the Apostle says) ends in confusion, the glory of this one on the contrary begins in death, in which his confusion ends: so also of all who are Christ's, according to that Ps. 116: precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his Saints. Glorious indeed is the death of Christ because of the glorious victory through death, resurrection, and ascension: and thus the Jews rendered it in the German Version, Und es wird seyn seine Ruhung ehrlich, just as they are accustomed to inscribe such things on tombs: may his rest be in the bundle of the living with the remaining righteous. Thus also Theod. Hackspan explains it: just as the death of the pious is precious, so precious, nay most precious, shall be the rest of Christ: so that there is an opposition between the death of Christ and of earthly kings. For these, consumed by death, have little glory; but his resurrection and ascension will be glorious. But because it is a matter of the calling of the Gentiles, that mention of death seems too abrupt: nor would the Prophet have indicated so great a mystery by this one word 'rest': nay, just as the banner is raised, so also is this rest glorious, by the force of the context. But by that word, reference is made to the calling of the Gentiles, who flow together to the root of Jesse, whence his rest and dwelling is very glorious in the Church and in the hearts of the faithful. If anyone wishes to introduce a discussion about the principal object of the Gospel, to the knowledge of which the Gentiles are called, that is indeed accustomed to be expressed by the name of the DEATH and CROSS of Christ, yet it is nowhere designated by the mention of REST in the sepulcher. Meanwhile, because that opinion detracts nothing from the analogy of faith, nor from the dignity of the matter in this magnificent promise, and the ancients judged that it refers to the death and sepulcher of Christ, we do not reject that explanation as pious. Grotius detracts not a little from this magnificent promise when he introduces such a gloss: Many from the Gentiles converted to the true God will flock to Hezekiah: And his dwelling will be full of glory. But we have here an infallible interpretation of the New Testament, that this passage is to be understood only of Christ, and of the calling and conversion of the Gentiles, Rom. 15, 4. And again Isaiah says: There shall be a root of Jesse and he who shall rise to rule the Gentiles, in him shall the Gentiles hope. The Apostle explains the shoot from the root as him who was to rise and rule the Gentiles. And that which is said about the Gentiles praying to him, he interprets as the trust and hope to be placed in Christ. In what way, therefore, can these things be twisted to apply to Hezekiah? Grotius warns that in the Hebrew it is THEY SHALL SEEK, which the Vulgate rendered, they shall pray. But what kind of seeking this is, is evident from the use of this phrase and other Prophetic passages. For it is used concerning the inquiry for the true God, who has revealed himself in the Church, concerning the worship of God, when God is sought so that worship may be rendered to him, and so that we may take refuge in him. 2 Chron. 12, 14. Ch. 15, 2. 4. Ch. 19, 3. Ch.

20, 3. Ch. 22, 9. Wis. 2, 3. and concerning the conversion of the Gentiles Is. 65, 1. Hos. 3, 15. Zech. 8, 22. then it is manifest from the Apostolic declaration. Added to this is the tenth, a fuller explanation of the propagation of this Kingdom, how the remnant of the people is to be gathered again. And it shall be IN THAT DAY, says the Prophet, hinting that he is continuing the discourse about THAT DAY, of which he had spoken in v. 10. Concerning which Jerome says: In that day, that is, in that time, of which it was also spoken above, when the root of Jesse shall have risen for a sign of the peoples, or to rule the Gentiles, the Lord shall apply his hand a second time, so that by no means, according to our Judaizers, at the end of the world, when the fullness of the Gentiles shall have entered, then all Israel may be saved: But let us understand all these things in the first advent: For we cannot, when one day is spoken of both now and above, refer that one to the first advent and this one to the second: lest through these things which follow and those which preceded, they should be referred to that Christ, whom the Jews contend has not yet come, but is to come. It follows in our Prophet: The Lord shall add a second time to possess the remnant of his people. Some wish that word A SECOND TIME to refer to the former liberation from the tyranny of Pharaoh, when they were led out of Egypt. Others [refer it to] the reduction from the Babylonian captivity; For then the Lord first brought back the REMNANT of his people. He led his entire people out of Egypt. Thus Osiander: Just as the Son of God, the Lord Jehovah, gathered (under the empire of Cyrus) the Jews dispersed into various nations, so that they might return to their fatherland from many regions, who had survived the former disasters; so a second time he will extend his hand like a standard-bearer, (He will let the little banner fly) and through the preaching of the Gospel he will gather the elect from the whole world into his Church: and indeed not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles: therefore he says: that the Lord would lift up a sign to the Gentiles. And thus John seems to explain this passage, Ch. 11. Jesus was to die for the nation, and not only for the (Jewish) nation, but so that he might gather into one the children of God (the elect) who were dispersed (among the Gentiles). Jerome seems to understand the word 'secondly' in another way: namely, that the remnant of the Israelites will only approach in a secondary way in the New Testament. Therefore, after the calling of the Gentiles, which were once considered the tail, Israel will be considered the tail, so that the Lord may set his hand a second time and possess the remnant of his people: concerning which we also read above, that not all Israel, but the remnant are to be saved, which shall have been left by the Assyrians and by Egypt, and by the various nations round about. The Lord is therefore said to be about to gather the remnant of his people, which shall be left by the Assyrians, and by Egypt, and by Pathros (Petraean Arabia) and by Ethiopia and by Elam (the Medes or Elamites, who are contiguous to the Medes) and by Shinar (from Babylon) and by Hamath (from Antioch) and from the islands of the sea (from Greece and the whole western part of the world: Grotius: From Cyprus, Crete, Macedonia and the maritime places of Asia. For all things situated by the sea are 'איים' to the Hebrews) and to lift up a banner to the nations and to gather the fugitives, or exiles of the people of Israel, and to gather the dispersed of the people of Judah from the four corners of the earth. For to these places the Israelites were dispersed partly by the Assyrian captivity, partly by the Babylonian captivity, partly by the persecution of Antiochus Epiphanes, and partly by other calamities, as Brentius [notes] in this place. Grotius acknowledges that this does not treat of the deliverance which took place in the time of Cyrus: although his reasoning is not solid: namely, that Isaiah had not yet reached the affairs of Nebuchadnezzar, nor, when he wrote these things, had he received a revelation of those matters. For whence is it certain to him that he had not yet had that revelation at that time? Had not the Prophet already received a revelation of those things which were to happen under the New Testament and prophesied them?

The reasoning of other interpreters is more certain and solid: because few returned to the land of Canaan under Cyrus; nor was that liberation such as is predicted here. For they remained miserably in the servitude of the Persian kingdom, by which they were afterwards oppressed to the very end. Grotius understands by the 'remnant of the people of Israel' certain of the ten tribes who, because of the incursions of Tiglath-Pileser and Shalmaneser, had retreated into various lands, and were to come again to Hezekiah: and by the 'dispersed of Judah' those who had fled under Sennacherib. But neither are the Israelites read to have been dispersed into such various regions and to have returned from them in the time of Hezekiah, nor were the Jews to be gathered from the four corners of the world under Sennacherib. And therefore, without doubt, the Prophet speaks of the liberation effected through Christ, and of the congregation which was to be in the New Testament. which was to be, with the Gospel spread throughout the world, when this sign or standard, having been erected, had to be made conspicuous among various nations, in the whole world, through these places, designated from different parts of the earth: As Jerome says excellently concerning this passage, how God has put His hand to the remnants of the people: That not all Israel, but the remnants were to be saved, which had been left by the Assyrians, and by Egypt, and by the various nations round about. For first the twelve Apostles, and the seventy, and the hundred and twenty souls believed in the Lord. James also speaks to the Apostle Paul, who himself was also of the remnants: 'You see, brother, how many thousands there are of Jews who believe? And they are all zealous for the law.' And in the same volume we read: 'Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven, who all wondered and said:' 'Are not these Galileans, and how do we hear, each one of us, our own language in which we were born? Parthians and Medes and Elamites and those dwelling in Mesopotamia and Syria, Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and Libya and Cyrene, and sojourners from Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs: we hear them speaking in our own tongues the mighty works of GOD.' From all these nations, therefore, the remnants of Israel will be saved through the Apostles. Ecclesiastical histories report that the Apostles, dispersed throughout the whole world, preached the Gospel: So that some penetrated to the Persians and Indians, and Ethiopia gave its hands to God, and beyond the rivers of Ethiopia gifts were brought thence to Christ. And lest it seem to signify only the Eastern peoples, he adds the rest: 'And from the islands of the sea.' But by the islands of the sea he signifies the western region, which is enclosed by the circuit of the Ocean. He will therefore lift up the sign of the cross to all nations, and will first gather the people of Israel from the Synagogues of the Jews, so that the Apostles might fulfill the command of the Savior, who had said, 'Go to the lost houses of Israel.' Finally, Paul also speaks to the unbelievers among the Jews: 'It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first, but since you have thrust it aside and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles, as the Lord commanded us.' Moreover, he signifies the four corners, the east and the west, the south and the north, so that through these the calling of the world might be demonstrated:

Eleventh, the union and Concord of the Israelites and the Jews had its fulfillment not in the time of Hezekiah, but in the New Testament, concerning which verse 13: 'And the jealousy of Ephraim shall depart: And the enemies of Judah shall perish.' Grotius rightly accepts these things concerning the hatred of the ten tribes against the Jews which was to cease; but he does not teach that it was fulfilled in the time of Hezekiah. The ten tribes did not return to the Jews, but remained divided: they did not fly with joined forces onto the shoulders of the Philistines. Nor are those nations, which are subsequently listed, read to have been in the auxiliaries of the Philistines, as Grotius thinks. And therefore these things are to be understood concerning the concord under the Gospel. For they are said to have flown onto the shoulders of the Philistines

and to have plundered the sons of the east, so that they might snatch them from the jaws of the Devil after the manner of the spiritual wars of the Lord. In which manner Philip flew onto their shoulders when he preached the Gospel in Azotus and other cities of the Philistines, Acts 8. By the sons of the east, Grotius understands the Arabs, who, with the Idumeans and Moabites as well as the sons of Ammon, also submitted themselves to the Gospel. Jerome in this place has it thus: 'At that time,' says Isaiah, 'Ephraim and Judah, who now, while I am prophesying, dissent among themselves with hostile hatred, will by no means be enemies: But according to the prophecy of Ezekiel, the two rods will be coupled into one rod, and will be joined into the Church of Christ, who had previously been separated, so that they may labor together among the nations, and fly onto the shoulders of the Philistines by sea, that is, first they shall preach to the maritime Palestinians, and through the sea they shall proceed with winged speed to the other nations; Or according to the Septuagint Interpreters' they shall fly in ships. They shall plunder the sea of the aliens together, i.e., they shall fly in the ships of the aliens, they shall plunder the sea together. Which we should understand from the example of the Apostle Paul alone, who was carried in the ships of aliens through Pamphylia and Asia and Macedonia and Achaia, and various islands and provinces, to Italy also and (as he himself writes) to the Spains. Therefore Ephraim and Judah, i.e., those who from the twelve tribes believed in Christ from among the Jews, shall together plunder the East: And they shall extend their hands into Idumea and Moab: According to that which Christ speaks mystically under the person of David: 'Into Idumea I will extend my shoe, the aliens are subject to me.' For these nations, at the time when Isaiah was prophesying, were adversaries to the people of the Jews. And therefore he now says, that after the root of Jesse has risen, that he may reign among the nations, and the banner of the cross has been raised for the salvation of the whole world, then also Idumæa and Moab, and the children of Ammon, that is, the whole breadth of Arabia, shall give their hands to the Apostles, and in the places of idolatry the Churches of Christ shall be raised up. Grotius could have consulted here his Jesuits Cornel. à Lapide, Menochius, and Tirinus; from whom the latter thus renders the sense at v. 14, as if to say: They shall subdue to Christ both Western and Eastern peoples, and shall gather spoils from them: Thus Peter is at Lydda and the Philistine towns: Thus Philip is at Azotus, having despoiled the satrapy of the Philistines. Others [mention] Gaza and Ascalon, where Athanasius and Chrysostom, according to Adrichomius and Baronius, teach that the Church of Christ flourished greatly. Thus the Apostle Thomas despoiled India, Bartholomew Armenia, Matthew Ethiopia, says Jerome, Basil, Cyril. Furthermore: And the Lord shall desolate, says the Prophet, the tongue, that is, the bay of the sea of Egypt (Brentius [says] the mouth of the Nile; Grotius understands that isthmus which is between the sea adjacent to Egypt and the Red Sea) and he says it will be consecrated, that is, untouched by all, because things sacred to God cannot be touched; others render it, YOU SHALL DRY UP. The matter comes to the same thing thus far, that it may be safely crossed or passed through. The following things, however, confirm the latter sense. And he shall lift his hand over the river, that is, the Nile, in the strength of his spirit, by his own power or even by a vehement wind: and he shall strike it in seven streams, that is, in its many branches, so that they may pass through it shod, i.e., he shall dry it up with a very strong wind, so that whoever wishes may be able to pass through it shod: and thus there will be a way without any obstacle for the remnant people to return to their homeland, just as the opportunity was given to Israel on that day on which he ascended out of Egypt, to pass through the Red Sea. That impediments will be removed, Grotius's explanation also implies, although he renders it otherwise in this way: He shall divide the Euphrates into seven streams, that is, the empire of the Assyrians into many parts. For the Medes defected from the Assyrians, the Chaldeans from the Medes. Thus those nations most hostile to the Hebrews, hindered by domestic strife, gave easy returns to those exiling among them.

However, it is not the return to the land of Canaan that is to be understood, but the entry into the Church of God and the heavenly kingdom, from which sin and death were holding us back. But through the Gospel it is shown that sin has been removed and death conquered. These were the deepest rivers, which no one could cross. But after Christ came and spread His Gospel throughout the whole world, these rivers were dried up, so that now a free access to the heavenly kingdom lies open, as Brentius, Osiander, the Vinarieans, and others explain these things. Jerome, however, Cyril, and Procopius take it concerning the Pelusian Gulf, which, when Augustus Caesar was pursuing Antony and Cleopatra, God dried up in the strength of His Spirit, i.e., by a most violent south wind, sent beyond custom, which drove all the waters, even of the seven streams of the Nile, as Tirinus has it in this place, for the most part into the sea, so that the soldiers of Augustus crossed on dry ground, and very quickly occupied Pelusium and the other keys of Egypt, and with Antony and Cleopatra extinguished, left the monarchy of the world to Augustus alone, as Strabo, Dio Cassius, and Plutarch testify. And this by divine counsel, so that in this way an approach to the Gospel of Christ might gradually be opened, both in Egypt and also in the rest of the world, now peaceful and reduced under the monarchy of one man. Something similar happened around the time of the reduction of the Jews from Babylon into Judea: For the Euphrates (which the Chaldean here understands by the river, and with him Sanchez) during the siege of Babylon was diverted by Cyrus through seven trenches and streams away from the city, as Herodotus, Xenophon, and Orosius testify, and thus the soldier was sent into the city on dry ground, and Balthasar the Chaldean King was taken from the midst with his men, and the monarchy was established for Cyrus, and liberty came to the Jews. These were figures of those things which Isaiah here predicts will happen to the Church in the times of Christ. Thus far Tirinus, who has the former from Corn. à Lapide: the latter, however, he took from Sanctius. But whom Cornelius à Lapide rightly refutes here: The oracles of Isaiah, he says, are more sublime, and do not look to the Jews returning from Babylon, but to Christ and the Christians: and that the Nile is understood here by the river is clear from the seven streams; for these are found in the Nile alone. The same drought of the Nile is predicted lower down in chapter 19, 5. But what St. Jerome indicates, that the Nile, previously flowing in one channel, was then first diverted into seven channels, that does not agree with the ancient historians. Our Grotius ought to have heeded here the warning of St. Jerome, which he left at the end of this chapter: Let the prudent and Christian reader have this rule for the promises of the Prophets: that those things which the Jews and our own—nay, not our own Judaizers—contend will be in the future in a carnal sense, we should teach have already been fulfilled in a spiritual sense, lest by the occasion of such fables and inextricable questions, according to the Apostle, we be forced to Judaize. Moreover, we do not disguise the fact that Cyril also, in explaining these things, compares the history of the reduction from the Babylonian captivity, even though he acknowledges that the genuine sense of the prophecies concerns the times of the New Testament: not that he thinks a double sense, literal and mystical, which Grotius calls more sublime, underlies them, but that the Holy Spirit alludes to those things which were done under the Old Testament in describing and explaining those things which were to be in the New Testament, and institutes a comparison of them. Whence at verse 12, Cyril has it thus: The Prophet wonderfully wove this discourse with these words. He takes what happened historically εἰς εἰκόνα πραγμάτων νοητῶν, for the image of describing a thing falling under the understanding. But the scope of the Prophet was to show the glorious deeds of the advent of our Savior from more evident things and from those which happened long ago. Finally, it is to be observed that the Chaldean Interpreter understands this prophecy concerning the Messiah the King, inasmuch as he renders it thus: And a King shall go forth from the sons of Jesse, and the Messiah shall be anointed from the sons of his sons: and that the Jews themselves acknowledge that the discourse here is about the Messiah, not only according to a more sublime sense, but κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, even if they understand most things carnally, and thus do not err concerning the subject of the prophecy, but concerning the predicates which are enunciated here about the Messiah: and concerning the explanation, because they understand a different Messiah than Jesus of Nazareth: as Abarbanel: Since this section cannot be explained according to any of those opinions (neither concerning Hezekiah, nor concerning Zerubbabel) it is clear that it treats of nothing but the Messiah our righteousness to be revealed quickly. I am forced, says R. Lipomanus, to explain this whole section concerning the King Messiah, even if these verses are otherwise hidden from some of our people; but I will show from the same that the Messiah has not yet come. See his Nizachon against the Christians. We add what Raimundus Martinus has concerning this place of Isaiah 11, v. 1, in the Dagger of Faith against the Moors and Jews, published at Paris by Joseph de Voisin in the year 1651, part III, dist. I, Chapter 11, § 6, p. 436. Note that in innumerable places in the Talmud this is explained concerning the Messiah, and never concerning another by anyone who has any authority among the Hebrews. Wherefore it is clear that our Judaizers err too much, who do not fear to explain this literally concerning Josiah: for it is shown that this is to be understood LITERALLY concerning the Messiah ALONE by R. Solomon, who explains this concerning him, not concerning Josiah; which, according to his custom, he would by no means have done if he could have explained it otherwise without injury to his Talmud and Targum and without prejudice to his predecessors. The words of R. Solomon on this place are as follows: The King Messiah will not judge according to the vision of his eyes, but with the wisdom of the holy and blessed God, who will be in his midst, he will know and understand who is guilty and who is innocent, and he will argue in equity, i.e., with a quiet and tender tongue. In Bereshith Rabba on Gen. 1, v. 2, The Spirit of Elohim: This is the Spirit of the Messiah, of whom it is said in Isaiah 11, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him. Many such things could be produced from the Rabbis: But there is no doubt among most recent Jews either concerning this passage, that it treats of the Messiah, although they understand most things carnally, and thus even contend that those words: the wolf shall dwell with the ram, are to be taken literally. Which things, however, R. Moses Maimonides in the Summa Talmud. tract. on Kings chap. 2, confesses are to be understood allegorically in this sense: that it will come to pass that the Israelites will dwell safely and without fear with the impious of the nations of the world, who are compared to the wolf and the leopard, Jerem. 5. v. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SVPER FORAMINA ASPIDIS] Aspides a- mant latebras. ET IN CAVERNA REGVLI] צפע Graeci modo κεράςην vertunt, modo ἀσπίδα, id est, genus quoddam aspidum ab aliis distinctum. Vers 10. IN DIE ILLA RADIX JESSE, QVI STAT IN SIGNVM POPVLORVM, IPSVM GEN- TES DEPRECABVNTVR] In Hebræo : quærent : id est, ad Ezechiam concurrent multi ex gentibus ad verum Deum converti. ET ERIT SEPVLCHRVM EJVS GLORIOSVM] Et erit requies ejus gloria : id est, gloriæ plena. Requies habitationem significat.

NOn actum fuit in antecedentibus de Ezechiæ, neque laudes ejus celebratæ, ut hic ad eas re- dire potuerit Propheta. Nam capite 9. non de Eze- chia, sed CHRISTO egit.
