Ita Vulgata: quam non male adsensum vocem Babylon addidisse ait Grotius, verba ita reddens ex Ebræo: Tempus noctis ample- xus mei (vel desiderii mei) posuit mihi in pavorem. (Nox illa, qua indulsi ego cum proceribus meis vo- luptatibus, & desideriis nostris, versa est mihi in maximum terrorem luctumque gravissimum.) Proinde age, inquit Propheta, pone mensam (instrue sumtuosa convivia) contemplare(tu vigil) in specula, comedendo, bibendo, surgite principes, ungite clypeos. Sensum ita reddit Grotius: Dum ponunt mensam (Babylonii) dum speculator (ab illis constitutus) speculatur, dum comedunt (illi) dum bibunt, surgite principes (vos Medi) & clypeos unctos habete. Im- perativo enuntiat, quod futurum videt, ut Babylonii in magno periculo securi, dum ipsi epulantur, vilissi- mis hominibus delegato excubandi munere, oppri- mantur subito! Alii verba: surgite principes ad con- vivatoresBabylonios Ironice dici volunt: q. d. Sur- gite è convivio, arma arripite, si forte queatis adhuc hostem repellere. In confesso est, hac hypotyposi depingi improvisam Babyloniæ cladem, quæ acci- dit, ipsis interim helluantibus & in summa securita- te voluptatibus operam dantibus. Quæ omnia ita impleta esse, cum urbs capta fuit à Cyro, è Da- niele Cap. V. ac prophanis Historicis constat. Et explicat Grotius ipse, visionem curruum duorum equitum, quorum alter mulis alter camelis vehebatur: Persas, qui mulis utebantur, & Medos qui came- lis, ut Bactris propiores. Per duos ergo illos currus speculatorem intellexisse, quæ gentes expugnaturæ es- sent Babylonem. Alii ita Cyrum ipsum Persam, & Darium Medum, per equites hac visione designa- tos, intelligunt. Plerique currum per Synecdo- chen & Enallagen numeri, de ingenti curruum nu- mero, & exercitu è curribus, ut antiquitus fieri so- lebat, pugnante intelligunt. Vid. Ex. 14, 6. 7. 1. Sam. 13, 5. Es. 36, 9. c. 43, 17. 1. Par. 20, 6. 7. Ps. 20, 8. Denique clamor ille, cecidit, cecidit Babylon, totalem rui- nam significat; quam (Babylonem) Medo futuram, ut id, quod in area à bobus calcatur, in explicatione vers. 10. fatetur Grotius: quod nullo tempore im- pletum legitur, nisi cum à Dario & Cyro urbs ex- pugnaretur. Hæc autem ruina hic prædicitur, tum ne Babyloniis forte innitantur Judæi, siquidem E- zechias multum fidebat Regi Babyloniæ, Legatis- que ejus omnes thesauros suos ostendebat: unde ab iisdem illos ablatum iri prædixit Propheta: tum ne in ipsaBabyloniorum potentia animum de- sponderent fideles, quod populus Domini plane delendus, regnumque Christi in ipso nunquam emersurum sit. Ideo vaticinatur, Babylonem tan- dem evertendam; regnum autem Christi erigendum, quod æternum manebit. Quod ad ruinam etiam mysticæ Babylonis Romæ, cujus typus Babylon e- rat, transfertur Apoc. 14, 8. siquidem de ista etiam clamor ille exaudiendus sit: Cecidit Babylon ista magna: Quod fatetur hic versu 9. Grotius. Eadem, inquit, verba de Roma usurpat Johannes. Quum ergo hæc ruina Romæ totalis ac finalis sit, de totali, ac finali etiam Babylonis ruina hic sermonem esse apparet.

## 21:8
Verse 8.

AND A LION CRIED OUT] The Greeks read אוּרִיָּה; i.e., that Uriah named above 8, 2. for who is more worthy to be placed on the watchtower than a priest!

But the authentic text is not to be corrected from a translation. Whatever, or however the Greeks may have read, the Hebrew text has it correctly: He cried out roaring like a lion. That Uriah was placed on the watchtower by the Prophet is not evident from any other document, nor does sacred history report that Uriah was a prophet. Jerome was so fortunate in guessing that he attained the mind of the LXX here, which Grotius thinks he has attained, therefore he confesses here, I do not sufficiently understand what the LXX interpreters intended in this place, that for a Lion which is called in Hebrew אַרְיֵה, they translated ὀξίαν i.e., Uriah, especially since the aforementioned priest Uriah, who is called as a witness, is written with different letters אוּרִיָּה.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET CLAMAVIT LEO] Legunt Græci אוּרִיָּה; i. e. Urias ille nominatus supra 8, 2. quis enim dignior in specula collocari, quam Sacerdos!

Sed non est corrigendus textus authenticus è translatione. Quicquid, aut quomodocunque legerint Græci, Ebræus textus recte habet: Clama- vit leonis instar rugiendo. Uriam in specula consti- tutum esse à Propheta nullo alias documento con- stat, neque Uriam Prophetam fuisse historia sacra perhibet. Tam felix in divinando fuit Hierony- mus, ut assequutus hic mentem LXX. sit, quam se assecutum putat Grotius, ideo fatetur hic, quid si- bi voluerint in hoc loco LXX. Interpretes, ut pro Leone qui Hebraice dicitur אַרְיֵה, ὀξίαν i. e. Uriam transtulerint, non satis intelligo, præsertim cum su- pra dictus sacerdos Urias, qui vocatur in testimonium, aliis literis scriptus sit אוּרִיָּה.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the destruction of Jerusalem joined with the destructions of other nations on account of a similar fault, to be inflicted likewise by the Assyrian on account of Epicurean security: and the rejection of Shebna, to whom Eliakim is to be substituted.

Ver. 1. THE BURDEN OF THE VALLEY OF VISION] That is, an admonition to the city of Jerusalem, which city is situated in a valley, and at that time was illuminated by the visions of the Prophets, which, although it was the greatest benefit of God, was held in low esteem by many.

WHAT ALSO IS TO THEE] When Isaiah pronounced and wrote these things, Eliakim was not yet master of the Lord's house, or κωροπολάτης, which dignity, according to those things which Isaiah prophesies here, he later received and held when Sennacherib came to the city, 2 Kings 18, 18.37. Wherefore these things were seen and said when Shalmaneser had taken Samaria, and Shebna, then still Master of the Lord's house, an impious man, and of the discipline of Ahaz, distrusting God and the Prophets, was of the opinion that a surrender should be made to Shalmaneser, and had many associates in his sloth. See above 8, 12.

IT is not sufficiently certain, what Grotius assumes as undoubted concerning Eliakim, that he was the same who is commemorated in 2 Kings 18, since Josephus b. X. c. 1, Abulensis in the book of 4 Kings c. 18. n. 33, and Torniellus at the year of the world 3322, judge that both Eliakim and Shebna, concerning whom Isaiah prophesies here, are different from those in the book of Kings: to whom also our B. Luther and the Jesuit Tirinus agree: and it seems to favor this, that in the time of Hezekiah, Shebna was only a Scribe; but Eliakim was Prefect of the palace: whereas this Eliakim, of whom Isaiah speaks, succeeded Shebna in the prefecture of the house. To others it seems that Eliakim was driven from that dignity, which he held in the time of Hezekiah as Prefect of the house under the impious King Manasseh, because he did not approve of his impiety, but was finally restored when the impious King was punished. Which is the opinion of Osiander. But Grotius seems to establish a double Shebna, even if it is the same Eliakim in the book of Kings and here: For there Shebna was only a Scribe at the time when Sennacherib came to the city, but here he was Master of the Lord's house already in the time of Shalmaneser, according to the opinion of Grotius; unless perhaps it is said with Junius, that Hezekiah, having perceived his impiety, made him an honorary scribe from being Prefect of the praetorium. But that does not fit this prophecy, in which the Prophet predicted that Eliakim would succeed this Prefect of the house who was to be cast out of the city, because when Shebna was Scribe, Eliakim is said to have been Prefect of the palace, 2 Kings 18. Nor is it read that Shebna advised that a surrender of the city be made to Shalmaneser after Samaria was taken by the same. Grotius invents histories and chronology according to his own genius, so that he may convince [the reader] of his commentaries: or certainly he received them as fabricated from the Jews, just as the Hebrew in Jerome said that these things pertain to the times of Sennacherib, when Shebna the Pontiff betrayed a great part of the city, and only Zion, that is, the citadel and the temple, and the nobles remained, in the example of the Roman city, when the Gauls were rushing in and he saved the patricians and the flower of the youth in the citadel. But that these things, which the Prophet predicts, did not happen under the Assyrian Shalmaneser, but under the Chaldean Nebuchadnezzar, is not obscure from the context, and most Interpreters agree: whatever may be the case concerning that Shebna, and concerning Eliakim. For this is a peculiar prophecy, which whether it was held at the same time as the burden of the valley of vision, or even concerns the same times, is not known from the conjunction. For often prophecies of very different times are joined together: nor does Grotius himself observe order here. For he had established predictions pertaining to the times of Sennacherib in the previous Chapters: but here he slips back to earlier times. But so that the prophecy concerning Shebna may cohere entirely with the present, which pleased B. Luther, it must be established that Shebna and Eliakim are DIFFERENT. Furthermore, I do not deny that Interpreters vary in the exposition of this Jerusalem burden, or threatening: Some understand it of the calamity under Sennacherib; to whom Junius agrees in this place. Others with Cyril and Jerome of the destruction under Nebuchadnezzar. The latter Interpretation seems preferable to us: to which B. Luther adds his vote, explaining it of the first Babylonian captivity under Jehoiakim: because only the Princes were carried away to Babylon. What is to thee, that thou hast ascended to the roofs either for fear of the enemy, to hide thyself, or to defend against the enemies; or to see the enemy placing camps before the city. For the Hebrews prepared such roofs, upon which one could walk. Thy slain are not slain by the sword, but destroyed by famine or pestilence. Which does not fit the siege of Sennacherib. Some understand it of civil death, that is, that they are about to surrender themselves with a womanish spirit. All thy princes have fled, they are bound together from the bow: they tried to flee, but could not escape the hand of the enemy. All who were found, fled far away together (they shall be led away far into Assyria) A day of tumult and of treading down and of weeping to the Lord (all things shall be full of mourning) And searching the wall, magnificent upon the mountain. Thus the Vulgate. But in the Hebrew it is: Digging through the wall, that there may be a cry or a shout to the mountain, as Avenarius explained in his Lexicon to the word קור. Osiander rendered: Because of the destruction of the wall and the cry to the mountain, i.e., the citizens of Jerusalem will see the wall being torn down by the enemies in the lower part of the city, and so they will cry out to their fellow citizens, who dwell in the upper part of the city toward Mount Zion, for help, so that they may protect the city from the enemy. B. Luther explains it thus: Therefore it is a day of slaughter, because the wall is undermined and the enemies are threatening the mountain. For the Assyrians, having besieged Jerusalem, had decided to lay it waste unless it surrendered. Junius renders: (A day) of the destruction of the wall (by which the towns of Judea are destroyed by engines of war) and of the shouting to the mountains (which each one, yielding to the enemy, seeks as a refuge by shouting in the mountains), which sense he confirms from the Hebrew distinctions. How, however, this whole prophecy was fulfilled in the time of Jeconiah (as B. Luther does with Cyril) is manifest from 2 Kings 24:10 ff. Grotius twists these and all the following things into a foreign sense, so that they may serve his preconceived explanation.

On the same verse 1.

BECAUSE YOU HAVE ASCENDED, EVEN YOU, ONTO THE ROOF] As if the enemy were already at the walls.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII. De Hierosolymæ clade aliarum gentium cla- dibus ob similem culpam juncta, ab Assy- rio itidem ob Epicuream securitatem infe- renda: ac rejectione Sobnæ, cui surrogan- dus Eliakim.

Vers. 1. ONUS VALLIS VISIONIS] Id est, admo- nitio ad civitatem Hierosolymorum, quæ urbs in valle est posita, & eo tempore Prophetarum visis illustrabatur, quod cum maximum esset Dei beneficium, à multis parvi fie- bat.

QUIDNAM QUOQUE TIBI EST] Cum hæc pronunciavit & scripsit Esaias, nondum Eliacim erat ma- gister domus dominicæ, sive κωροπολάτης, quam dignita- tem, secundum ea quæ hic vaticinatur Esaias postea accepit, eamque gessit, cum Sennacheribus venit ad urbem 2. Reg. 18, 18.37. quare hæc visa dictaque sunt, cum Salmanasar Sa- mariam cepisset, & Sobna, tunc adhuc Magister domus Do- minicæ, homo impius, & ex Achazi disciplina, Deo Prophe- tisque diffisus, deditionem faciendam Salmanasari censeret, multosque haberet ejus socordiæ socios. Vide supra 8, 12.

NON satis certum est, quod ceu indubium de Eliakim assumit Grotius, quod fuerit idem qui 2. Reg. 18. commemoratur, quum Josephus l. X. c. 1. Abulensis in lib. 4. Reg. c. 18. n. 33. & Torniel- lus ad ann. mundi 3322. tam Eliakim, quam Sebnam, de quibus Esaias hic vaticinatur, diversos esse ab il- lis in libro Regum, censeant: quibus etiam acce- dit B. Lutherus noster, & Jesuita Tirinus: & fave- re id videtur, quod tempore Ezechiæ Sebna fuerit tantum Scriba; Eliakim autem aulæ Præfectus: quum hic Eliakim, de quo Esaias, succefferit Sebnæ in præpositura domus. Aliis ita videtur, quod Eliakim ab illa dignitate, qua fungebatur tempore Ezechiæ ceu Præpositus domus sub impio Rege Manasse, quod impietatem ejus non approbaret, deterbatus, tandem autem, punito Rege impio, re- stitutus fuerit. Quæ sententia Osiandri est. Sebnam vero geminum videtur constituere Grotius, etsi i- dem Eliakim sit in libro Regum, & hic: Nam ibi Sobne erat tantum Scriba eo tempore, cum Senna- cherib ad urbem venit, hic vero fuit Magister do- mus Dominicæ jam tempore Salmanassaris, secun- dum Grotii sententiam; nisi forte cum Junio dica- tur, quod Hiskias, percepta ejus impietate, ex Præfe- cto prætorii scribam honorarium effecerit. Sed id non congruit huic vaticinio, quo huic Præfecto domus extra urbem projiciendo successurum Eliakim Propheta prædixit, quia cum Sebna Scriba esset, Præfectus aulæ fuisse Eliakim dicitur 2. Regum 18. Neque de deditione urbis Salmanassari facienda consuluisse Sebna legitur, post captam ab eodem Samariam. Historias & Chronologiam pro in- genio suo fingit Grotius, ut Commentariis suis fidem faciat: aut certe conficta à Judæis accepit, sicut Ebræus apud Hieronymum hæc ad tempora Sennacheribi pertinere dixit, quando Sebna Ponti- fex magnam partem prodidit civitatis, & tantum Sion, id est, arx & templum, ac nobiles remanse- runt, in exemplum Romanæ urbis, irruentibus Gallis patricios & florem juventutis in arce servavit. Quod autem hæc, quæ prædicit Propheta, non sub Salmanassare Assyrio evenerint, sed sub Nebucad- nezare Chaldæo, è contextu haud obscurum est, & consentiunt plerique Interpretes: quicquid de il- lo Sebna sit, & de Eliakim. Hæc enim peculia- ris Prophetia est, quæ an eodem cum onere visionis vallis habita sit tempore, aut eadem etiam concer- nat tempora, è conjunctione non innotescit. Sæpe namque conjunguntur vaticinia temporum maxi- me diversorum: neque ordinem hic observat ipse Grotius. Nam prædictiones ad Sennache- ribi tempora pertinentes in superioribus Capp. constituerat: hic vero ad superiora relabitur tem- pora. Ut vero omnino vaticinium de Sebna præ- senti cohæreat, quod B. Luthero placuit, DI- VERSOS esse Sebnam, & Eliakim, statuendum erit. Cæterum non diffiteor, quod varient In- terpp. in hujus oneris Hierosolymitani, vel com- minationis expositione: Nonnulli intelligunt de calamitate sub Sennacheribo; quibus accedit Junius in h. l. Alii cum Cyrillo & Hieronymo de clade sub Nebucadnezare. Nobis præferenda videtur po- sterior Interpretatio: cui calculum addit B. Luthe- rus de prima captivitate Babylonica sub Jojachim explicans: quia Principes tantum Babyloniam sunt translati. Quid est tibi, quia adscendisti in tecta vel metu hostium, ut te abscondas, vel ut defendas con- tra hostes; vel ut videas hostem castra ante urbem ponentem. Ebræi enim talia tecta parabant, qui- bus inambulari poterat. Interfecti tui non interfe- cti gladio, sed fame vel peste interemti. Quod non congruit obsidioni Sennacheribi. Nonnulli de morte civili, quod nempe muliebri animo sese de- dituri sint, intelligunt. Cuncti principes tui fugerunt, simul ab arcu ligati sunt: fugere conati sunt, sed manum hostis effugere nequiverunt. Omnes qui inventi sunt, pariter procul fugerunt (procul abdu- centur in Assyriam) Dies tumultus & conculcationis & fletuum Domino (omnia erunt plena luctu) Et scrutans murum magnificus super montem. Ita Vulgata. Sed in Ebræo est: Perfodiens parietem, ut clamor sit vel roboët ad montem, ut Avenarius in Lexic. ad verbum קור exposuit. Osiander red- didit: Propter destructionem muri & clamorem ad montem, i. e. cives Hierosolymitani videbunt ab hostibus dirui murum in loco inferiori civitatis, i- taque ad Concives suos, qui in superiori parte ur- bis ad montem Sion habitant, clamabunt pro auxi- lio, ut urbem ab hoste tueantur. B. Lutherus ita exponit: Ideo est dies interfectionis, quia murus sub- ruitur & hostes monti imminent. Assyrii enim obses- sam Hierusalem, nisi se dedisset, vastare decreverant. Junius reddit: (Dies) destructionis muri (quo oppi- da Judææ tormentis bellicis destruuntur) & vocifera- tionis ad montana (quosinguli cedentes hosti per- fugium vociferando in montanis quærunt,) quem sensum ab Ebraicis distinctionibus confirmat. Quomodo autem hæc tota Prophetia impleta sit Jechoniæ tempore (uti cum Cyrillo B. Lutherus) è 2. Reg. XXIV. 10. seqq. manifestum est. Grotius hæc & sequentia omnia in alienum sensum detorquet, ut suæ explicationi præconceptæ inserviant.

Eod. Vers. 1.

QUIA ASCENDISTI ET TU OMNIS IN TE- CTO] Quasi jam ad muros esset hostis.

## 22:2
FULL OF SHOUTING] On account of fear and consternation.

But the text does not sound of a cry of consternation, but of joy; not of the present time and state, but of the past. Full of shouting (you were, O Jerusalem), a crowded city (you were), an exulting city.

YOUR SLAIN ARE NOT SLAIN BY THE SWORD NOR DEAD IN WAR] They are lifeless from fear alone.

The prophet designates that many will truly perish, even if they do not die by the sword or in war. To be lifeless from fear alone does not sufficiently fit this phrase.

Latin:

CLAMORIS PLENA] Ob metum & consterna- tionem.

At non de clamore consternationis, sed gau- dii, non de tempore & statu præsenti, sed præterito textus sonat. Clamoris plena (eras ô Jerusalem) urbs frequens (eras) civitas exultans.

INTERFECTI TUI NON INTERFECTI GLA- DIO NEC MORTUI IN BELLO] Metu solo exani- mantur.

Propheta designat vere interituros plurimos, etsi non gladio vel bello intereant. Solo metu exa- nimandos phrasi huic non satis congruit.

## 22:3
Verse 3.

ALL YOUR PRINCES HAVE FLED TOGETHER] They flee, that is, they prepare a desertion.

DUREQUE] In the Hebrew: from the bow: which is to be connected with that 'they have fled.' From the bow: that is, for fear of the archers, who were very numerous in the Assyrian army.

LIGATI SUNT] That is, they conspired among themselves to take to flight. The following words signify the same. See a similar passage at 8, 12.

OMNES QUI INVENTI SUNT] Supply: in you. All, that is, most of the princes.

FUGERUNT] They prepare for flight, as above.

But these things agree neither with the manner of speaking nor with the text. The princes are said to have fled, or to have prepared a desertion, but they were captured in flight and bound. For they are reported to have been bound after their flight. And what need is there for a metaphorical meaning of conspiracy, when the word LIGATI SUNT can be taken literally? For it is certain that the best part of the people was led away captive. And the Prophet adds here: ALL WHO WERE FOUND WERE BOUND TOGETHER. Grotius perverts these things thus: Because all were found in you, i.e., most of the princes. But the text says that all who were found by the enemies were bound, not just some, nor were those who remained in the city bound, but those whom the enemy caught in flight; who had fled far outside the city.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

CVNCTI PRINCIPES TUI FUGERUNT SI- MUL] Fugiunt, id est, transfugium adornant.

DUREQUE] In Hebræo: ab arcu: quod conne- etendum cum illo fugerunt. Ab arcu: id est, metu sagit- tariorum, qui plurimi in Exercitu Assyrio.

LIGATI SUNT] Id est, conjurarunt inter se, ut fugam caperent. Idem significant verba sequentia. Vide simile 8, 12.

OMNES QUI INVENTI SUNT] Supple, in te. Omnes, id est, principum plurimi.

FUGERUNT] Fugam parant, ut supra.

Hæc vero neque modo loquendi, neque tex- tui conveniunt. Fugisse dicuntur Principes, vel adornasse transfugium, sed in fuga capti, ligati. Nam post fugam ligati perhibentur. Et quid opus Metaphorica significatione conjurationis, quum verbum LIGATI SUNT proprie accipi possit. Constat enim, optimam partem populi abductam esse captivam. Et subjungit hic Propheta: O- MNES, QUI INVENTI SUNT, VINCTI SUNT PARITER. Grotius hæc ita pervertit: Quia inventi sunt in te omnes i. e. principum plurimi. At textus omnes, qui ab hostibus in- venti sunt, non tantum nonnullos vinctos dicit, ne- que vincti fuêre, qui in urbe manserunt, sed quos in fuga hostis deprehendit; qui longe fugerant extra urbem.

## 22:4
Verse 4.

PROPTEREA DIXI] Here the City of Jerusalem answers the Prophet. That 'therefore,' however, is to be referred to what follows: 'Over the devastation of the daughter of my people.'

SUPER VASTITATE FILIÆ POPULI MEI] Because the ten tribes, which are of the same blood as I, are treated so cruelly, with slaughters, devastation, and exile.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

PROPTEREA DIXI] Hic respondet Prophetæ Civitas Hierosolyma. Illud autem, propterea referendum est ad id, quod sequetur, Super vastitate filiæ populi mei.

SUPER VASTITATE FILIÆ POPULI MEI] Quia decem tribus, quæ ejusdem mecum sunt sanguinis, ita sæve tractantur, cædibus, vastatione, exsilio.

## 22:5
DIES ENIM INTERFECTIONIS ET CONCULCATIONIS] Namely, for the Israelites.

ET FLETUUM DOMINO EXERCITUUM IN VALLE VISIONIS] But for me, Jerusalem continues to say, this matter is a cause for crying out to God with weeping.

SEARCHING THE WALL AND MAGNIFYING UPON THE MOUNTAIN] In the Hebrew: A digger of the wall and a cry upon the mountain, namely of Samaria 1 Kings 16:24.

Latin:

DIES ENIM INTERFECTIONIS ET CONCUL- CATIONIS] Nempe Israelitis.

ET FLETUUM DOMINO EXERCITUUM IN VALLE VISIONIS] Mihi autem, pergit dicere Hioroso- lyma, materia hæc est cum fletu clamandi ad Deum.

SCRUTANS MVRVM ET MAGNIFICANS SVPER MONTEM] In Hebræo: Suffossor parietis & clamor super montem, nempe Samariæ 1. Reg. 16, 24.

## 22:6
Verse 6.

AND ELAM TOOK THE QUIVER] The Elymaeans, who at that time still obeyed the Assyrians: for the secession happened afterwards.

AND THE SHIELD NAKED THE WALL] In the Hebrew: And Kir brought out the shield: That is, the Mede, a subject of the Assyrians at that time. See 2 Kings 16:9.

It does not appear that the city is answering these things. For the Prophet's discourse is continued. Depart from me, I will weep bitterly, (i.e., allow me to weep bitterly over the miseries of the city), do not press upon me to console me over the devastation of the daughter of my people. Grotius thinks these words are of Jerusalem speaking about the ten tribes, who were of the same blood as herself, being cruelly treated, with slaughters, devastation, and exile: But the inscription of the chapter teaches that this is not a discourse about the slaughter of the ten tribes, but about the valley of vision, i.e., Jerusalem herself. Nor had the Prophet dealt with the slain of the Israelites, but with Jerusalem before in verse 2: he had said that the Jews, not the Israelites, were taking flight in verse 3. Bitterness and weeping arise over them, not indeed over these, according to verse 4. Junius, although he introduces Judea speaking here in verse 4, nevertheless wishes to explain the gravity of her mourning, and by the devastation, he understands the slaughters, devastation, and exiles of the daughter of his people, not of the ten tribes, but of every town in Judea, which obeys Jerusalem as a mother. Which sense also has a place, even if the Prophet's discourse is said to be continued. And the following verses teach openly that it is not about the Israelites, but about Jerusalem, because it is a day of tumult and of treading down and of weeping to the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision in verse 5. Which, so that Grotius may distort it, since they speak manifestly about the calamity of Jerusalem, he tears apart thus: A DAY OF SLAUGHTER AND TREADING DOWN, namely for the Israelites. AND OF WEEPING TO THE LORD GOD OF HOSTS IN THE VALLEY OF VISION. To me, he continues to say, Jerusalem is the subject of this, with weeping to cry out to God. But who does not see that for those same people this day is the day of slaughter and treading down, for whom it is called a day of lamentation and weeping. Whence Grotius is wrong regarding those words SEARCHING THE WALL AND MAGNIFYING UPON THE MOUNTAIN: In the Hebrew: A digger of the wall and a cry upon the mountain, namely of Samaria 1 Kings 16:24. For there is nothing here about the mountain of Samaria.

There follows in the text verse 6. AND ELAM TOOK THE QUIVER. To which Grotius: The Elymaeans, who at that time still obeyed the Assyrians: for the secession happened afterwards. AND THE SHIELD NAKED THE WALL. In the Hebrew: And Kir brought out the shield, i.e., the Mede, a subject of the Assyrians at that time, see 2 Kings 16:9. The Vulgate is rightly corrected, and these things are understood concerning the Elymaeans and Medes. But they are not to be restricted to those times which Grotius intends. Even if in the time of Jeconiah the Elamites and Medes were not subjects to the Assyrians; they could nevertheless have served in the Assyrian army. Ludov. de Dieu wishes the whole passage to be translated thus from the sources: And Elam took the quiver: in the chariot there is a man, there are horsemen: (or also: for the chariot of a man there are horses) And Kir made naked (brought forth: or according to a comparison with the Ethiopic language, smoothed, polished) the shield.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET ÆLAM SUMSIT PHARETRAM] Elymæi, qui tunc adhuc Assyriis parebant: nam secessio postea fa- cta est.

ET PARIETEM NVDAVIT CLTPEVS] In He- bræo: Et Kir eduxit Clypeum: Id est, Medus Assyriorum subditus eo tempore. Vide 2. Reg. 16, 9.

Non apparet, civitatem hæc respondere. Pro- phetæ enim oratio continuatur. Recedite à me, a- mare flebo, (i. e. finite me acerbe deflere miserias urbis) nolite incumbere, ut me consolemini super va- stitate filiæ populi mei. Quæ verba Hierosolymæ esse de decem tribubus, quæ ejusdem secum erant san- guinis, sæve tractatis, cædibus, vastatione, exilio lo- quentis Grotius putat: Sed hic non de clade decem tribuum, sed vallis visionis h. e. ipsius Hierosoly- mæ sermonem esse, capitis inscriptio docet. Ne- que de interfectis Israëliturum, sed Hierosolymæ an- tea vers. 2. egerat Propheta: Judæos, non Israëlitas fugam capessere dixerat vers. 3. Super illis, non vero his amaritudo & fletus exoritur, juxta v. 4. Iunius etsi Judæam hic loquentem introducat vers. 4. eam tamen vult gravitatem luctus sui exponere, & per vastationem cædes, vastationem & exilia filiæ po- puli sui non decem tribuum, sed uniuscujusque oppidi in Judæa, quod Hierosolymæ velut matri paret, vastationem intelligit. Qui sensus etiam locum habet, licet Prophetæ sermo continuari di- catur. Et docent sequentia aperte, quod non de Israelitis, sed de Hierosolyma agatur, quia dies tu- multus conculcationis & fletuum Domino Deo exer- cituum in valle visionis vers. 5. Quæ ut detor- queat Grotius, quum manifeste de Hierosolyma b calamitate loquantur, ita discerpit: DIES IN- TERFECTIONIS ET CONCULCATIONIS nempe Israelitis. ET FLETUUM DOMI- NO EXERCITUUM IN VALLE VISIONIS. Mihi, pergit dicere Hierosolyma, materia hæc est cum fletu clamandi ad Deum. Quis vero non videt iisdem illis hanc diem esse diem interfectio- nis & conculcationis, quibus dies lamentationis & fle- tuum dicitur. Unde perperam ad illa SCRU- TANS MURUM ET MAGNIFICANS SU- PER MONTEM, Grotius: In Hebræo: Suffos- sor parietis & clamor super montem nempe Sa- mariæ 1. Regum 16, 24. Nihil enim hic de monte Samariæ.

Sequitur in textu vers. 6. ET ÆLAM SUM- SIT PHARETRAM. Ad quæ Grotius: Eli- mai, qui tunc Assyriis adhuc parebant: nam secessio postea facta est. ET PARIETEM NUDAVIT CLYPEUS. In Hebræo: Et Kir eduxit clypeum, i. e. Medus Assyriorum subditus eo tempore vid. 2. Reg. 16. vers. 9. Recte corrigitur Vulgata, & de Æ- limæis ac Medis hæc intelliguntur. Sed ad tem- pora illa, quæ intendit Grotius, ea restringen- da non sunt. Etsi Jechoniæ tempore Elamitæ & Medi subditi non fuerint Assyriis; in exercitu tamen Assyriaco militare potuerunt. Locum in- tegrum sic vertendum è fontibus vult Ludov. de Dieu: Et Elam sumsit pharetram: in curru vir est, equites sunt: (vel etiam: ad currum hominis equi sunt) Et Kir nudavit (depromsit: vel juxtà colla- tionem linguæ Æthiopicæ, levigavit, polivit) cly- peum.

## 22:7
Verse 7.

AND THY CHOSEN VALLEYS SHALL BE FULL OF CHARIOTS] Here the Prophet resumes his discourse, and foretells those things which were at some time to happen through Sennacherib. Even thy valleys, i.e., the suburban places, will be filled with the forces of that same nation. IN THE GATE] That is, at the gate.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ET ERUNT ELECTÆ VALLES TUÆ PLE- NÆ QVADRIGARVM] Hic Propheta sermonem resu- mit, & ea, quæ aliquando per Sennacheribum eventura erant, prænunciat. Etiam tuæ valles, i, e. loca subur- bana implebuntur copiis gentis ejusdem. IN PORTA] Id est, ad portam.

## 22:8
Verse 8.

AND THE COVERING OF JUDAH SHALL BE REVEALED] That is, the fortifications surrounding the city will be taken away. AND THOU SHALT SEE IN THAT DAY THE ARMORY OF THE HOUSE OF THE FOREST] Thou shalt perceive beautifully all things which can be provided by human means, but in vain, as long as thou shalt not have God propitious. This armory must have been in the city, but it has its name from that armory which Solomon had built in the forest of Lebanon 1 Kings 7:1. Because it had succeeded into its place. See 2 Chronicles 32:5.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET REVELABITVR OPERIMENTVM JVDÆ] Id est, munimenta circumsita urbi rapientur. ET VIDEBIS IN DIE ILLA ARMAMENTA- RIVM DOMVS SALTVS] Omnia quæ humanitus pro- videri possunt, pulchre perspicies, sed frustra, quam- diu Deum non habebis propitium. Armamentarium hoc necesse est in urbe fuerit, sed nomen habet ab eo arma- mentario, quod in Libani saltu Salomon struxerat 1. Reg. 7, 1. Quia ejus in locum successerat. Vid. 2. Par. 32, 5.

## 22:9
Ver. 9.

AND YOU SHALL SEE THE BREACHES OF THE CITY OF DAVID, BECAUSE THEY ARE MULTIPLIED] You will patch the gaping parts of the wall, which will be not a few through the negligence of former times. See the said passage in Chronicles. AND YOU HAVE GATHERED THE WATERS OF THE LOWER POOL] That is, you will lead those waters into the city, so that the enemy may not use them. For there were two lakes outside the city, which the Hebrews call pools, 2 Kings 18:17, above 7:3. There is mention of this diversion in 2 Chronicles 32:3 and Nehemiah 3:16.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ET SCISSVRAS CIVITATIS DAVID VIDE- BITIS, QVIA MVLTIPLICATÆ SVNT] Sarcietis mœnium hiantia, quæ non pauca erunt per superiorum temporum incuriam. Vide dictum locum Paralipome- non. ET CONGREGASTIS AQVAS PISCINÆ IN- FERIORIS] Id est, aquas illas in urbem ducetis, ne ho- stis ejus utatur. Nam duo erant extra urbem lacus, quos piscinas Hebræi vocant 2. Reg. 18, 17. Supra 7, 3. Est hu- jus derivationis mentio 2. Paral. 32, 3. & Nehem. 3, 16.

## 22:10
Ver. 10.

AND YOU HAVE NUMBERED THE HOUSES OF JERUSALEM] You will perhaps count the houses to a certain number, from which you may take material for building towers. See the said passage in Chronicles.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET DOMVS JERVSALEM NVMERASTIS] Ad certum numerum domos forte legetis, unde sumatis ma- teriam ad turres faciendas. Vide dictum locum Parali- pomenon.

## 22:11
Ver. 11.

AND YOU HAVE MADE A DITCH BETWEEN THE TWO WALLS FOR THE WATER OF THE OLD POOL] You will make a trench between the two walls, into which you will lead the water from the old, or upper, pool. See 2 Chronicles 32:30, 2 Kings 20:20. AND YOU HAVE NOT LOOKED TO HIM, WHO HAD MADE IT] Namely, the city of Jerusalem, the possession of which God gave to David, and at the same time all things that were necessary for increasing and defending the city.

AND ITS MAKER FROM AFAR] Him who was long ago the author of the founding of that city. YOU HAVE NOT SEEN] You will not care.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET LACVM FECISTIS INTER DVOS MV- ROS AD AQVAM PISCINÆ VETERIS] Inter duos muros fossam facietis, in quam deducetis aquam è piscina vetere, sive superiore. Vid. 2. Paralip. 32. vers. 30. 2. Reg. 20. vers. 20. ET NON SVSPIXISTIS AD EVM, QVI FE- CERAT EAM] Nempe urbem Hierosolyma, cujus pos- sessionem Deus dedit Davidi, simulque omnia quæ ad ur- bem augendam tuendamque erant necessaria.

ET OPERATOREM EJUS DE LONGE] Eum, qui pridem urbis ejus condendæ auctor fuit. NON VIDISTIS] Non curabitis.

## 22:12
Ver. 12.

AND THE LORD GOD OF HOSTS WILL CALL ON THAT DAY TO WEEPING] That is, when God is about to call you to weeping, etc. TO BALDNESS] That was forbidden in funeral mourning, not in a public calamity, Mic. 1:16.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET VOCABIT DOMINUS DEUS EXERCI- TUUM ILLA DIE AD FLETUM] Id est, cùm Deus vos ad fletum vocaturus est, &c. AD CALVITIVM] Id in luctu Funebri erat veti- tum, non in publico malo, Mich. 1, 16.

## 22:13
Ver. 13.

AND BEHOLD JOY AND GLADNESS] You meanwhile will not cease to hold banquets, as if acting in happy circumstances. LET US EAT AND DRINK: FOR TOMORROW WE SHALL DIE] That is, perhaps we shall die. Thus Horace: 'Seek not to ask what shall be tomorrow,' and 'Whatever day fortune shall give, count it as gain.' Likewise: 'Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in the morrow.' And elsewhere: '...he, master of himself, will live happy, who can say for the day, I have lived; tomorrow let the Father fill the sky either with a dark cloud or with pure sunlight.'

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ET ECCE GAVDIVM ET LÆTITIA] Vos in- terim non definetis convivia, tanquam in rebus lætis a- gitare. COMEDAMUS ET BIBAMUS: CRAS ENIM MORIEMUR] Id est, forte moriemur. Sic Horatius: Quid sit futurum cras fuge quærere, & Quem fors dierum cunque dabit lucro Appone. Item: Carpe diem, quam minimum credulo postero. Et alibi: - - - ille potens sui Lætusq; deget, cui licet in diem Dixisse, vixi cras vel atra Nube polum pater occupato Vel sole puro.

## 22:13
TO SLAY CALVES AND TO KILL RAMS, TO EAT FLESH AND TO DRINK (sweet and fragrant WINE.) These will be the exercises of your piety and the signs of your repentance: among which such songs will resound: LET US EAT AND DRINK. FOR TOMORROW WE SHALL DIE. Such security and impenitence did not prevail in the time of Hezekiah: nay, when the King was exhorting the whole people to trust in God, 'Be strong and courageous, do not fear, nor be dismayed before the King of Assyria and all the multitude that is with him: for there are more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh: with us is the Lord our God: who is our helper and fights for us'; the people were strengthened by the words of the king, and placed their trust in God their Lord, 2 Chron. 32. Finally, how does that threat in v. 4 fit the time of Hezekiah? IF IT SHALL BE FORGIVEN, that is, by no means shall THIS INIQUITY BE FORGIVEN YOU, UNTIL YOU DIE, that is, you will perish in your impiety. Since God was propitious to the Jews, and delivered them from the imminent slaughter, the army of Sennacherib having been destroyed. Grotius interprets it thus: Throughout their whole life, punishment will follow those who have done these things. But the discourse is about the Jews of that time, about whom the Prophet is prophesying, and their impenitence and destruction, which certainly do not agree with the time of the siege of Sennacherib. Whence it is manifest that the Grotian gloss does not hold. He observes that the Chaldean Paraphrast refers these things to the second death: and he does not disapprove. If, therefore, this is the sense of the Prophet, the Hebrews must have had knowledge of the second death and therefore also of eternal life at that time, which Grotius otherwise denies them. The Jews gather from the particle עד (until) that iniquity is forgiven in death, and that through death an expiation of sin is made. Maimonides, treatise on repentance. But that particle does not always affirm a thing after the time that is noted, where a negation has preceded. See 1 Sam. 15:35, 2 Sam. 6:22, Gen. 28:15.

Latin:

OCCIDERE VITULOS ET JUGULARE ARIETES, COMEDERE CARNES ET LI- BARE (suave fragransque VINUM.) Haec e- runt pietatis vestrae exercitia & poenitentiae signa: inter quae talia resonabunt cantica: COMEDA- MUS ET BIBAMUS. CRAS ENIM MO- RIEMUR. Talis securitas & impoenitentia tem- pore Ezechiae non viguit: imo cum Rex populum universum, ut in Deo confideret, cohortaretur, Viriliter agite & confortamini, nolite timere, nec pa- veatis Regem Assyriorum & universam multitudi- nem, quae est cum eo: multo enim plures nobiscum sunt, quam cum illo. Cum illo est brachium car- neum: nobiscum Dominus Deus noster: qui au- xiliator est noster pugnatque pro nobis; confor- tatus fuit populus verbis regis, inqueDeo Domino suo fiduciam collocavit 2. Par. 33. Denique quo- modo isti Ezechiae tempori convenit illa commi- natio v. 4. SI DIMITTETUR, id est, nequaquam dimittetur INIQUITAS HAEC VOBIS, DONEC MORIAMINI, id est, in impietate vestra peribitis. Siquidem Deus propitius fuerit Judaeis, eosque a clade imminente, deleto exercitu Sennacheribi, liberavit. Grotius ita interpretatur: Per totam vitam eos, qui haec fecerint, poena sequentur. Sed ser- mo est de Judaeis istius temporis, quo de vaticina- tur Propheta, eorumque impoenitentia & interitu, quae certe non congruunt tempori obsidionis Sen- nacheribi. Unde manifestum est, locum non ha- bere glossam Grotianam. Observat, haec ad mor- tem secundam referre Chaldaeum Paraphrasten: nec improbat. Si ergo hic sensus Prophetae, mortis secundae adeoque etiam vitae aeternae notitiam isto tempore habuisse Ebraeos oportet, quam alias illis derogat Grotius. Judaei e particula עד donec col- ligunt in morte dimitti iniquitatem, & per mor- tem expiationem peccati fieri. Maimonid. tr. de poenit. Sed ea particula non semper affirmat rem post tempus quod notatur, ubi praecessit negatio. Vid. 1. Sam. 15, 35. 2. Sam. 6, 22. Genes. 28, 15.

## 22:14
Ver. 14.

IF IT SHALL BE FORGIVEN] Aposiopesis. May I not be held as God, if I forgive this. UNTIL YOU DIE] Throughout their whole life, punishment will follow those who have done these things. The Chaldean Paraphrast refers it to the second death.

Grotius imagines a change of persons. And yet this Prophet has always spoken, nor does any evidence appear of a changed person. Furthermore, he separates what are joined in the text, for the things said about the quiver of Elam, about the chariots, about the horsemen, about the shield of Kir, cohere and are continued in the present verse: because those chosen, most fertile, and most pleasant valleys are to be filled with those archers, chariots, and soldiers with bared, flashing shields, and are to be full of the quadrigae from which it was customary to fight; and because the horsemen are to place (their tents) at the gate: which was fulfilled in 2 Kings 24:20. Therefore, this leap from the ten tribes to Judea is not to be imagined: from Shalmaneser to Sennacherib. Nor do those things which are in v. 11 agree with the time of Sennacherib. AND YOU HAVE NOT LOOKED TO HIM, WHO MADE IT. Namely, the city of Jerusalem, the possession of which God gave to David, and at the same time all things that were necessary for increasing and protecting the city.

Others understand IT [to mean] THE MATTER: because GOD had stirred up that war against Jeconiah. Which is not to be said so much of the war of Sennacherib. AND ITS MAKER FROM AFAR. Him who was long ago the author of the founding of that city. Others: who will bring enemies to you from a far land. Which interpretation is to be preferred. YOU HAVE NOT SEEN. You will not care. These things, I say, do not agree with Hezekiah and the people of that time. For the opposite is reported in 2 Chron. 32, namely that Hezekiah with the people had a refuge primarily in God during the siege of Sennacherib. Much less, therefore, can the rest be adapted to that time: AND THE LORD GOD OF HOSTS WILL CALL ON THAT DAY TO WEEPING. That is, when God is about to call them to weeping. TO BALDNESS. That was forbidden in funeral mourning, not in a public calamity. AND BEHOLD JOY AND GLADNESS. You meanwhile will not cease to hold banquets as if acting in happy circumstances. (You will do the opposite of that which God is about to command through the Prophets: with an Epicurean mind you will laugh at the prophetic admonitions)

Latin:

Vers. 14.

SI DIMITTETUR] Αποσιώπησις. Ne habear Deus, si id condono. DONEC MORIAMINI] Per totam vitam eos qui hæc fecerunt pœnæ sequentur. Ad mortem secundam refert Chaldæus Paraphrastes.

Fingit Grotius commutationem personarum. Atqui semper locutus hic Propheta est, nec indi- cium apparet mutatæ personæ. Adhæc separat ille, quæ in textu conjuncta sunt, nam quæ de pha- retra Elam, de curribus, de equitibus, de clypeo Kir dicta, cohærent, & continuantur versu præsenti: quod illis Sagittariis, curribus & militibus clypeis nudatis coruscantibus implendæ sint valles electæ, fertilissimæ, & amœnissimæ, plenæ futuræ quadri- garum, è quibus pugnari solebat; quodque equites posituri sint (tabernacula sua) ad portam: quod im- pletum 2. Reg. 24, 20. Non ergo saltus hic fin- gendus à decem tribubus in Judæam: à Salmanas- sare ad Sennacheribum. Neque congruunt ea, quæ v. 11. habentur, tempori Sennacheribi. ET NON SUSPEXISTIS AD EUM, QUI FE- CERAT EAM. Nempe urbem Hierosolyma, cu- jus possessionem Deus dedit Davidi, simulq; omnia quæ ad urbem augendam tuendamque erant necessa- ria.

Alii EAM REM intelligunt: quia DEUS bellum istud excitarat contra Jechoniam. Quod non adeo de bello Sennacheribi dicendum. ET OPERATOREM EJUS DE LONGE. Eum qui pridem urbis ejus condendæ auctor fuit. Alii: qui de longinqua terra vobis hostes adducet. Quæ interpretatio præferenda. NON VIDI- STIS. Non curabitis. Hæc, inquam, Ezechiæ & populo istius temporis non congruunt. Nam contrarium refertur 2. Par. 24. quod nempe cum- primis ad Deum in obsidione Sennacheribi pro- fugium habuerit Ezechias cum populo. Multo ergo minus aptari illi tempori possunt cætera : ET VOCABIT DOMINUS DEUS EXERCI- TUUM ILLA DIE AD FLETUM. Id est, cum Deus eos ad fletum vocaturus est. AD CAL- VITIUM. Id in luctu funebri erat vetitum, non in publico malo. ET ECCE GAVDIVM ET LÆTITIA. Vos interim non definetis convivia tan- quam in rebus lætis agitare. (Vos contrarium facie- tis ei, quod Deus per Prophetas jussurus est: animo Epicureo ridebitis admonitiones Propheticas)

## 22:15
Verse 15. GO, ENTER UNTO HIM, WHO DWELLS IN THE TABERNACLE] Better, who handles the money. OVER THE HOUSE] In the Hebrew: of a house not divine, but royal, as appears below 21:22. WHAT DOST THOU HERE?] What business have you here? He seems to have been an outsider like Doeg. Consider the opposite in Eliakim 21:23. OR AS IF ANY ONE HERE] In the Hebrew: or who is here for you? supply, is a kinsman. BECAUSE THOU HAST HEWN THEE OUT A SEPULCHRE HERE, HEWING IN THE HEIGHT A MEMORIAL DILIGENTLY] Great men were accustomed to build excellent monuments for themselves and their heirs. This man, inflated with riches, was imitating that.

Latin:

Vers. 15. VADE, INGREDERE AD EUM, QUI HABITAT IN TABERNACULO] Melius, qui pecunias tractat. PRAEPOSITUM TEMPLI] In Hebraeo: domus non divinae, sed regiae, ut apparet infra 21, 22. QUID TU HIC?] Quid tibi hic negotii est? vi- detur fuisse externus ut Doeg. Considera oppositum in Eliakimo 21, 23. AUT QUASI QUIS HIC] In Hebraeo: aut quis tibi hic? supple, cognatus est. QUIA EXCIDISTI TIBI HIC SEPULCHRUM, EXCIDISTI IN EXCELSO MEMORIALE DILI- GENTER] Viri magni solebant sibi haeredibusque suis monumenta egregia struere. Id iste homo divitiis infla- tus imitabatur.

## 22:16
Verse 16.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

## 22:17
BEHOLD THE LORD WILL CAUSE THEE TO BE CARRIED AWAY, AS A COCK IS CARRIED AWAY] In the Hebrew: The Lord will cast thee out by casting, O mighty man, i.e., He will cause you to live far outside the city. The sense is that he will be a leper, which the following also explains. AND AS A GARMENT SO HE WILL LIFT THEE UP] And by covering He will cover thee, namely your mustache according to the law concerning lepers, Leviticus 13:45. Where the same word is used as here, עטה.

Latin:

ECCE DOMINUS ASPORTARI TE FACIET, SICUT ASPORTATUR GALLUS GALLINACEUS] In Hebraeo: Dominus te projiciendo projiciet, o vir potens, i. e. efficiet, ut longe extra urbem habites. Sensus est, le- prosum fore, quod & sequentia explicant. ET QUASI AMICTUM SIC SUBLEVABIT TE] Et obtegendo obteget te, nempe mystacem tuum ex lege de leprosis Levit. 13, 45. Ubi idem verbum quod hic עטה.

## 22:18
Verse 18.

CROWNING HE WILL CROWN THEE WITH TRIBULATION] In the Hebrew: By rolling He will roll thee with wrappings: the same as 'He will cover'. AND AS A BALL HE WILL CAST THEE INTO A LARGE AND SPACIOUS LAND] Far outside the city, as a ball is accustomed to be thrown. The same as 'He will cast thee out by casting'. THERE SHALT THOU DIE] That is, you will be as one dead, which is accustomed to be said of lepers, Numbers 12:12. Josephus says of them: νεκρῶν μηδὲν διαφέροντας (differing in nothing from the dead). For Shebna did not die from leprosy, but returned to the city healed of it, not indeed having recovered that excellent dignity of the chamberlain, which in the meantime, as Isaiah predicts here, Eliakim, a most excellent man, had received, but nevertheless he was admitted to the royal council on account of his age and experience, which appears in 2 Kings 18:18, 26, 37.

Grotius wishes to foist upon us here again new commentaries concerning Shebna the leper, but one healed of leprosy and in turn admitted to the royal council: which he has devised, and has taken pains to insert into the text with his glosses, in order to maintain that this is the same Shebna who is introduced as the scribe of Hezekiah in 2 Kings 18. But in many ways he does violence to the Prophetic text, as will now be made clear. He correctly corrects the Vulgate from the Hebrew source and context. For the Hebrews have 'treasurer', and 'house' simply, not 'temple'. The text also in verses 21 and 22 clearly teaches that the royal house is to be understood. Whence Blessed Luther rightly translates: 'To the treasurer Shebna the steward.' But the Papists act foolishly while they wish to defend the Vulgate; and therefore they make him a priest, against the protest of the text. However, these things refute Grotius with his leper Shebna: First, because the Prophet testifies that he had built for himself in vain such a magnificent tomb in Jerusalem, because he is to be cast far away into foreign lands, and will die ingloriously. Then, because the Lord threatens him not with leprosy, but with exile. The Hebrew is thus correctly rendered by Osiander: 'Behold, the Lord will hurl you here and there, as a strong man hurls (something), and will cover you with covering.' (So that the sense may be: You will wander in exile; then you will die ingloriously without any honor of burial.) 'With a whirling he will whirl you away, like a ball into a spacious land,' i.e., you will be tossed about by various misfortunes in exile, nowhere standing safely, just as a ball is thrown now here, now there by those playing in a wide region. Blessed Luther in this place wishes it to be translated thus: 'Behold, the Lord will cast you, as a giant casts, and will cover you, and will whirl you, like a ball into a spacious land': i.e., after you have been cast out and have come to Babylon, there you will be tossed up and down, like a ball, no rest of body or soul will come to you. Which Grotius very badly perverts thus: 'And by covering he will cover you,' namely your mystic [covering], from the law concerning lepers in Lev. 13:45. 'By rolling he will roll you' with the wrappings of lepers, the same as 'he will cover'. The latter parts certainly can in no way be taken concerning the wrapping of lepers: since they speak openly of a whirling: 'By whirling he will whirl you with a whirling, like a ball.' Which in no way befit a leper. Grotius retains the copulative particle, 'AND AS A BALL HE WILL SEND YOU,' and thus tears those words from the preceding ones. But that [particle] is not in the sources, and so that comparison pertains to the former things and the verb must be repeated from the context, just as a ball is whirled by the hands. And what is that 'INTO A WIDE AND SPACIOUS LAND' to a leper? Grotius explains it as far outside the city. But the text speaks openly of a varied whirling into a spacious land. Finally, when it is added, 'THERE YOU WILL DIE,' what is more certain than that it is predicted that that Shebna must die in exile. Grotius, however, perverts it thus: 'THERE YOU WILL DIE,' i.e., you will be equal to a dead man, which is wont to be said of lepers in Num. 12:12. And he disguises his commentaries: For Shebna did not die from leprosy, but was healed of it and returned to the city, not indeed having recovered that excellent dignity of the chief steward, which in the meantime, as Isaiah predicts here, Eliakim the best of men had received, but yet was admitted to the royal council on account of his age and experience, which appears in 2 Kings 18:26, 27. But this is openly to contradict the text. For it is clearly predicted that Shebna is to be whirled about in exile, and that he himself will die there, and will not be worthy of his glorious monument, which he had taken care to have cut for himself in vain. But whence those things about leprosy, whence those things about a return to the city, Grotius? If he were indeed the same Shebna who is commemorated in 2 Kings 18, it would be better, so that violence is not done to the present text, to say with Osiander that he who was Secretary under Hezekiah ascended to a higher dignity under an impious successor, but on account of pride and impiety was cast off by God and died miserably in exile. But others, as I have said, believe he was a different person.

AND THERE WILL BE THE CHARIOT OF YOUR GLORY, THE DISGRACE OF THE HOUSE OF YOUR LORD.] Where you will be relegated from the city, ride, as much as you please, in your magnificent chariot, which you have prepared for yourself. That yields to the disgrace of Ahaz, who placed you, a man of no faith, in the highest position.

We add the explanation of Jerome: As a ball, if it is sent onto a slope, cannot stand, but rolls with a swift course: so also you will be led down to a very wide land, which we may understand as either Egypt or the plains of Babylonia; there you will die, and there will be the chariots of your glory, all the power and wealth with which you now walk supported, there you will feel the disgrace of your house: because you will suffer these things on account of evil works and the violated temple of your God.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

CORONANS CORONABIT TE TRIBULA- TIONI] In Hebraeo: Convolvendo convolvet te involucris: idem quod obteget. ET QUASI PILAM MITTET ET IN TERRAM LATAM ET SPATIOSAM] Longe extra urbem, ut pilae mitti solet. Idem quod projiciendo projiciet. IBI MORIERIS] Id est, eris par mortuo quod de leprosis dici solet Num. 12, 12. Josephus de iis: νεκρῶν μη- δὲν διαφέροντας. Nam Subna non mortuus fuit ex lepra, sed ab ea sanatus in urbem rediit, non quidem recuperata illa eximia dignitate κωροπαλάτε, quam interim, ut hic praedicit Esaias, Eliacim vir optimus acceperat, sed tamen admotus ob aetatem & experientiam consilio regio, quod apparet 2. Reg. 18, 18. 26. 37.

Nova hic iterum Commenta nobis obtrude- re vult Grotius, de Sebna leproso, sed à lepra sanato & consilio regio vicissim admoto: quæ excogita- vit, glossisque suis textui ingerere sategit, ut obtine- ret eundem esse Sebnam, qui ut scriba Ezechiæ tem- pore introducitur 2. Reg. 13. Sed multis modis vim textui Prophetico facit, uti jam patebit. Vulga- tam recte corrigit ex Ebræo fonte & contextu. Nam Ebræa thesaurarium habent, & domum simpli- citer, non templum. Textus etiam v. 21. 22. lucu- lenter docet, domum regiam intelligi. Unde B. Lutherus probe vertit: Zum Schatꝫmeister Seb- na den Hofmeister. Nugas vero agunt Papistæ, dum Vulgatam tueri volunt; ideoque eum Sacerdotem faciunt, reclamante textu. Grotium autem cum leproso suo Sebna hæc refellunt: Primo quod Pro- pheta testetur, frustra ipsum sibi sepulcrum Hie- rosolymis tam magnificum extruxisse, quia pro- cul in peregrinas terras projiciendus, & inglorius morietur. Tum quod non lepram, sed exilium minetur ei Dominus. Ebræa ita recte ab Osian- dro redduntur: Ecce Dominus hinc inde jactabit te, sicut jactat (aliquid) vir fortis, & operiendo operiet te. (ut sensus sit: Vagaberis in exilio; deinde inglorius morieris sine ullo honore sepulturæ.) Circumagitatione circumagit abit te, sicut pila in terram spatiosam, i. e. variis casibus in exilio jactaberis, nullibi tuto con- sistens, perinde ut pila in lata regione nunc huc, nunc illuc à ludentibus projicitur. B. Lutherus in h. l. sic verti vult: Ecce Dominus projiciet te, sicut projicit gigas, & operiet te, & circumagitabit te, sic- ut globum in terra spatiosa: i. e. postquam fueris projectus & veneris in Babylonem, ibi jactaberis sur- sum & deorsum, sicut globus, nulla tibi neque corpo- ris neꝫ animi quies continget. Quæ pessime ita per- vertit Grotius: Et obtegendo obteget te, nempe my- stacem tuum, ex lege de leprosis Lev. 13, 45. Convol- vendo convolvet te involucris, idem quod obteget. Posteriora certe nullo pacto de involucro leproso- rum accipi possunt: quum palam de circumagita- tione loquantur: Circumagitando circumagitabit te circumagitatione, sicuti pilam. Quæ nullate- nus leproso conveniunt. Grotius particulam co- pulandi retinet, ET QUASI PILAM MIT- TET TE, atque ita ista à præcedentibus divellit. Sed ea in fontibus non habetur, adeoque compara- tio ista ad priora pertinet & ἀπὸ κοινõ verbum re- petendum est, sicut pila manibus circumagitatur. Et quid illa IN TERRAM LATAM ET SPA- CIOSAM ad leprosum? Grotius exponit longe extra urbem. Sed textus de varia circumagitatio- ne in terram spatiosam aperte loquitur. Denique quum addatur, IBI MORIERIS, quid certius, quam quod Sebnæ illi in exilio moriendum esse prædicatur. Grotius autem ita pervertit: IBI MORIERIS, i. e. par eris mortuo, quod de leprosis dici solet Num. 12, 12. Et prætexit sua commenta: Nam Sebna non mortuus fuit ex lepra, sed ab ea sana- tus in urbem rediit, non quidem recuperata illa exi- mia dignitate ὑπερπαλάτε, quam interim, ut hic prædicit Esaias, Eliakim vir optimus acceperat, sed tamen admotus ob ætatem & experientiam consilio regio, quod apparet 2. Reg. 18, 26. 27. Sed hoc est pa- lam contradicere textui. Nam in exilio circum- agitandum esse Sebnam, ibique ipsum moriturum, nec monumento suo glorioso, quod frustra sibi excidi curarat, dignum futurum, luculenter prædicitur. Unde vero illa de lepra, unde illa de reditu in urbem Grotius? Si maxime idem Sebna foret, qui 2. Reg. 18. commemoratur, præstaret, ne textui præsenti vis inferatur, cum Osiandro dicere, quod qui sub Ezechia Secretarius, sub impio successore ad altiorem dignitatem adscenderit, sed propter superbiam & im- pietatem à Deo abjectus in exilio misere mortuus sit Sed alii,uti dixi, diversum eum fuisse credunt.

ET IBI ERIT CURRUS GLORIÆ TUÆ, I- GNOMINIA DOMUS DOMINI TUI.] Ubi eris rele- gatus ab urbe, vehere, quantum lubet, curru tuo magni- fico, quem tibi parasti. Cedit id dedecori Achazo, qui te hominem nullius fidei in summo loco posuit.

Addimus Hieronymi explicationem : Sicut pila, si mittatur in proclive, stare non potest, sed ve- loci cursu volvitur: ita & tu ad terram latissimam de- duceris, quam aut Ægyptum aut Babyloniæ campos intelligamus; ibid, morieris, & ibi erunt currus gloriæ tuæ,omnes potentiæ & opes,quibus nunc fultus incedis, ibi senties ignominiam domus tuæ: quia propter o- pera mala, & violatum templum Dei tui ista patie- ris.

## 22:19
Verse 19. AND I WILL EXPEL YOU FROM YOUR STATION] Namely, by the occasion of leprosy.

Lepers were not accustomed to be carried about at will in magnificent chariots. And therefore the words there, 'There will be the chariot of your glory,' mean nothing other than that his pride would have such an end, namely in exile, when he is about to perish with a miserable death, he will be honored with no glory of burial, he who had previously been accustomed to be carried in a magnificent chariot, and that this would result in his disgrace: or rather [the disgrace] of the family of the King of Lords; which plural Blessed Luther observes: 'There is here,' he says, 'to be divined who those Lords are.' He seems to have survived after Hezekiah under Manasseh, who was also led away captive. The Prophet adds for the sake of greater confirmation: 'I will expel you from your station, and I will depose you from your ministry.' Who therefore would presume that he was again admitted to the royal council?

Latin:

Vers. 19. ET EXPELLAM TE DE STATIONE TUA] Nempe per occasionem lepræ.

Leprosi non vehi solebant pro lubitu curri- bus magnificis. Ideoque verba ibi, Erit currus gloriæ tuæ, nihil aliud volunt, quam quod finem ta- lem habitura sit superbia ipsius, in exilio nempe, cum misera morte interiturus, nulla gloria sepul- turæ honorabitur, qui antea magnifico curru vehi consueverat, quodque ignominiæ ejus hoc cessu- rum sit: vel potius familiæRegis Dominorum; quem pluralem observat B. Lutherus: Est hic,inquit, di- vinandum,qui sint illi Domini. Videtur superstes post Ezechiam fuisse sub Manasse, qui quoque est captivus abductus. Addit Propheta majoris βεβαιώσεως ergo: Expellam te de statione tua, & de ministerio tuo deponam te. Quis ergo præsumat,eum denuo fuisse in consilium regium adscitum?

## 22:20
IN THAT DAY I WILL CALL MY SERVANT] ELIAKIM THE SON OF HILKIAH] It is most plain that this is he who was the chief steward at the time of Rabshakeh. See the cited place 2 Kings 18.

Latin:

IN DIE ILLO VOCABO SERVUM MEUM] ELIAKIM FILIUM HILKIÆ] Planissimum est, hunc eum esse, qui erat κεφοπαλάτης tempore Rabsacis. Vide dictum locum 2. Reg. 18.

## 22:21
Verse 21.

AND I WILL CLOTHE HIM WITH YOUR TUNIC AND WITH YOUR BELT I WILL STRENGTHEN HIM] For the highest of the nobles had excellent garments and belts.

AND HE SHALL BE AS A FATHER TO THE INHABITANTS OF JERUSALEM AND THE HOUSE OF JUDAH ] He expressed the duty of a good magistrate most excellently by the word father.

That this is indeed most plain does not appear, since it is nothing new to find different people whose names are the same and whose parents are of the same name. To Osiander, however, it seems that the same Eliakim, as we have said, who was set over the royal house under Hezekiah, was cast down from that dignity under the impious King Manasseh, but was finally restored, not in the former manner, but to a greater dignity. For he thinks it likely that this Eliakim governed the Kingdom of Judah in the meantime, while Manasseh returned from Assyrian captivity: and afterwards remained (on account of his faithful administration of the kingdom) in the highest dignity and power under King Manasseh, who had by then turned to God. Those magnificent promises which are subjoined here indicate that he was certainly not an ordinary prefect of the palace, but one of distinguished authority and more eminent power.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ET INDUAM ILLUM TUNICA TUA ET CIN- GULO TUO CONFORTABO EUM] Habebant enim summi procerum vestes & cinctus eximios.

ET ERIT QUASI PATER HABITANTIBUS JERUSALEM ET DOMUS JUDA ] Optime voce pa- tris expressit boni magistratus officium.

Id vero planissimum esse non apparet,quum nihil novi sit reperiri diversos, quorum nomina eadem & parentes ejusdem sint nominis. Osiandro tamen videtur eundem, uti diximus, Eliakim qui præpositus domus Regiæ sub Ezechia fuit, sub im- pio rege Manasse de ea dignitate deturbatum, tan- dem vero restitutum esse, non priori modo, sed ma- jori dignitati. Verisimile enim esse censet, hunc Eliakim gubernasse interim Regnum Juda, dum Manasses è captivitate Assyriaca rediit: & postea permansisse (propter fidelem regni administratio- nem) in summa dignitate & potentia apud Regem Menassem jam ad Deum conversum. Non vulga- rem sane prætorio præfectum, sed eum insigni au- toritate ac potestate eminentiori, magnificæ illæ promissiones, quæ hic subjunguntur, indicant.

## 22:22
Vers. 22.

AND I WILL LAY THE KEY OF THE HOUSE OF DAVID UPON HIS SHOULDER ] A figure of a key woven into the ephod, from which his office might be known.

It is a phrase of Scripture, to lay a key upon the shoulder, just as the government is said to be upon the shoulder in Isaiah 9:6, because by the key is uniquely understood the office of the key, which is imposed upon the shoulder of someone when he is placed in charge of an office, just as the fasces are said to be carried. There is no reason, therefore, to imagine such a figure of a key woven in. Thus, when in Revelation 3:7 Christ is said from this passage to have the key of David, it is certainly not understood that he has an ephod on which a key is woven.

AND HE SHALL OPEN HIM, AND THERE SHALL BE NONE WHO SHUTS, HE SHALL SHUT, AND THERE SHALL BE NONE WHO OPENS] That is, he shall perform his office with the highest approval of men, with no one contradicting. The mystical sense is in the Gospel of Matthew 16, 19.

Nay, with the highest authority and power. But why does he not seek a mystical sense in the passage of Apocalypse 3, 7, along with Cyril and others? Did he perhaps wish to gratify the Roman Pontiff, the adulterine and putative successor of Peter? Whom the Jesuits say is prefigured here, as can be seen in Tirinus. But they suppose that Eliakim was a Pontiff or Priest: whom Grotius, however, makes prefect of the court. How then will he be a type of the Roman Pontiff? And why do they not rather make Shebna, his predecessor, the type: whose predicates experience proves to belong more truly to the Roman Pontiff.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

ET DABO CLAVEM DOMUS DAVID SUPER HUMERUM EJUS] Clavis figuram intextam epomidi, unde functio ejus nosceretur.

Phrasis Scripturæ est, clavem super humerum dare, sicut super humerum esse principatum Es.9, 6. quia per clavem unice intelligitur munus clavis, quod humero alicujus imponitur, cum muneri præficitur,uti fasces geri dicuntur. Non ergo est, quod fingamus ejusmodi figuram clavis intextam. Sic cum Apoc. 3, 7. ex hoc loco Christus habere cla- vem David dicitur, non intelligitur certe habere epomida, cui clavis intexta.

ET APERIET EUM, ET NON ERIT QUI CLAU- DAT, CLAUDET, ET NON ERIT, QUI APE- RIAT] Id est, summa cum hominum approbatione fun- getur suo munere, nemine contradicente. Mysticus sen- sus in Evangelio Matth. 16, 19.

Imo summa cum autoritate ac potestate. Cur autem sensum mysticum non quærit in loco Apoc. 3, 7. cum Cyrillo & aliis? An gratificari for- taffis voluit Romano Pontifici, adulterino & puta- tivo Petri successori? quem hic figuratum dicunt Jesuitæ, ut apud Tirinum videre est. Sed illi sup- ponunt, Eliakim fuisse Pontificem vel Sacerdotem: quem vero aulæ præfectum facit Grotius. Quomo- do ergo typus erit Romani Pontificis? Et cur non potius Sebnam antecessorem ipsius typum faciunt: cujus prædicata verius Romano Pontifici compe- tere experientia comprobat.

## 22:23
Verse 23. AND I WILL FASTEN HIM AS A PEG IN A FAITHFUL PLACE] I will place him in an excellent state, θαυμαστῶ, as נאמן is translated in Deuteronomy 28, 59. Compare what is below in 25.

AND HE SHALL BE FOR A THRONE OF GLORY TO HIS FATHER'S HOUSE] Better: the truth; and he shall be for the honor of the throne: that is, for the king.

TO HIS FATHER'S HOUSE] Understand &: and he shall be for the honor of the king, so also for the house of Judah, from whence he arose: as above in 21.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ET FIGAM ILLUM PAXILLUM IN LOCO FI- DELI] Ponam illum in statu eximio, θαυμαστῶ ut נאמן vertitur Deut. 28, 59. Confer quod infra 25.

ET ERIT IN SOLIUM GLORIÆ PATRIS SUI] Melius veritas; & erit honori folio: id est, regi.

DOMUI PATRIS SUI] Subaudi &: & regi hono- ri erit, sic & domui Judæ, unde ortus est: ut supra 21.

## 22:24
Verse 24. AND THEY SHALL HANG UPON HIM ALL THE GLORY OF HIS FATHER'S HOUSE] All the courtly dignities of the house of Judah shall hang from him: for it returns to the simile of the peg.

DIVERS KINDS OF VESSELS, EVERY LITTLE VESSEL, AND FROM THE VESSELS OF THE CUPS, EVEN TO EVERY VESSEL OF MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS] For divers kinds of vessels, it is in the Hebrew: הצאצאים והצפעות which some translate as sons and grandsons. But the continuation of the translation makes it more credible that these are names of keys, one of which pertained to the exit from the house, the other πρὸς τὸν ἀφεδρῶνα. For that is what the Hebrew words sound like. Furthermore, by keys, as also by vessels, are understood the very ministries of the court, which were clearly to be in the power of Eliakim. For vessel of musical instruments you may well substitute vessel of flagons: that is, flagons: just as vessel of cups are cups: from the cups wine is poured into the flagons.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET SUSPENDENT SUPER EUM OMNEM GLORIAM DOMUS PATRIS EJUS] Ab ipso pende- bunt omnes dignitates aulicæ domus Judæ: redit enim ad similitudinem paxilli.

VASORUM DIVERSA GENERA, OMNE VAS PARVULUM, ET VASIS CRATERARUM, USQUE AD OMNE VAS MUSICORUM] Pro vasorum diversa genera, est in Hebræo: הצאצאים והצפעות quod nonnulli filios & nepotes vertunt. Sed continuatio transla- tionis magis facit credibile esse hæc nomina clavium, qua- rum altera ad exitum è domo pertinebat, altera πρὸς τὸν ἀ- φεδρῶνα. Id enim sonant Hebrææ voces. Porro per cla- ves, ut & per vasa, intelliguntur ipsa aulæ ministeria, quæ plane futura erant in Eliakimini potestate. Pro vas Musi- corum bene reponas vas lagenarum: id est, lagenas: sicut vas craterum sunt crateres: ex crateribus vinum funditur in lagenas.

## 22:25
Verse 25. THE PEG THAT HAD BEEN FASTENED IN A FAITHFUL PLACE SHALL BE TAKEN AWAY] Excellent. That is, Shebna shall be deposed on account of leprosy.

AND IT SHALL BE BROKEN, AND SHALL FALL, AND THAT WHICH HAD HUNG UPON IT SHALL PERISH] With him removed, all his clients shall be removed at the same time. For new masters of the court wish to have the ministers throughout the whole court beholden to themselves.

BECAUSE THE LORD HAS SPOKEN] This is the decree of God.

Latin:

Vers. 25. AUFERETUR PAXILLUS QUI FIXUS FUE- RAT IN LOCO FIDELI] Eximio. Id est, Sobna destitue- tur ob lepram.

ET FRANGETUR, ET CADET, ET PERIBIT QUOD PEPENDERAT IN EO] Ipso remoto, simul re- movebuntur omnes ejus clientelæ. Volunt enim novi magistri aulæ ministros per totam aulam habere sibi obno- xios.

QUIA DOMINUS LOCUTUS EST] Dei hoc est decretum.

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

The desolation of Tyre on account of pride for 70 years, and its trade once to be consecrated to the Lord.

THE BURDEN OF TYRE] Nothing is to be thought of here concerning Nebuchadnezzar, and much less concerning Alexander the Great. For all these prophecies cohere among themselves, and pertain to the nearest times. The prophecy which preceded was pronounced while Shalmaneser was besieging the city, and it contains both these matters and those which followed under Sennacherib. At the same time, it was both revealed by God and predicted and written down by the Prophet, which now follows concerning Tyre, and was fulfilled not long after. For as we learn from Menander of Ephesus, and from Josephus in the ninth book of his Antiquities, the King of the Assyrians, Shalmaneser, having subdued Samaria—which Menander includes under the name of the Phoenicians (we have shown, however, in Book I of De Veritate Religionis Christianae, that the name of the Phoenicians is extended quite broadly among the Greeks)—waged war upon the Tyrians, fought with a fleet, and caused the prices of goods among the Tyrians to be greatly increased. Finally, he himself departing, left guards at the rivers and aqueducts, who would keep the Tyrians from all water (and undoubtedly from commerce): and this was endured by the Tyrians for five years. If you add to these five years the two during which the King himself remained in those places, you will have seven years: which number I judge must be restored in all three places of this chapter, just as we said above at 7, 8 that שבע should be read instead of שבעים. Doubtless, the error is equal on both sides, with the י having been wrongly added by the scribes, or the signs of the septenary and septuagenary numbers, which were perhaps once distinguished—as they are now among the Arabs by the addition of a single dot, which would make tens out of units—having been confused.

Grotius again brings forth a new gloss, and for its sake accuses the Hebrew truth of corruption in three places in verse 15 and following. But if the sources are to be corrected because of a preconceived opinion, what certainty will be left in the Holy Scriptures? Nor is there any weight in the argument which he draws from the συνεχείᾳ (continuity) and the reason of time. For the thing itself teaches that not all prophecies in this or other Prophets cohere regarding Chronology: and even here the Interpreters observe the reason of the συνεχείας (continuity). Among these, St. Jerome says: As we read above concerning the divine threat against Babylon and the Philistines, and Moab, Egypt, and the Idumeans and the Israelites, that they insulted the captivity of His people. So also now, the prophecy is woven against Tyre, both an enemy and an insulter of the subversion of Jerusalem, because she herself is also to be destroyed by the same enemy. Let us read the histories of the Greeks, and especially of those who describe the wars of the Assyrian nation: and there we will find that after the captivity of Jerusalem, the Palestinians and Arabs, and Damascenes, and subsequently the Egyptians were subverted, etc. Furthermore, the history brought forward by Grotius does not fit the prophecy. For although Shalmaneser declared war on the Tyrians and fought with them with a fleet, the Tyrians were not nevertheless conquered; indeed, they obtained a notable victory against Shalmaneser and the Phoenician fleet, as Alexander the Tyrian testifies in Josephus, Book IX of the Jewish Antiquities. Here, however, it is predicted that the Tyrians would have to migrate to foreign seats, and that these would be brought to ignominy, and that Tyre would be devastated and would be in oblivion. Furthermore, the Prophet inculcates three times that Tyre would be cast down not just for five or seven, but for seventy years: nor is there any indication or trace of corruption of the text. For the Codices agree. The Hebrews, Chaldeans, Greeks, and Latins agree entirely. So that it would be utterly rash and profane to correct the sacred text here. Indeed, the Holy Spirit took care that there would be no room for correction, when after the words, 'And it shall be in that day, you will be in oblivion, O Tyre, seventy years,' He added, AS THE DAYS OF ONE KING. Which certainly are completely contrary to the Grotian commentary about the corruption of the text. For are seven years the days of one King? But seventy years are rightly called the days of one King, whether you look at the days of his life, as it is established that David lived for so many years; or even of his reign, as Oecolampadius explains: since at most no one reigned beyond seventy years in that age. Whence also Zwingli on this passage: It appears that a King among the Tyrians was sometimes made so advanced in age that he presided over affairs for LXX years. Others, with Piscator, understand the years of the Babylonian kingdom, during which it was still to stand. Grotius explains these words, 'as the days of one King,' i.e., how long the life of Shalmaneser will last. But that lacks a foundation, and does not fit. For did Shalmaneser live only seven years? To say nothing of the fact that the Hebrews were not accustomed to designate their numbers in the same way as the Arabs, which Grotius assumes gratuitously. Finally, we see how much the sense of the Prophet's words must be corrupted so that it may serve the Grotian hypothesis. For when it is held in the text that Tyre has been DEVASTATED, v. 1, Grotius explains it as stripped of wealth. Which are very different things. When the Prophet in v. 7 threatens that the Tyrians are to pass over into other lands, and that their feet will lead them far away to wander, so that they are forced to go into exile from their seat, which cannot happen when they are closed off from exit on all sides, Grotius invents that before the exits were closed, many migrated to maritime places, however distant. But it is manifest that captivity and exile are being predicted. Her own feet will lead her far away to wander: i.e., those who survive the slaughter in the captured city will migrate into a far-distant land into exile.

Where Grotius understands by 'feet' the feet of ships, or even oars: since the Latins call the ropes by which sails are stretched 'feet'. And Plautus calls the sailors themselves 'naval feet'. Nor do those words signify only a bare siege, but rather ruin and destruction; since it was added, 'they shall be in pain in Egypt, when they shall hear of Tyre,' viz. destroyed. This is a prophecy, says Jerome, that the Egyptians, after they feared a most powerful and neighboring nation destroyed by a long siege, might know that destruction also approaches themselves. 'Pass over the seas,' etc. Again, for 'sea and Tarshish' the LXX translated 'Carthage'. We read in the histories of the Assyrians that the besieged Tyrians, after they saw no hope of escaping, fled in ships to Carthage, and to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea. Whence it is also said in Ezekiel, 'No reward was given to him, nor to his army for Tyre': because all the wealth of the city was transferred, and the nobles also left it empty. This is Jerome. Who thought this over Tyre the crowned, which shone with royal majesty among other cities, whose merchants were princes and whose traffickers were the honorable of the earth? Who could have thought in his counsels to overturn so powerful a city, whose merchants were so rich that even one could have supported an entire army? The Lord of hosts has thought this, to bring down (weaken) the pride of all glory and to bring to ignominy all the honorable of the earth. 'Pass through thy land, as a river, O Tyre, daughter of the sea' (situated in the sea and as if born from the sea) 'because there is no girdle for thee any more.' Osiander explains these things thus: You will quickly depart into exile through your land (which you have on the continent): nor will you have any strength anymore, by which you can take care of your affairs. For they are said to gird themselves who are prepared to manage their affairs properly. Grotius interprets these things thus: PASS THROUGH THY LAND; into your land, that is, into one of your colonies. AS A RIVER, which is carried from a fountain into the sea. Thus you go as far as the Ocean, if you can. DAUGHTER OF THE SEA. In Hebrew: to the daughter (that is, the city) of Tarshish, that is, Tartessus, or Spain, which had frequent commerce with the Tyrian. THERE IS NO GIRDLE FOR THEE ANY MORE. By 'girdle' understand the fortifications placed around the city, which the enemy then held. Thus Grotius; but B. Luther more correctly [explains] these things: 'Pass into the land as a river': a notable figure, which signifies the future dispersion: just as a river is carried in its first course, leaving everything behind it: so you, being driven away, will leave your seats, your city. THERE IS NO GIRDLE ANY MORE. He calls the polity, the empire, the kingdom a 'girdle', as in Job ch. 12, 'He looseth the bond of kings.' And in the marginal gloss: 'Da ist kein Gurt (kein Regiment, und Oberkeit) mehr.' HIS HAND HE STRETCHED OUT OVER THE SEA, HE SHOOK THE KINGDOMS. In Hebrew: He terrified the kingdoms: namely, by the example of such a city.

To v. 13, which is very obscure, Grotius has annotated these things not inappropriately. BEHOLD THE LAND OF THE CHALDEANS. In which is the city of Babylon, whence Berosus's books are by some called Chaldaic, by others Babylonian. SUCH A PEOPLE WAS NOT. Better: This people is not. The Chaldeans were a people: now they are a province of the Assyrians. What wonder then, if the same Assyrians harass the Tyrians. ASSUR FOUNDED IT: THEY BROUGHT ITS STRONG ONES INTO CAPTIVITY. From the Hebrew you may translate best: The Assyrian filled that (land) with men of the desert: they erected its fortresses. The Assyrian led men of the 'skenitas' there: the Assyrians founded the fortresses that appear there. THEY DUG UP ITS HOUSES. Rather, they raised them up. For this meaning of the verb 'ur' coheres better with the preceding and following. THEY SET IT IN RUIN, that is, they made that land or people a servant to themselves, or made their towns into huts. For 'Mapalia' is a Punic word, as Festus and Servius note, which is written in Hebrew as here 'mapaliu'. The version and interpretation of Junius comes to almost the same thing: 'That land of the Chaldeans, this people was not, (now there is no Republic of theirs, but it has come into the power of another) since the Assyrian founded it, for the Barbarians (he established in it barbarian colonists unknown to the region). They had erected their exploratory watchtowers (Junius understands this of the Babylonians, that they confirmed themselves in every way) they raised its palaces: (the Assyrian) disposed it into ruin, (i.e., he overturned the whole region) so that they might exhibit that as the 'protasis', and the prophecy be confirmed by the example of the Babylonian Kingdom, which the ancestors of Sennacherib had occupied and overturned 2 Kings 17:24, C. 19:2, and the 'apodosis' be rendered in the following verse 14. HOWL, YE SHIPS OF THE SEA, FOR YOUR TYRE IS DEVASTATED.' Thus both that example and the application bring about ruin and devastation, but not a fruitless siege. Verse 14 certainly cannot be taken as referring only to a siege, that it was stripped of wealth: since the Prophet openly threatens desolation. B. Luther annotates these things on that verse: It is an obscure sentence, which if taken actively, is to be understood of the Chaldean devastation. But I take it passively, so that the sentence is: You will not be able to resist Alexander, who will conquer you. For he will also overturn Babylon, where there is not yet a people, (i.e., where there is not yet a Monarchy). The Hebrew sentence can be rendered thus: Behold the land of the Chaldeans, in which there is not yet a people whom Assur founded, so that it might be navigated, and he erected towers, and built palaces, and yet it is set in ruin. Whence in the German Bibles, as they are illustrated by that Weimar Paraphrase, these things are thus in v. 12, 13, 14.
