And truly, when it is a question here of a far most sumptuous feast, of a feast of fat things, of marrow and of wine on the lees, of foods most sumptuous, and of the purest wine, no more sumptuous feast has ever been prepared for all peoples than the preaching of the Gospel of Christ. Indeed, foods are not proposed in it which refresh the body: but foods are proposed which refresh the soul, indeed which preserve soul and body unto eternal life. External and worldly feasts satisfy for a short time, they do not cure perpetual hunger. But the Evangelical Feast so fills the faithful, that they never hunger for eternity. For in this feast is proposed the true heavenly manna John 6, 32. and water springing up into eternal life John 4. Christ himself is proposed to be eaten and drunk by faith, and in Christ the remission of sins, righteousness, salvation and eternal life. These are the dishes, these are the foods of the Evangelical feast. The Jews indeed dream of a carnal feast to be prepared by the Messiah, when he shall have gathered all the Jews from all nations and led them into a land flowing with milk and honey: at which he is to slaughter the greatest of all living creatures that God ever created, the bull Behemoth from the beasts, the Leviathan from the fishes, both of immense size, then also the bird Bar Juchne not much smaller, and is to provide the most generous wine, which was born in Paradise, and is still reserved there in the wine cellar of Adam: concerning which trifles see Buxtorf's Synag. Judaic. C. 36. p. 456. But those are altogether worthy of their authors, most foolish men. But they are unworthy of a lengthy review, much less a refutation. Let them wait for the bull, Leviathan, and that bird with the man from the cell of Adam, as long as they wish: for us it is certain that the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Rom. 14, 17. The Jews are nevertheless sounder thus far than Grotius, in that they acknowledge that a prophecy concerning the Messiah is held here, even if they interpret it carnally according to their custom.

Latin:

CONVIVIUM PINGVIUM) Vindicta Dei sæpe à Prophetis convivio comparatur, quia & consumit hostes, ut cibi consumuntur, & Deo gaudium parit.

VINDEMIÆ DEFECATÆ) Ex vino optimo.

Non desunt, qui de Convivio cruento expli- cent: quum in Sacris vindicta convivio compa- retur, & vinum iræ Dei, ac calix tribulationum & vindictæ non raro in Prophetis occurrunt. Luthe- rus ipse in Enarrat. quum credat, de excidio Judæo- rum novissimo antea actum esse, ita explicat. De mactatione impiorum dicit Dominus: Parabit Con- vivium in monte hoc: id est, totum populum con- gregabit in Hierusalem, ibi eos sinet per Romanos mactari. Pingues sunt divites. Medulla enim signi- ficat, quicquid est tenerrimum. Sic medulla tritici, id est, optimum triticum: vindemiæ defecatæ: re- cte, fecium expressarum; id est, ita delebit, ut ne fe- ces quidem relinquantur. Similiter Oecolampa- dius: Convivium pinguium & defecatorum ac me- dullatorum significat iram & indignationem Dei, si- cut frequenter Scriptura calicis nomine eandem indi- cat. Zach. 12. Ecce ego ponam calicem crapula omnibus populis in circuitu, h. e. calicem ebrieta- tis. Thren. 4. ad te quoq; perveniet calix & inebri- aberis. Et Jer. 21. Calix aureus in manu Domini. Nemo autem facile reperietur, qui de cæde Senna- cheribi cum Grotio explicarit. Neque obscurum est è verbis & contextu Prophetæ, de Convivio Ev- angelico sermonem hic esse: quod paratur fidelibus in regno Christi. Quia primo læta hic sunt omnia, & hilaritatem exprimunt convivii: Faciet Domi- nus exercituum omnibus populis in monte hoc convi- vium pinguium, convivium vindemiæ, pinguium, medullatorum, vindemiæ defecatæ. Neque vero de gaudio Deo ex vindicta hostium parando sermo est, sed de gaudio, quod populis obtinget per tam lautum convivium. Porro non uni tantum popu- lo id parandum à Domino, non Judæis aut Hiero- solymitanis, sed OMNIBUS POPULIS, dicente Propheta. Non ergo de vindicta adversus hostes, nedum de cæde Assyriorum hæc intelligi possunt: sed de Convivio, quod omnibus gentibus & popu- lis paratum est, quod nullum aliud est, quam Convi- vium Evangelicum. Adhæc parandum erat con- vivium istud in monte Zion, quem δεικτικῶς de- monstrat Propheta, IN MONTE HOC. Pa- ratum autem spirituale convivium est in monte Zi- on, quia in templo Hierosolymitano non tantum docuit Christus ipse, ac apparatum gratiæ & lauti- tias cœlestis epuli proposuit, sed ex monte Zion evulgandum etiam fuit Evangelium in universum mundum Esa. 2, 3. Et emittendum regni Christi sceptrum Psalm. 110, 4. Et quem habebimus cer- tiorem interpretem hujus lautissimi Convivii, quam eam, qui id nobis paravit? qui regnum Cæ- lorum convivio & Cœnæ magnæ ac nuptiis compa- rans, quodnam convivium prædixerit Esaias, pa- lam edocet Matth. 22. & Luc. 14. Quanquam etiam in V. T. Passim Convivium illud spirituale, & Evangelicum expositum sit Ps. 22, 27. Ps. 23, 5. Psalm 36, 9. Jerem. 9, 2. seqq. Cant. 6. imo ab ipso Propheta nostro c. 55, 1. seq. C. 65, 13. Ac profecto, quum hic de convivio longe lautissimo, de convivio pinguium, medullatorum & vini defecati, de cibis maxime opiparis, & vino purissimo agatur, nullum unquam lautius convivium populis omnibus para- tum est, quam prædicatio Evangelii Christi. Non proponuntur quidem in eo cibi, qui corpus refi- ciant: proponuntur autem cibi, qui reficiant ani- mam, imo qui conservent animam ac corpus ad vi- tam æternam. Externa & mundana convivia ad breve tempus exfatiant, perpetuæ fami non me- dentur. Convivium autem Evangelicum ita fide- les implet, ut nunquam esuriant in æternum. In hoc enim convivio proponitur manna cœleste ve- rum Joh. 6, 32. & aqua scaturiens in æternam vitam Joh. 4. proponitur ipse Christus fide manducandus & bibendus, & in Christo remissio peccatorum, justitia, salus & vita æterna. Hi sunt missus, hi sunt cibi Evangelici convivii. Judæi somniant quidem carnale convivium à Messia, ubi omnes Judæos ex omnibus nationibus congregaverit & in terram lacte & melle fluentem deduxerit, parandum: ad quod omnium, quæ Deus unquam creavit, maxima animantium, è jumentis taurum Behemoth, è pisci- bus Leviathan, utrumq; immensæ magnitudinis, tum avem quoq; Bar Juchne haut multo minorem mactaturus, ac generosissimum vinum adhibiturus sit, quod in Paradiso enatum, ibidemque adhuc in Adami cella vinaria reservetur: de quibus nugis vid. Buxtorfii Synag. Judaic. C. 36. p. 456. Sed dignæ illæ prorsus authoribus suis, hominibus ine- ptissimis. Indignæ autem prolixa recensione, ne- dum confutatione. Præstolentur illi taurum, Le- viathan & avem illam cum viro è cella Adami, quamdiu velint: nobis certum est, regnum Dei non esse cibum & potum, sed justitiam, pacem, & gaudium in Sp. Sancto. Rom. 14, 17. Saniores ta- men hactenus Judæi sunt Grotio, quod agnoscant, hic vaticinium de Messia haberi, etsi id pro more suo carnaliter interpretentur.

## 25:7
Vers. 7. AND HE WILL CAST DOWN ON THIS MOUNTAIN THE FACE OF THE COVERING CAST OVER ALL PEOPLE, AND THE VEIL THAT IS SPREAD OVER ALL NATIONS.) More correctly thus: The Lord will cast down on this mountain (that is, at this city) the face of the covering, which is wrapped over all peoples, and the covering, which is spread over all nations. By the name of covering and veil he denotes that terror from the Assyrian, which had as it were blinded all peoples.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET PRÆCIPITABIT IN MONTE ISTO FACIEM VINCVLI COLLIGATI SVPER OMNES POPVLOS, ET TELAM QVAM ORDITVS EST SV- PER OMNES NATIONES.) Rectius sic: Præcipitabit Do- minus in monte isto (id est, apud hanc urbem) faciem in volu- cri, quod involutum est super omnes populos, & operimentum, quod oppansum est omnibus gentibus. Involucri & operimen- ti nomine notat terrorem illum ab Assyrio, qui populos o- mnes velut excæcaverat.

## 25:8
Vers. 8. HE WILL SWALLOW UP DEATH.) That is, the dangers of death.

FOR EVER) That is, as long as Hezekiah shall live.

AND THE LORD GOD WILL TAKE AWAY THE TEAR FROM EVERY FACE.) Namely, of those who had been besieged.

A notable depravation of a famous Evangelical prophecy. For by this mountain is first to be understood not leaving the vicinity of the city, in which the camp of the Assyrians was placed. A mountain of such a kind is designated, on which all peoples can be gathered, so that they may enjoy the banquet of the Messiah. What, therefore, is more manifest than that some bodily mountain is not to be understood (for who will be of such capacity that he could contain all the nations of the earth?) but the spiritual mountain of the Church, Heb. 12, which has its name from Zion, because there was once an ordinary congregation, and because from there the Gospel also had to go forth into the whole world. Furthermore, by the face to wrap, that which is wrapped over all peoples, and the covering, which is spread over all nations, not the terror from the Assyrian, but a far more serious and universal evil is understood, which indeed had occupied not just certain peoples, or some nations, but all peoples and all nations universally. Upon all of whom, certainly, the terror from the Assyrian had not been struck. As a banquet and joy is prepared for all, so from all is the covering and sadness cast down. Which, therefore, the blessed Luther understands concerning the covering with which the dead are wrapped, which is common to all, because no one is exempt from death: especially because it is added; he will cast down death forever; which will be fulfilled when we are about to come forth from the coffin, and shall be raised from the dead. Whence in the marginal Gloss it has it thus: As the dead are wrapped, that is, He will make the dead alive. Which explanation, as it stands on its own footing, so not undeservedly these things, spoken generally about any covering with which all peoples are covered from the evils with which we are wrapped, are explained generally concerning the covering of ignorance, sins, calamities, ignominy, and concerning all the bonds of errors, sins, iniquities, miseries, death, corruption, since in Hebrew it is made הֲלוֹט הַלּוֹט a bond, a bond, or a wrapping, a wrapping, i.e., all bonds or wrappings. Every wrapping, every mournful habit shall be taken away, every mourning and cause for mourning shall be removed. Which phrase Brentius illustrates thus: He speaks of the mourning garment with which those who mourn dead friends are accustomed to be clothed: and which, when the time of mourning is finished, is accustomed to be laid aside again by its own rites, according to the custom of any nation. For all nations and peoples are said to be clothed in this garment, because death rules over them on account of sin, and by its tyranny takes away not only our friends, but also ourselves. Isaiah therefore teaches that this mourning garment is to be taken away and cast off on Mount Zion. But under that covering generally accepted there, it is certain that the sepulchral covering is also included. Whence Osiander: He will take away mortality. Nor does the blessed Luther deny, when with death also sin is designated by this word. For thus he has it in the Enarration of this place: AND HE WILL CAST DOWN; Translate it thus, and the face of all the wrapped ones will be devoured on that mountain, that is, he will destroy the wrapping with which all are wrapped. For death is before God as a wrapping with which the whole world is wrapped. This wrapping on Mount Zion, that is, in the Church, will be taken away from the pious. For this is the fruit and efficacy of the Gospel, that it may vivify the dead and take away death. Thirdly, when death is said to be cast down, it is not only about warding off the dangers of death, but the discourse is about death itself, which the Lord is said to be about to cast down, which certainly was not done when the Assyrians were struck down. Then the Israelites were indeed freed from the dangers of death at that time, but death itself was not cast down. Yet no one cast down and devoured it, except Christ, the death of death, just as he said in Hosea 13: O death, I will be your death, and O hell, I will be your plague. Fourthly, the distortion is to be detested, when the Prophetic words, He will cast down death forever, are thus perverted, until Hezekiah lives. The Prophet did not look to Hezekiah or his life by any little word, so far is it from being the case that, while he lived, he testified that the danger of death would be avoided: And how were the dangers of death cast down, as long as Hezekiah lived? For without doubt, not only the danger of death, but death itself was undergone by countless numbers among the people of God while he was living: although they escaped the danger of death at that time when the army of Sennacherib was struck down. Are they therefore to be said to have escaped it FOREVER, or at least while Hezekiah lived? The propriety of the letter must be retained entirely, concerning death cast down forever on Mount Zion, or in the Church. For he who keeps the word of Christ shall not see death forever, John 8, 15. What? That fifthly we have the Apostle as a clear interpreter of these words in 1 Cor. 15, with whose sense that most inept gloss of Grotius can in no way stand. For he explained the words of the Prophet both concerning Christ, and understood them concerning death forever overcome and devoured by him: DEATH IS SWALLOWED UP INTO VICTORY. For that which is swallowed up entirely into victory, that is not only for a certain time, but plainly totally and forever cast down. And the Apostle teaches that death is so swallowed up: as that which is forever defeated by the elect, whom they will be able to insult forever with a joyful song of victory: Where, O death, is your victory? Add that the Hebrew לנצח signifies both forever and into victory. Since, therefore, the Apostle proves the latter sense, it is manifest that it cannot be explained thus, UNTIL HEZEKIAH LIVES, without contradicting the Apostle. Sixthly, when the Prophet had prophesied concerning the covering, or bond and web in general, that it ought to be cast down on the holy mountain, now in particular he expresses the chief part of the bond and covering, namely death, which is to be cast down utterly: just as then he named another part of the covering, weeping, groaning, and tears, or the afflictions and calamities of this life which are the cause of them; since a heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day of their exit from their mother's womb, until the day of burial into the mother of all, Eccl. 14. Finally, the third, if I may so call it, part of the covering, namely ignominy and reproach, concerning which the Prophet: And he will take away the reproach of his people from the whole earth. For through sin we are wrapped in reproach, and clothed as if with ignominy: but through the Messiah all reproach, all ignominy and confusion had to be taken away. Therefore, St. Jerome is not inappropriately cited here: After the passion of the Lord, when He has delivered him from thirst and heat and whirlwind (for thus he explained the preceding parts), the Lord will make, not for the people of the Jews, but for all nations on Mount Sion, a feast of fat things, marrowy burnt offerings, and wine of the vintage refined, that He may cast down and cause to be absorbed the face of death and the bond by which all peoples shall be bound, and He shall break the net of death and the web with which He had caught all nations. And according to the Apostle: death shall be swallowed up forever. And the Lord shall take away the tear from every face, when, death being overcome, the kingdom of Christ shall have arrived, and the reproach of the human race, which had been created in the image of the Creator, shall have escaped the servitude of the Devil and of death. Hence, the wiping away of tears is also falsely restricted in the seventh place to the Jerusalemites besieged by Sennacherib. God is said to be about to take away the tear FROM EVERY FACE, just as He had indicated that there had been a mournful covering over all peoples and over all nations. Therefore, the discourse is not about the Jerusalemites alone. And just as the feast is to be prepared FOR ALL PEOPLES, so the mourning is to be taken away FROM EVERY FACE. Finally, it is interpreted concerning all the Elect

The Holy Spirit, Rev. 7:17. In these, the present prophecy will attain its full completion in the other life. The Lamb will rule them, and will lead them to the living fountains of waters, and will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more, nor will there be mourning, nor crying, nor will there be pain anymore. This is to cast down every trial by which we were enveloped, to cast down death forever, or into victory, and to take away every tear from every face, and every reproach of His people. Concerning which last point, our Brentius excellently says: The people of Christ glory from the Gospel in the great favor of GOD, in the many benefits which Christ obtained for them before God, in the liberation from all adversities, and thus from death itself. But behold, he is treated in this world as if he were most abject before God: he is exposed to all the most difficult dangers, he is oppressed by the impious, he is afflicted by extreme evils, he is held as filth and offscouring, and finally he is overwhelmed by a shameful death. But Christ, the Son of God, takes away this reproach throughout the whole earth, first by the preaching of His Gospel, because wherever the Gospel is preached, heavenly and perpetual glory is promised to all believers in place of worldly reproach: then He also takes it away in reality on the last day, so that the pious, freed from every reproach of this age, may enjoy heavenly and eternal glory. Wherefore, the Grotian gloss is also refuted in the eighth place from the subsequent confession and celebration of the faithful, verse 9. And the believers will say, namely, on that day: Behold, this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He will save us: This is the Lord, we have waited for Him; we will exult and rejoice in His salvation. For these words exhibit a faithful confession of the Messiah, who is God blessed forever: And He is our God or God with us because of the benefit of redemption; Whom all believers have awaited since the first promise in Paradise; who saves us, and in whose salvation בִּישׁוּעָתוֹ the faithful alone rejoice and exult: which joy is begun in this life, but will be consummated in the future life. For the discourse is about spiritual joy, with which we rejoice in God our Savior, and exult in His salvation: about that salvation which will come to pass, when death has been cast down or swallowed up forever, and mourning has been taken away, and every cause of mourning has been cast down, in that joy and salvation which will befall all peoples on Mount Zion through the Evangelical feast. Since the Prophet has explained the benefits of Christ thus far, he now proposes the duties of His people: which are trust in Him: Behold our Lord: We have waited for or we hope in Him. A confession declaring faith: They will say on that day: Behold, this is our God; this is the Lord. Finally, exultation and joy in the Lord: to which patience in adversities and obedience in works, which He demands, are required. Concerning which, Brentius can be compared here. Whence it is added: BECAUSE THE HAND OF THE LORD WILL REST ON THIS MOUNTAIN: For the hand of the Lord rests in the Church, there He obtains His kingdom; there He exerts His virtue and power; there He has His rest and delight. B. Luther, The hand of the Lord on this mountain. The virtue and power of God will be moved in the Church, because He liberates and gladdens it. Death being swallowed up forever, the people of God (so Jerome has it in this place) who shall have been liberated from the hand of death, will say to the Lord: Behold, this is our God, whom the incredulous thought to be only a man, and we have waited for Him, i.e., we have believed His words, because He has fulfilled His promises and will save us. Therefore, by His aid, having been snatched from the jaws of death, we will exult and rejoice in Him, and His hand and His power will rest on this mountain, of which we read above. When the Lord of Hosts has reigned on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has been glorified in the sight of His elders. Brentius not without reason warns that the hand of the Lord rested on Zion, i.e., the power and majesty of Christ, because He preached His Gospel in Jerusalem, and when He had ascended into Heaven, He sent the Holy Spirit there to His disciples, so that the rod of the Lord's power might go forth into the whole world, Ps. 110. It is too manifest that all these things sound of the benefits of the Messiah. Therefore also Calvin, who otherwise willingly perverts prophetic oracles, explains it of Christ: it is sufficiently certain, he says at verse 6, that destruction is not here denounced against the Gentiles or the Jews; but that both are invited together to a most sumptuous feast. And this is better established from the very words of Christ, while He compares the kingdom of Heaven to a wedding feast, which a King prepared for His Son, and to which He calls everyone indiscriminately, when those who had been invited before would not come. Nor is it doubtful to me that he speaks of the promulgation of the Gospel. And because it went forth from Mount Zion, he says that the Gentiles will come there to feast, because, where God proposed spiritual food to feed the souls of the whole world, it was the same as if He had prepared a common Table. And at verse 7, the true sense, in my judgment, is that the Lord promises that He will remove the veil by which they were held in blindness and ignorance. (That this sense is true, but not full, is evident from the above: for more things are comprehended under the name of the covering.) Therefore, by the light of the Gospel, these shadows have been dispelled. But he says that this will happen on Mount Zion: whence also the light of the word shone upon the whole world. Therefore, this passage must NECESSARILY be referred to the kingdom of Christ, for the light did not shine upon all men until Christ, the Sun of righteousness, arose, from whom all veils, coverings, and wrappings have been removed. At verse 8. He has destroyed death forever. The Prophet weaves together his argument. For in sum, he promises solid happiness under the kingdom of Christ. He therefore joins two things, which render happiness perfect and absolute. First, that life is perpetual, (for to those who are otherwise blessed for a time, it is miserable to perish.) Then, this life is joined with joy. For otherwise, death seems preferable to a sad and wretched life. He also adds that, with all ignominy removed, this life will be glorious, because otherwise the sad oppression of the people would have derogated from the faith of the prophecy. Concerning the time of fulfillment also, Calvin most correctly: Where, therefore, or when do these things have place? Undoubtedly these are to be referred to the universal kingdom of Christ: I say universal: because not only the beginning is to be regarded, but also the completion and the goal. And thus it ought to be extended to the second coming of Christ. Which is therefore called the day of redemption and restoration: since all things, which now seem confused, will be restored to their entirety and will put on a new form. This indeed pertains also to the redemption from Babylon, but since that was as it were a prelude and a slight taste of this, undoubtedly this promise is to be extended even to the last day.

Latin:

Vers. 8. PRÆCIPITABIT MORTEM.) Id est, peri- cula mortis.

IN SEMPITERNUM) Id est, donec vivet Eze- chias.

ET AVFERET DOMINVS DEUS LACHRY- MAM AB OMNI FACIE.) Eorum scilicet, qui obsefeffi fuerunt.

Insignis depravatio præclari vaticinii Evan- gelici. Nam per montem hunc primo intelligi ne- quit civitatis vicinia, in qua castra Assyriorum posita. Mons ejusmodi designatur, in quo omnes populi congregari possunt, ut convivio Messiae fruantur. Quid ergo manifestius, quam quod non intelligendus sit mons aliquis corporalis, (quis enim tantae erit capacitatis, ut omnes nationes terrae capere posset?) sed spiritualis mons Ecclesiae Ebr. 12. qui à Zione nomen habet, quod illic quondam congregatio ordinaria fuerit, quodq; inde etiam prodire debuerit Evangelium in orbem terrarum. Deinde per faciem involvere, quod involutum est super omnes populos, & operimentum, quod pansum omnibus gentibus, non terror ab Assyrio, sed longe gravius & universalius malum intelligitur, quod nempe non quosdam tantum populos, aut aliquas gentes, sed populos omnes, gentesq; universas occuparat. Quibus certe omnibus terror ab Assyrio incussus non erat. Ut convivium & laetitia paratur omnibus, ita ab omnibus praecipitatur operimentum & tristitia. Quod proinde B. Lutherus de operimento intelligit, quo involvuntur mortui, quod omnibus commune est, quia nemo à morte exemtus est: imprimis quia additur; precipitabit mortem in sempiternum; quod implebitur, cum è capulo prodituri sumus, & à mortuis excitabimur. Unde in Glossa marginali sic habet: Wie die Todten verhuͤllet werden, das ist, Er wird die Todten lebendig machen. Quae explicatio, uti suo stat talo, ita non immerito haec generaliter de quovis operimento dicta, quo omnes populi teguntur de malis, quibus involuti sumus, γενικῶς explicantur de operimento ignorantiae, peccatorum, calamitatum, ignominiae, & de vinculis omnibus errorum, peccatorum, iniquitatum, miseriarum, mortis, corruptionis, siquidem in Ebraeo fit הֲלוֹט הַלּוֹט vinculum, vinculum, vel involucrum, involucrum, h. e. omnia vincula vel involucra. Omne involucrum, omnis habitus lugubris auferetur, omnis luctus & causa lugendi tolletur. Quam phrasin ita illustrat Brentius: Loquitur de veste lugubri, qua indui solent hi, qui amicos mortuos lugent: & qua finito luctus tempore, iterum suis ritibus, pro more cujusvis gentis, deponi solet. Omnes enim gentes & populi hac veste induti dicuntur, quod mors dominatur in eos propter peccatum, & aufert sua tyrannide è vita non amicos tantum nostros, sed & nos ipsos. Docet igitur Esaias, quod hac lugubris vestis auferenda, & abjicienda sit in monte Zion. Sub illo autem operimento generaliter ibi accepto certum est, operimentum etiam sepulchrale comprehendi. Unde Osiander: Er wird die Sterbligkeit hinweg thun. Neque inficiatur B. Lutherus, cum morte etiam peccatum hac voce designari. Sic enim habet in Enarratione hujus loci: ET PRAECIPITABIT; Verte sic, & devorabitur in monte isto facies singulorum involutorum, id est, involucrum perdet, quo omnes sunt involuti. Est enim mors coram Deo, ceu involucrum, quo totus mundus involutus est. Hoc involucrum in monte Zion, id est, in Ecclesia, auferetur à piis. Hic enim Evangelii fructus est, & efficacia, ut mortuos vivificet & mortem tollat. Tertio cum precipitanda dicitur mors, non tantum de periculis mortis fugandis, sed de morte ipsa sermo est, quam praecipitaturus dicitur Dominus, quod certe non est factum, cum Assyrii caderentur. Tum à periculis mortis illo tempore liberati quidem sunt Israëlitae, mors autem ipsa praecipitata non est. Eam vero nemo praecipitavit, & devoravit, nisi Christus mors mortifactus, sicut dixit Ose. 13. O mors, ego ero mors tua, & ô inferne, ego ero pestis tua. Quarto στρεβλότης detestanda est, cum verba Prophetica, Praecipitabit mortem in sempiternum, sic pervertuntur, donec vivet Ezechias. Pro- pheta nullo verbulo Ezechiam aut vitam ejus re- spexit, tantum abest, ut dum vixerit ille, mortis pe- riculum declinatum iri testatus sit: Et quomodo mortis pericula præcipitata, donec vixit Eze- chias? Sine dubio enim non periculum tantum mortis, sed mortem etiam ipsam innumeri, eo vi- vente, subiere in populo Dei: licet periculum mortis tum temporis effugerint, cum Sennache- ribi exercitus cæsus fuit. Num ideo id IN SEM- PITERNUM, aut saltem dum vixit Ezechias, ef- fugisse dicendi sunt? Retinenda omnino est pro- prietas literæ, de morte in perpetuum præcipitata in monte Zion, vel in Ecclesia. Qui enim verbum Christi servat, mortem non videbit in æternum Joh. 8, 15. Quid? quod quinto Apostolum habeamus luculentum Interpretem horum verborum 1. Cor. 15. cum cujus sensu glossa illa ineptissima Grotii nullatenus consistere potest. Is enim verba Pro- phetæ & de Christo exposuit, & de morte in perpe- tuum ab ipso devicta & devorata intellexit: Ab- sorpta est MORS IN VICTORIAM. Quod e- nim in victoriam prorsus absorptum est, id non tantum ad certum tempus, sed plane totaliter & in sempiternum præcipitatum est. Et ita absorptam esse mortem docet Apostolus: ut quæ in æter- num profligata ab electis, cui in æternum illi insul- tare læto Epinikio poterunt: Ubi, mors, tua victo- ria? Adde quod Ebræum לנצח utrumque in per- petuum, & in victoriam significet. Quum ergo po- steriorem sensum probet Apostolus, manifestum est, non posse id ita explicari, DONEC VIVET EZECHIAS, quin contradicatur Apostolo. Sexto quum de operimento, vel vinculo & tela in genere Propheta vaticinatus fuerit, quod præcipitari in monte sacro debeat, nunc in specie præcipuam vin- culi & operimenti partem exprimit, nimirum mor- tem, quæ præcipitanda sit penitus: uti deinde ali- am partem operimenti, ploratus, gemitus & lacru- mas, vel quæ illarum causa sunt, afflictiones & cala- mitates hujus vitæ nominavit; siquidem jugum grave sit super filios Adam à die exitus de ventre ma- tris eorum, usq; in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium Eccl. 14. Denique tertia, ut ita vocem, pars operi- menti, nimirum ignominia & opprobrium est, de qua Propheta: Et opprobrium populi sui auferet de universa terra. Per peccatum enim involuti sumus opprobrio, & amicti quasi ignominia: sed per Messiam omne opprobrium, omnis ignominia & confusio auferri debuit. Ideoq; non incommode hic S. Hieronymus: Post passionem Domini, quan- do eum à siti & æstu ac turbine liberavit (sic enim exposuit antecedentia) faciet Dominus nequa- quam populo Judæorum, sed omnibus gentibus in monte Sion pingue convivium, holocausta medullata & vinum vindemiæ defæcatæ, ut præcipitet & ab- sorberi faciat faciem mortis & vinculi, quo omnes po- puli ligabuntur, disrumpetque rete mortis, & telam, qua omnes ceperat nationes. Et juxta Apostolum: absorbebitur mors in perpetuum. Et auferet Do- minus lacrumam ab omni facie, quando morte supe- rata, Christi advenerit regnum, & opprobrium gene- ris humani, quod ad imaginem conditum fuerat Crea- toris, Diaboli & mortis effugerit servitutem. Pro- inde septimo falso etiam restringitur lacrumarum abstersio ad Hierosolymitanos obsessos à Sennacheri- bo. AB OMNI FACIE lacrumam ablaturus Deus dicitur, quemadmodum super omnes populos & super omnes nationes operimentum lugubre fuisse, in- dicarat. Non ergo de solis Hierosolymitanis ser- mo est. Et uti convivium parandum OMNIBUS POPULIS, ita AB OMNI FACIE luctus aufe- rendus. Deniq; de omnibus Electis interpretatur id

Sp. Sanctus Ap. 7, 17. in quibus plenum comple- mentum in altera vita confequetur præsens vatici- nium. Reget illos agnus, & deducet eos ad vitæ fontes aquarum, & absterget omnem lacrumam ab oculis eorum, & mors ultra non erit, neq; luctus, neq; clamor, neq; dolor erit ultra. Hoc est præcipitare omne experi- mentum, quo involuti eramus, præcipitare mortem in sempiternum, vel in victoriam, & auferre omnem la- crumam ab omni facie, & omne opprobrium populi sui. De quo postremo eximie Brentius noster: Populus Christi gloriatur ex Evangelio de magno fa- vore DEI, de multis beneficiis, quæ Christus ipsis co- ram Deo impetravit, de liberatione ex omnibus ad- versis, adeog; ex ipsa morte. Sed ecce tractatur in hoc mundo, tanquam à Deo abjectissimus: objicitur dif- ficillimis quibusq; periculis, opprimitur ab impiis, af- fligitur extremis malis, habetur tanquam κάθαρμα & περίψημα, ac tandem obruitur turpi morte. Christus autem Filius Dei aufert hoc opprobrium, per univer- sam terram, primum prædicatione Evangelii sui, quia ubicunq; prædicatur Evangelium, promittitur omnibus credentibus pro mundano opprobrio cælestis & perpetua gloria: Deinde aufert id etiam reipsa in novissimo die, ut pii liberati omni opprobrio hujus seculi fruantur cælesti & æterna gloria. Quapropter refellitur etiam octavo glossa Grotiana è subjuncta Confessione & celebratione fidelium vers. 9. Et dicent credentes, sc. in die illa: Ecce Deus noster ipse, expectavimus eum & salvabit nos: Iste Dominus, sustinuius eum, exultabimus & lætabimur in Salu- te ejus. Hæc enim exhibent confessionem fiducia- lem Messiæ, qui Deus benedictus est in secula: Et Deus noster vel nobiscum Deus est ob redemtionis beneficium; Quem expectarunt inde à prima pro- missione Paradisiaca omnes credentes; qui salvat nos, & in cujus salute בִּישׁוּעָתוֹ lætantur & exultant unice fideles: quæ lætitia inchoatur in hac, consum- mabitur vero in futura vita. De spirituali enim læ- titia sermo est, qua lætamur in Deo salvatore no- stro, & exultamus in salute ejus: de illa salute quæ eveniet, præcipitata vel absorpta morte in sempiter- num, & ablato luctu, omniq; luctus causa præcipitata, in illa lætitia & salute, quæ omnibus populis in monte Zion per Evangelicum convivium obtinget. Quum beneficia Christi exposuerit hactenus Propheta, jam officia populi ejus proponit: quæ sunt fiducia in ipsum: Ecce Dominus noster: Expectavimus seu speramus in eum. Confessio fidem declarans: カス Dicent in illa die: Ecce, iste est Deus noster; iste est Dominus. Deniq; exultatio & lætitia in Domi- no: ad quam patientia in adversis, & obedientia in operibus, quæ exigit, requiritur. De quibus hic conferri Brentius poterit. Unde additur: QUIA REQUIESCET MANUS DOMINI IN MONTE ISTO: Nam in Ecclesia requiescit manus Domini, illic regnum suum obtinet; illic exerit virtutem & potentiam suam; illic requiem & delectationem suam habet. B. Lutherus, Ma- nus Domini in monte isto. Virtus & potestas Dei movebitur in Ecclesia, quia liberat & lætificat eam. Absorpta morte in perpetuum, populus Dei (sic ha- bet Hieronymus in h. l.) qui de manu mortis fue- rit liberatus, dicet ad Dominum: Ecce, Deus noster ipse, quem increduli hominem tantum putabant, & expectavimus eum, h. e. verbis ejus credidimus, quia sua promissa complevit & salvabit nos. Propterea ejus auxilio faucibus mortis erepti exultabimus & lætabimur in eo, & manus atq; ejus potentia requie- scet in monte isto, de quo supra legimus. Quum re- gnavit Dominus Exercituum in monte Zion & in Hierusalem, & in conspectu senum suorum fuerit glorificatus. Brentius haud præter rem monet, quod manus Domini in Zion requieverit, h. e. poten- tia & majestas Christi, quia in Hierusalem prædica- vit Evangelium suum, & cum adscendisset in Cœ- lum, misit ibi Sp. Sanctum discipulis suis, ut virga virtutis Domini exiret in orbem terrarum Psal. 110. Nimis manifestum est, de beneficiis Messiæ hæc omnia sonare. Ideo etiam Calvinus, qui lubenter alias oracula Prophetica pervertit, de Christo ex- plicat: satis constat, inquit ad vers. 6. hic non de- nunciari exitium gentibus aut Judæis; sed utrosq; una ad lautissimum convivium invitari. Idq; me- lius constat ex ipsis Christi verbis, dum regnum Cœlo- rum comparat nuptiis, quas Rex Filio suo apparavit, id quas omnes promiscue convocat, quum ii, qui prius fuerant invitati, venire nollent. Nec vero mihi du- bium, quin de promulgatione Evangelii loquatur. Et quia ex monte Zion prodiit, gentes illuc ad epu- landum venturas dicit, quia, ubi spiritualem cibum ad pascendas animas toti mundo proposuit Deus, per- inde fuit ac si communem Mensam parasset. Et ad vers. 7. verus, meo judicio, sensus est, quod Dominus promittit, se sublaturum velum, quo in cæcitate & ignorantia tenebantur. (Quem sensum verum, sed non plenum esse, è superioribus constat: plura enim operimenti nomine comprehenduntur.) Luce ergo Evangelii discussæ sunt hæ tenebræ. Hoc autem in monte Zion futurum esse dicit: unde etiam lux verbi toti mundo affulsit. Est igitur ad Christi re- gnum NECESSARIO referendus hic locus, nec enim lux affulsit omnibus hominibus, donec Sol justi- tiæ Christus exortus est, à quo omnia vela, integumen- ta & involucra sublata sunt. Ad vers. 8. Destruxit mortem in æternum. Propheta argumentum suum contexit. Nam in summa promittit solidam felicita- tem sub Christi regno. Duo igitur conjungit, quæ per- fectam & absolutam reddunt felicitatem, Primum, quod perpetua sit vita, (nam iis, qui beati alioqui sunt ad tempus, interire miserum est.) Deinde vi- ta hæc gaudio conjuncta est. Nam alioqui mœstæ & ærumnosæ vitæ mors videtur præferenda. Adjun- git etiam, omni ignominia sublata, gloriosam hanc vitam fore, quia Prophetiæ alioqui fidem derogas- set tristis populi oppressio. De tempore etiam im- pletionis rectissime Calvinus: Ubi igitur, aut quan- do hæc locum habent? Haud dubie ad universum Christi regnum referenda sunt: Universum dico: quia non tantum initium spectandum est, sed etiam complementum & meta. Atque ita ad secundum Chri- sti adventum extendi debet. Qui propterea dies re- demtionis & instaurationis vocatur: quoniam omnia, quæ nunc videntur confusa, restituentur in in- tegrum & novam formam induent. Hoc quidem ad redemtionem quoq; è Babylone pertinet, sed quum ea veluti præludium & tenuis gustus fuerit istius, haud dubie hæc promissio usq; ad ultimum diem prorogan- da est.

## 25:10
Vers. 10. AND MOAB SHALL BE THRESHED UNDER HIM, AS STRAW IS THRESHED IN A WAGON) Jerome: He speaks according to the custom of Palestine and many provinces of the East, which, on account of the scarcity of meadows and hay, prepare straw for the food of animals. There are, however, iron wagons with wheels revolving in the manner of saws, which crush and break up the stubble into straw. When this will happen, see above 11, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET TRITURABITUR MOAB SUB EO, SICUT TERVNTVR PALEÆ IN PLAU- STRO) Hieronymus: Hoc juxta ritum loquitur Palæstinæ & multarum orientis Provinciarum, quæ ob pratorum & fœni penuriam paleas præparant esui animantium. Sunt autem car- penta ferrata rotis in serracorum modum revolventibus, quæ sti- pulam conterunt & comminuunt in paleas. Quando hoc eve- nerit, vide supra 11, 14.

## 25:11
Vers. 11. AND HE SHALL SPREAD FORTH HIS HANDS IN THE MIDST OF THEM, AS HE THAT SWIMMETH SPREADETH FORTH HIS HANDS TO SWIM) Pressed by this burden, the Moabite will attempt everything to escape, in the way that those are accustomed to do who desire to swim out from a shipwreck, but in vain.

Above, the Prophet had it thus: IDUMEA AND MOAB THE PUTTING FORTH OF THEIR HAND. Which Grotius rendered, the sending in of their hands, that is, the Jews will send in their hand, they will make expeditions into their territories. But since he wishes there to be a discourse here concerning the praise of Sennacherib, how this sending of the hand into Moab coheres with him, if indeed he thinks the series of time is to be observed everywhere. But we have already shown that this hymn is to be expounded concerning the spiritual Banquet, the victory over death, the liberation from all mourning and reproach, and joy in the Lord. And therefore of the people having been set forth, now the punishments of the enemies of Christ and of his people are presented. For by Moab all the enemies of the Church are understood in general, because the Moabites were perpetual enemies of the Israelites, who had conspired for their destruction, Deut. 23. Therefore, this threshing or trampling will not be worldly: but it is to be understood according to the reason of the kingdom of Christ: that enemies are to be trampled spiritually from Mount Zion, because the Gospel, sent forth from Mount Zion, gathers the Church from every nation, against the will of all Moabites, Ammonites, Philistines, Greeks, and Romans, and its preaching is compared with the Church in the midst of enemies, until the Lord places them all as a footstool for his feet. Jerome understands spiritual enemies: from one idol and the demon who presided over this idol among the Moabites, he indicates all contrary powers to be humbled and led down into hell. Nor is there any doubt that, with the hand of the Lord resting upon the Church, it is protected and defended against all spiritual enemies alike and bodily ones. But here mention is made particularly of bodily enemies, who are designated by Moab. Since the Prophet has already sung before of spiritual enemies overcome and death swallowed up. But the emphatic description of the trampling of enemies is to be noted: who are said to be crushed first, as straw is accustomed to be by a wagon. Concerning which Jerome says: He speaks according to the rite of Palestine and many provinces of the East, which, because of the scarcity of meadows and hay, prepare straw for the food of animals. They are, however, carts shod with wheels revolving in the middle in the manner of saws, which crush and grind the stubble into straw. How, therefore, straw is crushed by iron wagons: so shall Moab be crushed under him, whether under the power of God, or in himself, so that nothing whole remains in him. In the Hebrew it is, במי מדמנה which Jerome rendered as 'in the wagon': others as 'in the dung'. Calvin thinks it is the name of a city from Jer. 48:2, so that there is an allusion to the fertility of the soil in which that city was situated; he translates it, however, with others, as 'in the dunghill'. Then a simile is applied from swimmers: to whom Grotius thinks they are compared, struggling in vain to emerge. Jerome explains it in this way: Just as one who swims is accustomed to extend his whole body: so Moab shall be dashed to the ground by his own power, and falling, shall make a path. Luther, Brentius, Osiander, the Vinarions, and others understand it of the Lord. As he who swims in water extends his hands and feet, and moves the water with his hands, wherever he wishes, and treads it with his feet, so that he may clearly dominate in the water: so also the Lord will extend his arm over the Moabites and will move or tread them according to his own will. Which explanation seems simpler and agrees more with the text. For as with the Lord's hand resting on the holy mountain, or protecting the Church, enemies are to be threshed and subjected to his feet: So when he shall extend his own hands IN THE MIDST OF IT (Moab, so it is held in the Hebrew, and not 'under Him'; which deceived Grotius: that is, in the midst of the enemies of the Church) just as one swimming extends to swim (so that he may grasp his enemies on every side) he is said to be about to humble its glory (or rather its pride and insolence), with the arms of his hands, as it is held in the source: about to overthrow it on every side with hands and arms. Which relation of the simile to God, approved also by Calvin, who explains the reason for the metaphor thus: Those who swim do not rush with their whole force, but lightly expand themselves, and calmly draw down their arms, only cutting through the waters, and overcoming them: So the Lord often does not exert great strength to cut through the impious, but without any effort, with no forces brought up, without any noise or tumult, he destroys and overthrows them, however strenuous and well-equipped they may seem. Thirdly, lest the Moabites, who were very proud of their fortifications, trust in their power and defenses in vain: for their cities were most fortified; and lest the faithful be terrified by them, the Prophet threatens their destruction, with his speech now turned to Moab: And the fortifications of your high walls will fall and be humbled. The Hebrew text has: he will cast down and humble. And he will pull down (in the Hebrew, and he will dash) to the ground even to the dust. Which words are joined for the sake of greater emphasis: He will cast down, he will humble, he will dash, finally with the addition of 'even to the dust': because the pride with which the Moabites were swollen needed to be beaten back: Cf. Isa. 19:6. For the fortifications of enemies, however powerful and proud, in which they trust, are easily cast down, humbled, and dashed to the ground by the Lord, nay, reduced to dust, provided we trust in the Lord and await his salvation. Calvin also acknowledges that by the name of the Moabites, synecdochically, all the enemies of the Church are comprehended; but because they were joined by kinship to the Israelites, he wishes them to be denoted in particular, with whom the Church has some connection. As those to whom none are more harmful.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET EXTENDET MANUS SUAS SUB EO, SICVT EXTENDIT NATANS AD NATAN- DUM) Pressus hoc onere Moabita omnia tentabit, ut evadat, quomodo illi solent, qui è naufragio cupiunt ena- tare, sed frustra.

Supra ita Propheta habuit: IDUMÆA ET MOAB PRÆCEPTUM MANUS EORUM. Quod Grotius reddidit, immissio manuum eorum, id est, Judæi manum immittent, expeditiones facient in fines eorum. Quum vero hic sermonem esse velit de laude Sennacheribi, quomodo cohæret illi hæc immissio manus in Moabitam, siquidem temporis seriem ubiq; observari putet. Cæterum de spiri- tuali Convivio, victoria mortis, liberatione ab omni luctu & opprobrio, de lætitia in Domino, hunc hy- mnum exponendum esse, jam ostendimus. Ideoq; propositis beneficiis Christi, & officiis populi nunc supplicia hostium Christi, & populi ejus sistuntur. Per Moab enim omnes Ecclesiæ hostes in genere intel- liguntur, quia Moabitæ perpetui fuêre hostes Israë- litarum, qui in exitium eorum conspirarant Deut. 23. Non ergo hæc trituratio vel conculcatio mun- dana erit: sed intelligenda est pro ratione regni Christi: quod spiritualiter conculcandi sint è mon- te Zion hostes, quia Evangelium emissum è monte Zion, colligit Ecclesiam ex omni natione, invitis omnibus Moabitis, Ammonitis, Philistinis, Græcis & Romanis, ejusque prædicatio cum Ecclesia com- paratur in medio hostium, donec illos universos Dominus ponat scabellum pedum suorum. Hie- ronymus intelligit hostes spirituales: Ex uno idolo & dæmone, qui huic idolo præsidebat apud Moabitas, omnes indicat contrarias fortitudines humiliandas & deducendas in tartarum. Neq; dubium est, ma- nu Domini quiescente in Ecclesia eandem protegi, ac defendi adversus hostes spirituales universos pa- riter & corporales. Sed hic peculiariter hostium corporalium mentio fit, qui per Moab designantur. Quum de devictis spiritualibus & morte absorpta antea jam cecinerit Propheta. Notanda autem est Emphatica descriptio conculcationis hostium: qui primo conterendi dicuntur, uti solent plaustro paleæ. De quo Hieronymus: Hoc juxta ritum loquitur Palæstinæ & multarum Orientis provinciarum, quæ ob pratorum & fœni penuriam paleas præparant esui animantium. Sunt autem Carpenta ferrata rotis per medium in serrarum modum se volventibus, quæ sti- pulam conterunt & comminuunt in paleas. Quomo- do igitur plaustris ferratis paleæ conteruntur: sic con- teretur Moab sub eo, sive sub Dei potentia, sive in se- metipso, ut nihil in eo integri remaneat. In Ebræo est, במי מדמנה quod Hieronymus reddidit in plau- stro: alii in fimo. Calvinus nomen urbis esse putat è Jer. 48, 2. ut alludatur ad ubertatem soli, in quo urbs illa sita erat; vertit tamen cum aliis in sterqui- linio. Deinde simile adhibetur à natantibus: qui- bus comparari putat Grotius, nequicquam emerge- re conantes. Hieronymus hoc modo explicat: Sicut solet, qui natat, totum corpus extendere: ita Moab de sua potentia allidetur in terram, & ruens semitam faciet. Lutherus, Brentius, Osiander, Vinarienses & alii de Domino intelligunt. Ut is qui in aqua natat, extendit manus & pedes suos, ac movet aquam ma- nibus, quo libet, & calcat eam pedibus suis, ut plane in aqua dominetur: ita etiam Dominus extendet brachium suum super Moabitas & commovebit seu calcabit eos pro suo arbitrio. Quæ explicatio simplicior videtur & textui magis congruit. Ut enim Domini manu quiescente in monte sacro, vel protegente Ecclesiam triturandi hostes ac pedibus ejus subjiciendi: Ita cum extendet idem manus suas IN MEDIO EJUS (Moab, ita in Ebræo habetur, non vero sub Eo; quod fefellit Grotium: id est, in medio hostium Ecclesiæ) sicut extendit natans ad natandum (ut circumquaq; hostes suos apprehen- dat) humiliaturus gloriam (vel superbiam & inso- lentiam potius) ejus dicitur, cum brachiis manuum suarum, ut in fonte habetur: manibus & brachiis undiquaq; eam profligaturus. Quæ similitudinis re- latio ad Deum probata etiam Calvino, metaphoræ rationem ita explicanti: Qui natant, non irruunt toto impetu, sed leviter sese expandunt, & brachia po- placide deducunt, aquas tantum proscindunt, & supe- rant : Ita Dominus sæpe haud magnas vires exercet ad proscindendos impios, sed absq; ullo negotio, nullis adductis copiis, sine ullo strepitu aut tumultu eos per- dit ac profligat, quantumcunq; strenui atq; instructi videantur. Tertio ne potentia & munimentis frustra confidant Moabitæ, qui valde superbiebant propugnaculis: erant enim urbes eorum munitis- simæ; ac ne terreantur iisdem fideles, destructio- nem eorum minatur Propheta, oratione nunc ad Moab versa : Et munimenta sublimium murorum tuorum concident & humiliabuntur. Ebræus tex- tus habet: prosternet & humiliabit. Et detrahet, (in Ebræo, & allidet) in terram usq; ad pulverem. Quæ verba ob majorem Emphasin conjunguntur: Prosternet, humiliabit, allidet, denique addito usq; ad pulverem: quia superbiam, qua turgidi erant Moabitæ, retundi oportebat: Conf. Esa. 19, 6. Hostium enim quantumvis potentium & superbo- rum munimenta, quibus confidunt, quæcunq; faci- le à Domino prosternuntur, humiliantur & in ter- ram alliduntur, imo in pulverem rediguntur, modo confidamus Domino, ejusq; salutem expectemus. Agnoscit etiam Calvinus, Moabitarum nomine συν- νεκδοχικῶς omnes Ecclesiæ hostes comprehendi; sed quia illi genere conjuncti erant Israëlitis, eos impri- mis denotari vult, quibuscum Ecclesia aliquid con- junctionis habet. Utpote quibus nulli sunt no- centiores.

## 26:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVI.

A spiritual song of Judah, concerning the protection of the Church, the destruction of enemies, the propagation of divine glory even among the nations, and the glorious resurrection of the faithful.

Vers. 1. IN THAT DAY IT SHALL BE SUNG) Let it be sung. For I composed it for that reason. THE CITY OF OUR STRENGTH SION SAVIOR, SHALL BE PLACED IN IT A WALL AND A BULWARK) Sion is not in the Hebrew, but added in the place of a gloss. You would translate it correctly: The city is firm for us. Salvation (which is God himself) has placed its walls and bulwark. Therefore, the city is invincible to us, because it was founded with the best omen, by God himself commanding. In a more sublime sense, you will correctly refer it to the heavenly city, whose founder is Jesus ישוע.

That it refers in the literal sense to Jerusalem, we by no means admit. Grotius is mistaken, as if this Canticle likewise pertained to the liberation from the army of Sennacherib. That it is not treated in the preceding [passages] is now in the open. Nor can the present Canticle be snatched away to that [interpretation], although it is introduced into the text. Whence by Grotius the dead are understood as those who were in the dangers of death, the corpse [as] a corpse held of the City, and many other things akin to these; which are indeed manifest proofs of the depravation of the text. Grotius spends all his effort on this, that he might introduce into the prophecies the sense which he had preconceived in his mind. Which is not [the mark] of a good interpreter. Moreover, with great consensus, the Doctors understand these things regarding the literal sense either of the spiritual or of the Heavenly Jerusalem: so that they may correspond to the preceding Canticle, which all acknowledge to be coherent with and analogous to this one. Nor is there need that a double sense be established here. With Grotius's version retained, JESUS himself is rightly said to have placed [himself as] the wall and bulwark of this city, in the literal sense. Because the discourse is about the preservation of the Church and spiritual salvation and peace. And how firm the earthly Jerusalem was with walls and bulwarks, its double devastation has sufficiently taught. Against Sennacherib also, wall and bulwark availed nothing: the City was liberated by the hand of God alone. Thus also the LXX render it, ἰδὲ πόλις ἰχυρὰ, καὶ σωτήριον ἡμῶν θή-

σωτὸ τεῖχος, & περὶ τεῖχος. Which Cyril explains: A fortified and saving city, the Savior of all, and a city having a wall, and a bulwark, that is to say, all safety. For cities, best girded with walls, do not have a simple fortification, and besides a great wall are also surrounded by another circummural defense. And it is furthermore consistent with the truth that those who sing this ode say of the Church of our Savior that: Behold a fortified and saving city. For the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, according to the voice of the Savior. For it is as if surrounded by a kind of double wall, both by the protection of the holy Angels, and by the heavenly one, and of GOD, who is the bulwark. For there is also the strength of the holy Spirits themselves: inasmuch as He alone is the Lord of all powers. Nor is the text poorly translated in this way; The Lord has placed salvation as walls and a bulwark. Which sense B. Luther expressed: Walls and defenses are salvation. Because the salvation of Christ and Jesus himself is truly the wall and bulwark of the Church. He not only establishes walls, but he himself is the wall, as the Lord promised in Zech. 2:5, I will be a wall of fire to it. Then the walls are also salvation, because they persist unshaken and are a victory even against the very gates of hell, as B. Luther explains in his Enarrations on this passage. Similarly, Brentius translates and explains: A strong city is for us, in which salvation itself has placed a wall and a bulwark, or, in which the Savior himself is placed as a wall and a bulwark of the wall. This city is the Church of Christ, the foundation of which city is Christ himself and his doctrine, Matt. 6:16; similarly, its wall and bulwark is Christ our true salvation. For nothing is firmer, nothing is stronger than Christ the Son of God. Thus the present hymn coheres excellently with the previous one. For since the Prophet has sung of the happiness and joy of the faithful, he exhorts them in this song to trust well in their adversities, and not to be offended by the external happiness of the impious. In that day, he says, namely at that time when the Gospel of Christ is propagated from Mount Zion into the world, this Canticle shall be sung in the land of Judah, that is, among all the pious who will acknowledge the Gospel of Christ, which was revealed in the land of Judah and confirmed by great miracles. Calvin explains these things regarding the return from the Babylonian exile: After the people have returned, they will be protected by God's guardianship and hand. But because this Canticle is of the same subject matter as the preceding one, and pertains to the same times, it is more correctly established that these things look primarily to the times of the New Testament. Which Oecolampadius also admits: He says, he wants the Prophet to say, such joy and such security will be for the saints, that they may truly sing these things. In that day, he says, in which those things will happen which were said above, namely when in this age we believe through the cross of Christ that the Devil is truly conquered, death and the curse abolished, and sin taken away. But especially also in the second coming of Christ, when, having conquered death, we will reign with Christ. The just, however, will sing spiritual songs, which proceed from the Holy Spirit, among whose fruits is also joy on account of trust in God.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVI.

Canticum spiritualis Juda, de præsidio Eccle- siæ, hostium exitio, gloriæ divinæ etiam inter gentes propagatione, & gloriosa fidelium resuscitatione.

Vers. 1. IN DIE ILLA CANTABITUR) Cantetur. Ideo enim id composui. URBS FORTITUDINIS NOSTRÆ SION SALVATOR, PONETUR IN EA MURUS ET ANTE- MURALE) Non est Sion in Hebræo, sed gloffematis vice additum. Recte verteris: Urbs nobis est firma. Salus (i- psa id est Deus) posuit muros & antemurale ejus. Ideo in- victa nobis urbs est, quia optimo omine, Deo ipso ju- bente, est condita. Sensu sublimiore recte referes ad civi- tatem cœlestem, cujus conditor Jesus ישוע.

SEnsu literali respicit Hierosolymam, nequaquam admittimus. Fallitur Grotius, quasi hoc Canti- cum itidem pertineat ad liberationem ab exercitu Sennacheribi. De ea in præcedentibus non agi, jam in aprico est. Neq; abripi potest eo præsens Canticum, quamvis inferatur textui. Unde à Gro- tio mortui de illis intelliguntur, qui in mortis peri- culis versabantur, cadaver de Civitate pro cadavere habita, & quæ his gemina alia plura; quæ vero de- pravationis text9 manifestæ τεκμήρια. In id omne studjum impendit Grotius, ut sensum, quem animo præconceperat suo, inferret vaticiniis. Quod nõ est boni interpretis. Cæterum magno Consensu Dd. quoad sensum literalem aut de spirituali aut de Cœ- lesti Hierosolyma hæc intelligunt: ut Cantico præcedenti, cui hoc cohærere atq; analogum es- se omnes agnoscunt, congruant. Neq; opus est, ut hic geminus constituatur sensus. Retenta versio- ne Grotii, JESUS ipse murus & Antemurale hu- jus civitatis, sensu literali, posuisse, recte dicitur. Quia de conservatione Ecclesiæ & spirituali salute ac pace sermo est. Et quam firma Hierosolyma terrena fuerit cum muris & antemuralibus, gemina ejus vastatio satis docuit. Adversùs Sennacheri- bum etiam murus & antemurale nihil profuit: sola Dei manu liberata est Civitas. Sic etiam LXX. red- dunt, ἰδὲ πόλις ἰχυρὰ, καὶ σωτήριον ἡμῶν θή-

σωτὸ τεῖχος, & περὶ τεῖχος. Quæ explicat Cyrill9: Urbs munita ac salutaris est, Servator omnium, & urbs murum habens, & propugnaculum, omnem sci- licet incolumitatem. Nam urbes, optime cinctæ mu- ris, non simplicem habent munitionem, & præter magnum murum etiam altero circummurali muni- mento obvallantur. Estq; præterea consentaneum veritati, illos qui hanc odam decantant, de Ecclesia Servatoris nostri dicere illud: Ecce urbs munita & salutaris. Portæ enim inferorum contra eam non in- valescent, juxta vocem Servatoris. Est enim veluti quodam gemino muro circumcincta, tum sanctorum Angelorum præsidio, tum superno, & DEI, qui est propugnaculum. Est enim & ipsorum sanctorum Spirituum robur: quippe qui solus est cunctarum potentiarum Dominus. Neq; male vertitur textus hoc modo; Salutem posuit Dominus muros & an- temurale. Quem sensum expressit B. Lutherus: Mauren und Wehre sind Heil. Quia salus Christi & ipse Jesus vere murus & antemurale Ecclesiæ. Non tantum constituit muros, sed ipse murus est, uti promisit Dominus Zach. 2, 5. ego ero ipsi igneus murus. Tum muri etiam salus sunt, quia inconcussi persistunt & victoria sunt adversus ipsas quoq; por- tas inferorum, uti explicat B. Lutherus in Enarrat. h. l. Similiter Brentius transfert & exponit: Fortis nobis urbs est, in qua salus ipsa posuit murum & ante- murale, vel, in qua Salvator ipse positus est in murum & propugnaculum muri. Hæc urbs est Ecclesia Christi, cujus urbis fundamentum est Christus ipse & doctrina ejus Matth. 6, 16. similiter murus & an- temurale ejus est Christus vera nostra salus. Nihil enim est firmius, nihil est fortius Christo Filio Dei. Sic cohæret optime præsens hymnus cum superio- ri. Quum enim felicitatem, & gaudium fidelium cecinerit Propheta, hortatur hoc carmine ipsos, ut in adversis suis bene confidant, neq; offendantur impiorum externa felicitate. In die illa, inquit, eo nempe tempore, quo Evangelium Christi è monte Zion in orbem terrarum propagatur, cantabitur istud Canticum in terra Juda, h. e. inter omnes pios, qui agnoscent Evangelium Christi, quod in terra Juda revelatum, & magnis miraculis confirmatum est. Calvinus explicat hæc de reditu ab exilio Baby- lonico: Postquam reversus fuerit populus, prote- ctum iri Dei tutela, & manu. Sed quia Canticum hoc ejusdem argumenti est cum præcedente, & ad eadem tempora pertinet, rectius hæc ad N. T. tem- pora præcipue spectari statuitur. Quod fatetur etiam Oecolampadius: Dicere, inquit, vult Pro- pheta, tale gaudium, & tantam securitatem futuram sanctis, ut vere hæc canere possint. Die illa, inquit, qua evenient ea, quæ superius dicta, nempe quum in hoc seculo per crucem Christi credimus vere victum Diabolum, abolitam mortem & maledictionem, sub- latum peccatum. Maxime autem & in secundo ad- ventu Christi, quando victa morte cum Christo re- gnabimus. Cantabunt autem justi spiritualia canti- ca, quæ à Spiritu Sancto proficiscuntur, inter cujus fructus & gaudium est ob fiduciam in Deum.

## 26:2
Vers. 2. OPEN THE GATES, AND LET THE NATION OF THE JUST ENTER, KEEPING THE TRUTH.) Those Jews, who fled from other towns and fields into distant places, rather than change their religion.

This is not a prophecy about the open gates of the earthly Jerusalem, nor about the entry of the Jews from other towns, but, as I said, about the spiritual Jerusalem, which is opened to all: and about the entry of the faithful: who are distinguished by this honorable epithet, the nation of the just, keeping the truth. For they believe in the word of God, which is truth itself, Psalm 119, John 17, and they keep it holily, Luke 8. The gates of this city are not in one part of the earth, but are where the Gospel is preached: where it is said to Christ: Behold our God, we will wait for him: where a feast of fat things is prepared, that is, among all peoples, and in the whole world, where the sound of the Apostles has reached; which is signified in Rev. 21 by the twelve gates of the heavenly Jerusalem. For the gates of this city are opened through the preaching of the Gospel: but they enter through these gates, as many as receive the Gospel by faith, and preserve faith in Christ. For these are the just nation, justified namely through faith in Christ: Therefore a nation שֹׁמֵר אֱמֻנִים keeping those faithful promises and faithful covenants, of which Isa. 55:3, Acts 13 speak. Which are the proper object of faith, and its foundation and chief support. For through faith those promises concerning the benefits of Christ are both received, and cherished in the mind, and kept: upon which faith also looks, by which it is itself nourished, supported, and sustained. Jerome wants this exhortation: Open the gates, to be said to the angels: that they may open the gates of Heaven to the elect; and he explains the whole chapter regarding the other life. Whom the Jesuits Cornelius, Tirinus, and Menochius follow; But most things in the text must be twisted in such a way. Grotius's version is also strange and contorted: the Osiandrian is far simpler; The decree (of yours) is stable: You will keep peace, peace. Because we have hoped in you. For Grotius acknowledges that יֵצֶר denotes a thought. But the thoughts of God are decrees, Isa. 55. B. Luther expressed the same sentiment: You always maintain peace according to a certain promise, for one relies upon you. This is to be understood concerning the decree and promise revealed in the Gospel, which is the basis of trust or confidence, and brings solid and true peace of conscience. For in the world there is no City whose walls are salvation: all can eventually be stormed: in none is there certain security, let alone true salvation and happiness. But the strength of this city is invincible: its walls are salvation and happiness. In it alone is true beatitude, which is sought in vain outside its walls. For outside the Church there is no salvation. In the cities of this world, the gates are open not only to the just and those keeping the truth, but many unjust are found everywhere, indeed they often dominate and prevail over the pious and occupy the very gates. The pious, however, are afflicted and oppressed. Calvin acknowledges this sense: namely, that the gate of the Church is founded upon the eternal and immutable counsel of God. In vain, therefore, does this Canticle pass over to the earthly Jerusalem, and to the inhabitants of the city renewed after the exile, on the grounds that they will be different from their predecessors because they will cultivate justice and faith. For the subject is the spiritual city, the Church. In this mystical City, however, the gates are opened only so that the just and the faithful may enter and enjoy its privileges. No one truly dwells in the heavenly Jerusalem except the pious and the just. 'There shall not pass through thee anymore the uncircumcised and the unclean' Isa. 52. 'This is the gate of the Lord: the just shall enter into it' Psalm 118. In the cities of the world there is no earthly peace nor true tranquility: but the city of God, the Church, enjoys true peace and tranquility, which the world can neither give to it nor take away from it John 16. 'Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.' And therefore the Prophet warns: 'Trust in the Lord forever.' Because in the Lord GOD is the rock of eternity, or the strength of the ages. Which Brentius thinks is more correctly translated thus: In God, that is, on account of God Christ (who is called יָהּ Psalm 68), the Lord is the rock of eternity or eternal strength. For the Father is our fortitude and our strength and our everlasting rock on account of his only-begotten Son, on account of whom the Father has become propitious to us and preserves us perpetually. Epiphanius against the Anonymous. He translates not dissimilarly, and explains concerning the divine περιχωρήσει: In God is the Lord: because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Yet the translation and explanation of the Blessed Luther is simpler: for God the Lord is a rock eternally. Do not fail in temptations, always hope. God is not broken by the weariness of helping: provided you are not broken by the weariness of hoping and calling upon Him. Because the Lord God is an eternal rock. Cyril says these things were spoken in this place especially to the holy mystagogues, the Apostles. Open the gates, that is, make the approach open through faith to those who wish, and through the blameless instruction of the mysteries, an entrance. And let the people keeping the truth enter. For divine and Evangelical and salvific preaching teaches believers justice above the law, so that they may constantly retain the truth. For it does not now introduce a typical or shadowy worship, as the ancient law certainly did, but a spiritual and true one.

Latin:

Vers. 2. APERITE PORTAS, ET INGREDIA- TVR GENS JVSTO RVM, CVSTODIENS VERI- TATEM.) Illi Judæi, quæ ex cæteris oppidis agrisque in loca longinqua profugere, quam religionem mutare malue- runt.

Non hic de apertis Hierosolymæ terrenæ portis, non de ingressu Judæorum è cæteris oppidis, sed, uti dixi, spirituali Hierosolyma, quæ omnibus aperi tur, vaticinium est: & de ingressu fidelium: qui honorifico isto elogio insigniuntur, gens justo- rum, custodiens veritatem. Illi enim verbo Dei, quod est ipsa veritas Psalm. 119. Joh. 17. credunt, illudque sancte custodiunt Luc. 8. Portæ hujus ur- bis non sunt in una parte terræ, sed ibi sunt, ubi pre- dicatur Evangelium: ubi dicitur Christo: Ecce Deus noster, expectabimus eum: ubi paratur con- vivium pinguium, h. e. inter omnes populos, & in toto orbe, quo pervenit sonus Apostolorum; quod significatur Ap. 21. per duodecim portas cæle- stis Hierusalem. Aperiuntur enim portæ hujus ur- bis per prædicationem Evangelii: ingrediuntur autem per has portas, quotquot recipiunt Evange- lium fide, & conservant fidem in Christum. Hi enim sunt gens justa, justificata videlicet per fidem in Christum: Ideo gens שֹׁמֵר אֱמֻנִים conservans fi- delia promissa illa & pacta fidelia, de quibus Efa. 55, 3. Act. 13. Quæ proprium fidei objectum, ac fun- damentum & fulcrum præcipuum ejusdem sunt. Per fidem enim & suscipiuntur, & animo foventur, ac custodiuntur illa promissa de Christi beneficiis: in quæ etiam respicit fides, quibus ipsa alitur, fulci- tur & sustentatur. Hieronymus hanc exhortatio- nem: Aperite portas, angelis dictam vult: ut ape- riant electis portas Cæli; totumq; caput de altera vita explicat. Quem sequuntur Jesuitæ Cornelius, Tirinus, Menochius; Sed pleraque ita torquenda sunt in textu. Mira etiam & contorta est versio Grotiana: simplicior longe Osiandrina; Decre- tum (tuum) stabile est: Servabis pacem, pacem. Quia in te speravimus. Nam יֵצֶר cogitatum notare agno- scit Grotius. Cogitationes autem Dei decreta sunt, Efa. 55. Eandem sententiam expressit B. Lu- therus: Du erhältest stets Friede nach gewisser Zu- sage, denn man verlässet sich auff dich. De decreto & promissione in Evangelio patefacta, quæ fiduciæ vel confidentiæ basis est, & pacem conscientiæ solidam ac veram adfert, id accipiendum. In mundo enim Civitas nulla est, cujus muri sint salus: omnes ex- pugnari tandem possunt: in nulla certa est securi- tas, nedum vera salus, & felicitas. At hujus urbis fortitudo invicta est: muri ejus salus & felicitas sunt. In ea sola vera est beatitudo, quæ extra muros ejus frustra quæritur. Extra Ecclesiam enim nulla est salus. In civitatibus hujus mundi non justis tan- tum portæ patent & veritatem custodientibus, sed plures passim reperiuntur injusti, quin dominantur sæpe ac prævalent piis ipsasq; portas occupant. Pii vero affliguntur & opprimuntur. Agnofcit Calvi- nus hunc sensum: æterno nempe Dei & immutabili consilio fundatam esse Ecclesiæ portam. Nequicquam ergo ad terrenam Hierosolymam transit hoc Can- ticum, & ad incolas renovatæ urbis post exilium, quod prioribus dissimiles futuri sint, quia justitiam & fidem colent. Agitur enim de civitate spirituali Ecclesia. In hac vero mystica Civitate portæ tan- tum aperiuntur, ut justi ac fideles ingrediantur, ejusque privilegiis fruantur. In cœlesti Hiersolo- lyma nemo vere habitat, nisi pius & justus. Non adjiciet ultra, ut pertranseat per te incircumcisus & immundus Efa. 52. Hæc porta Domini: justi intra- bunt in eam Psalm 118. In civitatibus mundi non est pax terrena neq; recta tranquillitas: ac civitas Dei, Ecclesia, vera pace & tranquillitate gaudet, quam mundus nec dare nec auferre ei potest Joh. 16. Justificati ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum. Ideoque mo- net Propheta: Sperate in Dominum in sempiter- num usq;. Quia in DEO Domino est petra æterni- tatis, vel robur fæculorum. Quod Brentius rectius ita transferri putat: In Deo, id est, propter Deum Christum (qui יָהּ vocatur Psalm. 68.) Dominus est petra æternitatis vel æternum robur. Pater enim est fortitudo nostra & robur nostrum & petra nostra sempiterna propter unigenitum filium suum, propter quem Pater nobis factus est propitius & conservat nos perpetuo. Epiphanius contr. Anonym. Non absimiliter transfert, & de περιχωρήσει divina ex- plicat: In Deo Dominus est: quia Pater est in filio & Filius in Patre. Simplicior tamen est B. Lutheri translatio & explicatio: denn Gott der Herr ist ein Fels ewiglich. Nolite deficere in tentationibus, semper sperate. Non frangitur Deus tædio juvan- di: modo vos non frangamini tædio sperandi & invocandi. Quia Dominus Deus est petra æterna. Cyrillus sanctis mystagogis Apostolis hæc præcipue hoc loco dicta ait. Aperite portas, id est, patefacite aditum per fidem his, qui volunt, & per inculpatam mysteriorum institutionem ingressum. Et ingredia- tur populus custodiens veritatem. Nam divina & Evangelica, & salvifica prædicatio docet credentes justitiam supra legem, ut constanter veritatem reti- neant. Nec enim jam typicum aut umbratilem, sicut certe antiqua lex, sed spiritualem & verum cultum inducit.

## 26:3
Verse 3. THE OLD ERROR HAS DEPARTED) The word יצר indeed signifies a figment, or a molded work: but among the Hebrews it is accustomed to be used for a thought. Therefore, let us translate it best: to a thought supported (supply, by trust in you, O God) you will provide prosperous things: prosperous things, I say, because it has trusted in you.

Latin:

Vers. 3. VETUS ERROR ABIIT) Vox יצר figmentum quidem, sive opus fictile significat: sed apud Hebræos poni solet pro cogitatione. Itaque optime vertamus: cogitatio- ni suffultæ (supple, tui fiducia, ô Deus) præstabis res prosperas: res prosperas, inquam, quia tibi confisa est.

## 26:4
Verse 4. YOU HAVE TRUSTED IN THE LORD IN ETERNAL AGES) Trust in the Lord unceasingly.

Latin:

Vers. 4. SPERASTIS IN DOMINO IN SÆCULIS ÆTERNIS) Fidite Domino indefinenter.

## 26:5
Verse 5. BECAUSE HE WILL BOW DOWN) He will bow down. For this song was made to be sung then, when the deed had been done.

Verse 5. THE SUBLIME CITY.) Nineveh. It is not specifically about Nineveh. But just as God is said generally to be about to bow down or depress and cast from the throne those who dwell on high, whatever enemies they may be, even the most eminent and powerful; so He is about to humble even a fortified city, however strong and fortified it may be. By which name not only cities, but also most powerful kingdoms and empires are designated. Which, although they may seem insuperable, will be overturned by the Lord when they oppose Him. It is not certain concerning Nineveh being humbled in the time of Sennacherib: therefore Grotius turns from that City to the Assyrians themselves: and he interprets the words of verse 6, THE FOOT SHALL TREAD IT DOWN, THE FEET OF THE POOR, THE STEPS OF THE NEEDY, even though they speak equally of the City, thus: The inhabitants of Jerusalem, held as lost, will despise the Assyrians. But this is not to bring out, but to bring in a meaning. The feet of the poor and the steps of the needy are said to be about to tread down the fortified city, the most powerful empires of the world. Which is not to be understood in a worldly, but in a spiritual way, according to the nature of the kingdom of Christ. For what are the poor and needy compared to the most flourishing kingdoms? They tread them down, therefore, by the power of the word; which happened when the Apostles and their successors, miserable and abject men, spread the Gospel in the world against the will of the princes and kingdoms of the earth, and gathered a Church for Christ from the subjects of impious Monarchs. Here the Prophet depicts Christ as a certain heroic warrior, who engages with none of his enemies whom he does not conquer, besieges no city which he does not take by storm, approaches no nation which he does not tread down, so that he may subject the most powerful Kings of the earth and the most fortified cities to his dominion. And there is no doubt that Christ, in the coming of His Majesty, will abolish even by external abolition all worldly kingdoms, and He alone will rule perpetually: but in the meantime, from that day especially on which the Holy Spirit was sent to the Apostles, Christ uses the humiliation and dejection of kingdoms and Cities, according to that reason which befits His kingdom in this world. Thus Osiander, as also Brentius, who observes also that this antithesis can be understood generally in this sense: All the kingdoms of this world are bowed down, decline toward destruction, and will at length be brought into dust, so that they may be trodden underfoot. For only the kingdom of Christ will last forever. Cyril understands the demons to be trodden down here, who are compared to fortified cities. But the former interpretation is to be preferred.

HE WILL HUMBLE) He has humbled: he has taken away its glory.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QVIA INCVRVABIT) Incurvabit. Fa- ctum est enim hoc canticum, ut tunc caneretur, cum res gesta esset.

Vers. 5. CIVITATEM SUBLIMEM.) Niniven. Non agitur in specie de Ninive. Sed uti gene- ratim Deus incurvaturus seu depressurus & de solio præcipitaturus dicitur habitantes in excelso quof- cunque hostes, etiam maxime eminentes ac poten- tes; ita humiliaturus etiam Civitatem munitam, utcunque fortissima & munitissima sit. Quo nomi- ne non tantum urbes, sed & regna ac imperia poten- tissima designantur. Quæ insuperabilia videri pos- sunt, evertentur à Domino, cum se illi opponent. De Ninive tempore Sennacheribi humiliata non constat: ideo à Civitate illa sese vertit Grotius ad Assyrios ipsos: & verba v. 6. CONCULCABIT EAM PES, PEDES PAUPERIS, GRES- SUS EGENORUM, etsi æque loquantur de Civitate, sic interpretatur: Contemnent Assyrios Hierosolymitæ pro perditis habiti. Verum hoc est non efferre, sed inferre sensum. Pedes pauperis & gressus egenorum conculcaturi dicuntur civitatem munitam, imperia potentissima mundi. Quod non intelligendum mundano, sed spirituali modo, pro ratione regni Christi. Quid enim pauperes & ege- ni sunt ad regna florentissima? Conculcant ergo ea verbi virtute; quod factum, cum Apostoli eo- rumq; successores, homines miseri & abjecti, invi- tis principibus & regnis terræ Evangelium sparsi- runt in terrarum orbe, & è Monarcharum impio- rum subditis Christo collegerunt Ecclesiam. De- pingit hic Propheta Christum quasi heroicum quen- dam bellatorem, qui cum nullo hostium congredi- tur, quem non vincat, nullam urbem obsidet, quam non expugnet, qui nullam gentem adit, quam non conculcet, ut potentissimos Reges terræ & muni- tissimas urbes suæ dominationi subjiciat. Ac du- bium non est, quin Christus in adventu Majestatis suæ abrogaturus sit etiam externa abolitione omnia mundana regna, & solus ipse perpetuo sit dominaturus: sed interea temporis ab eo cum- primis die, quo missus est Apostolis Spiritus San- ctus, Christus utitur humiliatione & dejectione re- gnorum ac Civitatum, pro ea ratione, quæ regno ejus in hoc mundo conveniat. Ita Osiander, ut & Brentius, qui observat etiam, posse hanc antithesin quoque generaliter intelligi hoc sensu: Omnia hujus mundi regna incurvantur, declinant ad interi- tum & deducentur tandem in pulverem, ut pedibus conculcentur. Solum enim regnum Christi perpetuo durabit. Cyrillus dæmonas hic conculcandos intel- ligit, qui munitis urbibus comparantur. Sed præ- ferenda prior interpretatio.

HVMILIABIT) Humiliavit: gloriam ei ab- stulit.

## 26:6
Verse 6. THE FOOT SHALL TREAD IT DOWN, THE FEET OF THE POOR, THE STEPS OF THE NEEDY) The inhabitants of Jerusalem, held as lost, will despise the Assyrians.

Latin:

Verf. 6. CONCVLCABIT EAM PES, PEDES PAVPERIS, GRESSVS EGENORUM) Contemnent Assyrios Hierosolymitæ, pro perditis habiti.

## 26:7
Verse 7. THE PATH OF THE UPRIGHT IS JUST, THE STRAIGHT WAY OF THE JUST TO WALK) The meaning is: that the path of the just is level: for his ways are made smooth by God. For it is an apostrophe to God.

Latin:

Verf. 7. SEMITA RECTI JVSTA EST, RE- CTVS CALLIS JUSTI AD AMBULANDVM) Sensus est: Semitam justi esse æquabilem: à Deo enim vias ejus complanari. Est enim Apostrophe ad Deum.

## 26:8
Verse 8. IN THE PATH OF YOUR JUDGMENTS.) Always obeying your law.

WE HAVE SUSTAINED YOU.) We have waited.

The discourse is not about the doctrine of the law, but rather about the Gospel. Those terms, judgments, the path of judgments, are used generally and denote the entire doctrine of the word of God, and thus even the Gospel itself, as is manifest even from Psalm 119. He had said before: THE PATH OF THE UPRIGHT IS JUST. He who has been justified through faith. THE UPRIGHT PATH OF THE JUST FOR WALKING. In the Hebrew there is an apostrophe to God, as Grotius acknowledges, you direct the path of the upright and just. For unless God by his Spirit should effect that we walk in the upright path and should direct our way, we would immediately fall away from the straight path. Some of our own explain the straight path as the very way by which one must go to heaven, which becomes known only through the Gospel; such as Brentius and Osiander. But when the faithful are said to wait for the Lord in the path of judgments, what other path can be understood than that of the Gospel?
