Deum non amplius rationem habe- re fœderis istius: projecisse civitates, non reputare homines miseros, neq; populi sui calamitate move- ri; his responsio Domini magis congruere videtur. Nunc consurgam, dicit Dominus, nunc exaltabor, nunc sublimabor. Etiamsi hucusq; videar irritum fecisse pactum, ac omnino projecisse Juda, non ta- men diutius deseram populum meum: nunc con- surgam, & accingam me ad liberandum eundem. Vers. 9. LUXIT ET ELANGUIT TERRA) Id est, Judæa in luctu & languore erat. CONFUSUS EST LIBANUS) Libanus mons ille superbus pudore perfundebatur. ET FACTUS EST SARON QUASI DESERTUM) Proxima Ba- sani arva squallebant. Vid. 1. Paral. 5, 16. CONCUSSA EST BASAN) Excussa. ET CARMELUS) Hic nomen est proprium. Memoran- tur enim loca, per quæ transierat Sennacheribus. Taci- tus Hist. 2. Est Judæam inter Syriamque Carmelus. Vid. & Plinium 5, 19. Nonnulli hic universam terram Judæam de- signari volunt, quæ istis quasi finibus suis terminata, quia Libanus ad Septentrionem, Saron ad Occi- dentem, Basan ad Orientem, Carmel ad Meridiem spectabat. Vers. 10. NUNC CONSURGAM, DICIT DOMINUS) Quasi dicat: nunc demum rebus omnibus deploratis tempus est me moveam. Vers. 11. CONCIPIETIS ARDOREM) Rectius: Quisquilias. PARIETIS STIPULAM) Id est, stulta consilia inanes habe- bunt eventus. Assyrios hic Deus alloquitur. SPIRITUS VESTER UT IGNIS VORABIT VOS) Ira vestra vobis exitio erit. Vers. 12. ET ERUNT POPULI QUASI DE INCENDIO CI- NIS) In Hebræo: & erunt populi incendia calcis. Id est, e- runt quasi positi in fornace calcaria. SPINÆ CONGREGATÆ IGNI COMBURENTUR) In Hebræo: Spinæ succisæ: præintelligendum quasi. Ita comburentur ut spinæ. Sæpe jam notavimus subitum illud malum, quod Assyriis immisit Deus, qualecunque tandem fue- rit, incendio comparari. Vers. 14 POSSEDIT TIMOR HYPOCRITAS) De illis lo- quitur, qui mutata religione salutem ab Assyrio quæri volebant. CUM ARDORIBUS SEMPITERNIS) Id est, cum igne, qui non exstinguitur. Talem putabant illi esse vim Assyriam. Sermo est de hypocritis in populo: non vero de apostatis. Illi simulant veram religionem & pie- tatem: hi vero à vera religione deficiunt. Conjun- guntur ergo hypocritæ cum aliis peccatoribus in Sion nondum resipiscentibus: utrique conterriti sunt, ut solent hypocritæ, & alii inpœnitentes pec- catores, in periculis esse timidissimi, quia fiducia in Deum carent. Hoc hominum genus in secundis rebus est securissimum, rursus in asperis rebus est despera- tissimum, ait B. Lutherus. QUIS, ajunt illi, POTE- RIT HABITARE DE NOBIS CUM IGNE DEVORANTE? QUIS HABITABIT EX NOBIS CUM ARBORIBUS (incendiis) SEM- PITERNIS. Hæc de Assyrio plerique accipiunt. Possent tamen de Deo ipso, qui ignis est consumens, Deut. 4, 24. Ebr. 12, 25. explicari, cujus iram in pu- blicis calamitatibus maxime horrent impii. Similis locus est Nah. 1, 6. Conf. 2. Chron. 34, 21. 26. Jerem. 44, 6. Atq; ita optime congruit responsio: utpote qua explicatur, quinam apud Deum habitaturi sint. Sentui huic nostro favent etiam autores notarum Belgicarum, imo etiam Hieronymus: Quis poterit habitare cum Deo?

## 33:15
Vers. 15. HE WHO WALKS IN JUSTICES) The Prophet responds to those words of the impious. Here is the character of a pious man, such as in Psalm 15. HE WHO CASTS AWAY AVARICE FROM CALUMNY) You may rightly translate: He who spurns gain from extortion. HE WHO STOPS HIS EARS, LEST HE HEAR BLOOD) He who is deaf to the calumnies through which the danger of another's life is plotted. AND SHUTS HIS EYES, LEST HE SEE EVIL) Evil, that is, ἀδικίαν, as the LXX here, the sense is: he turns away from every kind of injustice. Vers. 16. HE SHALL DWELL ON HIGH, HIS SUBLIMITY SHALL BE THE FORTIFICATIONS OF ROCKS) LXX. he shall dwell in a high cave of a strong rock: that is, he shall be no less safe than if he inhabited a tower on an inaccessible cliff. That happened to the pious Jerusalemites besieged by Sennacherib. BREAD IS GIVEN TO HIM) He shall be freed from hunger. LXX. bread shall be given to him. HIS WATERS ARE FAITHFUL) That which he may drink shall not be lacking to him. Vers. 17. HIS EYES SHALL SEE THE KING IN HIS BEAUTY) Sitting on the throne of majesty. THEY SHALL BEHOLD THE LAND FROM AFAR) Virgil: --- it pleases to go and see the Dorian camps and the deserted places. They shall not be shut up within the walls for long, but will wander wherever it pleases them.

Some interpreters explain this concerning King Hezekiah. But others have observed that this is a more sublime promise; who therefore understand it through Christ the King. For it concerns the benefit which falls to the pious and faithful, who walk in JUSTICES. By which plural noun Brentius understands a twofold justice, namely of faith and of works. But the vision of Hezekiah on the throne is not a benefit proper to the faithful: Furthermore, the previous benefits are also so arranged that they properly suit the faithful. He who walks in justices, who speaks right things, and abominates gain from calumnies, etc., he dwells on high, in the help of the most high God, Psalm 92, 1. nor are necessary foods ever lacking to him, Matthew 6. Ps. 36. Prov. 10. He who is such, says Jerome, shall himself dwell in the heights, that is, in the kingdom of heaven, or in the high cave of the most strong rock, in Christ Jesus, which rock followed the people of Israel, that they might drink from it, and be protected by its strength. The eyes of the faithful therefore see the King Messiah in his beauty, or majesty, reigning not only in a corner of the land of Judea, but in a far-off land, in the whole world, Ps. 72. THE HEART SHALL BE ASTONISHED AT THE WONDER (Thus the Hebrew is to be rendered: The Vulgate has, IT SHALL MEDITATE FEAR: which Grotius explains: The memory of the dangers passed will be sweet. But who does not see that this exposition is merely arbitrary!) AND YOU SHALL SAY WHERE IS THE SCRIBE, WHERE IS THE CENSOR, WHERE IS THE CHANCELLOR! For this is worthy of wonder, that in the kingdom of Christ the chief place is held not by the wise of this world, not by Censors, not by Chancellors, but by the humble, the simple, and the abject. For whom shall we give as a more certain Interpreter than the Apostle, who explains these things concerning the kingdom of Christ in 1 Cor. 1. The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who believe, it is the power of God. For it is written; I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the intelligence of the intelligent. Where is the wise man? Where is the Scribe? Where is the disputer of this world? To which also pertain those words of Christ in Matt. 11. I give thanks to you Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones. And the discourse seems to be about that king, whom he designated in ch. 31, 1: He who is such, says Jerome, shall behold King Christ in his brightness, of whom it is said above: Behold a just King shall reign, and Princes shall rule in judgment. Brentius pursues this interpretation at greater length: To whom Osiander also agrees in his Paraphrase. The ancient Doctors also explain it concerning Christ the King. Justin. in Dialogue with Trypho. Cyprian, book 2, against the Jews, ch. 28. Jerome, whom we have already cited: Prosper on Predestination, part 3, ch. 2. Procopius and others. Nor do Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus, and Menochius deny it. Those things which Grotius here brings forward from the sense of the Prophet—concerning the scribe of the Assyrians who inscribed the captives in a register, concerning their weigher or collector of tributes who exacted coins at the scale, concerning the one counting or measuring the towers, whom the Latin renders 'teacher of little ones,' and Luther and others interpret as 'Chancellor'—are foreign to the sense of the Prophet. I know that Piscator, Junius, and others explain it in almost the same way as Grotius, but how that interpretation agrees with the Pauline citation does not appear. Although Junius denies in Sacred Parallels, book 2, parallel 29, that the words of Isaiah were cited by the Apostle; yet Jerome and others are more correct, 1. Cor. 1, wish for this passage of Isaiah to be looked at, whence it is also brought forward in the margins of editions of the New Testament as a parallel to 1 Cor. 1:20. And the very words of the Apostle confirm this: πᾶ σοφὸς, πᾶ γραμματεύς; πᾶ ζητητής 8̂ αἰῶνος τέτε; He who is called ספר in Hebrew, and by the interpreter Paul γραμματεύς, is called a man of letters; because the experts in the law were so called in Ezra 7:6, whence the Syriac in 1 Cor. 1 rendered it 'expert in the law.' But he whom the Prophet calls a WEIGHER is an interpreter of the law, weighing words, called by the Apostle σοφὸς, who wishes to weigh all things in the balance of his own mind. Finally, what is in Hebrew ספר את המגדלים, counting or reviewing great and high or sublime things, and twin towers, is explained by Paul as συζητητὴς 8̂ αἰῶνῶ τέτε, a disputer of this age: for such are indicated who review and dispute the great and sublime things of this age.

Latin:

Vers. 15. QUI AMBULAT IN JUSTITIIS) Respondet Pro- pheta ad illa verba impiorum. Est hic χαρακτὴρ homi- nis pii, qualis Psal. 15. QUI PROJICIT AVARITIAM EX CALUMNIA) Recte vertas: Qui spernit lucrum ex concussione. QUI OBTURAT AURES SUAS, NE AUDIAT SANGVINEM) Qui surdus est ad calumnias, per quas vitæ alterius periculum struitur. ET CLAUDIT OCULOS SUOS, NE VIDEAT MALUM) Ma- lum, id est, ἀδικίαν, ut hic LXX, sensus est: aversatur o- mne genus injustitiæ. Vers. 16. ISTE IN EXCELSIS HABITABIT, MUNIMENTA SAXORUM SUBLIMITAS EJUS) LXX. ὗτος οἰκήσει ἐν ὑψηλῷ σπηλαίῳ πέτρας ἰσχυρᾶς: id est, erit non minus tutus, quam si turrem in inaccessa rupe inhabitaret. Id evenit Hiero- solymitis piis à Sennacheribo obsessis. PANIS EI DATUS EST) A fame liberabitur. LXX. ἄρτος δοθήσεται αὐτῷ. AQUÆ EJUS FIDELES SUNT) Non deerit ei, quod bibat. Vers. 17. REGEM IN DECORE SUO VIDEBUNT OCULI E- JUS) In solio majestatis sedentem. CERNENT TERRAM DE LONGE) Virgilius: --- libet ire & dorica castra Desertosque videre locos. Non erunt diu inclusi mœnibus, sed quaqua lubebit spa- tiabuntur.

Explicant nonnulli Interpp. de Rege Ezechia. Sed sublimiorem hanc esse promissionem, alii ob- servarunt; qui proinde per Regem Christum intel- ligunt. Agitur enim de beneficio, quod obtingit piis & fidelibus, qui ambulant in JUSTITIIS. Quo plurali nomine justitiam duplicem, fidei nempe & operum intelligit Brentius. At visio Ezechiæ in so- lio beneficium non est fidelium proprium: Adhæc priora etiam beneficia ita comparata sunt, ut fideli- bus proprie conveniant. Qui ambulat in justitiis, qui loquitur recta, & abominatur lucrum ex calu- mniis, &c. hic habitat in excelsis, in adjutorio Dei altissimi, Psal. 92, 1. nec unquam ei desunt alimenta necessaria Matth. 6. Ps. 36. Prov. 10. Qui talis est, inquit Hieronymus, ipse habitabit in excelsis, hoc est, in regno cælorum, sive in excelsa spelunca petræ fortissimæ, in Christo Jesu, quæ petra Israël populum sequebatur, ut biberet de ea, & ejus fortitudine prote- geretur. Vident itaq; oculi fidelium Messiam regem in decore, vel majestate sua dominantem non in an- gulo tantum terræ Judææ, sed in terra longinqua, in toto orbe terrarum, Psal. 72. COR PRÆ AD- MIRATIONE OBSTUPESCET (Sic reddenda Ebræa: Vulgatus habet, MEDITA- BITUR TIMOREM: quod Grotius exponit: Dulcis erit exactorum periculorum memoria. Sed quis non videt, mere arbitrariam esse illam expo- sitionem!) ET DICES UBI EST SCRIBA, UBI CENSOR, UBI CANCELLA- RIUS! Hoc enim admiratione dignum est, quod in regno Christi præcipuum locum non sapientes hujus seculi, non Censores, non Cancellarii, sed humiles, simplices & abjecti obtineant. Quem enim dabimus certiorem Interpretem, quam Apo- stolum, qui hæc de Christi regno explicat 1. Cor. 1. Sermo crucis est stultitia iis, qui pereunt, at nobis qui credimus, potentia Dei est. Scriptum est enim; per- dam sapientiam sapientum, & intelligentiam intelli- gentium rejiciam. Ubi sapiens? Ubi Scriba? Ubi dis- putator hujus seculi? Quo etiam faciunt illa Christi Matth. 11. Gratias ago tibi Pater Domine cæli & ter- ræ, quod absconderis hæc à sapientibus & prudenti- bus, & revelaris ea parvulis. Et de rege illo sermo videtur esse, quem c. 31, 1. designavit: Qui talis est, inquit Hieronymus, Regem Christum in sui clarita- te conspiciet, de quo supra dicitur: Ecce Rex justus re- gnabit, & Principes in judicio præerunt. Pluribus hanc interpretationem persequitur Brentius: Cui etiam adstipulatur Osiand. in Paraphrasi. De Chri- sto Rege etiam exponunt antiqui Doctores. Justin. in Dial. cum Triphone. Cyprian. lib. 2. contra Ju- dæos c. 28. Hieronymus, quem jam adduximus: Pro- sper de Prædest. part. 3. c. 2. Procopius & alii. Neque abnuunt Cornel. a Lap. Tirinus, Menoch. Aliena argo à sensu Prophetæ sunt, quæ hic Grotius de Assyriorum scriba, qui captivos matriculæ inscribebat, de eorum ponderatore, vel collectore tributorum, qui ad saco- mam nummos exegit, de numerante vel metiente tur- res, quem Latinus reddit, doctorem parvulorum, Lu- therus & alii Cancellarium interpretantur. Novi, quod ad eundem modum fere cum Grotio expli- cent Piscator, Junius & alii, sed quomodo ista inter- pretatio cum Paulina allegatione conveniat, non apparet. Quamvis vero Junius neget in Parallel. Sa- cris lib. 2. parall. 29. ab Apostolo allegata esse Esaiæ ver- ba; Rectius tamen Hieronymus, & alii, 1. Cor. 1. hunc Esaiæ locum respici volunt, unde etiam ad margi- nem in editionibus Novi T. ceu parallelus 1. Cor. 1. 20. adducitur. Idq; verba ipsa apostoli confirmant, πᾶ σοφὸς, πᾶ γραμματεύς; πᾶ ζητητής 8̂ αἰῶνος τέτε; Qui in Ebræo ספר, Interprete Paulo γραμ- ματεύς, literatus dicitur; quia ita vocabantur legis- periti Esd. 7, 6. unde Syrus 1. Cor. 1. legisperitum red- didit. Quem vero Propheta PONDERATOREM vocat, interpres legis est, verba ponderans, ab A po- stolo σοφὸς vocatus, qui omnia ponditare vult tru- tina mentis suę. deniq; quod in Ebręo est ספר את המגדלים numerans vel recensens res magnas, & al- tas, vel sublimes, turribqs geminas, à Paulo explica- tur, συζητητὴς 8̂ αἰῶνῶ τέτε, disquisitor seculi hu- jus: nam tales indigitantur, qui res magnas & subli- mes hujus seculi recensent, ac disquirunt.

## 33:18
THY HEART SHALL MEDITATE TERROR) The memory of dangers passed will be sweet.

Verse 18, where it is WHERE IS THE MAN OF LETTERS) ספר signifies a scribe. He understands him here as the one who inscribed the captives in a register, he names the chiefs of the Assyrian camps, and asks where they are, namely, they are gone.

WHERE IS HE WHO WEIGHS THE WORDS OF THE LAW?) In the Hebrew: Weigher: that is, a collector of tributes, who exacted coins at the scale.

WHERE IS THE TEACHER OF LITTLE ONES?) In the Hebrew: where is he who counts the towers: that is, measuring, like Capaneus at Thebes, of whom the old man says in the Phoenissae of Euripides: 'He calculates the seven approaches of the towers, measuring the walls up and down.'

Latin:

COR TVVM MEDITABITVR TIMOREM) Dulcis erit exactorum periculorum memoria.

Vers. 18. ubi EST LITERATUS) ספר scribam signi- ficat, Hic eum intelligit, qui captivos matriculæ inscrihe- bat, nominat castrorum Assyriorum præcipuos, & quærit ubi sint, nempe οἴχονται.

UBI LEGIS VERBA PONDERANS) In Hebræo: Ponde- rator: id est, collector tributorum, qui ad sacomam num- rios exigebat.

UBI DOCTOR PARVULORUM) In Hebræo: ubi nume- rans turres: id est, metiens, ut Capaneus ad Thebas, de quo senex in Euripideis Phœnissis: Ἐκεῖνῶ ἑπτὰ προσϐάσεις τεκμαίρεται Πύργων, ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω τείχη μετρῶν.

## 33:19
Verse 19. THOU SHALT NOT SEE A BRAZEN PEOPLE) The arrogant Assyrian.

A PEOPLE OF DEEP SPEECH) In the Hebrew: A people of speech too abstruse to be understood. The following words signify the same. If the people of the Jews did not understand the Syriac language, as you see in 2 Kings 18:26, much less the Assyrian.

Brentius also explains these, as a special blessing of the Church or the kingdom of Christ, as does Osiander, who renders them thus: 'A strong people (i.e., truculent, tyrannical, whom you cannot overcome) you shall not see, a people of deep lips, so that they cannot be heard, who is of a stammering tongue, and cannot be understood, i.e., the robust and barbarian peoples, whose language you cannot understand, will not afflict the Church.' Because, namely, the sending in of barbarian peoples is a curse, Deut. 28. Since those things which precede pertain to the kingdom of Christ, as do those which follow, therefore these intermediate things also seem to be taken in this way. Most, however, understand these things as not seeing the Assyrians, because they will not penetrate into the city. In which manner the Prophet then turns himself again from the earthly Jerusalem to the tabernacle of the Church. But the connection of the whole context will be clearer if you explain these intermediate things also concerning the kingdom of Christ. For the Prophet addresses the same just man of whom he had said, 'Thy heart shall be astonished with great wonder': to him, therefore, he also says: 'Thou shalt not see a strong people': and further: 'Look upon Zion,' etc. Let Brentius be consulted concerning the whole passage.

Latin:

Vers. 19. POPULUM IMPUDENTEM NON VIDEBIS) Arrogantem Assyrium.

POPULUM ALTI SERMONIS) In Hebræo: Populum sermonis abstrusioris, quam ut intelligatur. Idem significant verba sequentia. Si Syriacam linguam populus Judæorum non intelligebat, ut vides 2. Reg. 18, 26. multo minus Assyriam.

Explicat hæc etiam, ceu benedictionem pecu- liarem Ecclesiæ vel regni Christi Brentius, ut & O- siander, qui ea ita reddit: Populum fortem (i. e. tru- culentum, tyrannicum, quem superare non possis) non videbis, populum profundorum labiorum, quam ut audiri possit, qui blesæ est linguæ, nec intelligi po- test, i. e. non adfligent Ecclesiam populi robusti, & barbari, quorum linguam intelligere nequeas. quia sc. maledictio est populorum barbarorum immissio Deut. 28. Quum enim ea, quæ præcedunt, in regnũ Christi competant, ut & ea quæ sequuntur, idcirco etiam hæc intermedia ita accipienda videntur. Ple- riq; tamen ista de non videndis Assyriis intelligunt, quod in urbem penetraturi non sint. Quo pacto deinde sese iterum convertit Propheta à Jerusalem terrena ad Ecclesiæ tabernaculum. Sed συνέχεια cla- rior erit totius contextus, si intermedia hæc etiam exponas de Christi regno. Eundem enim justum al- loquitur Propheta, de quo dixerat, Cor tuum obstu- pescet præ magna admiratione: huic ergo etiam ait: Populum fortem non videbis: & porro: respice Sio- nem, &c. Videatur de toto loco Brentius.

## 33:20
Verse same. LOOK UPON ZION) That is, contemplate Zion with joy.

THE CITY OF OUR SOLEMNITY) The city to which people flock from all sides on feast days.

Verse 20.

TABERNACLE, WHICH SHALL BY NO MEANS BE MOVED) An immovable tent.

NOR SHALL THE NAILS THEREOF BE TAKEN AWAY FOR EVER) He calls those pegs nails, to which the ropes of the tents are fastened. For ever: that is, for a long time.

Latin:

Vers. eod. RESPICE SION) Id est, cum gaudio con- templare Sionem.

CIVITATEM SOLENNITATIS NOSTRAE) Urbem, ad quam undique diebus festis confluitur.

Vers. 20.

TABERNACULUM, QUOD NEQUAQUAM TRANSFERRI POTERIT) Tentorium immobile.

NEC AUFERENTUR CLAVI EJUS IN SEMPITERNUM) Clavos vocat paxillos illos, ad quos tentoriorum funes alligantur. In sempiternum: id est, in longo tempore.

## 33:21
Verse 21. A PLACE OF RIVERS AND BROAD STREAMS) God will be for us as a river surrounding the city. This metaphor pleased him. Therefore he pursues it.

NO GALLEY WITH OARS SHALL PASS THROUGH IT) That is, all things are tranquil for you.

NOR SHALL A GALLANT SHIP PASS THROUGH IT) A trieres is one thing, a trireme another: a trireme is driven by three oars, a trieres by three banks of oars: but often in Latin books the ignorance of scribes has confused these.

The ancient interpreters explain this not of Zion or earthly Jerusalem, but of the spiritual one. For it is customary for spiritual things and the antitype to be designated by the Prophets through words appropriate to the type or to bodily things. For SION, JERUSALEM, and THE CITY OF OUR SOLEMNITIES, as it is here in the Hebrew, is also called the Church, Heb. 12. THIS IS A SECURE HABITATION AND A TABERNACLE OF THE LORD, WHICH SHALL BY NO MEANS BE MOVED, because the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, Matt. 16. Nor is the name of tabernacle, not temple, used here without cause, so that it may be implied that the discourse is not about the Jerusalem temple, nor about that earthly city of Jerusalem: but about the Church of Christ, which, as the tabernacle of the Lord, is tied to no place, yet is perpetually preserved. And how could the Jerusalem temple be called a tabernacle, which SHALL BY NO MEANS BE MOVED, nor shall its nails be taken away FOR EVER, AND ALL ITS ROPES SHALL NOT BE BROKEN, if indeed it was afterwards destroyed by the Chaldeans and leveled to the ground! Therefore, these things must necessarily be explained of the immovable firmness of the Church: even though when the Prophet alluded to the city of Jerusalem and to the temple, the faithful could gather that in the city, if they walked in justice, and spoke uprightly, and cast away avarice, the temple and the seat of the Lord would be preserved among them, if indeed He wills to protect His own Church; and it is manifest that the Prophet continues to address the just man, and continues the promises made to him who strives for true piety. To whom he promised that his eyes would see the King Christ in his beauty, that their heart would admire the divine economy in the kingdom of Christ, that he would be safe from a barbarous people: to him he also promises that his eyes will see with pleasure the spiritual Jerusalem, a secure habitation, a tabernacle which will remain fixed and immovable for eternity. There is no reason, therefore, why we should take that FOR EVER as meaning only a long time. And since the temple had stood for scarcely a century and a half from this prophecy, how would the outcome have corresponded to so magnificent a promise, if it were to be understood of that? Those things are still subjoined which imply not only a temporary conversation, but a perennial one, and demonstrate that the Church will be invincible: BECAUSE THE LORD OUR GOD IS MAGNIFICENT THERE in preserving the Church, he wondrously shows his majesty and glory: A PLACE OF RIVERS AND BROAD STREAMS, NO GALLEY WITH OARS SHALL PASS THROUGH IT, the work of rowers, NOR SHALL A GALLANT SHIP PASS THROUGH IT. Triremes or other large ships cannot penetrate to that city to offer it violence, as it is surrounded by rivers and broad streams: the waters for they will indeed be so deep that they cannot be crossed on foot, nor will they support the burdens of ships, and therefore the city will be inaccessible and impregnable. Which does not fit Jerusalem: but that the Church will be invincible and impregnable is taught by this figurative discourse: the reason proper to the Church being adduced: FOR THE LORD IS OUR JUDGE, THE LORD IS OUR LAWGIVER, THE LORD IS OUR KING. HE WILL SAVE US. The most holy Trinity preserves and saves the faithful from all enemies; God the Father is our Judge and avenger, the Holy Spirit is our Lawgiver or Teacher: the Son of God is our King. By the grace and mighty work of this triune LORD we are saved, and secure against all our enemies. Thus Jerome on the words, Look upon Zion, O just one, to whom it was said above: Thy heart shall meditate on fear, and thou shalt not see the impudent people: And thou who hadst heard before, thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty, contemplate Zion the city of our solemnity: see the Church of Christ, in which is true solemnity, thine eyes shall discern the vision of peace, and unexpected riches, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man, and a tabernacle, which shall in no wise be moved. For the former tabernacle, which the people of the Jews had, was translated and taken away, nor shall its stakes be moved forever, and all its cords shall be firm, so that the Lord may dwell in it, which place is of all rivers and running streams, through which no one of the adverse party will be able to sail, nor will a great galley, which is interpreted as the Devil, be able to cross it: because the Lord himself is our judge and prince and King and Savior, and with him protecting we shall fear no snares. These things were said of Zion the city of our solemnity, and of Jerusalem the most wealthy habitation, which the Lord himself will surround and fortify with his rivers. Thus also Cyril: Behold Zion the city of OUR SALVATION (for so the LXX Interpreters have it). They signify by these things either the Church on earth, or the highest and beautiful city in the heavens, the nourisher of the Saints. Wherefore whether one names this Church on earth, or conceives that one in his mind, one thing will be demonstrated by both. For those who are in this lower one will in the progress of time be also in that highest and heavenly one. Thus Brentius of our own. It is manifest that these things cannot be understood of the external city of Jerusalem, which although it was not devastated by Sennacherib, yet was afterwards devastated by the Babylonians. Wherefore it ought to be understood of the true and heavenly Jerusalem, which is the Church of Christ, gathered through the Gospel from the whole world. This is the tranquil habitation. This is that true tabernacle of Moed, that is, of the pact, of the testimony, and of the assembly, which the tabernacle of Moses built in the desert shadowed forth. This can never perish forever, even if not only men, but even the Devils themselves should attack it. And a little later. What is it that makes Zion or the Church of God so firm? The Prophet answers: Because there is the magnificent Lord for us, a place of rivers and streams, which extend their hands or banks and shores very far, so that neither a ship of rowers, nor a great ship can pass through them. This is, the Church is so firm because it does not have any earthly man as a defender, nor is it situated in these lands after the manner of other cities, but has the Lord God himself as its defender, who in his magnificence and fortitude excels all worldly Kings and princes. And it is situated in the midst of the greatest rivers, through which no hostile fleet, whether of small or large ships, can pass, to storm and plunder it. The Church is said to be situated not on lands, but in the midst of the widest rivers, because it is so fortified by divine protection that it cannot be subverted and destroyed by any power of men or demons. Brentius wishes those words, Our Lord is our judge, the Lord is our leader, the Lord is our King, to be said of Christ, and indeed by antithesis to the government of the people of God performed by Judges, by Teachers and Priests, Eli and Samuel, by Kings, Saul, David and his descendants, inasmuch as they shadowed forth Christ the true judge, vindicating his people from all evils: the true Teacher and Priest, who offered himself for us, and the true King, who prepared and preserves for his people an eternal Kingdom in the heavens, whence it cannot happen that the Church should perish and be destroyed. He himself יושיענו WILL SAVE us. For this name was proper to Christ, who was called JESUS the SAVIOR of his people. B. Osiander, Calvin, Junius, the Authors of the Belgian notes, Amama, and others also explain this concerning the preservation of the kingdom of Christ. Tirinus notes that the Church is explained as the Church triumphant in heaven by Cyril, Procopius, Adam Sasbouth, Osorius, Haymo, and Cornel. à Lapide, and as the Church militant by Jerome, Theodoret, and Alvarez. Menochius, whom Grotius is accustomed to value highly, explained everything from verse 17 onwards as concerning the Church triumphant: and on v. 21 he has it thus: A PLACE OF RIVERS &c. i.e. in Jerusalem, not the earthly one (for this suffers from a scarcity of waters) but the heavenly one, there will be a huge river, like many rivers, from which the widest and open streams will flow down in every direction. St. John makes mention of THIS heavenly river, when in Rev. ch. 22 he says: And he showed me a river of water of life, bright as Crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb. This river signifies the exuberance of gifts, joys and pleasures, which God and Christ will pour out upon the blessed. IT SHALL NOT PASS &c. that is, no ship or hostile trireme shall pass through this river, which might disturb the peace of the city or plunder its wealth. This is Menochius. Concerning rivers in the Church, and its immovable firmness, David also sang in Ps. 46:5: The streams of the river make glad the city of God, he has sanctified his tabernacle in it, he himself is in the midst of it. And it shall never be moved. God shall HELP it in the morning, at the dawn, that is, timely, most quickly. Grotius connects v. 20 with this v. 21, or rather repeats the name of God from the same, and explains the place of rivers of very broad streams thus: God shall be for us instead of a river surrounding the city. Which fits the Church excellently. For to it God is instead of a river, while he inundates it with a river of grace and his gifts; and flows around it, so that it may be safe and secure from enemies. And thus Calvin not badly: NO SHIP SHALL PASS. Great rivers have this disadvantage, that they can provide access to enemies so that they may approach us by ship closer than is expedient. Thus, what seems to help greatly very often does harm. But the Lord says that he will be for us instead of a river, so that no such disadvantage is to be feared, nor shall access be open to enemies. He enumerates two species of ships, long ones and merchant ones, so that he may show that enemies will be prohibited in all ways. Ludovicus de Dieu confirms this opinion from the sources, namely that God is called here the place of rivers, in his Animadversiones on v. 21. כִּי אִם־שָׁם אַדִּיר יְהוָה לָנוּ מְקוֹם נְהָרִים. Pagninus and Junius distinguished these in such a way that אַדִּיר might be a description of the subject of the enunciation, and מְקוֹם might be the predicate. But in that sense, neither should לָנוּ have had a Zakeph, by which it would be distinguished from the following words, nor should the adjective אַדִּיר be placed before the substantive יְהוָה but after it. As the custom of the Hebrew language requires, that אַדִּיר should constitute the predicate, יְהוָה the subject, then again מְקוֹם the other predicate of the same subject: which the Vulgate and the Genevans rightly noted. I translate therefore: Truly there the magnificent Jehovah is for us like a lake of rivers, of broad streams, through which will not go &c. Verse 23. THY ROPES ARE LOOSED.) Because of the begun comparison of a river, he compares the Assyrian army to a ship, as Horace does the Roman Republic, whose passage corresponding to this is: - - - and without ropes the hulls can scarcely endure the imperious sea. SO SHALL THY MAST BE.) In the Hebrew: they will not make firm (that is, they will not have firm) the mast. In Horace: And the mast wounded by the swift South wind. THAT THOU CANST NOT SPREAD THE SIGN.) In the Hebrew: they will not expand the sail. Horace: Thy sails are not whole. THEN SHALL THE SPOILS OF MUCH PREY BE DIVIDED) See above 4. THE LAME SHALL TAKE THE PREY.) Proverbial: similar to 2 Sam. 5, 6. NOR SHALL THE NEIGHBOR SAY.) Rather, the inhabitant. I AM WEAK) I am weak from the siege. THE INIQUITY SHALL BE TAKEN AWAY FROM HIM.) The sense of all evil shall be taken away from the people. This interpretation concerning the Assyrians, who were attacking Jerusalem in vain, can be admitted, without prejudice to the explanation of the kingdom of Christ which precedes it. For thus the application is subjoined to that city in which God then had his hearth. And so Menochius explained it, whom Grotius followed in that part. THY ROPES ARE LOOSED, he says, he passed to the Assyrian, the enemy of the Jews, whom he addresses, with the allegory of the ship continued: the meaning is: The cables of thy ship are loosened, or broken. THEY SHALL NOT PREVAIL, having been made useless, and not able to keep the mast of the ship erect in its state. SO SHALL THY MAST &c. The mast of thy ship shall be overturned, nor wilt thou be able to spread thy banner at its top, as is wont to be done. THE SPOILS SHALL BE DIVIDED &c. By your army having been struck by the Angel. THE LAME SHALL TAKE THE PREY. So much so that there will be no one who can forbid it. NOR SHALL THE NEIGHBOR SAY I AM WEAK. But all those living in the surrounding places will be cheerful and erect in gathering the spoils. THE INIQUITY SHALL BE TAKEN AWAY FROM HIM. With the wicked Assyrians killed or put to flight, by whom he was oppressed: a better fortune will shine upon the people living in that region. Thus far the interpretation of Menochius. Cornel. à Lapide likewise wishes the Prophet to return to the argument of the chapter, to the times of Hezekiah and Sennacherib, but he wishes Zion to be addressed, thy tent ropes will only be loosened by the Assyrians (they will be broken) so that it may seem to be torn down: But they shall not prevail against thee. Thus that mast, which sustains the mass of the tent like a support (King Hezekiah) will fall forward, so that he cannot spread a military sign upon it, (his forces will be so collapsed that he cannot gather and array an army for the protection of the city) but then suddenly a wonderful conversion of things will happen &c. Calvin thinks the Assyrians are addressed, but that under their person the Prophet is simultaneously addressing any enemies whatsoever, and is pursuing his own simile, which he had used at the beginning. He had said, he says, that the Church is like a place fortified and surrounded by most ample rivers, through which access is not open to enemies, now he compares the state of the impious to ships: by which he signifies that they do not have a solid foundation, even though they show themselves formidable, burn with madness, and rage ferociously, and no one seems able to resist their fury. Although therefore they may have long ships and merchant ships, by which they join in a certain way the most widely separated regions, and obtain the empire of land and sea, yet nothing lasting or firm will be among them. The Lord will overturn their ships, and with ropes and masts broken, he will involve them in the same shipwreck. Amama [compares] the Hebrew text with Pagninus, the English, Genevan, Italian, and Spanish. The Tigurine [Bible] thinks it should be translated thus: thy ropes are loose, sind schlaff worden: (because they are not filled by the wind) nor can they rightly sustain their mast, nor will they expand the sail. And so also the Belgians rendered it in their Bibles. Franc. Junius interprets it thus, they will desert thy cables, (so that it is an apostrophe to the fleet of the enemies, with which they think to invade the Church) they have not yet confirmed their erect mast, they have not yet expanded the sail, then the prey of the spoil is seen &c. Others wish these things to be said to the Jewish Synagogue by way of contrast. But thou, O miserable Synagogue, thy ropes are loosened or broken, as the Chaldeans and Greeks have it, AND THEY SHALL NOT PREVAIL, they will no longer be able to sustain the tent. Thou wilt not be able TO SPREAD THE SIGN, (thy sail) on the MAST, let alone protect thyself: even the LAME themselves, and the blind Gentiles SHALL TAKE THE PREY. NOR shall thy NEIGHBOR, the Gentile people, say any longer, I AM WEAK, because all will be robust through Christ. For INIQUITY SHALL BE TAKEN AWAY FROM HIM. Thus Adam Sasbouth, and Tirinus. But because mention of the Jewish Synagogue had not been made, it is rashly introduced here. Nor can the former interpretations be admitted, because, namely, the Assyrian is addressed here; because the suffix in the word THY ROPES is of the feminine gender, whence it cannot be referred to anything other than to Zion, who was addressed before. Which I see also observed by our Brentius, an accurate interpreter of the Holy Scriptures. Whence he has these things regarding this rather difficult passage: Interpreters explain these things concerning the adversaries of the people of God: But because the suffix, which is added to the word for ropes in Hebrew, is of the feminine gender, and seems to look toward Zion, and the rest of the composition itself also agrees with that, we shall refer these things also to the Church. They ought, however, to be translated thus: Thy ropes are loosened, they are not strong. So also their mast (namely, it is not strong) they do not expand (on it) the banner. Then the prey of much spoil is divided, the lame take the prey. Nor does the inhabitant say, I am weak. And this is the meaning: When the Lord Christ, our Judge, Teacher, and King, is about to take up the administration of His Kingdom on earth, the ropes of the tent of Zion, or the Church (for above he called the Church a tent, whose ropes should not be broken) will indeed seem to be loosened, and not at all strongly to hold the constitution of the tent. The mast also, or the pole of this tent, will not seem to be firm enough, so that a sail can scarcely be hung upon it, yet then the greatest prey will be divided among the people of God, just as is wont to happen when victory is won. And the prey will be so obvious everywhere that even the lame will be about to seize it. Nor will anyone among the citizens and inhabitants complain any longer about his own weakness, but all will leap up healthy and firm for joy. To this also returns the Osiandrian Paraphrase: Thy cords are loosened, but they shall not (strongly) stretch (the tabernacle); so shall thy mast be, that thou canst not (sufficiently conveniently) spread the sail: that is, the affairs of the Church shall be in such a state as if someone were to fix a tabernacle or tent; whose mast (which ought to sustain the whole burden of the tabernacle) might appear so infirm that you would not believe it could bear for the sails of the Tabernacle to be hung, without either breaking or collapsing, and the cords on the sides not being well stretched, so that such a tent might appear at every moment to be meditating ruin, etc. Ludovicus de Dieu acknowledges that the Church is addressed in these words: and the Hebrew text, which is thus: נָטְשׁוּ חֲבָלָיִךְ בַּל יְחַזְקוּ כֵן תָּרְנָם בַּל פָּרְשׂוּ נֵס he rendered in this manner: Thy pains are left behind, they shall not strengthen the base of their mast, they shall not spread the banner. With this explanation added: In war, a mast was accustomed to be fixed in the ground, and to it a banner was appended, whence these two are also joined, Isa. 30:17. The sense is: there is no reason for you to grieve, O Church, your sorrows are left behind: which we say significantly in Dutch, 'Uwe droefheden syn achter ghelaten.' For although enemies stir up war against you, God will not permit them even to be able to strengthen the base of their evil, and to spread a banner in it set out against you, even then, as if they were conquered, the best spoils will be distributed, of which even the lame will be participants. But because mention was made earlier of ships and galleys, and it is manifest that the same allegory is continued here, this must be understood not of the evil of the earth fixed, but of the evil of a ship. For the word חבליך must be explained here not of sorrows but of ropes, just as it has been understood by all interpreters. The simplest sense therefore seems to be: YOUR ROPES ARE EXTENDED (O Zion). The Lord himself extends them. THEY WILL NOT STRENGTHEN, or they will be able to strengthen and fortify AGAINST YOU THE BASE of their evil (in their ships: the discourse is about the enemies of the Church) NOR WILL THEY SPREAD (will they be able to spread) A SAIL, or a banner; or if the word נטשׁ is to be rendered, THEY ARE LEFT BEHIND, the sense will be: Your ropes are indeed left behind, or deserted (as far as appearance in calamities is concerned): But the enemies will not be able to strengthen the base of their evil against you, or to spread a sail, much less to penetrate to you: nay, as soon as they attempt that, they will provide a partition even to much spoil, so that even the lame themselves will be about to plunder the prey. This is a bit more prolix concerning a sufficiently difficult passage. But the things that are subjoined explain the preceding things in summary, and in clear words: NOR SHALL THE INHABITANT of spiritual Zion, of which it has been treated thus far, SAY: I AM WEAK. From that danger, which the enemies had threatened, striving to strengthen evil and to spread a sail, so that they might penetrate to Zion, THE PEOPLE WHO DWELLED IN IT (ב in Zion) SHALL HAVE THEIR INIQUITY REMOVED FROM THEM. For all who are true citizens (through faith) of spiritual Zion, or Jerusalem, will obtain on account of the Messiah the remission of all their sins. The blessed Luther (whom the Weimar Paraphrase also illustrates) has therefore happily expressed the sense in these last two verses. Although he departs somewhat from the first words in the former clause of v. 23, and with most refers them to the Assyrians.

Latin:

Vers. 21. LOCUS FLUVIORUM RIVI LATISSIMI ET PATENTES) Deus nobis erit pro fluvio circumiente urbem. Placuit ei haec translatio. Itaque eam persequitur.

NON TRANSIBIT PER EUM NAVIS REMIGUM) Id est, omnia tibi tranquilla.

NEQUE TRIERIS MAGNA TRANSGREDIETUR EUM) A- liud trieres, aliud triremes: aliud triremes tribus remis aguntur: trieres ternis remorum ordinibus: sed saepe in libris Latinis inscitia librariorum haec confudit.

Non de Sione vel Hierosolyma terrena, sed spi- rituali explicant veteres Interpp. Solent enim ver- bis typo vel rebus corporalibus convenientibus designari penes Prophetas res spirituales, & anti- typus. SION enim HIERUSALEM & URBS CONVENTUS NOSTRI, ut hic in Ebraeo ha- betur, dicitur etiam Ecclesia, Ebr. 12. HAEC EST HABITATIO SECURA ET TABERNA- CULUM DOMINI, QUOD NEQUAQUAM TRANSFERRI POTEST, quia portae inferorum non praevalebunt adversus eam, Matth. 16. Nec prae- ter causam hic nomen tabernaculi, non templi adhi- betur, ut innuatur, sermonem esse non de templo Hierosolymitano, nec de terrena illa urbe Hierusa- lem: sed de Ecclesia Christi, quae sc. ut tabernaculum Domini nulli loco alligata est, perpetuo tamen conservatur. Et quomodo templum Hierosolymi- tanum dici poterat tabernaculum, quod NEQUA- QUAM TRANSFERRI poterit, nec auferentur clavi ejus IN SECULUM, ET OMNES FUNI- CULI EJUS NON RUMPENTUR, siquidem illud postmodum a Chaldaeis dirutum, & solo ae- quatum fuerit! Proinde necessario haec de Eccle- siae immota firmitate explicanda: etsi quum allude- rit Propheta ad urbem Hierosolymitanam, & ad templum, colligere poterant fideles in civitate, si ambularint in justitiis, & loquuti fuerint recta, & ava- ritiam projecerint, templum & sedem Domini penes se conservatum iri, siquidem Ecclesiam suam ipse tueri velit; & manifestum est, quod pergat Propheta al- loqui justum, & continuet promissiones illi, qui ve- rae pietati studet, factas. Cui promisit, quod oculi ejus visuri sint Regem Christum in decore suo, quod cor ipforum admiraturum sit divinam oixovouiav in re- gno Christi, quod tutus futurus sit a populo barbaro: ei etiam promittit, quod oculi ejus cum voluptate visuri sint spiritualem Hierosolymam, habitationem securam, tabernaculum quod fixum & immotum in aeternum manebit. Non ergo est, quod illud USQUE IN SEMPITERNUM de longo tempore tantum accipiamus. Et quum vix sesquiseculum ab hoc va- ticinio adhuc steterit templum, quomodo eventus tam magnificae promissioni respondisset, si de illo ea intelligenda? Subjunguntur adhuc ea, quae non temporariam solum conversationem, sed peren- nem inferunt, & Ecclesiam invictam fore, demon- strant: QUIA IBI MAGNIFICUS EST DO- MINUS DEUS NOSTER in conservanda Ec- clesia, mirifice ostendit majestatem & gloriam su- am: LOCUS FLUVIORUM RIVI LATISSIMI ET PATENTES, NON TRANSIBIT PER EUM NAVIS, opera remigum, NEQUE TRIE- RIS MAGNA TRANSGREDIETUR EUM. Non possunt ad eam urbem penetrare triremes, aut aliae naves magnae ad vim illi inferendam, utpo- te fluminibus rivisq; latissimis circumdatam:aquae enim ita profundæ quidem erunt, ut pedibus trans- mitti nequeant, neq; tamen onera navium sustine- bunt, ideoq; inaccessa erit urbs & inexpugnabilis. Quæ non conveniunt Hierosolymis: sed Eccle- siam invictam & inexpugnabilem fore, figurato hoc sermone docetur: adducta ratione Ecclesiæ propria: DOMINUS ENIM EST JUDEX NOSTER, DOMINUS EST LEGIFER NOSTER, DOMINUS EST REX NOSTER. IPSE SALVABIT NOS. Sa- crofancta Trinitas conservat & salvat fideles ab ini- micis omnibus, Deus Pater Judex, & vindex noster est, Spiritus Sanctus est Legifer vel Doctor noster: Filius Dei est Rex noster. Hujus trinunius DO- MINI gratia, & virtute salvi nos sumus, atq; securi adversus omnes inimicos nostros. Ita Hieronymus ad verba, Respice Sion, O juste cui supra dictum est: Cor tuum meditabitur timorem, & populum impu- dentem non videbis: Et qui antea audieras, regem in decore suo videbunt oculi tui, contemplare Sion ur- bem solennitatis nostræ: vide Ecclesiam Christi, in qua est vera solennitas, oculi tui cernent visionem pa- cis, & divitias insperatas, quas oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt, & ta- bernaculum, quod nequaquam transferri poterit. Prius enim tabernaculum, quod habuit populus Ju- dæorum, translatum est atq; sublatum, nec movebun- tur clavi ejus in sempiternum, & omnes funiculi ejus firmi erunt, ita ut Dominus habitet in eo, qui locus est omnium fluviorum rivorumque currentium, per quos nullus adversæ partis poterit navigare, neq; trieris magna, quæ interpretatur Diabolus, eum transgredi poterit: quia Dominus ipse est judex & princeps & Rex & Salvator noster, & illo prote- gente nullius metuemus insidias. Hæc dicta sunt de Sion urbe solennitatis nostræ, & de Hierusalem habi- tatione ditissima, quam ipse Dominus fluviis suis cir- cumdabit atq; vallabit. Ita & Cyrillus: Ecce Sion civitas SALUTARE NOSTRUM (sic enim habent LXX. Interpp.) Significant per hæc vel in terra Ecclesiam, vel in cælis summam & pulchram civitatem, altricem Sanctorum. Quare sive hanc in terris Ecclesiam nominet quis, sive illam animo con- cipiat, unum per utrumq; demonstrabitur. Qui enim in hac inferiori sunt, erunt progressu temporis etiam in illa summa atq; cælesti. Ita è nostris Brentius. Manifestum est, quod hæc non possunt intelligi de ex- terna urbe Hierusalem, quæ etsi non fuit vastata à Sennacheribo, tamen postea vastata est à Babyloniis. Quare intelligi debet de vera & cælesti Hierusalem, quæ est Ecclesia Christi, congregata per Evangelion ex toto orbe terrarum. Hæc est tranquillum habita- culum. Hæc est verum illud tabernaculum Moed, hoc est, pacti, testimonii, & collegii, quod tabernacu- lum Mosi in deserto architectatum adumbravit. Hæc nunquam in æternum perire potest, etiamsi non homi- nes tantum, sed etiam Diaboli ipsi eam oppugnent. Et paulo post. Quid est, quod Sionem seu Ecclesiam Dei tam firmam efficit? Respondet Propheta: Quia ibi est magnificus Dominus pro nobis, locus fluviorum & amnium, qui longissime porrigunt manus seu ripas & littora sua, ita ut nec navis remigum, nec navis grandis eos pertransire queant. Hoc est, Ecclesia ideo tam firma est, quia non habet terrenum aliquem ho- minem defensorem, nec sita est in his terris pro more aliarum civitatum, sed habet Dominum Deum ipsum defensorem, qui magnificentia & fortitudine sua omnes Reges & principes mundanos excellit. Et sita est in medio maximorum fluviorum, per quos nulla hostilis classis sive parvarum, sive magnarum navium trajicere possit, ad expugnandam & diripiendam eam. Dicitur autem Ecclesia ideo non in terris, sed in medio latißimarum fluviorum sita, quod sit divina prote- ctione ita munita, ut nulla nec hominum, nec dæmo- num potentia queat subverti & deleri. Verba illa, Dominus noster judex, Dominus ductor noster, Do- minus Rex noster, de Christo dicta esse vult Brentius, & quidem per antithesin ad gubernationem populi Dei factam per Judices, per Doctores & Sacerdotes, Eli & Samuelem, per Reges, Saulem, Davidem & posteros ejus, utpote qui adumbrarunt Christum ve- rum judicem, vindicantem populum suum ab omnibus malis: verum Doctorem & Sacerdotem, qui obtulit semetipsum pro nobis, verumq́; Regem, qui paravit & conservat populo suo æternum Re- gnum in cœlis, unde fieri non potest, ut pereat ac deleatur Ecclesia. Ipse יושיענו SALVABIT nos. Nomen enim hoc Christo proprium fuit, qui voca- tus est JESUS SALVATOR populi sui. De regni Christi conservatione explicant etiam B. Osiander, Calvinus, Junius, Autores notarum Belgi- carum, Amama, & alii. Tirinus de Ecclesia in cœ- lo triumphante à Cyrillo, Procopio, Adamo Sasbouth, Osorio, Haymone, & Cornel. à Lapide, de Ecclesia militante ab Hieronymo, Theodoreto, & Alvarez ex- plicari notat. Menochius, quem magui solet facere Grotius, omnia inde à versu 17. de Ecclesia trium- phante exposuit: & ad v. 21. ita habet: LOCUS FLUVIORUM &c. q. d. in Jerusalem non terrestri (hæc enim laborat aquarum penuria) sed cœlesti erit ingens fluvius, instar plurium fluviorum, ex quo rivi latißimi & patentes in omnem partem defluent. HUJUS cœlestis fluvii meminit S. Johannes, cum in Apoc. ait c. 22. Et ostendit mihi fluvium aquæ vi- tæ, splendidum tanquam Crystallum, procedentem de sede Dei & Agni. Fluvius hic significat exube- rantiam donorum, gaudiorum & voluptatum, quas Deus & Christus in beatos effundet. NON TRANSIBIT &c. id est, nulla navis, aut triremis hostilis per hunc fluvium transibit, quæ urbis pacem turbet, vel opes diripiat. Hæc Menochius. De flu- minibus in Ecclesia, ejusq́; immota firmitate etiam ce- cinit David Ps. 46, 9. Fluminis impetus lætificat ci- vitatem Dei, sanctificavit in ea tabernaculum suum, ipse in medio ejus. Neǵ; illa unquam commovebitur. ADJUVABIT eam Deus mane, diluculo, id est tempestive, citissime. Grotius connectit v. 20. cum hoc v. 21. vel repetit potius ex eodem nomen Dei, ac locum fluviorum rivi latißimi ita explicat: Deus nobis erit pro fluvio circuimiente urbem. Quæ opti- me conveniunt Ecclesiæ. Huic enim Deus est pro fluvio, dum inundat eam flumine gratiæ & dono- rum suorum; ac circumfluit eam, ut tuta ac secura sit ab hostibus. Atque ita non male Calvinus: NON TRANSIBIT NAVIS. Hoc in- commodi habent magni amnes, quod aditum hostibus præbere possint ut ad nos propius, quam expediat, na- vibus accedant. Ita sæpissime nocet, quod admodum juvare videtur. Dominus autem se ita pro fluvio futurum dicit, ut nullum tale incommodum metuen- dum sit, nec hostibus pateat aditus. Duas vero navi- um species enumerat, longas & onerarias, ut hostes modis omnibus prohibitum iri ostendat. Hanc sen- tentiam firmat è fontibus Ludovicus de Dieu, quod nempe Deus hic locus fluviorum dicatur, in Ani- madv. suis ad vers. 21. כִּי אִם־שָׁם אַדִּיר יְהוָה לָנוּ מְקוֹם נְהָרִים. Pagninus & Junius hac ita di- stinxerunt, ut אַדִּיר sit descriptio subjecti enuncia- tionis, prædicatum sit מְקוֹם. At eo sensu neque לָנוּ debebat habere Zakeph, quo distingueretur à sequentibus, neq; adjectivum אַדִּיר collocari ante substantivum יְהוָה sed post illud. Sicut ex more Hebraimi postulat, ut אַדִּיר constituat prædica- tum, יְהוָה subjectum, tum rursus מְקוֹם alterum prædicatum ejusdem subjecti: quod recte animadver- terunt Vulgatus & Genevenses. Verto ergo: Verum ibi magnificus est Jehovah nobis velut lacus fluviorum, rivorum latorum spatiis, per quem non ibit &c. Vers. 23. LAXATI SUNT FUNICULI TUI.) Ob cœptam comparationem fluminis, Assyriorum exercitum navi com- parat, ut Romanam Rempublicam Horatius, cujus locus huic respondens est: - - - ac sine funibus Vix durare carinæ Possunt imperiosius Æquor. SIC ERIT MALUS TUUS.) In Hebræo: non firmabunt (id est, non habebunt firmum) malum. Apud Hora- tium: Et malus celeri saucius Africo. UT DILATARE SIGNUM NON QUEAS.) In Hebræo: non expandent velum. Horatius. Non tibi sunt integra lintea. TUNC DIVIDENTUR SPOLIA PRÆDARUM MULTARUM) Vi- de supra 4. CLAUDI DIRIPIENT RAPINAM.) Proverbiale: cui simile 2. Sam. 5, 6. NEC DICET VICINUS.) Imo habitator. ELANGUI) Ex obsidione langueo. AUFERETUR AB EO INIQUITAS.) Omnis mali sensus à populo auferetur. Admitti potest hæc interpretatio de Assyriis, nequicquam oppugnantibus Hierosolyma, salva eorum, quæ antecedunt, explicatione de regno Christi. Sic enim applicatio subjungitur ad urbem illam, in qua Deus tum focum suum habebat. Atq; ita Menochius exposuit, quem sequutus ea parte est Grotius. LAXATI SUNT FUNICULI TUI, transiit, inquit, ad Assyrium, Judæorum hostem, quem alloquitur, continuata navis allegoria: sensus est: Rudentes navis tuæ laxati sunt soluti, aut fracti. NON PRÆVALEBUNT inutiles facti, & ma- lum navis in suo statu erectum retinere non valentes. SIC ERIT MALUS &c. Malus navis tuæ ever- tetur, nec in illius summitate, ut fieri solet, vexillum tuum explicare poteris. DIVIDENTUR SPO- LIA &c. Exercitu tuo ab Angelo percusso. CLAU- DI DIRIPIENT RAPINAM. Adeo nullus erit, qui prohibeat. NEC DICET VICINUS ELAN- GUI. Sed omnes circumjecta loca habitantes alacres erunt, & erecti in colligendis spoliis. AUFERETUR AB EO INIQUITAS. Occisis, vel fugatis Assy- riis iniquis, à quibus opprimebatur: populo in ea re- gione habitanti melior fortuna affulgebit. Hactenus interpretatio Menochii. Cornel. à Lapide pariter redire Prophetam ad argumentum capitis, ad tem- pora Ezechiæ & Sennacheribi, sed compellari vult Zionem, laxabuntur tantum tabernaculi tui funes ab Assyriis (rumpentur) adeo ut id convellendum videatur: Sed non prævalebunt illi tibi. Sic malus ille, qui quasi statumen molem tabernaculi sustinet (Rex Ezechias) pronus procumbet, ut in eo militare signum explicare non possit, (vires ejus ita prolapsæ erunt, ut exercitum in tutelam urbis cogere & in- struere non possit) verum subito tunc mira fiet re- rum conversio &c. Calvinus Assyrios compellari censet, sed sub eorum persona simul hostes quosvis Prophetam alloqui, ac similitudinem suam prose- qui, qua initio usus erat. Dixerat, inquit, Ecclesiam similem esse loco munito & circumdato fluviis amplis- simis, per quos hostibus accessus non pateat, nunc impi- orum statum navibus comparat: quo significat eos so- lidum fundamentum non habere, tametsi formidabi- les se præbeant, ardeant insania, & ferociter sæviant nec quisquam eorum furori resistere posse videatur Tametsi igitur naves eis longæ & onerariæ sint, quibu longissime disjunctas regiones quodammodo conjun gunt, terræq; & maris imperium obtinent, nihil ta men diuturni aut firmi apud ipsos erit. Evertet Do minus eorum naves, abruptisq; funibus & malis, eo dem naufragio ipsos involvet. Amama Ebræum tex- tum cum Pagnino, Angl. Genev. Ital. Hisp. Tigur: sic reddendum putat: funes tui laxi sunt, sind schlaff worden: (quia vento non implentur) neque recte sustinere possunt malum suum, neq; velum expandent. Atq; ita etiam reddidere Belgæ in Bibl. suis. Franc. Junius ita interpretatur, deserent rudentes tuos, (ut apostrophe sit ad classem inimicorum, qua Eccle- siam invadere cogitant) nondum confirmaverunt erectum malum suum, nondum expanderunt velum, tunc videtur præda spolii &c. Alii hæc dicta vo- lunt Synagogæ Judaicæ κατ᾽ ἀντίθεσιν. At tu, o mise- ra Synagoga, laxati vel rupti sunt, ut Chaldæi & Græ- ci habent, funiculi tui, ET NON PRÆVALE- BUNT, non amplius sustinere poterunt tabernacu- lum. Non poteris DILATARE SIGNUM, (ve- lum tuum) in MALO, nedum te tutari: ipsimet etiam CLAUDI, ac cæci gentiles DIRIPIENT RAPINAM. NEC amplius dicet VICINUS TUUS, populus gentilis, ELANGUI, quia omnes robusti erunt per Christum. Nam INIQUITAS AUFERETUR AB EO. Sic Adamus Sasbouth, & Tirinus. Sed quia Synagogæ Judaicæ mentio fa- cta non erat, temere ea hic ingeritur. Neq; admitti priores interpretationes possunt, quod sc. compel- letur hic Assyrius; quia affixum in voce FUNI- CULI TUI fœminini est generis, unde alio referri non potest, quam ad Zionem prius compellatam. Quod video etiam observatum Brentio nostro, accu- rato Sacrarum Literarum interpreti. Unde ad hunc locum satis difficilem ista habet: Interpretes exponunt hæc de adversariis populi Dei: Sed quia affixum, quod apud Hebræos vocabulo funiculo- rum additur, fœminini generis est, & respicere vi- detur ad Zionem, ac ipsa quoq; reliqua compositio eo convenit, referemus & hæc ad Ecclesiam. De- bent autem sic transferri: Laxantur funiculi tui, non sunt fortes. Sic & malus eorum (videlicet, non est fortis) non expandunt (in eo) vexillum. Tunc dividitur præda spolii multi, claudi diripiunt rapi- nam. Nec dicit habitator, elangui. Et est hæc sen- tentia: Cum Dominus Christus Judex, Doctor & Rex noster suscepturus est in terris administrationem Regni sui, videbuntur quidem funiculi tabernaculi Zionis, seu Ecclesiæ (supra enim vocavit Ecclesiam, tabernaculum, cujus funiculi non rumpantur) laxa- ti esse, ac minime fortiter constitutionem tabernaculi continere. Malus etiam, seu pertica hujus taberna- culi non videbitur satis firma esse, ut vix possit in ea velum suspendi, attamen tunc dividetur in populo Dei maxima præda, sicut parta victoria fieri solet. Et tam obvia ubiq; erit præda, ut etiam claudi eam sint rapturi. Nec quisquam inter cives & incolas con- queretur amplius de sua imbecillitate, sed omnes præ gaudio sani & firmi exilient. Quo etiam redit Osi- andrina Paraphrasis: Laxati sunt funiculi tui, sed non (fortiter) intendent (tabernaculum) sic erit ma- lus tuus, ut explicare velum non (satis commode) possis: id est, perinde se habebunt res Ecclesiæ, ac fi quis tabernaculum seu tentorium figat; cujus ma- lus (qui deberet totum onus tabernaculi sustinere) tam infirmus videatur, ut non crederes eum posse ferre, ut vela Tabernaculi appendantur, quin vel frangatur vel corruat, & funiculi in lateribus non bene intendantur, ita ut tale tentorium singulis momentis videatur ruinam meditari &c. Agnoscit Ludovicus de Dieu his compellari Ecclesiam: & tex- tum Ebræum, qui sic habet: נָטְשׁוּ חֲבָלָיִךְ בַּל יְחַזְקוּ כֵן תָּרְנָם בַּל פָּרְשׂוּ נֵס hoc pacto reddidit: Re- licti sunt dolores tui, non roborabunt basin mali sui, non expandent vexillum. Addita hac explicatio- ne: In bello malus terræ infigi solebat, eig; vexillum appendi, unde hæc duo etiam junguntur Esa. 30, 17. Sensus est, non est, quod doleas, o Ecclesia, relicti sunt dolores tui: quod Belgice significanter dicimus Uwe droefheden syn achter ghelaten, Nam etsi bellum in te moveant hostes, non permittet ipsis Deus, ut vel basin mali sui firmare possint, in eog; vexillum expandere: Sed simulac in te proficiscentur, jam tum tanquam de victis spolia optima distribuentur, quorum & claudi participes futuri. Verum quia navium & trire- mium antea mentio facta, & manifestum, hic ean- dem allegoriam continuari, non de malo terræ infi- xo, sed de malo navis hæc accipienda. Nam vox חבליך non de doloribus sed funiculis hic explican- da, quemadmodum ab Interpretibus omnibus in- tellecta. Sensus ergo simplicissimus videtur: EX- TENTI SUNT (ô Zion) FUNICULI TUI. Dominus ipse extendit eos. NON OBFIRMA- BUNT, vel obfirmare & roborare poterunt adver- sus te BASIN MALI sui (in navibus suis: de hostibus Ecclesiæ sermo est) NEQUE EXPAN- DENT (expandere poterunt) VELUM, vel vexillum; vel si verbum נטשׁ reddendum sit, RELICTI SUNT, sensus erit: Relicti qui- dem, vel deserti sunt (quoad apparentiam in cala- mitatibus) funiculi tui: Sed non roborare pote- runt hostes basin mali sui adversus te, aut velum ex- pandere, nedum ad te penetrare: imo tunc quam pri- mum id tentabunt, partitionem usq; ad spolium mul- tum præbebunt, adeo ut prædam etiam ipsi claudi præ- daturi sint. Hæc de loco satis difficili paulo proli- xius. Quæ vero subjunguntur, explicant antegressa summatim, ac luculentis verbis: NEC DICET HABITATOR Zionis spiritualis, de qua actum est hactenus: ELANGUI. Ex illo periculo, quod minitati erant hostes, malum firmare, ac velum ex- pandere satagentes, ut ad Zionem penetrarent PO- PULUS QUI HABITAVIT IN EA (בה in Zione) AUFERETUR AB EO INIQUI- TAS. Omnes enim, qui cives veri (per fidem) sunt spiritualis Sionis, vel Hierosolymæ, conse- quentur propter Messiam omnium suorum pecca- torum remissionem. Sensum ergo in his postremis duobus versibus feliciter expressit B. Lutherus (quem etiam Paraphrasis Vinariensis illustrat. Etsi à primis verbis in commate priori v. 23. nonnihil abeat, & cum plerisq; ea ad Assyrios referat.

## 34:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXIV. The vengeance of God against any infidels who are enemies of the Church, specifically the Edomites, both temporal and also eternal.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIV. Vindicta Dei adversus infideles quosvis Ec- clesiæ hostes, speciatim Idumæos, tum tem- poralis, tum etiam æterna.

## 34:2
Verse 2. THE INDIGNATION OF THE LORD IS UPON ALL NATIONS) Namely, those which were either subject to or allies of the Assyrians. An overly arbitrary determination. For, whence is it certain that these things were said against them, or if they were said against them at all, that these punishments concern them alone! Nor is it indeed beyond doubt that this discourse, as far as time is concerned, followed the preceding one: Nay, some, even of our own, Brentius and Osiander, think that this discourse was held not under King Hezekiah, but while his father Ahaz was reigning, at which time the Edomites poured themselves into the Kingdom of Judah, and afflicted the Israelites with rapine and slaughter, 2 Chron. 28. For since in such virulent hatred of the Edomites and other nations nothing else seemed to be expected by the Jews than total slaughter, from which the promise of the Messiah would have been at an end, they believe that Isaiah was therefore stirred up here to preach about the horrible destruction of all the enemies of the Church, and about the admirable preservation and expansion of the Church, and to lift up the faithful of his own time. Furthermore, we do not deny that diverse opinions occur concerning the argument of this discourse. Some wish it to be a prediction of the rejection of the Jews and the devastation of their land by the Romans, which they say is designated by Edom and Judea. Thus Cornelius à Lapide notes that Hugo, Lyranus, and Castrius explain it from Theodoret and Origen: But because the Edomites in the Scriptures are distinct and are distinguished from the Jews as their enemies, and open mention is made here of the land of Edom and the city of Bozrah in it, this discourse seems to be directed specifically against them. Under the word EDOMITES, however, Osiander wishes the Anti-Christian crowd to be noted, and he establishes a comparison of these among themselves, moved by the argument that the Prophet looks principally to the last day, when all the enemies of the Church, and especially the Anti-Christ, will be destroyed. Brentius asserts that by the name of Edomites all the enemies and persecutors of the Church of God are comprehended, whether Gentiles or Jews: since the Edomites pursued his brother Jacob, and the Edomites pursued the Jews, the people of God, with great hatred. He himself shows that the threats are general in his opening: DRAW NEAR, O NATIONS, AND HEAR, AND O PEOPLES, ATTEND. LET THE EARTH HEAR, AND ITS FULNESS, AND THE WORLD ITSELF, AND ALL ITS OFFSPRING. And the proposition subjoined: THE INDIGNATION OF THE LORD IS UPON ALL NATIONS. Although afterwards the lightnings of the threats are brandished in such a way that the Edomites are expressed and named. And most interpret these things concerning the final judgment and the consummation of the age. Which is primarily the opinion of the Fathers, and likewise of some of our own theologians and of almost all the Papist interpreters. Others, however, prefer to understand them of particular judgments: which explanation prevails especially among the Calvinists, led by Calvin himself, who wishes Isaiah to use hyperbolic speech: i.e., such great fear will confound you that the Heaven will seem to be falling upon your heads. Some indeed admit that particular judgments are treated here, but they think that the Prophet descends from them to the universal Judgment: which is the explanation of the Weimar Paraphrasts and of the blessed Dr. Gerhard in his Commonplaces on the consummation of the age.

Furthermore, all things considered, it seems to us that it must be established that: on the occasion of certain enemies of the people of God, a sentence is pronounced against all the enemies of the Church, and punishments are declared against them, but punishments both temporal and everlasting; yet for certain reasons the Edomites are named, because, namely, although they were kinsmen to the Jews, they were very hostile to the people of God, and gave the occasion for this discourse, and therefore similar enemies of the Church are comprehended together under them, and for that reason these things specifically also suit the Anti-Christian crowd, which the Prophet threatens with them. Thus, in our judgment, both the diverse explanations can be recalled to Harmony with a certain respect, and at the same time the force and integrity of the prophetic discourse and of the power of the words will be left. For these things cannot be restricted merely to particular judgments and temporal punishments, unless hyperbolic expressions are invented and the force of the Prophetic words is vehemently enervated. For in the very beginning of the discourse, not without cause, the nations and peoples are summoned (indefinitely): "Come near, ye nations, and hear; and hearken, ye people"; indeed, the whole earth, with all its fullness, and the universal world, with all its offspring, is called, because, to wit, the judgment of God against the enemies of the Church was to be instituted and described in the sight of all men, of all nations and peoples: and the whole earth and all its fullness, indeed the whole world with all its offspring, will be bound to submit itself to the wrath and judgment of God on the last day, where the end and consummation of all things will be, and the whole world is to perish, which, having been subjected to the abuse of the reprobate and to τῇ ματαιότητι, will at length be liberated ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς Φθορᾶς, Rom. 8, 20. 21. But then indeed the INDIGNATION OF THE LORD (in the προτάσει of the discourse) is proclaimed not only against certain enemies, but AGAINST ALL NATIONS, AND THE FURY OF THE LORD AGAINST ALL THEIR HOST, but the army of those who fight against the Church, which universality there is no reason why we should restrict, since the text itself does not restrict it. Judgment therefore against all the enemies of the Church, and that to be carried out in the sight of the whole world, but especially on that final pantocritical day, is designated, on which the indignation of the wrath and fury of the Lord will most fully pour itself out, and all nations are to perish. For the judgment of God is never exercised against all nations at once in this age. That will happen at the consummation of the age. Then it will be most fully fulfilled concerning all, what the Prophet says: HE HAS SLAIN THEM, AND GIVEN THEM TO THE SLAUGHTER. No one will then escape the hands of the Lord; all are to perish, death will then consume all, not only temporal, but eternal. We do not deny that the slaughter and even the temporal destruction of the enemies of the Church is included, but because all are said here to be slain, eternal death is especially understood: which none of them will escape who have died in impenitence; therefore, both temporal and, above all, eternal destruction is proclaimed to the same.

Latin:

Vers. 2. INDIGNATIO DOMINI SUPER OMNES GEN- TES) Nempe quæ Assyriorum erant aut subditæ, aut sociæ. NImis arbitraria determinatio. Nam, unde con- stat adversus eas dicta esse, aut si omnino ad- versus eas dicta sint, solis illas hæc supplicia concer- nere! Nec vero indubium est, hanc concionem quoad, tempus, præcedentem subsequutam esse: Imo censent nonnulli, etiam è nostris Brentius & Osiander, hanc concionem non sub Rege Ezechia, sed regnante Achas Patre ejus, habitam esse, quo tempore Idumæi in Regnum Juda se effuderunt, & Israelitas rapinis & cædibus afflixerunt 2. Par. 28. Quum enim in tam virulento Idumæorum & alia- rum gentium odio nihil aliud Judæis expectandum videretur, quam totalis internecio, unde actum fuisset de promissio Messia, Esaiam ideo hic excita- tum credunt, ut de horribili omnium hostium Ec- clesiæ interitu, & de admirabili conservatione ac dilatatione Ecclesiæ concionaretur, ac fideles su. temporis erigeret. Cæterum non diffitemur, di- verias de argumento hujus concionis occurrere sententias. Nonnulli eam prædici volunt Judæo- rum abjectionem & terræ ipsorum vastationem à Ro- manis factam, quam per Idumæam & Judæam desi- gnari ajunt. Ita ex Theodoreto & Origene, Hugonem, Lyranum & Castrium explicare notat Cornelius à Lapide: Sed quia Idumæi in Scripturis distincti sunt & distinguuntur à Judæis ceu hostes eorum, ac terræ Edom, & civitatis in ea Bozra aperta hic fit mentio, adversus eosdem directa peculiariter vi- detur hæc concio. Sub EDOMÆORUM tamen vocabulo Anti-Christianam turbam notari vult Osi- ander, ac collationem horum inter se constituit, eo motus argumento, quod Propheta principaliter in novissimum diem respiciat, quo omnes Ecclesiæ hostes, imprimis vero Anti-Christus perdentur. Brentius nomine Edomitarum comprehendi omnes hostes & persecutores Ecclesiæ Dei, sive gentes sive Judæos, asse- rit: siquidem Edom fratrem suum Jacobum, & Edo- mitæ Judæos populum Dei magno odio proseque- ti sunt. Generales esse comminationes ingressus ipse docet: ACCEDITE GENTES ET AUDI- TE, ET POPULI ATTENDITE. AUDIAT TERRA, ET PLENITUDO EJUS, ET OR- BIS IPSE, ET OMNE GERMEN EJUS. Et propositio subjuncta: INDIGNATIO DOMI- NI SUPER OMNES GENTES. Quamvis postea ita vibrentur fulmina comminationum, ut Idumæi exprimantur ac nominentur. Et de extre- mo judicio, ac consummatione seculi hæc interpre- tantur plerique. Quæ imprimis Patrum, Nostrorum item Theologorum quorundam ac Pontificiorum pene Interpp. est sententia. Alii tamen malunt ea de particularibus judiciis intelligere: quæ explicatio obtinet præcipue inter Calvinianos, præeunte Cal- vino ipso, qui hyperbolica Oratione Esaiam uti vult: q. d. tantus vos consternabit pavor, ut Cœlum in capita vestra ruere videatur. Nonnulli admittunt quidem de particularibus judiciis hic agi, sed ab illis descendere Prophetam ad Judicium universale cen- sent: quæ Paraphrastarum Vinariensium, & B. Dn. D. Gerhardi in LL. CC. de consummat. Seculi est explicatio.

Cæterum consideratis omnibus ita videtur no- bis statuendum esse: occasione hostium quorundam populi Dei adversus omnes Ecclesiæ hostes sententiam pronunciari, ac pœnas illis indici, sed pœnas tum temporales, tum sempiternas, certis tamen de causis nominari Edomæos, quod nempe illi etsi cognati Ju- dæis, tum populo Dei valde infensi fuerint, & occa- sionem huic concioni dederint, ideoq; similes ipsis Ecclesiæ hostes sub iisdem simul comprehendi, ea- que de causa speciatim etiam hæc Anti-Christianæ turbæ convenire, quæ illis minatur Propheta. Sic, nostro judicio, & diversæ explicationes certo re- spectu ad Harmoniam revocari poterunt, & relin- quetur simul Propheticæ concioni, verborumque δεινότητι sua vis atq; integritas. Non enim ad par- ticularia solum judicia, & pœnas temporales hæc re- stringi possunt, nisi hyperbolice loquutiones fingan- tur, ac vis verborum Propheticorum vehementer enervetur. Primo namque in exordio concionis, non præter causam, accersuntur gentes, & populi (indefinite) accedite gentes & audite, & populi atten- dite: imo terra tota, cum omni plenitudine sua, & orbis universus cum omni germine suo advocatur, quia sc. Judicium Dei adversus hostes Ecclesiæ in conspectu omnium hominum, omnium gentium & populorũ instituendum, describendum erat: ac ter- ra tota & omnis plenitudo ejus, imo tot9 orbis cum omni germine suo iræ & judicio Dei sese subjicere tenebitur in novissimo die, ubi finis & consummatio erit rerum omnium, totusq; orbis interiturus est, qui abusui reproborum, & τῇ ματαιότητι subjectus, tandem ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς Φθορᾶς liberabitur, Rom. 8, 20. 21. Tum vero INDIGNATIO DOMINI (in προτάσει concionis) non super quosdam tantum hostes indicitur, sed SUPER OMNES GENTES, ET FUROR DOMINI SUPER UNIVERSAM MILITIAM, sed exercitum eorum, qui adversus Ecclesiam decertant, quam universalitatem non est cur restringamus, quum textus ipse non restringat. Judicium ergo adversus omnes Ecclesiæ hostes, idq; in conspectu totius orbis, maxime vero in novissimo illo pantocritico die peragendum designatur, quo indignatio iræ & furoris Domini plenissime sese effundet, omnesq; gentes interituræ sunt. Nam adversus omnes gentes simul in hoc seculo nunquam exeritur judicium Dei. Fiet id in consummatione seculi. Tum maxime implebitur de omnibus, quod ait Propheta: INTERFECIT EOS, ET DEDIT EOS IN OCCISIONEM. Nemo tum effugiet manus Domini; omnes perituri sunt, omnes tum mors depascet, non temporalis tantum, sed æterna. Non inficiamur, interfectionem etiam atq; interitum temporalem hostium Ecclesiæ comprehendi, sed quia omnes interficiendi hic dicuntur, mors æterna maxime intelligitur: quam nemo eorum effugiet, qui in impœnitentia decesserint, interitus ergo tum temporalis tum imprimis æternus indicitur iisdem.

## 34:3
Vers. 3. THEIR SLAIN SHALL BE CAST OUT) They shall lie unburied.

AND FROM THEIR CARCASSES SHALL ASCEND A STENCH) Lucan, Pharsalia, Book 7: Why do you abandon the stinking fields?

THE MOUNTAINS SHALL MELT WITH THEIR BLOOD) Lucan: He looks upon the heaps sinking into decay.

But this punishment is particular, that the slain should lie unburied; therefore, Osiander's explanation does not seem to be rejected, that the impious enemies of the Church stink before God and his elect, in that they have been cast away by the Lord on account of their unbelief. For also in chapter 66, 24, Isaiah designated the eternal reproach and destruction of the impious with a similar phrase in the final words: And they shall go forth and look upon the carcasses of the men who have transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be to the satiety of vision for all flesh. Therefore, this is to be understood concerning the stench of the impious before God and his elect, both in this and especially in the future age. To which also Brentius's explanation tends: With very few words, he says, the most bloody battle against all the impious is committed. HE WHO DOES NOT BELIEVE, SHALL BE CONDEMNED, or, as it is in John: HE IS ALREADY CONDEMNED. How many myriads of impious men, you think, who despise the Gospel of Christ and persecute his Church, are truly and spiritually slaughtered by this one sentence, and damned forever! And although the impious do not die corporally immediately upon this sentence of divine wrath being heard and published, yet because they are already divinely destined for both death and eternal damnation, they are truly said to be lethally wounded, to flow with blood, and to breathe out their soul. And afterwards, when the Prophet says: their slain shall be cast out, and from their carcasses shall ascend a stench, it is fulfilled now always in the Church of God, after Christ has brought back victory from all his enemies, and sits at the right hand of God. For in the Church of God there is nothing more foul, nothing more abominable than the impious and unbelieving, since we know them to be cast away by God by the manifest sentence of the Gospel and destined for eternal damnation. Thus the Jews are filth and stink before all the pious, because they are to them like putrid carcasses. If all persecutors of the Gospel of Christ stink, until their damnation is publicly revealed. The Prophet adds: THE MOUNTAINS SHALL MELT, or liquefy, WITH THEIR BLOOD. By which figurative words they also think the horrible and eternal torments of the impious are depicted. It seems that those can be taken concerning the temporal slaughter of enemies, namely, that so much blood is to be shed everywhere, where the judgments of God exert themselves, that the dry mountains seem to melt, as it were, from the abundance of it, as Vatablus and others translate, the mountains shall melt because of the gore. Sanctius understands Princes by the mountains, so that it may be hinted that Princes as well as commoners are to be slaughtered. The former explanation, however, is simpler. For it is joined thus with ignominy and reproach, that they shall be for an abomination and a stench, here and in the age to come, the slaughter and killing of the enemies, with whose blood the mountains melt. For lest we should doubt that the final judgment is included here, therefore, which is to be noted in the third place, the Prophet wished to treat here with sufficiently clear words concerning the very liquefaction of the heavens, and thus the consummation of the age: AND ALL THE HOST OF HEAVEN SHALL MELT, AND THE HEAVENS SHALL BE ROLLED UP LIKE A BOOK, AND ALL THEIR HOST SHALL FALL AWAY, AS A LEAF FALLS FROM THE VINE AND FROM THE FIG TREE. Grotius explains the former thus: The air itself, from the blood and gore attracted, will be covered with foul clouds, and indeed so thick that they take away the sight of the stars:

And concerning that rolling up he has this: The LXX: Ἑλιγήσεται ὁ ὀυρανὸς ὡς βιβλίον, Rev. 6: and the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together. Just as in a rolled-up volume nothing can be read, so in heaven there will be nothing that is looked upon. See also Ezek. 32, 7.

But to those latter things he adds: A great abundance of blood gives off many hot exhalations, which, when they run into the clouds, make the appearance of falling stars, or, as Seneca speaks, flowing away. Here such stars are compared to a falling leaf, in the Apocalypse to a fig falling 6, 13.

These things he says. And thus also some others say that these things are spoken metaphorically and hyperbolically, and they think they are brought forward only to amplify the slaughter of the slain enemies. Others refer it to the perturbation of minds, because to those established in grief, light does not seem to be light. Which similar passages seem also to teach, Isa. 13, 9. Jer. 4, 23. c. 15, 9. Am. 8, 7. But the emphasis and propriety of words in divine oracles is not to be neglected without a most grave cause: Nor are hyperboles to be rashly invented in the Scriptures. Furthermore, the discourse here is not about the air, but about the heavens themselves, whose host are the stars, not about falling stars or meteors, but about the Stars in the firmament of heaven. Nor are the stars said to be covered by clouds and intercepted from view, but to melt or liquefy, and to fall away. Nor are only some stars said to waste away, BUT ALL THE MALICE OF THE HEAVENS; mention is made not only of some falling stars, but ALL THE HOST, or ARMY, OF THE HEAVENS is said to flow down. Thus, therefore, the Holy Scripture itself meets that gloss concerning the rolled-up scroll, in which nothing can be read: while it teaches that not only will the heavens be rolled up, the stars remaining safe, but that the whole army of the heavens also, all the stars, which are so called in Gen. 2:1, will flow down from heaven. Which things befit nothing but the consummation of the age.
