Add now the weight of the words: For the Hebrew נָמַק from מָקַק, to have been liquefied, dissolved, likewise to have been putrefied, corrupted, implies a total liquefaction, dissolution, and corruption, and Peter teaches that such a liquefaction and dissolution of the heavens will occur on the last day, 2 Pet. 3:10, 12. It is said of the heavens that they are to be rolled up like a book, נגלו, it looks to the rolling up of scrolls or books, which was customary among the Hebrews, which were not bound together from many pages, but consisted of one long and continuous page, which was rolled up around a piece of wood as if around an axis like a web. Therefore, just as Scripture expresses the creation of the heaven in such a way that it compares it to the stretching of a skin or a tent, Ps. 104:2, Is. 40:22, whence the heaven is called רקיע, an expanse: so, conversely, through the folding up of the heavens, their destruction and annihilation is to be understood. In what manner Justin in Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, q. 94, explained this passage: Just as the Holy Scriptures have sometimes compared the making of the firmament to the stretching of a skin, saying, 'stretching out the heaven like a skin'; sometimes to a fastened rope, 'The heaven,' he says, 'as a fastened rope'; sometimes to the roundness of a vaulted chamber, 'Stretching out,' he says, 'the heaven as a chamber': so also they have compared its dissolution sometimes to a book that is rolled up, sometimes to an element that is dissolved by fire, as the Apostle Peter says in his second catholic and universal epistle, sometimes to a garment growing old. This expanded heaven, says Cluverus on Apoc. 6, p. 259, will be folded up, by the command of God, by whose word it was previously dilated, Gen. 1:6, 7. It was a book in which the knowledge of Him shone forth written in golden characters, Ps. 19:1. But with the Creator himself appearing, that book will be folded up, and new heavens and a new earth will be created, Is. 65:17. and 66:22, 2 Pet. ch. 3, v. 13, Apoc. 21, v. 1. Concerning the stars, the verb יבול is used, which emanated from נבל, to flow down, which is rendered by the LXX Interpreters as ἐπαλαιώθησαν (they grew old) Ps. 18:46, as ἀποῤῥυήσεται (it shall flow away) Ps. 1:3, as Φθορᾷ (corruption) Exod. 18:18, as ἐφθάρη (it was corrupted) Is. 24:4, as ἐξέπεσε (it fell) Is. 40:7. And in this place by the word πίπτει (it falls). Therefore, just as the heavens themselves will be rolled up and destroyed, so also will all their host liquefy, waste away, wither, grow flaccid, and flow down. That simile of the leaf from the vine and the fig tree, which were most known and familiar in Canaan, implies total corruption: for those leaves wither and flow down in such a way that they are plainly corrupted. Thus, therefore, he predicts the corruption and destruction of the stars no less than of the heavens themselves: which certainly will not happen except on the last day. Finally, the parallel passage Apoc. 6:14 must also be compared here, which there is no doubt this oracle looks to: 'The stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind: and the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places.' Which are likewise explained by the Fathers concerning the consummation of the age: Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria on this passage of Isaiah, Eusebius in book 11 of the Preparation for the Gospel, Chrysostom to the Neophytes, Augustine in Ps. 103, Bede and Primasius in their Commentaries on the Apocalypse, from whose opinion one should not rashly depart. Nor does Johann Cluverus teach that there are reasons here to abandon the literal sense, in his Commentary on the Apocalypse, p. 258. The magnitude, he says, of the stars, believed in the judgment of astronomers, is not to be taken concerning some earthy mass of theirs, but that their very flame-like and most tenuous light encompasses so much space. However, it is certain that a flame-like substance is condensed and dilated, and what was just now occupying a huge space, is suddenly contracted and disappears entirely. Why then could the Stars not fall to the earth like coals, with their flame or light extinguished? So also Lactantius, Book 7 of the Institutes, ch. 15: 'The stars will fall very frequently, so that the whole heaven appears without any lights.' Indeed, Scripture itself explains the recession of the heaven in such a way that it teaches the destruction of its substance, Luke 21: 'Heaven and earth shall pass away,' 2 Pet. 3:10: 'The heavens shall pass away ῥοιζηδὸν (with a rushing noise),' Apoc. 20:11: 'from the face of him that sat on the throne the earth and heaven fled away, AND NO PLACE WAS FOUND FOR THEM.' Nor is the reasoning the same for the passages which others compare here as parallels: for in those it is open that the discourse is about particular judgments, and they are described in far different words; Thus Jer. 4:23, it is openly about the land of the Jews; 'I beheld the earth, and it was desolate of light, etc. For this shall the earth mourn, and the heavens above shall grow black.' Nothing there about the rolling up of the heavens, nothing about the liquefaction of the stars. Ezech. 32:6, the Prophet expressly indicates that the discourse is about the desolation of Egypt: 'I will water the land of thy swimming with thy blood to the mountains, and I will cover, while I extinguish thee, the heavens, and I will make their stars liquefy; I will make all the luminaries of light in the heavens grow dark OVER THEE, and I will give darkness upon thy land.' That these are much different from our passage, the comparison itself clearly shows. Add that Christ confirms in the most open words that the stars will truly fall from heaven, Matt. 24; and that Peter, having used the word τακήσεται, or τήκεται, as others read, 'they shall liquefy,' and shall perish, concerning the destruction of the heavens and the elements, 2 Pet. 3:12, seems to look to this passage. Whence there is no reason why it should be necessary to flee to a metaphor here, when it is not doubtful that the fulfillment will follow according to the letter in time. And thus Justin, l.c., and Jerome on this passage also explained it concerning the destruction and consummation of the heavens, who confirms his explanation with the same arguments that we have brought forward; After the overthrow of Jerusalem, and the shipwreck of a once most solid ship, and the plunder of all that furniture, it is said concerning the destruction of all nations, and concerning the consummation of the world, which is on the future day of judgment. Whence all nations and peoples of the earth and its fullness, the world and all its offspring, as well those places which are inhabited as those which are uninhabitable due to the excess of cold and heat, are commanded to hear, and to know with all trembling of mind what things are to come. For the indignation of the Lord is by no means described as coming upon only the one nation of the Jews and the Assyrians and the Chaldeans, the Egyptians, the Moabites, and the Ammonites and the Philistines: but also against all nations, and upon all their host, or as the Septuagint translated ἀριθμὸν αὐτῶν, that is, the number of them, which shall slay them, and cause the stench of putrefying bodies to ascend on high, signifying the sins of all nations, so that the mountains shall be filled with their blood and filth and gore, and the sublime powers also and the Angels, who presided over individual nations: and all the host or strength of the heavens shall waste away, the heavens shall be folded up, or rolled up like a scroll, and all their host and army: and as the Septuagint translated, ὰ ἄςρα πεσεῖτε ὡς φύλλα, that is, and the stars shall fall in the likeness of leaves, which, as cold approaches, dry and shriveled, fall from the vine and the fig tree. Which indeed the Savior also speaks of in the Gospel; The stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken, and then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven. Thus Jerome. Similarly, Cyril of Alexandria explains this concerning the final judgment in this place, as do Procopius, and Augustine in book 13 of the Confessions, chapter 15. Likewise Eusebius in book 11 of the Preparation for the Gospel, in the chapter on the renewal of the world, who adds that Plato transferred this passage of Isaiah into his own writings. From our own side, Osiander: All the host of the heavens shall waste away, that is, the luminaries and stars shall lose their vigor and splendor on the last day: and the heavens shall be folded up like a scroll: these heavens shall pass away, as if someone were to suddenly roll up an expanded scroll, and all their host (as above) shall fall away, or wither, just as a leaf falls from the vine, and something withered from the fig tree. For the Sun and Moon will lose their splendor, and the stars will fall from heaven: as Christ teaches in Matthew 24. The Weimar Paraphrase on verse 3 is this: God's judgment begins to go forth in this life against the enemies of God, but on the last day the final general judgment will be executed upon them all together, etc. Among the Reformed, Oecolampadius rejects the explanation of Grotius and Calvin regarding the Jews, who understand it as referring to the Gentiles falling in mutual slaughter and their unburied corpses left behind, corrupting everything with their stench, and who interpret the following verses according to that opinion by hyperbole, and he explains the slaughter of the nations as the death of souls; although he interprets it as the whole human race condemned by the law (which is his own peculiar opinion). Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges that it rises and flies away from the slaughter of Sennacherib, as is customary, to the destruction of the world at the end of the age: whom Tirinus and Menochius follow. Eman. Saa does not reject that explanation, but leaves it in the middle. (4.) They provide another argument according to the explanation of certain interpreters, which are further subjected by the Prophet concerning infernal punishments. For although verse 5, FOR MY SWORD IS DRUNK IN HEAVEN, BEHOLD IT SHALL DESCEND UPON IDUMEA, may concern a particular judgment against the Idumeans or even the twin enemies of the Church, and may be understood as referring to temporal punishment and destruction, it seems to some that the Prophet is not threatening them only with temporal punishments, but with eternal torments. But whatever may be the case regarding that, a new argument for our explanation certainly arises from the fact that the Prophet describes eternal punishment and everlasting horror, which hangs over all the impious and unbelieving, by mentioning pitchy rivers always burning, and unclean and ill-omened birds, and horrid desolation. For one should not think, as Brentius rightly warns here, that there will be any region on earth in which all rivers become pitchy and sulfurous, and always burn and smoke, and in which there is nothing but a lodging for all foul and horrible birds. For the fires or smokes of Etna and Vesuvius have nothing to do with this, but by these words is described the punishment of hellfire, and the perpetual terror and torment of all the impious enemies of Christ and His Church.

And thus (5.) this explanation agrees well with the continuity of this entire discourse: For in that manner, the description of the infernal punishments which will await the impious enemies of the Church in the present chapter is joined to the consummation of the age and the final judgment: then indeed, in the following chapter, the description of the happiness of the New Testament Church and the eternal blessedness of the faithful in the other life is added: and just as the Prophet had threatened the reprobate with temporal and eternal punishments, so he subsequently consoles the Church of Christ, or the faithful, and promises them spiritual and heavenly joy and happiness. But more on these later.

Latin:

Vers. 3. INTERFECTI EORUM PROJICIENTUR) Insepulti jacebunt.

ET DE CADAVERIBUS EORUM ASCENDET FOETOR) Lucanus 7. Pharsalicorum: Quid olentes deseris agros?

TABESCENT MONTES A SANGUINE EORUM) Lucanus: Sidentes in tabem spectat acervos.

Sed hæc pœna est particularis, quod occisi insepulti jaceant, proinde non rejicienda videtur Osiandri explicatio, impios Ecclesiæ hostes fœtere coram Deo & electis ejus, eo quod sint à Domino propter incredulitatem abjecti. Nam & cap. 66, 24. Esaias simili Phrasi æternum opprobrium & exitium impiorum designavit verbis ultimis: Et egredientur & videbunt cadavera virorum, qui prævaricati sunt contra me. Vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur, & erunt usq; ad satietatem visionis omni carni. De fœtore ergo impiorum coram Deo, & electis ejus, tum in hoc, tum etiam imprimis in futuro seculo hæc accipienda. Quo etiam tendit Brentii explicatio: Paucissimis, inquit, verbis committitur cruentissimum prælium adversus omnes impios. QUI NON CREDIDERIT, CONDEMNABITUR, seu, ut est apud Jobannem: JAM CONDEMNATUS EST. Quot putas myriadas impiorum hominum contemnentium Evangelion Christi & persequentium Ecclesiam ejus, hac una sententia vere & spiritualiter trucidari, ac in æternum damnari! Etsi autem impii non statim audita ac vulgata hac divinæ iræ sententia, corporaliter moriuntur, tamen quia jam sunt & morti & æternæ damnationi divinitus destinati, vere dicuntur lethaliter vulnerati, sanguine manare & animam efflare. Et postmodum, cum Propheta ait: interfecti eorum projicientur, & de cadaveribus eorum ascendet fœtor, impletur nunc semper in Ecclesia Dei, postquam Christus reportavit victoriam ab omnibus hostibus suis, & sedet ad dextram Dei. In Ecclesia enim Dei nihil est fœtidius, nihil abominabilius impiis & incredulis, quippe quos scimus manifesta Evangelii sententia à Deo abjectos & æternæ damnationi destinatos. Sic Judæi sor- des dent & fœtent coram omnibus piis, quia sunt ipsis tanquam cadavera putrida. Si fœtent omnes per- secutores Evangelii Christi, donec damnatio eo- rum publice reveletur. Addit Propheta : TA- BESCENT, vel liquefcent MONTES A SANGUINE EORUM. Quibus figuratis ver- bis etiam horribiles & æternos impiorum crucia- tus depingi censent. Accipi illa posse videntur de mactatione hostium temporali, quod nempe tantum sanguinis passim, ubi judicia Dei sese exerent, fun- dendum sit, ut aridi montes à copia ejus veluti li- quescere videantur, uti Vatablus, & alii vertunt, præ cruore montes liquefcent. Sanctius per montes in- telligit Principes, ut innuatur, æque Principes ac plebejos mactandos esse. Prior tamen explicatio sim- plicior est. Conjungitur enim ita cum ignominia & opprobrio, quod abominationi & fœtori futuri sint, hic, & in venturo seculo, mactatio, & occisio hostium, quorum sanguine tabescunt montes. Nam ne dubitaremus, judicium novissimum hic comprehendi, ideo, quod tertio loco notandum, de ipsa liquefactione cælorum, adeoq; consummatio- ne seculi hic verbis satis luculentis Propheta agere voluit: ET TABESCIT OMNIS MILITIA COELORUM, ET COMPLICABUNTUR, SICUT LIBER, COELI, ET OMNIS MI- LITIA EORUM DEFLUET, SICUT FO- LIUM DEFLUIT DE VINEA ET DE FI- CU. Grotius priora ita explicat: Aër ipse ex sanguine & tabo attracto obducetur turpibus nebulis, & quidem tam crassis, ut siderum conspectum adimant:

Et de illa complicatione hæc habet: LXX. Ἑλιγήσεται ὁ ὀυρανὸς ὡς βιβλίον, Apoc. 6. καὶ ὁ ὀυρανὸς ἀπεχωρίσθη ὡς βιβλίον ἑλισσόμενον. Sicut in vo- lumine complicato nihil legi potest, ita in cœlo nihil erit quod spectetur. Vide & Ezech. 32, 7.

Ad posteriora vero ista addit: Multa sanguinis copia multas exhalationes de se edit ca- lidas, quæ ubi in nubes incurrunt, faciunt speciem stella- rum cadentium, aut, ut Seneca loquitur, defluentium. Hic tales stellæ folio cadenti comparantur, in Apocalypsi groffo decidenti 6, 13.

Hæc ille. Atq; ita etiam alii nonnulli metapho- rice ac hyperbolice ista dicta ajunt, nec nisi ad stra- gem cæsorum hostium amplificandam proferri pu- tant. Alii ad animorum perturbationem referunt, quia in mœrore constitutis lux non videtur lux. Quod videntur loca similia etiam docere Esa. 13, 9. Jer. 4, 23. c. 15, 9. Am. 8, 7. Sed emphasis & pro- prietas verborum in oraculis divinis citra causam gravissimam negligenda non est: Neque fingen- dæ temere sunt hyperbolæ in Scripturis. Adhæc non de aëre hic sermo est, sed de cælis ipsis, quorum militia sunt sydera, non de stellis cadentibus, vel meteoris, sed de Sideribus in firmamento cœli. Nec obduci nebulis, & intercipi visui dicuntur si- dera, sed tabescere vel liquefcere, ac defluere. Ne- que aliquæ tantum stellæ tabescere dicuntur, SED OMNIS MALITIA COELORUM, non aliquarum tantum Stellarum cadentium mentio fit; sed defluere dicitur OMNIS COE- LORUM MILITIA, vel EXERCI- TUS. Sic ergo occurrit ipse S. S. glossæ illi de volumine complicato, in quo nihil legi po- test: Dum non tantum cælos complicatum iri, sal- vis sideribus, sed omnem etiam exercitum cœlo rum, omnia sidera, quæ ita vocantur Gen. 2, 1. cœlo defluxura docet. Quæ non nisi consummationi se- culi conveniunt. Adde jam verborum pondera: Nam Ebræum נָמַק à מָקַק liquefactus, dissolutus fuit, item putrefactus, corruptus fuit, totalem lique- factionem, dissolutionem ac corruptionem infert, ac talem liquefactionem & dissolutionem cœlo- rum Petrus in novissimo die futuram docet 2. Ep. 3, 10, 12. De cœlis dicitur, quòd convolventi sint, sicut liber, נגלו convolutionem voluminum vel li- brorum, apud Ebræos usitatam, spectat, quæ non ex multis paginis compingebantur, sed una pagina longa ac perpetua constabant, quæ circa lignum quasi circa axem instar telæ convolvebatur. Ut ergo creationem cœli ita exprimit Scriptura, ut ex- tensioni pellis, seu tabernaculi comparet Ps. 104, 2. Es. 40, 22. unde cœlum רקיע expansum dicitur: Sic ex adverso per complicationem cœlorum intelligen- da est eorundem destructio & annihilatio. Quo pa- cto Justinus in quæst. & Respons. ad Orthod. q. 94. hunc locum exposuit: Quemadmodum fir- mamenti facturam sanctæ literæ per collationem assi- milarunt quandoq; pellis extensioni, dicentes; cœ- lum extendens sicut pellem: aliquando funi firmato; Cœlum, inquit, veluti funis firmatus: nonnunquam rotunditati testudinis cameratæ; Extendens, inquit, cœlum tanquam cameram: sic & ejus solutionem per comparationem assimilarunt aliquando libro, qui convolvitur, quandoq; elemento, quod igne solvitur, sicut ait Apostolus Petrus in secunda catholica uni- versatique epistola, nonnunquam vestimento vete- rascenti. Cœlum hoc expansum, inquit Cluverus in Apoc. 6. p. 259. complicabitur, jubente Deo, cu- jus verbo antea dilatatum est, Gen. 1, 6. 7. Liber fuit, in quo notitia ejus aureis characteribus scripta enituit Psal. 19, 1. Sed apparente ipso creatore complicabitur liber ille, noviq; cœli ac nova terra creabuntur Es. 65, 17. & 66, 22. 2. Petr. cap. 3, v. 13. Apoc. 21. v. 1. De stellis adhibetur verbum יבול à נבל emanavit, defluit, quod redditur à LXX. In- terpp. per ἐπαλαιώθησαν Ps. 18, 46. per ἀποῤῥυή- σεται Ps. 1, 3. per Φθορᾷ Exod. 18, 18. per ἐφθάρη Es. 24, 4. per ἐξέπεσε Esa. 40, 7. Et hoc loco per ver- bum πίπτει. Ut ergo cœli ipsi convolventur & destruentur, sic liquefcet, tabescet, marcescet, flac- cescet, & defluet etiam omnis eorum exercitus. Simi- litudo illa folii de vinea & ficu, quæ in Cananæa ma- xime nota erant ac familiaria, totalem corruptionem infert: Nam folia illa ita marcescunt, & defluunt, ut plane corrumpantur. Sic ergo syderibus non minus, quam cœlorum ipsorum corruptionem & destructionem prædicit: quæ certe non fiet nisi novissimo die. Denique conferendus hic etiam locus parallelus est Ap. 6, 14. quem hoc oraculum respicere nullum est dubium: Stellæ cœli ceciderunt super terram, sicut ficus emittit grossos suos, cum à vento magno movetur: & cœlum recessit sicut liber involutus, & omnis mons & insulæ de locis suis motæ sunt. Quæ itidem de consummatione seculi expli- cantur à Patribus, Hieronym. Cyrill. Alexandr. ad hunc Esaiæ locum, Eusebio lib. 11. de præp. Evan- gelii, Chrysostomo ad Neoph. August. in Psal. 103. Beda & Primafio in Comment. ad Apoc. à quorum sententia temere discedendum non est. Neque causas hic esse, deserendi literam, docet Johann. Cluverus in Comment. Apoc. p. 258. Magnitudo, inquit, stellarum, Astronomorum judicio credita, non de mole quadam eorum terrea accipienda, sed quod ipsa eorum lux flammea & tenuissima tantum spatii comprehendat. Constat autem flammeam substan- tiam condensari, & dilatari, & quæ modo ingens spatium occupabat, subito contrahi, & disparere penitus. Quidni igitur Stellæ tanquam prunæ di- labi possint in terram, flamma seu luce earum ex- tincta? Sic etiam Lactantius Lib. 7. Instit. cap. 15. Stellæ creberrime cadent, ut cœlum omne sine ullis luminibus appareat. Recessionem vero cæli Scriptura ipsa ita explicat, ut interitum substantiæ ne lem ejus doceat Luc. 21. Cælum & terra transibunt 2. Petr. 3, 10. Cœli ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται præte- ribunt, Apoc. 20, 11. à facie sedentis in throno fugit terra & cælum, ET LOCUS INVENTUS NON EST EIS. Neque vero eadem ratio est locorum, quæ alii hic, ut parallela conferunt: nam in illis apertum est, sermonem esse de parti- cularibus judiciis, ac longe aliis ea verbis describun- tur; Ita Jerem. 4, 23. de Judæorum terra aperte agitur; Respexi terram, & luce erat desolata &c. Propter hoc lugebit terra, & nigrescent cæli desuper. Nihil ibi de cœlorum convolutione, nihil de Stella- rum liquefactione. Ezech. 32, 6. de vastitate Ægy- pti sermonem sibi esse, Propheta diserte indicat: Ir- rigabo terram natationis tuæ de sanguine tuo ad mon- tes, & operiam, dum extinguo te, cælos, & liquessere faciam stellas eorum; Omnia luminaria lucis in cælis tenebrescere faciam SUPER TE, & dabo caliginem super terram tuam. Multum hæc diversa esse à nostro loco, ipsa collatio liquido ostendit. Adde, quod Christus verbis apertissimis confirmet, vere de cœlo casuras esse stellas Matth. 24. quodq; Petrus adhibito verbo τακήσεται, vel τήκεται, ut alii legunt, colliquescent, ac interibunt, de cœlo- rum & elementorum destructione 2. Petr. 3, 12. hunc locum respicere videatur. Unde causa nulla est, cur hic ad Metaphoram confugere necessum sit, quum juxta literam complementum olim sequu- turum esse dubium non sit. Atque ita exposuerunt etiam de interitu ac consummatione cœlorum Ju- stinus l. c. Hieronym. in h. l. qui argumentis iisdem, quæ nos adduximus, explicationem suam firmat; Post eversionem Hierusalem, & naufragium quon- dam solidissimæ navis, prædamq; omnis supellectilis il- lius, de interitu omnium dicitur nationum, & de con- summatione mundi, quæ est in die futura judicii. Unde omnes gentes & populi terræ & plenitudo ejus, orbis & cuncta genimina ejus, tam quæ habitantur loca, quam quæ inhabitabilia sunt nimietate frigoris & caloris, jubentur audire, & quæ ventura sunt, cum omni mentis tremore cognoscere. Indignatio enim Domini nequaquam super unam gentem Judæam & Assyrios atq; Chaldæos, Ægyptios, Moabitas, & Am- monitas & Philistæos: sed & contra omnes gentes, & super universam militiam, sive ut Septuaginta transtulerunt ἀριθμὸν αὐτῶν, id est, numerum ea- rum, ventura describitur, quæ interficiat eas, & fœto- rem corporum putrescentium in altum ascendere fa- ciat, significans peccata omnium nationum, ita ut san gnie earum & spurcitia ac sanguine montes replean- tur, sublimes quoque virtutes & Angeli, qui singulis gentibus præsidebant: & tabescat omnis militia vel fortitudo cælorum, replicentur, sive complicentur cœli sicut liber, & omnis militia & exercitus eorum: atq; ut Septuaginta transtulerunt, ὰ ἄςρα πεσεῖτε ὡς φύλλα, id est, & Stella defluent in similitudine foliorum, quæ appropinquante frigore, arentia atq; contracta de vinea & ficu defluunt. Quod quidem & Salvator loquitur in Evangelio; Stellæ cadent de cælo, & virtutes cœlorum movebuntur, & tunc ap- parebit signum filii hominis in cælo. Hæc Hierony- mus. Similiter de judicio novissimo explicat Cyrillus Alexandr. in h. l. ut & Procopius, & Augustinus l. 13. Confess. c. 15. Nec non Eusebius lib. 11. de Præpar. Evangel. cap. de innovatione mundi, qui addit, Pla- tonem hunc Esaiæ locum in sua scripta transtulisse. E nostris Osiander: Tabescet omnis militia cælo- rum, id est, luminaria & stellæ vigorem & splendo- rem suum amittent in novissimo die: & complica- buntur sicut liber cæli: transibunt hi cæli, ac si quis rotulam expansam subito convolvat, & omnis mili- tia eorum (ut supra) defluet, seu marcescet, sicut defluit folium de vinea, & marcidum aliquid de ficu. Sol enim & Luna amittent splendorem suum, & stellæ de cœlo cadent: ut Christus docet Matth. 24. Paraphrasis Vinariens. ad v. 3. hæc est: Das Ge- richte Gottes fånget an in diesem Leben über die Feinde Gottes zu gehen, aber am jüngsten Tage wird das endliche allgemeine Gerichte über sie alle mit einander vollstrecket werden 2c. E Reformatis Oecolampadius Grotii & Calvini explicationem re- probat in Judæis, qui de gentibus mutuis cædibus cadentibus, & cadaveribus insepultis relictis, fœ- tore corrumpentibus omnia, intelligunt, & in eam sententiam sequentia per hyperbolen exponunt, & occifionem gentium explicat de animarum morte; quamvis te toto genere humano per legem conde- mnato (quæ ipsi peculiaris est sententia) interpre- tetur. Cornelius à Lapide, ex clade Sennacheribi as- surgere & avolare, de more, ad excidium orbis in fine seculi, agnoscit: quem sequitur Tirinus, & Me- nochius. Eman. Saa non reprobat illam explicatio- nem, sed in medio relinquit. (4.) Argumentum aliud juxta quorundam Interpp. explicationem sub- ministrant, quæ porro subjiciuntur à Propheta de pænis infernalibus. Etsi enim vers. 5. QUONIAM INEBRIATUS EST IN COELO GLA- DIUS MEUS, ECCE SUPER IDOMÆAM DESCENDET, de particulari judicio adversus Idumæos vel ipsis geminos hostes Ecclesiæ agatur, ac de pœna & exitio temporali ea accipi possint, non tamen solum temporalia supplicia ipsis minari nonnullis videtur Propheta, sed æternos cruciatus. quicquid vero de eo sit, novum certe argumentum nostræ explicationis inde nascitur, quod Propheta mentione piceorum fluminum semper ardentium, & immundarum ac inauspicatarum avium, vastitatis horridæ, ac sempiternæ describat æternam pœnam, & sempiternum horrorem, qui impendet omnibus impiis ac incredulis. Non enim, quod hic merito monet Brentius, sentiendum est, quod ulla regio in terris futura sit, in qua omnia flumina fiant picea & sulphurea, ac semper ardeant & fument, & in qua non sit, nisi omnium fœdarum & horribilium avium hospitium. Nam Ætnæ & Vefuvii ignes aut fumi nihil huc faciunt, sed his verbis describitur pœna ignis inferni, & perpetuus terror & cruciatus omnium impiorum hostium Christi & Ecclesiæ ejus.

Atq; ita (5.) congruit hæc explicatio probe cum συνεχείᾳ totius hujus concionis: Nam ea ratione consummationi seculi & judicio novissimo, descri- ptio pœnarum infernalium, quæ manebunt impios Ecclesiæ hostes præsenti capite: tum vero capite sequenti descriptio felicitatis Ecclesiæ N. T. & æter- næ beatitudinis fidelium in altera vita subjungitur: & uti minatus erat Propheta reprobis temporalia & æterna supplicia, ita consolatur deinde Ecclesiam Christi, vel fideles, ac promittit illis spiritualem & cœlestem lætitiam & felicitatem. Sed de his postea.

## 34:5
Verse 5. FOR MY SWORD IS DRUNK IN HEAVEN.) That is, it has begun to rage. Therefore it follows, it shall descend. Grotius neglects that phrase 'in Heaven.' Which some wish to be added on account of the judgment of God exercised against Lucifer in heaven: I, says the Son of God, as interpreted by Osiander, have already exercised an excellent vengeance in heaven, having cast down the evil spirits from there: and I have delivered them to eternal death: and now it is time that vengeance also be taken on earth for the impiety of men. Cornelius à Lapide thinks that Jerome's exposition also tends toward this. But most others wish to refer to a decree made in heaven, such as Lyranus, Vatablus, Calvin

and others in the same school, which opinion is not to be rejected, provided that some absolute decree is not invented. The explanation of Cornelius à Lapide, that vengeance will rage in heaven itself even to satiety, and as it were to drunkenness, even to the stars, is more clever than true.

UPON IDUMEA.) Idumea had followed the side of the Assyrians, as we said above in chapter 21. But the evil which is described here was brought upon the Idumeans by the Ethiopians, as we indicated in the same place.

The teachers of the Jews, as Jerome testifies, understand the Roman Empire, and wish for desolation to be predicted against it in vengeance for Zion: But the enemies of the Church are undoubtedly designated here, where some understand Judea specifically by Idumea, which had become similar to it in impiety: such as Cyril, Oecolampadius, and our B. Luther. He calls Judea Idumea, says Cyril, changing it a little, so that he might seem to mock it. Which opinion seems to be confirmed by the fact that in the following chapter the Prophet turns himself to the Church of the Gentiles. Brentius understands by the Edomites all the impious adversaries of Christ and His Church, generally, whether hypocrites among the Jews, or tyrants among the Gentiles, or any persecutors of pious doctrine: among whom, because the Roman Anti-Christ stands out under the New Testament, Osiander wishes him to be specifically designated here with his crowd: He threatens, he says, the Lord, under the name of the Idumeans, primarily the Roman Anti-Christ, and his flock and fellowship. For just as the Idumeans indeed used circumcision; but meanwhile raged most cruelly against the true people of God; so the Roman Pontiff, and his flock, have indeed received Baptism (the sign of the covenant), yet nevertheless they persecute the true Church of God nefariously and bloodily. As Esau (the Patriarch of the Edomites) had his name from redness, so the Anti-Christ and his followers are red with blood, namely that of the pious, which they have shed, Rev. 17. Osiander thinks that it is predicted here that Christ will kill him and destroy him at His glorious coming, and that the most severe vengeance against him and his accomplices is described in the words of this world, whose opinion Piscator also made his own, confirming the same from analogous places, Rev. 14, 16, 18. But we easily admit that this prophecy strikes the Edomites specifically, yet these were not brought forward here as an example without cause, where it concerns vengeance against the nations and peoples, the enemies of the Church, so that by their example it might be taught that those who are similar to them in guilt, by the persecution of the Church, will also be similar in punishment and divine vengeance. And therefore it should be established that these things are not rashly or wrongly applied even to the Roman Anti-Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QUONIAM INEBRIATUS EST IN COELO GLADIVS MEVS.) Id est, furere cœpit. Ideo sequitur, descendet. Negligit Grotius illud in Cælo. Quod non- nulli ob judicium Dei adversus Luciferum in cœlo exercitum, addi volunt: Ego, inquit Filius Dei, in- terprete Osiandro, jam exercui egregiam vindictam in cælo, dejectis inde spiritibus malis: ac tradidi illos æternæ morti: jamq; tempus est, ut etiam in terris ultio de hominum impietate sumatur. Quo etiam abire Hieronymi expositionem censet Cornelius à Lapide. Alii vero plerique decretum in cœlo fa ctum respici volunt, Lyranus, Vatablus, Calvinus

& alii in ejusdem Schola, quæ sententia non repro- banda, modo non fingatur absolutum aliquod decre- tum. Explicatio Cornelii à Lapide, quoniam in ipso cœlo ultio grassabitur usq́ ad satietatem, & quasi ad ebrietatem in ipsa astra, argutior est, quam verior.

SVPER IDVMÆAM.) Idumæa partes secuta erat Assyriorum, ut diximus supra XXI. Malum autem, quod hic describitur, illatum est Idumæis per Æthiopas, ut eodem loco significavimus.

Judæorum Magistri, teste Hieronymo, Ro- manum imperium intelligunt, eiq; vastitatem in ultionem Sion prædici volunt: Sed hostes Ecclesiæ sine dubio hic designantur, ubi nonnulli per Idu- mæam peculiariter Judæam intelligunt, quæ illi im- pietate facta erat similis: utpote Cyrillus, Oecolam- padius, & B. Lutherus noster. Idumæam, inquit Cy- rillus, vocat Judæam, paululum immutans, ut eam deridere videatur. Quæ sententia videtur inde fir- mari, quod cap. seq. se Propheta convertat ad gen- tium Ecclesiam. Brentius per Edomitas intelligit omnes impios adversarios Christi, ac Ecclesiæ ejus, generaliter, sive hypocritas inter Judæos, sive Tyran- nos inter gentes, sive quoscunq; persequutores piæ do- ctrinæ: inter quos quia sub N. T. eminet Anti- Christus Romanus, peculiariter illum hic cum tur- ba sua designatum vult Osiander: Minatur, inquit, Dominus sub Idumæorum vocabulo imprimis Anti- Christo Romano, ejusq́ gregi & sodalitio. Ut enim Idumæi circumcisione quidem utebantur; sed in- terim crudelissime in verum Dei populum grassa- bantur; Sic Pontifex Romanus, & grex ipsius, Baptismum quidem (fœderis signum) suscepe- runt, nihilominus tamen veram Ecclesiam Dei ne- farie & sanguinarie persequuntur. Ut Esau (Pa- triarcha Edomitarum) à rubidine nomen habuit, ita Anti-Christus, ejusq; asseclæ rubent sanguine, nimirum piorum, quem effuderunt Apoc. 17. Hunc ergo interfecturum Christum, & deleturum eum glorioso suo adventu hic prædici, & vindictam se- verissimam contra eum & complices ipsius, verbis hujus mundi, describi censet Osiander, cujus sen- tentiam suam quoq; fecit Piscator, confirmans ean- dem è locis analogis, Ap. 14. 16. 18. Sed admitti- mus facile Prophetiam hanc ferire peculiariter E- domitas, hos tamen non absq; causa in exemplum productos hic esse, ubi de vindicta adversus gentes & populos, Ecclesiæ hostes agitur, ut eorum exem- plo doceretur, illos, qui similes ipsis sunt in culpa, persequutione Ecclesiæ, similes quoque futuros in pœna & ultione divina. Ideoq; non temere aut perperam etiam ad Anti-Christum Romanum hæc applicari statuendum.

## 34:6
Ver. 6. HE IS FILLED WITH BLOOD, HE IS MADE FAT WITH FAT.) The slaughter is compared to sacrifices, and especially to those which were made for sin, in which the fat and the blood were yielded to God. Lev. 7.

OF THE BLOOD OF LAMBS.) Of the common people.

OF GOATS.) Of the priests.

OF THE BLOOD OF THE FAT RAMS.) Of the wealthy and the chief men. Lam. 1, 6.

FOR THE VICTIM OF THE LORD IN BOZRAH.) Which is Bosra in Ptolemy in Arabia Petraea, and likewise in Stephanus.

Latin:

Vers. 6. REPLETUS EST SANGUINE, IN- CRASSATVS EST ADIPE.) Cædes sacrificiis compa- ratur, & iis maxime, quæ pro peccato fiebant, in quibus adeps & sanguis Deo cedebant. Lev. 7.

DE SANGUINE AGNORVM.) Plebis.

HIRCORVM.) Sacerdotum.

DE SANGVINE MEDVLLATORVM ARIE- TVM.) Opulentorum ac summatum virorum. Thren. 1, 6.

VICTIMA ENIM DOMINI IN BOSRA.) Quæ Bósα Ptolemæo in Arabia Petræa, neque aliterStephano.

## 34:7
Ver. 7. AND THE UNICORNS SHALL COME DOWN WITH THEM.) That is, they also shall be conquered who were thought to be most invincible. See Job 39, 12. and following, and Psalm 22, 22.

AND THE BULLS WITH THE MIGHTY.) In the Hebrew: Bullocks with the robust: that is, bulls. Understand great and small, as Ps. 38, 31. 22, 13.

The reason is not to be rashly passed over, why the slaughter is compared to sacrifices, not so much because the slaying of the wicked and the impenitent is pleasing to God the just judge, like a sacrifice Ex. 32, 27. 29. as because this offering is to be performed in a similar manner: For as blood and fat were offered to God, so the destruction of the enemies would be bloody, and the sword of the Lord must be filled with their blood, so that whatever is in them by fatness and excellence, the sword of the Lord is to be fattened with it, no differently than knives were filled with blood in the offering of victims, and seemed to be fattened with fat. By the names of lambs, goats, and rams, you might perhaps not wrongly understand the common people, the priests, the wealthy, and the highest men. Others, however, observe that the word כָּרִים denotes pasture-rams that are leaping or kicking, not lambs: thus all those will signify leaders and princes and the chief men among the people, and that these are being dealt with specifically, the mention of unicorns, bulls, and the powerful in verse 7 also indicates. Whence it must be said that men of chief dignity and wealth are designated by the former names, which might perhaps be difficult to distinguish unless the distinction of such men is to be sought from external accidents. For all the names of PASTURE-RAMS, GOATS, STRONG RAMS, UNICORNS, BULLOCKS, AND BULLS are so arranged that they do not befit the common people, but the chief and principal men, and indicate the wealthy, the petulant, the strong, the sublime, the vigorous, the powerful; and the sons of the powerful with their progenitors: all of whom he says are to be slaughtered, so that the land may be drunk with their blood, and the soil with their fat: just as the Prophet had already embraced the common people and the populace in verse 5 under the name of the people of the Lord's slaughter. Piscator understands the first three names of lambs, goats, and rams as referring to common men, and the latter three of unicorns, bullocks, and bulls as referring to the more noble. All of whom are to be slaughtered like sacrifices. Which are to be understood concerning temporal punishments and plagues striking whole regions.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET DESCENDENT UNICORNES CVM EIS.) Id est, vincentur & illi qui maxime invicti pu- tabantur. Vid. Job. 39, 12. & sequentib9, & Psalm. 22, 22.

ET TAVRI CVM POTENTIBVS.) In Hebræo: Iuvenci cum robustis: id est, tauris. Intellige magnos & par- vos, ut Pf. 38, 31. 22, 13.

Causa non temere transmittenda, cur Sacri- ficiis comparetur cædes, non tam quod Deo justo ju- dici grata est impiorum & impœnitentium macta- tio, instar sacrificii Ex. 32, 27. 29. quam quod simi- li modo peragenda hæc oblatio: Nam ut sanguis & adeps Deo offerebantur, ita cruentum fore in- teritum hostium, ac gladium Domini Sanguine ipsorum implendum esse, ut & adipe ipsorum, quicquid in ipsis est per pinguedinem & præstan- tiæ, eo impinguatum iri Domini gladium, non se- cus atq; cultri in victimarum oblatione sanguine implebantur, ac adipe impingvari videbantur. A- gnorum, hircorum, arietum nomine Plebem, Sacerdo- tes, opulentos, ac summos viros forte non male intel- ligas. Alii tamen observant, vocem כָּרִים arietes pascuales saltantes, sive calcitrantes notare, non a- gnos: Sic omnia illa Duces ac principes, ac præcipuos in populo significabunt, ac de his peculiariter agi, etiam unicornium, & taurorum & potentium mentio indicat vers. 7. Unde dicendum, quod viri præci- puæ dignitatis & opulentiæ prioribus nominibus designentur, quæ distingui forte ægre possint, nisi ab accidentibus externis talium virorum distinctio petenda sit. Omnia enim nomina ARIETUM PASCUALIUM, HIRCORUM, ARIETUM FORTIUM, UNICORNIUM, JUVENCO- RUM, ET TAURORUM ita comparata sunt, ut non plebi, sed præcipuis, & principib9 viris con- veniant, ac opulentos, petulcos, fortes, sublimes, vege- tos, potentes; filiosq; potentum cum suis progenitori- bus indicent: Quos omnes mactandos dicit, ut in- ebrietur terra eorum sanguine, & humus eorum adipe: sicuti plebem ac populum jam promiscvum complexus erat Propheta v. 5. sub nomine populi interfectionis Domini. Piscator priora tria nomina agnorum, hircorum, arietum de hominibus vulgari- bus, posteriora tria unicornium, juvencorum, tauro- rum de nobilioribus intelligit. Qui omnes sacrifi- ciorum instar mactandi. Quæ de pœnis tempora- libus, & plagis totas regiones percutientibus intel- ligenda.

## 34:8
Vers. 8. YEAR OF THE RETRIBUTIONS OF THE JUDGMENT OF SION) The time for rendering a return to the adversary of Sion. The Idumeans were always most hostile to the Jews. Am. 1. 11. Obad. 10. seq. Lam. IV. 21. Ezek. XXV. 12. Ps. CXXXVII. 12.

Others explain it as against Sion. For they judge that the following prophecy directed against the Jerusalemites threatens a miserable destruction, which was to be inflicted by the Romans, as do Jerome, Cyril, Thomas, Forerius. But that the judgment for Sion is to be understood as being exercised against the Idumeans, the enemies of the Church, is manifest from the preceding verses, to which these are joined with the causal particle כִּי: FOR THE DAY OF THE LORD'S VENGEANCE, THE YEAR or time OF RETRIBUTIONS לְרִיב, which does not denote ADVERSARY, BUT OF THE CAUSE OR DISPUTE, or OF THE JUDGMENT OF SION. And thus the Chaldean, Lyranus, Arias Montanus, and Sanctius explain it as judgment or vengeance for Sion: Vatablus rendered it, The year of the repayments of the strife with Sion, by which GOD will repay retaliation to the Idumeans, who had constantly striven with the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ANNUS RETRIBUTIONUM JUDICII SION) Tempus reddendi vicem adversario Sionis. Idumæi semper infestissimi Judæis Am. 1. 11. Abdiæ. 10. seq. Thr. IV. 21. Ezech. XXV. 12. Ps. CXXXVII. 12.

Alii exponunt contra Sion. Nam sequens va- ticinium adversus Hierosolymitanos directum mi- serabile exitium minitari censent, quod à Romanis inferendum erat, utpote Hieronym. Cyrillus, Tho- mas, Forerius. Sed judicium pro Sione intelligen- dum esse contra Idumæos Ecclesiæ hostes exercen- dum, ex antecedentibus manifestum est, quibus hæc junguntur, cum particula causali כִּי: QUIA DIES ULTIONIS DOMINI, ANNUS vel tempus RETRIBUTIONUM לְרִיב, quod non notat ADVERSARIUM, SED CAUSÆ VEL DISCEPTATIONIS, aut JUDICII SION. Atque ita Chaldæus, Lyranus, Ariasmontanus, San- ctius exponunt per judicium, vel vindictam pro Sione: Vatablus reddidit, Annus repensionum rixæ cum Sion, quo DEUS rependet talionem Idumæis, qui cum Judæis jugiter rixati erant.

## 34:9
Vers. 9. ITS TORRENTS SHALL BE TURNED INTO PITCH, AND ITS SOIL INTO SULPHUR, AND ITS LAND SHALL BE INTO BURNING PITCH.) The cities will be set on fire, as if by pitch or sulphur.

Latin:

Vers. 9. CONVERTENTUR TORRENTES EJUS IN PICEM, ET HUMUS EJUS IN SUL- PHUR, ET ERIT TERRA EJUS IN PICEM ARDENTEM.) Urbes incendentur, quasi pix aut sul- phur.

## 34:10
Vers. 10. IT SHALL NOT BE EXTINGUISHED NIGHT AND DAY, ITS SMOKE SHALL ASCEND FOREVER.) That is, for a long time. For the embers and smoke of burned cities are accustomed to remain for a long time. Concerning smoke, Virg. 3. Aeneid: All Neptunian Troy smokes from the ground. Where Servius: The ruin may be brief, but the smoke remains for a long time. Seneca in the Troades: Ilium is there where smoke creeps high into the sky, and foul clouds. The Trojans will see their fatherland by this sign.

FROM GENERATION TO GENERATION IT SHALL BE DESOLATE.) That is, Idumea shall remain desolate.

FOR AGES OF AGES NO ONE SHALL PASS THROUGH IT.) For a very long time. εἰς χρόνον πολὺν, the Greeks here:

Latin:

Vers. 10. NOCTE ET DIE NON EXSTINGVE- TUR, IN SEMPITERNUM ASCENDET FUMUS EJUS.) Id est, diu. Solent enim incensarum urbium diu manere favillæ & fumus. De fumo Virg. 3. Æneid. Omnis humo fumat Neptunia Troja. Ubi Servius: Ruina sit brevi, fumus vero longo permanet tempore. Senec. Troadibus: Ilium est illic ubi fumus alte Serpit in Cælum, nebulæq; turpes. Troes hoc signo Patriam videbunt.

A GENERATIONE IN GENERATIONEM DESOLABITUR.) Id est, desolata manebit Idu- mæa.

IN SECULA SECULORUM NON ERIT TRANSIENS PER EAM.) Longissimo tempore. εἰς χρό- νον πολὺν, Græci hic:

## 34:11
AND THE PELICAN SHALL POSSESS IT) The Hebrews translate it as pelican; and the Latin interpreter Ps. 101, 7. AND THE HEDGEHOG) So also the Greeks: ἐχῖνοι. So also above 14, 23. THE IBIS) So also the Greeks. Some of the Hebrews wish it to be an owl. AND A MEASURING LINE SHALL BE EXTENDED OVER IT, SO THAT IT MAY BE REDUCED TO NOTHING, AND A PLUMB LINE INTO DESOLATION) Architects, when they wish to tear down some part of an old building, measure the width with a line, and the height with a plumb line.

Other interpreters also understand these things concerning temporal and long-lasting devastation: Cornel. à Lapide, Tirinus, Menochius: who nevertheless wish there to be a symbolic sense of the eternal punishments of hell. But since a double sense does not have a place in Holy Scripture, and the words of the Prophet are clear concerning eternal destruction, others have understood these according to the letter concerning the perennial destruction of the Jewish people, for whom no hope of restoration remains. Nor is there any doubt, indeed, that the punishments dictated for the enemies of the Church, of whom the Edomites provided an example, also await the Jews, after they have become enemies of the true Church. But that the eternal punishments of the wicked are described by these figurative words seems to be evident from these things: (1.) That the eternity and perpetuity of the punishments is described emphatically: IT SHALL NOT BE EXTINGUISHED NIGHT AND DAY; which signifies continuity: ITS SMOKE SHALL ASCEND FOREVER, which signifies eternity. (2.) Lest any doubt remain that eternity is denoted, it is added, IT SHALL BE DESOLATE FROM GENERATION TO GENERATION; FOR AGES OF AGES NO ONE SHALL PASS THROUGH IT. Which words לְנֵצַח נְצָחִים לְעוֹלָם thus joined together bring about a true and interminable eternity. (3.) Furthermore, towards the end of this chapter, a confirmation is added with words denoting proper eternity, עַד עוֹלָם they shall possess it unto the age, from generation to generation they shall dwell in it. Although the word generation may seem not to befit the other life, it is known, however, that Scripture is accustomed frequently to express things of the future life with words of the present: hence also the mention of nights and days is made in the description of eternity, even if nights and days have no place in the other life. (4.) By the same words, infernal punishments are depicted Ap. 14, 10. 11. HE SHALL BE TORMENTED WITH FIRE AND BRIMSTONE, AND THE SMOKE OF THEIR TORMENTS SHALL ASCEND FOR EVER AND EVER, and they have no rest DAY AND NIGHT. All of which are taken from this passage, and by the confession of all express the eternal punishments of hell. (5.) Since in other places of Scripture hell is described also by the mention of fire, pitch, and brimstone, and by the lake of fire burning with Brimstone Apoc. 19, 20. c. 20, 11. c. 21, 8. and the wicked are said to be tormented night and day for ever and ever, and the infernal fire is not extinguished Matth. 3, 12. Luc. 3, 17. Marc. 9, 44. 45. 46. 48. a comparison of them with the present prophecy confirms not obscurely that the fire of hell is signified here also. (6.) A horrible desolation is described in words altogether horrible, such as you would read nowhere else in Holy Scripture in such abundance: and not a temporary desolation only, but one that is to endure even unto the age. That such a thing happened to the land of Idumea is contrary to historical truth, and therefore it is to be judged that those horrible things were not undeservedly brought forward so prolixly to adumbrate the most horrible region of hell: as that whose horribleness can never be sufficiently described in words. (7.) An apocalyptic passage suggests an explanation concerning those ill-omened birds, which render that region horrible c. 18, 2.

where he reports similar things concerning the punishments of great Babylon: It has become a habitation of demons, and a guard of every unclean spirit, and a guard OF EVERY UNCLEAN AND HATEFUL BIRD. For here it is explained what those unclean and ill-omened birds are, and they are recounted at length. Therefore, the guard of every unclean and hateful bird has become Idumea, just as Babylon, that is, the guard of every unclean spirit, and the habitation of demons: since these explain each other. (8.) There is no region on earth in which all the rivers are pitchy and sulphurous; which burn and smoke perpetually and without end for ages, which is the habitation of all unclean and ill-omened birds. What Brentius explains concerning hell, not that the fire of hell is nourished and preserved by corporal pitch and sulphur, or that those ill-omened birds dwell in hell corporally, but that spiritual things are shadowed forth by the names of corporal things, and by the terms of ill-omened birds are signified the foulest demons and the gravest terrors, which will perpetually exercise the impious. But what he says, that that land will be desolate from generation to generation, and that no one will pass through it for ages of ages, does not signify, in the interpretation of Brentius, that no man is to be cast into hell, but by desolation and solitude he understands the horror which is in hell. Finally, that he recounts those ill-omened birds in hell, this clearly, according to the same, means for him what Christ says in very few words: Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the Devil and his angels. These are those ill-omened birds, which, so to speak, fly about in hell, and strike into the damned a terror by far the greatest of all and never to be ended for eternity. Thus also Osiander explains it concerning the region of darkness, horrors, and infernal torments. In which manner Blessed Gerhard also understands the passages concerning hell, §. 55, p. 622. This continuity of punishments is proved from the clearest assertion of Scripture, Ps. 34, 10. Night and day that (infernal) fire shall not be extinguished. Nor does Oecolampadius altogether deny it, when he understands it concerning punishments that will endure for eternity of eternities.

Although indeed these reasons do not seem to be disregarded, yet the arguments which can be brought forward from the other side that these things must be accepted concerning the perpetual desolation of Idumea are not to be concealed, such as that here (1.) mention is made not of the men themselves to be punished, but of the region and land of Idumea, which is said to be about to burn into pitch, and to be inhabited by those ill-omened birds (2.) that the Prophet notably says concerning the same, it shall be desolate from generation to generation, for ages of ages there shall be no one passing THROUGH IT. Which do not sound of Gehenna, but of the land of Idumea, because it was about this, not about that, that it was treated in the preceding. (3.) That it is said that a measuring line is to be extended over it, so that it may be reduced to nothing, and a plummet into desolation, just as Architects, when they wish to tear down some part of an old building, measure the width with a line and the height with a plummet, as Grotius rightly does here. (4.) That those things, its nobles shall not be there, they shall rather call the King, etc., do not fit Gehenna, but were said concerning the land of Idumea. (5.) That those things FROM GENERATION TO GENERATION are not easily found anywhere concerning the other world. (6.) That elsewhere also the desolation of regions and cities is described in such a way, as that of Babylon, Is. 13, 20. It shall not be inhabited even to the end, and it shall not be dwelt in even to generation and generation. But beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with Dragons, and Ostriches shall dwell there, and hairy ones shall dance there, and owls shall answer there in its houses, and Sirens in the temples of pleasure. And Jer. 50, 39. Therefore Ziim shall dwell with Ohim, and Ostriches shall dwell in it, and it shall not be inhabited anymore even to eternity, nor shall it be built even to generation and generation. As the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and its neighbors, says the Lord, a man shall not dwell there, and a son of man shall not inhabit it. And chap. 51, 37. And Babylon shall be into mounds, a habitation of Dragons, a stupor and a hissing, because there is no inhabitant. (7.) What of the fact that the passage in Rev. 18 also treats of the desolation of mystical Babylon, Rome: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and has become a habitation of demons. Whence a lengthy explanation of v. 4 seqq. concerning the destruction of Babylon is subjoined. For although Tartarus may be the proper Φυλακὴ of demons and unclean spirits, 2 Pet. 2, 4, Rev. 20, 3, 7, yet desolate cities, and other desert places, are also called their guard, in which they themselves are detained most unwillingly as if in a prison, desiring uniquely that, in order to fulfill their malice, and to indulge in human society with their machinations, a place might be left to them. See Luke 11, 24 seqq., Tob. 8, 3. (8.) Add that also the fire, by which Sodom and Gomorrah were overturned, is called eternal in Jude v. 7, and that those cities sustain the punishment of eternal fire (πυρὸς αἰωνίε δίκην). Induced therefore by these and other arguments, we do not deny that these things are to be understood concerning the perpetual desolation of Idumea. Furthermore, there is no doubt that that desolating fire, that horrible desolation, presents a type of the inextinguishable infernal fire, and of the horror in Gehenna, just as the fire by which Sodom burned, and their desolation, provides a type of Gehenna, which Jude v. 7 calls a specimen (δεῖγμα), and Peter 2 Epist. 2, 5 a pattern (ὑπόδειγμα). Whence also in the description of the infernal punishment and the fire and horror of Gehenna, Rev. 14, 10, 11, we judge that there is an allusion to this place. Thus, therefore, the eternal desolation and devastation of Idumea is predicted here, so that from the consummation of the age and the judgment which the Prophet had previously designated to be exercised upon the nations themselves on the last day, it could be gathered not obscurely that the Idumean peoples themselves would be punished by God much more, nay, that the torrents of the region of Edom would be into pitch, and its soil into sulphur, and its land into burning pitch, so that with pitch, sulphur, and fire, which will never be extinguished, the inhabitants of the region would be consumed night and day, and its smoke would ascend forever from the impious inhabitants of this land, and so they would be punished and tormented with fire and sulphur, and the smoke of their merits would ascend for ever and ever, and they would have no rest from those torments either by night or by day Ap. 22, 10. 11. The destruction of the land and the peoples of the land are therefore connected, so that the designation of one is not the exclusion of the other, but rather an inclusion; and the land is indicated as about to perish with the peoples.

Latin:

ET POSSIDEBUNT ILLAM ONOCROTA- LUS) קאת Pellicanum & Hebræi vertunt; & interpres Latinus Pfal. 101, 7. ET ERICIUS) Sic & Græci: ἐχῖνοι. Sic & su- pra 14, 23. IBIS) Sic & Græci. Hebræorum nonnulli noctuam esse volunt. ET EXTENDATUR SVPER EAM MENSV- RA, VT REDIGATVR IN NIHILVM, ET PER- PENDICVLVM IN DESOLATIONEM) Architecti, cum veteris ædificii partem aliquam dejicere volunt, me- tiuntur latitudinem linea, & altitudinem perpendiculo.

De vastitate temporali ac diuturna hæc intel- ligunt etiam alii Interpp. Cornel. à Lapid. Tirinus, Menochius: qui tamen fymbolicum sensum subesse volunt, æternorum suppliciorum inferni. Sed quum geminus sensus locum non habeat in S. Li- teris, ac verba Prophetæ luculenta sint de excidio æterno, alii secundum literam hæc de perenni exci- dio populi Judaici intellexerunt, cujus restaurandi Spes nulla superat. Neq; dubium sane est, pœnas hostibus Ecclesiæ, quorum exemplum præbebant Edomitæ, dictatas, etiam manere Judæos, post- quam illi veræ Ecclesiæ hostes facti sint. Quod au- tem figuratis hisce verbis impiorum æterna suppli- cia describantur, ex hisce constare videtur: (1.) Quod emphatice æternitas & perennitas pœna- rum describatur: NOCTE ET DIE NON EXTINGUETUR; quæ continuitatem: IN SEMPITERNUM ASCENDET FUMUS EJUS, quæ æternitatem significant. (2.) Ne du- bium supersit, æternitatem notari, additur, A GENERATIONE IN GENERATIONEM DESOLABITUR; IN SECULA SECU- LORUM NON ERIT TRANSIENS PER EAM. Quæ verba לְנֵצַח נְצָחִים לְעוֹלָם ita conjun- cta veram & interminabilem æternitatem infe- runt. (3.) Additur præterea sub finem capitis hujus, confirmatio, verbis æternitatem propriam notantibus, עַד עוֹלָם usq; ad seculum possidebunt eam, de generatione in gerationem habitabunt in ea. Licet vero generationis vox alteri seculo non convenire videatur, notum tamen est, quod Scri- ptura frequenter res futuri seculi verbis præsentis exprimere soleat: inde etiam noctium atq; dierum mentio fit in æternitatis descriptione, etsi noctes & dies in altero seculo locum non habeant. (4.) Ver- bis iisdem depinguntur pœnæ infernales Ap. 14, 10. 11. CRUCIABITUR IGNE ET SULPHU- RE, ET FUMUS TORMENTORUM EORUM ASCENDET IN SECULA SE- CULORUM, nec habent requiem DIE AC NOCTE. Quæ omnia ex hoc loco desumta, omniumq; confessione æternas gehennæ pœnas exprimunt. (5.) Quum in aliis Scripturæ locis etiam ignis, picis, & sulphuris mentione gehenna describatur, & per stagnum ignis ardentis Sulphure Apoc. 19, 20. c. 20, 11. c. 21, 8. ac nocte & die cruciari dicantur impii in secula seculorum, ignisq; infernalis non extinguatur Matth. 3, 12. Luc. 3, 17. Marc. 9, 44. 45. 46. 48. collatio eorum cum præsente vati- cinio haud obscure confirmat, hic etiam gehennæ ignem significari. (6.) Vastitas horribilis prorsus describitur verbis plane horribilibus, qualia nu- spiam in S. literis, tanta copia, legas: neque tem- poraria tantum vastitas, sed quæ usq; in seculum duratura sit. Qualem terræ Idumææ obtigisse, hi- storicæ veritati reclamat, ideoq; horribilia illa non immerito ad maxime horribilem inferni regione adumbrandam tam prolixe adducta esse, censen- dum est: utpote cujus horribilitas verbis nun- quam satis describi potest. (7.) Explicationem de infaustis illis avibus, quæ regionem illam horribi- lem reddunt, locus Apocalypticus suggerit c. 18, 2.

ubi de Babylonis magnæ pœnis similia tradit: Fa- cta est habitatio Dæmoniorum, & custodia omnis spiritus immundi, & custodia OMNIS VOLU- CRIS IMMUNDÆ ET EXOSÆ. Hic enim quænam illæ volucres immundæ & infaustæ sint, exponitur, ac prolixe eæ recensentur. Custodia er- go omnis volucris immundæ & odibilis Idumæa, perinde uti Babylon, facta, hoc est, custodia omnis spiritus immundi, & habitatio Dæmonum: siqui- dem hæc sese mutuo explicent. (8.) Regio in ter- ris nulla est, in qua omnia flumina sint picea & sul- phurea; quæ perpetuo ac sine fine ardeant ac fu- ment in secula, quæ omnium immundarum & in- auspicatarum avium habitatio sit. Quæ Brentius de inferno explicat, non quod ignis inferni nutria- tur & conservetur corporali pice & sulphure, aut quod habitent in inferno inauspicatæ illæ aves cor- poraliter, sed quod nominibus corporalium rerum adumbrentur res spirituales, & vocabulis inauspi- catarum avium significentur fœdissimi Dæmones & gravissimi terrores, qui impios perpetuo exer- cebunt. Quod autem dicit, terram illam desolandã de generatione in generationem, ac neminem in secula seculorum per eam transiturum, non significat, in- terprete Brentio, nullum hominem conjiciendum in infernum, sed per vastitatem & solitudinem in- telligit horrorem, qui est in inferno. Postremo quod recenset inauspicatas illas aves in inferno, hoc plane juxta eundem sibi vult, quod Christus paucissimis verbis dicit: Ite maledicti in ignem æternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis ejus. Hi sunt inauspicatæ illæ aves, quæ in inferno, ut ita dicam, circumvolitant, & incutiunt damnatis ter- rorem longe omnium maximum ac nunquam in æternum finiendum. Sic etiam Osiander exponit de regione tenebrarum, horrorum & cruciatuum Infernalium. Quo pacto intelligit quoq; B. Ger- hardus LL. CC. de inferno §. 55. p. 622. Hæc pœ- narum continuitas probatur ex clarissima Scripturæ assertione Ps. 34, 10. Nocte & die non extinguetur ignis ille (infernalis.) Neq; abnuit omnino Oeco- lampadius, cum de pœnis in æternitatem æternitatum duraturis intelligit.

Quamvis vero hæ rationes haud videantur insuper habendæ, non dissimulanda tamen argu- menta, quæ ab altera parte de vastitate Idumææ per- petua hæc accipi debere, adduci possunt, utpote quod hic (1.) non hominum ipsorum puniendorum, sed regionis ac terræ Idumææ, quæ in picem arden- tem futura, & ab avibus illis infaustis inhabitanda dicitur, mentio fiat (2.) quod de eadem notanter dicat Propheta, à generatione in generationem deso- labitur, in secula seculorum non erit transiens PER EAM. Quæ non de gehenna sonant, sed de terra Idumæa, quia de hac, non de illa actum erat in ante- cedentibus. (3.) Quod extendenda dicatur super eam mensura, ut redigatur in nihilum, & perpendi- culum in desolationem, sicut Architecti, cum vete- ris ædificii partem aliquam dejicere volunt, metiun- tur latitudinem linea & altitudinem perpendiculo, ut recte hic Grotius. (4.) Quod illa, nobiles ejus non erunt ibi, Regem potius invocabunt &c. non conveniant gehennæ, sed de terra Idumæa dicta sint. (5.) Quod illa DE GENERATIONE IN GENERATIONEM non facile de altero se- culo uspiam reperiantur. (6.) Quod alibi etiam vastatio regionum & civitatum ita describatur, ut pote Babylonis Es. 13, 20. Non habitabitur usque in finem, & non incoletur usque in generationem & gene- rationem. Sed requiescent ibi bestiæ, & replebuntur Domus eorum Draconibus, & habitabunt ibi Stru- tiones, & pilosi saltabunt ibi, & respondebunt ibi ulu- læ in ædibus ejus, & Sirenes in delubris voluptatis. Et Ier. 50, 39. Propterea habitabunt Ziim cum Ohim, & habitabunt in ea Strutiones, & non inhabitabitur ultra usq; in sempiternum, nec exstruetur usq; in ge- nerationem & generationem. Sicut subvertit Do- minus Sodomam & Gomorrham, & vicinos ejus, ait Dominus, non habitabant ibi vir, & non incolet eam filius hominis. Et cap. 51, 37. Et erit Babylon in tu- mulos, habitatio Draconum stupor & sibilus, eo quod non sit habitator. (7.) Quid quod locus etiam Ap. 18. de vastatione Babylonis mysticæ Romæ agat: Cecidit, cecidit Babylon magna, & facta est habitatio Dæmoniorum. Unde prolixa explicatio v. 4. seqq. de excidio Babylonis subjuncta est. Etsi enim tar- tarus Φυλακὴ propria sit Dæmonum & immun- dorum spirituum 2. Petr. 2, 4. Ap. 20, 3. 7. civitates tamen desolatæ, & alia loca deserta, custodia etiam eorum dicuntur, in quibus ipsi invitissimi detinen- tur velut in carcere, exoptantes unice, ut malitiam suam explendi, ac in societatem humanã molitio- nibus suis indulgendi locus ipsis relinquatur. Vid. Luc. 11, 24. seqq. Tob. 8, 3. (8.) Adde quod etiam ignis, quo Sodoma & Gomorrha eversa, æternus dica- tur Iudæ v. 7. & quod civitates illæ πυρὸς αἰωνίε δί- κην sustineant. His ergo aliisq; argumentis indu- cti de vastitate perpetua Idumææ, hæc intelligenda esse non abnuimus. Cæterum ignem istum deso- lantem vastitatem illã horribilem, typum exhibere ignis inextinguibilis infernalis, & horroris in gehen- na, dubium nullum est, perinde uti ignis, quo Sodo- ma conflagravit, & vastitas eorum typum gehennæ prębet, quem δεῖγμα vocat Iudas v. 7. & ὑπόδειγμα Petrus 2. Epist. 2, 5. Unde etiam in descriptione infernalis supplicii & ignis atq; horroris gehennæ Ap. 14, 10. 11. ad hunc locum alludi censemus. Sic ergo desolatio & vastitas æterna Idumææ hic prædi- cta, ut è consummatione seculi, & judicio, quod super gentes ipsas exercendum in novissimo die, antea Propheta designarat, haud obscure colligi potue- rit. populos ipsos Idumæos multo magis à Deo puni- tum iri, imo torrentes regionis Edomeæ in picem, & humum ejus in sulphur, & terram ejus in picem ardentem fore, ut pice, Sulphure atq; igne, qui nunquam extinguetur, nocte ac die consumantur incolæ regionis, & in sempiternum ascendat fumus ejus ab impiis terræ huj9 incolis, adeoq; puniantur & torqueantur illi igne ac sulphure, & fumus meri- torum ipsorum ascendat in seculum seculorum, ne- que noctes neq; dies requiem ab illis tormentis ipsi habituri sint Ap. 22, 10. 11. Connexa ergo sunt terræ, & populi terræ interitus, ut unius designatio alteri9 exclusio non sit, sed potius inclusio; ac peritura terra cum populis indicetur.

## 34:12
Vers. 12. THEY SHALL RATHER CALL A KING, AND ALL HIS PRINCES SHALL BE NOTHING.) In the Hebrew: They shall call a kingdom: that is, they shall indeed recall their ancient Kings to memory, but no one from that family shall exist. The Chaldean favors this interpretation.

Not only is the failure of Kings from the older Royal family noted, but a total anarchy, or rather the utter destruction of the kingdom itself. Piscator, Junius, the Anglican version: they shall call their nobles TO THE KINGDOM, but they shall not be (not one of them shall survive). D. Gomarus similarly: THEY SHALL CALL THEIR NOBLES (but they shall not be) to the kingdom, which version Sixtinus Amama prefers, but the translation of B. Luther is well-founded: חריה ואין שם מלוכה יקראו They shall call their heroes, but there will not be a kingdom for them. Ihre Herrn müssen heisse Herrn ohne Land(Reich) And all his Princes shall be אפס nothing. - Und alle ihre Fürsten müssen ein Ende haben. Brentius renders the same sense: This, he says, ought to be translated thus: His nobles shall be called without a kingdom, i.e., no more will be the kingdom in that land, even if mention is made of its nobles and princes, it is said that they are Kings or Princes without a kingdom, without a principality. For they will be Aphes, that is, a thing consumed, and clearly nothing. Thus also the Tigurines translated.

Latin:

Vers. 12. REGEM POTIUS INVOCABUNT, ET OMNES PRINCIPES EJVS ERVNT IN NIHI- LVM.) In Hebræo: Regnum vocabunt: id est, memoria quidem recolent veteres Reges suos, sed ex ea familia ne- mo exstabit. Favet huic interpretationi Chaldæus.

Non solum Regum è familia Regia vetustiori defectus notatur, sed totalis ἀναρχία, vel potius regni ipsius πανωλεθρία. Piscator, Iunius, Anglica- na versio, vocabunt nobiles suos AD REGNUM, sed non erunt (non supererit quispiam ex illis.) D. Go- marus similiter, NOBILES SUOS (sed non erunt illi) vocabunt ad regnum, quam versio- nem præfert Sixtinus Amama, sed bene se habet translatio B. Lutheri: חריה ואין שם מלוכה יקראו Heroes suos sed non ibi (illis) erit regnum, vocabunt. Ihre Herrn müssen heisse Herrn ohne Land(Reich) Et omnes ejus Principes erunt אפס nihil. - Und alle ihre Fürsten müssen ein Ende haben. Sensum eun- dem reddit Brentius: Hoc, inquit, sic debet verti: Nobiles ejus vocabuntur sine regno, h. e. nullum am- plius erit regnum in ea terra, etsi fiat mentio nobilium ac principum ejus, dicitur eos esse Reges seu Principes sine regno, sine principatu. Erunt enim Aphes, hoc est, res absumta, ac plane nihil. Sic etiam transtule- runt Tigurini.

## 34:13
Verse 13. AND THE PALIURUS.) Virgil: The thistle, and the paliurus rises with sharp thorns. IN ITS FORTIFICATIONS) Within the circuit of the walls which were there. PASTURES OF OSTRICHES) As above 13, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ET PALIURUS.) Virgilius: Carduus, & spinis surgit paliurus acutis. IN MVNITIONIBVS EJVS) Intra ambitum mœ- nium quæ fuere. PASCVA STRVTHIONVM) Vt supra 13, 21.

## 34:14
Verse 14. AND DEMONS SHALL MEET ONOCENTAURS) We said that ציים are wild beasts in the same place of chapter 13, where the Greeks have ὀνοκενταύρους. But איים are wild cats, as noted in the same place. AND THE HAIRY ONE SHALL CALL TO ANOTHER) See the said chapter 13, 21. THERE THE LAMIA SHALL LIE) A screech owl, as others translate: but what a screech owl is, Pliny denies is certain. The Hebrews record things similar about לילית to those which the Latins record about the screech owl. Ovid, Lucan, and Serenus mention the screech owl. Ovid also says it is named from its screeching.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ET OCCVRRENT DÆMONIA ONOCENTAVRIS) ציים esse feras diximus eodem loco capitis 13. ubi Græci habent ὀνοκενταύρους. איים autem sunt feles silvestres, ut ibidem notatum. ET PILOSVS CLAMABIT ALTER AD ALTE- RVM) Vide dicto capite 13, 21. IBI CVBABIT LAMIA) Strix, ut alii vertunt: quæ sit autem strix, negat constare Plinius. Paria autem de לילית Hebræi memorant iis, quæ Latini de strige. Strigis meminere Ovidius, Lucanus, Serenus. Ovidius & à stri- dendo dictam dicit.

## 34:15
Verse 15. THERE THE HEDGEHOG HAD A HOLE) It will build a nest safely, with no one forbidding. AND IT HATCHED YOUNG) It will bring forth. AND IT DUG AROUND) And it will break out: supply its offspring. AND IT CHERISHED IN ITS SHADOW) And its mother will rear it under the ruins. THERE THE KITES ARE GATHERED ONE TO ANOTHER) Kites will be gathered. Thus the interpreter also translated this Hebrew word in Deut. 14, 12, where the Greeks also have ἴκτινον.

Latin:

Vers. 15. IBI HABVIT FOVEAM ERICIVS) Ni- dificabit tuto, nemine prohibente. ET ENVTRIVIT CATVLOS) Pariet. ET CIRCVMFODIT) Et erumpet: supple fœtus ejus. ET FOVIT IN VMBRA EJVS) Et educabit eum mater sub ruinis. ILLVC CONGREGATI SVNT MILVI AL- TER AD ALTERVM) Congregabuntur milvi. Sic He- bræam hanc vocem transtulit interpres etiam Deut. 14, 12. ubi & Græci ἴκτινον.

## 34:16
Verse 16. SEEK DILIGENTLY IN THE BOOK OF THE LORD, AND READ) When that time shall have arrived, then take into your hands the volume of the prophecies, and read this chapter. NOT ONE OF THEM WAS WANTING, ONE DID NOT SEEK ANOTHER) Of those animals which I mentioned, none will be missing there. BECAUSE WHAT PROCEEDED FROM MY MOUTH, HE COMMANDED.) That is, he himself will give effect to my words. AND HIS SPIRIT.) His power. GATHERED THEM.) The aforementioned animals.

Latin:

Vers. 16. REQVIRITE DILIGENTER IN LI- BRO DOMINI, ET LEGITE) Vbi tempus illud adve- nerit, tunc in manus sumite volumen prophetiarum, & hoc caput legite. VNVM EIS NON DEFVIT, ALTER ALTE- RVM NON QVÆSIVIT) Illorum quæ dixi animantium nullum ibi desiderabitur. QVIA QVOD EX ORE MEO PROCE- DIT, ILLE MANDAVIT.) Id est, ipse effecta dabit mea verba. ET SPIRITVS EJVS.) Potentia ejus. CONGREGAVIT EA.) Ante dicta animantia.

## 34:17
Verse 17. AND HE HIMSELF CAST A LOT FOR THEM.) He attributed this land to them in such a way as those are accustomed to do who assign it by lots. See Num. 26, 56. AND HIS HAND DIVIDED IT TO THEM BY MEASURE.) Measurement precedes the lot. See Jos. 18. From these words Oecolampadius not inappropriately gathered the mystery of the Holy Trinity: The Father, he says, is signified when it is said, HIS. The Son indeed through the MOUTH: but the Holy Spirit through the Spirit, similar in Psalm 33. By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power. Where we read his, in the Hebrew is הוא, which the Kabbalists contend is the most excellent name of God, by which is signified his most perfect, immutable substance, and excelling all other things, and acting all things within itself, and remaining equally in itself. Finally, it is called his Spirit, although it proceeds from the Father and the Son: for it does not proceed as from two, but as from one principle, proceeding from both. AND WITH HIS HAND HE DIVIDED. The same who is the MOUTH of God, is also the hand of God, namely the Son, through whom he works, to whom also the Father has handed over all judgment. If this is taken as an affix in the word פיה as the Latin rendered it, this sense can be gathered: Because through my mouth he himself commanded, and through his Spirit he himself gathered them. And he himself cast a lot for them, and his hand divided it to them. Thus through the word הוא God the Father, through his SPIRIT, through whom it is gathered, the Holy Spirit, through his HAND, through whom the lot is divided, the Son of God is understood.

FOR EVER.) Interpret as above 10.

The eternal happiness of the faithful in the kingdom of Christ under his advent into the world, with which especially the Gentiles also are to rejoice, and the everlasting joy of the redeemed of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET IPSE MISIT EIS SORTEM.) Terram hanc illis ita attribuit, ut solent, qui per sortes eam as- signant. Vid. Num. 26, 56. ET MANVS EJVS DIVISIT' EAM ILLIS IN MENSVRAM.) Sortem præcedit dimensio. Vid. Jos. 18. Ex his verbis SS. Trinitatis mysterium non incommode collegit Oecolampadius: Pater, in- quit, signatur, cum dicitur, IPSIUS. Filius vero per OS: Spiritus autem S. per Spiritum, simile in Psal- mo 33. Verbo Domini firmati sunt cœli, & Spiri- tu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum. Ubi nos legimus ipsius, apud Heb. הוא, quod Cabalistæ conten- dunt esse Dei nomen excellentissimum, quo signi- ficetur perfectissima ejus substantia incommutabi- lis, & omnia alia excellens, & omnia intra se agens, & in seipso æqualiter manens. Deniq; dicitur Spi- ritus ipsius, quamvis à Patre & Filio procedat: non enim ut à duobus, sed ut ab uno procedit principio, ab utroque procedens. ET MANU DIVISIT. Idem qui est OS Dei, est & manus Dei, nempe Filius, per quem operatur, cui & omne judicium Pater tradidit. Si hoc ut affixum accipiatur in voce פיה quemadmodum reddidit Latinus, sensus hic col- ligi potest: Quia per os meum ipse præcepit, & per Spiritum suum ipse congregavit ea. Et ipse misit eis sortem, & manus ejus divisit eam illis. Ita per vo- cem הוא Deus Pater, per SPIRITUM ejus, per quem congregatur, Spiritus Sanctus, per MA- NUM ejus, per quam sors dividitur, Filius Dei intelligitur.

VSQVE IN SÆCVLVM.) Interpretare ut supra 10.

AEterna felicitas fidelium in regno Christi sub adventum ejus in mundum, qua cumprimis gavisuri sunt etiam gentiles, & lætitia sem- piterna redemtorum Domini.

## 35:1 Argument
Verse 1. THE DESERT AND THE PATHLESS SHALL BE GLAD.) While these judgments of God shall be exercised against Edom, Judea meanwhile which had been a desert, will be cultivated safely, and will reflourish under King Hezekiah.

Latin:

Vers. 1. LÆTABITUR DESERTA ET INVIA.) Dum hæc Dei judicia in Idumæam exercebuntur, Judæa in- terim quæ deserta fuerat, coletur tuto, & reflorescet sub Rege Ezechia.

## 35:2
THE GLORY OF LEBANON IS GIVEN TO IT) Loftiness.

THE BEAUTY OF CARMEL AND SHARON) Fruitfulness.

THEY SHALL SEE THE GLORY OF THE LORD) They shall experience his powerful protection in reality: for that is often what seeing means for the Hebrews.

Latin:

GLORIA LIBANI DATA EST EI) Celsitudo.

DECOR CARMELI ET SARON) Fœcundi- tas.

IPSI VIDEBUNT GLORIAM DOMINI) Po- tentem ejus tutelam reipsa experientur : id enim sæpe est videre Hebræis.

## 35:3
Ver. 3. STRENGTHEN THE WEAK HANDS) You prophets and all other good men, give courage to the Jews, lest they tremble at the memory of the siege they endured.

Latin:

Vers. 3. CONFORTATE MANUS DISSOLU- TAS) Vos Prophetæ omnes aliiqs viri boni addite animos Judæis, ne memoria toleratæ obsidionis pavescant.

## 35:4
GOD HIMSELF WILL COME, AND WILL SAVE YOU) He will ensure that the Ethiopian does not reach you.

Grotius explains these things as referring to the temporal happiness of the Jewish kingdom: following again the Jews, who likewise dream that external and temporal happiness is promised to them here. In this alone the blind Jews saw more than the Christian Grotius, in that they understood these things were to be taken as referring to the time of the coming of the Messiah, whereas Grotius twists them to the times of Hezekiah. For clear evidence of the Messiah stands in the text; but of King Hezekiah there appears not a jot, not a trace, although the Jews refer these things to their return to Palestine from their modern captivity, which they expect through their Messiah, and they invent wonders that he will perform at that time: namely, that no one will be so foolish then as not to walk the straight path even from the ends of the earth to the land of promise, and that, so they do not perish from thirst in desert places, God will stir up fountains everywhere, drive away savage beasts, and produce trees bearing leaves that will provide shade and refreshment for travelers, and whatever other trifles of theirs there are. St. Jerome also teaches that some have referred the latter part of this chapter to the second coming of the Messiah, and therefore he warns in his Commentary that we should not, in the Jewish manner, seek a golden Zion and a jeweled Jerusalem, which according to the prophecy of Daniel has been reduced to eternal ashes. For the Jews, he says, and our Judaizers refer it to the second coming, on the occasion of one verse: THEY SHALL BE CONVERTED AND SHALL COME TO ZION WITH PRAISE, desiring the blood of their enemies and the servitude of all nations. Among Christians, however, there has hitherto been no doubt that this prophecy must be taken as referring to our Lord and Savior Christ Jesus. Grotius alone thinks otherwise here, and with the Jews interprets it not of the spiritual flourishing of the kingdom of Christ, but of the temporal and external happiness of the kingdom of the Jews: which, however, he refers to the times of Hezekiah, and not to the coming of the Messiah. It will be worth the effort to vindicate this notable prophecy from this distortion, and to assert its genuine meaning, namely that it describes the happiness of the kingdom of Christ at the time of his coming into the world, which the Gentiles to be converted to the Gospel in the time of the New Testament were especially to enjoy, though the Jews were not excluded, except for those who excluded themselves through infidelity and deprived themselves of that blessedness. For it concerns the Church of the New Testament, which was gathered mostly from the Gentiles, whose joy and glory are therefore chiefly described here: yet not a few from the Jews belong to the same, who also came into Zion with exultation, as the redeemed of the Lord: indeed, the Church of the Gentiles was gathered to the remnant of the Jews, whence Blessed Luther understood this prophecy concerning the Church, born from the remnants of the Synagogue, and warned that all things which the Synagogue had were to be transferred into the Church gathered from the remnants of the Jews and the nations, was here predicted. These arguments can be noted: First, from the συνεχεία [continuity] and collation with the preceding chapter. For since there it was a matter of the enemies of the Church, and their destruction, and the final ruin of the impious and of the whole world, now it is a matter of the joyful propagation and happiness, both spiritual and heavenly, which will befall the same in this and the coming age. There he had predicted slaughter to the Idumeans and the perpetual desolation of their land: Here he predicts the vigor, joy, and salvation of the nations, which were like a desert and solitude, which they were to obtain through Christ. And therefore, to the evils which he had threatened there, he here opposes the goods which are to be expected; to the most horrible desolation, a joyful and flourishing vigor, since the deserts themselves will be like Lebanon, Sharon, and Carmel; to the multitude of wild beasts and ill-omened birds, the absence of evil beasts and demons; to perpetual sorrow and mourning, joy and everlasting exultation. Not badly, therefore, does Calvin here: After the Prophet has treated here of horrible slaughters and signified the miserable dissipation of the whole world, he consoles the pious with this promise, by which he declares that all things are to be restored. This, however, is done through Christ, by whom alone it is permitted to be renewed and exhilarated; since he alone restores all things and brings them back into true order, whereas outside of him there can be nothing but squalor and solitude, nothing but most miserable dissipation both in heaven and on earth.

We seek the second from the customary description of gentilism. For gentilism is wont to be described in the Holy Scriptures by a desert and an impassable land, whence the Church of the Gentiles is said to ascend from the desert, Canticles 8.
