Vers. 9. SCRIPTVRA EZECHIÆ REGIS JVDA Dictata ei, ut credibile est, ab ipso Esaia. UNde vero hoc credibile? Cur non credemus ab ipso Ezechia eam precationem esse profe- ctam, rege pio & Spir. S. repleto? Ne de eo dicam, quod quidam statuant, librum Judicum ab Ezechia esse conscriptum, teste Sixto Senensi lib. II. Bibl. ver- bo Ezechia, nonnulli collectos & digestos ab eo- dem libros Regum cum parabolis Salomoneis cre- dant. Rectius alii Ezechiæ Canticum id esse ajunt, etsi per Esaiam hisce verbis expressum, vel com- prehensum sit.

## 38:10
Verse 10. IN THE MIDST OF MY DAYS) In the middle of that age which most men are accustomed to live, and which the law promises. We see everywhere that premature death is seen as grievous, even by the good, when a better life has not yet been fully revealed.

The Socinian error recurs, which we have noted often, concerning a better life not yet fully revealed under the Old Testament, by which it is evident that the faith and hope of the pious ancients are undermined. For thus it would have to be said that the faithful of the Old Testament believed neither in the resurrection of the dead nor in eternal life, which are the στοιχεῖα τῶν λογίων τὣ Θεὣ [elements of the oracles of God], Heb. 6, 1: and how could they have had hope of a better life, destitute of the word of divine promise? Since the hope of the faithful rests, or certainly ought to rest, solely on the word of God. Furthermore, the Palatine, from the words, I SHALL GO TO THE GATES OF THE GRAVE, infers the limbo of the Fathers, lib. 6. de Arc. c. 9. But just as the gates of death can be understood of death itself, so the gates of hell can be understood of hell: Cf. Job 17, 13. 1 Sam. 2, 6. Wis. 16, 13. because the gates of hell are opposed to the land of the living, i.e., the sepulcher to the land in which one lives: and it is explained concerning the pit of corruption, where the body is consumed, verse 17. Furthermore, concerning this chapter of Isaiah 38, 17. we treated in Memor. Witeberg. Justor. Conc. 22. under the title: The healing of spiritual faintness.

Latin:

Vers. 10. IN DIMIDIO DIERVM MEORVM) In di- midio ejus ætatis, quam homines plurimi agere solent, & quam lex promittit. Videmus ubiqs mortem immaturā gra- vem visam etiam bonis, nondū plene revelata vita meliore.

Recurrit error Socinianus, quem notavimus sæpius, de vita meliore nondum plene revelata sub V. Test. quo fidem & spem piorum veterum labefa- ctari, in aprico est. Nam ita neque resurrectionem mortuorum, neq; vitam æternam credidisse fideles V. Test. quæ sunt στοιχεῖα τῶν λογίων τὣ Θεὣ, Ebr. 6, 1. dicendum erit: & quomodo spem habere vitæ melioris potuere, verbo promissionis divinæ desti- tuti? quum spes fidelium in verbo Dei recumbat, vel certe recumbere debeat unice. Cæterum Pala- tinus è verbis, VADAM AD PORTAS INFERI, colligit limbum Patrum lib. 6. de Arc. c. 9. At ut portæ mortis de ipsa morte, ita portæ inferni de inferno accipi possunt: Conf. Job. 17, 13. 1. Sam. 2, 6. Sap. 16, 13. quia opponuntur portæ inferni terræ vi- ventium, h. e. sepulcrum terræ, in qua vivitur: & explicatur de fovea putredinis, ubi corpus confu- mitur, vers. 17. Porro de cap. hujus Esaiæ 38. 17. egi- mus in Memor. Witeberg. Justor. Conc. 22. sub ti- tulo Lipothymiæ spiritualis sanatio.

## 38:11
Verse 11. I SHALL NOT SEE THE LORD GOD) The temple of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 11. NON VIDEBO DOMINVM DEVM) Tem- plum Domini.

## 38:12
Verse 12. MY GENERATION IS TAKEN AWAY) More correctly, as the following indicates, my dwelling.

AND IT IS ROLLED UP FROM ME) Removed from me.

MY LIFE IS CUT OFF AS BY A WEAVER) Thus the Latins say the threads of life are cut.

WHILE I WAS YET WEAVING, HE CUT ME OFF) דל πλόκιον is translated, Cant. 7, 5. Therefore the sense here seems to be, I am cut off from the web: which Festus and Nonius teach us are the covering of the woof: it has this, however, by the likeness of a braid.

FROM MORNING UNTIL EVENING YOU WILL FINISH ME) Supply 'I said', namely yesterday. Within this shining day I shall die.

Latin:

Vers 12. GENERATIO MEA ABLATA EST) Rectius, ut sequentia indicant, habitatio.

ET CONVOLVTA EST A ME) Translata à me.

PRÆCISA EST VELVTI A TEXENTE VITA MEA) Sic Latini dicunt vitæ stamina præcisi.

DVM ADHVC ORDIRER, SVCCIDIT ME) דל πλόκιον vertitur, Cantic. 7, 5. Itaque sensus hic videtur esse, abscissus sum à pano: quos esse tramæ involucrum docent nos Festus & Nonius: habet autem id πλοκῆς similitudine.

DE MANE VSQVE AD VESPERAM FINIES ME) Supple dixi, heri scilicet. Intra hunc diem lucentem moriar.

## 38:13
I HOPED EVEN UNTIL MORNING) When night had arrived, I did not think I would live beyond the dawn: and meanwhile, as if broken, I was suffering most grievous pains.

FROM MORNING EVEN UNTIL EVENING THOU WILT MAKE AN END OF ME) When the day had shone again, the severity of the disease was so great that I did not dare to hope I would see the evening.

Latin:

SPERABAM VSQVE AD MANE) Vbi nox adve- nerat, non ultra quam ad auroram victurum me putabam: atque interim, quasi fractus, gravissimos patiebar dolores.

DE MANE VSQVE AD VESPERAM FINIES ME) Cum dies iterum alluxisset, tanta erat morbi gravitas, ut vesperam me visurum sperare non auderem.

## 38:14
Vers. 14. AS A YOUNG SWALLOW, SO WILL I CRY) In Hebrew: Like a crane or a swallow, so I chirped.

I DID MEDITATE AS A DOVE) I groaned as a dove. Virgil: Nor shall the turtle dove cease to groan from the airy elm.

MINE EYES FAIL WITH LOOKING UPWARD) While I gaze at heaven during prayer, meanwhile the light of my eyes begins to fail.

O LORD, I AM OPPRESSED) He describes the disease under the guise of some wicked tax collector.

ANSWER FOR ME) Do what sureties are accustomed to do: for they prevent anyone from being thrown into prison.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SICVT PVLLVS HIRVNDINIS, SIC CLAMABO) In Hebr. Sicut grus vel hirundo ita pipiebam.

MEDITABAR VT COLVMBA) Gemebam ut co- lumba. Virgilius: Nec gemere aëria cessabit turtur ab ulmo.

ATTENVATI SVNT OCVLI MEI SPECTAN- TES IN EXCELSVM) Dum inter precandum cœlum in- tueor, interim deficere incipit lux oculorum.

DOMINE VIM PATIOR) Morbum describit sub specie improbi alicujus publicani.

RESPONDE PRO ME) Fac quod solent fidejus- sores: ii enim impediunt, ne quis in nervum ducatur.

## 38:15
Vers. 15. WHAT SHALL I SAY? OR WHAT HATH HE SPOKEN UNTO ME, AND HIMSELF HATH DONE IT?) In Hebrew: What shall I say? (supply: more); he himself has spoken to me, (namely, that I would recover? and that through Isaiah, before he departed from the sick man's chamber, 2 Kings 20:4) and he himself has done it, he has restored health to me.

I SHALL RECKON TO THEE ALL MY YEARS IN THE BITTERNESS OF MY SOUL) How the Greeks read these and the following words is difficult to conjecture. However, the sense in the Greek is not bad. If we follow the Hebrew, he says this: throughout the whole time of my life, the thought of this bitterness will recur to me.

Latin:

Vers. 15. QVID DICAM, AVT QVID RESPON- DEBIT MIHI, CVM IPSE FECERIT?) In Hebræo: Quid loquar? fupple amplius; ipse dixit mihi, (nempe fore ut convalescerem? idq; per Esaiam, antequam is de cubiculo ægrotantis egrederetur, 2. Reg. 20, 4.) & ipse fecit, Sanita- tem mihi reddidit.

RECOGITABO TIBI OMNES ANNOS MEOS IN AMARITVDINE ANIMÆ MEÆ) Quomodo hæc & sequentia legérint Græci, difficile est conjectu, Cæterum sensus in Græco est non malus. Si Hebræum sequamur, hoc dicit: toto vitæ meæ tempore cogitatio hujus amaritiei mi- hi recurret.

## 38:16
Vers. 16. O LORD, IF BY THESE THINGS MEN LIVE) O Lord, by these things one lives: by your promises, namely, and deeds.

AND IN ALL SUCH THINGS IS THE LIFE OF MY SPIRIT) By these things I have breathed again.

THOU WILT CORRECT ME, AND MAKE ME TO LIVE) In Hebrew: You heal me, and cause me to live.

Latin:

Vers. 16. DOMINE SI SIC VIVITVR) Domine per ista vivitur: per promissa scilicet tua & facta.

ET IN TALIBVS VITA SPIRITVS MEI) Per ista respiravi.

CORRIPIES ME, ET VIVIFICABIS ME) In He- bræo: Tu me sanas, & facis ut vivam.

## 38:17
Vers. 17. BEHOLD IN PEACE MY BITTERNESS MOST BITTER) That greatest bitterness was for my salvation.

YOU HAVE CAST BEHIND YOUR BACK ALL MY SINS) You do not wish to look upon my faults.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ECCE IN PACE AMARITVDO MEA A- MARISSIMA) Saluti mihi fuit ista maxima amarities.

PROJECISTI POST TERGVM TVVM OMNIA PECCATA MEA) Non vis ad culpas meas respicere.

## 38:18
Vers. 18. FOR THE GRAVE SHALL NOT CONFESS TO YOU) Your praise is not celebrated by the dead, Psalm 6, 6.

WHO GO DOWN INTO THE PIT) Into the ditch. LXX. οἱ ἐν ἅδᾳ.

Latin:

Vers. 18. QVIA NON INFERNVS CONFITEBITVR TIBI) Laus tua per mortuos non celebratur, Psal. 6, 6.

QVI DESCENDVNT IN LACVM) In foveam. LXX. οἱ ἐν ἅδᾳ.

## 38:21
Vers. 21. A LUMP OF FIGS) Which is believed to have been more harmful by its natural power.

UPON THE WOUND) Rather an ulcer, as it is in the Greek: that is, upon the most inflamed part.

Aquila, as Jerome reports here, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it ἕλκος: by which they wish to be understood the royal disease: since all things that are sweet are thought to be contrary, whether taken in food or applied to the body: but ἕλκος signifies an ulcer, an abscess, and a swelling, not the royal disease. Some think, as Hector Pinto reports, that the king's disease was a certain aposteme, which was cured by dried figs, which we call caricas. For according to the art of physicians, caricas are salutary for such diseases. Others think that these figs were not dried, nor naturally beneficial to wounds, but rather harmful, but that God wished to heal the king's ulcer with harmful and adverse things, so that He might declare His power more evidently. For God is accustomed to bring about great things by means that are repugnant to human judgment, so that His power may stand out and shine more clearly. Thus through Elisha He made the bitter waters of Jericho sweet with salt, and things that were harmful were made wholesome: when on the contrary, with salt sent, they ought to have become more bitter. When the waters of Mara in the desert were bitter, wood being cast into them, they were made sweet, although that wood was bitter, as some report. In the same way, the Hebrews injured by serpents recovered their health by seeing the bronze serpent, which God ordered to be erected. And some say that bronze seems harmful to those whom serpents have bitten. Thus Christ cured the blind man with clay, so that human reason might be confounded, and Christ might show His divinity. These things Pinto.

Latin:

Vers. 21. MASSAM DE FICIS) Quæ vi nativa magis nocitura fuisse creditur.

SVPER VVLNVS) Imo ulcus, ut est in Græco: id est, super parte maxime inflammata.

Aquila, referente Hieronymo hic, Symma- chus, & Theodotio ἕλκος interpretati sunt: per quod morbum regium intelligi volunt: cum contraria pu- tantur, vel sumpta in cibo, vel apposita corpori quæ- cunq; sunt dulcia: sed ἕλκος ulcus significat, vomi- cam, & tuber, non morbum regium. Nonnulli exi- stimant, Hectore Pinto referente, morbum regis fuisse apostema quoddam, quod ficis siccis, quos caricas appellamus, curatum sit. Nam juxta artem Medico- rum hujusmodi morbis sunt caricæ salutares. Alii ar- bitrantur hos ficus non fuisse siccos, neq; naturali- ter prodesse vulneribus, imo nocere, sed voluisse Deum rebus noxiis & adversis ulceri regis mederi, ut evidentius potentiam suam declararet. Solet enim Deus rebus hominum judicio repugnantibq res magnas efficere, ut ejus potentia emineat, & clarius illucescat. Sic per Elisæum aquas amaras Je- richo sale dulces reddidit, & quæ noxiæ erant, salu- bres factæ sunt: cum contra misso sale amariores fieri deberent. Aquæ Mara in deserto cum essent amaræ, ligno in eas conjecto, dulces redditæ fue- runt, cum lignum illud esset amarum, ut nonnulli referunt. Eodem modo læsi Hebræi à serpentibus viso serpente æneo, quem Deus erectum esse jus- sit, sanitatem recuperabant. Et ajunt nonnulli no- xium esse videri æs iis, quos serpentes momorde- rint. Sic Christus cœcum curavit luto, ut humana ratio confunderetur, & Christus suum numen ostenderet. Hæc Pintus.

## 38:22
Vers. same. WHAT SHALL BE THE SIGN, THAT I SHALL GO UP INTO THE HOUSE OF THE LORD) It seems more correctly translated: How great a miracle will it be that I go into the house of the Lord?

Others, how admirable is this sign (which, namely, the miracle God had offered to Hezekiah in the Sun) to be shown to me, that I am about to recover and go up again into the house of the Lord? But the prodigy was truly to be admired: because it was performed not in the shadow, or the sundial of Hezekiah alone, as Vatablus, Burgensis, Arias Montanus, Sanctius, and the Author of the Pre-Adamite fable say, as also Capellus in his History of the World to the year of the world 3283, but in the Sun itself, because Isaiah affirms it clearly in verse 8: And the Sun returned ten degrees; and for that reason also here, because of such a portent which had happened upon the earth, the Babylonian Legates are said to have been sent to Hezekiah, 2 Chron. 32, 31. Nor did the old Jewish Church understand it otherwise, as witnessed by Sirach ch. 48, 25, or the ancient Christian Church, with Cyril, Jerome, Procopius, and others as witnesses, so as to pass over the fact that Clavius, in his Fabrica instrumenti ad horologium, chapter 21, demonstrates that such clocks can be constructed by art in which the shadow alone moves backward: and that by this means the miracle can be easily explained away and denied, just as was done by Pedro Nunes, who asserted that that regression of the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz was natural this, inasmuch as they even assign one hour to every degree, and from this arose their fable that ten hours were subtracted from that day, which was dedicated to the funeral of the impious King Ahaz, so that he might not be buried with sufficient royal honor, which hours God therefore restored in the time of the pious King Hezekiah, so that nothing might seem to have been lost to nature. You will see various questions concerning this miracle in Cornelius à Lapide and others.

Latin:

Vers. eod. QVOD ERIT SIGNVM, QVIA ASCEN- DAM IN DOMVM DOMINI) Rectius videtur verti: Quantum erit miraculum me ire in domum Domini?

Alii, quam admirabile est hoc signum(quod scil. Deus obtulerat Ezechiæ miraculum in Sole) exhibendum mihi, quod convaliturus & ascensurq; denuo sim in domum Domini? Vere autem admi- randum erat prodigium: quod non in umbra, vel horologio solum Ezechiæ, uti Vatablus, Burgensis, Arias Montanus, Sanctius, & Autor Præ-Adamiti- cæ fabulæ, ajunt, ut & Capellus in hist. Aug. ad ann. mundi 3283. sed in Sole ipso patratum est, quia diser- te id affirmat Esaias v. 8. Et reversus est Sol decem lineis; & ea de causa etiam hic ob tantum porten- tum, quod super terram acciderat, Babylonii Le- gati ad Ezechiam missi dicuntur, 1. Par. 32, 31. Nec aliter id intellexit, aut vetus Judaica Ecclesia, teste Syracid. cap. 48, 25. aut Christiana Ecclesia antiqua, Cyrillo, Hieronymo, Procopio, aliisque testibus, ut taceam quod Clavius in Fabr. instrum. ad horolog. c. 21. demonstret, arte erigi posse talia horologia, in quibus sola umbra retrocedat:quodq; hoc pacto mi- raculum prorsus elidi ac negari facile possit, quem- admodum à Petro Nonnio factum, qui asseruit na- turalem fuisse illum regressum umbræ in Achazi horologio. Neque dubitant de eo Judæi, utpote qui gradui etiam cuivis unam horam tribuunt, atq; inde orta est eorum fabula, decem horas illi diei sub- tractas, qui dicatus erat exequiis impii regis Achazi, ne regiè satis sepeliretur, quas proinde Deus restitue- rit tempore pii regis Ezechiæ, ne quid naturæ decessis- se videretur. Quæstiones varias de hoc miraculo videfis apud Cornel. à Lapide, & alios.

## 39:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXIX. When Hezekiah had shown his treasures to the Babylonian envoys, the Prophet threatened their removal by the Babylonians and the abduction of his sons.

Verse 1. MERODACH) It seems that the passage in 2 Kings 20:12 should be corrected from this, where in the Hebrew it is written Berodach; the Greeks have Merodach in both places: Josephus only calls him Baladan, and says that mention of him was also made by Berosus in his Chaldean history. Now this man was a Mede: for the Medes held the Babylonian kingdom after Esarhaddon: of which change we have already had prophecies before; Nabopolassar, a Chaldean by birth and the father of Nebuchadnezzar, later expelled the Medes. This Merodach was numbered among the gods because of his benefits, as we shall say in our notes on Jeremiah 1, verse 2.

There is no necessity why we should be forced to admit an error in the writing of this word in the Hebrew source: since nothing is more frequent than for proper names to vary somewhat, or it could be said that this king was called Berodach as a proper name, and that he was the son of Baladan. Moreover, that Berodach is a common name for kings, just as the name of Ptolemy was among the Egyptians and the name of Caesar among the Romans—whence Nebuchadnezzar’s son was called Evil-Merodach, and Belshazzar is called Merodach in Jeremiah 50:2, perhaps from the first king of Babylon who was called Merodach and numbered among the gods—is observed by Cornelius à Lapide in this place. However, the Hebrew interpreters do not agree on who this Merodach was: they think it was Nebuchadnezzar, who transferred the monarchy from the Assyrians to the Chaldeans, but falsely; because he only began to reign a full century later. Most think he was the same person who is called Mardokempad by Ptolemy, such as Funccius, Mercator, Buntingius, Ubbo Emmius, and others; his parent Baladan was called by that name while he led a private life, but was later called Nabonassar, as Tirinus observes on 2 Kings 20:1, which is also the opinion of Cornelius à Lapide on this place.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXIX. Ezechias cum Legatis Babylonicis thesauros suos ostendisset, minatus est Propheta eo- rum per Babylonios ablationem, & filio- rum abductionem.

Vers. 1. MERODACH) Videtur hinc corrigendus locus 2. Reg. 20, 12. ubi in Hebræo Berodach scribitur, Græci utro- bique habent Μερωδὰχ: Josephus tantum Baladam vocat, aitque ejus mentionem factam & à Beroso iu Chaldaicis. Fuit autem hic Medus: Nam Medi post Asarhaddonem re- gnum Babylonicum tenuere: cujus mutationis jam ante vaticinia habuimus, Medos postea expulit Nabopolaffarus Chaldæus ortu, Nabuchodonosori pater. Hic Merodach ob beneficia in deos relatus, ut dicemus ad Jer. I. v. 2.

NUlla est necessitas, cur cogamur admittere er- rorem in hujus vocis scriptione in fonteEbræo: quum nihil frequentius sit, quam nomina propria nonnihil variare, aut dici posset, regem hunc appel- latum fuisse Berodach nomine proprio, filiumq; fuisse Baladam. Nomen autem Berodach esse commune regum nomen, sicut apud Ægyptios nomen Ptole- mei, apud Romanos Cæsaris nomen, unde filium Nabuchodonosor vocatum esse Evilmerodach, & Baltazarum Merodach Jer. 50, 2. vocari, forte à primo Babylonis rege Merodach dicto, & inter deos relato, observat Cornel. à Lapide in h. l. Quis- nam vero ille Merodach fuerit, non consentiunt Interpp. Ebræi: Nabuchodonosorem, qui Monar- chiam ab Assyriis ad Chaldæos transtulit, fuisse ex- iftimant, sed falso; quia integro seculo post hic de- mum regnare cepit. Plerique eundem fuisse, qui à Ptolemæo Mardo-Kempad vocatur, putant, utpote Funccius, Mercator, Buntingius, Ubbo Emmius & alii, Parentem ejus Baladam prius vocatum, cum privatam ageret vitam, sed postea Nabonassarem dictum, observat Tirinus ad 2. Reg. 20, 1. quæ etiam est sententia Cornelii à Lapide ad h. l.

## 40:1 Argument
PART II. CONTAINING THE MORE EVANGELICAL DISCOURSES OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH. SECTION I. CONSOLATIONS CONCERNING THE DELIVERANCE from the Babylonian captivity, with promises inserted and premised concerning Christ and His Church under the New Testament. CHAPTER XL. The consolation of the people from the advent and salvation of Christ, whose forerunner, the summary of the Evangelical discourse, and pastoral care are exhibited, and the incomparable greatness of God is commended against idolaters, those trusting in whom are clothed with strength.

Since the Prophet had already openly predicted that deportation which was to come about through Nebuchadnezzar and his general Nebuzaradan, he encourages those who would be partakers of that calamity, partly toward an amendment of life, and partly, if they perform it, he promises God’s severe judgments upon their enemies, and for them a return to their homeland, a flourishing state, safety against hostile neighbors, remarkable victories, and finally a great number of those who, by their example and instruction, would either accept the whole law or at least depart from idolatry and the wicked customs that usually accompany idolatry. These prophecies extend over a long period of time, from the times of the exile to the times of the restored temple and city, and indeed even to the times of the Maccabees and the following ages. For God did not wish any of the glories that were to happen to the people to be passed over in silence, so that there might be more consolation for the pious who were in exile through the fault of others. But why did he skip over the times of Manasseh, Josiah, and Jehoiakim? Because they contained nothing but the corruptions of the people, which gave cause for the deportation. For Josiah, although good, had not profited much by his example among the people, except that he had restored the rites in some way: but the spirit of most of the nobles and the people had remained removed from true piety. Now, since all the benefits of God contain within themselves a shadow of those things which Christ performed, then especially all those things which will henceforth be announced by Isaiah, with words very often directed by God in such a way that they might fit more simply and clearly into the things of Christ than into those which Isaiah originally intended to signify.

Now follows the second part of the prophecies of Isaiah: which Grotius likewise attempts to corrupt and to twist into a foreign sense, no less than the preceding one: And since that part is almost entirely occupied with describing the things of the New Testament, Grotius, in order to maintain that the literal sense does not regard the times of the New Testament, labors all the more vehemently the more illustrious these prophecies of the Prophet are here. He follows, however, the Jewish masters, blind guides, who trifle that this second part of the prophecy, up to the end of the book, deals with the glory of the Lord through the liberation of the people from the Babylonian captivity, by which they obscure the most evident prophecies concerning the Messiah, bringing upon themselves and others darkness rather than these most luminous oracles. Although Grotius himself could not deny that all those things which follow henceforth in this Prophet contain within themselves a shadow of those things which Christ performed, and indeed that the words were very often directed by God in such a way that they fit more simply and clearly into the things of Christ than into others. This confession, which arose from the truth itself, must be well observed: since the sense of the prophecies is to be derived primarily from the very words employed by God, and that sense is without doubt literal in prophecies which is the most simple, and is to be understood entirely as genuine and native to those things to which it fits more simply and clearly than to any others, according to hermeneutical rules and the sound opinion of all interpreters. Knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation, says Peter, 2 Epistle 1:20. That sense is sound and without danger, which is placed openly and without ambiguity in the very expressions in the Scriptures, says Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 46. But that Grotius, having neglected this perspicuity and simplicity of the sense of the prophecies when they are understood of Christ, still believes that another more literal and directly intended sense underlies these prophecies, nay, that he wishes that sense concerning Christ to be only shadowed forth by the proper sense, which he thinks is about entirely different matters, in that, I believe, no sensible interpreter will have him as an adherent. If, however, anyone should wish to contend on behalf of Grotius that the sense which he himself assigns is literal, and that the sense concerning Christ is mystical, he will first be able to be convinced by this Grotian concession which I have already observed: because the sense from which no other simpler or clearer sense flows from the words of Scripture, that without doubt is the literal, genuine, and native one: not merely mystical or indirectly and consequently intended. But Grotius grants that such is the sense concerning Christ in all these prophecies. Then, indeed, it must by no means be admitted that another sense should be attributed to those prophecies which are clear concerning Christ, and are explained as concerning Christ even in the New Testament by the Holy Scriptures themselves, much less that that [other sense] should be defended as the principal or literal one. For it is evident that this cannot be done without notable distortion and injury to the text and to the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures. Finally, that double sense of the same prophecy, namely literal and mystical, by no means agrees with the simplicity of Scripture, which is devoid of all ambiguity, and with its perspicuity and power of interpreting itself, since a sense is not to be brought into Scripture, but to be drawn out and brought forth from it. Nor is there any reason why we should gratify the Jews, who close their eyes against the clear light of the Prophetic oracles, by determining that those things speak of others rather than of Christ, which, according to the most simple and limpid sense, sound of no one else more than of Christ; and why we should invent another literal sense, and judge that Christ is hinted at only by some mystical reason and some shadowing forth. And whom could this zeal for Judaizing please, by which Grotius preferred to obscure with an admixture of Jewish glosses the prophecies placed in the clearest light and explained in the Scriptures of the New Testament concerning Christ, rather than to propose their native light, purified on all sides from the mists and darkness of the Rabbis, in the pious and praised manner of Christian interpreters! For those most illustrious oracles concerning John the Baptist, and concerning the passion of Christ in chapter 53, where Isaiah seemed to act the part of an Evangelist more truly than that of a Prophet, [are] Christian interpreters'. Christian interpreters, concerning the Prophetic office of Christ, Isaiah 61, and other things of this kind, which speak openly of Christ alone, and are explained by the Holy Scriptures as concerning Christ alone, he preferred to twist toward others with the Jews, rather than to leave them to Christ alone with the Christian Church. In the exposition of which he dwells only on Rabbinic glosses, and does not even make any mention of Christ; whence you might not undeservedly say that he inserted those annotations into his pages while drunk with a Jewish spirit. The argument which Grotius insinuates here, that the Prophet had already openly predicted the deportation which was to happen through the Babylonians, and therefore now encourages those who were participants in that calamity, and promises them the judgments of God upon their enemies, and a return to their fatherland, and a flourishing and safe state, and a great number of proselytes, is of no strength. For however it may be admitted that exhortations and consolations are intermingled in certain chapters, directed to that end, it does not follow that this whole remaining part of the prophecy is to be twisted solely to the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, not even excepting those prophecies which deal most clearly with Christ and the affairs of the New Testament. Are those things therefore to be taken as concerning bodily benefits, which evidently treat of spiritual ones, proper to the faithful? Nor is that continuity which is supposed here certain, as if Isaiah had proposed this consolatory discourse, which is held in chapter XL, immediately before the king, after he had denounced the Babylonian exile to him: since the circumstances teach rather that the Prophet meditated upon this prophetic discourse in the spirit much later. Which not even Calvin, although he Judaizes in these matters similarly to Grotius, and concedes that this deals literally with the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, could deny, since he judges that the present prophecy was proposed by Isaiah when he was already near death, whereas that conversation of the Prophet with the king, in which he had denounced the Babylonian captivity to him, had been held much earlier, so that he lived at least fifteen years after that conversation, as far as can be judged from the histories. Furthermore, there is no reason to ask why Isaiah skips over the times of Manasseh, Josiah, and Jehoiakim, because it is asserted gratuitously and without solid proof that he follows the times of the same kings step by step: just as it is also assumed precariously that this prophecy extends itself to the times of the Maccabees and the following periods. But these special points will be more correctly established from a special discussion of the Grotian misinterpretation.

Vers. 1. COMFORT YE, COMFORT YE MY PEOPLE) More correctly: my people, as the Chaldean also judged. God speaks, as the same Chaldean judges, to the Prophets who were to be in the time of the exile.

The Vulgate is correctly corrected. But that these things were said to the Prophets who were to be in the time of the Babylonian exile, as far as the genuine and native sense is concerned, is false. For they concern the times of the New Testament and the coming of Christ: which is most clear from the second verse: the voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert the paths of our God; Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain. That these things were predicted concerning the Proto-baptist John, interpreters greater than any exception testify. St. Matthew chapter 3, 1. 2. In those days, he says, came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea, and saying: Repent ye, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. For this is he who was spoken of by the Prophet Isaiah, saying: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. We have, therefore, who that is who was spoken of there by Isaiah: namely John the Baptist. St. Mark similarly testifies with a resounding voice that the proclamation of John in the wilderness, and not indeed of others who lived at the time of the Babylonian captivity, is dealt with here, chapter 1, 1. seqq. The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in the Prophet Isaiah: Behold I send my messenger before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight; John was in the WILDERNESS, baptizing and preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. From which allegation both things are evident: Both that Isaiah had prophesied there concerning John the Baptist who was to preach repentance in the wilderness, and that he did not deal with the Prophets who were to be in the time of the Babylonian exile: because he prophesied concerning one singular person, and indeed concerning the same one of whom Malachi dealt after the Babylonian captivity, concerning the messenger who was to prepare the way of the Lord; i.e., concerning John the Baptist. That the meaning is exactly the same, and the person the same, whom Malachi and whom Isaiah indicated, St. Mark openly teaches by the very fact that he brings forward these two prophecies as one, and cites the passage of Malachi as Isaiah's; because the Prophets not only wrote by the same spirit, but being occupied with the same subject, they mutually illustrate one another, and one confirms the other's meaning; and because Malachi explained Isaiah's prophecy, and teaches that it was to be understood only of the Angel, the precursor of the Lord, the Baptist, and that that voice of one crying in the desert had not yet been heard in his own time, but was finally to be heard in future times. Nor is the oracle of Isaiah to be taken otherwise, St. Luke has testified, chap. 3, 2. et seqq. The word of the Lord came upon John the son of Zechariah, in the desert. And he came into all the region about the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance, for the remission of sins, as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the Prophet: The voice of one crying in the desert, prepare ye the way of the Lord: make his paths straight, every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways plain, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God. He has here expressly taught Luke, that this prophecy is to be understood as concerning no one other than John, preaching repentance, when the word of the Lord came upon him in the desert, and that it does not look to past times, 'all flesh shall see the salvation of God,' but to future ones. The Proto-Baptist himself testified that these things were predicted of no one other than himself, and that that prophecy looks to the times of the New Testament, is sufficiently taught by the response which he gave to the Priests and Levites, which was then beyond doubt among the Jews; for when they asked, 'Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent me? What do you say about yourself?' 'I,' says St. John, 'am the voice of one crying in the desert, make straight the way of the Lord, as the Prophet Isaiah said.' And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees, as St. John the Evangelist reports in chapter I, 19 et seqq. Suppose the Pharisees believed what Grotius did, that Isaiah speaks literally of the prophets at the time of the Babylonian exile: how could St. John have dared to appeal so confidently to the prophecy of Isaiah before the legates of the Pharisees? Could the Pharisees not have replied? 'What is this to you, what was predicted about the prophets at the time of the Babylonian captivity?' Since, therefore, the Baptist assumes this as ὁμολογεμένως (admittedly) certain, that this concerned no one other than the forerunner of the Messiah, he testifies that he is the same, and thus presents the 'letters of his vocation,' as they are called, from the Prophetic pandects to the Legates of the Sanhedrin. And here this harmonious consensus of all the Evangelists deservedly has the force and weight of a great argument, so that we may conclude that the oracle concerning the prodromos of the Messiah, designated most evidently by certain marks, was produced and is not to be dragged or twisted elsewhere. Especially because so many faithful Interpreters mention only John the Baptist, and none of them makes any mention of a type with even one word. Which the blessed Hunnius not undeservedly urges against Calvin and Pareus, his hyperaspist. For it is not the case that one should object that it is not customary for the Evangelists, when alleging typical things, to express the types themselves. We see what custom Christ and the Evangelists and Apostles observe in the allegations of typical oracles, namely, that they make express mention of the type, and never easily omit it, unless it is already established beforehand what the type is, which is evident from the examples in Matt. 12 concerning Jonah, John 3 concerning the bronze serpent, John 6 concerning the manna, 1 Cor. 5 concerning the Paschal lamb, Heb. 7, 9, 10 concerning Melchizedek and the Aaronic sacrifices, the types of Christ: the explanation of whose signs is delivered διαρρήδην (expressly) in the Scriptures of the New Testament. But that the prophets comforting and exhorting the people at the time of the Babylonian captivity were types of John the Baptist comforting and exhorting the people under the auspices of the New Testament is nowhere taught in the Scriptures; so far is it from being taught anywhere that the Isaianic prophecy deals with those prophets as types of John, that all the Evangelists assert that it deals with a singular person, and indeed with the forerunner of Christ, St. John, whom Christ opposes to the prophets; 'The Law and the Prophets were until John' (Matt. 11:13), and he testifies that he is 'more than a prophet' (v. 9). It is therefore by no means to be tolerated that what is μοναδικῶς (uniquely) claimed for John, as the prodromos and forerunner of Christ, should be snatched away to the prophets of the time of the Babylonian destruction, let alone that it should be explained concerning them, as to its proper, native, and literal sense, against the mind of the Evangelists and the interpretation of John himself. It is added that a certain and singular person is described by individuating marks and characters, so to speak. For the Prophet designates the voice OF ONE CRYING, not indeed the voice of those crying: furthermore, he describes that one crying in such a way that he is to cry in the desert. Which Brentius paraphrases thus on p. 640: 'You, citizens of Jerusalem, are indeed terrified now by the prophecy of the subversion of Jerusalem, and you think that what has been promised concerning the coming of the Savior Messiah is most vain. But I not only announce to you that the Messiah will most certainly come, and will bring the benefits which I have already enumerated, but I will also signify to you by what argument your descendants may know the time of his coming. For he will not arrive unexpectedly, but will send before him a voice crying, that is, a preacher, who will not preach, according to custom, in the temple or synagogues, but will preach in the desert.' When, therefore, our descendants have heard that a preacher has arisen in the desert, then let them know that the Messiah, the true Lord our God, is near. Which the Evangelists understand μοναδικῶς (uniquely) and singularly concerning John crying in the desert. For what such voice of one crying in the desert was heard after this prophecy, which desert was so insignificantly known and celebrated, what voice produced such a clamor, just as the desert and the voice of John, because of which clamor the whole Sanhedrin sent a significant embassy to John, because of which a frequent crowd went out into the desert, so that Christ himself asked: 'What did you go out into the desert to see? A prophet? Yes, I say to you, and more than a prophet' (Matt. 11:9), because of whom not only Jerusalem, but all the land and region, all around the Jordan flocked to John, as Matthew testifies, when indeed that voice of one crying in the desert was heard (ch. 3:5). These are the very same words of the Prophet among the LXX Interpreters. Φωνὴ βοῶντος ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, which Matthew ch. 3 and Mark 1:20. And lest anyone doubt in any way what that voice of one crying in the desert is, St. John himself says, 'I am the voice of one crying in the desert, make straight the way of the Lord, as the Prophet said.' Therefore, the desert is not to be explained otherwise, nor is it lawful to interpret the Prophetic oracle concerning another crying in the desert. Nor is only the voice of one crying designated individually, but also those words of that voice are expressed, which suit no one as they do St. John, whence the Holy Evangelists, describing his clamor or voice and preaching, introduce that preaching or voice which, according to the Prophet, was to be heard in the desert: which is expressed by the LXX Interpreters ἑτοιμάσατε τὴν ὁδὸν κυρίε εὐθείας ποιήσατον τρίβες ἀυτẽ. Which Matthew and Mark the Evangelists repeat in the very same way. Those passages therefore treat of the way of the Lord in a peculiar sense, according to the Evangelical interpretation; of the way, I say, not of the return of the people from captivity, or of the visitation of the Lord, by which He was about to deign to visit the people in exile, but of the way of the Messiah, which was to be prepared for Him as the Lord of the people, whose advent He promises: and therefore He raises up the people with the consolation of the Lord's advent, to receive which they were to be awakened by the voice of one crying in the wilderness. There is added in the Prophet either a promise or a further exhortation, or rather a promise with an exhortation, because the Holy Spirit so exhorts that He is efficacious through the word of His exhortation, whence also those Prophetic words are to be understood not only παραινετικῶς (exhortatorily), but also ἐπαγγελτικῶς κὴ προφητικῶς (promissorily and prophetically), at once imperatively and promisively: πᾶσα Φάραγξ πληρωθήσεται, κὴ πᾶν ὄρος κὴ βυνὸς ταπεινωθήσεται, κὴ ἔσται πάντα σκολιὰ εἰς ἐυθεῖαν, & ἡ τραχεῖα εἰς ὁδὸς λείας. Thus the LXX Interpreters have it. Which Luke applies to the proclamation of John the Baptist, repeating the same Evangelical or promissory exhortation, joined with an exhortation, and adapting it to the time of the New Testament, or the advent of Christ, and citing those things in plainly the same words, except that the last ones vary a little, the sense remaining the same, as the promise concerning the manifestation of the glory of the Lord, which the Prophet here predicted would come to pass not through the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, but through the appearance of God in the flesh, Luke is witness: for he even wished to repeat that from Isaiah καὶ ὄψεται πᾶσα σὰρξ τὸ σωτήριον τῦ θεῦ & all flesh shall see the salvation of God, so that he might teach that the promise looked toward the times of the New Testament, as those in which the Jews not only saw the salvation of God, the Messiah, under a shadow, but ALL flesh was clearly to see this salvation of God. For thus is that revelation of the glory of the Lord explained, for whom the way was to be prepared, or at least it is taught that that vision would be joined with the manifestation of the glory of the Lord: all of which it is manifest look toward the times of the New Testament, or the advent of Christ. For then the way of the Lord was being prepared, then it was being revealed, nay, it could even be grasped as if by the eyes and the glory of the Lord was being beheld, as the LXX. ὀφθήσεται ἡ δόξα κυρίθ, which is evident from John 1:14, then all flesh could see the salvation of the Lord even with bodily eyes, as Simeon sings in Luke 2:30, 'my eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples'; then the mouth of the Lord was to speak, and it could be heard by all, כי פי יהוה דבר ὅτι κύριος ἐλάλησεν, that the mouth of the Lord or the Lord speaks: Then finally, it was to be announced especially to Jerusalem that iniquity has been dismissed. All of which so manifestly teach that this concerns the time of the advent of Christ, that even Fridericus Spanhemius, Dubior. Evang. Dub. XXI. f. 55, had to admit this, however much he contended in favor of his Judaizing Calvin, that as to the letter the times of the Babylonian captivity are designated here, but that the spiritual benefits of Christ lie hidden under a type. The words, he says, of the Prophet are too august to be restricted, both to a carnal benefit and to a benefit pertaining to one nation: many words of the Prophet are less conveniently referred to the type, most conveniently to the antitype: for the consolation, of which the Prophet speaks, pertains most especially to the time when not only the warfare of the people of God, or its pre-defined period was completed, but also when iniquity was discharged: which was indeed fulfilled when the πλήρωμα τῦ χρόνε came, and those weeks determined upon the people of God had elapsed, transgression was restrained, sins were sealed, iniquity was expiated, the righteousness of the ages was brought in, according to the prophecy of Daniel ch. 9. At that time also the glory of God was most especially revealed, when God was manifested in the flesh, and his glory was proven and established by so many excellent miracles. Add that the final words cannot be exhausted by a consideration of a typical and particular liberation, that all flesh would see the mouth of the Lord having spoken, which indeed pertain most especially to that liberation which was common to every flesh, to any nations whatsoever. Now if those things which were to be denounced and preached to the cities of Judah and Jerusalem at that time according to the Prophet are attended to, what is more certain than that the time of the Lord's advent is being looked to? For the Prophet speaking of it v. 9: 'Say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God, behold the Lord will come in strength, and his arm shall rule: behold his reward is with him, and his work before him, as a shepherd he will feed his flock.' The name 'your God' expresses the name of Christ, Immanuel: his advent was in strength, when he came as the ἰσχυρότερος, of whom Christ himself speaks in Luke 11:22. If a stronger one coming upon him (Beelzebub, that strong armed one, guarding his own atrium) shall have overcome him, etc. Then his arm ruled, by which he demonstrated infinite power, by the operation of various miracles, the overcoming of Satan, the omnipotent rule at the right hand of God, the conversion of the nations, the perfection of the Church, etc. What the Prophet has here, 'his reward is with him,' that Christ expressly professes of himself in Rev. 22:12: 'Behold I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according to his works.' And as the Prophet describes him as a shepherd feeding his flock, so Christ presents himself under this image, John 10:11 seqq. The evidence of the matter again compelled Spanh. to admit that these things which we have already adduced in v. 9 and 10 must necessarily be referred to the Messiah, and that in them the advent, offices, benefits, and efficacy of the Messiah are announced. By what right, therefore, are those things which must necessarily be referred to the Messiah κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, explained otherwise, and said to exhibit Christ only under a type! They are utterly ἀσύστατα, which Spanh. joins here, Φυλάττων τὴν ἔκθεσιν of his Master. For if the words of the Prophet are too august to be restricted to a carnal benefit, why are they explained concerning it, and what are those things which designate a carnal benefit, or restrict them to a benefit pertaining to one nation, why therefore are they expounded concerning the Jewish people and their liberation from the Babylonian exile, as regards the literal sense? What word is found in this prophecy, or even in the whole chapter, that sounds of the Babylonian captivity! If many words in this text are less conveniently referred to the liberation and the Babylonian captivity, certainly it ought to be a matter of conscience to refer them to the same, lest the words of the Prophet be accepted in a less convenient sense, especially because no necessity compels us to invent a type here. For although it may be admitted that the reduction from Babylon is a type of the liberation from the captivity of sin and Satan (which, however, where it has been handed down in the Scriptures has not yet been shown), yet how will it be proven that the things which are said here are typical? e.g. That the prophets consoling the people at the time of the exile were types of John the Baptist, that their voice is proposed here as a figure of the Johannine voice in the desert, that the completed warfare and the discharged iniquity at the time of the liberation from captivity typically adumbrated the expiation of iniquities made through Christ: that the glory of God revealed when the captivity was loosed, figured the glory of Christ, which shone forth in his miracles and exaltation! And what typical adumbration is there in the fact that the people received from the hand of the Lord for their sins double, i.e., as Spanhemius Dub. XXII. p. 62 renders it, manifold, or heavy punishments, at the time of the Babylonian captivity? How does this fit the antitype, or can it be applied? Here Spanhemius stuck in the mud. For that application, which he himself provides, is altogether unsuitable and incongruous; If, he says, we look to the antitype, the people of God truly received double from the hand of Jehovah in the time of the Messiah, sustaining the person of the Church, whether regarding the punishments inflicted upon it, or regarding the benefits which were bestowed upon the Church in the Messiah. Thus it can be shown far better in the antitype, how the iniquity of the Church was remitted, and yet it received double for its sins, than in the type. Indeed, who says these things about the type, which the Calvinists imagine? He wishes double to be taken for grave or manifold, as in Jerem. 16, 18. 1 Tim. 5, 12. Apoc. 18, 8. How therefore did the Jewish people receive double for their sins, as a type of the Church? Spanheim says that the people in the type received from the hand of Jehovah for all their sins כפלים double, i.e., manifold or grave PUNISHMENTS. But how now will the antitype respond, that the Church has received manifold PUNISHMENTS? What kind of argument of consolation will this be, which the Holy Scripture prescribes here: comfort, comfort my people: because the people received most grave punishments for their sins, and the Church will one day receive punishments, likewise manifold, or most grave? Behold the illustrious interpreters, the illustrious comforters! Spanheim is inept when he now obtrudes the Messiah sustaining the person of the Church in place of the people of God, perhaps by a Zwinglian alloeosis; for the Holy Scripture does not command the Messiah to be comforted, but its people, it does not predict that the Messiah will receive double for sins, but that its people will receive double: (P) He does not prophesy concerning the punishments inflicted upon the Messiah, but concerning the double benefits to be exhibited to the people; nor does Scripture testify, nor could it even testify, that the Messiah sustained the person of the Church when punishments were inflicted upon him, either here or anywhere else; because when the Messiah, as one substituted in our place, is subjected to punishment in our stead, there is as yet no Church, which emerges only after he has laid down his soul as a sacrifice for sins: For by this his redemptive and satisfactory passion, the Lord finally purchased for himself, with the incorruptible price of his Blood, the Church (Acts 20:28). How then could he have sustained the person of the Church in his passion, when there was as yet no Church, with Christ being substituted in the decree of God in place of the human race, and sustaining the punishment in its stead, which he therefore sustained in order to rescue the human race from the power of darkness, and to gather and build up the Church for himself from the same (Colossians 1:13, 14). Since the Prophet is entirely occupied here with the Paracletic genre, why then would he introduce punishment, why the most grievous torments, to be sustained either by the Jewish people or by the Church of God? But if double benefits are indicated, as it is most certain they are indicated, how is the Jewish people said to have received double benefits for their sins in the past, so that in that respect it was a type of the Church, which was to receive double? And was not that people, whom the Holy Spirit wishes to be raised up by consolation, the Church itself; why is it imagined to be only a type of the Church? For if the Jewish people in ancient times under the Babylonian captivity were to be designated in the highest degree, who does not know that the consolations which God applied to them were made primarily to the faithful, and to the Church of God which remained in that people, and were made to the whole people on account of the Church and the faithful who were in the people. It is therefore manifest that the type is imagined in vain, since the Holy Spirit commands the people of God to be consoled without any rationale for a type: It is also necessary to confess that those arguments by which the literal sense is recalled to the times of the Babylonian exile are in vain, which speak openly of the Church in the time of the New Testament without any involution of a type.

These things will be even clearer from a special discussion of the Grotian corruptions; for to these, where there is need, the Calvinian Φλυαρίαι (trifles) can also be joined. Spanheim himself indeed confesses, which some of the Jews also acknowledge, that MANY things are found here which pertain to the times of the Messiah. Why then does Spanheim drag them to the times of the Babylonian exile? Then, if many things in the text pertain to the times of the Messiah, why are they not rather convinced, from that very confession, that all things should be referred to the same? For this whole prophecy without doubt pertains to the same times, and is of the same subject matter, not a different one: nor is it right in one and the same prophecy, occupied with the same subject matter, to admit such a salvation, much less to imagine different objects, so that, for instance, most things indeed pertain to the times of the Messiah, yet the rest look to the times of the Babylonian exile. The text certainly does not indicate this, much less compel it; and are not the sounder Jews here to that extent superior to Grotius, Spanheim, and their accomplices, in that they acknowledge that many things in this prophecy, as far as the literal sense is concerned, pertain to the times of the Messiah? These men, however, labor to distort everything, as far as the literal sense is concerned, to the times of the Babylonian exile, and do not refer them to the times of Christ, except insofar as the benefit of Christ lay hidden in the liberation from Babylon, as in a type and a certain shadow, and was figured by it; which was not only the opinion of Spanheim, but also of Grotius, as is clear from his Annotations on Luke 3:4. Many things here, he says, Origen and others argue, in order to explain who are the mountains, who the valleys: when it ought to suffice, as I have said elsewhere, that the office of a herald is described, in type indeed in Isaiah, so that it may be signified that all things are now prepared for the people to be brought back to Judea from Babylon by postliminy: but in type for announcing the liberation from the servitude of sin and death, which were figured by that return. But that the Jews acknowledge no type, but refer most of those things according to the letter to the times of the Messiah, Spanheim again confesses not obscurely: The Jews, on the contrary, he says, contend that neither in the Babylonian captivity, nor in the liberation from it, can a type of either captivity or spiritual liberation be established without absurdity. Wherefore it is certain that the Jews explain these things according to the letter concerning the days of the Messiah. R. David Kimchi, to these words, 'comfort, comfort,' says that all these consolations will be in the days of the Messiah, and the repetition of the word is a mark of confirmation. What the opinion of the Christian Church is, you may learn from Cyril, who also shows the connection with the preceding chapters. The discourse, he says, passes to the times of Christ and introduces a clear prophecy of the grace through him: nor does it seem to wander outside of decorum, nor was it introduced untimely. For some, not sufficiently versed in the divine scriptures, will say: How does it happen that the Prophet here makes the prediction concerning Christ near to us by the speeches of Hezekiah? To this we shall institute a defense thus, saying this: Since the discourse had commemorated the final captivity of the Jewish land, and indeed of Jerusalem itself: it has now introduced, timely as it were, and usefully, the consolation subsequently made by God, and necessarily. But I shall say in a few words, and I shall explain accurately, what has just been said by us. For several invasions were made against Jerusalem, and the region of the Jews was often devastated, partly by the hand of the Assyrians, partly by neighboring Barbarians, and others who were ravaging it. The final captivity at last took place, through Nebuchadnezzar, in the times of the reign of Jeconiah, when Israel was led captive into the region of those whom we have mentioned. But in the times of the reign of Cyrus, it was released from captivity, and returned to Judea, and rebuilt the temple, and they dwelt not dispersed, until the advent of our Savior. When, therefore, he made mention of the final captivity, when the Babylonians, breaking into all the treasuries of the kings of Judah, returned to their own land: necessarily also after these things he makes a prediction of the consolation that has been made, namely through Christ, commanding and saying to those who administer the divine Gospel; Comfort, comfort my people, says God. We conclude with the words of B. Brentius. We must not look around anxiously to investigate what the meaning of this passage is. For the Evangelists, who are the true and divinely chosen interpreters of the Prophetic writings, manifestly show that this passage is to be understood not according to allegory, but κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, concerning John the Baptist, Matt. 3 & 11, Mark 1 & Luke 3 & John 1. Wherefore not even an angel is to be heard if anyone should interpret this passage otherwise than concerning John the Baptist. Finally, we have observed the confession of Grotius himself, who at Luke 24:47 refers this prophecy to the times of the N. Testament, and especially v. 9, from which he proves that the beginning of the Evangelical proclamation ought to have taken place in Jerusalem in the time of the N. T.

Latin:

PARS II. PROPHETÆ ESAIÆ CONCIONES MAGIS EVANGE- LICAS CONTINENS. SECTIO I. CONSOLATIONES DE LIBERA- tione è captivitate Babylonica, præmissis infertisque promissionibus de Christo, ejus- que Ecclesia sub Novo Testa- mento. CAPUT XL. Consolatio populi ab adventu & salute Chri- sti, cujus prodromus, Concionis Evangelicæ summa, ac cura pastoralis exhibetur, & contra Idololatras incomparabilis Dei ma- gnitudo commendatur, cui confidentes vir- tute induuntur.

Cum aperte jam prædixisset Propheta eam deportatio- nem, quæ per Nabuchodonosorum ejusque Ducem Nebu- zardanem erat eventura, liberaliter ejus calamitatis partici- pes futuros, partim ad emendationem vitæ excitat, partim si eam præstent, promittit severa Dei judicia in ipsorum ho- stes, ipsis vero reditum in patriam, statum florentem, tu- tumq; contra infestos vicinos, egregias victorias, magnum denique numerum eorum, qui ipsorum exemplo atque in- stitutione, aut legem totam susciperent, aut certe ab idolo- latria moribusque improbis, qui idololatriam plerumque comitantur, discederent. In longum autem tempus exten- dunt se hæc vaticinia à temporibus exilii, ad tempora templi & urbis restitutæ, imo & ad Maccabæorum & sequentia tempora. Nulla enim decora, quæ populo erant obventu- ra, taceri Deus voluit, quo plus solatii esset piis per aliorum culpam exulantibus. At cur transiliit tempora Manassis, Jo- siæ, Joakimi? quia nihil ea continebant, nisi corruptelas populi, quæ causam dedere deportationi. Josias enim, quamvis bonus, non multum exemplo suo apud populum profecerat, nisi quod ritus aliquo modo restituerat: sed ple- risq; & procerum & populi animus manserat remotus à ve- ra pietate. Cum autem omnia Dei beneficia umbram in se contineant eorum, quæ Christus præstitit, tum præcipue ista omnia, quæ deinceps ab Esaia prænunciabuntur, verbis sæpissime à Deo sic directis, ut simplicius limpidiusq; in res Christi, quam in illas, quas primo significare Esaias voluit, convenirent.

SEquitur jam altera parsProphetias Esaiæ: quam corrumpere itidem tentat Grotius, & in alie- num detorquere sensum, non minus, quam præ- cedentem: Et quum illa pene tota in rebus Novi Testamenti describendis occupata sit, Grotius, ut obtineat, sensum literalem non respicereNovi Te- stamenti tempora, tanto vehementius subinde la- borat, quanto illustriora hic sunt Prophetæ vatici- nia. Sequitur autem Judæorum Magistros, ducto- res cæcos, qui de gloria Domini per liberationem po- puli ex captivitate Babylonica in hac altera Prophe- tiæ parte agi, usq; ad finem libri, nugantur, quo va- ticinia evidentissima de Messia obfuscent, sibi & aliis caliginem potius, quam oraculis hisce lucu- lentissimis inducentes. QuamvisGrotius ipse dif- fiteri non potuerit, ista omnia, quæ deinceps in hoc Propheta sequuntur, umbram eorum in se contine- re, quæ Christus præstitit, imo verba sæpissime à Deo sic directa esse, ut simplicius, limpidiusq; in res Chri- sti, quam in alios conveniant. Quæ confessio ab ipsa veritate ei exorta probe observanda: siqui- dem sensus vaticiniorum è verbis ipsis à Deo adhi- bitis eruendus imprimis sit, & sensus ille sine du- bio literalis sit in vaticiniis, qui simplicissimus est, & de rebus illis omnino tanquam germanus & na- tivus intelligendus sit, quibus simplicius, limpi- diusque convenit, quam ullis aliis, juxta regulas Herminevticas, sanamque omnium Interpretum sententiam. Hoc primum scientes, quodnulla Pro- phetia Scripturæ sit propriæ interpretationis, ait Pe- trus 2. Epist. I. 20. Is sanus sensus & sine periculo, qui aperte & sine ambiguo ipsis dictionibus in Scri- pturis ponitur, inquit Irenæus lib. 2. cap. 46. Quod vero posthabita hac perspicuitate, & simplicitate sensus vaticiniorum, cum de Christo intelligun- tur, Grotius adhuc tamen alium in his vaticiniis credit subesse sensum magis literalem & directe in- tentum, imo sensum illum de Christo vult tantum adumbrari à proprio sensu, quem de aliis plane re- bus esse existimat, in eo neminem, credo, è corda- tis Interpp. habebit assentientem. Si quis tamen contendere velit pro Grotio, illum sensum, quem ipse assignat, esse literalem, sensum vero de Chri- sto mysticum esse, ille primum ex hac Grotiana concessione, quam jam observavi, poterit con- vinci: quia quo sensu nullus alius simplicior, lim- pidiorque è verbis Scripturæ fluit, ille sine dubio literalis, germanus & nativus est: non tantum my- sticus aut indirecte & consequenter intentus. At ta- lem in hisce vaticiniis omnibus esse sensum de Christo, largitur Grotius. Tum vero admitten- dum minime est, ut iis vaticiniis, quæ luculenta de Christo sunt, atque in Novo etiam Testamento de Christo explicantur ab ipso S. S. alius sensus af- fingatur, nedum ut ille pro principali aut literali vindicetur. Nam id sine insigni στρεβλότητι & in- juria textus, & interpretationis S.S. fieri non posse, in aprico est. Deniq; geminus ille sensus, ejusdem vaticinii, literalis nempe atque mysticus neutiquam convenit Scripturæ simplicitati, omnis ambiguita- tis experti, ac perspicuitati, & δεινότητι semetipsam interpretandi, cum non inferendus sit in Scriptu- ram sensus, sed ex ea eruendus, & efferendus. Ne- que est, quod Judæis id gratificemur adversus cla- ram vaticiniorum Propheticorum lucem oculos claudentibus, ut statuamus, de aliis potius, quam de Christo ea loqui, quæ juxta simplicissimum & limpidissimum sensum, de nullo alio, quam de Christo magis sonant; ac literalem sensum finga- mus alium, nec nisi mystica quadam ratione & ad- umbratione aliqua Christum subinnui censeamus. Et cui placere hoc Judaizandi studium poterit, quo vaticinia in clarissima luce posita, & in Scri- pturis Novi Testamenti de Christo exposita, ad- mistione gloffematum Judaicorum obfuscare po- tius maluit Grotius, quam pio, laudatoque more Interpp. Christianorum nativam eorum lucem à nebulis atque tenebris Rabbinorum undiquaque castigatam proponere! Nam & illustrissima illa oracula de Iohanne Baptista, de passione Christi cap. 53. quo Evangelistam verius quam Prophetam age- re visus est Esaias Interpp. Christianis, de officio Christi Prophetico, Esa. 61. aliaque hujusmodi, quæ aperte de uno Christo loquuntur, & à S.S. de uno Christo explicantur, ad alios detorquere maluit cum Judæis, quam cum Christiana Ecclesia uni Christo relinquere. In quorum expositione im- moratur tantum gloffematis Rabbinicis, ac Christi ne mentionem quidem ullam facit; unde spiritu Judaico Ebrium ea annotata Chartis inseruisse non immerito dixeris. Argumentum quod hic insinuat Grotius, quod aperte jam prædixerat Propheta de- portationem, quæ per Nabuchodonosorum eventura erat, ideoq; nunc calamitatis illius participes erigat, iisque judicia Dei in hostes, & reditum in patriam, & statum florentem ac tutum, magnumq; proselyto- rum numerum promittat, nullius roboris est. Nam utut hortamenta & solamina in quibusdam capiti- bus admisceri, eo directa, admittatur, non tamen ideo tota hæc reliqua parsProphetię detorquenda unice est ad liberationem de captivitate Babyloni- ca, ne exceptis quidem illis vaticiniis, quæ luculen- tissime de Christo, & rebus Novi Testam. agunt. Num ideo de corporalibus beneficiis accipienda sunt, quæ evidenter de spiritualibus, fidelibus pro- priis tractant? Neque vero certa est illa, quæ hic supponitur, συνέχεια, quasi Esaias concionem hanc consolatoriam, quæ cap. XL. habetur, proti- nus coram rege proposuerit, postquam ei denun- ciarat exilium Babylonicum: quum circumstantiæ doceant potius, multo post Prophetam demum hanc vaticidam concionem in spiritu meditatum esse. Quod ne Calvinus quidem, etsi similiter, ut Grotius in hisce Judaizet, ac de liberatione è ca- ptivitate Babylonica hic quoad literam agi conte- dat, diffiteri potuit, quum vaticinium præsens ab Esaia jam morti vicino propositum censeat, collo- quium vero illud Prophetæ cum rege, in quo eiBa- bylonicam denunciarat captivitatem, multo ante habitum fuerit, ita ut post eam collocutionem ad minimum ultra quindecim annos vixerit, quan- tum quidem ex Historiis judicari potest. Porro non est, quod quæratur, cur Esaias transiliat tem- pora Manassis, Josiæ, Jojakim, quia eundem regum tempora κατὰ πόδας persequi, gratis, & citra pro- bationem solidam, asseritur: Quemadmodum etiam illud precàrio assumitur, ad Maccabæorum, & sequentia tempora hanc prophetiam sese exten- dere. Sed hæc specialia è speciali discussione ψευδ- ερμηνείας Grotianæ constabunt rectius.

Vers. 1. CONSOLAMINI, CONSOLAMINI POPU- LE MEUS) Rectius: populum meum, ut & Chaldæus cen- suit. Loquitur Deus, ut idem Chaldæus censet, Prophetis futuris exsilii tempore.

Recte corrigitur Vulgata. Sed dicta hæc esse ad Prophetas, qui tempore exitii Babylonici futuri erant, quantum ad germanum & nativum sensum, falsum est. Nam concernunt ea tempora Novi Te- stamenti & adventus Christi: Quod luculentissi- mum est è versu secundo: vox clamantis in deserto, parate viam Domini, rectas facite in solitudine se- mitas Dei nostri; Omnis vallis exaltabitur, & omnis mons & collis humiliabitur, & erunt prava in dire- cta, & aspera in vias planas. Quæ de Protobaptista Johanne prædicta esse, interpretes omni exceptio- ne majores testantur. S. Matthæus cap. 3, 1. 2. In diebus autem illis, inquit, venit Johannes Baptista, prædicans in deserto Judææ, & dicens: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquavit enim regnum cœlorum. Hic est enim, qui dictus est per Esaiam Prophetam, di- centem: vox clamantis in deserto: parate viam Do- mini, rectas facite semitas ejus. Habemus ergo, quisnam ille sit, qui dictus est ibi per Esaiam: ni- mirum Johannes Baptista. S. Marcus similiter de Johannis præconio in deserto, non vero de aliis, qui jam tempore captivitatis Babylonicæ vixerunt, hic agi, sonora voce testatur cap. 1, 1. seqq. Initium Ev- angelii Jesu Christi, filii Dei, sicut scriptum est in Esaia Propheta: Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum ante faciem tuam, qui præparabit viam tuam ante te: Vox clamantis in deserto: Parate viam Domini, rectas facite semitas ejus; fuit Johannes in DE- SERTO, baptizans & prædicans baptismum pœni- tentiæ in remissionem peccatorum. E qua allegatio- ne utrumque constat: Et quod de Johanne Bapti- sta prædicaturo in deserto pœnitentiam vaticinato ibi fuerit Esaias, & quod non egerit de Prophetis futuris tempore exitii Babylonici: quia de una sin- gulari persona, & quidem de eadem, de qua Mala- chias post captivitatem Babylonicam egit, vatici- natus est, de Angelo, qui Domini viam paraturus erat; h. e. de Johanne Baptista. Eandem prorsus esse sententiam, eandem personam, quam Mala- chias, & quam Esaias indicavit, S. Marcus eo ipso aperte docet, quod hæc duo vaticinia tanquam unum, & Malachiæ locum pro Esaiano adducat, quod non solum eodem spiritu scripserint Prophe- tæ, sed in eodem argumento occupati se mutuo il- lustrent, & unus alterius sententiam confirmet, quodque Malachias Esaiæ vaticinium explicavit, ac non nisi de Angelo, præcursore Domini, Bapti- sta intelligendum fuisse, neq; suo tempore jam au- ditam esse vocem illam clamantis in deserto, sed demum futuris temporibus exaudiendam esse, do- ceat. Neq; aliter accipiendum esse oraculum Esaia- num, S. Lucas testatus est, cap. 3, 2. seqq. Factum est verbum Domini super Johannem Zachariæ filium, in deserto. Et venit in omnem regionem Jordanis, prædicans baptismum pœnitentiæ, in remissionem peccatorum, sicut scriptum est in libro sermonum Esaiæ Prophetæ: Vox clamantis in deserto, parate viam Domini: rectas facite semitas ejus, omnis val- lis implebitur, & omnis mons, & collis humiliabitur, & erunt prava in directa, & aspera in vias planas, & videbit omnis caro salutare Dei. Diserte hic docuit Lucas, non de alio, quam de Johanne, prædicante pœnitentiam, cum verbum Domini super eum fa- ctum est in deserto, hoc vaticinium exaudiendum esse, nec præterita tempora illud, videbit omnis ca- ro salutare Dei, sed futura respicere. Proto-Bapti- sta ipse non de alio, quam de seipso hæc prædicta esse, testatus est, illamque Prophetiam respicere Novi Test. tempora, tum penes Judæos extra du- bium fuisse responsum, quod Sacerdotibus & Le- vitis dedit, satis docet; Quum enim quærerent; Quis es, ut responsum demus his, qui miserunt me, quid dicis de te ipso? Ego, ait S. Johannes, vox cla- mantis in deserto, dirigite viam Domini, sicut dixit Esaias Propheta: Et qui missi fuerant, erant ex Pha- risæis, uti refert S. Johannes Evangelista cap. I. 19. seqq. Pone, Pharisæos id credidisse, quod Grotius, Esaiam de Prophetis, exilii Babylonici tempore, secundum literam loqui: quomodo tam confiden- ter ad Esaiæ vaticinium coram Pharisæorum lega- tis provocare ausus fuisset S. Johannes: Annon re- ponere potuissent Pharisæi? Quid hoc ad te, quod de Prophetis captivitatis Babylonicæ tempore præ- dictum? Quum ergo hoc tanquam ὁμολογεμένως certum assumat Baptista, quod hic non de alio, quam de præcursore Messiæ actum fuerit, se eun- dem esse testatur, adeoque vocationis suæ literas, quas vocant, ex pandectis Propheticis Legatis Sy- nedrii sistit. Atq; hic tam concors Evangelistarum omnium consensus merito vim & pondus habet magni argumenti, ut oraculum de prodromo Mes- siæ, certis notis evidentissime designatum, prodi- tum, non alio trahendum aut torquendum statua- mus. Præsertim quod tot fidi Interpretes solius Johannis Baptistæ meminerint, nullus eorum vel uno verbo typi mentionem ullam injiciat. Quod non immerito adversus Calvinum & Pareum, ejus Hyperaspistem, urget B. Hunnius. Nec enim est, ut objiciatur, usitatum non esse, ut Evangelistæ typi- ca allegando, typos ipsos exprimant. Videmus, quem morem observet Christus & Evangelistæ & Apostoli, in allegationibus oraculorum typico- rum, ut videlicet typi disertam mentionem faciant, nec facile unquam prætermittant, nisi de typo jam ante constet, quod ab exemplis constat Matth. 12. de Jona, Joh. 3. de serpente æneo, Joh. 6. de manna, 1. Cor. 5. de agno Paschali, Ebr. 7, 9, 10, de Melchi- sedeco & Aaroneis sacrificiis, Christi typis: Quo- rum fignoru explicatio διαρρήδην in Scripturis N. Test. tradita est. Prophetas autem tempore capti- vitatis Babylonicæ populum consolantes, & adhor- tantes typos fuisse Johannis Baptistæ sub auspicium Novi Testamenti consolantis & adhortantis po- pulum, nuspiam in Scripturis traditur, tantum ab- est, ut vaticinium Efaianum de Prophetis illis, ceu typis Johannis agere, alicubi doceatur, quod de sin- gulari quadam persona, & quidem de præcursore Christi S. Johanne videlicet agere, omnes Evange- listæ asseverant, quem Prophetis opponit Chri- stus; Lex & Prophetæ usq; ad Johannem Matth. 11, 13. & plus quam Prophetam esse testatur v. 9. Nulla- tenus ergo ferendum est, ut quod μοναδικῶς Jo- hanni vindicatum, ceu prodromo & præcursori Christi, ad Prophetas abripiatur, tempore exitii Babylonici, nedum ut de illis, quoad proprium & nativum, ac literalem sensum, contra mentem Ev- angelistarum, & interpretationem ipsiusmet Jo- hannis, explicetur. Accedit, quod notis & chara- cteribus individuantibus, ut ita loquamur, descri- batur certa & singularis persona. Nam vocem CLAMANTIS, non vero vocem Clamantium de- signat Propheta: adhæc clamantem illum ita descri- bit, quod clamaturus sit in deserto. Quæ Brentiu ita παραφράζῃ p. 640. Vos quidem cives Hierosolymitani exterriti estis nunc vaticinio subversionis Hierusalem, & existimatis vanissima esse, quæ de adventu Messiæ servatoris promissa sunt. Ego vero non tantum adnuncio vobis, Messiam certissime adventurum, & beneficia sua, quæ jam enumeravi, allaturum, sed etiam significabo vobis, quo argumento posteri vestri possint tempus adventus ejus cognoscere. Non enim adveniet ex improviso, sed præmittet ante se vocem clamantem, hoc est, concionatorem, qui non concionabitur, pro more, in templo, aut synagogis sed concionabitur in deserto. Cum ergo audierint posteri nostri exortum esse concionatorem in deserto, tunc sciant, Messiam verum Dominum Deum nostrum in propinquo esse. Quod Evangelistæ de Johanne in deserto clamante, μοναδικῶς & singulariter intelligunt. Quæ enim talis vox clamantis in deserto audita est post hoc vaticinium, quod tam insigniter notum atque celebre fuit desertum, quæ vox tantum clamorem edidit, sicuti desertum, & vox Johannis, ob quem clamorem totum synedrium legationem insignem ad Johannem misit, ob quem in desertum turba frequens exivit, ut Christus ipse quæsierit; Quid existis in desertum videre? Num Prophetam? Etiam dico vobis, & plusquam Prophetam, Matth. 11, 9. ob quem non tantum Hierosolyma, sed omnis terra & regio, omnes circa Jordanem confluxerunt ad Johannem, teste Matthæo, cum nempe vox illa clamantis in deserto exaudiretur, c. 3, 5. Eadem omnino verba sunt Prophetæ apud LXX. Interpp. Φωνὴ βοῶντος ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, quæ Matthæus c. 3. & Marc. 1, 20. Et ne quis ullatenus ambigat, quænam sit illa vox clamantis in deserto, S. Johannes ipse, Ego, inquit, sum vox clamantis in deserto, dirigite viam Domini, sicut dixit Propheta. Non ergo aliter desertum explicandum, aut de alio in deserto clamante interpretari fas est oraculum Propheticum. Neq; solum vox clamantis individualiter designatur, sed etiam verba illa vocis istiq exprimuntur, quæ nulli ita conveniunt, uti S. Johanni, unde clamorem vel vocem ejus ac concionem describentes S. Evangelistæ, concionem vel vocem illam, quæ exaudienda, secundum Prophetam, in deserto erat, introducunt: quæ à LXX. Interpretibus exprimitur ἑτοιμάσατε τὴν ὁδὸν κυρίε εὐθείας ποιήσατον τρίβες ἀυτẽ. Quæ eadem omnino ratione repetunt Matthæus & Marcus Evangelistæ. Agunt ergo illa de via Domini peculiari, juxta interpretationem Evangelicã, de via, inquam, non reditus populi è captivitate, aut visitationis Domini, qua populum in exilio dignaturus erat, sed de via Messiæ, quæ ei paranda ceu Domino populi, cujus adventum promittit: ideoq; populum consolatione erigit adventus Dominici, quem ut suscipiant, voce clamantis in deserto excitandi erant. Additur apud Prophetam sive promissio sive adhortatio ulterior, seu potius cum adhortatione pollicitatio, quia ita hortatur Spiritus Sanctus, ut per verbum adhortationis suæ efficax sit, unde etiã verba illa Prophetica non παραινετικῶς modo, sed ἐπαγγελτικῶς κὴ προφητικῶς imperative simul & promissive intelligenda: πᾶσα Φάραγξ πληρωθήσεται, κὴ πᾶν ὄρος κὴ βυνὸς ταπεινωθήσεται, κὴ ἔσται πάντα σκολιὰ εἰς ἐυθεῖαν, & ἡ τραχεῖα εἰς ὁδὸς λείας. Ita habent LXX. Interpret. Quæ Johannis Baptistæ præconio applicat Lucas, eandẽ sc. hortationem Evangelicam vel promissoriam, cum adhortatione conjunctam repetens, & tempori Novi Testamenti, vel Christi adventus accommodans, ac verbis plane iisdem illa adducens, nisi quod postrema paululum varient, sensu manente eodem, promissio de manifestatione gloriæ Domini, quam non per liberationem à captivitate Babylonica, sed per apparitionem Dei in carne futuram Prophetam hic prædixisse, Lucas testis est: nam ideo etiam illa repetita voluit ex Esaia καὶ ὄψεται πᾶσα σὰρξ τὸ σωτήριον τῦ θεῦ & videbit omnis caro salutare Dei, ut tempora Novi Testamenti promissionem illam spectare doceret, utpote quibus Judæi non solum sub umbra salutare Dei Messiam viderunt, sed O- MNIS caro hoc salutare Dei clare visura erat. Sic enim explicatur illa revelatio gloriæ Domini illius, cui via paranda, aut certe docetur conjunctam fore cum manifestatione gloriæ Domini visionem il- lam: quæ omnia spectare tempora N. Testamenti, vel adventus Christi manifestum est. Tum enim parabatur via Domini, tum revelabatur, imo velu- ti oculis usurpari poterat & conspiciebatur gloria Domini, uti LXX. ὀφθήσεται ἡ δόξα κυρίθ, quod è Joh. 1, 14. constat, tum videre poterat omnis caro etiam oculis corporeis salutare Domini, uti Simeon canit Luc. 2. 30. viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum, quod parasti ante faciem omnium populorum; tum loquu- turum erat os Domini, & audiri ab omnibus pote- rat, כי פי יהוה דבר ὅτι κύριος ἐλάλησεν, quod os Domini vel Dominus loquatur: Tum deniq; Hiero- solymæ cumprimis annunciandum erat, quod di- missa sit iniquitas. Quæ omnia tam manifeste do- cent, de tempore adventus Christi hic agi, ut fateri hoc debuerit etiam Fridericus Spanhemius Dubior. Evang. Dub. XXI. f. 55. utut in gratiam Calvini sui judaizantis contenderit, quoad literam tempora ca- ptivitatis Babylonicæ hic designari, sub typo autem la- tere beneficia Christi spiritualia. Verba, inquit, Pro- phetæ augustiora sunt, quam ut restringi possint, tum ad beneficium carnale, tum ad beneficium pertinens ad unam gentem: verba multa Prophetæ minus com- mode ad typum, commodissime ad antitypum referri: consolatio enim, de qua Propheta, pertinet potissimum ad tempus, quo non tantum militia populi Dei, vel pe- riodus ejus prædefinita completa fuit, sed & quo ex- soluta iniquitas: quod sane adimpletum, quando venit τὸ πλήρωμα τῦ χρόνε, & septimana illa decisa super populum Dei elapsæ fuere, cohibita defēctio, obsigna- ta peccata, expiata iniquitas, adducta justitia seculo- rum, secundum vaticinium Danielis cap. 9. Illo etiam tempore gloria Dei potissimum revelata, quando Deus manifestatus fuit in carne, & ejus gloria tot eximiis miraculis comprobata fuit, & constabilita. Adde verba ultima non liberationis typicæ & particularis consideratione exhauriri posse, omnem carnem visu- ram os Domini loquutum fuisse, quæ sane ad illam li- berationem potissimum pertinent, quæ cuivis carni, quibusvis gentibus communis fuit. Jam si ea, quæ de- nuncianda & prædicanda civitatibus Judæ & Hie- rosolymæ, isto tempore juxta Prophetam erant, at- tendantur, quid certius est, quam quod tempus ad- ventus Dominici respiciatur? De eo enim disente Propheta v. 9.
