Dic civitatibus Juda: Ecce Deus ve- ster, ecce Dominus in fortitudine veniet, & brachium ejus dominabitur: ecce merces ejus cum eo, & opus il- lius coram illo, sicut pastor gregem suum pascet. No- men Deus vester exprimit Christi nomen Immanu- el: ejus adventus in fortitudine erat, cum venit tan- quam ἰσχυρότερος, de quo Christus ipse Luc. 11, 22. Si fortior ei (Beelzebub, forti illi armato, atrium suum custodienti) superveniens, vicerit eum &c. Tum brachium ejus dominatum est, qua potentiam infinitam demonstravit, variorum miraculorum operatione, Satanæ devictione, omnipotenti ad dextram Dei regimine, gentium conversione, Ec- clesiæ perfectione &c. Quod hic Propheta habet, merces ejus cum eo, id diserte Christus de sese profi- tetur Apoc. 22, 12. Ecce venio cito, & merces mea me- cum est, reddere unicuig, secundum opera sua. Et uti Propheta eum, ceu pastorem gregem suum pascen- tem describit, ita Christus semetipsum sub hac effi- gie sistit, Joh. 10, 11. seqq. Rei evidentia iterum fateri coëgit Spanh. hæc quæ v. 9. & 10. jam adduximus, necessario ad Messiam referenda esse, iisq; Messiæ ad- ventum, officia, beneficia, & efficaciam prænunciari. Quo ergo jure illa, quæ necessario ad Messiam refe- renda κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, aliter explicantur, nec nisi sub ty- po Christum exhibere dicuntur! Prorsus ἀσύστατα sunt, quæ hic conjungit Spanh. Φυλάττων τὴν ἔκθε- σιν Magistri sui. Nam si augustiora sunt Prophetæ verba, quam ut restringi possint ad beneficium carnale, cur de eo explicantur, & quænam illa sunt, quæ car- nale beneficium designent, aut ad beneficium ad u- nam gentem pertinens ea restringant, cur ergo de populo Judaico, ejusq; liberatione è Babylonico exilio, quoad literalem sensum, exponuntur? Quod- nam vel verbulum in hoc vaticinio, aut etiam in to- to capite reperitur, quod Babylonicam sonet captivi- tatem! Si verba multa in hoc textu min9 commode referuntur ad liberationem, & captivitatem Baby- lonicam, certe religio esse debet, ad eandem ea re- ferre, ne verba Prophetæ sensu min9 commodo ac- cipiantur, imprimis quia nulla cogit necessitas, ut hic typum fingamus. Quamvis enim admitti possit, reductionem ex Babylone typum esse liberationis è captivitate peccati & Satanæ (quod vero ubi in Scripturis traditum sit, nondum ostensum fuit) ea tamen, quę hic dicuntur, typica esse, quomodo pro- babitur? e. g. Prophetas populum consolantes tempo- re exilii, typos fuisse Johannis Baptistæ, vocem eorum hic ceu figuram vocis Johanneæ in deserto proponi, completam militiam, & exsolutam iniquitatem tem- pore liberationis è captivitate typice adumbrasse ex- piationem iniquitatum per Christum factam: gloriam Dei revelatam, cum solveretur captivitas, figurasse gloriam Christi, quæ in miraculis & exaltatione ejus effulsit! Et quæ adumbratio typica in eo, quod popu- lus de manu Domini pro peccatis suis duplicia, h. e. ut Spanhemius Dub. XXII. p. 62. reddit, multiplicia, vel gravia supplicia suscepit, tempore captivitatis Ba- bylonicæ? Quomodo hoc antitypo congruit, aut ap- plicari potest? Spanhemio hic aqua hæsit. Nam ap- plicatio illa, quam ipse tradit, prorsus inconveniens & inconcinna est; Si antitypum, inquit, respiciamus, duplicia revera suscepit Dei populus de manu Jehovæ tempore Messiæ, Ecclesiæ personam sustinentis, sive quoad pœnas illi inflictas, sive quoad beneficia, quæ in Messia Ecclesiæ collata. Sic longe melius in antitypo ostendi potest, qui Ecclesiæ remissa sit iniquitas, & illa tamen duplum acceperit pro peccatis suis, quam in ty- po. Enimvero qui hæc de typo, quem fingunt Cal- vinistæ, dicta? duplum pro gravi vel multiplici sumi vult, uti Jerem. 16, 18. 1. Tim. 5, 12. Apoc. 18, 8. Quo- modo ergo pro peccatis suis populus Judaicus ac- cepit duplum, ceu typus Ecclesiæ? Dicit Spanhem. populum in typo suscepisse de manu Jehovæ pro omni- bus peccatis suis כפלים duplicia, h. e. multiplicia vel gravia SUPPLICIA. At quomodo jam respon- debit antitypus, quod acceperit Ecclesia multipli- cia SUPPLICIA? Quodnam hoc argumentum erit consolationis, quam hic præcipit S. S. consolamini, consolamini populum meum: quia populo accepit pro peccatis suis gravissima supplicia, & Ecclesia olim ac- ceptura est supplicia, itidem multiplicia, vel gravissi- ma? En præclaros interpretes, præclaros consola- tores! ineptus est Spanhemius cum Messiam Ec- clesiæ personam sustinentem nunc obtrudit loco po- puli Dei, per allæosin forte Zwinglianam; non e- nim Messiam consolari jubet S. S. sed populum su- um, non Messiam duplicia accepturum pro peccatis, sed populum suum duplicia accepturum prædicit: (P) non de pœnis Meffiæ inflictis, sed de beneficiis dupli- cibus populo exhibendis vaticinatur; neque Messiam Ecclesiæ personam sustinuisse, cum pœnæ illi infli- ctæ sint, vel hic vel alii uspiam testatur Scriptura, aut testari etiam potuit; quia cum Messias, ut in no- stri locum surrogatus, nostri vice pœnæ subjicitur, nulla adhuc est Ecclesia, quæ emergit demum, post- quam animam suam posuit sacrificium pro delictis: Nam per hanc passionem suam redemptoriam & satisfactoriam emit demum sibi Dominus, pretio Sanguinis sui incorruptibili, Ecclesiam Act. 20, 28. Quomodo ergo potuisset sustinere Ecclesiæ personam in passione sua, quum nulla adhuc Ecclesia fuerit, Christo in decreto Dei surrogato invicem generis humani, ejusq; loco pœnam sustinente, quam ideo sustinuit, ut eriperet genus humanum è potestate te- nebrarum, & Ecclesiam sibi ex eodem colligeret, atq; exstrueret Colof. 1, 13. 14. Quum hic in genere Paracletico totus occupatus sit Propheta, quid ergo ingereret pœnam, quid supplicia gravissima, sive populo Judaico, sive Ecclesiæ Dei sustinenda? Si vero beneficia duplicia indigitantur, uti indigitari certissimum est, quomodo pro peccatis suis olim ac- cepisse dicitur populus Judaicus beneficia duplicia, ut ea parte Ecclesiæ typus esset, duplicia accepturæ? Et annon populus ille, quem S. S. consolatione eri- gi vult, erat Ecclesia ipsa, cur solum is typus fingi- tur Ecclesiæ? Nam si maxime populus Judaicus an- tiquo tempore sub captivitate Babylonica designa- retur, quis nescit, consolationes, quas Deus eidem adhibuit, factas fuisse imprimis fidelibus, & Eccle- siæ Dei, quæ in illo populo supererat, ac universo populo factas propter Ecclesia, & fideles, qui erant in populo. Frustra ergo fingi typum, quum citra typi rationem populum Dei consolari jubeat S. S. in aprico est: Frustra etiam illa qua sensum litera- lem ad tempora Babylonici exilii revocari, quæ palam de Ecclesia tempore N. Test. sine ulla typi involutione loquuntur, fateri oportet.

Quæ clariora adhuc erunt è speciali discussio- ne Grotianarum corruptelarum; His enim jungi poterunt, ubi opus erit, Calvinianæ etiam Φλυα- ρίαι. Fatetur sane Spanhemius ipse, quod etiam nonnulli ex Judæis agnoscant, MULTA hic repe- riri, quæ ad tempora Meffiæ pertinent. Cur ergo ea ad tempora exilii Babylonici trahit Spanhemius? Tum si multa in textu pertinent ad tempora Mes- siæ, cur non omnia eodem referenda esse potius convincuntur, ex illa propria confessione? Tota enim hæc Prophetia ad eadem tempora sine dubio pertinet, ejusdemq; est argumenti, non diversi: ne- que fas est in uno eodemq; vaticinio, in eodem ar- gumento occupato, talem salutem admittere, ne- dum diversa objecta fingere, ut nempe pleraq; per- tineant quidem ad Messiæ tempora, cætera tamen respiciant tempora Babylonici exilii. Textus certe id non indicat, nedum cogit; Et annon sanio- res hic eatenus Judæi sunt Grotio, Spanhemio & complicibus, quod illi agnoscant, multa in hac va- ticinio, quoad sensum literalem, ad tempora Messiæ pertinere? Hi vero omnia, quantum ad sensum li- teralem ad tempora exilii Babylonici detorquere laborent, nec ad Christi tempora ea referant, nisi quatenus Christi beneficium in liberatione è Ba- bylone, ceu typo & umbra quadam latuit eaq; figu- ratum fuit. quam non Spanhemii tantum sententiam fuisse, sed etiam Grotii, ex Annotatis hujus ad Luc. 3, 4. liquet. Multa hic, inquit, Origenes & alii argu- tantur, ut explicent, qui sint montes, qui valles: cum illud sufficere debeat, quod alibi dixi, munitoris offi- cium describi, ἐν τύπῳ quidem apud Esaiam, ut signifi- cetur omnia jam parata esse ad populum è Babylonia in Judæam postliminio reducendum: διὰ τύπꙋ verò ad annuntiandam liberationem à servitute peccati & mortis, quæ reditu illo figurabantur. Nullum autem typum agnoscere Judæos, sed secundum literam pleraq; illa ad tempora Messiæ referre, iterum haud obscure fatetur Spanhemius: Judæi contra, inquit, pentendunt, nec in captivitate Babylonica, nec in libe- ratione ex ea sive captivitatis, sive liberationis spiri- tualis typum sine absurditate constitui posse. Quapro- pter Judæos, secundum literam hæc de diebus Mef- siæ explicare, certum est. R. David Kimchi ad hæc verba, consolamini, consolamini, omnes, inquit, istæ consolationes futuræ sunt in diebus Messiæ, & repeti- tio vocis conformationis nota est. Ecclesiæ Christianæ quę sit sententia, è Cyrillo addiscas, qui etiam nexum monstrat cum præcedentibus capp. Transit, inquit, oratio ad Christi tempora & gratiæ per ipsum clarum inducit vaticinium: neꙁ extra decorum videtur ex- spatiari, neꙁ intempestive introducta est. Dicent enim quidam in divinis literis non satis diligenter versati: Qui fit, ut Propheta hic sermonibus Ezechiæ prædi- ctionem de Christo nobis vicinam faciat? Ad hoc sic defensionem instituemus, illud dicentes: Cum ultimam Judaicæ terræ captivitatem, ipsorumꙁ, adeo Hieroso- lymorum commemor asset oratio: tempestive veluti, & utiliter deinceps factam à Deo consolationem jam in- duxit, & necessario. Sed paucis dicam, exponamꙁ, ac- curate, quæ à nobis modo dicta sunt. Plures enim im- pressiones contra Hierosolyma factæ sunt, & sæpe regio Judæorum vastata est, partim manu Assyriorum, par- tim finitimorum Barbarorum, aliorumꙁ, eam popu- lantium. Postrema demum facta est captivitas, per Nabuchodonosorum, temporibus regni Jechoniæ, quan- do Israël captivus est abductus in regionem eorum, quos diximus. Temporibus vero regni Cyri, à captivi- tate relaxata est, rediitꙁ, in Judæam, ac templum re- fecit, & habitaverunt non disperse, usꙁ, ad Servato- ris nostri adventum. Quando igitur ultimæ captivi- tatis mentionem fecit, cum in omnes regum Judææ the- sauros irrumpentes Babylonii redierunt in terram suam: necessario etiam post hæc consolationis factæ, videlicet per Christum, prædictionem facit, his qui di- vinum administrant Evangelium, præcipiens & di- cens; Consolamini, consolamini populum meum, dicit Deus. Concludimus B. Brentii verbis. Non est nobis solicite circumspiciendum, ut perscrutemur, quæ sit sententia hujus loci. Nam Evangelistæ, qui sunt ve- ri, ac divinitus electi Interpretes Propheticorum scri- ptorum, manifeste ostendunt, hunc locum non secun- dum allegoriam, sed κτ' τὸ ῥητὸν, de Johanne Baptista intelligendum esse Matth. 3. & 11. Marc. 1. & Luc. 3. & Joh. 1. Quare ne Angelus quidem audiendus est, si quis hunc locum aliter, quam de Johanne Baptista in- terpretaretur. Deniq; observavimus ipsius Grotii confessionem, qui ad Luc. 24, 47. hoc vaticinium ad tempora N. Test. refert, & imprimis v. 9. è quo probat initium præconii Evangelici N. T. tempo- re fieri debuisse in Jerusalem.

## 40:2
Vers. 2.

COMPLETA EST MALITIA EJVS.) The interpreter wrote militia; i.e., his labor will soon reach its end.

If the interpreter wrote militia, why then did neither Sixtus V nor Clement VIII, Supreme Pontiffs, amend the same, but confirmed it with Papal and Apostolic authority? Therefore, the advocate of the Roman See could not have patronized him here: but he judged that the authentic text, which has Militia, was altogether to be preferred. Furthermore, it is not the labor of the Babylonian exile, but of Diabolical servitude, than which no militia is heavier, that is pointed out: For when such a heavy militia in Paul, even though reborn, through the sin ἐκπεριςατον, καὶ πϱοσκείμενον still remained, so that under the same, it is a wonder how much, he groaned and exclaimed, 'Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?' Rom. 7. How much more grievous is that to be considered in the state of sin, and under the power of darkness, before man is transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God, Col. 1, and before the human race had yet been freed from that perpetual servitude, of which Heb. 2:15 says that through fear of death we were subject to bondage all our lives, but we have been freed by Christ, who destroyed him who had the power of death. Paul is somewhat better here [in the] LXX: 'her humiliation is fulfilled.' Yet they do not fully exhaust the emphasis of the Hebrew word, which Blessed Luther expressed more correctly: 'That her warfare may have an end.' Which Brentius explains excellently on p. 536: 'warfare' in this place is to be understood as spiritual warfare, namely that which was to be undertaken by the people of God under the law against Satan. For that bodily warfare was indeed grievous, which the citizens of Jerusalem sometimes found it necessary to undertake for their country against external enemies. But more grievous was that to which the victorious Babylonians compelled the citizens of Jerusalem, and by which they were led into captivity. But by far the most grievous of all was that which was exercised in the divine law against the enemy Satan. For the law of God was given and imposed upon men, that they might fight a good warfare in it, that they might fulfill it, that they might satisfy it, so that they might conquer death and Satan, and obtain eternal life. 'Keep,' he says, 'my laws and judgments, which if a man does, he shall live in them.' And Christ says, 'Do this, and you shall live.' But when men look into the law, and compare their own strength to it, then it is so far from the case that they can satisfy its will and obtain righteousness and life from it, that they rather recognize their sins from it, and understand and even feel that they are subject to eternal death. 'Through the law,' says Paul, 'is the knowledge of sin.' And, 'The law kills.' Thus it happens that in this warfare of the law, Satan our adversary conquers us and carries off the victory from us! But with this victor, what is more miserable, what more calamitous for us? For we are not only afflicted by the servitude of bodily curses, but also by the captivity of eternal punishments in the fire of hell. Wherefore, if the political warfare and its inconveniences are compared to this, the difference between them is so great that heaven and earth do not seem to be more distant from each other. But be of good courage, excellent citizens of Jerusalem. It is not all over for your salvation. For the time will come when this most grievous warfare shall be completed and finished. And this is so certain that I can deservedly say that this warfare is already completed and finished. Even if your descendants are led away into Babylonian captivity, and the city of Jerusalem is devastated, yet Christ the Son of God, who is promised to the Patriarchs, will not be captured by the Babylonians, nor will he be destroyed by them. For he will come in his own time, and will take away from his Church—indeed, he is even now taking away from all who believe in him—the yoke of such grievous warfare. Brentius teaches that Christ does this: First, while he exonerates the Church from the curse of the law. Then, when he conquers Satan and frees the Church from this warfare, by which it fights for Satan under the law. Therefore, the warfare of the flesh and of sin, by which we fight for our flesh at the instigation of Satan, is also included. Whence Flacius in Clav. Script. Col. 649. You might perhaps more correctly understand by 'warfare' the kingdom of the evil conscience of the old Adam, and of Satan himself over men, from whom they were then to be redeemed through the Messiah. It is certainly not without cause that this warfare is joined with sins. Those who understand 'warfare' as the burden of various laws which weighed upon the Jews, and bring in here the passages where the word צבא (warfare) is used for the functions of men and women serving in the temple (Exod. 38:8, Num. 34:14, 1 Sam. 2:22), do not exhaust the sense of the phrase. Meanwhile, you would not be wrong to say that this burden, by which various acts of worship (λατρείαι) pressed upon the Jews, is also included; on which see Blessed Hieronymus Weller.

Verse same. SHE HAS RECEIVED FROM THE HAND OF THE LORD DOUBLE FOR ALL HER SINS.) That is, as much as God judges to be enough.

He does not indicate whether he understands benefits or punishments. For Cyril and Jerome understood these, but less appropriately. Whence Jerome is here corrected by Blessed Luther. Nor does Grotius explain those 'doubles' correctly. For others prove that the gravity and multiplicity are rather noted by this phrase used in Scripture, from Jer. 16:18, 1 Tim. 5:17, Rev. 18:6. Blessed Luther understands those 'doubles' as the remission of sins, and the finished warfare or the abrogation of the law, under whose power and burdens the warfare is truly anxious and groaning. I like the explanation of Blessed Brentius, who excellently teaches on p. 538 that distinct benefits are indicated here. 'The Church,' he says, 'is not only exonerated from the warfare of the law, nor does it only receive the expiation of sins, but it also receives from the hand of the Son of God DOUBLE for all its sins.' And what, I ask, are those doubles which are rendered for sins? Are they the punishments which the law threatens for sins? But here benefits are enumerated, not punishments. Are benefits, therefore, repaid by the Son of God for sins? The Son of God does not indeed bestow benefits upon his Church on account of sins, to which punishments rather than benefits are owed, but what he says, that the Church receives from the hand of the Lord double for its sins, is clearly that which Paul, writing to the Romans, says: 'Not as the sin,' he says, 'so also is the gift. For if by the sin of one many died, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which was of the one man Jesus Christ, has abounded unto many.' And soon after: 'Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.' For the Son of God embraces Jerusalem, or the Church, with such clemency that even if you gather ALL the sins of men into one heap, yet he himself gathers into his Church far greater, and twice as many, benefits. For He does not only remit all his sins, but also grants him all His own righteousness, so that he may be able to trust in it before the tribunal of God no otherwise than if he himself had performed and fulfilled it by his own works. That which the law, says Paul, could not perform, in that part in which it was weak through the flesh, this God performed by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and condemned sin for sin, that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, that is: The perfect righteousness which the law demands of us is granted to us through Christ, who was made a victim for our sins, so that we possess as much righteousness in Christ through faith as is demanded by the law. What is more excellent than this benefit, what is even more desirable? And yet this is not yet the end of the benefits of the Son of God. For He also adds this benefit, that He co-opts His Church as a co-heir of all His heavenly inheritance. For those who truly believe in Christ are not only reckoned righteous before God, but are also adopted as children of God and as brothers of Christ. But if children, says Paul, then also heirs. Heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs of Christ. And they receive this benefit not from the hand of men, or from the merit of their own works, but they receive it from the hand of the Lord, that is, on account of the Son of God through faith. But what can be thought of that is greater than this benefit, what more august than it? This certainly is truly to receive from the Son of God benefits twice as great as all sins are. And thus others explain the double [benefits] as στέρησιν τꭣ κακꭣ ϗ θέσιν τꭣ καλꭣ, the abolition of evil and the bestowing of good: or grace and glory from Psalm 84:11, grace in the militant Church, glory in the triumphant. Justice, life, and eternal salvation. To some, this phrase here, and in Isa. 61:7, seems taken from the rite of the Old Testament, by which the firstborn received a double portion upon entering into an inheritance (Deut. 21:27); because the people of God, or the Church, is considered as the firstborn (Ex. 1:23), they judge that a portion of the heavenly inheritance is promised to it, ζωὴν καὶ περισσὸν, life and abundance (John 10:10).

But Musculus objects in vain here, that because it is added FOR HER SINS, it should be understood as obtaining the punishments which sins deserve. For it is not necessary to understand those words as referring to a meritorious cause, since they can be taken in the sense of exchange, to exaggerate the immense grace of God, because in place of sins He confers upon us double in Christ; or also τελικῶς, that for the sake of abolishing sins, so that they may not condemn us before God, we may obtain double.

But Brentius provides reasons why the Prophet speaks in the past tense—WARFARE IS ACCOMPLISHED: iniquity is pardoned, she has received from the hand of the Lord double—which are to be carefully observed not only here, but in other prophecies as well. He does this for two reasons: one is that this form of speaking signifies the certainty of this promise. For although what is promised is still to be fulfilled in the future, it is nevertheless as certain as if it were already fulfilled in reality. The other is that although in those times when Isaiah preached these things, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, had not yet come in the flesh, those who then believed in the One to come were no less partakers of His benefits than if He had already arrived and completed His course in these lands.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

COMPLETA EST MALITIA EJVS.) Scriptit inter- pres militia; i. e. labor ejus finem accipiet brevi.

Si interpres scripsit militia, cur ergo neq; Sixtus V. neq; Clemens IIX. PP. RR. eundem emendarunt, sed autoritate Papali & Apostolica confirmarunt? Non ergo advocatus Romanæ sedis hic ei patroci- nari potuit: sed pręferendũ textum authenticum, qui Militiam habet, omnino censuit. Cæterum non labor exilii Babylonici, sed servitutis Diabolicæ, quo gravior nulla est militia, indigitatur: Quum e- nim tam gravis militia in Paulo etiam renato per peccatum ἐκπεριςατον, καὶ πϱοσκείμενον reliqua adhuc fuerit, ut sub eadem, mirum quantum, gemeret & exclamaret, miser ego homo, quis me liberabit à corpore mortis hujus Rom. 7. quanto gra- vior illa censenda in statu peccati, & sub potestate tenebrarum, antequam homo transferatur in re- gnum Filii Dei Col. 1. & antequam adhuc libera- tum fuit genus humanum à servitute ista perpetua, de qua Ebr. 2, 15. quod timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxii fuerimus servituti, à Christo autem liberati sumus, destructo illo, qui mortis habebat imperium. Paulo melius hic LXX. ἐπλήσθη ἡ ταπείνωσις αὐ- τῆς. Nondum tamen plene emphasin Ebrææ vocis exhauriunt: quam rectius expressit B. Lutherus: Daß ihre Ritterschafft ein Ende habe. Quod egre- gie explicat Brentius p. 536. militia hoc loco intelli- genda est pro spirituali militia, videlicet pro eo, quæ populo Dei suscipienda erat in lege adversus Satanam. Nam gravis quidem erat ea corporalis militia, quam necesse habebant cives Hierosolymitani aliquoties pro patria adversus externos hostes suscipere. Gravior au- tem erat ea, ad quam victores Babylonii cogebant ci- ves Hierosolymitanos, & qua hi ad captivitatem ad- ducebantur. Sed longe omnium gravissima erat il- la, quæ in lege divina adversus hostem Satanam exer- cebatur. Lex n. Dei data est, & imposita hominibus, ut in ea militent bonam militiam, ut impleant eam, ut satisfaciant ei, quo vincant mortem & Satanam, & consequantur æternam vitam. Custodite, inquit, leges meas & Judicia, quæ faciens homo vivet in eis Et Christus ait, hoc fac, & vives. Sed cum homines intuentur in legem, & conferunt ad eam vires suas, tunc tantum abest, ut queant voluntati ejus fatisface- re, & consequantur ex ea justitiam ac vitam, ut po- tius agnoscant ex ea peccata sua, & intelligant ac e- tiam sentiant se æternæ morti obnoxios. Per legem, inquit Paulus, agnitio peccati. Et, Lex occidit, Itaq; fit, ut in hac legis militia Satan adversarius no- ster vincat nos, & reportet à nobis victoriam! Hoc autem victore, quid nobis miserius, quid calamito- sius? Non enim affligimur tantum servitute corpora- lium maledictionum, sed etiam captivitate æterno- rum suppliciorum, in gehenna ignis. Quare si poli- ticæ militiæ & incommoda ejus ad hanc conferantur, tantum est inter eas discrimen, ut cælum & terra non magis inter se distare videantur. Sed bono animo sitis optimi cives Hierusalem. De vestra salute non est conclamatum. Veniet enim tempus, quo hæc tam gravis militia compleatur, & finiatur. Quod & tam certum est, ut merito dicere possim eam militiam jam completam & finitam esse. Etsi etiam posteri vestri abducentur in captivitatem Babylonicam, & urbs Hierusalem devastabitur, tamen Christus filius DEI, qui est Patriarchis promissus, non capietur à Babylo- niis, nec delebitur ab eis. Veniet enim suo tempore, & tollet ab Ecclesia sua, imo nunc tollit ab omnibus cre- dentibus in eum, jugum tam gravis militiæ. Quod Christum facere docet Brentius; Primo dum exone- rat Ecclesiam maledictione legis. Deinde cum vin- cit Satanam & liberat Ecclesiam ab hac militia, qua sub lege militat Satanæ. Proinde & militia carnis, & peccati, qua militamus carni nostræ insti- gante Satana, comprehenditur. Unde Flacius in Clav. Script. Col. 649. Possis forte rectius per mi- litiam regnum malæ conscientiæ veteris Adami, & Satanæ ipsius super homines intelligere, à quibus per Messiam redimendi tunc forent. Non sane sine causa cum peccatis militia illa conjungitur. Qui mili- tiam intelligunt onus variarum legum, quod incu- buit Judæis, & huc conferunt loca, quibus verbum צבא militare, de functionibus virorum & mulie- rum templo servientium usurpatur Exod. 38. vers. 8. Numer. 34. vers. 14. 1. Sam. 2. vers. 22. sensum phra- seos non exhauriunt. Interim comprehendi etiam illud onus, quo variæ λατρείαι premebant Judæ- os, non male dixeris, quo de B. Hieran. Wellerus vi- deatur.

Vers. eod. SUSCEPIT DE MANV DOMINI DVPLICIA PRO OMNIBUS PECCATIS SUIS.) Id est, tantum quantum Deus satis esse judicat.

Non indicat, beneficiane, an supplicia intel- ligat. De his enim Cyrillus & Hieronymus, sed minus commode intellexere. Unde Hieronymus hic castigatur à B. Luthero. Neque recte illa du- plicia explicat Grotius. Nam gravitatem & mul- tiplicitatem alii potius phrasi Scripturæ usitatâ ita notari probant è Jerem. 16, 18. 1. Tim. 5, 17. Apoc. 18, 6. B. Lutherus duplicia illa intelligit de remissio- ne peccatorum, & finitam militiam seu abrogatio- nem legis, sub cujus vi & oneribus se exercere & ge- mere vere anxia est militia. Placet B. Brentii ex- plicatio, qui distincta hic beneficia indigitari, exi- mie docet p. 538. Non exoneratur tantum Ecclesia militia legis, inquit, nec accipit tantum expiationem peccatorum, verum etiam accipit de manu Filii Dei DUPLICIA pro omnibus peccatis suis. Ecque, obsecro, sunt illa duplicia, quæ pro peccatis redduntur? Num sunt supplicia, quæ lex peccatis minatur? At hic enumerantur beneficia, non supplicia. Num er- go pro peccatis rependuntur à Filio Dei beneficia! Non confert quidem filius Dei beneficia in Ecclesiam suam, propter peccata, quibus magis supplicia quam benefi- cia debentur, sed quod dicit, Ecclesiam suscipere de manu Domini duplicia pro peccatis suis, hoc plane il- lud est, quod Paulus ad Romanos scribens: Non ut peccatum, inquit, ita & donum. Nam si unius pec- cato multi mortui sunt, multo magis gratia Dei, & donum per gratiam, quæ fuit unius hominis Jesu Christi, in multos exuberavit. Ac mox: Ubi exuberavit peccatum, ibi magis exuberavit gra- tia. Filius enim DEI tanta clementia comple- ctitur Hierusalem seu Ecclesiam, ut etiamsi con- feras OMNIA hominum peccata in unum acer- vum, tamen ipse confert in Ecclesiam suam longe ma- jora, & duplo plura beneficia. Non enim tantum remittit ei omnia peccata, sed etiam donat ei omnem suam justitiam, ut possit ea coram tribunali Dei non aliter confidere quam si ipsa eam operibus suis præsti- tisset & implevisset. Quod lex, inquit Paulus, præsta- re non potuit, ea parte, qua imbecillis erat per car- nem, hoc Deus proprio filio misso in similitudine carnis peccatricis præstitit, ac de peccato conde- mnavit peccatum, ut justificatio legis impleretur in nobis, h. e. Quam perfectam justitiam lex à nobis exigit, donatur nobis per Christum, factum pro pecca- tis nostris victimam, ut tantum justitiæ possideamus in Christo per fidem, quantum à lege exigitur. Quid hoc beneficio excellentius, quid etiam optabilius? Et tamen hic nondum est beneficiorum filii DEI finis. Nam & hoc beneficium addit, quod cooptat Ecclesiam suam in cohæredem omnis suæ cælestis hæreditatis. Qui enim vere credunt in Christum, non reputantur tantum justi coram Deo, sed etiam adoptantur in Fi- lios Dei, & in fratres Christi. Si autem filii, inquit Paulus, ergo & hæredes. Hæredes quidem Dei, cohæredes autem Christi. Et hoc beneficium accipi- unt non de manu hominum, aut ex merito suorum operum, sed accipiunt illud de manu Domini, hoc est, propter filium Dei per fidem. Quid autem & hoc beneficio amplius, quid eo augustius excogitari potest? Hoc certe vere est à Filio Dei duplo majora beneficia accipere, quam sint omnia peccata. Atq; ita duplicia explicant alii στέρησιν τꭣ κακꭣ ϗ θέσιν τꭣ καλꭣ mali abolitionem, & boni elargitionem: vel gratiam & gloriam è Psalm. XXIV. vers. 12. gratiam in Ecclesia militante, gloriam in triumphante: Justitiam, vitam, & salutem æternam. Nonnullis phrasis ista hic, & Esa. 61, 7. desumta videtur ex ritu Vet. Test. quo in hæreditate adeunda primogenitus duplam partem accipiebat Deut. 21, 27. quia popu- lus Dei seu Ecclesia pro primogenito habetur Ex. 1, 23. ideo de illa portionem hæreditatis cœlestis ipsi promitti censent, ζωὴν καὶ περισσὸν vitam & a- bundantiam Joh. 10, 10.

Frustra autem hic objicit Musculus, quod ad- datur pro PECCATIS suis, ut obtineat supplicia, quæ peccata merentur, intelligi. Nam verba illa non est necessum de causa meritoria intelligere, cum sensu commutationis accipi possint, ad exaggerandam immensam Dei gratiam, quod loco peccatorum conferat nobis duplicia in Christo; vel etiam τελι- xῶς quod propter peccata abolenda, ne nos illa con- demnent coram Deo, duplicia consequamur.

Cur autem in præterito loquatur Propheta, COMPLETA est militia: dimissa est iniqui- tas, suscepit de manu Domini duplicia, causas reddit Brentius, quæ non hic tantum, sed in aliis etiam Pro- phetiis observandæ probe sunt. Facit hoc duabus de causis, una est, quod hæc loquendi forma significet hujus promissionis certitudinem. Etsi enim, quod promittitur, adhuc futurum est, ut impleatur, tamen tam certum est, quam si esset jam reipsa impletum. Altera est, quod etsi his temporibus, quibus Esaias hæc concionatus est, filius Dei, Jesus Christus non- dum venerat in carnem, tamen qui tum crediderunt in venturum, non minus fuerunt participes beneficio- rum ejus, quam si jam advenisset, & cursum suum in his terris complevisset.

## 40:3
Verse 3. THE VOICE OF ONE CRYING.) Supply, 'it happens.' It refers to what had preceded, 'cry to her': where the Interpreter here says, 'call to her.' He says, therefore, what the Prophets ought to cry at that time.

The sentence is not correctly supplied so that an imperative is designated; since a prophecy is held here, and thus signifies a future event, it is or will be THE VOICE OF ONE CRYING. Therefore, it does not refer to the preceding 'cry to her'; but the discourse is about the peculiar voice of one crying, as the interpretation of the New Testament infallibly holds, namely, concerning the proclamation of John the Baptist. For God here addresses first, in a general way, the Apostles and Ministers of the New Testament, that they may comfort the people. But afterwards, He introduces St. John specifically, when He speaks of the voice of one crying μοναδικῶς (singularly). Add that a specific place is designated in which the voice of one crying is to be heard: namely, IN THE DESERT, which does not agree with the Grotian gloss. For the Prophets were not commanded to cry in the desert: but John is foretold as crying in the desert, according to the unanimous explanation of the Evangelists. And although in the Hebrew text some refer the word במדבר not to the voice crying, but to the leveling because of the distinctive accent, it is nevertheless known that an accent does not always maintain its force, as is evident from the Zakeph-katon in the example of 2 Sam. 15:34, Isa. 5:30, Jer. 17:3, and even while that remains, the same sense is inferred. For it is predicted that he will cry where the way of the Lord was to be leveled. And therefore, with the LXX Interpreters, the holy Evangelists specifically observed here the place of the Johannine prediction. Add that the word itself במדבר (in the desert) also has a distinctive accent, by which it is distinguished from the following words. Nor are there lacking reasons why that voice had to be heard in the desert: partly because persons immediately raised up by God during corruptions of doctrine are accustomed to be separated in both manner and place of preaching from ordinary ministers (Amos 7); partly because the doctrine of John did not agree with the doctrine of the Pharisees and the learned in the law, who had occupied the temple and the synagogues; partly because it brought and predicted the destruction of the Levitical worship and the Hierosolymitan temple, and designated the conversion of the Gentiles, who were denoted by the desert; partly because he had to be distinguished from Christ even by this mark, whose the temple was, and who as Lord of the temple was to come to it (Mal. 3:2). Regarding the desert of the Gentiles, Jerome beautifully illustrates the whole passage at once: 'It must be noted,' he says, 'that the straight ways of the Lord and the paths of our God, the filling of the valleys and the humbling of the mountains and hills, and the correction of the crooked and the plains of the rough and rocky places, and the glory of the Lord and the salvation of our God are not preached in Jerusalem, but in the solitude of the Church, and in the desert multitude of the Gentiles, of which we read above: Rejoice, O desert that thirsts, let the solitude exult, and let it bloom like the lily; for this was a desert of the knowledge of God, and it was held by idols, humble in confession, erect in pride, rough and intractable in wildness.' But after the glory of the Lord appeared, and all flesh saw the salvation of God, everything was suddenly changed, and the way of the Lord was prepared, so that it appeared in the solitude of the glory of God, when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, and the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained upon Him: and the voice of the Father thundering from above was heard: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, hear him. And all flesh saw the salvation of God. Which is therefore called flesh, because it previously did not have the Holy Spirit. Of which the Lord also says: My Spirit shall not remain in those men, since they are flesh. But that flesh will see the salvation of God, of which He spoke the same through Joel: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy. Which John, who is the forerunner and precursor of the word of God, and is rightly called a voice, cried not only at that time, but even today in the desert of the Gentile churches, Masters cry out, so that we may make straight the ways and paths in our hearts for God, and be filled with mighty works and be inclined with humility, change the crooked into straight, turn the rough into soft, and thus deserve to see the glory of the Lord and the salvation of God.

Verse of the same.

IN THE DESERT PREPARE THE WAY OF THE LORD.) Desert places are accustomed to be very uneven. Through mountains, valleys, and forests, where a King was to travel, pioneers were sent who would cut down trees, level valleys, and remove the obstacles of mountains. See what was said on Matt. 3:3. Thus also God wishes it to be said to the exiled Jews, that they should take away the evil habits which were delaying their restoration.

Latin:

Vers. 3. VOX CLAMANTIS.) Supple, fit. Respicit id quod præcesserat, clamate ad eam: ubi hic Interpres, ad- vocate eam. Dicit ergo, quid clamare debeant eo tempo- re Prophetæ.

Non recte suppletur oratio, ut imperativus de- signetur: quum Prophetia hic habeatur, adeoque res futura significet, vox CLAMANTIS EST vel erit. Non ergo ad præcedens respicitur: clama- te ad eam; sed de peculiari voce clamantis sermo est: ut infallibilis habet interpretatio N. T. nimirum de præconio Johannis Baptistæ. Alloquitur enim Deus hic primum generatim Apostolos, & Ministros N. Testamenti, ut consolentur populum. Postmodum vero introducit peculiariter S. Iohannem, cum de voce clamantis μοναδικῶς loquitur. Adde quod lo- cus proprius designetur, in quo vox clamantis ex- audienda sit: IN DESERTO nempe, quod non congruit glossæ Grotianæ. Non enim Prophetæ jubebantur in deserto clamare: Sed Johannes cla- matus in deserto prænunciatur, juxta Evangeli- starum unanimem explicationem. Et quanquam in Ebræo textu nonnulli vocem במדבר non ad vo- cem clamantem, sed ad complanationem propter ac- centum distinctivum referant, notum tamen est, non semper vim suam obtinere accentum, uti de Za- kephkato exemplo 2. Sam. 15, 34. Esa. 5, 30. Ier. 17, 3. constat, & manente etiam illo sensus tamen idem infertur. Nam idi clamare prædicitur, ubi com- plananda erat via Domini. Ideoque cum LXX. In- terpp. sancti Evangelistæ peculiariter hic observa- runt locum prædictionis Joanneæ. Adde quod etiam ipsa vox במדבר in deserto accentum distin- ctivum habeat, quo à sequentibus vocibus distin- guitur. Neque desunt causæ, cur in deserto vox il- la exaudiri debuerit, tum quia personæ immediate à Deo in corruptelis Doctrinæ excitatæ sejunctæ esse solent & modo & loco prædicandi à ministris ordinariis Am. 7. tum quia Doctrina Johannis non conveniebat cum doctrina Pharisæorum & le- gis peritorum, qui templum occuparant & Synago- gas: tum quia interitum cultus Levitici, & templi Hierosolymitani adferebat & prædicebat, conver- sionemque gentium, qui per desertum notaban- tur, designabat: tum quia distinguendus erat à Christo etiam hac nota, cujus erat templum, & qui ceu Dominus templi ad illud venire debebat Mal. 3, 2. De deserto gentilitatis Hieronymus pulcre, to- tum simul locum illustrans: Animadvertendum, inquit, quod rectæ viæ Domini & semitæ Dei nostri, impletio vallium & montium, colliumq; humiliatio & pravorum correctio, & asperorum rupiumq; cam- pestria, & gloria Domini & salutare Dei nostri non prædicetur in Hierusalem, sed in solitudine Ecclesiæ, & in deserta gentium multitudine, de qua supra legi- mus: Lætare deserta sitiens, exultet solitudo, & floreat quasi lilium, hæc enim deserta erat notitia Dei, & ab idolis tenebatur humilis in confessione, ere- cta in superbia, aspera & intractabilis in feritate. Sed postquam apparuit gloria Domini, & vidit omnis caro salutare Dei, cuncta repente mutata sunt, & via Domini præparata, ita ut appareret in solitudine glo- riæ Dei, quando baptizatus est Dominus in Jordane, & aperti sunt cæli, & Spiritus Sanctus in specie co- lumbæ descendit & mansit in eo: voxq; Patris desu- per tonantis audita est: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui, hunc audite. Et omnis ca- ro vidit salutare Dei. Quæ propterea appellatur caro, quia prius sanctum Spiritum non habebat. De qua dicit & Dominus: Non permanebit Spiritus meus in hominibus istis, quum carnes sunt. Illa autem caro videbit salutare Dei, de qua per Joël idem loquebatur, effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem, & prophetabunt. Quod non solum illo tempore clamabat Johannes, qui sermonis Dei præ- cursor & prævius, & recte vox appellatur, sed usque hodie in deserto gentilium ecclesiarum clamant Ma- gistri, ut rectas faciamus vias & semitas in cordibus nostris Deo, impleamurq; virtutibus & inclinemur humilitate, prava mutemus in recta, aspera vertamus in mollia, & sic gloriam Domini & salutare Dei vide- re mereamur.

Vers. eod.

IN DESERTO PARATE VIAM DOMINI.) Loca deserta solent esse valde inæqualia. Per montes, valles, silvas, qua Rex incedere debebat, mittebantur munitores, qui arbores cæderent, valles adæquarent, montium obstan- tia tollerent. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. 3, 3. Sic etiam De- us vult exsulantibns Judæis dici, ut auferant mores malos qui restitutionem ipsorum morabantur.

## 40:4
EVERY VALLEY SHALL BE EXALTED) Let it be exalted: that is, let it be leveled. Understand the following in the same way.

Regarding the evil morals of the exiled Jews delaying their restoration, these things are wrongly taken according to the letter, which speak openly of preparing the way of the Lord coming in the flesh and are explained by the Holy Scriptures. For who is that Lord, if not Christ the true Son of God; whom Brentius also wishes to be designated in the previous verse. Comfort my people, says your God. For He is our God Immanuel, Is. 7:14, and the faithful are His people, whom He acquired for Himself with His blood, Acts 20:28. The same is also pointed out in v. 5. And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, of which an explanation is added, and all flesh shall see the SALVATION of God. For we know this salvation of God to be the Messiah, both from other places in the O.T., Gen. 49, Ps. 14, Ps. 95, Ps. 119, Is. 42, ch. 49, and especially from the Canticle of Simeon, Luke 2. Nor is this exaltation of valleys and humiliation of mountains only commanded here: But it is also predicted prophetically: since divine imperatives in Evangelical oracles are accustomed to include or imply a promise and an effect, just as Grotius admits that the things which follow in v. 5 imply a promise; and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, etc. But that in his annotations on Luke 3:4 he wishes those things which are stated in the Prophet and Luke in the future tense to be explained by an imperative, so that, to be sure, that command understood of the return from Babylon might signify the power of God, while in the Baptist's ministry human obedience is simultaneously required, in that there appears Grotius's customary ψευδερμηνεία (false interpretation), who attaches diverse meanings to the same saying: so that in this passage valleys are said to be exalted and mountains humbled, both in the sense that all things are prepared by divine power for leading the people back from Babylon, and also that men are to prepare themselves by free obedience so that they may be freed from the spiritual slavery of sin and death: both of which explanations Grotius handed down, asserting at the same time with the Pelagians and Papists that the τό ἑκόσιον (voluntary nature) of the human will has its part in conversion, even though it is compared now to creation, now to resuscitation from death, in which actions the human will has no part. But Scripture uses those expressions in describing conversion for the purpose of teaching that the powers of free will are nothing, concerning which elsewhere. We see, however, from these Grotian glosses, how disparate the meanings are that he attributes to the same sentence, which is to twist and pervert Scripture at one's own whim. Blessed Selneccer elegantly gathers from this proclamation the distinction of John from the Prophets. By this voice, he says, John shows that he is greater than the Prophets. The remaining Prophets said, if he delays, wait. But John does not command to wait, but to meet the coming Lord with joy, just as if the arrival of some King to his subjects is announced, the road is immediately prepared and adorned, so that it may be shown that the King is near, and the people may rejoice with the highest joy at his meeting. Moreover, the way of the Lord was to be prepared, not by an external leveling of a journey, as if there were talk about the ease of a journey, in the way that the Jews foolishly imagine that an easy journey, lacking all fatigue, is designated in the reduction of the Jews from the final captivity, from which Grotius does not depart much. Nor is it about a bare amendment of morals to a life that is honest and holy in external appearance: because these are human ways, as blessed Luther rightly says here, which we also see in some nations such as the Attic, Socrates, Xenophon, and others. The way of the Lord, therefore, is a manner of living and a divine life, so that He himself may live in us. If this way is to be prepared, let us thus cast away the presumption of righteousness and works, and let us acknowledge our sins. For although external crimes, adultery, fornication, thefts, etc., are also impediments on the way of the Lord, which it is necessary to remove, yet these are far greater and more serious: presumption and one's own righteousness. For they simply block the entrance to grace. Thus, therefore, the way is prepared, if we cast away these great rocks and those unmoved logs (I mean presumption and trust in works), and cling nakedly to receiving the double, with a simple confession of guilt. Therefore, let that preparation be by an internal change of mind and true repentance, of which, since there are two parts, Contrition and Faith, the interpreters wish the former to be designated by the humiliation of mountains and hills, and the latter by the exaltation of valleys, inasmuch as by the denunciation of divine wrath, the pride, depravity, and iniquity of human hearts, which lift themselves up like mountains, may be amended, and conversely, by the Evangelical promise concerning the free remission of sins and salvation to be obtained through Christ, the minds of the humble and poor in spirit, who are depressed like valleys, may be refreshed and raised up by heavenly consolation. He applies this to the sermon of John: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has approached, Wolfgang Musculus; The doctrine of repentance humbles mountains and hills, and makes straight the crooked and curved: that is: It amends the haughty, the depraved, and the iniquitous. The consolation of the kingdom of God, which is joined to the preaching of repentance, raises up the valleys, i.e.

consoles and refreshes the humble, the poor in spirit, and the abject. Christ is therefore to be received, as Brentius says in this place, not by leveling the physical mountains and hills of this world, but by uprooting the vices of minds, and correcting the impieties of hearts, and amending the depraved morals of life. Whence also John the Baptist rightly understood the meaning of these words, and proposed a commentary, as it were, when he says: Repent. And again, bear fruits worthy of repentance. And do not be of this mind, to say, We have Abraham as our father: And again, every tree not bearing good fruit will be cut down. And elsewhere he preaches the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins on account of Christ. Therefore, to repent and to believe the Gospel concerning the remission of sins on account of Christ is to level mountains and hills, and to rectify the crooked, so that we may receive Christ with due honor and enjoy his benefits. For a great and high and steep mountain is to trust in one's own righteousness, and to arrogate to one's own works the merits of eternal life. This is the arrogance which reaches even to heaven with its haughtiness: But this height and sublimity must be cast down and leveled, so that Christ may be reverently received. For one must not trust in the merits of one's own works, but only in the merit and righteousness of Christ. The highest mountain was when the Pharisees thought, we have Abraham as our father: But this mountain had to be cast down, the trust in external lineage had to be cast away, and trust had to be conceived only in Christ the Son of God, so that the fruit of his benefits might be perceived. On the contrary, however, the deepest valley and the most depraved and muddy path is to cast away the hope of one's salvation, to wallow in the mud of avarice, envy, lust, and other crimes. This valley must be leveled, and this muddy path must be purged, so that Christ may be reverently received. For repentance must be performed, sins must be acknowledged, hope must be conceived in Christ, through His Gospel. For thus it will come to pass that, with the valleys leveled and the ways cleared, Christ may walk and arrive without offense, and bring with Him all kinds of eternal benefits. And thus Cyril explains the way of salvation opened through Christ. Formerly, the excellent way was, so to speak, inaccessible to all men, and the path of evangelical conversation little trodden, because the mind of all was detained by worldly and earthly desires, and subjected to the flesh and its foul motions. But after He was made man, and flesh, according to the Scriptures, He abolished sin in the flesh, and demolished the principalities and powers and rulers of this world: He made for us a level way of piety, most fit for running, having nothing steep or raised on high, nothing hollow or downward, but rather leveled into plains. For all crooked things have been made straight.

Latin:

OMNIS VALLIS EXALTABITVR) Exaltetur: id est, complanetur. Sic accipe & sequentia.

De moribus malis exulantium Judæorum remo- rantibus restitutionem eorundem, perperam hæc κτ' τὸ ῥητὸν accipiuntur, quæ de via Domini, adveni- entis in carnem paranda aperte loquuntur & à S. S. explicantur. Quis enim ille Dominus, nisi Chri- stus Filius Dei verus; quem etiam versu priori desi- gnatum vult Brentius. Consolamini populum meum, dicit Deus vester. Ille enim est Deus noster Imma- nuel Es. 7, 14. & fideles sunt populus ejus, quem san- guine suo sibi acquisivit Act. 20, 28. Idem indigitatur quoque v. 5. Et revelabitur gloria Domini, cujus ἐπεξήγησις addita est, & videbit omnis caro SA- LUTARE Dei. Hoc enim salutare Dei Messiam esse novimus tum ex aliis V. T. locis Genes. 49. Psal. 14. Ps. 95. Ps. 119. Es. 42. c. 49. tum imprimis è Cantico Simeonis Luc. 2. Neque hic tantum imperatur hæc vallium exaltatio, & montium humiliatio: Sed præ- dicitur etiam προφητικῶς: quum imperativi divi- ni in Evangelicis oraculis promissione, & effectum includere, aut inferre soleant, quemadmodum fate- tur Grot. illa quæ sequuntur v. 5. promissionem infer- re; & revelabitur gloria Domini &c. Quod vero An- not. ad Luc. 3, 4. illa quæ apud Prophetam & Lucam futuro tempore enunciantur, per imperativum expo- ni vult, ut nempe imperium illud de reditu ex Baby- lonia acceptum Dei potentiam significet, in Bapti- stæ autem ministerio simul exigatur humanum obse- quium, in eo occurrit consueta Grotii ψευδερμηνεία, qui eidem dicto sensus diversos affingit: ut hoc lo- co valles exaltari, montes humiliari dicantur, tum hoc sensu, quod omnia divina virtute parata sint ad populum è Babylonia reducendum, tum etiam, quod homines libero obsequio se paraturi sint ad id, ut è spirituali servitute peccati & mortis liberen- tur: quam utramque explicationem tradidit Gro- tius simul cum Pelagianis & Papistis adserens, in con- versione suas partes habere humanæ voluntatis τό ἑκό- σιον, utut illa modo creationi, modo resuscitationi è morte comparetur, in quibus actionibus nullas partes habet humana voluntas. Sed Scriptura ideo illis utitur loquutionibus in conversione describenda, ut vires liberi arbitrii nullas esse doceat, de quo alias. Videmus autem ex istis glossis Grotianis, quam disparatos sensus eidem sententiæ tribuat, quod est, pro arbitrio Scripturam torquere ac per- vertere. Eleganter autem ex hoc præconio col- ligit B. Selneccerus distinctionem Johannis à Pro- phetis. Hac voce, inquit, Johannes ostendit se majo- rem esse Prophetis. Reliqui Prophetæ dixerunt, si moram fecerit, expectate. At Johannes non jubet expectare, sed venienti Domino occurrere cum gau- dio, perinde ac si Regis alicujus adventus ad subditos suos prænunciatur, statim via componitur, & ador- natur, ut Regem in propinquo esse ostendatur, & po- pulus in occursum ejus summo cum gaudio gestiat. Cæterum paranda via Domini erat, non externa itineris complanatione, ac si de itineris facilitate ser- mo esset, quemadmodum Judæi facile iter, & defa- tigatione omni carens in reductione Judæorum ex ca- ptivitate ultima designari, ineptiunt, à quibus non multum abit Grotius. Neque de nuda morum emen- datione ad vitam honestam & externa specie san- ctam: quia hæ sunt viæ humanæ, ut recte hic B. Lu- therus, quas etiam in aliquibus gentibus ut Attico, Socrate, Xenophonte & aliis videmus. Via Do- mini igitur est ratio vivendi, & vita divina, ut ipse in nobis vivat. Hæc via si paratur, sic abjiciamus præsumptionem justitiæ & operum, & agnoscamus peccata. Quanquam enim externa flagitia, adul- terium, scortatio, furta &c. etiam sint impedimenta in via Domini, quæ removere oportet, tamen hæc lon- ge majora & graviora sunt præsumptio & justitia propria. Præcludunt enim simpliciter gratiæ adi- tum. Sic igitur paratur via, si grandia hæc saxa, & immotos illos stipites (præsumptionem & fiduciam ope- rum dico) abjiciamus, & nudi hæreamus in suscipi- endis duplicibus, cum simplici confessione culpæ. Pro- inde sit illa præparatio interna mentis immutatione, veraq́; pœnitentia, cujus duæ quum sint partes, Con- tritio, & Fides, Interpp. illam per montium & col- lium humiliationem, hanc vero per vallium exalta- tionem designari volunt, siquidem denunciatione iræ divinæ, cordium humanorum, quæ instar montium se extollunt, superbia, pravitas, & iniquitas emen- detur, & vicissim promissione Evangelica de gratuita remissione peccatorum, & salute per Christum ob- tinenda, humilium pauperumq; Spiritu, qui instar vallium depressi sunt, mentes recreentur, & conso- latione cœlesti erigantur. Hæc applicat ad con- cionem Johannis: Pœnitentiam agite, Appropin- quavit enim regnum cælorum, Wolffg: Musculus; Doctrina resipiscentiæ humiliat montes & colles, & complanat prava & incurva: hoc est: Emendat ela- tos, pravos & iniquos. Consolatio regni Dei, quæ præ- dicationi resipiscentiæ adjungitur, erigit valles, h. e.

consolatur & recreat humiles pauperes Spiritu & ab- jectos. Excipiendus igitur Christus est, uti Brentius in h. l. non complanatis corporalibus hujus mundi montibus & collibus, sed exstirpatis vitiis mentium, & correctis impietatibus cordium, ac emendatis pra- vis vitæ moribus. Unde & Johannes Baptista recte intellexit sententiam horum verborum, & quasi com- mentarium proposuit, cum ait: Pœnitentiam agite. Et iterum, facite fructus dignos pœnitentiæ. Et ne sitis hac mente, ut dicatis, Patrem Abraham habe- mus: Ac rursus, omnis arbor non faciens fructum bo- num, excindetur. Et alias prædicat Baptismum pœ- nitentiæ in remissionem peccatorum propter Chri- stum. Agere ergo pœnitentiam, & credere Evangelio de remissione peccatorum propter Christum, est com- planare montes & colles, & rectificare curva, ut Chri- stum debito honore suscipiamus, & beneficiis ejus fru- amur. Magnus enim & altus, & præruptus mons est, confidere sua ipsius justitia, & arrogare suis operibus merita æternæ vitæ. Hæc est arrogantia, quæ elatione sua pertingit usq; ad cœlum: Sed hæc altitudo ac sub- limitas dejicienda est, & complananda, ut Christus re- verenter excipiatur. Non enim confidendum est me- ritis operum suorum, sed tantum merito & justitia Christi. Altissimus mons erat, cum Pharisæi cogita- bant, patrem Abraham habemus: Sed hic mons deji- ciendus erat, abjicienda erat fiducia externi generis, & concipienda fuit fiducia tantum in Christum Fi- lium Dei, ut fructus beneficiorum ejus perciperetur. E contra autem profundissima vallis & pravissimum ac lutosum iter est abjicere spem salutis suæ, volutari in cœno avaritiæ, invidiæ, libidinis, & aliorum scele- rum. Hæc vallis exæquanda, & hoc lutosum iter ex- purgandum est, ut Christus reverenter suscipiatur. Agenda enim est pœnitentia, agnoscenda sunt pecca- ta, concipienda est spes in Christo, per Evangelium ejus. Sic enim fiet, ut exæquatis vallibus & expurga- tis viis, Christus sine offensione incedat, & adveniat, atq; afferat secum omnia genera æternorum beneficio- rum. Atq; sic explicat Cyrillg de via salutis per Chri- stum patefacta. Olim omnibus, ut sic dixerim, homi- nibus inaccessa erat via eximia, & Evangelicæ con- versationis semita parum trita, quod mens omnium mundanis & terrenis esset detenta cupiditatibus, ac subjecta carnis, iisq; fœdis motibus. Postquam autem homo factus, atq; caro, secundum Scripturas, in carne abolevit peccatum, & principatus ac potestates, & rectores mundi hujus demolitus est: æquabilem nobis & ad currendum aptissimam viam pietatis effecit, ni- hil habentem acclive, vel in altum sublatum, nihil cavum aut deorsum, sed in campos magis complana- tum. Omnia enim obliqua facta sunt directa.

## 40:5
Vers. 5. AND THE GLORY OF THE LORD SHALL BE REVEALED.) If you do this, the help of God will appear, whatever men may eventually plot against it.

AND ALL FLESH SHALL SEE.) By the word flesh it is given to be understood that there is no strength in men when God wills this: the following words explain it more clearly.

That this discourse is not about the bodily help of God, which appeared in the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, but about a more illustrious manifestation of the glory of the Lord, is taught both by the preceding words concerning the times of the New Testament, and by the following, because He says that ALL flesh shall see the salvation of God, which was not fulfilled except under the New Testament. The word flesh, according to Jerome, designates the Gentiles, because they were called flesh, since they had not previously had the Holy Scriptures. Cyril explains the passage well, whose words it is helpful to transcribe: In what way, he says, and how does He say the glory will appear? For the only-begotten Word of God was and is, as existing God, and born of God the Father in an arcane manner in the substance of the Godhead, above every principality and power and throne, and dominions, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in the future, and He Himself is the glory of the Lord.

And we know his glory, even if we did not know it formerly: since, just as we also, having been made man by dispensation, he declared himself equal to God and the Father in power, operation, and glory, bearing all things by the word of his power, easily performing miracles, rebuking the creature, raising the dead, and accomplishing other wonderful things without labor. Therefore the glory of the Lord appeared, and all flesh beheld the salvation of God, namely of the Father. For he sent to us from heaven the Son as Savior and Redeemer. For since the law brought nothing to perfection, and typical sacrifices did not have the power of wiping away sins, we are perfected in Christ, and having been freed from every stain, we are honored with the spirit of adoption. This grace in him, as far as the scope and mind of the one saving is concerned, passed through all flesh, that is, through all men. For it is necessary to understand 'flesh' as man; if some seem to be devoid of this salvation, the word of the Prophet is nevertheless true, for the scope and purpose of the one honoring and wishing to save is attended to, not the sloth of those called is weighed. These latter things serve to prove the universal grace of God, which St. Cyril rightly asserted from this passage along with our churches.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET REVELABITUR GLORIA DOMINI.) Si hoc faciatis, apparebit Dei auxilium, quicquid tandem homines contra moliantur.

ET VIDEBIT OMNIS CARO.) Voce carnis dat intel- ligi, hominum nullas esse vires, ubi velit hoc Deus: Id sequentia clarius explicant.

Non de auxilo Dei corporali, quod in liberatione è captivitateBabylonica apparuit, sed de manifestatio- ne illustriori gloriæ Domini hic sermonē esse, tum an- tecedentia docent, de temporibus N. T. tum con- sequentia, quia OMNEM carnem visuram dicit sa- lutare Dei, quod impletum non est nisi sub N. T. Vox carnis juxta Hieronymum designat gentiles, quod caro appellati sint, quia prius S.S. non habue- rant. Explicat probe locum Cyrillus, cujus verba adscribere juvat: Quo pacto, inquit, & quomodo glo- riam dicit apparituram? Erat enim & est unigeni- tum Dei verbum, utpote Deus existens, & ex Deo Pa- tre, arcana ratione natus in Deitatis substantia, supra omnem principatum, & potestatem & thronum, & do- minationes, & omne nomen quod nominatur, non solum in hoc seculo, sed & in futuro, & ipse est gloria Domin.

& novimus nos gloriam ejus, etiamfi olim non nove- rimus: quando ficut & nos, factus homo dispensatio- ne, se potentia, operatione, gloria Deo & patri æqua- lem declaravit, omnia verbo potentiæ suæ ferens, mi- racula facile peragens, creaturam increpans, mor- tuos excitans, & cætera mirifica citra laborem perfi- ciens. Apparuit igitur gloria Domini, & contem- plata est omnis caro salutem Dei, scilicet Patris. Sal- vatorem enim & Redemptorem nobis misit de cælo Filium. Cum enim lex nihil consummaret, & typi- ca sacrificia non haberent vim abstergendi peccata, in Christo consummamur, & ab omni labe liberati, adoptionis spiritu honoramur. Hæc in illo gratia, quantum quidem ad scopum, & animum servantis, per omnem carnem meavit, id est, per omnes homines. Carnem enim intelligere oportet hominem, si quidam videantur hujus salutis expertes, verus tamen sic est Prophetæ sermo, scopus enim & propositum honoran- tis & servare volentis attenditur, non desidia vocato- rum expenditur. Quæ postrema ad universalem Dei gratiam probandam faciunt, quam cumEccle- siis nostris ex hoc loco asseruit recte S. Cyrillus.

## 40:6
Verse 6. ALL FLESH IS GRASS) Herbage. See what we said on Psalm 37:2. Add Psalm 103:15, above 15:6. AND ALL ITS GLORY AS THE FLOWER OF THE FIELD) So also the Greeks: καὶ πᾶσα δόξα ἀνθρώπου, as also 1 Peter 1:24; they read, of course, not חסדו, but הודו, and more correctly. THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD HAS BLOWN) Heat. James 1:11.

Latin:

Vers. 6. OMNIS CARO FOENUM) Gramen. Vide quæ diximus Psal. 37, 2. Adde Psalm. 103, 15. supra 15, 6. ET OMNIS GLORIA EJUS QUASI FLOS A- GRI) Sic & Græci: καὶ πᾶσα δόξα ἀνθρώπκ, ut & 1. Petr. 1, 24. legerunt nimirum non חסדו, sed הודו, & rectius. SPIRITUS DOMINI SUFFLAVIT) Æstus. Jac. 1. 11.

## 40:8
Verse 8. TRULY THE PEOPLE IS GRASS.) All people, as above, all flesh. BUT THE WORD OF OUR LORD REMAINS FOREVER) The predictions of the Prophets.

Two things must be seen here; the first is the accusation of the Hebrew text, that it now lies in error: because, namely, it was formerly written הודו and now is read חסדו. But whence will it be proven that it was formerly so written? The argument from the LXX translation is weak, as we have said quite often, even if St. Peter followed it as received. Because, namely, it made no difference to the sense. And why must הודו precisely be read, if it is to be rendered δόξα, could it not have been read כבוד? Therefore there is no certainty in it. But the Hebrew reading is both constant in all codices and does not oppose the Petrine allegation. For every good (because חסדו denotes his good) which flesh possesses, certainly embraces all the glory of the flesh. The other concerns the meaning of this proclamation. Grotius thinks that 'the word of the Lord' here denotes only the predictions of the Prophets, but whence is he going to prove that? Jerome more correctly unfolds the antithesis of FLESH and the word of the Lord here. The flesh is dried up and its beauty has fallen, because the Spirit of the fury of God and of his sentence has blown upon it, of him who bears the image of the earthly, and serves vices and luxury, and is grass and a passing flower. But he who has and keeps the image of the heavenly, that is the flesh which perceives the salvation of the Lord, which is daily renewed into knowledge according to the image of the creator, and receiving an incorruptible and immortal body, changes its glory, not its nature. But the word of our Lord, and those who are associated with the word, remain forever. Grotius is mistaken in that he refers these things only to the Jewish people, and to the predictions about the resolution of the captivity; for they sound generally about all men: All flesh is grass, and lest anyone perhaps exclude the people of Israel, whose were the promises of glory and the distinguished axioms (Rom. 9), he makes mention of it specifically. But he speaks about men, such as they are by their nature after the fall; for thus they are flesh with all their goods. And what word he understands is most clearly explained by Peter, certainly not the word about the resolution of the captivity, which looked to certain times and a certain people; but the word of the Gospel, which was announced especially by the Apostles, therefore bringing in the words of the Prophet he adds in 1 Epistle 1: 'And this is the word which has been evangelized to you': which is so firm that heaven and earth indeed are going to pass away, but this shall not pass away, but remain eternally, so powerful that, although by nature we are like hay and grass, with all the goods which we have by nature, through the virtue and efficacy of this word we live eternally and obtain eternal glory, and those who are born flesh from flesh are reborn through this word, as if from an incorruptible seed, to eternal life and glory. And this is the sum of the proclamation which is enjoined upon the teachers of the word, that they should preach and announce both the native corruption of men, ἀδυναμίαν, infirmity, vanity, and fleetingness, and the divine virtue of the word of God and the grace of regeneration to eternal life, and the salvation which we have through Christ in the word of the Gospel: which Brentius teaches was said specifically here to John, and how that was done by John, because that 'AND HE SAID' (verse 6) seems to be referred to the herald in the desert, when no mention of another precedes. For when John said to the Pharisees, 'Brood of vipers, etc.' and 'Do not say we have Abraham as our father,' he says nothing else than what was prescribed to him by the Prophet, that all flesh, and the very people of Israel themselves, were grass and a flower. With the Baptist: 'The Father loves the Son, and has handed over all things into his hand: He who believes in the Son has eternal life': That is the same thing that Isaiah says, 'the word of the Lord remains forever.' But any herald can be understood here: 'A voice was saying cry,' or 'preach,' whoever, namely, you are a herald, and whose duty it is to preach. For that name is contained and included in the word. Here, therefore, he answers, or asks: 'AND HE SAID,' any herald indefinitely, or whoever's ears that voice sounds into. For it is imagined, as it loves to happen in such dialogisms, as if someone is present, hearing that voice. The Vulgate wrongly rendered it in the first person, 'AND I SAID,' when in the source the third is held, וְאָמַר 'and he said.' 'What shall I cry!' etc. For this is the theme and subject matter of all heralds, to announce human misery, which is from the fall, and divine mercy, which is exhibited in Christ through the word of the Gospel; we do not deny that those things which are commanded to be preached in general about human misery are to be accommodated specifically to the Jewish people, for whose sake these things were inspired in the Prophet, inasmuch as he was sent to them, whose salvation God desired to be procured through him, and to whom, therefore, he was also manifesting the Messiah here in a peculiar way. And Grotius himself acknowledges that words placed indefinitely, e.g., 'the people is truly grass,' are to be explained universally: indeed, he provides this exegesis: 'every people, all flesh.'

Latin:

Vers. 8. VERE FOENUM EST POPULUS.) Omnis populus, ut supra, omnis caro. VERBUM AUTEM DOMINI NOSTRI MANET IN ÆTERNUM) Prædicta Prophetarum.

De Duobus hic videndum; Primum est textus Ebræi accusatio, quod is nunc in mendo cubet: quia sc. olim scriptum fuerit הודו nūc legatur חסדו. Sed unde olim ita scriptum fuisse probabitur? Argu- mentum è LXX. translatione infirmum est, uti sæ- pius diximus, etsi eam sequutus fuerit ceu rece- ptam S. Petrus. Quia sc. ad sensum nihil intererat. Et cur הודו præcisè legendum, si reddi debeat δό- ξα, annon legi potuit כבוד. Nulla ergo in eo cer- titudo. At lectio Ebræa & constans est in omnibus Codd. & Petrinæ allegationi non adversatur. Omne enim bonum (quia חסדו bonum ejus notat) quod caro possidet, complectitur utique omnem carnis gloriam. Alterum concernit sententiam hujus con- cionis. Verbum Domini tantum Prophetarum præ- dicta hic notare censet Grotius, sed unde id proba- turus est; Rectius antithesin CARNIS, & verbi Domini hic evolvit Hieronymus. Exsiccata est ca- ro & cecidit pulchritudo, quia Spiritus furoris Dei atq; sententiæ flavit in ea, ejus qui portat imaginem terreni, & servit vitiis atq; luxuriæ, fænumq; est & flos præteriens. Qui autem habet atq; custodit ima- ginem cælestis, illa caro est, quæ cernit salutare Domi- ni, quæ quotidie renovatur in cognitionem secundum imaginem creatoris, & incorruptibile atq; immortale corpus accipiens, mutat gloriam, non naturam. Ver- bum autem Domini nostri, & hi qui verbo sociati sunt, permanent in æternum. Fallitur in eo Grotius, quod ad populum solum Iudaicum hæc referat, & ad prædictiones de captivitatis solutione; Nam ge- neraliter sonant de omnibus hominibus: Omnis ca- ro gramen, & ne quis forte populum Israël, cujus e- rant promissiones gloriæ, & insignia axiomata Rom. 9. excipiat, peculiariter ejus mentionem fa- cit. Sed de hominibus loquitur, quales natura sua sint post lapsum; sic enim caro sunt cum omnibus bonis suis. Et quale verbum intelligit, clarissime explicatur à Petro, non certe verbum de solutione captivitatis, quod ad certa tempora, certumque po- pulum spectabat; Sed verbum Evangelii, quod præcipue ab Apostolis annunciatum est, ideo ad- ducens verba Prophetæ addit 1. Epist. 1. Hoc autem est verbum, quod Evangelizatum est vobis: quod ita firmum est, ut cœlum & terra quidem transitura sint, hoc autem non transeat, sed æternum maneat, ita potens, ut cum natura nos simus instar fœni & graminis, cum omnibus bonis, quæ natura habe- mus, per hujus verbi virtutem & efficaciam æternum vivamus & æterna gloria potiamur, & qui caro ex carne nati sunt, renascantur per hoc verbum, tanquam ex semine incorruptibi- li, ad vitam & gloriam æternam. Atque hæc est summa præconii, quod injungitur verbi Doctori- bus, ut nempe cum nativam hominum corruptio- nem, ἀδυναμίαν, infirmitatem, vanitatem & fuga- citatem, tum divinam verbi Dei virtutem & gra- tiam regenerationis ad vitam æternam, ac salutis, quam per Christum in verbo Evangelii habemus, præ- dicent & annuncient: quod peculiariter hic dictum esse Johanni, & quomodo à Johanne id factum sit, docet Brentius, quia illud & DIXIT vers. 6. ad præ- conem in deserto, quum nulla alterius mentio præ- cedat, referendum videtur. Quum enim Johan- nes ad Pharisæos, Genimina, inquit, viperarum &c. Item ne dicatis patrem habemus Abrahamum, nihil aliud dicit, quam quod à Propheta ei præscriptum est, Omnem carnem, ipsumque etiam populum Israëles- se gramen & florem. Cum Baptista: Pater diligit Fi- lium, & omnia tradidit in manum ejus: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam: Idem illud est, quod Esaias dicit, verbum Domini manet in æter- num. Sed subintelligi hic potest quivis præco: Vox dicebat clama, vel prædica, quicunque sc. præco es, & cujus id munus est prædicare. Nam nomen il- lud in verbo continetur, atque includitur. Hic er- go respondet, vel quærit: ET DIXIT, præco inde- finite quivis, vel cujuscunque auribus vox illa in- sonat. Fingitur enim, ut in talibus dialogismis fieri amat, ac si aliquis præsto sit, vocem illam exau- diens. Vulgata perperam reddidit, in prima per- sona, ET DIXI, cum in fonte tertia habeatur וְאָמַר & dixit. Quid clamabo! &c. Id enim the- ma & argumentum est quorumvis præconum, hu- manam miseriam, quæ à lapsu est, & divinam mise- ricordiam, quæ in Christo per verbum Evangelii ex- hibetur, annunciare, quæ vero in genere de huma- na miseria prædicari jubentur, speciatim accom- modari populo Judaico non inficiamur, cujus gra- tia hæc inspirata sunt Prophetæ, utpote ad quem ipse missus, cujus Salutem Deus per ipsum procu- ratam cupiebat, cui proinde hic etiam peculiariter Messiam manifestabat. Et agnoscit Grotius ipse verba indefinite posita, e. g. vere fænum est populus, universaliter explicanda esse: imo hanc tradit ἐξή- γησιν, omnis populus, omnis caro.

## 40:9
Vers. 9. GET THEE UP INTO THE HIGH MOUNTAIN)

See that you are heard from every side, whoever you are who will proclaim these words of mine in their own time.

O THOU THAT BRINGEST GOOD TIDINGS TO ZION.) That is, to Zion. Bringing good tidings

in Hebrew is מְבַשֶּׂרֶת, feminine in sound, common in sense, like קֹהֶלֶת. There is no need for us to take the feminine word in any other way than in the feminine gender. It is not one bringing good tidings to Zion that is designated, but Zion herself is established as the one bringing good tidings. The construction of the Hebrew words implies this, and it also appears from the feminine word itself. Get thee up into the high mountain, Thou, that bringest good tidings, O Zion, that bringest good tidings, O city of Jerusalem, lift up thy voice. For Zion and Jerusalem are commanded to promulgate the Gospel, so that it may be heard throughout the world. Therefore, she is commanded to preach from a high mountain, with a loud voice, which can be heard everywhere. Because as John was the voice of one crying in Judea, so Judea, and especially Zion, was bound to trumpet forth the voice of the Gospel, so that the sound of it might go out into all the earth. Which was done through the Apostles, and was completed in them. To this also goes the Commentary of Brentius, and the Paraphrase of Osiander: Now, says he here, the Prophet preaches about the publication of the Gospel, and figuratively addresses the Apostles, who were to make a beginning of the preaching of the Gospel at Jerusalem, i.e., You Apostles, make a beginning of preaching on Mount Zion, in the Jerusalem temple, nay, ascend the mountain of Zion, lift up your voice strongly, so that the sound of the Gospel may go out into all the earth, and that not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles may hear it, so that they may believe and be saved. Thus also Jerome: It is commanded to the choir of the Apostles, that they should ascend the heights for the preaching to all flesh, which is to see the salvation of God: and that they who are to speak of great things should dwell in high places. With which Cyril agrees in this place.

SAY TO THE CITIES OF JUDAH) That is, to the men dispersed from all the cities. Synecdoche.

Latin:

Vers. 9. SUPER MONTEM EXCELSVM ASCENDE TU)

Fac undique audiaris, quisquis hæc mea dicta suo tempore es prolaturus.

QUI EVANGELIZAS SION.) Id est, Sioni. Evangeli-

zans in Hebræo est, מְבַשֶּׂרֶת sono fœmininum, sensu commune, ut קֹהֶלֶת. Non opus est, ut vocem fœmininam aliter quam fœminino genere accipiamus. Non Evangelizans Sioni designatur, sed Sion ipsa Evangelizans con- stituitur. Id constructio verborum Ebræorum infert, & ex ipsa quoq; fœminina voce apparet. Su- per montem excelsum ascende, Tu, quæ Evangelizas, ô Sion, quæ Evangelizas ô civitas Hierusalem, exalta vocem tuam. Nam Zion, & Jerosolyma jubetur promulgare Evangelium, ut per orbem audiatur. Ideo de monte excelso, voce elata, quæ ubique audiri possit, prædicare jubetur. Quia ut Johannes in Ju- dæa vox erat clamantis, ita Judæa, & cumprimis Zion debebat vocem Evangelii ebuccinare, ut sonus ejusdem exiret in omnem terram. Quod per Apostolos factum est, in illis completum est. Quo abit etiam Commentarius Brentii, & Para- phrasis Ofiandri: Nunc, inquit hic, de publicatione Evangelii concionatur Propheta, & alloquitur figu- rate Apostolos, qui initium Jerosolymis facturi erant prædicationis Evangelii, q.d. Vos Apostoli initium facite prædicandi in monte Sion, in templo Jerosoly- mitano, imo afcendite in montem Sion, attollite forti- ter vocem, ut in omnem terram exeat sonus Evange- lii, idque audiant non modo Judæi, sed etiam gentes, ut credant & salventur. Sic etiam Hieronymus: Præ- cipitur Apostolorum choro, ut ad prædicationem o- mnis carnis, quæ visura sit salutare Dei, excelsa con- scendant: de magnisq́ue dicturi, in sublimibus commo- rentur. Cui consonat Cyrillus in h. l.

DIC CIVITATIBUS JUDA) Id est, hominibus disper- sis ex omnibus civitatibus. Συνεκδοχὴ.

## 40:10
Ver. 10.

HIS WORK BEFORE HIM) Metonymy: for work or works is put for the price of the work.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

OPUS ILLIUS CORAM ILLO) Μετωνυμία: nam o- pus sive opera posita est pro pretio operæ.

## 40:11
Ver. 11. HE SHALL GATHER THE LAMBS IN HIS ARM) The innocent.

HE SHALL CARRY THOSE THAT ARE WITH YOUNG) In the Hebrew: he shall lead. Virgil: -- this one also I scarcely lead, Tityrus, here among the dense hazels, for just now, having brought forth twins, the hope of the flock, she left them on the bare flint. By those that are with young, understand those who are weary with labor.

These things are not commanded to be said to those dispersed by the Chaldeans, but they look toward the times of the New Testament. Which the preceding things teach, concerning the proclamation of John v. 3, as also the subject matter of the discourse which is proposed here. For since the word of God remaining forever, by which God relieves our corruption and frailty, has as its object and principal argument the Messiah, the Savior of the human race, this subject matter is proposed here to him who ascends a high mountain and brings good tidings: Behold your God (who is the Messiah, Immanuel), behold the Lord God shall come in strength, and his arm (power) shall rule (against enemies, so that you may be delivered from their hand, Luke 1, 71, 74), behold his reward is with him, and his work before him: Which Christ acquires and offers at his first coming, but will distribute fully at his second coming: therefore these things are applied to him, Rev. 22, 12. Behold, he says himself, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to everyone according to his works. And to this Savior of ours likewise refer those things which follow in the Prophet: As a shepherd he shall feed his flock, he shall gather the lambs in his arm, and shall lift them in his bosom, he himself shall carry those that are with young. For this is that one Shepherd, of whom Ezek. 34, 25, 37. That good Shepherd, John 10, 11. This sense, which it is manifest flows from the very words and context, Jerome expressed: But what is that which they are commanded to say? Behold your God, whom you were always expecting: Behold, the Lord God shall come in strength, whom you despised as he came in humility. And his strength shall rule, he who had previously taken the form of a servant, being made obedient to the Father even unto death. Behold his reward is with him, and his work before him. According to what he himself says in the Gospel. The Son of man is also to come in the glory of his Father: and he shall render to everyone according to his work. As a shepherd he shall feed his flock. He, who is later to come in Majesty, first takes the form of a shepherd, and he says of himself: I am the good shepherd, and I know my own, and my sheep know me, and I lay down my life for my sheep.
