Of whom the Father speaks in Zechariah. I will strike the shepherd and the sheep shall be scattered. In his arm, he says, he shall gather the lambs: not the bulls, and rams, and he-goats, and great sheep, whom he threatens through Ezekiel, because they feed on milk and cover themselves with wool, and crush the weak flock, but the lambs still tender and raw in the infancy of Christ, who have recently been reborn in Baptism: of whom the Lord himself spoke to Peter: Feed my lambs. Whence also in the same Ezekiel it is written: I will raise up over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, my servant David, and he shall be their shepherd, and I the Lord will be their God, and David a prince in their midst. I the Lord have spoken; and I will make a covenant of peace with David. In which it is to be considered, that after much time, the gluttonous shepherds having been rejected, he says that our Lord, who is of the lineage of David, has been raised up, who may gather the lambs, and cherish them in his bosom, and he himself may carry the offspring of the sheep or the sheep with young on his shoulder. As we read in the Gospel, that he carried back on his shoulders the wandering sheep that remained from the usual flock to the folds. The sum therefore of the proclamation, which was to be announced to the cities of Judah by the Evangelists of the N.T. and the Apostles, is designated thus: Behold, your God is present, your Savior and your God Jesus Christ has been exhibited to you. Behold the Lord Jehovah shall come in strength, and his arm shall rule, i.e., preach that Jehovah the Lord himself has come into this world, who will exert his strength and power, as your God and Savior, about to overcome the Devil, death, and hell. Behold his reward is with him: his merit is so great that on account of it all believers are to obtain eternal life. This gracious reward he acquired for the human race, this he brings, and communicates through the word, this he has in his hand, so that he may confer it upon all who believe in him. His work, or works by metonymy, is the price of the work, which Grotius concedes. But the price of the work and labor of Christ is his merit. For the work or labor of Christ is his passion and death, by which he pays the ransom for our sins, the Father is so delighted by his work that in reward for it he grants to him that as many as believe in him may receive on his account the remission of sins, be reckoned righteous, be adopted as sons of God, and co-heirs of Christ. All of which the female evangelists of Zion and Jerusalem diligently explained to the cities of Judah. For from Zion and Jerusalem, after the Apostles preached there, these proclamations flowed out to the cities of Judah. Therefore with the word BEHOLD he commands those evangelizing to show as it were with the hand, as Cyril advises here, and to point out with the finger him who has been announced. But by the cities of Judah he designated not only those which were situated in Palestine, although this was to be announced to them first, but the universal Church of the N.T. is comprehended at the same time. For, as our Brentius beautifully says: In whatever place, in whatever region the Gospel of Christ is announced and received, which was first revealed of old in Jerusalem and the neighboring cities of the kingdom of Judah, there it is said to be a city of Judah, and a filial, as they call it, Church of the city of Jerusalem.

The things which are subjoined in this chapter, and constitute its other part from verse 12 to the very end, B. Brentius judges still to treat of Christ the eternal Son of God, and to set forth his majesty, wisdom and power, as well as his solicitude for his Church, so that on the occasion of the Babylonian captivity the people of God may be taught that, even if enemies are happy and the pious unhappy, the idolatry of the enemies is impious and abominable to God, but that the faithful, through the care of the Son of God, will attain eternal happiness. St. Cyril and St. Jerome, even though they think a new subject matter is proposed in this second part of the chapter, nevertheless show such a continuity with the preceding that they demonstrate from the coherence itself that these things are to be referred to the Son of God, which otherwise is undoubted among Christians from the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father. Lest anyone should think, says Jerome, that the calling of the Gentiles is difficult, and that all flesh should see the salvation of the Lord, and the Lord himself should come in strength, and render to everyone according to his work, like a shepherd he would cherish the lambs in his bosom, and he himself would carry those that are with young: his greatness is described, that nothing is impossible to him, and that he who created all things and is the creator of all, is able to accomplish even these things which, by comparison with them, are small. Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, etc. Cyril hands down this connection; From these things, which no mortal can attain to, and perform, nay perhaps not even the supernal and celestial powers, the (Prophet) attempts to show the excellent and incomprehensible force of divine wisdom. For the mystery of Christ is admirable, and this discourse of the τῆς ὀικονομίας is reckoned among the mysteries. Cyril nevertheless brings forward the opinion of others also, who explain those things which follow, who has measured the water with his hand, and the heaven with a span, concerning God the Father here, and adds: if anyone wishes to think this, he will offend nothing. Which opinion the blessed Osiander has embraced; There follows now ANOTHER DISCOURSE, which is directed against idolatry. In which, through the amplification of the divine majesty, it is shown how vehemently they rave who, when they make idols and worship them, by this very act think they are worshipping the true God. It is nevertheless certain through all these things that the first part of the chapter treats of the Messiah, and concerns his forerunner John. Since therefore not only the advent of the Messiah, but also the announcement of the same and of the Gospel in Sion, and by means of that is preached throughout the world among the Gentiles, the Prophet recalls the Jews from the idolatry, from which the Gentiles themselves, who served τοῖς μὴ φύσει οὖσι θεοῖς, were to be led to the recognition of the one true God in the time of the New Testament, lest among the Babylonians and wherever they may be dispersed, they be infected and contaminated by the same, and therefore he proposes the insanity of those who, in place of the immense God, who comprehends all the waters of the sea in the hollow of his hand, nay, embraces the whole heaven with a span, and sustains the whole globe of the earth with three fingers, who is truly great, nay, greatest, not in bulk, but in majesty and power, worship some little image, or attempt to express the majesty of God by the same, and wish to honor the best and greatest God with the worship of some image, which has nothing divine, and is far inferior not only to God, but even to man.

Latin:

Vers. 11. IN BRACHIO SVO CONGREGABIT AGNOS) Innocentes.

FŒTAS IPSE PORTABIT) In Hebræo: ducet. Virgilius: - - hanc etiam vix Tityre duco Hic inter densas corylos modo namque gemellos, Spem gregis, ab silice in nuda connixa reliquit. Per fœtas intellige, qui labore fessi sunt.

Non hæc dispersis à Chaldæis dici jubentur, sed tempora respiciunt Novi Testamenti. Quod ante- cedentia docent, de præconio Johannis v. 3. ut & ma- teria concionis, quæ hic proponitur. Nam quum verbum Dei in æternum manens, quo nostræ cor- ruptioni & fragilitati Deus subvenit, pro objecto & argumento præcipuo habeat Messiam Salvato- rem humani generis, super montem excelsum ascendenti, & Evangelizanti ea materia hic propo- sita est: Ecce Deus vester (qui Messias est, Imma- nuel) ecce Dominus Deus in fortitudine veniet, & brachium ejus (virtus) dominabitur (adversus ini- micos, ut de manu illorum liberemini, Luc. 1, 71. 74.) ecce merces ejus cum eo, & opus illius coram illo: Quæ acquirit & offert Christus primo adventu, plene autem distribuet adventu secundo: ideo de il- lo hæc usurpantur, Apoc. 22, 12. Ecce, inquit ipse, venio cito, & merces mea mecum est, reddere unicui- que secundum opera sua. Et hunc Salvatorem no- strum referunt pariter ea, quæ sequuntur apud Pro- phetam: Sicut pastor gregem suum pascet, in brachio suo congregabit agnos, & in sinu suo levabit, ipse por- tabit fœtas. Hic enim est Pastor ille unus, de quo Ezech. 34, 25. 37. Pastor ille bonus, Joh. 10, 11. Hunc sensum, quem ex ipsis verbis & contextu fluere ma- nifestum est, expressit Hieronymus: Quid est au- tem illud, quod jubentur dicere? Ecce Deus vester, quem semper expectabatis: Ecce, Dominus Deus in fortitudine veniet, quem contempsistis in humili- tate venientem. Et fortitudo ejus dominabitur, qui prius formam servi acceperat, factus Patri obediens usque ad mortem. Ecce merces ejus cum eo, & opus illius coram eo. Juxta quod ipse dicit in Evangelio. Venturus est etiam Filius hominis in gloria Patris sui: & reddet unicuiq; secundum opus suum. Sicut pastor gregem suum pascet. Iste, qui postea in Ma- jestate venturus est, prius formam pastoris accipit, & dicit ipse de se: Ego sum pastor bonus, & cognosco meas, & cognoscunt me oves meæ, & pono ani- mam meam pro ovibus meis. De quo in Zacharia Pater loquitur. Percutiam pastorem & oves disper- gentur. In brachio, inquit, suo congregabit agnos: non tauros, & arietes, & hircos, & grandes oves, qui- bus per Ezechiel comminatur, quod lacte vescantur & operiantur lanis, & infirmum conterant gregem, sed agnos adhuc tenellos & rudes in Christo infantia, qui nuper in Baptismo sunt renati: de quibus ipse Dominus loquebatur ad Petrum: Pasce agnos meos. Unde & in eodem Ezechiele scriptum est: Suscitabo super eos pastorem unum, & pascet eos, servum meum David, & erit pastor eorum, & ego Domi- nus ero eis in Deum, & David in medio eorum princeps. Ego Dominus locutus sum; & ponam cum David Testamentum pacis. In quo consideran- dum, quod post multa tempora David gulosis pastori- bus reprobatis, Dominum nostrum, qui est de stirpe Da- vid, suscitatum esse se dicat, qui congreget agnos, & foveat in sinu suo, & fœtus ovium sive fœtas oves ipse portet in humero suo. Sicut in Evangelio legimus, quod ovem erroneam & à grege solito remanentem, suis ad caulas humeris reportarit. Summa ergo præ- conii, quod civitatibus Judæ annunciandum ab Evangelistis N. T. & Apostolis erat, hæc designa- tur: Ecce, Deus vester adest, exhibitus est vobis Sal- vator & Deus vester Jesus Christus. Ecce Dominus Jehovah in fortitudine veniet, & brachium ejus do- minabitur, q. d. prædicate, Jehovam Dominum ipsum venisse in hunc mundum, qui fortitudinem ac potentiam suam exeret, ceu Deus & Salvator ve- ster, devicturus Diabolum, mortem & infernum. Ecce merces ejus cum eo: tantum est meritum ejus, ut propter illud omnes credentes vitam æternam consequuturi sint. Hanc gratiosam mercedem ac- quisivit humano generi, hanc affert, & communi- cat per verbum, hanc in manu sua habet, ut confe- rat omnibus, qui credunt in ipsum. Opus ejus, vel opera per metonymiam est pretium operæ, quod concedit Grotius. Operis autem & laboris Christi pretium est meritum ejus. Nam opus seu labor Christi est passio & mors ejus, qua persolvit λύτρον pro peccatis nostris, ejus opere ita delectatur Pater, ut in mercedem ejusdem concedat ei, ut quotquot in ipsum credunt, accipiant propter eum remissionem peccatorum, reputentur justi, ad- optentur in filios Dei, & cohæredes Christi. Quæ o- mnia Evangelizatrices Zion & Hierusalem, sedu- lo exposuerunt civitatibus Judæ. Nam è Zione ac Hierosolyma, postquam ibi prædicarunt Apostoli, hæc præconia dimanarunt ad civitates Judæ. Voce itaque ECCE jubet Evangelizantes manum velut ostendere, ut hic monet Cyrillus, & digito eum, qui prænunciatus est, indicare. Per civitates autem Ju- dæ non solum illas, quæ in Palæstina sitæ erant, de- signavit, etsi illis primum erat hoc annunciandum, sed universæ Ecclesiæ N. T. simul comprehendun- tur. Nam, ut pulchre Brentius noster: In quocunq; loco, in quacunque regione annunciatur & recipitur Evangelium Christi, quod primum olim in Jerusalem & finitimis urbibus regni Juda revelatum est, ibi di- citur esse civitas Juda, & filialis, ut vocant, Ecclesia urbis Hierusalem.

Quæ subjunguntur in hoc capite, ejusq; alte- ram partem constituunt à vers. 12. ad finem usq; de Christo æterno Dei filio adhuc agere, ejusq; majesta- tem, sapientiam & potentiam, nec non solicitudi- nem pro Ecclesia sua exponere, censet B. Brentius, ut occasione Babylonicæ captivitatis populus Dei doceatur, etsi hostes sunt felices, & pii infelices, idololatriam hostium impiam esse, Deoque abo- minabilem, fideles autem cura Filii Dei æternam felicitatem consecuturos. S. Cyrillus & S. Hie- ronymus, etsi novam in hac altera capitis parte ma- teriam proponi existiment, συνέχειαv tamen ita o- stendunt cum præcedenti, ut hæc ad Filium Dei re- ferenda esse, quod alias ex ὁμοουσία Filii cum Patre penes Christianos indubium est, è cohærentia ipsa ostendant. Ne quis putaret, inquit Hieronymus, difficilem esse vocationem gentium, & quod omnis ca- ro videret salutare Domini, & ipse Dominus veni- ret in fortitudine, & redderet unicuique secundum opus suum, instarᾶ, pastoris agnos foveret in sinu, & fœtas ipse portaret: describitur illius magnitudo, quod nihil ei impossibile sit, & qui universa condiderit, creatorq; sit omnium, etiam hæc quæ comparatione eorum parva sunt, valeat perpetrare. Quis mensus est pugillo aquas &c. Cyrillus hanc tradit conne- xionem; Ex his, quæ nullus mortalium assequi po- test, & præstare, imo fortassis nec supernæ cœlestesque potestates, conatur (Propheta) ostendere, præstan- tem & incomprehensam vim divinæ sapientiæ. Ad- mirabile est enim Christi mysterium, & inter arcana recensetur hic sermo τῆς ὀικονομίας. Adducit tamen Cyrillus aliorum etiam sententiam, qui illa, quæ se- quuntur, quis mensus est manu aquam, & cœlum palmo, de Deo Patre hic explicent, & addit: hoc si quis sentire velit, nihil offendet. Quam sententiam amplexus est B. Osiander; Sequitur nunc ALIA CONCIO, quæ directa est adversus idololatriam. In qua per amplificationem majestatis divinæ ostendi- tur, quam vehementer insaniant, qui, cum idola fa- ciunt, eaque colunt, hoc ipso verum Deum sese colere opinantur. Id tamen per es omnes certum est, prio- rem partem capitis de Messia agere, ejusque præcur- sorem Johannem concernere. Quum ergo non tan- tum adventus Messiæ, sed etiam annunciatio ejus- dem & Evangelii in Sion, & mediante illa per or- bem terrarum inter gentes prædicatur, ab idolo- latria, à qua gentes ipsæ, quæ servierunt τοῖς μὴ φύ- σει œσι θεοῖς, ad unius veri Dei agnitionem perdu- cendæ erant Novi Test. tempore, revocat Judæos Propheta, ne inter Babylonios & ubicunq; disper- gentur, eadem inficiantur, ac contaminentur, ideo- que insaniam eorum proponit, qui loco immensi Dei, qui universas aquas maris cava manu compre- hendat, imo palmo totum cœlum complectatur, ac tribus digitis totum terrarum orbem sustineat, qui vere magnus, imo maximus est, non mole, sed majestate & potentia, imagunculam aliquam co- lant, aut eadem majestatem Dei exprimere tentent, ac Deum optimum maximum honorare velint cul- tu imaginis alicujus, quæ nihil habet divini, neque tantum Deo, sed homine etiam longe est infe- rior.

## 40:12
Vers. 12. WHO HAS MEASURED THE WATERS IN THE HOLLOW OF HIS HAND) From his deeds he shows the immense power of God. He has measured in the hollow of his hand: that is, he contains the waters as if in the hollow of his hand, that is, the sea itself.

AND WILL WEIGH THE HEAVENS WITH A SPAN) In the Hebrew: He has disposed. A span, as a span. Thus also the following.

WHO HAS WEIGHED THE DUST OF THE EARTH WITH THREE FINGERS) In the Hebrew: Who has comprehended the dust of the earth in a tridental? For שׁליש is a tridental also in Ps. 80, 6.

AND HAS BALANCED THE MOUNTAINS IN A SCALE) In a balance. He sustains the mountains no less easily than a man sustains weights in a balance.

Latin:

Vers. 12. QUIS MENSUS EST PUGILLO AQUAS) Ex factis ostendit immensam Dei potentiam. Mensus est pu- gillo: id est, continet quasi pugillo aquas, id est, mare ipsum.

ET CŒLOS PALMA PONDERABIT) In Hebræo: Disposuit. Palma, quasi palma. Sic & sequentia.

QUIS APPENDIT TRIBUS DIGITIS MOLEM TERRÆ) In Hebræo: Quis comprehendit in tridentali pul- verem terræ? שׁליש enim tridental etiam Psal. 80, 6.

ET LIBRAVIT IN PONDERE MONTES) In statera. Non minus facile montes sustinet, quam homo pondera in statera.

## 40:13
Vers. 13. WHO HAS HELPED THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD) In the Hebrew: Who has instructed the Spirit of the Lord? The Greeks translated, τίς ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου, whom Paul follows in Rom. 11, 34, in the same sense, if I am not mistaken. For the Jews speaking Greek express words signifying a double action by one, so that ἔγνω here may be worth 'he made to know': that is, he taught. The following words explain this.

Latin:

Vers. 13. QUIS ADJUVIT SPIRITUM DOMINI) In Hebr. Quis instruxit Spiritum Domini? Græci verterunt, τίς ἔγνω νῦν κυρίυ, quos sequitur Paulus Rom. 11, 34. eodem, ni fallor, sensu. Nam Judæi Græce loquentes verba dupli- cem actionem significantia per unam exprimunt, ut ἔγνω hic valeat scire fecit: id est, docuit. Explicant id sequentia.

## 40:15
Vers. 15. BEHOLD THE GENTILES) Even those Chaldeans of your Lord now.

AS A DROP OF A BUCKET) Which if it falls, is cared for by no one.

AND AS THE MOMENT OF A BALANCE) He translates שׁחק very well, as also the Wise Man ῥοπὴν, 11, 23, which passage is a twin to this one. Understand a small weight.

BEHOLD THE ISLES AS SMALL DUST) דק signifies everything that is minute. The Greeks here translate it Σίελον, that is, spittle. Understand by isles the lands situated by seas or even rivers, in the Hebrew manner; he will cast them away like spittle where he wishes. Mesopotamia, Assyria, and Armenia seem to be understood especially.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ECCE GENTES) Etiam illi Chaldæi Do- mini nunc vestri.

QUASI STILLA SITULÆ) Quæ si decidat, à ne- mine curatur.

ET QUASI MOMENTUM STATERÆ) Optime ver- tit שׁחק, ut & Sapiens ῥοπὴν, 11, 23. qui locus huic loco geminus. Intellige scriptulum.

ECCE INSULÆ QUASI PULVIS EXIGUUS) דק omne, quod minutum est significat. Σίελον, id est, sputum, hic vertere Græci. Insulas intellige terras, maribus aut etiam amnibus ad sitas, more Hebræo; eas projiciet, ut spu- tum ubi velit. Præcipue videtur intelligi Mesopotamia, As- syria, Armenia.

## 40:16
Vers. 16. AND LEBANON SHALL NOT BE SUFFICIENT TO BURN, AND THE BEASTS THEREOF SHALL NOT BE SUFFICIENT FOR A BURNT OFFERING) They would not be sufficient, namely, if they were to be performed according to the sacred dignity.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ET LIBANUS NON SUFFICIET AD SUCCENDENDUM, ET ANIMALIA EJUS NON SUFFICIENT AD HOLOCAUSTUM) Non fufficerent, nempe si pro dignitate sacra e: facienda essent.

## 40:18
Vers. 18. TO WHOM THEN HAVE YE LIKENED GOD?) It is not without reason that he treats here of the place against images, which were erected to God or as if to God. For since the Israelites, having been deported by Tiglath-Pileser and by Shalmaneser, were already living among those who fashioned images for God, and likewise it was to happen to the Jews, whom Nebuchadnezzar was about to deport, both were to be forewarned, so that, mindful of the best and most wise law, they might beware of those customs which could imprint a thought less suitable to the divine Majesty upon their minds, and furthermore lead them away from the true God to false ones. Moses is praised by many because he constructed no images for God, lest God be believed to be similar to any animal, or even to the most perfect of animals, man. See what we have brought forward pertaining to this matter from Empedocles, Xenophanes, Tacitus, and Plutarch, at Deut. 4, 15. Add that saying of Antiphanes concerning God: Ὀφθαλμοῖς ἐχ ὁρᾶται, ὀδενὶ ἔοικε, διόπερ αὐτὸν ἐκμαθεῖν ἐξ εἰκόνος ὐδεὶς δύναται.

It can certainly be admitted that this most grave exhortation to avoid idolatry was most necessary both for the Israelites and for the Jews, for which reason the madness of idolaters is graphically depicted frequently not only by Isaiah, but by all the Prophets; yet it is by no means to be concluded from this, as Grotius does, as if those things which were premised concerning the consolation of the people at the beginning of the chapter were spoken at the time of the future Babylonian exile of the Prophets, which we demonstrated at the beginning of the chapter to pertain to the times of the N. T. For the people could be raised up most especially by the promise of the coming of the Messiah, who meanwhile was to be recalled from idolatry by the Prophets, until God, by sending His Son, should bathe not only the Jews but even the nations themselves in a more illustrious knowledge, and should exterminate all idolatry. Concerning the construction of images and the prohibition of Moses, who not only constructed no images for God, but also prohibited those to be constructed by which either a likeness of God is feigned or divine worship is attributed, we have spoken in its proper place, and we have exposed the τὸ ὔπηλον which Grotius fostered in that argument.

Latin:

Vers. 18. CUI ERGO SIMILEM FECISTIS DEUM?) Non abs re tractat hic locum contra imagines, quæ Deo aut quasi Deo erigebantur. Cum enim Israëlitæ à Theglath- phalasare, & à Salmanasare deportati, jam viverent inter eos, qui Deo fingebant imagines, itemque eventurum esset Judæis, quos deportaturus erat Nabuchodonosor, præmu- niendi fuêre utrique, ut, legis optimæ & sapientissimæ me- mores, caverent sibi ab iis moribus, qui minus convenien- tem divinæ Majestati cogitationem imprimere possent ani- mis, deinde & à vero Deo ad falsos abducere Laudatur à plurimis Moses, quod nullas Deo imagines struxerit, ne Deus aut animali alicui, aut etiam animalium pertiffimo, homini, similis crederetur. Vide, quę ad hanc rem pertinen- tia protulimus ex Empedocle, Xenophane, Tacito, Plutar- cho, ad Deut. 4, 15. Adde illud Antiphanis de Deo : Ὀφ- θαλμοῖς ἐχ ὁρᾶται, ὀδενὶ ἔοικε, διόπερ αὐτὸν ἐκμαθεῖν ἐξ εἰκό- νος ὐδεὶς δύναται.

Admitti sane potest, parænesin hanc gravissi- mam ad vitandam idololatriam, tum Israëlitus, tum Judæis maxime necessariam fuisse, quo nomine non ab Esaia tantum, sed ab omnibus Prophetis frequenter insania idololatrarum graphice depin- gitur, nequaquam tamen inde colligendum cum Grotio, ac si ea, quæ de consolatione populi præ- missa sunt initio capitis, Prophetis futuri exilii Ba- bylonici tempore dicta sint, quæ ad tempora N. T. pertinere, sub ingressum capitis demonstravimus. Nam adventus Messiæ promissione vel maxime eri- gi poterat populus, qui revocand⁹ interea per Pro- phetas erat ab idololatria, donec Deus misso filio illustriori cognitione non Judæos tantum, sed ipsas etiam gentes perfunderet, omnemq; idololatriam exterminaret. De imaginum structura & interdi- cto Mosis, qui non modo nullas Deo struxit ima- gines, sed eas etiam strui prohibuit, quibus vel si- militudo Dei affingitur, vel cultus divinus attribui- tur, suo loco diximus, & τὸ ὔπηλον, quod Grotius in illo argumento fovit, deteximus.

## 40:20
Vers. 20. HE HATH CHOSEN A TREE AND THAT WILL NOT ROT) In the Hebrew: He who is poor to offer, chooses wood that does not feel decay: that is, he who does not have gold and silver at hand. Such wood is especially cypress, so much so that Pliny 16, 41 reports that the image of Jupiter in the citadel lasted until his own age, having been dedicated in the six hundred and sixty-first year from the founding of the city. In the same place, Pliny praises the vine, juniper, and mulberry for those uses.

Latin:

Vers. 20. FORTE LIGNUM ET IMPUTRIBILE E- LEGIT) In Hebræo: Qui pauper est ad offerendum, lignum eligit, quod cariem non sentiat: is scilicet cui aurum & argen- tum non suppetit. Tale autem lignum præcipue est cupres- sus, adeo ut tradat Plinius 16, 41. simulacrum Jovis in arce è cupresso durasse ad suam ætatem, à condita urbe sexcen- tesimo sexagesimo primo anno dicatum. Laudat ibidem Plinius ad eos usus vitem, juniperum, morum.

## 40:21
Vers. 21. HAVE YE NOT UNDERSTOOD THE FOUNDATIONS OF THE EARTH) Namely, that they were made by Him, as below in verse 26. He says all these things so that those things which are worthy of Him may be thought concerning God.

Latin:

Vers. 21. NONNE INTELLEXISTIS FUNDAMEN- TA TERRÆ) Nempe ab ipso esse facta, ut infra 26. Hæc omnia dicit, ut de Deo ea, quæ ipso digna sunt, sentiantur.

## 40:22
Vers. 22. IT IS HE THAT SITTETH UPON THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH) Upon the orb of the earth.

AND THE INHABITANTS THEREOF ARE AS GRASSHOPPERS) As minute living creatures, if they are compared with Him.

THAT STRETCHETH OUT THEM AS A CURTAIN) See Psalm 104, 2 and Genesis 1, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 22. QUI SEDET SUPER GYRUM TERRÆ) Super orbem terræ.

ET HABITATORES EJUS SUNT QUASI LO- CUSTÆ) Velut minuta animantia, si cum ipso compa- rentur.

EXPANDIT EOS SICUT TABERNACULUM) Vide Psal. 104, 2. & Genes. 1, 6.

## 40:23
Vers. 23. THAT BRINGETH THE SEARCHERS OF SECRETS TO NOTHING) In the Hebrew: רוזנים, i.e., princes: the Greeks, ἄρχοντας: to the Arabs, وزن is heavy.

HE HATH MADE THE JUDGES OF THE EARTH AS VANITY) He blows them away, as follows.

Latin:

Vers. 23. QUI DAT SECRETORUM SCRUTATO- RES QUASI NON SINT) In Hebræo: רוזנים, i. e. principes: Græci, ἄρχοντας : Arabibus وزن est gravis.

JUDICES TERRÆ VELVT INANE FECIT) Dif- flat eos, ut sequitur.

## 40:26
Ver. 26. WHO BRINGS OUT THEIR HOST BY NUMBER) As if in ordered ranks.

AND CALLS THEM ALL BY NAME) As masters do their servants: hey Syrus, hey Geta: by way of command.

NOR WAS ONE MISSING) Not one of the stars flees from his command; they all rise according to his prescription.

Latin:

Vers. 26. QUI EDUCIT IN NUMERO MILITIAM EORUM) Velut ordinatis agminibus.

ET OMNES EX NOMINE VOCAT) Ut domini ser- vos: heus Syre, heus Geta: pro imperio.

NEQUE UNUM RELIQUUM FUIT) Nulla stella- rum defugit imper um, ex præscripto oriuntur omnes.

## 40:27
Ver. 27. WHY DO YOU SAY O JACOB) Why would you say, O posterity of Jacob? He warns them, lest when those calamities arrive, they think they are not a care to God.

Latin:

Vers. 27. QUARE DICIS JACOB) Quare diceres, ô Jacobi posteritas, Monet eos, ne cum eæ calamitates adve- nient, putent se Deo curæ non esse.

## 40:28
HE WILL NOT FAINT, NOR BE WEARY) That is, he is not fatigued by governing human affairs.

NOR IS THERE ANY SEARCHING OF HIS WISDOM) He means this: but his wisdom (which rules the world) is unsearchable. When he seems to cease, he is already arranging the causes of his actions in secret.

Latin:

Vers. 28. NON DEFICIET, NEQUE LABORABIT) Id est, non fatigatur gubernando res humanas.

NEC EST INVESTIGATIO SAPIENTIÆ EJUS) Hoc vult: sed sapientia ejus (quæ mundum regit) est im- perscrutabilis. Cum cessare videtur, jam causas actuum in occulto disponit.

## 40:29
Vers. 29. HE WHO GIVES STRENGTH TO THE WEARY) How could he be weary, who refreshes the weary? THE YOUTHS SHALL FAINT) נערים here are adolescents, as often elsewhere: The Greeks often translate them as νέοι & νεανίσκοι. It often happens, he says, that those who are of vigorous age faint under labor. Vers. 31. BUT THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD, SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH) That is, they shall receive new strength from time to time as God gives it. THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS AS EAGLES) New ones, clearly. See Ps. 103, 5.

Latin:

Vers. 29. QVI DAT LASSO VIRTVTEM) Quomodo lassaretur is, qui lassos recreat? DEFICIENT PUERI) נערים hic sunt adolescentes, ut sæpe alibi: Vertunt sæpe Græci, νέοι & νεανίσκοι. Sæpe evenit, inquit, ut qui vegetæ sunt ætatis, sub labore deficiant. Vers. 31. QVI AVTEM SPERANT IN DOMINO, MVTABVNT FORTITVDINEM) Id est, novas subinde vires Deo dante accipient. ASSUMENT PENNAS SICVT AQVILÆ) Novas scilicet. Vide Psal. 103, 5.

## 41:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLI.

The glory of Divine power and mercy, and the impotence and vanity of idols.

Vers. 1. KEEP SILENCE BEFORE ME, O ISLANDS) In the Hebrew: Be silent: but with the same sense: that is, admire with silence. But the LXX read not החרישו, but התחדשו: for they translate it ἐγκαινίζεσθε. AND LET THE NATIONS RENEW THEIR STRENGTH) When the peoples (that is, the Jews) shall acquire new strength: for it is a repeated expression, from that which preceded in 40, 31. It is frequent in the sacred writings to call the Jews לאמים, that is, λαὸς, and the others גוים, or as here איים. LET THEM THEN SPEAK) After the nations shall have been exhausted by wondering, then let them speak, and understand the causes. What God did in Abraham, he says he did the same in his descendants, and that deservedly, on account of the worship of the one God neglected by others. Vers. 2. WHO RAISED UP THE RIGHTEOUS MAN FROM THE EAST.) In the Hebrew it is, righteousness. But it is frequent for the Hebrews to put abstract nouns for concrete. He calls Abraham the worshiper of the one God the righteous man. For nothing is more righteous than that he should be held for God who created the world, not others, whom human audacity made gods. Chaldea and Mesopotamia are to the East of Judea. HE CALLED HIM TO FOLLOW HIM) He translates the sense of the Hebrew לרגלו well, at his feet. See Gen. 12, 1. Josh. 24, 3. Heb. 11, 8. HE SHALL GIVE THE NATIONS BEFORE HIS FACE) That is, he prostrated idolaters before him, Gen. 12, 1. for future tenses here stand for past, in the Hebrew manner. AND HE SHALL RULE OVER KINGS) In the Hebrew: He made him prevail over kings, Ps. 105, 14. HE SHALL GIVE THEM AS THE DUST TO HIS SWORD, AS DRIVEN STUBBLE TO HIS BOW) Thus those nations and Kings were scattered by the sword and bow of Abraham like dust or stubble. Vers. 3. HE SHALL PURSUE THEM, HE SHALL PASS IN PEACE, THE PATH SHALL NOT APPEAR UNDER HIS FEET) From the Hebrew you may translate it thus: Having pursued them, he arrived safely by that way which he had not entered (supply before) with his feet: that is, as far as Damascus, Gen. 14, 15.

Jerome, Cyril, and Procopius interpret the righteousness raised up from the East differently, understanding Christ, whose name is the East, Zech. 6, who was made righteousness for us, 1 Cor. 1, 30. Others, whom Jerome mentions, accepted it concerning Cyrus, King of the Persians, whom God stirred up from the East out of Persia against the Babylonians, prostrating many nations before him, so that their idols, which were made by human effort and raised up by the art of the silversmith, did not profit the Babylonians. Hugo, Adam, and Pagninus, in Cornelius à Lapide, made this their own opinion. But we grant that Abraham the righteous, as he is called in Wis. 10, 5, who was as it were the Father of faith and righteousness, by propagating it among the Canaanites and his descendants, is designated here, called forth from the East, or Chaldea, as Jerome reports that the Hebrews explained it, and as our people and most other interpreters commonly interpret it. Explicit mention of him was made later in v. 8. And thou Israel art my servant Jacob, whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend; in whom I have taken hold of thee from the ends of the earth. Which things teach that the former things concerning the vocation of Abraham, in whom the Israelites were taken hold of, who were in his loins, are to be accepted. Moreover, the example of Abraham is proposed for this reason, that since he himself professed his faith in Chaldea, the Jews as his seed should not fear to profess it in the Babylonian captivity, since God, who gave nations and Kings before his face, is about to protect them, so that all who oppose them may be confounded. Concerning the fact that the Prophet used the name of RIGHTEOUSNESS, there is a pious and elegant observation by B. Brentius; The Holy Spirit preferred to signify Abraham by the name of Righteousness (for the Hebrew truth has it thus: Who raised up Righteousness from the East?) rather than by the name of the righteous man, so that on this occasion he might subject to the auditor, or reader, that notable sentence which is written concerning Abraham: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness. For since Abraham was not only counted righteous through faith for the happiness of his own person, but was also proposed as an example to the whole Church of God, and as many as believe in Christ promised to Abraham, to them faith is counted for righteousness, it fits not ineptly that the name of righteousness rather than that of the righteous man should be attributed to Abraham. Vatablus's version and explanation contribute to this, as far as the following words are concerned: HE CALLED IT (Righteousness) to his foot: that is, Abraham preached righteousness in all the places through which he passed, and in which he stayed. Which, however, others explain more correctly concerning the reduction and obedience of Abraham, that God called him to follow, as the Vulgate rendered לרגלו, at his feet, as if he had gone before the way of Abraham, who was insisting upon his footsteps. See Gen. 12, 1. Josh. 24, 3. Heb. 11, 8. For Abraham followed God calling him, not knowing whither. Furthermore, if we consult the sources, the word יקרא does not refer to the person called, but is to be referred to the person calling. For the distinctive accent demands that, by the force of which the words are to be rendered thus: Who raised up from the east? Righteousness shall call him to his foot. Thus, by the name of righteousness, Christ, Jehovah our righteousness, can be understood, Jer. 23, 6. by whom Abraham was called, inasmuch as he was called so that he might be rendered a partaker of the righteousness of Christ.

Latin:

CAPUT XLI.

Gloria potentiæ & misericordiæ Divinæ, & idolorum impotentia ac vanitas.

Vers. 1. TAGEANT AD ME INSULÆ) In Hebræo: Tacete: sed sensu eodem: id est, cum silentio admiramini. At LXX. legerunt non החרישו, sed התחדשו: vertunt enim ἐγκαινίζεσθε. ET GENTES MVTENT FORTITVDINEM) Cum populi (id est, Judæi) novas acquirent vires: est enim repetita locutio, ex eo quod præcessit 40, 31. Frequens est sacris litteris לאמים, id est, λαὸς vocare Judæos, cæteros גוים, aut ut hic איים. TVNC LOQVANTVR) Postquam admirando defessæ erunt gentes, tunc loquantur, & causas intelligant. Quod in Abrahamo fecit Deus, idem se ait fecisse in ejus posteris, idqs merito, ob unius Dei cultum ab aliis neglectum. Vers. 2. QVIS SVSCITAVIT AB ORIENTE JV-STVM.) In Hebræo est, justitiam. Sed frequens Hebræis, abstracta ponere pro concretis. Justum dicit Dei unius cultorem Abrahamum. Nihil enim justius, quam eum pro Deo haberi, qui mundum condidit, non alios, quos humana audacia Deos fecit. Chaldæa & Mesopotamia ad Orientem Judææ. VOCAVIT EVM, VT SEQVERETVR SE) Bene vertit sensum Hebræi לרגלו, ad pedes suos. Vid. Gen. 12, 1. Jos. 24, 3. Hebr. 11, 8. DABIT IN CONSPECTVM EJVS GENTES) Id est, prostravit coram eo idololatras, Gen. 12, 1. nam futura hic valent pro præteritis, more Hebræo. ET REGES OBTINEBIT) In Hebræo: Regibus eum fecit prævalere, Psal. 105, 14. DABIT QVASI PVLVEREM GLADIO EJVS, SICVT STIPVLVAM VENTO RAPTAM ARCVI EJVS) Ita gentes & Reges isti gladio & arcu Abrahami disjecti sunt quasi pulvis aut stipula. Vers. 3. PERSEQVETVR EOS, TRANSIBIT IN PACE, SEMITA IN PEDIBVS EJVS NON APPARE-BIT) Ex Hebræo sic vertas: Persecutus eos pervenit incolumis ea via quam pedibus suis ingressus (supple ante) non fuerat: id est, Damascum usque, Gen. 14, 15.

ALiter justitiam ab Oriente suscitatam interpretantur Hieronymus, Cyrillus & Procopius, qui intelligunt Christum, cujus nomen est Oriens, Zach. 6. qui factus nobis est justitia, 1. Cor. 1, 30. Alii, quos refert Hieronymus, de Cyro Rege Persarum accepêre, quem adversus Babylonios ab Oriente è Perside excitabat Deus, prosternens ei gentes plurimas, ut Babyloniis non profuerint idola sua, quæ humano facta sunt studio, & arte ærarii excitata. Quam sententiam suam fecere Hugo, Adamus & Pagninus apud Cornel. à Lap. Sed largimur, Abraham justum, ut vocatur Sap. 10, 5. qui fuit quasi fidei & justitiæ Pater, eam in Chananæos & posteros suos propagando, hic designari, evocatum ab oriente, vel Chaldæa, ut Ebræos exposuisse refert Hieronymus, & communiter interpretantur Nostrates, ac cæteri pleriq; Interpp. Ejus postea mentio diserta facta est v. 8. Et tu Israël serve meus Jacob, quem elegi, semen Abraham amici mei; in quo apprehendi te ab extremis terræ. Quæ docent, priora de Abrahami vocatione, in quo apprehensi sunt Israëlitæ, qui erant in lumbis ejus, accipienda esse. Abrahami autem exemplum proponitur ideo, ut quum ipse fidem suam in Chaldæa professus fuerit, Judæi ceu semen ejus non timeant profiteri in captivitate Babylonica, siquidem Deus, qui dedit gentes & Reges in conspectu ejus, protecturus sit ipsos, ut confundantur omnes, qui oppugnant eos. De eo eo vero, quod JUSTITIÆ nomine usus est Prophe- ta, pia & elegans est observatio B. Brentii; Maluit Spiritus Sanctus Abrahamum nomine Justitiæ (He- bræa enim veritas sic habet: Quis expectavit ab O- riente Justitiam?) quam nomine justi significare, ut hac occasione subjiceret auditori, vel lectori illam in- signem sententiam, quæ de Abrahamo scripta est: Credidit Abraham Deo, & reputatum est ei ad justi- tiam. Nam cum Abraham non tantum ad suæ perso- næ felicitatem reputatus est justus per fidem, sed et- iam propositus est in exemplum universæ Ecclesiæ Dei, & quotquot credunt in Christum Abrahæ promissum, iis reputetur fides ad justitiam, non inepte congru- it, ut tribuatur Abrahamo justitiæ potius, quam justi cognomen. Quo facit Vatabli versio, & expli- catio, quantum ad verba sequentia: PROCLA- MAVIT ILLAM (Justitiam) ad pedem suum: id est, Abraham prædicabat justitiam in omnibus locis, per quæ transibat, & in quibus versabatur. Quæ tamen rectius de reductione & obsequio A- brahami cæteri explicant, quod vocaverit eum Deus, ut sequeretur, ut reddidit Vulgatus לרגלו, ad pedes suos, quasi præiverit viam Abrahami, vesti- giis suis insistentis. Vid. Gen. 12, 1. Jos. 24, 3. Ebr. 11, 8. Sequutus est enim Abraham Deum vocan- tem, nesciens quo. Cæterum si fontes consula- mus, vox יקרא, non refert personam vocatam, sed referenda est ad personam vocantem. Id enim po- scit accentus distinctivus, vi cujus verba ita redden- da: Quis suscitavit ab oriente? Justitia vocabit eum ad pedem suum. Ita nomine justitiæ Christus Jeho- va justitia nostra intelligi poterit, Jer. 23, 6. à quo vocatus est Abraham, utpote, qui vocatus est, ut justitiæ Christi particeps redderetur.

## 41:4
Vers. 4. CALLING THE GENERATIONS FROM THE BEGINNING) Commanding and about to command all peoples from the beginning of the world even to the end. Concerning this kind of speaking, see above 41, 4.

I THE FIRST AND THE LAST) In the Hebrew: with the last: i.e., I govern all things from the beginning even to the end.

That these things are to be understood not of the universal Empire of God, but of the calling to the kingdom of God, is manifest from the calling of Abraham, of whom mention was made before. Who did these things, if not He who calls the generations from the beginning, who has called and chosen all the Hebrews born from Abraham until now as His people, and from the beginning or the foundation of the world calls the generations, excluding no one from His kingdom? It is evident, however, with what purpose Grotius explains those words concerning the empire of God, namely, that he may likewise twist those things which follow, 'I am the first and the last,' to that same meaning. But it is one thing to call the generations, another to command and to rule. Nor do those words 'first and last' sound of empire, but they describe the eternity of God; therefore they are explained thus in Isaiah 43:10, 'I myself am, before me no God was formed, and after me there shall be none,' and Revelation 22:13, 'I am A and Ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.' Compare Isaiah 44:6, 48:12, Revelation 1:8, chapter 21:6. For the phrase 'WITH THE LAST,' how it is to be understood, is gathered from parallel passages in which God testifies that He is 'THE FIRST AND THE LAST,' and therefore the Vulgate rightly rendered it also in this place 'the first and the last'; B. Luther translated it, 'Ich bin der Erste und der Letzte,' provided that besides the designation of eternity, the care of GOD is simultaneously insinuated; for he did not wish that to be excluded, as the commentary of B. Luther teaches: all the generations of the earth pass away, I alone remain for eternity. There is no God of the first and the last, except the one only true and eternal God. Therefore, not badly, Osiander [says] by way of digression: I not only was before all creatures, and live for eternity, but I also give a beginning to all creatures, and to them, when it pleases, I put an end. Cyril of Alexandria on this passage says: God is the first and only, and without beginning, the maker of all things, nor will he be in any other way through infinite ages. For he himself is, and is alone. That this phrase indeed refers entirely to eternity, we have proven against the Socinians in our Disputation on the eternal pre-existence of the Son of God, chapter 27. Verse 5. THE ISLANDS SAW, AND FEARED) They will see the wondrous restoration of my people, and severe judgments upon other nations. Verse 6. EVERYONE WILL HELP HIS NEIGHBOR) They will gather together among themselves, like idolaters. Verse 7. THE METALWORKER STRENGTHENED THE ONE STRIKING WITH A HAMMER, WHO WAS FORGING AT THAT TIME) In the Hebrew: The metalworker strengthens the goldsmith: the polisher of the hammer [strengthens] him who strikes the anvil. SAYING IT IS GOOD FOR GLUE) Saying that this solder is good. Σύμβλημα to the Greeks. AND HE STRENGTHENED THEM) Some one of the gods. A NAIL SO THAT IT WOULD NOT MOVE) With rivets, as Arnobius speaks in this matter. The meaning is: as easily as they set up their idols, so easily do they think their empires can be set up by them. Verse 8. AND YOU ISRAEL) O Israel. For so אַתָּה is taken. SEED OF ABRAHAM MY FRIEND) Namely, you are, as if he were to say: remember that you are sprung from Abraham, to be treated likewise, if you do like things. It is a great honor for Abraham to be called the friend of God, 2 Chron. 20:7, James 2:23. A huge sign of his friendship is that for Abraham's sake God swore: Heb. 6:17. IN WHOM I HAVE APPREHENDED YOU FROM THE ENDS OF THE EARTH) In the Hebrew, although with transposed words: You are, whom I have apprehended. From the ends of the earth, from Egypt. He recalls old things, so that new ones may be hoped for. AND FROM ITS DISTANT PLACES I HAVE CALLED YOU) From its great places: In the Hebrew: that is, I rescued you from the king and princes of Egypt. Verse 9. I HAVE CHOSEN YOU, AND HAVE NOT CAST YOU AWAY) I have made you a peculiar people to myself, but I have not held you in contempt, as other nations. Verse 10. DO NOT DECLINE, BECAUSE I AM YOUR GOD) Do not lose heart. AND THE RIGHT HAND OF MY JUSTICE HAS UPHELD YOU) In the Hebrew: of my justice: that is, my just right hand: just as the Greeks also understood it here. Verse 11. THEY WILL BE AS IF THEY ARE NOT) In the Hebrew: they will be reduced to nothing. So also below 12. WHICH CONTRADICT YOU) That is, oppose you. See what is at Luke 2:34. YOUR REBELLIOUS MEN) Better: those who contend with you. Verse 13. APPREHENDING YOUR HAND) As a companion in battle. Verse 14. DO NOT FEAR WORM JACOB) You who are crushed by the nations like a worm, Ps. 22:7. YOU WHO ARE DEAD OF ISRAEL) Rather, men of Israel. For that is מְתֵי. But it is usually said of a few: therefore the Greeks here placed ὀλιγοστὸς. Verse 15. I HAVE PLACED YOU AS A NEW THRESHING WAGON) I will make you to be like a threshing sledge cutting deeply. HAVING SAWING TEETH) Well-toothed: Having mouths: in the Hebrew. YOU WILL THRESH THE MOUNTAINS AND CRUSH THEM, AND YOU WILL MAKE THE HILLS LIKE DUST) That is, by your prayers you will obtain that, just as once for Abraham's sake I crushed kings, and for the sake of Moses and those accompanying him the Egyptian king; so now also for your sake I will crush the Medes and Babylon, by whom you have been treated most wretchedly. Verse 17. THE NEEDY AND POOR SEEK WATERS, AND THERE ARE NONE: THEIR TONGUE HAS WITHERED WITH THIRST, I THE LORD WILL HEAR THEM) A Hebrew construction, which you may express in Latin thus: The needy and poor, who seek waters where there will be none, so that their tongue burns with thirst; I God will hear. Thirst and hunger, especially in scorching places, signifies every vehement desire, as 25:5. The following also show this. Verse 19. I WILL GIVE IN THE WILDERNESS THE CEDAR AND THE THORN, AND THE MYRTLE AND THE OLIVE WOOD: I WILL PLACE IN THE DESERT THE FIR, THE ELM AND THE BOX TREE TOGETHER) Another similitude taken from shadows in places which are not accustomed to have shadows. For if they appear suddenly, it is a great comfort. See above 25:4. What is a thorn here, in the Hebrew is שִׁטָּה. It is a proper kind of cedar. Whence the Shittim wood. It is called a thorn-bush by some, because it is not unlike the white thorn.

ELM) The Hebrews think it is another kind of cedar. It seems to be named from duration. For دهر to the Arabs is eternity.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VOCANS GENERATIONES AB EXOR- DIO) Imperans & imperaturus omnibus populis à mundi initio ad finem usque. De loquendi hoc genere vide su- prà 41, 4.

PRIMVS ET NOVISSIMVS EGO SVM) In He- bræo: cum novissimis: i. e. ab initio ad finem usque cuncta guberno.

Non de Imperio Dei universali, sed de voca- tione ad regnum Dei hæc intelligenda esse, è voca- tione Abrahami, cujus antea facta mentio, mani- festum est. Quis fecit hæc, nisi qui vocat genera- tiones ab exordio, qui Ebræos omnes ab Abraha- mo genitos hucusque vocavit & elegit in populum suum, & ab initio vel conditu mundi generationes vocat, neminem à regno suo excludens? Patet au- tem, quo fine de imperio Dei verba illa explicet Grotius, ut nimirum ea, quæ sequuntur, primus & novissimus ego sum, pariter eo detorqueat. At a- liud est generationes vocare, aliud imperare ac do- minari. Neque de imperio sonant illa primus & novissimus, sed æternitatem Dei describunt, ideo ita explicantur Es. 43, 10. Ego ipse sum, ante me non est formatus Deus, & post me non erit, & Apoc. 22, 13. Ego sum A & Ω, primus & novissimus, principium & finis. Conf. Es. 44, 6. 28, 12. Apoc. 1, 8. c. 21, 6. Phrasis enim CUM NOVISSIMIS, quomodo ac- cipienda sit, è locis parallelis colligitur, quibus Deus testatur se PRIMUM ET NOVISSIMUM esse, ideoq; recte Vulgatus reddidit etiam h.l. pri- mus & novissimus; B. Lutherus transtulit, Ich bin der Erste und der Letzte, siquidem præter æternita- tis designationem cura DEI simul insinuetur; istam enim non exclusam voluit, ut commentarius B. Lutheri docet: omnes generationes terræ præter- eunt, solus ego maneo in æternum. Non est primorum & novissimorum Deus, nisi unus solus verus & æternus Deus. Ideo non male παρεξ Οςιαν Osiander: Ego non modo fui ante omnes creaturas, atq; in æter- num vivo, sed etiam omnibus creaturis initium do, eisq́; quando libuerit, finem impono. Cyrillus Alex. in h. l. primus & solus, inquit, & sine principio Deus, univerforum opifex, nec alio modo erit per infinita secula. Ipse enim est & solus. Quod vero omnino æternitas ista phrasi inferatur, adversus Socinia- nos evicimus Disp. de æterna Filii Dei præexisten- tia, cap. 27. Vers. 5. VIDERUNT INSULÆ, ET TIMUERUNT) Videbunt miram populi mei restitutionem, & severa judi- cia in gentes alias. Vers. 6. UNUSQUISQUE PROXIMO SUO AUXI- LIABITUR) Coibunt inter se, ut idololatræ. Vers. 7. CONFORTAVIT FABER ÆRARIUS PER- CUTIENS MALLEO EUM, QUI CUDEBAT TUNC TEMPORIS) In Hebræo: Confirmat faber ærarius aurifi- cem: politor mallei eum, qui tundit incudem. DICENS GLUTINO BONUM EST) Dicens ferru- men hoc bonum esse. Σύμβλημα Græcis. ET CONFORTAVIT EOS) Deorum aliquem. CLAVIS UT NON MOVERETUR) Gomphis, ut loquitur in hac re Arnobius. Sensus est: quam facile simu- lacra sua statuminant, tam facile putant statuminari à se posse imperia sua. Vers. 8. ET TU ISRAEL) O Israël. Nam ita sumi- tur אַתָּה. SEMEN ABRAHAM AMICI MEI) Nempe es qua- si dicat: memento te ex Abrahamo ortum, pariter tractan- dum, si paria feceris. Magnus honos Abrahami amicum Dei dici, 2. Par. 20, 7. Jac. 2, 23. Ejus amicitiæ signum in- gens, quod Abrahami causa Deus juravit: Hebr. 6, 17. IN QUO APPREHENDI TE AB EXTREMIS TER- RÆ) In Hebræo, quanquam transpositis vocibus: Tu es, quam apprehendi. Ab extremis terræ, ab Ægypto. Vetera memorat, ut nova sperentur. ET A LONGINQUIS EJUS VOCAVI TE) A magnis ejus: In Hebræo: id est, regi & principibus Ægy- pti te eripui. Vers. 9. ELEGI TE, ET NON ABJECI TE) Te mi- hi feci populum peculiarem, non autem insuper habui, ut gentes alias. Vers. 10. NE DECLINES, QUIA EGO DEUS TU- US) Ne animo concidas. ET SUSCEPIT TE DEXTERA JUSTI MEI) In He- bræo: justitiæ meæ: id est, dextera mea justa: quomo- do & Græci hic accepere. Vers. 11. ERUNT QUASI NON SINT) In Hebræo: redigentur in nihilum. Sic & infra 12. QUÆ CONTRADICUNT TIBI) Id est, obstant. Vi- de quæ ad Lucam 2, 34. VIROS REBELLES TUOS) Melius: eos, qui tecum contendunt. Vers. 13. APPREHENDENS MANUM TUAM) Tan- quam pugnæ socius. Vers. 14. NOLI TIMERE VERMIS JACOB) Qui à gentibus tanquam vermis contereris, Psal. 22, 7. QUI MORTUI ESTIS EX ISRAEL) Imo, viri Israe- lis. Id enim מְתֵי. Sed solet de paucis dici: ideo Græci hic posuere ὀλιγοστὸς. Vers. 15. EGO POSUI TE QUASI PLAUSTRUM TRITURANS NOVUM) Faciam, ut sis velut tribula val- de incidens. HABENS ROSTRA SERRANTIA) Bene dentata: Ora habens: in Hebræo. TRITURABIS MONTES ET COMMINUES, ET COLLES QUASI PULVEREM PONES) Id est, precibus tuis obtinebis, ut, sicut olim Abrahami causa contrivi re- ges, & Mosis eumq; comitantium causa regem Ægyptium; ita nunc etiam vestri causa conteram Medos, & Babylo- nem, à quibus pessime tractati estis. Vers. 17. EGENI ET PAUPERES QUÆRUNT A- QUAS, ET NON SUNT: LINGUA EORUM SITI A- RUIT, EGO DOMINUS EXAUDIAM EOS) Constru- ctio Hebraica, quam Latine sic exprimas: Egenos & pau- peres, qui aquas quærunt ubi nullæ erunt, ita ut siti ardeat eo- rum lingua; ego Deus exaudiam. Sitis & fames, præsertim in locis æstuosis, omne vehemens desiderium significat, ut 25, 5. ostendunt id & sequentia. Vers 19. DABO IN SOLITUDINEM CEDRUM ET SPINAM, ET MYRTUM ET LIGNUM OLIVÆ: PO- NAM IN DESERTO ABIETEM, ULMUM ET BU- XUM SIMUL) Altera similitudo sumta ab umbris in lo- cis, quæ umbras habere non solent. Eæ enim subito fi appareant, magno id solatio est. Vide supra 25, 4. Quod hic est spina, in Hebræo est שִׁטָּה. Id cedri proprium est genus. Vnde ligna Setim. Spinus vocatur nonnullis, quod spinui albæ sit non dissimilis.

ULMUM) Hebræi putant aliud esse cedri genus. Di- ctum a duratione videtur. Nam دهر Arabibus est æter- nitate.

## 41:19
AND THE BOX TREE TOGETHER) For the Hebrews count this among the kind of cedars.

Latin:

ET BUXUM SIMUL) Hanc enim cedrorum gene- ri annumerant Hebræi.

## 41:20
Verse 20. AND THE HOLY ONE OF ISRAEL CREATED IT) The Greeks κατέδειξε: well. For ברא among the Hebrews is said of every miraculous deed.

The sentiment of v. 15 is more general, concerning the threshing of mountains and the reducing of hills to dust, which extends itself to any enemies of the Church whatsoever, and therefore we do not exclude the Medes and Babylonians, but we deny that they alone are noted. Brentius rightly: Mountains and hills are the great and mediocre empires and kingdoms of this world. These the Lord says are to be so crushed by the Church that not even their traces remain safe. The Church is said to have crushed the mountain or the Babylonian empire, because God for the sake of his Church took the Monarchy away from the Babylonians and the descendants of Nebuchadnezzar, and handed it over to Cyrus King of the Persians, so that on this occasion the Jews, who were the people of God, might be freed from captivity, and the Church might be restored in Jerusalem. Therefore in chapter 45:4 it is said to Cyrus: for the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my elect, I have called you by your name. Conf. Is. ch. 43:14. Then the Church is said to crush the mountains, or the kingdoms of this world, when the assembly of the Church of Christ is gathered through the Gospel, from all the kingdoms and empires of this world, with Kings and Princes resisting, and even against the gates of hell. Whence afterwards in chapter 43 he says: I will bring your seed from the East, and from the West I will gather you. I will say to the North, give, and to the South, do not forbid. Finally, the time will come at last, when all the empires of this world having been laid waste and trampled, the Church of Christ alone, having conquered death and Satan, shall triumph, and enjoy perpetual happiness in Christ its Savior. To which also verse 17 pertains: THE NEEDY AND POOR SEEK WATERS, AND THERE ARE NONE, THEIR TONGUE HAS WITHERED WITH THIRST, I THE LORD WILL HEAR THEM: which Grotius renders thus according to the Hebrew construction: The needy and poor, who seek waters, where there are none, so that their tongue burns with thirst, I God will hear. And what follows further. I WILL GIVE IN THE WILDERNESS THE CEDAR, &c. For by this metaphor of a desert of waters and fountains and trees, it is understood that God is about to establish among the nations a most abundant fountain of the preaching of His word, so that as many as thirst for true salvation may draw from that fountain heavenly and eternal blessedness. Which promise, as our Brentius observes, began to be fulfilled first of all in the Babylonian captivity itself, when the doctrine of the true religion was spread throughout the entire monarchy on the occasion of the dream explained by Daniel, Dan. 2 & 3, and from the miracle which was performed on Daniel among the lions, and from the public edict of Darius, Dan. 6. This spreading of the word of God is a river and a fountain, and a spring of waters on the tops of the mountains, in the fields and in the desert, from which not only the pious among the Jews, but also many among the nations drew true and eternal salvation. Then this promise was much more fulfilled in those times in which the Apostles spread the Gospel concerning Christ among all nations, and in which the true Church of Christ is gathered, as much from the Jews as from the nations. Finally, it is fulfilled in every single pious, needy, and afflicted person, calling upon God through faith in Jesus Christ, whom God does not so much desert as to stir up in him rivers of consolations, so that he may also be able to give others the water of consolation to drink. Heb. 1. Jerome comments thus: The people of the nations, poor and slight, who did not have the Scripture of truth, seeks through various teachers, and various

The dogmas of the philosophers [seek] healthy waters, and finds none, which are not: their tongue has withered with thirst, without law or Prophets. Therefore the Lord God of Israel did not utterly forsake them, nor suffer them to perish forever, but opened rivers on the bare hills or mountains, and fountains in the midst of the plains: Which rivers drew their beginning from that river which is read in the Psalms: The impetus of the river makes glad the city of God. And in another place: The river of God is filled with waters. Which water and fountains flowed from that fountain: which speaks through Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water. And above in this same Prophet it is said: they shall drink waters from the fountains of the Savior. Of which it is also sung in the Psalms: Bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel. And he placed, he says, the desert into a pool of waters, and the pathless land into streams of waters. Of which waters the Savior also spoke in the Gospel in mystical discourse: He who shall drink of the water that I shall give him, shall not thirst forever: But the water that I shall give him, shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into life eternal. And again, if any man thirst, let him come to me, and drink. He who shall drink of the water that I shall give him, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. This, however, says the Evangelist, he said of the Holy Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive. Because, therefore, the multitude of the Church, once a desert, had been irrigated with vital waters, therefore according to the LXX there are born in it the Cedar and the Box-tree, and the Myrtle, and the Cypress, and the Poplar according to the Hebrew, and the other Interpreters. The Cedar, the Setta and the Myrtle, and the wood of the Olive and the Fir and the Elm and the Box-tree together, which varieties of trees signify the diversity of spiritual grace. That all may understand and likewise know in their mind: that the hand of the Lord has performed all these things, so that in the aridity of the nations they might find streams of mighty works: And in the land once desert and full of salt, the Cedar and the Cypress, and other trees might be born: Whose loftiness and summit hastening to heavenly things, the wood of the olive might illuminate: which is the nourishment of light, and the rest of those who labor. Gregory the Great explains these species of trees in Homily XX on the Gospels. The Cedars are those whose hearts are so solidified in eternal love, that no rot of earthly love corrupts them. The Thorns are those who prick the hearts of the hearers, and thus pierce the mind with the pain of compunction. The Myrtles are those who temper the tribulation of their neighbors through compassion. The Olives are the merciful. The Firs are those who, placed in earthly bodies, contemplate heavenly things. The Elms, which support the vines, are the seculars, who sustain holy men full of spiritual gifts with their generosity. The Box-trees are those who, although they may not be able to bear good works due to the infirmity of age, nevertheless, following the credulity of faithful parents, hold the perpetual faith of greenness. It is evident from Cyril of Alexandria that the Greek Church understood this prophecy in the same way, namely that the desert and the land lacking water is the region of the nations: but the rivers are holy men, who have been enriched with divine and supernal discourse, and who, like a river and streams, pour out to those who thirst, and as it were gush forth, so that the desert once changes its face and in it marshes and forests appear, and the thirsting land is turned into aqueducts, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ET SANCTUS ISRAEL CREAVIT IL- LUD) Græci κατέδειξε : bene. Nam ברא apud Hebræos de omni facto mirabili dicitur.

Generalior est sententia v. 15. de montibus tri- turandis, & collibus in pulverem redigendis, quæ se ad hostes Ecclesiæ quoscunque porrigit, ideoque Medos & Babylonios non excludimus, sed eos solos notari negamus. Recte Brentius: Montes & colles sunt magna & mediocria imperia atque regna hujus mundi. Hæc dicit Dominus ab Ecclesia ita conterên- da, ut ne vestigia quidem eorum salva remaneant. Dicitur autem Ecclesia contrivisse montem seu im- perium Babylonicum, quia Deus propter Eccle- siam suam abstulit Monarchiam à Babyloniis & posteris Nebucadnezaris, ac tradidit eam Cyro Re- gi Persarum, ut hac occasione Judæi, qui erant po- pulus Dei, captivitate liberarentur, & Ecclesia in Jerusalem restauraretur. Ideo cap. 45, 4. ad Cyrum dicitur: propter servum meum Jacob, & Israëlem electum meum vocavit te nomine tuo. Conf. Es. cap. 43, 14. Deinde Ecclesia dicitur conterere montes, seu regna hujus mundi, cum cœtus Ecclesiæ Christi colligitur per Evangelium, ex omnibus regnis & imperiis hujus mundi, obsistentibus Regibus & Principibus, imo invitis etiam inferorum portis. Unde postea cap. 43. dicit: Ab Oriente adducam se- men tuum, & ab Occidente congregabo te. Dicam Aquiloni, da, & Austro, noli prohibere. Postremo veniet tandem tempus, quo vastatis & conculcatis omnibus imperiis hujus mundi sola Ecclesia Chri- sti, victa morte & Satana, triumphet, ac perpetua in Christo Salvatore suo fruatur felicitate. Quo etiam facit vers. 17. EGENI ET PAUPERES QUÆRUNT AQUAS, ET NON SUNT, LINGUA EORUM SITI ARUIT, EGO DOMINUS EXAUDIAM EOS: quæ ita juxta Ebraicam constructionem reddit Grotius: Egenos & pauperes, qui aquas quærunt, ubi nullæ sunt, ita ut siti ardeat lingua eorum, ego Deus exaudiam. Et quæ porro sequuntur. DABO IN SOLITUDI- NEM CEDRUM, &c. Hac enim deserti aquarum & fontium & arborum Metaphora intelligitur, quod Deus inter gentes largissimum fontem præ- dicationis verbi sui instauraturus sit, ut quotquot veram salutem sitiunt, hauriant ex eo fonte cœle- stem & æternam beatitudinem. Quæ promissio, observante Brentio nostro, primum omnium im- pleri cœpit in ipsa Babylonica captivitate, cum Doctrina veræ religionis divulgata fuit in univer- sam Monarchiam ex occasione somnii à Daniele expositi, Dan. 2. & 3. & ex miraculo, quod editum in Daniele inter Leones, & ex publico Darii edi- cto, Dan. 6. Hæc divulgatio verbi Dei flumen est & fons, & scaturigo aquarum in verticibus montium, in campis & in deserto, ex quibus non solum pii in- ter Judæos, verum etiam multi inter gentes hause- runt veram & æternam salutem. Deinde multo ma- gis impleta hæc promissio iis temporibus, quibus Apostoli divulgant Evangelium de Christo inter omnes gentes, & quibus congregatur vera Ecclesia Christi, tam ex Judæis, quam ex gentibus. Deniq; impletur ea in unoquovis pio, egeno & afflicto, Deum ex fide Jesu Christi invocante, quem adeo non deserit Deus, ut excitet in ipso flumina conso- lationum, ut & alios possit aqua consolationis po- tare Ebr. 1. Hieron. ita commentatur: Gentium po- pulus pauper & tenuis, qui non habebat Scripturam veritatis, quærit per diversos Magistros, & varia

Philosophorum dogmata aquas salubres, & non inve- nit, quæ non sunt: lingua eorum siti aruit, sine lege aut Prophetis. Propterea Dominus Deus Israël non eos penitus dereliquit, nec in æternum perire passus, sed aperuit in supinis collibus, sive montibus flumina, & in medio camporum fontes: Quæ flumina ex illo flu- vio duxere principium, qui in Psalmis legitur: Flu- minis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei. Et in alio loco: Fluvius Dei repletus est aquis. Quæ aqua & fontes de illo fonte manarunt: qui per Hieremiam loquitur: Me dereliquerunt fontem aquæ vivæ. Et supra in hoc eodem Propheta dicitur: bibent aquas de fontibus Salvatoris. De quibus & in Psalmis canitur: Bene- dicite Dominum Deum de fontibus Israël. Et posuit, inquit, desertum in stagnum aquarum, & terram in- viam in rivos aquarum. De quibus aquis & Salva- tor in Evangelio mystico sermone dicebat: Qui bibe- rit de aqua, quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum: Sed aquam, quam ego dedero ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ sa- lientis in vitam æternam. Et iterum, si quis sitit, ve- niat ad me, & bibat. Qui biberit de aqua, quam ego dabo ei, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ. Hoc autem, inquit Evangelista, dicebat de Spiritu Sancto, quem credentes in eo accepturi erant. Quia igitur de- serta quondam Ecclesiæ multitudo, aquis vitalibus fuerat irrigata, propterea juxta LXX. nascuntur in ea Cedrus & Buxus, & Myrtus, & Cyparissus, & Populus juxta Hebraicum, & cæteros Interpp. Ce- drus, Setta & Myrtus, & lignum Olivæ & Abies & Ulmus & Buxus simul, quæ varietates arborum di- versitatem significant gratiæ spiritualis. Ut omnes in- telligant & pariter mente cognoscant: quia manus Domini hæc universa perfecerit, ut in ariditate gen- tium invenirent fluenta virtutum: Et in terra quon- dam deserta plenag, Salsuginis Cedrus & Cyparissus, & aliæ arbores nascerentur: Quarum sublimitatem & verticem ad cælestia festinantem, illuminaret li- gnum olivæ: quod nutrimentum lucis est, & laboran- tium requies. Explicat has arborum species Grego- rius M. hom. XX. in Evang. Cedri sunt, quorum cor- da ita in æterno amore solidata sunt, ut eadem jam ter- reni amoris putredo nulla corrumpat. Spinæ, qui cor- da audientium pungunt, sicq; mentem dolore compun- ctionis perforant. Myrti, qui proximorum tribula- tionem per compassionem temperant. Olivæ sunt mi- sericordes. Abietes sunt, qui in terrenis corporibus positi, cælestia contemplantur. Ulmi, quæ vites susti- nent, sunt seculares, qui sanctos viros donis spiritua- libus plenos sua largitate sustentant. Buxi, qui licet ex ætatis infirmitate bona opera ferre non valeant, ta- men parentum fidelium credulitatem sequentes fidem perpetuam viriditatis tenent. Similiter hoc vatici- nium Græcam Ecclesiam intellexisse, è Cyrillo Ale- xandrino, constat, quod nempe desertum & terra a- quis carens gentium regio sit: flumina autem viri san- cti, qui divino & superno ditati sunt sermone, & qui fluviatilis ac rivorum instar, sitientibus effundunt, & quasi scaturiunt, ut desertum quondam mutet faciem & in eo paludes ac sylvæ appareant, & terra sitiens in aquæ ductus vertatur &c.

## 41:21
Vers. 21. BRING NEAR YOUR JUDGMENT) That is, now you idolaters, be present for your case.

BRING IF PERCHANCE YOU HAVE ANYTHING) In the Hebrew: Bring your strengths: that is, arguments.

Latin:

Vers. 21. PROPE FACITE JUDICIUM VESTRUM) Id est, jam vos idololatræ adeste causæ vestræ.

AFFERTE SI QUID FORTE HABETIS) In Hebræo: Adferte robora vestra: id est, argumenta.

## 41:22
Vers. 22. LET THEM APPROACH) Your gods.

THE FORMER THINGS, WHICH WERE ANNOUNCED) In the Hebrew: The former things which are (to happen, that is) announce. Tell us from the dictation of your gods, what things are about to happen.

Vers. 22. AND WE WILL SET OUR HEART) We will believe them to be Gods. It is a koinosis: for God here joins himself as it were to men.

There is no need for this koinosis, the Lord alone speaks here. But he uses the plural to designate the mystery of the plurality of the divine persons. Which we demonstrated in the invincible assertion of the plurality of persons.

chap. 15, §. 228. where Enjedinus, the Photinian, who likewise invented the figure of communication here, was satisfied.

AND WE SHALL KNOW THEIR LATTER THINGS) In the Hebrew: And let us know their posterior things, that is, let us know what things will be next following those first future things.

AND WHAT THINGS ARE TO COME TELL US) Namely, in the long term: as the following things explain. Thus it proceeds in order.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ACCEDANT) Dii vestri.

PRIORA, QUÆ FUERUNT NUNTIATE) In Hebr. Priora quæ sint (eventura scilicet) nunciate. Dicite nobis ex deorum vestrorum dictatu, quæ jamjam eventura sint.

Vers. 22. ET PONEMUS COR NOSTRUM) Crede- mus illos esse Deos. Est κοίνωσις: nam Deus hic se homi- nibus quasi adjungit.

Non opus est hac κοινώσει, Dominus solus hic lo- quitur. Plurali autem utitur ad designandum myste- rium pluralitatis personarum divinarum. Quod o- stendimus in assertione invicta pluralit. personarum.

cap. 15, §. 228. ubi Enjedino, Photiniano, qui itidem communicationis figuram hic commentus est, satis factum.

ET SCIEMVS NOVISSIMA EORVM) In Hebræo: Et sciamus posteriora eorum, id est, sciamus, quæ illis primis futuris proxime consequentia erunt.

ET QVÆ VENTVRA SVNT NVNCIATE NOBIS) Nempe in longum: ut sequentia exponunt. Ita ordine progreditur.

## 41:23
Vers. 23. DO WELL ALSO OR EVIL, IF YOU CAN) Overthrow your enemies, as I overthrew Pharaoh: save your worshippers, just as I saved the Israelites.

AND LET US SPEAK AND SEE) When you have performed these things, we will speak afterwards of other matters, and we will examine them as well.

Latin:

Vers. 23. BENE QVOQVE AVT MALE, SI POTESTIS FACITE) Evertite hostes vestros, ut ego Pharaonem everti: servate cultores vestros, quomodo ego Israëlicas servavi.

ET LOQVAMVR ET VIDEAMVS) Hæc ubi præstiteritis, agemus postea de rebus aliis, & eas quoque examinabimus.

## 41:24
Vers. 24. BEHOLD, YOU ARE FROM NOTHING) You might translate it better: less than nothing.

AND YOUR WORK FROM THAT WHICH IS NOT) You might translate it more correctly: Your work is worse than a viper's. For אפעה, which is pronounced here more briefly with a final ו, is a viper, as appears below 51, 5, and from the Arabic language. He understands the work of the gods to be that which concerns them, that is, idolatry.

IT IS AN ABOMINATION) It is abominable, by a Hebrew manner of speaking, of which we have already often treated.

WHO CHOSE YOU) Who takes you to himself to be worshipped.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ECCE, VOS ESTIS EX NIHILO) Melius vertas: minus nihilo.

ET OPVS VESTRVM EX EO, QVOD NON EST) Rectius vertas: Opus vestrum pejus viperino. Nam אפעה, quod hic fine ו brevius effertur, est vipera, ut apparet infra 51, 5. & ex sermone Arabico. Opus deorum intelligit id, quod circa eos sit, id est, idololatriam.

ABOMINATIO EST) Abominabilis est, loquendi genere Hebræo, de quo sæpe jam egimus.

QVI ELEGIT VOS) Qui sibi sumit vos colendos.

## 41:25
Vers. 25. I HAVE RAISED UP FROM THE NORTH, AND HE SHALL COME FROM THE RISING OF THE SUN) God explains through certain degrees more and more clearly the manner in which He is about to procure the restoration of the Jews. For 'I have raised up' one should put 'I will raise up'. The Medes are to the Jews toward the North. The Persians toward the East. Cyrus was a Medo-Persian, therefore called a mule in the oracle, a Persian through his father, Cambyses, a Mede through his mother Mandane, the daughter of Astyages.

HE SHALL CALL UPON MY NAME) He will worship me, and acknowledge me as the author of his happiness. See Ezra 1, 2. 7. Josephus 11, 1.

HE SHALL BRING MAGISTRATES AS CLAY, AND AS A POTTER TREADING THE DIRT) There is a certain transposition in the Hebrew, having this sense: He coming shall tread down princes like clay, or like a potter soft earth: princes, namely Astyages, Croesus, Nabonidus.

Lyranus and Vatablus and others also understand this of Cyrus; but Forerius and Sanctius, as also Corn. à Lapide, interpret it of Abraham, called from the East, or from Chaldea and from the North or Mesopotamia, who was a worshipper of the divine name, and who, both by himself and through his powerful royal descendants, defeated enemies, so that this is a kind of recapitulation. Others prefer to take it of Christ: whom Osiander says was raised up from the North and the East, because Nazareth, the fatherland of his upbringing, is situated to the North and East with respect to Jerusalem, but that explanation is more clever than solid. The authors of the Belgian notes say Christ was excited from the East and the North, because his empire extends from one end of the world to the other. But the word 'raising up' from the East does not sound of the extent of an empire, but rather indicates origin and source. Therefore the interpretation of the Weimar Paraphrasts might seem more convenient: that Christ was raised up from the East, because by reason of his Divinity he is the Dayspring from on high, Luke 1, 78. But from the North by reason of his human nature, because the two natures differ from each other, just as the North does from the East: Truly, the discourse is about the raising up as a future event, which could not have been predicted by idols, which does not fit the eternal generation of the Son of God, nor is the distance of natures in Christ ever expressed by the South and the East, nor can it be conveniently expressed. Oecolampadius also explains it of Christ, although he does not declare how he is said to be raised up from the East and the North, but wishes this to be said of the people of Christ. Musculus notes that Kimchi, among the Rabbis themselves, takes it of the Messiah, both Father and Son; he confesses, however, that he does not see how he can be said to be raised up from the North and the East. Wherefore others interpret this as referring to the nations and peoples being stirred up, that they may submit themselves to Christ. Thus Jerome, who nevertheless seems to have understood by those stirred up from the North, and by him who is from the rising of the sun, Christ himself: he says that he has stirred up a people of nations from the North. They are stirred up, however, from

from the North, so that they may believe in him who has come from the Rising of the Sun. Concerning whom we read above, who raised up the righteous one from the East, or righteousness? And in another place, Behold, the man whose name is the Rising. The explanation of Cyril is similar; he adds the reason, because if you look at the region of the Jews, which inclines mostly to the South, the land of the Gentiles is more Northerly. However, he seems to call Christ the one who is from the Rising of the sun, for the reason that it is written of him, Behold, the man whose name is the Rising. But B. Brentius refers both to the calling of the Gentiles, namely that the Gentiles are to be stirred up from the North and the Rising of the Sun, and are to come to the Church, just as it is said in chapter 9: From the East I will bring your seed, and from the West I will gather you, etc. Piscator explains it in this way also, and the authors of the Belgian notes do not deny it. But since the argument here is brought against the gods of the Gentiles and their worshippers, it does not seem that it could have been drawn from the fact that God alone can predict the calling of the Gentiles to the Church; rather, there was need in this case for such a prediction as would convince the Gentiles themselves at their own time, when it has been completed, so that they might be gathered to the Church. This gathering is the end. The means, therefore, from which they ought to recognize the truth of the heavenly doctrine, must be something else, distinct from the gathering of the Gentiles. Musculus also notes that it does not fit this exposition well enough that it is added, and he shall come upon princes as upon mortar, and as the potter shall tread the clay: Therefore B. Luther rendered another opinion; I understand 'from the North and the Rising of the Sun' distributively, i.e., from wherever they wish, whether from here or from there. From the East the Chaldean to save, from the North the Assyrian to destroy, etc. This you idols cannot do. Others, B. Luther continues, accept this passage concerning Christ, that he is to call some from the North, some from the East. It is indeed a good opinion, but I follow the general one concerning all who are called, whether to destroy or to save; however, Christ is also included in this general opinion. Furthermore, since the example introduced here by the Prophet is likely, by which the Lord shows not only his power but also his foreknowledge of future things, of which the gods of the Gentiles are devoid, we do not deny that something special is designated: what this might be here, because it is not defined who, but only from where he is to be stirred up, is ambiguous. Which is perhaps the reason why that explanation concerning Cyrus proved itself to the Hebrews and pleased some Christians; for the Hebrews, as Jerome says, interpret the one stirred up from the North and coming from the Rising of the Sun as the Assyrian and the Persians, who came to Jerusalem and had trampled all its princes, and none of the idols which they worshipped knew that this was going to happen, except the Lord alone, who avenged them for their sins. Calvin hands down yet another interpretation related to these latter ones, who understands those things from the North and the East separately: I think, he says, that two things are noted here by the Prophet. For when he says, from the North, he understands the Chaldeans; from the East, the Medes and Persians, as if he were saying, two changes worthy of memory will happen, for I will stir up the Chaldeans, whose kingdom I will raise on high. Then the Persians will arrive, who will transfer their power to themselves. The Lord teaches that these things, although they were to happen after a long interval, were already known to him and ordained by his counsel, so that their outcome might be a certain proof of his divinity. Meanwhile, in the first member he denounces punishment to terrify the Jews: in the second he commends his mercy, because he testifies that both the captivity and the liberation of the people will be his work, so that it may be manifest that both foreknowledge and power reside with him. Profane men distribute various duties among their gods. Apollo predicts future things, Jupiter executes them: and one does one thing, another another. But the parts of God are not only to predict or signify future things, but to dispose all things by his own will. For whatever there is of divinity belongs to God alone, nor can it be transferred to another. Therefore he claims for himself both to foreknow and to do, jointly. Saying that he calls from the North, as I recently touched upon, he issues a prophecy concerning the captivity, about which there was no opinion at that time, because the Jews were joined in friendship with the Chaldeans; at the same time he prophesies about the restoration of the people, who were led back into their homeland by Cyrus. Who in that state of affairs would have thought these things credible, especially since they followed after a long interval of time: For they happened about two hundred years after the Prophet had prophesied. The Lord testifies that he is the Author of these things: So that all may understand that the Chaldeans did not rush forth rashly, but were stirred up by the Lord, as if they were scourges for punishing the Jews: the Persians also and the Medes did not subdue the Chaldeans by their own power, except insofar as they were led by the hand of God and impelled. In this heap of opinions, everyone will be able to choose which he has judged the best. For the matter is ambiguous. We do not deny, however, that the two latter ones are sufficiently probable: provided that the Persians came from the East, and the discourse is not about paternal or maternal origin, but about the place from which they were to come. But since the Chaldeans are accustomed to be designated by the North, it seems that this most recent interpretation should rather be subscribed to. Which opinion I see Tirinus also chose, even though he otherwise gladly adheres to his Cornelius: I WILL STIR UP FROM THE NORTH a certain Monarch known to me alone, but unknown to the whole world, namely the Chaldean Nebuchadnezzar: AND HE SHALL COME, another also, FROM THE RISING OF THE SUN, namely Cyrus from Persia, for St. Thomas and Lorinus, Hugo, Pintus, Vatablus, Lyranus, Mariana and Saa explain all these things concerning them; both SHALL CALL UPON MY NAME as that of their Lord and master, that is, both will serve me in the expeditions which I shall demand of them, and both will also acknowledge and worship me, as is evident concerning Nebuchadnezzar from Dan. 3, 5, 9 and ch. 4, 31. Concerning Cyrus also, Ezra 1, 2. Both HE BRINGS MAGISTRATES AS CLAY, that is, he drives the nobles, princes, and all kings opposing him to such a state that they submit themselves to him as victor and are laid under him like the clay of a potter: But who of you, O Idols, HAS ANNOUNCED THESE THINGS, etc. Zwingli wishes to join together different opinions, but he does so in such a way that he tears the text apart and snatches away predicates that belong to the same subject to different ones. I, he says, judge this to be a sententious Synecdoche. So that it may be understood not only as Cyrus alone, as the Rabbis think, or Christ alone, as we do, but truly both Cyrus and Christ with his members. So that what pertains to the North and the East pertains especially to Cyrus and Christ. But as for the invocation, it pertains to the members of Christ, and because of this, to Christ himself.
