As for the trampling, it pertains to both, namely Christ and Cyrus, just as these things can pertain to Cyrus, and to Christ, and to the members of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 25. SVSCITAVI AB AQVILONE, ET VENIET AB ORTV SOLIS) Deus per gradus quosdam clarius clariusq; explicat modum, quo Judæorum restitutio nem sit procuraturus. Pro suscitavi ponendum suscitabo. Medi Judæis ad Septentrionem. Persæ ad Ortum. Cyrus Medopersa, ideo ημίονος in oraculo dictus, Persa per Patrem, Cambysem, Medus per matrem Mandanen Astyagis filiam.

VOCABIT NOMEM MEVM) Me colet, auctoremque suæ felicitatis agnoscet. Vid. Esdr. 1, 2. 7. Joseph. 11, 1.

ADDVCET MAGISTRATVS QVASI LVTVM, ET VELVT PLASTES CONCULCANS HVMVM) Est in Hebræo transpositio quædam, hunc habens sensum: Is veniens principes ut lutum conculcabit, aut ut figulus humum mollem: principes, nempe Astyagen, Crœsum, Nabonidum.

De Cyro intelligunt etiam Lyranus & Vatablus, aliique; at Forerius & Sanctius, ut & Corn. à Lapide de Abrahamo interpretantur vocato ab oriente, vel è Chaldæa & è Septentrione vel Mesopotamia, qui nominis divini cultor fuit, & tum per se, tum per Posteros suos Reges potentes debellavit, ut hæc sit quædam quasi ἀνακεφαλαίωσις. Alii de Christo malunt accipere: quem ab Aquilone & Oriente suscitatum dicit Osiander, quod Nazareth patria educationis ipsius, respectu Hierusalem sita sit ad Aquilonem & Orientem, sed ea explicatio argutior, quam solidior. Autores notarum Belgicarum Christum ab Oriente & Septentrione excitatum dicunt, quod imperium ejus ab uno mundi termino ad alterum sese porrigat. Sed non de imperii amplitudine sonat verbum EXCITANDI ab Oriente, verum ortum & originem indicat. Ideo convenientior videri possit Paraphrastarum Vinariensium interpretatio: Christum ab Oriente excitatum, quia ratione Deitatis Oriens est ex alto, Luc. 1, 78. A Septentrione vero ratione humanæ naturæ, quia duæ naturæ à se invicem discrepant, sicut Aquilo ab Ortu: Verum de excitatione ceu re futura sermo est, quæ prædici nequiverit ab Idolis, quod non congruit æternæ generationi Filii Dei, nec distantia naturarum in Christo per Austrum & Orientem uspiam exprimitur, aut commode exprimi potest. Exponit etiam de Christo Oecolampadius, etsi non declarat, quomodo ab Oriente & Aquilone ipse excitatus dicatur, sed hoc de populo Christi dictum velit. E Rabb. ipsis de Messia Kimchium Patrem, & Filium accipere notat Musculus; fatetur tamen se non videre, quomodo ille ab Aquilone & Oriente excitatus dici possit. Quapropter alii de gentibus & populis interpretantur excitandis, ut Christo se submittant. Ita Hieronymus, qui tamen videtur per excitandos ab Aquilone gentes, per eum, qui ab ortu solis est, Christum intellexisse: Suscitasse se dicit ab Aquilone populum nationum. Suscitantur autem ab

Aquilone, ut credant in eum, qui venerit ab Ortu So- lis. de quo supra legimus, quis suscitavit ab Oriente justum, seu justitiam? Et alio loco, Ecce vir Oriens nomen ejus. Similis est explicatio Cyrilli; addit ra- tionem, quia si regionem Judæorum respicias, quæ maxime ad Austrum vergit, magis est Aquilonaris terra gentium. Videtur autem eum, qui ab Ortu solis est, Christum dicere, eo quod scriptum sit de eo, Ecce, vir Oriens nomen ejus. B. Brentius vero utrumq; refert ad vocationem gentium, quod nempe gentes ab Aquilone & Ortu Solis excitandæ sint, & acces- suræ ad Ecclesiam, sicut cap. 9. dicitur: Ab Orien- te adducam semen tuum, & ab Occidente colligam te &c. Sic etiam Piscator explicat, neque abnuunt Autores notarum Belgicarum. Sed quum argumen- tum hic adversus gentium deos, & cultores eorum adducatur, non videtur id inde depromi potuisse, quod solus Deus prędicere queat vocationem gen- tium ad Ecclesiam, quin potius tali prædictione in hac causa opus fuerit, quæ gentes ipsas suo tempo- re, cum completa fuerit, convincat, ut aggregen- tur ad Ecclesiam. Hæc aggregatio finis est. Me- dium ergo, ex quo veritatem doctrinæ cælestis co- gnoscere debeant, aliud esse oportet, distinctum ab aggregatione gentium. Notat etiam Musculus expositioni huic non satis bene convenire, quod additur, & veniet super Principes quasi super lutum, & quemadmodum figulus calcabit lutum: Ideo aliam sententiam reddidit B. Lutherus; ab Aquilone & Ortu Solis distributive intelligo, i. e. undecunque voluere, sive hinc, sive isthinc. Ab oriente Chaldæum ad salvandum, ab Aquilone Assyrium ad perdendum &c. Hoc vos idola non potestis. Alii, pergit B. Lu- therus, de Christo hunc locum accipiunt, quod is quos- dam ab Aquilone, quosdam ab Oriente sit vocaturus. Bona quidem sententia est, sed ego generalem sequor de omnibus sive ad perdendum, sive ad salvandum vocatis, includitur autem in hanc generalem senten- tiam etiam Christus. Cæterum cum exemplum in- duci hic a Propheta verisimilem sit, quo non modo potentiam suam, sed etiam futurorum præscien- tiam ostendat Dominus, cujus expertes sunt genti- lium Dii, non abnuimus speciale quoddam desi- gnari: quod quale hic sit, quia non quis, sed tantum unde excitandus sit, definitur, ambiguum est. Quæ forte causa est, cur explicatio illa de Cyro Ebræis sese probarit, & Christianis nonnullis placuerit, Hebræi enim, ut Hieronymus ait, suscitatum ab A- quilone, & venire ab ortu Solis Assyrium interpre- tantur, & Persas, qui venerint Hierusalem, & o- mnes Principes illius conculcaverat, nullumque ido- lorum, quæ colebant, hoc scierit esse venturum, nisi so- lus Dominus, qui ultus est eos pro peccatis suis. Aliam adhuc interpretationem tradit Calvinus postremis istis cognatam, qui divisim illa ab Aquilone & O- riente intelligit: Ego, inquit, duas res hic a Prophe- ta notari existimo. Nam cum dicit, ab Aquilone, in- telligit Chaldæos, ab Oriente, Medos ac Persas, ac si diceret, duæ mutationes memoratu dignæ contingent, nam Chaldæos excitabo, quorum Regnum in sublime eveham. Deinde advenient Persæ, qui eorum poten- tiam ad se transferent. Hæc Dominus quamvis longo postea intervallo futura, jam sibi nota esse, suoq; consi lio ordinata esse docet, ut eorum eventus suæ divinita- tis certum sit documentum. Interea priore membro pænam denuntiat, ad terrendos Judæos: secundo com- mendat misericordiam suam, quia & captivitatem, & liberationem populi, opus suum fore testatur, ut pa- lam sit penes ipsum & præscientiam & potentiam esse. Profani homines varia inter Deos suos officia distri- buunt. Apollo prædicit futura, Jupiter exsequitur: atq; alius alia agit. Dei vero partes sunt non solum futura prædicere, aut fignificare, sed omnia disponere suo arbitrio. Quicquid enim divinitatis est, in solum Deum competit, nec alio transferri potest. Ideo tam præscire, quam facere conjunctim sibi vendicat. Ab Aquilone se vocare dicens, ut nuper attigi, vatici- nium edit de captivitate, de qua nunc nulla opinio erat, quia Judæi cum Chaldæis amicitia juncti erant, si- mul de restitutione populi vaticinatur, qui per Cyrum in patriam reductus est. Quis in illo rerum statu hæc credibilia esse existimasset, præsertim cum longo post temporis intervallo sequuta sint: Nam circiter du- centos postea annos evenerunt, ex quo Propheta vati- cinatus erat. Harum rerum Authorem se esse Domi- nus testatur: Ut omnes intelligant, Chaldæos non te- mere prosiliisse, sed à Domino fuisse excitatos, quasi flagella Judæis castigandis: Persas quoque & Medos non sua virtute Chaldæos subegisse, nisi quatenus du- cti manu Dei atq; impulsi sunt. In hoc cumulo sen- tentiarum eligere poterit quisque, quam judicarit optimam. Res enim ambigua est. Non diffitemur tamen duas posteriores satis probabiles esse: siqui- dem Persæ ab Oriente venerint, nec de origine pa- terna aut materna, sed de loco, unde venire debe- ant, sermo sit. Sed quum per Septentrionem Chal- dæi designari soleant, huic novissimæ interpretatio- ni potius subscribendum videtur. Quam senten- tiam video etiam elegisse Tirinum, etsi alias luben- ter adhærescat Cornelio suo: SUSCITABO AB AQUILONE CERTUM quendam Monarcham mihi uni notum, sed toti Orbi ignotum, nempe Chal- dæum Nabuchodonosarem: ET VENIET alter quo- que AB ORTU SOLIS, nempe Cyrus è Perside, de his enim exponunt hæc omnia S. Thomas & Lorinus, Hugo, Pintus, Vatablus, Lyranus, Mariana & Saa; uterq; VOCABIT NOMEN MEUM tanquam Domini & heri sui, id est, uterq; serviet mihi in ex- peditionibus, quas ipsis demandabo, uterq; etiam agno- scet & colet me, ut de Nabuchodonosare constat ex Dan. 3,5.9. & c. 4,31. de Cyro quoq; Esdr. 1, 2. uterq; ADDUCIT MAGISTRATUS QUASI LU- TUM, id est, eo adigit proceres, principes & Reges omnes sibi adversantes, ut sibi victori subdantur, & substernantur, sicut lutum figuli: Sed quis vestrum ô Idola, ANNUNCIAVIT HÆC, &c. Zwinglius conjungere vult diversas sententias, quod vero ita facit, ut textum discerpat, & prædicata, quæ ad eundem pertinent, ad diversa abripiat. Ego, inquit, sententiosam Synecdochen istam esse arbitror. Ut non modo vel Cyrum solum, quomodo Rabbini putant: vel Christum solum, quomodo nos, verum & Cyrum & Christum cum membris ejus intelligat. Ut quod ad Aquilonem atque Orientem attinet, maxime perti- neat ad Cyrum & Christum. Quod autem ad invoca- tionem, ad membra Christi, atq; propter hoc ad Chri- stum ipsum. Quod denique ad conculcationem, ad u- trumq; puta Christum & Cyrum, quomodo & ad Cy- rum, & ad Christum, & ad membra Christi hæc per- tinere possunt.

## 41:26
Verse 26. WHO HAS DECLARED FROM THE BEGINNING) Which of the gods predicted these things a long time before? that is, almost 150 years.

AND FROM THE BEGINNING) The same thing said twice.

THAT WE MAY SAY, HE IS JUST) That is, he justly claims the name of God for himself.

THERE IS NONE NEITHER ANNOUNCING) Any of the gods.

NEITHER PREDICTING) Any prophet serving those gods.

NOR HEARING YOUR WORDS) Namely, concerning that restoration of the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 26. QUIS SIGNIFICAVIT A PRIMORDIO) Quis deorum hæc prædixit longo ante tempore? id est, an- nis ferme 150.

ET A PRINCIPIO) Idem bis dictum.

VT DICAMVS, JVSTVS EST) Id est, juste ille si- bi Dei nomen vindicat.

NON EST NEQVE ANNVNTIANS) Deorum a- liquis.

NEQVE PRÆDICENS) Propheta aliquis illis diis serviens.

NEC AVDIENS SERMONES VESTROS) Nempe de illa Judæorum restitutione.

## 41:27
Verse 27. THE FIRST TO SION WILL SAY.) In the Hebrew it is not, he will say: but I say is to be understood. I, the first God, signify this.

BEHOLD THEY ARE PRESENT) The Jews will be present from all the ends of the earth.

AND I WILL GIVE JERUSALEM A PREACHER OF GOOD TIDINGS) I give now already Isaiah, who proclaims the restoration of the city.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected. Yet it does not correctly determine those whom the Lord predicts will be present; rather, that THEY SHALL BE PRESENT refers to the preceding. Behold THESE, to wit, shall be present, or are about to come to pass, which I have foretold. And I WILL GIVE JERUSALEM A PREACHER OF GOOD TIDINGS. Through these, many think Christ is designated, who in Isaiah 61:1 is introduced as a preacher of good tidings, with Cyril leading the way, and from the Reformed, Oecolampadius, Zwingli, as well as Piscator, the author of the Belgian notes. Of our own, Brentius, Osiander, and the Weimar Paraphrast, etc. But because a perpetual antithesis is instituted between the true God and the gods of the nations, since God testifies that He is the first to foretell these things to Zion, and to give a MESSENGER to Jerusalem, because God foretells these things not immediately, but through His messengers the Prophets, whereas on the contrary among the Gentiles there is no one who can enter into counsel, no one among those gods is so skilled in the future that he can answer anything certain to his consultants about that matter. Whence he concludes: Behold all are unjust (they undeservedly claim for themselves the name of gods, as Grotius not badly says) and their works are vain, wind, and their idols are empty; their opinion seems preferable, who do not indeed understand Isaiah precisely, but generally all through whom God foretold such things, which pleased not only Oecolampadius, Calvin, Musculus, Cornelius a Lapide, Tirinus, and Menochius, but was also handed down before them by the Blessed Luther, who takes these as a repetition, and explains the words we have discussed thus: I give my word, and the ministers of the word to my people. I therefore am the true God, but your religion and justice are nothing. Therefore, in the German translation, he rendered it in the plural, so that there might be an Enallage of the singular number for the plural, in the word מבשׂר, 'und gebe Jerusalem Prediger' (and I will give Jerusalem preachers).

Latin:

Vers. 27. PRIMVS AD SION DICET.) In Hebræo non est, dicet: sed subaudiendum dico. Ego Deus pri- mus id fignifico.

ECCE ADSVNT) Aderunt Judæi ex omnibus ter- ræ finibus.

ET JERVSALEM EVANGELISTAM DABO) Do jam nunc Efaiam, qui prædicat restitutionem urbis.

Recte castigatur Vulgatus. Non tamen recte determinat eos, quos adfore prædicit Dominus, imo illud ADERUNT respicit superiora. Ecce HÆC scil. aderunt, vel eventura sunt, quæ prædixi. Et urbi Jerusalem EVANGELISTAM DABO. Per hæc pleriq; Christum, qui Es. 61, 1. ceu Evan- gelista introducitur, designatum censent, præeun- te Cyrillo, & è Reformatis Oecolampadio, Zwinglio, utpote Piscatore, Autor. notar. Belgicarum. E no- stris Brentius, Osiander & Paraphrast. Vinariens. &c. Sed quia antithesis instituitur perpetua inter Deum verum & Deos gentium,quum testetur Deus se pri- mum hæc Sioni prædicere, & Hierosolymæ מבשׂר NUNCIUM dare, quia Deus non immediate, sed per nuncios suos Prophetas,hæc prædicit,quum ex adverso inter gentiles nullus sit, qui ineat consi- lium,nemo sit ex illis Diis ita futuri peritus,ut con- sultoribus suis de ea re certi quicquam respondere possit. Unde concludit: Ecce omnes injusti (imme- rito Deorum nomen sibi vendicant, ut non male Grotius) & vana opera eorum, ventus, & inania simulacra eorum; præferenda videtur eorum sen- tentia, qua non quidem Efaiam præcise, sed gene- ratim omnes, per quos Deus talia prædixit, intel- ligunt, quæ non tantum Oecolampadio, Calvino, Musculo, Cornel. à Lapide, Tirino, Menochio pla- cuit, sed etiam à B. Luthero ante hos tradita est,qui hæc pro repetitione habet,& verba, de quibus egi- mus, sic exponit: Ego do verbum meum, & mini- stros verbi populo meo. Ego igitur sum verus Deus, vestra autem religio & justitia nihil sunt. Ideo in Germanica translatione in plurali reddidit, ut E- nallage sit numeri singularis pro plurali, in voce מבשׂר, und gebe Jerusalem Prediger.

## 41:28
Verse 28. AND I SAW) However much I may look around.

THERE WAS NOT AMONG THEM ANYONE, WHO WOULD ENTER INTO COUNSEL, AND WHEN ASKED WOULD ANSWER A WORD) There is no one among those gods so skilled in the future that he can answer anything certain to his consultants about that matter.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ET VIDI) Quantumvis circumspectem.

NON ERAT EX ISTIS QVISQVAM, QVI INI- RET CONSILIVM, ET INTERROGATVS RESPON- DERET VERBVM) Nemo est ex illis diis ita futuri peri- tus, ut consultoribus suis de ea re certi quicquam respon- dere possit.

## 41:29
Verse 29. BEHOLD ALL ARE UNJUST) They undeservedly claim for themselves the name of gods.

AND THEIR WORKS ARE VAIN) The worship which is offered to them: as above in 24.

WIND AND EMPTY ARE THEIR IDOLS) They are worth nothing in themselves, nor do the spirits that use them have any power against God.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ECCE OMNES INJVSTI) Immerito deo- rum nomen sibi vindicant.

ET VANA OPERA EORVM) Cultus, qui eis ex- hibetur: ut supra 24.

VENTVS ET INANE SIMVLACRA EORVM) Nihil per se valent, nec qui iis utuntur spiritus quicquam contra Deum.

## 42:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLII.

The well-pleasedness of God the Father in the Messiah, and His meekness, and the illumination of the Gentiles, with an exhortation to thanksgiving, and a rebuke of ingratitude, especially of the Jewish people and their punishment.

Verse 1. BEHOLD MY SERVANT.) The Septuagint understood these things of the whole Jewish people: but to one looking at everything well, it will appear that the discourse of God returns to Isaiah, of whom above in 41:27. These things, however, were fulfilled more sublimely in Christ, whose figure Isaiah bore as much as he could, as did Jonah, Jeremiah, and certain others.

Grotius therefore establishes a double sense: a literal one concerning Isaiah, and a mystical one concerning Christ; but neither should a double sense be attached to the oracles of Scripture, nor does Grotius prove that these things should be accepted concerning Isaiah according to a literal sense; for that Isaiah is definitely understood by the 'preacher of good tidings' in chapter 41:28 has not yet been proven: nor if Isaiah were designated by that name there, would it follow that the same person is understood here: Whence it will be taught that the same is the מבשׂר of chapter 41:27, of whom the Lord speaks here, BEHOLD MY SERVANT. Sanctius concedes that there is an allusion here to those words in chapter 41:27, but in this way, as if God were saying: Behold, I will give them (the Prophets): nay, behold, I will give my servant, my elect, I am meditating on a GREATER thing than what I have bestowed upon you in the Prophets. And how does that passage square with Isaiah, 'He shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles' v. 1, 'He shall set judgment in the earth, and the isles shall wait for his law' v. 4, 'I have given thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles' v. 7. It is manifest that these and other things are snatched away to Isaiah not without σφάλματι (error). But the literal and proper sense of this prophecy does not concern Isaiah, but the Messiah, to whom these and all things in this discourse apply perfectly, and of whom those things were explained by the Holy Spirit Himself in the New Testament. The LXX Interpreters rashly added of their own the word Jacob and Israel, rendering it in this way: ἰακὼϐ ὁ παῖς μȣ, ἀντιλήψομαι ἀυτȣ̃. ἰσραὴλ ὁ ἐκλεκτός μȣ, πρόσεδέξατο ἀυτὸν ἡ ψυχή μȣ. For the Hebrew truth simply has: Behold my servant and my elect. Nor yet did the Greek Fathers, to whom it was not permitted to inspect the Hebrew text, through ignorance of the language, take the text of the LXX Interpreters concerning Jacob or Israel, but concerning Christ, whom they say was called Jacob and Israel because He was born of the blood of Jacob according to the flesh, as Cyril explains. In which sense Justin also understood it in Trypho. It is not therefore certain at all that the LXX took these things concerning the whole Jewish people. Furthermore, the Holy Scripture does not only interpret this concerning Christ in a mystical sense, but has openly testified that these things were predicted by Isaiah concerning Christ, and not concerning another. Thus Matthew, ὅπως πληρωθῇ, 'that it might be fulfilled' which was spoken by Isaiah, when he quotes the words of the Prophet at length in Matt. 12:18, 19, 20, 21, which he interprets concerning Christ performing miracles without clamor, and says they were fulfilled in Him: therefore it must be that they were predicted concerning Him, not concerning Isaiah. And thus also the description of this servant, in whom the soul of God was well pleased, was explained by God Himself, when with a public and illustrious manifestation He declared on two occasions that Christ Jesus was this servant of His, who was to fulfill all righteousness, crying from heaven, Matt. 3:17, ch. 17:2, etc., ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μȣ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα, i.e., this is that beloved of mine, in whom my soul was well pleased. For in no one except this servant does God have good pleasure, so that He might fully acquiesce: indeed, no one could please Him, nor even serve Him, unless this servant had merited that for us by his servitude and obedience. Therefore Calvin rightly says: By this testimony we understand that Christ is not only gracious to the Father, but that He alone is pleasing and acceptable to Him, so that there is no reason for obtaining grace from God except through Christ the intercessor. And in this sense this passage is cited by the Evangelists, just as Paul also teaches in the first chapter to the Ephesians, that we were so reconciled in the beloved that we are loved on account of Him. For although Calvin willingly snatches away oracles sounding of Christ to other things, yet in this so evident and illustrious prophecy he did not dare to do so. Concerning the firstborn himself, he says, and the head, it will be clear from the progress of the discourse: because those things which are said cannot be transferred to any other: and the Evangelists remove all controversy. Nor was there easily any doubt about it among Christian Interpreters, except that some took it concerning Cyrus: which opinion, however, was rejected by the rest as inept, and rejected by Grotius himself. Add that the Jews themselves acknowledged that the discourse here is not concerning the Prophet, but concerning the Messiah. R. David Kimchi to these words, 'behold my servant' הוא מלך משיח, he is King Messiah, it is so explained also in the Targum. הא עבדי משיח, Behold my servant Messiah. What of the fact that Grotius himself acknowledged that the oracle must be taken in this way, when he was engaged in the explanation of Matthew: For that wanton audacity of distorting almost all prophecies to ancient times had not yet bewitched his mind, which leaves almost no predictions regarding the times of the New Testament, looking at them in a literal sense. For he himself had corrected the LXX Interpreters in his annotations on the Gospel according to Matthew 12, 18. Nor do I doubt that this passage of the Prophet was understood by those same Interpreters as if it were dealing with the Hebrew people, and that because of those things which precede in chapter 41, 8, and those which follow in 43, 1; although, however, from other passages of Isaiah, and especially from those which are in the Prophet chapter 44, 6, they OUGHT to have observed that this deals with him who is to bring light both to the Jews and to the Gentiles; which the Chaldean Paraphrast rightly saw, who added the name of the Messiah here. Therefore, Grotius ought also to have observed the same, and not to distort the words of the Prophet to Isaiah. He made progress in writing, but towards Judaism.

Verse of the same. I WILL UPHOLD HIM) Better: upon whom I lean, whose work I wish to use.

Not only is work and ministry implied, but the εὐδοκία of God, or something similar, as the added words teach; therefore such a servant is designated, in whom God may thoroughly acquiesce, to whom He may hand over and commit all things into his hands. Whence the Lord calls him HIS ELECT, in whom His soul may have good pleasure. Which sound concerning Christ, according to the letter: For John the Baptist says of him in John 3: The Father loves the Son and has handed over all things into his hand. And Christ himself testifies in John 5, 22: The Father has given all judgment to the Son, so that they may also honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Other men, as many as are born of Adam, are cast away before God on account of sin; Christ alone is elect, because he knew no sin, although he does not wish to enjoy his election alone, but makes us participants in it. In Christ alone is good pleasure had, since all things outside of Christ are concluded under sin. Matthew 3, 17; chapter 17, 5; Ephesians 1, 6. Grotius himself taught that the passage in Matthew 3, 17 is parallel to this one of ours, Annotations on Matthew 3, 16. I think the appearance of the dove pertained to this, because he who was in Christ, the Spirit, had already been described long ago by Isaiah 42, 1, 2, 3 by a special mark of meekness, as is explained below in 12, to which Christ's words also seem to look, which are in Luke 9, 55, and to verse 17 of the same place, ἀγαπητὸς. Which in Isaiah is בחירי ἐκλεκτός μȣ: For ἐκλεκτος and ἀγαπητος are accustomed to be used for the same thing, see Psalm 2. Moreover, there is clearly the same sense in these words ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα, which is in those of Isaiah רצתה נפשי, just as some Greek Interpreters also have, εἰς ὃν εὐδόκησαν ἡ ψυχή μȣ. He observed there that the Greeks say εὐδοκεῖν τινι to signify a propense affection; but this εὐδοκεῖν ἐν τινι, here and in Matthew 17, 5; Mark 1, 11; Luke 3, 22; 1 Corinthians 10, 5, 38; or εἰς τίνα, Matthew 10, 11, 18, 2. Peter 1, 17, that it is a manifest Hebraism חפץ בו, as in Genesis 34, 14, or רצה בו, as in 1 Chronicles 28, 4, and that the interpreter of Irenaeus translates this ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα as 'in whom I have felt well,' book 3, chapter 11. Zwingli has this to say about the emphasis of this phrase at this place: The speech is not best rendered in Latin as 'in whom I have been pleased,' but it sounds more like this, 'in whom I am placid.' He who composed the hymn περὶ ᾿Επιφανείας understood this, when he sings thus: Truly you are my son pleasing to me, in whom I am appeased, etc. The Hebrew words רצתה נפשי, that is, 'my soul takes pleasure,' are too powerful to be exhausted by two words. But that paraphrase, 'In whom I am appeased,' comes very close. So much for him.

Verse of the same. HE SHALL BRING FORTH JUDGMENT TO THE GENTILES) He will announce my judgments against the Medes and Babylonians.

Grotius understands this as a judgment of punishment, which is to be announced against those nations, the Medes and Babylonians: But that denunciation of punishment does not fit this argument or eulogy of meekness: because the elect servant of the Lord is commended for grace, leniency, and meekness; and clamor is removed, such as is usually the case of those who flare up in anger and denounce the punishments and judgments of God: for then the Holy Scripture requires the raising of the voice, Isaiah 58, 1, which Grotius himself observed regarding those words, 'nor will his voice be heard outside': They are accustomed, he says, who flare up in anger, to speak so loudly that their voice is heard outside the house by passersby. Nothing here specifically about the Medes and Babylonians. But the announcement of judgment to the Gentiles is predicted generally, not for the terror, but for the consolation of the Gentiles. To whom this meekness and grace will be demonstrated. Grotius taught at Matthew 12, 18 that the law of God is to be understood here as being published among the Gentiles, not a judgment against the Medes and Babylonians: κρίσιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπαγγελεῖ. The origin of the word κτ̃ τὸ λεπτότατον, they had placed ἐξοίσει following the LXX. Moreover, it appears that ἐπαγγέλλειν is properly signified by that word in Deuteronomy 22, 19 and in many other places: from which it is also easy to gather which meaning of the polysemous word מִשְׁפָּט, which the Hellenists translate as κρίσιν everywhere, fits best here: namely, that which indicates a law or norm of living. For it is most proper for a law to be published: That this is true is shown by what follows immediately in the Hebrew. The distant nations will wait for his law. So much for Grotius there. But since the word of God is accustomed to be designated generally by the name of judgment and law, as is evident especially from Psalm 119, the word of the Gospel, which was announced by Christ and preached among the Gentiles by the Apostles, is more rightly understood here, because in it the grace and goodness of God are exhibited, and by it bruised reeds and smoking flax, prostrate and contrite hearts, are raised up and strengthened. For Grotius also wishes the Spirit of meekness and humility to be understood here properly and peculiarly, when the Lord says: 'I have put my Spirit upon him, he will bring forth judgment to the Gentiles,' designated by the visible sign of the dove, Matthew 3, and he observes in his annotations on Matthew 12, 18 that this sense is required both by what follows in the Prophet and by the occasion which led Matthew to cite the Prophet. But what the continuity might be, I have given my Spirit, the Spirit of meekness and humility, that he may bring forth judgment to the nations, that is, the law, or even the judgment of affliction and punishment. Although not only the Spirit of meekness and humility is indicated through Isaiah, or descended upon Christ in Baptism, to whom the Spirit was given not by measure, John 3:34, that is, the immense gifts of the Spirit, upon whom rests the Spirit of wisdom, of counsel, etc., Isaiah 11:2. Therefore, that phrase, 'he shall bring forth judgment,' the blessed Luther explains thus: There will be another person than Moses, who lay hidden in a Jewish corner: for this one spread Judgment, that is, the word of the Gospel, among the wandering nations, and those entangled in various sects and cults. He calls it judgment, because the Gospel simply condemns all righteousness, and commends and offers the judgment of Christ alone. The blessed Brentius thinks not otherwise: He shall bring forth judgment to the nations. This is said in such a way, just as if Christ were to rule among the nations by royal or worldly right. But the very nature of Christ's kingdom, and the deeds of Christ, interpret this saying. For to bring forth judgment to the nations in the kingdom of Christ is not to prescribe political laws to the nations, but it is to announce the Gospel concerning the remission of sins and eternal life. For this is the judgment by which the whole world is convicted of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment.

Latin:

CAPUT XLII.

Dei Patris complacatio in Messia, hujusque mansuetudo, & illuminatio gentium, cum exhortatione ad gratiarum actionem, & reprehensione ingratitudinis, imprimis po- puli Iudaici ejusq́; pœna.

Vers. 1. ECCE SERVVS MEVS.) LXX. hæc de toto populo Judaico intellexerunt: sed bene cuncta intuenti apparebit, Dei sermonem redire ad Esaiam, de quo supra 41, 27. Sublimius autem hæc impleta in Christo, cujus fi- guram, quantum potuit, gessit Esaias, ut & Jonas, Jeremi- as, & alii quidam.

Sensum ergo geminum constituit Grotius: Literalem de Esaia: Mysticum de Christo; sed neq; geminus sensus Scripturæ oraculis affingendus est, nec probat Grotius,quod secundum literalem sen- fum hæc de Esaia accipienda sint; Nam quod cap. 41, 28. per Evangelistam Esaias definite intelligatur, nondum evictum est: neque si ibi designaretur eo nomine Esaias,consequens esset, eundem etiam hic intelligi:Unde docebitur,quod idem sit מבשׂר cap. 41,27. de quo hic Dominus, Ecce SERVUS MEUS. Concedit Sanctius, allusum hic esse ad illa verba c. 41, 27. sed hoc modo, ac si dicat Deus: Ecce, ipsos (Prophetas) dabo: imo, ecce, ego dabo servum meum, electum meum, MAJUS quid medi- tor, quam quod in Prophetis vobis largitus sum. Et quomodo in Esaiam quadrat illud, Judicium gen- tibus proferet v. 1. ponet in terra Judicium, legem ejus insulæ expectabunt v. 4. dedi te in fœdus populi, in lu- cem gentium, v. 7. Manifestum est, hæc, & alia non absq; σφάλματι abripi adEsaiam. Sensus vero li- teralis & proprius hujus vaticinii non Esaiam con- cernit, sed Messiam, cui hæc & omnia in hac con- cione apprime conveniunt, & de quo illa explicata sunt ab ipso Spiritu S. in Novo Testamento. LXX. Interpp. de suo addidere temere vocem Jacob & Israël, hoc modo reddentes: ἰακὼϐ ὁ παῖς μȣ, ἀν- τιλήψομαι ἀυτȣ̃. ἰσραὴλ ὁ ἐκλεκτός μȣ, πρόσε- δέξατο ἀυτὸν ἡ ψυχή μȣ. Ebræa enim veritas sim- pliciter habet: Ecce servus meus & electus meus. Neq; tamen Græci Patres, quibus Ebræum textum inspicere non licuit, per linguæ ignorantiam, de Ja- cobo, aut Israële textum LXX. Interpp. accepere, sed de Christo, quem Jacobum & Israelem dictum a- junt, quia natus sit ex sanguine Jacob secundum carnem, ut explicat Cyrillus. Quo sensu etiam in- tellexit Justin. in Tryph. Non ergo certum omni- no, quod LXX. de toto populo Judaico hæc acce- perint. Porro S. S. non tantum sensu mystico de Christo interpretatur, sed palam testatus est, de Christo, non de alio hæc prædicta esse ab Esaia. Ita Matthæ9 ὅπως πληρωθῇ, ut impleretur, quod dictum est per Esaiam, cum prolixe verba Prophetæ addu- cit Matt. 12, 18. 19. 20. 21. quæ de Christo absq; clamo- re miracula patrante interpretatur, & in ipso im- pleta dicit: de ipso ergo prædicta esse oportet, non de Esaia. Atque ita etiam descriptio hujus servi, in quo sibi placuit animaDei, explicata est àDeo ipso, cum publica & illustri manifestatione binis vicib9 declararet, Christum Jesum esse hunc servum suum, qui omnem justitiam implere debebat, clamans de cœlo, Matth. 3, 17. c. 17, 2. &c. ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μȣ ὁ ἀ- γαπητὸς, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα, q. d. hic est ille dilectus me- us, in quo sibi placuit anima mea. In nullo enim præ- terquam in hoc servo beneplacitum habet Deus, ut penitus acquiescat: imo placere nullus illi pote- rat, ac ne servire quidem, nisi hic servus servitute & obedientia sua id nobis promeruisset. Ideo recte Calvinus: Hoc testimonio intelligimus Christum non solum gratiosum esse Patri, sed ipsum solum ei gra- tum, & acceptum esse, ut nulla sit ratio impetrandæ à Deo gratiæ, quam intercessore Christo. Atque hoc sen- su hic locus ab Evangelistis citatur, quemadmodum & Paulus primo ad Ephes. cap. docet, nos in dilecto sic fuisse reconciliatos, ut propter ipsum amemur. Etsi enim libenter oracula de Christo sonantia alio ab- ripiat Calvinus, in hoc tamen tam evidenti, & illu- stri vaticinio ausus id non fuit. De ipso quidem pri- mogenito, inquit, & capite nunc sermonem haberi ex progressu liquebit: quia neque ad alium quempiam transferri possunt, quæ dicuntur: & Evangelistæ controversiam omnem tollunt. Neq; facile de eo du- bium fuit inter Interpp. Christianos, nisi quod qui- dam de Cyro acceperint: quæ sententia tamen tan- quam inepta à reliquis reprobata, & à Grotio ipso rejecta est. Adde, quod agnovere ipsimet Judæi, non de Propheta, sed de Messia sermonem hic esse. R. David Kimchi ad hæc verba, ecce servus meus הוא מלך משיח, is est Rex Messias, ita exponitur etiam in Targ. הא עבדי משיח, Ecce servus meus Messias. Quid quod Grotius ipse agnoverit, ita acci- piendum esse oraculum, cum in Matthæi ex- plicatione versaretur: Nondum enim sibi men- tem excantarat proterva illa audacia, de vatici- niis plerisque omnibus ad tempora prisca detor- quendis, quæ nullas pene relinquit prædictiones, ad Novi Testam. tempora sensu literali spectantes. Castigarat enim ipse LXX. Interpp. annotationi- bus in Evang. ad Matth. 12, 18. Neque dubito ab iis- dem Interpp. hunc Prophetæ locum ita intellectum, quasi de Hebræo populo ageret, idque propter ea, quæ præcedunt cap. 41, 8. & quæ sequuntur 43, 1. cum ta- men ex aliis Esaiæ locis, præsertim vero ex iis, quæ sunt apud Prophetam cap. 44, 6. observare DE- BUISSENT, agi hic de eo, qui lucem allaturus sit tum Judæis, tum Gentibus; quod recte vidit Chal- dæus Paraphrastes, qui Messiæ nomen hic addidit. Idem ergo observare etiam debebat Grotius, nec verba Prophetæ detorquere ad Esaiam. Scribendo profecit, sed ad Judaismum.

Vers. eod. SUSCIPIAM EUM) Melius: cui innitor, cujus opera uti volo.

Non tantum opera & ministerium innuitur, sed εὐδοκία Dei, vel simile quid, ut verba addita docent; Ideoq; talis servus designatur, cui penitus acquie- scat Deus, cui omnia in manus tradat, & commit- tat. Unde ELECTUM SUUM vocat Dominus, in quo anima sua beneplacitum habeat. Quæ de Chri- sto sonant, quoad literam: De illo enim Johannes Baptista Joh. 3. Pater diligit Filium & omnia tradi- dit in manum ejus. Et Christus ipse testatur Joh. 5, 22. Pater omne judicium dedit Filio, ut etiam ho- norent Filium, sicut honorent Patrem. Alii homines quotquot ex Adamo nascuntur, abjecti sunt coram Deo propter peccatum, solus Christus est electus, quia non novit peccatum, etsi solus sua electione frui non velit, sed nos ejus participes reddat. In solo Christo beneplacitum habetur, quum omnia extra Christum sub peccato conclusa sint. Matth, 3, 17. c. 17, 5. Eph. 1, 6. Locum Matth. 3, 17. huic nostro parallelum esse docuit Grotius ipse, Annot. ad Matt. 3, 16. Columbæ speciem huc pertinuisse puto, quod is, qui in Christo erat Spiritus, speciali mansuetudinis nota jam olim descriptus esset ab Esaia 42, 1. 2. 3. ut in- fra explicatur 12. quo respicere etiam videntur Chri- sti verba, quæ sunt apud Luc. 9, 55. & ad v. 17. ejus- dem loci ἀγαπητὸς. Quod apud Esaiam est בחירי ἐκλεκτός μȣ: Nam ἐκλεκτος & ἀγαπητος pro eo- dem poni solent, vid. Psal. 2. Est autem plane idem sensus in his verbis ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα, qui in illis Esaiæ רצתה נפשי uti & Græci quidam Interpretes ha- bent, εἰς ὃν εὐδόκησαν ἡ ψυχή μȣ. Observavit ibi, ad affectum propensum significantem Græcos dicere εὐ- δοκεῖν τινι; hoc vero εὐδοκεῖν ἐν τινι, hic & Matth. 17, 5. Marc. 1, 11. Luc. 3, 22. 1. Cor. 10, 5. 38. aut εἰς τίνα, Matth. 10, 11. 18. 2. Petr. 1, 17. manifestum esse He- braismum חפץ בו, ut Gen. 34, 14. aut רצה בו, ut 1. Paral. 28, 4. & Irenæi interpretem hoc ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα vertere, in quo bene sensi, lib. 3. c. 11. Zwinglius de em- phasi hujus phraseos ad h. l. ita habet: Non optime redditur Latinis oratio, in quo mihi complacui, sed magis hoc sonat, in quo sum placidus. Id intellexit, qui hymnum περὶ ᾿Επιφανείας condidit, quum sic canit: Vere filius es tu meus mihi placitus, in quo sum pla- catus &c. Hebraica רצתה נפשי, id est, allubescit a- nima mea, potentiora sunt, quam ut duobus possint exhauriri verbis. At ea paraphrasis, In quo sum placatus, proxime accedit. Hæc ille.

Vers. eod. JUDICIUM GENTIBUS PROFERET) Ju- dicia mea in Medos, & Babylonios enunciabit.

De judicio pœnæ intelligit Grotius, quod adver- sus gentes istas, Medos & Babylonicos enuncian- dum sit: Sed illa pœnæ denunciatio non convenit huic argumento, vel elogio mansuetudinis: quia commendatur servus electus Domini à gratia, le- nitate, mansuetudine; ac removetur clamor, qua- lis esse solet eorum, qui ira excandescunt, ac pœnas & judicia Dei denunciant: tum enim vocis eleva- tionem requirit S. S. Ef. 58, 1. quod observavit ipse Grotius ad verba illa, nec audietur vox ejus foris: Solent, inquit, qui ira exardescunt, ita altum loqui, ut vox eorum extra domum a prætereuntibus exau- diatur. De Medis & Babyloniis speciatim hic nihil. Sed annunciatio judicii gentibus futura generaliter prædicitur, non in terrorem, sed in solatium gen- tium. Quibus hæc mansuetudo & gratia demon- strabitur. Legem Dei hic intelligendam esse inter gentes publicandam, non judicium adversus Medos & Babylonios, ad Matth. 12, 18. docuit Grotius: κρί- σιν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπαγγελεῖ. Originem vocis κτ̃ τὸ λεπτότατον, secuti LXX. posuerant ἐξοίσει. Cæterum proprie ἐπαγγέλλειν ea voce significari apparet Deut. 22, 19. aliisq; multis in locis: unde etiam collectu facile est, quæ significatio vocis πολυσήμου מִשְׁפָּט, quam κρίσιν passim vertunt Hellenistæ, hic maxime quadret: ea nempe, quæ legem sive normam vivendi indicat. Le- gis enim maxime proprium est, publicari: Verum hoc esse ostendit, quod mox in Hebræo sequitur. Ad le- gem ejus longinque gentes expectabunt. Hæc ibi Grotius. Quum vero judicii & legis nomine, gene- ratim verbum Dei designari soleat, ut è Psal. cum- primis 119. constat, rectius hic verbum Evangelii, quod à Christo annunciatum, & per Apostolos in- ter gentes prædicatum, intelligitur, quia in eo gra- tia & bonitas Dei exhibetur, eoque calami quassati & lina fumigantia, corda prostrata & contrita eri- guntur & corroborantur. Nam & Grotius vult, Spiritum mansuetudinis & humilitatis hic proprie & peculiariter intelligi, cum dicit Dominus: Dedi Spi- ritum meum super eum, judicium gentibus proferet, designatum visibili columbæ signo, Matth. 3. eumque sensum exigere tum quæ sequuntur apud Prophetam, tum occasionem, quæ Matthæum ad citandum Pro- phetam adduxit, observat annot. ad Matth. 12, 18. Quæ autem συνέχεια foret, dedi Spiritum meum, Spiritum mansuetudinis & humilitatis, ut judicium proferat gentibus, h. e. legem, vel etiam judicium af- flictionis & supplicii. Quanquam non solum man- suetudinis & humilitatis Spiritus per Esaiam indice- tur, aut in Baptismo super Christum descenderit, cui Spiritus datus non ad mensuram Joh. 3, 34. h. e. immensa Spiritus dona, super quem requiescit Spi- ritus sapientiæ, consilii, &c. Ef. 11, 2. Illud ergo, pro- feret judicium, ita explicat B. Lutherus: Erit alia persona, quam Moses, qui in angulo Judaico latuit: hic enim sparsit Judicium, h. e. Evangelii verbum in gentes errabundas, & variis sectis & cultibus impli- catas. Vocat judicium, quod Evangelium simpliciter damnat omnem justitiam, & solius Christi judicium commendat & offert. B. Brentius haud modo aliter: Judicium gentibus proferet. Hoc ita dicitur, perinde ac si Christus esset inter gentes dominaturus, jure Re- gio aut mundano. Sed & ipsa regni Christi ratio, & res gestæ Christi interpretantur hoc dictum. Proferre enim judicium gentibus in regno Christi, non est gen- tibus leges politicas præscribere, sed est Evangelium de remissione peccatorum & vita æterna annuncia- re. Hoc enim est judicium, quo universus mundus arguitur de peccato, de justitia, & de judicio.

## 42:2
Verse 2. HE SHALL NOT CRY OUT) He shall do nothing with a troubled mind.

NEITHER SHALL HE ACCEPT A PERSON) In the Hebrew, he shall not lift up, supply 'his voice,' more than the matter requires.

NOR SHALL HIS VOICE BE HEARD OUTSIDE.) Those who burn with anger are accustomed to speak so loudly that their voice is heard outside the house by those passing by.

These glosses are too meager. For there is here a litotes. He shall not cry out, he shall not lift up his voice, nor shall his voice be heard outside, that is, he will be meek, mild, placid, and humble. Christ will teach, but without clamor; he will not be a tumultuous preacher, but placid and sweet.

He will not make his voice heard, i.e., the voice of wrath and tumult, but he will make the voice of grace heard, as the blessed Luther explains, which exegesis is taken from the following words. These are opposed, according to Brentius, partly to the promulgation of the Decalogue, and partly to the promulgation of political laws in worldly empires. For in the promulgation of the Decalogue, such a clamor, such a horrible voice was heard, that the Israelite auditors drew back and were all but dead from fear. And in the promulgation of civil laws or edicts, a signal is usually given publicly, either by a trumpet or by the tumultuous sound of a drum. And a herald, with the most intense voice he can, cries out in the streets and threatens most severely that unless one obeys the edict, he shall be visited with extreme punishment. But Christ is a calm, gracious, and pleasant herald, so that as many as heard him were refreshed rather than terrified. Nor will his voice, he says, be heard outside; that is, he will not boast, he will not glory in his majesty, ineptly, importunately, and invidiously; but when he has performed miracles, he will threaten, as the Evangelist says, those who obtain health, not to make him manifest; so far is he from ambitiously, as the Princes of this world are wont to do, inculcating the titles of his majesty, etc. And as these things are said concerning the personal preaching of Christ, so they also hold their truth in the propagation of his Gospel. For Christ wishes it to be propagated for this reason, that we may understand that it is not wrath but grace, not destruction but salvation, not death but life, that is announced to us in the Gospel. Concerning the emphasis of the words, which he passed over here with dry feet, Grotius dealt with it at Matthew 12:19, rendering this sense and intention: that Christ was of such goodness that he did not wish the vices of those to be made public, of whom there remained some good hope. But it is evident that Matthew is not dealing with the vices of the Jews not being divulged, but with the miracles of Christ not being divulged. Thus, therefore, he teaches that meekness and humility will be joined with his calm and sweet preaching, devoid of all boasting: that his proclamation will be neither horrible or terrible, nor with ostentation, or μετὰ πολλῆς Φαντασίας, but will be sweet, calm, and humble. Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, Matt. 11:29.

Latin:

Vers. 2. NON CLAMABIT) Nihil aget perturbato animo.

NEQVE ACCIPIET PERSONAM) In Hebr. non eleva- bit, supple vocem, plusquam res exigit.

NEC AVDIETUR VOX EJVS FORIS.) Solent, qui i- ra exardescunt, ita altum loqui, ut vox eorum extra do- mum à prætereuntibus exaudiatur.

Glossæ hæ nimis jejunæ. Est enim hic λιτότης. Non clamabit, non elevabit vocem, nec audietur vox ejus foris, i. e. mansuetus, mitis, placidus atque hu- milis erit. Christus docebit, sed sine clamore, non erit tumultuosus prædicator, sed placidus & suavis.

Non audire faciet vocem suam, i. e. iræ & turbæ vo- cem, sed gratiæ vocem audire faciet, uti B. Lutherus explicat, quæ ἐξήγησις à verbis seqq. sumitur. Op- ponuntur hæc, juxta Brentium, partim promulga- tioni Decalogi, partim promulgationi legum Poli- ticarum in mundanis imperiis. Nam in Decalogi promulgatione tantus clamor, tam horrenda vox audita est, ut auditores Israëlitæ retrocederent, ac præ metu tantum non exanimarentur. Et in pro- mulgatione legum seu edictorum civilium solet publice signum dari aut buccina, aut tumultuoso sono tympani. Et præco, quam potest intentissi- ma voce, in plateis clamat, ac severissime minatur, ut nisi quis edicto pareat, extremo supplicio afficia- tur. Christus autem præco est placidus, gratus, & jucundus, ut quotquot audirent, magis recrearen- tur, quam exterrerentur. Nec vox ejus, inquit, au- dietur foris, hoc est, non jactabit, non gloriabitur de majestate sua, inepte, importune & invidiose, sed cum ediderit miracula, interminabitur, ut Ev- angelista ait, iis, qui consequuntur sanitatem, ne se manifestum facerent, tantum abest, ut ambitiose, sicut solent Principes hujus mundi, inculcet suæ majestatis titulos, &c. Quæ ut de personali Christi prædicatione dicta sunt; Ita etiam in Evangelii e- jus propagatione veritatem suam obtinent. Quod ea ratione propagari vult Christus, ut intelligamus in Evangelio annunciari nobis non iram, sed gra- tiam, non exitium, sed salutem, non mortem, sed vitam. De vocum emphası, quam hic sicco pede præteriit, egit Grotius ad Matth. 12, 19. sensum & intentionem hanc reddens: Christum ea fuisse boni- tate, ut palam fieri nollet eorum vitia, de quibus ali- quid superesset bonæ spei. At non de vitiis Judæorum haud propalandis, sed de miraculis Christi non di- vulgandis Matthæum agere in propatulo est. Ita ergo cum placida & suavi prædicatione, mansuetu- dinem & humilitatem conjunctam fore docet, o- mnis glorıationis expertem: quod præconium ej9 neq; horribile aut terribile, neq; cum ostentatio- ne, aut μετὰ πολλῆς Φαντασίας, sed suave, placi- dum atque humile futurum sit. Discite à me, quia mitis sum, & humilis corde, Matth. 11, 29.

## 42:3
Vers. 3. A BRUISED REED HE WILL NOT BREAK, AND SMOKING FLAX HE WILL NOT QUENCH.) It is a litotes. For he wishes to say that Isaiah would confirm with his prophecies the Hebrews, to whom some piety remained, but who were almost extinguished by calamities.

This is not the office of Isaiah, but of Christ, not to break a bruised reed and not to quench smoking flax. For he is not dealing only with confirmation in piety, but with the raising up of a terrified soul and the preservation of the little spark of faith, which is the work of Christ; nor does it look only to the Hebrews, but to men of any nation: and here it is referred primarily to the Gentiles, to whom the judgment was to be carried. The blessed Luther well explained the force of that sentence in his Commentary on this passage: that he does not cast away, does not oppress, does not condemn the bruised reed, that is, the wounded conscience, the faint-hearted, those terrified in respect of their sins, the weak in morals and in faith, but cherishes, heals, and lovingly embraces them. That proverbial expression is not explained in the same way: Hieronym. Epist. ad Algas. quaest. 2. He thinks the reed is a musical instrument, that is, a pipe, which, having been tuneful before, when it is broken, ceases to be useful, or if it sounds at all, it is discordant and unrefined, so that there is no patience, whether of the piper or the listener, that would not cast away or destroy such a reed. But others more correctly understand any reed or cane, which, when it is bruised, has no use and is therefore cast away, if indeed it is a matter of patience to sustain those things which lack utility; which is expressed even more in the smoking flax, which not only has no utility but is even a nuisance, whence August. lib. 1. Evang. qq. Q. 3. thinks the flax deserted by the light makes a stench, as we ourselves daily experience and suffer. But such will be the kindness in Christ that as long as there is something fiery in the flax, even if it does not shine so much as it smokes, he will not quench the flax. But concerning that figure of speech, see the blessed Luther on Matthew 12:40. Tom. 4. Jen. Latin. f. 330. There is another figure in these words, namely, tapinosis or emphasis, because it says less than it signifies, as 'he will not quench,' 'he will not break,' that is, he will greatly kindle and consolidate; and that figure is very sweet and powerful in its place for comforting, as if someone is faint-hearted and fears the Sacrament on account of reverence, etc., someone might persuade him with this figure: why do you fear, approach, for Christ will not give you poison. He is not standing behind you with a club. Likewise, he will not devour you. These negatives are very uplifting, because they most powerfully exclude the evil that is feared, and at the same time most opulently include the good that is sought, etc. Grotius had certainly explained the mind of these words much more correctly before: The sense is, he says at Matthew 12:19, he will not further break a reed already broken to some extent. And that is, he will not precipitate into ruin those who have fallen through some weakness, such as most of the Pharisees could be seen to be until that day; nay, on the contrary, he will bind up that which is broken, as it is in Ezekiel 34:16. He makes the same sense in the latter member concerning the wicks, in which the smoke recalls some trace of flame, not to be extinguished entirely. Which, as we have said, he understands of Christ. Although the allegorized meaning comprehends more, that not only are the fallen not to be precipitated into ruin, but also that those bruised by the conscience of sin are not to be utterly broken. For hearts prostrated by the judgment of sin and crushed by various afflictions and the horror of death and hell, what are they but bruised reeds, and when the spark of faith scarcely shines, nay, when scarcely a smoke is left, must they not be considered smoking wicks? Which distinct explanation is hinted at by the blessed Brentius and is retained in the Weimar Paraphrase. To B. Luther, however, it seems that these things can be conveniently distinguished in such a way that the former, concerning the bruised reed, is referred to the conscience, and the latter, concerning the smoking flax, to the instruction of morals and faith, so that both wounded consciences and those weak in morals may be regarded: who added this warning: The life of the brethren ought indeed to be bright and pleasant like light: But sometimes they are moved by Satan, sometimes by the flesh, to sadness, to anger, to moroseness; there they must be borne, there the flax is not to be extinguished, but cherished, etc. It is necessary in the holy Church that there be weak ones and such as those by whose deeds we are offended. Just as in the human body there are not only bones, but also weak and soft flesh. Wherefore the kingdom of Christ consists of those who bear and those who are borne. And our life is a certain composite of strength and infirmity.

Verse of the same.

IN TRUTH HE SHALL BRING FORTH JUDGMENT.) He shall faithfully declare the judgments of God, mixing in nothing of his own affection.

Latin:

Vers. 3. CALAMUM QUASSATUM NON CONTE- RET, ET LINUM FUMIGANS NON EXTINGUET.) Est λιτότης. Vult enim dicere, Esaiam vaticiniis suis con- firmaturum Hebræos, quibus pietatis restabat aliquid; sed pene extinctum calamitatibus.

Hoc non Esaiæ, sed Christi munus est, cala- mum quassatum non conterere, & linum fumigans non extinguere. Non enim id tantum de confirma- tione in pietate, sed de perterrefactæ animæ ere- ctione, & scintillulæ fidei conservatione, quæ opus Christi est, agit; Neq; tantum ad Ebræos spectat, sed ad cujusvis nationis homines: Et hic imprimis ad gentes, ad quas perferendum erat judicium, refertur. Vim sententiæ istius exposuit probe B. Lutherus in Comment. ad h. l. Quod concussum ca- lamum, h. e. sauciam conscientiam, pusillanimes, ex- territos respectu peccatorum suorum, infirmos in mo- ribus, & in fide non abjiciat, non opprimat, non da- mnet, sed foveat, sanet & amanter amplectatur. Pro- verbialis illa loquutio non eodem modo explica- tur: Hieronym. Epist. ad Algas. quæst. 2. calamum musicum instrumentum esse censet, h. e. fistulam, quæ cum canora prius fuerit, ubi frangitur, utilis esse desierit, aut si aliquid sonat, absonum illud est & incon- ditum, ut nulla tanta sit sive tibicinis, sive auditoris patientia, quin calamum ejusmodi abjiciat aut per- dat. Sed rectius alii quemvis calamum aut arundi- nem, quæ ubi quassata est, nullum usum habet, ad- eoque abjicitur, intelligunt, siquidem patientiæ sit ea sustinere, quæ utilitate vacent; quæ adhuc ma- gis exprimitur in lino fumigante, cujus non modo nulla est utilitas, sed etiam molestia, unde August. lib. 1. Evang. qq. Q. 3. linum à lumine desertum pu- torem facit, ut nos ipsi quotidie experimur & pati- mur. Sed ea erit in Christo benignitas, ut quamdiu aliquid igneum est in lino, licet illud non tam splen- deat, quam fumet, linum non extinguat. De figura vero illa sermonis B. Lutherus ad Matth. 12, 40. Tom. 4. Jen. Latin. f. 330. Inest his verbis alia figu- ra, sc. Tapinosis seu emphasis, quia minus dicit, quam significat, ut non extinguet, non confringet, h. e. ma- xime accendet & consolidabit, & est illa figura valde dulcis & potens in loco dicta ad consolandum, ut si pu- sillanimis aliquis sit, & metuat deinde Sacramentum, propter reverentiam &c. persuadeat aliquis hac figu- ra, cur metuis, accede, non enim Christus venenum tibi dabit. Er stehet ja nicht mit der Keule hinter dir. Item Er wird dich nicht fressen. Valde erigunt istæ negativæ, quia excludunt, quod metuitur malum po- tentissime, & simul includunt affirmative, quod peti- tur bonum opulentissime &c. Longe utique rectius antehac exposuerat Grotius mentem horum ver- borum: Sensus est, inquit ad Matth. 12,19. arundi- nem aliquatenus jam fractam non ultra franget. Id vero est, non præcipitabit in ruinam imbecillitate ali- qua lapsos, quales ad istum diem videri poterant Pha- risæorum pleriq;, imo contra τὸ συντετριμμένον καταδήσῃ, ut est apud Ezech. 34, 16. Eundem sensum in membro posteriori facit de Ellychniis, in quibus fumus aliquod flammæ vestigium refert, non extin- guendis penitus. Quæ de Christo, ut diximus, in- telligit. Quamvis plus comprehendat τὸ ἀλληγο- ρέμενον, quod non tantum lapsi haud præcipitandi in ruinam, sed quod etiam peccati conscientia quassati non prorsus conterendi sint. Corda enim judicio peccati prostrata variis afflictionibq & hor- rore mortis atq; inferni contrita, quid sunt nisi ca- lami quassati, & cum vix fidei scintilla lucet, imo vix fumus relictus est, annon ellychnia fumigantia ha- beri debent? Quæ distincta explicatio à B. Brentio innuitur, & in Paraphrasi Vinariensi retinetur. B. Luthero vero videntur ista ita commode distin- gui posse, ut prius de calamo quassato ad conscien- tiam, posterius de lino fumigante, ad morum & fi- dei informationem referatur, ut & sauciæ conscien- tiæ & infirmæ in moribus respiciantur: qui hoc ad- didit monitum: Debebat quidem fratrum vita can- dida & jucunda esse sicut lux: Sed nonnunquam à Satana, nonnunquam à carne eorum commoventur ad tristitiam, ad iram, ad morositatem, ibi ferendi sunt, ibi non est extinguendum linum, sed foven- dum &c. Necesse est in Ecclesia sancta esse infirmos & tales, quorum factis offendamur. Sicut in corpore humano non ossa tantum, sed etiam infirma & mollis caro est. Quare regnum Christi constat ex portanti- bus & portatis. Et vita nostra est compositum quod- dam ex fortitudine & infirmitate.

Vers. eod.

IN VERITATE EDUCET JUDICIUM.) Dei judicia fideliter enunciabit, nihil sui affectus permiscens.

## 42:4
HE SHALL NOT BE SAD, NOR TURBULENT.) In the Hebrew: He shall not grow dim, nor shall he be broken; i.e., he shall neither be deceived by ignorance, nor drawn back by fear from performing his duty.

UNTIL HE SET JUDGMENT IN THE EARTH.) So that he may not the less announce the judgments of God to the lands.

AND THE ISLES SHALL WAIT FOR HIS LAW.) Better: Let the isles await his teachings. That is, let those Assyrians, Mesopotamians, and others know for certain that the things which Isaiah says will come to pass.

A remarkable perversity again. First, the words do not sound concerning the faithful announcement of the judgments of God, but concerning the bringing forth of judgment, which is, that Judgment may be placed in the earth, as the Holy Scripture explains. Which is a divine result, not of any Prophet, but of Christ himself, who alone thus brings forth judgment, and places judgment and justice in the earth, Isa. 9, 7. Jerem. 23, 7. not only by the spreading of the Evangelical doctrine, but also by the erection of judgment and justice through the word in the Church in the hearts of men. B. Glassius indeed accepts it concerning the pronunciation of judgment, but that which is proper to Christ, in Gram. S. p. 453. Matth. 12, 20. The words of the Prophet are thus rendered ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν, until he shall cast forth judgment unto victory, i. e. until he shall pronounce a just sentence, by which he may declare himself the victor of all enemies, which is what happened when the Gospel was promulgated throughout the whole world. Grotius in his Annotations on Matthew explains it concerning the demonstration of the justice of judgment, but he describes it in such a way that it fits Christ alone. What Isaiah had said twice, he will bring forth judgment to truth, and until he shall place judgment in the earth, Matthew rightly contracted, and retained 'until' from the latter member, but from the former he placed that which the Greek Interpreter here translated as εἰς νῖκος, expressing the sense most fully: which I prefer to saying that the interpreter slipped through the ambiguity of the Syriac word, which the LXX had turned as εἰς ἀλήθειαν ἐξοίσει κρίσιν (thus the version of the LXX is to be amended from Justin, in which it is wrongly read as εἰς ἀληθῆ), our Interpreter said in the very same sense ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν. Indeed, Justin also cites in another place ἕως ἂν νῖκος ἐξοίσῃ, likewise expressing the sense, not counting the words. משפט or κρίσιν in this place I interpret otherwise than above, as a cause which is called into dispute, in the most accepted meaning. Therefore, to cast forth or to bring forth judgment (for these differ in nothing), unto truth, or unto victory, or unto an end, as in Job 23, 7, or even to bring forth victory, he is said to be one who makes his just causes so manifest that he can carry off the victory before any judge. See Psalm 51, 6. But Christ did this when he bore the evil customs of the Jews with that supreme gentleness and patience, and spared no effort in recalling them to a better way of life: Thus, in the same Prophet, God, recounting how many benefits he had bestowed upon his vineyard, and with how much patience he had awaited good grapes, challenges them to judgment, ch. 5, verse 3, which passage contributes wonderfully to explaining this. In which, however, he has not yet attained the goal: because these things are brought forward from Isaiah not only concerning the patience with which he bore the customs of the Jews, but so that, on the occasion of that withdrawal of Christ and the prohibition of the publication of miracles, the Holy Scripture might set forth the character of Christ and the manner of propagating his kingdom, and teach that the illustrious oracle is to be understood concerning him, but at the same time signify that, although he could accomplish nothing among the Jews with that humility, grace, and meekness of his, he would nevertheless truly bring forth judgment, and produce it unto victory: so that the judgment of Christ may prevail, and even triumph among the nations who will hope in his name, i. e. so that not only the doctrine of the Gospel may be carried forth to victory, and be established among the nations, but that judgment also may be erected, and obtain victory in the hearts of the faithful, and the kingdom of the Messiah be stabilized in justice and judgment. He himself will establish this kingdom, as Blessed Luther paraphrased, so that it may be firm, however much Satan may attempt to subvert it through the princes of the world. For he signifies the cross by the word of establishing. Furthermore, those words, he will not be sad, nor turbulent, do not sound concerning ignorance or fear, but commend again and again the gentleness, meekness, and kindness of Christ, in describing which the Holy Scripture is more prolix there because it can never be sufficiently preached, and thus those things are omitted by Matthew, because the former things only express the same in other words: whose intention here was to propose the gentleness and humility of our Savior from Isaiah, because he did not destroy the Pharisees who were forming a plan against Jesus, how they might destroy Jesus, but withdrew, and nevertheless healed the infirm from among the Jews, so that he might still win them over by his benefits and miracles, which he forbade to be divulged, lest he should seem to seek his own glory, through which, however, he wished those whom he solicited with such patience and gentleness to be led to the recognition of himself; inasmuch as he does not crush the bruised reed, and does not extinguish the smoking flax. Grotius thinks that the Hebrew words are to be rendered thus, with Pagninus and Arias Montanus: He will not grow dim, nor will he be broken. Others explain it otherwise. Aquila and Theodotion, he will not be obscured, and will not run. The Chaldean, he will not be fatigued, nor will he be affected with weariness, until he has ordained judgment in the earth, 'He shall not grow weary, nor let himself be annoyed.' So also the Spaniard and Sixtinus Amama. R. Kimchi explains the word כהה: he will fail; Piscator: 'He shall not faint nor grow weary.' Musculus, he will not fail, nor will he be broken. The English, he will not become remiss, nor will he be broken in spirit; The Italian, he will not be cut off, nor will he be broken, which he explained concerning death. Others with the old Spanish version, he will not be obscured, but will shine, by doctrine and miracles. Thus the Belgian version, he will not be obscured nor broken. Thus also the LXX Interpreters, he will shine, and will not be crushed. Which exposition D. Gomarus prefers: inasmuch as he thinks the splendor of Christ is here opposed to the smoking flax, and his unbroken virtue to the bruised reed. Zwinglius, he will not hallucinate, and will not be headlong. Our Brentius thinks the Vulgate does not oppose the Hebrew text. Others, he says, interpret this differently, but because the vulgar translation does not conflict with the meanings of the Hebrew expressions, we will now follow his opinion. He will not be sad, nor perturbed. Christ does not look upon those approaching with a hard, grim, and truculent countenance, nor does he give them answers with a perturbed spirit, but he himself calls all to himself most humanely, and dismisses them from himself most clemently. The Hebrew words imply that: he will not grow dim, he will not look with dim, sad, or turbid eyes, in the manner of those who scarcely deign to look at others, he will not be broken in spirit by the misdeeds of others; whence Blessed Luther rendered the sense thus: 'He will not be surly nor grim.' The word כהה, as Musculus notes, signifies to contract, to remit, to neglect, to be weak, to prohibit, to fail, to wrinkle, and to obscure; who therefore has handed down this sense of this sentence: He shall not fail, nor shall he be broken, until he sets judgment in the earth, that is, however much the world together with its prince may intend to contradict his word, and move every stone to impede its course, he shall nevertheless not desist from his undertaking, nor shall he rest, until he sets his seat, i. e., the Church of the pious, in the whole world. He does not simply say, until he brings forth judgment, as he had already said in the second [verse], but until he sets judgment in the earth. It is one thing to bring forth the Gospel from Zion, and another to set it in the earth. Thus Musculus. Calvin understood those words differently, he shall not fail, nor shall he be broken. He alludes, he says, to the next verse, and confirms that which was said before, namely that Christ will indeed be placid and gentle toward the weak, yet will have nothing effeminate or soft, because he will manfully execute the office commanded to him by the Father. Thus, both in the translation of the Hebrew text and in the sense of the same, the interpreters are carried off into different directions. Yet no one is easily found who has understood it of Isaiah, and believed that ignorance and fear were here taken away from him. We see no reason why we should depart from the Brentian explanation, which is also Osiander's, and with which the German version of the blessed Luther agrees, which not only agrees with the Vulgate version, but makes much of the commendation of the χρηστότητα [kindness] of the Messiah, in which the Prophet is entirely occupied, as interpreted by the Holy Spirit Himself in the New Testament. For the allegation of the Evangelist sufficiently teaches that this is the argument of the Prophet, who seems to have omitted those words for the reason that they express the same thing, in which sense Jerome also accepted the words of the Prophet, and he interpreted the translation of Aquila and Theodotion likewise: He will not be sad, nor turbulent, but will observe an equality of countenance at all times. For which Aquila and Theodotion interpreted: He will not obscure, and will not run, until he sets judgment in the earth. And the sense is: No sadness of countenance will deter him, nor will he hasten to punishment, who has reserved the truth of judgment for the last time. The LXX interpreters also Sanctius reduces the translation to this sense, so that the Septuagint signify that Christ will not be turbulent and sad; they declare this either by the lack of contrition of the mouth, or by his serenity and splendor, because these are signs of modesty and peace. Or certainly, while they say he is not to be crushed, they indicate that he is not to be overcome by turbulent motions of the mind, and in others they are accustomed to exterminate modesty and gentleness.

But above all they manifest the τρεβλότητα [perversity] of Grotius, which are added concerning the nations or the Islands: which among the LXX are thus: And in his name the nations will hope. Jerome translated, and the islands will wait for his law. Which Grotius thus perverts: Let them know for certain, the Assyrians, Mesopotamians, and others, that the things which Isaiah says will come to pass. Nothing here specifically about the Assyrians. Nor does the Prophet confirm only the certainty of those predictions. Nor are these words of a command, but words of a prediction: indicating what is to be, not what ought to be done. Finally, they do not concern a few Assyrians or Mesopotamians, but extend far more widely. For the Prophet comprehends all islands and lands. As Brentius rightly observed: The doctrine of the Gospel indicated by judgment is to be divulged as much in the cities of the earth as in the islands of the sea, and thus in the whole world. The interpretation of Musculus is almost identical. The word יחל signifies both to hope and to wait. By islands, however, he understands the nations, more remote from the peoples of the rest of the world, and separated by the circuit of the sea, so that the sense may be: he will set his word so far in the earth, i.e., in the world of lands, that the islanders also, divided and separated from the rest, will embrace his doctrine and place their hope in it; thus by islands he indeed understands the nations and peoples of the nations, but separated and secluded from the rest, of which he makes mention here for this reason, that he may express the amplitude of the kingdom of Christ. From which sense Grotius does not depart in his Annotations on Matthew; indeed, he proves the same from the preceding, from the emphasis of the words, and the allegation of the Evangelist. I will transcribe his passage in full: because it makes for the explanation of the words, as they have been adduced by Matthew: and ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι ἀυτõ ἔθνη ἐλπιõσι, it coheres best with the preceding. For the nations deservedly place their trust in the goodness of him who bore with the disobedient Jews with such gentleness; איים, which is in the Hebrew, does not always signify islands, but often any regions whatsoever, as Gen. 10, 5. Rightly, therefore, both the LXX and our interpreter rendered the sense with the word ἐθνῶν. Likewise ייחלו ἐλπιõσι is best, for thus both the LXX and the Hebrews explain it elsewhere. But that for לתורתו among the LXX men we have ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι, it is not a fault of the writers: for Justin also cites it twice thus. And our author here, who in this whole place has not followed the LXX, likewise renders it, ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι, or τῷ ὀνόματι, as some codices have. Doubtless תורה for the Hebrews frequently signifies that which the more elegant Greeks otherwise call דרך, a sect. The Hellenists, however, call the same ὄνομα, because it is the custom for followers to be named after the author of their institution. Thus Paul denies that he baptized anyone in his own name, indicating that he is the author of no new institution. The LXX, therefore, who interpreted this place concerning the Israelitic people, thought that the Prophet meant this, that foreign nations would place their trust in the profession of Judaism: whereas the sense is, as Matthew and the thing itself teaches us, that the nations would do that very thing in the profession of Christianity, which in itself contains the perfection of Judaism.

As for the words, UNTIL HE SETS JUDGMENT IN THE EARTH, some think that the time is defined by them, as if he were saying, he will be gentle and mild until death, because he announced the Gospel until death. As Hector Pintus explains, this gentleness will last until death, for then he will set judgment in the earth, reconciling man to the Father, dying for our sins. Sanctius is of a similar opinion. Christ is said to be about to be gentle and patient until, exalted on the cross and master of victory, he brings judgment. For Matthew recited those things thus: Until he casts forth judgment unto victory. But these things ought not to be restricted to the person and to the time of the life of Christ. For such as Christ was in the days of his flesh in setting judgment in the earth, such he is still, even if he does not do it now immediately, but through his ministers. Wherefore Brentius rightly: he did not exhibit this virtue in the lands only of the Church, but he still retains it, now sitting at the right hand of his Father. Because the description of the mighty works of Christ pertains to this, that all nations may be invited to believe in the Gospel of Christ, and may know that they cannot offer worship truly pleasing to God, nor obtain true salvation, unless they embrace this Christ with their faith, and follow the calling of his Gospel. Concerning which Calvin also had warned: This ought not to be restricted to the person of Christ, but to the whole course of the Gospel, because he not only performed the embassy enjoined upon him for three years, but continues the same daily through his ministers. It is said less conveniently that Christ now continues his embassy, because he has been exalted to the right hand of God; even if he still sets judgment in the earth through his legates, and will continue to do so until the consummation of the age. St. Irenaeus book 3 against. Hæres. chap. 2. reads these things thus: 'until he shall send forth judgment unto contention.' By which metaphor he indicates that the doctrine of the Gospel, which comes under the name of law and judgment, will come into contention with other laws, which lust, avarice, and ambition have raised into the world: which will all eventually fall, with the Gospel, or the judgment of Christ, conquering and triumphing everywhere in the world.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NON ERIT TRISTIS, NEQVE TURBU- LENTUS.) In Hebræo: Non caligabit, neq; frangetur; i. e. neq; ignorantia falletur, neque metu retrahetur à facien- do officio.

DONEC PONAT IN TERRA JUDICIUM.) Quo mi- nus Dei judicia terris annuntiet.

ET LEGEM EJUS INSULÆ EXPECTABUNT.) Melius: Documenta ejus insulæ exspectent. Id est, certo sciant illi Assyrii, Mesopotamienses, atque alii, eventu- ra, quæ dicit Esaias.

Insignis iterum ςρεβλότης. Primum non de annunciatione fideli judiciorum Dei verba sonant, sed de eductione judicii, quæ sit, ut ponatur in terra Judicium, ut explicat S. S. Quod est ἀποτέλεσμα divinum, non Prophetæ alicujus, sed ipsius Christi, qui solus ita educit judicium, & in terra judicium & justitiam ponit, Esa. 9, 7. Jerem. 23, 7. non solum Evangelicæ doctrinæ divulgatione, sed judicii et- iam atq; justitiæ per verbum in Ecclesia in cordi- bus hominum erectione. B. Glassius id accipit qui- dem de pronunciatione judicii, sed ea, quæ Christo propria est, in Gram. S. p. 453. Matth. 12, 20. Verba Prophetæ sic redduntur ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν, donec ejiciat in victoriam judicium, i. e. do- nec pronunciet sententiam justam, qua se victorem omnium inimicorum declaret, id quod factum est, cum Evangelium promulgaretur per universum orbem. Grotius in Annot. ad Matth. de justitiæ ju- dicii demonstratione explicat, sed eam ita describit, ut uni Christo conveniat. Quod bis dixerat Esaias ad veritatem judicium educet, & donec ponat in terra judicium, recte contraxit Matthæus, & donec retinuit ex posteriori membro, ex priori autem id po- suit, quod Græcus Interpres hic transtulit εἰς νῖκος, sensum plenissime exprimens: quod malo, quam am- biguitate vocabuli Syriaci lapsum dicere interpretem, quod LXX. verterant εἰς ἀλήθειαν ἐξοίσει κρίσιν (ita ex Justino emendanda versio LXX. in qua male legi- tur, εἰς ἀληθῆ) Interpres noster eadem plane senten- tia dixit ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τὴν κρίσιν. Imo & Justinus citat altero loco ἕως 8 νῖκος ἐξοίσῃ itidem sensum exprimens, non verba annumerans. משפט si- ve κρίσιν hoc loco aliter, quam supra interpretor pro causa, quæ in disceptationem vocatur, receptissima significatione. Ergo κρίσιν ἐκβάλλειν aut ἐκφέρειν, (hæc enim nihil differunt) εἰς ἀλήθειαν, sive εἰς νῖκος, sive εἰς τέλος, ut Jobi 23, 7. aut etiam ἐκφέρειν νῖκος is dicitur, qui justa sua ita manifesta facit, ut quovis judice victoriam referre possit. Vid. Psal. 51, 6. Hoc autem fecit Christus, cum summa illa lenitate ac pa- tientia malos Judæorum mores pertulit, nihilq; operæ pepercit eis ad meliorem frugem revocandis: Ita apud eundem Prophetam Deus referens, quanta beneficia vineæ suæ præstitisset, quantaq; cum patientia probas uvas exspectasset, ad judicium provocat c. 5. comm. 3. qui locus mire huic explicando facit. In quibus ta- men nondum assequutus est scopùm: quia non tan- tum de patientia, qua mores Judæorum pertulit, hæc ex Esaia adducuntur, sed ut occasione illius se- cessus Christi & vetitæ miraculorum propalatio- nis indolem Christi & modum propagandi regni ejus S. S. sisteret, atq; oraculum illustre de ipso ac- cipiendum esse doceret, simul autem significaret, quamvis ista humilitate, gratia ac mansuetudine sua nihil apud Judæos efficere posset, judicium tamen vere educturum, & εἰς νῖκος producturum: ut ob- tineat judicium Christi, atq; vel inter gentes trium- phet, quæ in nomine ejus sperabunt, h. e. ut non tan- tum doctrina Evangelii ad victoriam efferatur, & inter gentes constituatur, sed judicium etiam eri- gatur, ac victoriam obtineat in cordibus fidelium, & regnum Messiæ in justitia & judicio stabiliatur. Ipse statuet hoc regnum, ut B. Lutherus παρεφραζε, ut sit firmum, quantumvis Satan per principes mundi subvertere id conetur. Significat enim verbo statuendi crucem. Porro verba illa, non erit tristis, neq; turbulen- tus, non de ignorantia aut metu sonant, sed Chri- sti lenitatem, mansuetudinem & χρηστότητα ite- rum, iterumque commendant, in qua describenda prolixius est ibi S. S. quia nunquam illa satis prædi- cari potest, atque adeo prætermittuntur illa à Mat- thæo, quod priora solum aliis verbis efferant: cujus intentio hic erat πεισότητα Salvatoris nostri & hu- militatem ejus ex Esaia proponere, quod Phari- sæos consilium adversus Jesum ineuntes, quomo- do Jesum perderent, non perdiderit, sed fecesserit, & infirmos nihilominus e Judæis curarit, ut bene- ficiis & miraculis suis adhuc eos lucrifaceret, quæ divulgari vetabat, ne gloriam propriam quærere videretur, per quæ tamen eos, quos tanta patien- tia & lenitate solicitat, ad sui agnitionem perductos volebat; Siquidem calamum quassatum non con- terat, & linum fumigans non extinguat. Ebræa κα- τ᾽όδα ita reddenda esse, cum Pagnino, & Ariæmon- tano putat Grotius: Non caligabit, neq́; frangetur. Alii aliter exponunt. Aquila & Theodotio, non ob- scurabitur, & non curret. Chaldæus non fatigabi- tur, neque tædio afficietur, donec ordinaverit in terra judicium, Er sol nicht müde werden, noch sich ver- driessen lassen. Sic etiam Hispanus & Sixtinus Ama- ma. R. Kimchi verbum כהה exponit: יתושל defi- ciet; Piscator: Er sol nicht verschmachten noch mü- de werden. Musculus non deficiet, neq́; frangetur. Anglicus non remissus fiet, nec animo frangetur; I- talus, non exscindetur, nec frangetur, quod de morte exposuit. Alii cum Hispanica veteri versione, non obscurabitur, sed splendebit, doctrina & miraculis. Sic Belgica versio, non obscurabitur nec frangetur. Sic etiam LXX. Interpp. splendebit, neque conteretur. Quam expositionem D. Gomarus præfert: siqui- dem putet splendorem Christi lino fumiganti, e- jusq; infractam virtutem calamo quassato hic op- poni. Zwinglius, non hallucinabitur, & non erit præceps. Brentius noster Vulgatam Ebræo textui non adversari putat. Alii, inquit, alter hoc inter- pretantur, sed quia vulgata translatio non repugnat significatis Hebræarum dictionum, sequemur nunc sententiam ejus. Non erit tristis, nec perturbatus. Non aspicit Christus adeuntes duro, turvo ac trucu- lento vultu, nec dat eis responsa perturbato animo, sed vocat ipse ad se omnes humanissime, & dimittit à se clementissime. Id Ebræa inferunt: non caligabit, non aspiciet oculis caligantibus, subtristibus aut turbidis, more eorum, qui vix aspectu alios dignan- tur, non frangetur animo aliorum malefactis; un- de sensum ita reddidit B. Lutherus: Er wird nicht mürrisch noch greulich seyn. Verbum כהה, notante Musculo, significat contrahere, remittere, negligere, debile esse, prohibere, deficere, rugare & obscurare, qui proinde hunc sensum tradidit hujus sententiæ: Non deficiet, neq́; frangetur, donec ponat in terra ju- dicium, h. e. quantumvis verbo illius contradiceturus sit mundus una cum suo principe, omnemque lapidem moturus, quo cursum illius impediat, haud tamen cœ- pto desistet, nec quiescet, donec sedem illi, i. e.
