YOU ARE MY WITNESSES) You know these things were written down long ago. Above 43, 10.

It is not conveniently explained concerning the people of Israel, because the peoples of this world are to be understood, so that the singular is put for the plural, in this sense: since I appointed the peoples of this world, the plural pronoun למו indicates, which Musculus rightly observed, whom Grotius is accustomed to follow for the most part. Nor is it rightly said that the people in Israel were to endure forever, inasmuch as whose excision was frequently predicted, and who for so many centuries now has been no people: Therefore B. Luther rendered it in the plural: Die Völcker. We present this sense from the sources: And who like me shall call, and shall announce this, and shall set it in order for me, TO SET ME ASIDE a people of the age, or the nations of the world, that is, I call and bring to pass those things which are not: Rom. 4, 17. and announce them, before they come to pass, and set in order for me, in another manner than I have placed the peoples of the world, and things to come, and those things which are to be, let him announce to them. Jerome rendered it thus, and is like me. He calls those things which are not, as though they were, and explains the order of my creature, by which I have balanced all things with reason, from the time I made man upon the earth. DO NOT THEREFORE FEAR, NOR BE TROUBLED: Grotius adds, by this captivity: But this consolation extends more widely, and is not to be so restricted, AND THEN I MADE THEE HEAR, AND ANNOUNCED. Which Grotius accepts thus: Remember that this was already predicted to you long ago through Isaiah: Foreseen weapons do less harm. But GOD appeals to all the predictions by which He announced future events through the Prophets, which had their fulfillment with the Israelites themselves as witnesses. Is it not from that time, from which I made you hear future things, and announced them through the Prophets, that you are my witnesses, that is to say, that those things came to pass, and therefore that you may certainly believe that the rest will also come to pass.

Latin:

Vers. 6. EGO PRIMVS ET EGO NOVISSJ- MVS) Vide supra 41, 4. ABSQUE ME) In Hebræo: præter me. NON EST DEVS) sunt tantum λεγόμενοι θεοὶ, ut ait Paulus 1. Corinth. 8, 9. VOCET, ET ANNUNCIET, ET ORDINEM EXPONAT MIHI, EX QUO CONSTITVI PO- PVLVM ANTIQVVM) Ex Hebræo sic vertas: Quis, ut ego, significat & publicat, idque ordine sicut ego, qui disposui omnia populo perpetuum duraturo? Quis illorum, qui dicun- tur Dii, tuis populis omnia eventura suo quoque ordine præ- significat, ut ego ei populo, quem mirificis modis conservo? VENTVRA) Ex propinquo imminentia. Confer quæ supra 41, 22. 23. ET QVÆ FVTVRA SVNT) Multo post. Vers. 8. NOLITE TIMERE, NEQVE CONTVR- BAMINI) Hac captivitate. EX TVNC AVDIRE TE FECI, ET AN- NVNCIAVI) Memento per Esaiam pridem id tibi prædi- ctum. Tela prævisa minus feriunt. VOS ESTIS TESTES MEI) Scitis olim hæc præscripta. Supra 43, 10.

Non exponitur commode de populo Israëlis, quia populos hujus mundi intelligi, ut singularis pro plurali positus sit, hoc sensu, ex quo constitui populos hujus mundi, pronomen plurale למו in- dicat, quod recte observavit Musculus, quem ple- rumque sequi consuevit Grotius. Neque populus in Israel perpetuo duraturum esse recte dicitur, utpote cujus excisio frequenter prædicta, & qui per tot se- cula jam nullus fuit populus : Ideo B. Lutherus in plurali reddidit: Die Völcker. Sensum ex fon- tibus hunc exhibemus : Et quis sicut ego vocabit, & annunciabit hoc, & ordinabit illud mihi, PRÆ PONERE ME populum seculi, vel gentes mundi, hoc est, ut vocet atque efficiat, sicut ego vo- co, & efficio ea, quæ non sunt: Rom. 4, 17. & an- nunciet ea, antequam fiant, & ordinet mihi, alia ra- tione præterquam ego posui populos mundi, & ventura, & quæ futura sunt, annunciet illis. Hiero- nymus sic reddidit, & similis mei est. Vocat ea quæ non sunt, quasi sint, & exponit ordinem creaturæ meum, qua cuncta ratione libraverim, ex quo feci hominem in terra. NOLITE IGITVR TI- MERE, NEQVE CONTVRBEMINI: Addit Grotius, hac captivitate: Sed solatium hoc latius patet, nec ita restringendum, ET TVNC AVDIRE TE FECI, ET ANNNVCIAVI. Quod Grotius sic accipit: Memento per Esaiam id tibi pridem jam prædictum: Tela prævisa minus nocent. Sed provocat DEUS ad prædictiones uni- versas, quibus per Prophetas futura prænunciavit, quæ testibus ipsis Israelitis complementum suum habuere. Nonne ex eo tempore, quo audire te feci fu- tura, & prenunciavi per Prophetas, vos estis testes mei, quod sc. illa evenerint, ideoque & reliqua even- tura, certo credatis.

## 44:9
Vers. 9. AND THEIR MOST BELOVED THINGS SHALL NOT PROFIT THEM) The Interpreter wrote, if I am not mistaken, most loved things. For so it is in the Hebrew, and in the Greek τὰ καταθύμια αὐτῶν.

THEY THEMSELVES ARE THEIR WITNESSES) Those very best of shapers are witnesses, whence and how those things were made, which they call Gods: Since the uncertain craftsman was making whether a bench or a Priapus, He preferred it to be a God.

BECAUSE THEY DO NOT SEE NOR UNDERSTAND) Those idols have neither instruments of sensing nor of understanding.

THAT THEY MAY BE CONFOUNDED) Wherefore those who make and worship such things ought deservedly to be ashamed, Psal. 97, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ET AMANTISSIMA EORVM NON PRODERVNT EIS) Scripsit, ni fallor, Interpres ama- tissima. Sic enim in Hebræo, & in Græco τὰ καταθύμια αὐτῶν.

IPSI SVNT TESTES EORVM) Ipsi illi forma- tores optimi testes sunt, unde & quomodo facta sint ista, quæ Deos vocant: Cum faber incertus scamnum faceretne Priapum, Maluit esse Deum.

QVIA NON VIDENT NEQVE INTELLI- GVNT) Simulacra ista neque sentiendi neque intelligen- di instrumenta habent.

VT CONFVNDANTVR) Quare merito pudere debeat eos, qui talia faciunt & colunt, Psal. 97, 7.

## 44:10
Vers. 10. WHO HAS FORMED A GOD) That is, who, unless he is insane, would fashion a God for himself?

Latin:

Vers. 10. QVIS FORMATVIT DEVM) Id est, quis, nisi demens, Deum sib fabricet?

## 44:11
FOR THEY ARE CRAFTSMEN FROM AMONG MEN) Translate: false above others: they shall be ashamed, that is to say.

Vers. 11. THEY SHALL BE PUT TO SHAME.) The Interpreter wrote they shall stand, as it is in the Hebrew, and in the Greek ϛητάσωσαν. Let all those craftsmen of Gods arrive, and stand forth in the presence. They shall immediately fail in their cause.

Grotius rightly corrects the Vulgate version, whether the Interpreter wrote it so or not. He ought, however, to have tested the versions against the Hebrew truth in other places as well, and not, when they deviate, to argue that the Hebrew text is corrupt, which we have not infrequently observed him doing.

Latin:

FABRI ENIM SUNT EX HOMINIBVS) Ver- te: falsi præ cæteris: pudesient scilicet.

Vers. 11. FLABUNT.) Interpres scripsit stabunt, ut est in Hebræo, & in Græco ϛητάσωσαν. Adveniant cuncti illi fabri Deorum, & coram consistant. Statim causa cadent.

Recte corrigit Grotius Vulgatam versio- nem, sive ita scripserit Interpres, sive non. De- buisset autem in aliis etiam locis ad Ebraicam veri- tatem exigere versiones, non autem cum illæ de- viant, textumEbræum corruptiones arguere,quod non raro in ipso observavimus.

## 44:12
Vers. 12. HE HAS WORKED WITH A FILE) What he here calls a file, he perhaps better translates as an axe in Jeremiah 10, 3.

HE SHALL HUNGER AND SHALL FAIL) That is, unless he has food, his God will not be able to provide him with food, as I provided Manna for my people. And so it will be necessary that he fail.

HE SHALL NOT DRINK WATER, AND SHALL GROW WEARY) If there be no water present for him to drink, his god will not give it to him, as I do to mine from the rock. And so, before his god who is looking on, he will collapse from thirst.

Latin:

Vers. 12. LIMA OPERATVS EST) Quod hic li- mam, id Jeremiæ 10, 3. melius forte asciam vertit.

ESVRIET ET DEFICIET) Id est, nisi cibum ha- beat, Deus suus ei cibum præbere non poterit, ut ego meis Manna præbui. Itaque necesse erit deficiat.

NON BIBET AQVAM, ET LASSESCET) Si non adsit ei aqua quam bibat, Deus suus ipsi eam non da- bit, ut ego meis ex rupe. Itaque præ siti Deo suo inspe- ctante concidet.

## 44:13
Ver. 13. THE CARPENTER STRETCHETH OUT HIS RULE) A line, for a rule is that by which angular things are made.

HE FASHIONED IT WITH A PLANE) Better: He marks it out with a red-chalk line. Μιλτείῳ ϛάγματι in the Greek Epigram.

AS A BEAUTIFUL MAN DWELLING IN A HOUSE) About to dwell in a temple, just as a rich man dwells in his own house.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ARTIFEX LIGNARIVS EXTENDIT NORMAM) Lineam, nam norma est ad quam fiunt angulosa.

FORMAVIT ILLVD IN RVNCINA) Melius: Designat illud amussi miniata. Μιλτείῳ ϛάγματι in Epigram- mate Græco.

QVASI SPECIOSVM HOMINEM HABITAN- TEM IN DOMO) Habitaturum in templo, sicut homo dives domi suæ habitat.

## 44:14
Ver. 14. HE TOOK THE HOLM OAK) In Hebrew, תרזה: whence the Greek word θύρσος.

AND THE OAK WHICH HAD STOOD AMONG THE TREES OF THE FOREST) More correctly: Which had raised itself among the trees of the forest. The letter א often has the force of a relative pronoun: as in that which immediately follows, ואמצו.

HE PLANTED A PINE) The Hebrew ארן seems rather to signify a mountain ash. He planted, that is, he set it up before himself, so that he might hew it, and bestow upon it the form conceived in his mind.

Latin:

Vers. 14. TVLIT ILICEM) In Hebræo, תרזה: unde Græca vox θύρσος.

ET QVERCVM QVÆ STETERAT INTER LIGNA SALTVs) Rectius: Quæ extulerat se inter arbo- res sylvæ. א sæpe habet vim pronominis relativi: ut in eo quod statim sequitur ואמצו.

PLANTAVIT PINUM) ארן Hebræum videtur potius ornum fignificare. Plantavit, id est, destituit coram se, ut eam dedolaret, eique formam animo conceptam in- duceret.

## 44:15
AND IT BECAME FOR MEN A FUEL) Namely, the part which fell off by the hewing. The following words explain this.

Ver. 15. AND HE WORSHIPPED) The Hebrew word, which he uses here, signifies προσπίπτειν, to fall prostrate upon the ground.

AND HE IS BOWED DOWN BEFORE IT) He bent the knee. It is a Chaldean word, which Isaiah purposely used here. The Arabs also use it in the same sense. It exists often in Daniel. Other nations had other rites in worshipping idols: none of which Isaiah wished to pass over.

Latin:

ET FACTA EST HOMINIBUS IN FOCUM) Nempe pars quæ dolando decidit. Explicant id sequentia.

Vers. 15. ET ADORAVIT) Vox Hebræa, qua hic utitur, fignificat προσπίπτειν in terram procumbere.

ET CURVATUS EST ANTE ILLUD) Ge- nuaflexit. Vox est Chaldæa, quam de industria hic usurpa- vit Esaias. Usurpant eam eodem sensu & Arabes. Exstat apud Danielem sæpe. Aliarum gentium alii erant ritus in colendis idolis: quorum nullum præterire voluit Esaias.

## 44:16
Ver. 16. AND OF THE MIDST THEREOF HE EATETH FLESH) That is, he eats cooked flesh with the other part.

AHA) You might better translate: Well done: for it is an interjection of one rejoicing, as in Psalm 35:21.

I SAW A HEARTH) Namely, one shining brightly.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ET DE MEDIO EJUS CARNES CO- MEDIT) Id est, parte altera coctas carnes comedit.

VAH) Melius vertas: Euge: est enim lætantis In- terjectio, ut Psal. 35, 21.

VIDI FOCVM) Nempe bene lucentem.

## 44:17
Ver. 17. AND HE BESEECHES) He offers prayers to an image. That is the meaning of the Hebrew word. Heraclitus: ὅμοια, ὡς εἴ- τις τοῖς δόμοις λεχηνοίνετο, ποιεῦσιν οἱ προσιόντες ὡς θεοῖς τοῖς ἀψύχοις.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET OBSECRAT) Preces allegat imagini. Is est vocis Hebrææ significatus. Heraclitus: ὅμοια, ὡς εἴ- τις τοῖς δόμοις λεχηνοίνετο, ποιεῦσιν οἱ προσιόντες ὡς θεοῖς τοῖς ἀψύχοις.

## 44:18
Ver. 18. THEY HAVE NOT SEEN, NOR UNDERSTOOD) Not even a crumb of good sense remains for them.

FOR THEY HAVE SMEARED LEST THEIR EYES SEE) This 'obliti', which the interpreter has placed here, is from 'oblino' [to smear], not from 'obliviscor' [to forget]; both the Hebrew context and the Greek show this: more elegant Greeks would say λημῶσι [they have bleary eyes].

Latin:

Vers. 18. NON VIDERVNT, NEQVE IN- TELLEXERVNT) Ne mica quidem illis restat bonæ mentis.

OBLITI ENIM SVNT NE VIDEANT OCV- LI EORVM) Hoc obliti, quod hic posuit interpres, est ab oblino, non ab obliviscor, ostendit id & He- bræus contextus & Græcus: Græci elegantiores dicerent λημῶσι.

## 44:19
Ver. 19. I SHALL MAKE AN IDOL) They themselves would say, a god. But Isaiah, after the manner of his people, said βδέλυγμα [abomination], as the Greeks translate it here. See what [is written] at Matthew 24, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 19. IDOLVM FACIAM) Ipsi dicerent, Deum. Sed Esaias more suæ gentis dixit βδέλυγμα, ut hic vertunt Græci. Vide quæ ad Matth. 24, 15.

## 44:20
Ver. 20. A PART OF IT IS ASHES) He reads רבעו. For רבע properly signifies a fourth part, and improperly other parts as well. See Numbers 23, 10. The Greeks read רעה. The received reading does not seem bad in this sense: A deceived heart feeds on ashes: that is, on a thing of nothing. Whatever is wood can be turned into ashes.

HE ADORED IT) In the Hebrew it is: he causes that deceived heart to turn aside, namely from the truth, by a perverse custom, that is to say.

AND HE HAS NOT DELIVERED HIS SOUL) So that he could not extricate himself, namely from those bonds of idolatry.

NOR SHALL HE SAY) Nor think.

IS THERE A LIE IN MY RIGHT HAND) In the Hebrew: Surely it is a falsehood in my right hand: that is, that in which I labor is a mere deception.

Latin:

Vers. 20. PARS EJVS CINIS EST) Legit רבעו . Nam רבע quartam proprie, improprie etiam alias partes significat. Vide Num. 23, 10. Græci legerunt רעה . Vi- detur lectio recepta non mala hoc sensu: Pascitur cinere cor deceptum: id est, re nihili. Quicquid lignum est, ci- nesieri potest.

ADORAVIT ILLVD) In Hebræo est: divertere illum facit, nempe à vero, cor illud deceptum, prava scili- cet consuetudo.

ET NON LIBERAVIT ANIMAM SVAM) Ita ut se expedire non posset, illis scilicet idololatriæ vinculis.

NEQVE DICET) Neque cogitare.

FORTE EST MENDACIVM IN DEXTERA MEA) In Hebræo: Certe falsum est in dextera mea: id est, id in quo laboro, mera deceptio est.

## 44:21
Ver. 21. REMEMBER THESE THINGS O JACOB AND ISRAEL) Namely, when you are forced to live among idolaters and under idolaters.

I HAVE FORMED THEE) I have instructed.

Latin:

Vers. 21. MEMENTO HORVM JACOB ET ISRAEL) Nempe cum inter idololatras & sub idololatris vivere cogeris.

FORMAVI TE) Institui.

## 44:22
Ver. 22. I HAVE BLOTTED OUT AS A CLOUD THY INIQUITIES.) ἀπήλειψα ὡς νεφέλην i.e. I will cause thy crimes to disperse like a cloud or mist.

RETURN UNTO ME) That is, if only you correct yourself, and return to the true worship of me.

FOR I HAVE REDEEMED THEE) Better: that I may redeem thee: that I may free thee from this captivity: for this discourse is directed as if to those times as present. Thus also in the following, place 'he will do' and 'he will redeem'.

Latin:

Vers. 22. DELEVI VT NVBEM INIQVITATES TVAS.) ἀπήλειψα ὡς νεφέλην i. e. disperere faciam ut nu- bem aut nebulam tua crimina.

REVERTERE AD ME) Id est, si modo te corri- gas, & ad mei verum cultum redeas.

QVI REDEMI TE) Melius: ut redimam te: ut te ex hac captivitate liberem: nam ad illa tempora quasi præsentia, dirigitur hic sermo. Sic & in sequentibus pone, faciet, & redimet.

## 44:23
Ver. 23. SING, O YE HEAVENS) That is, the Angels.

SHOUT, YE LOWER PARTS OF THE EARTH) The lowest parts of the earth. The common people.

BREAK FORTH INTO SINGING, YE MOUNTAINS) The highest parts of the lands, that is, kings.

THE FOREST AND EVERY TREE THEREOF) The princes and companions of kings.

It had to be proven that this discourse is directed to those times. Nor is it held in the Hebrew, 'that I may redeem THEE,' BUT 'BECAUSE I HAVE REDEEMED THEE.' The cause is rendered, why they ought to turn to God, sought from the redemption, but the end is not indicated, as if, forsooth, he is redeemed on account of the conversion. This is therefore a mere perversion of the Sacred text. By REDEMPTION, however, is understood that on account of which we must turn to GOD OUR REDEEMER, having sent away idols, and look to Him in true faith as Redeemer, who by His merit and passion blots out all our sins, so that if we believe in Him, they vanish before the judgment of God, just as if a clearing wind dispels the clouds, so that not even a small cloud appears in the sky: or, where the Sun consumes the small clouds, or presses them down, and purifies the air. For all the Prophets bear witness to Christ, that through his name all who believe in him receive the remission of sins the sequence, is this, as the blessed Luther rightly observes: My office is to save: this I have done, I have conquered sins, death, Satan, and hell on the cross, I have overthrown the empire of the law. Now you also respond in turn to your office. Accept those things which I offer you, turn to me, your redeemer. Which sense is demanded not only by the emphasis of the word גאלתיך, I have redeemed you, which implies the redemption of Christ, accomplished by the price of his blood, but also by the eucharistic hymn to be sung on account of that redemption: Praise the heavens, etc. for the Lord has redeemed Jacob. Hence, it is easy to see without labor, says Cyril, that the future remission of sins, and the return, and the redemption of all through Christ, had been proclaimed by the holy Prophets in those times. For after God and Lord appeared to us, and dwelt together with the earth in the heavens, as man, the true lamb who takes away the sins of the world, the most holy victim: then, then it became a cause for a festival for the supreme and heavenly powers endowed with reason, or the orders of the holy Angels. (For they sang, they sang, on account of his carnal birth, I say, and said: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men.) And if it be true (and it is entirely true) according to the voice of the Savior, that there is joy in heaven before the holy Angels over one repenting sinner, is it to be doubted that, when Christ leads the whole world to the knowledge of the truth, when he calls to conversion, when he justifies by faith, and renders it illustrious through sanctification, there was joy and a panegyric among the highest spirits? Nor is this sense foreign to the preceding. For thus it is explained what that office is, which no gods of the nations, no idols, no merits of human justice can perform, and on account of which the name of the Son of God is never to be consigned to oblivion, but always to be celebrated privately and publicly: I have blotted out your iniquities as a cloud, and your sins as a mist. Turn to me, for I have redeemed you. For this is that benefit which the Son of God alone can bestow upon his worshipers, and does bestow. Nor can a greater or more useful benefit happen to them than that they should receive the remission of sins. And therefore, after Isaiah heard the sermon of the Son of God (we retain the words of our Brentius) concerning the deletion of sin, that is to say, the greatest benefit, he is so filled and exhilarated by the Holy Spirit that he cannot be restrained, but that not only does he himself exult with the greatest joy, but he also excites heaven, earth, valleys, mountains, woods, and trees to gladness and joy. For just as Abraham exulted with the greatest joy to see the day of Christ, he saw it and was glad: so also Isaiah, when he sees the day in the Spirit in this place, is suffused with such joy that he exhorts even other creatures to joy. Exult, he says, O heavens, that is, all heavenly creatures; jubilate, O lower parts of the earth, that is, those who dwell in the plains or in the valleys of the earth. Clap with joy, O mountains, that is, the inhabitants of the mountainous regions. Clap, O woods and all its trees, that is, all the inhabitants of the wooded places. But why must one exult and rejoice in this way? Is it because the Lord is about to deliver us from the Babylonian tyranny, and is about to restore to us our native land? This is indeed a huge benefit of God, most worthy of joy, gladness, and thanksgiving, but it is not the highest and greatest; rather, this is the greatest of all, which the Son of God confers upon his Church, namely, the deletion of sins: The Lord, he says, has done it. And the Lord has redeemed Jacob, and his glory is illustrated in Israel, that is, for this reason one must exult with joy, because the Son of God, who is our true Lord God, confers upon us this benefit, that all our sins may be remitted and blotted out. And the Son of God has redeemed us from all evils, from death and eternal damnation, and causes the glory of his name to be illustrated in his whole Church, which is the true Israel. Finally, it is manifest that this concerns that benefit of the Redeemer which pertains to all men, and is not peculiar to the Jewish people alone. For when Isaiah excites both heaven and earth to joy and gladness, he signifies that that benefit does not belong only to one human race enclosed in the land of Canaan; but to all nations, and not only to men, but also to the Angels. Which therefore ought to be explained not of the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, but of the spiritual redemption of Christ: For it pleased the Father, says the Apostle in Colossians 1, that in him all fullness should dwell, and by him to reconcile all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross by him, whether they be things on earth, or things in heaven. Which benefit, although it is of men, who are redeemed from death to eternal life, yet it pertains to the Angels, because when man is reconciled, they are affected with the highest joy, since they thus obtain companions who are to be ἰσάγγελοι (equal to the angels). Grotius, when he saw that this argument stood in the way of his false interpretation, understands by the heavens indeed the Angels, but by the EXTREMITIES OF THE EARTH, the lowest of the earth, that is, the common people; by the mountains, the highest of the earth, that is, Kings; by the FORESTS AND EVERY TREE THEREOF, Princes, the companions of Kings. But who does not see that that gloss is merely arbitrary? Nor indeed did the Kings and the highest of all lands, or at least the greatest part of them, rejoice on account of the released captivity of the Jewish people, and who are those Princes, companions of Kings, designated by the trees of the Forest, or where do they come under this name in the Scriptures? Wherefore the Interpretation which we have brought from Brentius holds itself more correctly, that all are excited to the praise of the Lord, who dwell in the lowest part of the earth, or in the valleys or mountains or hills, or in the forests: for just as by the heavens the inhabitants of heaven, so by the lowest parts of the earth, by the mountains and hills, by the forests, those who dwell in them are pointed out. And Grotius admits that these things pertain to the times of the coming of Christ, and his redemption, at Luke II. 14. But the Jesuits, Sanctius, and Corn. à Lapide are inept, who say that by the lowest parts of the earth, the saints established in the center of the earth, in limbo, are noted. For thus no inhabitants of the earth, except those who live in the hills, mountains, and forests, would have been called to this joy, which is discordant.

Latin:

Vers. 23. LAVDATE COELI) Id est, Angeli.

JVBILATE EXTREMA TERRÆ) Ima terræ. Plebeji.

RESONA ET MONTES) Summi terrarum, id est, reges.

SALTVS ET OMNE LIGNVM EJVS) Prin- cipes regum comites.

Probandum id erat, ad illa tempora hic sermo- nem dirigi. Nec in Hebræo habetur, ut redimam TE, SED QUIA REDEMI TE. Causa red- ditur, cur converti debeant adDeum à redemptio- ne petita, non vero finis indicatur, ut nempe ob conversionem redimatur. Mera ergo hæc est textus Sacri perversio. REDEMPTIO vero ea intelli- gitur, ob quam ad DEUM REDEMPTOREM NOSTRUM missis idolis nos convertere, in eum- que ceu Redemptorem vera fide respicere debe- mus, qui merito & passione sua delet omnia nostra peccata, ut si in ipsum credamus, evanescant illa coram Dei judicio, perinde ac si ventus serenator dispellat nubes, ut ne quidem nubecula in cælo ap- pareat: aut, ubi Sol nubeculas consumit, aut de- primit, aëremque purificat. Christo enim omnes Prophetæ testimonium perhibent, quod remissio- nem peccatorum propter nomen ipsius conse- quantur, quotquot in ipsum crediderint, Act. X. 43. Ratio ergo, quam hic adfert Dominus τῆς ἀκολυθείας, hæc est, ut recte observat B. Lutherus Officium meum est salvum facere: hoc feci, peccata, mortem, Satanam & infernum in cruce devici, pro- fligavi imperium legis. Jam tu quoque responde vicis- sim tuo officio. Accipe ea quæ tibi offero, convertere ad me, redemptorem tuum. Quem sensum postulat non tantum emphasis verbi גאלתיך redemi te, quæ redemptionem Christi, pretio sanguinis ejus fa- ctam importat, sed etiam hymnos eucháristicus, ob redemptionem istam decantandus: Laudate cæ- li &c. quoniam redemit Dominus Jacob. Hinc fa- cile nullo labore, inquit Cyrillus, perspicere licet, pro- clamatam fuisse per Prophetas sanctos, illis tempori- bus, futuram per Christum remissionem peccatorum, & reversionem, ac redemptionem omnium. Post- quam enim Deus & Dominus apparuit nobis, & ver- satus est simul cum terra in cælis, ut homo, agnus ve- rus, qui tollit peccata mundi, sacrosancta victima: tunc, tunc supremis ac cælestibus potestatibus ratione præditis, seu sanctorum Angelorum ordinibus, causa festi extitit. (Cecinerunt enim, cecinerunt, propter nativitatem ejus carnalem, inquam, & dixerunt: Gloria in excelsis Deo, & in terra pax, in hominibus bona voluntas.) Et si verum sit (est autem omnino verum) secundum servatoris vocem, gaudium esse in cælis coram sanctis Angelis super uno peccatore re- sipiscente, an dubitandum est, cum totum terrarum orbem ad veritatis agnitionem reducit Christus, cum ad conversionem vocat, cum fide justificat, & per sanctificationem illustrem reddit, gaudium & pa- negyrin in summis spiritibus fuisse. Neque alienus hic sensus est ab antecedentibus. Sic enim exponitur, quodnam illud officium sit, quod nulli Dii gen- tium, nulla idola, nulla humanæ justitiæ merita pos- sunt præstare, & propter quod nomen Filii Dei nunquam oblivioni tradendum, sed semper priva- tim & publice celebrandum: Delevi ut nubes ini- quitates tuas, & quasi nebulam peccata tua. Conver- tere ad me, quoniam redemi te. Hoc enim est bene- ficium illud, quod solus Filius Dei cultoribus suis præstare potest, & præstat. Nec potest his vel ma- jus, vel utilius beneficium contingere, quam quod accipiant remissionem peccatorum. Ideoque post- quam audivit Esaias concionem Filii Dei (verba Brentii nostri retinemus) de deletione peccati, maximo videlicet beneficio, Spritu S. ita impletur, & exhilaratur, ut teneri non possit, quin non solum ipse summa lætitia gestiat, verum etiam excitet ad lætitiam & gaudium, cælum, terram, valles, mon- tes, sylvas & arbores. Nam quemadmodum Abra- ham summo gaudio gestiit, ut videret diem Chri- sti, vidit & gavisus est: ita & Esaias cum hoc loco videat in Spiritu diem, tanta lætitia perfunditur, ut etiam alias creaturas ad lætitiam cohortetur. Exultate, inquit, cæli, h. e. omnes cælestes creatu- ræ, jubilate inferiora terræ, h. e. qui habitant in pla- nitie aut in vallibus terræ. Plaudite lætitia mon- tes, h. e. habitantes in montanis. Plaudite sylvæ & omnes arbores ejus, h. e. omnes sylvestrium lo- corum incolæ. Sed quamobrem sic exultandum & lætandum? Num quia Dominus liberaturus nos est ex Tyrannide Babylonica, & redditurus nobis terram Patriam nostram? Hoc quidem in- gens est beneficium Dei dignissimum gaudio, læ- titia, & gratiarum actione, non autem est summum & maximum, sed hoc demum maximum omnium est, quod Filius Dei in Ecclesiam suam confert, vi- delicet, Deletio peccatorum: Dominus, inquit, fecit. Et Dominus redemit Jacob, & gloria ejus il- lustratur in Israele, h. e. idcirco gestiendum est gaudio, quia Filius Dei, qui est verus Domi- nus Deus noster, confert in nos hoc beneficium, ut remittantur & deleantur nobis omnia peccata. Et Filius Dei redemit nos ab omnibus, malis, à morte & æterna damnatione, ac efficit, ut gloria nominis ejus in universa Ecclesia sua, quæ est verus Israel, illustretur. Postremo manifestum est de illo beneficio Redemptoris hic agi, quod omnes ho- mines concernat, non vero quod proprium sit solo populo Judaico. Quum enim Esaias excitet tam cœlum, quam terram ad gaudium & lætitiam, signi- ficat utique beneficium illud non tantum ad unum genus humanum in terra Canaan inclusum; sed ad omnes gentes, nec ad solos homines, verum etiam ad Angelos pertinere. Quod proinde non de liberatione è captivitate Babylonica, sed de spi- rituali Christi redemptione explicari oportet: Complacitum enim est Patri, inquit Apostolus Col. 1. inhabitare in illo universam plenitudinem, & per eum reconciliare cuncta erga se, pacificatis per san- guinem crucis ejus per eundem, sive quæ in terra sunt, sive quæ in cælis. Quod beneficium etsi hominum sit, qui redimuntur à morte ad vitam æternam, ad Angelos tamen pertinet, quod reconciliato homi- ne, summa ipsi afficiantur lætitia, siquidem ita so- cios consequantur, qui futuri sint ἰσάγγελοι. Gro- tius cum viderit argumentum hoc suæ ψευδερμη- νείᾳ obstare, per cælos intelligit quidem Angelos, per EXTREMA autem TERRÆ, ima terræ, h. e. plebejos, per montes, summos terrarum, id est, Reges, per SALTUS ET OMNE LIGNUM EJUS, Principes, Regum Comites. Sed glossam illam mere arbitrariam esse, ecquis non videt? Neque vero gaudebant Reges & summi terrarum quique, aut maxima saltem eorum pars ob solutam captivita- tem populi Judaici, & quinam illi sunt Princi- pes Regum comites, per arbores Sylvæ designa- ti, aut ubi hoc nomine veniunt in Scripturis? Quapropter rectius sese habet Interpretatio, quam è Brentio adduximus, quod omnes excitentur ad laudem Domini, qui in ima terra, vel valli- bus aut montibus vel collibus, aut in sylvis ha- bitant: perinde enim uti per cœlos incolæ cœli, fic per ima terræ, per montes & colles, per sylvas, qui habitant in illis, indigitantur. Et pertinere hæc ad tempora adventus Christi, & redemtionem ejus fatetur Grotius ad Luc. II. 14. Inepti autem sunt Jesuitæ, Sanctius, & Corn. à La- pide, qui per ima terræ, sanctos in centro terræ, in limbo constitutos notari ajunt. Sic enim nulli ha- bitatores terræ, nisi qui in collibus, montibus & sylvis degunt, convocati ad hoc gaudium essent, quod absonum.

## 44:24
Vers. 24. YOUR FORMER FROM THE WOMB) Who have been instructing you from the time of Abraham.

Latin:

Vers. 24. FORMATOR TUUS EX UTERO) Qui ab Abrahami tempore te institui.

## 44:25
Vers. 25. MAKING VOID THE SIGNS OF DIVINERS, AND TURNING SOOTHSAYERS INTO MADNESS) The Chaldeans, who cultivated the art of divining from the stars so much, and indeed without measure, that what had been the name of a nation, became the name of a profession. See Cicero, first book of De Divinatione, Tacitus, Annals 2. 3. 12. 14. 16. What follows pertains to the same.

Latin:

Vers. 25. IRRITA FACIENS SIGNA DIVINO- RUM, ET ARIOLOS IN FUROREM VERTENS) Chaldæos, qui ita artem ex astris divinandi, & quidem sine modo coluere, ut quod nomen gentis fuerat, factum sit no- men professionis. Vide Ciceronem primo de divinatione, Tacitum Annalium 2. 3. 12. 14. 16. Eodem pertinent, quæ sequuntur.

## 44:26
RAISING UP THE WORD OF HIS SERVANT) Who will make valid the prophecy of Isaiah.

AND FULFILLING THE COUNSEL OF HIS MESSENGERS) Such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

AND I WILL RAISE UP ITS DESOLATE PLACES) Its ruins.

Latin:

SUSCITANS VERBUM SERVI SUI) Qui ra- tum faciam Esaiæ vaticinium.

ET CONSILIVM NVNTIORVM SVORVM COMPLENS) Ut Jeremiæ & Ezechielis.

ET DESERTA EJVS SVSCITABO) Ruinas ejus.

## 44:27
Vers. 27. WHO SAY TO THE DEEP, BE DESOLATE)

LARE) In Hebrew: Dryer. This pertains to that which Cyrus did to capture Babylon: for he divided the river Euphrates, and having led a part of it into lakes, he entered the city through the old channel. The history is in Jeremiah 51:32 and in Herodotus. Verse 28. WHO SAY TO CYRUS, YOU ARE MY SHEPHERD) That is, I have set you over my people to shepherd them. It is truly wonderful that so long before, 210 years as Josephus thinks, the name of this king was openly announced in this place and in several following ones, to which you have a similar case regarding Josiah in 1 Kings 13:2. But indeed, God who had predicted these things, the same God instilled into those who had the right of giving the name the intention that they should give this name, and not another: Cyrus mentions this prophecy in Josephus 11:1. WHO SAY TO JERUSALEM YOU SHALL BE BUILT) Nehemiah 2. Personification. AND TO THE TEMPLE YOU SHALL BE FOUNDED) Ezra 7. The prophecy concerning the redemption to be performed through Cyrus is subjoined to the illustrious promise concerning the redemption of Christ. The reason for the continuity has been well rendered by B. Luther: He proposes this prophecy concerning Cyrus so that he may comfort the pious, lest they despair of the future kingdom of Christ, which he described in the previous eight chapters. For because the Babylonians were about to reduce the Jews almost to nothing, all the promises concerning the kingdom of Christ were in danger, and since the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews, along with the temple and the city of Jerusalem, had been devastated by the Babylonians, there was no hope for the kingdom of Christ. He promises, therefore, that he will lead the people back through Cyrus, and will restore the kingdom with the priesthood, so that the promised kingdom of Christ may be exhibited to a safe people. Although it may be admitted that the drying up of the Euphrates was signified by this prophecy, there are not lacking those who, with Cyril, wish these things to be said metaphorically: for he says thus, I am he who says to the abyss, you shall be desolate. He called the innumerable multitude of the Babylonians the abyss here, but its rivers the nations which flowed together to him, which were neighboring, summoned by them for aid. Because it is familiar to Scripture to compare many nations to rivers and the sea and waters. It was said also of Babylon itself and Nineveh, because its waters are like a pool. Thus also Brentius: The deep or abyss is Babylon, and its rivers are the kingdoms or cities subject to the Babylonians. Although he also adds that these things can also be understood of the drying up of the Euphrates itself, by which Babylon was conquered. But since that drying up of the Euphrates was a work of human industry, let us say that, even if some allusion is made to it, these things are nevertheless to be understood metaphorically rather as the desolation of the abyss of the Babylonian kingdom and the drying up of its rivers, because this work is claimed by God, or divine power, and God testifies that he is the one who says to the deep, be desolate, and dries up its rivers.

Latin:

Vers. 27. QVI DICO PROFVNDO, DESO- LARE)

LARE) In Hebræo: Siccator. Hoc pertinet ad id, quod Cyrus fecit, ut Babylonem caperet: Amnem enim Euphra- tem diffidit, & parte ejus in lacus abducta, per alveum vete- rem in urbem ingressus est. Historia est apud Jeremiam LI. 32. & apud Herodotum. Vers. 28. QVI DICO CYRO, PASTOR MEVS ES) Id est, te pascendo populo meo præfeci. Mirum vero tanto ante tempore, annis ante 210. ut Josephus putat, no- men hujus regis hoc loco & aliquot sequentibus aperte enuntiatum, cui simile habes de Josia 1. Reg. XIII, 2. Sed enim qui hæc prædixerat Deus, idem his qui jus habebant dandi nominis, eam mentem indidit, ut id nomen, non & aliud darent: meminit hujus prophetiæ Cyrus apud Josephum XI. 1. QVI DICO JERVSALEM ÆDIFICABERIS) Nehem. 2. Προσωποποιΐα. ET TEMPLO FVNDABERIS) Esdræ 7. Subjunctum est vaticinium de redemptione per Cyrum præstanda promissioni illustri, de re- demptione Christi. Ratio τῆς συνεχείας reddita probe est à B. Luthero: Ideo hoc vaticinium de Cyro proponit, ut consoletur pios, ne desperent de regno Christi futuro, quod bis quatuor Capp. descripsit. Quia enim fere in nihilum redacturi erant Babylonii Judæos, periclitabantur omnes promissiones de Chri- sti regno, & cum per Babylonios regnum & Sacerdo- tium Judæorum, una cum templo & civitate Hieru- salem essent vastata, nulla spes erat de Christi regno. Promittit igitur se reducturum populum per Cy- rum, & restituturum regnum cum Sacerdotio, ut promissum Christi regnum populo incolumi exhi- beatur. Quanquam vero admitti possit, vaticinio hoc significatam fuisse Euphratis exsiccationem: non desunt tamen, qui cum Cyrillo hæc per trans- lationem dicta velint: Ita enim ille, Ego sum qui dico abysso, desolabere. Abyssum hic innumerabilem Babyloniorum multitudinem nominavit, fluvios autem ejus gentes, quæ ad eum confluxerint, quæ finitimæ erant, ab ipsis in subsidium accersitæ. Quia familiare Scripturæ est, fluminibus & mari, & aquis multas gentes comparare. Dictum est & de ipsa Babylone & Ninive, quia piscinæ æquæ sunt aquæ ejus. Sic etiam Brentius: Profundum seu abyssus est Babylon, & flumina ejus sunt regna, vel ci- vitates Babyloniis subjectæ. Quamvis etiam addat, posse & hæc intelligi de ipsa Euphratis exsiccatione, qua Babylon expugnata est. Sed quum exsiccatio illa Euphratis opus fuerit industriæ humanæ, dica- mus, etsi ad eam allusio aliqua fiat, metaphorica ta- men hæc potius de desolatione abyssi regni Babylo- nici, & fluminum ejus arefactione intelligenda es- se, quia hoc opus vindicatur Deo, vel divinæ po- tentiæ, ac testatur Deus se esse, qui dicit profundo, desolare, & flumina ejus arefacit.

## 45:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLV.

A prophecy concerning Cyrus, who was about to occupy Babylon for the sake of the liberation of the Lord's people, with a sigh of the Prophet panting for Christ the true liberator. A rebuke of those disputing with God, and a confirmation of the liberation to be through Cyrus, as well as the eternal liberation of Christ, in whom alone is salvation.

Verse 1. THUS SAYS THE LORD TO MY CHRIST CYRUS) In the Hebrew it is not my, but his: that is, singularly beloved and consecrated for the work of God, no less than if he had been anointed by some Prophet in the manner of the Kings of the Jews. WHOSE RIGHT HAND I HAVE TAKEN HOLD OF) Whom I will confirm. AND I WILL SUBDUE NATIONS BEFORE HIS FACE) Medes, Lydians, Ionians, Babylonians. AND I WILL TURN THE BACKS OF KINGS) I will turn kings to flight, Astyages, Croesus, Nabonidus. Verse 2. AND I WILL OPEN DOORS BEFORE HIM

Latin:

CAPUT XLV.

Vaticinium de Cyro propter populi Domini li- berationem Babylonem occupaturo, cum su- spirio Prophetæ Christum verum liberato- rem anhelantis. Reprehensio disceptantium cum Deo, & confirmatio liberationis per Cy- rum futuræ, nec non æternæ liberationis Christi, in qua una est salus.

Vers. 1. HÆC DICIT DOMINVS CHRISTO MEO CYRO) In Hebræo non meo, sed suo est: id est, ad opus Dei singulariter dilecto ac consecrato, non minus quam si more Regum Judæorum per Prophetam aliquem unctus esset. CVJVS APPREHENDI DEXTERAM) Quem ego confirmabo. ET SVBJICIAM ANTE FACIEM EJVS GEN- TES) Medos, Lydos, Jonas, Babylonios. ET DORSA REGVM VERTAM) Vertam re- ges in fugam, Astyagem, Crœsum, Nabonidum. Vers. 2. ET APERIAM CORAM EO JANVAS

## 45:2
AND THE GATES SHALL NOT BE SHUT: I WILL GO BEFORE YOU, AND I WILL HUMBLE THE GLORIOUS ONES OF THE EARTH: I WILL CRUSH THE BRASS GATES, AND I WILL BREAK THE IRON BARS) All these things signify that God will act so that nothing may stand in his way. God provided almost equal good fortune to Alexander and Caesar, to the former for taming the ferocity of the Persians, to the latter for that of the Romans. The Latin interpreter, where we have הֲדוּרִים (uneven), which the Greeks translate as mountains, reads הֲרָרִים. The sense in the Hebrew is good: I will make uneven places level.

Latin:

ET PORTÆ NON CLAUDENTUR: EGO ANTE TE IBO, ET GLORIOSOS TERRÆ HUMILIA- BO: PORTAS ÆREAS CONTERAM, ET VE- CTES FERREOS CONFRINGAM) Hæc omnia signi- ficant facturum Deum ut ei nihil obstet. Parem ferme feli- citatem præstitit Deus Alexandro & Cæsari, illi ad Persa- rum, huic ad Romanorum ferociam edomandam. Latinus interpres ubi nos habemus הֲדוּרִים inæqualia, quod Græci vertunt ὄρη legit הֲרָרִים. Sensus in Hebræo bo- nus est: iniqua loca adæquabo.

## 45:3
Verse 3. HIDDEN TREASURES) Such as Sardis, where there was much wealth. Likewise of Asia, Ionia, Mesopotamia, the richest regions. Pliny 33.3. Cyrus, having conquered Asia, had found 34 thousand pounds, besides golden vessels, and wrought gold, and in it leaves and a plane tree and a vine: from which victory he brought back five hundred thousand talents of silver, and the crater of Semiramis, the weight of which amounted to 15 talents. Varro reports that an Egyptian talent weighs 80 pounds.

AND THE SECRETS OF SECRETS) Gems and necklaces kept most diligently.

WHO CALL YOUR NAME) Who even now give you a magnificent name. For Cyrus, if we believe Ctesias and Plutarch, signifies the Sun; if others, nourishment. Moreover, Cyrus was both a great light of the Persians, and a true nourisher of the peoples subject to him.

Latin:

Vers. 3. THESAUROS ABSCONDITOS) Ut Sar- dium, ubi gaza erat plurima. Item Asiæ, Joniæ, Mesopota- miæ, ditissimarum regionum. Plinius XXXIII, 3. Iam Cyrus devicta Asia pondo 34. millia invenerat, præter vasa aurea, au- rumque factum, & in eo folia ac platanum vitemque: qua victo- ria argenti quingenta millia talentorum reportavit, & craterem Semiramidis, cujus pondus XV. talentorum colligebat. Talen- tum autem Ægyptium pondo LXXX. patere, Varro tradit.

ET ARCANA SECRETORUM) Gemmas & mo- nilia diligentissime asservata.

QUI VOCO NOMEN TUUM) Qui tibi jam nunc indo nomen magnificum. Nam κῦρος, si Ctesiæ & Plutarcho credimus, Solem, si aliis, alimoniam significat. Fuit autem Cyrus & lux magna Persarum, & verus altos parentium sibi populorum.

## 45:4
Verse 4. FOR THE SAKE OF MY SERVANT JACOB, AND ISRAEL MY ELECT) Because I wish to use your efforts for his liberation.

I HAVE LIKENED THEE, AND THOU HAST NOT KNOWN ME.) Translate from the Hebrew: I will surname thee before thou knowest me. That is, while thou art still an infant, I will distinguish thee with that illustrious title of Cyrus: for his proper name was another, as Herodotus says.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PROPTER SERVUM MEUM JACOB, ET ISRAEL ELECTUM MEUM) Quia ad ejus li- bertatem tua opera uti volo.

ASSIMULAVI TE, ET NON COGNOVISTI ME.) Ex Hebræo verte: Cognominabo te priusquam me cognoscas. Id est, infantem adhuc insigniam egregio illo titulo Cyri: nam proprium ei nomen fuit aliud, ut ait Herodotus.

## 45:5
Ver. 5. I HAVE GIRDED THEE, AND THOU HAST NOT KNOWN ME.) The Greeks well [render it] ἐνίσχυσά σε: I have given thee strength: I will bring it about that thou shalt have an army from Harpagus, with which thou mayest attack Astyages. That God is the one creator of the world, Cyrus did not yet know at that time, but he learned it afterwards from the Hebrews. See above XLI. 25. as also the immortality of souls, which Xenophon and Cicero in the Cato Major testify was firmly believed by him.

That Cyrus not only had that general knowledge of God, that God is the one creator of the world, which is evident by the light of nature, but that he acknowledged and worshipped the true GOD, as God had predicted in Isaiah XLI. 25, is testified by the mandates which he himself published in 2 Chronicles XXXVI. v. 23, Ezra I. v. 2. Since this is clearer than light, who can doubt that he acknowledged the God of Israel to be the true God, and worshipped Him;

Latin:

Vers. 5. ACCINXI TE, ET NON COGNO- VISTI ME.) Græci bene ἐνίσχυσά σε: vires tibi dedi: Efficiam, ut Exercitum ab Harpago habeas, quo Astyagem oppugnes. Deum esse unum mundi opificem, nondum tunc norat Cyrus, sed id postea ab Hebræis didicit. Vide supra XLI. 25. ut & animorum immortalitatem, quam fir- me ab eo creditam testantur Xenophon & Cicero Catone majore.

NOn tantum generalem illam notitiam Dei ha- buisse Cyrump, quod Deus unus sit mundi opi- fex, quæ naturæ lumine constat, sed verum DEUM agnovisse & coluisse, quemadmodum prædixerat Deus Esa. XLI. 25. testantur mandata, quæ ipse pu- blicavit 2. Paral. XXXVI. v. 23. Esdr. I. v. 2. Quod cum luce clarius sit, ecquis ambigere potest, quod Deum Israëlis verum Deum esse agnoverit, eum- coluerit;

## 45:7
Ver. 7. MAKING PEACE.) Giving prosperity to peoples, such as the Persians.

AND CREATING EVIL) Sending evils upon peoples, such as the Medes and Babylonians.

Jerome more correctly judges that God signifies that He was both angry with His people, when it endured the darkness of captivity and the evils of servitude, and again merciful, when, having been sent back to their homeland, they received peace and joy. For these things are said on account of the people of God and therefore are to be applied to them.

Latin:

Vers. 7. FACIENS PACEM.) Dans salutem populis, ut Persis.

ET CREANS MALUM) Immittens mala in po- pulos, ut Medos, Babylonios.

Rectius Hieronymus significare Deum cen- set, se & iratum fuisse populo suo, quando tenebras captivitatis, malaque sustinuit servitutis, & rursum mifertum, quando remissi in patriam pacem & gau- dium receperunt. Dicuntur enim hæc ob populum Dei ideoque ad eum applicanda sunt.

## 45:8
Ver. 8.

DROP DOWN, YE HEAVENS, FROM ABOVE, AND LET THE CLOUDS RAIN DOWN THE JUST ONE: LET THE EARTH BE OPENED, AND BUD FORTH A SAVIOUR, AND LET JUSTICE SPRING UP TOGETHER: I THE LORD HAVE CREATED HIM) From the Hebrew: Flow, ye heavens, from on high, and let the heights of the ether distil justice: let the earth open itself, that salvation and justice may bring forth fruit: He whom I the Lord have created shall cause these to spring up together. The empire of Cyrus is described, whom all called the Father of peoples: namely, that it would come to pass that the earth would be full of justice and happiness, no otherwise than it is accustomed to be full of moisture when the heaven rains abundantly. A similar expression is in Psalm LXXII. 6, 7. Cyrus was, as appears from histories, just, magnanimous, clement, liberal: God had endowed him with so many and such great virtues. Which is what is said here, I have created.

A threefold explanation of this passage is found for the most part. Some explain it concerning Cyrus according to the letter, along with Grotius, because the Jews captive in Babylon panted for Cyrus as for a heavenly dew. But others take it concerning Christ, because more august things are said here than those which might suit Cyrus. Finally, it pleases some to retain both senses, so that the prophecy is understood literally of Cyrus, but allegorically or mystically of Christ. This is the explanation of Thomas, Lyranus, and Forerius. But since the laws of good interpretation, or the simplicity and perspicuity of the Holy Scriptures, do not admit a double sense of the same oracle of Scripture, nor does the present passage allow it, there does not appear to be a sufficient reason why that opinion, which is that of most of the Fathers, that the discourse is literally about Christ, should be dismissed, so that we might believe with Grotius and a few others that Cyrus is uniquely intended here, especially if it be said that the Prophet, when he was speaking about Cyrus, immediately flew to Christ here, and that the words of the present verse are to be read as a parenthesis, as if a brief sigh for Christ had been inserted on the occasion of the prophecy about Cyrus: because the pious were not longing so much for liberation from bodily captivity as that Christ, who was to redeem men from spiritual captivity, should be presented to the world. Therefore, most maintain that the Church seeks this benefit in that figurative mode of speech: partly because that bodily liberation and the remaining benefits came to the people on account of the promise concerning the Messiah, who otherwise had deserved by their sins to be left perpetually in captivity, v. 4; partly because the liberation of Cyrus exhibits an excellent figure of the liberation of Christ; and partly because the Prophet wished to rouse his hearers, so that they might not be fixed in their minds solely on that external liberation, but might seek the true liberator with more ardent vows and sighs. The words are also especially suited to describing him. For he, whom he desires, comes under the name of RIGHTEOUSNESS and SALVATION in the abstract. But these abstract names do not fit Cyrus in the least, but agree only with Christ, who is our righteousness, and is called ישע salvation everywhere, and from this word he obtained his name JESUS. And Christ is accustomed to be described in that manner, under the figure of a righteous sprout, or of righteousness. Jer. XXIII. 6, ch. XXXIII. 16: I will raise up to David a righteous sprout, and they shall call him Jehovah our righteousness. In those days, says the Psalmist, Ps. LXXII. 7, the righteous or righteousness shall flourish. The Messiah, says Daniel ch. IX. 24, shall bring in everlasting righteousness. Similarly, the Messiah is insinuated under the name of salvation and the savior, Gen. XLIX. 18, Jer. XXIII. 6, ch. XXXIII. 16. Then Israel shall be saved, Hos. I. 7: I will save them in the Lord their God. And here our Prophet, ch. XLIX. 6: That you may be my SALVATION unto the end of the earth. Whence in Luke II. 30 he is called SALVATION, which God has prepared in the sight of all peoples. Of whom, therefore, will the present sigh be more aptly understood, let the clouds rain down righteousness, and let the earth sprout salvation, than of the Messiah? Furthermore, this figure fits the mystery of the advent and incarnation of Christ concisely: because as herbs are born when the earth is made fertile with heavenly dew and moistened with rains, so that the hidden seeds of the herbs might be actuated: so the conception of Christ took place by the heavenly operation of the Spirit, so that that holy sprout might arise from the virgin. The sacred Psalmist described this mystery with a similar figure, Ps. LXXII. 6: He shall descend like rain upon the fleece, like showers falling gently and dropping bit by bit upon the earth. As dew does not descend sensibly, so the Holy Spirit worked this in the virgin secretly, so that the Son of God, descending from heaven, might assume human nature from those sanctified bowels. And what kind of opening of the earth and sprouting is denoted, a similar oracle of Isaiah teaches, ch. II: A rod shall go forth from the stem of Jesse, and a shoot shall sprout from his roots: because, namely, the shoot was to sprout from the root of Jesse of the Davidic stem. In the Council of Seville, Canon 13, the former, drop down, O heavens, was referred to the divine nature of Christ, the latter, let the earth open and sprout a Savior, to the human nature, because the Son of God descended like dew, Ps. LXXII. Others call Christ the sprout of heaven, because he was conceived from heavenly dew, i.e., from the Holy Spirit: the sprout of the earth, because he was born of a virgin. Therefore Vatablus explains it thus: drop down, O heavens from above, that is, let the Holy Spirit descend into the virgin, and bedew her, and make her fertile, so that she may bring forth Christ and the Savior. The heavens throughout the whole world were made honey-dropping, and the whole earth was filled with the mercy of the Lord: and therefore heavenly and earthly riches were made, and earth and heaven were reduced into one, as it were, sprout. Nor does the word צמח remit us obscurely to those places which used the same word concerning the birth of the Messiah, Is. IV. 1: in that day the sprout of the Lord shall be in beauty and glory, and the fruit of the earth in sublimity; Zech. III. 5. Behold I bring my servant, the sprout, cf. ch. VI. 12, Jer. XXIII. 5, ch. XXXIII. 16, in which locutions he explained צמח by the word Messiah. Let the earth open and sprout a Savior or let salvation and righteousness sprout, i.e., would that the earth might produce and bring forth into the light a Savior; Christ, however, was to be born from heaven, but on earth. Then salvation and righteousness were sprouting, because Christ is that sprout, our righteousness, and in him our salvation is situated. Sanctius says that almost no one doubts that this earth is the most blessed virgin, into whose womb that heavenly rain has slipped. Which, being made fertile by the divine spirit, poured forth the sprout so long desired. Let a metalepsis be observed in the word LET OPEN: since it is the same as to bring forth and produce like one opening: because the earth does not naturally sprout unless it opens itself. From Adam onwards the earth was sprouting the thorns and thistles of sins. The Prophet therefore desires that He may now sprout forth righteousness, or Him in whom alone we have righteousness. Finally, when the Lord is said to be about to create this, reference is made to that new thing of new things, which alone is new under the Sun, Jer. XXXI. 22. The Lord will create a new thing in the earth, a woman shall compass a man. The Vulgate reads, I the Lord have created HIM, but it should be read, I THE LORD CREATE HER, see RIGHTEOUSNESS AND SALVATION. Which words are God's response, given to the Church, which was so ardently seeking true righteousness and salvation. We will not say that those things which precede in this chapter are interpreted literally of Christ by not a few of the Fathers. Cyprian, book 4, Testim. Adv. Judæos. Tertullian, advers. Jud. c. I. Gregory of Nyssa, book de Testim. Select. Augustine, Vol. I, book de quinque hæres. and that Galatinus, book IV, c. XII, also brings forward testimonies from the Talmud in support of that same opinion. For we grant that those things concern Cyrus, which Jerome and some others of the ancients acknowledged. Although they did not doubt that these present things pertain to Christ. Which opinion Jerome reports and approves, referring also those things which follow this sigh to Christ. Cyril, although he accepts the preceding things concerning Cyrus without doubt, nevertheless teaches at length that these of ours are to be understood of Christ. It is solemn and familiar, he says, for divinely inspired Scripture often to extend its discourse from those things which were done individually and particularly concerning some, to the universal genus and to all: and as if from a clear image of historical events, to skillfully lead the mind of those who are being instructed to more arcane and mystical considerations. Which it is possible to see also in these verses which are at hand. Through mercy therefore and righteousness springing up from the earth, he understands Christ to be sprouting forth, and says that He is called the fruit and sprout of the earth, because He was born according to the flesh from a woman, who was one of the earthly ones. What of the fact that this is the common opinion of the Fathers, that this sigh pertains to Christ. St. Augustine, in the cited book, c. IV, thinks that these things are stated so plainly and openly concerning the incarnation of Christ, that they do not need interpretation. To these, almost all of our countrymen subscribe, as do all the Papists. Concerning Christ, says Sanctius, the common opinion of the Fathers and Interpreters accepts these things. And concerning others (with Grotius agreeing) he brings this ἐπίκρισιν (critique): That those who interpret these things concerning Cyrus, in such a way that he is stirred up by the ardent vows of the captive Israel, and that the desire is no otherwise; and as a sterile field, thirsting for the heavenly rain, are either Jews, or those studious of the Jewish faction, to whom Hugo strongly assents. But Hugo our Batavian more so. Our B. Brentius paraphrases thus: True justice, true salvation cannot come to us through another, whether that Cyrus, or some other Monarch, except through you, Son of God, our Lord: Act therefore, O heavens, act, O clouds, act, O earth: bring together all your strengths at once. You heavens and clouds give rain, you earth exhibit a fertile field, so that that best fruit may be produced, which is true justice and perpetual salvation. For these benefits are so necessary to us, that if we lack them, liberation from Babylon will profit us nothing, nor any other bodily goods. Wherefore, although we do not reject that benefit of external liberation from Babylon, yet we desire this most of all, this we ask, O heavens, O earth, that you may bring forth justice and salvation for us, that the Son of God, our Lord, may be sent from heaven, and may assume human nature on earth, so that we may be truly justified and saved through him and in him. The Reformed Belgian annotators to the vernacular Bible grant that the liberation here is to be understood not as bodily, but as spiritual. Similarly Oecolampadius, whose ἐξήγησιν (exegesis) I add: After the joyful message, by which he understood that the people were to be liberated from the captivity of Babylon through Cyrus, and afterwards much more blissfully through Christ, he desires with exceptional affections that the time be accelerated. With which affection he also prays below: Would that you would tear open the heavens, and descend! The sense, however, is this: Would that the celestial and terrestrial things might help, so that at last we might be made partakers of these vows. Away with the curse, by which because of our sins the heaven is bronze, and the earth iron: but let the celestial things give their grace, which the earthly things do not refuse to receive. Sins had divided between us and God, like clouds, so that prayer might not ascend: now let the rain of heavenly grace descend. We were hardened, so that we might not receive the word of the Lord: now let our earth be made fit for receiving grace; so that there may be salvation and justice. He prays, therefore, would that the time of salvation might come, and in which God might justly vindicate us from our enemies. Afterwards also, when he concedes that Christ is indicated as our justice and salvation, Oecolampadius acknowledges not obscurely that these things are not to be understood concerning Cyrus, but concerning Christ. Calvin himself, although he affirms that the double sense respects the liberation of the people from Babylon, adds however, that the Prophet does not restrict these promises to a few years, but pursues his benefits up to the advent of Christ, in whom all these things are abundantly fulfilled. There is no doubt, therefore, to him, but that he also commends eternal justice and salvation, which is brought to us through Christ. But since it is not permitted to establish a double sense in the same place of Scripture, and yet eternal justice and salvation cannot be excluded here, it is necessary that we accept this passage concerning the same alone. The Papists certainly, although they are studious of a double, nay, a multiple sense above others, are forced to acknowledge here that there is no room here for any other sense than that concerning Christ, so much so that Sanctius, their chief Interpreter, even opposes himself to the others on that account, who invent a double sense here. Cornelius à Lapide, while admitting that the beginning of the chapter deals with Cyrus, nevertheless warns that these things are predicted concerning Cyrus to this end, that he might give assurance to his own through the oracles of Isaiah concerning the remission of sins and the thanks to be brought through Christ, of which those were a type, to the Jews from this future liberation of Cyrus, just as from other ancient benefits of God conferred upon them, through experience. But those things which are had in verse 8, although they are accepted by Lyranus, Forerius, and Thomas himself literally concerning Cyrus, and allegorically concerning Christ, he acknowledges are too august to befit Cyrus. He says, therefore, that the Prophet, as is his custom, when he saw in Cyrus an image of Christ (in the preceding verses), here immediately flies to him, because Christ was his love, scope, and desire, whence he here breaks out into an ardent vow for him. Wherefore these things are to be accepted concerning Christ literally, according to Cornelius, and enclosed in a parenthesis, which separates this whole verse from the preceding and following ones, where the prophecy concerning Cyrus is continuous. And he says that the Fathers commonly explain it thus. These things similarly Casp. Sanctius in h. l. (in this place). When the species of Christ the redeemer appeared very closely in Cyrus the redeemer, Isaiah, an admirer and lover of Christ, rises from the middle of the course of his speech from Cyrus the Persian Christ, to Christ Jesus the Nazarene, and to the thought of eternal liberty. With a not dissimilar spirit and manner, Jacob, now about to die, when he beheld in his son Dan, from whom the great leader Samson arose, the ruler and vindicator of the Israelite nation, and the Prophetic Spirit did not rest in Samson the savior, turned to Christ the Author of greater liberty and said Gen. 49: I will wait for your salvation, O Lord. This is the common and true explanation. Afterwards he refutes others, who construct a double sense in this text: Others recognize Cyrus in these words historically, and in him, as in a shadow, they behold Christ, among whom are S. Thomas, Forerius, Lyra, and the Replicator. But how these things, which are so grave and illustrious, fit Cyrus historically, they labor greatly. Lyra therefore thinks that the heavenly dew and rain are invoked for the birth of Cyrus, and the name of the germinating earth is introduced, because, as Herodotus reports in book 1. To Cyrus's grandfather Astyages, there appeared in his sleep a certain vine springing from his daughter's genitals, which with a long growth of shoots would occupy all of Asia, and he learned from the interpreters what was to be, that a grandson born of his daughter would possess the empire of all Asia. Suitably, therefore, to the dream of Astyages, in which Cyrus, the assertor of Jewish liberty, is called a vine, he says that rain is desired, by which that vine may be born and grow from the maternal womb as if from a field. He thinks it can be called Just or Justice for this reason, because he was an administrator of divine justice against the Babylonians. But truly the very manner of speaking, and the magnitude of the matter, shows something above the capacity of Cyrus and the glory of the deeds performed by him. As far as the manner of speaking pertains, our Prophet often teaches, and others not rarely, whenever prophecy is concerned with a type, and is turned by apostrophe from it to one absent, the discourse is no longer about the type, but plainly about the thing figured and the truth. Certain oracles about Christ easily persuade us of this, Gen. 49. After Jacob recognized in his son Dan a shadow of Christ the Savior, 'Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a cerastes in the path, etc.' When he says by apostrophe, 'I will wait for your salvation, O Lord.' And Zech. 9, when a type had preceded, the Prophet, with his speech turned to those absent, says: 'Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; behold, your King comes.' And chap. 13, when a certain obscure shadow of Christ the Shepherd had preceded, making a step from there to Christ by apostrophe, he says, 'Awake, O sword, against my Shepherd, etc.' and 'strike the Shepherd.' As far as the matter itself is concerned, the name of the Just One, which is found here, is more illustrious and more august than that it should be attributed to Cyrus by Isaiah; which name is often attributed to Christ by this Prophet, and in the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Wherefore these things must be accepted entirely historically concerning Christ, and enclosed in a parenthesis, which separates this whole clause from the continuous thread of the prophecy. And indeed the common opinion of the Fathers and Interpreters accepts these things concerning Christ. This is Sanctius. Others follow these leaders, Cornel. à Lapide and Sanctius. Hector Pintus, Tirinus, Menochius, etc. Now if we examine the gloss of Grotius, how cold everything is: that the empire of Cyrus is described; when the earth is said to be about to bring forth salvation and justice, the earth full under him of his own justice and happiness: that Cyrus was just, magnanimous, clement, liberal. But this is the prayer of the Church, and of the faithful among the people of the Lord: whom Grotius will persuade that the empire of Cyrus was designated, when they prayed that the earth might bring forth salvation and justice? Then indeed it is one thing for a prince to be just and happy in any way: another, for true justice and salvation to germinate, which all the pious desire and long for. Furthermore, if the words are to be rendered thus, 'him whom I the Lord created will make this earth germinate,' by what means, pray, will these things suit Cyrus, did he make justice and salvation germinate at the same time? This belongs to God, not to any Prince or Monarch. Finally, if this passage of ours is similar to Psalm 72:6-7, which Grotius admits, nothing is more certain than that it treats of Christ. For we have invincibly proved that it treats of Christ when we discussed that passage. Oecolampadius, although he understands Cyrus as a type, nevertheless finds no way to attribute to him the praise and title of justice. Cyrus, he says, was not truly just, but most rapacious and most cruel, even though he was kind to the Jews. And therefore, as the histories have it, he was finally destroyed by Tomyris, Queen of the Scythians, with 200,000, his head thrown into a wineskin filled with blood, which she also said: ἐνεπλήσθητι αἱματοδιψάση κεφαλὴ, 'be sated with blood, O blood-thirsty head.' But our Christ is truly just, and justice itself, and he snatched us from the more atrocious Babylonians.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

RORATE COELI DESUPER, ET NV- BES PLVANT JVSTVM: APERIATVR TERRA, ET GERMINET SALVATOREM, ET JUSTITIA ORIATVR SIMVL: EGO DOMINUS CREAVI EVM) Ex Hebræo: Manate cœli de supernis, & summæ etheris stillent justitiam: aperiat se terra, ut fructum profe- rant salus & justitia: hæc simul germinare faciet is, quem ego Dominus creavi. Describitur Imperium Cyri, quem Patrem populorum appellarunt omnes: nempe fore, ut terra plena sit justitiæ ac felicitatis, non aliter quam plena humoris esse solet, cœlo large pluente. Similis locutio Psal. LXXII. 6. 7. Fuit Cyrus, ut ex historiis ap- paret, justus, magnanimus, clemens, liberalis: tot atque tantis virtutibus eum Deus instruxerat. Quod hic dicitur, creavi.

Triplex reperitur potissimum explicatio hu- jus loci. Nonnulli de Cyro eundem explicant se- cundum literam cum Grotio, quod Cyrum quasi rorem cælestem anhelarint Judæi in Babylone captivi. Sed alii de Christo accipiunt, quod au- gustiora hic dicantur, quam quæ Cyro conveniant. Denique nonnullis placet, utrumque sensum reti- nere, ut secundum literam de Cyro intelligatur va- ticinium, allegorice autem vel mystice de Christo. Quæ Thomæ, Lyrani, Forerii est explicatio. Sed quum geminum sensum ejusdem Scripturæ oraculi haud admittant leges bonæ interpretationis, aut Sacrarum literarum simplicitas & perspicuitas, ne- que præsens locus ferat, non apparet sufficiens cau- sa, cur sententia illa, quæ plerorumque Patrum est, quod de Christo secundum literam sermo sit, di- missa, cum Grotio, & paucis quibusdam aliis Cy- rum hic unice desiderari credamus, imprimis si di- catur Prophetam cum de Cyro verba faceret, mox ad Christum hic avolasse, ac verba præsentis versus per parenthesin legenda esse, ut insertum fuerit breve suspirium de Christo, occasione Prophetiæ de Cyro: quia non tam liberationem è captivita- te corporali anhelabant pii, quam ut Christus è spi- rituali captivitate homines redempturus mundo sisteretur. Ideo Ecclesiam hoc beneficium figura- to isto sermonis genere petere plerique statuunt: tum quod corporalis illa liberatio & reliqua bene- ficia ob promissionem de Messia populo obtige- runt, qui alias meruerat peccatis suis perpetuo re- linqui in captivitate v. 4. tum quod liberatio Cyri eximiam figuram exhibeat liberationis Christi, tum quod Propheta voluerit auditores suos excita- re, ne animis defixi unice in illam liberationem ex- ternam essent, sed verum liberatorem magis arden- tibus votis & suspiriis expeterent. Cui describen- do etiam apprime verba conveniunt. Nam is, quem desiderat, JUSTITIÆ & SALUTIS nomi- ne in abstracto venit. At hæc abstracta nomina minime quadrant in Cyrum, sed uni Christo con- gruunt, qui justitia nostra est, & ישע salus vocatur passim, atque ab hac voce nomen suum JESUS na- ctus est. Et solet ea ratione describi Christus, sub ger- minis justi, aut justitiæ figura. Jer. XXIII. 6. c. XXXIII. 16. suscitabo David germen justum, & vocabunt eum Jehovah justitia nostra. In diebus illis, inquit Psaltes Ps. LXXII. 7. florebit justus vel justitia. Messias, in- quit Daniel cap. IX. 24. adducet justitiam sempiter- nam. Similiter sub nomine salutis, & salutaris insi- nuatur Messias Gen. XLIX. 18. Jer. XXIII. 6. c. XXXIII 16. Tunc Israel salvabitur Hos. I. 7. Salvabo eos in Do- mino Deo suo. Et hic Propheta noster c. XLIX. 6. Ut sis SALUS mea usque ad extremum terræ. Unde Luc. II. 30. dicitur SALUTARE, quod paravit Deus in conspectu omnium populorum. De quonam ergo aptius suspirium præsens intelligetur, nubes pluant justitiam, & terra germinet salutem, quam de Mes- sia? Porro ad adventus & incarnationis Christi mysterium figura ista concinne quadrat: quia ut herbæ nascuntur, cum cœlesti rore terra fœcunda- tur, & pluviis humectatur, ut occulta herbarum se- mina actuarentur: Ita cœlesti Spiritus operatione conceptio Christi facta est, ut germen illud san- ctum è virgine oriretur. Simili figura hoc myste- rium descripsit Hieropsaltes Ps. LXXII 6. Descendet sicut pluvia in vellus, sicut imbres stillantes leniter & guttatim descendentes super terram. Ut ros non sensibiliter descendit, ita occulte S. S. in virgine hoc operatus est, ut Filius Dei de cœlo descendens ex sanctificatis illis visceribus humanam naturam as- fumeret. Et qualis apertio terræ ac germinatio de- notetur, simile Esaiæ oraculum docet c. II. Egre- dietur virga de stirpe Isai, & surculus de radicibus ejus germinabit: quia nempe surculus ex radice Isai progerminaturus erat stirpis Davidicæ. In Concil. Hispalensi Canon. 13. prius, rorate cæli, ad di- vinam, posterius, aperiatur terra & germinet Salva- torem, ad humanam Christi naturem relatum est, quia Filius Dei descendit sicut ros Ps. LXXII. Alii germen cœli Christum dicunt, quia ex rore cœlesti, h. e. ex Spirit. S. conceptus fuit: germen terræ: quia è virgine natus. Ideo Vatablus ita exponit, rorate cœli desuper, id est, descendat Spiritus S. in virginem, eamque irroret, & fœcundet, ut pariat Christum & Salvatorem. Cœli per totum orbem facti sunt melliflui, & terra tota impleta est misericordia Do- mini: Ideoque divitiæ cœlestes factæ sunt & terre- stres, terraque & cœlum in unum quasi germen re- dacta sunt. Neq; obscure nos remittit verbum צמח ad loca illa, quæ de Messiæ ortu idem verbum adhi- buere Es. IV. 1 in die illa erit צמח germen Domini in decore, & gloria & fructus terræ in sublimitate Zach. III. 5. Ecce adduco servum meum, צמח germen, Conf. c. VI. 12. Jer. XXIII. 5. c. XXXIII. 16. in quibus locu- tionibus צמח exposuit per vocem Messiæ. Aperia- tur terra & germinet Salvatorem vel germinent salus, & justitia, q. d. utinam terra producat & in lucem pro- ferat Salvatorem, Christus autem nasciturus erat cœlitus, sed in terris. Tum germinabant salus & ju- stitia, quia Christus germen illud est justitia nostra, & in eo est salus nostra sita. Sanctius, terram, inquit, hanc esse beatissimam virginem, in cujus uterum cœle- stis illa pluvia illapsa est, nemo fere dubitat. Quæ à di- vino spiritu fœcundata germen effudit tam diu deside- ratum. Observetur autem in voce APERIATUR metalepsis: quum idem sit, quod proferat & pro- ducat instar aperientis: quia terra naturaliter non germinat, nisi se aperiat. Ab Adamo inde terra ger- minabat spinas & tribulos peccatorum. Optat er- go Propheta, ut nunc justitiam germinet, vel eum in quo uno nobis est justitia. Denique cum Domi- nus id creaturus dicitur, ad novum illud novorum novissimum, quod solum sub Sole novum, respici- tur Jer. XXXI. 22. Creabit Dominus novum in terra, fœmina circumdabit virum. Vulgata legit, ego Do- minus creavi ILLUM, sed legendum, Ego DOMI- NUS CREO ILLAM vid. JUSTITIAM ET SALUTEM. Quæ verba responsoria sunt Dei, Ecclesiæ data, quæ tam ardenter veram justitiam & salutem expetebat. Non dicemus, quod ea et- iam, quæ antecedunt in hoc capite, de Christo ad literam interpretentur è Patribus non pauci. Cyprianus lib. 4. Testim. Adv. Judæos. Tertul. ad- vers. Jud. c. I. Gregorius Nyssenus lib. de Testim. Se- lect. August. Tom. I. lib. de quinque hæres. & quod in eam etiam sententiam Galatinus l. IV. c. XII. suf- fragia è Talmude adducat. Nam de Cyro illa age- re largimur, quod Hieronymus, & alii nonnulli è veteribus agnoverunt. Quamvis non dubitarint hæc præsentia ad Christum pertinere. Quam sen- tentiam refert & probat Hieronymus, etiam quæ se- quuntur hoc suspirium, ad Christum referens. Cyrillus etsi superiora de Cyro citra dubitatio- nem accipiat, hæc nostra tamen de Christo intel- ligenda esse prolixe docet. Solenne ac familiare, inquit, est divinitus inspiratæ Scripturæ, sæpenume- ro sermonem ab his, quæ sigillatim & particulatim de aliquibus facta sunt, ad genus universum & ad omnes producere: & velut à luculenta rerum historiæ ge- starum imagine, mentem eorum, qui instituuntur, ad considerationes magis arcanas ac mysticas scite tra- ducere. Quod etiam in his versibus, quæ præ mani- bus sunt, videre licet. Per misericordiam ergo & ju- stitiam ex terra enascentem, & germinantem Chri- stum intelligit, eumque terræ fructum & germen di- ci ait, quod natus sit secundum carnem ex muliere, quæ ex terrestribus una fuit. Quid quod com- munis Patrum hæc sententia sit, hoc suspirium ad Christum pertinere. S. August. lib. cit. c. IV. censet, hæc tam plane & aperte dicta esse de incarnation Christi, ut interpretatione non egeant. Quibus sub scribunt nostrates plerique omnes, ut & Pontifici omnes. De Christo, inquit Sanctius, hæc accipit com munis Patrum Interpretumque sententia. Et de alii (Grotio accedentibus) hanc fert ἐπίκρισιν: Qu hæc de Cyro interpretantur, ita ut ille ab Israele capti vo ardentibus excitetur votis, desideriumque non ali- ter; atque ager sterilis, sitiensque cœlestem desider pluviam, aut Judæi sunt, aut Judaicæ factionis studiosi quibus valde annuit Hugo. Sed magis Hugo noste Batavus. B. Brentius noster ita παραφράζει: Vera justitia, vera salus non potest nobis per alium, sive il- lum Cyrum, sive alium quemdam Monarcham, præ- terquam per te Filium Dei Dominum nostrum con- tingere: Agite igitur cœli, agite nubes, age terra: conferte simul omnes vires vestras. Vos cœli & nubes date pluviam, tu terra exhibe agrum fertilem, ut pro- ducatur optimus ille fructus, qui est vera justitia, & perpetua salus. Hæc enim beneficia nobis ita necessa- ria sunt, ut si his caruerimus, nihil nobis proderit libe- ratio ex Babylone, nec quicquam aliorum corpora- lium bonorum. Quare etsi non rejicimus beneficium illud externæ liberationis ex Babylone, tamen hoc ma- xime omnium desideramus, hoc petimus ô cœli, ô ter- ra, ut parturietis nobis justitiam & Salutem, ut de cœlo mittatur Filius Dei Dominus noster, & in terra assumat humanam naturam, quo nos per ipsum & in ipso vere justificemur & servemur. Reformati Bel- gici annotatores ad Biblia vernacula largiuntur pe- nes liberationem corporalem intelligendam hic esse spiritualem. Similiter Oecolampadius, cujus ἐξήγη- σιν adjicio: Post lætum nuncium, quo intellexit po- pulum è captivitate Babylonis liberandum per Cy- rum, & postea multo beatius per Christum, eximiis affectibus desiderat accelerari tempus. Quali affectu & infra optat: Utinam disrumperes cœlos, & descenderes! Sensus autem hic est: Utinam cœle- stia & terrestria adjuvent, quo tandem votorum isto- rum compotes efficiamur. Absit maledictio, qua pro- pter peccata nostra cœlum est æneum, & terra ferrea: sed gratiam suam dent cœlestia, quam suscipere non detrectent terrena. Diviserant inter nos & Deum peccata, ut nubes, ne ascenderet oratio: nunc descen- dat cœlestis gratiæ pluvia. Indurati eramus, ne reci- peremus verbum Domini: nunc idonea fiat terra nostra ad suscipiendum gratiam; ut sit salus & justi- tia. Orat igitur, utinam veniat tempus salutis, & quo juste vindicet nos Deus ab hostibus nostris. Post- ea etiam, cum Christum nostram justitiam & salu- tem indigitari concedit, hæc non de Cyro intelli- genda esse, sed de Christo, haud obscure agnoscit Oecolampadius. Calvinus ipse, etsi geminum sen- sum respicere liberationem populi è Babylone, af- firmet, addit tamen, non restringere Prophetam has promissiones ad paucos annos, sed beneficia sua prosequi usque ad adventum Christi, in quo hæc omnia impleta abunde sunt. Non dubium igitur ipsi, quin æternam quoque justitiam & salutem com- mendet, quæ nobis affertur per Christum. At quum geminum sensum in Scripturæ eodem loco consti- tuere non liceat, neque tamen æterna justitia & sa- lus hic excludi possit, necessum est, ut de eadem so- la hunc locum accipiamus. Pontificii certe etsi du- plicis, imo multiplicis sensus præ aliis studiosi sint, agnoscere hic coguntur, locum hic non esse alii sensui, quam de Christo, adeo ut Sanctius, præci- puus eorum Interpres, cæteris eo nomine etiam se opponat, geminum sensum hic fingentibus. Cor- nelius à Lapide initium capitis de Cyro agere ad- mittens, id tamen monet, hoc fine de Cyro ista prædi- ci, ut Judæis ex hac Cyri liberatione futura, æque atque ex aliis antiquis Dei beneficiis eis collatis, per expe- rientiam, fidem faceret suis per Esaiam oraculis de re- missione peccatorum gratiisque per Christum afferen- dis, quorum illa erant typus. At quæ vers. 8. haben- tur, etsi à Lyrano, Forerio ut & Thoma ipso literali- ter de Cyro, allegorice de Christo accipiantur, agnoscit, augustiora esse, quam ut Cyro conveniant. Dicit ergo, Prophetam de more, cum in Cyro videret imaginem Christi (in superioribus) hic mox ad eum avolare, quia Christus erat ejus amor, scopus, deside- rium, unde hic in ardens ejus votum erumpit. Quare hæc de Christo ad literam juxta Cornelium, accipien- da sunt, & claudenda parenthesi, quæ totum hunc ver- sum à præcedentibus & sequentibus, ubi continua est Prophetia de Cyro, separet. Atque ita communiter Pa- tres explicare ait. Hæc similiter Casp. Sanctius in h. l. Cum proxime appareret in Redemptore Cyro species Christi redemptoris, è medio sermonis cursu ad- mirator, & amator Christi Isaias à Christo Cyro Per- sa, ad Christum Jesum Nazarenum, & ad cogitatio- nem sempiternæ libertatis assurgit. Non dissimili spi- ritu, & modo Jacob jam moriturus, cum in filio Dan, à quo magnus Dux Samson ortus est, intueretur Israe- liticæ gentis rectorem & vindicem, neque in Samsone servatore acquiesceret Propheticus Spiritus, ad Chri- stum majoris libertatis Autorem conversus ait Gen. 49. Salutare tuum expectabo Domine. Hæc com- munis & vera explicatio est. Post refellit alios, du- plicem sensum adstruentes in hoc textu: Alii in his verbis Cyrum agnoscunt historice, in eo tanquam in umbra Christum intuentur, in quibus S. Thomas, Fo- rerius, Lyra, & Replicator. Quomodo vero hæc, quæ tam gravia sunt, & illustria historice conveniant Cy- ro, valde laborant. Lyra ideo putat ad Cyri nativita- tem advocari cælestem rorem, & pluviam & nomen induci germinantis terræ, quia, ut tradit Herodotus lib. 1.
