This is that iniquity, this the crime, on account of which the Jews were deleted from the catalog of the people of God, namely, that Christ Jesus the Son of God came into his own, and his own did not receive him, John 1.

to deliver them: But your impious obstinacy denies you my help. In both ways this assertion of the divine hand, or power, aptly fits the purpose. (We leave another still in the middle.) Jerome provides the reason for the συνεχείας [continuity]. We can say that he who is the performer of such great signs, who makes the heavens, the lands, and the seas serve his nod, could even himself have escaped the cross.

Latin:

QUIA VENI ET NON ERAT VIR) Quare venienti mihi nemo se sistit? Nemo mihi paret.

VOCAVI ET NON ERAT QUI AUDIRET) Vocanti nemo respondet? Id est, cur non recipitis facturos vos, ad quæ vos excitant Prophetæ?

De inobedientia Judæorum, quibus Prophetas misit Dominus, intelligit Grotius: Sed de causa pro- pria agitur reprobati populi Judaici, quæ fuit repro- batio Mesiæ. Ideoque de Mesliæ adventu & præco- nio hæc intelligenda sunt. Quod confirmatur porro, tum ex antegressis: Ibi enim loquutum esse Christum Redemptorem, è conclusione capitis præcedentis constitit. Quia orationem suam hic continuat: tum è consequentibus. Quia is venisse se testatur, cui Dominus dedit linguam eruditam, cui aurem aperuit & qui corpus suum percutientibus de- dit. Quem esse Christum, certum est. Veni igi- tur, inquit, id est, interprete Cyrillo, humanitatem indui & apparui Israelitis: & non erat inter illos homo, videlicet cordatus, & qui redemptionis tem- pus scire posset, vocavi, & non erat audiens. Etenim sic iterum Esaias Propheta in persona omnium no- strum Servatoris Christi inquit, (Inventus sum his, qui me non quærunt, conspicuus factus sum his, qui me non interrogant. Dixi: Ecce adsum genti, quæ mihi non credidit. Toto die expandi manus meas, ad populum incredulum & contradicentem) In Evangelicis etiam Scriptis sæpe inveniemus Do- minum vocantem ad fidem Judæos: (Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refi- ciam vos. Tollite jugum meum super vos- Rursus alibi: (Qui sequitur me, non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lucem vitæ.) Certe illis fru- ctuosum & utile esse declarat ut credant, inquiens: (Amen dico vobis, quia, qui credit, habet vitam æ- ternam.) Et complura alia congerere quis poterit, in eandem sententiam, si quidem voluerit prolixe rem persequi. Itaque vocavi, inquit, sed non erat audiens. Quæ causa propria & germana est, cur Judæi repro- bati sint. Hæc est illa iniquitas, hoc scelus, pro- pter quod Judæi sunt è populi Dei Catalogo deleti, vid. quod Christus Iesus Filius Dei in sua venit, & sui eum non receperunt, Joh. 1.

orum liberare: Sed vestra impia pertinacia vobis meam opem denegat. Utroque modo apte con- gruit hæc divinæ manus, vel potentiæ assertio insti- tuto. (Aliam adhuc in medio relinquimus.) Ra- tionem συνεχείας tradit Hieronymus. Illud possu- mus dicere, qui tantorum signorum patrator est, qui cælum, terrasque & maria suo facit servire nutui, etiam ipse crucem evadere potuerit.

## 50:2
Verse 2.

IS MY HAND SHORTENED AND MADE SMALL?) Perhaps you think that I, if you do your duty, will not perform my promises, as if they exceeded my powers. He refutes that.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

NVMQVID ABBREVIATA AC PARVVLA FA- CTA EST MANVS MEA?) Forte putatis me, si vos faciatis officium, promissa mea non præstiturum, quasi ea vires meas exsuperent. Id refellit.

## 50:2
BEHOLD AT MY REBUKE) By my command, as in Psalm 106:9.

I WILL MAKE THE SEA A DESERT) I will dry it up, as the Chaldean has here, and the Psalm in the aforementioned place. I can do this, if I wish. I showed this in the Red Sea.

I WILL PLACE THE RIVERS INTO DRY LAND.) As the Jordan once: and now the channel of the Euphrates.

Latin:

ECCE IN INCREPATIONE MEA) Imperio meo, ut Psal. 106, 9.

DESERTVM FACIAM MARE) Siccabo, ut hic Chaldæus habet, & Psalmus dicto loco. Facere hoc pos- sum, si velim. Ostendi hoc in mari rubro.

PONAM FLVMINA IN SICGVM.) Vt Jordanem olim: & nunc Euphratis alveum.

## 50:3
Verse 3.

I WILL CLOTHE THE HEAVENS IN DARKNESS.) As in Exodus 10, verse 21.

That God here shows His power, and looks back to the miracles performed in the liberation from Egypt, is beyond doubt: But because the Son of God is speaking, whose passion is primarily described here, how He gave His body to those who struck it, and His cheeks to those who plucked them, and did not turn His face from insults and spitting, because it concerns His advent and proclamation in these lands, and the cause of the reprobate Jewish people, because the power of the Son of God is illustrated by miracles, so that the blame for the evils of the people may be removed from Him, B. Brentius not badly observes four things, which Christ performed in His ministry among the Jews, and by which He testified that He both could and would save those who believe in Him, are proposed here: that He produced great and notable miracles, that He taught most salutary things, that He performed works divinely commanded most obediently, that He bore all evils most patiently. First, therefore, concerning miracles, He testifies that the power to redeem is not lacking to Him, where Brentius judges that by the species of Egyptian miracles, the genus is to be understood here, namely: that the Son of God testifies to His power in His ministry with such majesty that, just as formerly in the liberation of the Israelites from Egypt He produced such miracles that He inverted the nature of things, so now in the liberation of the human race from the power of Satan, He produces those miracles also by which He proves that He both rules over the nature of things and is by far the most powerful Savior of all. Known, however, are the miracles which Christ produced on earth when He preached His Gospel, which were also done no less above the powers of nature than those in Egypt. He restored sight to the blind, cleansed the lepers, made the mute speak, the deaf hear; and what exceeds all admiration, He raised the dead to life. By the mention of these miracles, the Son of God reproaches the Jews for their impiety, not only in this place of Isaiah, but also in the Gospel. If I do not, He says, the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do, and if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works. And afterwards the Evangelist says in wonder: Although He had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in Him, etc. Others interpret these things concerning the power of the Son of God to liberate the Jewish people from the power and yoke of the Romans. As if to say: Truly I could snatch you Jews as easily from the hands of the Romans as it was not difficult for me to snatch your ancestors long ago from the tyranny of Egypt. He takes these things from Isaiah with the Jews. But the Isaianic context resists. For He who speaks these things is Jehovah of infinite power, as is evident from verse 1 and following, since it is one continuous speech of the same person. But how is it fitting for Isaiah to say, Is my hand shortened? Furthermore, He who testifies: The Lord has given me a learned tongue: or if you prefer, one suitable for instructing others, is that same one whose head was struck, whose cheeks were plucked, whose face was troubled by spittle and insults. Which do not fit Isaiah, but Christ. Jerome therefore shuts the mouth of Grotius here, who Judaizes. The Jews, separating this chapter from the preceding ones, wish to refer it to the person of Isaiah: that he says he received the word from the Lord: how he sustains the weary and wandering people, and calls them back to salvation, and in the manner of children, who are instructed in the morning hours by the Holy Spirit, he hears what He speaks, and that he did not contradict His command, but when the Lord asked: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people, he answered Him: Behold me, send me. And because he said, Hear the word of the Lord, O Princes of Sodom, perceive with your ears the law of our God, O people of Gomorrah: having suffered such hard things, that he was exposed not only to the insults of words, but also to the pains of blows. Nevertheless, he was by no means terrified by the conscience of the commanding God, but according to that which is said to Ezekiel: Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads, like adamant and flint I have made your face, he had crushed all their attacks. These things would be said by those who strive by every reason to overturn the prophecies concerning Christ, and to twist them to a perverse understanding by a crooked interpretation, as if, even if these things were written about Isaiah, they could bring forward other testimonies concerning Christ, which are so clear that they infuse a bright light of themselves into the eyes of all. To the person of the Lord, therefore, in whom the previous book also ended, these things are also to be referred, that according to the dispensation of the assumed body he was instructed, and received the tongue of discipline, so that he knew when he ought to speak, when to be silent. Finally, He who was silent in His passion, now speaks throughout the whole world through the Apostles and Apostolic men. That periphrasis, by which Jerome notes the depravers of this illustrious place, if it fits anyone, is certainly most apt for Grotius, WHO BY EVERY REASON STRIVES to overturn the prophecies concerning Christ, and to twist them to a perverse understanding by a crooked interpretation. By the judgment of Jerome, therefore, which is that of the truth itself, this prophecy is so clear that it infuses a bright light of itself into the eyes of all.

Moreover, למודים denotes the language of those being taught rather than those teaching; this word, according to received usage, and as it is repeated at the end of this very verse, teaches this. For it is used of him who is taught by another, to whom he offers his ear. Which B. Luther rightly observed. There is an emphasis in the noun (eruditam linguam), i.e., a discipled language, which speaks nothing except what it has learned from God. It is not the language of a Master, but the language of a Disciple. Therefore, at the end of the clause, it should be translated not as if I hear as a Master, but as a disciple.

Verse of the same.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

INDVAM COELOS CALIGINE.) Ut Exod. 10. vers. 21.

Potentiam suam Deum hic ostendere, & ad miracula in liberatione ex Ægypto patrata respice- re, dubio vacat: Sed quia Filius Dei loquitur, cujus imprimis passio descripta hic est, quomodo corpus suum percutientibus dederit, & genas vellicantibus, nec averterit faciem suam à contumeliis & sputis, quia de adventu & præconio ejus in his terris, & de causa reprobati populi Judaici agitur, quia potentia Filii Dei miraculis illustratur, ut culpa malorum populi ab ipso removeatur, non male B. Brentius observat quatuor, quæ Christus in ministerio suo inter Judæos gessit, & quibus testatus est, se & pos- se, & velle eos, qui in ipsum credunt, servare, hic proponi, quod ediderit magna & insignia miracula, quod docuerit saluberrima, quod fecerit opera divini- tus præcepta obedientissime, quod tulerit mala omnia patientissime. Primum igitur de miraculis, non dees- se sibi testatur potentiam ad redimendum, ubi per species miraculorum Ægyptiacorum hic genus in- telligendum esse censet Brentius, videl. Filium Dei tanta majestate potentiam suam in ministerio testa- ri, ut sicut quondam in liberatione Israëlitarem ex Ægypto tanta miracula edidit, ut rerum naturam inverterit:ita nunc in liberatione humani generis è potestate Satanæ, ea quoque miracula edat, quibus se & naturæ rerum dominari, & longe omnium po- tentissimum Servatorem esse probet. Nota autem sunt miracula, quæ Christus in terris, cum prædica- ret Evangelium suum, edidit, quæ etiam non minus supra, quam naturæ vires efficere possunt, facta sunt, quam illa in Ægypto. Cæcis visum restituit, Leprosos mundavit, Mutos loqui, surdos audire fe- cit; & quod omnem admirationem excedit, mor- tuos ad vitam excitavit. Quorum miraculorum mentione Filius Dei exprobrat Judæis suam impie- tatem, non solum in hoc Esaiæ loco, verum etiam in Evangelio. Si non facio, inquit, opera Patris mei, nolite credere mihi. Si autem facio, & si mihi non vultis credere, operibus credite. Et postea Ev- angelista admirabundus dicit: Cum tanta signa fe- cisset coram eis, non credebant in eum &c. Alii de po- tentia Filii Dei liberandi populum Judaicum è pote- state & jugo Romanorum hæc interpretantur. q. d. Profecto possem vos Judæos tam facile è Romano- rum manibus eripere, quam non mihi difficile fuit vestrorum olim majores è Tyrannide Ægypti- De Esaia hæc cum Judæis accipit. Sed refra- gante contextu Esaiano. Is enim, qui hæc lo- quitur, Jehovah est infinitæ potentiæ, ut v. 1. seqq. constat, quum una sit continua oratio ejusdem per- sonæ. Quomodo vero Esaiæ convenit dicere, Nun- quid abbreviata est manus mea? Porro is qui testatur: Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam: aut si ma- lis, aliis instituendis idoneam, est idem ille, cujus ca- put percussum, genæ vellicatæ, facies sentis & con- tumeliis turbata. Quæ non Esaiæ, sed Christo conveniunt. Judaizanti itaque Grotio hic os ob- turet Hieronymus. Judæi, hoc capitulum à supe- rioribus separantes, volunt ad Esaiæ referre perso- nam: quod se dicat à Domino accepisse sermonem: quomodo lassum errantemque populum sustentet, & revocet ad salutem, & in morem parvulorum, qui matutinis horis erudiuntur à Spiritu S. audiat, quid loquatur, seque non contradixisse ejus impe- rio, sed Domino suscitante: Quem mittam, & quis ibit ad populum istum, respondisse ei: Ecce ego, mitte me. Et quia dixerit, Audite verbum Domini Principes Sodomorum, percipite auribus legem Dei nostri populus Gomorræ: in tantum dura perpessum, ut non solum verborum contumeliis, sed & plagarum doloribus fuerit expositus. Atta- men se conscientia jubentis Dei nequaquam esse per- territum, sed juxta id, quod Ezechieli dicitur: Ec- ce dedi faciem tuam valentiorem faciebus eorum, & frontem tuam duriorem frontibus eorum, ut Adamantem & Silicem dedi faciem tuam, univer- sos eorum impetus contudisse. Hoc illi dixerint, qui omni ratione conantur de Christo evertere Prophe- tias, & ad perversam intelligentiam prava interpre- tatione torquere, quasi, etsi hæc de Esaia scripta sint, possint alia super Christo afferre testimonia, quæ ita perspicua sint, ut clarum sui cunctorum oculis lu- men infundant. Ad personam igitur Domini, in quæ & superior finitus est liber, etiam ista referenda sunt, quod juxta dispensationem assumti corporis eru- ditus sit, & linguam acceperit disciplinæ, ut sciret, quando deberet loqui, quando reticere. Denique qui in passione tacuit, per Apostolos & Apostolicos viros in cuncto orbe nunc loquitur. Periphrasis illa, qua Hieronymus notat loci hujus illustris depra- vatores, si in ullum congruit, certe aptissima Grotio est, QVI OMNI RATIONE CONATVR de Christo evertere Prophe- tias, & ad perversam intelligentiam prava inter- pretatione torquere. Judicio ergo Hieronymi, quod ipsius veritatis est, hoc vaticinium ita perspicuum est, ut clarum sui cunctorum oculis lumen infundat.

Cæterum למודים notare potius eruditorum, quam docentium linguam, vox hæc ex usu recepto, & pro- ut hoc ipso versu in fine repetitur, docet. Nam de eo, qui ab alio eruditur, cui aurem præbet, adhi- betur. Quod recte observavit B. Lutherus. Epi- tasis est in nomine (eruditam linguam) q. d. linguam discipulatam, quæ nihil loquitur, nisi quod à Deo di- dicit. Non est lingua Magistri, sed lingua Disci- puli. Proinde in fine commatis vertendum, non ut audiam quasi Magistrum, sed quasi discipulum.

Vers. eod.

## 50:4
Verse 4.

THE LORD HAS GIVEN ME A LEARNED TONGUE.) Isaiah could indeed truly say this of himself, whose diction is the purest among all who were after Moses, and whose ἔννοιαi [thoughts] are most beautiful. But the interpretation of the seventy elders, γλῶσσαν παιδείας [tongue of instruction], is more congruent to this place, as also below in verse 5. The sense is, he gave me a tongue suitable for instructing others, the tongue of teachers, the Chaldean here.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

DOMINVS DEDIT MIHI LINGVAM ERVDI- TAM.) Vero quidem de se hoc dicere potuit Esaias, cu- jus dictio purissima inter omnes, qui post Mosem fuere, & ἔννοιαi pulcherrimæ. Sed loco huic congruentior est inter- pretatio senum LXX. γλῶσσαν παιδείας, ut & infra 5. Sensus est, dedit mihi linguam aliis instituendis idoneam, Linguam docentium, Chaldæus hic.

## 50:4
THAT I MIGHT KNOW HOW TO SUSTAIN HIM WHO IS WEARY WITH A WORD) In Hebrew: That I might know how to speak timely words to those who are weary: namely, by calamities.

Latin:

VT SCIAM SVSTENTARE EVM, QVI LAS- SVS EST VERBO) In Hebr. Vt norim loqui sermones op- portunos his, qui fessi sunt: calamitatibus scilicet.

## 50:4
HE WAKENS MORNING BY MORNING, HE WAKENS MY EAR TO HEAR AS A MASTER) In Hebrew: From morning to morning (that is, from day to day) he wakens my ear for me, that I may offer audience, just as Teachers are accustomed to do for their disciples. But the LXX connect the last word with the following ones, and seem to have read בלמודים: for ἡ παιδεία κυρίου ἀνοίγει μοι τὰ ὦτα is worth the same as ὁ κύριος ἐν παιδείᾳ ἀνοίγει μοι τὰ ὦτα.

Latin:

ERIGIT MANE, MANE ERIGIT MIHI AV- REM, VT AVDIAM QVASI MAGISTRVM) In He- bræo: A mane ad mane (id est de die in diem excitat mihi aurem, ut audientiam præbeam, sicut Doctores nempe discipu- lis facere solent. At LXX. ultimam vocem cum sequentibus connectunt, & videntur legisse בלמודים : idem enim valet ἡ παιδεία κυρίου ἀνοίγει μοι τὰ ὦτα, quod ὁ κύριος ἐν παιδείᾳ ἀνοίγει μοι τὰ ὦτα.

## 50:5
Verse 5.

BUT I DO NOT CONTRADICT: I HAVE NOT GONE BACKWARD.) I did not flee from the ministry, although it was hateful, as Jonah did.

Since these must necessarily be understood of the Messiah, it must be believed that his so-called active obedience is being described. And indeed, there is no mortal who can truly testify this of himself. The Lord wakens my ear morning by morning. I do not contradict his commands, and I have not gone backward. For we all in many things go backward and slip, James 3. Perfect obedience is noted, which Christ alone performed, and alone could perform, Rom. 8:3. The words MORNING, MORNING are not to be understood as from day to day, but according to the custom of the Hebrews they obtain the notion of a superlative, as if he were saying, most seasonably, which pertains to the perfection of the obedience by which he was obedient to his Father even unto the death of the cross.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

EGO AVTEM NON CONTRADICO : RE- TRORSVM NON ABII. ) Non defugi ministerium, quanquam odiosum, ut Jonas.

Quum de Messia accipienda hæc necessario sint, obedientiam ejus, quam vocant, activam describi credendum est. Et profecto nemo est mortalium, qui hoc de se vere testari possit. Dominus mihi eri- git mane aurem. Ego non contradico ipsius man- datis, & retrorsum non abii. Omnes enim in multis retrocedimus, atque labimur Jac. 3. Notatur perfe- cta obedientia, quam solus Christus præstitit, solus præ- stare potuit Rom. 8, 3. Verba MANE, MANE non est, ut intelligamus de die in diem, sed more Ebræis consueto superlativi notionem obtinent, ac si dicat, maxime tempestive, quod ad obedientiæ perfectionem pertinet, qua Patri suo usque ad mortem crucis obe- diens fuit.

## 50:6
Verse 6.

I GAVE MY BODY TO THE SMITERS, AND MY CHEEKS TO THEM THAT PLUCKED OFF THE HAIR.) To them that pluck the beard, which even among Latin Poets has a meaning of reproach or mockery. These things, however, and those which follow, are spoken figuratively by Isaiah, so that it might be understood that he was constant in executing the commands of God, even if he were much mocked by Shebna and his very powerful faction. Moreover, God willed that all these things also be fulfilled literally in Christ, so that the Jews, those hunters of letters, might have no excuse.

We have here again a notable example of the clearly Judaic crookedness of Grotius. He acknowledges that these things do not properly fit Isaiah, but Christ; he acknowledges that God willed to fulfill them literally, and that in Christ, and nevertheless he twists them toward Isaiah. But what, I pray, is that reasoning, 'God willed that all these things also be fulfilled literally in Christ, so that the Jews, those hunters of letters, might have no excuse'? For either those things were predicted of Christ according to the intention of the Holy Spirit, or they were not. If the former, why does Grotius not understand this discourse of Christ, why does he not accommodate his explanation to the intention of the Holy Spirit? If the latter, how could it be FULFILLED in Christ, which was not predicted of Christ, how are the Jews rendered without excuse, if nothing here was predicted of Christ by the Prophet from the intention of the Holy Spirit! But in order to beat back that depravity, because Calvin, Hyperius, Pelicanus, and Musculus also made it their own, as well as Thomas among the Papists, or whoever the author of that commentary is (for Corn. à Lapide denies it is Thomas's), we observe these arguments: (1.) From the continuity of the text. That Jehovah, who denies that he has repudiated the Jews or sold them, denies that his hand is shortened, by whose rebuke the sea is dried up, who turns rivers into a desert, who clothes the heavens with blackness, here speaks, and affirms that the tongue of the learned was given to him by the Lord, that his ear was opened, and testifies that he offered his body to be struck; who else can this be than the Son of God, clothed in a human body? For it is most manifest that all these things cohere and cannot be torn from one another, whatever the Jews and Judaizing Christians may yelp. (2.) And from the clause of the preceding chapter. Because the same Lord gives the reason for the rejected Jewish people, who professes himself to be the author of the calling and the snatching away of the Gentiles, as if they were prey to be freed from the hand of the strong. Who is none other than our Savior and Redeemer Christ Jesus, ch. 49:26. (3.) From the argument and subject matter of this treatment. Because there is talk of the bill of divorce and the rejection of the Jewish people, when the Gentiles were being taken in, and the cause of it is established as the fact that they did not receive him when he came, and refused to follow him when he called, to whom God gave a learned tongue, opened his ears, and who exposed his own body to passions and ignominies. But the arrival and calling of Isaiah was not the proper cause of the rejected people, but the rejection of the arrival and calling of the Messiah. (4.) From the prerogative of the learned tongue; for although Isaiah was also instructed in an eloquent and learned tongue, yet here it must be understood by way of excellence, which is sufficient for raising up any weary person at an opportune time: concerning which Brentius rightly says: Here is the learned and eloquent tongue of Christ, and the announcement of his Gospel, by which he so consoles and vivifies the poor, the miserable, and the afflicted, that they obtain joy in the midst of distresses, and life in death. Such a learned tongue Grotius does not leave to Isaiah, despoiling all his prophecies and promises of Christ of their kernel and marrow. Moreover, this eloquence is proper to Christ, so much so that no one participates in it at all, unless he receives from his fullness, in whose lips grace is poured out Ps. 45, whose throat is sweet Cant. 6, who is anointed with the Holy Spirit and sent to preach the gospel to the poor, and to bind up the brokenhearted Isa. 61, 1, whose sweetness and grace Isaiah had also preached above, ch. 42, 3. (5.) From the perfection of obedience. Because ears were awakened, pierced, and prepared for this Teacher for obedience, not of any kind, but by which the law might be perfectly fulfilled, as is manifest from the comparison of Ps. 40, 7, 8, 9, which Calvin acknowledges as parallel to this passage. (6.) From total innocence. Because he dares to challenge the judgment of God, that he can be accused or convicted by no one in any matter. He is near who justifies, who will contend with me? Let us stand together: Who will be able to bring a lawsuit against me by right? Let him approach me, let him come forth and bring forward, if he has anything, of which he can accuse me! Which refer to the grave, but unjust accusations of the chief priests and Pharisees, leveled against Christ in the days of his flesh, who indeed could publicly testify: Who will convict me of sin! John 8. Because he had not known sin 2 Cor. 5, 21, nor was guile found in his mouth Isa. 53. Therefore he pronounces concerning his adversaries: Behold, all (those adversaries of mine) shall be worn out like a garment, or rather shall rot, the moth shall eat them. Which applies to the chief priests and Pharisees. For these not only, when the innocence of Christ became known, were publicly confounded, but also finally perished eternally in their own sins. (7.) From the Hermeneutical Rule: For it is not permitted to depart from the literal meaning, where no necessity compels us. Since therefore it is evident from history by no document that the Prophet gave his body to those striking him, or to those plucking out his cheeks, and did not turn away his face from those rebuking and spitting upon him, and so Grotius, Calvin, and Musculus take refuge in figures, and thus against the rules of correct interpretation depart from the literal sense without necessity, their glosses are by no means to be admitted.

(8.) From the execution of divine judgment,

For he who speaks here at the end of the chapter claims for himself such an execution, not human, but truly divine: From my hand this has come to pass for you; whence it can in no way be doubted that Christ spoke throughout the whole chapter, since it is one and the same person who testifies that he gave his body to those who strike, and who threatens the most grievous judgment with these words: From my hand this has come to pass for you. Therefore these things by no means fit the Prophet, but Christ, as being he to whom God has given all judgment, John 5. On which account Corn. à Lapide not badly [says]: FROM MY HAND, i.e., I Christ, the just Judge and Avenger, whom you treated unworthily, I send you to this fire of damnation by my invincible and eternal hand, which therefore will feed and foster this fire for you forever. This is the lot of the impious, who would not hear the learned tongue of Christ, nor listen to him. Which argument Zwingli himself urges in this place. But from my hand this has come to pass for you. It is a note which properly attributes the preceding discourse to Christ God. But this is the meaning: you kindled the fire of your vengeance, but through my hand this has been done, that you may burn. (9.) From the analogy of the complement. For Christ himself refers us to the Prophets, when he predicts such things concerning his passion, Luke 18: Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written by the Prophet concerning the Son of man will be accomplished. For he will be delivered to the Gentiles, and will be mocked, and will be treated with insults and spat upon, and after they have scourged him, they will kill him. Since therefore he testifies that it was predicted by the Prophets that he would be spat upon, which was also fulfilled in the palace of the High Priest, when they covered his face and spat upon him, and struck him with blows, as also in the praetorium, when they mocking him spat in his face, as Matthew ch. 22 witnesses, but it is nowhere else read to have been predicted in the Prophets than in this oracle, what is more certain than that Christ pointed his finger at this! Concerning which Oecolampadius: He recounts notable insults, namely spitting, slaps, and blows, of which it is clearly read among the Evangelists. But he indicates spittle and the slap more than the crown of thorns and the cross: for when he spoke most wisely to him, he struck him with a slap as if he were a fool, which was a great ignominy for such a Doctor, for they testified that he was a vain, trifling impostor, while Christ patiently bore all those things. (19.) From the consensus of the Doctors of the Church. For all the Fathers explaining these things, did not expound them in a mystical sense, but according to the letter concerning Christ, whom Leo Castrius cites. See Cyprian, Adv. Jud., Athanasius, Epist. ad Epictet., Ambrose, de Incarn. Dom. c. V., Jerome and Cyril in this place, etc. With whom agree not only all our own, but also the Papists, from whom Corn. à Lapide says these words are so clear concerning Christ that they do not need explanation, but meditation, as well as from the Reformed, both the disciples of Calvin, Piscator, Junius, the authors of the summaries in the Herborn German Bibles and of the notes to the Belgian Bibles, and others, as well as the masters of Calvin himself, whom he himself ought to have heard here deservedly, as they rely on the text: I mean Zwingli; who has it thus in his Apolog. Compl.: The Hebrew has the tongue of the learned, in that idiom of theirs, about which it has already been said a thousand times, for, the learned tongue. We do not dwell on these things, and what follows, being taken in the person of the Prophet to some extent: for in general they do not fit him, but Christ alone, as the outcome will show. Just as these things which are Christ's also fit any Prophet to some extent, but not properly, but by concession. Therefore the Lord gave the Prophet a tongue learned to rebuke and to console. Hence it is that he insists strenuously. But he gave the most learned and most salutary [tongue] to Christ. As also Oecolampadius, whose words are thus to verse 1.

He predicts the blinding of Judea, because of Christ struck with slaps, and not heard. The Jews expound this chapter as referring to Isaiah, although they themselves testify that it is nowhere found written that Isaiah was struck with slaps. Nor is it true that the Jews were rejected because of Isaiah. It is certain therefore that they are seeking a way of escape, lest they confess Christ crucified! The whole explanation of this chapter is worthy to be read, and applied to refuting Calvin's Judaizing glosses. Whom Dav. Pareus did not dare to defend here at all, even if, so as not to be entirely silent, he snarled against the Calvin-Judaizing of B. D. Hunnius: I do not wish to set myself up as a judge: I WILLINGLY admit the PIOUS AND PROBABLE opinion of the adversary, but I cannot defend it as ENTIRELY CERTAIN, nor can the adversary. But Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Piscator, Junius, the Herbornenses, the Belgians, and others acknowledged it as entirely certain. The sole defender of Calvin, for the sake of his Teacher, preferred to hesitate and stumble, rather than profess certainty in an open matter. He admits that Pelican and Hyperius acknowledge that these things fit Christ the Lord more clearly and more properly, and thus he also acknowledges that it would be most simple to accept these things as spoken by the Prophet in the person of Christ, Calv. Orthod. p. 253. And yet he still hesitates whether this opinion is sufficiently certain, namely that those things were spoken by the Prophet in the person of Christ. But what explanation is not only PIOUS & PROBABLE, but also CLEARER & MORE PROPER, and furthermore SIMPLEST, how can one doubt that it is entirely certain! But B. Hunnius discussed these trifles in the second Anti-Pareus p. 284, seqq. We must return to Grotius.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

CORPVS MEVM DEDI PERCVTIENTIBVS, ET GENAS MEAS VELLENTIBVS. ) Vellentibus barbam, quod etiam apud Latinos Poëtas opprobrii, aut ludibrii habet significationem. Hæc autem, & quæ se- quuntur, dicta figurate sunt ab Esaia, ut intelligeretur con- stantem ipsum fuisse in exequendis Dei mandatis, etiam si à Sobna & factione ejus prævalida multum irrideretur. Cœ- terum voluit Deus hæc omnia etiam κατὰ λέξιν impleri in Christo, ut nihil excusationis haberent Judæi, literarum au- cupes.

Habemus hic iterum insigne documentum ςρεβλότητος Grotii plane Judaicæ. Agnofcit non convenire proprie hæc Esaiæ, sed Christo, agno- scit voluisse Deum ea implere κτ᾽ λέξιν, idque in Chri- sto, & nihilo secius ad Esaiam illa detorquet. Quæ- nam vero obsecro illa ratio, voluit Deus hæc omnia etiam κτ᾽ λέξιν impleri in Christo, ut nihil excusatio- nis haberent Judæi literarum aucupes ? Nam aut illa prædicta fuere de Christo, secundum intentionem Spiritus S. aut non. Si prius, cur non de Christo hanc concionem intelligit Grotius, cur intentioni Spiritus Sancti suam explicationem non accom- modat; Si posterius, quomodo IMPLERI in Chri- sto potuit, quod de Christo prædictum non fuit, quomodo Judæi ἀναπολόγητοι redduntur, si nihil hic de Christo à Propheta ex intentione S.S.prædi- ctum! Ut vero depravationem istam retundamus, quia suam etiam fecit eam Calvinus, Hyperius, Peli- canus & Musculus, nec non è Pontificiis Thomas, vel quisquis Autor Commentarii illius est, (Tho- mæ enim esse negat Corn.àLapide) Argumenta hæc observamus (1.) E textus συνεχείᾳ. Quod Jeho- vah, qui negat se repudiasse Judæos, aut vendidisse, negat manum suam abbreviatam esse, cujus increpa- tione exsiccatur mare, qui flumina ponit in desertum, cœlos induit caligine, hic loquatur, & à Domino si- bi linguam eruditorum datam, aurem apertam esse e- affirmet, testeturque se corpus præbuisse percutien- dum; qui quis alius esse potest, quam Filius Dei, cor- pus humanum indutus? Hæc enim omnia cohære- re, nec a se divelli posse, manifestissimum est, quic- quid ogganniant Judæi, & Judaizantes Christiani. (2.) Et capitis præcedentis clausula. Quia idem Do- minus causam reddit reprobati populi Judaici, qui vocationis & ereptionis gentium, ceu prædæ e ma- nu fortis liberandæ, autorem se profitetur. Qui nullus alius est, quam Salvator & Redemtor noster Christus Jesus c. 49, 26. (3.) Ab argumento & materia hujus tractationis. Quia de libello repu- dii, & reprobatione populi Judaici, cum gentes affu- merentur, sermo est, ejusque causa constituitur, quod illum, cum veniret, non receperint, cum vo- caret, sequi renerint, cui Deus linguam eruditam dedit, aures aperuit, & qui corpus suum passionibus & ignominiis exposuit. At Esaiæ adventus & vo- catio reprobata causa propria non fuit reprobati populi, sed adventus & vocationis Messiæ reproba- tio. (4.) E linguæ eruditæ prærogativa; Quam- vis enim & Esaias lingua eloquenti & erudita in- structus fuerit, hic tamen ea κατ' ἐξοχὴν intelligen- da, quæ lasso cuivis in tempore oportuno erigendo sufficiat: de qua recte Brentius: Hic erudita & elo- quens lingua Christi, & annunciatio Evangelii ejus, quo pauperes, miseros & afflictos ita consolatur & vi- vificat, ut in mediis angustiis lætitiam, in morte vi- tam consequantur. Qualem eruditam linguam non relinquit Grotius Esaiæ, omnia ejus vaticinia & promissiones de Christo nucleo & medulla spo- lians. Cæterum propria est hæc eloquentia Chri- sto, adeo ut nemo etiam de illa quicquam partici- pet, nisi e plenitudine ejus accipiat, in cujus labiis gratia diffusa Ps. 45. cujus guttur dulce est Cantic. 6. qui unctus est S. S. & missus ad Evangelizandum miseris, & ligandum corda contrita Esa. 61, 1. cujus suavitatem & gratiam etiam supra prædicarat Esaias c. 42, 3. (5.) Ex obedientiæ perfectione summa. Quia aures excitatæ, perforatæ & præparatæ huic Docto- ri sunt ad obedientiam non aliqualem, sed qua per- fecte lex impleretur, ut e collatione Ps. 40, 7. 8. 9. manifestum est, quem huic loco parallelum agno- scit Calvinus. (6.) Ex omnimoda innocentia. Quia provocare audet ad judicium Dei, quod a nemine accusari, vel convinci ulla in re possit. Juxta est, qui justificat, quis contradicit mihi? Stemus simul: Quis poterit mihi jure litem intendere? Accedat ad me, prodeat & proferat, si quid habet, de quo me accusare possit! Quæ respiciunt graves, sed iniquas accusa- tiones Pontificum & Pharisæorum, Christo in die- bus carnis intentatas, qui vero publice testari pote- rat; Quis me arguet peccati! Joh. 8. Quia non nove- rat peccatum 2. Cor. 5, 21. nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus Esa. 53. Ideo pronunciat de adversariis su- is: Ecce omnes (illi adversarii mei) quasi vestimen- tum conterentur, vel potius putrescent, tinea come- dent eos. Quod in Pontifices & Pharisæos qua- rat. Hi enim non modo, cum innotuit Christi innocentia, publice confusi sunt, sed in peccatis eti- am suis tandem æternum perierunt. (7.) E Regu- la Hermineutica: Nam a proprietate literæ disce- dere, ubi nulla nos cogit necessitas, integrum non est. Quum ergo ex historia nullo documento constet, Prophetam corpus percutientibus dedisse, aut genas vellentibus, faciemque ab increpan- tibus & conspuentibus in ipsum non avertisse, adeoque Grotius, Calvinus & Musculus ad fi- guras se recipiant, & ita contra regulas rectæ interpretationis præter necessitatem τὸ ῥητὸν re- linquant, glossæ eorum minime admittendæ erunt.

(8.) E Judicii exequutione divina,

Talem enim exæquutionem non humanam, sed ve- re divinam vindicat sibi, qui hic loquitur sub finem capitis: De manu mea factum est hoc vobis; unde dubitari nullatenus potest, per totum caput Chri- stum loquutum esse, siquidem una eademque per- sona est, quæ testatur, se corpus dedisse percutienti- bus, & quæ minatur judicium gravissimum his ver- bis: De manu mea factum est hoc vobis: Igitur hæc Prophetæ nullatenus conveniunt, sed Christo, utpote cui Deus dedit omne judicium Joh. 5. Quo nomine non male Corn. à Lapid. DE MANU MEA, q. d. Ego Christus, justus Judex & Vindex, quem vos indigne tractastis, vos ad hunc ignem da- mno manu mea invicta & æterna, quæ proinde ignem hunc vobis in æternum alet & fovebit. Hæc fors im- piorum, qui Christi linguam eruditam audire, illique auscultare noluerunt. Quod argumentum urget Zwinglius ipse in h. l. At à manu mea factum est hoc vobis. Nota est, quæ superiorem sermonem Christo Deo proprie tribuit. Est autem hæc senten- tia, vos ignem ultionis vestræ incendistis, sed per ma- num meam hoc est factum, ut ardeatis. (9.) E com- plementi analogia. Nam remittit nos Christus ipse ad Prophetas, cum prædicit talia de passione sua Luc. 18. Ecce ascendimus Hierosolymam, & con- summabuntur omnia, quæ scripta sunt per Prophe- tam de Filio hominis. Tradetur enim gentibus, & illudetur, & contumeliis afficietur & conspuetur, & postquam flagellaverint, occident eum. Quum ergo id prædictum à Prophetis testetur, fore, ut conspua- tur, quod etiam impletum in palatio Pontificis, cum faciem ejus contegentes exspuebant in ipsum, & colaphis cædebant eum, ut & in prætorio, cum illu- dentes ei exspuere in faciem ejus, teste Matthæo c. 22. nuspiam vero id in Prophetis alias prædictum legatur, quam in hoc oraculo, quid certius, quam quod digitum ad id intenderit Christus! De quo Oecolampadius: Insignes contumelias recitat, nem- pe conspuitionem, alapas & colaphos, de quibus mani- feste apud Evangelistas legitur. Magis autem in- dicat sputa & alapam, quam coronam spineam & crucem: nam quum sapientissime loqueretur illi, qua- si insipientem alapa percutiebat, quod tanto Doctori magna ignominia erat, testabantur enim vanum, nu- gacem impostorem, Christo illa omnia patienter fe- rente. (19.) E Doctorum Ecclesiæ ὁμοψηφίᾳ. Omnes enim Patres hæc explicantes, non mystico sensu, sed secundum literam de Christo exposuere, quos alle- gat Leo Castrius. vid. Cyprian. Adv. Jud. Athanasius Epist. ad Epictet. Ambrosius de Incarn. Dom. c. V. Hieronymus & Cyrillus in h. l. &c. Quibus conso- nant non tantum nostrates omnes, sed etiam Ponti- ficii, è quibus Corn. à Lap. hæc verba ita clara esse de Christo ait, ut explicatione non egeant, sed meditatio- ne, nec non è Reformatis tum Discipuli Calvini, Piscator, Junius, Autores summariorum in Bibliis Herbornens. German. & notarum ad Biblia Belgi- ca, & alii, tum Magistri quoque Calvini, quos ipse hic audire merito debuerat, utpote textui inniten- tes: Zwinglium dico; qui ita in Apolog. Compl. suæ habet: Linguam Doctorum habent Hebræa, suo isto idiotismo, de quo millesies jam est dictum pro, Linguam doctam. Nihil moramur ista, & quæ se- quuntur in Prophetæ persona capi aliquousque: nam in universum ei non competunt, sed soli Christo, quem- admodum successus patebit. Quomodo & cuivis Prophetæ ista quoque, quæ Christi sunt aliquousque competunt, at non proprie, sed precario. Dedit ergo Dominus Prophetæ linguam ad increpandum & con- solandum doctam. Hinc est, ut strenue instet. Sed doctissimam & saluberrimam Christo dedit. Ut & Oecolampadius, cujus verba sic habent ad vers. 1.

Excæcationem Judææ prædicit, propter Christum ala- pis cæsum, & non auditum. Judæi hoc caput in Jesaiam exponunt, tametsi ipsi testentur nusquam inveniri scriptum, alapis cæsum Jesaiam. Neque verum est, quod repudiati sunt propter Jesaiam Judæi. Certum igitur quærere illos evadendi viam, ne confiteantur Christum crucifixum! Digna est tota capitis hujus explicatio, quæ legatur, & ad Calvini Judaicas glos- fas refellendas applicetur. Quem Dav. Pareus defendere hic minime ausus fuit, etsi ne omnino ta- ceret, adversus B. D. Hunnii Calvinum Judaizan- tem ogganniret: Nolo me Judicem sistere: PIAM ET PROBABILEM adversarii sententiam LIBENTER admitto, sed ut OMNINO CER- TAM defendere non valeo, nec adversarius valet. At omnino certam agnovere Zvinglius, Oecolam- padius, Piscator, Junius, Herbornenses, Belgæ, aliique. Solus hyperaspistes Calvini, in gratiam Præcepto- ris, hærere ac titubare maluit, quam certitudinem in re aperta profiteri. Fatetur, agnoscere Pelica- num & Hyperium clarius & magis proprie hæc Christo sto Domino competere, adeoque agnoscit etiam, sim- plicissimum fore, ista accipere tanquam à Propheta in persona Christi dicta, Calv. Orthod. p. 253. Et ad- huc tamen hæret, an satis certa sit hæc sententia, quod nempe illa à Propheta in persona Christi dicta sint. At quæ explicatio non tantum PIA & PROBABILIS, sed etiam CLARIOR & MA- GIS PROPRIA, adhæc SIMPLICISSIMA est, eam omnino certam esse, quomodo ambigendum! Sed nænias istas discussit B. Hunnius in Anti-Pa- reo altero p. 284, seqq. Nobis redeundum ad Gro- tium.

## 50:7
Vers. 7.

THEREFORE I HAVE SET MY FACE, LIKE A VERY HARD ROCK, AND I KNOW THAT I SHALL NOT BE CONFOUNDED.) I also displayed the constancy of my mind by my countenance. Compare Ezekiel 3, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

IDEO POSUI FACIEM MEAM, UT PETRAM DURISSIMAM, ET SCIO, QUOD NON CON- FUNDAR.) Constantiarn animi etiam vultu prætuli. Con- fer Ezechielem 3, 8.

## 50:8
Vers. 8.

HE IS NEAR WHO JUSTIFIES ME, WHO WILL CONTRADICT ME) God will approve my words by the things themselves, wherefore I do not fear contradictors. Compare Rom. 8. v. 33.

There is noted not only the significance of exterior constancy, by which the same is displayed in the countenance, but boldness in taxing the most hostile and powerful adversaries, and the most constant fortitude, with which he approached the passion itself, more immovable than any flint, not ignorant that he would rise again, and would not be confounded in the least, whence Luke 19 he set his face firmly, that he might go to Jerusalem. Which Oecolampadius noted here.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

JUXTA EST QUI JUSTIFICAT ME, QUIS CONTRADICET MIHI) Deus rebus ipsis mea dicta ap- probabit, quare contradictores non metuo. Confer. Rom. 8. v. 33.

Notatur non tantum significatio constantiæ exte- rior, quo vultu eadem præfertur, sed παῤῥησία in ta- xandis adversariis infensissimis & potentibus, ac con- stantissima fortitudo, qua ipsam etiam passionem ag- gressus est quavis silice immobilior, non ignarus se re- surrecturum, & minime confusum iri, unde Luc. 19. obfirmavit faciem suam, ut iret Hierusalem. Quod notavit hic Oecolampadius.

## 50:9
Verse 9.

BEHOLD ALL SHALL BE WORN OUT LIKE A GARMENT, THE MOTH SHALL EAT THEM) The 'as' must be repeated in the latter clause: Thus they shall be worn out as a garment, which is eaten by a moth.

Jerome refers this to the worm of conscience. And as a moth, he says, shall eat them. See the conscience of sins and the zeal of the saved nations. Concerning which it is also said at the end of this volume: Their worm shall not die. Cyril, regarding the perpetual calamity of the Jewish nation: you shall go into old age, into corruption and destruction, worn out by many and inevitable evils, and an incurable calamity shall consume you like a moth.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ECCE OMNES QVASI VESTIMENTUM CON- TERENTVR, TINEA COMEDET EOS) Repeten- dum in posteriori membro quasi: Sic conterentur quasi ve- stimentum, quod à tinea comeditur.

Hæc ad vermen conscientiæ refert Hierony- mus. Et quasi tinea, ait, comedet eos. Conscientia vid. peccatorum & Zelus gentium salvatarum. De quo etiam in fine hujus voluminis dicitur: Vermis eorum non morietur. Ad perpetuam calamitatem gentis Judaicæ Cyrillus: in vetustatem, in corru- ptionem & interitum abibitis multis malis confecti & inevitabilibus, & vos consumet quasi tinea insa- nabilis calamitas.

## 50:10
Verse 10.

WHO IS THERE AMONG YOU THAT FEARETH THE LORD, OBEYING THE VOICE OF HIS SERVANT? HE THAT HATH WALKED IN DARKNESS, AND HATH NO LIGHT, LET HIM HOPE IN THE NAME OF THE LORD, AND LEAN UPON HIS GOD.) That is, if there is any pious person among you, let him not cease to expect God's help, even though he be in the midst of calamities.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

QVIS EX VOBIS TIMENS DOMINUM, AU- DIENS VOCEM SERVI SUI? QVI AMBULAVIT IN TENEBRIS, ET NON EST LUMEN EI, SPERET IN NOMINE DOMINI, ET INNITA- TUR SUPER DEUM SUUM.) Id est, si quis est ex vo- bis pius, is quamvis in mediis calamitatibus, ne desinat Dei opem expectare.

## 50:11
Ver. 11. BEHOLD, ALL YOU WHO KINDLE A FIRE) That is, you, who provoke divine wrath against yourselves,

GIRDED WITH FLAMES) Thus also the Greeks interpret זיקות, not badly: the Chaldean [interprets it as] a sword, just as the Latin interpreter [interprets it as] a lance. Prov. 26, 18.

WALK IN THE LIGHT OF YOUR FIRE) Better: hearth. To feel divine wrath.

YOU SHALL SLEEP IN SORROWS) You shall die as exiles.

Oecolampadius here observes the true cause of the people's reprobation: He also posits another sin of the Jews, namely impenitence. For pardon is promised to those who crucified [Him], provided they sinned through ignorance. For Christ also prayed to the Father for them: Father forgive them, for they know not what they do. Peter also says: And now brothers I know that you did it through ignorance, as did your Princes. Therefore repent and be converted. He says therefore, if anyone among you has walked in darkness, that is, has sinned through ignorance, and the light of faith has not shone upon him, and he has feared the Lord, and even after such ignominies has heard the voice of the servant of God, i.e., Christ, let him trust well in the name of the Lord, and lean with firm hope on God. For he shall not be forsaken. These are the words of Oecolampadius. This epiphonema concerns both those who fear the Lord, that they may hear the voice of His servant, i.e., Christ, Is. 42, and when they walk in darkness, i.e. afflictions, cross, and death, and have no light of happiness or tranquility, that they may hope in the name of the Lord, and lean upon their God, i.e., our Lord Jesus Christ, our only true Savior. But the others, whether Pharisees, or Chief Priests, or Princes, or commoners, or Jews, or Gentiles, who despise the voice of Christ, kindle for themselves by their impiety a fire, by whose sparks, flames, and lightning they are to perish. Which punishment, says the Son of God, will come upon you by my hand, by my power. For nothing is more certain than that you will lie overwhelmed in perpetual sorrows. Therefore, those who are girded with flames (thus Jerome infers) and surrounded, and have strengthened a conflagration for themselves, are provoked to salvation, and it is said to them: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames which you have kindled, that in punishments and torments they may learn the power of God, and return to salvation. Moreover, it signifies the desolation of the Jewish people, by which they were handed over to the Romans; and that they bear the yoke of captivity even until now. For all these things were done by the hand of Christ, and they shall sleep in sorrow and sorrows: because they were willing to receive the Son of God neither by benefits nor by torments. Whence He speaks to them: Go into the eternal fire, which God prepared for the devil and his angels. Therefore the Jews walk in the light of their fire, and in the flames which they have kindled for themselves, and when they undergo death, they sleep in sorrows. B. Luther refers this to the modern state of the Jews. In sorrows YOU SHALL LIE, i.e., you Jews, who were instructed with iron and flame against my Church, you shall suffer that which you wished others to suffer, and you shall be nothing but the miserable and laborious dregs of the people, you shall not stand or sit, but you shall lie never to rise again, without kingdom and priesthood. These things shall happen to you by my hand, whom you despise and reject as a weak God. Cyril interprets that sorrow concerning the fear of eternal punishments, in which they fall asleep. Grotius's gloss is too meager: YOU SHALL SLEEP IN SORROWS, you shall die as exiles. Which he understands in such a way that they are not to be led back with the others into Judea. For far graver punishments are designated for such great crimes, when they kindle a fire for themselves, that is, they provoke divine wrath against themselves, as Grotius himself explains. For God is a consuming fire to such, Deut. 4, Heb. 12. And therefore it must be believed that sorrows of destruction, both temporal and everlasting, are inflicted.

His descendants are commanded to hear GOD by the example of Abraham and are raised up with the consolation of lasting salvation, when the world is about to perish and the enemies are about to perish in sorrows, [salvation] being future for Zion through Christ, and [future] for the happiness and preservation of the same after it has drunk from the cup of wrath, by subsequently offering it to its oppressors.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ECCE, VOS OMNES ACCENDENTES IGNEM) Id est, vos, qui divinam iram in vos concitatis,

ACCINCTI FLAMMIS) Sic & Græci interpre- tantur זיקות, non male: Chaldæus gladium, sicut lan- ceam Latinus interpres. Proverb. 26, 18.

AMBVLATE IN LVMINE IGNIS VESTRI) Melius: foco. Sentire iram divinam.

IN DOLORIBVS DORMIETIS) Moriemini ex- torres.

Observat hic Oecolampadius veram causam reprobationis populi: Ponit & aliud peccatum Judæorum, nempe impœnitentiam. Nam crucifixo- ribus venia promittitur, siquidem per ignorantiam peccarint. Oravit enim & Christus pro eis Patrem: Pater dimitte illis, quia nesciunt, quid faciant. Pe- trus quoque dicit: Et nunc fratres scio, quod per ignorantiam fecistis, sicut & Principes vestri. Pœ- niteat igitur vos & convertimini. Dicit igitur, si quis è vobis ivit in tenebris, hoc est, peccavit per ignorantiam, & non fulsit ei lux fidei, & timuerit ille Dominum, & adhuc etiam post tantas ignominias audierit vocem servi Dei, h. e. Christi, bene confidat in nomine Domini, & innitatur firma spe in Deo. Non enim derelinquetur. Hæc Oecolampadius. E- piphonema hoc concernit tum timentes Domi- num, ut audiant vocem servi ejus, h. e. Christi, Es. 42. & cum ambulant in tenebris, h.e. afflictionibus, cruce & morte, & non habent lumen aliquod felici- tatis aut tranquillitatis, ut sperent in nomine Domi- ni, & innitantur Deo suo, h.e. Domino nostro Jesu Christo, solo vero Servatore nostro. Cæteri autem, si- ve Pharisæi, sive Pontifices, sive Principes, sive vul- gares, sive Judæi, sive Ethnici, qui contemnunt vo- cem Christi, accendunt sibi ipsis impietate sua ignem, cujus scintillis, flammis & fulgure perituri sunt. Quod supplicium mea manu, mea potentia, inquit Filius Dei, accedet vobis. Nihil enim certius est, quam quod jacebitis obruti perpetuis doloribus. Ergo qui accincti sunt flammis (ita infert Hieronymus) atque circumdati, & sibi incendium roboraverunt, provocantur ad salutem, & dicitur ad eos: Ambu- late in lumine ignis vestri, & in flammis quas suc- cendistis, ut in pœnis, atque suppliciis discant Dei po- tentiam, & redeant ad salutem. Signficat autem Ju- daici populi vastitatem, qua Romanis traditi sint; & captivitatis jugum huc usque sustineant. De manu e- nim Christi hæc facta sunt omnia, & in mœrore ac do- loribus dormient: quia nec beneficiis nec tormentis Dei Filium recipere voluerunt. Unde loquitur ad eos: Ite in ignem æternum, quem præparavit Deus diabolo & angelis ejus. Ambulant ergo Judæi in lumine ignis sui, & in flammis, quas accenderunt sibi, & cum mortem subeunt, in doloribus dor- miunt. B. Lutherus refert ad statum Judæorum modernum. In doloribus JACEBITIS, i. e. vos Ju- dæi, qui fuistis instructi ferro & flamma contra Ec- clesiam meam, patiemini id, quod alios voluistis pati, & nihil eritis nisi miserabilis & laboriosa fex populi, non stabitis aut sedebitis, sed jacebitis nunquam sur- recturi, sine regno & sacerdotio. Hæc vobis fient de mea manu, quem tanquam infirmum Deum conte- mnitis & repudiatis. Cyrillus de timore æternorum suppliciorum, in quo obdormiunt, mœrorem il- lum interpretatur. Nimis jejuna est Grotii glossa: IN DOLORIBUS DORMIETIS, moriemini extorres. Quod ita intelligit, quod reducendi non sint cum cæteris in Judæam. Longe graviora enim tantis delictis supplicia designantur, cum ignem sibi accendunt, id est, iram divinam in se concitant, ut Grotius ipse explicat. Deus enim talibus ignis con- sumens est, Deut. 4. Ebr. 12. Ideoque dolores exi- tii & temporalis & sempiterni inferri, credendum est.

Audire DEUM exemplo Abraha jubentur ejus posteri & solatio eriguntur de salute mansura, cum mundus interiturus hostes- que doloribus perituri sint, Sioni per Chri- stum futura, & felicitati ac conservatione ejusdem postquam è calice iræ bibit, oppres- soribus ejus deinceps propinando.

## 51:1 Argument
Ver. 1. LOOK TO THE ROCK, FROM WHICH YOU WERE HEWN) To that parent of your race, a man of unshaken faith, although צור can also be taken simply for origin, as Maimonides notes.

AND TO THE HOLLOW OF THE PLACE) The perforation of the cistern: that is, the womb, which God opened.

Latin:

Vers. 1. ATTENDITE AD PETRAM, VNDE EX- CISI ESTIS) Ad illum parentem generis vestri, virum in- concussæ fidei, quanquam צור etiam simpliciter pro origi- ne accipi potest, notante Maimonida.

ET AD CAVERNAM LOCI) Perforationem ci- sternæ: id est, uterum, quem Deus aperuit.

## 51:2
I CALLED HIM ONE) That is, Lacking all offspring.

AND I HAVE MULTIPLIED HIM) From him [came] the Israelites, the Idumeans, the tribes of the Israelites, the descendants of Keturah.

Latin:

VNVM VOCAVI EVM) Id est, Prole omni ca- rentem.

ET MVLTIPLICAVI EVM) Ab eo Israëlitæ, Idumæi, Israëlitarum tribus, Cheturæ posteri.

## 51:3
Verse 3. HE WILL MAKE HER DESERT.) As above 49, 19.

AS DELIGHTS.) Like Eden in the Hebrew. See Gen. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 3. PONET DESERTVM EJVS.) Ut supra 49, 19.

QVASI DELICIAS.) Quasi Hedenem in Hebræo. Vid. Gen. 2.

## 51:4
Verse 4. THE LAW SHALL GO FORTH FROM ME AND MY JUDGMENT SHALL REST FOR A LIGHT OF THE PEOPLES) תורת also signifies doctrine. I will teach, he says, the peoples that I am the true God, and they will acknowledge that when they have seen my judgments upon the impious.

Latin:

Vers. 4. LEX A ME EXIET ET JVDICIVM MEVM IN LVCEM POPVLORVM QVIESCET) תורת etiam doctrinam significat. Docebo, inquit, popu- los, me esse verum Deum, idque agnoscent, ubi judicia mea in impios viderint.

## 51:5
Verse 5. MY RIGHTEOUSNESS IS NEAR.) Cyrus will come, a worshiper of the one God.

MY SAVIOR HAS GONE FORTH.) Who will deliver my people.

THE ISLANDS SHALL WAIT FOR ME, AND THEY SHALL TRUST IN MY ARM.) In the Hebrew: They shall trust in my arm. The Persians, bordering on the sea, will hope for victory from me. The Persians, as we said before, had no images which they might worship.

Grotius again refers all these things to the dismissal of the people made through Cyrus. But this is against the mind of the Prophet, whom it cannot be proven—as Grotius wishes—to be prophesying specifically, or rather uniquely, about this dismissal. Our blessed Luther assigned the argument more correctly: that it shines forth from the coherence with the preceding chapter. He continues, he says, in the consolation of the Church, gathered from the remnants of the Jews and from the Gentiles, which is afflicted on account of the word. You, Church, think that you are a deserted widow and repudiated by me: But do not despair when you consider your fewness and your barrenness, because he in whom you believe is powerful to multiply you and to make you fruitful from being barren. Look back at the exhausted Abraham and the barren Sarah, into what a numerous posterity they grew. Furthermore, you are not yet as desperate as Abraham and Sarah were; do not therefore succumb, trust, etc. Thus he consoles with the notable example of Abraham all those who are solitary, abandoned, and barren in appearance on account of the word. Cyril also handed down this connection: When he has sufficiently objected to those who have hardened themselves against the truth, and has declared the punishment that will befall them unless they are willing to obey the Evangelical oracles and cease to raise the proud and stubborn neck of their mind, he conveniently transfers the speech of exhortation to those who have believed from the blood of Israel. For the nation of the Jews did not perish entirely, but remnants were preserved, according to the voice of the Prophet. Indeed, as it is written in the Acts of the holy Apostles, many embraced the word about Christ and acknowledged the appearance of his glory. These, therefore, he addresses. And thus the example of Abraham fits perfectly, which cannot be so applied to the time of the Babylonian captivity. For the people were not then reduced to such great fewness and solitude. LOOK TO THE ROCK, FROM WHENCE YOU WERE HEWN. Grotius notes that the word צור refers to unshaken faith, or simply, as Maimonides wishes, to the origin: But the impossibility of the thing is rather designated, as rightly observed after Cyril B. Luther observes: i.e., as it was impossible for a man to be born from a rock, so it was impossible for anything to be propagated from Abraham. And yet, from that one exhausted and desperate man, you have been propagated as such a great people. The πρωτοβαπτιςὴς also looked to this when he said that God could produce children for Abraham from stones, Matt. 3, 9, recalling this promise to memory, so that those who were solitary and in number clearly nothing might raise themselves up under the auspices of the N.T. He also introduces the same sense for what is added by the Prophet: AND TO THE CAVERN OF THE PIT, FROM WHICH YOU WERE CUT, i.e., to the barren Sarah. Grotius renders it from the Hebrew as the perforation of the cistern, that is, the womb, which God opened. For by nature it was exhausted and closed. BECAUSE I CALLED HIM ONE, AND BLESSED HIM. To which Megalander concisely says: The emphasis is on the word ONE, i.e., do not look at the multitude of the rejected and your own fewness, even if you are unique and solitary. For I can make you into a very great people. Without doubt, however, this example of Abraham was a great consolation to the Apostles, who were moved by the scandal of the rejected multitude. This is Luther. Therefore, these things fit this time conveniently, not equally the time of the Babylonian exile. Similarly, these things also about solitude and the desert; THE LORD WILL THEREFORE COMFORT (according to that ancient custom of His, and by the same reason) ZION (the spiritual one) AND WILL COMFORT ALL HER RUINS (or rather solitudes), AND WILL PLACE (or make) HER DESERT AS DELIGHTS (as a Paradise) AND HER SOLITUDES (wastes) AS THE GARDEN OF THE LORD (a Paradise planted by the Lord Himself). The Church was not so deserted, nor was such great solitude and waste discovered then, as under the advent of the Messiah. If Grotius understands this of the bodily waste of the place, he is being inept. For the consolation promised here is that which brings forth spiritual joy and gladness, thanksgiving, and the voice of praise. And the faithful took joy not so much from the recovery of the former place as from the happiness and increase of the Church. Consolation, says Cyril, is here a promise affecting joy; and bringing and introducing a certain hope as if to the listeners, with God gathering from everywhere those who are to be called through faith, that it will not be deserted and waste, but like a certain flowering paradise, and most fruitful with trees and having an intelligible fertility, i.e., joy and exultation and confession, and the voice of praise. The ruins of Zion, says Brentius, are the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Christ and His Apostles restored these ruins when, through the Gospel, they recalled the wandering Israelites to the true knowledge of God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and brought back the lost sheep to the fold of the Church. But the deserts and solitudes of Zion are the nations, which had already long ago deserted the true knowledge of God, and as Paul says, were alienated from the Commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of the promise, having no hope, and lacking God in the world. But through Jesus Christ, those who were once far off have been made near. And as the Prophet says, this desert has been made like a Paradise and like the garden of the Lord, in which there is always joy, thanksgiving, and jubilation. He distinguishes, therefore, RUINS AND SOLITUDES. But the Lord addresses those who were persecuting the just, and were seeking the Lord. Which can also be understood of the desire for the Messiah. For this is the Lord, whom the faithful were seeking, Mark 3, 1. whence His advent is promised. My justice is near, my Savior has gone forth. Wherefore, Jerome rightly disapproves of the sense of the Jews, which Grotius has followed here, whose explanation is worthy of being read here: HEAR ME, YOU WHO &c. To those sleeping in perpetual sorrow and pain, who kindled a fire for themselves, and made most robust flames; You, who pursue justice, and seek the Lord, (he signifies the choir of the Apostles, and of those believing through the Apostles) look to the rock, i.e., Abraham your Father: from whom you were cut: and to the cavern of the pit, from which you were cut, i.e., Sarah, who bore you. And consider this, that when he was one and a hundred years old, and had a barren wife, I multiplied his children, as the stars of heaven: so that the multitude surpassed number. If, therefore, from one man so many thousands of peoples were born, what is it great for me to restore the ruins of Zion, and change its deserts into a paradise of pleasure, and into the garden of the Lord, which God planted in Eden toward the East, and let there be found in it, instead of various trees, joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise? The Jews refer this to the times of Zerubbabel, because after the Babylonian waste Zion was restored, and the temple built, and the ancient religion returned. But how is it said above to Zion: They will carry your sons in their arms, and your daughters they will carry upon their shoulders. And Kings will be your nursing fathers, and queens your nursing mothers. And behold, these will come from afar, and those from the North and the Sea, and these from the southern land, when Zion will say: The place is too narrow for me, make space for me, that I may dwell: which exclude the mediocrity of those times, nor are they known to have been fulfilled over the earthly Jerusalem. Thus also here the Lord speaks to those who pursue what is just: according to that which is said elsewhere, Seek peace, and pursue it. And again: Pursuing hospitality. And they seek the Lord, so that they may conjecture the present from the former: since many more difficult things have already been done, they should not doubt these things which are promised to be future. He adds afterwards: And this is to be noted, that in Zion, which is compared to the Paradise of God, there ought to be nothing else except joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise, so that what the saints are going to do in heaven with the Angels of God, this they may also meditate upon on earth in the constant praise of the Lord.

Furthermore, the LAW & DOCTRINE, which he says will go forth from him, denotes not only the knowledge of the one God, but the entire doctrine of the Gospel, because it is accustomed to be understood of this when the going forth of the law is promised, Is. 2, 2. Mic. 4, 2. And Jews and Gentiles are summoned to hear it, as to a saving doctrine proper to those who pursue justice and seek the Lord. ATTEND TO ME MY PEOPLE, AND MY TRIBE HEAR ME; FOR THE LAW SHALL GO FORTH FROM ME. And afterwards: THE ISLANDS SHALL WAIT FOR ME, &c. Jerome says that the multitude of the Gentiles is summoned, which is the people of God, so that they may diligently hear what is said, concerning which Zechariah ch. 2. Many nations, he says, shall flee to the Lord, and shall be to him for a people. He also brings forward another exposition: Or as some wish, the people is called the remnant of believers from Israel, and the tribes or nations are those who have believed from the multitude of nations, Moses saying to the nations in the Song of Deuteronomy, (ch. 32.) Rejoice, O nations, for his people. B. Luther urges that a new law is promised: and therefore these things cannot be understood of the doctrine of the Mosaic law. Here he adds the manner and form of how the Church is to be multiplied and prepared into a garden, not by hands and any force, but by a new law, i.e., the Gospel, which not Moses to the Jews only, but Christ himself through his Apostles, is to spread throughout the whole world. Therefore it cannot be understood of the law of Moses. And it is a notable and clear passage concerning the abrogation of the law; for he promises a new Moses, a new law. That cannot be the law of works, because such was the law of Moses, but it is the law of grace and mercy, by which we are justified, when we apprehend it by faith. Nor indeed is the word of the law placed absolutely anywhere that it brings in doctrine only concerning the one God. And those things which are added are said by way of explanation: THE LAW shall go forth from me, and my judgment shall rest for a light to the peoples, or as the LXX have it, for a light to the nations, that is to say. Therefore, law and judgment are the same. Namely, the doctrine of the Gospel, which is wont to be described in such a way, as is known from Psalm 119 and other places, because it teaches the judgment of God, that is, righteousness, and brings to us justification, which is said to be about to go forth in such a way that it will be for a light to the nations; because through it the nations can be illuminated and led to the true light and the inheritance of the Saints in light. Here the law of the Gospel, says Jerome, is shown to be spiritual: which shall go forth from Zion, not that of Moses, which was once given at Sinai. The word אַרְגִּיעַ, because it properly signifies in Kal to cleave, to cut, to break, in Hiphil Dievius translates I WILL MAKE TO BREAK FORTH, because when the morning light rises, the sky seems as if it were being split, and from there light breaks forth in infinite rays. Thus he also renders it in Jer. 49:19. There is nothing here about knowing the judgment of God against the impious, which knowledge is certainly not the light of the nations, which the Prophets promise quite often.

Now, that Grotius understands Cyrus by the JUST ONE and Savior, or as it is held in the Hebrew and among the LXX, the RIGHTEOUSNESS AND SALVATION of the Lord, is entirely foreign to the Scriptures. For nowhere is Cyrus called the RIGHTEOUSNESS OF GOD, nowhere the SALVATION OF THE LORD. This name, both separately and conjunctively, is proper to the Messiah, and is claimed for him in ch. 49, Luke 2, Acts 13. And how insipid it is for Cyrus to be called the RIGHTEOUSNESS OF THE LORD because he was a worshiper of the one God! For thus all worshipers of the one God would have to be honored with this name. The observation of Brentius on this passage is worthy of note: Consider that the Son of God in this discourse preferred to say: My righteousness arrives, and my Salvation has gone forth, rather than, I have arrived, and I have gone forth: so that by these words he might signify what goods, what benefits he brings with him by his arrival. For he did not come naked and empty, but brings with him his righteousness and salvation. And the Lord himself explains whom he understands, while he adds MY ARMS SHALL JUDGE THE PEOPLES, that is, shall govern: For by the name of the arm you may rightly understand the Son of God, who is also called the power of God, to whom all judgment has been given, who is the Ruler and Governor of the peoples. But who will admit that Cyrus is to be understood by the arms of the Lord that will judge the peoples? Grotius ought to have listened here again to Jerome rather than to his Jews. For he has it thus: And lest we should think that what he promised was to come a long time after: he adds, my righteous one or my righteousness is near. For Christ was made for us by the Father wisdom and redeemer, holiness and righteousness and all things by which names power is called. And it is beautifully said that righteousness is about to go forth, so that by no means one nation, but the whole world may be saved. But that the Son of God, who was sent by the Father, is called Savior or salvation, which in Hebrew is called יְשׁוּעַ: Simeon holding the child in his arms speaks: Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, because my eyes have seen the salvation of the Lord, which you have prepared in the sight of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the nations. And what follows: And my arms shall judge the peoples, or according to the LXX, and in my arm the nations shall hope, that is, and in my arm the nations shall hope; either this signifies that all are judged by his power: or that all nations are to believe in Christ, who is the arm and strength of God. It is also said in another place: Your arm with power. Let your hand be strengthened, and your right hand be exalted: And again: Sing to the Lord a new song, his right hand and his holy arm shall save for him. For the right hand and the arm of the Lord is he himself, who previously saved for himself those who were lost, so that none of those whom the Father had given him should perish. For that by the arm of the Lord is denoted not some secular arm, but the infinite force and power of God, and that hypostatic, which is the Son of God himself, is clear from v. 9. Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Who will understand Cyrus here? But that the Son of God is being stirred up, who as the arm of the Lord in days of old had struck the proud (Pharaoh), had dried up the sea, and had delivered the people from Egypt, is an analogy of the Scriptures. Moreover, the plural name of the arms of the Lord is said either by enallage, or is used with emphasis to describe the infinite power of God. Therefore, in v. 5 it is immediately changed to the singular, so that Christ may be designated. THEY SHALL TRUST IN MY ARM. In! For in whom is one to trust, if not in Christ? Who is also thus named in Is. 40:10. And his arm shall rule. Those are parallel passages, and they declare one another. Therefore, there is no need for us to understand the Apostles with Augustine in his book on the Divine Essence through the ARM OF GOD the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, or with Haymo, Vatablus, and Lyranus, or to establish with others that there is an allusion to the arms of the Lord extended on the cross. The Scripture, says Cyril, everywhere calls the Son the ARM of the Father. For his is the power. Afterwards, to v. 10, having cited Ps. 97, his right hand and his holy arm have saved him: He adds; but the right hand and arm of God and the Father cannot be anyone else but our Lord Jesus Christ.

And that this is not about temporal salvation, but eternal, is sufficiently taught by those things which are said in verse 6 about the destruction of the heavens and the earth and the salvation of the faithful remaining forever, and in verse 11 about the eternal joy of the redeemed with all sadness put to flight. For these things do not befit a temporal liberation, which was neither devoid of all sadness and groaning, nor eternal, but they befit solely the blessedness of the elect in heaven, Rev. 21.

Finally, when the islands are said to be waiting for the Lord, it is wrongly restricted to the Persians situated by the sea, when it is known that by the name of ISLANDS the nations are generally indicated: and those things which treat of saving faith are very badly snatched away to the hope of temporal victory. For they are said to wait for the Lord in such a way, and to trust in the arm of the Lord, that they promise themselves righteousness and salvation from him, as well as everlasting joy. Jerome observes that the multitude of churches from the nations are called islands, or the souls of the saints, which in the persecutions of this world are solidified by firm faith in God. Similarly, Blessed Luther explains: That the Church is to be propagated among the nations. For islands are taken for the inhabitants of the islands, and for the Gentiles, who held all the islands in the Mediterranean Sea. Compare Is. 41. 42, 4. The islands, as I think, says Cyril, he calls the churches of the nations, which, placed in the middle as if in the sea, agitated by the incursions of things as if by waves, carry away the crown of praise through patience. For patience works probation, probation hope, but hope does not confound.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PROPE EST JVSTVS MEVS.) Veniet Cy- rus, cultor unius Dei.

EGRESSVS EST SALVATOR MEVS.) Qui populum meum liberabit.

ME INSVLÆ EXPECTABVNT, ET BRA- CHIVM MEVM SVSTINEBVNT.) In Hebræo: In brachio meo confident. Persæ mari adfiti à me sperabunt vi- ctoriam. Persæ, ut ante diximus, nullas habebant ima- gines, quas colerent.

REfert hæc iterum Grotius universa ad dimissio- nem populi per Cyrum factam. Sed contra men- tem Prophetæ, quem de hac dimissione peculiari- ter, imo unice vaticinari, quod Grotius vult, proba- ri nequit. Rectius assignavit argumentum B. Lu- therus noster: quod è cohærentia cum præcedenti capite elucescat. Pergit, inquit, in consolatione Ec- clesiæ, ex reliquiis Judæorum & ex gentibus collectæ, quæ propter verbum affligitur. Tu Ecclesia putas, te desertam viduam esse, & repudiatam à me: Verum ne desperes, cum paucitatem tuam & sterilitatem tuam consideras, quia is, cui credis, potens est te mul- tiplicare, & ex sterili fœcundam facere. Respice ef- fœtum Abraham & sterilem Saram, in quam nume- rosam posteritatem excreverint. Porro tu nondum ita desperata es, sicut Abraham & Sara fuerunt, noli igitur succumbere, confide &c. Sic consolatur insi- gni exemplo Abrahæ, omnes solitarios derelictos, & steriles in speciem propter verbum. Quem ne- xum etiam tradidit Cyrillus: Cum objecerit satis, his, qui adversus veritatem obduruerunt, & futu- rum illis supplicium declaraverit, nisi velint Evan- gelicis oraculis obsequi, desinantque superbum & præ- fractum mentis suæ collum erigere: commode exhor- tationis orationem transfert ad eos, qui ex sanguine Israël crediderunt. Non enim in totum periit gens Judæorum, sed conservatæ sunt reliquiæ, juxta Pro- phetæ vocem. Siquidem ut in Actibus sanctorum Apostolorum scriptum est, complures sermonem de Christo amplexati sunt, & apparitionem gloriæ ipsius agnoverunt. Hos itaque affatur. Atque ita apprime congruit exemplum Abrahæ, quod non adeo ap- plicari potest tempori captivitatis Babylonicæ. Ad tantam enim paucitatem & solitudinem tum reda- ctus non fuit populus. ATTENDITE AD PE- TRAM, UNDE EXCISI ESTIS. Vocem צור inconcussam fidem, vel simpliciter, ut Maimonides vult, originem respicere notat Grotius: Sed ἀδυνα- μίαν rei potius designari recte post Cyrillum ob- servat B. Lutherus: q. d. quam impossibile, ex saxo hominem nasci, tam impossibile erat ex Abrahamo aliquid propagari. Et tamen ex illo uno effœto & de- sperato viro vos tantus populus propagati estis. Quod etiam respexit πρωτοβαπτιςὴς, cum Deum Abraha- mo ex lapidibus filios producere posse dixit, Matt. 3, 9. in memoriam revocans hanc promissionem, ut ea- dem se erigerent, qui solitarii erant, & numero plane nullo, sub auspicium N. T. Sensum eundem infert quoque, quod additur apud Prophetam: ET AD CAVERNAM LACI, DE QUA PRÆCI- SI ESTIS, h. e. ad sterilem Saram. Grotius ex He- bræo reddit, perforationem cisternæ, id est, uterum, quem Deus aperuit. Natura enim effœtus & occlu- sus erat. QUIA UNUM VOCAVI EUM, ET BENEDIXI EI. Ad quæ concinne Megalander: Emphasis est in voce UNUM, q. d. noli spectare mul- titudinem repudiatorum & tuam paucitatem, etiam- si unica & solitaria sis. Possum enim te facere in ma- ximum populum. Sine dubio autem hoc exemplum Abrahæ magnæ consolationi Apostolis fuit, qui scan- dalo multitudinis abjectæ movebantur. Hæc Luthe- rus. Tempori ergo illi hæc commode congruunt, non perinde tempori exilii Babylonici. Similiter etiam ista de solitudine, ac deserto; CONSOLA- BITUR ERGO DOMINUS (pro antiquissimo illo suo more, atque eadem ratione) SION (spiri- tualem) ET CONSULABITUR OMNES RUI- NAS (vel potius solitudines) EJUS, ET PO- NET (seu faciet) DESERTUM EJUS, QUA- SI DELICIAS (quasi Paradisum) ET SOLITU- DINES (vastitates) EJUS QUASI HORTUM DOMINI (ab ipso Domino plantatum Paradi- fum.) Non adeo deserta erat Ecclesia, neque tanta solitudo & vastitas tum deprehensa est, quanta sub adventum Messiæ. De corporali vastitate loci si in- telligat Grotius, ineptit. Nam consolatio hic ea promittitur, quæ gaudium & lætitiam spiritualem, gratiarum actionem, & vocem laudis infert. Et fi- deles non tam è loci pristini recuperatione, quam ab Ecclesiæ felicitate atque incremento lætitiam capiebant. Consolatio, inquit Cyrillus, hic est promis- sio lætitia afficiens; & certam spem afferens & infe- rens quasi auditoribus, Deo undecunque congregante eos, qui per fidem vocandi sunt, non fore eam deser- tam & vastam, sed tanquam paradisum quandam florentem, & arboribus fructuosissimam & fertilita- tem habentem intelligibilem, i. e. lætitiam & exulta- tionem ac confessionem, vocemque laudis. Ruinæ Zio- nis, inquit Brentius, sunt oves perditæ domus Israë- lis. Has ruinas Christus & Apostoli ejus instaura- runt, cum per Evangelion revocaverunt errantes Israelitas ad veram agnitionem Dei Patris Domini nostri Jesu Christi, & reduxerunt perditas oves ad ovile Ecclesiæ. Deserta autem & solitudines Zio- nis sunt gentes, quæ jam olim deseruerant veram Dei agnitionem, & ut Paulus ait, abalienati à Re- publica Israëlis, extranei à testamentis promissionis, spem non habentes, Deoque carentes in mundo. Per Jesum Christum autem hi, qui quondam erant lon- ginqui, facti sunt propinqui. Et ut Propheta ait, hoc desertum factum est sicut Paradisus & sicut hortus Domini, in quo semper est lætitia, gratiarum actio & jubilatio. Distinguit ergo RUINAS ET SOLI- TUDINES. Alloquitur autem Dominus eos, qui persequebantur justum, & quærebant Dominum. Quod intelligi etiam potest de desiderio Messiæ. Hic enim est Dominus, quem quærebant fideles, Marc. 3, 1. unde ejus adventus promittitur. Prope est justus meus, egressus est Salvator meus.
