Quapro- pter sensum Judæorum, quem Grotius hic sequu- tus est, merito improbat Hieronymus, cujus expli- catio digna est, quæ hic legatur : AUDITE ME, QUI &c. Dormientibus in mærore ac dolore perpe- tuo, qui fuccenderunt sibi ignem, & flammas robustis- simas esse fecerunt; Vos, qui persequimini justitiam, & quæritis Dominum, (significat autem Apostolo- rum, & per Apostolos credentium chorum) respi- cite petram, i. e. Abrahamum Patrem vestrum: de quo excisi estis: & ad cavernam laci, de qua præcisi estis, i. e. Saram, quæ peperit vos. Et hoc considerate, quod cùm unius & centum esset annorum, & steri- lem haberet uxorem, multiplicavcrim filios ejus, qua- si stellas cæli: ita ut numerum vinceret multitudo. Si ergo de uno homine tanta populorum nata sunt millia, quid mihi grande est, ut instaurem ruinas Sion, & deserta ejus mutem in paradisum volupta- tis, & in hortum Domini, quem plantavit Deus in Eden contra Orientem, & inveniatur in eo pro diver- sis arboribus, gaudium atque lætitia, confessio & vox laudis? Hoc Judæi ad Zorobabel tempora referunt, quod post Babyloniæ vastitatem instaurata sit Sion, ædificatumque templum, & antiqua religio reddita. Sed quomodo supra dicitur ad Sion : Afferent filios tuos in ulnis, & filias tuas super humeros porta- bunt. Et erunt Reges nutritii tui, & reginæ nutri- ces tuæ. Et ecce, isti de longe venient, & illi ab A- quilone & Mari, & isti de terra australi, quando di- cet Sion: Angustus mihi est locus, fac mihi spa- tium, ut habitem : quæ mediocritatem excludunt il- lorum temporum, nec super terrena Hierusalem im- pleta noscuntur. Sic & hic loquitur Dominus ad eos, qui persequuntur, quod justum est: juxta illud, quod alibi dicitur, Quære pacem, & persequere eam. Et iterum: Hospitalitatem sequentes. Et quærunt Dominum, ut ex prioribus conjiciant præ- sentia: quum multa difficiliora jam facta sint, hæc, quæ promittuntur, futura,non dubitent. Addit post- ea: Et hoc notandum, quod in Sion, quæ comparatur Paradiso Dei, aliud esse non debeat, nisi gaudium & lætitia, confessio & vox laudis, ut quod in cælis fa- cturi sunt sancti cum Angelis Dei, hoc etiam in terra jugi in Domini laude meditentur.

Porro LEX & DOCTRINA, quam à se ex- ituram dicit, non modo cognitionem unius Dei, sed universam doctrinam Evangelii notat, quia de hac accipi solet, cum exitus legis promittitur, Es. 2, 2. Mich. 4, 2. & advocatur ad eam audiendam Judæi ac gentiles, ceu ad doctrinam salutarem pro- priam illis, qui justum persequuntur, & quærunt Dominum. ATTENDITE AD ME POPU- LUS MEUS, ET TRIBUS MEA ME AUDI- TE; QUIA LEX A ME EXIET. Ac postea: ME INSULÆ EXPECTABUNT, &c. Hiero- nymus provocari ait gentium multitudinem, quæ est populus Dei, ut diligenter audiant, quæ dicantur, de quo Zacharias cap. 2. Confugient, inquit, gentes multæ ad Dominum, & erunt ei in populum. Ad- ducit etiam aliam expositionem : Sive ut quidam volunt, populus appellatur reliquiæ ex Israël creden- tium, & tribus sive gentes hi, qui crediderunt ex mul- titudine nationum, dicente nationibus Mose in Deu- teronomii Cantico, (cap. 32.) Lætamini gentes pro populo ejus. B. Lutherus urget, quod nova lex pro- mittatur : adeoque de doctrina legis Mofaicæ hæc intelligi nequeunt. Hic modum & formam addit, quomodo Ecclesia sit multiplicanda & paranda in hortum, non manibus & vi aliqua, sed nova lege, h. e. Evangelio, quod non Moses in Judæos tantum, sed ipse Christus per Apostolos suos, in totum orbem sit di- vulgaturus. Ideo non potest accipi de lege Mosi. Et est insignis locus & clarus de abrogatione legis; Pro- mittit enim novum Mosen, legem novam. Ea non potest esse lex operum, quia talis erat lex Mosi, sed est lex gratiæ & misericordiæ, qua justificamur, cum eam fide apprehendimur. Nec vero uspiam vox le- gis absolute posita doctrinam tantum infert de uno Deo. Et quæ adduntur, κατʼ ἐπεξήγησιν dicta sunt LEX à me exiet, & judicium meum in lucem popu- lorum requiescet, vel ut LXX. in lucem gentium sci- licet erit. Idem ergo lex & judicium. Doctrina nem- pe Evangelii, quæ ita describi solent, ut è Psal. 119 aliisque locis notum est, quia docet Dei judicium, h. e. justitiam, nobisque affert δικαίωσιν, quæ ita ex- itura dicitur, ut in lucem gentium futura sit; Quia per illam gentes illuminari, & ad veram lucem & hæreditatem Sanctorum in luce perduci possunt. Hic lex Evangelii, inquit Hieronymus, ostenditur spiritualis: quæ exiet ex Sion, non Mosis, quæ olim in Sina data est. Verbum אַרְגִּיעַ, quia proprie in Kal significat scindere, fidere, rumpere, in Hiphil ver- tit Dievius ERUMPERE FACIAM, quia quando mane oritur lux, videtur quasi findi cœlum, indeque infinitis radiis lux erumpere. Sic etiam reddit Jer. 49, 19. Nihil hic de judicio Dei in impios co- gnoscendo, quæ certe notitia non est lux gentium, quam Prophetæ sæpius promittunt.

Jam quod per JUSTUM & Salvatorem, vel ut in Hebr. & apud LXX. habetur, JUSTITIAM ET SALUTARE Domini Cyrum intelligit Gro- tius, alienum à Scripturis prorsus est. Nuspiam enim Cyrus JUSTITIA DEI, nuspiam SALU- TARE DOMINI vocatur. Nomen hoc utrumque tum seorsim, tum conjunctim Messiæ proprium est, eique vindicatur c. 49. Luc. 2. Act. 13. Et quam jejunum est Cyrum dici JUSTITIAM DOMI- NI, quia cultor unius Dei fuit! Sic enim omnes u- nius Dei cultores isto nomine honorandi erunt. Notatu digna est observatio Brentii in h. l. Consi- dera, quod Filius Dei in hac concione maluit dicere: Mea justitia advenit, & mea Salus egressa est, quam, Ego adveni, & Ego egressus sum: ut his vocabulis significaret, quæ bona, quæ beneficia secum adventu suo afferat. Non enim venit nudus & inanis, sed af- fert secum suam justitiam & salutem. Et explicat Dominus ipse, quem intelligat, dum addit BRA- CHIA MEA POPULOS JUDICABUNT, h. e. gubernabunt: Nam brachii nomine Filium Dei, qui & virtus Dei dicitur, recte intelligas, cui omne judicium datum est, qui est Rector & Gubernator populorum. At Cyrum per brachia Domini populos judicatura intelligendum esse, quis admittet? Au- dire hic iterum potius debuerat Grotius Hierony- mum, quam Judæos suos. Ita enim habet ille: Ac ne putaremus longo post tempore, quod promisit, esse ven- turum: infert, prope est justus meus sive justitia. Christus enim à Patre factus est nobis sapientia & re- demptor, sanctitas & justitia & omnia, quibus virtus nominibus appellatur. Pulchreque dicitur justitia pro- cessura, ut nequaquam una gens, sed omnis salvetur orbis. Quod autem Salvator sive salus, quod Hebraice dicitur יְשׁוּעַ appelletur Filius Dei, qui missus à Patre est: Simeon tenens puerum in ulnis suis loquitur: Nunc dimittis servum tuum Domine, quoniam vi- derunt oculi mei salutare Domini, quod præpara- sti in conspectu omnium populorum, lumen in re- velationem gentium. Quodque sequitur: Et brachia mea populos judicabunt, sive juxta LXX. καὶ εἰς τὸν βραχίονά με ἔθνη ἐλπιῶσιν, id est, & in brachio meo gentes sperabunt; Vel hoc significat, quod omnes vir- tute illius judicentur: vel quod in Christum, qui est brachium & fortitudo Dei, omnes credituræ sunt na- tiones. Dicitur & in alio loco: Tuum brachium cum potentia. Confortetur manus tua, & exaltetur dex- tera tua: Et iterum: Cantate Domino canticum novum, salvabit sibi dextera ejus, & brachium san- ctum illius. Dextera enim & brachium Domini ipse est, qui prius perditos salvavit sibi, ut nullus periret de his, quos ei Pater dederat. Quod enim per brachium Domini non seculare aliquod brachium, sed vis & potentia infinita Dei, eaq; hypostatica, quæ est ipse Filius Dei notetur, è v. 9. liquet. Consurge, consur- ge, induere fortitudine brachium Domini. Quis hic Gyrum intelliget? Filium Dei autem excitari, qui ut brachium Domini in diebus antiquis percusse- rat superbum (Pharaonem,) exsiccarat mare, ac li- berarat populum ex Ægypto, Scripturæ analogon est. Brachiorum autem Domini nomen plurale vel per enallagen dicitur, vel ad infinitam potentiam Dei describendam cum emphasi adhibetur. Ideo v. 5. statim cum singulari commutatur, ut designe- tur Christus. IN BRACHIO MEO CONFI- DENT. In! quo enim confidendum, nisi in Chri- sto? qui sic etiam nuncupatus est Es. 40, 10. Et bra- chium ejus dominabitur. Parallela loca illa sunt, & mutuo se declarant. Ideo non opus est, ut cum Au- gustino lib. de Essent. Div. per BRACHIUM DEI Patris Filium & S. S. vel cum Haymone, Vatablo & Lyrano Apostolos intelligamus, vel ad brachia Do- mini in cruce extensa alludi, cum aliis statuamus. BRACHIUM Patris, inquit Cyrillus, Scriptura passim vocat Filium. Ejus enim est potentia. Postea ad v. 10. adducto Ps. 97. servavit eum dextra ejus, & brachium sanctum ejus: Addit; dextra autem & brachium Dei ac Patris non esse potest alius quis- quam, nisi Dominus noster Jesus Christus.

Nec de salute temporali, sed æterna hic agi ea, quæ de interitu cælorum & terræ, salute fidelium in sempiternum manente dicuntur vers. 6. & de lætitia sempiterna redemptorum omni fugata tristitia v. 11. satis docent. Hæc enim non conveniunt liberatio- ni temporali, quæ nec omnis tristitiæ, & gemitus expers fuit, nec æterna, sed unice conveniunt bea- titudini electorum in cælis, Apoc. 21.

Denique quum Insulæ expectaturæ dicuntur Do- minum, perperam id restringitur ad Persas mari af- sitos, quum notum sit INSULARUM nomine ge- neratim gentes indigitari: & quæ de fiducia salvifi- ca agunt, pessime ad spem victoriæ temporalis abri- piuntur. Expectare enim ita dicuntur Dominum, ac confidere in brachio Domini, ut justitiam & salu- tam ab ipso sibi promittant, nec non lætitiam sem- piternam. Hieronymus Ecclesiarum ex gentibus multitudinem insulas dici, observat, vel animas San- ctorum, quæ in persequutionibus mundi istius, firma in Deum fide solidatæ sunt. Similiter B. Lutherus ex- plicat: Propagatum iri Ecclesiam in gentes. Insulæ enim pro insularum incolis sumuntur, & pro genti- libus, qui in mari mediterraneo omnes insulas te- nebant. Confer Es. 41. 42, 4. Insulas, ut opinor, in- quit Cyrillus, dicit gentium Ecclesias, quæ in medio tanquam mari positæ, rerum incursionibus quasi flu- ctibus agitatæ, collaudationis coronam per patien- tiam auferunt. Operatur enim patientia probatio- nem, probatio spem, spes autem non confundit.

## 51:6
Vers. 6. THE HEAVENS SHALL VANISH LIKE SMOKE) The stars in the heaven now appear, now lie hidden. THE EARTH SHALL WEAR OUT LIKE A GARMENT) Great parts of the lands are swallowed up by the sea. AND ITS INHABITANTS SHALL DIE IN LIKE MANNER) Many places become uncultivated, which were full of inhabitants. BUT MY SALVATION SHALL BE FOREVER, AND MY RIGHTEOUSNESS SHALL NOT FAIL) My promises remain always firm.

A remarkable perversion of the words, which are clearer than the sun concerning the destruction of heaven and earth. The stars in the heaven are not said to be sometimes hidden, when, namely, they are below the horizon, but the HEAVENS themselves are said to VANISH

VANISH LIKE SMOKE, which differ as much as heaven and earth. It is not said that the earth is consumed by the sea, as regards its parts, but the whole earth is designated as about to perish, THE EARTH SHALL WEAR OUT LIKE A GARMENT, or rather, it shall rot, it shall be dissipated: In Hebrew the consummation of the heavens is expressed by the verb נִמְלָחוּ they shall be consumed, which is explained by Aquila as μεωθήσε- ται they shall be ground into nothing; by Symmachus as ἁλιωσον- ται they shall be crushed like salt and vanish, to which opinion Jerome is witness that the version of the LXX can also be adapted: ὁ ὐρανὸς ὡς καπνὸς ἐςερεώθη, the heaven was established like smoke, which means that the entire firmness and strength and fortitude of the heavens is made equal to a most empty wind and smoke, which is dissolved into the air. Which in Ps. 102, 27, the other [phrase], here applied to the earth, is designated by the phrase: they shall grow old like a garment. But by Christ in a place parallel to this, the destruction of heaven and earth is expressed by the same word, Matt. 24, 35. Mark 13, 31. Luke 21, 33. heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not perish. By which word παρέρχε- θαι such a passing away is noted, which leaves no trace of the thing passing, such as is that of time, Matt. 14, 15. etc. And therefore the interpreters understand the words of the Prophet as concerning the destruction and consummation of heaven and earth, with Irenaeus leading the way, lib. 4. c. 6. Chrysost. in homil. on Rom. 8. Whence that which is subjoined concerning the inhabitants of the earth, AND ITS INHABITANTS SHALL PERISH LIKE THESE, is wrongly explained as concerning the places being deprived of their cultivators, because not only the destruction of the inhabitants of the earth, but also of the earth itself, and not of the earth alone, but also of the heaven, is expressed by the Prophet. Therefore no place will remain, if indeed the consummation of the universe is designated. Although indeed these things are so joined, that the inhabitants are said to perish, and the heaven to melt, and the earth to grow old, yet those things are not going to be in the same way for men and for the destruction of the universe, but what the reason for each is, must be learned from the Scriptures, and therefore, that we may touch upon this in passing, it is not permitted to conclude with Jerome that heaven and earth do not perish and are not reduced to nothing, because the inhabitants do not perish in that way, but are to be changed for the better. But of that elsewhere.

The words LIKE THESE, does not refer to the preceding heaven and earth, or to smoke and garments, but B. Luther wishes τὸ HÆC to be demonstrative, as if the Prophet were pointing to a louse or a flake. Sixtinus Amama with others prefers that כְּמוֹ כֵן be rendered LIKE SO, that is, SIMILARLY. But because smoke and a garment are not rightly said to die, and because he gave his own simile to the heavens, and his own to the earth, Ludov. de Dieu thinks that a peculiar simile of its own is also attributed to the inhabitants of the earth; and therefore he translates thus: Because the heavens shall vanish like smoke, and the earth shall grow old like a garment, and its inhabitants shall die like a louse. For even if it is not found elsewhere except in the plural כִּנִּים, because indeed it was not in use to speak of one louse, it is certain, however, that its singular is כֵּן, the notion of which seems to fit best in this place. Thus Dievius. But the version and interpretation of B. Luther can be conveniently retained, even if כְּמוֹ זֹאת is not present. For we can also understand the word כֵּן demonstratively: They shall perish like so. Osiander: Like a little gnat. But the inhabitants of the earth are understood as the impious, who are not indeed to be annihilated, as are the heaven and the earth, yet they shall perish eternally. Opposed to these in antithesis is the perpetuity of salvation and justice. For even if heaven and earth perish, even if the reprobate perish כְּמוֹ כֵן, yet MY SALVATION SHALL BE FOREVER, AND MY JUSTICE SHALL NOT FAIL. Which Grotius perverts as if only the promise of liberation from Babylon, certainly to be fulfilled, were designated. But the Prophet points out the perpetuity of THE JUSTICE OF THE LORD AND THE SALVATION OF THE LORD, which, with heaven and earth perishing, shall not fail, but shall be everlasting: because the salvation and justice of those who believe in Christ are eternal. Therefore not the firmness of the promises themselves, but the eternity of the promised salvation is hinted at here: so that the trust of the nations in Christ the Lord may be strengthened, whose end is eternal salvation, 1 Pet. 1. Moreover, it is of a great spirit, which B. Luther warns of here, of huge assurance, to believe that the justice which is promised to us in the bare word is greater and more stable than heaven and earth. Compared to which, heaven and earth are nothing. St. Cyril wishes the Son of God to be understood again through the justice and salvation of the Lord, just as his eternity is opposed by the divine Lyricist in Ps. 102, 26 to the mutability and destruction of the heavens and the earth. And he observes that the nations are ordered to lift their eyes to heaven, and the destruction of heaven is predicted, because they thought heaven was the Lord, and they worshipped the stars, and they worshipped the very earth subject to the feet of all, so that they might not be ignorant that those things which were produced, so that they might be, are again to be dissolved.

Latin:

Vers. 6. COELI SICUT FVMVS LIQVESCENT) Sidera in Cælo modo apparent, modo latent. TERRA SICVT VESTIMENTVM ATTERE- TVR) Magnæ terrarum partes hauriuntur à Mari. ET HABITATORES EJVS SICVT HÆC IN- TERIBVNT) Multa loca inculta fiunt, quæ plena fuere cultoribus. SALVS AVTEM MEA IN SEMPITERNUM ERIT, ET JVSTITIA MEA NON DEFICIET) Pro- missa mea manent semper firma.

Insignis perversio verborum, quæ Sole cla- riora sunt de interitu cæli & terræ. Non sidera in cælo dicuntur aliquando latere, cum scil. infra ho- rizontem sunt, sed COELI ipsi dicuntur LI-

quæ toto cœlo differunt. Non dicitur terra hauriri a mari, quoad partes, sed universa terra interitura designatur, TERRA SICUT VESTIMENTUM ATTERE- TUR, vel potius, putrescet, dissipabitur: In Ebræo consummatio cælorum exprimitur verbo נִמְלָחוּ consumentur, quod ab Aquila exponitur μεωθήσε- ται in nihilum comminuentur; à Symmacho ἁλιωσον- ται in Salis modum conterentur & evanescent, in quam sententiam etiam versionem LXX: Interpp. accipi posse ὁ ὐρανὸς ὡς καπνὸς ἐςερεώθη, cælum sicut fumus firmatum est, Hieronymus autor est, quod nempe omnis cælorum firmitas & robur & fortitudo vento inanissimo & fumo, qui in auras solvitur, coæ- quetur. Quæ Ps. 102, 27. altera, hic de terra adhibi- ta phrasi designata est: veterascent ut vestimentum. A Christo vero in loco huic parallelo interitus cæ- li & terræ eadem voce exprimitur, Matth. 24, 35. Marc. 13, 31. Luc. 21, 33. cælum & terra transibunt, verba autem mea non peribunt. Qua voce παρέρχε- θαι talis præteritio notatur, quæ nullum rei transeun- tis relinquit vestigium, qualis est temporis, Matth. 14, 15. &c. Ideoque de interitu & consummatione cœli & terræ Prophetæ verba Dd. Ecclesiæ intelli- gunt, præeunte Irenæo lib. 4. c. 6. Chrysost. in homil. ad Rom. 8. Unde quod de habitatoribus terræ sub- jungitur, ET HABITATORES EJUS SICUT HÆC INTERIBUNT, perperam de locis privan- dis cultoribus exponitur, quia non tantum interi- tus habitatorum terræ, sed etiam terræ ipsius, nec terræ solum, sed etiam cœli à Propheta exprimitur. Non ergo locus ullus supererit, siquidem consum- matio universi designetur. Quanquam vero hæc ita conjungantur, ut interire dicantur habitatores, & cælum liquefcere, & terra veterascere, non tamen eodem modo se illa habitura sunt hominum, & uni- versi interitus, sed quæ utriusque ratio sit, è Scriptu- ris discendum, ideoque, ut obiter id attingamus, non licet concludere cum Hieronymo, cælum & terram non perire, & in nihilum redigi, quia habita- tores ita non dispereunt, sed in melius commutatum iri. Sed de eo alias.

Verba SICUT HÆC, non ad antecedentia cælum & terram, aut ad fumum & vestimenta re- fert, sed τὸ HÆC δεικτικὸν esse vult B. Lutherus, quasi pilum aut floccam ostendat Propheta. Sixtinus Amama cum aliis mavult כְּמוֹ כֵן reddi SICUT SIC, id est, SIMILITER. Sed quia fumus & vestis non recte dicuntur mori, & quia cœlis suum dedit simile, terræ quoque suum, existimat Ludov. de Dieu, habitatoribus terræ etiam peculiare suum tribui simile; ideoque sic vertit: Quia cæli tanquam fumus evanescent, & terra tanquam vestis inveteraf- cet, & habitatores ejus tanquam pediculus morientur. Etsi enim alibi non inveniatur nisi in plurali כִּנִּים, quia nempe usu non veniebat, de uno pediculo a- gere, certum tamen est, singulare ejus esse כֵּן, cujus notio videtur hoc loco optime convenire. Sic Dievius. Sed commode retineri potest B. Lu- theri versio, & interpretatio, etiamsi non habeatur כְּמוֹ זֹאת. Nam δεικτικῶς intelligere possumus etiam vocem כֵּן Interibunt sicut sic. Osiander: Als ein Schniplin. Habitatores terræ autem intelligun- tur impii, qui non annihilandi quidem sunt, uti cœ- lum & terra, æternum tamen peribunt. Opponi- tur istis in antithefi perennitas salutis & justitiæ. Etsi enim cælum & terra intereant, etsi reprobi כְּמוֹ כֵן pereant, SALVS tamen MEA IN SEMPITER- NUM ERIT, ET IVSTITIA MEA NON DEFICIET. Quæ ita pervertit Grotius, ac si pro- missio solum liberationis è Babylone certo im- plenda designetur. At Propheta JVSTITIÆ DO- MINI ET SALUTIS DOMINI perennitatem, quæ cœlo & terra pereunte, non deficiet, sed sem- piterna erit, indigitat: quia salus & justitia eorum, qui in Christum credunt, æterna sunt. Non ergo promissionum ipsarum firmitas, sed promissæ salu- tis æternitas hic innuitur: ut gentium fiducia in Christo Domino roboretur, cujus finis est æterna salus, 1. Petr. 1. Est autem magni animi, quod hic monet B. Lutherus, ingentis plerophoriæ, credere, quod justitia, quæ nobis in nudo verbo promittitur, major & stabilior sit quam cælum & terra. Ad quam comparatum cælum & terra nihil sunt. S. Cy- rillus per justitiam & salutem Domini iterum Fi- lium Dei intelligi vult, perinde uti ejus æternitas à divino Lyrico Psal. 102, 26. opponitur cælorum & terræ mutabilitati & interitui. Et observat, ideo tollere in cælum oculos juberi gentes, & interitum prædici cæli, quia opinatæ sunt cælum esse Dominum, & Stellas adorarunt, ipsamque terram omnium pedi- bus subjectam coluerunt, ne nescirent, quæ producta sint, ut sint, rursum dissolvenda esse.

## 51:7
Ver. 7.

HEAR ME, YOU WHO KNOW JUSTICE) He addresses the pious, who were among the Hebrews.

MY PEOPLE, MY LAW IS IN THEIR HEART.) In whose heart is my law.

DO NOT FEAR THE REPROACH OF MEN, AND DO NOT BE AFRAID OF THEIR BLASPHEMIES) Do not fear the revilings of the idolaters, who will call you worshippers of clouds, circumcised, sparing of pigs, unsociable.

He understands these things concerning the pious among the Hebrews at the time of the Babylonian captivity. But although these things also contributed to their consolation, the connection with the preceding [verses] teaches that the times of the New Testament are being looked to. And therefore the interpreters have observed that the Lord addresses the Apostles and other first believers under the New Testament: whom Christ in the days of his flesh addressed and consoled in the same way, so much so that he seems to have drawn his words from this oracle, certainly having testified that the promised παράκλησιν (consolation) was already being provided by him. Whence Tertullian lib. 4. cap. Marc. 14. believes that Christ alludes to this and says the same thing, when he says in Luke 6, 22: Blessed are you, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you, and shall reproach you. For as Christ declares them blessed, promising them a most abundant reward in heaven: so here he promises them eternal salvation and justice. For since the impious persecutors must perish, who shall be delivered to perpetual torments, the worm shall eat them, and the moth like a garment and wool, the pious, through the righteousness of Christ received by faith, and through his salvation, shall be perpetually happy and blessed. MY RIGHTEOUSNESS SHALL BE UNTO GENERATIONS OF GENERATIONS, that is, it shall be perpetual. Because nothing else is accustomed to be denoted by that phrase than perpetuity: and therefore it is not to be vexed, as if it did not accord with eternity and the future age. For it is certain from verse 11 that the discourse is about this: Everlasting joy upon their heads, etc. And the same thing is said here concerning righteousness and eternal salvation, which was promised in verse 6. Jerome understands by this salvation and righteousness the Lord, remaining for eternity, or in both generations of the former and the latter people, who received his advent.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

AVDITE ME, QVI SCITIS JVSTVM) Pios, qui inter Ebræos erant, alloquitur.

POPVLVS MEVS, LEX MEA IN CORDE EO- RVM.) In quorum corde lex mea est.

NOLITE TIMERE OPPROBRIVM HOMI- NVM, ET BLASPHEMIAS EORVM NE METVA- TIS) Ne timete convitia idololatrarum, qui vos vocabunt nubium adoratores, recutitos, parcentes porcis, insocia- biles.

De piis inter Ebræos tempore captivitatis Babylonicæ hæc intelligit. At quanquam eorum consolationi hæc etiam cedebant, respici tamen Novi Testamenti tempora nexus cum superiori- bus docet. Ideoque Dominum Apostolos & alios fideles primos sub Nov. Test. alloqui, Interpp. ob- servarunt: quos eodem modo Christus in diebus carnis suæ allocutus & consolatus est, adéo ut ver- ba sua ex hoc oraculo depromsisse videatur, testa- tus certe sit, promissam παράκλησιν jam abs se præ- stari. Unde Tertullianus lib. 4. cap. Marc. 14. credit, Christum huc alludere idemque dicere, cum ait Luc. 6, 22. Beati estis, cum vos oderint homines, & cum separaverint vos, & exprobraverint. Nam ut bea- tos illos prædicat Christus promittens illis mer- cedem in cælis copiosissimam: Ita hic salutem & justitiam æternam ipsis pollicetur. Quum enim impiis persequutoribus pereundum sit, qui perpe- tuis tradentur cruciatibus, vermis eos comedet, & tinea sicut vestimentum & lanam, pii per justitiam Christi fide acceptam, & per salutem ejus perpe- tuo felices & beati erunt. JUSTITIA MEA IN GENERATIONES GENERATIONUM, id est, perpetua erit. Quia nihil aliud quam perpe- tuitas illa phrasi denotari consuevit: ideoque ve- xanda non est, ac si æternitati & futuro seculo haud congruat. De hoc enim sermonem esse è vers. 11. certum est: Lætitia sempiterna super capita eo- rum &c. Et idem dicitur hic de justitia & salute æ- terna, quod vers. 6. promissum erat. Hieronymus per hanc salutem & justitiam Dominum intelligit, permanentem in æternum, sive in utraque generatio- ne prioris, & posterioris populi, qui adventum ejus receperunt.

## 51:9
Vers. 9.

PUT ON STRENGTH, O ARM OF THE LORD.) Arm here is in the vocative case.

AS IN THE ANCIENT DAYS, IN THE GENERATIONS OF AGES) In the Hebrew: Awake as in the ancient days, in the ages of the centuries: that is, which were many centuries ago.

THOU HAST OVERTHROWN THE PROUD ONE) In the Hebrew רהב, which signifies proud, and is accustomed to be used for Egypt, as in Psalm 87:4.

THOU HAST WOUNDED THE DRAGON) The sea beast, Pharaoh. The prophets call tyrants by that name, especially the Egyptians. See Ezek. 29, 3. 33, 2. and what is to be said there THOU HAST DRIED UP THE SEA) The Red Sea.

Grotius is correct here. Therefore, the arm of the Lord is stirred up here by the Prophet. AWAKE, AWAKE: For what is added in the LXX version, JERUSALEM, they added that of their own accord. Whence the Greeks twist themselves (being ignorant of the Hebrew text) as to how what follows fits Jerusalem, 'hast thou not struck the proud one!' But the matter is plain from the source. For those things are said concerning the arm of the Lord, i. e., concerning Christ, who led out the Israelites and performed those miracles, just as He had promised Moses from the burning bush, when He appeared to him, that he might lead out the people, Exod. 3. Christ is therefore stirred up, that by His mighty power He may defeat the infernal Dragon, just as He once struck down Pharaoh, the proud enemy and sea dragon, who ruled over Egypt, constrained on one side by the sea, on the other by the streams of the Nile, whence he thought himself invincible. Compare Is. 27, 1. Thus Jerome: The Lord had encouraged those believing in Him, saying: Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not dread their blasphemies, and He had promised them His salvation and everlasting justice for their aid, which is none other than Christ, the arm of the Lord, of whom He had spoken above, and in my arm shall the nations hope. Whence the people speak to the arm of the Lord, and entreat His coming and implore the promised aid, saying: Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Awake as in the days of old, and exert all Thy strength, that Thou who for many ages hast delivered Thy saints from dangers, mayest also protect us with Thy strength. For Thou art He who struck the proud one, wounded the Dragon, namely Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who is also called the great Dragon in Ezekiel. Thou didst dry up the Red Sea, that Thy people might find a way through the most violent waters and the depths of the sea, and might escape the pursuing Egyptians. Thou, therefore, who didst these things, now also bring back those redeemed and liberated by Thy blood into Sion, and into the heavenly Jerusalem, or into the Church, which Thou hast prepared for Thyself with Thy blood: in which, when they shall be, they will rejoice with everlasting joy, and will say: O Lord, as with a shield of Thy good will Thou hast crowned us. For they shall have joy and gladness, with sorrow and sighing fleeing away.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

INDUERE FORTITVDINEM BRACHIVM DO- MINI.) Brachium hic est casu vocandi.

CON SVRGENTIBVS IN DIEBVS ANTIQVIS, IN GENERATIONIBVS SÆCVLORVM) In Hebræo: Suscita te sicut in diebus antiquis, in ætatibus sæculorum: id est, quæ ante multa secula fuere.

PERVERTISTI SVPERBVM) In Hebræo רהב, quod superbum significat, & solet pro Ægypto poni, ut Psal. 87, 4.

VULNERASTI DRACONEM) Belluam marinam Pharaonem. Tyrannos Prophetæ eo nomine appellant maxime Ægyptios. Vide Ezech. 29, 3. 33, 2. & ibi dicenda SICCASTI MARE) Rubrum.

Recte hæc Grotius. Excitatur ergo hic bra- chium Domini à Propheta. CONSURGE, CONSURGE: Nam quod in versione LXX. ad- ditur JERUSALEM, id illi de suo adjecere. Unde Græci se torquent (Ebræi textus ignari) quomo- do Hierosolymæ conveniant, quæ sequuntur, nun- quid non percussisti superbum! Sed res plana est è fonte. Nam illa de brachio Domini dicuntur, h. e. de Christo, qui eduxit Israëlitas, & miracula ista pa- travit, quemadmodum è rubo ardenti Mosi, cum ei appareret, ut populum educeret, promiserat Exod. 3. Excitatur ergo Christus, ut virtute po- tenti debellet Draconem infernalem, uti Pha- raonem olim prostravit, superbum hostem & Draconem marinum, qui Ægypto dominaba- tur hinc mari, inde rivis Nili coactæ, unde se insuperabilem putabat. Confer Es. 27, 1. Ita Hieronymus: Dominus credentes in se fuerat cohor- tatus, dicens: Nolite timere opprobrium hominum, & blasphemias eorum ne metuatis, Salutemque suam & justitiam sempiternam eis promiserat in au- xilium, quæ non est alia præter Christum, brachium Domini, de quo supra dixerat, & in brachio meo gentes sperabunt. Unde populus loquitur ad bra- chium Domini, & ejus deprecatur adventum & pro- missum implorat auxilium dicens: Consurge, con- surge, induere fortitudine brachium Domini. Con- surge sicut in diebus antiquis, & omnem tuam ex- erce fortitudinem, ut qui per multa secula sanctos tuos de periculis liberasti, etiam nos tua fortitudi- ne protegas. Tu es enim, qui percussisti superbum, vulnerasti Draconem, regem videlicet Ægypti Pharaonem, qui & in Ezechiel Draco magnus appel- latur. Tu siccasti mare rubrum, ut per aquas vehe- mentissimas & profunda maris viam tuus populus reperiret, & Ægyptios fugeret persequentes. Qui igitur ista fecisti, nunc quoque redemptos & liberatos sanguine tuo reduc in Sion, & in cælestem Hierusa- lem, sive in Ecclesiam, quam tibi tuo sanguine præpa- rasti: in qua, quum fuerint, gaudebunt lætitia sem- piterna, & dicent: Domine ut scuto bonæ volun- tatis tuæ coronasti nos. Habebunt enim gaudium atque lætitiam, fugiente dolore & gemitu.

## 51:11
Ver. 11. AND NOW,) Even now. EVERLASTING JOY UPON THEIR HEADS.) Crowns always fresh.

In the text it is held: And now, they that are redeemed by the Lord shall return, and shall come into Sion praising. A comparison is therefore instituted with the liberation from the hand of Pharaoh. And now they shall return in this way. Just as the arm of the Lord liberated the Hebrews from the hand of Pharaoh when he was drowned, and led them with joy and jubilation as far as Judea, into Sion, so now the same arm of the Lord, Christ Jesus, shall redeem us from the power of the infernal Dragon, that we may come into Sion and jubilate, here inchoately, but perfectly in Heaven: because it is added, everlasting joy upon their heads, they who are redeemed by the Lord shall come into Sion, they shall hold joy and gladness, sorrow and sighing shall flee away. Which cannot be drawn, as far as the literal sense is concerned, to the liberation from Babylon. Because the liberated had neither EVERLASTING joy, nor PURE and true GLADNESS, devoid of all sorrow, of all sighing, which the faithful never have in this world, but will obtain at last in the future age, where death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor shall there be any more pain, Apoc. 21, 4. In which place we have an interpretation of the words of Isaiah that is beyond all exception. Therefore Christ now responds to this stirring up of the Prophet or of the faithful people as if by an antistrophe, ver. 12. I, I MYSELF WILL CONSOLE YOU, I will be present with you, I will bring aid and solace, nay rather salvation and joy by My coming, and your joy no one shall take from you, John 16, 22. For I come into the world for your sake, and although I shall leave the world again in such a way that you will no longer (after the ascension into heaven) see and touch Me, nevertheless I will be present with you, all the days even unto the consummation of the age, Matth. 28. as Osiander here. Who, even if he acknowledges that this consolation could also have been rightly applied to the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, nevertheless understands it concerning the redemption made through Christ. Cyril says that there is an allusion to that liberation, but teaches that the subject here is properly the liberation of Christ. For they shall be brought back, he says, by the Lord, and shall come into Sion, which is understood as the Church, rejoicing and glad. For there shall be praise and joy upon their head, and exultation shall take hold of them. For He crowns, as it were, the souls of the believers, and fills them with all joy and exultation, and gladness, the Savior of all being celebrated by them, and having become for them as a chord and a lyre. But where there is a calling that calls to repentance and conversion, and to the wiping away of sin, namely through faith in Christ; where there is the ministry of the Holy Spirit, and grace, and the honor of adoption, and the enjoyment of infinite goods, and the hope of the kingdom of heaven, there is always that from which we may rejoice, and sorrow, mourning, and sighing also flee away. For what place is left for sorrow? And for what causes would there be sighing, where there is absolutely no occasion for sighing and sorrowing, nay where hope holds and possesses exultation, gladness, pleasure, which cannot be lost, in its own power, as it were. Let Grotius's gloss about always fresh crowns therefore depart, which agrees neither with the text nor with history. For the Hebrews did not always have fresh victories after their return, but were subject to many afflictions, as is evident from the books of the Maccabees.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET NUNC,) Etiam nunc. LÆTITIA SEMPITERNA SUPER CAPITA EO- RUM.) Coronæ semper recentes.

In textu habetur: Et nunc, qui redempti sunt à Domino, revertentur, & venient in Sion laudan- tes. Collatio ergo instituitur cum liberatione è ma- nu Pharaonis. Et nunc ita revertentur. Sicut bra- chium Domini liberavit Ebræos de manu Pharao- nis eo submerso, illosque cum gaudio & jubilo de- duxit usque in Judæam, in Sion, ita nunc idem Do- mini brachium Christus Jesus à Draconis inferna- lis potestate redimet nos, ut in Sion veniamus & jubilemus, hic inchoate, perfecte vero in Cœlo: quia additur lætitia sempiterna super capita eorum, qui redempti à Domino in Sion veniunt, gaudium & lætitiam tenebunt, fugiet dolor & gemitus. Quæ tra- hi non possunt, quod ad sensum literalem attinet, ad liberationem è Babylone. Quia liberati neque SEMPITERNAM habebant lætitiam, neque GAUDIUM MERUM & verum, omnis doloris, omnis gemitus expers, quod in hoc mundo nun- quam habent fideles, sed obtinebunt demum in fu- turo seculo, ubi mors ultra non erit, neque luctus, neq; clamor, neque dolor erit ultra, Apoc. 21, 4. Quo loco verborum Esaiæ interpretationem habemus omni exceptione majorem. Ideo Christus ad hanc exci- tationem Prophetæ vel populi fidelis veluti per an- tistropham nunc respondet vers. 12. EGO, EGO IPSE CONSOLABOR VOS, adero vobis, o- pem & solatium, imo salutem & gaudium afferam adventu meo, & gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis, Joh. 16, 22. Nam & vestri causa in mundum venio, & tametsi mundum ita iterum relinquam, ut non amplius (post ascensum in cœlum) videatis & palpetis me, tamen nihilo minus adero vobis, o- mnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi, Matth. 28. ut hic Osiander. Qui etiamsi agnoscat consolationem hanc recte etiam applicari potuisse ad liberationem e captivitate Babylonica, intelligit tamen eam de redemptione per Christum facta. Cyrillus alludi ad istam liberationem dicit, sed agi proprie hic de liberatione Christi, docet. Reducen- tur enim, inquit, a Domino, & venient in Sion, quæ scil. intelligentia percipitur, i. e. Ecclesiam, lætantes & gaudentes. Erit enim in capite eorum laus & læti- tia, & exultatio eos apprehendet. Coronat enim quasi animas credentium, omnique eas replet gaudio & exultatione, & lætitia, universorum Servator ab ipsis celebratus, illisque quasi chorda & lyra factus. Ubi autem vocatio est vocans ad pœnitentiam & conver- sionem, & ad peccati abstersiorem, per fidem videli- cet in Christo; ubi Spiritus S. Ministerium est, & gratia, & adoptionis honor, ac infinitorum bonorum fruitio, & regni cælorum spes, ibi semper est, unde lætemur, fugitque etiam dolor, mæror & gemitus. Quis enim locus relictus est dolori? Et quibus de causis ge- mitus esset, ubi gemendi & dolendi nulla prorsus est occasio, imo ubi spes exultationem, lætitiam, volupta- tem, quæ amitti non potest, atque gaudium in sua quasi potestate obtinet & possidet. Facessat ergo glossa Grotii de semper recentibus coronis, quæ neque tex- tui, neque historiæ congruit. Non enim semper re- centes habebant victorias Ebræi, post reditum, sed multis subjecti fuere afflictionibus, ut e libris Mac- cabæorum constat.

## 51:12
Ver. 12. WHO ART THOU, THAT THOU SHOULDST FEAR A MORTAL MAN?) Is your spirit so little, that you fear men, having God as your helper?

Latin:

Vers. 12. QVIS TU, UT TIMERES AB HOMINE MORTALI?) Ita parum tibi sit animi, ut homines timeas, Deum habens adjutorem?

## 51:13
Ver. 13. WHERE NOW IS THE FURY OF THE OPPRESSOR?) That power of the Chaldeans?

Latin:

Vers. 13. UBI NUNC EST FUROR TRIBULAN- TIS?) Vis illa Chaldæorum?

## 51:14
Ver. 14. HE SHALL QUICKLY COME MARCHING TO OPEN.) In the Hebrew: The bound one has hastened, that he may be loosed. The captive people, through Zerubbabel: for he will carry his prayers to Cyrus.

HE SHALL NOT KILL EVEN TO DESTRUCTION.) In Hebrew: He shall not die in the pit: he shall not perish in miseries.

NOR SHALL HIS BREAD FAIL) His provision shall not be lacking.

Grotius again applies these things to Cyrus, and to the Chaldeans. But the preceding context teaches that Pharaoh is rather indicated by the name of the oppressor: as if to say, just as the fury of Pharaoh pursuing the Hebrews was swallowed up by the sea, so also the fury of those pursuing you will soon be swallowed up and vanish. Therefore, these things are not to be drawn to the liberation from the Babylonian captivity with the Jews, but, since the preceding verses treat of the liberation of Christ, these must be explained in a similar way, with most Christian interpreters. The Hebrew words concisely placed מִהַר צֹעֶה לְהִפָּתֵחַ are variously explained, concerning which see Amama on this passage. Even if the translation of Grotius were assumed to the greatest extent, with which the Pagnini, Italian, and Spanish versions agree; yet the haste of a captive people in offering prayers to Cyrus would not be noted, since nothing has been handed down about Cyrus before: if indeed it can be understood as hastening to God with prayers. Munster on this passage: This passage is very obscure. Some of the Hebrews think this contains the meaning: He who is thus pressed by a tyrant, and is held bound as if in a prison of sand, let him patiently endure; after a little time the prison will be opened, he will escape death, and he will have wherewith to live. Kimchi explains צועה as טלטול, a wandering or nomadic dwelling, such as the Jews have today, who nowhere have a certain and safe habitation. And that too is captivity. And such was almost the state of Christians long ago among the nations, of whom the Prophet seems to make mention here. Jerome interpreted it as 'the one walking,' because צועה also denotes one who is roaming: and he understood this of Christ. Where then is the pride of the persecutors now? Where is the secular power with which they raged against you with rabid mouth? My son will come quickly, walking and trampling upon your adversaries, so that he may open to you the way of victory, or that he may unlock the underworld, who will not kill to the point of extermination, but wishes to save those who are converted. Finally, that bread which is interpreted, with the Gospel proving it, as Doctrine, will never fail, but will always be open to those wishing to eat. Which sense is not inelegant, and seems to favor that which is said in verse 15, THE LORD OF HOSTS IS HIS NAME שמו. For so it is held in the Hebrew, not שמי 'my name.' Corn. à Lapide explained it thus: the arm of the Lord will come quickly, that is, Christ the powerful warrior, walking and trampling upon your adversaries, so that he may open prisons, and from there lead you out, already condemned to death, as he did for Peter in Acts 12:11. HE WILL NOT KILL, that is, he will not permit the Tyrants to kill the faithful to the point of extermination. Vatablus renders it thus: FOR HE WILL HASTEN (or will devote effort, namely when Christ has arrived) WALKING (wandering, exiled, understanding in the kingdom of Christ) so that IT MAY BE OPENED (that is, loosened from the bonds of sins) AND HE SHALL NOT DIE (bound) IN THE PIT, NOR SHALL HIS PROVISION FAIL (his bread, that is, the word of the Lord and doctrine.) B. Luther, however, refers these things to Pharaoh. This passage, he says, translate thus: Where now is the fury of the oppressor? While he was hastening and running to open (that is, to dismiss the people of Israel), they themselves (namely the people of Israel) were not dying in the pit, nor was bread failing them (that is, the people). So also Brentius: But I ask you, where now is the fury of that oppressor! Did I not restrain him remarkably! For I drove him to such a necessity by punishments that, although he could be persuaded by no words to let you go free, at length he ran in haste, so that he might not only let you go free, lest you perish to the point of extermination, but also bestow great wealth upon you, so that bread or provision might not be lacking to you. And Osiander: Where (now) is the fury of the oppressor, I mean Pharaoh, King of Egypt, who had once most grievously afflicted the people of God? He will come quickly, Hebr. 'He hastened walking to open,' i.e., He hastened at last to dismiss the Israelites, and he not only permitted them to leave Egypt, but also compelled them, and he will not kill to the point of extermination (i.e., the Israelite people did not die with the firstborn of the Egyptians) nor will his bread fail, more correctly 'nor did his bread fail' (the people of God, i.e., although the Israelites were leaving Egypt in haste, yet in the desert they did not have need to perish from hunger. For when the provision which they had carried with them from Egypt was consumed, the heavenly Manna soon followed). Musculus himself, although prone to Jewish glosses, rejected that Jewish explanation which Grotius seized upon: It can be read: Where is, or where will be the fury of the one afflicting? i.e., It will vanish, it will be nowhere, it will be rendered void. In this sense it will have to be understood concerning the future overthrow of Babylon, by which all its fury was to be extinguished. Some others, however, refer it to the slaughter of the Assyrians, by which their fury was extinguished by the hand of an Angel. And these read: Where is now the fury of the oppressor, namely the Assyrian? To me, however, the exposition of those who refer it to the fury of Pharaoh pleases more, to which sense the following things seem to favor: 'Who was hastening walking to open, that he might not die by extermination, nor did his bread fail.' He speaks of Pharaoh, who had afflicted the people of Israel in Egypt with the harshest captivity, concerning whose fury he asked and said, 'And where is the fury of the oppressor?' He adds, 'who was hastening walking to open.' The little word שׁוֹעֶה i.e., 'who,' is missing in the Hebrew. But how Pharaoh, struck by so many plagues after the slaughter of the firstborn, hastened to open, i.e., to dismiss the captive Israelites, so that they might not die by extermination, one may see in Ex. 12, where it is read thus: And the Egyptians urged the people of Israel, that they might go out of the land speedily, saying: We shall all die. Without a doubt, they were hastening, walking, that is, the couriers who were sent to urge the Israelites to leave most quickly. For they feared, if this were not done, that it would come to pass that they would all die to the point of extermination. The Israelites had seen this, but neither the elders had kept it in mind, nor did their descendants think about it. 'Nor did his bread fail,' he says. He understands it of that which did not cease to provide bread from heaven for the redeemed people during all that time they stayed in the desert. It is too narrow that some refer it to the flour which the people carried with them from Egypt. This verse is obscure. I have expressed the sense, which to me, after some others, including the German Interpreter, seemed to be the simpler one. Lyranus explains it concerning the Anti-Christ in this manner: 'He will come quickly,' i.e., he will swiftly reach the degree of his power, 'walking to open,' his own most wicked intent against Christ. 'And he will not kill to the point of extermination,' namely the Christians, being prevented by sudden death, 'nor will his bread fail,' i.e., he will not die of hunger, just as he will not by the sword, but by the word of our Lord Jesus Christ. There are those who explain it concerning the hastening of the liberation of the exiles from Babylon. And these read: 'The exile will hasten, that he may be loosened, nor will he die in the pit, nor will his bread fail.' 'And I am the Lord your God, who divides the sea.' He attaches the history of the divided Red Sea, so that he may recall to their memory how their ancestors were liberated from Egypt and led across the bottom of the sea on dry feet. He refreshes these histories for them, so that they may better accommodate themselves to future events. That, that its waves may roar, is added to this end, that it may express the vehemence of this dividing, which had been done by a vehement and burning blast, just as one may see in Ex. 14: Without doubt that dividing of the sea was not done without the greatest roaring and raging of its waves. Thus Musculus. We therefore judge that this sense, handed down by the blessed Luther as the most simple, should be retained, and therefore we render v. 15 thus according to the customary Hebraism: I the Lord thy God, who divide the sea &c. Whose name, the Lord of hosts, should not be referred to any other person than the one speaking. Grotius erred, in that he snatched away to the future things which are said in the past, and which by the force of the context look to those things which were done long ago, and indeed even transferred them into the future, against the duty of a good interpreter: HE SHALL HASTEN THE BOUND that he may be loosed: Because in the Hebrew it is מִהַר HE HASTENED.

Latin:

Vers. 14. CITO VENIET GRADIENS AD APE- RIENDUM.) In Hebræo: Festinavit vinctus, ut solvatur. Populus captivus, per Zorobabelem: nam preces suas ad Cyrum deferet.

NON INTERFICIET USQVE AD INTERNE- CIONEM.) In Hebr. Non morietur in fovea: non interibit in miseriis.

NEC DEFICIET PANIS EJUS) Viaticum illi non deerit.

Iterum ad Cyrum hæc rapit Grotius, & ad Chaldæos. At tribulantis nomine Pharaonem po- tius indigitari, superiora docent: q. d. ut furor Pha- raonis Ebræos persequentis absorptus est a mari, ita & furor persequentium te mox absorbebitur, & eva- nescet. Non ergo cum Judæis ad liberationem e ca- ptivitate Babylonica hæc trahenda, sed, quum an- tecedentia de liberatione Christi agant, hæc simili- ter explicanda erunt, cum plerisque Christianis In- terpp. Ebræa concise posita מִהַר צֹעֶה לְהִפָּתֵחַ va- rie exponuntur, quo de videatur Amama ad hunc locum. Etiamsi autem maxime assumeretur trans- latio Grottii, cui congruit Pagn. Italica, & Hispanica versio; non tamen populi captivi festinatio in pre- cibus ad Cyrum deferendis notaretur, quum nihil de Cyro antea traditum sit: siquidem ad Deum festi- nare precibus intelligi possit. Munsterus ad h. l. Est locus iste multum obscurus. Quidam Ebræorum pu- tant hunc continere sensum: Qui sic premitur a Ty- ranno, & quasi in arena carcere vinctus tenetur, fi- patienter sustineat, post modicum tempus aperietur carcer, evadet mortem, & habebit unde vivat. Kimchi exponit צועה pro טלטול discursu, vel vaga habi- tatione, qualem hodie Judæi habent, qui nullibi certam & tutam habent mansionem. Et id quoque est captivitas. Et tales fere olim fuit status Christia- norum inter gentes, quorum Propheta hic memi- nisse videtur. Hieronymus gradientem interpreta- tus est: quia צועה notat etiam grassantem: Idque intellexit de Christo. Ubi est ergo nunc persequuto- rum superbia? ubi potentia secularis, qua in te ore rabido sæviebant? Cito veniet filius meus, gradiens & conculcans adversarios tuos, ut aperiat tibi viam victoriæ, sive ut inferos reseret, qui non interficiat us- que ad internecionem, sed velit salvare conversos. Denique panis illius, qui interpretatur, Evangelio pro- bante, Doctrina, nunquam deficiet, sed semper volen- tibus ad vescendum patebit. Qui sensus non inele- gans est, & favere videtur ei, quod vers. 15. dicitur DOMINUS EXERCITUUM NOMEN EJUS שמו. Sic enim habetur in Ebræo, non שמי nomen meum. Corn. à Lapide sic exposuit, cito veniet bra- chium Domini, id est, Christus potens bellator, gra- diens & conculcans adversarios tuos, ut carceres a- periat, indeque te jam ad mortem damnatum educat, ut fecit Petro Actor. 12, 11. NON INTERFI- CIET, id est, non permittet Tyrannos interficere fi- deles usque ad internecionem. Vatablus ita reddit: QUIN FESTINABIT (vel dabit operam, nempe ubi advenerit Christus) DISCURRENS (vagus exulans, subintell. in regno Christi) ut APERIA- TUR (solvatur à vinculis scil. peccatorum) ET NON MORIATUR (vinctus) IN FOVEA, NEQUE DEFICIAT EUM COMMEATUS (panis ejus, id est, verbum Domini & doctrina.) B. Lutherus tamen ad Pharaonem hæc refert. Hunc locum, inquit, sic verte: Ubi nunc est furor tribu- lantis? Dum acceleraret & discurreret ad aperien- dum, (h. e. ad dimittendum populum Israël) ipsi au- tem (scilicet populus Israel) non moriebantur in fo- vea, nec deficiebat ea (idest, populum) panis. Sic etiam Brentius: Sed quæso te, ubi nunc est furor istius tribulatoris! Annonne compescebam eum egregie! Eo enim necessitatis adigebam eum suppliciis, ut cum nullis verbis persuaderi potuerit, quo te liberum dimit- teret, tandem festinabundus discurrerit, ut non so- lum te liberum, ne ad internecionem perires, dimitte- ret, verum etiam magnas opes in te conferret, ne tibi panis seu commeatus deesset. Et Osiander: Ubi (nunc) est furor tribulantis, Pharaonis dico, Regis Ægyptiaci, qui populum Dei gravissime olim afflixe- rat? Cito veniet, Hebr. Festinavit gradiens ad ape- riendum, i. e. Festinavit tandem, ut dimitteret Israë- litas, neque tantum Ægypto egredi eos permisit, sed & coëgit, & non interficiet usque ad internecionem (i. e. Israëliticus populus non moriebatur cum primogeni- tis Ægyptiorum) nec deficiet, rectius nec deficiebat panis ejus (populi Dei, i. e. quamvis festinanter Æ- gypto excederent Israëlitæ, tamen in deserto non ne- cesse habebant fame perire. Cum enim consumptus essêt commeatus, quem ex Ægypto secum exporta- vant, successit mox Manna cœlestis. Musculus ipse, etsi pronus in Judaicas glossas, illam Judaicam ex- plicationem, quam arripuit Grotius, reprobavit: Potest legi: Ubi est, vel ubi erit furor affligentis? q. d. Evanescet, nusquam erit, irritus reddetur. Hoc sensu intelligendum erit de futura Babylonis eversione, qua omnis illius furor erat extinguendus. Referunt tamen alii nonnulli ad cladem Assyriorum, qua fu- ror illorum manu Angeli extinctus est. Et hi legunt: Ubi est jam furor affligentis scilicet Assyrii? Mihi tamen eorum expositio magis placet, qui referunt ad furorem Pharaonis, cui sensui sequentia favere videntur: Qui festinabat gradiens ad aperiendum,ne moreretur internecione, nec defecit panis ejus. Loquitur de Pharaone, qui populum Israël in Ægypto durissima captivitate afflixerat, de cujus furore percontans dixit, & ubi furor affligentis? Subjicit, qui festinabat gradiens ad aperiendum. Vocula שׁוֹעֶה i. e. qui,desideratur in Ebræo. Quomodo autem Pharao tot plagis percussus post cædem primogenitorum festinaverit ad aperiendum,h.e.dimittendum captivos Israëlitas, ne morerentur internecione, Ex.12.videre licet, ubi sic legitur: Urgebantque Ægyptii populum Israël em, ut de terra velociter exirent, dicentes: Omnes moriemur. Dubio procul, festinabant gradientes, id est, cursores, qui mittebantur, ut urgerent Israëlitas ad egrediendum celerrime. Timebant enim, nisi hoc fieret, futurum ut ad internecionem usque morerentur omnes. Viderant hoc Israëlitæ, verum nec ipsi majores mente retinuerant, nec posteri de illo cogitabant. Nec defecit panis ejus, inquit. Intelligit de eo, quod redemptum populum toto illo tempore, quo commoratus est in deserto, panis de cœlo non destituit. Angustius est, quod nonnulli referunt ad farinam,quam populus ex Ægypto secum asportavit. Est hic versus obscurus. Sensum expressi, qui mihi post nonnullos alios, Germanicum etiam Interpretem, visus est esse simplicior. Lyranus exponit de AntiChristo ad hunc modum: Cito veniet, i. e. velociter attinget gradum suæ potestatis, gradiens ad aperiendum,pessimum sc. intentum suum contra Christum. Et non interficiet ad internecionem, Christianos scilicet, morte repentino præventus,nec deficiet panis ejus, i. e. non morietur fame, sicut nec gladio, sed Domini nostri Jesu Christi verbo. Sunt, qui exponant de acceleranda liberatione exulum è Babylone. Et hi legunt: Festinabit exul, ut solvatur, nec morietur in fovea, nec deficiet panis ejus. Et ego Dominus Deus tuus dissefans mare. Annectit historiam dissecti maris rubri, ut in memoriam illis revocet, quomodo majores ipsorum ex Ægypto liberati sicco pede per maris fundum fuerunt traducti. Has illis historias refricat, quo futuris sese rebus melius accommodent. Illud, ut sonent fluctus ejus, ad hoc est adjectum, ut dissectionis hujus vehementiam exprimat, quæ facta fuerat per vehementem urentemque flatum, sicuti Ex.14. videre licet: Dubio procul non est ista dissectio maris sine maximo fluctuum illius sonitu ac fremitu facta. Hæc Musculus. Hunc ergo sensum à B. Luthero traditum ceu simplicissimum, retinendum censemus, ideoque v. 15. ita reddimus juxta usitatum Ebraismum: Ego Dominus Deus tuus findens mare &c. Cujus nomen, Dominus exercituum, ne ad aliam, quam loquentis personam referatur. Erravit Grotius, quod quæ in præterito dicuntur, & ad ea, quæ facta sunt olim, respiciunt vi contextus, ad futura abripuit,imo etiam in futuro transtulit contra officium boni interpretis: FESTINABIT VINCTUS ut solvatur: Quia inHebræo est מִהַר FESTINAVIT.

## 51:15
Vers. 15.

WHO DIVIDE THE SEA, AND ITS WAVES ROAR) From the Hebrew: Who divide the sea, although its waves are raging.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

QVI CONTVRBO MARE, ET INTVMESCVNT FLVCTVS EJVS) Ex Hebræo: Qui findo mare, quamvis frementibus ejus fluctibus.

## 51:16
Vers. 16. I HAVE PUT MY WORDS IN THY MOUTH) Through the Prophets I have given my promises to thee, which thou mayest recite in turn.

It does not appear to whom Grotius believed this v. 16 was properly directed. The Jews, Hugo, and Musculus wish these things to be said to the Prophet. The Chaldean to the Prophets, Jerome and Vatablus, Forerius, Adam to Christ, Cyril, Procopius and Sanctius, from Christ to the Apostles and Apostolic men; Corn. à Lap. wishes them to be said to Christ, but as if under Christ the faithful of Christ and the Apostles are understood. Our blessed Luther, Brentius, Osiander, and Pappus, however, judge that these things are said of the Church or the Ministry of the word in the New Testament. Which opinion is to be preferred, as being consonant with the Prophetic text and the office of the ministers of the word. Grotius seems to refer it to the Jewish people promises, which he subsequently recites; but God is said to PUT THE WORD IN THE MOUTH, not when we recall the word of God, or when those who have heard it recite it, but when he puts it into the ministers of the word, and suggests how they ought to speak it, Acts 2:4. For he does not only imprint concepts upon their minds, but also puts words into their mouths, with which they ought to utter them, which is primarily and immediately in those extraordinarily sent, such as were the Prophets and Apostles, and secondarily and mediately in those who are sent ordinarily. Cf. Exod. 4, Matt. 10:16.

IN THE SHADOW OF MY HAND I HAVE PROTECTED THEE, THAT THOU MAYEST PLANT THE HEAVENS AND FOUND THE EARTH) It seems to me that the LXX translated it best: ἐν ᾗ ἔστησα τὸν ὀρανὸν καὶ ἐθεμελίωσα τὴν γῆν. I will protect thee with that hand which was strong enough to establish the heaven and to make firm the earth. There is a not insignificant ellipsis in the Hebrew.

The text is clearly perverted by this not insignificant, as he calls it, ellipsis, which is truly fictitious. Which is refuted even by the fact that the effect of the word of God, placed in the mouth of the Ministers, is here established as no less the planting of the heaven and the founding of the earth than the constitution of the people of the Lord. In vain, therefore, is that planting and founding distorted to the first creation of heaven and earth. Brentius, however, explains this beautifully: For the Ministry of the Gospel is that instrument by which the Son of GOD plants the heaven and founds the earth. What could be said more excellently about this ministry? For the Son of God gathers to himself by this ministry heavenly citizens and co-heirs of heavenly goods. This is truly to plant the heavens. For as many as receive the Gospel of Christ through faith become as it were new plants of paradise and the kingdom of heaven, so that they may bear the fruit of eternal life. But he also founds the earth by this ministry, because he constitutes, orders, and even transfers the kingdoms of this earth. Which are usually accustomed to meditate upon the destruction of the Church and its Gospel. But it always happens by divine dispensation that they serve the Gospel more, even against their own will. But if indeed any kingdom of this earth tends only to this, that it may take the Gospel of Christ out of the world, then nothing is more certain than that its ruin is near. For the nation and kingdom, the Prophet says elsewhere, that will not serve thee, shall perish, and the nations shall be laid waste in solitude.

Verse of the same.

AND SAY TO SION: THOU ART MY PEOPLE.) And to say to Sion: thou (again) shalt be my people.

Here Grotius inserts the word AGAIN of his own accord, so that he may obtain that the discourse is about the rebuilding of the city. But it is a question of the spiritual Sion, because while it is said that the heaven is to be planted and the earth to be founded, then you will say to Sion, THOU ART MY PEOPLE. For when he gathers a people to himself, the heaven is planted and the earth is founded. Therefore blessed Osiander paraphrases thus: I will reform and restore the earth, and I will plant the heaven as a paradise, by gathering, namely, through the ministry of the Gospel from the kingdoms of the earth a Church, by which the heaven may be filled, so that my elect may be like the most beautiful trees in the paradise of God. Whence also I will profess before the heavenly Father that these are my elect, for whom the heaven is prepared. Nay, even in this age I will confirm them in faith, so that they may be certain that they are the Sons of GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 16. POSVI VERBA MEA IN ORE TVO) Per Prophetas promissa mea tibi dedi, quæ subinde recites.

Non apparet,ad quem hic v.16. sermonem dirigi proprie crediderit Grotius. Judæi, Hugo & Musculus ad Prophetam hæc dici volunt. Chaldæus ad Prophetas,Hieronymus & Vatablus, Forerius, Adamus ad Christum, Cyrillus, Procopius & Sanctius, à Christo ad Apostolos, virosque Apostolicos; Corn. à Lap. ad Christum dicta vult, sed ut sub Christo intelligantur Christi fideles & Apostoli. Nostri au- tem B. Lutherus, Brentius, Osiander, Pappus, ad Ec- clesiam vel Ministerium verbi in Novo Test. dicta censent. Quæ sententia præferenda, utpote textui Prophetico & Ministrorum verbi officio consen- tanea. Ad Judaicum populum referre videtur Gro- tius, cui promissa dedit Deus, quæ subinde recitet; sed VERBVM PONERE IN ORE DEVS di- citur, non cum nos verbum Dei recolimus, aut qui id audivere, recitant, sed cum verbi Ministris id in- dit, & quomodo eloqui id debeant, suggerit, Act. 2, 4. Non enim tantum animo ipsorum conceptus imprimit, sed etiam verba ori indit, quibus eos ef- ferre debeant, quod πρώτως immediate sit in ex- traordinarie missis, quales erant Prophetæ, & Apo- stoli, δευτέρως & mediate in illis, qui ordinarie mit- tuntur. Conf. Exod. 4. Matth. 10, 16.

IN VMBRA MANVS MEÆ PROTEXI TE, VT PLANTES CŒLOS ET FVNDES TERRAM) Videntur mihi LXX. optime vertisse: ἐν ᾗ ἔστησα τὸν ὀρανὸν καὶ ἐθεμελίωσα τὴν γῆν. Illa manu te protegam, quæ sa- tis valida fuit ad constituendum cœlum, firmandamque terram. Est in Hebræo ellipsis non magna.

Textus plane pervertitur per istam non ma- gnam, ut vocat, ellipsin, vere fictitiam. Quæ vel ex eo refellitur, quod effectus verbi Dei, in ore Mini- strorum positi, non minus hic constituatur planta- tio cæli & fundatio terræ, quam constitutio populi. Domini. Frustra ergo illa plantatio & fundatio ad primam creationem cœli & terræ detorquetur. Pulchre autem ista explicat Brentius: Ministerium enim Evangelii organon illud est, quo Filius DEI plantat cœlum & fundat terram. Quid posset de hoc ministerio excellentius dici? Nam Filius Dei colligit sibi hoc ministerio cælestes cives & cohæ- redes cœlestium bonorum. Hoc vere est plantare cœlos. Quotquot enim recipiunt Evangelion Christi per fidem, fiunt quasi novæ plantæ paradisi & regni cœlorum, ut ferant fructum perpetuæ vi- tæ. Sed & terram fundat hoc ministerio, quia con- stituit, ordinat, ac etiam transfert regna hujus ter- ræ. Quæ solent plerumque meditari exitium Eccle- siæ & Evangelii ejus. Fit autem semper divina dis- pensatione, ut magis Evangelio, etiam præter vo- luntatem ipsorum, serviant. Quod si vero regnum aliquod hujus terræ eo tantum propendet, ut tol- lat è mundo Evangelion Christi, tunc nihil certius est, quam quod ruina ejus sit in propinquo. Gens enim & regnum, inquit alias Propheta, quod non servierit tibi, peribit, & gentes solitudine vasta- buntur.

Vers. eod.

ET DICAS SION: POPVLVS MEVS ES TV.) Et ad dicendum Sioni: tu (rursus) mihi eris populus.

Hic de suo interferit Grotius vocem RVRSVS, ut obtineat, sermonem esse de readificatione urbis. Sed de spirituali Sione agitur, quia dum cœlum plantandum, fundanda terra dicitur, tum Sioni di- ces, POPVLVS MEVS ES TV. Quum enim populum sibi colligit, plantatur cœlum & funda- tur terra. Ideo B. Osiander ita παραφράζει: Ego re- formabo & restaurabo terram, & cœlum tanquam paradisum plantabo, colligendo nimirum per Ev- angelii ministerium è regnis terræ Ecclesiam, qua repleatur cœlum, ut sint electi mei instar pulcher- rimarum arborum in paradiso Dei. Vnde & profi- tebor coram Patre cœlesti, hos esse meos electos, quibus paratum sit cœlum. Quin & in hoc seculo confirmabo eos in fide, ut certi sint, se esse Filios DEI.

## 51:17
Verse 17. THOU HAST DRUNK EVEN TO THE DREGS OF THE CUP OF STUPOR) For stupor in the Hebrew is התרעלה from רעל, which for the Chaldeans is to tremble: a horrible cup, by which the whole body is shaken.

AND THOU HAST DRUNK EVEN TO THE DREGS) Thou hast drained it all.

Latin:

Vers. 17. VSQVE AD FVNDVM CALICIS SOPO- RIS BIBISTI) Pro soporis in Hebræo est התרעלה à רעל, quod Chaldæis est tremere: horribile poculum, quo totum corpus concutitur.

ET POTASTI USQUE AD FÆCES) Totum exhausisti.

## 51:18
Verse 18. THERE IS NONE TO SUSTAIN HER FROM ALL THE SONS WHOM SHE HATH BROUGHT FORTH, AND THERE IS NONE TO TAKE HER BY THE HAND FROM ALL THE SONS WHOM SHE HATH NOURISHED) When thou wast most grievously shaken by that horrible cup, and wast as it were paralyzed, none of thine led thee by the hand: namely, because no one had the strength for it, not the king, not the prince, not the priest.

Latin:

Vers. 18. NON EST QUI SUSTENT ET EAM EX OMNIBUS FILIIS QVOS GENUIT, ET NON EST QVI APPREHENDAT MANUM EJUS EX OMNI- BUS FILIIS, QVOS ENUTRIVIT) Cum gravissime concutereris ex illo horribili poculo, &ēses quasi παραλε- λυμένη, nemo tuorum te manu duxit: nempe quia nulli id erat virium, non regi, non principi, non sacerdoti.

## 51:19
Verse 19. THERE ARE TWO THINGS WHICH HAVE HAPPENED TO THEE) Which have rushed upon thee. These two things are famine and slaughter: but he names each twice: for devastation and famine are the same: likewise contrition and the sword.

Others explain the word two or DOUBLE in verse 19 as MULTIPLE, whom Osiander follows: because here not only two, but more evils are recounted, DEVASTATION AND CONTRITION AND FAMINE AND THE SWORD: Nor is it necessary that we take devastation and the sword, famine and contrition, by way of explanation. For neither do famine and contrition, nor the sword and devastation, extend equally widely. And other calamities are added besides: THY SONS HAVE BEEN CAST FORTH (they failed in strength) THEY HAVE SLEPT (they lay half-dead) AT THE HEAD (beginning) OF ALL THE STREETS, etc. How these calamities had their fulfillment, Cyril explains. The wicked, he says, have perished wickedly: partly because their whole region was devastated, and at the same time with Jerusalem the most celebrated temple itself was burned: then also falling away from hope in God, and expelled from the flock of the saints, to these, he says, all these things happening to you, and as if intoxicated with the fullest fury, none of your children was present to you, there was no one who would take hold of your hand, no one who would console you. And further: It is permitted to enumerate very many evils which happened to the Jews, in the time of the captivity: under Vespasian, I say, and Titus: when the whole region of the Jews burned, and no kind of calamity was lacking to them, but they reached as it were the highest pinnacle of every evil.

WHO WILL BE SORROWFUL OVER YOU) And yet who grieved for you?

WHO WILL CONSOLE YOU?) That is, what human being has consoled you? No one.

Latin:

Vers. 19. DUO SUNT, QVÆ OCCURRERUNT TIBI) Quæ in te irruerunt. Hæc duo sunt famies & cæ- des: sed utrumque bis nominat: idem enim sunt vastitas & fames: item contritio & gladius.

Alii v. 19. vocem duo vel DVPLICIA expli- cant MVLTIPLICIA, quos sequitur Osiander: quia hic non tantum duo, sed plura recensentur mala, VASTITAS ET CONTRITIO ET FA- MES ET GLADIVS: Neque necessum est ut vastitatem & gladium, famem, & contritionem κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν accipiamus. Namque neque fames & contritio, neque gladius & vastitas æque late pa- tent. Et adjiciuntur præterea aliæ calamitates: FI- LII TVI PROJECTI SVNT (defecerunt viri- bus) DORMIERUNT (jacuerunt semianimes) IN CAPITE (principio) OMNIVM VIARVM, &c. Hæ autem, calamitates quomodo complementum habuerint, explicat Cyrillus. Mali, inquit, male perierunt: Partim devastata cuncta eorum regione, & simul cum Hierosolymis incenso ipso templo cele- bratissimo: deinde etiam à spe in Deum decidentes, & à grege sanctorum expulsi, his, inquit, omnibus tibi accidentibus, & plenissimo furore velut inebriatæ ti- bi nemo tuorum liberorum adfuit, non erat, qui ma- num tuam apprehenderet, nemo qui consolaretur. Et porro: Plurima mala, quæ Judæis contigerunt, enumerare licet, captivitatis tempore: sub Vespasia- no, inquam, & Tito: quum tota Judæorum regio con- flagravit, & nullum calamitatis genus illis defuit, sed ad summum quasi omnis mali fastigium perti- gerunt.

QVIS CONTRISTABITUR SUPER TE) Et ta- men quis tibi indoluit?

QVIS CONSOLABITUR TE?) Id est, quis ho- minum te consolatus est? nemo.

## 51:20
V. 20. AS AN ORYX SNARED) In Hebrew it is תוא, which is also written תאו Deut. 14, 5. It seems to be the same animal which Aristotle calls Thoa in the History of Animals 2. 17. Pliny 8. 34. Oppian on Hunting 3. I wonder who read the LXX, who have, ὡς σευτλίον ἡμίεφθον: or the Chaldean who placed, as broken little flasks.

Latin:

V. 20. SICUT ORTX ILLAQVEATUS) In Hebræo est תוא, quod & תאו scribitur Deut. 14, 5. Videtur idem esse animal quod Thoa vocant Aristoteles historia Animalium 2. 17. Plinius 8. 34. Oppianus de Venatu 3. Miror qui legerint LXX. qui habent, ὡς σευτλίον ἡμίεφθον: aut Chaldæus qui posuit, ut lagunculæ confractæ.

## 51:21
Vers. 21. DRUNK NOT WITH WINE) For, as Alexis says: Λύπη μανίας κοινονίαν ἔχει τινα. Fear has made some run about like those who are insane and thunderstruck, says Seneca in Natural Questions 6. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 21. EBRIA NON A VINO) Nam, ut Alexis ait: Λύπη μανίας κοινονίαν ἔχει τινα. Aliquos insanis attonitisque similes discurrere fecit metus, ait Seneca naturalium quæstionum 6. 29.

## 51:23
Vers. 23. I WILL PUT IT INTO THE HAND OF THOSE WHO HAVE HUMBLED YOU) Who have afflicted you.

Jerome accepts these promises in v. 23 hypothetically, if, that is, Jerusalem were to convert herself. THEREFORE HEAR, &c. O Jerusalem, to whom I said: Arise, arise, stand up and do penance, because you have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury, and have drained it to the dregs, and your children who are scattered in the whole world, and led captive, have lain in the streets, and at the heads of the ways, know that you are poor and humbled and drunk, not with wine, but with the fury of the Lord. Therefore if you do penance, and having been raised up you stand, you will know that the cup of sleep and ruin, or according to Symmachus and Theodotion, of maceration and commotion, is to be taken from your hand: and the condy, for which also in this place Symmachus has interpreted a crater, you will no longer drink, but it is to be handed over to your adversaries, who said to your soul, bow down that we may pass over, and with them saying so, you were bowed down by your own will. And you have placed your body or back as the earth: Or according to the LXX, your middle and your necks outside to those passing over. Let this be said according to history; that Jerusalem, if she wishes to raise herself and stand up, ne- although she may drink the cup of the Lord's fury, nor suffer further what she previously endured. There is no need, however, for it to be understood hypothetically. It is certain that this chapter deals with the primitive Church gathered in Jerusalem, as has been shown thus far, and most Interpreters Jerome, Cyril, Haymo, Vatablus, Luther, Brentius, Osiander, and others agree. But because there were in the city both unbelievers and the faithful remnants of Israel, what the Prophet threatens regarding drinking the cup UP TO THE BOTTOM AND UP TO THE DREGS, and regarding calamities, bereft of all help and consolation, must be understood with respect to them. THERE IS NONE TO SUSTAIN HER FROM ALL THE SONS WHOM SHE BORE, AND THERE IS NONE TO TAKE HER HAND FROM ALL THE SONS WHOM SHE NURTURED. Which must be understood regarding the most recent calamity. For in the Babylonian exile there were Zorobabel, Nehemiah, Ezra, and other leaders of liberation. There were also consoling Prophets, Ezekiel, Daniel, and later Haggai and Zechariah. But as regards the faithful, the Prophet consoles them in the final verses, and towards the beginning of the following chapter: because even if the Republic and Synagogue of the Jews is clearly destroyed, the Church nevertheless began to flourish from their remnants, for which the Prophet exclaims: ARISE, ARISE, STAND UP O JERUSALEM. Which was a restoration of Jerusalem and Zion, not indeed a physical one, but a spiritual one. Thus it passes from the unbelieving and destroyed Jerusalem to the one believing and growing in Christ, or from the Jewish to the Christian. For just as the Roman people is the same, once pagan, now Christian, so Jerusalem is the same, once Jewish, now Christian, especially because this began and was gathered initially from the Jews, as Cornelius à Lapide explains from Jerome, Cyril, Haymo, Dionysius, Forerius, Adam Sasbouth, and Vatablus, and others, concerning which Jerome.

on Isaiah 52:9. With the people of the Jews led into captivity, and the city burned, either there was a rare inhabitant in Jerusalem, or none. But after He who was speaking before in the Prophets, and was in the beginning with God, God the Word dwelt among us, and was made flesh: the deserts of Jerusalem were restored, and He came of whom it is written: He shall build my city, and shall bring back the captivity of my people; so that it may by no means be lamented by Jeremiah: How does the city sit solitary, that was full of people, she is become as a widow that was great among the nations: but let her hear David singing: When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that comfort. And a little later: We were made glad. And so that we may know that these things are by no means said of the people of the Jews, but of all who are to believe in the Lord through the Apostles, he posits and says: He who has comforted her, or has had mercy on her, and who has rescued or redeemed her, He Himself has prepared, or revealed His holy arm, in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. From which it is clear that, with the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church, built up through the Apostles, which had been abandoned by the Jews, the arm of the Lord is revealed to all nations, and all the ends of the earth see His salvation. What is said, AND I WILL PUT IT (THE CUP) INTO THE HAND OF THEM THAT HUMBLED THEE, was fulfilled when the authors of the Jerusalemite destruction perished miserably. See Leo Castrius.

AND THEY SAID TO THY SOUL) To thee.

BOW DOWN THAT WE MAY PASS OVER) To prostrate so that we may pass over.

AND THOU HAST LAID THY BODY AS THE GROUND, AND AS A WAY TO THEM THAT PASS OVER) It was the pride of the kings of the East to walk over human bodies, Josh. 10:24, Ps. 110:1. Some kings in India still retain this.

Latin:

Vers. 23. PONAM ILLUM IN MANU EORUM, QVI TE HUMILIAVERUNT) Qui te afflixerunt.

Hieronymus promissiones hasce v. 23. ὑποθε- τικῶς accipit, si scilicet Hierosolyma se converteret. IDCIRCO AUDI, &c. ô Hierusalem, cui dixi: Elevare, elevare, consurge & age pœnitentiam, quia bibisti de manu Domini calicem furoris ejus, & epo- tasti eum usque ad fæces, & filii tui qui in toto orbe di- spersi sunt, ductique captivi jacuerunt in plateis, & in capitibus viarum, scito te esse pauperculam & humi- liatam & ebriam, non à vino, sed furore Domini. Idcirco si egeris pœnitentiam, & elevata surrexeris, scies calicem soporis & ruinæ, sive juxta Symmachum & Theodotionem, macerationis & commotionis, de manu tua esse tollendum: & condy, pro quo & in hoc loco Symmachus craterem interpretatus est, te ultra non esse bibituram, sed tradendum adversariis tuis, qui dixerunt animæ tuæ, incurvare ut transea- mus, illisque dicentibus voluntate propria incurvata es. Et posuisti quasi terram corpus sive dorsum: Vel juxta LXX. media & cervices tuas foris trans- euntibus. Hoc juxta historiam dictum sit; quod Hie- rusalem, si elevare se voluerit atque consurgere, ne- quaquam bibat calicem furoris Domini, nec patia- tur ultra quæ prius sustinuit. Non opus autem est, ut hypothetice intelligatur. Certum est, quod de primitiva Ecclesia in Hierusalem collecta agatur hoc capite, uti ostensum hactenus, & plerique In- terpretes Hieronymus, Cyrillus, Haymo, Vatablus, Lutherus, Brentius, Osiander, aliique consentiunt. Quia vero in urbe erant tum increduli, tum fideles reliquiæ Israelis, istorum respectu intelligenda, quæ de ebibendo calice USQVE AD FVNDVM ET USQVE AD FECES minatur Propheta, & de calamitatibus, omnis auxilii & solatii experti- bus. NON EST, QVI SVSTENTET EAM EX OMNIBUS FILIIS QVOS GENUIT, ET NON EST, QVI APPREHENDAT MANUM EJUS EX OMNIBUS FILIIS QVOS ENUTRIVIT. Quæ de novissima cala- mitate intelligere oportet. In exilio enim Baby- lonico fuerunt Zorobabel, Nehemias, Esdras & alii Duces liberationis. Fuerunt & Prophetæ conso- latores, Ezechiel, Daniel, & postea Haggæus & Za- charias. Quod vero ad fideles attinet, illos consola- tur Qropheta versibus postremis, & sub initium se- quentis capitis: quia etsi plane deleatur Judæorum Respublica & Synagoga, florere tamen ex reliquiis eorum cœpit Ecclesia, ob quam exclamat Prophe- ta: ELEVARE, ELEVARE, CONSURGE HIERUSALEM. Quæ fuit restauratio Hierosoly- mæ & Sionis non quidem corporalis, sed spiritua- lis. Transit itaque è Jerusalem non credente & ex- cisa ad credentem Christo succrescentem, sive à Ju- daica ad Christianam. Sicut enim idem est populus Romanus olim gentilis, nunc Christianus, sic eadem est Hierusalem, olim Judaica, nunc Chri- stiana, præsertim quia hæc è Judæis primitus cœpit, & collecta est, ut ex Hieronymo, Cyrillo, Haymone, Dionysio, Forerio, Adamo Sasbouth & Vatablo expli- cat Cornelius à Lapide, & alii, quo de Hieronym.

ad Es. 52, 9. ducto in captivitatem populo Judæorum, & urbe succensa, aut rarus erat in Hierusalem ha- bitator, aut nullus. Postquam autem prius loque- batur in Prophetis, & erat in principio apud Deum, Deus verbum habitavit in nobis, & caro factus est: instaurata sunt deserta Hierusalem, & venit ille de quo scriptum est: Hic ædificabit civitatem meam, & captivitatem populi mei reducet; ut nequaquam plangatur ab Hieremia: Quomodo sedet sola civi- tas, quæ erat plena populis, facta est quasi vidua quæ erat multiplicata in gentibus: sed audiat Da- vid canentem: In convertendo Dominum captivi- tatem Sion, facti sumus tanquam consolati. Et post paululum: Facti sumus lætantes. Et ut scia- mus nequaquam hæc dici de populo Judæorum, sed de omnibus, qui per Apostolos in Dominum credituri sunt, ponit & dicit: Qui consolatus est eam, sive misertus est ejus, & qui eruit vel redemit eam, ipse paravit, sive revelavit brachium sanctum suum, in conspectu omnium gentium, & videbunt omnes fines terræ salutare Dei nostri. Ex quo perspicuum est, exstructa per Apostolos spirituali Hierusalem, id est, Ecclesia, quæ à Judæis fuerat derelicta, revelari brachium Domini cunctis gentibus, & videre salu- tare ejus omnes fines terræ. Quod dicitur, & PO- NAM ILLUM (CALICEM) IN MANU EORUM, QVI TE HUMILIAVERUNT, impletum fuit, cum auctores excidii Hierosolymi- tani misere perierunt. Vid. Leo Castrius.

ET DIXERVNT ANIMÆ TVÆ) Tibi.

INCVRVARE VT TRANSEAMVS) Sternere ut transeamus.

ET POSVISTI VT TERRAM CORPVS TVVM, ET QVASI VIAM TRANSEVNTIBVS) Fa- stus hic erat regum Orientis super corpora humana in- cedere, Jos. 10, 24. Psal. 110, 1. Retinent adhuc quidam in India reges.

## 52:1 Argument
