To whom it is commanded that they depart from Jerusalem, and preach the Gospel in the whole world, the Lord Savior saying: Go and teach all nations: baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that they may by no means remain with the blaspheming Jews, for whose slaughter the Roman army is being prepared, but that they may abandon the polluted, and be separated from them, and be cleansed, who carry the vessels of the Lord: they are also the temple of the Holy Spirit and the great house of gold and silver vessels. Such was the Apostle Paul, who is called a vessel of election, he had also prepared himself as a precious vessel, fit for the service of God. Or at least this must be said, that the vessels of the Lord are the armor of God, which is spiritual. Of which the Apostle Paul also spoke: Put on the armor of God, and he enumerates them one by one: the breastplate of righteousness, and the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is interpreted as the word of God. To this he adds the belt of truth, and feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace. And in another place: Laying aside therefore the works of darkness, let us put on the armor of light. Thus, St. Jerome did not only discuss the invention of the Jews, but also explained the meaning of the Prophet's words. Which he understood to refer to the Apostles and the choir of all the Saints: For the Apostle teaches in 2 Cor. 6 that this also applies to other Saints. B. Brentius compared this passage with our own in such a way that it is by no means ambiguous, from the Apostolic interpretation, that these things do not pertain to the Levites, or to Sassabasar and his companions, nor do they concern either Levitical pollution or purification, but the sanctification enjoined upon all the faithful. It will be worth the effort to cite his words. But the excellent interpreter of Scripture, divine Paul, explains what meaning this exhortation has and to what it refers, who, writing to the Corinthians, uses this exhortation: Do not, he says, bear the yoke with unbelievers. For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? Or what communion has light with darkness? etc. And soon after: Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing. You see that Paul not only transcribed this exhortation from Isaiah into his Epistle, but also interpreted it. For the Son of God exhorts the pious, who believe in the Apostolic preaching, that, since He has redeemed them from sins and has brought it about that there is no longer any place for any uncircumcised or unclean person among His people, they should not bear the yoke with the uncircumcised and unclean: that is, with unbelievers, as Paul interprets: Depart, he says, depart. I do not grant you any delay or remission in departing, but I command you to depart immediately, and I urge it again and again: Depart, depart, and go away from there. From where? From the midst of the unbelievers, from the midst of a perverse nation. And lest you be contaminated, I command you not even to touch the contaminated or polluted thing. Come out therefore quickly from the impious, so that you, who carry the vessels of the Lord, may be clean and pure from all the filth of the impious. But this departure has a far different character than that departure from Egypt. For then the Israelites had a necessity to leave Egypt bodily, and to go out in haste, and in a way to flee. For the Scripture says, the Egyptians urged the people of Israel to go out of the land quickly. And again: The flour could not be leavened, as the Egyptians forced them to leave, and allowed them to make no delay, etc. But now I do not demand a bodily departure from the land of the impious. For where would you have to go, if it were not permitted for you to dwell in any land of the impious? But I want a spiritual departure, namely, that you do not mingle, as Paul explains: If any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner, with such a one do not even eat, etc. In the departure from Egypt, Moses went before, and the leaders ordained by Moses forced, or gathered, the hosts of the Israelites. But in this spiritual departure, no legislator or external Prince goes before, but the Lord Himself, the God of Israel, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, goes before and gathers the host of the Church. I am, He says, with you always, even unto the end of the world. And, I will come again, and take you unto myself, that where I am, there you may be also. I add also the interpretation of St. Cyril, which is in agreement. This speech seems to have been addressed by God either to those who have been gathered through faith and are called children of the Church, or to the holy mystagogues, namely the Apostles and Evangelists, who were the light of the whole earth under the vault of heaven, carrying the word of the Evangelical preaching to all the inhabitants of the earth like ambassadors. He commands these to withdraw and to depart from the infidels, as from those who are defiled, because they were unwilling to believe in Christ, and indeed even implicated their own heads in the crime of the Lord's murder. Go out therefore, touch not the unclean thing, that is, be separated from communion with them, so that you touch nothing of theirs. For he who touches pitch, he says, shall be defiled. For it is necessary that those who have believed in Christ, and have been called through Him to the cleansing of sin and to the participation of sanctification, should be far removed from Jewish ignorance, and be of a completely different opinion from them, and be entirely separated. For there is no communication of light with darkness, nor any part for the believer with the infidel. For those who have worshipped Emmanuel with a solid faith, and have been made partakers of His divine nature, because they are companions of the Holy Spirit and filled with His holy gifts, carry the vessels of God. But when He commands them to go out from the midst of it, He says: you shall not go out with a tumult, nor shall you begin a flight. For He does not command them to withdraw from the Jewish order as if fleeing and afraid, but rather quietly, and as if endowed with authority, as though refusing to associate with those who are so defiled, and to be numbered with the profane and the wicked. Thus far Cyril. Even the Papist interpreters acknowledge, and among them those who have attempted to attach a double sense, literal and mystical, to the previous verses, that here the discourse is uniquely about spiritual matters, even if they wish to allude to the Levites carrying the vessels, and those who were to carry the same from Babylon, in which they have no contradiction from us, provided that a mere allusion is established, and a double sense is not introduced. Even if it alludes to that, says Cornelius, yet the Prophet does not here lose his point, I mean the sharpness of his mind, and his own meanings. For from verse 6 and onwards, he does not treat of Babylon, but of Jerusalem and the Church. The meaning therefore is, as if to say: I said, that all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. Wherefore, O Apostles, that this may be fulfilled through you, and that you may evangelize this very thing to all nations, depart and go out from the unfaithful, polluted, and blasphemous Jerusalem, soon to be laid waste by the Romans. Go and preach throughout the whole world, you who carry the vessels of the Lord, i.e., who, as mystagogues, handle and administer the Holy Scripture and the Holy Sacraments: wherefore you yourselves also be pure and holy, that you may handle holy things holily. Thus St. Jerome, Cyril, Haymo, Procopius, Adam, and Tertullian, lib. 3, against Marcion, c. 22. Wherefore the Apostle aptly cites this passage in 2 Cor. 6:17, and from it proves and commands that the faithful should avoid excessive dealings with infidels, such as marriages. Similarly, Cornelius says that by those words, TOUCH NO UNCLEAN THING, allusion is made to the law of the ancients, from which he who touched unclean things, such as corpses, menstruous women, flesh torn by wild beasts, etc. was considered unclean and had to be purified, all of which signified the uncleanness of sin, which the Prophet understands here: whence he says, be cleansed, and depart. Finally, by the words FOR YOU SHALL NOT GO OUT IN A TUMULT, the Jesuit thinks an allusion is made to the Hebrews going out from Egypt, who, with the Egyptians pressing them on account of the slaughter of the firstborn, went out fearfully, hastily, and tumultuously, as if fleeing, so that they did not have time to leaven the mass of flour from which they were to bake bread. And on the contrary, an ALLUSION is made to the Hebrews going out from Babylon; for they, with Cyrus favoring, or rather commanding it, prepared themselves for the departure peacefully, gradually, and conveniently, and had time to purify themselves and the Levites, if any had touched anything unclean. An allusion, I say, to this Cornelius admits, whom others follow. Indeed, he refutes Thomas and Hugh, who think this is the literal sense which Grotius assigned. It is more true, he says, that it is only alluded to him. For the literal sense is about the Apostles. That is to say: I said, O Apostles, go out from impious Jerusalem, go to the nations, but first be cleansed, because you will have leisure to cleanse yourselves and to prepare yourselves holily for such a holy duty of preaching. For you will not go out tumultuously, as if defeated or fleeing and timid, like the Jews from Egypt, but as eager and fearless victors, as those who have overcome and laughed at the threats or blows of the Jews, as is clear in Acts 4, 5, etc. He adds the reason, because God will be your Leader, the Lord will go before you, and will protect and direct you.

Now, regarding the final verses of this chapter of Isaiah 52, it is pleasing to prefix to them a certain preface, previously set before a special Disputation on those verses, defending the Isaianic Acropolis of the Christian Faith against the attack of Hugo Grotius, which is as follows:

PREFACE.

That the satisfaction and merit of Christ is the acropolis of the Christian faith, no one who receives and venerates Christ with true faith doubts. This mystery of faith, if it is proposed in clear and perspicuous words in any oracle of the Old Testament, has been expounded by Isaiah, the most eloquent of the Prophets, in the final verses according to the Latin Vulgate version, from v. 13 of chapter 52, as well as the entire following chapter—which cohere not only in the German version of B. Luther, but also in Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho, and Augustine, book 18 of The City of God, chapter 29, and are referred to chapter 53—nay, even according to the Greek translation of the LXX, and thus according to the entire Greek Church, they constitute the 53rd chapter, in language most luminous and truly august, by the common sense and consensus of the Christian world. For it has been the unanimous opinion and faith of all until now that this is to be understood of no one else but Christ, that just servant of God, and of his humiliation and his exaltation. And the Christian world has truly judged with St. Jerome in his Prologue to Paul and Eustochium, and with Augustine in the cited place, that St. Isaiah acts more as an Evangelist here than as a Prophet. Nor did the ancient teachers of the Hebrews doubt that Isaiah was speaking of no one else but the Messiah, as witnessed by the most ancient writings and the Targum of R. Jonathan, son of Uzziel, which is esteemed by the Jews at almost the same value as the Sacred Code. Grotius alone, although he has dared everything until now in this most august Prophet, so that his advocacy would not be lacking to the modern circumcised ones, to whom this Isaianic chapter is a thorn in the eye—which one might not undeservedly call the torture of the Rabbis—has attempted to snatch away, nay, to undermine and overturn this acropolis of the Christian faith. Abraham Hulsius testifies in Jewish Theology, part 1, p. 318, that certain Jews confessed to him that their Rabbis would easily have extricated themselves from the Prophetic Scriptures, had Isaiah only kept silent. But Grotius, surpassing the trickery of the Rabbis by a great distance, was able to extricate himself easily, not only from the other Prophetic scriptures, but also from the oracles of Isaiah, and this most luminous prophecy of all. That many from among the Jews have been converted to the faith of Christ from the reading of this chapter alone, not a few who have dealt with them have reported. We call to witness B. Helvicus, who in Appendix III of the Jewish Index, § 39, says: I know, he says, among the Jews, those who were moved by this single passage of Isaiah to begin to favor Christianity. And Johannes Isaacus Levita provided an example of this matter, who was led to the Christian faith by the study of this chapter, which he himself testifies about himself in the Defense of the Truth of the Holy Hebrew Scripture, book 2, p. 82. I ingenuously confess, he says, that that very chapter led me to the Christian faith.

Christian faith. For I read that chapter more than a thousand times, compared it accurately with many translations, and discovered a hundred times more mysteries about Christ contained in the Hebrew text than are found in any other translation. The same Rabbi adds how he stopped the mouths of other Rabbis from this chapter. We present his words. At these last Frankfurt assemblies, he says, I met with five Rabbis, whom I reduced to such straits from the same chapter, and stopped their mouths, that they could not answer a single word against my arguments and reasons. But what of our Grotius? He not only dares to answer, but so perverts this whole chapter that he does not leave a word in it that pertains to Christ in its proper and native sense, twisting everything to JEREMIAH, with such distortion as I believe has not easily been heard or explored among Christians. And thus, just as before in other Prophetic prophecies, so now especially in this most luminous prediction about Christ, he has testified that he is of the number of those who, as St. Peter says in 2 Ep. 3, 16, twist the scriptures to their own destruction. The glutton of books could scarcely produce one from the entire assembly of both Jews and Christians who has snatched this prophecy away to Jeremiah, except R. Saadia Gaon, whom he leaves far behind in twisting it. Yet we can still grant him another Socinian, but of the same, if not worse, bran, who indeed did not dare to prefix his name to this impiety, and thus appeared in public anonymously, but gave this title to his most profane and detestable book: The Origin and Foundations of the Christian Religion. Whether Grotius read that writing of most profligate impiety, I would not easily say. Certainly, a crow is not so similar to a crow as the Grotian depravation of the prophecies of the latter part of the book of Isaiah is to that anonymous one: which the Anonymous contends, especially and primarily from chapter 40 to the end, promises liberation from the Babylonian captivity, similarly twisting the entire 53rd chapter to the Prophet JEREMIAH. I had already finished these defenses against the Grotian perversity, when, doing something else, I happened by chance upon the profane trifles of an Anonymous author: otherwise I would have brought together a deduction of the individual verses, and both walls, as the saying goes, could have been whitewashed with the same bucket. But our B. Jacobus Martini long ago relieved me of this labor against the Anonymous author, who devoted a great part of the Third book concerning the Three Elohim to his wicked distortions. Who, however, that person was, appears from the scope of the treatise, in which he attempts to demonstrate that all the prophecies in the O.T. promising the Messiah are conditional: and because the descendants of David did not fulfill that condition, neither was the Messiah exhibited to them, nor do the 'reguli' (thus he calls Christians by way of a cavil) acknowledge Jesus as the Messiah except falsely. Grotius therefore has these leaders and authors of his depravity; one a Jew, and the other a semi-Jew, or even worse than any Jews whatsoever: when he has added his own effort to theirs, does he not deserve the detestation of all Christians, in whom there is even a crumb of piety, because he dared, with great exertion and such impiety, to corrupt the chief chapter of the whole Old Testament codex, and its oracles so clear, with glosses and commentaries more than Rabbinical, and to twist them toward Jeremiah, so that he left nothing in it proper to the MESSIAH, and snatched away all the sentences, all the words, by the neck, toward Jeremiah? A deed unheard of in the Christian world, and utterly unworthy of a Christian man. For that this chapter cannot be explained of any other than the one Messiah, and cannot That this is in no way to be understood of Jeremiah, shines forth more clearly than the midday sun from the verses and almost every single word. And this has been expounded even ten times in the New Testament concerning Christ, by all the Evangelists, and also by the Apostles, St. Paul and St. Peter, as well as St. Philip, so that it openly contradicts the interpretation of the Holy Spirit, who snatches it away to another, in the literal sense. If, however, the authority of the New Testament or the Apostles did not happen to move the Judaizing Grotius, which he trusts he can refute with his customary evasion—that the Holy Spirit applies it mystically only to Christ, while the words of the Prophet himself, which deal according to the letter with Jeremiah, not with Christ, ought to have been weighed—the Holy Spirit has so confronted that depravation that no place is left for it. For as many words as there are, so many weights of reasons and arguments occur, which repress and exclude the Jewish gloss. It will be worth the effort to bring them forward, and at the same time to overthrow the Grotian corruptions, so that the glory of Christ may be vindicated, and the acropolis of the Christian faith asserted: May the Lord Jesus, the A and Ω, both of our salvation and of the Prophetic writings, which He has consecrated for our salvation, grant that this may be done happily!

But thus the Grotian Annotations have word for word on the latest verses of chapter 52 of Isaiah:

Latin:

Vers. 11. RECEDITE, RECEDITE, EXITE INDE) Chaldæus: Separamini, separamini: id est, cavete vobis ab omni immunditie legali, & si quam contraxistis, eam eluite secundum legem: omnia accurate agite, cum exibitis. Satis erit temporis; nec quisquam vobis obstabit.

QVI FERTIS VASA DOMINI.) Vos Sassabasat & ejus comites, Esdræ 1. 8. 9. 10. 11.

Glossam hanc mere Judaicam, ex iis, quæ dicta sunt, facile est refellere: solum quomodo ea in Ju- dæis ab Hieronymo profligata sit, videbimus. Et hoc Judæi, inquit, sic differere conantur: exite de Babylone, & idola illorum derelinquite. Exite de medio illius, & vasa, quæ Nabuchodonosor capta Hierosusalem tulerat, Cyro laxante captivos sub Zo- robabel & Esdra referte in templum, nec sicut prius de Ægypto cum tumultu & timore fugistis, ita egre- dimini de Babylone, sed cum pace & voluntate Re- gis Persarum atque Medorum, in quo Domini vo- luntas apparuit, qui protexit & congregavit vos. Alii quæ de Babylone diximus, de Romano Regno interpretantur, quod in adventu Christi, qui eos li- beraturus sit, hæc omnia compleantur. Nos autem audientes supra: Quam pulchri super montes pedes annuntiantis, & prædicantis pacem? Et: Revelabit Dominus brachium suum in conspectu omnium gentium, & videbunt omnes fines terræ salutare Dei nostri: nequaquam hoc de Judæis, sed de Apo- stolorum omniumque Sanctorum intelligimus choro. Quibus præcipitur, ut recedant de Hierusalem, & in toto mundo Evangelium prædicent, dicente Domi- no Salvatore: Ite & docete omnes gentes: bapti- zantes eas in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. ut nequaquam cum Judæis blasphemantibus maneant, in quorum necem Romanus paretur exercitus, sed pollutos derelinquant, & separentur ab eis, atque mun- dentur, qui portant vasa Domini: Templum etiam sunt Spiritus Sancti & magna domus vasa aurea & argentea. Qualis fuit Apostolus Paulus, qui vas electionis dicitur, præparaverat etiam se in vas pretiosum & aptum in ministerium Dei. Vel cer- te hoc dicendum, quod vasa Domini, armatura Dei sit spiritualis. De qua & Paulus Apostolus loqueba- tur: Induite vos armatura Dei, & per singula enu- merat: Loricam justitiæ, & clypeum fidei, & ga- leam salutis, & gladium Spiritus, qui interpretatur verbum Dei. Adhæc addit, cingulum veritatis, & calceatos pedes in præparatione Evangelii pacis. Et in alio loco: Deponentes ergo opera tenebra- rum, induamus arma lucis. Ita non discussit tantum commentum Judæorum, sed sensum etiam verbo- rum Prophetæ expedivit S. Hieronymus. Quæ de Apostolis, omniumque Sanctorum choro intellexit : Nam & Sanctis cæteris hæc convenire docet Apo- stolus 2. Cor. 6. Quem locum B. Brentius ita cum hoc nostro contulit, ut ambiguum ex interpreta- tione Apostolica minime sit, hæc non pertinere ad Levitas, vel ad Sassabasarem, ejusque comites, neque concernere sive pollutionem, sive mundationem Le- viticam, sed sanctificationem fidelibus omnibus in- junctam. Operæ pertium erit verba ejus adducere. Sed quam sententiam habeat ista exhortatio, & quo respiciat, exponit optimus Scripturæ Interpres, Divus Paulus, qui ad Corinthios scribens, hac exhortatione utitur: Ne ducatis, inquiens, jugum cum in- credulis. Quod enim consortium justitiæ cum injustitia ? aut quæ communio luci cum tene- bris: &c. Et mox: Quapropter exite de medio illorum, & separamini ab illis, dicit Dominus, & immundum ne tetigeritis. Vides, Paulum hanc co- hortationem non solum ex Esaia in Epistolam suam transcripsisse, verum etiam interpretatum esse. Hor- tatur enim Filius Dei pios, qui credunt Apostolicæ prædicationi, ut, cum redemerit ipsos a peccatis, & ef- fecerit, quod amplius nulli incircumciso aut immun- do sit locus in populo suo, non ducant jugum cum in- circumcisis & immundis: hoc est, cum incredulis, sicut Paulus interpretatur: Discedite, inquit, discedite. Non concedo vobis aliquam discedendi moram, aut remissionem, sed jubeo vos statim discede- re, & urgeo iterum atque iterum: Discedite, discedi- te, & abite inde. Unde? De medio incredulorum, de medio pravæ nationis. Et ne vos contamine- mini, jubeo vos, contaminatum seu pollutum ne tangere quidem. Exite igitur cito ab impiis, ut vos, qui fertis vasa Domini, sitis mundi & puri ab omnibus sordibus impiorum. Hic autem exitus longe aliam habet rationem, quam exitus ille ex Ægy- pto. Tunc enim Israëlitæ necesse habebant corporali- ter deserere Ægyptum, & festinanter exire, & quo- dammodo fugere. Urgebant enim, inquit Scriptura, Ægyptii populum Israël de terra exire velociter. Et iterum: Farina non poterat fermentari, cogen- tibus exire Ægyptiis, & nullam facere finentibus morem &c. Nunc autem non exigo corporalem exi- tum de terra impiorum. Quo enim abeundum vobis esset, si in nulla impiorum terra commorari vobis lice- ret? Sed volo exitum spiritualem, videlicet, ne com- misceamini, sicut Paulus exponit: Siquis, cum fra- ter appelletur, fuerit scortator, aut avarus, aut simu- lacrorum cultor, aut convitiator, aut ebriosus, aut rapax, cum ejusmodi ne cibum quidem capiatis &c. In exitu ex Ægypto præcedebat Moses, & cogebant, seu colligebant agmina Israëlitarum duces à Mose or- dinati. In hoc autem spirituali exitu non præcedit Moses quispiam legislator, aut externus Princeps, sed præcedit & cogit agmen Ecclesiæ Dominus ipse, Deus Israëlis, h. e. Dominus noster Jesus Christus. Ego, in- quiens, vobiscum sum, omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Et, iterum veniam, & as- sumam vos ad me ipsum, ut ubi ego sum, illic & vos sitis. Addo & interpretationem S. Cyrilli ὁμόψηφον. Videtur hac Oratio habita esse à Deo, vel ad eos, qui per fidem congregati sunt, & Ecclesiæ filii nuncupati sunt: vel ad Sanctos mystagogas, nimirum Apostolos & Ev- angelistas, qui universæ sub cæli complexu terræ lux extiterunt, Evangelicæ prædicationis verbum ad omnes terræ incolas velut legati portantes. Hos jubet re- cedere, & ab infidelibus abire, tanquam ab inqui- natis, eo quod noluerint Christo credere, imo & suæ ipsorum capita Dominicæ cædis crimine implicave- rint. Exite ergo, immundum ne tangite, id est, à communione cum illis segregamini, ut eorum nihil contingatis. Qui enim tangit picem, inquit, inqui- nabitur. Est enim necesse, ut, qui in Christum credi- derunt, & per ipsum vocati sunt ad emundationem peccati, & ad participationem sanctificationis, procul absint ab inscitia Iudaica, & diversa prorsus ab illis sint sententia, omninoque separentur. Nulla enim com- municatio luci cum tenebris, nec pars fideli cum infideli. Nam qui solida fide Emanuelem coluerunt, & divinæ ipsius naturæ participes facti sunt, eo quod con- sortes sint sancti Spiritus sanctisque ejus donis repleti, vafa portant Deo. Verum cum exire de medio ejus præcipiat, ait: non exibitis cum tumultu: neque fu- ga initis. Nec enim quasi fugientes & timentes ab or- dine Judaico recedere præcipit, sed quiete potius, & quasi authoritate præditos, velut detrectantes cum his adeo inquinatis versari, & cum prophanis ac impro- bis connumerari. Hactenus Cyrillus. Agnoscunt etiam Pontificii Interpp. & inter hos illi quoque, qui geminum sensum, literalem & mysticum verfibus prioribus allinere conati sunt, hic unice de spiritua- libus sermonem esse, etsi alludi velint ad Levitas va- sa portantes, eosque qui è Babylone eadem asporta- turi erant, in quo nos contradicentes non habent, si nuda scilicet allusio statuatur, non geminus intro- ducatur sensus. Etsi eo alludat, inquit Cornelius, ta- men hic non fugit suum acum, mentis inquam aciem, suaque sensa Propheta. A versu enim 6. & deinceps non agit de Babylone, sed de Jerusalem, & Ecclesia. Sensus ergo est, q. d. Ego dixi, quod videbunt omnes fines terræ salutare Dei nostri. Quocirca ô Apostoli, ut per vos hoc impleatur, utque idipsum evange- lizetis omnibus gentibus, recedite & exite de infi- deli, polluta & blasphema Jerusalem, mox à Ro- manis vastanda. Ite & prædicate per totum orbem, qui fertis vasa Domini, i. e. qui quasi mystagogi sa- cram Scripturam & S. Sacramenta tractatis, & mi- nistratis: quare & vos ipsi estote puri & sancti, ut sancte sancta tractetis. Ita S. Hieronymus, Cyrillus, Haymo, Procopius, Adamus, & Tertull. lib. 3. contra Marcion. c. 22. Quocirca apte hunc locum citat Aposto- lus 2. Cor. 6, 17. ex eoque probat, jubetque, ut fideles ni- mia infidelium commercia, uti sunt connubia, vitent. Similiter verbis illis, POLLUTUM NOLITE TANGERE, alludi ait Cornelius ad legem vete- rum, ex qua, qui tangebat immunda, ut cadavera, menstruata, carnem à feris laniatam &c. censebatur immundus, debebatque purificari, quæ omnia immun- ditiem peccati significabant: quam hic intelligit Pro- pheta: Unde ait, mundamini, & recedite. Deni- que verbis QUONIAM NON IN TUMULTU EXIBITIS, alludi censet Jesuita ad Ebræos ex Ægy- pto exeuntes, qui urgentibus Ægyptiis ob cædem pri- mogenitorum trepide, præpropere, & tumultuarie, quasi fugientes exierunt, ita ut non haberent tempus fermentandi massam farinæ, ex qua cocturi erant pa- nes. Atque ex adverso ALLUDI ad Ebræos Babylone exeuntes; illi enim favente, imo jubente Cyro, placide, sensim & commode se ad egressum compararunt, habue- runtque spatium purificandi se, & Levitas, si qui im- mundum quid tetigissent. Alludi, inquam, eo admit- tit Cornelius, quem alii sequuntur. Imo Thomam & Hugonem, qui hunc sensum literalem esse putant, quem Grotius assignavit, refellit. Verius, inquit, est, ad eum tantum alludi. Sensus enim literalis est de Apostolis. q. d. dixi, o Apostoli, exite ex impia Hieru- salem, ite ad gentes, sed prius mundamini, quia habe- bitis otium vos mundandi, & sancte vos aptandi ad tam sanctum munus prædicationis. Nam non exibi- tis tumultuarie, quasi victi aut fugientes & timidi, uti Judæi ex Ægypto, sed quasi victores alacres, & im- pavidi, utpote qui Judæorum minas aut plagas su- peraveritis & riseritis, ut patet Act. 4, 5. seqq. Ratio- nem subdit, quia Deus erit Dux vester, præcedet vos Dominus, vosque proteget & diriget.

Quod jam ad postrema Commata Cap. hujus Esaiæ 52. placet iisdem præmittere præloquium quoddam, antehac speciali Disputationi super illa præmissum, Fidei Christianæ Acropolin Esaianam contra impugnationem Hugonis Grotii defendens, quod ita sese habet:

PRÆLOQVIUM.

Acropolin fidei Christianæ esse satisfactio- nem & meritum Christi, nemo, qui vera fide Chri- stum suscipit & veneratur, ambigit. Hoc mysteri- um fidei si in ullo Veteris Testamenti oraculo ver- bis claris & perspicuis propositum, ab Esaia Prophe- tarum disertissimo commatibus postremis juxta Vulgatam versionem Latinam, à v. 13. capite 52. nec non integro sequenti, quæ non modo in Germa- nica B. Lutheri versione, sed etiam penes Justinum in Dialogo cum Tryphone, & Augustinum l. 18. de Civitate Dei cap. 29. cohærent, & ad cap. 53. re- vocantur, imo juxta Græcam LXX. viralem trans- lationem, adeoque juxta universam Græcam Ec- clesiam LIII. caput constituunt, oratione perquam luculenta, & vere augusta, communi orbis Chri- stiani sensu & consensu, expositum est. Non enim de alio, quam de Christo, servo illo Dei justo, ejus- que tum exinanitione, tum exaltatione id intelli- gendum esse, unanimis omnium sententia & fides hactenus fuit. Et Evangelistam verius hic, quam Prophetam agere S. Esaiam cum S. Hieronymo in Pro- logo ad Paul. & Eustoch. & Augustino loco lauda- to, ex vero censuit orbis Christianus. Neque de eo dubitarunt antiqui Ebræorum Magistri, Esaiam de nullo alio, quam de Messia agere, testibus scriptis vetustissimis, & Targum R. Jonathan, Ben Uzielis, quod pari ferme cum Codice Sacro æstimatur pe- nes Judæos pretio. Solus Grotius cum omnia ha- ctenus ausus fuerit in hoc augustissimo Propheta, ut ne deesset advocatura sua recentioribus verpis, quibus hoc caput Esaianum sudes in oculis est, quod carnificinam Rabbinorum non immerito quis dixerit, acropolin hanc fidei Christianis eripere, imo subruere atque evertere conatus est. Te- statur Abraham Hulsius in Theologia Judaica par- te 1. p. 318. confessos sibi Judæos quosdam esse, Rabbinos suos in Propheticis Scripturis se facile extri- catures fuisse, modo Esaias tacuisset. At Grotius longissime Rabbinorum superans κυβείαν facile se extricare potuit, non tantum cæteris Propheticis scripturis, sed etiam oraculis Esaiæ, & hoc omnium luculentissimo Vaticinio. Multos è Judæis ex hu- jus solius capitis lectione ad fidem Christi conver- sos esse, non pauci, qui cum ipsis egere, perhibue- runt. In testimonium vocamus B. Helvicum, qui Appendice III. Elenchi Judaic. §. 39. Novi ego, in- quit, inter Judæos, qui hoc solo ferme loco Esaiæ per- moti fuerunt, ut Christianismo favere ceperint. Et exemplum ejus rei præbuit Johannes Isaacus Levita, qui ad Christianam fidem hujus capitis evolutio- ne perductus est, quod defensione veritatis He- braicæ S. Script. l. 2. p. 82. ipse de se testatur. Inge- nue, inquit, profiteor, illud ipsum caput ad fidem

Christianam me adduxisse. Nam plus millies caput illud perlegi, contuli accurate cum multis translatio- nibus, deprehendi centies plus de Christo mysteria in textu Hebræo contineri, quam ulla alia conversione reperiantur. Addit idem Rabbi, quomodo aliis Rabbinis ex hoc capite os oppilarit. Verba ejus sistimus. His, inquit, proximis Comitiis Franco- fortensibuscum quinque Rabbinis sum congressus, quos ex eodem capite in eas angustias redegi, osque illorum obturavi, ut ne verbum quidem adversus argumenta & rationes meas respondere potuerint. Quid vero Grotius Noster? Ille non modo respondere au- det, sed totum hoc caput ita pervertit, ut nec ver- bum in eodem relinquat, quod sensu proprio & na- tivo ad Christum spectet, omnia ad JEREMIAM detorquens, tanta sρεβλότητι, quantam non facile inter Christianos auditam vel exploratam credo: Adeoque sicuti antea in aliis Propheticis vaticiniis, ita nunc imprimis in hac tam luculenta prædictio- ne de Christo testatum reddidit, se ex eorum esse numero, qui dicente S. Petro 2. Ep. 3, 16. sρεβλῦsin τὰς γραφὰς πρὸς τὴν ἰδιαν αὐτῶν ἀπώλειαν. Vix unum producere potuit librorum heluo ex uni- verso tum Judæorum tum Christianorum cætu, qui ad Jeremiam hoc vaticinium abripuerit, R. Saa- dia Gaon, quem vero in eo detorquendo lon- gis post se relinquit intervallis. Largiri tamen adhuc alium ei possumus Sociennum, sed ejus- dem, si non pejoris furfuris, qui vero ausus non fuit nomen suum huic impietati præfigere, itaque ἀνώνυμῶ in lucem prodiit, libro autem suo maxi- me prophano & detestando hunc titulum fecit, Origo & fundamenta religionis Christianæ. Num scriptum illud profligatissimæ impietatis legerit Grotius, non facile dixerim. Certe non corvus corvo tam similis est, quam depravatio vaticinio- rum posterioris partis libri Esaiani Grotiana illi τῶ ἀνωνύμῳ: quam à capite 40. usque ad finem potis- simum ac præcipue promittere liberationem à captivi- tate Babylonica contendit Anonymus, totum caput 53. similiter ad JEREMIAM Prophetam detor quens. Absolveram jam hasce vindicias adversus Grotianam sρεβλότητα, cum aliud agens forte in Anonymi nugas prophanas inciderem: alias con- tulissem singulorum commatum deductionem, atq; eadem fidelia uterque, quod dicitur, paries de- albari potuisset. Sed levavit me hoc labore adver- sus Anonymum jam pridem Noster B. Jacobus Martini, qui magnam partem libri Tertii de Tri- bus Elohim improbis ejus detorsionibus impendit. Quis autem ille fuerit, è tractatus scopo apparet, quo demonstrare conatur, omnia vaticinia in V. T. Messiam promittentia conditionalia esse : & quia conditionem illam non impleverunt posteri Davidis, nec Messiam ipsis exhibitum esse, nec nisi falso regulos (fic per cavillum nominat Christianos) Jesum pro Messia agnoscere. Hos ergo Duces & Autores ha- bet Grotius suæ depravationis; Judæum unum, & semi-Judæum, vel Judæis etiam quibusvis deterio- rem alterum: Quibus cum operam suam adjunxe- rit, annon detestationem Christianorum omnium, quibus vel mica pietatis inest, meretur, quod præ- cipuum caput totius codicis Veteris Testamenti, & oracula tam luculenta ejusdem, glossis & commen- tis plusquam Rabbinicis corrumpere, & ad Je- remiam detorquere, magno molimine, eaque im- pietate ausus sit, ut nihil in eo MESSIÆ pro- prium reliquerit, omnes sententias, omnia verba, ad Jeremiam obtorto collo abripuerit? Quod faci- nus in orbe Christiano inauditum, & homine Christi- ano prorfus indignum. Nam non posse de alio quam de uno Messia hoc caput explicari, non posse de Jeremia id ullatenus accipi, sole meridiano cla- rius è commatibus & verbis penè singulis elucel- cit. Et expositum id vel decies in Novo Testamen- to est de Christo, ab Evangelistis omnibus, nec non ab Apostolis, S. Paulo & S. Petro, ut & S. Philippo, ut palam Spiritus S. interpretationi reclamet, qui ad alium, sensu literali, id abripit. Si tamen Judai- zantem Grotium forte non movit autoritas Novi Testamenti vel Apostolorum, quam elidere con- sueto effugio se posse confidit, Spiritum Sanctum mystice solum ad Christum applicare, quæ secundum literam de Jeremia, non de Christo agunt, verba ipsa Prophetæ ponderasse debebat, quibus deprava- tioni illi sic obviam ivit Spiritus Sanctus, ut nullus ei locus reliquus sit. Quot enim verba, tot rationum & argumentorum pondera occurrunt, quæ Judai- cam glossam reprimunt, & excludunt. Operæ pre- tium erit ea in medium producere, & corruptelas Grotianas simul profligare, ut Christi gloria vindi- cetur, fideique Christianæ acropolis adseratur: Quod ut feliciter fiat, largiatur Dominus Jesus, A & Ω & salutis nostræ, & literarum Propheticarum, quas nostræ saluti consecravit!

Sic autem αὐτολεξεὶ habent Annotata Gro- tiana ad novissima commata cap. 52. Esaiæ:

## 52:13
Ver. 13. BEHOLD MY SERVANT SHALL UNDERSTAND.) Jeremiah shall know that all these things are most clearly revealed to him: a figure of Christ, to whom the Chaldean refers these things.

HE SHALL BE EXALTED AND LIFTED UP, AND SHALL BE VERY HIGH.) He shall be in great honor among the Chaldeans themselves. See Jerem. 39 at the end and 40.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ECCE INTELLIGET SERVUS MEUS.) Hæc omnia clarissime sibi revelata cognoscet Jeremias: fi- gura Christi, ad quem hæc refert Chaldæus.

EXALTABITVR ET ELEVABITVR, ET SV- BLIMIS ERIT VALDE.) In magno honore erit apud ipsos Chaldæos. Vide Jerem. 39. in fine & 40.

## 52:14
Ver. 14. AS MANY WERE ASTONISHED AT THEE, SO SHALL HIS APPEARANCE BE INGLORIOUS AMONG MEN, AND HIS FORM AMONG THE SONS OF MEN.) Now the second, now the third person speaks of Jeremiah, which is frequent among the Hebrews. Just as many had wondered that a man so excellent should be treated so foully, thrust into prison, then into a muddy pit, and there waste away from both filth and lack of food, so on the contrary, with things changed, the honor held for him will be a source of admiration.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SICVT OBSTVPVERVNT SVPER TE MVLTI, SIC INGLORIVS ERIT IN VIROS ASPE- CTVS EIVS, ET FORMA EIVS INTER FILIOS HOMINVM.) Modo secunda, modo tertia persona de Jeremia loquitur, quod frequens Hebræis. Sicut multi mirati erant hominem tam egregium tam fœde tractari, detrudi in carcerem, deinde in lacum lutosum, ibique & pædore & cibi inopia contabescere, sic contra rebus mu- tatis admirationi erit honos ipsi habitus.

## 52:15
Ver. 15. HE SHALL SPRINKLE MANY NATIONS.) In the Hebrew: he shall so sprinkle, that it may correspond to that 'as' which preceded. He shall turn many from the nations away from the worship of idols. A similitude taken from legal sprinklings: whence also to the Chaldeans כרז is to rebuke. But the 70 have οὕτω θαυμάσονται ἔθνη πολλὰ ἐπὶ αὐτῷ, not badly. For to wonder is as it were to be sprinkled by the brilliance of someone.

KINGS SHALL SHUT THEIR MOUTHS.) Kings, such as Nebuchadnezzar of the Chaldeans, Necho of the Egyptians, and their Satraps shall wonder in silence, when they shall see all the things which Jeremiah shall say, so fulfilled to a hair and in their own times.

BECAUSE THEY TO WHOM IT WAS NOT TOLD, THEY HAVE SEEN OF HIM.) In the Hebrew: Because what had not been explained to them (supply: by anyone else) that they saw: most openly predicted by him himself.

THEY WHO HAVE NOT HEARD HAVE CONTEMPLATED.) In the Hebrew: What they have not heard (from their astrologers and magi) these things they understood: foreseen by him.

It is manifest that Grotius understands these things of Jeremiah. He indeed makes Jeremiah a figure of Christ, but he acknowledges no literal sense, which the Holy Spirit intended, other than that which he has handed down concerning Jeremiah. Therefore he understands this Servant of God to be Jeremiah, nor does he interpret the predicates, which are uttered concerning that servant of God, of Christ, but of Jeremiah, even though he says that this man was a figure of Christ.

But that it may be clear how much Grotius agrees entirely with the recent apostate Jews, I transcribe the explanation of Lipomanus, from the Disputation instituted against the Christians from the Prophet Isaiah and the XII Minor Prophets §. CCXXXVI, who after he had depraved the sense of the Prophet, and twisted it to the Israelites, added these things: Finally, this same reading (Prophetic) is expounded in an ALLEGORICAL sense concerning the Messiah: but I intended to prefer the literal. Which is the evasion of recent Apellas, since they are not unaware that the text was expounded by the ancient Rabbis concerning the Messiah, from whom, lest they seem to dissent, they pretend that they applied them to that Messiah only in a mystical sense. But if the ancient Rabbis expounded this prophecy in a mystical sense, what then, according to them, was its literal sense, and of what subject did they understand it according to the letter? Certainly, none can be brought forth from their mind. And in what sense did they locate the mystery, or what mystery did they locate, which they established as its foundation? One may compare here Abrah. Hulfius p. 1. Theol. Jud. p. 442, teaching that that opinion concerning the mystical sense of Scripture, which belongs to the recent Rabbis, did not even enter the minds of the ancients, nor does it have a place in the explanation of the ancient Rabbis. Furthermore, the Chaldean in his version, when he converts the Hebrew text into his own idiom, did not by any means hand down a mystical sense, but translated the words of the text literally, or at least explained their literal sense, in which he truly interpreted the passage concerning the Messiah. Which Grotius reported here, and nevertheless used that similar evasion of the blind Jews, as if the Chaldean had only understood it mystically in that way. Concerning which Hulfius truly says: Nothing is more foolish than to say that Jonathan understood this prophecy concerning the Messiah in a mystical sense removed from the mind of Isaiah: By the same right you would call his entire paraphrase mystical and alien to the mind of Scripture; indeed, he would have been clearly ridiculous, who for that purpose translated the Hebrew Scripture into the Chaldean dialect almost word for word, so that those accustomed to that dialect might better perceive the mind of the Prophets; if indeed he had substituted an inept and fictitious sense in its place; could that mode of writing have been called a Targum, or a paraphrastic exposition? These are his words. Furthermore, that what is handed down in the very ancient book PESIKTA concerns only a mystical sense is repugnant to the very words by which it is taught from this Prophecy that the Messiah is to be subjected to afflictions and pains. We shall bring forward the passage later, which will clearly convince one of the vanity of the Grotian exception. What is held in Midrasch Tillim on Ps. 2, 7, in the same opinion concerning the mind of the Prophet, certainly cannot be snatched away to a mystical sense alone, but concerns the proper and literal sense of the oracle: The matters of King Messiah, he says, are narrated, and his mysteries in the Scripture of the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. In the Scripture of the Prophets, as it is said (Is. 52, 13.) Behold my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up and shall be very high. What is written afterwards: Behold my servant, I will uphold him, and it is hinted in him (Is. 42, 1.) Finally, in the Scripture of the Hagiographa, as it is said (Ps. 110, 5.) The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, etc. And another Scripture says (Dan. 7, 13.) And behold with the clouds of heaven there is one like the son of man. Do these also speak of Christ only in a mystical sense! In what literal sense, therefore, are they to be taken? The gloss of R. Solomon must be added: I have heard how this Scripture is explained in a certain Midrasch, HE SHALL BE EXALTED AND LIFTED UP MY SERVANT: in this way: The holy and blessed God shall exalt the Messiah more than Abraham, and he shall be exalted more than Moses, and he shall be very high more than the Angels. Which tradition is held in Bereschith, as noted by Raimundus Martini in Pugio Fidei Sect. II. c. 9. §. 25. Who art thou, O great mountain? (Zech. 4, 7.) That great mountain is the Messiah. And why does he call him a great mountain? Because he is greater than the Patriarchs, as it is said (Is. 52, 13.) Behold my servant shall understand, that is, the Messiah, who shall be lifted up more than Abraham, etc. In the book Sanhedrin chapter Chelek, various opinions are brought forward concerning the Messiah, but from the house of the Rabbi, a certain one answers that the Messiah is he of whom they are about to speak: Truly he himself bore our infirmities, therefore his name is said there to be future חיוורא [leprosus] leprous. Similarly in Rabboth, in the book of Ruth, at ch. 4, 14, this chapter is explained concerning the Messiah, the Son of David, concerning which see Constantinus Lempereur in his refutation of Abrabanel, fol. 51 seqq. That R. Moses Hadarschan at Gen. 1, 3 explains this chapter concerning the Messiah, as also R. Juda in the book Nezack Israel, the last chapter. B. Helvicus observed in Elench. 4 against the Jews. R. Tanchum has it thus in this place: זה מלך המשיח This is King Messiah. R. Abarbenel himself cites Jonathan and R. Moses Maimonides to that opinion, and says that it is the opinion of the sages of blessed memory in their various expositions. The author of Alkoth Rochel, R. Machir, part 2, from the book Itsitra, brings these things forward: When God created his world, he extended his hand under the throne of grace, and produced the soul of the Messiah, and his company, and said to him, do you wish to heal and redeem my children, after six thousand years? He answered him, will you also endure chastisements to wipe away their iniquities, according to that which is written (Isa. 53, 4) surely he himself bore our diseases? He answered: I will endure them with joy. These things savor of the mystery concerning the decree of redemption, even if the Rabbis have involved it in fables and trifles according to their custom. Abraham Hulfius inserted this book of R. Machir into his Jewish Theology, part 1, and those things are produced more prolixly from the ancient book PESIKTA in the book Malkuth, which passage we shall exhibit more fully at Isa. 61. He also praises this illustrious sentiment from the book PESIKTA Aggada Sam., nor is there anyone who calls its authority into doubt, concerning which see Buxtorff in Biblioth. Rabbin. From all of which, however, it is manifest that this chapter was understood by the Ancients concerning the Messiah κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν [according to the literal sense], and therefore R. Alschech in this place. Behold, he says, our Rabbis of blessed memory with one mouth establish, and have received from their ancestors, that the discourse is concerning King Messiah.

Indeed we do not deny that modern Rabbis go into all other things, but to reconcile these with the sounder ancients is to wish to connect the arctic and antarctic poles. Those opinions are not subordinate, but opposite. The ancients, with R. Jonathan Ben Uziel in the Targum, who interpreted this whole chapter concerning the Messiah, translating it, and thus delivering the literal, not mystical, sense, accepted it concerning the Messiah according to the letter: but the moderns wish it to be understood according to the letter, not concerning the Messiah, but concerning others. Of whom some understand the Israelitic people here by the servant of the Lord, such as R. Solomon, R. Joseph and David Kimchi, R. Isaac Ben Abraham ch. 22, R. Lipomanus and others, also R. Isaac Abrabaneel, who however is not consistent with himself, but having changed his opinion explains the passage concerning King Josiah. Others accept it concerning Ezra, some concerning Zerubbabel: R. Alschech explains it concerning Moses; some understand it concerning Abraham: by some it is explained concerning the ministering Angels. Others admit that it treats of the Messiah, but they invent another Messiah besides the Son of David, namely the Son of Joseph who is to die in war. R. Saadia Gaon, whom Grotius followed, accepts it concerning Jeremiah. Wherefore Grotius could have learned even from the Jews themselves that the present chapter is not to be understood otherwise, as far as the literal or proper sense is concerned, than concerning the Messiah, both because the sounder and ancient ones among them acknowledged it, and because the more recent ones going into other things have nothing certain, and attach most inept senses to the Prophet, and destroy themselves with mutual conflicts, and because they themselves acknowledge that they cannot extricate themselves from this prophecy. Now to the arguments by which it is to be proved that this prophecy treats not of Jeremiah, but of Christ, according to the literal sense. We draw the first from the name of the servant. Thus God calls him: BEHOLD MY SERVANT. Who that servant may be is not to be invented from our own wit, but to be learned from the Prophet himself. Namely, he to whom he had said in ch. 49, 3: You are my servant, and v. 6: it is a small thing for you to be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob. He, concerning whom he had said in ch. 42, 1: Behold my servant, I will uphold him, my elect, my soul has delighted in him. But this was not Jeremiah, or any other, Moses, Abraham, Josiah, or the people of God, much less any of the Angels: but as Don Isaac Abarbenel confesses, and proves against R. Solomon, the Messiah. Therefore, just as in ch. 42, 1 he pointed him out as if with a finger, BEHOLD my servant, so here the Lord similarly indicates him, BEHOLD my servant, so that there might be no doubt that the discourse is concerning the same subject, to whom this name MY SERVANT is peculiarly vindicated. Hence Zech. 3, 6: I will bring, says God, MY SERVANT Zemah. He is called a servant because he assumed the form of a servant Phil. 2, 7. He served God the Father by doing his will John 6, 38, Ps. 40, 8, and men, by promoting their salvation, because he came to minister, and to give his soul for us Matt. 20, 28. Therefore in Midrash Tillim on Ps. 2, 7 those things are explained jointly concerning the Messiah Isa. 42, 1 and ch. 52, 13. Behold my servant understands, which is what is written elsewhere, Behold my servant, I will uphold him; and in both places in the Targum the name of the Messiah is added.

We seek the second argument from the epithet of this servant. He is called THE SERVANT OF THE LORD THE JUST ONE ch. 53, 11, which epithet is proper to Christ, who alone is called absolutely just, as one who is alien from all injustice and sin Heb. 7, 2, 2 Cor. 5, 21, in whom it pleased God Isa. 42, 1. No man can otherwise be called simply just: There is none that does good, there is not even one Ps. 14, 3. And it is to be observed that the Holy Scriptures describe Christ peculiarly by this epithet, while it calls him the JUST branch Jer. 23, 6, ch. 33, 15, and honors the same with the eulogy of JUSTICE in the abstract Isa. 51, 5, my justice is near.

The third argument can be sought from wise action. Behold my servant ישכיל, which word denotes from intelligence to direct all things rightly in one's affairs, so that a prosperous and favorable outcome follows. Whence the LXX rendered it συνήσει, Jerome understands it, and the Targum יצלח will prosper. R. David Kimchi הצליח: compare Jos. 1, 7. 8. 1. Sam. 8, 30. Which certainly does not suit Jeremiah: for he did not always act from intelligence, he did not direct all things so that a prosperous outcome followed. He did many things less wisely, many things less prosperously, and in such a way that he even cursed the day of his birth c. 20, 14. Since therefore Grotius understands that this predicate does not suit him, he perverts it with an unheard-of rationale: as if it signified only the revelation of the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, and of those things which Isaiah predicted concerning it: Jeremiah will know all these things most clearly revealed to himself. Who ever, even in a dream or a fever, conceived that such a meaning was in this word? It does not sound of the intelligence of revealed things, much less of a clearer revelation of future things, least of all of the manifestation and knowledge of a future bodily liberation, but it points out something peculiar proper to this SERVANT. That in all things which are to be done, he will act only wisely and happily. Which is to be understood uniquely of Christ, who is the very wisdom of the Father Prov. 8. upon whom the Spirit of wisdom and intelligence rested Es. 11, 1. who administered all things most prudently, did all things best Marc. 7, 37. brought all things most happily to an end Luc. 24, 26. and is to bring them to an end 1. Cor. 15, 24. And it is to be observed that in this verse a preposition is contained, so that to the prior word ישכיל the servant's actions, which as a servant he executed, are designated, as most prudently and most happily expedited: But let the reward of exaltation be described for the others by the Prophet, who here has embraced the sum of the whole chapter. For this is entirely occupied in the most laborious actions of the servant, who had to minister to God even unto death Phil. 2, and to men, so that he might lay down his soul for them Matt. 20, 28, and in the exaltation of the same. Cyril explained the emphasis of the word properly. He will understand, he says, for all divine intelligence and wisdom, and he will do and will speak. Moreover, it is the work of divine wisdom, besides other things, that the only-begotten Word of God should become flesh, and that he should be poor together with the inhabitants of the earth: so that we might be enriched by his poverty, so that believing in him, we might wipe away the defilements of sin, since the Mosaic law was not sufficiently fit for taking away sins, so that by the death of his flesh he might abolish death, destroy destruction, refashion those held by death unto immortality, make man, an inhabitant of the earth, a citizen of heaven, and join the once fugitive to God and the Father through himself: that he might preach liberation to the captives, sight to the blind, and heal the broken in heart, and extinguish hell, and deprive Satan of his empire and tyranny against all. He will understand, therefore, he says, my child. For there is nothing that was not done intelligently, nothing that was not done wisely for our sake.

Therefore we draw the fourth argument from the exaltation. Which, described in very emphatic words, fits Christ perfectly, but by no means Jeremiah or others. HE SHALL BE EXALTED, HE SHALL BE LIFTED UP, AND HE SHALL BE VERY HIGH. For by this epexegesis the highest dignity and exaltation is insinuated, since the repetition of a matter in different words serves to corroborate the meaning, as the Rabbis observe. But what, I ask, was such a great exaltation of Jeremiah? Grotius says he was held in great honor among the Chaldeans ch. 39, at the end, and ch. 40. But nothing else is handed down there than that he was preserved in life and dismissed free. What is this to such a great EXALTATION described so magnificently? What kind of exaltation this was is explained in the following, namely that even Kings shall shut their mouth over him: that he shall sprinkle many nations v. 15: that he shall see his seed, justify many, divide the spoils of the strong, and that he shall have an ineffable generation. Things which are proper to the Messiah do not fit Jeremiah in any way. Therefore the Rabbis themselves acknowledge in Bereschith Rabba on Gen. 28, 10, that this indicates that this servant will be greater than the Fathers, Abraham and Moses, indeed much more sublime than the Angels, and that no other than the Messiah is understood.

The fifth argument may be taken from the contemptible form. Which is described in verse 14. That many are astonished at him, as Jerome rendered it. Forster notes that the word שמם is properly said of a person or thing that, because of guilt or punishment, is worthy of an abominable breath. Which meaning emphatically expresses the state of Christ, who was abominable because of the guilt of sin, which he took upon himself, and was made κατάρα for us Gal. 3, 13, and because of the punishment which he sustained. Although some refer these things to the Israelites by way of comparison, just as many were astonished at you, O Israel, in the Babylonian captivity, such as Calvin, Musculus, Marloratus, Tirinus, and even our Tarnovius, yet because the captivity, of which no mention is made, is rashly introduced, and the permutation of persons is frequent in this chapter: as the blessed Osiander observes, that here, as in a Comedy, the persons vary; it must be believed that these things pertain immediately to the servant of the Lord. For such apostrophes are neither infrequent nor lacking in emphasis. And כאשר, as Schindler notes in his Lexicon, when the particle כן follows, it is to be taken as 'how much more, so much more', see Ex. 1, 12; Hos. 4, 7; whence the sense will be this: The more contemptible you will be, or the more they will be astonished at you, the more you will sprinkle the nations. Which Dr. Weller explained in his Erudite Explication of ch. 53: The more many will fall into a kind of delirium and devastation of mind over you, the more you will be deformed. This apostrophe could also be understood simply as Jerome rendered it: AS MANY WERE ASTONISHED AT YOU. And the LXX Interpreters: ὃν τρόπον ἐκστήσονται ἐπί σὲ πολλοὶ, so that it refers to the preceding, i.e.: MY SERVANT will act INTELLIGENTLY, AND HE SHALL BE EXALTED (as many were astonished at you, or will be astonished), as if God the Father, as if in wonder, were asserting this in direct speech to Christ, 'wie denn über dir viel sich entsezen werden', so that the truth is confirmed more illustriously by this apostrophe, and the stupendous event of things and the admiration of those beholding are placed more before the eyes. Grotius admits this Enallage: 'Now,' he says, 'it speaks in the second, now in the third person about Jeremiah, which is frequent among the Hebrews.' And he thinks a comparison of afflictions and glory is instituted. But that application to Jeremiah does not fit the words of the Prophet in any way. For how were they astonished at the glory of him whom they threatened to cast into prison? And what was there to admire in Jeremiah, whether you look at the ignominy and affliction, which was common to him with other Prophets and men of God, or at the glory, which did not befall him so greatly that it would turn men into astonishment? But the passion of Christ and his exaltation surpasses all admiration. The LXX Interpreters retain the comparative sense in this way: As many SHALL BE ASTONISHED at you, so shall your appearance be marred by men. Whence they also admitted that Enallage. Nor does any of the Ancients introduce the Israelite people here, which we observe in favor of Calvin, who wrongly followed the Targum here. Cornelius à Lapide renders this meaning: Just as the common people at first admired Christ's miracles, doctrine, and life, so soon seeing him inglorious, that is, captured, condemned, bruised, bloody, spat upon, disfigured, and crucified, they despised him. What is added: so inglorious will be his appearance among men, and his form among the sons of men. In the Hebrew it is: his appearance will be corrupted beyond a man, AND HIS FORM BEYOND THE SONS OF MEN. A comparison is indeed instituted, so that the contemptible form, such as that of no man, and not even of any son of man, that is, of a commoner and of the lowest sort, was ever, which that opposition of man and son of man implies in Ps. 49:3, that is, of the highest objection and ingloriousness, may be expressed. Whence R. Kimchi explains: And they shall wonder, because they shall see, as if to say, his appearance is more corrupted than any man. It descends from שחת which is to be corrupted from the foundation, to be depraved, Jer. 13:7. These things again do not fit Jeremiah, who was not the most despised and most inglorious beyond other men and sons of men, but Christ, than whom no one has been affected with greater ignominy and contempt.

We deduce the sixth argument from the sprinkling of the nations. For by whom were the nations sprinkled, if not by Christ, or how could it be said of Jeremiah or another, this one or that one shall sprinkle many nations? Grotius says this was done when Jeremiah turned the nations from the worship of idols: But how did Jeremiah do this more than other Prophets? R. David Kimchi explains, he shall make them speak, that is, the fame of his name shall sprinkle many nations, and he shall propagate his name far and wide. But the reason for the special sprinkling of the nations is explained afterwards by the Prophet. For since sprinklings were accustomed to be made among the Jews through the blood of victims, and the Prophet treats of a victim for all slaughtered, he indicates that the nations are to be sprinkled, not with the blood of Levitical victims, but with the blood of that expiatory victim of whom he prophesies. Whence Jerome explained it thus: He shall sprinkle many nations, cleansing them with his blood, and in baptism consecrating them to the service of God. Conf. Heb. 9, 13.

We draw the seventh argument from the veneration of Kings: KINGS SHALL SHUT THEIR MOUTHS AT HIM. The LXX render it συνάξoσι, they shall contract, that is, they shall no longer contradict or open their mouths, but shall contract and shut them out of veneration and submission. Therefore, repentance and shame are also indicated by that phrase, and acquiescence in him, and thus honor, as Tarnovius observes in this place. Which things befit not Jeremiah, but Christ alone. Grotius’s gloss is very frivolous and empty, that the Kings of the Chaldeans and of the Egyptians, Necho, with their satraps, saw fulfilled what Jeremiah had predicted. The things promised are far greater than the knowledge of the fulfilled liberation predicted: because the conversion of Kings converted to the Kingdom of Christ is indicated by the salutary knowledge of him. The Jews, most audacious, says Cyril, although they are to be held in no account, yet dared to mock him, and often to attack him with an unbridled tongue, and to utter blasphemous words. But many Kings, as fearing God and offering glory to the King of all, shall shut their mouths, that is, they shall say nothing discordant, nor shall they utter anything that could undermine the glory of Christ. For just as opening the mouth is a symbol of audacity, impudence, and shamelessness, so closing the mouth is a sign of shame, subjection, repentance, observance, and sometimes admiration, as Forerius says. Similar things were predicted of Christ in Ps. 72, 10. 11. Is. 49, 23.

Let the eighth argument follow from the description and conversion of the nations, which is presented in these words: FOR THEY TO WHOM IT WAS NOT TOLD CONCERNING HIM, HAVE SEEN: AND THEY WHO HAVE NOT HEARD, HAVE CONTEMPLATED, namely, that those who have not heard of the Gospel, which consists of divine revelation alone, are to know it and receive it through faith. For we have the Holy Spirit himself as the author that these things treat of the preaching of the Gospel among the Gentiles and their conversion to the faith of Christ, who in Rom. 15, 21 explained these words in this way. Therefore, Grotius’s gloss is by no means to be borne: That the things which then happened were not explained to the Chaldeans and Egyptians by anyone other than Jeremiah, nor heard by the Astrologers and Magi. How, I ask, will these things be reconciled with the Apostolic interpretation? Oecolampadius rightly says against that Jewish gloss: In John 12 and to the Romans we are sufficiently taught that the Gentiles would believe, while the Jews, to whom it was prophesied concerning Christ, were blinded. The Jews, however, now explain it otherwise, namely that they shall see what has not been announced, and shall hear more than they have contemplated, i.e., they shall hear more in reality than was predicted by the Prophets. They prevaricate everywhere and do not want to hear of their own blinding, which itself serves the confirmation of our faith, for by attacking this prophecy, they fulfill it.

And these arguments, drawn from the clause of chapter 52 according to the Vulgate division of chapters, are sufficiently clear: But the following chapter will provide even more evident ones, in which Grotius acknowledges that there is a continuous discourse with those that preceded, and a prophecy concerning the same person. Concerning which, therefore, we shall now treat. The meaning of this passage, therefore, is this, according to Brentius: The Son of God will lower himself by his servitude and obedience into such deformity of appearance that he will surpass all other men in the foulness or filthiness of his face, and therefore many, when they see him, will be astonished and offended. Nor can they be induced to believe that his Majesty is as great as is attributed to him by the preaching of the Gospel. But the more servile his appearance is, the more illustrious will be the glory of his dominion. He shall sprinkle many nations. He will not be preached only among the Jews, but his Gospel will be scattered among many nations, in the whole world. And not only private men will surrender themselves as subject to him by their faith, but even Kings and Monarchs shall shut their mouths before him, they will not dare to contradict him: They will revere him, and adoringly acknowledge his majesty, because his glory will be published not only among the Jews, to whom the name of Messiah or Christ was already sufficiently known from the beginning, but also among other nations, among whom nothing had previously been preached, heard, or known concerning Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ISTE ASPERGET GENTES MVLTAS.) In Hebræo: sic asperget, ut respondeat illi sicut quod præ- cessit. Multa ex gentibus ab idolorum cultu avertet. Si- militudo sumta ab aspersionibus legalibus: unde & Cal- dæis כרז est objurgare. At 70. habent ὕτω θαυμάσονται ἔθνη πολλὰ ἐπὶ ἀυτῷ non male. Nam mirari est veluti aspergi fulgore alicujus.

CONTINEBVNT REGES OS SVVM.) Reges, ut Nabuchodonosor Chaldæorum, Nechos Ægyptiorum, eorumque Satrapæ admirabuntur cum silentio, ubi vide- bunt omnia quæ dicet Jeremias, ita ad amussim, & suis tem- poribus impleta.

QVIA QVIBVS NON EST NARRATVM, DE EO VIDERVNT.) In Hebræo: Quia quod explicatum illis non fuerat (supple ab alio quoquam) id viderunt: per ipsum apertissime prædictum.

QVI NON AVDIERVNT CONTEMPLATI.) In Hebræo: Quæ non audierunt (ab astrologis & magis suis) hæc intellexerunt: ab ipso prævisa.

Manifestum est hæc de Jeremia intelligere Grotium. Figuram quidem Christi Jeremiam fa- cit, sed sensum literalem, quem intendit Spiritus Sanctus, nullum agnoscit, quam eum, quem de Je- remia tradidit. Ideo Servum hunc Dei intelligit Jeremiam, nec prædicata, quæ de illo servo Dei ef- feruntur, de Christo interpretatur, sed de Jeremia, etsi hunc figuram Christi fuisse dicat.

Ut autem constet, quam conspiret ex asse cum recentioribus Judæis apostatis Grotius, adscribo Lipomani explicationem, è Disp. advers. Christia- nos è Propheta Esaia, & XII. Minor. Prophet. in- stituta §. CCXXXVI. qui postquam depravarat sensum Prophetæ, ac detorserat ad Israelites, hæc subjecit: Tandem eadem hæc lectio (Prophetica) ALLEGORICO sensu exponitur de Messia: sed ego literalem præferre intendi. Quod effugium est recentium Apellarum, quum non nesciant ab anti- quis Rabbinis de Messia textum expositum esse, à quibus ne dissidere videantur, sensu mystico solum eos ad Messiam illum applicasse fingunt. At si in sensu mystico veteres Rabbini hoc vaticinium ex- posuere, quis ergo secundum ipsos sensus ejus fuit literalis, & de quonam id subjecto intellexere se- cundum literam? Nullum utique ex mente ipsorum proferri potest. Et in quonam sensum mysticum aut mysterium illi locarunt, quod fundamentum ejus constituerunt? Conferri hic poterit Abrah. Hulfius p. 1. Theol. Jud. p. 442. docens, sententiam illam de sensu mystico Scripturæ, quæ Rabbino- rum est recentium, ne in mentem quidem venisse veteribus, neque in explicatione veterum Rabbi- norum locum habere. Porro Chaldæus in versione sua, cum convertit textum Ebræum in suum idio- ma, non utique sensum mysticum tradidit, sed verba textus ad literam transtulit, aut certe literalem sen- sum eorum exposuit, in qua vero locum de Messia interpretatus est. Quod hic retulit Grotius, & ni- hilo secius simili isto cæcorum Judæorum effugio usus est, ac si tantum mystice ita intellexerit Chal- dæus. De quo vere Hulfius: Nihil stultius est, quam dicere, Jonathanem id sensu mystico à mente Esaiæ remoto intellexisse vaticinium hoc de Messia: Eodem jure totam ipsius paraphrasin dixeris mysti- cam & à mente Scripturæ alienam, imo plane ridicu- lus fuisset, qui eum in finem Scripturam Hebraicam in Dialectum Chaldaicam verbotenus fere transfunde- bat, ut isti dialecto asveti Prophetarum mentem melius perciperent; si vero sensu præterito ineptum & ficti- tium loco ejus supposuisset; an iste scribendi modus potuisset dici Targum, seu expositio paraphrastica? Hæc ille. Ulterius quæ in libro PESIKTA anti- quissimo traduntur, sensum mysticum tantum con- cernere, verbis ipsis repugnat, quibus ex hac Pro- phetia docetur, Messiam afflictionibus ac dolori- bus subjiciendum esse. Locum adducemus postea, qui vanitatem exceptionis Grotianæ luculenter convincet. Quæ in Midrasch Tillim super Ps. 2, 7. in eandem sententiam de mente Prophetæ habentur, non certe ad sensum mysticum solum abripi pos- sunt, sed proprium & literalem sensum oraculi con- cernunt: Narratæ, inquit, sunt materiæ Regis Messiæ, & mysteria ejus in Scriptura legis, Prophetarum & Ha- giographorum, In Scriptura Prophetarum, sicut di- ctum est (Es. 52, 13.) Ecce intelliget servus meus, exalta- bitur & elevabitur & sublimis erit valde. Quod postea scriptum est: Ecce servus meus, suscipiam eum, & in- nuitur in eo (Es. 42, 1.) In Scriptura denique Hagio- graphorum, sicut dictum est (Ps. 110, 5.) Dixit Domi- nus Domino meo, sede ad dextram meam &c. Et alia Scriptura dicit (Dan. 7, 13.) Et ecce cum nubibus cœli sicut filii hominis est. Num hæc etiam sensu mystico tantum de Christo loquuntur! De quo ergo sensu literali accipienda sunt? Addenda est glossa R. Salomonis: Audivi quomodo in quodam Midrasch exponitur hæc Scriptura, EXALTABI- TUR ET ELEVABITUR SERVUS MEUS: hoc modo: Exaltabit Deus sanctus & benedictus Messiam plusquam Abraham, & exaltabitur plus- quam Moses, & sublimis erit valde plusquam An- geli. Quæ traditio habetur in Bereschith, notante Raimundo Martini in Pugione Fidei Sect. II. c. 9. §. 25. Quis tu mons magne? (Zach. 4, 7.) Mons magnus iste est Messias. Et quare vocat eum montem magnump? Quia est major quam Patres, sicut dictum est (Es. 52, 13.) Ecce intelliget servus meus, id est, Messias, qui levabitur plusquam Abraham &c. In libr. Sanhedrin cap. Chelek adducuntur variæ opiniones de Messia, è domo vero Rab. quidam respondet, Messiam illum esse, de quo dicturi: vere languores nostros ipse tulit, ideo dicitur ibi nomen ejus futurum חיוורא leprosus. Similiter in Rabboth, in libr. Ruth. ad c. 4, 14. exponitur hoc caput de Messia Davidis Filio, quo de vid. Constan- tinus Lempereur in refutat. Abraban. fol. 51. seqq. R. Mosen Hadarschan ad Gen. 1, 3. hoc caput expli- care de Messia, ut etiam R. Juda in lib. Nezack Israel c. ultim. B. Helvicus observavit Elench. 4. contra Jud. R. Tanchum ita habet in h.l. זה מלך המשיח Hic est Rex Messias. R. Abarbenel adducit ipse in eam sententiam Jonathanem & R. Mosen Maimoni- den, eamque esse ait sapientum p. m. in variis illorum expositionibus. Auctor Alkoth Rochel, R. Machir part. 2. ex libr. Itsitra hæc adfert: Quando creavit Deus mundum suum, extendit manum suam sub solio gratiæ, & produxit animam Messiæ, ejusque cater- vam, dixitque ipsi, visne tu sanare & redimere filios meos, post sex millia annorum? Respondit ipsi, an etiam sustinebis castigationes ad abstergendum ini- quitates eorum, juxta illud, quod scriptum est (Esa. 53, 4.) certe morbos nostros ipse tulit? Respondit: Sustinebo illas cum gaudio. Mysterium de decreto redemptionis ista sapiunt, etsi fabulis & nugis in- volverint illud pro more suo Rabbini. Librum istum R. Machir inseruit Abraham Hulfius Theol. suæ Judaicæ p. 1. & producuntur illa prolixius ex antiquo libro PESIKTA in libr. Malkuth, quem locum ad Es. 61. plenius exhibebimus. Laudat etiam illustrem istam sententiam, è libr. PESIKTA Aggada Sam. neque est qui in dubium autoritatem ejus vocet, de quo vid. Buxtorff. in Biblioth. Rab- bin. Ex quibus vero omnibus manifestum est, de Messia intellectum ab Antiquis fuisse hoc caput κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, ideoque R. Alschech in h.l. Ecce, inquit, Rabbini nostri p. m. uno ore statuunt, & à majoribus acceperunt, de Rege Messia sermonem esse.

Equidem non diffitemur, Rabbinos moder- nos in omnia alia ire, sed hos cum antiquis saniori- bus conciliare, est polum arcticum & antarcticum connectere velle. Non subordinatæ sunt, sed op- positæ illæ sententiæ. Antiqui cum R. Jonathan Ben Uzielis in Targum, qui totum hoc caput de Messia interpretatus est, id transferens, adeoque sensum literalem, non mysticum tradens, de Messia se- cundum literam id accepere: Moderni autem se- cundum literam, non de Messia, sed de aliis id intel- lectum volunt. Quorum alii populum Israeliticum per servum Domini hic intelligunt, utpote R. Salo- mon, R. Joseph. & David Kimchi, R. Isaac Ben Abraham c. 22. R. Lipomanus & alii, etiam R. Isaac Abrabaneel, qui vero sibi non constat, sed mutata sententia locum de Rege Josia explicat. Alii de Efra, nonnulli de Zorobabel accipiunt: R. Alschech de Mose exponit; nonnulli de Abrahamo intelligunt: A quibusdain de Angelis ministris explicatur. Alii de Messia agere admittunt, sed fingunt, alium Mef- siam præter Filium Davidis, nempe Filium Josephi bello interiturum. De Jeremia autem accipit R. Saadia Gaon, quem sequutus est Grotius. Qua- propter vel ab ipsis Judæis discere poterat Grotius, non esse caput præsens aliter, quantum ad litera- lem, seu proprium sensum intelligendum, quam de Messia, tum quod saniores & antiqui ex iisdem id agnoverint, tum quod in alia euntes recentiores nihil certi haabeant, & ineptissimos sensus Prophe- tæ affingant, mutuisque pugnis se conficiant, tum quod agnoscant ipsi, sese expedire ab hac Prophetia non posse. Jam ad argumenta, quibus probandum, non de Jeremia, sed de Christo hoc vaticinium age- re, secundum literalem sensum. Primum è servi nomine depromimus. Ita vocat eum Deus: EC- CE SERVUS MEUS. Quis ille servus sit, non ex ingenio nostro fingendum, sed e Propheta ipso discendum. Ille nempe, cui dixerat c. 49, 3. Tu es servus meus, & v. 6. parum mihi est, ut sis mihi servus ad suscitandas tribus Jacob. Ille, de quo cap. 42, 1. dixerat: Ecce servus meus, suscipiam eum, electus meus, complacuit sibi in illo anima mea. At hic non Jeremias fuit, aut ullus alius, Moses, Abra- ham, Josias, aut populus Dei, nedum Angelorum ul- lus: sed ut Don Isaac Abarbenel fatetur, & adver- sus R. Salomonem convincit, Messias. Ideo, uti c. 42, 1. velut digito demonstrabat ipsum, ECCE ser- vus meus, ita hic similiter eum indicat Dominus, ECCE servus meus, ut ne dubium esset de eodem subjecto sermonem esse, cui nomen hoc SERVUS meus peculiariter vindicatur. Inde Zach. 3, 6. Ad- ducam, inquit Deus, SERVVM MEUM Ze- mah. Qui servus dicitur, quia formam servi assum- sit Phil. 2, 7. Deo Patri servivit voluntatem ejus fa- ciendo Joh. 6, 38. Ps. 40, 8. & hominibus, salutem eorum promovendo, quia venit ut ministraret, & animam suam daret pro nobis Matth. 20, 28. Ideo in Midrasch Tillim super Psal. 2, 7. illa conjunctim de Messia explicantur Es. 42, 1. & c. 52, 13. Ecce intel- ligit servus meus, quod est quod scriptum est alibi, Ecce servus meus, suscipiam eum; Et utrobique in Targum additur nomen Messiæ.

Alterum argumentum petimus e servi hujus epithero. Dicitur SERVUS DOMINI JUSTUS c. 53, 11. quod epitheton Christo proprium est, qui solus absolute justus dicitur, utpote qui alie- nus est ab omni injustitia & peccato Ebr. 7, 2. Cor. 5, 11. in quo Deo placuit Esa. 42, 1. Nullus homi- num simpliciter justus dici alias potest: Non est, qui faciat bonum, non est usque ad unum Ps. 14, 3. Et observandum, quod Christum hoc Epitheto pecu- liariter describat S. S. dum eum vocat germen JU- STUM Jer. 23, 6. c. 33, 15. & JUSTITIÆ elogio in abstracto eundem honorat Esa. 51, 5. justitia mea prope est.

Tertium argumentum peti potest a sapienti actione. Ecce servus meus ישכיל quæ vox notat ex intelligentia recte in suis negotiis omnia ita dirigere, ut prosper, ac secundus eventus sequatur. Unde LXX. reddidere συνήσει, Hieronymus intelligit, & Targum יצלח prosperabitur. R. David Kimchi הצליח : confer. Jos. 1, 7. 8. 1. Sam. 8, 30. Quod Jere- miæ utique non convenit: nam non egit is semper ex intelligentia, non direxit omnia ita, ut prosper eventus sequeretur. Multa egit minus sapienter, multa minus prospere, atque ita, ut diei etiam nati- vitatis suæ maledixerit c. 20, 14. Quum ergo hoc prædicatum ei haud convenire intelligat Grotius, pervertit id inaudita ratione: quasi significaret tantum revelationem liberationis captivitatis Ba- bylonicæ, & eorum quæ circa illa prædixit Esaias: Hæc omnia sibi clarissime revelata cognoscet Jere- mias. Quis unquam vel per somnium, aut febrim huic verbo talem sensum inesse concepit? Non de intelligentia revelatorum, nedum de clariori revela- tione futurorum, minime omnium de manifesta- tione & cognitione futuræ liberationis corporalis id sonat, sed peculiare quid SERVO huic proprium indigitat. Quod in omnibus, quæ agenda sunt, non nisi sapienter & feliciter acturus sit. Quod de Christo unice intelligendum est, qui est ipsa sapien- tia Patris Prov. 8. super quo Spiritus sapientiæ & in- telligentiæ requievit Es. 11, 1. qui omnia prudentissi- me administravit, omnia optime fecit Marc. 7, 37. omnia felicissime ad finem perduxit Luc. 24, 26. & perducturus est 1. Cor. 15, 24. Et observandum quod hoc versu præpositio contineatur, ut verbo priori ישכיל servi actiones, quas ut servus exe- quutus est, designentur, ceu prudentissime & feliciss- sime expedite: Cæteris vero præmium exaltationis describatur à Propheta, qui hic complexus est sum- mam totius capitis. Hoc enim in actionibus servi laboriosissimis, qui ministrare debuit Deo usque ad mortem Philip. 2. & hominibus, ut animam suam pro ipsis poneret Matth. 20, 28. & in exaltatione ejusdem totum occupatum est. Cyrillus emphasin vocis exposuit probe. Intelliget, inquit, pro omni intelligentia & sapientia divina, & faciet & loque- tur. Opus autem divinæ sapientiæ præter alia est, ut unigenitum Dei verbum caro fieret, & ut una cum terræ incolis pauper esset: quo nos ipsius paupertate ditaremur, quo credentes in ipsum, peccati inquina- menta abstergeremus, cum Mosaica lex satis non esset ad tollenda peccata idonea, ut morte carnis suæ mor- tem aboleret, interitum deleret, morte detentos ad im- mortalitatem refingeret, hominem terræ incolam cæli civem efficeret, quondam fugitivum, per se Deo ac Pa- tri conjungeret: captivis liberationem, cæcis visum prædicaret, & contritos corde sanaret, orcumque ex- tingueret, & Satanam imperio ac tyrannide contra omnes privaret. Intelliget ergo, inquit, puer meus. Nihil enim non intelligenter, nihil non sapienter fa- ctum est nostra causa.

Ideo quartum argumentum depromimus ab exaltatione. Quæ verbis valde emphaticis descripta Christo apprime congruit, neutiquam vero Jere- miæ, aut aliis. EXALTABITVR, ELEVA- BITVR, ET SVBLIMIS ERIT VAL- DE. Hac enim epexegesi summa dignitas & ex- altatio insinuatur, quum repetitio rei diversis vo- cibus ad corroborandam significationem faciat, ut Rabbini observant. Quænam vero obsecro tanta fuit Jeremiæ axaltatio? Grotius in magno honore dicit habitum apud Chaldæos c. 39. sub finem, & c. 40. At nihil ibi aliud traditur, quam quod in vita con- servatus, & liber dimissus fuerit. Quid hoc ad tan- tam EXALTATIONEM tam magnifice descri- ptam?
