Qualis hæc fuerit, exponitur in sequenti- bus, quod nempe etiam Reges os suum super ipsum contineant: quod gentes multas aspergat v. 15. quod semen videat, multos justificet, fortium spolia dividat, quodque genus habeat inenarrabile. Quæ Messiæ propria sunt, Jeremiæ nullatenus congruunt. Ideo agnoscunt ipsimet Rabbini in Bereschith Rabba super Gen. 28, 10. quod hic indigitetur, majorem hunc servum fore, quam Patres, Abraham & Moses, imo sublimiorem multo, quam Angelos, nec alium, quam Messiam intelligi.

Quintum argumentum desumere licet à for- ma contemptibili. Quæ vers. 14. describitur. Quod multi super ipsum obstupescant, ut Hieronymus red- didit. Forsterus notat vocem שמם proprie dici de persona, aut re, quæ propter reatum aut pœnam afflatu abominabili digna sit. Quæ significatio emphatice exprimit statum Christi, qui abominabilis fuit pro- pter reatum culpæ, quem in se suscepit, & factus xa- τάρα pro nobis Gal. 3, 13. & ob pœnam, quem susti- nuit. Quamvis vero hæc nonnulli referant ad Israe- litas per modum comparationis, quemadmodum super te ô Israel in captivitate Babylonica multi ob- stupuerunt, utpote Calvinus, Musculus, Marlora- tus, Tirinus, etiam Tarnovius noster, tamen quia captivitas, cujus nulla facta mentio, temere inferi- tur, & permutatio personarum in hoc capite fre- quens est: ut observat B. Osiander, hic veluti in Comœdia personas variare; ad servum Domini hæc immediate pertinere, credendum est. Nam ta- les Apostrophæ nec infrequentes sunt, nec em- phasi carent. Et כאשר notante Schindl. in Lex. cum sequitur particula כן sic accipi, quanto magis, tanto magis, vid. Ex. 1, 12. Hof. 4, 7. unde sensus hic erit: Quando magis contemptibilis eris, aut obstu- pescent super te, tanto magis asperges gentes. Quod Dn. D. Wellerus in Erudita explicatione c. 53. ex- posuit: Quanto vero plures super te in animi quasi delirium & vastationem incident, tanto magis tu de- formaberis. Apostrophe etiam hæc simpliciter ita intelligi posset, ut reddidit Hieronymus, SICUT OBSTUPUERUNT SUPER TE MULTI. Et LXX. Interpp. ὃν τρόπον ἐκστήσονται ἐπί σὲ πολ- λοὶ, ut nempe referatur ad præcedentia h. m.: IN- TELLIGENTER aget SERVVS MEUS, ET EXALTABITUR (sicut super te obstupuerunt multi, vel obstupescent) quasi admirabundus dire- cto sermone ad Christum Deus Pater id asseveret, wie denn über dir viel sich entsezen werden, ut tum veritas hac Apostrophe illustrius confirmetur, tum stupendus rerum eventus, & conspicientium ad- miratio magis ob oculos ponatur. Admittit hanc Enallagen Grotius: Modo secunda, inquit, modo tertia persona de Jeremia loquitur, quod frequens He- brais. Et comparationem afflictionum & gloriæ in- stitui censet. Sed applicatio illa ad Jeremiam nullatenus verbis Prophetæ congruit. Quomodo enim obstupuere illi gloriam ejus, qui in carcerem minati sunt eum detrudere: Et quidnam erat ad- mirandi in Jeremia, sive ignominiam & afflictio- nem respicias, quæ ipsi cum aliis Prophetis & viris Dei communis fuit, sive gloriam, quæ ipsi tanta non obtigit, ut in stuporem homines converteret: At Christi passio, ejusdemque exaltatio omnem admi- rationem superat. LXX. Interpp. retinent compa- rativum sensum hoc modo: Quemadmodum OB- STUPESCENT super te multi, sic vituperabitur ab hominibus species tua. Unde etiam Enallagen il- lam admiserunt. Nec quisquam Veterum ingerit hic populum Israëlitioum, quod in gratiam Calvini observamus, qui perperam hic Targum sequutus est. Cornelius à Lapide sensum hunc reddit: Sicut plebs initio admirata fuit Christi miracula, doctri- nam & vitam, ita mox videns eum inglorium, puta captum, damnatum, lividum, cruentum, consputum, defiguratum & crucifixum despexit. Quod additur: sic inglorius erit in viros aspectus ejus, & forma ejus inter filios hominum. In Hebræo est: corruptus erit præ viro aspectus ejus, ET FORMA EJVS PRÆ FILIIS HOMINVM. Comparatio nempe insti- tuitur, ut contemptibilis forma talis, qualis nullius viri, ac ne ullius quidem filii hominis, h. e. plebeji, & infimæ sortis fuit unquam, quod illa oppositio viri & filii hominis infert Ps. 99, 3. h. e. summæ objectio- nis & ingloriæ exprimatur. Vnde R. Kimchi ex- ponit: Et admirabuntur, quia videbunt, q. d. cor- ruptus magis sit præ omni viro aspectus ejus. Descen- dit à שחת quod est funditus corrumpi, depravari Jer. 13, 7. Hæc iterum non conveniunt Jeremiæ, qui non præ alii viris & filiis hominum despectissi- mus fuit, & maxime inglorius, sed Christo, quo ma- jori ignominia & contemptu affectus nemo est.

Sextum argumentum deducimus à gentium aspersione. Nam à quonam aspersæ gentes sunt, nisi à Christo, aut quomodo de Jeremia aut alio dici poterat, iste vel hic asperget gentes multas? Grotius id factum ait, cum Jeremias gentes à cultu idolorum avertit: At quomodo præ aliis Prophetis hoc ma- xime Jeremias fecit: R. David Kimchi explicat, faciet loqui, h. e. fama sui nominis multas gentes asperget, & nomen suum longe lateque propagabit. Sed specialis aspersionis gentium ratio explicatur post- ea à Propheta. Quum enim per sanguinem victi- marum aspersiones fieri consueverunt apud Ju- dæos, & Propheta de victima agat pro omnibus mactata, gentes afpersum iri non victimarum Levi- ticarum sanguine, sed sanguine illius expiatoriæ vi- ctimæ, de quo vaticinatur, indicat. Unde Hiero- nymus ita exposuit: Iste asperget gentes multas, mun- dans eas sanguine suo, & in baptismate Deo conse- crans servituti. Conf. Ebr. 9, 13.

Septimum argumentum depromimus à Regum veneratione: SUPER IPSUM CONTINE- RUNT REGES OS SUUM. LXX. reddunt συνάξoσι, contrahent, id est, non contradicent am- plius, aut aperient os, sed contrahent & continebunt ex veneratione ac submissione. Ideo & pœnitentia ac pudor ea phrasi indicatur, & acquiescentia in ipso, adeoque honor, ut observat Tarnov. in h.l. Quæ non Jeremiæ, sed Christo unice conveniunt. Perquam frivola & jejuna est Grotii glossa, quod Nabuchodo- nosor Chaldæorum, & Nechos Ægyptiorum Reges cum Satrapis viderint impleta, quæ prædixerat Jere- mias. Longe ampliora sunt quæ promittuntur, quam cognitio impletæ liberationis prædictæ: quia conversio Regum ad Regnum Christi conversorum sa- lutari ejus cognitione indicatur. Judæi audacissimi, inquit Cyrillus, etsi nullo in numero habendi, eum ta- men deridere ausi sunt, linguaque eum effræni sæpenu- mero impetere, ac blasphemas voces emittere. Com- plures autem Reges ut Deum timentes & ut Regi uni- versorum gloriam offerentes os suum continebunt, id est, nihil dicent absonum, nec quicquam quod gloriam Christi labefactare possit, sonabunt. Nam sicut aperi- re os Symbolum est audaciæ, procacitatis & invere- cundiæ, sic claudere os, est signum pudoris, subjecti- onis, pœnitentiæ, observantiæ, & interdum admi- rationis, dicente Forerio. Similia de Christo præ- dicta sunt Ps. 72, 10. 11. Ef. 49, 23.

Succedat argumentum octavum è gentium de- scriptione & conversione, quæ hisce verbis exhibe- tur: QUIA QUIBUS NON EST NARRA- TUM DE EO, VIDERUNT: ET QUI NON AUDIERUNT, CONTEMPLATI SUNT, quod nempe, qui de Evangelio, quod sola revela- tione divina constat, non audiverint, id cognituri, & per fidem suscepturi sint. Nam hæc de prædica- tione Evangelii inter gentiles, eorumque conver- sione ad fidem Christi agere, autorem habemus i- psummet Spiritum S. qui Rom. 15, 21. hæc verba ita exposuit. Nullatenus ergo ferenda Grotii glossa: Quod non explicata Chaldæis & Ægyptiis fuerint ab alio, quam Jeremia, quæ tum acciderunt, nec audita ab Astrologis & Magis sint. Quomodo hæc obsecro cum interpretatione Apostolica conciliabuntur? Recte adversus glossam illam Judaicam Oecolam- padius: Joh. 12. & ad Romanos satis docemur, Ju- dæis, quibus de Christo prophetatum est, excæcatis cre- dituras gentes. Judæi autem nunc secus exponunt, nempe quod visuri sint, quod non est annunciatum, & audituri plus quam contemplati sunt, h. e. plus audi- turi reipsa, quam per Prophetas prædictum sit. Ter- giversantur ubique & excæcationem suam audire no- lunt, quod & ipsum fidei nostræ confirmationi servit, impugnando enim vaticinium istud, ipsum implent.

Atque hæc argumenta è clausula c. 52. juxta vul- gatam capitum recensionem, deprompta, satis lu- culenta sunt: Sed longe adhuc evidentiora caput sequens subministrabit, in quo cum illis, quæ præ- cesserunt, continuum sermonem, & de eadem per- sona Prophetiam haberi, agnoscit Grotius. De quo proinde nunc agemus. Sententia itaque hujus perico- pes hæc est, interprete Brentio; Filius Dei demittet se servitute & obedientia sua in tantam aspectus de- formitatem, ut turpitudine seu fœditate faciei suæ su- peret omnes alios homines, ideoque multi, cum viderint eum, obstupescent & offendentur. Nec induci possunt, ut credant, quod tanta sit ejus Majestas, quanta ei prædicatione Evangelii tribuitur. Sed quo servilior est aspectus ejus, eo illustrior erit gloria dominationis ejus. Asperget gentes multas. Non prædicabitur tantum inter Judæos, sed Evangelion ejus spargetur inter multas gentes, in toto orbe terrarum. Nec pri- vati tantum homines tradent sese ei subditos fide sua, sed etiam Reges ac Monarchæ continebunt coram eo os suum, non audebunt ei contradicere: Reverebun- tur eum, & agnoscent adorabundi majestatem ejus, quia gloria ejus vulgabitur non tantum inter Ju- dæos, quibus nomen Messiæ seu Christi jam inde ab initio satis cognitum fuit, sed etiam inter alias gen- tes, inter quas antea de Christo nihil nec prædica- tum, nec auditum, nec cognitum fuerat.

## 53:1 Argument
CHAPTER LIII. The contemptible form of Christ, his passion and death for the sins of the human race, as also his resurrection from death, and his generation, as also the seed, which through faith in his satisfaction will obtain righteousness.

Vers. 1. WHO HAS BELIEVED OUR REPORT, AND TO WHOM IS THE ARM OF THE LORD REVEALED?) It is a continuous discourse with those things which preceded in the previous chapter and verse 7. Do you wish to know, he says, who that person is to be, of whom I have begun to treat, who will both have full faith in my prophecies, and will himself receive most exact revelations concerning the greatest things which the power of God will perform, with all circumstances added? I will give you his twin marks, from which he may be known. These marks indeed agree with Jeremiah first, but rather more sublimely, and often more literally, with Christ.

We see with what a wavering conscience Hugo has pleaded the cause of the Jews here. For he confesses that not only do the marks by which this person is designated agree RATHER AND MORE SUBLIMELY with Christ, but also that they OFTEN MORE LITERALLY befit Christ, and he treats the literal sense in such a way that he substitutes Jeremiah in the place of Christ, and contends that these things were said first of JEREMIAH, i.e., as regards the literal sense, for he makes this the prior one. Thus, therefore, because the sense is prior, when things are said literally of someone, the literal sense here will treat of Christ; and it will not treat of Christ in the literal sense, but only in the mystical, which are contradictory, and betray a reprobate mind. To which must be entirely ascribed the fact that he has twisted this whole chapter, as regards all the verses, all the clauses and words, to Jeremiah. For in no chapter throughout the whole Scripture was he so laboriously occupied with all the verses and almost all the members as in this one of Isaiah, lest, namely, an advocate for the perfidy of the Jews was lacking. Thus, therefore, the busybody makes progress in the Holy Scriptures. For when he was publishing annotations on the Gospels, he acknowledged that these things concern Christ, and not indeed anyone else, at John 12:34 & 38, as also in the annotations to Mark 15:28, Luke 24:47, and likewise in De Veritate Religionis Christianae, book 5, section 19, which passage we shall adduce later. But now he twists this whole chapter to Jeremiah: according to that saying of the Apostle, 2 Timothy 3:9. Furthermore, see for me a marvelous gloss on these words: WHO HATH BELIEVED OUR REPORT? AND TO WHOM IS THE ARM OF THE LORD REVEALED? that is, do you wish to know who that future person is, of whom I have begun to speak, who will both have full faith in my prophecies, and will himself receive most exact revelations concerning the greatest matters which the power of God will perform, with all circumstances added! Which, I believe, never came into the mind of any mortal. namely, that Jeremiah is understood, who alone believed the report of Isaiah, and to whom alone the arm of the Lord was revealed, that is, His power in liberating the people, and in the manner of liberation. Whom, therefore, now by genuine marks has decided to describe. But here the faith of no one is commended, but those words have the force of denial, as questions of that kind are wont to have among the Hebrews, and therefore the unbelief (ἀπιστίαν) of the Jews is argued, and their blindness because they do not believe the prophetic report, and so the arm of the Lord has not been revealed to them, whereas on the contrary the Gentiles, who had heard nothing before about the Messiah, are about to know and believe him.

Therefore, against that gloss, one must first observe this antithesis (ἀντίθεσις) between the faith of the Gentiles and the unbelief (ἀπιστίας) of the Jews, because it concerns the dispersion and conversion of the Gentiles, and the incredulity of the Jews is argued. Next, one must note the subject matter of the Prophet's report, which was not about deliverance from captivity, but about the servant of the Lord who would act intelligently and be exalted. The Chaldean rendered 'report' as announcement, from בשׂר, which is properly used of the Gospel, and above in chapter 52, 7; chapter 61, 1; as it is also used in chapter 41, 27. Thirdly, the faith designated here is not historical, but salvific, or that which is the cause of salvation: because by that faithful knowledge this just servant makes us just, Isaiah 53, 11. Fourthly, the emphasis is on the word 'arm of the Lord,' which here designates not the power of the Lord in delivering the people, but Christ, and his power in our redemption, and therefore Cyprian (lib. 11, test. advers. Jud.) understands the Son of God by the arm of the Lord. Tertullian, lib. 1, against Praxeas, chapter 13; Augustine, tractate 53 on John; Cyril of Alexandria on this passage, and others. Fifthly, the underlying subject matter, about which he began to treat in verse 31, 'you were sold for nothing, you shall be redeemed for nothing and without silver,' is proof that the discourse here is not about the signs for recognizing Jeremiah, in whose knowledge little was situated, whether you look at the people to whom Isaiah was then preaching, or his descendants, but that the REDEEMER and REDEMPTION are being described, which was accomplished not with corruptible gold and silver, but with his own most precious blood, 1 Peter 1, 18; because in that verse 3 the proposition of what was to be said was contained: since the Prophet had then set out to describe both the most miserable sale of the people, and especially the most gracious redemption of Christ, by the power of which we have been freed from every evil. Sixthly, the subsequent translation sufficiently teaches that it is not about the signs of Jeremiah, but about the judgment of the people and of God himself that is being treated here, about the Messiah, in what place the people would hold him, to whose perverse judgment is opposed the true opinion of the Prophet or rather of the Holy Spirit concerning him. And therefore these complaints are properly about the unbelief of the people, that most of the Jews would not believe: 'Who has believed or is about to believe' (in the prophetic manner the past is used for the future) 'our report,' that is, the word which we have received through hearing from the Lord, and which ought to have been heard by all, as being 'worthy of all acceptance' (πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιον), which is called the 'word of hearing' (λόγος ἀκοῆς) in 1 Thessalonians 2, verse 13, Hebrews 4, 2; because nothing is equally worthy of hearing as the word of the Gospel: whence 'our report' is the same as 'our preaching,' because it is the same word which they heard, and which the Prophets preached. He does not entirely deny that anyone of them would believe, but the Prophet laments that very few would believe at all, that the greatest part would reject the benefit of the Lord through unbelief (ἀπιστίαν), as if it had not been revealed to them, so that the number of the faithful in respect to the unfaithful would be nothing, as Cyril, or rather Clichtoveus (lib. 8 in John, chapter 20), observes: The Prophet placed the particle WHO not for an absolute negation, but for rarity, because very few believed what the holy Prophets heard from God and announced to the people. So also Jerome, who at the same time explains the reason for the connection (συνεχείας): After the words of the Father, by which he had announced to the world that his Son was to come, and before the scandal of the cross, about which he was about to speak: 'His appearance will be inglorious, and his form beyond the sons of men,' he had prefixed the glory of the resurrection: 'He shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high,' so that by the humility of the cross he might anticipate the glory of the resurrection. The chorus of the Prophets replied that they had fulfilled their duty, and as much as was in them, had announced his arm and power to all. But in that which he says: 'Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?' he signifies the rarity of believers from among the Jews. Seventhly, we have an infallible interpreter of this passage, St. John, who in chapter 12, 38 says that the Prophet's word was fulfilled when the Jews did not believe in Jesus, whom he said (chapter 53, 1) 'Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed!' John teaches, therefore, that this was predicted about the Jews, who were NOT TO BELIEVE in Christ: Grotius, on the contrary, contends that these things refer to the FAITH applied to the prophetic sermon by JEREMIAH; which are most disparate, nay, clearly contrary meanings. And St. John explains not obscurely that this ARM OF THE LORD is Christ, because he adds that the Prophet SPOKE ABOUT HIM, that is, about Christ: which can be taken about both passages which he brought from the Prophet, chapter 6 and 53. Finally, the holy Apostle interpreted the prophetic sentence in the same way in Romans 10, 16. 'But not all obey the Gospel. For Isaiah says: Lord, who has believed our report.' The Apostle speaks of salvific faith, of faith in Christ, 'how shall they call on him in whom they have not believed,' of the proclamation of the Gospel, of the word of Christ, or of Christ, and he explains the cause of the rejected Jewish people, and argues their unbelief (ἀπιστίαν). How then can there be any doubt that the discourse is about the Jewish people, and especially in the time of the New Testament, who rejected Christ and the word of Christ, which had already been preached long ago by the Prophet, and was announced to them by Christ and the Apostles? Which differ as widely as heaven and earth from the gloss of Grotius, concerning Jeremiah who was to believe the report of Isaiah. The Apostles explain the Prophet's question negatively, Grotius affirmatively: the Apostles concerning the unbelieving Jewish people, Grotius concerning the one believing Jeremiah: the Apostles concerning the time of the New Testament, Grotius concerning the time of the Babylonian captivity: the Apostles concerning the hearing and the word of the Gospel, Grotius concerning the prediction of liberation from the Babylonian captivity. Although Grotius is not consistent in these commentaries: for while he interpreted these things here concerning the FAITH OF JEREMIAH, elsewhere, namely in his Annotations on Romans 10:17, he explained it concerning the few from the people who would believe in the time of Jeremiah: of which this is the note: κύριε τίς ἐπίςευσε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν; as if he were saying, few. What had happened in the time of Jeremiah was to happen again for similar reasons. But that the discourse is about the time of Jeremiah is neither evident from the words of Isaiah, and it is repugnant to the interpretation of St. John and Paul, who do not merely institute some application by way of similarity, but testify that that predicted unbelief of the people of the latest time of the Jews had been by Isaiah. And therefore these things were brought forth from the person of the Apostles: Who has believed our report, as our Brentius rightly observed among others.

Latin:

CAPUT LIII. Christi forma contemtibilis, passio & mors pro peccatis generis humani, ut & è morte ere- ptio, Ejusdemque generatio, ut & semen, quod per fidem in ipsius satisfactionem ju- stitiam consequetur.

Vers. 1. QVIS CREDIDIT AVDITVI NOSTRO, ET BRACHIVM DOMINI CVI REVELATVM EST?) Est continuus sermo cum iis quæ præcesserunt ca- pite præcedente & commate 7. Vultis scire, inquit, quis ille sit futurus, de quo cœpi agere, qui & meis Prophetiis plenam habebit fidem, & ipse de maximis rebus, quas Dei potentia peraget, revelationes accipiet exactissimas, omnibus cir- cumstantiis additis? Dabo vobis geminas ejus notas, unde cognosci possit. Hæ notæ in Jeremiam quidem congruunt prius, sed potius sublimiusque, sæpe & magis κατὰ λέξιν, in Christum.

VIdemus, quam titubante conscientia hic Judæ- orum causam egerit Hugo. Fatetur enim non tantum POTIVS ET SUBLIMIUS notas, quibus hæc persona designatur, congruere in Christum, sed etiam SÆPE MAGIS κατὰ λέξιν Christo convenire, & literalem tantum sensum ita tractat, ut Jeremiam Christi loco substituat, ac prius de JEREMIA, h. e. quoad literalem sensum, hunc enim priorem facit, ea dici contendat. Sic ergo quia sensus prior est, cum κατὰ λέξιν aliqua de aliquo dicuntur, sensu li- terali hic de Christo agetur; & non agetur de Chri- sto sensu literali, sed tantum mystico, quæ sunt ἀντι- φατικὰ, produntque νοῦν ἀδόκιμον. Cui adscriben- dum omnino, quod totum hoc caput, quoad omnes versus, omnia commata & verba ad Jeremiam de- torserit. In nullo enim capite per Scripturam totam tam operose circa omnes versus, & omnia pene membra occupatus fuit, ut in hocEsaiano, ne sc. Ju- dæorum perfidiæ advocatus deesset. Ita proficit er- go ὁ πολυπράγμων in S. literis. Nam quum anno- tata in Evangelia ederet, agnovit de Christo hæc a- gere, non vero de alio quopiam ad Joh. 12, 34. & 38. ut & annot. ad Marci 15, 28. Luc. 24, 47. nec non in de Verit. Relig. Christ. l. 5. §. 19. quem locum postea adducturi sumus. Jam vero ad Jeremiam totum hoc caput detorquet: juxta illud Apostoli 2. Tim. 3, 9. Porro vide mihi mirabilem glossam horum verborum. QUIS CREDIDIT AUDITUI NOSTRO, ET BRACHIUM DOMINI CUI REVELATUM EST? h. e. vultis scire quis ille sit futurus, de quo cœpi agere, qui & meis Prophetiis plenam habebit fidem, & ipse de maximis rebus, quas Dei potentia peraget, revelationes accipiet exactis- simas, omnibus circumstantiis additis! Quæ, credo, nunquam ulli mortalium in mentem venit. Jere- miam nempe intelligi, qui unus crediderit auditui Esaiæ, & cui uni revelatum fuerit brachium Domi- ni, id est, potentia ejus in liberando populo, & modo liberationis. Quem proinde nunc genuinis notis describere constituerit. At hic non ullius fides commendatur, sed verba illa vim negandi habent, uti solent interrogationes ejusmodi apud Ebræos, ideoq; ἀπιστίαν Judæorum arguitur, & excœcatio quod auditui Prophetico non credant, adeoque bra- chium Domini revelatum illis non sit, quod ex ad- verso gentes, quæ nihil antea audierant de Messia, ipsum cognitutæ & credituræ sint.

Observanda ergo adversus glossam illam pri- mo ista ἀντίθεσις fidei gentilium & ἀπιστίας Iudæo- rum, quia agitur de gentium aspersione & conversio- ne, ac Iudæorum incredulitas arguitur. Deinde no- tanda materia auditus Prophetæ, quæ fuit non de li- beratione è captivitate, sed de servo Domini intel- ligenter acturo & exaltando. Auditum reddidit Chaldæus annunciationem, a בשׂר, quod de Evan- gelio proprie usurpatur, & sup. cap. 52, 7. cap. 61, 1. ut & cap. 41, 27. ita adhibitum est. Tertio fides de- signata hic est non historica, sed salvifica, vel quæ salutis causa est: quia cognitione illa fideli servus hic justus justos nos facit, Esa. 53, 11. Quarto emphasis est in voce brachii Domini, quæ hic non potentiam Domini in liberando populo, sed Christum designat, ejusque virtutem in nostra redemptione, ideoque per brachium Domini Filium DEI intelligit Cy- prian. lib. 11. test. advers. Jud. Tertull. lib. 1. contr. Prax. cap. 13. Augustin. tract. 53. in Joh. Cyrill. Ale- xandr. in h. l. & alii. Quinto, substrata materia, de qua agere cœpit v. 31. gratis venundati estis, gratis & sine argento redimemini, documento est, hic non de notis dignoscendi Jeremiam, in cujus cognitio- ne parum situm erat,sive populum spectes,cui tum prædicabat Esaias, sive posteros ejus, sermonem esse, sed REDEMPTOREM & REDEMPTIO- NEM describi, quæ facta est non corruptibili au- ro & argento, sed pretiosissimo sanguine ipsius, 1.Pet. 1, 18. quia illo v. 3. propositio continebatur dicen- dorum: quum instituerit Propheta tum venditio- nem populi miserrimam, tum imprimis redemtio- nem Christi gratiosissimam describere, vi cujus ab omni malo liberati simus. Sexto translatio sub- sequens satis docet,quod non de notis Jeremiæ, sed de judicio populi ac Dei ipsius hic agatur, de Messia, quo loco populus ipsum habiturus sit, cujus per- verso judicio opponitur vera Prophetæ vel potius Spirius Sancti de ipso sententia. Ideoque hæ que- relæ proprie sunt de incredulitate populi, quod plerique è Judæis credituri non sint: Quis credidit vel crediturus est (more Prophetico pro futuro præteritum adhibetur) auditui nostro,hoc est,verbo, quod per auditum accepimus à Domino,quodque audiri omnino debebat, utpote πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιον, quod λόγος ἀκοῆς dicitur 1. Thessal. 2. v. 13. Ebr. 4, 2. quod nihil æque dignum sit auditu, quam verbum Evangelii: unde idem est auditui nostro, quod prædicationis nostræ, quia idem verbum est, quod audivere, & quod prædicarunt Prophetæ. Non omnino negat, quenquam ex illis creditu- rum, sed dolet Propheta, quod pauci omnino cre- dituri sint, maxima pars per ἀπιστίαν reprobatura sit beneficium Domini, ac si revelatum ipsis non esset, adeo ut fidelium numerus respectu infide- lium nullus futurus sit,ut Cyrill. vel Clichtoveus po- tius l. 8. in Joh. cap.20. observat: Particulam QVIS Propheta non pro omnimoda negatione,sed pro rarita- te posuit,quia quod S. Prophetæ à Deo audierunt, & po- pulo denunciasunt, paucissimi crediderunt. Sic etiam Hieronymus, qui simul rationem συνεχείας expo- nit: Post verba Patris, quib. Filium suum mundo nun- ciaverat esse venturum, & ante scandalum crucis, de quo dicturus erat: Inglorius erit aspectus ejus,& for- ma ejus præfiliis hominum: gloriam præmiserat re- te surrectionis? Exaltabitur & elevabitur, & sublimis erit valde, ut humilitate crucis resurrectionis gloriam præveniret. Respondit Prophetarum chorus, se im- plesse officium, & quantum in se fuit, brachium illius atque virtutem omnibus nunciasse. In eo autem quod dicit: Quis credidit auditui nostro, & brachium Domini cui revelatum est? raritatem credentium significat ex Judæis. Septimo habemus interpre- tem hujus pericopes infallibilem S. Johannem, qui cap. 12, 38. impletum dicit Prophetæ sermonem, cum non crederent Judæi in Jesum, quem dixit (cap. 53, 1.) Domine quis credidit auditui nostro, & brachium Domini cui revelatum est! Id ergo prædictum fu- isse de Judæis, NON CREDITURIS sc. in Chri- stum Johannes docet: Grotius contra FIDEM adhibitam sermoni Prophetico à JEREMIA hæc sonare contendit; qui maxime disparati, imo pla- ne contrarii sensus sunt. Et explicat haud obscure S. Johannes BRACHIUM DOMINI hoc esse Christum, quia addit LOCUTUM ESSE Pro- phetam DE EO, hoc est, de Christo: quod de utroque loco, quem adduxit è Propheta cap. 6. & 53. accipi potest. Denique eadem ratione inter- pretatus est: sententiam Propheticam S. Apostolus Rom. 10, 16. Sed non omnes audiunt Evangelium. Isaias enim dicit: Domine quis credidit auditui no- stro. Loquitur Apostolus de fide salvifica, de fide in Christum, quomodo invocabunt, in quem non cre- diderunt, de præconio Evangelii, de verbo Chri- sti, vel de Christo, & causam exponit reprobati po- puli Judaici, ejusque ἀπισίαν arguit. Quomodo ergo dubium esse potest de populo Judaico, & im- primis tempore Novi Testam. sermonem esse, qui Christum, & verbum Christi reprobavit, quod jam olim prædicatum fuit à Propheta, & per Christum & Apostolos ipsis annunciatum? Quæ toto cœlo distant à glossa Grotiana, de Jeremia auditui Esaiæ credituro. Apostoli negative explicant Prophetæ interrogationem, Grotius affirmative: Apostoli de Judaico populo incredulo, Grotius de uno Jere- mia credente: Apostoli de tempore Novi Testam. Grotius de tempore captivitatis Babylonicæ: Apo- stoli de auditu & verbo Evangelii, Grotius de præ- dictione liberationis è captivitate Babylonica. Quan- quam non constet sibi in his commentis Grotius: Nam quum hic de FIDE JEREMIÆ ista inter- pretatus sit, alibi, nempe Annotat. ad Rom. 10, 17. de paucis ex populo tempore Jeremiæ credituris expo- suit: Cujus hæc nota est: κύριε τίς ἐπίςευσε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν; quasi diceret pauci. Quod Ieremiæ tempore evenerat, iterum erat eventurum paribus de causis. At de Jeremiæ tempore sermonem esse, nec ex Esaiæ verbis constat, & interpretationi S. Johan- nis & Pauli repugnat, qui non tantum applicatio- nem aliquam per similitudinem instituunt, sed præ- dictam illam incredulitatem populi novissimi Ju- dæorum temporis ab Esaia fuisse testantur. Ideoque hæc ex persona Apostolorum prolata sunt: Quis credidit auditui nostro, ut recte observavit inter alios Brentius noster.

## 53:2
Vers. 2. AND HE SHALL GROW UP AS A TENDER PLANT BEFORE HIM) And here 'and' is put for 'namely'. The sense is: Jeremiah, still a boy, will begin to serve God in the Prophetic office. You have testimony concerning him in Jerome, in the beginning of his commentary on Jeremiah. See also Jeremiah himself, chap. 1, v. 6. Thus the Lord Jesus at the age of 12 taught the Doctors.

AND AS A ROOT OUT OF A DRY GROUND) Born in the poor little village of Anathoth, Jer. 1, v. 1, with the addition of what we had here above 10, 30. Thus also Bethlehem in the time of Jesus was a village, closer to a village than a town, John 7, 42.

New distortions again. There is no need for us to speak about the particle AND, although here its sense is rather causal. Because a reason is rendered, why the Jews did not believe: Namely, the lowly origin of the Messiah, and his contemptible appearance, as the Christian world has hitherto believed with one mind. But from this, Grotius, it appears, has not scrupled to depart in favor of the Jews. He understands it properly of Jeremiah, or according to the literal sense, even though he subsequently adds the Lord Jesus, but only after he had corrupted the sense of the Prophet, so that in this and the following verses this prophecy can no longer be of any use against the Jews. But what do these things have to do with the beginning of the prophetic office at a childish age, while he is said to grow up like a sapling before him? And how did the Prophet join the birth in a poor village to the beginning of the office? The words themselves teach that both must be understood of the origin, and that these things declare themselves mutually. עלה (ascendit) is used for those born from the earth, Deut. 29:22, Prov. 24:31, Is. 32:13, Hos. 10:8. Am. 7:1. In the Targum it is rendered יתרבא (he will grow up), which sense the word 'Surculi' (of a shoot) also demands. For such a phrase does not suit an office, HE SHALL GROW UP LIKE A SAPLING, but rather an origin, as appears from similar passages. Is. 11:1, A flower shall grow up from his root; Jer. 23:6, c. 33:16, I will cause a righteous branch to sprout. The Targum rendered it כרבלבין (like sprouts/shoots), from the root לבלב, he sprouted from the heart or marrow of a tree. He grows up like a sapling לפניו (before him), i.e., the Lord, because the name יהוה precedes it: but just as powerful, wealthy, and splendid men are compared to tall cedars and oaks, Dan. 4:17, Jer. 22:15, so Christ, poor and abject, is compared to a tender sapling, which is indeed pleasant, but is held as nothing on account of its weakness, as our Dr. Weller does here, referring to Augustine, Tom. 10, Serm. 36. The words AS A ROOT OUT OF A DRY GROUND Grotius himself refers to a humble origin, which he nevertheless wrongly drags to the city of Anathoth; for it is not the fatherland that is designated, but the stock and family: A root arises from a dry ground as a certain offspring of it; for the dry ground is not only his native soil, but provides him with an origin like a mother: Therefore, what is said here about the ground of dryness, Is. 11:2, is expressed thus: מגזע, which word, as Kimchi observes, denotes properly a cut-down tree, which is evident from Job 14:4; because the Davidic family was like a dry ground and a cut-down tree, so attenuated and worn away was it when that righteous branch arose from it. Some wish to look to the virginity of the mother, concerning which Jerome says: Symmachus interpreted it as a branch instead of a sapling, to show that the man was assumed who proceeded from a virginal womb; concerning which he infers: As a root out of a dry ground. For 'dry' (sitienti), Aquila interpreted it as 'pathless' (invia), to demonstrate the privilege of virginity, because he was created from the earth, previously pathless, without any human seed. This is he of whom we also read above: A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall grow up from his root, to signify his birth and ascent in the world. Therefore our Dr. Weller renders this from the emphasis of the words as a paraphrase. For my servant will not be august like a cedar, but like a most tender sapling, which, growing up from a tree, seems to everyone to be ripe for eradication, lest by drawing the sap of the tree it ruin the whole tree; he will rise, and just as a root cannot arise from a desert and thirsty land, or if one has arisen, it cannot reach proper maturity, for the necessary nourishment is lacking: So also my servant will arise from such a land, from which naturally no fruit is to be hoped for, nay, the tabernacle of David will be so collapsed that no one will estimate that it will reach any maturity. How a childish age at the time of the assumption of the office is deduced from these words, there will be need of an Oedipus.

Verse of the same. HE HATH NO FORM NOR COMELINESS) He will present nothing magnificent in his countenance, lean and sorrowful.

AND WE SAW HIM) Here Isaiah attributes the speech to the Jewish men who were to live with Jeremiah, and to see that those things which he had said were true.

AND THERE WAS NO APPEARANCE AND WE DESIRED HIM) The interpreter followed a Hebraism, but AND is equivalent to THAT. The sense is: his countenance will not be lovely.

He understands these things of the external view and appearance, and explains them of Jeremiah alone. For who will apply these things mystically to Christ, that he presented nothing magnificent in his countenance, was lean and sorrowful, and that he had no lovely countenance? Since he pleaded the cause of the Jews, he ought to have dealt with the Targum, which explains these things of the Messiah in a completely contrary sense: His appearance will not be like a common appearance, nor his authority like the authority of an idiot; which sense, if it were conformable to the text, would respond more correctly to the truth and fulfillment than the Grotian invention. But we admit that he of whom the discourse is, is said to be devoid of form and comeliness, and that the judgment of the Jews who lived in his time is set forth: We saw him, and there was no appearance THAT WE SHOULD DESIRE HIM, as Symmachus, Vatablus, Tirinus, and B. Tarnovius explain, with whom B. Luther almost agrees, taking 'die uns gefallen hätte' for ונ. Others, with Leo Castrius, Salmeron, and Sanctius, repeat the particle of negation from the common, AND WE DID NOT DESIRE HIM. Dr. Weller, not inelegantly, understands the ה of interrogation, which ellipsis is very common, and not without emphasis: AND SHOULD WE DESIRE HIM! Which interpretations easily agree as to the sense. Furthermore, that the subject is Jeremiah, and that his external form, his natural appearance, is signified as deformed and devoid of comeliness, is too thin and frivolous; nor is there anything certain about the deformity, the gloomy and lean and unlovely form of Jeremiah; nay, that these things are predicted of Christ is, from the infallible interpretation of the Holy Spirit and the whole prophetic context, beyond doubt among all Christians: but that his passion is designated, and the defacement of his face, which he contracted in it, when he was all horrid with blows, stained with blood, and pierced with scourges. For his face was so disfigured that Pilate himself said in wonder: Behold the man! Whence Jerome here distinguishes the beautiful form, which the Psalmist attributes to the Messiah, from this deformity, which the Jews ascribe to the same, namely that he contracted this during the passion. But if he had no form nor glory, but his appearance was ignoble and failing beyond the sons of men: or as it is held in the Hebrew, despised and the last of men: how is it said in the Psalms: Gird thyself with thy sword upon thy thigh, O most mighty, with thy beauty and thy comeliness. Which is easily solved: He was despised and ignoble when he hung on the cross, and having been made a curse for us, he bore our sins. And he was speaking to the Father: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me. But he was renowned and comely in appearance when at his passion the earth trembled, the rocks were rent, and the elements feared an eternal night as the Sun fled. Of whom also the bride in the Song of Songs: My kinsman is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands. White in the fullness and purity of virtues: ruddy in his passion.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET ASCENDET SICUT VIRGULTUM CORAM EO) Et hic positum est pro nimirum. Sensus est: Jeremias adhuc puer Deo servire in Prophetico munere in- cipiet. Habes testimonium de eo apud Hieronymum, in principio ad Jeremiam. Vide & ipsum Jeremiam cap. I. v. 6. Sic Dominus Jesus anno ætatis 12. Doctores docuit.

ET SICUT RADIX DE TERRA SITIENTI) Na- tus in paupere viculo Anathoth, Jer. 1. v. 1. addito quod habuimus hic supra 10, 30. Sic & Bethlehem Jesu tempore vico, quam oppido propior, Joh. 7, 42.

Novæ iterum detorsiones. De particula ET non est quod dicamus, quamvis hic sensus ejus po- tius causalis sit. Quia redditur ratio, cur non cre- diderint Judæi: Nempe vilis ortus Meßiæ, & con- temptibilis aspectus, ut hactenus unanimi mente Christianus orbis credidit. A quo vero Grotio in gratiam, ut apparet, Judæorum recedere, religio non fuit. DeJeremia proprie, vel juxta sensum li- teralem intelligit, etsi attexat deinde Dominum Je- sum, sed postquam sensum Prophetæ corruperat, ita ut in hoc & sequentibus versibus nulli plane usui amplius esse possit hoc vaticinium adversus Judæos. Quid vero hæc ad initium muneris Pro- phetici in puerili ætate, dum ascendere dicitur sicut virgultum coram eo? & quomodo initio muneris subjunxit Propheta nativitatem, in paupere viculo? Verba ipsa docent, utrumque de ortu accipiendum esse, ac mutuo ista se declarare. עלה ascendit, de terra nascentibus adhibetur Deut. 29, 22. Prov. 24, 31. Es. 32, 13. Hos. 10, 8. Am. 7, 1. a Targum redditur יתרבא succrescet, quem sensum etiam ortus postu- lat vox Surculi. Nam de munere talis phrasis non convenit, ASCENDET SICUT VIRGULTUM, sed de ortu, ut è similibus locis apparet. Es. 11, 1. Flos de radice ejus ascendit Jer. 23, 6. c. 33, 16. germi- nare faciam germen justum. Targum reddidit כרבלבין sicut germina propagines, à Rad. לבלב ex corde arboris seu medulla pullulavit. Ascendit sicut virgultum לפניו coram eo, sc. Domino, quia nomen יהוה præcedit: sicut vero homines potentes opulenti & splendidi comparantur altis cedris & quercubus, Dan. 4, 17. Jer. 22, 15. ita Christus pauper & abje- ctus tenero virgulto, quod quidem amœnum est, sed propter imbecillitatem nihili habetur, ut hic Dn. D. Wellerus noster, remittens ad Augustin. Tom. 10. Serm. 36. Verba SICUT RADIX DE TERRA SITIENTI Grotius ipse ad ortum tenuem refert, quæ tamen perperam trahit ad civitatem Anathoth; non enim patria designatur, sed stirps & familia: Radix de terra sitienti oritur tanquam proles quæ- dam ejus; non enim terra sitiens est tantum natale solum illius, sed matris instar originem ipsi præbet: Ideo quod hic dicitur de terra siccitate, Esa. 11. v. 2. ita effertnr מגזע, quæ vox observante Kimchio no- tat proprie lignum excisum, quod è Job. 14, 4. con- stat; quia familia Davidica erat instar terræ sitien- tis, & ligni excisi, sic attenuata & attrita erat, cum inde oriretur germen illud justum. Nonnulli ma- tris virginitatem respici volunt, quo de Hierony- mus: Pro virgulto Symmachus ramum interpreta- tus est, ut assumptum ostenderet hominem, qui pro- cessit de utero virginali; de quo infert: Sicut radix de terra sitienti. Pro sitienti Aquila interpretatus est invia, ut virginitatis privilegium demonstraret, quod absq; ullo bumano semine de terra prius invia sit crea- tus. Iste est de quo & supra legimus: Exiet virga de ra- dice Jesse, & flos de radice ejus ascendet, ut nativi- tatem ejus & ascensum significet in mundo. Ideo Dn. D. Wellerus noster hanc è verborum emphasi red- dit παραφρασιν. Etenim non instar cedri augustus erit servus meus, sed instar virgulti tenuissimi, quod ex arbore succrescens omnibus eradicandum mature videtur, ne succum arboris attrahens totam arborem pessundet, surget, & sicut radix è terra deserta & siti- culosa oriri nequit, vel si quæ orta est, ad maturita- tem justam pervenire nequit, alimentum enim neces- sarium deficit: Sic & servus meus ex ejusmodi orie- tur terra, unde naturaliter fructus sperandus nullus, quin adeo tabernaculum Davidis erit collapsum, ut nemo ipsum ad aliquam maturitatem perventurum æstimaturus sit. Quomodo ætas puerilis tempore suscepti officii ex his verbis deducatur, Oedipo opus erit.

Vers. eod. NON EST SPECIES EI NEQUE DECOR) Nihil magnificum in vultu præferet, macer & mœstus.

ET VIDIMUS EUM) Hic Esaias sermonem tribuit hominibus Judæis, qui cum Jeremia victuri erant, & visuri, vera esse, quæ dixerat.

ET NON ERAT ASPECTUS ET DESIDE- RAVIMUS EUM) Hebraismum sequutus est interpres, sed ET valet UT. Sensus est: non erit vultus illi amabilis.

Hæc de externo intuitu & aspectu intelligit, ac de uno jam tantum Jeremia explicat. Qui enim Christo mystice ista applicabit, quod nihil magnifi- cum in vultu prætulerit, macer & mœstus fuerit, & quod non fuerit ei vultus amabilis? Quum Judæo- rum causam egerit, transigere debuerat cum Tar- gum, quod de Messia prorsus contrario sensu hæc explicat: Non erit aspectus ejus sicut aspectus com- munis, nec autoritas ejus sicut autoritas idiotæ, qui sensus si textui conformis esset, veritati & comple- mento rectius responderet, quam commentum Grotianum. Sed admittimus speciei & decoris ex- pertem dici eum, de quo sermo est, & judicium ex- poni Judæorum, qui ejus tempore vixere: Vidimus eum, & non erat aspectus UT DESIDERARE- MUS EUM, ut Symmachus, Vatablus, Tirinus, B. Tarnovius explicant, quibus fere consonat B. Lu- therus, die uns gefallen hätte, pro ונ accipiens. Alii cum Leone Castrio, Salmerone, Sanctio particu- lam negandi ἀπὸ κοινῶ repetunt, ET NON DE- SIDERAVIMUS EUM. Dn. D. Wellerus non ineleganter ה interrogandi subintelligit, quæ elli- psis usitatissima est, nec emphasi caret: ET DE- SIDERAREMUS EUM! Quæ interpretationes quoad sensum facile conveniunt. Cæterum subje- ctum illud esse Jeremiam, ac significari externam formam, naturalem speciem deformem ac decoris ex- pertem, nimis jejunum, atque frivolum est, neque de Jeremiæ deformitate, tetrica, ac macra nec ama- bili forma quicquam constat; imo de Christo hæc prædici, ex interpretatione Spiritus S. infallibili, rotoque contextu Prophetico, penes omnes Chri- stianos indubium est: sed ut passio ejus designetur ac faciei defœdatio, quam in illa contraxit, cum totus colaphis horridus, sanguine fœdatus, flagris confi- tus esset. Facies enim ejus ita defœdata fuit, ut Pi- latus ipse admirabundus diceret: Ecce homo! Unde formam speciosam, quam Messiæ Hieropsaltes tri- buit, Hieronymus hic distinguit ab hac deformita- te, quam Judæi eidem adscribunt, quod nempe hanc in passione contraxerit. Sin autem non habebat speciem neque gloriam, sed forma ipsius erat ignobi- lis & deficiens præ filiis hominum: sive ut habetur in Hebræo, despectus & novissimus virorum: quo- modo in Psalmis dicitur: Accingere gladio tuo su- per femur tuum potentissime pulchritudine & de- core tuo. Quod facile solvitur: Despectus erat & ignobilis, quando pendebat in cruce, & factus pro no- bis maledictum peccata nostra portabat. Et loqueba- tur Patri: Deus Deus meus, quare me dereliquisti. Inclytus autem erat & decorus aspectu, quando ad passionem ejus terra contremuit, saxa dirupta sunt, & fugiente Sole æternam noctem elementa timuerunt. De quo & sponsa in Cantico Canticorum: Fratruelis meus candidus & rubicundus, electus de millibus. Candidus plenitudine ac puritate virtutum: rubi- cundus in passione.

## 53:3
Vers. 3. DESPISED AND THE LAST OF MEN) Rejected by men, حذل is also to cast away among the Arabs.

The Hebrew word does not imply only a simple rejection: For בזה, as Forster notes, is to cast away in one's mind to be trampled upon, to disdain with a high brow, and to hold as a thing of nothing 1 Sam. 10 v. 27, Esth. 3 v. 6, 2 Sam. 12, 9. Therefore the LXX rendered it ἄτιμον, which word is used of one ennobled by a notable crime, who was excluded from public offices, and whom it was permitted to kill with impunity, is employed. Whence Christ is also called in Ps. 22, בזוי [despised]. But he is called THE MOST ABJECT OF MEN, because he is held to be extremely vile, because contracted adjectives before plurals denote the highest eminence, whence by comparing the places of Scripture Ps. 22, 8. 109, 25. Matth. 27, 39. Mark 15, 39. the learned Dr. Weller collected this emphasis of the words: nay, the Messiah will be cast out like immature and sour fruit, he will be exposed to be trampled by feet, as one publicly infamous, inscribed as one to be killed with impunity on the pillory Job 12. & 9. by no one not lower than any lowest person, from whose company all good men guard themselves, lest they contract the stain of ignominy, he is held, he is neglected with a high eyebrow, and the order of men ceases in him, so that he is not a man, but a worm. There is added A MAN OF SORROWS, that is, according to the custom of speaking of the Hebrews, a most afflicted man, full of sorrow and miseries in every way, both in body and soul, the prince and leader of all those who are and ever were most miserable, so that he seems to be a kind of sea of sorrows, as our praised Theologian paraphrases. Which things certainly do not come to Jeremiah in this emphasis and collection of synonyms. Nor is it ever read that this was the judgment of the Jews concerning him, nor was there need for it to be predicted by another Prophet: of which thing a similar example will hardly be found.

AND ACQUAINTED WITH INFIRMITIES) Such as that one in Homer: 'For he is not ignorant of blows, nor of missiles.' R. Jonathan & R. Jehuda render: Broken by infirmity. Although we grant that one acquainted with infirmity is indicated, who has experienced the same, and to whom it has become familiar and domestic. What are added, AND AS ONE HIDING HIS FACE, our learned Dr. Weller, the most eminent of theologians today, has rendered best from the Hebrew for those skilled in the holy tongue, with Mercer and Pagninus, taking מסתר as a substantive: A HIDING OF FACES FROM US, in that sense in which shepherds are called an abomination of the Egyptians Gen. 46, 34. i.e., And in truth we all turn away and hide the face from him as from an abominable thing, and which you could not look upon without disgust and nausea, DESPISED WHEREFORE WE DID NOT REPUTE HIM. LXX. he was dishonored and was not accounted, i.e., his face. Therefore, that the vile, abject, and contemptible appearance of the Messiah in his birth, ministry, passion, and cross is commemorated by these things, can be ambiguous to no one. Certainly those things do not fit any mortal, nor was any people affected by the appearance and affliction of anyone with as much scandal as by the passion and cross of the Messiah.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DESPECTUM ET NOVISSIMUM VIRO- RUM) Rejectum ab hominibus, حذل etiam Ara- bibus est abjicere.

Ebræa vox non simplicem tantum rejectionem infert: Nam בזה notante Forstero, est animo abjecit conculcandum, alto supercilio dedignatus est, & ut rem nihili habuit 1. Sam. 10. v. 27. Estr. 3. v. 6. 2. Sam. 12, 9. Ideo LXX. reddidere ἄτιμον, quæ vox de insigni facinore nobilitato, qui à publicis munerib. excludehatur, & quem impune licebat occidere, adhibetur. Unde Christus etiam Pf.22. בזוי dicitur. NOVISSIMUS VIRORUM autem vocatur, quod extreme vilis habeatur, quia adjectiva contra- cta ante pluralia summam eminentiam notant, unde collatis Scripturæ locis Pf. 22, 8. 109, 25. Matth. 27, 39. Marc. 15, 39. hanc verborum emphasin collegit Dn. D. Wellerus: imo Messias instar fructus im- maturi & acerbi projicietur, pedibus conculcandus exponetur, ut publice infamis instar, cippo impune oc- cidendus inscriptus Job. 12. & 9. à nemine non infra quemvis infimum, à cujus consortio boni quique sibi ca- vent, ne maculam sibi contrahant ignominiæ, habea- tur, alto negligatur supercilio, & ordo hominum in ipso cesset, ut non homo, sed vermis sit. Additur VIR DOLORUM, id est, ex Ebræorum loquendi con- suetudine, vir afflictissimus, dolore & miseriis qua corpus, qua animam undiquaque plenus, princeps & choragus omnium omnino quicunque sunt & fue- runt unquam miserrimorum, ita ut pelagus quasi quoddam dolorum videatur, ut Theologus noster laudatus παραφράζει. Quæ certe Jeremiæ non veniunt in hac emphasi & congerie Synonymo- rum. Neque Judæorum hoc de ipso judicium aut fuisse unquam legitur, aut opus erat id prædici ab alio Propheta: cujus rei simile exemplum vix in- venietur.

ET SCIENTEM INFIRMITATVM) Qualis ille apud Homerum: Ὃν γάρ τι πληγέων ἀδαήμων, ὐδὲ βολάων. R. Jonathan & R. Jehuda reddunt: Contri- tum infirmitate. Quamvis largiamur indigitari gnarum infirmitatis, qui expertus sit ejusdem, & cui illa familiaris & domestica facta. Quæ adduntur, ET QUASI ABSCONDITUS VULTUS EJUS, ex Ebræo optime reddidit linguæ sanctæ peritis- simus Dn. D. Wellerus noster, Theologorum hodie eminentissimus, cum Mercero & Pagnino מסתר ha- bens pro substantivo: ABSCONSIO FACIE- RUM A NOBIS, eo sensu, quo pastores abomi- natio Ægyptiorum dicuntur Gen. 46, 34. q. d. Et revera nos omnes faciem ab eo tanquam re abomina- bili, & quam sine fastidio & nausea aspicere haud pos- sis, avertimus & abscondimus, DESPECTUS UNDE NEC REPUTAVIMUS EUM. LXX. ἠτιμάσθη καὶ ὐκ ἐλογίσθη, despecta & non reputata facies sc. ejus. His ergo vilem, abjectam & con- temptam speciem Messiæ in ortu, ministerio, passio- ne ac cruce commemorari, nemini ambiguum esse potest. Nulli certe mortalium ea omnia conveni- unt, nec ullius specie & afflictione tanto affectus est populus scandalo, quanto Messiæ passione ac cruce.

## 53:4
Ver. 4. SURELY HE HAS BORNE OUR GRIEFS.) He bore such evils not deserved by him, which we had deserved. He says the Jews will say all these things after the city was taken.

Grotius has corrupted these things, and what further follow in this chapter, which are most full of life-giving consolation, in a wonderful manner, so that we must believe entirely that not the Holy Spirit, but the Demon, the author of all lies and error, directed the pen and mind of the man, so that he might bring darkness upon a most clear prophecy, and that he might twist it by the help of that very one as the Spirit of darkness toward Jeremiah. For what is clearer than that these things treat of Christ the Savior? What is more certain than that these things do not fit Jeremiah, nor any other mortal, but are proper to Christ alone, if they are accepted according to the sense which the words bring, without distortion, and understood according to the interpretation handed down by the Holy Scriptures! The bearing of our griefs teaches this at least in the first place. For who of the human race bore, or could bear, our griefs, except Christ alone? Griefs are punishments inflicted for sins, and therefore to bear the griefs of the human race is to pay and sustain the punishments which we have deserved for our sins. Who is capable of this, except Christ, who alone satisfied for our sins! For it is not signified that he took upon himself our diseases, so that he himself was subject to diseases, but that he derived into himself the guilt of sin, by which we were bound, and he himself bore the evils which we deserved, which sense Grotius admits. But how could they have professed, or been able to profess, to the Jews after the city was taken concerning Jeremiah, that he sustained the evils which they themselves had deserved, when they all themselves, as a punishment for their sins, underwent captivity and notable slaughter, and Jeremiah did not sustain the evils in their place; nay, when the city was occupied, the Jews killed and led into captivity, he was dismissed free. And does not Grotius openly contradict his own gloss to the interpretation of the Evangelist Matthew 8, v. 6. and he healed all who were ill, that it might be fulfilled which was said by Isaiah the Prophet saying, He took our infirmities, and bore our sicknesses. Grotius contends that what Matthew explains concerning Christ, who healed all who were ill, and cast out demons, is to be understood concerning Jeremiah, sustaining certain evils around the imminent Babylonian captivity. There is indeed some difficulty concerning the application of the prophecy to the diseases cast out by Christ, but that the subject in the Prophet is Christ, he calls into question, which Grotius acknowledged before he was demented by the ravings of the Jews. For in the Annotations on the books of the Gospels on Matthew 8, 17, he wrote thus concerning this matter: Just as the deeds of the ancients had the figure of the things of Christ, so also the actions of Christ himself served to denote others. For there can be no doubt that the benefit of health restored to bodies bore the figure of the remission of sins and healed minds. Therefore the prophecy was fulfilled twice: first when Christ, tiring himself until evening, occupied himself in relieving the diseases of others, as Matthew shows here: later, when, enduring the punishment of the cross, he obtained for us the remission of sins, as Peter teaches 2 Epist. 2, 24. For the collation of the LXX version, which Peter follows almost step by step, teaches that the same place of Isaiah is looked to by Peter. He obscured the reason for the application there, that the labor in curing diseases was a figure or type of the labor in enduring the punishment of the cross, and the benefit of health restored to bodies was a figure of healed minds. Which reason, however, is neither rightly enough proposed, and is less sufficient, and cannot even be held as primary. It is certain that Christ wished to prefigure by this healing of bodies that salvation which He provides for our souls, but because the prophecy of Isaiah is said to be fulfilled here, the question arises as to its meaning: to which, indeed, a double meaning ought by no means to be assigned. Wherefore it had to be determined, what is the proper sense of these words intended by the Holy Spirit? That, however, is none other than the one indicated by St. Peter, as the entire συνέχεια of the text together with the ἁρμονία of the Petrine passage establishes. It is therefore a matter of the punishments of our sins borne and endured by Christ, who took and sustained the infirmities and sorrows, and all the evils which we had deserved by our sins, so that He might obtain for us the remission of sins, and liberate us completely from them. St. Peter therefore teaches this; indeed, St. Matthew also teaches this, if we examine the matter more accurately. For if Christ so took upon Himself our infirmities and sorrows, that He languished and suffered for us, not only by sustaining infirmities and sorrows in His soul, as He Himself testifies, 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death'; but also in His body, not indeed by sustaining natural diseases and sicknesses, yet by sustaining various wounds and sufferings, and that to this end, that he might deliver us from the pains and languors of soul and body; nor did Peter depart from the true meaning of the prophecy, who taught that we are taught by the Prophetic oracle to have been delivered from the languors and pains of the soul, nor did St. Matthew, who [taught we were delivered] from the languors and pains of the body. St. Matthew, however, did not express the manner by which he delivered us, which Isaiah there explained clearly, if any other of the holy men of God did, as he was most highly illuminated by the Spirit of Christ, namely, that this was done by the substitution of Christ in our place, and by his taking upon himself and paying for our guilt and punishment. For it was enough to show him of whom Isaiah spoke, and to refer to that Prophet, and also to teach and explain the deliverance which we have from Christ. For we have truly been delivered by him not only from our sins, which he himself testified as often as he imparted the remission of sins and preached about the spiritual grace which he provides to us; but especially when he entrusted to his ministers the power of remitting sins, but also from the punishments and penalties of sins, such as are diseases, possessions of demons, and death. Therefore he gave specimens of that deliverance in the days of his flesh, and by the very act demonstrated that he was such a Savior, when he cured all who were afflicted with diseases, cast out demons, and delivered the possessed, and even raised some from death; because Matthew was reporting this there and was about to report further, he taught most correctly that the prophecy of Isaiah had been fulfilled then, which is fulfilled further as often as we are delivered even today from diseases or the power of Satan, and it will be fulfilled in the most perfect manner when the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed, when we shall be delivered from death and corruption, and also from eternal condemnation. Then it will be manifest openly and most fully that Christ took our languors and bore our pains. For although already in this age, as many of us as obtain the remission of sins by the merit of Christ are delivered from any punishments and penalties whatsoever, and thus even from the diseases of the body, yet because it pleases God sometimes to send such things to us not as τιμωρίαν and punishment, but as δοκιμασίαν, a fatherly chastisement, then our deliverance, which we owe to Christ, will be established far more perfectly when we shall be entirely free and immune from all evils in the other life. Meanwhile, that poisoned fountain of sins being obstructed, from which diseases and all the evils that press upon us spring, these are not undeservedly considered to be washed away, because with the remission of guilt obtained, which Christ merited by his passion, no place remains for punishment, and it must be believed that we are truly delivered from it. When the Son of God had come, says Brentius p. 671, into this world, to cure our infirmities, he undertook to expiate sin, which was the cause of all our infirmities and evils. But this being expiated, all our infirmities were spiritually and truly cured. For although infirmities still remain corporally and afflict the pious in this age, yet they can neither be perpetual, nor can they bring any harm to true salvation, because sin being expiated, God is more propitious to those who believe and call upon him, on account of his Son, and adopts them as heirs of his goods, and saves them in death, that they may have celestial and eternal life. And these things [are said] concerning the application of our text made by Matthew.

Therefore, it is clear that the meaning which Grotius makes the second is the only one, which he himself also acknowledged to be the fuller one. Therefore, on Matthew 8:17, explaining ἀσθενείας as חליינו, he says: the LXX and Peter, looking to the second and FULLER meaning, interpreted it quite properly as ἁμαρτίας: the LXX rendered it ὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει. St. Peter, 1 Epist. 2:24, ὃς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν. Since therefore Grotius acknowledges here that the words of Isaiah are referred to by St. Peter, and that the FULLER meaning is being explained, and St. Peter openly teaches that Christ HIMSELF bore our sins in his body upon the wood of the cross, when he sustained the punishment of our sins, this meaning of our prophecy must be the FULLER one. Which we say is the only one, and the only true one. Now, that he wishes the troubles endured in curing diseases to be also included in the words of the Prophet, this can be admitted so far as those troubles were meritorious. For whatever labors, troubles, languor, pain, passion, and torments Christ sustained, it pertains to his merits, since he sustained all those for our sake, and performed all obedience, both active and passive, for the sake of our salvation. To the explanation of the scribe Grotius. On the word ἐβάστασεν in Matthew chapter 8:17, he notes thus: Tertullian interprets it as HE TOOK AWAY. But there is in this word, as also in the Hebrew סבל and in the similar מען which the Syrian used here, a certain signification of a burden, that is, of trouble: just as also that which preceded, ἀνέλαβε, is, as if you were to say, he took up onto his shoulders. The meaning is therefore that Christ, in order to remove diseases from men, did not avoid any labors, however untimely. For that here, and no less in Mark and Luke, the time is expressed after the sun set, that it has its own emphasis has been noted not badly by Theophylact. But neither is the other circumstance to be omitted, that Christ was almost oppressed among these things by the crowd of people coming together, which Mark and Luke thought should be noted when they were reporting the history of the healed paralytic. Certainly, Isaiah also, besides death, describes the many troubles and miseries of Christ in fulfilling his office. Paul expressed the same force of the word סבל when he said in Rom. 15:1, τὰ ἀσθενήματα τῶν ἀδυνάτων βαστάζειν, and Gal. 6:2, Ἀλλήλων βάρη βαστάζετε. For this is what he means, that others are to be relieved even with some inconvenience to ourselves. Therefore, the prophecy of Isaiah was fulfilled twice: first in the healing of diseases, not without trouble to Christ, then much more perfectly in his very death, by which he took away the diseases of the soul. We have already stated our opinion concerning the double meaning. However, it does not appear that Isaiah intended that trouble was to be created for Christ in curing diseases, and that his labors were untimely: whence, even if it be said that he embraced γενικῶς whatever Christ endured for the sake of expiating our sins, under which name all troubles and fatigues are also included; yet when I speak of the genus, I do not immediately express a certain species: nor does Isaiah the Prophet, or Matthew citing him, contemplate under this formal aspect that our ἀσθενείας were borne, in the sense that he would undergo labor and fatigue in curing various diseases; and therefore this expression of time after the setting of the sun contributes nothing to this oracle of Isaiah: nor does that circumstance pertain here, that he was almost crushed by the crowd of men: both of which circumstances Mark and Luke alone express, not Matthew, who cited the oracle of Isaiah. For since Grotius acknowledges that חליינו is properly AD MODUM by the LXX Interpreters and is rendered here by Peter as ἁμαρτίας, that word cannot denote here either bodily sicknesses or the troubles of labor. By which word sins are properly denoted, by that same word in the same place TROUBLES are certainly not denoted. Moreover, it can be added that the Chaldean himself understood the word חליינו in no other way, because he interpreted it as חובנא, i.e., debts. And that the LXX Interpreters emphatically designated the passion of Christ, when they rendered those words: he himself bore our sorrows, as: περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται, he suffers pain for us, by which word the most exquisite pains, even infernal torments themselves, are expressed in Luke 16:24, 25.

Meanwhile, it is rightly observed that the word סבל signifies a burdensome carrying, but it must be placed in the context of our sins being borne and expiated, according to St. Peter and the Prophet's own intention. And although Isaiah, besides death, also designated many of Christ's miseries and troubles in the fulfilling of his office, he could not, however, by these words which we are now treating, signify both those SINS and MISERIES and the PASSION endured in his body, as the punishment of sin, and the MISERY devoured in curing evils: since those meanings are most disparate and cannot underlie the same words. Grotius himself, when he was writing against Socinus concerning the satisfaction of Christ, ch. 1, p. 11, had taught that the word סבל is to sustain, to carry, and as often as it is placed with the name of SIN or INIQUITY, and especially in Hebraism, it signifies to bear punishments. What then remains, but that we conclude that it was indicated by the Prophet that Christ bore our punishments, and therefore bore the penalty for our sins. Grotius acknowledges in the same place that Peter, in citing the words of Isaiah, had regard to sacrifices, and that his words are to be understood in a sacrificial sense; just as, indeed, expiatory victims were said to carry sins, because, to wit, they were slaughtered for sins, and were delivered into death in the place of those who had sinned, to figure the satisfaction of Christ. It is helpful to transcribe the entire passage, since it contributes to explaining the Prophetic and Apostolic passage παράλληλον, and to confounding Grotius, who now sails for the Jews and Socinians, no less than Socinus, against whom he once defended the Catholic faith. For thus it stands in Defens. fid. Cathol. de satisfact. Christi, ch. 1, p. 9: The form of the satisfaction of Christ is the payment of punishments for our sins: which Socinus strictly denies. Wherefore we shall briefly prove this very thing. The Hebrews, to signify that which the Latins call paying penalties, have no phrase more accepted than this: to bear sin: to which the expression of the Latins is similar, to pay for crimes, that is, the punishments of crimes. If anyone shall not have informed against a blasphemer, he shall bear his sin. Levit. 5, 1. He who has uncovered the nakedness of his sister, let him bear his sin. Levit. 20, 17. Thus expiatory victims are said to carry the iniquities of those who offer them, Lev. 10, 17. Because their blood is for the human soul, Lev. 17, 1. Nor are these words found only together, but also separately in the same sense. Thus βασάζειν τὸ κρίμα is said in Gal. 5, 10; to bear sins, Ezech. 18, 20. And for sin to come upon someone, that is, the punishment of sin, 2 Kings 7, 9. In the very same phrase Peter said that Christ bore our sins up in his body to the tree, 1 Pet. 2, 24. He could have said ἤνεγκε, but because he wished to signify at the same time the ascent onto the cross, ἀνήνεγκε, that is, he bore by going up: which diminishes nothing from the said phrase, but adds something to it. Therefore the Syrian translated: he carried and made to ascend. Socinus, in order to enervate the force of this passage, first says that ἀνήνεγκε signifies he took away: but this is against the nature and usage of the word. For neither does the particle ἀνά suffer that interpretation, nor has any Greek writer used the word in that way. In the New Testament also it never occurs with that meaning: but it signifies either to carry up, Luke 24, 51, or to lead up, Matt. 17, 1, Mark 9, 2. And because victims were brought to a higher place, that is, to the altar, therefore they also are said to be ἀναφέρεσθαι, Heb. 7, 27, Jas. 2, 21. Whence also Christ himself is said to have offered himself, ἀνενέγκας, Heb. 7, 27, and we are said to offer praises or spiritual sacrifices, ἀναφέρειν, Heb. 13, 15, and 1 Pet. 2, 28. Socinus cites only one passage, Heb. 9, 28, where he wishes ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας to be nothing other than to take away: but undeservedly, and without example, and not as the sense of the passage demands. For two comings of Christ are opposed to each other: the former, by which he bore our sins, the other by which he is to come χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, that is, not burdened, not loaded with any sins, but released and immune from them. However, these are not ἀντίστοιχα, to be χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας and to take away sins, but to be χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας and to be burdened with sins. Whence it appears that in that passage to the Hebrews also, ἀνενεγκεῖν is either to carry up, namely to the cross, as in the passage of Peter (and that aptly, because here too there is an allusion to sacrifices: and the cross was as it were an altar) or simply to endure, as in Thucydides κινδύνους ἀναφέρειν. Therefore ἀναφέρειν is to bear, not to take away, which the context of Peter himself proves. For it is not a question of just any benefit of Christ, but of his supreme patience, which is shown not by taking away, but by bearing. What Socinus adds, that what follows—that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness—does not cohere well with this sense in which Christ is said to have borne our sins, is said without any cause. For Peter manifestly indicates that Christ so bore our sins that he might at the same time free us from punishment: whence he adds immediately: by whose stripe you were healed. These cohere excellently: if Christ underwent such harsh things so that you might obtain the forgiveness of sins, surely, having obtained it through faith, you ought to beware of sins in the future. God has granted us, that being delivered out of the hand of our enemies, we might serve him in all holiness and righteousness, Luke 1, 74, 75. Behold, you have been made whole, sin no more hereafter, John 5, 14. You were bought with a price. Glorify therefore God in your body, 1 Cor. 6, 20. Nor does Paul do anything else in chapter 7 and the following chapters to the Romans, than to show that we ought to be stirred up by the supreme benefits of God and Christ to live holily. These are the words of Grotius, before he had yet been seduced by the Jews: And these things concerning the first argument.

A second argument, that the discourse here is uniquely about Christ, is provided by the unfavorable judgment concerning the blows of him who is described here. For it is a question here of him who was falsely believed to have been struck and afflicted with blows on account of his own sins. That, however, in no way fits Jeremiah or any other mere man. For there is no mortal who, if he is afflicted by God, is entirely innocent; all are subject to sins, therefore if they are afflicted, it is certain that this happens not on account of the sins of others, but on account of their own sins, since the rule of divine justice requires it; Christ alone suffered for sins not his own, when he took our sins upon himself. 2 Cor. 5:21. Let us now hear the judgment of the Jews concerning him, along with the gloss of Grotius.

Verse same. AND WE ESTEEMED HIM AS A LEPER AND STRUCK BY GOD AND HUMBLED) The Hebrew word נגוע is indeed taken also to mean a leper, but by itself it signifies nothing other than the following word, struck. From this passage arose the fable among the Jews that the Messiah dwells among lepers. But the sense is: we believed Jeremiah was deservedly cast into prison and the mire, with God holding him in hatred as an enemy of the city and the Temple, and a false prophet. See Jer. 26.

The Messiah, therefore, whom the Jews themselves acknowledge to be indicated here by the Prophet, even though they have invented that fable to crush the Christian faith, Grotius, a Christian, does not admit is to be understood here, and renders such a sense as refers only to Jeremiah, which is not to Judaize, but to be worse than the Jews. We admit that the word נגוע, which Jerome, following Symmachus and Aquila, rendered as leper, denotes in general one wounded or struck: the LXX rendered it: εἶναι αὐτὸν ἐν πόνῳ, that he is in labor. The other word נכה from מכה אלהים, to kill, to strike, does not denote a God struck, as Bellarmine lib. 2 de verbo Dei c. 11, Andrade, Cornelius à Lapide after Gorlatinus wish, but because מכה is placed in the construct state, and a substantive in construction always precedes an adjective, it ought to be explained as struck

of God. The third וּמְעֻנֶּה and signifies humbled or afflicted by tyranny, servitude, or force; see Ps. 102 v. 24, Ps. 119 v. 26, Lam. 3 v. 33. The judgment of the Jews is therefore referred to here, because they thought that he was both wounded for his own transgressions and struck with blows by God, and was exceedingly depressed and humbled, as the words clearly teach. Certainly he himself bears our infirmities and carries our sorrows, but we thought that he was struck and afflicted by the blow of God: when we saw him to be so deformed, so foul, so abominable, it immediately came into our mind not of our own infirmities and iniquities, but of divine severity toward his own transgressions. For we judged, according to the bent of human reason, that he was divinely afflicted so horribly because of his own sins. But when we considered the matter itself, as it is, having been taught by the Holy Spirit, we acknowledge that he is so foully lacerated, not by his own fault, not by the merits of his own sins, of which he has none, but by our fault and the merits of our sins, and that he suffers our infirmities.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VERE LANGVORES NOSTROS IPSE TVLIT.) Ille non talia meritus mala tulit, quæ nos era- mus meriti. Hæc omnia ait dicturos Iudæos post captam urbem.

Hæc, & quæ porro sequuntur in hoc capite, vivificæ consolationis plenissima, mirum in mo- dum corrupit Grotius, ut omnino credamus, non Spiritum S. sed Dæmonem, mendacii & erroris omnis auctorem, calamum animumque hominis direxisse, ut vaticinio luculentissimo tenebras in- ferret, idque ope ipsius ceu Spiritus tenebrarum ad Jeremiam detorqueret. Quid enim clarius, quam quod hæc de Christo Salvatore agant? Quid certius, quam quod neque in Jeremiam, neque in ullum alium mortalium hæc conveniant, sed soli Christo propria sint, si juxta sensum, quem verba inferunt, sine στρεβλότητι accepta & juxta interpretationem à S. S. traditam intelligantur! Id docet utique primo Languorum nostrorum portatio. Quis enim huma- ni generis languores tulit, aut ferre potuit, præter unum Christum? Languores sunt pœnæ pro pecca- li- tis inflicte, ideoq; languores humani generis ferre, est pœnas, quas peccatis promeriti sumus, luere, & sustinere. Quis hoc valet, nisi Christus, qui solus pro peccatis nostris satisfecit! Non enim signifi- catur, quod morbos nostros susceperit, ita ut mor- bis subjectus ipse fuerit, sed quod reatum peccati, quo nos obstricti eramus, in se derivarit, & mala, quæ meriti sumus, ipse pertulerit, quem sensum Grotius admittit. Quomodo autem Judæis post captam urbem de Jeremia professi sunt, aut profi- teri potuere, quod mala, quæ ipsi erant meriti, su- stinuerit, quum omnes ipsi, in pœnam peccato- rum, captivitatem & cladem insignem subierint, neque eorum loco Jeremias mala sustinuerit; imo occupata urbe, cæsis, & in captivitatem abducti Judæis, liber dimissus fuerit. Et annon glossa sua palam refragatur Grotius interpretationi Evange- listæ Matth. 8. v. 6. & omnes male habentes curavit, ut adimpleretur quod dictum est per Esaiam Prophe- tam dicentem, Ipse infirmitates nostras accepit, & ægrotationes nostras portavit. Quod de Christo, qui curavit omnes male habentes, & Dæmonia ejecit, explicat Matthæus, id de Jeremia, mala quæ- dam sustinente circa imminentem captivitatem Babylonicam intelligendum esse, contendit Gro- tius. Difficultas quidem aliqua est circa applica- tionem vaticinii ad morbos à Christo profligatos, sed subjectum apud Prophetam esse Christum, omni dubietate vocat, quod agnovit Grotius, priusquam Judæorum deliriis dementaretur. Nam in Annot. ad libros Evangel. ad Matth. 8, 17. ita hac de re scri- psit: Sicut veterum res gestæ rerum Christi figuram habuerunt, ita & ipsius Christi actiones aliæ aliis de- notandis inservierunt. Nam beneficium corporibus redditæ sanitatis, quin figuram remissionis peccato- rum & sanatarum mentium tulerit, dubitari non potest. Bis ergo impletum est vaticinium: prius cum Christus semet fatigans ad vesperam usque alio- rum morbis levandis vacavit, ut hic ostendit Mat- thæus: posterius, cum crucis supplicium perferens re- missionem peccatorum nobis impetravit, ut docet Petrus 2. Epist. 2, 24. Nam eundem locum Esaiæ à Petro respici, docet collatio versionis LXX. quam ferme κα- τὰ πόδας Petrus sequitur. Applicationis rationem stiscuit illic eam, quod labor in curandis morbis figura vel typus laboris in exantlando supplicio cru- cis, Beneficium corporibus redditæ sanitatis figura sa- natarum mentium fuerit. Quæ vero ratio nec recte satis proposita, & minus sufficiens est, ac ne pro pri- maria quidem haberi potest. Certum est, figurare voluisse Christum hac corporum sanatione illam, quam animabus nostris præstat salutem, sed quia impletum hic dicitur vaticinium Esaiæ, de illius sen- su quæritur: cui utique geminus sensus assignari minime debet. Quapropter constituendum erat, quisnam proprius & à S. S. intentus horum verbo- rum sensus sit? Is vero nullus alius est, quam qui à S. Petro indicatur, utpote quem tota συνέχεια tex- tus cum ἁρμονίᾳ loci Petrini statuminat. Agitur itaque de pœnis peccatorum nostrorum à Christo por- tatis & exantlatis, qui languores & dolores, omnia- que mala, quæ meriti eramus peccatis nostris, tulit ac sustinuit, ut remissionem peccatorum nobis im- petraret, nosque ab illis liberaret penitus. Id ergo docet S. Petrus, imo id etiam docet S. Matthæus, si rem accuratius inspiciamus. Nam si Christus ita lan- guores, & dolores nostros suscepit, ut pro nobis langueret ac doleret, animo non tantum languores & dolores sustinendo, uti testatur ipse, Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem; sed etiam corpore, non quidem morbos & ægritudines naturales, varias ta- men plagas & perpessiones sustinendo, idq; ea fini, ut nos ab animæ & corporis doloribus & languori- bus liberaret, neq; Petrus à vera sententia vaticinii abiit, qui ab animæ languoribus & doloribus nos li- beratos doceri Prophetico oraculo tradidit, nec S. Matthæus, qui à languoribus & doloribus corporis. Modum autem, quo nos liberavit, non expressit S. Matthæus, quem ibi Esaias plane, si quisquam alius sanctorum Dei virorum exposuit, ut fuit maxime à Christi Spiritu illuminatus, quod nempe surroga- tione Christi in vicem nostri, & culpæ atque pœnæ no- stræ susceptione ac luitione id factum sit. Satis enim erat, ostendere illum, de quo Esaias egerit, & ad Prophetam istum remittere, nec non liberationem, quam à Christo habemus docére, atque expone- re.
