Vere enim liberati sumus ab ipso non modo à peccatis nostris, quod toties ipse testatus est, quo- ties remissionem peccatorum impertiit, & de gratia spirituali, quam nobis præstat, concionatus est; maxime autem cum potestatem remittendi pecca- ta ministris suis credidit, sed etiam à peccatorum suppliciis & pœnis, ceu sunt morbi, Dæmonum obses- siones, & mors. Ideo specimina liberationis istius edidit in diebus carnis, & facto ipso demonstravit, se esse talem Servatorem, cum omnes qui morbis affecti erant curavit, Dæmones expulit, ac obsessos liberavit, nonnullos etiam à morte suscitavit, quod quia ibi Matthæus referebat & porro relaturus erat, rectissime impletum vaticinium Esaiæ tum fuis- se docuit, quod impletur porro, quoties nos hodie- que liberamur à morbis aut potestate Satanæ, & implebitur perfectissima ratione, cum novissimus hostis mors destruetur, cum liberabimur à morte, & corruptione, nec non ab æterna condemnatione. Tum enim constabit palam & plenissime, Christum languores nostros suscepisse, ac dolores nostros tulisse. Quanquam enim jam in hoc seculo, quotquot con- sequimur remissionem peccatorum, Christi merito, à pœnis ac suppliciis quibusvis, adeoque à corporis etiam morbis liberamur, quia tamen placet Deo, ta- lia nobis non ceu τιμωρίαν & pœnam, sed tanquam δοκιμασίαν, castigationem paternam quandoque immittere, tum longe perfectius constabit nostra liberatio, quam Christo debemus, cum ab omnibus malis prorsus liberi & immunes futuri sumus in al- tera vita. Interim obstructo illo fonte venenato peccatorum, unde scaturiunt morbi, & mala quæ nos premunt universa, non immerito hæc abluta censentur, quia impetrata remissione culpæ, quam meruit Christus passione sua, pœnæ nullus superest locus, & ab illo liberatos nos vere esse credendum est. Cum venisset Filius Dei, inquit Brentius p. 671. in hunc mundum, ad curandas nostras infirmitates, suscepit expiandum peccatum, quod erat omnium in- firmitatum & malorum nostrorum causa. Hoc au- tem expiato, infirmitates nostræ omnes spiritualiter, ac vere curabantur. Etsi enim manent infirmitates adhuc corporaliter, & affligunt pios in hoc seculo, ta- men nec possunt esse perpetuæ, nec possunt afferre ali- quod veræ salutis incommodum, quia expiato peccato, Deus est credentibus & invocantibus ipsum propi- tius, propter Filium suum, & adoptat eos in suorum bonorum hæredes, ac servat eos in morte, ut habeant cœlestem & æternam vitam. Atque hæc de applica- tione dicti nostri à Matthæo facta.

Sensum ergo, quem secundum facit Grotius, unicum ejusdem esse liquet, quem etiam ipse agno- vit pleniorem esse. Ideo ad Matth. 8, 17. ἀσθενείας explicans חליינו, inquit, proprie admodum LXX. & Petrus, ἁμαρτίας, respicientes sensum secundum ac PLENIOREM: ὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει reddidere LXX. S. Petrus 1. Epist. 2, 24. ὃς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν. Quum ergo hic verba Esaiæ referri agnoscat Grotius à S. Petro, sensumque PLENIOREM exponi, aperte doceat S. Petrus, quod tulerit Christus peccata nostra IPSE in corpore suo super lignum crucis, cum pœnam pec- catorum nostrum sustinuit, sensum hunc vaticinii nostri PLENIOREM esse oportet. Quem nos dicimus unicum, uniceque verum. Jam quod mole- stias in morbis curandis exantlatas etiam compre- hendi vult verbis Prophetæ, hactenus admitti potest, in quantum molestiæ illæ erant meritoriæ. Quicquid enim laborum, molestiarum, languoris, doloris, passionis, cruciatuum sustinuit Christus, ad merita ejus pertinet, quum omnia illa nostri causa sustinuerit, omnem obedientiam tum activam, tum passivam nostræ salutis ergo præstiterit. Ad scribam Grotii explicationem. Ad verbum ἐβά- sασεν Matthæi capite 8, 17. ita notat: ABSTU- LIT interpretatur Tertullianus. Sed est in hac voce, ut & in Hebræa סבל & in simili מען quam hic Syrus posuit, oneris quædam, id est molestiæ, signifi- catio: sicut & quod præcessit ἀνέλαβε est, quasi dicas, in humeros sustulit. Sensus est ergo Christum ut morbos hominibus demeret, nullos labores quantum- vis intempestivos defugisse. Nam quod hic, neque mi- nus apud Marcum, & Lucam, tempus exprimitur post solem occasum, habere suam ἔμφασιν non male à Theophylacto notatum est. Sed neque altera circum- stantia omittenda est, quod Christus inter hæc pene op- pressus sit hominum concurrentium turba, quod Mar- cus & Lucas annotandum putaverunt, cum paralytici sanati historiam referrent. Sane Esaias etiam præ- ter mortem, molestias ærumnasque multas Christi in obeundo munere, describit. Eandem vim verbi סבל Paulus expressit cum dixit Rom. 15, 1. τὰ ἀσθενήματα τῶν ἀδυνάτων βαστάζειν, & Gal. 6, 2. Ἀλλήλων βάρη βαστάζετε. Hoc enim vult, sublevandos alios etiam cum nostro aliquo incommodo. Bis igitur imple- tum est Esaiæ vaticinium, primum in morborum sa- natione, non sine Christi molestia, deinde multo per- fectius in ipsa morte, qua animi morbos sustulit. De sensu gemino sententiam jam diximus. Molestiam autem in morbis curandis Christo creandam, ac labo- res ejus intempestivos Esaiam intendisse non appa- ret: unde etiamsi dicatur, quod complexus fuerit γενικῶς, quicquid Christus peccatorum nostrorum expiandorum causa sustinuit, quo nomine omnes molestiæ ac defatigationes etiam comprehendun- tur; non tamen cum genus dico, statim certam speciem exprimo: nec sub hoc formali intuetur sive Esaias Propheta, sive eum adducens Matthæus portatas ἀσθενείας nostras, quod laborem & defa- tigationem subiturus esset in curandis morbis va- riis; ideoque hæc temporis post Solem occasum ex- pressio ad hoc Esaiæ oraculum nihil facit: neque huc pertinet illa circumstantia, quod ab hominum turba pene oblisus fuerit: quam utramque circum- stantiam Marcus & Lucas soli exprimunt, non Mat- thæus, qui oraculum Esaiæ adduxit. Quum enim a- gnoscat Grotius חליינו proprie AD MODUM à LXX. Interpp. & Petro hic reddi ἁμαρτίας, non potest illa vox vel ægritudines corporis, vel mole- stias laboris hic notare. Qua voce proprie no- tantur peccata, ea utique eodem in loco non notantur MOLESTIÆ. Addi autem potest, quod etiam ipse Chaldæus vocem חליינו non ali- ter intellexerit, quia interpretatus est חובנא h. e. debita. Et quod LXX. Interpp. passionem Christi emphatice designarint, cum verba illa: dolores nostros ipse portavit, sic reddidere: περὶ ἡ- μῶν ὀδυνᾶται, pro nobis dolet, qua voce dolores ex- quisitissimi, cruciatus etiam ipsi infernales expri- muntur Luc. 16, 24. 25.

Interim voce סבל molestam portationem si- gnificari, recte observatur, sed ea in peccatis nostris ferendis, & luendis ponenda est juxta S. Petrum, & propriam intentionem Prophetæ. Et quamvis Esaias præter mortem etiam ærumnas, & molestias Christi multas in obeundo munere designarit, non ta- men his verbis, quæ nunc tractamus, & PECCA- TA & MOLESTIAS illas & PASSIONEM in corpore suo exantlatam, ceu pœnam peccati, & MOLESTIAM in curandis malis devoratam si- gnificare potuit: quum sensus illi maxime disparati sint, & iisdem verbis subesse non possint. Docuerat Grotius ipse, cum adversus Socinum de satisfactio- ne Christi scriberet, c. 1. p. 11. vocem סבל esse susti- nere, bajulare, ac quoties bajulare ponitur cum nomi- ne PECCATI aut INIQUITATIS, & maxime in Ebraismo, significare pœnas ferre. Quid ergo restat, quam ut concludamus, id indicatum fuisse per Pro- phetam, Christum tulisse pœnas nostras, adeoque tulisse supplicium pro peccatis nostris. Agnofcit Grotius ibidem, Petrum adducentem verba Esaiæ, respexisse ad sacrificia, & verba ejus sensu sacrificiali esse intelligenda; uti nempe victimæ expiatoriæ pec- cata dicebantur portare, quia sc. pro peccatis macta- bantur, & vice eorum, qui peccarant, in mortem tra- debantur ad figurandam satisfactionem Christi. Ad- scribere juvat locum integrum, quum faciat ad ex- plicandum locum Propheticum & Apostolicum παράλληλον, & confundendum non minus Gro- tium nunc Judæis & Socinianis velificantem, quam Socinurn, adversus quem fidem Catholicam quon- dam defendit. Sic enim habet defens. fid. Cathol. de satisfact. Christi c. 1. p. 9. Forma satisfactionis Chri- sti est pœnarum pro peccatis nostris persolutio: quod districte negat Socinus. Quare hoc ipsum breviter probabimus. Hebræi ut significent id quod Latini di- cunt pœnas pendere, nullam habent phrasin magis receptam, quam hanc, ferre peccatum: cui similis & Latinorum locutio, luere delicta, hoc est, delictorum supplicia. Si quis blasphemum non indicaverit, fe- ret peccatum ipsius. Levit. 5, 1. Qui nuditatem so- roris suæ retexit, peccatum suum ferto. Levit. 20, 17. Sic expiatoriæ victimæ dicuntur portare iniqui- tates offerentium, Lev. 10, 17. Quia sanguis ipsa- rum est pro animâ humanâ, Lev. 17, 1. Neque tantum conjunctim, sed & separatim istæ voces inveniuntur sensu eodem. Sic βασάζειν τὸ κρίμα dicitur Gal. 5, 10. ferre peccata, Ezech. 18, 20. Et supervenire alicui peccatum, id est, pœna peccati, 2. Reg. 7, 9. Ea- dem plane phrasi dixit Petrus, Christum peccata nostra sursum tulisse in corpore suo in lignum 1. Pet. 2, 24. Poterat dixisse ἤνεγκε, sed quia simul signi- ficare voluit ascensum in crucem, ἀνήνεγκε, hoc est, tulit sursum eundo: quod de dicta phrasi nihil immi- nuit, sed ei addit aliquid. Itaque Syrus transtulit: por- tavit & afcendere fecit. Socinus ut vim hujus loci enervet, primo ait, ἀνήνεγκε, significare abstulit: sed contra naturam, usumque vocis. Nam nec particula ἀνά eam patitur interpretationem, nec quisquam Græcus Scriptor ita usus est ea voce. In Novo quoque Testamento nusquam occurrit eo significatu: sed aut sursum ferre significat, Luc. 24, 51. aut sursum duce- re, Matth. 17, 1. Marc. 9, 2. Et quia victimæ in lo- cum superiorem, hoc est, in aram adferebantur, ideo illa quoque dicuntur ἀναφέρεσθαι, Ebr. 7, 27. Jac. 2, 21. Unde & Christus ipse dicitur se ἀνενέγκας, Hebr. 7, 27. & nos laudes sive spiritualia sacrificia ἀναφέρειν dicimur. Hebr. 13, 15. & 1. Petr. 2, 28. Unum dunta- xat locum citat Socinus, Hebr. 9, 28. ubi vult ἀνενεγ- κεῖν ἁμαρτίας nihil aliud esse quam auferre: sed im- merito, & citra exemplum, & non id exigente loci sententia. Nam opponuntur inter se duo Christi ad ventus: prior, quo peccata nostra tulerit, alter quo venturus sit χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, hoc est, non gravatus, non oneratus ullis peccatis, sed ab iis solutus & immu- nis. Non sunt autem ista ἀντίστοιχα, esse χωρὶς ἁμαρ- τίας, & peccata auferre, sed esse χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας & peccatis oneratum esse. Unde apparet illo quoque ad Hebraeos loco ἀνενεγκεῖν esse aut sursum ferre, in crucem scilicet, ut in loco Petri (idque apposite, quia hic quoque ad sacrificia alluditur: crux autem fuit velut ara) aut simpliciter perpeti, ut apud Thucydidem κινδύνους ἀναφέρειν. Est ergo ἀναφέρειν ferre, non auferre, quod ipse Petri contextus evincit. Agitur enim non de quovis Christi beneficio, sed de summa ejus patien- tia, quæ non auferendo, sed ferendo ostenditur. Quod addit Socinus, cum hoc sensu, quo Christus di- catur tulisse peccata nostra, non satis recte cohærere, quod sequitur, ut peccatis mortui justitiæ vivamus, sine ulla causa dicitur. Manifeste enim indicat Pe- trus, Christum ita tulisse peccata nostra, ut nos simul à pœna liberaret: unde addit statim: ipsius vibice sanati estis. Optime autem hæc cohærent: si Chri- stus tam dura subiit, ut peccatorum veniam conse- queremini, sane eam adepti per fidem, à peccatis cave- re debetis in posterum. Dedit nobis Deus, ut libera- ti ex manu inimicorum nostrorum ipsi serviamus in omni sanctitate & justitia Luc. 1, 74. 75. Ecce sa- nus factus es, ne pecces posthac. Joh. 5, 14. Pretio emti estis. Glorificate ergo Deum in corpore ve- stro 1. Cor. 6, 20. Nec aliud agit Paulus cap. 7. & sequentibus ad Romanos, quam ut ostendat, summis Dei & Christi beneficiis excitari nos debere, ut sancte vivamus. Hæc Grotius, priusquam adhuc à Judæis seductus esset: Atque ista de primo argu- mento.

Alterum argumentum, quod hic unice de Christo sermo sit, præbet sinistrum judicium de pla- gis ejus, qui hic describitur. De eo enim hic agitur, qui falso credebatur propter peccata sua percussus, plagisque affectus. Id vero in Jeremiam, aut alium hominem merum nullatenus quadrat. Nemo enim est mortalium, qui si affligatur à Deo, innocens prorsus sit; omnes peccatis obnoxii sunt, ideo si affligantur, non ob aliena, sed ob propria ipsorum peccata id fieri certum est, quum id divinæ justitiæ regula requirat; solus Christus ob peccata non sua passus est, cum nostra peccata in se derivavit. 2. Cor. 5, 21. de quo Judæorum nunc judicium cum glossa Grotiana audiamus.

Vers. Eod. ET NOS REPUTAVIMUS EUM QVA- SI LEPROSUM AC PERCUSSUM A DEO ET HUMILIATUM) Vox Ebræa נגוע sumitur quidem & de leproso, sed nihil aliud per se significat, quam vox se- quens percussum. Ex hoc loco orta inter Iudæos fabula, Messiam inter leprosos morari. Sed sensus est: nos cre- dimus Ieremiam merito conjectum in carcerem & lutum, Deo illum exosum habente, ut hostem urbis & Templi, ac pseudo-Prophetam. Vid. Ierem. 26.

Messiam ergo, quem Judæi ipsi agnoscunt à Propheta hic notari, etsi fabulam istam commenti sint ad elidendam fidem Christianam, Grotius Christianus hic intelligi non admittit, sensumque talem reddit, qui solum Jeremiam referat, quod non Judaizare est, sed deteriorem esse Judæis. Ad- mittimus vocem נגוע quam Hieronymus, Symma- chus & Aquilem sequutus, leprosum reddidit, in genere notare vulneratum, vel percussum: LXX. reddidere: εἶναι αὐτὸν ἐν πόνῳ, esse ipsum in labore. Altera vox נכה à מכה אלהים necare, percutere, non percussum Deum notat, ut Bellarm. lib. 2. de verbo Dei c. 11. Andrad. Cornel. à Lap. post Gorla- tinum volunt, sed quia מכה in regimine est posi- tum, & substantivum semper in constructione præcedit adjectivum, explicari debet, percussum

Dei. Tertia וּמְעֻנֶּה & humiliatum vel afflictum tyrannide, servitute vel vi depressum designat; vi- de Psal. 102. v. 24. Psalm. 119. v. 26. Thren. 3. v. 33. Judicium ergo Judæorum hic refertur, quod pu- taverint ipsum ob delicta propria & vulneratum, & à Deo plagis percussum, summopere depressum, atque humiliatum esse, ut verba diserte docent. Cer- te langvores nostros ipse suffert, & dolores nostros ipse portat, nos vero putabamus ipsum cæsum esse & afflictum percussione Dei: cum videremus eum tam deformem, tam fœdum, tam abominabilem esse, statim venit nobis in mentem non nostrarum infirmitatum & iniquitatum, sed divinæ severita- tis erga ipsius prævaricationes. Judicabamus enim pro humanæ rationis ingenio, eum divinitus pro- pter sua ipsius delicta tam horribiliter afflictum. Sed cum rem ipsam, ut est, per Spiritum S. edocti, consideraremus, agnoscimus eum, non sua culpa, non suorum peccatorum, quorum nullum habet, meritis, sed nostra culpa & meritis nostrorum pec- catorum tam fœde lacerari, ac nostras ipsum infir- mitates sufferre.

## 53:5
Verse 5. BUT HE WAS WOUNDED FOR OUR INIQUITIES) In Hebrew: But truly he was wounded (that is, he was treated badly) by our crime. The fault was in us, not in him. Thus also what follows: he was bruised by our fault. We thought most unjustly of him, and therefore we treated him cruelly? That now appears by the things themselves. Similar things were said by the Jews who converted on the day of Pentecost and thereafter.

THE CHASTISEMENT OF OUR PEACE WAS UPON HIM) With him; that is, he brought us salutary warnings, if we had received them.

AND BY HIS STRIPE WE ARE HEALED) By his stripe (i.e., his own patience) we would have been healed: i.e., freed from impending evils, if we had had faith in his words, confirmed by such great tolerance of evils. The Hebrews cannot express the potential mood otherwise than by the indicative. Therefore, much attention must be applied to obtain the meanings.

Grotius continues in perverting the most evangelical oracle. Since he does not find Jeremiah wounded, he weakens that word, so that it denotes nothing other than treated badly. But from there the third argument against his distortion. Because, namely, he who is treated of here was not only treated badly, but was wounded vehemently, and sustained most grievous sorrows. For the word חיל denotes vehement sorrows, as Avenarius observes, in the intestines, and is generally taken for the pain of a woman in labor, see Isa. 23 v. 4, ch. 26 v. 18, Jer. 41 v. 31, etc. Kimchi says the pain is such as that of a woman in labor or one castrating himself; whence this meaning is elicited: He himself was most miserably vexed with most exquisite pains, and in the very intestines like a woman in labor, because of our transgressions, as interpreted by our Dr. Weller. The Prophet adds מְדֻכָּא HE WAS BRUISED, he is confused and broken or oppressed, for thus the word דכא is used concerning oppression to the ground, Job 6 v. 9, Lam. 3 v. 12, etc. Kimchi explains it by Ps. 143 v. 3, he has broken my life to the ground. Forster in his Commentary observes that it properly means to crush in a mortar. Such wounding, the suffering of most exquisite pains, breaking, and crushing, truly fits Christ most accurately, but not Jeremiah, as History testifies. Furthermore, he is said to be wounded מִפְּשָׁעֵינוּ for our iniquities: Bruised מֵעֲוֹנוֹתֵינוּ for our crimes. The former word from מרד signifies a sin committed knowingly and contumaciously, such as rebellion is, and פשעים according to Aben Ezra in Hos. 14 v. 3 are called those who depart from authority, who remove themselves from the authority of a legitimate Lord, and oppose themselves to him through rebellion, which they gather from Gen. 31, 36; 1 Sam. 24, 12; 1 Kings 12, 18; Isa. 2, 3; ch. 20 v. 38. Such are our sins, for which Christ was struck and wounded, inasmuch as we transgress against God the creator and our Lord, withdraw ourselves from his Dominion, nay, oppose ourselves to it. The other word עָוֺן iniquity and depravity comes from עָוָה which is properly to be bent, to be crooked; and then transferred to the mind to act iniquitously and perversely. Some refer the former word to actual sin, the latter to original. Grotius depraves it thus: But truly he was wounded by our crime, bruised by our fault, that is, we treated him so iniquitously: as if the meritorious cause, why he was so wounded and bruised here, were not expressed, but the quality and injustice of that affliction and bruising. Which distortion is most to be detested. For the preposition מִ here is to be rendered FOR, as it is taken in Deut. 7 v. 8, Ps. 12 v. 6, Ps. 39 v. 9, Isa. 1 v. 29, Obad. v. 10, Zech. 9 v. 10, and is explained by the LXX Interpreters: αὐτός δὲ ἐτραυματίσθη διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, he was wounded for our sins, μεμαλάκισται διὰ τὰς ἀνομίας ἡμῶν, he was infirm for our iniquities: as also by Jerome: he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our crimes, which meaning the whole context demands, because he bore our infirmities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him: God laid upon him all our iniquities: for the crime of the people he was struck, he laid down his soul for sin, he carried our iniquities, and bore the sins of many. Whence an invincible argument, that this chapter cannot be understood of Jeremiah according to the letter. For it treats of him according to the letter, who was wounded and struck FOR the sins of others, so that the sins were not his own, but another's, as the meritorious cause of the wounding and striking. But that which cannot be said of Jeremiah, but applies uniquely to Christ, and must be accepted uniquely concerning Him, is here. Which sense a parallel passage also confirms, Romans 4, v. 25. He was delivered for our offenses. Nor has the Christian Church hitherto accepted it otherwise: Crellius the Socinian himself, against Grotius, page 15, acknowledges that NO OTHER cause can be understood here than the impulsive procatarctic cause. Socinus confesses in his Theological Lectures, page 121, part II, on the Savior Christ, chapter 7, that it is implied that Christ was in a certain way killed by our sins, that is, that our sins were the antecedent cause of Christ's death, from which it is easy to gather (whatever the Socinian crowd may yelp) that if an antecedent efficient cause is noted, no other is understood here than the impulsive, procatarctic, or meritorious one. For our sins could not kill Christ otherwise than by meriting death, or because they were the meritorious cause of Christ's death. Add that the phrases to suffer or to die for sins, and similar ones, import the punishment and chastisement of sins, nor have the Socinians been able to prove the contrary by any example. See Lev. 26, 18. Deut. 18, 12. 1 Kings 16, 14. 2 Kings 23, v. 6. ch. 24, v. 1. Psalm 107, 17. Isaiah 7, 17. Jer. 13, 22. Lamentations 4, 13. Dan. 9, 16, etc. Wherefore this foundation of the Catholic faith concerning the satisfaction of Christ was believed to be immovable, which Grotius himself, when he was disputing against Socinus for the Catholic faith, gravely opposed to the heretic! For after he had brought forward arguments from the phrase of the Apostle, He was delivered for our sins, Romans 4, verse 25, and others, chapter 2, page 3 of the Defense of the Catholic Faith. Catholic faith, he added these things: Since also the particle מִ among the Hebrews denotes an antecedent or impulsive cause, as Psalm 38, v. 9, and often elsewhere: the passage of Isaiah 53 cannot be translated better, and more congruently with other scriptures, than he is afflicted with pain for our transgressions, he is bruised for our iniquities: but sins are the cause of punishment in no other way than by way of merit.

Nor indeed can it be shown that those words, 'on account of sins' or 'because of sins,' especially where they are joined to sufferings, are taken anywhere in the Holy Scriptures in any other way than in this meaning of merit. So much for Grotius there. But now, for the sake of a Jewish gloss on Jeremiah, he does not hesitate to overturn this distinguished bulwark of the faith himself, and to weaken completely the former defense of the faith! What of the fact that even in those annotations which he adorned in later years, having already completed the annotations to the Old Testament, he acknowledged that these things concerning Christ must be explained according to the literal sense, even though for the sake of Socinus, to whom in his final years he approached in not a few things, and to whom he conformed his own glosses, he did not refrain from ςρεβλότητι; for example, Annot. on 1 Pet. 2:23: 'Who himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree.' Ἀνήνεγκεν here is 'took away,' as the following words show, just as we noted the same word is taken in Heb. 9:28; in the same sense αἴρει ἁμαρτίαν, John 1:29, and סבל and נשא in Isa. 53:4, where the Greeks say 'he bears.' He killed our vices just as those who are fixed to a cross are accustomed to be killed. A similar manner of speaking is in Col. 2:14. See also Rom. 6:6, Gal. 2:20, 5:24; but this is a μετάληψις. For Christ did not properly take away our vices when he was crucified, but he gave the causes through which they might be taken away. For the cross of Christ is the foundation of preaching; but preaching is of repentance. Repentance, however, takes away vices, ἐν τῷ σώματι ἀυτῦ, 'with his body.' In a locution such as is in Matt. 6:29, Rom. 15:29, Eph. 5:1-2, and elsewhere. Just as his body was driven onto the cross, so also our life is as it were driven onto the cross. Particles signifying a likeness are often omitted, and thus the speech becomes more effective. So much for Grotius there.

Now who will endure that distortion of the golden sentence of the Prophet: 'THE DISCIPLINE OF OUR PEACE WAS UPON HIM'? Or 'with him,' that is, he brought us salutary things, if we have received them. From an absolute statement he makes a hypothetical one; from discipline, doctrine, mere information, or admonition. For the word מוסר denotes punishment and chastisement, which is certain from the perpetual use of the word: whence not even the Socinians deny that it brings about the same affliction, inasmuch as they only deny that that affliction is penal and has the nature of a punishment; see Socinus in Praelect. ch. 31, p. 133, and Crellius against Grot. p. 67. Therefore a distinction is made between תוכחת, rebuke or correction, and מוסר, chastisement; the former is done with words and arguments, Prov. 12:1, ch. 6:23, but the latter implies real discipline and affliction, Job 5:17, Prov. 13:24, Jer. 30:18, etc. Just as also from this word descend מאסרים, bonds and thongs of chastisement. Thus that word is used concerning the punishment of the Egyptians, Deut. 11:2, and concerning divine punishments, Ps. 39:12. Which sense the word PEACE also confirms: because it is called the chastisement of peace, because through that very chastisement peace and immunity from punishment were acquired for us, just as it is called the chastisement of intelligence in Prov. 1:3, which is done for the sake of intelligence. Since, therefore, our peace is composed by his chastisement, and he himself is said to be chastised so that there might be peace for us, it is most manifest that it does not designate doctrine and warnings brought by this subject, but punishment and torments endured by him of whom the discourse is. And thus both ancient and more recent interpreters have rendered it. Among them, Jerome in the Latin Church handed down this paraphrase: 'What we ought to have sustained for our crimes, he suffered for us, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether those things which are on earth or those which are in heaven.' From these, Blessed Luther is especially to be heard: 'He himself was chastised so that we might have peace, that is, the remission of sins and a quieted conscience. If, therefore, we wish to have peace, it is necessary that it be done through his discipline. He by merit ought to have had peace, and we the punishments of our sins, but here all things are inverted: another sins, and another is punished.' Zwingli agrees, and Alexander Morus proves that opinion more broadly in his Notes and Diatribes on this chapter, among other things urging on p. 53 the particle על. It is plain here that שלום is opposed to war or enmity and hatred, as often elsewhere. Which the preposition על added confirms. For it is most apt for designating a surety: as in Jud. 19:20, in the tragic history of that concubine. 'And that old man said: Peace be to thee: all thy lack be עלי upon me,' that is, I constitute myself a debtor, and I bind myself to provide all necessary things. Paral. 24. upon this age, that is, upon Israel: that is, it is incumbent upon him as a debt to offer sacrifices, and he is held to this by an everlasting obligation. Thus Gen. 27. v. 15. upon me be thy curse, that is, I shall pay for you. As in the Gospel: his hand upon me; so here our chastisement upon him. I pass over that Sanctius explains the word שלום as retribution, explaining it thus: The discipline of our retribution upon him, that is, the punishment which we ought to have rendered and paid back for our sins, God has laid upon him; that is, whatever penalties God ought to have exacted from us for our sins, the Father exacted that from the innocent Son. Paul seems to have alluded to this reading in Colossians ch. 2. Forgiving you all trespasses, blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us; and he took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. The handwriting is the same as a debt, or retribution, that is, what divine law compelled one to pay for sins. But to nail it to the cross is nothing other than to have placed it upon himself. Therefore, from these words, Catholics have demonstrated satisfaction against the Socinians. Which argument Grotius also holds as solid in his Defensio Fidei Catholicae, p. 15. There had preceded in the same Prophet, 'the chastisement of our peace is laid upon him, and by his stripe healing is made for us.' In the Hebrew, chastisement is called מוסר, which word does not signify affliction of any kind, but that which has the nature of a punishment, whether it be παραδειγματικὴ or only νουθετικὴ, by which words Taurus the Philosopher once conveniently distinguished the kinds of punishments. And from there it happened that any νουθεσία was signified by the word musar by catachresis. But since the meaning of νουθεσίας has no place in Christ, especially when it concerns afflictions that include death, it remains that we understand an affliction which has a παράδειγμα joined to it. For it is not possible to find a use of that Hebrew word set apart from any consideration of guilt. It is true that the name of peace among the Hebrews signifies any good whatsoever, but if we understand here from the subject matter the good of impunity, it will appear that the punishment of Christ and our impunity are most excellently opposed to one another: although nothing prevents reconciliation from being understood by the name of peace, even with no mention made of enmity, which the matter itself and the following words of the Prophet sufficiently indicate had preceded. For neither did the Angels make mention of enmity when they proclaimed that peace was to come upon the earth, Luke 2:14, nor did the Apostle when he said that we have peace with God, Rom. 5:1. ἐκ τῆς πληγῆς αἱματώδης τύπος. Therefore πληγὴ μαστίγας is said to make μώλωπας, Sir. 28:18. The Syrian translated it as 'by his spots': because his whole body was sprinkled and stained with the blood of the wounds! What of the fact that the Jews also acknowledged this? R. Solomon Jarchi rendered it here: 'let the chastisements of peace come upon him, which was for us': because he himself was chastised, so that there might be peace for the whole world.

This argument is strengthened from those things which are subjoined for the sake of explanation by the Prophet, 'and by his stripes we are healed.' For the meaning of these words here is that he himself was affected by the bruising of a wound from clotted blood, so that we might be healed from our wounds. That this is the Prophet's meaning, lest we should by chance doubt, the Holy Spirit himself has handed down at 1 Pet. 2:24. For from this passage it is certain that these things are to be understood not of Jeremiah, but of Christ, and that they concern not only the Jews, but the whole human race, that is, the Gentiles equally as well as the Jews, because this Epistle of Peter was written to the Gentiles converted to Christ, of whom Peter says: By his (Christ's) wounds you have been healed. For since the LXX rendered it τῷ μώλωπι αὐτõ ἡμεῖς ἰάθημεν, Saint Peter makes the application to the Gentiles by merely changing the person: ᾧ τῷ μώλωπι αὐτõ ἰάθητε. Μώλωψ is a swelling rising from a blow, or the mark of a blow on the skin. Therefore, the perversity of Grotius is to be detested, who twists it to Jeremiah and attaches to them a meaning that is clearly different. By his bruising, that is, by his patience, we would have been healed, that is, freed from the evils hanging over us, if we had had faith in his words. What Peter says of Christ, Grotius says of Jeremiah; what the former says of the passion of Christ and the μώλωψ, that is, a blow of such a kind on the skin as has been bruised by the striking of lashes, the latter says of the patience of Jeremiah: what the former says of healing procured for us through Christ, the latter says of a possible liberation from evils hanging over us: what the former takes absolutely and in the indicative mood, the latter takes hypothetically and in the potential mood: if this is not perverting the text, what then will it be? A great deal of attention, indeed a great deal of twisting, is needed to elicit such a meaning, which hardly came into the mind of any of the Jews, whom the judgment of God blinded and delivered over to a perverse mind. But Grotius was, without doubt, convinced by the force of truth when he arrived at his annotations on the Petrine passage: whence he acknowledged, not obscurely, that the word expressly spoken by Isaiah is to be understood not of Jeremiah, but of Christ, and that the bruising does not denote patience, but passion. For after he had noted that these words were taken from Isa. 53:5, he added: חבורה, which is translated μώλωψ, properly signifies a bruise from a contusion, but figuratively it is taken for any pain whatsoever, as Gen. 5:22, Exod. 21:26, Ps. 38, Isa. 50:1, Prov. 20:19, Sir. 23:11, ch. 28:21, Judith 9:13. In many ways, indeed, the pains of Christ have healed us from vices, but here the example is especially regarded which he gave us of obedience, patience, and gentleness of love in the midst of pains, as the preceding things show: This is false, which Grotius added in favor of the Socinians, that the example is especially regarded here. For he himself previously taught against Socinus that the passion of Christ is regarded here as merit and satisfaction. Nor did Peter exhort only to patience, but to righteousness, so that, having been made far from sins, we might live to righteousness, and he sought arguments not only from the example of Christ, but especially from his merit and the benefit of conversion. For since Christ himself, in the manner of servants, willed to be beaten with lashes for our sake, why should we not endure blows and lashes if they are inflicted by harsh masters? Since he himself willed to be affected by blows so that we might be healed from the wounds of the soul, we must certainly live not to the sins by which the wounds of the soul and the blows themselves were procured, but to righteousness; because he was wounded and died not only for the expiation of sins, but also so that he might mortify sin in us. Let us live to him, says Ambrose in 2 Cor. 5, who did not spare his own Son, so that he might crucify our passions in his body. For Christ died for us, so that we might die in his revived body. Therefore, it is not our life that died in him, but our guilt. Meanwhile, Grotius ought to have acknowledged here that these things treat of the bloody passion of Christ, not of the patience of Jeremiah. Blessed Luther says beautifully on these words: It is a most joyful consolation, his bruises are our plaster: But we had deserved the bruises, and health was owed to him. If anyone, therefore, desires health, let him not consider his own chastisement and cross, but let him only look to Christ and believe, then he will be healed, that is, he will have eternal righteousness. Which were also the pious meditations of the pious Tauler, Meditations on the Life of Christ, ch. 8: so that we might live, it was necessary for him to die; so that we might be gladdened, he was saddened; so that we might be healed, he was wounded; so that we might be cleansed, he shed his blood. The blood of the Physician was shed, and it became the medicine of the sick man. Nor does Cornelius a Lapide speak badly: By his bruising we are healed. Vatablus translates, and in his bruising we have been medicated. This is the precious medicine, which Christ prepared not from the juices of herbs, not from the fat of beasts, not from another's body and blood, but from his own. He stored this medicine in the Holy Sacraments instituted by himself, for whence do the Sacraments have the power of justifying and healing the diseases of the soul? Namely, from the bruising, blood, and wounds of Christ. They follow in this the ancient faith of the Church: which Cyril expressed in this place. Formerly we were at variance with God through hatred and enmity, resisting his most holy laws, and not subject to the yoke of obedience, and refusing to serve him. But it was necessary, he says, that we, who had fallen into such audacity, should be chastised with a blow, so that, receding from vices, we might dissolve the enmity and enter into peace with God by submitting our neck to him and doing that which pleases him. But this discipline, he says, which was to be inflicted rather upon those sinning, so that they might cease to wage war against GOD, fell upon him. And that, I think, is: The discipline of our peace was upon him. But he explains the meaning of these words more plainly, immediately subjoining: By his bruising we are healed. For he suffered, as I said, for us. Thus far Cyril.

Latin:

Vers. 5. IPSE AUTEM VULNERATUS EST PRO- PTER INIQVITATES NOSTRAS) In Hebræo: At ve- ro ipse vulneratus (id est, male tractatus est) nostro crimine. In nobis culpa fuit, non in ipso. Sic & quod sequitur: attri- tus est per nostram culpam. Iniquissima de eo sensimus, & propterea crudeliter eum tractavimus? id nunc rebus ipsis apparet. Similia dixerunt Judæi, qui se converterunt die Pentecostes & deinceps.

DISCIPLINA PACIS NOSTRÆ SUPER EUM) Apud eum; id est, monita nobis attulit salutaria, si ea rece- piffimus.

ET LIVORE EJUS SANATI SUMUS) Livore ejus, (i.e. ipsius patientia) nos sanati fuissemus: i.e. liberati ab im- pendentibus malis, si verbis ipsius, tanta malorum tolerantia confirmatis, habuissemus fidem. Hebræi potentialem mo- dum aliter, quam per indicativum exprimere nequeunt. Ideo multa adhibenda attentio ad consequendos sensus.

Pergit Grotius in pervertendo εὐαγγελικωτάτῳ oraculo. Quum Jeremiam non in veniat vulnera- tum, verbum illud enervat, ut nihil aliud notet, quam male tractatum. Inde vero tertium argu- mentum contra πρεβλότητα ejus. Quia sc. is, de quo hic agitur, non solum male tractatus, sed vulnera- tus fuit vehementer, doloresque gravissimos su- stinuit. Nam vox חיל dolores notat vehementes, observante Avenario, in intestinis, & plerumque accipitur de dolore parturientis, vide Esa. 23. v. 4. cap. 26. v. 18. Jerem. 41. v. 31. &c. Kimchi dicit, do- lorem esse, qualis est parturientis aut castrantis se; unde sensus hic eruitur: Ipse vero exquisitissimis do- loribus, & in intestinis ipsis instar parturientis mi- serrime propter prævaricationes nostras divexatus fuit, interprete Dn. D. Wellero nostro. Addit Pro- pheta מְדֻכָּא ATTRITUS EST, confusus est & confractus vel oppressus, sic enim usurpatur verbum דכא de oppressione ad terram Job. 6. v. 9. Thren. 3. vers. 12. &c. Kimchi explicat per Psalm. 143. v. 3. confregit ad terram vitam meam. Forster. in Com- mentar. observat, quod proprie sit contundere in mortario. Qualis vulneratio, dolorum exquisitissi- morum perpessio, confractio & contusio Christo qui- dem verissime convenit, non autem Jeremiæ, teste Historia. Porro vulneratus ille dicitur מִפְּשָׁעֵינוּ pro- pter iniquitates nostras: Attritus מֵעֲוֹנוֹתֵינוּ propter scelera nostra. Vox prior à מרד significat peccatum scienter & contumaciter admissum, quale rebellio est, & פשעים juxta Aben Ezram in Hos. 14. v. 3. di- cuntur illi, qui egrediuntur è potestate, qui è potestate legitimi Domini se eximunt, eique se opponunt per re- bellionem, quod è Gen 31, 36. 1. Sam. 24, 12. 1. Reg. 12, 18. Esa. 2, 3. cap. 20. v. 38. colligunt. Talia peccata sunt nostra, ob quæ Christus percussus & vulnera- tus fuit, siquidem contra Deum creatorem & Do- minum nostrum prævaricemur, ejus Dominio nos subducamus, imo opponamus. Altera vox עָוֺן ini- quitas & pravitas ab עָוָה quod proprie est incur- vari, curvum esse; ac deinde ad animum transla- tum inique ac perverse agere. Nonnulli priorem vocem ad peccatum actuale, posteriorem ad origi- nale referunt. Grotius ita depravat: At vero ipse vulneratus est nostro crimine, attritus est per no- stram culpam, id est, inique ipsum ita tractavimus: quasi non causa meritoria, cur hic ita vulneratus, & attritus fuerit, exprimeretur, sed qualitas & inju- stitia afflictionis & attritionis istius. Quæ vero στρεβλότης est maxime detestanda. Nam præpositio מִ hic reddenda est PROPTER, uti accipitur Deut. 7. v. 8. Psal. 12. v. 6. Psal. 39. v. 9. Esa. 1. v. 29. Obad. v. 10, Zach. 9. v. 10. & exponitur à LXX. Interpp. αὐτός δὲ ἐτραυματίσθη διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, ipse vulneratus est propter peccata nostra, μεμαλά- κισται διὰ τὰς ἀνομίας ἡμῶν, infirmatus est propter iniquitates nostras: ut & ab Hieronymo: ipse vul- neratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra, quem sensum esse postulat totus contextus, quia langvores nostros tulit: disci- plina pacis nostræ super eum: Deus posuit in eum omnes iniquitates nostras: propter scelus populi per- cussus est, animam posuit pro peccato, iniquitates nostras portavit, & peccata multorum tulit. Unde invictum argumentum, non posse hoc caput de Je- remia secundum literam intelligi. De eo enim agit quoad literam, qui PROPTER peccata aliorum vulneratus & percussus est, ita ut peccata non pro- pria, sed aliena, causa fuerint meritoria vulneratio- nis & percussionis. Quod vero de Jeremia dici ne- quit, sed unice in Christum convenit, deque eo unice accipiendum hic est. Quem sensum etiam locus parallelus statuminat, Roman. 4. v. 25. Tra- ditus est propter, delicta nostra. Nec aliter acce- pit hactenus Christiana Ecclesia: Crellius ipse So- cinianus contra Grotium pag. 15. agnoscit, NUL- LAM ALIAM intelligi hic posse causam, quam im- pulsivam procatarcticam. Socinus fatetur prælect. Theolog. pag. 121. part. II. de Servat. Christo cap. 7. id innui, Christum à peccatis nostris quodam- modo occisum esse, id est, peccata nostra Christi mor- tis antecedentem causam fuisse, unde promtum est colligere, (quicquid etiam ogganniat Sociniana turba) si notatur causa efficiens antecedens, aliam nullam hic intelligi quam impulsivam, procatar- cticam vel meritoriam. Non enim aliter peccata nostra Christum occidere poterant, quam mor- tem promerendo, vel quod causa meritoria fue- rint mortis Christi. Adde quod phrases pati, vel mori propter peccata, ac similes, peccatorum supplicium & punitionem importent, neque ullo exemplo contrarium probare potuere Sociniani. Vide Lev. 26, 18. Deut. 18, 12. 1. Reg. 16, 14. 2. Reg. 23. v. 6. c. 24. v. 1. Psal. 107, 17. Esa. 7, 17. Jer. 13, 22. Thren. 4, 13. Dan. 9, 16. &c. Quapropter immo- tum creditum fuit hoc fidei Catholicæ de satis- factione Christi fundamentum, quod Grotius ipse, cum adversus Socinum disputaret, pro fide Catholica, graviter hæretico opposuit! Post- quam enim è phrasi Apostoli, traditus est propter peccata nostra. Roman. 4. vers. 2. & aliis argumen- ta adduxisset cap. 2. pag 3. Defens. Fid. Cathol. hæc subjunxit: Quum & particula מִ apud Ebræos cau- sam antecedentem sive impulsivam denotet, ut Psal. 38. v. 9. & alibi sæpe: locus Esa. 53. melius, & scri- pturis aliis congruentius transferri non potest, quam dolore afficitur ob defectiones nostras, atteri- tur ob iniquitates nostras: peccata autem pœnæ causa sunt non aliter, quam per modum meriti.

Neque vero oftendi poterit, voces iftas, ob pec- cata, vel propter peccata, præsertim ubi perpessioni- bus junguntur, aliter sumi usquam in sacris literis, quam in hoc meriti significatu. Hæc ibi Grotius. Nunc vero in gratiam glossæ Judaicæ de Jeremia, insigne hoc fidei propugnaculum ipse evertere, pristinamque fidei defensionem penitus enervare non dubitat! Quid quod in annotatis etiam illis, quæ posterioribus annis adornavit, absolutis jam annotatis ad Vetus Testamentum, hæc de Christo secundum literalem sensum explicanda esse agno- verit, etsi in gratiam Socini, cui annis extremis in non paucis appropinquavit, & glossemata sua con- formavit, à ςρεβλότητι sibi non temperarit; puta Annot. ad 1.Pet. 2,23. Ὅς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν ἀυτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν ἐν τῷ σώματι ἀυτῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον. Ἀνήνεγ- κεν hic est abstulit, quod sequentia ostendunt, quomodo idem verbum sumi notavimus Ebr. 9, 28. eodem sensu αἴρει ἁμαρτίαν, Joh. 1, 29. & סבל & נשא Esa. 60, 4. ubi Græci Φέρε. Vitia nostra ita interfecit, sicut qui cruci affiguntur, interfici solent. Simile loquendi ge- nus Coloss. 2, 14. Vide & Rom. 6, 6. Gal. 2, 20. 5, 24. est autem hic μετάληψις. Non enim proprie Christus, cum crucifigeretur, vitia nostra abstulit, sed causas dedit, per quas auferrentur. Nam crux Christi fun- damentum est prædicationis; prædicatio vero pœni- tentiæ. Pœnitentia vero aufert vitia, ἐν τῷ σῶματι ἀυτῦ cum corpore suo. Locutione, qualis est Matth. 6. v. 29. Rom. 15. v. 29. Eph. 5. v. 1. 2. & alibi. Sicut corpus ejus in crucem actum est, ita & vita nostra quasi in crucem acta. Particulæ similitudinem signi- ficantes sæpe subticentur, sitque sic oratio efficacior. Hæc ibi Grotius.

Jam quis feret illam detorsionem sententiæ Prophetæ aureæ: DISCIPLINA PACIS NO- STRÆ SUPRA EUM. Vel apud eum, id est, no- bis attulit salutaria, si ea recepissimus. Ex absoluta facit hypotheticam, è disciplina doctrinam, meram informationem, vel admonitionem. Vox enim מוסר pœnam & castigationem notat, quod ex per- petuo vocis usu certum: unde ne Sociniani quidem negant eandem afflictionem inferre, utpote qui inficiantur solum, eam afflictionem pœnalem esse, & pœnæ rationem habere, vide Socin. in prælect. cap. 31. p. 133. & Crellius contra Grot. p. 67. Ideo distingui- tur inter תוכחת increpationem, correptionem, & מוסר castigationem; illa fit verbis & argumentis, Prov. 12. v. 1. cap. 6. v. 23. hæc vero realem discipli- nam, & afflictionem importat Job. 5. v. 17. Prov. 13. v. 24. Jer. 30. v. 18. &c. Quemadmodum etiam ab hac voce descendunt מאסרים vincula & lora ca- stigationis. Sic usurpatur vox ista de pœna Ægyptio- rum, Deut. 11. v. 2. de suppliciis divinis, Psal. 39. v. 12. Quem sensum etiam confirmat vox PACIS: quia castigatio pacis dicitur, quod per eam ipsius casti- gationem nobis pax, & immunitas à pœna acqui- sita sit, uti castigatio intelligentiæ dicitur Prov. 1. v. 3. quæ fit ob intelligentiam. Quum ergo pax nostra componatur ipsius castigatione; & castigatus di- catur ipse, ut nobis pax esset, manifestissimum est, non doctrinam, & monita ab hoc subjecto allata, sed pœnam & supplicia ab illo, de quo sermo est, exantlata designari. Atque ita reddidere cum ve- teres, tum recentiores Interpretes. Ex illis Hiero- nymus in Ecclesia Latina hanc paraphrasin tradidit: Quod nos pro nostris debebamus sceleribus sustinere, ille pro nobis passus est, pacificans per sanguinem cru- cis suæ, sive quæ in terris, sive quæ in cælis sint. Ex hisce B. Lutherus inprimis audiendus: Castigatus ipse est, ut nos haberemus pacem, id est, remissionem peccatorum & conscientiam sedatam. Si igitur ha- bere pacem volumus, necesse est, id fieri per discipli- nam ipsius. Ipse merito pacem, nos nostrorum pec- catorum pœnas habere debebamus, sed sunt hic in- versa omnia: Alius peccat, & alius plectitur. Con- sentit Zwinglius, ac latius eam sententiam probat Alexand. Morus in Notis & Diatr. ad hoc cap. in- ter alia urgens p. 53. particulam על. Planum est hic שלום opponi bello sive inimicitiæ ac odio, ut sæpe ali- bi. Quod præpositio על adjecta confirmat. Aptissima enim est designandæ fidejussioni: ut Jud. 19. v. 20. in historia tragica concubinæ illius. Et dixit vir ille se- nex: Pax esto tibi: omnis defectus tuus עלי super me, id est, ego me constituo debitorem, ac me obligo ad præbendum omnia necessaria. Sic 2. Paral. 24. in sæculum hoc est super Israëlem: hoc est, ei incumbit quasi debitum sacrificia offerendi, & ad id obligatio- ne tenetur sempiterna. Sic Gen. 27. v. 15. super me maledictio tua, id est, ego pro te luam. Ut in Evan- gelio: manus ejus super me; ita hic castigatio nostra super eum. Taceo quod Sanctius vocem שלום exponat retributionem, sic explicans: Disciplina retributionis nostræ super eum, id est, supplicium, quod nos retribuere, ac rependere debuimus pro peccatis nostris, super eum imposuit Deus; id est, quicquid pœnarum Deus à nobis exigere de- buit pro peccatis, id ab innocenti filio pater exe- git. Ad hanc lectionem allusisse videtur Paulus ad Coloss. cap. 2. Donans vobis omnia delicta, delens quod adversum nos erat Chirographum decreti, quod erat contrarium nobis; & ipsum tulit de me- dio, affigens illud cruci. Chirographum idem est quod debitum, seu retributio, id est, quod pro peccatis exolvere jus cogebat divinum. Affigere autem illud cruci, nihil aliud est, quam posuisse super se. Ideo ex hisce verbis satisfactionem adversus Socinianos demonstrarunt Catholici. Quod argumentum etiam pro solido habet Grotius in defens. fid. Cal- thol. p. 15. Præcesserat apud eundem Prophetam, ca- stigatio pacis nostræ imponitur ei, & livore ejus fit curatio nobis. In Hebræo castigatio dicitur מוסר quæ vox afflictionem non qualemcunque significat, sed eam, quæ pœnæ habeat rationem, sive sit παραδειγ- ματικὴ sive νουθετικὴ tantum, quibus vocabulis com- mode pœnarum genera olim distinxit Taurus Philo- sophus. Atque inde factum, ut quælibet νουθεσία voce mufar per κατάχρησιν significaretur. Cum vero νουθε- σίας significatio in Christo locum non habeat, præser- tim cum de afflictionibus agatur, mortem includen- tibus, restat afflictionem intelligamus, quæ conjun- ctum habeat παράδειγμα. Nam ab omni culpæ re- spectu sepositum vocis istius Ebrææ usum non est re- perire. Verum est, pacis nomine apud Ebræos bonum qualecunque significare sed: hic si ex subjecta materia intelligamus bonum impunitatis, apparebit inter se optime opponi punitionem Christi, & impunitatem nostram: quanquam nihil vetat pacis nomine re- conciliationem intelligi, etiam nulla facta inimicitiæ mentione, quam præcessisse res ipsa & sequentia Prophetæ verba satis indicant. Nam nec inimicitiæ mentionem fecerunt Angeli, cum pacem super ter- ram promulgarunt venturam, Luc. 2. v. 14. nec Apo- stolus, cum pacem nos dixit habere apud Deum, Rom. 5. v. 1. ἐκ τῆς πληγῆς αἱματώδης τύπος. Ideo πληγὴ μαστίγας dicitur facere μώλωπας, Syr. 28, 18. Sy- rus exposuit maculis ejus: quia sanguine plaga- rum corpus ejus totum conspersum & commacu- latum fuit! Quid quod Judæi etiam id agnoverint. R. Salomo Jarchi hic reddidit: veniant super eum castigationes pacis, quæ fuit nobis: quia ipse castiga- tus fuit, ut esset pax omni mundo.

Roboratur hoc argumentum ex iis, quæ ἐξη- γήσεως ἕνεκα subjunguntur penes Prophetam, & livore ejus sanati sumus. Horum enim verborum hic sensus est, ipsum livore plagæ ex sanguine concreto affectum, ut nos à vulneribus nostris sanaremur. Quam Prophetæ mentem esse, ne forte ambigere- mus, tradidit eam ipse Spiritus S. 1. Pet. 2. v. 14. Ex hoc enim loco constat, non de Jeremia, sed Christo hæc intelligenda esse, nec tantum Judæos illa con- cernere, sed totum genus humanum, hoc est, gentes pariter atque Judæos, quia hæc Epistola Petri scripta est ad gentes conversas ad Christum, de quibus Pe- trus: Per ipsius (Christi) vulnera vos sanati estis. Quum enim LXX. reddiderint τῷ μώλωπι αὐτõ ἡμεῖς ἰά- θημεν, mutata tantum persona applicationem facit ad gentes S. Petrus: ᾧ τῷ λώλωπι αὐτõ ἰάθητε. Μώ- λωψ est tumor ex plaga surgens, vel vestigium pla- gæ in cute. Detestanda itaque ςρεβλότης Grotii, qui ad Jeremiam detorquet, & sensum plane alium iis affingit. Livore ejus, id est, ipsius patientia nos sana- ti fuissemus, id est, liberati ab impendentibus ma- lis, si verbis ipsius habuissemus fidem. Quæ de Christo Petrus, de Jeremia Grotius; quæ ille de passione Christi & μώλωπι, hoc est, plaga ejusmodi cutis, quæ ex verberum incussione sugillata sit, hic de pa- tientia Jeremiæ: quæ ille de sanatione per Christum nobis conciliata, hic de possibili liberatione ab im- pendentibus malis: quæ ille absolute & in modo in- dicativo, hic hypothetice & in modo potentiali accipit: quod si non est textum pervertere, quid tandem erit? Multa omnino attentione, imo multa detor- sione opus ad eruendum ejusmodi sensum, qui vix Judæorum ulli in mentem venit, quos judicium Dei excæcavit, & in sensum perversum tradidit. Sed convictus, sine dubio, vi veritatis fuit Gro- tius, cum in annotatis suis ad locum Petrinum per- venit: unde ῥητῶς dictum Esaiæ non de Jeremia, sed de Christo intelligendum esse, neque livorem patientiam notare, sed passionem, haud obscure agnovit. Postquam enim notasset, verba hæc ex Esa. 53. v. 5. sumpta esse, addidit. חבורה quod μώλωψ vertitur, proprie livorem ex contusione significat, at figurate pro quovis dolore sumitur, ut Gen. 5. v. 22. Exod. 21, 26. Psal. 38. Esa. 50, 1. Prov. 20. v. 19. Syr. 23, 11. cap. 28, 21. Judith. 9, 13. Multis quidem modis Christi dolores nos à vitiis sanarunt, sed hic maxi- me respicitur exemplum, quod nobis dedit obedien- tiæ, patientiæ, mansuetudinis dilectionis in mediis doloribus, ut antecedentia ostendunt: Falsum hoc est, quod in gratiam Socinianorum attexit Gro- tius, quod exemplum hic maxime respiciatur. Nam passionem Christi hic ut meritum & satisfactionem respici, adversus Socinum ipse antea docuit. Ne- que tantum ad patientiam, sed ad justitiam, ut lon- ge facti à peccatis justitiæ vivamus, hortatus est Petrus, nec ab exemplo solum Christi, sed maxime à merito & conversionis beneficio argumenta petiit. Quum enim Christus ipse servorum more propter nos flagris cædi voluerit, quidni sustineremus plagas & verbera, si à dominis duris inferantur? quum ipse plagis affici voluerit, ut nos sanaremur à vulne- ribus animæ, utique non peccatis, quibus animæ vulnera, & ipsi plagæ conciliatæ, vivendum, sed justitiæ; quia non solum ob peccatorum expiatio- nem vulneratus, & mortuus, sed etiam ut pecca- tum in nobis mortificaret. Vivamus ei, inquit Am- brosius in 2. Cor. 5. qui proprio Filio non pepercit, ut in illius corpore nostras crucigeret passiones. Pro nobis enim mortuus est Christus, ut nos in illius cor- pore redivivo moreremur. Mortua est ergo in illo non vita nostra, sed culpa. Interim agnoscere de- buit hic Grotius, hæc de passione Christi cruenta, non de patientia Jeremiæ agere. Pulchre B. Lu- therus ad hæc verba: Est jucundissima consolatio, livores ipsius sunt nostrum emplastrum: Atqui nos meriti eramus livores, & ipsi debebatur sanitas. Si quis ergo sanitatem optat, ille non suam castigatio- nem & crucem consideret, sed tantum respiciat in Christum & credat, tum sanabitur, hoc est, habebit justitiam æternam. Quæ etiam pia meletemata fu- ere pii Tauleri meditat. vit. Christi cap. 8. ut nos vi- veremus, ipsum mori oportuit; ut nos exhilararemur, ipse tristatus est; ut nos sanaremur, ipse vulneratus est; ut nos mundaremur, ipse fudit sanguinem. Fu- sus est sanguis Medici, & factum est medicamen- tum ægroti. Nec male Cornelius a Lap. Livore ejus sanati sumus. Vatablus vertit, & in livore ejus nobis medicatum est. Hoc est pretiosum pharma- cum, quod non ex herbarum succis, non ex adipe be- stiarum, non ex alieno corpore & sanguine, sed ex proprio confecit Christus. Hoc pharmacum in S. Sa- cramentis a se institutis recondidit, unde enim Sa- cramenta habent vim justificandi, sanandique animæ morbos, scilicet ex livore, sanguine & vulneribus Christi. Sequuntur in eo antiquam Ecclesiæ fidem: quam expressit Cyrillus in h. l. Olim odiis & simul- tate a Deo dissidebamus, sacrosanctis ejus repugnan- tes legibus, & obedientia jugo non subjecti, ac ei servi- re renuentes. Sed erat, inquit, necesse, verbere ca- stigari nos, qui eo audaciæ prolapsi eramus, ut a vi- tiis recedentes, inimicitiam dirimeremus, pacemque cum Deo iniremus, submittendo ei cervicem, & id, quod ei placet, efficiendo. Sed hæc, inquit, discipli- na, quæ inferenda erat potius peccantibus, ut DEO bellum inferre desinerent, in ipsum devenit. Idque, opi- nor, est: Disciplinæ pacis nostræ super eum. Sed planius horum verborum sensum exponit, mox sub- jungens: Livore ejus nos sanati sumus. Passus enim est, ut dixi, pro nobis. Hactenus Cyrillus.

## 53:6
Vers. 6. ALL WE LIKE SHEEP HAVE GONE ASTRAY) We have gone astray now from the times of Manasseh. EVERYONE HAS TURNED TO HIS OWN WAY) Some to one idol, others to another. AND THE LORD HAS LAID ON HIM THE INIQUITY OF US ALL) God permitted that he should suffer most unworthy things because of our grave crime.

Latin:

Vers. 6. OMNES NOS QVASI OVES ERRAVI- MVS) Erravimus jam a Manassis temporibus. VNVSQVISQVE IN VIAM SVAM DECLI- NAVIT) Alii ad alia idola. ET POSVIT DOMINVS IN EO INIQVITA- TEM OMNIVM NOSTRVM) Permisit Deus, ut ille nostro gravi crimine indignissima pateretur.

## 53:7
Ver. 7. HE WAS OFFERED BECAUSE HE HIMSELF WILLED IT, AND HE OPENED NOT HIS MOUTH) In the Hebrew: He was oppressed and afflicted and he opened not his mouth. The LXX express the sense well: κ' αυτός διὰ τὸ κεκακῶσθαι ἐκ ἤνοιξεν τὸ ςόμα ἀυτᾶ. Even then, when he was being driven into prison and into a muddy place, he did or said nothing angrily. The Chaldean strangely inverts all these things, so that he may depict for us a Messiah such as the Jews desire. AS A SHEEP) A sheep is a most gentle animal. AND AS A LAMB) With which Jeremiah himself compares himself in chapter 11, 18.

Again a most unworthy and truly diabolical perversion of a most illustrious passage, one filled with life-giving consolation. For whose work is it, if not the Devil's, to obstruct the fountains of life-giving consolation? Whose, if not the Devil's, to weaken the Evangelical Oracles, which are spirit and life to us, and to deprive them of all the juice of saving refreshment? If the Chaldean strangely inverts it, so that he may depict a Jewish Messiah, Grotius no less strangely perverts it, so that he may exclude the Christian Messiah from this most noble passage. For he does not say a single word here about our Messiah: indeed, he perverts the text for that reason, so that it no longer fits the Messiah in any way. For those words which speak of the passion of Jeremiah from the intention of the Holy Spirit, which he sustained on account of the idolatry of the Jewish people, frequented from the times of Manasseh, those cannot, from the intention of the Holy Spirit, treat of Christ, who suffered for the sin of the human race. And since from the very evidence of the words, which in these and other verses are so clear that they could not be clearer, and also from the Apostolic interpretation, it is absolutely certain and ἀμετακίνητον [unshakable] that it treats of our sins cast upon him, the gloss concerning Jeremiah, who suffered most unworthily on account of the crime of idolatry of the Jewish people, is in no way to be tolerated; nor can it with the truth of historical, or even with divine justice, be in any way reconciled, that Jeremiah suffered for the crime of the people. For God either inflicted those sufferings upon him himself, or at least permitted them. A bare permission cannot be understood, because the Prophet says, the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. But that God himself inflicted them is repugnant to His justice. Furthermore, how did Jeremiah suffer most unworthy things because of the grave crime of the people? Is it so that this was the meritorious cause of the Prophet's sufferings, for which he was afflicted by God, or does it pertain to the efficient cause inflicting the sufferings upon him, that the Jews wickedly and with grave crime afflicted him? The former cannot be maintained, because for God to have afflicted the Prophet for another's fault does not accord with the rule of divine justice. Although the latter may be true, it is nevertheless irrelevant: because sins are introduced here as the meritorious cause of the passion, but the manner is not determined, whether he was afflicted wickedly or unjustly, or indeed justly? Nay, since the iniquities were placed upon this subject by God, it could not have been done unjustly, but it was done most justly. Finally, what is there in this text that restricts the error of the sheep to the times of Manasseh, or to the idolatry of the Jews? Nothing of the sort can be shown in this chapter. That gloss, therefore, brings something else into the text, and is thus falsely sold as the literal sense.

But lest any doubt remain that these things are to be accepted of no one else but Christ, we observe (1) that the universal corruption of the whole human race is indicated here. ALL WE like sheep have gone astray. And again: everyone has turned to his own way: and finally, He has laid the iniquity of ALL of us upon him. Who are those all? If you say they are the Jews, because they have fallen into idolatry, you are mistaken: because not ALL Jews fell abruptly into idolatry. And there was without doubt only a remnant in the people of God. For the Church could not utterly perish. And that this is to be understood not only of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles, the Petrine interpretation teaches, because 1. Pet. 2. v. 25. is explained concerning the Gentiles: nay, that the Jews and Gentiles are all understood together, that is, absolutely all men, the antecedents and consequents prove, since it is implied that he bore the sins of all men, was wounded for the iniquities of all of us, and was chastised for the sake of the peace of all of us: then the words themselves, placed universally, confirm this, which therefore are to be understood universally and without restriction. To these are added other sayings of Catholic Scripture, such as those which openly teach that all men are subject to sin, that all men have gone astray like sheep, have turned to an evil way, and that there is no distinction here, and conclude all under sin by the voice of the law, Rom. 3 and 11, Gal. 3. Whence it is easy to conclude that these things can be understood of none but Christ. Who is the Redeemer and Savior of the whole human race, after it had failed, and all had turned aside, Ps. 14, v. last. Cyril paraphrases these things thus: All we like sheep have gone astray, everyone has gone his own way, and the Lord delivered him for our sins. Therefore we have gone astray, we have fallen away from the living God, pursuing our own pleasures. But the Lord of all, that is, God and Father, delivered him for our sins, that He might absolve us from punishment, and preserve those who believe.

(2) The tacit exemption of the present subject. For since the iniquity of ALL has been placed upon this subject, it must be distinct from all those, in such a way that it is immune from iniquity. For those who are subject to iniquity, their iniquity was placed upon this subject. Since, therefore, in this transfer, or substitution, there are, so to speak, two persons, one from whom the sin was transferred, the other to whom it was transferred, and the former is the whole human race: for there is no distinction there; certainly this one must not be any one of the men subject to sin, but Christ, who is free from sin, of whom the Prophet says later, that he did no iniquity: not a mere man, perhaps from the common sort, but the God-man.

(3) The breadth of the transferred guilt. For not just some guilt, but every aberration, every turning into a wicked way, every iniquity, i.e., whatever at all has the nature of sin, is said to be transferred by the Lord onto this bearer of sin. That, indeed, can be said or understood of no one else but Christ, that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29.

(4) The truth of the transfer. As truly as we have all gone astray, as we have all turned like sheep from the path of justice, and are thus all sinners before the judgment of God, so truly have our iniquities been transferred to this bearer of sin before the divine tribunal. But how can that be said of any mere man? How can one be substituted into the place of another, and indeed an innocent one into the place of a guilty one, if the discussion is about mere men? But that our iniquities have been most truly transferred to Christ, the Mediator of God and men, that he was substituted in the most holy judgment of God into our place as guilty ones, although he was innocent, the whole Holy Scripture testifies: the just died for the unjust, 1 Pet. 3:18. If one died for all, it is the same as if we had all died, 2 Cor. 5:14.

(5) The reason for the transfer, because that transfer of iniquities was made both by reason of imputed guilt, because in the judgment of God all sins whatsoever were imputed to him, and by reason of the punishment endured, because he had to sustain the punishment in our place. For that phrase implies, the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all, as we have shown more fully in the refuted Socinianism. The Lord made them rush as if with force and impetus, made them meet him, and made them strike upon him, the iniquities of all. For פגע is to strike by meeting, to meet and strike upon someone by impelling, with a hostile mind, with the mind of destroying, Exod. 5:3, Num. 35:19, Josh. 8:21. Which, indeed, can be understood of no one else but Christ alone, who both derived our guilt and punishment upon himself, or received them imposed by the Father, bore them, and paid for them. (6) The meritorious cause of the passion. For since affliction and punishment are brought in by this phrase, the meritorious cause of that punishment is also expressed here, namely that he sustains it not by the merit of his own iniquities, but of our aberrations, deviations, and iniquities. Which indeed cannot be said of others: since no one pays for the fault of another, and is punished on account of the merit of another's sin, without his own fault: this is fitting only for Christ the Mediator and sponsor, or surety of the human race, who took upon himself our punishment along with the guilt, and was punished for the merit of our sins, having been made sin for us, when he himself knew no sin, 2 Cor. 5:21.

(7) The principal efficient cause of that translation and affliction. This is established as Jehovah; the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. But for God to have laid the iniquity of other men upon a mere man, so that he was under the necessity of paying for it, is both unheard of and contrary to divine justice. But indeed concerning Christ, with Scripture as witness, that is most true, nor is it alien to divine justice; nay, it is confessedly a great tempering of divine justice and clemency. (8) The final cause of that translation itself. Why did the Lord lay our iniquities upon him? Those things which precede concerning our error and deviation indicate this, namely that the erring sheep might be converted, and those who had each declined into his own way might be brought back into the way of the Lord: the phrase itself indicates this, which is sacrificial, so that, to wit, our iniquities having been transferred onto Him, they might be expiated, and we might be freed from iniquities. To this effect are similar passages Ps. 108, 6. 7. Isa. 34, 8. Matt. 15, 24. Luke 15, 4. And the Targum of Jonathan renders this verse, 'The Lord caused the iniquity of our whole number to strike upon Him,' thus: 'And before the Lord it was well-pleasing to remit the sins of our whole number for His sake.' Whence St. Peter points out that end thus: 'You were as sheep going astray, but are now converted to the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.'

(9) A typical foreshadowing, which was done both in other sacrifices and especially in the scapegoat (ἀποπομπαίῳ). For in it was figured what is explained here. To that, therefore, Isaiah looks, as the phrase itself teaches. As, therefore, the sins and iniquities of all were laid upon that goat, that they might be expiated, typically according to the divine law Lev. 16, so upon this Lamb, of whom it is treated, who takes away the sins of the world, are laid the iniquities of us all to be borne, that they may be expiated in the antitype and the body itself. Therefore both Isaiah and Peter used sacrificial phrases to explain this mystery, that they might refer us to this illustrious figure, by which the expiation of the iniquities of the whole number was foreshadowed. And it has been rightly observed by Grotius himself against Socinus, p. 126, that in Acts 8, 32, the word ἀμνὸν was used from the Greek interpretation, and that Peter looked to this passage of Isaiah, 1 Pet. 1, 18. where Grotius also teaches that Christ is called a lamb because He bore our sins. To the same, he says, look the passages in which Christ is called a lamb. Nor would it matter much to the point, even if they were not accustomed in the law to sacrifice lambs for sin. For even so, it would have been permitted to holy men to name one animal for another, so that at once the comparison might consist in the general meaning of an animal, and yet, by naming a lamb rather than a ram or a goat, the innocence of the victim might be expressed. For that reason also Peter added ἀμώμꙋ ϰ ὰσπίλꙋ 1 Pet. 1, v. 19, and it could at once, and by a certain brevity of words, look to the prophecy of Isa. 53, 7, in whose Greek interpretation there was the word ἀμνꙋ, as appears in Acts 8, v. 32. But furthermore, it is clear that a lamb was used in expiating contaminations, Lev. 14, v. 12, Num. 6, 12, which contaminations in the old law were so far equated to sin that they even received the name of sin. Whence also that lamb is said to be offered for guilt or transgression, and in the other place it is expressly added, because he sinned concerning a corpse, Num. 6, v. 11. The effect also is the same to some extent. For the contaminated were not admitted to the society of the Jewish polity (πολιτείας) except through such an expiation. Indeed, even the paschal victim (which it is agreed was for the most part a lamb, Exod. 12, v. 5) had something of an expiatory nature in its first institution. For God says that He, looking to its blood, would turn away from the Hebrews that destruction which they would otherwise have had in common with the Egyptians (in whose imitation they had contaminated themselves), Exod. 12, 13, Heb. 11, 28. But also for sin, say of a rash oath, the law shows that a lamb was accustomed to be offered, Lev. 5, 4, 6. But when Christ is called a lamb, that a sacrifice is signified, not only Peter shows, saying we were redeemed by the blood of the lamb, 1 Pet. 1, v. 18, 19. but also John in the Apocalypse in many places, and among others, where he says He was slain, Apoc. 5, 6, 9, 12, c. 13, 8. But a sacrifice cannot be understood as other than for sin, because, by the testimony of Peter, it was redemptive. Such is only a sacrifice for sin; whence it is more than manifest that when the Baptist said that Christ was the lamb who would take away the sins of the world, John 1, 29, it is a matter of sins there past, not of future ones; and of taking away guilt through the obtaining of remission before God, but not through the generation of faith.

(10) The fruit of that imposition of sins. Which the very connection (συνέχεια) in these words shows. For it is a matter of that imposition which is the cause of our peace or reconciliation with God, and of spiritual healing, and of our justification and salvation. Of an imposition that is reconciling, pacifying, healing, justifying, saving; because by the power of this imposition of our sins, the discipline of our peace is upon Him, and by His stripe we are healed; by the power of the same we are justified by the knowledge of this just servant of God, that is, through faith in Him. Finally, we add the explanation of Grotius himself, which he delivered in Defens. Fid. Cathol. advers. Socin. p. 13 seq. In the same Isaiah, v. 6 and 7, it is: 'God cast, or struck upon Him the punishment of us all. He is exacted and He is afflicted.' Here Socinus moves every stone to extort a genuine sense from the words: and invents a new interpretation: God meets through Him (or with Him) the iniquity of us all. But the Hebrew word hiphgiah of that conjugation, which signifies not a single but a double action, openly protests. Wherefore, since pagah properly signifies to meet, it follows that hiphgiah is 'caused to meet,' and by metaphor, 'he interceded': because an intercessor as it were interposes his prayers. To intercede has no place here. For then it would be said that God interceded for Christ: for that is the meaning of this word with the following particle ב, Jer. 15, 11. Nor does 'caused to intercede' fit here, both because 'bo' follows, which is 'upon him,' whereas otherwise it should have been said, 'he caused him to intercede,' and because all things which immediately precede and follow pertain to affliction, not to intercession. These words, therefore, do not bear any sense other than this: God caused to meet upon Him, that is, struck, drove into Him the sin of us all.

All of which things are further strengthened by the appended clause, which in the Vulgate is poorly rendered: 'he was offered, because he himself willed it': that Calixtus followed this imprudent transcription of his words from Maldonatus in his Concord. Evangel. on John 6:51, Theod. Hackspan observes here; but B. Luther rightly corrected the Vulgate in his Comment. on this passage. Grotius, however, translates the Hebrew text thus: 'He was oppressed and afflicted.' But he twists it to Jeremiah, because he was to be thrust into prison and into a muddy place. To that end he praises the version of the LXX Interpreters, in which, however, nothing about Jeremiah is held. He says that they expressed the sense well, κ᾿ αὐτὸς διὰ τὸ κεκακῶσθαι ἐκ ἤνοιξε τὸ ςόμα ἀυτό: but the LXX Interpreters omit that נגַשׂ and add the preposition διὰ of their own. More correctly B. Luther: 'Da er gestrafft und gemartert war.' For in Hebrew it properly denotes, 'he was exacted, and he himself is afflicted' נגשׂ, as was rightly observed by Mr. D. Weller, our [colleague], it is by force to drive someone to pay a debt or tribute, as public exactors are wont to do violently, or to perform some other troublesome work: and in the New Testament it is expressed by ἀγγαρεύειν. Whence in Exod. 3:7, ch. 5, 6, 14, it is used concerning the tyrannical exaction of Pharaoh. See also Job 3:17, Isa. 9:3, ch. 14:2, Dan. 11:20. And therefore it is emphatically noted that, by Christ, when he had once taken our sins upon himself, the penalty and payment of the debt, which we, but not he, had contracted, was exacted with great rigor, Ps. 69. Ludov. de Dieu has it thus concerning these words, in his animadvers. on this passage, p. 546. The Prophet had said in verse 6 that the iniquities of us all had been cast upon Christ. Therefore נגשׂ is added, which here, as also elsewhere in many places, I judge should be referred to the person from whom the payment is exacted, rather than, with the illustrious Junius, to the penalty or payment which is exacted. I translate, 'he was exacted,' het is hem as-gheeuscht, that is, the payment and performance of those iniquities, which had been cast upon him, was demanded from him.

Nor did he refuse, or act stubbornly, but on the contrary, he was exacted וְהוּא נַעֲנָה and he was humble, וְלֹא יִפְתַּח פִּיו and he did not open his mouth. נַעֲנָה is not here for me, afflicted, but humble, meek: as in the Kal עָנָה, to be humbled, עָנִי humble, עֲנָוָה humility. In that meaning it also exists in the Niphal Infinitive Exod. 10, 3. you refused לֵעָנֹת to be humbled from my face. The clear and most learned Mr. Joh. Cloppenburg takes נִגַּשׂ impersonally, it is exacted, that is, an exaction is demanded and he is afflicted, or, let there be an exaction, and he is afflicted. The sense is, when it was a matter of exacting the penalty of sins, it was exacted from none other than him, he had to be afflicted. נִגַּשׂ is taken then just as verse 5. נִרְפָּא לָנוּ healing is given to us, that is, healing is granted. Although therefore this word is explained in different ways, the best interpreters nevertheless agree in this, that the same satisfaction of Christ is being set forth. Grotius himself also observed this emphasis and force of the word against Socinus: That sin is exacted, that is, according to the PHRASE of Scripture, THE PENALTY OF SIN, and he himself is afflicted. Thus, therefore, the noun of iniquity must be repeated from the previous words, as if to say, whatever of our iniquities was laid upon him by God, that is exacted from him in a strict sense, he is bound to pay for it. Grotius continues there on p. 14 as follows: The word Nagas in Isaiah is also to be noted. For it is most certain that nagas (with the shin point on the left horn) properly signifies to exact, as appears in 2 Kings 23:35, Zech. 9:8. Metaphorically, however, it is taken for to oppress. The passive, therefore, niggas is either he is oppressed or it is exacted. To be oppressed has no place here, because there follows in the same verse vehu, and he himself is afflicted. For there will be no sense if one says of the same person: he is oppressed, and he himself is afflicted. It remains, therefore, that that word be taken properly, or signify, it is exacted, and be referred to the noun immediately preceding, which is sin: To exact sin, however, is nothing else, or can be nothing else, than to exact the penalty of sin. The exaction of the penalty and the affliction of Christ therefore cohere. Which sense we defend against the exceptions of Crellius, the hyperaspist of Socinus, in Socinismo Proflig. p. 453.

Nor is the likeness of the sheep and the lamb used without cause, not only because it is apt for expressing patience, which is the only reason Grotius brings forward, but so that we may be referred to the Levitical sacrifices, and thus be made more certain that here the Prophet is presenting that Lamb of God, and the sheep, whose many figures were daily exhibited in the Levitical sacrifices, namely the Messiah, who was prefigured by the countless beasts which were offered all day long in the Old Testament by his satisfaction, by which he had to transfer our guilt and penalty onto himself, to bear the guilt, and to pay the penalty, which was shadowed forth in those figures. Most poorly, therefore, are these things understood again of Jeremiah. Elegantly, however, does Jerome speak of this lamb in this place. This is the lamb, in whose type the lamb was sacrificed, whose blood smeared on the doorposts put the destroyer of Egypt to flight, who not only redeemed us with his blood, but also covered us with wool: so that he might warm those shivering in their infidelity with a garment, and we might hear the Apostle speaking to us: as many of you as have been baptized into Christ, have put on Christ. And in another place: Put on the Lord Jesus Christ. We have here also an Interpreter above all exception, the Holy Spirit, who points out with his finger who that lamb is, not only through the forerunner (πρωτοβαπτιςὴν) pointing him out openly before them, as one who had been sent for that purpose: Behold that Lamb of God, who bears the sin of the world, John 1:29, as if to say, Behold, this is that Lamb of God, upon whom God placed the iniquities of us all, who bears our sins, and from whom the sin of the whole human race is exacted, as the Prophet foretold; but also through St. Peter, who expressly (διαρρήδην) explained this prophecy of Isaiah concerning that most patient lamb,

Christ, and taught that he bore our sins in his body upon the wood of the cross, 1 Ep. 2:23, 24, and as the Syriac interpreter explained, caused our sins imposed and imputed to him (by God) to ascend with him onto the cross, as also through Philip, who demonstrated that that silent lamb was Jesus, Acts 8:35.

Latin:

Vers. 7. OBLATVS EST QVIA IPSE VOLVIT, ET NON APERVIT OS SVVM) In Hebræo: Oppressus & afflictus fuit & non aperuit os suum. Sensum bene exprimunt LXX. κ' αυτός διὰ τὸ κεκακῶσθαι ἐκ ἤνοιξεν τὸ ςόμα ἀυτᾶ. Etiam tunc cum in carcerem ageretur, & in locum lutosum, nihil fecit dixitve iracunde. Mire hæc omnia invertit Chaldæus, ut Messiam nobis depingat, qualem Iudæi volunt. SICVT OVIS) Ovis mitissimum animal. ET QVASI AGNVS) Cum quo ipse Ieremias se comparat cap. 11, 18.

Iterum indignissima, & vere diabolica perver- sio loci illustrissimi & consolatione vivifica refer- tissimi. Cujus enim est nisi Diaboli, fontes vivificæ consolationis obstruere? cujus, nisi Diaboli, Evan- gelica Oracula, quæ nobis spiritus & vita sunt, ener- vare, omnique succo salvificæ refectionis privare? Si mire invertit Chaldæus, ut Messiam Judaicum de- pingat, non minus mire pervertit Grotius, ut Mes- siam Christianum ex hoc loco nobilissimo excludat. Nam de Messia nostro hic nec ullum verbum facit: imo ea ratione textum pervertit, ut ad Messiam amplius nullo modo quadret.
