Quæ verba enim de passione Jeremiæ loquuntur ex intentione Spiritus S. quam sustinuit ob idololatriam populi Judaici, inde a Manassis temporibus frequentata, illa non possunt ex intentione Spiritus Sancti agere de Chri- sto, propter peccatum generis humani passo. Et quum ex ipsa verborum evidentia, quæ in his & aliis commatibus tam luculenta sunt, ut luculentio- ra esse nequeant, nec non Apostolica interpretatio- ne certum omnino sit, & ἀμετακίνητον, de pecca- tis nostris in eum conjectis agi, nullo modo ferenda est glossa de Jeremia, ob crimen idololatriæ populi Ju- daici indignissima passo; neque id cum veritate hi- storica, vel etiam cum justitia divina regula ullate- nus conciliari potest, Jeremiam ob populi crimen passum esse. Nam vel inflixit Deus ipsi eas passiones, vel permisit saltim. Nuda permissio intelligi non potest, quia Propheta, posuit, inquit, Dominus in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Inflixisse autem ipsummet Deum, justitiæ ejus repugnat. Porro quomodo gravi crimine populi perpessus est indi- gnissima Jeremias? Num ita, ut illa causa fuerit me- ritoria passionum Prophetæ, ob quam à Deo affli- ctus fuerit, an vero ut ad caussam efficientem pas- siones eidem inferentem id pertineat, quod scele- rate & cum gravi crimine Judæi ipsum afflixerint? Prius statui non potest, quia ob culpam alienam af- flixisse Deum Prophetam regulæ justitiæ divinæ non congruit. Posterius etsi verum sit, ἀλλότριον tamen est: quia peccata hic introducuntur, ut me- ritoria passionis causa, non vero determinatur mo- dus, sceleratene vel injuste afflićtus sit, an vero ju- ste? imo, quum à Deo positæ sint in hoc subjectum iniquitates, non id injuste fieri potuit, sed factum est justissime. Denique quid in hoc textu est, quod ad Manassis tempora ovium errorem restringat, aut ad idololatriam Judæorum? Nihil tale in hoc capite ostendi potest. Glossa ergo ista aliud è tex- tui infertut, adeoque pro literali sensu falso ven- ditatur.

Ne autem supersit dubium, de nullo alio, quam de Christo hæc accipienda esse, observamus (1) universalem totius generis humani corruptionem hic indigitari. OMNE NOS quasi oves erravi- mus. Et iterum: unusquisque in viam suam declina- vit: ac denique posuit OMNIUM nostrum iniqui- tatem in eum. Quinam illi omnes sunt? Si dicas Ju- dæos esse, quia prolapsi in idololatriam sunt, falleris: quia non OMNES ἀποτόμως Judæi in idololatriam prolapsi. Et fuit sine dubio tantum semen aliquod in populo Dei. Non enim penitus interire pote- rat Ecclesia. Nec de Judæis solum, sed etiam genti- libus id intelligendum esse, Petrina interpretatio docet, quia 1. Pet. 2. v. 25. de gentibus explicatur: imo Judæos & gentes simul omnes, hoc est, absolute omnes homines intelligi, cum antecedentia & conse- quentia evincunt, siquidem omnium hominum pec- cata portarit propter omnium nostrum iniquitates vulneratus, omniumque nostrum pacis causa castiga- tus, innuatur: tum verba ipsa universaliter posita confirmant, quæ proinde universaliter ac sine re- strictione sunt intelligenda. Quibus accedunt alia scripturæ Catholicæ dicta, utpote quæ omnes homi- nes peccato obnoxios esse, omnes homines instar ovium errasse, in viam malam declinasse, nullamque hic esse διαςολὴν palam docent, omnesque voce legis sub peccatum concludunt, Rom. 3. & 11. Gal. 3. Unde in proclivi est concludere, non nisi de Christo hæc intelligi posse. Qui totius generis humani, post- quam defecerat, omnesque declinaverant, Re- demtor & Salvator est, Psal. 14. v. ult. Cyrillus hæc ita παραφράζει: Omnes nos ut oves erravimus, quis- que via sua erravit, & Dominus eum tradidit pro no- stris peccatis. Itaque erravimus nos, à Deo vivente de- fecimus, voluptates nostras consectantes. Atqui uni- versorum Dominus, id est, Deus & Pater, propter pec- cata nostra tradidit eum, ut nos à pœna absolveret, cre- dentesque conservaret.

(2) Tacitam subjecti præsentis exemtionem. Nam quum OMNIUM iniquitas in hoc subjectum posita sit, oportet id ab istis omnibus distinctum esse, ea ratione, ut immune sit ab iniquitate. Qui enim iniquitati obnoxii, eorum iniquitas in hoc subjectum posita fuit. Quum ergo in hac transla- tione, vel surrogatione duæ sint, ut ita dicam, per- sonæ, una, à qua translatum est peccatum, altera, in l quam id translatum fuit, illa autem genus huma- num universum sit: ibi enim nulla διαστολή; utique hanc oportet esse non aliquem ex hominibus pec- cato obnoxium, sed Christum peccati expertem, de quo Propheta postea, quod iniquitatem non fe- cerit: non ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον è communiori forte, sed θεάνθρωπον.

(3) Culpae translatae latitudinem. Non enim quae- dam saltim culpa, sed omnis aberratio, omnis in viam pravam declinatio, omnis iniquitas, h. e. quicquid omnino peccati rationem habet, translatum dici- tur à Domino in hunc peccati latorem. Id vero de nullo alio dici, aut intelligi potest, quam de Chri- sto, agno illo Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi, Joh. 1, 29.

(4) Translationis veritatem. Quam vere aberravi- mus omnes, sicut oves declinavimus omnes, à trami- te justitiae, adeoque peccatores sumus omnes co- ram judicio Dei, tam vere iniquitates nostrae in hunc peccati latorem translatae sunt coram tribu- nali divino. Id vero quomodo de ullo ψιλανθρώ- πῳ dici potest? Quomodo surrogari in alterius lo- cum, & quidem nocentis alter, isque innoxius pot- est, si de meris hominibus sermo sit? At in Chri- stum, Mediatorem Dei & hominum, translatas ve- rissime esse nostras iniquitates, illum in judicio Dei sanctissimo in nostrum ceu nocentium locum, etsi innocentem, surrogatum esse, tota Scriptura S. te- statur: mortuus est justus pro injustis, 1. Pet. 3, 18. Si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, idem est, ac si mortui essemus omnes, 2. Cor. 5, 14.

(5) Translationis rationem, quia translatio ista iniquitatum facta est tum ratione imputatae culpae, quod in judicio Dei illi omnia omnino peccata im- putata sint, tum ratione exantlatae poenae, quod no- stri loco poenam sustinere debuerit. Id enim infert phrasis illa, posuit Dominus in eo iniquitatem nostrum omnium, uti in Socinismo profligato plenius osten- dimus. Irruere fecit Dominus veluti cum vi atque im- petu, occurrere ei fecit, & impingere fecit in ipsum o- nium iniquitates. Nam פגע est impegit occurrendo, occurrit & impegit in aliquem impellendo, animo ho- stili, animo perdendi Exod, 5, 3. Num. 35, 19. Jos. 8, 21. Quod vero de nullo alio, nisi de solo Christo, qui & culpam & poenam nostram in se derivavit, vel à Patre impositam suscepit, portavit, & luit, in- telligi potest. (6) Passionis causam meritoriam. Quum enim afflictio ac poena inferatur hac phrasi, causa meritoria etiam poenae istius hic expressa est, nimirum quod non merito suarum iniquitatum, sed nostrarum aberrationum, declinationum & ini- quitatum ipse eam sustineat. Quod vero de aliis dici nequit: quum nemo alterius culpam luat, & ob meritum peccati alieni puniatur, citra propriam culpam: uni Christo Mediatori & sponsori, vel vadi generis humani hoc convenit, qui cum culpa poe- nam nostram suscepit, & merito peccatorum no- strorum punitus est, factus pro nobis peccatum, quum ipse non nosset peccatum, 2. Cor. 5, 21.

(7) Translationis istius & afflictionis causam effi- cientem principalem. Constituitur haec Jehovah; Do- minus posuit in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. In ho- minem autem nudum aliorum hominum iniquita- tem Deum posuisse, ita ut ille luere necessum habu- erit, & inauditum, & justitiae divinae contrarium est. At vero de Christo, Scriptura teste, id verissimum, nec à divina justitia alienum, imo ὁμολογουμένως μέγα temperamentum divinae justitiae atq; clemen- tiae est. (8) Causam translationis ipsius finalem. Cur posuit Dominus nostras iniquitates in ipsum? Id indicant, quae praecedunt de nostro errore, ac deviatione, ut nempe oves errantes converteren- tur, & qui in suam quique viam declinarant, in viam Domini reducerentur: indicat id ipsa phrasis, quae facrificialis est, ut sc. iniquitatibus à nobis translatis in ipsum illæ expiarentur, nosque ab iniquitatibus liberaremur. Quo faciunt loca similia Pf. 108, 6. 7. Esa. 34, 8. Matth. 15, 24. Luc. 15, 4. & Targum Jo- nathan hunc versum, Dominus fecit impingere in ipsum iniquitatem universitatis nostræ, ita reddens: Et coram Domino fuit beneplacitum remittere pecca- ta universitatis nostræ propter ipsum. Unde S. Pe- trus finem illum sic indigitat: Eratis sicut oves er- rantes, sed conversi nunc estis ad Pastorem & Episco- pum animarum vestrarum.

(9) Typicam adumbrationem, quæ tum in aliis sa- crificiis facta, tum imprimis in hirco ἀποπομπαίῳ. In eo enim figuratum fuit, quod hic explicatum est. Ad illum itaq; respicit Esaias, quod phrasis ipsa do- cet. Ut ergo hirco isti peccata populi, & iniquitates omnium imponebantur, ut expiarentur, typice juxta legem divinam Lev. 16. ita huic, de quo agitur, agno, qui tollit peccata mundi, portandæ impo- nuntur omnium nostrum iniquitates, ut expientur in antitypo, & corpore ipso. Ideo & Esaias, & Petrus phrasibus sacrificialibus usi sunt ad explicandum hoc mysterium, ut nos remitterent ad illustrem hanc figuram, qua adumbrata fuit expiatio iniqui- tatum totius universitatis. Et recte observatum est ab ipsomet Grotio contra Socin. p. 126. Act. 8, 32. è Græca interpretatione vocem ἀμνὲ adhibitam es- se, & ad hunc Esaiæ locum respexisse Petrum 1. Pet. 1, 18. ubi docet etiam Grotius, quod Christus agnus dicatur, quia peccata nostra portavit. Eodem, in- quit, respiciunt loci, in quibus Christus agnus dicitur. Neque multum ad rem faceret, etiamsi non soliti essent in lege agni pro peccato immolari. Nam etiam sic licuis- set viris sanctis pro pecude pecudem alteram nomina- re, ut simul & in generali pecudis significatione com- paratio consisteret, & tamen agno potius, quam ariete aut capra nominato innocentia victimæ exprimeretur. Ideo enim & Petrus addidit ἀμώμꙋ ϰ ὰσπίλꙋ 1. Pet. 1. v. 19. potuitque simul & quodam verborum compen- dio respici ad vaticinium Esa. 53, 7. in cujus interpre- tatione Græca erat vox ἀμνꙋ, ut apparet Act. 8. v. 32. Verum insuper liquet, agnum in contaminationibus expiandis fuisse usurpatum, Lev. 14. v. 12. Num. 6, 12. quæ quidem contaminationes in lege veteri peccato eousque æquabantur, ut & peccati nomen accipe- rent. Unde & agnus ille in reatum sive delictum offerti utroque dicitur, & altero loco diserte addi- tur, quia peccavit circa cadaver Num. 6. v. 11. Effe- ctus quoque idem aliquatenus. Nam contaminati non admittebantur ad societatem πολιτείας Judaicæ, nisi per talem expiationem. Quin & paschalis victima (quam plerumque agnum fuisse constat, Exod. 12 v. 5.) in prima institutione aliquid habuit expiatorii. Ait enim Deus, se respicientem ad ejus sanguinem aver- surum ab Ebræis id exitium, quod alioqui cum Ægy- ptiis (quorum imitatione se contaminaverant) habi- turi erant commune Exod. 12, 13. Heb. 11, 28. Sed & pro peccato, puta temerarii juramenti, agnam offer- ri solitam ostendit lex, Lev. 5, 4. 6. Agnus autem cum dicitur Christus, sacrificium notari, non tantum Petrus ostendit, redemptos nos dicens agni sanguine 1. Pet. 1, v. 18. 19. sed & Johannes in Apocalypsi multis locis, atque inter cæteros, ubi mactatum eum dicit, Apoc. 5, 6. 9. 12. c. 13, 8. Sacrificium autem aliud, quam pro peccato intelligi non potest, quia Petro teste, fuit redemptorium. Tale est solum sacrificium pro pec- cato; unde plus quam manifestum est, cum dixit Ba- ptista, Christum esse agnum, qui auferret mundi peccata, Joh. 1, 29. de peccatis ibi præteritis agi, non de futuris; & de auferendo reatu per remissionis impe- trationem apud Deum, non autem per fidei ingene- rationem.

(10) Fructum istius peccatorum impositionis. Quem ipsa συνέχεια in hiscce verbis ostendit. Nam de ea impositione agitur, quæ causa est nostræ pacis vel reconciliationis cumDeo,& sanationis spiritua- lis, nostræq; justificationis & salutis. De impositio- ne reconciliatrice, pacificatrice, curatrice, justificatri- ce, salvatrice; quia vi impositionis hujus peccato- rum nostrorum,disciplina pacis nostræ est super illum, & livore ejus sanati sumus, vi ejusdem justificamur nos cognitione servi istius Dei justi, hoc est, per fi- dem in ipsum. Denique addimus ipsam Grotii ex- plicationem: quam tradidit defens. fid.Cathol. ad- vers. Socin. p. 13. seq. Apud eundem Esaiam vers. 6. & 7. est: Deus conjecit, sive impegit in eum pœ- nam omnium nostrum. Exigitur & ipse affligitur. Hic nullum non lapidem movet Socinus, ut sensum ge- nuinum verbis extorqueat: novamque interpretatio- nem comminiscitur: Deus occurrit per ipsum (vel cum ipso) iniquitati omnium nostrum. Sed recla- mat aperte vox Hebræa hiphgiah ejus conjugationis, quæ non unicam, sed duplicem actionem significat. Quare cum pagah proprie significet occurrere, sequi- tur ut hiphgiah sit fecit occurrere, & per metapho- ram, deprecatus est: quia deprecator preces suas quasi interponit. Deprecari hic locum non habet. Nam tum diceretur Deus pro Christo esse deprecatus: ea enim est hujus vocis sequente ב particula significatio, Jer. 15, 11. Neque fecit deprecari hic convenit, tum quia sequitur bo, quod est in illum, cum alioqui dici debuisset, fecit illum deprecari,tum quia omnia, quæ proxime antecedunt & sequuntur, ad afflictionem, non ad deprecationem pertinent. Non ferunt ergo verba hæc sensum alium, quam hunc: fecit Deus illi occurrere, hoc est, impegit, incussit in illum pecca- tum omnium nostrum.

Quæ omnia ulterius roborantur è subjuncto commate, quod in Vulgata male redditur: oblatus est, quia ipse voluit: quam imprudenti verborum suorum è Maldonato transcriptione sequutum esse Calixtum in Concord.Evangel. ad Joh.6,51. obser- vat hic Theod. Hackspan. recte autem castigavit Vulgatam B.Luther. in Comment. ad h. l. Ebræum autem textum ita transfert Grotius: Oppressus & afflictus fuit. Sed ad Jeremiam torquet, quod in car- cerem & in locum lutofum detrudendus esset. Ea fine laudat LXX.Interpp. versionem, inqua tamen nihil de Jeremia habetur. Sensum bene expressisse ait, κ᾿ αὐτὸς διὰ τὸ κεκακῶσθαι ἐκ ἤνοιξε τὸ ςόμα ἀυτό: sed omittunt LXX. Interpretes illud נגַשׂ & de suo addunt præpositionem διὰ. Rectius B. Lutherus: Da er gestrafft und gemartert war. Nam Ebrai- ce proprie notat, exactus est, & ipse affligitur נגשׂ, ut recte observatum Dn. D. Wellero nostro, est vi adigere aliquem ad solvendum debitum vel tribu- tum, ut solent violenter exactores publici, vel aliud aliquod opus malestum efficiendum: & in Novo Te- stamento per ἀγγαρεύειν exprimitur. Unde Exod. 3.v.7. c. 5, 6.14. de tyrannica Pharaonis exactione adhibetur. Vide etiam Job. 3, 17. Esa.9, 3. cap. 14, 2. Dan. 11. v. 20. Ideoque emphatice notatur, à Chri- sto, cum semel peccata nostra in se susceperit, magno rigore exactam esse pœnam solutionem debiti, quod nos, non autem ipse, contraxeramus Ps. 69. Ludov. de Dieu de his verbis ita habet, in animadvers.ad h. l. p. 546. Dixerat Propheta vers. 6. conjectas fuisse in Christum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Additur itaque נגשׂ quod hic, ut & alibi passim, ad personam potius, à qua solutio exigitur, quam cum Cl. Junio ad pœnam aut solutionem, quæ exigitur, referendum ar- bitror. Verto, exactus fuit, het is hem as-gheeuscht, id est postulata ab ipso est solutio & præstatio ista- rum iniquitatum, quæ in ipsum conjectæ fuerant.

Nıq;recusavit,aut refractarium egit,quin contra,exa- ctus fuit וְהוּא נַעֲנָה & ipse humilis fuit, וְלֹא יִפְתַּח פִּיו neque aperuit os suum. נַעֲנָה non est mihi hic,af- flictus,sed humilis,mansuetus: ut in Kal עָנָה, humi- liari, עָנִי humilis, עֲנָוָה humilitas. Ea significa- tione & in Infinitivo Niphal extat Exod. 10, 3. renui- sti לֵעָנֹת humiliari à facie mea. Clar. & Doctiss. Vir Joh. Cloppenburgius נִגַּשׂ impersonaliter accipit, exactum est, id est, exactio postulata est & ille affli- ctus est, vel, exactio sit, & ille affligitur. Sensus est, quum de pœna peccatorum exigenda ageretur, non ab alio, quam ab illo exacta est, ille affligi debuit. Su- mitur tum נִגַּשׂ sicut vers. 5. נִרְפָּא לָנוּ anatum est nobis, id est sanatio data. Etsi ergo diversis mo- dis verbum istud explicetur, consentiunt tamen optimi Interpretes in eo, quod eadem satisfactio Christi exponatur. Quam emphasin & vim vocis ipse etiam Grotius contra Socinum observavit: Exigitur id peccatum, hoc est, secundum PHRA- SIN Scripturæ, POENA PECCATI, & ipse affli- gitur. Sic ergo è prioribus verbis repetendum no- men iniquitatis, q. d. quicquid iniquitatum nostra- rum ipsi impositum est à Deo, id exigitur ab ipso di- stricta ratione, pro eo solvere tenetur. Pergit ibi Grotius p. 14. ita : Notanda quoque est apud Esaiam vox Nagas. Certissimum enim est, nagas (schin pun- ctum habente in cornu sinistro) proprie significare, exigere, ut apparet 2. Reg. 35. Zachar. 9, 8. Meta- phorice autem sumi pro opprimere. Passivum ergo niggas est aut opprimitur aut exigitur. Opprimi- tur hic locum non habet,quia sequitur in eodem Com- mate vehu, & ipse affligitur. Nullus enim erit sen- sus, si quis de eodem dicat : opprimitur, & ipse affli- gitur. Restat ergo, ut vox illa proprie sumatur, aut significet, exigitur, & referatur ad nomen proxime antecedens, quod est peccatum : Exigere autem pec- catum, nihil aliud est, aut esse potest, quam exigere pœnam peccati. Cohærent ergo exactio pœnæ & Christi afflictio. Quem sensum adversus exceptio- nes Crellii Socini hyperaspistæ defendimus Soci- nismo Proflig. p. 453.

Nec absque causa similitudo ovis & agni adhi- betur,non solum, quod ea ad patientiam exprimen- dam apta sit, quam causam Grotius solum adfert, sed ut remittamur ad sacrificia Levitica,adeoq; cer- tiores reddamur, hic sisti à Propheta agnum illum Dei,atq; ovem, cujus tot figuræ in sacrificiis Levi- ticis quotidie exhibebantur, Messiam nempe, qui per pecudes innumeras, quæ tota die offerebantur in V.T. præfiguratus fuerit satisfactione sua, qua culpam & pœnam nostram in se transferre,culpam portare, pœnam luere debuit, quod in illis figuris adumbratum fuit. Pessime ergo hæc iterum de Je- remia intelliguntur. Eleganter autem de hoc agno Hieronymus in h. l. Hic agnus est, in cujus typo im- molabatur agnus, cujus cruor linitus in postibus, ex- terminatorem fugabat Ægypti, qui non solum sanguine suo nos redemit, sed & lanis operuit : ut algentes infi- delitate sua veste calefaceret, & audiremus Aposto- lum nobis loquentem : quotquot in Christo baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Et in alio loco: Induimini Christo Jesu. Habemus & hic Interpretem omni ex- ceptione majoremSpir.S.qui quisnam agnus ille sit, digito demonstrat, non tantum per πρωτοβαπτι- ςὴν eundem exerto digito coram ostendentem,ut- pote qui ad id missus erat: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui portat peccatum mundi, Joh. 1, 29. q. d. Ecce, hic est agnus ille Dei, in quem Deus posuit omnium nostrum iniquitates,qui fert peccata nostra,& à quo exigitur peccatum totius generis humani, ut prædixit Pro- pheta; sed etiam per S. Petrum, qui διαρρήδην hoc Esaiæ vaticinium de agno illo patientissimo,

Christo exposuit, illumq; pertulisse peccata nostra in corpore suo super lignum crucis docuit 1. Ep. 2, 23. 24. & ut Syrus interpres exposuit, peccata nostra sibi im- posita & imputata (à Deo) in crucem secum ascende- re fecisse, ut & per Philippum, qui agnum illum ob- mutescentem Jesum esse, demonstravit Act. 8, 35.

## 53:8
Verse 8. HE WAS TAKEN AWAY FROM DISTRESS AND FROM JUDGMENT) He was taken away from prison and from judgment: that is, liberated at last. He calls this judgment, because under the guise of judgment these very evils had been imposed. See Jer. 32:3, but he was liberated by the Babylonians.

WHO SHALL DECLARE HIS GENERATION?) Who will be able to count the days of his life? i.e., he will be very long-lived.

FOR HE WAS CUT OFF FROM THE LAND OF THE LIVING) Namely, when he was first cast into prison, then into that muddy pit, and again into prison.

FOR THE TRANSGRESSION OF MY PEOPLE I STRUCK HIM) In the Hebrew it is, a blow to him, supply happened, by the supreme error and crime of the people, as was also said before. Some Hebrew codices had לו here, but למו signifies the same thing: for it is not without examples of the ם (mem) used for emphasis (ὑπερβολικόν).

Many things show that violence is being done to this most august text. First, that it is snatched away to the liberation effected by the Babylonians: of whom there is neither a trace nor a footprint in this whole chapter. Nor indeed was Jeremiah then liberated from distress when he was released from prison by the Babylonians; but he was forced to experience new adversities afterwards, when he was held as a liar and a seducer, chap. 43:2. Second, that the ineffable generation is explained as the long life of Jeremiah. For generation is not the same thing as life, nor is life, even if it be very long, such as even that of Methuselah was, ineffable. Third, that Jeremiah is imagined to have been struck for the transgression of the Lord's people: which we have often pointed out is contrary to divine justice. Fourth, that the cutting off from the land of the living is twisted to the thrusting of Jeremiah into prison and a muddy place. For this was not a cutting off from the land of the living, because he lived still, and passed a long life in the land of the living, as Grotius notes, such a life whose days, as he himself trifles, are indescribable. For a cutting off from the land of the living, as the phrase itself teaches, and all interpreters agree, brings about death, and it is so explained in v. 10 when it is said that he laid down his soul for a transgression. For these things are written as mutually explaining one another by way of an epexegesis familiar to Scripture: he is cut off from the land of the living, stricken for the wickedness of the people, but who shall declare his generation? And: if he had laid down his soul for a transgression, he shall see a long-lived seed, it is by no means obscure. I pass over the fact that killing is also indicated, when he is said to be led as a sheep to the slaughter or to be killed, v. 7. Fifthly, it is diametrically opposed to the explanation of Philip, who denies that these words ought to be understood of the Prophet himself, or of anyone else, than of Jesus: Acts 8:34. I pray you, of whom does the Prophet say this: of himself, or of some other man? For when the Eunuch was stuck in his questioning, Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this scripture (of Isaiah) he preached Jesus unto him. He taught, therefore, that they were to be understood not of the Prophet himself, nor of any other man, but of Christ alone. Which most clearly contradicts the Grotian corruption. And yet Grotius still attempted to insert his Jeremiah, such is the unbridled and impious impudence of the man, in his Annotations on Acts 8, that perhaps Philip thought of Jeremiah; for thus he trifles at verse 34: περὶ ἑαυτοῦ (whether Isaiah speaks of himself) For Isaiah also endured many evils in the time of Manasseh, ἢ περὶ ἑτέρου τινός. Perhaps he thought of Jeremiah. But if he thought of him, he certainly removed and excluded him as well. For that interrogation is so formed that both Isaiah and any other person is excluded, and Christ alone is left. Therefore it is added in verse 35: he preached unto him Jesus. But there are not lacking a thousand arts of perverting things here also. For he says that Philip explained these things of Jesus, because all these words agree with him in an excellent manner, that is, as he himself understands, in a mystical sense: Thus, therefore, he thinks that those things can still be understood according to the literal sense concerning Jeremiah (perhaps also that Philip had Jeremiah in mind), even though mystically they speak of JESUS. But Philip did not know that a single saying could have a double sense, and therefore he spoke simply and of one sense, and judged that the discourse was about one subject, while he asked: I pray thee, of whom speaketh the Prophet this? of himself, or of some other man? And, if Philip, or the Holy Scriptures, had understood it in the literal sense concerning Jeremiah, but had taught that in the mystical sense it should be transferred to Jesus, how would he have found faith in the Eunuch, whom Grotius reports to have been instructed in the Jewish religion? Could the Eunuch not have reasoned, what have these things to do with Jesus, since they were fulfilled long ago in Jeremiah? Therefore it is manifest that these things are so explained by Philip concerning Jesus, that it is denied that they should be understood in any way concerning Jeremiah or any other person, since the words do not even allow for it. For no one else was cut off from the land of the living for the wickedness of the people, or after he was cut off, had a generation which cannot be declared.

Now if we examine the Prophetic words further, more arguments will be available for refuting the Grotian distortion and for confirming the uniquely genuine interpretation concerning Christ. HE WAS TAKEN AWAY FROM DISTRESS AND FROM JUDGMENT. These do not denote liberation from prison or from human judgment, but liberation from the distress and judgment of God himself. The word עצר does not signify a prison but a prevailing and a predominating, as Forster notes in his Lexicon, and thus it brings about distress, as Jerome rendered it. The LXX translated it as ταπείνωσιν (humiliation), which Philip retained in Acts 8:33, by which humiliation he was made humble even to the death of the cross, Phil. 2. The Hebrew word is used for the distress of the womb in Prov. 30:16 and for the distress of affliction in Ps. 57:39. And since the highest degree of distress and humiliation is designated on account of the added word of judgment, our Lord Dr. Weller rightly understands the infernal pains, which most greatly constrained him and affected him with the highest distresses. By the word משפט (judgment), every judgment in which he was affected by distress and was constrained is understood, because he was exempted from all that judgment. Which was especially the judgment of God, because God made him sin for us, 2 Cor. 5:21, and a curse, Gal. 3:13, whence the highest distresses and truly infernal pains occupied his soul. In this judgment, the penalty was exacted from him, and he was wounded and bruised for our sins: which is attributed to God by the Apostle, Rom. 4 and 8, and indeed even by Isaiah: who testifies that the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all. Therefore, the Prophet signifies that he was taken away from the judgment of God, whom he had taught to have been so gravely afflicted in the judgment of God. The sense of the LXX Interpreters In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: thus Jerome explained it. In humility his judgment was taken away, that signifies that he ascended to the Father as a victor from tribulation and judgment. Although he was subject to tribulation and distress, and was in the judgment of God, when he sustained condemnation in our place, yet he was taken away from that judgment and asserted into liberty. The Chaldean rendered those words from distress and judgment as מיסרהין ומופלענו (from chastisement and from punishment): Of the more recent ones, Stephanus, he was taken away from bonds and from sentence. Oleaster and Münster, from the prison of the sepulchre. Tremellius, he shall be taken away through constraint and judgment. Piscator, from the constraint of the soul and the judgment of God.

WHO SHALL DECLARE HIS GENERATION? Which some understand concerning the eternal generation, others concerning the admirable and ineffable birth from the Virgin Mary, as Cyril and Jerome had observed, and indeed concerning the former Athanasius in his exposition. See Aug. Tr. 31 in John ch. 7, and concerning the latter Justin, Dial. c. Tryph.

Tertullian adv. Jud. ch. 14, book 3 adv. Marc. ch. 7, but others concerning the everlasting duration of life after the resurrection, as for instance from the more recent ones, B. Luther, Tarnov, Rivet. The Targum explains it concerning the wonders performed in the days of the Messiah, i.e., and the wonders which he did for us in his days, who shall be able to declare! Corn. à Lapide takes it for an exclamation, by which the Prophet inveighs against that generation, or the men of that age. But because here a prophecy concerning future things is held, and indeed concerning that which follows the rescue of the Messiah from constraint and judgment, and the word דור nowhere denotes birth, nor is there any discussion here of miracles, and much less does an invective exclamation have a place here. There remains the interpretation concerning the ineffable duration of the life of the Messiah, which seems to agree both with the whole context and particularly with the preceding verse, so that it may be an antithesis of the constraint and judgment in the state of humiliation, and also of the happiness and joy of another eternal life in the state of exaltation. To which explanation, left to its own weight, we judge that the explanation of those who interpret it concerning the seed of Christ, and the pious who are to be born from him in a number and manner unspeakable to us, is to be preferred, and we give this sense to these words: That no one can express by speaking the generation, race, family, posterity, children of the Messiah, and furthermore the children of those born, and those who will be born from them. We urge most of all the force of the words and the Biblical usage: And first indeed the interrogation, such as occurs here, often insinuates the great difficulty of a matter, it is evident from 1 Sam. 2:25, Ps. 15:1, Prov. 31:10. and here in verse 4, it is sometimes also an undeniable fact that it imports some impossibility. Who shall declare, i.e., No one shall easily declare, or no mortal can declare. Then the word דור properly denotes a series of men succeeding one another, where one thing is born from another, and thus it returns as it were into itself in the manner of a sphere, Is. 41:4, see Schindler in his Lexicon. When דור ודור is doubled, it is accustomed sometimes to denote duration and eternity. But where דור is placed simply, it perpetually and everywhere denotes generation, children, race, family, posterity, but it is never taken for duration and eternity. I have examined all the places which occur in the Concordances, and I have discovered what I said. It is not worth the effort to write down each one here. It is taken in this way in Gen. 7:1, ch. 17:7, 9, 12, Exod. 12:14, 16, 42, ch. 16:32, 33, ch. 17:21, ch. 30:21, Lev. 23:21, Num. 9:20, ch. 35:21, Deut. 1:38, ch. 2:14, ch. 29:22, Josh. 22:27, 28, Jud. 2:16. & c. 3, 2. 1 Chron. 16, 14. Ps. 12, 8. Ps. 14, 5. Ps. 22, 31. Ps. 24, 6. Ps. 49, 14. 71, 18. 63, 15. 78, 4. 6. 8. 109, 13. 112, 2. 102, 19. Prov. 30, 11. 12. et seqq. Isa. 41, 4. Jer. 2, 31. c. 7, 29. Joel 1, 3. nor is any dissimilar example given. Finally שוח, (from which descends יְשׂוֹחֵחַ) is to meditate, to speak, and is attributed as much to the mind as to the mouth. Avenarius compares it with שָׁחָה to swim, and wishes it to signify properly to swim, as it were, in a spacious subject. In this form it exists only twice. Ps. 143, 5, I will meditate on the works of your hands: or I will recount and declare. So many and so stupendous are the works of the hands of God, that he who recalls the same to memory seems to swim in his mind as if in a vast and most spacious Ocean: and in this place: where it can be rendered in the same way. Such is the generation of the Messiah, and such that family, that whoever presumes to investigate it by meditating, he casts himself as it were into a vast sea, which no mortal can overcome by swimming. Which paraphrase, born from the proper meaning of the words and Biblical usage, the context admits very well. For the fact that in this verse the prophecy begins concerning the exaltation of Christ and the fruits acquired by his emptying, both the thing itself teaches, and the learned interpreters observe. But the chief fruit, and not the last degree of his exaltation, is that with Christ resurrected, children are generated throughout the whole world, and that his name is propagated in a continuous series, from generation to generation, to late posterity, so that there is neither measure nor number of the faithful serving Christ. Furthermore, for this reason Christ suffered himself to be reduced to the greatest straits of soul and body, and to be condemned to death, that, being lifted up from these straits and snatched from judgment, he might no longer live for himself, but for his generation; and that he might perpetually beget sons and daughters for himself in the Church. For this purpose, Christ was violently cut off as the tree of life, so that we, who were dry wood, might be grafted into him, and be able to draw sap from him, lest we be consumed by unquenchable fire. Which word גָזַר in the following verse implies, see Gen. 15, 17. 1 Reg. 3, 25. 26. 2 Reg. 6, v. 4. Ps. 136, 13. Hab. 3, 17. Let these passages be compared with one another: Gen. 2, 9. Apoc. 2, 7. chap. 22, 2. Luc. 23, 31. Job 15, v. 2. 3. Matth. 3, 10. 12. And as all the fruit of the passion of Christ redounds to the Church of Christ, so while it is said that through his passion he obtained this, that he might gather a Church to himself, by this one word is comprehended whatever benefits are acquired by the death of Christ. Which is the reason why the clearer herald of the Gospel, as St. Augustine calls Isaiah, explains this fruit again and again here and derives it from the passion of Christ. Therefore, what he says in v. 13, that the Messiah would see a spiritual seed, because his soul, i.e., he himself (for נֶפֶשׁ soul sometimes in Oriental languages is the same as he himself, cf. Jer. 51, 14. Amos 6, 8. with Gen. 22, 16. Heb. 6, 16. 17. likewise Matth. 20, 28. Mark 10, 45. with 1 Tim. 2, 6.) placed or gave himself as a sacrifice for the guilt of sins: What he says in v. 15, Jehovah says, I will give him a portion for the many, that is, for the salvation of the Church. Cf. Ps. 68, 19. Eph. 4, 8. so that ב may be taken for מ, just as elsewhere in Gen. 11, 4. Levit. 16, 22. Psal. 18, 50. Psal. 12, 6. or if the emphasis of the word יַחֲלֹק is heeded, I will give him an inheritance among the many, as R. Solomon explains אחלק לו נחלה וגוחר I will distribute to him a possession and the strong, and the LXX, διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸς κληρονομήσει πολλοὺς, therefore he himself shall possess many as if by inheritance, because he delivered his soul to death and bore the sins of many (i.e., of all, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 5, 19, with whom Calvin agrees in this place against Musculus and others who have the name from themselves): The Prophet seems to indicate the very same thing in v. 11, when he says the generation and posterity of the Messiah will be ἀνάριθμον (innumerable), since he was afflicted on account of the transgression of the people of God, and cut off from the land of the living. The same effect here, the same cause, the same coherence of effect and cause. At least the words are different, which present the same thing with elegant variety.

There follows now in the text: HE WAS CUT OFF FROM THE LAND OF THE LIVING. FOR THE TRANSGRESSION OF MY PEOPLE I STRUCK HIM. Which explain the cause of the spiritual generation of the Messiah, and are then explained by the Prophet in this way: The Lord willed to crush him in infirmity, if he shall have placed his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed. For what else is: He struck him for the transgression of the people, than, the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity for sin, or on account of sin? What else is cut off from the land of the living, than he placed his soul? What else is his generation no one shall recount, than he shall see a long-lived seed! Indeed, concerning this eighth verse, in which we are engaged, about the straits and judgment, etc., the interpreters vary in rendering the literal sense concerning Christ: some understand it still of the passion, others of the exemption from the passion through resurrection and glorification. From these, some explain it thus: he was condemned without any fault, by the sedition of the Jews and the voice of Pilate, as it is in Jerome: Others, he was snatched and dragged by the people or the Synagogue, and from the judgment or the Pharisees, as Forerius and Castalio explained; he was dragged or led from the assembly of the people and the Synagogue. And Vatablus; he was snatched without delay and without judgment, etc. But those explanations are forced. Simpler is that which takes it as an exemption from straits and judgment: For the word לקח he was accepted, taken, although it signifies various things, responds best to the Apostolic word ἀνέληψον, and emphatically notes that he was liberated by ASCENSION and assumption into heavenly glory, and the Holy Scriptures did not take it otherwise in Acts 8. ἤρθη ἡ κρίσις (the judgment was taken away), which words cannot be drawn to the passion, but pertain entirely to glory, because the judgment was taken away; and there is no sense if you say he was taken away from the midst of the straits: nor will what follows concerning the ineffable generation cohere in that way; which also does not seem to begin the description of the resurrection and glory quite aptly, because the victory over death and the ascension into heaven preceded that generation and spiritual posterity. And all things will flow more correctly if it is said that, being snatched from every strait, especially of the soul, and lifted up from the judgment of God into heaven, he had a race which no one could express or enumerate by speaking: so that ineffable glory follows the ineffable strait in that judgment, when he is liberated from it, and happiness and success follow; and the cause of it is here inculcated anew (because it can never be sufficiently inculcated for our edification and consolation), because, namely, he was cut off from the land of the living, when the Lord so struck him for the transgression of the people; when therefore he had thus placed his soul for the sin of men as a sacrifice, crushed by the Lord, he now sees a long-lived seed and an ineffable race; and he is exhilarated for that anxiety by this most joyful fruit of his spiritual seed, and race, as his highest delights. Rightly therefore B. Luther: This Prophet confesses him to have been resurrected, because he previously said he was slaughtered like a victim. Up to this point the words were only of death, now it turns to the opposite side, and says, Christ is not dead, he has been taken up by God. But he would not speak thus of a dead man, remaining in the sepulcher. It is necessary therefore that we understand this concerning the resurrection. By Pilate he was judged but again he was taken up from judgment. And those things concerning the land of the living etc. pertain also to the resurrection. Nor is it in vain that he repeats both the passion of Christ and the end of the passion, that he suffered for our sake. For he wishes this article to be deeply impressed upon our souls, so that we do not hear the passion of Christ as we hear another history, but rather that we look to the use and the end, that he suffered for our sins. But what he says, that he was cut off from the land of the living, signifies that there is a twofold life: One of those who live here on earth, and another of Christ, namely eternal and new. Therefore the Jews expect him in vain: For he is cut off from this life, when he was afflicted with the punishment of the cross. Thence he passed into another life, as he says: I go to my Father. Thus the passion of Christ was nothing else than an acceptance from anguish, and a way to immortal life, in which he is now established as King, and head of his Church, which he rules and preserves through his word and Spirit. Not inelegantly has Alex. pursued this sense. Morus, although he errs in that he takes צער for a sepulcher, which Piscator and B. Luther more correctly explained as all anguish, because when he was buried in the sepulcher, all things were already CONSUMMATED, nor did he stick any longer in the judgment of God, nor was the sepulcher for him a prison or penal confinement, and because Christ being dead is δεδικαίωται ἀπό τ̑ ἁμαρτίας, as Morus himself confesses, how however can he who is justified from sin still be confined by a just judge in penal confinement? Concerning the συνεχείᾳ in the text, the things he hands down are neat: The generation (of the Messiah), he says, is wonderful, not only on account of the number of the blessed seed like the number of the Stars: But also on account of the manner. For commonly indeed none generate except the living. For generation is the production of a living being from a living being to the likeness of nature. But the Messiah does not generate unless slain and dead, according to that in John 12. Amen amen I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground shall have died, it alone remains: But if it shall have died, it will bring forth much fruit. This interpretation agrees also with those things which precede: For only after the resurrection and ascension into heaven, with the Spirit poured out for the calling of the Gentiles, did he beget an innumerable offspring; and with those things which are placed below, he shall see a long-lived seed; but especially with those things which immediately follow: Because he was cut off from the land of the living. The word נגזר shows that the simile is taken from trees. The branches of trees, when cut off, sprout again, and are therefore cut off so that they may sprout again. And indeed other trees, when their roots are cut off, are both sterile and dead. Whence, in this same Prophet, the Eunuch is compared to a dry stick, which draws no sap from the earth. But the Messiah, not only after his death, will see a long-lived seed, but even then will most especially beget sons, and like new shoots and shrubs will produce them. The not unusual paronomasia of our Prophet also holds a pleasant contemplation. For he who said in ch. 11, 1, 'And a branch (נצר) shall go forth, and a shoot (מגזע) from the stump of Jesse,' now says 'cut off' (נגזר), as if he were saying 'the stump is rooted out' (נגע נגזר). Theophylact elegantly calls Christ a fruit-bearing, ever-flourishing, ever-living tree (ξύλον ἔγκαρπον, ἀειθαλὲν, ἀείζωον). Just as his birth is compared to a root and a shoot, so his death is called an excision, Dan. 9, 25: 'After LXII weeks Christ shall be cut off,' and Luke 23, 31: 'If they do this in the green wood.' That root, which earlier arose from a thirsty or living earth, now torn up from the depths of the earth, both lives and begets, and fills the whole world with an innumerable abundance of fruits. Nor does Mr. Dr. Wellerus poorly observe that to be cut off from life is indeed to be taken from the midst, cut off, Ps. 88, 6. Lam. 3, 54. but it is noted, however, at the same time that the life of Christ was vivid, because he was not to depart from this collection of miseries and the bonds of the body by natural dissolution, but was to depart by violence inflicted, not otherwise than if a tree, before it reaches its proper height, is cut down, Luke 23, 39.

There follows 'for the transgression of my people a plague to him' (מפּשׁע עמי נגע למו). Or as the Vulgate has it in the same sense, 'for the wickedness of my people I struck him.' Thus also the LXX express the meaning: 'for the iniquities of my people he was led to death' (ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνομιῶν τοῦ λαοῦ μου ἤχθη εἰς θάνατον). Others take that 'to him' (למו) in the plural, but Grotius rightly recognizes it as singular, and by epenthesis of the ם it is placed for 'to him' (לו). Others like to distinguish the text thus: 'He was cut off from the land of the living for the wickedness of my people, a plague was due to them,' but this is too clever, and does not agree with the punctuation in the source. More subtle, and also more far-fetched, is the sense of Morus, which he proposes thus: 'Thus therefore, with all respect to everyone, we interpret: He was cut off from the land of the living, and for this wickedness of my people, a plague will lie upon them (the living).' That the land of Canaan is understood by the land of the living, Ezek. 26 and 31 and elsewhere, there should be no doubt. Now indeed, from that heart of the earth, Jerusalem, Christ was cut off, and hence a plague to those Jerusalemites, the Jews living at that time, who think others dead in comparison to themselves, and the destruction of the whole land of the living. There is a double explanation by Cocceius; to the people (who held Christ for 'plagued' (מנוגע), that is, affected by a plague, and abominable) happened a 'plague' (נגע), that is, such a plague that they themselves are utterly abominable. But the Prophet is occupied not with the destruction of the Jews, but with the destruction of the Messiah, and he spends his divine Rhetoric solely on figuring its cause in various ways and 'in many parts and in many manners' (πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως) to exhibit that passion of our salvation in a way that brings it forth and seals it. Morus ought to have recalled with a mindful heart what he had said most truly and not inaptly in the preface, that these things are pure Gospel, having no burdens. I repeat his words, because, being extorted from the truth, they strangle other glosses also, which are clearly

intruded into this Evangelical chapter: In other oracles, certain streaks as it were of the Gospel are seen mixed and inserted into legal doctrines: here it is PURE Gospel. Other Prophets, and Isaiah himself elsewhere, are carried away and indeed fly up from earthly and legal things to Evangelical and heavenly ones, but they do not endure; rather, as if their flight were failing, they slip down to the earth and to the law, and are revolved back to their BURDENS. But this Isaiah perseveres in his state, and so adheres to the Messiah once found, that he cannot be torn away before he has proclaimed his whole course from the starting gates to the finish line. Hackspanius refutes Cocceius more fully in this place. St. Jerome expressed the sense best, even while explaining the words of the LXX: 'Because of the magnitude of the sins of the people, whom he always held as his own, he was led to death, so that he might recall them to life by his own death.'

Latin:

Vers. 8. DE ANGUSTIA ET DE IUDICIO SUB- LATUS EST) De carcere & de judicio ablatus est: id est, li- beratus tandem. Iudicium vocat hoc, quia specie judicii ipsa hæc mala imposita fuerant. Vide Ier. 32, 3. liberatus autem per Babylonios.

GENERATIONEM EIVS QVIS ENARRABIT?) Quis numerare poterit dies vitæ ejus ? i. e. erit valde longævus.

QVIA ABSCISSVS EST DE TERRA VIVENTI- VM) Nempe cum actus fuit primum in carcerem, deinde in lacum illum cænosum, ac rursum in carcerem.

PROPTER SCELVS POPVLI MEI PERCVSSI EVM) In Hebræo est, plaga ipsi, supple evenit, populi summo errore ac crimine, ut & ante dictum est. Quidam Codices Ebræi hic habuerunt לו, sed למו idem significat: neque enim exemplis caret ם ὑπερβολικόν.

Vim fieri textui augustissimo multa docent. Pri- mo, quod is ad liberationem per Babylonios factam abripitur: de quibus nec vola, nec vestigium in hoc toto capite. Nec vero tum ab angustia liberatus Je- remias, cum à Babyloniis è carcere dimitteretur; sed novas postmodum adversitates experiri coa- ctus fuit, cum pro mendaci ac seductore habitus est cap. 43, 2. Secundo, quod generatio inenarrabi- lis de vita Jeremiæ longæva exponitur. Nam nec generatio idem est, quod vita, nec vita etsi valde longæva sit, qualis vel ipsa Methusalæ erat, inenar- rabilis est. Tertio, quod Jeremias fingitur propter scelus populi Domini percussus: quod justitiæ divinæ contrarium esse, sæpius monuimus. Quarto, quod abscissio de terra viventium ad detrusionein Jeremiæ in carcerem & locum lutosum detorquetur. Hæc enim non fuit abscissio de terra viventium, quia vi- xit adhuc, & in terra viventium longævam vitam transegit, notante Grotio, talem, cujus dies, ut ipse nugatur, inenarrabiles. Abscissio enim de terra vi- ventium, ut phrasis ipsa docet, omnesq; Interpretes consentiunt, mortem infert, atq; ita exponitur v. 10. cum dicitur pro delicto animam suam posuisse. Hæc enim sese exponere mutuo κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν scri- pturæ familiarem, abscissus de terra viventium est, propter scelus populi percussus, sed generationem ejus quis enarrabit? Et: si posuisset pro delicto animam su- am, videbit semen longævum, minime obscurum est. Taceo, quod occisio etiam indicetur, cum sicut ovis ad mactationem vel ad occidendum ductus dicitur v. 7. Quinto refragat ur καδδιάμετρον explicationi Phi- lippi, qui hæc verba negat de Propheta ipso, aut de quoquam alio, intelligi debere, quam de Jesu: Act. 8, 34. Obsecro te, de quo Propheta dicit hoc: De se, an de alio aliquo: Quum enim hæreret rogatus Eunuchus, aperuit Philippus os suum, & incipiens à scriptura ista (Esaiæ) evangelizavit illi Jesum. Docuit ergo non de Propheta ipso, non de alio aliquo, sed de Christo solo intelligenda esse. Quod apertissime contrariatur depravationi Grotianæ. Et adhuc tamen inserere Jeremiam suum conatus est Grotius, quæ effrenis & impia viri impudentia, in Annot. ad Act. 8. quod forte de Jeremia cogitarit Philippus; sic enim ad vers. 54. nugatur: περὶ ἑαυτῦ (num de seipso lo- quitur Esaiæ) Nam & Esaias multa pertulit mala Manassis tempore, ἡ περὶ ἑτέρω τινί. Forte de Jere- mia cogitavit. At si de illo cogitavit, removit utique & exclusit etiam illum. Nam interrogatio illa sic formatur, ut tum Esaias, tum quivis alius exclu- datur, solus Christus relinquatur. Ideo additur vers. 2. ἐυαγγελήσατο ἀυτὸν τὸν Ιησῦν. Sed non defunt mille artifici hic etiam pervertendi artes. Nam de Jesu hæc exposuisse Philippum, ait, quod in ipsum omnia ista verba congruant eximio modo, hoc est, ut ipse intelligit, sensu mystico: Sic ergo putat adhuc intelligi ea secundum sensum literalem posse de Ieremia (forte etiam in animo Jeremiam habuisse Philippum) etsi mystice ea de JESU loquuntur. Sed Philippus nescivit unius dicti geminum esse sen- sum, ideoque simpliciter & de uno sensu loquutus est, & de uno subjecto sermonem esse judicavit, dum quæreret: Obsecro, de se, an de alio aliquo loqui- tur Propheta. Et, si sensu literali intellexisset Philip- pus, vel S. S. de Jeremia, sensu autem mystico id transferendum esse ad Jesum tradidisset, quomodo fidem invenisset apud Eunuchum, quem in Reli- gione Judaica informatum fuisse, tradit Grotius? Annon regere poterat Eunuchus, quid ista ad Je- sum, quia jam pridem impleta sunt in Jeremia! Ideoq; manifestum est, ita de Jesu hæc à Philippo explicari, ut negetur, de Jeremia aut alio quopiam ea ullate- nus intelligenda esse, siquidem nec ferant id verba. Nemo enim alius de terra viventium abscissus est propter scelus populi, vel postquam abscissus fuit, generationem habuit, quæ enarrari nequeat.

Jam si verba Prophetica ulterius scrutemur, plu- ra suppetent refellendæ στρεβλότητι Grotianæ & confirmandæ unice genuinæ interpretationi de Christo argumenta. DE ANGUSTIA ET DE JUDICIO SUBLATUS EST. Hæc non libera- tionem è carcere, aut è judico humano notant, sed libe- rationem ex angustia & judicio ipsius Dei. Vox עצר non carcerem sed prævalescentiam, & predominatio- nem significat, ut Forsterus in Lex. notat, adeoque angustiam infert, ut Hieronym. reddidit. LXX. τα- πείνωσιν exposuere, quem ἔνθεον Philippus reti- nuit Act. 12, 38. qua ταπεινώσει humilis factus usque ad mortem crucis est Philip. 2. Adhibetur Ebræa vox de angustia uteri Prov. 30, 16. & de angustia affli- ctionis Ps. 57, 39. Et cum supremus gradus angustiæ & ταπεινώσεως propter additam vocem judicii de- signetur, recte Dn. D. Wellerus noster dolores infer- nales intelligit, qui maxime constrinxerunt, sum- misque angustiis ipsum affecerunt. Voce משפט judicium omne, in quo angustia affectus, & coarcta- tus fuit, intelligitur, quia omni illo judicio exem- ptus est. Quod præcipue fuit Dei judicium, quia Deus fecit eum pro nobis peccatum 2. Cor. 5, 21. & ma- ledictum Gal. 3, 13. unde summæ angustiæ & dolo- res vere infernales animam ejus occuparunt. In judicio hoc exacta est pœna ab ipso, & vulneratus at- que attritus est propter peccata nostra: quod Deo tri- buitur ab Apostolo, Rom. 4. & 8. imo etiam ab Esaia: qui testatur Dominum posuisse in ipsum omnium no- strum iniquitatem. Ex judicio ergo Dei subla- tum Propheta significat, quem in judicio Dei tam graviter afflictum fuisse docuerat. Sensum LXX. Interpp. ἐν ταπεινώσει ἡ κρίσις αὐτῶ ἤρθη: sic exposuit Hieron. In humilitate judicium ejus ab- latum est, illud significat quod de tribulatione atque judicio ad Patrem victor ascenderit. Etsi tribula- tioni & angustiæ obnoxius, & in judicio Dei fue- rit, cum nostri loco condemnationem sustinuit, è judicio tamen illo sublatus est, & in libertatem as- sertus. Chaldæus voces illas ex angustia & judicio reddidit מיסרהין ומופלענו A castigatione & à pœ- na: E recentioribus Stephanus, à vinculis & à sen- tentia sublatus est de medio. Oleaster, & Münsterus de carcere sepulchri. Tremellius per coarctationem & judicium tolletur. Piscator è coarctatione animi & judicio Dei.

GENERATIONEM EJUS QUIS ENAR- RABIT? Quod de generatione æterna alii, alii de nativitate admiranda & ineffabili è Maria virgine intelligunt, ut Cyrillus & Hieronymus observa- rant, & de illa quidem Athanas. in expos. Vid. Aug. Tr. 31. in Joh. c. 7. de hac vero Justin. Dial. c. Tryph.

Tertul. adv. Jud. c. 14. l. 3. adv. Marc. c. 7. alii vero de fempiterna vitæ post resurrectionem duratione, utpo- te è recentioribus B. Luth. Tarnov. Rivet. Thar- gum de mirabilibus in diebus Messiæ patratis expli- cat, h. m. & marabilia quæ fecit nobis in diebus ejus quis poterit enarrare! Corn. à Lapide pro exclama- tione habet, qua Propheta in istam generationem, vel homines istius ætatis invehatur. Sed quia hic Prophetia de futuris habetur, & quidem de eo, quod ereptionem Messiæ è coarctatione & judicio subse- quitur, verbumque דור nuspiam notat nativitatem, nec de miraculis hic agitur, & multo minus excla- matio invectiva locum hic habet. Restat inter- precatio de duratione vitæ Messiæ inenarrabili, quæ & toti contextui congruere videtur, & peculiariter commati antecedenti, ut sit ἀντίθεσις coarctationis & judicii in statu exinanitionis, nec non felicitatis & gaudii alterius æternæ vitæ in statu exaltationis. Cui explicationi suo ponderi relictæ præferendam censemus eorum explicatioem, qui de semine Christi, & piis ex eo nascituris numero modoque nobis indicibili interpretantur, & sensum horum verbo- rum damus istum: Neminem fando efferre posse gene- rationem, genus, familiam, posteritatem, liberos Mes- siæ, & porro natorum natos, & qui nascentur ab illis. Urgemus potissimum verborum δεινότητα & usum Biblicum: Et primo quidem interrogationem, qua- lis hic occurrit, sæpe magnam rei difficultatem insi- nuare, patet è 1. Sam. 2, 25. Ps. 15, 1. Prov. 31, 10. & h. l. v. 4. nonnunquam etiam ἀδυναμίαν aliquam im- portare ἀναμφίλεκτον est. Quis enarrabit, h. e. Nemo facile enarrabit, vel nullus mortalium enarrare potest. Deinde vox דור notat proprie hominum sibi succedentium seriem, ubi aliquid ex alio nascitur, & ita in morem sphæræ in se quasi redit Es. 41, 4. vid. Schindlerus in Lex. Quum geminatur דור ודור so- let nonnunquam durationem & æternitatem notare. Sed ubi simpliciter דור ponitur, perpetuo & ubique notat generationem, liberos, genus, familiam, posterita- tem, nusquam autem sumitur pro duratione & æter- nitate. Examinavi loca omnia, quæ in Concordantiis occurrunt, & quod dixi, deprehendi. Singula huc adscribere non est operæ pretium. Accipitur ita Gen. 7, 1. c. 17, 7. 9. 12. Exod. 12, 14. 16. 42. c. 16, 32. 33. c. 17, 21. c. 30, 21. Lev. 23, 21. Num. 9, 20. c. 35, 21. Deut. 1, 38. c. 2, 14. c. 29, 22. Jos. 22, 27. 28. Jud. 2, 16. & c. 3, 2. 1. Paral. 16, 14. Ps. 12, 8. Ps. 14, 5. Ps. 22, 31. Ps. 24, 6. Ps. 49, 14. 71, 18. 63, 15. 78, 4. 6. 8. 109, 13. 112, 2. 102, 19. Prov. 30, 11. 12. seqq. Esa. 41, 4. Jer. 2, 31. c. 7, 29. Joel. 1, 3. nec ullum datur dissimile exemplum. Demum שוח, (à quo descendit יְשׂוֹחֵחַ) est medita- ri, eloqui, & tam animo quam ori tribuitur. Avenarius id confert cum שָׁחָה natare, & vult proprie signifi- care in materia spatiofa quasi natare. In hac forma bis tantum extat. Ps. 143, 5. opera manuum tuarum meditabor: vel recensebo & enarrabo. Tot sunt & tam stupenda opera manuum Dei, ut qui eadem memoria recolit velut in vasto & spatiosissimo Oceano natare animo videatur: & hoc loco: ubi eodem modo reddi potest. Ea est Messiæ generatio, eaque familia, ut quicunque meditando eam indagare præsumit, is velut in vastum mare sese præcipitet, quod enatando superare nemo queat mortalium. Quam pa- raphrasin è verborum propria significatione & u- surpatione Biblica enatam optime admittit contex- tus. Etenim quod hoc versu incipiat Prophetia de Christi exaltatione & fructibus exinanitione ejus ac- quisitis, tum res ipsa docet, tum observant doctio- res Interpp. Præcipuus autem fructus, nec postre- mus exaltationis gradus est, quod Christo resuscitato per totum terrarum orbem generentur filii, quod- que nomen ejus propagetur continuata serie, de gene- ratione in generationem, ad seram posteritatem, ut nec modus, nec numerus sit fidelium Christo servi- entium. Adhæc ideo Christus passus est sese ad sum- mas animi & corporis angustias redigi, & ad mor- tem condemnari, ut sublatus ex his angustiis & ere- ptus è judicio non jam sibi viveret, quam generationi suæ; Et ut perpetuo in Ecclesia sibi gigneret filios filias- que. Hoc sine violenter excisus est Christus arbor vitæ, ut nos, qui eramus arida ligna, ipsi inferi, & ex eo succum trahere possemus, ne igne inextincto com- bureremur. Quod verbum גָזַר in sequenti com- mate infert, vid. Gen. 15, 17. 1. Reg. 3, 25. 26. 2, Reg. 6. v. 4. Ps. 136, 13. Hab. 3, 17. Conferantur inter se hæc loca Gen. 2, 9. Apoc. 2, 7. cap. 22, 2. Luc. 23, 31. Job. 15. v. 2. 3. Matth. 3, 10. 12. Et ut omnis fructus passionis Christi redundat in Ecclesiam Christi, sic dum dici- tur per passionem id obtinuisse, ut sibi colligeret Ecclesiam, hoc uno verbo comprehenditur, quic- quid est beneficiorum morte Christi acquisitorum. Quæ est causa, quod hic iterum iterumque fructum istum explicet & è passione Christi deducat Evan- gelii prænunciator apertior, ut Esaiam vocat D. Au- gustinus. Quod itaque v. 13. ait Messiam semen visu- rum spirituale, quia anima ejus h. e. ipse (nam נֶפֶשׁ anima quandoque in linguis Orientalibus idem est quod ipse, conf. Jer. LI, 14. Amos 6, 8. cum Gen. 22, 16. Ebr. 6, 16. 17. item Matth. 20, 28. Marc. 10, 45. cum 1. Tim. 2, 6.) sese posuit, vel dedit sacrificium pro reatu peccatorum: Quod v. 15. Jehovah dicit, par- tem dabo ei pro multis, hoc est, in salutem Ecclesiæ. Conf. Ps. 68, 19. Eph. 4, 8. ut ב pro מ accipiatur, quemadmodum alias Gen. 11, 4. Levit. 16, 22. Psal. 18, 50. Psal. 12, 6. vel si emphasis vocis יַחֲלֹק atten- datur, dabo ei hæreditatem inter multos, quomodo R. Salomo explicat אחלק לו נחלה וגוחר distri- buam ei possessionem & fortes, & LXX. διὰ τοῦτο αὐ- τὸς κληρονομήσει πολλοὺς, ideo ipse possidebit multos quasi hæreditario, quia tradidit morti animam suam & peccata multorum (h. e. omnium, teste Apostolo Rom. 5, 19. cum quo facit Calvinus in h. l. adversus Musculum, & alios, qui à se nomen habent) ipse tu- lit: Idem omnino indicare videtur Propheta v. 11. cum generationem & posteritatem Mesiæ dicit fore ἀνάριθμον, quoniam propter prævaricationem populi Dei afflictus fuit, & de terra viventium abscissus. Idem hic effectus, eadem causa, eadem effectus & causæ cohærentia. Saltim verba diversa sunt, quæ eleganti varietate rem eandem exhibent.

Sequitur nunc in textu: QUI ABSCISSUS EST DE TERRA VIVENTIUM. PRO- PTER SCELUS POPULI MEI PERCUS- SI EUM. Quæ causam exponunt generationis Messiæ spiritualis, & explicantur deinde à Prophe- ta hoc modo: Dominus voluit conterere eum in in- firmitate, si posuerit pro peccato animam suam, vide- bit semen longævum. Quid enim aliud est: Percuf- sit eum propter scelus populi, quam, Dominus voluit eum conterere in infirmitate pro peccato, vel propter peccatum? Quid aliud est abscissus de terra viven- tium, quam posuit animam suam? quid aliud gene- rationem ejus nemo enarrabit, quam videbit semen longævum! Equidem circa hoc comma octavum, in quo versamur, de angustia & judicio &c. variant Interpp. in reddendo sensu literali de Christo: alii de passione adhuc intelligunt, alii de exemptione è passione per resurrectionem & glorificationem. Ex il- lis nonnulli ita exponunt, absque ulla culpa, seditione Judæorum & Pilati voce damnatus est, ut est apud Hieronymum: Alii raptus & tractus est à populo seu Synagoga, & à judicio seu Pharisæis, uti Forerius & Castalio exposuit; A cætu populi & Synagoga pro- tractus vel ductus est. Et Vatablus; absque dilatione citraque judicium raptus est &c. Sed contortæ sunt il- læ explicationes. Simplicior est, quæ de ereptione ex angustia & judicio accipit : Nam vox לקח acceptus, assumtus est, etsi varia significet, optime respondet voci Apostolicæ ἀνέληψον, ac emphatice notat libe- ratum esse ASCENSU & assumptione in cœlestem gloriam, nec aliter accepit S.S. Act. 8. ἤρθη ἡ κρίσις, quæ voces trahi non possunt ad passionem, sed o- mnino pertinent ad gloriam, quod sublatum sit judi- cium ; & nullus est sensus, si dicas, de angustia sub- latus est de medio : neque cohærebit ita quod sequi- tur de generatione inenarrabili ; quod etiam non satis apte videtur inchoare descriptionem resurre- ctionis & gloriæ, quia generationem illam & po- steritatem spiritualem præcessit victoria de morte ac ascensio in cœlum. Et omnia rectius fluent, si di- catur ereptus ex omni angustia, imprimis animi, & è judicio Dei sublatus in cælum genus habuisse, quod ne- mo fando exprimere vel enumerare possit : ut inenar- rabilem angustiam in illo judicio inenarrabilis glo- ria, cum inde liberatus est, & felicitas ac succeslus consequatur; ejusque causa hic denuo inculcetur, (quia nunquam satis ad nostri erectionem & conso- lationem inculcari potest) quia sc. abscissus est de ter- ra viventium, quando Dominus ita ipsum percussit propter scelus populi ; quum ergo ita animam suam posuerit pro peccato hominum in sacrificium, attri- tus à Domino nunc semen longævum & genus in- enarrabile videt ; & exhilaratur pro ista anxietate fructu isto lætissimo spiritualis sui seminis, & ge- neris, ceu summis delitiis suis. Recte ergo B. Luthe- rus : Confitetur hic Propheta eum resuscitatum, quia ante dixit eum sicut victimam mactatum esse. Hactenus mortis verba tantum fuerunt, jam in contrariam par- tem vertitur, & dicit, Christus non est mortuus, est susce- ptus à Deo. Sic autem non loqueretur de mortuo homi- ne, manente in sepulchro. Necesse igitur est, ut de resur- rectione hac intelligamus. Per Pilatum est judicatus sed rursus sublatus de judicio est. Et ad illa de terra non vi- ventium &c. Pertinent & hæc ad resurrectionem. Non autem frustra est quod repetit tum passionem Christi tum finem passionis, quod propter nos passus est. Vult e- nim hunc articulum alte nostris animis impressum, ut non sic audiamus Christi passionem, sicut aliam histo- riam audimus, sed potius ut usum ac finem spectemus, quod propter nostra peccata sit passus. Quod autem di- cit, eum abscissum de terra viventium, significat du- plicem esse vitam : Aliam eorum, qui hic vivunt in ter- ra, & aliam Christi, æternam scilicet & novam. Ergo Iu- dæi frustra eum expectant : Est enim de hac vita abscis- sus, cum supplicio crucis afficeretur. Inde transivit in aliam vitam, sicut dicit : Vado ad Patrem meum. Sic Christi passio nihil fuit aliud, quam acceptio de angu- stia, & via ad immortalem vitam, in qua nunc est con- stitutus Rex, & caput Ecclesiæ suæ, quam per verbum & Spiritum suum regit & servat. Non ineleganter hunc sensum persequutus est Alex. Morus, etsi in eo aberret quod צער de sepulchro accipiat, quod de angustia omni rectius exposuit Piscator, & B. Lutherus, quia cum in sepulchro conderetur, jam CONSUMMATA erant omnia, nec hærebat am- plius in judicio Dei, neque sepulchrum ipsi pro carcere aut pœna carceraria fuit, & quod mortuus Christus est δεδικαίωται ἀπό τ̑ ἁμαρτίας, ut Mo- rus ipse fatetur, quomodo autem justificatus à pec- cato, pœna carceraria à justo judice adhuc con- cludi potest? De συνεχείᾳ in textu concinna sunt, quæ tradit : Mirabilis, inquit, generatio (Messiæ est) non tantum ob numerum benedicti seminis instar nu- meri Stellarum : Sed etiam ob modum. Nam vulgo quidem non generant nisi viventes. Est enim generatio productio viventis à vivente ad similitudinem naturæ. At Messias non generat nisi occisus & mortuus, jux- ta illud Joh. 12. Amen amen dico vobis, nisi gra- num frumenti cadens in terram mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet: Si autem mortuum fuerit, fru- ctum multum afferet. Convenit hæc interpretatio & cum iis, quæ præcedunt: Nam post resurrectionem de- mum & ascensionem in cælum effuso Spiritu ad voca- tionem gentium innumerabilem sobolem procreavit; & cum iis quæ subjiciuntur, videbit semen longæ- vum; sed maxime cum iis, quæ statim sequuntur: Quoniam excisus est de terra viventium. Vox נגזר ostendit ab arboribus desumptam esse similitudinem. Rami arborum excisi repullulant atque ideo ex- scinduntur ut repullulent. Et cæteræ quidem arbo- res, excisæ radices, & steriles, & mortuæ sunt. Vn- de apud hunc ipsum Prophetam arido ligno compa- ratur Eunuchus, quod succum ex terra nullum tra- hit. At Messias non tantum post mortem suam videbit semen longævum, sed etiam tunc maxime generabit filios, & tanquam novella germina, fruticesque produ- cet. Jucundam etiam contemplationem habet non in- solens Prophetæ nostri paronomasia. Nam qui dixit c. 11, 1. Et egredietur נצר, & מגזע surculus de stipite Isaia, nunc dicit נגזר quasi diceret נגע נגזר stipes ex- stirpatus est. Theophylactus eleganter vocat Christum ξύλον ἔγκαρπον, ἀειθαλὲν κ, ἀείζωον frugiferum, semper floridum, semper vivum. Ut nativitas ejus cum radice ac surculo comparatur, ita mors ejusdem excisio dicitur Dan. 9, 25. Post LXII. hebdomadas exscindetur Christus, & Luc. 23, 31. Si hoc in viridi ligno faciunt. Radix illa superius orta è terra sitienti seu viventi nunc avulsa funditus è terra & vivit & generat, & universum implet orbem innumera fru- ctuum copia. Nec male observat Dn. D. Wellerus è vita abscindi esse quidem è medio tolli, excidi Psal. 88, 6. Thren. 3, 54. sed notari tamen simul ætatem Christi vividam, quod non ex hac colluvie & ærum- nis vinculis corporis naturali dissolutione digredien- dum, sed vi illata decedendum fuerit, non secus ac si arbor antequam ad justam perveniat proceritatem, excidatur Luc. 23, 39.

Sequitur מפּשׁע עמי נגע למו à prævaricatione populi mei plaga ipsi. Vel ut Vulgata habet sensu eo- dem propter scelus populi mei percussieum. Sic etiam exprimunt sententia LXX. ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνομιῶν τοῦ λαοῦ μου ἤχθη εἰς θάνατον A peccatis, vel propter peccata po- puli mei adductus est in mortem. Alii in plurali accipi- unt illud למו, sed recte agnoscit Grot. singulare ac per Epenthesin ם id positum pro לו. Aliis placet ita textum distinguere: Excisus est de terra viventium propter scelus populi mei, plaga illis sc. debebatur, sed hoc argutius est, nec congruit distinctioni in fonte. Subtilior est, & longius petitus etiam est sensus Mo- ri: quem ita proponit: Sic igitur pace omnium inter- pretamur: Excisus est à terra viventium & propter hoc scelus populi mei plaga illis (viventibus) in- cumbet. Quin terra Canaan per terram viventium intelligatur Ezech. 26, & 31. & alibi, dubitari non debet. Iam vero ex illius corde terræ Hierosolymis exci- sus est Christus & hinc plaga Hierosolymitanis illis, viventibus illo tempore Judæis, qui cæteros præ se mortuos putant, & excidium totius terræ viventium. Gemina explicatio est Cocceji; populo (qui Chri- stum pro מנוגע id est, plaga affecto, & abominando habuit) contigit נגע id est, ejusmodi plaga, ut ipsi sint abominabiles prorsus. At Propheta non in exi- tio Judæorum, sed in excidio Messiæ occupatur, ejus- que causam ut variis figuret modis atq; πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως passionem illam salutis nostræ pro- mam condam exhibeat, unice Rhetoricam suam divinam impendit. Memori mente recoluisse debe- bat Morus, quod in præfatione verissime, nec in- concinne dixerat, merum hæc Evangelium, nulla onera habere. Repeto ejus verba, quia à veritate extorta, alias etiam glossas, quæ in hoc caput plane

Evangelicum intruduntur, jugulant : In aliis oracu- lis quædam velut Evangelii stricturæ legalibus doctri- nis permixtæ ac insertæ visuntur : hic MERUM Evangelium est. Alii Prophetæ, ipseque adeo Esaias alibi, rapiuntur & subvolant quidem à rebus terre- nis, & legalibus ad Evangelicas, & cælestes, at non perdurant, sed volatu quasi fatiscente dilabuntur in terram & ad legem, adque ONERA sua revolvuntur. Hic vero Esaias perseverat in statu, & ita Messiæ se- mel invento inhæret, ut ante non possit avelli, quam totum ejus cursum à carceribus ad metam præconia- verit. Coccejum plenius refellit Hackspanius in h. l. Optime autem sensum expressit S. Hierony- mus, etsi τῶν ὁ verba explicans : Propter magni- tudinem peccatorum populi, quem semper peculiarem habuit, ductus ad mortem est, ut illos ad vitam sua morte revocaret.

## 53:9
Ver. 9.

AND HE SHALL GIVE THE WICKED FOR HIS BURIAL, AND THE RICH MAN FOR HIS DEATH.) They had wanted to kill him too, as we read in Jer. 26. But God, in his place, gave to death through the Chaldeans men who were indeed powerful, but wicked, namely the Priests who had plotted the death of Jeremiah, 2 Kings 25, 18, 19, 20, 21. Their riches, by which they had hoped they could be redeemed, profited them nothing. The Greeks expressed this sense well. BECAUSE HE HAD NOT DONE INIQUITY, NEITHER WAS DECEIT IN HIS MOUTH.) Although he had said nothing other than what God had commanded him.

We will not adhere to an impious distortion of the text. For however in any way the Priests could be understood by the 'wicked' (which gloss, however, is merely precarious), however they could also be understood by the name of the 'rich man' (which, however, is not proven, nor can it be proven), it is most false that this deals with the Chaldeans here, and the destruction made by them: it is impious to distort those words, which sound of Christ alone, to Jeremiah: and no less impious to accept as referring to the rightly administered office of the Prophet those things which exhibit the total innocence and sinlessness (ἀναμαρτησίαν) of Christ. For nothing is more evident than that those words, BECAUSE HE HAD NOT DONE INIQUITY, NEITHER WAS DECEIT IN HIS MOUTH, remove every sin, whether committed by deeds, or by words, or by the mind, from this subject. For he who neither did any iniquity, nor any deceit, he is truly devoid of all sin. Nor does Holy Scripture interpret this sentence otherwise than concerning absolute innocence, 1 Pet. 2; indeed, in this text it is asserted as many times as He Himself is said to have been wounded for our sins, struck for the transgression of the people, and things similar to these: for there it is denied that He was struck for His own sins, and His innocence is asserted. Therefore, these things can be understood of no one else but the Messiah, who alone is ἀναμάρτητος. This, says Jerome, can be understood of no man at all, that he has sinned neither in deed nor in word, the Scripture saying: No one is clean from filth, even if his life has been but one day long, and we all like sheep have gone astray, everyone has turned aside to his own way, except for Him who bore our sins, and suffers for us, and was wounded for our iniquities, and was afflicted for our crimes, by whose death we are healed. He now excuses Christ, says Blessed Luther, and says He was most innocent, who harmed no one either in word or in life. For this is the highest innocence, to have harmed no one, neither by word nor by deed. Most innocent, therefore, judged for the most guilty. But since we have an interpreter superior to every exception, St. Peter, who in 1 Epist. 2, with a clear voice testified that no one else is to be understood here than CHRIST, who suffered for us, left us an example, that we may follow his footsteps: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth; what need is there of other arguments to slaughter the στρεβλότητα [perversity] of Grotius? who finally in his Annotations on the Petrine passage seems not obscurely to acknowledge that these things must be taken κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν [according to the letter] concerning Christ, expressing this meaning of the words brought from Isaiah: Christ was led to death by no crime of his own, Luke 23:41, John 8:46.

Since, therefore, there ought to be no doubt about the subject, nor should any Christian be in doubt; one must labor more on the true meaning of these words, concerning which opinions vary greatly. The LXX Interpreters rendered it, 'And I will give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death': to whom Grotius appeals in vain, as they have nothing concerning Jeremiah, nor perhaps did they dream of him. Cyril interprets them thus: 'It seems in these words he wishes to signify, and to show that to be true which we have already said, in that they were very impious and most iniquitous who were incited against the people of God, and therefore Christ was taken away to death.' For, he says, since they raged impiously against him, and killed the Prince of life, inconsiderately exercising impiety even against him who saves: hence also, and indeed very deservedly, the wicked and the rich, he says, I will give for his burial, and for his death, into the hands of enemies. For in two ways the Jews had offended, both because they killed the Lord, and because they slandered his burial. Jerome rendered a nearly similar meaning, that God, after the Lord's passion, handed over to the Romans and subjected to eternal servitude the Scribes and Pharisees and Sadducees, the Priests and High Priests, who formerly reigned among the people and abounded in various riches, and in that sense the wicked and the rich were handed over for his burial and death. Analogous is Hackspan's gloss about the crowd of the wicked being thrust into the sepulcher which they had prepared for the innocent (Messiah), and about the rich (assessors of the Sanhedrin) paying the judgment of death and similar punishments for his (Messiah's) death. But even if the Jews were handed over because of the crucifixion and killing of CHRIST, they are not to be said to have been handed over because of his burial. Nor is a change designated in the Hebrew text, as the Vulgate rendered it with the LXX Interpreters. that the wicked are to be given for the burial, whence the foundation of that and the Grotian gloss collapses. Furthermore, the matter here is not about the final destruction of the Jews, but about the passion, death, and burial of Christ, whose emptying and exaltation the Prophet describes. Finally, it does not appear how that gloss squares with the words of the Prophet: 'he gave the wicked his sepulcher,' that is, because of his death he handed over the wicked to the avenging hands of enemies, or thrust the wicked into the sepulcher which they had prepared for the innocent, 'and the rich in his deaths,' that is, those rich men from among the Jews who were assessors of the Sanhedrin, into the judgment of death for his death, as Hackspan encrusts that gloss. That it is brought into the text, not brought out of the same, is too clear. And Theodoret ought to have recognized this. Hackspan's own words, who to verse 8 [adds] a similar depravation (To the people who held Christ as one afflicted by a plague and abominable, such a plague happened that they themselves are utterly abominable:) 'It is certain,' he says, 'that in this chapter two things are mainly treated, namely who pays the penalties, and for what cause. The former is the Messiah, the latter the sins of all men, even of the Jews.' Therefore, the punishment which awaits the Jews because of the contempt of Christ is not predicted here. No one, at any rate, elicits this meaning from those words. Others wish the burial and death of the wicked to be indicated here, to be inflicted upon them by Christ the judge, and to that end they snatch away the Chaldean paraphrase: 'he will hand over the wicked to Gehenna and the rich of riches, who have done iniquitously, to the death of perdition.' Raymond Martin does not deny this in Pugio Fidei, page 430. Note: just as the Prophet described him through the merit of his passion as the Redeemer of the faithful; so he described him through the power of his Deity as the damner of the unfaithful, where he says in chapter 53, ויתן את־רשעים קברו, 'and he will give the wicked into the sepulcher, or into his pit.' Explaining which, the Targum of Jonathan says, וימסר ית רשיעיא לגיהנם, 'and he will hand over the wicked to Gehenna.' But since those things are twisted, most acknowledge that these things pertain to the sepulcher and death of Christ. But some refer them to the manner, others to the fruit of the burial and death. The former vary again: Zwingli explains it thus: 'A sepulcher will be given to him with the wicked.' Sepulcher is put for slaughter by synecdoche. For he was killed among thieves. AND EXALTATION AMONG ROBBERS, i.e., whose punishment or authority and dignity will find an end with the fortune of robbers. Which, however, anyone can see to be intricate and twisted. For the sepulcher is distinguished here from death, and does not denote death. Nor can exaltation be chiseled out of the word במותיו, much less crucifixion, or dignity or authority. Finally, how will it be taught that עשיר denotes robbers? Therefore, no one among the Zwinglians has followed that perplexed gloss. Oecolampadius translates it thus: 'and he gave his sepulcher with the wicked, and his high places with the rich, i.e., Mausoleums.' He gives this interpretation, however: 'he will kill by crucifying, as the wicked, and he will kill as the rich, who are killed not because of crimes, but because of riches': but who will draw any certain meaning from that! I believe that Oecolampadius hardly understood himself. And why does he mention a sepulcher with a Mausoleum, if he wishes to indicate nothing other than death! This is the ἐξήγησις [exegesis] of Junius: The people of the Jews gave the sepulcher of Christ to the wicked, i.e., to the Gentiles, i.e., handed him over to the nations to be killed, and to the rich, i.e. to Pilate, that he might put him to death, not because they saw anything in him worthy of death, but on the contrary, because they could not endure his justice and integrity. But that [interpretation] is rightly rejected by Rivet: Because it can hardly be shown from any other similar phrase that TO GIVE BURIAL is understood as to deliver to death. Furthermore, the name of the rich man is in no way restricted to Pilate: therefore he considers that interpretation forced. We add that the word HE GAVE is wrongly referred to the people of the Jews, when it ought rather to be referred to Christ. What Calvin explains concerning God the Father, in this way, that God delivered Christ into the hands of the wicked, and of the rich or of the rich violators, so that by the wicked and the rich the same thing is signified, and the Pharisees and Priests, Pilate and the Roman soldiers are noted. But he accepts SEPULCHRE metaphorically, because the wicked and violent overwhelmed him as it were, so that he could be considered buried between them and their bloodstained hands, but this is forced. Not much different is the interpretation of Grotius, which he delivered in his book on the truth of the Christian religion, V. n. XIX: He was given even unto death and burial into the hands of the powerful and the wicked, when nevertheless he had done injury to no one.
