Asyndeton est, non absque emphasi, adhibetur autem illa figura ad commotiores & ce- leriores animi affectus judicandos, quasi dicas, sta- tim & largissime omnibus circumfundetur bonis. שבע non de quacunque saturitate explicandum, sed peculiari modo & stylo Scripturæ gaudium expri- mit, quo satiabuntur electi in altera vita, Ps. 16, 3. 17, 15. 22, 27. 65, 6. 91, 16. ut recte notavit B. Tar- novius: Unde hanc paraphrasin elicit Dn. D. Wel- lerus: Laborandum quidem erit animæ ejus ob pri- mævam Adami transgressionem, veruntamen ereptus singulari delectatione & suavitate bona intuebitur usque sine tædio abunde in vita æterna perfruetur. Quæ tamen de gaudio, quod percipit ex semine suo spirituali Messias, præcipue intelligenda censemus. Nam non ob suam adeo felicitatem lætatur, sed ob successum prosperum in opere & beneplacito Domini, in propagatione Ecclesiæ, quemadmodum sua passio- ne non sibi, sed nobis gaudia parare voluit, ac no- stra salus summæ ejus deliciæ. Quem sensum con- sequentia firmant: VIDEBIT ET SATURA- BITUR IN SCIENTIA SUA, JUSTIFICA- BIT IPSE JUSTUS SERVUS MULTOS. Per resurrectionem Christus non modo ipse immen- sis bonis ditatus, & satietate gaudii cœlestis perfu- sus est, sed communicat ea cum suis, & ex eo gau- dia summa percipit.

## 53:11
Vers. eod. IN HIS KNOWLEDGE.) Through the knowledge of God which he has.

HE THE JUST SERVANT HIMSELF SHALL JUSTIFY MANY.) By his example and instruction he shall correct many even from the Gentiles. This is the most proper signification of the verb הצדיק, and of the Greek δικαιοῦν, which appears from Dan. 12:3, Apoc. 22:11, and often elsewhere. From this proper signification others flow by a certain similarity.

AND HE HIMSELF SHALL BEAR THEIR INIQUITIES.) That is, they take away, by metonymy, because those who take away some filth are accustomed to carry it by placing it upon their neck. Thus also you have נשא for to take away, Num. 16:15, 2 Kings 20:17, and it is translated by ἴκοσπᾶι, ἀνάιρειν, ἀφαιρεῖν. Jeremiah took away the sins of many, in such a way as we have said, by correcting them.

The more evident the words of the truly Evangelical Prophet are here again concerning the manner of our justification before God, the more is the Grotian κενοδοξία [vainglory] to be detested. For the cause of justification, both organic, and meritorious, and formal, is so designated here that this Evangelical aphorism seems written by the very rays of the Sun. The organic and instrumental cause is faith. IN HIS KNOWLEDGE. For parallel passages prove that the suffix is to be translated passively, Job 17:3, Luke 1:17, 1 John 4:12, Jer. 9:33, 1 Cor. 1:30, 31, just as it is taken in Hos. 13:14, provided that, as Kimchi notes, suffixes fall both into the agent and the patient, but according to the diversity of the matter are taken now actively, now passively. That knowledge, however, according to the custom of the Hebrews, brings in an affection of trust, not bare and theoretical, but joined with trust and practical, as is evident from the Pauline explanation in the proper seat of the doctrine concerning justification. Rom. 3:24 ff. Since the act of justification is attributed to this knowledge, it is necessary that the fiducial knowledge of Christ be understood, to which alone justification is actually attributed. Doctrine indeed also contributes to justification, but because not all who are taught are justified, and faith immediately touches justice and procures it for us, therefore faith is understood here, to which justification is perpetually ascribed. And Kimchi himself confesses that knowledge of him ought to be rendered here, comparing Is. 11:9, The earth is filled with the knowledge of Jehovah. The meritorious cause is THE JUST SERVANT, as the explanation is added, he himself shall bear their iniquities. Who cannot be understood as Jeremiah. For the JUST man is designated as such, who is entirely innocent, devoid of all sin, in whom neither any iniquity nor deceit is found: and thus God the Father here pronounces Christ, whom He had reckoned with the wicked, now just: nay, he is called the JUST SERVANT on account of the perfect obedience, both active and passive, which he rendered to God in this service, for the sake of our salvation, to expiate our injustice, and to bring back eternal righteousness Ps. 40. Who is also called the righteous branch and our righteousness by Jeremiah ch. 23, 6. And Jeremiah himself was not absolutely righteous by himself, nor did he justify others by the knowledge of himself as the righteous servant of God. This is proper to the Messiah alone. Brentius rightly says: God the Father had many other servants from the very beginning of the world, Abraham, Moses, David, and other Patriarchs and Kings, but none of them was so faithful a servant that he fulfilled the whole will of God, and performed all righteousness and obedience. Wherefore none of them could by his own virtue attain righteousness, so far was it from the case that he could render others righteous by the knowledge of himself. But Christ alone, the Son of God, was so faithful a servant that he completed all parts of righteousness and obedience in the commands of God his Father, both by doing and by suffering. Wherefore he alone obtained that not only he himself should be pronounced righteous before the tribunal of God his Father, but also that all who know him should be reckoned righteous before God. This is most strongly convinced by those things which the Prophet adds: AND HE HIMSELF BORE THEIR INIQUITIES. For this does not apply to Jeremiah, or to any other, but to Christ alone. He very badly per verts that phrase, Grotius translates it as if סבל denotes removal here, and as if the removal of iniquity were effected in no other way than the Prophet indicates, as if by way of correction. But here the word נשא is not used, which sometimes occurs with the meaning of taking away, but סבל, which is 'he bore' and is used regarding a burden imposed upon the shoulders, Is. 46, 4. 7, and also regarding the burden of sin, Lam. 5, 17. Nor is there any doubt that where the word סבל of bearing is joined with sin, the suffering of punishment is implied. Since Grotius himself inculcated this rule against Socinus, he now cuts the nerve of the same, explaining the bearing of iniquities as mere doctrinal correction, that is, perverting the mind of the Prophet against his own conscience, which is the mark of those who are τῶν αὐτοκατακρίτων (self-condemned). We repeat his own words from Defens. fid. Cathol. p. 11. In the Hebrew it is ועונתם הוא יסבל. Moreover, the word עון signifies iniquity, and also the punishment of iniquity, as in 2 Kings 7, 9. Moreover, the word סבל is to sustain, to bear; and as often as 'to bear' is placed with the noun of sin or iniquity, in every language, and especially in Hebraism, it signifies to bear punishments. For while nasa indeed sometimes signifies to take away, sabal, however, never does. Therefore, it is expressly said here that Christ will bear the punishments of those who are justified. This phrase admits no other interpretation. Nor is it an objection that this bearing of iniquity in the Prophet seems to be placed after the resurrection. For the Prophet opposes the glory of Christ, as it were, to his preceding passions, sometimes in a natural order, sometimes in an inverted order, because by placing the effect, he renders the cause. Thus, after the mention of eternal duration, destruction, and the plague, there is a mention in v. 8. Then in v. 10, after the contrition and disease and sacrifice, the seed, longevity, and prosperity are named, to which are joined deliverance from trouble and the justification of many in v. 11. The Prophet returns again to the punishments endured for sins, and adds that it would therefore come to pass that he would divide the spoil, because, namely, he had given himself to death, being numbered with the transgressors. For it was fitting that he who had borne the sins of many should have the right of interceding for them, verse 12. But what Socinus says, that this word sabal, when joined to sin, does not always include some imputation, but that it is enough if it designates that someone is afflicted on the occasion of any deed of another, he proves by no example, nor does Holy Scripture ever speak in that way. Indeed, even Greek and Latin authors, when they use that phrase, always include imputation. To strengthen this exception, Socinus cites a passage from Jeremiah, which is as follows: Our fathers have sinned, and are not; and we have borne their punishments, Lam. 5, 7; nor does this allow any imputation to be understood here. But by what argument does he prove that this phrase signifies something else here than in all other places where it appears? Socinus himself is forced to admit that as often as sons follow the footsteps of their fathers, not only their own but also their fathers' sins are imputed to them. For it is the manifest voice of God, Exod. 20, 5. That those, however, with whom Jeremiah deals were similar to their parents is shown by what follows in the Prophet: Woe to us, for we have sinned, v. 16. Nor is this foreign to Jeremiah's purpose. For in order to exaggerate the misery of those who were living at that time, he says that the punishments of both their own and their ancestors' crimes redound upon them: and that therefore the lot of their parents was perhaps much better than theirs, who, though equally guilty, had nevertheless been removed from life before these most bitter torments were finally poured out all at once, as if stored up in the treasury of divine wrath. Even if the meaning of these words, 'to bear sins,' were ambiguous in the sacred writings, nevertheless, both this passage of Isaiah and that of Peter would make the interpretation certain by the added mention of the sufferings of Christ and our liberation. For to bear sins by suffering, and in such a way that others are liberated thereby, can judge nothing else than the taking upon oneself of another's punishment. These are Grotius's words there, which we have abundantly demonstrated to be entirely solid against the heresy of Socinus in our vindications for Grotius against Crellius, undertaken at Königsberg 24 years ago, the summary of which we subsequently presented in 'Socinismo profligato' in the article on the satisfaction of Christ. The formal cause of justification is designated both by the word HE SHALL JUSTIFY, which is forensic, and which justification is opposed to condemnation; and by the knowledge of Christ are justified those whose iniquities he bore, that is, they are absolved from iniquities; and Christ justifies many by his knowledge, as the just servant of God, bearing their iniquity, that is, by his obedience, both active, by which as a just servant he fulfilled all righteousness, since by the obedience of this one many are justified, Rom. 5, 18, and passive, by which he bore our sins, by sustaining their punishment, whence they are not imputed to us, because they were imputed to him in the judgment of God, 2 Cor. 5, 21. This most illustrious sentiment of the Prophet, Grotius tries in vain to obscure with his dark glosses. For even if perhaps elsewhere the word for justifying were used regarding erudition and justice, here, however, the forensic sense is so clear that it cannot be understood as mere erudition or correction. Although he has not even proved that it is used anywhere for correction or doctrine alone. Certainly, those passages cited do not prove it. For in Dan. 12, 3, the word can properly be taken regarding those who have justified others, namely, regarding the teachers of the word, to whom it is attributed ministerially that they justify, regenerate, and save others, whence they are also called Saviors in the Scriptures. In the other saying, however, Apoc. 22, 11, that notion of justifying as correction has no place at all. For it is not a matter of teachers, but of the just, who are warned to devote effort so that they may continue to remain just, and be justified, and be preserved in justice. But what Grotius says, that that meaning, to justify by correction or instruction, is proper to this word, and that other meanings flow from it by a certain similarity, that is at least gratuitously invented, and enjoys no plausibility; how does the forensic meaning, when it denotes absolution, flow from that fictitious meaning?

Latin:

Vers. eod. IN SCIENTIA SUA.) Per eam, quam habet, Dei cognitionem.

IVSTIFICABIT IPSE IVSTVS SERVVS MEVS MVLTOS. ). Exemplo & institutione sua corriget mul- tos etiam ex gentibus. Hæc est maxime propria verbi הצדיק, & Græci δικαιοῦν significatio, quæ apparet ex Dan. 12, 3. Apoc. 22, 11. & alibi sæpe. Ab hoc significatu pro- prio alii per similitudinem quandam fluunt.

ET INIQVITATES EORVM IPSE PORTABIT.) Id est auferunt, per Metonymiam, quia qui sordes aliquas auferunt, solent eas collo supposito portare. Sic & נשא pro auferre habes, Num. 16, 15. 2. Reg. 20, 17. vertiturque per ἴκοσπᾶι, ἀνάιρειν, ἀφαιρεῖν. Abstulit Ieremias multorum peccata, ita ut diximus eos corrigendo.

Quo evidentiora hic iterum sunt verba Prophe- tæ vere Evangelici de ratione justificationis nostræ coram Deo, eo magis detestanda est Grotiana κενοδοξία. Nam designatur hic ita justificationis causa tum organica, tum meritoria, tum formalis, ut aphoris- mus iste Evangelicus ipsis Solis radiis scriptus vi- deatur. Causa organica & instrumentalis est fides. IN SCIENTIA SUI. Affixum enim passive ver- tendum esse, loca parallela evincunt Job. 17. 3. Luc. 1, 17. 1. Joh. 4, 12. Jer. 9, 33. 1. Cor. 1, 30. 31. uti accipi- tur Hos. 13, 14. siquidem Kimchio notante affixa ca- dant & in argentem & in patientem, sed pro diversi- tate materiæ modo active, modo passive accipiantur. Cognitio autem illa, more Ebræis usitato, affectum fiduciæ infert, non nuda, & theoretica, sed cum fi- ducia conjuncta & practica, ut è Paulina explica- tione in propria sede doctrinæ de justificatione constat. Rom. 3, 24. seqq. Quum enim tribuatur justificationis actus huic cognitioni, necessum est cognitionem fiducialem Christi intelligi, cui soli actu justificatio tribuitur. Facit quidem etiam do- ctrina ad justificationem, sed quia non omnes, qui docentur justificantur, & immediate attingit justi- tiam fides, eamque nobis conciliat, ideo fides hic intelligitur, cui perpetuo justificatio adscribitur. Et fatetur ipse Kimchi, hic scientiam sui reddi de- bere, conferens Es. 11, 9. Repleta est terra scientia Jehovæ. Causa meritoria est SERVUS JUSTUS, ut additur explicatio, iniquitates eorum ipse porta- bit. Qui non potest intelligi Jeremias. Nam JU- STUS talis designatur, qui prorsus innocens, omnis peccati expers, in quo nec iniquitas ulla, nec dolus invenitur: adeoque Deus Pater hic Christum, quem cum iniquis reputarat, justum nunc pronunciat: imo SERVUS JUSTUS dicitur ob perfectam obe- dientiam tum activam, tum passivam, quam in hoc servitio Deo præstitit, nostræ salutis ergo, ad ex- piandam 'nostram injustitiam, & reducendam æ- ternam justitiam Ps. 40. Qui etiam germen justum & justitia nostra nuncupatur à Jerem. c. 23, 6. Ac Je- remias nec ipse per se absolute justus fuit, nec alios ceu servus Dei justus, sui cognitione justificavit. Hoc uni Messiæ proprium est. Recte Brentius: Habuit Deus Pater multos alios servos jam inde ab initio orbis terræ, Abrahamum, Mosen, Davidem, & alios Patriarchas ac Reges, sed nullus eorum tam fidelis servus fuit, ut impleverit omnem voluntatem Dei, & præstiterit omnem justitiam ac obedientiam. Quare nullus eorum potuit sua virtute consequi ju- stitiam, tantum abfuit, ut alios ex sui cognitione ju- stos redderet. Solus autem Christus filius Dei, tam fidelis servus fuit, ut in mandatis Dei Patris sui ab- solverit omnes partes justitiæ & obedientiæ tam fa- ciendo, quam patiendo. Quare solus hic impetravit, ut non ipse tantum pronunciaretur coram tribunali Dei Patris sui justus, verum etiam, ut omnes cogno- scentes ipsum reputarentur coram Deo justi. Quod maxime convincunt ea, quæ addit Propheta: ET INIQUITATES EORUM IPSE PORTA- VIT. Non enim Jeremiæ, aut ulli alii, sed soli Christo hoc convenit. Phrasin eam pessime per- vertit Grotius, ac si סבל ablationem hic notet, nec alia ratione ablatio iniquitatis facta sit, quam indi- gitat Propheta, quasi per correctionem. At hic non habetur verbum נשא quod quandoque auferendi significatu occurrit, sed סבל, quod est bajulavit & de onere humeris imposito adhibetur Ef. 46, 4. 7. nec non de onere peccati, Thren. 5, 17. Neque dubium est, ubi vox סבל bajulandi cum peccato jungitur, pænæ luitionem inferri. Quam regulam cum ipse Grotius inculcarit adversus Socinum, nunc ner- vum eidem incidit, de sola doctrinali correctione portationem iniquitatum explicans, h. e. mentem Prophetæ contra propriam conscientiam perver- tens, quod est τῶν αὐτοκατακρίτων. Repetimus verba ipsius è defens. fid. Cathol. p. 11. In Hebræo est ועונתם הוא יסבל. Vox autem עון iniquitatem si- gnificat, atque etiam iniquitatis pœnam, ut 2. Reg. 7, 9. Vox autem סבל est sustinere, bajulare, quoties au- tem bajulare ponitur cum nomine peccati, aut ini- quitatis, id in omni lingua & maxime in Hebrais- mo significat pœnas ferre. Nam nasa quidem inter- dum significat auferre, sabal autem nunquam. Di- serte igitur hic dicitur Christus laturus pœnas eorum, qui justificantur. Hæc phrasis nullam aliam inter- pretationem recipit. Neque obstat, quod hæc portatio iniquitatis apud Prophetam videatur post resurre- ctionem poni. Gloria enim Christi Prophetæ quasi al- terius opponit antecedentes passiones, modo naturali, modo inverso ordine, quia effectu posito causam red- dit. Ita post mentionem æternæ perdurationis, excidii & plagæ sit mentio v. 8. Deinde v. 10. post contritio- nem & morbum & sacrificium semen, longævitas, & prosperitas nominantur, quibus conjunguntur libera- tio à molestia & multorum justificatio v. 11. Redit iterum Propheta ad pœnas pro peccatis toleratas, & subjungit, ideo fore ut prædam partiatur, quia scil. morti se dederit, annumeratus defectoribus. Decere enim, ut is, qui peccata multorum tulerit, jus habeat pro eis intercedendi vers. 12. Quod vero ait Socinus, hanc quoque vocem sabal peccato adjunctam non semper includere imputationem aliquam, sed satis esse, si designet affligi quempiam occasione qualicunque facti alieni, id nullo exemplo probat, neque unquam S. Scri- ptura ita loquitur. Imo Græci etiam Latinique auto- res, cum ea phrasi utuntur, semper imputationem in- cludunt. Citat firmandæ huic exceptioni Socinus Je- remiæ locum, qui sic habet: Patres nostri peccave- runt, & non supersunt: nos vero pœnas eorum fe- rimus Thren. 5, 71. neque hic patitur ullam imputatio- nem intelligi. At quo argumento probat, aliud hic si- gnificare eam phrasin, quam aliis omnibus in locis, u- bi exstat. Fateri cogitur ipse Socinus, quoties filii Pa- trum sequuntur vestigia, non propria tantum, sed & paterna peccata ipsis imputari. Est enim manifesta Dei vox, Exod. 20, 5. Eos autem, de quibus agit Je- remias, parentibus suis fuisse similes, ostendit id, quod apud Prophetam sequitur, Væ nobis, qui peccavi- mus, v. 16. Neque vero hoc alienum est à Jeremiæ insti- tuto. Ut enim eorum, qui tum vivebant, miseriam exaggeret, ait in ipsos redundare & propriorum & avitorum scelerum pœnas: eoque multo meliorem ipso- rum forte fuisse parentum sortem, qui pariter rei, an- te tamen exempti essent vitæ, quam ista acerbissima supplicia velut in iræ divinæ thesauro coacervata tandem simul effunderentur. Etiamsi vero ambigua esset harum vocum, ferre peccata, in sacris literis significatio; tamen tum hoc Esaiæ, tum isto Petri loco certam faceret interpretationem adjuncta mentio perpessionum Christi & liberationis nostræ. Pec- cata enim ferre patiendo, atque ita, ut inde liberentur alii, aliud judicare non potest, quam pœnæ alienæ sus- ceptionem. Hæc ibi Grotius, quæ omnino solida c esse adversus Socini hæresin vindiciis nostris pro Grotio adversus Crellium Regiomonti ante hos 24. annos susceptis abunde demonstravimus, quo- rum summam deinceps in Socinismo profligato in articulo de satisfactione Christi exhibuimus. Caufa formalis justificationis designatur tum verbo JUSTIFICABIT, quod forense est, quæ justificatio condemnationi opponitur; & per scien- tiam Christi justificantur ii, quorum iniquitates ba- julavit, id est, ab iniquitatibus absolvuntur; & Chri- stus justificat scientia sua multos, ceu servus Dei ju- stus, portans ipsorum iniquitatem, h. e. obedien- tia sua tum activa, qua ut servus justus omnem justitiam implevit, siquidem per hujus unius obe- dientiam justificantur multi, Rom. 5, 18. tum pas- siva, qua peccata nostra bajulavit, pœnam eorum sustinendo, unde nobis non imputantur, quia ipsi in judicio Dei imputata sunt, 2. Cor. 5, 21. Quam illustrissimam sententiam Prophetæ glossis suis tenebricofis obfuscare frustra nititur Grotius. Nam etsi forte alibi vox justificandi de eruditione & justitia adhiberetur, hic tamen tam clarus est fo- rensis sensus, ut non possit de nuda eruditione vel correctione intelligi. Quamvis ne id quidem pro- barit, quod de sola correctione vel doctrina uspiam usurpetur. Loca certe illa adducta id non probant. Nam Dan. 12, 3. proprie accipi vox potest, de illis, qui alios justificarunt, de verbi nempe Doctoribus, qui- bus διακονικῶς tribuitur, quod alios justificent, rege- nerent, salvent, unde etiam Salvatores in Scriptu- ris dicuntur. In altero vero dicto Apoc. 22, 11. nul- lum plane locum habet illa justificandi notio pro correctione. Agitur enim non de doctoribus, sed de justis, qui monentur, operam dent, ut porro ju- sti maneant, ac justificentur, & in justitia conser- ventur. Quod autem dicit Grotius, illam signifi- cationem, justificare per correctionem, vel institutio- nem, esse huic verbo propriam, & ab ea alia signi- ficata per similitudinem quandam fluere, id gratis saltim confictum est, nec ulla verisimilitudine gau- det, quomodo etiam significatio forensis, cum ab- solutionem notat, ab illo commentitio significatu fluit?

## 53:12
Vers. 12. THEREFORE I WILL DISTRIBUTE TO HIM MANY,) I will give him a portion among many. That is: the Chaldeans will save many for his sake. See Jerem. 39, 17. AND HE SHALL DIVIDE THE SPOILS OF THE STRONG) That is, Nebuzaradan, the Master of the soldiers, after the city was captured, sends him gifts from the booty, Jerem. 40, 5. There was also offered to him by the Chaldeans as much of the land as he wished. See also below 15, 11. BECAUSE HE HATH DELIVERED HIS SOUL UNTO DEATH.) In the Hebrew: Because he poured out his soul unto death. That is, he exposed himself to the dangers of death by cultivating the truth, which begets hatred. See the history appropriate to this matter, Jer. 26, 13. Thus we said at John 10, 11 that τιθέναι ψυχὴν is used for exposing oneself to the danger of death. AND WAS RECKONED WITH THE TRANSGRESSORS) He was treated in the way that transgressors are accustomed to be, in prison, in chains, and in the pit. AND HE BARE THE SINS OF MANY) He was treated very badly through the wickedness of many, as above 5. AND HE MADE INTERCESSION FOR THE TRANSGRESSORS) יפגיע means to pray, as the Hebrew writer concerning the life and death of Moses explains, looking to this passage. The sense is: At that very time, when he was suffering such harsh things from the people, he did not cease to pour out prayers to God for them, as Moses once did in the desert. See Jer. 14, 7. 37, 3. 38, 17. 42, 2.

We hear nothing here but mere distortions again without any proof, just as if Grotius were exercising a dictatorship over the sacred Oracles, and all were bound to venerate his bare dictates, because αὐτὸς ἔφα. For if it were lawful to apply Prophecies to any sort of historical convenience, and to twist those things which do not fit in that application, would not the Scriptures be like a waxen nose? Which Grotius perhaps intended with the Papists. He could have felt with his very hands that all these things are dragged away and twisted to Jeremiah only by force, and that all the same things are best attributed, even from the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures themselves, to the one Messiah. For as to that distribution mentioned first, it scarcely entered anyone's mind even in a dream that it was indicated that many would be saved from the Chaldeans thanks to Jeremiah, although this would be most certain, which nevertheless cannot be demonstrated: for in the cited passage Jer. 39:17, there is mention of none but Ebed-Melech alone, to whom it is promised by the Lord that he will save his soul as prey, because he had trust in the Lord, but not that he was to be saved from the Chaldeans thanks to Jeremiah, which are vastly different. But these things refer to the preceding, because he bore the iniquities of men, THEREFORE I WILL GIVE HIM A PORTION AMONG THE MANY OR OVER THE MANY, because it is noted by the blessed Tarnovius and Dr. D. Weller that 'pro' is sometimes used for 'SUPER', so that indeed by his knowledge many may be justified. Jerome rendered it, 'therefore I will distribute to him the many,' and the same sense was expressed by the LXX; διὰ τ̃το αὐτὸς κληρονομήσῒ πολλὲς, 'therefore he himself shall possess the many,' and the Targum: 'he divides for himself the prey of the many.' Nor does the gloss of R. Solomon depart from this: 'I will distribute to him the possession and the strong among the many with the ancient Fathers.' Most explain it, therefore, concerning the donation of men as an inheritance, whence the sense will be that not only among a few, such as the Jews, but among many, even the Gentiles themselves, the possession and inheritance are to be given to him, just as God the Father promised to his Son, Ps. 2. For the consequence of the passion and exaltation of Christ is the calling of the Gentiles, and the possession of many as an inheritance and peculiar treasure. To which the version of the blessed Luther tends: 'Darumb wil ich ihm grosse Menge zur Beute geben.' Others understand it of goods received from God the Father for the use of men; but the former explanation is simpler and more accepted. We have the great Brentius agreeing: 'This is to be read thus: I will give him a great multitude for spoils, and the strong shall be his prey.' Although these things can be understood of the victory which the Son of God carried off from Satan, and which plundered all the power of Satan as prey, showing openly the despoiled principalities and powers, and triumphing over them by himself, as Paul speaks: Of which victory also, and the distribution of spoils, Christ himself speaks in Luke ch. 11. Where he says, 'the stronger one, coming upon him, overcomes him, takes away all his armor in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils': yet he seems here to speak especially of the multitude of the Church collected from all nations and kingdoms, which itself is also a part of the prey which the Son of God took away from Satan. Therefore, what is said: 'I will give him a great multitude for spoils, and the strong shall be his prey,' is clearly that very thing which is said in the Psalm: 'Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession.' And again: 'He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth. Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the dust, the Kings of Tarshish and the isles shall offer gifts, etc., all Kings shall worship him, all nations shall serve him, etc.' This certainly is to receive a great multitude for spoils, and the strong for prey. But it began to be fulfilled when the Apostles, having received the Holy Spirit, carried around the Gospel of Christ with their preaching, beginning from Jerusalem even to the ends of the earth, and collected a Church from all the nations and kingdoms of the earth. So also Jerome: 'Therefore I will divide to him the many, so that for the portion of the Lord Jacob, and the cord of his inheritance Israel, they may believe in him coming from the east and the west, and recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.' That being fulfilled which is written: 'Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession.' Concerning which it is also read in this same Prophet: 'There shall be a Root of Jesse, and he who shall rise to rule over the Gentiles, in him shall the Gentiles hope.'

What therefore (2) the Prophet hands down concerning the strong being distributed as prey, Grotius most poorly drags away to Jeremiah. And how jejune that is: 'provisions were given to Jeremiah, some little gifts were given; Therefore in him was fulfilled what is held here: AND HE SHALL DISTRIBUTE THE ROBUST AS PREY.' It is not of spoils, or other little gifts of the strong of any kind that there is speech here, but the STRONG themselves are the PREY, which God distributes to this servant of his: As the blessed Luther most rightly rendered it. 'Und er sol die Starcken zum Raub haben.' More subtle is Alex. Morus's interpretation concerning the partition of Christ's garments. To me, he says p. 101, it seems more convenient to refer it to the following (he speaks of this part of the last verse, in which we are now occupied) but so that 'אֶת' is taken for 'לְ', the sign of the Dative, which seemed so to Oleaster: 'He shall divide the spoils to the strong.' But the authority of the Syrian interpreter is greater with me: 'לְעַשִׁינֵי שׁלל'. But that it signifies garments, spoils, is conceded by all: 'To the strong therefore or the quarrelsome (for this is the power of the word 'עֲצוּמִים' in Prov. 18 and elsewhere: than which epithet I know not if any fits soldiers better) he shall divide the garments, and indeed by lot, as Job 21:17.' Nor does it stand in the way that he himself did not divide his garments; for neither did he himself shed his own blood, which follows immediately. The sense will be: 'And I will impart to him the many, i.e., I will give to him the Gentiles, since (no one is ignorant that 'כּ' is often causal) he divided the garments to the strong or quarrelsome, and for that, because he poured out his soul unto death, i.e., he suffered the garments to be divided, and his soul to be poured out, and was numbered with the transgressors, the robbers.' But neither does that stand in the way, that in the former member we take אֶחֱלַק in the sense of imparting and giving simply: but in the latter, of dividing: For that figure of speech full of elegance, which they call ἀντανάκλασιν, is well known. It is added that this word חָלַק is said of the participation of those things which are not divided or cut, just as that seamless tunic of Christ was not divided. Yet it does not disapprove of our exegesis, but illustrates and confirms it. Nor, however, he says, do we so please ourselves in this interpretation, that we either disapprove of the received one, or omit to illustrate it: according to which the Messiah is compared to a victorious and triumphing leader, who, having captured great booty, divides it among his own, as Exod. 15, 9. Jud. 5, 30. and even Isaiah 9, 2. As victors exult over captured booty, when they divide the spoils. Although, not to conceal anything, I do not think that any partition of booty must necessarily be understood: which neither the force and nomenclature of the Hebrew words demand, nor the thing itself. I will simply give to him, or, I will impart through many, that is, he will receive or attain, will possess the booty of the nations and all the strongest: so that the first member may be an explanatory one of the second: or that the former may refer to men, the latter to the Angels, whose strength and multitude are known, and concerning them the triumph of Christ, in the Epistle to the Colossians. Which latter concerning the Angels is too frivolous. Thirdly, the cause of this donation openly refutes those Grotius trifles, FOR HE POURED OUT HIS SOUL UNTO DEATH. For what, did Jeremiah pour out his soul unto death? He indeed tries to pervert it, as if only the danger of death were noted, but the words expressly bring in death itself, from which one must not depart; and the Prophet had predicted that same thing before in equally most open words, that this righteous servant would lay down his soul for sin as a sacrifice, and not otherwise than concerning death even the LXX Interpreters.

or the Targum, or whoever else the translators and commentators understood. R. Salom. Jarchi and Kimchi also noted an emphasis in the word הערה, which they explain as the pouring out of the soul unto death, by comparing Gen. 24, 20. In this way, both the readiness of Christ in undergoing his passion, which Brentius also noted, and the abundance of his sufferings are indicated, in which he was poured out like water, Ps. 22. Morus wishes to indicate αἱματεκχυσίαν [blood-shedding], without which there is no sacrifice, since the soul was poured out when his veins were emptied and his blood was shed, and when water and blood flowed from his side. Nor indeed is τιθέναι ψυχὴν [to lay down one's soul] merely to expose oneself to the danger of death, John 10, 11, but to undergo death itself, since Christ, that good Shepherd, underwent death itself for us, and did not merely expose himself to the danger of death.

Fourthly, because this righteous servant of God is said to be reputed with the wicked, in the Hebrew, AND WAS NUMBERED WITH THE TRANSGRESSORS, LXX. ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη [he was reckoned among the lawless], that is dragged off to Jeremiah only impiously, because in this he is openly contradicted by the Holy Spirit, who most explicitly testifies that these things were predicted concerning Christ in his passion and crucifixion, when he was reputed with the transgressors, Matt. 15, 25. And they crucify with him two thieves, one on his right hand and another on his left; And the Scripture was fulfilled, which says: And he was reputed with the iniquitous. He is also contradicted by Christ himself, who teaches that this was written concerning himself, Luke 22, 37. For I say to you, that this which is written must yet be fulfilled in me: And he was reckoned with the iniquitous. For those things which are concerning me have an end. Since these things are most evident, Grotius himself confessed, when he was preparing annotations on the Evangelical books, that the whole prophecy must be explained concerning Christ, and to that opinion he also praised the Chaldean paraphrast. On the passage in Mark he has this: ϗ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη, ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη [and with the lawless he was reckoned, among the lawless he was reckoned] the LXX have in Isaiah. But Christ had predicted that this prophecy was to be fulfilled in himself, Luke 22, 37. Let it be permitted to translate: he was numbered with the criminals. Hebrew grammarians wish those to be called פשׂעים [transgressors] who sin both deliberately and with a certain notable perfidy: Ἄνομοι [lawless] are elsewhere called οἱ ἀλλόφυλοι [the foreigners]: but here those who are held by no reverence for divine or human law or rights, δίκην ἐν χέρσιν ἔχοντες [having justice in their hands]. But the whole of that prophecy of Isaiah, just as Philip did in the Acts, so also the ancient Chaldean Paraphrast explains concerning the Messiah. As to פושעים [transgressors] being noted as rebels and seditious persons, it is gathered from 1 Kings 22, 19, 2. Kings 1, 1, and therefore it was indicated that Christ was to be numbered with such criminals, villains, rebels, and seditious persons: which was most especially done when he was suspended among men of such a stamp: For although he was treated as a criminal immediately when he was captured in the garden of olives and bound and dragged around in a circle, in the courtyard of the High Priest, the praetorium of the Roman Governor, the hall of King Herod, and was subjected to injuries both verbal and real, and compared to Barabbas the thief, nay, held to be worse than him, yet the Holy Spirit looked primarily to the fact that he was to be crucified in the middle between thieves, because he dealt most with the ignominious death of Christ and the supreme punishment for sins, which he paid for us, whence he is said to have delivered his soul unto death, and to have prayed for the transgressors, and to have borne sins, all of which he accomplished on the cross, when he hung among the transgressors, in which sense the Holy Spirit also interpreted it, Mark 15, 28. Among the LXX and the Evangelists the verb ἐλογίσθη [was reckoned] is used, whereas in the Hebrew it is ומנה, which denotes not only to be reputed, but is also rightly translated as to be computed, to be numbered, and it was fulfilled when Christ was not only reputed as a thief, but also numbered among thieves, when he was crucified in the midst of them. With what face, therefore, with what conscience he [Grotius] dragged that to Jeremiah

(he is treated, as criminals are wont to be, in prison, in chains, and in the pit) is in the open.

Fifthly, he again very badly perverts the words of the Prophet concerning the punishment which the servant of the Lord paid for us: AND HE HIMSELF BORE THE SINS OF MANY, attaching to them this meaning which is clearly foreign: he was treated very badly through the wickedness of many. But it has been proven before that these words imply not only affliction, but the payment of a penalty, and do not designate wickedness as the efficient cause προηγεμένην [primary], but as an external, προκαταρκτικὴν [preparatory] and meritorious cause. It is truly to be wondered at that Grotius should be so blind in such great light, since nowhere in any chapter of the whole Holy Scripture has this argument concerning the satisfaction of Christ, which is the fountain and foundation of all life-giving consolation, been handed down more diligently, more copiously, and more clearly than in this one of ours; and because we cannot better πρὸς ὄμμα ποιεῖν [bring it before the eyes] than it was done by the blessed Brentius, for the sake of a sweet recapitulation, we shall set it forth in his words, not neglecting the grave and full admonition of that man of God, the late lamented, concerning that most honeyed abundance of words. But I ask you, says our Brentius to v. 6, count for me diligently how often in this one, and very small, passage it is repeated and reiterated that the Son of God was afflicted on account of our sins, and overwhelmed by our iniquities. And why should we not show this diligence to this discourse, when it has been commended to us so often by heavenly testimonies? Let us count, therefore: 1. 1. Surely he himself bore our infirmities. 2. He himself carried our sorrows. 3. He was wounded on account of our iniquities. 4. He was bruised on account of our crimes. 5. The discipline of our peace was upon him. Or the punishment upon him, that we might have peace. 6. By his stripe we are healed. 7. The Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all. 8. He was cut off from the land of the living. For the crime of my people I struck him. 9. He gave the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death. 10. If he shall lay down his soul as an offering for sin, he shall see, etc. 11. He himself shall bear their iniquities. 12. He bore the sins of many.

What, then, is the meaning of the repetition of the same thing so often iterated? This tautology would be abominable to some little learned rhetorician. But neither does the Holy Spirit delight in empty babbling. And yet, since in this chapter He appears to be a babbler and a tautologist, there is no doubt that He is treating a matter most necessary of all to be known. For the literature of the nations also hands down that those things which are beautiful must be repeated again and again: 'Twice and thrice the beautiful things.' And someone else asks that not ornate things be told to the citizens, but necessary ones: 'Do not tell me elegant things, but those of which the city has need.' Let there be told to us, too, not words artfully composed, but things useful for the salvation of the Church. In this chapter, therefore, it is repeated so often that the Son of God undertook to expiate the sins of the human race: First, because for our true and eternal salvation nothing is more necessary to us than the knowledge of this matter. For unless we know and believe that the Son of God took our sins upon Himself, we are not justified before God, we are not adopted as sons of God, we are not saved in death, but we must necessarily perish in our sins and in death forever. What can be more miserable and more pernicious than this destruction? The same thing is therefore repeated so often, so that we may be excited and awakened to place all our effort in knowing the benefit of the Son of God. Next, experience itself teaches that the mind of man, terrified by the judgment of God on account of sins, stands in need of abundant consolation. For although you have commanded him once and even again to trust well, because sins have been forgiven on account of Christ, yet because he is too terrified by the horrible wrath of God, he thinks these things are said not seriously, but only for the sake of common and solemn consolation. Wherefore it seemed good to the Holy Spirit to repeat so often in this one chapter that the Son of God took upon himself our sins to be expiated, so that he might signify that this sentiment was not devised by human vanity, but is most true, most certain, most firm, and corroborated by a heavenly decree, than which nothing is more immutable. Let us not therefore despise, but rather receive with a most serious mind that battologia, which renders us so clearly more certain of the will of God, and helps the weakness of our faith. But this most holy battologia and tautologia could not yet suffice for Grotius to believe that the discourse here is about Christ according to the literal sense, much less to determine that the sentiment, which has been so abundantly and with such care expounded by the Holy Spirit concerning the expiation of our sins made through Christ, in which our eternal salvation is situated, is contained here.

The last member in this Epilogue of the Prophet is the prayer of this just servant of God for transgressors, which he again snatches away to Jeremiah, with not a word of mention made of Christ, concerning whom this prophecy treats, as is evident both from the preceding parts and from the fulfillment itself, since he also prayed for transgressors when, numbered among the wicked, he was crucified in their midst. The LXX certainly rendered it so that it cannot be understood except of Christ: καὶ διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀυτῶν παρεδόθη, and the Chaldean Paraphrast also: And it shall be forgiven to the rebellious on account of him. This is a consequence of the intercession of Christ, where it was previously connected with the same in the office of Christ. Whom the Prophet thus wished to demonstrate would fully discharge the duties of a Priest, because he would both bear his sins and lay down his soul as a sacrifice for the sin of the human race, and by his intercession for us would obtain the grace of the Father, just as it was the duty of the Priest in the Old Testament both to offer sacrifices and to pray for the people. And since his intercession was not only made on the altar of the cross, but is even now being carried out in the heavens, Rom. 8:34, Heb. 9, not without cause does the Prophet here repeat again that Christ bore the sins of many, but teaches that he who bore our sins and offered the victim of his own body, having entered into the holy of holies with that very blood which he shed upon the altar of the cross, intercedes for the people, which is, in truth, to fulfill whatever was foreshadowed in the High Priest. We add the explanation from Bereschith Rabba on Gen. 24:67. And the King Messiah was in the generation of the wicked, and he gave his heart to seek mercies for Israel, and to humble himself for them as it is said (Isa. 53:5), and he was afflicted for our crimes. And he (the Messiah) seeking mercies or pieties for them when they sin: as it is said, and by his labor we are healed: And he says, And he bore, or lifted up, the sin of many, and interceded for the transgressors.

And these things concerning this remarkable chapter, in which, by the common judgment of the Christian world, Isaiah acted more as an Evangelist than a Prophet. But that Grotius so enervated, corrupted, and distorted it, that he snatched the palm from the Socinians, those shifty masters of corrupting the Scriptures, and opened a way for the Jews, enemies of the Christian name, to attack this part of the faith, nay, he attacked it with all the battering rams that the gates of hell provided, as a champion of Jewish perfidy. Socinus certainly, although he was of a most crafty disposition and born to twist the Scriptures, and had never easily found an equal, much less a superior, seems to have wished that he could devise some [interpretation], or find one devised by others, to which the things handed down in this chapter could be adapted in some way, but it was not of his sharpness to fashion such a one for himself, nor of such reading or erudition to dig it out from the inventions of the Jews, being entirely ignorant of Hebrew literature. Whence in part II of De Serv. Christ. chap. 5, he wrote thus: Although as regards the explanations of this chapter of Isaiah brought forward by the Jews, which I have not yet seen, or read, or examined, I do not doubt that the Prophet there, no less than elsewhere, as is the custom of almost all the other Prophets, expounded that prophecy concerning Christ under some type, concerning which if it were certain to us, then without doubt it would appear how the meaning of those words, insofar as I say they ought to be understood of Christ, differs from the common interpretation today. For it is necessary that the figure correspond in some way to the thing figured, and that the interpretation of the words, which is accommodated to the figure, be able to admit of a certain similarity.

Among the Jews, however, although some, but rarer ones, have dreamed of Jeremiah here, they will nevertheless undoubtedly be rendered more expert if they are to read those Grotian things in perverting the mind of the Prophet, certainly they will be more hardened in error, impiety, and hardness of heart; having neglected both the letter of the Prophetic evidence and the authority of the sounder Rabbis. For these have interpreted this chapter concerning the Messiah with great consensus, whether we consult the Paraphrasts, such as Jonathan in the Targum, whose exposition is held among the Jews in a place equal to the authentic text, or the Midrashim and commentators, such as Bereschith Rabba or the great exposition on Gen. 28, the dialogue of Jehovah and the Messiah in R. Moses Hadarschan on Gen. 1:3, Midrash Tillim on Ps. 2, Midrash Ruth on Ruth 2:14, the commentary of the great commentator among the Jews, R. Moses Hadarschan, not only on this chapter of Isa. 53, but also on Gen. 24:67 and on Ps. 49. Tanchuma on this passage: Behold my servant shall prosper, this is King Messiah, he shall be extolled above Abraham, he shall be lifted up above Moses, and he shall be high above the Angels of the Ministry, concerning whom see more at length Abrah. Hulfius in Theol. Jud. part I. p. 434. Whether the Talmudic writers authentic to the Jews, as in the book Sanhedrin chapter Chelek, etc., or other ancient Rabbis, who can be read in Raimund. Martin. in Pug. Fid., Petr. Galatinus in Arcan. Cathol. veritatis, Helvic. in Elench. Judaic., and a good part have been brought forward before. The fragments of ancient authors, of the books Tanchuma and Siphre, were collected by R. Simeon, author of the book Jalkut, which Constantin L’Empereur produced from it. From which it is exceedingly manifest that the ancient Rabbis, that is, those who lived either around the times of Christ or not long after, interpreted this prophecy concerning Christ. Whence R. Alschech confessed at the beginning הנה רז״ל בהאחד קיימו וקבלו כי על מלך המשיח ידבר. Our Rabbis of blessed memory with ONE MOUTH establish, and have received by tradition from their ancestors, that the discourse is about KING MESSIAH. R. Solomon was also forced to confess this in his Commentary: OUR MASTERS of blessed memory affirm that these things are said concerning Messiah. Behold, for they say that Messiah was stricken, as it is said (Is. 53, 4) Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows. They also assert that he sits at the gate of Rome, among those having infirmities, as it is said in the book Sanhedrin in the distinction Chelek. But as for what was said concerning Messiah (Is. 52, 15) he shall be exalted, and lifted up, and be very high, I have heard that it is a certain gloss of the annunciation, which explains this Scripture thus: The holy and blessed God shall exalt Messiah more than Abraham, etc. Lipomanus was also obliged to confess the same in these words: This section is also explained concerning MESSIAH, But I have given only his simple meaning. The same Isaac Don Abarbanel confesses: Whose words are these: And certainly Jonathan Uzielides interprets it concerning the future Messiah, and it is also the opinion of the WISE MEN of blessed memory IN THEIR VARIOUS EXPOSITIONS. He also grants us there the agreement of R. Nachmanides, because he himself explains this Prophecy concerning the Messiah, etc. Grotius, however, preferred to attribute the praise of truth to more recent words than to the ancient Rabbis, to the whole Christian world, to the Apostles, and to Christ himself, the unique Teacher of truth. What of the fact that the Grotian opinion has already been refuted and defeated by the Rabbis themselves in R. Saadia Gaon: who seems to have been the first to invent it. For R. Aben Ezra, who praised that author of the same opinion, refutes the same from the context: and Don Isaac Abarbanel, whose words are worthy to be read here for the confounding of Grotius, has prolixly disapproved of that gloss; IN TRUTH, he says, I see NOT even ONE verse which can be explained concerning him (Jeremiah) (Grotius, however, teaches that all can be explained concerning Jeremiah, being far more crafty than the Jewish Masters themselves in corrupting the oracles themselves) by what reason will it be said of Jeremiah; He shall be exalted and shall be very high! Likewise that: Because of him Kings shall shut their mouth! for that age was accustomed to have prophets. How also can it be said, that he bore our diseases, and carried our sorrows, and that by his wound there is healing for us, that God made the sins of all of us to fall upon him, as if the punishment had rested upon him, and Israel had been immune! Then that: for the sins of my people the plague למו. Likewise, he gave his grave with the wicked, cannot be referred to him, much less that, he shall see seed, he shall prolong his days. Likewise, he shall divide the spoil with the strong. In all of which there is nothing that can be conveniently affirmed concerning him. Whence I VEHEMENTLY WONDER, how R. Haggaon could have been led into this opinion, and that there are WISE MEN (Rabbis) who praise this exposition, when yet THAT WHOLE manner of explaining IS PLAINLY ALIEN, AND NOT SUPPORTED BY SCRIPTURE. But those glosses which the most learned of the Rabbis wonder that any of their own could have thought of, those Grotius embraces with both arms, and adorns in wondrous ways, as he is well able to do, as if he were a hired advocate of the Jews, against the Christian faith! But so that it may become manifest how greatly Grotius has degenerated from himself in the opinion of this whole chapter, it is helpful, as if in place of an appendix, to bring forward both the paraphrase which he once gave in book V of De Verit. Relig. Christ. §. XIX., and the Refutation which he instituted against the fiction of the Jews, which he invented here concerning the Jewish people dispersed among all nations, so that by their example and speech they might make many proselytes everywhere: But it holds thus in the l.c. No one who is willing to turn his mind to these words of Isaiah in chapter 53 will be able to deny that the Messiah himself had to arrive at his kingdom through hardships and death, and at the power of adorning his family with the highest goods. Who has believed our report, and has recognized the power of God? And that is because he rose up, with God looking on, like a tender shoot, like a herb from sandy soil: in his countenance there was nothing beautiful, nothing comely, nor if you looked, was there anything that would delight; he was exposed to contempt, and was among men as the most abject, having experienced many sorrows, many sicknesses: all turned themselves away from him: he was in such great contempt, and of no value. But truly he bore our diseases, he tolerated our evils. We held him as if struck from heaven, smitten and depressed by God: but he was wounded for our sins, crushed for our crimes. The punishment which might procure salvation for us was imposed upon him: his stripes were given to us for a remedy. For certainly we all were wandering like sheep here and there: God inflicted upon him the punishment which was owed to our crimes: And yet when he was oppressed and most grievously tortured, he did not emit a voice, like a lamb to be slaughtered, or a sheep, which is shorn, they are silent and mute. After bonds, after judgment he was taken from the midst: but who will be able to worthily speak of the duration of his life? Truly he was taken from this place, in which we live: but this evil happened to him because of the crimes of my people. Even to death and burial he was given into the hands of the powerful and the impious, although he had done injury to no one, nor had any evil deceit ever been detected in his speech. But although God suffered him to be crushed to such an extent, and to be affected with sorrows, yet because he constituted himself a piacular sacrifice, he shall see posterity, he shall lead a durable life, and those things which are pleasing to God will be happily managed through him. Seeing himself liberated from evil, says God, he shall be satisfied with pleasure, especially in this, that my just servant himself shall absolve many by his teaching, taking away their crimes. I will give him an excellent portion, where spoils shall be divided among the warriors, because he gave himself to death, and was numbered with the wicked, and while he himself bore the punishments of the crimes of others, he constituted himself a sinner for the guilty. Who can be named, either of Kings or Prophets, to whom these things correspond? No one, surely. But as for what the more recent Jews have invented, that this is about the Hebrew people themselves dispersed among all nations, so that by their example and speech they might make many proselytes everywhere, that meaning first of all is repugnant to very many testimonies of the sacred scriptures, which cry out that nothing of evil has happened to the Jews, which they had not deserved by their own deeds, and in addition much greater things. Then the very series of the Prophetic discourse does not bear that interpretation. For the Prophet, or God, which seems more convenient in this place, says: this evil happened to him because of the crimes of my people. But the people of Isaiah, or even the peculiar people of God, is the Hebrew people. Wherefore he, who is said by Isaiah to have suffered such heavy things, cannot be the same people. This is what Grotius says, who further appeals to the confession of the Hebrews and counters the objection of others regarding a twofold Messiah: The ancient teachers of the Hebrews better acknowledged that these things were said of the Messiah; when some of the later ones saw this, they invented two Messiahs, of whom they call one the son of Joseph, who would suffer many evils and a bloody death, and the other the son of David, to whom all things would turn out prosperously; (the authors of which invention he cites, besides the Talmud under the title Succah, R. Solomon and R. Kimchi) when it would have been much easier, and more consistent with the writings of the Prophets, to acknowledge one who would arrive at the kingdom through adversities and death, (which he observes Abarbanel himself follows in more than one place regarding this chapter of Isaiah) which we believe concerning Jesus, and the thing itself teaches to be true. In the Annotations to book V of De Ver. Rel. Christ. p. 186. he has these memorable things brought forward from the writings of the Hebrews to illustrate the sense of the Prophet: namely, that the Chaldean Paraphrast and the Babylonian Gemara under the title Sanhedrin interpret this chapter 53 of Isaiah concerning the Messiah, that Abarbanel teaches at this place that by the word DISEASES in verse 4 any evils whatsoever are to be understood, that Rabboth and Solomon Jarchi explain verse 5 concerning the punishment imposed upon him regarding the Messiah to the Gemara under the title Sanhedrin, that Alseck understands that he constituted himself a piacular victim from evils willingly tolerated, and through this name understands disciples, that Abarbanel refers VOLUPTATE (with pleasure) he shall be satisfied in verse 11 to the future age, that the Babylonian Gemara under the title סימה (Sotah) teaches that verse 12, where spoils shall be divided among the warriors, is to be understood in a spiritual way, and that Alseck wishes honors and rewards to be understood by spoils at this place. Since these things are so by the judgment of the Hebrews themselves, why did Grotius fear to go in all other directions and to obscure the text written by the rays of the Sun with commentaries, not even daring to approve of the blind guides themselves, he will render a most grave account to God. We certainly show that the Christian faith stands unmoved and unshaken against the very gates of hell from this Prophetic prophecy, now with Christ as Leader and avenger, to whom, having been both emptied and exalted for us, be glory, praise, and honor forever! Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 12. IDEO DISPERTIAM EI PLVRIMOS,) Dabo ei partem in multis. Id est: multos servabunt Chaldæi in ipsius gratiam. Vid. Jerem. 39, 17. ET FORTIUM DIVIDET SPOLIA) Id est, Na- buzardan Magister militum capta urbe de præda ipsi dona mittit, Jerem. 40, 5. Oblatum etiam ipsi à Chaldæis terræ quantum vellet. Vid. & infra 15, 11. PRO EO, QVOD TRADIDIT IN MORTEM ANIMAM SVAM.) In Hebræo: Quia effudit in mortem animam suam. Id est, periculis mortis semet objecit, colen- do veritatem, quæ odium parit. Vide historiam ad hanc rem appositam, Jer. 26, 13. Sic τιθέναι ψυχὴν dici pro peri- culo mortis semet objicere, diximus ad Joh. 10, 11. ET CVM SCELERATIS REPUTATVS EST) Ita est tractatus, quomodo scelerati solent, in carcere, cate- nis & barathro. ET IPSE PECCATA MULTORVM TVLIT) Pessime tractatus fuit per multorum improbitatem, ut su- pra 5. ET PRO TRANSGRESSORIBVS ROGAVIT) יפגיע est deprecari, ut exponit ad hunc locum respiciens scriptor Hebræus de vita & morte Mosis. Sensus est: Eo ipso tempore, cum tam dura pateretur à populo, non cessavit ad Deum preces pro eo fundere, ut olim Moses id deserto. Vid. Jer. 14, 7. 37, 3. 38, 17. 42, 2.

Nil hic nisi meras iterum detorsiones audi- mus sine ulla probatione, non secus, ac si dictatu- ram exerceret Grotius in sacra Oracula, omnesque venerari ejus nuda dictata tenerentur, quia αὐτὸς ἔφα. Nam si ob qualemcunque historiæ conveni- entiam Prophetias applicare, & ea, quæ in illa appli- catione non quadrant, torquere fas esset, annon instar cerei nasi erunt Scripturæ? Quod fortassis voluit cum Papistis Grotius. Poterat vel manibus ipsis palpare, hæc omnia non nisi per vim abripi, & detorqueri ad Jeremiam, eademque universa opti- me, etiam ex interpretatione ipsius S. S. uni Messiæ tribui. Quod enim primo ad dispertitionem illam, vix per somnium ulli in mentem venit, id indica- tum esse, multos servatum iri à Chaldæis in gratiam Jeremiæ, quamvis hoc certissimum foret, quod ta- men demonstrari non potest: nam in laudato loco Jer. 39,17. non nisi unius EbedMelechi mentio sit, cui promittitur à Domino, quod ipse prædæ instar ani- mam salvaturus sit, quia in Domino habuit fiduciam, non vero quod à Chaldæis in gratiam Jeremiæ con- servandus sit, quæ maximopere diversa sunt. Re- ferunt autem hæc sese ad antecedentia, quia iniqui- tates hominum portavit, IDCIRCO DABO EI PARTEM IN MULTIS VEL SUPER MUL- TOS, quia etiam pro SUPER quandoque adhiberi notatum B. Tarnovio & Dn. D. Wellero, ut nempe ipsius scientia justificentur multi. Hieronymus red- didit, ideo dispertiam ei plurimos, eundemque sen- sum expressere οἱ ὀ; διὰ τ̃το αὐτὸς κληρονομήσῒ πολλὲς, ideo ipse possidebit multos, & Targum: ipse di- videt sibi prædam multorum. Nec R. Salomonis glos- sa abit: Distribuam illi possessionem & fortes in multos cum Patribus antiquis. Explicant ergo plerique de donatione hominum in hæreditatem, unde sensus e- rit, non tantum inter paucos, utpote Judæos, sed inter multos, ipsos etiam gentiles ipsi possessionem & hære- ditatem dandam, uti pollicitus est Deus Pater Filio suo, Ps. 2. Consequens enim passionis & exaltrationis Christi est vocatio gentium, & possessio plurium in hæreditatem & peculium. Quo abit B. Lutheri ver- sio: Darumb wil ich ihm grosse Menge zur Beute geben. Alii de bonis à Deo Patre acceptis in usum hominum intelligunt; sed prior explicatio simpli- cior & receptior est. Adstipulantem habemus ma- gnum Brentium: Hoc sic legendum est: Dabo ei pro spoliis magnam multitudinem, & fortes erunt ei præda. Etsi hæc intelligi possunt de victoria, quam Filius Dei ex Satana reportavit, & quæ diripuit in prædam omnem Satanæ potentiam, ostentans palam exspoliatos principatus ac potestates, & triumphans de illis per semetipsum, ut Paulus loquitur: De quali etiam victoria, & spoliorum distributione loquitur Christus ipse apud Lucam c. 11. Ubi fortior, inquit, superveniens vicerit eum, aufert universa arma e- jus, quibus confidebat, & spolia ejus distribuit: ta- men præcipue hic loqui videtur de multitudine Eccle- siæ ex omnibus gentibus & regnis collectæ, quæ & ipsa est pars prædæ, quam Filius Dei à Satana abstulit. Itaque quod dicitur: Dabo ei pro spoliis magnam multitudinem, & fortes erunt ei in prædam, plane illud ipsum est, quod in Psalmo dicitur: Postula à me, & dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam, possessio- nem tuam terminos terræ. Et iterum: Dominabi- tur à mari usque ad mare, & à flumine usque ad ter- minos orbis terrarum. Coram illo procident Æ- thiopcs, & inimici ejus terram lingent, Reges Tharsis & insulæ munera offerent, &c. adorabunt eum omnes Reges, omnes gentes servient ei, &c. Hoc certe est magnam multitudinem pro spoliis, & fortes in prædam accipere. Cœptum autem est imple- ri, cum Apostoli, acceptu Spiritu S. circumtulerunt prædicatione sua Evangelion Christi, initio facto ab Hierosolymis usque ad extrema terræ, collegerunt Ec- clesiam ex omnibus terræ nationibus & regnis. Sic etiam Hieronymus: Propterea dividam ei plurimos, ut pro parte Domini Jacob, & funiculo hæreditatis illius Israël, credant in eum de oriente & occidente venientes, & recumbant in regno Dei, cum Abra- ham, Isaac & Jacob. Impleto illo, quod scriptum est: Postula a me, & dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terræ. De quo & in hoc eodem Propheta legitur: Erit Radix Jesse, & qui resurget, ut principetur gentibus, in ipso gentes sperabunt.

Quod ergo (2) de fortibus distribuendis in præ- dam tradit Propheta, pessime ad Jeremiam abripit Grotius. Et quam jejunum illud est: data sunt Je- remiæ cibaria, data aliqua munuscula; Ergo in eo impletum, quod hic habetur: ET ROBUSTOS DISPERTIETUR PRÆDAM. Non de spoliis, aut aliis qualibuscunque munusculis fortium hic ser- mo est, sed FORTES ipsi sunt PRÆDA, quam distribuit Deus huic servo suo: Uti rectissime B. Lutherus reddidit. Und er sol die Starcken zum Raub haben. Subtilior est Alex. Mori interpreta- tio de partitione vestimentorum Christi. Mihi, inquit p. 101. commodius videtur ad sequentia refer- ri (loquitur de hac parte commatis ultimi, in qua nunc occupamur) sed ita ut אֶת pro לְ nota Dativi sumatur, quod hic Oleastrio visum: Fortibus divi- det spolia. Sed major apud me Syri interpretis autori- tas: שׁלל .לְעַשִׁינֵי At significare vestes, exuvias, ab omnibus conceditur: Fortibus ergo sive rixosis (hæc enim Prov. 18. & alibi potestas est vocis עֲצוּמִים: quo Epitheto nescio an ullum militibus conveniat ma- gis) dividet vestes, & quidem forte, ut Job. 21, 17. Nec obstat, quod ipse vestes non divisit suas; nam nec ipse sanguinem effudit suum, quod statim sequitur. Sensus erit: Et ego impertiar ipsi multos, h. e. dabo ipsi gentes, quoniam (כּ sæpe αἰτιατικὸν esse nemo ignorat) fortibus aut rixosis divisit vestimenta, & pro eo, quod effudit in mortem animam suam, h. e. dividi vestimenta, & effundi animam passus est, & peccatoribus, latronibus annumeratus est. At nec illud obstat, quod in priori membro sumimus אֶחֱלַק in significatu impertiendi ac dandi simpliciter: in po- steriori vero dividendi: Notum enim schema illud ple- num elegantiæ, quod ἀντανάκλασιν vocant. Accedit, quod hæc vox חָלַק de participatione rerum earum di- citur, quæ non dividuntur aut scinduntur, quemad- modum nec divisa est illa inconfutilis Christi tunica. Non tamen improbat nostram ἐξήγησιν, sed eam il- lustrat & confirmat. Neque tamen, inquit, in hac ita nobis placemus interpretatione, ut receptam vel im- probemus, vel omittamus illustrare: juxta quam comparatur Messias victori ac triumphanti duci, qui capta ingenti præda, dividit eam inter suos, ut Exod. 15, 9. Jud. 5, 30. atque adeo Esaiæ 9, 2. Sicut exultant victores capta præda, quando dividunt spolia. Quan- quam, ne quid celem, non necessario putem partitio- nem prædæ aliquam intelligi oportere: quod nec vis & nomenclatura vocum Hebraicarum postulat, nec res ipsa. Simpliciter dabo ipsi, seu, impertiar per multos, id est, gentes & fortissimos quosque accipiet vel consequetur, potietur prædam: ut sit prius membrum alterius ἐξηγητικὸν: vel ut prius ad homi- nes, posterius ad Angelos referatur, quorum & forti- tudo & multitudo nota, deque iis Christi triumphus, ad Colossenses Epistola. Quod posterius de Angelis nimis frivolum. Tertio palam næniis istis Grotia- nis refragatur causa hujusce donationis, PRO EO, QUOD TRADIDIT IN MORTEM ANIMAM SUAM. Quid enim, an Jeremias ani- mam suam in mortem tradidit. Depravare quidem id conatur, ac si tantum periculum mortis notare- tur, sed verba διαρρήδην ipsam mortem inferunt, à quibus discedendum non est; & prædixerat id an- tea itidem apertissimis verbis Propheta, quod ani- mam positurus sit hic servus justus pro peccato in sacri- ficium, nec aliter, quam de morte vel LXX. Interpp.

vel Targum, vel alii quicunq; translatores & com- mentatores intellexere. R. Salom. Jarchi & Kimchi notarunt etiam emphasin in verbo הערה, quod de effusione animæ in mortem emplicant, conferendo Gen. 24, 20. Quo pacto tum promptitudo Christi in subeunda passione, quod notavit etiam Brentius, tum passionum copia indigitatur, in quibus ipse sicut aqua effusus fuit, Ps. 22. Morus vult αἱματεκχυσίαν nota- ri, sine qua nullum sacrificium, quum anima effusa sit, cum ejus vacuarentur venæ sanguisque funderetur, & cum ei aqua & sanguis ex latere fluitaret. Nec vero τιθέναι ψυχὴν tantum est periculo mortis sese expone- re Joh. 10, 11. sed mortem ipsam subire, siquidem Chri- stus Pastor ille bonus mortem ipsam pro nobis sub- ierit, non tantum periculo mortis sese exposuerit.

Quarto, quod cum sceleratis hic servus Dei justus reputatus dicitur, in Ebræo, ET CUM PRÆVA- RICATORIBUS NOMINATUS EST, LXX. ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη, id non nisi impie ad Jere- miam abripitur, quia in eo aperte contradicitur Spiritui S. qui hæc de Christo in passione & crucifi- xione cum prævaricatoribus reputato prædicta esse disertissime testatur, Matth. 15, 25. Et cum eo cru- cifigunt duos latrones, unum à dextris & alium à sini- stris ejus; Et impleta est Scriptura, quæ dicit: Et cum iniquis reputatus est. Contradicitur etiam ipsi Christo, qui hoc de sese perscriptum esse docet Luc. 22, 37. Dico enim vobis, quoniam adhuc hoc, quod scriptum est, oportet impleri in me: Et cum ini- quis deputatus est. Etenim ea, quæ sunt de me finem ha- bent. Quæ cum maxime evidentia sint, fassus est Gro- tius ipse, cum ad libros Evangelicos annotationes adornaret, totum vaticinium de Christo explican- dum esse, inque eam sententiam laudavit quoque Chaldæum paraphrastren. Ad Marci locum hæc ha- bet: ϗ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη, ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλο- γίσθη habent LXX. apud Esaiam. Implendum autem hoc vaticinium in se Christus prædixerat Luc. 22, 37. ver- tere liceat: facinorosis annumeratus est פשׂעים He- bræi Grammatici eos dici volunt, qui & deliberato, & cum insigni quadam perfidia delinquunt: Ἄνομοι alibi dicuntur οἱ ἀλλόφυλοι: hic vero ii, qui nulla ju- ris aut legum divinarum humanarumve reverentia te- nentur, δίκην ἐν χέρσιν ἔχοντες. Totum autem illud E- saiæ vaticinium, sicut in Actis Philippus, ita & vetus Chaldæus Paraphrastes de Messia exponit. Quod ad פושעים notari rebelles & seditiosos è 1. Reg. 22, 19. 2. Reg. 1, 1. colligitur, ideoque indicatum fuit, Chri- stum annumeratum iri ejusmodi sceleratis, facino- rosis, rebellibus ac seditiosis: quod maxime factum, cum inter ejusmodi furfuris homines suspensus est: Quanquam enim pro facinoroso tractatus fue- rit statim, cum in horto oliveti captus & vinctus in orbem pertractus, in atrio Pontificis, prætorio Ro- mani Præsidis, aula Regis Herodis, injuriis & ver- balibus & realibus affectus, Barrabæ latroni com- paratus, imo deterior eodem habitus fuit, im- primis tamen eo respexit S. S. quod medius inter latrones crucifigendus fuerit, quia de morte Christi ignominiosa, & pœna peccatorum suprema, quam pro nobis luit, maxime egit, unde tradidisse dici- tur animam in mortem, & orasse pro transgressoribus, & peccata portasse, quæ omnia in cruce peregit, cum inter prævaricatores penderet, quo sensu id interpretatus etiam est S. S. Marc. 15, 28. Apud LXX. & Evangelistas adhibetur verbum ἐλογίσθη, quum in Ebræo sit ומנה, quod non tantum repu- tari notat, sed recte etiam vertitur computari, nu- merari, & impletum est, cum non solum reputa- tus est pro latrone Christus, sed etiam numeratus inter latrones, quando in medio ipsorum crucifixus est. Qua ergo fronte, qua conscientia illa ad Jerem.

pertraxerit Grot. (ita est tractatus, quomodo scelerati solent, in carcere, catenis, & barathro) in aprico est.

Quinto pessime iterum pervertit verba Prophe- tæ de pœna, quam luit servus Domini pro no- bis: ET IPSE PECCATA MULTORUM TU- LIT, hanc plane alienam mentem ipsis affingens: pessime tractatus fuit per multorum improbitatem. Quæ vero verba non solum afflictionem, sed pœnæ luitionem inferre, nec improbitatem ceu causam ef- ficientem προηγεμένην, sed ut causam externam προ- καταρκτικὴν & meritoriam designare, antea pro- batum est. Mirandum profecto est, quod in tanta luce cæcutierit Grotius, siquidem nuspiam in ullo capite totius Scripturæ S. hoc de satisfactione Chri- sti argumentum, quod fons & fundus est omnis vi- vificæ consolationis, diligentius, copiosius, & lucu- lentius traditum sit, quam in hoc nostro; quod quia non possumus melius πρὸς ὄμμα ποιεῖν, quam à B. Brentio id factum est, suavis ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως gratia, verbis ejus expediemus, non neglecto gravi & succiplena viri Dei τοῦ μακαρίτου commonefa- ctione, de ista verborum copia mellitissima. Quæso autem te, inquit ad v. 6. Brentius noster, numera mi- hi diligenter, quoties in hac una, eaque parva admodum περικοπῇ repetatur & iteretur, Filium Dei afflictum esse propter nostra peccata, & obrutum nostris iniqui- tatibus. Et cur hanc diligentiam isti concioni non præstaremus, cum ea toties nobis cœlestibus testi- moniis sit commendata: Numeremus igitur: 1. Vere languores nostros ipse tulit. 2. Dolores nostros ipse portavit. 3. Vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras. 4. Attritus est propter scelera nostra. 5. Disciplina pacis nostræ super eum. Vel sup- plicium super eum, ut nos pacem haberemus. 6. Livore ejus sanati sumus. 7. Posuit Dominus in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. 8. Abscissus est de terra viventium. Propter sce- lus populi mei percussi eum. 9. Dedit impios in sepulturam suam, & divitem in mortem suam. 10. Si posuerit animam suam hostiam pro pec- cato, videbit &c. 11. Iniquitates eorum ipse portabit. 12. Peccata multorum tulit.

Quid ergo sibi vult repetitio ejusdem rei toties itera- ta? Hæc ταυτολογία esset eruditulo cuidam rhetori ab- ominabilis. Sed nec Spir. S. delectatur inani βαττολο- γίᾳ. Et tamen cum in hoc capite videatur βαττολό- γος καὶ ταυτολόγος esse, dubium non est, quin tractet rem cognitu maxime omnium necessariam. Nam & gentium literæ tradunt ea, quæ pulcra sunt, iterum atq; iterum repetenda: Δὶς & τρὶς τὰ καλὰ. Et alius quis- piam petit civibus dici non ornata, sed necessaria Μή μοι λέγε τὰ κομψὰ, ἀλλ᾽ ὧν δεῖ πόλις. Dicantur & nobis, non verba artificiose composita, sed saluti Ecclesiæ utilia. In hoc igitur capite toties repeti- tur, quod Filius Dei susceperit peccata humani ge- neris expianda: Primum quia cognitione hujus rei ad nostram veram & æternam salutem nihil magis nobis necessarium est. Nisi enim cognoscimus & credimus, Filium Dei sustulisse in se peccata nostra, non justificamur coram Deo, non adoptamur in Filios Dei, non servamur in morte, sed necesse ha- bemus in peccatis nostris, & in morte in æternum perire. Quo exitio quid potest esse miserius, & per- niciosius? Repetitur ergo toties eadem res, ut ex- citemur, & expergiscamur ad collocandum omne studium nostrum in cognoscendo beneficio Filii Dei. Deinde experientia ipsa docet, mentem homi- nis, judicio Dei, propter peccata territam, indigere- copiosa consolatione. Etsi enim semel ac etiam iterum jusseris eum bene confidere, quod remissa sint pec- cata propter Christum, tamen quia horribili Dei ira nimium est exterritus, putat hæc non serio, sed tan- tum vulgaris & solemnis consolationis gratia dici. Quare visum est Spiritui S. toties in hoc uno capite iterare, Filium Dei suscepisse in se peccata nostra ex- pianda, ut significet, hanc sententiam non esse hu- manæ vanitate excogitatam, sed esse verissimam, certif- simam, firmissimam, & cælesti decreto, quo nihil est immutabilius, corroboratam. Non contemnamus igi- tur, sed potius gravissimo animo excipiamus eam bat- τολογίαν, quæ nos devoluntate Dei tam perspicue cer- tiores reddit, & imbecillitati fidei nostræ succurrit. Sed hæc βαττολογία & ταυτολογία sanctissima nondum sufficere potuit Grotio, ut crederet hic se- cundum literalem sensum de Christo sermonem ef- se, nedum eam sententiam, quæ tam copiose & tan- ta cum cura exposita est à S. S. de expiatione pecca- torum nostrorum per Christum facta, in qua æterna nostra salus sita est, hic comprehendi statueret.

Postremum membrum in hoc Epilogo Pro- phetæ est Oratio servi hujus Dei justi pro transgesso- ribus, quod iterum ad Jeremiam abripit, nullo ver- bulo mentione facta Christi, de quo hoc vaticinium agere, tum ex antecedentibus constat, tum è com- plemento ipso, siquidem etiam pro transgressori- bus oraverit, cum inter facinorofos numeratus in medio eorum crucifixus est. LXX. certe ita reddi- dere, ut non nisi de Christo intelligi possit: καὶ διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀυτῶν παρεδόθη, Chaldæus etiam Paraphrastes: Et rebellantibus remittetur propter eum. Hoc consequens intercessionis Christi, ubi prius connexum est cum eodem in officio Christi. Quem ita demonstrare voluit Propheta plene Sacerdotis partibus defuncturum, quod & peccata ejus porta- turus sit, animamque suam positurus in sacrificium pro peccato humani generis, & intercessione sua pro nobis gratiam Patris impetraturus, quemadmo- dum Sacerdotis in V. T. erat, tum offerre sacrificia, tum orasse pro populo. Et quum intercessio ejus non tantū facta sit in ara crucis, sed etiamnum per- agatur in cœlis, Rom. 8, 34. Ebr. 9. non præter causam Propheta denuo hic repetit, quod Christus peccata multorum tulerit, sed docet, eum, qui peccata nostra tulit, & victimam proprii corporis obtulit, ingref- sum in sanctū sanctorū cum illo proprio sanguine, quem effudit super altari crucis, intercedere pro populo, quod est, revera implere quicquid in sum- mo Sacerdote adumbratum est. Addimus explica- tionem è Bereschith Rabba ad Gen. 24, 67. Et fuit Rex Messias in generatione impiorum, deditq́; cor suum ad requirendas misericordias pro Israële, & ad humilian- dum se pro illis sicut dictum est (Esa. 53, 5.) & ipse tri- bulatus est propter scelera nostra. Et ipse (Messias) petens misericordias vel pietates pro ipsis cum peccant: sicut dictum est, & per laborem ejus medi- catum est nobis: Et dicit, Et ipse peccatum multorum tulit, vel elevavit, & pro transgressoribus intercessit.

Atque hæc de hoc insigni capite, in quo com- muni orbis Christiani judicio, verius Evangelistam quam Prophetam egit Esaias. Quod vero ita ener- vavit, corrupit, detorsit Grotius, ut Socinianis, ver- sipellibus illis corrumpendi Scripturas Magistris, palmam præripuerit, Judæis autem, Christiani no- minis hostibus viam aperuerit, hanc fidei partem oppugnandi, imo arietibus omnibus, quoscunque portæ infernales subministrarunt, eandem, ceu hy- peraspistes Judaicæ perfidiæ, impugnarit. Socinus certe, etsi ingenio vaferrimo fuerit, & ad torquen- das Scripturas natus, haud facile parem, nedum su- periorem habuerit unquam, optasse quidem vide- tur excogitare posset aliquem, aut ab aliis excogita- tum invenire, cui aptari aliqua ratione queant, quæ in hoc capite traduntur, sed acuminis ejus non fuit, ut talem sibi fingeret, nec tantæ lectionis aut eruditionis, ut è Judæorum commentis erueret, Ebraicæ literaturæ prorsus ignarus. Unde part. II. de Serv. Christ. cap. 5. ita scripsit: Quanquam quod attinet ad ejus capitis Esaiæ explanationes à Judæis allatas, quas ego nondum vel vidi, vel legi, vel examinavi, non dubito quin Prophetæ non minus ibi, quam alibi mos est fere cæterorum Prophetarum, sub aliquo typo eam de Christo Prophetiam expo- suerit, de quo si nobis constaret, tunc procul dubio ap- pareret, quam eorum verborum sententia, quatenus inquam de Christo intelligi debent, à communi hodie interpretatione distet. Necesse est enim figuram fi- gurato aliqua ratione respondere, & verborum in- terpretationem, quæ figuratæ accommodatur, per si- militudinem quandam admittere posse.

Inter Judæos vero, etsi nonnulli, sed rariores hic Jeremiam somniarint, peritiores tamen sine dubio reddentur, si Grotiana ista lecturi sunt in pervertenda mente Prophetæ, magis certe in erro- re, impietate, cordisque duritie obfirmabuntur; posthabita cum litera Propheticæ evidentiæ, tum autoritate saniorum Rabbinorum. Hi enim ma- gno consensu hocce caput de Messia interpretati sunt, sive Paraphrastes consulamus, utpote Jona- thanem in Thargum, cujus expositio apud Judæos parili loco cum textu authentico alias habetur, sive Midraschim & commentatores, utpote Bereschith Rabba seu expositionem magnam in Genes. 28. Dialogismum Jehovæ & Messiæ apud R. Mose Ha- darschan super Gen. 1, 3. Midrasch Tillim in Psal. 2. Midrasch Ruth in Ruth. 2, 14. magni apud Judæos commentatoris R. Mosis Hadarschan Commentar. non tantum in hoc caput Es. 53. sed etiam in Gen. 24, 67. & in Ps. 49. Tanchuma in hunc locum: Ec- ce prosperabitur servus meus, hic Rex Messias est, extolletur supra Abraham, elevabitur supra Mosen, & altus erit supra Angelos Ministerii, de quo vid. prolixius Abrah.
