Hulfius in Theol. Jud. part. I. p. 434. Sive Thalmudicos Scriptores Judæis authenti- cos, utpote in libro Sanhedrin cap. Chelek. &c. sive alios Rabbinos antiquos, qui legi possunt apud Raimund. Martin. in Pug. Fid. Petr. Galatinum in Arcan. Cathol. veritatis. Helvic. in Elench. Judaic. & bonam partem antea adducti sunt. Fragmenta au- torum veterum, librorum Tanchuma & Siphre col- legit R. Simeon autor libri Jalkut, quæ ex illo pro- duxit Constantin. L’Empereur. E quibus oppido manifestum est Rabbinos veteres, h. e. illos, qui vel circa tempora Christi, vel non multo post vixerunt, de Christo hanc Prophetiam interpretatos esse. Un- de R. Alschech fassus est sub initium הנה רז״ל בהאחד קיימו וקבלו כי על מלך המשיח ידבר. Rabbini nostri p. m. UNO ORE statuunt, & à majori- bus per traditionem acceperunt, de REGE MESSIA Sermonem esse. Fateri id etiam coactus fuit R. Salo- mo in Comment. MAGISTRI NOSTRI p. m. af- firmant hæc de Messia dici. Ecce, dicunt enim, quod Messias plagatus est, sicut dictum est (Es. 53, 4.) Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse por- tavit. Asserunt etiam, quod sedeat in porta Romæ, in- ter habentes infirmitates sicut dictum est in libro San- hedrin in distinctione Chelek. Quod vero de Messia di- ctum est (Es. 52, 15.) exaltabitur, elevabitur, & subli- mabitur valde, audivi, quod quædam glossa annuncia- tionis est, quæ Scripturam hanc sic exponit, exaltabit Deus sanctus benedict. Messiam plus quam Abra- hamum, &c. Fateri idem quoque debuit Lipomanus hisce verbis: Exponitur etiam sectio hæc de MESSIA, at ego sensum ejus simplicem tantum dedi. Fatetur i- dem Isaac Don Abarbaniel: Cujus hæc sunt verba: Et certe Jonathan Uzielides interpretatur de futuro Messia, atq; etiam est sententia SAPIENTUM p. m. IN VARIIS ILLORUM EXPOSITIONIBUS, Largitur etiam illic nobis consensum R. Nachma- nidis, quod ipse hanc Prophetiam de Messia expo- nat &c. Grotius vero maluit verbis recentioribus, quam antiquis Rabbinis, universo Christiano or- bi, Apostolis, Christoque ipsi, unico veritatis Ma- gistro, laudem veritatis tribuere. Quid quod Gro- tiana sententia ab ipsis Rabbinis confutata & pro- fligata jam sit in R. Saadia Gaon: qui eam primus effinxisse videtur. Nam & R. Aben Ezra, qui istum ejusdem sententiæ autorem laudavit, refellit ean- dem è contextu: & prolixe improbavit glossam i- stam, Don Isaac Abarbenel, cujus verba digna sunt, quę hic ad confundendam Grotiilegantur; REVERA, inquit, NE UNUM quidem versiculum video, qui de ipso (Jeremia) exponi possit (Grotius vero omnes de Jeremia exponi posse docet, in depravandis oraculis ipsis Judæorum Magistris lon- ge versutior) qua ratione de Ieremia dicetur; Ex- tolletur & altus erit valde! Item illud: Propter eum obdent Reges os suum! nam ætas illa Prophetas ha- bere consueverat. Quomodo etiam dici potest, mor- bos nostros portasse, & dolores nostros bajulasse, & vulnere ejus curationem nobis esse, Deum in ipsum incurrere fecisse peccata omnium nostrum, quasi ipsi pœna incubuisset, & Israël fuisset im- munis! Tum illud: propter peccata populi mei plaga למו. Item dedit cum improbis sepulcrum e- jus, ad ipsum referri nequit, multo minus illud, vide- bit semen, prolongabit dies. Item, cum robustis par- tietur spolium. In quibus omnibus nihil est, quod de ipso commode affirmari possit. Unde VEHEMENTER MIROR, quomodo R. Haggaon in hanc sententiam perduci potuerit, & SAPIENTES (Rabbinos) DARI, qui hanc expositionem laudent, quum tamen TOTA ista exponendi ratio PLANE ALIENA SIT, ET SCRIPTURA NON FULTA. Sed quas glossas Rabbinorum doctissimi mirantur ulli suorum in mentem venire posse, illas ambabus ulnis amplectitur Grotius, & miris, ut egregie po- test, modis ornat, ac si conductitius advocatus esset Judæorum, adversus fidem Christianam! Ut autem quantopere à seipso degenerarit in totius hujus ca- pitis sententia Grotius, palam fiat, juvat mantissæ veluti loco cum paraphrasin, quam olim lib. V. de Verit. Relig. Christ. §. XIX. tradidit, tum Elen- chum, quem adversus commentum Judæorum, quod hic de populo Judaico in omnes gentes dis- perso, ut suo exemplo ac sermone multos ubique proselytos faceret, instituit, adducere: Ita autem habet l. c. Ipsum vero Messiam debuisse per ærumnas & mortem pervenire ad regnum suum, & ad potesta- tem summis bonis ornandi familiam suam, negare nemo poterit, qui ad ista Esaiæ verba capite 53. ani- mum volet attendere. Quotusquisque credidit ser- moni nostro, & vim Dei agnovit? Idq; ideo, quia surrexit ille, Deo adspectante, tanquam tener surcu- lus, tanquam herba ex solo arenoso: in vultu ejus nihil pulchri, nihil decori, nec si aspiceres, quic- quam erat, quod oblectaret; contemtui patebat, & inter homines erat velut abjectissimus, multos do- lores, multas ægritudines expertus: omnes se ab eo avertebant: tanto erat despicatui, nulloq; in pretio. Sed vere nostros ille morbos pertulit, nostra mala toleravit. Nos illum habuimus tanquam de cœlo tactum, à Deo ictum atq; depressum: sed ob nostra peccata vulneratus est, attritus ob nostra crimina. Pœna, quæ nobis salutem pareret, ipsi imposita est: tumices ipsius dati sunt nobis pro remedio. Certe enim nos ut oves aberrabam9 omnes huc atq; illuc: ipfi Deus inflixit poenam, quæ nostris criminibus debebatur: Et tamen cum opprimeretur & gravif- fime cruciaretur, vocem non emifit, ficut agnus ma- ctandus, aut ovis, quæ tondetur, filent muta. Post vincula, post judicium è medio fublat9 est: fed rur- fus vitæ ejus durationẽ quis digne eloqui poterit? Nimirum ex hoc loco, in quo nos vivimus, ereptus est: sed hoc malum ei evenit ob populi mei fcelera. Ad mortem usque & sepulturam datus est in man9 potentium atq; impiorum, cum tamen nemini fe- ciffet injuriam, neq; in sermone ejus deprehensus fuiffet unquam dolus malus. Sed quamquam Deus eousq; eum passus est conteri, doloribusq; affici, ta- men quia fe constituit hostiam piacularem, videbit posteritatem, vitam aget durabilem, & quæ Deo sunt placita, per ipsum feliciter curabuntur. Libe- ratum se à malo conspiciens, ait Deus, voluptate sa- tiabitur, eo maxime, quod dogmate suo ipse justus servus meus multos absolvet, eorum crimina aufe- rens. Dabo ei partem eximiam, ubi inter præliato- res spolia dividentur, quia morti se dedidit, & sce- leratis annumeratus est, cumq; pœnas aliorũ crimi- num ferret ipse, pro fontibus se constituit peccato- rem. Quis potest nominari aut Regum, aut Propheta- rum, in quem hæc congruant? Nemo sane. Quod au- tem recentiores Judæi commenti sunt, agi hic de ipso populo Hebræo disperso in omnes gentes, ut suo exem- plo ac sermone multos ubiq; proselytos faceret, is sensus primum plurimis facrarum literarum testimoniis re- pugnat, quæ clamant, Judæis nihil mali accidisse, quod non ipsum, & insuper majora multo suis factis essent promeriti. Deinde ipsa Prophetica orationis series eam non fert interpretationem. Dicit enim sive Prophe- ta, quod isto loco videtur convenientius, sive Deus: hoc malum illi evenit ob populi mei scelera. Populus autem Esaiæ, aut etiam populus Dei peculiaris est po- pulus Hebraicus. Quare is, qui tam gravia perpessus ab Esaia dicitur, non potest idem populus esse. Hæc Grotius, qui porro ad confessionem Ebræorum provocat, & exceptioni aliorum de gemino Mes- sia occurrit: Melius antiqui Hebræorum Magistri fa- tebantur hæc de Messia dici: quod cum viderent qui- dam posteriorum, duos Messias commenti sunt, quo- rum alterum vocant Josephi filium, qui mala multa & mortem cruentam pateretur; alterum Davidis fi- lium, cui cuncta prospere fuccederent; (cujus com- menti autores adducit præter Thalmud titulo Suc- ca R. Salomonem, & R. Kimchium) cum multo faci- lius esset, & Prophetarum scriptis congruentius, u- num agnoscere, qui per adversa & mortem ad regnum esset perventurus, (quod ipsum non uno in loco ad hoc Esaiæ caput Abarbanielem sequi observat) quod nos de Jesu credimus, & verum esse res ipsa docet. In Annotatis ad libr. V. de Ver. Rel. Christ. p. 186. hæc habet ἀξιομνημόνευτα è Scriptis Ebræorum ad sensum Prophetæ illustrandum producta: quod nempe hoc c. 53. Ef. de Messia interpretentur Chaldæus Pa- raphrastes, & Gemara Babylonica titulo de Syne- drio, quod v. 4. MORBORUM voce quævis ma- la intelligi doceat ad hunc locum Abarbaniel, quod v. 5. de pœna ipsi imposita de Messia explicet Rab- both, & Salom. Jarchi ad Gemaram titulo de Syne- drio v. 10. quod se constituerit hostiam piacularem de malis volenti animo toleratis accipiat Alseck, & per hoc nomen discipulos intelligat v. 11. VOLU- PTATE satiabitur ad futurum feculum referat A- barbaniel, v. 12. ubi inter præliatores spolia dividen- tur, spirituali modo intelligendum doceat Gemara Babylonica titulo סימה, per spolia sapientum ho- nores & præmia intelligi velit ad hunc locum Al- seck. Quæ quum ipsorummet Ebræorum judicio ita se habeant, cur Grotius in alia omnia ire veritus non sit, & textum Solis radiis scriptum obscurare commentis,ne ipsis quidem cæcis ductoribus pro- batis ausus sit, Deo rationem gravissimam reddet. Fidem certe Christianam ex hoc vaticinio Prophe- tico immotam & inconcussam stare adversus ipsas etiam inferorum portas, nunc Duce, ac vindice Christo ostendimus, cui pro nobis & exinanito, & exaltato, gloria, laus, & honor sit in secula! Amen.

## 54:1 Argument
ORATION III. How widely the fruit of Christ's redemption extends, and his Seed. CHAPTER LIV.

The Church is invited to joy, because under the New Testament it will be more numerous from the nations than it had once been, and is to be propagated throughout the world, secure by the protection of the Lord, having forgotten its old calamity: to be built from precious stones, founded in justice: in which all will be taught by God, about to enjoy much peace.

Ver. 1. REJOICE, O BARREN ONE, WHO DOST NOT BEAR] He returns to that discourse which he had begun at the beginning of chapter 52, and had interrupted with the mention of JEREMIAH. The city of Jerusalem had for a long time been barren, and without birth, i.e., deserted, desolate, as that expression is explained above 49, 21.

MANY ARE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ONE, MORE THAN OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND] You will become fuller than those cities which have always been inhabited, and have had Kings among them. Jerusalem, by far the most famous of the cities of the East, according to Pliny.

Here the water stuck for Grotius. Although he has otherwise boasted of a perpetual συνέχειαν (continuity) in the prophecies of Isaiah, and has exhibited to us various specimens of distortions in order to serve a preconceived opinion—that he prophesied about events before the coming of the Messiah, which were fulfilled either while Isaiah was alive or not long after—now he himself could not find the reason for the coherence, but established an INTERRUPTED series of prophecies, so that he might just insert his JEREMIAH, and eliminate Christ from the letter of the prophecies. But if we attend to the voice of the Holy Scriptures, dismissing the glosses of the blind Jews, there is no interruption here, but all things cohere most sweetly. Let this, therefore, be the first argument against that Jewish gloss concerning the earthly Jerusalem. For since the Prophet has hitherto described both the emptying and the exaltation of the Messiah, and has prophesied especially about the fruit of the labors of this just servant, that he will act prosperously and will be very sublime, and although very few of the Jews will believe the report of faith, he will nevertheless sprinkle many nations, so that even Kings will hold their mouths, and those to whom it has not been told about him will see, so that he himself will have an ineffable generation, and will see his spiritual seed with the highest pleasure and satiety of joy, about to justify many more by the knowledge of himself, and about to receive a portion in many, and the strong as spoil, after he has delivered his soul unto death, bearing the sins of men, and interceding for them before God the heavenly Father: the most clear-sighted prophet now provokes the Gentiles with a most joyful call, he commands them to enlarge the place of the tent, he promises a frequent influx of nations to the Church from the right and from the left, and describes the happiness and glory of the Church, which will be in the time of the New Testament, in magnificent words, most worthy of such splendor. Concerning which Jerome has this: After the birth of the Savior, and the order of his life and virtues, the passion of the cross, and the glory of the resurrection, when, laying down his soul, he saw a long-lived seed, and in his knowledge he, the just one, justified many, and divided the spoils of the strong, and prayed for the transgressors, giving a place for repentance, he passes to the calling of the Gentiles, and describes in full discourse those who are to believe in him. Cyril also agrees: Having explained most beautifully how the true lamb, i.e., Christ, bore the precious cross for us and the slaughter for the world: and having also predicted that he would possess many, he turns the speech of the prophecy to those who have now been given to him by God as a lot, that is, the Gentiles. Therefore, the subject matter of this Prophetic discourse provides us with a second argument against the Gloss of Grotius, in which purely spiritual things resound: spiritual joy, spiritual generation, spiritual Jerusalem, spiritual tabernacle, spiritual betrothal and union, spiritual structure and edification, and to say it in a word, all things refer to a spiritual promise. There is no reason, therefore, why we should think of bodily things here, or with the blinded Jews, distort to the erection of a city which was desolate what is said about the fruitfulness and expansion of the Church, or imagine with the Jews a jeweled Jerusalem, built from precious stones, Sapphires and Jaspers; which indeed Grotius also dreamed of here, but what else did he reveal than that, with the reprobate nation, he was deprived of the true light of faith and blinded, and had completely closed his eyes to the light shining in the New Testament! Since, which will be a THIRD argument for us, this chapter has been clearly explained by the Holy Scriptures concerning the times of the New Testament and the calling of the Gentiles. The passage is Gal. 4, 27, where the Apostle of the Gentiles taught most openly that the present prophecy is not to be taken concerning the Jerusalem which serves with her children, but that which is above and is free, which is our mother, and that that joy concerns not the rebuilding of Jerusalem, but the amplification of the Church and the conversion of the Gentiles. But that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is our mother. For it is written, rejoice, O barren one, who dost not bear, break forth and cry, thou who dost not travail: for many are the children of the desolate one, more than of her who has a husband. For these are the very words of the LXX elders in Isa. 54, 1, as Grotius observes in his Annotations on Gal. 4. If, therefore, the vessel of election (these are the words of Jerome), taking the testimony from Isaiah which we now have in our hands, referred it to the children of promise, and to the Church gathered from the Gentiles or from both peoples, which had been desolate and abandoned among the Jews, which had not had a husband, God, nor had received the law, nor the Prophets, we are compelled by the same reason to follow the footsteps of our predecessor: and to call her desolate, of whom we read above: Rejoice, O desolate one, and the rest similar to these.

In vain did he again profit from his Papistical κρησφυγέτῳ, because these things are said about the city of Jerusalem, long deserted and destitute of a kingdom, that its offspring would be greater than that of lands always inhabited and ruled, but mystically and most elegantly adapted to the Gospel by Paul, because while Christ was preaching it brought forth few, but once he was removed from mortal life it brought forth many, so that the Jews were few compared to the Christians. For not to speak of that new ἐυρήματι, that by the name Jerusalem the Evangelical covenant is understood, which can neither be taught from the Scriptures nor in any way agrees, whence will it be proven, I pray, that by that old city the Gospel was mystically signified? And shall we believe that the Gospel is called upon μυστικῶς to joy and praise, that the Gospel is called a mother and a city, which is from heaven, that by the barren and deserted primordial Church of the New Testament is here understood in a mystical sense! Is it not sufficiently manifest that by her who had few children, the Jewish Church is designated, which under the Old Testament, in comparison with the Church of the New Testament diffused and disseminated throughout the whole world, had few children? Nor indeed does the Apostle here put forth a new sense, or one latent and hidden, but he appeals to Prophetic testimony, according to a common sense and one by no means unknown in the Church. But who, indeed, would have admitted that the Apostle was revealing entirely new meanings alien to the letter, and had allowed the Prophet, who in the literal sense directly intended by the Holy Spirit prophesied concerning the rebuilding of the city, to be snatched away to the Gospel and its power under the guise of a mystical sense! And are not the Jews and those who Judaize strongly confirmed in their perverse opinions by such corruptions? Concerning which Jerome says in this place: The Jews and our Judaizers refer this passage and the rest that follow to Jerusalem, which they say is to be restored in the kingdom of a thousand years, and that it is the same which previously had a husband, and afterwards ceased to have one, and will have many more children after the divorce than it had before under a husband. Since a comparison of two women is clearly set forth, of her who had a husband and was dismissed, and of her who was always deserted and without a husband. Nor is it to be wondered at concerning the Jews, whose eyes and ears are closed, if they do not see the manifest truth. What shall I say of Christians, I do not know, who, when the Apostle says that these things are allegorical and refer to the two testaments, the old and the new, by referring to Sarah and Hagar, hand over the victory to the Jews, out of a desire for earthly pleasures in the thousand years. Add fourthly, that Christ himself taught that this Prophetic chapter proposed not corporal but spiritual goods, and promised the heavenly instruction of God, and urged that sense, as received and common, in a public sermon against the Jews, John 6:45. It is written in the Prophets, and they shall all be taught of God διδακτοι Θεᢏ, which is taken from this chapter, verse 13. And from Jer. 31:33. Everyone who has heard from the Father, and has learned, comes to me. Whence it is also manifest that, according to the interpretation of Christ and the common opinion of the Jews themselves of that time, these things are by no means to be restricted to the times of the Old Testament, as Grotius was persuaded along with the Jews, but that they pertain primarily to the faithful under the New Testament, where a fuller knowledge of God ought to have flourished. Grotius himself certainly acknowledged this, when he was occupied with the Evangelical books, that ALL in the Prophet are understood as all those to whom the word of the Gospel is announced, whose passage we are about to cite. Why then has he now allowed himself to be imposed upon by blind leaders, so that he should go in all other directions here! What of the fact that, fifthly, some have acknowledged from the very words themselves that these things are to be understood concerning the times of the Messiah. For in Midrash Shir Hashirim on that Cant. 1:5, I am black, these things are held: they are said concerning the Jerusalem of the Messiah: Rejoice, O barren one (Isa. 54:1) who does not bear children into Gehenna, etc. And in Midrash Tillim on that Psalm 21, O Lord, in thy strength the King shall rejoice, it is read thus: This is as if Scripture had said (Isa. 11:10) and it shall be in that day the root of Jesse, which shall stand as a sign for the peoples. Rabbi Chanina said: The King Messiah is not to come except to give commandments to the nations, but Israel will learn the law from God the holy and blessed, just as it is said (Isa. 54:15). And all thy children shall be taught of God. And why? Therefore, because it is said (Isa. 11:10) to him shall the nations seek. Finally, the Targum of R. Jonathan also interprets this whole prophecy from chapter 52:13 up to the end of chapter 54 concerning the Messiah. And these are the general arguments which can be opposed to the Grotian commentary; the sermon itself provides several special ones. In which, first, the proposition of the sermon is to be observed: Rejoice, O barren one, who does not bear, sing praise, and cry aloud, you who do not travail. Which can be explained either concerning the Gentiles in particular, whose conversion is predicted, or concerning the Church in general. The former sense pleases some, for the reason that the Gentiles seem to be described properly by these names: Barren, and she who does not bear, and deserted, as is known from other similar prophecies. Thus Cyril: He says that they are many. For those from the Gentiles can be understood to be much more frequent and more numerous in count, comparisons of those who are of the blood of Israel, who are considered as one single nation. He deigns to compare the multitude of the Gentiles to a barren and abject woman, namely one destitute of a husband, and addresses her: Rejoice, O barren one, who does not bear. Others, however, comprehend at the same time Judea, such as it was under the auspices of the New Testament, because it had then been reduced to the utmost barrenness, and was very much deserted, and truly bereft of the faithful, so that thus the people of God and the Church in these beginnings of the New Testament such as it was, let it be observed that solitude and barrenness appeared, but [was] soon to be converted into joyful fruitfulness: How Jerome explains it: The Jewish Synagogue, as long as it had God as a husband, and the divine word, and was joined to the law, was bearing many children to God: but when it received a bill of divorce, and would not answer the calling husband, and heard: You are the daughter of your mother, who has forsaken your husband. And again: You did not call me as Lord, nor as Father and the prince of your virginity. Therefore, in this same Prophet it is lamented: How has the faithful city become a harlot, Sion full of judgment, in which justice slept, but now thieves. But also this is to be noted, that when he says: More are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband, the Synagogue is not entirely excluded from childbirth, but the multitude of the Gentiles is preferred to it: And it itself also, in the Apostles and through the Apostles, first brought forth a people from the Jews. Whence the two princes of the Apostles divided the hosts of those believing in Christ for themselves, of the circumcision and of the Gentiles, so that from both peoples they might build up the previously deserted and poor Jerusalem. To which also the explanation of Blessed Luther goes: He calls the Church barren by comparison with the Synagogue, it is not a fruitful people. As also the Osiandrian paraphrase: The Lord consoles the Church, because although before his advent into this world it was to be very thin and afflicted, nevertheless through the preaching of the Gospel he would bring it about that it should become most copious and most happy. Praise, or celebrate the Lord by jubilating, in the Church of Christ, O barren one, who dost not bear, that is, who seemest at the beginning as if barren, in respect to the Jewish Church, which has innumerable disciples, or sons: sing praise, or more correctly: rejoice, jubilate, and sing, laugh joyfully, exult, you who in the beginning did not bear, who in the beginning seemedst barren, like the mother of the Israelites, Sarah. For many shall be the children of the desolate, more than of her who had a husband, says the Lord, i.e., the Church of Christ, which is gathered through the Gospel, in the progress of time will be much more copious than the Jewish Synagogue, or Church, which then still boasted in the Law and Levitical worship, and had an innumerable multitude of disciples or sons. For the Church of Christ, gathered from the nations, although its beginnings were small, nevertheless became far greater than the Jewish ever was, even when it was most numerous. To this sentiment this saying of the Prophet is alleged by Paul in Galatians 4. Others extend this discourse to the Church of all times: For all the faithful are the spiritual seed of the Messiah, and the fruit of his labors extends itself to all times. Whence our Brentius interpreted it generally, as a consolation made to the Church, which in a miserable and afflicted state fears lest, on account of its fewness and calamity, it might entirely perish, and he applies the same also to the afflicted state of the Church in the Babylonian captivity: You, O Church, who now art in the times of Ahaz or Hezekiah, or Manasseh, grievest in a wonderful manner that there are so few who follow true piety from the heart. You, O Church, who art to be in the Babylonian captivity, liest oppressed with huge grief, because you neither bear nor bring forth, because you see neither any happiness of the Church in the present, nor any hope of salvation for the future left behind. Which he similarly applies afterwards to other times, after the return from Babylon in the times of Antiochus, in the times of Herod, and afterwards of Annas and Caiaphas, etc. Meanwhile, however, an argument of consolation is subjoined: For many are the children of the desolate more than of her who has a husband, says the Lord, Brentius refers this to the calling of the Gentiles. Thus, therefore, the Church will indeed be addressed commonly in the proposition: praise, O barren one, who do not bear, break forth into joy and jubilation, you who do not travail; but the argument, by which the Church is excited to gladness, is drawn from the conversion of the Gentiles, as if to say: You complain of the paucity of your assembly, and you fear lest the Church should at length perish entirely, but take heart, because many more are about to come to the true Church from the Gentiles than from the Jews. Which Brentian analysis is pious and learned. For thus the address is directed to the Church in general, and afterwards, where she is commanded to enlarge her tents, those things pertain peculiarly to the Jewish Church; then an application also can be made, sweet and pleasant, to the paucity of the faithful of any times: because it is said of the Church generally: rejoice, you who do not bear, etc. Finally, it is thus referred peculiarly to the Church and the times of the N.T., even if the address is general: because it is appropriated to this time, through the first argument of consolation, concerning which Brentius therefore rightly observes that it treats of the conversion of the Gentiles. The text of this saying manifestly preaches about the calling of the Gentiles, and about the multiplication of the Church from the Gentiles. For the Jewish nation is as a woman having a husband, because the Law and the promise concerning Christ were given to it, as a husband to a wife, so that from that nation many children of God and heavenly citizens might be procreated. Whence also Paul, Rom. 7, compares the law to a husband. Do you not know, he says, that the law has dominion over a man as long as he lives? For a woman subject to a husband is bound by the law to her living husband, etc. But the Gentile and uncircumcised nation is as a woman deserted and repudiated by her husband, because she had neither the law nor the promises. Therefore, children of God could not be born from that nation, as far as its laws and polity were concerned. But what happened? When Christ had come, and spread His Gospel through the Apostles among the Jews and the Gentiles, many more were gathered to the Church from the Gentiles. More, he says, are the children of the desolate, namely of the Gentile nation, than of her who was joined to a husband, i.e., the Jewish nation. To this also Paul looks when he says, The Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have attained righteousness. But that righteousness which is by faith. On the contrary, Israel, who pursued the law of righteousness, did not arrive at the law of righteousness. For what reason? Because not by faith, but as if by the works of the law. Since this is the case, that you, little flock of the Church among the Jews, are to be multiplied by the accession of the Gentiles, there is no reason why you should despond in spirit and grow weary in building the Church: but rather enlarge the place of your tent. Nor does Wolfgang Musculus dissent from this explanation. The fulfillment, he says, of this prophecy we ought not to refer to that time of restored Zion, which intervened between the liberation from Babylon and the time of Christ the Savior, but to the time of the kingdom of Christ, in which the remnants of Zion grew immensely through the accession of the Gentiles. For as many as came to Christ from the Gentiles became children of Zion, a little before desolate and barren. By Zion, however, I understand not the carnal Jerusalem, which spurned Christ its Savior: but the spiritual one, namely the Church of the elect and the faithful, which perpetually, both in Babylon and liberated from Babylon, and afterwards in the time of Christ, adhered with a sincere heart to the Lord its God, which we rightly call the firstfruits of the Church of Christ. And in this sense the Apostle used the present passage, Gal. 4.

where he does not compare the churches of Israel and the Gentiles, but the carnal and spiritual Israel. We ought not, however, to exclude believers from the circumcision from the Church of the spiritual Israel, since they were the firstfruits of it. Thus he.

Now if we weigh the emphasis of the words, it will be by no means obscure that a joy not carnal and worldly, but spiritual and divine, is intimated here. The Prophet addresses the barren one, who does not bear, who does not travail. Which look to barrenness and fecundity regarding spiritual generation; for it will not easily be taught that, when a certain city is described as bereft of citizens, it is called both one that does not bear and one that does not travail on account of desolation. But that spiritual barrenness, birth, and regeneration are so described is not new, Ps. 68, 7. Isa. 49, 22. 60, 4. 66, 9. 53, 10. Nor did the Apostle understand it otherwise, when he taught that the mother of the faithful is designated by Jerusalem, Gal. 4, and the heavenly Jerusalem, which is from above. Whence it is manifest that he who takes it concerning the earthly Jerusalem, and concerning an external city and polity, contradicts the Apostolic explanation. For this is not the mother of the faithful. Which, just as it begets us spiritually through the word and sacraments, so it is in the open that spiritual barrenness is designated by the Prophet, which also the mention of spiritual marriage v. 5, and the denomination of children who are taught by God v. 13, and the explanation of Christ Himself John 6, 45, implies. Nor indeed does the Prophet provoke to such great joy on account of an external restoration. For although that restoration was a notable benefit, yet the cause of joy for the faithful is far greater when the enlargement and propagation of the Church is promised. Therefore he uses that apparatus of words which the Holy Scriptures are accustomed to employ in spiritual gladness and exaltation, as can be seen primarily from the Davidic odes, then also from the Isaianic ones. Rejoice, break forth into joy, jubilation. St. Cyril notes a peculiar emphasis in the word BREAK FORTH, ῥῆξον ὴ βόησον. There was, he says, in God a barren one of all, bringing forth none, who ought or could be reckoned and enumerated among the children of God on account of faith and virtue. But behold, it is commanded to break forth and cry out. Now women who are in the birth-stool and are giving birth are accustomed to do this: whom they say excite the midwives, to cry out with an undaunted and loud voice, so that the infant may be extracted from the womb, the bowels being dilated by the cry. This, I think, is: Break forth and cry out. Begin, he says, to bring forth, and as if one travailing with many, give forth from time to time a cry always suitable to those giving birth, as a mother truly about to be of innumerable peoples, perceive spiritual pleasure. But God, the creator of all things, declaring the meaning of this saying, infers, saying: Because more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband. It is therefore familiar to divinely inspired Scripture to call a widow desolate. But the multitude of the Gentiles was a widow. For she had no commerce with the Word, with the Word, I say, the sower of all true knowledge and of studies pertaining to piety. Grotius indeed, in his Annotations on Galatians 4, prefers that an eruption of the voice be implied: ῥήγνυσθαι can indeed signify the birth itself: But the Hebrew text requires more that an eruption of the voice be understood, in the way we have ῥῆξες φωνὴν in Job 6:5, and the word itself, which is here in the Hebrew פצח, is translated by βοᾶν in Isaiah 14:7, 44:23. Even if we admit this, it is nevertheless manifest from the Pauline interpretation that the subject matter of the joy is not earthly, but spiritual and heavenly.

This is indeed further confirmed from the principal argument of this joy. Which is the second special reason for us against the Grotius commentary. BECAUSE MANY ARE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE MORE THAN OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND. What that desolate one is, becomes clear from the opposition.

For the interpretation that by her who is said to have a husband are understood cities ruled by their own princes or kings, is a mere precarious gloss, which, I think, has occurred to no one except Grotius, who was born for such εὑρήματα (inventions). It is manifest, however, that the Church is understood, whose husband and spouse the Lord is, as is openly said in v. 5, 'your Maker is your husband,' and v. 6, 'because as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit the Lord has called you, and a wife rejected from her youth.' And therefore, by the name of the forsaken, the interpreters understand the Gentile world, which was previously utterly forsaken, just as they judge the Jewish Church to be designated by her who has a husband. If, however, she who has a husband is the Jewish Church, when it was in its pristine vigor, but the same is called forsaken about the time of the coming of Christ, the Gentiles are here included under the name of many children, because it is added: 'your seed shall inherit the Gentiles,' not by a corporal inheritance, but by a spiritual one, as B. Luther says. We add this on account of Grotius, who wishes to understand by ἔρημον (desert) and שׁוממה (desolate) in the cited place a widow, as it is taken in Lamentations 1:13. Although his objection is weak from the opposite member. For to her who has a husband is opposed she who does not have a husband, whether she had one and is a widow, or has not had one. And Grotius acknowledges that the Hebrew and Greek word can signify one bereft of children, forsaken by friends, and many similar things. Cyril explains it concerning the Gentile world: 'Before the Savior's coming,' he says, 'she was a widow and barren, and for that reason bereft of children.' But after she received the heavenly bridegroom through faith, she received more children than she who had a husband, that is, the Synagogue of the Jews. We have previously cited the opinion of Jerome. The expansion of the Church, concerning which the following verse speaks, provides a third reason. Which Grotius again strives in vain to corrupt.

Latin:

ORATIO III. Quam late pateat fructus redemtionis Christi, ejusque Semen. CAPUT LIV.

Ecclesia invitatur ad lætitiam, quod ex genti- bus sub N. T. futura sit numerosior, quam olim fuerat, & per orbem propaganda, protectione Domini secura, veteris oblita calamitatis : ædificanda ex pretiosis lapi- dibus, fundata in justitia : in qua omnes e- runt à Deo docti, multa pace fruituri.

Vers. 1. LAUDA STERILIS, QUÆ NON PARIS] Redit ad eum sermonem, quem cœperat initio capitis 52. & mentione injecta JEREMIÆ interruperat. Urbs Hiero- solyma longo tempore fuerat sterilis, ac sine partu, h. e. de- serta, desolata, ut illa locutio exponitur supra 49, 21.

MULTI FILII DESERTÆ, MAGIS QUAM EJUS, QUÆ HABET VIRUM] Plenior fies illis urbi- bus, quæ semper habitatæ sunt, & Reges apud se habuere. Hierosolyma longe clarissima urbium Orientis Plinio.

HÆsit hic aqua Grotio. Quum συνέχειαν per- petuam in vaticiniis Esaiæ alias creparit,eaq; fini præconceptæ opinioni, quod de rebus gestis ante Messiæ adventum, quæ vel vivente Esaia, vel non ita longe post impleta sunt, vaticinatus sit,ve- lificaturus,varia detorsionum specimina nobis ex- hibuerit, nunc ipse cohærentiæ rationem invenire non potuit, sed INTERRUPTAM seriem vatici- niorum statuit, ut modo ingereret suum JERE- MIAM, Christumque è litera vaticiniorum elimi- naret. At si S.S. vocem,missis cæcorum Judæorum glossis attendamus,nulla hic interruptio,sed suavif- sime cohærent omnia. Hoc ergo primum argu- mentum esto adversus glossam illam Judaicam, de terrena Hierosolyma.Quum enim Propheta descri- pserit hactenus tum exinanitionem, tum exaltatio- nem Messiæ, & imprimis de fructu laborum servi hujus justi vaticinatus sit, quod prospere acturus, & sublimis valde futurus sit, & quamvis pauci admo- dum è Judæis auditui fidei credituri, multas tamen gentes adspersurus sit, ut Reges etiam os suum conti- neant, & quibus de eo non est narratum, videant, adeo ut ipse genus inenarrabile habiturus, semenque visu- rus sit spirituale, cum summa voluptate & gaudii saturitate, justificaturus cognitione sui multo pluri- mos, & accepturus partem in multis, fortesque in prædam, postquam tradiderit animam suam in mor- tem, ferens peccata hominum, & pro iisdem interpel- lans apud Deum Patrem cælestem : provocat genti- litatem nunc vates oculatissimus κελεύσματι lætif- fimo,ad laudem & lætitiam, dilatare jubet locum ten- torii, promittit frequentem à dextris & à sinistris confluxum gentium ad Ecclesiam, & felicitatem ac gloriam Ecclesiæ, tempore N. T. futuram, magnifi- cis verbis describit, splendore tanto dignissimis. Quo de Hieronymus ita habet : Post nativitatem Sal- vatoris, & ordinem vitæ atq; virtutum, passionem cru- cis, & resurrectionis gloriam, quando ponens animam suam vidit semen longævum, & in scientia sua ipse justus justificavit plurimos, & fortium divisit spolia, & pro transgressoribus rogavit, dans locum pœniten- tiæ, transit ad vocationem gentium, & qui in illo sint credituri, pleno sermone describit. Consonat & Cy- rillus: Exposito pulcherrime, quemadmodum precio- sam pro nobis crucem & mactationem pro mundo ve- rus agnus, i. e. Christus tulerit: & prædicto etiam, eum multos possessurum: Prophetiæ orationem ad eos jam, qui illi in sortem à Deo dati sunt, id est, Gentes, convertit. Alterum itaque argumentum nobis ad- versus Glossam Grotii præbet materia hujus con- cionis Propheticæ, in qua mere spiritualia resonant, spirituale gaudium, spiritualis generatio, spiritua- lis Hierosolyma, spirituale tabernaculum, spiritua- lis desponsatio & copulatio, spiritualis structura & ædificatio, & ut verbo dicam, omnia spiritualem promissionem referunt. Non ergo est, quod hic corporalia sapiamus, aut cum excæcatis Judæis, ad erectionem urbis, quæ desolata erat, detorquea- mus, quæ de Ecclesiæ fœcunditate atq; dilatatione dicuntur, aut Hierosolymam gemmatam, è lapidibus pretiosis Sapphyris & Jaspidibus constructam cum Judæis comminiscamur; quam utique Grotius hic etiam somniavit, sed quid aliud prodidit, quam quod, cum gente reproba, vero lumine fidei or- batus, & excæcatus fuerit, oculosq; ad lucem in N. T. fugentem penitus occluserit! Siquidem quod TERTIUM nobis erit argumentum, & hoc caput à S. S. luculenter expositum sit de temporibus N. T. & vocatione gentium. Locus est Gal. 4, 27. ubi A- postolus gentium non de Hierosolyma, quæ servit cum filiis suis, sed illa, quæ sursum & libera est, quæ mater nostra est, vaticinium præsens accipiendum esse, & lætitiam illam, non reædificationem Hiero- solymæ, sed Ecclesiæ amplificationem & gentium conversionem concernere, apertissime docuit. Illa autem, quæ sursum est Jerusalem, libera est, quæ est mater nostra. Scriptum est enim, lætare sterilis, quæ non paris, erumpe & clama, quæ non parturis: quia multi filii desertæ magis, quam ejus, quæ habet virum. Hæc enim sunt ipsa verba LXX. senum Esa. 54, 1. ut observat Grot. Annot. ad Gal. 4. Si igitur vas electio- nis (verba sunt Hieron.) assumens de Es. testimoniũ, quod nunc habemus in manibus, ad repromissionis re- tulit filios, & ad Ecclesiam de gentibus seu ex utroq; po- pulo congregatam, quæ deserta in Judæis fuerat & re- licta, quæ virum non habuerat Deum, nec legem acce- perat, nec Prophetas, ipsa ratione compellimur, sequi vestigia præcessoris: & desertam eam dicere, de qua supra legimus: Lætare deserta, & reliqua his similia.

Nequicquam iterum suo Papistico κρησφυγέ- τῳ profecit, quod hæc dicantur de urbe Hierosolymo- rum diu deserta, & regno destituta, majorem ejus fo- re sobolem, quam terrarum semper inhabitatarum ac regnatarum, μυστικῶς autem & perquam eleganter ad Evangelium aptentur à Paulo, quod Christo præ- dicante paucos peperit, eo vitæ mortali exempto plu- rimos, ita ut Judæi præ Christianis pauci essent. Nam ne de novo illo ἐυρήματι dicamus, quod no- mine Jerusalem fœdus Evangelicũ intelligatur, quod neq; è Scripturis doceri potest, neq; ullatenus con- gruit, unde evincetur, obsecro, per urbem illam veterem mystice significatum fuisse Evangelium? Et num credemus Evangelium provocari μυστικῶς ad lætitiam & laudem, Evangelium vocari matrem & civitatem, quæ de cælo est, per sterilem & desertam primordialem Ecclesiam Novi Testamenti hic in- telligi sensu mystico! Annon manifestum satis est, per eam, quæ paucos habuit filios, Judaicam Eccle- siam designari, quæ sub V. T. ἐν συγκρίσει cum Ec- clesia N. T. per totum terrarum orbem diffusa, & disseminata paucos filios habuit! Neque vero sen- sum novum promit hic Apostolus, aut latentem & occultum, sed provocat ad testimonium Prophe- ticum, secundum sensum communem & in Ec- clesia minime ignotum. Ecquis vero Aposto- los novos prorsus sensus à litera alienos pandente admisisset, & quæ sensu literali, à S. S. directe in- tento de reædificatione urbis vaticinatus est Pro- pheta, ad Evangelium, ejusque virtutem, sub sche- mate sensus mystici abripi permisisset! Et annon talibus corruptelis oppido confirmantur Judæi, & Judaizantes in suis perversis opinionibus! De quo Hieronymus in h. l. Hunc locum & cætera, quæ se- quuntur, Iudæi & nostri Iudaizantes ad Hierusalem re- ferunt, quam dicunt in mille annorum regno instau- randam, & eandem esse, quæ prius habuit virum, & postea habere desierit, multoq; plures habitura sit filios post repudium, quam prius habuit sub viro. Cum perspicue duarum mulierum ponatur compara- tio, ejus, quæ virum habuit, & dimissa est, & ejus, quæ semper deserta & absq; viro fuit. Nec miran- dum de Judeis, quorum oculi auresq; sunt clausæ, si apertam non videant veritatem. De Christianis quid loquar, nescio, qui dicente Apostolo, quæ sunt allegorica, & ad duo testamenta vetus & novum, Saram Agar- que referente, Judeis tradunt manus, terrenarum in mille annis desiderio voluptatum. Adde Quarto, quod Christus ipse hoc caput Propheticum non corporalia, sed spiritualia bona proposuisse, ac cœlestem Dei informationem promisisse, docue- rit, eumque sensum, ceu receptum atque com- munem in publica concione adversus Judæos urse- rit Joh. 6, 45. Scriptum est in Prophetis, & erunt omnes docibiles Dei διδακτοι Θεᢏ, quod ex hoc cap. v. 13. depromptum est. Et è Jer. 31, 33. Omnis, qui audi- vit à Patre, & didicit, venit ad me. Unde manife- stum etiam est, quod juxta Christi interpretatio- nem, Judæorumque ipsorummet istius temporis communem sententiam ista minime restringenda sint ad tempora Vet. Test. uti Grotius cum Judæis persuasus fuit, sed ad fideles sub N. Test. ubi ple- nior Dei cognitio vigere debuit, imprimis perti- neant. Agnovit certe id Grotius ipse, cum in li- bris Evangelicis versaretur, OMNES APUD PROPHETAM intelligi omnes eos, quibus sermo Evangelii annunciatur, cujus locum deinde addu- cturi sumus. Cur ergo nunc imponi sibi passus est à cœcis Ductoribus, ut in alia omnia hic iret! Quid quod quinto è verbis etiam ipsis nonnulli agnove- rint, hæc de temporibus Messiæ intelligenda esse. Nam in Midrasch Schir Haschirim ad illud Cant. 1, 5. nigra sum, hæc habentur; de Jerusalem Messiæ di- cuntur: Lætare sterilis (Esa. 54, 1.) quæ non paris filios in gehennam &c. Et in Midrasch Tillim super illud Psal. 21. Domine, in virtute tua lætabitur Rex, ita legitur: Hoc est, ac si dixerit Scriptura, (Esa. 11, 10.) & erit in die illa radix Isai, quæ erit stans ad signum populorum. Dixit R. Chanina: Non est Rex Messias venturus, nisi ad dandum præcepta gentibus, Israël autem discet legem à Deo sancto benedicto, sic- ut dicitur (Es. 54, 15.) Et omnes filii erunt docti à Deo. Et cur? Idcirco, quia dictum est (Es. 11, 10.) ad eum gentes studebunt. Denique Targum etiam R. Jo- nathani totum istud vaticinium inde à cap. 52, 13. usque ad capitis 54. finem de Messia interpretatur. Atq; hæc sunt generalia argumenta, quæ Grotiano opponi possunt commento; specialia plura submi- nistrat ipsa concio. In qua primo concionis proposi- tio observanda: Lauda sterilis, quæ non paris, decan- ta laudem, & hinni, quæ non parturis. Quæ expli- cari possunt vel de gentilitate in specie, cujus con- versio prædicitur, vel de Ecclesia generatim. Prior sensus nonnullis placet, ideo, quia gentilitas vide- tur describi proprie istis nominibus: Sterilis, & quæ non paris, & deserta, ut ex aliis similibus vati- ciniis notum est. Ita Cyrillus: Multos eos esse dicit. Multo enim frequentiores, & numero plures illi ex gentib9 intelligi possunt esse, comparationes eorum, qui sunt ex sanguine Israël, qui pro una sola gente haben- tur. Mulieri sterili & abjectæ, viro scilicet destitutæ comparare dignatur Gentium multitudinem, eamq́; alloquitur : Lætare sterilis, quæ non paris. Alii ta- men comprehendunt simul Judæam, qualis ea fuit sub auspicium N. T. quia tum redacta erat ad sum- mam sterilitatem, valdeq; deserta fuit, & orba vere fidelibus, ut ita conjunctim populus Dei & Eccle- sia in istis primordiis N. Testament. qualis fuerit spectetur, quod solitudo & sterilitas apparuerit, verum mox convertenda in lætam fœcunditatem: Quomodo explicat Hieronymus : Synagoga Judai- ca, quamdiu virum habebat Deum, sermonemq́; di- vinum, & legi juncta erat, generabat Deo plurimos filios : quando autem accepit libellum repudii, & vo- canti viro noluit respondere & audivit : Filia matris tuæ tu es, quæ dereliquisti virum tuum. Et iterum : Non ut Dominum me vocasti, neque ut Patrem & principem virginitatis tuæ. Propterea in hoc eodem Propheta plangitur : Quomodo facta est meretrix civitas fidelis, Sion plena judicii, in qua justitia dor- mivit in ea, nunc autem latrones. Sed & hoc notan- dum, quod quando dicit ; Plures filii desertæ, magis quam ejus, quæ habet virum, non penitus Synagoga excludatur à partu, sed multitudo ei gentium præfe- ratur : Et ipsa etiam in Apostolis & per Apostolos pri- mum populum genuit de Judæis. Unde duo Apostolo- rum principes, agmina sibi credentium in Christo, cir- cumcisionis & gentium diviserunt, ut ex utroque po- pulo desertam prius atque pauperculam ædificarent Hierusalem. Quo etiam B. Lutheri abit explicatio : Ecclesiam vocat sterilem collatione Synagogæ, non est populus fœcundus. Ut & Osiandrina paraphrasis : Consolatur Dominus Ecclesiam, quòd licet ante ad- ventum ipsius in hunc mundum admodum tenuis & afflicta sit futura, tamen per prædicationem Evange- lii se effecturum, ut copiosissima & felicissima fiat. Landa, seu jubilando celebra Dominum, in Eccle- sia Christi sterilis, quæ non paris, id est, quæ videris initio quasi sterilis, respectu Ecclesiæ Judaicæ, quæ in- numerabiles habet discipulos, seu filios : decanta lau- dem, rectius : gaude, jubila, & hinni, lætabunda ride, exulta, quæ initio non pariebas, quæ in princi- pio videbaris sterilis, sicut mater Israëlitarum Sara. Quoniam multi erunt filii desertæ, magis quam e- jus, quæ habebat virum, dicit Dominus, i. e. Eccle- sia Christi, quæ per Evangelion colligitur, progressu temporis multo erit copiosior, quam Iudaica Synago- ga, seu Ecclesia, quæ tum adhuc Lege & cultu Levitico gloriabatur, & innumeram discipulorum seu filiorum multitudinem habebat. Ecclesia enim Christi, ex gentibus collecta, etsi exigua ejus initia erant, tamen longe major evasit, quam Iudaica unquam fuit, etiam cum esset frequentissima. In hanc sententiam hoc Pro- phetæ dictum allegatur à Paulo ad Gal. 4. Alii ex- tendunt hanc concionem ad Ecclesiam omnium temporum : Omnes enim fideles sunt semen spiri- tuale Messiæ, & fructus laborum ejus ad omnia se- se porrigit tempora. Unde Brentius noster gene- raliter interpretatus est, ceu consolationem Eccle- siæ factam, quæ in misero & afflicto statu metuit, ne propter paucitatem & calamitatem tota inter- eat, & applicat eandem quoque ad afflictum sta- tum Ecclesiæ in captivitate Babylonica : Tu Eccle- sia, quæ nunc es Achazi vel Ezechiæ, vel Manasse tem- poribus, mirum in modum doles, quod tam pauci sint, qui veram pietatem ex animo sectentur. Tu Ecclesia, quæ futura es in captivitate Babylonica, jaces oppressa ingenti dolore, quod nec paris, nec parturis, quod nec in præsentia vides aliquam Ec- clesiæ felicitatem, nec spes aliqua salutis in futurum relicta sit. Quod similiter postmodum ad alia tempora applicat, post reditum è Babylone temporibus Antiochi, temporibus Herodis, & post- ea Annæ & Caiphæ &c. Interim tamen argumen- tum consolationis subjunctum: Quoniam multi fi- lii desertæ magis, quam ejus, quæ habet virum, dicit Dominus, refert Brentius ad vocationem gentium. Sic ergo compellabitur quidem Ecclesia commu- niter in propositione: lauda sterilis, quæ non paris, prorumpe in gaudium & jubila, quæ non parturis; Sed argumentum, quo Ecclesia excitatur ad læti- tiam, depromitur à conversione gentium, q. d. Con- quereris de paucitate vestri cœtus, & metuis, ne Ec- clesia tandem prorsus intereat, Sed confide, quia mul- to plures concessuri sint ad veram Ecclesiam ex genti- bus, quam ex Judæis. Quæ ἀνάλυσις Brentiana pia & erudita est. Nam ita προσφώνησις dirigitur ad Ecclesiam in communi, ac postmodum ubi dilatare jubetur tentoria sua, peculiariter ea attinent Eccle- siam Judaicam; tum applicatio quoq; suavis ac ju- cunda fieri potest, ad paucitatem fidelium quo- rumvis temporum: quia de Ecclesia γενικῶς dici- tur: lætare quæ non paris, &c. Denique peculiariter ita ad Ecclesiam & tempora N. T. refertur, etsi ge- neralis sit compellatio: quia appropriatur huic tempori, per primum consolationis argumentum, de quo proinde recte Brentius observat, quod id agat de conversione gentium. Τὸ ῥητὸν hujus dicti manifeste concionatur de vocatione gentium, & de mul- tiplicatione Ecclesiæ ex gentibus. Nam gens Judai- ca est quasi mulier, habens maritum, quia data est ei Lex & promissio de Christo, tanquam mulieri maritus, ut ex ea gente multi filii Dei & cives cœlestes procrea- rentur. Unde & Paulus Rom. 7. confert legem mari- to. An ignoratis, inquiens, quod lex tantisper do- minetur homini, quoad is vixerit! Nam viro ob- noxia mulier, viventi viro alligata est per legem &c. Gens autem Ethnica, & incircumcisa est velut mulier à viro deserta & repudiata, quia nec habuit legem, nec promissiones. Itaque non potuerunt ex ea gente, quantum quidem ad leges, & politiam ejus attine- bat, filii Dei nasci. Sed quid factum est? Cum venis- set Christus, & vulgaret per Apostolos Evangelion suum inter Judæos & gentes, multo plures collecti sunt ad Ecclesiam ex gentibus. Plures, inquit, sunt filii desertæ, videlicet gentis Ethnicæ, quam ejus, quæ marito juncta erat, h. e. gentis Judaicæ. Huc & Pau- lus respicit, cum ait, Gentes, quæ non sectabantur justitiam, apprehenderunt justitiam. Justitiam au- tem eam, quæ est ex fide. Contra, Israël, qui secta- batur legem Justitiæ, ad legem Justitiæ non perve- nit. Propter quid? quia non ex fide, sed tanquam ex operibus legis. Quod cum ita se habeat, ut tu pu- sille grex Ecclesiæ inter Judæos multiplicandus sis ac- cessione gentium, non est, quod despondeas animum, & defatigeris in ædificanda Ecclesia: sed potius dilata locum tentorii tui. Neque abnuit huic explicatio- ni Wolfgangus Musculus. Adimpletionem, inquit, vaticinii hujus non debemus referre ad tempus illud restitutæ Sionis, quod inter liberationem è Babylone & tempus Christi Servatoris intercessit, sed ad tempus regni Christi, in quo reliquiæ Sionis, per accessionem gentium creverunt in immensum. Quotquot enim ex gentibus Christo accesserunt, facti sunt filii Sionis, paulo ante desolatæ ac sterilis. Per Sionem autem in- telligo non carnalem Hierusalem, quæ Christum Ser- vatorem suum sprevit: Sed spiritualem, Ecclesiam videlicet electorum ac fidelium, quæ perpetuo tum in Babylone, tum è Babylone liberata, & postea tempo- re Christi, corde sincero Domino Deo suo adhæsit, quam recte primitias Ecclesiæ Christi vocamus. Et hoc sensu præsentem locum usurpavit Apostolus, Gal. 4.

ubi non confert Israëlis & gentium, sed carnalis & spiritualis Israëlis Ecclesias. Non debemus autem cre- dentes ex circumcisione secludere ab Ecclesia spiritua- lis Israëlis, cum illi hujus fuerint primitiæ. Hæc ille.

Jam si verborum emphasin expendamus, gau- dium non carnale & mundanum, sed spirituale & divinum hic intimari, minime obscurum erit. Compellat Propheta sterilem, quæ non parit, quæ non parturit. Quæ respiciunt sterilitatem, & fœ- cunditatem, quoad generationem spiritualem; Non enim facile docebitur, cum civibus orba quæ- dam urbs describitur, eam & quæ non parit, & quæ non parturit ob desolationem vocari. At spiritualem sterilitatem, partumque & regenerationem ita de- scribi novum non est, Psal. 68, 7. Esa. 49, 22. 60, 4. 66, 9. 53, 10. Nec aliter intellexit Apostolus, cum matrem fidelium per Hierosolymam designari do- cuit Gal. 4. & cœlestem Hierosolymam, quæ ἄνω- θεν est. Unde manifestum est explicationi Aposto- licæ contrariari, qui de terrena Hierosolyma acci- pit, & de urbe ac politia externa. Hæc enim non est mater fidelium. Quæ uti gignit nos spiritualiter per verbum & sacramenta, ita in aprico est, sterili- tatem spiritualem à Propheta designari, quod etiam mentio conjugii spiritualis v. 5. & denominatio fi- liorum, qui à Deo docti sunt v. 13. ipsiusque Christi explicatio Joh. 6, 45. infert. Neque vero ob exter- nam restaurationem Propheta ad tantum gaudium provocat. Quamvis enim insigne beneficium fue- rit illa restauratio, longe tamen major gaudii causa est fidelium, cum Ecclesiæ ampliatio & propagatio promittitur. Ideo isto utitur verborum apparatu, quem in lætitia & exaltatione spirituali adhibere solet S. S. ut imprimis ex odis Davidicis, tum Esaia- nis quoque videre est. Lætare, prorumpe in gaudium, jubila. S. Cyrillus peculiarem emphasin notat in voce PRORUMPENDI ῥῆξον ὴ βόησον. Erat, inquit, in Deo omnium sterilis, nullum pariens, qui deberet aut posset in filiis Dei reputari, & recenseri propter fidem & virtutem. Sed ecce jussum est erum- pere & clamare. Solent autem id facere mulieres, quæ in sella sunt & pariunt: quas ajunt excitare ob- stetrices, interrita & alta vox exclamare, quo infans è matrice extrahatur, visceribus ad clamorem dila- tatis. Hoc, opinor, est: Erumpe & clama. In- cipe, inquit, parere, & quasi parturiens multos, pa- rientibus convenientem semper clamorem subinde ede, tanquam mater vere futura innumerabilium popu- lorum, voluptatem percipe spiritualem. Declarans vero hujus dicti sensum universorum Deus, infert, dicens: Quia plures filii desertæ, quam haben- tis virum. Familiare est igitur Scripturæ divinitus inspiratæ, desertam appellare viduam. Vidua autem fuit gentium multitudo. Non enim quicquam ei commercii fuit cum Sermone, cum Sermone, in- quam, omnis veræ cognitionis & studiorum ad pieta- tem pertinentium satore. Grotius vero Annot. ad Galat. 4. mavult eruptionem vocis innui: ῥήγνυσθαι potest quidem & ipsum partum significare: Sed He- bræus textus magis exigit, ut eruptio vocis intelliga- tur, quomodo ῥῆξες φωνὴν habemus Job. 6, 5. & ver- bum ipsum, quod hic in Hebræo est פצח per βοᾶν ver- titur Es. 14, 7. 44, 23. Quod etiamsi admittamus, è Paulina tamen interpretatione manifestum est, materiam gaudii non terrenam esse, sed spiritua- lem & cœlestem.

Id vero ulterius confirmatur è præcipuo hu- jus gaudii argumento. Quæ secunda nobis ratio specialis est adversus Grotianum commentum. QUONIAM MULTI FILII DESERTÆ MA- GIS QUAM EJUS, QUÆ HABET VIRUM. Quænam deserta illa sit, ex oppositione elucescit.

Per eam enim, quæ virum habere dicitur, intelligi civitates à principibus aut regibus suis regnatas, mere precaria glossa est, quæ nemini, opinor, præter Grotium ad talia εὑρήματα natum, in mentem ve- nit. Manifestum autem est intelligi Ecclesiam, cujus vir & maritus est Dominus, ut v. 5. aperte dicitur, qui te fecit maritus tuus, & v. 6. quia ut mulierem derelictam & mœrentem spiritu vocavit te Domi- nus, & uxorem ab adolescentia abjectam. Ideoque desertæ nomine gentilitatem intelligunt Interpp. quæ prius plane derelicta erat, uti per eam, quæ vi- rum habet designatam Ecclesiam Judaicam cen- sent. Si tamen ea, quæ virum habet, sit Ecclesia Judaica, cum in pristino vigore esset, deserta autem eadem dicatur sub tempus adventus Christi, gentes hic sub filiorum multorum nomine comprehen- dentur, quia additur: semen tuum gentes hæredita- bit, non corporali hæreditate, sed spirituali, ut B. Lutherus. Hoc ob Grotium addimus, qui per ἔ- ρημον & שׁוממה l. c. vult intelligi viduam, uti sumi- tur Thren. 1, 13. Quamvis objectio ejus infirma sit ex opposito membro. Nam illi, quæ virum habet, op- ponitur, quæ virum non habet, sive habuerit & vidua sit, seu non habuerit. Et agnoscit Grotius, Ebræam & Græcam vocem posse significare orbam liberis, desertam ab amicis, & multa similia. Cyrillus de gen- tilitate explicat: Ante Servatoris, inquit, adventum vidua erat & sterilis, ob eamque causam orba liberis. Sed postquam per fidem cælestem sponsum accepit, plu- res liberos suscepit, quam ea, quæ virum habuit, id est, Judæorum Synagoga. Hieronymi sententiam an- tea adduximus. Tertiam rationem præbet dilatatio Ecclesiæ, de qua vers. sequenti. Quem iterum frustra cor- rumpere satagit Grotius.

## 54:2
Verse 2. ENLARGE THE PLACE OF YOUR TENT] Cities are compared to a tent, see Ezekiel 23. AND STRENGTHEN YOUR STAKES] Fix the pegs well, to which those ropes that support the tent are tied. See above 33:20. Verse 3. FOR YOU SHALL SPREAD TO THE RIGHT AND TO THE LEFT] To the North and to the South. YOUR SEED SHALL INHERIT THE GENTILES] You shall extend your empire even beyond the old borders, into Idumea, Moab, and Syria.

It will have to be proven that material cities are being regarded, but we have already shown that the Apostle and Christ himself interpret it concerning the Church. For this is the mother of us all. And in this all are taught by God, all who hear from the Father and learn, who come to Christ, John 6. But here she is commanded to enlarge the place of her tent because of the multitude of the Gentiles who are gathered. It teaches, therefore, that the boundaries of the Church are to be widened. And there is an allusion to the Mosaic tent or tabernacle, which was a certain type of the Church. It is also signified that the Church in the New Testament is not tied to a certain place. Therefore, he used the name of a tent rather than a temple. It is evident, however, even from this name, how absurd Grotius's opinion concerning the Evangelical covenant or the Gospel is. For since he understands the Evangelical covenant by Jerusalem, what would be denoted by the tent! His words in Galatians 4:26 are as follows. By the name Jerusalem here is understood the other covenant, namely the Evangelical, and that on account of the etymology. For Jerusalem signifies a vision of peace, which name fits the Gospel accordingly, Luke 2:14, Romans 5:1, chapter 10:15, 1 Corinthians 7:15, Ephesians 2:17. The Hebrews expect a more beautiful Jerusalem. Zohar on Numbers, Jarchi on the Song of Songs: But truly that beautiful Jerusalem has already arrived, Revelation 21:2. It is said, however, to have come from above, because God the Father revealed it not by descending onto a mountain, but by remaining in heaven and sending His Son. The writer to the Hebrews 12:25 teaches us this sense. Trifles. Nowhere is the Gospel denoted by the word Jerusalem, nor is that taught in Hebrews 12:25, to which place this meaning does not fit at all. For is the Gospel denoted by Mount Zion, to which we have approached? You would equally ineptly understand the Gospel in Revelation 21:2. For is the bride who comes from heaven the Gospel! Such glosses are worthy of the author Hugo, or Nugone (Trifler). Although the Gospel is a messenger of peace, it is not, however, a vision OF PEACE, much less does it come by the name of Jerusalem. And is the Gospel the mother of the faithful! Grotius thinks so, because, forsooth, διαθήκη (covenant) is a feminine noun, as he seems to infer in the same place. Which, however, is not to infer, but to play with a serious and sacred matter. By the Gospel, indeed, we are begotten spiritually, but the mother who generates us is the Church. The Gospel and the word of truth is the medium through which we are begotten; it is the incorruptible seed from which we are reborn, 1 Peter 1:21, James 1:18, but we are referred to the tents, the enlargement of which denotes the expansion of the Church, not of a city, because the tent was a type of the Church. Whence St. Cyril: 'Enlarge the place of your tent, and your tabernacle.' For because she was endowed with good and numerous offspring beyond expectation, having received the word or bridegroom from heaven, she is necessarily commanded to extend her tabernacles in breadth and length, and to fix the stakes, so that you may understand from this the unshaken base of the Church of the Gentiles. To stretch out the cords indicates the spacious and incomparably rich amplitude of the holy Churches, even if the first tent was altogether small and had very narrow courtyards. Nevertheless, even in that workmanship, one can see, as in a figure and type, the breadth, length, and looseness of the Church of the Gentiles described. For around the ten curtains, made of goats' hair, the courtyards were placed on all four sides, as if cutting the individual parts of the world, one hundred in length, fifty in breadth. Therefore he says: 'Expand further to the right and to the left,' that is, let your cords be widened on all sides. The whole world is full of holy Churches: for they are also quite large, spacious, and very long on all sides and most beautiful. For thus says the God of all concerning the Jerusalem temple built after the first was burned down by the hands of the Assyrians: Who is there among you who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now, he says, as if it were not in your eyes? As I live, says the Lord: Because the glory of this latter house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord almighty. For many more and more opulent temples, i.e., Churches, have been built throughout the whole world than the temple that was at Jerusalem, having an altar august to the glory of Christ. Enlarge therefore, he says, the place of your tent, and of your tabernacles. Thus Cyril. Likewise also St. Jerome: To whom he had said: Praise, O barren one, who do not bear, break the bonds by which you were held bound, and cry out in confession of the Lord, you who did not have children. Now she is commanded, in the likeness of the tabernacle of Moses which it once had in the desert, to enlarge her tent, and stretch out her skins, and make her cords longer, and drive the pegs, by which every tent is fastened, deep into the ground, and strengthen them, lest it be dissipated by the blasts of the winds. And let it penetrate to the right and to the left, and by no means imitate the narrowness of the Jewish tabernacle, which encompassed a length of one hundred cubits and a breadth of fifty: nor let it be enclosed by the brevity of the temple, which had sixty cubits in length and twenty in breadth. But let it not cease to take up space to the right and to the left. He adds (refuting Grotius regarding the Jews) what follows: And lest we think this is said according to the frivolous contention of the Hebrews concerning Zion, which is to be restored by the Lord to its ancient state, he sets forth more clearly what was hidden: And your seed shall inherit the nations. Concerning which also in the Gospel we read: He went out who sows to sow. And again: Did you not sow good seed in your field? Which seed will also cause deserted cities to be inhabited, so that the Churches of the nations may arise in the whole world. Or certainly, the seed must be said to be the Apostles and the remnants of the Jewish people. Concerning which it is said in this same Prophet seed, we would have been as Sodom, and we would have been like Gomorrah. But the Apostle says: The remnants, he says, have been saved. This is about the magnitude of the Churches, which, instead of one place of Judea and that a very narrow one, will dilate their borders in the whole world.

The fourth reason, therefore, is sought from the inheritance of the nations. THY SEED, it is said to the Church, SHALL INHERIT THE NATIONS. These things are rightly referred to the remnants of Israel by Jerome. For when the Prophet addresses the Church, those things by which he commands her to dilate the place of her tent pertain to the Jewish Church. In whose possession was the tent, but it was too narrow. Through the borders TO THE RIGHT AND TO THE LEFT, the propagation of the Church into all parts of the earth is insinuated. Therefore, she is said to inherit the NATIONS. That is, not only a few in Idumea, Moabitis, Syria: But indefinitely and generally, as this inheritance is explained in Ps. 2 and Isa. 60. Furthermore, it is not only alien but also false, both what Grotius assumes, and that the empire extended itself beyond the old borders of the Jews after the captivity, which was certainly far larger under David and Solomon, and that it extended itself into Idumea, Moabitis, and Syria, which is repugnant to history. The sense, however, which we have given concerning the spiritual tents, agrees no less with the text than with experience and historical truth: which Brentius expressed very well: Dilate the place of your tent, and extend the curtains of your tabernacles. Do not spare. Do not grow sluggish. Do not describe the place with narrow borders, but stretch out your ropes as far as possible, and firmly consolidate the nails by which the ropes are fixed to the earth. For so great will be the assembly of the Church that it can no longer be contained by the Mosaic tent or tabernacle. A new and sufficiently ample tabernacle will have to be built, which may lie open in every direction, as much to the right as to the left. For your seed will inherit the nations, and will inhabit the deserted cities, i.e. The Apostles, and a few others from the Jews, who were selected as seed from the remaining crowd, will beget by their preaching, for the receiving of the heavenly inheritance, a great multitude of nations, and will cause these regions and cities, which now seem entirely alien and deserted by the people of God, to become the hospices of the children of God and of the true Church of the Lord. Cyril believed that the Church of the nations was addressed in these words; therefore, since the Church of the nations was at first small, he judged it to be indicated that it would afterwards rule over many nations and regions, in this manner: Thy seed will possess the nations, and you will inhabit the devastated cities. For the Church of the nations was the mother and nurse of very many holy and good men, and she brought forth many princes and prefects of peoples, so that she ruled over many nations, and was able to hand down the uncorrupted sermon of the mystery, and did not lack the art of shepherding. For such a great multitude of your seed, he says, will there be, that cities full of inhabitants will not suffice, but that they will be able to fill the vast ones.

Latin:

Vers. 2. DILATA LOCUM TENTORII TUI] Ur- bes tentorio comparantur, vid. Ezech. 23. ET CLAVOS TUOS CONSOLIDA] Paxillos bene defige, ad quos deligantur funes illi, qui tentorium sustinent. Vide supra 33, 20. Vers. 3. AD DEXTERAM ENIM ET AD LÆ- VAM PENETRABIS] Ad Aquilonem & Austrum. SEMEN TUUM GENTES HÆREDITABIT] Et- iam extra veteres fines imperium porriges, in Idumeam, Moabitidem, Syriam.

Urbes materiales respici probandum erit, de Ecclesia vero interpretari Apostolum, Christumq; ipsum jam ostendimus. Hæc enim est omnium no- strûm mater. Et in hac omnes sunt à Deo docti, omnes, qui audiunt à Patre, & discunt, qui ad Christum ve- niunt, Joh. 6. Jubetur autem dilatare locum tentorii hic ob multitudinem gentium, quæ aggregantur. Docet ergo pomæria Ecclesiæ amplianda esse. Et alluditur ad tentorium vel tabernaculum Mosaicum, quod typus quidam erat Ecclesiæ. Significatur etiam Ecclesiam non esse in N. T. ad certum locum alligatam. Ideo potius tentorii, quam templi nomen adhibuit. Patet autem vel ex hoc nomine, quam ab- surda sit Grotii de fœdere Evangelico, vel Evangelio sententia. Nam quum per Hierosolymam intelligat fœdus Evangelicum, ecquid per tentorium notabi- tur! Verba ejus ita habent Gal. 4, 26. Nomine Jeru- salem hic intelligitur alterum fœdus, nempe Evangeli- cum, idque ob ἐτυμολογίαν. Nam Jerusalem signifi- cat visionem pacis, quod nomen Evangelio exinde competit Luc. 2, 14. Rom. 5, 1. cap. 10, 15. 1. Cor. 7, 15. Eph. 2, 17. Hebræi pulchriorem Jerusalem expectant. Zohar ad Numeros, Jarchi ad Canticum: Sed vere illa pulchra Ierusalem jam advenit Apoc. 21, 2. Dici- tur autem superne venisse, quia Deus Pater eam non in montem descendens, sed in cælo manens misso Filio suo revelavit. Hunc sensum docet nos scriptor ad Heb. 12, 25. Nugæ. Nuspiam voce Jerusalem Evangelium notatur, nec id docetur Ebr. 12, 25. cui loco plane non congruit haec significatio. Num enim per mon- tem Sion, ad quem accessimus, Evangelium nota- tur? Aeque inepte Apoc. 21, 2. Evangelium intelli- gas. Num enim sponsa, quae de caelo venit, Evange- lium est! Dignae tales glossae sunt autore Hugone, vel Nugone. Quamvis Evangelium pacis nuncium sit, non tamen visio PACIS est, nedum Hierosoly- morum nomine venit. Et num Evangelium est ma- ter fidelium! Id putat Grotius, quia scilicet διαθήκη nomen foemininum est, ut ibidem colligere vide- tur. Quod vero non colligere est, sed in re seria & sacra ludere. Per Evangelium quidem gignimur spiritualiter, sed mater, quae nos generat, Ecclesia est. Evangelium & verbum veritatis medium est, per quod gignimur, semen est incorruptibile, ex quo renascimur 1. Pet. 1, 21. Jac. 1, 18. sed remittimur ad tentoria, quorum dilatatio Ecclesiae ampliationem, non civitatis denotat, quia tentorium typus erat Ecclesiae. Unde S. Cyrillus: Dilata locum tentorii tui, & tabernaculum tuum. Nam quia bona & nu- merosa sobole praeter opinionem praedita fuit, accepto de caelo sermone sive sponso, necessario jubetur taber- nacula sua in latitudinem & longitudinem extendere, & clavos figere, ut inconcussam Ecclesiae gentium basim inde intelligas. Protendere funiculos, spacio- sam & incomparabiliter divitem sanctarum Eccle- siarum amplitudinem subindicat, etiamsi primum tentorium omnino parvum fuerit, & atria habuerit angustissima. Veruntamen vel in illo opificio videre licet tanquam in figura ac typo descriptam Ecclesiae gentium latitudinem, longitudinem, & laxitatem. Nam circa decem aulaeas, ex pellibus cilicinis confe- ctas, aulae positae erant undiq; quatuor, veluti singulas orbis partes secantes, longitudine centum, latitudine quinquaginta. Propterea dicit: Adhuc in dextris & in sinistris expande, id est, undiquaq; funiculi tui amplientur. Plenus est sanctarum Ecclesiarum orbis terrarum: etenim sunt quoq; bene magnae, spacio- sae, & bene longe undique & pulcherrimae. Sic enim dicit universorum Deus templo Hierosolymitano ex- structo post primum manibus Assyriorum exustum. Quis ex vobis est, qui vidit domum hanc in gloria sua priore? Et quomodo nunc, inquit, videtis ipsam, quasi non esset in oculis vestris? Vivo ego, dicit Dominus: Quia major erit gloria domus hu- jus ultimae, quam primae, dicit Dominus omnipo- tens. Nam templo, quod Hierosolymis fuit, multo plu- ra & opulentiora per universum orbem terrarum aedi- ficata sunt templa, i. e. Ecclesiae, habentes altare in gloriam Christi augustum. Dilata igitur, inquit, lo- cum tentorii tui, & tabernaculorum tuorum. Haec Cyrillus. Ita & S. Hieronymus: Cui dixerat: Lau- da sterilis, quae non paris, rumpe vincula, quibus tenebaris adstricta, & clama in confessionem Domini, quae liberos non habebas. Nunc eidem praecipitur in si- militudinem tabernaculi Moysi, quod quondam ha- buit in deserto, ut dilatet tentorium suum, pellesq; di- stentet, & funiculos faciat longiores, & claves, quibus firmatur omne tentorium, in altum defigat, & roboret, ne ventorum flatibus dissipetur. Ad dextramq; pene- tret & sinistram, & nequaquam judaici tabernaculi imitetur angustias, quod centum cubitorum longitu- dinis, & quinquaginta latitudinis ambiebat: nec tem- pli brevitate claudatur, quod sexaginta cubita habe- bat in longum, & viginti in latum. Sed ad dexteram & sinistram locum capere ne cesset. Addit (Grotium in Judaeis refellens) quae sequuntur: Ac ne putemus hoc juxta frivolam Hebraeorum contentionem dici de Sion, quae in antiquum statum a Domino restituen- da sit, ponit manifestius, quod latebat: Et semen tuum gentes haereditabit. De quo & in Evangelio legimus: Egressus est qui seminat seminare. Et iterum: Nonne bonum semen seminasti in agro tuo? Quod semen etiam civitates desertas faciet in- habitari, ut Ecclesiæ gentium in toto orbe consurgant. Vel certe semen dicendum est Apostolorum & Judæi- ci populi reliquiæ. De quo in hoc eodem Propheta dicitur: Nisi Dominus Sabaoth reliquisset nobis semen, sicut Sodoma essemus, & similes Gomorræ fuissemus. At Apostolus: Reliquiæ, ait, salvæ factæ sunt. Hoc de Ecclesiarum magnitudine, quæ pro uno Judææ loco & ipso angustissimo, in toto orbe terrarum, suos terminos dilatabunt.

Quarta itaque ratio ab hæreditate gentium pe- titur. SEMEN TUUM, dicitur Ecclesiæ, GENTES HÆREDITABIT. Hæc recte ad reliquias Israëlis referuntur ab Hieronymo. Nam cum Ecclesiam compellet Propheta, ea, quibus ju- bet dilatet locum tentorii, ad Judaicam Ecclesiam pertinent. Penes quam erat tentorium, sed nimis angustum. Per terminos AD DEXTRAM ET AD SINISTRAM propagatio Ecclesiæ in omnes terræ partes insinuatur. Ideo GENTES hæredi- tare dicitur. Hoc est, non paucos tantum in Idu- mæa, Moabitide, Syria: Sed indefinite & genera- liter, uti exponitur Ps. 2. hæc hæreditas, & Esa. 60. Adhæc non modo alienum, sed etiam falsum u- trumque est, quod assumit Grotius, & quod extra ve- teres fines Judæorum imperium sese porrexerit post ca- ptivitatem, quod utique longe amplius sub Davide ac Salomone fuit, & quod in Idumæam, Moabiti- dem, Syriam sese extenderit, quod historiæ repu- gnat. Sensus autem quem dedimus de spirituali- bus tentoriis, non minus textui congruit quam ex- perientiæ ac veritati historicæ: quem optime ex- pressit Brentius: Dilata locum tentorii tui, & ex- tende cortinas tabernaculorum tuorum. Ne par- cas. Ne torpescas. Ne describas locum angustis finibus, sed diduc funes tuos quam longissime, & consolida firmiter clavos, quibus funes terræ insi- guntur. Tantus enim erit cœtus Ecclesiæ, ut non possit amplius contineri tentorio seu tabernaculo Mo- saico. Novum & satis amplum tabernaculum æ- dificandum erit, quod quaquaversum tam ad dextram quam ad sinistram pateat. Nam semen tuum hæredi- tabit gentes, & inhabitabit civitates desertas, h. e. Apostoli, & pauci alii ex Judæis, qui tanquam semen ex reliqua turba selecti sunt, gignent prædicatione sua ad accipiendam cælestem hæreditatem, magnam gentium multitudinem, & efficient, ut hæ regiones & civitates, quæ modo videntur à populo Dei prorfus alienæ & deser- te, fiant hospitia filiorum Dei & veræ Ecclesiæ Domini. Gentium Ecclesiam compellari his verbis credidit Cyrillus, ideo cum exigua primum fuerit gentium Ecclesia, postmodum gentibus & regionibus mul- tis dominaturam fuisse indicari censuit h. m. Se- men tuum gentes possidebit, & civitates vastatas in- habitabis. Plurimorum namq́; virorum sanctorum & bonorum mater nutrix Ecclesia gentium fuit, ac multos principes atq́; præfectos populorum peperit, ad- eo ut multis gentibus dominaretur, & quod illibaturn mystagogiæ sermonem tradere potuit, & artificio pa- scendi non caruit. Tanta enim, inquit, multitudo seminis tui erit, ut civitates plenæ habitatoribus non suffecerint, sed ut vastas replere possint.

## 54:4
Vers. 4.

YOU WILL FORGET THE CONFUSION OF YOUR YOUTH] The time of youth, which when these things happen will have long since passed. Thus also shortly 6.

But here again the inept Commentary of Grotius is confounded. For in her youth Jerusalem, or earthly Judea, was not confounded, but enjoyed the best flower. Therefore, the fifth reason can be fixed here, to refute his Jewish commentaries. That widow is to be understood here, who suffered confusion in her youth. But the earthly Jerusalem did not suffer this in her youth. Jerome, however, raises a doubt here from the mind of the Jews and Judaizers, how the Church of the nations can be understood by the barren woman, since she was not a widow, to which there is no reason for us to bring forward his own responses: since there is no place for doubt if by the barren woman, who is addressed here as the Church, it is understood generally, not restrictedly as the Church of the nations, as we observed from Brentius. By which method all things are easy and plain. Who also interpreted this promise happily: YOU WILL NOT BE CONFOUNDED, YOU WILL NOT BE ASHAMED, you will not be affected by ignominy, YOU WILL NOT BLUSH, BUT YOU WILL FORGET THE CONFUSION OF YOUR VIRGINITY (For instead of Youth in the Hebrew is alumaich, which properly signifies, Your virginity) and you will no longer remember the reproach of your widowhood. He persists in the begun metaphor of a woman, of whom there are three species. One is a virgin, another a widow, the third a wife who has a husband. And this one is indeed in that kind of life in which she may conceive and bring forth children. But a virgin is barren, and a widow is deserted, because the former neither had nor has a husband: the latter, even if she had a husband, nevertheless lost him. He says therefore: You, O Church, have been seen until now as a virgin and a widow, i.e., plainly barren and deserted, and therefore subject to confusion and reproach.
