Et quamvis respiceretur terrena Hierusalem, quæ sedes fuit Ecclesiæ, ratione derelictionis, & abje- ctionis, quod protrita & abominationi habita fue- rit, ac ratione vastationis Babylonicæ, non ta- men externa solum ejusdem reparatio hic designa- ta fuerit, sed Ecclesiæ in eadem restauratio & per ean- dem propagatio: quia ideo restaurata fuit, ut pro- pagaretur Ecclesia, quæ in statu presso erat sub ser- vitute Babylonica. Postea autem extructo tem- plo illustrior facta, & longe amplius propagata, imo & in superbiam feculi & gaudium in generatio- nem & generationem posita, non per materiale templum, sed quando ex Hierusalem prodiit doctrina Evangelii per totum orbem. Ad tempora enim N. T. & vocationem gentium hæc imprimis pertinere, ea quæ adjecit Propheta, palam testantur, Et SU- GES Lac gentium & mammilla Regum lactaberis: Filiæ enim Hierusalem mysticæ vel Ecclesiæ edu- cantur & foventur sumtibus Gentium & Regum: qui nutritii sunt Ecclesiæ, ut loco parallelo Esa. 49, 23. habetur. B. Brentius refert hæc peculiariter ad juventutem, quæ fovetur sumtibus Regum, donec adoleverit, & impletum dicit, cum Reges, Princi- pes & civitates, Scholas, in quibus juventus docea- tur pias literas, & in catecheticis instituatur, κοινό- βια, & collegia studiosorum, in quibus doctrina Evangelii Adolescentiæ tradebatur, & ad posteros propagata est, & Academias instituêre, ut sumtibus eorum tanquam mammillis & lacte educentur ado- lescentes ad ministeria tam Politica quam Eccle- siastica. Non hic de attrahendis divitiis vel opi- bus tantum terrenis, sed de spontanea gentium & Regum beneficentia in Ecclesiam, qua nutritii e- jusdem alentur & fovebuntur, sermo est. LXX. Interpp. cum Chaldæo divitias habent: sed recte Hieronymus: Hæ divitiæ secundum Hebraicam veritatem ubera sunt Regum atq; Doctorum, qui- bus nascentium in CHRISTO eruditur & nutritur infantia. Quæ cum fuxeris & perveneris ad soli- dum cibum, tunc scies, quod ego sum Salvator tuus, qui te redemi sanguine meo, sive DEUS fortis Jacob. PRO ÆRE AFFERAM AURUM. Hæc non de operibus terrenis, aut iis, quæ ademta terrenæ urbi, restituendis cum augmento, accipienda sunt. Analogæ tales gloffæ somniis sunt Judæorum, qui ubique terrenas divitias & opes ac carnalem prospe- ritatem sibi fingunt: Quod si τῷ ῥητῷ præcise in- hærere velis, ostendatur, quando hoc vaticinium juxta τὸ ῥητὸν impletum sit: quod certe si literam spectes, non de restitutione ablatorum loquitur, sed immensas promittit divitias, quia pro ære pollicetur aurum, pro ferro argentum, pro lignis æs, pro lapidi- bus ferrum. Quomodo vero, non dicam Judæorum exulum restituta Politia, sed Monarchia potentis- sima sub cœlo tantas unquam habuit divitias, tan- tos thesauros? Manifestum ergo iterum est, spiri- tualiter hæc intelligenda esse de regno Christi, quod à regnis terrenis describi solet, illis sub ma- gnificentissimo statu etiam propositis, ut majestas ejus quodammodo nobis, quibus terrena hæc ante oculos solum versantur, cœlestia ἀόρατα καὶ ἄῤῥητα sunt, adumbretur. Uno verbo, omnia in Re- gno Christi dicuntur fore splendida, omnia gloriosa, & vere majestatica. Sed splendor ille internus est, non externus, splendor spiritualis est & cœlestis, etsi terreno & mundano splendore adumbretur, qualis nempe filiæ Regis splendor erit, auro fulgentis, cujus gloria omnis ab intus est Pf. 44, 10. 13. Divitiæ hæ spi- rituales Ecclesiæ sunt Christus ipse, qui est omnium bonorum thesaurus, cum quo donata sunt ei remif- sio peccatorum, justitia & salus æterna & omnia bona cœlestia, quibus nihil in ullo unquam regno præstantius fuit, nihil pretiosius. Deinde præter has generales divitias, quæ cuivis fideli donantur, in Ecclesiam per Christum conferuntur aliæ etiam opes & dona, quibus corpus Ecclesiæ non solum a- litur, sed etiam ornatur, & vegetum redditur, ut sunt: Prophetia, linguæ &c. Denig, prospicit etiam DEUS Ecclesiæ & fidelibus quibusvis de opibus ne- cessariis, imo efficit, ut Ecclesia etiam juxta æternas opes ditissima sit. Dives enim est, non qui mul- tum auri & argenti possidet, sed qui paucis est con- tentus. Magnus enim quæstus pietas, cum animo sua sorte contento. Hoc autem est opus fidei in piis, ut minuat cupiditatem terrenarum divitiarum & impleat animum cœlestibus opibus, præ quarum multitudine & magnitudine non reputet terrenas opes, sed optime contentus sit iis, quas Dominus dederit, & è quibus etiam, quantumvis alioqui paucissimis, tantum necessariarum rerum accipit, quantum Crœsus quispiam ex omnibus reditibus regni sui. Hieronymus alia ratione hæc expli- cat spiritualiter: Ergo in instauratione spiritualis Hie- rosalem ligna vertentur in æs: & lapides mutabun- tur in ferrum, id est, bruti quondam & insensibiles homines, in eas materias mutabuntur, quæ utilitatem aliquam præbeant civitati. Ipsumque æs aut fer- rum per augmenta virtutum, in aurum argentumq, mutabuntur; ut nequaquam utilitatis speciem, sed pretium quoq, habeant ac decorem.

Vers. eod.

PONAM VISITATJONEM TUAM PACEM] פְּקֻדָּה Hebræis præfecturam significat, & μετωνυμικῶς pro ipsis præfectis sumitur, quomodo hic acceperunt & Græci & Chaldæus. Sensus est: clementer gubernaberis ac Es- dra, Zorobabele, Nehemia & horum similibus,

Vers. eod.

ET PRÆPOSITOS TUOS JUSTITIAM] In He- bræo: Exactores tuos justitiam: id est, summa cum æqui- tate ac moderatione tributa abs te exigentur. Vide Es- dram 10. v. 32.

His verbis præfectos & præpositos vel exactores Hierosolymæ describi ac celebrari dubio vacat, sed non describuntur à Politicis virtutibus, clementia, æquitate, ac moderatione, in gubernatione aut tribu- torum exactione. Tota enim tractatio docet, longe sublimior hic spectari, ad quorum majestatem illa exigui sint momenti, si quis clemens in guberna- tione, moderatus in tributorum exactione sit: & verba ipsa ABSTRACTIVA plus important: Nam non præfectos CLEMENTES ET PACI- FICOS promittunt, sed ponam, inquit, PRÆ- FECTURAM aut PRÆFECTOS PACEM: non PRÆPOSITOS moderatos, sed PONAM PRÆPOSITOS TUOS JUSTITIAM. Quam emphasin recte expressit Brentius, quod allusio ad Regnum Salomonis fiat: In regno Christi sunt etiam sui præpositi & exactores, quos vo- camus præsides, Præfectos, Scultetos & Publi- canos, sed longe tolerabiliores ac meliores, quam fuerunt præfecti Israëlitarum in Ægypto, aut et- iam in Regno Salomonis. Hi enim Israëlitas du- rissimis suis exactionibus ita perturbarunt, ut non ingemiscerent tantum; verum etiam præ Tyran- nidis gravitate vociferarentur: Cur ita agis con- tra servos tuos? Et, Pater tuus durissimum jugum imposuit nobis. Quod si vero de Ecclesiasticis præ- positis, ac præfectis Israëlitarum loquendum est, non fuerunt politicis illis tolerabiliores, sed gra- viores. Alii enim qui urgebant humanas tradi- tiones, non afferebant conscientiis pacem sed tantum perturbationem ac desperationem. Alii qui urgebant legem ipsam, non afferebant justi- tiam, sed potius injustitiam. Lex enim auget non aufert peccatum. Et quanquam lex neces- sario prædicanda & recte explicanda est, ut agni- to peccato ad consequendam justitiam Christi properetur, tamen si lex prædicatur absque Christo, quod solenne est doctoribus legis, ducit potius ad agnitionem injustitiæ, quam justitiæ, & facit peccatum majorem in modum peccans. Chri- stos autem ponit præpositos suos Pacem, & Scul- tetos suos justitiam, hoc est, constituit in admini- strando regno suo tales præfectos qui afferant pa- cem & justitiam. Hoc præcipue respicit in A- postolos & Apostolicam prædicationem. Christus enim legit Apostolos suos, & misit eos in univer- sum orbem, ut prædicarent Evangelion omni crea- turæ. Evangelion autem de JESU CHRISTO affert veram pacem conscientiæ, & veram co- ram Deo justitiam. Annunciat enim Deum patrem esse nobis reconciliatum & placatum, per filium suum Jesum Christum, & docet justitiam Fi- lii Dei omnibus, qui in ipsum credunt, donari ac imputari, ut reputentur, propter Christum, co- ram Deo tam justi, quam si legem suis ipsorum o- peribus implevissent. Justificati igitur ex fide, ut Paulus ait, pacem habemus erga Deum per Domi- num nostrum Jesum Christum. Apostolos sequuti sunt alii præpositi & præfecti, qui doctrinam ab i- psis traditam propagarunt, ac pacem & justitiam Ecclesiæ afferunt, per doctrinam ab Apostolis tra- ditam, & S. S. confirmatam, ut etiamsi Apostoli vi- vita defuncti sint, maneant tamen per doctrinam suam, quam solam suscipit Ecclesia, præfecti ac præ- positi Ecclesiæ. De his Psal. 55. Pro patribus tuis nati sunt tibi filii, constitues eos principes super o- mnem terram. Et iterum Ps. 68. Principes Juda duces eorum, Principes Zabulon & Principes Naph- thalim. Et supra c. 52. Quam pulcri super montes pedes adnunciantis & prædicantis Pacem, & in Joh. c. 15. Constitui vos, ut eatis & fructum afferatis, & fructus vester maneat &c. Manet autem fructus A- postolicus in vera Ecclesia perpetuo. Recte igitur di- cimus eos esse perpetuos Ecclesiæ Principes, præpositos ac præfectos: præsertim quum & alias Christus ad ipsos dicit: Vos qui secuti estis me in regeneratio- ne, cum sederit filius hominis in sede majestatis suæ, sedebitis & vos super sedes duodecim, judi- cantes duodecim tribus Israël. Hæc autem non eo re- spiciunt, ut invocemus Apostolos, tanquam deos tutela- res, aut patronos & defensores in judicio Dei, sed ut cognoscamus nobis non esse aliam salutis doctrinam propositam, præter Apostolicam, & secundum eam doctrinam universum humanum genus coram Deo judicandum esse, ut qui crediderit Apostolicæ doctri- næ, salvus fiat, qui vero non crediderit ei, condemne- tur perpetuo. Ita Brentius noster: non abnuimus tamen etiam ad alios Ecclesiæ doctores hoc vatici- nium referri: de quo ita Hieronymus habet: Po- nam, inquit, Principes tuos in pacem, & episcopos tuos in justitiam: Pro quo scripturæ sanctæ admi- randa majestas, quod principes futuros Ecclesiæ epi- scopos nominavit: quorum omnis visitatio in pace est, & vocabulum dignitatis in justitia: ut nequaquam accipiant personam in judicio: nec audiatur quippiam iniquum in terra Ecclesiæ, neq; contritio, & infelicitas in terminis ejus. Justitiam tamen, & pacem de ju- stitia & pace quam annunciat Evangelium, acci- piendam censemus: quia omnia ita comparata hic sunt, ut spiritualia bona, quæ in regno Christi florent, exhibeant. Unde decimum argumentum nostræ sententiæ emergit à Præsidum & Præfecto- rum in hac urbe descriptione. In qua enim terrena civitate, in quo regno hujus seculi præpositos ponit Deus pacem, & præfectos justitiam? Ne de Esdra quidem, Zorobabele, Nehemia, ac similibus, qua in Politico regimine spectantur, dixeris, quod PAX, & JUSTITIA fuerint, siquidem nullum tam perfectum regimen sit, in quo tantum PAX vigeat, & JUSTITIA, nulla odia aut con- tentiones, nulla injustitia, aut iniquitas reperian- tur. Soli regno Christi hoc proprium est. Con- fer. Esa. 11.

## 60:18
Vers. 18.

NON AUDIETUR ULTRA INIQUITAS IN TERRA TUA] Rapine: the Chaldean rightly.

VASTITAS ET CONTRITIO] Spoliation and concussion; which are wont to be frequent under external empires.

ET OCCUPABIT SALUS MUROS TUOS] He seems to have read קרוא from קרא: but as we have it, both the Greeks and the Chaldean read it. You shall call your walls salvation, because, namely, no enemy shall afflict them.

ET PORTAS TUAS LAUDATIO] You shall call your gates praise, namely because the watchmen in them will not signify the arrival of enemies, but in total security will sing the praises of God.

Thus Grotius understood all these things regarding external tranquility with the Jews, that no robbery, no spoliation and extortion took place in Judea, no enemy besieged the walls, and that in total security the watchmen sang the praises of God; but when was there such tranquility in Judea! Here the histories fail, nor did the Polyhistor have anything he could bring forward for the fulfillment of the prophecy. Therefore, a new argument, which will be the eleventh in order, from the tranquility, justice, and salvation promised here to the city and the land about which the Prophet prophesies. For since it was never fulfilled by reason of temporal and external tranquility and salvation, I will not say in Judea, but in any Republic ever, it is manifest that these things must be understood of spiritual tranquility and salvation, and thus that the prophecy treats of the Church or the Kingdom of Christ. Jerome also notes the name of JESUS expressed here by the Prophet: which in such prophecies is not to be rashly neglected. Because the Spirit of Christ, which was in the Prophets, desired to express from time to time this saving name, outside of which there is no salvation in any other name, through the holy men of God, until it should be openly revealed from heaven. Nothing iniquitous shall be heard in the land of the Church, nor contrition and unhappiness in its borders; for wherever iniquity is, and justice is not observed, and peace is lost: all these things will follow. But for all these (he says) SALVATION shall occupy your walls, or the Savior, which is read in Hebrew ישועה, which properly sounds the name of the Lord. For He himself is the strength of the walls of the Church, which has gates in the praise of the Lord, so that those who enter it may …first learn to praise the Lord and confess his name. To which pertains what is had in Isaiah 26: a city of our strength. Sion, a Savior shall be placed in it as a wall and a bulwark. The city of Jerusalem and its entire region was entirely exposed to the invasion, plundering, devastation, and condition of enemies. But the Church of Christ is immune from that, nor is it exposed to the lust of enemies, but salvation is in its walls, jubilation is in its gates, so that as many as dwell in it may have salvation and eternal joy: indeed, while worldly cities and regions perish by plunderings and devastations, the spiritual city and land is helped by these adversities rather than destroyed, because the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church, nor can the very gates of hell prevail against it. Matt. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

NON AUDIETUR ULTRA INIQUITAS IN TERRA TUA] Rapina: Chaldæus recte.

VASTITAS ET CONTRITIO] Spoliatio & con- cuffio; quæ frequentia solent esse sub externis imperiis.

ET OCCUPABIT SALUS MUROS TUOS] Vi- detur legisse קרוא à קרא: sed ut nos habemus, legerunt & Græci & Chaldæus. Muros vocabis salutem, quia scilicet nullus hostis eos affiliet.

ET PORTAS TUAS LAUDATIO] Portas tuas laudem vocabis, nempe quia vigiles in illis non hostium ad- ventum significabunt, sed in summa securitate Dei laudes canent.

Ita de externa tranquillitate hæc omnia intel- lexit Grotius cum Judæis, Quod nulla rapina in Ju- dæa, nulla spoliatio & concuffio locum habuerit, nullus hostis muros affilierit, quodque in summa securitate vigiles in portis Dei laudes cecinerint, sed quando illa tranquillitas in Judæa fuit! Hic de- ficiunt Historiæ, neque habuit, quod pro comple- mento vaticinii adduceret Polyhistor. Argumen- tum ergo novum, quod in ordine erit undecimum,à tranquillitate, justitia & salute, urbi ac terræ, de qua vaticinatur Propheta, hic promissa. Quum e- nim temporalis & externæ tranquillitatis & salutis ratione nunquam id impletumfuerit, non dicam in Judæa, sed in nulla unquam Republ. manifestum est, de spirituali tranquillitate ac salute hæc acci- pienda esse, adeoque de Ecclesia vel Regno Christi vaticinium agere. Hieronymus notat etiam nomen JESU à Propheta hic expressum: quod in talibus vaticiniis non temere negligendum. Quia Spiritus Christi, qui in Prophetis fuit, nomen hoc salutife- rum, extra quod non est in ullo alio nomine salus, subinde exprimere per Sanctos Dei viros gestiit, donec illud palam revelaretur de cœlo. Non audie- tur quippiam iniquum in terra Ecclesiæ, neq; contri- tio & infelicitas in terminis ejus, ubicunq; enim iniqui- tas est, & justitia non servatur, & pax perditur: hæc omnia consequentur. Sed pro his (ait) omnibus oc- cupabit SALUS muros tuos, sive Salvator, qui in Hebraico legitur ישועה quod proprie nomen Domini sonat. Ipse enim fortitudo murorum Ecclesiæ, qua ha- bet portas in laude Domini, ut qui ingrediuntur eam, primum discant laudare Dominum, & nomen illius confiteri. Quo facit quod Ef. 26. habetur: urbs for- titudinis nostræ. Sion Salvator in ea ponetur murus & antemurale. Urbs Hierusalem & universa ejus regio patebat omnino hostium invasioni, dire- ptioni, vastationi, & conditioni. At Ecclesia Christi immunis ab illa est, nec patet hostium libi- dini, sed in muris ejus salus, in portis ejus jubilatio est, ut quotquot in ea habitant, salutem habeant, & æ- ternum gaudium : imo quum mundanæ urbes & regiones direptionibus & vastationibus pereant, spiritualis urbs, & terra juvatur potius his adversis, quam deletur, quia sanguis Martyrum semen est Ecclesiæ, nec prævalere adversus eam possunt ipsæ inferorum portæ Matth. 16.

## 60:19
Vers. 19. THE SUN SHALL NO LONGER BE FOR THEE TO SHINE BY DAY, NOR SHALL THE SPLENDOR OF THE MOON ILLUMINATE THEE] In the Hebrew: And for splendor (nocturnal, that is) the moon shall not illuminate thee. The sense is: Thou shalt not derive joy from the fact that thou seest the sun by day and the moon by night: since a much greater joy, and that a perpetual one, shall be thine from the perpetual favor of God. We have often seen that joy is signified by the name of light: yet the learned among the Hebrews draw these things mystically to the better life.

Latin:

Vers. 19. NON ERIT TIBI AMPLIUS SOL AD LUCENDUM PER DIEM, NEC SPLENDOR LU- NÆ ILLUMINABIT TE] In Hebræo : Et pro splendore (nocturno scilicet) luna non illustrabit te. Sensus est : Non inde gaudium capies quod solem de die, & noctu lunam videas: cum multo majus gaudium, idque perpetuum ti- bi sit futurum, ex Dei perpetuo favore. Sæpe jam vidimus lucis nomine gaudium significari : mystice tamen hæc ad vitam meliorem trahunt Hebræorum eruditi.

## 60:20
Vers. 20. THY SUN SHALL NOT SET ANY MORE, AND THY MOON SHALL NOT WANE] There shall no longer be for you that anxiety of mind which casts down the countenance to the ground and forbids one to look at the stars. See above 13, 10, and consider that which follows in this place.

THE DAYS OF THY MOURNING SHALL BE COMPLETED] They shall be finished.

These things look not only according to the mystical sense to happiness and spiritual and heavenly gladness, but according to the literal and primarily intended meaning of the Holy Scriptures. For no external city, much less a land or region, can boast of the perennial light of the Sun, without the alternation of darkness, of the perennial favor of God or happiness and gladness, on account of the perpetual vicissitudes which are in this world, which the sins of men beget and the divine justice extorts. And so necessity itself demands that we understand these things, as regards the literal sense itself, concerning the spiritual happiness and gladness which is promised to the Church of God, which it enjoys in this age partially, but in the other it shall enjoy it wholly. Let this, therefore, be the twelfth argument from the perpetual happiness and gladness of the city of which the Prophet speaks. Which is confirmed by the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures. For John followed no other than the very genuine sense of this prophecy, Apoc. 20. v. 23. The city has no need of the Sun, nor of the Moon, to shine in it. For the brightness of God illuminates it, and its lamp is the Lamb. And v. 25. And its gates shall not be shut by day: for there shall be no night there. And Apoc. 22, 5. And there shall be no night any more, and they shall not need the light of a lamp, nor the light of the Sun, because the Lord God shall illuminate them, and they shall reign for ever and ever. For the discourse is about that city to which the LORD is for AN EVERLASTING LIGHT, and to which ITS GOD is for ITS GLORY, that is, which the Lamb Christ Jesus illuminates, as John interprets, who is both the LIGHT and the GLORY OF HIS PEOPLE, our GOD, and Immanuel. For this is that true light which illuminates every man, the Sun of righteousness, the light of the world. Joh. 1. Mal. 4, 1. Joh. 8. & 12. It is manifest that these things are to be understood not of the external Jerusalem, but of the Church of Christ. Worldly and external kingdoms need this worldly Sun and Moon, so that days and nights may be illuminated by the splendor of these luminaries, and men may complete their works, and the earth may bring forth its fruit. But the kingdom of Christ does not need the splendor of these luminaries; but it has a greater and more illustrious light, which is Christ himself. The worldly kingdom is not being built up, but the heavenly and spiritual one. And since the name of light in the Hebrew manner implies happiness and darkness implies unhappiness, nothing else is signified than that Christ, the Sun of righteousness and the true light, because he never sets upon the Church, brings to it a light of happiness which is never extinguished, but remains perpetually. Therefore it is added: THE DAYS OF THY MOURNING SHALL BE COMPLETED, for where the Lord shines without end, how can mourning remain there? And therefore the pious, because they have Christ the true light, do not grieve even in external mourning, which for them is not properly mourning, but an instrument of joy: provided they are most certain in adversities of liberation, in death of life, in the horrors of hell of the joy of the heavenly kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 20. NON OCCIDET ULTRA SOL TUUS, ET LUNA TUA NON MINUETUR] Non erit vobis amplius ea anxietas animi, quæ vultus in terram dejiciat, & astra aspectare vetet. Vide supra 13, 10. & considera id quod sequitur hoc loco.

COMPLEBUNTUR DIES LUCTUS TUI ] Finiti erunt.

Non secundum mysticum sensum tantum ad fe- licitatem & lætitiam spiritualem ac cœlestem hæc spectant, sed secundum literalem & primo intentam S.S.sententiam. Nam nulla externa urbs, nedum ter- ra aut regio de perenni luce Solis, sine tenebrarum alternatione, de perenni favore Dei aut felicitate, ac lætitia gloriari potest, ob perpetuas vicissitudi- nes, quæ in hoc mundo sunt, quas peccata homi- num pariunt, & justitiæ divinæ extorquent. Adeoq; necessitas ipsa postulat, ut hæc quoad ipsum sensum literalem de spirituali felicitate & lætitia intelliga- mus, quæ Ecclesiæ Dei promittitur, qua in hoc se- culo fruitur μερικῶς, in altero autem fruetur ὀλι- κῶς. Hoc ergo esto argumentum duodecimum à perpetua felicitate ac lætitia urbis, de qua sermo est Prophetæ. Quod ab interpretatione S.S. confirma- tur. Non enim alium, quam ipsummet genuinum sensum hujus vaticinii sequutus est Johannes Apoc. 20. v. 23. Civitas non eget Sole, neque Luna, ut luceant in ea. Nam claritas Dei illuminat eam, & lucerna ejus est Agnus. Et v. 25. Et portæ ejus non claudentur per diem : Nox enim non erit illic. Et Apoc. 22, 5. Et nox ultra non erit, & non egebunt lumine lucernæ, neq́; lu- mine Solis, quoniam Dominus Deus illuminabit illos, & regnabunt in secula seculorum. De illa enim civita- te sermo est, cui DOMINUS est in LUCEM SEM- PITERNAM, & cui DEUS EJUS est in GLORIAM IPSIUS, hoc est, quem Agnus Christus Jesus illumi- nat, interprete Johanne, qui & LUX est & GLO- RIA POPULI SUI, DEUS noster, & Immanuel. Hic enim est lux illa vera, quæ omnem hominem illu- minat, Sol justitiæ, lux mundi. Joh. 1. Mal. 4, 1. Joh. 8. & 12. Quæ non de externa Jerusalem, sed de Eccle- sia Christi intelligenda esse manifestum est. Mun- dana & externa regna indigent hoc mundano So- le, & Luna, ut splendore horum luminarium dies & noctes illustrentur, hominesque opera sua confi- ciant, & terra fructum suum proferat. Regnum au- tem Christi non eget horum luminarium splendo- re; sed habet majorem & illustriorem lucem, quæ est Christus ipse. Non erigitur regnum mundanum, sed cœleste & spirituale. Et cum lucis nomen more Ebræo felicitatem & tenebrarum infelicitatem in- ferat, nihil aliud fignificatur, quam Christum Solem justitiæ ac lucem veram, quia nunquam occidit Ec- clesiæ, afferre eidem felicitatis lucem quæ nun- quam extinguatur, sed perpetuo maneat. Ideo ad- ditur : COMPLEBUNTUR DIES LUCTUS TUI, ubi enim Dominus lucet sine fine, quomodo ibi reliquus esse potest luctus ? Ideoque pii, quia Christum veram lucem habent, ne in luctu quidem externo dolent, qui ipsis proprie non est luctus, sed organon gaudii: siquidem certissimi sint in ad- versis de liberatione, in morte de vita, in horrori- bus inferni de gaudio regni cœlestis.

## 60:21
Vers. 21. BUT THY PEOPLE, ALL JUST, SHALL INHERIT THE LAND FOREVER] All those in the people who shall be just shall possess the land by perpetual right. Compare what is above 57, 19. 20. 21. 59, 20.

THE SPROUT OF MY PLANTING, THE WORK OF MY HANDS FOR GLORIFICATION] He reads מַטָּעוֹ, as the Masoretes placed in the margin, thinking, no doubt, that this is signified, that those who return are as if planted by God in their ancestral land. But the reading which is in the text מַטָּעַי can be retained in this sense, which certain interpreters have posited: That the sprout of his plantings may glory in the work of my hands (that is, because of my benefits). The sprout of his plantings, that is, his posterity.

Latin:

Vers. 21. POPULUS AUTEM TUUS, OMNES JUSTI, IN PERPETUUM HÆREDITABUNT TER- RAM] Illi omnes in populo, qui justi erunt, perpetuo jure terram possidebunt, Confer quod supra 57, 19. 20. 21. 59, 20.

GERMEN PLANTATIONIS MEÆ, OPUS MA- NUS MEÆ AD GLORIFICANDUM] Legit מַטָּעוֹ, ut Masoretæ in margine posuerunt, putantes nimirum id significari, istos reduces à Deo velut consitos in terra avita. Sed potest retineri lectio quæ est in textu מַטָּעַי hoc sensu, quem quidam interpretes posuêre: Ut surculus plantarum ejus in opere manuum mearum (id est, ob mea beneficia) glo- rietur. Surculus plantarum ejus, id est, posteritas.

## 60:22
Vers. 22. THE LEAST SHALL BE A THOUSAND] In the Hebrew: The very few: as also in Greek ὀλιγοστὸς, namely the number of the family.

AND THE LITTLE ONE INTO A MOST STRONG NATION] The same sense as that which preceded.

IN HIS TIME] In the Hebrew: In his time. After they shall have returned home.

These things cannot be snatched away to the people and the land of Canaan. All are called righteous who inherit the land, not as Grotius perverts it, all among the people who are righteous. For he saw that not all who returned into Judah were righteous. But the Prophet describes the whole people thus: all of them righteous. Nor did they inherit the land לְעוֹלָם for an age. But they possessed it only for a time. For now, for 16 centuries, they have been exiled from that inheritance. Finally, not all were the shoot of the Lord's planting: indeed, there were many evil plantings among them. And therefore these things must necessarily be understood of the Church. Whose citizens are righteous, the shoot of the Lord's plantings to glorify the Lord, who possess the land as an inheritance for ages, not this worldly one, but that of the other life. Whence the thirteenth argument arises, from the holiness of all the citizens in this city, which the Prophet asserts here expressly. Nothing is more certain, says Brentius, than that which the Prophet says thus, that all the people of the Church are righteous as well as holy, namely on account of Christ through faith. For although sin still adheres in the flesh of the people of the Church, by the desire of which sin they sometimes even slip into manifest crimes, nevertheless if they repent, the inherent sin is not imputed, and the committed crime is forgiven, so that there is no condemnation for those who are grafted into Christ Jesus. And furthermore. Formerly the land of Canaan was promised and given to the Church of the people of God as an inheritance. But that people was either led away from that land by captivity, or snatched from it by death, and finally even cast off by God, so that it is no longer the people of God. But after Christ came, and gathered the Church from Jews and Gentiles by the spreading of the Gospel, He gathered the whole world into the land of His Church, and first indeed He gave it the whole earth as a perpetual inheritance, because as long as this world shall stand, there will always be a Church of Christ on earth. No persecution, no tyranny can be so great that it might remove the Church of the Lord from the earth. For although the Apostles are cruelly killed, and the martyrs are inhumanly slaughtered, nevertheless the Church grows and expands all the more. The blood, he says, of Christians is seed. The more the blood of the pious is shed by the impious, the more fertile the field of the Church becomes, and it also brings forth more fruit. Upon this Rock (which is both Christ Himself, and the preaching of the Gospel concerning Christ) I will build, He says, My Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And Paul: Built, he says, upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with the chief cornerstone being JESUS CHRIST Himself. Therefore, just as no tyranny can move this cornerstone from its place, and overturn this foundation, so also the building of the Church can no longer be demolished in these lands, and utterly destroyed. Furthermore, the Church is said to be an inheritance of the earth forever, also for this reason, that it may never again be cast away by God, just as the people of Israel were cast away before. For although after the Gospel has been proclaimed, the nations, which now acknowledge Christ, and a little later follow, sometimes having rejected Christ and His Gospel on account of impiety, are themselves rejected by Christ, yet the true Church, wherever it is in the world, is never rejected. The mountains, he says, were moved, and the hills shall tremble, but my mercy shall not depart from thee, and the covenant of my peace shall not be moved, says the Lord who has mercy on you. Finally, it is manifest that the cause is given here, why there is such stability of the Church. The sprout or flower of my planting. THE WORK OF MY HANDS for glorification. This is, the Church has not rashly arisen from itself, but is my own planting, and the workmanship of my hand, established for this purpose, that it may enjoy eternal glory with me in the heavenly kingdom. But who could eradicate the planting of GOD? Who would be able to destroy the workmanship of GOD? Human plantings are indeed not accustomed to be long-lasting. Every planting, he says, which my heavenly Father has not planted, shall be eradicated. But the planting of the Church is divine. The Prophet now subjoins, THE LEAST SHALL BE IN A THOUSAND, AND THE SMALL ONE INTO A MOST STRONG NATION. Concerning which Jerome says: Then he who was small shall be in thousands, and hearing from the Lord, Be having power over five or ten cities, so that he may be called χιλιάρχης: And he who with the Apostle had said; to me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, shall be a Prince of a great nation in the heavens, when at the appointed time God shall have sent his angels, and shall have gathered to him all the saints from the extremity of heaven even to its extremity, not only from Israel; but also from the people of the nations, whom he was signifying when he spoke: And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold, and them I must gather, that there may be one fold and one Shepherd. This, however, he will do suddenly, so that when all things have been despaired of, then they may be gathered into a most strong nation. Which, although we see them being fulfilled daily in the Church in part, yet they shall be more fully completed in the consummation of the world, and in the second coming of the Savior. Cyril also referred these to the future age. For now, that is, in this age, the glorious [state] of the saints is hidden, and if you look at the pride of the world, they seem to be the least, who do not have illustrious glory. But again when Christ shall have shone from Heaven, then even he who was held to be the least and small, shall be into a great nation. For he shall be set over peoples, and shall rule over many, inasmuch as his praiseworthy course has been finished in this life. But as the rest speak about the Church in this life, even if some things attain perfection in the other life, so above others the explanation of Brentius pleases in this place: The Church shall not only be preserved in these lands, but shall also be so increased and multiplied, that from one small one a thousand may arise, and from one meager one a great multitude of a nation may be made. The final argument here for us, therefore, will be from the remarkable fortitude and spiritual blessing of the faithful; by which virtue of the spirit they are clothed from on high, and irrigated by divine blessing, they are thus strengthened to propagate the Church, so that the least may be in a thousand, and the small one into a most strong nation. Which was fulfilled under the auspices of the New Testament, and is still often fulfilled in the Church. Did not Peter seem a small one: but from his one sermon on the day of Pentecost there arise not only a thousand, but three thousand men. Was not Paul small and meager, of whom the Psalm says: There is Benjamin the little one, or the small one, ruling among them? And he himself proclaims concerning himself: I am the least of the Apostles. And yet this least one proclaimed, or as he himself speaks, fulfilled the Gospel of Christ from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions, even unto Illyricum. How many thousands of men, do you think, in such a great space of lands, have come to the Church by the ministry of Paul? And although he himself has departed from this bodily life, yet his writings still live in the Church, from which such a great offspring of the Church grows up, that it cannot be numbered. Since therefore we discover in reality that those things which Isaiah proclaims in this chapter concerning the kingdom of Christ are truly fulfilled in the Church, now that the Gospel has been proclaimed, and we certainly know that the majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ is to be revealed from heaven in its own time, by which all these things shall be most perfectly fulfilled, let us also arise, which the Prophet said at the beginning, and let us be illuminated by the light of Christ and His Gospel, so that by the splendor of this light we may be led through the darkness of death to the glory of the heavenly life!

Latin:

Vers. 22. MINIMUS ERIT IN MILLE] In Hebræo: Paucissimus: ut & Græce ὀλιγοστὸς, nempe familiæ numerus.

ET PARVULUS IN GENTEM FORTISSI- MAM] Idem sensus qui præcessit.

TEMPORE EJUS] In Hebræo: Tempore suo. Post- quam domum redierint.

Non possunt hæc abripi ad populum, & ter- ram Canaan. Omnes justi dicuntur, qui hæreditant terram, non ut pervertit Grotius, omnes in populo, qui justi sunt. Vidit enim non omnes, qui rediêre in Judam, justos fuisse. At Propheta populum uni- versum ita describit: omnes illi justi. Neque לְעוֹלָם in seculum acceperunt hæreditate terram. Sed ad tempus tantum possederunt. Nunc enim per 16. se- cula exulant illa hæreditate. Denique non omnes virgultum plantationis Domini fuere: quin multæ plantationes malæ inter ipsos. Ideoq; hæc necessa- rio de Ecclesia intelligenda. Cujus cives justi sunt, virgultum plantationum Domini ad glorifican- dum Dominum, qui in secula terram hæreditate possident, non hanc mundanam, sed alterius vitæ. Unde decimum tertium argumentum nascitur, à ci- vium omnium in hac urbe sanctitate, quam hic διαρ- ῥήδην asserit Propheta. Nihil certius est, ait Brentius, quam quod, sic Propheta ait, omnis populus Ec- clesiæ sit justus ut & sanctus, videlicet propter Chri- stum per fidem. Etsi enim peccatum hæret adhuc in carne populi Ecclesiæ, cujus peccati cupiditate nonnunquam etiam in manifesta scelera prolabun- tur, tamen si resipiscunt, peccatum inhærens non imputatur, & commissum scelus remittitur, ut nulla fit condemnatio his, qui insiti sunt in Christo Jesu. Et porro. Olim promissa & data est terra Canaan Ecclesiæ populi Dei in hæreditatem. Sed is populus aut captivitate ex ea terra abductus est, aut morte ab ea abreptus, ac postremo etiam à Deo abjectus, ne sit amplius populus Dei. Postquam autem Chri- stus venit, & collegit divulgato Evangelio Eccle- siam ex Judæis & Gentibus, congregavit univer- sum orbem in terram Ecclesiæ suæ, ac primum qui- dem dedit ei totam terram in perpetuam hæredi- tatem, quia donec hic orbis steterit, semper erit Ec- clesia Christi in terris. Nulla persecutio, nulla tyran- nis tanta esse potest, quæ Ecclesiam Domini è ter- ris tollat. Etsi enim Apostoli crudeliter interficiun- tur, & martyres immaniter trucidantur, tamen eo magis crescit & dilatatur Ecclesia. Sanguis, inquit, ille, Christianorum semen est. Quo plus sanguinis piorum ab impiis effunditur, eo fertilior fit ager Ecclesiæ, & plus quoq; fructus profert. Super hanc Petram (quæ est & Christus ipse, & prædicatio Ev- angelii de Christo) ædificabo, inquit, Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam. Et Paulus: Superstructi, inquit, super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum, summo angulari la- pide ipso JESU CHRISTO. Sicut ergo nulla tyran- nis potest hunc angularem lapidem de loco suo dimovere, & hoc fundamentum subvertere, ita et- iam non potest ædificium Ecclesiæ in his terris de- moliri, ac penitus destruere. Deinde Ecclesia dici- tur hæreditate terram in perpetuum, etiam hac ra- tione, quod nunquam amplius abjiciatur à Deo, si- cut jam ante abjectus est populus Israël. Etsi enim post divulgatum Evangelion gentes, quæ nunc a- gnoscunt Christum, & paulo post sequuntur aliquo- ties rejecto Christo & Evangelio ejus ob impieta- tem, rejiciuntur & ipsæ à Christo, tamen quæ vera Ecclesia ubivis terrarum, nunquam rejicitur. Mon- tes, inquit, commovebantur, & colles contremiscent, misericordia autem mea non recedet à te, & fœdus pa- cis meæ non movebitur, dicit miserator tuus Dominus. Denique manifestum est hic causam reddi, cur tan- ta Ecclesiæ sit stabilitas. Germen seu flos plantationis mea. OPUS MANUS MEÆ ad glorificandum. Hoc est, Ecclesia non à seipso temere exorta est, sed mea ipsius plantatio, & manus meæ opificium, in hunc usum constitutum, ut æterna gloria mecum in cœ- lesti regno fruatur. Quis autem plantationem DEI eradicare posset? Quis opificium DEI destruere valeret? Humanæ quidem plantationes non so- lent esse diuturnæ. Omnis plantatio, inquit, quam non plantavit Pater meus cœlestis, eradicabitur. Plantatio autem Ecclesiæ est divina. Subjungit nunc Propheta, MINIMUS ERIT IN MILLE, ET PARVULUS IN GENTEM FORTISSIMAM. Quo de Hieronymus: Tunc qui parvulus fuit, erit in millia, & audiens à Domino, Esto habens po- testatem super quinque vel decem civitates, ut appel- letur χιλιάρχης: Et qui cum Apostolo dixerat; mihi minimo omnium sanctorum data est gratia hæc, Princeps erit magnæ gentis in cœlestibus, quando tempore constituto miserit Deus angelos suos, & con- gregaverit ad eum omnes sanctos à summitate cæli us- que ad summam ejus, non solum de Israël; sed & de gentium populo, quem significans loquebatur: Et alias o- ves habeo, quæ non sunt de grege isto, & illas opor- tet me congregare, ut fiat unus grex & unus Pastor. Hoc autem subito faciet, ut quando omnia fuerint de- sperata, tunc in gentem fortissimam congregentur. Quæ licet ex parte in Ecclesia quotidie videamus expleri, tamen in mundi consummatione plenius complebuntur, & in secundo salvatoris adventu. Ad futurum seculum hæc etiam retulit Cyrillus. Nunc enim, id est, in hoc seculo, occultata est gloriosa sanctorum, & si fastum mundi respicias, minimi esse videntur, qui illustrem non habent gloriam. Sed rursus ubi illuxerit de Cælo Christus, tunc etiam qui habitus est minimus & par- vus, erit in magnam gentem. Præficietur enim popu- lis, & imperitabit multis, utpote in hac vita confecto cursu laudabili. Sed ut cætera de Ecclesia in hac vita loquuntur, etsi nonnulla perfectionem consequan- tur in altera vita, ita præ aliis placet hoc in loco ex- plicatio Brentii: Ecclesia non tantum servabitur in his terris, verum etiam ita augebitur & multiplicabi- tur, ut ex uno parvulo oriantur mille, & ex uno exi- guo fiat magna gentis multitudo. Argumentum ergo postremum hic nobis erit à fidelium insigni fortitudi- ne & spirituali benedictione; qua virtute spiritus ex alto induti, & benedictione divina irrigati sic ro- borantur, ad propagandam Ecclesiam, ut minimus sit in mille, & parvulus in gentem fortissimam. Quod impletum est sub auspicia Novi Testamenti, & ad- huc sæpe impletur in Ecclesia. Annon parvulus vi- debatur Petrus: sed ex una ejus concione in die Pentecostes oriuntur non mille tantum, sed tria millia hominum. Annon parvulus & exiguus fuit Paulus, de quo Psalmus ait: Ibi Benjamin adolescen- tulus, seu parvulus dominatur inter eos? Et ipsemet de se prædicat: Ego sum minimus Apostolorum. Et tamen hic minimus vulgavit, vel sicut ipse loquitur, implevit Evangelium Christi à Hierosolymis & cir- cumjacentibus regionibus, usq́; ad Illyricum. Quot, putas, millia hominum, in tanto terrarum spatio, ministerio Pauli ad Ecclesiam accessisse? Et quan- quam ipse hac vita corporali defunctus est, tamen vivunt adhuc in Ecclesia Scripta ejus, ex quibus tanta soboles Ecclesiæ succrescit, ut dinumerari non queat. Cum igitur reipsa comperiamus, ea quæ Esaias in hoc capite de regno Christi concionatur, vere in Ecclesia, divulgato jam Evangelio, impleri, ac certo sciamus revelandam esse suo tempore ma- jestatem Domini nostri Jesu Christi de cœlo, quo hæc omnia perfectissime implebuntur, Surgamus & nos, quod Propheta initio dixit, & illuminemur luce Christi ac Evangelii ejus, ut splendore hujus lu- cis perducamur per tenebras mortis ad gloriam cœlestis vitæ!

## 61:1 Argument
CHAPTER LXI.

Christ himself testifies that he is anointed by the Holy Spirit to be sent to announce the Gospel concerning redemption and the Jubilee of grace, and describes his own ministers: whence the faithful exult in him, adorned with garments of righteousness and his Priestly attire.

Vers. 1. THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME] Isaiah speaks here of himself, as the Chaldean notes. But in whom we see a not obscure image of Christ. Therefore, he says, GOD has breathed upon me with his spirit.

LEST anything of the remainder should survive, which the text speaks of concerning Christ according to the letter, he distorts this prophecy also, otherwise most illustrious, and understands it with the Jews concerning Isaiah. By which error he was already occupied, when he was adorning the Annotations to the Evangelist. For thus to Luke 4, 18. Πνεῦμα κυρίε ἐπ' ἐμέ. Just as the liberation from the Babylonian captivity was both an image and a pledge of the liberation of souls, which the Messiah was about to perform, so also those things which Isaiah had said concerning himself were so directed by God, that they would more excellently fit the Lord Jesus. Kimchi also adapts these to the Messiah. But in this place, when he treats of Isaiah, so that we may first warn of this, he was unmindful of the συνεχείας, which he himself wished to hand down as perpetual and concatenated in this Prophet. For since the preceding discourse dealt with the return into Judea according to Grotius, how does the speech concerning the office of the Messiah cohere now? Is it not thus necessary for the Holy Spirit to slip back to Jeremiah, which concerning chapter LIII. Grotius dreamed, provided it refers to Isaiah himself, which he pretends is happening here with the Jews. Which certainly do not at all agree with that coherence which Grotius has set out to deliver. But if this prophecy is understood according to the letter concerning Christ, it will cohere perfectly with the preceding. Since, indeed, it has been treated concerning the spiritual structure and inhabitants of the mystical city, the Church of Christ, especially under the times of the New Testament, Christ is introduced in the days of his flesh about to preach the doctrine of the Gospel, through which the Church is to be built. Since mention has been made of prefects and presidents, who are to be placed in peace and justice, now their supreme president, who was about to bring peace and justice, and for that reason was anointed by the Holy Spirit, is presented as the savior, who was about to occupy the walls, the Lord, who was about to illuminate the city. Isaiah had described the people in that city, the citizens and inhabitants, that they would be righteous; that they would rejoice with perennial happiness and joy, that they would be the sprouts of the planting of the Lord for celebration, that they would be strong, and would propagate themselves copiously: Now therefore he teaches more abundantly that Christ is about to bestow these benefits: inasmuch as he places upon those mourning in Zion a crown, oil for ashes, joy for mourning, so that they who are in it may be called strong ones or trees of righteousness, priests of the Lord, and may be clothed with garments of salvation, and that righteousness and praise may sprout before all nations.

Furthermore, secondly, if we investigate the speaking person from the connection of the discourse, he who had spoken at the end of the preceding chapter, I THE LORD in his time will suddenly do that, now continues the discourse, the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, therefore he has anointed me. Since, therefore, he upon whom the Spirit of the Lord is, is Jehovah, who is about to effect those things which Isaiah predicted, it is most manifest that these things cannot be understood of Isaiah, but that Christ is introduced as speaking. Concerning which Cyril: He who in the preceding said concerning those to be called through faith: I the Lord in time will gather them, as if in the now instant time in which he promised that he would gather them, and as if having now become man, and taking on our likeness, and submitting himself to emptying, says: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me: since by nature being God, the only-begotten, he is the holy of holies, and he himself sanctifies every nature, as being born of a holy father, and since he sends forth the spirit proceeding from himself upon his heavenly powers, and furthermore upon those acknowledging his appearance, how then is he sanctified? For when he is God and the same man, he gives the spirit to the creature by reason of his Deity, but he receives it from God and the Father by reason of his humanity. This we say is the anointing. Which was also observed by Jerome: He who had said above: I THE LORD in time will gather them; or according to the Hebrew: I the Lord in his time will suddenly do this, speaks consequently: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, not that the Lord God has a Lord God, but that according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh he says those things which are humble. Which is further confirmed Thirdly from other things, which we showed in the preceding chapter that Christ professed concerning himself: Indeed, with David Pareus admitting, he is undoubtedly the same who speaks in the preceding chapter, THE ISLANDS HAVE WAITED FOR ME: and who here says: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; but he himself is Christ, as is clear from the context. Fourthly from the consequences. For that same one, who testifies that he is anointed and sent to preach the Gospel, speaks of himself thus: FOR I THE LORD loving judgment and hating robbery in a burnt offering. Therefore the Prophet does not speak of himself, but Christ the Lord is introduced by the Prophet as speaking. Which also Fifthly the anointing, of which he treats, testifies. The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, for the reason that the Lord has anointed me. Because the Spirit of the Lord is upon Christ, as Isaiah taught in ch. 11, 1. The Lord anointed Christ with the Spirit, so that not absolutely, and κατ' αὐτονομασίαν, he is called משיח, χρισὸς and the Anointed of the Lord: who also alone among the Prophets obtained the name from the anointing, as one whom he anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows Ps. 45. Which passage is parallel to this one of ours. For also by David the Messiah is called God anointed by GOD Ps. 45, and here Jehovah is said to be anointed by Jehovah, and as there he is celebrated by David with such an eulogy, you have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness: so here the anointed one testifies of himself: I the Lord loving judgment and hating robbery in a burnt offering. Add that Calvin himself admits that this is not a discourse about just any anointing, but about the fullness of the spirit and about an anointing above all fellows ἄνευ μέτρου, which belongs to Christ alone. Sixthly, the discourse in this place is about him who was sent, not only to preach the Gospel to the meek; but also that he might heal the brokenhearted. But this cannot be said of the Prophet: For the healing of the brokenhearted is a θεόεργημα, a divine work, which does not befit a mere man, but is proper to the Messiah. Seventhly, because these benefits, which are announced by this anointed one of the Lord, are also in reality conferred by the same, all of which cohere in an inseparable connection and are attributed to one and the same Person, by what reason, I ask, can they be snatched away to Isaiah? Calvin had to acknowledge this again, that indeed Christ alone performs these things for the Church, which he here as a herald promises that he will perform. It is added that, with Pareus likewise admitting, God in almost the same words above in ch. 42, 7, addressed not the Prophet, but the Messiah. I have given you for a covenant of the people, for a light of the nations, that you may open the eyes of the blind and bring the prisoner out of the prison, and from the house of the prison those sitting in darkness etc. For this anointed one of the Lord professes concerning himself here, that he was sent, that he might heal the brokenhearted, and preach indulgence to the captives, and opening to those who are shut up etc. Eighthly, the prophetic words clearly imply that the proclamation of redemption, healing and illumination, as well as joy, praise and glorification is designated here as such, whose herald he himself is about to effect that redemption, healing, illumination, joy, praise, glorification, because he says he was sent to announce these things in such a way that he might at the same time heal the brokenhearted, that he might effectively comfort all who mourn, that he might place for those who mourn in Zion, and give them a crown for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the mantle of praise for the spirit of heaviness, that they may be called in it oaks of justice, the planting of the Lord for glorification. Ninthly, he who speaks here, and calls himself the Lord, and openly distinguishes himself from the Lord, that is God the Father, as well as from the Spirit of the Lord: whence it is necessary that no one else is speaking here, according to the very letter of the text, except Christ, who alone is the Lord ὑποsατικῶς distinguished from the Father and the Holy Spirit. For thus he speaks in v. 1: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, for the reason that the Lord has anointed me. And 8: For I THE LORD loving judgment and hating robbery in a burnt offering: and I will give their work in truth, and I will strike a perpetual covenant for them. He who promises that he will give their work in truth and will place a perpetual covenant for them, distinguishes himself afterwards in v. 9 again from God the Father. All, he says, who see them, shall know them, that these are the seed, which THE LORD has blessed. Therefore THE LORD, upon whom is the Spirit of the Lord, and who wishes to strike a perpetual covenant with his people, speaks of THE LORD, who has blessed him, that is Christ, the true GOD, speaks of the Father, the true GOD and LORD. Tenthly, when the Church, full of thanks, responds to this remarkable promise to the Lord in v. 10. and rejoices and exults that she is clothed by the LORD with the garments of salvation and the robes of righteousness, what else does she testify, than that he, who gives to Zion a crown for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the mantle of praise for the spirit of heaviness, has clothed himself with the garments of righteousness and salvation? Because this congratulation and exultation in the Lord looks back to the preceding promise, from which that joy results among the faithful. Concerning which Jerome: according to the Hebrews, it is the beginning of another chapter, in which the Church of Christ is introduced to respond to the words: I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God. By no means in the fathers, as the Jews boasted saying: We are the seed of Abraham, and have never been in bondage to any man, but in God, the scripture saying: and the heart and soul of the multitude of the believers was one. And he renders the causes of joy; because he has clothed me with the garments of salvation and with the robe or tunic of righteousness and joy, which in Hebrew is called מעיל, he has adorned and surrounded me. For as many of us as have been baptized into Christ, have put on Christ, and we have the tunic of righteousness, who has been made for us holiness, righteousness and redemption. Eleventh, since here the conversion of the nations is connected with this announcement of the Gospel, just as the earth brings forth its sprout and as a garden causes its seed to germinate, so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to germinate before ALL NATIONS, how can this proclamation of Isaiah be vindi cated? Is it not manifest that the same Lord God, who clothes the faithful with garments of salvation and robes of righteousness, so that they may rejoice in this Lord, so that they may exult in this their God, is designated when it is said THE LORD GOD will cause RIGHTEOUSNESS AND PRAISE to spring forth? Who therefore is none other than He whom the faithful celebrate with this confessional title: Jehovah our righteousness Jerem. 23. & Is. 45, 14. In Jehovah is my righteousness and strength. Twelfth, we have an interpreter greater than any exception, Christ Jesus, who explains this prophecy concerning Himself, not in a mystical sense, but as to the literal sense. For He testifies with a clear voice that it is fulfilled in Him, nor does He acknowledge any other subject of this prophecy. For if it had been fulfilled in Isaiah, if it concerned the liberation from the Babylonian captivity predicted by Isaiah, the Jews could have replied, what is that to You, which speaks of the Prophet Isaiah, and which was predicted concerning the liberation from captivity, and was fulfilled long ago? But it was admittedly certain among the Jews at that time that these things did not concern Isaiah, but had been predicted concerning the Messiah, nor did anyone raise any doubt or controversy about it. For thus it is read in Luke 4, 15. And He Himself was teaching (having returned, that is, from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit and after He had returned from the desert, and had come in the power of the Spirit into Galilee) in their synagogues, and was glorified BY ALL. And He came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up, and entered according to His custom on the Sabbath day into the Synagogue and stood up to read. And there was delivered to Him the book of the Prophet Isaiah, and as He unrolled the book, He found the place where it was written: The Spirit of THE LORD IS UPON ME, because He has anointed me, He has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, to set at liberty those who are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of retribution. And when He had folded the book, He gave it back to the minister and sat down: And the eyes of all in the Synagogue were fixed upon Him. And He began to say to them: That TODAY this Scripture is fulfilled in your ears. And ALL bore witness to Him, and wondered at the words of thanks which proceeded from His mouth. Add what is contained in v. 43. That I must PREACH the kingdom of God to other cities also, because FOR THIS PURPOSE I have been SENT. What is clearer than that Christ, by His own proper interpretation and the Evangelist's narrative, is He who according to this prophecy of the Prophet (1.) was anointed with the Holy Spirit, which was publicly declared in the Jordan when the Holy Spirit came upon Him: (2.) Was sent by the Lord to preach the Gospel, because He came for that purpose in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and testified that He must preach the kingdom of God, because FOR THIS PURPOSE HE WAS SENT. (3) That He is the same one who speaks in the Prophet: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me etc. (4.) and that it was fulfilled in Him, in the days of His flesh, which is predicted here, because He Himself testifies with a sonorous voice, TODAY this Scripture is fulfilled. (5.) That Christ is this HERALD & EVANGELIST sent to preach to the poor etc., not Isaiah. For when Christ was preaching the Gospel, He testified clearly: TODAY this scripture is fulfilled IN YOUR EARS, i.e., by this very proclamation of the Gospel, which now resounds in your ears, that scripture is fulfilled. (6.) He teaches that this scripture is fulfilled not only by reason of the proclamation; but also by reason of the other mighty works which the Prophet had predicted there, as being things which He had read to them from the Prophet, and had explained concerning Himself, namely, that He was sent to heal the brokenhearted, which He was actually performing as a divine work, that He was sent to preach deliverance to the captives, which certainly cannot be understood of the Babylonian captivity, or any other bodily salvation. For the Messiah was not sent for the sake of that, nor ought He to have been sent; but for spiritual captivity and liberation; and therefore it is a violent distortion when Grotius snatches away what Christ Himself explained concerning spiritual liberation to a bodily liberation. Similarly Christ testifies: TODAY this scripture is fulfilled, that He was sent to preach sight to the blind, which, since He explains it concerning spiritual illumination, is distorted against Christ's mind and exposition to the opening of those shut up in Babylon. He testifies that it was predicted of Himself that He was sent TO SET AT LIBERTY those who are bruised, which He concludes from the words of the Prophet; this, however, can BY NO MEANS be applied to Isaiah. Whence it is most manifest that this illustrious prophecy is most perversely distorted to Isaiah. For how did Isaiah set at liberty those who are bruised? He testifies that He was sent to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of retribution. That acceptable year, therefore, that day of retribution cannot be understood of the year of the Babylonian liberation, which Christ had no need to preach, since it had passed long ago. (7.) That these things were irrefutably certain and indubitable among the Jews at the time of Christ, namely that these predictions are to be understood not of Isaiah, but of the Messiah, is manifest from the fact that all of them bore witness, and no one opposed Him in that interpretation and thesis, that these things concern the Messiah. Add that Christ also preaches from this passage in Matthew 11 to the messengers of John, and assumes it as undoubtedly prophetic, predicting His own office, when He ordered it to be announced to John, the poor have the Gospel preached to them. By which words He signifies that these words of the Prophet look to Himself: Since therefore the Son of God Himself interprets this His own sermon, which He gave so many years before concerning His own office, there is no other interpretation contrary to this for us to hear, not even that of an angel, but this alone is to be respected and held, as Brentius gravely warns. Since all these things are most clear, his champion Pareus could not defend his Calvin here, without yielding the victory here to our B. Hunnius, who had refuted the Judaizing Calvin on the grounds that he said the Prophet was speaking of himself, that he was sent and anointed by the Lord, that is, equipped with the necessary things. He prefers, however, he says, to concede to the received opinion, that Christ himself is introduced preaching about the calling of his office and his benefits. For first, Christ clearly shows the fulfillment in himself; if anyone objects that he does not say CHRIST: Today for the first time, and in me alone is it fulfilled, but simply: Today this scripture is fulfilled: it is not very firm: since Christ openly restricts the fulfillment to the PRESENT time, and indeed to ALL of it. For it could be fulfilled in NO OTHER, because it properly applies to NO OTHER, except to Christ ALONE, especially since it is certain that it is not about typical, but about eternal redemption, and about the proper office and benefit of the Messiah that is being treated here: whence indeed the consequence is firm: It is fulfilled in Christ: Therefore not in the Prophet. Although he still wishes to help his Calvin, Pareus nevertheless makes mere games of it, which B. Hunnius taught clearly before our eyes. For that hiding-place about a double literal sense is most absurd, one historical, according to which this herald is the Prophet, announcing the benefits of the Messiah, the other Prophetic, according to which it is the Messiah himself, proclaiming these things about himself through the mouth of the Prophet. For thus everywhere, when a prophecy about the Messiah occurs, it will be permissible to invent a double literal sense: the Historical one of the Prophet announcing these things about the Messiah, and the Prophetic one about the Messiah, whose benefits these are. The question is not whether the Prophet spoke or wrote these things through the Spirit of CHRIST, so that

CHRIST uttered these things through the mouth of the Prophet, but concerning what subject they treat, and who this person is who is introduced here by the Prophet as speaking: whether he speaks of himself, or indeed of the Messiah. Here, at any rate, Pareus could not escape the force of the truth, but that he confirmed our explanation with his own vote, and pronounced that the Jewish gloss, which is that of Calvin and Grotius himself, ought to be exploded: This prophecy, he says, Christ of Nazareth applied to himself in the Synagogue, and closed its explanation with this epiphonema: Today this scripture is fulfilled in your ears, therefore it cannot be doubted that it pertains to Christ! Therefore, the JEWISH CORRUPTION must be exploded, which is, that this must be expounded LITERALLY in the person of Isaiah, as if he were preaching about himself, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, for the reason that he anointed me. For neither are TEMPORAL benefits or BODILY DELIVERANCE from Babylon treated here, but spiritual and eternal goods, which no one provides EXCEPT Christ, concerning whom the Jews are convinced by CLEAR arguments from the text. He sent me, says this herald, to preach good tidings to the meek, to bind up the brokenhearted, to give them beauty for ashes, that they may be called trees of righteousness: that all may be called priests of Jehovah, ministers of God: that they may have perpetual joy: that he may make a perpetual covenant with them. These and other things CANNOT BE UNDERSTOOD EXCEPT as the benefits of the Messiah. These things Pareus says most truly. But by these he openly refutes Calvin, whom he had undertaken to defend. Finally, the consensus of the Interpreters is to be noted in this place. Pareus grants him to us: I see that all Christian Interpreters CONCUR in this, that Christ himself is here preaching about his own vocation and anointing to the office of the Messiah, and about giving eternal benefits to the Church, which, once exhibited in the flesh, he actually brought with him, and provides to the Church forever. But even the Jews themselves confess that this oracle, according to its proper and literal sense, must be understood of the Messiah: Thus R. Saadia Gaon explains it in the book Haemunoth, ch. 8. The son of David (the Messiah) will meet them, to confirm their heart, and heal their fracture, and raise up their spirits, which is said in Is. 61, 1. The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, etc. R. David Kimchi in the Book of Roots, root משח, the Prophet spoke in the person of the Messiah, as if the Messiah had said thus, and therefore GOD anointed me, etc. From which it is manifest that Grotius also perverts the opinion of Kimchi, when he attributes to him that he at least adapts these to the Messiah in some mystical sense, even if they were said of Isaiah in the literal sense. For Kimchi acknowledges that Isaiah SPEAKS THESE THINGS IN THE PERSON OF THE MESSIAH, as if the Messiah had said these things. Thus also Biblical interpreters explained it in the Midrash of Canticles concerning the exultation in the days of the Messiah, which are in verse 10, and in the Midrash Tillim concerning the conversion of the Gentiles, which are held in verse 11. Which we will adduce later. The blind Doctors of the Jews therefore saw the true meaning, which the Christian Grotius could not see, or rather, when he had seen it long ago, when he was adorning his annotations to the Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles, as is clear from the annotations to Luke 24, 47 and to Acts 10, 38, he did not wish to see it any longer, after he was blinded by the blind Doctors. For there he acknowledged that the κήρυγμα of repentance among the nations, entrusted to the Disciples of Christ, had been predicted in this place.

Verse of the same. FOR THE REASON THAT THE LORD HAS ANOINTED ME TO PREACH TO THE MEEK] The sense is: therefore he gave his spirit to me, because he imposed upon me a magnificent office, such as that of those anointed into a kingdom or priesthood. That to preach in Hebrew is, to carry a joyful message: to whom? to the meek, that is, to the good, and to those patiently tolerating the evils inflicted upon them. The LXX [translate] πτωχοῖς by the change of one letter, concerning which see at Luke 4, 18.

He understands the word משח not of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, but of the imposition of an office, such as that of those anointed into a kingdom and priesthood. But that such an office, as that of those anointed to a kingdom and priesthood, was imposed upon Isaiah, is false. Since he was neither King nor priest. And it is not established that Isaiah obtained the prophetic office through anointing. Nor is any Prophet ever distinguished by the name of Messiah or Anointed. Which is proper to Christ κατ' ἐξαίρετον λόγον, who is said here to be anointed by the Lord not through the imposition of an office, which is the end of anointing, but through the communication of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Nor is it observed without reason that the word משח is distinguished from נסך, in that the former signifies primarily the smearing of oil, and consequently consecration: but the latter, when added to a Person, obtains the meaning of appointing and setting over. Since therefore the former, not the latter, is used, it must be believed that the discourse is not about the appointment to an office, but about the anointing itself, by which the Messiah was anointed with the oil of the Spirit on account of his office. For which he is distinguished by the name of Messiah, which is also treated in the parallel passages Ps. 45, 7. Rom. 9, 24. Acts 4, 24. and 10, 38. Cyril, in the book on the true faith to Theodosius, at the end: When the word was made flesh, then we also say that he himself was named CHRIST Jesus. For since he was anointed with the oil of gladness, i.e., with the Holy Spirit, by God the Father, for that reason he was also named Christ. And St. Athanasius taught in Oration 2 against the Arians that in that sense also that anointing was declared, when the Holy Spirit came upon Christ in Baptism. When these things, the spirit of the Lord is upon me, and GOD anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit, were pronounced and said concerning him, were they declared publicly, except then, when, established in the flesh, he was being baptized in the Jordan, and the Spirit was descending upon him? And Hilary, book 11 on the Trinity: Jesus was anointed with the Spirit and power of God, then when, as he was ascending from the Jordan, the voice of GOD the Father was heard, Thou art my Son, today I have begotten thee, so that through this testimony the anointing of spiritual power of the flesh sanctified in him might be recognized. Which Jerome also observed in his Commentary on this passage: The anointing of Christ was completed at that time, when he was baptized in the Jordan, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. Which things are to be understood concerning the signification and declaration of the anointing, as Hilary and Athanasius warned. For the anointing itself, or the communication of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, took place in the incarnation itself. Concerning which Chrysostom, homily. Of the Holy Spirit. From the time that the Savior deigned to assume our creature, Christ was filled with the Holy Spirit. And Augustine, book 15, On the Trinity, chapter 46: 'Christ was not anointed with the Holy Spirit when he descended upon him as a dove after he was baptized, but he is to be understood as having been anointed with this mystical and invisible anointing when the Word of God was made flesh.' This was also noted by Remigius in Explanation of Hebrews 1, 9; Albinus Alcuinus, book 11, against Felix of Urgell; Hugo Etherianus, book 3, On Heresies, chapter 10; Theophylact, Commentary on Mark 1. All agree on this, that the anointing is to be understood as the communication of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, no one is easily found who has explained the anointing through the imposition of an office. The sense, therefore, in the words of the Prophet is that which the words themselves convey: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to announce the Gospel,' that is, the Spirit of the Lord, the Spirit of Wisdom, the Spirit of power, etc., rests upon me, for the reason that the Lord has anointed me with the Holy Spirit, as with the oil of gladness and his gifts, ἐκ τοῦ μέτρου [without measure], to the end that I might announce the Gospel, and that I might heal the brokenhearted. Where it is manifest that the anointing is the cause why the Holy Spirit rests and remains upon Christ.

and that the end of this anointing is the Prophetic office, and the redemptive or salvatory one, to which it is established that the parts of the Priestly and Royal office pertain. This sense is confirmed by the explanation of Grotius on Luke 4:18. ὅ ἕνεκεν ἔχρισέ με; it seems, he says, that ὅ ἕνεκεν designates something consequent: whereas on the contrary, from the usage of the Hellenists, it signifies an antecedent: for it answers to the Hebrew יַעַן, which word does not signify 'because of this,' but 'in that,' as in Genesis 22:16, ὅ ἕνεκεν ἐποίησας τὸ ῥῆμα τῦτο καὶ ἐκ ἐ- φείσω τῦ ὑῖ σκ τῦ ἀγαπητῦ, ἦ μὴν εὐλογῶν εὐ- λογήσω σε. Where likewise, as here, there is יַעַן in the Hebrew, which word the LXX elsewhere translate by ἀνθ' ὧν. Nor is the reasoning which Grotius brings forward of any value; ἔχρισϵ here does not signify the donation of the Spirit (for the same would be rendered for the sake of itself) but an enjoined office. For the same is not rendered for the sake of itself; but it is because he was anointed with the Holy Spirit, that the Spirit rests and remains upon him, with the immense fullness of his gifts. Others say that the discourse here is about the revealed and manifest mission of the Holy Spirit into Christ the Son of God, when, having now been made man, he was publicly consecrated in Baptism, for the undertaking and perfecting of his vocation, which indicates that the Holy Spirit was in him for this end, that he might be anointed: or also for the reason that, because he was anointed with the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit descended upon him publicly, so that that anointing might be openly demonstrated.

As to the Object of the proclamation, to whom namely he announces the Gospel, there is no reason why we should admit that the word עֲנָוִים ought to be read otherwise, or that it was read otherwise by the LXX: since not only when it is written עֲנָוִים, but also when it occurs as it is written in this place, עֲנָוִים signifies the miserable and the needy, and therefore could rightly be rendered by the LXX Interpreters as πτωχοῖς, even if they did not read it otherwise than we do. Therefore, not with the Vulgate as MEEK, not with Grotius as GOOD, and those who patiently endure inflicted evils, but with the LXX Interpreters and with St. Luke, and indeed with Christ himself, they are understood as POOR and MISERABLE, just as in Matthew 11 this object is defined as ᾖ πτωχοὶ εὐαγγε- λίζονται. And Grotius acknowledges in his Annotations on Luke that this meaning corresponds more correctly. We add the entire passage of his: (πτωχοῖς) Among the diversities of readings which occur in the Hebrew codices, there is none more frequent than that which has arisen from the interchange of the letters ו and י between themselves. Wherefore this very word, which stands here in the Prophet, is written in Psalm 34:3, 9:13, and 19, and Proverbs 16:19 by some as עַנְיֵי and by others as עֲנָוִים, with the Masoretes acknowledging it, whose authority the Jews follow. But also elsewhere, where nothing but עֲנָוִים is read, as we have it written in this place of the Prophet, the LXX translate it as πένητες. As in the place of the Psalm among the Hebrews 10:17, 22:27. Truly the origin of the word shows that misery is properly signified by this word: but afterwards it was transferred to the denotation of modesty and a submissive mind, which we also said regarding the word ταπεινῶν. And that meaning of a miserable state is much more suitable to this place than the meaning of a modest mind.

Verse of the same. HE SENT ME, THAT I MIGHT HEAL THE BROKEN IN HEART] In the Hebrew: That I might bind up the broken in heart: namely, just as good surgeons bind up wounds, so I have been commanded to mitigate their pain with my prophecies.

But the matter here is not primarily about pain and contrition on account of some bodily evil, nor about a binding which is only in a wound, but about a spiritual evil, by which hearts are especially crushed and we are rendered συντετριμμένοι τὴν καρδίαν on account of the power of sin, the anguish of conscience, and the curse of the law, which evils the Messiah (of whom the discourse is) heals, not by prophecies, nor by preaching alone, but by efficacious healing and the curing of the wounds of conscience. For such a Physician is needed in Matthew 9, and such is the medication of Christ in Isaiah 53, 1 Peter 2; compare Isaiah 25:4. Nor indeed are those πτωχοὶ, to whom the Gospel is preached, those who lack the external riches of the world, or who are miserable on account of bodily calamities and miseries, since the Prophet previously called even Kings and princes, who are to be converted to Christ through the Gospel, and there is no respect of persons in the kingdom of Christ (Acts 10), but they are to be understood as spiritually miserable, needy, and poor, as is evident from Matthew 5 and 11, and also Revelation 3. Origen, Ambrose, and Theophylact in Luke 4 understand by the poor primarily the Gentiles, who are impoverished on account of sins, that is, destitute of grace and salvation, especially those who acknowledge themselves as such. For to such did Christ preach the Gospel. Who are then called the broken in heart. The poor, says Brentius, are called in this place those who, by the gravity and magnitude of their sins, have been cast into such humility and destitution that they feel they must perpetually perish from a hunger for righteousness. For wherever they turn themselves, they find no righteousness by which they may be satisfied and saved: In the law, many pious and honest things are indeed commanded, but they discover that the flesh is too weak to be able to truly perform those things which the law demands. In human traditions, various things are proposed, having indeed the appearance of piety, but which cannot stand against the gates of hell and save the maker. What then should they do? Whither should they turn? Certainly, since they find sin in themselves, and can attain no righteousness neither from the divine law nor from human traditions, nothing else remains but that they should perish from a hunger for righteousness. This is a huge destitution, this is the most grievous poverty, which so depresses the soul that it feels it must be thrust down even to hell. But let us be well confident and let us awake. For the Son of God was anointed with the Holy Spirit, and sent that he might discharge the office of the true Priest, namely, that he might announce the Gospel to the poor. What then is that Gospel of Christ the Son of God? It is certainly not such a Gospel that promises bodily goods. For the poor in spirit do not require such goods. Nor are they refreshed by such things, even if many and the greatest should happen. They find not without difficulty that with which they may feed their belly, but they do not find that with which they may sustain the hunger and destitution of the mind. For here there is need not of bodily, but of spiritual and heavenly goods. The Gospel, therefore, of Christ, the Son of God, is this, that it promises and brings true and heavenly goods. For Christ announces that he himself is the true expiator of sins, that he is the true reconciler between God and man, that he grants his own righteousness to all who believe in him, so that as many as believe in him may be reckoned righteous before God and be saved. Hence Symmachus, as noted by Jerome, and Theodotion, expressed the sense when they expounded: TO BIND UP THE WOUNDS OF SINS. Nor did Christ interpret it otherwise in Luke 4. He certainly did not look to those broken by captivity. He taught that it was to be understood concerning spiritual evils and the medicine which he brought to them. Regarding that healing, Brentius rightly says: The Son is anointed and sent to this office, that he may heal, that he may bind up the wounds of the broken heart, and cure them with his poultice. What, therefore, is that poultice with which the Son of God cures the contriteness of the heart? It is not from some earthly apothecary, nor from Babylon or Rome, but brought down to us from heaven itself, namely the Gospel concerning the expiation of sin through Christ, concerning the righteousness of Christ granted to us, concerning the appeasement of the wrath of God through Christ, concerning the mitigation of the divine sentence on account of Christ. The Father, he says, has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. And soon after: Amen, amen I say to you: He who hears my word, and believes him who sent me, has eternal life, and shall not come into condemnation, but has passed from death to life. You have a poultice, which the Son of God has brought. If you apply this to a heart wounded by the sentence of eternal condemnation, true and eternal health will immediately follow. It must not be passed over in this place, that Grotius would gladly wish this particle to be expunged from the Code of St. Luke. For thus he has it at Luke 4:18. this word ἰάσασθαι τοὺς συντετριμμένους τὴν καρδίαν does not appear to have been in the ancient Greek books from Origen. But neither is it easy to collect that it appeared in the most ancient Latin Codices from the explanation of Ambrose on this place.
