Vers. 6. I HAVE MADE THEM DRUNK IN MY INDIGNATION] I gave them the cup of my wrath to drink. See Ps. 75, 9. above 51, 21. 22. 23. But the Chaldean reads אשברם instead of אשכרם, which is, I have broken them.

AND I HAVE DRAWN DOWN THEIR STRENGTH TO THE EARTH] That is, their blood. For here in the Hebrew is the same word as above 3. The Greeks here [translate] κατήγαγον τὸ αἷμα αὐτῶν εἰς γῆν: I have made a great slaughter.

The entire 63rd chapter ought to have been written down, just as it was distinguished by the Blessed Luther, who referred the remaining part in the Vulgate version to Chapter 64: because the matter itself demanded and required such a distinction. But here Grotius has again devised a completely new gloss on this illustrious prophecy, which has hitherto never been heard in the Church of God, so that it may be sufficiently evident from this what is to be thought of the commentary of this illustrious, if it pleases God, Interpreter of Holy Scripture. And although various interpretations are read elsewhere concerning this prophecy, it never occurred to anyone to have this dream, that Judas Maccabeus was exhibited to the Prophet in a vision. In which, however, Grotius, because it came into his mind (perhaps through a fever), was so pleased with himself that, for the sake of it, he did not hesitate to twist all the prophecies that follow up to the end of the Prophet to those times, with a huge daring, and worthy only of the genius of GROTIUS. But the vanity of this commentary is easily detected. For first, there is no connection of it with the preceding [passages]: which connection Grotius is accustomed to urge most strongly in these prophecies of Isaiah. For what is that leap from Cyrus to Judas Maccabeus? Since, however, the preceding [passages] dealt with Christ, and these also suit the same, they are most correctly explained concerning him. Who then, says Jerome, is the Savior who comes to the daughter of Zion: whose reward is with him, and his work before him, and the just one has gone forth as brightness, and the Savior has been kindled as a lamp: and the bridegroom has rejoiced over his bride the Church, nay, his God has exulted over her, who is himself both Bridegroom and Lord: Therefore, according to the assumption of flesh and the passion of the cross, it is said to him: that thy foot may be dipped in blood. And under the name of Judah it is prophesied in Genesis: Judah, thy brethren shall praise thee: Thy hands shall be on the necks of thy enemies, the sons of thy father shall worship thee: Judah is a lion's whelp, to the prey, my son, thou art gone up: resting thou hast couched as a lion, and as a lioness: who shall rouse him? And again: Binding his foal to the vineyard, and his ass, O my son, to the vine: he shall wash his robe in wine and his blood of the grape his mantle. By which he makes in a certain way the continuation handed down by Musculus: These verses were not to be torn away from the end of the preceding chapter. For they pertain to the argument of those things which are said there. He said: Behold your savior comes, behold his reward is with him, and his work before him. And they shall call them the holy people, the redeemed of the Lord, etc. Here he explains that, Behold your savior comes, behold his reward is with him, and his work before him. By the little word Behold, which he repeated, he thus prophesied concerning the future redemption, as if it were already at the doors, and could be pointed out with a finger: which he did for the sake of certainty. Now for the amplification of that he uses a figure of speech, suitable to prophetic visions. For he speaks with admiration, just as if he sees in the spirit a certain distinguished hero, clothed in a red garment, and bravely advancing with much might, and wondering who he might be, he asks, saying: Who is this, who comes from Edom? with red garments from Bozrah, this one glorious in his garment, walking in the multitude of his might? Thus by hypotyposis he describes the Lord the avenger, comparing him to a hero endowed with singular strength, and clothed in a bloody garment: so that he may allude to the future vengeance, which he was about to take upon his enemies.

Then there is nothing which even slightly persuades that these things are to be explained concerning Judas Maccabeus. And therefore the gloss of Grotius ought to be held as a mere ἰδία ἐπίλυσις (private interpretation). For it can be reconciled with no faith either from the text of the Prophet, or from the New Testament, and not even from any explanation of the ancients. Thirdly, those names are far more august than what would suit Judas, or any ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ (mere man), I am he who speaks justice, and I am a defender or Master to save. Which the Christian Church has hitherto believed to be proper to the Messiah. I am, says Jerome in the paraphrase of this place, he to whom the Father has delivered all judgment, of whom also the Psalmist was saying: O God, give thy judgment to the King and thy justice to the son of the King. Who speak justice: that I may repay evils to the evil, and goods to the good: who have come to fight against the opposing powers, and to preach remission to the captives, and to free the bound from prison, so that both the adversaries may feel the punishments and the captives the liberty. For he judged, says Cyril, the world and Satan, who had oppressed it with injury, and saved those burdened by an intolerable tyranny, and by his command over them he cast down the apostate and the alien. Fourthly, the treading of the winepress is claimed for this one alone, so much so that he expressly denies that anyone is with him. But Judas Maccabeus did not fight alone, but had associates. Which Grotius does not deny. Nor indeed is he said to have trodden the winepress alone without the help of others or of nations; but absolutely I HAVE TRODDEN THE WINEPRESS לבדי ALONE (Symmachus in Justin, Dial. with Trypho, rendered it μόνῳ ἑαυτῷ, i.e., uniquely Alone.) He adds the negative for the sake of emphasis, so that he may more strongly deny that anyone was present with him: THERE WAS NO MAN OF THE PEOPLES WITH ME. Fifthly, that is further established, when he not only removes a helper ἀρνητικῶς (negatively): I LOOKED ABOUT AND THERE WAS NO HELPER, I SOUGHT AND THERE WAS NONE TO HELP; but also θετικῶς (positively) affirms that the victory was obtained by himself alone: MY ARM HAS SAVED FOR ME, AND MY INDIGNATION ITSELF HAS HELPED ME. Which do not suit Judas Maccabeus. For even if he had not then entered into any leagues with any nation, yet it is not said here that alone, nor is the discourse about the zeal of the law alone: but it is ἀποτόμως (sharply) denied that a helper was present, and salvation and victory are attributed to the arm of this Hero alone. This winepress, says Jerome, in which both punishments for the evil and rewards for the good are trodden by the Savior, he himself trod alone, and had no helper. For neither Angel, nor Archangel, thrones, dominions, or any of the heavenly powers, assumed a human Body, and suffered for us, and trod down and crushed the adversaries and strengths, except him who speaks in the Psalm: Save me O Lord, for the Holy one has failed: Inasmuch as even the most confident and in the truth of the faith most firm Apostle Peter, terrified by fear, fled, nay, denied the Lord. Sixthly, since it has been treated before concerning the advent of Jesus the Savior and those redeemed by the Lord, now this Hero testifies here concerning the year of redemption, or of his redeemed, and therefore no other year of redemption is understood than that of this Savior. Seventh, what this day of vengeance is, what the year of redemption, which this Hero says is in his heart, is by no means obscure from chapter 61; that I might preach the acceptable year to the Lord and the day of vengeance to our God. Which certainly cannot be twisted to the times of Judas Maccabeus. Eighth, what that red garment of this Hero is, is known from the prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob, Gen. 49, 11, which Cyril therefore compares here: Why are thy garments red? and thy clothing as from a full trodden winepress? Here recall to my memory what the Patriarch Jacob said: He shall wash his robe in wine, and his mantle in the blood of the grape. For the garments appeared stained with blood, and colored as if with must by redness. Which is the almost common interpretation of Christians. Ninth, the adornment and strength of this Hero, which the Prophet admires: Who is this beautiful in his robe, walking in the multitude of his strength, is described in almost a similar way by the Hieropsalmist Ps. 45, whose description when compared with this Prophetic one teaches that the discourse is about no one else than the Messiah. Tenth, there is added the very ἐξήγησις (explanation) of the Holy Spirit, for who that HERO is, is clearly expressed in Rev. 19, 11. And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse, and he who sat upon him was called FAITHFUL & TRUE, and with JUSTICE he judges, and FIGHTS. His eyes are as a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, having a name written, which no one knows but he himself, and he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called THE WORD OF GOD. And v. 15. And HE TROD THE WINEPRESS of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God almighty, and he has on his garment and on his thigh written: King of Kings, and Lord of Lords. We have [it], who that Hero is, who was seen by Isaiah. Not Judas Maccabeus, but Christ Jesus, who was seen by John in the same manner: who is likewise described there by JUSTICE, by BATTLE with enemies, by a GARMENT sprinkled with blood, and the treading of the WINEPRESS, by HIS POWER, and also by WRATH and indignation, because his eyes are like a flame of fire, so that it is permitted to no Christian to doubt that this Hero is none other than Christ our Lord, King of Kings, and Lord of Lords. Nor is there any reason to say that only a figure of Christ is held here, which Grotius asserted regarding the place in the Apocalypse: For the same words and the same description of this Hero testify that the same subject is being dealt with in both places, nor is it ever hinted that Judas Maccabeus bore the figure of Christ by reason of his battle, and all things which Isaiah expresses are too august to befit a Jew. But all things agree entirely with the Messiah, especially if this Johannine vision is compared with the vision of Isaiah. But Scultetus objects in vain: that it cannot be concluded from the translation of certain phrases to Christ that the discourse is about Christ. For not only of the phrases, but of the thing itself, a translation is made from the Prophetic text into the Apocalyptic; which the evidence of the thing does not so much teach as proclaim. Since indeed concerning the same thing, and concerning the same that in both places the same subject is described, the same kind of discourse is used, so that no place for escape is left. What of the fact that in the Eleventh [chapter] the ancient Rabbis themselves even acknowledged that it is not Judah, nor any other hero, but the Messiah alone who is described in Isaiah? Concerning which we have a clear testimony in Bereshith Rabba of R. Moses Hadarschan upon that [verse] Gen. XLIX. 11. 'He shall wash his garment in wine': When King Messiah comes, he will be clothed in purple, beautiful to behold, which in color will be like wine. And in the blood of grapes his garment. The garment of King Messiah will be red silk, like blood, and it will be embroidered with other colors above. And he himself will be the head of Israel. And this is what is written in Gen. XLIX. 11. 'He shall wash his garment in wine,' as it is said in Isa. LXIII. 2. 'Why is thy garment red, and thy clothing like [the blood of] grapes,' as it is said (Isa. LXIII. 2.) And thy garments like one treading in the winepress. Although these [passages] teem with fables mixed in by more recent Jews, yet the true tradition and faith of the older Rabbis shines through, that they understood this prophecy of no one else but King Messiah, the Head of Israel. In which Twelfth [point] we have almost all Christian interpreters agreeing, except that Calvin, according to his own arrogance, departs from the rest out of a desire to innovate, decreeing with dictatorial authority: 'CHRISTIANS HAVE VIOLENTLY TWISTED THIS CHAPTER,' as if these things pertained to Christ (Why does he not also say that the Holy Spirit, whom Christian interpreters follow, has TWISTED them?) when the Prophet speaks simply of GOD HIMSELF, and they have FASHIONED here a red Christ, because he was soaked in his own blood, which he shed on the cross. But the Prophet intended NOTHING OF THE SORT. The simple sense is that the Lord here comes forth into the sight of the people in red garments, so that all may understand that he is the avenger and vindicator of his own. Which teacher Musculus followed: as also Abraham Scultetus in Idea Concion. super Esaiam. But B. Hunnius stopped Calvin's mouth: whom the exegeses of his own associates also sufficiently refute: Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Pellican, Gualther, Junius & Tremellius, Tossanus, who are of one mind with the other Christians here. See from the Fathers Origen in Matth. tr. 15. Cyprian, or rather Rufinus in Symbol. Ambrose de Instit. Virgin. Athanasius q. LXXVIII. Jerome, & Cyril in h. l. &c. Yet Calvin acknowledged, Musculus acknowledged, Scultetus acknowledged, that the subject here cannot be established as a mere man, but God, and that the predicates of eminence belong to him, so that they do not fall upon a man. And Musculus refutes that explanation concerning the victory against the Edomites: It is indeed known that Edom is the Idumeans, and Bosrah a city of the Idumean region. But it is at the same time known to those who know Hebrew that Edom signifies red, and Bosrah a vintage. Wherefore, in my judgment, those who, because of these two words, explain the present prophecy as concerning vengeance taken upon the Idumeans, write without sufficient consideration. For the Prophet does not speak of this, but of the future subversion of the Babylonians and the redemption of the captive people. He mentions Edom and Bosrah in this sense: Who is this that comes thus clothed in red garments, so that he can be said to come from Edom: and whose garments are thus reddened with the blood of grapes, as if he were coming from Bosrah? Since Edom signifies red and Bosrah a vintage; he says that the hero coming in a red garment and one sprinkled with the redness of grapes comes from Edom and Bosrah by allusion. And I prefer to retain this sense than to depart from the consistency of the same argument without necessity.

Although indeed these things easily suffice against Grotius's fiction regarding the person who is treated here: yet concerning the genuine sense of those things which are proposed here, because they are explained in diverse ways by interpreters, something must still be examined. Musculus embraces the diverse opinions of any interpreters thus: The Hebrews explained it concerning the oppression of the Roman nations, understanding Rome by Bosrah. Jerome refers it to the triumph of Christ, ascending after his passion to heaven with the admiration of the angels, saying: 'Who is this' &c. After him, others explain it concerning the vengeance of God against the Edomites, since mention is made of Edom and Bosrah: others concerning the triumph of Christ, which he took over the Synagogue of the Jews, which they understand by Edom. Lyranus [explains it] concerning the destruction of the Anti-Christ, Jerome cites the exposition of certain ones who refer these things to the end of the world. But Musculus himself interprets it concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity. B. Glassius thus reviews the various explanations in Explanat. Colloq. Passion. which he appended to Onomatologiæ Messiæ Propheticæ p. 403. Having now dismissed the opinion of certain ones who explain this excellent prophecy only concerning the temporal liberation of the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity and the violence of the Edomites (since it is evident from the preceding chapters 60, 61, 62, & following 65, 66, that the Prophet speaks of the Church of the N.T.), we shall hear the opinions of others who interpret it concerning Christ. For some explain it concerning Christ triumphing gloriously against the enemies of the Church (Tossanus, & others), some concerning Christ ascending into heaven (as Hector Pintus in Comment. h. l. from Dionysius, Jerome, Cyril, Haymo), some concerning Christ utterly cutting off the Jewish synagogue (as Luther Tom. 3. Lat. Jen. in expl. h. l.), some concerning Christ finally redeeming the Church (as Piscator of Herborn, who however is inconsistent here. For in his Latin scholia he refers it to the final redemption, which we have mentioned: but in his German version he refers it to the passion itself), some finally explain it concerning Christ coming gloriously to judgment (as Lyranus in h. l.). Which interpretations, however, he judges not to be opposed, but rather to be subordinated in a series, and to agree amicably, thus exhibiting the sense of the place briefly: Christ struggling most bitterly in his passion, and triumphantly victorious after his passion, and all breaking the power of the enemies, the sense and understanding of our Prophetic oracle, is the prow and the stern, namely that there is contained in this chapter a clear σκιαγραφία [sketch] of the passion and death of Jesus Christ and especially of his joyful catastrophe, that is to say, that he, emerging as victor over his enemies, the Devil, death, and hell, who were plotting his plenary destruction, celebrated a triumph by rising from the dead, ascending to the heavens, and sitting at the right hand of the Father, and still carries off a trophy over any adversaries whatsoever until the end of the age, and asserts his Church from them, about to destroy the whole hostile troop by a plenary excision at last.

Moreover, this most noble vision proposed is in a dialogistic form, so that it may affect more, and imprint more strongly those things which are exhibited. As far as the questioner is concerned first, some ancients suppose that they are Angels who ask: Who is this that comes from Edom, inasmuch as they congratulate Christ ascending into heaven. Thus Justin Dial. c. Tryph., Origen Com. 15 in Matth., Ambrose lib. de Institut. Virgin. 5, Jerome and Cyril in this place, Augustine Serm. 5 de Ascens., Dionysius de Cœlest. Hier. C. 7, Haymo, etc. Others, however, say that the Prophet asks, inasmuch as this vision happened to him, others Sion, of whom mention was made before c. 62 v. 11, or the Sionides: In the thing itself, however, they agree, that they admire here the habit, appearance, or fortitude of Christ the hero. Whence it matters little, whether the Prophet himself by himself, or whether another institutes this question. He asks, however, who that Hero is, whom he describes partly by the habit of his garments, partly by his appearance and heroic gait. Do those things concern the habit of garments, who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? Which Grotius accepted regarding the place, i.e., that he came from the land of Edom, and from its metropolis Bozrah. fought against the Edomites and that metropolis. But since he falsely understands Judas Maccabeus through this Hero, so that however he might apply these things to him, he draws here the battle which Judas undertook against the Idumeans: concerning which, however, nothing else is handed down in the cited place 1 Macc. 5, 3 according to Grotius's own interpretation, than that Judas brought war upon the descendants of Esau in Idumean Acrabatane (which was a part of Idumea) because they were besieging the Israelites, that is, making incursions, and he struck them with a great slaughter. But to gather that from those bare names Edom and Bozrah is too weak. Since it is known that names of such a kind for the enemies of the people of God are not rarely placed generally for any enemies whatsoever. Whence Brentius understood these things mystically: whose opinion I am pleased to explain in his own proper words. There is a twofold method of consoling the afflicted and oppressed by enemies. One is led from liberation from enemies: the other from the destruction of enemies. Since, therefore, the Prophet has consoled his hearers in the previous sermons by the former method of consolation, terrified by the prophecy of the Babylonian captivity and other calamities which are accustomed to happen to the people of God: he undertakes now in this sermon to console them by the latter method, and preaches to them about the destruction of the enemies of the people or Church of God, and about the signal victory which Christ carries off from all the enemies of His Church. For although he seems to speak only of the Edomites, yet he signifies not obscurely that he understands by the name of the Edomites all the enemies and adversaries of His Church. For a little later it is said: The year of my retribution comes. Which is to be read thus: The year comes, in which mine are redeemed: signifying clearly that He is redeeming His Church from all enemies. And soon: I have trodden down the peoples in my fury, which certainly pertains not to one nation only, but to all adversary nations. And there exists above in chapter 34 a sermon of the same argument, in which by the name of the Edomites all the enemies of the Church are understood, just as we explained in that place. Wherefore it must be thought that this sermon also was instituted concerning the destruction of all the enemies of the people of God, whether they existed before Christ was born, or came after Christ was born, and whether they are uncircumcised Gentiles, or carnal and impious Jews. These things Brentius, whom Osiander, Junius and Tremellius, Glassius, and others follow. Moreover, it does not seem inconvenient, in our judgment, the explanation of those who refer Edom and Bozrah, according to the signification of the words, to the habit in which this Hero was seen, as if coming from Edom, because that word denotes redness or red, and as if from Bozrah, which word signifies vintage: i.e., who is this, who thus comes clothed in reddish garments, so that he can be said to come from Edom, and whose garments are thus reddened with blood, as if he comes from Bozrah, or vintage. Which opinion seems to be confirmed from the fact that those things are joined by way of explanation; Who is this, who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah, so that to come from Edom is to come with dyed garments, from Bozrah, to come with reddish garments, but those same ones reddened through the vintage. Thus Cornelius à Lapide: he comes from Bozrah, that is, from the vintage and the winepress, for he has garments dyed with red must, that is, with blood. Zwingli agrees: Edom signifies red, and is the proper name of a place. See therefore how pleasantly the spectators of the triumph marvel, when they murmur that Christ, reddened with His own blood, comes from Edom, and this on account of the purple in which those who were triumphing were clothed. Bozrah signifies both vintage and is the name of a place. He makes Christ therefore wet, sticky, and squalid, as those are who, in tending the vintage, neglect the care of the body, because he was badly treated, beaten with scourges, crowned with thorns, crucified, pierced with a lance, and all soaked, imbued with all his blood. Nor are such allusions to names unusual in Scripture: and it is also not infrequent that the particle of similitude כ or כמו is understood, which some say is done here, as Sanctius and others. As if he comes from Edom, as if from Bozrah. And the word אדום is used immediately afterwards in v. 2 concerning the redness, from which Edom has its name. And by that reason an occasion is given to inquire more abundantly afterwards not only in general about redness, but specifically about such redness, which is of those treading in the winepress in verse 2, so that thus in the second verse we have an explanation of the preceding, or of the first verse: For what was asked in figurative words: Who is this, who comes from Edom, that, with the person of this Hero known, so that the cause of that habit may be investigated, is now expressed more explicitly, why therefore is your garment red? Similarly, what was asked there, who is that one with dyed garments from Bozrah, is explained in this way, and your garments like those of one treading in the winepress. Finally, neither the battle nor the victory against the enemies could be commemorated here yet, because it was still being asked about that one whom the Prophet saw, who he is, and what that redness means for itself. The Prophet did not see him returning immediately from the battle and victory against the enemies, but only afterwards understood it from the response of the Hero who was seen. Nor is inquiry made only about the color of the habit, but also about the heroic form of the same and the gait worthy of such a Hero, who shone with heroic fortitude. THIS ONE BEAUTIFUL IN HIS STOLE, MARCHING IN THE MULTITUDE OF HIS STRENGTH. Who is that one so honorably, so splendidly clothed, marching in the great majesty of his strength! To which are twin the things which are held in Ps. 45, 3 and following concerning this Hero beautiful in form above the sons of men, gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty, with your splendor and your beauty proceed, proceed prosperously and reign: Myrrh, Aloes, and Cassia from your garments. An illustration of both prophetic places, as regards this habit and appearance of our Hero, is held in Revelation 19, 11. His eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many crowns, and he was clothed with a garment sprinkled with blood, and out of his mouth proceeds a sword sharp on both sides, that with it he might smite the nations. All of which things pertain to the habit, clothing, form, and majesty of our Hero, and mutually illustrate one another. Thus, therefore, the Prophet expressed both the redness and the comeliness of the same Hero, worthy of him. The redness, while he said he was from Edom and from Bozra חמוץ בגדים, sprinkled with garments, as Tremellius and Junius explain, having red garments, as Vatablus explains. The word חמץ denotes 'is fermented,' 'is sprinkled with leaven,' it has a kinship with צמת 'he made bloody,' 'he stained with blood,' which is sour like leaven; therefore also in Apoc. 19:13 this word is explained concerning the redness of blood sprinkled on garments. The comeliness is expressed by הדור בלבושו 'comely in his apparel': because הדר is to decorate and to adorn. Although blood otherwise defiles and renders us foul, Ez. 16:6, yet for warrior heroes it is glorious to have a garment sprinkled with blood, because their magnanimity is perceived from it. And that garment was representatively the human nature, which grew red with the blood poured out, but nothing of its glory departed from it; nay, rather, the human nature of Christ was magnificently adorned with glory and honor, as John ch. 1:14 testifies. Thus that blood-staining contributed not a little to the splendor of that glory, because his clemency, love, and ineffable grace made it conspicuous to us, nay, demonstrated the magnanimity and heroic fortitude of that Hero. Although, therefore, this sprinkling of blood seemed to be a pollution according to the external aspect, as it is said in verse 3, 'I have defiled all my garments,' yet in truth this was the signal glory of our most august Both are predicated of Christ suffering in human nature, says the Blessed Glassius, l. c. p. 440, both pollution and decoration or glory; the former according to appearance, the latter according to truth: the former by reason of the passion itself, the latter by reason of the victory brought back from the enemies and performed in the very shedding of blood as a satisfaction for our sins, from which we are cleansed through the blood of Christ. Therefore, those things which are diverse only by reason of different objects are not to be opposed. Christ defiled Himself by taking upon Himself the filth of our sins through the imputation made, and by expiating them in His own body, 1 Pet. 2:24, by sustaining the wrath of the Father and the sting of death and hell, and finally by miserably shedding His blood. But the same One, by this shedding of His most precious blood, made for US the purgation of sins by Himself, Heb. 1:3, and His blood CLEANSES US from all sin, 1 John 1:7. Both are joined in 2 Cor. 5, last verse: GOD made Him, who knew no sin, to be SIN for US, that we might become the righteousness of GOD in Him.

The Prophet thus describes the gait of the victor: צֹעֶה בְּרֹב כֹּחוֹ. For the word צֹעֶה is to be taken intransitively and neutrally, nor is it used otherwise; nay, the Prophet's inquiry demands this sense: because he had not yet understood about His heroic actions. And therefore, from those external things, namely from the color and decoration of the garments, as well as from the manner of the gait in which He was seen to be described in this vision, he could as yet only describe Him as we are accustomed to describe someone from such external things when we inquire into his person. It is therefore no less foreign to the usage of the word than to the sense of this question that Calvin interprets this verb transitively, concerning the nations which the Lord transfers elsewhere, and Schindler in Lex. p. 1558, MOVING AND EXPEL- LING peoples, as well as Vatablus and Marloratus, making Israel migrate from all the places of its captivity into which it is dispersed, as if not the gait, but the action of the Triumpher were being expressed. More correctly, therefore, Jerome renders it 'walking,' others 'advancing,' others 'running.' For it denotes moving oneself from one place to another by migrating, whence Avenarius in Lex. derives the Greek σείω 'I move,' and the Latin cieo, and the German ziehen/umziehen/einen Zug. The interlinear gloss explains the words 'in the multitude of His strength' concerning military forces; thus those things in Rev. 19:11 agree: 'And the armies which are in heaven followed Him on white horses.' Surrounded by whom He could appear, even if meanwhile He Himself alone, not the companions and ministers now surrounding Him, trod the winepress in His passion. Which also that explanation of Grotius seems to imply: 'Leading a host, and He Himself like a great host.'

Others, however, prefer to refer these things to the heroic gait of the One coming. Thus Glassius, comparing the passage Prov. 30:29-30. Thus also Cornelius à Lapide: 'Walking with an imperatorial, strong, powerful, and magnificent step, and by his very gait, habit, form, and gesture, bearing before him strong forces, great spirits, and heroic courage.' Just as Agesilaus, King of the Lacedaemonians, seeing Epaminondas, the Theban general, walking nobly with his battle line, exclaimed: 'O magnificent man!' says Plutarch in Epaminondas.

There now follows the Answer to the former question, by which it is explained what that Person is, who that Hero is, whom the Prophet saw: I

- WHO SPEAK RIGHTEOUSNESS AND AM A DEFENDER TO SAVE. From which answer the Prophet certainly could not understand that it was Judas Maccabaeus, nor did that ever easily come into anyone's mind. But he could easily understand that it was the Messiah, as it was not unknown that He was described by this and a similar periphrasis: whom the Holy Spirit everywhere celebrates for righteousness and mercy, to whom it is vindicated that He announces to us the true righteousness obtained by Himself, Ps. 40:11, Isa. 42:1, ch. 45:27, ch. 48:17-18, ch. 50:4, ch. 53:11, ch. 60:17, ch. 61:1, and that He Himself is a Master, or great and abundant to save: because the word רב signifies both 'much' and 'Master,' both of which suit Christ, with whom is plenteous redemption, Ps. 130:7. and infinite wisdom, by which He knows how to succor the human race, and in the very word לְהוֹשִׁיעַ the Lord revealed His name to the Prophet, namely that He is JESUS, and that this is to be His name, by which name He was already insinuated to him in ch. 49:6, ch. 44, and recently ch. 62:11. We have here, therefore, truly a speaker of words and a doer of deeds, a Hero powerful both in words and works, 'mighty in deed and word,' Luke 24:19. To which it contributes that in Rev. 19:11 He is thus described: FAITHFUL AND TRUE, who judges and fights with RIGHTEOUSNESS. Brentius rightly: 'By this periphrasis Christ describes Himself. Nor is there any other to whom this description applies except Jesus Christ.' For first, He speaks in righteousness, that is, He teaches His Gospel, by which it is revealed that He alone is our righteousness, by which He also bestows all His righteousness on those who believe in Him. For as many as believe in Him enjoy His righteousness in such a way that, on account of it, they themselves are reckoned righteous before God and receive all the rewards of the righteous. Next, He is a defender to save, that is, a master of salvation. For He is the One who can and knows and wills to save, who has much and great power, knowledge, and will to save. For there is no other name, as Peter says, given among men under heaven by which we must be saved. Similarly other Interpreters; Corn. a Lapide from the Papists: 'Christ answers: I am the Messiah, who have obtained the righteousness and salvation which I promised by defending and conquering.'

The Prophet's second question is as follows: WHY THEN IS THY APPAREL RED, AND THY GARMENTS LIKE THOSE OF THEM THAT TREAD IN THE WINEPRESS. He had been sufficiently instructed concerning the Person of the Hero, whom the Prophet had understood from that response in such a way that he had no further need to ask about the same. For the response given was a clear περίφρασις of the Messiah, from which, in truth, he could in no way understand Judas Maccabeus, about whom he had not yet received a single word by report. And therefore he now wishes to be taught about this habit and gait of the Messiah, which was done so that the passion and triumph of the Messiah might be placed more clearly before the eyes of the faithful. If you are the Master of salvation (thus Brentius paraphrases), why is it that you have such bloody garments? You seem to come more from a battle, or a slaughterhouse, where much carnage has been done and much blood shed, than from that place where great salvation has been obtained. For just as those who tread grapes in a winepress are accustomed to bring back garments splattered with must and dregs, so you walk, your clothes splattered with much blood. What, therefore, does this habit mean for you? Or how does it agree with your Epithet, by which you call yourself Rabbi, or Master of salvation? Jerome's very pleasant paraphrase is as follows: Whence, O Christ, O immaculate Lamb, did you stain your snowy and virginal flesh? Whence did you redden it with blood? For clemency becomes you more than cruelty, whiteness more than gore. Similar is the Dialogismus in Ps. 25, 9, whose explanation, most sweetly delivered by Augustine, excellently illustrates this interrogation of ours; he ascen- ded, says the Bishop of Hippo in sermon 178 on the Season, which is the 5th on the Ascension of the Lord, suffused with the redness of blood, and crowned with victorious trophies. All the heavenly beings saw Christ beautiful in his wounds, the spoils brought back from the tyrannical camps, and admiring the shining banners of divine power, they resound with such hymns, and lead him on rejoicing: Who is, they say, this King of glory? And they answer, The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. This is that white and ruddy one, pierced by the multitude. This is he who had no form nor comeliness. Weak in the snare, strong in the spoil: vile in his little body, armed in battle, foul in death, beautiful in resurrection; white from the virgin, red on the cross, dark in reproaches, bright in heaven.

The answer given to this question does not only explain the cause of the redness of the garment, and the similarity to those who have trodden in the winepress, but it provides a more abundant account of his victorious progress, or why he appears walking in the greatness of his power; I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the peoples there is no man with me. He teaches that he has trodden the winepress entirely, and indeed alone, without any assistant or helper, so that in this struggle he did not have even one helper. But he explains at the same time what kind of winepress this is, namely, not of grapes, but of enemies: And how he trod them. I trod them in my fury, and trampled them in my wrath, and their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I have stained all my raiment. Although a winepress is properly an instrument of expression, not of the treading of grapes, yet, because that vessel in which grapes are trodden by the feet before they are subjected to the press to be expressed does not have a peculiar name in the Holy Scriptures, it is commonly expressed by the word for winepress פּוּרָה: by this vat, however, are metonymically understood the grapes or clusters cast into the winepress, by which he is said to have trodden enemies, and peoples, as is had in verse 6: I have trampled the peoples in my fury: He uses the word for trampling, both because victors were accustomed to trample enemies with their feet, no differently than clusters are trodden by the vintner in the winepress, as was done in Josh. 10:24. Indeed, enemies were even trampled and threshed by carts and iron-wheeled wagons, 2 Sam. 12:31, 1 Chron. 20:2, Judg. 8:16, Amos 1:3, and the same mode of speaking occurs concerning God in Lam. 1:16. Rev. 14:19, that he tramples in the winepress those upon whom he exercises vengeance: and because he looked to the first promise concerning the treading of the serpent's head with his feet, in which is simultaneously designated the wounding of the heel of the foot, through which the ὁ Ὀφιόμαχος (serpent-fighter) had to be reddened with his own blood, Gen. 3:15. By which pact also the trampling of the Demon is described in Ps. 91:13, you shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk and you shall trample the lion and the dragon, and a similar phrase is applied to Christ in Ps. 110:6, he shall crush the head of many lands. Therefore the enemies of Christ are said to be subjected to his feet as his footstool, Ps. 110:1, 1 Cor. 15:25, 26, indeed even to be crushed under the feet of his faithful, Rom. 16:20. The sense therefore is: as vintners are accustomed to tread the gathered vintage vehemently and with great effort, so I prostrate my enemies, subject them to my feet, trample them, and destroy them in my wrath. That he testifies that he performs this alone, and as Symmachus emphatically rendered it, μονώτατον, uniquely alone: and lest anyone add any allies to him in this work: there is, he says, no man of the peoples, or any with me: indeed, so that he may deny as an agent that any σύνεργον (co-worker) was present with him, he adds: I looked around and there was no helper, I sought, and there was none who would help. Therefore the Papists are foolish, and recently Hector Pintus: There is no MAN with me, so that he would not exclude the Virgin Mary. The very manner of speaking refutes such a frivolous exception. From the kind of expression, says Sanctius, it is signified quite significantly that no one at all provided auxiliary work to Christ.

God speaks in the human manner, and says that he had surveyed every place with his eyes, and had attentively searched through everything, and that there was no one who had enough strength for such a work, as Adam explains, or whose work he needed for its happy outcome. Which explanation in the spiritual sense, that is, the procuring of the salvation of souls, is easy and manifestly true; since the procurement and gift of that salvation pertains to him who is truly and properly the savior. Finally, he testifies with a sonorous voice that he accomplished this alone by his own power, and obtained that victory, when he adds in verse 5: And it saved for me, not a stranger, not an ally and assistant of any kind, not some superior, but MY ARM, my own virtue and power, and MY VERY INDIGNATION has helped me. As my fortitude was for my salvation: so besides my heroic zeal nothing was for my help and assistance, by my fortitude and my Zeal this whole victory was uniquely obtained.

We have a Hero, a warrior and victor; But who are those enemies whom he conquered and trampled? He says simply in verse 3: I trod THEM in my fury, and trampled THEM in my wrath, with no mention made of who they are. Naturally, since he described his person beforehand, and thus now testifies to his wrath and fury in this work of treading and trampling, and teaches that he executes it alone, he wishes it to be gathered from that, who the enemies are with whom he had to deal? Namely those whom the Messiah, that Master, had to defeat in order to save, whose trampling could not be done except by this Master alone, whom that one, and he alone, was able to overcome, and whose head he was about to trample with such Zeal and fury, in whose trampling, finally, he was about to stain his garment with his own blood. Who these are, the Prophet [shows] from the Proto-Evangelium Gen. 3:15. & by the Jacobite prophecy Gen. 49, 10, and other prophecies, especially Davidic ones, then by the revelation made to him in ch. 53, it could not be hidden, even if express mention of them were not made here. Namely, that he had to fight with the ancient serpent, and the serpentine seed, with the whole Diabolical rabble, with that strong armed man, as he is called by Christ in Luke 11, with that robust and giant one, of whom above in ch. 49, 24. For the sake of destroying whom he had to appear 1 John 3, 8. For against no one else did the Savior become so inflamed with that fury and wrath of his, inasmuch as he came not against any one of men, but for the sake of delivering all men. But what is said of the same in Rev. 19, 13: And he himself treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty, does not contradict this sense of ours, but illustrates the same, because those spiritual enemies are the winepress of the fury of God, whom God in his fury subjects to the press, so that they are like a press or clusters and grapes, subjected to the press not of wine, but of the fury of God, because they are trodden by Christ in fury and wrath: whom he indeed trod in his passion, but because his power lasts perpetually, he is still said to tread them. Nor indeed is the wrath of God one thing, and the wrath of Christ another: and it is the same thing in reality to tread enemies in his wrath as in a press or vat, and to tread the vat or winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty. For this treading of the divine winepress of wrath is so called only with respect to the enemies, whom the wrath of God presses. Nor does anything stand in the way of the fact that the discourse is about the same enemies in both places, by this phrase, because when Christ is introduced as the victor over corporal enemies, one ascends to the source and origin of this victory, and the cause of that victory is exhibited, that he himself is the one who strikes the nations: since he also trod the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty, and vanquished Satan himself, the Prince of the world, whom in his instruments he also never ceases to vanquish, until he places all his enemies as a footstool for his feet. Ps. 110, 1. 1 Cor. 15, 25.

It follows in the Prophet: And their blood is sprinkled upon my garments, and I have stained all my raiment. The LXX rendered the word נִצְחָם (their strength) as τὸ αἷμα ἀυτῶν, and similarly the Vulgate, their blood, either because blood is the redness and life of the body, as some wish, or because mention had been made of a red color; but since that Hebrew word never denotes blood, as Forster observed in his Lexicon, it must be believed that they looked more to the sense than they interpreted the word. That word signifies strength and excellence, whence Junius and Tremellius wish the abstract to be put for the concrete, and they posit an ellipsis in this way: thus is sprinkled (the blood) of whose and of their most robust ones upon my garments. Which ellipsis and interpretation, however, seems too arbitrary. The explanation of the blessed Luther pleases as the simplest, which Piscator and the Dutch also retained, 'Daher ist ihr Vermögen auf meine Kleider gesprützt' [Therefore their power is sprinkled upon my clothes]: But how was he sprinkled with the virtue and power of the enemies, so that all his garments were stained, and indeed reddened or dyed with a red color? That is to be understood in this way, that the battle was so fierce that the enemies exerted all their strength, whom he indeed tramples, but in such a way that their power is sprinkled upon his garments, or appears on the garments of Christ, how much power they applied. Since this Hero had to fight even to blood, and the enemies fought with such virtue and force that he necessarily had to shed his blood most copiously, and stain his whole garment with his blood, until he conquered them. For in stained garments the abundance of shed blood is noted, as in Gen. 49, 11. He will wash his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape. And B. Glassius rightly observes that the word נִצְחָם agrees beautifully with the thing itself: For the power of the enemies, with whom Christ had to struggle, was so great that it seemed for a time to have a certain appearance of victory, superiority, and predominance, when Christ, pressed by the sense of the wrath of God and infernal punishments, emitted bloody θρόμβους [clots] through his sweat, and, driven to the cross, complained most gravely of divine dereliction, and was afterwards delivered to bodily death itself. This was that נִצְחָם, that power and bitterness of the enemies, which was sprinkled on the clothes of Christ, so that he himself was entirely soaked with shed blood. Other interpreters understood that this sense underlay the words of the Prophet, although they attempted to gather the same otherwise from the words: where it is to be seen in the interlinear Gloss: And their blood (mine) (poured by them) is sprinkled upon my garments (limbs). In the Glossa Ordinaria, the blood is called the blood of the Jews, because they shed it, and thence sustained vengeance. Burgensis: Their blood is said to be sprinkled, not because it is their blood properly, but because it was shed through their procurement, or also because they made themselves liable for this blood, saying, his blood be upon us, etc.

But furthermore, the reason is subjoined why he fought with such zeal against the enemies, until he powerfully overcame them: And why he performed this alone. The reason for the former is this; for the day of vengeance is in my heart, the year of my redemption has come. A twofold reason is contained here: the one is divine vengeance against the enemies, which was to be exercised on that great day of Christ's passion. For then was the judgment of the world, by which the prince of this world was to be cast out, John 11. To this end he had to exercise vengeance against the diabolical troop, because it had drawn the human race away from God. The other is divine thanks toward men, for the exercising of which he assigns not only a day, but a year. By which not only is the Jubilee year referred to, Lev. 25, 9, but also the perennial duration of that Jubilee is designated: Because that year lasts perpetually, if you look at its effect, from the Proto-Evangelium until the consummation of the age, namely the announcement of thanks and good pleasure, which however was made especially in the New Testament; therefore this time is strictly called the time of good pleasure, 2 Cor. 2, 2. For although on the same day both the vengeance against Satan and the redemption of the human race were accomplished, because however that redemption is to be applied to us, and that is done through that mystical Jubilee year, in which thanks is announced and dispensed to us, therefore that time is said to have come to Christ, in which Christ had to acquire that thanks by his death, but that year lasts for us as long as the kingdom of thanks lasts. Let those things be compared which are said concerning the time of good pleasure at Is. 61, 2 and c. 49, 8. The reason for the latter is explained by these things, namely why he performed this work alone? And I looked, or rather I looked around, I turned my eyes everywhere, as men are wont to do when about to attack their enemies, to seek out forces from everywhere, but there was no helper who could assist me either in vengeance against the enemies or in the redemption of the human race. I sought in the Hebrew, ואשתומם, I was astonished, I was amazed, or also I was devastated, I was in anxiety, as the blessed Luther says, 'Ich war in Schrecken' [I was in terror], which was fulfilled when he began to be sorrowful, distressed, and sore amazed, and when his soul was περίλυπος [exceeding sorrowful] even unto death, Matt. 26, 37, 38, and there was no one supporting, who could support or sustain among men. AND MY ARM SAVED FOR ME, as salvation is sometimes taken for a thing strenuously and happily managed, and to do salvation is to obtain victory, so also to save is to conquer, or to act prosperously against enemies, 1 Sam. 14, 6. Ps. 97, 2. Ps. 112, 25. The sense is, because of the greatest force of the enemies I would have succumbed while suffering and agonizing, had not my divine omnipotence sustained me and overthrown the hostile troop. AND MY WRATH UPHELD ME. Divine power and zeal for redeeming the human race sustained the human nature of Christ, lest it succumb under the immense burden. Finally, the συμπέρασμα (conclusion) is added v. 6. AND I TROD DOWN THE PEOPLES IN MY WRATH, AND MADE THEM DRUNK IN MY FURY, AND BROUGHT DOWN THEIR STRENGTH TO THE EARTH. He explains more fully the similitude taken from the winepress, that he trod down the hostile peoples, just as grapes are trodden, that he drew down their strength to the earth and subjected it to his feet, just as grapes are subjected to the feet: that he made them drunk with the wine of the wrath of God, just as wine is pressed out from trodden grapes, by which men are made drunk. Cf. Ps. 75, 9. Is. 29, 9. c. 51, 17. 21. Jer. 25, 15. Lam. 3, 18. Hab. 3, 16. Inebriavi: Junius and Tremellius explain, I offered great and unusual cups of afflictions and of my wrath to be drunk. The word עמים denotes peoples, but עם (people) is said not only of men, but also of other collective things metaphorically, such as of ants Prov. 30, 25, of locusts Joel 2, 2. 25. And therefore here it can be referred to the whole troop of enemies, with whom Christ had to struggle, both corporal, and especially spiritual. Thus Ps. 110, 6. Glassius says that גוים (nations) are called, who in v. 1 are called enemies, who are not only earthly, but also spiritual. 1 Cor. 15, 25. 26. Luke 1, 71, comparing also Matt. 13, 28, where the Devil is called ἐχθρὸς ἄνθρωπος (an enemy man). Zwingli also acknowledged this, I attacked the beast sin, relying on my arm and my strength. The slaughter of peoples, which is held here, is a periphrasis of sin and death overcome.

Latin:

Vers. 6. INEBRIAVI EOS IN INDIGNATIONE MEA] Iræ meæ calicem eis potandum dedi. Vide Psal. 75, 9. supra 51, 21. 22. 23. At Chaldæus pro אשכרם legit אשברם, quod est, confregi eos.

ET DETRAXI IN TERRAM VIRTUTEM EO- RUM] Id est, sanguinem. Est enim hic in Hebræo vox eadem quæ supra 3. Græci hic κατήγαγον τὸ αἷμα αὐτῶν εἰς γῆν : ingentem occidionem feci.

ADscribendum fuit integrum caput 63. quem- admodum id à B. Luthero distinctum, qui re- liquam in versione vulgata partem ad C. 64. retu- lit : quod res ipsa talem distinctionem posceret ac requireret. Excogitavit autem hic iterum Grotius novam plane illustris vaticinii glossam, quæ hacte- nus in Ecclesia Dei nunquam audita, ut quid de commento hujus præclari, si Deo placet, S. Lite- rarum Interpretis habendum sit, exinde satis constet. Et traditæ quidem alias de hoc vaticinio leguntur variæ interpretationes, sed nemini un- quam in mentem venit hoc somnium, quod in vi- su exhibitus Prophetæ fuerit Judas Maccabæus. In quo tamen Grotius, quia ipsi, (forte per febrim) in mentem id venit, ita sibi placuit, ut ejusdem gratia non dubitarit, omnia quæ sequuntur vati- cinia usque ad finem Prophetæ ad ista tempora detorquere, ausu ingenti, nec nisi GROTII in- genio digno. Vanitas autem commenti istius facile detegitur. Nam primo nullus nexus ejusdem est cum præcedentibus : quem vero in hisce vaticiniis Esaiæ vel maxime urgere solet Grotius. Quis enim saltus ille à Cyro ad Judam Maccabæum? Quum vero præcedentia de Christo egerint, hæc eidem etiam conveniant, rectissime de ipso ea explicantur. Quis igitur, inquit Hieronymus, venit filiæ Sion Salva- tor : cujus merces cum eo est, & opus illius coram illo, & egressus est justus ut splendor, & Salvator accensus est ut lampas : gavisusque sponsus super sponsa sua Ecclesia, imo exultavit super eam Deus suus, qui ipse & Sponsus & Dominus est : Propterea secundum assumptionem carnis & passionem crucis dicitur ad eum : ut intingatur pes tuus in sanguine. Et sub Judæ vocabulo in Genesi prophetatur : Juda te laudabunt fratres tui : Manus tuæ in cervicibus inimicorum tuorum, adorabunt te filii patris tui: Catulus leonis Juda, ad prædam Fili mi, ascen- disti, requiescens accubuisti ut leo & quasi leæna: quis suscitavit eum? Et iterum: Ligans ad vi- neam pullum suum, & ad vitem, ô Fili mi a- sinam suam: lavabit vino stolam suam & san- guine uvæ pallium suum. Quo facit certa ratione συνέχεια à Musculo tradita: Hi versus non erant di- vellendi à calce præcedentis capitis. Pertinent enim ad argumentum eorum, quæ ibi dicuntur. Dixit: Ecce servator tuus venit, ecce merces ejus cum eo, & opus ejus ante ipsum. Et vocabunt eos populum sanctum, redemptos Domini &c. Hic illud, Ecce servator tuus venit, ecce merces ejus cum eo, & opus ejus ante ipsum, exponit. Per voculam Ecce, quam ingeminavit, sic vaticinatus est de futura redemptione, quasi jam esset in foribus, ac digito mon- strari posset: id quod certitudinis gratia fecit. Jam ad illius amplificationem utitur sermonis figura, visio- nibus propheticis accommoda. Perinde enim cum admiratione loquitur, ac si videat in spiritu heroem quendam insignem, veste rubicunda indutum, mul- taque virtute fortiter grassantem, & admiratus quisnam sit, interroget, dicens: Quis est iste, qui ve- nit de Edom? vestibus rubicundis de Bosrah, decorus iste in veste sua gradiens in multitudine virtutis suæ? Sic per hypotyposin Dominum ultorem describit, comparans eum heroi singulari robore prædito, ac veste cruenta induto: ut alludat ad futuram ultio- nem, quam sumpturus erat de inimicis.

Deinde nihil est, quod vel leviter persuadeat, hæc de Juda Maccabæo explicanda esse. Ideoq; me- re ἰδία ἐπίλυσις haberi debet glossa Grotiana. Nam ei neque è textu Prophetæ, neque è Novo Testa- mento, ac ne è veterum quidem explicatione ulla fides conciliari potest. Tertio nomina illa augu- stiora longe sunt, quam quæ Judæ, aut ulli ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ conveniant, Ego sum qui justitiam loquor, & propugnator vel Magister sum ad salvandum. Quæ Messiæ propria esse, hactenus credidit Ecclesia Christiana. Ego sum, inquit in paraphrasi hujus loci Hieronymus, cui Pater tradidit omne judicium, de quo & Psalmista dicebat: Deus judicium tuum Re- gi da & justitiam tuam filio Regis. Qui loquor ju- stitiam: ut malis mala, & bonis retribuam bona: qui veni pugnare contra adversarias potestates, & ca- ptivis prædicare remissionem, & vinctos de carcere liberare, ut & adversarii pœnas & captivi sentiant libertatem. Judicavit enim, inquit Cyrillus, orbem & Satanam, qui eum injuria oppresserat, fervavit- que intolerabili tyrannide gravatos, & imperio in illos suo dejecit apostatam & alienum. Quarto tor- cularis calcatio huic soli vendicatur, adeo ut neget diserte quenquam secum esse. At Judas Macca- bæus non pugnavit solus, sed habuit socios. Quod non diffitetur Grotius. Nec vero solus fine adju- tu externorum vel gentium torcular calcâsse di- citur; sed absolute TORCULAR, inquit, CAL- CAVI לבדי SOLUS (Symmachus apud Justinum Dial. cum Tryph. reddidit μόνῳ ἑαυτῷ, q. d. unice Solus.) Negativam addit emphaseos causa, ut fortius neget, quemquam sibi adfuisse: NON FUIT VIR DE POPULIS MECUM. Quin- to stabilitur id ulterius, cum non modo ἀρνητικῶς auxiliatorem removet: CIRCUMSPEXI ET NON ERAT AUXILIATOR, QUÆSIVI ET NON ERAT QUI ADJUVARET; sed etiam θετικῶς affirmat, à se solo victoriam ob- tentam: SALVAVIT MIHI BRACHIUM MEUM, ET INDIGNATIO MEA IPSA AUXILIATA EST MIHI. Quæ Judæ Macca- bæo non conveniunt. Nam etsi is nulla cum gente fœdera tum inierit, non tamen id solum hic dicitur, neq; de solo legis zelo sermo est: sed ἀποτόμως ne- gatur, adfuisse auxiliatorem, ac soli Herois hujus brachio tribuitur salus, & victoria. Hoc torcular, inquit Hieronymus, in quo & malis supplicia, & bo- nis præmia à Salvatore calcantur, solus ipse calcavit, quis nullumq; habuit adjutorem. Neq; enim Angelus, aut Archangelus, throni, dominationes, aut ulla cœle- stium potestatum, humanum Corpus assumpsit, & pro nobis passus est, & conculcavit adversarios fortitudines atq; contrivit, nisi ille qui loquitur in Psalmo: Sal- vum me fac Domine, quoniam defecit Sanctus: In tantum ut etiam confidentissimus & in fidei veritate firmissimus Apostolus Petrus, timore territus fugerit, imo Dominum negarit. Sexto quum actum fuerit antea de adventu Jesu Salvatoris & redemtis a Do- mino, jam de anno redemtionis, vel redemtorum suo- rum testatur hicHeroes, ideoq; non alius redemtio- nis annus, quam hujus Salvatoris intelligitur. Septi- mo, quis hic dies ultionis, quis annus redemtionis, quem hic Heros dicit esse in corde suo, e capite 61. minime obscurum est; ut prædicarem annum pla- cabilem Domino & diem ultionis Deo nostro. Quæ certe ad Judæ Maccabæi tempora detorqueri non possunt. Octavo rubrum illud vestimentum, quale sit hujus Herois e Patriarchæ Jacobi vaticinio no- tum est Gen. 49, 11. quod proinde hic confert Cy- rillus: Quare rubra sunt vestimenta tua? & indu- menta tua, velut ex torculari pleno calcato? Hic mihi repete memoria, quod Patriarcha Jacobus dixit: Lavabit in vino stolam suam, & in sanguine uvæ amictum suum. Tincta enim sanguine indumenta apparebant, & tanquam musto colorata rubore. Quæ communis fere Christianorum est interpretatio. Nono Herois hujus ornatus & fortitudo, quam ad- miratur Propheta: Quis est iste formosus in stola sua, gradiens in multitudine fortitudinis suæ, simili fere ratione descripta est ab Hieropsalte Pf. 45. cujus de- scriptio cum hac Prophetica collata docet de nul- lo alio, quam Messia sermonem esse. Decimo acce- dit ipsa Spiritus Sancti ἐξήγησις, quis enim HE- ROS ille sit, luculenter expressum est Apoc. 19, 11. Et vidi cœlum apertum, & ecce equus albus, & qui se- debat super eum, vocabatur FIDELIS & VE- RAX, & cum JUSTITIA judicat, & PUGNAT. Oculi ejus sicut flamma ignis, & in capite ejus diade- mata multa, habens nomen scriptum, quod nemo no- vit nisi ipse, & vestitus erat veste aspersa sanguine, & vocatur nomen ejus VERBUM DEI. Et v. 15. Et IPSE CALCAVIT TORCULAR vini furoris iræ Dei omni- potentis, & habet in vestimento & in femore suo scri- ptum: Rex Regum, & Dominus Dominantium. Ha- bemus, quis ille Heros sit, qui ab Esaia conspectus. Non Judas Maccabæus, sed Christus Jesus, qui ea- dem ratione visus Johanni est: qui pariter ibi de- scribitur a JUSTITIA, a PUGNA cum hostibus, a VESTE sanguine aspersa, & conculcatione TORCULARIS, a POTENTIA SUA, nec non ab IRA & indignatione, quia oculi ejus sicut flamma ignis, ut nemini Christianorum ambigere liceat, huncHeroem nullum alium esse, quam Chri- stum Dominum nostrum, Regum Regem, & Do- minum Dominantium. Nec est, quod dicatur figu- ram Christi solum hic haberi, quod ad locum Apo- calyps. Grotius asseruit: Nam verba eadem & de- scriptio hujus Herois eadem testantur, de eodem subjecto utrobiq; agi, neq; ratione pugnæ suæ Ju- dæam Maccabæum Christi figuram gessisse unquam innuitur, & augustiora omnia sunt, quæ Esaias ex- primit, quam ut Judæ conveniant. Ex asse autem conveniunt omnia Messiæ, imprimis si visio hæc Jo- hannea cum visione Esaiæ componatur. Nequic- quam vero excipit Scultetus: ex phræsium quarun- dam translatione ad Christum concludi non posse, quod de Christo sermo sit. Nam non phræsium modo, sed rei quoq; ipsius ex textu Prophetico in Apocaly- pticum fit translatio; quod rei evidentia non tam docet, qua clamat. Siquide de eadem re, deq; eodem quod utrobiq; describitur subjecto idem ufurpetur sermonis genus, ut effugii nullus relictus sit locus. Quid quod Undecimo ipsimet etiam Rabbini ve- teres agnoverint penes Esaiam describi non Ju- dam, non alium quemquam Heroem sed Messiam unice. Quo de luculentum habemus testimo- nium in Bereschith Rabba R. Mosis Hadarschan super illud Gen. XLIX. 11. Lavabit in vino vesti- mentum suum : Quando veniet Rex Messias, vesti- tus erit purpura pulchra visu, quæ in colore similis erit vino. Et in sanguine uvarum indumentum suum. Indumentum Regis Messiæ erit sericum ru- beum, ut sanguis, & erit acupictum aliis coloribus superius. Et ipse erit caput Israël. Et hoc est, quod scribitur Gen. XLIX. 11. Lavabit in vino vestimen- tum suum, sicut dictum est Es. LXIII. 2. Quare ru- beum est vestimentum tuum, & in sanguine uva- rum indumentum tuum, sicut dictum est (Esa. LXIII. 2.) Et indumenta tua sicut calcantis in tor- culari. Quæ quamvis fabellis à recentioribus Ju- dæis admistis scateant, pellucet tamen vera tra- ditio ac fides antiquiorum Rabbinorum, quod de nullo alio quam de Rege Messia, Capite Israel, hanc Prophetiam intellexerint. In quo Duodecimo consentientes habemus Christianos Interpretes facile omnes, nisi quod Calvinus pro supercilio suo à cæteris novaturiendi studio abeat, pro auto- ritate dictatoria decernens: Hoc Caput VIOLEN- TER TORSERUNT CHRISTIANI, quasi ad Christum hæc pertinerent (Cur non etiam TOR- SISSE Spiritum Sanctum ait, quem sequuntur Christiani Interpp.) cum Propheta simpliciter de IPSO DEO pronunciet, atque FINXERUNT hic rubicundum Christum, quòd sanguine proprio madidus esset, quem in cruce fuderit. Atqui NIHIL TALE voluit Propheta. Simplex sensus est, Dominum hic rubicundis vestibus prodire in po- puli conspectum, ut omnes intelligant ipsum ultorem suorum ac vindicem esse. Quem præceptorem sequutus est Musculus: ut & Abraham Scultetus in Idea Concion. super Esaiam. Sed Calvino os oppilavit B. Hunnius : quem etiam satis refellunt ἐξηγήσεις sociorum propriorum: Zuvinglii, Oe- colampadii, Pelicani, Gualtheri, Junii & Tre- mellii, Tossani, qui Christianis cæteris hic ὁμό- ψηφοι sunt. Vid. è Patribus Origenes in Matth. tr. 15. Cyprianus, vel Ruffinus potius in Symbol. Ambros. de Instit. Virgin. Athanasius q. LXXVIII. Hieronymus, & Cyrillus in h. l. &c. Agnovit tamen Calvinus, agnovit Musculus, agnovit Scultetus, non posse subjectum hic constitui nudum homi- nem, sed Deum, ejusque esse eminentiæ prædi- cata, ut non cadant in hominem. Et refutat Mu- sculus illam explicationem de victoria adversus E- domitas: Notum quidem est, Edom esse Idumæos, & Bosrah civitatem regionis Idumææ. Verum simul notum est Ebræa scientibus, Edom significare ru- beum, & Bosrah vindemiam. Quare meo judicio, non satis considerate scribunt, qui propter duas hasce voces vaticinium præsens de ultione sumpta ab Idu- mæis exponunt. De hac enim Propheta non loquitur, sed de futura Babyloniorum subversione, ac populi captivi Redemptione. Meminit autem Edom & Bosræ hoc sensu: Quis est iste, qui sic venit vestibus ru- bicundis indutus, ut dici possit venire de Edom: & cujus indumenta sic sunt sanguine uvarum ru- bricata, ac si veniat de Bosrah? Quoniam Edom rubeum & Bosrah vindemiam significat; Heroem in veste rubicunda & rubedine uvarum aspersa ve- nientem, per allusionem de Edom & Bosrah venire dicit. Et hunc sensum retinere malo, quam ab ejusdem Argumenti constantia præter necessitatem discedere.

Quanquam vero hæc facile sufficiant adversus Grotii commentum, quod ad personam, de qua hic agitur: de sensu tamen genuino eorum, quæ hic proponuntur, quia diversimode ab Interpp. ex- plicantur, nonnihil adhuc dispiciendum erit. Di- versas sententias quorumvis Interpp. ita comple- ctitur Musculus: Ebræi exposuerunt de oppressione gentium Romanorum, per Bosrah Romam intelligen- tes. Hier. refert ad triumphum Christi, ascendentis post passionem suam ad cælum cum admiratione angelo- rum, dicentium: Quis est iste &c. Post illum exponunt alii de ultione Dei contra Edomitas, quoniam mentio fit Edom & Bosrah: alii de triumpho Christi, quem tulit de Synagoga Judæorum, quam intelligunt per E- dom. Lyranus de Anti-Christi deletione, Hieron. citat quorumdam expositionem, qui referunt hæc ad finem mundi. Musculus vero ipse de liberatione è ca- ptivitate Babylonica interpretatur. B. Glassius sic recenset varias explicationes in Explanat. Colloq. Passion. quam subjunxit Onomatologiæ Messiæ Propheticæ p. 403. Missa jam quorumdam sen- tentia, qui de temporali solum populi Judaici ex ca- ptivitate Babylonica, Edomitarumque violentia, li- beratione, præclaram hanc Prophetiam exponunt (cum ex capp. præced. 60. 61. 62. & seqq. 65. 66. con- stet, de Ecclesia N. T. Prophetam loqui) aliorum, qui de Christo interpretantur, sententias audiemus. Qui- dam enim de Christo gloriose contra hostes Ecclesiæ triumphante (Tossanus, & alii) quidam de Christo in cælum ascendente (ut Hector Pintus in Comment. h. l. ex Dionysio, Hieronymo, Cyrillo, Haymone) qui- dam de Christo synagogam Judaicam funditus exscin- dente (ut Lutherus Tom. 3. Lat. Jen. in expl. h. l.) quidam de Christo finaliter Ecclesiam redimente (ut Piscator Herbornensis, qui tamen hic inconstans est. In scholiis enim Latinis ad redemptionem, quam di- ximus, finalem: in germanica vero versione ad ipsam passionem refert) quidam demum de Christo ad judi- cium gloriose veniente (ut Lyranus in h. l.) exponunt. Quas vero Interpretationes non oppositas, sed po- tius ἐπαλλήλως subordinatas esse, & amice con- cordare censet, ita συντόμως loci sententiam ex- hibens; Christus acerrime in passione sua luctans, & victoriose post passionem triumphans, omnemq; hostium potentiam frangens, oraculi nostri Prophetici sensus & intellectus, prora & puppis est, quod nempe con- tineatur in hoc capite luculenta passionis & mortis Je- su Christi ejusque cumprimis jucundæ Catastrophes σκιαγραφία, quod scilicet is victor evadens de hosti- bus suis, Diabolo, morte, inferno, qui plenariam ipsi moliebantur deletionem, triumphum egerit, resurgen- do à mortuis, ascendendo ad cælos, & sedendo ad dex- tram Patris, & adhuc de quibusvis adversariis ad fi- nem usq; seculi trophæum ferat, ab eisq; Ecclesiam suam asserat, totam hostilem catervam plenaria tan- dem excisione deleturus.

Proposita autem hæc visio nobilissima est in forma Dialogistica, quo magis afficiat, & fortius imprimat ea, quæ exhibentur. Quod primum ad interrogantem attinet, veteres nonnulli Angelos es- se, qui quærant: Quis est iste, qui venit de Edom, autumant, utpote, qui Christo ascendenti in cœlum gratulentur. Sic Justinus Dial. c. Tryph. Origenes Com. 15. in Matth. Ambrosius lib. de Institut. Vir- gin. 5. Hieronymus & Cyrillus in hoc loco, Augusti- nus Serm. 5. de Ascens. Dionysius de Cœlest. Hier. C. 7. Haymo &c. Alii vero Prophetam, utpote cui contigit hæc visio, quærere dicunt, alii Sionem, cu- jus antea facta mentio c. 62. v. 11. vel Sionidas: In re ipsa tamen conveniunt, quod admirentur hic Chri- sti herois habitum, speciem aut fortitudinem. Unde parum refert, num Propheta ipse per se, num vero alius quæstionem hanc institual? Quærit autem, quis ille Heros sit, quem partim ab habitu vestium, partim à specie & incessu heroico describit. Vestium habitum illa concernunt, qui venit de Edom, tinctis vestibus de Bosrah? Quæ de loco accepit Grotius q. ex terra Edom, & è metropoli ejus Bosrah venerit. Utpote, qui adversus Edomitas & metropolim illam pugnarit. Sed quum Judam Maccabæum falso per hunc Heroa intelligat, ut quomodocunque hæc ei applicaret, pugnam, quam Judas adversus Idumæos suscepit, huc trahit: de qua vero nihil aliud loco ci- tato 1. Macc. 5, 3. traditur juxta ipsius Grotii inter- pretationem, quam quod Judas bellum intulerit E- savi posteris in Idumæa Acrabatane (quæ pars Idu- mææ fuit) quia circumsedebant Israelitas, id est, in- cursabant, & percusserit eos plaga magna. At ex nu- dis istis nominibus Edom & Bosra id colligere, ni- mis infirmum est. Quum notum sit nomina ejus- modi specialia hostium populi Dei, non raro gene- ratim poni pro quibusvis hostibus. Unde Brentius hæc senikῶς intellexit: cujus sententiam verbis ipsius propriis explicare lubet. Duplex est ratio consolandi afflictos & oppressos ab hostibus. Una ducitur à libe- ratione ab hostibus: altera ab interitu hostium. Cum igitur Propheta consolatus sit in superioribus concio- nibus priori consolationis ratione auditores suos, terri- tos vaticinio Babylonicæ captivitatis & aliarum cala- mitatum, quæ populo Dei evenire solent: suscipit nunc hac concione consolandos eos posteriori ratione, & concionatur eis de interitu hostium populi seu Ec- clesiæ Dei, & de insigni victoria, quam Christus ab o- mnibus Ecclesiæ suæ hostibus reportat. Etsi enim vide- tur de Edomitis tantum loqui, tamen baud obscure significat, se Edomitarum nomine intelligere omnes hostes & adversarios Ecclesiæ suæ. Nam paulo post di- citur; Venit annus retributionis meæ. Quod ita le- gendum est: Venit annus, quo mei redimantur: si- gnificans videlicet, se Ecclesiam suam ab omnibus ho- stibus redimere. Et mox: conculcavi populos in fu- rore meo, Quod certe non ad unam tantum gentem, sed ad omnes adversarias gentes pertinet. Et extat su- pra cap. 34. concio ejusdem argumenti, in qua no- mine Edomitarum omnes Ecclesiæ hostes intelligun- tur, quemadmodum eo loco exposuimus. Quare sen- tiendum & hanc concionem institutam esse de interitu omnium hostium populi Dei, sive illi ante natum Chri- stum fuerint, sive post natum Christum venerint, ac sive sint Gentes incircumcisæ, sive carnales & impii Judæi. Hæc Brentius, quem sequuntur Osiander, Junius & Tremellius, Glassius, & alii. Cæterum non inconveniens, nostro judicio, videtur eorum expli- catio, qui Edom & Bozra referunt juxta vocum si- gnificationem, ad habitum, quo conspiciebatur hic Heros, quasi de Edom veniens, quod vox illa rube- dinem s. rubrum notet, & quasi de Bozra, quæ vox vindemiam significat: q. d. quis est iste, qui sic venit vestibus rubicundis indutus, ut dici possit venire de Edom, & cujus indumenta sic sunt Sanguine rubri- cata, ac si veniat de Bozra, seu vindemia. Quæ sen- tentia videtur ex eo confirmari, quod ista κατ' ἐπε- ξήγησιν conjuncta; Quis est iste, qui venit de Edom, tinctis vestibus de Bozrah, ut de Edom venire, sit ve- nire tinctis vestibus, de Bozra, venire rubicundis ve- stibus, sed rubricatis iisdem per vindemiam. Sic Cor- nelius à Lapide: venit de Bozra, id est, de vindemia & torculari, habet enim vestes rubro musto, id est, sanguine tinctas. Annuit Zvvinglius: Edom russum significat, & loci proprium nomen est. Vide igitur quam amœniter mirentur spectatores triumphi, cum Christum Sanguine suo rubricatum, de Edom venire murmurant, atque hoc propter purpuram, qua in- duebantur triumphantes. Bozra & vindemiam significat, & loci nomen est. Christum ergo uvidum, glutinosum & squalidum facit, quomodo hi sunt, qui vindemiam curando, curam corporis negligunt, pro- pterea quod male tractatus, flagris cæsus, spinis coro- natus, crucifixus, lancea penetratus, ac totus toto san- guine imbutus maduit. Neque insolentes sunt in Scriptura tales allusiones ad nomina: & subaudiri quoq; particulam similitudinis כ vel כמו haud in- frequens, quod hic fieri nonnulli dicunt, ut San- ctius, & alii. Quasi de Edom, quasi de Bozra veniat. Et usurpatur postea statim v. 2. verbum אדום de ru- bedine, è quo Edom nomen habet. Atque ea ratione occasio datur uberius deinde quærendi non tan- tum in genere de rubedine, sed speciatim de tali ru- bedine, quæ est calcantium in torculari versu 2, ut ita versu secundo habeamus explicationem præce- dentis, vel primi versus: Nam quod figuratis verbis quærebatur: Quis est iste, qui venit de Edom, id co- gnita persona hujus Herois, ut indagetur causa i- stius habitus, explicatius nunc exprimitur, quare ergo rubrum est indumentum tuum? Similiter, quod ibi quærebatur, quis ille tinctis vestibus de Bozra, explicatur hoc modo, & vestimenta tua sicut cal- cantium in torculari. Denique nondum hic com- memorari poterat sive pugna, sive victoria contra hostes, quia adhuc quærebatur de isto, quem vidit Propheta, quisnam sit, & quid illa rubedo sibi velit. E pugna & victoria adversus hostes ipsum redire non videbat statim Propheta, sed postmodum de- mum à responso Herois conspecti intelligebat. Ne- que solum de colore habitus, sed de forma etiam he- roica ejusdem & incessu tanto Heroe digno, qui co- ruscabat Heroica fortitudine, inquiritur. ISTE FORMOSUS IN STOLA SUA, GRADIENS IN MULTITUDINE FORTITUDINIS SUÆ. Quis est ille tam honorifice, tam splendi- de vestitus, incedens magna fortitudinis suæ ma- jestate! Quibus gemina sunt, quæ Ps. 45, 3. & seqq. habentur de hoc Heroe specioso forma præ filiis ho- minum, accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum po- tentissime, specie tua, & pulchritudine tua intende, prospere procede & regna: Myrrha, Gutta, & Casia à vestimentis tuis. Utriusque loci prophetici illustra- tio, quoad hunc habitum & conspectum Herois nostri habetur Apocalyps. 19, 11. Oculi ejus sicut flamma ignis, & in capite ejus diademata multa, & vestitus erat veste aspersa sanguine, & de ore ejus pro- cedit gladius ex utraq; parte acutus, ut in ipso percu- tiat gentes. Quæ omnia ad habitum, vestitum, for- mam & majestatem nostri Herois faciunt, ac se mutuo illustrant. Sic ergo Propheta & ruborem & decorem ejusdem tanto Heroe dignum expressit. Ruborem, dum eum de Edom, & de Bozra חמוץ בגדים conspersum vestibus dixit, ut Tremell. & Junius, rubras vestes habentem, ut Vatablus ex- ponunt. Verbum חמץ notat fermentatus est, consper- sus est fermento, cognationem habet cum צמת cru- entavit, infecit sanguine, qui acetosus est instar fer- menti, ideo etiam Ap. 19, 3. hæc vox de rubedine san- guinis vestibus aspersa explicatur. Decor exprimi- tur הדור בלבושו decorus in veste sua: quia הדר est decorare & ornare. Quanquam vero sanguis a- lias collutulet, & fœdos nos reddat Ez. 16, 6. He- roibus tamen bellatoribus gloriosum est habere vestem respersam sanguine, quia magnanimitas eo- rum inde conspicitur. Et erat vestis illa repræsen- tative) humana natura, quæ affuso sanguine rubuit, sed eo nihil decessit gloriæ ejusdem, imo uti gloria & honore magnifice decorata fuit humana natura Christi, teste Joh. c. 1, 14. Sic cruentatio illa ad gloriæ istius splendorem non parum fecit, quia cle- mentiam, amorem, & gratiam ejus inenarrabilem nobis conspicuam reddidit, imo Herois istius ma- gnanimitatem & fortitudinem Heroicam demon- stravit. Quamvis ergo pollutio videretur hæc san- guinis aspersio secundum externum aspectum, ut versu 3. dicitur omnia vestimenta mea inquinavi, ta- men revera hæc insignis fuit gloria nostri augustis- simi Herois, quod ad sanguinem usque pro nobis certavit & sanguine fuso hostes nostros superavit. Utrumque, de Christo in humana natura passo prædi- catur, inquit B. Glassius l. c. p. 440. & pollutio & decor sive gloria, prius κατ' δόξαν, posterius κατ' ἀλήθειαν: prius ratione ipsius passionis, posterius ra- tione victoriæ ab hostibus reportatæ & præstitæ in ipsa etiam sanguinis fusione satisfactionis pro peccatis no- stris, à quibus per sanguinem Christi mundamur. Non igitur opponenda, quæ tantum ratione diversorum objectorum diversa sunt. Christus seipsum contami- navit, peccatorum nostrorum sordes facta imputatio- ne suscipiendo, & in proprio corpore expiando 1. Pet. 2, 24. Patris iram, mortisq, & inferni stimulum susti- nendo, sanguinem demum miserabiliter effundendo. Idem vero hac sui sanguinis pretiosissimi effusione fe- cit NOBIS peccatorum purgationem per seipsum, Heb. 1, 3. & sanguis ejus MUNDAT NOS ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. 1, 7. Utrumque conjungitur 2. Cor. 5, ult. DEUS illum, qui non noverat peccatum, pro NOBIS PECCATUM fecit, ut nos fieremus ju- stitia DEI in ipso.

Incessum victoris ita describit Propheta צֹעֶה בְּרֹב כֹּחוֹ Nam vox צֹעֶה intransitive ac neutraliter accipienda est, neque aliter usurpatur, imo hunc sensum postulat Prophetæ ζήτημα: quia nondum de actionibus ipsius Heroicis intellexerat. Ideoq; ab externis istis, nempe a colore & decore vestimen- torum, nec non à modo incessus, quo conspiciebatur in hac visione describi adhuc tantum potuit, ut so- lemus aliquem ab ejusmodi externis describere, cum in ejus personam inquirimus. Alienum er- go non minus à vocis usu, quam à quæstionis hujus sensu est, quod verbum hoc transitive interpretatur Calvinus, de gentibus quas Dominus alio transfert, & Schindler. in Lex. p. 1558. MOVENS ET EX- PELLENS populos, nec non Vatablus & Marlora- tus, demigrare faciens Israelem ex omnibus locis ca- ptivitatis suæ, in quos dispersus est, quasi non inces- sus, sed actio Triumphatoris exprimeretur. Re- ctius itaque reddit Hieronymus gradiens, alii ince- dens, alii discurrens. Notat enim sese movere de loco ad alium migrando, unde Græcum σείω moveo, & La- tinum cieo, ac Germanicum ziehen/umziehen/einen Zug derivat Avenarius in Lex. Verba in multitudi- ne virtutis suæ, glossa interlinearis de militiaris co- piis explicat; Sic congruent illa Ap. 19, 11. Et exer- citus, qui sunt in cælo sequebantur eum in equis albis. Quibus stipatus apparere potuit, etsi interim ipse solus, non comites & ministri eum nunc stipantes, in passione torcular calcavit. Quod etiam illa Gro- tii explicatio inferre videtur: Agmen agens, magniq; ipse agminis instar.

Alii tamen malunt ad ipsum Heroicum venien- tis incessum hæc referre. Sic Glassius conferens locum Prov. 30, 29. 30. Sic etiam Cornelius à Lapi- de: Incedens gradu imperatorio, valido, potenti & magnifico, ipsoq; gressu, habitu, forma & gestu præ se ferens vires validas, spiritus ingentes, animosq; heroi- cos. Quomodo Agesilaus Rex Lacedæm. videns E- paminondam ducem Thebanorum cum sua acie gene- rose incedentem, exclamavit: O virum magnifi- cum! ait Plutarchus in Epaminonda.

Sequitur jam Responsio ad priorem interroga- tionem, qua explicatur, quænam illa Persona, quis- nam ille Heros sit, quem Propheta vidit: EGO

- QUI LOQUOR JUSTITIAM ET PROPU- GNATOR sum AD SALVANDUM. E qua certe responsione id intelligere non poterat Pro- pheta, Judam Maccabaeum esse, neq; id unquam ulli facile in mentem venit. At intelligere facile pote- rat Messiam esse, utpote quem describi hac & simi- li περιφράσει non ignotum erat: quem celebrat passim Spir. S. a Justitia & misericordia, cui vindi- catur, quod annunciet nobis veram justitiam a se partam Pf. 40, 11.
