Ef. 42, 1. c. 45, 27. c. 48, 17. 18. c. 50, 4. c. 53, 11. c. 60, 17. c. 61, 1. u. quodq; ipse sit Magister, vel multus, & copiosus ad salvandum: quia vox רב & multum & Magistrum significat, quod utrumque Christo convenit, penes quem est copiosa redemtio Pf. 130, 7. & infinita sapientia, qua novit generi hu- mano fuccurrere, & in ipsa voce לְהוֹשִׁיעַ Prophe- tae nomen suum aperuit Dominus, quod nempe JESUS sit, quodque hoc nomen suum futurum sit, quo nomine insinuatus ipsi jam fuit c. 49, 6. c. 44. & proxime c. 62, 11. Habemus ergo hic vere ῥητῆρα λό- γων πρηκτῆρά τε ἔργων, Heroem potentem & ver- bis & operibus δυνατὸν ἐν ἔργῳ & λόγῳ Luc. 24, 19. Quo facit, quod Ap. 19, 1. ita describitur: FIDELIS & VERAX, qui cum JUSTITIA judicat & pugnat. Recte Brentius: Hac periphrafi Christus se ipse de- scribit. Nec est alius, in quem haec descriptio com- petat, praeterquam Jesus Christus. Primum enim loquitur in justitia, hoc est, docet Evangelion suum, quo revelatur, quod ipse solus sit justitia nostra, quo etiam donat omnem suam justitiam his, qui credunt in ipsum. Quotquot enim credunt in eum, justitia ejus ita fruuntur, ut propter eam reputen- tur & ipsi coram Deo justi, & accipiant omnia prae- mia justorum. Deinde propugnator est ad salvan- dum, hoc est, magister salutis. Is enim est, qui po- test & novit & vult servare, qui multam & magnam habet potentiam, notitiam & voluntatem servandi. Non enim aliud nomen, ut Petrus ait, sub caelo da- tum inter homines, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri. Si- militer alii Interpretes; Corn. a Lapide e Pontificiis; Respondet Christus: Ego sum Messias, qui justitiam & salutem, quam promisi, propugnando & expu- gnando comparavi.

Altera Quaestio Prophetae ita habet: QUARE ERGO RUBRUM EST INDUMENTUM TUUM, ET VESTIMENTA TUA SICUT CALCANTIUM IN TORCULARI. Sufficienter instructus erat de Persona Herois, quam ex isto re- sponso ita intellexerat Propheta, ut opus non ha- beret amplius de eadem quaerere. Nam responsio data luculenta erat περίφρασις Messiae, e qua vero Judam Maccabaeum, de quo fando nullum adhuc verbum acceperat, intelligere minime poterat. Id- eoque nunc de habitu & incessu isto Messiae edoceri vult, quod factum, ut clarius fidelibus ob oculos passio & triumphus Messiae poneretur. Si es Magister salutis (ita παραφράζει Brentius) quid est, quod tam cru- entas habes vestes? Videris magis ex praelio, aut lanie- na, ubi multa caedes sit facta, & multus sanguis effusus, venire, quam ex eo loco, ubi magna sit falus parta. Nam quemadmodum hi, qui calcant uvas in torculari, solent vestimenta musto & fecibus aspersa reportare, ita tu incedis, vestes multo sanguine aspersus. Quid ergo sibi vult hic habitus? aut quomodo convenit cum Epitbeto tuo, quo te vocas Rabbi, aut Magistrum salutis? Hie- ronymi paraphrasis perjucunda ita habet: Unde carnem niveam & virgineam, o Christe, o Agne imma- culate, cruentasti? Unde sanguine rubricasii? Magis enim tibi clementia convenit quam crudelitas, magis candor quam cruor. Similis est Dialogismus Pf. 25, 9. cuj9 explicatio ab Augustino suavissime tradita no- stram hanc interrogationem eximie illustrat; Ascen- debat, inquit Hipponensis Episcopus serm. 178. de Tempore, qui est V. de Ascens. Domini, cruoris ru- bore perfusus, & trophæis victricibus laureatus. Vide- runt cælites cuncti speciosum vulneribus Christum, spo- lia castris tyrannicis reportata, & admirantes fulgen- tia divinæ virtutis vexilla, talibus concrepant hymnis, deducuntque lætantes: Quis est, inquiunt, iste Rex gloriæ? Et ajunt, Dominus virtutum, ipse est Rex gloriæ. Hic est ille candidus & roseus, compunctus a multitudine. Hic est ille, qui non habuit speciem neq; decorem. Infirmus in laqueo, fortis in spolio: vilis in corpusculo, armatus in prælio, fœdus in morte, pul- cher in resurrectione; candidus ex virgine, rubicundus in cruce, fuscus in opprobrios, clarus in cælo.

Responsio huic quæstioni reddita non exponit tantum causam rubedinis indumenti, & similitudi- nis cum iis, qui in torculari calcarunt, sed rationem uberiorém tradit incessus victoriosi, vel cur appareat gradiens in multitudine virtutis suæ; Torcular calcavi solus, & de gentibus non est vir mecum. Do- cet, se omnino torcular calcasse, & quidem solum, sine ullo parastata, aut auxiliatore, ita ut in hoc a- gone ne unum quidem adjutorem habuerit. Sed explicat simul, quale hoc torcular sit, sc. non uva- rum, sed hostium: Et quomodo calcarit eos. Cal- cavi eos in furore meo, & conculcavi eos in ira mea, & aspersus est sanguis eorum super vestimenta mea, & omnia indumenta mea inquinavi. Quanquam torcular proprie instrumentum sit expressionis, non calcationis uvarum, tamen, quia vas illud, in quo pedibus calcantur uvæ, priusquam subjiciantur torculari, ut exprimantur, non habet peculiare nomen in S. literis, communiter voce torcularis פּוּרָה exprimitur: per hunc autem lacum metony- mice uvæ sive racemi intelliguntur torculari injecti, quo hostes calcasse dicitur, & populos, ut v. 6. habe- tur: Conculcavi populos in furore meo: Conculcatio- nis autem voce utitur, tum quia victores solebant hostes pedibus conculcare, non secus ac racemi à vinitore in torculari calcantur, uti Ios. 10, 24. factum. Imo carpentis etiam, plaustrisque ferrantibus con- culcabantur inimici & triturabantur 2. Sam. 12, 31. 1. Par. 20, 2. Jud. 8, 16. Am. 1, 3. & de Deo occurrit idem loquendi modus Thr. 1, 16. Ap. 14, 19. quod in torculari conculcet, in quos vindictam exercet: tum quia respexit primam promissionem de cal- cando pedibus capite serpentino, in qua simul vulne- ratio calcanei pedis designatur, per quam sanguine rubrefieri proprio debuit ὁ Ὀφιόμαχος Gen. 3, 15. Quo pacto etiam conculcatio Dæmonis describi- tur Ps. 91. 13. super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis & conculcabis leonem & draconem, ac similis phra- sis adhibetur de Christo Ps. 110, 6. conquassabit ca- put terræ multæ. Ideo hostes Christi dicuntur pedi- bus ejus subjici ceu scabellum pedum ipsius Ps. 110, 1. 1. Cor. 15, 25. 26. imo sub pedibus etiam fidelium i- psius conteri Rom. 16, 20. Sensus ergo est: ut colle- ctam vindemiam vehementer & magno conatu vinde- miatores calcare solent, sic ego hostes meos prosterno, pedibus subjicio, conculco, & in ira mea deleo. Quod se solum, & ut Symmachus emphatice red- didit μονώτατον unice solum præstare testatur: ac ne quis socios ipsi ullos adjungat in hoc opere: non est, inquit, de gentibus vir, vel ullus mecum: imo ut efficiarius neget, ullum σύνεργον sibi adfuisse, ad- dit: Circumspexi & non erat auxiliator, quæsivi, & non fuit, qui adjuvaret. Inepte ergo Papistæ, & nuper Hector Pintus: Non est VIR mecum, ut non exclude- ret Mariam Virginem. Quam frivolam exceptio- nem refellit ipsa loquendi ratio. Ex dicendi genere, inquit Sanctius, satis significanter ostenditur, nul- lum omnino Christo auxiliarem operam præstitisse.

Loquitur vero humano more Deus, & dicit lustraf- se oculis se omnem locum, attenteque pervestigasse omnia, neque fuisse ullum, qui ad tantum opus satis haberet virium, ut exponit Adamus, vel cujus opera ad felicem ejus exitum indiguerit. Quæ explicatio in spirituali sensu, id est, procuranda animorum sa- lute, facilis est, & manifeste vera; cum ejus salutis procuratio & donum ad illum pertineat, qui vere & proprie salvator est. Denique se solum pro- pria virtute sua hoc effecisse, ac victoriam illam obtinuisse, sonora voce testatur, cum subjicit v. 5. Et salvavit mihi, non peregrinus, non socius ac parastates quicunque, non superior aliquis, sed BRACHIUM MEUM, mea virtus & potentia propria, & INDIGNATIO MEA IPSA auxi- liata est mihi. Ut fortitudo mea saluti mihi fuit: ita præter zelum meum heroicum nihil adjutorio mihi fuit ac auxilio, fortitudine mea & Zelo meo tota hæc victoria unice obtenta est.

Habemus Heroem bellatorem & victorem; Sed quinam illi hostes sunt, quos vicit & concul- cavit? Simpliciter ait vers. 3. Calcavi Eos in furore meo, & conculcavi Eos in ira mea, nulla mentione facta, quinam illi sint. Nimirum cum personam suam descripserit antea, adeoque; nunc iram & furo- rem suum in hoc calcandi & conculcandi opere te- stetur, seque solum id exequi doceat, colligi inde vult, quinam hostes sint, cum quibus ipsi res fuerit? Illi nempe quos Messias Magister ille ad salvandum debellare debebat, quorum conculcatio non nisi ab hoc solo Magistro fieri poterat, quos unus ille, ac solus superare valebat, & quorum caput tanto Zelo & furore calcaturus erat, in quorum denique conculcatione vestimentum suum sanguine pro- prio inquinaturus erat. Qui qualesnam sint, Pro- phetam è Prot-Evangelio Gen. 3, 15. & Jacobæo va- ticinio Gen. 49, 10. aliisque vaticiniis imprimis Davidicis, tum revelatione sibi c. 53. facta latere non poterat, etsi hic expressa eorum mentio non fieret. Quod nempe pugnandum ei fuerit cum serpente antiquo, & semine serpentino, cum tota col- luvie Diabolica, cum forti illo armato, uti à Chri- sto nuncupatur Luc. 11. cum robusto & gigante isto, de quo supra c. 49, 24. Cujus destruendi causa apparere debuit 1. Joh. 3, 8. Nam adversus nemi- nem alium Salvator isto furore & ira sua ita excan- duit, utpote qui non adversus ullum hominum, sed omnium hominum liberandorum causa venit. Quod vero de eodem Ap. 19, 13. dicitur : Et ipse cal- cat torcular vini furoris Dei omnipotentis, non re- pugnat huic nostro sensui, sed illustrat eundem, quia hostes illi spirituales sunt torcular vini furoris Dei, quos Deus in furore suo subjicit torculari, ut instar torcularis vel racemorum, & uvarum sint, torculari non vini, sed furoris Dei subjecti, quod à Christo in furore & ira conculcantur : quos con- culcavit quidem in passione sua, sed quia virtus e- jus perpetuo durat, adhuc conculcare dicitur. Neque vero alia est ira Dei, alia ira Christi: & i- dem reipsa est calcare hostes in ira sua tanquam in torculari seu lacu, & calcare lacum seu torcular vini iræ Dei omnipotentis. Hæc enim torcularis iræ divinæ calcatio non nisi respectu hostium, quos ira Dei premit, ita dicitur. Neque obstat quic- quam, quo minus de iisdem hostibus utrobique, hac quidem phrasi, sermo fit, quia cum introduci- tur Christus ceu victor hostium corporalium, ad fontem & originem hujus victoriæ ascenditur, & causa istius victoriæ exhibetur, quod ipse sit, qui percutit gentes: siquidem etiam torcular calcavit furoris iræ Dei omnipotentis, ac Satanam ipsum mundi Principem debellavit, quem in organis suis etiam debellare nunquam desinit, donec ponat o- mnes inimicos suos Scabellum pedum suorum. Pf. 110, 1. 1. Cor. 15, 25.

Sequitur apud Prophetam: Et aspersus est san- guis eorum super vestimenta mea, & omnia indu- menta mea inquinavi. Vocem נִצְחָם Robur (eorum) LXX. reddidêre τὸ αἷμα ἀυτῶν, ac similiter vulga- tus, sanguis eorum, sive quia sanguis est rubor & vi- ta corporis, ut nonnulli volunt, sive quia rubri co- loris mentio facta erat, sed cum nunquam vox illa Ebræa sanguinem notet, ut observavit Forster. in Lex. credendum est, sensum eos magis respexisse, quam vocem interpretatos esse. Vox ista signifi- cat robur & excellentiam, unde Abstractum pro Concreto poni volunt Junius & Tremellius, & elli- psin statuunt, hoc modo: ita inspersus est (sanguis) cujus & robustissimi illorum vestimentis meis. Quæ ta- men ellipsis & interpretatio nimis arbitraria vide- tur. Placet B. Lutheri explicatio ceu simplicissima: quam etiam Piscator & Batavi retinuêre, Daher ist ihr Vermögen auf meine Kleider gesprützt: Quo- modo autem virtute & potentia hostium consper- sus fuit, ut inquinata omnia ejus indumenta, & qui- dem rubefacta, vel rubeo colore tincta sint? Id in- telligendum ea ratione, quod nempe tam acris pugna fuerit, ut hostes omnem suam vim exercue- rint, quos ipse quidem conculcat, sed ita, ut po- tentia eorum sparsa super vestimentis sit, vel in ve- stimentis Christi appareat, quantam illi potentiam adhibuerint. Siquidem huic Heroi ad sanguinem usque pugnandum fuerit, & hostes ea virtute, ac vi pugnaverint, ut sanguinem ipse copiosissime ef- fundere, totumque suum vestimentum sanguine suo inquinare necessum habuerit, donec eos vin- ceret. Nam in vestimentis coinquinatis copia ef- fusi sanguinis notatur, uti Gen. 49, 11. Lavabit in vi- no stolam suam & in sanguine uvæ vestimentum suum. Et recte observat B. Glassius, congruere vocem נִצְחָם pulcre cum re ipsa: Potentia enim hostium, quibuscum Christo colluctandum erat, tanta fuit, ut victoriæ, superioritatis & prædominationis quandam speciem ad tempus habere videretur, cum Christus iræ Dei & infernalium pœnarum sensu pressus sanguineos θρόμβους per sudorem e- mitteret, & in crucem adactus de divina derelictio- ne gravissime conquereretur, & postea morte ipsi corporali traderetur. Hic fuit ille נִצְחָם, illa po- tentia & amarulentia hostium, quæ vestibus Chri- stir inspersa est, ut totus ipse effuso maderet san- guine. Hunc sensum subesse verbis Prophetæ alii Interpp. intellexêre, etsi eundem aliter è ver- bis colligere conati sunt: ubi videre est in Glossa interlin. Et aspersus est sanguis (mens) eorum (ab eis fusus) super vestimenta (membra) mea. In Gloss. Ord. Sanguis Christi Judæorum dicitur, quia fude- runt, & inde vindictam sustinuerunt. Burgensis: A- sperfus dicitur sanguis eorum, non quia est sanguis eo- rum proprie, sed quia per procurationem eorum fuit effusus, vel etiam quia ipsi fecerunt se obnoxios hujus sanguinis, dicentes, sanguis ejus super nos &c.

Subjungitur autem porro ratio, cur tanto cum zelo pugnarit adversus hostes, donec eos poten- ter expugnaret: Et cur solus hoc peregerit. Prio- ris ratio hæc est; dies enim ultionis in corde meo, annus redemtionis meæ venit. Gemina hic contine- tur ratio: altera divina adversus hostes vindicta, quæ illo die passionis magno Christi exercenda e- rat. Tum enim erat judicium mundi, quo princeps hu- jus mundi foras ejiciendus erat Joh. 11. Hac fini ad- versus Diabolicam catervam vindictam exercere debebat, quod abstraxerit à Deo genus humanum. Altera divina erga homines gratia, cui exercendæ non diem tantum, sed annum tribuit. Quo non modo ad annum Jubilæum respicitur Lev. 25, 9. sed etiam duratio perennis istius Jubilæi designatur: Quia annus ille perpetuo durat, si ef- fectum ejus respicias, inde à Prot-Evangelio us- que ad consummationem seculi, annunciatio nem- pe gratiæ & beneplaciti, quæ tamen præcipue in N. T. facta est; ideo hoc tempus κυρίως dicitur tempus beneplaciti 2. Cor. 2, 2. Nam quamvis eo- dem die & vindicta adversus Satanam & redemtio humani generis peracta sit, quia tamen redemtio illa applicanda nobis est, & id fit per mysticum il- lum Jubilæum annum, quo gratia nobis annuncia- tur & dispensatur, ideo tempus istud venisse qui- dem Christo dicitur, quo Christus morte sua gra- tiam eam acquirere debuit, sed nobis durat ille an- nus quandiu regnum gratiæ durat. Conferantur quæ de tempore beneplaciti ad Es. 61, 2. c. 49, 8. Posterioris ratio hisce exponitur, cur nempe solus hoc opus præstiterit? Et aspexi vel potius cir- cumspexi, oculos undiquaque circumtuli, uti solent homines, hostes suos aggressuri, conquirere undi- que copias, sed non erat auxiliator, qui vel in ultio- ne adversus hostes, vel in redemtione humani ge- neris mihi assistere posset. Quæsivi in Ebr. ואשתומם obstupui, demiratus sum, vel etiam devastatus sui, in anxietate fui, ut B. Lutherus, Ich war in Schre cken/ quod impletum est cum cœpit λυπεῖσθαι, ἀδη- μονεῖν, ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι, & cum anima ejus περίλυπος undique tristis erat usq́; ad mortem Matth. 26; 37. 38. & non erat fulciens, qui inter homines fulciret aut sustentaret. ET SALVAVIT MIHI BRA- CHIUM MEUM, uti salus pro re strenue & feli- citer gesta quandoque sumitur, & facere salutem est obtinere victoriam, sic etiam salvare est vincere, seu prospere contra hostes agere 1. Sam. 14, 6. Ps. 97, 2. Ps. 112, 25. Sensus est, ob maximam hostium vim suc- cumbendum mihi patienti & agonizanti fuisset, nisi divina mea omnipotentia me sustinuisset & hostilem catervam evertisset. ET IRA MEA FULCIVIT ME. Divina virtus & zelus pro redimendo ge- nere humano sustentarunt humanam Christi natu- ram, ne sub immenso onere succumberet. Additur deniq; συμπέρασμα v. 6. ET CON- CULCAVI POPULOS IN IRA MEA, ET INEBRIAVI EOS IN FURORE MEO, ET DESCENDERE FECI IN TERRAM FOR- TITUDINEM EORUM. Explicat uberius simi- litudinem à torculari desumtam, quod populos ho- stiles conculcarit, sicut calcantur uvæ, quod vir- tutem eorum in terram detraxerit & pedibus sub- jecerit, uti uvæ pedibus subjiciuntur: quod vino fu- roris Dei inebriarit, uti ex uvis calcatis vinum ex- primitur, quo homines inebriantur. Conf. Ps. 75, 9. Es. 29, 9. c. 51, 17. 21. Jer. 25, 15. Thr. 3, 18. Hebr. 3, 16. Inebriavi Junius & Tremellius exponunt, magna pocula atq́; insolita afflictionum & iræ meæ epotanda præbui. Vox עמים populos notat sed עם populus di- citur non de hominibus solum, sed etiam de aliis rebus collectivis metaphorice, utpote de formicis Prov. 30, 25. de Locustis Joel. 2, 2. 25. Ideoque hic ad totam catervam hostium, cum quibus colluctari Christus necessum habuit, tum corporalium, tum im- primis spiritualium referri potest. Ita Ps. 110, 6. גוים gentes dici ait Glassius, qui v. 1. inimici dicti, qui non terreni solum, sed & spirituales sunt. 1. Cor. 15, 25. 26. Luc. 1, 71. conferens etiam Matth. 13, 28. ubi Diabo- lus dicitur ἐχθρὸς ἄνθρωπος inimicus homo. Agnovit id etiam Zwinglius, beluam peccatum fretus brachio & fortitudine mea adortus sum. Cædes populorum, quæ hic habetur, periphrasis est superati peccati & mortis.

## 63:8
Ver. 8. NEVERTHELESS MY PEOPLE IS] In the Hebrew: Truly. CHILDREN NOT DENYING] In the Hebrew: Children not lying: That is, children not false, such as are those who insert themselves into foreign families by a lie. Brentius explains this correctly, that here the benefit of the adoption of the Israelites is celebrated, as if to say: GOD chose the Israelites as His own peculiar people, above all other nations, and adopted them as His children, not spurious, not adulterine, but true, legitimate, and genuine. For as to what the Vulgate reading has: Children not denying, or not lying: the constant piety of the Israelites is not commended: for as far as they themselves are concerned, they were always a stiff-necked people, and as Isaiah said above, a people provoking to anger, and lying children, children unwilling to hear the law of God: but the immense clemency of God is commended, that although the Israelites never kept a true and constant faith to God, yet He Himself acknowledged them as His own peculiar people, and not as false, spurious, and adulterine, but as true and legitimate children. For thus Moses says in Deut. 7: The Lord thy God hath chosen thee: to be a peculiar people unto himself above all people that are upon the face of the earth: and Exod. 4: Israel is my son, even my firstborn. AND HE BECAME A SAVIOUR] At length He brought salvation to them.

Latin:

Verf. 8. VERUNTAMEN POPULUS MEUS EST] In Hebræo: Vere. FILII NON NEGANTES] In Hebræo: Filii non mentientes: Id est, filii non falsi, quales sunt illi, qui se in familias alienas mendacio inferunt. Explicat id Brentius recte, quod hic cele- bretur beneficium adoptionis Israëlitarum, q. d. DEUS elegit Israëlitas in peculiarem suum popu- lum, præ omnibus aliis gentibus, & adoptavit eos in filios suos, non spurios, non adulterinos, sed veros, legitimos & genuinos. Nam quod vulgata lectio habet: Filii non negantes, seu non mendaces: non commendatur constans pietas Israëlitarum: quippe quod quantum ad ipsos attinet, semper fue- rint populus duræ cervicis, & ut supra dixit Esaias, populus ad iracundiam provocans, & filii menda- ces, filii nolentes audire legem Dei: sed commen- datur immensa Dei clementia, quod etsi Israëlitæ nullam unquam servaverunt veram & constantem fidem Deo, tamen ipse agnovit eos pro peculiari suo populo, & non pro falsis, spuriis & adulteri- nis, sed pro veris & legitimis filiis. Sic enim dicit Moses Deut. 7. Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus: ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram: & Exod. 4. Filius meus primogenitus Israël. ET FACTUS EST SALVATOR] Tandem illis salutem attulit.

## 63:9
Ver. 9. IN ALL THEIR AFFLICTION HE WAS NOT AFFLICTED] That is, He was not wearied in helping them. Thus Jerome notes that לו is read for לא, so that the sense may be: in all their distress, there was distress to Him: that is, He Himself grieved for their evils. A statement made κατ’ ἀνθρωποπάθειαν (after the manner of men), as are many.

A second benefit is now celebrated. He not only adopted them as His people and children, but also saved and preserved them. According to the כתיב (the reason for which the Vulgate, Vatablus, and Arias Montanus took into account in their translation), according to Brentius, it is implied: that God defended the people with such care that their affliction was not an affliction or destruction, because it was only an aid toward good. Grotius prefers to refer it to God, that He was not afflicted or fatigued. But the former sense seems simpler. According to the קרי, the meaning is clear. In all their affliction there was affliction to Him, that is, He considered Himself to be afflicted rather than them: inasmuch as He transfers the calamities of His own people onto Himself, Jud. 10:16, Zach. 2:8. Acts 9:4, and therefore Luther, Osiander, Münster, Pagninus, and the Belgic translation observed the קרי לו: as if GOD Himself were afflicted in the affliction of the Israelites: which, however, to Him (as the כתיב indicates) ὄντως, and in reality, was not an affliction, but is only attributed to Him ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (after the manner of men). Thus this sense is subordinated to the sense of the Keri, or explains it. For the notes of the Masoretes of this kind, when they add a Keri לו, do not so much explain a different sense of the author, the Holy Spirit Himself (who must everywhere be the same and consistent with Himself), as they resolve difficulties that have arisen in the reading, or teach a subordination of sense which an unusual writing seemed to imply, or which a comparison of a different reading indicated. Jerome refers this to the Son of God: In all their affliction He is afflicted, that is, God, so that He might bear not only our sins, but also our afflictions. For He Himself bears our infirmities, He grieves for us.

AND THE ANGEL OF HIS FACE SAVED THEM] The LXX here tacitly take the negation as repeated: as if He were saying, not through an Angel, but He Himself made them safe. But the Chaldean is otherwise: and the Hebrews say that not just any Angel is called the Angel of the face of God, but him whom they call מטטרון, a word taken from the Latin, that is, metator (a measurer): concerning which see what we have said in the fourth book for the truth of the Christian Religion. They call the same one סערא רבא, a great preceptor: likewise שדי, the powerful one, because of the power communicated to him by God. Thus Solomon Jarchi. This Angel seems to be he whom Daniel names Michael, whom God had given as a protector to the Israelite people, who is one of the seven great Angels, or of the face, that is, the highest Satraps of the heavenly kingdom. See what we have said on Matt. 18:10.

IN HIS LOVE, AND IN HIS INDULGENCE HE HIMSELF REDEEMED THEM] He did not only commit them to the protection of that great Angel, but He Himself also did what the Angel could not; He moved the heart of Cyrus to liberate them.

AND HE BORE THEM AND CARRIED THEM ALL THE DAYS OF OLD] For a long time He kept them safe and illustrious, namely from the time of Zerubbabel.

Grotius understands it of a created Angel, following the Papists, Photinians, and especially the Jews, with whom also Calixtus, whom we have corrected, agrees. Harnon. Calixt. Hæret. p. 909. Hackspan, a disciple of Calixtus, fluctuates, and argues almost on both sides, whether a created or uncreated angel is to be understood, providing excuses for the Socinians and Jews, by which they render the illustrious testimony of the Holy Trinity ambiguous. For he thinks, with Calixtus leading, that the Spirit of God and the face of God can be held to be the same, and that it is not necessary that the Spirit of Holiness be a person distinct from the Father, and that he is called the angel of the face just as the bread of the faces, which is in the sight of God, because it does not apply to Christ, as He is God. In which, however, he is not sufficiently consistent with himself. For elsewhere, namely on Ps. 11:7, Notar. Philolog. Theol. part 2, p. 54, he interprets this angel of the faces not of any created angel, but of Christ, as He is God, and that by the same phrase compared with the bread of the faces: because just as that was placed in the sight of the ark of the covenant, so Christ is that angel, who is placed in the sight, that is, the bosom of the Father. He also rashly understands Moses as the spirit of holiness; which gloss does not easily come to the mind even of the Anti-Trinitarians themselves. But leaving these aside, let us proceed here primarily against Grotius: for we have already satisfied the Socinians, Calixtines, and others elsewhere. Many things teach that the Son of God is to be understood here: First, that peculiar name of the Angel of the face of the Lord, which belongs to no created Angel: For it is one thing when Angels are said to see the face of God in heaven, Matt. 18, which befits all Angels and is common to the elect with them; (Nor does the difference, which the Jews handed down between the Angels of the face, the great and highest Satraps, have any foundation anywhere, but is to be reckoned among their inventions.) It is another thing when he is called here the Angel of the face of the Lord; for that is proper to this one alone, namely, to him who is the ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης & χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ πατρὸς, Heb. 1. v. 3, whom he who sees, sees the Father, John 14, 9, as one who rendered the face of God as it were visible, when he led the Israelites with a visible appearance, Exod. 23, 10, ch. 33, 14, and exhibits the grace of God, which is accustomed to be designated by the face of God, (see Num. 6, 29, Ps. 67, 2). Next, there is attributed to this Angel a work proper to Christ, from whom he himself has his proper name, ישוע, because he saved the Israelites. Which is nowhere attributed to any created Angel. Thirdly, the same one who saved them is said to have redeemed the same. For the discourse is continued concerning the same Subject. And therefore it is not necessary that the pronoun הוּא be referred to God, since it can be understood of the Angel himself, whose mention was made immediately before. Add that the work of redemption is attributed to the Angel by this same verb, Gen. 48, 16, The Angel who REDEEMED ME from all evil, for the verb גאל is used there also; indeed, this verb is proper to the Son of God, because it signifies such a Redeemer who delivers by right of kinship, which Grotius himself confessed above, ch. 59, 20. גואל, he says, properly is to redeem by right of kinship. Fourthly, he who in his love and in his indulgence redeemed the Israelites is without doubt true GOD. But the Angel of the face in the love and indulgence he redeemed them: E. The Angel of the face is the true GOD, and thus is understood not as a created Angel, but as the uncreated Son of GOD. Fifth, he who carried them and lifted them up all the days of old cannot be a created Angel, because this work is proper to GOD alone. Since, therefore, this is attributed to the Angel of the face, because all the aforementioned things cohere and pertain to one subject, the Angel of the face, it is manifest that the Angel of the face is not some created being, but the uncreated Son of God himself. Sixth, that Angel is indicated here, whose Spirit the Israelites tempted. But this is none other than the Son of God, as whose Spirit is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him and is sent. Seventh, from the history of the leading out, if we compare it, it is not obscure that no other Doctor of the people, who saved him from Egypt, and redeemed him and carried him, was any other than the Son of God, that Angel who appeared to Moses in the burning bush, Ez. 3, who led the people in the pillar of cloud and fire, Exod. 14, whom they were commanded to revere lest he be provoked, from whom they obtained indulgence and remission of sins, Ex. 23, 20, from whom JACOB prayed for a blessing for his grandsons, and Moses for the Israelites, Gen. 48, 16, Deut. 33, 16. Therefore the Apostle teaches 1 Cor. 10, 4, 9 that Christ led the Israelites, and was tempted by them: and St. Jude v. 4 that he saved his people from Egypt. Which, finally, the Jews also acknowledged, the older ones indeed, at Exod. 14, ch. & we have observed elsewhere: indeed, when the Jews called that Angel of the face Metatron, the great teacher, likewise שדי the Almighty (which is a name proper to the one God), they do not obscurely confess that that Angel is the Messiah, the Angel of the covenant. The older ones certainly, from whom they received those ἐξαγγέλω names, there is no doubt that they thought this. To this Angel Metatron they also attribute the work of mediation and intercession before GOD, whom they make the supreme intercessor, whom Moses used, in Midrash Elle Haddebarim c. 3, 26.

These things concerning the Subject. The predicates, which pertain to the same history of the leading of the Israelites according to the tenor of the words and parallel passages, on which all Interpreters have hitherto agreed, Grotius alone has torn apart, referring part of them to the time of the leading out of the Israelites (if I am not mistaken), part to the liberation made through Cyrus, part to subsequent times from Zerubbabel onwards, and part specifically to the times of Antiochus. All of which it is manifest proceed from his own private interpretation. For no reason is given for any of them. But that the Israelites are said to be saved here is explained when the Prophet adds, in his love and in his indulgence he redeemed them, which pertain to the impulsive cause of salvation, namely the grace and love of the Lord; and when he subjoins: he carried them and lifted them up all the days of old, which look to the manner of salvation and concern their leading, as is evident from a similar canticle, namely that of Moses, Deut. 32, 11, 12. As an eagle stirring up its young to fly, and fluttering over them, spread its wings, and took him and carried him on its shoulders, the Lord alone was his Guide, and there was no strange god with him. Nor is it to be understood of any other time than that time of the leading, because the Israelites are said to have provoked the Lord to anger; which we know happened often in the desert, and therefore it is wrongly snatched away to the times of Antiochus. For this is not a prophecy about future things, but the mercies of the Lord are sung because of past benefits. Whence those Grotian Glosses vanish into smoke, the new inventions of his wit, born to devise anything, concerning v. 10, which now follow.

Latin:

Verf. 9. IN OMNI TRIBULATIONE EORUM NON EST TRIBULATUS] Id est, non est defatigatus, eos adjuvando. Sic Hieronymus notat legi pro לא pof- se לו ut sensus sit: in omni eorum angustia, ipsi angustia fuit: id est, ipse indoluit illorum malis. Dictum κατ’ ἀνθρωπο- πάθειαν, ut multa.

Alterum beneficium jam celebratur. Non solum adoptavit eos in populum & filios suos, ve- rum etiam salvavit & servavit eos. Juxta τὸ כתיב (cujus rationem in translatione habuit vulgatus, Vatablus, Arias Montanus,) secundum Brentium innuitur: Deum tanta cura populum defendisse, ut afflictio ejus non esset afflictio vel pernicies, quia erat tantum adjumentum in bonum. Grotius mavult ad Deum referre, quod non tribulatus vel fatigatus fuerit. Prior autem sensus simplicior videtur. Jux- ta קרי in aprico est sententia. In omni tribulatione eorum ipsi erat tribulatio, id est, reputabat se potius quam ipsos affligi: siquidem calamitates suorum in se transferat Jud. 10, 16. Zach. 2, 8. Act. 9, 4. atque ideo קרי לו observarunt Lutherus, Osiander, Mün- sterus, Pagninus, Belgica translatio: ac si DEUS ipse tribulatus esset in tribulatione Israëlitarum: quæ tamen ipsi (quod τὸ כתיב indicat) ὄντως, & re- vera non fuit tribulatio, sed tantum ἀνθρωποπαθῶς eidem tribuitur. Subordinatur ita hic sensus τῷ Ke- uibh sensui ί Keri, aut eundem explicat. Masori- tarum enim notæ ejusmodi cum לו Keri adjiciunt, non tam sensum diversum autoris, ipsius Spiritus S. explicant (quem oportet ubivis eundem esse, ac sibi constare) quam difficultates in lectione ortas expediunt, sensumve subordinationem docent, quam inusitata scriptio innuere visa, aut collatio di- versæ lectionis indicavit. Hieronymus id ad Fi- lium Dei refert: In omni tribulatione eorum ipse est tribulatus, id est, Deus, ut non solum peccata, sed & tribulationes nostras ipse portaret. Ipse enim infir- mitates nostras portat, pro nobis dolet.

ET ANGELUS FACIEI EJUS SALVAVIT EOS] LXX. hic negationem tacite pro repetita habent: quasi dicat, non per Angelum, sed ipse eos salvos fecit. Verum aliter Chal- dæus: & dicunt Hebræi non quemvis Angelum dici An- gelum à facie Dei, sed eum quem ipsi vocant מטטרון, vo- ce ex Latina desumta, id est metatorem: de qua vide quæ diximus ad librum quartum pro veritate Religionis Chri- stianæ. Vocant eundem סערא רבא magnum præcepto- rem: item שדי potentem, propter potentiam ei à Deo communicatam. Ita Salomon Jarchi. Videtur hic An- gelus esse is quem Michaelem nominat Daniel, quem Deus populo Israelitico dederat protectorem, qui unus est se- ptem Angelis magnis, sive faciei, id est, summis Satrapis re- gni cœlestis. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. 18, 10.

IN DILECTIONE SUA, ET IN INDULGEN- TIA SUA IPSE REDEMIT EOS] Non tantum Ange- li illius magni tutelæ ipsos commisit, sed ipse etiam fecit quod Angelus non poterat, movit cor Cyri ad illos libe- randos.

ET PORTAVIT EOS ET ELEVAVIT EOS CUNCTIS DIEBUS SÆCULI] Longo tempore eos tu- tos clarosque præstitit, à tempore nempe Zorobabelis.

De Angelo creato intelligit Grotius, Papistas, Photinianos & cumprimis Judæos sequutus, cum quibus etiam facit Calixtus à nobis castigatus Har- non. Calixt. Hæret. p. 909. Hackspan. Calixti discipulus fluctuat, & fere in utramque partem disputat, creatusne angelus an increatus intelli- gatur, Socinianis & Judæis exceptiones sufficiens, quibus illustre testimonium SS. Trinitatis ambi- guum reddant. Nam & Spiritum Dei ac faciem Dei pro eodem haberi posse, nec necesse esse, ut distincta sit persona à Patre Spiritus Sanctitatis e- jus, & angelum faciei dici ita sicut panis facierum, qui est in conspectu Dei, præeunte Calixto cen- set, quod in Christum, qua Deus est, non cadat. In quo tamen sibi ipsi non satis constat. Nam alibi, nimirum ad Ps. 11, 7. Notar. Philolog. Theol. part, 2. p. 54. non de angelo aliquo creato, sed de Chri- sto hunc angelum facierum interpretatur, qua Deus est, idq; eadem phrasi de pane facierum col- lata: quia sicut ille positus fuit in conspectu arcæ fœderis, ita Christus est angelus iste, qui positus est in conspectu, id est, sinu Patris. Temere etiam Spi- ritum sanctitatis Mosen intelligit; Quæ glossa ne ipsis quidem Anti-Trinitariis facile in mentem ve- nit. Sed istis missis, imprimis adversus Grotium hic pergamus: Socinianis enim, Calixtinis & aliis alias satisfecimus. Intelligendum hic esse Filium Dei multa docent: Primum nomen illud peculiare An- geli faciei Domini, quod nullius Angeli creati est: Nam aliud est, cum Angeli dicuntur faciem Dei videre in cælis, Matth. 18. quod Angelis omnibus convenit, & electis cum ipsis commune est; (Ne- que enim differentia, quam Judæi tradiderunt in- ter Angelos faciei, Satrapas magnos & summos, ali- cubi fundamentum habet, sed inter commenta eo- rum reputanda est.) Aliud cum hic vocatur Ange- lus faciei Domini; id enim huic uni proprium est, illi nempe, qui est ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης & χαρακ- κτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ πατρὸς Ebr. 1. v. 3. quem qui videt, patrem videt Joh. 14, 9. ut qui faciem Dei quasi conspicuam reddidit, cum visibili specie Israelitas deduxit Exod. 23, 10. c. 33, 14. & gratiam Dei, quæ per faciem Dei designari solet, (vid. Num. 6, 29. Ps. 67, 2.) exhibet. Deinde tribuitur huic Angelo opus Christo proprium, à quo ipse nomen pro- prium habet, ישוע, quod salvos fecerit Israelitas. Quod nulli Angelo creato uspiam tribuitur. Ter- tio idem, qui salvavit eos, redemisse eosdem dici- tur. Nam de eodem Subjecto continuatur ora- tio. Ideoque non necessum est, ut pronomen הוּא ad Deum referatur, quum de ipso Angelo, cujus proxime mentio facta, intelligi possit. Adde, quod Angelo redemtionis opus eodem hoc verbo tri- buatur Gen. 48, 16. Angelus qui REDEMIT ME ab omni malo, nam & ibi verbum גאל adhibetur, imo hoc verbum proprium est filio Dei, quia si- gnificat talem Redemtorem, qui jure propinqui- tatis liberat, quod supra c. 59, 20. Grotius ipse professus est. גואל, inquiens, proprie est redimere jure propinquitatis. Quarto qui in dilectione sua, & in indulgentia sua redemit Israelitas, sine du- bio est verus DEUS. At Angelus faciei in Di- lectione & indulgentia sua redemit eos: E. An- gelus faciei est verus DEUS, adeoque non An- gelus creatus, sed increatus Filius DEI intelligi- tur. Quinto qui portavit eos & elevavit eos cunctis diebus seculi, non potest esse Angelus creatus, quia hoc opus Solius DEI proprium est. Quum ergo id Angelo faciei tribuatur, quia cohærent prædicta omnia & ad unum pertinent subjectum, Angelum faciei, manifestum est Angelum faciei esse non creatum quendam, sed ipsummet increatum Dei Filium. Sexto is Angelus indigitatur hic, cujus Spiritum tentarunt Israëlitæ. At hic alius nullus est, quam Filius Dei, utpote cujus Spiritus est Spi- ritus Sanctus, qui ab eo procedit & mittitur. Se- ptimo ex historia eductionis, si eam conferamus, haud obscurum est, quod nullus alius Doctor po- puli, qui salvavit eum ex Ægypto, & redemit eum & portavit eum, fuerit, quam Filius Dei, Angelus ille qui in rubo ardente Mosi apparuit, Ez. 3. qui in columna nubis & ignis populum deduxit, Exod. 14. quem revereri jubebantur ne irritaretur, à quo in- dulgentiam & remissionem peccatorum conse- quebantur, Ex. 23, 20. à quo benedictionem pre- catus est nepotibus suis JACOB, & Israëlitis Moses Gen. 48,16. Deut. 33, 16. Ideo docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 10, 4. 9. quod Christus duxerit Israëlitas, & ab iis tentatus sit: & S. Judas v. 4. quod populum suum salvarit ex Ægypto. Quod denique Judæos etiam agnovisse, antiquiores nempe, ad Exod. 14. cap. & alias observavimus: imo quum Judæi An- gelum illum faciei dixêre Metatorem, præceptorem magnum, item שדי omnipotentem (quod est no- men uni Deo proprium) Angelum illum Messiam esse, Angelum fœderis, haud obscure fatentur. Antiquiores certe, à quibus illa ἐξαγγέλω nomina accepêre, id sensisse minime dubium est. Huic etiam Angelo Metatori tribuunt opus mediatio- nis ac intercessionis apud DEUM, quem interces- sorem supremum, quo Moses usus sit, faciunt in Midrasch Elle Haddebarim c. 3, 26.

Hæc de Subjecto. Prædicata, quæ ad eandem historiam deductionis Israëlitarum juxta tenorem verborum & loca parallela pertinent, de quo o- mnes Interpp. hactenus consensêre, unus Grotius discerpsit, partem eorum referens ad tempus edu- ctionis Israëlitarum (nisi fallor) partem ad libera- tionem per Cyrum factam, partem ad tempora sub- sequentia inde à Zorobabele, partem in specie ad tempora Antiochi. Quæ omnia ex idiᾳ ἐπιλύσει proficisci manifestum est. Nulla enim eorum red- ditur ratio. At quod salvati hic dicuntur Israë- litæ, explicatur, cum addit Propheta, in dilectione sua & in indulgentia sua redemit eos, quæ pertinent ad causam impulsivam κεχαριτωμένην salvationis, gratiam nempe, & amorem Domini; & cum sub- jungit: portavit eos & elevavit eos cunctis diebus se- culi, quæ spectant ad modum salvationis, & de- ductionem eorum concernunt, ut è simili canti- co, Mosis nempe, constat, Deut. 32,11.12. Sicut A- quila provocans ad volandum pullos suos, & super eos volitans, expandit alas suas, & assumsit eum atq; por- tavit eum in humeris suis, Dominus solus Dux ejus fuit, & non erat cum eo Deus alienus. Nec de alio tem- pore intelligendum, quam de illo deductionis tempore, quia dicuntur Israëlitæ Dominum ad iracundiam provocasse; quod in deserto sæpius fa- ctum esse novimus, ideoque perperam id abripi- tur ad tempora Antiochi. Non enim hic Prophe- tia habetur de rebus futuris, sed misericordiæ Do- mini cantantur ob beneficia præterita. Unde in fumum abeunt Glossæ illæ Grotianæ, nova εὑ- ρήματα ingenii ejus ad quævis excogitanda nati, circa v. 10. quæ jam sequuntur.

## 63:10
Vers. 10.

BUT THEY PROVOKED TO ANGER] Namely around the times of Antiochus, see what we shall say concerning Daniel.

AND THEY AFFLICTED HIS HOLY SPIRIT] In the Hebrew: The Spirit of his Holiness. LXX. παρώξυναν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀυτῶ. Naturally God, because he is holy, cannot bear impiety. Cf. Eph. 4, 30, where, however, in a slightly different sense, the Holy Spirit is taken for gifts.

AND HE TURNED AGAINST THEM AS AN ENEMY, AND HE HIMSELF FOUGHT AGAINST THEM] By handing them over into the hand of Antiochus, and his leaders.

For how they afflicted the Holy Spirit, who was placed in their midst in the desert, is most well-known from history, concerning which also Nehemiah in his prayer c. 9, 16, 17, 20, as well as David Ps. 95, 8, as also the Apostle Heb. 3, 7 seqq. and 1 Cor. 10, 6 seqq. Nor do the things which Isaiah subjoins concerning divine indignation and punishment look to other times: AND HE TURNED AGAINST THEM AS AN ENEMY, AND HE HIMSELF FOUGHT AGAINST THEM. Concerning which there is a great consensus of Interpreters. Certainly no one has been found hitherto who has referred these to the times of Antiochus. This is Grotius's own invention.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

IPSI AUTEM AD IRACUNDIAM PROVOCA- VERUNT] Nempe circa tempora Antiochi, Vide quæ ad Danielem dicemus.

ET AFFLIXERUNT SPIRITUM SANCTI E- JUS] In Hebræo: Spiritum Sanctitatis ejus. LXX. παρώξυ- ναν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀυτῶ. Nimirum Deus, quia san- ctus est, impietatem ferre non potest. Conf. Eph. 4, 30. ubi tamen sensu paulo alio Spiritus Sanctus pro donis su- mitur.

ET CONVERSUS EST EIS IN INIMICUM, ET VERE DEBELLAVIT EOS] Tradendo eos in ma- num Antiochi, & ejus ducum.

Quomodo enim Spiritum Sanctum afflixe- rint, qui in medio ipsorum positus erat in deserto, ex historia notissimum est, de quo etiam Nehemias in precatione sua c. 9, 16. 17. 20. nec non David Ps. 95, 8. ut & Apostolus Ebr. 3, 7. seqq. & 1. Cor. 10, 6. seqq. Neque ad alia tempora spectant, quæ de indignatione & pœna divina Esaias subjicit: ET CONVERSUS EST EIS IN INIMICUM, ET VERE DEBELLAVIT EOS. De quo magnus est Interpp. consensus. Nemo certe in- ventus hactenus est, qui ad Antiochi tempora hæc retulerit. Grotii commentum hoc proprium est.

## 63:11
Vers. 11.

AND HE REMEMBERED THE DAYS OF OLD OF MOSES] And here it is placed for 'nevertheless': although they were of the worst merit, God nevertheless delivered them even from Antiochus, and did for them such things as He had once done in the time of Moses.

There is no trace of the times of Antiochus to be found here. And he is still occupied with the recounting of benefits once shown, because although GOD had indeed turned into an enemy to the people on account of their sins, He nevertheless remembered the days of old, of Moses and of His people, and in turn showed grace to them. Others connect 'days of old' with Moses, in which way Brentius: Although God was provoked to such great wrath by the impiety and crimes of the Israelites in the desert, that He would now hand them over to be conquered by enemies, now think to take them away entirely from the earth and destroy them; saying to Moses, 'Let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them and that I may consume them.' And again: 'I will smite them with the pestilence and consume them'; yet having remembered that Moses, whom He Himself had chosen as their leader, and had promised that He would deliver them through him, was spending the days of old, or of his life, among them, and was interceding for them with such ardor of piety that he would rather be blotted out of the book of life than abandon the salvation of this people, He remitted His wrath, and being reconciled with the people, continued to protect and preserve them. 'I have pardoned,' He says, 'according to thy word: but as truly as I live, all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord.' Others propose these as distinct arguments or incentives of divine grace: namely, that GOD remembered both the days of old and Moses His servant, as B. Luther translated: 'He thought again of the former time, of Moses.' We add, then also of His people. The days of old are the ancient days in which God had made a promise to Abraham concerning the taking up of his posterity and seed. Thus, therefore, Isaiah says that grace was shown to the Israelites on account of the promises made from ancient days, on account of the intercession and prayers of Moses the man of God, and because they themselves were the people of the Lord and His peculiar treasure. Compare Deut. 7. c. 9, 18. seqq. Ezech. 20, 13. seqq.

Verse of the same.

WHERE IS HE THAT BROUGHT THEM UP OUT OF THE SEA?] He introduces God reflecting on His benefits. But the Chaldean thinks it is to be understood here: lest the nations say, namely, 'Where is that God now?'

WITH THE SHEPHERDS OF HIS FLOCK] Under the shepherds Moses and Aaron. But the Chaldean translates it, as shepherds are accustomed to lead their flock, supply, [the word] lead. WHERE IS HE WHO PUT THE SPIRIT OF HIS HOLY ONE IN THE MIDST OF IT] And here in the Hebrew: of his holiness, that is, as the Chaldean understands it, who gave the gift of prophecy to Moses and the seventy elders. See Num. XI. v. 25. 26. 27. 28. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET RECORDATUS EST DIERUM SECULI MOSIS] Et hic positum pro attamen: quanquam illi pes- sima erant meriti, Deus tamen etiam ab Antiocho eos li- beravit, fecitque illis qualia olim Mosis tempore fecerat.

De Antiochi temporibus hic nullum deprehen- dere est vestigium. Et versatur adhuc in depræ- dicatione beneficiorum olim exhibitorum, quod conversus quidem DEUS populo fuerit in inimi- cum ob peccata, sed recordatus tamen dierum seculi, Mosis & populi sui, gratiam iisdem vi- cissim exhibuerit. Dies seculi alii connectunt cum Mose, quo pacto Brentius: Etsi Deus impie- tate & sceleribus Israëlitarum in deserto ad tantam iracundiam provocatus est, ut nunc traderet eos hostibus vincendos, nunc cogitaret eos prorsum de terra tollere & delere; Dimitte me, inquiens ad Mosen, ut irascatur furor meus contra eos & deleam eos. Et iterum: Feriam eos pestilentia at- que consumam; tamen recordatus, quod Moses, quem ipse in ducem eorum elegerat, & promis- rat se eos per ipsum liberaturum, ageret dies se- culi, seu vitæ suæ inter eos, & intercederet pro eis tanto pietatis ardore, ut mallet de libro vitæ de- leri, quam salutem hujus populi deferere, remi- sit iram suam, & reconciliatus cum populo per- rexit eum tueri, & conservare. Dimisi, inquiens, juxta verbum tuum: Vivo ego, implebitur gloria Domini universa terra. Alii ceu distincta argu- menta vel incitamenta gratiæ divinæ ea propo- nunt: quod nempe DEUS recordatus fuerit tum dierum seculi, tum Mosis servi sui, uti B. Lutherus transtulit: Er gedachte wieder an die vorige Zeit/ an den Mose. Addimus, tum etiam populi sui. Dies seculi sunt dies antiqui, quibus promissionem fecerat Deus Abrahamo, de assumenda posteri- tate ac semine ejus. Ita ergo gratiam exhibitam Israëlitis Esaias dicit ob promissiones à diebus an- tiquis factas, ob intercessionem & preces Mosis viri Dei, & quia erant ipsi populus Domini, ac peculium ejus. Confer. Deut. 7. c. 9,18. seqq. E- zech. 20, 13. seqq.

Vers. eod.

UBI EST QUI EDUXIT EOS DE MARI?] Deum inducit recogitantem sua beneficia, At Chaldæus putat hic subintelligi: ne dicant gentes, nempe ubi nunc ille Deus?

CUM PASTORIBUS GREGIS SUI] Sub pasto- ribus Mose & Aarone. At Chaldæus vertit, ut pastores pe- cus suum, supple, deducere solent. UBI EST QUI POSUIT IN MEDIO EJUS SPI- RITUM SANCTI SUI] Et hic in Hebræo : sanctitatis suæ, id est, ut accipit Chaldæus, qui donum prophetiæ dedit Mosi & senibus LXX. Vide Num. II. v. 25. 26. 27. 28. 29.

## 63:12
Ver. 12.

WHO LED MOSES TO THE RIGHT HAND BY THE ARM OF HIS GLORY] More correctly: who led Moses by his magnificent arm, to the right hand: that is, taking hold of his right hand, as fathers are accustomed to do with children.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

QUI EDUXIT AD DEXTERAM MOSEN BRACHIO GLORIÆ SUÆ] Rectius : qui brachio magnifico suo deduxit Mosen, ad dexteram: id est, dex- teram ejus apprehendens, ut patres pueris solent.

## 63:13
Ver. 13.

AS A HORSE IN THE DESERT NOT STUMBLING] You might translate it better: As a horse in the fields they did not stumble. מדבר often signifies fields, in which there are neither houses nor trees, but wide spaces for running. The Israelites went through the bed of the sea no less securely than a horse leaps through such fields. Ver. 14. AS AN ANIMAL DESCENDING INTO THE FIELD, THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD WAS HIS LEADER] The Spirit of the Lord (that is, God himself, in the Hebrew manner) led them gently in the same way as cattle that descend into a valley. This is because cattle, when they descend from a mountain along a slope, are accustomed to be led very gently. THUS DIDST THOU LEAD THY PEOPLE] Here, with the words of God which he had interjected finished, Judas Maccabeus continues his discourse. If God is introduced reflecting on these things, GOD the Father speaks about the Son, the Leader of the people, to whom the liberation of the people from Egypt is peculiarly attributed. Others, however, wish these words to be not of God, but of the people, complaining that their former grace is not being shown to them. Formerly God led (thus Brentius paraphrases) the Israelites through the abysses of the Red Sea; and just as a horse walking in the desert, or on firm and non-watery ground, does not easily stumble, or fall, or drown, so God preserved the Israelites, so that even though they walked in the abysses of the sea, they nevertheless proceeded no less constantly and firmly than if they were walking on dry land. And just as cattle descend or are driven to the valley, and are refreshed by the Spirit of the Lord, i.e., by a gentle breath of wind, so you, O Lord, drove your people with the greatest gentleness and mildness, so that the glory of your name might be illustrated. But where are you now, O God, the savior of your people and the driver of your flock? For see the inversion of things. In past centuries you led your people safely through the abysses of the sea, and kept your flock safe and secure from all wild beasts. But now your people have been cast into the deepest abysses of all, and your flock lies open to the ravages of all wild beasts. Regarding the rest, there is no reason for us to be anxious. For the sense is in the open and beyond controversy, that these things concern that leading of the people which was done through Moses, and that those former times and benefits are to be compared with the state about which the Prophet here repeats, where is your zeal (that former one) and your fortitude, the multitude of your bowels and of your mercies? But those words above, where is he who led them? Grotius does not show that they are of God (not of the people, or of the Prophet sighing, or praying for the people, or introducing the faithful who could use such a prayer in afflicted circumstances, so that he might place the future state as if before their eyes, and lead the words for the faithful if there were to be any). That Judas Maccabeus either spoke above, or is now continuing the discourse, or that this is his prayer, is supported by no evidence, not even an obscure one. This interpretation of Grotius is purely arbitrary. But as to which times these properly belong, the interpreters vary. Brentius, as we have seen, and others think they look to the time of the Babylonian captivity. Which opinion Jerome attributes to the Jews: but he himself prefers to refer them to the present times. Another pericope begins, says Jerome, at those words, I will remember the mercy of the Lord, in which the Prophet speaks in the person of the people; recounting the benefits of God toward himself and the hardness of his own heart, on account of which both Jerusalem was handed over to fire and Israel to captivity. Which the Jews refer to the Babylonian times. We, however, have shown by order and reason that it is spoken of the present time, in which they serve the Romans, and with Israel excluded, a crowd of Gentiles has succeeded. Which explanation of Jerome does not seem to be despised. For many things favor the same: First and especially the connection with the preceding, where it was a matter of those things which look primarily to the times of the New Testament, such as the Prophetic office of Christ, ch. 61, the preaching of the Gospel through the whole world, ch. 62, the Advent of the Messiah, and his battle against sin, death, and Satan, and his glorious triumph, ch. 63. Furthermore, if we look at the consequences, ch. 65. & 66, it is a matter of the calling of the Gentiles, and of other things which likewise pertain to the times of the New Testament, and also of the consummation of the age and other last things. And therefore it is better to interpret these in such a way that they are referred to the latest dissipation of the Jews and the overthrow of the city rather than to the Babylonian captivity. Furthermore, since this has already been dealt with above, and the promise of liberation through Cyrus was made to the people of God, it seems more convenient to accept the present complaints regarding the latest destruction and total ruin of the Jewish state. Nor is there any doubt that the same is more fitting to this, whether we look at the complaint of the passion: Where is your zeal and your fortitude? The multitude of your bowels and of your mercies? They have restrained themselves over me: or whether we attend to the most grave blinding and hardening of the Jewish people: Why have you made us err, O Lord, from your ways. You have hardened our heart so that we would not fear you? Or the state and condition of the people and the Jewish polity: As if they possessed nothing, your holy people: enemies have trampled your sanctification. We have become as in the beginning, when you did not rule over us, nor was your name invoked over me. To which state one did not arrive from the Babylonian captivity. For then the people of the Lord still remained, then God still ruled over them: then the name of God was still invoked over them. But now, ever since the latest destruction, they are no longer a people, nor is God any longer their Lord, nor is the name of the Lord invoked over them: but they have become as in the beginning, before they were assumed into the people of God. And because they were already verging toward that state upon the impending arrival of the Lord, because all things were already threatening the ruin of the Jews, therefore in the midst of these complaints the Prophet is resolved into a most ardent sigh, that the heavens being rent, the Lord might descend, the true savior, and the only hope and confidence of the pious, who were awaiting the salvation of the Lord, who was about to prepare by his arrival eternal joys, which eye has not seen nor ear heard. Furthermore, to what time do those things more rightly correspond, which occur here concerning the universal apostasy of the people, and the total rejection of the same: We have all fallen as a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away: THERE IS NONE, who calls upon your name, who rises up and takes hold of you: To establish the truth of which, there is need of great hyperbole, if these are referred to the Babylonian captivity, or to the times of Antiochus. Finally, the overturning of the city, the temple, and the polity of the Hebrews is connected here with the calling of the Gentiles, which uniquely corresponds to the most recent Destruction. It in no way corresponds to the times of Antiochus, nor of the Babylonian captivity, The city of your sanctuary has become a desert, Sion has become a desert, Jerusalem desolate, the house of our sanctification, and of our glory, where our fathers praised you, has become a burning of fire, and ALL OUR DESIRABLE THINGS have become a ruin (which certainly did not happen in the times of Antiochus, and not even under the Babylonian captivity;) They sought me, who did not ask before, they found me, who did not seek me. Which pertain to the calling of the Gentiles. preceding: To the prayer of the people mixed with complaints, in which he had said: Why have you made us wander, O Lord, from your way, have hardened our hearts, so that we would not fear you; He answered, as the Jews wish, God the Father, as we prove, the Lord and Savior: I am not so rigid and cruel, who prefers the repentance of a sinner to his death: nor do I repel repenting children, who nevertheless have preserved the dignity of their name: that I should even wish to save strangers. When I weigh all these things and each one, I see that nothing stands in the way of Jerome's explanation, which is also Cyril's, and that everything fits perfectly, I add my vote, that these complaints agree with the most recent destruction and the most miserable state in which the Jews still are, having become from a people not a people, and such as they were before, when they had not yet been taken up by the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

QUASI EQUUM IN DESERTO NON IM- PINGENTEM] Vertas melius : Sicut equus in campis non impegerunt. מדבר sæpe significat campos, in quibus nec domus sunt, nec arbores, sed lata ad cursum spatia. Israëlitæ non minus secure per maris alveum ivêre, quam equus per tales campos desultat. Vers. 14. QUASI ANIMAL IN CAMPO DESCEN- DENS, SPIRITUS DOMINI DUCTOR EJUS FUIT] Spiritus Domini (id est, Deus ipse, more Hebræo) ita eos leniter duxit, quomodo pecus, quod in vallem descendit. Id ideo, quia pecora cum à monte per clivum descendunt, leniter admodum duci solent. SIC ADDUXISTI POPULUM TUUM] Hic ab- solutis Dei verbis, quæ interjecerat, Judas Maccabæus ser- monem suum prosequitur. Si Deus hæc recogitans introducitur, DEUS Pater de Ductore populi Filio loquitur, cui liberatio populi ex Ægypto peculiariter vindicatur. Alii tamen hæc verba non Dei, sed populi esse volunt, querentis sibi pristinam non exhiberi gratiam. Quondam eduxit Deus (ita παραφράζει Brentius) Israëlitas per abyssos maris rubri ; & sicut equ9 am- bulans in deserto, seu in terra firma & non aquosa, non facile impingit, aut corruit seu demergitur, ita conservavit Deus Israëlitas, ut etsi ambulabant in Abyssis maris, non minus tamen constanter & fir- miter pergerent, quam si in arida terra proficisce- rentur. Et quemadmodum pecus descendit seu mi- natur ad vallem, & refocillatur Spiritu Domini, h. e. leni afflatu venti, ita tu Domine minasti populum tuum summa mansuetudine & lenitate, ut gloria nominis tui illustraretur. Ubi autem nunc es Deus, populi tui servator & gregis tui minator ? Vide enim rerum inversionem. Superioribus seculis eduxisti populum tuum salvum per abyssos maris, & serva- sti gregem tuum ab omnibus silvestribus feris tu- tum ac securum. Nunc autem populus tuus conje- ctus est in profundissimas quasque abyssos, & grex tuus patet omnium ferarum dilacerationibus. De cæteris non est quod soliciti simus. Sensus enim in aprico & extra controversiam est, de illa populi de- ductione, quæ per Mosem facta hæc agere, & tem- pora ac benficia ista priora componi cum statu, de quo hic ingeminat Propheta, ubi est zelus tuus (il- le pristinus) & fortitudo tua, multitudo viscerum tuorum, & miserationum tuarum ? Sed verba ista superiora, ubi est qui eduxit eos ? Dei esse (non po- puli, aut Prophetæ suspirantis, aut precantis pro popu- lo, vel introducentis fideles, qui rebus afflictis tali oratione uti possent, ut statum futurum quasi ob oculos poneret, & fidelibus si qui futuri sint verba præiret,) non ostendit Grotius. Judam autem Mac- cabæum vel supra locutum esse, vel nunc continua- re sermonem, aut hanc ejus esse precationem, nul- lo, ne obscuro quidem constat indicio. Mere ar- bitraria est hæc Grotiana interpretatio. Ad quæ- nam vero tempora proprie hæc pertineant, va- riant Interpp. Brentius, ut vidimus, & alii ad tempus captivitatis Babylonicæ ea spectare existi- mant. Quam sententiam Hieronymus Judæis tribuit: mavult autem ipse ad tempora præsen- tia referre. Incipit alia περικοπὴ, ait ad verba isla, Miserationem Domini recordabor, Hierony- mus nius, in qua ex Persona populi Propheta loquitur; enarrans beneficia in se Dei & sui cordis duritiam, ob quam & Hierusalem incendio & Israël captivitati traditus sit. Quod Judæi ad Babylonica referunt tempora. Nos autem ordine & ratione monstravi- mus, de præsenti dici tempore, in quo Romanis ser- viunt, & excluso Israële gentium turba successit. Quæ explicatio Hieronymi non videtur contemnenda. Favent enim eidem multa: Primo ac præcipue συν- έχει cum superioribus, ubi de iis actum est, quæ ad Novi Testamenti tempora imprimis spectant, ut- pote de munere Christi Prophetico, cap. 61. de prædicatione Evangelii per totum orbem c. 62. de Adventu Messiæ, & pugna ejusdem adversus pec- catum, mortem, & Satanam, ac glorioso ejusdem triumpho c. 63. Porro si consequentia spectemus, cap. 65. & 66. de vocatione gentium agitur, & de aliis, quæ ad tempora itidem Novi Testamenti fa- ciunt, nec non de consummatione seculi aliisq́; novis- simis. Ideoque præstat hæc ita interpretari, ut ad no- vissimam Judæorum dissipationem & urbis eversionem potius referantur, quam ad Babylonicam captivita- tem. Porro, cum de hac jam superius actum, & promissio liberationis per Cyrum populo Dei fa- cta sit, convenientius videtur, querelas præsentes de novissimo excidio & πανωλεθρίᾳ status Judaici accipere. Neque dubium est eandem magis huic convenire, sive querelam τὸ πᾶθῷ respiciamus: Ubi est Zelus tuus & fortitudo tua? multitudo vi- scerum tuorum & miserationum tuarum? super me continuerunt se: sive gravissimam cæcationem & indurationem populi Judaici attendamus: Qare errare nos fecisti Domine in viis tuis. Indurasti cor nostrum ne timeremus te? sive statum, & conditio- nem populi & politiæ Judæorum: Quasi nihilum pos- sederunt populum sanctum tuum: hostes conculcave- runt sanctificationem tuam. Facti sumus quasi in principio, cum non dominaveris nostri, neque invoca- retur nomen tuum super me. Ad quem statum non perveniebatur à captivitate Babylonica. Tum enim adhuc manebat populus Domini, tum adhuc Deus dominabatur ipsis: tum adhuc nomen Dei invocabatur super ipsos. At jam inde à novissimo excidio non sunt amplius populus, nec amplius Deus est Dominus ipsorum, nec invocatur nomen Domini super ipsos: sed facti sunt quasi in princi- pio, antequam in populum Dei assumerentur. Et quia ad eum statum jam vergebant sub ingruen- tem adventum Domini, quia Judæ jam ruinam minabantur omnia, ideo in mediis istis querelis resolvitur in suspirium ardentissimum Prophe- ta, ut disruptis cælis descendat Dominus, ve- rus salvator, & unica spes & fiducia piorum, qui expectabant salutare Domini, qui paraturus erat adventu suo æterna gaudia, quæ oculus non vidit nec auris audivit. Ulterius, cuinam tem- pori rectius conveniunt illa, quæ de apostasia universali populi, ac rejectione ejusdem totali hic occurrunt: Cecidimus quasi folium UNIVERSI, & iniquitates nostræ, quasi ventus abstulerunt nos: NON EST, qui invocet nomen tuum, qui con- surgat & teneat te: Ad quarum veritatem ad- struendam, opus est magna hyperbole, si ad ca- ptivitatem Babylonicam, aut ad Antiochi tem- pora hæc referantur. Denique connectitur hic eversio civitatis, templi, politiæ Ebræorum cum vocatione gentium, quod novissimo Excidio unice congruit. Temporibus Antiochi nulla- tenus convenit, nec Babylonicæ captivitatis, Civitas sancti tui facta est deserta, Sion deserta facta est, Hierusalem desolata, domus sanctifica- tionis nostræ, & gloriæ nostræ, ubi te laudaverunt patres noftri, facta est in exustionem ignis, & O- MNIA DESIDERABILIA NOSTRA facta sunt in ruinam (quæ certe facta non sunt temporibus Antiochi, ac ne quidem sub captivitate Babylo- nica;) Quæsierunt me, qui ante non interrogabant, invenerunt, qui non quæsiverunt me. Quæ ad vo- cationem gentium pertinent. Ad quæ verba Hiero- nymus recte ita annotat, concinne συνέχειαν often- dens cum præcedentibus: Ad orationem populi mixtam cum querimoniis, in qua dixerat: Quare nos errare fecisti Domine de via tua, indurasti corda nostra, ut timeremus te; Respondit, ut Ju- dæi volunt, Deus Pater, ut nos probamus, Dominus atq; Salvator: in tantum non sum rigidus, & crude- lis, qui malo pœnitentiam peccatoris, quam mortem: nec repello filios pœnitentes, qui tamen sui nominis ser- vaverint dignitatem: ut etiam alienos salvare velim. Hæc omnia & singula ubi expendo, Hieronymi ex- plicationi, quæ etiam Cyrilli est, cui nihil obstare, omnia apprime congruere video, calculum adji- cio, querelas hasce convenire excidio novissimo, & miserrimo statui, in quo adhuc sunt Judæi è po- pulo facti non populus, & quales antea erant, quum nondum assumti erant à Domino.

## 63:15
Verse 15.

MULTITUDE OF YOUR BOWELS] The abundance of your kindness, as the Chaldean here,

HAVE RESTRAINED THEMSELVES OVER ME] Better: They have poured themselves out over me with force. For from the word אָפַק are derived אֲפִיקִים torrents. Just as waters long held back burst forth more abundantly and powerfully, so also the goodness of God, long repressed, opened itself most powerfully in Judas Maccabeus.

The words are twisted into a clearly contrary sense, for אָפַק means he used force, made an attack, acted violently, and in the 4th conjugation he forced himself, restrained himself with great force, as is said of Joseph in Gen. 45:1. Joseph could not restrain himself; and ch. 43:31. And he restrained himself with a certain force. See also Isa. 42:14, ch. 64:12, Esth. 5:10, nor is it found anywhere in the scriptures in the sense of pouring out. But אָפַק is used of torrents, because they rush with violence and force, so that they cannot be contained. And it is manifest that the complaint is being continued. Therefore all interpreters have explained it as the mercy of the Lord being restrained, not poured out. And there is great emphasis in it to express the goodness of God, that he is, as it were, compelled with force and a certain violence to restrain his mercies, and to do a strange work, when it is his own proper work to have mercy, with sins and the hardening of men imposing necessity upon him. Nothing here about Judas Maccabeus.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

MULTITUDO VISCERUM TUORUM] Copia benignitatis tuæ, ut hic Chaldæus,

SUPER ME CONTINUERUNT SE] Melius: In me se effuderunt cum impetu. Nam à verbo אָפַק dicun- tur אֲפִיקִים torrentes. Sicut aquæ diu retentæ ube- rius & validius erumpunt, ita & Dei bonitas, diu repressa, in Juda Maccabæo potentissime se aperuit.

In sensum plane contrarium verba torquen- tur, nam אָפַק est vim intulit, impetum fecit, violenter egit, & in 4. Conjugatione impetum sibi fecit, con- tinuit se impetu magno, uti de Josepho dicitur Gen. 45, 1. Non potuit se Joseph continere; & c. 43, 31. Et continuit se vi quadam. Videatur etiam Esa. 42, 14. c. 64, 12. Esth. 5, 10. nec uspiam reperitur in scripturis sensu effundendi. De torrentibus vero u- surpatur אָפַק, quia cum violentia & impetu, ut contineri nequeant, ruunt. Et manifestum est continuari querelam. Ideo interpp. omnes de re- tenta, non effusa miseratione Domini exposuere. Estq; in eo magna emphasis ad exprimendam Dei bonitatem, quod quasi cum impetu & vi quadam cogatur cohibere miserationes suas, & alienum opus facere, quum proprium ejus opus sit misere- ri, necessitatem ei imponentibus peccatis & indu- ratione hominum. Nihil hic de Juda Maccabæo.

## 63:17
Verse 17.

WHY HAVE YOU MADE US WANDER, O LORD, FROM YOUR WAYS] Translate: why did you make us? For why would you allow us, oppressed by a long tyranny, to fall away from your law? See Ps. 125, v. 3.

YOU HAVE HARDENED OUR HEART, LEST WE SHOULD FEAR YOU] And here translate: you hardened, namely by prolonging our evils too much.

There is no reason why we should admit another version. Indeed, there is a reason why we should not admit it. Because the faithful are asking about the afflicted and miserable state of the people, such as it is at present, by the just judgment of God, not such as it could have been. Namely, about the hardening of the people, which happened to them at the coming of the Messiah, John 12. God is not established here as the cause of this, nor is the divine prolongation of evils, but since they themselves hardened their hearts by sins and impenitence, God by a just judgment permitted this, and left them to their own malice. Concerning which Cyril in this place. But since, because of much disobedience and perverse malice, they raved against Christ, they fell away from the union which is with him, namely the spiritual one, and were deprived of his gifts, and did not know the way of evangelical conversation. Hence, weeping most deservedly, they say: Why have you led us astray, O Lord, from your way? Have you hardened our hearts, lest we should fear you? For they hardened their own hearts. Therefore it was said to them by the voice of the Prophet: Rend your hearts and not your garments. But although God could have softened everyone, he permitted them to have a broken and stubborn mind. For this reason, because he did not render them tender and soft, he is said to harden them. But to those to whom this happens, it is altogether necessary that something else should befall them: that is to say, that they should lack the fear of God. Conf. Ps. 81, 13. Acts 14, 16. The Israelite Church is certainly praying for the forgiveness of sins. How then could it accuse God, or establish him as the cause of its sins in the acknowledgment of its own guilt and in its prayer? B. Luther in his Commentary explains this by permission: because we did not want to hear your word, you permitted us to wander and to sin, just as it is, the sin is the punishment of sin. Whom Junius and Tremellius followed. But Cornelius a Lapide rightly notes Can. 23 in the Epistle of Paul. God permits evil in one way, man in another: man negatively, God positively: man often with sin, because he is bound to prevent it: God justly and holily, because as the supreme Lord of all he permits secondary causes to himself, so that they may use their own liberty in any direction. For he would inflict violence on nature if he necessitated it to good. Pareus's gloss in book 2, on the loss of grace and the state of sin, ch. 14, is impious, that because of the force of the Hiphil conjugation it is inferred that God moves and impels to action, that is, to sin: because in this way he is openly established as the cause of sin. But the comparison of passages teaches that Scripture itself interprets active verbs concerning permission, 2 Chron. 15, 2. Ps. 81, 13. Hos. 4, 12. Acts 14, 16.

Same verse.

RETURN FOR THE SAKE OF YOUR SERVANTS] Look upon us mercifully for the sake of those fathers from whom we derive our origin. Thus the Chaldean.

THE TRIBES OF YOUR INHERITANCE] Tribes are taken here for the heads of the tribes. He explains whom he understands by saints, namely those from whose shoot (for that is what שבט properly means) those branches have come forth.

They do not allege the merits or justice of the Patriarchs, which one is never allowed to find in sacred writings or in the prayers of the saints, but they call themselves servants of the Lord, so that the Lord may turn from anger to grace for his own sake, to help them, and in view of the misery of the servants of his. Concerning which Cyril in this place. Again they ask that he return to them, by his serenity, I say, and humanity. They say they are his servants and inheritance, not as if they had done anything that befits servants, or were placing his neck under a yoke, nor that they were rendering obedience because they had obtained that inheritance. But because they were once called his, and from the beginning had an intimate and close relationship with him, for this reason and for this alone they ask to be saved. Let us know therefore, (so Brentius advises) that when a sinner asks God to show favor on account of the tribes of Israel, he does not boast of any righteousness or holiness of these tribes, which God might regard. For nothing was more impious than these: Since you are, says Moses, a stiff-necked people. And Stephen: You always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you. But he appeals to the promises of God, which were spoken here to the tribes, and to the truth and mercy of God. For God said concerning these tribes: I will be their God: And: Israel is my firstborn son. And elsewhere the Israelites are called the peculiar people of God and the inheritance of God: because he chose them out of all nations, that they might be the guardians of his promises concerning the Messiah, and might propagate them to posterity, and that the Messiah might be born from their own nation.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

QUARE ERRARE NOS FECISTI DOMINE DE VIIS TUIS] Verte faceres? Cur enim sineres nos lon- ga tyrannide oppressos deficere a lege tua? Vide Ps. 125. v. 3.

INDURASTI COR NOSTRUM, NE TIME- REMUS TE] Et hic verte indurares, nempe prorogando nimium nostra mala.

Non est causa, cur aliam versionem admitta- mus. Imo causa est, cur non admittamus. Quia quaerunt fideles de statu afflicto & miserabili popu- li, qualis in praesenti est, justo Dei judicio, non qua- lis esse poterat. De induratione nempe populi, quae ipsi contigit sub adventum Messiae Joh. 12. Cujus causa non constituitur hic Deus, aut prorogatio malorum divina, sed quum ipsi peccatis & impoe- nitentia corda sua indurarint, Deus justo judicio id permisit, & malitiae propriae ipsos reliquit. De quo Cyrillus in h. l. At quoniam propter multam inobe- dientiam & sinistram malitiam in Christum bacchati sunt, exciderunt conjunctione, quae cum ipso est, spi- rituali videlicet, & ejus donorum expertes fuerunt, viamque Evangelicae conversationis haud noverunt. Hinc meritissimo flentes dicunt: Quare seduxisti nos Domine a via tua? Obdurasti corda nostra, ne timeremus te? Obdurarunt enim sua ipsorum corda. Itaque dictum est illis voce Prophetae: Disrum- pite corda vestra & non vestimenta vestra. Verum cum emollire potuisset universorum Deus: permisit illis, ut mentem perfractam haberent, & contuma- cem. Hac de causa, quia tenera & mollia ipsa non reddidit, ipse obdurare dicitur. Quibus autem hoc accidit, his omnino necesse est aliud obvenire: ut in- quam Dei metu careant. Conf. Ps. 81, 13. Act. 14, 16, Veniam utique precatur Ecclesia Israelitica peccato- rum. Quomodo ergo Deum accusaret, aut ipsum causam peccatorum suorum constitueret in culpae suae agnitione, ac deprecatione? B. Lutherus in Comment. de permissione exponit h. m. quia nolui- mus audire verbum tuum, permisisti nos errare, & peccare, sicuti sit, peccatum peccati est poena. Quem sequuti sunt Jun. & Tremell. Recte autem notat Cornel. a Lapide Can. 23. in Epist. Paul. Aliter per- mittit malum Deus, aliter homo: homo negative, Deus positive: homo saepe cum peccato, quia tenetur impedire: Deus juste & sancte, quia summus omnium Dominus causas secundas sibi permittit, ut libertate sua in quamlibet partem utantur. Vim enim naturae inferret, si eam necessitaret ad bonum. Impia est Parei glossa l. 2. de amiss. grat. & stat. peccat. c. 14. quod ob vim conjugationis Hiphil inferatur Deum movere & impellere ad agendum, hoc est, ad pec- candum: quia ita aperte causa peccati constitui- tur. Scripturam autem ipsam verba activa de per- missione interpretari collatio locorum docet 2. Par. 15, 2. Psal. 81, 13. Hos. 4, 12. Act. 14, 16.

Vers. eod.

CONVERTERE PROPTER SERVOS TUOS] Respice nos clemens propter illos patres, ex quibus or- tum ducimus. Sic Chaldaeus.

TRIBUS HAEREDITATIS TUAE] Tribus hic pro capitibus tribuum sumuntur. Explicat quos sanctos intel- ligat, illos scilicet, ex quorum surculo (id enim proprie שבט) rami isti prodiere.

Non allegant Patriarcharum merita aut justi- tiam, quod nunquam in sacris reperire licet, aut in sanctorum orationibus, sed se servos Domini di- cunt, ut convertatur Dominus ab ira ad gratiam propter se, ad se juvandos, & intuitu miseriae ser- vorum suorum. De quo Cyrillus in h. l. Iterum pe- tunt ut redeat ad se, per serenitatem, inquam, & humanitatem. Servos & hæreditatem dicunt esse se, non quasi aliquid quod servos decet egerint, aut cervi- cem ejus jugo fupponerent, nec quod hæreditate illa po- titi præstarent obedientiam. Sed quia semel ejus di- cti sunt, & conjunctionem cum ipso ab initio intimam- que necessitudinem habuerunt, propter hoc & quidem solum servari petunt. Sciamus igitur, (ita monet Brentius) quod cum peccator rogat Deum, ut fa- veat propter tribus Israelis, non jactat aliquam ha- rum tribuum justitiam aut sanctitatem, quam Deus respiciat. Nihil enim his magis impium fuit: Cum sis, inquit Moses, durissimæ Cervicis populus. Et Stephanus: Vos semper Spiritui sancto resistitis, sicut Patres vestri ita & vos. Sed appellat ad pro- missiones Dei, quæ hic tribubus dictæ sunt, & ad veritatem atque clementiam Dei. Dixit enim Deus de his tribubus: Ego ero Deus eorum: Et: Filius meus primogenitus Israel. Et alias vocantur Israe- litæ peculiaris populus Dei & hæreditas Dei: pro- pterea quod ex omnibus gentibus elegerit eos, ut essent custodes promissionum ejus de Messia, & propagarent eas ad posteros, & ut Messias ex ipso- rum gente nasceretur.

## 63:18
Verse 18. AS IF THEY POSSESSED NOTHING YOUR HOLY PEOPLE] You might translate more correctly: For a short time they possessed the people of your holiness: namely, the Syro-Macedonians under King Antiochus Epiphanes held Jerusalem for three years and six months.

Although the word לִמְעַר may be understood concerning time, it will not, however, indicate that the people were possessed by enemies for a short time. For neither is the mark of the accusative found here, as if they possessed the people, nor does any word occur concerning the Syro-Macedonians, nor does that possession of Jerusalem for 312 years have any bearing here, where the discourse is about the possession of the entire people, and about the total destruction of the Jewish polity. But we rightly prefer the version of the blessed Luther with Mr. Brentius, which is as follows: Some translate this thus: For a little time your holy people possessed, namely the sanctuary or the inheritance which you gave them, but because it follows immediately concerning the enemies who trampled the sanctuary of the Lord: Therefore it seems more correct that our teacher of holy memory, Dr. Luther, translated it thus: They have almost possessed (our enemies) your holy people. Sie besitzen dein heiliges Volck schier gar. Which were truly fulfilled under the times of the latest Jewish polity: when the scepter was taken away from Judah, and the people were possessed by enemies. The evils which are contained in these complaints are certainly more serious and more constant than to be able to be referred to that short time of three years, and the evils which then happened to the people. Whence Jerome understands these things and those which follow as concerning the Romans: Our enemies, says the Prophet, have trampled your sanctuary. There is no doubt that he signifies the temple: which the victorious Romans trampled. And we have become as in the beginning, before we were called into Abraham and while we were in Egypt, not having God, nor kings, nor princes, nor prophets, nor the law of the commandments of God, all of which were completed after the passion of the Lord, and are being completed today.
