For as they say: His blood be upon us and upon our children, the eternal curse remains: And God does not rule over them, nor is his name invoked over them, while they are by no means called the people of God. These are Jerome's words, which we think are evident. But Grotius likewise perverts them according to his custom, and twists them to Judas Maccabeus.

Verse of the same. OUR ENEMIES HAVE TRAMPLED YOUR SANCTIFICATION] They profaned your sanctuary with impure rites. That had happened a little before Judas Maccabeus invaded Idumea. 1 Maccabees 1. 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 57.

Latin:

Vers. 18. QUASI NIHIL POSSEDERUNT POPU- LUM SANCTUM TUUM] Rectius vertas: Ad breve tem- pus possederunt populum sanctitatis tuæ: nempe Syromace- dones rege Antiocho Epiphane Hierosolyma tenuere per annos tres & menses sex.

Etsi de tempore vox לִמְעַר intelligatur, non tamen populum ad breve tempus possessum fuisse ab hostibus indicabit. Nam neque nota accusationis hic habetur, quasi populum possederint, neq; de Syro-Macedonibus ullum occurrit verbum, neq; illa Hierosolymorum per 312. annos possessio huc facit, ubi de populi integri possessione sermo est, & de πανωλεθρίᾳ politiæ Judaicæ. Sed præfe- rimus merito B. Lutheri versionem cum Dn. Bren- tio, qui ita habet: Nonnulli hoc sic vertunt: Parvo tempore possedit populus tuus sanctus, videlicet sanctuarium seu hæreditatem, quam dedisti eis, sed quia mox sequitur de hostibus, qui conculcave- runt sanctuarium Domini: Ideo rectius videtur Præ- ceptor noster sanctæ memoriæ D. Lutherus sic vertis- se: Propemodum possederunt (hostes nostri) populum sanctum tuum. Sie besitzen dein heiliges Volck schier gar. Quæ vere impleta sunt sub no- vissimæ politiæ Judaicæ tempora: cum sceptrum de Ju- da auferretur, & populus ab hostibus possideretur. Gra- viora certe ac constantiora sunt mala, quæ his que- relis continentur, quam ut ad breve istud tempus triennii, & mala, quæ tum populo acciderunt, re- ferri possint. Unde Hieronymus hæc & quæ se- quuntur, de Romanis intelligit: Hostes nostri, ait Propheta, conculcaverunt sanctuarium tuum. Haud dubium, quin templum significet: quod victores cal- cavere Romani. Et facti sumus sicut in principio, antequam vocaremur in Abraham & dum essemus in Ægypto, non habentes Deum, nec reges, nec principes, nec Prophetas, nec legem mandatorum Dei, quæ o- mnia post passionem completa sunt domini, hodieq́; complentur. Dicentibus enim illis: Sanguis ejus super nos & super filios nostros, manet maledictio sempiterna: Et non dominatur eorum Deus, neq; invocatur nomen illius super eos, dum nequaquam Dei populus nuncupatur. Hæc Hieronymus, quæ evidentia esse putamus. Sed pervertit ea itidem pro more suo Grotius, & ad Judam Maccabæum detorquet.

Vers. eod. HOSTES NOSTRI CONCULCAVERUNT SAN- CTIFICATIONEM TUAM] Sanctuarium tuum profa- narunt sacris impuris. Id acciderat paulo antequam Idu- mæam invaderet Judas Maccabæus. 1. Macc. 1. 45. 46. 47. 48. 49. 57.

## 63:19
WE HAVE BECOME AS IN THE BEGINNING, WHEN YOU DID NOT RULE OVER US, NOR WAS YOUR NAME INVOKED OVER US] These are expressed from the Greek: But in the Hebrew and Chaldean the sense is better: We have been from every age: (yours, that is) but you have not ruled over them (the Greeks, that is) nor has your name been pronounced over them: that is, they have never been called the people of God.

He takes these things only concerning the profanation of the sanctuary. Whereas they treat of the trampling and destruction, indeed of the total destruction of the entire ecclesiastical polity of the Jews: as the words themselves sound. Which, so that Grotius may refute it, he brings forward a new version and explanation, entirely alien to the LXX interpreters, Jerome, the Vulgate version, and the common explanation of interpreters. Vatablus rendered the Hebrew text word for word thus: We have become AS of old, over whom you did not rule, and over whom your name was not invoked. Also in this way, as those over whom you have not ruled from the age, (i.e., you have forsaken us O Lord, as those over whom you have never ruled) I say, we have become like those over whom your name was not invoked. That is, who have never been called yours. There is nothing in the text about the Greeks. They are rashly inserted by Grotius, who everywhere sails for his preconceived opinion, and strives to force it into the text.

Latin:

FACTI SUMUS QUASI IN PRINCIPIO, CUM NON DOMINARERIS NOSTRI, NEQUE INVO- CARETUR NOMEN TUUM SUPER NOS] Hæc de Græco expressa sunt: Sed in Hebræo & Chaldæo melior est sensus: Nos fuimus ab omni ævo: (tui scilicet) non an- tem dominatus es illis (Græcis scilicet) neq; pronunciatum est nomen tuum de eis: id est, nunquam vocati sunt Dei populus.

De prophanatione tantum sanctuarii ea acci- pit. Quum de conculcatione & deletione agant, imo de πανωλεθρίᾳ universæ politiæ Ecclesiasti- cæ Judæorum: ut verba ipsa sonant. Quæ ut e- lidat Grotius, novam versionem & explicationem adfert, à LXX. Interpp. Hieronymi, vulgatæ ver- sionis & communi Interpp. explicatione prorsus alienam. Vatablus ad verbum Ebræum textum ita reddidit; Facti sumus UT olim, quibus non do- minabaris, & super quos non invocabatur nomen tuum. Item hoc modo, ut ii quibus à seculo non es dominatus, (q. d. deseruissti nos Domine, ut eos, quibus nunquam fueris dominatus) similes inquam iis facti, super quos non fuit invocatum nomen tuum. Id est, qui tui nunquam vocati sunt. De Græcis nihil est in textu. Temere ingeruntur à Grotio, qui præconceptæ opinioni ubique velificatur, e- amque textui inferre satagit.

## 64:1 Argument
CHAPTER LXIV.

A sighing for the coming of Christ the liberator with a deprecation of guilt, and an imploring of commiseration and grace in calamity, and of miserable desolation.

Verse 1.

O THAT THOU WOULDST REND THE HEAVENS] The discourse of Judas Maccabeus is continued. That לוּ, which this interpreter translates as 'O that', the Greeks took as ἐὰν, and the Chaldean not badly as הֲלוֹא, which is 'is it not', and in the sense of words not of one wishing, but of one indicating, in this manner: Didst not thou (the Chaldean adds 'for our sake') rend the heavens, and descend? From thy face the mountains were melted? As fire makes water boil from branches, so that fire: that thou mightest make thy name manifest to thine enemies, and the nations might tremble before thee? He looks back to the history of those things which God did on Mount Sinai. See Exod. 19, 18. Add Ps. 18, 8. 96, 5. where the Greeks have τὰ ὄρη ὡσεὶ κηρὸς ἐτάκησαν, as here ὡς κηρὸς ἀπὸ πυρὸς τήκεται.

Latin:

CAPUT LXIV.

Suspirium pro adventu Christi liberatoris cum deprecatione culpæ, & imploratione com- miserationis & gratiæ in calamitate, ac de- solationis miserabilis.

Vers. 1.

UTINAM DISRUMPERES CŒLOS] Continua- tur sermo Judæ Maccabæi. Illud לוּ, quod utinam In- terpres hic vertit, Græci ἐὰν, Chaldæus sumpsit non male pro הֲלוֹא, quod est nonne, & verba non optantis, sed indicantis sensu, hunc in modum: Nonne tu (propter nos addit Chal- dæus) dirupisti cælos, & descendisti? à facie tua liquefacti sunt montes? sicut ardente igne ex ramalibus aquas ebullire facit is ignis: ut manifestares nomen tuum hostibus, & coram te formi- darent gentes? Respicit historiam eorum, quæ fecit Deus in monte Sinai. Vide Exod. 19, 18. Adde Ps. 18, 8. 96, 5. ubi Græci habent τὰ ὄρη ὡσεὶ κηρὸς ἐτάκησαν, ut hic ὡς κηρὸς ἀπὸ πυρὸς τήκεται.

## 64:3
Ver. 3. WHEN THOU DIDST TERRIBLE THINGS WE SHALL NOT ABIDE] That is, when thou hast done such wonderful things for our sake, is it not fair that thy help should be patiently awaited by us?

THOU CAMEST DOWN, AND FROM THY FACE THE MOUNTAINS FLOWED DOWN] He repeats what he had said above, so that he may the more impress the matter upon their minds.

We leave the dream concerning the prayer of Judas Maccabeus to Grotius. But it must not be conceded that לוּ 'O that' should be converted into הֲלוֹא 'is it not', with both letters and points changed. By which method the speech is plainly perverted, and from Optative becomes Indicative. Furthermore, most ancient Christian interpreters accepted that optative prayer as a sigh of the Prophet, or of the faithful people for the coming of the Messiah. Let us hear Jerome, explaining the whole passage: O THAT THOU WOULDST REND THE HEAVENS, AND WOULDST COME DOWN. Since enemies have trampled upon thy sanctuary, and we have become as in the beginning, when thy name was not called upon us: therefore we pray and say: O that thou wouldst rend the heavens, and wouldst come down: and that thou, who art always promised, wouldst at length fulfill those promises! This, however, was said at that time, when the Savior had not yet arrived: nor had he assumed man from the virginal womb of our nature and substance, whom he might save: that as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear the image of the heavenly. But if you were to do this, they say, and the heavens were opened, or heaven at the coming of your majesty, the mountains would flow down, or a tremor would seize the mountains: and they would be consumed, just as wax is consumed from the face of the fire. And to Ezekiel and he saw a great vision. But also Moses in the blessings of Deuteronomy prays: May the Lord open to you his good treasure, the heaven, that it may give you a blessing. And in the Gospel, John the Baptist is narrated to have seen the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit descending upon the Lord in the form of a dove. But the MOUNTAINS, which from the coming of the Lord, of whom it is written, GOD is a consuming fire, SHALL BE CONSUMED AND MELT LIKE WAX, are the opposing powers, and all who raise themselves against the knowledge of GOD. Of whom it is also sung in the 96th Psalm: The earth saw and was moved. The mountains melted like wax from the face of the Lord, from the face of the God of all the earth. For if you were to descend, and fulfill your promises, THE WATERS OF THE SEA WOULD WASTE AWAY (according to Symmachus), AND THAT FIRE WOULD CONSUME ALL THEIR SALTNESS. Of which it is also written in another Psalm: As smoke vanishes, let them vanish. As wax is consumed from the face of the fire, so let sinners perish from the face of God: And this is to be noted, that when the waters of the sea shall have been consumed by divine fire, then LET THE NAME OF THE LORD Savior BE MADE KNOWN TO HIS ENEMIES: of whom it is said in the 67th Psalm: The tongue of your dogs from the enemies by him: that whom they had not perceived by benefits, they may recognize by the subversion of their city and their own captivity. AND FROM HIS FACE THE NATIONS SHALL BE TROUBLED, or as it is said more significantly in Hebrew, THEY SHALL BE MOVED, so that those which were previously immovable, MAY COME to salvation, and when HE SHALL HAVE DONE WONDERS and shown signs in the Gospel, which he once showed in Egypt and in the wilderness: they shall confess that they CANNOT BEAR the glory of his coming, or that a tremor (as the LXX have) has seized the mountains. And beautifully according to the Hebrew, as if they had been heard, who had prayed above: O THAT YOU WOULD REND THE HEAVENS AND DESCEND, FROM YOUR FACE THE MOUNTAINS WOULD FLOW DOWN: afterwards they infer: YOU DESCENDED, the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, truly Immanuel, which is interpreted God with us. AND THEREFORE FROM YOUR FACE all the MOUNTAINS FLOWED DOWN. Of which we spoke above. This is Jerome. Gaspar Sanctius, although he asserts in the preceding that the discourse is about the Babylonian captivity, nevertheless teaches that these words look toward the coming of the Messiah, which a great conversion of souls would follow, and explains it thus: In the mountains, he says, it is sufficiently known that proud men or insolent Spirits are understood: because these think themselves to be raised above the rest of the crowd, just as high mountains above a depressed valley. These therefore, when that mountain, which is situated above the summit of all mountains, shall have lowered itself to the depths, and shall have descended to it, so that he is called the last of men by Isaiah; and by David a worm and no man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people, they will cast away (if there is any mind or shame) their arrogant spirits, and will altogether waste away from their inflated Spirit. Waters are called minds, both soft and cold, and which after the delights of the flesh and the remaining blandishments of an intemperate mind thus melt and flow down, just as waters are carried along a sloping place. These, therefore, the fiery power of Christ will cause to effervesce, which inflames minds, just as water boils and seethes from a fire placed beneath; and the moisture being consumed, from which the mind is fluid and slippery, it assumes manly and constant Spirits: So that in water you see nothing less than the nature of water, which the divine spirit burns up, and what is muddy and soft, it brings into the hardness and firmness of iron. FROM YOUR FACE THE NATIONS WOULD BE TROUBLED. Now he explains the Metaphor, and compares the time of Christ and the liberty of the world with the ancient time of Moses and the liberty of the Jewish people. The nations, he says, would be troubled, that is, moved by benefits, or shaken by fear, they would think of better things. For they would fail from themselves, so that as far as possible they might be unraveled, that is, they would put off the old man, namely themselves, and put on the new. Which is to depart from themselves into another nature as it were, so that those who previously had been of the earth earthly, may now begin to be of heaven heavenly. WHEN YOU SHALL HAVE DONE WONDERS, WE SHALL NOT SUSTAIN. Such will be the ardor, such in Christ, when he shall have vibrated the rays of his doctrine, when he shall have produced the admirable proofs of divine power, when by the example of his life, and the holiness of his morals, he shall have brought force almost to the form of a better life to men, so that no one would not succumb to such doctrine, and to such a weight of prodigies. Nor is Cornelius à Lapide entirely alien from this explanation; FROM YOUR FACE THE MOUNTAINS WOULD FLOW DOWN. He alludes to the descent of the Lord on Sinai, when he gave the law to Moses and the Hebrews, in which that mountain trembled and was as it were melted before the Lord, from a certain mute and natural reverence for God, Ex. 19, 18. The whole mountain of Sinai, he says, was smoking, for the reason that the Lord God had descended upon it in fire, and smoke ascended from it as from a furnace. Indeed, the Apostle teaches that Mount Sinai was shaken by an earthquake, Heb. 12, 26. and the Psalmist in Psalm 67, 9. For this descent of the Lord to the Hebrews was a type of the descent of Christ to men, who softens and bends the mountains, that is, the proud hearts of mortals, by the power of his grace, as well as of his example, to humility, patience, and every virtue, so that they seem to be dissolved and melted. Thus St. Jerome and Tertullian, book on the Resurrection of the flesh, chap. 26. St. Justin, and from him Leo Castrius, who teaches that all these things were fulfilled both in the Baptism of Christ and at Pentecost: for then, by the face of Christ and the Holy Spirit, the proud hearts of the Jews were softened and melted, and they accepted the faith of Christ preached by the Apostles: then also the waters, that is, their cold and sluggish hearts, as well as those of the Apostles, burned with the fire of charity: then the nations were troubled, when, hearing the preaching of the Gospel, they condemned their infidelity and former ways through fear of God and hell; and, being pricked in heart, they entered upon a new and pious life, so that from earthly they might become heavenly. This is Cornelius, who likewise explains the following verses concerning the coming of Christ, nay, he brings forward very many authors for this opinion at verse 4. For concerning the incarnation, he says, and the present life of Christ, and of the Christians to be converted to him, he has treated thus far, and St. Paul 1 Cor. 2:9, and St. Jerome, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius accept it concerning that. Anselm likewise, as well as Adam, Forerius, Leo Castrius, and Sanchez here, likewise Tertullian, Cyprian, Tatian, Theophilus of Antioch, etc. Similarly Hector Pintus, Tirinus, Menochius, and others. From the Reformed, the Dutch Paraphrasts; from our own, Pappus, and the Weimar Paraphrasts. Lyranus, Alexander of Hales, and Zwingli indeed explain it concerning the coming of Christ, but refer it to the second coming. Oecolampadius, although he goes in a different direction here, nevertheless acknowledges that Paul in 1 Cor. 2 explains these things concerning Christ. For the Apostle, he says, teaching how we have received the Spirit of God, which supplies the knowledge of such great mysteries, so that it can even make foolish the wisdom of the world, wishes the desire of the Prophet and of the pious to be heard, having received the Holy Spirit, and thus that Christ did not do lesser but greater things through the word of the cross than formerly on Mount Sinai. Wherefore others also explain it in this sense as having been desired with ineffable longings, the coming of Christ and the kingdom of the Church. But if the Apostle interpreted these things in this way, how can a gloss different from his own explanation be proven? But that will have to be examined now.

Latin:

Vers. 3. CUM FECERIS MIRABILIA NON SU- STINEBIMUS] Id est, cum tam mira nostri causa feceris, nonne æquum est, tuam opem à nobis patienter exspe- ctari?

DESCENDISTI, ET A FACIE TUA MON- TES DEFLUXERUNT] Repetit quod supra dixerat, quo magis rem inculcet animis.

SOmnium de oratione Judæ Maccabæi Grotio relinquimus. Non autem concedendum erit, ut לוּ utinam convertatur in הֲלוֹא annon, mutatis & literis & punctis. Quo pacto pervertitur plane oratio, & ex Optativa sit Indicativa. Cæterum In- terpretes Christiani veteres optativam illam ora- tionem pleriq; acceperunt, ceu suspirium Prophe- tæ, aut populi fidelis pro adventu Messiæ. Audia- mus Hieronymum, locum integrum enarrantem: UTINAM DISRUMPERES COELOS, ET DESCENDERES. Quoniam hostes nostris con- culcaverunt sanctuarium tuum, & facti sumus qua- si in principio, quando non invocabatur nomen tuum super nos: propterea deprecamur & dici- mus: utinam disrumperes cœlos, & descenderes: & qui semper promitteris, ea aliquando promissa compleres! Hoc autem eo tempore dicebatur, quan- do nec dum salvator advenerat: nec de utero virgina- li natura nostræ atq; substantiæ assumpferat hominem, quem salvaret: ut sicut portavimus imaginem terre- ni, portemus imaginem supercœlestis. Quod si fa- ceres, inquiunt, & aperirentur cœli, sive cœlum ad adventum majestatis tuæ, montes defluerent, vel tremor apprehenderet montes: & consume- ren-tur, sicut cera à facie ignis consumitur. Et Ezechie- li aperti sunt cœli, & vidit visionem magnam. Sed & Moyses in Deuteronomii benedictionibus impreca- tur: Aperiat tibi Dominus thesaurum suum bo- num cœlum, ut det tibi benedictionem. Et in Evangelio Baptista Johannes vidisse narratur cœlos apertos, & Spiritum Sanctum super Dominum in specie columbæ descendentem. MONTES au- tem, qui ab adventu Domini, de quo scriptum est, DEUS ignis consumens est, INSTAR CERÆ CONSUMENTUR ET LIQUEFIENT, ad- versariæ potestates sunt, & omnes qui se erigunt ad- versum scientiam DEI. De quibus & in 96. Psalmo canitur: Vidit & commota est terra. Montes li- quefacti sunt, sicut cera à facie Domini, à facie Dei universæ terræ. Si enim tu descenderes, & tua pro- missa compleres, TABESCERENT (juxta Sym- machum) AQUÆ MARIS, ET OMNEM SALSUGINEM EARUM IGNIS ILLE CON- SUMERET. De quo & in alio Psalmo scriptum est: Sicut deficit fumus, deficiant. Sicut con- sumitur cera à facie ignis, sic pereant peccatores à facie Dei: Et hoc notandum, quod cum aquæ ma- ris divino fuerint igne consumtæ, tunc NOTUM FIAT NOMEN DOMINI Salvatoris INIMI- CIS ejus: de quibus in 67. Psalmo dicitur: Lingua canum tuorum ex inimicis ab ipso: ut quem bene- ficiis non senserant, urbis suæ subversione & propria captivitate cognoscant. ET A FACIE illius GENTES TURBABUNTUR, sive ut signifi- cantius in Ebræo dicitur, MOVEBUNTUR, ut quæ prius immobiles erant, VENIANT ad salutem, cumque MIRABILIA FECERIT & ostenderit si- gna in Evangelio, quæ quondam ostendit in Ægypto & in solitudine: confitebuntur se gloriam adventus e- jus FERRE NON POSSE, sive quod tremor (ut LXX. habent) apprehenderit montes. Pulchrèq; jux- ta Hebraicum, quasi exauditi essent, qui supra fuerant deprecati: UTINAM DISRUMPERES COE- LOS ET DESCENDERES, A FACIE TUA MONTES DEFLUERENT: postea inferunt: DESCENDISTI, verbum caro factum es & habi- tasti in nobis, vere Immanuel, quod interpretatur nobiscum Deus. ET IDEO A FACIE TUA omnes MONTES DEFLUXERUNT. De quibus supra diximus. Hæc Hieronymus. Gaspar Sanctius, etsi in superioribus de Babylonica ca- ptivitate sermonem esse asseruerit, hæc tamen verba adventum Messiæ respicere, quem magna a- nimorum conversio sequutura sit, docet atque ita explicat: In montibus, inquit, principes viros aut Spi- ritus insolentes intelligi, satis est notum: quia hi su- pra reliquam turbam attolli se putant, sicut excelsi montes super depressam vallem. Hi ergo ubi mons il- le, qui supra montium omnium verticem situs est, se ad ima depresserit, eog; descenderit, ut novissimus vi- rorum dicatur ab Esaia; & à Davide vermis & non homo, opprobrium hominum & abjectio ple- bis, abjicient (si quid mentis aut pudoris est) arro- gantes animos, & ab inflato Spiritu omnino tabescent. Aquæ dicuntur animi, & molles & frigidi, & qui post carnis delitias & reliqua intemperantis animi blandimenta sic liquescunt & defluunt, sicut per decli- vem locum feruntur aquæ. Has ergo effervescere fa- ciet vis Christi ignea, quæ mentes inflammat, sicut aqua exæstuat, ac fervet ab igne subjecto; & consum- pto humore, à quo animus fluxus est & lubricus, Spi- ritus assumit viriles & constantes : Ita ut in aqua ni- hil minus videas quam aquæ naturam, quam divinus spiritus exurit, & quod luteum est & molle, in ferri duritiem & firmitatem adducit. A FACIE TUA GENTES TURBARENTUR. Jam explicat Metaphoram, & tempus Christi libertatisq́; mundi cum antiquo tempore Moysis & populi Judaici liber- tate componit. Gentes, inquit, turbarentur, id est, adductæ beneficiis, vel metu concussæ meliora co- gitarent. Deficerent enim à se ipsis, ut quoad fieri posset, retexerentur, id est, veterem exuerent ho- minem, nempe seipsos, & novum induerent. Quod est à seipsis abire in aliam quasi naturam, ut qui prius fuerant de terra terreni, incipiant jam esse de cælo cæ- lestes. CUM FECERIS MIRABILIA, NON SUSTINEBIMUS. Is erit ardor, eavis in Christo, cum doctrinæ suæ radios vibraverit, cum admiranda ediderit divinæ virtutis documenta, cum vitæ exem- plo, morumq́; sanctitate vim prope ad melioris vitæ formam hominibus attulerit, ut nemo tali doctrinæ, & tanto prodigiorum ponderi non succumbat. Neque a- lienus est plane ab hac explicatione Cornelius à Lapide; A FACIE TUA MONTES DE- FLUERENT. Alludit ad descensum Domini in Sina, cum legem dedit Mosi & Hebræis, in quo mons ille contremuit & quasi liquefactus est coram Domi- no, ex muta & naturali quadam Dei reverentia, Ex. 19, 18. Totus, inquit, mons Sinai fumabat, eo quod descendisset Dominus Deus super eum in igne, & ascenderet fumus ex eo quasi de fornace. Quin ex terræ motu concussum fuisse montem Sina docet Apo- stolus Hebr. 12, 26. & Psaltes Psalmo 67, 9. Hic enim descensus Domini ad Hebræos typus erat descensus Christi ad homines, qui montes, id est, superba morta- lium corda, vi gratiæ suæ, æque ac exempli sui, emollit & inflectit ad humilitatem, patientiam & omnem virtutem, ut solvi & liquari videantur. Ita S. Hie- ronymus & Tertull. lib. de Resurrectione carnis. cap. 26. S. Justinus, & ex eo Leo Castrius, qui hæc omnia impleta docet tum in Baptismo Christi, tum in Pente- coste: tunc enim à facie Christi & Spiritus Sancti, su- perba Judæorum corda, mollita & liquata sunt, fi- demq́; Christi ab Apostolis prædicatam susceperunt: tunc etiam aquæ, id est, frigida & torpida eorum, æque ac Apostolorum corda, igne charitatis arserunt: tunc gentes turbatæ sunt, cum audientes prædicatio- nem Evangelii, metu Dei & inferni damnarunt suam infidelitatem & mores pristinos; ac compuncta no- vam piamq́; vitam inierunt, ut ex terrestribus fierent cœlestes. Hæc Cornelius, qui sequentia de adventu Christi itidem exponit, imo in eam sententiam plu- rimos autores adducit ad v. 4. Nam de incarnatione, inquit, & præsenti vita Christi, & Christianorum ad eum convertendorum, hactenus egit, de eaq́; accipiunt S. Paulus 1. Cor. 2, 9. & S. Hieron. Chrysost. Theophy- lact. Oecum. Anshelmus itidem, atq́; Adamus, Forerius, Leo Castrius & Sanchez hic, item Tertull. Cyprian. Tatianus, Theophilus Antioch. &c. Similiter Hector Pintus, Tirinus, Menochius, aliiq́;. E Reformatis Pa- raphrastæ Batavi, è nostris Pappus, Paraphrastæ Vi- narienses. Lyranus, Alexan. ab Ales, & Zwinglius de Christi adventu quidem explicant, sed ad se- cundum adventum referunt. Oecolampadius etsi in alia omnia hic eat, agnoscit tamen Paulum 1. Cor. 2. hæc de Christo explicare. Docens enim, inquit, Apostolus, quomodo spiritum Dei acceperimus, tanto- rum mysteriorum cognitionem suppeditantem, ut & mundi sapientiâ infatuare queat, exauditum vult Pro- phetæ atq́; piorum desiderium, accepto spiritu Sancto, atq́; adeo non minora sed ampliora fecisse Christum per verbum crucis, quam olim in monte Sina. Qua- propter & alii in hunc sensum exponunt ineffabilibus desideriis optatum fuisse Christi adventum & Ecclesiæ regnum. Si autem Apostolus hæc ita interpretatus est, quomodo diversa ab ejusdem explicatione glossa probari potest? Sed de eo jam dispicien- dum erit.

## 64:4
Ver. 4.

FROM OF OLD THEY HAVE NOT HEARD, NOR PERCEIVED WITH EARS: THE EYE HAS NOT SEEN, O GOD, BESIDE THEE, WHAT THOU HAST PREPARED FOR THOSE WHO WAIT FOR THEE] The Greeks express the simplest sense here, by following which one may translate this passage thus: Never has it been heard, never, I say, perceived by ears, never has it been manifest to eyes that there is any God beside thee, who does such things for those who trust in him. There is no one who has seen the gods of the Gentiles provide such things for their own; indeed, there is no one who has heard even by probable authority anything of the sort about them.

But this is a gloss clearly different from the mind and interpretation of the Apostle. He is not comparing God with the gods of the Gentiles, nor is he speaking of the miracles which God performed for the sake of the Israelites, or of the wonders on Mount Sinai: if that were the Prophet's meaning, the passage would be brought forward by the Apostle in 1 Cor. 2 entirely beside the point. But Grotius, unconcerned about that, only strives to twist everything to fit a preconceived opinion. Indeed, when we turn over the Annotations of Grotius on the Pauline Epistles, one must marvel at the most vain and inept fabrication of this man, by which he has attempted to escape the authority of Paul. He pretends, namely, that Paul did not derive his sentiment in 1 Cor. 2:9 from the present passage of Isaiah—which is the constant opinion of all interpreters, as the very comparison proves—but from the writings of I know not which Rabbis, and that these had the same from an ancient tradition, or from the Apocrypha of Elias, which have now perished. Here, therefore, Grotius preferred to take refuge in the Apocrypha of Elias and the Rabbis rather than grant a place to the manifest truth, even though he acknowledges that the sense of the things which Paul alleges is found in Isaiah; as if, indeed, the Holy Spirit in the New Testament ever looked to anything other than Canonical Scripture with the phrase καθὼς γέγραπται, or anywhere, when he says, 'as it is written,' or uses a similar phrase, pointed his finger at the writings of the Rabbis or at an Apocryphal book. This could be taught by no example, and has been unheard of in the Church until now, unless I am entirely mistaken. But I will transcribe the entire passage of Grotius, so that I may not seem to have attributed these things to him: ὃ ὀφθαλμὸς ὀυκ εἶδε, καὶ ὄυς ὀυκ ἤκουσε, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου ὀυκ ἀνέβη, ἅ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἀυτόν. The sense indeed is in Isaiah 64:4, where the Greeks have: ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος ὀυκ ἠκούσαμεν, ὀδὲ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἡμῶν εἶδον θεὸν πλὴν σ̃υ καὶ τὰ ἔργα σου, ἅ ποιήσεις τοῖς ὑπομένωσιν ἔλεος. The Rabbis also explain these words as referring to the other life in a more arcane sense: but since Origen, Jerome in his work to Pammachius on the best kind of interpreting, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, and Gregory Syncellus report that the very words which Paul uses here existed in the Apocrypha of Elias, it is entirely credible that Paul derived this from the writings of the Rabbis, who had them from ancient tradition: concerning which kind of sayings, see what we have brought forward at Matt. 27:9. Chrysostom says in this place that many ancient books have perished: Jerome has already refuted what he brings forward from Origen in this place, and has at the same time exposed the fruit of such commentaries, whence it is helpful to repeat them here, if by chance anyone is delighted by these trifles of a great trifler. He says: 'The Apostle Paul, as a Hebrew of Hebrews, assumes a paraphrase of this testimony from authentic books in the Epistle which he writes to the Corinthians: not rendering word for word, which he entirely disdains to do, but expressing the truth of the meanings which he uses for that which he wished to strengthen.' Whence let the ravings of the apocryphal books be silent, which are thrust upon the Churches of Christ on the occasion of this testimony. Of which it can truly be said that the Devil sits in ambush with the rich, in the apocrypha, so that he may kill the innocent. And again, he lies in wait in the apocryphal book as a lion in his den: he lies in wait to seize the poor. For the Ascension of Isaiah and the Apocalypse of Elias have this testimony. And by this occasion, many such thorns, and the deceived little women of Lusitania, burdened with sins, who are led by various desires, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth, were led to accept the monstrosities of names such as Basilides, Balsamus, and Thesaurus, and also Barbelion and Lenfibora, and the rest. Concerning whom the Apostolic man Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons and martyr, writes most diligently, explaining the many heresies of Origen: and especially those of the Gnostics, which, through the Egyptian Marcus, first deceived the noble women of the Gauls around the Rhone, and then those of the Spains, mixing pleasure with fables, and claiming for their own ignorance the name of knowledge. But having dismissed Grotius, whom we judge unworthy of further refutation here, we do not deny that different opinions occur concerning the sense of the Apostolic allegation. But two of them are the principal ones. The first is that those words deal with gifts divinely prepared for the faithful, and indeed with eternal happiness and glory. This is confirmed both by the evidence of the words, because the discourse is about those things which God has prepared for those who wait for him, i.e., the faithful, and indeed such things as no mortal has seen, heard, or comprehended with the mind, such as are the goods of the future life, as they far surpass every sense, every intellect, and every natural concept: and also by the coherence of the text, for this is not foreign, since the Prophet, dealing with the incarnation of Christ, flies forward to those things which were obtained through the same; and the eternal glory of the faithful of Christ is the term, end, and effect of the incarnation of Christ. Thus St. Jerome.

The second is that it concerns the mode and manner and οἰκονομία of the preparation of grace and the glory of the faithful through Christ: which does not exclude the former, but includes it. Which it is permitted to confirm first and chiefly from the explanation of the Apostolic [writings]. For this is sufficiently clear in this opinion. Indeed, it does not easily admit another sense. Since in that second chapter of the first to the Corinthians and a great part of the first chapter, it treats of that divine οἰκονομία in Christ, of the wisdom of God, which shines forth in this mystery, which although it may be mere foolishness to the Gentiles and a scandal to the Jews, yet to the faithful it is the wisdom and power of God, besides which wisdom Paul wished to know nothing else, just as he had demonstrated from Jer. 9 that the faithful ought not to glory in any other thing. Which wisdom he calls hidden from the princes of worldly wisdom, which neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has the human heart ever comprehended, because the natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him and he cannot understand them. But which wisdom God revealed to the Apostles through His Spirit, and which they themselves delivered in words which the Holy Spirit teaches. For that this discourse is about this wisdom shines forth more clearly than the sun from the whole chapter. Let the immediate coherence of the words be weighed first. We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory: which none of the princes of this age knew. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But as it is written, that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love Him. A distinction is made here manifestly between the glory, to which that hidden wisdom is directed, inasmuch as God predestined it unto glory, and the wisdom, which God predestined to that end before the ages; and that wisdom It is called ἀποκεκρυμμένη, hidden, not known to the princes of the world, which if the princes of the people, the Pharisees, the Priests, had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But they did not know: because it is written, eye has not seen; ear has not heard, etc. Whence it is ὀφθαλμοφανῶς evident that that most wise economy of salvation in Christ and through Christ was predestined by God from eternity, that which no eye has seen, ear has not heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man. Which Caspar Sanctius also observed in this place, having brought forward the words of the Apostle already cited, adding these: Which words if anyone weighs attentively, he will surely find, unless he wishes to offer violence to himself and to the text, that the discourse is about Christ; for he treats of that wisdom which, because the princes were ignorant of it, they delivered the Lord of glory to death: but that wisdom, which is said to be in a mystery, is Christ. But why they did not know that wisdom, that is, Christ, Paul teaches, because it is written, indeed, in this place of Isaiah, eye has not seen, etc. Hence I seem to myself to gather that the discourse here is about Christ rather than about the happiness of the blessed. Then it is confirmed by the perspicuity of the Prophetic words. For the discourse is about those things which from the age they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears: eye has not seen. Which are primarily mysteries concerning Christ. Inasmuch as they are ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν τῆς κτιστῆς φύσεως, as Justin says. Then the Apostle himself exclaims, confessedly great is the mystery of godliness, 1 Tim. 3:16. And Peter testifies that the Angels desired to παρακύψαι, 1 Epist. 1:10, concerning which also St. Paul, 1 Cor. 2, says that they are σοφία Θεοῦ ἐν μυστηρίῳ ἡ ἀποκεκρυμμένη & τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος θεοῦ v. 6 & 14, and also c. 1:18. The word of the cross is to them that perish foolishness, to us who are saved the power of God, v. 25. τὸ μῶρον τοῦ θεοῦ σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐστί. The Prophet speaks of those things which no one heard or saw except Christ. For he addressed Christ here, O that you would rend the heavens. He alone manifested these things to us: No one has seen God at any time: the only begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him, ἐξηγήσατο, 1 John 1:14. No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him, Matt. 11:27. Therefore the Son of God, as the interpreter of the will of God, and the herald and Evangelist of these mysteries, was sent into the world, and anointed with the Spirit of God, Isa. 61:1, that he might announce them. Who, John 3:11, testifies that he has heard and seen those things which, to wit, the ear has not heard, the eye has not seen except him. Which he also revealed to the Apostles through the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Apostle says that he has the MIND OF CHRIST, 1 Cor. 2:16. The discourse is about those things which Christ prepared for those who wait for him, i.e., was about to prepare, because in the prophetic manner future things are expressed in the past, for the sake of preparing which he had to descend from heaven. But lest anyone say that these things do not pertain to the mysteries concerning the mode of salvation, but to the salvation itself prepared for us by Christ, it must be known that Christ not only prepared salvation for us, but also all things that make for salvation. For all things have been prepared through him. Therefore the entire economy of salvation is expressed thus, πάντα ἕτοιμα ALL THINGS ARE PREPARED, Matt. 22:4, ἅ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ Θεός. Which the Apostle said before were predestined before the ages by God, so that, to wit, they might be prepared by Christ for our glory, 1 Cor. 2:7. For he had to prepare for us the remission of sins, true righteousness, saving faith, and all things that pertain to salvation, and therefore salvation itself, and as the Apostle spoke a little before, 1. Cor. 1:30, he had to become for us from God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, that he who glories, may glory in the Lord, who does or prepares mercy, judgment, and righteousness in the earth, Jer. 9:24. Christ prepares us for himself as a people, Luke 1:17, that we may be rendered ready for every good work, ἑτοῖμοι, Tit. 3:1, 2 Tim. 2:21; he prepares us as his bride, Ap. 21:2. He prepares for us good things, not only of glory but also of grace. Because from him, in him, through him are all things that pertain to our salvation. And the Apostle himself explains what those things are which God has prepared for us, which no one has known, nor any eye has seen, which indeed God revealed to the Apostles through the Holy Spirit, that they might know τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ χαρισθέντα ἡμῖν, which are given to us by God, 1 Cor. 2:12. And therefore all the gifts and goods of grace are comprehended in those things which have been prepared for us by Christ. Thirdly, this opinion is confirmed from the connection and cohesion of the words. For it treats of those things which he performed when he rent the heavens and descended from the heavens, that the mountains might flow down at his presence. Primarily spiritual enemies, who are great mountains, for the sake of destroying whom he came, 1 John 3:8, and that all nations might be converted to him, when he did wonderful, or glorious things, as the LXX Interpreters have, not only by performing bodily miracles, which run into the senses, but primarily by wonderfully delivering us from the power of Satan, sin, death and hell, by overcoming and defeating our enemies with wonderful power and an admirable method, concerning which the preceding chapter LXIII had treated. In which the economy of salvation truly hidden and admirable consists. Fourthly, those things which follow in the Prophet pertain to this: YOU MET HIM THAT REJOICES AND WORKS RIGHTEOUSNESS, BEHOLD YOU ARE ANGRY: Which some explain thus: You met the nations rejoicing in you, but you are angry with us. It certainly pertains to the admirable economy of divine grace that Christ prepared grace and salvation for those who wait for and love him, who receive him through faith, and that he meets him who rejoices and works righteousness, or who works with joy, who rejoice in his grace and coming, and believe in him and embrace his righteousness. Similarly Menochius explains that he met the Gentiles embracing him with joy. Fifthly, the consensus of certain Interpreters is added: Sanctius in this opinion praises Jerome, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius and Primasius on Paul, as also certain Greek Scholia, likewise from his own, Gagnejus, Forerius and Leo Castrius on Isaiah. Nor does he think Cyril's words are inconsistent, just as he does not think Procopius's are. Thus Chrysostom on 1 Cor. 2: What need is there to speak of the princes of this age, when no man, no heavenly power knows these things? What are those things? Because through that which seems to be the foolishness of preaching, he will overcome the world, and the nations will be enticed, and there will be a reconciliation of God to men, and such great goods will come to us. How then did we know, he says? Through the Spirit. And Theodoret: Since he mentions the ignorance of the Jews, and said that the mystery of the economy was revealed, he necessarily added that neither has any heard, nor ever seen, nor has an insatiable mind conceived what the God of all has prepared for those who ardently love him. Similarly Theophylact on the passage of the Apostle: What has he prepared for those who worship him? Namely, the knowledge of Christ and the salvation which has been sought for us through his incarnation. These things indeed neither has the human eye inspected, etc. Among the Papists, besides Sanctius, Estius defends this opinion in his notes on this passage. This sentence is commonly brought forward to teach that the goods which have been prepared for the elect in the kingdom of heaven are incomprehensible. But the Apostle Paul indicates another sense to us. For he refers it to the mysteries of the Christian religion; namely, those things which before Christ lay hidden and were obscurely contained in the Law, in the Psalms, and in the Prophets, but after Christ were manifested to believers, through the ministry of the Apostles. And he thinks it is manifest from the Apostolic text that this sentiment does not pertain properly to the goods of the future age, but to the mysteries of the Christian faith. In his commentary on 1 Cor. 2, he has it thus: The sense, however, is of this kind; but we speak those things which, according to the Prophet, were neither seen by the eyes of men, nor heard by ears, nor thought of by the mind, that is, known to no men at all; namely, those things which God prepared and predestined for those who love and wait for Him. These are the salvation and glory of adoption and eternal happiness, to be procured by such a wonderful order of divine wisdom. For the Prophet in that place treats of the benefits of Christ, of which these are the chief. Nor is Calvin a stranger to this sentiment: He discusses in that place the doctrine of the Gospel, which he shows to surpass the comprehension of human genius. For it contains knowledge quite foreign and remote from the sense of our flesh: In short, it is a secret wisdom. Whence it happens that Paul is deservedly carried away into admiration of it, and as the Prophet, weighing with himself the admirable benefits of God, exclaims as if astonished that nothing such had ever been heard: so in the most excellent of all benefits, where namely Christ is offered to us through the Gospel, one may exclaim in the same manner, Lord, what You provide for Your people is greater than any grasp of human genius: no eye, no ear, no sense, no mind can reach to such a height. Therefore, Paul adapts this passage excellently to his own argument, nor does he abuse the Prophet's sentiment while he places the peculiar grace with which God deigns to honor His Church above the world. Pareus is clearer on 1 Cor. 2. WHAT EYE HAS NOT SEEN. A periphrasis of Evangelical wisdom. For instead of what he could have said, but we preach such wisdom as the eye has not seen, and which God prepared for those who love Him: he says in the words of Scripture, we preach those things which the eye has not seen, and which God has prepared. Who nevertheless teaches how both sentiments can be joined. He describes, he says, that wisdom both from its nature, because it is not naturally grasped by anyone through sensual or mental knowledge, and from its salutary effect, because it is concerning heavenly and eternal goods, prepared for those who love God. He joins these two to declare what he had said in verse 7, that the wisdom of God is hidden in a mystery: and predetermined by God for our glory. For what is this glory? Which God prepared for us in the heavens: The glory, namely, of eternal life, with which the Lord of glory, Christ Himself, shines in the heavens: and which He promised to His own. To whom? Not to the princes of the world, who crucified Him, who hate Him, who persecute Him in the world: but to those who love Him, that is, believers, as Ambrose expressly interprets. Finally, Blessed Gerhard does not oppose this explanation, but joins both in his Loci Communes on eternal life, number 48. It is possible, he says, for both interpretations to be conveniently joined. For the doctrine of the Gospel itself is wisdom hidden from all human reason, and the goods offered in the Gospel exceed all sense, experience, and natural thought, and those things which Christ did and suffered for us, in order to acquire those goods, are more sublime than all human thought. Which is certainly better than to say with others that the Apostle abused the testimony of the Prophet, or twisted it into another meaning, or to have recourse to the Apocrypha with Grotius. We do not deny that eternal salvation is looked at here, but that which was to be prepared by the wonderful economy of divine wisdom, which no one knew, and which was revealed to the Apostles through the Holy Spirit. For the goods of eternal life were not revealed there, which the Apostle brings forward concerning them were unspeakable words.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

A SECULO NON AUDIERUNT, NEQUE AURIBUS PERCEPERUNT: OCULUS NON VIDIT DEUS ABSQUE TE, QUÆ PRÆPARASTI EXPE- cTANTIBUS] Sensum simplicissimum hic Græci expri- munt, quem sequendo licet hunc locum sic vertere: Nun- quam auditum est, nunquam, inquam, auribus perceptum, nunquam oculis patuit esse Deum præter te, ullum qui in se con- fidentibus talia faciat. Nemo est qui viderit Deos Gentium talia suis præstare, imo nemo est, qui vel probabili autori- tate tale aliquid de illis audierit.

Hæc vero plane diversa glossa est à mente, & interpretatione Apostoli. Non comparat Deum cum gentiumDiis,non de miraculis, quæ Israelita- rum causa fecit Deus, aut de miris in monte Sinai agit: Quæ si Prophetæ mens esset, prorsus utique præter rem locus ab Apostolo 1. Cor. 2. adducere- tur. Sed Grotius de eo nihil solicitus, id tantum agit, ut ad præconceptam opinionem detorqueat omnia. Ipsa vero ubi revolvimus Annotata Gro- tii ad Epistolas Paulinas, mirari oportet vanissi- mum & ineptissimum hujus commentum,quo au- ctoritatem Paulinam effugere conatus est. Fingit nempe, non ex Esaiæ præsenti loco, quæ constans est omnium Interpp. sententia, quam ipsa collatio comprobat, sed ex scriptis, nescio quibus, Rabbi- norum Paulum sententiam suam 1. Cor. 2, 9. de- promsisse, hos vero eandem habuisse è veteri tradi- tione, vel Apocryphis Eliæ,quæ jam interierunt. Hic ergo confugere ad Apocrypha Eliæ & ad Rabbi- nos maluit Grotius, quam veritati apertæ locum concedere, etsi agnoscat sensum eorum, quæ Pau- lus allegat,apud Esaiam haberi; Quasi vero uspiam Spiritus Sanctus in Novo Testamento voce καθὼς γέγραπται ad aliam,quam ad CanonicamScriptu- ram respiciat,aut ullibi, cum ait, sicut scriptum est, aut simili voce utitur, ad scripta Rabbinorum, aut ad Apocryphum librum digitum intendat. Quod nullo exemplo doceri poterit,& inauditum hacte- nus in Ecclesia,nisi me omnia fallunt, fuit. Sed ad- scribam locum integrum Grotii,ne hæc ei affinxif- se videar, ὃ ὀφθαλμὸς ὀυκ εἶδε, καὶ ὄυς ὀυκ ἤκουσε, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου ὀυκ ἀνέβη, ἅ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἀυτόν. Sensus quidem est apudEsaiam 64, 4. ubi Græci: ἀπὸ τ τοῦ αἰῶνος ὀυκ ἠκούσαμεν, ὀδὲ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἡμῶν εἶδον θεὸν πλὴν σ̃υ καὶ τὰ ἔργα σου, ἅ ποιήσεις τοῖς ὑπομένωσιν ἔλεος. Quæ verba etiam Rabbini de vita altera exponunt sensu arcanio- re: sed cum ipsa verba, quibus hic utitur Paulus, ex- stitisse in Apocryphis Eliæ tradat Origenes, Hieronymus ad Pammachium de optimo genere interpretandi, Za- charias Chrysopolitanus, & Gregorius Syncellus, cre- dibile omnino est, deprompsisse hoc Paulum ex scriptis Rabbinorum, qui ea habuerunt ex traditione veteri: de quo genere dictorum vide quæ attulimus ad Matth. 27, 9. Multos veteres libros periisse dicit hoc lo- co Chrysostomus: Quæ ex Origene adducit, pro- fligavit jam Hieronymus in h. l. qui fructum simul talium commentorum exposuit, unde juvat ea hic repetere, si quis forte istis nugis magni Nugonis delectetur. Paraphrasin, inquit, hujus testimo- nii, quasi Hebræus ex Hebræis assumit Apostolus Paulus de authenticis libris in Epistola, quam scribit ad Corinthios: non verbum ex verbo reddens, quod facere omnino contemnit, sed sensuum exprimens veritatem, quibus utitur ad id, quod voluit robo- randum. Unde apocryphorum deliramenta conticescant, quæ ex occasione hujus testimonii inge- runtur Ecclesiis Christi. De quibus vere dici potest, quod sedeat Diabolus in insidiis cum divitibus, in Apocryphis, ut interficiat innocentem. Et iterum, insidiatur in Apocrypho quasi leo in spelunca sua: in- sidiatur, ut rapiat pauperem. Ascensio enim E- saiæ & Apocalypsis Heliæ hoc habent testimonium. Et per hanc occasionem, multæq; hujusmodi spina- rum, & Lusitaniæ deceptæ sunt mulierculæ, oneratæ peccatis, quæ ducuntur desideriis variis, semper discen- tes, & nunquam ad scientiam veritatis pervenientes: ut Basilidis, Balsami atq;, Thefauri, Barbelionis quoq; & Lenfiboræ, ac reliquorum nominum portenta susci- perent. De quibus diligentissime vir Apostolicus scri- bit Hirenæus Episcopus Lugdunensis & martyr, mul- tarum explicans Origenes Hæreseon: & maxime Gnosticorum, quæ per Maxum Ægyptium, Gallia- rum primum circa Rhodanum, deinde Hispaniarum nobiles fœminas deceperunt, miscentes fabulis volu- ptatem, & imperitiæ suæ nomen scientiæ suæ vendi- cantes. Misso autem Grotio, quem hic ulteriore refutatione indignum judicamus, de sensu allega- tionis Apostolicæ non diffitemur diversas occur- rerefententias. Duæ autem earum præcipuæ sunt. Prior est, quod verbis illis agatur de donis divinitus præparatis fidelibus, & quidem de æterna felicitate & gloria. Quæ confirmatur tam è verborum evi- dentia, quia sermo est de iis, quæ præparavit Deus expectantibus sese, h. e. fidelibus, & quidem tali- bus, quæ nemo mortalium vidit, audivit aut mente comprehendit, qualia sunt bona futuræ vitæ, utpo- te omnem sensum, omnem intellectum, omnem naturalem conceptum longe exsuperantia: tam è textus cohærentia, hæc enim aliena non est, siqui- dem Propheta de Christi incarnatione agens, ad ea, quæ per eandem parta sunt, avolet; gloria autem fidelium Christi æterna est terminus, finis & effe- ctus incarnationis Christi. Ita S. Hieronymus.

Altera est, quod agatur de modo & ratione ac οἰκονομίᾳ præparationis gratiæ, & gloriæ fidelium per Christum: quæ priorem non excludit, sed com- prehendit. Quam confirmare licet primo ac præ- cipue ex Apostolicæ explicatione. Hæc enim lucu- lenta satis est in hac sententia. Imo alium non ad- mittit facile sensum. Siquidem isto capite secundo prioris ad Corinthios & magnam partem capitis pri- mi agitur de illa οἰκονομίᾳ divina in Christo, de sa- pientia Dei, quæ in hoc mysterio elucet, quæ etsi Gentibus stultitia, Judæis scandalum merum sit, fide- libus tamen sapientia & virtus Dei est, præter quam sapientiam nihil aliud scire volebat Paulus, uti neq; fideles in ulla alia re gloriari debere, è Jer. 9. de- monstraverat. Quam sapientiam absconditam di- cit principibus sapientiæ mundanæ, quam neq́; ocu- lus viderit, neq́; auris audiverit, neq́; cor humanum comprehenderit unquam, quia animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei, stultitia illi sunt & non potest intelligere. Quam vero sapientiam Deus Apostolis per spiritum suum patefecit, quamque ipsi tradidêre verbis, quæ Spiritus Sanctus docet. De hac sapientia enim sermonem esse ex toto capite Sole clarius effulget. Expendatur imprimis verborum immediata cohærentia. Loquimur Dei sapientiam in mysterio, quæ abscondita est, quam prædestinavit Deus ante secula in gloriam nostram: quam nemo principum hujus seculi cognovit. Si enim cognovis- sent, nunquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. Sed sicut scriptum est, quod oculus non vidit, nec auris au- divit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quæ præparavit Deus iis, qui diligunt illum. Distinguitur hic manifeste inter gloriam, ad quam directa est sapien- tia illa abscondita, utpote quam prædestinavit Deus in gloriam, & sapientiam, quam Deus ea fini ante secula prædestinavit; & sapientia illa dicitur ἀποκεκρυμμένη, abscondita, non cognita Principibus seculi, quam si cognovissent principes populi, Pharisæi, Sacerdotes, nunquam Domi- num gloriæ crucifixissent. Sed non cognovêre: quia scriptum, oculus non vidit; auris non audivit &c. Undè ὀφθαλμοφανῶς constat, sapientissimam il- lam οἰκονομίαν salutis in Christo & per Christum à Deo ab æterno prædestinatam esse, id quod oculus nullus vidit, aurit non audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit. Quod observavit etiam Caspar Sanctius in h. l. adductis verbis Apostoli jam allegatis, hæc sub- jiciens: Quæ verba si quis attente expendat, inveniet profecto, nisi vim sibi, ac textui afferre velit, sermonem esse de Christo; agit enim de ea sapientia, quam quia principes ignorarunt, Dominum gloriæ morti tradi- derunt: illa vero sapientia, quæ in mysterio esse dici- tur, Christus est. Cur vero sapientiam illam, id est, Chri- stum non cognoverint, docet Paulus, quia scriptum est utig, hoc Esaiæ loco, oculus non vidit &c. Hinc ego colligere mihi videor de Christo potius esse sermonem hic, quam de beatorum felicitate. Deinde confirma- tur è verborum Propheticorum perspicuitate. Nam de illis sermo est, quæ à seculo non audiverunt, neǵ, au- ribus perceperunt: oculus non vidit. Quæ imprimis sunt mysteria de Christo. Utpote quæ ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν τῆς κτιστῆς φύσεως dicente Justino, sunt. Deinde Apostolus ipse exclamat ὁμολογουμένως μέγα τ’ εὐσεβείας μυστήριον, 1. Tim. 3, 16. Et Petrus testatur quod An- geli desiderarint παρακύψαι 1. Epist. 1, 10. de qui- bus etiam S. Paulus 1. Cor. 2. quod sint σοφία Θεᾶ ἐν μυστηρίῳ ἡ ἀποκεκρυμμένη & τὰ τᾶ πνώματος θεᾶ v. 6. & 14. nec non c. 1, 18. Sermo crucis est illis, qui pereunt, stultitia nobis, qui salvamur virtus Dei v. 25. τὸ μῶρον τᾶ θεᾶ σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐςί. De illis loquitur Propheta, quæ nemo au- divit aut vidit præter Christum. Nam Christum hic compellavit, utinam disrumperes cœlos. Hic solus ea nobis manifestavit: Deum nemo vidit un- quam: Filius Dei unigenitus, qui in sinu Patris est, enarravit ἐξηγήσατο 1. Joh. 1, 14. Nemo novit pa- trem nisi Filius, & cui voluerit Filius revelare Matth. 11, 17. Ideo Filius Dei, ut interpres voluntatis Dei, & horum mysteriorum præco & Evangelista, in mundum missus est, & unctus Spiritu Dei Esa. 61, 1. ut ea annunciaret. Qui Joh. 3, 11. ea se audivisse, & vidisse se testatur, quæ sc. auris non audivit, o- culus non vidit præter ipsum. Quæ per Spiritum S. etiam Apostolis revelavit. Ideo Apostolus ait se ha- bere MENTEM CHRISTI 1. Cor. 2, 16. De illis sermo est, quæ præparavit Christus expectantibus i- psum, h.e. præparaturus erat, quia more prophetico futura efferuntur in præterito, quorum præparan- dorum gratia de cœlo descendere debebat. Ne ve- ro quis dicat, hæc non mysteriiis de modo salutis, sed ipsi saluti à Christo nobis paratæ convenire, sciendum, quod non tantum salutem nobis Christus præpa- ravit, sed etiam omnia, quæ ad salutem faciunt. Omnia enim per ipsum præparata sunt. Ideo uni- versa salutis οἰκονομία ita effertur, πάντα ἕτοιμα OMNIA PRÆPARATA SUNT Matth. 22, 4. ἅ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ Θεὸς. Quæ Apostolus antea di- xit prædestinata ante secula à Deo, ut sc. à Christo præpararentur ad gloriam nostram. 1. Cor. 2, 7. Parare enim nobis debuit remissionem peccato- rum, veram justitiam, fidem salvificam, & omnia, quæ ad salutem pertinent, ideoq; ipsam salutem, & ut Apostolus paulo ante locutus est, 1. Cor. 1, 30. fieri debuit nobis à Deo sapientia, justitia, sanctifica- tio & redemtio, ut qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, qui facit vel parat misericordiam, judicium, & ju- stitiam in terra Jer. 9, 24. Præparat Christus nos nos sibi in populum, Luc. 1, 17. ut reddamur ad omne opus bonum ἑτοῖμοι Tit. 3, 1. 2. 2. Tim. 2, 21. præparat nos ut sponsam suam. Ap. 21, 2. Præparat nobis bona, non tantum gloriæ sed etiam gratiæ. Quia ab ipso, in ipso, per ipsum omnia, quæ ad nostram salutem pertinent. Et explicat Apostolus ipse, quænam sint illa, quæ præparavit nobis Deus, quæ nemo cognovit, nec oculus ullus vidit, quæ vero Deus per Sp. S. Apostolis revelavit, ut cognosce- rent τὰ ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ χαρισθέντα ἡμῖν, quæ nobis à Deo donantur 1. Cor. 2, 12. Ideoq; omnia gratiæ dona & bona comprehenduntur illis, quæ nobis à Chri- sto præparata sunt. Tertio confirmatur hæc sen- tentia è verborum συνεχείᾳ & cohæsione. Nam de illis agitur, quæ præstitit, cum cælos disrumperet & de cælis descenderet, ut montes à facie ejus deflue- rent. Hostes imprimis spirituales, qui sunt magni montes, quorum destruendorum causa advenit 1. Joh. 3, 8. utque gentes omnes ad ipsum converte- rentur, cum fecit mirabilia, vel gloriosa, ut LXX. In- terpp. habent, non tantum miracula corporalia, in sensus incurrentia patrando, sed imprimis mirabi- liter nos à potestate Satanæ, peccati, mortis & in- ferni liberando, hostes nostros mirabili potentia & admiranda ratione superando & debellando, de qua cap. præcedente LXIII. actum erat. In quo oἰκονομία salutis vere abscondita & admiranda con- sistit. Quarto huc faciunt, quæ sequuntur apud Prophetam: OCCURRISTI LÆTANTI ET FACIENTI JUSTITIAM, ECCE TU IRA- TUS ES: Quæ ita explicant nonnulli: Occur- risti gentibus lætantibus in te, at nobis iratus es. Ad œconomiam certe admirandum gratiæ divinæ per- tinet, quod Christus præparavit gratiam & salutem expectantibus & diligentibus ipsum, qui per fidem ipsum suscipiunt, quodq; occurrat lætanti & facien- ti justitiam, vel cum lætitia facienti, qui de gra- tia & adventu ejus lætantur, eique credunt & ju- stitiam ejus amplectuntur. Similiter Menochius explicat, quod occurrerit Gentibus cum lætitia i- psum amplectentibus. Quinto accedit Interpp. quorundam consensus: Sanctius in hanc sententiam laudat Hieronymum, Ambrosium, Chrysostomum, Theophylactum, Oecumenium & Primasium in Paulum, ut & Græca quædam Scholia, item ex suis Gagnejum, Forerium & Leonem Castrium in Esaiam. Nec abhorrere putat Cyrilli verba, sicut nec Proco- pii. Sic Chrysostomus in 1. Cor. 2. Quid opus est di- cere de Principibus seculi hujus, quando nemo homi- num, nulla cælestium virtutum hæc novit? Quænam illa? Quoniam per eam, quæ videtur esse stultitia prædicationis, orbem terræ superabit, & gentes al- licientur, & Dei ad homines erit reconciliatio, & tanta nobis accedent bona. Quomodo igitur cogno- vimus, inquit? per Spiritum. Et Theodoretius: Quoniam Judæorum ignorationis meminit, & œco- nomiæ mysterium revelatum esse dixit, necessario ad- jecit, quod neque ullus audiverit neque unquam vidit neque mens insatiabilis cogitavit quæ universorum Deus iis præparavit, qui eum ardenter diligunt. Si- militer Theophylactus ad locum Apostoli: Quid ille se colentibus præparavit? Christi sc. notionem & salutem, quæ nobis est per ejus incarnationem quæsita. Hæc quidem neg; oculus humanus inspe- xit &c. E Pontificiis præter Sanctium Estius hanc sententiam propugnat in notis ad h. l. Solet vulgo hæc sententia proferri ad docendum, incompre- hensibilia esse ea bona, quæ electis præparata sunt in regno cælorum. Sed alium sensum indicat nobis Apo- stolus Paulus. Refert enim ad mysteria Religionis Christianæ; scilicet quæ ante Christum latebant & obscure continebantur in Lege, in Psalmis & Prophe- tis, post Christum autem manifestata sunt credenti- bus, ministerio Apostolorum. Et manifestum esse putat ex Apostolico textu, non pertinere hanc sententiam proprie ad bona futuri seculi, sed ad mysteria fidei Christianæ. In comment. ad 1. Cor. 2. ita habet: Sensus autem hujusmodi est; sed loqui- mur ea, quæ juxta Prophetam nec oculis hominum vi- sa, nec auribus audita nec animo cogitata fuerunt, id est, nulli prorsus hominum cognita; nimirum ea, quæ præparavit ac prædestinavit Deus diligentibus & exspectantibus se. Ea sunt salus, & gloria adoptio- nis atq; æternæ felicitatis, tam mirabili ordine sa- pientiæ divinæ procuranda. Nam de Christi benefi- ciis, quorum hæc præcipua sunt, agit eo loco Prophe- ta. Nec alienus est ab hac sententia Calvinus: Dif- ferit eo loco de Evangelii doctrina, quam ostendit humani ingenii comprehensionem superare. Nam alienam admodum & remotam à sensu carnis nostræ scientiam continet: Denique arcana sapientia est. Quo fit, ut merito Paulus in admirationem ejus ra- piatur, atque ut Propheta beneficia Dei admirabilia secum expendens, quasi attonitus exclamat, nihil us- quam tale fuisse auditum:ita in præstantissimo omnium beneficio, ubi scilicet per Evangelium nobis offertur Christus, eundem in modum exclamare licet, Do- mine, quod præstas populo tuo, omni captu humani ingenii majus est: nullus oculus, nulla auris, nul- lus sensus, nullus animus ad tantam altitudinem per- venire potest. Itaq; Paulus optime ad suam disputa- tionem accommodat hunc locum, nec abutitur Pro- phetæ sententia, dum peculiarem, qua Deus Eccle- siam suam dignatur, gratiam supra mundum locat. Clarius Pareus in 1. Cor. 2. QUÆ OCULUS NON VIDIT. Periphrasis sapientiæ Evangelicæ. Pro eo enim, quod dicere poterat, sed prædicamus talem sa- pientiam, quam oculus non vidit, & quam Deus paravit diligentibus eum: dicit scripturæ verbis, prædicamus ea, quæ oculus non vidit, & quæ Deus præparavit. Qui tamen docet, quomodo utraque sententia conjungi possit. Describit, inquit, sapien- tiam illam tum ab ejus natura, quod sensuali aut mentali notitia a nemine capiatur naturaliter, tum à salutari effectu, quod sit circa cælestia & æterna bo- na, diligentibus Deum præparata. Conjungit hæc duo ut declaret, quæ dixerat vers. 7. sapientiam Dei esse occultam in mysterio: & præfinitam à Deo ad nostram gloriam. Quæ enim est hæc gloria? Quam pa- ravit nobis Deus in cœlis: Gloria nempe vitæ æter- næ, qua ipse Dominus gloriæ Christus refulget in cœ- lis: & quam suis promisit. Quibusnam? Non prin- cipibus seculi, qui eum crucifixerunt, qui oderunt, persequuntur in mundo: sed diligentibus eum, hoc est, credentibus, ut Ambrosius expresse interpretatur. Denique non adversatur huic explicationi B. Ger- hardus, sed utramque conjungit in LL. CC. de vi- ta æterna num. 48. potest, inquit, utraque interpre- tatio commode conjungi. Nam & ipsa doctrina Evan- gelii est sapientia ab omni humana ratione abscondi- ta, & bona in Evangelio oblata excedunt omnem sen- sum, experientiam & cogitationem naturalem, & ea, quæ Christus pro nobis fecit, ac passus est, ut bo- na illa acquireret, omni hominis cogitatione sunt sublimiora. Quod utique præstat, quam cum aliis dicere, quod Apostolus abusus sit Prophetæ testimonio, vel in aliam sententiam detorserit, vel ad Apocrypha cum Grotio recurrere. Salutem ergo æternam hic spectari non abnuimus, sed quæ præparanda fuit mirabili οἰκονομίᾳ divinæ sapientiæ, quam nemo cognovit, quaq; per Spiritum Sanctum re- velata est Apostolis. Nam bona æternæ vitæ isthic revelata non sunt, quæ adducit de illis Apostolus ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα fuêre.

## 64:5
YOU MET HIM WHO REJOICES AND DOES JUSTICE: THEY WILL REMEMBER YOU IN YOUR WAYS] You may translate it correctly thus: You met with joy (that is, patience, as the Greeks explain it here) him who does what is right: those, I say, who in all their acts remembered You. You met, that is, you bestowed the greatest benefits upon them of your own accord when they were not hoping for them, as to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, the Judges, David, Elijah, and others.

BEHOLD YOU WERE ANGRY, AND WE HAVE SINNED] That is, But You were angry with us, because we have sinned: because we were not like those ancestors of ours.

IN THEM WE WERE ALWAYS, AND WE SHALL BE SAVED] The best version is: If we had always been in them (in those ways of theirs, of which I spoke above), we too would have been saved.

That meeting of God is referred by others, as I said, to the nations. Brentius, however, refers it also to past times, and even to the holy Patriarchs. The happiness of the former time and the calamity of the present time are opposed to each other. So happy, he says, were the times formerly, that as many as called upon You with a joyful conscience, and did justice, and glorified You, walking in Your calling, You would meet them with Your favor, hear their prayers, and help them in all adversities. I will say something more: You saved not only the just, but also the unjust. For although you were sometimes angry because we had sinned, and had persisted in sins for a long time: yet we were saved by You, and we obtained salvation at last. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and many others were just Patriarchs, and they called upon You with lively faith and a joyful conscience. Wherefore You met them with Your help, in all their adversities. Our ancestors the Israelites, when they were still in Egypt, sinned most gravely, not only with common crimes; but even with idolatry. And yet You delivered them. When they had come into the desert, they became no more just: and yet You saved them. When they had already received their land, and were dwelling in it, they provoked You to most grave anger by their wicked deeds. And although You were destroying them, to be afflicted by enemies on account of their impiety; yet as soon as they turned to You, and cried out to You, You heard them, and restored them to their former liberty. This was the happiness of former times. But now see how everything is changed to the contrary. Neither explanation contradicts our sentiment delivered before. Let each one follow whichever he deems most convenient.

Vers. 5.

AND WE HAVE BECOME, AS ALL OF US UNCLEAN] Like lepers. For so טמא is accustomed to be taken, Levit. 13, 45. Thus we have become filthy with sins, as lepers with leprosy.

Latin:

OCCURRISTI LÆTANTI ET FACIENTI JU- STITIAM: IN VIIS TUIS RECORDABUNTUR TUI] Recte sic vertas: Occurristi cum gaudio (id est, patientia, ut hic explicant Græci) recta facienti: iis, inquam, qui in omnibus actibus suis tui meminerunt. Occurristi, id est, ul- tro illis nec sperantibus beneficia maxima contulisti, ut Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo, Josepho, Mosi, Judicibus, Davidi, Eliæ & aliis.

ECCE TU IRATUS ES, ET PECCAVIMUS] Id est, At nobis iratus fuisti, quia peccavimus: quia similes illis majoribus nostris non fuimus.

IN IPSIS FUIMUS SEMPER, ET SALVABI- MUR] Optima versio est: Si in ipsis (in illorum viis, de quibus supra) fuissemus semper, etiam nos salvi fuissemus.

Occursus ille Dei ab aliis, ut dixi, ad gentes re- fertur. Brentius tamen ad tempora præterita quoq; refert, & ad sanctos etiam Patriarchas. Oppo- nuntur inter se superioris temporis felicitas & præ- sentis temporis calamitas. Tam felicia, inquit, tem- pora fuerunt quondam, ut quotquot te invocabant læta conscientia, & faciebant justitiam, & glorificabant te, ambulantes in tua vocatione, iis occurreres tuo favore, exaudires preces eorum, & juvares eos in omnibus adversis. Plus aliquid dicam: servabas non tantum justos, sed etiam injustos. Etsienim aliquoties ira- scebaris, quod peccassemus, & in peccatis diu perse- veraremus: tamen servabamur a te, & consequeba- mur vel tandem salutem. Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, & multi alii fuerunt justi Patriarchæ, & invocaverunt te alacri fide & læta conscientia. Quare occurrebas eis auxilio tuo, in omnibus adversis ipso- rum. Majores nostri Israëlitæ, cum essent adhuc in Ægypto, peccabant gravissime, non solum vulgari- bus sceleribus; verum etiam idolatria. Et tamen liberasti eos. Cum venissent in desertum, nihilo ju- stiores fiebant: & tamen servasti eos. Cum jam ter- ram suam accepissent, & in ea habitarent, concitabant te flagitiis suis in gravissimam iram. Etsi autem per- debas eos, propter impietatem hostibus affligendos; tamen quamprimum ad te converterentur, & ad te clamarent, exaudisti eos, & restituisti eos in pristi- nam libertatem. Hæc fuit felicitas superiorum tempo- rum. Nunc autem vide, quam omnia sint in diversum mutata. Neutra explicatio nostræ sententiæ an- tea traditæ refragatur. Sequatur quisque, quam censuerit convenientissimam.

Vers. 5.

ET FACTI SUMUS, UT IMMUNDI OMNES NOS] Ut leprosi. Ita enim solet sumi טמא, Levit. 13, 45. Ita peccatis obsorduimus, ut leprosi lepra.

## 64:6
AND AS A CLOTH OF A MENSTRUOUS WOMAN] He followed the Greeks, who have ὡς ῥάκος ἀποκαθημένης. That noun עדים is not found elsewhere in the sacred scriptures. But to the Chaldeans it is עדוין, which is to the Hebrews מרחק, to Theodotion ἐκβρασμός, as we said at Lev. 13, 6. Therefore, a patch will be signified, which is accustomed to be placed upon pustules, and then cast away. Therefore, the Chaldean did not poorly place here a cast-off rag.

ALL OUR RIGHTEOUSNESSES] He speaks by imitation, and calls those things righteousnesses which wicked men call by that name, namely sacrifices and similar rites. A similar expression is above 57, 12. They would do badly who refer these to a life composed according to the law of Moses: much worse, those who refer these words to martyrdom, and other works congruent with the Gospel. Πᾶ πᾶ φρένας ἐκπεποτᾶσδε;

AND WE HAVE FALLEN AS A LEAF ALL OF US, AND OUR INIQUITIES AS THE WIND HAVE TAKEN US AWAY] Cf. Ps. 1, 3. 4.

The matter here is not about wicked men, who have become filthy with sins. It is the complaint of those who invoke God as their Father, and acknowledge that all their righteousnesses are unclean. Because in truth, if our righteousness is compared with the divine rule, and is estimated according to strict justice, it is imperfect, and very unclean; even life, if it be compared to the law of Moses, never responds to it so exactly that many imperfections and many impurities do not intervene. Prov. 20. 1. Reg. 8. Psal. 32. 1. Job. 1. Nor is there any other norm of good works than the divine Law. That the Gospel proposes a new law or a more perfect obedience to the commandments of God smells of the lamps of the Socinians and Papists. Jerome explains this phrase thus be saved by your mercy, who are unclean through ourselves: and whatever we seem to have of righteousness is compared to the cloth of a sitting woman, or of a menstruous woman. For which Theodotion [used] the Hebrew word itself עדים, which Symmachus interpreted as κυσέων, that is, of those giving birth. Aquila [used] μαρτυρίων, that is, of testimonies: when the blood is approved in the first marital intercourse of a virgin. And we have fallen away, he says, like leaves from trees: which, on account of our iniquities, are scattered by the blasts of the winds. In which it must be considered that the righteousness which is in the law is called impurity by comparison with Evangelical purity. For that which was previously glorified was not glorified, on account of the excellent glory. Whence also the Apostle Paul, who had fulfilled everything according to the righteousness which is in the law, says that he counted all things as loss, that he might gain Christ, and on account of the eminent knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whom he considers all things as dung, that he may gain Christ: and be found in him, not having his own righteousness, which is from the law, but through the faith of Christ, which is righteousness from God. Indeed, the righteousness which is in the law, insofar as it is performed by us, must be held to be unclean and dung-like with respect to the most perfect and most pure righteousness of Christ, which is exhibited in the Gospel to be apprehended through faith.

The same explanation is that of Bernard, sermon 1 on the Feast of All Saints: What can all our righteousness be before God? Will it not be reckoned, according to the Prophet, as a menstruous cloth? If it be judged distinctly, all our righteousness will be found unjust and lacking. And sermon 5 on the dedication of the Church: If even all our righteousnesses, when inspected in the light of truth, are found to be like a menstruous cloth, what then will our injustices be reckoned? Therefore, the Remonstrants are not to be heard here, when in the Scripta Synodalia Dodracena they note that this passage is ineptly cited to prove that even the most excellent works of the regenerate are deservedly said to be defiled by sins: nor is their censure to be approved, as if by this explanation the text is perniciously corrupted so that it may serve to foster vices. To whom not only Grotius, but also Hackspan lent an ear, furthermore provoking [others] to the consensus of the Pontificians. Bellarm. book II de Monachis, chapter 13; book 4 de justificatione, chapter 2. Felicianus Capito in Vindic. V. T., Becanus in Manuali, Forerus in Manual. Luth. p. 442, and others. The arguments of Hackspan are of no moment: The first is as follows: Such a thing must be understood in this place, on account of which the Jews were led away into the Babylonian captivity: But they were led away on account of grosser sins, which deserved exclusion from the land of Canaan. Resp. Those who acknowledge that even their own righteousness is like a menstruous cloth do not deny or conceal grosser sins. And the Israelites speak of themselves as a whole: in whose assembly there were not only the just and regenerate, but also the reprobate. Since, therefore, they confess their own sins as well, and their impurity, it is clear that others, who most deserved that abduction, were subject to graver ones. Nor indeed is there any adult believer who has not at some time contaminated himself with grave sins. Therefore, that which Hackspan urges with the Remonstrants, that the good works of the regenerate are not a cloth or the garment of a menstruous woman, but are adorned with distinguished praises by the Holy Scriptures, and are called now clean garments, now undefiled religion, now purple and fine linen, and hence it is also denied of those living piously that they have defiled their garments Apoc. 19:8, Is. 61:10, Apoc. 3:4, Jas. 1:27, 2 Pet. 3:15, that does not conflict with the former: but it must be understood rightly: Indeed, those praises belong to good works when they are considered first Evangelically, as they redound from faith, and are esteemed on account of faith, and shine in the eyes of God: secondly, by reason of the principle, as they proceed from the Holy Spirit and are done by the regenerate man: thirdly, by reason of the form: as they harmonize with the divine law and are good: fourthly, by reason of the end, as they are directed to the glory of God. But those which, on account of the adhering imperfection and impurity, are nevertheless, if God wishes to deal with us according to the rigor of His law, deservedly acknowledged to be like a menstruous cloth, by which name Blessed Luther, Tom. I. Lat. Jen. p. 286, teaches from this passage that there is sin in a good work, and Tom. II. in Commentar. Latin. p. 585, calls every good work (not viewed formally, but materially, or as having imperfection joined to it) sin: which orthodoxy all genuine Lutherans have hitherto sacredly guarded against the Remonstrants and the Pontificians alike; indeed, not a few even of the Papists themselves have acknowledged it. Joh. Gerson, book 4 de consolatione Theologiae, pr. 1, that Isaiah, involving himself with the rest and becoming vile to himself, brought forth with humble confession: all our righteousnesses are as a menstruous cloth. Who, therefore, would have boasted his own righteousnesses to God as more than the cloth of his own confusion, like a woman to her husband? Adrian of Utrecht, later Roman Pontiff, in 4 sentent., as reported by Cassander in Consultatio, p. 924, says: Like a menstruous cloth, he says, are all our righteousnesses. For we continually drip the pus of various crimes upon the cloth of life, which we weave with works of righteousness. Georgius Cassander observes that it is taught by the universal Church that the righteousness which is placed in the obedience of the divine commandments is in itself impure and imperfect. Joh. Hofmeister, however, in Harmon. A. C. art. 6, p. 121, does not think anyone is so stupid as to dare to say that our works do not need mercy and the propitiator Christ. Cf. the explanation of Luther on 1 John 1, T. 6, Altenb. p. 1190.

Verse 6.

Latin:

ET QUASI PANNUS MENSTRUATÆ] Secu- tus est Græcos, qui habet ὡς ῥάκος ἀποκαθημένης. No- men illud עדים non reperitur alibi in sacris literis. Sed Chaldais עדוין est, quod Hebræis מרחק, Theodotioni ἐκβρασμός, ut diximus ad Lev. 13, 6. Significabitur ergo pit- tacium, quod pustulis imponi, ac deinde abjici solet. Ideo panniculum abjectum non male hic posuit Chaldæus.

UNIVERSÆ JUSTITIÆ NOSTRÆ ] Loquitur κατὰ μίμησιν, & justitias vocat id, quod homines improbi eo nomine appellant, sacrificia scilicet & ritus similes. Similis locutio supra 57, 12. Male facerent, qui hæc re- ferrent ad vitam compositam ad legem Mosis: multo pe- jus, qui hæc verba referunt ad martyrium, & alia opera Ev- angelio congruentia. Πᾶ πᾶ φρένας ἐκπεποτᾶσδε;

ET CECIDIMUS QUASI FOLIUM UNIVER- SI, ET INIQUITATES NOSTRÆ QUASI VEN- TUS ABSTULERUNT NOS] Conf. Ps. 1, 3. 4.

Non de hominibus improbis hic res est, qui peccatis obsorduêre. Querela est eorum, qui Deum ut Patrem suum invocant, & agnoscunt, u- niversas justitias suas immundas esse. Quia revera si comparetur justitia nostra cum regula divina, & quoad ἀκριβοδίκαιον æstimetur, imperfecta, & im- munda valde est; vita etiam, si componatur ad le- gem Mosis, nunquam ei tam exacte respondet, ut non multæ interveniant imperfectiones, multæ immundities. Prov. 20. 1. Reg. 8. Psal. 32. 1. Job. 1. Neque alia norma est bonorum operum, quam Lex divina. Evangelium novam legem aut perfectio- rem obedientiam mandatorum Dei proponere, Socinianorum & Papistarum lucernas olet. Phra- sin hanc ita explicat Hieronymus: Juxta Hebrai- cum, qui semper fuimus in peccatis, tua tamen salva- bimur misericordia, qui per nos immundi sumus: & quicquid videmur habere justitiæ, panno sedentis, si- ve menstruatæ mulieris comparatur. Pro quo Theo- dotio ipsum verbum Hebraïcum עדים, quòd Symma- chus interpretatus est κυσέων, id est, parientium. A- quila μαρτυρίων, hoc est, testimoniorum: quando sanguis in primo coitu maritali virginis approbatur. Et defluximus, inquit, quasi folia de arboribus: quæ propter iniquitates nostras, ventorum flatibus disperguntur. In quo considerandum, quod justi- tia, quæ in lege est, ad comparationem Evangelicæ pu- ritatis immunditia nominetur. Etenim non est glo- rificatum, quòd prius glorificatum fuit, propter ex- cellentem gloriam.
