Ex his qui electi erant Christum venientem susceperunt, atque ita vere reducti sunt ad Deum. Post quos etiam alii Israelitæ in dispersione gentium manentes, per Evan- gelium reducti sunt ad Deum, quæ est reductio spi- ritualis, omnibus tribubus promissa & per Christum præstita; in hanc reductionem spiritualem Israe- litarum, sive decem tribuum solum respiciunt expo- sitores. Sed oportet nos etiam meminisse illius cor- poralis reductionis, propter quædam verba Prophe- tarum, & propter ipsam historiam, quam indica- vimus. Quando vero leguntur non reducendæ de- cem tribus, aut restituendæ, notum est illis, qui sacris literis assueti sunt, qui intelligatur, ut dixi ca- pite 9. ubi dicitur Cubilia Draconum &c. & capi- te 25. ubi dicitur, Solitudines sempiternas &c. Nam Israel non restituitur ut Juda. Non enim simul re- dit, sed paulatim ex omnibus tribubus redeunt pau- ci, qui tamen pauci postea intra quingentos aut qua- dringentos annos (nam quidam serius redierunt) multiplicabantur supra modum usq; ad Christum. Deinde, nunquam resurgunt in Regnum & poten- tiam, & illam politiam, quam antea habuerunt, sed sed reguntur sub Juda, ut taceam de alienigenis domina- toribus, id quod sæpe utriq; populo erat postea com- mune malum, ut discerent promissum Messiam spera- re & desiderare. Præterea non restituuntur suis urbibus & pagis & agris & vineis, ut Juda. Nam optima quæq; in Regno Samariæ occupaverant Sa- maritani: Sed habitant ubi loca vel occupare vel emere licebat absq; ordine, absq; tribuum discrimi- ne, ut supra dixi, non ut Domini terræ, sed ut exu- les, qui cupiebant ibi esse cives, id quod licuit tunc eis sub Regno Persarum, nec solis licuit, sed etiam gentilibus tunc hoc ibi licuisset, tamen hoc ipsum pro- spere cessit eis, ut totam Galilæam occuparent præter alia loca. Ex his vides sic abjectas fuisse decem tri- bus, ut ad pristinam gloriam, atq; adeo ad patrum suorum agros & possessiones nunquam redierint, ut nunc rursum non repetam, quod maxima pars eorum nunquam rediit ad illas terras, atque ita intelligenda sunt verba Josephi, quæ legis 10. Antiqq. libro cap. 5. Quam ergo gratiam habuerunt sic reversi? Dixi jam ante magnam gratiam fuisse, quod ita redie- runt ad veram Dei sui religionem, atq; adeo ad Deum Patrum suorum, & quod electi ex eis præsentem in carne Dominum Christum postea susceperunt, se- cundum verbum Christi: Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis &c. Quapropter concludit ex his omnibus B. Antecessor noster, fidelis παραστάτης S. Lutheri, de pace spirituali hæc intelligenda esse, & tempore Nov. Testam. complementum suum obtinuisse: Igitur quæ hic de pace Israelis dicuntur, intelligat aliquis ut velit, etiam de illa quantula- cumq; temporali pace, qua post captivitatem reversi fruebantur & gaudebant se rediisse ad fratres suos & ad cultum Dei. Quando autem hæc pax sæpe in- terrupta est, ut supra diximus, & non toti Israeli ex- hibita, certum est hac pace non complete præstitam es- se quod hic promittitur. Nam finis hujus capitis de- clarat, æterna esse quæ hic promittuntur, quorum, quæ simul corporalia promittuntur, vix umbra fuerunt & initia beneficiorum Dei post Babylonicam capti- vitatem. Ideoq; hæc in Christo completa sunt Judæis & Gentibus. Unde ait Paulus Eph. 2. Veniens pacem evangelizavit vobis qui longe fuistis, & pacem iis qui prope: quoniam per ipsum habemus accessum ambo in uno Spiritu ad Patrem. Et Es. cap. 9. manifestis verbis hanc pacem, super solium David & super Regnum ejus, in Christo dicit æternam, cum ait: Et pacis non erit finis super solium David & super Regnum ejus, ut corroboret illud in judicio & ju- stitia a modo & usque in sempiternum. Rom. 5. Ju- stificati ex fide pacem habemus erga DEUM per Jesum Chrtistum &c.

Nullatenus ergo glossa Grotiana admittenda, RURSUM ÆDIFICABO TE, ubi conversa fueris ad me, faciam rursus habeas domos. ET Æ- DIFICABERIS, Et tuto eas possideas. Non enim de materialibus ædificiis, sed de ædificatione Ecclesiæ ac propagatione ejusdem vaticinium agere, ex his, quæ dicta sunt, manifestum est. Argumenta è tex- tu hæc colligi possunt (1.) A subjecto, cui facta pro- missio, UNIVERSIS COGNATIONIBUS ISRAEL vers. 11. Omnes enim illæ corporaliter non redierunt. (2.) A nomine, quo ornatur VIRGO ISRAEL, quod Ecclesiæ est σημαν- τικόν. (3.) A loco, in quo plantandæ vineæ, adhuc plantabis vineas in montibus Samariæ. Omnes autem Israelitæ vineas in montibus Samariæ mini- me plantarunt, quos occuparunt potius gentiles Samaritani. Quapropter de spirituali plantatio- ne hæc accipienda, quæ in Samaria facta est Joh. 4. Actor. 8. (4.) A custodum excitatione: Surgite & ascendamus in Sion ad Dominum Deum nostrum. Quam exhortationem concernere congregatio- nem ad Ecclesiam & tempora Nov. Testam. è lo- cis parallelis Esa. 2, 3. Mich. 4, 2. constat. (5.) à Lætitia descriptione, quæ populo imperatur, ob quam sese mutuo ad Ecclesiam invitant : EXUL- TATE IN LÆTITIA JACOB ET HIN- NITE SUPER CAPUT GENTIUM, PER- SONATE ET CANITE ET DICITE : SALVA DOMINE POPULUM TUUM RELIQUIAS ISRAEL. Quæ referunt spiri- tualem lætitiam in Domino, & votum pro succes- su Regni Domini, ut è parallelo loco Matth. 21. liquet. (6.) E connexa gentium vocatione, versu 10. AUDITE GENTES VERBUM DOMINI. GENTES &c. (7.) Abonorum conditione, quæ hic promittuntur : ERO DEUS IPfIS, & ipsi erunt mihi populus, anima eorum erit quasi hortus irriguus, & ultra non efiurient, inebriabo animam Sacerdotum pinguedine, & populus meus bonis im- plebitur. (8.) E gaudio communi & universali eoque mero & vero: Tunc lætabitur virgo in choro, juvenes & senes simul: & convertam luctum eorum in gaudium & consolabor eos & lætificabo à dolore suo. Tale gaudium nullum est in hoc mundo, so- lum gaudium in Domino spirituale verum est, & perfectum gaudium. (9.) E subjuncto vaticinio de cæde Bethlehemitica. Quod cum aliis connexis ad tempora Nov. Testam. pertinet.

## 31:15
Vers. 15. A VOICE WAS HEARD ON HIGH OF LAMENTATION.) It is better that רמה be taken as a proper name, as the Chaldean and the Greeks also took it here. Rama is a city in the Tribe of Benjamin, Josh. 18:25, 1 Kings 15:17. Into it Nebuzaradan gathered all the Jews bound in chains, to be deported to Babylon, as we learn below in 40. It is no wonder, therefore, if there was a great lamentation there at that time.

AND THE WEEPING OF RACHEL WEEPING FOR HER CHILDREN, AND REFUSING TO BE COMFORTED FOR THEM, BECAUSE THEY ARE NOT) This seems to be a personification of Rachel, long since dead and buried not far from Rama, such a personification of the dead as we also had in Isaiah 14; although by Rachel the matrons of the tribe of Benjamin may also be understood, just as Jacob is said for the Israelites, and David for the descendants of David. These wept inconsolably when they saw their children being torn away from them.

Thus, indeed, the word רמה is taken as a proper name by the LXX Interpreters, and their translation is retained by Matthew, as being received by usage. Others, however, prefer to take it appellatively, since it is not new for the Evangelists and Apostles to cite the version of the LXX Interpreters, even if it differs in words from the Hebrew text, provided the sense and scope of the oracles alone remain the same; whence Jerome translates 'on high,' and thus also Blessed Luther translated it, not only here in Jeremiah, but also in Matt. 2:18. 'On high, a lamentation was heard,' some understand that it was heard in the highest heaven; others that it resounded in the mountains, like those things which resound from on high. But in this there is a greater difficulty: whose lamentation is this? We dismiss the opinion of those who refer it to the slaughter of the Benjaminites described in Judg. 20, which is the author of the Questions on the Old and New Testament and is attributed to Origen. For it would be absurd for Rachel to be introduced weeping now at last, because of a crime committed some centuries before. Some, as reported in the parallels—though not approved, as Spanheim attributes to him—explain it with Francis Junius as referring to some singular calamity nowhere described. But why should we flee to that, when we have the fulfillment at hand? Some of the Jews understand it of the lamentation under Titus, others of the lamentation under Hadrian, as Jerome notes. But the context fits neither calamity. Others, therefore, interpret it of the Assyrian abduction, most of the time of the Babylonian captivity. To which Grotius adds his support. But we know from the infallible interpretation of the Holy Spirit in Matt. 2 that the gathering of the Jews by Nebuzaradan is not being predicted, but the infanticide of Herod is designated. Concerning which Grotius was entirely silent here. For the Evangelist openly says: THEN, when Herod killed the infants, that it was FULFILLED which was spoken by Jeremiah the Prophet saying: A voice was heard in Rama. Therefore, what was fulfilled by Herod was not fulfilled by Nebuzaradan; what the Prophet speaks of concerning infanticide and weeping because of infanticide, those things do not deal with abduction into captivity and weeping because of that abduction. Nor does that weeping of Rachel, mourning for her children without the admixture of consolation, fit the history of the abduction: because it is nowhere read that the Jewish matrons in Rama wept for the captivity of their children more than others; which weeping, as a fulfillment of the prophecy, the Prophet would not have neglected to mention in his historical description. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit explicitly interprets the prophecy concerning the lamentation heard because of the killing of the infants, but nowhere explains it as concerning the lamentation because of the abduction of the Jews into captivity, why, having set aside this interpretation which was openly delivered by the Holy Spirit Himself, should we embrace one that was not delivered by Him, or admit a double meaning in place of one undoubted exposition of the Holy Spirit, when there is no trace of the other in Scripture? Junius also urges this, that mothers are introduced here only as weeping over the calamity of their children, whereas in a general slaughter, such as the Assyrian and Babylonian ones were, all ranks of the Israelites would have wept over the common calamity of all. That most grievous lamentation certainly fits the weeping of the slaughtered infants better, because the immense cruelty toward children moved the maternal bowels most vehemently. Nor was it beside the point for it to be noted by Junius; if the Prophet had wished to deal with the calamity of the entire Kingdom, he would not have accumulated so many singular circumstances. For although, as Spanheim objects in part 2 of the Evangelical Doubts, Doubt 82, page 564, it is not new for general events to be represented by Prophets through certain persons and certain places, yet mention of special places and persons is never made without a special cause, nor would he have made mention here of Rama as a special place, nor of Rachel weeping, if he had described the calamity of the abduction in general. For it is not established that the lamentation was heard more in Rama, or that the stock of Benjamin, originating from Rachel, was affected by a greater slaughter and had a greater cause for weeping. But in the Herodian infanticide Rachel is deservedly introduced weeping, by which it is signified that that tyranny would rage even to the borders of Benjamin, and in those confines, where Rachel closed her eyes and was buried, her posterity also was to be slaughtered by cruel savagery. Moreover, Rachel's tomb existed in the field of Bethlehem, Gen. 35, 19, and thus in the place where that slaughter was committed; as Spanheim has it on page 567, who adds: That Matthew wished to say that the calamity inflicted upon the Bethlehemites was then so great that there was need even for the mourning of the dead, since the wailing of the living could by no means be equal to the grief, nay, that the wailing of the living had reached even to the ears of the dead, and had stirred them to a like mourning. But it is not to be thought that Matthew wished to say only that, but he introduced the prophecy of Jeremiah in that sense also, and taught that it was fulfilled in this slaughter; nay, Spanheim acknowledges that this could have been said more fittingly concerning the Bethlehemitic slaughter, in that there was a need for the lamentation of the deceased Rachel, rather than for the abduction of the people, since the guilty people of God were indeed subdued and abducted by enemies, but those innocent little children were slaughtered. And to this point contribute those things which the same Spanheim argues for the sake of defending the sense of the oracle handed down by Matthew, against the Jews concerning the place of the lamentation against the Jews concerning the place of the lamentation, which I am pleased to append. But if the Jews insist, what does the lamentation uttered in Rama have in common with the Bethlehemite slaughter, and the mourning that arose over it, for Rama was situated in the lot of the tribe of Benjamin, but Bethlehem in the lot of the tribe of Judah? Resp. It is known that the tribes of Judah and Benjamin were joined together from the time of the schism of the Kingdom, and one scepter was forged from both, whence it ought not to seem strange that what happened to one is ascribed to the other. A synecdoche of this kind is frequent among the sacred writers. Thus, under Judah, Benjamin is included 1. Kings 22:20, when it is established from chapter 11:31, 32 that the ten tribes, designated by ten fragments, had yielded to Jeroboam. For 2 Chronicles 11, they are read to have persisted in the faith of Judah and Benjamin under Rehoboam, who nevertheless in 1 Kings 11:32 are called one tribe. Thus R. Levi says that by the name of Judah, Benjamin is simultaneously connoted, because the region of Benjamin was within the circuit of the region of Judah, or according to others, because the region of Judah, assigned in an oblong tract toward the South, extended itself into the lot of the tribe of Benjamin. See the learned commentary of the distinguished man Constantine l'Empereur on the Codex Middoth. chapter 3, who notes in the same place that the Jerusalem temple itself was situated partly in the portion of the tribe of Judah, and partly in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin according to the opinion of the Talmudists, namely, that the anterior parts of the temple, the court of the women and the court of the people and of the Priests, were in the portion of Judah up to the front of the altar, but the שכינה or the habitation of the divinity and other holier places were בחלק הבנימין in the portion of Benjamin. Is it a wonder, therefore, that what happened in the tribe of Judah was expressed through a neighboring place situated in the lot of the Benjaminites, since there was such a conjunction of both tribes that prosperity and adversity pertained to both? 3. Add that Rama was very close to Bethlehem, which is gathered from Judges 19:1, 3, and 16, to be taken for one or the other, or that the Prophet implies that such a lamentation was excited in the tribe of Judah, which reached as far as Rama in the tribe of Benjamin. Thus Maldonado, born with sufficient acuteness, notes that τὸ ברמה in Rama can be taken for 'as far as Rama,' as if the lamentation of the Bethlehemite mothers was heard that far. 4. It can also be said that the Holy Spirit thus indicated that that mourning and lamentation extended to both tribes, for the infants were killed at Bethlehem and yet the lamentation was simultaneously excited in Rama. It is also no wonder that in a place bordering on two tribes, Benjaminites lived mixed with Judeans, since they had coalesced with the tribe of Judah, especially from the return from the Babylonian captivity, and no longer held a distinct name. It is harsher that Justin, in his Dialogue with Trypho, reports that Rama is a place in Arabia, to which the cry of the Bethlehemites reached. 5. It could also be said that not only the cry, but also the slaughter of Herod perhaps reached that far, which pleased Origen long ago, since not only are the Bethlehemite infants said by the Evangelist to have been slaughtered, but also the massacre was made at the same time ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆς in all its borders. 6. Add that it is not infrequent for the sacred writers, by the commemoration of some place, to imply something else by allusion through the proper name of that place itself. Thus Matthew, speaking after the Prophet about the mourning excited in Rama, simultaneously implies mourning heard in a high place, and thus diffused far and wide, both because Rama signifies such a thing, and because it was undoubtedly situated in a high place, from which it also drew its name, which is gathered partly from the custom of the Hebrews, and partly from 1 Kings 15:17, where Baasha, King of Israel, ascending against Judea, is said to have built Rama, so that he might not allow anyone to go out or come in to Asa, King of Judah. Hence it is probable that Rama was a place fortified by nature as well as by art. Thus Theophylact, ἡ Ῥαμὰ τόπ ἦν τῆς παλαιστήνης ὑψηλός. Τῦτο γὰρ σημαίνει τὸ ὄνομα. And as all these things contribute entirely to defending our opinion, so there is no need for us to take refuge in the idea that the Prophetic prediction was brought in only by assumption, about which later. Furthermore, what is objected, that it is absurd for Rachel to be introduced weeping, and not Leah, when nevertheless the slaughter was carried out not among the descendants of Rachel, but of Leah, from whom Judah was born, and the Bethlehemite citizens, is sufficiently resolved by Spanheim, even without calling into aid the response concerning the sense of analogical accommodation. For he answers in three other ways on page 571. 1. It is not absurd that the lamentation for this slaughter is ascribed to Rachel, not because of envy of the happiness of the sons of Leah who were decorated with the crown of martyrdom, which once pleased the Author of the Questions on the Old and New Testament, but 1. because the tomb of Rachel was near Bethlehem, Genesis 35:19, 20; 1 Samuel 10:2. Rachel is introduced through an excellent personification, weeping for the slaughter of the infants carried out near her. 2. And this all the more, because not only did a close right of kinship and proximity intervene between Rachel and the children of Leah, but also because the Benjaminites, the descendants of Rachel, constituted one body only, as was said above, with the tribe of Judah, which is from the descendants of Leah. 3. Add that the executioners of Herod undoubtedly also broke into the neighboring border of the Benjaminites, and drew the wicked sword against some also of the descendants of Rachel, since the Evangelist expressly testifies that that slaughter was carried out ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὀρίοις ἀυτῆς in all its borders. But if anyone objects that Jerusalem was situated between Rama and Bethlehem, and therefore it does not seem likely that the infants were killed in Rama also; he answers that Herod dared in ignoble villages what he did not dare in the metropolis of the Kingdom. To which response must be added: that Herod understood well enough that CHRIST was not born in the metropolis, but in some more ignoble village. There is, therefore, no reason for us to exempt Rama from the slaughter of Herod with Spanheim, since Matthew, citing the Prophetic passage, testifies that in it mourning and lamentation were heard.

Furthermore, the cause of the lamentation is expressed in such a way that it fits the Herodian παιδοκτονίᾳ (child-slaughter) better than the Babylonian deportation: since they are said to grieve over their children, BECAUSE THEY ARE NOT. For through captivity they did not cease to be children, but they did cease to be through the slaughter of the tyrant. Spanheim himself explains this phrase in this place in this way. It is not, he says, to be taken ἁπλῶς (simply) in this way, but κατά τι (in a certain respect): that Rachel did not weep over her children as if they were clearly not survivors, or as if they were utterly cut off, but because they were not, namely, among the living, having been nefariously slaughtered, without hope of their restoration to this present life. Thus Theophylactus: ἐκ εἰσὶν, ἐν τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ, ἐκ εἰσὶν ἐπὶ αἱ ψυχαὶ ἀθάνατοι (they are not in this life, they are not, although the souls are immortal). Therefore, not to be here means only not to survive, to be deprived of life, to cease to be among men. Thus the term אֵינֶנּוּ is read frequently among the sacred writers. See among other places Psalm 39:14, Jeremiah 49:10. And indeed, Scripture speaks in this way according to human perception; for those seem not to survive who do not survive among the living, or are no longer survivors. Thus the world judges that it is all over for those who are slaughtered or cut off, although often, if they are slaughtered for the sake of God, then at last they truly begin both to be and to live. Nor for that reason from mourning & We abstain from all lamentation, although we are persuaded that our own have been sent ahead to the blessed seats, whom either natural death or violent death has torn from us. Those two things, however, stand out remarkably in the Prophet. 1. The human and carnal affection of mothers: who do not wish to admit consolation on account of the slaughter of their sons. 2. Divine correction: let your voice cease from weeping, etc. So he. Similarly Grotius in Annot. on Matt. 2, 18. That 'not to be' here means the same as 'not to live,' just as the dead are said to have been among the Latins, that is, to have lived. And Sophocles calls the dead οὐκ ἔτι ὄντας: just as we say that has perished which has escaped our sight or knowledge: to which that in Psalm 39, 14 seems to look, 'before I go away, so that I am no more.' And Psalm 37, 36, concerning the impious, 'he was not': the Psalmist himself interprets, 'I sought him and he was not found.' So also Gen. 5, 24, concerning Enoch, 'he was not,' the LXX translate οὐχ εὑρίσκετο. So also Sirach 17, 25. ἀπὸ νεκρῦ ὡς μηδὲ ὄντος, ἀπόλλυτε ἐξομολογήσης. Unless we prefer that 'not to be' is said strictly of a man, because a body separated from the soul, or a soul from the body, is not properly called a man. Josephus speaks in this manner also: 'For we have received from Him (God) our being, and we give back to Him again our no longer being.' Soon follows 'the soul is always immortal.' But if these who are mourned were killed, the prophecy will certainly not be understood concerning those who were carried away. Moreover, such a great lamentation is instituted here, (which also deserves observation,) not for children in general of both sexes; but for sons, just as consolation is also added concerning sons: 'And your sons will return to their borders,' but the Babylonian slaughter affected both sexes; yet the Herodian tyranny subjected only sons to cruel death.

To these reasons let the Junian observation be added, l. 1. parallel. 7. that the Prophet wished to propose by those words some clear sign of that coming in which the Kingdom of God was to have its completion, therefore Jeremiah proposes that sign as to be exhibited in its own time, Matthew describes it as already exhibited. And that this sign is, that a great lamentation is to be excited in Rama and a wicked and bloody deed is to be committed. The end, says Junius page 1305, in both places is one and the same, namely that by some certain, notable, and clear sign it might be publicly shown and demonstrated that He had arrived in whom the kingdom of God was to be revealed and to receive its completion, with the preaching of the Gospel instituted: and both conveniently narrate this sign, Jeremiah indeed showing it as future, but Matthew demonstrating it as done. The sum, therefore, is that the Kingdom of our Lord JESUS Christ in this world is infected with very many calamities, and that the children of the kingdom are to enter into it through many afflictions: but that that most singular sign of that coming Kingdom and first arising in the Person of Christ, the King and supreme Savior, was signified by God long ago, and completed in its own time, of which sign there was to be an undoubted testimony. For although many and unworthy slaughters have been committed since the memory of man, yet nowhere is it read (unless my mind deceives me) an example of such a crime: by which only little children, not even excepting (if we believe Macrobius) the King's own son, were slaughtered against right and wrong in the whole region, without any inquiry, at the will of one tyrant and indeed acting under the power of another, among the people of God. Nor does the continuity of the text suggest otherwise. For when the Prophet had prophesied concerning the happiness of the Kingdom of Christ, he indicates that it would not be without calamity in these lands, when under the very beginnings of the New Testament, with Christ the Savior scarcely born, his citizens

of Bethlehem with their neighbors are to be subjected to a grave persecution. Osiander delivered this coherence in his Paraphrase: 'Lest anyone should think that the Kingdom of Christ in this world would be without any persecution, and should imagine for himself mere and perpetual bodily joys: the Prophet inserts a prophecy concerning that slaughter which the pious parents in Bethlehem of Judah, and those borders, sustained when their boys were killed by Herod.' Which history is described in Matt. chap. 2: where this text of the Prophet is also alleged. Yet the Prophet speaks in figurative language in such a way that at first glance he seems to deal with the miseries of the Babylonian exile. But we most safely follow the interpreter, the Holy Spirit, explaining this passage for us through the Evangelist and Apostle Matthew. THUS SAYS THE LORD: A VOICE HAS BEEN HEARD ON HIGH OF LAMENTATION, OF MOURNING AND OF BITTEREST WEEPING, OF RACHEL THE MATRON WEEPING FOR HER SONS, AND REFUSING TO BE CONSOLED FOR THEM: (not admitting consolation) BECAUSE THEY ARE NOT: that is, because it was all over with them: This is, the Jewish matrons in the city of Bethlehem and in the border (where once the most pious matron Rachel, wife of the Patriarch Jacob, died and was buried, Gen. 35) will lament with a loud voice, and will bewail their boy children, who were being slaughtered by the satellites of Herod: (hoping that he would also kill Christ among them) nor will they wish to admit consolation: because with great grief they will see them lying lifeless. Similarly Junius and Tremellius; The excellence of the kingdom of Christ having been set forth, lest anyone think that all things in this age will be most perfect in body and soul, the Prophet resolves two occupations of grave inconveniences, which the faithful experience here in the kingdom of Christ, as we said in verse 10. The former is that external sufferings in the Kingdom of Christ will not cease, but that it will come to pass that Satan will exercise his fury immediately upon Christ being born, in three verses: The latter is that the consciousness of their own internal infirmity will also remain in the pious, which is explained in the following. The occupation of the former is held, this indeed will be solved by the two following; but the occupation of the latter is contained in verse 18 and 19, the solution in the three following. B. Hulsemannus resolves the whole chapter thus: There are three parts: The first, up to verse 15, is as it were a hypotyposis of the benefits to be exhibited with the exhibited Christ, which are prefigured by the liberation from the Babylonian captivity. The second part is a description of both the adversities and the pleasures which will happen to the Jews when Christ is exhibited, from verse 15 to 31. The third is the promise of the grace proper to the New Testament, which was to follow the merit of Christ, from verse 31 to the end. Concerning this second part, therefore, in which we are now occupied, he has it thus: The second part describes both the evils of punishment from verse 15 to 41, and the goods of grace from verse 21 to 31. The evils of punishment can be distributed according to times, so that some are said to be about to happen when Christ is born, such as the infanticide of Herod, which is described by the accompanying weeping in verse 15 and the present divine consolation in verses 16 and 17; others when Christ is taken from the earth, namely the destruction by the Romans in verse 18. The consequent fruit, the goods of grace, are described from the procreative cause, namely Christ, 20, 21; from the consequent effect, happiness, by prosopopoeia in verse 23; from the form in verse 24; from the principal efficient cause, the grace of God, which is described by the attribute of vehemence, as if it had acquired new strength through sleep, verses 25, 26; from the removal of the cause, and the contrary effect, etc. These, therefore, we have in agreement with Jerome and other ancient ὁμοψήφες; to whom we also add B. Pappus: Although to many interpreters this prediction seems to look primarily to some other calamity of the Jewish people, & only secondarily represented rather than fulfilled in the infants of Bethlehem, yet for us, among whom the authority of the Gospel is beyond controversy, the citation of the Evangelist Matthew ought to give assurance that the words here are spoken most especially concerning that Herodian slaughter of infants. The Prophet, moreover, by prosopopoeia, rouses Rachel, buried near Bethlehem, so that she may lament those infants most cruelly killed by Herod: and then, turning his speech to them, he consoles the mothers of the infants themselves. We add, moreover, the Blessed Hunnius the Elder in his Commentary on Matthew, ch. 2: Although these words can also be explained according to the letter concerning the miserable slaughter of the Hebrew people, which occurred at the time of the Babylonian captivity, yet by reason of the type, or rather indeed principally, the Lord there treats of and prophesies concerning that infanticide. For there are many things in that 31st chapter which openly argue that the whole matter is to be understood concerning the times of the advent and Kingdom of the Messiah. Of which kind also is this: I create a new thing in the earth, says the Lord, a woman shall encompass a man. Similarly, there exists there a famous promise of a new covenant, under which the Lord wills to remit their sins to them, and to remember their iniquities no more: which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 8, refers to the kingdom of Christ under the New Testament. Indeed, many other things occur there which can in no way be accommodated to the times of Jeremiah, especially those things which are mentioned concerning the benefits to be provided to the Gentiles themselves as well. Thus all the circumstances, and the context of the whole of the preceding and following parts, show that the words of the Prophet were alleged by the Evangelist in their true sense. By Rachel, however, in figurative speech, the city of Bethlehem is denoted, since in its borders Rachel, the primary wife of the Patriarch Jacob, once died and was buried in the same place. So that the sense is that the matrons of Bethlehem, having raised a cry, lamentation, and wailing to heaven, are lamenting the most mournful lot of their little ones, so much so that the magnitude of the sudden grief rejects every medicine of sorrow and every consolation, for the reason that they are not, that is, because those mothers see that it is all over for their sweetest little children in this life, since they see them lying before them lifeless and nefariously slaughtered by the bloodstained hands of their executioners. These are the words of the Blessed Hunnius. Which he likewise asserted in his Calvinus Judaizans, and afterwards in his Anti-Paeus he repeated the sum of them thus on page 215: I have shown, he says, that the Christian sense squares most aptly with the peristasis of the whole chapter. For the Lord is prophesying about that desired time when God will be propitious to all Israel, when He wills to lead back His people, so that they may return to Zion rejoicing and with jubilation. Which, according to the common custom of the Prophets, is to be accepted concerning a spiritual reduction to the communion of the Church of the New Testament. And that the Prophet is speaking entirely of things which were to be at the advent of Christ. And I said that this is indicated more clearly by the added notation of the grief and lamentation of Rachel over her sons: which the Evangelist Matthew declares to pertain to the tragedy of the infanticide or most miserable slaughter of the boys of Bethlehem. After which promises the Lord thus consoles His people and inserts into the consolation a prophecy concerning the birth of the Messiah, testifying that He is about to create a new thing in the earth, namely that a woman shall encompass a man, and that it will come to pass then that the Lord will satisfy the weary soul and every hungry soul: indeed that the Lord will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, the old one being removed, just as the Epistle to the Hebrews interprets it through the scope of the prophecy, and pronounces that it looks to the time of the exhibited Messiah. Thus far again our Blessed Hunnius. Although the Blessed Gerhard refers this prophecy to the calamity of the ten tribes when they were led away into captivity,

in his Notes on Matthew, he nevertheless corrects his opinion afterwards, or at least does not deny that the Holy Spirit looked to the Herodian infanticide, page 137. It is said that at the time of the infanticide that oracle was fulfilled either by a certain similarity, because in that infanticide an equally great, if not greater, calamity oppressed the Bethlehemites and their neighbors than the Israelite tribes at the time of the abduction into captivity, or perfectly, with respect had to the intention of the Holy Spirit, because when the Holy Spirit proposed this oracle through Jeremiah, He looked not only to the abduction of the ten tribes, but also to this infanticide of Bethlehem. Therefore, by a pathetic plasis, Rachel, buried some centuries before in the vicinity of Bethlehem, is introduced as lamenting her children, killed then both by the Assyrians and Babylonians and by King Herod. Which opinion seems more convenient than if you were to say, with some, that the prophecy was brought forward by the Evangelist in a mystical sense; or even in an accommodative sense, with Jansenius, Bucer, and Spanheim. Spanheim himself refutes the mystical sense along with Cornelius a Lapide: Since indeed it does not appear how the slaughter of a whole people can be called a type of the slaughter of the children of one or another village, the deportation of the slaughter, the deportation of a rebellious and impious people for their crimes, the slaughter of children extinguished in the first flower of age for Christ and His cause. Spanheim strives hard to prove in many ways that the sense is accommodative, yet he could produce no example of it from the Scriptures by which he might teach that when Scripture says something was fulfilled which was predicted by a Prophet, only a bare allusion or accommodation is taking place. That distinction of phrase by Spanheim, that Matthew did not say, 'that it might be fulfilled, which the Lord said through the Prophet, saying,' but only 'then was fulfilled, which the Lord said through Jeremiah, saying,' is more subtle than it is true. For anyone can easily see that the sense of both phrases is the same, and their scope the same, whether it is said, 'that it might be fulfilled,' or 'then that was fulfilled, which was predicted.' The examples which Spanheim produced in doubt 72 are less clear, and do not prove what he himself intends: namely, that Scripture is sometimes said to be fulfilled improperly and secondarily, analogically or exemplarily, when something similar happens to that which was already long ago either done or said or predicted, whether it happens narratively, or correctionally or disparagingly by way of correction or rebuke. For the passage in Isaiah 29:13 refers to those very people to whom it is applied in Matthew 15:8. and the prophecy of Isaiah 6 was fulfilled not merely by accommodation, but directly in the hearers of Christ in Matthew 13:14, which we noted in the explanation of those passages of Isaiah. Nor is Psalm 78:2 brought forward by the Evangelist in Matthew 13:34-35 by mere accommodation and transfer. For that same one who says in the Psalm, 'I will open my mouth in a parable,' spoke in parables in Matthew. This is not applied only to Christ, but Christ spoke through the mouth of the Psalmist. Since the Spirit of Christ spoke through the Prophets, as Peter testifies in 1 Epistle 1:11, on which see blessed Gesner's Commentary on the Psalms. We deny that Romans 9:29 is merely an accommodation of the passage in Isaiah 1:9: we showed the contrary in the explanation of the passage of Isaiah. As for Matthew 21:13, when what was said long ago by Jeremiah in chapter 7:11 about the Jews of his age is applied by Christ to the merchants of his own time, that phrase is not used, 'that it might be fulfilled,' or 'then was fulfilled, which was predicted by Jeremiah,' as in this place, but it is said simply, 'it is written.' No other examples are brought forward by Spanheim. Nor is there any need for us to invent that improper mode of fulfilling Scripture while, since no necessity compels one to have recourse to impropriety.

Latin:

Vers. 15. VOX IN EXCELSO AUDITA EST LAMEN- TATIONIS.) Melius est, ut רמה sumatur pro proprio nomine, ut hic etiam Chaldæus & Græci sumsere. Ra- ma urbs est in Tribu Benjamin Josuæ 18, 25. 1. Reg. 15, 17. In eam Nabuzaradan collegit omnes Judæos vinctos ca- tenis, ac deportandos in Babylonem, ut discimus infra 40. Non mirum ergo, si magna ibi tum fuit lamentatio.

ET FLETVSRaCHEL PLORANTIS FILIOS SVOS, ET NOLENTIS CONSOLARI SVPER EIS, QVIA NON SVNT) Videtur esse προσωποποιϊα Rache- lis pridem mortuæ, & non longe à Rama sepultæ, qualem mortuorum προσωποποιῖαν etiam habuimus Esaiæ 14. quam- quam possint & per Rachelem matronæ intelligi tribus Benjaminis, sicut Jacob pro Israelitis dicitur, & David pro Davidis posteris. Hæ inconsolabiliter fleverunt, cum viderent á se abstrahi liberos suos.

Ita sane vox רמה sumitur pro nomine proprio à LXX. Interpp. & retinetur à Matthæo illorum translatio, utpote usu recepta. Alii tamen ma- lunt appellative accipere, quum non novum sit Evangelistis & Apostolis versionem LXX. Interpp. adducere, utut verbis à textu Ebræo discrepantem, dum sensus & scopus solum oraculorum idem ma- neat; unde Hieronymus vertit in excelso, atque ita etiam transtulit B. Lutherus non modo hic in Jeremia, sed etiam Matth. 2, 18. In excelso, plan- ctum auditum, nonnulli intelligunt, quod in cælo altissimo exauditus sit; alii quod in montibus per- crebuerit, ut ea quæ ex alto resonant. Sed in eo major difficultas, quisnam hic planctus? Mitti- mus eorum sententiam, qui ad Stragem Benjami- nitarum, Jud. 20. descriptam referunt, quæ autoris est Quæst. Vet. & Nov. Testam. & Origeni tribui- tur. Absurde enim nunc demum Rachel plorans introduceretur, ob facinus ante aliquot secula commissum. Nonnulli, referente in parallelis, non probante, ut ei affingit Spanhemius, Franc. Junio de singulari aliqua calamitate nuspiam de- scripta explicant. Cur vero eo confugeremus, quum in promtu habeamus complementum ? E Judæis nonnulli de planctu sub Tito, alii de planctu sub Hadriano intelligunt, notante Hieronymo. Sed contextus neutri calamitati congruit. Alii ergo de abductione Assyriaca, plerique de captivitatis Ba- bylonicæ tempore interpretantur. Quibus calcu- lum adjicit Grotius. Non autem collectionem Judæorum à Nabuzaradan futuram prædici, sed in- fanticidium Herodis designatum esse ex infallibili interpretatione Spiritus Sancti Matth. 2. novimus. De qua hic prorsus tacuit Grotius. Nam aperte Evangelista : TUNC, cum Herodes interficeret infantes, ADIMPLETUM esse, quod dictum est per Jeremiam Prophetam dicentem : Vox in Rama audita est. Quod ergo impletum est per He- rodem, id non per Nebuzaradan impletum est; Quæ Propheta loquitur de infanticidio & ploratu ob infanticidium, ea non de abductione in capti- vitatê & ploratu ob illam abductionem agunt. Ne- que congruit ille ploratus Rachelis, lugentis filios suos, sine admistione consolationis, historiæ ab- ductionis : quia nuspiam leguntur matronæ Judai- cæ in Rama præ aliis deplorasse liberorum suorum captivitatem; quem ploratum ceu complementū vaticinii non neglexisset Propheta in historica de- scriptione commemorare. Quum ergo Spiritus S. diferte de planctu ob interfectionem infantum exaudito interpretetur vaticinium, nuspiam au- tem id exposuerit de planctu ob abductionem Ju- dæorum in captivitatem, cur ista interpretatio- ne posthabita, quæ ab ipso Spiritu S. aperte tra- dita est, eam, quæ ab ipso tradita non est, ample- ctamur, aut loco unius indubitatæ expositionis Spiritus Sancti geminam admittamus, quum de altera nullum in Scriptura sit vestigium. Junius urget etiam hoc, quod matres hic tantum intro- ducantur lugentes super filiorum calamitate, in clade vero generali, qualis erat tum Assyriaca, tum Babylonica, omnes Israelitarum ordines super com- muni omnium calamitate luxisse. Magis certe convenit luctus ille gravissimus planctui occiso- rum infantum, quia immanis erga liberos crude- litas materna imprimis viscera commovit vehe- mentissime. Neque præter rem à Junio moni- tum fuit; Prophetam si de calamitate Regni univer- si agere voluisset, haud ita cumulaturum fuisse tot cir- cumstantias singulares. Etsi enim, quod Spanhe- mius excipit part. 2. Dubior. Evangel. Dubio 82. pag. 564. novum non sit, eventus generales à Prophetis repræsentari per certas personas & certos locos, tamen specialiunı locorum & personarum nunquam sine speciali causa mentio fit, neque vel Rama loci specialis,neque Rachel plorantis hic fe- cisset mentionem, si in genere abductionis cala- mitatem descripsisset. Magis enim in Rama planctum exauditum esse, aut stirpem Benjamin è Rachele oriundam majori clade affectam esse, & majorem plangendi causam habuisse, non con- stat. At in Herodiano infanticidio merito Rachel plorans introducitur, quo designetur usque in fines Benjamin tyrannidem illam sævituram, & in illis confiniis, ubi Rachel oculos clausit, ac sepulta est, posteritatem etiam ejus crudeli sævitia interimun- dam esse. Rachelis autem sepulcrum in agro Beth- lehemitico exstabat, Gen. 35, 19. adeoque in loco ubi committebatur carnificina illa; ut habet Spanhe- mius pag. 567. qui addit : Id dicere voluisse Mat- thæum, tantam tum fuisse calamitatem inflictan Bethlehemiticis, ut vel mortuorum luctu opus esset, cum viventium planctus baud quaquam dolori par esse posset, imo viventium planctum ad mortuorum usque aures pertigisse, & eos ad parem luctum exci- tasse. Atqui non id tantum dicere voluisse Mat- thæum censendum est, sed eo etiam sensu Jeremiæ vaticinium induxit, atque in hac strage id imple- tum esse docuit; imo agnoscit Spanhemius conve- nientius hoc dici potuisse de strage Bethlehemitica, quod nempe Rachelis demortuae planctu opus fuerit, quam de abductione populi, siquidem populus Dei nocens subactus & abductus fuerit ab hostibus, pueruli vero illi innoxii jugulati. Atq; huc faciunt, quae idem Spanhemius pro vindicando oraculi sensu à Matthaeo tradito, adversus Judaeos de loco planctus disputat pag. 569. quae subjungere placet. Si vero instent Iudaei, quid planctui in Rama edito commune sit cum strage Bethlehemitica, & luctui super illa oborto, Ramam enim sitam fuisse in sorte tribus Benjamin, Bethleemum vero in forte tribus Iuda, Resp. Notum esse, tribus Iudae & Benjaminis conjunctas fuisse inde à scissione Regni, & unum ex utraque sceptrum conflatum, unde mirum videri non debet, quod uni accidit, alteri adscribi. Synecdoche ejusmodi frequens sacris Scriptoribus. Sic sub Iuda Benjamin comprehenditur 1. Reg. 22, 20. quum constet ex cap. 11, 31. 32. decem tribus per decem fragmenta designatas cessisse Ieroboamo. Nam 2. Chron. 11. in Rehabeam fide Iuda & Benjamin perstitisse leguntur, qui tamen 1. Reg. 11, 32. tribus una vocantur. Sic R. Levi Iuda nomine Benjaminem simul connotari ait, quod Benjaminis regio fuerit intra ambitum regionis Iuda, secundum alios quod regio Iuda assignata tractu oblongo Meridiem versus in sortem tribus Benjamin se exporrexerit. Vide Commentarium eruditum Constantini l' Empereur Viri Cl. in Codicem Middoth. cap. 3. qui ibidem notat ipsum templum Hierosolymitanum ex parte in portione tribus Iuda, ex parte in portione tribus Benjamin situm fuisse ex Talmudistarum sententia, anteriores videlicet templi partes, atrium mulierum & atrium populi ac Sacerdotum, idque ad altaris usque frontem in Iuda portione fuisse, שכינה vero sive divinitatis habitationem & alia loca sanctiora fuisse בחלק הבנימין in portione Benjamini. An mirum ergo quod in tribu Iuda contigit, per locum vicinum in forte Benjaminitarum situm expressum fuisse, cum tanta utriusque fuerit tribus conjunctio, ut prospera & adversa ad utramque pertinerent? 3. Adde Ramam propinquam admodum fuisse Bethleemo, quod colligitur ex Jud. 19, 1. 3. & 16. pro alterutra sumi, vel Prophetam innuere, planctum talem excitatum fuisse in tribu Iuda, qui pertigerit Ramam usque in tribum Benjamini. Sic Maldonado natus acute satis notat τὸ ברמה in Rama posse accipi pro usque ad Ramam, quasi planctus matrum Bethleemiticarum eousque fuerit exauditus. 4. Potest etiam dici, sic Spiritum S. indicasse Luctum & planctum illum ad utramque tribum se extendisse, infantes enim occisos fuisse Bethleemi & tamen planctum simul excitatum in Rama. Non mirum etiam in loco duabus tribubus contermino permixtos habitasse Benjamitas Iudaeis. quippe qui cum tribu Iuda coaluerant, vel imprimis à reditu è captivitate Babylonica, nec distinctum amplius nomen obtinebant. Durius est, quod Iustinus Dialogo cum Tryphone refert, Ramam locum esse in Arabia, ad quem pertigerit Bethleemitarum clamor. 5. Posset etiam dici non clamorem tantum, sed & carnificinam Herodis forte eousque pertigisse, quod Origeni jam olim placuit, quum non tantum infantes Bethleemitici jugulati dicantur ab Evangelista, sed & strages simul facta ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆς in omnibus finibus ejus. 6. Adde non infrequens esse sacris Scriptoribus loci alicujus commemoratione per allusionem aliud quid nomine proprio ipsius loci innuere. Sic Matthaeus post Prophetam loquens de luctu excitato in Rama, simul innuit luctum in excelso auditum, adeoque longe lateque diffusum, tum quia Rama tale quid significat, tum quia in loco edito sita dubio procul fuit, unde & nomen traxit, quod colligitur partim ex consuetudine Hebræorum, partim ex 1. Reg. 15, 17. ubi Bahasa Rex Israelis ascendens con- tra Iudeam dicitur ædificasse Ramam, ne sineret ad Asam Regem Iudæ egredi aut regredi quenquam. Hinc probabile, Ramam fuisse locum munitum na- tura simul & arte. Sic Theophylactus, ἡ Ῥαμὰ τόπ ἦν τῆς παλαιστήνης ὑψηλός. Τῦτο γὰρ σημαίνει τὸ ὄνομα. Quæ omnia uti omnino faciunt pro vin- dicanda nostra sententia, ita non opus est, ut eo confugiamus, tantum per assumptionem adductum esse vaticinium Propheticum, de quo postmo- dum. Cæterum quod objicitur absurdum esse Rachelem induci plorantem, non Leam, cum tamen strages edita fuerit non inter posteros Rachelis, sed Leæ, ex qua natus Iuda, & Bethlehemitani cives, satis expeditur à Spanhemio, etiam non vocata in subsidium responsione de sensu accommodationis analogicæ. Respondet enim tribus aliis modis pag. 571. 1. Non absurdum, Racheli planctum ob hanc carnificinam adscribi, non ob æmulationem fe- licitatis filiorum Leæ martyrii corona decoratorum, quod placuit olim Authori quæstionum in Vetus & Novum Testamentum, sed 1. quia sepulchrum Ra- chelis Bethleemo propinquam erat Gen. 35, 19. 20. 1. Sam. 10, 2. Rachel per προσωποποιίαν egregiam introducitur, plorans stragem infantum prope se edi- tam. 2. Idque eo magis, quia non tantum cognatio- nis & proximitatis jus arctum intercedebat inter Rachelem & Leæ liberos, verum etiam quia Benja- minitæ Rachelis posteri unum duntaxat corpus con- stituebat, ut supra dictum, cum tribu Iuda, quæ est è Leæ posteris. 3. Adde carnifices Herodis dubio pro- cul in vicinum Benjamitarum limitem etiam irrupis- se, & nefarium ferrum in aliquos quoq; è Rachelis po- steris strinxisse, quum diserte testetur Evangelista, stragem illam editam ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὀρίοις ἀυτῆς in o- mnibus finibus ejus. Quod si autem quis objiciat, Hierosolymam interjectam fuisse inter Ramam, & Bethlehem, non ergo verisimile videri in Rama quo- que occisos infantes; respondet; Herodem ausum fuisse in vicis ignobilibus, quod non audebat in me- tropoli Regni. Cui responsioni addendum: quod in- tellexerit satis Herodes, CHRISTUM non natum esse in metropoli, sed in vico aliquo ignobiliori. Non ergo est, quod eximamus Ramam à carnificina Herodis cum Spanhemio, siquidem in ea omnino luctum & planctum exauditum fuisse, Matthæus locum adducens Propheticum testatur.

Porro causa planctus ea exprimitur, quæ magis παιδοκτονίᾳ Herodianæ, quam transporta- tioni Babylonicæ convenit: cum dolere dicuntur super filiis, Eo QUOD NON SINT. Nam per captivitatem non desierunt esse filii, desie- runt autem per interfectionem tyranni. Ex- plicat Spanhemius ipse ita hanc phrasin hoc in loco. Id non esse, inquit, ἁπλῶς sic sumendum, sed κατά τι: Rachelem non plorasse super libe- ris suis, quasi plane non forent superstites, vel quasi funditus excisi forent, sed quod non essent sc. in vivis, nefarie scilicet jugulati, sine spe restitutionis illorum in vitam præsentem. Sic Theophylactus ἐκ εἰσὶν, ἐν τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ, ἐκ εἰσὶν ἐπὶ αἱ ψυχαὶ ἀθάνατοι. Non esse ergo hic tantum est non superesse, vita privari, de- sinere esse inter homines. Sic τὸ אֵינֶנּוּ legitur frequen- ter apud Scriptores sacros. Vide inter loca alia Psal. 39, 14. Ierem. 49, 10. Et sane sic Scriptura loquitur ex sensu humano; Illi enim videntur non superesse, qui non supersunt in vivis, vel non am- plius sunt superstites. Sic judicat mundus, actum esse de iis, qui jugulati vel excisi, quamvis sæpe, si ob Dei causam jugulentur, tunc demum vere in- cipiant & esse, & vivere. Nec ob id à luctu & planctu omni abstinemus, quamvis persuasum habeamus, nostros ad beatas sedes præmissos, quos vel mors naturalis à nobis avulsit, vel violen- ta. Duo vero illa egregie se excipiunt apud Pro- phetam. 1. Affectus humanus & carnalis matrum: quæ nolunt admittere consolationem ob filiorum suorum stragem. 2. Correctio divina : quiescat vox tua à ploratu, &c. Hæc ille. Similiter Grotius oster in Annot. ad Matth. 2, 18. Esse autem hic va- let idem quod vivere, quomodo mortui Latinis fuis- se, id est, vixisse dicuntur. Et Sophocles mortuos di- cit οὐκ ἔτι ὄντας : sicut periisse dicimus id quod conspe- ctum aut notitiam nostram effugit : quo spectare vi- detur illud in Psalmo 39, 14. antequam abeo, ut non sim amplius. Et Psal. 37, 36. de impio, non fuit: i- pse Psalmographus interpretatur, quæsivi eum & non est inventus. Sic & Gen. 5, 24. de Enocho, non erat, LXX. vertunt οὐχ εὑρίσκετο. Sic & Siraci- des 17, 25. ἀπὸ νεκρῦ ὡς μηδὲ ὄντος, ἀπόλλυτε ἐξο- μολογήσης. Nisi malimus illud non esse κυριολέκτως dici de homine, quia non corpus ab animo separatum, neque à corpore animus homo proprie dicitur. Lo- quitur hunc in modum & Josephus : καὶ γὰρ εἰλήφα- μεν παρ᾽ ἐκείνε (τῦ Θεῦ) τὸ εἶναι καὶ τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι πάλιν ἐκείνῳ δίδομεν. Mox sequitur ψυχὴ ἀθάνα- τος ἀεί. Si autem hi, qui lugentur, occisi sunt, non certe intelligendum erit vaticinium de transpor- tatis. Instituitur autem hic tantus planctus, (quod etiam observationem meretur,) non ob liberos in universum utriusque sexus; sed ob filios, quem- admodum etiam de filiis additur consola tio : Et revertentur filii tui ad terminos suos, Babylonica au- tem clades utrumque sexum affecit; at tyrannis Herodiana filios tantum crudeli neci subjecit.

Hisce rationibus accedat observatio Iunia- na l. 1. parallel. 7. quod Propheta voluerit verbis illis proponere signum aliquod luculentum adven- tus illius, in quo complementum esset habiturum Regnum Dei, Jeremjam ergo proponere signum illud ut exhibendum suo tempore, Matthæum de- scribere illud, ut jam exhibitum. Hoc vero si- gnum esse, planctum ingentem excitandum esse in Rama & nefandum & sanguinosum facimus pa- trandum esse. Finis, inquit Junius pag. 1305. in utroque loco unus & idem est, nempe ut certo ali- quo insigni & luculento signo publice ostenderetur, ac demonstraretur eum advenisse, in quo regnum Dei patefieri & complementum sortiri oportuit, in- stituta prædicatione Evangelii : atque hoc signum uterque convenienter narrat, Ieremias quidem fu- turum ostendens, Matthæus vero demonstrans fa- ctum. Summa igitur est, Regnum Domini nostri JESU Christi in hoc mundo infectum esse quam plu- rimis calamitatibus, & filios regni per multas affli- ctiones in illud ingressuros esse : sed illud maxime sin- gulare signum aventantis illius Regni & primum exorientis in Persona Christi, Regis & Servatoris summi, à Deo significatum olim, & suo tempore com- pletum esse, cujus signi indubitatum futurum esse te- stimonium. Nam etsi multæ & indignæ strages post hominum memoriam fuerunt editæ, nusquam ta- men legitur (nisi me animus fallit) facinoris ex- emplum ejusmodi : quo soli parvuli, ne excepto quidem (si Macrobio credimus) Regis ipsius fi- lio, contra jus & fas in regione tota fuerint trucida- ti, sine quæstione ulla, ad tyranni unius volunta- tem & quidem agentis sub potestate alterius, in po- pulo Dei. Neque vero aliud suadet συνέχεια textus. Quum enim de Regni Christi felicitate vaticinatus fuerit Propheta, id non absque calamitate fore in his terris indicat, quum sub ipsa Nov. Testamenti primordia, vix nato Christo Salvatore cives ejus

Bethlehemitici cum vicinis gravi persequutioni subjiciendi sint. Quam cohærentiam tradidit O- siander in Paraphrasi: Ne quis autem existimaret, Regnum Christi in hoc mundo fore absque omni per- sequutione, sibique mera & perpetua corporalia gau- dia imaginaretur: inserit Propheta vaticinium de illa clade, quam sustinuerunt pii parentes in Bethle- hem Juda, & finibus illis, cum ab Herode ipsorum pueri interficerentur. Quæ historia Matth. 2. cap. est descripta: ubi & hic textus Prophetæ allegatur. Ita tamen loquitur figurato sermone Propheta, ut prima fronte videatur de miseriis exilii Babylonici agere. Sed sequimur tutissime interpretem Spiri- tum Sanctum per Evangelistam & Apostolum Matthæum nobis hunc locum explicantem. HÆC DICIT DOMINUS : VOX IN EXCELSO AUDITA EST LAMENTATIONIS, LU- CTUS ET FLETUS amarissimi, matronæ RA- CHEL PLORANTIS FILIOS SUOS, ET NOLENTIS CONSOLARI SUPER EIS: (non admittentis consolationem) QUIA NON SUNT: id est, propterea quod actum de illis esset: Hoc est, matronæ Iudaicæ in urbe Bethlehem & in confinio (ubi olim piissima matrona Rachel, uxor Patriarchæ Jacobi, mortua & sepulta est, Gen. 35.) alta voce lamentabuntur, atq; deplorabunt pueros filios suos, qui per satellites Herodis trucidaban- tur: (sperantis, se inter eos etiam interfectu- rum Christum) nec volent admittere consola- tionem: quia cum ingenti dolore videbunt eos ja- centes exanimes. Similiter Junius & Tremellius; Exposita regni Christi præstantia, ne quis existimet, omnia in hoc seculo corpore & animo fore absolutissi- ma, duas occupationes gravium incommodorum, quæ fideles in regno Christi hic experiuntur, Prophetæ di- luit, ut diximus vers. 10. Prior est, externas tamen perpessiones in Regno Christi non esse desituras, sed fore ut statim à Christo nato furorem suum Satanas ex- erceat, tribus versibus: Posterior est, etiam reman- suram in piis suæ infirmitatis internæ conscientiam, quæ exponitur sequentibus. Prioris occupatio habe- tur, hoc vero solvetur duobus sequentibus; posterioris vero occupatio continetur vers. 18. & 19. solutio tribus seqq. B. Hulsemannus totum caput ita resolvit: Partes tres sunt: Prima usque ad vers. 15. est velut hypotyposis beneficiorum cum exhibito Christo exhi- bendorum, quæ præfigurantur per liberationem è captivitate Babylonica.Secunda pars est Descriptio tum adversitatum tum voluptatum, quæ cum exhi- bito Christo Judæis contingent, à vers. 15. ad 31. Tertia est promissio gratiæ Novi Testamenti propriæ, quæ meritum Christi erat consecutura, à vers.31. ad finem. De parte ergo hac secunda, in qua jam oc- cupamur, ita habet: Pars secunda describit tum mala pœna à vers. 15. ad 41. tum bona gratiæ à vers.21. ad 31. Mala pœna secundum tempora distribui pos- sunt, ut alia dicantur eventura Christo nato, ut in- fanticidium Herodis, quod describitur ab adjun- cto ploratu vers. 15. & præsenti divina consolatione vers. 16. 17. alia Christo è terris sublato, videlicet excidium per Romanos vers. 18. Consequens fru- ctus, Bona gratiæ describuntur à causa procreante, nimirum Christo 20. 21. ab effectu consequente, feli- citate, per prosopopœiã vers.23. à forma vers. 24. à causa efficiente principali gratia Dei, quæ describi- tur ab attributo vehementiæ, quasi per somnum novas vires acquisiverit vers.25 26. à remotione cau- sæ, & effectus contrarii &c.Hos ergo habemus juxta cum Hieronymo & aliis antiquis ὁμοψήφες; qui- bus addimus etiam B. Pappum: Etsi autem multis Interpretibus videtur prædictio hæc aliam quandam Iudaici populi calamitatem principaliter respicere, & secundario tantum in infantibus Bethlehemiticis representata potius quam impleta esse, nobis tamen, apud quos autoritas Evangelica extra controversiam est, Matthæi Evangelistæ citatio fidem facere debet, de illa infantum Herodiana cæde verba hic potissi- mum fieri. Excitat autem Propheta κτ' προσωπο- ποΐαν Rachelem prope Bethlehem sepultam, ut ea in- fantes illos, ab Herode crudelissime necatos, deplo- ret: ipsasg; infantium deinde matres, converso ad eas sermone consolatur. Addimus insuper B. Hun- nium Seniorem in Comment. in Matth. c. 2. Hæc verba etsi possint secundum literam etiam exponi de populi Hebræi miserabili clade, qua occidit tempore captivitatis Babylonicæ, tamen ratione typi, imo ve- ro principaliter, de infanticidio isto agit & vaticina- tur ibi Dominus. Multa quippe sunt in eo capite 31. quæ palam arguunt, de temporibus adventus & Regni Messiæ id totum esse intelligendum. Cujusmo- di etiam est hoc: Novum creo in terra, dicit Do- minus, fœmina circumdabit virum. Similiter ex- stat ibi præclara promissio novi fœderis, sub quo Do- minus remittere illis velit peccata, & iniquitates illo- rum non recordari amplius: quæ ad regnum Christi sub novo testamento refert auctor Epistolæ ad Hebr. 8. Quin & alia complura occurrunt ibi, quæ ad Je- remiæ tempora neutiquam accommodari possunt, im- primis quæ memorantur de beneficiis præstandis ipsis quoque gentibus. Sic omnes circumstantiæ, totius- que antecedentium & consequentium contextus o- stendit, verba Prophetæ vero sensu ab Evangelista esse allegata. Per Rachelem autem sermone figurato civitas Bethlehem notatur, quippe in cujus finibus olim mortua est Rachel Jacobi Patriarchæ uxor pri- maria, ibidemque sepulta. Ut sensus sit, matronas Bethlehemiticas sublato in cœlū clamore, planctu & ejulatu, deplorare luctuosissimam sortem par- vulorum suorum, adeo, ut magnitudo subiti lu- ctus omnem doloris medicinam, omnemque consolationem respuat, eo quod non sint, hoc est, quod videant matres illæ, de suis dulcissimis filiolis in hac quidem vita actum esse, quippe quos videant coram se jacentes exanimes. & carnificum illorum sanguinariis manibus nefarie contrucidatos. Hæc Beatus Hunnius. Quæ in Calvino Judaizante iti- dem asseruit, & postmodum in Anti-Pareo sum- mam eorum ita repetiit pag. 215. Ostendi, inquit, sensum Christianorum quam aptissime quadrare ad totius capitis περίστασιν. Vaticinari enim Dominum de optato illo tempore, quo futurus sit propitius Deus totius Israelis, quo reducere velit populum suum, ut lætantes & cum jubilo redeant in Zion. Id quòd juxta per vulgatum morem Prophetarum de spiritua- li reductione ad communionem Ecclesiæ Novi Testa- menti sit accipiendum. Et omnino loqui Prophetam de rebus, quæ sub adventum Christi futuræ essent. Id- que dilucidius indicari dixi, addita notatione luctûs & planctus Rachelis super filios suos: quod ad traga- diam infanticidii seu miserrimæ trucidationis puero rum Bethleemiticorum pertinere Matthæus Evan gelista perhibeat. Post quæ sic promissa Dominus con soletur populum suum & consolationi inserat vatici nium de nativitate Messiæ, testificans se novum qui creaturum in terra, nimirum ut fœmina circunde virum, & futurum esse tunc, ut Dominus inebrie animam lassam & omnem animam esurientem satu ret: imo ut Dominus feriat domui Israel & domu Juda fœdus novum, sublato veteri, sicut eam per copen vaticinii Epistola ad Hebræos interpretatur, & ad tempus exhibiti Messiæ spectare pronunciat. Ha ctenus iterum B. Hunnius noster. B. Gerhardu etsi referat hoc vaticinjum ad calamitatem decer tribuum, cum abducerentur in captivitatem,

Not. ad Matth. corrigit tamen postea sententiam, vel certe non abnuit, respexisse Spiritum Sanctum ad Herodianum infanticidium pag. 137. Dicitur tempore infanticidii oraculum illud impletum vel per quandam similitudinem, quia in illo infanticidio æque magna, sinon major, calamitas Bethlehemitas & eorum vicinos oppressit quam Israeliticas tribus tempore abductionis in captivitatem, vel perfecte re- spectu ad intentionem Spiritus Sancti habito, quia cum Spiritus Sanctus hoc oraculum per Jeremiam proponeret, respexit non solum ad abductionem decem tribuum, sed etiam ad hoc infanticidium Bethleemi- ticum. Introducitur igitur per patheticam πλάσιν Rachel ante aliquot secula in vicinia Bethlehem, se- pulta, liberos suos tum ab Assyriis & Babyloniis, tum ab Herode Rege interemptos deplorare. Quæ senten- tia commodior videtur, quam si mystico sensu ab Evangelista adductam Prophetiam dicas, cum nonnullis; vel etiam sensu accommodativo, cum Jansenio, Bucero, & Spanhemio. Sensum mysticum refellit ipse Spanhemius cum Cornelio a Lapide: Si- quidem non appareat, qui strages totius populi di- catur typus in specie cædis puerulorum unius vel al- terius vici, deportatio occisionis, deportatio populi re- bellis & impii ob scelera sua cædis puerulorum in pri- mo ætatis flore extinctorum ob Christum & ejus cau- sa. Sensum vero accommodativum esse probare multis satagit Spanhemius, nullum tamen ejus e Scripturis exemplum producere potuit, quo do- ceret, cum Scriptura aliquid impletum dicit, quod prædictum fuit per Prophetam, nudam tantum al- lusionem vel accommodationem fieri. Illa phraseos distinctio Spanhemiana, quod Matthæus non dixe- rit, ut impleretur, quod ait Dominus per Prophetam, dicentem, sed tantum tunc impletum fuisse, quod ait Dominus per Jeremiam dicentem, argutior est, quam verior. Quivis enim facile videt, utriusqs; phraseos eundem esse sensum, eandem latitudinem, sive di- catur, ut impleretur, sive tunc impletum illud fuit, quod prædictum est. Exempla, quæ produxit Span- hemius, dubio LXXII. minus luculenta sunt, neque hoc, quod ipse vult, probant: nempe impleri quan- doq; dici Scripturam improprie, & secundario, ἀναλο- γικῶς vel παραδειγματικῶς, quando simile quid contingit illi, quod jam olim vel factum vel dictum vel prædictum, sive id fiat διηγητικῶς vel narrative, sive ἐπανορθωτικῶς aut διασυρτικῶς correctionem vel traductionem. Nam locus Es. 29,13. respicit illos i- psos, quibus applicatur Matth. 15,18. & vaticinium Es. 6. non per accommodationem tantum, sed dire- cte impletum fuit in auditoribus Christi Matth. 13, 14. quod in explicatione istorum locorum Esaiæ notavimus. Neque per meram accommodationem & transsumptionem adducitur Psalmus 78, 2. ab Evan- gelista Matth. 13, 34. 35. Nam idem ille, qui in Psal- mo ait: aperiam per parabolam os meum, loquutus est apud Matthæum in parabolis. Non applicatur hoc tantum Christo, sed Christus locutus est per os Psaltis. Siquidem Spiritus Christi per Pro- phetas locutus fit teste Petro 1. Epist. 1, 11. de quo videatur B. Gesnerus Comment. in Psalm. Rom. 9, 29. meram tantum accommodationem esse lo- ci Esai. 1, 9. negamus: Contrarium in explicatio- ne loci Esaiæ oftendimus. Quod ad Matth. 21, 13. cum ad institores sui temporis a Christo applicatur, quod de Judæis suæ ætatis jam olim a Jeremia di- ctum cap. 7, 18. non adhibetur phrasis illa, ut im- pleretur, aut tum impletum est, quod per Jeremiam prædictum, ut hoc loco, sed simpliciter dicitur γέγραπται scriptum est. Alia exempla a Spanhe- mio non adducuntur. Neque opus est, ut fin- gamus improprium illum Scripturæ implendæ mo- dum, cum nulla cogat necessitas ad improprieta- tem recurrere.

## 31:16
Verse 16. THERE IS A REWARD FOR YOUR WORK.) Because of your piety, O Rachel, I will treat your descendants mercifully. Or because of your prayers, O mothers.

Latin:

Vers. 16. EST MERCES OPERI TUO.) Propter tuam pietatem, ô Rachel, posteros tuos clementer tracta- bo. Vel propter vestras preces, ô matres.

## 31:17
Verse 17. AND THERE IS HOPE FOR YOUR LATTER END,) That is, eventually it will be: that is, your hope will be fulfilled.

The consolation which the Lord provides for mothers lamenting their children, THERE IS A REWARD FOR YOUR WORK, is not promised on account of Rachel's merits or piety, nor on account of the merits of the Bethlehemite mothers, but He promises a reward that is purely gratuitous, which is not given on account of works, but to the work or affliction: so that the mere consequence of the reward to the work is indicated, but no regard for merit intervenes, just as children are called a reward, but a gratuitous one, Psalm 127:4. Nor is work denoted here by the name of labor, but affliction: just as this word is used elsewhere regarding affliction, Gen. 5:29, Matt. 11:28. But when the return from the land of the enemy is promised in verse 16, and again in verse 17. Your children will return to their own borders, these things indeed seem to imply a return from the Babylonian captivity to the land of Canaan, from which they had been cast out, and we do not deny that these phrases look to and allude to the same; but in the manner of the Prophets, who are accustomed to present spiritual things under the veil of earthly ones, something else is signified than the words suggest: which, if it is not heeded in most of the oracles concerning the Kingdom of the Messiah, Jewish dreams about a bodily Kingdom and temporal happiness will easily prevail. Furthermore, that return from the land of the enemy is explained by some as a conversion to the kingdom of Christ: Thus Junius and Tremellius in their notes on this passage. Solution of the preceding objection: however much Satan may rage and attack the life of the Saints, the Church will nevertheless have new children daily, both among the Israelites and from the co-opted Gentiles, who lie hidden in the land of the enemy, that is, in the Kingdom of Satan and in the power of darkness, until they return to the Church, called by Christ. This zeal of yours toward your children will not be in vain; but it will be compensated by a greater benefit from God, because others will be acquired and will join themselves to you. But because new children are not promised in the text, but the children are said to be about to return to their border, and this consolation is opposed to the weeping for the slain children, Osiander more correctly explains it concerning the restoration of the children in the heavenly fatherland: And your children will return from the land of the enemy into their fatherland, and there is hope for your latter end. Your children will return to their borders, that is, they will be restored to you. Be of good cheer, you parents whose children have been slain. For the Lord will give eternal joy for that sorrow. For your children have not perished, but have been sent ahead into the heavenly fatherland and will rise again in their bodies on the last day. For that HOPE is FOR YOUR LATTER END, and it is not inappropriately said to look to the last things of the world. But they are said to return TO THEIR BORDER, because the border destined for the faithful is the heavenly fatherland: and the phrase is taken from the type of the heavenly fatherland, namely the promised land, in which the Israelites had their borders. If you ask how the children are said to return from the land of the enemy, when the discourse is about those who have been slain, who are no more, for this is given as the cause of the lamentation, it is manifest that a bodily return cannot be understood, nor that the border from which they return is the land of the enemy, Chaldea, because those slain were in Judea, but the slain children are said to return when they are awakened from death, as is found in Psalm 90:3: You turn man to destruction, and say, RETURN, O children of men. Those who are in the land of the enemy are in the region of death, when death, the last enemy, 1 Corinthians 15:26, detains them and treads upon them, as the King of terrors, Job 18:14, in the land of darkness and oblivion, or remote, Psalm 88:12, which in Job 10:21.

is called a land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror. Jerome has this to say about them: We understand it better of the little ones, who have the reward of blood shed for Christ, and instead of the land of Herod the enemy, they possess the kingdoms of heaven, and will return to their former seat when, for the body of humility, they have received a glorious body. This is the hope of the latter end, when the righteous will shine like the sun, and infants, once little ones and sucklings, without the increase of age and the injuries and labor of the body, will rise again into a perfect man, into the measure of the fullness of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET EST SPES NOVISSIMIS TUIS,) Id est, tandem erit: id est, implebitur spes tua.

Consolatio, quam matribus filios suos deplo- rantibus sufficit Dominus, EST MERCES OPERI TUO, non ob Rachelis merita aut pie- tatem, neque ob merita matrum Bethleemiticarum promittitur, sed mercedem spondet mere gratuitam, quæ non propter opera datur, sed operi vel afflictio- ni: ut nuda consequutio indicetur præmii ad opus, non vero meriti respectus interveniat, quemadmo- dum liberi merces dicuntur, sed gratuita Psal. 127, 4. Neq; etiam laboris nomine opus hic notatur, sed afflictio: uti alias de afflictione hæc vox usurpatur cap. Gen. 5, 29. Matth. 11, 28. Cum autem promit- titur reditus è terra inimici vers. 16. & iterum vers. 17. Filii tui revertentur in terminos suos, videntur quidem ista reditum è captivitate Babylonica in terram Canaan, è qua ejecti erant, inferre, neque abnuimus phrasibus istis ad eandem respici, atque alludi; sed more Prophetarum, qui solent sub invo- lucro bonorum spiritualia exhibere, aliud signifi- catur, quam verba præ se ferunt: quod nisi in ple- risque de Regno Messiæ oraculis attendatur, facile Judaica somnia de corporali Regno, & temporali feli- citate obtinebunt. Cæterum reditus ille è terra ini- mici de conversione ad regnum Christi à nonnullis explicatur: Ita Junius & Tremellius in notis ad h. l. Solutio præcedentis occupationis: utcumq; furat Sa- tanas, & Sanctorum vitam appetat, Ecclesiam ta- men liberos novos indies habituram esse, tum in Israe- litis, tum ex cooptatis gentibus, qui in terra inimici la- tent, id est, in Regno Satanæ, & in potestate tenebra- rum, donec revertantur ad Ecclesiam, vocati à Chri- sto. Non erit irritum tuum hoc studium erga li- beros; sed ampliore beneficio à Deo compensabi- tur, quod alii comparabuntur & se adjungent tibi. At quia non novi liberi promittuntur in textu, sed reversuri dicuntur filii ad terminum suum, & con- solatio hæc opponitur ploratui ob interfectos filios, rectius Osiander de restitutione filiorum in cælesti patria explicat: Et revertentur filii tui de terra ini- mici in patriam, & est spes novissimis tuis. Rever- tentur filii tui ad terminos suos, id est, restituentur ti- bi. Bono animo estote vos parentes, quorum in- terfecti sunt liberi. Dominus enim pro isto mœ- rore dabit perpetuum gaudium. Etenim liberi ve- stri non perieruut, sed præmissi sunt in patriam cœ- lestem & corporibus suis resurgent in novissimo die. Illud enim SPES est NOVISSIMIS TUIS, novissima mundi respicere non incommode di- citur. AD TERMINUM autem suum redire dicuntur, quia terminus fidelibus destinatus est pa- tria cælestis: & desumta est phrasis à typo cœ- lestis patriæ, terra nempe promissa, in qua Israeli- tæ terminos suos habebant. Si quæras, quomodo de terra inimici reverti dicantur filii, quum sermo sit de interfectis, qui non sunt amplius, hæc enim causa planctus redditur, manifestum est, reditum corporalem intelligi non posse, neque terminum a quo Chaldæam inimici terram esse, quia interfecti illi sunt in Judæa, sed reverti dicuntur filii inter- fecti, cum excitantur à morte, uti Psal. 90, 4. habe- tur: Redigis hominem ad interitum, & dicis, RE- VERTIMINI filii hominum. Qui in terra inimici sunt, in regione mortis, cum mors hostis novissimus 1. Corinth. 15, 22, ipsos detinet, & calcat super eos, quasi Rex interitus Job. 18, 14. in terra tenebrosa, & oblivionis, vel remota, Psal. 88, 13. quæ Job. 10, 21.

vocatur terra tenebrosa, & operta mortis caligine, ter- ra miseria & tenebrarum, ubi umbra mortis & nul- lus ordo, sed sempiternus horror. Hieronymus ita de his habet: Melius de parvulis intelligimus, qui mercedem habeant effusi sanguinis pro Christo, & pro terra Herodis inimici teneant regna cælorum, & reversuri sint in sedem pristinam quando pro corpore humilitatis, corpus receperint gloriosum. Ista est spes novissima, quando justi fulgebunt sicut sol, & infantes quondam parvuli atq; lactantes, absq; ætatum incre- mento & injuriis ac labore corporeo resurgent in vi- rum perfectum, in mensuram plenitudinis Christi.

## 31:18
Verse 18. HEARING I HAVE HEARD EPHRAIM LAMENTING) The sense of this passage seems to me to be far different from that which has appeared to most. God gives the reasons why He is not about to bring back the ten tribes, but is about to bring back Judah; because the Israelites of the ten tribes (who are named from Ephraim, because the kingdom was in his lineage) were unwilling to repent in captivity. Understand 'lamenting' as 'exiled'.

YOU HAVE CHASTISED ME AND I WAS INSTRUCTED AS AN UNTAMED CALF) You indeed punished me, but I have become no better; like an untamed calf. That 'I was instructed as an untamed calf' signifies: I was not instructed, I was not corrected, as the Chaldean rightly understood here. Chrysostom cites this passage thus, from which the Greek copies that we have seem to need correction: ἐπαίδευσάς με κύριε, καὶ ἐκ ἐπαιδεύθην, ἀλλ' ἐγενόμην ὡς μόσχος ἀδίδακτος. ἐπίστρεψόν με καὶ ἐπιστραφήσομαι. The passage is in Volume 6, in the sermon, 'That God is the same in the Old and New Testament'.

TURN ME AND I SHALL BE TURNED) The sense is that they said this: Make it so that I return to my fatherland, and then I will repent.

Latin:

Vers. 18. AUDIENS AUDIVI EPHRAIM TRANSMI- CRANTEM) Sensus hujus loci longe alius mihi videtur esse, quam is qui plerisq; visus est. Causas reddit Deus, cur decem tribus non sit reducturus, Judam autem reducturus; quia Israelitæ decem tribuum (qui ab Ephraimo nominan- tur, quod regnum in ejus stirpe fuerit) noluerint resipisce- re in captivitate. Transmigrantem intellige exsulantem.

CASTIGASTI ME ET ERUDITUS SVM QVASI JUVENCVLVS INDOMITVS) Tu quidem me punivisti, sed ego nihilo melior factus sum;quam juvencus indomitus. Illud eruditus sum ut juvencus indomitus, significat, non sum eruditus, non sum correctus,ut hic recte accepit Chaldæus. Chrysostomus hunc locum sic citat, unde corrigenda vi- dentur exemplaria Græca quæ habemus: ἐπαίδευσάς με κύριε, καὶ ἐκ ἐπαιδεύθην, ἀλλ' ἐγενόμην ὡς μόσχος ἀδίδακτος. ἐπίστρεψόν με καὶ ἐπιστραφήσομαι. Locus est Tomo 6. ser- mone, eundem esse Deum Veteris & Novi Testamenti.

CONVERTE ME ET CONVERTAR) Sensus est, hoc illos dixisse: Fac ut redeam in patriam, & tunc re- sipiscam.

## 31:19
Vers. 19. FOR AFTER THOU HAST CONVERTED ME, I DID PENANCE) Translate: When thou shalt have brought me back, I will do penance.

AND AFTER THOU HAST SHOWN ME) When thou shalt have shown me: Supply thy benefits.

I STRUCK MY THIGH) I will strike my thigh: namely in the days of כפריס.

I AM CONFOUNDED, I HAVE BLUSHED, BECAUSE I HAVE BORNE THE REPROACH OF MY YOUTH.) As if he were to say: Now I cannot be free to do penance: I am so ashamed of these evils, through which my old sins are so severely punished.

Latin:

Vers. 19. POSTQVAM ENIM CONVERTISTI ME, EGI POENITENTIAM) Verte: Ubi me reduxeris, agam pœnitentiam.

ET POSTQVAM OSTENDISTI MIHI) Ubi ostenderis mihi: Supple beneficia tua.

PERCVSSI FEMVR MEVM) Percutiam femur meum: nempe in diebus כפריס.

CONFVSVS SVM, ERVBVI, QVONIAM SVSTINVI OPPROBRIVM ADOLESCENTIÆ MEÆ.) Quasi diceret: Nunc non possum vacare agendæ pœnitentiæ: adeo me pudet horum malorum, per quæ ve- tera mea delicta tam severe puniuntur.

## 31:20
Vers. 20. IF EPHRAIM IS AN HONORABLE SON TO ME, IF A DELICATE CHILD) God answers: Is not Ephraim a precious son to me, is he not a delicate child? Certainly it is necessary that he believe that I cannot be without him, because he is so delicate that he is unwilling to do penance unless his return is first obtained.

SINCE I SPOKE OF HIM, I WILL STILL REMEMBER HIM) When I shall have spoken enough with him, (that is, when I shall have sufficiently admonished him) I will altogether remember him, namely, I will be mindful of that stubbornness of his.

THEREFORE MY BOWELS ARE TROUBLED FOR HIM) On this account I am vehemently angry with him. The word for bowels among the Hebrews refers to every more serious emotion.

I WILL SURELY HAVE PITY ON HIM) I think these should be read as a question. Could I possibly have pity on him who is unwilling to correct himself, as long as he is in evil circumstances?

Grotius perverts the text with his new interpretation, nor is he sufficiently consistent with himself. For if these things are to be understood concerning the desertion of the ten tribes, how in verse 21 are the two tribes addressed, since the discourse is so constructed that there is no doubt that the same, not different, people are being addressed? Furthermore, since we are certain from the preceding that these things pertain to the times of the New Testament, our blessed Hulsemann refers these to the final destruction wrought by the Romans. It is manifest that the miserable state and groaning of Ephraim and the virgin of Israel are presented here, when the Israelites, confounded because of their crimes, bear the reproach of their youth: and that the bowels of divine mercy are opened, by which He did not disdain to console Ephraim and Israel and to recall them to penance. Although indeed God's grace was in vain among most Israelites, He nevertheless wished to testify it to all, and to recall all to the way, for which cause also that new thing, which the Lord was about to create on the earth, is proposed, since it was created to that end, and the Son of God was born of a virgin, that what had perished might be sought, and sinners might be called to repentance. the Lord bless you, O habitation of justice! Since some remnants shall be snatched from the Jews, and from them the beginnings of the Christian Church shall arise, which will then be greatly increased and multiplied. Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah.
