## 52:11
Ver. 11.

IN THE HOUSE OF THE PRISON) The Hebrew properly has 'house of inquiry,' where inquiry is made into the accused. 'House of the bound,' says the Chaldean; the LXX more harshly, ἐὶς ὀικίαν μύλωνος.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

IN DOMO CARCERIS) Hebræum proprie habet, domum inquisitionis, ubi in reos inquiritur. Domum vin- ctorum, Chaldæus; LXX. durius ἐὶς ὀικίαν μύλωνος.

## 52:12
Ver. 12.

TENTH OF THE MONTH) It is the seventh in the book of Kings. The error is undoubtedly from old numeral notes, either here or there. Josephus has the ninth day of the month.

No error is to be admitted here: Johannes Wolphius in the book of Kings says this about these matters: This discrepancy, if the matter is considered more correctly, will be none at all: For it is credible that on the ninth day of the fourth month some hope of taking the city had shone upon the Chaldeans, when the besieged, exhausted by labor and starvation, defended themselves more slackly, a considerable part of the walls having collapsed, and perhaps having already lost some ramparts, and finally around the beginning of the fifth month the city was captured, with the king having turned to flight. Just as our author himself also says in the preceding verses, that on the ninth of the month, namely the fourth, as Jeremiah says, the city was broken through. Wherefore, since the city was broken through on the ninth day of the fourth month, and it was finally completely stormed on the seventh day of the fifth month, while the inhabitants were still defending it even after it was broken; since the Chaldeans occupied the city with no uncertain hope once the walls were breached, it is not surprising that the former time was noted by Jeremiah. The Hebrews report that the Chaldeans entered the sacred temple on the seventh day, and held assemblies and celebrated feasts in it, but then finally set it on fire on the ninth day. It is credible, however, that the burning of such a great city and temple lasted not a few days, since a certain part of Rome, once burned by Nero, burned for six days and seven nights. The Hebrews also think it should be observed that by those numbers of days and months it is represented to us how well the punishment corresponds with their sins: since in the fifth month the violation, and on the seventh day the pollution of the Sabbath are signified, etc. The Jesuit Sanctius says, the solution of this discrepancy is not difficult. For since Riblah, from where Nebuzaradan departed, was distant from Jerusalem by no small interval, in the fourth book of Kings the seventh day is set, on which the journey was begun; in Jeremiah the tenth, on which it was finished: nor is it incredible that three days were consumed in traversing that space by the military march.

Verse of the same.

PRINCE OF THE MILITIA) In Hebrew: Prince of the slayers. Thus they always call Egyptian, Babylonian, and other foreign soldiers, whose wars were either unjust or immoderate.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

DECIMA MENSIS) Septima est in libro Regum. Er- ror haud dubie ex veteribus notis numeralibus, aut hic, aut illic. Nonam diem mensis habet Josephus.

Nullus hic error admittendus: Johannes Wol- phius in lib. Regum ita de his: Hæc discrepantia, si res reputetur rectius, nulla erit: Credibile est enim, mensis quarti nona die spem urbis obtinendæ Chal- dæis aliquam affulsisse, cum obsessi, labore & inedia exhausti, remissius se tuerentur, aliquanta muro- rum parte collapsa, aliqua jam fortasse propugnacu- la amisisse, tandem circa mensis quinti initium ur- bem, rege in fugam verso, captam esse. Veluti superio- ribus versibus author noster ipse etiam dicit, nona mensis, puta quarti, ut inquit Ieremias, urbem per- ruptam esse. Quamobrem cum urbs nona quarti mensis die perrupta sit, hanc etiam fractam adhuc propugnantibus incolis, quinti mensis die septimo tota demum fuerit expugnata: quoniam perruptis muris urbem Chaldæi minime dubia jam spe occupa- runt, non mirum est, prius illud tempus à Ieremia notatum esse. Tradunt Hebræi Chaldæos ædem sa- cram die septima igressos, in eaque conventus egis- se, & convivia celebrasse, tum autem nona demum die incendisse. Credibile est autem, incendium tan- tæ urbis & ædis non paucos dies durasse, cum quædam pars Romæ à Nerone quondam incensa dies sex & noctes septem arserit. Observandum etiam Hebræi censent, numeris illis dierum atque mensium repræ- sentari nobis, quam bene pœna cum illorum peccatis conveniat: quando mense quinto violatio, septimo die sabbathi pollutio significentur &c. Jesuita San- ctius, solutio, inquit, hujus discrepantiæ difficilis non est. Cum enim Reblata, unde egressus est Nebu- zardan, à Hierosolymis distaret intervallo non mo- dico, in libro quarto Regum dies ponitur septimus, in quo inchoatus; apud Ieremiam decimus, in quo finitus est cursus: neque incredibile est, à militari progressu tres dies in spatio illo decurrendo fuisse con- sumptos.

Vers. eod.

PRINCEPS MILITIÆ) In Hebræo: Princeps inter- ficientium. Ita semper appellant milites Ægyptios, Baby lonios, & alios externos, quorum bella erant aut injusta aut immoderata.

## 52:16
Verse 16.

VINE-DRESSERS AND HUSBANDMEN) In Hebrew: And vine-dressers and husbandmen; that is, who were to be vine-dressers and husbandmen. The Greeks: εἰς ἀμπελόεργυς κὶ εἰς γεωργύς. The Chaldean: that they might cultivate fields and vineyards.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

VINITORES ET AGRICOLAS) In Hebræo: I vinitores & agricolas; id est, qui essent vinitores & agricola Græci: εἰς ἀμπελόεργυς κὶ εἰς γεωργύς. Chaldæus: ut coleren agros & vineas.

## 52:17
THE CHALDEANS BROKE) So that they could be carried more easily.

Latin:

CONFREGERVNT CHALDÆI) Quo facilius portari possent.

## 52:18
Verse 18.

FLESH-HOOKS) It is wonderful in how many ways the word יעים is translated. The Greeks and the Latin have placed 'creagras' here: the Greeks elsewhere [translate it as] καλυπτῆρα, φιάλην, θέρμας, πυρεῖα: the Latin now [as] creagras, as here, now [as] tongs, now [as] tridents, now [as] platters, now [as] ladles. I would believe anything rather than that they were brooms, as some translate. For they were not of such value that the Chaldeans would carry them away on such a long journey. יעי in Hebrew, and יעא in Chaldean, is to remove. That makes me think they were shovels.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

CREAGRAS) Mirum quot modis vertatur vox יעים. Creagras hîc posuere Græci & Latinus : Græci alibi καλυ- πτῆρα, φιάλην, θέρμας, πυρεῖα: Latinus modo creagras, ut hîc, modo forcipes, modo tridentes, modo scutra, modo trullas. Quidvis potius crediderim, quam scopas fuisse, ut quidam vertunt. Neque enim tanti erant, ut eas tanto itinere auferrent Chaldæi. יעי Hebraice, & יעא Chal- daice, est removere. Id facit, ut palas fuisse existimem.

## 52:19
AS MANY AS WERE GOLDEN, GOLDEN: AND AS MANY AS WERE SILVER, SILVER) That is, of both materials, solid-hammered, with no hollowness, with no admixture.

Latin:

QVOTQVOT AVREA, AVREA: ET QVOT- QVOT ARGENTEA, ARGENTEA) Id est, utriusque materiæ ὁλόσφυρα, nulla inanitate, nulla admixtione.

## 52:20
Verse 20.

AND ONE SEA, AND TWELVE BRAZEN BULLS, WHICH WERE UNDER THE BASES WHICH KING SOLOMON HAD MADE) Nay, they were not under the bases, but under the Sea, 1 Kings 7:24, 25, compared with 27. Wherefore a transposition must be supplied entirely in this way: One Sea and twelve bulls which were under (the Sea and) the bases which King Solomon had made. The LXX: οἱ μόχοι δώδεκα χαλκοῖ ὑποκάτω τῆς θαλάσσης.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ET MARE VNVM, ET VITVLOS DVODE- CIM ÆREOS, QVI ERANT SVB BASIBVS QVAS FECERAT REX SOLOMON) Imo non sub basibus e- rant, sed sub Mari, 1. Reg. 7, 24. 25. collato 27. Quare omnino supplenda ὑπερθεσις hoc modo: Mare unum & vitu- los duodecim qui erant subter (mare &) bases quas fecerat rex Salomon. LXX. οἱ μόχοι δώδεκα χαλκοῖ ὑποκάτω τῆς θαλάσσης.

## 52:21
Verse 21.

EIGHTEEN CUBITS WERE ON ONE PILLAR, AND A LINE OF TWELVE CUBITS WENT ROUND IT) They were eighteen common cubits high, which, if you subtract the base, make the 35 cubits mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:15. This line signifies the circumference.

MOREOVER THE THICKNESS OF IT WAS FOUR FINGERS) That is, the diameter. It is absolutely necessary that the scribes erred here in the number, for four fingers cannot make the diameter of a circumference of twelve cubits on a pillar.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

DECEM ET OCTO CVBITI ERANT IN CO- LVMNA VNA, ET FVNICVLVS DVODECIM CV- BITORVM CIRCVIBAT IPSAM) Decem & octo cu- bitos communes altæ erant, qui, si demas basim, faci- cunt 35. cubitos memoratos 1. Paral. 3, 15. Funiculus hic significat τὴν περίμετρον.

PORRO GROSSITVDO EJVS QVATVOR DIGITORVM) Id est, ἡ δυάμετρος. Omnino necesse est scribæ hîc erraverint in numero, nam quatuor digiti non possunt facere dimetientem ambitus octo cubitorum in co- lumna.

## 52:23
Verse 23.

NINETY-SIX POMEGRANATES) Namely on the half-side of each pillar, which all joined together from the two sides of the two pillars, make four hundred, as it is in 2 Chronicles 4:13, with one pomegranate added to each side to distinguish the sides. But that here 100 are said immediately instead of 95 was done to round the number, unless the scribe also erred here.

Grotius is quite ready with accusations against the Authentic codex, as if it had suffered corruption. But this is by no means to be conceded. Junius and Tremellius rendered the former words thus: 'Moreover its thickness was four fingers.' I do not see how these can be argued to be an error in number. In the latter, Grotius himself showed a way of reconciling them: and so also Junius: 'Ninety-six, excluding the four individual ones, which if you include, they will make a hundred in each row' 1 Kings 7:20, 2 Chronicles 4:13. Osiander rendered and reconciled them from the Hebrew text thus: 'And there were ninety-six pomegranates in their space, for the remaining four facing the wall of the temple could not be seen.'

Latin:

Vers. 23.

MALA GRANATA NONAGINTA SEX) Nem- pe in cujusque columnæ dimidiato latere, quæ omnia jun- cta ex duobus lateribus duarum columnarum, faciunt qua- dringenta, ut est 2. Paral. 4, 13. addito scilicet ad quodque latus, uno malo Punico distinguente latera. Quod autem hîc statim pro XCV. dicuntur C. factum est ad rotundan- dum numerum, nisi & hîc scriba erraverit.

Admodum promptus est Grotius ad ἐγκλήμα- τα adversus codicem Authenticum, quasi is cor- ruptionem passus sit. Quod vero nequàquam con- cedendum. Priora verba ita reddidere Iunius & Tremellius: Densitas autem ejus quatuor digitorum erat. Quæ quomodo erroris in numero argui pos- sint, non video. In posterioribus modum conci- liandi Grotius ipse monstravit: atque ita etiam Ju- nius: Nonaginta sex, exceptis singularibus quatuor, quæ si comprehenderis, efficientur centena singulis or- dinibus 1. Reg. 7, 20. 2. Chron. 4, 13. Ea è textu E- bræo sic reddidit & conciliavit Osiander : Et fue- runt mala granata nonaginta sex in spatio suo, nam quatuor reliqua ad parietem templi vergentia non poterant conspici.

## 52:24
Verse 24.

AND THE CAPTAIN OF THE HOST TOOK) Namely from the temple, as the following opposition shows.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ET TVLIT MAGISTER MILITIÆ) Nempe de templo, ut ostendit oppositio sequens.

## 52:25
Verse 25.

SEVEN MEN OF THOSE WHO SAW THE KING'S FACE) Five in the book of Kings. But Josephus has seven.

Under that number seven is included that courtier having command over the forces, and the scribe of the army, who is mentioned later, as Junius and Tremellius reconcile it. Osiander thus: In the history of 1 Kings 25, fewer persons are counted, but only those who were principal. This reconciliation is more convenient, because that Sopher and the courtier are named here specifically, besides those seven men.

THE SCRIBE, THE PRINCE OF THE SOLDIERS) Rather, the scribe of the prince of the soldiers just mentioned. It is better to take this than as a proper name, as this interpreter did in 1 Kings 24:19.

WHO WAS PROVING THE TROOPS) In Hebrew: Who was making the people serve, of the land: that is, who was enrolling citizens in the registers and was present for the levy. See a not dissimilar office in the Assyrian camps by the same name ספר Isaiah 33, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

SEPTEM VIROS DE HIS QVI VIDEBANT FACIEM REGIS) Quinque in libro Regum. At septem habet Josephus.

Sub nomine illo septenario comprehenditur ille aulicus imperium in copias habens, & scriba ex- ercitus, cujus postea mentio sit, ut Iunius & Tre- mellius conciliant. Osiander ita: In historia 1. Reg. 25. pauciores personæ, sed illæ præcipuæ tantum nu- merantur. Quæ conciliatio commodior est, quia Sopher ille, & aulicus peculiariter hic nominan- tur, præter istos septem viros.

SCRIBAM PRINCIPEM MILITVM) Imo, Scribam principis militum modo dicti. Melius hoc quam pro nomi- ne proprio accipere, ut fecit hic interpres 1. Reg. 24, 19.

QVI PROBABAT TTRONES) In Hebræo: Qui militare faciebat populum, terræ: id est qui cives asscribebat numeris & delectui aderat. Vide non dissimile officium in castris Assyriis eodem nomine ספר Esaiæ 33, 18.

## 52:28
Ver. 28.

IN THE SEVENTH YEAR [OF THE] REIGN OF NEBUCHADNEZZAR, as the following indicate. It is that very first deportation which is narrated in 2 Kings 24:12, 13, 14, 15, 16. But here too the numbers differ. It is a small matter that this event is said there to have happened in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar: for it could have happened partly in the seventh year, partly in the eighth. But in the book of Kings you have more than ten thousand abducted. Yet the sum placed here below agrees with the numbers of the three deportations placed here.

There will be no difficulty if you say that 3023 were Jews of the common sort abducted at that time, but 7000 were men of principal dignity, which number is expressed in 2 Kings 24:16.

Ussher, however, in Chron. S. p. 36, judges that that deportation which took place under Jeconiah, of which 2 Kings 24 speaks, is different, and that this number 3023 pertains not at all to the same; and with James Capellus in Chronol. at the year M. 3398 and 3414, he observes that some deportations were greater, others smaller. He assigns three of the former kind. The first in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar in the captivity of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, 2 Chron. 36:6. The second in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar in the transmigration of Jeconiah, of which 2 Kings 24:12. The third in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar in the destruction of the city and Temple under Zedekiah, of which 2 Kings 25. He likewise makes three of the latter kind, namely these, of which Jeremiah speaks here: made in the seventh, eighteenth, and twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar came, to be sure, in the first year of his reign, and wished to abduct Jehoiakim bound in chains: but after he was made tributary, he left him in Jerusalem, 2 Chron. 36:6, though some of the more distinguished families were deported, especially Daniel with his companions, Dan. 1:1, at the end of the third year of Jehoiakim, beginning of the fourth, Jer. 25:1. Furthermore, in the seventh year of his reign he abducted again, because Jehoiakim had revolted from him, 2 Kings 24:1, 2, 3023 from Judea. Then in the following year, the eighth, after the death of Jehoiakim, while Jeconiah was reigning, who presided for only three months, Nebuchadnezzar made an expedition again, and carried off the King with a great multitude, 2 Kings 24:14 seqq. The fourth expedition happened in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar: in which, as Jeremiah testifies, he abducted 832 souls. But in the following year, the 19th, Zedekiah himself was captured, deprived of his eyes, abducted, and the Temple with the Palace was burned, 2 Kings 25:8. Which was the fifth deportation. The sixth and final deportation was made in the 23rd year of Nebuchadnezzar, by Nebuzaradan, 745, as Jeremiah teaches here. Concerning which, see more in Chron. S. Biblico Sect. 6, q. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

IN ANNO SEPTIMO JVDÆOS 3. MILLIA 23.) Regni Nabuchodonoforis, ut sequentia indicant. Est ea ipsa abductio prima, quæ narratur 2. Reg 24, 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. Sed & hic discrepant numeri. Parum est, quod ibi facta hæc res dicitur anno octavo Nabuchodonosoris: potuit enim id accidisse partim anno septimo, partim o- ctavo. Sed in libro Regum habes abductos plus decem millibus. Summa tamen hic infra posita cum trium abdu- ctionum numeris hic positis congruit.

Nulla erit difficultas, si dicas 3023. fuisse vulgaris generis Judæos tum abductos, 7000. vero præcipuæ dignitatis viros, qui numerus expressus est 2. Reg. 22, 16.

Usserius tamen in Chron. S. p. 36. diversam censet esse deportationem illam sub Jechonia fa- ctam, de qua 2. Reg. 24. numerumque hunc 3023. nihil omnino ad eandem attinere; & cum Jacobo Capello in Chronol. ad Ann. M. 3398. & 3414. ob- servat, deportationum alias fuisse majores, alias minores. Prioris generis tres assignat. Primam an- no Nebucadnezaris primo in captivitate Jojakimi, filii Josiæ 2. Par. 36, 6. Secundam anno Nebu- cadnezaris octavo in transmigratione Jechoniæ, de qua 2. Reg. 24, 12. Tertiam anno Nebucadneza- ris decimo nono in urbis & Templi excidio sub Zede- kia, de qua 2. Reg. 25. Posterioris generis itidem tres facit, has nempe, de quibus hic Jeremias: an- no Nebucadnezaris septimo, decimo octavo, & vi- gesimo tertio factas. Venit nempe Nebucadnezar primo regiminis sui anno, & catenis vinctum Jo- jakimum abducere voluit: sed post tributarium fa- ctum reliquit Hierosolymis, 2. Paral. 36, 6. depor- tatis tamen quibusdam ex insignioribus familiis, Daniele imprimis cum sociis, Dan. 1, 1. anno Jo- jakimi tertio exeunte, quarto ineunte, Jer. 25, 1. Porro septimo regiminis sui anno abduxit iterum, quia Jojakim defecerat ab ipso, 2. Reg. 24, 1. 2. è Judæa 3023. Dehinc anno sequente octavo post obitum Jojakimi, regnante Jechonia, qui per tres menses tantum præfuit, expeditionem iterum fe- cit Nebucadnezar, Regemque cum magna multi- tudine traduxit, 2. Reg. 24, 14. seqq. Quarta ex- peditio contigit anno Nebucadnezaris decimo o- ctavo: quo, teste Jeremia, abduxit 832. animas. Anno autem sequente 19. Zedekias ipse captivatus, oculis privatus, abductus, & Templum cum Re- gia combustum est, 2. Reg. 25, 8. Quæ quinta fuit deportatio. Sexta & postrema deportatio anno 23. Nebucadnezaris facta, per Nebusar Adanem, 745. docente hic Jeremia. De quibus pluribus Chron. S. Biblico Sect. 6. q. 20.

## 52:29
Ver. 29.

IN THE EIGHTEENTH YEAR) that is, at that time when the city was captured, although above 12, and 2 Kings 25:8, that year is said to have been the 19th, whence this passage seems to need correction,

There is no need for correction. For it happened at the end of the eighteenth, and at the beginning of the nineteenth. v. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

IN ANNO OCTAVO DECIMO) id est, eo tem- pore, cum urbs capta est, quamquam supra 12, & 2. Reg. 25, 8. is annus dicitur fuisse 19. unde corrigendus videtur hic locus,

Non opus est correctione. Nam accidit ad finem Decimi octavi, & sub initium noni. v. 12.

## 52:30
Ver. 30.

IN THE TWENTY-THIRD YEAR.) This is not in the history of Kings and Chronicles. But it is entirely credible. That was done when, after Gedaliah was killed, new disturbances were feared. See in Jeremiah 40 and the following, 2 Kings 25:23.

ALL SOULS THEREFORE FOUR THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED) This number seems to me to be smaller than it should be: and therefore both the sum and the preceding numbers are suspect. The notes, which were once used in books, are easily confused with one another.

That suspicion is groundless. For this number is collected only from those who were placed here from the three abductions, omitting the seven thousand Jews of primary rank, and the thousand craftsmen. Of whom special mention is made in the book of Kings. If these are added, the sum of those abducted emerges as 12,600, according to the opinion of those who think Jeremiah is dealing with that deportation which is recounted in the book of Kings: But it is more correctly established that other and different deportations are designated here.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

IN ANNO VIGESIMO TERTIO.) Hoc in histo- ria Regum & Paralipomenis non est. Sed omnino credibi- le est. Id factum, cum post interfectum Godoliam, novi motus metuerentur. Vide in Jeremia 40. & poster. Reg. 25, 23.

OMNES ERGO ANIMÆ QVATVOR MILLIA SEXCENTÆ) Videtur mihi hic numerus æquo minor esse: ideoque suspecta & summa & numeri præcedentes. Notæ, quæ olim in libris usurpatæ, facile inter se mutantur.

Suspicio illa nulla est. Nam colligitur hic tan- tum numerus eorum, qui hic positi erant è tribus abductionibus, prætermissis septem millibus prima- riæ dignitatis Judæis, & mille fabris. Quorum pe- culiaris in libro Regum mentio facta. Qui si ad- dantur, summa emergit abductorum 12600. se- cundum eorum sententiam, qui Jeremiam de illa deportatione agere putant, quæ in libro Re- gum recensita est: Sed rectius statuitur, hic alias & diversas deportationes designari.

## 52:31
Ver. 31.

IN THE TWENTY-SEVENTH YEAR OF THE TRANSMIGRATION OF JOACHIN) Of the first abduction, in which Joachin or Jechonias was abducted.

TWENTY-FIFTH OF THE MONTH) The twenty-seventh in the book of Kings. Concerning the rest, see what we have said at the end of the latter book of Kings.

The discrepancy of this day arises from the fact that while it was indeed proposed in the assembly of the nobles on the 25th day, it was deliberated upon for two days. Therefore, the beginning of the liberation was on the 25th day, the completion occurred on the 27th. Others say he was led out of prison on the 25th day, but raised up on the 27th. Dionysius, Lyra. Josephus himself, book 10, ch. 12, reconciles it thus: that the decree concerning the freeing of the King was made on the 25th day of the month, but the execution took place two days later on the 27th. Therefore, there is no dissonance here. And these things regarding Jeremiah; whose exhortation derived from this passage we conclude with Theodoret: The Lord shows mercy while punishing, and uses chastisement to console: and He tempers the sentence of justice with clemency. Wherefore we ought to fear the just judgment: and relying on His benevolence, not to despair of salvation: expecting true divine mercy, we ought to walk in the straight path, so that we may be able to attain a blessed end, through Jesus Christ our Lord; with whom may there be glory to our Father, together with the most holy Spirit, both now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

IN VIGESIMO SEPTIMO ANNO TRANS- MIGRATIONIS JOACHIN) Primæ abductionis, in qua abductus Joachin sive Jechonias.

VICESIMA QVINTA MENSIS) Vicesima septi- ma in libro Regum. De cæteris vide, quæ diximus ad finem posterioris Regum.

Discrepantia diei istius inde est, quod 25. die quidem id in procerum conventu propositum sit, sed biduo deliberatum fuerit. Initium ergo libera- tionis 25. die, complementum 17. factum. Alii eductum dicunt die 25. de carcere, elevatum autem 27. Dionysius, Lyra. Josephus ipse lib. 10. c. 12. sic conciliat, quod decretum de liberando Rege die 25. Mensis, exequutio autem biduo post die 27. facta. Nulla ergo hic dissonantia. Atque hæc ad Jere- miam; Quem parænesi ex hac pericopa deducta cum Theodoreto concludimus: Puniens miseretur Dominus, & castigatione utens consolatur: justitiæ que sententiam clementia temperat. Quare nos ju- stumn judicium formidare debemus : & benevolentia ejus freti de salute non desperare: veram misericor- diam divinam expectantes, recta via debemus ince- dere, quo beatum finem adipisci queamus, per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum; cum quo Patri nostro sit gloria, una cum sanctissimo Spiritu, & nunc & semper & in sæcula sæculorum. Amen.

# Ezekiel

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON EZEKIEL.

Ezekiel was a Priest, as he himself will soon say: he was strong in learning and talent, so that (setting aside the gift of Prophecy, which is incomparable) you would not unjustly compare him to Homer, because of his beautiful ἐννοίας (thoughts), illustrious comparisons, and great knowledge of many things, especially Architecture.

We said at 2 Kings 22:14 that this Ezekiel was among those who were the first of all to be carried away from the tribe of Judah in the times of Jechonias. He was carried away, as he himself testifies, to the bank of the river כבר. That river is the Χαβώρας in Ptolemy in his description of Mesopotamia, and the Ἀβόῤῥας to Strabo. Pliny 5.25 indicates the reason for the name. There are those who report that the Euphrates was diverted by the work of the prefect Cobar, where we said it is split, so that it would not infest Babylonia with a headlong course.

Observations on the Grotian Preface, and what else is ἀξιομνημόνευτα (worthy of memory) concerning the τὰ προλεγόμενα (prolegomena).

Grotius touches upon the status of the prophet, the place of the vision, his office, and his character. In status he was a συναιχμά-

λωτος, which is evident from chapter 1, 2. But the first abduction to Babylon took place under Jehoiakim, not under Jeconiah: although Ezekiel crossed over under the latter, from which abduction he also calculates the years, chapter 1, 2. and elsewhere. And therefore he prophesied in a foreign region: whence the boasting of the Jews is false: that the gift of prophesying is restricted to the borders of Palestine. Nazianzen, in oration 47, thinks he was previously a servant of Jeremiah. The Hebrews make him the same person as his son: but Scripture contradicts this, which calls him the son of Buzi. Some talk nonsense that he was Pythagoras; but he was a Greek, not a Jew, and much later than Ezekiel.

The place of the vision is at the bank of the Chebar. By which name Menochius, Tirinus, and Maldonatus wish the Euphrates to be designated; Grotius, along with Prado, Villalpando, Pinto, and Cornelius à Lapide, seems to understand a stream diverted from the Euphrates by the labor of Chabor. Others, with Junius, Tremellius, Piscator, and Polanus, understand a river flowing through Mesopotamia into the Euphrates. Which river is called Χαβώρας by Ptolemy in Geography book 5, chapter 18, and Strabo book 5, chapter 16, and is erroneously called Aborras by Ammianus in book 14, chapter 23. Which opinion Franciscus Junius confirms with not-to-be-despised arguments in his Commentary on Ezekiel 1 and at the end of chapter 2. Epiphanius says his homeland was Sarara.

Grotius says that the office of the Prophet was priestly: others prefer to say he was called a priest because of his priestly lineage, concerning which Epiphanius and Jerome write. As for the talent of the Prophet, he compares him with Homer: but such comparisons are rash and unworthy, even if they are customary for Grotius. For the Spirit of Ezekiel differs from the Homeric genius as much as heaven from earth; but we do not wish to dwell on these things. According to Jerome, in chapter 47, Ezekiel is the Ocean of the Scriptures and the labyrinth of the mysteries of God. According to his name יחזקאל, he is the strength of God, who was truly strong against the obstinate, and according to Gregory the Great, a hard preacher against the hard-hearted: he also proved his strength by martyrdom, as Epiphanius testifies.

Moreover, the chronology, the summary, and the economy of the book must be observed. As for the former, Ezekiel began to preach in the 5th year of Zedekiah, chapter 1, 2, which was the year of the world 3409, the 30th year of the sins of the house of Judah from the beginning of Jeremiah, who began to prophesy in the 13th year of Josiah, year 34. Ezekiel ceased in the year of the migration of Jeconiah, and in the 25th from the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, see chapter 40, 1, or rather in the 27th year of the migration, as is found in chapter 29, 17, so that he prophesied for at least 22 years: ending in the year of the world 3432, from which time, shortly after, Daniel—who had been carried off as a very young boy eight years earlier, at the end of the third year of Jehoiakim in Babylon—began to prophesy in the year of the world 3434, explaining the dream of Nebuchadnezzar. This is the chronotaxis of Ezekiel:

In the 5th year of the migration of Jeconiah and the reign of Zedekiah, Ezekiel is called to his ministry with a singular rite and divine testimony, chapter 1, 2, 3. And the vision of the four wheels and the living creatures, chapter 1, occurred: repeated in chapter 10: signifying the chariot of the Gospel of Christ, in which, through the ministry of the Gospel, by the breath of the Holy Spirit, He is carried into all parts of the earth. Chapters 4, 5, 6, and 7: the siege of Jerusalem, and the horrible famine, war, and plague, and the total destruction of the Jewish kingdom are predicted.

Migration of Jeconiah 6. He had the discourses described from chapter 8 up to 20, in which he argues against the idolatry and other sins of the people, exhorts them to repentance, and predicts the destruction of the kingdom and the King.

Migration 7. The Prophet had the discourses from chapter 20 to 23 inclusive, in which he argues against idols, lusts, contempt for the ministry, the usury of the prophets, priests, princes, and the sins of the people, and predicts the destruction of the whole kingdom and the neighboring Ammonites.

Migration 9. The wife of the Prophet dies, chapter 24, and punishments are denounced against the neighboring peoples, chapter 25.

Migration 10. The Prophet threatens Egypt with desolation, ch. 29, 30.

Migration 11. At the beginning of the year he announces the destruction of Tyre, ch. 26, 27, 28, as also in the third month to Pharaoh King of Egypt, ch. 31. In the fourth month the city of Jerusalem was captured, and the Jews were led away into the Babylonian exile.

Migration 12. Ezekiel in Babylon receives the news of the devastated city of Jerusalem, ch. 33, and prophesies concerning the office of watchmen or faithful Pastors, and concerning Christ the best Pastor, ch. 33, 34, and also concerning the future liberation of the Israelites through Christ, ch. 36, and treats of the resurrection of the dead, ch. 37. Again he also predicts destruction to Pharaoh, ch. 32.

Migration 25. Ezekiel describes the building of the mystical Jerusalem from ch. 40 to the end.

Migration 27. He predicts that Egypt will be captured by Nebuchadnezzar, ch. 39, 17.

As regards, therefore, the summary and argument of the book, the occasion is primarily to be observed, which was given for this Prophecy both by the False Prophets in Judea, Hananiah and others, and by the people, both those who were left in Judea and those who had crossed over into Chaldea with Jeconiah: for those who had remained in Judea held those who had crossed over to the Chaldeans as traitors, or as timid and cowardly, as those who preferred to accept the yoke of servitude rather than to defend their liberty bravely: but some of these desired to persuade the Jews left in their homeland that they would shortly return to Jerusalem with the vessels that had been carried away. For the False Prophets boasted that the Jews, who were still living in Jerusalem under the new King Zedekiah, would be invincible against the Babylonians, and that the Babylonian kingdom would shortly fall, so much so that the captives began to regret that they had listened to Jeremiah and had surrendered themselves into the power of the Babylonian Monarch, Jer. 28, 4. 29, 25. For this reason God raised up Ezekiel among the captives in Babylon, to confirm the authority of Jeremiah, that a greater captivity, indeed the destruction of Judea, still remained: whence Jerome on Is. 12, 7 says, the prophecy of the former (Jeremiah) was sent to the captives in Babylon, and that of the latter (Ezekiel) to those who dwelt in Jerusalem, so that the providence of God might be proven in different regions, and the hearers might understand that whatever was happening to the people did not consist in the power of idols, but by the command of the Lord. Ezekiel therefore prophesies concerning the captivity of King Zedekiah and the people, and concerning the destruction of the city, and the huge calamities that would precede it, so that those who were in Babylonia might understand that they had consulted their own interests rightly because they had obeyed the Prophecy of Jeremiah: and at the same time he promises that the Jews would be led back in turn to their Homeland, liberated from Babylonian servitude; and at the same time, just as Jeremiah predicts, he speaks concerning certain other kingdoms, that they were to be converted by the Babylonian Monarch, so that the Jews might know that the Babylonian King was the scourge of God, which no one could escape or restrain by rebellion: but above all he also comforts the faithful with promises concerning Christ, through whom they were to be restored into the kingdom of God and the heavenly homeland: and thus he subjoins the sweetest Evangelical promises to his most severe legal sermons, so that the people might be stirred to repentance and confirmed in the divine grace and the forgiveness of sins.

As to the general economy of this book

The Prophetic [book], its parts are two, after the investiture, so to speak, of the Prophet, made in the three prior chapters. The first is completed by threatening, the second by consolatory discourses. To the investiture and authority of the Prophet pertains the first vision, in which partly the authority of the one sending is so exhibited, that the chief scope concerning the propagation of the Gospel and the glory of Christ in the time of the New Testament is simultaneously figured, ch. 1. partly the legitimation of the one sent or the legate is held: whose calling and fortune is described in ch. 2. and what he ought to announce is indicated, the glory of Christ being manifested again, and confirmed by the sign indicated of closing and opening the mouth, ch. 3. Furthermore, the Prophetic threatenings, which make the former part, some concern the Jewish people, others concern foreigners.

In the threatenings against the Jewish people occurs (1.) A schematic figuration of the future siege and captivity of the Jews, with an exposition of the same: which siege is adumbrated with the years of sins, and famine, and calamity in the city, ch. 4. and by the figure of hairs to be shaved off and scattered, the slaughter and dispersion of the Jews is signified, ch. 5. the punishment of idolaters and the impenitent is figured by the gesture of the Prophet, ch. 6. the overthrow of the Jewish kingdom is predicted and adumbrated by chains, ch. 7. All of which seem to pertain still to the first apparition up to ch. 8. exclusive.

In the second apparition various visions of the Prophet are shown, such as those four in ch. 8. exhibiting the abomination of the people, the Levites, the Priests, and others, with divine threatening: and in ch. 9. by the fifth vision, six men armed for killing; to whom, however, Christ the Priest intervenes, exempting his own marked with a sign: to whom in ch. 10. are committed burning coals to fill the house of the Lord with the splendor of glory, whence the Majesty of Christ appears, expressed again by the Evangelical chariot being led through the world: which was the sixth vision.

In the third revelation, first, he presents the supreme security of the people with imminent punishments, yet the return of the exiles with the benefits of the Gospel is promised, ch. 11. Then, ch. 12. the Prophet, ordered to walk with a packed bundle, predicts migration and exile, ch. 12. and against the Pseudo-Prophets of both sexes, promising all other things, he prophesies, ch. 13. and detects the hypocrisy of certain elders given to idolatry, with the punishments of the people not to be averted by any intercession unless they repent, ch. 14. and the people is compared to an unfruitful vine, useless, to be cast into the fire, ch. 15. Furthermore, the divine benefits having been recounted, their ingratitude and spiritual fornication are exhibited, and most grave punishments are denounced; with the addition, however, of consolation concerning the remission of sins and the renewal of the covenant, ch. 16. By an enigma proposed through the Babylonian King, the future abduction of the Jewish King is presented, with his vain confidence in the Egyptians, the propagation of the kingdom of Christ being depicted at the same time, ch. 17. There follows ch. 18. a divine protestation, that a pious son is not to be punished for an impious parent, and that God does not delight in the death of the impious, ch. 18. and a special threnody because of Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, the last King of the Jews, ch. 19.

In the fourth revelation, ch. 20. because of the men prominent in the Babylonian captivity, a judgment is made concerning the outcome of that captivity, the prevarications of both the present ones and their ancestors having been recounted, denouncing even graver punishments, with the addition, however, of a promise concerning those who, having performed repentance, are about to serve God: and ch. 21. concerning the triple exterminating sword, and concerning the way of the Babylonian King against Jerusalem chosen by augury, with the addition also of the punishments of the Ammonites (enemies of the people of God): and also ch. 22. concerning the sins of the people against both tables, and the impiety of the Magistrate and Priests: and specifically ch. 23. concerning the spiritual fornication of the Jews, a twin to the idolatry of the Israelites, on account of which they are to be overthrown by the Babylonians.

The fifth revelation, a parable concerning the pot in which meats are cooked, gives the distresses of the citizens of Jerusalem, and by the sign of the Prophet's wife dying suddenly and not to be mourned, that it will not even be granted to them to lament their evils, ch. 24. And thus far the threatenings against the Jews.

There follow now PREDICTIONS AGAINST FOREIGNERS.

I. Against foreign peoples, such as the Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites & Philistines, chap. 25.

II. Against Tyre, whose overthrow, and indeed its final future devastation by Alexander the Great, is predicted in chap. 26, with a description of its insane luxury, and destruction in chap. 27, and the pride and ruin of the King of Tyre: where vengeance of God is also intimated to the Sidonians, and restoration is promised to the Israelites.

III. There follows the Sixth revelation, in which a threat is held against the Egyptian King: where, however, restoration is again promised to Egypt, as is the return of the Israelites, in chap. 29, with the SEVENTH revelation added in the same chapter, the reason why the land of Egypt is to be given to the Babylonians, and in chap. 30, the depopulation of Egypt and its cities is amplified. In the Eighth revelation, instituted in chap. 31, a comparison of the power of the Egyptians and Assyrians is made, and destruction is predicted for both. In the Ninth revelation, the ruin of the Egyptian King and the King is again treated in chap. 32. And thus far the first part of the Prophetic threats.

There follows now the latter part of the consolations 1. concerning the gracious will of God, that the wicked should turn and live, not perish, for whose sake watchmen, the ministers of the word, are appointed, by which the faithful are fortified against the news of the capture of Jerusalem; and concerning the prediction of destruction denounced because of hypocrites, chap. 33.

2. Concerning the Good Shepherd Christ, after woe is denounced against the bad shepherds, chap. 34.

3. Consolation concerning the joy of the people of God because of the punishment of ἐπιχαιρεκακία (malicious joy) inflicted upon the Edomites, chap. 35.

4. Consolation in the affliction of the nations from the return, and gathering to the kingdom of Christ, and the conversion of the nations and the benefits of the N. T., chap. 36.

5. Consolation concerning the resurrection of the dead, and the union of the Israelites and Jews under Christ, ch. 37.

6. Consolation concerning the destruction of Gog in the mountains of Israel, ch. 38 and 39.

In the final discourse, consolation is presented on account of the destruction of the city and temple, from the promised new temple and the holy land: where first concerning the new temple, as regards the exterior of the temple, the three vestibules, ch. 40, and as regards the interior of the temple, ch. 41, as also as regards the chambers adhering to the temple, ch. 42; thereafter concerning divine worship in this temple and the laws of the same, ch. 43, and also the order of the Priests, and the rules to be observed by them, ch. 44. Finally, concerning the holy land in the remaining chapters, and indeed concerning its general partition and rights, ch. 45; concerning ecclesiastical and ceremonial laws, ch. 46; concerning the mystical water overflowing from the temple and the borders of the holy land, ch. 47; concerning the special partition of the same, and the new Jerusalem, ch. 48 and last.

This, however, is to be observed: in the numbering of these revelations, the order is not that of the time in which the divine revelations were made, which is had from the Chronotaxis, but the order of the chapters of the book, in which order they are recounted in the book.

The principal scope of the whole Prophetic book is the same as that of the other Prophets, namely Christ, and his kingdom. Therefore, at the beginning, Christ is presented as about to carry the chariot of the Gospel and of his kingdom through the world, and the glory of the same is again halted in its progress, ch. 10 & 11. v. 23. And towards the end of the chapter, in three whole chapters, the image of the temple and the city and the spiritual state is shadowed forth: therefore also in the very destruction of the city, Christ is introduced marking his own with a sign, so that they do not perish at the same time, ch. 9. And the promised liberation from captivity and the restoration of the people for the sake of preserving the kingdom of Christ in Judea, until Christ by his advent propagates it from there through the whole world. Therefore the mystical union of Israel and Judah is promised in chapters 11, 20, 29, and 37, and the remission of sins in chapter 16, and the propagation of the kingdom of Christ in chapter 17, and the gracious will of GOD confirmed by oath in chapters 18 and 33; therefore also CHRIST is promised as that good Shepherd in chapter 34, and the conversion of the nations to the same in chapter 36, as also the resurrection of the faithful to eternal life in ch. 37, and the destruction of the enemies of the Church, in chapters 38 and 39.

PART I. Containing the Comminations after the calling of the Prophet.

VISION I. The preparation concerning the calling of the Prophet.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD EZECHIELEM.

Fuit Ezechiel Sacerdos, ut mox ipse dicet: valuit erudi- tione, & ingenio, ita ut (seposito Prophetiæ dono, quod incomparabile est) non immerito Homero eum com- pares, ob pulchras ἐννοίας, comparationes illustres, ma- gnam rerum multarum, præsertim Architecturæ, cogni- tionem.

DIximus ad 2. Reg. 22, 14. hunc Eze- chielem fuisse inter eos, qui de Judæ tribu primi omnium avecti fuere Je- choniæ temporibus. Fuit autem ave- ctus, ut testatur ipse, ad ripam amnis כבר. Is amnis est χαβώρας Ptolemæo in Mesopotamiæ descriptione, Stra- boni Ἀβόῤῥας. Nominis causam indicat Plinius 5. 25. Sunt qui tradunt Euphratem Cobaris præfecti opere deductum, ubi eum diximus findi, ne præcipiti cursu Babyloniam infestaret.

Observationes ad Procœmium Grotia- num, & quæ præterea sunt ἀξιομνημόνευτα circa τὰ προλεγόμενα.

PRophetæ statum, visionis locum, officium, & ingenium tangit Grotius. Statu fuit συναιχμά-

λωτος, quod è cap. 1, 2. constat. Sed prima abdu- ctio in Babylonem sub Jojakimo facta fuit, non sub Jechonia: etsi sub hoc Ezechiel transierit, à qua et- iam abductione annos computat, cap. 1, 2. & alias. Ideoq; in exotica regione prophetavit: unde falsa est Judæorum gloriatio: quod prophetandi donum ad limites Palæstinæ adstrictum sit. Servum prius Je- remiæ fuisse Nazianzenus orat. 47. putant. Cujus filium eundem faciunt Ebræi: sed refragante Scri- ptura, quæ filium Buzi eum dicit. Nonnulli ine- ptiunt eum Pythagoram fuisse; sed hic Græcus fuit, non Judæus, & Ezechiele longe posterior.

Locus visionis est ad ripam Chebar. Quo no- mine Euphratem designari volunt Menochius, Ti- rinus, Maldonatus; rivum ex Euphrate deductum opera Chabori, Grotius intelligere videtur cum Prado, Villalpando, Pinto & Cornelio à Lapide. Alii cum Junio, Tremellio, Piscatore, Polano fluvium per Mesopotamiam in Euphratem redundantem, intelligunt. Qui fluvius Ptolem.co l. 5. c. 18. Geogr. Strab. lib. 5, c. 16, Χαβώρας, Ammiano vitiose Abor- ras lib. 14, c. 23. dicitur. Quam sententiam argu- mentis non contemnendis firmat Franciscus Ju- nius in Commentario ad Ezech. 1. & sub finem 2. cap. Patriam Epiphan. Sararam dicit.

Officium Prophetæ Sacerdotale fuisse, Gro- tius dicit: Alii malunt Sacerdotem vocatum ob prosapiamsacerdotalem, de quo Epiphanius & Hie- ronymus. Quantum ad ingenium Prophetæ, con- fert cum Homero: Sed temerariæ & indignæ sunt ejusmodi comparationes, etsi solemnes Grotio. Toto enim cœlo Spiritus Ezechielis à genio Home- rico differt; Sed his immorari nolumus. Hieronymo autore, in c. 47. Ezechiel Scripturarum est Oceanus & mysteriorum Dei labyrinthus. Juxta nomen suum יחזקאל est fortitudo Dei, qui vere fortis fuit contra obstinatos, & secundum Gregorium M. durus præ- dicator contra duros: fortitudinem etiam martyrio probavit, teste Epiphanio.

Observanda autem præterea Chronologia, sum- ma & οἰκονομία libri. Quod ad illam, cœpit Eze- chiel prædicare anno 5. Zedeziae c. 1, 2. qui fuit Mundi 3409. peccatorum domus Judæ 30. à Jere- miæ initio, qui 13. Josiæ vaticinari cœpit, ann. 34. De- siit Ezechiel anno transmigrationis Jechoniæ, & à regiminis Zedexiæ initio 25. vid. c. 40, 1. vel potius anno transmigrationis 27. ut habetur c. 29, 17. ut ita per 22. annos ad minimum vaticinatus sit: finiens ann. M. 3432. ex quo paulo post Daniel, octennio antea Babylonem Jojakimi tertio finiente, valde puer, traductus, vaticinari cœpit anno M 3434. Ne- bucadnezari somnium exponens. Chronotaxis E- zechielis hæc est:

Migrationis Jechoniæ & regniZedekiæ 5. E- zechiel ad ministerium suum singulari ri- tu, & testimonio divino vocatur c. 1.2.3. & Visio quatuor rotarum & animalium c. 1. contigit: c. 10. repetita: significans cur- rum Evangelii Christi, in quo per mini- sterium Evangelii flatu Spiritus S. vehi- tur in omnes terræ partes. Cap. 4. 5. 6. & 7. obsidio Hierosolymæ, & horrenda fames, bellum & pestis, ac παν- ωλεθρία regni Judaici prædicitur.

Migrat. Jech. 6. Conciones à c. 8. usque ad 20. descriptas habuit, in quibus idololatriam & alia peccata populi arguit, ad pœniten- tiam hortatur, & excidium regni & Regis prædicit.

Migration. 7. Conciones à c. 20. ad 23. inclus. habuit Propheta, in quibus idola, libidi- nes, comtemtum ministerii, usuras Pro- phetarum, Sacerdotum, Principum & po- puli peccata arguit, totique regna, & vi- cinis Ammonitis excidium prædicit.

Migration. 9. uxor Prophetæ moritur c. 24. & vicinis populis pœnæ denunciantur, c. 25.

Migrat. 10. Ægypto vastitatem minatur Pro- pheta c. 29, 30.

Migrat. 11. initio anni Tyro excidium de- nunciat cap. 26. 27. 28. ut & mense tertio Pharaoni Regi Ægypti, c. 31. Mense quarto urbs Jerusalem capta, & Judæi in exilium Babylonicum abducti sunt.

Migrat. 12. Ezechiel in Babylone accipit nun- cium de vastata urbe Hierusalem, c. 33. & de officio speculatorum seu Pastorum fi- delium, ac Christo Pastore optimo vati- cinatur, c. 33. 34. nec non de liberatione Israelitis per Christum futura c. 36. & de resuscitatione mortuorum c. 37. agit. Rur- sus etiam Pharaoni exitium prædicit, c. 32.

Migrat. 25. Jerosolymæ mysticæ ædificium describit Ezechiel à c. 40. usque ad finem.

Migrat. 27. Ægyptum à Nebucadnezare ca- ptam iri prædicit c. 39, 17.

Quod ergo summam & argumentum libri atti- net, occasio imprimis observanda, quæ Prophetiæ huic data tum à Pseudoprophetis in Judæa, Hana- ni & aliis, tum à populo & qui relicti in Judæa, & qui in Chaldæam cum Jechonia transierant: illi enim, qui in Judæa remanserant, hosce qui ad Chaldæos transierant, pro proditoribus habe- bant, aut timidis, & ignavis, ut qui jugum servitu- tis accipere, quam libertatem fortiter tueri malue- rint: horum vero nonnulli persuadere Judæis in pa- tria relictis cupiebant brevi se cum vasibus trans- portatis Hierosolymam redituros. Jactitabant enim Pseudoprophetæ, Judæos, qui Hierosolymis adhuc sub novo Rege Zedekia degebant, invictos fore ad- versus Babylonios, brevique Babylonicum regnum ruiturum, adeo ut pœnitere captivos cœperit, quod Jeremiæ auscultarint, & se in potestatem Mo- narchæ Babylonici tradiderint, Jer. 28, 4. 29, 25. Idcirco excitavit Deus penes captivos in Babylone Ezechielem, quo Jeremiæ autoritatem firmaret, majorem adhuc captivitatem imo excidium Judææ restare: unde Hieronymo in Es. 12, 7. dicente, illius (Jeremiæ) prophetia mittebatur ad captivos in Ba- bylone, & hujus (Ezechielis) ad eos, qui habita- bant in Jerusalem, ut unius in diversis regionibus Dei providentia probaretur, & intelligerent audi- entes quæcunque accidebant populo, nequaquam idolorum potestate, sed Domini jussione consistere. Vaticinatur ergo Ezechiel de regis Zedekiæ & po- puli captivitate, deque urbis excidio, & ingentibus calamitatibus illud præcessuris, ut qui in Babylonia erant, intelligerent se rebus suis recte consuluisse, quod Prophetiæ Jeremiæ paruissent: ac promittit simul, reductum iri Judæos vicissim in Patriam, libe- ratos è Babylonica servitute; simulque de aliis qui- busdam regnis, perinde ut Jeremias prædicit, quod per Babylonicum Monarcham ea convertenda sint, ut scirent Judæi Babylonicum Regem esse fla- gellum Dei, quod nemo rebellione effugere, aut cohibere possit: sed imprimis etiam fideles solatur promissionibus de Christo, per quem restituendi e- rant in regnum Dei, & patriam cœlestem: adeoque concionibus legalibus severissimis subjungit suavif- simas promissiones Evangelicas, ut ad pœnitentiam excitetur populus, & de divina gratia, ac condona- tione peccatorum confirmetur.

Quod ad œconomiam universam hujus libri

Prophetici , partes ejus duæ sunt , post investitu- ram, ut ita dicam, Prophetæ, tribus prioribus capp. factam. Prima comminatoriis , consolatoriis alte- ra concionibus absolvitur. Ad investituram & au- toritatem Prophetæ pertinet prima visio, in qua partim mittentis autoritas sic exhibita, ut præcipuus scopus de Evangelii propagatione, ac gloria Christi tempore N.T. simul figuretur , cap. 1. partim legi- timatio missi vel legati habetur : cujus vocatio & fortuna describitur cap. 2. & quid annunciare de- beat,indicatur, manifestata iterum gloria Christi,& signo indicato oris occludendi & aperiendi confirma- tur c. 3, Porro Comminationes Propheticæ,quæ par- tem priorem faciunt , aliæ populum Judaicum , aliæ exoticos concernunt.

In comminationibus adversus populum Judai- cum occurrit ( 1. ) Schematica futuræ obsidionis & captivitatis Judæorum figuratio, cum expositione ejusdem: quæ obsidio , cum peccatorum annis, & fa- me, ac calamitate in urbe adumbratur cap. 4. & fi- gura pilorum abradendorum & dispergendorum, Ju- dæorum internecio & dispersio significata cap. 5. ido- lolatrarum & impœnitentium pœna gestu Prophe- tæ figuratur cap. 6. eversio regni Iudaici prædicta & catenis adumbrata cap. 7. Quæ omnia adhuc ad primam apparitionem pertinere videntur usque ad cap. 8. exclusive.

In secunda apparitione variæ visiones Prophe- tæ ostenduntur, utpote quatuor illæ cap.8. abomi- nationem populi, Levitarum, Sacerdotum & alio- rum cum comminatione divina exhibentes : & 9. cap. visione quinta sex viri ad occidendum arma- ti; quibus vero Christus Sacerdos intervenit suos signo notatos eximens : cui in cap. 10. committun- tur carbones igniti ad implendam domum Domini splendore gloriæ, unde Majestas Christi apparet curru Evangelico per orbem deducendo iterum expressa : quæ sexta fuit visio.

In tertia revelatione primum summam po- puli securitatem cum pœnis imminentibus sistit, promittitur tamen exulum reditus cum Evangelii beneficiis cap. 11. Deinde cap. 12. Propheta sarcina compacta ambulare jussus migrationem, & exilium prædicit, cap.12. & contra Pseudo-Prophetas utrius- que sexus , alia omnia promittentes , vaticinatur cap. 13. ac Seniorum quorundam idololatriæ dedi- torum hypocrisin detegit, cum pœnis populi nulla intercessione , nisi resipuerint, avertendis cap. 14 & comparatur populus viti infrugiferæ , inutili, in ignem abjiciendæ cap. 15. Porro recensitis bene- ficiis divinis, ingratitudo, & fornicatio eorum spi- ritualis exhibetur, ac pœnæ gravissimæ denuncian- tur ; addito tamen solatio de remissione peccatorum, & fœderis renovatione cap. 16. Ænigmate proposito per Babylonicum Regem futura Regis Judaici ab- ductio, cum hujus in Ægyptios vana confidentia sistitur, depicta simul regni Christi propagatione, cap.17. Succedit cap. 18. protestatio divina, quod non puniendus filius pius sit ob impium parentem, quodque Deus morte impiorum non delectetur cap. 18. & threnodia specialis ob Ioachazum, & Ze- dekiam ultimum Judæorum Regem c. 19.

In quarta revelatione cap.20. ob viros in Babylo- nica captivitate præcipuos facta de eventu capti- vitatis illius , recensitis prævaricationibus tum præsentium , tum majorum ipsorum, pœnas de- nuncians adhuc graviores, addita tamen promis- fione de illis , qui pœnitentia acta Deo servituri sunt : & cap. 21. de gladio exterminatorio triplici, & de via Babylonici Regis adversus Jerosolymam per augurium electa, additis etiam pœnis ( hostium populi Dei) Ammonitarum : nec non cap. 22. de peccatis populi contra utramque tabulam, ac Ma- gistratus & Sacerdotum impietate: & speciatim cap. 23. de fornicatione spirituali Judæorum, gemi- na idololatriæ Israëlitarum, ob quam per Babylo- nios evertendi sint.

Quinta revelatio parabola de olla, in qua coquuntur carnes, angustias civium Hierusalem, & signo uxoris Prophetæ subito morientis non lu- gendæ, ne id quidem concessum iri, ut mala sua defleant, donet, cap. 24. Atque hactenus commi- nationes adversus Judæos.

Sequuntur jam PRÆDICTIONES AD- VERSUS EXOTICOS.

I. Contra populos exteros, utpote Ammoni- tas, Moabitas, Idumæos & Philistinos cap. 25.

II. Contra Tyrum, cujus eversio, imo & ul- tima per Alexandr. M. futura vastatio prædicitur cap. 26. descripto insano ejus luxu, & exitio cap. 27. ac Regis Tyrii superbia, & excidio: ubi Sidoniis e- tiam vindicta Dei intimata, promissa contra Israe- litarum restitutione.

III. Succedit Sexta revelatio, in qua commi- natio habetur contra Regem Ægyptium: ubi tamen Ægypto iterum restauratio, ut & Israëlitis reductio simul promissa c. 29. addita eodem capite SEPTI- MA revelatione, causa, cur terra Ægypti Babylo- niis danda, & cap. 30. amplificata Ægypti & urbium ejus depopulatione. Revelatione Octava, instituta c. 31. comparatione potentiæ Ægyptiorum & Assy- riorum, utrique interitus prædicitur. Nona revela- tione iterum de ruina Regis Ægyptiaci & Regis a- ctum cap. 32. Atque hactenus pars prior commina- tionum Propheticarum.

Sequitur jam pars posterior consolationum 1. de gratiosa Dei voluntate, ut convertatur & vivat, non pereat impius, cujus gratia vigiles constituan- tur ministri verbi, qua muniuntur fideles adversus nuncium de capta Hierosolyma; & de excidii prædi- ctione ob hypocritas denunciati, cap. 33.

2. De Bono Pastore Christo, post væ malis pa- storibus denunciatum cap. 34.

3. Solatium de gaudio populi Dei ob pœnam ἐπιχαιρεκακίας Idumæis inflictam c. 35.

4. Solatium in afflictione gentium è reditu, & congregatione ad regnum Christi, ac conversione gentium & beneficiis N. T. c. 36.

5. Solatium de resuscitatione mortuorum, & unione Israëlitarum & Judæorum sub Christo, c. 37.

6. Solatium de interitu Gogi in montibus I- sraelis cap. 38. & 39.

Postrema concione solatium exhibetur ob ex- cisionem urbis & templi è promisso novo templo, & terra sancta: ubi primo de novo templo, quoad exte- riora templi tria vestibula cap. 40. & quoad templi interiora cap. 41. ut & quoad conclavia templo adhæ- rentia cap. 42. dehinc de cultu divino in hoc templo & legibus ejusdem cap. 43. nec non ordine Sacerdo- tum, & regulis ipsis observandis cap. 44. Denique de terra sancta reliquis capitibus, & quidem de ejus generali partitione, ac juribus cap. 45. de legibus Ec- clesiasticis, & ceremonialibus cap. 46. de aqua my- stica è templo redundante & finibus terræ sanctæ cap. 47. de speciali partitione ejusdem, & nova Hieroso- lyma cap. 48. & ultimo.

Id autem observandum, in numeratione harum revelationum spectari ordinem non temporis, quo factæ sunt divinæ revelationes, qui è Chronotaxi habetur: sed capitum libri, quo ordine in libro re- censitæ illæ sunt.

Scopus præcipuus totius libri Prophetici idem est, qui aliorum Prophetarum, nimirum Christus, ejusque regnum. Ideo sub initium exhibetur Chri- stus currum Evangelii & regni sui per orbem pro- vecturus, ejusdemque gloria in progressu iterum si- stitur, cap. 10. & 11. v. 23. & sub finem cap. tribus in- tegris, templi & urbis, ac civitatis spiritualis effigies adumbrata: ideo & in ipso exitio urbis Christus in- troductus suos signo notans, ne simul pereant cap. 9. & promissa liberatio è captivitate ac reductio populi propter regnum Christi in Judæa conservandum, do- nec Christus adventu suo id per totum orbem inde propaget. Ideo conjunctio Israelis, & Judæ mystica promissa capp. 11. 20. 29. & 37. & peccatorum remissio cap. 16. ac regni Christi propagatio cap. 17. & gratiosa DEI voluntas jurejurando firmata cap. 18. & 33. ideo & CHRISTUS Pastor ille bonus cap. 34. promit- titur, ac conversio gentium ad eundem cap. 36. ut & resuscitatio fidelium ad æternam vitam c. 37. ho- stiumque Ecclesiæ deletio, cap. 38. & 39.

PARS I. Post vocationem Prophetæ Commina- tiones continens.

VISIO I. Parasceve vocationem Prophetæ con- cernens.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. The place and time being designated, the vision of the four living creatures and the wheels is explained, and of the firmament, in which the son of man sits upon a throne with fiery splendor and the brightness of a rainbow.

Ver. 1. AND IT CAME TO PASS IN THE THIRTIETH YEAR) From the book of the law found by Hilkiah: concerning which 2 Kings 22, 10, 11, 12. Thus the Chaldean here.

Thus not only the Chaldean, but also Piscator and Polanus from the Reformed, and Osiander from our own. But because no example is given of an epoch assigned from the time of the discovered law, Junius says that the epoch was indeed instituted from that time, but not when the book of the law was found, but when the restoration of the public covenant was made by Josiah. He refutes those who attached this opinion to the Prophet, and the opinions of others who think the thirtieth year is designated from the Jubilee year, with R. Dav. Kimchi and Jerome, or from the birth of the Prophet with Origen, Gregory the Great, Victorinus, Lyranus, Hugo, Torniellus, and Cramer. Since the calculation of the Jubilees does not agree. And that the Prophet should have mentioned his own private age in this argument, there is no reason, nor can that matter be confirmed by any example. He rejects Scaliger's opinion, that the era is computed from the reign of Nabopolassar, although he thinks it agrees with the calculation of time, by this strongest argument, that it was completely unknown to the Jews still living in their homeland: for whose benefit, however, this prophecy was published. Calvisius defends Scaliger's opinion in his Chronological Isagoge, ch. 33, p. 181, with whom agrees the Blessed Dn. D. Behmius in Chronolog. Manuduct. lib. 2, Tit. 4, ch. 3, p. 202, and in the Themate Chronolog. on the first year of Cyrus. Let those things which are brought forward on Jer. 29, 10 be compared. Theodoret makes the beginning of the counting from the divine oracle concerning the captivity to be terminated in 70 years, 2 Kings 22, 17. Whom Pintus, Maldonatus, and others follow: for all those things, namely the divine oracle, the beginning of the reign, and the time of the found law and the restored covenant, fall into the same year, namely the 18th year of Josiah's age. Wilhelmus Langius, in book 2 de ann. Christ. c. 13, p. 314, rejects Scaliger's opinion that the 30th year is designated from the beginning of the reign of Nabopolassar, and determines that the 30th year of the Prophet's age is rather designated, as that in which he reached the full priestly age, when he first became worthy of the visions of God. But I do not see a solid reason for rejecting his opinion brought forward. For what he brings from Berosus, that Nebuchadnezzar reigned 43 years, does not hinder that opinion at all, as he indeed thinks. For since his reign ended in the 37th year of the deportation of Jeconiah, as witnessed by Jer. 52, 31, and the fifth year of Jeconiah after the deportation is here collected with the thirtieth year from the reign of Nabopolassar, as Scaliger judges, thirty-two years must have elapsed from that thirtieth year which Ezekiel designated in this place. Let these 32 years therefore be added to those 30, and 62 years will emerge, counted from the beginning of the reign of Nabopolassar. Furthermore, since he reigned into the 21st year, and Nebuchadnezzar into the 43rd year according to Ptolemy's Canon, 64 years will indeed arise from the beginning of Nabopolassar to the end of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, which number exceeds the former by two years: But if the years of Nabopolassar, as also of Nebuchadnezzar, are understood as current, not completed, or even if the 30th year in Ezekiel is not current but finished, and similarly the 32 years collected by Jeremiah are noted as whole and completed, the sum of the years will easily agree, and no contradiction will remain. The observation of Ptolemy, confirmed by the celestial character, will also agree in this way. For the fifth year of the reign of Nabopolassar, distinguished by a celestial character, namely an eclipse of the Moon, according to Ptolemy, is the 127th Nabonassarean. Whence it is clear that he began to reign in the 122nd Nabonassarean year, and thus the thirtieth year from the beginning of his reign will be 152. Nabonassarean, which agrees and is collected with the fifth year from the deported Jeconiah: as also the fifth of Zedekiah. Wherefore the eleventh year of the deported Jeconiah and of the reign of Zedekiah will be the 158th Nabonassarean year, and the thirty-seventh year from the deportation of Jeconiah, which was the year of Nebuchadnezzar's death, will be the 184th Nabonassarean year. Since therefore Nabopolassar reigned until the 143rd Nabonassarean year, and Nebuchadnezzar his son spent forty-two whole years in a solitary reign, and died in the forty-third, it is gathered from this that the year of Nebuchadnezzar's death was the current 185th, that is, the completed 184th of the Nabonassarean era. We add what the Blessed D. Joh. Behmius has concerning these in the discuss. Theol. Hist. Chronolog. instituted in the year 1633 at Königsberg, thesis 17. We insert this mention of Nabopolassar, the parent of Nebuchadnezzar, in passing, that Joseph Scaliger in his golden books on the emendation of times learnedly gathers that the Babylonians fixed an epoch from this Nabopolassar, a most famous King, on account of his outstanding merits and the royal expansion of the Babylonian kingdom, which Ezekiel uses, who, being stationed in Babylonia at the river Chebar or Chaboras (as Ptolemy calls it in his Geographies), makes mention of the thirtieth year without a certain determination, and connects this thirtieth year with the 5th of Jehoiachin, son of Jeconiah, c. 1, 1. & 2. We warned in the preceding thesis that Nabopolassar in the 17th year of his reign sent his son Nebuchadnezzar for the first time into Syria, Phoenicia, and Judea against the rebels. The first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Judea is the third year of Jehoiakim completed, Dan. 1, v. 1, the fourth beginning, Jer. 25, 1. Therefore, the first year of Nabopolassar arises from the 18th year of Josiah, which is clearly notable in sacred history. For in that very year, Josiah, a most pious King, purges, repairs, and restores the temple violated by his grandfather and parent, publishes the authentic books of Moses found in the ruins, and causes them to be read publicly, and also celebrates the Passover with such great magnificence, 2 Kings 22, 2 Chron. 34 & 35. From this 18th year of Josiah to the end of his reign remain 14 years (for he reigned for 31 years, 2 Kings 22, 1, 2 Chron. 34, 1). With the addition of the 11 years of Jehoiakim, 2 Kings 23, 36, 2 Chron. 36, 5, and the five of Jeconiah, there arise 30 years from the first of Nabopolassar to the fifth of Jeconiah. It is likely that Ezekiel, being stationed in Babylonia, followed the era used by the Babylonians. These things we have thus discussed according to the mind of Calvisius and Behm heretofore: But because Mr. Behm presupposes that the years of Nebuchadnezzar began in the 17th year of Nabopolassar, from his arrival in Syria and Judea which took place in that year: but a more accurate calculation commands that arrival to be placed in the 20th year of Nabopolassar, which we have shown with Ussher in our Biblical Chronicle: it is better to understand the 30th year from the restored covenant, which is the same as the 30th in the years of the sins of the house of Judah. In which year also the divine oracle concerning the calamities about to befall Judea, 2 Kings 22:17, occurred: for they prove that it is not unusual for years to be calculated from the time of a divine forewarning, by the example of the 400 years in Genesis 15:13, which they say are to be numbered not from the time of the actual entry into Egypt, but from the time of the divine oracle. Compare concerning this year question 22, section 5, of our Biblical Chronicle.

WHEN I WAS IN THE MIDST OF THE CAPTIVES) When I was among those deported in the times of Jeconiah.

THE HEAVENS WERE OPENED) Which is a θεοσημασία (sign from God) of a heavenly vision. We have spoken to Matthew 3:16.

Latin:

CAPUT I. Designato loco & tempore visio explicatur quatuor animalium & rotarum, ac firma- menti, in quo throno insidet filius hominis igneo splendore, iridisque nitore.

Vers. 1. ET FACTVM EST IN TRIGESIMO AN- NO) Ab invento legis libro per Helciam: de quo 2. Reg. 22, 10. 11. 12. Ita hic Chaldæus.

ITa non Chaldæus tantum, sed è Reformatis e- tiam Piscator & Polanus, è nostris Osiander. Quia vero nullum datur exemplum epochæ à tempore repertæ legis assignatæ, Junius ab eo quidem tempo- re epocham institutam dicit, sed non qua inventus liber legis, sed qua fœderis publici facta est per Josiam instauratio. Qui hanc sententiam Prophetæ adstru- xit, aliorumque opiniones, quæ ab anno Iubilæo, cum R. Dav. Kimchi & Hieronymo, vel à nativitate Pro- phetæ cum Origene, Gregorio M. Victorino, Lyrano, Hugone, Torniello. Cramero, annum trigesimum de- signari putant, refellit. Siquidem non conveniat sub- putatio Jubilæorum. Quod autem Propheta in hoc ar- gumento privatæ suæ ætatis meminerit, causa nulla sit, neque res illa exemplo ullo confirmari possit. Scali- geri sententiam, quod à regno Nabopolassaris æra computetur, etsi temporis calculo convenire pu- tet, hoc potissimum argumento reprobat, quod Ju- dæis in patria adhuc versantibus, ea penitus ignota fuerit: Quorum tamen bono hæc Prophetia edita. Tuetur a. Scaligeri sententiam Calvisius in Isagoge chronologica cap. 33. pag. 181. cui consonant B. Dn. D. Behmius Chronolog. Manuduct. lib. 2. Tit. 4. cap. 3. pag. 202. & in Themate Chronolog. de primo anno Cyri. Conferantur, quæ ad Jer. 29, 10. adducta sunt. Theodoretius numerandi initium fa- cit ab oraculo divino de captivitate 70. annis ter- minanda 2. Reg. 22, 17. Quem Pintus, Maldonatus, & alii sequuntur: illa enim omnia, oraculum nempe divinum, initium regni, & tempus inventæ legis & re- staurati fœderis in eundem annum incidunt, nimi- rum in annum ætatis Josiæ 18. Scaligeri sententiam quod 30. annus ab initio regni Nabopalasari desi- gnetur, reprobat Wilhelmus Langius l. 2. de ann Christ. c. 13. pag. 314. annumque ætatis Prophetæ 30 potius designari statuit, utpote quo plenam sacerdo talem ætatem attigerit, cum primum dignus visioni bus Dei fieret. Sed non video adductam solidam e- jus reprobandæ causam. Nam quod ex Beroso ad- fert, Nebucadnezarem 43. annos regnasse, senten- tiæ illi nihil,uti quidem putat, officit. Quum enim regnum ejus defierit anno translationis Jechoniæ 37. teste Jer. 52, 31. Jechoniæ autem annus quintus post translationem hic colligetur cum anno trige- simo,à Regimine Nabopalassari, ut Scaliger censet, triginta duos annos effluxisse oportet inde ab illo trigesimo, quem designavit hoc loco Ezechiel. Ad- dantur ergo hi 32. anni istis 30. & prodituri sunt 62. anni, numerati ab initio regiminis Nabopalassaris. Porro quum hic imperarit in 21. annum, Nebucad- nezar autem in 43. annum juxta Ptolemæi Cano- nem,exurgent quidem inde ab initio Nabopalassa- ris usque ad finem regiminis Nebucadnezaris anni 64. qui numerus priorem biennio superat : Sed si anni Nabopallassaris, ut & Nebucadnezaris intelli- gantur currentes,non completi,vel etiam annus 30. apud Ezechielem non currens,sed exactus,ac simi- liter 32. anni à Jeremia collecti integri, & completi notentur, facile summa annorum conveniet, nec ulla remanebit contradictio. Congruet quoque ita observatio Ptolemæi, Charactere cœlesti firmata. Nam quintus annus regiminis Nabopallassaris,insig- nis cœlesti Charactere, deliquio nempeLunæ,apud Ptolemeum,est centesimus vigesimus septimusNa- bonazaræus. Vnde liquet, ipsum anno 122. Nabona- zaræo regnare cœpisse, adeoque tricesimus annus ab initio regni ipsius erit 152. Nabonazaræus, qui convenit, & colligatur cum quinto anno à depor- tato Jechonia : ut & quinto Zedekiæ, Quapropter undecimus annus deportati Jechoniæ & regiminis Zedekiæ erit annus Nabonazaræus 158. & trigesi- mus septimus annus à deportatione Jechoniæ, qui emortualis fuit Nebucadnezari, erit annus Nabo- nassaræus 184. Quum itaque Nabopallasar regna- rit usque ad annum centesimum quadragesimum tertium Nabonazaræum, ac Nebucadnezar filius ipsius integros quadraginta duos annos in regno solitario exegerit, ac quadragesimo tertio obierit, colligitur inde,annum emortualem Nebucadneza- ris fuisse currentem centesimum octuagesimum quintum, hoc est, exactum centesimum octuagesi- mum quartum æræ Nabonazarææ. Addimus quæ habet de his B. D. Joh. Behmius in discuss. Theol. Hist. Chronolog. Ann. 1633. Regiomonti instituta th. 17. Mentiome Nabopallassari parentis Nebucadne- zaris obiter id inserimus, Josephum Scaligerum in aureis suis de temporum emendatione libris erudite colligere, Babylonios ab hoc Nabopallassaro, famosissi- mo Rege, ob egregia merita & Regiam Babylonici re- gni amplificationem Epocham fixisse,qua Ezechiel uti- tur,qui in Babylonia ad fluvium Cebar vel Ceboræ (uti Ptolemæus vocat in Geographicis) constitutus, mentio- nem facit anni tricesimi sine certa determinatione, huncque tricesimum connectit cum 5. Jojacini f. Jecho- niæ c.1,1. & 2. Monuimus in præcedente thesi Nabopal- lassarum anno 17. sui regiminis filium Nebucadneza- rem primum in Syriam,Phœniciam & Judæam contra rebelles misisse.Primus Nebucadnezaris in Judæam ad- ventus est annus Jojakimi tertius absolutus Dan, 1. v. 1. quartus iniens Jer. 25, 1. Primus ergo Nabopallassari exurgit à 18. Josiæ anno in sacris plane notabili. Eo ipso namque anno Josias Rex pientissimus templum ab avo & parente violatum purgat, reficit, instaurat, libros Mosis Authenticos in parietinis repertos divulgat, pu- bliceque prælegi curat, Pascha quoque tanta celebrat magnificentia, 2. Reg. 22. 2. Chr. 34. & 35. Ab hoc 18. Josiæ anno ad finem regiminis restant 14.anni(nam per 31. annos regnavit 2.Reg.22, 1.2. Chr.34,1.) Additis 11. annis Iojakimi 2.Reg.23,36.2.Ch.36,5.& quinque Iecho- niæ exurgunt 30. anni à primo Nabopallassari ad quin- tum Jechoniæ. Verisimile est Ezechielem in Babylo- nia constitutum æram Babyloniis usitatam sequu- tum esse. Hæc ita ex mente Calvisii & Behmii dis- putavimus antehac: Sed quia præsupponit D. Beh- mius anno 17. Nabopallassari inchoari Nebucad- nezaris annos, ab adventu ejus in Syriam, & Ju- dæam eo anno facto: accuratior vero computus in 20. annum Nabopallassari adventum illum col- locari jubet, quod cum Usserio ostendimus in Chronico Biblico: præstat annum 30. à restaurato fœdere, qui idem 30. est in annis peccatorum do- mus Judæ intelligere. Quo etiam anno oraculum divinum de calamitatibus Judææ eventuris 2. Reg. 22, 17. contigit: non enim insolitum esse à tempore divinæ prænunciationis annos computari, exem- plo 400. annorum Gen. 15, 13. probant, qui non à tempore realis in Ægyptum ingressus, sed à tem- pore oraculi divini numerandos dicunt. Confe- rat. de hoc anno quæst. 22. Sect. 5. Chronici nostri Biblici.

CVM ESSEM IN MEDIO CAPTIVORVM) Cum essem inter illos Jechoniæ temporibus deportatos.

APERTI SVNT COELI) Quæ est θεοσημασία visi cælestis. Diximus ad Matth. 3, 16.

Verse 3. AND THE HAND OF THE LORD WAS THERE UPON HIM) God acted powerfully in me. Below 3:14.
