Ver. 27. AND WHEN I HAVE BROUGHT THEM AGAIN] I would have brought them again. AND AM SANCTIFIED IN THEM IN THE SIGHT OF MANY NATIONS] I would have been. Many foreign nations acknowledged my power in the restoration of the Jews: and yet many of them forgot me.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ET REDUXERO EOS] Reduxissem eos. ET SANCTIFICATUS FUERO IN EIS IN O- CULIS GENTIUM PLURIMARUM] Fuissem. Gen- tes plurimæ extraneæ potentiam meam agnoverunt in re- stitutione Judæorum: & ipsorum tamen multi mei obliti sunt.

## 39:28
Ver. 28. AND THEY SHALL KNOW] They will remember once the temple is cleansed.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ET SCIENT] Reminiscentur repurgato templo.

## 39:29
Ver. 29. NEITHER WILL I HIDE MY FACE ANY MORE FROM THEM] From them, who have seriously performed penance. FOR I HAVE POURED OUT MY SPIRIT UPON THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL] Because I will pour out my spirit upon the whole house of Israel. For it coheres with the preceding. To pour out one's spirit upon someone, to the Hebrews signifies to pursue with love, as Isaiah 32:15. A similar manner of speaking 1 Sam. 18:1, Exod. 35:20. Not dissimilar Isaiah 58:10.

THE LAST VISION IN THIS BOOK, CONCERNING THE NEW TEMPLE AND THE NEW HOLY LAND.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ET NON ABSCONDAM ULTRA FACIEM MEAM AB EIS] Ab eis, qui pœnitentiam serio ege- rint. EO QUOD EFFUDERIM SPIRITUM MEUM SUPER OMNEM DOMUM ISRAEL] Quoniam effun- dam spiritum meum super omnem domum Israël. Cohæret e- nim cum superioribus. Effundere spiritum suum super aliquem, Hebræis significat amore profequi, ut Efa. 32, 15. Simile loquendi genus 1. Sam. 18, 1. Exod. 35,20. Non dissimile Ef. 58,10.

VISIO IN HOC LIBRO ULTIMA, DE TEMPLO NOVO ET NOVA TERRA SANCTA.

## 40:1 Argument
CHAPTER XL.

A man seen with a measuring line, who measured the breadth and height of the new temple, and the three courts, namely the outer, the middle in which are 30 chambers with tables, and the innermost, in which are the altar and two columns.

Ver. 1.

IN THE TWENTY-FIFTH YEAR OF OUR EXILE, IN THE BEGINNING OF THE YEAR, THE TENTH OF THE MONTH, [THE FOURTEENTH YEAR AFTER THE CITY WAS STRUCK] In the beginning of the year, that is, of the month TISRI, which is the most ancient beginning of the year. Thus Jerome wishes it in these matters.

We have spoken elsewhere about the beginning of the year. Now we must look into the connection of the 25th year of exile and the 14th from the striking of the city, from which non-vulgar chronologists—especially those who follow the side of Scaliger (from whom Grotius is not alien, as he has revealed elsewhere)—gather, having compared chapter 33:21, where the eleventh year of the captivity is connected with the year of the extermination of the city, that the captivity began with the deportation of Jeconiah, and that from there also the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity, defined in Scripture, take their beginning. And the matter seems too manifest. For if the year of the destruction and πανολεθρίας (total destruction) of the city was the eleventh of the captivity, and the same was the eleventh of the reign of Zedekiah, and of the abduction of Jeconiah, to whom he was substituted, and both years of the 25th of the migration were the 14th of the struck city, what is more certain than that the beginning of the captivity must be fixed at the voluntary deportation of Jeconiah? But we have demonstrated this with reasons, as we believe, invincible, at chapter 29 of Jeremiah. that the beginning of the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity must be taken from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and not from the deportation of Jeconiah. Which was most clearly established from the passages of Jeremiah. What then? Shall we set Ezekiel, who in both these places, ch. 33 and 40, is likewise extremely clear, against Jeremiah? In the year, he says, ch. 33:21, the twelfth לגלותינו, of our exile. And here he openly says the twenty-fifth year of exile was the fourteenth of the struck city. Therefore, in the eleventh year of exile, the city was struck.

B. Behmius, no mean champion of the Scaligerian sect, also saw these things, without a doubt, whom, however, we observed above, when we treated the passage of Jeremiah, to have deserted the day after the opinion which he had followed the day before. Wherefore he certainly acknowledged in his later age that the argument which is sought from these passages of Ezekiel for that opinion is not sufficiently valid, even though he once held it to be most valid, namely when he was publishing his Chronological Manuduction, in which, book 2, title 2, chapter 2, page 108, it is held thus: The whole of Ezekiel is on our side, in different places ch. 1:2, 24:1. He refers the ninth year of the captivity to that time when Nebuchadnezzar began to besiege Jerusalem. But that was done in the 9th year of King Zedekiah, 2 Kings 25:1, Jer. 39:1 and 52:4. Thus he refers the 12th year of the captivity to that time when, the year having passed, the city of Jerusalem had been struck, that is, devastated, ch. 33:21. But the same Prophet most clearly of all refers the 25th year of the captivity to the 14th year of the πανολεθρίας [total destruction] of the temple, chap. 40, 1. and very often elsewhere he carefully counts the years from the migration of Jeconiah, chap. 8, 1. c. 20, 1. chap. 26, 1. c. 29. c. 31, 1. c. 32, 1.

He delivered these things there, as ἀναντιῥῥήτως [irrefutably] certain in the year 1616, but, a more accurate investigation having been instituted, in later years he began to be rendered doubtful, and therefore in the disputation which he held on this theme at Königsberg on September 30, 1633, he so far did not adhere to that epoch of the beginning from the deportation of Jeconiah, that he asserted that the beginning was assigned by the Holy Spirit Himself in Jer. 25, 12 to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, which in that place is concatenated with the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, not from the death of his parent, but from his first arrival into Syria, made while his father Nabopolassar was still living (concerning which see Berosus in Josephus, book 10 of Antiquities, chap. 11, and book 1 in the Appendix, as also Eusebius, book 9 of Evangelical Preparation, chap. 4). By which Nebuchadnezzar, on account of the rebellion of the Satrap of Egypt and Coelesyria and Phoenicia against the Kingdom

Babylon, the expedition having been made, and the rebels defeated, and the Syro-Egyptian region subdued, having advanced to Jerusalem, he made Jehoiakim, King of Judah, a vassal and tributary to the Babylonian King, who was a tributary to Pharaoh Necho (whom Nebuchadnezzar had defeated) 2 Kings 23:33, 2 Chron. 36:3, 2 Kings 24:1, Jer. 46:2, Dan. 1:1, 2, with Daniel the Prophet and his companions and others being led away at the same time into Babylon, and also a good part of the instruments of the House of the Lord. That was the third year of Jehoiakim completed, Dan. 1:1, but the fourth current, Jer. 25, c. 46:2. Concerning which Eusebius in the Chronical Canon at the 4th year of the 54th Olympiad. The whole time of the captivity of the Jews is gathered to be 70 years. Which, however, according to some, is from the third year of Eliakim (who is Jehoiakim) up to the 29th of King Cyrus. Whence it appears that this opinion had prevailed even before Eusebius.

It pleases me to propose this opinion in the words and arguments of the blessed D. Behm, brought forward from the cited disputation, which by chance is in no one's hands here. From the first, he says in thesis 27, of Nebuchadnezzar according to Scripture, to the last of Nabonidus the Mede, whom Cyrus conquered (to us he is Darius the Mede in Daniel ch. 9, v. 1), precisely 70 years have elapsed. This is to be proven not from light conjectures, but from historical truth and the mathematical Canon of Ptolemy. The true Berosus in Josephus in the first book against Apion, and Eusebius lib. 9, praepar. evang. c. 4, counts 66 years from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the last of Nabonidus the Mede. The mathematical Canon of Ptolemy does the same. Behold the deduction! 43 years are attributed to Nebuchadnezzar in both, namely from the death of his parent Nabopolassar: to Avarodamus (Evil-Merodach) 2, to Niricassolassar (Belshazzar) 4, to Nabonadius the Mede (Darius the Mede) 17. The sum is 66. The same golden fragment from the true Berosus is cited in Josephus, book 10 of the Antiquities, c. 12. But there the numbers are corrupted. 18 are attributed to Evil-Merodach instead of 2, 40 to Neriglissar instead of 4. There remain 4 years to the 70 years of captivity, to be completed from the first of Nebuchadnezzar. These are completed from historical collation in this way. Scripture counts the years of King Nebuchadnezzar one way, Berosus with Josephus another. These from the death of the parent: that from the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Syria and Palestine, which occurred while the parent was still alive, as we saw above from Berosus. Therefore, more years of reign are to be attributed to this most famous King according to Scripture. But how many years are to be added? That is indeed contained nowhere expressed in any history. Would that we had the full history of the Babylonian Kings from Nebuchadnezzar to Cyrus by Berosus, Megasthenes, Diodorus Siculus, and other historians! Nothing is left to us except desire. Yet from diligent examination and mutual collation of histories, we have judged: that Nabopolassar sent his son Nebuchadnezzar, flourishing and strong in age and vigor, into Syria and Palestine for the first time in the 17th year of his reign, and consequently that he reigned for four solid years with his parent. We confirm this calculation in three ways. 1. From the annals of the Phoenicians in Josephus in the first book against Apion, which count 49 years from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the first of Cyrus of the Persian Monarchy. See above in thesis 14; with the 30 years of the reign of Cyrus added, they become 79 years from the first of Nebuchadnezzar according to Scripture and the annals of the Phoenicians to the last of Cyrus. But the mathematical Canon of Ptolemy has only 75 years from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the last of Cyrus: 66 from the first of Nebuchadnezzar to the last of Nabonidus the Mede, 9 of Cyrus from the defeat of Babylon. The sum is 75 years. A difference of four solid years. We prove this very thing in another way. The last of Cyrus in the mathematical Canon of Ptolemy is the 218th of Nabonassar, the 7th of Cambyses, the 225th of Nabonassar, marked with a celestial character. Therefore, the first of Cyrus of the Persian Kingdom is the 188th of Nabonassar, for he reigned for 30 years. But we said in the preceding calculation that the annals of the Phoenicians count 49 years from the first of Cyrus to the first of Nebuchadnezzar, which, subtracted from the 188th of Nabonassar, leave 139 years of Nabonassar to the first of Nebuchadnezzar according to Scripture. But Ptolemy in the Canon counts 143 years to the first of Nebuchadnezzar, with autopsia as witness. Behold again an interval of four years! (3) The same is evident from the Eusebian enumeration, which itself also counts 79 years from the first of Nebuchadnezzar according to Scripture to the last of Cyrus: 19 years of Nebuchadnezzar to the burning of the Solomonic temple: from this to the beginning of the Persian Kingdom of Cyrus 30 years, with 30 of the Persian reign. The sum is 79 years. But the mathematical Canon of Ptolemy, as was just said, has only 75 years. Again a difference of four solid years. This is a most excellent guidance, which dissipates the sandy conjectures of chronologers and curbs the license of many. Therefore, by the grace of God, we have this: that Nebuchadnezzar reigned for 47 years from his first arrival into Syria and Palestine, four with his parent, 43 alone. This having been obtained, the defect of 4 years in the mathematical Canon of Ptolemy is thus supplied. Therefore, from the first of Nebuchadnezzar according to Scripture and the annals of the Phoenicians to the last Babylonian King, whom Cyrus conquered, there are precisely 70 years, agreeing with the 70 years of captivity. But Ptolemy in the Canon attributes 9 years of Babylonian dominion to Cyrus. He would have conquered the last Babylonian King in the 21st year. of his Persian Kingdom, and immediately upon the occupation of Babylon, he would have relaxed the captivity for the Jews, they requesting it from Cyrus by way of information. Moreover, this guidance provides us with a torch for the chronological connection of the years of Nabonassar to the years of Scripture. If the first of Nebuchadnezzar from his first arrival into Palestine is the fourth of Jehoiakim, with Jeremiah as witness, ch. 25:1. Therefore, the first of Nebuchadnezzar after the death of his parent arises from the 8th of Jehoiakim: and the 19th of the same according to Scripture would be the 15th according to the Canon of Ptolemy. But the mathematical Canon of Ptolemy connects the first of Nebuchadnezzar with the 144th of Nabonassar. Therefore, it will agree with the 158th of Nabonassar, which year is to be connected with the year of the extermination of the Solomonic temple not conjecturally, but historically. Which connection wonderfully refreshes and confirms the chronological mind of man. According to this term, therefore, of 70 years of Babylonian servitude, every difficulty which is accustomed to be raised concerning these years is removed. Thus the release from captivity took place while Cyrus was living, nine full years before his death. And indeed, Scripture speaks almost everywhere of the Babylonian servitude of the Jews having taken its true beginning from the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Palestine, and having continued from thence even to the times of Cyrus. For from that time, when Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Necho in a great battle at the Euphrates in the 4th year of Jehoiakim (Jer. 46:2) and occupied a good part of Egypt, Judea (which Pharaoh Necho had previously made tributary, 2 Kings 23:33 and following; 2 Chron. 36:3) came under the tribute of the Babylonian kingdom: For Nebuchadnezzar, returning from Egypt, besieged Jerusalem and made Jehoiakim tributary for three years (2 Kings 24:1), and at the same time sent Daniel with his companions and many others to Babylon. Behold the beginning of the Babylonian servitude! In the course of time, when Jehoiakim, King of Judah, rebelled and defected from Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar, at the end of the seventh year of his reign, came to Jerusalem again, and having seized the rebellious King of Judah, he cast him into chains with the intention of leading him to Babylon, but he died in chains and was cast out unburied Jer. 22, 19. c. 36, 30. 2. Chron. 36, 6. Thus far B. Behmius.

Although these things are indeed sufficiently firm and solid, yet the most excellent Chronologist held a preconceived opinion, which he had drawn from Scaliger and Calvisius, so that he preferred to fluctuate in doubt, at that time, rather than to abandon it entirely, and he left the whole matter in the middle. He confesses, however, his hallucination, that he was formerly less fair to this opinion. In our Chronological Introduction, he says in Thesis 33, we were somewhat unfair to this opinion concerning the starting point (A QUO) of the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity from the first arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Syria, from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, King of Judah. But with the passage of time, having considered the matter and the circumstances of the matter more deeply, having become fairer, we have determined that from this starting point (A QUO) to the last year of Nabonidus, the Median King of Babylon, whom Cyrus conquered, precisely 70 years have elapsed. Which most sweet agreement leads me to this, that I easily add my calculation to those who make this the starting point (A QUO) of the 70 years of servitude.

He therefore adds his calculation to this opinion, but, as I said, he does not wish to renounce the former, although both cannot stand together. There remains the FOURTH OPINION (so he continues in thesis 34) which begins these 70 years with the Prophet Ezekiel seven years later from the spontaneous abduction of Jeconiah to Babylon, most solemn and famous, as indicated above. I defended this opinion in the Chronological Introduction, following Clement of Alexandria, Scaliger, Tremellius, Calvisius, and other most excellent Chronologists, and even today I cannot set it aside entirely. For the careful enumeration of Ezekiel is sacrosanct to me, and the consolatory Epistle of the Prophet Jeremiah, which he sent to those twice deported to Babylon, and promises them deliverance by divine power at the end of 70 years, chapter 29. Finally, thesis 39. he testifies to indecision in this case: Having therefore rejected the two prior opinions, which begin the 70 years of Babylonian servitude either from the thirteenth year of Josiah, or from the burning of the temple, and terminate them either in the first year of the Persian kingdom of Cyrus, or in the second of Darius Hystaspis, we give a free option to all and each of the lovers of Historical-Chronological study, which of the two later ones they wish to choose; whether that which begins the years of servitude from the 4th year of Jehoiakim, from the 1st arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Syria, and finishes in the 21st year of the Persian kingdom of Cyrus: or the other, which makes the starting point (A QUO) of the years of captivity the spontaneous deportation of Jeconiah to Babylon, and the terminal point (AD QUEM) the 28th year of the Persian kingdom of Cyrus. Both opinions can certainly subsist very well, without confusion of the Chronological system.

What the cause was, why he did not approach with boldness (μετὰ παῤῥησίας) the opinion which begins the 70 years from the fourth year of Jehoiakim, I think he has sufficiently indicated, namely that he had not yet seen how that careful enumeration of Ezekiel, which is deservedly sacrosanct to all, and the consolatory Epistle of Jeremiah chapter 40, might agree with that beginning, since both seem to constitute the transportation of Jeconiah rather as the beginning of the captivity. The most recent Disputation on this matter, held nine years later at Königsberg, testifies that he had finally resolved this doubt, by which he defined without hesitation; that they depart from the Prophet Jeremiah c. 25, 1, who do not begin the 70 years of Babylonian pressure from the fourth year of Jehoiakim. Why do they depart, he says, from the Prophet Jeremiah, who begins the 70 years of Babylonian pressure from the fourth year of Jehoiakim and the first

arrival of Nebuchadnezzar into Judea, chapter 25? Did not the abduction of the Jews to Babylon begin immediately from that time? Were not the three last Kings of the Jews, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, Zedekiah, made vassals of the Babylonian King Nebuchadnezzar from that time? Did not Judea become tributary to the Babylonian King from that time? We have adduced to Jer. 29 other arguments of the late lamented (τῶ μακαρίτη) which he proposed for this opinion from Chronological and Historical documents.

But how he resolved those things which had previously held him in doubt, is not clear. For he has nothing about them in this most recent disputation. But what is to be held concerning the passage Jer. 29, 10, we have already said there. No connection of the 70 years of captivity with the time of the spontaneous deportation is established there. It is only said that the Epistle was written to the abducted, and the time when it was written is expressed; after Jeconiah with the Queen (mother) and the courtiers, and other Princes, had been abducted. But if anyone should strongly urge: that the time of the written consolatory Epistle, not of the deportation that had taken place, is expressed there, yet the beginning of the 70 years of Babylonian servitude is not fixed at that time. Only in verse 10 is liberation promised when the 70 years are completed. But the beginning of those 70 years is not assigned there, as it had already been assigned in c. 25, 1. 11.

But what shall be done with Ezekiel, who so solicitously, in so many places, counts the years of the captivity, as no other of the Prophets does, namely ch. 1, 1. ch. 8, 1. ch. 20, 1. ch. 24, 1. 2. ch. 26, 1. ch. 29, 1. ch. 31, 1. ch. 32, 1. ch. 33, 21. ch. 40, 1. There is no reason why those should recall us from a most solidly founded opinion. For they teach only this, that the years are counted by Ezekiel from the deportation of Jeconiah, with which the years of the reign of Zedekiah began. Which he counted so solicitously, so that the account of the chronology might be consistent. Nowhere, however, did Ezekiel even slightly indicate that he was counting the 70 years of Babylonian servitude and oppression. Of that, there is neither a trace nor a footprint in the whole book of Ezekiel, so that one must wonder that men of the highest rank so confidently collect from that enumeration of Ezekiel the calculation of the years of Babylonian servitude, and the beginning of this epoch. Wherefore one must acquiesce in the designation of Jeremiah and Daniel, as regards the beginning of the epoch. For Daniel, a most accurate observer of times, taught by his own example that Jeremiah was to be looked to in this epoch of 70 years: concerning which Dan. 9, 2. In the first year of his reign I, Daniel, understood by books the number of the years, concerning which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the Prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem should be accomplished in 70 years. And those 70 years were defined not by Ezekiel, but by Jeremiah. And therefore the beginning of the epoch is to be sought in Jeremiah, not in Ezekiel.

Furthermore, it is absolutely necessary to distinguish between the deportation that took place under Jehoiakim, and the transmigration of Jeconiah. The former happened in the third year of Jehoiakim, King of Judah, as Daniel most clearly has it, ch. 1, 1. In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim, King of Judah, came Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, unto Jerusalem, and besieged it, and the Lord delivered Jehoiakim, King of Judah, into his hand, and part of the vessels of the House of God, etc. Which history is described in 2 Kings 24. Whence Cornelius à Lapide errs, when he wishes to conclude from Jer. 52, 28 that there was no captivity in the fourth year of Jehoiakim. Since in that year Jehoiakim was made tributary, and Daniel himself was carried away with his companions. But this deportation of Jeconiah happened after the death of Jehoiakim, to whom he had been substituted. Namely, seven years after the abduction of Daniel. And since that oppression and abduction under Jehoiakim was the first, from it certainly of the seventy years of oppression and Babylonian servitude beginning. Furthermore, if they were only to begin after seven years, a longer captivity would have remained for those who were abducted under Jehoiakim, and they would have had to remain there for a full seven years longer. Nor could it have been clear to them from where the beginning of the seventy-year epoch should be taken, if that first abduction and the subjection of Jehoiakim were not to be included in the calculation. Added to this is that Jeremiah, who defined those seventy years, nowhere starts them from the transmigration of Jeconiah: and that Holy Scripture speaks distinctly of this transmigration, which Ezekiel designates with the word גלותה (c. 1, 2; c. 33, 2; c. 40, 1), and of the oppression, for which he defined seventy years, under King Nebuchadnezzar and his successors: They shall serve the King of Babylon, Jer. 25, 11. And that consolation in Jer. 29, 10. When the seventy years of Babylon are fulfilled, I will visit you and I will perform for you that excellent word of mine concerning bringing you back to this place, gave hope of restoration to all those abducted by the King of Babylon, no less to those who had been transferred there in the first abduction than to the rest; otherwise, the latter would have been in a worse condition. And therefore, the beginning of the counting of the years of captivity is deservedly to be taken from the first abduction. Restoration and abduction look to each other mutually. To the abducted, restoration had been promised. But those who were transferred to Babylon in the first incursion of Nebuchadnezzar were also abducted. As abduction is the terminus a quo of the captivity, so restoration, when it was first made, is deservedly established as the terminus ad quem of the same. They are therefore hallucinating who, led by mere conjecture, assert that the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity are to be calculated from Ezekiel, and that the beginning of that most famous epoch and the years succeeding it in it are designated [by him]. For although he calculates the years from the transportation of Jeconiah, yet that the years of captivity began to flow from then, and that that solemn epoch of the seventy years of captivity has the same beginning as the epoch of the transmigration of Jeconiah, is affirmed merely precariously, and is a petitio principii. Therefore, let the years of the epoch of servitude and oppression defined by Jeremiah, and accurately observed by Daniel, who was transferred at that time, remain distinct from the years of the spontaneous transmigration of Jeconiah, counted by Ezekiel, who the Jews assert was abducted to Babylon at the same time, concerning whom also Josephus [writes in] book 10, Antiquities, c. 8.

THE HAND OF THE LORD WAS UPON ME] The divine power seized me.

AND BROUGHT ME THITHER] in a vision, so that I might see all past things as if they were present, as above in chapter 8; 'thither' refers to the city, that is, Jerusalem.

Latin:

CAPUT XL.

Vir cum mensura conspectus, qui dimensus est latitudinem & altitudinem novi templi, & atria tria, exterius nempe, medium in quo 30. cameræ cum mensis, & intimum, in quo altare & duo columnæ.

Verf. 1.

IN VIGESIMO QUINTO ANNO TRANSMIGRATIONIS NOSTRÆ, IN EXORDIO ANNI, DECIMA MENSIS, [QUARTODECIMO ANNO POSTQUAM PERCUSSA EST CIVITAS] Principio anni, id est, mensis TISRI, qui initium anni antiquissimum. Ita his vult Hieronymus.

DE initio anni alias diximus. Jam de colligatione 25. anni transmigrationis, & 14. à percussa civitate dispiciendum, è qua colligunt Chronologi non vulgares, maxime qui Scaligeri partes sequuntur (à quibus alienus non est Grotius, uti alias prodidit) collato cap. 33,21. ubi annus undecimus captivitatis connectitur cum anno exterminii urbis, Captivitatem cepisse cum deportatione Jechoniæ, atque inde etiam initium capere annos 70. captivitatis Babylonicæ, in Scriptura definitos. Et res videtur nimis manifesta. Nam si annus excidii & πανολεθρίας urbis fuit undecimus captivitatis, idemque undecimus fuit regiminis Zedekiæ, & abductionis Jechoniæ, cui ille surrogatus est, & annus uterque migrationis 25. fuit 14. percussæ urbis, quid certius, quam quod captivitatis initium in Jechoniæ spontanea deportatione figendum sit. Sed demonstravimus rationibus, uti arbitramur, invictis ad c. 29. Jerem. initium 70. annorum captivitatis Babylonicæ capiendum esse à quarto Jojakimi anno, non vero à Jechoniæ deportatione. Quod è Jeremiæ locis luculentissime constitit. Quid ergo? num committemus cum Jeremia Ezechielem, qui in utroque hoc loco, c. 33. & 40. itidem perquam luculentus est? In anno, inquit, c. 33, 21. duodecimo לגלותינו, transmigrationis nostræ. Ethic Vigesimum quintum annum transmigrationis aperte dicit decimum quartum fuisse percussæ urbis. Undecimo ergo transmigrationis anno urbs percussa fuit.

Vidit hæc etiam, sine dubio, B. Behmius, Scaligerianæ sectæ propugnator non postremus, quem tamen supra, cum locum Jeremiæ tractavimus, istius sententiam, quam pridie sequutus erat, postridie deseruisse, observavimus. Quapropter agnovit utique posteriori ætate, non esse satis validum argumentum, quod ex his Ezech. locis pro illa sententia petitur, etiamsi olim pro validissimo id habuerit, cum nempe Manuductionem Chronologicam ederet, in qua lib. 2. tit. 2. cap. 2. pag. 108. ita habetur: Ezechiel totus est a nostris partibus, diversis in locis cap. 1, 2. 24,1. Nonum captivitatis annum rejicit in id tempus, quo Nebucadnezar Jerosolymam obsidere cepit. Id autem factum est anno 9. Regis Zedekiæ, 2. Reg. 25, 1. Jerem. 39, 1. & 52, 4. Ita 12. captivitatis annum rejicit in id tempus, quo præterito anno civitas Jerosolyma percussa erat, id est, desolata cap. 33, 21. Omnium autem clarissime idem Propheta 25. annum captivitatis rejicit in 14. πανολεθρίας templi cap. 40, 1. & alibi sæpissime à Jechonia migratione sollicite annos numerat cap. 8, 1. c. 20, 1. cap. 26, 1. c. 29. c. 31, 1. c. 32, 1.

Hæc ibi, tanquam ἀναντιῥῥήτως certa An. 1616. tradidit, sed, accuratiori inquisitione instituta, posterioribus annis dubius reddi cepit, ideoque disputatione, quam de hoc themate Regiomonti Anno 1633. 30. Sept. habuit, adeo non inhæsit illi Epochæ initio à deportatione Jechoniæ, ut ab ipso Spiritu Sancto Jer. 25, 12. initium quarto anno Jojakim! assignari, asseruerit, qui illic loci cum primo anno Nebucadnezaris non à morte parentis, sed à primo sui in Syriam adventus, vivente adhuc Patre Nabopolassare facti, (de quo Berosus apud Josephum lib. 10. Ant. cap. 11. & 1. in App. ut & Eusebium lib. 9. præpar. Evang. cap. 4.) concatenatur. Quo Nebucadnezar, ob Satrapæ Ægypti & Cælosyriæ & Phœniciæ rebellionem adversus Regnum

Babyloniæ, expeditione facta, & rebellibus devi- ctis, ac regione Syrio-Ægyptiaca subacta, Hiero- solymam progressus, Jejoakimum Judæ Regem, Pharaonis Necho (quem Nebucadnezar device- rat) ante tributarium 2. Reg. 23,33. 2. Chron. 36, 3. Regi Babylonico parenti Vasallum, & tributarium fecit, abductis simul in Babyloniam Daniele Pro- pheta, cum sociis, & aliis, bona quoque parte in- strumentorum Domus Domini, 2. Reg, 24, 1. Jer. 46, 2. Dan. 1, 1. 2. Erat is tertius annus Jojakimi completus Dan. 1, 1. quartus vero currens Jer. 25. c. 46, 2. De quo Eusebius in Canone Chronico ad annum 4. Olymp. 54. Colligitur omne tempus capti- vitatis Judæorum anni 70. Qui vero secundum quos- dam à tertio anno Eliakim (qui est Jojakim) usq; ad 29. Cyri Regis. Unde apparet, eam sententiam jam ante Eusebium invaluisse.

Proponere placet hanc sententiam verbis, & ar- gumentis B. D. Behmii è disputatione laudata ad- ductis, quæ hic forte in nullius manibus est. A primo, inquit thes. 27. Nebucadnezaris secundum Scripturam, ad ultimum Nabonidi Medi, quem Cyrus vicit (Nobis est Darius Medus apud Danielem cap. 9. v. 1.) præcise 70. anni elapsi sunt. Id probandum non ex levibus conjecturis, sed ex historica veritate, & Mathematico Ptolemæi Canone. Verus Berosus apud Josephum priore in Appionem, & Eusebium lib. 9. præparat. Evang. c. 4. à primo Nebucadnezaris ad ultimum Nabonidi Medi numerat annos 66. Idem facit Mathematicus Ptolemei Canon. En deductio- nem! Nebucadnezari tribuuntur anni 43. utrobique, à morte scilicet Parentis Nabopallassaris: Avaroda- mo (Evilmerodacho) 2. Niricassolaffari, (Belthasari) 4. Nabonnadio Medo (Dario Medo) 17. Sum- ma 66. Idem aureum fragmentum ex vero Beroso apud Josephum citatur lib. 10. Αρχαιολογ. c. 12. Verum ibi numeri corrupti sunt. Evilmerodacho tribuuntur 18. pro 2. Neriglifsorori 40. pro 4. Restant. 4. anni ad 70. annos captivitatis, complendi à primo Nebucadne- zaris. Hi ex historica collatione hoc modo complen- tur. Scriptura aliter numerat annos Regis Nebucad- nezaris, aliter Berosus cum Josepho. Hi à morte pa- rentis: illa à primo Nebucadnezaris in Syriam & Palæstinam adventu, facto vivente adhuc parente, ut supra vidimus ex Beroso. Plures ergò anni regiminis tribuendi sunt huic famosissimo Regi secundum Scri- pturam. Quot vero anni superaddendi? Id quidem nullibi expressum in aliqua historia continetur. Uti- nam plenam Berosi, Megasthenis, Diodori Siculi, & aliorum Historicorum Historiam Babylonicorum Re- gum à Nebucadnezare ad Cyrum haberemus! Nil præter desiderium nobis relictum est. Ex sedula ta- men historiarum scrutatione & mutua collatione ide- ruimus: Nabopallassarem filium Nebucadnezarem, ætate & robore virentem & valentem in Syriam & Palæstinam prima vice misisse anno 17. sui regiminis, & consequenter cum parente annos quatuor solidos regnasse. Hanc supputationem tripliciter firmamus. 1. ex Phœnicum annalibus apud Josephum priore in Appion. qui à primo Nebucadnezaris ad primum Cyri Monarchiæ Persicæ numerant annos 49. Vi- de supra thesi 14. additis 30. annis Regiminis Cyri fiunt 79. anni à primo Nebucadnezaris secundum Scripturam & annales Phœniciorum ad ultimum Cyri. Mathematicus vero Ptolemæi canon à primo Nebucadnezaris ad ultimum Cyri 75. tantum annos habet: 66. à primo Nebucadnezaris ad ultimum Nabonnidi Medi 9. Cyri à devicta Babylone. Sum- ma 75. anni. Differentia annorum quatuor solido- rum. Hoc ipsum alio modo probamus. Ultimus Cyri in Mathematico Ptolemæi Canone est 218. Nabona- diano zaraeus, 7. Cambysis, 225. Nabonazareus, cœlesti charactere notatus. Ergo primus Cyri Regni Persici est 188. Nabonazaræus, per 30. namq; annos regnavit. Diximus autem in præcedente supputatione annales Phœnicum à primo Cyri ad primum Nebucadneza- ris numerare annos 49. qui à 188. Nabonazaræo subtracti remanent 139. anni Nabonazaræi ad pri- mum Nebucadnezaris secundum Scripturam. At- qui Ptolomæus in Canone ad primum Nebucadneza- ris annos 143. numerat, ἀυτοψίᾳ teste. En iterum intervallum quatuor annorum! (3) Idem patet ex Eusebiana enumeratione, quæ & ipsa à primo Nebu- cadnezaris secundum Scripturam ad ultimum Cyri 79. annos numerat: 19. annos Nebucadnezaris ad Salomonici templi conflagrationem: Ab hac ad ini- tium Persici Regni Cyri 30. anni cum 30. Persici Re- giminis. Summa 79. annis. Atqui Mathemati- cus Ptolomæi Canon, uti modò dictum, annos tantum 75. habet. Iterum differentia quatuor solidorum an- norum. Excellentissima hæc est manuductio, quæ are- nosas Chronologorum conjecturas dissipat, multorumq; licentiam frænat. Id ergo per Dei gratiam habemus, Nebucadnezarem à primo sui in Syriam & Palæsti- nam adventu per 47. annos regnâsse, quatuor cum parente, 43. solum. Hoc obtento defectus 4. annorum in Mathematico Ptolomæi Canone ita suppletus est. A primo ergo Nebucadnezaris secundum Scripturam & Phœnicum annales ad ultimum Babyloniorum Regem, quem Cyrus vicit, præcisè 70. anni sunt, convenientes cum 70. annis captivitatis. Ptolemæus vero in Canone Cyro 9. annos tribuit Babylonici Do- minatus. Vicisset ergo ultimum Babyloniorum Re- gem anno 21. Persici sui Regni, & statim ab occupa- ta Babylone, Iudæis id à Cyro per informationis modum petentibus captivitatem laxasset. Hæc insuper ma- nuductio nobis facem præbet Chronologicæ alligatio- nis annorum Nabonassaræorum ad annos Scripturæ. Si primus Nebucadnezaris a primo sui in palæstinam adventu est quartus Jojakimi, Jeremia teste c. 25, 1. Ergo primus Nebucadnezaris post parentis mortem exurgit ab 8. Jojakimi: & 19. ejusdem secundum Scripturam esset 15. secundum Ptolemæi canonem. Atqui Mathematicus Ptolemæi canon primum Nebu- cadnezaris connectit cum 144. Nabonassaræo. Er- go conveniet cum 158. Nabonassaræo, qui annus cum anno exterminii Solomonici templi Chronologice connectendus non στοχαστικῶς, sed ἱστορικῶς. Quæ con- nexio Chronologicum hominis animum mirifice re- creat & confirmat. Secundum hunc ergo terminum 70. annorum Babylonicæ servitutis omnis difficultas, quæ circa annos hosce moveri solet, sublata est. Ita laxatio captivitatis facta est vivente Cyro novem solidis annis ante suam mortem. Et sane a primo Nebucadne- zaris in Palæstinam adventu Babylonicam Judæo- rum servitutem verum initium sumpsisse, indeque ad Cyri usq; tempora continuasse, Scriptura ubivis fe- re locorum loquitur. Ab eo namq; tempore, quo Nebu- cadnezar Pharaonem Necho magno prælio ad Eu- phratem vicit anno 4. Jojakimi Jer: 46, 2. & bonam Ægypti partem occupavit, Judæa (quam Pharao Necho ante tributariam fecerat 2. Reg. 23, 33. & seq. 2. Chron. 36, 3.) sub tributum Babylonici regni venit: Nam Nebucadnezar ex Ægypto redux Hierosoly- mam obsedit, & Jehojakimum tributarium fecit tri- bus annis 2. Reg. 24, 1. simul & Danielem tum sociis & aliis plurimis Babylonem misit. En Babylonicæ servitutis initium! Successu temporis cum Jojakim Rex Judæ contra Nebucadnezarem rebellaret & de- ficeret, Nebucadnezar anno septimo sui regni ferè desinente, Hierosolymam iterum venit, & rebellem Judæ Regem comprehensum in vincula conjicit, animo Babylonem abducendi, verum in vinculis mor- tuus abjicitur insepultus Jer. 22, 19. c. 36, 30. 2. Chron. 36, 6. Hactenus B. Behmius.

Quanquam vero hæc satis firma sint, atque solida, hæsit tamen Chronologico præstantissimo opinio præconcepta, quam à Scaligero & Calvi- sio hauserat, ut fluctuare dubius, isto quidem tem- pore, maluerit, quam illam omnino deserere, ac rem omnem in medio reliquerit. Fatetur tamen hallucinationem suam, quod minus æquus huic sententiæ olim fuerit. In Chronologicæ nostræ ma- nuductione, inquit Thesi 33. nonnihil iniquiores fuimus in hanc sententiam de termino A QUO 70. annorum Babylonicæ captivitatis a primo Nebucadne- zarıs in Syriam adventu, à quarto Jojakimi Regis Judæ. Verum successu temporis, re & rei circum- stantiis altius consideratis, æquiores facti, statuimus, ab hoc termino A QUO ad ultimum Nabonnidi Medi Babylonici Regis, quem Cyrus vicit, præcise 70. annos elapsos esse. Quæ suavissima convenientia me eo adducit, ut facile meum calculum iis adjiciam, qui hunc terminum A QUO faciunt 70. annorum servitutis.

Addit ergo calculum huic sententiæ, sed, ut dixi, priorem abdicare non vult, quum ta- men utraque consistere simul nequeat. Restat QUARTA OPINIO (ita pergit thes. 34.) quæ 70. hosce annos cum Ezechiele Propheta septennio post inchoat à spontanea Jechoniæ in Babylonem abductio- ne, maxime solenni & famosa, ut supra indicatum. Hanc sententiam in Chronologica Manuductione de- fendi, secutus Clementem Alexandrinum, Scali- gerum, Tremellium, Calvisium, & alios præstantis- simos Chronologos, & etiamnum hodie eam in totum seponere non possum. Solicita namq; Ezechielis nu- meratio mihi sacrosancta est, & consolatoria Jere- miæ Prophetæ Epistola, quam bisce deportatis in Babyloniam misit, ipsisque decursu 70. annorum re- ditum divinitus promittit cap. 29. Denique thes. 39. ἐπαμφοτερισμὸν in hac causa testatur: Abje- ctis ergo duobus prioribus opinionibus, quæ 70. annos Babylonicæ servitutis inchoant vel à decimo tertio Jo- siæ, vel à templi conflagratione, terminant vel in pri- mo Cyri Persici regni, vel in secundo Darii Hystaspis, liberam omnibus & singulis Historico-Chronologici stu- dii amatoribus optionem damus, quam ex duabus po- sterioribus eligere velint; num eam, quæ annos servi- tutis incipit à 4. Jojakimi à 1. Nebucadnezaris in Sy- riam adventu, finit in 21. Cyri Persici regni: num alteram, quæ terminum A QUO annorum captivi- tatis facit spontaneam Jechoniæ in Babylonem depor- tationem, terminum AD QUEM 28. Cyri Persici regni. Utræq; sane opinio optime subsistere potest, si- ne Chronologici systematis confusione.

Quid causæ fuerit; cur non μετὰ παῤῥη- σίας accesserit sententiæ, quæ auspicatur 70. an- nos à quarto Jojakimi, satis opinor, indicavit, quod nempe nondum viderit, quomodo sollicita illa Ezechielis numeratio, quæ merito omnibus sa- crofancta est, & consolatoria Jeremiæ Epistola cap. 40. cum illo initio conveniat, quum Jechoniæ po- tius transportationem initium captivitatis utraque constituere videatur. Atexuissetandem ipsum hanc dubitationem novissima de hac materia Dis- putatio, novennio post Regiomonti habita testa- tur, qua citra hæsitationem definivit; eos à Jeremia Propheta c. 25, 1. discedere, qui non incipiant annos 70 Babylonicæ pressuræ, à quarto Jojakimi. Quare dis- cedunt, inquit, à Propheta Jeremia, qui annos 70. Ba- bylonicæ pressuræ incipit à quarto Jojakimi & prim

Nebucadnezaris adventu in Iudæam cap. 25? An- non ab eo statim tempore incepit Iudæorum in Baby- loniam abductio? Annon ab eo tempore tres ultimi Iudæorum Reges Iojakim, Iechonia, Zedekia facti sunt vasalli Babylonici Regis Nebucadnezaris? Annon ab eo tempore Iudæa Babylonico Regi facta est tribu- taria? Argumenta τῶ μακαρίτη alia, quæ in hanc sententiam ex Chronologis & Historicis docu- mentis proposuit, ad Jer. 29. adduximus.

Quomodo autem expediverit illa, quæ du- bium ipsum antea tenuerant, non constat. Nihil enim in hac novissima disputatione de illis habet. Quid vero de loco Jerem. 29, 10. habendum sit, il- lic jam diximus. Nulla ibi 70. annorum captivi- tatis instituiturcum tempore spontaneæ deporta- tionis colligatio. Exarata solum dicitur Epistola ad abductos, & tempus, quo exarata fuit, exprimi- tur; postquam Iechonias cum Regina (matre) & au- licis, Principibus aliisŕ, abducti fuere. Quod si ma- xime quis urgeat: istic non exaratæ Epistolæ conso- latoriæ, sed factæ deportationis tempus exprimi, non tamen initium in illo tempore figitur 70. annorum Babylonicæ servitutis. Solum vers. 10. completis 70. annis liberatio promittitur. Initium autem illorum 70. annorum ibi non assignatur, utpote quod c. 25, 1. 11. assignatum jam erat.

Sed quid fiet Ezechieli, qui tam sollicite, in tot locis numerat annos captivitatis, ut nullus Pro- phetarum alius, utpote cap. 1, 1. c. 8, 1. c. 20, 1. c. 24, 11. 12. c. 26, 1. c. 29, 1. c. 31, 1. c. 32, 1. c. 33, 21. c. 40, 1. Non est, quod illa nos à sententia solidissime fundata re- vocent. Id enim solum docent, annos ab Ezechie- le numerari à Iechoniæ deportatione, cum qua cœpe- re anni Regiminis Zedekiæ. Quos ita sollicite nu- meravit, ut Chronologiæ ratio constaret. Nuspiam autem Ezechiel vel leviter saltem indicavit, sese numerare annos 70. servitutis ac pressuræ Babylonicæ. De eo nec vola, nec vestigium in toto Ezechielis libro, ut mirari oporteat, adeo ex Ezechielis ista enumeratione viros præcipui commatis tam con- fidenter supputationem annorum servitutis Baby- lonicæ, atque initium Epochæ hujus colligere. Quapropter Jeremiæ ac Danielis designationi ac- quiescendum, quod ad Epochæ initium. Nam Daniel, temporum observator accuratissimus, Jere- miam in hac 70. annorum Epocha respiciendum esse, suo exemplo docuit: de quo Dan. 9, 2. An- no uno regni ejus Ego Daniel intellexi in libris nume- rum annorum, de quo factus est sermo Domini ad Ie- remiam Prophetam, ut complerentur desolationis Ie- rufalem 70. anni. Nec ab Ezechiele, sed a Ieremia definiti sunt illi 70. anni. Et in Jeremia ergo quærendum Epochæ initium, non in Ezechiele.

Porro distinguere omnino oportet inter de- portationem sub Iojakimo factam, & transmigratio- nem Iechoniæ. Illa accidit tertio anno Ioakim Regis Iu- da, ut apertissime Daniel habet cap. 1, 1. Anno tertio Regni Ioakim Regis Iuda venit Nebuchadonosar, Rex Babylonis in Ierusalem, & obsedit eam, & tradidit Dominus in manus ejus Iojakim Regem Iudæ, & partem vasorum Domus Dei &c. Quæ historia de- scripta est 2. Reg. 24. Unde errat Cornelius à La- pide, cum è Jerem. 52, 28. concludere vult, nullam captivitatem fuisse anno quarto Iojakim. Siquidem illo anno tributarius Iojakim factus, & Daniel ipse abductus fuerit cum sociis. Hæc vero Iechoniæ deportatio post mortem Jojakimi, cui surrogatus fuit, evenit. Septennio scilicet post Danielis abductionem. Et quum illa pressura, & ab- ductio sub Jojakimo prima fuerit, ab ea utique inchoandi anni LXX. pressuræ, & servitutis Ba- bylonicæ. Adhæc si post septennium demum in- choarentur, illos,qui sub Jojakimo abducti, diu- turnior captivitas mansisset, ac per integrum se- ptennium longius iisdem ibi hærendum fuisset.Ne- que constare potuisset ipsis, undenam Epochæ LXX. annorum initium sumendum sit, si prima i- sta abductio, & Jojakimi subjectio in computum ve- nire non debuit. Accedit, quod Jeremias, qui LXX. annos illos definivit, nuspiam eosdem ordiatur à Jechoniæ transmigratione: quodq; distincte loqua- tur Scriptura Sacra de hac transmigratione, quam voce גלותה designat Ezechiel c.1,2.c.33,2.c.40,1. & de pressura,cui LXX. annos definivit, sub Rege Nebucadnezare, & successoribus: Servient Regi Ba- bylonis, Jer. 25, 11. Et consolatio illa Jer. 29,10. Ubi implebuntur Babyloniæ 70. anni, visitabo vos & præ- stabo erga vos verbum meum illud optimum de redu- cendo vos in locum hunc, omnibus abductis à Rege Babyloniæ, non minus illis,qui prima abductione eo translati erant,quàm reliquis, spem faciebat re- ductionis; alias isti deterioris fuissent conditionis. Ideoque merito inde à prima abductione initium numerandorum annorum captivitatis est capien- dum. Reductio & abductio respiciunt sese mutuo. Abductis promissa erat reductio. Abducti autem etiam erant,qui prima Nebucadnezaris incursione Babylonem traducti sunt. Ut abductio terminus à quo est captivitatis,ita reductio, cum primum facta illa est, merito terminus ad quem ejusdem con- stituitur. Hallucinantur ergo, qui ab Ezechiele annos LXX. captivitatis Babylonicæ supputari, & Epochæ istius celeberrimæ initium, annosque in ea succedentes designari,nuda conjectura ducti,as- serunt. Etsi enim annos à Jechoniæ transportatio- ne supputet, annos tamen captivitatis inde fluere cepisse, atque captivitatis illam solemnem Epo- cham LXX. annorum idem initium habere cum E- pocha transmigrationis Jechoniæ mere precario affirmatur, & αἴτησις eστ ἐν ἀρχῇ. Distincti ergo maneant anni Epochæ servitutis & pressuræ à Jere- mia definiti, & à Daniele, qui tum traductus est, ac- curate observati, ab annis spontaneæ transmigratio nis Iechoniæ, ab Ezechiele numeratis, quem simul isto tempore Babylonem abductum esse, Judæi asse- runt, de quo etiam Josephus lib. 10. Antiq. c. 8.

FACTA EST SUPER ME MANUS DOMINI] Vis divina me arripuit.

ET ADDUXIT ME ILLUC] ἐν ὀπτασίᾳ, ut omnia præterita viderem quasi præsentia, ut supra 8. illuc refer- tur ad civitatem, id est, Hierosolyma.

## 40:2
Verse 2. IN THE VISIONS OF GOD] Not in the body.

HE SET ME DOWN UPON A VERY HIGH MOUNTAIN] Namely, to Mount Moriah.

UPON WHICH WAS AS IT WERE THE BUILDING OF A CITY] To which mountain was built as it were another city; it signifies the Temple, which had the appearance of a city. Tacitus: The Temple in the manner of a fortress, its own walls. See Josephus, Jewish War 5, 14. There have always been various opinions concerning this temple which Ezekiel saw, both of Jews and Christians, as Jerome notes, and this whole passage of the Prophet has been held to be very difficult. I, however, side with those who think that a view of the temple, such as it had been when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it, was offered to the eyes of Ezekiel, and that for two reasons. First, so that the Jews might understand how great a glory of their nation they had lost by their crimes: second, so that once they had returned, they might have a specimen which they could imitate as much as they were able. As much as they were able, I say: for neither did extreme haste allow them to imitate it perfectly, nor were their resources equal to the resources of Solomon. Thus Ezra 3, 12 teaches us. & Josephus in these words: 'But the priests and Levites, and the elders of the families, recalling the former temple in their memories, and seeing the greatest and most expensive one having been made, [and seeing] the one being constructed now to be more lacking due to poverty, and considering how much it had fallen from the ancient prosperity and the worth of the temple, they were saddened, and being unable to control the grief at this, they were led to wailing and tears.'

If anyone should object that this description does not fully agree with that which we had in the reign of Solomon, I will answer that so many kings after Solomon, over such a long time, from the huge tributes and gifts which were brought into the temple, added much to the Temple and its ornaments: they also changed some things out of usage, which Josephus teaches us also happened in Herod's Temple. Not all such changes are prescribed, but for an example see 2 Kings 12, 35. Furthermore, since that man of admirable diligence, and besides most expert in architecture and the Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldean languages, Villalpandus, has accurately explained this whole passage of Ezekiel concerning the Temple to us, I urge all who are desirous of learning to approach him, and at the same time I wish that those things which the man of rare erudition, Capellus, has observed after him, and which he has hitherto kept back, might also be published. That will be the reason why we shall touch upon these things only in passing.

TOWARD THE SOUTH] Namely, with respect to Mount Moriah: for the Temple was to the north of the city.

That the Solomonic temple, such as it was when it was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, does not correspond to this διατύπωσις [delineation] has been sufficiently shown by others. For (1) the location does not correspond: the temple of Ezekiel was outside the city, and removed from the city by 15,000 reeds, that is, 27,000 paces, or, if the reeds are Sacred, 30,000, and therefore 27 or 30 Italian miles, as Cornel. à Lap. calculated at chapter 48, 11. Which is a journey of one day. (2) The capacity does not correspond. For otherwise Jerusalem, according to the Rabbinic measurement, would be larger than the whole world. For this city of Ezekiel is eighteen thousand leagues, as the Rabbis count in chapter 48, 35; compare chapter 47, 22. It is certain that, whether we measure the circuit of the city or of the temple, they would be far larger than would befit that ancient city or temple. The circuit of the city is designated as 36 German miles according to the observation of B. Luther. Nor does the division of the land handed down here correspond to the ancient division of the land of Canaan: (1) For that first land of Canaan, as B. Haffenreffer has it in 'The Temple of Ezekiel' page 109, promised to the sons of Israel, was distributed among the tribes in such a way that whichever tribe was larger and more numerous also had a larger inheritance: but in our vision the possession is equal for all, chapter 47, verse 14. You shall possess the land, one as well as another, and indeed even to the strangers who sojourn in this land, their own portion is to be attributed to each. Ibidem verse 22. Then (2) by reason of site and shape, the division of the vision also differs from that ancient one: for the individual tribes had their possessions in different spaces and terminated in different ways: this one was longer than it was wide; that one round, this one more angular; that one was situated toward the east, this one toward the west. But the division of our land is equal and uniform: for all the portions, from the east to the west, extend in an even stretch through the whole breadth of the land, chapter 48. But neither does the order and arrangement of things correspond to the ancient one. For the old Jerusalem was situated in the Tribe of Benjamin, Josh. 18, verse 28. In our vision, the city and temple are situated in the holy portion or oblation. In the old division, the tribe of Judah, as the most populous and most powerful in strength, occupied the extreme position toward the south to more successfully receive the incursions of enemies; in our vision, with the city and temple and the whole holy oblation, it is more northerly. And many more differences of this kind could be shown, by which our vision is distinguished from that ancient state of affairs. (3) The structure does not correspond. Solomon's temple was 120 cubits high. See 2 Chron. 3, 4. But that of Zerubbabel, which according to Grotius was to be adorned according to this διατύπωσις [delineation], was only 60 cubits. (4) The inhabitants of the city do not correspond, who here are not only two tribes, but all the tribes of Israel, both Samaritans and Jews, chapters 47, 48. (5) The manner of worship does not correspond. For although sacrifices and worship, as B. Haffenreffer has it on page 109, of this temple, a great part are described by the phrases and ceremonies of the ancient religion: yet the number and manner of these are many times changed, innovated, diminished, or augmented. From all of which it is manifest that our vision is not to be understood of those ancient Jerusalems, Temple, or the land of Canaan, but of a certain new Temple, a new land, a new city. (6.) The name of the city does not fit. For the name of Ezekiel's temple is Jehovah Shammah, The Lord is there, which properly fits only the Christian Church. (7.) The waters going out from the temple, entering into the dead sea, and sweetening all of it, do not fit, which the whole Jordan could not sweeten everywhere. (8) The gate of the east being perpetually closed does not fit, with the reason subjoined in chapter 44, 2: Because the Lord God of Israel has gone out through it. (9) Those fruitful trees arranged on both sides of the waters, and bringing forth fruit every month, do not fit; to say nothing of many other things which do not fit at all. Whence Papists, even if they believe the temple of Solomon to be magnificently restored by Zerubbabel is described here literally, yet they confess that it is signified more allegorically that the Jewish Synagogue is to be restored through the Church of Christ. Because the one Church, which was once of the Jews, is now of the Christians. But this one is more ample, more august, more laborious, more glorious, more perfect, more beautiful, more gracious. Compare Athanasius, Oration V against the Arians; Chrysostom, homily on Psalm 14. Blessed Luther teaches that these things are to be understood merely mystically. For the nature of one and the same subject, of which it is necessary to understand either all or no predicates in this place, does not permit some things to be understood mystically, others κατὰ το ῥητὸν, others of the spiritual house of the Church, others of the material Jerusalem temple. But since we cannot understand all things of a worldly and material city or temple, as both Papists and Jews are forced to confess, it must be concluded that no predicates can be understood of a material city or temple, whether one to be built to the form of Solomon's by Zerubbabel, as Grotius does with some ancient Rabbis and Papists, or the Utopian and fictitious one of the modern Jews, which they themselves dream is the third. Blessed Megalander has nervously embraced these in his preface to Ezekiel, who should be seen. But since Grotius refers to Villalpandus (it is not certain whether Capellus has published anything), we likewise refer our reader to the temple of Ezekiel by Dn. D. Matthias Hafenreffer, where he will find the mystical meaning handed down, which Osiander also synoptically embraced in his Paraphrase, and which Gregory the Great and Lyranus also handed down in their own way, and Cornelius à Lapide exhibits from the same in his Commentary.

Blessed Hafenreffer has already refuted in the Rabbis the gloss of Grotius, which is clearly taken from them. For the Hebrew doctors, as he has on page 1, dreamed that this vision was a designation, description, and delineation of the city and temple, as they were to be restored and rebuilt after the Babylonian captivity by Zerubbabel and Nehemiah. But after they could not demonstrate the fulfillments of this vision from the histories of those times, they therefore prepared for themselves this hiding place and refuge of dreams: that all those structures could not have been completed at one time, nor under one prince, but that many, even foreign Kings, had to communicate and spend their effort and wealth on this restoration. And so that this vision was nothing other than a comfort for the captives in Babylon; that they should hope for the best, because not only the solution of that captivity, but a magnificent and most splendid reintegration of both city and temple was to be expected. And so carnal men, beyond wood and stones, know nothing, understand nothing, attain nothing. Blessed Hafenreffer urges the arguments which we have brought forward; and so he concludes: Therefore, it is not an external Jerusalem city, but a heavenly or spiritual city that is described, whose name is: The Lord is there. Last chapter, last verse. It is not the temple of Zerubbabel, but the temple, or Church of Christ, that is described: not Levitical worship, but Evangelical: Finally, not buildings, not external dwellings, but the benefits of the kingdom of Christ, and its flower, beauty, and amplitude are painted before our eyes in this Prophetic vision. But our Prophet wished to write down all these things under shadows and typical words taken from the circumstances of the times, places, and worship of that people to whom he accommodates this vision offered to him. He deals first with the restoration of the Temple in chapters 40, 41, and 42. Secondly, with the worship itself, chapters 43 and 44. Thirdly, with the reformation of the whole kingdom, chapters 45, 46, 47, and 48. In describing all of which, as has been said, the Prophet, or rather the Lord who exhibited this vision to the Prophet, uses words and phrases accommodated to the state of the Hebrews, that is, he describes as if it were the temple of the Hebrews, he describes as if it were the worship of the Hebrews, he describes as if it were the land of the Hebrews, when yet he wished to designate nothing of their understanding, but the spiritual and Evangelical kingdom of Christ. Yet he interposes many things which had a discrepancy from that ancient form, so that even from that it might be gathered that the vision is to be understood of another matter than the words of the same description would sound.

Latin:

Vers. 2. IN VISIONIBUS DEI] Non corpore.

DIMISIT ME SUPER MONTEM EXCELSVM] Ad montem nempe Moriæ.

SUPER QUEM ERAT QUASI ÆDIFICIUM CIVITATIS] Cui monti inædificata erat velut urbs altera, Templum significat, quod urbis habuerat speciem. Taci- tus: Templum in modum arcis propriǫ, muri.Vide Josephum Belli Judaici 5, 14. Variæ semper de hoc templo,quod vi- dit Ezechiel,fuere sententiæ, tum Judæorum, tum Chri- stianorum, ut notat Hieronymus, habitusque est totus hic locus Prophetæ perdifficilis. Ego vero iis accedo, qui pu- tant Ezechielis oculis oblatum conspectum templi, quale fuerat,cum id destruxit Nabuchodonosor, idq; duabus de causis. Primum, ut intelligerent Judæi, quantum gentis suæ decus criminibus suis amisissent: deinde, ut olim re- versi specimen haberent,quod imitarentur, quantum pos- sent. Quantum possent,inquam: nam perfecte ut imitaren- tur, neque summa festinatio permisit,neque opes multo o- pibus Solomonis impares. Ita nos docet Esdras 3, 12. & Josephus his verbis: οἱ δὲ ἱερεῖς καὶ λευῖται, καὶ τῶν πατριῶν οἱ πρεσβύτεροι τῷ πρότερον ναὸν ταῖς μνήμαις ἀναπολῶντες μέγιστόν τε κὴ πολυτελέσατον, κέ τ̓ γεγενημένοι ὁρῶντες ὑπὸ πτωχείας ἐν- δεέστερον τῷ πάλαι κατασκευαζόμενον, ὅσον ἐκ τῆς ἀρχαίας εὐ- δαιμονίας ὑποβεβηκός, κὴ τῆς ἀξίας τῷ ναῶ λογιζόμενοι κατήφου, κέ τῆς ἐπὶ τούτῳ λύπης κρατεῖν ἐδυνάμενοι μέχρις ἑστίων κέ δακρύων

προήγοντο. Si quis objiciat non convenire plane hanc de- scriptionem cum illa quam habuimus in imperio Solomo- nis, respondebo tot à Solomone reges tanto tempore ex ingentibus quæ in templum inferebantur tributis ac donis, multum adjecisse Templo, ejusq; ornamentis: mutasse et- iam quædam ex usu, quod & in Herodis Templo contigisse docet nos Josephus. Non omnes mutationes tales præ- scriptæ sunt, sed in exemplum vide 2. Reg. 12, 35. Cæterum cum totum hunc Ezechielis de Templo locum accuratè nobis exposuerit vir admirabilis diligentiæ, præterea archi- tecturæ, linguarumq; Latinæ, Græcæ, Hebraicæ, & Chaldai- cæ peritissimus Villalpandus, omnes discendi cupidos hor- tor eum ut adeant, simulq; opto, ut edantur etiam quæ vir raræ eruditionis Capellus, post eum observata premit ha- ctenus. Ea causa erit cur hæc nonnisi in transcursu attacturi simus.

VERGENTIS AD AUSTRUM] Nempe respectu mon- tis Moriæ: nam urbi Templum ad Septentrionem erat.

Templum Solomoneum quale id fuit, cum de- strueretur à Nebucadnezare, huic διατυπώσει non congruere ab aliis satis ostensum est. Nam (1) non congruit locus: templum Ezechielis extra urbem fuit, & remotum ab urbe per 15. millia calamorum, hoc est, 27000. passuum, vel, si calami sint Sacri, 30000. adeoq; 27. vel 30. miliaria Italica, ut com- putum inivit Cornel. à Lap. ad c. 48, 11. Quod est iter unius diei. (2.) Non cogruit capacitas. Nam alias Jerusalem major foret, juxta Rabinicam di- mensionem, toto orbe. Nam hæc Ezechielis urbs octodecim millium Leucarum est, uti Rabini nu- merant cap. 48, 35. confer. cap. 47, 22. Id certum est, sive civitatis, sive templi circuitum metiamur, longe majores fore, quam priscæ illi urbi aut tem- plo conveniant. Urbis circuitus 36. miliarium Germanicorum designatur juxta B. Lutheri obser- vationem. Neque terra divisio hic tradita con- venit pristinæ terræ Canaan divisioni: (1.) Prim enim terra illa Canaan, ut habet B. Haffenrefferus in Templo Ezechielis pag. 109. filiis Israel promis- sa, sic inter tribus fuit tributa, ut quæ tribus amplior & copiosior esset, ampliorem etiam haberet hære- ditatem: sed in visione nostra omnibus æqualis est possessio cap. 47. vers. 14. Possidebitis terram, unus æque ac alter, quin etiam peregrinis, qui in hac terra peregrinantur, sua singulis est attribuenda portio. Ibidem vers. 22. Deinde (2) situs & formæ ratione, etiam differt visionis divisio, à pristina illa: diversis namq; spatiis, & diversimode terminatis, possessiones suas habuerunt singulæ tribus: hæc longior quam latior; illa rotunda, hæc angulata magis; illa ad ortum, hæc ad occasum sita fuit. Sed nostræ terræ divisio æqualis & uniformis est: omnes enim portiones, ab ortu in occasum, per totam amplitudinem terræ æquabili tractu porri- guntur cap. 48. Verum neque ordo & dispositio rerum pristinæ respondet. Nam Hierosolyma ve- teres sitæ fuerunt in Tribu Benjamin. Jos. 18. vers. 28. In nostra visione sita est urbs & templum in portione sive oblatione sancta. In veteri divisione tribus Juda, ut populosissima & viribus potentissi- ma, ad hostium incursiones felicius excipiendum, extremum locum versus meridiem occupavit; in nostra visione, & urbe & templo, & tota oblatione sancta, est Septentrionalior. Et hujusmodi diffe- rentiæ plures etiam monstrari possent, quibus vi- sio nostra ab antiquo illo rerum statu discrimina- tur. (3.) Non congruit structura. Salomonis templum altum fuit cubitus 120. Vid. 2. Par. 3, 4. At Zorobabelis, quod juxta hanc διατύπωσιν ador- nandum secundum Grotium, cubitorum solum 60. erat. (4.) Non congruunt urbis incolæ, qui hic non sunt duæ tantum tribus, sed omnes tribus Israelis tam Samaritæ quam Judæi capp. 47. 48. (5.) Non congruit ratio cultus. Nam licet sacrifi- cia & cultus, ut habet B. Haffenrefferus pag. 109. hujus templi, magnam partem phrasibus & cere- moniis antiquæ religionis describantur: multis tamen vicibus eorundem numerus ac modus mu- tantur, innovantur, diminuuntur, vel adaugentur. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum est, visionem no- stram, non de antiquis illis Hierosolymis, Tem- plo, aut terra Canaan, sed de novo quodam Tem- plo, nova terra, nova civitate accipiendam esse. (6.) Non congruit nomen civitatis. Nam Ezechie- lis templo nomen est, Jehovah Schammah, Domi- nus ibi, quod proprie soli Ecclesiæ Christianæ con- venit. (7.) Non congruunt aquæ è templo egre- dientes, in mare mortuum ingredientes, idque to- tum edulcorantes, quod totus Jordanus ubiq; edul- corare non posset. (8) Non congruit perpetuo clausa orientis porta, cum ratione subjuncta cap. 44, 2. Quoniam Dominus Deus Israel egressus est per eam. (9) Non congruunt arbores illæ fæcundæ utrinque ad aquas dispositæ, & per singulos menses fructus proferentes; ut multa alia taceamus, quæ minime congruunt. Unde Papistæ, etsi templum Salomonis magnifice à Zorobabele instaurandum ad literam hic describi credant, magis tamen allego- rice significari restaurandam Synagogam Judaicam per Ecclesiam Christi, fatentur. Quia una Eccle- sia, quæ olim fuit Judæorum, jam est Christiano- rum. Sed hæc illa amplior, augustior, operosior, gloriosior, perfectior, pulchrior, gratiosior. Con- fer Athanasium Orat. V. contra Arian. Chryso- stomum homil. in Psal. 14. B. Lutherus mere mysti- ce intelligenda hæc esse docet. Nam alia mystice, alia κατὰ το ῥητὸν, alia de Ecclesiæ domo Spirituali, alia de materiali æde Hierosolymitana intelligi non permittit unius ejusdemque subjecti ratio, de quo oportet aut omnia, aut nulla prædicata hoc in loco intelligere. Omnia autem quum de terrena & materiali urbe aut templo accipere non possimus, ut cum Papistæ, tum Judæi fateri coguntur, con- cludendum est, nulla prædicata de materiali urbe aut templo sive Zorobabelis ad formam Salomonei ex- struendo, uti Grotius cum Rabbinis veteribus non- nullis, & Papistis, sive Utopico & fictitio Judæorum modernorum, quod tertium ipsi somniant, intel- ligi posse. Nervose complexus est hæc B. Mega- lander præfat. in Ezech. qui videatur. Sed cum remittat Grotius ad Villalpandum, (num Capel- lus aliquid ediderit, non constat) lectorem no- strum pariter remittimus ad Dn. D. Matthiæ Hafen- refferi templum Ezechielis, ubi mysticam signifi- cationem traditam inveniet, quam Synoptice quoque complexus est Osiander in Paraphras. ac suo modo etiam Gregorius Magnus ac Lyranus tra- didêre, & ex iisdem exhibet Cornelius à Lapide in Commentario.

Refutavit B. Hafenrefferus jam in Rabbinis Grotii glossam, quæ plane ex iisdem desumpta. Hæbræi namq; doctores, uti habet pag. 1. somniarunt hanc visionem fuisse designationem, descriptionem & delineationem urbis & templi, sicut post captivita- tem Babylonicam per Zorobabelem & Nehemiam restituenda & restauranda essent. Posteaquam au- tem ex historiis illorum temporum hujus visionis com- plementa demonstrare non potuerunt; Ideo hoc so- mniorum sibi latibulum & refugium compararunt, non uno tempore, nec sub uno principe, omnes illas structuras perfici potuisse, sed plures, etiam extra- neos Reges, operam & opes suas, huic restaurationi communicare & insumere debuisse. Adeoque visio- nem hanc nihil aliud fuisse, quam solatium capti- vorum in Babylonia; optime nimirum sperandum, quia non tantum captivitatis illius solutio, sed magni- fica splendidissimag; & urbis & templi redintegratio expectanda sit. Adeoq́; carnales homines, ultra lignum & lapides, nihil sapiunt, nihil intelligunt, nihil assequuntur. Argumenta urget B. Hafenref- fer. quæ nos adduximus; adeoq; concludit: Non igitur externa civitas Hierosolymitana, sed civitas cœlestis aut spiritualis describitur, cui nomen est: Dominus ibi. cap. ult. v. ult. Non templum Zoro- babelis, sed templum, sive Ecclesia Christi describitur: non cultus Leviticus; sed Evangelicus: Denique non ædificia, non mansiones externæ, sed beneficia regni Christi, ejusq́; flos, pulchritudo, & amplitudo in hac visione Prophetica ante oculos nostros depingitur. Isthaec omnia vero sub umbris & verbis typicis ex cir- cumstantiis temporum, locorum, cultuum istius po- puli desumptis, cui visionem hanc sibi oblatam accom- modat, Propheta noster voluit exarare. Agit pri- mum de restitutione Templi capp. 40. 41. & 42. Secundo de ipso cultu, capp. 43. & 44. Tertio, de reformatione totius regni capp. 45. 46. 47. & 48. in quibus omnibus describendis, ut dictum est, utitur Propheta, vel Dominus potius, qui hanc visionem Prophetæ exhibuit, verbis ac phrasibus stalui Hebræorum accommodatis, hoc est, de- scribit quasi templum Hebræorum, describit quasi cultum Hebræorum, describit quasi terram He- bræorum, cum tamen nihil eorum intellectum, sed regnum Christi Spirituale & Evangelicum desi- gnatum voluisset. Plura tamen interferit, quæ à pris- ca illa forma discrepantiam habebant, ut vel inde colParent, de alia re visionem accipiendam esse, quam ejusdem descriptionis verba sonarent.

## 40:3
Vers. 3.

BEHOLD A MAN] An Angel, as in Apoc. 11, 1. Angels are called men, where they appear in that form, Daniel 10, 5. Most of our people determine that this Demonstrator of Ezekiel is not some created angel, but the Son of God: For it is not an angel, but Christ who is the architect of his Church, Matthew 16, 18. Who is called a man because of his human nature; for his appearance is as of most lucid brass. Compare Ezekiel 1, 7. By which is expressed both his purity and Holiness according to his human nature, and his most pure, most holy divine nature, much more durable than any steel, and brass, and iron. Which is confirmed primarily from a similar place, Zechariah 2, 1, where Christ is likewise seen in the form of a man, having in his hand a measuring line, whose property it also is to be the measurer and judge in the Church. For he has a balance and a measuring rod, with which that man measures and distributes all things, the smallest and the greatest, at the gate of the house of the Lord: Because he is the inspector and keeper of the house of the Lord, and through him alone the entrance is open; John 14:6, chapter 10:9. Jerome on chapter 47 of Ezekiel. That man, he says, who was clothed in linen (בדים) and was the leader of the Prophet, passed through clearly; he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

WHOSE APPEARANCE WAS AS THE APPEARANCE OF BRASS] Namely, shining, which the Greeks add here. Both the strength and the splendor of the angels are signified.

AND A LINE OF FLAX IN HIS HAND] The Septuagint: a builder's measuring line. Craftsmen used it for larger spaces. Zech. 2:1.

AND A MEASURING REED IN HIS HAND] Thus a reed (κάλαμος) is also taken in Rev. 11:1, and is called by apposition a measuring reed (κάλαμος μέτρον) in Rev. 21:15, in which way the measuring rod is also to be understood here from the Septuagint, which in those places was accustomed to be made from a reed. Its use is in exact dimensions. By both these instruments, however, it is signified that that angel will perform the office of a surveyor, and will exactly demonstrate all heights, lengths, and breadths.

Moreover, Osiander thinks that this temple signifies Christ primarily, yet also shadows forth the Church as the mystical body of Christ. We admit this latter point, that the Church is shadowed forth, but not the former; much less both. The steps by which one ascends, v. 6, progress in the knowledge of God; the chambers, in which the priests ought to put on their sacred vestments, v. 7, of the faithful, who put off the old man and put on the new, the Priesthood 1. Petr. 2, the vestibule of the gate, v. 9, the preparation of those who are about to perform the ministry of the Gospel; the breadth and height of the gate, that the gates of the world must be opened to Christ, the King of glory; the seat before the chambers, that some space must be granted to the ministers of the Church, so that they may rest from their labors and take breath, v. 12, the windows narrower on the inside, so that those who are in the room may see further and more broadly than those standing outside who desire to look into the room through the windows, signify that a more abundant knowledge of divine mysteries becomes the ministers of the Church, v. 16, the pavement paved with stone, the firm foundation of the faith of Christians, v. 17, the North gate, that even the Northern nations will arrive at the knowledge of Christ, v. 20, the windows, however, being similar, noted the same manner of entering into the kingdom of heaven, v. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ECCE VIR] Angelus, ut Apoc. 11, 1. Angeli viri vocantur, ubi ea specie apparent Daniel 10, 5. PLeriq; nostrates Demonstratorem hunc Eze- chielis, non esse angelum quendam creatum, sed Filium Dei statuunt: Namque non angelus, sed Christus est architectus Ecclesiæ suæ, Matth. 16, 18. Qui vir dicitur ob naturam bumanam; species enim ejus quasi æris lucidissimi. Confer Ezech. 1, 7. Quo tum puritas & Sanctitas ejus secundum naturam humanam, tum divina ejus natura purissima, san- ctissima, omni Chalybe, atque ære, & ferro mul- to durabilior exprimitur. Quod imprimis con- firmatur è loco simili Zach. 2, 1. ubi visus itidem in forma viri est Christus, habens in manu funiculum mensuræ, cujus etiam proprium hoc est, quod sit mensurator & judex in Ecclesia. Stateram enim ha- bet, & perticam, quibus omnia, minima, maxima metitur & distribuit vir ille, in porta domus Do- mini: Quia ille inspector & conservator est Do- mus Domini, & per eum solum ingressus patet; Joh. 14, 6. cap. 10, 9. Hieronymus ad cap. 47. Ezech. Vir ille, inquit, qui indutus erat בדים & du- ctor Prophetæ liquido pertransiit, peccatum non fecit, nec dolus inventus est in ore ejus.

CUJUS ERAT SPECIES QUASI SPECIES Æ- RIS] Fulgentis scilicet, quod hic Græci adjiciunt. Si- gnificatur & fortitudo & splendor Angelorum.

ET FUNICULUS LINEUS IN MANU EJUS] LXX. σπαρτίον οἰκοδόμων. Eo utebantur fabri ad majora spatia. Zach. 2, 1.

ET CALAMUS MENSURÆ IN MANU EJUS] Sic κάλαμος sumitur etiam Apoc. 15, 1. & vocatur per ap- positionem κάλαμος μέτρον Apoc. 21, 15. quomodo & hic à LXX. intelligenda pertica, quæ in illis locis fieri solebat ex calamo. Usus ejus in exactis dimensionibus. Utroque autem hoc instrumento significatur, illum angelum men- soris functurum officio, & omnes altitudines, longitudines & latitudines exacte demonstraturum.

Cæterum templum hoc imprimis Christum significare, Ecclesiam tamen etiam ceu corpus Christi mysticum adumbrare putat Osiander. Posterius hoc admittimus, quod Ecclesia adumbretur, non item prius; nedum utrumque. Gradus per quos ascenditur v. 6. profectus in agnitione Dei; thala- mi, in quibus Sacerdotes sacrum vestitum assumere debeant, v. 7. fidelium, veterem hominem exuen- tium, novum induentium, Sacerdotium 1. Petr. 2. vestibulum portæ v. 9. præparationem eorum, qui ministerioEvangelii functuri sunt; portæ latitudo & altitudo, aperiendas esse Regi gloriæ Christo por- tas mundi; Sedile ante thalamos, concedendum esse aliquod spatium ministris Ecclesiæ, ut à labori- bus requiescant, & respirent, v. 12. fenestræ intus an- gustiores, ut qui in conclavi sunt, longius & latius spiciant, quam, qui extra stantes per fenestras in conclave inspicere cupiunt, ministros Ecclesiæ co- piosiorem decere mysteriorum divinorum cogni- tionem significant, v. 16. pavimentum lapide stra- tum firmum fundamentum fidei Christianorum v. 17. porta Aquilonaris etiam Septentrionales gentes ad agnitionem Christi perventuras v. 20. fenestræ autem similes eandem rationem ingrediendi in re- gnum cœlorum v. 22. notabant.

## 40:43
Vers. 43. AND THE LIPS THEREOF A HANDBREADTH] Hooks or pegs from which the meat hung, as the Chaldean understands it here, and as we said at Psalm 67:14. Osiander rendered it thus: And the lips of those tables were of the breadth or height of a handbreadth, turned inward all around, that is, these four tables had edges or rims of the height of a handbreadth: so that none of the instruments could easily fall from the tables. But upon the tables (the remaining four) they placed the meat of the offering (already duly prepared). [These tables signify the ministry of the word of the Gospel. And they were placed in the four corners of the vestibule; because the Gospel (concerning Christ offered for us on the cross) was to be spread into the four parts of the world. But where the Gospel of Christ is sincerely preached, there the believers mortify the old Adam, and offer themselves as a sacrifice pleasing to God, Rom. 12. chap. For that mortification the Lord uses various instruments, that is, the cross and afflictions: which nevertheless are very salutary to the pious.]

Latin:

Vers. 43. ET LABIA EARUM PALMI UNIUS] Crema- thræ sive unici unde pendebant carnes, quomodo hic ac- cipit Chaldæus, & nos diximus ad Psalm, 67, 14. Osiander ita reddidit: Et labia earum mensa- rum erant latitudine seu altitudine palmæ unius, re- flexa intrinsecus per circuitum, id est, he quatuor mensæ habebant margines seu limbos altitudine pal- mi: ne quid instrumentorum facile de mensis cadere posset. Super mensas autem (reliquas quatuor) car- nes oblationis (jam rite præparatas) ponebant. [Hæ mensæ ministerium verbi Evangelii significant. Et positæ sunt in quatuor angulis vestibuli; quia Evange- lium (de Christo pro nobis in cruce oblato) divulgan- dum erat in quatuor partes orbis terrarum. Ubi autem Evangelion Christi sincere prædicatur, ibi cre- dentes mortificant veterem Adamum, & offerunt se- ipsos hostiam gratam Deo, Rom. 12. cap. Ad eam mortificationem utitur Dominus variis instrumentis, hoc est, cruce & afflictionibus: quæ tamen sunt piis admodum salutares.]

## 40:45
Ver. 45. THIS CHAMBER] More correctly the room, which faces the southern way, shall be for the Priests, who keep watch in the guards of the temple, i.e., who are prepared to serve the Lord in the temple, singing His praises. Such Singers are all the faithful Eph. 5. Col. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 45. HOC GAZOPHYLACIUM] Rectius cubiculum, quod respicit viam meridia- nam, Sacerdotum erit, qui excubant in custodiis templi h. e. qui parati sunt, ut serviant Domino in templo, decantantes ipsius laudes. Quales Can- tores sunt omnes fideles Eph. 5. Col. 3.

## 40:46
Ver. 46. THESE ARE THE SONS OF SADOC] You shall translate: These are of the sons of Sadoc, the chief Priests, of whom mention is made below 43, 19. 44, 15. 48, 11. namely, their assistants.

The posterity of the Priest Sadoc (who anointed Solomon as King) is destined above all Levitical families to sacrifice to the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 46. ISTI SUNT FILII SADOC] Vertes: Hi sunt fi- liorum Sadoc, præcipuorum Sacerdotum, quorum infra mentio 43, 19. 44, 15. 48, 11. adjutores scilicet.

Posteritas Sacerdotis Sadoc (qui unxit Salo- monem in Regem) præ omnibus Leviticis familiis destinata, ut Domino sacrificet.

## 41:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLI. The interior parts in the temple are described, the door, the walls, the windows, the Holy of Holies, the Cherubim, the wooden altar, the table & the entrances in the temple, & the sanctuary.

Latin:

CAPUT XLI. Interiora in templo describuntur, janua, pa- rietes, fenestræ, Sanctum Sanctorum, Cherubim, altare ligneum, mensa & ostia in templo, & sanctuario.

## 41:3
Ver. 3. AND HE WENT INWARD AND MEASURED THE FRONT TWO CUBITS, AND THE DOOR SIX CUBITS. In the Hebrew thus: the front of the door two cubits; that is, the door (through which the entrance lay into the Holy of Holies) had a front on both sides, & each front was of two cubits: these fronts stood out for the sake of ornament, so that the form of the door might be more elegant. But the Prophet describes the doors so often and so diligently, so that the door which leads into the kingdom of heaven may never be forgotten. Now Christ is that door. John 10.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET INTROGRESSUS INTRIN- SECUS MENSUS EST IN FRONTE DUOS CUBITOS, ET PORTAM SEX CUBITO- RUM. IN Ebræo ita: frontem portæ duos cubitos; id est porta (per quam ingressus patebat in Sanctum Sanctorum) utrinque habebat frontem, & quælibet frons erat duorum cubitorum: hæ frontes ornatus gratia prominebat, ut elegantior esset forma portæ. Toties autem & tam diligen- ter Propheta portas describit, ut nunquam obli- viscantur portæ, quæ ducit in regnum cœlorum. Christus autem est illud ostium. Joh. 10.

## 41:7
Ver. 7. AND THE SIDE-CHAMBER WAS ROUND ABOUT &c.

In the Hebrew: and the walkways, which were higher, were wider and surrounded (the temple.) Because the house was surrounded in the upper parts all around: (this is to be understood of only three sides of the house) because the house was wide in the upper part, (i.e., there was enough space in the upper part of the house, so that the upper walkways could be wider than the lower ones:) & thus one ascended from the lower to the higher places. [Next to those walkways, moreover, were rooms, in which those who performed the Ministry rested. For the Lord provides some lodging for the pious in the World, until they complete the course of their calling.] As Osiander has it here.

Latin:
