Vers. 7. ET PLATEA ERAT IN RO- TUNDUM &c.

In Ebr. & deambulatoria, quæ erant altiora, eo latiora & circumdabant (templum.) Quia circum- dabatur domus in superioribus partibus circumcirca: (hoc de tribus tantum lateribus domus est intelligen- dum) quia domus in superiori parte lata erat, (i. e. satis erat spatii in superiori parte domus, ut deambu- latoria superiora possent esse latiora, quam inferio- ra:) & sic ab inferioribus adscendebatur ad superio- ra loca. [Juxta illa autem deambulatoria erant cu- bicula, in quibus quiescebant, qui Ministerio funge- bantur. Dominus enim piis in Mundo hospitium ali- quod procurat, donec vocationis suæ cursum absolvat.] Ut hic habet Osiander.

## 41:8
Ver. 8. AND I SAW IN THE HOUSE THE HEIGHT ROUND ABOUT &c.

In the Hebrew: And I saw in the house the height, founded all around & the walkways, by the fullness of a reed, namely they were separated by six cubits, (that is, as regards height one walkway was distant from another by six cubits: for a full reed had six cubits.) But the width from the wall, to which the walkway was attached, to the extremity (of the walkway) was five cubits: (I think this was the lowest walkway: for thus it agrees with the building of the temple, which Solomon built, 2 Kings 6.) And what remained had rooms, which belonged to the house, (i.e., the walkway occupied five cubits: the remaining space belonged to the temple & its rooms.) & between the chambers there was a width of twenty cubits all around about the house: (i. e. between those chambers there was a space below in the temple of twenty cubits: for those chambers or rooms occupied no space of the lower temple. But the temple had twenty cubits in width; as Osiander again.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET VIDI IN DOMO ALTI- TUDINEM PER CIRCUITUM &c.

In Ebr. Et vidi in domo altitudinem, circum- quaq; fundata & ambulatoria, calami plenitudine, nempe sex cubitis distincta erant, (id est, quoad al- titudinem unum deambulatorium ab altero distabat sex cubitis: calamus enim plenus sex cubitos habe- bat.) Latitudo autem à pariete, cui adjunctum erat deambulatorium, ad extremitatem (deambulatorii) erat quinq; cubitorum: (hoc puto fuisse infimum de- ambulatorium: sic enim congruit cum ædificio tem- pli, quod Salomon ædificavit, 2. Reg. 6.) Et quod reliquum erat, habebat cubicula, quæ pertinebant ad domum, (i. e. deambulatorium occupabat quinq; cubitos: reliquum spatium ad templum & ejus cubi- cula pertinebat.) & inter gazophylacia erat latitudo viginti cubitorum circumquaq; circa domum: (i. e. in- ter illa conclavia erat spatium infra in templo viginti cubitorum: gazophylacia enim seu cubicula illa nul- lum inferioris templi spatium occupabant. Templum autem habebat in latitudine viginti cubitos; ut ite- rum Osiander.

## 41:13
Ver. 13. AND THAT WHICH WAS SEPARATED &c.

Osiander renders it thus: And the porch and its structure and its walls were one hundred cubits in length: (for such was the length of the walls, which surrounded the porch on both sides.) This amplitude of the temple signified that the Church of God is open to all who are truly penitent.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ET QUOD SEPARATUM E- RAT &c.

Osiander ita reddit: Et solarium & structura ejus & parietes ejus erant in longitudine centum cubi- torum: (tanta enim fuit parietum longitudo, qui utrinq; solarium cingebant.) Hæc amplitudo templi significabat, Ecclesiam Dei patere omnibus vere pœ- nitentibus.

## 41:16
Ver. 16. BUT THE GROUND EVEN TO THE WINDOWS &c.

In Hebrew: And (he measured how much space there was) from the ground even to the windows (namely) the windows covered from the door (vestibule) even to the inner house, and outside: and every wall round about inside and outside, by their measures: (i.e. Everything had its own certain measure, so that there was nothing that was not excellently arranged.) For although in the Church many things seem to our eyes to be confused or fortuitous: yet before God individual things are so ordered and measured, that He even has the hairs of our head numbered, Matt. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 16. TERRA AUTEM USQUE AD FENESTRAS &c.

In Ebr. Et (mensus est, quantum spatii es- set) à terra usq; ad fenestras (nimirum) fenestras con- tectas ab ostio (vestibulo) usq; ad domum interiorem, & extra: & omnem parietem circumcirca interiùs & exteriùs, suis mensuris: (i. e. Omnia habebant certam suam mensuram, ut nihil non esset optime dis- positum.) Etsi enim in Ecclesia multa videntur co- ram oculis nostris esse confusa aut fortuita: tamen coram Deo ita singula sunt ordinata & mensurata, ut etiam capillos capitis nostri in numerato habeat Matth. 10.]

## 41:18
Ver. 18. AND HAD TWO FACES CHERUB] Two forms which were most prominent. For otherwise there were four forms in each Cherub.

Concerning the signification of the Cherubim, Osiander says thus: The angelic forms signify the ministers of the Church: for these are often called angelic in Scripture. It behooves them to be most humane toward the flock committed to them (especially toward troubled consciences), but against Heretics and Tyrants to be endowed with a most brave and clearly leonine spirit: so that they may in no way allow themselves to be deterred from professing the truth of the word of God. And those who are such will obtain the palm, that is, a glorious victory. Therefore, the crown of righteousness is laid up for them, as Paul says 2 Tim. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DUASQUE FACIES HABEBAT CHE- RUB] Duas formas quæ maxime eminebant. Erant enim alioqui in quoque Cherub formæ quatuor.

De significatione Cherubim Osiander ita: Formæ Angelicæ ministros Ecclesiæ significant: Hi e- nim in Scriptura sæpe Angelici vocantur. Hos oportet er- ga gregem sibi commissum (præsertim erga consterna- tas conscientias) esse humanissimos, adversus vero Hæ- reticos, Tyrannos fortissimo & plane leonino animo præditos: ut à veritate verbi Dei profitenda deter- reri sese nequaquam patiantur. Et qui tales sunt, palmam, hoc est, præclaram victoriam, obtinebunt. Itaq; reposita est illis corona justitiæ, ut Paulus ait 2. Tim. 3.]

## 41:22
Ver. 22.

AND HE SPOKE TO ME] Transferred, that is, to that part where the table was, on which were the loaves of the showbread.

That table stood before the Lord, so that the censer might be placed upon it and the sacred incense burned before the Lord. The altar, however, signified Christ, because of whom our prayers are heard and praises are acceptable to God, Heb. 13:10. There is nothing acceptable to God except Christ the son, the altar.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

ET LOCUTUS EST AD ME] Translatum sci- licet in eam partem, ubi erat mensa, in qua panes προ- θέσεως.

Mensa illa stabat coram Domino, ut in ea poneretur thuribulum atq; adoleretur coram Do- mino thymiama sacrum. Altare autem significa- bat Christum, propterquem audiuntur preces nostræ & laudes Deo sunt gratæ Ebr. 13, 10. Nul- la est grata Deo nisi Christus filius ara.

## 41:25
Ver. 25.

WHEREFORE ALSO THE TIMBERS WERE THICKER &c.

In Hebrew: And the timber was thick toward the porch on the outside: (i.e., a bar of great strength closed the doors from the outside: so that no one could break the doors by force.) [For the Church of Christ is impregnable, Rom. 8.] And the windows were narrow (in the temple) [For we know in part in this life, and we prophesy in part, 1 Cor. 13. i.e., The knowledge of God in this life is not entirely perfect.] And palms were carved here and there on the sides of the vestibule: and on the sides of the house (of the Lord) and on the beams. [For the whole Church of Christ obtains certain victory against Satan.] as Osiander explains these.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

QUAMOBREM ET GROSSIORA E- RANT LIGNA &c.

In Ebræo: Et densum lignum erat versus porticum extrinsecus : (i. e. Vectis magnæ firmitatis extrinsecus claudebat ostia : ne quis vi fores effringe- re posset.) [Est enim Ecclesia Christi inexpugnabilis Rom. 8.] Et fenestræ angustæ erant (in templo) [Ex parte enim in hac vita cognoscimus, & ex parte pro- phetamus 1. Cor. 13. i. e. Agnitio Dei in hac vita non est omnino perfecta.] Et palmæ erant sculptæ hinc & hinc in lateribus vestibuli : & in lateribus domus (Do- mini) & in trabibus. [Tota enim Ecclesia Christi certam victoriam adversus Satanam obtinet.] uti hæc explicat Osiander.

## 42:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLII. Concerning the treasuries, and other things pertaining to sacred use, to be built.

Latin:

CAPUT XLII. De Gazophylaciis, cæterisq; quæ ad sacrum usum pertinent, ædificandis.

## 42:5
Ver. 5.

WHERE THE TREASURIES WERE LOWER IN THE UPPER PARTS] The Rabbis Solomon and David Kimchi say these verses and the two following are of difficult interpretation. Something may be corrupt in the reading. But see Villalpandus.

Grotius could show no trace of corruption, and yet he boldly pronounces or suspects: something may be corrupt in the reading. He is so well-fed and prepared to disparage the integrity of the authentic text that where the Rabbis only complain of a difficulty, he easily dreams of corruption. Osiander amends the Vulgate version from the Hebrew thus: And the upper chambers were narrower: because the supports projected more than the lowest and middle parts of that building: for those (chambers) were triple and did not (however) have such columns as were in the courts: and therefore they were distinct from the lowest and middle ones, from the ground: (i. e. the upper chambers were narrower than the lowest: because the supports occupied a certain part, which sustained the walkways, by which one could reach the middle and highest chambers: for there were three rows of chambers placed one above the other.] And he explains the following two verses, v. 7, 8, thus: And the outer enclosure according to the treasuries: which were in the way of the outer court before the treasuries: which were in the way of the outer court before the treasuries, its length was fifty cubits. Heb. and the outer wall, which was next to the treasuries, toward the outer court, before the treasuries (or chambers) had in length fifty cubits. Because the length of the chambers, towards the space of the outer court, was fifty cubits: but there were two such rows of chambers: and [the length] before the face of the temple (the space between the Temple and the chambers) was one hundred cubits, as was also said a little before. In these chambers, however, were to be stored the things necessary for the preservation and exercises of divine worship. [By these buildings, therefore, it was signified that the Lord would provide those things which are necessary for preserving the ministry of the Gospel.]

Latin:

Vers. 5.

UBI ERANT GAZOPHTLACIA IN SUPERIO- RIBUS HUMILIORA] Hæc commata & duo sequentia difficilis esse interpretationis ajunt Rabbini Salomo & Da- vid Kimchi. Potest aliquid corruptum esse in lectione. Sed vide Villalpandum.

NUllum monstrare potuit Grotius vestigium corruptionis, & tamen audacter pronun- ciat vel suspicatur : potest aliquid corruptum esse in lectione. Tam pransus & paratus est ad derogan- dum integritati textus authentici, ut ubi de diffi- cultate vel queruntur solum Rabbini, corruptio- nem facile somniet. Osiander versionem vulgatam ita emendat exEbræo: Et cubicula superiora angustio- ra erant : quia fulcra prominebant præ infimis & me- diis illius ædificii : triplicia enim erant illa (cubicula) & non (tamen) tales habebant columnas, quales e- rant in atriis : ideoq; distincta erant ab infimis & a mediis, à terra : (i. e. superiora cubicula angustiora e- rant,quam infima : quia fulcra quandam partem occu- pabant,quæ sustinebant deambulatoria,quibus ad me- dia & summa cubicula perveniri poterat : tres enim fuerunt cubiculorum ordines sibi invicem superimposi- ti.] Et sequentia duo commata v. 7. 8. ita expli- cat : Et peribolus exterior secundum gazophyla- cia : quæ erant in via atrii exterioris ante gazo- phylacia : quæ erant in via atrii exterioris ante gazophylacia, longitudo ejus quinquaginta cu- bitorum. Hebr. & murus exterior, qui erat juxta gazophylacia, versus atrium exterius, coram gazo- phylaciis (seu cubiculis) habebat in longitudine quin- quaginta cubitos. Quia longitudo erat gazophy- laciorum, versus spatium atrii exterioris,quinqua- ginta cubitorum : duo autem erant tales ordines ga- zophylaciorum : & [longitudo] ante faciem tem- pli (spatium inter Templum gazophylacia) fuit cen- tum cubitorum, ut paulo ante etiam dictum est. In his autem gazophylaciis reponenda erant necessaria ad conservationem & exercitia cultus divini. [His itaq; ædificiis significabatur, Dominum subministra- turum ea, quæ ad conservandum ministerium Evange- lii sunt necessaria.]

## 42:13
Verse 13. WHO APPROACH THE LORD IN THE HOLY OF HOLIES;

In the Hebrew: When they offer most holy sacrifices to the Lord: when they shall eat the remains of those most holy sacrifices in those sacred chambers.) [But just as the priests also used to eat of the same sacrifice by which God was appeased: so Christians (who are all priests before God) eat the same Christ, who on the altar of the cross was a sacrifice for the expiation of the sins of the world, in the Supper of the Lord: in memory of his passion, and that they may be preserved in a new spiritual life; but Christ is eaten in a holy place: that is, let us not approach the Supper of the Lord with a profane and impenitent heart.]

Latin:

Vers. 13. QUI APPROPINQVANT AD DOMI- NUM IN SANCTA SANCTORUM;

In Hebræo: Quando offerunt Domino sanctissi- ma sacrificia: cum reliquias illorum sanctissimo- rum sacrificiorum comedent in cubiculis illis sacratis.) [Ut autem de eodem sacrificio, quo placabatur De- us, comedebant etiam sacerdotes: ita Christiani (qui omnes sunt coram Deo sacerdotes) eundem Christum, qui in ara crucis fuit sacrificium pro expiandis Mun- di peccatis,in Cœna Domini comedunt: in memoriam passionis ejus, & ut in nova spirituali vita conserven- tur; Comeditur autem Christus in loco sancto: hoc est non accedamus ad Cœnam Domini prophano & impœnitenti corde.]

## 42:20
Verse 20. DIVIDING BETWEEN THE SANCTUARY AND THE PLACE OF THE COMMON PEOPLE.

In the Hebrew: To divide between the holy and the profane, i.e., this wall distinguished the holy place for the people of God from the external non-holy space. [Moreover, the great amplitude of the outer court (in which the people were to assemble) signified that the way to Christ the Savior is open to all believers, in whatever region of the world they may dwell. And the distinction of the holy from the profane shows that all men who are outside the Church of God are profane and abominable to God, however much they may excel in learning, wisdom, or virtue, or power.]

Latin:

Vers. 20. DIVIDENTEM INTER SANCTUA- RIUM ET VULGI LOCUM.

In Ebr. Ad dividendum inter sanctum & pro- phanum, i. e. hic murus distinxit sanctum locum pro populo Dei ab externo spatio non sancto. [Cæterum tanta atrii exterioris, (in quo populus convenire de- bebat) amplitudo significabat, omnibus credentibus patere aditum ad Christum Salvatorem, in quacunq; mundi plaga habitent. Et distinctio sancti à pro- phano ostendit omnes homines, qui sunt extra Ec- clesiam Dei, esse prophanos & Deo abominabiles, quantacunq; eruditione, sapientia, aut virtute, po tentiave polleant.]

## 43:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLIII. While the glory of the Lord is appearing, the Prophet hears that the children of Israel will no longer pollute the name of the Lord: and what the measurements of the altar are, and the sacrifices, concerning which laws are prescribed.

Latin:

CAPUT XLIII. Gloria Domini apparente audit Propheta, quod filii Israel amplius nomen Domini non polluent: & quæ sint mensuræ altaris, ac sacrificia, de quibus præscribuntur leges.

## 43:2
Verse 2. AND BEHOLD THE GLORY OF THE GOD OF ISRAEL WAS GOING FORTH BY THE WAY OF THE EAST]

Just as it had once gone forth from the Temple, deserting the Temple, chap. 10. So it was to be that it would return to the Temple, that is, it would again have that seat accepted, and the sacred things, and would show its protection to them.

Osiander gives this meaning: Through that Eastern gate entering in his Triumphal chariot, Christ to be incarnate in great Majesty (such a vision as I had also seen some years before). For Jesus Christ is the true God of Israel, that is, of all who believe in his Gospel.] Cf. what is above concerning the vision at the river Chebar. Therefore, verse 7, the Son of God promises his presence and gracious governance to the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET ECCE GLORIA DEI ISRAEL EGREDIE- BATUR PER VIAM ORIENTALEM]

Sicut exierat o- lim ex Templo, Templum deserens cap. 10. Ita futurum erat in Templum rediret, id est, rursus acceptam haberet eam sedem, ac sacra, iisque suam tutelam exhiberet.

Osiander hanc reddit significationem: Per portam illam Orientalem ingredientem in cur- ru suo Triumphali, Christum incarnandum in ma- gna Majestate (qualem visionem etiam ante aliquot annos videram.) Est enim Jesus Christus verus Deus Israelis, hoc est,omnium Evangelio ipsius credentium.] Conf. quæ supra de visione ad fluvium Chobar. Ideo vers. 7. promittit Filius Dei Ecclesiæ præ- sentiam suam & gubernationem gratiosam.

## 43:12
Verse 12. THIS IS THE LAW OF THE HOUSE. &c.

This will be the condition of this house of God, that the whole of it on every side, as far as the mountain extends, and as far as its boundaries reach, the whole of it shall be held most holy, as if it were the innermost part of the Temple. [For the whole true Church of Christ is sanctified by the blood of Christ through faith: so that God may dwell in it. Therefore, let it also study holiness, purity, and piety from every side (in the whole conversation of its life): let it be seen to be holy on every side. But this last thing will finally be perfected in the other century.]

Latin:

Vers. 12. ISTA EST LEX DOMUS. &c.

Hæc erit hujus domus Dei conditio, ut tota un- diquaq; quatenus mons patet, & quousq; pertingunt ejus termini,id totum habeatur sanctissimum, ac si es- set intima pars Templi. [Tota enim Christi vera Ecclesia sanguine Christi per fidem est sanctificata: ut Deus in ea habitet. Itaq; etiam ex omni parte (in tota vitæ suæ conversatione) sanctitati, puritati & pietati studeat: undiquaque sancta conspiciatur. Hoc vero postremum in altero seculo demum perficie- tur.]

## 43:13
Verse 13. BUT THESE ARE THE MEASUREMENTS OF THE ALTAR.

Namely of the burnt offerings, which was in the court of the Priests. The things which follow are translated partly badly, partly too obscurely. In the cubit most truly, which had a cubit and a palm, in its bosom was a cubit, and a cubit in breadth, and its boundary up to its lip round about was one palm: this also was the trench of the altar. And from the bosom of the earth up to the lowest ledge were two cubits, the breadth of one cubit, and from the lesser ledge up to the greater ledge four cubits and the breadth of one cubit. The Ariel itself was of four cubits, and from the Ariel up to the top were four horns. And the Ariel was of twelve cubits in length by twelve cubits in breadth: foursquare with equal sides. And the ledge was of fourteen cubits in length, by fourteen cubits in breadth, at its four corners; and the border round about it was half a cubit: and its bosom was one cubit round about: and its steps were turned toward the East. In Hebrew: One must take such cubits (in measure), each of which exceeds the common cubit by the breadth of one palm. And the base (of the altar) was (in height) one cubit, and in breadth one cubit, and it reached to its lip, which was round about one palm: and this was the projection of the altar. (The altar had many ledges, up to the top leaf; just as one offsets a building with beautiful molding: where some moldings go around the outside, and some are elegantly recessed inward.) And from the base, which was placed on the ground up to the lower support were two cubits, and the breadth of one cubit: (A broad, thick molding went around again:) and from that lesser support up to the greater, there were four cubits, and (that upper support) also had a cubit in breadth. And thus the Harel (i.e., the altar on that part was of four cubits) in height: And from the Ariel (i.e. from the altar) upward stood out four horns (or small columns, which for the sake of ornament were at the four top corners: just as we are accustomed to place skillfully crafted apples or globes.) And the Ariel (around the top part, yet not entirely at the summit:) was of twelve cubits in length, and twelve cubits in breadth, and the altar was square. And the top of the altar (which was to support the sacrifices and the fire) had fourteen cubits in length, and fourteen cubits in breadth, and was entirely square. And a certain border surrounded the altar (on the top surface) which was of half a cubit (in height, prepared for this purpose, so that nothing might fall off, either from the sacrifices or from the fire.) And the base (the lowest, of which it was spoken a little before) had a cubit in circuit (whether you look at the height or the breadth; this is a brief and customary repetition.) And its steps were toward the East: (by these steps the Priests ascended to the altar. How those steps were formed, and how they adhered to the altar, so that they would not nevertheless deform the rest of the altar's structure, Scripture does not express. There is no doubt, however, that they adhered to the rest of the building skillfully and elegantly. I think, however, that the words Harel and Ariel are to be taken in one and the same meaning. For the Prophets sometimes omit one letter. But Ariel signifies the Lion of God. And the Prophet Isaiah calls the city of Jerusalem by this name, chap. 29. & the altar of burnt offerings by this name: because the city was unconquered, like a divine lion, as long as sincere religion stood.) [But the altar denoted Christ, by whose (the Lion of the tribe of Judah) victory we also are unconquered against death, the Devil, and hell, if we have applied to ourselves by true faith the sacrifice of Christ performed on the cross. The four small columns at the four corners signified: the Gospel about Christ immolated for us to be propagated into the four parts of the world. For Christ was denoted not only by the sacrifices, but also by the altar itself; because our spiritual sacrifices (such as prayers, mortification of the flesh, alms) are not acceptable to God unless we rely by faith on Christ the Savior: for on his account we, together with our new obedience, are accepted by God. Moreover, such a great mass and artificial structure of the altar (which not only had elegance, but also provided firmness) signified that the Gospel about Christ crucified could not be extirpated by any human power.] All of which are contained in the Osiandrian Paraphrase.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ISTÆ AUTEM SUNT MENSURÆ ALTARIS.

Holocaustorum nempe, quod erat in atrio Sacerdotum. Quæ sequuntur, partim male, par- tim nimis obscure sunt conversa. In cubito verissi- mo, qui habebat cubitum & palmum, in sinu ejus erat cubitus, & cubitus in latitudine, & definitio ejus usque ad labium ejus in circuitu palmus unus: hæc quoque erat fossa altaris. Et de sinu terræ usq; ad crepidinem novissimam duo cubiti, latitudo cu- biti unius, & à crepidine minore usque ad crepi- dinem majorem quatuor cubiti & latitudo cubiti unius. Ipse autem Ariel quatuor cubitorum, & ab Ariel usque ad sursum cornua quatuor. Et Ariel duodecim cubitorum in longitudine per duode- cim cubitos latitudinis: quadrangulatum æquis lateribus. Et crepido quatuordecim cubitorum longitudinis, per quatuordecim cubitos latitudi- nis, in quatuor angulis ejus; & corona in circuitu ejus dimidii cubiti: & sinus ejus unius cubiti per circuitum: gradus autem ejus versi ad Orientem. Hebraice: Ejusmodi autem cubitos (in mensura) accipere oportet, quorum quisq́ vulgarem cubitum latitudine unius palmi excedat. Et basis (altaris) fuit (altitudine) unius cubiti, & latitudine unius cu- biti, & pertinebat ad labium ejus, quod erat cir- cumcirca unius palmi: & hæc fuit prominentia al- taris. (Es hat der Altar viel Absätze gehabt, biß an das oberste Blatt; gleich wie man mit schönem Gesimbs ein Gebäu absetzt: da etliche Gesimbs aussen herumb gehen, etliche einwarts zierlich ver- tieffet seyn.) Et à basi, quæ terræ imposita erat usq́ ad fulcrum inferius erant duo cubiti, & latitudo unius cubiti: (Es ist wiederumb ein breit dick Leisten- werck herumb gangen:) & à fulcro illo minore usq́ ad majus, erant quatuor cubiti, & (illud superius fulcrum) habebat etiam cubitum in latitudine. Et sic Harel (i.e. altare ea parte erat quatuor cubitorum) in altitudine: Et ab Ariel (i.e. ab altari) sursum emi- nebant quatuor cornua (seu columnulæ, quæ ornatus gratia in quatuor angulis supremis erant: quemad- modum nos poma scite fabrefacta aut globos impone- re solemus.) Et Ariel (circa supremam partem, non tamen omnino in summo:) erat duodecim cubitorum in longitudine, & duodecim cubitorum in latitudine, eratq́ altare quadratum. Et supremum altaris (quod sacrificia & ignem sustinere debebat) quatuor- decim cubitos habebat in longitudine, & quatuorde- cim cubitos in latitudine, eratq́ omnino quadra- tum. Et corona quædam circumdabat altare (in suprema superficie) quæ erat dimidii cubiti (altitudi- ne, in eum usum parata, ne quid vel de sacrificiis, vel de igne decideret.) Et basis (infima, de qua paulo ante dictum est) habebat cubitum in circuitu (sive altitudinem sive latitudinem spectares; hæc est brevis & usitata repetitio.) Et gradus ejus erant versus Orientem: (per hos gradus adscendebant Sacerdotes ad altare. Quomodo autem illi gradus formati fue- rint, & quomodo altari adhæserint, ut nihilo minus reliquam altaris structuram non deformarent, Scri- ptura non exprimit. Non tamen dubium est, quin scite & eleganter reliquo ædificio adhæserint. Puto autem vocabula Harel & Ariel in una & eadem significatione accipienda. Prophetæ enim interdum omittunt unam literam. Ariel autem Leonem Dei si- gnificat. Et Propheta Isaias urbem Jerusalem, cap. 29. & altare holocaustorum hoc vocabulo appellat: propterea quod invicta erat urbs, tanquam divinus leo, quamdiu syncera religio constabat.) [Altare autem Christum denotabat, cujus (Leonis de tribu Juda) victoria etiam nos invicti sumus adversus mor- tem, Diabolum, & infernum, si sacrificium Christi in cruce peractum, vera fide nobis applicuerimus. Quatuor columnulæ in quatuor angulis significabant: Evangelion de Christo pro nobis immolato propagan- dum in quatuor orbis partes. Christus enim non tan- tum per sacrificia, sed etiam per ipsum altare denota- bantur; quia nostra sacrificia spiritualia (ut sunt preces, mortificatio carnis, eleemosynae) non sunt Deo grata, nisi fide innitamur Christo Salvatori: propter ipsum enim nos una cum nova nostra obedientia Deo sumus accepti. Tanta autem altaris moles & arti- ficiosa structura (quae non mo elegantiom habebat, sed etiam firmitatem praebebat) significabat Evange- lion de Christo crucifixo, nulla potentia humana ex- tirpari posse.] Quae omnia habentur in Paraphrasi Osiandrina.

## 43:15
Ver. 15.

BUT THE ARIEL ITSELF] See the things said in Isaiah 29, ver. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

IPSE AUTEM ARIEL] Vide dicta Esaiae 29. vers. 1.

## 43:19
Ver. 19.

AND YOU SHALL GIVE THE PRIESTS AND THE LEVITES, WHO ARE OF THE SEED OF ZADOK, WHO APPROACH UNTO ME, SAITH THE LORD, TO OFFER ME A BULLOCK FROM THE HERD FOR SIN] In the Hebrew it is, To the Priests the Levites: that is, who are of the Levitical race, the legitimate Priests. Nor otherwise the LXX and the Chaldean. Whence it can be believed that there is here a scribe's error in the Latin. All these things were done in a vision, so that the rites commanded in Exod. 24, Levit. 28 might be the more retained in their minds. For Ezekiel here takes the role of a private person. The Rabbis foolishly say that Ezekiel will do this after the first resurrection in the third temple.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ET DABIS SACERDOTES ET LEVITAS, QUI SUNT DE SEMINE SADOC, QUI ACCE- DUNT AD ME, AIT DOMINUS, UT OFFERANT MIHI VITULUM DE ARMENTO PRO PECCATO] In Hebraeo est, Sacerdotibus Levitis: id est, qui ex Levitico sunt genere, legitimis Sacerdotibus. Nec aliter LXX. & Chaldaeus. Unde credi potest, hic vitium esse scribae in Latino. Omnia haec facta sunt ἐν ὀπτασίᾳ, quo magis animis retinerentur ritus praecepti Exod. 24. Levit. 28. Nam Ezechiel hic refert personam ἰδιώτε. Rabbini inepte Ezechielem hoc facturum ajunt post resurrectio- nem primam in templo tertio.

## 44:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLIV.

The gate of the Sanctuary closed, which the Lord alone enters: the uncircumcised in heart shall not enter the sanctuary, nor the Levites who have followed idols. But these shall be ministers of the house: but the Priests shall enter, and the laws of these are set forth.

Latin:

CAPUT XLIV.

Porta Sanctuarii clausa, quam solus Domi- nus ingreditur: incircumcisi corde non ingredientur sanctuarium, nec Levitae, qui idola sequuti sunt. Sed hi ministri domus erunt: Sacerdotes autem ingre- dientur, & horum leges ponuntur.

## 44:2
Verse 2.

THIS GATE SHALL BE SHUT, IT SHALL NOT BE OPENED] Here follow the precepts which God gives to be observed after the restoration of the temple. BECAUSE THE LORD GOD HATH ENTERED IN BY IT] That is, that image representing the judgments of God above 43, 2. By it, that is, in that place in the vision. AND IT SHALL BE SHUT FOR THE PRINCE] Even for the prince or Ethnarch of the Jews.

The Doctors of the Church wish to be shadowed forth by this gate, shut to all except the Prince, through which God entered, the Θεοτόκε womb, of which the Church also sings in the Hymn concerning the virgin mother of God: The gate becomes passable for Christ, filled with grace, and the King passes through and remains, shut as it was for ages. Therefore they say it is shut to the people, not to the priest, or the prince, who represented the person of Christ. St. Augustine, sermon 2 on the Nativity. The shut gate is the seal of modesty, the integrity of immaculate flesh. For she was not violated by the birth, who was rather sanctified by the conception. Compare Ambrose, book on the Institution of Virgins, chapter 8. Rufinus in the exposition of the Creed.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

PORTA HAEC CLAUSA ERIT, NON APE- RIETUR] Hic sequuntur praecepta, quae Deus dat obser- vanda post templi restitutionem. QUONIAM DOMINUS DEUS INGRESSUS EST PER EAM] Id est, imago illa judicia Dei reprae- sentans supra 43, 2. Per eam, id est, eo loco in visione. ERITQUE CLAUSA PRINCIPI] Etiam principi sive Ethnarchae Judaeorum.

Doctores Ecclesiae per portam hanc omnibus clausam, praeterquam Principi, per quam Deus ingressus, adumbratum volunt Θεοτόκε ute- rum, de quo etiam Ecclesia canit in Hymno de matre Dei virgine: Fit porta Christi pervia, refer- ta plena gratia, transitque Rex & permanet, clausa ut fuit per secula. Ideo clausam populo dicunt, non sacerdoti, aut principi, qui Christi personam referebant. S. Augustinus serm. 2. de nativit. Por- ta clausa est signaculum pudoris, immaculatae carnis integritas. Non enim violata est partu, quae ma- gis est sanctificata conceptione. Confer Ambros. lib. de Institution. Virg. cap. 8. Ruffin. in exposi- tione Symb.

## 44:10
Verse 10.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

## 44:11
THEY SHALL BE IN MY SANCTUARY AS MINISTERS] They shall be thrust down to the lower ministries.

Latin:

ERUNT IN SANCTUARIO MEO AEDITUI] Ad inferiora ministeria detrudentur.

## 44:22
Verse 22.

AND THEY SHALL NOT TAKE A WIDOW OR A DIVORCED WOMAN AS WIVES] See what we have said at Leviticus 21, verse 14.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

ET VIDUAM ET REPUDIATAM NON AC- CIPIENT UXORES] Vide quae diximus ad, Levit. 21. vers. 14.

## 45:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLV.

In the division of the land, with the firstfruits of the Lord separated, a certain portion is to be assigned to the Priests, the Le-

of the vines, the cities, and the Prince, equity is to be observed in weights, measures, first fruits, and sacrifices, which sacrifices shall be offered on the first and seventh day of the first month, and in the solemnities of the Passover and of Tabernacles.

Latin:

CAPUT XLV.

In terrae divisione separatis Domini primitiis assignanda certa portio Sacerdotibus, Le-

vitis, civitatibus, ac Principi, servandag æquitas in ponderibus, mensuris, primitiis & sacrificiis, quæ sacrificia offerentur primo ac septimo die primi mensis, & in solemnitatibus Paschæ, ac Tabernaculorum.

## 45:7
Verse 7. ALSO TO THE PRINCE, etc.

Osiander interpreted these things thus: Also to the Prince, (a space of land shall be given:) on this side and on that: (so that the Temple and the city may be contained within the possession of the Prince:) and let it look (one part of his possession) toward the territory of the sanctuary: and the other toward the city: from the Western corner indeed let it be extended (the possession of the Prince) toward the west: but from the Eastern corner let it be extended (the possession of the Prince) toward the East: and let the length according to each of the aforementioned parts (namely of the Temple and of the city) be extended from the Western boundary even to the Eastern boundary: (Thus the possession of the Prince encompassed on every side, from all sides, the Temple and the city together. For toward the West and the East he had possessions: then from the left side of the Temple and the city his possession reached from the West to the East: so also from the right side of the city and the Temple his possession reached from the West even to the East. Thus the Temple and the city were surrounded by the possessions of the prince.) [For the possession of the Prince of peace, our Lord Jesus Christ, is by far the most ample: since all power has been given to him in heaven and on earth, Matt. 28. He also surrounds and protects his Church on every side.]

Latin:

Vers. 7. PRINCIPI QUOQUE &c.

HÆc ita interpretatus est Osiander: Principi quoq́;, (spatium terræ dabitur:) hinc & hinc: (ita ut Templum & urbs contineantur inter possessionem Principis:) & respiciat (una ejus possessionis pars) versus territorium sanctuarii: & altera versus urbem: ab angulo quidem Occidentali protendatur (Principis possessio) versus occidentem: ab angulo vero Orientali protendatur (Principis possessio) versus Orientem: & longitudo juxta unamquamque supradictarum partium (Templi scilicet & urbis) protendatur à Termino Occidentali usq́; ad terminum Orientalem: (Sic principis possessio complexa est undiquaq́; ab omnibus lateribus, Templum & urbem simul. Versus Occidentem enim & Orientem habuit possessiones: deinde à sinistro latere Templi & urbis pertingebat ejus possessio ab Occidente in Orientem: sic etiam à dextra parte urbis & Templi pertingebat ejus possessio ab Occidente usque ad Orientem. Ita Templum & urbs possessionibus principis circumdabantur.) [Est enim possessio Principis pacis, Domini nostri Jesu Christi, longe amplissima: quippe cui data est omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, Matth. 28. Is etiam undiquaq́; suam Ecclesiam circumdat & tuetur.]

## 45:17
Verse 17. HE SHALL MAKE A SACRIFICE FOR SIN, etc.

In the Hebrew: He himself shall offer a sacrifice for expiating sin, and a meat offering, and a burnt offering, and peace offerings to reconcile the house of Israel (to God). [Although priests (not princes) were accustomed to sacrifice: yet the Holy Spirit in this place speaks thus of set purpose: so that he might signify that our Prince Jesus Christ would be a Priest, who would perform all the duties of a Priest, and fulfill all the requirements of the high Priest: so that he might reconcile us to the heavenly Father.]

Latin:

Vers. 17. IPSE FACIET PRO PECCATO SACRIFICIUM &c.

In Ebræo: Ipse offeret sacrificium pro peccato expiando, & sacrificium cibarium, & holocaustum & tributoria ad reconciliandam (Deo) domum Israël. [Etsi autem Sacerdotes (non principes) sacrificare solebant: tamen Spiritus Sanctus hoc loco data opera sic loquitur: ut significet, quod Princeps noster Jesus Christus futurus esset Sacerdos, qui omnia Sacerdotis officia obiret, omnesq́; numeros summi Pontificis impleret: ut nos Patri cœlesti placaret.]

## 45:18
Verse 18. IN THE FIRST MONTH, ON THE FIRST OF THE MONTH, YOU SHALL TAKE A BULLOCK FROM THE HERD]

This is commanded to the Prince, as the preceding things show. The Rabbis refer this also to Ezekiel, who is to do this after the first resurrection.

Those Rabbinical commentaries are not worthy of being refuted.

Latin:

Vers. 18. IN PRIMO MENSE UNA MENSIS SUMET VITULUM DE ARMENTO]

Principi hoc præcipitur, ut præcedentia ostendunt. Rabbini & hoc ad Ezechielem referunt, qui id facturus sit post primam resurrectionem.

Commenta illa Rabbinica digna non sunt, quæ confutentur.

## 45:20
Verse 20. FOR EVERY ONE WHO HAS SINNED THROUGH IGNORANCE, etc.

In the Hebrew: And you shall expiate the house, just as a man is accustomed to be expiated who has sinned through ignorance or imprudence: and you shall expiate for the house: that is, thus you shall consecrate the Temple. [The Lord commands the Sanctuary (which was a type of the Church) to be expiated, as if it had been contaminated by some sin: so that he might signify that the Church had to be cleansed by the blood of Christ, who cleanses us from all iniquity, 1 John 1. And we are daily expiated and cleansed, when (doing penance) we sprinkle our hearts through faith with the blood of Christ.] These are Osiander's words. The rest is already clear from Leviticus, namely what those things foreshadowed.

Latin:

Vers. 20. PRO UNOQUOQUE QUI IGNORAVIT &c.

In Ebræo: Et expiabitis domum, quasi vir expiari solet, qui per ignorantiam aut imprudentiam peccavit: & expiabitis pro domo: id est, sic consecrabitis Templum. [Jubet autem Dominus Sanctuarium (quod erat typus Ecclesiæ) expiari, quasi peccato aliquo fuisset contaminatum: ut significaret, Ecclesiam fuisse emundandam Christi sanguine, qui emundat nos ab omni iniquitate, 1. Johan. 1. Et quotidie expiamur & emundamur, cum (pœnitentiam agentes) per fidem corda nostra sanguine Christi aspergimus.] Hæc Osiander. Cætera è Levitico jam constant, quidnam scilicet ea adumbrarint.

## 46:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLVI.

The gate of the sun to be opened on Sabbaths and New Moons, and what burnt offerings the Prince shall offer on these days, and by which gate he himself or the people shall enter or leave the temple: concerning the voluntary and daily burnt offering of the prince; the places in which the Priests shall cook the sacrifices, and the ministers the victims of the people.

Latin:

CAPUT XLVI.

Porta solis Sabbatis, ac Calendis aperienda, & quæ holocausta his diebus offeret Prin- ceps, quave porta ipse aut populus templum ingredietur vel egredietur: de spontaneo, & quotidiano principis holocausto; loca in quibus Sacerdotes coquant sacrificia, & ministri victimas populi.

## 46:15
Vers. 15. THE CONTINUAL BURNT OFFERING.

That which is always in use. [But it is always sacrificed when the Gospel concerning Christ crucified is preached until the end of the world, and his memory is preserved by the communion of his body and blood in the Lord's Supper. The Papists are ridiculous, who attempt to establish the sacrifice of the Mass from similar passages: just as if the shadows of the Old Testament were to be brought back into the light of the Gospel of Christ.]

Latin:

Vers. 15. HOLOCAUSTUM SEMPITERNUM.

Quod semper sit in usu. [Tum autem semper sacrificatur, cum Evangelion de Christo crucifixo ad finem Mundi usq; prædicatur, & memoria ejus, communicatione corporis & sanguinis ejus in Cœna Domini, conservatur. Ridiculi sunt autem Papi- stæ, qui ex similibus locis sacrificium Missæ stabilire conantur: perinde ac si umbræ veteris Testamenti in lucem Evangelii Christi essent reducendæ.]

## 46:17
Vers. 17. BUT IF HE SHALL GIVE A LEGACY]

A gift, in the Hebrew: and so the Chaldean and the LXX. We learn from this that estates even given as a gift returned at the time of the Jubilee to the old possessors and their heirs.

The mystical meaning according to our Osiander is this: Christ is the Prince of peace. He gave to his sons (believers): but he also gives some gifts to servants (that is: the impious). But the gifts of the impious are sometimes taken away from them again; since they have not used them well. But to the pious they are confirmed and increased: until in the other life they possess all things most perfectly.] In the eternal Jubilee, of course.

Latin:

Vers. 17. SI AUTEM DEDERIT LEGATUM]

Donum, in Hebræo: & sic Chaldæus & LXX. Discimus hinc prædia etiam dono data Jubilæi tempore rediisse ad possessores ve- teres, eorumque hæredes.

Significatio mystica juxta Osiandrum nostrum hæc est: Christus est Princeps pacis. Is filiis suis (credentibus donabat: sed & servis (hoc est: impiis) dat aliqua dona. At impiorum dona, ab ipsis iterum aliquando aufferuntur; quippe qui iis non bene sunt usi. Piis autem confirmantur & au- gentur: donec in altera vita omnia perfectissime possideant.] In æterno scilicet Jubilæo.

## 46:24
Vers. 24. THIS IS THE HOUSE OF THE KITCHENS IN WHICH THE MINISTERS OF THE HOUSE OF THE LORD SHALL COOK THE VICTIMS OF THE PEOPLE.

These four small courts are kitchens, in which the Levites shall cook the remains of those sacrifices, which the people are also permitted to eat. For after the sacrifices, honest feasts were instituted. [But in the Church of Christ, the meats of the sacrifices are cooked when the ministers of the Church do not cast at the hearers Evangelical sermons about Christ that are unpremeditated, raw, and poorly arranged, but teach the people about Religion solidly and skillfully.] As Osiander has it here.

Latin:

Vers. 24. HÆC EST DOMUS CULINARUM IN QUA COQUENT MINISTRI DOMUS DOMINI VICTIMAS POPULI.

Hæc quatuor atriola sunt culinæ, in quibus Levitæ coquent reliquias eorum sacrificiorum, de quibus etiam populo vesci licet. Instituebantur e- nim post sacrificia honesta convivia. [In Ecclesia autem Christi coquuntur carnes sacrificiorum, cum Ecclesiæ ministri Evangelicas de Christo conciones non impræmeditatas & crudas, maleque dispositas auditoribus objiciunt, sed solide & dextre populum de Religione docent.] Ut hic habet Osiander.

## 47:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLVII.

Waters flowing out from under the threshold of the house will create a torrent, which finally cannot be waded across: but it heals all things to which it reaches, having fish and fruit-bearing trees. The boundaries of the holy land, which is to be divided to the 12 tribes of Israel, and to the strangers.

Vers. 1. WATERS WERE FLOWING OUT FROM UNDER THE THRESHOLD OF THE HOUSE]

Conducted through underground channels, they burst forth into the open court of the priests, for washing the victims, cleansing the ground from blood, and casting out filth.

Latin:

CAPUT XLVII.

Aquæ subter limen domus egredientes effi- cient torrentem, qui tandem transvadari non potest: Sanat autem omnia, ad quæ pertingit, habens pisces & arbores frugi- feras. Termini terræ sanctæ, quæ 12. tri- bubus Israel, & advenis dividenda est.

Vers. 1. AQUÆ EGREDIEBANTUR SUBTER LIMEN DOMUS]

Per canales subterraneos ductæ erumpebant in subdiale sacerdotum, ad lavandas victimas, purgandum à sanguine solum, & sordes ejiciendas.

## 47:7
Ver. 7. BEHOLD ON THE BANK OF THE TORRENT VERY MANY TREES

Where that torrent, or rather fountain, goes out from the temple, it will nourish with its moisture excellent trees of every kind, so that there will always be some fruits there, whether early or late. See below 12.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ECCE IN RIPA TORRENTIS LIGNA MULTA NIMIS]

Ubi ille torrens sive fons potius, extra templum egreditur, humore suo educabit arbores optimas omnis ge- neris, ita ut semper aliqui ibi fructus sint futuri aut præ- coces, aut serotini. Vide infra 12.

## 47:8
Ver. 8. THEY SHALL ENTER THE SEA

The Dead [Sea].

AND THEY SHALL GO FORTH AND THE WATERS SHALL BE HEALED

The swiftness of that torrent will be so great that, passing through the Dead Sea, nothing will be corrupted by it, just as certain rivers pass through lakes: the Abdua through Lake Larius, the Ticinus through Verbanus, the Mintius through Benacus, the Ollius through Sevinus, the Rhodanus through Lemanus, as Pliny testifies, 2, 100. They shall be healed, that is, they shall remain wholesome, nor will they retain anything of those pestilential waters.

Latin:

Vers. 8. INTRABUNT MARE]

Mortuum.

ET EXIBUNT ET SANABUNTUR AQUÆ]

Tanta erit rapiditas illius torrentis, ut mare mortuum per- transiens, nihil ab eo corrumpatur, quomodo transeunt, quidam amnis Fucinum lacum, Larium Abdua, Verbanum Ticinus, Benacum Mintius, Sevinum Ollius, Lemanum Rhodanus, teste Plinio 2, 100. Sanabuntur, id est, mane- bunt salubres, neque retinebunt quicquam de aquis illis pestilentibus.

## 47:9
AND EVERY LIVING SOUL THAT CREEPS]

That is, swims, for it concerns fish. שׁרץ is said of any movement of an animal, as Levit. 11, 29, wherefore it is also translated by κινεῖν. Gen. 7, 21.

SHALL LIVE]

It shall not perish, like those fish which are put into the Dead Sea. Tacitus says of it: It suffers neither fish nor birds accustomed to the waters.

THEY SHALL BE HEALED]

That is, they shall be sound.

These uses of the waters are not recounted here, but others. For they served primarily for the healing of the waters of the Dead Sea, verse 8, then for fertility, as we shall say later. But these marvelous waters signify without doubt something singular. For no such waters were found either in the temple of Solomon or in that of Zerubbabel. But these are proper to the mystical temple of Ezekiel, through which some say, with the blessed Hafenreffer, that divine thanks and blessings are shadowed forth, while others judge that the waters of Evangelical doctrine are signified, concerning which waters of refreshment, Ps. 23, Isa. 12, chap. 35, 6, John 4, chap. 7. These, therefore, are designated (1) As to their origin, that they went forth from under the threshold of the House, then that they proceed primarily from Christ, who is the door and the only gate of salvation, John 14, then that they proceed secondarily from the ministers of the word, nor is their spring found except in the Church: Ambrose in Apoc. chap. 21, 1. By the torrent we must understand the divine Scripture, which goes forth from the temple, that is, from the Church, namely from the mouth of the preachers. But they proceed as 'phialantes' [trickling], as the blessed Hafenreffer rendered the Hebrew word on page 318, because there is no external pomp, striking the eyes, as those things which are in the world are great and dazzle the eyes. The ocean of the world foams and roars: the waters of the temple trickle, that is, they flow softly and gently. (2) As to their increase, because they first reach the ankles, afterwards they ascend to the knees, thirdly they reach to the loins, finally they become higher than the stature of the Prophet, and are to be crossed by swimming. By which the increase of thanks, or also the depth of the word of God and of divine mysteries is noted, because the more we rush into the mysteries of the word, the deeper they are, so that at last the searcher of majesty is overwhelmed by it. The torrent, says Ambrose, he could not cross, because no one can search out the depth of divine and heavenly mysteries as it is. For we know in part, we prophesy in part. Considering that he himself could not cross this torrent, Paul said, O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! (3) As to the effect; which is primarily twofold: The first is the admirable healthfulness of the waters, the other is the admirable power of fertility and fruitfulness. Concerning the former, verse 8. For when these waters flowing from the temple through Galilee and the plains descend and are discharged into the Dead Sea, not only are the waters of that sea cured by these waters flowing into them, but all living creatures also, to which these waters arrive, are made alive. Grotius, in order to strip this effect from the waters, introduces a meaning entirely foreign to the words of the Prophet, that they do not corrupt the Dead Sea, even if they pass through it, and that they remain healthful. But in the text they are said to enter the Dead Sea in such a way that it is healed. For the Dead Sea is the Sodomitic lake: it is also called the salt sea, on account of the nitrous matter of sulfur, which it perpetually exhales. In which, because of its pestilent nature, because it is always smoking and exhales a dark and foul vapor, no fish, nor any animal can live in it, whence they say that the fish of the Jordan, as soon as they arrive at it, either die in it or turn back. This sea, therefore, is said to be healed by the inflowing waters, but not that these remain healthful: Nay, such is the healthfulness of those waters that they not only heal that pestilent sea, but also make alive all living creatures, which could not live there. By which the effect of the divine word is excellently expressed, through which the Dead Sea, the whole world, which lies in the evil one, 1 John 5, 19. The ungodly, who are like a raging sea, whose waves overflow into trampling and mire, as witnessed by Isa. 57, 20, are healed and made alive: concerning which Hafenreffer says thus on page 331. What is the Dead Sea? A harmful and horrible lake of our crimes and sins, into which we have been cast through manifold defections from the Lord, and have been condemned: here all things are foul, all things are dead and destructive, hence pestilent and destructive vapors exhale, devastating every neighboring region even to the heavens, here are no healthful fruits, but either eternal sterility, or a species feigning fruit with useless beauty. For by nature we are children of wrath, Eph. 2, 3. We are dead in our trespasses and sins. Ibid. v. 1. The waters flowing from the temple, and coming into the Dead Sea, heal the dead waters, and wherever the rivers arrive, all living creatures are made alive, Ezekiel 47, 8. 9. This is, without a doubt, the power and virtue of spiritual thanksgivings and blessings, which most perfectly repair and restore all damages whatsoever, both those inflicted upon us and those hanging over us, from sin, death, and hell. Those are the waters, as has been demonstrated in the preceding, of divine grace and mercy, the remission of sins, sanctification, justification, and all the merits of the Savior, the word of salvation, the washing of regeneration, the Lord's Supper, and the power of the Holy Spirit dwelling within us. These, therefore (all and each of which come under the name of spiritual waters), remove all the damnable viscosity of the Asphaltite lake or Dead Sea, that is, they purge the foulness of sin, dissipate the pestiferous exhalations which draw forth the wrath of God and the thunderbolts of eternal perdition, extinguish the flames of hell, of which the Asphaltite is an exemplar, drive away the ashes and smoke, and to that extent kill death itself, and restore life to all, wherever they may come. For the Blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from all sin 1 John 1:7. And when we were dead in our trespasses and sins, God (who is rich in mercy) made us alive together in Christ, and raised us up together, and made us sit in the heavenly places in Christ JESUS, that He might show in the ages to come the exceeding riches of His grace, in His kindness toward us in Christ Jesus, that He might show in the ages to come the exceeding riches of His grace, in His kindness toward us in Christ Jesus Eph. 2:4 ff. Such you once were (rotten, to be sure, foul, wicked, and damned sinners), but you were washed, but you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God 1 Cor. 6:11. And again to the Colossians: When you were once alienated and enemies in your mind, in wicked works, yet now He (GOD) has reconciled you in the body of His flesh, through death, to present you holy, and blameless, and irreproachable in His sight Col. 1:21. Thus the blessed Hafenreffer. But that muddy and marshy places are not healed by the health-giving nature of these waters, but remain condemned to eternal sterility by their own vice, is not because the waters are not sufficiently health-giving, or not sufficiently effective for purging and healing everyone, but because many prefer to wallow in the mud and mire of sins without repentance, like swine, rather than, having abandoned the dung of their crimes, to hasten to the healing waters through faith and true repentance.

From this prophecy, 'and there shall be many fish,' arose the fact that Christians were called fish among the ancients, because, reborn by the waters of Baptism, they have obtained the spiritual life of grace. Which name ἰχθὺς refers to an acrostic about Christ by its initial letters, according to Nazianzen: Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior. See Augustine, book 18, On the City of God, chapter 13. This admirable change, says Cornelius à Lapide, namely the vivification of the Dead Sea, that is, of the sinner, proceeds from the waters which that is, from Christ, who is the gate of heaven, and flow into the right side, that is, through the right side of the crucified Christ opened and wounded by a lance, for from it blood and water, and the Sacraments of the Church, flowed; says Saint Augustine. Where note, it is the common opinion of the ancients that the side of Christ on the cross was pierced by the soldier on the right, and some think this is predicted here by Ezekiel when he says in verse 2: and behold, waters overflowing from the right side. We add Jerome's explanation: We have already said that the waters signify either the grace of Baptism or evangelical doctrine. Which if they go forth from the threshold of the temple of the Lord, and hold to the Apostolic discipline: they make the mounds of sand, previously sterile and infertile, to be fruitful: and all the plains and deserts are so irrigated that they express in themselves the sacrament of the Jericho river: which Elisha cured with evangelical and apostolic salt: to such an extent that where there had previously been sterility and death, there might be abundance and life. And they not only healed the deserts, but they enter the eastern sea: namely the dead sea, in which nothing could be vital, and the most bitter sea, which in Greek is called λίμνη ἀσφάλτου, that is, the pool of bitumen. And in a wonderful way the dead waters are healed by the evangelical waters: which have obtained the name of death from the fact that they have nothing vital in them. For they did not know him who says: I am the life and the truth. And in truth, according to the letter up to this point, nothing that breathes and can move can be found in this sea because of the excessive bitterness, not even little snails and small worms and eels and other kinds of living creatures or serpents: whose little bodies we can know better than their names. Finally, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, carries fish flowing into it, they die immediately and float on the oily waters. Since these things therefore have no utility, as the simple text testifies, even if they have been done, which the foolish superstition of the Jews believes; according to the spiritual understanding, cured by the torrent of the Lord, they will have very many fish, and everything will live to which that torrent shall arrive.

Latin:

Verf. 9. ET OMNIS ANIMA VIVENS QUÆ SERPIT]

Id est, Natat, nam de piscibus agitur. שׁרץ de quovis motu animalis dicitur, ut Levit. 11, 29. quare & per κινεῖν vertitur. Gen. 7, 21.

VIVET]

Non interibit, ut illi pisces, qui in mare mortuum immittuntur. Tacitus de eo : Neque pisces aut suetas aquis volucres patitur.

SANABUNTUR]

Id est, sanæ erunt.

Non hic recensentur hi usus aquarum, sed a- lii. Faciebant enim potissimum ad sanationem aquarum maris mortui vers. 8. tum ad fœcundita- tem, uti postea dicemus. Significant autem si- ne dubio aliquid singulare aquæ hæ mirabiles. Nullæ enim tales aquæ vel in templo Salomoneo, vel in Zorobabelis repertæ. Sed propriæ hæ sunt templo mystico Ezechielis, per quas aliqui gratias & benedictiones divinas adumbratas esse, cum B. Hafenreffero dicunt, alii significatas aquas doctrinæ Evangelicæ censent, de quibus refectionis aquis, Ps. 23. Esa. 12. cap. 35, 6. Joh. 4. cap. 7. Hæ ergo de- signantur (1) Quoad ortum, quod egressæ sint sub- ter limen Domus, tum quod πρώτως à Christo, qui est porta & janua salutis unica Joh. 14. tum quod à ministris verbi δευτέρως procedant, nec nisi in Ecclesia inveniatur earum scaturigo: Am- brosius in Apoc. cap. 21, 1. Per torrentem Scripturam divinam intelligere debemus, quæ de templo, id est, de Ecclesia egreditur, ab ore scilicet prædicatorum. Procedunt autem quasi phialantes, ut verbum He- bræum B. Hafenrefferus reddidit pag. 318. quia nulla est externa pompa, in oculos incurrens, u- ti ea, quæ in mundo sunt, magna sunt, & ocu- los perstringunt. Oceanus mundi spumat & fre- mit: aquæ templi phialantes, hoc est, molliter & leniter manant. (2) Quoad incrementum, quia primum attingunt talares, postea adscendunt ad genua, tertio ad lumbos pertingunt, postremo staturæ Prophetæ altiores evadunt, & natatu traji- ciendæ sunt. Quo incrementum gratiarum, vel etiam profunditas verbi Dei & mysteriorum divino- rum notatur, quia quo magis in verbi mysteria nos incurrimus, eo profundiora illa sunt, ut tan- dem scrutator majestatis opprimatur ab ea. Tor- rentem, inquit Ambrosius, non potuit transva- dere, quia profunditatem divinorum cælestiumque mysteriorum nullus, sicut est, perscrutari potest. Ex parte enim cognoscimus, ex parte prophetamus. Hunc torrentem idem Paulus transmeare se non posse considerans, dicebat, ô altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei! (3) Quoad effectum; qui duplex potissimum: Primus admiranda aqua- rum salubritas, alter admiranda fœcunditatis vir- tus, & fertilitas. De priori versu 8. Quum enim aquæ hæ è templo promanantes per Gali- læam & campestria descendentes in mare mor- tuum exonerentur, non tantum aquæ istius maris influentibus hisce aquis curantur, sed o- mnes quoque animantes, ad quas hæ aquæ perve- niunt, vivificantur. Grotius ut hunc effectum aquis eripiat, plane alienam verbis Prophetæ mentem inducit, quod mare mortuum non corrum- pant, etsi id pertranseant, quodque salubres ma- neant. At in textu dicuntur ita intrare mortuum mare, ut id sanetur. Mare enim mortuum lacus est Sodomiticus : dicitur & mare salsum, ob nitro- sam sulphuris, quod perpetuo exhalat, materiam. In quo propter pestilentem naturam, quia semper fumans est, & tenebrosum, tetrumque vaporem exhalat, nullus in eo piscis, nec ullum animal vive- re potest, unde ajunt, Jordani pisces, quam primum ad ipsum perveniunt, aut emori in eo- q dem, aut retrocedere. Hoc ergo mare sanari di- citur aquis influentibus, non vero hæ salubres ma- nere: Imo tanta est aquarum istarum salubritas, ut non solum pestilens illud mare sanent, sed o- mnes quoque animantes, quæ nullæ ibi vivere pos- sint, vivificet. Quo effectus verbi divini egregie exprimitur, per quod mare mortuum mundus uni- versus, qui in maligno jacet 1. Joh. 5, 19. Impii, qui quasi mare fervens sunt, cujus fluctus in conculcatio- nem & lutum redundat, teste Esa. 57, 20. sanantur, & vivificantur: de quo ita Hafenreff. pag. 331. Quid mare mortuum? Noxius & horribilis scelerum & peccatorum nostrorum lacus, in quem per multipli- ces defectiones à Domino præcipitati, damnatiq; su- mus: hic omnia fœtida, omnia emortua & exitiosa sunt, hinc vapores exhalant pestilentes & exitiosi, o- mnem vicinam regionem ad cælos usque devastantes, hic nulli salubres fructus, sed vel æterna sterilitas, vel inutili pulchritudine fructum ementita species. Na- tura enim filii iræ sumus Ephes. 2, 3. Mortui sumus in delictis & peccatis nostris. Ibid. v. 1. Aquæ pro- manantes è templo, & venientes in mare mortuum sanant aquas mortuas, & quocunque perveniunt flumina, omnia animantia vivificantur Ezechielis 47, 8. 9. Hæc nimirum vis & virtus est gratiarum & benedictionum spiritualium, quæ omnia omnino da- mna, à peccato, morte & inferno nobis & illata, & im- pendentia perfectissime resarciunt & restaurant. Illæ aquæ sunt, ut in superioribus demonstratum est, gra- tia & misericordia divina, remissio peccatorum, san- ctificatio, justificatio, & omnia merita Salvatoris, verbum salutis, lavacrum regenerationis, Cœna Do- minica, & virtus in nobis habitantis Spiritus Sancti. Hæc igitur (quæ omnia & singula aquarum spiritua- lium nomine veniunt) omnem Asphaltitis lacus seu maris mortui damnatam viscositatem tollunt, hoc est, peccati fœditatem expurgant, pestiferas exhalatio- nes, quæ iram Dei, & æternæ perditionis fulmina eli- ciunt, dissipant, orci flammas, cujus Asphaltites exem- plar est, extinguunt, cineres & fumos abigunt, ad- eoque ipsam mortem enecant, & omnibus, quocunq; venerint, vitam restituunt. Nam Sanguis Jesu Christi, Filii Dei, emundat nos ab omni peccato 1. Joh. 1, 7. & cum mortui essemus in delictis & pecca- tis nostris, convivificavit nos Deus (qui dives est in misericordia,) in Christo, & conresuscitavit & con- sidere fecit in cælestibus in Christo JESU, ut o- stenderet in seculis supervenientibus abundan- tes divitias gratiæ suæ, in bonitate super nos in Chri- sto Jesu, ut ostenderet in seculis supervenientibus ab- undantes divitias gratiæ suæ, in bonitate super nos in Christo Jesu Eph. 2, 4. seqq. Hæc aliquando fuistis (pu- tidi nimirum, fætidi, scelerati & damnati peccatores) sed abluti estis, sed justificati estis, in nomine Domi- ni Jesu, & in Spiritu Dei nostri 1. Cor. 6, 11. & rur- sus ad Colossenses: Cum essetis aliquando alieni, & inimici sensu, in operibus malis, nunc reconciliavit (DEUS) in corpore carnis Christi, per mortem, ex- hibere vos sanctos, immaculatos, irreprehensibi- les coram ipso Coloss. 1, 21. Hæc B. Hafenreffer. Quod autem cænosa & palustria loca aquarum istarum salubritate non sanantur, sed vitiositate sua æterna sterilitate damnata permaneant, non inde est, quod aquæ non satis salubres sint, vel ad purgandum & sanandum omnes non satis efficaces, sed quod multi in cæno lutoque peccatorum sine pœnitentia, por- corum instar, volutari malunt, quam relictis scele- rum stercoribus ad sanantes properare aquas, per fi- dem & veram pœnitentiam.

Ex hac Prophetia, & erunt pisces multi, ortum, quod pisces dicti sint Christiani, penes antiquos, quia renati aquis Baptismi, vitam spiritualem gratiæ adepti sunt. Quod nomen ἰχθὺς refert ἀκροστιχὶς de Christo literis initialibus, apud Nazianz. ἰησοῦς χριστὸς θεοῦ ὑἱὸς σωτὴρ. Vide Aug. lib. 18. de Civit. Dei, cap. 13. Hæc admirabilis mutatio, inquit Cor- nelius à Lapide, puta maris mortui, id est, peccato- ris, vivificatio provenit ex aquis, quæ manant à limi- ne & ostio Sancti Sanctorum, id est, à Christo, qui est porta cæli, fluuntque in latus dextrum, id est, per Christi crucifixi latus dextrum lancea apertum & vulneratum, ex eo enim sanguis & aqua, atque Ecclesiæ Sacramenta fluxerunt; ait sanctus Augu- stinus. Ubi nota, communis veterum sententia est, latus Christi in cruce à milite perfossum fuisse dex- trum, idque putant aliqui hic prædici ab Ezech. cum ait vers. 2. & ecce aquæ redundantes è latere dextro. Addimus Hieronymi explicationem: Aquas vel Baptismi Gratiam, vel Evangelicam significare doctrinam, dudum diximus. Quæ si egrediantur de limine templi Domini, & Apostolicam teneant disciplinam: tumulos sabuli, steriles prius & in- fertiles, faciunt esse frugiferos: & omnia plana at- que deserta ita irrigantur, ut exprimant in se Hieri- chontini fluvii sacramentum: quem Helisæus Evan- gelico & Apostolico curavit sale: in tantum, ut ubi prius sterilitas fuerat, & mors, ibi ubertas esset & vita. Nec solum deserta sanarunt, sed intrant mare orientale: mare videlicet mortuum, in quo nihil po- terat esse vitale, & mare amarissimum, quod Græce λίμνη ἀσφάλτου, id est, stagnum bituminis vocatur. Mirumque in modum aquis Evangelicis aquæ sanan- tur mortuæ: quæ ab eo, quod nihil in se vitale ha- beant, nomen mortis sortitæ sunt. Non enim no- verant eum, qui dicit: Ego sum vita & veritas. Et revera juxta literam hucusque, nihil quod spiret & possit incedere, præ amaritudine nimia in hoc mari reperiri potest, nec cochleolæ quidem parvique vermiculi & anguilli & cætera animantium sive serpentium gene- ra: quorum magis corpuscula possumus nosse quam nomina. Denique, si Jordanis auctus imbribus pisces illuc influens rapuerit, statim moriuntur, & pingui- bus aquis supernatant. Cum hæc itaque nihil uti- litatis habeant, ut simplex sermo testatur, etiamsi facta fuerint, quod stulta Judæorum superstitio cre- dit; juxta intelligentiam spiritualem, Domini tor- rente curatæ, habebunt pisces plurimos, & vivent o- mnia, ad quæ torrens iste pervenerit.

## 47:10
Verse 10.

AND FISHERMEN SHALL STAND UPON THEM] In that part where that torrent shall flow. FROM ENGEDI EVEN UNTO ENEG LAIM] Jerome: En-eglaim is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters, but Engedi is where it ends and is consumed. THERE SHALL BE A DRYING OF NETS] See above 26, 5.

These things concerning the fishermen likewise regard the times of the New Testament: those fishermen are the Apostles and their successors, Matt. 4, 19; Luke 5, 10. Whose duty it is to draw men out of the sea of the world and the mud of sins, with the net of the divine word, so that they may be gathered to the Church. They are said to stand from the small town of Engedi even unto the small town of En-eglaim, from one extremity of the sea to the other, because they do this throughout the whole dead sea of the world, so that men may be enclosed by the net of the word, and drawn to the port of the Church and of eternal life; whence various species of fish extracted, various kinds of men, Gal. 3, 28; Col. 3, 10. Concerning which Jerome: There shall be fishermen, to whom the Lord Jesus speaks: Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men, of whom also Jeremiah: Behold, I, he says, will send fishers. And very many species: indeed, kinds of fish shall be in the sea that was once dead. Which fish, at the command of the Lord, he drew to the right side

Peter, and they were one hundred and fifty-three, so that because of their multitude the nets were breaking. But those who have written about the nature and property of living creatures, who have learned the ἁλιευτικὰ in both the Latin and Greek language, of whom Oppian the Cilician is one, a most learned poet, say that there are one hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish, all of which were caught by the Apostles: and nothing remained uncaught, while both noble and ignoble, rich and poor, and every kind of man is drawn out of the sea of this age to salvation. But what follows: on its shores and in its marshes, or in those waters which go out beyond the shores, they shall not be healed: that secretly shows that he who has not been in the ark of Noah perishes, while the flood reigns, and those whom this river has not reached do not receive health. This is Saint Jerome.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET STABUNT SUPER ILLAS PISCATORES] Illa parte, qua ille torrens fluet. AB ENGADDI USQUE AD ENGALIM] Hie- ronymus: Engalim in principio est maris mortui, ubi Iorda- nis ingreditur, Engaddi vero ubi finitur, atque consumitur. SICCATIO SAGENARUM ERIT] Vide supra 26, 5.

Hæc de piscatoribus respiciunt itidem tem- pora Novi Testamenti: Piscatores isti Apostoli sunt, eorumque successores Matth. 4, 19. Luc. 5, 10. Quorum officium est homines extrahere è mari mundi & luto peccatorum, reti verbi divini, ut colligantur ad Ecclesiam. Stare autem dicuntur ab oppidulo Engaddi usque ad oppidulum Engalim, ab una maris extremitate, usque ad alteram, quia per totum mare mortuum mundi hoc agunt, ut concludantur verbi sagena homines, & ad por- tum Ecclesiæ, & vitæ æternæ extrahantur; unde variæ species piscium extractæ, varia hominum genera Gal. 3, 28. Colos. 3, 10. de quo Hierony- mus: Erunt piscatores, quibus loquitur Dominus Jesus: Venite ad me, & faciam vos piscatores ho- minum, de quibus & Hieremias: Ecce ego, inquit, mittam piscatores. Et plurimæ species: imo gene- ra piscium erunt in mari quondam mortuo. Quos pi- sces ad dextram partem, jubente Domino, extraxit

Petrus, & erant centum quinquaginta tres, ita ut præ multitudine eorum retia rumperentur. Ajunt autem, qui de animantium scripsere natura ac pro- prietate, qui ἁλιευτικὰ tam Latino, quam Græco didicere sermone, de quibus Oppianus Cilix est, Poë- ta doctissimus, centum quinquaginta tria esse genera piscium, quæ omnia capta sunt ab Apostolis: & nihil remansit incaptum, dum & nobiles & ignobi- les, divites & pauperes, & omne genus hominum de mari hujus seculi extrahitur ad salutem. Quod au- tem sequitur: in littoribus ejus & in palustribus, sive in his, quæ extra littora egrediuntur aquæ, non sanabuntur: illud latenter ostendit, quod, qui in Noë arca non fuerit, pereat, regnante diluvio, & quos iste fluvius non attigerit, non suscipiant sani- tatem. Hæc S. Hieronymus.

## 47:11
Verse 11.

BUT ON ITS SHORES, AND IN THE MARSHES THEY SHALL NOT BE HEALED] The littoral and marshy places (of the sea) shall not be wholesome. The rest of the Dead Sea shall remain as they had been before.

These things are rightly rendered from the Hebrew by Osiander, and explained; Heb. but its outlets and its marshes shall not be healed, but shall be salt, (that is, when water flows from that sea into neighboring places and makes marshes: those marshes do not become wholesome, but will keep a certain bitterness and virulence, and will even progress for the worse) For heretics (who go out from the Church), spurning pious admonitions, do not return to a sound mind: but are altogether incurable, especially the heresiarchs, whence Paul says: Avoid a heretical man after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a one is subverted, and sins, being condemned by his own judgment, Tit. 3.

BECAUSE THEY SHALL BE GIVEN TO SALT] In the Hebrew there is not 'because', but 'they shall be given to salt', that is, they shall be left. See what we said in Gen. 14, 3. Tacitus on the Asphaltite, which is the same Dead Sea: A lake of immense circumference, in appearance like a sea, but more corrupt in taste.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

IN LITTORIBUS AUTEM EJUS, ET IN PA- LUSTRIBUS NON SANABUNTUR] Littoralia autem, & palustria (maris) non erunt salubria. Manebunt cæ- tera maris mortui, qualia ante fuerant.

Recte hæc ab Osiandro redduntur ex E- bræo, & explicantur; Hebr. exitus autem ejus, & paludes non sanabuntur, sed salsæ erunt, (id est, quando de mari illo effluit aqua, in loca vi- cina, & efficit paludes: illæ paludes non fiunt sa- lubres, sed servabunt amaritudinem & virulen- tiam quandam, & in deterius etiam proficient) Hæretici enim (qui ab Ecclesia egrediuntur) pias admonitiones spernentes, non redeunt ad sanam mentem: sed sunt omnino insanabiles, præser- tim Hæresiarchæ, unde Paulus dicit: Hæreticum hominem post unam atque alteram admonitio- nem devita, sciens: quia subversus est ejusmo- di, qui ejusmodi est, & delinquit, cum sit pro- prio judicio condemnatus, Tit. 3.

QUIA IN SALINAS DABUNTUR] In Hebræo non est quia, sed sali dabuntur, id est, relinquentur. Vide quæ diximus Gen. 14, 3. Tacitus de Asphaltite, qui idem mare mortuum: Lacus immenso ambitu specie ma- ris sapore corruptior.

## 47:12
Ver. 12.

ITS LEAVES FOR MEDICINE] It is a wonder if this water is that which Pliny calls Callirrhoe in the chapter on the Asphaltite, and calls a fountain, no doubt because, covered for some time, it bursts forth again, of medicinal health. Solinus teaches us that it comes from Jerusalem: Callirrhoe is nearest to Jerusalem, a fountain most approved for its medicinal heat, and is so named from the very proclamation of its waters. Martianus Capella: The second elevation is Judea from Jerusalem, in which side is the fountain Callirrhoe.

It does not appear what that fountain has to do with the water seen by Ezekiel. The text teaches that it has entirely peculiar effects, and that it is a purely mystical water. To this also contributes that fruitfulness, that on the banks of that torrent on both sides there is fruit-bearing wood of a different kind, whose leaves do not fall off, nor are the fruits corrupted, because it brings forth new fruits every month, because its waters go out from the Sanctuary, and its fruits for food, and its leaves for medicine: which it is manifest are truly mystical. Osiander has conveniently expressed the meaning: From the preaching of the Gospel and the administration of the Sacraments, very many Christians will be born everywhere, who are good and fruitful trees: And as various species of trees produce various good fruits: so they, according to the diversity of gifts, will serve their neighbor in various and different ways. Yet directing all things to the praise of God. The leaves will not fall off, that is, they will not perish in the heat of temptations, but will be preserved green (the faithful). Their fruits will not be corrupted: their labor will not be in vain in the Lord: but they will bring forth the greatest and permanent benefits and he shall have a most ample (by grace) reward. Every month they shall produce fruits: that is, they shall be most rich in good works, they shall never cease to bring forth good fruits abundantly. But they shall be so fruitful because they are cherished and refreshed by the Ministry of the Gospel, which does not spring from the pools of human wisdom, but from the inner chambers of heavenly mysteries, and thus has flowed to us from the bosom of the Father through Christ, John 1. Moreover, it refreshes and strengthens the labors and duties of Christians (such as are all works of charity, among which the consolations of the afflicted proposed from the word of God are not the least), and provides medicine for the soul to the sick, so that they themselves may recover. B. Hafenreffer treats this more lengthily and elegantly on page 353 et seqq. But above all, the cause of that fertility is to be noted. The Prophet makes the demonstrator of this to be that those waters proceed from the Sanctuary. The fruits of the faithful, of course, are the effects of spiritual waters through the Holy Spirit or the Evangelical doctrine, and are produced by the power of the divine word, not by our own strengths. Let us not think, says Jerome, that the abundance of such great fruits belongs to the banks, or the trees, or the months; he gives the causes of the fertility, and infers: Because its waters shall go forth from the Sanctuary: It is not therefore of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy. But that we may be recalled to the first source of this torrent, which is the Holy Spirit, like a river of living water, crystalline, proceeding from the Father and the Son, or from the glory and throne of God and the Lamb (the glory of God, however, is the very essence of God) ἐκπορευόμενον, who diffuses himself most greatly in the heavenly Jerusalem among the blessed, and irrigates them with his far most copiously flowing waters, and fills even the head of the Elect himself, our Savior Christ Jesus, as the tree of life, with immense gifts, these things are shown to St. John in Apoc. 22, 1, and are described in almost the same manner as they were shown here to Ezekiel and described. He showed me a river of water of life, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb in the midst of its street, and on either side of the river the tree of life bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit every month, and the leaves of the tree for the healing of the nations. We must be conformed to this tree of life, as fruit-bearing trees, and from this tree of life is all our fertility, by which spiritual trees of righteousness bring forth various fruits, pleasing to God, wholesome to our neighbor, Isa. 61, Phil. 1. But Christ, the tree of life, gives immortal life to the blessed by the vision and fruition of himself, and is for them food and fresh pleasure, through 12 months, that is, for all eternity. The leaves of the tree are the words of Christ, with which he will soothe and comfort the blessed of all nations forever. Thus Beda, Rupertus, Ansbertus, Riebera, and others. Compare Apoc. 2, 7. And the Holy Spirit is the most abundant fountain of both grace and glory, happiness, and all pleasure, of which Ambros. lib. 3. de Spiritu Sancto cap. 3. This river, certainly, proceeding from the throne of God is the Holy Spirit, whom he drinks who believes in Christ: and therefore the very gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified thus by the name of a river, which abound in the blessed from God and the Lamb, so that they may be satisfied with the torrent of pleasure, Ps. 35, 9, Isa. 66, 12. But for Cornelius à Lapide to dream of the river, trees, and apples literally, as they were in the earthly paradise, approaches Jewish delusions. Ambrose, however, not unaptly compares both the Apocalyptic and the Prophetic passage in Apoc. 22, whose words we add: Two banks, he says, signify the two testaments. Between these two banks runs the great torrent of the Scriptures, which has been edited by the holy Fathers; but by the trees are designated the teachers of the Church, who are said to be planted on both banks, that is, in the doctrine of the Old and New Testament, whence drawing the waters of true knowledge they bring forth both fruits and leaves; for by fruits are designated good works: but by leaves the words of preaching; fruits are profitable for food, and leaves for medicine: Because every doctor then ministers the healing medicine of words to a languishing soul, when he has first fed it with the examples of good works. Behold, Ezekiel said he saw the torrent go out from the temple, but John says that not a torrent, but a river proceeding from the throne of God and the Lamb was shown to him. A torrent is wont to be dried up by the excessive heat of the sun, but a river is dried up by no heat. Not inappropriately, therefore, is divine Scripture expressed by a torrent, which, when the sun comes, that is, the Lord, for judgment, will be dried up: because after the resurrection divine Scripture will not be necessary. Furthermore, by the river, which will be dried up by no heat of the sun, is understood the perpetual glory of the saints: which is said to proceed from the throne of God and the Lamb, because from him will proceed the river of the glory of the saints, from whom the stream of all good things proceeded to them while they were placed in the flesh: which river is said to be bright as crystal.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

FOLIA EJUS AD MEDICINAM] Mirum si hæc aqua ea sit, quam Callirrhoën Plinius vocat in capite de Asphaltite, fontemque appellat, nimirum quia tectus a- liquamdiu rursus erumpit, medicæ salubritatis. Ab Hie- rosolymis eum venire Solinus nos docet: Callirrhoë Hiero- solymis proxima, fons calore medico probatissimus, & ex ipso aquarum præconio sic vocatus est. Martianus Capella: Se- cunda elatio Judæa ab Hierosolymis, in quo latere est fons Challirrhoe.

Non apparet, quid fons ille ad aquam faciat ab Ezechiele visam. Quam prorsus peculiares ha- bere effectus, & mere mysticam aquam esse, textus docet. Quo etiam facit illa fæcunditas, quod in ripis torrentis illius ex utraque parte lignum fru- ctiferum diversi generis sit, cuius folia non diffluunt, nec fructus corrumpuntur, quod per singulos menses novos gignit fructus, quia aquæ ejus de Sanctuario egrediuntur, & fructus ejus in cibum, & folia ejus in medicinam: quæ vere mystica esse, manifestum est. Significationem commode expressit O- siander: Ex Evangelii prædicatione & Sacramento- rum administratione nascentur passim plurimi Chri- stiani, qui sunt bonæ & fæcundæ arbores: Et ut variæ arborum species, varios bonos fructus gignunt: ita illi pro diversitate donorum, variis & diversis rationi- bus proximo inservient.
