Omnia tamen ad laudem Dei dirigentes. Folia non defluent, id est, non peribunt in æstu tentationum, sed virentes con- servabuntur (fideles) Fructus ipsorum non corrum- petur: labor eorum non erit inanis in Domi- no: sed maximas & permanentes utilitates affe- ret: & habebit amplissimam (ex gratia) remune- rationem. Singulis mensibus fructus producent: id est, erunt ditissimi in bonis operibus, nunquam ces- sabunt bonos fructus copiosè gignere. Tam autem foecundi erunt, quia foventur & recreantur Mini- sterio Evangelii, quod non ex humanae sapientiae lacunis scaturit, sed ex adytis coelestium arcano- rum, atque adeo è sinu Patris per Christum ad nos emanavit, Joh. 1. Christianorum autem labores & officia, (qualia sunt omnia charitatis opera, inter quae afflictorum consolationes è verbo Dei propo- sitae non sunt postrema) valentes reficiunt, & confirmant: aegris vero medicinam animae prae- stant, ut & ipsi convalescant. Quae prolixius & ele- ganter exequitur B. Hafenrefferus pag. 353. seqq. Sed cumprimis notanda causa istius fertilitis. Hanc Prophetae demonstrator facit, quod aquae illae è Sanctuario prodeant. Fructus nimirum fide- lium, aquarum spiritualium, per Spiritum Sanctum vel doctrinae Evangelicae effectus sunt, & virtute verbi divini procreantur, non propriis nostris vi- ribus. Neputemus, inquit Hieronymus, riparum esse, vel arborum aut mensium tantarum frugum a- bundantiam, reddit causas ubertatis, & infert: Quia aquae ejus de Sanctuario egredientur: Non ergo volentis, neǵ; currentis, sed miserentis Dei est. Ut vero ad primam scaturiginem hujus torren- tis revocemur, qui est Spiritus Sanctus, instar fluvii aquae vivae crystallini, à Patre & Filio, vel è gloria & sede Dei & agni (gloria autem Dei est ipsa Dei essentia) ἐκπορευόμενον, qui sese maxime in coelesti Hierosolyma in beatos diffundit, & lon- ge copiosissime fluentis suis illos irrigat, ipsumque etiam caput Electorum, Salvatorem nostrum Chri- stum Jesum, ceu lignum vitae, immensis dotibus re- plet, ostenduntur haec S. Johanni Apoc. 22, 1. & describuntur eadem fere ratione, uti hic ostensa Ezechieli, & descripta sunt. Ostendit mihi fluvium aquae vitae splendidum, tanquam Crystallum, proce- dentem de sede Dei, & agni in medio plateae ejus, & ex utraque parte fluminis lignum vitae afferens fru- ctus duodecim, per menses singulos reddens fructum suum, & folia ligni ad sanitatem gentium. Huic ligno vitae conformari oportet nos, ceu arbores frugiferas, & ab hoc vitae ligno omnis nostra est fertilitas, qua spirituales arbores justitiae varios fructus ferunt, Deo gratos, proximo salubres E- sa. 61. Phil. 1. Sed Christus lignum vitae beatis, vi- sione & fruitione sui vitam dat immortalem, & in cibum eis est, & voluptatem recentem, per 12. menses, id est, in omnem perpetuitatem. Ligni folia sunt verba Christi, quibus beatos omnium gentium mulcebit, & consolabitur in aeternum. Sic Beda, Rupertus, Ansbertus, Riebera & alii. Confer Apoc. 2, 7. Et Spiritus Sanctus est tum gratiae, tum gloriae, felicitatis, ac voluptatis omnis fons uberri- mus, de quo Ambros. lib. 3. de Spiritu Sancto cap. 3. Hic utiq́; fluvius de sede Dei procedens est Spiritus San- ctus, quem bibit, qui credit in Christum: Ideoque significantur ita per fluvii nomen ipsa dona Spi- ritus Sancti exuberantia, quae redundant in bea- tos à Deo & agno, ut torrente voluptatis poten- tur Psal. 35, 9. Esa. 66, 12. Fluvium vero, arbo- res, & poma ad literam, uti erant in paradiso ter- restri, dum Cornelius à Lapide somniat, ad Ju- daica deliria accedit. Non inconcinne autem Am- brosius in Apoc. 22. locum utrumque Apocalypti- cum, & Propheticum confert, cujus verba adjici- mus: Duae ripae, ait, duo testamenta significant. Inter has duas ripas magnus torrens Scripturarum, qui à san- ctis Patribus editus est, decurrit, per ligna vero Eccle- siae doctores designantur, qui in utrisque ripis, id est, in doctrina Veteris ac Novi Testamenti plantati esse dicuntur, unde aquas veræ scientiæ trahentes & fru- ctus gignunt & folia; per fructus namque opera bo- na: per folia autem verba prædicationis designantur; fructus in cibum, & folia in medicinam proficiunt: Quia unusquisque doctor languenti animæ medici- nam verborum salutiferam tunc ministrat, cum eam prius exemplis bonorum operum paverit. Ecce Eze- chiel torrentem de templo exiisse se vidisse dixit, Joan- nes autem non torrentem, sed fluvium à sede Dei & agni procedentem sibi ostensum fuisse dicit. Torrent ex nimio ardore solis solet siccari, fluvius vero nullo ar- dore exsiccatur. Non inconvenienter ergo per torren- tem divina Scriptura exprimitur, quæ veniente sole, id est Domino, ad judicium, siccabitur: quia post resurrectionem divina Scriptura necessaria non erit. Porro per fluvium, qui nullo ardore solis exsiccabitur, gloria sanctorum perpetua intelligitur: qui à sede Dei & agni procedere dicitur, quia ab illo fluvius glo- riæ sanctorum procedet, à quo illis in carne positis processit rivus omnium bonorum: qui fluvius splendi- dus tanquam Crystallus esse dicitur.

## 47:13
Vers. 13.

THIS IS THE BORDER BY WHICH YOU SHALL POSSESS THE LAND, IN THE TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL] This assignment, and what follows in the last chapter, would have had a place if the ten tribes had converted themselves to God no less than Judah and Benjamin. For thus they would have equally obtained a return. Now only a few, mixed with Judah and Benjamin, returned, and they had seats in common with them. In the course of time, however, by the gift of the Kings, even that land which had belonged to the ten tribes was conceded to the Jews, as we have shown elsewhere from Josephus.

Grotius assumes this prophetic vision as if it were made under a hypothesis, or shadowed forth the Holy Land and the possessions of the tribes in it, under a condition, namely, what possession each tribe would have had if they had indeed converted themselves to God. But here the possessions are simply assigned to all the tribes. Not the least trace of any hypothesis or condition appears here. Nor would there have been need for an accurate designation of all the borders if GOD had understood that those tribes would never return. Not returning, they were in need of no possessions. But that God, who foresaw all things from eternity, should have wished to determine these limits in vain is in no way consistent. Wherefore we have here a manifest argument that these things cannot be understood of the land of Canaan, and of the twelve tribes of Israel according to the letter, as they sound, but must be understood of the spiritual Canaan, the Church of Christ, and of Israel according to the promise, the true believers. The twelve tribes therefore are all believers and Christians. The three gates indeed from the individual sides, and the four quarters of the world signify that the entrance into the Church is open from all sides and from all quarters of the world. Because the ternary is the number of perfection. Add that by a similar reason the heavenly Jerusalem, the Church of the triumphant elect, is described, Ap. 21, 10, which has twelve gates, marked with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel: where it is certain that not only Israelites according to the flesh belong to that supernal city. Nor do these gates of Ezekiel correspond at all to the ancient Jerusalem. Because the gate of Ephraim is placed here to the East, which however was situated there to the North, as can be seen in Adrichomius and Villalpandus. Jerome also notes at chapter 48 that the names of the forty-eight cities, which in the volume of Numbers are given to the Levitical tribe for dwelling with their suburbs, are passed over in silence here, and the cities of the fugitives, of which three were given beyond the Jordan, namely Bosor and Ramoth and Gaulon in the two and a half tribes: and three within the Jor dan, namely Cades and Sichem and Cariatharbe. For there was no need in the description of the Saints and perfect conversation to describe the aids of fugitives. Which Israel needed while still placed on earth, and hastening through many labors and dangers to come to this city, and saying in each of the Saints: I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were. This is Jerome. Finally, the distinction between Jews and Gentiles is removed here, which, during the Old Testament, had to remain intact. Which is manifest from chapter 47, 22. Through this chapter, says Jerome, we learn, and the pride of the Jews is shaken off, that there is nothing divided between Israel and the people of the Gentiles; for if the land is divided to sojourners and aliens, together with those who are of the people of Israel, that is, the natives: it is doubtful to no one that the inheritance of the people of the Gentiles and the people of the Jews is the same: if, however, they have been converted to the worship of the God of Israel, which the name Christian properly possesses, the Jews having the letter of the law and we the spirit: they holding the parchments, and we Him who is written in the parchments. And among Moses the land is divided by lot: here, however, as we have said, it is assigned by the judgment of the Lord: and there is one possession for the sojourner and the Israelite, and in each tribe an inheritance is given, by the command of the Lord God. Vers. 15. FROM THE GREAT SEA] See on this place the man of greatest learning, John Selden, in the Appendix to Mare Clausum. WAY OF HETHALON] It is in the Damascus region of Syria: below 48, 1. VENIENTIBUS SEDADA] In the same tract, Num. 34, 8. Vers. 16. EMATH] Num. 13, 22. 24, 8 1. Reg. 8, 65. 2. Reg. 18, 34. BEROTHA] 2. Sam. 8, 8. Barathema in Ptolemy. SABARIM] Sora, as it seems to Ptolemy. HOUSE OF TICHON] Some take תיכון commonly, so that the middle tract is understood. But the Chaldean took it for a proper name, and rendered it the pool of Agbra. NEAR THE BORDER OF AURAN] LXX above the borders of Auranitis, as this land is called by Ptolemy. Vers. 17. AS FAR AS THE COURT OF ENON] You would translate more correctly, the village of Enan: as this interpreter is in Num. 34, 9. for Enon and Enan are the same, as appears by comparing the place below c. 48. It could also, with the former Hebrew word retained, be called Adrenan, as חצר עינון is ἀδράμυτῖ©. THAMAR] Thamaro in Ptolemy. Vers. 19. TO THE WATERS OF CONTRADICTION CADES] So that place is also called in Num. 27, 48. from the history which is in Num. 20. Vers. 22. TO YOU AND TO THE SOJOURNERS WHO HAVE COME TO YOU] After the example of that which had once been granted there to the Kenites. Jud. 1, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

HIC EST TERMINUS IN QUO POSSIDEBI- TIS TERRAM, IN DUODECIM TRIBUBUS ISRAEL] Hæc assignatio, & quæ sequitur capite postremo, locum habitura fuisset, si decem tribus non minus, quam Judæ & Benjaminis, se ad Deum convertissent. Sic enim pari- ter impetrassent reditum. Nunc pauci tantum permixti Judæ & Benjamini rediere, iique sedes cum illis habuere communes. Procedente tamen tempore, dono Regum etiam illa terra, quæ decem tribuum fuerat, Judæis con- cessa est, ut ex Josepho alibi ostendimus.

Assumit Grotius hanc visionem Propheti- cam, ac si facta sub hypothesi sit, vel adumbraret terram Sanctam, & possessiones tribuum in ea, sub conditione, qualem nempe habitura quæque tri- bus fuisset possessionem, si nimirum se ad Deum con- vertissent. At hic simpliciter assignantur possessio- nes tribubus omnibus. Nullius hypotheseos vel conditionis hic apparet vel minimum vestigium. Neque vero opus fuisset accurata designatione o- mnium terminorum, si intellexisset DEUS, tri- bus illas nunquam redituras. Non redeuntes nul- lis indigebant possessionibus. Deum vero, qui o- mnia prævidit ab æterno, frustra determinare i- stos limites voluisse, nullatenus consentaneum. Quapropter manifestum hic argumentum habe- mus, non posse hæc intelligi de terra Cananæa, & de duodecim tribubus Israel secundum literam, pro- ut sonant, sed de spirituali Cananæa, Ecclesia Christi, deque Israele secundum promissionem, ve- ris fidelibus, intelligenda esse. Duodecim ergo tri- bus sunt omnes fideles & Christiani. Portæ vero tres à singulis lateribus, & plagis mundi quatuor si- gnificant, undique ab omnibus plagis mundi patere ingressum in Ecclesiam. Quia ternarius est nume- rus perfectionis. Adde, quod simili ratione de- scribatur cælestis Hierosolyma, electorum trium- phantium Ecclesia, Ap. 21, 10. quod portas duode- cim, nominibus duodecim tribuum Israel insigni- tas habeat: ubi certum est, non Israelitas solum se- cundum carnem ad illam supernam civitatem per- tinere. Neque consonant hæ portæ Ezechielis o- mnino antiquæ Hierosolymæ. Quia porta Ephraim po- nitur hic ad Orientem, quæ vero ibi sita fuit ad Se- ptentrionem, ut apud Adrichomium, & Villalpandum videre est. Notat quoque Hieronymus ad c. 48. quod quadraginta octo civitatum, quæ in Numerorum vo- lumine tribui Leviticæ dantur ad habitandum cum suburbanis suis, hic silentur nomina, & civitates fugitivorum, quarum tres trans Jordanem, Bosor scilicet & Ramoth & Gaulon in duabus & di- midia tribu datæ sunt: & tres intra Jor- dantem, Cades videlicet & Sichem & Cariatharbe. Neque enim opus erat in descriptione Sanctorum & conversatione perfecta, fugitivorum describi auxilia. Quibus Israel indiguit adhuc in terra positus, & per multos labores atq; discrimina adhanc civitatem ve- nire festinans, & in singulis Sanctis loquens: Adve- na sum, atque peregrinus, sicut omnes patres mei. Hæc Hieronymus. Denique tollitur hic discrimen Judæorum & gentium, quod, durante Veteri Test. sartum tectum manere oportebat. Quod è cap. 47, 22. manifestum est. Per hoc capitulum, inquit Hieronymus, disci- mus, & decutitur supercilium Judæorum, nihil inter Israel & gentium populum esse divisum; si enim ad- venis & alienigenis, cum his, qui sunt de populo Israel, hoc est, indigenis, terra dividitur: nulli dubium, ean- dem esse hæreditatem populi gentium & populi Judæo- rum: si tamen conversi fuerint ad cultum Dei Israel, quod proprie nomen possidet Christianum, habentibus Judæis legis literam & nobis spiritum: illis tenentibus membranas, & nobis eum, qui scriptus est in membra- nis. Et apud Moysen sorte terra dividitur: hic au- tem ut diximus, Domini judicio delegatur: unaq; pos- sessio est advenæ & Israeli, & in singulis tribubus da- tur hæreditas, jubente Domino Deo. Vers. 15. A MARI MAGNO] Vide ad hunc locum maximæ eruditionis virum Joannem Seldenum in Appen- dice maris clausi. VIA HETHALON] Est in Syria Damascena: in- fra 48, 1. VENIENTIBUS SEDADA] In eodem tractu, Num. 34, 8. Vers. 16. EMATH] Num. 13, 22. 24, 8 1. Reg. 8, 65. 2. Reg. 18, 34. BEROTHA] 2. Sam. 8, 8. Barathema Ptolemæo. SABARIM] Sora, ut videtur Ptolemæo. DOMUS TICHON] Quijdam תיכון sumunt com- muniter, ut intelligatur tractus medianus. At Chaldæus pro nomine sumsit proprio, reddidque piscinam Agbræam. JUXTA TERMINUM AURAN] LXX ἐπάνω ὁρίων Αὐρανίτιδος, quomodo hæc terra vocatur à Ptolemæo. Vers. 17. USQUE AD ATRIUM ENON] Rectius vertas, villam Enan: ut hic interpres Num. 34, 9. est enim idem Enon & Enan, ut apparet collato loco infra c. 48. Pos- set etiam retenta voce priore Hebræa dici Adrenan, quomo- do חצר עינון est ἀδράμυτῖ©. THAMAR] Thamaro Ptolemæo. Vers. 19. AD AQUAS CONTRADICTIONIS CA- DES] Sic vocatur is locus etiam Num. 27, 48. ex histo- ria quæ est Num. 20. Vers. 22. VOBIS ET ADVENIS QUI ACCESSE- RVNT AD VOS] Ad exemplum ejus, quod ibi olim Ci- næis concessum fuerat. Jud. 1, 16.

## 48:1 Argument
CHAPTER XLVIII.

The division of the Holy Land into twelve tribes: where the firstfruits and the sanctuary are: the place of the Priests and Levites; the measure of the city in a square with its suburbs: the possession of the prince and the twelve gates of the city according to the twelve tribes.

Latin:

CAPUT XLVIII.

Divisio terræ Sanctæ in duodecim tribus: ubi sunt primitiæ & sanctuarium: locus Sa- cerdotum ac Levitarum; mensura civita- tis in quadro cum suburbanis: possessio prin- cipis & duodecim portæ civitatis juxta duodecim tribus.

## 48:15
Vers. 15. ROUND ABOUT EIGHTEEN THOUSAND] Which sum the sides taken four times make: for each side was commanded to be four thousand and five hundred cubits. Some say they were as many leagues, to which Lyranus accedes: whence Finus, lib. 2. Flagell. Judæorum cap. 8. concludes that by Jerusalem the congregation of the Gentiles to Christ, or the universality of Christians, is to be understood: because otherwise, he says, this city would equal the magnitude of the world, if it did not exceed it: but however that may be opposed to the Jews κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον, who understand 18,000 leagues here; we admit, however, that not leagues, but reeds are to be understood: which according to Jerome's computation make forty-four thousand paces, and three hundred and forty paces.

Latin:

Vers. 15. PER CIRCUITUM DECEM ET OCTO MILLIA] Quam summam faciunt quater sumta latera: nam latus unumquodque jussum erat esse quater mille & quingentorum cubitorum. Abbini totidem leucarum fuisse dicunt, qui- bus accedit Lyranus: unde Finus lib. 2. Fla- gell. Judæorum cap. 8. concludit, per Jerusalem congregationem gentium ad Christum, seu universi- tatem Christianorum intelligendam esse: quia alio- quin, inquit, civitas hæc mundi magnitudinem adæ- quaret, si non superaret: sed utut κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον Judæis id opponi possit, qui 18000. leucarum hic intelligunt; Admittimus tamen non leucas, sed calamos subaudiri: qui juxta Hieronymi compu- tationem efficiunt quadraginta quatuor millia pas- suum, & trecentos quadraginta passus.

## 48:35
THE NAME OF THE CITY FROM THAT DAY THE LORD IS THERE] The Lord is there, supply, dwells: not that it is called by this name, but that this epithet will most rightly belong to it. You have similar things in Jer. 23, 6. and 33, 16. where see.

From that epithet, however, it is evident that that city is not earthly, the metropolis of Judea, whose name is Jerusalem; but spiritual, the Church of Christ, to which this is proper and perpetual; that the Lord dwells in it; who never departs from it, as He departed from that earthly city: Matt. 23, 38. 39. Concerning which name, let the blessed Hafenreffer be seen at length, lib. 1. cap. 150. seqq. And Rabbi Solomon acknowledges on this place that all things which are written in Ezekiel concerning Jerusalem are to be understood of the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem. And hence the holy Bernard received that holy city with this greeting, serm. 6. to the knights of the temple: Hail, holy city, which the Most High Himself sanctified as His own tabernacle, by which so great a generation might be saved in you and through you. Hail, City of the great King, from which new and pleasant miracles for the world have never been lacking from the beginning. Hail, Mistress of the Gentiles, prince of provinces, possession of the Patriarchs, mother of the Prophets and Apostles, imitator of the faith, glory of the Christian people, which God has always allowed to be attacked from the beginning; so that for brave men, as it was an occasion of virtue, so it might also be of salvation. Hail, land of promise, which once flowing with milk and honey for your inhabitants alone, now offers the remedies of salvation and the food of life to the whole world. A land, I say, good and best, which in that most fruitful bosom of yours, receiving the heavenly grain from the ark of the Father's heart, have brought forth such great harvests of Martyrs from the heavenly seed, and nevertheless, from all the rest of the race of the faithful, you have produced fruit, a fertile soil, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold, multiplied over all the earth. Whence also, most sweetly satisfied and most opulently satiated from the great multitude of your sweetness, those who have seen you belch forth the memory of the abundance of your pleasantness everywhere, and even to the end of the earth they speak of the magnificence of your glory to those who have not seen you, and they recount the wonders which are done in you. Glorious things are said of you, O City of God.

A twin name to this, which the spiritual Jerusalem is said to be going to have, is THE LORD IS THERE, which the heavenly Jerusalem received in Rev. 21:3: BEHOLD THE TABERNACLE OF GOD IS WITH MEN, AND HE WILL DWELL WITH THEM. How great its happiness, how great its glory is, we perceive as if through a lattice, when we look upon the Apocalyptic διατύπωσιν [delineation], yet ἀναποκάλυπτον & ἀκατάληπτον [unrevealed and incomprehensible]. Because eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man. And they are mere ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα [unspeakable words] even to him who has usurped them with his own eyes, and drunk them in with his own ears. Ah, when shall we arrive there, so that we may see eternally, hear eternally, and celebrate with eternal praises, and confess: as we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God. The Lord has founded it forever Ps. 48:8. יהוה שמה Jehovah is there; there Jehovah SHALL BE ALL IN ALL. Come Lord Jesus, Come, and lead us there. You who by your blood have initiated for us a new and living way through the veil, that is, your flesh.

Jesus, sweetness of hearts, living fountain, light of minds, exceeding every joy and every desire. I desire you a thousand times; My Jesus, when will you come! When will you make me joyful, when will you satisfy me with yourself!

Jesus, angelic glory, in the ear a sweet song, in the mouth a wondrous honey, in the heart heavenly nectar. Now I see what I have sought; I hold what I have longed for, I languish with the love of Jesus. And I see the whole with my heart.

Glory to You Lord Jesus! AMEN.

Latin:

NOMEN CIVITATIS EX ILLA DIE DOMI- NUS IBIDEM] Dominus ibi, supple, habitat: non quod hoc nomine appelletur, sed quod hoc ἐπίθετον jure opti- mo ipsi sit competiturum. Similia habes Jer. 23, 6. & 33, 16. ubi vide.

Ex eo vero Epitheto constat, civitatem illam non esse terrenam, Judææ Metropolin, cui nomen Hierusalem; Sed spiritualem, Ecclesiam Christi, cui proprium est hoc, atque perpetuum; Quod Dominus in ea habitet; Qui nunquam ab ea rece- dit, uti à terrena ista civitate discessit: Matth. 23, 38. 39. De quo nomine prolixe videatur B. Ha- fenrefferus lib. 1. cap. 150. seqq. Et agnoscit Rabbi Sa- lomo in hunc locum, omnia quæ in Ezechiele de Jerusalem scribuntur, de sancta civitate superna Jerusalem intelligenda esse. Et hinc sanctam illam civitatem hac salutatione excepit sanctus Bernhar- dus serm. 6. ad milites templi: Salve civitas sancta, quam ipse sanctificavit sibi tabernaculum suum Altis- simus, quo tanta in te & per te generatio salvaretur. Salve Civitas Regis magni, ex qua nova, & jucunda mundo miracula nullis temporibus defuere ab initio. Salve Domina gentium, princeps provinciarum, Pa- triarcharum possessio, Prophetarum mater, & Apo- stolorum, imitatrix fidei gloria populi Christiani, quam Deus semper a principio passus est oppugnari; ut viris fortibus sicut virtutis, ita foret & occasio salutis. Salve terra promissionis, quæ olim fluens lac & mel tuis duntaxat habitatoribus, nunc universo orbi re- media salutis, vitæ porrigis alimenta. Terra, in- quam, bona & optima, quæ in fœcundissimo illo sinu tuo, ex arca paterni cordis cœleste granum suscipiens, tantas ex superno semine Martyrum segetes protuli- sti, & nihilominus ex omni reliquo fidelium genere fructum, fertilis gleba, trigesimum & sexagesimum & centesimum super omnem terram multipliciter pro- creasti. Unde & de magna multitudine dulcedinis tuæ jucundissime satiati, & opulentissime saginati, me- moriam abundantiæ suavitatis tuæ ubique eructant, qui te viderunt, & usque ad extremum terræ ma- gnificentiam gloriæ tuæ loquuntur eis, qui te non vide- runt, & enarrant mirabilia, quæ in te fiunt. Glorio- sa dicta sunt de te, Civitas Dei.

Geminum huic nomen, quod spiritualis Hie- rosolyma habitura dicitur, DOMINUS IBI est, quod cœlestis Hierosolyma Ap. 21, 3. accepit: EC- CE TABERNACULUM DEI CUM HOMI- NIBUS, ET HABITANT CUM EIS. Quanta à. illius felicitas, quanta gloria sit, veluti per transen- nam perspicimus, cum Apocalypticam διατύπωσιν, sed ἀναποκάλυπτον & ἀκατάληπτον respicimus. Quia oculus non vidit, auris non audivit, neque in cor hominis ascendit. Et mera sunt ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα etiam illi, qui oculis suis ea usurpavit, auribusq; suis hau- sit. Ah quando eo deveniemus, ut æternum videa- mus, æternum audiamus, æternisque elogiis cele- brcmus, & confiteamur: sicut audivimus, sic vidimus in civitate Domini virtutum, in civitate Dei nostri. Dominus fundavit eam in æternum Psal. 49, 7. יהוה שמה Iehovah ibi; ibi Jehovah OMNIA ERIT OMNIBUS. Veni Domine Jesu, Veni, & eo nos perducito. Qui sanguine tuo initiasti nobis viam novam, & viventem per velamen, vel carnem tuam.

Jesu dulcedo cordium Fons vivus lumen mentium Excedens omne gaudium Et omne desiderium. Desidero te millies; Mi Jesu quando venies! Me lætum quando facies Me de te quando saties!

Jesu Decus angelicum, In aure dulce canticum, In ore mel mirificum, In corde nectar cœlicum, Jā quod quæsivi video; Quod concupivi teneo, Amore Jesu langueo. Et corde totum video.

Gloria Tibi Domine Jesu! AMEN.

# Daniel

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
GROTIUS' PREFACE.

The Greeks say that Metrodorus of Scepsis was a man of rare erudition and eloquence, but that he reached such a degree of friendship with King Mithridates that the king made the greatest use of his counsels: but that through the arts of rivals he fell into the king's anger, a harbinger of death, as Solomon says: and so he perished by an evil fate. Daniel, strong in talent, instructed in all the arts that were valued among the Chaldeans, and furthermore distinguished by great gifts from God, was in high favor with the Chaldean kings: but he too incurred an offense which would have brought him certain death, had not the power of God intervened. "These are the rewards of tyrannical friendship," said Aratus of Sicyon. We have stated elsewhere the reason why the Hebrews do not count Daniel among the Prophets, namely that he led a life not Prophetic, but satrapal, just as David led a royal one. Wherefore they say that they indeed wrote through the Holy Spirit, but were not Prophets. Nevertheless, both Christ and Josephus call Daniel a prophet, and Maimonides, in the second part of the Guide for the Perplexed, affirms that he can be called so in a more general sense. The Church, however, as Jerome warns us, uses in Daniel not the version of the LXX Interpreters, but that of Theodotion, because it seems to have expressed the sense more correctly, which Origen, a diligent reader of the versions, had also judged. The same Jerome says that for understanding the final parts of Daniel, the manifold history of the Greeks is necessary: namely that of Sutorius Callinicus, Diodorus, Jerome (the Egyptian, who wrote the history of the Phoenicians), Polybius, Posidonius, Claudius, Theon, and Andronicus surnamed Alypius, whom, he adds, Porphyry also says he followed, namely in explaining Daniel, whose authority he said the books were written after the event in order to evade: how impudent this is, we have said elsewhere. Jerome continues, and among those whom he says are necessary, he also places the books of Josephus, and those whom Josephus cites: and especially, he says, those of Livy, and Pompeius Trogus, and Justin, who all narrate the history of the final vision, and describe the wars of Syria and Egypt, that is, of Seleucus and Antiochus and the Ptolemies, from after Alexander up to Caesar Augustus. Since nothing of all these whom Jerome names has reached us, except Josephus and Justin, we must use these: and to these must be added Strabo and Appian, who undoubtedly also used the books of those who perished. Then indeed, in place of Porphyry, and all those books read by Porphyry, we must use those things which Jerome teaches us from Porphyry. Among the Greeks, however, Polychronius, a diligent reader of Porphyry, and Chrysostom, approached most closely to the sense of these prophecies. It matters a great deal that these prophecies be well understood: first, so that the providence and foreknowledge of God may appear the more clearly: then, so that a perverse interpretation, confusing the times, may not hinder the Jews from recognizing the times of the Messiah: which is done most of all by those who drag things that have a manifest sense when spoken of Antiochus Illustris to the Antichrist, like Hippolytus and many others.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM GROTII.

METRODORUM Scepsium ajunt Græci virum fuisse raræ eruditio- nis & eloquentiæ, pervenisse au- tem eum ad amicitiæ gradum a- pud regem Mithridatem, ut rex ejus maxime consiliis uteretur: sed æmulorum artibus incidisse in iram regis, prænuntiam mor- tis, ut loquitur Solomon: itaque eum malo fato periisse. Daniel ingenio valens, omnibus institutus, quæ apud Chal- dæos valebant artibus, præterea magnis à Deo donis egre- gius, in flagrante fuit gratia apud reges Chaldæos: sed is quoque offensam incurrit, quæ ei certam attulisset mor- tem, nisi Dei potentia intervenisset. Ταῦτά ἐστι τὰ ἐπίχει- ρα τῆς τυραννικῆς φιλίας, ajebat Aratus Sicyonius. Cur Da- nielem Prophetis non accenseant Hebræi causam alibi di- ximus, nempe quod vitam egerit non Propheticam, sed satrapicam, ut David regalem. Quare eos ajunt scripsif- se quidem per Spiritum Sanctum, sed Prophetas non fuis- se. Attamen & Christus & Josephus Danielem vocant Prophetam, & sic eum dici posse significatu generaliore af- firmat Maimonides parte secunda Ductoris dubitantium. Utitur autem Ecclesia, ut Hieronymus nos monet, in Da- niele non LXX. Interpretum versione, sed Theodotio- nis, quod ea sensum rectius expressisse videatur, quod & Origenes lector versionum diligens judicaverat. Ait i- dem Hieronymus, ad intelligendas extremas partes Da- nielis, multiplicem Græcorum historiam esse necessariam: Sutorii videlices Callinici, Diodori, Hieronymi, (nempe Ægyptii, qui res Phœnicum scripsit) Polybii, Posidonii, Claudii, Theonis, & Andronici cognomento Alypii, quos, addit, & Porphyrius secutum se dicit, nempe in explican- do Daniele, cujus ille auctoritatem ut eluderet, scriptos dixit libros post eventum: quod quam sit impudens alibi diximus. Pergit Hieronymus, & inter eos quos dicit ne- cessarios, etiam Josephi ponit libros, & eorum quos po- nit Josephus: præcipueque, ait Livii, & Pompeii Trogi, atque Justini, qui omnes extremæ visionis narrant histo- riam, & post Alexandrum usque ad Cæsarem Augustum, Syriæ & Ægypti, id est, Seleuci & Antiochi & Ptolemæo- rum bella describunt. Horum omnium, quos nominat Hieronymus, cum ad nos nihil pervenerit, præter Josephum & Justinum, his nobis utendum est: addendusque his Stra- bo & Appianus: qui haud dubie etiam illorum qui perie- runt usi sunt libris. Tum vero pro Porphyrio, & tot illis libris Porphyrio lectis, utendum nobis iis quæ ex Porphyrio nos docet Hieronymus. Inter Græcos autem ad sensum ho- rum vaticiniorum proxime accessit Polychronius Porphy- rii lector diligens, & Chrysostomus. Bene autem intelli- gi hæc vaticinia refert plurimum: primum ut eo lucidius appareat Dei providentia & præscientia: deinde ne prava interpretatio tempora confundens impediat Judæos Mes- siæ tempora agnoscere: quod vel maxime illi faciunt, qui quæ de Antiocho illustri dicta sensum habent manifestum, ad AntiChristum trahunt, ut Hippolytus, multique alii.

## 1:1 Introduction: To the Grotian Preface and Other Prolegomena. Why Is Daniel Among the Hagiographa? Are the
TO THE GROTIAN PREFACE AND OTHER prolegomena. Why is Daniel among the Hagiographa? Are the Jews to be excused here? Concerning the interpretation of Porphyry: and that which is akin to it by Grotius. His own judgment concerning the Porphyrian matters. The name, and the time of the Prophet, and his excellence: as well as the scope and economy of the writing.

Setting aside the comparison of Daniel with Metrodorus of Scepsis, which he provides concerning the authority of Daniel according to the Hebrews, the better interpreters of prophecy, and the use of the German interpretation, let us examine the matter. The opinion of the Hebrews, by which they remove Daniel from the number of the Prophets and count him among the books of כתובים, or Hagiographa as they call them, is adorned with this color, that they do not count him among the Prophets for the reason that he did not lead a Prophetic life, but a Satrapal one. But life does not make a prophet, but rather Prophetic inspiration; nor were the authors of books such as Ruth and Chronicles excluded from the number of the Prophets and counted among the Hagiographa by the Jews because of a non-Prophetic life. And why are the Lamentations of Jeremiah counted among the Hagiographa, which were certainly written by a Prophet who led a Prophetic life? There must therefore be another reason why they distinguished the Hagiographa. Which they derive not from the institution of life, but from the mode of revelation. Namely, that revelation by the Holy Spirit is one thing, and revelation by Prophecy is another. This distinction, most accepted among the Rabbis, had by no means escaped Grotius. For they say that the Hagiographers indeed wrote by the Holy Spirit: but not by prophecy, although they do not explain the sense of this distinction in the same way. Most wish prophecy to be when revelation comes to one either sleeping, or to one awake, but in such a way that he is deprived of his senses, and being rapt out of himself, hears and sees something. They say the Holy Spirit is when the Spirit of the Lord invades a man who is awake, with his senses remaining intact, so that he speaks like another man, but with the Holy Spirit agitating him and dictating his words to his tongue, so that he may sing the praises of God: as Laurentius Fabricius in Partit. Codicis Ebr. c. 19 and Hottinger in Thesauro Philolog. lib. 2. c. 1. p. 491 teach.

But it is easily seen that this distinction is frivolous. For do all things that are written in the Mosaic books, do all things that occur in the historical books, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, nay, do all things that occur in the Prophets, contain revelations which were manifested to those sleeping through dreams, or to those awake through ecstasy? And who will admit that such revelations happened less to Daniel, whose book is certainly no less filled with visions and dreams than those of the other Prophets?

But perhaps there lies in it something treacherous; that the Jews do not count Daniel among the other Prophets, because they do not deem him worthy of the Prophetic seat, if indeed they see that his oracles too manifestly refute their impiety and their vain expectation of a future Messiah. Just as Theodoret inveighs in a long speech against the Jews, because they remove Daniel from the number of the Prophets. Whence also, as Hottinger notes l. c. pag. 510, they not only keep others from the reading of Daniel, but they themselves abstain from it, because, forsooth, the time of the arrival of the Messiah is defined too clearly in it. They prefer, indeed, that Daniel never be read: than that from the reading the same [things] lead others to the saving knowledge of Jesus of Nazareth. Maldonatus, however, excuses the Jews against Theodoret in the preface of his commentary on Daniel, p. 595. Nor do the Hebrews, when they place Daniel not among the Prophets, but among the Hagiographa, deny that he is a Prophet. Moreover, since they make eleven degrees of prophecy, they do not place [anyone] among the Prophets unless they have at least reached the third. That, however, is when it is said that the word of the Lord came to someone, just as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the other minor Prophets are accustomed to say: because Daniel does not say this, they do not place him among the Prophets of the first rank, but place him in the second [rank] of Prophets, in which they say David, Solomon, and many others are, whom they call prophets not in that singular way by which they call Isaiah and Jeremiah, but in a certain general way; but as far as authority is concerned, they attribute to him no less than to the others of the first rank of Prophets. Whatever, however, may be the case here regarding the opinion of the Jews, it certainly cannot be denied that Daniel was full of the Prophetic Spirit, that he had illustrious visions and prophetic dreams, and that whatever ἀξιώματα (axioms/dignities) belonged to other prophets, they applied to Daniel in a remarkable way, who, as Josephus says, book 10 of Antiquities, ch. 12, § 7, 'did not only continue to prophesy things to come, as did the other prophets, but also set the time at which these things would come to pass.' Nor was there any doubt about this in the time of Josephus among the Jews, as these words of his at the end of book 10 teach: ὅτι τὸ θεῖον αὐτῷ πνεῦμα συμπαρῆν: 'The Spirit of God,' he says of Daniel, 'was present with him'; likewise: ὡς πάντα γὰρ αὐτῷ παραδόξως ὡς ἑνί τινι τῶν μεγίστων εὐτυχήθη προφητῶν. 'For all those things happened to him beyond belief, as to one of the greatest prophets': τὰ γὰρ βιβλία ὅσα δὴ συγγεγραμμένα καταλέλοιπεν, ἀναγινώσκεται παρ’ ἡμῖν ἔτι καὶ νῦν, καὶ πεπιστεύκαμεν ἐξ αὐτῶν, ὅτι ὡμίλει τῷ θεῷ. For the books which he left behind, written by himself, are read among us to this day, by whose testimony we believe that Daniel had communion with God. Nor did Maimonides speak improperly when he called Daniel a prophet in part 2 of the More Nevochim, ch. 45. Indeed, he says, 'Daniel, the volume of Ruth and Esther, all were written through the Holy Spirit, and thus all are called prophets in a general sense.' Therefore, he does not oppose the Holy Spirit to Prophecy. And in the Foundations of the Law, ch. 7, he assigns to Daniel the mark of a true Prophet. Abarbanel, however, refutes even the opinion of those in his commentary on Daniel who wish for Solomon and Daniel to be called prophets only על דרך העברה, by way of metaphor. Jacchiades also, in book 1, ch. 18, testifies concerning Daniel that he attained the highest limit of a prophet, even though he attributes the book itself to the Great Synagogue, and that according to the opinion of the Talmudists in Baba Bathra, ch. 1. which, however, others more correctly claim for Daniel, which is clear from ch. 8, 1; ch. 9, 2; 10; 11; 12. See Constantin l'Empereur in the Paraphrase of Jacchiades, p. 7. Now, as far as the interpreters of Daniel are concerned, Grotius praises Porphyry above all, whom he also followed in explaining the prophecies of Daniel, and for that reason he also commends Polychronius, who approached the meaning of these prophecies most closely, because he was a diligent reader of Porphyry. But it is unworthy, having abandoned Christian interpreters, to follow a pagan apostate, a most bitter enemy of the Christian faith, as Porphyry is called by Augustine, Tom. 10, sermon 143, de tempore, who, puffed up by the swelling of vain knowledge, recoiled from the most saving humility of Christ, as Augustine speaks in book 10 of the City of God, ch. 28. For he was previously imbued with our piety, from which he later fell away, and attacked it with such great rage, as Ludovico Vives notes on this passage of Augustine.

Whom Grotius rashly excuses, acting as an advocate not only for Rabbinic ἀπαισία (ignorance/folly), but also for pagan impiety (by which that infamous apostate Porphyry is certainly very celebrated among venerable antiquity): when at ch. 11 of Daniel, verse 45, he says this about him: 'Porphyry was, as we know from his writings which are extant, and from the fragments which remain among other writers, neither impious nor ignorant of history, but while he wishes to encrust paganism, which God willed to destroy, by following the counsels of human prudence, he pays great penalties for his contumacy.' But is this not extreme impiety, to fall away from the Christian faith, and to attack it most bitterly, and to encrust paganism, and conversely to attack the Christian faith with great rage? Is it not extreme impiety that he harasses the sacred writers, such as the holy Evangelists, St. Paul, whom he calls impudent, St. Peter, and others: nay, that he argues that Christ himself was inconsistent, as Jerome noted in various places; that he also traduces our Daniel, as the same Jerome testifies, Tom. 3, preface to Daniel, p. 28, and T. 5, preface to the Commentary on Daniel to Pammachius and Marcellus, where Jerome speaks thus about Porphyry: 'Against the prophet Daniel, Porphyry writes the twelfth book, not wishing it to have been composed by him whose name is inscribed upon it, but by someone who was in Judea in the times of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, and that Daniel did not so much speak of things to come as he narrated things past. Finally, whatever he said up to Antiochus, he says contains true history, but what he opined beyond that, because he did not know the future, he lied.' To whom Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea, responded most skillfully in three volumes, that is, the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth. Apollinarius also, in one large book, that is, the twenty-sixth, and before this, in part, Methodius. But because our purpose is not to respond to the calumnies of an adversary, which require a long discourse, but to discuss those things which were spoken by the Prophet for our own benefit, that is, for Christians; I advise this in the preface, that no one of the prophets has spoken so openly about Christ. For he does not only write that he is to come, which is common to the others: but he also teaches at what time he is to come, and arranges the kings in order, and enumerates the years, and announces the most manifest signs. These, because Porphyry saw them all completed and past, he could not deny, and overcome by the truth of history, he burst into this calumny: that those things which are said to be about to happen at the consummation of the world concerning the Antichrist, he contends were fulfilled under Antiochus Epiphanes because of the similarity of the deeds in certain respects. Whose attack is a testimony of the truth. For such was the credibility of the words, that to incredulous men the Prophet seems not to have spoken of future things, but to have narrated past ones. And yet, where the occasion offers itself in the explanation of the same volume, I shall endeavor to respond briefly to that calumny, and to oppose with a simple explanation the arts of philosophy, or rather secular malice, through which he strives to subvert the truth and to take away the clear light of the eyes with certain deceptions. This pious and praiseworthy intention was Jerome's; but Grotius preferred to assume those things which Jerome refuted in Porphyry, and to make them his own, and to defend the parts of Porphyry, or rather to absolve that rabid enemy of the Christian name from impiety. Whence we leave it to the wise to judge what should be thought of his commentaries on this Prophet, and with what spirit he approached the most holy prophecies. Nevertheless, the use of his interpretation, and that double [use] Grotius presents to us, that from it the providence and foreknowledge of God may appear more clearly, and that the same may be guarded against, lest a perverse interpretation, by confounding the times, prevents the Jews from recognizing the times of the Messiah. But the providence and foreknowledge of God can be most excellently established from these prophecies, even if they are not snatched away to Antiochus Epiphanes, as they are by the blasphemous Apostate and encruster of paganism, regarding the little horn in ch. 7, 8, and the King doing according to his own will and exalting himself against every god. Nor is the designation of the time of the Messiah's advent endangered, even if we, with the ancient Doctors, establish that this King is not Antiochus, but Antichrist. [2] But Grotius preferred, having abandoned the Doctors of the Church, to follow a pagan, an enemy of the Christian name, certainly not for the sake of the Christian faith, which suffers no loss regarding the calculation of Daniel, even if the latest prophecies are explained concerning the Antichrist; but, if the truth must be told, for the sake of the Roman Antichrist himself, so that he might not seem to lack his advocacy and patronage, since he has enervated with great effort the most celebrated passages of the New Testament which deal with the Antichrist, and indeed twisted the Pauline oracle partly to Caligula, partly to Simon Magus; but he snatched away the Johannine ones from Epist. ch. 2 and 4 and Apoc. 13 and 18 to Bar Kokhba, Apollonius, Trajan, and Domitian; then indeed he tries to prove that this illustrious prophecy of Daniel is to be accepted as being only about Antiochus Epiphanes, having also called Porphyry to his aid. [3] However, how much weight should be given to the trifles of Porphyry, by which he went about detracting from the authority of the Prophecy, was not unknown to Grotius, who had already once written these things about the same matter when he was writing on the Truth of the Christian Religion, book 1, § 18, for the vindication of the oracles of Daniel: The translation of the empire from the Assyrians to the Medes and Persians, and thence to Alexander the Macedonian, (predicted) by Daniel; whose successors would then be the Lagidae and Seleucidae in part; and what evils the Hebrew people would receive from all these, but especially from Antiochus Epiphanes, so clearly, that Porphyry, who compared the Greek histories existing in his own time with those prophecies, could not extricate himself otherwise than by saying that those things which were attributed to Daniel were written after the event; which is just as if someone were to deny that the works which exist under the name of Virgil, and have always been held as Virgilian, were written by him in the age of Augustus. [4] For there was never more doubt among the Hebrews about that which we are saying than there was about this among the Romans. Why, therefore, did Grotius allow himself to be seduced by this scoundrel? The Learned will not wonder without cause.

[Neb]uchadnezzar, yet he was divinely raised to such great honors, in the most powerful Empires, as have never befallen any other Jew, as B. Luther rightly observed in his German preface: and he was the wisest of all the men of his age, Ezek. 28:3, and the most pious, Ezek. 14:14, and not undeservedly called by Jerome, Epist. 103 to Paulinus, the one conscious of all times and a Polyhistor of the whole world. Whom the Papists confidently assert remained a celibate, but against the open text of Ezek. 14:16. But Daniel reached, according to the calculation of Pererius, 138 years: born in the 25th year of Josiah, died in the first year of Darius Hystaspis: according to others, however, he is believed to have lived about one hundred years: if indeed that age of 130 years was unusual at that time, and not more than 95 years elapsed from the 25th of Josiah until Darius, in whose first year Isidore says he died, in his book on the Life and Death of the Prophets.

The principal scope of this book, which the Savior himself in Matt. 24:15, Mark 13:14, asserted to be in the Prophetic Canon, with this warning added, ὁ ἀναγινώσκων νοείτω, is the kingdom of Christ, for the sake of which the Prophet presented the kingdoms of the World, so that he might teach that they were to perish, but the kingdom of Christ would remain forever, ch. 2:44 and ch. 7:14; concerning the preservation and propagation of which he dealt historically under the empire of the Chaldeans and Medo-Persians, as far as the last of its Monarchs, and the beginnings of the latter under Darius the Mede and Cyrus; but prophetically under other subsequent Emperors and empires and Monarchies and kingdoms up to the end of the Jewish Polity, indeed up to the consummation of the age, and he accurately defined the time of the advent of the Messiah in chapter 9; whence there are two parts of it: the former Historical, in the first 6 chapters: the latter Prophetic, in the remaining chapters, or the six latter ones. [12] The historical part is about Daniel the captive, and his education and the Babylonian School, ch. 1; then about Daniel with his companions raised up in the court, the occasion of whose exaltation, the revelation and explanation of Nebuchadnezzar's dream concerning the four Monarchies, is described in ch. 2; and the consequences first in the Chaldean Empire partly under Nebuchadnezzar, namely the liberation of Daniel's companions from the fiery furnace, ch. 3; as well as Nebuchadnezzar, whose rejection from the kingdom, predicted here according to the explanation of his new dream made by Daniel, and his wonderful restoration and conversion, is described in ch. 4; partly under Belshazzar: whose writing seen on the wall Daniel explained, confirmed by the event, the killing of the King, and the translation of the kingdom to the Medes, ch. 5. Then under the empire of the Medes and Persians, especially in the time of Darius the Mede, by whom he was cast into the den of lions, and from the same was in turn divinely liberated: The King having been converted to the acknowledgment of the true God, and Daniel having been more and more exalted under Darius and Cyrus.

Furthermore, some things must still be premised as προλεγόμενα concerning the Prophet and his present Prophecy, or the Prophetic writing: primarily regarding the Chronology, and the scope, and the οἰκονομίαν of the book.

The name DANIEL, by which also one of the sons of David was distinguished (1 Chron. 3:1) and one of the descendants of Ithamar (Ezra 8:2), is related to the name Dan, the etymology of which is explained in Gen. 30:5: 'He has pleaded my cause'; so that Daniel is 'He has judged for me,' or 'God is my judge and avenger.'

The prophetic part presents the prophecies revealed to Daniel partly under Belshazzar in the first year of his reign concerning the 4 Monarchies and Christ the King, established by the Ancient of Days (ch. 7), and partly in the third year with the explanation of Gabriel concerning the destruction of the Persian kingdom and the beginning of the Monarchy of the Greeks, and the time of Antiochus Epiphanes (ch. 8); then under Darius the Mede, concerning the LXX mystical weeks until Christ the Leader and the confirmation of the covenant (ch. 9); then under Cyrus, in the remaining three chapters, which exhibit first the preparation for the revelation made through the Son of God and an angel (ch. 10): then the revelation itself concerning future things, namely concerning those things which, under the Old Testament after the end of the three Persian Monarchs and the empire of Alexander the Great divided into the Kings of Syria and Egypt, were to happen primarily under Antiochus Epiphanes (ch. 11, up to v. 35), as well as concerning those things which [are] in the New Testament. Daniel lived at about the same time that Jeremiah and Ezekiel flourished: and he described some deeds of his own time, deeds, I say, of the Chaldeans, Medes, and Persians (following the history of the books of Kings to that extent) from the third year of Jehoiakim to the …third year of Cyrus, that is, about 73 years, from the deportation of Jehoiakim, from which the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity are counted to the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus, whose third year is designated in ch. 10:1. He who was born of the tribe of Judah and of royal lineage, as seems to be hinted at in ch. 1:3 and 2 Kings 20:18, although he was captured with King Jehoiakim, by Nebuchadnezzar

In Christ the Great, ch. 11. [the rest] will happen toward the end of the world, ch. 12. Cornelius a Lapide adds, with Maldonatus, that the third part of the Prophet is likewise historical in the two final chapters, 13 and 14, in the Greek and Latin Vulgate text, concerning Susanna and Bel: But that is rather fabulous, as it is called by Origen, Eusebius, and Apollinaris, as Cornelius admits, and is entirely alien to the divine Canon: inasmuch as it does not exist in the Hebrew Canon, as Jerome testifies in his prologue; hence Lyranus and Dionysius the Carthusian deny that these belong to the Canon, to whom Cornelius a Lapide says this should be forgiven, because they lived before the Council of Trent. But it is not to be forgiven to the Council of Trent that it defined that a book, which was never in the Hebrew Canon and is contrary to the Canonical books, as has been demonstrated elsewhere, should be reckoned among the Canonical books of the Old Testament. And Bellarmine himself, in book 1 of On the Word of God, ch. 9, judges that the Daniel who delivered Susanna, destroyed Bel, and killed the Dragon, and sat in the lions' den for six days, is not the same as our Prophet, but was from the tribe of Levi, according to Jerome. Concerning which, elsewhere. But we shall now proceed to the annotations themselves, and we shall endeavor both to illustrate the Prophecy and to respond to the calumny and distortion of Grotius—as Jerome did to that of Porphyry—and to oppose with a simple explanation the arts of philosophy (or philology), nay, the secular malice through which he strives to subvert the truth and to take away the clear light of the eyes with certain prestidigitations. With the same Jerome leading the way, however, we vow and pray that the Lord and Savior may respond for his own cause, in his own sense, through our mouth, who says to the Prophet: Open your mouth and I will fill it. For if, when we have been seized before judges and tribunals, he warns us not to think about what we ought to answer, how much more is he able to fight his own battles against blaspheming adversaries and to conquer in his servants. May this be done, Lord Jesus, for the manifestation of the heavenly truth and for the praise and glory of your one name. AMEN.

Latin:

AD PRÆLOQVIUM GROTIA- NUM ET ALIA προλεγόμενα. Daniel cur inter Hagiographos? An excusandi hic Judæi? De interpretatione Porphyrii: & ei gemina Grotii. Hujus judicium pro- prium de Porphyrianis. Nomen, & tem- pus Prophetæ, ejusque præstantia: nec non scopus & οἰκονομία scripti.

Missa collatione Danielis cum Metrodero Sce- psio, quæ de auctoritate Danielis secun- dum Ebræos, interpretibus Prophetiæ melioribus & interpretationis Germanæ usu tradit, dispicia- mus. Ebræorum sententiam, qua Danielem Prophetarum numero eximunt, & libris כתובים, vel hagiographis, quos vocant, accensent, hoc colore ornat, quod ipsum ideo Prophetis non an- numerent, quod vitam non egerit Propheticam, sed Satrapicam. Sed Prophetam non facit vita, ve- rum inspiratio Prophetica; neque ob vitam non Propheticam librorum ex. grat. Ruth & Paralipo- menorum auctores exclusi e Prophetarum nume- ro, & hagiographis annumerati sunt a Judæis. Et cur hagiographis Threni Jeremiæ accensentur, qui utique a Propheta, qui vitam Propheticam ges- sit, scripti sunt? Aliam ergo causam subesse opor- tet, cur Hagiographa distinxerint. Quam non a vitæ instituto, sed a revelationis modo depro- munt. Quod nempe alia sit revelatio per Spi- ritum Sanctum, alia per Prophetiam. Quæ distin- ctio apud Rabbinos receptissima minime latue- rat Grotium. Dicunt enim scripsisse hagiographos quidem per Spiritum Sanctum: Sed non per pro- phetiam, quamvis istius distinctionis sensum non eadem ratione explicent. Plerique Prophetiam esse volunt, cum revelatio vel dormienti obtingit, vel vigilanti, sed ita ut sensibus privetur, & ex- tra se raptus aliquid audiat & videat. Spiritum Sanctum esse dicunt, cum Domini Spiritus homi- nem vigilantem integris manentibus sensibus in- vadit, ut loquatur instar alius hominis, sed Spi- ritu Sancto ipsum agitante & verba ejus lingua di- ctante, ut laudes Dei decantet: uti Laurentius Fa- bricius in partit. Codicis Ebr. c. 19. & Hottingerus Thesauro Philolog. lib. 2. c. 1. p. 491. docent.

Quam vero distinctionem frivolam esse, fa- cile constat. Num enim omnia, quæ in libris Mosaicis, num quæ in Historicis, Josuæ, Judicum, Samuelis, Regum, imo num omnia, quæ in Pro- phetis occurrunt scripta, revelationes continent, quæ dormientibus per somnia, per ecstasin vigi- lantibus manifestatæ sunt? Et quis admittet, Da- nieli minus tales revelationes obtigisse, cujus cer- te liber visionibus, somniisque non minus refer- tus est, quam cæterorum Prophetarum?

Sed in eo latet forte ὕπουλόν τι; quod Judæi Danielem aliis Prophetis non accensent, quod nempe sede Prophetica non dignentur ipsum, si- quidem videant, nimis manifeste ejus oracula impietati ipsorum & inani expectationi Messiæ futuri refragari. Quemadmodum Theodorelus longa oratione invehitur in Judæos, quod Danie- lem de Prophetarum numero demant. Unde etiam, notante Hottingero l. c. pag. 510. non alios tantum a Danielis lectione arcent, sed & ipsi ab eadem abstinent, quia nimirum tempus adven- tus Messiæ nimis clare in eo definitur. Malunt u- tique Danielem nunquam legi: quam ex lectione eadem alios ad salutarem Jesu Nazareni notitiam deduci. Excusat tamen Judæos adversus Theodore- tum Maldonatus in procœmio commentarii in Da- niel. p. 595. Neque Hebræi, cum Danielem non inter Prophetas, sed inter hagiographos ponunt, Prophe- tam esse negant. Cæterum cum undecim Prophetiæ gradus faciant, non ponunt inter Prophetas, nisi qui saltem ad tertium pervenerunt. Is autem est, cum dicitur verbum Domini ad aliquem factum esse, quemadmodum Isaias, Jeremias, Ezechiel, cæterique minores Prophetæ solent dicere: quod quia Daniel non dicit, non collocant inter Prophetas primige- neris, sed in secundo Prophetarum ponunt, in quo Davidem, Salomonem multosque alios esse dicunt, quos non singulari illo, quo Isaiam & Jeremiam, sed generali quodam modo Prophetas appellant; quod au- tem attinet ad auctoritatem, non minorem illis, quam cæteris primi generis Prophetis attribuunt. Quic- quid vero hic de sensu Judæorum sit, negari certe non potest, Danielem plenum fuisse Spiritu Pro- phetico, habuisse illustres visiones & somnia Prophe- tica, & quæcunque ἀξιώματα Prophetarum alio- rum fuere, insigni ratione Daniele convenire, qui, Josepho dicente, lib. 10. antiquit. c. 12. 8 τὰ μέλλον- τα μόνον προφητεύων διετέλει καθάπερ καὶ οἱ ἄλ- λοι προφῆται, ἀλλὰ κὴ καιρὸν ὥριζειν, εἰς ὃν ταῦτα ἀποβήσεται. Neque de eo dubium fuisse Jo- sephi tempore penes Judæos hæc ejus in fine libri 10. docent: ὅτι τὸ θεῖον αὐτῷ πνεῦμα συμπαρῆν: Spiritus Dei, inquit de Daniele, aderat ei; Item: ὡς πάντα γὰρ αὐτῷ παραδόξως ὡς ἑνί τινι τῶν μεγί- στων εὐτυχήθη προφητῶν. Omnia illa supra fidem, & quantum maximorum Prophetarum ulli fuccedebant: τὰ γὰρ βιβλία ὅσα δὴ τυγγεγραψάμλνος καταλέ- λοιπεν, ἀναγινώσκεται παρἡμῖν ἔτι κὴ νῦν, καὶ πε- πιστεύκαμλν ἐξ αὐτῶν, ὅτι ὡμίλει τῷ θεῷ. Legun- tur enim apud nos in hunc diem libri, quos à se conferi- ptos reliquit, quorum testimonio credimus fuisse Da- nieli cum Deo commercium. Neque vero Maimoni- des improprie solum Danielem Prophetam dixit part. 2. More Nevochim cap. 45. Imo, Daniel, inquit, volumen Ruth. & Esther, omnia per Spiritum Sanctum scripta sunt, & sic etiam omnes vocantur in genere Prophetæ. Non ergo opponit Spiritum San- ctum Prophetiæ. Et in fund. Leg. cap. 7. assignat Danieli veri Prophetæ notam. Abarbanael vero refellit etiam eorum sententiam commentat. in Danielem, qui Salomonem & Danielem tantum על דרך העברה per modum Metaphoræ Prophe- tas dici volunt. Jacchiades etiam lib. 1. c. 18. testatur de Daniele, quod summum Prophetæ terminum af- secutus sit, etsi librum ipsum tribuat Synagoga ma- gnæ, idque ex sententia Thalmudistarum inBara Ba- thra cap. 1. quem vero rectius alii Danieli vendi- cant, quod è cap. 8, 1. c. 9, 2. 10. 11. 12. liquet. Vide Constantin. l'Emper. in Paraph. Jacchiad. p. 7. Jam quod ad Interpretes Danielis attinet, lau- dat Grotius imprimis Porphyrium, quem etiam in vaticiniis Danielis explicandis sequutus est, atque ideo etiam Polychronium commendat, qui ad sen- sum horum vaticiniorum proxime accesserit, eo quod Porphyrii lector diligens fuerit. At indignum, re- lictis Christianis interpretibus, sequi Apostatam paganum hostem fidei Christianæ acerrimum, ut vo- catur ab Augustino Porphyrius Tom. 10. sermon. 143. de tempore, qui à saluberrima Christi humili- tate tumore inflatus vanæ scientiæ refiluit, ut Augusti- nus loquitur lib. 10. de Civit. Dei cap. 28. Fuit enim prius imbutus pietate nostra, à qua postea defcipit, ma- gnaq́; rabie in eam invectus est, ut Ludov. Vives in hunc Augustini locum habet.

Quem temere excusat Grotius, non Rabbi- nicæ tantum ἀπαισίας, sed paganæ etiam impieta- tis, (qua certe infamis ille Apostata Porphyrius penes antiquitatem venerandam valde celebris est,) Advocatus: cum ad cap. 11. Danielis vers. 45. ita de eo : Erat Porphyrius, ut ex scriptis ejus, quæ extant, & ex fragmentis quæ apud scriptores restant alios, cognoscimus, neq́; impius, neq́; historia- rum ignarus, sed dum consilia sequens humanæ pru- dentiæ incrustare vult paganismum, quem Deus vo- lebat destruere, magnas dat contumaciæ pœnas. At annon hæc extrema impietas est, à fide Christiana desciscere, eandemque acerrime insectari, ac pa- ganismum incrustare, atque ex adverso in fidem Christianam magna rabie invehi? Annon extrema impietas quod sacros scriptores exagitet, utpote S. Evangelistas, S. Paulum, quem procacem dicit, S. Petrum, & alios: quin ipsum Christum incon- stantiæ arguat, ut passim notavit Hieronymus; quod Danielem etiam nostrum traducat, eodem Hieronymo teste, Tom. 3. præfat. in Dan. pag. 28. & T. 5. præfat. in Comment. Daniel. ad Pamma- chium & Marcell. ubi ita de Porphyrio habet Hie- ronymus: Contra Prophetam Danielem duodeci- mum librum scribit Porphyrius, nolens eum ab ipso, cujus inscriptus est nomine esse compositum, sed a quodam, qui temporibus Antiochi, qui appellatus est Epiphanes, fuerit in Judæa, & non tam Danielem ven- tura dixisse, quam illum narrasse præterita. Deni- que quicquid usq́; ad Antiochum dixerit, veram hi- storiam continere, quod autem ultra opinatus sit, quia futura nescivit, esse mentitum. Cui solertissime responderunt Eusebius Cæsariensis Episcopus tribus voluminibus, id est, octavodecimo, & nonodecimo, & vigesimo. Apollinarius quoq́;, uno grandi libro, hoc est, vicesimo sexto, & ante hoc ex parte Methodius. Verum quia nobis propositum est, non adversarii ca- lumniis respondere, quæ longo sermone indigent: sed ea, quæ à Propheta dicta sunt, nostris disserere, id est, Christianis; illud in præfatione commoneo, nul- lum Prophetarum tam aperte dixisse de Christo. Non enim solum scribit eum esse venturum, quod est commune cum cæteris: sed etiam, quo tempore venturus sit docet, & Reges per ordinem digerit, & annos enumerat, ac manifestissima signa prænunciat. Quæ, quia vidit Porphyrius universa completa & transacta negare non poterat, superatus historiæ ve- ritate, in hanc prorupit calumniam: ut ea, quæ in consummatione mundi de Antichristo futura dicun- tur, propter gestorum in quibusdam similitudinem sub Antiocho Epiphane impleta contendat. Cujus impugnatio testimonium veritatis est. Tanta enim dictorum fides fuit, ut Propheta incredulis homini- bus videatur non futura dixisse, sed narrasse præteri- ta. Et tamen sic ubi se occasio in explanatione ejusdem voluminis dederit, calumniæ illius strictim respondere conabor,& Philosophiæ artibus, imo malitiæ seculari, per quam subvertere nititur veritatem, & quibusdam præstigiis clarum oculorum lumen auferre, explana- tione simplici contraire. Hoc Hieronymi institutum pium ac laude dignum fuit; Sed Grotius maluit ea, quæ in Por- phyrio refutavit Hieronymus, assumere, ac sua facere, partesque Porphyrii tueri, imo rabio- sum illum hostem nominis Christiani ab impietate absolvere. Unde quid de ejus in hunc Prophetam commentis habendum, & quo Spiritu aggressus sit vaticinia sanctissima, cordatis judicandum relin- quimus. Usum tamen suæ interpretationis eumq; ge- minum fistit nobis Grotius, quod ex ea appareat lucidius Dei providentia & præscientia, quodque caveatur eadem, ne prava interpretatio tempora confundens impediat Judæos Messiæ tempora agnosce- re. At Dei providentia & præscientia constare ex his vaticiniis optime potest, etiamsi non cum blas- phemo Apostata, & paganismi incrustatore va- ticinia de cornu parvulo cap. 7, 8. & de Rege jux- ta voluntatem suam faciente & elevante se adversus omnem Deum ad Antiochum illustrem abripiantur. Neque temporis adventus Messiæ designatio pericli- tatur,utut cum antiquis Doctoribus hunc Regem non Antiochum, sed Antichristum esse statuamus. Sed maluit Grotius relictis Doctoribus Ecclesiæ paganum sequi, hostem nominis Christiani, non certe in gratiam fidei Christianæ, quæ quoad calculum Danielis nullam jacturam facit, etiamsi novissima vaticinia de Antichristo explicentur, sed si dicendum quod res est, in gratiam ipsius AntiChristi Romani, cui ne deesse videatur advo- catura & patrocinio suo, cum celeberrima loca Novi Testamenti, quæ de Anti Christo agunt, magno molimine enervavit, & Paulinum quidem oraculum partim ad Caligulam, partim ad Simo- nem Magnum detorsit; Johannea vero ex Epist. c. 2. & 4. & Apoc. 13. & 18. ad Barchochebam, Apol- lonium, Trajanum & Domitianum abripuit; tum vero hoc Danielis illustre vaticinium, non nisi de solo Antiocho illustri accipiendum esse, advocato etiam in subsidium Porphyrio, evincere conatur. Quantum autem nugis Porphyrii tribuendum sit, quibus autoritati Prophetiæ derogatum ivit, non ignotum erat Grotio, qui hæc de eodem jam o- lim, cum de Verit. Relig. Christ. scriberet l. 1. §. 18. tradiderat, ad vindicandum oracula Danielis: A Daniele (prædicta) translatio imperii ab Assyriis ad Medos ac Persas, inde ad Alexandrum Macedo- nem; cujus deinde ex parte successores forent Lagi- dæ, & Seleucidæ; quæque mala populus Hebræus ab his omnibus, maxime vero ab Antiocho illustri accepturus esset, adeo perspicue, ut Porphyrius, qui historias Græcas suo adhuc tempore exstantes cum vaticiniis istis contulit, aliter se expedire non po- tuerit, quam ut diceret ea, quæ Danieli tribueban- tur, post eventum fuisse scripta; quod perinde est, quasi quis neget, quæ sub Virgilii nomine exstant, & pro Virgilianis habita sunt semper, ab ipso scri- pta Augusti ævo. Non enim de isto, quod dicimus, magis unquam dubitatum inter Hebræos fuit, quam de hoc apud Romanos. Cur ergo ab hoc empæcta seduci se passus est Grotius? non immerito Do- cti mirabuntur.

bucadnezare, ad tantos tamen evectus divinitus honores fuit, in Imperiis potentissimis, quanti nulli unquam Judæo obtigêre, ut B. Lutherus in præfat. Germanica probe observavit: omnium- que seculi sui hominum sapientissimus fuit Ezech. 28, 3. & pientissimus Ezech. 14, 14. omnium tempo- rum conscius & totius mundi Polyhistor ab Hierony- mo non immerito vocatus Epist. 103. ad Paulin. Quem cælibem quidem mansisse confidenter asse- runt Papistæ, sed contra apertum textum Ezech.14, 16. Attigit autem Daniel juxta Pererii calculum 138. annos: natus Josiæ 25. denatus primo Darii Hy- staspidis: juxta alios vero centum circiter annos vixisse creditur: siquidem ista ætâs 130. annorum illo tempore inusitata fuerit, nec à Josiæ 25. usque ad Darium, cujus primo anno mortuum ipsum di- cit Isidorus l. de Vit. & obit. Prophet. effluxerint plures quam 95. anni.

Scopus præcipuus libri hujus, quem Salvator ipse Mattb. 24,15. Marc. 13,14. Canoni Prophetico asseruit, addita hac monitione ὁ ἀναγινώσκων νοείτω, regnum Christi est, cujus gratia regna Mun- di exhibuit Propheta, ut ea peritura,regnumChri- sti autem semper mansurum, doceret c. 2, 44. & c. 7, 14. de cujus etiam conservatione, ac propagatio- ne, sub imperio Chaldæorum, & Medo-Persarum, quoad illius extremos Monarchas, hujus vero pri- mordia sub Dario Medo, & Cyro bistorice; sub a- lis autem sequuturis Imperatoribus & imperiis, & Monarchiis, ac regnis usque ad finem Poli- tiæ Judaicæ, imo usque ad consummationem seculi Prophetice egit, & imprimis tempus adven- tus Messiæ accurate definivit cap. 9. unde duæ ejus sunt partes: Prior Historica, capp. 6. prioribus: posterior Prophetica capp. reliquis,vel sex posterio- ribus. Historicatum de Daniele captivo, ejusque informatione,& Schola Babylonica c. 1. tum de Da- niele cum sociis in aula evecto, cujus exaltationis occasio, somnii Nebucadnezaris de quatuor Mo- narchiis revelatio, & explicatio c. 2. describitur; & consequentia primum in Imperio Chaldaico par- tim sub Nebucadnezare, Sociorum nempe Danielis è fornace igneo liberatio cap. 3. nec non Nebucadneza- ris, cujus hic prædicta juxta expositionem novi e- jusdem somnii à Daniele factam, à regno rejectio, ejusdemque mirabilis restitutio & conversio c.4. par- tim sub Belsazare : cujus Scripturam in pariete visam expossuit Daniel ab eventu, interfectione Regis, & translatione regni ad Medos comprobatan cap. 5. Deinde sub imperio Medorum & Persarum,tempo- re imprimis Darii Medi, à quo in foveam leonum conjectus, & ex eadem vicissim divinitus liberatus fuit: Rege ad agnitionem veri Dei converso, & Da- niele sub Dario & Cyro magis magisque exaltato.

Cæterum præmittenda adhuc nonnulla προ- λεγόμενα de Propheta, & Prophetia ejus præsen- te, vel scripto Prophetico: imprimis quoad Chronologiam, & scopum, ac οἰκονομίαν libri.

Nomen DANIEL, quo etiam insignitus fuit unus è Davidis filiis 1. Par. 3, 1. & unus è po- steris Ithamar Esdr. 8, 2. cognatum est nomini Dan, cujus etymologia exponitur Gen. 30, 5. Causam meam egit; ut ita Daniel sit judicavit pro me, vel judex & vindex meus est Deus.

Prophetica pars sistit Prophetias tum sub Bel- sazare Danieli revelatas partim primo regni ejus anno de 4. Monarchiis, & Christo Rege, ab antiquo dierum constituto c. 7. partim anno tertio cum ex- plicatione Gabrielis de interitu regni Persici, & ini- tio Monarchiæ Græcorum, ac tempore Antiochi Epiphanis c. 8. tum sub Dario Medo, de LXX.heb- domadibus mysticis usque ad Christum Ducem, & ad confirmationem fœderis c. 9. tum sub Cyro, cæte- ris tribus capp. quæ exhibent primo præparatio- nem ad revelationem c. 10. per Filium Dei & ange- lum factam: deinde ipsam de futuris revelationem, utpote de iis, quæ sub Veteri Testamento post trium Persicorum Monarcharum exitum, & Alexandri M. imperium in Syriæ & Ægypti Reges divisum sub An- tiocho Epiphane imprimis eventura sint, cap. 11. usque ad v. 35. nec non de iis,quæ in N. T. sub Anti- Vixit autem Daniel eo fere tempore, quo floruit Jeremias, & Ezechiel: & gesta nonnulla sui temporis, gesta, inquam, Chaldæorum, Me- dorum & Persarum (historiam librorum Regum eatenus prosequens) à tertio Jojakimi ad tertium Cyri, hoc est, annorum LXXIII. circiter descri- psit, inde à deportatione Jojakimi, à qua LXX. captivitatis Babylonicæ anni ad primum Monar- chiæ Cyri numerantur, cujus tertius annus desi- gnatur cap. 10,1. Qui è tribu Iuda, & slemmate Regio procreatus, ut innui videtur cap. 1, 3. 2. Reg. 20, 18. etsi cum Rege Jojakimo captus fuerit, à Ne-

Christo Magno, cap. 11. reliquo, & sub finem Mundi evenient, cap. 12. Cornelius à Lapide addit cum Maldonado ter- tiam Prophetæ partem itidem Historicam duobus postremis capp. 13. & 14. in Græco & Latino Vulgato textu, de Susanna, & Bele: Sed ea fabulosa potius est, uti ab Origene, Eusebio, Apollin. faten- te Cornelio vocatur, & a Canone divino prorsus a- liena: utpòte in Ebræo Canone non extans, teste Hieronymo in prolog. proinde Lyranus & Dionys. Carthus. hæc ad Canonem pertinere negant, quibus id condonandum esse ait Cornelius à Lapide, quia fuerunt ante concilium Tridentinum. Sed condo- nandum Concilio Tridentino non est, quod li- brum, qui nunquam in Ebræo Canone fuit, & Canonicis, ut alibi demonstratum, contrariatur, Canonicis Veteris Testamenti accensendum esse de- finierit. Et censet Bellarminus ipse lib. 1. de Verbo Dei c. 9. non eundem esse Danielem, qui Susannam liberavit, Bel destruxit, ac Draconem interfecit, & in lacu leonum sex diebus sedit, cum Propheta no- stro, sed è tribu Levi, juxta Hieronymum. Quo de alias. Sed accedemus nunc ad ipsa annotata, ac tum illustrare Prophetiam, tum etiam calumniæ, & detorsioni Grotianæ, uti Hieronymus Porphyria- næ, respondere conabimur, & Philosophiæ (vel Philologiæ) artibus, imo malitiæ seculari, per quam subvertere nititur veritatem, & quibus dam præstigiis clarum oculorum lumen auferre, explanatione sim- plici contraire. Præeunte autem eodem Hierony- mo, vovemus & precamur, ut Dominus atq́ Sal- vator pro causa sua, suo sensu, nostro ore respondeat, qui loquitur ad Prophetam: Aperi os tuum & im- plebo illud. Si enim, cùm apprehensi fuerimus ante Judices & tribunalia, monet ne cogitemus, quid respondere debeamus, quanto magis contra ad- versarios blasphemantes sua potest bella bellare, & in servis suis vincere. Fiat id Dominé Jesu ad verita- tis cœlesti manifestationem, & unius nominis tui Laudem atque gloriam. AMEN.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. HISTORICAL. CHAPTER I.

Daniel, transferred into Chaldea with his companions, is committed to the instruction of Melzar, abstains from the King's food, makes successful progress in the Chaldean language and all-embracing wisdom, is also adorned with the gift of Prophecy, and is presented to Nebuchadnezzar and employed in his service along with his companions.

Verse 1.

IN THE THIRD YEAR OF THE REIGN OF JOAKIM KING OF JUDAH] At its end; because this expedition of Nebuchadnezzar fell for the greatest part into the fourth year of Joakim. Therefore Jeremiah 21:1 names the fourth year. But this is the eleventh year of Joakim reigning in the history of the Kings, namely because from that time he had received the kingdom from the Chaldeans. But the Hebrews did not consider him king until after the death of his brother Joahaz, who had been carried off to Egypt and was expected to return.

In a similar way Pererius, Ribera, Junius, and Ussher reconcile it, that the first year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar coincided almost entirely, or at least for the most part, with the third, and meanwhile also in some part with the fourth year of the reign of Joakim, and that he came about the beginnings of his reign, which still fell within the third year of Joakim. But Torniellus, at the year 3429, no. 3, attempts to prove that the first year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar did not touch the third year of Joakim at all, but began only in the fourth year, and thus he seeks a solution

Vol. 2 of the Annals, page 134, from the account of Berosus in Josephus, book 1 against Apion, and book 10 of the Antiquities, ch. 11, from which he concludes that Nebuchadnezzar, about one year before he succeeded his father in the kingdom of Babylon, waged war against the Jews and led certain captives to Babylon. To this, B. Walther adds his calculation in the Harmony on Daniel 1. B. Dn. D. Behm, in Chronol. Decad. 2, observation 6, page 248, notes: If anyone wished to connect the first year of Nebuchadnezzar immediately with the third of Joakim, he would fall into a manifest absurdity: for by this reasoning he would connect the ninth of Nebuchadnezzar with the eleventh of Joakim, which is against the Scripture, which connects the eleventh of Joakim with the seventh of Nebuchadnezzar ending and the eighth beginning, 2 Kings 25:8, Jer. 52:29. Daniel, therefore (and indeed alone), places the arrival of Nebuchadnezzar in the third year of Joakim. The latter part of the Kings, along with Jeremiah, begins the first year of Nebuchadnezzar from the taking of Jerusalem, which occurred when the fourth year of Joakim was well advanced, so that the first year of Nebuchadnezzar must be concatenated with the fourth and fifth of Joakim, and so on consequently. Whoever does not attend to this, as B. Behm judges, will cast himself headlong into various difficulties. Ussher, however, showed in his Sacred Chronology, p. 30, how those difficulties might be resolved. And in later and wiser meditations, B. D. Behm, in the Disputation on the term from which and to which of the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity, held at Königsberg in the year 1633, thesis 17, acknowledged that the first year of Nebuchadnezzar's arrival in Judea was the third year of Joakim begun, and the fourth entering.

Lyra, Tostatus, and Gesner initiate a different calculation, as does B. Meisner in his Babylonian Schol. part 1, § 12, so that the third year is understood as the one from which he began to pay tribute. By a contrary reasoning, Maldonatus on this passage, with R. Saadia, wishes the third year of Joakim to be indicated, from which he made a rebellion against the King of Babylon, and did not reign under tribute, but as a free man. He thinks he can prove this interpretation from four clear passages of Scripture compared with one another; but let these be read there (in Maldonatus). According to them, the eleventh or last year of Joakim is understood. But to count years from the payment of tribute, or even from rebellion and defection from the King of Babylon, when no mention of either this or that has preceded, is clearly unusual; furthermore, it seems too harsh that the third year of the REIGN should be said and understood as the eleventh year of the reign. And therefore the first reconciliation is to be preferred above all: according to which B. Meisner acknowledges that all things are plain, so that we are not forced to calculate the third year from elsewhere than from the beginning of the reign, as the letter itself requires. But as for what he thinks stands in the way of the same, that Daniel here speaks of that expedition of Nebuchadnezzar, by which he led away himself and other sons of princes as captives (which term we easily acknowledge is being referred to), that does not seem to us to stand in the way: for we do not concede that in Jer. 52:28 that abduction is designated, which is here assumed without proof. For there, another expedition of Nebuchadnezzar is being discussed. See what we have said regarding Jer. 52:28.

Latin:

PARS I. HISTORICA. CAPUT I.

Daniel in Chaldæam translatus cum sociis Melzaris informationi commissus à Regio cibo abstinens feliciter proficit in Chaldai- ca lingua, & sapientia omnigena, dono etiam Prophetiæ ornatus, ac sistitur Ne- bucadnezari, ejusque Ministerio una cum Sociis adhibetur.

Vers. 1.

ANNO TERTIO REGNI JOACIM REGIS JU- DA] Exeunte; quia hoc iter Nabuchodonosori maxima fui parte in annum quartum Joachimi incidit. Ideo quar- tam annum nominat Jeremias 21, 1. At undecimus hic an- nus est regnantis Joachimi in Regum historia, nempe quia ab eo tempore regnum à Chaldæis acceperat. At Hebræi eum pro rege non habuerunt, nisi post fratris Joachazi, qui in Ægyptum avečtus fuerat, & rediturus sperabatur, mortem.

SImili modo conciliant Pererius, Riebera, Iunius, Usserius, Primum regni Nabuchodonosaris annum concurrisse fere totum, vel saltem magna parte cum tertio, interim etiam ex aliqua parte cum quarto regni Jojakimi, eumque venisse circa initia regni sui, quæ adbuc in tertium annum Joakimi inciderunt. Sed Torniellus ad annum 3429. n. 3. probare conatur, annum primum regni Nabuchodonosaris, nul- latenus attigisse tertium Joakimi annum, sed anno quarto demum cœpisse, adeoque solutionem petit

Tom. 2. Annal. pag. 134. ex relatione Berosi apud Josephum lib. 1. contra Appion. & lib. 10. antiqui- tat. c. 11. unde colligit, Nebucadnezarem uno circiter anno, antequam Patri in regno Babylonis succede- ret, intulisse Judæis bellum, & captivos quosdam duxisse Babyloniam. Cui calculum adjicit B. Wal- therus in Harmon. ad Dan. 1. B. Dn. D. Behm. in Chronol. Decad. 2. observat. 6. pag. 248. notat: Si quis cum tertio Jojakimi primum Nebucadnezaris sta- tim colligare vellet, in manifestam lapsurum absurdi- tatem: hac enim ratione cum undecimo Jojakimi nonum Nebucadnezaris colligabit, quod est contra scripturam; quæ undecimum Jojakimi cum septimo Nebucadnezaris finiente, & octavo ineunte 2.
