In the History, Daniel took his name as it was commonly pronounced: In the visions, however, as was fitting for a prophet. Concerning this custom of the Jews of turning the names of false gods into reproach, with letters changed or transposed, see Moses of Coucy, in the 32nd prohibitive commandment. HE SAW A DREAM] As Joseph did once. For even in that way, no less than through inspiration, or divine visions, or a voice, God opens future things to those dear to him. HE COMPREHENDED IN A BRIEF DISCOURSE] In Chaldean: he said the head of the words: that is, he comprehended the sum of the matters in writing. AND SUMMARIZING, HE SAYS] In Chaldean: But Daniel having spoken, said.

Latin:

PARS II. PROPHETICA. SECTIO I. VISIONES DANIELIS SUB BELSAZARE. VISIO I. CAPUT VII.

Daniel vidit quatuor animantia, & in quar- to imprimis cornu parvum observavit. Vi- dit & ad antiquum dierum adductum Fi- lium hominis gloriam & potestatem divi- nam, & regnum æternum accipientem: Et impetravit explicationem istius visionis de quatuor Monarchiis, & regno Christi, & peculiariter de quarto imperio & parvo cornu contra sanctos obtinente usq; ad ju- dicium regnoq́ altissimi sempiterno.

Vers. 1.

ANNO PRIMO BALTASSAR REGIS BABY- LONIS] Hactenus Historia. Sequuntur nunc visa Danie- lis oblata divinitus, quæ quia variis temporibus contigêre, cogitur retrorsum ire, & repetere tempora, quæ in historia jam erat prætervectus, quod & aliis Prophetis evenit. Pro בלשאצר quod supra habuimus, codices Hebræi emen- datiores habent בלאשצר litera transposita, sensuque mu- tato. Id enim significat, Belum esse ignis hostici, id est, u- rendum flamma hostili, quod & Jeremias prædixerat L. 2. LI, 44. Ita prophetæ nomina in honorem idolorum re- perta levi flexu in eorundem contumeliam deterquebant. In Historia Daniel ejus nomen sumpsit, ita ut vulgo pro- nuntiabatur: In visis vero ita, ut prophetam decebat. De hoc more Judæorum nomina falsorum Deorum in con- tumeliam vertendi, literis mutatis aut transpositis, vide Mosem de Kotzi, præcepto vetante 32. SOMNIUM VIDIT] Ut olim Josephus. Nain etiam eo modo non minus quam per afflatum, aut visa divina, aut vocem, Deus futura dilectis sibi aperit. BREVI SERMONE COMPREHENDIT] In Chal- dæo: caput verborum dixit: id est, summam rerum scripto comprehendit. SUMMATIMQUE PERSTRINGENS, AIT] In Chaldæo: Effatus autem Daniel dixit.

## 7:2
Ver. 2. AND BEHOLD THE FOUR WINDS OF HEAVEN] A description of a huge storm: such as that; 'The East wind and the South wind rush together, and the South-West thick with storms.' Ovid, Tristia I, 2. 'For now the East wind gathers strength from the purple sunrise, now the West wind sent in the late evening is present. Now the cold North wind rages from the dry Bear: now the South wind wages battles with opposing front.' Lucan: 'First, O North-East wind, you raise your head from the Atlantic Ocean, stirring the tides: now as you lift, the sea was raging, and had raised all its waves against the crags: The cold North wind meets it and beats it back from the sea: And the surface hangs in doubt, by which wind it may fall. But the madness of the Scythian North wind conquered, and twisted the waves, and made the depths into hidden sands. Nor does the North wind carry the sea to the rocks, and it breaks its own sea in the flows of the North-East wind: and the stirred seas can even clash with the winds withdrawn. I would not believe that the threats of the East wind had ceased, nor that the South wind, dark with rains, had lain under the prison of the Aeolian rock.' Valerius Flaccus: 'The Thracian horses pour themselves out joyfully from the prison, and the West wind, and the South wind, the color of night on its wings, with its offspring of storm clouds, and the East wind, shaggy with storms and yellow-haired on its head with much sand.' But by the storm, understand wars. IN THE GREAT SEA] That is, not in some lake, such as the Asphaltite and the Gennesaret, which the inhabitants call seas: But in that sea which washes Syria, Egypt, and Judea. Thus also the Poets: 'Sweet it is in the great sea, when the winds are troubling the waters.' Likewise: '...just as a small ship caught in the great sea when the wind is raging.' By the sea, understand the peoples, as in Rev. 17, 15.

B. Gesner correctly explained these things after Albertus Magnus, Disp. VII. 17. 27. Theodoret and others understand seditions and tumults by the winds, for the reason that great disturbances preceded the rise of all kingdoms and empires, but since winds move the sea, which commotion is a symbol of disturbances and seditions: Therefore the winds, which cause it, cannot denote it itself. For as winds and waves or storms sent in differ, as cause and effect, Matt. 8, so it is necessary that the cause of the disturbances be shadowed forth by the winds. It is therefore most convenient that we understand by the winds the devils and their instruments, wicked men, by whose efforts and machinations movements, wars, and seditions are stirred up in Empires, just as importunate, violent, and pernicious enemies are sometimes designated by winds, Jer. 4, 11, 12; ch. 49, 36; 51, 1; Hos. 13, 15. Whence also sins break forth, on account of which the kingdom is transferred from nation to nation. As the son of Sirach says in chapter 10: A kingdom is translated from one people to another because of injustices, and wrongs, and injuries, and riches gotten by deceit. These things certainly are from the Devil, and from the own will of the wicked. And similar to that is what appears in Apoc. 6, a fiery horse, to whom power is given to take peace from the earth. Wherefore a vehement commotion of the sea preceded the apparition of the four living creatures, which is nothing other than the disturbance of the Republic brought in by the Devil. By the great sea nothing else is signified here than the image of many waters, or of some huge sea, which denotes the human race. Just as also in the Apocalypse ch. 17 the angel says: The waters which you saw are peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues. These, therefore, the winds, that is, the Devils, disturb, and out of those disturbances new kingdoms emerge.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET ECCE QUATUOR VENTI COELI] Ingentis tempestatis descriptio: qualis illa; Una Eurusq́, Notusq́, ruunt, creberq́, procellis Africus. Ovidius I. Tristium II. Nam modo purpureo vires capit Eurus ab ortu, Nunc Zephyrus sero vespere missus adest. Nunc gelidus sicca Boreas bacchatur ab Arcto: Nunc Notus adversa prælia fronte gerit. Lucanus: Primus ab Oceano caput exseris Atlanteo Core, movens æstus: jam te tollente furebat Pontus, & in scopulos totas erexerat undas: Occurrit gelidus Boreas pelagoq́, retundit: Et dubium pendet, vento cui concidat, æquor. Sed Scythici vicit rabies Aquilonis, & undas Torfit, & abstrusas penitus vada fecit arenas. Nec perfert pontum Boreas ad Saxa, suumq́ In fluxus Cori frangit mare: motaq́, possunt Æquora subductis etiam concurrere ventis. Non Euri cessasse minas, non imbribus atrum Æolii jacuisse Notum sub carcere saxi Crediderim. Valerius Flaccus: ---- Fundunt se carcere læti Thraces equi, Zephyrusq́, & nocti concolor alis Nimborum cum prole Notus, crinemq́, procellis Hispidus & multa flavus caput Eurus arena. Per tempestatem autem bella intellige. IN MARI MAGNO] Id est, non in lacu aliquo, qualis Asphaltites & Genezerethanus, quæ maria vocant accolæ: Sed in mari illo, quod Syriam, Ægyptum, Ju- dæam alluit. Sic & Poëtæ: Suave mari magno, turbantibus æquora ventis. Item: --- sicut minuta magno Deprensa navis in mari vesaniente vento. Per mare populos intellige, ut Apoc. 17, 15.

REcte hæc post Albertum M. exposuit B. Gesne- rus Disp. VII. 17. 27. Per ventos Theodoretus, & alii seditiones, & tumultus intelligunt, eo quod ortum omnium regnorum & imperiorum magnæ turbæ antecesserunt, sed cum venti mare commo- veant, quæ commotio turbarum & seditionum symbolum est: Ideo venti, qui eam efficiunt, non possunt ipsam denotare. Nam ut venti & fluctus sive procella immissæ differunt, tanquam causa & effectus Matth. 8. Ita necesse est, ut causa turbarum per ventos adumbrata sit. Commodissimum pro- inde est, ut per ventos intelligamus diabolos, & eo- rum instrumenta impios homines, quorum studiis & machinationibus motus, bella, & seditiones in Imperiis concitantur, uti hostes importuni, violen- ti & perniciosi per ventos designantur quandoque Jerem. 4, 11. 12. c. 49, 36. 51, 1. Ose. 13, 15. Unde et- iam peccata prorumpunt, propter quæ regnum de gente in gentem transfertur. Sicut Syracides cap. 10. ait: Regnum à gente una ad alteram traducitur propter injuste facta, & contumelias & divitias in- juste partas. Hæc certe à Diabolo sunt, & proprio impiorum arbitrio. Et simile est illud, quod A- poc. 6. apparet equus igneus, cui datur potestas auferendi pacem de terra. Quamobrem appari- tionem quatuor animalium antecessit maris vehe- mens commotio, quæ nihil aliud, quam turbatio Rei- publ. à Diabolo invecta. Per mare magnum nihil a- liud hic significatur, quam imago multarum aqua- rum, seu ingentis alicujus maris, quæ notat genus humanum. Sicut etiam in Apocalypsi c. 17. dicit an- gelus: Aquæ quas vidisti, sunt populi, & turbæ & gentes, & linguæ. Has itaque venti, id est, Diaboli turbant, & ex illis turbis nova regna emergunt.

## 7:3
Verse 3. AND FOUR GREAT BEASTS] Beasts, because the empires were idolatrous, as Jacchiades notes here. The Prophet sees this, which Nebuchadnezzar did not see. See the things said above 2, 31.

COMING UP FROM THE SEA] Having obtained great force from their own respective peoples, they were carried against others.

DIFFERENT FROM ONE ANOTHER] Which diversity is explained in the following.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET QUATUOR BESTIÆ GRANDES] Ideo bestiæ, quia idololatricæ erant imperia, ut notat hic Jacchia- des. Aspicit hoc Propheta, quod non videbat Nabuchodo- nosor. Vide dicta supra 2, 31.

ASCENDEBANT DE MARI] A populis quisque suis magnam vim nacti, in alios ferebantur.

DIVERSÆ INTER SE] Quæ diversitas in sequen- tibus explicatur.

## 7:4
Verse 4. THE FIRST WAS LIKE A LIONESS] Like a Lion.

AND IT HAD WINGS OF AN EAGLE] It was moved very swiftly under him: swifter than eagles. Jer. 4, 13. Whence also it is compared to an eagle, Jer. 48.40.

I WAS BEHOLDING UNTIL ITS WINGS WERE PLUCKED] The course of its empire was slowed under Evil-Merodach, Neriglissar, and Labashi-Marduk.

AND IT WAS LIFTED UP FROM THE EARTH] That is, the wings by which it was carried above the earth. For often among the Chaldeans, as also among the Hebrews, the conjunction has the force of a relative pronoun.

AND IT STOOD UPON ITS FEET AS A MAN] It kept itself in quietness,

AND A MAN'S HEART WAS GIVEN TO IT] Knowledge of the true God was given to Nabonidus. Above 6,20. Therefore God, when He wished to destroy Babylon, nevertheless spared him.

This figure of the first Monarchy, although it is rightly applied to Nebuchadnezzar and his successors, yet the earlier monarchs are not to be excluded. Therefore the first Monarchy bears the symbol of a Lion, on account of the noble monarchs endowed with heroic greatness, which can be understood also of Nimrod, Ninus, and Semiramis, who, although a woman, surpassed men in virtue, as Justin, Curtius, and others testify. They are said to be lifted up from the earth because, on account of their pride, they flew as it were in the air, and even aspired to divine honors, as is evident concerning Sennacherib, Isa. 37, 17; Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 3, v. 4; and Belshazzar, Dan. 5. They stood upon their feet, and a man's heart was given to them, because that leonine heart was taken from them, and because they experienced the human lot, as is commemorated in a monument concerning Sennacherib, erected after that notable slaughter with this inscription: εἰς ἐμέ τις ὁρέων εὐσεβὼς ἔστω. See Herodotus, book 2. Concerning Nebuchadnezzar, after he had returned to himself, see Dan. 4, 29. Concerning the humiliation of Belshazzar, Dan. 5. Therefore these things are not to be restricted to Nabonidus or Darius alone. Indeed, that Darius in Dan. 6, 20 is not Nabonidus, nor did he hold Babylon before the occupation, but rather Belshazzar was cut off on account of his blasphemies and impiety, whom Darius the Mede, having occupied Babylon under the auspices of the second Monarchy, succeeded in the government, c. 5, 30; c. 6, 1. By the eagle's wings, not only speed is noted, but also the eminence and majesty of the empire, Job 39, 30; Prov. 23, 5. By the plucking of the wings, not a retardation of the course, but a decrease of the kingdom and its beauty, since unfledged wings exhibit deformity; Sanctius interprets this as the loss of the army, of the provinces of Media, Persia, and Lydia, and also the defection of the leaders Gadaras and Gobryas: Nor is there any reason why we should depart from the native signification of the conjunction Vav, because it could be considered lifted from the earth when the form of monarchical government was removed, as Mr. Dr. Geier rightly observes. The blessed Gesner writes thus concerning these in Disp. VII, th. 47: Since they previously flew in the air and were eminent above all the kingdoms of the world, afterwards it behooved the Assyrians, like other princes, to walk upon the ground and be content with the human condition, and a human heart was given to them, which is fearful, Jer. 17. But the heart endowed with leonine ferocity and aquiline swiftness was entirely taken away from them. Jerome writes thus concerning this first beast: The Babylonian kingdom, on account of its savagery and cruelty, or on account of its luxury and life serving lust, is called not a lion, but a lioness. For those who have written about the natures of beasts say that lionesses are more ferocious, especially if they are nursing cubs, and are always eager for mating. But that it had the wings of an eagle signifies the pride of a most powerful kingdom: whose prince speaks through Isaiah, 'I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High.' Whence it is said to it: 'If it be carried high as an eagle, I will pull it down.' Otherwise, as the lion holds the kingdom among beasts, so the eagle holds it among birds. But this also must be said, that the eagle lives for a long time, and the kingdom of the Assyrians dominated for many ages. But that its wings were plucked, that is, of the lioness or eagle, signifies the other kingdoms over which it previously ruled and flew in the world. And it was lifted up, he says, from the earth, namely, with the subversion of the empire of the Chaldeans. And what follows: 'And it stood upon its feet as a man, and its heart was given to it': If we understand this of Nebuchadnezzar, it is clear that after he lost the kingdom and his power was taken away, he was restored again to his former state, and learned that he was not a lioness but a man, and received the heart which he had lost. But if we understand it generally of the kingdom of the Chaldeans, it must be felt that, with Balthasar killed and the Medes and Persians succeeding to the empire, the Babylonians understood themselves to be men and of a humble and fragile nature.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PRIMA ERAT QUASI LEÆNA] Quasi Leo.

ET ALAS HABEBAT AQUILÆ] Celerrime sub illo movebatur: velocius aquilis. Jer. 4, 13. Unde & Aquilæ comparatur, Jer. 48.40.

ASPICIEBAM DONEC EVULSÆ SUNT ALÆ EJUS] Tardati cursus ejus imperii sub Evilmerodacho, Negriglassorsoro, Laborosoardocho.

ET SUBLATA EST DE TERRA] Vertē, و per quas efferebatur supra terram. Sæpe enim Chaldæis ut & Hebræis, copula vim habet relativi.

ET SUPER PEDES QUASI HOMO STETIT] Quiete se continuit,

ET COR HOMINIS DATUM EST EI] Cognitio veri Dei data Nabonnedo. Supra 6,20. Ideo Deus, cum vellet destruere Babylonem, ipsi tamen pepercit.

Figura hæc primæ Monarchiæ, etsi Nebucadnezari & successoribus recte accommodetur, non tamen excludendi priores Monarchæ. Leonis ergo Symbolum prima Monarchia gerit, ob generosos, & Heroica magnitudine præditos Monarchas, quod de Nimrodo etiam, Nino, ac Semiramide, quæ etsi fœmina, viros virtute anteivit, Justino, & Curtio teste, aliisque intelligi potest. Supra terram elati dicuntur, quod ob fastum velut in aërë volitarint, ac divinos etiam affectarint honores, ut de Sennacheribo Esa.37,17. Nabuchodonosare Dan.3. v. 4.Belsazare Dan. 5. constat. Super pedes stetêre, & cor hominis datum eis est, quod cor illud leoninum exemptum ipsis, quodque sortem humanam experti sunt,uti de Sennacheribo monumentum commemoratur, post insignem illam cladem cum hac Ἐπιγραφῇ exstructum: εἰς ἐμέ τις ὁρέων εὐσεβὼς ἔσω. Vid. Herodot. l. 2. De Nebucadnezare, postquam ad se rediisset, videatur Dan. 4,29. De Belsazari humiliatione Dan. 5. Non ergo ad solum Nabonnedum vel Darium hæc restringenda. Imo Darius ille Dan. 6,20. non Nabonidus est, nec Babylonem tenuit ante occupationem, sed Belsazar potius ob blasphemias & impietatem excisus, quem sub auspicium secundæ Monarchiæ occupata Babylone Darius Medus in regimine excepit, c.5 30. c. 6,1.Per alas aquilinas non tantum velocitas, sed etiam eminentia & majestas imperii notatur Job.39,30. Prov. 23, 5. Per avulsionem alarum non cursus retardatio, sed decrementum regni & pulchritudinis ejus quum alæ implumes deformitatem exhibeant; Sanctius de exercitus amissione, provinciarum Mediæ, Persæ, Lydiæq;, nec non Ducum Gadaræ, & Gobryæ defectione interpretatur: Neque est cur à nativa significatione copulæ Vav discedamus, quia sublata de terra censeri poterat, cum sublata Monarchici regiminis forma fuit, ut recte observat Dn. D. Geierus. B. Gesnerus ita de his Disp.VII. th.47. Cum antea in aëre volitarent, & super omnia regna mundi eminerent, postea Assyrios ut alios principes humi incedere, & humana conditione contentos esse oportuit, datumq; illis est cor humanum, quod est pavidum Jer.17. Cor vero leonina ferocia & aquilina celeritate præditum penitus illis ademptum fuit. Hieronymus ita de hac prima bestia: Regnum Babylonicum propter sævitiam & crudelitatem, sive propter luxuriam & vitam libidini servientem non leo,sed Leæna appellatur. Ajunt enim hi, qui de bestiarum scripsere naturis, leænas esse ferociores, maxime si catulos nutriant, & semper gestire ad coitum. Quod autem habebat alas aquilæ, superbiam significat regni potentissimi: cujus princeps loquitur per Esaiam, super sydera cœli ponam thronum meum, & ero similis altissimo. Unde dicitur ad eam: si alte feratur ut aquila, inde detraham. Alioquin ut leo inter bestias, ita aquila inter aves regnum tenet. Sed & hoc dicendum, aquilam multo tempore vivere, & regnum Assyriorum multis ætatibus fuisse dominatum. Quod autem evulsæ sunt alæ ejus,id est, leænæ, sive aquilæ, cætera regna fignificat: quibus prius impera- bat & volitabat in mundo. Et sublata est, inquit, de terra subverso videlicet imperio Chaldæorum. Quodque sequitur: Et super pedes, quasi homo ste- tit, & cor ejus datum est ei: Si de Nabuchodonosor intelligimus, perspicuum est, quod postquam perdidit regnum, & potentia ejus ablata est, rursus in pri- stinum statum restitutus sit, & non Leænam, sed homi- nem se esse didicerit, & cor receperit, quod amiserat. Sin autem generaliter de regno Chaldæorum, hoc sen- tiendum est, quod interfecto Balthasar & Medis, Per- sisć, imperium succedentibus, Babylonii homines & humilis fragilisć, naturæ se esse intellexerint.

## 7:5
Vers. 5.

AND BEHOLD ANOTHER BEAST LIKE A BEAR] A bear is an omnivorous animal, says Aristotle 8, 5. Thus the Medo-Persians were great plunderers, robbers, Jer. 51, 48. 56. A bear, according to the Persians, signifies a wealthy enemy, says Achmetes.

IN ONE PART IT STOOD] In the Chaldean: It stood at one side: that is, apart, namely from Judea. The sense is: It did no harm to Judea: How Jerome here interprets it most excellently, having followed the Hebrews, as he himself says.

AND THREE ROWS WERE IN ITS MOUTH, AND IN ITS TEETH] In the Chaldean: and three ribs were in its mouth between the teeth. These three ribs are the Persian, Median, and Chaldean Empires. Ribs signify the strength of a man, Achmetes 12.

AND THUS THEY WERE SAYING TO IT] Thus it was said.

ARISE, EAT MUCH FLESH] For it willingly practices σαρκοφαγεῖ; Aristotle in the cited place.

By the three teeth they understand three distinguished and principal Kings: Cyrus, Darius son of Hystaspes, and Xerxes, who increased the power of the kingdom above the others, as witnessed by Herodotus and Justin. Jerome, however, understands three empires: we ought to take the three rows in the mouth of the Persian kingdom, and in its teeth, as three kingdoms: the Babylonian, the Median, and the Persian; which were reduced into one kingdom. And we read of Ahasuerus that he held 127 provinces, Esth. 1, 1. This Monarchy is said to have eaten much flesh, on account of its victories and the peoples it conquered: whence in Dan. 8, 4, it is called a ram pushing with its horn to the west, (Persia was situated in the East), the North, and the South. It attacked the West when it subdued Syria, Palestine, and Babylon; the North when it subdued the Scythians. Which was done by Cyrus and Darius son of Hystaspes. Herodotus also teaches that Lydia was subdued by Cyrus. It pushed to the South when Cambyses subjugated Egypt, and Xerxes recovered it when it rebelled, as did Artaxerxes Longimanus, and also Ochus, as witnessed by Herodotus and Diodorus.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ET ECCE BESTIA ALIA SIMILIS URSO] Ur- sus ζῶον παμφάγον ait Aristoteles 8, 5. Sic Medopersæ ra- ptores magni, prædones, Jer. 51, 48. 56. Ursus secundum Persas hostem significat opulentum, ait Achmetes.

IN PARTE STETIT] In Chaldæo: Stetit ad la- tus unum: id est, seorsum, nempe à Judæa. Sensus est: Judææ nihil nocuit: Quomodo Hieronymus hic optimè interpretatur secutus Hebræos, ut ipse dicit.

ET TRES ORDINES ERANT IN ORE EJUS, ET IN DENTIBUS EJUS] In Chaldæo: & tres costæ e- rant in ore ejus inter dentes. Hæ tres costæ sunt, Imperium Persicum, Medicum & Chaldaicum. Costæ vires homi- nis significant, Achmetes XII.

ET SIC DICEBANT EI] Sic dicebatur.

SURGE, COMEDE CARNES PLURIMAS] Nam usus libenter σαρκοφαγεῖ; Aristoteles dicto loco.

Per tres dentes intelligunt tres insignes ac præci- puos Reges Cyrum, Darium Hystaspis, & Xerxem, qui præ cæteris regni potentiam auxerunt, teste Herodoto & Justino. Hieronymus tamen tria im- peria intelligit: tres ordines in ore regni Persarum, & in dentibus ejus tria regna debemus accipere: Babylonicum, Medorum atć, Persarum: quæ in u- num redacta sunt regnum. Et legimus de Asvero quod CXXVII. provincias tenuerit Esth. 1, 1. Co- medisse dicitur hæc Monarchia canes plurimas, ob victorias & populos debellatos: unde Dan. 8, 4. dicitur aries ventilans cornu in occidentem, (Sita e- rat Persia in Oriente) Aquilonem & meridiem. Oc- cidentem autem impugnavit, cum Syriam, Palæsti- nam, Babylonem subegit; Aquilonem cum Scythas. Quod à Cyro & Dario Hystaspis factum. Herodo- tus etiam Lydium à Cyro subactum docet. Meri- diem ventilavit, cum Ægyptum Cambyses subju- gavit, & rebellem Xerxes recepit, item Arta- xerxes Longimanus, ut & Ochus teste Herodoto, & Diodoro.

## 7:6
Vers. 6.

AND BEHOLD ANOTHER LIKE A LEOPARD] A LEOPARD is a variegated animal. Thus Alexander was of variegated character, now clement, now cruel: now temperate in his way of life: now drunken: now abstinent, now indulging in loves. A leopard among the Persians and Egyptians signifies an irreconcilable enemy, says Achmetes.

AND IT HAD WINGS, AS A BIRD, FOUR UPON IT] That is, this power will be swifter, by Chaldean force, which had only two wings. See below 8, 5. Lucan about Alexander: 'And a thunderbolt that would strike all peoples equally.' And his mother had dreamed that a thunderbolt was born from her womb.

The leopard, a wild animal familiar to Africa and Asia, shadows forth the third Monarchy; it breathes an excellent odor from its whole body, by the sweetness of which it seizes and devours other beasts. See Pliny, book 8, ch. 9; Aristotle, book 8, History of Animals, ch. 6. Plutarch says that a pleasant odor emanated from the skin and limbs of Alexander the Great.

is the author, and he certainly attracted more by the scent of his fame than he subdued by arms. And the Leopard is by itself a most swift animal, and ὁρμητικόν, which rushes headlong into blood, but here in addition to this, wings are attributed to it, and indeed four, to denote the highest speed. Alexander the Great, as Jerome says in this place, ran from the Illyrian and Adriatic sea as far as the Indian Ocean and the river Ganges, not so much by battles as by victories, and in six years he subjugated a great part of Europe and all of Asia to himself. And Justin says it is uncertain whether it is more admirable that Alexander conquered the world or that he attempted to conquer it.

AND FOUR HEADS WERE ON THE BEAST] Four heads had grown up in place of one. These are the four highest leaders after Alexander: Perdiccas, Seleucus, Ptolemy, Meleager; of whom Perdiccas was in charge of the Macedonian cavalry; Seleucus of the foreign [troops]; Meleager of the royal bodyguard; Ptolemy of the infantry. See below 8, 22, and add 1 Maccabees 1, 7, and what will be said there.

AND POWER WAS GIVEN TO IT] A huge one, of course, from God, the arbiter of kingdoms.

If four heads grew up in place of one, as Grotius acknowledges, this must be understood not of the four highest leaders of Alexander, but rather of his successors: Ptolemy, Seleucus, Philip, and Antigonus. For these had divided his empire into four kingdoms. Therefore also in chapter 8, the horn of the he-goat is said to be broken, and four horns arise from it toward the four winds of heaven: one taking Syria, another Egypt, the third Asia, the fourth Greece. If anyone raises a scruple as to how four kingdoms constitute one Monarchy, the blessed Helvicus answers in his Synopsis of Universal History, p. 40, that they are not considered separately by themselves, but taken together they merit this axiom, just as when a prince is dead, all the prefects together represent the Prince, so that if any part of the dominion is torn away by some outsider, it is lost not to the prefect, but to the whole Principality. Thus the Romans also, having snatched away Asia, and occupied Macedonia, Greece, and Syria, are indeed said to have diminished the Monarchy of the Greeks, but they cannot properly be said to have extinguished it and transferred it to themselves until they had subdued the last part, Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET ECCE ALIA QUASI PARDUS] PARDUS varium animal. Sic Alexander moribus variis, modo cle- mens, modo crudelis: modo victus temperati: modo e- briosus: modo abstinens, modo indulgens amoribus. Pardus apud Persas & Ægyptios hostem significat irrecon- ciliabilem, ait Achmetes.

ET ALAS HABEBAT, QUASI AVIS, QUA- TUOR SUPER SE] Id est, celerior erit hæc vis, vi Chaldaica, quæ duas tantum habebat alas. Vide infra 8, 5. Lucanus de Alexandro ---- Fulmenć, quod omnes Percuteret pariter populos. Et mater ejus somniaverat ex utero suo enasci fulmen.

Pardus animal ferum Africæ Asiæque fami- liare tertiam Monarchiam adumbrat, spirat toto corpore præstantem odorem, cujus suavitate be- stias alias corripit, ac devorat. Vid. Plin. lib. 8. c. 9. Aristot. lib. 8. Hist. anim. c. 6. E cute & membris Alex. M. jucundum odorem emanasse Plutarch.

autor est, & attraxit sane plures odore famæ quam armis subegerit. Et est Pardus per se ani- mal velocissimum, & ὁρμητικόν, quod præceps ruit in sanguinem, sed hic adhæc tribuuntur ei alæ, & quidem quatuor, ad celeritatem summam notan- dam. Alexander M. ut h. l. Hieronymus, ab Illy- rico & Adriatico mari usq́, ad Oceanum Indicum & Gangem fluvium non tam præliis quam victoriis per- currit, & sex annis magnam partem Europæ, & o- mnem sibi Asiam subjugavit. Et Justinus ait, in- certum esse, utrum admirabilius sit, Alexandrum vi- cisse orbem, quam vincere aggressum esse.

ET QUATUOR CAPITA ERANT IN BE- STIA] Quatuor capita succreverant loco unius. Hi sunt quatuor summi post Alexandrum duces, Perdicca, Seleu- cus, Ptolemæus, Meleager; quorum Perdicca equitatui Macedonico; externo Seleucus; Meleager Satellitio re- gio; Ptolemæus peditatui præerant. Vide infra 8, 22. & adde 1. Maccab. 1, 7. & quæ ibi dicentur.

ET POTESTAS DATA EST EI] Ingens scilicet, à Deo regnorum arbitro.

Si quatuor capita loco unius succrevere, uti agnoscit Grotius, non de summis Alexandri duci- bus quatuor, sed potius de successoribus hæc acci- pienda, Ptolemæo, Seleuco, Philippo, & Antigono. Nam hi imperium ipsius diviserant in quatuor regna. Ideo etiam c. 8. cornu hirci caprarum fran- gi dicitur, & oriuntur inde quatuor cornua per quatuor ventos cæli: Uno Syriam, altero Ægyptum, tertio Asiam, quarto Græciam adipifcente. Si quis scrupulum moveat, quomodo quatuor regna u- nam Monarchiam constituent. Respondet B. Hel- vicus in Synopsi Hist. univers. p. 40. ea non per se se- paratim considerata, sed conjunctim hoc axioma me- reri, haud secus ac de mortuo principe, omnes præfe- cti conjunctim repræsentant Principem, adeo, ut si qua pars ditionis ab extero quodam avellatur, illa non præfecto, sed toti Principatui decedat. Ita Romani etiam, erepta Asia, occupata Macedonia, Græcia, Syria diminuisse quidem Monarchiam Græcorum di- cuntur, extinxisse vero & ad se transtulisse dici pro- prie non possunt, antequam ultimam partem Ægy- ptum subegerint.

## 7:7
Verse 7.

THE FOURTH BEAST TERRIBLE AND WONDERFUL] The legs of the image: which are described here under the name of one wild beast, because the Macedonian Kings were of both Syria and Egypt, and within certain borders sometimes these, sometimes those, reigned more widely: furthermore, because Judea, which is especially looked to here, was held or harassed now by these, now by those. Even now the Hebrews call those empires by one name מלכות יון.

IT HAD GREAT IRON TEETH, EATING AND CRUSHING] The same as the iron in the image in II. 40. The greatest cruelty toward the Jews is denoted, as I have said.

AND TRAMPLING THE REST WITH ITS FEET] If it had left any alive, it treated them foully.

BUT IT WAS DISSIMILAR TO THE OTHER BEASTS WHICH I HAD SEEN BEFORE IT] That is, much more savage.

The fourth beast adumbrates the fourth Monarchy, just as the first three beasts were figures of the three prior empires. And therefore it is explained by great consensus among interpreters, historians, and chronologists as the Roman empire, if you except some Calvinists, Piscator, Rollock, Polanus, Junius, and Tremellius in this place, Chamier in Panstratia, Vol. II, 17, 14, and Pezel in Mellificium. Nor indeed can it be understood of the successors of Alexander; for they had already been adumbrated under the third beast, through the four heads which had grown up in place of one. Whence I conclude: The fourth beast is entirely other and different from the preceding Beasts. As is evident in chapter 5, verses 7, 10, 19, 23. But the successors of Alexander are not other or different from the preceding beasts. Therefore they will not be the fourth beast. Furthermore

The fourth beast is to endure until the final Judgment, under the end of which the Saints of the most high God are to receive the kingdom. But the kingdom of the successors of Alexander was not to endure until the final judgment. Therefore the kingdom of Alexander is not the Fourth beast. The proposition is Daniel 7, 9, 10, 13, 14, 22, 26, 27. The assumption is manifest. For the kingdom of Egypt was finally taken away by the Romans, when it had stood for 294 years from the death of Alexander. Ptolemy, book III, chapter 8; Clement of Alexandria. Further: In this judgment, the period of the four beasts having been completed, the kingdom is given to the Saints, and the majesty and greatness of the Kingdoms under the whole heaven, which they will possess until the age, and until the ages of ages, chapter 7, 18, 22, 27. But the Maccabees did not hold the kingdom for more than 126 years, which Josephus counts up to Herod. Wherefore the kingdom of the saints after the four beasts cannot be explained as the Maccabees. Furthermore, since Grotius concedes that the same thing is signified by the iron teeth eating and crushing of this beast as by the iron feet in the Danielic Colossus in chapter 2, and since in that place it is not the successors of Alexander but the monarchs of the fourth empire that are shadowed forth, it is necessary that we accept this figure also as concerning the fourth empire, not the successors of Alexander. And that false interpretation of Grotius has already been refuted by Jerome in the author of this discovery, the scourge of Christians, Porphyry, whom Grotius does not deny he has followed here. It has also been refuted by most excellent historians and chronologists in Bodin, who illustrated the same in his Method, chapter 7. But as for those among the Reformed who patronize the same, Calvin’s commentary on Daniel, whom they otherwise venerate as their teacher and master, easily refutes them.

AND IT HAD TEN HORNS] That is, there will be ten kings, as below in verse 24, namely those who are about to rage against the Jews, both from Syria and from Egypt, all of whom Porphyry enumerated from history. Horns are prominent in living creatures, and so are kings in a people. We see, however, that those ten horns can be found in the eleventh chapter below, namely these: Ptolemy Lagi, Seleucus Nicator, Ptolemy Eupator, Ptolemy Euergetes, Seleucus Callinicus, Antiochus the Great, Ptolemy Philopator, Ptolemy Epiphanes, Seleucus Philopator, Antiochus Epiphanes.

Thus, therefore, those horns according to Grotius are ten kings succeeding one another, not, however, coexisting kingdoms. But if you consider the force of the text, it is not kings but kingdoms that are understood by the horns. For as Maldonatus rightly observes: in this place, and wherever there is talk of future monarchies, it is not so much a matter of persons as of things. And the beast was seen to have the horns simultaneously, not successively, and therefore they must be understood as supreme existing kingdoms. Add that ten kings cannot be found who successively held dominion after Alexander the Great up to Antiochus in Syria. For these were they: Seleucus Nicanor, Antiochus Soter, Antiochus Theos, Seleucus Callinicus, Seleucus Ceraunus, Antiochus the Great, Seleucus Philopator, Antiochus Epiphanes, who therefore was the eighth in order. But this little horn follows the ten previous horns. But that Grotius, with Porphyry, weaves together one order of kings from the different kingdoms of Syria and Egypt is too gross an error. Furthermore, the opponents do not agree concerning the ten horns. For Franciscus Junius explains those horns one way, others another way, but the count of neither Grotius, nor Junius, nor others rests on a solid foundation. Grotius, however, appeals to the authority of Porphyry, which we do not begrudge him. But, not to speak of others, why does he number among them Seleucus Nicanor and Callinicus, who afflicted the Jews, when they had no business in interceding with the Jews, nor are they read to have infested them; indeed, Nicanor was most beneficent to the Jews, as Josephus testifies, book 12, chapter 3. Why does he omit those whom Junius enumerates, who brought forward several Antiochi here, namely Soter, Theon, and Hierax, whom he confuses with the Great? Clearly, that enumeration is too arbitrary, and it contributes nothing to those horns of the fourth beast. For the Prophet did not intend to describe only the enemies of the Jews here, but proposed to himself to shadow forth the Empires of the world. Nebuchadnezzar, certainly, Darius, Cyrus, and other Monarchs showed great benefits to the Jews, and propagated the true worship of God, and for His sake procured the liberation of the people; whom, indeed, not even Grotius himself said were excluded from this figure of living creatures. Wherefore Blessed Luther, Osiander, Gesner, and Helvicus understand here the ten following kingdoms: Syria, Egypt, Asia, Greece, Africa, Spain, Gaul, Italy, Germany, England. Philippus Nicolai, under the name of Asia, having included Egypt and Syria, substituted Hungary and Poland in their place, book 2, On the Kingdom of Christ, chapter 8.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

BESTIA QUARTA TERRIBILIS ATQUE MI- RABILIS] Crura imaginis: quæ hic sub unius feræ no- mine describuntur, quod tam Syriæ, quam Ægypti Reges Macedones essent, & in certis finibus modo hi, modo il- li latius regnaverint: præterea Judæam quod hic maxime respicitur, nunc hi, nunc illi tenuerint, aut vexaverint. Etiam nunc Hebræi ista imperia uno nomine appellant מלכות יון.

DENTES FERREOS HABEBAT MAGNOS, COMEDENS, ATQUE COMMINUENS] Idem quod ferrum in imagine II. 40. Sævitia denotatur in Judæos maxima, ut dixi.

ET RELIQUA PEDIBUS SUIS CONCUL- CANS] Si quos vivos reliquerat, eos fœde tractabat.

DISSIMILIS AUTEM ERAT CÆTERIS BE- STIIS, QUAS VIDERAM ANTE EAM] Id est, mul- to sævior.

Bestia quarta quartam Monarchiam adumbrat, ut priores tres bestiæ figuræ erant trium priorum imperiorum. Ideoque magno consensu ab inter- pretibus, Historicis, & Chronologis de Romano imperio explicatur, si Calvinianos nonnullos, Pi- scator Rolloc. Polan. Jun. & Tremell. in h. l. Chamie- rum Panstrat. Tom. II. 17, 14. Pezel. in Mellif. exci- pias. Neque vero de successoribus Alexandri intelli- gi potest; nam illi jam sub tertia bestia adumbrati erant, per quatuor capita, quæ loco unius ipsi succreverant. Unde concludo: Quarta bestia prorsus alia ac diversa est à præcedentibus Bestiis. Ut c. 5. v. 7. 10. 19. 23. constat. At successores A- lexandri non sunt alii aut diversi à præcedentibus bestiis. Non ergo erunt quarta bestia. Porro

Quarta bestia duratura est ad Judicium usq́; extre- mum, sub cujus finem Sancti Dei altissimi regnum suscepturi sunt. At regnum successorum Alexandri non erat duraturum usque ad extremum judi- cium. E. regnum Alexandri non est Quarta be- stia. Propositio est Dan. 7, 9. 10. 13. 14. 22. 26. 27. Assumtio est manifesta. Nam Aegypti regnum postremo à Romanis sublatum est, cum stetisset à morte Alexandri annis 294. Ptol. lib. III. cap. 8. Clemens Alexandr. Ulterius : In hoc judicio, ex- acta quatuor bestiarum periodo, Sanctis datur regnum, & majestas & amplitudo Regnorum sub toto cœlo, quod possidebunt usque in seculum, & usque in secula seculorum c. 7, 18. 22, 27. Atqui Maccabæi non tenuerunt regnum amplius annis 126. quos Josephus numerat usque ad Herodem. Quare regnum sanctorum post quatuor bestias non potest exponi de Maccabæis. Adhæc, cum largiatur Grotius per ferreos dentes comedentes at- que comminuentes hujus bestiæ idem figuratum es- se, quod cap. 2. in Colosso Danielitico per ferreos pedes, illic autem non successores Alexandri, sed quarti Imperii Monarchæ adumbrati sint, neces- sum est, ut hanc etiam figuram de quarto Impe- rio, non de Alexandri successoribus accipiamus. Et refutata est Grotiana ista ψευδερμηνεία jam ab Hie- ronymo in autore hujus εὑρήματος, empacta Christianorum, Porphyrio, quem hic se sequutum esse non diffitetur Grotius. Refutata etiam est ab Historicis & Chronologis præstantissimis in Bodi- no, qui in Methodo sua c. 7, eandem illustravit. Qui verò è Reformatis eidem patrocinantur, eos Calvini, quem ceu præceptorem & Magistrum suum alias venerantur, Commentarius in Danie- lem facile redarguit.

ET HABEBAT CORNUA DECEM] Id est, de- cem erunt Reges, ut infra 24. nempe qui sævituri sunt in Judæos, tum ex Syria, tum ex Ægypto, quos omnes ex hi- storia numeravit Porphyrius. Cornua eminent in animan- tibus sic in populo Reges. Videmus autem decem ista cor- nua reperire posse in capite infra undecimo, hos scilicet, Ptolemæum Lagi, Seleucum Nicatora, Ptolemæum Eupa- tora, Ptolemæum Evergeten, Seleucum Callinicum, Antio- chum Magnum, Ptolemæum Philepatora, Ptolomæum Epi- phanem, Seleucum Philopatora, Antiochum Epiphanem.

Ita ergo cornua illa secundum Grotium, sunt decem Reges sibi invicem succedentes, non verò regna coëxistentia. At si vim textus respicias, non Re- ges, sed regna per cornua intelliguntur. Nam ut recte Maldonatus observat : hoc in loco, & ubicunq́; de futuris Monarchiis sermo est, non tam de personis, quam de rebus agitur. Et visa est cornua simul ha- bere bestia, non vero successive, ideoque de regnis summis existentibus ea intelligenda. Adde quod non inveniantur decem Reges, qui successive domi- nium obtinuerint post Alexandrum Magnum us- que ad Antiochum in Syria. Hi enim fuere; Se- leucus Nicanor, Antiochus Soter, Antiochus, Theos, Seleucus Callinicus, Seleucus Ceraunus, Antiochus Magnus, Seleucus Philopator, Antiochus Epipha- nes, qui proinde octavus fuit ordine. Hoc autem cornu parvum decem cornua priora sequitur. Quod autem Grotius cum Porphyrio de diversis regnis Syriæ & Ægypti unum contexit Regum ordinem, id nimis crassus error est. Porro non conveniunt οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας de decem cornibus. Aliter enim e- narrat illa cornua Franciscus Junius, aliter alii, sed nec Grotii, nec Junii, nec aliorum numerus solido nititur fundamento. Ad autoritatem Por- phyrii tamen provocat Grotius, quam ipsi non invidemus. Cæterum ne de aliis dicamus, cur Seleucum Nicanora, & Callinicum illis annumerat, qui Judæos afflixere, quum ipsis nihil negotii in- tercesserit cum Judæis, neque eosdem infestasse le- gantur, imo Nicanor Judæis benefissentissimus fue- rit, teste Josepho l. 12. c. 3. Cur omittit illos, quos Ju- nius recenset, qui plures hic Antiochos nempe So- tera, Theon, & Hiracem, quem cum Magno confun- dit, adduxit. Scilicet nimis arbitraria est illa enu- meratio, neque ad illa quartæ bestiæ cornua quic- quam facit. Non enim tantum hostes Judæorum hic describere voluit Propheta, sed Imperia mun- di adumbrare sibi proposuit. Nebucadnezar cer- te, Darius, Cyrus & alii Monarchæ Judæis beneficia magna exhibuere, & cultum Dei verum propaga- runt, ejusque causa populi liberationem procura- runt; quos vero ab hac animantium figura exclu- di nec ipse Grotius dixit. Quapropter B. Luthe- rus, Osiander, Gesnerus, Helvicus intelligunt hic de- cem regna sequentia, Syriam, Ægyptum, Asiam, Græciam, Africam, Hispaniam, Galliam, Italiam, Germaniam, Angliam. Philippus Nicolai sub A- siæ nomine Ægyptum & Syriam complexus in ea- rum locum substituit Ungariam & Poloniam lib. 2. de Regno Christi cap. 8.

## 7:8
Verse 8.

AND ANOTHER LITTLE HORN SPRANG UP FROM THE MIDST OF THEM] It is called a little horn because, although it was of royal lineage, it nevertheless had no right to the kingdom, namely Antiochus Epiphanes. See 11, 21.

AND THREE OF THE FIRST HORNS WERE PLUCKED UP FROM BEFORE IT] That is, by him, or by his command. Seleucus, his elder brother, was killed; Demetrius, the son of the same Seleucus, but the cousin of Antiochus, was indeed despoiled; likewise Ptolemy Philopator, King of Egypt, was despoiled. Demetrius was the son of Seleucus, who was the brother of Antiochus. And therefore in Justin, where Demetrius is called the uncle of this Antiochus's son, it should be read cousin: which Appian and the abbreviator of Livy, book 46, teach us. See what will be said below on chapter 11.

AND BEHOLD, EYES LIKE THE EYES OF A MAN WERE IN THIS HORN] That is, he will be sharp-sighted for matters to be done. See 8, 23.

AND A MOUTH SPEAKING GREAT THINGS] For he was very arrogant. Whence also he was called ἐπιφανὴς. See below 20.

Here the falsity of the Porphyrio-Grotian interpretation reveals itself more. For three horns out of those are said to have been cast down by the little horn growing up. He brings forward Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, despoiled by Antiochus. Likewise Ptolemy Philopator: But here the matter is about plucked up and cast down horns, not about despoiling: Nor is that Demetrius found in the number of the ten horns brought forward by Grotius. And Demetrius reigned after Epiphanes. But the horns ought to have been cast down before he reigned, chapter 7, 8. Furthermore, that little horn of Daniel, which grew up among the ten horns, is distinct from the ten horns, and is not of the number of those horns. For it is said to have ascended בֵּינֵיהוֹן among them. But Antiochus Epiphanes is not a horn distinct from the ten horns, but is one of the number of them, according to Grotius. Therefore Antiochus is not the little horn with which the Prophet deals. After the rise of the ten horns, the little horn came forth, and those ten horns are distinctly called the former ones in respect to this one, v. 8. קַרְנַיָא קַדְמָיָתָא concerning the ten former horns. That King signified by the little horn is said to be about to rise after the rest, v. 24. AND ANOTHER SHALL RISE AFTER THEM: and he shall differ from the FORMER. Which can in no way be understood of Antiochus. For he was not another rising after the ten Kings, but one from the number of the ten Kings: he does not differ from those ten former Kings as a new and different King, but belongs to their number, according to the Grotian explanation. Add that that little horn ought to have ascended or come forth AMONG those ten horns of the fourth beast, v. 8, 20, 21, and thus its exit pertains to the Fourth empire, not indeed to the third. But Antiochus Epiphanes did not come forth from the fourth beast, but from the third, Dan. 8, 9, 22, 25, having arisen from Seleucus. And therefore Antiochus Epiphanes is not that little horn which grew up among the ten horns. Furthermore, the little horn of the Fourth beast, which grew up among the ten horns, is greater than the others after it acquired strength, verse 20. But Antiochus Epiphanes was never greater or more powerful than the others. Which Helvicus proves from histories, page 5. Besides the fact that the Parthian nation had long before this defected from the Seleucids under Seleucus Callinicus, and Syria had been greatly weakened by internal wars (See Appian, Syr., Just. book 27), it is known to what straits Antiochus the Great, the father of Epiphanes, was reduced, and of how great a part of his kingdom he was stripped by the Romans, and moreover with how heavy a tribute he was burdened: See Livy, dec. 4, book 7, Flor. book 2, chapter 8, etc. How then could Epiphanes be called greater and more powerful than the kings before him? Finally, the little horn was to prevail against the saints until the Ancient of days came for judgment, and thus that empire is to last until the very last day. But the Empire of Antiochus has already been overturned for many centuries.

But if it be objected that Antiochus is represented by the little horn in the following chapter, the answer is easy: that it is different from this one, which is evident even from the fact that that little horn arises on the forehead of the Goat of the goats, that is, of Alexander the Great. But the present κεράδιον is born from the fourth beast, verse 22.

These arguments, therefore, convince us that Antiochus is not to be understood here, as Grotius and most Calvinists maintain. Whence Calvin himself supports us here, as does John Napier with the interpreter Leo de Dramma in prop. 24, p. 86, acknowledging that the fourth beast is necessarily the Roman Monarchy. If, therefore, you ask, who then is designated here? I answer: The Papists wish to indicate the Antichrist, whom they imagine is yet to arise: Maldonatus, Pererius, Cornelius à Lapide in h. l., Rebera in Apoc. 12, 11, Josephus à Costa lib. 11. de temp. noviss. cap. 9, Bellarminus lib. 3. de Pontifice Romano c. 16, Gretserus in defens. Bellarm., Schoppius de Antichristo, Lessius demonstrat. 12. de Antichrist., Becan. Tom. 2. opusc. 1. But since they find their Utopian Antichrist nowhere else in Holy Scripture, and dream things about him that are in no way consistent with the Scriptures, this passage is not distorted to refer to him except rashly. For that Antichrist invented by the Papists is a mere being of reason and a Papistical chimera. And not a few things in the text stand against this opinion, which are urged by Gesner, th. 134. For first, this little horn denotes a secular prince, or king, in that it arises from the ten little horns, that is, from the midst of kings or princes: and the angel below expressly names this horn a king, who would be more powerful than the former ones. The Antichrist, however, although he claims royal eminence for himself, Dan. 11, yet in his own character, 2 Thess. 2 and elsewhere, is introduced not as a monarch and king, but as a pseudo-apostle and impious doctor of the Church. Then it is handed down concerning this King that he will cast down three horns and will wage war against the Saints of God, which prophecy signifies nothing else than that the tyrant who is signified by this image will be outside the Church: but the Antichrist sits in the midst of the Church, 2 Thess. 2, nor does he cast down the horns, but sits upon the whole beast unharmed, Apocal. 17. Finally, the coming of the Antichrist is with prodigies and miracles, Matt. 24 and Luke 21, 2 Thess. 2. But to this little horn no miracles, but force, cruelty & blasphemy are attributed.

Although, however, Jerome and other Fathers seem to have interpreted this type concerning the Antichrist; it is nevertheless certain that they did not even dream in a fever of such an Antichrist as the Papists imagine for themselves. And whatever they hand down concerning this little horn, all of that can most correctly be transcribed to the Eastern Antichrist, who is outside the Church. Nor is it a wonder that the Fathers speak more obscurely about the Antichrist, since the oracles of the Prophets derive their light from the event, and we finally today, after both Antichrists, Eastern and Western, have been revealed, can rightly judge concerning them.

And therefore our people understand the little horn of Daniel to be about the Antichrist indeed, but a true one, not a feigned one, about the Eastern one, not the Western one, that is, about the Turk, who is described here with unmistakable γνωρίσμασι (marks) and characters. For he is called (1.) a little horn, because at the beginning he was very small. For Mahomet, from parents of the lowest rank, Adele, or as the Alcoran calls him in Geifreus, lib. IV. Aul. Turc. p. 163. ABBALLA, and born of his mother Emina in the territory of the city of Mecca in the year of Christ 560, a servant at the beginning, then manumitted, he took into marriage his mistress, the wife of Abdimeneptis, a rich merchant, and she having died, he joined to himself in marriage the daughter of Prince Bubaris, and when the Ishmaelites had fought brilliantly under the standards of Heraclius against Cosroes the Persian, but their pay was not being paid to them, and they were defecting from the Emperor, he became their leader, and Mahomet called them Saracens: and the little horn passed through Arabia, Syria, and other kingdoms, and thus grew into great power. Furthermore (2.) that little horn had to arise under the fourth Monarchy, which was fulfilled in the Mahometan empire. God judges the Turkish empire unworthy, as Osiander rightly says here, that one should speak of it as if it were a peculiar Monarchy. For the Turk is not truly a Monarch, but he has occupied certain parts of the Roman Empire: in which he sticks, just as a cancer (disease) in a body. (3.) That little horn had to tear away three from those kingdoms. That was done when Egypt, Asia, and Greece were reduced under the power of Mahomet. See B. Luther, preface to Daniel, Osiander in the Paraphrase, B. Gesner on this passage, B. Balduin, Tom. II. disput. Witteberg. disp. VI. B. Gerhard, Tom. IX. LL. CC. 191. He extorted Parthia, Armenia, and Mesopotamia not from the Romans, but from the Persians. (4.) The eyes of this horn, like the eyes of men, designate the craftiness and cunning of Mahomet, which B. Gesner expresses here at length from his history and the Alcoran. Although the barbarity of the Saracens and Turks was and is great, as Osiander says here (for they do not care for letters or the studies of humanity), yet in increasing their Empire they are most sharp-sighted; they seize all opportunities by which they may occupy and subjugate neighboring territories. And without doubt the Turk knows better what is happening in the Roman Empire than any of the estates of the Empire. (5.) A mouth speaking great things notes the lies and Mahometan blasphemies, with which the Alcoran is most full. A compendium of this was exhibited by Geifreus, lib. IV. Turc. Aulæ, and brother Richard, Tom. II. Witebergens. Luth. And the Alcoran itself boasts that it indeed contains 22,000 sayings, but that nine thousand of them are false. (5.) That horn makes war against the Saints, and prevails over them v. 21. Which sad experience has sufficiently taught to have been fulfilled concerning the Mahometan beast. (6.) To attempt to change times. The Turks observe neither the Sabbath of the Jews nor the Lord's Day, but celebrate the day of Venus in its place, both in insult to Christ, who was crucified on that day, and in honor of Venus, whom the Hagarenes once worshipped, as Cedrenus testifies. (7.) That horn also changes the law. Thus Mahomet cast away the law or heavenly doctrine, and having invented another law diametrically opposed to it, he included it in the Alcoran. (8.) The duration of that kingdom is defined by a time, times, and half a time. Similarly also Apoc. 12, 12. The woman shadowing the Church is said to flee for a time, times, and half a time, and the same exile is described later by the space of 1260 days, and further Apoc. 11, 23. c. 13, 5. the same time is circumscribed by 42 months, which complete three years and a half; from which comparison it appears that this phrase was used by Daniel in the same sense: and thus designates three years and a half or 1260 days. Most understand solar years, each of which comprises as many years as it otherwise comprises days; which fit the Mahometan Kingdom very well. For Mahomet arose in the year of Christ 560, from which time to the present year 1672, 1112 years have elapsed: thus therefore 148 would still remain, which Christ promised would be shortened for the sake of the elect, Matt. 24. Others assign the beginning of the Mahometan kingdom to about the year of Christ 613, by which agreement the end would be in the year 1873. (9.) That horn is said to be great before its fellows, among those ten horns v. 20. Which there is no doubt fits the Mahometan empire. For it is greater than any of those seven remaining Empires. (10.) Finally, that horn is said to be destroyed at the coming of the Lord to Judgment. Nor will the power of the Eastern Antichrist be abolished except with the glorious coming of Christ, which will also bring an end to the Roman Antichrist, 2 Thess. 2. Osiander says, I think this text should be understood thus: that the Lord, shortly before the last day, will overturn the power of the Turk (that Gog and Magog of Ezek. 29, 39): then I think the end of this world will soon be present. He notes, however, later that the last day will finally abolish the whole power of the Turks entirely. (11.) We add the consensus of Joh. Annius of Viterbo, lib. de quæstion. in Apoc. c. 17. Cantapretensis l. 1. Hypoth. Genebr. in Chron. ad Ann. Chron. 590. Hector Pinti, Vatablus, as also Joh. Langius in Justin. Dial. c. Triph. Fevardentius in Iren. l. V. c. 26. Clichtov. in l. 4. Damasc. de O. F. c. 27. and also from our own B. Luther, preface to Dan., Philipp. Melancht., B. Osiand. on this passage, B. Ægidius Hunnius T. 1. oper. f. 1428. B. Gesner on this passage, B. Balduin T. 2. disp. Witeb. disp. 2. c. 1. th. 6. B. D. Gerhard T. VI. de Magistr. th. 137. T. IX. de Extr. Jud. th. 91. B. D. Brochmand. See P. R. against Bellarmine, p. 323. Mr. D. Geier on this passage, and the Paraphrast of the Weimar theologians, and most other orthodox theologians, who refer these things which are told of the little horn to Mahomet, the founder of the Turkish empire, which Mr. D. Svaningius acknowledges may not inconveniently be done, although with Oecolampadius he draws these to both: but which must necessarily be taken of one only, whether an Eastern or Western Anti-Christ, since only one little horn is designated, not a twin one. He rightly urges the patrons of the Porphyrian-Grotian opinion, which Polanus also, Tremellius, and Piscator have embraced, that they should count in proper order those three kings whom the little horn cast down, and show them to have been broken by the beast with many horns through the agency of Antiochus, and that they should teach how it is consistent that the fourth beast, which they make the empire of the Seleucids, is said to survive until the last day.

See also what B. Gesner has opposed to this opinion in this place, B. Gerhard Vol. VI. on the Magistrate, thesis 136, B. Helvicus in his Historical Synopsis, page 5 et seqq. The opinion of Calvin, that Julius Caesar and his successors are denoted by the little horn, as also that of R. Saadia, that Titus Vespasianus is designated, does not agree with the marks expressed here; those who, along with other Jews, blasphemously twist the little horn toward Christ the Savior, one will be able to see refuted in D. Suaningius, if it pleases anyone. That the Roman Pontiff is not understood here is also taught by Andr. Vilettus against Bullinger with certain arguments, not all of which are so easily dissolved. Jerome refutes the Porphyrian opinion of Grotius from the text and the consensus of the interpreters in this way: In vain does Porphyry suspect that the little horn, which arose after the ten horns, is Antiochus Epiphanes, and that the three horns plucked out from the ten horns are the sixth, Ptolemy surnamed Philometor, and the seventh, Ptolemy Euergetes, and Artaxias, King of Armenia, the former of whom died long before Antiochus was born. We know, however, that Antiochus did indeed fight against Artaxias, but that he remained in his original kingdom. Therefore, let us say what all ecclesiastical writers have handed down: at the consummation of the world, when the Roman kingdom is to be destroyed, there will be ten kings who will divide the Roman world among themselves: And that an eleventh little king will arise, who will overcome three kings out of the ten: That is, the King of the Egyptians, and of Africa, and of Ethiopia.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET CORNU ALIUD PARVULUM ORTUM EST DE MEDIO EORUM] Parvulum cornu dicitur, quia etsi genere erat regio, nullum tamen jus habebat ad regnum, Antiochus scilicet Epiphanes. Vide 11, 21.

ET TRIA DE CORNIBUS PRIMIS EVULSA SUNT A FACIE EJUS] Id est, per ipsum, aut ex ipsius jussu. Seleucus frater ipsius major occisus; spoliatus ve- ro Demetrius ejusdem Seleuci filius, Antiochi autem Pa- truelis: spoliatus item Ptolomæus Philopator Rex Ægypti. Demetrius fuit filius Seleuci, qui frater Antiochi. Ac pro- inde apud Justinum, ubi filio hujus Antiochi Demetrius dicitur Patruus, legendum patruelis: quod nos docent Ap- pianus, & Livii breviator lib. 46. Vide quæ dicentur infra ad cap. 11.

ET ECCE, OCULI QUASI OCULI HOMI- NIS ERANT IN CORNU ISTO] Id est, perspicax e rit ad res agendas. Vide 8, 23.

ET OS LOQUENS INGENTIA] Erat enim ar- rogans admodum. Unde & ἐπιφανὴς dictus. Vide infra 20.

Hic magis se prodit falsitas interpretationis Porphyrio-Grotianæ. Nam tria cornua ex illis di- cuntur à succrescente parvo cornu dejecta. Ad- fert Demetrium filium Seleuci spoliatum ab Antio- cho. Ptolomæum item Philopatorem: Sed hic de a- vulsis, & disjectis cornubus, non de spoliatione res est: Neque Demetrius ille in numero decem cor- nuum à Grotio adductorum reperitur. Et regna- vit Demetrius post Epiphanem. At cornu dejecta oportuit ante regnare cap. 7, 8. Porro parvum illud cornu Danielis, quod inter decem cornua enatum, distinctum est à decem cornubus, non vero est ex numero istorum cornuum. Nam dicitur ascendis- se בֵּינֵיהוֹן inter ea. At Antiochus Epiphanes non est cornu distinctum à decem cornubus, sed unum est ex illorum numero, juxta Grotium. Ergo An- tiochus non est parvum cornu, de quo Propheta agit Post ortum decem cornuum prodiit parvum cornu, & illa decem cornua hujus respectu difer- te dicuntur priora v. 8. קַרְנַיָא קַדְמָיָתָא de decem cornubus prioribus. Dicitur Rex ille per parvum cornu significatus post reliquos surrecturus v. 24. ET ALIUS CONSURGET POST EOS: & diffe- ret ipse à PRIORIBUS. Quæ nullatenus de An- tiocho intelligi possunt. Ille enim non fuit alius consurgens post decem Reges, sed unus ex decem Re- gum numero: non differt à prioribus illis decem Regibus, ceu novus & alius Rex, sed ad eorum numerum pertinet, juxta Grotianam explicatio- nem. Adde quod cornu illud parvum ascendere vel prodire debuerit INTER desem illa cornua quartæ bestiæ v. 8. 20. 21, adeoque exitus ejus per- tinet ad Quartum imperium, non vero ad tertium. Atqui Antiochus Epiphanes non prodiit ex quarta bestia, sed ex tertia Dan. 8, 9. 22. 25. ortus è Seleuco. Ideoque Antiochus Epiphanes non est cornu illud parvum, inter decem cornua enatum. Præterea Cornu parvum Quartæ bestiæ, quod exortum est inter decem cornua, majus est cæteris, postquam vires acquisivit vers. 20. At Antiochus Epiphanes non fuit unquam major, aut potentior cæteris. Quod ex historiis probat Helvicus pag. 5. Præter- quam quod Parthica gens dudum antehac sub Se- leuco Callinico à Seleucidis defecerat & Syria in- testinis bellis plurimum debilitata fuerat (Vide Appian. Syr. Just. lib. 27.) notum est, ad quantas angustias Antiochus M. pater Epiphanis redactus, & quanta regni parte à Romanis exutus fuerit, & quam gravi insuper tributo oneratus: Vide Liv. dec. 4. lib. 7. Flor. l. 2. c. 8. &c. Qui ergo Epi- phanes cæteris ante se regibus major potentiorq; dici possit? Denique prævaliturum erat cornu par- vum sanctis, donec veniret antiquus dierum ad ju- dicium, adeoque ad novissimum diem usque dura- turum est illud imperium. At Antiochi Impe- rium jam per plura secula eversum.

Quod si vero objiciatur; Antiochum sequen- te capite per parvulum cornu repræsentari; facilis est responsio; id ab hoc diversum esse, vel ex eo con- stare, quod illud corniculum oriatur in fronte Hir- ci Caprarum, hoc est, Alexandri Magni. Præsens autem κεράδιον ex quarta bestia nascatur, vers. 22.

Hæc ergo argumenta convincunt non intel- ligendum hic esse cum Grotio, & Calvinianis ple- risque Antiochum. Unde Calvinus ipse hic no- bis suffragatur, ut & Johannes de Napejr cum Inter- prete Leone de Dramma propos. 24. p. 86. agno- scens, quartam bestiam necessario esse Monarchiam Romanam. Si ergo quæras, ecquis denique hic de- signatus fuerit? Resp. Pontificii Antichristum, quem adhuc oriturum fingunt, indicari volunt: Maldonatus, Pererius, Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. Rebera in Apoc. 12, 11. Josephus à Costa lib. 11. de temp. noviss. cap. 9. Bellarminus lib. 3. de Pontifice Romano c. 16. Gretserus in defens. Bellarm. Schop- pius de Antichristo, Lessius demonstrat. 12. de An- tichrist. Becan. Tom. 2. opusc. 1. Sed cum Utopi- cum suum Antichristum nuspiam alias inveniant in S. Literis, & ea de illo somnient, quæ Scripturis nullatenus consentanea sunt, non nisi temere hic locus ad eundem detorquetur. Merum enim est Ens rationis, & Chimæra Papistica Antichristus ille à Papæis confictus. Et obstant non pauca huic sententiæ, in textu, quæ urgentur à Gesnero th. 134. Primo enim hoc parvulum cornu denotat secula- rem Principem, seu Regem, eo quod oritur è decem corniculis, id est, è medio Regum vel Principum: & angelus infra expressè nominat cornu istud Re- gem, qui potentior sit futurus prioribus. Anti- christus autem licet regiam eminentiam sibi ven- dicet, Dan. 11. attamen in proprio suo habitu 2. Thess. 2. & alibi non ut Monarcha, & Rex, sed ut Pseudo-Apostolus, & Impius Ecclesiæ Doctor induci- tur. Deinde de hoc Rege traditur, quod tria cor- nua sit dejecturus, & Sanctis Dei bellum illaturus, quod vaticinium nihil aliud significat, quam eum tyrannum, qui hac imagine signatur, fore extra Ecclesiam: Antichristus autem sedet in media Ec- clesia, 2. Thess. 2. neque dejicit cornua, sed toti be- stiæ illæsæ insidet Apocal. 17. Denique adventus Antichristi est cum prodigiis & miraculis, Matth. 24. & Luc. 21. 2. Thess. 2. Huic autem corniculo nulla miracula, sed vis, sævitia & blasphemia tri- buuntur.

Etsi autem Hieronymus, & alii Patres viden- tur hunc typum de Antichristo interpretati; cer- tum tamen est, quod illi talem Antichristum, qua- lem Pontificii sibi imaginantur, ne per febrim quidem somniaverint. Et quicquid illi de hoc corniculo tradunt, illud omne Anti Christo orienta- li, qui est extra Ecclesiam, rectissime transcribi po- test. Nec mirum est, Patres obscurius de Anti- Christo loqui, cum oracula Prophetarum lucem suam ab eventu fortiantur, & nos demum hodie, postquam uterque AntiChristus, orientalis atque occidentalis, revelatus est, recte de illis judicare possimus.

Ideoque Nostrates de Antichristo quidem, sed vero, non ficto, de orientali, non occidentali parvum cornu Danielis intelligunt, hoc est, de Turca, qui hic non dubiis γνωρίσμασι & Characteribus de- scribitur. Namque dicitur (1.) parvum cornu, quia sub initium valde exiguum fuit. Mahomedes e- nim infimæ sortis parentibus Adele, vel ut Alcora- nus apud Geifreum eum vocat lib. IV. Aul. Turc. p. 163. ABBALLA, & matre Emina in agro urbis Mechæ Anno Christi 560. procreatus, servus initio, deinde manumissus in matrimonium duxit heram suam Abdimeneptis divitis Mercatoris conjugem, eaque defuncta Bubaris Principis filiam sibi matri- monio copulavit, & cum Ismaëlitæ sub Heraclii si- gnis præclare militassent adversus Cosroëm Per- sam, sed stipendia ipsis non solverentur, & ab Impe- ratore deficerent, Dux eorum factus est, & Sarace- nos illos vocavit Mahumetes: transiitque parvum cornu Arabiam, Syriam, & alia regna, adeoque ex- crevit in magnam potentiam. Porro (2.) par- vum illud cornu sub quarta Monarchia oriri de- buit, quod in Mahumetano impletum imperio. In- dignum judicat Deus Turcicum imperium, ut re- cte hic Osiander, ut de eo, tanquam de peculiari Monarchia, loquatur. Turca enim non est vere Mo- narcha, sed occupavit quasdam partes Romani Im- perii: In quibus hæret, sicut cancer (morbus) in corpore. (3.) Parvum illud cornu à regnis istis tria avellere debuit. Factum id, cum Ægyptus, Asia, & Græcia sub potestatem Mahometis redacta. Vide B. Lutherum præfat. in Danielem, Osiandrum in Paraph: B. Gefnerum ad h. l. B. Balduinum Tom. II. disput. Witteberg. disp. VI. B. Gerhard. Tom. IX. LL. CC. 191. Parthiam, Armeniam & Mesopota- miam non Romanis, sed Persis extorsit. (4.) Oculi hujus cornu tanquam oculi hominum designant vafriciem & versutiam Mahometis, quam ex histo- ria ejus, & Alcorano hic prolixe exprimit B. Ges- nerus. Tametsi magna fuit, & est Saracenorum & Turcarum barbaries, ut hic Osiander, (neque enim literas aut studia humanitatis curant) tamen in au- gendo Imperio suo sunt oculatissimi, omnes occa- siones captant, quibus vicina territoria occupent & subjugent. Et procul dubio Turca melius quid in Romano Imperio fiat, novit, quam aliqu status Imperii. (5.) Os loquens grandia mendaci & blasphemias Mahomedicas notat, quibus Alcora nus est refertissimus. Hujus compendium Gei- fræus lib. IV. Turc. Aulæ & frater Richardus Tom II. Witebergens. Luth. exhibuit. Et jactitat Al- coranus ipse, se quidem continere 22000. dicta, sed novem millia eorum falsa esse. (5.) Præliatu cornu illud contra Sanctos, & prævalet illis v. 21 Quod de bestia Mahometana impletum esse, tristi experientia satis docuit. (6.) Mutare conatu tempora. Turcæ neque Sabbathum Judæorum neque diem Dominicam observant, sed diem Vene- ris ejus loco celebrant, tum in Christi contume- liam, qui eo die crucifixus, tum in Veneris, quam Hagareni olim coluerunt, teste Cedræno, hono- rem. (7.) Mutat cornu illud etiam legem. Ita Mahomed legem seu doctrinam cœlestem abjecit, & aliam legem ei è diametro oppositam commen- tus, eamq; Alcorano complexus est. (8.) Duratio regni illius per tempus, tempora & dimidium tempo- rum definitur. Similiter etiam Apoc. 12, 12. Mulier Ecclesiam adumbrans fugere dicitur tempus, tempo- ra, & dimidium temporum, atque idem exilium describitur postea 1260. dierum spatio, ac porro Apoc. 11, 23. c. 13, 5. tempus idem mensibus 42. cir- cumscribitur, qui tres annos cum dimidio absol- vunt; ex qua collatione apparet, eodem sensu hanc phrasin à Daniele adhibitam: adeoq; tres an- nos cum dimidio vel 1260. dies designare. Pleri- que intelligunt annos solares, quorum quilibet tot annos, quot alioquin dies complectatur; qui ap- prime conveniunt Regno Mahumetano. Nam Mahometh exortus est an. Christi 560. ex quo tem- pore in præsentem annum 1672. elapsi sunt 1112. anni: Sic ergo restarent adhuc 148. quos propter electos abbreviatum iri, Christus promisit Matth. 24. Alii initium regni Mahumedani circa ann. Christi 613. assignant, quo pacto finis foret anno 1873. (9.) Cornu illud magnum dicitur præ so- ciis suis, in decem illis cornibus v. 20. Quod Ma- hometano imperio convenire nullum dubium est. Majus enim est, quam ullum ex septem illis reliquis Imperiis. (10.) Denique cornu istud destructum dicitur sub adventum Domini ad Judicium. Ne- que AntiChristi Orientalis potestas abolebitur, ni- si cum glorioso Christi adventu, qui finem etiam Anti-Christo Romano adferet 2. Thess. 2. Osian- der, existimo, inquit, hunc textum sic accipiendum: quod Dominus paulo ante novissimum diem, poten- tiam Turcæ (Gog illius & Magog Ezech. 29, 39.) sit e- versurus: deinde puto, mox adfuturum & finem hu- jus mundi. Notat tamen postea novissimum diem totam omnino Turcarum potestatem demum abo- liturum. (11.) Addimus consensum Joh. Annii Viterbiensis lib. de quæstion. in Apoc. c. 17. Canta- pretensis l. 1. Hypoth. Genebr. in Chron. ad Ann. Chron. 590. Hector Pinti. Vatabli, ut & Joh. Langii in Justin. Dial. c. Triph. Fevardentii in Iren. l. V. c. 26. Clichtov. in l. 4. Damasc. de O. F. c. 27. nec non è nostris B. Lutheri præfat. in Dan. Philipp. Melancht. B. Osiand. in h. l. B. Ægidii Hunnii T. 1. oper. f. 1428. B. Gesner. in h. l. B. Balduin. T. 2. disp. Witeb. disp. 2. c. 1. th. 6. B. D. Gerhard. T. VI. de Magistr. th. 137. T. IX. de Extr. Jud. th. 91. B. D. Brochmand. de P. R. contr. Bellarm. p. 323. Dn. D. Geier. in h. l. ac Paraphrast. Vinariensium & plero- rumq́; aliorum orthodoxorum Theologorum, qui hæc ad Mahometem imperii Turcici conditorem referunt, quæ de parvo cornu perhibentur, quod non incommode fieri agnoscit D. D. Svaningius etsi cum Oecolampadio ad utrumq́; hæc trahat: Quæ vero necessario de uno tantum accipienda sive O- rientali, sive Occidentali Anti-Christo, quum u- num tantum minutum cornu designetur, non ge- minum. Urget autem recte Porphyrio-Grotianæ sententiæ, quam Polanus etiam, Tremellius & Pisca- tor amplexi sunt, Patronos, ut tres illos Reges, quos parvum cornu disjecit, justa serie numerent, eosq́; An- tiochi opera à bestia multicorni fractos ostendant, ut- que doceant, quomodo conveniat, quod usque ad extremum diem supersesse quarta bellu, quam faciunt Seleucidarum imperium, dicatur.

Vid. etiam, quæ huic sententiæ opposuit B. Gesn. in h. l. B. Gerhard. T. VI. de Magistr. th. 136. B. Helvicus Syn. Histor. pag. 5. seqq. Calvini sententia, quod Julius Cæsar, & ejus successores per parvum cornu notentur, ut & R. Saadiæ, quod Titus Vespa- sianus designetur, non convenit notis hic expressis; quos cum aliis Judæis blaspheme parvulum cornu ad Christum servatorem detorquentibus refutatos videre poterit apud D. Suaningium, cui libuerit. Pontificem Romanum hic non intelligi adversus Bullingerum etiam Andr. Vilettus argumentis qui- busdam docet, quæ non adeo εὐδιάλυτα sunt o- mnia. Porphyrianam Grotii sententiam ita è textu & Interpretum consensu refellit Hierony- mus; Frustra Porphyrius cornu parvulum, quod post decem cornua ortum est, Epiphanem Antiochum su- spicatur, & de decem cornubus tria evulsa cornua, sextum Ptolomæum cognomento Philometorem, & septimum Ptolomæum Evergetem & Artaxiam Re- gem Armeniæ, quorum priores multo antequam An- tiochus nasceretur, mortui sunt. Contra Artaxiam vero dimicasse quidem Antiochum novimus: sed illum in regno pristino permansisse. Ergo dicamus, quod omnes scriptores Ecclesiastici tradiderunt: in consum- matione mundi, quando regnum destruendum est Ro- manorum, decem futuros Reges, qui orbem Romanum inter se dividant: Et undecimum surrecturum esse Regem parvulum, qui tres Reges de decem Regibus superaturus sit: Id est, Ægyptiorum Regem, & A- phricæ, & Æthiopiæ.

## 7:9
Verse 9.

I WAS LOOKING UNTIL THE THRONES WERE PLACED] The seats of the judges, namely of God, as King and of the Angels, as the satraps of the kingdom. See what is above 4, 14. 21. Matt. 19, 28. Rev. 4, 2. 4. 5, 1. 20, 4.

AND THE ANCIENT OF DAYS SAT] He saw the form of a man of advanced age, by which it was signified that the judgments of God would be well-matured, such as those of old men are wont to be.

HIS GARMENT WHITE AS SNOW] Not only is He Himself incorrupt, but also all things that are around Him.

AND THE HAIR OF HIS HEAD AS PURE WOOL] Tinged with no color. Thus the judgments of God are pure from turbulent affections.

HIS THRONE FLAMES OF FIRE] That is, like a flame. Fire is a most effective thing: so also is God most powerful for executing His judgments.

HIS WHEELS A BURNING FIRE] As it were a burning fire. Seats were accustomed to be transported in the East: therefore they had wheels, like the curule chairs of the Romans. It is signified that power accompanies God wherever He wills.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ASPICIEBAM DONEC THRONI POSITI SUNT] Sedilia judicum, Dei scilicet, ut Regis & An- gelorum, ut Satraparum regni. Vide quæ supra 4, 14. 21. Matth. 19, 28. Apoc. 4, 2. 4. 5, 1. 20, 4.

ET ANTIQUUS DIERUM SEDIT] Formam vi- dit viri provectæ ætatis, quo significabatur bene cocta fo- re Dei judicia, qualia esse senum solent.

VESTIMENTUM EJUS CANDIDUM QUASI NIX] Non ipse tantum incorruptus, sed & omnia quæ cir- cum eum sunt.

ET CAPILLI CAPITIS EJUS QUASI LANA MUNDA] Nullo colore tincta. Sic Dei Judicia pura à turbidis affectibus.

THRONUS EJUS FLAMMÆ IGNIS] Id est; tanquam flamma. Ignis res efficacissima: sic & Deus ad Judicia sua exequenda potentissimus.

ROTÆ EJUS IGNIS ACCENSUS] Quasi ignis ardens Sedilia in Oriente transportari solebant: Ideo ro- tas habebant, ut sellæ curules Romanorum. Significatur potentia Deum comitari quocumque voluerit.

## 7:10
Verse 10.

A FIERY AND RAPID RIVER WAS GOING FORTH FROM HIS FACE] In the Chaldean: A fiery river was flowing, going forth from His mouth. Perpetual force was present in all His decrees.

Thus also B. Gesner wishes the opinion of the Judge to be indicated, which will truly be fiery to the impious. Rupert of Deutz, however, wishes the Holy Spirit to be shadowed forth by the river, whose opinion is not inappropriate: For just as God the Father is presented by the Ancient of Days, and the Son in the likeness of the Son of Man, so in this illustrious theophany it was fitting that the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the divinity, should also be exhibited. And since the Holy Spirit is otherwise exhibited in the Scriptures under the likeness and appearance of a river, John 7, Rev. 22, and loves a fiery form, and presents Himself to be seen in that way, Acts 2, furthermore, this personal character is expressly held here in the word ἐκπορευόμενον, which occurs in the Greek text and is appropriated to the Holy Spirit, John 15, 26, Rev. 21, 1. (In the Chaldean text occurs the word נפק, which the Syrian uses in John 15:26.) Finally, let it be called ἐκπορευόμενον [proceeding] FROM THE FACE of the Ancient of Days, which is proper to the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord ἐκπορευομένῳ παρὰ τ̃ πατρὸς [proceeding from the Father], and therefore not undeservedly are these things expounded concerning the Holy Spirit. Just as a river is of the same nature as its source, so is the Holy Spirit with the Father. The face of the one sitting is like fire; the river from the face is also fiery. See B. Gerhard, Chapter 178 of the Harmon. Evang. The blessed Wilh. Lyserus more fully confirmed this interpretation in a Pentecostal Program, A.D. 1633, publicly proposed here in the name of the Rector, according to the custom of the Academy: This river of Daniel is fire, and indeed not a culinary one, to which Vitruvius attributes the first associations of men in book 2, chapter 1, or an elemental one, about which there is still a dispute among philosophers, but clearly supercelestial and divine, which is conspicuous even in the very throne of the one sitting, whence he is said to inhabit unapproachable light 1 Tim. 6,16. it is said, he shows his supreme wisdom and knowledge, infinite justice and immense power. For this river of fire goes forth from the face of him who sits upon the throne, whence his divine origin and nature are conspicuous. For this river of fire מִן־קֳדָמוֹהִי from the face, or the front of him who sits upon the throne, the ancient of days, arises, not from the back, as an effect produced by him outside of himself follows. Concerning the angels it is immediately subjoined that they stood קָדָמוֹהִי before him: But when the Holy Scripture speaks of this river, it adds the particle מן, which, when added to rivers, is wont to recall us to their origin and source Ex. 17, 6. Jud. 15,19. Thus, therefore, the source of this river is in the very face of the Ancient of Days, in which, because there is nothing that is not God himself, this river also emanating from him will be a participant in the divine nature: for a river is of the same nature as the source from which it flows, according to that well-known saying of Bede, book 1, in Morum, chapter 1: We know that a living fountain, a pool, and a stream contain such equality that if you pour from any one of them into another, you find no dissimilarity in them: provided that no impurity enters from the outside. Who, therefore, knowing these things on visible earth, cannot believe in the Trinity and unity of the invisible Creator? Who, knowing the one and same substance of the fountain, the stream, and the pool—that is, water—cannot understand that which the Lord says in the Gospel: he who sees me, sees also the Father. Although, indeed, this fiery river is of the same nature and essence as the face of the one sitting on the throne and the Ancient of Days himself; yet it is distinguished from him by way of emanation. For this river of fire is called נָפֵק [going out]. נפק is properly rendered by ἐκπόρευσιν [procession], whence the seventy elders explained Daniel in this place thus: ποταμὸς πυρὸς εἷλκεν ἐκπορευόμενος [a river of fire was drawing, proceeding]: Indeed, the Holy Spirit himself, in the commentary which he caused to be recorded above through John in the Apocalypse concerning this vision of Daniel, uses the same word regarding the egress of this river, chapter 22:1: he showed me a pure river of water of life, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. But we know and profess from the Athanasian Creed that ἐκπόρευσιν [procession] and the procession from the Father and the Son is the personal property of the Holy Spirit: The Holy Spirit is not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. We have the foundation of this faith in the words of Christ, John 15:26. the Spirit of truth which proceeds from the Father; which the Syrian renders thus: רוּחָא דִשׁוּרָא הוּ דְמִנְלוּת אָבִי נָפֵק [the Spirit of truth which goes out from the Father], retaining clearly the same word which Daniel has here. So that by this word the internal and eternal emanation of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son may be insinuated to us, and the otherwise ineffable and incomprehensible mystery in a liken ess of the fiery river emanating from the fiery face and yet remaining conspicuously in the same, contrary to the nature of other rivers, which recede from the source by flowing, is in some way shadowed forth to us.
