In- terim peccavimus: & tu nos ejecisti. Sed memor pacti tui simul fuisti, & promisisti nobis restitutionem politia & reditum ex hac captivitate Babylonica, si- mulque productionem Messiæ salvatoris. Cum igitur tempus servituti à te destinatum effluxerit, ego vehe- menter te oro, liberes nos ex Babylone, restituas nobis Judæam, & jam tandem in Judæa mittas Dominum Messiam. Qui totum caput Danielis, imo totam hi- storiam electi hujus populi in lineam Christi, & pro- missionem certæ terræ, propter eundem finem attribu- tæ, consideraverit, hunc verum scopum petitionis Da- nielis esse fatebitur. Adde quod Scripturæ sacræ hic mos sit in similibus locis exprimere ita Personarum divinarum pluralitatem, cum a Domino propter Do- minum aliquid petitur, aut Dominus à Domino ali- quid fecisse dicitur, aut simili ratione Domini ac Do- mini mentio fit, quemadmodum id alias ex profes- so contra Judæos & Socinianos ostendimus. Distin- cte ergo hic monstratur Dominus, Deus Pater, qui exaudit preces, & faciem suam illuminat super Jeru- salem, & Dominus propter quem exaudit, Filius Dei mediator & intercessor unicus, propter quem Dominus faciem suam illuminat. Neque temere observatur mysterium in trina repetitione vocis Domini vers. 19. Domine esaudi, Domine placare,

Domine attende : qua nonnulli credunt Sacram Trinitatem Personarum divinarum indicari; cui subjungitur; inclina aurem tuam Deus meus, ut ostendatur tres illas personas esse unum Deum, quemadmodum etiam Seraphim in hymno suo Esa. 6. trina vocis SANCTUS repetitione S. S. Trinitatem celebrant, essentiae vero divinae uni- tatem voce Jehovah Zebaoth designant.

## 9:18
Vers. 18. AND THE CITY UPON WHICH YOUR NAME IS CALLED] That is, which is called by your name. Thus also Jer. 25, 29. Jerusalem was called the city of God Ps. 48, 2. 9. 101, 8.

FOR WE DO NOT PRESENT OUR PRAYERS BEFORE YOUR FACE IN OUR OWN JUSTIFICATIONS] That is, we do not say that we have been innocent: we do not deny that we have deserved this punishment: we do not use defense, but supplication, as before a father: forgive: if ever hereafter.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ET CIVITATEM SUPER QUAM INVO- CATUM EST NOMEN TUUM] Id est, quae de tuo no- mine vocata est. Sic & Jer. 25, 29. vocabatur Hieroso- lyma urbs Dei Ps. 48, 2. 9. 101, 8.

NEQUE ENIM IN JUSTIFICATIONIBUS NO- STRIS PROSTERNIMUS PRECES ANTE FACIEM TUAM] Id est, non dicimus nos fuisse innocentes : non negamus nos poenam hanc promeritos : non defensione u- timur, sed deprecatione, ut apud patrem : ignosce: si un- quam posthac.

## 9:19
Vers. 19. FOR YOUR OWN SAKE] He repeats the same things often, as is wont to happen in vehement emotion.

Latin:

Vers. 19. PROPTER TEMET IPSUM] Saepe eadem repetit, ut fieri solet in affectu vehementi.

## 9:20
Vers. 20. AND WHILE I WAS CONFESSING MY SINS] It is the mark of the pious not to dissemble their faults before God, even if committed through ignorance or by surprise. In exile, such a confession took the place of expiatory sacrifices.

Latin:

Vers. 20. CUMQUE CONFITERER PECCATA MEA] Piorum est culpas suas, quamvis ex ignorantia, aut per subreptionem admissas apud Deum non dissimulare. In exsilio talis confessio erat vice victimarum expiantium.

## 9:21
Vers. 21. BEHOLD THE MAN GABRIEL] That angel, the messenger of great things, in a manly appearance.

WHOM I HAD SEEN IN THE VISION FROM THE BEGINNING] Already before 8, 16.

FLYING SWIFTLY] The swiftness of the ministry is signified, as in others of the Cherubim and Seraphim: thus also the Indians have long since depicted angels.

HE TOUCHED ME] To add strength. See above 8, 18.

AT THE TIME OF THE EVENING SACRIFICE] That is, the ninth hour, which, as formerly, while the Temple stood, was dedicated to sacrifices, so now it was dedicated to prayers.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ECCE VIR GABRIEL] Angelus ille rerum magnarum nuntius, virili specie.

QUEM VIDERAM IN VISIONE A PRINCI- PIO] Jam ante 8, 16.

CITO VOLANS] Celeritas ministerii significatur, ut in aliis Cherubinorum & Seraphinorum : sic etiam In- di jam olim Angelos pingunt.

TETIGIT ME] Ad robur addendum. Vide su- pra 8, 18.

IN TEMPORE SACRIFICII VESPERTINI ] Id est, hora nona, quae, ut olim, stante Templo, sacrificiis, ita nunc orationibus erat dicata.

## 9:22
Vers. 22. NOW I HAVE COME FORTH TO TEACH YOU, AND THAT YOU MIGHT UNDERSTAND] That you may understand as I teach, namely what is to become of that city which you love so much.

Latin:

Vers. 22. NUNC EGRESSUS SUM UT DOCE- REM TE, ET INTELLIGERES] Ut me docente intelli- gas, nempe quid futurum sit de urbe illa, quam tantum di- ligis.

## 9:23
Vers. 23. FROM THE BEGINNING OF YOUR PRAYERS THE WORD WENT FORTH] That is, as soon as you began to pray, I immediately received the command.

I, however, have come to indicate to you] That I might come to indicate to you: namely, those things which pertain to the city.

BECAUSE YOU ARE A MAN OF DESIRES] Thus also below 10, 11. It is, moreover, a Hebrew manner of speaking, which is explained now actively, now passively. Symmachus translates well here ἀνὴρ ἐπιθυμητέ. Daniel is so called in the same sense as Mary is κεχαριτωμένη, Luke 1, 28.

YOU THEREFORE HEED THE WORD] Attend to those things which I shall say.

AND UNDERSTAND THE VISION] That you may understand the prophecy. For as prophets are seers, so every kind of prophecy, in whatever way it becomes known to man, is called a vision.

Latin:

Vers. 23. AB EXORDIO PRECUM TUARUM E- GRESSUS EST SERMO] Id est, simul atque precari coe- pisti, statim mandatum accepi.

EGO AUTEM VENI UT INDICAREM TIBI] Ut veniens tibi indicarem: nempe ea quae ad urbem pertinent.

QUIA VIR DESIDERIORUM ES ] Sic & infra 10, 11. Est autem loquendi genus Hebraeum, quod modo active, modo passive exponitur. Symmachus hic bene vertit ἀνὴρ ἐπιθυμητέ. Ita vocatur Daniel pari sensu quo Ma- ria κεχαριτωμένη, Luc. 1, 28.

TU ERGO ANIMADVERTE SERMONEM] Attende iis quae dicam.

ET INTELLIGE VISIONEM] Ut intelligas Prophe- tiam. Nam ut Prophetae videntes, ita omne Prophetiae ge- nus, quocunque modo homini innotescat, visio dicitur.

## 9:24
Ver. 24. SEVENTY WEEKS] Of years. For such was the custom of speaking, and it remains among the Talmudists. Therefore, where a week of days is treated, the name of days is accustomed to be added, Ezek. 45, 21. Below 10, 2. & 3. in the Hebrew.

This is almost the only oracle which Grotius leaves us concerning the Messiah in the Old Testament. In which, however, he also wished not to be entirely wanting to the Jews. For first, he maintains that no mention of the benefits of Christ is made here, if you correctly weigh his mind: he wishes only the punishments of the Jews to be predicted, namely the destruction of the Jewish polity, so that iniquity might be atoned for, just as he interprets verse 24 concerning their punishments, and he leaves only the publication of the Gospel, which, however, he himself turns into law in the Socinian, Papistic, and indeed even Jewish manner. Then, he denies that the term of the coming of the Messiah is defined here. And by that reasoning, he acts as a midwife to the Jews again. For if nothing other than the destruction of the Jewish polity is predicted, and the term of the coming of Christ is not defined here, how will the Jews be able to be solidly convinced from this oracle that Christ has already arrived, which, however, has hitherto been believed by all Christians as a solid and invincible foundation against Jewish unbelief, especially because at verse 27 it is said that the desolation of the land of the Jews must occur, even until the consummation, as defined by God. However, he denies that this devastation and destruction will have an end. Indeed, with the Jews, he makes the Messiah a worldly Prince, who ought to have liberated Jerusalem and the Jews as his people from impending evils, if, that is, he had been obeyed. For the Jews believe in such a Messiah, who was promised to liberate them from temporal evils, and who was promised as such a liberator under the hypothesis of obedience: whereas, on the contrary, the Prophetic Scripture establishes the Messiah as a spiritual liberator, who ought to save his people from their sins, nor does it promise the liberation of Christ under a hypothesis, but absolutely, since both the advent of the Messiah and the satisfaction for the sins of the whole world, which he had to provide, were promised absolutely, without a hypothesis. As for that defined time of seventy weeks, weeks are rightly understood by Grotius not of days, but of years. Some Jews understand the week not of years, but of Jubilees, each of which is completed in 49 years, whence they think a space of 3430 years is designated by 70 weeks. But nowhere in the sacred writings do 49 years come under the name of a week, nor did the second temple stand for so many years. Origen attributes decades of seven years to a week in Homily 29 on Matthew, so that 70 weeks make up 4900 years. But that acceptance of a week occurs nowhere in Scripture, and the years are dragged in irrelevantly from the beginning of the world up to the consummation of Christ, of which there is no trace in this place. Finally, 4900 years are falsely counted from the creation to the advent of Christ. Wherefore it is undoubted among all Christians that weeks of years, not of days, or otherwise, are designated. For Scripture knows no other weeks than either of days (Ex. 34:22, Lev. 12:1) or of years (Lev. 30:8). But weeks of days cannot be understood here, because it is notoriously false that within seven such weeks, that is, 49 days, the streets and walls were built, and within seventy weeks of days, that is, the space of one year and 18 weeks, all those things which are predicted here to be fulfilled were fulfilled. And the Jews themselves acknowledge that weeks of years are understood. R. Aben Ezra on this passage: The venerable R. Saadia said that these seventy weeks are of years. R. Levi, R. Solomon, R. Joseph Jachiades, and R. Isaac Abarbinel agree; Menasse Ben Israel, *de term. vit.* p. 160. And the same is taught in the Talmud, in the tract Sanhedrin, Chapter Chelec, from R. Saadia, that these LXX weeks make up 490 years. Furthermore, although there are not wanting those who understand lunar years here, such as Africanus in the fifth volume of his *Tempora* apud Jerome on this passage, and Theodoret on this passage, Bede, and others, who make them 475 years, nevertheless, the usual and commonly received ones are entirely to be understood, because there is no evidence that lunar ones are designated, nor should one depart from the received meaning, by which sacred Chronology is defined, without cause. The Jews indeed had a lunar year, but one of such a kind that, according to the insertion of an intercalary month, it coincides with the solar, as was proved by B. D. Behm, *Lib. 1. Chron. Manud. Tit. 3. c. 2.* For unless they had had a lunar year mixed with a solar one, their feasts would have been cast into another time within a short space of years.

ABBREVIATED ARE UPON THY PEOPLE] They are defined. When these are finished, the people will no longer exist, that is, the Jewish polity, which you perhaps hitherto hoped would be everlasting.

AND UPON THY HOLY CITY] That is, so beloved by you.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected, which the Papists excuse here in vain. But the Hebrew word is rendered 'are defined.' Because נחתך and גזר are synonyms according to the Rabbis, as can be seen in R. Solomon on this passage and R. Mardochai Nathan in his Concordance: but this signifies 'decreed' (Job 22:38, Isa. 9:20), and it is manifest that a defined space of time is being dealt with here. But as for Grotius understanding 'defined upon the people' in such a way that, when they are finished, the Jewish polity or people should no longer exist, that tends to the same point as if this space of LXX weeks were defined up to the destruction of the Jewish people and the total ruin of the city. Which opinion, although not a few embrace it, who, that is, assign the term to which of these LXX weeks to the destruction of the Jerusalemites, others however say that this term is more rightly fixed at the Lord's passion, or shortly after it: and thus they wish the people to be considered here, insofar as they were chosen by God as a holy people, and the city, insofar as it had to provide a seat for the worship of God, and a workshop for Christ for the perfection of his work. Since it is notably said 'upon the people, place, and holy city': and the angelic scope is to console the people: but he would not be consoling if, at the very outset, before any announcement of the benefits of the Messiah, he were to threaten final destruction.

THAT THE TRANSGRESSION MAY BE CONSUMMATED] that it may receive its end, namely, the punishment. For it is frequent for the Hebrews to call punishments by the word פשע and similar terms.

Daniel was most anxious about the restoration of the city, not for the sake of the city, but for the sake of the promises concerning the Messiah made to be fulfilled in that city. Therefore, Gabriel informs him not about the destruction of the city, but about the defined fullness of those things which were to be consummated there. Nor does he simply say that seventy weeks are determined upon that people and upon the city, but with a certain relation and intention: that they are defined, not for the preservation or consummation of the city, or for the time of the consummation, but for shutting up the transgression and consummating the sin. And this is the term to which of the LXX weeks; which the Angel expresses with a clear and sonorous voice. He makes mention of the city and the people, however, not in defining the term to which of the years, but in determining that place and people in which those things were once to be done. Whence it is tacitly involved at the same time that the city and people will be repaired, and that it is to be preserved until those things are completed in that city and in that people.

AND THAT SIN MAY RECEIVE AN END] In the Hebrew, 'to seal up sin': That is, the punishment of sins. Things which are completed are accustomed to be sealed. Thus Cicero in the second book of *De Divinatione*.

AND LET INIQUITY BE BLOTTED OUT] In Hebrew it is כפר. Which is also accustomed to be placed in this way, just as piare [to atone] is used among the Latins:

And they will atone for the guilt of the wretched with death. That is, they will cause it to be paid. Thus the Hebrews say, תהי מיתתו כפרה עליו. Therefore, consistently with those things which precede, you may rightly translate, and let iniquity be paid for; most fully, that is to say.

But this is a notable depravation of an illustrious Evangelical promise, while it is transmuted into a most grave threatening. But (1.) the propriety of the words stands in the way, for פשע properly denotes prevarication, and therefore sin, not the punishment of sin, and likewise there is no doubt that the other words חטאת & עון properly denote sin, and it is not right to depart from the proper signification without a compelling reason. Furthermore, the discourse is concerning that consummation of prevarications and sealing of sin, which happens when iniquity is blotted out or expiated, since those words are joined exegetically. Thirdly, that consummation, sealing, and blotting out of sins is understood here, which is joined with eternal righteousness. But the punishment of sins and iniquities is not joined with eternal righteousness: but the expiation of sin and the bringing in of true righteousness are connected. Fourthly, concerning that confirmation, and sealing, and blotting out of iniquities, which is the end and fruit of the passion and death of Christ, or which Christ, by his coming, passion, and death, was to effect for us, for which also the Holy of Holies was to be anointed. Therefore, this is not to be understood concerning the penalty and plenary payment of iniquity. For its end was not the punishment of the Jews, but the expiation of the sins of the whole world. Is. 53. Zach. 14, 10. Fifthly, the benefits which Christ bestowed upon us are clearly expressed, both privative, whereby the consummation of transgressions, lest they should condemn the human race, nor could they even dominate; the sealing of sins, lest they accuse us, just as an open handwriting accuses us of debts Col. 2, 14. but a sealed book cannot be read Is. 29. v. 11. and iniquities blotted out, because expiation was made for the sins of the whole world, 1. Joh. 2, 2. and sins are said to be covered here as it is here in the Hebrew, because our iniquities are covered by the merit of Christ, so that they do not appear in the sight of God Rom. 4. then positive, that eternal righteousness has been brought and procured for us. Sixthly, the words לכל הפשע are more correctly rendered, to restrain, than to consummate the transgression. For although כלה may be to consummate, כלא however is to restrain and imprison. Because Christ restrained and broke the power of sin against us, by which it accuses us before God. Finally, the common consensus of all interpreters can be opposed to this Jewish-Grotian gloss: who interpret ὁμοθυμαδὸν concerning the expiation of iniquities made through Christ. But Grotius was led astray here by the Jews: for thus R. Joseph Jacchiades explains it: that LXX weeks still remain, so that Jerusalem may be destroyed, and the Jews sent into exile, so that an end may be put to their transgression.

AND EVERLASTING RIGHTEOUSNESS BE BROUGHT IN] Within that time the Gospel shall be published, which is righteousness, not that which was to last for a time, as that of the law, which you, Daniel, above 9, 15, did not wrongly call righteousness, but without end.

Righteousness is one thing, but the Gospel is another, which announces righteousness, and is a proclamation of the grace of the remission of sins, of righteousness, and of eternal salvation. Righteousness is the object of the Gospel, but this is not itself Righteousness, but a proclamation, or promise, or announcement of eternal righteousness. Which Grotius very badly confuses with the Photinians, as if Christ only brought Righteousness by announcing the Gospel, and was the first herald of the Gospel: both of which claims of the Socinians we have refuted in their proper place. Grace and the remission of sins were preached, along with eternal righteousness, even in the Old Testament. Indeed, all the Prophets announced it, as Peter testifies Acts 10, 43. Therefore, the bringing in of righteousness in the time of the New Testament is left as something far different than that which is accomplished by preaching alone: namely, true and eternal righteousness had to be acquired in the fullness of time through the Messiah, and the angel expresses this with the word BRINGING IN. The Apostle explains ἑυρίσκειν as to find, because he teaches that Christ found eternal redemption Heb. 9, 12. Therefore Christ is also called in Jerem. 23, 6. Jehovah our Righteousness. Which R. David Kimchi explains thus: The Messiah shall be called by this name Jehovah our righteousness, because in his days the righteousness of Jehovah, always enduring or perpetual, shall be obtained by us. R. Moses Hadarsan & R. Levi in this place have it thus: Everlasting righteousness is none other than the Messiah, of whom it is written (Is. 56, 1.) Establish judgment and do righteousness, for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. Similarly R. Barachai in the book on the order of the world on Isaiah 56, 1. explains: My salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. That is the Messiah, of whom it is written Dan. 9. that everlasting righteousness may be brought in.

Nor indeed does that Grotian opposition of Legal and Evangelical Righteousness hold together; that the legal was to last for a time, but the evangelical is eternal. For the legal also ought to have been eternal, provided it could have been performed, according to that: he who shall do them, shall live in them.

AND THE VISION AND PROPHECY BE FULFILLED] Within that time the ancient prophecies of Jacob, David, Isaiah, and others will be fulfilled. Matth. 11, 13. Only to Daniel were those things revealed which were to exist after that time. Matth. 24, 15. Vision and prophecy, that is, prophetic visions.

AND THE HOLY OF HOLIES BE ANOINTED] The Lord Jesus becomes the Christ, through his resurrection and ascension into the heavenly palace. Acts 2, 36. But he is rightly called the Holy of Holies, that is, the Most Holy of all: just as κατ' ἐξοχὴν the Holy One. Acts 3, 14. c. 4, 30. Apoc. 3, 7. Joh. 2. verse 20. Thus Moses Gerundensis explains these things concerning the Messiah.

Grotius explains these things thus, that within the time of those LXX weeks, the publication of the Gospel, the fulfillment of visions, and the anointing of the Holy of Holies must take place. Others, who establish the term to which as the passion and death of Christ, say that the particle ל prefixed to the infinitive verbs expresses the final term. Because according to the style of scripture, the prefix ל added to an infinitive is accustomed to denote not the term through which, as they say, or within which, but the term to which, and that the LXX weeks are said to be decided for the performing of these benefits: and so these seem to be established as their term. And because below v. 26, the Prophet seems to have placed those benefits in the last week. Moreover, by the HOLY OF HOLIES some here understand the Sanctuary, or the Mosaic and Solomonic holy of holies, which is so called Exod. 26, 33. with Junius and Vatablus. Others understand not the typical, but the heavenly Holy of Holies, of which Heb. 8, 11. 12. 24. 25. with Piscator, others the Church, as Mr. D. Anan. Weberus in his dissertation 2 on the salvation of Christ concerning the seventy weeks of Daniel, page 32, interprets this anointing as the real sanctification of the temple and its principal part, the typical Sanctuary, by which it, with all its worship and apparatus of sacrifices, through the offering and blood of the victim and immaculate lamb Jesus Christ in his passion and death, was truly anointed, i.e., so consecrated in its office and conferred duty, that its divine authority, which it had in the O.T., is fully confirmed: or also concerning the entry of the high priest into the heavenly and eternal Holy of Holies, when he opened it to us and destined and dedicated it as an eternal dwelling. But that anointing is understood in that way in the scriptures will scarcely be taught, and it is sufficiently known what is denoted by anointing when the discourse is about Christ, who obtained his name from anointing. And therefore we confess that by the Holy of Holies, Christ must be understood entirely, who was also made Christ through the resurrection, so that there is no need to invent new meanings for the word anointing, or to explain these things concerning the typical or heavenly sanctuary, even if this is the term to which the LXX weeks were to be expressed. But that this is expressed here, we do not yet see solidly proven by these words. For the little word ל can be taken in the sense of a final cause, as it is very often taken, namely that the LXX weeks were established by divine decree so that these things might finally come to pass while those weeks are being fulfilled: whence those who say they are completed in the destruction of the city, meanwhile, and before the city is destroyed, judge that this anointing has taken place; with whom Grotius also agrees. It seems entirely certain to us that by the Holy of Holies, Christ is understood. Which is also [the opinion of] Tertullian in book 4 against the Jews, Jerome, Theodoret on this passage, Galatinus, Luther in volume 8 of the Jena edition, folio 83, and Helvicus in his special disquisition, thesis 120.

It is the opinion of the Tigurines, Cornelius à Lapide, and others. The Arabic version agrees, rendering it thus: to Christ, who is the holiness of holinesses; and R. Moses Gerundensis in Galatinus, book 6, on the truth of the Catholic mysteries, chapter 18, as also R. Lusitanus in the colloquy of Mittelburg, fol. 103.

Latin:

Vers. 24. SEPTUAGINTA HEBDOMADES] Anno- rum. Ita enim mos erat loquendi, & manet apud Thalmu- dicos. Ideo ubi de dierum hebdomade agitur, solet adji- ci dierum nomen Ezeh. 45, 21. Infra 10, 2. & 3. in Hebraeo.

Hoc fere unum est oraculum, quod de Messia relinquit nobis Grotius in Veteri Testamento. In quo tamen etiam non omnino deesse voluit Judaeis. Nam primo nullam hic de beneficiis Christi men- tionem fieri statuit, si recte ejus mentem expen- das: solum praedici vult poenas Judaeorum, πο- λιτείας nempe Judaicae destructionem, ut lua- tur iniquitas, quemadmodum vers. 24. de poenis eorum interpretatur, solamq; Evangelii publica- tionem relinquit, quod tamen ipse in legem vertit more Sociniano, Papistico, imo & Judaico. Dein- de terminum adventus Messiae hic definitum esse negat. Atque ea ratione Judaeis iterum obstetri- catur. Nam si nihil aliud, quam Politiae Judaicae de- structio praedicta, adventus vero Christi terminus nullus hic definitus est, quomodo Judaei ex hoc oraculo convinci solide poterunt, quod Christus jam advenerit, quod tamen hactenus solidum & in- victum contra Judaicam ἀπιστίαν creditum est ab universis Christianis fundamentum, maxime quia ad vers. 27. vastitatem terrae Judaeorum contingere debere, usque ad consummationem à Deo DEFI- statuit. Non autem vastitatem & con- summationem istam finem habituram negat. Imo cum Judæis Messiam Principem terrenum facit, qui Hierosolymam & Judæos ceu populum suum à malis impendentibus liberare debuerit, si scili- cet ei paritum fuisset. Talem enim Messiam Judæi credunt, qui ut malis temporalibus ipsos liberet, promissus sit, & qui ut liberator talis promissus sit, sub hypothesi obedientiæ: quum ex adverso Scriptura Prophetica Messiam liberatorem spiri- tualem constituat, qui populum suum à peccatis salvare debeat, neq; sub hypothesi liberationem Christi promittat, sed absolute, siquidem & adven- tus Messiæ & satisfactio pro peccatis totius mundi, quam præstare is debuit, absolute, citra hypothe- sin, promissa sint. Quod ad tempus illud definitum septuaginta hebdomadum, recte hebdomades non dierum, sed annorum intelliguntur à Grotio. Judæi nonnulli hebdomadem non annorum, sed Jubilæo- rum intelligunt, quorum quisq; 49. annis absolvi- tur, unde spatium 3430. annor. per 70. septimanas designari putant. Sed nuspiam in sacris 49. annis nomine hebdomados veniunt, neq; templum se- cundum tot annis stetit. Origenes septimanæ tribuit septem annorum decades Hom. 29. in Matth. ut 70. Septimanæ conficiant 4900. annos. Verum ea acceptio septimanæ nullibi occurrit in scriptura, & ἀπροσδιονύσως trahuntur anni ab exordio mundi, usq; ad consummationem Christi, quorum nullum hoc loco est vestigium. Deniq; falso numerantur à creatione ad adventum Christi 4900. anni. Qua- propter indubitatum penes Christianos omnes est, hebdomadas annorum, non dierum, aut alias desi- gnari. Nam scriptura non novit alias septimanas, quam vel dierum Ex. 34, 22. Lev. 12, 1. vel annorum Lev. 30, 8. At hebdomades dierum hic intelligi nequeunt, quia intra septem ejusmodi septima- nas, hoc est, 49. dies ædificatas esse plateas & mu- ros, & intra septuaginta septimanas dierum, hoc est, anni unius & 18. hebdomadum spatium, ista omnia quæ hic implenda prædicta sunt, impleta esse noto- rie falsum est. Et agnoscunt ipsimet Judæi Septi- manas annorum intelligi. R. Aben Ezra ad h.l. Di- xit venerabilis R. Saadia, quod istæ septuaginta septi- manæ annorum sint. Annuit R. Levi, R. Salomo, R. Joseph Jachiades, R. Isaac Abarbinel; Menasse Ben Israel de term. vit. p. 160. Idemque docetur in Thalmud. in tract. Sanhedrin C. Chelec ex R. Saa- dia, has LXX. septimanas conficere 490. annos. Por- ro quamvis non desint, qui annos plane lunares hic intelligant, utpote Africanus in Quinto volum. tempor. apud Hieronymum in hunc locum, Theo- doretus in h. l. Beda, & alii, qui efficiant 475. anni, tamen usuales & communiter recepti omnino intel- ligendi, quia Lunares designatos esse, nullo constat indicio, nec à recepta significatione, qua Chrono- logia sacra definita est, citra causam discedendum est. Habuerunt quidem Judæi annum Lunarem, sed ejusmodi, qui juxta Embolimæi mensis inser- tionem cum solari coincidit, uti à B. D. Behmio probatum lib. 1. Chron. Manud. Tit. 3. c. 2. Nisi enim annum Lunarem mixtum cum solari conve- nientem habuissent, festa eorum brevi spatio an- norum in aliud tempus conjecta fuissent.

ABBREVIATÆ SUNT SUPER POPULUM TUUM] Definita sunt. Iis exactis non ultra erit populus, id est, πολιτεία Judaica, quam tu forte hactenus sperasti fore sempiternam.

ET SUPER URBEM SANCTAM TUAM] Id est, tibi adeo amatam.

Recte corrigitur vulgata, quam nequicquam hic Pontificii excusant. Redditur autem vox Ebræa definitæ sunt. Quia נחתך & גזר secundum Rabbi- nos synonyma sunt, ut apud R. Salomon. in h. l. & R. Mardochai Nathan in Concord. videre est: hoc autem significat decrevit Job. 22, 38. Esa. 9, 20. & manifestum est de definito temporis spatio hic agi. Quod vero Grotius definitas super populum ita in- telligit, quod, iis exactis, non ultra πολιτεία Judai- ca, aut populus superesse debeat, illud eo tendit, ac si definitum sit istud spatium LXX. hebdoma- dum usque ad excidium populi Judaici & πανωλε- θρίαν urbis. Quam sententiam, etsi non pauci amplectantur, qui scilicet terminum ad quem harum LXX. Septimanarum assignant excidio Hie- rosolymitanorum, alii tamen eatum terminum re- ctius figendum dicunt in passione Dominica, vel paulo post eandem: adeoque populum hic confi- derari volunt, quatenus erat à Deo electus in populum sanctum, & civitatem, quatenus cultui Dei sedem, & Christo ad operis sui perfectionem officinam præ- bere debebat. Siquidem notanter dicatur super populo, loco & civitate sancta: & scopus angelicus sit populum consolari: non autem consolaretur, si in ipsa fronte ante ullam beneficiorum Messiæ an- nunciationem finalem interitum minaretur.

UT CONSUMMETUR PRÆVARICATIO] ut finem suum accipiat, pœna scilicet. Nam pœnas פשע, & similibus vocabulis appellare frequens Hebræis.

Solicitus erat maxime Daniel de restauratio- ne urbis, non ob urbem, sed ob promissiones de Messia factas in urbe illa complendas. Ideo non de urbis excidio, sed definito πληρώματι eorum, quæ ibi erant consummanda, Gabriel ipsum infor- mat. Neque simpliciter dicit Septuaginta hebdoma- das determinatas esse super populum istum, & super urbem, sed cum certa σχέσει & intentione: definitas esse, non ad conservationem, vel consummationem urbis, vel ad tempus consummationis, sed ad oc- cludendam prævaricationem, & consummandum pec- catum. Atque hic est terminus ad quem LXX. he- bdomadum; quem clara & sonora voce exprimit Angelus. Mentionem autem urbis & populi fa- cit, non in termino ad quem annorum definiendo, sed in loco & populo isto determinando, in quo i- sta olim agenda erant. Unde tacite id simul in- volvitur, reparatum iri urbem & populum, atque eo usque conservandum esse, donec ista in urbe illa, & populo isto compleantur.

ET FINEM ACCIPIAT PECCATUM] In He- bræo, ad obsignandum peccatum: Id est, pœnam pecca- torum. Quæ completa sunt, obsignari solent. Ita Ci- cero secundo de Divinatione.

ET DELEATUR INIQUITAS] In Hebræo est כפר. Quod etiam sic poni solet, quomodo piare apud Latinos:

Et culpam miserorum morte piabunt. Id est, lui facient. Sic dicunt Hebræi, תהי מיתתו כפרה עליו. Ergo congruenter iis quæ præcedunt re- cte vertas, & luatur iniquitas; plenissime scilicet.

Hæc vero est insignis depravatio illustris pro- missionis Evangelicæ, dum illa transmutatur in com- minationem gravissimam. At obstat (1.) verborum proprietas, nam פשע proprie prævaricationem, adeoq; peccatum notat, non pœnam peccati, atque ita cætera verba חטאת & עון peccatum proprie notare dubium non est, à significatione autem pro- pria recedere citra prægnantem causam integrum non est. Deinde de illa consummatione prævarica- tionum & obsignatione peccati sermo est, quæ fit, cum deletur vel expiatur iniquitas, quum illa verba ἐξηγητικῶς conjuncta sint. Tertio ea hic intelligi- tur peccatorum consummatio, obsignatio, deletio, quæ conjuncta est cum justitia æterna. At pœna pec- catorum & iniquitatum non conjuncta est cum æterna justitia: sed expiatio peccati, & justitiæ veræ adductio connexa sunt. Quarto de illa con- firmatione, & obsignatione & deletione iniquita- tum sermo est, quæ finis, & fructus est passionis & mortis Christi, vel quam Christus adventu, pas- sione & morte sua nobis efficere debebat, ob quam & sanctus Sanctorum ungendus erat. Non ergo de pœna & luitione iniquitatis plenaria hæc intelligen- da. Finis enim erat ejus non pœna Judæorum, sed expiatio peccatorum totius mundi Es. 53. Zach. 14, 10. Quinto exprimuntur præclare beneficia, quæ Christus præstitit nobis, tum privativa, qua præva- ricationum consummationem, ne genus humanum condemnarent, nec etiam dominari possent; pec- catorum obsignationem, ne accusent nos, prout Chi- rographum apertum accusat nos de debitis Col. 2, 14. liber autem obsignatus legi nequit Es. 29. v. 11. & iniquitates deletæ, quia expiatio facta pro pec- catis totius mundi, 1. Joh. 2, 2. & tecta dicuntur hic peccata ut hic est in Ebræo, quia teguntur Christi merito, ne appareant in conspectu Dei iniquitates nostræ Rom. 4. tum positiva, quod nobis adducta & parta sit æterna justitia. Sexto verba לכל הפשע rectius redduntur, ad cohibendum, quam ad consummandum prævaricationem. Nam etsi כלה sit consummavit, כלא tamen est cohibuit & incarce- ravit. Quia Christus coercuit & infregit vim pec- cati adversus nos, qua accusat nos coram Deo. De- nique opponi glossæ isti Judaico-Grotianæ com- munis omnium interpretum consensus potest: qui ὁμοθυμαδὸν de iniquitatum expiatione per Chri- stum facta interpretantur. Seductus autem hic à Ju- dæis Grotius est: sic enim R. Joseph Jacchiades exponit: restare adhuc LXX. septimanas, ut de- struatur Jerusalem, & Judæi in exilium mittantur, ut ipsorum prævaricationi finis imponatur.

ET ADDUCATUR JUSTITIA SEMPITERNA] Intra id tempus publicabitur Evangelium, quæ est justi- tia, non illa ad tempus duratura, ut legis, quam tu Da- niel supra 9, 15. justitiam non male appellasti, sed sine fine.

Aliud est justitia, aliud vero Evangelium, quod annunciat justitiam, & concio est gratiæ re- missionis peccatorum, justitiæ & salutis æternæ. Justitia objectum Evangelii, hoc autem non ipsa est Justitia, sed concio, vel promissio aut annuncia- tio justitiæ æternæ. Quæ cum Photinianis con- fundit Grotius pessime, quasi Christus solum ad- duxerit Justitiam Evangelium annunciando, & pri- mus Evangelii præco fuerit: quod utrumque aἴ- τημα Socinianorum suo loco profligavimus. Præ- dicata fuit gratia, & remissio peccatorum, cum ju- stitia æterna etiam in Veteri Testamento. Imo omnes Prophetæ eam annunciarunt, teste Petro Act. 10, 43. Adductio ergo longe alia justitiæ tem- pore Novi Testamenti relicta est, quam quæ sola prædicatione tantum absolvatur: nimirum acqui- renda erat in plenitudine temporum per Messiam vera & æterna justitia, atque hoc exprimit angelus voce ADDUCTIONIS. Apostolus exponit ἑυρίσκειν invenire, quia Christum docet invenis- se æternam λύτρωσιν Ebr. 9, 12. Ideo Christus etiam dictus est Jerem. 23, 6. Jehovah Justitia nostra. Quod ita exponit R. David Kimchi: vocabitur Messias hoc nomine Jehovah justitia nostra, propter- ea quod in diebus ejus obtingat nobis justitia Jehovah semper durans seu perpetua. R. Moses Hadarsan & R. Levi h. l. ita habent: Justitia sempiterna non est nisi Messias, de quo scriptum est (Es. 56, 1.) Constituite Judicium & facite justitiam, quia proxime est sa- lus mea ut veniat, & justitia mea reveletur. Simi- liter R. Barachai in libro de ordine mundi Esa. 56. 1. exponit: Prope est salus mea ut veniat, & ju- stitia mea ut reveletur. Illa est Messias, de quo scri- ptum est Dan. 9. ut adducatur justitia sempiterna.

Neque vero sibi constat illa oppositio Justitiæ Le- galis & Evangelicæ Grotiana; Quod legalis ad tem- pus durare debuerit, Evangelica autem æterna sit. Nam & legalis æterna esse debebat, modo præstari potuisset, juxta illud; qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis.

ET IMPLEATUR VISIO ET PROPHETIA] Intra id tempus implebuntur prophetiæ veteres Jacobi, Davidis, Esaiæ, & aliorum. Matth. 11, 13. Soli Danieli revelata, quæ post id tempus erunt exstitura. Matth. 24, 15. Visio & prophetia, id est, visa prophetica.

ET UNGATUR SANCTUS SANCTORUM] Dominus Jesus fiat χριστὸς, per resurrectionem & ascensum in cœlestem regiam. Actor. 2,36. Recte autem ille San- ctus Sanctorum, id est, omnium Sanctissimus dicitur: Quemadmodum κατ' ἐξοχὴν ὁ ἅγιος. Act. 3, 14. c. 4, 30. Apoc. 3, 7. Joh. 2. vers. 20. Sic explicat hæc de Messia Moses Gerundensis.

Explicat hæc ita Grotius, quod intra tempus illarum LXX. septimanarum, publicatio Evangelii, impletio visionum & unctio Sancti Sanctorum fieri debeat. Alii, qui terminum ad quem constituunt passionem & mortem Christi, particulam ל ex verbis infinitis præfixam terminum finalem exprimere a- junt. Quod juxta stylum scripturæ præfixum ל infinitivo additum non terminum per quem, uti lo- quuntur, vel intra quem, sed terminum ad quem no- tare soleat, quodq; LXX. septimanæ decisæ dicantur ad præstanda hæc beneficia: Adeoque hæc ita vi- deantur terminus earum constitui. Et quod infra v. 26. ea beneficia in ultimam septimanam locasse videatur Propheta. Cæterum per SANCTUM SANCTORUM nonnulli hic intelligunt Sanctua- rium, vel sanctum sanctorum Mosaicum & Salo- monem, quod ita vocatur Exod. 26, 33. cum Iunio & Vatablo. Alii non typicum, sed cæleste Sanctum Sanctorum, de quo Eb. 8, 11. 12. 24. 25. cum Piscato- re, alii Ecclesiam, uti Dn. D. Anan. Weberus disp. 2. de salvat. Christ. de septuaginta Septimanis Danie- lis pag. 32. hanc unctionem de reali sanctificatione templi & præcipuæ ejus partis, Sacrarii typici inter- pretatur, qua illud cum omni suo cultu & sacrifi- ciorum apparatu per oblationem & sanguinem vi- ctimæ & agni immaculati Jesu Christi in passione & morte vere inunctum, h. e. ita in officio suo ac col- lato munere consecratum est, ut authoritas ejus di- vina efficacia, quam in V. T. habuit, plene con- firmata sit: vel etiam de ingressu summi sacerdotis in Sanctum Sanctorum cæleste & æternum, quando nobis illud aperuit & ut habitaculum æternum de- stinavit & dedicavit. Sed unctionem ea ratione in scripturis accipi, vix docebitur, & notum satis est, quid per unctionem notetur, cum de Christo ser- mo est, qui ab unctione nomen obtinuit. Ideoque per Sanctum Sanctorum fatemur, omnino intelli- gendum esse Christum, qui etiam per resurrectio- nem Christus factus est, ut opus non sit novas significationes vocis unctionis invenire, aut de sanctuario typico, vel cœlesti hæc explicare, etiamsi hic terminus ad quem exprimeretur LXX. Septi- manarum. Quem vero hic expressum esse, istis qui- dem verbis nondum videmus solide probari. Nam vocula ל sensu causæ finalis accipi potest, uti sæ- pissime accipitur, constitutas nempe esse LXX. Septimanas decreto divino, ut hæc tandem fiant, dum implentur illæ septimanæ: unde qui eas com- pleri ajunt in excidio urbis, interea tamen, & antequam urbs excidatur, hanc unctionem factam censent; cum quibus etiam Grotius facit. Id nobis omnino certum videtur per Sanctum San- ctorum Christum intelligi. Quæ etiam Tertul- liani lib. 4. contr. Jud. Hieronymi Theodor. in hunc locum, Galatini, Lutheri Tom. 8. Je- nensi fol. 83. Helvici disquisitione pecul. th. 120.

Tigurinorum, Cornelii à Lap. & aliorum est sen- tentia. Consonat Arabicus uterque ita reddens; ad Christum, qui est sanctitas sanctitatum, & R. Mos. Gerundensis apud Galat. lib. 6. de verit. Cath. Ar- can. cap. 18. ut & R. Lusitanus in colloq. Mittel- burg. fol. 103.

## 9:25
Verse 25.

KNOW THEREFORE AND ATTEND] Learn and retain.

FROM THE GOING FORTH OF THE WORD] From the promulgation of the edict. For that is what it means to go forth, as above 6, 7; Luke 2, 1.

THAT JERUSALEM MAY BE BUILT AGAIN] Understand the edict of that Darius, who is mentioned in Ezra 6, for after that there was to be no other edict on that matter. Whoever wishes to know more arguments for this interpretation, let him read what Scaliger has in book 6 of the Emendation of Times, and what Junius has on this passage.

UNTIL CHRIST THE LEADER] The Hebrew word עַד here and elsewhere does not signify the final limit, but something contained within the limits, as if he were saying, including also the visible life of Christ, who, having been appointed by God as the prince of his people, would have delivered them from the impending evils forever, if he had been obeyed.

Grotius, in book 5 of the Truth of the Christian Religion, § 14, defined the term from which the seventy weeks began differently and more correctly: the edict not about the restoration of the temple, but about the restoration of the city, which edict was promulgated under Artaxerxes Longimanus; where at the same time he rightly observed against the Jews that the marks of the Messiah were fulfilled in our Jesus: Daniel, he says, at the dictation of an angel, left it written in chapter 9, that after the promulgation of the edict to restore the city of Jerusalem, five hundred years would not elapse before the Messiah was present. But to this day, more than two thousand years have elapsed since that time, and he whom the Jews expect is not present: nor can they name anyone else to whom that time corresponds: But it fits Jesus so well that the Hebrew Master Nehumias, who preceded him by fifty years, openly said even then that the time of the Messiah signified by Daniel could not be drawn out beyond those fifty years. With this mark of time agrees another, which we touched upon above, concerning the empire being given divinely to all nations after the posterity of Seleucus and Lagus had ceased to reign, the latter of which ended in Cleopatra, not long before Jesus was born. The third mark is in the said chapter 9 of Daniel, that after the coming of the Messiah the city of Jerusalem was to be destroyed, which prophecy concerning the destruction of the city Josephus himself refers to his own age: whence it follows that the time set for the coming of the Messiah had already passed even then. The passage indicated from Josephus, in book 10, chapter 12, reads as follows: At the same time Daniel also wrote about the empire of the Romans, and that it would come to pass that our nation would be devastated by it. All these things he left written down as God indicated, so that those who read these things and consider the events cannot but admire Daniel for the honor received from God. Jachiades himself taught that the seventy weeks of years end in the destruction of the second Temple, at Dan. 9, 24. This is correct against the Jews. But more on the term from which and to which these mystical weeks belong later. Furthermore, regarding that condition which Grotius here hints was added to the promises about the Messiah for the sake of the Jews, concerning the Messiah being the future LEADER of the people, if the people were to obey him, he discussed it soundly himself when he asserted the Truth of the Christian Religion against the Jews: Why then does he pour cold water on the Jews here? Thus there, book 5, § 15. The Jews feel themselves pressed by these arguments concerning the coming of the Messiah: to evade them, some say that their sins were the cause why he did not arrive at the promised time. To omit that it is indicated in the said prophecies that the decree was fixed, not suspended by any condition: how could the coming be delayed because of sins, when this also had been predicted, that because of the many and greatest sins of the people the city was to be destroyed shortly after the times of the Messiah? Add that the Messiah was to come for this reason also, to provide a remedy for a most corrupt age, and at the same time to bring forgiveness of crimes along with rules for amending one's life, whence it is said of his times in Zechariah, chapter 13, that there would then be a fountain opened to the house of David, and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for washing away sins: and among the Hebrews themselves it is accepted to call the Messiah isch copher, that is, a placator. But it is clearly abhorrent to reason to say that what was precisely destined for a certain disease was delayed because of that disease. These arguments also militate against the invention of the Judaizing Grotius concerning the promise of the Messiah the Leader made under a CONDITION: since the promise concerning the Messiah the Leader is fixed in the prophetic oracles, not suspended by any condition, nor can it be hindered by sins, because it was promised for the sake of providing a remedy for sins. Concerning that name Isch Copher, which is placator, Grotius praises the Chaldean paraphrast on Cant. 1, 24, and observes that R. Judah in Chasidim and R. Simeon in Bereschith Rabba say that the Messiah would bear our sins.

SEVENTY WEEKS, AND SIXTY WEEKS SHALL BE] Two things are to be noted here; that the Hebrews split a perfect number into parts, as in Ezek. 45, 12. Then, that they place the smaller number before the larger, as in Gen. 5, very often, Gen. 8, 3, and often elsewhere.

AND THE STREET AND WALLS SHALL BE BUILT AGAIN] Turn; after the street and trench shall have been built again.

IN THE STRAIT OF TIMES] That is, into that space of time many evils will fall: the slaughter of kings, civil wars mixed with foreign ones, a venal priesthood, and other things of this kind.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

SCITO ERGO ET ANIMADVERTE] Disce & retine.

AB EXITU SERMONIS] A promulgatione edi- cti. Id enim est egredi, ut supra 6, 7. Luc. 2, 1.

UT ITERUM ÆDIFICETUR JERUSALEM] E- dictum intellige Darii illius, cujus mentio 6. Esdr. post id enim nullum erat aliud exstiturum ea de re edictum. Qui plura hujus interpretationis argumenta volet cognoscere, legat, quæ Scaliger habet libro 6. Emendationis tempo- rum, & quæ Junius ad hunc locum.

USQUE AD CHRISTUM DUCEM] עַד He- bræum hic & alibi, non ultimum terminum significat, sed aliquid intra terminos contentum, quasi dicat, inclusa et- iam Christi vita aspectabili, qui constitutus a Deo populi sui princeps in perpetuum impendentibus malis eum li- berasset, si ei paritum fuisset.

Aliter & rectius terminum à quo LXX. hebdo- madum definiverat Grotius l. 5. de Ver. Rel. Christ. §. 14. edictum non de restauratione templi, sed de restauratione urbis, quod edictum sub Artaxerxe Longimano promulgatum est; ubi simul contra Judæos recte observavit notas Messiæ in Jesu no- stro impletas: Daniel, inquit, angelo dictante cap. 9. conscriptum reliquit, post promulgatum edictum de instauranda urbe Hierosolymorum non elapsuros annos quingentos, quin adesset Messias. Atqui in hunc diem elapsi sunt ab eo tempore plus bis mille an- ni, nec adest is, quem Judæi exspectant: nec quem- quam alium nominare possunt, in quem id tempus quadret: In Jesum autem tam bene convenit, ut Magister Hebræus Nehumias, qui annis quinquagin- ta eum præcessit, aperte jam tum dixerit, non pos- se ultra eos quinquaginta annos protrahi tempus Messiæ à Daniele significatum. Cum hac temporis nota congruit altera, quam supra attigimus, de im- perio in omnes nationes dando divinitus, postquam Seleuci & Lagi posteritas regnare desiisset, quarum posterior in Cleopatra desiit, non multo antequam Jesus nasceretur. Tertia nota est dicto cap. 9. a- pud Danielem, quod post Messiæ adventum ex- scindenda esset urbs Hierosolyma, quod de excidio urbis vaticinium ipse Josephus ad suam refert æta- tem: unde sequitur, tempus Messiæ adventui præ- stitum jam tum præteriisse. Locus è Josepho indi- catus ita habet l. 10. c. 12. Eodem tempore Daniel etiam de Romanorum scripsit imperio, & fore ut ab eo gens nostra vastetur. Hæc omnia ille Deo indican- te præscripta reliquit, ita ut non possint qui ista le- gunt, & eventus considerant, non admirari Danie- lem ob honorem à Deo acceptum. Septuaginta anno- rum hebdomadas finire in excidio Templi secun- di Jachiades ipse docuit ad Dan. 9, 24. Hæc contra Judæos recte. De termino autem à quo & ad quem hebdomadum istarum mysticarum po- stee exquisitius. Cæterum quod ad conditionem illam, quam promissionibus de Messia additam Grotius in Judæorum gratiam hic innuit de Mes- sia DUCE populi futuro, si ei pariturus sit populus, solide eam ipse discussit cum contra Judæos Ve- ritatem Religionis Christianæ asseruit: Cur ergo hic Judæis frigidam suffundit! Ita ibi l. 5. §. 15. Sen- tiunt se premi his argumentis de Messiæ adventu Ju- dæi: quæ ut eludant, nonnulli ajunt sua peccata in causa fuisse, quo minus promisso tempore adveniret. Ut omittam, in dictis vaticiniis definitum, non aliqua conditione suspensum decretum indicari: quomodo ob peccata differri adventus potuit, cum hoc quoq; præ- dictum esset, ob plurima & maxima populi peccata urbem exscindendam paulo post Messiae tempora? Adde quod Messias venturus erat hac quoque de cau- sa, ut corruptissimo seculo medicinam faceret, simul- que cum emendandae vitae regulis criminum veniam adferret, unde de ejus temporibus apud Zachariam dicitur cap. 13. fore tunc fontem apertum domui Da- vidis, & Hierosolymitis omnibus, ad peccata abluen- da: & apud ipsos Hebraeos receptum est Messiam ap- pellare isch copher, hoc est placatorem. Plane au- tem a ratione abhorret, dicere ob morbum aliquem dilatum id quod praecise ei morbo erat destinatum. Quae argumenta militant etiam adversus commen- tum Grotii Judaizantis de promissione Messiae Du- cis sub CONDITIONE facta: siquidem promis- sum de Messia Duce in propheticis vaticiniis de- finitum, non aliqua conditione suspensum sit, nec ob peccata impediri possit, quod ob medicinam peccatis praestandam fuit promissum. De nomine illo Isch Copher, quod est placator, laudat Grotius Chaldaeum paraphrasten Cant. 1, 24. & observat Messiam peccata nostra portaturum dicere R. Iu- dam in Chasidim, & R. Simeonem in Bereschith Rabba.

HEBDOMADES SEPTEM, ET HEBDOMADES SEXAGINTA ERUNT] Duo hic notanda; Hebraeos nu- merum perfectum in particulas scindere, ut Ezech. 45, 12. Deinde vero numerum minorem praeponere majori, ut Ge- nes. 5. saepissime, Gen. 8, 3. & alibi saepe.

ET RURSUM AEDIFICABITUR PLATEA ET MURI] Verte; postquam jam rursus aedificata fuerit pla- tea & fossa.

IN ANGUSTIA TEMPORUM] Id est, in illud spatium temporis multa incident mala: regum caedes, bel- la civilia mixta externis, sacerdotium venale, & alia ejus- modi.

## 9:26
Vers. 26.

AND AFTER SIXTY-TWO WEEKS] Those, namely, which will follow the first seven that were sufficiently prosperous.

CHRIST SHALL BE KILLED] Christ himself looks to this in Luke 24:46.

AND HIS PEOPLE SHALL NOT BE, WHO ARE ABOUT TO KILL HIM] In the Hebrew it is only ואין לו, that is, not to him, supply, shall that people be obedient, whom he had come to redeem. This is the cause of the destruction, that the Jews did not obey Christ, nay, and even took care to have him killed.

AND THE CITY AND THE SANCTUARY] Both the city and the temple.

HE SHALL DESTROY] He shall overturn.

THE PEOPLE] The army.

WITH THE LEADER WHO IS TO COME] In the Hebrew: Of the leader who is to come: Namely, Titus Vespasianus. Thus many of the Hebrews.

AND HIS END SHALL BE DEVASTATION] In the Hebrew: His end with a cleansing; that is, after the city is overturned, the army of Titus shall flood the whole of Judea; which you see in Josephus.

AND AFTER THE END OF THE WAR THE APPOINTED DESOLATION] For the end of the war there shall be a defined desolation. עד often signifies FOR, as Joel 2:8, Jeremiah 11:14, 2 Chronicles 30:8. God predetermined this outcome for that war, the devastation of the land.

## 9:27
Verse 27.

HE SHALL CONFIRM THE COVENANT WITH MANY FOR ONE WEEK] That is, the beginning of the last week of years (for the following exposition demands this sense) will draw many into a league of the Jews, and they will give hope of a successful war. 20 thousand Idumeans are about to arrive to their aid. See Josephus, Jewish War, 3, 16. But all these things are in vain.

AND IN THE MIDST OF THE WEEK] In the latter part of the last week of years.

THE OBLATION AND THE SACRIFICE SHALL FAIL] The temple having been burned before the city was captured. Josephus, Jewish War, 6, 26.

AND THERE SHALL BE IN THE TEMPLE THE ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION] כנף to the Hebrews is everything that is spread out. Malachi 4:2. שקוצים to the Hebrews are idols. Therefore he says this: through spread-out idols will come desolation, or the destruction of the city. Those spread-out idols are the military standards of the Romans, exposed to the sight of all, as we said at Matthew 24:15.

AND EVEN UNTO THE CONSUMMATION AND THE END THE DESOLATION SHALL PERSEVERE] And even unto the consummation, and indeed a determined one (by God, as above 24, 26) the devastation will happen. So great will be the devastation and slaughter, that nothing of that state, so noble, will remain, so God has determined protecting, whose decrees must not be gainsaid. Consummatio is the same as συντέλεια 1 Macc. 3, 42. Among the many expositions of this passage concerning the Weeks, which Jerome recites from Africanus, Eusebius, Hippolytus, Apollinaris, Clement, Origen, Tertullian, and the Hebrews, this one which I have set forth seems to me the plainest. Of the ancients, Chrysostom 2 against the Jews has always approached closest to the truth.

I. N. THEOLOGICAL EXAMINATION CONCERNING THE SEVENTY WEEKS OF DANIEL. THE OUTSET.

§. I.

Among the sacred Oracles, which the Prophets, searching into what or what manner of time the Spirit which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, as St. Peter witnesses in 1 Ep. 1, 11, brought forth, without doubt, that one stands out and is the prize, which was brought down from heaven by the Angel GABRIEL, and described by the man of desires DANIEL, the greatest of the Prophets: whose profound wisdom in divine secrets, celebrated throughout the world, was proclaimed by Ezekiel himself, the great Prophet, c. 28, 3: Behold, thou art wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that is hidden from thee. We point to the prophecy concerning the seventy Weeks, proposed in Dan. 9, 24 and following, than which no prophecy has defined more clearly, no prophecy more accurately, the time for finishing the transgression, making an end of sins, and bringing in everlasting righteousness.

§. II.

But since this most illustrious oracle, especially as regards the designation of the time divinely defined, is exposed to the greatest difficulties—which have been produced not so much by the obscurity of the Angelic words, which are clear enough provided they are weighed piously and accurately, as is fitting, without preconceived opinion, as by the contentions and private interpretations of Interpreters and Chronologers in explaining and applying them—we have determined in this inaugural disputation to weigh and consider a little more accurately the most famous and most vexed controversy concerning the LXX weeks.

§. III.

We shall do this in such a way that, having brought forward and discussed the various opinions of others concerning the same, we may exhibit and assert the true one, which is consistent with the words of the text. For these words of the Interpreter of celestial mysteries, hidden from all the wise of the world, are deservedly sacrosanct to us, so that we judge that not one iota, and not even one tittle, should be held lightly; to these, every Chronological computation must be recalled as to an infallible Canon, and not, vice versa, this celestial and divine canon twisted, as is done by many, to a preconceived system or emendation of times.

§. IV.

The celestial Chronologer and definer of times himself requires attention in a matter of the greatest moment, which God foreordained before the ages, which we neither know nor can investigate outside of this revelation: Now I have come forth to teach thee, and that thou mightest understand. And these things pertain to Chapter 9 of Daniel. We have previously proposed in a public Disputation a certain Theological examination concerning the LXX Weeks recorded in this chapter by Daniel, which therefore, since it contributes greatly to the illustration of that most illustrious oracle, we have thought fit to subjoin here.

I. THEOLOGICAL EXAMINATION CONCERNING THE SEVENTY WEEKS OF DANIEL. THE OUTSET.

teach thee, and that thou mightest understand. Do thou therefore heed the word, and understand the vision. Whence St. Jerome on this passage: If it is said to Daniel, 'diligently attend, that you may hear and understand what you see,' what ought we to do, whose eyes are blinded by the shadows of ignorance and the darkness of vices? Cornelius à Lapide reports of a certain noble and learned Pontiff that he spent many years in investigating this question, and since he could not resolve it, and it became more intricate day by day, he unfortunately fell into madness and a mad Judaism. Wherefore, what is the truth concerning these mystical weeks, and what is the opinion concerning the term from which and to which they belong, must be learned by religious attention and investigation, primarily from this oracle, when accurately considered and diligently compared with other Biblical and Exotic Chronological documents, and with how these harmonize with the infallible Chronology of the Holy Spirit! That we may piously weigh, rightly understand, and dexterously apply this, he alone provides who searches the deep things of God, through whom these things have been revealed to us, whom we receive by divine gift, that we may know the things that are freely given to us by God. Which Christ promised that the heavenly Father would give to those who ask Him, Luke 11, 13; and therefore we pray from the heart that He may be willing to give it to us now also, that through Him we may obtain understanding in all things.

CHAPTER I. Various opinions concerning the LXX Weeks, but entirely incongruous and discordant.

§. V. Concerning the seventy weeks, there are almost as many opinions, both among the Ancients and among the moderns, as there are heads. In which it seems difficult and arduous to touch the truth. St. Jerome certainly did not dare to define anything certain: 'I know,' he says, 'that this question has been variously disputed by most learned men, and that each one has said what he felt according to the capacity of his own genius.' Since, therefore, it is dangerous to judge the opinions of the Masters of the Church, and to prefer one to another, I will say what each one has felt, leaving it to the judgment of the reader whose exposition he ought to follow. Yet the attainment of truth is not to be despaired of, provided we show ourselves teachable to the celestial Teacher. We shall therefore review most of the opinions, adding, where it will be worth the effort, a judgment from the Divine oracle, for perhaps no one will be able to enumerate all of them. But we shall first bring forward those which are less suitable, nay, even discordant, and will not be easily defended by anyone today.

§. VI. Among these, the opinion of Origen must be numbered first, who in his 29th treatise on Matthew makes these weeks not of years, but of decades, and traces the beginning from the first-formed man. 'I think, however,' he says, 'that the seventy weeks cut short upon the people and upon the holy city, so that sin may be finished, are four thousand nine hundred years from Adam up to the seventy years which were after the dispensation of Christ.' Which opinion is absurd in many ways, since not only are such weeks of decades entirely unusual in sacred calculation, and everyone agrees that weeks of years are to be understood in this place, but that beginning of Origen is also clearly ἀλλότριον (alien), and has no connection with the present oracle, and the calculation itself, that 4900 years have elapsed from the creation of the world to the birth of Christ, does not harmonize at all; whence Origen in book 10. of the Stromata defined these weeks far otherwise, as will be said later.

§. VII. Another opinion is that which Cornelius à Lapide reports, that some begin the weeks from the 13th year of Josiah, in which Jeremiah began (ch. 1, 11) to prophesy concerning the destruction and the fall of Jerusalem. But the outcome of the word here is not about the destruction, but about the rebuilding of the city. This opinion, therefore, in no way fits the text, and as it is ἀδέσποτον (ownerless), we do not think it should be refuted here more fully.

§. VIII. The third is that of those who take the beginning of this epoch from the fourth year of King Zedekiah, namely seven years before the overthrow of the city, because then the word went forth through Jeremiah promising liberation after 70 years of the Babylonian captivity (ch. 29). So Nicolaus Lyranus, Paulus Burgensis, Vatablus in this place, as also Petrus Galatinus in book 4 of 'De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis', ch. 15. Which opinion is likewise deservedly rejected. For if the beginning is to be made from the promise of liberation, what reason is there why it should not be taken from another earlier promise, such as is found in Jeremiah 25, or from that most ancient one which exists in Isaiah 45? Furthermore, in that promise of Jeremiah 29, it is indeed a matter of the resolution of the captivity, but no mention is made of the building of the city, which the Angel designates here. Finally, from the fourth year of Zedekiah, not 490 years, which these 70 weeks make, but more than six hundred years have flowed until the term of the epoch defined here.

§. IX. Fourthly, some Jews begin these weeks from the devastation of the first city, such as R. Isaac Ben Abraham, R. Abarbinel, R. Joseph Jachiades. Finus (book 1, 'Flagellum Judaeorum', ch. 5) and Petrus Galatinus (book 4, 'De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis', ch. 14) propose the opinion of R. Solomon thus: namely, that the first ten weeks are to be counted from the destruction of the temple until its rebuilding, but the remaining ones from the second temple built until its destruction. But this opinion is inept. For the destruction of the temple and its or the city's rebuilding cannot be calculated from the same term. And since they count four hundred and twenty years of the second temple, to which they add seventy years of desolation, where will the time be left that had to be spent on the construction of the temple? Besides, it is false that the second temple stood for only 420 years. The Talmudists in Megilla ch. 1 observe that 78 years elapsed from the destruction of the first until the construction of the second: But to the destruction of this second temple from the destruction of the first, according to Josephus (book 7, 'De Bello Judaico', ch. 18), 709 years are counted, concerning which see Cornelius à Lapide in this place.

Furthermore, the beginning of the epoch is not established here by the Angel as the destruction of the temple, but the going forth of the word concerning the rebuilding; and the Angel announces joyful and consolatory things here, concerning the prayers of Daniel being heard, not sad ones. Whence R. Moses Gerundensis, R. Ozia, R. Josue, R. Barnahaman, R. Barachias, and others praised by Finus and Galatinus, say that at the end of these 70 weeks the Messiah will come. Finally, R. Aben-Ezra also rejects and refutes this opinion from among the Jews.

§. X. Fifthly, others among the Jews are more inept, who fix the beginning of this epoch at the second devastation, because it is openly established here by the Angel Gabriel at the going forth of the word concerning the rebuilding.

§. XI. Sixthly, those among the Hebrews are extremely absurd who understand by each week a Jubilee, or even, as others trifle, 49 years, or even a hundred, so that 70 weeks make 3430 or 7000 years, upon the completion of which they say Christ will come. For where is a week taken in such a way in the Scriptures? And how does that fit either Haggai, who promises that the Messiah will come after a little time (ch. 2, 7), or the event itself? Since the destruction of the temple is connected with the end of these weeks, as if to follow shortly after, and the cessation of the oblation and sacrifice is predicted before their expiration. For sixteen centuries ago the sacrifice already ceased, and the temple was destroyed. Finally, in the Talmud itself, in the treatise Sanhedrin, chapter Chelec, it is taught that 70 weeks make 490 years, and not seventy Jubilees.

§. XII. Seventhly, Hippolytus the Martyr thinks these weeks began fifty years before the resolution of the captivity, and he places the end of the 69 weeks at the advent of Christ, but refers the last week to the consummation of the age, dividing it into the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, and into the kingdom of the Anti-Christ. But in that opinion there is οὐδὲν ὑγιές (nothing sound). For that beginning is clearly arbitrary, and does not in any way agree with the words of the angel concerning the going forth of the word, nor does the calculation fit, nor finally is it right to separate the last week in such a way, or to drag it to the end of the world, about which nothing occurs here.

§. XIII. Eighth, Tertullian, in his book against the Jews, and Origen in book 10 of the Stromata, as Jerome notes in this place, place the beginning of these weeks in the first year of Darius the Mede, or at that time when Daniel had this vision, which opinion Jerome also attributes to the Hebrews. But they did not observe that the time between Darius the Mede and the birth of Christ greatly exceeds 70 weeks of years: indeed, Tertullian was mistaken in the chronology of the Persian Kings, of whom he enumerates only six, and to whom he assigns only one hundred years; not to mention other manifest errors of his in that calculation. The Hebrews, terminating sixty-two weeks at the destruction of the city, and the remaining eight at the extermination which took place under the Emperor Hadrian, did not calculate correctly, since not 70 weeks, but nearly one hundred have elapsed, up to the disaster which befell them in the time of Hadrian.

§. XIV. Ninth, Cyril of Jerusalem, in Catechesis 12, likewise thinks that these weeks began in the time of Darius the Mede: but he confuses him with the Darius under whom the temple was built, and when he says that Jerusalem was built in the eighth year of Darius, he does not distinguish between the structure of the temple and the structure of the city: nor does Cyril correctly calculate the times from the beginning of the reign of Darius to the birth of Christ.

§. XV. To these add, tenth, those who, following Megasthenes and Philo, begin these weeks from the second year of Darius Longimanus, as they call him, against whom better chronologists have long since demonstrated that Megasthenes, as well as the series of Persian Kings which they produce from him, are the inventions of Johannes Annius of Viterbo, a monk who, with unheard-of recklessness, created Darius Longimanus and other Persian Kings such as never existed in the nature of things. Not by Herodotus and Thucydides, whence we have judged that these trifles also should be referred to the former class of opinions which we have assigned.

§. XVI. To these, moreover, let those eleventh ones be added, who refer the beginning to the second year of Cambyses, and end the weeks with the auspices of the reign of Herod, when he invaded the kingdom of the Jews, having killed the legitimate King Antigonus, the last of the Hasmonean line. Which year of the beginning of Herod in the Julian period 4773, by counting backward 490 years, leads us to the second year of Cambyses. These are clearly ἀλλότρια (alien) to this oracle. For what do the weeks of Daniel have to do with the beginning of Herod, and how does the second year of Cambyses fit here?

§. XVII. A new and unheard-of method of explaining the 70 weeks (so the author himself calls it) was attempted to be introduced by Hervart in his Chronology inscribed 'Against the incredible errors of others' c. 276, namely that the 62 weeks are to be begun from the same term from which the first 7 weeks begin, which he wishes to define at the completion of the walls, Nehemiah 6:15, in the 31st year of Artaxerxes Mnemon: but that the end of those 62 weeks is the fourteenth year of the incarnate Son of God. Finally, that the 70 weeks are terminated in the extermination of Jerusalem, and that this is at the same time the middle of the last week. But it is no wonder that that method of calculating is unheard-of: it is a wonder, however, that Hervart found a follower in Mr. Dr. Gravius, who in his inaugural oration in the year 1657 held at Jena, makes the term from which the same seven and the remaining 62 weeks with him: but he establishes the term to which of these as the 12th year of Christ, not referring that one week to the 70 weeks themselves, but beginning it only from the last year of the seventieth week, when Jerusalem was surrounded by a siege. But these εὑρήματα (inventions) are easily refuted. For the term from which of the seven weeks cannot possibly be the same as the term from which of the sixty-two, since those intervals are distinct and follow one another, and from those combined 7 and 62 weeks, with that one specially named, the 70 weeks themselves, defined by the angel, are produced. Nor does the building of the walls fall into the years of Artaxerxes Mnemon, but of Longimanus: since if 49 years, or seven weeks, are counted backward from the 31st year of Mnemon, the beginning of them (that is by hypothesis) falls at the same time as the 62 weeks into the 24th year of Longimanus, notable for no distinguished character: to which also the issue of the edict does not correspond, from which Gabriel wished the beginning of the numbering to be made, but the end of the 70 weeks will thus fall into the year of Christ 68, in which year neither did the extermination of Jerusalem happen, nor can the term of the confirmation of the covenant be fixed, even if the siege of Jerusalem began at that time. But how can it be denied that that one week specially named by the angel pertains to the 70 weeks, or be affirmed that it begins from the last year of the seventieth week, when the whole space of time defined by the angel does not exceed the Epoch of the 70 weeks? Not to mention that in the fifth year after the desolation of the city, no notable character corresponds that would fit here. Finally, there will not be had in this way, with that new interpretation standing, a designation of the time of the passion of Christ, which is the principal object of the angelic discourse, whence interpreters and chronologists hunt with great zeal in this prophecy for the time of the passion. For Dr. Gravius contends that Christ is said to be killed after 62 weeks, yet this is to be understood as only afterward, that the sixty-sixth week was fulfilled, of which certainly neither a trace nor a footprint is found in the text. But Theobald Meuschius led the way for Gravius, whom he followed almost κ̉ πόδα (step by step). For his opinion in the System of the Chronology of the Old Testament, published at Speyer in 1612, succinctly proposed on p. 83, is as follows: The seven weeks begin from the edict of Darius Nothus, and end in the 32nd year of Artaxerxes Mnemon. But the sixty-two weeks begin from the same principle of the edict of Darius Nothus, and are terminated with the twelfth year of the born Messiah: after these sixty-two weeks the Messiah was cut off, but not immediately after, rather with 22 full years interposed. The third part of the weeks or one week neither coheres with the 62, nor do its halves cohere with each other in time. For the former half pertains to the confirmation of the covenant through the preaching of the Messiah done 4 years before his death: but the latter half pertains to the time of the Jewish war, which lasted about three years, as witnessed by Josephus, during which Jerusalem was desolated.

§. XVIII. Finally, in the thirteenth place, the invention of Isaac Vossius must also be recalled to this class of absurd opinions, who, preferring the account of Josephus to the Holy Scripture, refers the completion of the temple to the ninth year of Darius (whom Ezra calls the sixth, c. 6:15); but he makes the beginning of the 70 weeks from the 25th year of Xerxes (whom he pretends is the Artaxerxes of Ezra and Nehemiah), but he establishes the end as the nativity of Christ, and adding some half to the sixty-two weeks, having dismissed the Hebrew text, which he translates very poorly, from the 70 Interpreters 'ἐξολεθρευθήσεται χρίσμα' (the anointing shall be destroyed), he fashions for himself this sense: when 62 and a half weeks have elapsed, the anointing will cease, that is, the Kings who were truly of the Jewish line will cease, the power having been transferred to the Romans. To have recited these ravings is to have refuted them. For they deserve no other refutation, these profane and impiously injurious absurdities against the Holy Code.

§. XIX. These opinions, therefore, as openly false and absurd, are all deservedly rejected, nor do I think they will easily find any patron today. Besides these, however, others occur, with a greater appearance of probability, and asserted by authors of the highest rank, even if they do not deserve the calculation, which must now be further weighed.

CHAPTER II.

Opinions concerning the 70 Weeks that are more probable, but not consonant with the divine oracle.

§. XX. Before we bring those forward, the cause of the discrepancy among authors in assigning the terminus a quo of the seventy weeks must be adduced. This is chiefly that the latter is fixed by the Angel at the GOING FORTH OF THE WORD concerning the building of Jerusalem, and that various edicts are read in the sacred scriptures to have been promulgated concerning it: the first by Cyrus, Ezra 1:1; the second in the second year of the reign of Darius, Ezra 4; the third in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, Ezra 7:7; and finally the fourth in the twentieth year of the same, Nehemiah 2. Whence authors have been divided into parties concerning this Going forth of the word, some assigning the first, others the second, some the third, and finally certain people the fourth as the beginning of this Epoch. Who, however, each one again departs into different opinions, nor do they extricate themselves in the same way.

§. XXI. Those who refer the beginning to the times of Cyrus differ in their opinions about the end of this Epoch, and thus they also disagree in the calculation itself. Clement of Alexandria in book 1 of the Stromata and Johannes Mariana indeed place the beginning in the first year of Cyrus, but they refer the end to the destruction, which took place under Titus. Which therefore will be the fourteenth opinion here.

§. XXII. Eusebius, however, in book 8 of the Demonstratio Evangelica, beginning the weeks from the first year of Cyrus and the release from captivity, terminates the sixty-ninth in Alexander the King and likewise Pontiff: because the Pontiffs ruled the Jewish people up to that point, whom he thinks were called Christs by Gabriel, and he places the end of the weeks in Jerusalem captured by Pompey. Although Eusebius is not consistent with himself, but also begins the weeks of Daniel from the sixth year of Darius Hystaspes, and finishes the 69 weeks at the death of Hyrcanus, whom he says was the last Pontiff of the Maccabean line to be called Christ, and was slaughtered by Herod in the 186th Olympiad, separating the last week, and attributing half of it to the proclamation of Christ, and the other half to the proclamation of the Apostles in Judea; nay, with yet another new interpretation, assigning seventy years to the seventieth week, from the Baptism of Christ to the Principate of Trajan. This, therefore, shall be the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth opinion concerning this Epoch.

§. XXIII. In the sixteenth place, others indeed place the beginning of the weeks likewise in the release from captivity made by Cyrus, but they place the end in the passion of Christ. Because this opinion has certain patrons from among our Theologians, and is wonderfully pleasing even for the reason that it deduces the entire Chronology from the creation of the world up to the death of Christ from the θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) scriptures alone, we shall examine it particularly.

CHAPTER III. Concerning the Beroaldists who begin the weeks from the edict of Cyrus, and finish them in the passion of Christ.

§. XXIV. This opinion is defended primarily by Matthaeus Beroaldus, the Frenchman Dionysianus, in book 3 of his Chronology, chapters 7 and 8, whom Philip Mornay, Johannes Haslerus, Isaac Genius have subsequently followed, and David Pareus has contended for this opinion especially sharply in his Chronological treatise on the LXX weeks of Daniel. Robert Baillie, Professor at Glasgow, in his historical and chronological work, book 1, question 11, also alleges Broughton, Rainolds, Howe, Nisbet, and the English annotators for this opinion. Among our own, M. Georgius Stempelius in his Delineatio Sacrae Chronologiae, as well as Dr. Ananias Weber in a disputation on this passage of Daniel held at Leipzig, and others, have embraced the same.

§. XXV. They urge these reasons for this beginning of the Epoch: First, that the mandate of Cyrus was the first edict concerning the release from captivity. Second, that it looked to the return of the people and the building of Jerusalem, which Gabriel clearly designates here. Third, that the parallel passages Is. 44:28, Jer. 29:10 agree. Fourth, that what was promised here was fulfilled in 2 Chron. 36:22-23, Ezra 1:1. Fifth, they add that a doubt is left regarding the beginning of the LXX weeks, and the Prophet is not sufficiently informed about that beginning by the heavenly messenger unless the first edict of Cyrus is regarded.

§. XXVI. To this opinion, however, Joseph Scaliger, and those who follow him, and other more accurate Chronologists, oppose primarily the interval of the Persian kingdom, which, contrary to the faith of all historians and the truth of celestial motion, would have to be compressed by about 100 years by that agreement. This is also urged by Africanus in Jerome on this passage: If from Cyrus, and his first indulgence by which the captivity of the Jews was relaxed, the LXX weeks are counted, we shall find a hundred and more years, which exceed the set number of LXX weeks, and much more if from the day on which the Angel spoke to Daniel, and a larger number is added if you wish to have the beginning of the captivity as the beginning of the weeks. For the kingdom of the Persians remained until the beginning of the Macedonians for two hundred and thirty years, and the Macedonians themselves reigned for three hundred years, and from then until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ suffered, 60 years are counted, which together make 590 years, so that one hundred years remain over. This is Africanus. The Kings of the Persians are listed by historians with unanimous consent, as Calvisius has it in Isagog. Chronolog. c. 42, as follows: The first King Cyrus reigned for 30 years. Cambyses 7. The Interregnum of the Magi is one year. Darius Hystaspes ruled for 36 years. Xerxes 21. Artaxerxes Longimanus 41. Darius Nothus 19. Artaxerxes Mnemon 43. Ochus 23. Arses 3. Darius Codomannus 6. But there is no doubt among chronologists concerning the three hundred years of the Macedonians; whence Jerome on this passage.
