He refutes Hippolytus, who counts 62 weeks up to the advent of Christ, from these intervals, because the times do not correspond at all: since two hundred and thirty years of the Persian kingdom are calculated, and three hundred of the Macedonians, and after them thirty years up to the Nativity of the Lord; that is, 560 years from the beginning of the King of the Persians up to the advent of the Savior. Similarly, he refutes Clement of Alexandria from the fact that, according to the MOST DILIGENT CALCULATION, from the first year of Cyrus, King of the Persians and Medes, in which Darius also ruled, up to Vespasian and the destruction of the temple, 630 years are calculated. Eusebius book 8. εὐαγγελικῆς ἀποδείξεως (Demonstratio Evangelica), and from him Jerome on this passage, joins the times of the Pontiffs with the years of the Persian and Greek empire, and calculates 483 years from the first year of King Cyrus and the return of the captives to the death of Alexander the King and Pontiff, from which it is manifest that far more than 70 weeks of years have passed from the released captivity to the advent of the Messiah.

§. XXVII. Since the Beroaldists cannot untie this knot, they cut it, and they do not fear to assert that all Greek historians—Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Diodorus Siculus, and others who ever wrote about past events—wrote their accounts of Persian affairs, as far as the designation of times is concerned, with Greek, that is, with fictitious, credibility. Therefore, our blessed teacher, and subsequently my colleague at the University of Königsberg, the Lord Doctor Johann Behm, refutes them at length in his Manuductio ad Chronologiam, book 2, title 3, vindicating the Greek historians from Beroaldist injuries and demonstrating, from the firmness of celestial motion and from eclipses, and from the evidence brought forward from Ptolemy, Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, and Diodorus Siculus, that the kingdom of the Persians lasted for more than 130 years; concerning which, see Scaliger, book 6, De Emendatione Temporum, page 585 of the edition in my possession. The Greek writers recorded the years of all the kings of Persia so truly and faithfully that, from the beginning of Cyrus to the death of Alexander the Great, not even a single year has been lost. For all the times during which those kings reigned are marked by some notable character, which cannot be contradicted. For either by some defect of the luminaries, as in the years of Cambyses and Darius: or by some most certain interval, as the beginning of Cyrus from the Olympiads, the end of Artaxerxes Longimanus from the Peloponnesian War, the beginnings of Darius Nothus and Artaxerxes Mnemon. These are Scaliger's words.

§. XXVIII. It will be easy to reply to the arguments opposed by the Beroaldists: As to the first, that here the discourse is not about the mandate for releasing the captivity, but about the going forth of the word: that it is to be understood concerning the word that went forth for the sake of building the city, not concerning the dissolution of the captivity, nor concerning a bare mandate, which was not joined with the effect of building Jerusalem, as the edict of Cyrus was, but concerning the word joined with the effect.

§. XXIX. As to the second argument, there is nothing in the words of the angel about the return of the people, but about the reiterating of the building of the city לְהָשִׁיב וְלִבְנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלַם which words can be rendered: to restore or repair and build Jerusalem, because the word שׁוּב in Piel and Hiphil denotes restoration, 2 Kings 14:22, 26. Or if you prefer, τὸ הָשִׁיב can be taken adverbially by the customary idiom of the holy language, so that the sense may be, to reiterate and build, that is, to build the city again, as the Vulgate and B. Luther rendered it, by which reasoning the Angel also spoke afterwards, v. 25. תָּשׁוּב וְנִבְנְתָה it shall return and be built, the street, that is, it shall be built again. See similar locutions in Josh. 5:2, Job 6:18, Ps. 24:7, Ez. 8:13, Zech. 8:16. And that word is not used without cause, if you listen to the opinion of others. For they wish the mention of the word הָשִׁיב for reiterating the building to be made so that it may be indicated that the first building would not succeed upon the first edict, but that the building, having been hindered and interrupted for some time, would have to be reiterated. But those who are of the contrary opinion are too bold in supplementing the sacred text at their own discretion: but if it is permissible to insert the word 'people' into the words of Gabriel, in this way, 'to bring back (the people),' will it not be permissible with equal ease to understand the word 'edict,' in this manner: 'to bring back or restore (the edict) and build Jerusalem.' Because the going forth of the divine Prophetic word was about renewing the edict for the rebuilding of the temple, which had been rendered void, and thus annihilated, through the wickedness of the enemies. Furthermore, if those words 'to bring back or cause to return the people' are retained at all, the sense will be this: to permit that (the people) may return, not to their homeland, but to build. For since he had been hindered before, and recalled from the work of construction, it was necessary that he be brought back and recalled to the pursuit of it, so that the King, by his edict, might cause the people to return to the work of construction. Which was also observed by Scaliger, lib. 6, de Emend. temp., p. m. 604. The Jews, who were building again, are said to return and build: Kings, who allowed or ordered this, are said to cause to return to construct, that is, to order to construct again. Therefore דְבַר לְהָשִׁיב וְלִבְנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלַם is an edict commanding to construct Jerusalem again. The Jews are said to be שָׁבִים לִבְנוֹת returning to build. But the King is said to be מֵשִׁיב הַיְהוּדִים לִבְנוֹת causing the Jews to return to build: That is, ordering them to build again. Finally, not only did Cyrus cause the people to return by relaxing the captivity, but also Artaxerxes, as Ezra testifies, ch. 7. and 8, where a not insignificant sum is reported, which returned by his permission with Ezra, and to all those wishing to return to their homeland of their own accord, that liberty was granted by the King.

§. XXX. The third argument assumes the places in Isa. 44:28, Jer. 29:10 as parallel to our text, when they are not parallel. Isaiah testifies that Cyrus alone would promulgate an edict concerning Jerusalem and the building of the temple. Jeremiah, after the 70 years of captivity had elapsed, promises the relaxation of the captivity and the return to Judea. But that that edict of Cyrus and the release of the captivity are looked to here, when the going forth of the word is defined as the beginning of Daniel's Epoch, that stood in need of demonstration.

§. XXXI. The same must also be held concerning the fourth argument about the completion of this prophecy. Namely, it is assumed as an agreed point in 2 Chron. 36:22, 23, Ezra 1:1, that the word or edict is proposed, concerning the going forth of which Daniel prophesied in this place, which, however, is the very thing in question, which now comes into controversy.

§. XXXII. But as to what is urged fifthly, that unless the angel looked to the edict of Cyrus, there would be no determined beginning, that cannot move us; since a certain beginning is fixed in the going forth of the word concerning the return to the works of repair and construction of Jerusalem: whence it could be understood that the first concession was not looked to, nor would the work succeed, but that there would be need of another and new edict, as the explanation of some holds, or at least that that permission is indicated which granted the repair not only of the Ecclesiastical state, but also of the Political, and provided the means, and autonomy, if we may so call it, for the same. Then if you understand the going forth of the word not of a Royal edict, but of a Prophetic one, as some wish, the Angel must be considered to have referred to other Prophets, and to have promised that the open word of God would go forth at some time, namely at that time when Jerusalem is built with success, and that the calculation of the 70 weeks is to be begun from this going forth of the word. But it is hardly credible that the angel wished to refer this of ours, or even the people of the Lord, to another Prophet, from whom they might receive clearer light concerning this Epoch, who was sent from heaven for the very reason that he himself might reveal the beginning and end of this Epoch, and not to indicate that it was to be revealed long ago.

§. XXXIII. These things, therefore, concerning that opinion which begins Daniel's weeks from the edict of Cyrus, concerning which B. Behmius says: We ourselves would certainly wish that the beginning of these 70 weeks could be taken from this time: for thus we would labor less in Chronology, and we would have the interval of years from the creation to the death of the Messiah from the sacred writings alone. But because this opinion shortens the interval of the Persian kingdom to 100 years, against the truth of celestial motion, it must be said that the weeks cannot begin from the return of the Jews from Babylon, or from the edict of Cyrus.

CHAPTER IV. Concerning the same opinion, but slightly interpolated.

§. XXXIV. Therefore, seventeenthly, in order that these difficulties may be avoided, another way of angelic calculation is entered upon: while indeed that Beroaldian beginning from the edict of Cyrus is retained, the final term of the weeks is slightly extended, so that they may not end in the year of the crucifixion; but the passion may fall in the middle of the last week, and its end may be about the admission of the Gentiles to the kingdom of Christ, and the name of Christians, Acts 10 and 11. But lest they should find it necessary to compress the interval of the Persian kingdom so greatly, they say that in the angelic computation of the 70 weeks, 49 continuous years were not numbered in the prior interval of seven weeks; but that the same were computed by a method of intercalation. Which, having been done by Constant l'Empereur with no appearance of probability, has been recently adorned above all by Mr. Matth. Wasmuth, Professor at the Academy of Rostock, in Vindiciae Hebraicae scripturae, part 2, chapter 1, page 800.

who strives to teach that the Angel (as a mystical-chronological prophet rather than a purely historical one) does not compute continuous years by that number of 7 weeks (nor, therefore, all those years which flowed from Cyrus to the 1st year of Mnemon), but only those years, intermittently and successively, in which, by the restoration of the temple and city granted by some Persian kings, the affairs of the Jews flourished with whatever success.

§. XXXV. In these matters, Constantine L'Empereur, as it seems, led the way in part in his annotations to R. Jacchiades' commentary on Daniel 6. For he maintains that Daniel computes only the years in which progress was made in the work, omitting all those in which it ceased; and from the beginning of Cyrus to the seventh of Artaxerxes Mnemon, although he admits that more than one hundred and forty years had flowed, he nevertheless maintains that Daniel counts only forty-nine, that is, seven weeks, in this manner: from the first of Cyrus to the first of Xerxes, he says, the construction of the temple continued for forty-six years (of which he thinks the Jews spoke to Christ in John 2); then he judges that the first interruption of the work occurred in the first year of Xerxes, so that the work continued through all the days of Cyrus, Cambyses, Smerdis, and Darius Hystaspis, yet the finishing touch was not put on the temple during all that time; afterwards, he maintains that the work was interrupted during the entire life of Xerxes and Artaxerxes Longimanus, and that it was resumed in the second year of Darius Nothus and proceeded until his sixth, for three years, but incomplete. For he says that in the sixth year of Nothus, due to the negligence of the Jews themselves, not by any external force, it ceased again from the work until the seventh of Artaxerxes Mnemon, for eighteen years; when, from Ezra, it was completed in a few months to the temple: so that these months added in the seventh of Artaxerxes, to those which were lacking in the sixth of Darius, make only one year, and that the forty-ninth, and the last of the seventh week, in which the temple was built: he wishes the remaining sixty-three to be counted continuously from the seventh of Artaxerxes to the passion of Christ: where, however, he finds only four hundred and thirty-four years, which, added to the previous 49, make only 483. So that of the total sum of four hundred and ninety, seven are still missing. He supplies these, not as Africanus and others do with the fiction of their lunar years, but from Scaliger and Selden by Egyptian years (which the Jews sometimes, though very rarely, used), consisting of twelve months of thirty days: such Egyptian years exceed the common and solar years by a week in four hundred and eighty-three. Thus L'Empereur: Dr. Wasmuth differs from him in this, that the latter introduced Egyptian years so that he might finish the calculation in the year of Christ's passion: the former places the end of Gabriel's epoch in the fourth year after Christ's passion, and counts 434 years not from the seventh of Artaxerxes to the passion of Christ, but from the 1st of that Artaxerxes Mnemon to the baptism of Christ and the beginning of his ministry. Nor do they agree in the calculation of the first seven weeks, even though both wish to exclude the years in which there was a cessation from the work of building the temple. For Constantine maintains that the work of construction succeeded through all the days of Cyrus, Cambyses, Smerdis, and Darius Hystaspis, but that during the entire reign of Xerxes and Artaxerxes Longimanus, up to the second of Darius Nothus, and thus for 21 years of Xerxes, 41 of Longimanus, and 2 of Darius Nothus, or for 64 years, the work rested, being resumed in turn for the following three years. But these things concerning the progress of the work through the entire time of Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius I do not agree with the chronology: for Cyrus reigned 7 years from the time of the edict, Cambyses 8, Darius Hystaspis 36, which make 51, and thus, with the three years under Darius Nothus added, there result not 49 years only, or seven weeks, but 54 years and almost eight angelic weeks: Nor does the progress of the work through the entire time of the monarchy of Cyrus, Cambyses, Smerdis, and Darius Hystaspis agree with the historical truth of the divine Canon in Ezra. Therefore, Dr. Wasmuth initiated another method of calculation, in order to extract 49 discontinuous years of the construction of the temple. Namely, that the work succeeded for three years under Cyrus (it rested during the remaining years of the monarchy, as also throughout the entire reign of Cambyses and Smerdis, which from Ezra 4 and the consensus of historians and chronologists are certain), it was resumed again in the years of Darius Hystaspis, throughout the entire time of his reign, that is, thirty-six years: under Xerxes, however (although the Jews were prohibited for the first 14 years, yet in the later years of his reign, with Xerxes having been reconciled to the Jews through the intercession of Esther), the work flourished for six years: (it was inhibited again, throughout the entire reign of Artaxerxes Longimanus, for over 40 years); finally, under Darius Nothus, for about four years, from the second to the sixth of his empire, the building of the temple was completed: he judges that the Jews promoted nothing further in the remaining 13 years of the same empire, up to the reign of Artaxerxes Mnemon: whence, from these years of the temple's construction, although discontinuous, collected into a sum, he makes up seven weeks for the first angelic interval: And he begins the second, which is of 62 weeks, from the first of Artaxerxes Mnemon. These are the views of Dr. Wasmuth, whom Mr. Christian Ravius followed in his recently published Chronology, who, however, began the 62 weeks not from the first of Artaxerxes Mnemon, but immediately from the sixth of Darius Nothus. But both, as we have said, followed primarily Alsted in his Thesaurus Chronologiae, section 17, under the Chronology of the Persian Monarchy, Observation 4, who says that the foundations were laid in the second year of Cyrus, but then immediately ceased under Cambyses (because he assigns only two years to the monarchy of Cyrus with some months) and continued for 36 years of Darius Hystaspis: but under Xerxes he assigns another cause for the work from the 46th year of the return from Babylon to the 60th year, and further teaching that construction succeeded in the final 6 years of the Empire of Xerxes, whom he makes Ahasuerus, to the 65th year of the return, which itself is the 42nd year of construction; and under the Empire of Artaxerxes Longimanus he establishes a third cause of 41 years, up to the second of Darius Nothus, and the 107th of the return. But as in this calculation many things are assumed precariously, and some are entirely alien to historical truth, both Sacred and profane, so the collection of discontinuous years can in no way be proven, being entirely contrary to the opinion of Gabriel: whence to Robert Baillie, whom Mr. Wasmuth celebrates in historical and chronological matters as the chief and most accurate of all moderns (though without reason), that opinion of L'Empereur concerning discontinuous years seemed so entirely new and singular, and so improbable, that he did not think it necessary to dwell on refuting it, which he wished to cite at least for this reason, that it might serve as a document of how widely a small error at the beginning deviates at the end, and to what absurdity the deduction of the weeks from the first year of Cyrus has even today carried away very learned men.

§. XXXVI. Lest, however, others might perhaps be led into the same (as there is nothing so absurd that it does not find supporters), we observe these few things for the present; first, that such a method of intercalating years, and of counting them, and of collecting into one sum those which at such long and diverse intervals are divided, is entirely unusual and clearly unknown to Holy Scripture. Whence also, as far as is known, no such calculation ever came into the mind of anyone before Alsted and L'Empereur. The case of the passage of Ezra chapter 5:16, 'from that time (of Cyrus) until now it is being built,' is a different matter, and nothing favors those discontinuous years for there no calculation of years is subtracted; nor is it asserted that it was built continuously from that time, but only that it was built until now, and the work was not brought to an end. Therefore, that phrase is not to be tortured: for it implies nothing other than that the temple was indeed begun to be built in the times of Cyrus; but that it was not yet completed by those times: from which, however, it cannot be inferred that they continued in the construction throughout all those years, nor that they labored always until those times, when it was whole, nor that they were forced to desist from the work by prohibitions. For concerning those alternating periods of work or cessations, unless it is known from elsewhere, it certainly cannot be known from that phrase. Nor does that passage help that opinion at all: for it does not treat there of Darius Nothus, but of the first of that name, the son of Hystaspes, as is evident from the preceding chapter of Ezra 4:24. But as for the fact that Scaliger with his followers begins the calculation in the last week with a number of intercalated years joined together, but separated in time, in that neither are such various disjointed epochs of years, or accumulations, concluded into one sum, and that gap, although it is a single one, Mr. Wasmuth himself noted with just censure in Scaliger on page 282, because although he correctly made the middle of the last week (by referring the death of Christ to it), without any reason (though quite imperiously) he inserted a GREAT GAP of 34 years after that middle, and postponed the remaining half after the 70 weeks were completed, which even to have recounted is to have refuted. Furthermore, it does not at all suit the angelic speech to join years separated in time in such a number: because the angel Gabriel wished to designate an exact and adequate number of years from the term from which to the term to which, which is precisely completed by 70 weeks, 490 years, without intercalary years. Which Mr. Wasmuth concedes, urging the emphasis of the word נחתך, which implies a precisely defined interval. But if you omit the 76 intercalary years of cessation (which he himself demands), the number of weeks from the going forth of the word to the end, which the Angel designates, will not be precisely defined either: for thus almost eleven weeks will have been omitted: since at that term according to that calculation, not 490, but 566 years according to Mr. Wasmuth (but according to others even more) will have elapsed. Nor could it have been known for certain to any mortal, nor could it even now be known, how to calculate the interval of the 70 weeks: because no traces of intercalating years, or of the distinction between years of cessation and construction to be observed, are found either in this prophecy or anywhere else in the Holy Scriptures, even slightly obscurely. And Mr. Wasmuth himself admits this in his presupposition 1, page 242. In this prophecy, the 70 annual weeks make only 490 years, and with that left uncertain, there would be no certain account of time. Whence Alsted indeed discontinues the years of the building of the temple, but leaves the weeks of Daniel continuous, and begins them from the edict promulgated at the beginning of Darius Nothus, the thirty-seventh

ending with Artaxerxes Memnon. Thirdly, just as in the second partial interval of 62 weeks the years are to be understood as continuous or joined, as those authors admit and all interpreters agree, and no less in the third interval of one week the seven years are to be taken as not disjointed: so in the first interval of seven weeks, and in the total sum of 70 weeks, it is necessary to understand the years as joined, not disjointed, unless one wishes to render everything uncertain. For with the same ease that discontinuous years are imagined in the first interval, another would imagine discontinuous years in the second, and another in the third interval, which the latter was also done by Scaliger. What certainty, therefore, will remain?

§. XXXVII. Fourthly, the collection of seven weeks, so that a complete sum of 49 years may emerge, is too arbitrary, and not made by anyone in such a way as perhaps by those three authors, who nevertheless differ greatly among themselves, and are not provided with suitable documents concerning the years of construction and cessation, with regard to their number or the method of calculation which each one follows. Those 46 years of the construction of the temple, which they draw hither from Jewish tradition, John 2:20, do not agree with that calculation: because 49 years ought to have been numbered: whence for their supplement three years of Cyrus are snatched hither, but since the structure had already begun in them, how will the Jewish tradition stand for itself; 'Forty and six years was this temple in building,' why did the Jews omit a full three-year period, and indeed that first one, under which the building began, by the edict of a most august Monarch, and by what authority is it taught that that three-year period was passed over? since a bare assertion can easily be judged rash? Furthermore, it is asserted by no document that the structure of the Temple was promoted for a full 36 years under Darius Hystaspes. For that which Ezra ch. 5, 5. The inhibition said to have been made in the time of Cyrus until the reign of Darius, must be understood of that Darius, under whose empire in the sixth year, after the work was resumed in the second, the building was completed, as is clearly held in Ezra 2:24, ch. 6:14, 15. But whom Mr. Wasmuth determines is not Darius Hystaspes, but Nothus, appealing to the consensus of other historians? although he is vehemently mistaken in this: Since indeed not Nothus, but the son of Hystaspes is to be understood in those places of Ezra: under whose reign historians, chronologists, and interpreters teach with great consensus that the structure of the temple was completed, Wasmuth himself admitting it. For he praised these on page 258: Eusebius in his Chronicle, Josephus in Antiquities of the Jews 2, ch. 4, Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of Stromata, Jerome, Basil, and Theodoret in their Commentary on Haggai, Augustine, book 18 of The City of God, ch. 20, Gordon in his Chronicle, pp. 53, 231, Reusner in his True Computation of the Years of the World. Vorstius in his dissertation on the time of the restoration of the Temple, Heinrich Philipp in his Questions and Chronological Notes, pp. 218, 249, Robert Baillie in his Historical and Chronological work, p. 187, David Chytraeus in his Sermons on the Times of the World, p. 298, Grotius in this place, Isaac Vossius in his dissertation on the LXX Interpreters, p. 144, Laurentius Eichstadt in his Chronological Studies, letter R. 2. and T. 2. and 4. Likewise Capellus, James Ussher, Petavius, Pererius, Sanctius, Torniellus, with the added sign of others of the same opinion, etc.

Nor indeed is it to be conceded (which he takes for himself gratuitously) as if two different Dariuses are understood in Ezra 2:4 and 24, and in the former place indeed Darius Hystaspes is designated, but in the latter Darius Nothus. For the text most evidently teaches that it concerns one and the same: inasmuch as in it the work is said to have been hindered in the last times of Cyrus until the reign of Darius, verse 5, and afterwards it refers specifically, how, as had been reported before concerning Cyrus, under Ahasuerus (the king next to Cyrus, that is, Cambyses) at his beginning the Jews were falsely accused, v. 6, as also in the days of his successor Artaxerxes (Smerdis, for example, for he was the successor of Cambyses) v. 7, and from there v. 24, it is repeated what had been said, that the work had been hindered until the reign of Darius, and the year of Darius is designated, namely the second, in which the work succeeded again. Nor finally is it to be admitted, Ezra 5 v. 16 (which he calls a famous passage) that the temple is said to have been built from the time of Cyrus until the times of Darius Nothus, and that in the sense that there was no cessation from the structure of the temple in continuous ages from Cyrus to Darius Nothus, but only intermittently under Cambyses, Smerdis Magus, Ahasuerus, and Artaxerxes Longimanus. For thus it would have ceased for far longer and for more years, namely for 64 years, than it was worked upon in the structure, seeing that it was done only in 45 years according to this latest calculation. How then is it said that Sheshbazzar (Zerubbabel) came under Cyrus and laid the foundations of the house, and from that time until now (to the times of Nothus) it was built, when under so many kings, Cyrus, in the final times, Cambyses, Smerdis, Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes Longimanus, and at the beginning of Darius, it had ceased for 64 years from the work of the structure?

§. XXXVIII. Furthermore, that in the fifth place, under Xerxes, the structure was continued for the last 6 years, but the work ceased for the first 14 years, is said gratuitously and without a suitable witness; and it is falsely assumed that the Ahasuerus of Esther is Xerxes, which opinion will be discussed below. For whence is that number of 14 years of cessation obtained, or what trace occurs in sacred or profane histories of a six-year structure granted under Xerxes? The authority of Alsted, stating this without a suitable witness, just as it is otherwise very slight in these matters, so in this novel discovery it ought not to be of such weight that for its sake such things are admitted and sold as indisputably certain, which are read nowhere among sacred or exotic writers.

§. XXXIX. Furthermore, in the sixth place, that under Artaxerxes Longimanus the Jews were again forbidden, during the whole time of his same empire, to proceed with the work of the structure, is said to be maintained by the principal historians and chronologists; but no one is called as a witness, and perhaps no one can easily be brought forward, unless you wish to admit those who, having followed Scaliger primarily, substitute Darius Nothus for Hystaspes in Ezra. For that Artaxerxes in Ezra 4, 7 and 23 is to be understood as Longimanus is asserted rashly, since the text sufficiently indicates that the closer successor of Cyrus is designated, between whom (namely Cyrus and this Artaxerxes) only Ahasuerus (and not several) intervened: nor does the name of Artaxerxes prove anything. For as he admits in Chronolog. Alsted. p. 182, that name was common. The kings of the Persians, he says, were almost all called Darius and Artaxerxes. Thus the Egyptians called their kings Pharaohs and Ptolemies. The Parthians, Arsacids; the Latins, Murrani; the Albans, Sylvii; the Romans, Caesars; the Philistines, Abimelech and Achish; the Scythians, Scholothi; the Danes, Skioldungos; the Turks, Ottomans. And Ravius concedes that Artaxerxes Longimanus is not understood there, but another far earlier than him.

§. XL. Furthermore, in the seventh place, it is falsely asserted that the temple was completed under Darius Nothus: and it is assumed precariously that under that king the Jews promoted nothing for the last 13 years, until the reign of Artaxerxes Mnemon. For if this Darius of Ezra, under whom he testifies in chapters 5 and 6 that the work proceeded, is Nothus, how will it be taught, I pray, that a king who with such diligence, such liberality, I add also such piety, as that edict reviewed in chapter 6 breathes, took care that the structure of the temple should be finished, hindered, or permitted that the works of the Jewish people should be hindered, whose sacrifices and prayers for his life and that of his children he desired greatly and valued most highly, Ezra 4, 10? And whence will it be demonstrated that the Artaxerxes of Darius, the promoter of divine worship, patronized the divine worship and the Jewish polity more fully immediately at the beginning of his empire? The contrary is rather clear from chapter 7. Ezra v. 7, that namely only in the seventh year was the king's mind reconciled to them. Which Artaxerxes other more accurate chronologists more correctly maintain was not Mnemon, but Longimanus.

§. XLI. Now eighth, since in that calculation, although merely arbitrary, the cited author has mostly followed Alstedius (to whom he attributes a great deal in these matters), he will nevertheless be reconciled with him with difficulty. For the latter finishes the building of the temple in the sixth year of Darius Nothus, and counts only 46 years: namely 36 under Darius Hystaspes, 6 under Xerxes, and 4 under Darius Nothus, and under Cyrus, to whose entire Monarchical reign he ascribes only two years and a few months; he maintains that only the foundations of the temple were laid in the second year of his monarchy, and that work was not done on the structure of the temple for three years, from which seven full weeks cannot emerge, unless the two or three prior years of Artaxerxes Mnemon are added; which years Wasmuth draws to the second interval of the Angelic computation.

§. XLII. Therefore, ninth, as regards the other interval, it is merely precarious that its beginning falls in the first year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, to whom, however, the connection with the preceding interval does not agree if that ended in the sixth year of Nothus: because the empire of Mnemon did not follow the sixth year of Nothus, but the nineteenth: but the first and second interval in the computation of Gabriel cohere in immediate connection: nor do they admit that interval of 13 years, or from the sixth year of Darius Nothus to the first of his successor. Furthermore, that does not agree with the history of Ezra and Nehemiah, in which the beginning of the privilege and concession given to the Jews under Artaxerxes for restoring Jerusalem is not reduced to the beginning of his reign, but to his seventh year, Ezra 7:7, and regarding the repair of the streets and walls, to the 20th year. Nehemiah 1:1, whence one must wonder why it is said that no necessity appears why that beginning should be restricted to that [time] (since it was done by the Holy Spirit Himself) and why it should not be referred to the very beginning of the reign of Artaxerxes (contrary to the express letter)? For it is not permitted, on account of our calculation which we have conceived in our mind, to recede from the express letter of the Holy text, or to oppose it.

§. XLIII. Tenth, Mr. Wasmuth makes a double completion of that second interval, and he attempts to carve it out of the text; namely, one broader, at the beginning, the repair of the street and the moat: the other in the succession, sadder, expressed through the distress of the times: But in the words of the Angel these are not referred to a successive state; but they look to the same times, that the streets and walls ought to be built, but in distress of times, 'Then the walls and streets will be built again, yet in a miserable time,' Mr. Wasmuth renders.

The times of the building of the streets and walls are not, therefore, distinct from the times of distress, following one another successively: but these were to be at the same time τῷ χρόνῳ [in time]: namely, the distress and the construction of the streets and trenches or walls: and consequently, this distress of times is rashly drawn to the state under the Seleucid Kings and Antiochus, given this explanation: because the streets and trenches had already been repaired long before, under the Persian Monarchs, which repair happened in the distress and σενοχωρια [narrowness/distress] of times under the same. And here Ravius departs from his Wasmuth, interpreting this distress as the time of intercalation, and distinguishing it by a parenthesis from those things which are said about the construction of the streets and trenches, so that the distress is snatched away to the times of the disturbed building of the temple, which Mr. Wasmuth applies to the state under the Seleucid Kings and Antiochus.

§. XLIV. Eleventh, it is assumed without sufficient proof that the seven weeks and the sixty-two are to be distinguished in this way regarding the completion of events, so that within the former the temple, and within the latter the streets and trenches, must have been repaired. For there is no express word about the construction of the temple; but generally about the construction of Jerusalem: with special mention also made of the streets and trenches, so that it might be indicated that the edict referred to, not Cyrus, but Artaxerxes. Nor does the history agree; for the temple was not built in the 49 years next after the edict; but rather the history of the streets and trenches, or they were repaired, and the Polity was restored, and thus the whole of Jerusalem was built again, which the angel had hinted at. Nor were sixty-two weeks spent on that restoration of the city, which were rather designated and defined after the seven weeks of restoration had elapsed, unto Messiah the Prince. Finally, how would the arrival of Messiah, the Prince, who was exhibited only long after the times of the restorations, be connected with the restoration of the city? Therefore, that distinction of intervals cannot stand in any way.

§. XLV. Lastly, from the first of Artaxerxes Mnemon to Messiah the Prince, declared through Baptism and the solemn θεοφανειαν [theophany], there did not intervene precisely sixty-two weeks, or 434 years. If we follow the canon of Ptolemy, 46 years belong to Artaxerxes Mnemon, 21 to Ochus, 2 to Arses, 4 to Darius Codomannus, which years of the Persians make 73. But the years of the Greek Kings according to Ptolemy are counted as 302. From the Roman Kings, the 43 years of Augustus and the 14 of Tiberius pertain to this, which all collected into one sum produce 432 years; whence, so that he may obtain the exact number of 434 years, Mr. Wasmuth does not set Christ as baptized after the 14th of Tiberius, or in the current 15th year, but in the seventeenth year of Tiberius, openly protesting against St. Luke, who in chapter 3, verse 1, reports that Christ received baptism in the 15th year of Tiberius. If one wishes to follow the calculation of Alsted, he will find from the first of Artaxerxes Mnemon, which he made the year of the World 3546, to Augustus, whose beginning of empire he placed in the year of the World 3907, 361 years; to which if 56 years are added, which he attributes to Augustus Caesar, and 14 full years of Tiberius, 431 years will be produced, and thus Christ would have been baptized in the 432nd year from the auspices of Artaxerxes Mnemon; and since it pleased Alsted to place the end of the seven weeks not in the first of that Artaxerxes, but in the 30th and in the year of the World 3576, it must be said that not 434, but 402 years had elapsed until Christ the Prince, and thus 32 years will be lacking for the integrity of the 62 weeks, and only 57 weeks with three years will have elapsed, provided that Alsted refers the baptism of Christ to the year of the World 3978; whence in the calculation of the LXX weeks he differs greatly from Mr. Wasmuth, referring their beginning not to the first of Cyrus, but to the second of Darius Nothus (which are distant from each other by 108 years) and assigning their end not to the time of the naming of Christians at Antioch, or the fourth year after the death of Christ, but to the destruction of the second temple.

§. XLVI. These things, therefore, clearly teach that that new explanation of the weeks of Daniel deserves no calculation. For which, as the most powerful foundation, the accentuation of the words is placed underneath, namely that under the word שִׁבְעָה, seven (weeks), the Athnach is found, which cuts the middle into two parts, of which the former has the express first interval of the whole space of the LXX weeks (v. 24), namely 7 weeks with its completion of the event, so that the latter part recounts the second interval, namely 62 weeks, with its own completion of the event likewise. But this is too slippery and weak a foundation to sustain such a great mass. For it is known that the Athnach does not always distinguish in such a way that it separates words, or cuts the verse, as far as the sense is concerned, into two parts: which is evident even from the first verse of the Bible: where we know that it is indeed placed there, the sense having it with emphasis: In the beginning created GOD, He created, I say, the heaven and the earth; but it does not at all do what is intended by such a division here, that the determination of the object, the creation of heaven and earth, should be torn apart or separated from the act of creation: for the same sense emerges as if the Athnach were not present, namely that in the beginning GOD created the heaven and the earth: it is not said that GOD first created, or created indefinitely, so that afterwards the creation of heaven and earth is indicated (as if it were something distinct or a different act). And why could not a repetition of that kind be posited here likewise? Know therefore and take note, from the publication of the edict to cause to return and to build Jerusalem (so its version has it) until Messiah the Prince are seven weeks. And sixty-two weeks, I say, that is to say, I do not say only that seven weeks will flow until then; but also another sixty-two (namely, until Messiah the Prince;) but it will return and be built, or they will return and build the street, and the moat, (that I may explain what kind of repeated building I understand to be granted by the solemn edict, from which the beginning of the calculation is to be taken:) but in the distress of times. Or perhaps it may not be inconveniently said with Grotius, that those words, and the street and walls shall be built again, are to be translated thus: after the street and moats have already been built again; so that the term to which the first, and from which the second interval, is expressed by the construction of the streets and moats. But what necessity compels us here to imagine that seven weeks are defined for building the temple, of which no mention at all is made, and sixty-two are indeed assigned for building the street and the moat? Can the Athnach distinction alone cause these intervals of weeks to be restricted in that manner to such objects and completions? And let us suppose that the Athnach is used so that it may be observed that those seven weeks are different from the sixty-two: nothing else can be gathered from it than that for a certain reason those seven weeks were peculiarly distinguished, and for the sake of a clearer distinction that distinctive accent has been applied. The cause, however, of that distinction is not the one which is feigned here, but that those seven weeks were defined for the rebuilding of the street and the moat, of which rebuilding mention was expressly made; but sixty-two [weeks] (those seven not being passed over or excluded, but premised and included) remain until the Messiah the leader. For also in the word וְשָׁנִים there is a sub-distinctive accent, the major leader, which he calls Rebhia: which was not to be neglected. Furthermore, if the completions of the events of the interval are to be gathered from the accentuation, why will it not be concluded from verse 26 that after sixty-two weeks, before the last week and the excision of the Messiah and the dissipation of the sanctuary, it is predicted, because both completions are joined in one verse and are commemorated before the completions of the last week? Is it not also so from the Athnach accent. v. ult. [verse last], would someone gather that that week, by which the covenant was to be strengthened for many, is distinct because it is separated by that great accent, with its completion, from that half-week by which the sacrifice was to cease, but that the same is joined into the half-week of the wing of abominations, which in the other clause of the last verse is joined with the cessation of the sacrifice, and is not so distinct and separated from it (as far as the accents are concerned) as the strengthening of the covenant. But what monstrous explanations would emerge from that? Wherefore, having dismissed those laws of the accents, and those perhaps entirely novel, born yesterday or the day before, and not yet recalled for more accurate examination, let alone approved by a Senate of Philologists, in which certainly the first author, B. Bohlius, frankly professed to me and solemnly testified that he had not yet been able to find any proof when he published his own, but his disciple M. Caspar Ledebuhr, formerly my fellow-boarder, to whom most of those rules after B. Bohlius are owed, was so entangled in those difficulties that in the principal oracles he was against the faith of the Christian world, indeed sometimes against the authority of the New Testament, from his doctrine and invention of accentuation, he would stubbornly dispute, and would plead the cause of the Jews against our Theological College in the University of Königsberg in letters and public writings; which we therefore leave to be examined by the sons of the Grammarians, although in the meantime we do not reject all of them, nor do we wish that the effort which is expended on this study be deprived of its praise; it remains that we should rather weigh the entire prophecy than stick in the accents. From which it is gathered in summary that there are four intervals of the seventy weeks, distinctly designated by the Angel: The first of seven weeks, the second of sixty-two, with those seven weeks included, the third of the last week: and the fourth in the last week also, namely of the half of the same. Whose completions are not distinguished by accents, but are gathered from the speech of the Angel, with a collation of history instituted at the same time, which is the best interpreter of prophecy, in which these completions of events are to be detected: the first of the rebuilding of Jerusalem, concerning which both the edict as the term from which the weeks are introduced, and the structure is explained, which does not look to the temple, but to the city, because the streets and the moat are commemorated, and the time is hinted at: because the first seven weeks are without doubt to be referred to the first completion. Now since sixty-two weeks are subjoined to them, and mention is made further of the coming of the Messiah the leader, with history confirming it, the term to which they belong is the public inauguration of Christ; especially because after those sixty-two weeks he is said to be cut off, and in the middle of the week the sacrifices are to cease, which correspond to the abolition of sacrifices through his death; whence the events of the third and fourth interval can be gathered; that the death of Christ is placed in the middle of the week: but the confirmation of the covenant is attributed to the entire last week, to be instituted through the middle of the week before his death, through the time of the ministry of Christ, which was 3 1/2 years, or a half-week, as also through the other half of the week after the death of Christ through the ministry of the Apostles, all of which will be explained and confirmed more clearly hereafter. And so much for that novel opinion.

CHAPTER V. Concerning the opinion of those who refer the beginning to the times of Darius Hystaspis.

§. XLVII. Eighteenth, others refer the beginning to the times of Darius, concerning whom Ezra 4:24. And they understand Darius the son of Hystaspes, which is the opinion of Johannes Driedo in book 3 of De Scripturis et Dogmatibus Ecclesiasticis, ch. 5, and Cornelius Jansenius in his Concordia Evangelica, ch. 122, and according to Tirinus it was approved by Eusebius and Cyril of Jerusalem. We do not, however, oppose to this opinion what the Scaligerians do: namely, that that Darius, concerning whom Ezra speaks there, is not Darius Hystaspis, but Darius Nothus, which seems manifest to them from the series of Persian Kings, if indeed that Darius is the middle one between two Artaxerxeses, or Artaxerxes one, who is commemorated in ch. 4, v. 7, as the predecessor of Darius, and another the successor of Darius in ch. 7, v. 1. But no Darius is found in the history of the Persian Kings between the two Artaxerxeses, except Darius, whom they call Nothus, who was the middle one between Artaxerxes Longimanus and Artaxerxes Mnemon. For we acknowledge that this opinion and reasoning of Scaliger does not stand on a very firm footing, and therefore it may suffice for refuting the opinion of Driedo that the truth of chronology and celestial motion does not agree if you refer the beginning to the times of Darius Hystaspis. For from his second year (or as others prefer, the sixth), far more than 490 years have elapsed until the Messiah. Therefore Eusebius, beginning these years from the sixth of Darius Hystaspis, terminates them at the death of Hyrcanus, whom he says was killed by Herod in the 186th Olympiad, in the 10th year of the reign of Augustus, although the slaughter of Hyrcanus should be referred not to the 10th year of the Monarchy of Augustus, but to the first year.

CHAPTER VI. The opinion of Scaliger, that the beginning should be led from the 11th year of Darius Nothus, and its foundations.

§. XLVIII. Wherefore others trace the beginning of the weeks of Daniel back to the nineteenth year of Darius Nothus, among whom is Sulpitius Severus, lib. 2. Histor. Sacr., who indeed terminated the 69 weeks at the destruction of Jerusalem, but passed over the seventieth in silence. Rupertus in Tabb. Chronolog. at the year of the World 3527, established the beginning of the LXX weeks in the 2nd year of Darius Nothus, and the end at the destruction of the City. This opinion concerning the 2nd year of Darius Nothus as the initial Epoch of this period, besides Mæstlin the Tubingen Astronomer, was championed especially by the illustrious man Joseph Scaliger, whom not a few of the modern Chronologers & Interpreters follow, Sethus Calvisius, Dn. D. Joh. Behm, Dn. D. Helvicus, M. Martinus Helvicus diatrib. de LXX. hebdom. Dan., Ubbo Emmius, Junius, Polanus, Angelocrator, Mo lineus, Alstedius, Coccejus, L'Empereur, Joh. Tarnov. in Hagg. Calixtus, Majerus, Georg. König in Vindiciis Sacr. disp. 3. Franckenberger, Wagnerus, Strauchius, Schubertus, & others. Added to them is also Hugo Grotius, who nevertheless is not sufficiently consistent with himself in this, in that he declares in the annotations at the end of chapter 9 of Daniel that Chrysostom, in book 2 against the Jews, approached the truth most closely, who certainly did not begin the weeks from the times of Darius, but from the 20th of Artaxerxes.

§. XLIX. These arguments seem to favor Scaliger in particular: First, that the angel speaks of the going forth of the word to rebuild Jerusalem. Which word, because it is placed simply and absolutely, seems to be understood ἐξοχικῶς and in a more famous sense concerning the divine and Prophetic word, since no mention of a King is made, nor is any trace of a Royal diploma detected in the text, whence in the judgment of certain Scaligerians, that going forth of the word is most correctly referred to the prophecies of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah; since after Daniel the Jews had no prophet before these. But through those men, excited by God in a singular and magnificent manner, the going forth of the Divine word and the impulse was made concerning the building of the House of the Lord, Hagg. 2, 4. Zach. 1, 16. c. 8, 9. concerning which thus B. D. Behmius, lib. 2. Chron. Manud. Tit. 3. c. 6. p. 161. This going forth is clearly singular, and the most magnificent of all, and that by reason both of God, who through the prophets Haggai and Zechariah promulgated a singular and divine mandate concerning the rebuilding of the house of the Lord: and of the Persian King himself, who by a singular and most magnificent promulgation commanded the Jews again to build the interrupted temple, with a dire imprecation upon those who would impede this work, Esdr. 6. and by reason of the happy succession of this work. For from the second year of this Darius to the sixth of the same, the structure of the temple was continued and completed without impediment: Esdr. 6, 15. Furthermore, if we accurately weigh the History, the building was instituted not by the edict of the King, but by the word of the Lord. For by the edict of Cyrus the Captivity was indeed loosened, and the building of the temple promised, but this edict was impeded, while Cyrus was still living, and for some time after his death. But under Darius the word of the Lord went forth through the prophets to build Jerusalem, and at this exit of the word of the Lord, without waiting for the King's edict, the work which had hitherto been impeded was promoted. Therefore, for the foundation of the structure, the edict of the King is not alleged by the Holy Spirit, but the word of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, Esdr. 5, 1. which they brought forth in the name of the God of Israel. Then, therefore, the WORD went forth concerning the building of Jerusalem. Nor did they wait for the consent of the King, but relying on the word of the Lord they undertook the work, and were strengthened in the work by the prophets of the Lord, v. 2. Furthermore, when Thatnai the provincial prefect, and the other ministers of Darius, inquired about the work, they testified that they had undertaken it, that they were servants of the God of heaven and earth, even though they also appealed to the indulgence of King Cyrus, made previously; and Ezra testifies that the eyes of the Lord were upon the elders of the Jews, so that they might not be hindered; and finally, afterwards, the consent of Darius was added, when the Jews were already occupied in the work at the word of the Lord, so that they might not be impeded in the same, Esdr. 6, 7. Therefore Ezra again adds, v. 14, that the work succeeded through the prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah; And that they built according to the mandate of the GOD of Israel and the mandate of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, because God was the primary author of the structure through the mandates of the prophets, but the Royal edicts, and especially that of Darius, served the same, which was never impeded and had the desired success.

§. L. Then Haggai 1, 1 seems to mark the beginning of this Epoch, defining the second year of Darius, the first day of the sixth month, on which the word of the Lord came to the prophet, and the spirit of Zerubbabel the Prince of Judah was excited, and the spirit of the rest of the people, so that they might come or return and build the house of the Lord, v. 13, 14. By which God promised assistance, v. 13. Which also happened again on the 24th day of that Month, as also on the 21st of the following, cap. 2, 1, 2. Which seem to demonstrate openly and as if with a pointing finger the EXIT of the WORD of the Lord concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem; with God himself both commanding and advancing the work of the structure by his Spirit.

§. LI. Thirdly, they also establish the same from Zach. 1, 6, when God promises there that he will again turn his mercy to Jerusalem, so that the house of God may be built. Which also happened in the second year on the 24th day of the eleventh month. Therefore, they conclude that the exit of the Word of the Lord is not undeservedly referred to the second year of Darius, in which the word of the Lord went forth again and again concerning this structure. Compare Zach. 8, 2, 9. seqq.

§. LII. Fourthly, this is a most valid weapon, in Scaliger's judgment, that seventy years before the second year of this Darius, the fasts of the fifth and seventh Months had been instituted, which could not have been instituted except by the Church, and therefore nowhere except in Jerusalem, with the use of sacrifices prevailing. Certainly, they did not institute solemnities or fasts in the deportation, but in Palestine, with the altar already standing and the daily sacrifice prevailing, those were instituted. Therefore, says Scaliger p. 602, Zach. 7, 5 it is said: How you lamented in the fifth and seventh months these LXX years. He says those fasts were instituted 70 years ago, when it was the second year of Darius. The second year of Darius Hystaspis is 4194 in the Julian period. Seventy years counted backwards end in the fourth year of the captive Zedekiah, when there was no Church in Palestine. And yet it is said in Zechariah, both that it is the seventieth year from the institution of their fasts, and that in that place, i.e., in Jerusalem, they were celebrated for 70 years, and that by those very people whom the Prophet addresses. How can this be Darius son of Hystaspes? But 70 years reckoned back from the 2nd year of Darius Nothus end in the 28th year of Darius Hystaspes, at which time the Jews were in no better condition than when they were still in Babylon: inasmuch as they were not permitted to build the temple of God and to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. Therefore the fasts were instituted then. For this reason the Angel in the same Zechariah ch. 1, 12, thus beseeches God concerning the most calamitous state of the Jews: O Lord of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years? Or does he say that God does not have mercy on the cities which they were then permitted to rebuild by the edict of Cyrus? He complains, therefore, of the interruption of the work: which had been brought about seventy years from this time by a greater effort of the enemies than before. Wherefore Darius, he in whose second year an edict was issued concerning the restoring of the temple from the prior edict of Cyrus, he, I say, is a different Darius from Darius son of Hystaspes: he is therefore Nothus.

§. LIII. Fifthly, when the Angel speaks of the rebuilding of Jerusalem, he clearly seems to point out the continuation of the interrupted structure. For while from the going forth of the word to return again to build Jerusalem, that which was hindered for a time, so that they might return, God procured through edicts and commands, made both through His Prophets and promulgated by Darius. Therefore in Ezra 5, 2, the going forth of the word is taught through Haggai and Zechariah, that Zerubbabel and Joshua had begun to build the house of the Lord, or to return to the works of the structure, previously begun.

§. LIV. Sixth, the time spent on the structure is appropriate. For 70 weeks, that is, 49 years, are defined for it by the Angel. Now, if the building was begun anew in the second year of Darius, who reigned for 19 years, the end and completion of the building will fall in the 32nd year of Artaxerxes, in whose 20th year he was sent for the repair of Jerusalem, and he presided over the work, both regarding the construction of the walls and regarding the restoration of the polity, up to the 32nd year of Artachsashtha, as is held in Neh. 5, 14.

§. LV. Seventh, Chronologists observe that the interval from the second year of Darius Nothus to the desolation of the later temple is quite singular, both with respect to the beginning and with respect to the end, and it fits perfectly with this definition of 70 weeks, concerning which D. Behm says the following on page 161: The Angel calls that interval of 490 years by the singular appellation of 70 annual weeks; by the number 70, he alludes to the years of captivity; by weeks, he looks to the Sabbatic and Jubilee years, and he intends that the beginning of that departure for the rebuilding of Jerusalem should be taken from a completed Sabbatic and Jubilee year, from the beginning of an annual week. The whole interval of time is to be included precisely within 70 weeks, that is, 70 Sabbatic years and 10 Jubilee years. If now the calculation of times is instituted, and the whole chronological system from the world to the second year of Darius Nothus is examined, we will find that both the time and the singular appellation of time agree exactly, and that the second year of Darius Nothus falls in its earlier part into the Sabbatic and Jubilee year of the Jews, so that with the sixth month, in which Haggai begins in chapter 1, verse 1, that year of rest is completed: With the following, therefore, if we take the beginning of the 70 annual weeks according to Daniel from the Autumn by divine sanction, we will arrive with the end of those same weeks at the Sabbatic and Jubilee year, upon the completion and expiration of which, in the following year, Jerusalem was desolated by the just judgment of God through Vespasian.

§. LVI. Eighth, they urge this, that the most recent destruction of Jerusalem is defined by this oracle, which they think is most clear from the words of Daniel: whence it will be appropriate for the Epoch to be initiated from the building of Jerusalem, which was to end in its desolation: namely, from the structure of the holy city, not from the foundations of the temple having been laid: And therefore, the beginning is to be made not from the time of Cyrus, but finally from the reign of this Darius, so that it may begin from the edict for the restoration of the city and end in its destruction. For it is not in vain that the head of the weeks pertains to the restoration of the State of Jerusalem, since their end is referred to the fall and deletion of that same city.

§. LVII. Ninth, the angel indicates this openly when he teaches in verse 25 that the streets and walls are to be built again. Therefore, the terminus a quo is to be established not from the foundations of the temple having been laid, but from the building of the city.

§. LVIII. Tenth, the same is testified by the manifest designation of this Epoch, which the angel made Ἀσυνδέτως in verse 24: 70 weeks נֶחְתַּךְ are precisely defined over your people and over your holy city, that is, over the Republic and over the city. Therefore, the terminus cannot be placed in the reign of Cyrus, where only the foundations of the temple began to be laid, and the work itself was hindered; but from the time when not only did the works in building the temple succeed again, so that they were completed without hindrance, but the city itself also began to be rebuilt (with walls and streets), and thus the people also began to be reduced to a certain form of polity, so that it might be the holy people of God, in both civil and ecclesiastical polity: which works were then advanced by Ezra and by Nehemiah, under the rule of Darius Nothus and Artaxerxes Memnon.

§. LIX. Eleventh, the beginning of the Angelic prophecy thus harmonizes with the end. For just as he said in verse 24 that 70 weeks were decided over the people and over the holy city, so he is to be considered to have established the end of these weeks afterward, when he designated the end of the people and the city through the final desolation: The people of the Prince [the Roman Emperor] who is to come will destroy the city itself and the sanctuary, and he will destroy it in such a way that its end will be in a flood [so that the city may be extirpated as if by a certain deluge], and up to the end of the war of desolations, which is fixed, that is, with the end of the war the city will be precisely desolated, through that desolating abomination, that is, through the winged Roman army. Compare Matt. 24, 25; Luke 21, 22. What else do these imply, other than that the city is to be desolated again after the passage of 70 weeks: just as it began to be built at their beginning?

§. LX. Twelfth, it is not rashly observed that the scope of this divine revelation is entirely consistent with this interpretation. For when Daniel asked that the Lord might be willing to have mercy again on the holy city and the people, for the sake of the Lord (the Messiah), the Angel promised not only its restoration, so that the Messiah might be able to perform the work of redemption there, within these 70 Weeks, but lest the Prophet should dwell only on this people and this city, whose restoration he desired, he also prophesies that the people and the city will indeed be destroyed with the Sanctuary and the Levitical cult, but that it would not therefore be over with the Church; nay, then finally, with the most recent desolation of the city and Sanctuary imminent, the Messiah is to be anointed, so that he may be the Prince or King of his chosen people, who may serve the Lord in spirit and truth without corporal offerings and sacrifices, and not be restricted to any certain place, so that the Prophet might thus be recalled to the prophecies which had been produced concerning the special kingdom of the Messiah, and be confirmed concerning their most certain fulfillment. Just as it was accustomed to be done in other prophecies.

§. LXI. The event corresponds most exactly to the thirteenth oracle. For chronologists agree on this, that the desolation of Jerusalem occurred in the first year of the 212th Olympiad, that is, at the end of the 845th Olympic year. If, therefore, 490 years are counted backward, we shall arrive at the 355th Olympic year, or the third year of the 89th Olympiad, which is to be established as the terminus a quo of this epoch. That this is the second year of Darius Nothus, D. Behm teaches on p. 160. What the state of this time was in Persia and the Jewish Church is manifest from Haggai, Zechariah, Ezra, and Greek history. At the beginning of the 2nd year of the 87th Olympiad, the Peloponnesian War began, as was ἀποδεικτικῶς (demonstratively) confirmed in the preceding chapter: in the 7th year of that war, in winter, Artaxerxes Macrocheir died, according to Thucydides, book 4. Therefore, he died in the 4th year of the 88th Olympiad, with half of it elapsed. Artaxerxes Longimanus was succeeded by a certain Xerxes, who, having completed one year of his reign, or, as others write, two months, ended his life, according to Diodorus, book 12. But Diodorus inclines toward a one-year span based on other historians, with whom we also agree. Xerxes was succeeded by Sogdianus for seven months, as Diodorus has it in the aforementioned place, and likewise Sulpitius Severus, Ctesias, Eusebius in his Chronicle, and many others. Sogdianus having been killed, Darius Nothus came to the helm of the kingdom. He therefore began around spring, (as much as can be gathered from the prophecies of Zechariah and Haggai who connect the 6th and 11th Hebrew month with the 2nd year of Darius (Hag. 1, 1. Zachar. 1, 7.) when the first year of the 89th Olympiad had almost passed. Therefore, any year of Darius Nothus shares with two Olympiadic years, the first with the first and second, and the second with the second and third of the 89th Olympiad. But the third year of this Olympiad, according to our calculation, gives us the beginning of the weeks. Whence we firmly conclude that these weeks are to be started from the second year of Darius Nothus.

§. LXII. To these reasons is finally added the authority of certain Ancients, to which Scaliger also appeals. Neither do we alone, he says, deduce the beginning of the weeks from the second year of Darius Nothus, since many of the ancients order those weeks from the same head. We were not a little gladdened when we saw that the Ancients also felt the same as we do. It was previously observed that Sulpitius Severus orders the same from the 2nd year of Darius Nothus: Eusebius and Cyril of Jerusalem also order them from the times of Darius, even if they wish him to be the Darius of Hystaspes, whom Ezra c. 4, 24 commemorates. Blessed Luther also agrees, as to the beginning of the Weeks, as far as the matter itself is concerned, because he orders them from the edict of Darius, of which Ezra 4 speaks, even if he calls him Darius Longimanus, and terminates the Weeks in the seventh year after the resurrection of Christ in his preface to Daniel. Blessed Franzius Disp. 10. Sch. Sacrif. th. 75. has it thus: If only a uniform calculation of the years of the World and of Kings could be procured according to all Historians, no beginning of the LXX weeks would be more aptly assigned than that which Luther also makes, in the second year of Darius, to which the Prophet Haggai c. 1, 1 and Zach. 1, 11 also seems to look. For thus God himself would be established as both the author of the Babylonian Captivity and at the same time the first announcer of the departure from the Babylonian Captivity through the Prophets.

CHAPTER VI. A discussion of the opinions of Scaliger and his followers.

§. LXIII. Although Scaliger's opinion is indeed very specious, and is received with great applause by most illustrious men, it can by no means be reconciled with the divine Oracle and the words of the Angel, and other divinely inspired Scriptures. Therefore, we cannot add our calculation to it. For it is a matter of conscience for us to depart from the manifest meaning of the Holy Scriptures. Nor is it fitting to accept, for the sake of any man, however great, what applauds at first sight, without accurate investigation and comparison with other places of Scripture, which is everywhere consistent with itself. The beginning of the Babylonian captivity assigned by Scaliger, which he starts from the deportation of Jeconiah, has now made us more cautious. For however much nothing may seem more manifest from the very connection of St. Ezekiel c. 33, 20 and c. 40, 1, we have nevertheless demonstrated with irrefutable arguments in the Anti-Grotian annotations to Jer. 29 that the beginning of the 70 years of captivity is to be taken not from the deportation of Jeconiah, but from the fourth year of Jehoiakim. But what is to be held concerning the connection of Ezekiel, we have said at c. 41, which, if they are accurately considered, will easily allow no one to doubt that that Scaligerian opinion is to be rejected entirely, unless we wish to do violence to Holy Scripture and chronological truth. Although Scaliger, as is his wont, very confidently pronounces that those who deny that the words of Jeremiah are most clear for that opinion of taking the beginning from the captured Jeconiah wish to 'light a lamp at midday.' Similar is the illustrious man's boldness in these LXX weeks. There remains, he says in the Epilogism of the Weeks of Daniel, that last struggle and labor, as it seems to some, Herculean, as I judge it most light, to discover the head and beginning of the Weeks of Daniel. But whether this task was most light for the Great Man, and how successfully he has defined this arduous controversy, let the matter itself teach.

§. LXIV. But before all things it must be examined how he treated this heavenly oracle, concerning which he errs from the very threshold. For since the angel defined seventy weeks, and no one has ever doubted that the number was defined precisely, which the Hebrew expression also implies, Scaliger alone dared to increase that number, fearing nothing of that thunderbolt which the Lord threatened in Ap. 22, 15 against those adding anything to those things which are written in the book of prophecy. For thus he has it in the later edition of his work De Emend. temp. p. 606. The partition of the weeks according to Daniel is therefore half, one, seven, sixty-two. There are therefore 493 1/2 years. That half-week running beyond the sum of seventy escaped the most sharp-sighted vigilance of all, both ancients and moderns. But we rightly assert it, and restore it to its Author. These are his words: but who took it away, so that there is need of restitution, or how can that be taken away which is nowhere to be found? This is truly an unbearable audacity, to add three and a half years to an angelic, nay, divine computation! And shall we believe that ALL, both ancients and moderns, among whom there were certainly many far more sharp-sighted than Scaliger, could not see what he alone saw? But excessive self-confidence brings it about that all others are believed to be blind, or destitute of eyes. How could anyone, whether of the ancients or the moderns, see a half-week beyond seventy, where Holy Scripture precisely determined only LXX Weeks?

§. LXV. For although the Angel made mention of a half-week, he nevertheless indicated openly that it was not separated from that number, or different from that one week, but is contained in it, and included in the seventy, while he defined the whole time adequately by the space of LXX weeks. Nor did anyone ever doubt this, whether from the Jews or the Christians. After sixty-two weeks the Prophet adds seven and one, and the half of the week shall abolish the sacrifice. The half of the singular week, of which mention was just made, is to be understood here: the Angel also indicated this by the fact that he emphatically used the article ה, and the half of that week: since indeed all Interpreters [agree] that that recently named week is thus defined. Let those whom Scaliger rashly contradicts acknowledge it, denying the force of that article without any reason, and thus defining it by a dictatorial authority which is granted to no one treating of Holy Scripture. But with all respect to the most serious and learned men, this article does nothing, nor is it to be understood definitively (ὁριστικῶς) concerning the immediately preceding week, but indefinitely as half of one week. Clearly, in order to introduce his new and hitherto unheard-of half-week over and above the 70 weeks, he evacuates the customary force of the article acknowledged here by everyone. But he himself had once perceived it more correctly, when in the prior edition of his work he did not deny the force of the article, with this interpretation handed down, that Christ preached for half a week and for half the daily sacrifice was taken away. What then, I pray, is the cause now of that strange interpretation (ἐπιλύσεως), and of the addition made to the angelic 70 weeks? Because, forsooth, from the second year of Darius Nothus to the destruction of Jerusalem, 493 years are completed in number ed. But this is to twist Scripture to a preconceived amendment of the times, and not to amend the times from Scripture. Which no pious person will approve. And let this be the first proof of how the illustrious man handles the Angelic oracle!

§. LXVI. The mystical division of the Angel will provide a second. For since we are taught, even by the Rabbi Masters themselves, that not a single apex in the Scriptures is to be held as rash, Scaliger defines and openly declares that this distinction of weeks made with care by the Angel has nothing mystical in such an august and vigorous oracle, because he finds nothing in his ὑποθέσει that corresponds to it: This partition of weeks has no more secret a meaning than the division of a mina into 25, 20, 15 shekels in Ezech. chap. 45, 12, which sum to 60 shekels. But even there the division of the mina is not in vain, as our blessed Franzius shows in disp. 10, Schol. Sacrif. th. 16. For it is taught that a mina must consist of 60 shekels, the numbers of which are placed minutely for the reason that at that time many committed great fraud in the number of the shekel, some forcing 20 upon the poor for a mina, some 25, some scarcely 15. See Am. 8, 5. 6. And since Scaliger acknowledges that the LXXII weeks are not placed in vain, why does he assert of the others that their partition has nothing in reserve?

§. LXVII. Nor is it to be approved, thirdly, that the intervals of the weeks are torn apart by Scaliger, if indeed the words of the Angel require a continuation in them, and a whole number of LXX weeks, or 490 years, cannot be collected from years that are not continuous or are torn apart. Why then did Scaliger deny the continuation? Clearly this was done because he saw well that it did not suit his opinion, which is truly again to snatch the sacred text to his own view. The continuation, he says, of the intervals through this division of weeks cannot happen, it follows from this, because the division is also arbitrary, like the division of the mina in Ezekiel, and the intervals of the times are one thing in the history of the weeks, another in the division of the weeks. For in the weeks there is mention of the passion of Christ, likewise of the destruction of Jerusalem. Which interval is of 37 years only. But there is no mention here of 37 years, nor is the 37th year a septenary number, but it is a biennium above five weeks. Therefore, there is no reason to have regard for the partition, nor is there any continuation of intervals here. These are Scaliger's words: who truly rashly assumes that which can neither be demonstrated from the words of the Angel, and is by no means conceded to him by others, namely that the destruction of Jerusalem is comprehended within the scope of those weeks. Nor is he consistent with himself: since he himself collected all the numbers into a sum, in order to elicit 493. For that could not be done unless the continuation of the seven and sixty-two weeks, and also that one which he adds on, the half-week, had a place. For how will you collect scattered years into a sum so that they flow in order and follow one another, how will you have 490 years following one another in order, if 49 of them are not flowing in a continuous flow with the 62 Weeks or 432 years, if you admit both of those joined and continuously flowing with the remaining 7 years or the last week, but some of them outside the series of continuation or continuous flow, or continuous succession, I do not know to what times you would relegate them. Furthermore, what is clearer than that the time of the passion of Christ has been defined here by the Angel: After sixty-two weeks the Messiah shall be killed. Nor could Scaliger deny that, but since the illustrious man was stuck here, and did not think that these years should be connected with the seven preceding, against the open opinion of the Angel (because he himself collected the years into a sum), he felt it necessary to confess concerning these seven weeks that he did not know to what they point in a special commemoration, and indeed he did not even find that which he invented about the half-week, to what he should refer it. For they who fix the end of the weeks at the destruction of Jerusalem have no mystery of that half-week, named separately, to bring forward. It is helpful to hear Scaliger himself. The year, he says, of the passion in the Julian period is 4746. From which, if 434 years are unraveled, which are sixty-two weeks, one will arrive at the year 4313 of the Julian period, which is the fifth year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, who gave the third rescript after Cyrus to the Satraps of Syria concerning the restoring of Jerusalem and the expenses to be paid for the sacrifices of the temple. Wherefore, without any doubt, Artaxerxes Mnemon gave that rescript in the 5th year of his reign, from which time until the end of the sixth year Ezra proclaimed the departure to his countrymen: Thus, for all the preparation of the journey, for collecting the vessels, for calling out the Jews from everywhere, there was need of at least two years. To what the seven remaining weeks pertain, neither Daniel defined, nor do I know; but that these intervals are interrupted, and not continuous, we have both demonstrated above, and the thing itself speaks. From the year 4290 of the Julian period to the year 4313, that is, from the Edict of Darius Nothus to the Rescript of Artaxerxes Mnemon, there are 23 years, which are far smaller than seven weeks, and they themselves are not septenary. I do not doubt that they are 49 vacant, that is, they do not have an epoch to which they are referred. But that week, in which he will confirm the covenant, can be taken in two ways. Either as a whole, or divided, not indeed in time, but in cause. A whole after the passion; divided, half before, the other half after the passion. But what acts or deeds should be attributed to that time, let the more learned see. These are his words. But truly, is it not inconvenient that the end and the term to which is assigned by the Angel to the LXII weeks, namely in the passion of Christ, but the term from which is not expressed? Which Scaliger calls the fifth year of Artaxerxes Mnemon: but where is any trace of it here, if indeed according to Scaliger, the beginning of Daniel's Epoch is fixed here not in the times of Artaxerxes Mnemon, but of Darius Nothus, nor is any other designation of the term from which found here? Is it not inconvenient that in the prophecy of the Angel the 49 years are entirely vacant, that is, have no Epoch to which they may be referred? If the 62 weeks are not vacant, but have an Epoch here, why must it be said of the 7 weeks that they are vacant, and have been distributed by the Angel in vain?
