Fourthly, the beginning of the 70 weeks is not correctly fixed at the going forth of the Royal edict concerning the building of the temple. For the angel defines the beginning otherwise, and designates the going forth of the word not concerning the building of the temple, but concerning the restoration of Jerusalem, as the words of the oracle most clearly hold. And therefore it is manifest that those who begin the Epoch from the edict concerning the structure of the temple are hallucinating, and openly depart from the words of the Angel. By no means, however, is it permitted to us to fix the beginning at will, but it is necessary to assume the one defined by the heavenly messenger, and to seek no other. Rightly here our blessed Pappus: The edicts of Cyrus and Darius Hystaspes are refuted from the beginning of the Weeks by this argument, that they speak not of the restoration of the city, but only of the temple. Therefore, even though the second year of Darius is joined with the beginning of Zechariah and Haggai; yet, because, as can be seen in Ezra 5 and 6, it treats only of the temple, not of the restoring of the city, therefore it is snatched away from those who refer the beginning of the word to this point, even against their will.

Although they themselves have that by which they hope they can defend themselves somewhat: since not only do the Satraps beyond the Euphrates openly accuse the Jews, because they are not restoring the temple, but because they are building the city, finishing the walls, and joining the very foundations, but also because, on account of the intermission of the restoration of the temple and the care for private houses in the second year of Darius, the Jews are most gravely rebuked by the Prophets Zechariah and Haggai, from which it is certainly concluded that even then the city itself had also begun to be restored. But although it is sufficiently proven by those testimonies that the city and private houses had also begun to be restored at that time; yet the outcome of the word, by which such a restoration had been permitted or commanded, does not yet appear. For the exhortations of Haggai and Zechariah urge the restoration of the temple, not of the city or the Polity. This is D. Pappus.

§. LXVIII.

Fifth, the sixty-two and seven weeks, i.e., sixty-nine, are openly terminated in the Messiah the Leader, verse 25. And you shall know and understand from the going forth of the word to cause to return, and to the building of Jerusalem עַד־מָשִׁיחַ until the Messiah the Leader, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, the street shall return and be built, and the wall, and in the distress of times. And after the sixty-two weeks the Messiah shall be cut off. What could have been said more clearly, so that it might be signified that LXIX weeks are to be numbered until the Messiah? They twist themselves greatly, or to speak more correctly, they twist the Scripture, who stand on the side of Scaliger. Grotius retreats to the particle עַד, because it, both here and elsewhere, does not signify the final limit, but something contained within the limit, as if he were saying, including also the visible life of Christ, who was constituted by God as Prince of His people forever. But such an explanation of the Hebrew עַד has no place where, as happens here, the limit of time is defined ἀποτόμως (abruptly/precisely); therefore others quibble over the word מָשִׁיחַ, that by the anointed one in this place is understood not Christ, who is called so ἐξοχικῶς (by way of eminence), and in v. 26, where there is talk of the excision of Christ, is called by this name, but the Roman Emperor, so that just as Cyrus is called the anointed of the Lord, who was destined to execute the judgments of God against the Babylonians: So Vespasian might also be called the anointed of the Lord, ordained for judgments against the perfidious and wickedly evil and obstinate Jewish nation. But it is absurd that Vespasian the destroyer should be introduced here as if ἀπὸ μηχανῆς (from a machine), before any promise had been made of the advent of the Messiah, about whom Daniel was primarily concerned: Nor can the name of Messiah, placed absolutely, be snatched away to Vespasian, especially where no necessity compels one to accept it otherwise than in the famous sense. What of the fact that the angel immediately explains himself, which Messiah he points out, namely the one whom he predicts is to be cut off, or about whose passion he prophesies here. If anyone says that in the following verse it is also explained who the Messiah נָגִיד (Leader) is, where mention is made of the people of the נָגִיד הַבָּא (Leader TO COME), who was about to destroy the city: that the Messiah Christ Jesus is distinguished from the Messiah נָגִיד, because the latter is said to be coming after the LXII and VII weeks, but the former is to be cut off within those weeks. Resp. That that coming Leader is openly distinguished from the Messiah the Leader, who is the primary subject of this prophecy. For that COMING LEADER is not called Messiah, nor is he ever called so: But our Christ, about whose passion the Angel prophesies, is openly called Messiah. Furthermore, our Christ is not said to be cut off within these defined weeks, but the time of the death or excision of Christ is expressed ἀποτόμως & ἀκριβῶς (abruptly and accurately). But concerning the coming Leader χρονικῶς or χρονολογικῶς (chronologically)

nothing is defined, nor is the time of his advent determined, which certainly did nothing for the consolation of the elect and the βεβαίωσιν (confirmation) of faith concerning the Messiah. Furthermore, lest anyone object that thus the same limit will be for the advent of our Messiah and his passion, the Angel accurately distinguishes them. For he precisely counts seven and sixty-two weeks until the advent of the Messiah, i.e., to the doctoral office, by which he wished to show himself as Leader and teacher to his people. But he says that his excision or passion and death will be after the sixty-two (and seven) weeks, i.e., when those have already been completed, in the middle of the last week, as he declares himself afterwards.

§. LXIX. Whence the Calvinists adhering to Scaliger, since they see clearly that no one else can be understood here by the Messiah the Leader than our Christ, in order that they may be able to φυλάττειν (preserve) their thesis, they wish Christ to be viewed here as the judge of the people: Thus Tremellius and Junius in their notes on this passage: until Christ the predecessor, that is, until that time when Christ will demonstrate himself as Lord by a most severe judgment upon his city and people, and by the benefit of the Gospel as Prince and head of the Church, who reigns in the house of David forever. Similarly Polanus on this passage: until the Messiah the predecessor, that is, for so long until the Messiah the leader of this people is to come, and by an evident, public, and manifest sign will make the rejection attested. Which B. D. Bebm. also followed in Manuduct. Chronol. p. 168. We respond that the phrase of Daniel (until the Messiah) is general, and that we understand nothing from this in isolation, whether the Angel is speaking in those words of his advent into the flesh, or of his death, or of some singular and punitive advent. We understand the punitive advent of Christ upon the city of Jerusalem. For when God wishes to punish some place, then Scripture attributes an advent to God ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (in a human manner). But this interpretation deserves no consideration. For it is, first, merely precarious, and supported by no reason. Then, when the time of the Messiah is defined, to whom can it come into mind, unless he is driven to it by a preconceived opinion, to believe that a particular divine judgment is being designated? For prophetic Scripture does not like to speak in such a way. Third, it is not taught here simply that the Messiah will come, but a certain interval of time is established, UNTIL THE MESSIAH THE LEADER, with no determination added. By what right, therefore, is this advent determined to a particular judgment? Fourthly, since the time decided and indicated according to these authors has already been pointed out up to the destruction, will it not be περισσολογία [redundancy] to define it again here? For whether the interval of time is defined up to the devastation of the city, or up to the advent of the Leader who is to devastate the city, the same thing will be said, which in such a vigorous and succinct oracle is not to be admitted. Fifthly, indeed, there will thus be an ἀντιλογία [contradiction] in the words of the Angel, while he now said that seventy weeks were defined up to the destruction of the city, as those authors wish, but now says that sixty-nine weeks are up to the judgment of extermination. That these things are ἀσύστατα [inconsistent], everyone sees. Sixthly, it was inconvenient for the time to be commemorated up to the particular judgment of Christ demonstrating Himself as Judge and Lord from heaven, before the destruction and passion of Christ are commemorated, which exaltation finally followed: indeed, seventhly, it will again be ἀντιφατικὸν [contradictory] for Christ to be said to be cut off after the sixty-second (that is, including the seven prior, finally the sixty-ninth week), and for only LXII and VII weeks to be numbered up to the judgment of Christ already exalted at the right hand of God. For did He, after He came as Judge to destroy Jerusalem, finally get cut off Himself?

§. LXX. §. LXX. Fifthly, the time of Christ's passion is determined here, not generally and confusedly, that Christ is to be cut off within the space of these weeks; but ὀριστικῶς (definitively) and accurately, since the Angel openly says in v. 26 that after sixty-two weeks (not neglecting the seven previously named) the Messiah is to be cut off. If those times are not taken as joined, but the LXII weeks are to be understood separately, which Scaliger wants, how can Christ be said to be cut off after LXII weeks or 434 years, taking the beginning of the numbering from the 2nd year of Darius Nothus? For from that time until the year of the passion, not only LXII weeks have elapsed, but LXV. What, therefore, was the reason why the angel, in designating the time of Christ's passion, named seventy-two weeks rather than LXV, or if it be said to us precisely that he intended to refer to that time, only wishing to indicate the future passion before the destruction of Jerusalem, why did he not use the round number of LX weeks instead? Whence Calixtus despairs here in his Dissert. de LXX. Septim. of a solution in the angelic partition of time, and a sufficient answer as to which events and deeds this Epoch and particle of time correspond. Without ambiguity I say that all those who labor to accommodate these intervals of time also to histories and deeds are wasting their effort. From wherever, therefore, you take the beginning, the calculation will fall into those years which have contributed nothing significant to history. And so that it may become manifest that it CANNOT be accommodated, I order only that what is said by the Angel be considered: From the going forth of the word unto Christ the Leader are VII and LXII weeks, that is LXIX. But immediately: And after LXII weeks Christ shall be cut off. Up to Christ are LXIX weeks, and Christ shall be cut off after LXII weeks. If you wish to apply this to history, it is such an ἄπορον (impasse) that it can be explained by no genius, however great. Thus Calixtus. Because, namely, according to his own opinion, he could make no application: although he also incorrectly separates the LXII weeks, after which Christ was to be cut off, from the VII weeks, which together with them make LXIX. He had need to acknowledge and confess that his own opinion, by which the terminus is established at the destruction of Jerusalem, carries such ἄπορα (impasses) with it. Therefore he does not deny here that the Angelic partition is in vain for Scaliger: thinking that an integral number is divided into arbitrary parts, from which, when joined, it is again integrated, which he thinks is done in the scriptures so that the numbers are understood to be true and customary numbers, not ἀναγωλικοὶ (anagogical) or μυςηριώδεις (mysterious). Which reasoning is inept and unworthy of such a Critic. Furthermore, the Scaligerians here also retreat to the Hebrew idiom, who fix the end of the weeks at the destruction, namely that the words of the Angel are to be taken thus: And after sixty-two weeks, Christ having been cut off, the people of the coming leader will dissipate the city or the sanctuary. For Hebrews are accustomed to use two copulative constructions, when among the Latins ablatives of consequence are employed. Thus Junius, Tremellius, Polanus, Behmius, Calvisius, and others explain it. But this Zeugmatic construction, as Polanus calls it, first, neither the scope of the Angel bears, nor does the Athnach accent allow, which regularly makes a colon, and separates the words after LXII WEEKS from the word ישחית, and thus they testify that a distinct enunciation is completed by this former member. Furthermore, secondly, the interposition of the Vav copula and the distinct designation of subject and predicate openly prove that different propositions are contained there: And after LXII weeks Christ shall be cut off. This is the first proposition, whose subject is Christ. And the people of the COMING LEADER shall dissipate the city and the sanctuary; which is the other proposition, whose subject is other and different; namely, the people of the coming Leader. Therefore the prior proposition is absolute because of the interposed Vav, and is in itself integral and separate.

§. LXXI. Furthermore, thirdly, since the Messiah is the principal subject of the whole text, it does not appear how it is to be admitted that his mention was made παρεμβλαδικῶς (parenthetically) and incidentally, and as if only in a parenthesis in the particular exposition. Wherefore others, when they see that the designation of the time of the ςαυρώσεως (crucifixion) cannot be denied, pretend that God extended that interval from the passion of Christ until the desolation, which they think is circumscribed here by the space of one week, as a παρεμβολημα (intercalation) or to 35 years. But by this method any divine prophecies in which certain times are defined can be rendered uncertain with the same ease. Some dare to define this one week by a period of 4 years, so that it does not consist of seven years like the rest. Oecolampadius also agrees with them: who indeed introduced a clearly singular opinion about these weeks, and in our judgment the most absurd of all others. But who will bear a new meaning of the word WEEK being devised here, where it is too manifest that all weeks are in the same condition.

§. LXXII. Fourthly, if the angelic designation of the term refers to the Messiah being cut off, that one and final week will most correctly be referred to the confirming of the Evangelical covenant of Christ, which he not only confirmed himself by miracles to the Jews, to whom he was especially sent, but also intended to gather the Church through the Apostles after his ascension into heaven, primarily in Judea, but all things were in vain because of the stupendous and incredible blindness of this people, whence a final πανωλεθρία (total destruction) is predicted for them at the same time.

§. LXXIII. Fifth, the half of the week will correspond especially well, as being defined for the cessation of sacrifices. Some refer both this member concerning one week, and concerning the half of this week, to the seven-year period after the resurrection of Christ, because for a full seven-year period the evangelical covenant was still confirmed to the Jews, in which many were converted to faith in Christ, and because in the half of that week the sacrifice failed; since the Levitical sacrifices and ceremonies did not cease immediately from the resurrection of Christ, but the Jewish Synagogue had to be buried with honor first, lest the weaker in faith be offended, and the curable Jews be deterred from the Gospel of Christ. Whence only in the fourth year from the resurrection of Christ did the sacrifices begin to cease, and thus the Levitical shadows were not abrogated immediately, but gradually. Thus Lucas Osiander in his paraphrase & B. Luther, if you look at his δευτέρας φροντίδας, as is evident from his preface to Daniel. Others, however, according to the former opinion of B. Luther, divide the last week in such a way that they attribute its first half to the proclamation of Christ up to the passion, which lasted for 3½ years, and they wish him to be called נגיר, because as an authentic Teacher he instructed the people, and refuted their false dogmas and impiety, as was fitting; but they begin the other half from the passion and resurrection of Christ; in which way the Messiah or Christ will be considered to have strengthened the covenant among the Jews throughout the week, because in the one half he did it αὐτοπροσώπως, and immediately by teaching, and by confirming his doctrine with miracles: but in the other half mediately and through the Apostles; Whence not a few say that the cessation of the sacrifice occurred in the first half of the week, through the passion and death of Christ, which brought an end to the sacrifices, and the other Levitical shadows, as being those which, upon the appearing of the body had to disappear, because having obtained their completion they had no place, which even the tearing of the veil in the temple testified; and they understand by the cessation of sacrifices, not a total ending, as far as the external work is concerned, for thus they lasted after the death of Christ, but as far as a definite time and a legitimate manner of acting is concerned, as also the use by which they prefigured the future sacrifice of Christ. They also urge that by the copula this abrogation is attributed no less to the Messiah himself than the confirmation of the covenant: and that it is by no means certain that Vespasian, a full three years before the destruction, abolished the rites of the sacrifices. Since indeed the Jews, as Josephus testifies in the Jewish War, were still sacrificing at the Passover of the last year. That is immovable, says Franzius, Disput. 10. Schol. Sacrif. th. 57, that Christ must be cut off at the end of the sixty-ninth week, and at the beginning of the seventieth. For the text of Daniel says expressly, until Christ the leader seven weeks, sixty-two weeks. And these weeks together make sixty-nine weeks. Then he repeats: after the sixty-two weeks Christ shall be cut off, namely, because those things which are expressed before this AFTER must happen when the former weeks are singularly separated from the sixty-two weeks, namely HE SHALL RETURN, the street and the wall shall be rebuilt in the distress of times. This exposition must necessarily be admitted, otherwise the opinion which would emerge from comparing both would be most absurd, or contradictory to itself, in this manner: Until Christ the Leader seven weeks, sixty-two weeks. But after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be cut off. The hearer would be left uncertain whether he ought to embrace the former or the latter proposition. From the going forth therefore of the word unto Christ the leader, or the exalted one, there are intervals of sixty-nine weeks, and indeed of seven weeks for the streets to be rebuilt and the walls to be repaired. But after the sixty-two weeks elapsed from the end of the preceding seven weeks, Christ shall be cut off (but also at the same time he shall be exalted), namely, precisely at the beginning of the last week, which contains seven years. Therefore, the Messiah will not be killed at the end of all the last seven years, but at the beginning of the last seven years, and at the same time he will be exalted. For Luther teaches beautifully and truly that Christ is not called Leader by the Angel until after his full exaltation has followed.

§. LXXIV. Sixth, the LXX weeks will be said most conveniently to be defined thus for finishing the transgression, and sealing up sins, and for atoning for iniquity and bringing in everlasting righteousness, since all these things were done through the passion of Christ, and for anointing the holy of holies, who was fully constituted Christ through his exaltation. Seventh, it will also fit conveniently that it is said that the LXX weeks are determined upon the people of Daniel, and upon his holy city; because the people were holy until that time, until the kingdom of God was transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles.

§. LXXV. Eighth, the principal scope of the angelic prophecy, which most people place here, will thus be obtained, that a definite term was set for the passion and death of Christ, whereas if the opinion of others stands, that this term is fixed on the destruction of Jerusalem, no definite time would be left for the passion and death of Christ. Whence our people, following the ancient Doctors, especially defend this opinion concerning the term of the passion of Christ: Blessed Luther, Gesner, Osiander, Franzius, Weber; likewise Funccius with his followers; although, as was observed before, they do not agree on the exact definition of the term of these weeks; since some wish them to end precisely in the passion and death of the same, with Blessed Gesner: Others, with Blessed Luther, refer the passion of Christ to the end of the sixty-ninth week: and conclude the last, or seventieth, week in the seven years from the resurrection of Christ, as Franzius.

§. LXXVI. Ninth, it does not appear what that one week concerning the strengthening of the covenant means, or what that half of the week concerning the cessation of the sacrifice implies, if the term to which of this Epoch is the destruction of the city. The followers of Scaliger do not find here what to say. For that Junius in his lectures on Daniel, and with Tremellius in the notes to this place, as also Polanus, refer this confirmation of the covenant to the oracle by which Christ could migrate from the city at the impending destruction, as Josephus, Egesippus, and Eusebius testify, that is too insipid, nor was it done for an entire week, that is, for seven years, or at least for half a week. And what does that voice of Jesus son of Ananias, 'let us depart hence,' have to do with the confirmation of the covenant? Grotius therefore, with the felicity he had, devised a new opinion concerning the one week, not referring it with the other Interpreters to the Evangelical covenant strengthened by Christ, but to the covenant of the Jews, when he interprets the beginning of the last week of years thus: he will draw many into the covenant of the Jews, and 20,000 Idumaeans, coming to their aid, will give hope of a successful war, but I fear whether this interpretation will easily prove itself to anyone. That is truly just as ridiculous as that invention of the Jews, who interpret the strengthening of the covenant as the truce between the Romans and the Jews, which they pretend was made after the war. For the discourse is not about the beginning of the last week of years, but about an entire week: nor is the week said to be about to draw into a covenant, nor is there anything here about a military covenant, but he is said to be about to confirm the covenant for one week, he of whom, as the principal subject, it is treated here, i.e., the Messiah. How this corresponds to the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, I do not find explained. Concerning that intermediate week, however, D. Behmius says: We interpret the words of Daniel plainly according to the letter, 'in the middle of the week' (the last one, that is) 'he shall abolish the sacrifice and the offering,' that is, sacrifices will cease as the devastation of the city encroaches. For thus Daniel explains this phrase in ch. 11, v. 31, and ch. 12, v. 11. That it is to be taken literally is testified by the first book of Maccabees, 1. 7, c. 4, 54. For there should be no doubt for us that one, or two, or even three years before the plenary desolation of the city and temple, sacrifices had ceased amidst such internal dissensions and external wars by which Jerusalem was oppressed. But the issue here is not the necessity of the cessation of sacrifices, which the calamity of war imposes and which enemies were about to impose, but rather the abolition of sacrifices, which he is to perform who was to confirm the covenant for half a week. Who is the πρῶτον δεκτικὸν, or the primary subject in this oracle. It is not about the abolition of violence and coercion, but the abolition of the completion and exhibition of that which was prefigured by those rash and shadowy sacrifices, through which sins were to be expiated, eternal righteousness brought back, and prophecies sealed and fulfilled, as the Angel teaches. And from where are we made certain that no Jew at all offered any sacrifice for three years before the desolation of the city, which are said to be entirely gratuitous and are in no way likely. Finally, the discussion is about the abolition not of the act, but of the right, as being about to happen by the Messiah, and connected with the corroboration of the Evangelical covenant and the cutting off of the Messiah; and therefore better interpreters understand it as the abolition made through the death of Christ as the true sacrifice.

§. LXXVII.

§. LXXVII. Tenth, if we say that the Epoch of the destruction of the city, along with others, was intended to designate the Epoch of the passion of Christ—an opinion which has great and weighty authors—most things in the archangel's prophecy will be more straightforward. For thus, first, the simplest sense will emerge, which the words themselves bear in verse 29: that there are sixty-seven weeks until the Messiah the Prince, who, through the proclamation of the Gospel, was made Leader of the people, and indeed through his death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven and session at the right hand of God, was fully made Prince, and had presented himself to that end, and had also been inaugurated from heaven, at that limit of sixty-seven or sixty-nine weeks. Nor, secondly, will the sense be any less clear in the following words of verse 26, 'after sixty-two (and the seven preceding) weeks the Messiah shall be cut off,' and the literal meaning will be able to be preserved. For thus, if the final week, which is specifically commemorated, is joined to the middle, a fixed limit will be expressed for the passion and death of Christ. And because this was the primary cause of the destruction of the city—that they killed the promised Messiah—therefore, thirdly, it is most correctly subjoined, not as something connected immediately by reason of time, but because it coheres by reason of causality, and the destruction of the city and the people, which they brought upon themselves by their own anathemas at the passion of Christ—'his blood be upon us and upon our children!'—will certainly and shortly follow the cutting off of Christ.

§. LXXVIII. Eleventh, the first falsehood of Scaliger's opinion regarding the term to which the 70 weeks belong is that persuasion that by Darius in Ezra 4:24 one must understand Darius Nothus, from whose second year 70 weeks, or rather, as he himself counts, seventy and a half, have flowed until the total destruction of the people. We shall show later that this persuasion rests on no foundation, and indeed that it is false. Wherefore, this hypothesis collapsing, Scaliger's opinion regarding the term to which this Epoch belongs collapses entirely. For if it is Darius Hystaspis whose second year is celebrated in Ezra, and if the beginning or the term from which this Epoch is established is in that same second year of his reign, how can its end be established in the Jerusalemite total destruction?

§. LXXIX. Finally, in Scaliger's opinion, it is not without reason that it is desired that it should agree neither with the angel's oracle nor with the Evangelical history in assigning the Passovers of Christ. Since five Passovers of Christ have been counted by him. But there is no reason for us to discuss this hypothesis in this place: for there will be another occasion to deal with it, God willing. And therefore we leave him alone with his own disciples and followers, who here desert their teacher.

§. LXXX. And so much for the opinion of Scaliger. For the reasons brought forward for it will be more correctly discussed when we have brought the remaining opinions into the middle and have asserted the truer one with more solid arguments. For the straight is the index of itself and of the crooked. Moreover, the blessed Helvicus reports yet another opinion of a certain Scaligerian author anonymously, in his vindication of passages from the Scriptures of the Old Testament, p. 332, who also begins the seven weeks for building the walls and the 62 until Christ and the entire 70 weeks from the same beginning, namely the second year of Darius Nothus, and refers the end of the 62 weeks to the 12th year of the Christian era, in which Christ as a 12-year-old boy stood present in the temple. But he confesses that this opinion is urged by the firmest arguments: nor does it appear how it agrees either with the text of Daniel or with the chronology. It certainly does not need a laborious refutation; yet let it complete the number, and let it be the 20th opinion.

It agrees, in some part, as far as the same beginning of the 7 and 62 weeks is concerned, with the twelfth opinion, which we discussed above.

CHAPTER VII. Concerning those who refer the beginning of the Epoch to the times of Artaxerxes.

§. LXXXI. After we have shown that the beginning of the mystical Epoch is to be referred neither to the times nor to the edicts of Cyrus or Darius, there now remain the opinions of those who reduce it to the times and edicts of Artaxerxes. In reviewing these, through the removal of those things which do not agree with our oracle, we proceed to the position of the true opinion, which agrees with this oracle. They are again of various orders. First occur those who reduce this Epoch to the 32nd year of Artaxerxes. Which is therefore the twenty-first opinion in this our enumeration, which the Jesuit Suarez brings forward in part 3, disp. 1, sect. 2, which Tirinus notes is not entirely disapproved of even by him, but it enjoys no probable appearance of truth, and seems unworthy of refutation; since neither did any edict of any celebrity go forth at that time which agrees with this oracle, nor does the term to which it belongs agree in any way.

§. LXXXII. Next, the opinion of Jac. Tirinus in his Sacred Chronicles, chapter 38, must also be rejected here, which is the twenty-second in order here, making the beginning from the 23rd year of Artaxerxes, as he himself says, from the city clearly built and restored, when Nehemiah celebrated the dedication of the new or restored city, Nehemiah 12:42. To have commemorated it is to have refuted it. For neither does that rest on any foundation. Tirinus distorts, in a new and unheard-of way, the Word of Gabriel, FROM THE GOING FORTH OF THE WORD, that it may be built again, in order to extort this sense. Understanding by THE END of the word, not the end of the word by which it is promised, commanded, or permitted that the city be built again, but by which it is in fact built again, not only inchoatively, but completely, so that the word is taken for the thing. But who would bear such a gloss, from the going forth of the word that it may be built, that is, from the end of the thing, or of the city: likewise that it may be built, this is, from the completed building! This depravation is also unworthy, that it should be laboriously refuted. I pass over the errors of calculation, which chronologists may discuss. Certainly, it cannot be solidly taught from the book of Nehemiah that the city was fully built and entirely restored in the 23rd year of the reign of Longimanus; whence Tirinus called into aid the apocryphal writing Ecclesiasticus 49:15 and the fictitious miracle in 2 Maccabees 1:33.

§. LXXXIII. Moreover, Tirinus does not depart much from the definition of the true limit when he declares his opinion, even though he clearly errs, as we have seen, in explaining the oracle of Daniel. For he wishes the 23rd year of Artaxerxes, from which he began to rule together with Xerxes for the first time, to be the eighth year from the death of Xerxes, from which he ruled alone. Whence he adds on page 44: And Ezra 1, 1. c. 7, 8 would strongly favor them, where he says that he returned to Jerusalem from Persia in the 7th year of Artaxerxes, if it were certain that that Artaxerxes was our μακρόχειρα or Longimanus. For we would then readily concede that that seventh year was his year of reigning alone from the death of Xerxes. Therefore, Tirinus proposed his conclusion thus on page 45: The 23rd year, from which Artaxerxes μακρόχειρ began to rule together with Xerxes for the first time, or the 8th year from which he ruled alone, or the 28th from the beginning of the reign of Xerxes, coincides with the 4th year of the 80th Olympiad and the 297th of the city of Rome. And from the 7th month, Tisri, of this year is taken the beginning of the 70 weeks of Daniel. This (conclusion) is that of the authors cited for the 7th opinion, and furthermore of Basil of Seleucia: and Chrysostom favors it:

And regarding the matter, most others hold this, at least those who fix the Baptism of Christ with St. Luke in the 15th year of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ was proclaimed by the heavenly Father as leader and teacher of the people, and the 69th week of Daniel, that is, 483 years, came to an end. For the 15th year of Tiberius concurs with the 3rd year of the 201st Olympiad and the 780th of the city. Now perform the calculations and you will find the intervening 483 years from the 8th year of Artaxerxes alone to the 15th of Tiberius. What is to be thought of these things will be clear from those things which are to be said next. Cornelius à Lapide himself refutes this opinion in his Commentary on this passage, because it may indeed be cleverly invented, but it is not free from difficulty, and it seems that the words 'from the going forth of the word' are somewhat twisted.

§. LXXXIV. Twenty-third, Funccius in his Chronology starts this epoch from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus (whom he calls Darius Longimanus), but he places the end of the weeks of Daniel at the passion of Christ. In which opinion Funccius is entirely pleased with himself in his Commentary, book 1, on Chronology, having begun his Dissertation on the 70 weeks of Daniel thus: If ever a certain calculation of these weeks had existed, whatever I have spent of both labor and vigils on my entire Chronology would be superfluous. But since, as far as I know, none has yet been found which would agree exactly with the words of the Angel, and would rest on probable reasons founded in the New and Old Testament, it was not so much useful as it was necessary to have devoted very much effort to investigating the truth of this matter. Funccius was followed by others, even among our own, especially B. Gesner in his Commentary on Daniel, as well as Henric. Bunting. in his Chronology and in his Itinerarium Sacrum, p. 692. Funccius explains the text thus: That seventy weeks were precisely defined by God, but that when this space of weeks was finished, it would come to pass that the transgression of the law of God would be taken away, sins would be covered, and iniquity would be expiated, and that immediately the righteousness of the ages would succeed, that visions and prophecies would be fulfilled (these, namely, which are about Christ the Lord), and the most holy, who is Christ the Son of God anointed with the oil of gladness, Ps. 45, would be anointed. But transgression or prevarication could not be taken away except through the innocence and satisfaction of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor could sins be covered or iniquity expiated except through the death and shedding of his own blood, as both Testaments demonstrate most copiously. So also neither could the righteousness of the ages be brought back, nor could visions and prophecies be fulfilled, unless the Lord were resurrected, who was delivered up for our sins and raised for our righteousness, Rom. 4. For the Prophets also predicted his resurrection, etc. Wherefore, since these things had to happen immediately after the 70 weeks (as the word נחתך, which is 'is precisely determined,' compels), it is necessary that the weeks themselves came to an end at the time when Christ undertook to satisfy for our sins by his death. When the 62 weeks were finished, יכרות the Messiah (i.e., AFFIXED) will be cut off, to whom neither the city nor the sanctuary (will belong). Which explanation of the words וְאֵין לוֹ, that neither the city nor the sanctuary any longer belong to him, he professes to have received from Erasmus Aichler: concerning the true sense of which words it has been treated elsewhere. But he will confirm the covenant with many for one week; in the middle of the week he will CAUSE TO CEASE the oblation and the sacrifice. Which indeed he thinks was done not so much by the death of Christ as by his baptism.

§. LXXXV. But in the opinion of Funccius these things are deservedly missed: first, that he establishes the year of the passion as the limit of these seventy weeks. For Funccius takes this for himself as undoubted without proof: namely, that the Angel said that Christ would only then suffer and rise again when all these weeks were precisely finished. If the Angel means this, why then does he say, after sixty-two (and seven) weeks Christ will be cut off? Should he not have thus included that last week as well? Then, that definition of time up to Christ the Leader will be in vain if Christ the Leader did not appear openly at that limit, but only later in the middle of the week, having been divinely proclaimed by a public voice from heaven? Third, Funccius does not find how he could assign an entire week to the confirmation of the covenant made by Christ before his death. He acknowledges that the covenant was confirmed by Christ inaugurated in Baptism for only half a week: yet, so that he does not say nothing about the other half, which he counts backward, he says that through it Christ excited a great desire for himself among the pious, and then indeed that Christ, at the time when he entered his manly age, say the twenty-seventh year, could have confirmed the Testament with his blameless life to those who knew they could not be saved by the law but had need of a Messiah. But if the seventieth week is to be begun from when he entered his manly age and could confirm the Testament to the pious desiring the Messiah with his blameless life, why is the beginning not taken from the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth year of his age, and what is the certainty of this definition? It is manifest that these things are too arbitrary and do not even agree with the accurate definition of the Angel. Fourth, that cessation of oblations and sacrifices does not agree with the Baptism of Christ. For how did he cause the oblation and sacrifice to cease through baptism? Funccius says: That Christ on that day, which fell in the middle of the week, namely in the one hundred and seventy-ninth year, the fourth of the seventieth week, entered the holy of holies and began to perform the office of priest, when he took upon himself baptism and in it all the sins of the whole world to be washed away, and afterwards to be expiated by his blood. But if the middle of the week falls on that day of the great expiation and the entry of the high priest into the holy of holies, anyone can see that it is not the baptism of Christ, but his passion and death, through which he entered the holy of holies as the true High Priest, when the veil of the temple was torn, that corresponds to it. Which is certain from Heb. 9.

§. LXXXVI. Therefore others, although they may embrace the beginning of the weeks according to Funccius's opinion, nevertheless do not place their end in the passion of Christ, but after his passion and death. They attribute the first half of the week to the covenant confirmed by Christ from the Baptism up to the passion and death of Christ, and they place the other half of the week after the cutting off of Christ. And this is the twenty-fourth opinion concerning the weeks of Daniel. Which Cornelius à Lapide embraces at this place, p. 1362. I say that it seems certain from the latter, that these 70 weeks must be begun from this 7th year of Artaxerxes, for if you begin from elsewhere, you will not complete the number of 490 common or solar years, as all agree. Therefore, since this 7th year of Artaxerxes concurs with the 4th year of the 70th Olympiad and with the 297th year of the city founded, but the baptism of Christ fell in the 15th year of Tiberius, which year concurs with the 4th year of the 201st Olympiad. and with the 781st year of the city, from this it follows that from this 7th year of Artaxerxes up to Christ the Leader, that is, up to this time of the baptism of Christ, in which Christ was constituted and declared the Leader of the people of God, or the guide and teacher of the Church (God the Father saying: This is my beloved Son, hear him), 69 weeks had flowed, that is, 483 years; then in the middle, as the angel says, of the seventieth and last week, that is, in the 487th year, which was

18. [In the reign] of Tiberius Caesar, Christ was killed, and three years after the death of Christ the 70 weeks, that is, 490 years, are finished. For this is truer than that which Africanus, Rupertus, and Beda think: namely, that the 70 weeks are finished precisely in the very year of the passion of Christ. For thus Gabriel ought to have said: At the end (not in the middle) of the week, Christ being killed, the oblation and sacrifice shall fail. Cornelius à Lapide praises for his opinion Cedrenus, Fuuccius, Bucholzer, Angelocrator, Helvicus, Capellus, to whom Tirinus also attributes that opinion: but that they do not agree in all things regarding the term of the Epoch is evident. Helvicus also disagrees in the beginning of the Epoch, which he places in the 2nd year of Darius; nor does he make Artaxerxes, of whom Ezra ch. 7 speaks, μακρόχειρα, but ἢ μνήμονα.

§. LXXXVII. Most recently, above others, Philippus Lansbergius has excellently constructed this opinion in Chronol. Sacr. lib. 2. cap. 11. First, how the Angel generally encompassed all the benefits which Christ performed in the last week, v. 24. For in the beginning of the seventieth week, that holy of holies Jesus Christ was anointed by the Holy Spirit as the Redeemer of his people. But in the middle of that week he satisfied for us on the cross, and indeed by his death he closed our wickedness, restrained sin, and expiated iniquity; but by his resurrection he restored eternal righteousness to us. Finally, at the end of the seventieth week, when he had finished all things which were written and prefigured concerning him in the Law and the Prophets, he sealed the vision and the Prophecy, i.e., he imposed an end to the law and prophetic visions, and as the Author to the Hebrews writes, he made the old covenant obsolete and introduced the new. Then, how the Angel divided that time which God had prefixed. Lansbergius therefore refers the seven weeks to the restoration and rebuilding of Jerusalem. The sixty-two weeks, which are to be joined with those seven up to Christ the Leader, he counts from the seventh year of Longimanus up to the Baptism of Christ, when he was inaugurated as the Leader or prince of his Church: which make 483 years and almost ten months according to his own calculation, so that the beginning of the principate of Christ falls in the year 775 Julian from Nabonassar. He constitutes the half of the last week as the death of Christ, through which he was to abolish all the sacrifices of the Old Testament and the entire legal worship, but he makes the exit of the same the end of the confirming of the covenant among the Jews, in the year 491 from the edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus, 781 Nabonassarean, the twenty-first of Tiberius. What is to be thought of this opinion will be manifest from what follows.

§. LXXXVIII. The twenty-fifth opinion is that of those who lead the beginning of this Epoch from the 20th year of Artaxerxes Μακρόχειρος, Nehem. 1 and 2, but constitute the end in the year of the passion of Christ, but they judge that lunar years are to be understood, each of which contains 12 lunar months, but 354 days, so that it is shorter than the solar year by eleven days. Whence 475 solar years make 490 lunar years, which they say have elapsed from the 20th of Artaxerxes to the passion of Christ. It is observed that Julius Africanus in book 5 of his annals was the first to hand down this opinion. Which Cornelius à Lapide also attributes to Chrysostom, Rupertus, Gordonus Huntlaeus, and Torniellus. Benedictus Pererius defends it primarily in his Commentary on Daniel, whom Torniellus in his annals for the year of the World 3609, n. 4, judges to have treated this whole matter concerning the LXX weeks most copiously and accurately in two entire books. But that opinion is deservedly to be rejected, primarily because it injects years into this computation that are clearly unused by the sacred Scriptures. For nowhere, as Cornelius à Lapide admits, does it use lunar years, but solar ones. But if indeed the Hebrews used lunar ones, nevertheless every third year they added a month from the days that had accrued, and intercalated it, so that thus through embolismic months they might equate lunar years to solar ones, both so that they might accommodate themselves to the chronicles and chronology of other nations, and because of the Passover and Pentecost, so that they might celebrate those at the appropriate time, as the same Cornelius observes: indeed Lyranus, a Jew by origin and most versed in the affairs of the Jews, denies that the Jews used lunar years. They are mistaken, he says, who think that the Hebrews used such (lunar) years at any time, otherwise the WHOLE series of the Old Testament wavers. Which R. Aben-Ezra also confirms in Levit. 25. Our months correspond to the moon, and our years at the end return to the years of the sun. Whence it is evident that the Jews defined only the months by the motion of the moon, but not the years, but rather measured these by the course of the sun, and for the sake of that matter intercalated an entire month at a certain time. Which their modern computation also confirms. Therefore, no other than solar years can be understood. And what, I ask, would remain certain in the Scripture of the Old Testament in the computation of years, if sometimes lunar years, and not always solar ones, were to be understood? Furthermore, the term to which of Daniel's weeks is not correctly fixed in the year of the Lord's passion, since it was rather established by the Angel in the middle of the last week. To say nothing, finally, of the fact that it is doubtful whether 13 years are to be counted from the 7th of Artaxerxes designated by Ezra up to the 20th of the same Artaxerxes named by Nehemiah, of which we are to speak afterwards. Which the patrons of this opinion assume as indubitably certain.

§. LXXXIX. Others, therefore, in the twenty-sixth [year] retain indeed that beginning of our Epoch, namely the year of Longimanus, but more correctly they count solar years, and they finish the 70 weeks in the seven-year period after the Lord's passion. This is the opinion of B. Osiander in his paraphrase: In the twentieth year of Darius Artaxerxes Longimanus (he calls him this, with certain others, because the name Darius was common to the Persian Kings) Nehemiah was sent into Judea, so that he might restore the walls and gates of the city of Jerusalem, Nehem. chap. 2. For although the temple had been begun much earlier, and finally completed; nevertheless the city of Jerusalem had more the appearance of a village than of a city: Nehemiah, however, restored the walls and gates: and this was to rebuild the city: from the departure of Nehemiah into Judea, up to the passion and resurrection of Christ, there are gathered about four hundred and seventy-seven years. But because by that reasoning six years are still missing up to the final week, which he attributes to the confirmation of the covenant after the passion and resurrection of the Lord, Osiander appended this warning about it: Nor let it disturb the pious reader that according to the customary computation six years are lacking. For since the reckoning of times must of necessity be sought in large part from profane historians; it ought not to seem a wonder if they, through carelessness, neglected those six years (especially in a history of nearly five hundred years). For more belief is to be given to the divine Oracle, uttered through the Angel Gabriel, than to Heathen writers: in whom many historical errors are found everywhere. Moreover, if the words of the Angel are attended to more diligently, they do not teach that the final week is to follow the cutting off of Christ, but they place his death in the middle of the final week, because they predict that the Jewish sacrifices would be abolished through his death, which in reality was also thus fulfilled.

Nor is there need that we should admit such a defect in the history of the Kings of a full six-year period, as will be evident later. §. XC. Wherefore others, having retained the beginning of the 20th year of Longimanus as the twenty-seventh, and having counted the years not as lunar but as solar, and not having cast the excision of the Messiah to the end of the sixty-ninth week, but to the middle of the seventieth, finish the entire weeks in the four-year period after the excision of the Messiah. Which opinion is defended today primarily by Dionysius Petavius and Mr. Wilhelmus Langius. The former seeks the beginning of the weeks from the 20th year of Artaxerxes, not from the death of Xerxes, but counted from the first auspices of his reign with his parent, which he makes the tenth year of his sole reign: and thus he establishes that the first year of the weeks corresponds to the year before Christ 455, of the Julian period 4259, of the world 3529, and that the seventieth week began in the very year in which Christ was baptized. See part 2, book 2 of the Rationarium temporum, ch. 10. But this is his opinion in book 2 of his work on the years of Christ, ch. 9: that a double beginning must indeed be established for Artaxerxes Longimanus, the former depending on the year of the Julian period 4241; but the latter on the year 4248, whence from the former beginning he counts the years designated by Nehemiah, so that thus the first of Daniel's week depends on Nisan of the Julian period 4260, and at the beginning of the 487th year of this epoch, at the beginning of the fourth year of the seventieth week, in the month of Nisan, that is, in the middle of the 70th week of the Julian period 4746, Christ, having been offered for us, abolished the legal sacrifices and offerings. Which opinion, differing somewhat from the former, may be counted as the twenty-eighth.

CHAPTER VIII. The review of opinions is concluded: with the judgment of the blessed Franz and a refutation of the Jews.

§. XCI. And thus stand most of the opinions concerning the seventy weeks. Furthermore, St. Jerome observes in the preface to book 11 of his Commentary on Isaiah that Josephus and Porphyry discussed this question at length, and in his catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers he reports that a certain Jew, who flourished in the time of the Emperor Severus, wrote most fully concerning these seventy weeks: But nothing of these has reached our age. St. Augustine, in Epistle 80 to Hesychius, reports that some have made the 70 weeks double, and taught that the former were fulfilled at the first coming of Christ, but that the latter are to be fulfilled at his final coming. Which will be the twenty-ninth opinion. Thirtieth, Apollinaris of Laodicea, the Bishop, as Jerome reports in this place, counted the 70 years of the weeks from the going forth of the word, when Christ was generated from the Virgin Mary, up to the 49th year of the expected repentance of the Israelites. But after sixty-two weeks he designated the coming of Elijah, and said that in the last week Jerusalem and the temple would be built over 3 and a half years, and that the Antichrist would come: but to recite these inventions is to refute them. §. XCII. It seems difficult and arduous, however, to define which of the reviewed opinions should be chosen. The primary cause of this difficulty is easily the intricate nature of the chronology and the times. Concerning which Funccius complains greatly here. Whence it seems safest to our blessed Franz in his Schol. Sacrific. Disp. 10, thesis 58, that, having abandoned these chronological disputes, the sixty-nine weeks should be counted backward in some most sincere and correct Chronicle, which, regarding the Kings between Cyrus and Tiberius, under whom suffered

Christ, so that one may arrive at the true beginning of the weeks, or the term from which the going forth of the word, of which Daniel speaks. But what sort of most correct Chronicle is to be hoped for, though not to be expected, the blessed one judges. To whom Mr. D. Muller adds his calculation in his work on the refutation of Judaism, having adduced several causes whence the diversity in the calculation and in the opinions of the authors has arisen.

§. XCIII. Moreover, nothing at all is lost by this chronological contention from the argument of our faith against the Jews taken from this oracle. Which both the blessed Franz and Mr. D. Muller have clearly demonstrated. In short, from whatever going forth of the word concerning the restoration of the city and the Babylonian captivity the beginning is taken, it is certain that the 70 weeks have long since elapsed; and since the Messiah ought to have come before the destruction of the city, while the sacrifices were still standing, our argument remains irrefutable that he came sixteen centuries ago, if indeed for so many centuries the city has been devastated, which had been restored 70 years after the Babylonian captivity, and the Levitical sacrifices have utterly ceased, nay, the entire Levitical cult has expired with the whole Jewish polity. It is memorable what Dionysius the Carthusian reports in his Commentary on this place. That a letter was written six hundred years ago by a certain Rabbi Samuel to Rabbi Isaac, in which he confessed that it is evidently confirmed by this prophecy that the Messiah has already come, and that the responses of the Jews are altogether weak and absurd. Wherefore he does not see how the Jews even now expect the Messiah to come: a part of which it is helpful to transcribe here: It seems, he writes, my Lord, that the prophecy of Daniel, which is written in the ninth chapter, has already been completed, where it is thus said: After sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed, and the people shall come with the prince who is to come, and shall destroy the city and the house, and the destruction of perpetual desolation shall be finished. And there is no doubt, my Lord, that the destruction of perpetual desolation is this captivity in which we now are. For it is now a thousand years, and the Lord says openly through the Prophet that there will be a perpetual desolation on account of the killing of Christ, just as our desolation is after the killing of Christ. For He did not threaten a perpetual desolation except after the killing of Christ. And if we should wish to say that before the killing of Christ we were in desolation, the Christians answer us that before that death there was no desolation except for seventy years, and after this we were brought back into the land of promise, and we were in grace and honor before God. Certainly, my Lord, I see no escape: for in fact it is proven to us that after seventy weeks of years were completed from the rebuilding of the temple, then Jesus was killed by our fathers: and afterwards came the leader, namely Titus, and the people, namely the Romans, and they did to us according to this prophecy. Today it is a thousand years, and nevertheless we are in the wrath of God, and yet we hope in Him, still expecting the Messiah to come, and that we shall return to the land of promise, and shall restore the city and the temple, and shall be in grace and honor before God: and that this desolation will not be perpetual, but temporal. Alas, my Lord, that is not a consistent excuse and escape, and such an expectation seems vain. Thus far the Epistle of the Rabbi.

§. XCIV. Our B. Franzius also mentions in his Schola sacrif. Disp. 10. thes. 82. how he convinced a certain learned Jew, brought to him by Martin Trost of Hoxar in Westphalia, from this oracle: who, at the mention of Daniel, trembled all over, signifying that from Daniel it is not to be disputed, otherwise someone would become either a madman or a heretic, and he was reduced to such a state that he could answer nothing else to the argument from this article than this: perhaps one week in Daniel denotes 100 or 1000 years. To this, says B. Franzius, I answered him that I was willing to admit and concede his objection (hypothetically for the time being) that one week comprises either 100 or 1000 years; meanwhile, however, I most courteously requested of him, if he does not yet think the weeks of Daniel have elapsed, to show me where in the world the Jews are sacrificing today. For since Daniel expressly teaches that the Messiah must be exhibited before the abrogation of the sacrifices restored after the resolution of the Babylonian captivity, it would certainly be impossible to deny that the sacrifices must still stand if the Messiah has not yet come. By the strength of this he felt himself constrained, and submitted nothing else than this, that he was not equal to this discussion of ours, although it appeared from the whole conversation that he was most experienced. And when he was asked to think more about this matter in the following days, he replied that the Jews do not do this, for otherwise that would be the way to heresy and defection. Thus B. Franzius. Mr. Dr. Muller, our friend and brother most closely joined in Christ, observes in Rabb. Confut. ch. 10, p. 356, that the Jews evade discussing this text, and that he has experienced this with several Rabbis, who excused themselves with this pretext, that Daniel is δυςνόητος and difficult to understand: also citing the saying of R. Lusitanus in the Colloquy of Mittelb. fol. 102: It is rash to interpret Daniel, I will insinuate my interpretation with fear. But this discussion might seem alien to our purpose, therefore we return to the proposed question.

CHAPTER IX. Confirmation of the true opinion concerning the Epoch of Daniel from this oracle.

§. XCV. After we have therefore brought forward all the opinions that occurred to us concerning this most grave chronological difficulty, and have exhibited their reasons, with the addition sometimes of new weights of arguments, we judge that, all moments having been weighed, the calculation must be added to those who establish the term from which the 70 annual weeks begin as the 7th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, and place the passion of Christ in the middle of the last week. But the modern ἕυρημα of Scaliger, that the beginning of the Epoch should be taken from the 2nd year of Darius Nothus, and the completion should be placed in the destruction of the city, can by no means be approved, of which we are most certain, even if it pleased Dr. Calixtus so much that he judged it could not be doubted, unless ineptly, that the weeks take their beginning from the edict of Darius Nothus, that is, his 2nd year, and end in the 120th of the Christian era, when the sacrifices were removed, the temple burned, the city overturned, and the Jewish polity destroyed. That Dr. Calixtus was too precipitate in his judgment can be taught both by those things which we have discussed before, and it will be clear from those things which are now to be said further.

§. XCVI. Various arguments confirm our opinion, both those which a more accurate scrutiny of the text suggests, and those which can be drawn from Sacred chronology and History, and the collation of the same with exotic writers. Nor is it involved in those difficulties by which others are, but rather it contributes most greatly to discussing Biblical-Chronological difficulties.

§. XCVII. These textual arguments can be observed. First, from the scope of the Angel's information, which was to console Daniel, to raise him up, and to make him more certain about the fulfilling of the promises, not so much concerning Jerusalem and the people, as concerning the Messiah, and his apotelesmata, and works most necessary of all, which are the cause and fountainhead of all salvation, namely, that he was to expiate the sins of the whole world in Jerusalem and in the midst of the people, and was to bring back eternal righteousness. Wherefore he teaches that it is so far from the case that any doubt should arise concerning the restoration of the city and the people, that in the more secret divine council it is absolutely defined that that most salutary work, in which the hinge of the salvation of the whole human race turns, which all the faithful have expected and desired, is to be accomplished in that place, and that a certain time has also been divinely determined and decided, in which it must be accomplished there, which is now announced and expressed by the angel. For the chief scope of such solemn embassies and angelic revelations has almost always been this: to render that principal and supreme promise concerning the Messiah as certain as possible; which was the A and Ω of divine revelations, and the σκόπος σκοπιμώτατος of the whole Scripture, the time of which the Prophets searched into above all, as St. Peter testifies, 1. Epist. 1, 11. And that Daniel is to be reckoned among these in the first place, who, intent upon this, was most solicitous about the same, no one will easily doubt. Furthermore, the Angel also alludes here, as Lansbergius rightly says in l. 2. Chron. c. 11. p. 81, to the seventy years of the captivity of the people and the desolation of Jerusalem, which God had predicted through the Prophet Jeremiah, and teaches that for those 70 years, God had defined seventy weeks of years, that is, 490 years, upon the completion of which the true liberation of the Israelite people and the holy city would be at hand. The angel also concedes to the Prophet that that liberation, which he so greatly desired, was at that time at the door, but he denies that it is that true liberation which God had promised to his people through the hand of the Messiah. The Angel therefore draws the Prophet back from the meditation of that momentary liberation, and commands him to direct his mind to the seventy times seven years that follow, or the ten subsequent Jubilees, by which all the prophecies of the Prophets concerning the Messiah were to be concluded, and the true redemption of the Church was to be perfected, and an eternal Jubilee was to be introduced into the Church, in which the remission of sins and eternal righteousness would flourish. And the Angel himself seems to allege this cause of the revelation, while he says: I have come, that I might indicate to you, because YOU ARE A MAN OF DESIRES. Therefore the Angel now indicates and reveals that which the Prophet most desired to know. But what did he desire more than the time of the sufferings of the Lord, searching into what or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in him did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ. Which divine promise the same heavenly messenger, who defined the time here, also indicated would be fulfilled in the fullness of times, Luke 1. Wherefore the matter here is not primarily about the definition of the period of rebuilding the city or restoring the people, but about that time most desired of all, which even Daniel, the man of the Lord's desires, panted for. For what consolation would that be, if the heavenly messenger primarily intended that, that there was defined in the council of God another, and that a most grievous, and final, and ultimate destruction of the city and people, which the Scaligerian opinion desires?

§. XCVIII. We seek the second argument from the express mention of that thing for which those LXX weeks are defined. For the Angel does not say absolutely that they are defined over the city and people, as Scaliger and his followers, but especially Calixtus, assert this confidently; but they are defined, he says, upon this holy city, and upon this thy people. Therefore, the discourse is not simply about the duration of the city and the people, but insofar as this holy city and this holy people could still be called such in any way, or even σχετικῶς (relatively) at that time: for while Christ was still teaching in it, that Holy of Holies, while the Apostles were striving to sanctify it by the public proclamation of the word, that title was not to be denied to it entirely. But when they drove Christ to the cross and cast the Apostles out of the temple, the inhabitants of Jerusalem rendered themselves utterly unworthy of it. And lest any doubt should remain as to what this determination of time refers, Gabriel expressly added that seventy weeks were defined upon this holy city and upon this holy people לְכַלֵּא to finish or close the transgression, which was done by the Passion of the Lord. Therefore, mention is made of the people and the city as the seat and place where this ought to happen: but the finishing of the transgression, the sealing of sins, the expiation of iniquity, and the bringing in of the righteousness of the ages are mentioned as the thing itself, most desired and salutary to the whole world, which ought to have been accomplished in that people and in that city. They are therefore mistaken, and do not weigh the text as is proper, who say that this period was decided for the city in order to destroy it, because the words of Gabriel do not allow for this. They treat of the destruction of sin, not of the destruction of the city. And that thing, which is said to be defined here, is described by the heavenly messenger with such apparatus that one is led to wonder that this definition could have been snatched away to the city and its final destruction. For that ל (to), which those of the opposite party have confused with τῷ על (upon) through a notable hallucination (since the former designates the thing defined, the latter the place in which the defined thing ought to have been done), is repeated SIX TIMES in one verse, so that we might not be ignorant of what the LXX weeks are defined for, and what ought to happen at the end of them. For since the Angel explicitly and laboriously testifies that those weeks are defined to finish the transgression, to restrain sin, to expiate iniquity, to bring in eternal righteousness, to seal the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Holy of Holies, it is clearer than light that those weeks are not defined to destroy the Israelite people and to wipe out the holy city. Because these are as far apart as heaven and earth: to expiate sins and bring in eternal righteousness, and to destroy the Israelite people and wipe out the Holy City.

§. XCIX. The permutation of the particle ל and עַד provides the third argument. For so that we might be most certain that that ל refers to the end to which those LXX weeks are defined, and thus the term is defined to which this πληρώματος τοῦ χρόνου (fullness of time) belongs, עַד מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד (unto Messiah the Prince) is added, which cannot be taken otherwise than as a determination of the term to which. But the Messiah was Leader, or King, not in the desolation of Jerusalem, but when he began to rule with his doctrine and the scepter of the word, and sent it forth through Judea, powerfully commanding even nature itself, the sea, the winds, and all manner of diseases, and even death itself, which he put to flight, and the demons, which he cast out from all who were possessed with authority, so that they even acknowledged him as Lord and openly confessed it with horror; then also when he himself entered Jerusalem as King, was put on the cross under the title of King, and as a spiritual King gathered his forces to send them into the world, and, trusting in the right hand of the Lord, began to rule more illustriously in the midst of his enemies. Indeed, he declared himself Prince and the Lord's anointed when he undertook his office, and when he was proclaimed the Son of God from heaven, in whom God was well pleased. Was this not his most illustrious declaration as נָגִיד (Prince)? Those who make the destruction of the city the term to which cannot find why Christ should be called Prince when that city was to be destroyed, or what this, UNTO MESSIAH THE PRINCE, has in common with destruction! §. C. We seek the fourth argument from the explicit designation of the passion of Christ. What is clearer than that the time of the passion of Christ is defined when Gabriel says, and after sixty-two weeks (with the seven weeks previously named computed before) the Messiah shall be cut off: which openly imply not an indefinite time, but one certainly determined and defined by the just number of so many weeks. We are therefore compelled to confess that Gabriel here expressed exactly the time of the passion of Christ, which Daniel, along with other Prophets, searched out most religiously when he counts the weeks, upon the completion of which the Messiah was TO BE CUT OFF. And B. Behmius acknowledges that this is the common opinion, that the scope of the angel was precisely to determine the time of the passion of Christ. D. Calixtus is therefore mistaken when he considers this most accurate determination of time to be no determination at all; nor does he think that the time of the passion of Christ is hinted at except indefinitely and generally: namely, that IN THE MEANTIME, AT HIS OWN TIME, the Holy of Holies will be anointed, and will obtain the remission of sins and eternal righteousness. §. CI. The fifth is from the work of the last week. 'And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week.' What does that corroboration of the covenant mean, and what is that last week, if one fixes a different term than the one designated by us? Those who go elsewhere here can certainly define nothing. They say that only one week out of the LXX is meant, but they cannot say which one it is, or which number, or where its beginning and end ought to be placed, or indeed that such a week ever existed, let alone where it is to be sought. But if the passion of Christ is fixed as the primary scope, that last week will comprehend the time of the crucifixion, and indeed the years of Christ's ministry, during which he himself confirmed the covenant of grace with many, and committed it to his Apostles so that it might be further confirmed in that city and in that people. Which was done successively throughout one week. For then, with the Holy Spirit also sent, and the public preaching of the name of Jesus in that city and among the Jewish people especially, the covenant of grace was confirmed by word and miracles. §. CII. The sixth argument can be drawn from the definition of the middle of the last week. For in order that the Angel might define even more accurately the very year of Christ's passion, he distributed the last week into two halves, and thus indicated that, one half having elapsed, that is, three years and a half beyond the sixty-nine weeks, Christ would be cut off. In the half, he says, of the (last) week, (the Messiah) shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, which is not more rightly said to have been done than by the passion of Christ, since with the veil rent, an end was in reality brought to the Levitical ceremonies, and by the oblation of the body of Christ, those typical sacrifices were bound to cease, and were no more. Rightly Pererius lib. 10. in Daniel. Immediately after the death of Christ those sacrifices failed, not indeed according to use and exercise, but according to virtue and efficacy, and as theologians now speak in the schools, according to value. For after that time, although they were not immediately deadly, until the truth of the doctrine of Christ should become known to the world by the promulgated Gospel; they were nevertheless dead: for they ceased to be pleasing and acceptable to God and salutary to men. Thus the beginning and the end of this angelic prophecy, v. 24 and 27, elegantly explain each other. At the beginning, the time is defined in general Of the seventy weeks: Towards the end the time is expressed specifically, so that the middle year might also be designated: namely, that the passion of Christ falls in the last week, in the middle of it. Towards the beginning it is predicted that the expiation of sins would be joined with the sealing of the vision, because then sins were to be expiated in one day through the death of CHRIST, and the visions and prophecies, whose principal goal was this expiation through the death of CHRIST, were to be sealed. Towards the end it is indicated what he is to do then, so that the sacrifice may cease, because the expiatory offering of Christ brought an end both to the prophecies and to the types, but especially to the sacrifices. Thus the middle also fits the beginning and the end most excellently, and the whole Prophecy is most elegantly consistent with itself; which in other expositions is greatly obscured. For since the Holy of Holies is said to be anointed, in order to expiate sins and bring in eternal righteousness, v. 24, seven and sixty-two weeks are defined until that anointing, and after these have elapsed his excision is predicted. Now Christ is said to be anointed when he undertook his office, because then he declared himself to be the Lord's anointed, and was declared so by a heavenly voice. Thus, therefore, the time of the Lord's office and ministry is accurately defined, which had previously been indicated in a general way: Indeed, since the year of the passion and death is expressed afterwards, it is openly shown how much time Christ ought to spend in teaching until he is cut off and makes the sacrifices cease by his own sacrifice, namely, the middle week: Such a determination is nowhere else read in the prophecies. Since, therefore, all other things concerning Christ have been accurately defined in the Prophets, it was fitting to define this also, which was the principal thing; and as Peter testifies, it was defined, 1. Epist. 1, 11. and therefore it is not to be permitted that this angelic computation be understood otherwise than concerning the time of Christ's passion, lest so significant a character be obscured.

§. CIII. The seventh argument is provided by the accurate distribution of that last week, whose beginning, middle, and end the Angel defines exquisitely. In the beginning that Holy of Holies was anointed with the Holy Spirit at his Baptism, as the Redeemer of his people; he came as נָגִיד, Leader of his people, and proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord, and began to confirm that covenant of grace among his people. In the middle of the week he completed the work of his redemption, and indeed by his death he expiated iniquity, but by his resurrection he brought back eternal righteousness to us. Nor, however, did he cease to confirm the covenant for MANY among his people, but what he had done personally in the days of his ministry, he deigned to continue doing through the Apostles after his ascension into heaven, until the end of the week; and when he had completed all things which were written in the Law and the Prophets, he sealed the vision and the prophecies, imposed an end upon the Law and the prophetic visions, and thus abolished the old covenant and introduced and established the new.

§. CIV. The eighth argument we seek from the going forth of the word. Which is expressly defined here. But the going forth of the word is not understood concerning the rebuilding of the temple, which we know Cyrus, and afterwards (with the work interrupted) Darius, took care of; because there is no mention made here by any word of restoring the temple. But it is about the restoration of the polity, both Ecclesiastical and civil, and the rebuilding of Jerusalem; as the words of the Angel openly have it: From the going forth of the word, that Jerusalem be built again, just as the Vulgate rightly expressed the Hebrew phrase, for returning and building Jerusalem. For the Hebrews are accustomed to express the repetition of an action with the verb שׁוּב, as examples teach, Zech. 5, 1; Jon. 1, 13. The Hebrews, says Calixtus, do not have a word by which they may express repeated building in isolation; therefore it will be necessary for them to use a circumlocution and say: He shall return, and it shall be built. Now to the rebuilding and restoration of Jerusalem pertains partly the restoration of the polity of the city, for instance both Ecclesiastical and civil, which is the internal form of the city, and partly the repair of the buildings, streets, and walls of the city, which is its external form. Wherefore the second year of Darius cannot be established as the terminus a quo, in which year indeed the word went forth, both prophetic and Royal, but concerning the building of the temple, not the restoring of the city. For terms are not to be assigned according to our own judgment, but we must adhere strictly to the declaration made by the Angel.

§. CV. Ninth, a still clearer definition is had in those things which the Angel added for the sake of explanation; it shall return and be rebuilt, that is, it shall be built again (by the same Hebrew phrase) the street and the wall. Which teach that it is not a matter of the structure of the temple, but of the rebuilding of the city and the ramparts, and that the beginning is established from this Epoch, not from that. What could have been said more clearly against the opinion of Beroaldus and Scaliger? For both begin it from the restoration of the temple, the former from the permission which Cyrus had granted, which did not succeed; the latter, however, from the concession of Darius, which was carried into effect. If the Angel had looked to the restoration of the temple, he would undoubtedly have made mention of it: he would not have denoted the building of the city and the streets and the walls in an accurate definition of the terminus a quo. For in order that it might be more correctly established from whence the Epoch ought to be begun, the angel was not content with that general reparation of Jerusalem, but added an express mention of the ramparts and streets, lest by chance someone might refer the same to the first foundations of the temple and the first structure of certain huts or shanties at the time of the relaxed captivity, or even to the building of the temple itself, which was separated by a long interval from the reparation of the city and the adornment of the streets.

§. CVI.
