Statim post Christi interitum defecerunt illa sa- crificia, non sane secundum usum & exercitium, sed secundum virtutem & efficaciam, & ut nunc in scholis loquuntur Theologi, secundum valorem. Namque post id temporis, licet non statim fuerint mortifera, quoad promulgato Evangelio veritas do- ctrinæ Christi mundo innotesceret; fuere tamen mor- tua: desierunt enim Deo esse grata & accepta homini- busque salutaria. Ita explicant sese mutuo eleganter v. 24. & 27. initium, ac finis hujus prophetiæ ange- licæ. Sub initium tempus in genere definitum septuaginta hebdomadum: Sub finem expressum specifice tempus, ita ut annus medius etiā designa- retur: passionem nempe Christi cadere in septima- nam ultimam, in medietatem illius. Sub initium prædicitur, expiationem peccatorum conjunctam fore cum obsignatione visionis, quia tum uno die ex- pianda peccata erant per mortem CHRISTI, visionesque & prophetiæ, quarum præcipuus sco- pus erat ista per mortem CHRISTI expiatio, obsignandæ. Sub finem indicatur, quid facturus tum sit, ut sacrificium cesset, quia & prophetiis complementum & typis, imprimis vero sacrificiis finem attulit Christi oblatio expiatoria. Optime etiam ita medium initio & fini congruit, sibique constat elegantissime tota Prophetia; quæ in aliis expositionibus valde obscuratur. Nam cum San- ctus Sanctorum ungendus dicatur, ut expiet peccata, & adducat æternam justitiam v. 24. septem, & sexa- ginta duæ septimanæ usque ad unctionem illam de- finiuntur, & post has elapsas excisio ejus prædicitur. Unctus autem Christus dicitur, cum officium ag- gressus est, quia tum unctum Domini esse se decla- ravit, ac voce cœlesti declaratus fuit. Sic ergo tempus officii, & ministerii Domini accurate defi- nitur, quod antea generatim indicatum erat: Imo quum passionis & mortis annus exprimatur postea, aperte monstratur, quantum tempus Christus do- cendo conficere debeat, donec excindatur, & ces- sare sacrificia faciat suo sacrificio, nimirum mediam septimanam: Qualis determinatio nuspiam in va- ticiniis legitur. Quum itaque omnia alia accura- te definita sint in Prophetis de Christo, etiam hoc, quod præcipuum erat, definire conveniens fuerat. ac teste Petro, definitum fuit, 1. Epist. 1, 11. adeoque non permittendum, ut hic computus angelicus ali- ter, quam de passionis Christi tempore intelligatur, ne tam insignis character obscuretur.

§. CIII. Septimum argumentum submini- strat accurata septimanæ istius ultimæ distributio, cujus & initium & medium & finem Angelus ex- quisite definit. In principio unctus est ille San- ctus Sanctorum Spiritu Sancto in Baptismo, in po- puli sui Redemtorem, venit ut נָגִיד, Dux populi sui, & promulgavit annum acceptum Domino, cœ- pitque confirmare fœdus illud gratiæ in populo suo. In medio septimanæ perfecit opus redemtionis suæ, & per mortem quidem expiavit iniquitatem, per resurrectionem vero suam æternam nobis re- duxit justitiam. Neque tamen desiit MULTIS in populo suo pactum confirmare, sed quod αὐτοπρο- σώπως fecerat in diebus ministerii sui, post ascen- sionem in cœlos per Apostolos porro facere digna- tus est, usq́ ad exitum septimanæ, & ubi consummas- set omnia, quæ in lege & Prophetis scripta erant, obsignavit visionem, & prophetias, legi & prophe- ticis visionibus finem imposuit, adeoque antiqua- vit ita vetus pactum, & induxit ac stabilivit novum.

§. CIV. Octavum argumentum ab exitu sermonis petimus. Qui definitus hic expresse est. Non autem exitus sermonis intelligitur de reædifi- catione templi, quam Cyrum, ac postmodum (ope- ris interruptis) Darium curasse novimus; quia de templo restaurando, nullo hic verbo mentio facta. Sed de restauratione politiæ tum Ecclesiasticæ, tum civilis & reædificatione Hierosolymæ; uti verba Angeli aperte habent: Ab exitu sermonis, ut ite- rum ædificetur Jerusalem, quemadmodum recte E- bræam phrasin, ad revertendum & ædificandum Hie- rosolyma expressit Vulgarius. Siquidem Ebræi so- lent iterationem actionis verbo שׁוּב exprimere, ut exempla docent Zach. 5, 1. Jon. 1, 13. Hebræi, inquit Calixtus, vocabulum non habent, quo solitario ite- ratam ædificationem exprimant, circumlocutione igitur eos uti oportebit, & dicere: Revertetur, & ædi- ficabitur. Ad reædificationem autem & restau- rationem Hierosolymæ pertinet partim restaura- tio politiæ civitatis, puta tum Ecclesiasticæ, tum civilis, quæ est interna forma civitatis, partim repa- ratio ædificiorum, platearum & murorum civitatis, quæ ejusdem forma externa est. Quapropter non potest terminus à quo constitui annus secun- dus Darii, quo verbum quidem exiit tum propheti- cum, tum Regium, sed de ædificando templo, non de restauranda urbe. Non enim pro nostro arbitrio termini assignandi sunt, sed declarationi ab Angelo factæ ἀποτόμως inhærendum est.

§. CV. Nono luculentior adhuc definitio habetur in iis, quæ ἐξηγήσεως gratia addidit Ange- lus; revertetur & reædificabitur, hoc est, iterum æ- dificabitur (eadem Ebræa phrasi) platea & murus. Quæ docent non de structura templi, sed de reædifi- catione urbis, & mæniorum agi, & ab hac Epocha initium constitui, non ab illa. Quid luculentius adversus Beroaldi, & Scaligeri sententiam dici po- terat? Nam uterque inchoat eam à templi restau- ratione, ille à permissione, quam Cyrus indulserat; quæ non succefsit: hic autem à Darii concessione, quæ in effectum deducta est. Si templi restaura- tionem respexiffet Angelus, sine dubio ejus men- tionem fecisset: non vero urbis & platearum, & murorum ædificationem denotasset, in accurata termini à quo definitione. Ut enim constaret re- ctius, undenam iniri Epocha debeat, non generali illa Hierosolymorum reparatione contentus fuit an- gelus, sed addidit disertam mæniorum & platearum mentionem, ne forte quis ad prima templi funda- menta, & primam casularum, aut tuguriolorum quo- rundam structuram tempore laxatæ captivitatis eandem referat, aut etiam ad ipsam templi ædifi- cationem, à qua longo intervallo distabat à repara- tione urbis, ac platearum adornatione.

§. CVI. Decimo quum Angelus urbem hanc SANCTAM, & populum in ea SANCTUM vocet, ac postmodum HIEROSOLYMAM ædi- ficandam, denique ipsa etiam mœnia cum plateis restauranda prædicat, haud obscure indicat, ibi E- pocham esse inchoandam, cum sc. urbs illa in for- mam eam redigi cœpit, quæ pristino quadantenus similis esset statui, ac imprimis politia & Ecclesiafti- ca plene adornari cœperit, & civilis, constitutis Magistratibus, in ordinem redigi, atque omnia κτ' τάξιν καὶ ἐυσχημοσύνην disponi debuere, non absque successu, simulque externa etiam forma ci- vitati respondens aliquo pacto priori, platearum, portarum, murorum adornatione concilianda fuit. Nam per politiam ujusmodi civilem urbs facta de- mum est, & per ἐυσχημοσύνην & πολιτείαν Eccle- siasticam cœpit non nihil ad nitorem pristinum, ceu URBS sancta adspirare.

§. CVII. Undecimo ea sine dubio sententia de LXX. hebdomadis præferenda est, quæ partitio- ni temporis Angelicæ consonat, eandemque accura- te observat: quod in nostra fit, qua VII. hebdoma- dæ, & LXII. & UNA, ultima vel septuagesima septi- mana, & in hac utraq; medietas seorsim sua habent σημασίαν, ut VII. hebdomadæ ad ædificationem, & restaurationem civitatis, LXII. à civitate restaurata ad exhibitionem Christi Ducis, residuæ unius dimi- dium ad passionis tempus, & confirmationem pacti per Messiam ipsum, alterum dimidium, ad ejusdem pacti inter Judæos confirmationem post excisionem Messiæ per discipulos ejus instituendam deputentur. In Scaligeriana vero sententia istæ partes nullam habent significationem, sed vacare censentur.

Nam quod Calixtus dicit, hac partitione angelum solum interpretationibus Symbolicis & Cabalisticis viam obstruere voluisse atque indicare, quod veri, & usitati intelligantur numeri, futile est atque exem- plo Scripturae caret, neque huic tam exquisito computo coelesti ullatenus convenit: ut taceam, quod summa hinc non prodeat 70 1/2. septimana- rum, quas Calixtus numerat. Ita enim partes illas ipse colligit in summam: VII. & LXII. & I. confi- ciunt LXX. Ad locum Ezech. 45. v. 21. quem pro exemplo simili adducit, responsum antea est. Et respondent etiam illi, qui caeteroquin Scaligero in hac causa adhaerent, uti exemplo est disputatio Dorscheana §.XXXIII. quod utrinque ratio dispar sit. In Daniele enim singulis periodis sua specialia fata assignantur, sed eorum nihil in testimonio E- zecheliano occurrit. Et annotarunt hujus divisio- nis causam R. Jarchi, David Kimchi, maxime A- barbinel, cujus haec sunt: Quod eam (minam) di- vidat in istas partes, id sit, quia unaquaeque pars pon- dus, sive moneta erat per se. Moneta quaedam erat 20. siclorum, alia 25. alia 15. Quae cum simul mi- nam constituerent, Deus jubens, ut singulis sua constaret quantitas, ad minam examinari manda- bat, ut an singulis suum inesset pondus, per minam, quam simul conficere debebant, innotesceret. Ut ergo non temere illa divisio instituta, ita etiam hic non sine gravi causa periodos hebdomadum adhi- bitas fuisse, merito censeri judicat laudata dispu- tatio. Quam vero causam juxta suam opinionem reddere non possunt Scaligeri sectatores.

§. CVIII. Atque haec argumenta e textu facile persuadent, non esse aliter explicandu hoc oracu- lum; ac cogunt etiam, si forte difficultas in Chro- nologia suboriatur, non torquendum esse ad Chro- nologia, quae alias multis obsita est difficultatibus, oraculum angelicum, sed ex oraculo angelico po- tius emendandum esse calculum Chronologicum.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X.

Chronological arguments, and those taken from the fulfillment.

§. CIX. Now indeed, if we also adapt the Chronology and the fulfillment of the oracle to the words, just as they sound most clearly, we shall find the outcome more easily according to the thread of this our opinion than if we enter into the meanders of any other opinions. Therefore, the twelfth argument is provided by the fulfillment of the Prophecy concerning the going forth of the Word. Which is recorded in Ezra 7 and Nehemiah 2, verse 1, et seqq., where it is related, in the book of Ezra first, how Ezra undertook the restoration of both the ecclesiastical and civil polity in Jerusalem at the special command and diploma of the King. But in the book of Nehemiah, how, at the prayers poured out by Nehemiah to God and his supplication before King Artaxerxes, the rebuilding of the city was obtained, and Nehemiah was dismissed with letters of safe conduct and a supply of horsemen, as well as mandates that the necessary equipment should not be denied. And the divine historian is extremely painstaking in distributing the rebuilding of the walls and gates and the repair of the entire city over several chapters, so that the fulfillment of the illustrious prophecy might not be touched upon lightly, but exhibited περιστατικῶς (circumstantially). For what need would there have been for that most prolix description, unless the Holy Spirit had wished to make the fulfillment of the Angelic prophecy thus πρὸς τὸ ὄμμα (before the eyes)?

Therefore, the Holy Scriptures indicate the beginning of the weeks not obscurely in those places, namely that they began in the 7th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus; First, because Ezra's plan, undertaken on the 1st day of the month for the journey, is painstakingly described, v. 9, Ezra 7. (2) The direction of the hand of God, which was with Ezra, v. 6. (3) The decree and rescript of the King, v. 10 et seqq., is brought forward. (4) The consent of the 7 supreme counselors of the King, v. 14. (5) The royal expenses for the restoration, especially of divine worship, without which no polity of the Republic is safe. Which was the piety and religion of the King. (6) Permission to do whatever he pleased, or whatever he judged to make for the εὐταξίαν (good order) for his brethren, v. 18. (7) The concession that those who wished might journey there with the priests and Levites, verse 13. (8) The remarkable multitude of those who set out: who, with those who had been brought from Caspia, were about 1700, enumerated in chapter 8. Therefore, there was need for the construction of buildings, so that they could live there with their families. (9) Divine guidance, chapter 7, v. 3. (10) The appointment of Judges, as well as the ordination of elders. For then King Artaxerxes granted power by his royal diploma, nay, he demanded this of Ezra: But you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God, which is in your hand, appoint (from the Jews) Judges and magistrates, that they may judge, or administer justice to all the Jewish people who are beyond the river Euphrates in the land of Canaan, chapter 7, v. 25. Similarly, one may read about the appointment of Elders in Ezra 10, 14. And how Ezra labored with the utmost zeal to restore everything to the εὐταξίαν (good order) of both polities, so that the holy city might be raised to its former splendor in some measure, the history of Ezra abundantly testifies, which, since it is the principal repair of Jerusalem, the beginning of the Angelic Epoch is deservedly to be sought from thence, if indeed it was undertaken at the edict of the King. For the Angel speaks of the return for the building of Jerusalem, which phrase, whether it denotes the return of the People, which others wish, along with the repair of Jerusalem, fits the history of Ezra perfectly, if indeed those two, the return of the people and the repair of the city, are taken together, and likewise this repair alone, or if it is viewed separately, it fits no edict more correctly, which was indeed joined with effect, than this one, which was entrusted to Ezra, as all the περιστάσεις (circumstances) show. Which succeeded in such a way that afterwards, by the same King Artaxerxes (whether within the next three years, or within thirteen years, which does not matter much to the sum of the matter), the most gracious permission was granted for the external form of the city to be repaired, and through Nehemiah the gates, walls, and streets could be adorned, and those things which pertained to εὐταξίαν (good order) could also be further ordered and disposed.

§. CX. Thirteenth, if you compare the condition and state of the times, such as the Angel foretold, with this history, it will correspond in every respect. For Gabriel had foretold that the street and the walls would be built in a time of distress: ἐν στενοχωρίᾳ τῶν χρόνων, as the LXX have it. That we might not be in doubt that this came to pass, Nehemiah explains this στενοχωρίαν and distress at length, describing the persecution and conspiracy of Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the Ammonite, as also of Geshem the Arabian, against the Jews, how they attempted to hinder the construction of the walls and the repair of the city, and received the architects and builders with mockery and reproaches, and having entered into a league, attacked the city, and strove to involve it in internal dissensions, so that they might check the work. chap. 2. & 4. Which and other difficulties of those times, such as the scarcity of provisions that had arisen, the new snares of Sanballat and his accomplices, the false accusation of Nehemiah, the hiring of Shemaiah the traitor, and the false brethren and traitors among the Jews themselves, are described at length up to Chapter VII.

§. CXI. The period of seven weeks defined by the angel also corresponds to the fourteenth. For although the time of that distress (σενοχωρίας), and of the completed building and restoration of the city, is not expressed by Ezra or Nehemiah, yet just as the Angel assigned the full seven weeks, i.e., 49 years, to this restoration, so it is easy for the reader of the book of Nehemiah to have no doubt that it lasted for as many years. The whole of which was occupied with the difficulty of the times, and the rebuilding of the walls and gates, and the adorning and restoration of the whole city, so that a full description of the fulfillment of the prophecy would not be lacking. For no other scope seems to have been set for the book of Nehemiah. For the census of the people, and the celebration of the feast of tabernacles, and the sanctioning of both ecclesiastical and political laws, so that the divine covenant might be renewed and all things ordered for good order (εὐταξίαν), belong to this restoration, Ch. 7, 8, 9, 10; as well as the distribution of the parts and streets of the city by lot, ch. 11; the inauguration of the walls, ch. 12; and the visitation and reformation instituted by Nehemiah, last chapter. Although Nehemiah restored the walls in the space of 50 days, he was nevertheless occupied for a full 12 years—namely, from the 20th year of Artaxerxes until the 32nd (Neh. 13:6)—in building up the city, increasing the number of citizens, and performing other things that looked to the safety of the people and the city, after those things which had been expedited by Ezra for the sake of the polity. But in that year he returned to the King and remained with him until the end of the years, or the last year, i.e., the 41st of the reign of Longimanus, for a period of nine years: and then, having obtained leave from the King again, he returned to Jerusalem, where he found the greatest confusion in the Republic he had established; to amend which, and thus to fully restore the city and the Republic, he is to be believed to have spent the remaining seven years of the seven weeks. The blessed Gesner does not deny this, disp. 9, §. 158. The restoration of the streets and walls of the city is announced to be within the course of 7 weeks. Now seven weeks constitute 49 years. Within which the city and the Jerusalem Republic were repaired, albeit with great distress of times. For how great was the affliction of the Jews while repairing the city and the walls is evident in Neh. 4, where Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, and other enemies so harassed the Jews that it was necessary for half of the men building to stand guard with arms, while the other half did the work in the meantime. How great also was the difficulty with which Ezra, the Doctor of the Law, and Nehemiah, the Royal cupbearer, raised up the collapsed Republic and accustomed the people to the divine law, is most clearly written in Ezra 9 & 10 and Neh. 5, 8, 9. Others explain the distress of time as a short time. For the wall was completed by Nehemiah within 50 days, Neh. 6; but the Hebrew word צוק does not signify a short space of time, but calamity, pressure, and affliction. This is from the blessed Gesner. Others refer the distress of times not to those seven weeks, but only to the following LXII; indeed, they argue from the ellipsis of the contrary, that since the LXII are said to have been in distress, and thus the former are tacitly denied to have been such, they judge them to have had a happier state due to the presence and authority of Nehemiah, whereas they felt the other distresses most under the Maccabees. Which explanation is also praised by the blessed Jacob Martini in book III, de tribus Elohim, c. 32. Which we weighed above in ch. 4; that the received explanation is more consonant is by no means obscure.

§. CXII. If anyone objects that those 49 years or seven weeks are not found in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which describe the reparation of the city, if the beginning of the counting is made from the seventh year of Artaxerxes, much less are so many years counted up to the building of the streets and walls, which seems to constitute the term of the former weeks. Resp. That the adorning of the streets and walls indeed pertains to the cycle of seven weeks, but the term is not fixed in it. Then, if the words of the Angel are accurately weighed, he made mention not only of external reparation and material buildings, even though that is also commemorated here, so that those times are designated more certainly, but the 'going forth of the word to build Jerusalem,' so that, namely, there may be a city, and indeed a HOLY CITY, and a PEOPLE in it reduced to a certain order, is looked to, so that in that city and in that people the Messiah may perform those things for whose sake he himself had to come primarily: that he may expiate sins, bring back eternal justice, make sacrifices cease, and that by his own excision, or his passion and death. Because seventy weeks are said to be decided upon the PEOPLE and upon the HOLY CITY: And the Epoch of this decided or determined time is fixed as to its beginning in the going forth of the word to build Jerusalem, so that, namely, there may again be a city governed by ecclesiastical and political laws, and that it may be enclosed by walls and gates. All of which pertain to the cycle of the first seven weeks. The beginning of which Nehemiah makes from the 20th of Artaxerxes, c. 11, and proceeds thereafter to recount in order all that he himself did for the sake of repairing Jerusalem; those things are also woven in which contributed to that reparation and restoration, both as to external and internal form, up to the 32nd year of Artaxerxes. Nor does Nehemiah indeed hand down that all those things which were desired for the good order (ἐυταξίαν) of the city and its full restoration were expedited in that year. Nor does any reason appear why we should believe that Nehemiah was the Royal leader or governor in Palestine only up to the 32nd year of Artaxerxes. For although he was ordered to perform this office up to that time from his first mission, for 12 years, he nevertheless obtained a dismissal from the King again afterwards, so that he might return to Palestine, and thus the time during which he remained there is not defined. However, he did not return without the mandate of the Duke or governor; otherwise, he could not have executed with authority those things which he expedited in chapter 13 concerning the polity and sacred ecclesiastical matters, from which it is gathered that, having seen King Artaxerxes again after that twelve-year period had elapsed, Nehemiah had been confirmed in that dignity of Jewish Duke. But however the matter may stand regarding him, nothing prevents it from being said that such was the unhappiness of the times that thereafter, for thirty-seven whole years, there was always a need to labor until the city was restored to some likeness of its former splendor and was repaired again in both sacred and civil polity. Finally, this also is to be observed, that the angel adds in the periphrasis of the former seven weeks the word צוק, a constriction of times or στενοχωρίαν [distress], and therefore, even if that city had been repaired sooner and restored to full order, that στενοχωρία and constriction nevertheless lasted until that point, namely to the ninth year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, in which the first seven weeks are finished, and a happier state of the city of Jerusalem seems to have followed. Some extend the age of Nehemiah up to the times of Alexander the Great, which fall into the thirteenth week of Daniel. What wonder, if Nehemiah was occupied for seven annual weeks in order to restore the state of Jerusalem in its entirety during those difficult times, even if his history is not woven through to that point in the sacred texts? And does not the king The mention of Darius Nothus is made in the history of his reign, ch. 12, v. 22, because at that time there was still labor being done on those things which pertained to the order of the priestly and Levitical families and the ecclesiastical state! B. Luther in Dissert. de LXX. septim. Dan. T. IV. Oper. Lat. Jen. f. 616. In so many years (49) Jerusalem was barely restored, so that it had a street and a trench (thus the Angel speaks), so that it had a polity established in the street and in peace. And the trench, that is, the wall and fortification against war and enemies, for that time is required, so that a city may be built, both for government and against enemies, so that both may be in full swing and stand. Those years were completed in the 5th year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, while Nehemiah was still governing, and Joiakim the priest, etc. At the term or end of the years of the first VII weeks, Megalander differs from our calculation by only four years, referring it to the 5th year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, which we refer to the 9th of the same. For in the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, Nehemiah began the work. There still remained XXI years of the reign of that Artaxerxes: Darius Nothus reigned for XIX years, whose successor was Artaxerxes ὁ μνήμων. Therefore, the end of the seven weeks or XLIX years falls into the ninth year of this man.

§. CXIII. The chronology of the subsequent weeks corresponds remarkably well to the fifteenth. For from the designated year of Artaxerxes Longimanus (which Artaxerxes we shall teach later is indicated by Ezra ch. 7, and it is confessed by almost everyone that he is no other than the Artaxerxes of Nehemiah, who is the Artaxerxes of Ezra), so many weeks and years have flowed, up to the defined term, which were designated by the Angel. Three intervals are counted here: Of the first, of seven weeks, we have already said that it aptly agrees with the beginning of the Epoch proven by us. The second is of sixty-two weeks, to be begun from the end of those seven: or sixty-nine from the beginning of the Angelic Epoch: which is completed in CCCCLXXXIII years. So many years, therefore, are to be counted to Christ the Leader solemnly proclaimed. If we compare profane history to this, Petavius begins the reasoning in this way, who fixes the beginning of the Epoch in the 20th year of Longimanus, Artaxerxes ὁ μακρόχειρ began to reign in the 1st year of the LXXVII Olympiad. LXXIX, as is gathered from Diodorus Siculus, book XI of the Bibliotheca, that is, 4250 of the Julian period. Therefore, his twentieth year coincides with the year 4269 of the Julian period. Furthermore, the fifteenth year of Tiberius, according to the Julian period, is the year 4742, in which Christ was baptized and undertook his office. Therefore, between the twentieth year of Longimanus and the fifteenth of Tiberius, CCCCLXXIII years intervened according to the calculation of Petavius; and thus X years are missing to complete those sixty-nine weeks. But because the angelic calculation cannot be wrong by any reason, it is necessary that the deficiency of that decade be supplied from elsewhere, in whatever way that may be done through chronological truth. For the calculation of the heavenly messenger is above all exception, to which chronology must be recalled, and not the reverse and perverse way of examining the heavenly calculation by the calculations of chronologists. But in order for Petavius to resolve this, he says that Artaxerxes reigned for a decade with his father Xerxes, and that Scripture counts the twentieth year of Artaxerxes from the time that his reign was undertaken with his father; since it sometimes counts the years of sons from the time they began to reign with their fathers. But Diodorus Siculus designates the beginning of his own reign. Thus, therefore, the beginning of the proper reign of Artaxerxes would have been the year

of the Julian Period 4250, the beginning of the reign undertaken with his father (which Scripture may respect) would have been the year 4240 of the Julian Period, and thus the XX year of the reign of Longimanus according to Scripture will coincide with the year 4259 of the Julian Period, from which up to the year 4742 of the Julian Period are counted 483 years, that is, sixty-nine weeks. Dionysius Petavius gathered this double beginning of the reign of Artaxerxes Longimanus from the fact that the flight of Themistocles from Greece and his arrival in Persia is conjectured by Diodorus Siculus to be in the 2nd year of the LXXVII Olympiad, which preceded the slaughter of Xerxes by seven years. The same Themistocles, according to the narrative of Thucydides, had then given letters to Artaxerxes νεωστὶ βασιλεύοντα (newly reigning). He was therefore νεωστὶ βασιλεύων already 7 years before the slaughter of his parent, and thus was admitted to the kingdom at least seven years before the death of his father. Similar is the reconciliation of Mr. Wilhelm Langius, book II, on the years of Christ, ch. 15, p. 326, who likewise teaches that Artaxerxes reigned with his father for at least 7 years. Jacobus Tirinus also, in Chron. Sacr. ch. 28, confirms from many authors of proven faith that Artaxerxes did not administer the empire only from the death of his father, but for many years before together with his father.

§. CXIV. Although Petavius and Langius differ somewhat in the beginning of the years of the reign of Artaxerxes, they agree perfectly, however, on the term from which and to which the Epochs of Daniel belong. Langius judges the opinion of Petavius thus: If Petavius had not followed a false reasoning in the year of the passion, he would have produced the most true things. But now he has both pushed back the things preceding the Epoch of Artaxerxes by one year, and he assigns the year of the passion to the beginning of the third year of the seventieth week. But the beginning of the third year is not the middle of the annual week, but the fourth. The decision of that dispute, which opinion is to be preferred, depends in large part on the true reasoning of the year of the crucifixion and the definition of the years of the ministry of Christ. Which matter would require a special examination. But lest we err in it, the heavenly measurer of times took care, when he assigned half a week to the office of Christ in these lands, up to the passion of Christ, the time of which it was most fitting to be assigned by this so illustrious and august oracle. For since other more minute things were accurately defined concerning Christ in the Old Testament, it was altogether fitting that this matter of such great moment, how many years Christ should have spent in undertaking his office, should not be neglected by the Prophets, which, since it is defined nowhere else, had to be set forth in this most exquisite calculation of times by Gabriel. But Mr. Langius refutes Petavius, because he referred the passion of Christ to the beginning of the third year of the last week. Which opinion he [refutes] in part II, book IV, ch. 4, p. 226, of the Rationarium temporum. Thus Petavius had proposed: We assert that Christ suffered in the third year of his preaching, and that he survived his baptism for two full years and some months. Whence he assigned to the passion of Christ the Julian year 76, and the second year of the 202nd Olympiad drawing to a close, of the Julian period 4744. But since these things do not agree with the observation of Phlegon of Tralles, that in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad there was an eclipse of the sun, the greatest of all those known before, μεγίστη τῶν ἐγχωρισμένων πρότερον (which was the eclipse on the day of Christ’s death, Matt. 27, Luke 23, v. 44), the opinion of Petavius is not undeservedly rejected, as far as the designation of the year of the crucifixion, σταυρωσίμου, is concerned. Furthermore, by the same argument with which Mr. Langius presses Petavius, namely that the third year beginning is not the middle of the annual week, but the fourth, he is himself also pressed, because, to wit, four com- Full years and what exceeds them do not make half a week. For Mr. Langius maintains that it is necessary and clearly certain that five Passovers were celebrated during the ministry of Christ, book 2, on the years of Christ, ch. X, p. 477. He maintains that Christ preached for four full years, namely from the Passover of the Julian year 47 to the Passover of 78, ch. IX, p. 420. Therefore, he is not consistent with himself. He assigns the Passion of Christ to the 4th of the Nones of April, and the 15th day of the month of Nisan or the second of April; however, he refers the baptism of Christ to January 6th, ch. 2, p. 356. If those things which were done concerning Christ after his baptism up to the first Passover are considered more accurately, it will be manifest that January 6th suits that time better than (as many do with Epiphanius) November 8th. And therefore Christ would have completed almost three months beyond the four years in his ministry. But how will 4 years and 3 months be the middle of a week, which is attributed to the confirmation of the covenant by Christ, up to his excision and the removal of sacrifices? And how did Christ suffer in the fourth year at the beginning of the seventieth week, which Langius asserts in ch. 9, page 420, if he spent four full years and three months teaching? Thus the beginning of the ministry of CHRIST will not fall into the term of the 69 weeks, but into the 6th year (inclusive) of the sixty-ninth week. But the Angel defined accurately the time of the coming of the Messiah נגיד: indeed, neither will the time of the Passion of Christ be established so ἀκριβῶς (accurately) from the Angelic oracle. Which contradicts the opinion of Langius himself. For thus he says in ch. 10, p. 424: For no prophecy predicted the time of the birth accurately, so that for this reason the birthday had to be inquired into most accurately: which had to be done in the time of the Passion. For Daniel stated the time of this MOST ACCURATELY, and therefore it ought to be inquired into with the greatest zeal and the greatest diligence, so that it may be demonstrated both that Daniel predicted true things and that Jesus is the true Messiah. Furthermore, neither will the account of the last week of Daniel hold up if the opinion of Langius prevails in all respects. For according to the oracle of Daniel, the other half of it extends itself up to the cessation of sacrifices, which was brought about by the death of Christ. Concerning which Langius says in his explanation of the Oracle of Daniel: He (the Angel) further says that the Messiah is to be taken away after those 62 weeks, i.e., those which followed the first seven. And so after the 69 weeks had finished from the issuing of the edict, Christ had to be taken away. And indeed in the MIDDLE OF THE 70TH WEEK. For then he caused the sacrifice and the oblation to cease. Which indeed was not done in any other way, except that sacrifices and oblations had no use after that time. For it is clear from Josephus that victims were sacrificed up to the final destruction of the city, but these had to be removed before the destruction. Therefore, Daniel speaks of the use or fruit of the sacrifices, which Christ rendered useless by his death, having been offered once for our sins. Therefore, there will be 486 full years from the going forth of the edict to the death of CHRIST, and he will have suffered at the beginning of the 487th. These things Lord Langius, book II, on the years of Christ, ch. 9, page 417. Now as to the other half of the last week, it does not appear how it can be held with certainty according to the Langian opinion. Thus four full years will remain; because he places the beginning in the month of Nisan, and again the end also in the same month of the weeks. But Langius counted only two or three years in the confirmation of the covenant among the Jews after the Passion of Christ. How then would four full years, or even more, have remained? For Langius also grants more years, and thus does not rest with the interval of 70 weeks defined by Daniel, l. c. p. 420. His words are these: Christ indeed confirmed the covenant with many for one week. Naturally, this whole prophecy looks to the Jews: therefore the word 'many' also pertains to the Jews, with whom Christ confirmed the new covenant for SEVEN AND BEYOND (NB. BEYOND, which how it may harmonize with the words of the Angel, defining the time most accurately, let the author see) years up to the last year of the 70th week. (That will not be the last term, if the last week is extended BEYOND, if indeed the rest are complete in themselves.) For since he himself had preached to the Jews for four full years, namely from the Passover of the Julian year 74 to the Passover of 78, he ordered his disciples to announce the Gospel afterwards. Who in the two or three years next after the ascension admitted only the Jews. Indeed, they even argued if anyone preached to the Gentiles. But finally, when that time which had been decided upon the Jews was finished, the Apostles, since the Jews were unwilling to listen and were rejecting grace, turned themselves to the Gentiles. Finally, that Langian calculation deserves no assent, because it invents in a new and unheard-of way that the day of the Passion of Christ was not Friday, which everyone has believed until now, if by chance you except one Paulus Forosemproniensis, but Thursday; in which persuasion he so pleases himself that he uses the same even to refute the opinion of the Blessed Chemnitz, whom he says the theologians of Germany follow, with τῆς παῤῥησίας (boldness): That, however, he says in ch. 10, page 422, is sufficiently manifest, that Christ according to the opinion of Chemnitz was baptized after the Passover of the Julian year 73. And therefore the first Passover is of the year 74, the second 75, the third 76, the fourth 77. But in this year it is IMPOSSIBLE that Christ suffered. For neither would Chemnitz himself deny that Christ suffered on the preparation day of the Passover on a Thursday. Because those things are demonstrated from the Scriptures in such a way that it is not open to a Christian man to speak against them. But these two can never agree in the year 74: as we have clearly demonstrated before. Therefore, neither did Christ suffer in this year. But this is not the place to speak of this novel opinion of his. And it was eruditely refuted by Mr. Wandalinus, now a theologian at Copenhagen, our singular friend, in his Historical-Theological Diatribe on the day of the Passion and the three days of the death of Christ, opposed to the new and paradoxical Langian opinions, and published with the approval of the Venerable Theological Faculty in the Academy of Leipzig in the year 1651.

§. CXV. Thus much concerning the opinion of Petavius and Langius, neither of which can be simply approved, since the former openly errs in the designation of the year of Christ's passion, which the latter indeed correctly assigns, along with Phlegon of Tralles, to the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad (the 4746th of the Julian period, in which Scaliger and Calvisius agree), but in the explanation as well as the application of the angelic oracle, as has been shown, he is mistaken in more than one way. Nevertheless, both designate the beginning of our epoch more correctly than others, when they establish it as the 20th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, and judge that the middle of the last week falls upon the passion of Christ; although they differ at the beginning in that Langius makes the 20th year of Longimanus the 4241st of the Julian period; but Petavius makes it the 4240th year of the Julian period, which is a difference of one year.

§. CXVI. Lansbergius easily agrees concerning the beginning of the reign of Artaxerxes, which he linked likewise with the 313th of Iphitus and the 284th of Nabonassar in Chronol. S. lib. II. cap. 9. p. 69. Xerxes, he says, was killed by Artabanus, according to Diodorus, in the fourth year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad, that is, in the three hundred and twelfth year of Iphitus. Therefore, Artaxerxes Longimanus began to reign alone in the three hundred and thirteenth year of Iphitus, that is, in the two hundred and eighty-fourth year and a half from Nabonassar, Julian. However, Petavius does not refer the beginning of our epoch to the tenth year of the solitary reign of Artaxerxes, but to the seventh year, counting from the beginning of his reign until the edict six full years with nine months, so that it falls in the year 291 from Nabonassar, Julian with three months. He adds, therefore, 486 full years until the year of the passion of Christ, from which emerges the year of Nabonassar 777. Which year, however, is not for Petavius σταυρώσιμος, but rather the inaugural and auspicious year of Christ's office, the year, I say, of his Baptism, not of his passion. But in truth, Lansbergius does not deserve support regarding the year of the passion of Christ. For the Nabonassarean year 777 according to the Julian period is 4742. Iphitean 805. But Christ was undoubtedly crucified in the Iphitean year 808, according to the observation of Phlegon, which is noted in the Chronicles of Eusebius, and explained by Tertullian, Africanus, Origen in book II against Celsus, Jerome, Paul the Deacon in History of the Miscellanies, book II, chapter 2, and other Fathers regarding that extraordinary eclipse on the day of Christ's passion. Three years are therefore missing. Next, in the explanation of the oracle of Daniel, we also observe a certain ἑαυτομαχίαν or αντιλογίαν in Lansbergius. He admits in book II of Chronology, chapter 11, page 81, that in the beginning of the seventieth week that Holy of Holies, Christ Jesus, was anointed, and that the Principate of Christ had begun: and as he speaks on page 87, that he himself proclaimed to the Israelite people the acceptable year of the Lord: He admits that in the middle of that week Christ satisfied for us on the cross, and by his death abolished all the sacrifices of the Old Testament, whence the veil was torn into two parts at his death, Matt. 27, 51. Concerning which he further speaks thus on page 87. Furthermore, the Angel also defines the time in which Christ is to abrogate the legal sacrifices and offerings by his death, namely in the half of the seventieth week, that is, in the fourth year of the same week. That year was 487 from the edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus, but 777 from Nabonassar. For the edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus was promulgated in the year 291 from Nabonassar. Therefore, if sixty-nine weeks are added to this year, with the half of one week, that is, 486 years, the middle of the seventieth week will fall in the year 777 from Nabonassar, in which the Angel says Christ will die, and by his death will put an end to the legal sacrifices and offerings. But since he asserts that only two full years with three months intervene between the Baptism of Christ and his passion, I do not see how that entirely agrees with the prophecy of the Angel. For the Angel assigns a half-week from the beginning of his office until his passion. But how can two years with three months make a half-week?

§. CXVII. But these things being set aside, let us see primarily about that which is the main point here, whether Lansbergius correctly establishes the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus as the term from which our epoch begins? The doubt is especially that such an edict did not go forth in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, such as is indicated here by Gabriel. For the discourse here is expressly about the edict concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and its streets, and its walls. But what is read as promulgated in the seventh year of Artaxerxes in Ezra 7 seems to have nothing about the building of Jerusalem, its streets or walls, but only about certain things pertaining to sacred worship, about transferring the sacred vessels, about contributing royal expenses for sacrifices and divine worship, about the privileges and exemptions of the Priests and Levites, and likewise about appointing judges and curators throughout Judea. Which Mr. Langius also urges in book II, chapter 9. Lansbergius begins to count from the VII year of Artaxerxes, but at that time an edict was not made for building the city, which he falsely supposes, but only for the temple and those things which concern sacrifices. And Sulpitius Severus already noted this long ago in book II of Sacred History. I, he says, find that Ezra did nothing regarding the rebuilding of the city; I believe his greater concern was to reform the people of corrupt morals. But in truth, Lansbergius himself notices this well, and therefore he joined both edicts of Artaxerxes in book II, chapter 11 of Chronology, page 83. Among these edicts, he says, there is none that agrees with the description of the Angel than the edict of Artaxerxes Longimanus. For Cyrus and Darius Hystaspis promulgated edicts in such a way concerning the building of the temple, but not concerning restoring and building Jerusalem. But Artaxerxes Longimanus published both, and accomplished the first indeed through Ezra, the other through Nehemiah. He distinguishes these, concerning RESTORING AND BUILDING Jerusalem. He refers the former to the first edict of Artaxerxes concerning RESTORING Jerusalem, its ecclesiastical and political state, through Ezra the scribe, Ezra 7. He refers the latter to the second edict concerning building the walls of Jerusalem through Nehemiah the King's cupbearer, Nehemiah 2, 1. Thus, therefore, almost all of Ezra, as from chapter 7, and all of Nehemiah will be occupied in that both-fold edict, concerning restoring and rebuilding Jerusalem and its execution. Whatever, however, may be the case regarding that explanation of the Hebrew words of the Angel concerning RESTORING AND BUILDING Jerusalem, we retain the simple exposition concerning the going forth of the word TO CAUSE TO RETURN AND TO BUILD Jerusalem, for which rebuilding of Jerusalem certainly the mere decoration of walls and streets was not required, even if that is also mentioned, so that it might be established that it falls into the times of the seven former ones, but primarily there was a need for the reparation of the polity, both ecclesiastical and civil, which pertained entirely to the internal form of the city, and so that it might truly be a city, and a people, and indeed a holy city, and the people in it a holy people. Therefore, those things which Ezra accomplished are not foreign to this prediction. For by the power of the royal diploma he brought back the Jewish citizens into Jerusalem, and received immunity, and laws for the city, and magistrates and judges to be appointed, whence there is no doubt that the city was rebuilt at that time. Before that time, says Funccius, it was only permitted to the Jews to build the temple and to administer sacred rites according to the law of the Lord. But now, when Ezra is sent, there is added the confirmation of the Republic and the liberty of living under their own magistrates, which, by Hercules, is the true building of a city. For if any city is destitute of these, however much it may be fortified with a rampart and wall, yet it cannot deservedly be called a city. To say nothing of the fact that those two μανρέχεια, the edicts concerning the Republic and the city, may appear to have followed one another closely and within a three-year period, and may be considered as one; both because they proceeded from one and the same King, and because they concern the restoration of the state, both as to its internal and external form, and because they followed one another almost immediately. Concerning which also B. Gesner, disp. IX. on Daniel, §. 147. Because these two mandates were issued by the same King Longimanus, and concerning the same matter, namely the restoration not of the temple, but of the city and the polity, therefore for the same merit they are held to be correct. Which seems to that extent more consistent, if it be said that Ezra counted the seventh year of the solitary reign of Artaxerxes, which also, if I am not mistaken, is the opinion of Lansberg regarding the former edict: but that Nehemiah, in commemorating the 20th and 32nd year of the same Artaxerxes, looked not to the years of his solitary reign, but to the 20th and 32nd year from when he was admitted into the partnership of the kingdom by his father Xerxes. Which latter point regarding Nehemiah's computation Lansberg did not indeed notice, yet Petavius and Langius observed; just as, conversely, the former point regarding Ezra, that he counted the years of the solitary reign of Artaxerxes, Petavius or Langius did not observe, but Lansberg rightly noticed, and from historical observations and chronological characters elicited and proved, in Book II of his Chronology. S. chap. IX, p. 68, demonstrating by a calculation of eclipses that the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus was the two hundred and ninety-first from Nabonassar. Thus, therefore, those two edicts of Artaxerxes will differ by only three years. But we leave this to be weighed by chronologists and other learned men. For the sum of the matter does not consist in this. And whether it be said that Nehemiah follows the same reckoning of years as Ezra, or, as we observe sometimes happens in the comparison of the reign of the Kings of Israel and Judah designated in the Books of Kings, and the computation of the same Kings observed in the Books of Chronicles, that one counts the years of the solitary, the other of the joint reign, nothing is lost to the certainty of our opinion. Although Tirinus in his Sacred Chronology, chap. XXXVIII, observes that Cedrenus, Cornelius à Lapide, Bucholzer, Capellus, Funccius, and Angelocrator also look to this seventh year of the solitary reign of Artaxerxes. Which he also noted regarding Basil of Seleucia, namely that for this reason he derived the beginning of the 70 weeks of Daniel from the 8th year of the reign of Artaxerxes; provided that Xerxes reigned for 20 years, and that after the seven years of the reign assumed by his son Artaxerxes had elapsed, that edict went forth at the beginning of the eighth year.

§. CXVIII. The time of the passion of Christ, defined by the Angel, will correspond so exactly with the sixteenth [year] in chronological computation. But the best method of computing is that which is instituted by Olympiads, concerning which Julius Africanus, in Book III of his Annals, as reported by Eusebius in Book X of the Preparation for the Gospel, last chapter, judged thus: up to the Olympiads nothing certain is found in the history of the Greeks, but all things are written in confused times; but after the Olympiads, since all things were noted most diligently by the four-year period, no confusion of times appears at all. Scaliger, in his Chronological Elenchi against Pareus, honored this method of computing with this eulogy: The Olympiad is the guardian of times, the vindicator of historical truth, the restrainer of the fanatical license of chronologists. Neither in the Holy Scriptures nor in history is any interval better explained than that from the first Olympiad to Alexander, and from here to the Julian epoch of the Antiochians, which indeed is of such importance that whatever we have discovered in sacred history up to the destruction of the temple ought to be referred to that interval. If, therefore, we use this computation here, it is evident from Diodorus Siculus, Book XI of his Library, that the reign of Artaxerxes Longimanus began in the 1st year of the 79th Olympiad, or the 313th of Iphitus. The seventh year, therefore, according to Ezra, will be the 326th of Iphitus. If now 486 years, that is, sixty-nine weeks and a half, are added to the current three hundred and twenty-first year of Iphitus, there will result the 807th year of Iphitus. And thus the annotation of Phlegon agrees, that Christ suffered in the fourth year of the two hundred and second Olympiad. Dr. Pappus begins his reasoning thus in his Commentary on Daniel: The death of Alexander the Great falls in the 1st year of the 114th Olympiad, that is, the 453rd of Iphitus; the interval, therefore, is 356 years up to the 808th of Iphitus, or the year of the passion of Christ. To which you add: Artaxerxes Longimanus 33, Nothus 19, Mnemon 41, Ochus 23, Codomannus 6, Alexander 6 after the defeat of Codomannus. These 130 years, therefore, added to the previous 356, make a sum of 486 years, which, to wit, flowed from the seventh year of Longimanus up to the passion of the Lord, to which if you add 3 1/2 years up to the end of the epoch of Daniel, the end will fall in the 490th year from the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus. If we follow the manuscript canon of the Kings of Claudius Ptolemy, as it is exhibited in the Chronology of Dr. Behm, p. 260, this computation will be: 33 years remain from the 8th year of Artaxerxes I, whom he calls Darius II; there are 19 years of Artaxerxes II, 46 of Ochus, 21 of Arses, 2 of Darius III, 4; which years of the Kings of Persia joined together make 125. The years of the Greek Kings, according to that Canon, are 302. Of Alexander the Great 8. Of Philip Aridaeus 7. Of Alexander Aeus 12. Of the Greek Kings in Egypt, Ptolemy Lagus 20, Ptolemy Philadelphus 38, Ptolemy Euergetes I 25, Ptolemy Philopator 17, Ptolemy Epiphanes 24, Ptolemy Philometor 35, Ptolemy Euergetes II 29, Ptolemy Soter 36, Dionysius 29, Cleopatra 22. Finally, the 65 years of the Roman Emperors look to this, namely the 43 years of Augustus, 22 of Tiberius, the last of which concurs with the end of the last week, provided that the 15th year of Tiberius, in which Christ was baptized, concludes the 69th week. Those years 125, 302, 65, collected into a sum, make 492, which the mystical weeks complete. That two-year period which remains over is easily explained by the customary distinction of inclusive and exclusive numbering. Thus, therefore, the Chronology of the Kings also agrees, according to the observations of Ptolemy. Lansberg begins his reasoning thus: He makes the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus the 291st of Nabonassar. To these he adds sixty-nine weeks, that is, 483 years. They emerge as 774 from Nabonassar to the principate of Christ; with the final seven-year period added, the LXX weeks end in the year 781 from Nabonassar, in which manner both the initial and final years of our Epoch would have been Sabbatical and Jubilee. Which seems very harmonious. Abraham Bucholzer fixes the beginning with us in his Chronological Index in the 7th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus from the creation of the world 3514. If 486 years are added to these up to the middle of the last week, or the σταυρώσιμον year, the death of Christ will fall in the year of the world according to his computation 4600: the 80th Jubilee of the world, the 30th of Moses, because by his death Christ abrogated the Old Testament and made its sacrifices cease and acquired for us an everlasting Jubilee of life, and brought it back. This year of the world 4600 Bucholzer thinks was indicated by Ezekiel through the 4000 cubits in the description of the mystical temple, although Bucholzer departs from our opinion in this, that he makes that year of the world 4000 not the year of the passion but of the Baptism of Christ and ends the weeks of Daniel at the passion of Christ.

§. CXIX. On the other hand, the Scaligerians do not find in their hypothesis concerning the going forth of the word made in the second year of Darius Nothus up to the extermination of Jeru- folyma: The LXX weeks, when they compare the history and the completion. For Scaliger himself counts the years not as 490, but as 403 and a half. And therefore they invent that a half-week must still be added, and they even strive to twist the words of the angel into that sense. Which is especially to be noted, says Calixtus in the loc. cit., to the LXX weeks thus distributed into parts, he (the Angel) still adds a half of a week. And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the half of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease. The sum collected makes not only precisely LXX weeks, but LXX with a half, which half certainly is by no means to be neglected, and ought also to come into the number with the rest. And afterwards: since therefore the second year of Darius Nothus falls into the year of the World 3027, before the birth of Christ 421, if from that year 493 years are counted, how many LXX weeks and a half they make up, it will happen that that year 493 will begin in the current year after the birth of Christ 72. But of the Dionysian Era 70, in which very year the daily sacrifice ceased due to the scarcity of priests, on the 17th day of July (as Josephus writes, book VII of his history, ch. 4), the temple was set on fire and burned on the 10th of August (ibid. ch. 9), the upper city was captured on the eighth of September (ibid. ch. 18), and thus Jerusalem was overthrown, and the Jewish polity destroyed, and the desolation and consummation occurred, which the Angel had predicted. Since these things agree exactly, we have need of no other argument, as we said before, to prove that the beginning of the weeks must be made from the second year of Darius Nothus. How inept that twisting of the Angel's words is, we have already said above. Here is to be noted especially the self-contradiction of Calixtus: for he makes this the sense of the Angelic words: LXX weeks CUT OFF, DETERMINED or CONSTITUTED are said to be over the people and the city, which is the same as that just so much is predetermined, during which the city and people may remain until their destruction. And here Calixtus counts X Jubilees, each of which contains 49 years: LXX, he says, weeks are cut off, those indeed constitute 490 years and contain 7 cut off weeks, i.e., they make up X Jubilees. How therefore can a half-week be added? Are 493 and a half years X Jubilees or 70 cut off weeks, i.e., cut off and accurately defined? In the blessed Dorscheus's disputation on the LXX weeks, held by M. Johan. Frid. Heilbrunner, although the same beginning and the same terminus ad quem as that of Scaliger is designated and asserted, regarding this determination, thesis XX of Seder Olam is praised. Rabbi Jose said: that which is said, LXX weeks are cut off, teaches that they were PREDETERMINED beforehand by LXX years: And thus it is said in Gen. 7, v. 3. And his days shall be 120 years. It could not be said thus unless it was defined and cut off with precision beforehand by the Lord. These things we thought should be pointed out against Scaliger, that that precision pertains not only in general to the total sum, but also particularly to the individual weeks.

§. CXX. But as for what Calixtus objects, that if we begin the epoch of the weeks from the time of Artaxerxes, whether the VIIth year with Abraham Bucholzer, or the XXth year with Johannes Temporarius, the end is produced more than XX years beyond the destruction of the city; a hypothesis assumed precariously, not granted, nor to be granted, because it is far most false, it deceived him, namely that Artaxerxes Mnemon is understood by Ezra and Nehemiah in the designation of the VIIth and XXth year. Otherwise, the Scaligerians acknowledge that the chronological calculation is correct if the years are counted from the times of Artaxerxes Longimanus, just as Bucholzer, Temporarius, and others do, and thus our opinion also holds. The blessed Behmius argues thus in book II, IV, III, ch. VII of his Chronological Manual. If those LXX weeks end in the Sunday passion, it is necessary that the terminus a quo falls into the times of Artaxerxes Longimanus in about the sixth or seventh year. The major premise, he says, is manifest. The Messiah was crucified in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad or the 808th Olympiad year drawing to its end. In which matter there is a COMMON CONSENSUS of chronologists. With 490 years subtracted, there remain 318 or the second year of the 89th Olympiad. At which time the truth of celestial motion confirms that Artaxerxes Longimanus reigned in Persia, against the Beroaldists, and the Funccians and others do not deny it. These things from D. Behmius.

§. CXXI. The Angel does not end the weeks in the passion of Christ, as not a few wish: but he places the passion abolishing the sacrifices in the middle of the last week. For he does not say: In the end of the week, but IN THE MIDDLE the host and sacrifice shall fail, when, namely, that one true expiatory sacrifice would be offered. And thus the years of Christ's ministry will agree exactly with the oracle of Daniel, as they are commonly counted by our people. For Gabriel assigned to the confirmation of the covenant of grace to be made through Christ a half-week, i.e., three years and a half. Thus, therefore, a triennium and a half will have to be assigned to the ministry of Christ, namely from the baptism of Christ until his excision, or passion, abolishing and mortifying the Levitical sacrifices: where, however, it must be pointed out that there is no need that we assign a half-year, i.e., six precisely months beyond the triennium to the ministry of Christ, but that it is necessary, however, that it be said that Christ did not preach for only a year, or die in the same year in which he was baptized, as Pererius observes that Tertullian in his book against the Jews, Clement of Alexandria in book 1 of the Stromata, Julius Africanus in book V of the Annals, and Lactantius in book IV of the Institutes, ch. X, maintain, book XI on Daniel, q. VII; nor even only for a biennium, as the same Pererius notes that Apollinaris of Laodicea and some others thought, which we previously observed was also the opinion of Petavius and Lansberg, but that he required a full triennium in the office of teaching, with some months, which, namely, flowed from the time of the Baptism until the Passover. Furthermore, for the angelic calculation to be consistent, it is necessary that four complete years not be assigned to the ministry of Christ, with Langius and those who attribute five Passovers to Christ. Wherefore it shall suffice if he has spent a full three years in teaching, with some months added. Which opinion is wont to be confirmed from the Evangelical history, because it has distinguished the whole time of Christ's preaching through four Passovers from His Baptism down to His death. The first, John 2, which was the one immediately after His baptism. The second, John 5, which is understood as the Passover by Irenaeus in book II, chapter 39, by Eusebius in his Chronicles and in chapter 8 of the Demonstratio Evangelica, likewise by Jerome and Theodoret in this place, and by Rupert on John 5. Which opinion is also approved by the blessed Chemnitius in his Harmonia Evangelica, Prolegomena chapter 3, teaching that either that feast in John 5:2 is the Passover, or at least that another intermediate Passover must be conceded between that which is described in John 2:13 and that which follows in John 6:4. Others seek a second Passover in Matthew 12, Mark 2, Luke 6; see Bucholtzer in his Chronology, the third chapter, John. Finally, the fourth in chapters 11, 13, 18. To which also no light weight is added by the authority of the Ancients; since it was the almost common opinion of the Fathers that Christ preached the Gospel after His Baptism for three full years and somewhat more. For this was the opinion of Evodius, a disciple of the Apostles, as Nicephorus testifies.

Book II of the Ecclesiastical History, ch. 3. Ignatius the Martyr established this in his Epistle to the Trallians; Eusebius reports that this was the ancient tradition of the Church in Book VIII of the Demonstratio Evangelica, and he himself embraces that opinion in his Chronicles, and derives it from the Evangelical history of St. John; Chrysostom also fostered this opinion in Homily XXIII on Matthew, as did Theodoret on Daniel, ch. IX, and others. Finally, many of the moderns also follow them: B. Luther, Funccius, Chemnitius, and most others. And by that reasoning, the words of the Angel are also explained by the author of the Scholastic History in the history of Daniel, ch. X, as well as by Dionysius the Carthusian in his Commentary on Daniel IX, cited by Pererius toward the end of Book X on Daniel. Which opinion is approved by our B. Chemnitius; indeed, it is praised as common and received. Learned, he says, are the thoughts of Luther and others, who gather from Daniel such a calculation, for the Prophet says (he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease), namely, by the offered victim of his own body. Now, half a week makes three years and a half. From this is taken the common and received opinion, which also exists in the fragments of Theophilus, that Christ spent three years and as many months, or days, as intervened from his Baptism to the first Passover in his ministry. And foreign histories also support this opinion. For Eusebius recites from the commentaries of the Gentiles that that eclipse of the Sun, which occurred at the time of Christ's passion, was noted, and that it happened in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad. And that that time fell in the 18th year of Tiberius, in whose fifteenth year Christ had begun his ministry. Add also the consensus from the Papists of the Jesuit Tirinus, Sacred Chronology, ch. 47, p. 61. I do not see how anyone can solidly doubt the year of his death, since we have it both from the Evangelists and from perpetual tradition that Christ preached for no more than three years and a quarter, or survived his Baptism for that long, as will be clear from ch. 49. Nor is there any of the ancients who attributes a full four-year period to the preaching of Christ. And how otherwise shall we demonstrate that Christ was killed in the middle of the 70th week, which Daniel predicted?

§. CXXII. The eighteenth year of the latter half of the last week also consistently holds its ground in this way, if we compare the fulfillment with the prophecy. For thus three years and some months will remain to complete the newest week and to finish this mystical Epoch, during which time the covenant was confirmed to the Jews after the ascension of Christ, and many of the Jews were converted through the preaching of the Apostles. To this also contributed the first Council of the New Testament, which was celebrated at Jerusalem for the confirmation of the covenant of thanksgiving, Acts 15:11. Cf. Jer. 30:30. For this was the primary scope of the Council. Which was convened about four years after the resurrection, as some please. And B. Luther, Vol. IV. Jena Latin edition, f. 617, asserts that almost in the 3rd or 4th year after the resurrection of Christ, in the Council of the Apostles, Acts 15, it was decreed by public opinion that the burden of the law should be removed from the necks of the disciples. For this confirmation of the newest week concerns the Jewish nation, just as it is said concerning the entire 70 weeks that they were determined upon the Israelite people and upon the holy city, but not upon the Gentiles: and the Messiah was promised in the first place to the Jews, whom he also served before other peoples. Therefore, while the 70th week was running, he preached the Gospel to the Israelites alone, and not openly to the Gentiles as well, and

caused it to be preached. Toward the end of the weeks, it is also read that St. Paul, the Teacher of the Gentiles, came to Jerusalem and conferred with Peter, from whence he set out from there to the regions of Syria and Cilicia, Acts 15, Gal. 1. Which opinion is not disapproved by Pererius, Book XI on Daniel, p. 734. In the remainder of this week, the Apostles preached the Gospel in Judea with great zeal and ardor of spirit: And it was previously assumed by our B. Luther, although he later placed the entire newest week after the excision of Christ. Jacob Tirinus, Petavius, Lansbergius, Langius, and others among the moderns also explain it thus. Pererius is mistaken, however, when he judges that the entire Epoch of the 70 weeks from the 20th year of Artaxerxes to the 4th year after the Lord's passion makes not 490 years, but 493: But by the Angel, not 70 1/2 weeks, but only 70 in a round number, he judges, because the Angel was content to have expressed that maximum and at the same time full and complete number of 70 weeks. Which opinion both protests against the words of the Angel, inasmuch as he teaches that 70 weeks are appointed and cut off, and furthermore divides them into 7, 62, and one, and accurately executes even the fractions of half a week: and it deviates from chronological reasoning, as was shown before. But if it pleases others to relegate the Jerusalem Council to later times, the fourth year after the death of Christ is certainly notable for other reasons, to which some refer, and among these Tirinus in his Sacred Chronicle, the conversion of Saul, who became the TEACHER OF THE GENTILES, Acts 9 (which others say happened in the first year after the death of Christ) and the tranquility gained for Christians in all of Judea, Galilee, and Samaria, the first fury of the Jews having been calmed, and the Emperor Tiberius threatening death by public edict to the accusers of Christians, Acts 8. But especially in this last year of the weeks, St. Peter learned by the vision of the sheet full of serpents that the Gospel was to be preached also to the Gentiles, Acts 10:9, and thus, the middle wall of partition having been broken down, the Gentiles coalesced with the faithful Jews into one Church. In this year also, as Bucholzer correctly observes in his Chronological Index, the name of Christians first arose at Antioch, Acts 11. The name of the Jews, he says, was the appellation of the people of God, which was then rejected because of that people's contempt for the Messiah, and it is changed into the sweetest name of Christians (that is, ANOINTED ONES), and thus the Church of God receives from Christ, in whom it believes, both the name and the benefits signified by the name itself. These things fit the end of our Epoch very well; for its beginning was the restoration or repair of Jerusalem and of the holy people of God to a legitimate form of polity: but its end is, after the Evangelical covenant had been abundantly, but in vain, confirmed in Jerusalem and among the Jews, the assumption of the Gentiles into the peculiar possession of God, and the ecclesiastical polity of the remnants of Israel made by Peter. It took its beginning when, by the edict of the King, with the hand of God directing and Ezra promoting, concerning the repairing of the earthly Jerusalem, and the holy people of God, it obtained there a new form, as it were. The end falls upon the heavenly edict sanctioned by divine vision and committed to the Apostle who was a servant, concerning the expanding of the spiritual Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, through the gathering of the Gentiles, and into a new denomination of the people of the Lord; because it has obtained from Christ a new and far sweeter name. Finally, into that conference of those great lights and pillars of the Church, namely St. Paul, the Teacher of the Gentiles, and St. Peter, as also St. James the brother of the Lord, Acts 9, Gal. 1, 18, 19, which contributes greatly to the propagation of the Gospel, and the expansion of the boundaries of the Church, whence it is manifest that the beginning and end of the Epoch agree remarkably in the very completion, and that it elegantly corresponds to the words and calculation of the heavenly messenger.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

Argumenta Chronologica, & a complemen- to petita.

§. CIX. Jam vero si Chronologiam etiam, atque complementum oraculi verbis, prout claris- sime sonant, aptemus, facilius exitum inveniemus juxta filum hujus nostrae sententiae, quam si mean- dros aliarum quarumvis opinionum ingrediamur. Duodecimum itaque argumentum subministrat Vaticinii de exitu Verbi complementum. Quod Esdr. 7. & Nehem. 2. vers. 1. seqq. consignatum est, ubi refertur, in libro Esdrae primum, quomodo Esdras ad peculiare mandatum & diploma Regis aggressus sit politiae cum Ecclesiasticae tum civilis restitutionem in Jerusalem. In libro autem Nehe- miae quomodo ad preces Nehemiae ad Deum fusas, & supplicationem penes Regem Arthasashtha im- petrata fuerit urbis reaedificatio, dimissusque Ne- hemias, cum literis salvi conductis, & equitum co- pia, nec non mandatis ad apparatum necessarium non denegandum. Et perquam operosus est di- vinus historicus, in murorum & portarum reaedifica- tione, & universae civitatis reparatione per aliquot capita distribuenda, ut illustris vaticinii comple- mentum non leviter attingeretur, sed περιστατι- κως exhiberetur. Ad quod enim illa tam prolixa descriptione opus fuisset, nisi Spiritus Sanctus ita προς το ομμα ποιειν voluisset complementum va- ticinii Angelici?

Hebdomadum ergo initium haud obscure S. S. indicat in istis locis, quod nempe anno VII. Ar- taxerxis Longim. ceperint; Prima quia operose deseribitur Esdræ consilium 1. die mensis de profe- ctione susceptum v. 9. Esdr. 7. (2.) Manus Dei directio, quæ cum Esdra fuit v. 6. (3.) Decretum & rescriptum Regis v. 10. seqq. adducitur. (4.) Con- sensus 7. consiliariorũ summorum Regis v. 14. (5.) Im- pensæ Regiæ ad restaurationẽ cumprimis cultus di- vini, sine qua salva nulla est politiaReipubl. Quæ pietas fuit & Religio Regis. (6.) Permissio, ut agat, quicquid libuerit, aut quicquid judicaverit fratri- bus ad εὐταξίαν facere v. 18. (7.) Concessio, ut qui voluerint, eo proficiscantur cum sacerdotibus & Levitis vers. 13. (8.) Insignis multitudo eorum, qui profecti sunt: qui cum illis, qui è Caspia adducti 1700. circiter erant, cap. 8. enumerati. Opus ergo fuit ædificiorum extructione, ut cum familiis suis ibi agere possent. (9.) Divina deductio cap. 7. v. 3. (10.) Constitutio Iudicum, ut & ordinatio seniorum. Nam potestatem tum concessit Rex Artachsashtha diplomate suo Ragio, imo demandavit hoc Esdræ: Tu autem Esdra, secundum sapientiam Dei tui, quæ est in manu tua, constitue (ex Judæis) Iudices & præsides, ut judicent, seu jus dicant omni populo Iu- daico, qui est trans flumen Euphratem in terra Ca- naan cap. 7. v. 25. Similiter de Seniorum constitu- tione legere est Esdr. 10, 14. Et quomodo omnia Esdra ad utriusque politiæ εὐταξίαν restaurare, ut aliqua ratione ad pristinum nitorem eveheretur urbs sancta, summo studio allaborarit historia Es- dræ abunde testatur, quæ quum sit præcipua Hie- rosolymæ reparatio, inde merito Epochæ Angeli- cæ initium petendum est, siquidem ad edictum Re- gis ea suscepta sit. Loquitur enim Angelus de re- ditu ad ædificationem Hierusalem, quæ phrasis sive reditum Populi, quod alii volunt cum reparatione Hierosolymæ notet, historiæ Esdræ apprime con- gruit, siquidem illa duo reversio populi & reparatio urbis, si conjunctim accipiantur, itemque hæc re- paratio solitaria, vel si seorsim spectetur, ad nullum edictum rectius congruat, quod quidem cum ef- fectu conjunctum fuerit, nisi ad hoc, quod Esdræ creditum fuit, ut omnes περιστάσεις docent. Quod ita succesflit, ut postmodum ab eodem etiam Rege Artachsastha (sive intra proximum triennium, seu intra tredecim annos, quod ad summam rei non multum refert) externæ formæ civitatis reparan- dæ gratiosissima permissio concessa sit, ac per Ne- hemiam portæ, mœnia, plateæ adornari, atq; ea, quæ ad εὐταξίαν pertinebant etiam ordinari, ac dispo- ni amplius potuerint.

§. CX. Decimo tertio si temporum conditio- nem & statum, qualem prædixit Angelus, cum hac historia contendas, ex asse congruet. Nam ædi- ficatum iri plateam & muros in angustia temporum prædixeratGabriel: ἐν στενοχωρίᾳ τῶν χρόνων, ut ha- bent LXX. Quod ita evenisse ne ambigui esse- mus, Nehemias hanc στενοχωρίαν & angustiam pro- lixe exponit, describens Saneballat Horonitæ, & To- biæ Ammonitæ, ut & Gosemi Arabis insectationem, & conspirationem adversus Judæos, quomodo im- pedire conati sint murorum structuram & repara- tionem urbis, fannisque & probris exceperint ar- chitectos, & structores, ac fœdere inito civitatem oppugnarint, & intestinis dissidiis involvere satege- rint, ut opus sufflaminarent. cap. 2. & 4. Quæ & aliæ difficultates temporum istorum, utpote ob exor tam annonæ caritatem, ob novas insidias Sannebal- lat & complicum, falsam κατηγορίαν Nehemiæ, conductum Semajam proditorem, falsosque fra- tres & proditores inter ipsos Judæos, describuntur prolixe usque ad VII. Caput.

§. CXI. Decimo quarto congruit etiam pe- riodus ab angelo definita septem hebdomadum. Quanquam enim tempus σενοχωρίας istius, & con- summatæ ædificationis & instaurationis urbis non exprimatur ab Esdra, aut Nehemia, tamen uti An- gelus integras septem septimanas h. e. XLIX. annos ad hanc instaurationem assignavit, ita non dubium facile est, tot annis eandem durasse legenti Nehe- miæ librum. Qui totus in difficultate temporum, ac rædificatione murorum ac portarum & adorna- tione, ac restauratione totius urbis ideo occupatus fuit, ne deesset plena complementi vaticinii de- scriptio. Nullus enim videtur alius scopus libri Ne- hemiæ præfixus. Nam ad hanc instaurationem pertinet etiam populi recensio, & celebratio festi ta- bernaculorum, & legum tum Ecclesiasticarum, tum politicarũ sanctio, ut fœdus divinum renovaretur, & omnia ad εὐταξίαν ordinarentur, C. 7. 8. 9. 10. nec non partium, & platearum civitatis per sortem di- stributio c. 11. murorum inauguratio c. 12. & institu- ta à Nehemia visitatio ac reformatio. Cap. ultimo. Quanquam vero muros restauravit Nehemias spa- tio 50. dierum, in urbe tamen extruenda, & civium numero augendo, aliisque rebus præstandis, quæ ad populi & urbis incolumitatem spectabant, post illa quæ ab Esdra politiæ causa expedita erant, oc- cupatus fuit totos annos 12. puta à 20. Artaxerxis usque ad 32. Neh. 13, 6. Eo autem anno ad Regem reversus est, mansitque apud ipsum usque ad finem annorum, vel ultimum annum h. e. 41. imperii Lon- gimani, per novennium scilicet: atque tum impe- trata iterum à Rege venia rediit Hierosolyma, ubi invenit maximam Reipubl. à se constitutæ confu- sionem, ad quam emendandam, adeoque plene re- staurandam urbem & Rempublicam reliquos an nos septem hebdomadum impendisse credendus est. Non abnuit B. Gesnerus, disp. 9. §. 158. Re- stauratio platearum & murorum urbis intra 7. heb- domadum decursum futura nunciatur. Septem autem hebdomades constituunt annos 49. Intra quos civitas & Resp. Hierosolymitana reparata est, licet magna temporum angustia. Quanta enim in affli- ctione fuerint Judæi reficientes urbem & mœnia, id Neh. 4. patet, ubi Sanaballat, Tobias, Arabes, & alii hostes Judæos adeo divexant, ut dimidia pars viro- rum ædificantium armis in excubiis stare necessum haberet, altera dimidia parte interim opus faciente. Quanta item cum difficultate Esdras legis Doctor & Nehemias Regius pincerna collapsam Rempubl. ere- xerint, populumque ad divinam legem assuefecerint Esdr. 9. & 10. Neh. 5. 8. 9. clarissime perscriptum est. Angustiam temporis alii de brevi tempore exponunt. Nam murus intra 50. dies à Nehemia completus est. Neh. 6. sed Hebræorum vocabulum צוק non significat breve temporis spatium sed calamitatem, pressuram & afflictionem. Hæc B. Gesnerus. Alii angu- stiam temporum referunt non ad septem istas heb- domadas, sed ad sequentes solum LXII. imo istas ex ellipsi contrarii, quum LXII. dicantur fuisse in angustia, adeoque tacite priores tales fuisse negen- tur, feliciorem statum habuisse arbitrantur, ob præ- sentiam & authoritatem Nehemiæ, cæteras vero maxime sub Maccabæis angustias sensisse. Quæ explicatio etiam laudatur à B. Jacob. Martini libro III. de tribus Elohim c. 32. Quam supra expendi- mus cap. 4. illam vero receptam explicationem magis consonam esse, minime obscurum est.

§. CXII. Si quis objiciat, non inveniri in li- bris Esdræ & Nehemiæ, qui reparationem urbis de- scribunt XLIX. illos annos vel septem hebdomadas, si initium numerationis fiat à septimo Artaxerxis, multo minus tot annos numerari usq; ad platearum & murorum ædificationem, quæ terminum priorum hebdomadum constitui videtur. Resp. Ad circu- tum septem hebdomadum pertinere quidem pla- tearum & murorum adornationem, sed in ea non figi terminum.
