Tum, si accurate expendantur ver- ba Angeli, non solum externæ reparationis & ædifi- ciorum materialium mentionem fecit, etsi ea hic etiam commemoretur, adeo certius tempora illa designanda, sed Exitum sermonis ad ædificandum Ierusalem, ut nempe urbs sit, & quidem URBS san- cta, ac POPULUS in ea in certā turmam redactus, respici, ut in illa urbe, & in illo populo Messia ea peragat, quorū causa imprimis venire ipse debuit, peccata expiet, æternam justitiam reducat, cessare faciat sacrificia, idque excisione sui, vel passione & morte sua. Quia decisæ dicuntur septuaginta septi- manæ super POPULUM, & super URBEM SANCTAM: Et Epocha ejus decisē vel determi- nati temporis figitur quod ad initium in egressu ver- bi ad ædificandum Hierosolymam, ut sc. iterum urbs sit legibus Ecclesiasticis ac politicis gubernata, utque ea mœniis & portis claudatur. Quæ omnia perti- nent ad cyclum septem priorum hebdomadum. Quarum initiū à XX. Artaxerxis facit Nehem. c. 11. & pergit deinceps ordine recensere omnia, quæ fecerit ipse reparandæ Hierosolymæ gratia, perte- xuntur etiā illa, quæ ad reparationem & restaura- tionem istam faciebant tum qua externam, tum qua internam formam usque ad XXXII. Artaxerxis an- num. Nec verò tradit Nehemias illa anno omnia illa, quæ ad ἐυταξίαν urbis, ejusque plenam restau- rationem desiderabantur, expedita esse. Neque apparet ratio cur Nehemiam tantum usq; XXXII. Annum Arthasastæ Ducem seu gubernatorem fu- isse Regium in Palæstina credamus. Etsi enim eo usque à prima missione juberetur hoc officio de- fungi per XII. sc. annos, impetravit tamen postea denuo à Rege dimissionem, ut reverteretur in Palæ- stinā, adeoque non definitur tempus, per quod ibi substiterit. Non autem reversus est citra axioma Ducis seu gubernantis, alioquin ea, quæ expedivit c. 13. circa politiam & Ecclesiastica sacra, cum au- toritate exequi non potuisset, unde colligitur, viso Rege Artachsasta iterū post exactum illud duodecen- nium confirmatum fuisse Nehemiam in dignitate illæ Ducis Iudaici. Utut autem de eo sese res habeat, nihil obstat, quo minus dicatur, eam fuisse tempo- rum infelicitatem, ut deinceps adhuc per integros XXXVII. annos semper laborandum fuerit, donec urbs ad aliquid instar prioris nitoris restituta, & qua politiam sacram & civilem iterum reparata fuerit. Denique & hoc observandum, quod angelus ad- dat in Epochæ priorum septem hebdomadum περιφράσει צוק coarctationem temporum vel sevo- χωρίαν, ideoque etiamsi citius reparata fuisset illa urbs, & in plenum restituta ordinem, illa tamen sevoχωρία, & coarctatio eo usque duravit, ad annum nempe Artaxerxis Memoris nonum, quo finiuntur septem priores septimanæ, & felicior videtur suc- cessisse status urbis Hierosolymitanæ. Nehemiæ ætatem nonnulli extendunt usque ad Alexandri M. tempora, quæ in Decimam tertiam septimanam Danielis incidunt. Quid mirum, si Nehemias per septem hebdomadas annales occupatus fuit, ut in integrum restitueret difficilibus istis tempori- bus statum Hierosolymorum, utut eo usque non pertexatur ejus historia in sacris. Et annon regi- minis Darii Nothi mentio in historia ejus facta est c. 12. v. 22. quod tum adhuc laboratum fuerit in iis, quæ ad familiarum sacerdotalium & Leviticarum ordinem & statum Ecclesiasticum faciebant! B. Lutherus in Dissert. de LXX. septim. Dan. T. IV. Oper. Lat. Jen. f. 616. Tot annis (49.) vix est restituta Ierusalem, ita ut plateam & fossam ha- beret (sic Angelus loquitur) ut haberet politiam constitutam in platea & pace. Et fossam, id est, mu- rum munitionem contra bellum & hostes, da gehöret Zeit zu, daß eine Stadt angericht werde, beyde zum Regiment, und wider die Feinde, daß beydes im Schwang gehe und stehe. Isti anni sunt impleti an- no 5. Artaxerxis Mnemonis, adhuc gubernante Ne- hemia, & Iojakim sacerdote, &c. In termino seu fi- ne annorum priorum VII. hebdomadum quadri- ennio solum ibi discrepat à calculo nostro Mega- lander referens illum ad V. Artaxerxis Mnemonis, quem nos ad Nonum ejusdem referimus. Nam anno 20. Artaxerxis Longimani cepit opus Nehe- mias. Superabant adhuc XXI. anni regiminis istius Artaxerxis: XIX. annis vero regnavit Darius No- thus, cujus successor fuit Artaxerxes ὁ μνήμων. In hujus ergo nonum annum incidit finis septem he- bdomadum vel XLIX. annorum.

§. CXIII. Decimo quinto congruit egregie Chronologia subsequentium hebdomadum. Nam à designato anno Artaxerxis Longimani, (quem Artaxerxem ab Esdra c. 7. indicari postea docebi- mus, neque alium esse Nehemiæ, quam Esdræ Ar- taxerxem penes omnes fere in confesso est) fluxere tot septimanæ, & anni, usque ad terminum defini- tum, quos ab Angelo designatæ. Tria intervalla hic numerantur: De primo septem septimanarum jam diximus, quod apte conveniat initio Epochæ nobis probato. Alterum est sexaginta duarum septimanarum, à fine istarum septem inchoandum: vel sexaginta novem ab initio Epochæ Angelicæ: quod absolvitur annis CCCCLXXXIII. Tot ergo anni ad Christum Ducem solenniter proclamatum numerandi. Huic si conferamus prophanam Hi- storiam, rationem ita init Petavius, qui in XX. Lon- gimani Epochæ initium figit, regnare cepit Arta- xerxis ὁ μακρόχειρ anno I. Olympiad. LXXIX. ut è Diodoro Siculo l. XI. Bibl. colligitur, h. e. periodi Julianæ 4250. Annus itaque ejus vigesimus con- currit cum anno periodi Julianæ 4269. Porro an- nus decimus quintus Tiberii, secundum periodum Julianum est annus 4742. quo Christus baptizatus & munus suum aggressus est. Intervenere ergo inter vigesimum annum Longimani, & decimum quintum Tiberii anni CCCCLXXIII. juxta Peta- vii computum; adeoque desiderantur X. anni ad complendum sexaginta novem illas hebdomadas. Quia vero falli calculus angelicus nulla ratione po- test, necessum est, decennii illius defectum aliunde suppleri, quacunque tandem id ratione fieri queat per Chronologicam veritatem. Nam computus cœlestis nuncii omni exceptione superior est, ad quem Chronologia revocanda, non vice inversa & perversa cœlestis computus ad Chronologorum calculos examinandus. Id autem ut expediat Pe- tavius, Artaxerxem per decennium cum Patre Xerxe regnasse, atque inde à regiminis cum Patre suscepti tempore Scripturam Artaxerxis vigesimum annum numerare ait; quum filiorum annos ita nonnun- quam ab eo tempore, quo cum Patribus regnare ceperint, numeret. Diodorum Siculum vero pro- prii regiminis initium designare. Sic ergo ini- tium proprii regiminis Artaxerxis fuerit annus

Periodi Julianae 4250. initium regiminis cum Patre suscepti, (quod Scriptura respiciat) annus Periodi Julianae fuerit 4240. adeoque annus XX. regiminis Longimani secundum Scripturam concurret cum anno Periodi Julianae 4259. a quo usque ad annum Per. Jul. 4742. numerantur 483. anni h. e. septi- manae sexaginta novem. Quod geminum ini- tium regiminis Artaxerxis Longimani Dionysius Petavius collegit ex eo, quod Themistoclis fuga ex Graecia, & adventus in Persiam a Diodoro Siculo in annum II. Olymp. LXXVII. conjiciatur, qui Xerxis caedem septennio antecessit. Idem v. Themistocles juxta Thucydidis narrationem ad Artaxerxem tum literas dederit νεωστὶ βασιλεύοντα. Fuit ergo νεωστὶ βασιλεύων jam 7. annis ante caede parentis, adeoque ad regnum septem annis ad mi- nimum ante obitum patris adscitus est. Similis est conciliatio Dn. Wilhelmi Langii l. II. de annis Christi c. 15. p. 326. qui itidem docet 7. annis ad minimum Artaxerxem cum Patro regnasse. Ja- cobus etiam Tirinus in Chron. Sacr. c. 28. e mul- tis autoribus probatae fidei confirmat, Artaxerxem non a morte demum Patris, sed multis ante annis una cum Patre imperium administrasse.

§. CXIV. Quanquam vero nonnihil discrepent Petavius & Langius in initio annorum Imperii Ar- taxerxis, in termino tamen a quo & ad quem Epo- chae Danielis apprime consentiunt. De Petavii sententia ita judicat Langius: Petavius nisi falsam rationem in anno passionis sequutus fuisset, verissima prodidisset. Nunc vero & uno anno minus Epo- cham Artaxerxis antecedentia detrusit, & annum passionis in tertium hebdomadis septuagesimae ineun- tem confert. At tertius annus incipiens non est me- dium hebdomadis annalis sed quartus. Decisio li- tis istius, utra sententia praeferenda? magnam par- tem a vera ratione anni σταυρωσίμου, & definitione annorum ministerii Christi dependet. Quae res peculiarem ἐξέτασιν requireret. Ne autem in ea aberremus, cavit coelestis temporum metator, cum dimidiam hebdomadam muneri Christi in his ter- ris assignavit, usq; ad passionem Christi, cujus tem- pus hoc tam illustri & augusto oraculo assignari maxime conveniebat. Quum enim alia minutio- ra accurate de Christo in Vetero Testamento defi- nita sint, congruum omnino erat, ut res haec tanti momenti, quot annos Christus in officio subeundo con- ficere debuerit, haud negligeretur a Prophetis, quae quum nuspiam alias definita fit, in hac exquisitiffi- ma Gabrielis temporum supputatione expediunda erat. Refellit autem Petavium Dn. Langius, quod in tertium incipientem hebdomadis ultimae passionem Christi retulerit. Quam sententiam part. II. libr. IV. c. 4. p. 226. Rationar. tempor. ita proposuerat Petavius: Nos anno praedicationis tertio passum esse Christum asserimus, ac biennium integrum cum men- sibus aliquot supervixisse baptismo. Unde passioni Christi assignavit annum Julianum LXXVI. & O- lympiadis 202. annum secundum exeuntem, perio- di Julianae 4744. Quum vero haec non conveniant cum Phlegontis Tralliani observatione, quod anno quarto Olympiadis CCII. Eclipsis Solis fuerit omniu prius cognitarum maxima μεγίστη τῶν ἐγχωρισμέ- νων πρότερον (quae fuit diei emortualis Christi ecli- psis Matth. 27. Luc. 23. v. 44.) non immerito, quan- tum ad designationem anni σταυρωσίμου, reprobatur Petaviana opinio. Caeterum quo argumento Dn. Langius Petavium premit, quod tertius annus in- cipiens non sit medium hebdomadis annalis, sed quar- tus, eodem premitur & ipse, quod sc. quatuor com- Pleti anni & quod excurrit, non faciant medium heb- domadis. Statuit enim D. Langius, necessarium ac plane certum esse, quinq; paschata in ministerio Christi acta fuisse l. 2. de ann. Christ. c. X. p. 477. statuit Christum solidos quatuor annos prædicasse, a Paschate nempe anni 47. Juliani ad Pascha 78. c. IX. p. 420. Non ergo sibi satis constat. Passioni Christi IV. Nonas Aprilis assignat, & diem XV. Men- sis Nisan sive primi (vel secundæ Aprilis) Baptismum autem Christi refert ad VI. Januar. c. 2. p. 356. Si ea, quæ de Christo post baptismum usq; ad primum Pa- scha gesta sunt, accuratius considerentur, manifestum erit VI. Januarii magis isti tempori convenire, quam (ut multi cum Epiphanio) VIII. Novembris. Ideoq; adhuc tres fere menses ultra quadriennium confe- cisset Christus in ministerio. Quomodo autem 4. anni cum 3. mensibus medium erunt septimanæ, quod tribuitur confirmationi pacti per Christum, usque ad ejus excisionem, & sacrificiorum ablatio- nem? Et quomodo anno quarto ineunte hebdoma- dis septuagesimæ passus est Christus, quod asserit Lan- gius c. 9. pag. 420. si integros quatuor annos, & tres menses docendo consumsit? Sic ministerii CHRISTI initium non incidet in terminum LXIX. hebdomadum, sed in annum VI. (inclusive) hebdomadis sexagesimæ nonæ. At Angelus defi- nivit accurate tempus adventus Messiæ נגיד: imo neque constabit ita ἀκριβῶς ex oraculo Angelico tempus passionis Christi. Quod repugnat ipsius Langii sententiæ. Sic enim ille c. 10. p. 424. Non enim ulla Prophetiæ nativitatis tempus accurate præ- dixit, ut hujus causa natalis accuratissime necessario inquirenda esset: quod in passionis tempore faciendum fuit. Hujus enim tempus Daniel ACCURATISSIME dixit, ideoq; illud summo studio, summaque diligentia inquiri debet, ut & Daniel vera prædixisse, & Jesus verus Messias esse demonstretur. Porro nec septi- manæ ultimæ Danielis ratio constabit, si Langii sententia per omnia obtineat. Nam juxta ora- culum Danielis medietas ejus altera porrigit sese usque ad sacrificiorum cessationem, morte Christi factam. De quo Langius in explicatione Ora- culi Danielis: Dicit porro (Angelus) Messiam tol- lendum esse post istas 62. hebdomades, h. e. istas, quæ septem priores sequebantur. Adeoque post finitas ab edicto emisso 69. hebdomadas tolli Christus de- bebat. Et quidem MEDIA HEBDOMADE LXX. Tum enim sacrificium & oblationem quiesce- re fecit. Quod quidem alia ratione factum non fuit, nisi quod sacrificia & oblationes post illud tempus nul- lum usum haberent. Nam ex Josepho patet, victi- mas immolatas fuisse usq; ad supremum urbis exci- dium, at ante excidium hæc tolli debebant. De usu ergo sive fructu sacrificiorum Daniel loquitur, quæ morte sua Christus inutilia reddidit, semel pro nostris peccatis oblatus. Erunt ergo ab egressu edicti ad mortem CHRISTI anni solidi 486. & 487. ineunte Dominus passus erit. Hæc Dominus Langius l. II. de ann. Christi cap. 9. pag. 417. Jam quod ad alteram medietatem ultimæ septimanæ, non apparet, quomodo ea ex Langiana sententia certo haberi possit. Restabunt ita quatuor solidi anni; quia in mense Nisan initium, & rursus finem quoque in eodem mense ponit hebdomadum. Nu- meravit autem Langius in confirmatione pacti pe- nes Judæos post Christi passionem duos solum aut tres annos. Quomodo ergo restitissent adhuc quatuor solidi anni, aut etiam plures? Nam & plu- res annos largitur Langius, adeoque LXX. hebdo- madum intervallo a Daniele definito non acqui- escit l. c. p. 420. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Confirma- vit vero Christus pactum cum multis hebdomade una. Nimirum tota hæc Prophetia ad Judæos spectat: vox ergo multi etiam ad Judæos pertinet, cum quibus no- vum pactum Christus confirmavit SEPTEM ET ULTRA (NB. ULTRA, quod quomodo con- fonet verbis Angeli, accuratissime tempus defini- entibus, autor viderit) annis usque ad ultimum an- num hebdomadis LXX. (ille non erit ultimus termi- nus, si ULTRA extendatur ultima septimana, fi- quidem reliquæ per se completæ sint) Quippe cum ipse solidos quatuor annos Judæis prædicasset, à pa- schate nempe anni 74. Juliani ad pascha 78. discipu- los suos Evangelium postea annunciare jussit. Qui annis duobus aut tribus proximis post ascensionem so- los Judæos admittebant. Imo & altercabantur, si quis gentilibus prædicaret. Sed tandem, finito isto tempore, quod supra Judæos decisum erat, Apostoli à Judæis audire nolentibus, & gratiam respuentibus, se converterunt ad gentes. Denique nullum mere- tur assensum computus ille Langianus, quod nova & inaudita ratione fingat, diem passionis Christi fuisse feriam non VI. quod hactenus credidere o- mnes, si forte unum Paulum Foro semproniensem excipias, sed quintam; in qua persuasione ita sibi placet, ut eandem etiam ad B. Chemnitii senten- tiam, quem Theologos Germaniæ sequi ait, re- fellendam τῆς παῤῥησίας adhibeat: Illud tamen, inquit c. 10. pag. 422. satis manifestum est, Christum juxta Chemnitii opinionem baptizatum esse post pa- scha anni Juliani 73. Ideoque primum pascha est anni 74. alterum 75. tertium 76. quartum 77. Sed hoc anno IMPOSSIBILE est Christum passum fuis- se. Neque enim ipse Chemnitius negaverit, Chri- stum in parasceve Paschatis feria V. passum esse. Quia ista ita ex Scripturis demonstrantur, ut homini Christiano contra fari integrum sit. At hæc duo nun- quam anno 74. convenire possunt: ut antea manife- ste demonstravimus. Ergo neque hoc anno Chri- stus passus est. Sed de hac ejus novella opinione non est hic dicendi locus. Et profligavit eam erudite Dn. Wandalinus, Theologus nunc Haffnien- sis, Amicus noster singularis Diatrib. Historicâ Theologicâ de feria passionis & triduo mortis Christi, novis & paradoxis opinionibus Langia- nis opposita, & cum approbatione Vener. Fa- cult. Theolog. in Academia Lipsiensi Anno CIO IOC LI. edita.

§. CXV. Hæc itaque de Petavii & Langii sententia, quæ neutra probari simpliciter po- test, siquidem ille in designatione anni passionis Christi aperte erret, quem hic recte quidem, cum Phlegonte Tralliano, Olympiades CCII. quartum (periodi Julianæ 4746. in quo Scaliger & Calvisius consentiunt) assignat, sed in oraculi angelici tam explicatione, quam applicatione, ut ostensum, non uno modo fallitur. Rectius tamen uterque initium Epochæ nostræ designat, quam alii, cum id annum XX. Artaxerxis Longimani constituunt, mediumque septimanæ ultimæ in- cidere in passionem Christi judicant; etsi in initio in eo discrepent, quod annum XX. Longimani 4241. Periodi Julianæ faciat Langius; Petavius vero annum 4240. Per Julian. quæ unius anni est differentia.

§. CXVI. Lansbergius facile consentit de initio Regni Artaxerxis, quod colligavit pariter cum Iphiti 313. & Nabonassaræo 284. in Chronol. S. l. II. c. 9. p. 69. Xerxes, inquit, interfectus est ab Arta- bano, teste Diodoro, Olympiadis septuagesimæ octavæ anno quarto, hoc est, anno Iphiti trecentesimo & duo- decimo. Itaq; Artaxerxes Longimanus solus re- gnare cœpit anno Iphiti trecentesimo & decimo tertio, hoc est, anno à Nabonassare Juliano ducentesimo octu- agesimo quarto cum dimidio. Non autem in deci- mum annum solitarii regiminis Artaxerxis Epo- chæ nostræ initium cum Petavio refert, sed in an- num septimum, numerans ab initio regiminis ejus usque ad edictum annos solidos sex cum mensibus no- vem, ut id cadat in annum à Nabonassare 291. Julia- num cum mensibus tribus. Addit ergo annos so- lidos 486. usque ad annum passionis Christi, unde prodit annus Nabonassaris 777. Qui vero annus Petavio non est σταυρώσιμος, sed inauguralis po- tius & auspicalis muneris Christi, annus, inquam, Baptismi, non passionis ejus. Verum enim vero de anno passionis Christi suffragium haud meretur Lansbergius. Nam annus Nabonassareus 777. secundum periodum Julianam est 4742. Iphiteus 805. At crucifixus indubie est Christus anno Iphiteo 808. juxta observationem Phlegontis, quæ in Chronicis Eusebii annotata est, ac à Tertulliano, A- fricano, Origene l. II. contra Cels. Hieronymo, Pau- lo Diacono Histor. Mils. II. l. 2. & aliis Patribus de Eclipsi illa extraordinaria diei passionis Christi ex- plicata. Deficit ergo triennium. Deinde in explicatione oraculi Danielis observamus etiam quandam ἑαυτομαχίαν vel αντιλογίαν in Lansber- gio. Fatetur l. II. Chronol. c. 11. p. 81. In princi- pio septimanæ septuagesimæ unctum esse Sanctum il- lum Sanctorum Christum Jesum, & Principatum Christi inivisse: & uti pag. 87. loquitur, promulgas- se ipsum populo Israelitico annum acceptum Domino: Fatetur in medio illius septimanæ satisfecisse Christum pro nobis in cruce, & per mortem abolovisse omnia V. T. sacrificia, unde aulæum scissum in duas partes in morte ipsius Matth. 27, 51. Quo de porro ita loqui- tur pag. 87. Porro & tempus definit Angelus, in quo Christus sacrificia & oblationes legales, per mortem suam abrogaturus sit, nimirum dimidia septimana septuagesima, hoc est, anno quarto ejusdem septimanæ. Erat is annus ab edicto Artaxerxis Longimani 487. sed à Nabonassare 777. Edictum enim Artaxerxis Longimani promulgatum est anno à Nabonassare 291. Itaque si ad hunc annum addantur septimanæ sexaginta novem, cum unius septimanæ semisse, hoc est, anni 486. cadet medium septimanæ septuagesimæ in annũ à Nabonassare 777. in quo Angelus Christum moriturum esse dicit, & per mortem suam finem im- positurum sacrificiis & oblationibus legalibus. Sed quum inter Christi Baptismum & ipsius passionem intercedere solidum tantum biennium cum mensi- bus tribus asserat, non video, quomodo id prorsus cum Angeli vaticinio conveniat. Nam Angelus à principio muneris ejus septimanam dimidiam as- signat usque ad passionem ejus. At quomodo bi- ennium cum tribus mensibus potest dimidiam septi- manam efficere?

§. CXVII. Sed hisce missis, de eo imprimis videamus, quod hic præcipuum est, anne annum septimum Artaxerxis Longimani recte constituat Lansbergius terminum à quo Epochæ nostræ? Du- bium potissimum est, quod tale edictum anno se- ptimo Artaxerxis Longimani non exierit, quale à Gabriele hic indigitatur. Nam expresse sermo hic est de edicto de reædificatione Hierosolymæ, & platearum, & murorum ejus. Quod vero anno septimo Artaxerxis promulgatum legitur Esdr. 7. nihil videtur habere de ædificatione Hierosolymæ, platearum aut murorum, sed tantum de quibus- dam ad cultum sacrum pertinentibus, de transfe- rendis vafis sacris, de conferendis sumtibus Regiis ad sacrificia &cultum divinum,de privilegiis & ex- emptionibus Sacerdotum & Levitarum, de consti- tuendis item judicibus & curatoribus per Judæam. Quod urget etiam Dn. Langius l. II. c. 9. Lansber- gius a VII. anno Artaxerxis numerare incipit, sed tum non de urbe ædificanda edictum factum fuit, quod falso supponit, sed tantum de templo,iisque quæ sacrificia concernunt. Et notavit id jam olim Sul- pitius Severus l. II. Histor. Sacr. Ego, inquit, Esdram nihil super reficienda urbe egisse comperio, credo potiorem ei fuisse curam plebem corruptis mo- ribus reformandi. Verum enim vero probe id ad- vertit Lansbergius ipse, ideoque conjunxit edi- ctum utrumque Artaxerxis l. II. c. 11. Chron. S. p. 83. Inter hæc edicta, inquit,nullum est, quod cum An- geli descriptione convenit, quam edictum Artaxerxis Longimani. Cyrus enim & Darius Hystaspis edi- cta ita promulgarunt de ædificando templo,non autem de restituendis & de ædificandis Hierosolymis. At Artaxerxes Longimanus utrumque publicavit, at- que effecit primum quidem per Esdram, alterum per Nehemiam. Distinguit hæc, de RESTITU- ENDIS, ET ÆDIFICANDIS Hierosolymis. Prius refert ad edictum primum Artaxerxis de RESTITUENDIS Hierosolymis, Ecclesiastico & politico statu,per Esdram legis peritum, Esdræ 7. Posterius ad alterum edictum refert de ædifican- dis Hierosolymorum muris per Nehemiam Regis Pincernam Nehem. 2, 1. Sic ergo Esdras pene to- tus,utputa inde à Cap. 7. ac totus Nehemias in edi- cto illo utroque,de restituendis & de reædificandis Hierosolymis ejusque exequutione occupabitur. Quicquid vero sit de illa verborũ Ebræorũ Angeli explicatione de RESTITUENDIS & ÆDIFI- CANDIS Hierosolymis,retinemus simplicem ex- positionem de exitu sermonis AD REVERTI FACIENDUM & ÆDIFICANDUM Hierusa- lem, ad quam reædificationem Hierosolymæ cer- te non requirebatur sola murorũ & platearum ad- ornatio, etsi ea etiam commemoretur, ut in se- ptem priorum tempora eandem incidere consta- ret, sed imprimis opus erat reparatione politias cum Ecclesiastica, tum civilis, quæ ad formam in- ternam civitatis,& ut vere sit civitas, ac populus,& quidẽ civitas sancta,ac populus in ea populus san- ctus,omnino pertinebat. Non ergo ab hac præ- dictione aliena sunt ea,quæ Esdras expedivit. Re- duxit enim vi diplomatis Regii Judæos cives in Je- rusalem,& immunitatem accepit leges civicas,Ma- gistratus & judices constituendi,unde dubium nul- lum est, civitatem reædificatam tum fuisse. Ante id tempus, inquit Funccius, tantummodo permissum erat Judæis, ædificare templum, & sacra secundum legem Dominis administrare. Nunc autem cum Esdras mittitur, accedit Reipubl. confirmatio, & li- bertas sub propriis Magistratibus vivendi, quæ me Hercule, vera urbis ædificatio est. Nam si qua his destituta erit, utcunque sit vallo muroque munita, tamen urbs dici merito non potest. Ut taceam,quod illa duo μανρέχεια, edicta Rempubl. & urbem concernentia videri possint proxime & intratrien- nium se consequuta, & quasi pro uno æstimari pos- sint; tum quod ab uno eodemque Rege profecta sint,tum quod concernant restitutionem civitatis, qua formam internam & externam ejusdem, tum quod immediate fere sese exceperint. De qui- bus etiam B. Gesnerus disp. IX. in Dan. §. 147. Quia hæc duo mandata ab eodem Rege Longimano, deque eadem re, nimirum de restauratione non tem- pli,sed urbis & politiæ sunt edita, ideo pro eodem me- rito habentur. Quod eatenus videtur magis con- sentaneum, si dicatur, Esdram septimum annum numeraffe solitarii Regiminis Artaxerxis, quæ e- tiam ni fallor est Lansbergii de priori edicto sen- tentia : Nehemiam autem annum XX. & XXXII. ejusdem Artaxerxis commemorantem, respexisse non annos solitarii Regiminis, sed XX. & XXXII. annum ex quo à Parente Xerxe in societatem regni adscitus fuit. Quod posterius de Nehemiæ com- puto non advertit quidem Lansbergius, observa- vit tamen Petavius, & Langius; quemadmodum vicissim prius de Esdra, quod numerarit annos solitarii regiminis Artaxerxis, non observavit Pe- tavius, aut Langius, sed recte animadvertit, & ex historicis observationibus & Characteri- bus chronologicis eruit ac probavit Lansbergius, libr. II. Chron. S. cap. IX. pag. 68. per calculum Eclipsium demonstrans septimum annum Artaxerxis Longimani fuisse ducentesimum nonagesimum pri- mum a Nabonassare. Sic ergo duo illa edicta Ar- taxerxis tribus annis solum distabunt. Sed hoc Chronologis aliisque eruditis expendendum re- linquimus. Neque enim in eo summa rei consi- stit. Et sive dicatur Nehemias eandem prosequi annorum rationem, quam Esdras, sive, ut quando- que fieri observamus in collatione regiminis Re- gum Israelis & Judæ in libris Regum designa- ti, & computi eorundem Regum in libris Chronicorum observati, alter annos numeret solitarii, alter socii regiminis, nostræ sententiæ certitudini nihil decedit. Quamvis hunc septi- mum annum solitarie regnantis Artaxerxis respice- re etiam Cedrenum, Cornelium à Lapide, Buchol- zerum, Capellum, Funccium, Angelocratorem ob- servet Tirinus in Chronol. Sacr. cap. XXXVIII. Quod etiam de Basilio Seleuciensi notavit, quod nempe idcirco ab anno 8. regni Artaxerxis 70. hebdomadum Danielis initium duxerit; siqui- dem Xerxes per XX. annos regnarit, & septen- nio suscepti ab Artaxerxe filio regiminis elapso, octavo anno ineunte, edictum illud exierit.

§. CXVIII. Decimo sexto congruet ita exacte tempus passionis Christi definitum ab An- gelo, cum chronologico computo. Optima autem computandi ratio est, quæ per Olympiadas instituitur, de qua Iulius Africanus, libro III. an- nalium, referente Eusebio libr. X. de præparat. Evangel. cap. ult. ita judicavit: usque ad Olympia- des nihil exploratum in Græcorum historia inveni- tur, sed omnia sunt confusis scripta temporibus, post Olympiades autem, quoniam quadriennio diligentis- sime omnia notabantur, nulla penitus confusio tem- porum apparet. Scaliger in Chronologic. con- tra Pareum Elenchis hoc illam computandi ratio- nem mactavit elogio: Olympias custos temporum, vindex historicæ veritatis, frenatrix fanaticæ Chro- nologorum licentiæ. Neque in S. S. neque in historia Epochis ullum intervallum melius explicatum est, quam illud à prima Olympiade ad Alexandrum, & hinc ad Epocham Antiochenorum Iulianam, quod quidem tanti est, ut quidquid nobis ad templi exicidium in historia sacra compertum est, totum illi intervallo acceptum referri debeat. Hoc ergo computo si hic utamur, constat è Diodoro Siculo l. XI. Bibl. Artaxerxis Longimani regnum cœpis- se anno 1. Olympiadis LXXIX. vel 313. Iphiteo. Annus ergo septimus apud Esdram erit Iphiti 326. Si jam ad trecentesimum vigesimum primum Iphi- teum currentem addantur anni 486. hoc est, sexa- ginta novem hebdomadæ, cum dimidia, prodi- bunt 807. anni Iphiti. Atque ita consonat an- an- notatio Phlegontis, quod Christus passus sit anno quarto Olympiadis ducentesimae secundae. D. Pap- pus ita rationem init in Comment. in Dan. Mors Alexandri Magni incidit in annum 1. Olymp. 114, id est, Iphiti 453. intervallum ergo est annorum 356. usque ad Iphiti 808. vel passionis Christi an- num. Quibus addas: Artaxerxis Long. 33 Nothi 19 Mnemonis 41 Ochi 23 Codomanni 6 Alexandri 6 post devictum Codomannum. Hi ergo 130. anni superioribus 356. additi, summam efficiunt annorum 486. quot sc. a septimo Longimani fluxe- re usque ad passionem Domini, quibus si 3 1/2. an- nos usque ad finem Epochae Danielis adjicias, in- cidet finis in annum 490. ab anno Artaxerxis Lon- gimani septimo. Si canonem Regum ma- nuscriptum Claudii Ptolomaei, uti exhibetur in Chronolog. D. Behm. pag. 260. sequamur, com- putus hic erit: Anni 33. restant ab VIII. Artaxer- xis I. quem vocat, Darii II. anni sunt 19 Artaxer- xis secundi 46. Ochi 21. Arogi 2. Darii tertii 4. qui anni Regum Persarum juncti efficiunt 125. Graecorum Regum, secundum illum Canonem, anni sunt 302. Alexandri Beati 8. Philippi Ari- daei 7. Alexandri Aei 12. Graecorum Regum in Aegypto, Ptolomaei Lagi 20. Ptolom. Philadel- phi 38. Ptolomaei Evergetis primi 25. Ptolomaei Philopatris 17. Ptol. Epiphanis 24. Ptol. Philo- matris 35. Ptolom. Everg. secundi 29. Ptol. Soteris 36. Dionysii 29. Cleopatrae 22. Denique Ro- manorum Regum huc spectant anni 65. utpote Augusti anni 43. Tiberii 22. quorum ultimus concurrit cum septimanae ultimae exitu, siquidem XV. Tiberii, quo baptizatus Christus, exeat 69. Septimana. Anni illi 125. 302. 65. in summam collecti efficiunt 492. quos complent hebdoma- des mysticae. Biennium illud, quod redundat, fa- cile expeditur usitata distinctione inclusive & ex- clusive numerationis. Sic ergo consonat etiam Chronologia Regum, juxta Ptolomaei observa- tiones. Lansbergius ita rationem init: Septi- mum annum Artaxerxis Longimani facit 291. Na bonassar. his addit sexaginta novem septimanas, h. e. annos 483. emergant 774. a Nabonassare ad principatum Christi; septennio postremo addito, exeunt LXX. hebdomadae anno 781. a Nabonassa- re, quo pacto & initialis, & finalis Epochae nostrae annus fuisset Sabbaticus & Iobeleus. Quod val- de concinnum videtur. Abraham Bucholzerus nobiscum in Indice Chronologico initium figit in anno VII. Artaxerxis Longimani a conditu Mun- di 3514. quibus si addantur anni 486. usque ad me- dium septimanae ultimae, vel annum σταυρώσιμον, cadet mors Christi in annum mundi juxta ejus computum 4600: Jubilaeum mundi 80. Mosis 30. quia morte sua abrogavit Christus Vet. Testam. & sacrificia ejus cessare fecit & vitae Jubilaeum sempi- ternum nobis acquisivit, & reduxit. Quem annum M. 4600. putat Bucholzerus ab Ezechiele indica- tum esse per 4000. cubitos in templi mystici de- scriptione, etsi Bucholzerus in eo a nostra abeat sententia, quod annum illum M. 4000. faciat non passionis sed Baptismi Christi annum ac hebdo- madas Danielis finiat in passione Christi.

§. CXIX. Ex adverso Scaligeriani non in- veniunt in hypothesi sua de exitu verbi anno secun- do Darii Nothi facto usque ad exterminium Hiero- folyma: LXX. hebdomadas, cum historiam ac com- plementum conferunt. Numerat enim Scaliger ipfe annos non 490. sed 403. & dimidium. Ideo- que fingunt addendam esse dimidiam adhuc septi- manam, atque in eum sensum etiam detorquere sa- tagunt verba angeli. Quod inprimis notandum est, inquit Calixtus l. c. LXX. septimanis ita in partes di- stributis adhuc subjungit (Angelus) semissem septi- manæ. Et roborabit pactum multis septimana una, & dimidio septimanæ cessare faciet sacrificiũ&ob- lationẽ. Summa collecta facit non tantũ præcise septi- manas LXX. sed LXX. cü semisse, quæ certe semissis neu- tiquam negligenda, in numerum quoque cum reliquis venire debet. Et postea: cum igitur annus secun- dus Darii Nothi incidat in annum Mundi MMMIƆ XXVII. ante natum Christum CCCCXXI. si ab eo an- no putentur anni CCCCXCIID. quot septimanæ LXX. & dimidia conficiunt, fiet, ut CCCCXCIII. ille annus incipiat currente anno post natum Christum LXXII. Eræ autem Dionysianæ LXX. quo ipso desiit juge sa- crificium ob penuriam sacerdotum, die XVII. Jul. (ut scribit Josephus l. VII. hist. c. 4.) incensum & exustum est templum die 10. Augusti (ibid. c. 9.) superior urbs capta octavo Septembris (ibid. c. 18.) atque ita eversa est Jerusalem, & deleta politia Judaica, & facta de- solatio & consummatio, quam prædixerat Angelus. Cum hæc exacte conveniant, nullo alio, ut ante dixi- mus, argumento nobis opus est, ut probemus, à secun- do anno Darii Nothi initium septimanarum facien- dum esse. Quam inepta sit illa verborum Angeli στρεβλότης, supra jam diximus. Hic notanda im- primis ἑαυτομαχία Calixti: Angelicorum enim verborum hunc facit sensum: Septimanas LXX. DECISAS, DETERMINATAS sive CONSTI- TUTAS dici super populum & urbem idem esse, quod tantundem præfinitum esse, quo maneant urbs & po- pulus usꝙ ad excidium suum. Et numerat hic Ca- lixtus X. Jubilæos, quorum quisque 49. annos con- tinet: LXX. inquit, Septimanæ decisæ sunt, illæ vero constituunt annos CCCCXC.& VII. septimanas deci- sas continent, i. e. X. Jubilæos conficiunt. Quomodo ergo addi potest dimidia septimana? Anne 493½. anni sunt X. Jubilæi aut 70. septimanæ decisæ h. e. ἀποτόμως & accurate definitæ? In B. Dorschei dis- putatione de LXX. hebdomad. à M. Johan. Frid. Heilbrunner habita, etsi idem initium idemq; ter- minus ad quem, qui à Scaligero, designetur & adse- ratur, de hac determinatione laudatur th. XX. Se- dor Olam. Dixit R. Jose: quod est dictum, septimanæ LXX. præcisæ sunt, docet quod fuerint PRÆDE- TERMINATÆ ante per LXX. annos: Et sic dictum Gen. 7. v. 3. Et erunt dies ejus 120. anni. Non potuit sic dici nisi quod fuit definitum & præcisione præcisum ante apud Dominum. Hæc monenda duximus contra Scaligerum, illam præcisionem non in genere duntaxat ad summam totam, sed particulariter etiam ad singu- las septimanas pertinere.

§. CXX. Quod autem objicit Calixtus, ab Artaxerxis tempore, sive VII. cum Abrahamo Bu- cholzero, sive XX. anno cum Johanne Temporario Epocham incipiamus septimanarum, finem produci plusquam XX. annos ultra excidium urbis; hypothe- sis assumta precario, non concessa, neque conce- denda, quia longe falsissima, ipsum fefellit, nempe quod Artaxerxes Mnemon ab Esdra & Nehemia, in VII. & XX. anni designatione intelligatur. Cæ- teroquin agnoscunt Scaligeriani, recte se habere computum chronologicũ, si putentur anni à tem- poribus Artaxerxis Longimani, quemadmodum Bucholzeri, Temporarii, & aliorum, adeoque e- tiam nostra fert sententia. B. Behmius ita argumen- tum tatur l. II. IV. III. c. VII. Chronolog. manuduct. Si LXX. illæ hebdomades finiuntur in Dominica pas- sione, necesse est terminum à quo incidere in Artaxer- xis Longimani tempora in annum quasi sextum vel septimum. Major, inquit, manifesta. Messias crucifixus anno quarto Olympiadis 202. vel Olym- piadico 808. ad finem decurrente. Qua in re COM- MUNIS Chronologorum CONSENSUS est. De- tractis 490. annis, remanent 318. vel annus secundus Olympiadis 89. Quo tempore Artaxerxem Longi- manum in Perside regnasse veritas cœlestis motus contra Beroaldistas firmat, & Funcciani aliiq́, id non negant. Hæc D. Behmius.

§. CXXI. Non finit Angelus septimanas in passione Christi, ut non pauci volunt: sed passionem abolentem sacrificia locat in medium septimanæ novissimæ. Non enim dicit : In fine hebdoma- dæ, sed IN MEDIO deficiet hostia & sacrifi- cium, cum sc. offeretur unicum illud verum expia- torium sacrificium. Atque ita convenient cum oraculo Danielis exacte anni ministerii Christi, ut communiter à nostris numerantur. Nam assigna- vit confirmationi fœderis gratiæ per Christum fu- turæ Gabriel dimidium septimane, h. e. annos tres cum dimidio. Ita ergo triennium cum dimidio assignandum erit ministerio Christi, à baptismo sc. Christi usque ad excisionem, vel passionem ejus, abolentem & mortificantem sacrificia Levitica : ubi tamen monendum, non opus esse, ut ἀποτόμως annum dimidium, h.e. sex præcise menses ultra tri- ennium assignemus ministerio Christi, sed neces- sum tamen esse, ut dicatur Christum non per annum solum prædicasse, aut eodem anno, quo ba- ptizatus est, mortuum esse, quemadmodum Tertul- lianum libr. advers. Jud. Clementem Alexandrinum l. 1. Stromat. Julium Africanum l. V. Annal. Lactan- tium libr. IV. Institut. c. X. statuere observat Pere- rius l. XI. in Daniel. q. VII. neque etiam solum per biennium, uti Apollinarem Laodicen. & alios non- nullos sensisse notat idem Pererius, quam etiam Pe- tavii & Lansbergii fuisse mentem, antea observa- vimus, sed triennium solidum exegisse in docendi munere, cum aliquot mensibus, qui sc. inde à tem- pore Baptismi usque ad Pascha effluxere. Adhæc ut constet calculus angelicus, necessum est, ut mini- sterio Christi non assignentur quatuor anni com- pleti, cum Langio & illis, qui quinq́ Paschata Chri- sto tribuunt. Quapropter suffecerit, si solidum triennium docendo consumserit cum mensibus aliquot. Quæ sententia ex historia Evangelica confirmari solet, quod ea omne tempus prædica- tionis Christi per quatuor paschata distinxerit à Baptismo usque ad mortem. Primum Joh. 2. quod post baptismum proximum fuit. Alterum Joh. 5. quod festum ἐξοχικῶς nominatū ab Irenæo lib. II. cap. 39. Eusebio in Chronicis & in c. 8. Demonstr. Evang. Hieronymo item & Theodoreto in h. l. ac Ruperto in Joh. 5. de Paschate intelligitur. Quam sententiam etiam probat B. Chemnitius in Harmon. Evange- lic. Proleg. c. 3. docens aut festum illud Joh. 5. v. 2. Pascha esse, aut certe concedendum esse aliud pa- scha intermedium, inter illud quod Joh. 2, 13. descri- bitur, & quod sequitur Joh. 6, 4. Alii secundum Pa- scha quærunt Matth. 12. Marc. 2. Luc. 6. vid. Bucholtzer. in Chronolog. Tertium cap. 6. Johan. Quartum denique c. 11. 13. 18. Cui etiam pondus non leve accedit à Veterum autoritate; Siquidem communis fere Patrum sententia fuerit, Christum post Baptismum prædicasse Evangelium tribus an- nis integris & aliquanto plus. Hoc enim sensit Evodius Apostolorum discipulus, teste Nicephoro

Libr. II. Hist. Eccl. c. 3. hoc Ignatius Martyr statuit Epist. ad Trallianos, hanc veterem Ecclesiæ traditio- nem fuisse Eusebius perhibet l. IIX. demonstr. Ev- angel. & sententiam illam amplectitur quoque i- pse in Chronicis, atque è S. Johannis historia Evan- gelica deducit; hanc etiam sententiam fovit Chry- sostomus hom. XXIII. in Matth. ut & Theodoretus in Dan. IX. cap. & alii. Quos denique etiam multi è recentioribus sequuntur B. Lutherus, Funccius, Chemnitius & plerique alii. Et ea ratione expli- cantur quoque verba Angeli ab auctore Historiæ Scholasticæ in historia Danielis c. X. ut & à Dionysio Carthusiano in Commentar. ad Daniel. IX. apud Pererium sub finem libr. X. in Daniel. Quæ sen- tentia probatur B. Chemnitio nostro, imo ceu communis & recepta laudatur. Eruditæ sunt, in- quit, cogitationes Lutheri & aliorum, qui ex Danie- le colligunt talem supputationem, dicit enim Propheta (confirmabit pactum multis hebdomada una, & in dimidio hebdomadis cessare faciet hostiam & sacrifi- cium) scilicet oblata victima sui corporis. Facit au- tem dimidia septimana tres annos & dimidium. Hinc sumta est communis & recepta sententia, quæ etiam in Theophili fragmentis extat, Christum in ministe- rio suo, dicendo & faciendo versatum esse annos tres & totidem menses. seu dies, quot intercesserunt à Ba- ptismo ad primum Pascha. Et huic sententiæ etiam exteræ historiæ suffragantur. Eusebius enim ex Eth- nicorum Commentariis recitat, defectiionem illam So- lis, quæ tempore passionis Christi facta est, annotatam esse, quod contigerit quarto anno 202. Olympiadis. Et quod tempus illud inciderit in 18. annum Tyberii, cujus anno decimo quinto Christus ministerium suum inchoaverat. Adde & è Pontificiis consensum Tiri- ni Jesuitæ Chron. S. c. 47. p. 61. Non video quod so- lide quis possit dubitare de anno mortis, cum tam ex Evangelistis, quam ex perpetua traditione habea- mus, Christum non nisi tribus annis cum trimestri prædicasse, seu à Baptismo supervixisse, ut patebit ex cap. 49. Neque ullus est veterum qui prædica- tioni Christi solidum quadriennium tribuat. Et quomodo alioquin in medio 70. hebdomadis, quod prædixit Daniel, occisum Christum demon- strabimus?

§. CXXII. Decimo octavo posterioris me- dietatis septimanæ ultimæ ratio ita etiam recte sibi constat, si complementum cum vaticinio confe- ramus. Nam ita triennium & aliquot menses re- stabunt ad complendam novissimam septimanam, & absolvendam Epocham hanc mysticam, per quod tempus confirmatum fuit fœdus Judæis post ascensionem Christi, & conversi sunt multi è Judæis per Apostolorum præconium. Quo etiam facie- bat primum Concilium Nov. Test. quod Hieroso- lymis celebratum fuit ad fœderis gratiæ confirma- tionem Act. 15, 11. Conf. Jer. 30, 30. Hic enim præci- puus Concilii scopus fuit. Quod circiter qua- driennio post resurrectionem coactum est, ut non- nullis placet. Et B. Lutherus V. IV. Jenensi La- tin. f. 617. asserit fere 3. aut 4. anno post resurrectio- nem Christi in Concilio Apostolorum Act. 15. pu- blica sententia decretum esse, tollendum esse legis onus à cervicibus discipulorum. Nam confirma- tio hæc novissimæ septimanæ gentem respicit Ju- daicam, quemadmodum de universis LXX. hebdo- madis dicitur, quod decisæ sint super Israeliticum po- pulum & super urbem sanctam, non autem super gentes: & promissus fuit Messias primo loco Judæis, quibus etiam inserviit ante alios populos. Ideo currente septimana LXX. Israëlitis solis, non autem palam etiam gentibus Evangelium prædicavit, &

prædicari curavit. Sub finem etiam hebdoma- dum legitur S. Paulus, gentium Doctor, Hierofo- lymam venisle, & cum Petro contulisle, unde in Syriæ & Ciliciæ regiones ex eo profectus est Act. 15. Gal. 1. Quæ sententia non improbatur Pererio, libr. XI. in Daniel p. 734. Refiduo hujus hebdomadis Apostoli magno studio & ardore animi Evangelium in Judæa prædicarunt: Et à B. Luthero nostro prius assumta fuit, etsi postea totam hebdomadam novissimam post excisionem Christi collocarit. Explicant ita etiam è recentioribus Jacob. Tirinus, Petavius, Lansbergius, Langius & alii. Fallitur ta- men Pererius, dum universam Epocham LXX. he- bdomadum ab anno XX. Artaxerxis ad annum IV. post Dominicam passionem, non annos CCCCXC. sed CCCCXCIII. efficere arbitratur: Ab Angelo autem non 70 1/2. hebdomadas sed numero rotundo 70. tan- tum constitui censet, quod contentus fuerit Angelus maximum illum eundemque plenum atque integrum LXX. hebdomadum numerum expressisse. Quæ opi- nio & verbis Angeli reclamat, utpote qui consti- tutas & ἀποτόμως decisas docet LXX. hebdoma- das, easque insuper tribuit in VII. LXII. & unam, ac minutias etiam dimidiæ septimanæ accurate exe- quitur: & à chronologica ratione aberrat, quem- admodum antea ostensum. Si vero cum aliis pla- ceat Hierosolymitanum Concilium in posteriora tempora rejicere, notabilis certe aliis ἀξιώμασι est quartus à motre Christi annus, in quem referunt nonnulli, & inter hos Tirinus in Chronico sacro Saulis conversionem, qui DOCTOR GEN- TIUM evasit Act. 9. (quam vero alii anno pri- mo post mortem Christi factam ajunt) & tranquil- litatem Christianis in tota Judæa, Galilæa & Sama- ria,sedato primo Judæorum furore, ac Tiberio Im- peratore accusatoribus Christianorum publico e- dicto mortem comminante, conciliatam Actor. 8. sed imprimis hoc anno ultimo hebdomadum, S. Pe- trus visione lintei pleni serpentibus didicit prædican- dum Evangelium etiam gentibus Act. 10,9. adeoq; rupto pariete intergerino in unam Ecclesiam coa- luere gentiles cum fidelibus Judæis. Hoc etiam anno, uti recte observat Bucholzerus in Indice Chronologico, nomen Christianorum primum or- tum est Antiochæ Act. 11. Judæorum inquit, nomen erat appellatio populi Dei, ea tunc definit rejecto po- pulo illo propter contemtum Messiæ, & mutatur in dulcissimum nomen Christianorum (id est, UNCTO- RUM) atque ita Ecclesia Dei à Christo, in quem cre- dit, & nomen & beneficia nomine ipso significata ac- cipit. Quæ optime fini Epochæ nostræ conveniunt; Nam initium ejus erat restitutio vel reparatio Hie- rosolymæ & populi Dei sancti ad legitimam politiæ formam: finis vero ejus est, postquam abunde, sed frustra confirmatum fuisset in Hierusalem & inter Judæos pactum Evangelicum assumtio gentilium in peculium Dei, & politiam Ecclesiasticam reliquia- rum Israelis per Petrum facta. Initium cepit, cum edicto Regis, manu Dei dirigente, Esdra provehente, de reparanda terrena Hierosolyma, & populi Dei sancto, novam quasi formam illic consequeretur. Finis incidit in cæleste edictum visione divina sanci- tum servo Apostolo commissum de amplianda spi- rituali Hierosolyma, quæ omnium nostrum mater est, per aggregationem gentilium, inque novam denominationem populi Domini; quia consequu- tus est à Christo nomen novum, longeque suavif- fimum. Deniq; in collationem istam magnorum illorum luminum & columinum Ecclesiæ S. Pauli nempe gentium Doctoris & S. Petri ut & S. Jacobi fratris Domini Act. 9. Gal. 1, 18. 19. quæ plurimum facit ad propagationem Evangelii, & ampliatio- nem pomœriorum Ecclesiæ, unde manifestum est, egregie convenire Epochæ initium & finem in ipso complemento, illudque eleganter respondere verbis & calculo cœlestis nuncii.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

The Consensus of the Doctors.

§. CXXIII. These reasons, therefore, support our opinion, to which also some weight is added by the authority of great Doctors and Chronologers. For although they do not all provide assent to the same thing in all parts, nor explain themselves in the same way, nor calculate by the same method, yet the principal Doctors and Chronologers agree with us, first regarding the term from which, that it ought to be referred to the times of Artaxerxes mentioned by Ezra and Nehemiah: some also in that it should be referred to the 7th year of Longimanus, which Ezra designates. Cedrenus, Luther, Funccius, Bucholcerus, Bullinger, Capellus, Rob. Baillie, Wendel. Lansbergius, Reusner, Bünting, Gesner, Joh. Cluverus, Vogelius, Edvard. Samsonius, Salmero, Henricus Philippi, etc. But those who refer it to the 20th year of Longimanus, regarding the matter itself, since most of them present lunar years, they easily agree with this Epoch of the 7th year, and seem to differ only in the mode of explanation. Which opinion is defended by the most ancient writer Julius Africanus in book V of the Annals, cited by Jerome in this place; Chrysostom in Orat. II against the Jews; Theodoret in this place; Bede in book II of the Exposition of Ezra, ch. 16, and in the book on the reckoning of time, ch. VI; Rupert in the book of Daniel, ch. 15; the author of the Historia Scholastica in the history of Daniel, ch. 10; Dionysius the Carthusian in this place; Comestor, ch. 10; Johannes Zonaras, Vol. I of the Annals; Antoninus in part 1 of the Chronicle, Tit. III, ch. VIII; Petrus Galatinus, book IV of the arcana of the catholic truth, ch. 16; Johannes Lucidus, book VII of the Emendation of Time, last book; Cornel. à Lapide in this place; Benedict Pererius, Commentary on Daniel, books X and XI; August. Torniellus in the Annals for the year of the world 3609, no. 4, and the year of the world 4084, no. 20. Dionysius Petavius, book XII of the doctrine of Time, ch. 32 et seqq., as also part II, book III of the Ration. temp., ch. X. Salianus likewise in the Annals, Gordon Huntlæus, Suarius, Vilalpandus, Melanchton likewise, Jac. Usserius, Thomas Lydiat the Englishman, Isaac Vossius, Vorstius, and also Wilhelmus Langius and many others. Although indeed the reason escapes some of these in that they indicate lunar years: yet we have already shown that the calculation is perfectly consistent if we retain our beginning, and understand the years as used in the manner of Scripture, from which the Hebrews do not depart (since not they, but the Hagarenes use lunar years) and as solar. Scaliger himself fixes the Epoch of the 62 weeks in the times of Artaxerxes. Although he is mistaken in that he wishes Artaxerxes Mnemon to be designated by Ezra and Nehemiah, and does not calculate the years correctly. It is evident that the calculation and opinion of Lansbergius, an excellent Chronologer, differ little from ours. Abraham Bucholzerus also agrees, and others praised above, Angelocrator, Capellus, etc. Nor is the opinion of Funccius, and those who follow him, B. Gesner, and others, any different regarding the beginning of the Epoch. Which Cornelius à Lapide, cited earlier, also defends at length, praising the votes of Cedrenus, Theodoret, and by a certain reasoning even of Eusebius himself, and other Chronologers. Nicolaus Abraham, and from the same, Rob. Baillie, praises for this opinion Basil, Eusebius (who has several opinions), Gualter, Bullinger, Funccius, Bucholcerus, Capellus, Helvicus, Cornel. à Lapide, Sanctius, Henr. Philippi, and Tirinus.

§. CXXIV. Secondly, regarding the term to which, most both ancient and recent agree that it is not to be placed at the destruction of Jerusalem, and almost only Scaliger with his followers defends this modern opinion about placing the term to which at the destruction of the city: but the Doctors also assert with great consensus that it looks to the Passion of the Lord, even if some fix these weeks in the Passion itself, and some end them seven years after the Passion of the Lord: And therefore also from our side, those who have hitherto acceded to our opinion include B. Luther, who at first made the end of these weeks the same as we did, the middle of the week after the Passion and resurrection of the Lord (although later in the Preface to Daniel he placed the entire last week after the excision of the Lord, which is also the opinion of B. Jac. Martini), B. Gesner and B. Franzius, who end them in the Passion of the Lord, and other Chronologers, Funccius, Bucholzerus, etc. Regarding B. Chemnitius, Petavius, Lansbergius, and Langius, who favor our opinion, we have already spoken. But especially Cornelius à Lapide, with Tirinus not dissenting, as we said in th. LXXI and LXVIII, defends and supports our opinion, both regarding the beginning of the Epoch and the end, from the Papists; from the Reformed, Philippus Lansbergius; from our side, B. Dn. D. Pappus, who has it thus in his Commentary on Daniel at this place: 'Artaxerxes Longimanus himself in the 7th year of his reign again permitted the people to be led back from Babel under the leadership of Ezra the Priest in the year of the world 3514, and in the 62nd year after the edict of Darius Hystaspis.' To this seventh year, those who have now published MORE ACCURATE Chronologies, almost all refer the beginning of the weeks. And afterwards: 'Although, however, as far as the first 7 weeks are concerned, their end, that is, the 49th year, is concluded by no memorable end; which indeed might be noted in the history of Ezra or Nehemiah; yet the same Ezra and the history of Nehemiah testify abundantly enough to the straits by which the Jews were oppressed in the restoration of both the Temple and the city: And thus it remains true what Daniel predicted: That in the straits of times the streets and walls of Jerusalem were to be restored. The history of the sixty-two weeks extends to the time of the baptism of Christ: provided that half of the last week be added. And there are also manifest testimonies among foreign writers, by which the same years are traced from the seventh year of Longimanus, to the death of Alexander the Great, and thence through the Olympiads to the death of Christ. For his death is assigned to the last year of the two hundred and second Olympiad.' The death of Alexander, however, [falls] in the first year of the 114th Olympiad. The difference, therefore, is 89 Olympiads, which constitute 356 years. If you add to these the 33 years of Artaxerxes, the 19 of Darius Nothus, the 43 of Artaxerxes Mnemon, the 23 of Darius Ochus, the 6 of Darius Codomannus, and as many for Alexander after Darius was defeated, the sum we mentioned will emerge, namely 490 years. The late lamented ought to have said 486. The calculation demands it, and thus it also approaches our computation, as was warned before, even if in the enumeration or calculation that oversight carried him away to other things.

§. CXXV. Similarly, D. Matthias Wasmuth of Kiel, now Extraordinary Professor of Theology at the Academy, explains the term to which, [in] Hebrew

& Ordinary of Oriental Languages in his Vindications of Holy Hebrew Scripture, part II, chapter 1, page 292, asserting that the end of those weeks must be set at 3 1/2 years after the death of the Savior, in the notable confirmation of the New Covenant (v. 27), exhibited in the Church of the Gentiles or the New Testament, first at Antioch, professing the Messiah by the public symbol of the Christian name: to which also, by at least a few months, preceded that illustrious vision of Peter of the animals to be slaughtered (Acts 10), by which the admission of the Gentiles to the kingdom of Christ (without circumcision or the rigor of the law) was prefigured, and soon began to be fulfilled in Cornelius and the converted Antiochenes. The same [author] on the completion of those things which the Angel assigned to the middle of the last week, page 309. Expressly, he says, v. 26, the excision or death of the Messiah the Prince is said to be future after those (7 and 62) weeks, namely, in the very middle of the seventieth week. Thus, therefore, the end of the second interval, the Messiah the Predecessor, as is shown clearly enough in the text, and is asserted and confirmed by the harmony of Histories so precisely by the very lapse of 434 years, namely in the 17th year of Tiberius, that it [is supported by] the chief Chroniclers and interpreters, Theodoret, Zonaras, Calvisius, Helvicus, Alstedius, Wilhelm Lang, Pererius, Salmeron, Salianus, Baillie, Suarez, etc. The excision of the Messiah, however (he has on page 311), falls in the 20th year of Tiberius. In which calculation and consensus of Chronologists, the reason indeed escaped the most learned man, when he asserted that the time of the Messiah the Predecessor, in which he undertook his office, should be referred to the 17th year of Tiberius, since Luke openly refers it to the 15th year, chapter 3, 1: yet in the sum of the matter, regarding the term to which, he agrees with us: Although he goes into all other things regarding the term from which: whose opinion we therefore weighed above. Ludovicus Capellus in Chronol. page 24, with his brother Jac. Capellus in Histor. Sacr. & Exot. makes the beginning the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, the end the year of Christ σταυρώσιμον [the year of the crucifixion], yet he admits that that time from the beginning to the death of Christ can be numbered in such a way that only 487 years intervened, which, since we judge them to have intervened, we have thus far the very ὁμόψηφον [agreement in calculation]: even if he thinks (which has its use in its own place) that to quibble about one or another year in such a variety of authors who have written about the Persian and Greek Kings is idle and superfluous.

§. CXXVI. Finally, we have recently observed how from these parts the opinions of the ancients and the moderns also stand, as far as the years of the ministry of Christ and the half of the weeks of Daniel are concerned. All of which procure some authority κατ' ἔξω [externally] for this opinion, however solid and firm it may be in itself.

§. CXXVII. But since no small difficulty remains concerning Artaxerxes, especially in Ezra, and also concerning Darius, whose 2nd year the same commemorates, and Scaliger with his followers relies chiefly on that hypothesis, that in Ezra 4 Darius Nothus is to be understood, and thus in Ezra 7 Artaxerxes μακρόχειρ [Longimanus] cannot be understood, but Artaxerxes Memoriosus is designated, so that the meaning of the scripture may not be doubtful here, nor should we be stuck in this illustrious oracle, it will now be necessary to treat these things ἀκριβέστερον [more accurately]. For Scaliger confidently, and those who follow him in Chronology, as well as D. Georg. Calixtus in his Exposition of the Oracle concerning the LXX weeks of Daniel, affirm that that Darius is not Hystaspes, but Nothus, and Artaxerxes not Longimanus but Memoriosus. Who that Darius is, says Calixtus, up to whose second year the building of the temple is written to have been hindered, it is easy to gather. For Darius, who is between the two Artaxerxes, cannot be other than Darius Nothus, and the former Artaxerxes must be Longimanus, but the latter Mnemon, or Memoriosus.

Which is also the opinion of Barthol. Maier in his Dissertation on the LXX weeks of Daniel, annexed to the exposition of Calixtus.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

Consensus Doctorum.

§. CXXIII. Hæ ergo rationes sententiam no- stram statuminant, cui etiam pondus aliquod acce- dit ab autoritate magnorum Doctorum & Chrono- logorum. Quamvis enim non quoad omnes par- tes omnes eidem assensum præbeant, nec eodem modo sese explicent, aut calculum eadem ratione ineant, consentiunt tamen nobiscum præcipui Do- ctores & Chronologi, primo qua terminum à quo, quod ad Artaxerxis ab Esdra & Nehemia com- memorati tempora referri debeat: nonnulli etiam in eo, quod ad VII. annum Longimani, quem Esdras designat, referendus sit. Cedrenus, Lutherus, Func- cius, Bucholcerus, Bullingerus, Capellus, Rob. Bai- lius, Wendel. Lansbergius, Reusnerus, Büntingius, Gesnerus, Joh. Cluverus, Vogelius, Edvard. Samso- nius, Salmero, Henricus Philippi &c. Qui vero ad annum XX. Longimani referunt, quoad rem ipsam, quum plerique annos intermedios luna- res sistunt, facile cum hac Epocha VII. anni con- veniunt, atq; in modo explicandi solum discrepa- re videntur. Quam sententiam defendit Scriptor Antiquissimus Julius Africanus lib. V. Annal. a- pud Hieron. in h. l. Chrysostom. in Orat. II. advers. Jud. Theodoret. in h. l. Beda lib. II. Exposit. Esdr. cap. 16. & lib. de ratione temp. c. VI. Rupert. in libr. Dan. c. 15. Autor histor. Scholast. in hist. Dan. c. 10. Dionysius Carthusianus in h. l. Comestor. c. 10. Johan- nes Zonaras T. I. Annal. Antoninus in 1. part. Chro- nic. Tit. III. c. VIII. Petrus Galatinus lib. IV. de ar- can. cath. verit. c. 16. Johannes Lucidus lib. VII. de Emend. Temp. lib. ult. Cornel. à Lapide in h. l. Be- nedict. Pererius Comment. in Daniel. lib. X. & XI. August. Torniellus in Annal. ad annum mundi 3609. n. 4. & annum mundi 4084. n. 20. Dionysius Peta- vius lib. XII. de doctr. Temp. c. 32. seqq. ut & part. II. lib. III. Ration. temp. c. X. Salianus item in An- nal. Gordonus Huntlæus, Suarius, Vilalpandus, Me- lanchton item, Jac. Usserius, Thomas Lydiat Anglus, Isaacus Vossius, Vorstius, nec non Wilhelmus Langius aliique multi. Quamvis vero nonnullos istorum ratio in eo fugiat, quod annos lunares indigitent: optime tamen sibi constare calculum, si nostrum initium retineamus, annosque more scripturæ, à quo non discedunt Ebræi, (cum non illi, sed Ha- gareni annos Lunares adhibeant) usitatos & sola- res intelligamus, jam ostendimus. Scaliger figit ipse in temporibus Artaxerxis Epocham he- bdomadum LXII. Quamvis in eo fallatur, quod ab Esdra & Nehemia Artaxerxem Memorem designa- tum velit, neque annos recte putet. Lansbergii excellentis Chronologi calculum & sententiam parum à nostra distare, in aprico est. Consentit etiam Abraham Bucholzerus, & alii supra laudati, Angelocrator, Capellus &c. Neque alia est, quod ad initium Epochæ, Funccii, & qui eum se- quuntur, B. Gesneri, aliorumque sententia. Quam prolixe tuetur quoque Cornelius à Lapide antea adductus, laudans suffragia Cedreni, Theodoreti, ac certa ratione ipsius etiam Eusebii, aliorumq; Chro- nologorum. Nicolaus Abraham, & ex eodem Rob. Bailius laudat pro hac sententia Basilium, Eusebium (qui plures habet sententias) Gualterum, Bullingerum, Funccium, Bucholcerum, Capellum, Helvicum, Cornel. à Lapide, Sanctium, Henr. Phi- lippi, & Tirinum.

§. CXXIV. Secundo, quod ad terminum ad quem, non in destructione Hierosolymæ collocan- dum eum esse plerique tum veteres, tum recentio- res consentiunt, ac fere solus Scaliger cū suis neo- tericam hanc opinionē de termino ad quem in ex- cidio urbis locando propugnat: Spectare autem eundem ad passionem Dominicam itidem magno consensu Doctores adstruunt, etsi nonnulli in ipsa passione has septimanas figant, nonnulli septennio post passionem Domini easdem finiant: Ideoque etiam è nostris accedunt hactenus sententiæ nostræ cum B. Luthero, qui primo terminum harum septi- manarum eundem nobiscum fecerat, mediam septi- manam post passionem & resurrectionem Domini (etsi postea Præfatione in Daniel. septimanam to- tam postremam collocarit post excisionem Domi- nicam, quæ etiam B. Jac. Martini est sententia,) B. Gesnerus & B. Franzius, qui in passione Domi- nica easdem finiunt & alii Chronologi Funccius, Bucholzerus &c. De B. Chemnitio, Petavio, Lans- bergio, & Langio nostræ sententiæ faventibus jam antea diximus. Sed imprimis nostram senten- tiam, tum quoad initium Epochæ, tum quoad fi- nem tuentur ac propugnant è Pontificiis Cornelius à Lapide, non abnuente Tirino, uti th. LXXI. & LXVIII. diximus, E Reformatis Philippus Lans- bergius, è nostris B. Dn. D. Pappus, qui ita habet Comment. in Dan. ad h. l. Ipse autem Longimanus Artaxerxes anno VII. regni sui iterum permisit re- duci populum ex Babel duce Esdra Sacerdote anno mundi 3514. & anno 62. post Darii Hystaspis edi- ctum. Ad hunc septimum annum, qui nunc AC- CVRATIORES ediderunt Chronologias, principi- um septimanarum ferme referunt. Et postea: Et- si autem, quoad primas 7. hebdomadas attinet, finis earum, hoc est, annus 49. nullo memorabili fine con- cluditur; Qui quidem in Esdræ aut Nehemiæ histo- ria notatus sit; tamen quibus angustiis Judæi in re- stitutione & Templi & urbis oppressi fuerint, eadem Esræ ex Nehemiæ historia satis abunde testantur: At- que ita verum manet id, quod Daniel prædixit: In angustia temporum plateas & muros Hierosoly- mæ restituendos esse. Septimanarum sexaginta duarum historia usque ad tempus baptismi Christi protenditur: Siquidem dimidium postremæ septima- næ adjiciatur. Et sunt apud exteros quoque scripto- res manifesta testimonia, quibus iidem anni ab anno septimo Longimani, ad mortem usque Alexandri Magni, & inde per Olympiadas ad Christi usque mortem deducuntur. Nam mors ejus in annum ul- timum Olympiadis ducentesimæ secundæ confertur. Alexandri autem interitus in annum primum Olym- piadis 114. Differentia igitur est, Olympiadum 89. quæ annos constituunt 356. Quibus si addas Artaxer- xis annos 33. Darii Nothi 19. Artaxerxis Memoris 43. Darii Ochi 23. Darii Codomanni 6. & Alexan- dri post devictum Darium totidem, ea quæ dixi- mus summa emerget, annorum videlicet 490. Dice- re debuit 486. ὁ μακαρίτης. Id calculus poscit, atq; ita etiam nostræ acceditur computationi, ut antea monitum, etsi in numeratione vel calculo παρόρα- μα illud ad alia eundem abripuerit.

§. CXXV. Explicat similiter terminum ad quem D. Matthias Wasmuth Kiloniens. nunc Aca- demiæ Professor Theologus Extraordinarius, Ebrææ

& Orientalium Linguarum Ordinarius in vindiciis S. Hebrææ Scripturæ part. II. cap. 1. p. 292, afferens, finem earum hebdomadum constituendum esse 3 1/2. an- nis post mortem Salvatoris, in notabili Novi Fœderis (v. 27.) confirmatione, in Ecclesia gentium seu Nov. Test. Antiochiæ primum, publico Christiani nominis symbolo, exhibitum Messiam professa: cui & paucis mensibus saltim præcesserit illustris illa Petri visio al- tilium mactandorum (Act. 10.) qua gentium ad re- gnum Christi (citra circumcisionem aut legis rigo- rem) admissio præfigurata, mox in Cornelio, & Antio- chenis conversis impleri cœpit. Idem de comple- mento eorum, quæ mediæ septimanæ ultimæ affi- gnavit Angelus, pag. 309. Expresse, inquit, v. 26. Messiæ ducis excisio seu mors post illas (7. & 62.) hebdomadas futura dicitur, scil. ipso septuagesimæ hebdomadis medio. Ita ergo finis secundi intervalli, Messias Antecessor, uti aperte satis in textu monstra- tur, & ab Historiarum concordia adeo præcise ipso- rum 434. annorum defluxu, anno scil. Tiberii 17. assertus confirmatur, ut præcipuorum Chronicorum & interpretum, Theodoreti, Zonaræ, Calvisii, Hel- vici, Alstedii, Wilhelmi Langii, Pererii, Salmero- nis, Saliani, Bailii, Suarii &c. Excisio autem Mes- siæ (pag. 311. habet) incidit in annum Tiberii 20. In quo calculo, & consensu Chronologorum ratio quide virum doctissimum fugit, cum tempus Mes- siæ Antecessoris, quo officium suum aggressus est, referri asseruit ad Tiberii annum 17. siquidem Lucas aperte ad annum 15. cap. 3, 1. referat: in rei tamen summa, quoad terminum ad quem nobiscum con- venit: Quanquam in alia omnia eat, quod ad termi- num a quo: cujus sententiam supra ideo expendi- mus. Ludovicus Capellus in Chronol. pag. 24. cum fratre Jac. Capello in Histor. Sacr. & Exot. initium facit septimum Artaxerxis Longimani, finem an- num Christi σταυρώσιμον, fatetur tamen tempus il- lud ab initio ad mortem Christi sic numerari posse, ut intervenerint solum 487. anni, quos intervenisse quum censeamus, hactenus habemus ipsam ὁμόψη- φον: etsi existimet (quod suo loco usum habet) vitilitigare de uno vel altero anno in tanta autorum, qui de Regibus Persicis, & Græcis scripsere, varietate otiosum esse ac supervacaneum.

§. CXXVI. Denique quomodo ab his par- tibus etiam sententiæ veterum & recentiorum, quantum ad annos ministerii Christi & dimidiam hebdomadum Danielis stent, proxime observavi- mus. Quæ omnia huic sententiæ, quantumvis per se solidæ ac firmæ, aliquam autoritatem κατ' ἔξω conciliant.

§. CXXVII. Sed quum difficultas non exigua supersit de Artaxerxe, imprimis apud Esdram, nec non de Dario, cujus annum II. idem commemo- rat, ac Scaliger cum sectatoribus suis illa præcipue nitatur hypothesi, quod Esdr. 4. Darius Nothus in- telligendus sit, adeoque Esdr. 7. non possit Arta- xerxes μακρόχειρ intelligi, sed Artaxerxes Memo- riosus designetur, ne dubia hic sit scripturæ senten- tia, nec in oraculo hoc illustri hærendum nobis sit, ἀκριβέστερον de his agendū nunc erit. Confidenter enim Scaliger, & qui eum in Chronologia sequun- tur, nec non D. Georg. Calixtus Exposit. Oraculi de LXX. hebdomad. Daniel. affirmant, Darium illum non Hystaspida esse, sed Nothum, & Artaxerxem non Longimanum sed Memoriosum. Quis Darius ille, inquit Calixtus, sit, ad cujus usq; annum secundum ædificatio templi impedita scribitur, facile est colli- gere. Darius enim, qui medius est inter duos Ar- taxerxes, alius esse non potest, quam Darius Nothus, & priorem Artaxerxem oportet esse Longimanum, posteriorem vero Mnemonem, sive Memoriosum.

Quæ etiam Barthol. Maieri Differt. de LXX. heb- dom. Danielis, expofitioni Calixtinæ annexa, est fententia.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. Darius in Ezra 4, 5, 24 is one and the same, namely the son of Hystaspes; nor is Artaxerxes in Ezra 7 to be understood as any other than Longimanus.

§. CXXVIII. This, therefore, we must show, that the Darius whom Ezra names in chapter 4 is not different, but one and the same in verses 5 and 24. Nor is the Darius in the latter verse, whom they call Νόθον [Nothus], but Darius Hystaspes to be understood, and that in his second year the structure of the temple was resumed; whence it follows that in Ezra 7 not Artaxerxes Mnemon, but Artaxerxes Longimanus is designated. These arguments, however, move us chiefly not to rise to Scaliger here, who preferred to substitute Darius Nothus, even though not a few Chronologists of great name have made that their opinion. First, because Ezra, describing the times and causes of the hindered structure of the temple, where he wished to designate those Kings under whom the Cuthæi obstructed the work, named no others than Cyrus, Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes, and Darius. He testifies that it was in their times that the delay was injected. If others had intervened from Cyrus to Darius, under whose rule the work had suffered delay, the Divine Historian would by no means have omitted them. Wherefore by this Darius must necessarily be understood the Son of Hystaspes, the fourth from Cyrus, whence it also remains that no other intermediate ones can be understood here by Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes than those Kings who followed Cyrus most closely and preceded the King named Darius. Who, according to exotic history, were Cambyses the son of Cyrus, and Smerdis the Magus, his impersonated or supposed son. The former, when he had received the less august name of Cambyses from his grandfather, being raised to the kingdom, assumed the title of Ahasuerus; which according to Herodotus signifies a warrior and is believed to have been common to Kings: For also the husband of Esther was distinguished by the name of Ahasuerus, who without doubt had another proper name. Since in the entire series of Persian Monarchs the name Ahasuerus does not appear, according to the canon of Ptolemy. But what Scaliger with his followers attempts to make of Ahasuerus, namely Xerxes, is utterly absurd. For what does the name Ahasuerus have in common with the appellation of Xerxes? Smerdis, indeed, when he was feigning the person of the son of Cyrus, wishing also to gain authority for himself by the name, wanted to be called Artaxerxes: which Grotius observes was a gentile name for the Kings of the Persians, along with the name of Xerxes. Nor is it new or unusual for Holy Scripture, omitting the proper name of Kings, to call them by those names which they imposed upon themselves, even if those are common and used by many. Which is done without confusion of persons, when the circumstances of the text sufficiently designate the person. Thus that King, whom Ptolemy called by his proper name Nabonidus, Scripture names Belshazzar, which he assumed for himself in honor of Bel, whom he worshipped as God; for בלטשאצר is said as if 'hiding the treasure of Bel,' or 'priest of the mysteries of Bel.' Others wish that King to have been called by his own name Laborosoarchod, in whose place his associate Niricassolassar presided. Some say he was called Evil-Merodach, as can be seen in Cornelius à Lapide. Certainly the name Belshazzar was not proper, but common, which was also imposed upon Daniel (Dan. 1, verse 7); similarly the King of the Persians is called [so] (Dan. 8, verse 28).

Chap. 9. Concerning the name of Darius, which was certainly not a proper name, but a common name, just as besides this Darius the Mede, three other Dariuses are mentioned in the Persian Monarchy. And that the proper name for that Darius was Nabonadius, the followers of Scaliger strive to prove from Ptolemy's canon, the fragment of Berosus, and Megasthenes. We pass over other examples in a matter sufficiently clear.

§. CXXIX. Furthermore, it is manifest that the time of the reign of Darius is established as the limit of the hindered building of the house of the Lord. For the enemies of Judah and Benjamin are said to have corrupted the counselors and to have hindered the plan of building the temple, all the days of Cyrus, and UNTIL the reign of Darius, King of the Persians. If, therefore, Darius Nothus is designated, it will be necessary that the work was hindered not only during the times of Cambyses and Smerdis, but also of Darius Hystaspis, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes Longimanus (whom Darius Nothus succeeded). But how would Ezra have concealed those, and made mention of only two Kings, while passing over the others who succeeded Cyrus? Why would he have skipped over that entire interval, namely the seven years of Cambyses and the seven-month space of Smerdis, and the 36 years of Darius Hystaspis, that is, 44 years, without a pause? In no way, certainly, is it likely that the divine historian would pass over in silence those Kings by whom the structure seems to have been most hindered, when he is pursuing a history full of the inhibited and hindered structure.

§. CXXX. Thirdly, the Holy Scripture wished to define not only the reign, but also the year of that same reign, for the sake of sacred Chronology, and to demonstrate the Prophetic truth, at which time the building of the temple was resumed. Since, therefore, it said that it was hindered until the Empire of Darius, and recounted the Kings under whom it was hindered, and the slander cast upon the Jews, and the Royal interdict, it now designates the year of the reign of Darius in which the counsels of the adversaries finally had an end, verse 24. The work of the Lord was interrupted UNTIL the second year of Darius, so that, if the matter is properly weighed, nothing can be more manifest than that it is a matter of one and the same Darius in both verse 5 and verse 24. For the intermediate verses explain only the manner and the stratagem of the informers, and report the interdict which the enemies of the Jews obtained through slander. Therefore, the copulative particle in v. 6. ובמלכות in a causal sense is correctly rendered by B. Luther, which it is not rarely accustomed to obtain, so that this is the continuity of the text: They hired counselors against them to destroy their counsel all the days of Cyrus until the Reign of Darius. For in the reign of Ahasuerus (Cambyses), in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Benjamin, and in the days of Artaxerxes (likewise Smerdis) wrote Bishlam, Mithridates, etc., whence it is clear that these deeds just mentioned were before the times of that Darius, in whose second year the work succeeded. For if those things had happened after the Darius named in the fifth verse, and the accusations had been brought to Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, that report would be very inconsistent: They hindered the counsel all the days of Cyrus UNTIL the reign of DARIUS (Hystaspis); And afterwards, in the time of Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, Xerxes and Longimanus, they wrote an accusation. For thus, with the final limit of the hindrance already indicated at the beginning of the reign of Darius, the hindrance would be referred to as occurring under the successors of Darius. Which is absurd.

§. CXXXI. Fourthly, it is not likely that Xerxes and Artaxerxes Longimanus hindered the work of the restoration of the temple, and hindered it in such a way that they resisted more than others, and especially, for instance, that they deserved to be reported by that name by Ezra more than Cambyses and Smerdis Magus, especially if Xerxes, as Scaliger wishes, is Ahasuerus, the husband of Esther, and Artaxerxes Longimanus is his son by Esther or Amastris. For how would it be consistent with their piety to hinder the structure of the temple so greatly?

§. CXXXII. Fifthly, Chronology contradicts it. For if the restoration of the temple was hindered until the times of Darius Nothus, it is necessary that the Israelites, after they returned to their homeland by the indulgence of Cyrus, were deprived of the temple for an entire century and more. Let the calculation be subtracted, whether from the 21st or, as others prefer, from the 29th year of Cyrus, until the second year of Darius the Bastard, and an interval of 110 or 118 years will emerge. But who would believe that they lacked a temple for such a long time, or how would that be consistent with divine promises? Therefore, it is better to establish that hands were set to the work of the structure of the temple again in the time of Darius Hystaspis; according to which hypothesis they would have been deprived of the temple, the ordinary seat of divine worship, for barely 20 years after their return to Palestine.

§. CXXXIII. Sixthly, the words of the letter of accusation, which is had in Ezra 4, verse 14, must be weighed. Since therefore we have destroyed the temple, B. Luther rendered the sense more emphatically: Now that we are all here who have destroyed the temple. Whence it appears that the informers, who then sent letters to Artaxerxes, had once been present at the destruction of the temple; which, since it happened in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar, and from that time until the second year of Darius Hystaspis 70 years had flowed, and from there to the Empire of Artaxerxes Longimanus 55, it would be necessary for them, if they were only 8 years old at the time of the destruction, to have been 143 years old. Which age was then utterly unusual: but that some had eighty-odd years in that century is far more likely, such as could have been present both at the destruction of the former temple and at these accusations before Smerdis.

§. CXXXIV. Seventhly, since Joshua held the Pontificate at that time when the Israelites returned to Palestine by the tenor of the decree of Cyrus, that is, in the 21st year of the reign of Cyrus, which was the first of the Monarchy of Cyrus, it is necessary that he held the Pontificate at the time the temple was built, for at least 121 years, and thus by living over 150 years he would have completed it, if that time falls in the sixth year of Darius Nothus. For from the 21st year of Cyrus until the 6th of Darius, 121 years are counted. But if the limit of the built temple is established as the sixth year of Darius Hystaspis, only 23 years will have elapsed from the first of Cyrus until the completion of the work. Therefore, it is again more likely that the time of the former, not the latter, Darius is to be understood.

§. CXXXV. Eighthly, this passage of Hag. 2, 4 is to be compared. Where the Prophet speaks thus: Who is among you that saw this House in her first glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing? From whence it is gathered that in the time of Haggai there still survived those who had seen the first house in its glory. These would have had to be nearly two hundred years old, if the structure of the temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius Nothus. For from the time of the destruction until the second year of Hystaspes, seventy years are counted: from this, however, one hundred and two years elapsed until the sixth of Darius Nothus, namely thirty-four remaining of Darius Hystaspes, twenty-one of Xerxes, forty-one of Longimanus, and six of Darius Nothus, which, when added together, make one hundred and two years. If you add to these seventy years, one hundred and seventy-two years are produced. If there were any who were already ten years old when they saw the first house, it is necessary that they were one hundred and eighty-two years old in the time of Haggai. years, which were ordered to compare the glory of another house with the former. Which μακροβιότης (long-livedness) does not suit that age.

§. CXXXVI. Ninthly, the Prophetic passage Zech. 1:12 confirms our opinion most solidly. For in the second year of Darius, Zechariah is said to have prayed: O Lord of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation? This is now the seventieth year! For the Prophet received a divine response in these words: I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy, and I will return to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it. Therefore, the restoration of the temple was promised divinely in the second year of Darius. That it was completed in the sixth year of the same Darius is most manifest from a collation of Ezra and Haggai. But that Darius in Zechariah cannot be any other than Darius Hystaspis. For the chronology does not fit Darius Nothus in any way, but it fits the former perfectly. Since from the destruction of the city until the second year of Darius Hystaspis, 70 years elapsed. For that happened in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar at its beginning, which was the 158th of the Nabonassarian Era. Since, therefore, the seventh year of Cambyses, according to Ptolemy, was the 225th Nabonassarian, the second of Darius will have to be connected with the 228th year of that era. From these, however, subtracting the 158th year of the destruction, there remain 70 years, which is exactly how many elapsed from the destruction of the city to the restoration of the temple. And just as many years of this interval will also emerge according to the Eusebian calculation of the years of Iphitus. For Eusebius in his Chronicles places the destruction in the second year of the 47th Olympiad, or the 186th of Iphitus. Since, therefore, Cyrus reigned for 30 years, who began in the 1st year of the 55th Olympiad, or the 217th of Iphitus, that is, the 31st year after the destruction, to these 31 years must be added 29 (which followed the first year of Cyrus), as well as 8 of Cambyses, and Smerdis, and two of Darius Hystaspis, and the sum of 70 years will again be produced exactly. If the second year of Darius Nothus is assumed, 167 years will intervene from the extermination of the city. Which interval no one will be able to reconcile with the oracle of Zechariah.

§. CXXXVII.
