Here the Scaligerians twist themselves; and since they see that the words of Zechariah in no way agree with the chronology of the destruction and devastation of the city if the oracle is referred to the age of Darius Nothus, they invent that the years of devastation are not being looked at, but times that followed long after, namely the years of other calamities, which, however, they cannot count or define from the sacred texts, since neither a trace nor a footprint of them is found anywhere. Dr. Behm admits this in lib. 2. Chron. Manud. Tit. 2. cap. 3. p. 111. We probably conclude that Zechariah by the 70 years did not understand the years of captivity, but others; indeed, no trace of this matter appears elsewhere in the sacred texts. But that does little to infringe upon our opinion. That century suffered from a scarcity of Prophets, so that we have only Haggai as a contemporary (σύγχρονον) with Zechariah, etc. Not to mention that he accuses Zechariah here of NOT HAVING ATTENDED to an accurate calculation of those 70 years. Let Scaliger himself also be heard in his animadversions on Eusebius, p. 91. For the Angel is not speaking of the seventieth year of the deportation, but that from the Edict of Cyrus the Jewish nation was so often infested by its neighbors that it was given no opportunity to inhabit cities safely or to raise walls, during which interval, which is 106 years, it experienced every kind of calamity during the last 70 years, so that no opportunity was given to restore cities in Judea. But as we readily grant that the seventieth year of the deportation is not meant: so it is entirely manifest from the Prophet that the seventieth year from the destruction of the city, in which the House of the Lord lay in ashes, is indicated. On account of which also those fasts of the fifth and seventh month, about which Zech. 7:5, were instituted, because in the fifth month the temple was burned, 2 Kings 25:8. In the seventh, Gedaliah, who was set over the remnant of the Jews, was killed, verse 25. On account of which total destruction (πανωλεθρίαν) the fasts of the fourth and tenth month were also instituted, Zech. 8:19, because in the fourth the city was taken, Jer. 39. But in the tenth it began to be besieged, 2 Kings 25. And thus Eusebius interpreted the passage of Zechariah in his Chronology, page 151. That the seventieth year of the desolation of the temple was completed in the second year of Darius, the Prophet Zechariah is witness, when he speaks thus of the second year of Darius: O Lord Almighty, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which thou hast despised? This is the seventieth year, or these seventy years. For these are equivalent (ἰσοδυναμῶντα). Jerome explained it similarly, as did Clement of Alexandria, cited by Jerome in this place of Zechariah: that in the second year of Darius, son of Hystaspis, the seventieth year of the desolation of the temple, which was predicted by Jeremiah, was completed, Zechariah himself is witness, saying: O Lord of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy? Therefore, the 70 years of the captivity, which begin in the fourth year of Jehoiakim and end in the first year of the Monarchy of Cyrus, are to be distinguished: as we have clearly shown with the blessed Dr. Behm regarding Jer. 29, and the 70 years of the destruction of the city and temple, which are to be started in the 19th year of Nebuchadnezzar and reach their end in the second year of Darius Hystaspis. Zechariah speaks of these, not of those. But the Holy Scripture knows of no other seventy years of desolation, and thus they are vainly invented by Scaliger, who could produce no witness for them, but like many other things, he invented them out of his own head (ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων).

§. CXXXVIII. Ninth, the weeks add some further strength to this mystical opinion of ours, which is in itself sufficiently firm, as we have seen thus far. For since Gabriel established the beginning of them at the going forth of the word concerning the restoration of Jerusalem, which occurred in the 7th year of Artaxerxes, as Ezra testifies, as we have clearly proven, and that Artaxerxes is none other than μακρόχειρ (Longimanus), it is necessary that Darius, his predecessor, be the son of Hystaspes, under whose second year the temple began to be restored. This consequence is clear from the collation of chapters 4 and 7 of Ezra with Nehemiah 2, and is acknowledged by all. For Darius Nothus did not precede Longimanus, but succeeded him. Scaliger indeed thinks that the beginning of the weeks of Daniel favors his own opinion; nay, this has undoubtedly arisen from the fact that it was observed that 70 weeks of years, or 490 years, had intervened between the 2nd year of Darius Nothus and the destruction of Jerusalem. For from that, a conjecture could easily arise for one indulging in his own στοχασμοῖς (conjectures), neglecting the testimonies of Scripture, that that Darius, in whose 2nd year the temple began to be restored, is τὸν Νόθον (the Bastard) and that the end of the weeks of Daniel ought to be established at the destruction of Jerusalem. But since the words of the angel do not bear this, there is no place for that conjecture. On the contrary, the beginning of the Epoch of the 70 weeks is clearly fixed at the going forth of the word concerning the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem, which, according to Ezra and Nehemiah, must be referred to the times of Artaxerxes Longimanus. Therefore, so that the passages of Scripture may harmonize with themselves in all things, which in no part of itself can ἐαυτομαχεῖν (fight against itself), that second year of Darius so celebrated in the Scriptures is none other than that of Darius Hystaspes.

§. CXXXIX. Tenth, the passage of Ezra ch. 6, 14 makes for our opinion, in which the Kings under whom the work of the Lord succeeded in restoring the temple are expressed and celebrated in this order: Cyrus, Darius, and Artachsashta. For if Darius Nothus, and Artaxerxes

If Mnemon is to be understood, as Scaliger wishes, there will be an excessively long interval from the first edict of Cyrus, whether it be considered promulgated in the penultimate year or the eighth year from his death, up to the seventh year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, namely 132 or 139 years; nor will the truth be easily able to be established by those words in Ezra ch. 6, 14: 'and they built and founded it by the command of the God of Israel, and according to the mandate of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, Kings of the Persians.' For did they indeed still build the temple, of which there is speech there, for 139 years after the edict of Cyrus, and indeed according to the mandate of Cyrus?

§. CXL. Nor does that objection of Scaliger and Dr. Behm from chapter 6 of Ezra move us in any way; that a quite long interval seems to have intervened from the edict of Cyrus up to the second year of this Darius, because it was necessary to search for the concession of Cyrus in the archives of Achmetha, or Ecbatana, the metropolis of Media, and it does not appear likely that within 13 years (the number that elapsed from the edict of Cyrus to the 2nd of Darius) the memory of it could have so slipped away that it had to be searched for in the archives. For things are sometimes searched for in archives that were done and commanded within a lustrum, or even within a shorter space, for the sake of more certain knowledge of the matter, so that there may be an unchangeable certainty regarding both the edict and the causes of the edict, and other circumstances. It is known to those who are engaged in public offices, or who are in charge of archives, that nothing happens more frequently. So that I wonder that any strength is placed in this argument. Nor did only 13 years elapse from the mandate of Cyrus to the second year of Darius Hystaspes, but eighteen: and two other Kings intervened, and indeed a contrary interdict also intervened: which had to be inquired into entirely, especially by a new King; since two others had intervened in the government, so that the causes of both the concession and the inhibition might be weighed in a just balance.

§. CXLI. Most recently we add the authority of the ancients, who with great consensus acknowledge that the restoration of the temple made under Darius is to be referred not to the reign of Darius Nothus, but of Hystaspes. Which not only Josephus does from the Jews, lib. 11. antiq. c. 4. and lib. 1. against Apion, but also not a few of the principal rank among Christian Doctors, both in the Greek Church, Clement of Alexandria lib. 1. Strom., Eusebius in Chron. lib. 1., Theodoret comment. on Haggai and Zechariah, Cyril of Alexandria, Basil of Seleucia, etc., and in the Latin, Jerome on Haggai and Zechariah, and Augustine lib. 18. de Civit. Dei c. 26., Bede, Marianus Scotus, etc. Whose consensus, supported by reasons, is deservedly held by us in higher regard than the opinion of some moderns born yesterday or the day before, who have chosen to go against us in all other matters here without grave cause. Nor are there lacking, however, among the recent authors, those of great name who are of the same mind as us. Among the Papists, Bellarmine, Genebrard, Salianus, Tornielli, Pererius, Sanctius, Petavius, Gordon, Henr. Philippi, etc.; among the Reformed, Rob. Baillie, Cappel, James Ussher, Isaac Vossius, Joh. Vorstius; among our own, David Chytraeus, Reusner, Christian Matthiae, Wilh. Langius, Vogelius in compend. Chronol. p. 159. and 182., Laurentius Euchstadius, etc.

§. CXLII. Nor indeed is the argument of any moment which those of the opposite side hold as their masterpiece, derived from names, namely Scaliger, Calvisius, and others: Which they are accustomed to propose thus: That Darius is understood by Ezra, and his second year is indicated, who is the middle one between two Artaxerxes: But not the son of Hystaspes, but the Nothus is the middle one between two Artaxerxes, according to the testimony of History and the series of Persian Kings; because Artaxerxes Longimanus preceded him, and Artaxerxes Mnemon followed him. Therefore, not Darius Hystaspes, but the Nothus is understood by Ezra, when his second year is indicated. In which comparison, if the middle position is understood according to rigor, so that the immediate predecessor and immediate successor of Darius is called Artaxerxes, the major proposition cannot be demonstrated from sacred history. For although after Artaxerxes, whose edict is referred to in Ezra 4, mention of Darius is made in verse 24 of the same chapter, and afterwards another Artaxerxes is commemorated in ch. 7, yet this other Artaxerxes is not established by Ezra as the immediate successor of Darius. For could not some one of the successors have been omitted in that History? But if that middle position is not taken so strictly, the minor proposition does not stand on firm footing. For Artaxerxes followed Darius Hystaspes (with Xerxes intervening), and Smerdis the Magian preceded him, whom nothing prevents us from believing to have assumed the name of Artaxerxes out of pride and desire for glory, having laid aside the vile name of Smerdis; indeed, the series of Ezra altogether compels us to believe that that former Artaxerxes of Ezra is Smerdis. For he is referred to as the third from Cyrus, since in this order the Persian Kings (of whom he himself made mention) follow one another in Ezra: Cyrus, Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes, Darius, Artaxerxes, who are commonly called by exotic writers Cyrus, Cambyses, Smerdis, Darius Hystaspes, Artaxerxes Longimanus. But he who is missing in that series, the immediate successor of Hystaspes, Xerxes, can easily be supplied from Daniel ch. 11, 2: 'Behold, three more kings shall stand in Persia, and the fourth shall be far richer than them all.' But that fourth one is without doubt Xerxes. Between whom and Darius the Mede there are three intermediaries: Cyrus, Cambyses (Smerdis was held unworthy by the Holy Scriptures to be numbered among other genuine Kings and Monarchs), and Darius Hystaspes. Nor indeed can those who follow the side of Scaliger object to the diversity of names. For who is unaware that Kings assumed other names when they were moved to the fasces, a custom which Scaliger, in book 6 of De Emendatione Temporum, proved to have been observed by the Kings of the Persians. Thus Darius Nothus was previously called Ὤχος and Ὦχος, Artaxerxes Mnemon was called Ἀρσίκας and Ὀάρσης. And Codomannus was so called, who obtained the name of Darius. What wonder is it, therefore, if the name of Ahasuerus was attributed to Cambyses, and that of Artaxerxes to Smerdis during their reign, or if they themselves chose more illustrious names of this kind in preference to baser names? And how do Labynitus in Herodotus, Nabonadius in the Canon of Ptolemy, and Darius the Mede in Daniel agree, which nevertheless designate the same person according to Scaliger! How futile is the objection concerning names, so that when all other things agree, the single difference prevents Mavius from being Mavius, says Scaliger in Animadversiones ad Eusebium, page 85.

§. CXLIII. I find one more reason, which the blessed D. Behmius, along with Scaliger, strongly urges, taken from the chronological series, namely that it is gathered from Ezra and Nehemiah that both Ezra and Nehemiah lived until the times of Alexander the Great. Because Jaddua, who is mentioned in Neh. 12:22, went out to meet Alexander the Great as he was arriving at Jerusalem in his pontifical robes, as Josephus testifies in book 11 of the Antiquities, chapter 8. But it cannot be concluded from the history of Ezra and Nehemiah that both reached the times of Alexander. Concerning Ezra, nothing else is held than that he lived in the time of the high priest Johanan, and entered his chamber, Ezra 10:6. But not that he was still alive in the time of the pontificate of Johanan's son, Jaddua, much less in the time of Alexander the Great. Nehemiah, however, only mentions Jaddua the high priest in chapter 12:22. Where there is no reason for us to deny with the Temporarius that this Jaddua went out to meet Alexander; since, even if that were granted, it would not yet follow that Nehemiah, who reached the pontificate of Jaddua, also lived in the time of Alexander the Great, because he could have died at the beginning of that pontificate, having died. Then, even if he had lived right up to the times of Alexander, which is indeed established by no certain document concerning Nehemiah, nothing absurd will arise in the chronological series. For let us suppose Nehemiah was 20 years old in the 30th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus; therefore, in the sixth year of Darius Codomannus, in which he was defeated by Alexander the Great, he would have been 142 years old. Therefore, those things could be replied to the Scaligerians which they themselves reply to the Beroaldists in a similar case. The absurdity, says Dr. Behmius, lib. 2, Tit. cap. 10, page 175, which the Beroaldists assume from the longevity of Zerubbabel the Prince and Joshua the High Priest, we say is so constituted that an absurdity is feigned where there is no absurdity. Is this an absurdity, for a man to live 140 or 150 years? This argument proceeds from the short-livedness of the Germans to that of other peoples. This is Dr. Behm.

§. CXLIV. Now, to add something concerning Ahasuerus, the husband of Esther, various opinions occur regarding him. Four are recounted by Grotius on Ezra ch. 4, 6, because some make him Cambyses, others Darius Hystaspis, others Artaxerxes Mnemon, others Artaxerxes Longimanus. But Grotius omits a fifth, which today is almost the principal one; namely, that he was Xerxes, which Scaliger, Calvisius, Dr. Behm, Tremellius, Junius, and others defend; as also a sixth, that he was Artaxerxes Ochus, which is that of Serrarius and Gordon, and also a seventh, which has pleased not a few, that he was Astyages, the father-in-law of Cyrus; whom Melchior Canus (l. 11, Loc. c. 6), Gerhardus Mercator in his Chronology, Temporarius (l. 3, Demonstrat. Chronol. p. 185), and Wanckelius, formerly a professor of this Academy in a solemn Academic Dissertation, make the Ahasuerus of Daniel and Esther, and the father of Darius the Mede. R. Solomon, Lyra, Vatablus, Genebrardus, Petavius, Tirinus, and Wilb. Langius say he was Cambyses, as do the Jews in Seder Olam, etc. Methasthenes, B. Luther, Philippus, Brentius, Osiander, Joh. Carion, Funccius, Ussher, and many others say he was Darius the son of Hystaspis; as do Aben-Ezra among the Jews, and Corn. à Lapide and Joh. Benedictus among the Pontificials. Josephus (l. 11, Antiqq. c. 6), Sulpitius Severus, Nicephorus, Cajetanus, Bellarmine, Salianus, and Sanctius say Artaxerxes Longimanus. Eusebius, Marianus Scotus in his Chronicle, and Bede in his 'On the Six Ages of the World' at the year of the world 3588, say Artaxerxes Mnemon. Therefore, some place this history before the resolution of the Babylonian captivity, who fight for Astyages; others after the resolution of the captivity, who fight for the rest: Cambyses, Darius, Xerxes, Longimanus, Mnemon, and Ochus.

§. CXLV. The blessed Dr. Behmius brought forward the arguments for both opinions in Decad. 2, Observ. 10, in Chronol. Manuduct. p. 251. But the latter are of greater weight, because the husband of Esther ruled from India even to Ethiopia (Esth. 1:1). But no one before Cambyses held Egypt, which is adjacent to Ethiopia. Nor did the Persians rule over the Medes before Cyrus. Nor did the Medes worship the God of the Hebrews; nor did they have a royal residence at Susa. Nor is it plausible that the Jews, during the Babylonian captivity, went into Persia in such a great multitude, or enjoyed such liberty there, that, as is narrated in ch. 9:16, they could slaughter 75,000 of their enemies in one day there, and kill 800 in the royal residence.

§. CXLVI. These reasons for Xerxes are brought forward by Scaliger: that Ahasuerus is mentioned after Cyrus and Darius, and before Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:6); that the extent of the kingdom of Ahasuerus agrees especially with the rule of Xerxes in Herodotus lib. 7, c. 9; that the name of the wife of Xerxes in Herodotus is A'μηστρις or A'μεστρις, which is the same as חֲמַאסתַּר; that the time fits, because Kish the Benjamite was taken into Babylon in the time of Jeconiah (Esth. 2:46), from whom up to Esther three generations are counted, about 120 years: Kish, Shimei, Jair, Mordecai, which is the interval from the voluntary deportation of Jeconiah to Xerxes. What Wanckelius produced to the contrary is weighed by Dr. Behm in the aforementioned place.

§. CXLVII. I confess, however, that neither the family nor the origin of Xerxes' wife fits, since Amestris was Persian, not Hebrew; nor do those things which Herodotus reports about Amestris agree with the piety of Esther and those things which are handed down about her in the book of Esther; and Dr. Behm does not deny this. But he thinks that some things could have been sprinkled into the narrative of Herodotus which, by reason of the circumstances, deserve some correction; indeed, he even goes so far as to say that the book of Esther was written after the times of the Prophets, and that in it not everything should be dissected to the quick—in which, however, it would have been better to have chosen to suspend judgment (τὸ ἐπέχειν), until some Elias solves the knot, as he himself speaks with Scaliger, than to render the authority of a Canonical book doubtful and suspect; since he does not hide that some human error can be detected in Scaliger's opinion: but to call into doubt the Hebrew Canon, to which the book of Esther belongs, is by no means fitting.

§. CXLVIII. To us, in an uncertain matter, it does not seem advisable to define anything certain. For the rest, there is no solid reason why the modern opinion of Scaliger should be preferred to the opinions of any of the ancients (if you except the opinion of the Jews concerning Cambyses, which does not fit for the reason that in the book of Esther 3:7 the twelfth year of the reign of Ahasuerus is mentioned, but Cambyses ruled for only eight years), or that of Josephus and Sulpitius concerning Artaxerxes Longimanus, or that of the blessed Luther concerning Darius Hystaspis. To which opinion James Ussher also added his calculation in Chronol. p. 160, establishing the queen, the wife of Darius Hystaspis, named Vashti, as the daughter of Cyrus, called Atossa; to which opinion concerning Darius Hystaspis we do not deny that we incline. For (what they urge for Xerxes) that Ahasuerus, whose mention is in Ezra 4, lived after Darius (Hystaspis), is established by no indubitable criterion (κριτηρίῳ). Although if you look at the words, Darius is named before Ahasuerus; yet he is not said to be prior to him, but it is not obscurely signified that he is later than the same. And whence will it be proved that the Ahasuerus of Ezra chapter 4 was the husband of Esther? This is assumed gratuitously, for the mere agreement of names proves nothing solidly. Nor indeed did Xerxes alone have a large kingdom: and the Persian Amestris of Xerxes is entirely different from the Hebrew Esther, who is called Atossa by the Hebrews, and Artygtona by Herodotus (lib. 3. c. 88. l. 7. c. 69. compared), that maiden whom he narrates that Darius loved most dearly, and whose image he had fashioned from solid gold; finally, whether Mordecai, or rather his great-grandfather Kish, is said to have been carried away with Jeconiah in Esther 2:6, might seem doubtful, nay, it should rather be determined that this carrying away is to be understood of Mordecai; inasmuch as he is the primary subject of the historical narrative there, whose genealogy and status or condition are described. For that it treats of the transportation of him whose parent, grandfather, and great-grandfather are commemorated, and who was the foster-father of the daughter of his brother, Edissa, is by no means obscure, if verses 5, 6, and 7 are weighed: whence Bellarmine, in book 2 of the Word of God, chapter 7, acknowledges that Mordecai had been carried away to Babylon with King Jehoiachin, but carried away not in himself, but in his parents or ancestors. Which is indeed to be considered a twisting of the text in this place: nor does it agree with chapter 11, verse 2. Moreover, Mordecai was of that number of captives whom Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, had carried away from Jerusalem with Jeconiah, King of Judah; not to mention that Mordecai is expressly commemorated among those carried away who returned with Zerubbabel.

Ezra 2:2. Therefore the opinion concerning Artaxerxes Mnemon has no place; much less concerning Artaxerxes Ochus: for thus Mordecai would have had to have completed more than two hundred years in living. However, we do not see what reason there is why one should depart from the opinion of the blessed Luther, which also pleased most of our own after Carion, Brentius, Philippus, Osiander, Funccius, etc., that the husband of Esther was Darius Hystaspis.

§. CXLIX. We see, however, to what end the love and patronage of the Scaligerian opinion finally leads; since, as we have said, for its sake the blessed Lord Dr. Behmius himself did not hesitate to challenge the canonical authority of the book of Esther, towards the end of his Chronological Guide: From these we conclude that the book of Esther was written after the times of the Prophets, and that in it not everything is to be taken literally. What if it had been written after the model of Judith? Which book is not historical, but poetic. But such ill-advised statements occur more frequently in that Guide, such as p. 18, 19, that St. Stephen in Acts 7 followed false opinions, and p. 50, that in the Pauline passage Acts 13:20 there lies a great suspicion of corruption: and also p. 246, that in Jer. 27 there is an error of person, and that the name of Zedekiah should be placed instead of Jehoiakim, and that a similar σφάλμα (error) has crept into Matthew ch. 27:9: Likewise p. 227, concerning the term of 70 years of captivity shortened by the power of divine mercy; and other things of this kind. These we have thought worthy of note, both so that such things, which are contrary to the canonical authority, purity, and integrity of the sacred books, or to the truth of divine prophecies, may not be accepted by readers imprudently, and so that we may learn to conduct ourselves religiously in the Holy Code, and not for the sake of a preconceived opinion abandon even a single apex of Scripture, or call it into doubt.

CHAPTER XIII. An examination of the argument for the opinion of Scaliger.

§. CL. It remains that we resolve the arguments which were brought forward in ch. 5 for the opinion of Scaliger. Although from those things which have been said, they now seem to be εὐδιάλυτα (easily dissolved). In the first, we deny that the going forth of the prophetic word is understood by Gabriel. Nor does any reason prove this. For the word 'going forth' is general, and can be taken as much of the word of the King as of the word of God. For although no King is mentioned, the edict is nevertheless described so περιστατικῶς (circumstantially) that it does not allow us to be ignorant of the King. Nor can the word of Haggai or Zechariah concerning the building of the house of the Lord be understood; for the discourse is not about a word which was to go forth for the sake of the building of the house of the Lord, but which was to go forth concerning the restoring and rebuilding of Jerusalem, and the restoring of the streets and walls of the city: Such a word is not read to have gone forth through Haggai or Zechariah: and therefore, since in Ezra 6:14 the command of God made through the Prophets is joined with the command of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, these are to be taken σχετικῶς (relatively), so that the command of God and the command of Cyrus and Darius look to the building of the temple. But the command of Artaxerxes [looks to] the arrangement of those things which pertained to Ecclesiastical Polity, as is evident from the tenor of this command. Which is brought forward in ch. 7, even if by ὑσερολογίαν (hysteron proteron) it was joined to the others in the preceding chapter.

§. CLI. The second argument from Hagg. 1:1 suffers from a double fault: first, of a doubtful, nay, false comparison, as if the passage of Haggai were parallel to ours and corresponded to that going forth of the word of which Gabriel speaks here; then, of an erroneous application of the year of Darius 2 mentioned by the Prophet to the reign of Darius Nothus, which not so

Nothus, but the reign of Hystaspis, we proved in the preceding chapter.

§. CLII. In the third, from Zech. 1:6, the same faults lie hidden, and the building of the house of the Lord, of which Zechariah speaks, is confused with the building of the city, of which Daniel speaks, and likewise Darius Nothus with Darius the son of Hystaspis.

§. CLIII. The things which are brought forward fourth from Zech. 7 provide a most valid weapon, but against Scaliger. For the seventy years reckoned back from the second year of Darius Hystaspis end not in the fourth year of the captivity of Zedekiah, as Scaliger says, but in the last or eleventh year of King Zedekiah, which was the year of the πανωλεθρίας (total destruction) of the Solomonic temple, from which to the last of Cyrus, Eusebius counts 60 solid years: Let 8 of Cambyses and Smerdis be added, and two of Darius, and 70 emerge. Thus, if you look at the Nabonassarean years, the first of Nebuchadnezzar in Judea is 140 from Nabonassar, and therefore the 18th of Nebuchadnezzar is 159 Nabonassarean, the last of King Zedekiah. Wherefore Zech. 1:12 rightly complains: O Lord of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these seventy years? Because so many years had flowed from the total destruction of the city, for the sake of which the fasts had been instituted. But if you count the seventy years back from the 2nd of Darius Nothus, the beginning will fall into the thirtieth of Darius Hystaspis, which year is not notable by any character. Nor do the Scaligerians have even a probable cause why an epoch of such a kind should be cast into that year. But what Scaliger urges, that fasts could not have been instituted except in the city of Jerusalem alone and while the use of sacrifices obtained, and therefore that in the Babylonian exile, with the temple destroyed, fasts had by no means been instituted, that cannot be proven. For why could fasts not have been instituted in exile? For Scaliger himself admits that the Church remained in exile, even if he wishes it to have remained without the arguments or insignia of the Church. Which we readily grant concerning some more eminent insignia. Moreover, if the Church remained, it does not appear what could have prevented them from being able to celebrate fasts; nay, in the most fervent persecution under Haman, the Church could still assemble even in the very metropolis and Royal city, namely Susa, outside of Jerusalem—all the Jews living there, that is—and celebrate fasts; as the book of Esther ch. 5:10 testifies. The Jews also instituted solemn feasts there in exotic places, namely the days of Purim, which the whole Jewish Church dispersed there celebrated outside of Palestine. There are also no arguments which Scaliger uses here to prove that fasts could not have been instituted outside of Palestine. He says that no solemnities were celebrated because the Feast of Tabernacles was as it were instituted anew in the 20th year of Artaxerxes, because its observance had not only ceased, but had also been consigned to oblivion. But what kind of consequence is that: The Jews neglected, or rather consigned to oblivion for a time, the feast of Tabernacles in Palestine itself. Therefore, no solemnities could be celebrated by them in the Babylonian exile? Therefore, neither were fasts instituted or celebrated there? For whatever reason they consigned the feast of Tabernacles to oblivion, which was not free from fault, they could certainly have celebrated it, and indeed they even celebrated it once under Joshua, son of Jozadak, after their return, Ezra 3:4. From this negligence and fault of the Jews in Palestine, therefore, it is not permitted to infer that they could not have celebrated any solemnities at all in exile, and not even have instituted fasts. But Scaliger has yet another argument for this matter, namely, that they could not have celebrated the Passover. Again, he says in lib. 6. de emend. tempor. pag. 602: Daniel fasts from the fourth day of Nisan until the 24th of the same month. Therefore, Daniel did not celebrate the Passover on the 14th of Nisan, Dan. 10:2, 3, 4.

Furthermore, Ezra migrates on the 12th of the month of Nisan from the river Ahava, nor does he celebrate the Passover, or at least he does not even eat unleavened bread, as all Jews and Samaritans do today, wherever they are in the world, who call the eating of unleavened bread and endives παχαζιζειν. Therefore, they instituted no solemnities or fasts during the deportation. But who does not see that there is more in the conclusion than in the premises? For even if they did not celebrate the Passover outside of Palestine, which was tied to a certain place, namely Jerusalem, does it follow that they did not celebrate fasts, which were not tied to Palestine at all? Does it follow that they instituted absolutely no solemnities in foreign lands? The contrary is manifest from the fast celebrated in Susa and from the feast of Purim.

§. CLIV. The fifth argument from the reiteration of the Jerusalem structure does not hold, unless it is assumed that the discourse is about the structure of the temple, which, having been interrupted for a time, was to be continued in turn. But in the text, there is nothing about the interrupted structure of the temple being reiterated, but about the city being built again. Of all the interpreters, says Scaliger himself, this is the meaning, so that they understand it thus: From the going forth of the word to restore and build Jerusalem: that is, from the publication of the edict concerning the restoring and building of Jerusalem. And indeed, Daniel intended nothing else. Thus Scaliger.

§. CLV. The sixth errs in its application, and, like others, confuses the structure of the temple with the building of the city. The former was begun in the 2nd year of Darius, not the latter. But the angel speaks of the latter, not the former. Therefore, that interval of 49 years from the second year of Darius to the 32nd of Artaxerxes, mentioned by Nehemiah, is of no help. For this is not Artaxerxes Mnemon, but he who obtained the name 'Longimanus' (Long-handed). Finally, the followers of Scaliger cannot designate the epoch of the 62 weeks; what point is there, then, in applying the smaller number of seven weeks, when they fail in the more important and larger one! What of the fact that Scaliger does not even know how to apply those seven weeks, whence he does not hesitate to say they are vacant, that is, they have no epoch to which they may be referred.

§. CLVI. The seventh, that the beginning of the 70 weeks was initiated from a completed Sabbatical and Jubilee year, and that the end likewise falls in a Sabbatical and Jubilee year, upon the completion of which Jerusalem was desolated, is more clever and specious than solid and firm. For whence will it be apodictically taught that the Lord willed the beginning to be made here from a Sabbatical and Jubilee year, or if that be so, that the beginning must be fixed precisely in that way, and that Scaliger's calculation is to be preferred to all others in that matter? How many hypotheses must be assumed, which are by no means free from controversy, in order for those things to be proven? What of the fact that Lansbergius, also beginning these weeks from the 7th of Longimanus, makes not only the initial but also the final year not only Sabbatical, but also a Jubilee! We certainly cannot safely rely on these topics in explaining the oracles of Scripture.

§. CLVII. Eighth, while we do not deny that the final destruction of Jerusalem is defined in this oracle, since the desolation is predicted in open words and is demonstrated by Christ from this oracle in Matthew 21, we nevertheless deny absolutely that the term of the seventy weeks is set in that ἐρημώσῑ (desolation). Nor does it follow that if the beginning of the epoch is the building of the city, the end of the same must be constituted as the desolation of the city. And the end of the confirmation of the covenant in the city and among the holy people corresponds very well to the restoration of both the ecclesiastical and civil polity: because that restoration was made on account of the covenant of grace, for the sake of which not only were those ecclesiastical matters expedited by Ezra, but afterwards the city also had to be repaired by Nehemiah, so that it might provide a lodging for the Church, until the kingdom of God was to be taken away from this people, which began to happen after the weeks were completed; from which time also both the ecclesiastical and civil polity inclined toward an end, until the final πανολεθρία (total destruction) should shortly follow.

§. CLVIII. The ninth fights against the Beroaldists, that the epoch is not to be begun from the laying of the temple foundations and the Kingdom of Cyrus: but it does not make for Scaliger that it should be referred to the second year of Darius Nothus: indeed, because the angel openly deals with the building of the streets and walls, how does Scaliger snatch those things away to the repeated building of the temple and the continuation of a work begun but interrupted?

§. CLIX. Tenth, when 70 weeks are said to be defined over the people and over the holy city, it is indeed rightly concluded that the term cannot be fixed in the reign of Cyrus, where only the foundations of the temple were laid, but it cannot be inferred from that that the epoch is to be begun from the time when the works in building the temple, having been hindered for many years, succeeded again. For there is nothing in the text about the construction of the temple. But it is more correctly gathered from these words of Gabriel that the beginning designated is that at which a certain form of polity, both ecclesiastical and civil, began to be instituted in the city of Jerusalem by public authority or at the going forth of the royal word, which falls not in the times of Darius Nothus, nor of Artaxerxes Mnemon, but in the times of Artaxerxes Μακρόχειρ (Longimanus).

§. CLX. Eleventh, when 70 weeks are said to be decreed over the people and over the holy city, Gabriel does not mean that the end of these weeks will be the destruction of the city and the people, but that the holy people with the holy city will cease, with the confirmation of the covenant, which is said to be in the final week, so that it can no longer be considered the holy people of God and the holy city: because from then on the kingdom of God will be taken away from them, and the total destruction of the city will begin to impend. Which, however, is not included in the space of the seventy weeks, but is designated as being about to happen shortly after their expiration. Nor indeed, according to Scaliger's opinion, did the city either begin to be restored at the beginning of the epoch, or was it destroyed at the end of the same: for the restoration of the city began not in the time of Darius, but of Artaxerxes, and the city was destroyed not at the end of the weeks, but in the fourth year after the 70 weeks had elapsed, according to the calculation of Scaliger, Calixtus, and others. Therefore, this explanation is consistent with itself in no part.

§. CLXI. The twelfth argument can be opposed to Beroaldus, but it opposes our opinion in nothing; indeed, it confirms the same and teaches that it is entirely consistent with the scope of Gabriel: for the restoration of the people and the city, as witnessed by Ezra and Nehemiah, began not in the time of Darius, but of Artaxerxes.

§. CLXII. As regards the thirteenth calculation of B. D. Behm, which counts precisely 490 years from the second year of Darius Nothus until the destruction of Jerusalem, it does not agree with the Scaligerian computation. For according to this, the second year of Darius Nothus is 4290 of the Julian Period, as can be seen in book 5 of De emendatione temporum, page 412. But the year of the final destruction of Jerusalem is 4783 of the Julian Period, according to the same author. Therefore, 493 years intervene. But let the followers of Scaliger reconcile these things. We know that those who wish to define the mystical weeks must look not only to the chronological count of years, but primarily to the words of the divine oracle; from which, however, it is clearer than the midday light that they depart.

§. CLXIII. Finally, Scaliger rejoices without cause concerning the consensus of the ancients, for he could produce none: Eusebius and Cyril do not agree with him: because they understand with us the 2nd year of Darius in Ezra not as the reign of Darius Nothus, but of Hystaspes. Sulpitius Severus alone is brought forward from all of antiquity, who indeed does not agree in calculation with Scaliger. For he does not count 70 and a half weeks to the destruction of Jerusalem, but sixty-nine, and he is silent about the last and also about the half-week after the last, that is, the seventieth. Therefore, Scaliger did not receive this from his antiquity, but against the consensus of antiquity he invented that the Darius of Ezra is Darius Nothus, and he devised that designation of our mystical Epoch. And these things concerning the 70 weeks of Daniel. To the Triune God, the Best and Greatest arbiter of times, who is above and outside all time, be praise and perennial glory!

Latin:

CAPUT XII. Darius Efdr. 4, 5. 24. unus est, idemq́; Hystaspis nempe filius; neque Efdr. 7. Artaxerxes alius, quam Longimanus intelligendus est.

§. CXXVIII. Id ergo oftendendum nobis est, Darium quem nominat Efdras cap. 4. neque diver- fum effe, sed unum eundemque verf. 5. & 24. Neq; pofteriori commate Darium, quem vocant Νόθον, sed Darium Hystaspida intelligi, ejusque anno se- cundo templi structuram reassumptam effe; unde confequitur Efdr. 7. non Artaxerxem Mnemona, sed Artaxerxem Longimanum defignari. Argu- menta autẽ hæc nos præcipue movent, quo minus Scaligero hic affurgamus, qui Darium Nothum sub- stituere maluit, etsi non pauci Chronologi magni nominis eam fententiam fuam fecerint. Primo quod Efdras defcribens tempora, & caufas impe- ditæ structuræ templi, ubi Reges illos, sub quibus opus fufflaminarint Cuthæi, defignare voluerit, nullos alios nominavit, quam Cyrum, Ahasverum, Arthasasthba, & Darium. Horum nempe tempo- ribus remoram injectam fuiffe teftatur. Si alii in- terceffiffent à Cyro ad Darium, sub quorum regimi- ne opus remoram paffum fuiffet, neutiquam illos prætermififfet Divinus Hiftoricus. Quapropter per Darium hunc neceffario intelligendus Hyfta- fpis Filius, quartus à Cyro, unde relinquitur etiam quod non alii intermedii hic intelligi poffint per Ahasverum & Artasasthba, quam Reges illi, qui Cyrum proxime fequuti funt, & Regem, Darium nuncupatum, antecefferunt. Qui tefte exotica hi- storia fuere Cambyses Cyri filius, & Smerdis Magus, filius ejus perfonatus, vel putatitius. Prior quũ ab avo minus auguftum Cambysis nomen accepiffet, in regnum evectus Afveri ἐπωνυμίαν affumfit; quæ juxtaHerodotũ ἀῤῥήϊον bellicosum fignificat & com- munis Regibus fuiffe creditur: Nam & Estheræ maritus nomine Ahasveri infignitus fuit, qui fine dubio aliud nomen proprium habuit. Siquidem in univerfa ferieMonarcharumPerficorum nomen Ahafveri non compareat, tefte Ptolomæi canone. quod vero exAhafvero Xerxem facere conaturSca- liger cum fectatoribus fuis, prorfus ineptum est. Quid enim commune est nomini Ahasveri cum Xerxis appellatione? Smerdis vero, quum perfo- nam filii Cyri fingeret, nomine etiam fibi autorita- tem conciliaturus, Arthachfasta dici voluit: quod cum nomine Xerxis gentilitiumRegibus Perfarum fuiffe, Grotius obfervat. Neque vero novum aut infolens Scripturæ facræ est, omiffo nomine proprio Regum ipfos iis appellare nominibus, quæ fibi im- pofuerint, etfi communia illa fint, & à pluribus u- furpata. Quod citra confufionem perfonarum fit, cum circumstantiæ textus perfonam fatis defi- gnant. Ita Regem illum, quem nomine proprio appellavit Ptolomæus Nabonidum, nuncupat fcri- ptura Baltafar, quod ille fibi affumfit in honorem Beli, quem pro Deo colebat; nam בלטשאצר di- citur quafi recondens thefaurum Beli, seu facerdos mysteriorum Beli. Alii Regem illum dictum nomine suo fuiffe Laboroffardochum volunt, cujus loco fo- cio nomine præfuit Niricaffalaflarus. Nonnulli ipfum Evilmerodach vocatum ajunt, uti videre est apud Cornelium à Lapide. Nomen certe Balthafar non fuit proprium, fed commune quod ipfi etiam Dario impofitum Dan. 1. verf. 7. similiter appellatur Rex Perfarum Dan. 8. verf. 28.

cap. 9. Darii nomine, quod utique non erat pro- prium, sed commune nomen, quemadmodum præter hunc Darium Medum adhuc tres alii Darii in Monarchia Persarum commemorantur. Et proprium illi Dario nomen fuisse Nabonadii è Pto- lomæi canone, Berosi fragmento & Megisthene Scaligeriani probare satagunt. Alia Exempla ta- cemus in re satis liquida.

§. CXXIX. Porro manifestum est, tempus regni Darii terminum constitui præpeditæ ædifica- tionis domus Domini. Nam hostes Judæ & Ben- jamin consiliarios corrupisse, & consilium extru- endi templi impedivisse dicuntur, omnibus die- bus Cyri, & USQUE ad regnum Darii Regis Per- sarum. Si ergo Darias Nothus designetur, ne- cessum erit, non tantum Cambysis & Smerdis, sed etiam Darii Hystaspis, Xerxis, & Artaxerxis Lon- gimani, (quem Darius Nothus excepit,) tempo- ribus opus impeditum fuisse. Quomodo vero illos dissimulasset Esdras, & duorum solum Re- gum mentionem fecisset, cæteris qui Cyro succef- fere, præteritis? Cur totum istud intervallum, se- ptennium nempe Cambysis & Smerdis septime- stre spatium, & Darii Hystaspidæ XXXVI. annos, hoc est XLIV. annos sicco pede transiliisset? Nul- lo certe modo hoc verisimile est, Reges illos, à qui- bus maxime impedita videtur structura silentio transiturum divinum historicum, ubi historiam in- hibitæ & impeditæ structuræ plenam persequitur.

§. CXXX. Tertio non regnum tantum, sed regni etiam ejusdem annum definire voluit Scri- ptura sacra, in gratiam Chronologiæ sacræ, & ad demonstrandam veritatem Propheticam, quo re- assumpta est iterum ædificatio templi. Quum er- go impeditam eam, usq; ad Imperium Darii dixerit, ac Reges, sub quibus impedita fuit, & calumniam in Judæos vibratam, atque interdictum Regium recensuerit, annum regiminis Darii nunc designat, quo adversantium consilia finem tandem habuere vers. 24. Intermissum est opus Domini USQUE AD secundum annum Darii, ut adeo, si res probe pensi- tetur, nihil manifestius esse possit, quam quod de uno eodemque Dario & versu 5. & versu 24. actum sit. Nam versus intermedii exponunt solum mo- dum, & stratagema delatorum, referuntque inter- dictum, quod per calumniam hostes Judæorum ob- tinuere. Particula ergo copulativa v. 6. ובמלכות sensu causali recte redditur à B. Luthero, quem non raro obtinere solet, ut hæc sit textus συνέχεια: Con- duxerunt adversus eos consiliarios ut destruerent con- silium eorum omnibus diebus Cyri usq; ad Regnum Darii. Nam in regno Ahasveri, (Cambysis) in principio regni ejus conscripserunt accusationem ad- versus habitatores Iuda & Benjamin, & in diebus Arthasasthæ (Smerdis similiter) scripserunt Bese- lam, Mithridates &c. unde liquet hæc modo com- memorata gesta esse ante Darii illius tempora, cu- jus anno secundo successit opus. Nam si post Da- rium versu quinto nominatum accidissent illa, & ἐγκλήματα ad Asverum, & Arthachsastha delata es- sent, valde absona foret illa relatio, Impedierunt consilium omnibus diebus Cyri USQUE AD DA- RII (Hystaspis) regnum; Et postea, Ahasveri & Artahsastæ, Xerxis & Longimani tempore scripse- runt accusationem. Sic enim, indicato jam finali termino impeditionis, initio regni Darii, referetur impeditio sub successoribus Darii. Quod ἄτοπον.

§. CXXXI. Quarto non verisimile est, Xer- xem & Artaxerxem Longimanum impedivisse opus instaurationis templi, & ita impedivisse, ut præ aliis etiam obstiterint, ac præcipue, ut puta præ Cam- byse, atque Smerde Mago eo nomine ab Esdra re- ferri meruerint, imprimis, si Xerxes, uti vult Scali- ger, Ahasverus sit Estheræ maritus, & Artaxerxes Longimanus ejusdem ex Esther vel Amastride filius. Qui enim ipsorum pietati hoc congrueret, tanto- pere structuram templi sufflaminare?

§. CXXXII. Quinto repugnat Chronologia. Nam si templi instauratio præpedita fuit usque ad Darii Nothi tempora, necessum est, Israelitas, post- quam Cyri indulgentia in patriam reversi sunt, per integrum Seculum, & quod excurrit, templo desti- tutos fuisse. Subducatur calculus, sive à XXI. si- ve, ut alii malunt, à XXIX. Cyri anno, usque ad se- cundum Darii τẽ νόθε, & prodibit intervallum CX. vel CXVIII. annorum. Quis vero credat, tanto tempore ipsos templo caruisse, aut quomodo id promissis divinis consentaneum fuerit? Quapro- pter præstat statuere, iterum operi structuræ tem- pli manus admotas esse tempore Darii Hystaspis; juxta quam hypothesin vix per XX. annos destitu- ti fuissent post reditum in Palæstinam templo, sede cultus divini ordinaria.

§. CXXXIII. Sexto expendenda sunt verba E- pistolæ delatoriæ, quæ Esdr. 4. habetur vers. 14. Quandoquidem igitur templum destruximus, B. Lu- therus ἐμφατικωτέρως sensum reddidit: Nun wir aber alle dabey sind, die wir den Tempel zerstöret haben. Unde apparet, delatores, qui tum literas ad Artachsashtha dederunt, templi destructioni quon- dam interfuissse; quæ quum facta sit anno Nabu- chodonosoris XIX. ex eo autem tempore usque ad annum Darii Hystaspis secundum LXX. anni efflu- xerint, & inde ad Artaxerxis Longimani Imperium LV. oportet istos, si tantum VIII. annos habuere excidii tempore, annos natos fuisse CXLIII. Quæ ætas tum prorsus inusitata fuit: Octuaginta autem aliquot annos habuisse nonnullos isto seculo, longe verisimilius est, quales proinde & destructioni pri- oris templi, & hujus delationibus apud Smerdem interesse potuissent.

§. CXXXIV. Septimo quum Josua Pontifica- tum gesserit illo tempore, quo in Palæstinam, teno- re diplomatis Cyri, rediere Israelitæ, hoc est, XXI. regni Cyri anno, qui primus Monarchiæ Cyri fu- it, oportet ipsum, tempore exædificati templi Pontificatu functum fuisse, ad minimum per CXXI. annos, adeoque vivendo ultra CL. an- nos confecisse, si tempus istud incidit in sextum Darii Nothi. Nam ab XXI. anno Cyri usque ad Darii VI. numerantur CXXI. anni. At si terminus extructi templi sextus Darii Hystaspis constitua- tur, XXIII. anni tantum à primo Cyri usque ad consummationem operis elapsi erunt. Quapro- pter iterum vero est similius prioris, non posterio- ris Darii tempus intelligendum esse.

§. CXXXV. Octavo conferendus erit hic locus Hag. 2, 4. Ubi ita Propheta: Quis inter vos est, qui vidit Domum istam in gloria sua prima? Et quid videris hanc? Numquid non ita est, quasi nihil sit in oculis vestris? Unde colligitur, Haggæi tempo- re adhuc fupersse, qui primam domum in gloria sua viderint. Quos oportebat ducentorum pene fuisse annorum, si templi structura VI. Darii Nothi consummata est. Nam à destructionis tempore usque ad secundum Hystaspis annum numerantur LXX. anni: ab hoc vero CII. anni effluxere ad Sex- tum Darii Nothi, ut puta XXXIV. reliqui Darii Hy- staspidæ, XXI. Xerxis, XLI. Longimani, & VI. Da- rii Nothi, qui in summam redacti centum & duos annos conficiunt. His si addas annos LXX. prodi- bunt CLXXII. anni. Si qui jam fuerint X. an- norum, cum viderunt primam domum, necessum est, ut illi habuerint Haggæi tempore CLXXXII. annos, qui comparare alterius domus gloriam cum priori jubebantur. Quæ μακροβιότης ætati isti non congruit.

§. CXXXVI. Nono solidissime sententiam no- stram confirmat locus Propheticus Zach. 1, 12. An- no enim secundo Darii Zacharias precatus dicitur : Domine exercituum usq́; quo non misereberis Jeru- salem, & urbium Judæ, quibus iratus es. Iste jam se- ptuagesimus annus est! Accepit enim Propheta re- sponsum divinum hisce verbis : Lætatus sum super Jerusalem, & cum Zelo magno revertar ad Jerusa- lem in misericordia: Domus mea ædificabitur in ea. Promissa ergo divinitus fuit secundo Darii anno templi instauratio. Quam completam Sexto Darii ejusdem anno fuisse è collatione Esdræ & Haggæi manifestissimum est. At Darius ille apud Zacha- riam alius esse nequit, quam Darius Hystaspis. Nam de Dario Notho nullo pacto congruit Chronolo- gia, optime autem de priori. Siquidem ab excidio urbis usq́; ad annum secundum Darii Hystaspis efflu- xere 70. anni. Illud enim accidit anno 19. Nabu- chodonosaris ineunte, qui fuit Æræ Nabonazarææ 158. Quum ergo septimus Cambysis annus, juxta Ptolomæum fuerit Nabonazaræus 225. secundus Darii colligandus erit cum anno istius æræ 228. Ab his autem subtractis juxta annum excidii 158. rema- nent 70. anni, quot scilicet ab excidio urbis, ad re- stauracionem templi elapsi. Et totidem anni hujus intervalli prodibunt quoq; juxta calculum anno- rum Iphiti Eusebianum. Ponit enim Eusebius in Chronicis excidium in secundum Olympiadis 47. vel Iphiti 186. Quum ergo Cyrus per 30. annos re- gnarit, qui cœpit anno 1. finiente Olympiadis 55. seu Iphiti 217. hoc est 31. anno post excidium, ad- dendi hisce annis 31. erunt 29. (qui primum Cyri annum sequuti sunt) nec non 8. Cambysis, & Smer- dis, ac duo Darii Hystaspis, & proditura iterum ex- acte est summa 70. annorum. Si annus secundus Darii Nothi assumatur, 167. anni intervenient inde ab exterminio urbis. Quod intervallum nemo cum oraculo Zachariæ conciliaturus est.

§. CXXXVII. Torquent hic sese Scaligeria- ni; & quum videant nullatenus verba Zachariæ, si ad Darii Nothi ætatem oraculum referatur, con- gruere Chronologiæ excidii & devastationis urbis, fingunt, non respici annos devastationis, sed tempora longe post sequuta, annos nempe aliarum calamita- tum, quos vero numerare, aut definire è sacris ne- queunt, quum eorum nec vola nec vestigium us- piam habeatur. Fatetur id D. Behm. lib. 2. Chron. Manud. Tit. 2. cap. 3. p. 111. Probabiliter colligimus Zachariam per annos 70. non annos captivitatis, sed alios intellexisse, nullum quidem hac de re in sacris a- libi vestigium apparet. Verum id ad nostram senten- tiam infringendam parum facit. Laboravit id secu- lum penuria Prophetarum, ut unicum Haggæum ha- beamus cum Zacharia σύγχρονον &c. Ut taceam, quod accuset hic Zachariam, quod accuratam illo- rum 70. annorum supputationem NON ATTEN- DERIT. Audiatur & Scaliger ipse in animadvers. ad Euseb. p. 91. Non enim Angelus loquitur de anno septuagesimo deportationis, sed quod ab Edicto Cyri toties Judæa gens à finitimis infestata fuerit, ut nullas urbes tuto habitare, nullos muros excitare facultas ei data fuerit, quo intervallo, quod est annorum 106. per ultimos 70. annos nullum non calamitatis genus experta fuerit, ut nullas urbes in Judæa instaurandi copia facta sit. Sed uti facile largimur, non intelligi annum septuagesimum deportationis : Sic manife- stum omnino est è Propheta, annum septuagesi- mum ab excidio urbis, quo Domus Domini in cine- ribus jacuit, indigitari. Ob quod etiam jejunia illa illdo quinti & septimi mensis, de quibus Zach. 7,5. insti- tuta, quia quinto mense templum exustum, 2. Reg. 25, 28. Septimo Gedalia reliquiis Judæorum præfe- ctus occisus fuit vers. 28. Ob quam πανωλεθρίαν in- stituta quoq; jejunia quarti & decimi mensis Zach. 8,19. quia quarto urbs expugnata est Jerem. 39. De- cimo autem obsideri cœpit 2. Reg. 25. Atque ita in- terpretatus est Zachariæ locum Eusebius in Chro- nol. pag. 151. Quod autem septuagesimus annus de- solationis templi altero Darii anno fuerit expletus, testis est Zacharias Propheta, cum de secundo anno Darii ita loquitur, Domine omnipotens, quousq; non misereberis Jerusalem, & civitatibus Juda, quas de- spexisti? hic septuagesimus annus est, vel his septua- ginta annis. Hæc enim ἰσοδυναμῶντα sunt. Similiter exposuit Hieronymus, ut & Clemens Alexandrinus ab Hieronymo in h. l. Zachariæ adductus: secundo anno Darii, filii Hystaspis septuagesimum desolatio- nis templi annum, qui ab Jeremia prædictus est, fuis- se completum, ipse Zacharias testis est, dicens: Do- mine exercituum, usq; quo non misereberis? Distin- guendi itaque anni 70. captivitatis, qui à Jojakimi quarto incipiunt, & in primo Monarchiæ Cyri an- no desinunt: uti circa Jerem. 29. luculenter cum B. D. Behmio monstravimus, & anni 70. excidii urbis & templi, qui anno Nebucadnezaris 19. in- choandi, finem consequuntur secundo Darii Hy- staspis anno. De his loquitur Zacharias, non de il- lis. Alios autem septuaginta annos desolationis ignorat Scriptura sacra, adeoque frustra illi fingun- tur à Scaligero, qui nullum de illis testem produ- cere potuit, sed ut multa alia ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων illos com- mentus est.

§. CXXXVIII. Nono hebdomada nostræ mysti- cæ huic sententiæ per se satis, ut hactenus vidimus, firmæ adhuc robur aliquod addunt. Quum enim exitum verbi de Hierosolymæ restauratione initium earum constituit Gabriel, qui Artaxerxis 7. anno, teste Esdra, accidit, quemadmodum luculenter probavimus, neque alius Artaxerxes ille sit, quam μακρόχειρ, necessum est Darium ejus prædecesso- rem, esse Hystaspis filium, sub cujus secundo anno templum restaurari cœptum est. Quæ consequentia è capitis 4. & 7. Esdræ cum Nehem. 2. collatio- ne aperta, & penes omnes in confesso est. Nam Darius Nothus non præcessit Longimanum, sed successit eidem. Existimat quidem Scaliger, ini- tium hebdomadum Danielis suæ potius favere o- pinioni, imo hæc enata sine dubio inde est, quod observatæ fuerint 70. hebdomades annorum seu 490. anni intercessisse inter annum 2. Darii Nothi & excidium Hierosolymitanum. Ex eo enim con- jectura oriri facile potuit στοχασμοῖς suis, neglectis Scripturæ testimoniis, indulgenti, Darium illum, cuj9 anno 2. templum instaurari cœpit, τὸν Νόθον esse & terminum septimanarum Danielis constitui de- bere in excidio Hierosolymitano. Sed quum hoc an- geli verba non ferant, locus illi conjecturæ nullus est. Ex adverfo vero luculenter initium Epochæ 70. Septimanarum figitur in exitu sermonis de Hierosolymitana murorum instauratione, qui jux- ta Esdram & Nehemiam ad Artaxerxis Longima- ni tempora referendus. Ut ergo per omnia con- sonent sibi Scripturæ loca, quæ nulla sui parte, po- test ἐαυτομαχεῖν, Darii ille secundus annus tanto- pere in Scripturis celebratus non alterius est, quam Darii Hystaspis.

§. CXXXIX. Decimo pro nostra sententia facit locus Esdræ c. 6, 14. quo exprimuntur & celebran- tur Reges, sub quibus opus Domini successerit, in restaurando templo, hac serie, Cyrus, Darius, & Artachsashta. Si enim Darius Nothus, & Artaxerxes

Memor intelligantur,uti vult Scaliger, nimis lon- gum intervallum erit à primo edicto Cyri, sive id anno penultimo, seu octavo à morte ejus promul- gatum censeatur, usque ad septimum annum Arta- xerxis Memoris, annorum nempe 132. vel 139. neq; facile constare poterit verbis istis Esdr. c. 6, 14. veri- tas: & ædificaverunt & fundaverunt ex præcepto Dei Israël, & juxta mandatum Cores, Darii, & Artach- sastæ Regum Persarum. Num enim annis 139. post edictum Cyri adhuc ædificarunt templum, de quo ibi sermo est & quidem juxta mandatum Cyri?

§. CXL. Neq; ullatenus nos movet illa Scalige- ri & D. Behmii objectio è cap. 6. Esdræ; quod in- tervallum bene longum ab edicto Cyri usque ad secun- dum annum hujus Darii intercessisse videatur, quia necesse fuit, Cyri concessionem in Archivis Achmetæ, vel Ecbatanis, Metropoli Mediæ inquirere, non au- tem verisimile appareat, intra 13. annos (quot ab edi- cto sc. Cyri ad 2. Darii elapsi) memoria id adeo exci- dere potuisse, ut inquirendum in Archivis fuerit. In- quiruntur enim quandoque in Archivis, quæ intra lustrum, imo quæ intra brevius spatium gesta, ac mandata sunt, ob certiorem rei notitiam, ut tam de edicto, quam de causis edicti, aliisq; circumstantiis ἀμεταπτώτως constet. Nihil frequentius accidere, notum, qui in muneribus publicis versantur, aut qui archivis præfecti sunt. Ut mirer, aliquod in hoc argumento robur collocari. Neq; 13. tantum anni elapsi sunt à mandato Cyri ad Darii Hystaspidæ se- cundum annum, sed octodecim: & intervenere duo alii Reges, imo contrarium etiam interdictum in- tercessit: quæ inquirenda omnino erant, novo Re- gi maxime; quum duo alii in regimine intercesse- rint, ut causæ tum concessionis, tum etiam inhibi- tionis justa lance ponderarentur.

§. CXLI. Novissime addimus autoritatem vete- rum, qui magno consensu instaurationem templi sub Dario factam agnoscunt, non ad Darii Nothi, sed Hystaspidæ Imperium referendum esse. Quod non solum è Judæis Josephus lib. 11. antiq. c. 4. & l. 1. contra Appionem facit, sed etiam è Christianis Do- ctoribus præcipui commatis non pauci, tum in Græca Ecclesia, Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 1. Strom. Euseb. in Chron. lib. 1. Theodoretius comment. in Haggæum & Zachariam, Cyrillus Alexandrinus, Basilius Seleuciensis &c. tum in Latina Hieronym. in Hagg. & Zach. & Augustinus lib. 18. de Civit. Dei c. 26. Beda, Marian. Scot. &c. Quorum utiq; consensus, rationibus stipatus, nobis potiori loco merito habetur, quam Neotericorum nonnullorū χθὲς ἡ πρώην enata opinio, quibus in omnia alia hic ire libuit citra gravem causam. Nec desunt tamen è recentiorib9 autores nobis ὁμόψηΦοι magni no- minis. E Pontificiis Bellarminus, Genebrard. Salia- nus, Torniell. Pererius, Sanctius, Petavius, Gordon. Henr. Philippi &c. è Reformatis Rob. Bailius, Ca- pellus, Jacob Usserius, Isaac Vossius, Joh. Vorstius, è nostris David Chytreus, Reusnerus, Christianus Matthiæ, Wilh. Langius, Vogelius in compend. Chronol. p. 159. & 182. Laurentius Euchstadius &c.

§. CXLII. Neq; vero ullius momenti est argu- mentum, quod à nominibus deductū οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας ceu palmarium habent, Scaliger nempe, Calvisius, alii: Quod ita proponere ipsi solent: Ille Darius ab Esdra intelligitur, ejusq; annus secundus indi- gitatur, qui medius est inter duos Artachsastas, vel Artaxerxes: At non Hystaspis filius, sed ὁ Nόθος est inter duos Artachsasthas medius, teste Historia, & serie Regum Persicorum; quia hunc præcessit Arta- xerxes Longimanus, & sequutus est Artaxerxes Mnemon. Ergo non Darius Hystaspis, sed ὁ Nόθος ab Esdra intelligitur, cum annus ejus secundus in- digitatur. In qua collatione si medietas secundum rigorem intelligatur, ita ut immediatus antecessor & immediatus successor Darii Artaxerxes dictus sit, major propositio ex sacra historia demonstrari non potest. Quamvis enim post Artachsasthæ, cujus edictum Esd. 4. refertur, Darii mentio fiat vers. 24. ejusdem capitis, ac postmodum Artachsashtha alius c. 7. commemoretur, non tamen hic alter Artach- sastha immediatus Darii successor constituitur ab Esdra. Annon enim potuit in illa Historia aliquis successorum prætermitti? Si vero ita stricte non sumatur illa medietas, propositio minor firmo non stat talo. Nam Darium Hystaspidis sequutus est (me- diante Xerxe) Artachsashtha, & antecessit Smerdis Magus, quem Artachsashthæ nomen sibi ex fastu & cupiditate gloriæ vili Smerdis nomine deposito, sumsisse ut credamus, nihil vetat; Imo series Esdræ omnino cogit, Artachsashtham illum priorem Es- dræ Smerdem esse. Nam refertur ut tertius a Cyro, quum hoc ordine in Esdra Reges Persici (quorum mentionem ipse fecit) sese consequantur, Cores, Asverus, Artachsashtha, Darius, Artachsashtha, qui vulgo appellantur ab exoticis scriptoribus Cyrus, Cambyses, Smerdis, Darius Hystaspis, Artaxerxes Longimanus. Qui vero desideratur in ista serie im- mediatus Hystaspis successor Xerxes, suppleri faci- le potest e Daniele cap. 11, 2. Ecce adhuc tres Reges stabunt in Perside, & quartus ditabitur opibus nimis super omnes. Quartus vero ille sine dubio Xerxes est. Inter quem & Darium Medum tres intermedii sunt, Cyrus, Cambyses, (Smerdis indignus habitus est a S. S. qui aliis annumeraretur γνησίοις Regibus & Monarchis) & Darius Hystaspis. Neq; vero nomi- num diversitatem objicere possunt, qui Scaligeri partes sequuntur. Nam quis ignorat, Reges no- mina alia assumsisse, cum ad fasces admoti sint, quem morem Persarum Regibus observatum fuis- se Scaliger lib. 6. de Emendat. temp. probavit. Ita Darius Nothus prius vocatus Ὤχος & Ὦχος, Ar- taxerxes Mnemon dictus Ἀρσίκας & Ὀάρσης. Et Codomannus dictus, qui Darii nomē obtinuit. Quid ergo mirum, si Asveri nomen Cambysi, & Artaxer- xis Smerdi in regimine tributum sit, vel ipsi præ vi- lioribus nominibus illustriora ejusmodi nomina elegerint? Et quomodo conveniunt Λαβύνιτος a- pud Herodotum, Nabavídiος in Canone Ptolemæi, & Darius Medus in Daniele, quæ tamen eandem personam Scaligerianis designant! Quam futilis objectio de nominibus, ut cum reliqua omnia conve- niant, discrimen unicum faciat, ne Mavius sit Mavius ait Scaliger Animadvers. ad Euseb. pag. 85.

§. CXLIII. Unam adhuc reperio rationem, quam cum Scaligero B. D. Behmius valde urget, e Chronologica serie petitam, quod nempe & Es- dram & Nehemiam ad tempora Alexandri M. vi- xisse ex Esdra & Nehemia colligitur. Quia Jaddua, cujus Neh. 12, 22. mentio fit, Alexand. M. Hierosoly- mam advenienti in Pontificali habitu obviam pro- cessit, teste Josepho lib. 11. Orig. cap. 8. Sed ex historia Esdræ & Nehemiæ concludi non potest, quod A- lexandri tempora uterq; attigerit. De Esdra nihil aliud habetur, quam quod Johannis Pontificis tem- pore vixerit, ejusque cubile ingressus sit Esdr. 10, 6. Non vero quod tempore Pontificatus filii Johan- nis Jaddua, nedum quod Alexandri M. tempore in vivis adhuc fuerit. Nehemias vero refert solum Jadduam Pontificem cap. 12, 22. Ubi non est, quod cum Temporario negemus, hunc Jadduam obviam factum esse Alexandro; Siquidem eo concesso nondum sequatur, Nehemiam qui Jadduæ Pontifi- catum attigit, etiam Alexandri M. tempore vixisse, quia potuit sub initium Pontificatus istius diem obiisse, obiisse. Tum si maxime etiam usque ad Alexandri tempora vixisset, quod vero nullo certo documen- to de Nehemia constat, nihil absurdi in Chrono- logica serie orietur. Nam ponamus Nehemiam 20. Artachsasthæ Longimani anno 30. egisse an- num, sexto ergo anno Darii Codomanni, quo ab Alexandro M. devictus est, annorum fuisset 142. Reponi itaq; Scaligerianis possent ea, quæ ipsi in si- mili Beroaldistis reponunt. Absurditatem, inquit D. Behmius lib. 2. Tit. cap. 10. pag. 175. quam ex longævitate Zerubabelis Ducis & Iehosuæ Pontificis Beroaldistæ sumunt, dicimus, ita comparatam esse, ut absurdum fingatur in eo, ubi nihil absurdi est. Est- ne hoc absurdum, hominem 140. vel 150. annos vive- re? Argumentum hoc procedit à βραχυβίᾳ Germa- norum ad reliquorum populorum. Hæc D. Behm.

§. CXLIV. Jam ut de Ahasvero Estheræ ma- rito aliquid adjiciam?, variæ de illo occurrunt sen- tentiæ. Quatuor recensentur à Grotio ad Esdr. cap. 4, 6. quod alii Cambysem, alii Darium Hystaspis, alii Artaxerxem Memoriösum, alii Artaxerxem Lon- gimanum eum faciant. Sed omittit Grotius quin- tam, quæ hodie fere præcipua est; quod nempe Xerxes fuerit, quam Scaliger, Calvisius, D. Behm. Tremellius, Iunius, & alii tuentur; ut & sextam, quod fuerit Artaxerxes Ochus, quæ est Serrarii & Gordoni, nec non septimam, quæ non paucis pla- cuit, quod Astyages fuerit, Socer Cyri; quem Da- nielis & Estheræ Ahasverum, Darii Medi Patrem faciunt Melchior Canus l. 11. Loc. c. 6. Gerhardus Mercator in Chronologia, Temporarius l. 3. De- monstrat. Chronol. p. 185. Wanckelius, Professor quondam hujus Academiæ in Dissert. Acad. sole- mni. Cambysen fuisse dicunt R. Salomo, Lyra, Vata- blus, Genebrardus, Petavius, Tirinus, VVilb. Lan- gius, ut & Iudæi in Seder olam &c. Darium Hysta- spis Filium Methasthenes, B. Lutherus, Philippus, Brentius, Osiander, Ioh. Carion, Funccius, Usserius, & alii plurimi: nec non è Judæis Aben-Ezra; è Pon- tificiis Corn. à Lapide, Ioh. Benedictus. Artaxerxem Longimanum Iosephus l. 11. Antiqq. c. 6. Sulpitius Severus, Nicephorus, Cajetanus, Bellarm. Salianus, Sanctius: Artaxerxem Memorem Eusebius, Maria- nus Scotus, in Chronico, Beda de sex ætatibus Mun- di ad annum mundi 3588. Alii ergo ante captivita- tis Babylonicæ solutionem hanc historiam collo- cant, qui pro Astyage pugnant: alii post captivita- tis solutionem, qui pro reliquis Cambyse, Dario, Xerxe, Longimano, Memore, Ocho.

§. CXLV. Utriusque sententiæ argumenta ad- duxit B. D. Behmius Decad. 2. Observ. 10. in Chro- nol. Manuduct. p. 251. Sed posteriora majoris pon- deris sunt, quia maritus Esther dominatus est ab India usq; ad Æthiopiam Esth. 1, 1. At nemo ante Cambysem Ægyptum Æthiopiæ conterminam obtinuit. Neq; Persæ imperarunt Medis ante Cy- rum. Neq; Medi Deum Ebræorum coluerunt: Ne- que Susis Regiam habuerunt. Neq; vero affine est, Judæos durante Babylonica captivitate tanta mul- titudine in Persidem profectos, aut tanta libertate ibi gavisos esse, ut, quod c. 9, 16. narratur, una die 75000. hostium ibi trucidare, & in Regia 800. in- terficere potuerint.

§. CXLVI. Rationes pro Xerxe hæ à Scaligero adferuntur: quod Ahasveri post Cyrum, & Dari- um, & ante Artaxerxem mentio facta Esdr. 4, 6. quod Regni Ahasveri amplitudo cum Xerxis regi- mine apud Herodotum lib. 7. c. 9. imprimis conve- niat, quod nomen uxoris Xerxis apud Herod. A'μη- στρις A'μεστρις item sit, quod חֲמַאסתַּר, quod tem- pus congruat, quia Kis Benjamita abductus est in Babyloniam Iechoniæ tempore Esth. 2, 46. à quo usq; ad Esther tres generationes recensentur, anni quasi 120. Kis, Simei, Jair, Mardochæus, quantum inter- vallum est à spontanea Jechoniæ deportatione ad Xerxem. Quæ Wanckelius in contrarium produ- xit, expenduntur à D. Behm. l. c.

§. CXLVII. Fateor tamen, uxori Xerxis neque familiam, vel ortum congruere, cum Amestris Per- sica, non Ebræa fuerit; Neq; Estheræ pietati, & iis, quæ de ea tradita sunt in libro Esther, convenire il- la, quæ Herodotus de Amestri refert; nec id diffite- tur Dn. D. Behm. sed Herodoti narrationi nonnulla aspergi potuisse putat, quæ circumstantiarum ratione correctionem aliquam mereantur : imo eo etiam a- bit, quod Estheræ liber post Prophetarum tem- pora scriptus sit, in eoque omnia ad vivum resecari non debeant, in quo tamen præstabat τὸ ἐπέχειν ele- gisse, donec Elias aliquis nodum solvat, quemadmo- dum ipse cum Scaligero loquitur, quam autorita- tem libri Canonici dubiam & suspectam reddere; quum in Scaligeri sententia humanum aliquem la- psum deprehendi posse, non dissimulet: Canonem au- tem Ebræum, ad quem liber Esther pertinet, in du- bium revocare, minime par sit.

§. CXLVIII. Nobis in re incerta certi aliquid definire non videtur consultum. De cætero causa solida nulla est, cur ulli vetustiorum sententiæ (Ju- dæorum de Cambyse opinione si excipias, quæ ideo non congruit, quod in libro Esther c. 3, 7. comme- moretur duodecimus Regni Ahasveri annus. Cam- byfes autem per octennium tantum regno præfue- rit) seu Josephi & Sulpitii de Artaxerxe Longimano, seu B. Lutheri de Dario Hystaspis, præferri neote- rica Scaligeri opinio debeat. Cui etiam calculum adjecit Jac. Usserius in Chronol. p. 160. Reginam Darii Hystaspis uxorem, Vasthi nominatam, Cyri filiam statuens, Atossam dictam: in quam de Dario Hystaspide sententiam, nos inclinare haud diffite- mur. Nam (quod pro Xerxe urgent) Ahasverum, cujus meetio sit Esdr. 4. post Darium (Hystaspida) vixisse, nullo κριτηρίῳ indubio constat. Quamvis si verba respicias, Darius prius nominetur, quam Asverus; Non tamen hoc prior esse dicitur, sed non obscure eodem posterior esse significatur. Et unde probabitur Asverum Esdræ cap. 4. maritum Esther fuisse? Gratis hoc assumitur, sola enim no- minis convenientia solide nihil probat. Neq; vero solus Xerxes Regnum amplum habuit: & Amestris Xerxis Persica ab Ebræa Esther prorsus diversa est, quæ Ebræis Atossa, Herodoto (lib. 3. c. 88. l. 7. c. 69. collato) Artygtona, virgo illa, quam Darium ma- xime adamasse, & cujus imaginem ex auro solido compactam habuisse narrat, nuncupata; denique num Mardochæus, an vero proavus ejus Kis trans- latus cum Jechonia dicatur Esth. 2, 6. dubium vi- deri possit, imo de Mardochæo hanc translationem intelligendam esse, potius statuendum; utpote qui primarium ibi historiæ narrationis subjectum est, cujus & genealogia, & status vel conditio describi- tur. Nam de illius transportatione agi, cujus pa- rens, avus, & proavus commemoratur, & qui nutri- tius filiæ fratris sui Edissæ erat, minime obscurum est, si v. 5.6.7. expendantur: unde Bellarminus l. 2. de verbo Dei c. 7. agnoscit, Mardochæum transla- tum fuisse in Babyloniam cum Rege Joachin, ve- rum translatum non in se, sed in parentibus, aut ma- joribus suis. Quod hoc quidem loco pro detorsione textus habendum: neque cum 11. cap. 2. convenit. Erat autem Mardochæus de illo numero captivo- rum, quos transtulerat Nabuchodonosor, Rex Baby- lonis de Jerusalem cum Jechonia Rege Judæ; ut ta- ceam quod Mardochai inter illos translatos expref- se commemoretur, qui cum Zorobabel reversi sunt

Esdr. 2, 2. Ideo sententia de Artaxerxe Memore locum non habet; Multo minus de Artaxerxe O- cho: Sic enim Mardochæum oportuisset vivendo plus quam ducentos annos confecisse. Non videmus autem quid causæ sit, cur à B. Lutheri sententia, quæ etiam plerisq; nostris post Carionem, Brentio, Phi- lippo, Osiandro, Funccio &c. placuit, discedi debeat, quod maritus Esther Darius Hystaspis fuerit.

§. CXLIX. Videmus autem quorsum tandem expediat Scaligerianæ sententiæ amor, ac patroci- nium; quum etiam ut diximus, in ejus gratiam ipse B. Dn. D. Behmius non dubitarit autoritatem Ca- nonicam libri Esther solicitare, sub finem Chrono- logicæ suæ manuductionis : Ex his colligimus, E- stheræ librum post Prophetarum tempora scriptum, in eoque omnia ad vivum resecanda non esse. Quid si ad exemplar Judith fuisset conscriptus? qui liber non est historicus, sed Poëmaticus. Sed talia impro- vide dicta in illa Manuductione plura occurrunt, utpote p. 18. 19. quod S. Stephanus Actor. 7. falsas opiniones sectatus sit, & p. 50. quod in Paulino loco Actor. 13, 20. magna subsit corruptionis suspicio: nec non pag. 246. quod Ier. 27. erratum personæ, & pro Jojakimi Zedekiæ nomen locandum sit, quodq́; consi- mile σφάλμα in Matthæum c. 27, 9. irrepserit: Item p. 227. de termino 70. annorum captivitatis vi mi- sericordiæ divinæ decurtato; & quæ hujus generis alia sunt. Quæ notanda duximus, tum ne impru- denter talia, quæ canonicæ autoritati, puritati, & integritati librorum sacrorum, aut vaticiniorum divinorum veritati adversa sunt, à lectoribus susci- piantur, tum ut in Sacro Codice religiose versari discamus, nec in gratiam præconceptæ opinionis vel ullum apicem Scripturæ dimittamus, aut in dubium vocemus.

CAPUT XIII. Rationem pro Scaligeri sententia examen.

§. CL. Restat, ut argumenta, quæ c. 5. pro sen- tentia Scaligeri adducta sunt, expediamus. Quan- quam ex iis, quæ dicta sunt, ea εὐδιάλυτα nunc vi- deantur. In primo negamus exitum verbi Prophe- tici à Gabriele intelligi. Neq; ulla id evincit ratio. Nam vox egressus verbi generalis est, & tam de ver- bo Regis, quam de verbo Dei accipi potest. Etsi enim Rex nullus commemoretur, edictum tamen ita πε- ριστατικῶς describitur, ut Regem nos ignorare non patiatur. Nec intelligi potest verbum Haggæi aut Za- chariæ de exstruenda domo Domini; non enim de verbo sermo est, quod ædificationis domus Domini causa, sed quod de restituendis, & reædificandis Hie- rosolymis, de plateis & muris civitatis restaurandis exiturum erat: Quale verbum non legitur exiisse per Haggæum, aut Zachariam : ideoque cum Esdr. 6, 14. conjungitur mandatum Dei per Prophetas factum, & mandatum Cyri, Darii & Artachsastæ, σχετικῶς hæc accipienda, ut mandatum Dei, ac mandatum Cyri & Darii templi ædificationem re- spiciant. Artachsastæ autem mandatum dispositio- nem de iis, quæ ad Ecclesiasticam Politiam pertine- bant, quemadmodum ex tenore hujus mandati constat. Quod cap. 7. adductũ est, etsi per ὑσερολο- γίαν præcedenti capite cæteris adjunctum fuerit.

§. CLI. Alterum argumentum ex Hagg. 1, 1. du- plici laborat vitio, tum dubiæ, imo falsæ collationis, ac si Haggæi locus nostro parallelus sit, & respon- deat egressui illi verbi, de quo hic Gabriel: tum er- ronæe applicationis anni Darii 2. à Propheta com- memorati ad regnum Darii Nothi, quem non tā

Nothi, sed Hystaspis regimen designare, capite præ- cedenti evicimus.

§. CLII. In tertio è Zach. 1, 6. eadem latent vi- tia, ac confunditur ædificatio domus Domini, de qua Zacharias, cum ædificatione urbis, de qua Daniel, nec non Darius Nothus cum Dario Hystaspis filio.

§. CLIII. Quæ quarto adferuntur è Zach. 7. va- lidissimum telum, sed adversus Scaligerum præbent. Nam septuaginta anni à secundo Darii Hystaspis retexti retro desinunt non in quartum annum capti Zedekiæ, ut ait Scaliger, sed in ultimum vel undeci- mum Regis Zedekiæ annum, qui erat annus πανω- λεθρίας Salomonici templi, à quo ad ultimum Cyri Eusebius numerat 60. solidos annos: Addantur 8. Cambysis & Smerdis, ac duo Darii & emergunt 70. Ita si annos Nabonassaræos respicias, primus Nebucadnezaris in Judæa est 140. à Nabonassare, ideoque 18. Nebucadnezaris est 159. Nabonaza- ræus, ultimus Regis Zedekiæ. Quapropter merito conqueritur Zach. 1, 22. Domine Deus exercituum quousque non miseraberis Hierosolyma & urbes Juda, quibus iratus es jam his septuaginta annis. Quia tot anni effluxerant ab urbis πανωλεθρίᾳ, cujus gratia jejunia instituta erant. Si autem septuaginta annos à Darii Nothi 2. retro numeres, initium incidet in trigesimum Darii Hystaspis, qui annus nullo cha- ractere notabilis est. Neq; habent Scaligeriani vel probabilem solum causam, cur epocha ejusmodi in illum annum conjiciatur. Quod autem urget Sca- liger, jejunia institui non potuisse, nisi in sola urbe Je- rusalem & sacrificiorum usu obtinente, adeoque in exilio Babylonico everso templo minime instituta fuis- se jejunia, id probari non potest. Quidni enim in exilio institui poterant jejunia? Nam & in exilio mansisse Ecclesiam, fatetur Scaliger, etsi sine argu- mentis aut insignibus Ecclesiæ eam mansisse velit. Quod de nonnullis eminentioribus insignibus faci- le largimur. Cæterum, si mansit Ecclesia, quidnam obstare potuerit, quo minus jejunia celebrare qui- verint, nõ apparet, imo in ferventissima persequu- tione sub Hamane adhuc coire potuit Ecclesia e- tiam in ipsa metropoli, & Regia, Susis scilicet extra Hierosolymam, omnes nempe ibi degentes Judæi, ac jejunia celebrare; teste libro Esther cap. 5, 10. In- stituerunt etiam ibi in exoticis locis festa solemnia Judæi, dies scil. Purim, quos tota illic dispersa Ec- clesia Judaica celebravit extra Palæstinam. Nulla etiam sunt argumenta, quibus hic utitur Scaliger, ut probet, extra Palæstinam institui non potuisse je- junia. Dicit, nulla solemnia celebrata fuisse, quia sce- nopegia anno 20. Artachsastæ quasi denuo instituta, quod cultus ejus non solum desitus fuerit; sed etiam oblivioni traditus. At quænam illa est consequen- tia: Judæi intermiserunt imo oblivioni tradiderunt ad tempus in ipsa Palæstina festum scenopegias. Ergo nulla solemnia ab ipsis celebrari potuere in exilio Babylonico? Ergo nec jejunia ibi instituta aut celebrata sunt? Quacunq; de causa ipsi Sceno- pegias festum oblivioni tradiderint, quod culpa non vacabat, potuere certe illud celebrare, imo e- tiam sub Jesu, filio Josedeck, semel celebrarunt id post reditum Esdr. 3, 4. Ab hac itaque negligentia & culpa Judæorum in Palæstina non licet colligere, quasi in exilio prorsus non potuerint ulla solemnia celebrare, ac ne quidem jejunia instituere. Sed ha- bet aliud adhuc argumentum ejus rei Scaliger, quod nempe Pascha celebrare non potuerint. Rur- sus, inquit lib. 6. de emend. tempor. pag. 602. Da- niel à quarta die Nisan ad 24. ejusdem mensis jejunat. Ergo 14. Nisan pascha non celebravit Dan. 10, 2. 3. 4.

preterea Esdras migrat 12. mensis Nisan ex fluvio A- hava, neque celebrat Pascha, saltim ne Azyma qui- dem comedit, ut hodie omnes Judæi faciunt & Sama- ritæ, ubicunq; terrarum sunt, qui azyma & Intyba comedere vocant παχαζιζειν. Nulla ergo solemnia aut jejunia in deportatione instituerunt. Sed quis non videt, plus esse in conclusione, quam in præmissis? Nam etsi pascha non celebrarint extra Palæstinam, quod erat alligatum ad certum locum, Hierosoly- mam nempe, num ideo non celebrarunt jejunia, quæ minime ad Palæstinam alligata erant? Num ideo nulla plane in exoticis locis instituerunt sole- mnia? Contrarium è jejunio Susis celebrato, & è festo Purim manifestum est.

§. CLIV. Quintum argumentum à reiteratio- ne structuræ Hierosolymitanæ non stringit, nisi assumatur, de structura templi sermonem esse, quæ interrupta ad tempus, vicissim continuanda. At in textu nihil habetur de structura interrupta templi reiteranda, sed de iterum ædificanda urbe. Omnium interpretum, inquit Scaliger ipse, hæc est mens, ut ita intelligant: Ab exitu verbi ad reducendurn & ædi- ficandum Hierosolyma: hoc est, à publicatione e- dicti de instaurandis & ædificandis Hierosolymis. Et sane nihil aliud voluit Daniel. Hæc Scaliger.

§. CLV. Sextum errat in applicatione, atque, ut alia, confundit structuram templi cum ædifica- tione urbis. Illa cœpta est anno 2. Darii, non hæc. At angelus de hac loquitur, non de illa. Nil igitur juvat intervallum istud annorum 49. à secundo an- no Darii ad 32. Artaxerxis à Nehemia comme- moratum. Naniq; hic non est Memoriofus Arta- xerxes, sed ille, qui à longis manibus nomen conse- quutus est. Deniq; non possunt Scaligeri Sectato- res Epocham hebdomadum 62. designare; quid ergo attinet numerum minorem septem hebdo- madum applicare, quum in potiori, & majori defi- ciant!
