Quid quod septem etiam illas hebdomadas applicare nesciat Scaliger, unde non dubitat eas vacare, hoc est, non habere Epocham, ad quam re- ferantur.

§. CLVI. Septimum, quod initium 70. hebdo- madum initum sit a completo Sabbatico & Jubi- læo, & finis itidem cadat in annum Sabbatarium & Jubilæum, quo exacto Jerusalem desolata fuerit, magis argutum & speciosum, quam solidum & fir- mum est. Nam unde apodictice docebitur, quod hic à Sabbatico & Jubilæo initium fieri voluerit Dominus, aut si id sit, quod præcise ita figi initium debeat, calculusq; Scaligeri cæteris omnibus ea in re præferendus sit. Quam multæ hypotheses su- mendæ sunt controversia minime vacantes, ut illa evincantur? Quid quod Lansbergius etiam à 7. Longimani septimanas hasce inchoans, ut initia- lem, ita & finalem annum non modo Sabbaticum, sed Jubilæum quoque faciat! Istis certe Topicis in explicandis Scripturæ oraculis tuto inniti haud possumus.

§. CLVII. Octavo uti non negamus in hoc ora- culo excidium Hierusalem novissimum definiri, quũ apertis verbis desolatio prædicatur, & à Chri- sto ex hoc oraculo Matth. 21. demonstretur; ita ter- minum septuaginta hebdomadum in ista ἐρημώσῑ constitui ἀποτόμως inficiamur. Neq; consequens est, si initium Epochæ sit urbis ædificatio, finẽ ejus- dem desolationẽ urbis constitui debere. Et appri- me restitutioni politias tum Ecclesiasticæ tum civilis, respondet finis confirmationis pacti in urbe, & a- pud populum sanctũ: quia illa restitutio facta est ob pactum gratiæ, cujus causa non tantum Ecclesiasti- ca illa expedita sunt per Esdram, sed postmodum etiam per Nehemiã civitas reparanda fuit, ut præ- beret hospitium Ecclesiæ, donec regnum Dei au- ferendum ab hoc populo erat, quod post comple- tas hebdomadas fieri cœpit; ex quo tempore etiam tum Ecclesiastica, tum civilis politia ad finem in- clinavit, donec brevi sequeretur finalis πανολεθρία

§. CLVIII. Nonum adversus Beroaldistas militat, non esse à jactis templi fundamentis, Regnoq; Cy- ri inchoandam Epocham: non autem pro Scalige- ro facit, quod adDariiNothi secundum initium re- ferri debeat: imo quia aperte angelus de ædifica- tione platearum & murorum agit, quomodo Sca- liger ea abripit ad iteratam templi ædificationem, & operis incepti, sed interrupti continuationem?

§. CLIX. Decimo cum definitæ dicuntur 70. he- bdomades super populum & super civitatem san- ctam, recte quidem concluditur, terminum in re- gnoCyri figi non posse, ubi solum templi jacta fun- damenta, sed inferri inde non potest, Epocham ex eo tempore inchoandã esse, ex quo operæ in tem- plo extruendo per multos annos impeditæ iterum successerunt. Nihil enim de templi exstructione in textu habetur. Rectius vero colligitur è verbis istis Gabrielis, initium designatum esse illud, quo certa Politiæ tum Ecclesiasticæ, tum civilis in urbe Hie- rosolymitana forma, autoritate publica, vel ad e- gressum verbi Regii institui cœpit, quod non inDa- rii Nothi, nec in Artaxerxis Memoris, sed in Ar- taxerxis Μακρόχειρ℔ tempora incidit.

§. CLX. Undecimo cum 70. septimanæ super populum & super sanctam urbem decretæ dicun- tur, non id vult Gabriel, finem harum hebdoma- dum fore excidium urbis & populi, sed defiturum, cum confirmatione pacti, quæ novissima septima- na futura dicitur, populum sanctum cum urbe sancta, ut non amplius sanctus Dei populus, & urbs san- cta haberi possit: quia exinde regnumDei aufere- tur ab iis, ac incipiet imminere totale urbis exci- dium. Quod vero non includitur septuaginta he- bdomadum spatio, sed post decursum earum brevi futurum designatur. Neque vero juxta Scaligeri sententiam civitas vel restaurari cœpit sub initium Epochæ, vel excisa sub exitum ejusdem fuit: nam non Darii, sed Artaxerxis tempore cœpit urbis restauratio, & deleta urbs fuit non sub finem he- bdomadum, sed quarto anno post elepsas 70. he- bdomadas juxta calculum Scaligeri, Calixti, & aliorum. Nulla ergo sui parte sibi constat ista ex- plicatio.

§. CLXI. Duodecimum argumentum Beroaldo opponi potest, nostræ vero sententiæ nihil adver- satur, imo confirmat eandem, docetque scopo Ga- brielis illam prorfus consentaneam esse: Nam re- stauratio populi & urbis, teste Esdra & Nehemia, non Darii, sed Artaxerxis tempore cœpit.

§. CLXII. Quod decimo tertio calculum B. D. Behmii attinet, qui à Darii Nothi 2, usq; ad exci- dium Hierosolymitanum præcise numerat 490. annos, non congruit ille Scaligerianæ computa- tioni. Nam juxta hanc secundus Darii Nothi est 4290. Per. Jul. uti videre est lib. 5. de emendat. tem- por. pag. 412. Annus vero novissimi exterminii Hierosolymitani est 4783. Per. Jul. eodem autore. Intercedunt itaq; 493. anni. Sed hæc componant sectatores Scaligeri. Nos novimus, non computum tantum annorum Chronologicum, sed imprimis verba oraculi divini respicere debere, qui definire hebdomadas mysticas cupiunt; a quibus vero illos abire luce meridiana clarius est.

§. CLXIII. Denique de consensu veterum sine causa lætatur Scaliger, nullum enim producere po- tuit: Eusebius & Cyrillus non faciunt cum ipso: quia annum 2. Darii apud Esdram non de regi- mi-ne Darii Nothi, sed Hystaspis nobiscum intelli- gunt. Solus Sulpitius Severus adfertur ex universa antiquitate, qui vero in calculo non convenit cum Scaligero. Non enim 70. hebdomadas cum dimi- dia numerat ad excidium Hierosolymitanum, sed sexaginta novem, & de ultima nec non de dimidia septimana supra ultimam, hoc est, septuagesima ta- cet. Non ergo ab antiquitate sua accepit Scaliger, sed adversus antiquitatis consensum Darium Es- dræ commentus est Darium Nothum esse, illamq; Epochæ nostræ mysticæ designationem excogita- vit. Atq; hæc de 70. hebdomadibus Danielis. Deo Triuni, arbitro temporum Optimo Maximo, qui supra & extra omne tempus est, laus sit & perennis gloria!

# Hosea

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON HOSEA. PREFACE.

HOSEA derives his name from הוֹשֵׁעַ [he saved], so called partly for the sake of a good omen, because he was to bring some salvation to the people ministerially or in the capacity of a servant, which was also accomplished by his proclamation; partly, that it might be held as a memorial of the desired Savior, who was to be called by a similar name, Matt. 1:21. He preached primarily to the Israelites, while at the same time Isaiah and Micah were teaching among the Jews, whose synchronism is apparent from the inscription and the mention of the kings, since under Jeroboam II, while the Kingdom of Israel was flourishing greatly, idolatry and other sins were also most rampant, from which he wished to recall the Israelites to repentance by the threat of the devastation of the kingdom, with gracious promises and notable predictions concerning the kingdom of Christ interspersed for the sake of the faithful and the penitent. The prophecy of Hosea, which is completed in seven sermons, can be distributed into sermons clothed in a type, which are two in the first three chapters, and

those proposed naked without a type, of which five are contained in the remaining eleven chapters. Regarding the first two: in the first, by the commanded taking of a harlot wife, the spiritual harlotry of the Israelites and the punishment of it, the rejection of the people, is figured, yet with the promise subjoined concerning the increasing of the remnant of the Israelites by the calling of the Gentiles, chap. 1. Which are further explained at greater length in chap. 2. In the second, by the new reconciliation of the harlot wife after the long abandonment of the Israelites, the conversion to GOD and King David, the Messiah, is designated, chap. 3.

Of the latter kind, some sermons are legal (comparatively), showing the disease, while others are Evangelical, proposing the remedy; there are three legal ones: of which two are made simply and without contention, namely the third sermon containing a rebuke, both general because of the sins of the Israelites, and special because of their spiritual harlotry, chap. 4; and the fourth, both setting forth a threat of ejection and devastation to all estates, chap. 5, and prescribing true and serious conversion with a promise of grace, chap. 6, while complaining of their hypocritical conversion and confidence in treaties with foreigners, chap. 7. The third, which is fifth in order, is instituted by way of contention, concerning which B. Tarnovius should be consulted: by which are compared with one another in chap. 8, the judgments of God and the misdeeds of the people: and further in chap. 9, the wickedness of men and the justice of God, shining forth in poverty, deportation, the removal of divine worship, and devastation. Finally, chap. 10 again [treats of] the crimes of the Israelites and the counsels of God. Since in this sermon a proposition of the trumpet of divine judgment to be exercised through the Assyrian because of the violated divine covenant is prefixed to these chapters, it is better to follow the same, and thus we have: chap. 8, the threatening trumpet; chap. 9, the trumpet refuting the people's boasting; chap. 10, the trumpet exciting to repentance, so that the fifth sermon may now sound forth the imminent punishment.

The Evangelical sermons are the two last, in the four remaining chapters. And the former indeed, chap. 11, exhibits the divine love shown to the Israelites in Christ the Son of God, and the mercy, because of which He cannot utterly destroy Ephraim. The latter, however, first promises to the Israelites the continuation of ancient benefits, provided they convert themselves to the Lord, chap. 12; then it teaches that salvation is from Himself, destruction from Israel, with a subjoined prophecy concerning the Redemption of Christ who is to deliver us from hell and death, chap. 13. Finally, it exhorts again to repentance, with the sweetest promises of grace and blessing made, chap. 14. Such is the economy. But that we may not have need of various subdivisions, we shall treat the same in the explanation of the Prophet according to this septenary number of sermons.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD HOSEAM. PRÆFATIO.

HOSEAS nomen habet ab הוֹשֵׁעַ salvavit, dictus ita partim ominis boni causa, quod salutem aliquã populo allaturus sit διακονικῶς vel ministerialiter, quod etiam præconio ejus factum; partim, ut memoriale haberetur desiderati Salvatoris, qui simili nomine nuncupandus sit Matth. 1, 21. Prædicavit autem imprimis Israëlitic, quum eodem tempore apud Judæos docerent E- saias & Micheas, quorum Synchronismus ex in- scriptione ac Regum mentione apparet, cum sub Jerobeamo II. admodum florente Regno Israëlis idololatria & alia peccata etiam maxime vigerent, à quibus Israëlitus, comminatione devastationis regni ad pœnitentiam revocare volebat, admixtis in gratiam fidelium & pœnitentium gratiosis pro- missionibus & insignibus de regno Christi predictioni- bus. Distribui autem potest Prophetia Hoseæ, quæ septem absolvitur concionibus, in conciones typo ve- stitas, quæ duæ sunt in tribus prioribus capitibus, &

nudas sine typo propositas, quarum habentur quinque reliquis undecim capitibus. Quoad prio- res duas: in prima demandata assumptione mulie- ris scortatricis culpa scortatio spiritualis Israëlicarum ejusque pœna abjectio populi figuratur, subjuncta tamen promissione de Israëliturum reliquiis augen- dis vocatione gentium cap. 1. Quæ porro prolixius explicantur c. 2. in altera nova conciliatione mu- lieris scortatricis post diuturnam derelictionem If- raëlicarum conversio ad DEUM & Regem David, Messiam, designatur cap. 3.

Posterioris generis conciones aliæ (συγκριτι- xῶς) legales sunt morbum ostendentes, aliæ vero Evangelicæ remedium proponentes; Legales tres habentur: è quibus duæ simpliciter & citra con- tentionem factæ, utpote concio tertia increpatio- nem continens, & generalem ob peccata Israelita- rum, & specialem ob scortationem spiritualem c. 4. & quarta tum comminationem omnibus statibus fi- stens ejectionis nempe ac devastationis c. 5. tum veram & seriam conversionem cum pollicitatione gra- tiæ præscribens c. 6. cum de hypocritica eorum con- versione & confidentia in fœderibus cum peregrinis conquerens c. 7. tertia, quæ ordine quinta est, per contentionem, de qua conferendus B. Tarnovius, in- stituta: qua comparantur inter se C. IIX. Dei judi- cia & populi maleficia: ac porro C. IX. hominum nequitia & Dei justitia, in egestate, deportatione, cultus divini ablatione ac devastatione elucescens. Denique C. X. iterum Israelitarum crimina & Dei consilia. Quibus capitibus in hac concione quum præfixa sit propositio tubæ judicii divini per Assyrium exercendi ob violatum fœdus divi- num, præstat eandem sequi, atque ita habemus c. 8. Tubam comminatoriam: c. 9. tubam glorianonis populi confutatoriam: cap. 10. tubam ad pœniten- tiam excitatoriam, ut sic quinta concio imminen- tem jam pœnam ebuccinet.

Evangelicæ conciones sunt duæ postremæ, quatuor residuis capitibus. Et prior quidem c. 11. Amorem divinum in Christo Filio Dei Israelitis ex- hibitum, & misericordiam, ob quam Ephraimum non possit penitus perdere, exhibet, Posterior vero primum Israelitis beneficiorum antiquorum conti- nuationem promittit, modo se ad Dominum con- vertant C, 12. tum salutem ex sese perditionem ex If- rael esse docet, subjuncto vaticinio de Redemptione Christi nos ex inferno & morte liberaturi Cap. 13. Denique ad pœnitentiam denuo hortatur, factis suavissimis gratiæ & benedictionis promissionibus C. 14. Ita sese habet οἰκονομία. Ne autem subdivi- sionibus variis opus habeamus, in explicatione Prophetæ juxta septenarium hunc concionum nu- merum eundem pertractabimus.

## 1:1 Argument
SERMON I. And that, clothed in the type of the harlot, is completed in the first two chapters, partly legal, partly Evangelical. CHAPTER I. The time of the prophecy having been indicated, the taking of a harlot is commanded to figure the spiritual harlotry of the people, from whom three children are to be born, called by names designating the punishments of the same: Jezreel, namely, because of the devastation of Israel; Lo-ruhamah because of the rejection of the same without mercy, which, however, is to be shown to Judah in Christ; and Lo-ammi, the exclusion of the carnal people from the Church, yet with the promise of the notable gathering of the spiritual Israelites to Christ the head. Hosea took the wife of whoredoms as he was commanded.

Ver. 1.

IN THE DAYS OF UZZIAH, JOTHAM, AHAZ, HEZEKIAH] Hosea lived a long time, and acted as a prophet, as the Hebrews maintain, for 90 years. Therefore he had many prophets contemporaneously, such as Isaiah, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, as Jerome notes here: and he saw the people of the ten tribes flourishing, and he saw no small part of the same carried away by Tiglath-Pileser.

Jerome erred in his chronology when he said that at the time when Uzziah began to reign over Judah, Jeroboam had reigned for twelve years over Israel: whereas it was not the twelfth but the twenty-seventh year, as can be seen in 2 Kings 15, 1. Moreover, the reign of Uzziah coincides in its first 26 years with the reign of Jeroboam: and since the beginning of the prophecy is fixed in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam, it must be placed within the last years of Jeroboam and the first of Uzziah. Therefore, that tradition of the Hebrews is uncertain: that Hosea acted as a prophet for a full 90 years. Because its beginning is not defined precisely. Furthermore, that Jonah prophesied before Hosea from

The chronology is by no means obscure, nor can Joel and Obadiah be placed as contemporaries of that state.

Latin:

CONCIO I. Eaque typo vestita scortatricis duobus primis capitibus absoluta, partim lega- lis, partim Evangelica. CAPUT I. Indicato Prophetiæ tempore demandatur as- sumtio scortatricis ad populi scortationem spiritualem figurandam, è qua tres filii no- minibus pœnas ejusdem designantibus ap- pellandi, procreantur: Jefreel nempe ob Israelis devastationem: Loryhamo ob re- jectionem ejusdem sine misericordia, quæ vero Judæ in Christo exhibenda: & Loam- micarnalis populi ab Ecclesia exclusionem, promissa tamen Israelis spiritualis insigni ad Christum caput aggregatione. Accepit uxorem machis Osea reprensis.

Vers. 1.

IN DIEBUS OZIÆ, JOATHAN, ACHAZ, EZE- CHIÆ] Diu vixit Osee, & Prophetam egit, ut volunt Hebræi per annos XC. itaque multos habuit Prophetas συνχρόνως, ut Esajam, Joelem, Amosum, Abdiam, Jonam, Micheam, ut hic notat Hieronymus: viditque populum decem tribuum florentem, vidit ejusdem partem non exi- guum translatam per Teglathphalasfarum.

In Chronologia erravit Hieronymus, cum di- xit eo tempore, quo regnare cœpit Ozias super Ju- dam, duodecimum annum super Israel regnasse Je- roboamum: Siquidem non duodecimus sed vigesi- mus septimus annus fuerit, uti videre est 2. Reg. 15, 1. Regnum autem Oziæ primis 26. annis cum Re- gno Jeroboami concurrit: & cum initium Prophe- tiæ figatur in diebus Uziæ & Jeroboami, intra po- stremos Jeroboami, & primos Uziæ id collo- candum. Incerta itaque est illa Ebræorum tradi- tio: Oseam per integros XC. annos Prophetam egisse. Quia initium ejus ἀποτόμως definitum non est. Porro Jonam ante Hoseam prophetasse è

Chronologia minime obscurum est, nec σύγχρονοι illi statui possunt Joel & Obadias.

## 1:2
Verse 2.

THE BEGINNING OF THE LORD'S SPEAKING IN HOSEA, AND THE LORD SAID) That is, when God first began to address Hosea, He said to him. Compare Gen. 1:1. Regarding the passage in Gen. 1:1, we have spoken there. Some gather from these words that God made the beginning of prophetic predictions through Hosea, so that he is the first of all the prophets, but the chronology does not agree, nor do the words imply it, which are rightly rendered concerning the first prophecy of Hosea by the LXX, the Chaldean, and Vatablus. B. Luther translated: 'And when the Lord began to speak through Hosea; He said to him.' GO AND TAKE UNTO THEE) Bring into your house. See what we said regarding Matt. 1:20. A WIFE OF WHOREDOMS) That is, a harlot, who has offered herself to many. Maimonides wishes these things to have happened only in a vision: but both the sequence of the passage and other similar passages require that it be believed that those things which were being transacted between God and the Hebrew people were expressed by some sign occurring before the eyes of men. To take a wife who had been a harlot was not illicit, except for priests, Deut. 21:7. It might indeed have seemed quite base: but whatever God commands, He makes honest by the very act of commanding it.

Not only Maimonides (p. 2, Director Dub. c. 45), but also Jerome in his preface and on chapter 4 of Ezekiel, as well as Rufinus, think that these things happened in spirit and in vision: indeed, Rufinus reports that Palestine, Egypt, and all who follow Origen maintain this, and Junius, Tremellius, Polanus, and Drusius explain it no differently. B. Luther, in his preface to Hosea, judges that these things happened only typically and that the name of a harlot was imposed upon the legitimate and chaste wife of Hosea only for the sake of signification; this is also the opinion of Osiander, Winkelmann, and Andreas Schaffmann (l. 2, de Caus. peccat. c. 4, p. 204). Others say it is a mere parable (not a historical event), the sum of which is: Go concerning the Israelites, they are as much a wife and children to me as if a wife were to go away and commit whoredom with another. Which is the explanation of Pareus and Zanchius: for Zanchius judges this merely allegorical interpretation, which he says is the Chaldean one, to be the simplest; although he does not condemn the one he acknowledges to have been that of the Fathers, and especially of Irenaeus and Augustine, that it is a true and certain history, nor is he averse to the one that maintains these things happened only in a vision with the Hebrews, which he still prefers to the explanation of the Fathers. On the other hand, there have not been wanting those, as B. Meisner notes, who have judged that the Prophet himself committed whoredom and took Gomer, not for the sake of marriage, but of whoredom, an act they called similar to the theft of the Jews, who despoiled the Egyptians at the command of the Lord: but this is not to be admitted, nor can it be gathered from the text. That was the opinion of Thomas (1. Secundae q. 10, art. 4, ad 3, and 22, q. 154, art. 2, ad 3), that Gomer was not joined to the Prophet in true marriage, but was given to him by God's dispensation so that he might beget children from her. The example concerning the spoils of the Israelites does not fit. For in taking the goods of the Egyptians by divine authority, the law of nature also intercedes for them, because it establishes wages for mercenaries with divine law.

However, the words and the circumstances of the text do not allow for this to be a mere vision, figure, or parable. Therefore, we give our assent to Grotius, that the Prophet had to take a harlot at the command of the Lord, to adumbrate the spiritual whoredom of the people. This is also maintained by Irenaeus among the Fathers, Basil on C. 8 of Isaiah, Augustine (l. 3, de doctr. Christi c. 21, and the book against Secundinus the Manichaean, cap. 21, l. 22, against Faustus, c. 80 and 89), Cyril, Theodoret, and others, as well as by our own B. Gesner, Pappus, and Meisner, and among the Papists, Ribera, Burgensis, and others.

The letter of the text is clear. For the command of the Lord is expressed, the obedience of the Prophet, the name of the woman, along with the names of the children. Finally, the command is repeated in c. 3:1. And the Lord wished to exaggerate the turpitude of spiritual whoredom not only with words, but also to represent it with a deed, whence Irenaeus (l. IV, c. XXXVII): 'Not only through visions which were seen, and sermons which were proclaimed, but also in operations, it was seen by the prophets, so that through them he might prefigure and pre-demonstrate future things. For which reason the Prophet Hosea also took a wife of whoredom, prophesying through an operation, because by whoring she will commit whoredom against the Lord.' Theodoret on c. 1 of Hosea. The God of all things, he says, after speaking to men laboring under an old and robust disease, did not persuade them with words, but showing future things by certain adumbrated deeds, he draws those who had become deaf and hardened to sins toward speculation and consideration by the admirability of the things seen. This opinion is so certain to Theodoret that he does not hesitate to write: 'I cannot sufficiently marvel at the audacity of those who do not fear to say that the words are devoid of deeds, and that while God ordered those things to be carried out, the Prophet did not receive them, and did not exhaust the commands.'

What Grotius advises, that it might indeed have seemed quite base, but whatever God commands, He makes honest by the act of commanding it, is indeed true in this case, because to take a harlot was not evil and illicit by nature, but yet it was illicit for priests by decree on account of the command of God, Lev. 21:7; but it is by no means to be extended to other things which are by their nature and intrinsically evil. Jerome objects in his preface to Hosea to Pammachius: 'God commands nothing except what is honest, nor does He make things that are base honest by commanding them.' Answer: Some things are base by their own nature, which God neither commands, nor can they be made honorable by being commanded: But some things, even if they are less honorable in a certain respect and positively with regard to some law, are nevertheless not base and dishonorable by their own nature, which can be made honorable by the addition of a command and authority, just as from illegitimate children themselves, through legitimation, that which is base can be removed, and through subsequent marriage, antecedent baseness can be made honorable. Therefore, it is one thing to commit fornication, which is in itself a vice: it is another to marry a harlot, which is not a vice, nor is it simply base, but in certain cases and for certain reasons can be honorable: just as it was not base when Salmon, one of the princes of the Israelites, took Rahab, a famous harlot, as his wife, or when David took Bathsheba, whom he had made an adulteress, as his wife, which marriages God himself honored with the lineage of the Messiah. And there were here grave reasons for the most wise God why He commanded it, both public, namely, that He might not only more vehemently reproach the people for idolatry, but also move them, and set before their eyes His own kindness and μακροθυμίαν [long-suffering], in that He bears with them, even though they are fornicators, and bestows benefits upon them: and private; namely, that He might call that harlot away from her suitors and convert her through the Prophet. Nor is this contrary to the holiness of the Prophet. For if the God of all, which are the words of Theodoret, took up the Synagogue, an adulteress lost to lust, and the fountain of holiness was not contaminated by this impure and execrable one, neither did the Prophet receive a stain from that wife full of lewdness. For the association with her did not occur for the sake of serving immoderate desire, but in obedience to the commands of God. Indeed, Jerome himself absolves the Prophet here in his Commentary, where he agrees with our opinion in part, or at least does not judge it to be so inconvenient, as indeed some Calvinists have noted it with sharp censure. Nor is the Prophet to be blamed, he says, the prophet meanwhile, TO FOLLOW THE HISTORY, if he converts a harlot to chastity, is rather to be praised, because he made a good woman out of a bad one. For he who remains good is not himself polluted if he is associated with a bad person, but he who is bad is turned into a good person if he follows the example of a good one. From which we understand that the Prophet did not lose his chastity by being joined to a harlot, but that the harlot assumed the chastity which she did not have before. Especially since the blessed Hosea did not do this for the sake of luxury, nor of lust, nor of his own will, but obeyed the command of God, so that what we read carnally in him, we might prove to be done spiritually in God, who receives the Synagogue, that is, the people of the Jews serving fornication and lust.

Rivetus, however, raises a doubt here, following the footsteps of Zanchius and Pareus. That point indeed, which others urge, that it was not appropriate for the Prophetic office, he does not entirely deny can be excused by an extraordinary divine mandate; but he thinks that there is something else that stands in the way. For if that woman was made thrifty when she was taken by the Prophet, then the children taken with her were not children of fornications. Some dissolve this doubt thus: that they were called children of fornications because, although they were legitimate, they nevertheless imitated their mother, who had been a harlot. We do not deny that this is indeed quite harsh, and little in agreement with the words: since it is indicated that they were such from their very birth; it is simpler and entirely consistent with the text if we say that those were called children of fornications whom the Prophet had to take with the harlot mother, and not those whom he subsequently begot in the marriage entered into with the same woman at the command of God. For it is not found in the sources, as the Vulgate translated: Take to yourself a wife of fornications. AND MAKE children of fornications. The Hebrew text does not recognize this word of making. Since, therefore, the single word ACCIPE or take governs both nouns, so that the Prophet was commanded to take the children of fornications just as much as the wife of fornications, the children begotten by the Prophet can in no way be understood, but the children of the harlot taken with the mother. For although that Hebrew word might elsewhere sometimes denote to take a wife, or to marry, and sometimes to receive, or to beget children, yet that word should not be resolved into two meanings in this place due to the diversity of the object, in such a sense: Go take a harlot by marrying, and receive children by begetting, as B. Meisnerus wishes; for the sense of one and the same word in the same sentence cannot be so disparate; that it denotes both acceptance into marriage and reception through procreation, although this latter meaning has not been proven for this word from other places either. Those, therefore, who were subsequently begotten as the Prophet's children are not to be confused with these whom he took with the harlot mother. In the latter, the spiritual fornication of the Israelites was adumbrated; in the former, however, the Lord figured the various states of the people, and the various punishments of the same, through symbolic names imposed upon the children of the Prophet. But how, you will ask with Rivetus, did that woman represent the Church of Israel, and how will that reasoning hold together for itself; because the land will commit fornication? For what would this be: take to yourself a wife, who, having been taken by you, ceases to fornicate, and is made chaste by your marriage, so that she may represent the Israelite land which fornicates by fornicating. I answer: The added reasoning holds together for itself very well, as the scope of the figure. For the woman, who had fornicated, represented the Israelite land, which had hitherto fornicated. For it does not look to her future fornication; but the spiritual fornication practiced and continued up to this point is adumbrated. Whence Rivetus himself renders the words thus, the land will fornicate by fornicating: that is:

it is continually fornicating. Indeed, through this figure of the harlot woman to be taken by the Prophet, the divine μακροθυμία is exhibited, because He desires that the Israelites, even though they have fornicatingly fornicatied, should still be joined to Him, and indeed to that end, that they might desist from spiritual fornication, just as the Prophet, taking a harlot, had to recall her from fornication, and render her chaste by his marriage. This certainly was the intention of the Lord, both in the marriage of the Prophet with the harlot and in the Israelites being, as it were, betrothed to Him anew, so that the former might be drawn away from bodily, and the latter from spiritual, fornication. But that gloss which Rivetus provides is very inept: The Prophet takes Gomer the daughter of Diblaim, i.e., departing, he went to the Israelites, so that he might announce to them the parable which he had received from God, i.e., so that he might announce to the Israelite Church that it is Gomer, that is, destruction, or about to be destroyed shortly; and the daughter of Diblaim, that is, of aridity, of drying up, or of attenuation, or that that kingdom is to be so destroyed that the land is rendered desert. It is certain that no example of such a parable will be given in the whole of Scripture. For here there is both the command of God, and the circumstantial execution of the command, and the symbolic explanation of both, and since that harlot woman, from whom the Prophet received three children, is said to have fornicatied after the marriage entered into with the Prophet (Ch. III. 1), whom nevertheless the Prophet took again, and bound to himself for a certain price (ver. 2 seqq.) to adumbrate the character of the Israelites and the divine μακροθυμία, what is more evident than that these things are narrated not otherwise than historically as deeds done: since no trace, or only an obscure one, appears that a mere parable is handed down here.

AND MAKE FOR YOURSELF CHILDREN OF FORNICATIONS] In the Hebrew it is not make, but and those born of fornications, that is, take. Bring into the house with the mother those bastards whom she bore in that harlot life. For there are other children, whom Hosea later begot from her, and they were used for other meanings,

They commonly understand it as referring to children begotten by the Prophet, but we have previously warned that it is more correctly taken as the taking of illegitimate children: and therefore we admit that this Grotian explanation is genuine. And it is now clear from the genuine sense of the prophet how greatly Rivetus, along with Polanus, is mistaken when he sells that argument for his gloss as if it were insoluble: The Prophet took children of whoredoms. Therefore he did not beget them himself. The Prophet is commanded, says Polanus, to take with him children of whoredoms, who if they were born before the marriage, could not have been conceived first by Gomer, which is stated in the text: if they were conceived after the marriage, they were certainly legitimate, not children of whoredoms, which title nevertheless is likewise held in the text. B. Meisnerus replies: We concede that these children were born not before, but after the marriage contract of the Prophet, and were therefore legitimate. Nevertheless, they are rightly called children of whoredoms (1.) on account of their mother, a harlot, whose infamous mark they retained, especially since she committed adultery even within the marriage itself, as is hinted in chapter 3. (2.) on account of their future whoredom, because the children themselves, bearing the character of their mother, after they grew up, undoubtedly began to commit whoredom. But this is not to be conceded to Polanus: that these children were born after the Prophet's marriage. For they are expressly said to have been TAKEN. If, therefore, they were taken by the Prophet with their mother, the children of whoredoms were neither begotten by the Prophet nor born in wedlock, but in the very act of whoredom; otherwise they could not be called children of whoredoms: which name indicates that they are such by birth, does not denote that they became whoremongers, and expresses the condition of the children, not of the mother.

FOR THE LAND WILL SURELY COMMIT WHOREDOM FROM THE LORD) Better, plays the whore: for since the Hebrews do not have a present tense, they express it now by the past, now by the future. For 'from the Lord', it is 'from after the Lord': that is, it ceased to follow God, adhering to idols as if they were paramours: - - - your care Lycoris / Followed another through the snows, and through the horrid camps. The land here is the people of the ten tribes.

This explanation, concerning the present time, confirms our opinion which we delivered at verse 2. Nor indeed was the Prophet required to designate by this symbol what kind of people they would be hereafter, but what kind they had been, and even now are: nay, that they might not persevere in being such hereafter, they were warned here by the symbol of the harlot turned into a wife.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

PRINCIPIVM LOQVVENDI DOMINO IN HOSEE, ET DIXIT DOMINVS) Id est, Cum primum Deus Oseen alloqui cœpit, dixit ei. Confer Gen. 1, 1. De loco Gen. 1, 1. ibi diximus. Nonnulli ex hisce verbis colligunt, Deum prædictionum Propheticarum initium fecisse per Hoseam, ut ita sit Prophetarum omnium primus, sed Chronologia non congruit, neque verba id inferunt, quæ recte redduntur de prima Hoseæ prophetia à LXX. Chaldæo, Vatablo. B. Lutherus transtulit; Vnd da der HErr ansieng zu reden durch Hoseam; Sprach Er zu ihm. VADE ET SVME TIBI) In domum tuam deduc. Vide quæ ad Matth. 1, 20. UXOREM FORNICATIONUM) Id est meretricem, quæ multis admodum sui copiam fecerit. Maimonides hæc vult contigisse ἐν ὀπτασίᾳ tantum: sed & series loci, & alia loca similia magis id credi exigunt, signo aliquo in hominum oculos occurrente, expressas eas res quæ inter Deum & Hebræum populum agebantur. Uxorem ducere, quæ meretrix fuerit, non erat illicitum, nisi sacerdotibus Deut. 21, 7. Videri quidem id poterat subturpe: sed quicquid jubet Deus, idem jubendo honestum facit.

Non Maimonides solum p. 2. director. dub. c. 45. sed & Hieronym. in procem. & ad cap. 4. Ezech. ut & Ruffinus putant, in spiritu & visione illa gesta esse: imo refert Ruffinus Palæstinam, Ægyptum, omnesque Origenem sequentes ita statuere, nec aliter explicat Iunius, Tremellius, Polanus, Drusius. B. Lutherus typice tantum illa accidisse ac legitimæ castæque uxori Hoseæ solum nomen scorti significationis causa impositum fuisse censet in Præfat. sup. Hos. quæ etiam Osiandri, Winkelman. ut & Andreæ Schaffmanni l. 2. de Caus. peccat. c. 4. p. 204. est sententia. Alii meram esse parabolam (non rem gestam) ajunt, cujus summa sit: Vade de Israëlitis, æque illos mihi uxorem esse, & filios, ac si uxor abiret & scortaretur cum alio. Quæ est Parei, & Zanchii explicatio: hanc enim interpretationem mere allegoricam quam Chaldæi esse dicit, Zanchius censet esse simplicissimam; etsi nec eam damnet quam Patrum & imprimis Irenæi & Augustini fuisse agnoscit, quod vera & certa sit historia, neque ab ea alienus sit quæ in visione hæc tantum cum Ebræis contigisse statuit, quam Patrum explicationi adhuc præfert. Ex adverso non defuerunt, B. Meisnero notante, qui censuerint, Prophetam ipsum esse scortatum, & affumpsisse Gomeram, non matrimonii, sed fornicationis causa, quod factum simile dixere furto Judæorum, Ægyptios ad mandatum Domini spoliantium: sed hoc admittendum non est, neque è textu colligi potest. Fuit ea Thomæ sententia 1. Secundæ q. 10. art. 4. ad 3. & 22. q. 154. art. 2. ad 3. Gomeram non fuisse copulatam Prophetæ, vero matrimonio, sed dispensante Deo traditam ei, ut filios ex ea procrearet. Non congruit exemplum de Israëlitarum spoliis. Nam in Ægyptiorum bonis autoritate divina capiendis jus etiam naturæ interpellat pro iis, quod mercenariis statuit mercedem cum lege divina.

Meram tamen ὀπ]ασίαν, figuram aut parabolam hic esse, non ferunt verba, nec circumstantiæ textus. Ideo assensum præbemus Grotio, quod ad mandatum Domini meretricem assumere debuerit Propheta, ad adumbrandam spiritualem scortationem populi. Quod etiam è Patribus Irenæus, Basilius in C. 8. Efa. Augustinus l. 3. de doctr. Christi c. 21. & lib. contra Secundin. Manich. cap. 21. l. 22. contra Faust. c. 80. & 89. Cyrillus, Theodoretus, & alii, nec non è nostris B. Gesnerus, Pappus, Meisnerus, è Pontificiis Ribera, Burgensis, & alii statuunt.

Litera textus clara est. Exprimitur enim præce- ptum Domini, obfequium Prophetæ, nomen mulieris, cum nominibus filiorum. Repetitur denique præce- ptum c. 3, 1.Et volebat Dominus turpitudinem spi- ritualis fornicationis non modo verbisexaggerare, sed facto etiam repræsentare, unde Irenæus l. IV. c. XXXVII. Non solum per visiones quæ videbantur, & sermones, quæ præconiabantur, sed & in operatio- nibus visus est Prophetis, ut per eos præfiguraret, & prædemonstraret futura. Propter quod & Prophe- ta Hosea accepit uxorem fornicationis per operatio- nem prophetans, quod fornicando fornicabitur con- tra Dominum. Theodorelus in c. 1. Hos. Universõ- rum Deus, inquit, posteaquam ad homines in vetera- to & robusto morbo laborantes verba faciens, non verbis persuasit rebus quibusdam adumbratis futura ostendens, visorumq; admirabilitate ad speculationem & considerationem eos, qui ad peccata obsurduerant, & percalluerant, trahit. Quæ sententia adeo certa Theodoreto est, ut scribere non dubitet; Eorum audaciam mirari satis non queo, qui non verentur di- cere, verba esse rebus destituta, & quod ea quidem Deus exequenda jusserit, non tamen Propheta rece- perit, ac non jussa exhauserit.

Quod Grotius monet, videri id quidem potuis- se subturpe, sed quicquid Deus jubet,id jubendo hone- stum facit, id in hoc casu quidem verum est, quia scortatricem ducere malum & illicitum non erat τῇ Φύσει, sed tamen quoad sacerdotes illicitum e- rat θέσει ob mandatum Dei, Lev. 21, 7. sed ad alia, quæ natura sua & intrinsece mala sunt, extendendũ minime est. Objicit Hieronym. in Præfat. in Ose- am ad Pammach. Nihil Deus præcepit, nisi quod bone- stum est, nec jubendo turpia facit honesta, quæ tur- pia sunt. Resp. Turpia quædam sunt natura sua, quæ neque præcipit Deus, neque præcipiendo honesta fieri possunt: Quædam vero etsi secun- dum quid & positive cujusdam legis respectu minus honesta sint, natura tamen sua turpia & inhonesta non sunt,quæ accedente jussione & au- toritate cohonestari possunt, quemadmodum ab ipsis spuriis per legitimationem id quod turpe est, tolli potest, & per matrimonium subsequens turpi- tudo antecedanea cohonestari. Aliud ergo est scor- tari, quod per se in vitio est: aliud scortatricem du- cere, quod non in vitio, nec simpliciter turpe est, sed in certis casibus & ob certas causas honestum esse potest: quomodo turpe non erat, cum Salmon unus ex principibus Israëlitarum Rahab famosam meretricem, aut cum David Bathsebam, quam adul- teram fecerat, in uxorem duxit, quæ conjugiaDeus ipse prosapia Messiæ honoravit. Et fuerunt hic Deo sapientissimo causæ graves, cur id mandarit, tum publicæ, ut nempe populo idololatriam non tantum vehementius exprobraret, sed etiam eun- dem commoveret, suamq; benignitatem ac μακρο- θυμίαν, quod ipsos, etsi fornicarios ferat, & benefi- ciis afficiat, ob oculos poneret: tum privatæ; ut nempè scortum illud à procis suis avocaret, & per Prophetam converteret. Neq; id Sanctitati Pro- phetæ adversum. Nam si universorum Deus, quæ verba Theodoreti sunt, libidine perditam adulte- ram suscepit Synagogam, & non contaminatus est fons sanctitatis ex impura hac & execrabili, neq; Prophe- ta ex illa stupri plena uxore maculam suscepit. Non enim appetitioni immoderatæ inservienti, sed Dei im- periis obtemperanti cum illa consuetudo intercessit. Imo absolvit hic Prophetam ipse Hieronymus in Commentar. ubi ad sententiam nostram accedit ex parte, aut certe tam inconvenientem eam non ju- dicat, prouti quidẽ acri censura eandem Calvinia- ni nonnulli notarunt. Nec culpandus, inquit, Pro- pheta interim, UT SEQUAMUR HISTORIAM, si meretricem convertit ad pudicitiam, sed potius lau- dandus, quod ex mala bonam fecerit. Non enim, qui bonus permanet, ipse polluitur, si societur malo, sed qui malus est, in bonum vertitur, si boni exem- plum sectetur. Ex quo intelligimus non Prophetam perdidisse pudicitiam, fornicariæ copulatum, sed for- nicariam assumsisse pudicitiam, quam antea non ha- bebat. Præsertim cum beatus Oseas non ob causam luxuriæ, non libidinis, non propria fecerit voluntate, sed Dei paruerit imperio, ut quod in isto carnaliter le- gimus, in Deo factum spiritualiter probaremus, qui suscipit Synagogam, hoc est, populum Judæorum for- nicationi & libidini servientem.

Dubium autem hic movet Rivetus, Zanchii & Parei legens vestigia. Illud sane, quod alii ur- gent, quod non conveniens id fuerit muneri Prophe- tico, excusari mandato divino extraordinario non o- mnino abnuit; sed esse præterea quod obstet, exi- stimat. Si enim mulier illa facta est frugi, cum à Propheta ducta est, utique filii ab ea ducti non fue- runt filii fornicationum. Quod dubium dissol- vunt nonnulli ita: dictos fuisse filios fornicationum, quod etsi legitimi essent, adulti tamen matrem, quæ fu- erat fornicatrix imitati sint. Id vero durum pror- sus esse, & verbis parum conveniens, non diffite- mur: siquidem tales fuisse eos ab ipso ortu indice- tur; simplicius est & textui prorsus congruum, si dicamus filios fornicationum dictos esse, quos cum matre fornicaria assumere debuit Propheta, non vero quos deinde in conjugio ad mandatum Dei cum eadem inito procreavit. Neq; enim in fon- tibus habetur, uti vulgatus transtulit: Sume tibi uxorem fornicationum. ET FAC filios fornica- tionum. Verbum hoc faciendi non agnoscit tex- tus Ebræus. Quum ergo unicum τὸ ACCIPE vel sume utrumq; nomen regat, ut ita Propheta æ- que filios scortationum, uti mulierem scortationum sumere jussus fuerit, nullatenus intelligi possunt fi- lii à Propheta procreati, sed filii scortatricis cum muliere matre assumti. Etsi enim vox illa Ebræa alibi notaret nonnunquam maritam accipere, vel in uxorem ducere, nonnunquam suscipere, vel liberos procreare, non tamen vox illa ob diversitatem obje- cti in duo significata resolvenda esset hoc in loco, tali sensu, Vade accipe fornicariam ducendo, & suscipe liberos procreando, uti vult B. Meisnerus; nam u- nius ejusdemq; vocis in eadem sententia non po- test tam disparatus esse sensus; ut & notet acceptione in matrimonium, & susceptionem per procreationem quamvis nec ex aliis locis hæc posterior significatio de hac voce probata sit. Qui ergo deinde procre- ati sunt Prophetæ filii, non confundendi cum his- ce quos accepit cum matre scortatrice. In hisce adumbrata fuit spiritualis Israëlitarum fornicatio, in illis v. figuravit Dominus varios status populi, & varias ejusdem pœnas per nomina symbolica, libe- ris Prophetæ imposita. Sed quomodo, quæres cum Riveto, mulier illa repræsentabat Ecclesiam Is- raelis, & quomodo ratio illa sibi constabit; quia for- nicabitur terra? Quid enim hoc esset: accipe tibi u- xorem, quæ à te ducta desinat scortari, & conjugio tuo pudica efficiatur, ut repræsentet terram Israëliti- cam quæ scortando scortatur. Respondeo: Optime sibi constare adjunctam rationem, ut figuræ sco- pum. Nam mulier, quæ scortata erat, repræsen- tabat terram Israëliti cam, quæ hactenus scortata fuit. Neque enim respicitur futura ejus scortatio; sed adumbratur hucusque frequentata, & continu- ata fornicatio spiritualis. Unde Rivetus ipse ita reddit verba, fornicando fornicabitur terra: id est:

continuo fornicatur. Imo per figuram istam mu- lieris scortatricis a Propheta ducendæ exhibetur divina μακροθυμία quod Israelitas, etsi scortando scortati sint, sibi adhuc copulatos cupiat, & qui- dem eo fine, ut a scortatione spirituali desistant, quemadmodum Propheta scortatricem ducens a scortatione revocare debebat, ac conjugio suo pu- dicam reddere. Hæc certe erat intentio Domini, & in matrimonio Prophetæ cum scortatrice & in Israelitis sibi quasi denuo desponsandis, ut illa a corporali hi a spirituali fornicatione abstraherentur. Perquam autem inepta est illa glossa, quam tradit Rivetus: Propheta assumit Gomer filiam Dibelaim, i. e. abiens profectus est ad Israelitas, ut ipsis denuntiaret parabolam, quam a Deo acceperat h. e. ut denuncia- ret Israeliticæ Ecclesiæ eam esse Gomer, id est, destru- ctionem, vel brevi destruendam; & filiam Diblaim, id est, ariditatis, exsiccationis, vel attenuationis, vel re- gnum illud ita destruendum esse, ut terra reddatur de- serta. Talis parabolæ, certum est, nullum dabitur in universa Scriptura exemplum. Habetur enim hic & mandatum Dei, & περιστατικὴ mandati exe- quutio, & utriusque symbolica explicatio, & cum for- nicatrix illa mulier, e qua tres liberos suscepit Pro- pheta, post conjugium cum Propheta initum scor- tata dicatur C. III. 1. quam tamen Propheta denuo assumsit, ac mercede certa sibi devinxit vers. 2. seqq. ad adumbrandam indolem Isralitarum, & μακρο- θυμίαν divinam, quid evidentius est, quam quod i- sta non aliter, quam historice ceu gesta narrantur: Siquidem nullum, vel obscurum solum, appareat vestigium, meram hic traditam esse parabolam.

ET FAC TIBI FILIOS FORNICATIONUM] In Hebræo non est fac, sed & natos fornicationum, sume scilicet. In domum deduc cum matre spurios illos, quos in vita illa meretricia genuit. Alii enim sunt filii, quos Oseas postea ex ea genuit, & ad alias significationes adhibiti,

Communiter intelligunt de filiis a Propheta procreatis, sed rectius de assumtione filiorum spu- riorum accipi, antea monuimus: ideoque Gro- tianam hanc explicationem germanam esse admit- timus. Et patet nunc e genuino prophetæ sensu, quantopere fallatur Rivetus cum Polano, cum ra- tionem illatn pro sua glossa, ceu insolubilem, ven- ditat: Filios fornicationum assumsit Propheta. E. ipse non genuit. Jubetur Propheta, inquit Polanus, filios fornicationum una assumere, qui si ante conjugium fuerunt nati, non primum a Gomera concipi potue- runt, quod in textu dicitur: si post conjugium conce- pti fuerunt, utiq; legitimi fuerunt, non filii fornicatio- num, qui tamen titulus itidem in textu habetur. Re- spondet B. Meisnerus: Concedimus, quod non an- te, sed post contractum conjugium Prophetæ, libe- ri isti prognati, adeoque legitimi fuerint. Recte ni- hilominus dicuntur filii fornicationum (1.) ob ma- trem meretricem, cujus infamem notam retinue- runt, præsertim cum illa in ipso etiam matrimonio fuerit scortata, ut c. 3. innuitur. (2.) ob futuram scortationem, quia & ipsi liberi, matris indolem ge- rentes, posteaquam adoleverunt, procul dubio scortari cœperunt. Sed concedendum id non est Polano: quod hi liberi post conjugium Prophetæ nati sint. Expresse enim dicuntur ASSUMTI. Si ergo a Propheta cum matre assumti scortatio- num filii nec procreati sunt a Propheta nec in ma- trimonio nati sunt sed in ipsa scortatione; alias scortationum filii vocari non possent: quod nomen ortu tales esse indicat, non factos scortatores notat, & liberorum, non matris conditionem exprimit.

QUIA FORNICANS FORNICABITUR TERRA A DOMINO) Melius, scortatur: nam Hebræi cum præsens non habeant, modo id per præteritum, modo per futurum exprimunt. Pro à Domino, est à post Dominum: id est, Deum sequi desiit, idolis quasi moechis adhærens: - - - tua cura Lycoris Perq; nives alium, perq; horrida castra sequuta est. Terra hic est populus decem tribuum.

Confirmat hæc explicatio, de præsenti tempo- re, nostram, quam ad v. 2. tradidimus sententiam. Nec vero qualis deinceps futurus sit populus de- signare debebat hoc symbolo Propheta, sed qualis fuerit, atque etiamnum sit: imo ne deinceps talis esse perseveret, hic symbolo scortatricis conver- sæ in conjugium monebantur.

## 1:3
Ver. 3. AND HE TOOK GOMER) This word signifies one who is failing: by that name it is indicated that the people of the ten tribes would suffer a grievous fainting.

DAUGHTER OF DIBLAIM) Diblaim are two cakes of figs. It is signified that just as some figs are good and others bad (see Jerem. 24), so also there were others good, but many bad, among the ten tribes.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET ACCEPIT GOMER) Deficientem hæc vox significat: eo nomine indicatur, populum decem tri- buum grave deliquium passurum.

FILIAM DEBELAIM) Debelaim sunt duæ ficutim massæ. Significatur sicut ficus aliæ sunt bonæ aliæ malæ (vi- de Jerem. 24.) ita etiam alios bonos, sed multos malos fuisse in decem tribubus.

## 1:4
Ver. 4. CALL HIS NAME JEZREEL) The three names of the children of Hosea signify the three punishments of the ten tribes. Jezreel is a noble city in the territory of the ten tribes, 1 Kings 21, 2 Kings 9, 10, 10, 6.

YET A LITTLE WHILE) Within a short time.

AND I WILL VISIT THE BLOOD OF JEZREEL UPON THE HOUSE OF JEHU) Better, for the blood of Jezreel: in which sense the particle את is often taken. The sense is, such slaughter as Jehu wrought upon the house of Ahab, and upon Jezebel in the city of Jezreel, with such slaughter will I punish the posterity of Jehu, when, namely, Zechariah shall be killed with his own, Jehu indeed being his great-great-grandfather, but his son being Jeroboam, under whom this vision of Hosea occurred. 2 Kings 15, 10.

The sense is simpler if the ordinary meaning of the word את is retained. For God threatens that He will visit the blood of Jezreel, or bloods, as it is held in the Hebrew, i.e., the slaughters committed in Jezreel, the primary city of the Israelite kingdom, and especially those which were committed by Jehu, who destroyed Joram the son of Ahab, and his whole family; which, although he did it with a divine command, and in that manner in which the action commanded by God is viewed, for executing His justice against the impiety of the house of Ahab and for avenging the blood of Naboth, it may be just: yet if we attend to the intention and the manner of the execution, it is manifest that he neither observed the due manner, nor had a legitimate end, because he raged against the family of Ahab more out of cruelty and lust for reigning than out of a zeal for avenging God's glory; nay, although he boasted with words of zeal for the Lord 2 Kings 10, 16. he did not act by that very deed so that idolatry might be extirpated, but so that the worship of the calves might be retained. v. 30, 31. See B. Meisner, p. 48. Thus Jerome: Israel is the metropolis city of the ten tribes, in which Naboth was killed, for whose blood Jehu is raised up, who destroyed the house of Ahab and Jezebel; but because Jehu himself also, the avenger of innocent blood, entered into the ways of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who had made Israel to sin, and fashioned the golden calves in Dan and Bethel, his kingdom also is said to be about to be subverted: under whose great-grandson Jeroboam, Hosea began to prophesy, upon whose death his son Zechariah succeeded to the kingdom, who was killed in the sixth month of his reign. The mind of Jonathan the paraphrast does not seem to have been otherwise: I will visit the blood of those who worship idols, which Jehu shed in Israel, whom he killed because they worshipped Baal: and afterwards they themselves also turned to wander after the calves that were in Bethel and Dan. Therefore I will reckon that blood as innocent upon the house of Jehu. The opinion of R. David Kimchi was certainly the same: Although he did in this matter what was pleasing to the Lord, because he himself did not devote effort to live according to the prescription of the divine law, nor did he depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the blood which he had shed was imputed as innocent blood.

AND I WILL CAUSE TO CEASE THE KINGDOM OF THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL) To cease, namely, in the house of Jehu. For the killer of Zechariah, and his successor, Shallum, was from another lineage.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VOCA NOMEN EJUS JEZRAHEL) Tria nomina liberum Oseæ tres pœnas decem tribuum signifi- cant. Jezrahel nobilis urbs in decem tribuum solo 1. Reg. 21, 1. 2. Reg. 9, 10. 10, 6.

ADHUC MODICUM) Intra breve tempus.

ET VISITABO SANGUINEM JEZRAHEL SVPER DOMUM JEHU) Melius, per sanguinem Jezrahel: quo sensu את sæpe sumitur. Sensus est, qualem stragem edidit Jehu in domum Achabi, & in Jezabelem in urbe Jezrahelis, tali strage puniam posteritatem Jehu, cum scilicet interfi- cietur cum suis Zacharias, Jehu quidem abnepos, filius au- tem ejus Jeroboami, sub quo hoc visum Oseæ contigit. 2. Regum 15, 10.

Sensus simplicior est retento ordinario signi- ficatu vocis את. Minatur enim Deus visitaturum sese sanguinem Jezrahel, vel sanguines, ut in Ebræo habetur, h. e. cædes in Jezrahel factas, primaria urbe regni Israelitici, & imprimis quæ à Jehu factæ, qui Joram filium Achabi, ejusq; totam familiam dele- vit, quod cum mandato divino fecerit, atq; ea ra- tione, qua spectatur actio à Deo imperata, ad justitiam ejus exequendam, contra impietatem domus A- chabi & ad vindicandum sanguinem Nabot justa sit: tamen si intentionem & modum exequutionis at- tendamus, manifestum est, eum neque modum de- bitum observasse, nec finem legitimum habuisse, quia crudelitate & regnandi libidine in Achabi fa- miliam magis sæviit, quam studio vindicandi Dei gloriam, imo cum verbis jactavit zelum pro Domi- no 2. Reg. 10, 16. id facto ipso non egit, ut idolola- tria extirpareiur, sed ut cultus vitulorum retine- retur. v. 30. 31. Vid. B. Meisner. p. 48. Sic Hierony- mus: Israel est civitas metropolis decem tribuum, in qua interfectus est Naboth, ob cujus sanguinem suscita- tur Iehu, qui delevit domum Achab, & Iesabel, verum quia & ipse Iehu, ultor sanguinis justi, ingressus est per vias Ieroboam filii Nebath, qui fornicari fece- rat Israel, & conflavit vitulos aureos in Dan & Be- thel, regnum quoq; ejus dicitur subvertendum : sub cujus pronepote Ieroboamo prophetare cæpit Hosee, quo mortuo filius ejus Zacharias succeffit in regnum, qui sexto mense imperii sui occidit. Non alia videtur mens fuisse Ionathani paraphrastæ: visitabo sangui- nem colentium idola, quem effudit Iehu in Israele, quos occidit quod colerent Baal: & postea conversi sunt etiam ipsi, ut errarent post vitulos, qui erant in Bethel & Dan. Ideo reputabo illum sanguinem innocen- tem super domum Iehu. Eadem certe sententia R. David Kimchi fuit: Quanquam fecit hac in re quod gratum erat Domino, quia tamen ipse non dedit ope- ram, ut ex præscripto legis divinæ viveret, neq; ab o- mnibus peccatis Ieroboam, filii Nebath recessit, impu- tatus est sanguis, quem effuderat, pro sanguine inno- cente.

ET QUISCERE FACIAM REGNVM DOMVS ISRAEL) Cessare, nempe in domo Jehu. Nam Zachariæ interfector, idemque successor Sallumus ex alia stirpe fuit.

## 1:5
Ver. 5. I WILL BREAK THE BOW OF ISRAEL IN THE VALLEY OF JEZREEL) I will break the strength of that people by civil wars. By the name of the bow, strengths are signified to the Hebrews, as 2 Sam. 2, 4. It seems that that slaughter is especially indicated which Menahem was about to give, 2 Kings 15, 16. Near Jezreel the fields extend beyond ten thousand paces. Thus Jerome here.

Latin:

Vers. 5. CONTERAM ARCUM ISRAEL IN VALLE JEZRAHEL) Vires populi illius frangam bellis civilibus. Arcus nomine Hebræis vires significantur, ut 2. Sam. 2, 4. Videtur præcipue indicari strages illa, quam daturus erat Manahemus 2. Reg. 15, 16. prope Jezrahelem campi se ul- tra decem passuum millia extendunt. Ita hic Hieronymus.

## 1:6
V. 6. CALL HIS NAME WITHOUT MERCY) The Greek word better expresses the Hebrew sense: οὐκ ἠλεημένη.

I WILL NO LONGER HAVE MERCY ON THE HOUSE OF ISRAEL) That is, I will no longer extend my mercy toward the ten tribes.

BUT I WILL FORGET THEM BY OBLIVION) He has used it as if it were from נשׁה and נ had been placed for ה, as often happens. But it is more correctly interpreted, I will take them away: that is, I will utterly remove them from this land: them, that is, the Gileadites, the Galileans, the Naphtalites, the Reubenites, the Gadites, a part of Manasseh 2 Kings 15:29, 1 Chronicles 5:26.

Latin:

V. 6. VOCA NOMEN EJUS ABSQUE MISERICOR- DIA) Græca vox melius exprimit sensum Hebræum : οὐκ ἠλεημένη.

NON ADDAM ULTRA MISERERI DOMJU ISRAEL) Id est, non ultra extendam adversus decem tri- bus miserationem meam.

SED OBLIVIONE OBLIVISCAR EORUM) Sumsit quasi esset à נשׁה & positum esset נ pro ה, ut sit sæ- pe. Sed rectius interpretari, tollendo tollam eos : id est, omni- no eos auferam ab hac terra : eos, id est, Galaaditas, Galilæ- os, Nephtalitas, Rubenitas, Gaditas, partem Manassis 2. Reg. 15, 29. 1. Paralip. 5, 26.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. AND I WILL HAVE MERCY ON THE HOUSE OF JUDAH) I will grant this to the piety of Hezekiah, so that the people who are under him may not suffer the same things as the ten tribes.

AND I WILL SAVE THEM IN THE LORD THEIR GOD) By myself, by my own power: it is the custom of the Hebrews to place a noun for a pronoun. The Chaldean [paraphrast] says by the word of the Lord their God: for the Chaldean is accustomed in the great actions of God to make mention of the word of God.

Although we do not deny that custom of the Hebrews; yet it is not necessary here that we should have recourse to it. Since God the Father may rightly be said to save us in the Lord our God, his only-begotten Son: so that a plurality of persons in God is designated. Which explanation is proved first, expressly. Because it flows from the letter itself, and is therefore most simple; for who is it that speaks here, if not God the Father, who, when he is said to save the house of Judah in the Lord their God, the Messiah is shown, through whom all salvation comes to them, so that they may worship the same as their Lord God, and place their trust in him. Wherefore it is confirmed secondly by the acts of grace, which are commemorated here. I will have mercy, says the Lord, on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God. This mercy is not absolute, but founded in the Messiah, who is the source and foundation of all mercy and grace. Salvation, which is exhibited to the people, is granted to them on account of the Messiah, outside of whom there is no salvation, Acts 4:12. Thirdly, by parallel passages, where the Lord speaks of the Lord, and the Lord to the Lord, or is said to do something through the Lord: which passages have been produced elsewhere in great number, and a plurality of divine persons is asserted against the Socinians from them. Fourthly, by the Chaldean paraphrase, which understands the λόγον ὑποστατικὸν by the word, and thus points out the Son of God here and in similar places. Fifthly, by the fulfillment, namely the liberation of the house of Judah from Rezin King of Syria, and Pekah King of Israel through the Messiah their Lord God: whom they therefore worshipped by this name עמנואל our God, or God with us, Is. 7:1, 14. The liberation from the hand of Sennacherib also pertains to the fulfillment of the prophecy, when 185,000 were slain by the Angel of the Lord, by which Angel B. Meisner in this place, page 6, understands the Son of God. But the fulfillment is rashly restricted to the sole liberation from the Babylonian captivity, and this is rendered as a paraphrase: I will have mercy on the house of Judah: that is, I will grant this to the piety of Hezekiah, so that the people who are under him may not suffer the same things as the ten tribes. That this explanation is too restricted is clear from Grotius himself: because a little later he cited the passages 2 Kings 16, Is. 7:1, which certainly concern histories carried out before Hezekiah under Uzziah. To which we add, most recently, an argument from the authority of the ancient Church, inasmuch as it believed that the distinction of the Father and the Son was designated in this and other similar places, as from Hi lary in De Trinitate and Jerome on this passage is certain. Moreover, we have dealt with this and other oracles concerning Christ from Hosea in a certain Academic program, which it will not be tedious to add here. It holds that matter thus:

Although the Prophets of the Old Testament, whom St. Athanasius on the incarnation of the Word rightly calls not teachers of the Jewish people, but of the whole world, and a public sacred school, saw our Lord JESUS only from afar as one who WAS TO COME, they nevertheless not rarely present His advent, incarnation, preaching, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension into heaven, Redemption, and other benefits of that kind, as if they had beheld the Son of God ἐνσώματον, καὶ ἔνσαρκον (in the body and in the flesh) close at hand, and had usurped with their own eyes what He did or suffered for the sake of our salvation, and had drawn from His most holy mouth what He brought forth from the bosom of the Father. Nor is there any doubt that the Prophets showed such things, having seen them with the eyes of the mind by the Spirit of Christ which was in them, who are also called SEERS, because they beheld future things as if they were present, as St. Basil interprets in the preface to Isaiah. And that they heard the Son of God explaining the same things to them in person, just as the prophetic oracles concerning the Messiah are primarily called by the name of HEARING, Isa. 53, 1. Rom. 10, 16. because the Prophets were hearers of God in receiving the oracles, so that they might in turn teach their own hearers. Therefore Obadiah c. 1, 2 says, we have heard a report from the Lord, or we have heard the Lord speaking openly, and Habakkuk ch. 3, 1. O Lord, I have heard your report, and was afraid. Although it seemed to St. Basil in Isa. ch. 11, that neither was a vision proposed to the eyes of the Prophets to be looked upon, nor knowledge to be heard by the ears, but that a brilliant radiance flowing from the Holy Spirit insinuated itself into their hearts, either by exhibiting things present or by announcing things future; and that the splendor of light, as he speaks in ch. 7 of Isaiah, preoccupied the mind, serving for illumination. Theodoret, however, did not hesitate to assert at the beginning of Nahum that the kindness of the most holy Spirit infused into certain Prophets what He wished by means of a sound, so that they thought they heard someone speaking, just as likewise certain visions were presented to their eyes, so that they might behold them in person. But the chief object of the vision and hearing of the Prophets was Christ the God-man, in person and office, whose day they all desired to see with the patriarch Abraham, John 8, 56. Luke 10, 23. 1 Pet. 1, 11. whatever may seem otherwise here to Julian the Apostate, old or new. Theodoret speaks excellently in 'On the Cure of Greek Affections': Just as other paths from villages and fields converge into the royal road, so the Prophets showed that this (CHRIST) is the way for believers, through whom alone access is open to life. All the Prophets were sent before the face of Christ, and were called Angels, says St. Chrysostom in ch. 2. Matt. hom. XXVII. St. Augustine teaches in book VII of the City of God, ch. XXXII, that all prophecies announce those things which, for the sake of the eternal life of the faithful, we believe to have been fulfilled in Christ, and see being fulfilled, and trust will be fulfilled; nor does he hesitate to assert that all things which are contained in the books of the Prophets were said either about Christ or for the sake of Christ, book XII against Faustus, ch. VII. He gives the reason in Psalm CXLII. Christ Himself, he says, was preaching Himself in the Prophets, since He Himself is the Word of God, nor did they say any such thing unless they were full of the Word of God. Therefore they announced Christ, being full of Christ, and they preceded Him who was to come, whom He did not abandon as they preceded Him. Clement of Alexandria brings forward to that effect a certain testimony of St. Peter, accepted by tradition from the fathers, truly worthy of mention, in book VI of the Stromata, p. 314. Whence also Peter, speaking of the Apostles in the preaching, says: But we, when we had unrolled the books which we had of the Prophets, who partly indeed through parables, partly through enigmas, but partly by their own express authority and in their very words name Christ Jesus, we found His advent, and death, and cross, and all the other punishments with which the Jews afflicted Him, and the resurrection, and the assumption into heaven, before Jerusalem was founded, as it is written. All these things, which it was necessary for Him to suffer, and after Him those things which shall be. When, therefore, we had recognized these things, we believed in God through those things which were written about Him. From which Petrine preaching also, Clement shortly after observed that apophthegm of the leader of the Apostles, 'nothing without Scripture.' Which tradition entirely agrees with those things which the holy Apostle left written about the Prophets in his 1st Epistle, 1, verses 10, 11. But how the holy men of God announced Christ, Augustine explained distinctly and by parts in book 18 of the City of God, ch. 28 and following; and long before him St. Irenaeus taught by an elegant comparison in book 4, ch. 66. For since they (the Prophets) themselves were members of Christ, each one of them, according to what he was a member, according to this also manifested the prophecy, all and many prefiguring one, and announcing the things which are of one. For just as through our members the operation of the whole body is indeed shown, but the figure of the whole man is not shown by one member, but by all; so also all the Prophets indeed prefigured one, but each one of them, according to what he was a member, according to this fulfilled the disposition, and prophesied the operation of Christ which was according to that member. Which he illustrates at length with various examples. But what we have said in general about the Prophets, that can be specifically detected in the first of them whose writings were consecrated to the Canon with the law of Moses and the Psalms of David, HOSEA, (for Athanasius in the Synopsis, and Augustine in the place cited, make him the first among them): who, with his contemporary ISAIAH, bore not so much the name of Jesus the Savior, as Jesus Himself in his heart, on his lips, and in his pen, so much so that what St. Athanasius said of the greater part of Isaiah can also be judged of no small part of the prophecies of HOSEA: that it is indeed more a Gospel concerning the advent of the Word of God into the flesh than a prophecy, if you look at the clarity of the oracles, however they may be uttered in the manner in which those who, according to Tertullian, are called by the office of FORETELLING, were accustomed to utter theirs. For what else does it sound forth from the very beginning, promising from the person of God the Father: & I will have mercy on the House of Judah, & I WILL SAVE them IN JEHOVAH their LORD GOD, ch. 1, 7. where indeed the Chaldean interpreter acknowledged the Messiah, rendering it, I will save them in the WORD of the Lord their GOD, whom Christians, here worse than the Jews, are unwilling to acknowledge. How clearly that supreme benefit of the Messiah concerning our calling to the kingdom of grace does this illustrious prophecy present, ch. 2, 10. & the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which is without measure, & shall not be numbered, & it shall be in the place where it shall be said to them, you are not my people, it shall be said to them: Sons of the living GOD. How pleasant, how sweet and honeyed is that promise of CHRIST our Bridegroom! & I will betroth thee unto me for ever: I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness and in judgment, and in grace, and in mercies, in faithfulness I will betroth thee unto me, & thou shalt know the Lord. ch. 2, 19. Indeed, these abundant divine graces cannot be explained in words, says the great man Luther, explaining clearly the gems of the marriage ring, which Christ gives to His Bride the Church, and the gold of faith, from which this ring is made, and which encompasses these precious gems, with this epiphonema: Thus the Prophets elegantly and learnedly commended to their hearers and to posterity their doctrine: But they have simply stripped the glory of justification entirely from the Law and our works. Furthermore, how full of consolation that discourse on the adulterous woman beloved by God in chapter 3 is, and how it properly pertains to the description of the kingdom of Christ, our same Hero has taught better than others: What, he says, could be imagined more sweet? By what other similitude could the mercy of GOD be equally commended? Most sweet is what Christ himself says about the lost little sheep, but this illustration of guilt shows the abysses of divine mercy more clearly. But how solidly and powerfully are the Jews, and all who refuse to acknowledge Christ as the true God with the Father, convinced in chapters 3 and 5? Let us hear the Blessed Luther again on page 508: Let the Jews answer here, why is that worship, which is attributed to God, also attributed to King David? Do we therefore worship many Gods? Or will God give his glory to another? For he not only says, they will seek God, but promises that it will come to pass that they will also seek their King David. This testimony is therefore CLEAR, that King David is to be sought with the same zeal and affection with which the true God is sought. But if this seems absurd to the impious (for God is one God), necessity will force the Jews to define that God (Jehovah) and this King David are one and the same God. Since they are to be worshipped with the same worship. Moreover, the Prophet in chapter 6 exhibited our resurrection with such a wonderful brevity of words that he simultaneously insinuated the resuscitation of Christ, of which that is the fruit. Concerning which the Blessed Luther says excellently: The Prophet rightly changes the persons. For it had to be said, Christ will be brought to life after two days, and on the third day he will rise again. But the Prophet says, we will be brought to life after two days and on the third day, on which Christ rose again, we will rise. And that is why; for because we, plunged into death by sin, were to remain in death forever, the Son of God transferred our sins onto himself, and satisfied for them on the cross, and rising afterwards, conquered the death which he had undergone for us. Therefore, we began to rise and live when Christ rose again. For through him our death was overcome, and the life which we had lost was restored. The Prophet also describes the struggle of Jacob and his antagonist so clearly in chapter 12 that it is a wonder that anyone can be found who cannot find Christ in it. Regarding the Jews, perhaps that is not a wonder, who have eyes and do not see, but it is truly to be lamented that Christians are so very blind here. I will not be reluctant to cite the Blessed Luther again, whom our adversaries oppose to us in this cause without any merit of his own: The Jews, he says, trifle in their own way, and even interpret Elohim as an Angel. But the truth teaches us otherwise; for we know that Christ, because of the ministry which he was to have in the Church and in the flesh, is called an Angel in Genesis 48, Isaiah 63, Malachi 3. Therefore it is CLEAR that this Angel, who is also called Elohim, was the Son of God, and Jacob, who conquered in that struggle, is called Israel, because he conquered God. And a little later: Here again remember the mystery of the Trinity; he calls him God and Angel, and then adds, in Bethel he found him and there he spoke to us. Who? Doubtless he who was God and Angel (Maleach Elohim); but so that you may have absolutely no doubt who that GOD and Angel is, he adds LORD GOD of hosts, LORD is his memorial, or his name: Here the august name of God (Jehovah) is attributed to our Lord Jesus Christ, which he takes upon himself when he says, Philip, he who sees me, sees my Father. The blind Jews are not worthy to see this light. Therefore, when they read these things, they do not know what they are reading, and it is impossible for them to extricate themselves from this passage, or to explain it correctly. But if it is true that the Prophets spoke from the Holy Spirit, what clearer testimony of the Trinity can be shown? But so that we may now wrap in silence many other truly Evangelical things occurring in this Prophet, the illustrious promise in chapter 13, 14 shines forth truly like a most splendid star: I will redeem them from the hand of hell, I will vindicate them from death. I will be your plague, O death, I will be your destruction, O hell. Concerning which the distinguished interpreter of the Prophets, St. Jerome, says excellently: The Lord liberated all, and redeemed them in the Passion of the cross and the shedding of his blood: when his soul descended into hell, and his flesh did not see corruption, and he spoke to death itself and to hell: I will be your death, O death, for I died for this reason, that you might die by my death. I will be your bite, O hell, you who devoured all with your jaws. To which other Doctors agree with great consensus, and among the Jews themselves R. Moses Hadarschan in Galatinus book 8, chapter 21. But we have here primarily the best interpreter, and one above all exception, the Holy Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15, who, regarding how he simultaneously showed the most wholesome practice of this prophecy, it is better to explain in the words of the Blessed Luther than my own: Paul, he says, because of his excellent knowledge, weaves the most beautiful and full consequences of consolation from this place of prophecy; If, he says, death has lost its sting or its power, it follows that sin also has been expiated through Christ, and we have been liberated by him. For where there is sin, there death must necessarily exist. Just as, on the contrary, where there is no sin, there life and justice must necessarily be present. But thus sin has been removed through this victory, the power of sin also, that is, the law, has been removed at the same time, so that it cannot condemn or accuse us. This, he says, is that famous victory which we have through Christ, and we deservedly give thanks to our God for it, who gave it to us, so that we may enjoy it.

AND I WILL NOT SAVE THEM BY BOW, AND BY SWORD, AND BY WAR, AND BY HORSES, AND BY HORSEMEN) I will cause that neither the Syrians, nor the rest of the ten tribes will be able to harm them at all: by the fear of the Assyrian cast upon them, 2 Kings 16, Isaiah 7, 1.

If this history concerning Rezin and Pekah is regarded, how did the Lord give this liberation to the piety of King Hezekiah? Although we do not deny that that liberation also pertains here; yet the words not by bow, nor by sword, etc., seem primarily to refer to that salvation which happened to the Jews under Hezekiah, which was entirely miraculous and truly divine, with the army of Sennacherib struck down by the hand of the Angel, 2 Kings 19, Isaiah 38, concerning which Jerome also explained this prophecy in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET DOMUI JUDA MISEREBOR) Dabo hoc pietati Ezechiæ, ne qui sub eo est populus, eadem pati- atur quæ decem tribus.

ET SALVABO EOS IN DOMINO DEO SUO) Per me mea vi : mos Hebræorum ponendi nomen pro pronomine. Chaldæus per verbum Dei Domini sui : solet enim Chaldæus in magnis Dei actionibus verbi Dei facere mentionem.

Quanquam morem illum Ebræorum non negemus; non tamen hic necessum est, ut ad eum nos recipiamus. Siquidem Deus Pater recte di- catur nos salvare in Domino Deo nostro, Filio suo unigenito : ut ita pluralitas personarum in Deo de- signetur. Quæ explicatio probatur primo ῥητῶς. Quia ex ipsa litera fluit, adeoq; simplicissima est, ec- quis enim est, qui hic loquitur, nisi Deus Pater, qui cum salvare domum Juda in Domino Deo ipsorum dicitur, monstratur Messias, per quem omnis salus ipfis obtingit, ut eundem ceu Dominum Deum suum colant, ac fiduciam in ipsum collocent. Qua- propter confirmatur id secundo ex actibus gratiæ, qui hic commemorantur. Miserebor, inquit Do- minus, Domui Juda, & salvabo eos in Domino Deo suo. Misericordia hæc non est absoluta, sed funda- ta in Messia, qui omnis misericordiæ & gratiæ fons est, & fundus. Salus, quæ exhibetur populo, ob Messiam ei præstatur, extra quem nulla est salus Actor. 4, 12. Tertio locis in parallelis, ubi Dominus de Domino loquitur, & Dominus Domino, vel per Dominum aliquid facere dicitur : quæ loca alias producta sunt magno numero, & adserta adversus Socinianos ex iisdem pluralitas divinarum perso- narum. Quarto Chaldæa paraphrasi, quæ per ver- bum intelligit λόγον ὑποστατικὸν, adeoque Filium Dei ita hic indigitat, & in similibus locis. Quinto complemento, liberatione nempe domus Juda à Re- zin Rege Syriæ, & Peka Rege Israelis per Messiam Dominum Deum ipsorum : quem proinde cole- bant hoc nomine עמנואל Deus noster, vel Deus no biscum Es. 7, 1, 14. Pertinet etiam ad complemen- tum vaticinii liberatio à manu Sennacheribi, cum per Angelum Domini 185000 cæsi sunt, per quem Angelum B. Meisnerus in h. l. pag. 6. intelligit Fi- lium Dei. Temere autem restringitur comple- mentum ad solam liberationem è captivitate Ba- bylonica, & hæc redditur paraphrasis: Domui Juda miserebor : id est, dabo hoc pietati Ezechiæ, ut qui sub eo est populus, eadem patiatur quæ decem tribus. Quam explicationem nimis restrictam esse ex ipso Grotio liquet : quia paulo post adduxit loca 2. Reg. 16. Es. 7, 1. quæ utique historias concernunt ante Ezechiam sub Ozia gestas. Quibus novissime addimus argumentum ab autoritate veteris Eccle- siæ, utpote quæ in hoc & aliis similibus locis distin- ctionem Patris & Filii designari credidit, ut ex Hi- lar. de Trinit. & Hier. in h. l. constat. Cæterum egimus de hoc & aliis oraculis de Christo ex Hosea in programmate quodam Academico, quod hic adjicere non pigebit. Sic autem habet illud:
