Conf. Ef. 11, 6.7. Joh. 5,23. Nonnulli subtilius per agri bestias tyrannos, per volucres cæli sapientes hujus mundi & superbos, per reptilia promiscuum & dolosum vulgus intelligunt, quæ B. Gesneri explicatio est.

## 2:19
Verse 19. AND I WILL BETROTH THEE UNTO ME FOREVER) You who have been a harlot, if you keep faith hereafter, I will betroth: that is, I will treat you as a bride and wife. IN RIGHTEOUSNESS) That is, by doing good. For this noun is very often used in this way. AND IN JUDGMENT) מִשְׁפָּט is said, because it is owed to someone by law, such as cohabitation, food, and clothing to a wife. AND IN MERCY, AND IN COMPASSIONS) By forgiving sins.

Latin:

Vers 19. ET SPONSABO TE MIHI IN SEMPI- TERNUM) Te quæ meretrix fuisti, si posthac fidem ser- ves, sponsabo: id est, ut sponsam atque uxorem tractabo. IN JUSTITIA) Id est, benefaciendo. Ita enim hoc nomen sæpissime usurpatur. ET IN JUDICIO) מִשְׁפָּט dicitur, quod alicui ex lege debetur, ut uxori cohabitatio, victus, vestitus. ET IN MISERICORDIA, ET IN MISERA- TIONIBUS) Condonando peccata.

## 2:20
Verse 20. IN FAITH) By performing all promises: for that is אֱמוּנָה.

This promise is spiritual and Evangelical: by which God promises that He will betroth Himself to us: as He who is the true bridegroom of our soul. I say it is an Evangelical promise, because it was made without any condition of works, in which is to be noted: (1) The author of the betrothal: Jehovah God; where some observe the threefold repetition of the word, which was done not so much for the certainty of the spiritual marriage, as for the insinuation of the mystery of the Holy Trinity, as if to say: I, God the Father, will betroth you to me. I, God the Son, will betroth you to me. I, God the Holy Spirit, will betroth you to me, just as we are baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, which action is nothing other than a certain mystical betrothal. (2) The act of the betrothal. Which pertains to the new covenant, which God has struck with us. For if it were understood as the simple reception of a fornicating people into grace, this would not be a new betrothal: but only a continuation of the prior covenant and marriage. For a husband is not said to betroth to himself anew a wife to whom he does not impute crimes. Since, therefore, the Lord uses the word for betrothing here, He looked without doubt to the new covenant with the Church of the New Testament, as the blessed Meisner says in this place. By the power of this covenant, therefore, God promises us, in a most eminent way, what belongs to a bridegroom. A bridegroom joins his bride tightly to himself, loves her intimately, provides for her necessities, adorns her as much as he can, defends her, leads her into his house, and makes her a participant in all his goods: Thus God, our bridegroom, joins us to Himself through a gracious union, loves, cares for, adorns, covers, and finally leads us into heaven, the house of glory, and blesses us with heavenly and eternal gifts. Apoc. 19, 7. This conjunction in spiritual marriage is attributed in a special way to the Son of God, our Messiah, Is. 61. Joh. 3.

2 Cor. 11. Eph. 5, 26. because as a bridegroom and bride are united in both bodies and souls, so that they are one flesh and one Spirit, so the Son of God wished to be joined to us both by reason of flesh, when He assumed our flesh into the unity of His person, and coupled it to Himself, and through the incarnation betrothed Himself to us, and by reason of Spirit, because He communicates His Spirit to us, and unites and joins ours to His, so that we may be one Spirit with the Lord, 1 Cor. 6, 17. (3) The duration of the covenant. It is not a temporary covenant, but I will betroth you to me forever, says the Lord. Therefore, the covenant does not look to temporal goods, nor only to the Israelite people according to the flesh, but to spiritual, heavenly, and eternal goods, and to the people of Israel according to the promise and the Spirit. (4) The attributes and conditions of the divine covenant. For here four conditions of the covenant on the part of God are touched upon. I will betroth you to me on the part of God. Both in righteousness and judgment, or in such a way that through gratuitous justification I may grant you true righteousness, and through gracious defense I may assist you, so that by the former against sin, and by the latter against Satan and his satellites, I may vindicate and assert you for myself: and in mercy and compassions: that is, through the exhibition of manifold spiritual and corporal grace, which the word חֶסֶד brings, as also through commiseration in all necessities, which we especially need because of daily infirmities and various temptations and adversities to which we are subject. All of which testify that the covenant is merely gratuitous, by the power of which everything we need is graciously administered and exhibited to us. (5) The condition of the covenant on our part. Which is none other here than faith and the acknowledgment of God. I will betroth you to me in faith, and you shall know the Lord.

Which are synonymous, and explain one another mutually, and are joined by ἐπεξήγησιν (epexegetical explanation). For faith is described through the knowledge of the Lord, Is. 53:11, John 17:3; the knowledge of the Lord is included in faith, for which awareness, assent, and trust are required: whence its first degree is ἐπίγνωσις (full knowledge). Therefore, trust is joined with acknowledgment, so that we may understand it to be neither a bare nor a theoretical awareness, but a practical awareness, which is directed toward trust and brings it about, just as in practical matters γνῶσις (knowledge) ought to be directed toward πρᾶξιν (action), nor should we think trust to be blind, which is without the knowledge of that toward which it is directed, but a trust more than ἐπιστημονικὴν (scientific) arising from awareness, omniscience, and a more certain demonstration, since it rests upon the immovable truth of God: in which scientific trust, if we may so call it, and fiducial knowledge it behooves us to glory uniquely, to such an extent that we prefer it to all wisdom, all fortitude, and all riches; indeed, that we place in it all divine wisdom, all spiritual fortitude, and all our heavenly riches, as we are admonished in Jer. 9:24, where the same conditions of divine betrothal are held to be proposed. Cf. 1 Cor. 1:31, 2 Cor. 10:17. Therefore, by faith here is not understood fidelity or constancy in keeping promises, but trust, because the word synonymous with knowledge, which is used concerning saving faith, demands this, Job 19:25, Is. 53:11, in the manner of the Hebrews, which words include the affection of knowledge. The very word for faith demands it, because אֱמוּנָה (emunah) is taken for trust and justifying faith, Hab. 2:4, Rom. 1:17. Its correlate demands it. Because in this reciprocal betrothal, faith is to be accepted in such a way that it looks toward divine mercy. For since on the part of God nothing is offered to us …except grace, and that which is merely gratuitous—gratuitous justification, gratuitous vindication of us, gratuitous communication of gifts, gratuitous exhibition of mercies—faith is certainly required on our part, which accepts this grace of God, apprehends it, and appropriates it to us. Finally, the nature of this covenant demands it. Which, just as it is truly Evangelical, so it requires in us trust also. Because the Gospel, and any Evangelical promise, and the Evangelical covenant requires faith, and for that reason is distinguished from the legal covenant, in that the latter introduces the condition of works, but the former requires faith alone. Gal. 3, 11. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 20. IN FIDE) Omnia promissa præstando : id enim est אֱמוּנָה.

Promissio hæc spiritualis est, & Evangelica : qua Deus pollicetur sese desponsaturum se nobiscum : utpote qui verus animæ nostræ sponsus est. Evan- gelicam dico promissionem, quia facta est sine omni conditione operum, in qua notandus. (1) Desponsa- tionis autor : Jehovah Deus; ubi observant non- nulli trinam verbi repetitionem, quæ facta sit non tam ob connubii spiritualis certitudinem, quam ob mysterii S. S. Trinitatis insinuationem, q. d. Ego Deus Pater desponsabo te mihi. Ego Deus Filius despon- sabo te mihi. Ego Spiritus S. desponsabo te mihi, quem- admodum in nomine S. S. Trinitatis baptizamur, quæ actio nihil aliud est, quam mystica quædam de- sponsatio. (2) Desponsationis actus. Qui pertinet ad novum fœdus, quod Deus nobiscum pepigit. Nam si de simplici receptione populi fornicarii in gra- tiam intelligatur, hæc non foret nova desponsatio : sed prioris tantum fœderis & conjugii continuatio. Non enim maritus dicitur uxorem sibi de novo de- sponsare, cui flagitia non imputat. Quum ergo hic desponsandi verbo utatur Dominus, ad novum fœ- dus cum Ecclesia Novi Testamenti dubio procul respexit, ut B. Meisnerus in h. l. Vi ergo fœderis hu- jus Deus, quæ sponsi sunt, eminentissima ratione nobis promittit. Sponsus sponsam suam arcté sibi conjungit, intime amat, de necessariis prospicit, pro virili ornat, defendit, in domum suam deducit, omniumque suorum bonorum participem reddit : Sic Deus sponsus noster conjungit nos sibi per gra- tiosam unionem, amat, curat, ornat, tegit, & tan- dem in cælum, gloriæ domum deducit, ac cœlesti- bus & æternis donis beat. Apoc. 19,7. Tribuitur au- tem hæc conjunctio in spirituali connubio pecu- liari ratione Filio Dei Messia nostro, Ef. 61. Joh. 3.

2. Cor. 11. Ephef. 5, 26. quia ut sponsus & sponsa & corporibus & animis uniuntur, ut una caro sint, & unus Spiritus, ita Filius Dei jungi nobis voluit tum ratione carnis, dum nostram carnem in unitatem personæ assumsit, sibiq; copulavit, & per incarna- tionem se nobis desponsavit, tum ratione Spiritus, quia Spiritum suum nobis communicat, & nostrum suo unit, ac conjungit, ut simus unus Spiritus cum Domino, 1. Cor. 6, 17. (3) Fœderis duratio. Non est fœdus temporarium, sed desponsabo te mihi in sem- Fæderis piternum, inquit Dominus. Non ergo fœdus respi- duratio. cit bona temporalia, non populum tantum Israëli- ticum secundum carnem, sed bona spiritualia, ca- lestia & æterna, ac populum Israël, secundum promis- sionem & Spiritum. (4.) Fœderis divini attributa & Fæderis conditiones. Tanguntur enim hic conditiones fœ- conditiones. deris ex parte Dei quatuor. Desponsabo te mihi Ex parte tum in justitia & judicio, vel ita, ut per gratuitam Dei. justificationem veram justitiam tibi donem, ac per gratiosam defensionem tibi assistam, ut illa adversus peccatum, hac adversus Satanam, ejusque satellites te mihi vindicem, atq; adseram: tum in misericor- dia, & miserationibus : h. e. per gratiæ spiritualis & corporalis multivariæ exhibitionem, quam vox חֶסֶד infert, ut & per commiserationem, in omnibus ne- cessitatibus, qua imprimis opus habemus ob infir- mitates quotidianas, variasq; tentationes, & adver- sitates, quibus obnoxii sumus. Quæ omnia testan- tur fœdus mere gratuitum esse, vi cujus nobis o- mnia, quibus nobis opus est, gratiose administran- tur & exhibentur. (5.) Fœderis conditio ex parte no- stri. Quæ nulla alia hic, quam fides, & agnitio Dei. Desponsabo te mihi in fide, & cognosces Dominum.

Quæ synonyma sunt, ac se mutuo explicant, & per ἐπεξήγησιν conjunguntur. Nam fides per cognitio- nem Domini describitur Ef. 53, 11. Joh. 17, 3. cognitio Domini in fide includitur, ad quam notitia, assensus, & fiducia requiritur : unde primus ejus gradus επί- γνωσις est. Ideo fiducia cū agnitione conjungitur, ut neq; nudam aut theoreticam notitiam esse intelli- gamus, sed notitiam practicam, quæ ad fiduciam di- recta est, eandemq; infert, uti in practicis γνῶσις ad πρᾶξιν directa esse debet, neq; fiduciam cæcam esse existimemus, quæ sine cognitione ejus sit, in quod fertur, sed fiduciam plusquam ἐπιστημονικὴν ex no- titia, omniscientia & apodixi certiori, quippe im- mota Dei veritate nitente, oriundam : in qua fiducia scientifica, ut ita vocitemus, & scientia fiduciali unice nos gloriari decet, adeo, ut eam omni sapientiæ, omni fortitudini, omnibus divitiis præferamus, imo in ea- dem omnem sapientiam divinam, omnem fortitudi- nem spiritualem, omnesq; divitias nostras cælestes col- locemus, uti Jer. 9, 24. monemur, ubi eædem divi- næ desponsationis conditiones propositæ haben- tur. Conf. 1. Cor. 1, 31. 2. Cor. 10,17. Non ergo per fidem hic intelligitur fidelitas, aut constantia in ser- vandis promissis, sed fiducia, quia hoc poscit ver- bum synonymum cognitionis, quod de fide salvi- fica adhibetur Job. 19, 25. Ef. 53, 11. more Ebræo- rum, quæ verba notitiæ affectum includunt. Poscit id ipsum fidei vocabulum, quia אֱמוּנָה de fiducia & fide justificante accipitur Hab. 2, 4. Rom. 1,17. Poscit id correlatum. Quia in sponsione hac reciproca fi- des ita accipienda est, ut respiciat divinam miseri- cordiam. Quum enim ex parte Dei nil nisi gratia, & quod mere gratuitum sit, offeratur nobis, gra- tuita justificatio gratuita vindicatio nostri, gratuita donorum communicatio, gratuita miserationum ex- hibitio, fides utique ex parte nostra requiritur, quæ hanc Dei gratiam acceptet, apprehendat, nobisq; appropriet. Poscit deniq; fœderis hujus ratio. Quod uti vere Evangelicum est, ita requirit in nobis fidu- etiam. Quia Evangelium, & quævis promissio Evangelica, ac fœdus Evangelicum fidem postulat, eaque ratione à fœdere legali distinguitur, quod hoc conditionem operum inferat, illud autem solam fidem requirat. Gal. 3, 11. 12.

## 2:21
Vers. 21. I WILL HEAR THE HEAVENS) a personification, such as are many in the Prophets: that is, I will give the heaven an optimal constitution, such as it would desire, thus it would have the sense.

AND THEY SHALL HEAR THE EARTH) The heaven will make the earth fruitful. Ἐρᾷ μὲν ὄμβρου γαῖ᾽, ὅταν ξηρὸν πέδον Ἄκαρπον αὐχμῷ νοτίδος ἐνδεως ἔχει· Ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ σεμνὸς οὐρανὸς πληρούμενος Ὄμβρου πεσεῖν εἰς γαῖαν ἀφροδίτης ὕπο· Ὅταν δὲ συμμιχθῆτον εἰς ταὐτὸν δύο Τίκτουσι ἡμῖν πάντα κἀκτρέφουσ᾽ ἅμα, Ὅθεν βρότειον ζῇ τε κᾀ θάλλει γένος. says Euripides.

Latin:

Vers. 21. EXAUDIAM COELOS) προσωποποιΐα, quales multæ in Prophetis: id est, dabo cœlo constitutio- nem optimam, qualem optaret, sic sensum haberet.

ET ILLI EXAUDIENT TERRAS) Terram fœ- cundam faciet cœlum. Ἐρᾷ μὲν ὄμβρου γαῖ᾽, ὅταν ξηρὸν πέδον Ἄκαρπον αὐχμῷ νοτίδος ἐνδεως ἔχει· Ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ σεμνὸς οὐρανὸς πληρούμενος Ὄμβρου πεσεῖν εἰς γαῖαν ἀφροδίτης ὕπο· Ὅταν δὲ συμμιχθῆτον εἰς ταὐτὸν δύο Τίκτουσι ἡμῖν πάντα κἀκτρέφουσ᾽ ἅμα, Ὅθεν βρότειον ζῇ τε κᾀ θάλλει γένος. ait Euripides.

## 2:22
Vers. 22. AND THE EARTH SHALL HEAR THE CORN, AND THE WINE, AND THE OIL) It will open itself to the fruits wishing to break forth.

AND THESE SHALL HEAR JEZREEL) The seed of God; the pious, namely, as above 1, 11.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ET TERRA EXAUDIET TRITICUM, ET VINUM, ET OLEUM) Pandet se frugibus erumpere volentibus.

ET HÆC EXAUDIENT JEZRAHEL) Semen Dei; pios scilicet, ut supra 1, 11.

## 2:23
Vers. 23. AND I WILL SOW HER UNTO ME IN THE EARTH) I will scatter widely, as seeds that are cast.

AND I WILL HAVE MERCY UPON HER THAT HAD NOT OBTAINED MERCY) That was οὐκ ἠλεημένη, as above 1, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ET SEMINABO EAM MIHI IN TERRA) Late spargam, ut quæ jaciuntur semina.

ET MISEREBOR EJUS, QUÆ FUIT ABS- QUE MISERICORDIA) Quæ fuit οὐκ ἠλεημένη, ut supra 1, 6.

## 2:23
Vers. 24. AND I WILL SAY TO THEM WHICH WERE NOT MY PEOPLE) And to the people, who for a long time had not been mine; above 1, 9.

THOU ART MY PEOPLE) The same sense as above 1, 10.

AND HE SHALL SAY, THOU ART MY GOD) The same sense as above 1, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET DICAM NON POPULO MEO) Et populo, qui diu meus non fuerat; supra 1, 9.

POPULUS MEUS ES TU) Idem sensus, qui su- pra 1, 10.

ET IPSE DICET, DEUS MEUS ES TU) Idem sensus, qui supra 1, 6.

## 3:1 Argument
SERMON II. LIKEWISE CLOTHED IN A SIMILAR TYPE, EVANGELICAL. CHAPTER III.

The Prophet is again commanded to win back the love of the Adulteress with a new gift to indicate the new grace of GOD, because after the long abandonment of the people, in which they remained without a Polity and without divine worship, they are to be converted in the time of the N. Testament to their King David (i.e., the Messiah from the lineage of David), and will truly celebrate his grace. God loves those who hate Him, and seeks those who have turned away.

ADHUC VADE) God wishes another type to be employed, by which His supreme leniency toward a people whom He could have utterly destroyed by right is signified, but He preferred to prolong its life and await repentance, like a husband who does not bring an adulterous wife before a judge to be condemned to the punishment of death, but bears it patiently, while nevertheless abstaining from her bed in the meantime.

DILECTAM AMICO) To her husband.

SICUT DOMINUS DILIGIT FILIOS ISRAEL) An explanation of the type, which is clearer below in verses 4 and 5.

ET DILIGUNT VINACIA UVARUM) The correct version seems to be, flagons of wine. For so it is in 2 Sam. 6:19, Cant. 2, and often in the Talmudic writings. Certain Rabbis say it is the sixth part of an Ephah. They used to offer wine to the gods, then drink from it.

Latin:

CONCIO II. ITIDEM TYPO SIMILI VESTITA, EVANGELICA. CAPUT III.

Propheta denuo jussus amores Scortatricis sibi conciliare novo munere ad indicandam no- vam DEI gratiam, quod post diuturnam derelictionem populi, in qua sine Politia & sine cultu divino mansit, N. Test. tempore convertendus sit ad Regem suum David (h. e. Messiam è Davidis stemmate,) ejus- que gratiam celebraturus vere. Diligit osores Deus, aversosque requirit.

Vers. 1. ADHUC VADE) Alterum typum vult adhiberi Deus, quo significetur summa ejus lenitas in populum, quem jure perdere omnino potuisset, sed maluit vitam ejus producere, & pœnitentiam exspectare, par marito, qui u- xorem adulteram non ad judicem defert, mortis supplicio adjudicandam, sed fert patienter, à concubitu tamen ejus interim abstinens.

DILECTAM AMICO) Marito suo.

SICUT DOMINUS DILIGIT FILIOS ISRAEL) Explicatio typi, quæ est planior infra v. 4. 5.

ET DILIGUNT VINACIA UVARUM) Recta versio videtur, lagenas vini. Sic enim 2. Sam. 6, 19. Cant. 2. & in Thalmudicis sæpe. Quidam Rabbini dicunt esse partem sextam Ephæ, Libabant vinum diis, deinde ex eo bibebant.

## 3:2
Vers. 2. ET FODI EAM MIHI) I bought her for myself. For כרה signifies this also. But just as coemption was a type of marriage among the Romans, so also among the Hebrews men acquired wives for themselves by a gift for the sake of marriage, or by labor, Gen. 29:18, 2 Sam. 3:14.

QVINDECIM ARGENTEIS) Namely, shekels.

ET CORO HORDEI) The LXX keep the Hebrew word γομόρ. See Lev. 28:16, Ezek. 45:11.

ET DIMIDIO CORO HORDEI) That which is here in the Hebrew as לתך is also found in the Talmudic writings, and is said to hold fifteen seahs, five Ephahs: but the codices which the seventy elders used held it far otherwise: for they translate it νῆβελ οἴνε, and that is indeed a flagon of wine. Jer. 13:12.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET FODI EAM MIHI) Emi eam mihi. Nam כרה & hoc significat. Sicut autem cœmito matrimonii erat genus apud Romanos, sic & apud Hebræos viri dona- tione ob nuptias, aut operis uxores sibi acquirebant, Ge- nes. 29, 18. 2. Sam. 3, 14.

QVINDECIM ARGENTEIS) Siclis scilicet.

ET CORO HORDEI) LXX. Hebraicam vocem servant γομόρ. Vide Lev. 28, 16. Ezech. 45, 11.

ET DIMIDIO CORO HORDEI) Quod hic in Hebræo est לתך, etiam in Thalmudicis invenitur, & dici- tur tenere quindecim seas, quinque Ephoth: sed longe ali- ter habuere codices, quibus usi sunt LXX. senes: vertunt enim νῆβελ οἴνε, id vero est lagenam vini. Jer. 13, 12.

## 3:3
Vers. 3. DIES MULTOS EXSPECTABIS ME) That is, I wish you to wait for me in a widow's bed, before I am fully reconciled to you,

Verf. eod. NON FORNICABERIS, ET NON ERIS VIRO) And you must abstain from both illegitimate and legitimate intercourse.

SED ET EGO EXSPECTABO TE) In the Hebrew: I also for your sake, supply, will abstain from marriage.

Some interpreters expect me to explain this phrase in a completely contrary sense. Some understand the Hebrew words תשבי לי, 'You shall sit for me,' as referring to widowhood, as if it were a punishment for a harlot, like Vatablus: 'You shall sit for me,' namely, as a widow: so that by this very thing the rejection of the people for many days is proclaimed, which is later explained in the exposition of the type. Others take it as referring to marital adherence: 'you shall sit for me,' that is, you shall adhere to me alone and cohabit, which sense B. Luther also expressed, and the command of the Lord openly demands it: 'Go again and love the woman.' For God commands not the rejection of the woman, but the taking of her. Nor does the new contract, by which he bought her or acquired her for himself again for a certain price, imply anything else. By the word כרה, to pierce or dig through, Gefner, along with Oecolampadius and Montanus, thinks that the custom is being referred to, by which they were accustomed to bore the ear of slaves, Deut. 15, 17. That contract implies not rejection, but cohabitation, by which she was bound to adhere to him alone. Finally, the reciprocal stipulation teaches the same thing. For as the Prophet demands from the woman: 'You shall not be for a man,' namely, another, concerning which way of speaking compare Rom. 6, 3. So, conversely, you promise to the same: 'And I also to you.' Which words cannot have a negative sense, but contain a matrimonial promise, by which the Prophet wished to entice the adulteress, so that she would not have relations with others. B. Luther says thus on this passage: The Prophet is right to love the adulteress, but the beginnings of love are very tenuous. He spends on her not as much as was spent on a maidservant injured by a bull that was wont to push. For her master, according to the Law, had to be paid thirty shekels. This is half the price. Then, why does he give barley so sparingly, and not complete two homers? Jerome follows the opinion of the Jews, who think that there are mysteries in these numbers, and transfer them to the ancient people, liberated from Egypt, and adorned on the forty-fifth day with the law. Although I do not entirely condemn these, yet it is certain that they are not proper. For the simple and true meaning is that the Lord, being about to scatter Israel among the nations, will have them live there sparingly and harshly, so that in this way He may force them to desist from idolatry. For fifteen pieces of silver and a half-homer of barley are nothing but daily bread and a sad exile among the nations. He shows, however, the reason why God is going to do this, and why He will cast His people into the nations, and will suffer them to be treated harshly there. 'There,' he says, 'you shall sit for me, and you shall not play the harlot, you shall not join yourself with another husband,' that is, I am handing you over to the Assyrians for this reason, that you may be forced to desist from that shameful idolatry, which you retained so pertinaciously while the kingdom was quiet. Therefore, this sentiment pertains to teaching us about the punishments which God inflicts upon us because of sins, namely, that we should conclude that they are not inflicted upon us as if God wishes to reject us and for us to perish in our sins, but so that, compelled by evils, we may cease to sin, and be called by these harsh means to repentance. Just as Paul says: 'We are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world.' So far B. Luther. If anyone should urge verse 4: 'Because the children of Israel shall sit for many days,' we answer: those words pertain to the explanation of the prior state before the taking of the adulteress in the antitype: but the rest, v. 5, 'And after this the children of Israel shall return,' refers to the later state of the woman returning into favor and adhering to her husband, as a new covenant.

Latin:

Vers. 3. DIES MULTOS EXSPECTABIS ME) Id est, volo expectes me in thoro vidua, antequam tibi plene re- concilier,

Verf. eod. NON FORNICABERIS, ET NON ERIS VIRO) Et illegitimo & legitimo concubitu abstinere debebis.

SED ET EGO EXSPECTABO TE) In Hebræo: Ego etiam propter te, fupple, abstinebo à conjugio.

Phrasin hanc expectabis me prorsus contrario sensu exponunt Interpp. Nonnulli verba Ebræa תשבי לי Sedebis mihi, de viduitate, ceu pœna forni- cariæ intelligunt, ut Vatablus: Sedebis mihi scil. vi- dua: ut hoc ipso prædicatur abjectio populi ad dies multos, quæ postea explicatur in typi ἐκθέσει. Alii de adhæsione connubiali accipiunt: sedebis mihi, id est, mihi uni adhærebis & cohabitabis, quem sensum etiam expressit B. Lutherus, eumq; aperte manda- tum Domini postulat: Adhuc vade & dilige mulie- rem. Præcipit enim Deus non abjectionem mulieris, sed affumtionem. Neque aliud infert contractus no- vus, quo fodit eam, vel comparavit sibi denuo certo pretio mulierē. Verbo כרה perforare, perfodere re- spici ad consuetudinem, qua solebant servis auri- culam terebrare Deut. 15, 17. putat cum Oecolampad. & Montano Gefnerus. Ille contractus non abjectio- nem, sed cohabitationem, qua ipsi soli adhærefcere debebat, infert. Deniq; reciproca stipulatio idem docet. Nam ut à muliere poscit Propheta: Non eris viro scil. alteri, de quo modo loquendi conferatur Rom. 6, 3. Sic vice versa promittis eidem: Et ego etiam ad te. Quæ verba sensum negativum habere nequeunt, sed promissionem matrimonialem conti- nens, qua allicere voluit Propheta adulteram, ne cum aliis rem haberet. B. Lutherus ita hoc loco: Justus est Propheta amare adulteram, sed initia a- moris admodum sunt tenuia. Impendit in eam non tantum, quantum impendebatur in ancillam à bove cornupeta læsam. Nam ejus hero ex Lege numerandi erant sicli triginta. Hic dimidium pretium est. Deinde cur ita parce donat hordeum, & non complet duos coros? Hieronymus sequitur Judæorum senten- tiam, qui in hisce numeris mysteria esse censent, & transferunt eos ad populum veterem, liberatum ex Ægypto, & ornatum die quadragesimo quinto lege. Hæc etsi non omnino damno, tamen certum est, non esse propria. Simplex enim & vera sententia est, quod Dominus Israëlem inter gentes disseminatu- rus, & ibi habiturus sit parce ac duriter, ut hoc mo- do cogat desistere ab idololatria. Nam quindecim argentei, & sesquicorus tritici nihil sunt quam panis quotidianus, & triste exilium inter gentes. Ostendit autem causam, cur hoc facturus sit Deus, & projectu- rus suum populum in gentes, & passurus, ut ibi duri- ter habeatur. Ibi, inquit, mihi sedebis, & non forni- caberis, non conjunges te cum alio marito, hoc est, ideo te trado Assyriis, ut cogaris desistere ab illa turpi idololatria, quam dum regnum quietum fuit, tam pertinaciter retinuisti. Pertinet igitur hæc sen- tentia ad docendos nos de pœnis, quas infligit nobis Deus propter peccata, ut scilicet statuamus, eas nobis non infligi ideo, quasi abjicere nos Deus & in peccatis perire velit, sed ut coacti malis desinamus peccare, & vocemur hisce duris mediis ad pœnitentiam. Sicut Paulus dicit: A Domino corripimur, ne cum hoc mundo damnemur. Hactenus B. Lutherus. Si quis versum 4. urgeat: Quia dies multos sedebunt filii Israel, respondemus: ea verba ad priorem statum ante assumptionem adulteræ in antitypo explican- dum, pertinere: Cætera vero v. 5. Et posthæc re- vertentur filii Israel, referre statum posteriorem re- deuntis in gratiam mulieris, & viro adhærescentis, ut novi pacti.

## 3:4
Vers. 4. BECAUSE) For. This is a plainer explanation of the type: therefore a new period begins here.

FOR MANY DAYS THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SHALL SIT) In places under the dominion of Assyria. WITHOUT A KING) Namely, of their own nation. AND WITHOUT A PRINCE) That is, not only shall they not have their own King, but not even anyone endowed with jurisdiction from among their own people. שר The Greeks rightly translate as ἄρχοντα, the Chaldean as שלטן. AND WITHOUT SACRIFICE) Whether legitimate or idolatrous. AND WITHOUT AN ALTAR) מצבה, the Greeks are accustomed to translate as στήλην. By this word are signified those small pillars which were lawful before the law. Gen. 28, 18. 22. 31, 13. 45, 51. 52. 35, 14. 20. By the law, because they were frequent in idolatrous use, they began to be forbidden to the Hebrews Exod. 23, 24. c. 34, 13. Levit. 26, 1. Deut. 7, 5. 12, 3. 16, 22. 1 Kings 14, 23. AND WITHOUT AN EPHOD) The Greeks [translate] ἐδὲ ἱερατείας: a figure well explained. For that breastplate, which is called an Ephod, is the mark of the high priest. Exod. 28. AND WITHOUT TERAPHIM) The LXX translated [it] ἐδὲ δήλων, that is, without Urim: but Teraphim everywhere signifies idols. Moreover, the name is in itself neutral: and therefore it can signify not badly the images of false worship, as in the histories of Laban, and elsewhere, but also the Cherubim themselves, as Jerome noted here and we noted on Judges 17, 5.

That the former [phrases] WITHOUT A KING, AND WITHOUT A PRINCE pertain to the political state is undoubted, because they shall have no head of their own, neither a King, just as they had lived before under a King, nor even any Prince; that is, because they shall have not only no monarchical, but not even any other form of government. Which describe their miserable condition with respect to Polity and the Republic. The latter [phrases] exhibit a miserable condition with respect to the Church, because they shall have neither Sacrifice nor Ephod: nor a statue or teraphim. From which most [commentators] judge that the cessation of true worship is inferred from the former, and the impediment of false worships as well from the latter: so that it is hinted that absolutely all worship, whether true or false, will cease: but because false worship is not a care to God, and the people were never easily without all worship, I would rather say it is hinted only [to be] the cessation of worship instituted by God, so that they shall have neither sacrifice nor מַצֵּבָה altar, as the Vulgate renders it (the LXX explain it with the word θυσιαστήρια); nor an Ephod; which the LXX rendered ἱερατείαν, Aquila ἐπένδυμα [meaning] over-garment, Luther rendered Leibrock: such as the Ephod was then common, made of linen, of any priests 1 Sam. 2, 18. c. 14, 3. 2 Sam. 6, 4. then the singular one of the high priest, woven of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet Exod. 28, 5. c. 39, 5. Finally, they were also without Teraphim: the Targum explains: Nor shall there be one who returns an answer, ὀὐέ δηλώσεως υσης without manifestation. Jerome handed down the general sense. Teraphim are properly called μορφώματα, that is, figures and simulacra, provided that even sacred and lawful images are noted by that word, such as the Cherubim were in the temple, yet not idolatrous, such as those of Rachel Gen. 31, 49. and Micah Jud. 17, 5. were, which Blessed Meisner also acknowledges, even though he takes Teraphim and the statue in this place in a bad sense; but Blessed Gesner took it in a good sense with us in his commentary on this place, to which opinion it favors that these are introduced as punishments. But is the removal of idolatrous statues and images a punishment?

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVIA) Namque. Hæc est planior explica- tio typi: itaque nova hic periodus inchoatur.

DIES MULTOS SEDEBUNT FILII ISRAEL) In locis Assyriæ ditionis. SINE REGE) Nempe suæ gentis. ET SINE PRINCIPE) Id est, non modo Regem suum non habebunt, sed nec ullum è suis jurisdictione, præ- ditum. שר Græci recte vertunt ἄρχοντα, Chaldæus שלטן. ET SINE SACRIFICIO) Sive legitimo, sive ido- lolatrico. ET SINE ALTARI) מצבה, στήλην solent vertere Græci. Significantur hac voce columellæ istæ, quæ ante legem licitæ. Genes. 28, 18. 22. 31, 13. 45, 51. 52. 35, 14. 20. per legem, quod frequentes essent in usu idolola- trico, vetari Hebræis cœpere Exod. 23, 24. c. 34, 13. Le- vit. 26, 1. Deut. 7, 5. 12, 3. 16, 22. 1. Reg. 14, 23. ET SINE EPHOD) Græci ἐδὲ ἱερατείας: bene ex- plicata figura. Nam pectorale illud, quod Ephod dicitur, nota summi sacerdotis. Exod. 28. ET SINE TERAPHIM) ἐδὲ δήλων verterunt LXX. id est, sine Urim: sed Teraphim ubique simulacra significat. Est autem nomen per se medium: Ideoque significare po- test non male imagines falsi cultus, ut in Labanis historiis, & alibi, sed & ipsos Cherubinos, ut hic notavit Hierony- mus & nos notavimus ad Jud. 17, 5.

Priora illa SINE REGE, ET SINE PRIN- CIPE ad statum politicum pertinere indubium est, quod nullum habituri proprium caput sint, neque Regem, quemadmodum antea sub Rege vixerant, neq; etiam Principem aliquem; hoc est, quod non solum non monarchicam, sed nec ullam aliam re- giminis formam habituri sint. Quæ miseram for- tem eorum respectu Politiæ & Reipubl. describunt. Posteriora miseram conditionem respectu Eccle- siæ exhibent, quod neq; Sacrificium neq; Ephod ha- bituri sint: neque statuam aut teraphim. E quibus istud veri cultus cessationem, hoc falsorum quoque cultuum impedimentum inferri pleriq; censent: ut innuatur prorsus omnem cultum, seu verum seu falsum desiturum: sed quia Deo curæ non est fal- sus cultus, neque unquam absque omni cultu facile fuit populus, dixerim potius innui solum cessatio- nem cultus divinitus instituti, ut neque sacrificium neq; מַצֵּבָה altare, ut Vulg. reddit (LXX. θυσιαστη- ρία voce exponunt) habituri sint; neque Ephod; quod LXX. ἱερατείαν, Aquila ἐπένδυμα super indu- mentum, Lutherus Leibrock reddidere: quale Ephod tum vulgare erat ex lino, sacerdotum quorumvis 1. Sam. 2, 18. c. 14, 3. 2. Sam. 6, 4. tum singulare summi sa- cerdotis, ex auro, hyacintho, purpura & coccino con- textum Exod. 28, 5. c. 39, 5. Denique etiam sine Te- raphim erant: Targum exponit: Nec erit, qui re- sponsum reddat, ὀὐέ δηλώσεως υσης sine manifesta- tione. Hieronymus sensum generalem tradidit. Tera- phim proprie appellantur μορφώματα, id est, figuræ & simulacra, siquidem etiam sacræ & licitæ imagi- nes ea voce notentur, quales in templo Cherubim erant, non tamen idololatricæ, quales Rachelis Gen. 31, 49. & Michæ Jud. 17, 5. fuere, quod agno- scit etiam B. Meisnerus, etsi Teraphim & statuam hoc loco in malam partem accipiat; in bonam au- tem partem nobiscum accepit B. Gesnerus com- ment. in h. l. cui sententiæ favet, quod hæc tan- quam pœnæ inducantur. Num autem statuarum & imaginum idololatricarum ablatio pœna est?

## 3:5
Verse 5.

AFTERWARDS) When they have lived for a long time in that state, deprived of kingdom, temple, sacrifices, and idolatry, weary of the cruelty of idolaters toward them. AND THEY SHALL SEEK THE LORD THEIR GOD) That is, and they shall apply themselves to God. Thus בקש is rightly translated as προσκοπᾶσι [seek] Lev. 19, 31. AND DAVID THEIR KING) They shall adhere to Zerubbabel, who shall be of the family of David, and therefore shall be called David, as all [descendants] from Jacob [are called] Israel Ezech. 34, 23. The Chaldean paraphrast and many Rabbis acknowledge that these things are to be referred eminently to the Messiah. AND THEY SHALL FEAR) More correctly, they shall be astonished: LXX. ἐκστήσοντα TO THE LORD AND TO HIS GOODNESS) [...] διὰ αὐτοῖς. The sense is; because of such great beneficence of God.

IN THE LATTER DAYS) In times to come. For the Hebrew באחרית הימים signifies neither more nor less than that.

Grotius, Judaizing, rashly snatches this promise away to Zerubbabel and the worship of the Jewish people after the resolution of the Babylonian captivity. The very denomination of the subject refutes this gloss. The text clearly indicates who those are who are said to be about to return: namely, the children of Israel, who, just as they were openly distinguished from the Jews in the preceding [chapters], so there is no cause why they should be taken in another sense here. For the fact that some think the Jews are indicated by this general name in this place does not agree with the speech of the Prophet, who accurately distinguished the Kingdom of Judah from the kingdom of Israel. And here he speaks of the kingdom of the ten tribes and the children of Israel. For it is not for us to mix together what the Prophet distinguished. The reason of coherence also demands this; which Brentius rightly explained: In the previous two chapters, it was declared both by signs and words that the Lord would reject carnal Israel, first by devastation through Shalmaneser: then, by blinding through Christ; but these things, however they may happen to carnal Israel, yet it was shown that the spiritual [Israel] would not fail to such an extent that it would rather come to be gathered as much from the Jews as from the Gentiles, and the number of true Israelites would become as the sand of the sea: for whose sake the Lord would be willing to hear the heaven, the earth, the grain, the wine, the oil: that is, He would be willing to affect them with every kind of benefit: And these things indeed shall happen to the true and spiritual Israelites, etc.

That this prophecy is to be understood not of Zerubbabel, but of the Messiah, these things clearly teach, besides the arguments already adduced: namely (1) The designation of the term of the return. They are said to return not into Judea, which was a bodily return, but to the Lord, which is a spiritual conversion. The term from which, therefore, is not the Babylonian captivity, but the diabolical tyranny and servitude of sin. For from this are they liberated who are converted to the Lord. But they are said to SEEK the Lord their God who, by true repentance and faith, desire and seek the grace of the Lord their God, that the Lord himself may be their God, whose grace and favor alone they desire and long to enjoy. For we lose this Lord our God through sin and turning away from God. He must therefore be sought through repentance and conversion to God; just as in Hos. 6:1 the Israelites mutually exhort one another to repentance, 'Come, let us return to the Lord,' so here they are said to be about to return through true repentance: about to return seeking the Lord: which two things explain each other: because by both modes of speaking repentance is accustomed to be designated. Compare Is. 4:6, 7. And by the phrase, THEY SHALL SEEK the Lord their God, the parts of repentance seem to be indicated: (1) acknowledgment of sin, and contrition: since the appetite and desire for the Lord comes from nowhere else than from the knowledge of evil and the anguish of the heart; just as a sick man does not seek a physician unless he feels his disease, so those who languish in soul on account of sin and the sense of divine wrath flee to the Lord, Ps. 42:1, Matt. 9:12. (2) True confidence, which lies hidden in the pronoun THEIR God, inasmuch as they rely on the grace of the Lord, and seek the same through faith, so that they may be designated as those who are about to place their confidence solely in Jehovah, the true Lord and their God.

II. The divine veneration of the Messiah. Because the faithful are said to be about to seek both the Lord their God and David their King; the same worship and the same confidence are deferred to both Jehovah and King David, because by the one and same word SEEK placed there, a double worship, religious and civil at the same time, of the first and second table, cannot be designated. Since, therefore, with the same worship and the same confidence they must pursue that King David, our Lord God, by King David is by no means understood King Zerubbabel, but the Messiah, whose type and progenitor David was, and to whom the throne of David was promised, Is. 9, 6. who alone is to be pursued with the same honor as God the Father, John 5, 19. ch. 14, 1. Which argument the blessed Luther pursues in Tom. 4. Jen. Lat. p. 508. but here observe diligently the words: They shall seek, he says, the Lord their God, and David their King. What new thing arises here? For the word of seeking in this place properly signifies internal worships, just as Psalm 69 testifies. Let not those who wait for thee, O Lord, be ashamed for my sake. Let not those who seek thee, O God of Israel, be confounded for my sake. That these worships are attributed to God no one will take unfairly, just as the Prophet here uses the true name of God (Jehovah), but here let the Jews answer, why is that worship, which is attributed to God, also attributed to King David? Shall we therefore worship many Gods? Or will God give his glory to another? For he not only says they will seek God, but promises that it will come to pass that they will also seek their King David; this is therefore a clear testimony that King David is to be sought with the same zeal and affection with which the true GOD is sought. But if this shall seem absurd and impious (for God is one God), necessity will compel the Jews to define God (Jehovah) and this King David as one and the same God. Since they are to be worshipped with the same worship. But here let them answer, who that King David is.

III. The peculiar denomination of the Messiah. For since by the name of King David, David αὐτοπροσώπως (in person) cannot be understood, and the name of David is not taken in its proper sense, it is undoubted (since he had long since yielded to fate) that the sprout and son of David, called κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence), or metaphorically, as others wish, King David the similar, whose figure David was, is to be understood. For this name is appropriated to him, since it cannot be taken of David himself. But it is nowhere attributed to Zerubbabel. Which those same places that Grotius alleges, Ezek. 34, 23. 24. 37, 24. 25. confirm, which we have shown in the annotations on Ezekiel to treat of no other than the Messiah. To which add the place in Psalm 132, 10. Turn not away the face of thine anointed for David thy servant, that is, for Christ, preserve the rule of thine anointed, Is. 55, 3. I will join with you an everlasting covenant, the sure mercies of David, in which place although the benefits promised by God to David can be understood, some nevertheless wish to understand the Messiah, even among the Jews. R. David Kimchi and among the Reformed Wolffg. Musculus (who otherwise does not easily leave room for the prophecies of the Messiah) calls David, saying, Christ, the son of David, he calls his mercies, firm and faithful, the grace, benevolence, and all that salvation which he was about to exhibit through him not only to Israel, but also to the whole world. The blessed Glassius assented in Rhetor. S. p. 415. and judges that this sense is most clearly of all evident from v. 4: Behold I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander of the people. Finally, there is added a place similar to this of ours,

Jer. 30, 8. They shall serve the Lord their God, and David their King, whom I will raise up for them: in which the Chaldean version acknowledges that the Messiah, the son of David, is designated. And so also the Targum interprets in this place: They shall obey the Messiah, the Son of David, their King. When there is speech of a temporal Prince arising from the seed of David, who is similar to David in piety and holiness of life, the name of David is not attributed to him simply, but he is said to be like David, to walk in the ways of David, etc. 1 Kings 18, 3. ch. 22, 2. Jer. 13, 13. Therefore Christians interpret of the Messiah ὁμοθυμαδὸν (with one accord), Jerome in this place, Augustine T. 4. book on the eight questions of Dulcitius q. 5. Hugo, Vatablus, Isidorus, Arias Montanus, Galatinus book 3 on the arcana of the Catholic truth, ch. 23. etc.

IV. The negation of a temporal King; for they are said to be about to seek King David, long after the kingdom was taken away, when they had sat for a long time without King and Prince. How therefore can this be taken of an earthly King, which had to happen after the earthly kingdom was clearly taken away?

V. The description of the worship of the New Testament. And they shall revere the Lord and his goodness. Vatablus explains it adjectivally as the good Lord, and understands it of Christ. But the blessed Luther explains it beautifully of the worship under the N. T.: But because the Prophet expressly adds, they shall tremble at his goodness, who does not see that this fear is more truly reverence, and an eager zeal, lest so beneficent a God be offended. Therefore the true meaning is, that in the New Testament nothing else will be preached through the Gospel than the immense goodness of God, which has been shown through Christ the Son of God, and that the remnant of Israel, as well as those scattered among the nations, will embrace this with admiration.

VI. Mention of the last days. Grotius has recently translated it as "in the times to come," and says that the Hebrew conveys nothing more. But the Septuagint interpreters, who rendered it ἐπ’ ἐχάτῳ τῶν ἡμέρων, and the Vulgate, in novissimo dierum, have without doubt grasped the sense of the Hebrew phrase more correctly. And such a phrase is accustomed to designate a specific time, not indefinitely any future time whatever: for who would doubt that things which are predicted to happen will happen in the times to come? That is understood of its own accord. Scripture, however, expresses in this way the last times in which those things are to be, whence the interpreters with great consensus understand these things to be about the last days. Furthermore, since it is said here that the Israelites will seek their King Messiah, which, if the Israelites are to be understood according to the flesh, we think has not yet been done, we judge it to be evident from this very fact that the last times are designated here. Although it must be observed that the last times are spoken of in two ways, either simply with respect to the whole universe, or in a qualified sense, with respect to a certain people, and especially the Jewish people; however, whether the prophecy is taken in that sense or in this, it is manifest that it cannot be referred to the times of Zerubbabel, which could in no way be called the last times.

As to what times this prophecy properly refers, interpreters vary greatly. Some, with the Jews mentioned by Jerome and Grotius, refer it to the restoration of the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity, such as Theodoret, Theophylact, and others, although most of them differ from Grotius in that they understand by that King David not Zerubbabel, but Christ. Others judge that its fulfillment pertains to the times of the New Testament: and indeed some of these assert that the prophecy looks toward the final times of the world, while others believe that the final times of the Jewish people are designated. Furthermore, those people do not explain themselves in the same way. For those who dream of a thousand years of earthly happiness after, I know not what, particular resurrection of the dead, such as Piscator, Alsted, and Bisterfeld, drag this prophecy off to that as well. Others, having exploded this Chiliastic error, nevertheless promise some happiness to the Jews toward the final times of the world (namely, that they are to be converted to the Church of Christ in great and remarkable numbers in their own time before the last day, concerning which they also wish Hosea to prophesy in this place). Which opinion concerning the future conversion of the Jews most people cherish only as probable, but others defend it ἀποτόμως, and among these especially D. Calixtus, tract. de supremo judicio, de signis ante diem extremum pag. 30. Concerning the great conversion of the Jewish people, which I mentioned, he also treats Hosea the Prophet, ch. 3. Calixtus also brings forward in support of this opinion Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, Rupert of Deutz, Nicholas of Lyra, Paul of Burgos, likewise Augustine, book 18 of The City of God, ch. 28, and Julianus Pomerius of Toledo in book 1 against the Jews. Modern Hebrew commentators observe that this passage is to be interpreted concerning the servitude also to which they were so long subject, and the liberation which they hope for in these last times from the dignity of the Messiah. Solomon Jarchi indeed does so more obscurely, but Aben-Ezra and David Kimchi do so fully and clearly; nay, that some Jews even in the time of Jerome, or before him, applied this prophecy to the future time, as noted in this place. by Jerome: but the commentaries of the Jews are by no means to be heeded here, for they dream of some general conversion of their nation, not to Christ, whom they reject, but from the sins by which they imagine the coming of the Messiah is hindered, and of a liberation from their present dispersion and captivity through their Messiah, whom they hope for: concerning which see Menasseh Ben Israel, book 3 on the resurrection, ch. 3. And indeed it is most true that if the Israelites had seriously repented of their deeds, the coming of the Messiah would not have been delayed; but now, because they lie deeply immersed and remain fixed in their vices and sins, hence it is that their blessedness is deferred until the end of days, according to Hosea ch. 3, 18. Nay, they even imagine that the ten tribes still survive, and that they will be converted in the time of their Messiah, whom they await, which is in the Mishnah, Sanhedrin ch. 11, s. 31. R. Eliezer seems to have indicated this: As the day is darkened and illuminated, so for the ten tribes, for whom there is now darkness, it will come to pass that it will shine for them. Thus R. Aben-Ezra on Isaiah 11, 12, 13, understands by Israel the ten tribes distinct from the tribe of Judah, and says that they will likewise return to their lands. The trifles of Benjamin of Tudela concerning the Israelites beyond the Caspian Sea are unworthy of being cited. It is no wonder that Lyra and Burgensis were perplexed as to the opinions of the Jews. But in Jerome, Augustine, and Cyril, almost nothing certain is held concerning the conversion of the Jews: for they speak of it in various ways. Origen himself seizes upon the τὸ ἐπέχειν [suspension of judgment] in his Commentary on Romans 11. Who this 'all Israel' is that will be saved, and what this 'fullness of the Gentiles' will be, only one knows, and his only-begotten Son. There is no reason, therefore, for Calixtus to boast of the consensus of the Fathers here. The contrary opinion is in Augustine, Ep. 59; Jerome on ch. 11 of Isaiah; as also in Caesarius in Nazianzen. Voetius attributes [this] to Dial. 4, although he himself still expects a notable conversion of the Jews, Disp. select. part 2, p. 126. Calixtus could have more rightly praised the Papists, especially the more recent ones, Cornelius à Lapide, Mariana, and most others, who here with great effort perform great trifles. At the end of the world, toward the coming of the Antichrist (that Utopian one, whom they have invented will come from the tribe of Dan), especially after he is slain, the Israelites and Jews who adhered to him while he was living and reigning, partly mindful of the sermons and miracles of Elijah and Enoch, and partly by the exhortation of other preachers, will be converted to Christ, as Cornelius Lapideus has it in this place. Nor would followers have been lacking in the school of Calvin, such as those whom Voetius praises in the place cited, and Hornbeck, De convinc. Jud. p. 35, Hottinger, Thes. Phil. p. 9, to whom, however, Calvin himself, Marloratus, and Hyperius are opposed, as is also Wollebius in his Compendium. Theology, who do not admit that such a general conversion of the Jews is still to be expected, nor do Bullinger, Zwingli, and Hemmingius hold it as certain; and there occur among the Calvinists not a few other things here which even Calixtus himself would not have approved: such as the Chiliastic error of Alsted and his associates, the fiction of Brightman concerning the assault of the Antichrist, as also of the Turks by the newly converted Jews, and the total extirpation of the Turkish empire. The opinion of Forbes, book 4 of his Inst. Historico-Theol. ch. 33, concerning the conversion of the Jews and at the same time the Mahometans after the Roman idolatry has been exploded and the Antichrist reduced to order. The conjecture of Lambert Daneau, which he brings forward at the end of his commentary on Augustine's De haeresibus, that perhaps the Jews are not to be gathered into the Christians, but the Church is to be transferred from the Christians to the Jews. Archer and Godwin, the English Independents, as also Batroveus, citing Robert Baillie in his Oper. Histor. & Chronol. book 2, p. 247, not only bring Christ down from heaven and bind the resurrection of the martyrs to 1,000 years before the end of the world, but also send Gog and Magog with their army against Christ in the midst of the saints. Piscator says that the martyrs will rise again and ascend into heaven, so that they may reign there with Christ, etc. But the arguments which Calixtus draws from our text for that purpose prove nothing other than that the discourse here is not about the state of the Jews under the Babylonian captivity, which we readily admit: although indeed some of our own, Brentius in his Commentary on this place, Flacius in his gloss, Dr. Aegidius Hunnius, Dr. Georg Mylius, Winckelm, Balthasar Mentzer in his Analysis of Romans 11, Tom. 1, Disp. Giess. § 60, Dr. Gesner and Balduinus on Romans 11, Dr. Meisner in his Commentary on Hosea 3, Haffenreffer in Templ. Ezech. p. 313. those now among the saints, from the apostolic passage especially in Romans 11, 25, 26, 27, think that toward the end of the world some notable conversion of the Jews will take place; yet most others, for reasons not light, do not agree, B. Luther himself, Tom. 8, Jen. Germ. fol. 110, Phil. Melanchthon, Osiander, Dr. Daniel Cramer on the Kingdom of Christ, part 2, ch. 4, q. 6, B. Hoe in his commentary on the Apocalypse, Tom. 2, p. 605, B. Pappus in his commentary on Hosea 3, Dr. Brochmand in System. quaest. 13, De extr. Judic., Dr. Joh. Cluver on Romans 11, the Weimar Paraphrast on Romans 11, B. Jac. Weller in his commentary on Romans 11, B. Dn. Dr. Hülsemann, B. Dn. Dr. Georg Grossshain in his Diatribe on the Catholic conversion of the Jews, etc. B. Wigandus in his commentary on this place has it thus: 'IN THE LAST OF DAYS' signifies the time of the manifestation of Christ. For he teaches that those things will not happen so quickly, but that God will observe a predetermined time. Although this phrase also refers to those things which were promised, namely, that they would be without King and Priest. For both were undermined when Christ appeared. B. Winckelmannus on this passage IN THE LATTER DAYS, i.e., after the advent of the Messiah. That whole time from the advent of the Messiah is called the latter time, the end of the age, the final hour. Therefore, these things pertain to the consolation of the pious in the ten tribes, although they were few. The blessed Lord Doctor Pappus discusses this prophecy and others like it in his commentary on this passage as follows: In the beginning, we deny that when it is said among the Prophets that something will be in the latter days, it must be referred to the final advent of CHRIST or His return for the universal judgment. And we contend that it can be clearly shown that all those passages which mention the latter days among the Prophets are to be understood concerning the first advent of Christ, and were fulfilled in it. Unless, therefore, a necessary cause is brought forward why we should follow another interpretation in this place: we shall also maintain this Prophecy, that there are also some things among the Prophets concerning the end of the world and the times preceding the end of the world: But we deny this, that those predictions are marked by the note of the last times: for the reason that that whole time, which is from the birth of the Lord and the manifestation of the Messiah until the end of the world, is the latter time to the Prophets. We say, therefore, that this Prophecy was fulfilled at the very beginning of the New Testament; when many thousands

of the Jews were converted to Christ, as the whole history of the Acts of the Apostles teaches, and especially the twenty-first chapter: where not only Paul narrates how great things God has done among the Gentiles through his ministry: but James also and the other elders of Jerusalem admonish Paul that thousands of the Jews have believed. And with a few words interposed, he continues thus: But as for that question concerning the universal conversion of the Jews who are to survive before the last day, I judge it to be a fiction of the same sort as that concerning the Anti-Christ, who is to arise from the stock and tribe of Dan, and to reign for three years and a half. It is not indeed for us to deny repentance to any man, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles, but neither is it for us to invent a story about the universal conversion of any nation, which the Holy Scriptures have not predicted. For that passage to the Romans, if it is looked into more deeply, not only does not confirm this opinion for which it is brought forward, but clearly even overturns it, Rom. 11:25. For in this lies that great mystery, which Paul also preaches in other Epistles: That all Israel which is to be saved consists of the remnant of the Jews and the fullness of the Gentiles: nor does Paul affirm that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, others from carnal Israel are still to be enlightened; but he announces that immediately after the fullness of the Gentiles, all Israel will be saved: that is, according to the doctrine of the 9th and also of this 11th chapter, that the spiritual Israel is to be considered, and its gathering from Jews and Gentiles. To the same effect is the fact that in the very prediction of our Prophet, not only is the return of the children of Israel predicted, but also the duration of that Church, which duration cannot be understood as the end of the world. Thus Dn. D. Pappus.

From which review of opinions it is manifest that D. Calixtus had no cause to argue against our B. Hülsemann, because in this question concerning the conversion of the Jews he made a divorce from his teachers B. Rungius and B. Hutterus, to whom our o̔ μακαρίτης [blessed one] replied thus in his Calixtinische Gewissens-Wurm, ch. 8, p. 1173: If Calixtus had indicated the future conversion of some, and indeed a considerable number of Jews, as probable, as Dd. Rungius and Hutterus do, he would not be to blame for that; only that he (1.) extended the conversion of the Jews in such a way as a divine and indubitable sign, which should precede the approaching last day and be believed, (2.) that as one now says of Germany: All Germany has accepted the Christian faith, so one should also say of the whole Jewish people before the last day: All Israel has been saved (as he indeed extends it once more), that D. Hülsemann censures as inconsistent with the Word of God and all orthodox teachers, including D. Rungius and Hutterus. To which also B. Dn. D. Wellerus inclines, in Commentar. ad Rom. XI, p. 644. The Apostle indicates that some from the Jews are to be converted perpetually, and that all Israel, i.e., the son of promise, is at some time to receive the inheritance together with the Gentiles. That Jews were baptized in great numbers at different times and enrolled in the college of the Church, Osiander testifies, cent. 5, lib. 1, cap. 24; cent. 6, lib. 4, cap. 4 & 5, pp. 244, 245; cent. 7, lib. 2, cap. 7, p. 95. We do not deny (which, however, cannot be proven demonstratively from this passage, but is known to God alone) that it may still happen, by the singular mercy of God, that some notable number of Jews may come to the kingdom of the Messiah before his glorious return, for which we pray with all our heart that it may certainly come to pass. B. Gerhard had anticipated this moderation in LL. CC. T. IX, p. 111. What kind and how great precisely the conversion of the Jews will be, before the fulfillment of this oracle, cannot be known demonstratively. Which is far safer than the rashness of Balthasar Willius in his commentary on Zach. ch. 14:5, p. 515, defining the conversion of the Jews as more certain than certain under the Philadelphian period (he invents for himself wonderful dreams about periods from a distortion of the Apocalypse, ch. 2 & 3), to happen not long after these (our) times. But these things are by occasion of our Prophetic passage; we shall discuss these more fully, if it seems good to God, at Rom. 11:25; where Grotius proposed a new interpretation of the Apostolic oracle, no less clearly different from that which he himself delivered in his book 2 de Verit. Relig. Christ. sect. VIII, than from the interpretations of others.

But if you ask, what then is the meaning of the Prophetic oracle concerning the conversion of the Israelites to the Lord; the explanation of our B. Luther in his commentary on this passage seems the simplest (from which the interpretations of Wigand, Winckelmann, and Pappus, nor the paraphrases of Osiander or the Vinarieans, are not alien): The people of Israel remained disseminated among the Gentiles until the Gospel had been published among the Gentiles by the Apostles; finally they began to be converted and to seek the Lord their God and David their King. And in the marginal gloss: Israel did not come to the king again after the captivity, until the true David, Christ, came, the King of all the world. Voëtius certainly, although he is industrious in asserting the general conversion of the Jews, denies himself in the cited place, p. 133, that the ten tribes are to be converted in the same way, if the discourse is about the tribes considered under the species and form of that nation, both ecclesiastically and politically: and he observes that the men of those tribes can be distributed into three classes. 1. Of those who, through wars from the time of Jeroboam up to the Assyrian captivity, sought other seats, partly among neighboring nations, partly in Judea (of whom those either joined themselves to Jewish synagogues erected in the lands of the Gentiles, and thus were incorporated into the Church and the Jewish people; or were mixed with the Gentiles, coalesced with them, and degenerated into them: the latter in the land of the Jews coalesced with the body of the Church and the Jewish people, not only before the Babylonian captivity, 1 Kings 11:20, 21, 23; 2 Chron. 2:13, 14 & 15:9 & 30:11; Luke 2; Philipp. 3, 5. collated with Rom. 9. 2. but also after the return from captivity, Ezra 1, 5. & 4, 1. 2. Of those who, through the Assyrian captivity and the invasions preceding it, were transported into the lands of the Gentiles, 2. Kings 17. All of whom must be said, partly to have degenerated into Gentiles; partly to have joined themselves there to Jewish Synagogues and διασποραῖς (James 1. verse 1.) and to have united with them; partly to have returned into the land of the Jews, when the Jews returned from Babylon, and from the neighboring nations the Ammonites, Moabites, &c. partly to have returned into the land of the ten tribes, and to have united with the Cutheans or Samaritans. 3. Of those who, at the time of the Assyrian deportation, were left in the land of the ten tribes, and united with the colonies of the Gentiles brought there, or at least were intermixed, 2. Kings 17. From which distribution it is evident that the descendants of those Israelites, if any are converted, or are to be converted, are not converted by a general conversion (such as that of the Jews) nor as Jews or Israelites, constituting a nation apart; but partly as these or those Gentiles, with whom they united, or into whom they degenerated, partly as Jews, partly as Samaritans. To these, therefore, since the Israelites are to return, there is no doubt that, with the Gentiles, Jews, and Samaritans converted at the time of the New Testament, very many from the Israelites (or ten tribes) That those who had long sat without a King, had been converted to King David the Messiah.

that it could have come into the mind of a sane person, we are utterly amazed. They ought to have been mindful of what Calvin, their common master, warned elsewhere, but not in the place of Hos. 4:2: We must always look to this, that we do not flutter in the air. Subtle speculations please at first glance, but afterwards they vanish.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

POSTHÆC) Ubi diu vixerint in illo statu, privat regno, templo, sacrificiis, & idololatriæ, ob idololatrarum in se sævitiam pertæsi. ET QVÆRENT DOMINUM DEUM SUUM Id est, & ad Deum se applicabunt. Ita בקש recte pe προσκοπᾶσι vertitur Lev. 19, 31. ET DAVID REGEM SUUM) Adhærebunt Zo robabeli, qui erit ex familia Davidis, & propterea David ap pellabitur, ut omnes ex Jacobo, Israël Ezech. 34, 23. a Messiam eminenter hæc referenda agnoscunt paraphrast Chaldæus, & Rabbini multi. ET PAVEBUNT) Rectius, stupebunt: LXX. ἐκστήσοντα AD DOMINUM ET AD BONUM EJUS) […] διὰ αὐτοῖς. Sensus est; ob tantam Dei beneficentiam.

IN NOVISSIMO DIERUM) In post venturis tem- poribus. Id enim nec quicquam amplius significant He- bræa באחרית הימים.

Temere hanc promissionem ad Zorobabelem & cultum populi Judaici, post solutionem captivitatis Babylonicæ abripit Judaizans Grotius. Glossam hanc refellit ipsa subjecti denominatio. Quinam illi sint, qui reversuri dicuntur, textus luculenter in- dicat: nimirum filii Israël, qui uti in superioribus aperte discernebantur à Judæis, ita nulla causa est, cur hic alio sensu accip antur. Quod enim nonnul- li putant Judæos hoc generali nomine hoc loco in- digitari, non convenit orationi Prophetæ, qui ac- curate distinxit Regnum Juda à regno Israëlis. Et hic de regno decem tribuum & filiis Israël loquitur. Quæ enim Prophetâ distinxit, nostrum non est commiscere. Poscit id etiam cohærentiæ ratio; quam recte exposuit Brentius: In prioribus duobus capitibus, & signis & verbis declaratum est, Domi- num rejecturum Israëlem carnalem, primum deva- statione per Salmanassar: deinde, excæcatione per Christum; sed hæc, utcunque carnali Israëli accidant, tamen ostensum est, spiritualem, usque adeo non defecturum, ut potius colligendus veniat tam ex Judæis, quam ex gentibus, & fiat numerus vero- rum Israëvitarum sicut arena maris: propter quos Dominus exaudire velit cœlum, terram, triticum, vinum, oleum: hoc est, velit eos omni genere be- neficiorum afficere: Et hæc quidem veris & spiri- tualibus Israëvitis contingent &c.

Non autem de Zorobabele, sed de Messia hoc vaticinium accipiendum esse, præter argumenta jam adducta, hæc luculenter docent: utpote (1) Termini reditus designatio. Non redituri dicuntur in Judæam, quæ corporalis fuit reversio, sed ad Do- minum, quæ conversio est spiritualis. Terminus ergo à quo est non Babylonica captivitas, sed Dia- bolica tyrannis, & peccati servitus. Ab hac enim li- berantur, qui ad Dominum convertuntur. QUÆ- RERE autem Dominum Deum suum dicuntur, qui vera pœnitentia, & fide Domini Dei sui gratiam desiderant, & ambiunt, ut ipse Dominus sit Deus ipforum, cujus unius gratia, & favore frui discupi- unt, & exoptant. Hunc enim Dominum Deum nostrum amittimus per peccatum, & aversionem à Deo. Quærendus ergo est per pœniteneiam, & conversionem ad Deum; quemadmodum Hos. 6, 1. mutuo se exhortantur Israëlitæ ad pœnitentiam, venite, revertamur ad Dominum, ita hic reversuri dicuntur per veram pœnitentiam: reversuri quæ- rentes Dominum: quæ duo sese explicant: Quia utroque loquendi modo pœnitentia designari so- let. Confer Es. 4, 6.7. Et indigitari videntur phra- si, QUÆRENT Dominum Deum suum, partes pœnitentiæ (1) peccati agnitio, ac contritio: Siqui- dem appetitus, & desiderium Domini non aliun- de sit, quam ex mali notitia, & cordis angustia; sicut ægrotus Medicum non quærit, nisi cum morbum sentit, sic qui languent animo ob peccatum, & iræ divinæ sensum, ad Dominum confugiunt, Ps. 42, 1. Matth. 9, 12. (2) Vera fiducia, quæ in pronomine Deum SUUM latet, siquidem Domini gratia ni- tantur, eandemque per fidem ambiant, ut in Je- hovam verum Dominum ac Deum suum unice fiduciam collocaturi designentur.

II. Divina Messiæ veneratio. Quia & Dominum Deum suum, & Regem David quæsituri dicuntur fi- deles; idem cultus, eadem fiducia & Jehovæ & Re- gi David defertur, quia una eademque voce posita QUÆRERE non potest cultus geminus, religio- sus simul & civilis, primæ & secundæ tabulæ designa- ri. Quum ergo eodem cultu, eadem fiducia prose- quendus sit Rex ille David, Dominus Deus noster, nequaquam Rex Zorobabel per Regem David in- telligitur, sed Messias, cujus typus & progenitor David fuit, & cui thronus Davidis promissus erat, Es. 9, 6. qui solus eodem honore cum Deo Patre prosequendus est, Ioh. 5, 19. cap. 14, 1. Quod argu- mentum exequitur B. Lutherus Tom. 4. Jen. Lat. p. 508. sed hic observa diligenter verba: Quærent, inquit, Dominum Deum suum, & Regem suum David. Quid hic novi oritur? Nam verbum quæ- rendi hoc in loco proprie significat internos cultus, sic- ut testatur Psal. 69. Non erubescant propter me, qui te exspectant Domine. Non confundantur propter me, qui te quærunt, DEUS Israël. Hos cultus Deo tribui nemo inique feret, sicut Propheta hic utitur vero Dei nomine (Iehova) sed hic re- spondeant Judæi, cur is cultus, qui Deo tribuitur, etiam tribuitur Regi David? Num igitur colemus plures Deos? Aut Deus dabit gloriam suam alteri? Non solum enim dicit Deum quærent, sed promittit futurum, ut etiam quærant Regem suum David, cla- rum igitur hoc testimonium est, eodem studio & af- fectu Regem David quærendum, quo verus DEUS quæritur. Hoc autem si absurdum & impium videbi- tur (Deus enim Deus unus est) coget Judæos neces- sitas, ut definiant Deum (Jehova) & hunc Regem David esse unum & eundem Deum. Siquidem eo- dem cultu sunt colendi. Sed hic respondeant, quis ille Rex David sit.

III. Peculiaris Messiæ denominatio. Nam cum Re- gis Davidis nomine intelligi David αὐτοπροσώπως nequeat, ac proprio sensu Davidis nomen non acci- pi, indubium sit, (qui jam pridem fatis concesserat) metonymice germen & filius Davidis κατ' ἐξοχὴν dictus, vel metaphorice, quod alii volunt, Rex David similis, cujus figura David fuit, intelligendus est, Huic enim illud nomen, cum de ipso Davide non potest accipi, appropriatur. Nuspiam autem Zoro- babeli tribuitur. Quod eadem illa loca, quæ Gro- tius allegat, Ezech. 34, 23. 24. 37, 24. 25. confir- mant, quæ non de alio, quam Messia agere, in an- not. ad Ezech. ostendimus. Quibus adde locum Psal. 132, 10. Non avertas faciem uncti tui propter David servum tuum, id est, propter Christum, conserva regimen uncti tui, Es. 55, 3. Jungam vobis- cum fœdus perpetuum, benignitates Davidis certif- fimas, quo loco etsi intelligi possint beneficia Davi- di à Deo promissa, nonnulli tamen Messiam intel- ligit volunt, etiam è Judæis. R. David Kimchi & è Reformatis Wolffg. Musculus (qui alias non facile in vaticiniis Messiæ locum relinquit) Davidem, in- quiens, vocat Christum, Davidis filium, misericor- dias illius, firmas & fideles, gratiam, benevolentiam, ac omnem eam salutem vocat, quam erat per illum non Israëlï modo, sed etiam toti orbi exhibiturus. An- nuit B. Glassius in Rhetor. S. p. 415. & clarissime o- mnium hunc sensum ex v. 4. patere arbitratur: En testem populorum dedi eum ducem & præceptorem populi. Accedit denique locus huic nostro similis,

Ier. 30, 8. Servient Domino Deo suo, & David Regi suo, quem suscitabo illis: in quo Chaldaica versio Messiam filium Davidis designari agnoscit. Atq; ita etiam interpretatur Targum h. l. Obedient Messiæ, Filio David, Regi suo. Cum de Principe temporali è semine David oriundo sermo est, qui Davidi si- milis sit pietate, ac vitæ sanctimonia, non tribuitur ipsi nomen Davidis simpliciter, sed esse dicitur sicut David, ambulare in viis David, &c. 1. Reg. 18, 3. cap. 22, 2. Ier. 13, 13. De Messia itaq; interpretantur Christiani ὁμοθυμαδὸν, Hieron. in h. l. August. T. 4. lib. de octo Dulcitii quæst. q. 5. Hugo, Vatablus, Isi- dorus, Arias Montanus, Galatinus lib. 3. de arcan. Cath. verit. cap. 23. &c.

IV. Regis temporalis negatio; dicuntur enim quæ- situri Regem David, longe post ablatum regnum, ubi diu absq; Rege atq; Principe sederant. Quomodo ergo de Rege terreno hoc accipi potest, quod eve- nire debuit post ablatum plane regnum terrenum?

V. Cultus Novi Testamenti descriptio. Et reve- rebuntur Dominum & bonitatem ejus. Vatablus ad- jective exponit bonum Dominum, & de Christo in- telligit. B. Luth. vero pulchre de cultu sub N. T. explicat: Quia autem Propheta diserte addit, pave- bunt à bonitate ejus, quis non videt, pavorem hunc verius reverentiam esse, & acre studium, ne tam be- neficus Deus offendatur. Ergo vera sententia est, quod in N. Testamento per Evangelium prædicabitur aliud nihil, quam immensa Dei bonitas, quæ per Chri- stum Filium Dei ostensa est, & quod hunc cum admi- ratione amplexuræ sint reliquiæ Israël, tum inter gen- tes sparsæ.

VI. Dierum novissimorum mentio. Grotius no- viter vertit in postventuris temporibus, nec quic- quam amplius Ebræa inferre, ait. Sed rectius sine dubio assequuti sunt sensum Ebrææ phraseos LXX. Interpp. qui reddidere ἐπ’ ἐχάτῳ τῶν ἡμέρων, & Vulgatus in novissimo dierũ. Et designari tali phrasi solet certum tempus, non indefinite quodcunq; fu- turũ tempus: nam quæ eventura prædicuntur, ec- quis ambigat postventuris temporibus eventura. Id ultro intelligitur. Exprimit autem ita Scriptura tempora novissima, quibus illa futura sint, unde In- terpp. magno consensu de novissimis diebus hæc in- telligunt. Porro quum hic dicantur Israëlitæ Mes- siam Regem suum quæsituri, quod ab ipsis, si Israe- litæ secundum carnem intelligendi sint, nondum fa- ctum putant, vel ex eo constare arbitramur, tempo- ra novissima hic designata esse. Quanquam obser- vandum sit, novissima tempora duobus modis dici, vel simpliciter respectu totius universi, vel secundum quid, respectu certi populi, & imprimis populi Judai- ci. Cæterum sive isto, sive hoc sensu vaticinium ac- cipiatur, manifestum est, ad tempora Zorobabelis id referri non posse, quæ nullo pacto novissima di- ci potuere.

Ad quænam vero tempora hoc vaticinium pro- prię spectet, de eo valde variant interpretes. Non- nulli cum Judæis apud Hieron. & Grotio, id refe- runt ad reductionem populi Judaici è captivitate Babylonica, utpote Theodoretus, Theophylactus, & alii, etsi in eo à Grotio pleriq; abeant, quod per Re- gem illum David non Zorobabel intelligant, sed Christum. Alii complementum ad tempora N. T. spectare censent: & horum quidem nonnulli ad novissima mundi tempora vaticinium respicere au- tumāt, nonnulli vero novissima Judaici populi tem- pora designari credunt. Illi porro non eodem mo- do sese explicant. Nam qui mille annos felicitatis terrenæ, post, nescio quam, particularem resurre- ctionē mortuorum somniant, utpote Piscator, Al- stedius, Bisterfeldius, hoc etiam vaticinium eo abri- piunt. Alii Chiliastico hoc errore exploso, aliquam tamen felicitatem Judæis pollicentur sub extrema mundi tempora (quod scil. magna & insigni fre- quentia ipsi ante novissimum diem suo tempore ad Ecclesiam Christi convertendi sint, de qua e- tiam hic loci Hoseam vaticinari volunt.) Quam vero sententiam de futura Judæorum conversio- ne plerique ceu probabilem solum fovent, alii ve- ro ἀποτόμως tuentur, & inter hos imprimis D. Calixtus tractat. de supremo judicio, de si- gnis ante diem extremum pag. 30. De magna, quam dixi, populi Iudaici conversione agit quoque Hoseas Propheta c. 3. In quam sententiam adducit etiam Calixtus Hieronymum, Cyrillum Alex. Rupertum Tuitiensem, Nicolaum Lyranum, Paulum Burgensem, item Augustinum l. 18. de civ. Dei c. 28 & Julianum Pomerium Toletanum libro 1. contra Judæos, De servitute etiam, cui tam diu obnoxii fuerunt, & liberatione, quam ultimis hisce temporibus à Messiæ dignitate sperant, interpretari hunc locum hodiernos Ebræos, commentatores observant. Salomonem quidem Jarchiadum obscurius, at Aben-Ezra & David Kimchi plene & perspicue, imo in futurum tempus Judæos quoq; nonnullos tempore Hieronymi, vel ante ipsum, hoc vaticinium detulisse, notante in h. l. Hieronymo: sed Judæorum commenta hic curanda minime sunt, somniant enim illi generalem aliquam conversionem gentis suæ, non ad Christum, quem reprobant, sed a peccatis, quibus impeditum fingunt adventum Messiæ, & liberationem à præsenti dispersione ac captivitate per Messiam suum, quẽ sperant: de quo Menasse Ben Israel lib. 3. de resurrect. cap. 3. Et profecto verissimum est, si Israëlitæ serio factorum suorum pœnitentiam egissent, Messiæ adventus non fuisset procrastinatus, at nunc, quia profunde immersi jacent, hærentq; defixi in vitiis & peccatis suis, hinc est, quod differatur beatitudo illorum usque ad finem dierum juxta Oseam c. 3, 18. Imo fingunt etiam decem tribus adhuc superesse, easdemque conversum iri tempore sui, quem exspectant, Messiæ, quod in Mischnajoth Sanhedrim cap. 11, s. 31. R. Eliezer hisce indicasse videtur: Sicut dies obtenebratur & illuminatur, ita decem tribus, quibus nunc caligo est, futurum est, ut luceat ipsis. Ita R. Aben-Ezra Es. 11, 12. 13. per Israel intelligit decem tribus distinctas à Judæ tribu, easq; pariter reversuras dicit in terras suas. Benjam. Tudelensis nugæ de Israëlitis ultra mare Caspium, indignæ sunt, quæ referantur. Lyrano & Burgensi hæsisse quid de Judæorum opinionibus non mirum. Penes Hieronymum vero, Augustinum & Cyrillum nihil fere certi habetur de Judæorum conversione: nam varie de illa loquuntur. Origenes ipse τὸ ἐπέχειν arripit in Commentar. in Rom. 11. Quis sit iste omnis Israel, qui salvus fiet, & quæ erit ista plenitudo etiam gentium, unus solus novit, & unigenitus ejus. Non est ergo, quod Patrum consensum hic jactitet Calixtus. Contrariam sententiam Augustino Ep. 59. Hieronymo in c. 11. Es. ut & Cæsario apud Nazianz. Dial. 4. tribuit Voëtius, etsi Judæorum insignem conversionem ipse etiamnum exspectet, Disp. select. part. 2. p. 126. Pontificios rectius laudare poterat Calixtus, imprimis recentiores Corn. à Lapide, Marianam, & plerosque alios, qui hic magno conatu magnas nugas agunt. In fine mundi, sub adventum Antichristi (Utopici illius, quem è tribu Dan venturum commenti sunt) maxime post eum occisum, Israëlitas & Judæos, qui ei viventi & regnanti adhæserunt, partim memores concionum & miraculorum Eliæ & Enochi, partim aliorum concionatorum exhortatione conversum iri ad Christum, ut habet Corn. Lapideus in h. l. Neq; in Calvini schola defuissent asseclæ, quales plurimos laudat Voëtius l. c. & Hornbeck de convinc. Jud. p. 35. Hottinger. Thes. Phil. p. 9. quibus tamen reluctatur Calvinus ipse, Marloratus, Hyperius, ut & Wollebius in Compend. Theol. qui ejusmodi generalem conversionem Judæorum adhuc expectandam esse, non admittunt, neque pro certa eam habent Bullinger, Zvinglius, Hemmingius, & occurrunt penes Calvinianos non paucoshic alia, quæ nec ipse Calixtus probasset: ut pote Alstedii, & sociorum Chiliasticus error, Brigthmanni commentum de oppugnatione Antichristi, ut & Turcarum per Judæos noviter conversos, & imperii Turcici totali extirpatione. Forbesii lib. 4. Inst. Historico- Theol. cap. 33. opinio de conversione Judæorum si- mul & Mahomedistarum post explosam idolola- triam Romanam, & Antichristum in ordinem re- dactum. Lamberti Danæi conjectura, quam in fi- ne comment. ad August. de hæresibus, adfert, quod forte non Christianos aggregandi sint Judæi, sed Ecclesia à Christianis transferenda ad Judæos. Ar- cherus, & Godvinus, Angeli independentes, ut & Ba- troveus citante Rob. Bailio, in oper. Histor. & Chronol. l. 2. p. 247. non tantum Christum de cœ- lo deducunt, & resurrectionem Martyrum 1000. annis ante mundi finem adstringunt, sed &Gog & Magog cum suo exercitu contra Christum in me- dio sanctorum immittunt. Piscator Martyres resur- recturos, in cœlum ascensuros dicit, ut ibi cum Christo regnent, &c.
