For this ἐκθέσει (exposition), the following arguments may be observed; the first from the explicit mention of the third day. For one must not depart from the literal meaning unless necessity urges. Since, therefore, the third day is here expressly commemorated for the future resuscitation, one must not understand an indefinite short time, but rather one must adhere to and acquiesce in the definition of the Holy Spirit Himself, who did not without cause express the third day. He did not express the day without mystery, by the mention of the third day, which even the Jews themselves understood, and therefore, as we have seen, they anxiously sought various things which they might adapt to the third day. Why, therefore, should we rashly abandon the designation made by the Holy Spirit, rather than believe that the third day of Christ's resurrection is defined? To which one alone this commemoration of the third day aptly corresponds. Certainly, the interpreters could bring forward no other three-day period, no third day of resuscitation, that fits. Cyril, indeed, in book 1 on John, chapter 26, interpreted the third day otherwise: namely, concerning the last times, but he understood it nevertheless concerning Christ: God healed us again on the third day, having been struck by corruption and death, that is, not in the first, nor in the middle, but in the last times, because, having been made man for our sake, He raised up and healed the whole nature in Himself. The last times, therefore, are signified by the appellation of the third day. But this indefinite signification does not agree with the definite number of the third day, nor does it have a foundation in Scripture, and therefore the third day is to be understood properly, as it sounds.

The second from the distinct commemoration of the two days. Lest it be ambiguous that the third day is designated precisely, the Prophet wished to express it in two distinct ways. For there is no doubt that these words are an epexegesis: He will revive us after two days and on the third day He will raise us up. What need would there have been to express the third day so specifically and distinctly if not the third day, but a short interval of time, were being signified indefinitely? Blessed Luther also notes something mysterious in that commemoration of the two days, Vol. 4, Jena. There is no need to inquire anxiously why it is not enough for the Prophet to have said: 'He will make us rise on the third day,' but he also adds about the two days: 'After two days he will revive us.' For although it could be said that the third day and after two days are the same thing, or at least that the two days are included in the third day, yet nothing prevents, since these two articles of our faith are distinct, 'He descended into hell' and 'He rose again on the third day,' from transferring what he says about the two days to the descent into hell: for it must be believed that this descent was something other than that he was buried.

The third is from the comparison of the Apostolic passage. For the Apostle teaches clearly in 1 Cor. 15:4 that Christ rose again on the third day according to the Scripture. Since, therefore, this is nowhere expressly predicted in the Scriptures concerning the THIRD DAY, unless this passage is admitted, we cannot doubt that he referred to this passage, where mention of the future resurrection on the third day expressly occurs, and thus this passage is to be understood concerning the resurrection of Christ which took place on the third day. For Jonah's three days in the belly of the whale was only a type, albeit an illustrious one, not an express prophecy.

The fourth is from the meritorious vivification of Christ. For truly Christ on the third day (of his resurrection) raised and vivified us by reason of merit, and being recalled to life, he restored us to life. Concerning which Eph. 2:6: 'He has made us alive together with Christ, and raised us up together, and made us sit in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.' And 1 Cor. 15:22: 'As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.' For Christ was not the only one vivified and raised. We have all been vivified and raised in Christ. The resurrection of Christ is our resurrection: the life of Christ is our life. 'I live,' says Christ, 'and you shall live,' John 14. Which argument, along with the previous ones, the blessed Luther urges no less solidly than elegantly in this place. He adds the time, 'After two days he will revive us, and on the third day he will raise us up.' How, or why? Surely so that we may live before his face, that is, in the life in which he himself lives. These things, when diligently weighed, prove that the Prophet speaks clearly about the resurrection of Christ, and that this is the passage which Paul hints at in 1 Cor. 15, where he says: 'Christ rose again on the third day, according to the Scripture.' For it can be urged not only because he says 'after two days' and 'on the third day,' but because he adds: 'The Lord will revive us and we shall live before him.' These things can only be referred to the resurrection of our flesh and eternal life. But you will say, 'He does not speak of the resurrection of Christ, or his return to eternal life, but of ours. For he says, "He will revive us after two days," etc.' I answer: this very thing is most worthy of observation. For he shows in this way the fruit of the resurrection of Christ. For Christ alone is the one who was vivified after two days and rose again from the dead on the third day. But the Prophet shows that the fruit of this resurrection pertains to us as well. And so he makes Christ's life our life and his resurrection our resurrection, just as the Apostles are also accustomed to do. Paul in Col. 3 says we are dead, and our life is hidden with Christ in God. In chapter 15 of the first to the Corinthians, he says: 'If Christ is preached that he rose from the dead, how do some say that there is no resurrection of the dead?' Likewise, 'Christ has risen, and has become the firstfruits of those who sleep. For since by one man came death, and by one man came the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so all shall be made alive through Christ.' These sentences show that this is the fruit of the resurrection of Christ: that we also may rise and live. Therefore the Prophet rightly changes the persons. For it should have been said: 'Christ will be vivified after two days, and will rise again on the third day,' just as Peter says: 'being put to death in the flesh, but made alive by the Spirit.' For it so happened that Christ rose again on the third day. But the Prophet says: 'We are to be vivified after two days, and on the third day, on which Christ rose, we are to rise.' And that for this reason: Because we, having been plunged into death by sin, were to remain in death forever, the Son of God transferred our sins onto himself, and made satisfaction for them on the cross, and afterwards rising again, he conquered the death which he had undergone for us. And so we began to rise and live when Christ rose again. For through him our death was overcome, and the life which we had lost was restored. But diligent effort was to be taken that we might apply the resurrection of Christ to ourselves in this way, so that when you hear that Christ rose again on the third day, you may firmly conclude that you have risen together with him. As it truly is, although it is not yet revealed. For this is why Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who sleep, because he was the first to rouse himself from death into life, and we are to follow him. But he says that victory over death and sin was given to us by God through Christ. This is our blessed Luther.

The fifth is from the Prophet's scope and intention. For since he predicted the plundering and captivity to Ephraim, or Israel and Judah, because they would not repent, even though they felt the blow, and seemed to be consumed by a slow decay as if by the erosion of woodworm and moths, whence the Lord had to attack them not as a weak little worm, but as an untamed Lion and Panther, and the Prophet testified that the Lord, having led them into exile, would leave them in calamity and go to his own place, and would desert them, until, having performed penance, they are converted to the Lord, which was not fulfilled so much under the Old Testament or in Ephraim and Judah, in those ten and two tribes, as regards the conversion predicted here, since the ten tribes are not read to have returned to the Lord with the two, having acknowledged their guilt through penance, but rather remained in that dispersion among the Gentiles and Samaritans, with a few exceptions who were mixed with the Jews, nor did the distinction of those ten tribes, or of Ephraim, remain after the Assyrian abduction. Whence whatever is said here concerning the conversion of Ephraim, or the ten tribes, and of Judah, or the two tribes, is to be understood in the prophetic manner, by which they are accustomed to embrace the Church of the New Testament through the denomination of the Israelites, not excluding Israel according to the flesh, but gathered into the same assembly of converted Gentiles, to which Church collected from Israelites and Gentiles, most of the Evangelical promises of the Old Testament properly pertain. Which if we should wish to understand concerning merely corporal benefits, we shall easily lapse into Judaism, which savors of nothing but carnal things in its Messiah. Which matter our blessed Hunnius has already executed against Calvin's defender Pareus, whom it is pleasant to hear here p. 235. It is not denied that the Prophet introduces the people, testifying to their repentance, and sustaining themselves by the confidence of the goodness and mercy of God who remits sins. But because the Spirit, who governed the mouth and pen of the Prophet, as Peter attests, in those matters especially where mention is made of the remission of sins, was accustomed to look not only to external liberation (which was a benefit of short duration) but chiefly to spiritual: therefore Christians rightly determine that the Prophet, illuminated by that divine spirit, here beyond and above external vivification and liberation from temporal destruction, raises the minds of the repenting people to that vivification which was to be through Christ. Certainly the sound of the words argues that the finger is pointed at Christ, struck for our sins; and raised on the third day: whose resurrection is not his own private one, but (by reason of its fruit) common to all who believe in him. For since (as the Apostle Paul, the most faithful interpreter of the Prophets, writes) we were dead through our transgressions, he made us alive together with Christ, and raised us up together with him, and made us sit together with him among the heavenly beings Eph. 2. Which words so harmonize with the testimony of Hosea, that the Apostle seems to have looked hither while writing. Therefore, what is read concerning the people repenting and expecting the remission of sins from God does not detract from our opinion, but rather fits most aptly into the principal scope of all the Prophets (which is to bear witness to Christ, that that remission of sins is given through his name, Acts 10). And here is found the foundation of confidence, which is the chief part of repentance, from which, indeed, the faithful can raise themselves up in the striking and wounds by which they have been injured, and conceive hope of healing and salvation, namely from the meritorious vivification and resuscitation, done in the ζωοποιήσει [making alive] and excitation of Christ; for since salvation was procured for us when Christ was delivered up for our sins and raised for our justification Rom. 4, 25, and we were made alive and raised together in him when we were dead in sins, Eph. 2, 5 (as far as merit is concerned), from thence and therefore we have to hope with confidence in any striking whatsoever, and we can conceive a solid and indubitable hope of healing, insofar as it has seemed salutary to us. This argument and foundation is therefore not undeservedly laid down here for the mutual consolation of the faithful, outside of which no place for hope, no place for any consolation remains. Acts 4, 12.

Sixth, from the universality of the promise. For this vivification does not pertain only to certain Israelites, nor only to two tribes, but all Israelites can raise themselves up by it: nor are those looked at here so much as they pertained to the people of Israel according to the flesh, as those who, performing true repentance, betake themselves to the Lord with true confidence; and therefore it is certain that it applies to all the faithful, nay, that the same consolation can be applied to themselves by all men, so that when they feel the hand of God striking them, they should raise themselves up primarily by this divine benefit, that in Christ, who was raised on the third day, he raised us all together, and life and salvation were then prepared for all of us. That this is not to be restricted to a bodily restoration is certain even from the fact that God did not bring back all the tribes of the Israelites, but only the Jews from captivity. Therefore, the day of the release from captivity is not understood here.

Seventh, from the hope and expectation of eternal life. The discourse is about such a vivification as includes eternal life. But the hope of liberation from bodily miseries or from the Babylonian captivity does not at the same time include the gift of eternal life, but that vivification which comes to us in Christ, who was raised on the third day, embraces eternal life at the same time, which Christ acquired for us all by his resurrection: therefore it is said that by his resurrection he destroyed death and brought life and incorruption to light 1 Pet. 1, 1. Rightly Blessed Luther: what he says: we shall live (Lipanaf) before his face, although otherwise they refer it to the life of the pious in this age, yet it certainly includes eternal life, which we begin to possess by faith while we live here, just as John says: Now we are children of God, but it has not yet been revealed, but when it is revealed, we shall be as he is. Especially Psalm 16, 11 can be compared. For what Christ there professes concerning his own resurrection, that happens to us at the same time in Christ and on account of Christ: You have made known to me the paths of life, you will fill me with joy with your countenance, delights are in your right hand forever. How also Christ in John 14: I live, and you shall live. For just as Adam lost life for himself and his descendants, so Christ received the same for himself and for us. But when Rivetus objects that what is said here cannot be referred proximately and immediately to the life of glory, since those things which are added in the following verse do not pertain to the condition of life, from which he concludes that temporal life and that a prosperous one is understood, but with the condition of the cross; especially, however, and absolutely the life of grace, namely through the manifestation of divine favor, which life and blessedness in heaven necessarily follows, that does not hinder our opinion: If we understand the life of grace here primarily in such a way that it, from the intention of God and the power of the merit of Christ, at the same time includes and embraces, and does not exclude, the blessed life of glory: just as also those things which are subjoined pertain to the condition of life in such a way that that knowledge of the Lord, which is of travelers, tends toward the recognition which we are to have in the fatherland, which is called that of those who have arrived, and has it as its end and complement: we therefore admit that sense thus far, we shall live before his face, raised with Christ, who was raised on the third day, and living forever we shall live before GOD, and we shall enjoy the life of grace through the manifestation of his faith or grace (since GOD is said to favor, when he does not turn his face away, but directs it toward us, or looks upon us graciously, Num. 6. Ps. 67. Ps. 33, 18. and the antithesis of chapter 5, 15 confirms that sense: I will go and return to my place, until they repent) from which not only will happiness of every kind redound to us in this life, especially spiritual, but we shall be preserved most of all for a more blessed life, so that we may live eternally before his face in heaven, just as Christ raised is filled with life and eternal joy with the countenance of God: therefore Rivetus could not here despise the Chaldean paraphrase, which looked to that, explaining it: he will give us life in the days of consolation, which are to come in the day of the resurrection of the dead, he will raise us up, and we shall live before him: and he himself constructs this document from these words of the Israelites, page 214. Since those who promise themselves life in the face of God have previously confessed that they had been torn away and as it were rent asunder, we learn by their example that in death itself life is to be hoped for, in the sepulcher resurrection, in the very jaws as it were of the underworld the contemplation of the divine face, and heavenly glory.

Eighth, from the knowledge of the Messiah. This fruit, moreover, is both of repentance and of vivification. And we shall know, and we shall follow, that we may know the Lord: the Lord (the Lord Father) will raise us up (with the Messiah) on the third day, and we shall know, and we shall follow, that we may know the Lord (the Messiah, whom, having been raised, we profess with Thomas to be our Lord and our God, John 20:28), since a greater knowledge arises for us when we are converted to the Lord by true repentance; nor does the blessed Luther note without reason that this passage pertains (especially) to the times of the New Testament: the phrase in the word (Jada) is well known. For it embraces the knowledge of God, and the mystery of the word, by which the true knowledge of God is propagated. Therefore, this passage pertains to the time of the revealed Gospel, after Christ's resurrection, when both the Holy Spirit was given to the Apostles, and by their ministry the knowledge of God, that is, the benefit of Christ, was scattered into all parts of the world. For then, minds inflamed by the Holy Spirit embraced the word with great zeal. As the history of the Apostles shows. This is the blessed Luther. The word WE SHALL KNOW can be referred to the knowledge of this life, so that both the purity of doctrine and its clarity may be noted, because in the New Testament Christ is to be known fully and plainly, not under the wrappings of oracles and types; the rest, and we shall follow, that we may know the Lord, not only the zeal of learning,

and perseverance, but also embrace the end and completion of knowledge, namely intuitive knowledge, which, in order for us to attain, it is necessary that we persist in doctrine, that we pursue it in this life, until we attain the same in the other life. Since, therefore, spiritual benefits are celebrated here, the knowledge of God, the coming forth of the Messiah, the dissemination of the Gospel, it is manifest that that prophecy ought not to be restricted to a temporal liberation.

through the preaching of the Gospel (says the Church) like the dawn, spreading itself far and wide: which no one can prohibit. And Christ refreshes our thirsty hearts (exhausted and languid in the sense of sins and the wrath of God) with his Gospel like a most welcome rain: and renders us fruitful for doing good works, like rain does the earth. Nor will anyone be able to stop the course of the Gospel by any arts or persecutions. For the same reason the Vinarian Paraphrasts explain: 'Then we will pay attention to it, and be diligent, that we may know the Lord. When Christ after his resurrection will let the Gospel be preached in all the world, we will hear the same with diligence, and arrive at the soul-saving knowledge of God:' For He (the Messiah) will (not only from the grave in his resurrection, but also through the preached word of the Gospel with his grace and benefits) break forth like the beautiful dawn, (as the dawn goes before the rising of the sun, so the light of divine knowledge will be kindled through the light of the Gospel in the heart of men, going before the full knowledge of God in eternal life, 2 Pet. 1, verse 19. As no one can hinder the dawn, so no one will be able to hinder the course of the Gospel. As the dawn drives away the darkness of the night, so Christ will powerfully drive away the darkness of ignorance, of sins, of tribulation, and of damnation through the word of the Gospel, Is. 9, verse 7, chap. 60, 1. As the dawn, when it breaks forth, gladdens everyone, so also Christ with his word will gladden everything) and will come to us like a rain, like a latter rain, that moistens the land (Likewise, as the rain refreshes the dry earth and makes it fruitful, Ps. 65, verse 11. So Christ will refresh our dry and thirsty hearts, make them fruitful for good works, and rich in heavenly joy. Blessed Luther had also handed down this sense in his Commentary on Hosea in the year 1545. AS THE DAWN HIS GOING FORTH IS ESTABLISHED. These things pertain to the ministry of the word and the doctrine of the Gospel. For the Prophet uses the similitude of the dawn for this reason, to show that this light of the word, which is the knowledge of the Lord, is to be scattered into the whole world. Nor is there any doubt to me that the Prophet in this place imitated the prophecy of David in Ps. 19. where he compares the doctrine of the Gospel to the sun, 'from the end of the heavens,' he says, 'is his going forth, and his circuit to the end of them, and there is no one hidden from his heat.' But because our Prophet prophesies about the beginnings and, as it were, the cradles of the Gospel, the similitude of the dawn was more apt than that of the sun. For this, as if showing itself from afar to the world, gradually takes on those increments, so that the rising sun may illuminate the whole world with its light. And further: but to what does the word (Nachon) pertain, which we translate 'is established,' others translate 'to be prepared,' but it is true. It signifies (chon) to be prepared, but in such a way that it is stable and firm, and cannot be either overturned or hindered. In this manner the Prophet speaks here of Christ and the Gospel, in which the benefit of Christ is proposed: 'His going forth is prepared.' For just as no one can prohibit the rising dawn, nor wrap up its light so that it cannot be seen, so it signifies that the ministry of the Gospel cannot be hindered or oppressed, even if Satan and the world are going to attempt it with great effort. The sentiment therefore agrees with that saying of Christ: 'The gates of hell shall not prevail.' The reason is, because his going forth is prepared and firm. From the preparation of the Messianic going forth: concerning which the Prophet says thus: 'As the dawn his going forth is prepared, and he will come like the early and latter rain to the earth.' Grotius, so that he might serve his hypothesis, neglects the Hebrew distinctions, joined those things which are not joined, inserted foreign things which do not appear in the text, and converted a simple promise of grace into a hypothetical one, thus annotating on this: 'WE SHALL KNOW AND WE SHALL FOLLOW, THAT WE MAY KNOW THE LORD: AS THE DAWN HIS GOING FORTH IS PREPARED.' You may translate it best thus, by supplying what are often wont to be omitted in the Hebrew: If we know the Lord, and by knowing him we follow him, his help will be as prompt for us as the dawn is, AND HE WILL COME LIKE THE EARLY AND LATTER RAIN TO THE EARTH.) The early rain is called that which is at the time of sowing, the latter, that which is at the ripening of the crop, as we said in Deut. 11:14. The sense is: at every time all prosperous things will happen to them from God. But according to the Hebrew truth the text stands thus: as Jerome rendered it: 'we shall know and we shall follow, that we may know the Lord: As the dawn (morning) his (the Lord's) going forth is prepared, and he will come like rain to us (as it were) the latter and early rain to the earth,' and as Blessed Luther: 'Then we will pay attention to it, and be diligent, that we may know the Lord, for He will break forth like the beautiful dawn, and will come to us like a rain, like a latter rain, that moistens the land.' In the manuscript papers of Blessed To the writings of Luther, which I possess upon this Prophet, from the communication of the most noble and most learned Mr. Joh. Martin Luther, great-grandson of the Great Man, Electoral Councilor, Dean of Zeitz, and also Canon of Meissen, my honorable kinsman and godfather (which evidently testify to the great diligence and fidelity applied by Luther in translation, and teach that he often changed and variously attempted the same word, phrase, or sentence two or three times while translating, until that metaphrasis which he approved emerged), this note was added by his own hand: Concerning Christ and the Gospel. From this autograph of his, even though it was so variously emended, the first edition of the Old Testament was printed, which appeared here in Wittenberg in the year 1532 from the workshop of Joh. Lufft, and a marginal gloss was added: Here he prophesies of Christ and the Gospel. Whence Osiander rightly interpreted these in his paraphrase: Then the Church of Christ will not be stupid toward the word of God, as before, but will learn the Gospel of Christ with great zeal: so that from it it may properly acknowledge its God. (And indeed it is known from the Acts of the Apostles with what alacrity both Jews and Gentiles received the Gospel of Christ, and made excellent progress in the knowledge of God: which zeal it behooves us to imitate. And many so loathe the word of God that they attend sermons unwillingly, and deign scarcely to look at the Holy Bible) As the dawn is prepared or established is his going forth: and he shall come as the early rain to us: more correctly: the timely, and the latter rain of the earth, (that is, Christ the Savior arises for us as the going forth of this King through the Gospel, like the dawn, which cannot be hindered, but little by little pours itself more brightly upon the world. AND HE SHALL COME TO US AS THE RAIN, AS THE LATTER RAIN TO THE EARTH. This is the second consolation, that the word, just as it cannot be hindered, so also will it bring forth certain fruit. For this is the reason why the Prophet compares the Gospel to rain, and indeed to the latter rain, which refreshes the crop, almost exhausted by the constant heat of the sun, at the time of harvest, so that it may be able to take on growth. B. Meisner thinks that a triple going forth can be understood. 1. Of the Nativity, when the Messiah came forth from the womb of Mary into the world. 2. Of the Resurrection, when He came forth alive from the sepulchre. 3. Of the Preaching, when He went forth through the Gospel into the whole world, and applied the benefits, acquired by His merit, to believers, Psalm 19, 3. 6. But here the third going forth is properly designated, which is compared both to the daybreak, or dawn, because just as this drives away the night and scatters the darkness, so Christ, going forth through the Gospel as the sun of righteousness, Mal. 4, and the long-awaited dawn, put to flight all the darkness of ignorance, affliction, and damnation; and to the timely rain, or morning and evening rain (concerning which Deut. 11, Joel 2, 23, James 5, 7), of which the former, sent immediately after the sowing, causes the seed to take root in the earth, but the latter falls when the crop grows up into ears and stalks, so that the fruit may reach maturity, because Christ, by His Gospel preached everywhere, refreshed dry and thirsty hearts, quickened the dead, and caused them to grow in good works, and rendered them ripe for the heavenly harvest, as B. Meisner himself explained.

The promise is not, therefore, to be taken only in a general sense, with Grotius, that prosperous things will happen to the pious in time, nor with the Calvinists is it to be restricted to the captives under the Babylonian power, that God wishes to show Himself propitious to them, as Rivetus contends with a weak argument, that the going forth of God is opposed to the departure by which He had returned to His own place; for even if this opposition had a place here, does it not stand more illustriously when that gracious visitation, which occurred under the New Testament, is opposed to the abandonment of the Israelites? To which, just as this notable eulogy, shadowed forth by the double figure of the dawn and the timely rain, more aptly agrees, so interpreters commonly, with the ordinary and interlinear gloss, and also Lyranus, refer these things to the time of the New Testament. Above, says B. Gesner, the Lord hid Himself, and because of the sins of the people went away to His own place, that is, He withdrew His help and aid, and even the consolatory sermons of the Gospel, from the obstinate for some time, so that the Israelite people seemed utterly deserted by God, and the coming of the Messiah clearly denied. But now the penitent exclaim with joy: that the Lord Messiah is coming forth again from His hiding place and arriving. For although those who were not to attain to these times seem to be introduced as saying these things, yet they are predicted by those who are one people and sustain themselves with the same hope, and in the spirit.

We draw the tenth argument from the gratuitous forgiveness of sins on account of Christ.

The Prophet subjoins this benefit to the preaching of the Gospel: WHAT SHALL I DO UNTO THEE, EPHRAIM? WHAT SHALL I DO UNTO THEE, JUDA? YOUR MERCY IS AS A MORNING CLOUD, AND AS THE DEW THAT GOES AWAY EARLY. Grotius takes it in a bad sense, that is, what good could I do for you, while you are such? Mercy, that is, your probity, fails quickly, just as the dew or the cloud, having arisen in the morning, are dissipated when the sun arrives: and concerning the word MERCY, he notes this: חסד is indeed usually translated as ἔλεος and ἐλεημοσύνη, both among the Greek interpreters of the Old Testament and among the writers of the New: but in truth the meaning of the word includes this part, but extends more widely, and reaches to all duties of piety and probity: whence חסידים are called ἀσιδαῖοι in the Maccabees, who solicitously fulfilled all parts of their duties, whence it happened later that the name ἐσσαίων or ἐσσηνῶν was derived from ח. And it is believed that there is something more in it than in the word צדק. But whatever may be the case regarding that nomenclature of the Hasideans and Essenes, they certainly ought not to have been corrected or marked with censure, since even the writers of the New Testament, who wrote moved by the Holy Spirit, used the Greek interpreters of the Old Testament. Nor is your mercy to be taken here in an active sense, but in a passive one, the mercy to be shown to you: because the Prophet is occupied in the promises of benefits, by which the penitent are to be raised up, not in the reproof of vices: and the comparison of the similitude of the morning cloud and the dew passing away in the morning, with the former one of the dawn and the morning or timely rain, sufficiently teaches that the Prophet persists in the paracletic genre, and these things are not to be dragged to the corrective genre. Wherefore your mercy is to be understood passively concerning the gratuitous forgiveness of sins. For just as the morning rain tempers the sultriness of summer nights, and dew refreshes drooping herbs and crops, so too does nothing else but the immense mercy of God recreate and vivify the terrified consciences of men, scorched by the act of divine wrath. Therefore, what B. Luther had rendered in the cited αὐτογράφῳ: Was soll ich dir doch thun Ephraim, he corrected with his own hand ἐμφατικωτέρως, interpreting it in a good sense, in this way: Wie will ich dir so wohl thun Ephraim? And what he had rendered before: Denn die Güte so euch gebühret, ist wie eine Morgen-Wolcke, und wie ein Thau, der früh morgens dahin fähret: this he later amended through φροντίδας δευτέρας as follows: Denn die Gnade so ich euch erzeigen will, wird seyn wie eine Morgen-Wolcke, und wie ein Thau, der früh morgens fället: concerning which he himself is to be heard from the commentary p. 520. The Prophet spoke of the time of the New Testament, that the liberation from death by the resurrection of Christ, and eternal life, will be preached, and then men will truly acknowledge God. For they will not fear him, as those are compelled to fear to whom he is not rightly known, but they will rest in his mercy. And although the Synagogue and the nations will oppose this doctrine, yet he says it will come to pass that, just as the dawn cannot be restrained, but rather illuminates the world more and more, not without immense fruit, so neither will the course and fruit of the word be able to be hindered. Thus far the Prophet has spoken concerning the kingdom of Christ. Now he adds an amplification of these benefits: What shall I do to you, O Ephraim? What shall I do to you, O Judah? as if comparing them with the benefits exhibited to the ancient people. It was a great thing to be liberated from the servitude of Egypt, to be adorned with glorious victories against the nations, to possess the land promised to the Fathers, but all these things were temporal, and they were only helped for the present. The New Testament, however, brings to us spiritual and eternal riches, namely reconciliation with God, the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. Therefore the Prophet adds: Your grace will be like the morning cloud. Here, not only ambiguity but also the nature of the simile has misled interpreters. For almost all the more recent ones take 'beneficence' or 'piety' actively, by which the Jews did good to others, and they think it is compared to dew, because they suddenly turned away from it to impiety and sins. Jerome takes it passively, but thinks the nature of the simile is the same, that the beneficence by which the Lord helped them was soon to fail.

situra. For those to be led away into captivity by the Assyrians and Babylonians, etc. But I approve of neither opinion. It is indeed true that piety or beneficence is taken passively, as God is about to use it toward this people. But the Prophet does not use the similitude of dew because it vanishes quickly, but rather he looks to the fact that the earth is refreshed by dew. For in great heat, even the nights are hot to the point of human exhaustion. But when the dawn is about to break, cool breezes are stirred up, and dewy clouds distilling moisture restrain the heat and cool the earth. Just as, therefore, hot and thirsty bodies are refreshed when they drink cold water and resume their lost liveliness, so too the earth is refreshed, and languishing plants, as it were, resume their strength and stand upright when they drink the morning dew. But what is this heat in men? Nothing other than the sense of sin, of the wrath of God, and of eternal punishments. For when these things occupy the soul, they all but shut out the Spirit, just as this very temptation is excellently described in Ps. 38: O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury, nor chasten me in thy wrath. For thine arrows are stuck fast in me, and thy hand is heavy upon me. There is no soundness in my flesh because of thy wrath, nor is there peace in my bones because of my sin. For my sins have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they are weighed down upon me. I am bowed and brought very low, and I go about mourning all the day. For my loins are filled with dryness, and there is no soundness in my flesh; I am crushed and broken exceedingly, I howl because of the anxiety of my heart. Lord, all my desire is before thee, and my groaning is not hidden from thee. My heart trembles, my strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes is not with me. In these sorrows and dangers, nothing lifts up languishing and all-but-dead souls except the doctrine of the Gospel, which teaches: that Christ has transferred our sins onto Himself, has made satisfaction for them, and by His death has opened for us the way to life. When souls hear these things, they conceive the hope of pardon, and like flowers that are nearly dead, they return to their former liveliness and brightness.

The eleventh argument may be sought from the uncertainty of other expositions. For those who depart from the literal meaning in the designation of time, 'after two days and on the third day,' which produces a certain sense, have nothing certain on which to fix their foot. For others, 'after two days' is the same as 'shortly,' with Grotius, in which sense Rivetus wished to collect similar passages, but found none, except those that were little similar and heterogeneous, as is clear from his Commentary. Others take it in a completely contrary sense, for a long time, as if God were saying: 'Think and resolve thus among yourselves, and in turn persuade one another, even if God does not immediately at the very first moment heal your wounds, but lets the dead lie for two days, that is, for a time, so that you may be like rotting corpses, yet you must not doubt concerning your redemption, because He can restore life in a moment to those who have long been dead.' To this they refer what is said about Lazarus in John 11:39. Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days, as Rivetus observed on p. 209. But while he assumes the former sense, he satisfies neither himself nor others. For at one moment he understands the third day as the time of liberation from captivity and miseries, and at another as the time of the New Testament, and he explains it thus: 'After a few days, having sent His Son in human flesh, He will endow us with spiritual life, and thus will raise us up.' But how will 'two days' and 'a short time' denote at the same time the passage of some centuries, and how can it be said to happen 'after a few days' what happens after the lapse of about eight hundred years?

Christian interpreters, who, although they do not all agree on the manner of explaining, nevertheless easily agree on the substance of the matter, that this prophecy speaks of the third day of Christ's resurrection. Rivetus could not conceal this: 'It is certain that many of the Fathers explain this passage concerning the resurrection of Christ, which took place on the third day, some of whom contend for this directly.' Others, however, wish the resurrection of men to be promised in the resurrection of Christ, as in the cause and prince of those to be raised, among whom are Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. 14; Gregory of Nyssa, book on the knowledge of God, chapter on the resurrection of Christ; and Rufinus in the Creed, no. 17, who think these words: 'He will quicken us after two days, in the third He will raise us up, and we shall live in His sight,' are said in the person of those who rose together with Christ and came into the holy city and appeared to many, Matt. 27:53. Others understand it of all those to be raised who were raised on the third day in Christ the head, because by His resurrection He generated in us the hope of our own. This is Rivetus. Theodoret explained it most conveniently: 'By these things,' he says, 'he designates the resurrection of the Savior which took place after three days, which procured the public resurrection and gave to all of us the hope of immortality generated from the knowledge of God.' Nor does Zanchius, among the Calvinists, altogether deny it in his Commentary on this passage: 'Because the Israelites and the elect Jews, who were to be quickened, were to have this from Christ the head rising for our justification, therefore it is necessary to understand it PRINCIPALLY of Christ.' And these things for the present concerning this prophecy.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVID FACIAM TIBI EPHRAIM? QUID FACIAM TIBI JUDA?) Id est, quid boni vobis pos- sem facere, dum tales estis?

MISERICORDIA VESTRA) חסד, έλεος quidem & ἐλεημοσύνη verti solet, tum apud Græcos Interpretes Vete- ris Testamenti, tum apud scriptores Novi; Sed revera signi- ficatio vocis hanc quidem partem complectitur, sed latius patet, extenditrq; se ad omnia pietatis & probitatis & offi- cia: unde חסידים Ἀσιδαῖοι in Maccabaicis dicuntur, qui omnes officiorum partes sollicite explebant, unde factum postea extrito ו nomen ἱσσιαίων vel ἐσσηνῶν, & aliquanto plus in eo esse creditur, quam in voce צדיק.

QUASI NUBES MATUTINA, ET QUASI ROS MANE PERTRANSIENS) Brevi defecit vestra probitas, quomodo ros, aut nubes mane exorta, sole ad- ventante dispereunt.

Recte Judæorum commenta hic deser it Gro- tius, quos utinam in aliis plerisq; non sequutus es- set! Aliter tamen figmentum Judæorum refert Hieronymus, (nisi forte id aliud aut aliorum sit: nullum enim κατ'ὄνομα vel Grotius vel Hierony- mus expressit) quod nempe per diem secundum tempus Messiæ, per tertium tempus judicii intelli- gant, quo se ab omnibus malis liberatum iri, & per mille annos variis deliciis fruituros somniant. Quæ Chiliastarum phantasia insipida est. Et urget hic Hieronymus Judæos: Respondeant nobis, quæ sit dies prima: hoc est: primus Salvatoris adventus: Et cum respondere non potuerint, inferamus primum diem esse, juxta quod ipsi volunt in humilitate Salva- toris adventum: secundum in gloria: tertium in habitu judicantis. Qui autem secundum, tertiumq; suscipiunt: primum se perdidisse testantur: quia secundus & tertius sine primo non potest appellari. Alii per diem primum tempus liberationis è captivi- tate Babylonica, per tertium liberationis è præsenti discrimine, cui in hunc diem subjacent, intelligunt, sed hic non agitur de vivificatione primo & secun- do die facta, & quæ tertia die speranda sit. Vivifi- cabit, inquit Propheta, nos post duos dies: in tertia die suscitabit nos. Et Expectatio Messiæ liberaturi eos è moderna dispersione, vanissima est. Veniet Messias, sed judicatum illos, qui eum, cum venit, re- cipere noluerunt. Aliorum interpretatio de tribus templis, primo à Salomone exstructo, ab Assyriis destructo, altero post captivitatem erecto, à Ro- manis devicto, tertio à Messia restaurando, quæ etiam R. Salomonis est, & ineptior & alienior hic est, quam ut refutatione egeat; quam tamen inter- polavit Abarbenel hoc pacto: post duas vindictas, quæ transierunt super nos, post duo templa, quæ destru- cta sunt, & die tertio, h. e. sub templo futuro exsuscitavit bit nos, & vivemus coram ipso, quin neg cademus imposterum, neque captivi abducemur, quæ est mors intellectualis: sed eo tempore faciet nos stare, & perse- verabimus in eo statu omnibus diebus terræ, & vive- mus coram ipso, h. e. perseverabimus in cultu ejus, & non moriemur, & terra non desolabitur. Et tunc, in tempore illius salvationis, cognoscemus, persequemur cognoscere Dominum, &c. Ex ipsius sensu primus dies esset status templi primi, secundus status tem- pli secundi, tertius erectio tertii : de quo vid. Coc- cejus in h. l. p. 61. Cæterum non defuere è Rabbi- nis, quibus Grotius ipse hîc aures præbuisse debue- rit : qui & locum præsentem de resurrectione Mes- siæ & nostra explicarint, de quibus vid. Galat. l. 3. arcan. cath. verit. c. 12. l. 8. c. 22. l. 12. c. 3.

Quanquam vero diffiteri non potuerit Gro- tius, Verba Prophetæ APERTISSIME præfigurare tempus, intra quod Christus vitam, & Ecclesia ejus spem erat receptura, sensum tamen literalem longe alium facit, nimirum hunc, quod brevi Deus Ebræos ex tantis miseriis, quæ morti comparari solent, restituturus sit : unde illum de Christo & Ecclesia sensum mysticum, vel eminentem, ut alias loqui a- mat, esse oportet. Ita scilicet extenuanda est Scri- ptura, ut quid eminenter notet, adipiscamur, ut in si- mili de Grotio questus est Coccejus. Qui vero hîc non aliter tractavit insignem locum, ut juxta præ- conceptam novam ac mirabilem Prophetæ οἰκονο- μίαν, ad sensum multo ineptiorem abriperet, quẽ nemo ante Coccejum unquam in Propheta somni- avit, nec quisquam temere post eundem admiserit. Nimirum fatetur Coccejus, fieri non posse, ut ad Christi resurrectionem non sit hoc loco respectus, & ta- men explicat hæc secundum sensum literalem de Ecclesia Christiana per Assyrios, h. e. Saracenos & Turcas contruncata & lacerata, manuq́; Anti-Christi (Romani) percussa, hoc pacto : ille vivificabit nos, & excitabit, ut vivamus coram ipso, q. d. Cer- tum est, Deum non defuturum nostris conatibus, & etiamsi videatur aliquamdiu deesse conatibus nostris successus, tamen non intermorietur semen, quod est in nobis, & semen, quod ipsi recensebitur in seculum, non intercidet, quippe dictum est c. 2, 21. Desponsabo te mihi in seculum. Igitur si maxime videamur cadere & tradi in manum hostium nostrorum, nihilominus tamen aliquando surgemus in posteris nostris, & vi- vet Ecclesia coram ipso. Ita significatur consolatio, quam habuerunt Martyres, qui restiterunt Anti- Christo, in suis passionibus, quod certi essent, tandem suo labori ex suis passionibus responsurum esse fru- ctum Ecclesiæ, in emendatione & pace & amplifica- tione. Quis hæc unquam in textu prophetico sub- odorari aut divinando assequi valuit, sive quod de Saracenis & Turcis, sive quod de Anti-Christo Ro- mano hîc ullum vestigium sit ! Et quomodo Chri- sti resuscitationem hæc respicient, si non de resurre- ctione à morte, nedum de resurrectione ipsius Christi agant, sed fideles in posteris surrecturos solum do- ceant? Dicis : temporis, quo iterum surgent, & non cadent amplius, brevitas per analogiam tempus, quo Christus in sepulchro jacuit, exprimit ; sed quis Oe- dipus analogiam illam inveniet, nisi qui ad Sacra- mentariorum analogiam forte affuefactus fuerit? Audiamus tamẽ analogiæ istius mysteria enarran- tem Coccejum : Id illam vim habet, q. d. Christus caput nostrum non eo fine resurrexit è mortuis, ut pa- tiatur suos succumbere, & regnum tradat hostibus. Significatur autem etiam interim debere bis vel ter elucescere testimonium veritatis contra Anti-Chri- stum; vivificabit nos à diebus duobus, sive ultra duos dies, q. d. Longius durabit Ecclesia, & re- gnum Christi, quam ut una vel altera emicatione fi- niatur. Excitabit nos tertio die. Simplex mens Prophetiæ est, hanc ipsam & similes prophetias fore consolationi fidelibus ad patientiam in certamine cum Antichristo, ut etiamsi videant se premi, & ante- cessores suos cecidisse, nihilominus tamen haud despe- rent, aut confessionem spei abjiciant. Hussius fertur in ultimo agone de oritura post seculum pugna & re- formatione prædixisse. Certe potuerunt pii etiam ex Apocalypsi eam spem concipere, ubi ostenditur, vi- ctum iri Sanctos per tempus & tempora & dimidium temporis. Quo modulo temporis non tantum deter- minatur intervallum ab ortu Bestiæ ad separationem Ecclesiæ ab ea, sed etiam vices ostenduntur contradi- ctionum, & quartæ vicis non abrumpenda continua- tio, sive victoriæ initium in quarto tempore. Hoseas dicit die tertio, intelligens tertium diem resuscitati- onis, sive resuscitationem tertio iterandam q. d. lu- ctaturos cum Regno Antichristi post primum ca- sum tribus vicibus resuscitabit, & tum vivemus co- ram ipso, ut Rege & præceptore nostro unico, & lætabimur in ipso. Hæ tres vices excitationis Ecclesiæ oppressæ, de qua oppressione est Es. 57, 1. sunt in Wal- densibus, Wicklefi & Hussi discipulis & Reformato- ribus ultimis, Luthero, Melanchthone, Calvino, & Col- legis ipsorum, comprobatæ. Et post aliquam multa: In Ecclesia Christiana tradita in manum Antichristi dies illos tres post primum tempus agnoscimus; & jam tertio die cum duobus testibus à Bestia interfectis ipsam Ecclesiam revixisse vidimus, & quamvis coar- ctatam, tamen nec dum supprimi potuisse, comperi- mus, certi q; sumus, minante vesperam die lucem ori- turam, & messe finita, jacturas esse reparandas. Sed satis de affanis Coccejanis: quas recitasse est solidis- sime refutasse, in his enim commentis ὀδὲν ὑγιὲς.

Præceptor Cocceji Joh. Calvinus, Christi re- suscitationem hic spectatam esse à Propheta nullus concessit: imo illum sensum ceu nimium argutum & evanidum habuit, eosq; in aere volitare judicavit, qui ita intelligunt. Solet hic locus exponi de Christo, quod post triduum & die tertio suscitabit Ecclesiam suam, quia scimus Christum non sibi privatim, sed suis membris resurrexisse: Est enim primitiæ resurgen- tium. Videtur ergo hic sensus non male quadrare, quod Propheta hic erigat fideles in spem salutis, quia Deus excitabit filium suum primogenitum, cujus resurrectio communis erit, & totius Ecclesiæ vita. Sed sensus ille videtur mihi NIMIUM ARGUTUS. Et sem- per hoc spectandum est nobis, ne volitemus in aere. Pla- cent argutæ speculationes primo intuitu, sed postea eva- nescunt. Ergo quisquis volet proficere in scripturis, sem- per hanc regulam teneat, ut solidum sit, quicquid colli- git, sive in Prophetis, sive in Apostolis. Calvinum sequuti sunt alii ejus discipuli, & de liberatione ex captivitate, ac reparatione Ecclesiæ post biduum, id est, breve tempus futura, vaticinium exposuere, ad eundem fere modum uti Grotius: utpote Gualte- rus, Mollerus, Tremellius, Polanus, Drusius & alii, nisi quod in liberatione è miseriis corporalibus sensu eminenti, Grotiano posthabito, pleriq; subsi- stant. Paræus tamen Calvini adversus B. Ægid. Hun- nium, qui Calvinum ἰsdaΐζειν etiam hic arguit, ὑπερασπισης de Christo duobus modis exponi pos- se hoc vaticinium tradidit, ne sc. videretur plane à veterum abiisse sensu (1.) ratione typi, quia liberatio ex captivitate fuit typus liberationis per Christi re- surrectionem futuræ. Vaticinium ergo debere in- telligi tum de typo literaliter & primo, tum de an- titypo mystice & secundario. (2.) Per necessarium nexum effectus cum sua causa. Nulla enim Ecclesiæ redemptio sive sit temporalis sive æterna contin- git, nisi per Christum, ideoq; & hoc sensu oraculum istud ad Christum, tanquam ad causam necessario referri opinatur. Sed quod ad posteriorem modum, nemo prudens admittit, hoc esse Scripturam ex- ponere. Nam aliud est declarare cujusnam me- rito suscitatio tertia die futura obtingat Israe- litis, de quo ejus merito nihil in textu illo habe- tur; aliud vero est explicare textum, quemnam suscitatum iri prædicat Spiritus S. & quisnam ille dies tertius sit, quo is suscitandus sit. Scripturæ enim textum exponere censeri non possumus, cum aliquid aliunde è Scripturis demonstratum expo- nimus & adducimus, sed cum aliquid in illo textu Scripturæ, qui sub manu est, contineri, seu ῥητῶς, seu διανοητικῶς, docemus, etiamsi ad id ex textu eruendum aliis locis opus sit, sed parallelis, non plane ἀλλοτρίοις, seu heterogeneis. Quod vero ad priorem, qua vocat Pareus, expositionem at- tinet, qua cum Grotiana conspirat: nequaquam admittendum, ut uni eidemque oraculo geminus, isque tam disparatus sensus tribuatur, quod nec perspicuitas Scripturæ, nec docendi ratio Spiritus S. simplicissima, minimeque ambigua, aut intricata admittit. Nam eo pacto subjectum vivificationis u- num geminatur, ut aliud objectum sit in sensu lite- rali, nim. Israëlitæ, aliud in sensu mystico, nimirum Christus; sic prædicatum, etsi unum idemque ge- mino etiam sensu accipitur, vivificatio nempe & suscitatio, ut notet tum veram à morte resuscitatio- nem & vivificationem proprie, tum metaphorice re- stitutionem è miseriis morti similibus. At vocem eandem & proprie & figurate in eodem loco, cum semel tantum occurrit, adhiberi, ἄτοπον est, & à Scripturæ more alienum. Similiter & tertius dies longe aliter in eminenti erit intelligendus. Ibi enim figurate notabit breve tempus: hic vero proprie, uti sonat, tertium diem post elapsum biduum signi- ficabit: quem sensum potius primum obvium quis dixerit, quia proprietati literæ inhæret. Quapro- pter cum simul consistere geminus ejusmodi sen- sus nullatenus possit, restat, ut alteruter sensus hic solum retineatur.

Quem ergo germanum & nativum sensum hu- jus vaticinii statuemus, quam illum, quem & Eccle- siastici Doctores, & Judæorum Rabbini nonnulli in verbis Prophetæ pro nativo habuere nec exclude- re hic ausi sunt vel Grotius, vel Pareus, aut Cocce- jus, aliique recentiores nonnulli Calvinistæ? Quem tamen non eodem semper modo proponunt. B. Meisnerus noster de interpretatione vera & litera- li in Commentario differens, ita eam exponit p. 597. Hæc non est alia, quam Prophetiam loqui de resur- rectione tum Christi, tanquam capitis, tum nostra vel- uti membrorum. In confesso enim est, quod hic sermo fiat, non de liberatione ex captivitate temporali, sed potius de actu quodam Messiæ & beneficio Novi Test. Actus ille Christi resurrectio, beneficium nostra resu- scitatio est. Quod enim Christum attinet, suum pecu- liare triduum ille habuit. Primum die nuncupamus passionis & mortis: Secundum sepulturæ & quie- tis: Tertium gloriosæ resurrectionis, quo è sepul- chro prodiit secundum Scripturam 1. Cor. 15, 4. Nulla vero Scriptura de tertio die præter hanc Hoseæ inve- nitur in toto Veteri Testamento, uti Dorotheus obser- vat. Nos quod spectat, duobus modis resurgimus (1.) Anima, quum regeneramur, & in novitate viæ ambulare incipimus, de qua Rom. 6, 8. dicitur: Si mortui sumus cum Christo, credimus, quia simul & vivemus cum illo. Et clarius Ephes. 2, 4. 5. DEUS cum essemus mortui in peccatis, convivificavit nos in Christo, & conresuscitavit, quæ verba cum Ho- seæ vaticinio prorsus coincidunt. (2) Corpore, quod iterum fit bifariam 1. in spe & ratione juris, quo pa- cto tertia die cum Christo vivificati sumus, 1. Cor. 15, 22. quia tunc jus resurrectionis nostræ accepi- mus: 2. in re & ratione ipsius facti, quando in extre- mo die vitam reipsa recuperabimus. Hæc resuscita- tio fit etiam post biduum. Nam & Christiano cui- libet sunt quoque tres dies. Primus est crucis, quam diu in hac terra vivimus. Secundus est quietis, quando in sepulchro jacemus. Tertius est resurre- ctionis, quum glorificati ad novam vitam prodibi- mus. Hæc quamvis pia & jucunda sint, suumque usum rite adhibita in homileticis habere possint, ta- men si arctius textum urgeamus, quodnam biduum, & quis tertius dies intelligatur à Propheta, non cer- te huc faciet Christianorum illud triduum crucis, quietis & resurrectionis, sed unice Christi: Ideoque B. Meisnerus ipse, cum postea in eodem commen- tario ἀγωνιστικῶς & exquisite de sensu disputat, num Hoseas de resurrectione Christi tertia die futu- ra vaticinetur, hunc, non alium sensum reddit, eumque literalem esse adstruit pag. 616. Nos vere tertio die resurrecturos, sed non in propria persona, verum in Christo. Quod ad genuinam status forma- tionem observari cupit Pareus p. 123. in Hoseam, sub- dole nobiscum agit, & talem absurdam interpretatio- nem nobis tribuit, quod duplex adhibenda sit figura, nimirum Enallage numeri pluralis pro singulari, & Synecdoche totius pro parte, quasi dixerit Propheta: Tertio die suscitabit nos per Christum, & nos cum eo. Quasi vero tam stolidi essemus, ut pluralem mu- temus in singularem, quin potius pluralem retinemus & sine figura tropoque dicimus: Nos vere tertio die resurrecturos, sed non in propria persona, verum in Christo. Hæc B. Meisnerus. Quem sensum etiam tradiderat B. Gesnerus, quod nempe præsens lo- cus non possit de externa saltem & corporali libera- tione accipi, sed quod de redemptione per Christum è mortuis die tertia resurrecturum præstanda neces- sario exponi debeat. Et ante hosce Doctores no- stros imprimis Megalander Commentario in h. l.

Pro hac autem ἐκθέσει, sequentia observari possunt argumenta; primum à diserta mentione ter- tiæ diei. Non enim est à proprietate literæ difceden- dum, nisi urgeat necessitas. Quum ergo tertius dies hic expresse commemoretur futuræ resuscitationis, non indefinite tempus breve intelligendum, sed definitioni potius ipsius Spiritus Sancti, qui non sine causa tertium diem expressit, inhærendum & acquiescendum est. Non sine mysterio diem ex- pressit, tertiæ diei mentione, quod vel Judæi ipsi in- tellexere, ideo tam anxie, uti vidimus, varia con- quisivere, quæ tertio diei aptarent. Qui itaque nos temere designationem à S. S. factam relinquamus, quin tertium diem resurrectionis Christi defini- tum esse credamus? Cui uni apte respondet hæc tertiæ diei commemoratio. Nullum certe aliud triduum, nullum tertiũ resuscitationis diem, quod congruat, adferre potuere interpretes. Cyrillus sa- ne l. 1. in Joh. c. 26. aliter tertium diem interpreta- tus est: nempe de novissimis temporibus, sed intel- lexit tamen de Christo: corruptione morteque per- cussos Deus tertio die rursus nos curavit, id est, non primis, neq; mediis, sed novissimis temporibus, quia propter nos factus homo, totam naturã in seipso susci- tavit, atque sanavit. Novissima igitur tempora tertiæ diei appellatione significantur. Verbũ hæc significatio indefinita, neque definito tertiæ diei numero con- venit, neque in Scriptura fundamentum habet, ideoq; proprie tertius dies, uti sonat, intelligendus.

Secundum è distincta bidui commemoratione. Ne ambiguum esset, ἀποτόμως tertiũ diem designari, duobus distinctis modis exprimere eum voluit Propheta. Nam hæc dici καὶ ἐπεξήγησιν dubium nullum est: Vivificabit nos post duos dies & in tertia die suscitabit nos. Quid opus fuisset tam specifice diem tertium distinctim exprimere, si non dies ter- tius, sed breve temporis intervallum indefinite si- gnificaretur? B. Lutherus notat etiam aliquid μυ- sτηριῶδες in illa commemoratione bidui T. 4. Jen. Lat. fol. 519. Non opus est sollicite inquirere, cur non satis sit Prophetæ dixisse: Tertia die surgere nos faciet, sed etiam addat de biduo: Post biduum vivificabit nos. Etsi enim poterat dici: Tertiam diem & post biduum idem esse, aut saltem biduum includi in tertiam diem, tamen nihil prohibet, cum bi duo articuli fidei nostræ distincti sint, Descendit ad inferna & tertia die resurrexit, hoc quod de biduo dicit, transferre ad descensum ad inferna: oportet enim credi hunc descensum fuisse aliud quiddam quam quod sepultus est.

Tertium è loci Apostolici collatione. Diserte enim docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 15, 4. Christum tertia die resurrexisse juxta Scripturam. Quum ergo nullibi in Scripturis expresse hoc prædictum sit, de TERTIO DIE, nisi hic locus admittatur, dubitare non possumus, quin hunc locum, ubi expresse resuscitationis tertia die futuræ mentio occurrit, respexerit, adeoque locus hic de resuscitatione Christi tertia die facta intelligendus sit. Nam Jonæ triduum in ventre ceti typus tantum fuit, etsi illustris, non expressum vaticinium.

Quartum è meritoria Christi vivificatione. Vere enim Christus tertia die (resuscitationis suæ) nos resuscitavit & vivificavit ratione meriti, & in vitam revocatus, vitæ nos reddidit. De quo Eph. 2, 6. Convivificavit nos in Christo, & corresuscitavit & sedere fecit in cælestibus in Christo Jesu. Et 1. Cor. 15, 22. Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. Non enim Christus solus vivificatus est, & resurrexit. Vivificati sumus, & resurreximus in Christo omnes. Christi resuscitatio nostra est resuscitatio: Christi vita nostra est vita. Vivo ego, inquit Christus, & vos vivetis, Joh. 14. Quod argumentum cum prioribus urget non minus solide, quam eleganter B. Lutherus in h. l. Addit tempus, post biduum vivificabit nos, & tertia die suscitabit nos. Quomodo, aut cur? Nimirum ut vivamus ante faciem ejus, hoc est, in vita, in qua ipse vivit. Hæc diligenter æstimata arguunt Prophetam diserte loqui de Christi resurrectione, & hunc esse locum, quem Paulum innuit 1. Cor. 15. ubi dicit: Resurrexit Christus tertia die, secundum Scripturam. Non enim solum urgeri potest, quod dicit post biduum & tertia die, sed quod addit: Dominus vivificabit nos & vivemus coram ipso. Hæc non nisi ad resurrectionem carnis nostræ, & vitam æternam referri possunt. Sed inquies, Non loquitur de Christi resurrectione, seu reditu in vitam æternam, sed de nostra. Nos enim, inquit, vivificabit post biduum, &c. Respondeo: hoc ipsum maxime dignum est observatione. Ostendit enim hoc modo fructum resurrectionis Christi. Christus enim solus est, qui post bidunm vivificatus est, & tertia die resurrexit à mortuis. Ostendit autem Propheta hujus resurrectionis fructum ad nos quoque pertinere. Itaque Christi vitam nostram vitam & ejus resurrectionem nostram resurrectionem facit, sicut Apostoli quoque solent. Paulus Coloss. 3. dicit nos mortuos, & vitam nostram cum Christo in Deo absconditam. In cap. 15. primæ ad Corinth. dicit: Si Christus prædicatur resurrexisse cum mortuis, quomodo dicunt quidam resurrectionem mortuorum nihil esse? Item, Christus resurrexit, & factus est primitiæ dormientium. Quia per unum hominem mors, & per unum hominem resurrectio mortuorum venit. Sicut enim per Adam omnes moriuntur. Ita vivificabuntur omnes per Christum. Hæ sententiæ ostendunt fructum resurrectionis Christi hunc esse. ut nos quoq; resurgamus, & vivamus. Itaque Propheta recte mutat personas. Dicendum enim erat: Christus vivificabitur post biduum, & ter- tia die resurget, sicut Petrus dicit: vivificatum Spi- ritu. Nam ita accidit, ut Christus tertia die resurgeret. At Propheta inquit: Nos vivificandos post biduum, & tertia die, quo Christus resurrexit, resurrecturos. Idque ideo: Quia enim peccato demersi in mor- tem, perpetuo eramus in morte mansuri, Filius Dei nostra peccata in se transtulit, & pro eis fatisfe- cit in cruce, ac postea resurgens, mortem, quam pro nobis obierat, vicit. Itaque nos tum resurgere & vivere cœpimus, cum Christus resurgeret. Per eum enim nostra mors devicta, & vita, quam amisera- mus, reddita est. Danda autem diligens opera erat, ut ad hunc modum resurrectionem Christi nobis appli- caremus, ut cum audis, Christum tertia die resurre- xisse, certo statuas, te una cum ipso resurrexisse. Sicut revera est, quanquam nondum revelatum est. Ideo enim Paulus Christum vocat primitias dormi- entium, quod primus in vitam ex morte seipsum exci- tavit, & nos eum secuturi sumus. At dicit, nobis à Deo datam victoriam mortis & peccati per Christum. Hæc B. Lutherus noster.

Quintum è Prophetæ scopo & intentione. Quum enim Ephraimo, vel Israeli & Judæ direptionem & captivitatem prædixerit, quia resipiscere nolue- runt, etsi plagam sentirent, & lenta quasi tabe tere- dinis & tinearum erosione consumi viderentur, unde Dominus non ut imbecillis vermiculus, sed ut indo- mitus Leo, & Panthera ipsos aggredi necessum ha- buit, ac testatus sit Propheta, Dominum abductis illis in exilium, in calamitate ipsos relicturum, & in locum suum abiturum, eosq; deserturum esse, do- nec pœnitentia acta, ad Dominum convertantur, quod non adeo sub V. Test. aut in Ephraimo & Ju- da, in decem illis, & duobus tribubus impletum est, quantum ad conversionem hic prædictam, siqui- dem non legantur decem tribus cum duabus, agni- ta culpa, per pœnitentiam ad Dominum reversæ, sed in dispersione illa quide manserunt inter gen- tiles & Samaritanos, paucis exceptis, qui Judæis ad- mixti fuere, neque decem illarum tribuum, vel E- phraimi distinctio post abductionem Assyriacam manserit. Unde quicquid hic de conversione Ephraimi, seu decem tribuum, & Judæ, seu duarum tribuum dicitur, intelligendum more prophetico, quo per Israelitarum denominationem Ecclesiam N. Test. complecti solent, non excluso Israele se- cundum carnem, sed aggregato ad eundem genti- lium conversorum cœtu, ad quam Ecclesiam ex I- sraelitis & gentilibus collectam, pleræque promif- siones Evangelicæ V. T. proprie spectant. Quas si de mere corporalibus beneficiis intelligere veli- mus, in Judaismum, nil nisi carnalia penes Messiam suum sapientem, facile prolabemur. Quam rem e- xequutus jam adversus Calvini hyperaspistem Pa- reum B. Hunnius noster est, quem hic audire juvat p. 235. Non negatur, Prophetam inducere populum, testificantem suam resipiscentiam, & sese fiducia boni- tatis ac misericordiæ Dei remittentis peccata susten- tantem. Quia vero Spiritus, qui regebat os & cala- mum Prophetæ, attestante Petro, in iis maxime, ubi remissionis peccatorum fit mentio, non ad externam solummodo liberationem (quæ beneficium erat exi- gui temporis) sed potissimum ad spiritualem respicere solitus est: ideo recte statuunt Christiani, Prophetam divino illo spiritu collustratum, hic ultra & supra vivificationem externam, ac liberationem à tem- porali exitio, mentes resipiscentis populi ad eam vivificationem extollere, quæ per Christum futura erat. Certe sonus verborum arguit digitum intendi ad Christum, ob peccata nostra percussum; & die tertia resuscitatum: cujus resurrectio non est ipsius privata, sed (fructus ratione) communis tis omnibus, qui in illum credunt. Cum enim (ut Pro- phetarum fidissimus interpres Apost. Paulus scribit) essemus mortui per delicta, convivificavit nos una cum Christo, simulque cum eo resuscitavit, & simul cum eo sedere fecit inter cœlestes Eph. 2. Quæ ver- ba cum Oseæ testimonio ita concordant, ut inter scri- bendum Apostolus huc respexisse videatur. Proinde quæ de populo resipiscente, & remissionem pecca- torum à Deo expectante, leguntur, nihil derogant sententiæ nostræ, quin potius ad principalem scopum omnium Prophetarum (qui est testimonium per- hibere Christo, quod illa remissio peccatorum per ipsius nomen detur, Act. 10.) quam appositissime quadrant. Et fundamentum hic habetur fiduciæ, quæ præcipua pars est pœnitentiæ, unde nempe fi- deles sese in percussione, & vulneribus, quibus sauciati sunt, erigere, & spem sanationis & salutis concipere possint, è meritoria videlicet vivificatio- ne, & resuscitatione, in ζωοποιήσει & excitatione Christi facta, quum enim Christo propter peccata no- stra in mortem tradito, propter justitiam nostram re- suscitato Rom. 4, 25. nobis salus parta sit, nos in ipso convivificati simus & conresuscitati, cum mortui esse- mus peccatis, Eph. 2, 5. (quantum ad meritum) in- de atque ideo cum fiducia sperare habemus in quacunque percussione divinam gratiam, & sana- tionis, prouti quidem ea salutaris nobis visa fuerit, spem concipere possumus solidam & indubitatam. Hoc ergo argumentum & fundamentum consolatio- ni mutuæ fidelium hic non immerito substerni- tur, extra quod nullus spei, nullus consolationi ulli locus superat. Act. 4, 12.

Sextum, è promissionis universalitate. Vivifica- tio enim hæc non ad quosdam solum Israelitas, nec ad duas tantum tribus pertinet, sed ea se erigere Israelitæ omnes possunt: nec tam hic respiciuntur illi, ut ad populum Israelis secundum carnem per- tinebant, quam qui pœnitentiam veram agentes, ad Dominum vera fiducia se recipiunt; ideoque fidelibus omnibus eam convenire, imo ab omnibus hominibus eandem consolationem sibi applicari posse, certum est, ut cum manum Dei percutientis sese sentiunt, hoc imprimis beneficio divino sese erigere habeant, quod nos in Christo tertia die re- suscitato, suscitavit simul omnes, nobisque omnibus vita & salus parata tum sit. Ad reductionem certe corporalem hæc restringenda non esse, vel ex eo constat, quod non omnes Israëlitarum tribus, sed solum Judæos Deus è captivitate reduxerit. Non ergo dies solutionis captivitatis hic intelligitur.

Septimum è vitæ æternæ spe atque expectatione. De tali vivificatione sermo est, quæ æternam inclu- dit vitam. At spes liberationis ex miseriis corpora- libus, vel è Babylonica captivitate non includit si- mul donationem vitæ æternæ, sed illa vivificatio, quæ in Christo tertio die resuscitato nobis obtin- git, vitam æternam simul complectitur, quam no- bis omnibus Christus resurrectione sua acquisivit: ideo dicitur resurrectione sua mortem destruxisse, vi- tam & incorruptionem illuminaffe 1. Petr. 1, 1. Recte B. Lutherus: quod dicit: vivemus (Lipanaf) ante faciem ejus, etsi alioqui referunt ad vitam piorum in hoc seculo, tamen certo includit æternam vitam, quam incipimus fide possidere, dum hic vivimus, sicut Joh. dicit: Nunc sumus filii Dei, sed nondum revelatum est, cum autem revelabitur, erimus sicut ipse est. Conferri imprimis potest Psal. 16, 11. Nam quod ibi Christus de sui resurrectione profitetur, id no- bis in Christo, & propter Christum simul obtinge- re: Notas mihi fecisti vias vitæ, adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo, delectationes in dextra tua usque in finem. Quomodo etiam Christus Joh. 14. Vivo ego, & vos vivetis. Ut enim Adamus sibi & posteris amisit vitam, sic Christus pro se & nobis accepit eandem. Quum vero Rivetus obvertit, quæ hic dicuntur, proxime & immediate ad vitam gloriæ referri non posse, siquidem ea, quæ versu sequ. adduntur, pertineant non ad conditionem vitæ, unde concludit vitam temporalem eamque prosperam intelligi, sed cum conditione crucis; præsertim vero & absolute vitam gratiæ, nempe per manifestationem favoris divini, quam necessario sequatur vita, & beata in cælis, id nostræ sententiæ non officit: Si vitam gratiæ ita hic imprimis intelligamus, ut ea ex intentione Dei, & vi meriti Christi simul includat, & complectatur, non excludat vitam gloriæ beatam: quemadmodum etiam ea, quæ subjunguntur, ita ad vitæ pertineant conditionem, ut ea notitia Domini, quæ viatorum est, tendat ad agnitionem, quam in patria habituri sumus, quæ comprehensorum dicitur, eamque pro termino & complemento habeat: sensum ergo illum admittimus hactenus, vivemus ante faciem ejus, resuscitati cum Christo, tertio die resuscita- to, & in æternum vivente vivemus coram DEO, & vita gratiæ fruemur per fidei vel gratiæ ejus manifestationem (siquidem favere dicatur DEUS, cum faciem suam non avertit, sed dirigit ad nos, seu gratiose nos respicit, Num. 6. Psal. 67. Psal. 33, 18. & eum sensum antithefis cap. 5, 15. confirmet: Vadam & revertar ad locum meum, donec resipiscant) unde non solum omnis generis felicitas in hac vita ad nos redundabit, spiritualis imprimis, sed conservabimur maxime ad beatiorem vitam, ut æternum ante faciem ejus in cælis vivamus, quemadmodum Christus resuscitatus adimpletur vita & lætitia æterna cum vultu Dei: ideo aspernari hic Rivetus non potuit paraphrasin Chaldæam, quæ eo respexit, id exponens: vita donabit nos in diebus consolationis, qui venturi sunt in die resurrectionis mortuorum, suscitabit nos, & vivemus coram eo: & hoc documentum extruit ipse ex his verbis Israelitarum pag. 214. Quandoquidem qui sibi pollicentur vitam in facie Dei, antea fassi sunt, se fuisse raptos, & velut discerptos, discimus eorum exemplo, in ipsa morte sperandam esse vitam, in sepulchro resurrectionem, in ipsis velut inferorum faucibus contemplationem faciei divinæ, & gloriam cælestem.

Octavum è Messiæ cognitione. Hic autem fructus & pœnitentiæ & vivificationis est. Et sciemus, & sequemur, ut cognoscamus Dominum: Dominus (Dominus Pater) resuscitabit nos (cum Messia) tertio die, & sciemus, & sequemur, ut cognoscamus Dominum (Messiam, quem resuscitatum cum Thoma profitemur Dominum nostrum, & Deum nostrum, Joh. 20, 28.) siquidem major agnitio nobis oriatur, cum ad Dominum vera pœnitentia convertimur; nec abs re notat B. Lutherus pertinere hunc locum (imprimis) ad N. Test. tempora: Nota est phrasis in verbo (Jada.) Complectitur enim notitiam Dei, & mysterium verbi, quo vera Dei notitia propagatur. Pertinet igitur hic locus ad tempus revelati Evangelii, post Christi resurrectionem, cum & Spiritus Sanctus Apostolis datus, & ministerio eorum notitia Dei, hoc est, Christi beneficium in omnes partes terrarum sparsa est. Tum enim accensi animi per Spiritum S. magno studio verbum amplexi sunt. Sicut ostendit historia Apostolorum. Hæc B. Lutherus. Verbum SCIEMUS referri potest ad cognitionem hujus vitæ, ut cum doctrinæ puritas, tum perspicuitas notetur, quod plene & plane in Novo Test. non sub involucris oraculorum & typorum, Christus cognoscendus sit; Reliqua & persequemur, ut cognoscamus Dominum, non tantum studium discendi,

& perseverantiam, sed etiam terminum & comple- mentum cognitionis complectuntur, intuitivam nempe cognitionem, quam ut assequamur, opus est, ut insistamus doctrinæ, ut consectemur eam in hac vita, donec consequamur eandem in altera vita. Quum ergo hic celebrentur beneficia spiri- tualia, cognitio Dei, egressus Messiæ, dissemina- tio Evangelii, manifestum est, non debere illud vaticinium ad liberationem temporalem restringi.

per Evangelii prædicationem (inquit Ecclesia) tanquam aurora, longe lateque sese diffundens: quam nemo prohibere potest. Et Christus Evangelio suo sitibunda corda nostra (sensu peccatorum & iræ Dei exhausta & languida) tanquam imber gra- tissimus recreat: & nos ad bona opera facienda fœcundos reddit, tanquam imber terram. Neque quisquam ullis artibus, aut persecutionibus Evan- gelii cursum sistere poterit) Eadem ratione Vina- rienses Paraphrastæ exponunt: Denn werden wir acht darauff haben, und fleissig seyn, daß wir den HErrn erkennen. Wenn Christus nach seiner Aufferstehung das Evangelium in aller Welt wird predigen lassen, werden wir denselben mit Fleiß hören, und zum seligmachenden Erkänt- nuß GOttes gelangen: Denn Er (der Messias) wird (nicht allein aus dem Grabe in seiner Auffer- stehung, sondern auch durch das gepredigte Wort des Evangelii mit seiner Gnad und Wolthaten) herfürbrechen wie die schöne Morgenrõ- the, (wie die Morgenröthe vor der Sonnen Auff- gang hergehet, also wird das Licht der Göttlichen Erkändtnuß durch das Licht des Evangelii im Herzen der Menschen angezündet, vor der völli- gen Erkändtnuß GOttes im ewigen Leben herge- hen, 2. Petr. 1. vers. 19. Wie die Morgenröthe niemand hindern kan, also wird auch der Lauff des Evangelii niemand hindern können. Wie die Mor- genröthe die Finsternüß der Nacht vertreibet, also wird Christus durchs Wort des Evangelii die Fin- sternüß der Unwissenheit der Sünden, des Trübsals und der Verdamnuß kräfftiglich vertreiben, Es. 9. vers. 7. cap. 60, 1. Wie die Morgenröthe, wenn sie herfür bricht, jederman erfreuet, also wird auch Christus mit seinem Worte alles erfreuen) und wird zu uns kommen, wie ein Regen, wie ein Spat-Regen, der das Land befeuchtet (Gleicherweise, wie der Regen das dürre Erd- reich erquicket und fruchtbar machet, Ps. 65. vers. 11. Also wird Christus unsere dürre und durstige Herzen erquicken, zu guten Wercken frucht- bar, und zur himmlischen Freude reich machen. Quem sensum tradiderat etiam B. Lutherus in Comment. in Hos. An. 1545. QUASI AURORA FIRMATUS EST EGRESSUS EJUS. Hæc ad ministerium verbi & doctrinam Evangelii perti- nent. Ideo enim auroræ similitudine Propheta uti- tur, ut ostendat hanc verbi lucem, quæ est notitia Domini, spargendam in totum orbem terrarum. Nec dubium mihi est, Prophetam in hoc loco imita- tum Davidi vaticinium Ps. 19. ubi doctrinam Ev- angelii comparat soli, ab extremo cœlorum, inquit, egressus ejus, & circuitus ad extremum eorum, & ne- mo est absconditus à calore ejus. Quia autem noster Propheta de initiis & quasi cunabulis Evangelii va- ticinatur, aptior auroræ similitudo fuit, quam solis. Hæc enim tanquam procul se ostendens orbi, paulatim ea incrementa sumit, ut ascendens sol lumine suo to- tum mundum illustret. Et porro: sed quorsum perti- net verbum (Nachon) quod vertimus firmatus est, alii vertunt paratum esse, at verum est. Significat (chon) paratum esse, sed sic ut stabile & firmum sit, nec possit aut everti, aut impediri. Ad hunc modum Propheta hic de Christo & Evangelio dicit, in quo Christi beneficium proponitur: Paratus est egressus ejus. Sicut enim auroram surgentem nemo pro- hibere, nec ejus lumen involvere potest, ne possit conspici, ita significet ministerium Evangelii im- pediri aut opprimi non posse, etsi id magno conatu Satan & mundus acturus sit. Convenit igitur sen- tentia cum illo Christi dicto: Portæ inferorum non prævalebunt. Ratio est, qui paratus & firma- Nonum è Messiani egressus præparatione: de quo ita Propheta: Quasi diluculum præparatus est egressus ejus, & veniet quasi imber nobis tempora- neus & serotinus terræ. Grotius ut posset τῇ ὑποθέ- σει δουλεύειν, distinctiones Ebræas negligit, ea, quæ non conjuncta sunt, conjunxit, aliena, quæ in textu non comparent, inseruit, & promissionem gratiæ simplicem in hypotheticam convertit, ita de hoc annotans: SCIEMUS SEQUEMURQUE, UT COGNOSCAMUS DOMINUM: QUA- SI DILUCULUM PRÆPARATUS EST EGRESSUS EJUS. Optimè sic vertas, supplendo quæ in Hebræo sæpe omitti solent: Si cognoscamus Dominum, & cognoscendo eum sectemur, tam promptum nobis erit ejus auxilium, quam est au- rora, ET VENIET QUASI IMBER NOBIS TEMPORANEUS, ET SEROTINUS TERRÆ.) Imber temporaneus dicitur, qui est se- mentis tempore, serotinus, qui adulta segete, ut diximus Deut. 11,14. Sensus est: omni tempore o- mnia ipsis à Deo prospera eventura. Sed juxta Hebræam veritatem textus ita habet: ut Hiero- nymus reddidit: sciemus sequamurque, ut cognosca- mus Dominum: Quasi diluculum (aurora) præpa- ratus est egressus ejus (Domini) & veniet quasi im- ber nobis (veluti) serotinus & temporaneus terræ, & uti B. Lutherus; Denn werden wir acht darauff haben, und fleissig seyn, daß wir den HErrn er- kennen, denn Er wird herfür brechen wie die schö- ne Morgenröthe, und wird zu uns kommen wie ein Regen, wie ein Spat-Regen, der das Land feuchtet. In schedis manu B. Lutheri scriptis, quas super hunc Prophetam, è communicatione Nobilissimi, & Consultissimi Dni. Joh. Martini Lutheri, Megalandri Pronepotis, Consiliarii E- lectoralis, Decani Zicensis, nec non Canonici Mise- nensis, Domini Affinis & Compatris mei honoran- di, habeo (quæ de summa Lutheri diligentia, & fide in translatione adhibita, evidenter testan- tur, & sæpe eandem vocem, phrasin aut senten- tiam, bis, terve inter vertendum mutatam, va- rieque tentatam, donec ea, quæ probaretur me- taphrasis, prodiret, docent) adjecta hæc nota est ejusdem manu: De Christo & Evangelio. Ex hoc ejusdem ἀυτογράφῳ, etiamsi ita varie emen- dato, typis exscripta est prima editio Vet. Test. quæ hic Wittebergæ Anno cIɔ Iɔ XXXII. ex offi- cina Joh. Lufft prodiit, additaque est glossa margi- nalis: Hier weissaget er von Christo, und dem Ev- angelio. Unde recte Osiander ea interpretatus in sua paraphrasi: Tunc Ecclesia Christi non erit ad verbum Dei stupida, ut antea, sed magno Zelo Evan- gelium Christi discet: ut ex eo Deum suum probe à- gnoscat. (Et sane ex actis Apostolicis notum est, quanta alacritate tum Judæi, tum gentes Evange- lion Christi receperint, & in agnitione Dei egre- gios progressus fecerint: quem Zelum nos imita- ri decet. Ac multi verbum Dei adeo fastidiunt, ut conciones inviti frequentent, & sacra Biblia vix aspicere dignantur) Quasi diluculum præparatus seu firmatus est egressus ejus: & veniet quasi imber nobis temporaneus: rectius: tempestivus, & serotinus terræ, (id est, exoritur nobis Christus Salvator tus est hujus Regis egressus per Evangelium, sicut auroræ, quæ impediri non potest, sed paulatim il- lustrior infundit se orbi. ET VENIET NOBIS SICUT PLUVIA, SICUT SERA PLUVIA TERRÆ. Hæc est altera consolatio, quod verbum, sicut non poterit impediri, ita etiam certum pariet fructum. Hæc enim causa est, cur Prophet a Evan- gelium pluviæ comparet, & quidem seræ, quæ se- getem, æstu solis assiduo pene exhaustam, sub messis tempus recreat, ut incrementum possit su- mere. B. Meisnerus triplicem egressum subintel- ligi posse censet. 1. Nativitatis, quum Messias ex utero Mariæ in mundum prodiit. 2. Resurrectio- nis, cum è sepulchro vivus exiit. 3. Prædicationis, cum per Evangelium in totum mundum egressus est, & beneficia, suo merito acquisita, credenti- bus applicavit, Psalm. 19, 3. 6. Sed hic proprie ter- tius egressus designatur, qui comparatur tum dilu- culo, vel auroræ, quia uti hæc noctem pellit, & te- nebras discutit, ita Christus per Evangelium egre- diens tanquam sol justitiæ, Mal. 4. & aurora diu expectata, fugavit omnes ignorantiæ, afflictionis & damnationis tenebras; tum pluviæ tempestivæ, seu matutinæ, & serotinæ (de qua Deut. 11. Joel. 2, 23.
