Vide ad Rom. 1. Verf. 11. EPHRAIM QUASI AVIS, AVOLAVIT GLORIA EORUM) Coharentia sunt haec, & est Hebraica locutio, pro Ephraimi gloria ut avis ebolabit. Gloriam intelligie hic foecunditatem, de qua se jactabant. A PARTU) Id est, infantes à matre recentes morientur. ET AB UTERO) Abortient feminae. ET A CONCUBITU) Concubitus erunt infecundi. Verf. 12.

## 9:12
Verf. 12. FOR THOUGH THEY HAVE BROUGHT UP THEIR CHILDREN) If it should happen to any to bring up children to some age. I WILL MAKE THEM CHILDLESS AMONG MEN) That is, I will cause them to be carried away into the places of the Assyrian empire. BUT ALSO WOE TO THEM) Furthermore, many evils shall befall them: namely in that exile. WHEN I SHALL DEPART FROM THEM) When I shall have utterly forsaken them. The LXX and Theodotion read 'basari' instead of 'basari', as Jerome notes.

Latin:

QUOD ETSI ENUTRIVERINT FILIOS SVOS) Si quibus contingat liberos ad aliquam aetatem educere. ABSQUE LIBERIS EOS FACIAM IN HOMINIBUS) Id est, faciam in loca Assyriaci imperii avehantur. SED ET VAE EIS) Praeterea multa mala eis obvenient: nempe in isto exilio. CVM RECESSERO AB EIS) Ubi eos penitus dereliquero. LXX. & Theodotion pro בשרי legerunt בשרי, ut notat Hieronymus.

## 9:13
Verf. 13. EPHRAIM AS I SAW, TYRE WAS FOUNDED IN BEAUTY) The Ephraimite nation, as if I were regarding Tyre, was so established in pleasant places. See Ezech. 28, 12. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion for Holem, for Schurec: ar LXX. Tsor, theran, which I say for this reason, that the old variety of Scripture may appear. AND EPHRAIM SHALL LEAD HIS CHILDREN TO THE SLAUGHTER) That is, he shall be forced by the enemies to produce them.

Latin:

Verf. 13. EPHRAIM UT VIDI, TYRUS ERAT FUNDATA IN PULCHRITUDINE) Gens Ephraimitica, quasi adficerem Tyrum, ita stabilita erat in amoenis locis. Vide Ezech. 28, 12. Aquila, Symmachus, & Theodotion pro Holem, pro Schurec: ar LXX. צור, θηραν, quod ideo dico, ut vetus Scripturae varietas appareat. ET EPHRAIM DUCET AD INTERFECTORUM FILIOS SVOS) Id est, ab hostibus cogetur producere.

## 9:14
Verf. 14. GIVE THEM O LORD, WHAT WILT THOU GIVE THEM?) Give them O Lord what Thou art about to give; that is, in the way Thou hadst said Thou wouldst give, namely sterility, or infants that are miscarried. The prophet, when he heard it would come to pass that parents would betray their children to the enemies, prayed to God that He might be content with a lesser punishment. --- or to be born Never or to die immediately upon being born) Miscarrying: for that is 'shakol'.

AND DRY BREASTS) Let there not be any whom they may suckle, infants. Verf. 15. ALL THEIR WICKEDNESS IN GILGAL) They do not now begin to sin for the first time in Gilgal, concerning which above 4, 15. Long ago they did that, when they despised Samuel, 1. Sam. 11, 15. and so deservedly I hate that place. The mystical sense is: that the Jews would bring it about through the highest crime that Christ be crucified in Golgotha: for this name is the same as Gilgal, except that it is a Syriac pronunciation.

We have often denied that a mystical sense, or one distinct from the literal, can exist at the same time in the same place. And here one must marvel at Grotius seeking a mystery where no one could easily have suspected it, and in countless places where mysteries are spontaneously obvious, and well observed by all, he does not recognize the mysteries, or certainly mixes in another entirely alien sense, which he sells as literal.

That savors of the singular genius of the man; but in expounding the scriptures, singularity was not so much to be affected as to be avoided. For they are not of private interpretation, and what, besides the affinity of letters, is common to Gilgal, that place near the Jordan Jos.

5, 9, which was once holy, but afterwards became a place where sins were accumulated, and idols were erected especially Hos. 2, 11, with Mount Golgotha, on which Christ was put upon the cross? THERE I HATED THEM) Even of old. FROM MY HOUSE I WILL CAST THEM OUT) God calls His house here the whole land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I WILL NO MORE LOVE THEM) I will no longer love them.

Latin:

Verf. 14. DA EIS DOMINE, QVID DA BIS EIS?) Da eis Domine quod daturus est; id est, quomodo daturum te dixeras, nempe sterilitatem, aut infantes ἀκυομένους. Propheta cum audivit futurum, ut parentes hostibus filios suos proderent, oravit Deum ut minore poena contentus esset. --- ἡ τὸ γενέσθαι Μηδέποτ' ἢ τὸ θανεῖν αὐτίκα τικτόμενον) Abortientem: id enim est שכל.

ET VBERA ARENTIA) Non sint ulli quos lactent, infantes. Verf. 15. OMNES NEQUITIAE EORUM IN GILGAL) Non nunc primum incipiunt peccare in Gilgale, de quo supra 4, 15. jam dudum id fecerunt, cum Samuelem contemferunt, 1. Sam. 11, 15. itaque merito eum locum odi, Mysticus sensus est: Judaeos per summum scelus effecturos, ut Christus crucifigatur in גלגלת: nam hoc nomen idem est cum גלגל, nisi quod Syriaca est pronunciatio.

Mysticum sensum, feu distinctum à literali, simul in eodem loco locum habere, faepius negavimus. Et mirari hic oportet Grotium mysterium quaerentem, ubi nemo facile id suspicari potuit, & innumeris locis, ubi ultro obvia sunt mysteria, & ab omnibus bene obfervata, mysteria non cognoscentem, vel certe alium plane ἀλλοτριον sensum, quem pro literali venditat, commiscentem.

Sapit id genium viri singularem; at in scripturis exponendis non tam affectanda, quam vitanda erat singularitas. Non enim sunt ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, Et quid praeter literarum affinitatem commune est Giligali, loco isti prope Jordanem Jof.

5, 9. quae sancta quondam fuit, sed postmodum locus factus est, ubi cumulata peccata, & erecta imprimis idola Hof. 2, 11. cum monte Golgatha, in quo Christus in crucem actus est? IBI EXOSOS HABUI EOS) Etiam olim. DE DOMO MEA EJICIAM EOS) Domum hic suam vocat Deum totam terram promissam Abrahamo, Ifaaco, Jacobo. NON ADDAM UT DILIGAM EOS) Non ultra eos amabo.

## 9:15
ALL THEIR PRINCES ARE REVOLTERS) They have fallen away from me, either by worshipping false deities, or by assimilating me to calves. Verf. 16. EPHRAIM IS SMITTEN) He shall be smitten, namely with sterility, as above 2. See Psalm 102, 5. THEIR ROOT IS DRIED UP) The generative power. FOR THOUGH THEY BRING FORTH, I WILL SLAY THE MOST BELOVED OF THEIR WOMB) He had written, I think, the interpreter 'most beloved', the 'inimnumata': that is, children long desired.

Latin:

OMNES PRINCIPES EORUM RECEDENTES) Defecerunt à me, aut falfa numina colendo, aut me assimilando vitulis. Verf. 16. PERCUSSUS EST EPHRAIM) Percutietur, nempe sterilitate, ut supra 2. Vide Pfalm. 102, 5. RADIX EORUM EXSICCATA EST) Vis genitrix. QUOD ETSI GENUERINT, INTERFICIAM AMANTISSIMA UTERI EORUM) Scripserat, puto, interpres amatiflima, τὰ ἰνιμνύματα: id est, liberos diu optatos.

## 9:17
Verf. 17. MY GOD WILL CAST THEM AWAY) God who will henceforth be the God of the prophets, but not also of the people. AND THEY SHALL BE WANDERERS AMONG THE NATIONS) Dispersed among the gentiles. See 2. Kings 15, 29, 16, 6. 1. Chronicles 5, 26.

Latin:

Verf. 17. ABJICIET EOS DEUS MEUS) Deus posthac futurus Prophetarum, non & populi. ET ERUNT VAGI IN NATIONIBUS) Disperfi inter gentes. Vide 2. Reg. 15, 29, 16, 6. 1. Para. lip. 5, 26.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. Penitential Trumpet.

The idolatrous altars of the Israelites are to be destroyed, covenants to be changed into gall: the idols of the calves, with the King, are to be carried away, the high places to be laid waste, with the eternal despair of the worshippers. Therefore he predicts a punishment more grievous than that of the Gibeonites was, and the humiliation of the proud calves of Ephraim, and they are warned to bear justice, not iniquity: and the confidence of the strength of their Heroes is announced, and the destruction of their fortifications and of the King himself, which will be shortly. He shall subvert the idol's crops of the plow. Verf. 1. ISRAEL IS AN EMPTY VINE) From the Greek LXX, a vine putting forth branches.

Aquila translates 'a vine', Symmachus 'a vine', the Chaldean 'laid waste': which agrees best with the Hebrew. The sense is: that the land of Israel shall be empty of cultivators. Isaiah 5, 6. FRUIT ACCORDING TO IT) In the Hebrew: He set fruit for himself. That is, whereas it was formerly fruit-bearing. ACCORDING TO THE MULTITUDE OF HIS FRUIT, HE HATH INCREASED THE ALTARS: ACCORDING TO THE FAT

THE ABUNDANCE OF HIS LAND, HE HAS ABOUNDED WITH IDOLS) The more prosperous his affairs were, the more he indulged in idolatry.

Latin:

CAPUT X. Tuba Poenitentialis. Idololatrica altaria Ifraelitarum destruenda, foedera in fel mutanda: idola vitulorum, cum Rege, abducenda, excelfa desolanda, cum aeterna cultorum desperatione.

Pradicit itaque gravior, quam Gibeonitarum erat, poena, & Ephrajmi vituli superbi humiliatio, ac monentur ad ferendum justitiam, non iniquitatem: & fiduciam fortitudinis Heroum fuorum de nunciatur & munitionum & Regis ipfius exitium, brevi futurum. Subruet idoli segetes olvarum. Verf. 1. VITIS FRONDOSA ISRAEL) Ex Graeco LXX, fenum ἐκκληματῦσα.

Aquila vertit ἦνδρον, Symmachus ἐλομαξᾶσαν, Chaldaeus vastatam: quod optime cum Hebraeo convenit. Senfus est: fore ut terra Ifraelis fit cultoribus vacua. Efaiz 5, 6. FRUCTUS ADAEQUATUS EI) In Hebraeo: Fructum sibi pofuit. Id est, antehac frugifera cum esset. SECUNDUM MULTITUDINEM FRUCTUS SUI, MULTIPLICAVIT ALTARIA: JUXTA UBER

UBERTATEM TERRÆ SVÆ, EXUBERAVIT SI- MULACRIS) Quo res habuit prosperiores, eo magis in- dulsit idololatriæ.

## 10:2
Ver. 2.

THEIR HEART IS DIVIDED) He has departed from the law. Thus the Chaldean. The Hebrews, as Jerome relates, say that the people dissented from King Hoshea, who was calling them back to piety; for the king was less evil than his predecessors, even if not entirely good. 2 Kings 17:2. That this is predicted here. AND HE SHALL BREAK THEIR IDOLS) God, of whom it was treated a little before 9:17; but He will do this through the Assyrians. For idols, in the Hebrew it is altars. HE SHALL LAY WASTE THE ALTARS) Here in the Hebrew it is statues, מַצֵּבוֹת from נָצַב, concerning which word Stephanus says thus: Νάσιβ, signifies pillars as Philo says. To whom also Ouranius, Nesaibis, he says, signifies in the Phoenician language a stone put together.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

DIVISUM EST COR EORVM) A lege recessit Ita Chaldæus. Hebræi, ut narrat Hieronymus, ajunt po- pulum dissensisse à rege Osea, qui eos ad pietatem revoca- bat, erat enim rex minus malus quam priores, etiam si non plane bonus. 2. Reg. 17, 2. id hic prædici. ET CONFREGIT SIMULACRA EORVM) Deus, de quo actum paulo ante 9, 17. faciet autem hoc per Assyrios. Pro simulacra, in Hebræo est aras. DEPOPULABITUR ARAS) Hic in Hebræo est statuas, מַצֵּבוֹת à נָצַב, de qua voce sic Stephanus: Νάσιβ, σημαίνει τὰς στήλας ὥς φησι Φίλων. οἷς δὲ Ουράνι@, Νέσαιβις, φησὶ, σημαίνει τῇ Φοινίκων γλώττῃ λίθ@ συγκείμεν@.

## 10:3
Ver. 3.

FOR NOW THEY SHALL SAY: WE HAVE NO KING) That is, we do not care for the rule of King Hoshea: this they are about to say. FOR WE DO NOT FEAR THE LORD) In the Hebrew: we have not feared. That is, we have long since abandoned the worship of God. AND WHAT SHALL THE KING DO FOR US?) What has he done? That is, what could he do to harm us? For whatever is sinned by many is much.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

QUIA NUNC DICENT: NON EST REX NOBIS) Id est, non curamus imperia Oseæ regis: hoc il- li dicturi sunt. NON ENIM TIMEMUS DOMINUM) In He- bræo: non timuimus. Id est, pridem deseruinus Dei cultum. ET REX QVID FACIET NOBIS?) Quid fecit? Id est, quid nocere nobis potuit? nam Quicquid multis peccatur multum est.

## 10:4
Ver. 4.

YOU SPEAK WORDS OF A USELESS VISION, AND YOU SHALL STRIKE A COVENANT) They will speak words of a false oath when they strike a covenant. When they promise loyalty to the king by oath, as was the custom, they will think of nothing less than observing it. AND JUDGMENT SHALL SPRING UP LIKE BITTERNESS UPON THE FURROWS OF THE FIELD) There is also here a transposition of words, such as we have often had. The meaning is: punishment will abound just as darnel is wont to do in fields. רֹאשׁ to the Hebrews signifies both poison and bitterness, and that word is wont by similarity to be transferred also to other pernicious things. The LXX here have placed ἄγρωστιν, a kind of herb harmful to crops, concerning which see Jerome on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

LOQVIMINI VERBA VISIONIS INUTILIS, ET FERIETIS FEDUS) Loquentur verba juramenti falso cum pangent fœdus. Cum regi fidem juramento pollicebun- tur, ut moris erat, nihil minus cogitabunt, quam de eo observando. ET GERMINABIT QUASI AMARITUDO JU- DICIVM SVPER SVLCOS AGRI) Est & hic traje- ctio verborum, qualem sæpe habuimus. Sensus est: pœna ita abundabit, ut solet in agris lolium. רֹאשׁ Hebræis & venenum & amaritiem significat, soletque per similitudi- nem ea vox & ad alia perniciosa transferri. LXX. hic po- suere ἄγρωστιν herbæ genus frugibus nocens, de quo vide Hieronymum ad hunc locum.

## 10:5
Ver. 5.

THE INHABITANTS OF SAMARIA HAVE WORSHIPPED THE COWS OF BETHAVEN) The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear for the calves of Bethaven. The history which is referred to here is not only in Jerome in this place, but also in the Seder Olam Rabbah, part four. BECAUSE HIS PEOPLE MOURNED OVER IT) He shall mourn. To Shalmaneser (whom the Hebrews often confuse with Sennacherib) two calves were sent, which the people thought were those very golden calves which Jeroboam had made. The Hebrews call both calves and cows ἐπικοίνως (in common). AND HIS PRIESTS REJOICED OVER IT) The priests were glad about it, namely because they had substituted gilded bronze ones for the golden ones. Grotius feeds on Rabbinical fables from the Seder Olam and Jerome, that the priests had removed the calf and substituted one of bronze covered with gold, and that the people therefore mourned because they thought the golden calf had been taken away, but the priests were glad because they knew the Babylonian King had been deceived. But if, setting aside the Vulgate, the Hebrew text is attended to, it will be manifest that there is no need for such trifles: in the Hebrew it is יָגִילוּ which signifies both to fear and to go into exile. Therefore it is rightly translated thus: The Samaritans shall go into exile because of the calves of Bethaven; if the sense of fearing is retained, they are said to fear because of the incursions of the Assyrians, lest they should destroy the idols, as B. Luther: The inhabitants of Samaria worry about the calves of Bethaven. B. Gesner with the Chaldean and Jerome rendered: they worshipped the cows of Bethaven, i.e., Up to this point the citizens of Samaria worshipped the golden calf, but his people mourned (shall mourn) over it: The priests rejoiced over it in its glory: but it has migrated (shall migrate) from it. They shall not have, therefore, anything to rejoice over anymore. Which meaning is plain, so that there is no need at all to leave the passage to the fables of the Jews. Add that Joh. Cocceius notes, that not even a jot of these things is found in the Commentaries of the Hebrews, nor does the Seder Olam of the Frobenian edition consist of four, but of three parts, and where the exile of the calf is treated, nor is a word found about the gilding.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

VACCAS BETHAVEN COLVERVNT HABI- TATORES SAMARIÆ) Ob vitulas Bethaven pavebunt habitatores Samariæ. Historia, quæ hic respicitur, est non tantum apud Hieronymum hoc loco, sed & in Seder Olam majore, parte quarta. QUIA LUXIT SVPER EUM POPULUS EJUS) Lugebit. Ad Salmanassarem (quem cum Sennacheribo sæ- pe confundunt Hebræi) missi sunt duo vituli, quos popu- lus putabat esse illos ipsos vitulos aureos, quos fecerat Je- roboam. Hebræi & vitulos & vitulas dicunt ἐπικοίνως. ET ÆDITUI EJUS SVPER EVM EXSVLTA- VERUNT) Sacerdotes de eo lætabantur, nempe quia pro aureis supposuerant æneos deauratos. Pascitur Grotius fabulis Rabbinicis è Seder Olam & Hieronymo, quod Sacerdotes vitulum sub- duxerint, æneum vero auro obductum substituerint, populum ergo luxisse, quia ratus est aureum vitulum sublatum esse, sed Sacerdotes lætos fuisse, quia sciebant Regem Babylonicum esse delusum. Si autem post- habita vulgata, textus Ebræus attendatur, opus non esse talibus nugis, manifestum erit: in E- bræo est יָגִילוּ quod & pavere & exulare significat. Ideo ita vertitur recte: Exulabunt Samaritani pro- pter vitulos Bethaven; si retineatur pavendi sen- sus, pavere dicuntur propter irruptiones Assyrio- rum, ne idola destruerent, uti B. Lutherus: Die Einwohner zu Samaria sorgen für die Kälber zu Bethaven. B. Gesnerus cum Chaldæo & Hierony- mo reddidit: coluerunt vaccas Bethaven q. d. Huc- usque cives Samariæ aureum vitulum coluerunt, at luxit (lugebit) super eum populus ejus: Sacrificuli super eum exultarunt in gloria ejus: at migravit (migrabit) ab eo. Non habebunt ergo, quod lætentur amplius super eo. Qui sensus planus est, ut minime necesse sit locum fabellis Judæorum relinquere. Adde quod Joh. Cocce- jus notet, nec in Commentariis Ebræorum vel γρὺ de his haberi, nec Seder Olam editionis Fro- benianæ quatuor, sed tribus partibus constare, & ubi de exilio vituli agitur, de deauratione item nec μῦ reperiri.

## 10:6
Ver. 6. FOR HE HIMSELF ALSO SHALL BE CARRIED INTO ASSYRIA) He shall be carried. Both calves shall go into Assyria. A GIFT TO THE AVENGER KING) Here again in the Hebrew is ירב, as above v. 13, that is, to the helper, the protector. They called by this name the lesser kings, the greater ones, to whose faith and protection they had given themselves. See 2 Kings 17:3. CONFUSION SHALL TAKE EPHRAIM, AND ISRAEL SHALL BE ASHAMED OF HIS OWN WILL) The king, the fraud having been detected, shall treat the Israelites with insults: because of their own counsel: that is, the fraud of the priests.

Latin:

Vers. 6. SIQUIDEM ET IPSE IN ASSVR DELATVS EST) Deferetur. Uterque vitulus in Assyriam ibit. MUNUS REGI ULTORI) Est hic iterum in He- bræo ירב, ut supra v. 13. id est, adjutori, protectori. Appel- labant hoc nomine reges minores, alios majores, quorum se in fidem clientelamque dederant. Vide 2. Reg. 17, 3. CONFUSIO EPHRAIM CAPIET, ET CON- FUNDETUR ISRAEL IN VOLUNTATE SUA) Rex fraude deprehensa, contumeliis afficiet Israelitas: propter consilium suum: id est, fraudem sacerdotum.

## 10:7
Vers. 7. SAMARIA HAS MADE HER KING PASS AWAY LIKE FOAM UPON THE FACE OF THE WATER) In the Hebrew: Samaria has perished, her king: that is, and her king, as the Chaldean rightly understood. That which is like foam (ἐπίζεμα in Symmachus) on the surface of the water, namely that which is in the pot, signifies swiftness.

Latin:

Vers. 7. TRANSIRE FECIT SAMARIA REGEM SVVM QVASI SPUMAM SUPER FACIEM AQUÆ) In He- bræo: Periit Samaria, rex ejus: id est, & rex ejus, ut recte accepit Chaldæus. Illud ut spuma (ἐπίζεμα Symmacho) in superficie aquæ, nempe ejus quæ in olla est, celeritatem significat.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. AND THE HIGH PLACES OF THE IDOL SHALL BE DESTROYED) Those hills on which idols were worshipped. AND THEY SHALL SAY TO THE MOUNTAINS, COVER US: AND TO THE HILLS FALL UPON US) They will seek to hide even in the most secluded caves. Isaiah 2:9. Luke 23:30. Revelation 6:16.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET DISPERDENTUR EXCELSA IDOLI) Col- les illi in quibus idola colebantur. ET DICENT MONTIBUS, OPERITE NOS: ET COLLIBVS CADITE SVPER NOS) Quærent latere vel in abstrusissimis specubus. Esaiæ 2, 9. Lucæ 27, 30. Apoc. 6, 16.

## 10:9
Vers. 9. FROM THE DAYS OF GIBEAH ISRAEL HAS SINNED) You have sinned, in the Hebrew. It is not a new thing that crimes, however great, are observed in the descendants of Jacob. It appeared long ago in Gibeah. See above 9:9. THERE THEY STOOD) At that time, however, because there were those who punished the crimes, the people remained in their land. GIBEAH SHALL NOT OVERTAKE THEM, THE BATTLE AGAINST THE SONS OF INIQUITY) The battle in Gibeah did not overtake them against the sons of iniquity. That is, they were not made captives, since they were severe avengers of crimes. For in the final battle they were the victors. Judges 20.

Latin:

Vers. 9. EX DIEBUS GABAA PECCAVIT ISRAEL) Peccasti, in Hebræo. Non novum est quod scelera quam- vis magna conspiciantur in posteris Jacobi. Apparuit id jam pridem in Gabaa. Vide supra 9, 9. IBI STETERVNT) Illo tamen tempore, quia erant qui scelera puniebant, mansit populus in terra sua. NON COMPREHENDET EOS GABAA, PRÆ- LIUM SUPER FILIOS INIQUITATIS) Non compre- hendit eos prælium in Gabaa contra filios iniquitatis. Id est, non facti sunt captivi, cum severi essent scelerum vindices. Nam ultimo prælio victores fuere. Jud. 20.

## 10:10
Vers. 10. ACCORDING TO MY DESIRE I WILL CHASTISE THEM) Now it is in my mind to bind them. That is, that they may become captives. PEOPLES SHALL BE GATHERED AGAINST THEM) Since they themselves did not punish the crimes, foreign peoples will do it. WHEN THEY SHALL BE CHASTISED FOR THEIR TWO INIQUITIES) Then they shall be bound for their two sins. That is, the two calves, in whose worship they sinned.

Latin:

Vers. 10. JVXTA DESIDERIUM MEUM CORRIPIAM EOS) Nunc in animo mihi est ut vinciam eos. Id est, ut fiant captivi. CONGREGABUNTUR SUPER EOS POPU- LI) Quandoquidem ipsi scelera non puniere, facient id populi externi. CUM CORRIPIENTUR PROPTER DVAS INIQVITATES SUAS) Tunc vincientur propter duo pecca- ta sua. Id est, duos vitulos, in quorum cultu peccavere.

## 10:11
Vers. 11. EPHRAIM IS A HEIFER TAUGHT TO LOVE THRESHING) Because they had compared God to a calf, God himself more justly compares them to that calf or young bull. Ephraim is a docile heifer: that is, she seemed to me to be capable of being well taught. Because the Hebrews almost entirely lack verbal nouns, they use their participles in their place. I loved threshing: God, of course, who is speaking. I loved, he says, the produce of the field, which is in the threshing. Other interpreters have taken this here as a causative, about which we have spoken elsewhere. AND I PASSED OVER THE BEAUTY OF HER NECK, I WILL RIDE UPON EPHRAIM) I made (supply yoke, as Jerome does here) pass over her beautiful neck: and I myself have been carried by Ephraim: namely, as rustics are sometimes accustomed to sit upon oxen. The sense is: I imposed a law upon them, and I myself was their ruler. JUDAH SHALL PLOW) יעבוד יה instead of: I said, Judah shall plow. He continues in the metaphor of agriculture, which he will pursue for a long time. חרש both here and below in 13. Jerome noted here that the LXX wrongly took it in the sense of keeping silent. JACOB SHALL BREAK HIS FURROWS) Jacob shall harrow. See Job 39:13.

Latin:

Vers. 11. EPHRAIM VITULA DOCTA DILIGERE TRI- TURAM) Quia illi Deum vitulo comparaverant, ipse Deus justius illo vitulo aut juvenco comparat. Ephraim vitula docilis: id est, visa est mihi bene edoceri pos- se. Hebræi quia verbalibus ferme carent, participiis eorum vice utuntur. Diligebam trituram: Deus scilicet qui loqui- tur. Amabam, inquit, ruris proventum, qui est in tritura. Alii Interpretes hic sumserunt, ut παραγωγικὸν, de quo diximus alibi. ET EGO TRANSIVI SVPER PULCHRITU- DINEM COLLI EJUS, ADSCENDAM SUPER E- PHRAIM) Transire feci (supple jugum, ut hic Hierony- mus) super pulchras cervices ejus: & ipse vectus sum Ephrai- mo: nempe, ut solent interdum rustici insidere bubus. Sen- sus est: legem eis imposui, & ipse rector eorum fui. ARABIT JUDAS) יעבוד יוה pro: dixi, aret Judas. Pergit in similitudine agriculturæ, quam diu persequetur. חרש & hic & infra 13. LXX. male sumpsisse in tacendi sensu notavit hic Hieronymus. CONFRINGET SIBI SULCOS JACOB) Occet Jacob. Vide Job. 39, 13.

## 10:12
Vers. 12. SOW FOR YOURSELVES IN RIGHTEOUSNESS) God continues to relate what he commanded them, and mixes the comparison taken from agriculture with the apodosis. To sow is to do good: to reap is to receive a reward, as we have already seen several times before. AND REAP IN THE MOUTH OF MERCY) That you may reap according to mercy, namely, of GOD. על־פי and לפי are often the same to the Hebrews as κατὰ is to the Greeks. BREAK UP FOR YOURSELVES A FALLOW FIELD) Plow for yourselves a field. BUT THE TIME TO SEEK THE LORD) Better, For the time: for ו receives both senses. WHEN HE SHALL COME WHO SHALL TEACH YOU RIGHTEOUSNESS) Until he comes who shall rain down righteousness upon you. Who shall irrigate you with his benefits.

Latin:

Vers. 12. SEMINATE VOBIS IN JUSTITIA) Per- git Deus referre quid ipsis imperaverit, & miscet compara- tionem ab agricultura sumtam cum τῇ ἀποδόσει. Seminare est bene agere: metere est referre mercedem, ut jam ante vidimus aliquoties. ET METITE IN ORE MISERICORDIÆ) Ut metatis secundum misericordiam, nempe DEI. על־פי & לפי sæpe idem est Hebræis, quod Græcis κατὰ. INNOVATE VOBIS NOVALE) Arate vobis arvum. TEMPVS AVTEM REQVIRENDI DOMI- NVM) Melius, Tempus enim: nam ו utrumque sensum recipit. CUM VENERIT QVI DOCEBIT VOS JU- STITIAM) Donec veniat qui depluat super vos justitiam. Qui vos irriget suis beneficiis.

## 10:13
Vers. 13. YOU HAVE PLOWED WICKEDNESS) You have done the opposite of what I hoped: you have devoted effort to impious things,

INIQVITATEM) That is, the punishment of sins, in which way עוֹלָה is often taken.

MESSVISTIS) You will reap.

COMEDISTIS FRUGEM MENDACII) Feed on false fruit: specious, but not nourishing.

QUIA CONFISVS ES IN VIIS TUIS IN MULTITUDINE FORTIUM TUORUM) It shifts from the plural to the singular. For we are accustomed to use both when we address some body consisting of many. This was, however, the beginning of a new sense, to which the following things cohere: A tumult will arise. The sense is: God being despised, your own ways pleased you, and you thought you had the fate of your strength in your youth and your allies. For דַרְכְּךָ the LXX read רִכְבְּךָ, ἐν τοῖς ἅρμασί σε, which Jerome also teaches us, for which some codices wrongly have: ἁμαρτήμασί σε.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ARASTIS IMPIETATEM) Contra fecistis quam sperabam: operam dedistis rebus impiis,

INIQVITATEM) Id est, pœnam peccatorum, quo modo sæpe sumitur עוֹלָה.

MESSVISTIS) Metetis.

COMEDISTIS FRUGEM MENDACII) Pasce- mini fruge falsa: speciosa, sed non alente.

QUIA CONFISVS ES IN VIIS TUIS IN MULTITUDINE FORTIUM TUORUM) Transit a plurali ad singularem. Nam utroque uti solemus cum cor- pus aliquod ex multis constans alloquimur. Fuit autem hic initium novi sensus, cui cohærent sequentia: Consurget tumultus. Sensus est: Deo comtemto, tui mores tibi placue- re, fatisque virium in juventute tua & sociis habere putasti. Pro דַרְכְּךָ LXX. legerunt רִכְבְּךָ, ἐν τοῖς ἅρμασί σε, quod & Hieronymus nos docet, pro quo quidam codices male habent: ἁμαρτήμασί σε.

## 10:14
Vers. 14.

CONSV RGET TVMVLTVS IN POPVLO TUO) Therefore it arises. For such is the force here of the particle ו. The word שָׁאוֹן, which is translated here as tumult, signifies a hostile sound.

ET OMNES MUNITIONES TUÆ VASTA- BVNTVR) All places, even the most fortified. There is also here in the Hebrew a singular verb constructed with a plural noun.

SICVT VASTATVS EST SALMAN A.) King of the Midianites, Jud. 8, 5. etc.

A DOMO EJUS QVI JVDICAVIT BAAL IN DIE PRÆLII) In Hebrew בֵּית אַרְבֵאל, which the Greeks translated ἐκ τᾶ οἴκυ Ἰεροβαάλ: for Jerome teaches us well that it should be read thus, for which the vulgate codices corruptly have Ἰεροβοάμ. Jerobaal is the surname of Gideon. It is written in Hebrew יְרֻבַּעַל Jud. 6, 31. which the Latin here explains by periphrasis, he who judged Baal, expressing the origin of the name. Moreover, א is accustomed to be placed at the beginning for י & ע, or to be omitted, as בֵּל for בַּעַל, or to be changed into a softer letter, as here אַרְבֵאל. The Greek version adds here ἐκ, as if supplying the Hebrew defect of the letter ב. Then it seems to take οἶκον for an army; which inconveniences can be avoided if for בֵּית one writes בִּיר, that is, by Jerobaal. Some understand Salmanassarus here by Salman, and think that some victory was obtained by him from Arbala. But these things were written before the time of Shalmaneser, if indeed the notation of time at the beginning of the written book pertains to the whole book. The Chaldean does not take שַׁלְמָן as a proper name, but as "peaceful," and translates אַרְבֵאל as "by ambushes," taking א as paragogic: for אֹרֶב means ambushes. He explains: as a man living in peace is devastated by ambushes in time of war.

MATRE SUPER FILIOS ALLISA) A proverbial kind of speaking, signifying such a slaughter in which neither sex nor age is spared, Gen. 32, 11.

Note here again the rashness and audacity of Grotius regarding the authentic text, because he attempts to make בִּיר out of בֵּית. But who gave him this power of changing the sacred Code? Nor does the history of Jerubbaal fit the place. For first, the names Arbel and Jerubbaal are different, not only as to the letters, but especially as to the points, which are not to be neglected. Then, the Salma of this place is written with ש, but Zalmunna in Jud. 8, 11 with צ; the former denotes peaceful, the latter a shadow or a minute image. Third, the history to be compared was not about a slaughtered King, but about some city being razed, since the Prophet prophesies that the cities of the Israelites would likewise be razed. Fourth, the verb of laying waste does not fit a person, or Zalmun, but a city or fortification. Fifth, the object of the devastation is not Salmon, but Arbel. Therefore, those are not to be inverted. In Hebrew it is: as to laying waste Salman Beth Arbeel, and not as the Vulgate has it, as Salman was laid waste by the house, etc. And therefore others rightly understand by Beth Arbel not the house or family of some Arbel, but a town in the land of Samaria, which Jerome in the Hebrew places calls the border of Judea, a village beyond the Jordan in the borders of Pella, who also observes that another place in a very large field was called by this name. The Vulgate therefore deserved correction here again: which Grotius, in order to defend, dared to corrupt the authentic text. Ribera complained about this, Rivet p. 336. It is wonderful how those who have sworn by the words of the Vulgate twist themselves to defend it, especially Ribera, who not only transforms ש into שׁ; and elides the ע at the end of the name of the Prince of the Midianites, but also considers אל Ael and באל Baal to be the same. And he thinks there is no difference between Beth Arbel and Jerubbaal; because he does not want to force his Church to unlearn after so many centuries; while otherwise he acknowledges that his interpretation can hardly be defended. Grotius had not sworn by the words of the Vulgate, nor yet does he acquiesce to those corruptions to support it, but rather amends the text of the Holy Spirit, and converts בית into ביר.

However, the history referred to is commonly known, even if not commemorated in the Holy Scriptures, concerning the slaughter that took place in the town or field of Galilee, Arbel, or Beth Arbel, in which mothers were cruelly slaughtered with their infants. Which is believed to have been done by Shalmaneser in the first incursion into Samaria, so that Salman is called Salmanasser, adding the epithet Asser, also used for other Kings, as is the example of Tiglath-Pileser, 2 Kings 15, 29.

As to the doubt of Grotius from Chronology, B. Gesner shows rather that the time fits very well here: For Hosea, as was said in the first chapter, preached in the time of Ahaz and Hezekiah, Kings of Judah: but in the twelfth year of Ahaz, Hoshea son of Elah became King of Israel, against whom Shalmaneser ascended, and first made him a tributary, in his seventh year, and the fifth of Hezekiah; then he shut him in prison, and finally in the ninth and last year of his reign, he led away the ten tribes, which falls into the seventh year of Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18, verse 9. The Prophet therefore proposes a sad spectacle, which was still in everyone's eyes, ears, and memory, and threatens that what had happened to Arbela or Betharbel would happen to the remaining cities of Samaria and Galilee, unless they repent.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

CONSV RGET TVMVLTVS IN POPVLO TUO) Ideo consurgit. Ea enim vis hic est particulæ ו. Vox שָׁאוֹן, quæ hic vertitur tumultus, significat hostilem so- nitum.

ET OMNES MUNITIONES TUÆ VASTA- BVNTVR) Omnia loca etiam munitissima. Est & hic in Hebræo verbum singulare constructum cum nomine plurali.

SICVT VASTATVS EST SALMAN A.) Rex Madianitarum, Jud. 8, 5. &c.

A DOMO EJUS QVI JVDICAVIT BAAL IN DIE PRÆLII) In Hebræo בֵּית אַרְבֵאל, quod Græci verterunt ἐκ τᾶ οἴκυ Ἰεροβαάλ: nam sic legendum bene nos docet Hieronymus, pro quo vulgati codices cor- rupte habent Ἰεροβοάμ. Jerobaal est cognomen Gedeonis. Scribitur Hebraice יְרֻבַּעַל Jud. 6, 31. quod hic Latinus pe- riphraseice explicat, qui judicavit Baal, originem nominis exprimens. Solet autem & א in initio poni pro י & ע, aut omitti, ut בֵּל pro בַּעַל, aut in leniorem literam mutari, ut hic אַרְבֵאל. Græca versio addit hic ἐκ, quasi supplens He- bræum defectum literæ ב. Deinde οἶκον videtur sumere pro exercitu; quæ incommoda vitari possunt, si pro בֵּית scriba- tur בִּיר, id est, per Jerobaalem. Quidam per Salmanem Sal- manassarem hic intelligunt, & ei putant victoriam aliquam ab Arbala obtigisse. Verum hæc scripta sunt ante Salma- nassaris tempus, si modo notatio temporis initio scripti libri ad totum librum pertinet. Chaldæus שַׁלְמָן non pro pro- prio nomine sumit, sed pro pacifico & אַרְבֵאל vertit per insidias, ut א sit παραγωγικόν: nam אֹרֶב insidiæ. Explicat: sicut vastatur homo in pace vivens, per insidias, in belli tempore.

MATRE SUPER FILIOS ALLISA) Loquendi Genus proverbiale, significans occidionem talem, in qua non sexui, non ætati parcitur, Gen. 32, 11.

Notanda hic iterum temeritas, & audacia Grotii in textum authenticum, quod ex בֵּית facere conetur בִּיר. At quis ei hanc potestatem dedit mu- tandi sacrum Codicem? Neque convenit loco hi- storia Jerubaal. Nam primo nomina diversa sunt Arbel & Jerubaal, non modo quod ad literas, sed imprimis quoad puncta, quæ negligenda non sunt. Deinde Salma hujus loci per ש scribitur, at Zalmu- na Jud. 8, 11. per צ, illud pacificum notat, hoc um- bram vel imaginem minutam. Tertio non de Rege trucidato conferenda historia erat, sed de excisa ur- be aliqua, siquidem pariter urbes Israëlitarum exci- sum iri vaticinetur Propheta. Quarto verbum va- standi non convenit personæ, seu Zalmoni, sed urbi aut munitioni. Quinto objectum vastationis non est Salmon, sed Arbel. Non ergo illa invertenda. In Ebræo est: secundum vastare Salman Beth Ar- beel, non vero ut vulgata, sicut vastatus est Salman à domo, &c. Ideoque recte alii per Beth Arbel non domum, aut familiam Arbeli cujusdam, sed oppi- dum in terra Samariæ, intelligunt, quod Hierony- mus in locis Ebræis terminum Judæ dicit, vicum trans Jordanem in finibus Pellæ, qui etiam obfervat alium locum in campo prægrandi hoc vocabulo nuncupatum esse. Castigationem ergo merebatur hic iterum vulgata: quam ut tueretur Grotius, corrumpere textum authenticum ausus est. Que- stus est hic de Ribera Rivetus pag. 336. vulgatam versionem, ut defendant, qui in ejus verba jurarunt, mirum quam se torqueant, inprimis Ribera, qui non solum ש in שׁ transformat; & ע in fine nominis Prin- cipis Madianitarum elidit, sed etiam אל Ael & באל Baal pro eodem habet. Et inter Beth Arbel, & Jerubbaal nihil discriminis esse putat; quia non vult cogere Ecclesiam suam ut dediscat post tot anno- rum centurias; cum alioquin agnoscat aegre posse de- fendi suam interpretationem. Non jurarat in verba vulgata Grotius, nec tamen pro ea sustinenda illis acquiescit corruptelis, quin textum Spiritus sancti emendet, & בית in ביר, convertat.

Historia autem respicitur in vulgus nota, etsi in S. literis non commemorata, de clade in oppido vel campo Galilaeae Arbel, vel Beth arbel facta, in qua matres cum infantibus crudeliter jugulatae. Quod à Salmassare in prima irruptione in Samariam fa- ctum creditur, ut Salman dictus sit Salmanasser, ad- dido Epit heto Asser, aliis quoque Regibus usitato, ut exemplo est Tiglath Pelasser 3. Reg. 15, 29.

Quod ad dubium Grotii è Chronologia, ostendit potius B. Gesnerus, optime hic tempus convenit: Nam Oseas, ut capite primo dictum est, concionatus est tempore Achasi & Ezechiae Regum Iudae: anno autem duodecimo Achasi, Oseas filius El- la factus est Rex Israelis, contra quem ascendit Sal- manasser, eumque primo tributarium fecit, anno ipsius septimo, & Ezechiae quinto; deinde carceri inclusit, & tandem anno nono ac ultimo ejus regni, decem tri- bus abduxit, quod in annum Ezechiae septimum inci- dit, 2. Reg. 18. vers. 9. Proponit itaque Propheta triste spectaculum, quod in omnium adhuc oculis, auribus & memoria versabatur, & quod Arbela seu Bethar- belae acciderat, idem reliquis urbibus Samariae & Ga- lilaeae eventurum minatur, nisi resipiscant.

## 11:1 Argument
Vers. 1.

SO HAS BETHEL DONE TO YOU) That is, idolatry, whose seat is Bethel, will be the cause that a similar calamity may happen to you.

FROM THE FACE OF THE MALICE OF YOUR WICKEDNESSES AS THE MORNING PASSES, ISRAEL HAS PASSED) These are to be connected in such a way that, as in the Hebrew, they are divided in the Latin, not only by period, but also by chapters. In Hebrew: From the face of the malice, the malice, I say, of your wickedness, in the dawn the King of Israel will be cut off by destruction: That is, in the very beginnings of the kingdom, King Hoshea son of Elah will be uprooted from the kingdom and the fatherland.

Grotius [says] these things not badly. But it pleases me to add the commentary of Cocceius, so that we may have an example again, by which the private interpretation of a man in treating the Holy Scriptures is made clear. For he dreams here of the killing of the King of Sweden, Gustavus Adolphus, and the slaughter of the King of England, Charles, and the destruction of the cities of Germany. This pericope, he says, p. 110, comprises the chastisement of the Evangelical Church. It consists in the calamity or slaughter of armies, in the occupation of places after fortifications have been overcome or broken through. Just as we have seen the Palatinate, Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia, Pomerania, Upper and Lower Saxony, Holstein, the Cimbrian Chersonese, and thus from the Baltic Sea to the Northern Sea, and again the Rhine, to which also Wesel and other fortresses [belong], all to have come into power. In the end he adds a terrible example of calamity, which he calls the elision of the mother over the children. Thus Scripture is accustomed to speak of a nest or a bird brooding over its chicks, Deut. 22, 6. Thence a proverbial way of speaking is used, Gen. 32, 11. Lest she come and strike me, the mother over the chicks, that is, the father with the children. It seems to me that this same proverb is used in this place in this way, not to signify that all will be utterly extirpated (for the Dawn, of which presently, does not permit that) but that after calamities and huge slaughters, and the storming of fortifications, and indeed with the most dire and savage devastation, it will be that even safely and beyond the persecution of those suffering, as of unfledged birds, he who is called the patron, Isa. 19, v. 20, may be killed in that way, by which after Germany was conquered, and especially Magdeburg, the King of Sweden was slaughtered. And to v. 15. In the first clause he expresses the efficient and meritorious cause of this evil. Bethel, i.e., the seat of superstition, Rome, and its masters, to whom the peoples surrounding the Church on all sides (v. 10) obey, thus did to you. Above, chapter 6, 9. The society of priests, with the spikes of the men of the legions, i.e., of the Emperor, corrupts life. The impulsive cause is malice, and indeed evil malice. Because of the malice of your malice. In the second clause he adds to the heap of evils a new evil, and that a more bitter one, the more the Church at that time was about to dwell in the hope of some good, as some light of peace had shone forth (which was concluded A.D. 1646, January 30, between the King of Spain and the Dutch, and between the Emperor and the Kings of France and Sweden on the 24th of October of the same year), the King of Israel kills. Formerly I thought here of an opposing king, of whom (verse 6.) but sad experience compels us to count among the chastisements of the Church the slaughter of some king (besides that one who was signified in the parable of the mother concerning the chicks) in the Evangelical Church, and indeed the only one in that part which professes the reformation; who was also called the head of the Church in his kingdoms. That was done A.D. 1649, January 30. The word here is the same as that which appears in verse 7, where it treats of the abolition of the Constantinopolitan Emperors. Scripture did not keep silent about this chastisement, and elsewhere as Apoc. 14, 20. Ps. 107, 40. Cant. 8, 7. Deut. 32, 42. Thus Cocceius, of which kind are the rest in these and other Commentaries. From the claw, the lion.

SERMON VI. EVANGELICAL, THE FIRST IN THIS ORDER. CHAPTER XI.

Concerning the love of God toward the Israelites, for whose sake the Son of God will be called out of Egypt, and whom God led sweetly long ago, who, because of impenitence, were indeed to be subjected to the Assyrian, but because of God's mercy were not, like Admah, to be utterly overthrown, provided that in the time of the N.T. the pious Israelites are at last to follow the Lord, with the Lord roaring through the voice of the Gospel, about to call the peoples also from the west, nay, about to gather the Egyptians and Assyrians themselves. God argues against the ungrateful, and continues to show mercy.

Verse 1.

BECAUSE ISRAEL WAS A CHILD, AND I LOVED HIM) When Israel was a child, I loved him. The first age of the people was in Egypt, Ezek. 16, 5. c. 23, 3. AND OUT OF EGYPT I CALLED MY SON) Israel is called the Son of GOD, and indeed the firstborn, Ex. 4, 22, a figure in this of Christ. See what is at Matt. 1, 25. c. 2, 15. Out of Egypt I called: that is, I ordered to come out. Jerome notes here that those things which typice precede in others are referred, according to truth and fulfillment, to Christ.

CONCERNING this passage, various opinions occur, especially because of the allegation made in the New Testament, Matt. 2, 15. Some understand it only of the Israelites, especially the more recent Rabbis, R. David Kimchi, and others with Julian the Apostate in volume VII, who slandered Matthew for this reason, that he twisted what was said of Israel to Christ, in order to mock the simplicity of those who believed from the Gentiles. Yet all Christians detest this impiety. Therefore they reconcile Matthew with Hosea, because he does not allege the Prophet, but only alludes to this place, in the same manner as Acts 13, 11, where an allusion is made. Which is the explanation of Jansenius, just as if someone speaking of some part concerning anxiety for a son's safety were to say: you would have seen the father unable to stand still because of his desire for his son, and neglecting everything, so that that of Maro might be fulfilled in him: All care of the dear parent rests in Ascanius.

But Barradius rightly rejects the opinion of Jansenius, T. I. Conc. Evangel. p. 188. That which is fulfilled is not said by way of accommodation, but by way of prediction. And the allegation of Matthew is manifest: because he expressly says that this scripture of Hosea has been fulfilled when Christ returned from Egypt, he does not merely hint that something similar happened. And this is what Rivetus observes here, p. 343. When the writers of the New Testament bring forward some place for direct proof, not for accommodation, then by the very mode of citing they sufficiently show the difference between a similarity and an example brought forward, and the proper fulfillment of the thing predicted: for when they do not bring forward some place for the sake of similarity or general confirmation, but plainly to show that that which they narrate or affirm was entirely predicted, and because it had been predicted, it was necessary that it should exist: and then that it existed when that which is narrated or affirmed by them happened: they are accustomed to use such words, from which this mind of theirs is openly established, as in this place, that it might be fulfilled which was said.

Others accept all these things both of Israel and of Christ: in the literal sense of Israel, in the mystical of Christ; thus Calixtus in Concord. p. 75, and most Calvinists. Which method of interpreting Grotius followed here, being pleasing to the Papists. For he understood it of Israel according to the letter: but he judged that it should be referred to Christ in a more sublime sense, as is evident from the collation of those things which he annotated on Matthew. Which is also the opinion of Spanheim: that oracles often occur in Prophetic writings having a double fulfillment: one in the subject itself, another in the antitype: that nothing prevents the word בֶּן from being understood both collectively of the people, and individually and antonomastically of the Messiah, part II. Dub. Evangel. LXII. p. 478. Which things, however, can by no means be proven, firstly, because a double sense is thus attached to the same oracle, contrary to the simplicity, perspicuity, and certainty of scripture, and beyond the custom of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, that it is altogether inconsistent for the same word 'son' in the same passage to be understood both in an improper sense concerning a son metaphorically so called by adoption, and in a proper sense concerning the true and natural Son of God. For one and the same word to be taken at one and the same time both properly and tropically or figuratively is absurd, nay, clearly impossible. For he who speaks of an adopted son in an improper sense, by that very fact, while he speaks improperly, certainly does not speak properly: while he speaks of an adopted son, he does not speak of a true and natural son. Similarly, thirdly, it is inconsistent for the name 'son' to be taken both collectively and in a summary fashion concerning the Israelites, and individually or singularly concerning Christ. Fourthly, it is furthermore inconsistent for the verb 'I have called' to be understood both in the sense of the past and in the sense of the future: 'I am about to call' hereafter; the former concerning Israel, the latter indeed concerning Christ. Nor does blessed Joh. speak ill here. Tarnovius: If the Calvinists obtain this, why will they not also obtain that, in the words of the Supper, the words of Christ, 'Eat, drink,' can be rightly explained properly with respect to the symbols, but improperly with respect to the heavenly thing or the body and blood of Christ? Fifthly, Matthew is intent on rendering the reason why God permitted His Son to be driven into Egypt, and again recalled Him from Egypt, and he seeks it from the prediction made through the Prophet, so that, namely, that prophecy might obtain its fulfillment. But what does the migration of the Israelites into Egypt, in which not even the principle of a type holds with respect to the flight of Christ into Egypt, and their leading out of Egypt, have to do with that?

Somewhat more convenient is the opinion of those who do not precisely establish a double sense of the same sentence here, but, having retained a single sense concerning Israel,

They wish to show that Matthew alone pointed out a type, just as St. John, ch. 19, 36, when he refers us to Exod. 12, 46, 'you shall not break a bone of it,' points out a type. Where, however, it must be noted that by that very fact St. John does not teach that a double sense exists in the words of Moses; for it does not suit the place in Exodus that the subject designated by the pronoun 'IT' [illi] is both the paschal lamb and also Christ, since no word about Christ is contained therein, nor does the underlying subject matter admit that Christ is understood there along with the paschal lamb. And it is a very different thing for a type to be pointed out, or the correspondence of an antitype with a type, and for another sense different from the literal—namely, a mystical one—to be exhibited. For it is possible that words in their proper place retain a simple sense, but the thing itself which is expressed by them is taught to have had a typical respect to the antitype to be exhibited under the N.T., and that the work does not introduce a duality of sense into the same statement. And for that reason the observation of Jerome and Theophylact could be admitted here more easily than the Grotian double sense: of whom the former, on Hos. ch. 11, says: 'There is a wonderful depth of scripture: those things which precede typically are referred in others, according to truth and fulfillment, to Christ.' The latter, however, says that what was said through a figure about the people was truly fulfilled in Christ. But since Matthew does not refer us to history or some typical fact, but rather renders the cause why Christ had to be recalled from Egypt—which certainly is not so clear in that typical reasoning—that reconciliation does not satisfy. For although the liberation of the Israelites from the power of Pharaoh and from Egypt was a type of our spiritual liberation from the power of Satan and from hell, accomplished through the active and passive obedience of Christ, yet the liberation of the Israelites themselves from Egypt was not therefore a type of the recall of Christ the Son of God from the Kingdom of Egypt. There, the Israelites bore the type of us and of the whole human race, not of Christ; but Moses, leading them out of Egypt, bore the figure of Christ. Nor is the reason for that type established from elsewhere; just as, indeed, we are sufficiently taught from the scriptures concerning the paschal lamb, that it was a type of Christ. Nor, finally, is it so clear from the present passage of Hosea that some respect of a type intervened in that recall of Israel in faith [in πίσει] for the reduction of Christ from Egypt, just as, concerning the type of the paschal lamb, the matter was an undoubted fact among the Jews, brought forward by John in ch. 19 from Exod. ch. 12 itself. That comparison is therefore very different. Furthermore, Rivetus rightly warns here that types must be distinguished: 'Types,' he says, 'and allegories then at last produce firm consequences when they are concerned with a question of law, that is, if it is ever asked whether something is said to be just or unjust. But if they pertain to a question of fact—that is, if it is asked whether something will happen or not—then one must distinguish among types; because since some types are given and commanded by God, while others are merely facts: because those given or commanded by God, since they properly look to the thing shadowed forth and have a perpetual and necessary relation, they absolutely conclude that what they were given to shadow forth will happen, because types are nothing other than signs of the divine will, which in truth is a certain ineluctable and absolute necessity.' But those types which were facts, and not properly and peculiarly destined for some certain signification; since they follow the nature of examples, the proofs from these are not of necessity, but only of contingency. And so they can delight and illustrate in teaching, but prove very little. If, therefore, the coming of the Israelites from Egypt was a type of the coming of the Messiah from Egypt, since it was not a type of Law, but of fact; not given, but only performed by deed; not a proper proof, but a common one, as are all examples, it can bring forward no firm proof. This is Rivetus, following F. Junius, whose words he also made his own from lib. parall. cap. 6. Finally, when certain proofs of the literal sense can be given, and the correspondence of the oracle with its fulfillment, one must not depart to the reasoning of a type. For prophecies are more powerful and clearer testimonies than types and figures, which, lest we seem to introduce them into the scriptures, it is necessary to show from the scriptures themselves before an application is made.

Others here betake themselves to the closest conjunction of head and body. Christ is the head, the Church the mystical body. Therefore, what happens to this is not undeservedly thought to be referred to the head itself. And so, as Israel was going out of Egypt, Christ went out at the same time, as the head and bridegroom of the Church. This is the opinion of Gesner: concerning which, however, B. Meisnerus adds this critique: 'This is indeed a pious and true opinion, but beside the point. For Matthew does not intend this, that Christ went out with Israel, as the head, long ago in the time of Moses, as regards his divinity, but that after his birth and flight into Egypt, he was recalled in his own person as regards his humanity, and by this very fact, in this time of the N.T., the scripture of Hosea was fulfilled.' Add that Matthew does not relate an analogy, but a history historically, nor is that analogy concerning the head firm. For how many things were done in the desert, in the land of Canaan, under the judges and Kings, which, although they can be said to have pertained to the head in its members, could in no way be fulfilled in the head itself?

Fifthly, therefore, others understand these things of Christ alone, and indeed in such a way that they refer the preceding things also to Christ. Thus Eusebius, Demonstrat. Evangel. l. 9, demonstr. 9, understands all the preceding things which were said about the King of Israel of Christ literally, and asserts that these same words were said and are to be understood not of Israel in any way, but of Christ alone. The same opinion was expressed in the notes to the N. Test. ch. 2 of Matthew by Isidorus Clarius Brixianus; as if the Lord were admonishing his people through the Prophet that when Christ the Teacher of righteousness arrived, they should not fail to admit him through drowsiness, or let the occasion slip by, because Christ's conversation on earth would be like the dawn, after, namely, the King of Israel was cut off by the cutting off after the three years of preaching. Although he foresaw, however, that the Jews would demand Christ for death, along with Herod, and would do so not so much out of malice as out of imprudence, because they were children; that he had led his son away into Egypt, lest the foolish people, by killing Christ before the time, should deprive themselves of the fruit which they ought to have received from him. Finally, Herod having died, and the people having for the most part forgotten the birth of Christ, that he had called his son out of Egypt, so that, while they were ignorant, he might grow up among them, etc. But Rivetus rightly refutes this opinion. For the fact that he understands the Christ to be cut off by the King of Israel is utterly absurd. Furthermore, the claim that Christ was led away into Egypt for that reason, because the child Israel was going to demand him for death along with Herod, lacks all reason. For the people were not guilty of that cruelty which Herod exercised; indeed, he incurred the worst thanks from the people, who ordered so many infants to be slaughtered in a miserable massacre, and abolished the royal blood among the Jews. Furthermore, since the question here is about the ten tribes, no reason can be devised why the name of Israel in this passage ought to be taken for the Jews, among whom Herod reigned. So he.

Sixth, Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, in his Commentary on this passage, thinks that the Prophet is speaking about King Herod and about Christ. That he said the King of Israel had passed through, is to be understood of King Herod, whose The kingdom quickly had an end, which are subjected, because 'Israel is a child and I loved him' etc., to sound literally concerning Christ, who, Herod being dead, was recalled from Egypt. Spanheim does not approve of that opinion, especially because what is said about King Hosea is absurdly understood of Herod, but how much more absurdly did Cocceius interpret those things concerning the King of England?

The seventh opinion is that of those who establish that the whole first verse of this chapter is to be understood literally of Christ, but by no means of the Israelite people, so that the sense is: when Christ was an infant, or a child, I loved him, and I called him out of Egypt: which Spanheim notes is the explanation of many in the cited place, p. 487. But in this explanation, it is desired: 1. That it wishes the child of Israel to denote nothing other than an infant: since the discourse is not about a child simply, but about the child of Israel, as those wish who say that the word נער is placed in the construct state. 2. That it makes Christ the subject in the first clause, whereas Israel is rather the object there, which is to be taken in the nominative case, not to be rendered by the genitive. 3. That the name of Christ is clearly not had in the first clause, nor even implicitly; but if it is derived from the second clause, the explanation seems hyperbolic and contorted to some: which, however, others go about excusing through the character of the Hebrew language.

The eighth is that of Fr. Junius, that the words of the first verse likewise refer to Christ according to the letter, but in another manner, which he explains in his Parallels, book 1, p. 6. The Prophet begins in chapter 9 to turn his discourse to the true Israel, so that partly by the remembrance of the benefits of God, partly by the harshness of the judgments, partly by the arguments of divine mercy, he may raise the pious to the expectation of the coming of Christ, in whom and through whom God was about to fulfill the truth of his prophecies. Therefore, he makes hope of salvation here for the remnants of Israel in Christ Jesus, and establishes that the elect remnants are to be snatched from the common conflagration on account of his son, and in him: 1. As in the head and firstborn among many brothers, from whom life and salvation is derived to all his members. 2. As in the son of love, in whom the infinite love of GOD rests. Moreover, that the principles of this salvation are to be demonstrated, at the time when the son of God, despised by the people of the Jews and harassed by Herod, is to be recalled from Egypt, so that the work of salvation promised to the Church in Judea might be executed in reality. Thus the Prophet designated 1. the source and causes of salvation, when he says, because he is the child of Israel, I love him. 2. The sign of the appearing and coming grace is explained by those words: 'Out of Egypt I called my son.' For it is just as if God had said, even if I were about to destroy the whole of Israel, I will not do it on account of my son; for since he is the child of Israel, that is, the firstborn, performing the eternal priesthood (for thus the children of Israel are said to be in Exod. 24), furthermore since he is my only-begotten son, although the Israelites have expelled him from their midst, and are unworthy that grace should be shown to them, nevertheless on account of the elect, and for their salvation, I am about to call my son from Egypt, that he may bring salvation to the sheep of Israel. Spanheim repeats these things from Junius in the cited place. In the Junius-Tremellius notes, these are presented thus at this place: The Prophet passes to the narration of the gracious promises concerning the reconciliation of the Israelites with GOD, that is, of the holy remnants according to the election of grace in Christ. The sense, therefore, is that the love of GOD toward his people is eternal, and since the foundation of that gratuitous love and the good pleasure of God is in Christ (whom, exhibited and born in the flesh, neither the Jews nor the Israelites had acknowledged), although it would not have been alien to the justice of God that they should be deprived of it forever (which his withdrawal into Egypt seemed to portend), yet that God is consistent with himself in his love toward his people, and therefore that Christ (whom they had not at all received when he came to his own) is to be recalled from Egypt, to which he had been withdrawn, into the land of Israel. Moreover, this is the argument of God: I love this one, and therefore whomsoever he loves, and for whom he intercedes, them I am about to love: But he loves Israel: for he is the firstborn child of Israel, legitimately interceding for him before me: wherefore I am about to do good to Israel in him whom I love, and to this end I am about to recall the same from Egypt. Which interpretation Joh. Piscator also embraced in his notes on Matt. 2, verse 15. Observing that the preceding name (of the son) is postponed according to the custom of the Hebrews: for this is the regular collocation of the words, because 'My Son is a child,' that is, a minister of Israel, i.e., of the Israelite people, therefore I love him, and on account of both causes I called him out of Egypt, so that, namely, having returned to his fatherland and been educated at Nazareth, he might go forth from there to preach the Gospel. Which, however, Spanheim judges to be clever and ingenious rather than solid. And yet those things which he opposes to them are not so solid. For what he says first, that it is too hyperbatic and contorted in the words, Piscator already meets that through that custom of the Hebrews. What he says next about the anaclasis in the sense and connection, and that the ingenious analysis of Junius from the transition after the comminations to the correction, from the correction to the concession, does not satisfy, the patrons of that opinion will settle that in a similar manner of scripture, to which such a transition is not unusual. Thus the apology of Junius in the Parallels holds: But we cannot see how the adjuncts are repugnant to this interpretation: For on the contrary, they have the greatest agreement with this interpretation of ours; chapter 10 preceded with the most just sentence of God concerning the destroying of the Israelites. To this sentence, a certain correction, as it were, is subjected for the consolation of the holy remnants, the foundation of which is Christ, as we said before. Therefore, there is the greatest agreement with the preceding matters. But what will become of the following ones? They also agree perfectly with that proposition. For in the following words there is a concession, and a kind of forensic contention, as it were, and a disputation: by which God most vehemently exaggerates the wickedness of the Israelites, so that He may then further illustrate His mercy. Why should I not have called my son out of Egypt? says the Lord: For otherwise it would have been all over with this whole nation of the Israelites: which, however much it may have been recalled by the Prophets, deserted to idols: however much I may have demonstrated myself by works, it was willfully blind, and could not be tamed thus far by my guidance or healing, nor by my most loving services, deliverances, nourishment, administration, or finally by scourges, nor has it yet lifted its eyes to the supreme God. What else, therefore, was I to have done here, than to bring back my son who was living abroad? For how was I to hand you over, Ephraim? &c. Thus the sentence concerning the salvation of the pious is finally delivered, as if the Lord suddenly emerged from the most grievous heat of those contentions. I will not do it, He says, &c. as if He were saying; nevertheless you are my child, dear to me: damnable indeed because of your sins, but to be saved because of my nature, truth, holiness, and mercy in the son of my love, whom I called out of Egypt. The very sequence of the discourse will show to those who are attentive that this is the genuine understanding of the passage. Rivetus, who has what are considered sharp points, is without doubt stronger than Spanheim. But the analysis is far plainer, in Spanheim's judgment, if the commemoration of both the benefits of God and the ingratitude of the people is subjected to the proposed threats. We admit it. But is it not the greatest benefit that God recalled his son for the Israelites from Egypt? Which is certainly far greater than that leading of the Israelites out of Egypt. As to what thirdly seems absurd to Spanheim, that the word נער here is referred only to the primogeniture or the ministry of the Messiah, with the foundation of the application to the antitype removed, they do not admit that this is absurd for him, and they will not unjustly say that it labors under a begging of the question, since the question is: Does any rationale of a type have a place here? Furthermore, fourthly, that the word ישׂראל cannot be explained otherwise than violently in the genitive case, when Spanheim proves from that, that it is certain and clear from an inspection of the text that the word בני here is literally the predicate of Israel, in that Spanheim is vehemently mistaken, and he does nothing but beg the question, which is very familiar to him. Which is also detected in the fifth reason. He says it is harsh and crude, with the plain and literal sense completely rejected (for it is asked concerning it, whether that is the literal sense?), to sub-understand the word בני my son, or to draw it back from the end of the verse to the beginning. But Piscator deduces that from the custom of the Hebrews, especially since בני does not occur there, but לבני with a prefix. Such prefixes are accustomed to be no obstacle to words being drawn back to what precedes: because only the noun is regarded, which is to be drawn back, as is known to those learned in Hebrew. Finally, as to what Spanheim asks, why mention was made here of the calling of the Son of God out of Egypt, rather than of his destination or mission into the world? That seems to us a trifle. Since it is not right to prescribe to the Holy Spirit which benefits He wishes to allege, and since that benefit of the destination of the Messiah has been inculcated often elsewhere, that recall of the Son out of Egypt, done for the sake of the Jews, ought also to have been commemorated somewhere; since the ancient Scripture has not been silent even about other more minor things concerning the Messiah; and St. Matthew has testified that this recall was predicted here. Add that the mission into the world is a common benefit, but this recall, done for the sake of the Jews, is a gift proper and peculiar to them: whence its commemoration is highly suitable for reproaching them for their ingratitude. These things against Spanheim.

However, Rivetus also urges that scruple concerning the BOY ISRAEL, and that more pressingly, if I am not mistaken; yet that, he says, seems forced, that Junius wishes the Son of God to be called the Messiah at the beginning נער ישראל that is, as he interprets, the firstborn son of Israel. He brought forward for proof a passage from Exod. ch. 24, v. 5. Where Moses is said to have sent נערי naarei, that is, the boys of the children of Israel, who made burnt offerings ascend, in which place Lyranus thinks it more true that the firstborn of the Israelites are understood, and those the firstborn of the twelve princes of Israel, because the priesthood was then annexed to the primogeniture, than that others refer it to Nadab and Abihu, the future priests; but since the interpretation of this passage is not certain, and they can be understood as the young men of the Israelites, their ministers who brought the cattle fit for immolation: otherwise possessing no authority among them; as 1. Sam. 2, verse 13, the boy of the priest is mentioned, who ministered to him, in an inferior rank; it does not seem that this word can or ought to be understood of Christ. These things Rivetus. And not unjustly. For it will never be taught that the word נער is the same as firstborn son. Nor is it conveniently accepted here for a minister, as Piscator wished. For neither has that use of the word been demonstrated, nor ought it to be admitted in this place, since one should not depart from the proper sense of a word to an improper one beyond necessity: nor is this the cause of the paternal love of Christ, that he is a minister of Israel, nor should one rashly depart from the common consensus of interpreters, who take the word Israel here in the nominative case, not the genitive: which consensus, however, Spanheim wrongly tries to disprove here by the mark of the genitive case. Finally, that the word boy is more rightly applied to Israel here in the nominative case is confirmed by a comparison of the passage Luke 1, v. 54, ἀνελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ, he has helped Israel his servant.

This is the ninth explanation, that the former colon pertains to Israel: but the latter, which Matthew alleged, to the Messiah. Which has always been approved by us: since it is easy and ready, and accords with the interpretation handed down by the Holy Spirit. The sense therefore will be this: Although Israel is and remains נער, i.e., a boy, or rather crude, precipitous in actions, shaking off (the yoke) and a transgressor: yet I loved him, and because of the love with which I embrace him, I recalled my Son out of Egypt, for his sake, that he might instruct, bring into order, and amend him. For the word נער denotes that by the force of its etymology, and it is taken for a sinner in Isa. 65:20, but it is interchanged with the word חוטא, a sinner who has turned aside from the way (by which a notable sin and transgression is denoted, Num. 15:29, Ps. 4:5, Ps. 41:5, Lam. 1:8, Isa. 1:4), a boy a hundred years old shall die, and וְהַחוֹטֶא the sinner a hundred years old shall be cursed. Rivetus renders it thus: although Israel is a boy, crude and tender, yet I love him, adducing the version of the LXX Interpreters, διότι νήπιος Ἰσραὴλ: because a child cannot be left to himself without danger: therefore, lest he perish entirely left to himself, I recalled my Son out of Egypt, who might take him up and preserve him in his remnants, lest he should precipitate himself entirely by his imprudence and crudity. Others in the same sense render the word כִּי with the more accepted meaning BECAUSE, in this way: because Israel is a boy, i.e., tender, crude, in need of care, laboring both under childish ignorance and weakness, I loved him, and because of the love with which I embrace him, I recalled my Son out of Egypt, namely to teach, rule, and recall him to his duty, lest for lack of a ruler he should cast himself headlong into destruction. But since the Prophet has rebuked Israel most vehemently, that explanation does not seem to fit this passage so well, by which the sins of Israel are extenuated as if they proceeded from childish ignorance and infirmity, rather than being committed with a high hand; therefore, retaining the adversative sense, the word נער is to be understood not of one who is raw, tender, and infirm, but rather of a transgressor or one shaking off the yoke, so that the divine grace which He deigned to show to this prevaricating Israel might be the more ample. I see that this opinion, which I approve, was also held by the blessed Tarnovius, when I compare the same, inasmuch as he rendered it thus: although Israel is a boy, shaking off the paternal yoke more often.

This oracle, therefore, as regards the latter clause, is to be understood literally of Christ, not of the Israelite people, as these things confirm: First, the evidence of this interpretation: for all things are so clear; nor is there anything harsh, forced, or twisted in that interpretation. Spanheim acknowledges that it is far more probable than the Junian explanation, and that the construction of both words and sense is easier when the latter clause is referred only to Christ. Nor is there need for such hyperbaton, and all the words flow in order and retain their native sense. Tarnovius teaches on page 361 that all and each of the words admit this sense most excellently. כִּי is very often taken adversatively for 'although,' which they translate here as 'because' or 'when'; see Exercit. Bibl. p. 63 et seqq. The noun נער, although it is general in meaning and denotes one inferior to others either by age or ministry, yet by reason of its origin, because it is from נער, i.e. he shook off, and by the rebellion joined to most, nay, of a certain innate ignorance and malice, it signifies him who frequently shakes off the yoke of a parent or master, and is unskilled, foolish, stupid. Prov. 1, 4. & 22, 15. Isa. 3, 3. Eccles. 10, 16. Jer. 1, 6. compare the word νήπιος 1 Cor. 13, verse 11. Eph. 4. verse 11. &c. in the New Testament, where let Aben Ezra be noted on this passage & a gloss on this name. He refers, he says, to chapter 10. v. 11. where עֶגְלָה מְלֻמָּדָה & above c. 4, 16. פָּרָה סֹרֵרָה; weigh also those things which are said about this boy below v. 3. & you will understand these things more correctly. Vau is used in various ways, so much so that it is called Proteus by many. Yet it notes Exod. 5, 16. straw is not given to your servants, yet bricks וּלְבֵנִים he says complete for us, Job 3, 26. וְלֹא yet the commotion did not arrive Hos. 1, 10. וְהָיָה yet the number of the sons will be. Eccles. 9, 15. וְאָדָם לֹא זָכַר yet the man did not remember. Thus καὶ Luke 7, 8. in the New Testament, Phil. 4, 10. thus a little later the same Vau is used for therefore, for that reason, wherefore in וּמִמִּצְרַיִם, let other similar places cited in Commentar. Psal. 12. v. 10. page 59 be seen, where the same is also proven concerning the particle καὶ. So he.

Then the distinction of the words בְּנִי & נַעַר. Which, as they are of very different meaning, so according to this interpretation they are rendered most conveniently and are assigned to their subject most correctly. For no one doubts that the name נַעַר fits Israel perfectly for describing his character, such as it was. For he was always either crude or headstrong, and not rarely shaking off the yoke, & a stubborn transgressor: such as Hosea especially depicted this people. That name therefore fits Israel, not Christ. But the other name of my Son, together with that one, if the meaning of a contumacious sinner and prevaricator holds, such as the Israelites were for the most part, is not joined so conveniently, and is not attributed to the same person in one and the same discourse in the way it is here, conjunctively. And therefore both are not to be taken of Israel, but rather the former only is to be explained of Israel, but the latter of Christ.

Thirdly, the propriety of the word MY SON. For the name of the Son of GOD, taken properly, fits none but Christ. But it is a rule of sound Theology, the Socinians themselves say, that the proper meaning of a word is to be retained where we are not forced to descend to an improper one, and that one should not have recourse to a figure unless necessity compels. Since therefore there is no necessity here, nay rather all things are in good order, for us to assign the august name of Son of God, proper to the Messiah, placed absolutely and simply, to the stubborn Israel, when we can understand Christ himself, it is a matter of conscience for us to interpret it of another than Christ.

Fourthly, the diversity of Israel, whom GOD loved although a boy, and the Son of God, whom He called out of Egypt, for the sake of Israel. For if it persisted in the same subject, the Prophet would speak rather thus: Although Israel is a boy, I loved him, and I called him out of Egypt. But because he introduces another subject here, and I called MY SON GOD, he teaches not obscurely that he is said to be called the Son of God for the sake of Israel, and because of his love for him, rather than that Israel himself was called.

Fifthly, also the interpretation of the Holy Spirit in the N. T., which is above all exception, and by far the most luminous. For Matthew gives the reason why Christ did not remain in Egypt, but was recalled from Egypt, namely that it might be fulfilled which was said by the Prophet saying: Out of Egypt I called my son. What therefore the Holy Spirit interprets concerning the Son of God, it is not for us to snatch away to Israel; what the Evangelist explains concerning the calling of Christ out of Egypt, and says was fulfilled in it, that cannot and ought not to be understood of the leading of the Israelite people out of Egypt. What was fulfilled finally in the New Testament, that was not done long ago in the time of Moses. If you say that these things are explained thus by Matthew only in a transumptive or accommodative sense, Spanheim refutes this opinion at length in doubt LXIV. LXV., not only in Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, but also in his Bucer and Mercer. The places cited by Jansenius from Matt. 13, 14. 15. & c. 15. another says are of a general kind, and either deal with vices, or with common arts, where the same reason is ordinarily found in many. That there is a different reason where the Messiah is concerned, to whom it is only alluded by such a citation, and indeed contrary to the mind of the Holy Spirit, is foreign to all reason. But if you object to him with Spanheim that these things are alleged by Matthew in a mystical sense, most of Spanheim's arguments which are opposed to Jansenius will stand in the way: such as that the citations which concern the Messiah, studiously gathered by Matthew, are not for the sake of illustration only, but also of proof, that this Jesus of Nazareth is the true Messiah, in that those things are read to have been fulfilled by him, in him, and around him, which were predicted concerning the Messiah in the Old Testament: and that it is little fitting for a sacred writer, having left the true sense of the Prophetic passage, to catch at a mere allusion (a mystical sense only), nay that the style of the Evangelists is far different from the style of the Prophets; the latter is involved, the former is evolved; in the latter are allegories, figures, types, in the former the declaration of figures and types, not a crop of new allusions. And Spanheim wishes it to be referred here, which Junius aptly notes, that the disciples of Christ were not allegorists, but true leaders or analysts of the old allegories and types, and therefore an injury is done to them if they are said to overwhelm old types and allegories with new allegories, and to distort the most sacred words of the Law and the Prophets to that use, who are the most solid interpreters of them all. Add that the reason of a type and a mystical sense of that kind does not fit here, which has also been noted by Rivet: Nor does the consequence hold, which some connect: that no pious person doubts that the Egyptian liberation was a type of spiritual liberation: Therefore this calling out of Egypt is deservedly referred to Christ, the author of spiritual liberation. For what is this to the return of Christ from Egypt, not spiritual, but temporal and corporal, if I may so speak? Or because the liberation from the Babylonian captivity was a figure of spiritual liberation, was Christ therefore bound to be sent into Babylon, and afterwards called out, so that the truth might correspond to the type? Rivet has this on p. 343. On which matter Tarnovius has more in this place on p. 356.
