Let these also be weighed: 1. although the miraculous liberation from Egypt was a certain type of spiritual liberation through Christ from hell, as from spiritual Egypt in Rev. 11:8, yet neither was that liberated people a type of the liberating Christ (for the people were being liberated, Christ was liberating: the people were being oppressed by hard servitude in Egypt, Christ was living safe and secure in Egypt from the violence of Herod, which had expelled him from Judea) nor was that liberation [a type] of Christ the liberator. 2. Israel was not called out from Egypt by voice alone, but was led out by a mighty hand, Christ by the sole voice of an Angel, Matt. 2:19, 20. III. How can we not attribute ingratitude to Christ, if we interpret both parts of the first verse literally concerning him as the antitype? IV. How will one word signify both past tense and future in one place? Nor are those who fight for the mystical sense sufficiently consistent with themselves. Pareus certainly sometimes understands these things literally only concerning Israel, mystically concerning Christ, and sometimes says they were also literally fulfilled in Christ: Matthew, he says in Tarnovius p. 350, writes that this oracle was then fulfilled in Christ. Therefore, similarity alone is not the cause. It must be granted, therefore, literally concerning the adoption and liberation of the Jews tion from Egypt these things are now said. For the scope and all the circumstances demand this. Nevertheless, it is most correctly applied to Christ under the name of a double type. And a little later: just as the body of the Church was now called out of Egypt, so the head itself, Christ, had to be recalled thence into Judea, so that what was done in the body might also be LITERALLY fulfilled in the head. What kind of uncertainty is this, is applied and is literally fulfilled? He refutes the similarity, and he himself establishes it in this explanation. Piscator, however, although when he first explained Hosea, he accepted these things concerning Israel in a literal sense, and explained them concerning Christ only according to a mystical sense, nevertheless later corrected this opinion in his Commentaries on Matthew and interpreted these words, with which we are now dealing, according to the letter concerning CHRIST alone. Other things, which exclude that mystical sense, were indicated before.

Sixthly, it is added, which Andreas Osiander and Franc. Junius did not warn of rashly (which Argument moves Rivet), that Matthew wished to prove almost every single circumstance that occurred in the History of Christ, by instituting a comparison of the predictions of the Old Testament with the event, so that from the fulfillment of all the circumstances he might show that Jesus is the Christ. However, for such a proof, a type of the kind they place here could by no means suffice. The reason is that types and allegories only then produce firm consequences when they are engaged in a question of law, that is, if it is ever asked whether something is said to be just or unjust. Concerning which we warned above. Thence Rivet concludes; Since therefore I see that all who think these words cited by Matthew are either allegorical or analogical, and think they refer primarily to the liberation of the people of Israel from Egypt, involve themselves; and that it does not satisfy this reason, because from such a type, or such an analogy as they establish, no firm argument can be elicited: and that Matthew wished to prove the fulfillment of the Prophecy by light conjectures, was alien to the prudence of so great an Apostle: I cannot take refuge in this interpretation to a Type, or analogy.

Seventhly, the divine grace and the stubbornness of the Israelites are so exaggerated, that the love of God toward the Israelites is merely gratuitous, and therefore persists, even if they have nothing in themselves worthy of love, and many things that deserve hatred; of which gratuitous love, which is also proclaimed elsewhere in Deut. 7, 7. chap. 9, 10. the chief proof is in the mission of the Son, when he himself testified that he was sent especially to the lost sheep, namely of Israel, Matth. 15.

Thus eighthly, those things which follow cohere correctly. For this is the reason why God does not utterly reject the Israelites, even if they are most refractory, because He destined to send them the Messiah, who might recall them from their path: whence He could not yet destroy the whole of Israel. For although He had decided to overturn the kingdom of Israel, yet the hope of restoration remained under the Messiah, who, summoned from Egypt, might gather the scattered Israelites from here and there by the word of preaching. But those things which follow from the second to the eighth verse showed how unworthy they rendered themselves of the gratuitous love of God, and thus on the contrary they testify how constant God was in His mercy, who, so often provoked, had not yet laid aside the care of that people, and after so many remedies attempted, but neglected and rejected by them, had decided at length in His own time to prepare and apply that last and most salutary one by giving them Christ the teacher. There is therefore a certain anticipation, as Rivet rightly says, and a concession, by which, while he compares the testimonies of his kindness with the most ungrateful misdeeds of the Israelites, he indeed concedes that they are unworthy of his dealing with them so mercifully thereafter: yet he wills to show the fullness of grace and truth in Christ, by manifesting him in his own time. Similarly, B. Tarnovius: I think this first verse is a proleptic proposition of all those things which are explained thereafter. But those things are of two kinds primarily, namely the benefits bestowed upon the ungrateful people of Israel and the crimes committed by them, and the grace which comes to it through Christ. He notes the crimes with these words, although Israel is a child often shaking off the paternal yoke, yet he designates the benefits with these words, 'yet I love him,' and he lays the foundation of this love and connivance and remission of sins in this clause, 'therefore I called my only-begotten son out of Egypt,' into Judea, so that by teaching rightly there, living piously, and perishing by a hard death, he might sufficiently satisfy for the sins of the human race, and effectively for the faithful Israel (I use that distinction in the Lutheran sense, not the Calvinian) and bring forth salvation, so that thus through his intercession God the Father, whose son he is, moved, might not deal with men by strict law in all things, but that those whom I could have destroyed for their sins, as Sodom and Gomorrah, I might love those believing in Christ and hold them in the place of sons.

Ninthly, the same Tarnovius, on the occasion of speaking, confirms this explanation thus: These were the last things (which for that reason are also added to this chapter in many books, see the Vulgate version and the Papist Commentators, and others who follow it) the King of Israel was suddenly and unexpectedly cut off entirely. Hence now immediately arises (1) this question, why does God punish Israel so severely? The Prophet answers in one word, because Israel is a disobedient child. (2) Therefore, when God takes away the King, does He cast off His people entirely? Not so, He takes away the kingdom, He does not utterly deny His love, because He says, 'yet I love him.' (3) Will you therefore give no king? Certainly Christ my son, whose kingdom is eternal although not of this world, he is the one in whom alone I am well pleased, and I love Israel, so that I may not utterly destroy them. This is B. Tarnovius page 360.

Tenth, to these is added the authority of the Doctors and Interpreters, who, although they do not all agree on the method of explanation, nevertheless unanimously consent in this, that according to the letter the discourse here is about Christ; not a few also support our interpretation, as far as the substance of the matter is concerned. We praised Eusebius before from book 9 of the Demonstratio, p. m. 426, as well as Isidorus Clarius in his notes on Matthew 2, with whom Lyranus and Dionysius likewise understand this passage according to the letter concerning Christ, as do also Andr. Osiander in his Harmonia, Franciscus Junius in his Parallela, the same and Tremellius in their notes, Piscator on Matthew 2, Joh. Tarnovius in his Commentaries, Andr. Rivetus in his Commentary, and Johannes Cocceius in his Commentary on this passage. Fridericus Spanhemius says that it is the opinion of most interpreters and has great authors; from whom he professes to dissent unwillingly, yet certain things intervene which prevent him from thinking that this opinion should be subscribed to. But those things are by no means of such importance that they should move us from this so solidly founded opinion, and therefore it will be worth the effort to examine them.

The first is: that that כִּי does not seem to be causal, but only temporal, to be rendered as 'when' or 'at the time that Israel was a child', that is, in a tender state I loved him; but whence will it be proven that this particle should be rendered thus here? He teaches this by no argument, Spanhemius says it only nakedly and doubtfully, 'IT SEEMS', and he does not even bring forward places in which the particle כִּי is designative of time. But that it is causal is undoubted from its usual sense: That it is also used in an adversative sense, places everywhere obvious teach; nor does anything here stand in the way of this interpretation, but everything agrees perfectly.

The second point is what is evident from an inspection of the text, that the same subject is called in the literal sense both נער and בן, a boy and a son, and this cannot be denied without manifest violence being done to the words of the Prophet: This, however, was not evident to Rivet nor to other most sharp-sighted men, nor did Spanheim teach how violence is done to the words of the Prophet. He therefore begs the question, as is customary and solemn for him, τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ. I would rather say it is evident that the name is not applied here to the same subject, and that violence is done to the words of the Prophet if it is dragged to the same subject; certainly, one departs from the propriety of the prophetic voice, and the Apostle is openly contradicted, if the latter clause is taken as referring to anyone other than Christ. And here we oppose Cocceius to Spanheim: We accept the Son of God in emphasis and ἐν δυνάμει (i.e., in all the value of signifying, so that it may denote the power of τοῦ ἰδίου, but not the infirmity of υἱοῦ Θεοῦ) as referring to the only-begotten Son of God, as in Ps. 2, 1. 12. Is. 9, 5. Ezek. 21, 15. Prov. 30, 4. The reason for understanding it thus is because it is said in ἀντιδιαστολῇ to Israel. And words must be explained in their propriety, unless an evident reason prevents it. And that exposition is conformable to the promises and prophecies, and especially to that which is in Hos. 1, 7. I will save them in Jehovah their God, and ch. 2, 1. They shall be called the sons of the living God. This exposition also has the Holy Spirit as its author, Matt. 2, 15, and the history of subsequent events supports it. LXX: ἐξ Αἰγύπτου μετεκάλεσα τὰ τέκνα αὐτοῦ. Therefore they judged that it should be read לבניו as if the י at the end had perished. Indeed, they thought it inconvenient to take 'my son' as referring to Israel by antonomasia. Let it be observed here that Matthew amended the version of the LXX interpreters. This is Cocceius.

The third point is that the commemoration of the Messiah would be too abrupt and concise if the Messiah alone were said to be understood by those latter words, such as would hardly be found elsewhere. The Prophet ends the preceding chapter with a commination, he adds a commemoration of a benefit known to the common people, and which is solemn among the Prophets: and immediately in the verse following he returns to reproaching the people for their ingratitude; I ask, how can the mere mention of the calling of the Messiah out of Egypt cohere with the preceding and following parts? Everything will be connected together most excellently if we admit the literal sense concerning the Israelite people and the benefit shown to them at the same time. Thus Spanheim. But what is new in the Scripture of the Old Testament about a concise commemoration of the Messiah? We do not concede, however, that it is too abrupt. For a reason is given why he called his son out of Egypt for the good of Israel, and the doubt is removed by κατ' ἀνθυποφορὰν from the malice of Israel. Cocceius accumulates still more in his commentary. He says the Prophet recapitulates the entire government of Israel, and shows I. its first state in childhood, i.e., the state of pedagogy and the servitude of the elements of the world. For this is the childhood of Israel, Gal. 3, 24. 4, 1. 2. 3. This state of Israel is from the leading out of Egypt until the Kingdom of God or of Christ, under the first covenant. Jer. 31, 32. II. The mission of the Son of GOD to him in that state, so that he might become even lower than those who are called gods, a servant of those who dominate, a servant of circumcision under the law, Ps. 8, 6. Is. 49, 7. Is. 53, 11. Rom. 15, 8. Gal. 4, 4. III. The recall of the Son, who had been withdrawn by flight into Egypt, to the people. See Matt. 2, 13. 14. 15. Jeremiah 31, 15. 16 speaks of this flight and the consequent slaughter of the children in Bethlehem, and the return from flight. A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, most bitter weeping: Rachel (the Bethlehemite mothers) weeps over her children, she refuses to admit consolation over her children who were killed; because he is not, He demonstratively, or from the verse above, that טוּב my good. A greater cause for weeping, that Christ, the good of the Lord, did not appear, than that the children were killed. Otherwise, if he had appeared, it would have been for consolation. Thus said Jehovah: Restrain your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears. For there is a reward in your work, and my son, my salvation, will return with his mother and Joseph from the land of the enemy: and there is expectation for your end, and the children will return to their border: even Israel will be recalled through the Gospel. This flight is a specimen of the sufferings of Christ. He makes his Love the cause of this reduction. For it is of the love of God that he gave, nay, delivered his son as a victim for us. John 3, 16. Again we warn here, and the word of love is taken in emphasis far better concerning the gift of the son for salvation than concerning any benefits whatsoever which were bestowed upon Israel before that time, which do not prevent him from being left in his infancy, devoid of that adoption which is given through Christ. IV. The calling of the Israelites made through Christ, Mic. 6, 9. Jer. 23, 6. 33, 16. Ps. 2, 7. and the Apostles, Ps. 8, 3. 68, 12. Compare Hos. 11, 4. Contend with your mother, etc. V. Disobedience, and indeed with contumacy: Thus they went away from their face. Thus it is placed in the apodosis, so that in the protasis a particle of assimilation is to be understood, i.e., The more and more ardently they called them, with the greater disdain they went away from the face of them, the callers, so as not to hear them. A similar ellipsis in Is. 55, 9. Ps. 48, 6. This is what he says, who also wishes other things there to pertain to the times of the New Testament, in which, although we do not vote with him, but admit that those things which the Prophet complains about regarding the ingratitude of the people pertain to the people of that time, nothing nevertheless stands in the way of the benefit to be shown to this people in the time of the New Testament being shown here: because it is the same people, just as it was also the same people who were led out of Egypt, and who lived in the time of Hosea and thereafter, nay, even he whose fates he designated after some time. Furthermore, is it not better that we say the Prophet adds a commemoration of a singular benefit, rather than a benefit known to the common people, and thus returns to reproaching the people for their ingratitude! For the more eminent the benefit is, the more grievous is the vice of ingratitude! But who, I ask, of mortals (says Spanheim) among the Israelites could have anticipated in his mind that calling of the Messiah out of Egypt, whom they all believed was to be called not out of Egypt, but out of Israel, or rather out of Judah. Resp. It is no wonder that Spanheim maintains the Israelites did not believe what was predicted concerning the Messiah, since he asserts that the meaning of the predictions was indeed perceived by the mouths of the Prophets. pag. 486. Moreover, they could have understood the calling of Christ out of Egypt entirely; for it is predicted here in clear words: I have called (I will call, according to the solemn manner of the Prophets) my Son out of Egypt: which, taken as they sound, produce no other meaning than that Christ was to be called out of Egypt, with which prediction the raising up of the Messiah out of Judah does not conflict in the least. For his birth, or raising up, which took place out of Judah, is one thing, and his recall out of Egypt is another: which are not to be opposed to one another.

Fourthly, he argues thus: Thus the last words of the first verse could be referred to the Messiah alone with a far greater appearance of probability, if it had been said by the Holy Spirit, because Israel is a child, I have loved him, and I have given or sent or destined my son to him, or I am about to send a savior to him, or something of that sort. But I reply: With the same appearance of probability, nay, with the same certainty, those words pertain to the Messiah alone, when it is said, therefore I have called my son out of Egypt, nay, this is more fit ting in this place: because it was a benefit proper to the Israelites, as was said above. Nor is there any reason for him to say that his calling out by the Jews could not be foreseen, any more than its cause, and the mention of something more foreign to his faith, because the Messiah did not immediately upon his arrival from Egypt gird himself for the governance of the boy Israel: For there was no need for it to be foreseen from elsewhere: Since from this prophecy that calling out could have been known, and by the interpreter of the Holy Spirit that aforementioned thing was predicted, even if the flight, and the cause of the flight, were not indicated. Nor is the mention of the recall of the Messiah into the land of Israel foreign for that reason, because he did not immediately govern Israel. For that too must be attributed to his love for Israel, that he wished to be brought up among them, and there is no doubt that the little boy πληρούμενος σοφίας, with whom was χάρις Θεoῦ, Luke 2:40, was a joy and pleasure and a notable example to the faithful: who at twelve years old publicly instructed even the great doctors themselves.

That (5) Israel is often called a boy, the son of God, the firstborn of God, Eph. 4:22, Jer. 31:9, has nothing to do with the matter: for that appellation of son of God and firstborn is improper and figurative. And it is manifest that the discourse there is about Israel. But that it is treated of the same in the other passage, no document proves; indeed, we know by the interpreter of the Holy Spirit that it speaks not of Israel, but of Christ, whom God forbid that we should contradict. Nor is it right to descend from the proper meaning of the word בני, which is left to our discretion, to an improper one.

That (6) which is objected regarding the insoluble knot presented to the Jews, concerning the birth of the Messiah, who did not come out of the tribe of Judah or Bethlehem, because he is understood to be called out of Egypt, that is of no account: For there is no conflict between a birth from Bethlehem, or from the tribe of Judah, and a calling out from Egypt; indeed, both ought to have been believed, because both had been revealed. And since Spanheim himself maintains that the calling of Christ is exhibited here in a mystical sense, certainly if that was known to the Prophet and other faithful, they ought to have believed the calling from Egypt no less than the birth from Judah. And what, I pray, is this knot, I will not say insoluble to the Jews, but of any perplexity at all? Was it not easy to think that he who was certainly to be born from Bethlehem, because he was to be called at some time from Egypt, would pass into Egypt, so that he might be called from there by divine nod?

And these are the things which have been brought forward by Spanheim in a refutatory manner against our explanation, which did not seem to be ignored or passed over, since they have drawn even a certain excellent Theologian into that view, so that it might be clear what strength resides in them. Now, in order to construct his own opinion regarding the double sense of this oracle in a constructive manner, he seeks his first argument from the words and the context of the Prophet, which most clearly teach that he is speaking of the Jewish people and the benefit in their leading out from Egypt. We concede that he is speaking of the Israelite people and of a divine benefit: but of a far more eminent one, namely, the destination of the only-begotten Son to the same. The second from the scope of the Old Testament. and the custom of the Holy Scriptures, he assumes that among them the person, times, office, benefits, actions, passions, and other things of that kind of the Messiah are found expressed by most frequent types: but this proceeds from the undistributed to the distributed, a vicious consequence. For it does not follow that if types sometimes occur in the Scriptures, a type is held here also; that method of exhibiting things by express oracles is no less frequent among the sacred writers of the Old Testament; whence a stronger argument will hold in this way: Since all things which Christ did and suffered, even the more minute ones, and all his benefits were predicted in the Old Testament by prophetic oracles, is it a wonder if this most notable work was not predicted here? And since, by the interpreter of the Holy Spirit, we have it that this also was predicted long ago by Hosea, it would be a sin to strip that prophecy, by which the Holy Spirit predicted it, of this sense, and to attribute another sense to it, and to betake oneself to the bare notion of a type, especially in that place where no one could ever think of a type. For who among mortals of the Israelites, to use the argument and words of Spanheim here, could have anticipated in his mind that calling out of the Messiah (typically adumbrated in the leading out from Egypt)? And what need was there to have alleged those words of Hosea, if nothing else was to be indicated than the calling out from Egypt figured by the leading out of the people? Thus, indeed, the Evangelist would have spoken otherwise, and would have asserted, rather than Christ proposing the sign of Jonah, that a sign had been given to the Israelites of the future calling out of Christ in their own leading out, or at least it ought to have been clear from elsewhere regarding that figure.

Spanheim seeks a third reason in analogy and manifold convenience, but in those 14 members of comparison he could not find even one that taught the nature of a type or figure, such as was required here. For it is one thing for certain members of comparison and similarity to intervene, which occur in many histories if they are compared with other deeds, and another for a thing done under the New Testament to have been a type by the intention of the Holy Spirit of a thing to be done under the New Testament: so that while the latter happens, the statement dealing with the former can rightly be said to be fulfilled. Which Spanheim could have already learned from Tarnovius, when he replied to Ribera, who was investigating some members of comparison in his Commentary: Although there are certain things in which a certain comparison could be instituted, yet who will prove from that that they were adumbrated and predicted by the Prophet, and therefore fulfilled in that way. It is certain that the Son of God (1) is called both the people of Israel and Christ, but was the people of Israel a type of the υἱότητος of Christ in that? Who would say this? (2) Israel fled into Egypt, the same happened regarding Christ. But where is the departure of Israel into Egypt established as a type of the departure of Christ into Egypt? (3) Israel fled compelled by famine, Christ compelled by the sword: there is some comparison here, but shall we immediately call it a figure and a type? (4) There the extraordinary prudence of God exercised itself, similarly also here; but who will admit that a type of the preservation of Christ was exhibited in that? (5) As Israel, so also Christ had a safe reception in Egypt, but whether the safe reception of Israel was a type of the safe reception of Christ is being investigated. (6) As through that migration of Israel God became known to Egypt, so also it should not be doubted that the name of Christ became known in Egypt through the proclamation of Joseph and Mary. Be it so: this will be some comparison, not immediately a type. (7) The servitude of Israel in Egypt was a type of the servitude of the people of God, which they are often compelled to undergo in this world: thus also the flight of Christ is a certain likeness of our exile. But by that reasoning, the servitude of Israel in Egypt is not established as a type of Christ acting in Egypt, who is not read to have served there, but rather that the stay of both, namely of Israel and of Christ in Egypt, was a figure of the other, namely of the people of God and the Church. (8) As Israel in Egypt had a nourisher and kinsman from his own people, so also Christ had Joseph and Mary. But here there is a dissimilarity rather than a similarity. For Christ did not have to flee into Egypt for the sake of the former, in order to find a nourisher and kinsman there, in the way that the Israelites descended for that reason. It is a wonder that Spanheim did not also establish a type in Joseph, who was so fortunate in finding types. For Israel was with Joseph in Egypt: Christ also had his Joseph there. (9) As Israel was called out of Egypt by the special guidance of God, so also was Christ. (10) As Israel remained there until he was led out by God, so also Christ. In this, however, he ought to have shown the rationale of the types primarily, namely that that leading out of the people from Egypt prefigured the calling forth of the Messiah. Which until now has occurred to no one of the Jews, even though they, as Spanheim admits, contend that the Messiah is very often designated under the shell of external sayings and deeds. What? That Christ himself led out the Israelites, and was the author of their leading out, and the figure is not to be sought in the Israelites, but in Moses, in the liberator of the people, if it is a matter of a figure. (11) as Israel was led out by the angel addressing Moses, so also Christ by the warning of an angel. Here again a dissimilarity shines forth or a contrary. For the Angel leading out Moses was not a type of a created angel, but the Son of God himself. (12) as the people after the departure from Egypt were introduced into the holy land, which they had inhabited before, so also Christ. A mere comparison here. (13) As Israel, so also Christ was led out, with the infanticidal King removed. The former with Pharaoh removed, the latter with Herod removed. Here again a mere and forced comparison. (14) as there the love of God toward Israel, so here it was proven toward Christ. But who will say that Israel, beloved of God, was a type of Christ, beloved of God, and the love of God toward Israel a type of the love of God toward Christ? That indeed is κρινόμενον, for the proving of which in such prolixity I do not detect even a γρὺ or a μὺ in Spanheim.

But he proceeds further (4) to the places which he calls parallel regarding a double fulfillment, concerning the bone of the paschal lamb not being broken, John 19:36, and in that oracle 2 Sam. 7:14, Heb. 1:5, likewise those which, spoken typically concerning Isaac, Ishmael, Sarah, and Hagar, are referred mystically to the mysteries of the New Testament. But those places are nothing less than parallel to our oracle, nor do they prove a double sense of the same statement, which they ought to have proven. For that the paschal lamb was a type of Christ was established from elsewhere, whence also that περίστασις concerning the not breaking of the bone could easily be applied to it: And that the Israelite people was a type of Christ, whence, I ask, is it established? And who of the Jews constituted the Israelites as a type of the Messiah? The oracle 2. Sam. 7 is altogether perversely snatched away to Solomon, as far as the literal sense is concerned: since such things were not said to any of the angels, as the Apostle testifies in Heb. 1:5, it speaks of Christ alone: as we have shown there against Grotius. Isaac is constituted a type of Christ by the Holy Spirit in the sacrifice in Heb. 11. But is the whole Israelite people therefore a type of Christ? The figures which are taken from Isaac and Israel, Sarah and Hagar, have a foundation in the Scriptures, yet they do not teach a double sense of the same statement. Here, however, we desire the foundation of the type, and we are inquiring about a double sense of the same oracle.

Therefore, Spanheim appeals to the arrows of Jonathan and their shooting, 1 Sam. 20, to show that in some way different things can be designated by the same words or things. But these are as different as heaven and earth: that a single word and statement has a double sense from the intention of the Holy Spirit, and that one thing is a figure and sign of another. There the matter is about the signification of words, here about the designation or shadowing forth of some thing. That one thing and another is designated by some symbol is not new, especially if the symbols are assumed by convention, and their declaration is made. But that such disparate senses underlie the same words in the same oracle, this indeed we deny ἀποτόμως. But while Spanheim objects that it is neither new nor absurd for the same word to be taken both collectively and individually, by the example of the first promise, he begs the question in that very absurdly, for the crushing of the serpent's head is attributed to nothing but the seed of the woman understood μοναδικῶς, i.e. to the Messiah: that the Church is also noted there by the seed of the woman is new, and equally discordant as when the Papists say that Mary is also noted by it. For the race of mortals is to be liberated through this seed of the woman, through the crushing of the serpent, but it cannot be the seed of the woman itself. Furthermore, he says that nothing prevents the same word from being taken historically in one way, prophetically in another, of a past act in one way, of a future in another. But it is entirely an obstacle that the same word in the same place obtains such disparate significations, nor will that be taught by any example from the Scriptures. But that which is drawn in here concerning the Holy Spirit, to whom future things are also present, is again very discordant, for past things are also simply present to Him. Must we therefore conclude from that that when the Holy Spirit speaks of the future, He is simultaneously speaking of the present and of the past? Ἄτοπον ἀτοπώτατον! from which nothing but mere uncertainty and confusion will arise in the Scriptures. He says that it is indeed absurd for several senses of the same kind, namely literal, to agree to the same place, but not so if it is a matter of senses of a different kind, e.g., literal and mystical (which he trusts he will prove ἀναντιῤῥήτως both by reason and by examples, but we hold both to be absurd, and the reasons adduced by him militate against both, i.e., they teach that there cannot be different senses of the same oracle of a different kind, just as of the same kind, inasmuch as any statement of Scripture has only one form: Therefore also only one sense; likewise that not one enunciation but several enunciations are given, where not one but several things are enunciated, since one and true are convertible among themselves: likewise that thus Scripture is rendered ἀμφιδέξιος, ἀμφίλοξος, equivocal, obscure, uncertain; The force of which he strives in vain to elide, as if the unity of the form of Scripture remained, even if a double sense, literal and mystical, is established in the same statement, for the reason that the mystical sense is signified not so much by words as by things, and that there is given a harmony and σχέσις of the literal sense to the mystical, of the type to the antitype, and finally from both an entire and complete sense arises. Whence they call those composite oracles: and because a double enunciation is found implicitly in such, even if only one is explicit, nor is Holy Scripture therefore ambiguous and uncertain when that sense is indicated by the Holy Spirit. For how does the unity of form remain, if such disparate significations, nay often contrary ones, are attributed to one word in the same place, the signification of past and future, the signification of proper and metaphorical, the signification of an individual and of a whole multitude, etc. That which is signified not so much by words as by things, no one would call the sense of the words. For the sense is ultimately what words render and signify. It is one thing, therefore, to seek the signification of words, but another thing what some thing signified by the words has shadowed forth. Thus in the bronze serpent erected, the words in the history of Moses have only one signification, but by that history of the erected bronze serpent historically handed down by Moses, God intended to signify and shadow forth something else. Therefore Spanheim ought not to have confused words and the things themselves. Nor indeed is that harmony detected in the words or enunciations in relation to diverse, disparate, and contrary significations, but in the things indicated by the words. If, however, through the same words, by the intention of the principal author, the Holy Spirit, both the leading out of the Israelites from Egypt is signified, and at the same time the calling back of Christ from Egypt is indicated, how will the unity of the form of Scripture remain, how the unity of the enunciation, how will the speech of the Holy Spirit not be ambiguous and obscure from the very intention of the Holy Spirit, concerning which Spanheim himself doubts whether even the Prophet himself perceived that sense? That this can certainly be asserted and proved, he acknowledges on page 513. But the more ambiguous the speech of the speaker is, than that which, on the part of the primary speaker, has a double sense, one open, the other involved and obscure, which not even the minister himself, in bringing it forth or referring to it, understands, focusing his mind solely on the former. Whence Spanheim finds it necessary to invent COMPOSITE oracles, or to seek them from his Pareus, from one enunciation from one subject, so that he supposes one thing to be clearly different, and interprets the predicate also in a diverse way, even though there is only one in the sacred text: which is not to explain Scripture, but to pervert it: just as the Sacramentarians are accustomed to feign both a proper and a metaphorical sense in the one word 'edite' [eat], so that there might not be only one object of eating, nor one eating, but a double one commanded by the same word in the Holy Eucharist. Which we all, as many as adhere to the literal sense, consider a notable depravation of the words of that Testament.

But what reason, what examples does he bring forward for this equivocation, which are so irrefutable? It cannot be denied (so it stands word for word) that that is the sense of Scripture which the Holy Spirit, its author, proposes, which the God-breathed writers, and for that very reason self-evident, declare. But besides the literal sense, a mystical one is very frequently proposed by the Holy Spirit and His amanuenses in the New Testament. This is his argument: in which, the major being granted, the minor is to be proved. But which one, he does not prove as he had received it, both by reason and examples, but only by examples, concerning the not breaking of the bones of the paschal lamb, and from the words: 'I will be to him a father,' and 'The wives of Abraham,' to which, however, an answer has already been given. He adds the types of Melchizedek, the bronze serpent, Jonah, etc., but he errs by ignorance of the point at issue. For it is not to be proved that types are given in the Old Testament, but that besides the literal sense, a mystical sense also underlies one and the same oracle, 'behold the rose, behold the foot,' in the proving of which Spanheim clearly failed, and thus with great effort he truly accomplished nothing. The rest, in which Spanheim is still verbose, luxuriating in distinctions and according to his custom, do not deserve this effort, that they should be unraveled, and from these they can be judged sufficiently. But these things here ought not to seem foreign, since Grotius himself also fights for the same opinion concerning the double sense of Scripture here and in many other places of Scripture with the same weapons as Spanheim.

And these things concerning that oracle: which the Holy Spirit Himself interpreted in the New Testament concerning Christ, whence that sense is to be holily guarded by us. Which was also the reason why he did not bring forward the version of the Seventy Interpreters, as he otherwise usually does for the most part, because that version wrongly rendered it in the plural, and did not attain the genuine sense 'I called my children,' but according to the Hebrew truth, which Aquila also expressed, 'I called my son,' so that it might be certain that the Prophet spoke concerning the Son of God. Concerning which Dr. Luther in this place: 'This is more to be observed, since the Apostles almost always follow the translation of the Seventy, that Matthew in this place wished to follow the Bible of the Hebrews. For the Seventy have not the singular but the plural number: Out of Egypt I called his children.' The Evangelist corrects this error and by his authority wishes to show by this testimony that this Jesus, born of Mary and called out of Egypt by an angel, is the true eternal Son of God, begotten from eternity. Therefore this testimony of the Prophet applies more truly to Him than to the ancient people, who were sons not by nature, but by adoption. This is the simple and genuine meaning. Thus Blessed Luther. Nor was this sense altogether unknown to the Jews, even though they covered it with their own wrappings, as they are accustomed to do. For those words in Psalm 80:9, 'Thou shalt transplant the vine from Egypt,' they interpret concerning the Messiah in the book Bereshith in section

Harvel. Makom. But that those words of the Psalm treat of the same thing of which Hosea chapter 11:1 treats here, they profess in Schemoth Rabba section 43, whence it can be gathered that they themselves also accepted the words of Hosea concerning the Messiah. Compare Pugio Fidei of Raimund Martini, pp. 125, 432.

Latin:

Vers. 1.

SIC FECIT VOBIS BETHEL) Id est, idolola- tria, cujus sedes Bethel causa erit, ut similis vobis eveniat calamitas.

A FACIE MALITIAE NEQVITLARVM VE- STRARVM SICVT MANE TRANSIT, PERTRAN- SIIT ISRAEL) Haec ita connectenda sunt, ut in Hebraeo, quae in Latino, non periodo tantum, sed & capitulis discer- pta sunt. In Hebraeo: A facie malitiae, malitiae, inquam, ve- strae, in aurora excidio exscindetur Rex Israel: Id est, in ipsis regni initiis evelletur è regno & patria rex Osees filius Elae.

Haec non male Grotius. Addere autem pla- cet commentum Cocceji, ut exemplum habeamus iterum, quo expediat hominis ἰδία ἐπίλυσις in tra- ctandis Scripturis sacris. Somniat enim hic occi- sionem Regis Sueciae Gustavi Adolphi, & mactatio- nem Regis Angliae Caroli, atque excisiones urbium Germaniae. Haec pericopa, inquit, p. 110. complecti- tur castigationem Ecclesiae Evangelicae. Ea consistit in calamitate sive clade exercituum, in occupatione locorum superatis aut perruptis munimentis. Quem- admodum vidimus Palatinatum, Bohemiam, Mora- viam, Silesiam, Pomeraniam, Saxoniam Superiorem & Inferiorem, Holsatiam, Cimbricam, Chersone- sum, & sic à mari Balthico ad mare Septentrionale, & rursus Rhenum ad quem etiam Vesalia & aliae arces, omnia fore in potestatem venisse. In fine addit terribi- le exemplum calamitatis, quod dicit Elisionemma- tris super filiis. Ita solet loqui Scriptura de νεοττιᾷ sive ave pullis incubante Deut. 22, 6. Inde παροιμιῶδες loquendi genus usurpatur, Genes. 32, 11. Ne veniat & percutiat me matrem super pullis, hoc est, pa- trem cum liberis. Mihi videtur eadem haec pa- raemia hoc loco sic usurpari, non, ut significet omnes omnino extirpatum iri (id enim non permittit Aurora, de qua mox) sed post calamitates & clades ingentes, & expugnationes munitionum, & quidem cum dirissima & saevissima vastatione fore, ut etiam tuto & praeter patientium persecutionem, tanquam avium implumium, is, qui patronus dicitur, Esa. 19. v. 20. interficiatur. Isto modo, quo post expugnatam Germaniam, & imprimis Magdeburgum, rex Sueciae mactatus est. Et ad v. 15. Primo colo exprimit causam efficientem & meritoriam hujus mali. Bethel, h. e. Sedes superstitionis Roma, & ejus domini, quibus populi undiquaq́; cingentes Ecclesiam (v. 10.) parent, sic fecit vobis. Supra cap. 6, 9. Societas Sacerdotum muricibus viri legionum, h. e. Imperatoris, vitam corrumpunt. Causa impulsiva est malitia, & quidem mala. Propter malitiam malitiæ vestræ. Secundo colo adjungit ad cumulum malorum novum malum, idq́; & acerbius, quo magis eo tempore Ecclesia in spe alicujus boni versatura erat, simul aliqua lux pacis affulserit (quæ A. C. 1646. 30. Januar. conclusa est inter Regem Hispaniæ & Belgas, & inter Cæsarem ac Galliæ Suediæq́; Reges eodem anno 24. Octobris) occidit Rex Israelis. Olim cogitavi hic de rege adversario, de quo (vers. 6.) sed tristis experientia nos cogit inter castigationes Ecclesiæ numerare interemptionem regis alicujus (præter illum, qui in parcemia matris super pullis fuit significatus) in Ecclesia Evangelica, & quidem unici in ea parte, quæ reformationem profitetur; qui etiam caput Ecclesiæ in suis regnis dictus fuit. Id factum A. C. 1649. 30. Januar. Verbum hic idem est cum eo, quod extat vers. 7. ubi de abolitione Imperatorum Constantinopolitanorum agitur. Non tacuit hanc castigationem Scriptura, & alibi ut Apoc. 14, 20. Psal. 107, 40. Cantic. 8, 7. Deut. 32, 42. Hæc Coccejus, cujus generis sunt cætera in his & aliis Commentariis. Ex ungue leonem.

CONCIO VI. EVANGELICA IN HOC OR- DINE PRIOR. CAPUT XI.

De amore Dei erga Israelitas, quorum gratia ex Ægypto vocabitur Filius Dei, quosq́; suaviter jam olim duxit Deus, qui ob impœnitentiam Assyrio quidem subjiciendi, sed ob Dei misericordiam non, instar Adamæ, penitus evertendi, siquidem tempore N. T. Dominum sectaturi tandem sint pii Israelitæ, Domino per vocem Evangelii rugiente, ab occasu etiam populos advocaturo, imo ipsosmet Ægyptios, & Assyrios aggregaturo. Arguit ingratos Deus, & miserescere pergit.

Vers. 1.

QVIA PVER ISRAEL, ET DILEXI EVM) Cum puer esset Israel, dilexi eum. Prima ætas populi fuit in Ægypto Ezech. 16, 5. c. 23, 3. ET EX ÆGYPTO VOCAVI FILIVM MEVM) Israel DEI Filius, & quidem primogenitus, dicitur Ex. 4, 22. figura in hoc Christi. Vide quæ ad Matth. 1, 25. c. 2, 15. Ex Ægypto vocavi: id est, exire jussi. Notat hic Hieronymus quæ τυπικῶς præcedunt in aliis, juxta veritatem & adimpletionem referri ad Christum.

DE hac pericopa sententiæ occurrunt variæ, inprimis ob allegationem in Novo Testam. factam Matth. 2, 15. Nonnulli solum de Israelitis intelligunt, Rabbini imprimis recentiores R. David Kimchi, & alii cum Juliano Apostata in volum. VII. qui calumniatus ideo Matthæum est, quod de Israele dictum ad Christum detorserit, ut simplicitati eorum, qui de gentibus crediderunt, illuderet. Quam tamen impietatem omnes detestantur Christiani Ideo Matthæum conciliant cum Hosea, quod non alleget Prophetam, sed alludat tantum ad h. l. ad eundem modum uti Act. 13, 11. allusio facta. Quæ Jansenii est explicatio, perinde ac si quis de parte aliqua loquens solicito de filii salute, diceret: vidisses patrem præ filii desiderio non posse consistere, & omnia negligere, ut impleretur in eo illud Maronis:

Omnis in Ascanio chari stat cura parentis. Sed recte Jansenii sententiam reprobat Barradius T. I. Conc. Evangel. p. 188. Quod impletur, per accommodationem non dicitur, sed per prædictio- nem. Et manifesta est Matthæi allegatio: quid di- serte dicit hanc Hoseæ scripturam impletam esse, cum Christus ex Ægypto rediret, non simile tantum quid accidisse innuit. Et hoc est quod hic observat Rivetus p. 343. Quando scriptores Novi Testamen- ti ad directam probationem, non ad accommodatio- nem locum aliquem adducunt, tunc ex ipso citandi modo satis ostendunt differentiam, inter similitudi- nem & exemplum adductum, & propriam rei prædi- ctæ adimpletionem: cum enim non adducunt locum aliquem aut similitudinis, aut generalis confirmatio- nis gratia, sed plane ut ostendant id, quod ipsi narrant aut affirmant, fuisse omnino prædictum, & quia præ- dictum fuerat, necesse fuisse ut existeret: tunc autem extitisse, cum illud evenit, quod ab ipsis narratur aut affirmatur: solent ejusmodi verba adhibere, unde hæc ipsorum mens aperte constet, ut hoc loco, ut adim- pleretur quod dictum est.

Alii tum de Israele, tum de Christo hæc omnia accipiunt: sensu literali de Israele, mystico de Chri- sto; ita Calixtus in Concord. p. 75. & Calviniani plerique. Quam interpretandi rationem Papistis gratam Grotius hic sequutus est. Nam de Israele secundum literam intellexit: sensu autem subli- miori ad Christum referendum esse, censuit, ut e collatione eorum quæ annotavit ad Matthæum constat. Quæ etiam Spanhemii sententia: in scri- ptis Propheticis occurrere sæpe oracula composita, ge- minam impletionem habentia: unam in ipso, alte- ram antitypo: nihil obstare τὸ בֶּן, & collective de populo, & individualiter ac antonomastice de Messia intelligi, part. II. Dub. Evangel. LXII. p. 478. Quæ vero probari minime possuut. primo, quod ita sen- sus geminus eidem oraculo affingatur, contra scri- pturæ simplicitatem, perspicuitatem & certitudi- nem, ac præter Sp. S. morem. Deinde quod incon- veniens omnino sit, eandem vocem filii in eodem loco tum sensu improprio de filio metaphorice ita di- cto per adoptionem, tum proprio de filio vero & na- turali Dei intelligi. Nam unam eandemque vocem simul & semel & proprie & tropice seu figurate accipi ἄτοπον, imo plane ἀδύνατον. Nam qui loquitur de filio adoptivo sensu improprio, is eo ipso dum impro- prie loquitur, certe non loquitur proprie: dum de filio adoptivo loquitur, non loquitur de filio vero & naturali. Similiter tertio inconveniens est nomen filii & συλλεπτικῶς ac collective accipi de Israelitis, & μοναδικῶς vel singulariter de Chri- sto. Quarto inconveniens insuper est, verbum vo- cavi & sensu præteriti intelligi & sensu futuri: vo- caturus deinceps sum; illo de Israele, hoc vero de Christo. Nec male hic B. Joh. Tarnovius: Si id obtinent Calviniani, quidni etiam obtinebunt, in ver- bis Cœnæ verba Christi, Edite, bibite respectu symbo- lorum proprie, respectu autem rei cælestis seu corporis & sanguinis Christi improprie recte posse explicari. Quinto Matthæus in eo est, ut causam reddat, cur Deus Filium suum in Ægyptum fugari permiserit, ac rursus ex Ægypto revocarit, atque eam petit e prædictione per Prophetam facta, ut scilicet vatici- nium illud suum complementum sortiretur. Quid vero eo facit migratio Israelitarum in Ægyptum, in qua ne typi quidem ratio respectu fugæ Chri- sti in Ægyptum obtinet, & eductio eorum ex Ægypto?

Commodior nonnihil est eorum sententia, qui non duplicem præcise sensum hic constituunt ejus- dem sententiæ, sed retento unico sensu de Israele,

Matthæum solum typum monstrasse volunt, quemadmodum S. Johannes Cap. 19, 36. cum nos remittit ad Exod. 12, 46. os non frangetis illi, typum monstrat. Ubi tamen monendum, quod eo ipso S. Johannes non doceat, geminum sensum verbis Mofis inesse; Nam nec subjectum pronomine ILLI designatum esse, cum agnum paschalem, tum etiam Christum, loco Exodi convenit, utpote in quo nullum verbum de Christo habetur, nec sub- strata materia admittit, ut Christus cum agno pa- schali ibi intelligatur. Et multum diversa sunt, ty- pum monstrari, vel convenientiam antitypi cum ty- po, & alium sensum à literali diversum, mysticum nempe exhiberi. Illud enim fieri potest, ut verba in sede propria simplicem sensum retineant, res autem ipsa, quæ illis expressa est, doceatur typicum respectum habuisse ad ἀντίτυπον sub N. T. exhi- bendum, utque opus non διττότητα sensus in ean- dem sententiam invehere. Atque ea ratione Hie- ronymi & Theophylacti observatio hic facilius admitti posset, quam Grotianus duplex sensus: è quibus ille ad cap. 11. Hos. Est mira, inquit, scriptu- ræ profunditas: Ea quæ typice præcedunt, in aliis jux- ta veritatem & adimpletionem referuntur ad Chri- stum. Hic vero quod per figuram, inquit, dictum est de populo, impletum est vere in Christo. Sed quum Matthæus non ad historiam aut factum aliquod ty- picum nos remittat, verum potius causam reddat, cur Christus debuerit ex Ægypto revocari, quæ certe in typica ista ratione non adeo luculenta est, non satisfacit illa conciliatio. Nam etsi liberatio Israëlitarum à potestate Pharaonis, & ex Ægypto typus fuerit liberationis nostræ spiritualis ex pote- state Satanæ, & ex inferno, per Christi activam & passivam obedientiam factæ, non tamen ipsa libera- tio Israëlitarum ex Ægypto ideo typus fuit revoca- tionis Christi Filii Dei è Regno Ægypti. Ibi Israe- litæ nostri & totius humani generis typum gessere, non Christi: Moses vero deducens eos ex Ægy- pto figuram Christi gessit. Nec aliunde typi illius ratio constat; quemadmodum quidem de agno paschali, quod typus fuerit Christi affatim edoce- mur è scripturis. Nec denique ex Hoseæ loco præ- senti id adeo liquet, quod respectus typi aliquis in- tervenerit in ea revocatione Israelis in πίσει ad re- ductionem Christi ex Ægypto, quemadmodum de typo agni paschalis ex ipso cap. 12. Exod. à Johanne cap. 19. adducto penes Judæos res indubia fuit. Disparrima ergo est illa collatio. Porro non male monet hic Rivetus distinguendos esse typos: Typi, inquit, & allegoriæ tum demum firmas consequentias pariunt, cum in quæstione juris versantur, hoc est, si quando quæratur utrum justum aut injustum aliquid dicatur esse. Quod si ad quæstionem facti pertine- bunt: id est, si quæratur, utrum aliquid futurum sit nec ne; tum inter typos distingui oportet; quia cum typorum alii sint dati, & imperati à Deo; alii vero facti: Quia dati seu imperati sunt à DEO, ii cum proprie ad rem adumbratam spectent, & perpetuam relationem ac necessariam habeant, omnino conclu- dunt futurum id, cujus adumbrandi causa dati sunt, quia typi non sunt aliud quam divinæ voluntatis si- gna, qua in veritate est ineluctabilis quædam & abso- luta necessitas. Qui autem typi facti fuerunt, nec ad certam aliquam significationem proprie & peculiari- ter destinati; ii cum naturam exemplorum sequan- tur, horum documenta non sunt necessitatis, sed tan- tum contingentiæ. Itaque delectare & illustrare in docendo possunt, probare autem minime. Si ergo ac- cessio Israëlitarum ex Ægypto typus fuerit accessionis Messiæ ex Ægypto, cum non fuerit typus Juris, sed fa- cti: non datus, sed tantum opere præstitus; non pro- ba- prius, sed communis, ut sunt exempla omnia, nullam probationem firmam adferre potest. Hæc Rivetus F. Junium sequutus, cujus verba etiam sua fecit è libr. parall. cap. 6. Denique cum certa dari possunt sensus literalis documenta, & oraculi ejusdem complemento convenientia, non est ad typi rationem discedendum. Vaticinia enim potiora & illustriora sunt testimonia, quam typi & figuræ, quas ne in scripturas inferre videamur, è scripturis ipsis ostendere prius oportet, quam fiat applicatio.

Alii hic se recipiunt ad arctissimam capitis corporisquæ conjunctionem. Christus caput est, Ecclesia corpus mysticum. Huic ergo quod contingit, ad ipsum caput non immerito putatur referri. Ideoque exeunte Israele & Ægypto Christus una egressus est, ut caput & sponsus Ecclesiæ. Quæ est Gesneri sententia : de qua vero hanc addit B. Meisnerus ἐπίκρισιν: Pia quidem & vera hæc sententia, sed præter scopum. Matthæus enim non hoc intendit, quod Christus cum Israele, veluti caput, olim tempore Mosis exierit, quoad divinitatem, sed quod post nativitatem & fugam in Ægyptum in sua persona quoad humanitatem revocatus, & hoc ipso N. T. tempore scriptura Hoseæ impleta fuerit. Adde quod Matthæus non analogiam, sed historiam referat historice, nec illa analogia firma sit de capite. Quam multa enim fuerunt gesta in deserto, in terra Canaan, sub judicibus & Regibus, quæ etsi ad caput possunt dici pertinuisse in suis membris, in capite ipso minime impleri potuerunt?

Quinto itaque alii de solo Christo hæc intelligunt & quidem ita, ut præcedentia etiam ad Christum referant. Ita Eusebius Demonstrat. Evangel. l. 9. demonstr. 9. Omnia præcedentia, quæ de Rege Israelis dicta sunt, de Christo ad literam intelligit, & hæc eadem verba, non de Israele ullo modo, sed de solo Christo dicta fuisse & intelligenda asserit. Eandem sententiam expressit in notis ad N. Test. cap. 2. Matth. Isidorus Clarius Brixianus; quasi Dominus populum suum admoneret per Prophetam, ut cum Christus Doctor justitiæ advenerit, ne per oscitationem eum non admitteret, aut occasionem præterlabi sineret, quia Christi conversatio in terris auroræ similis esset, postquam nempe post prædicationis triennium, succidendo succideretur Rex Israel. Cum tamen prævideret Judæos Christum ad mortem postulatuos, cum Herode, idque facturos, non tam ex malitia, quam ex imprudentia, quia pueri essent; in Ægyptum abduxisse filium suum, ne stultus populus Christum ante tempus occidendo, se privaret fructu, quem ex eo capere debebat. Tandem Herode mortuo, & populo nati Christi magna ex parte oblito, vocasse filium suum ex Ægypto, ut ipsis ignorantibus apud eos adolesceret &c. Sed hanc sententiam recte refellit Rivetus. Nam quod per Regem Israelis succidendum Christum intelligit, prorsus est absurdum. Deinde quod ea de causa abductum fuisse Christum in Ægyptum dicit, quia Israel puer illum ad mortem cum Herode erat postulaturus, omni ratione caret. Populus enim non fuit reus crudelitatis illius, quam exercuit Herodes; imo pessimam inivit gratiam à populo, qui tot infantes miserabili carnificina obtruncari jussit, & sanguinem regium apud Judæos abolevit. Præterea cum hic quæstio sit de decem tribubus, nulla ratio excogitari potest, cur nomen Israelis hoc loco accipi debeat pro Judæis, apud quos Herodes regnabat. Hæc ille.

Sexto Rupertus Abbas Tuitiensis in Comment. ad h. l. existimat Prophetam loqui de Rege Herode, & de Christo. Quod dixit pertransiisse Regem Israelis, de Herode Rege intelligendum esse, cujus Regnum cito finem habuit, quæ subjiciuntur, quia puer Israel & dilexi eum &c. de Christo ad literam sonare, qui Herode mortuo revocatus ex Ægypto. Non probat eam opinionem Spanhemius, impri- mis quod quæ de Hosea Rege dicuntur, de Herode absurde intelligantur, sed quanto absurdius Cocce- jus de Rege Angliæ ea interpretatus est?

Septima sententia eorum est, qui totum ver- sum primum hujus capitis de Christo literaliter in- telligendum esse statuunt, nullatenus vero de po- pulo Israëlítico, ut sensus sit: cum Christus esset in- fans, vel puer, dilexi eum, & evocavi eum ex Ægy- pto: quam multorum esse explicationem, notat Spanhemius loco citato p. 487. sed in hac explica- tione desideratur, 1. quod puerum Israelis nihil a- liud quam infantem notare velit: quum non de puero simpliciter, sed de puero Israelis, ut illi vo- lunt, qui vocem נער in regimine positam esse di- cunt, sermo sit. 2. Quod Christum subjectum fa- ciat in primo colo, quum potius objectum ibi sit Israël, quod in nominandi casu accipiendum est, non per genitivum reddendum. 3. Quod nomen Christi in primo colo plane non habeatur, nec im- plicite quidem, si vero è secundo colo derivetur, hyperbolica & contorta nonnullis videtur expli- catio: quod tamen alii per Ebrææ linguæ indo- lem excusatum eunt.

Octava Fr. Junii est, Verba primi Versus iti- dem ad Christum referentis secundum literam, sed alia ratione, quam in Parallelis ita explicat l. 1. p. 6. Propheta incipit cap. 9. ad verum Israelem conver- tere orationem suam, ut partim recordatione bene- ficiorum Dei, partim Judiciorum asperitate, par- tim misericordiæ divinæ argumentis erigat pios ad exspectationem adventus Christi, in quo & per quem Deus Prophetiarum suarum veritatem erat comple- turus. Reliquiis ergo Israelis hic spem facit salutis in Christo Jesu, & statuit electas reliquias ex incendio communi eripiendas propter filium suum, & in ipso: 1. Ut in capite & primogenito inter multos fratres, à quo in membra sua omnia derivatur vita & salus. 2. Ut in filio dilectionis, in quo amor DEI infinitus conquiescit. Hujus autem salutis principia demon- stratum iri, quo tempore filius Dei à populo Judæorum contemptus, & ab Herode infestatus ex Ægypto sit re- vocandus, ut opus salutis promissum Ecclesiæ in Judea reipsa exequeretur. Sic designavit Propheta 1. salu- tis fontem & causas, quando dicit, quia puer Israelis est, diligo eum. 2. signum apparentis & adventan- tis gratiæ exponitur illis verbis: Ex Ægypto voca- vi filium meum. Perinde enim est, ac si dixisset Deus, totumne Israelem perditurus essem, non faciam propter filium meum; nam cum puer Israelis sit, id est, primogenitus, æternum sacerdotium obiens, (sic enim pueros Israelis dici Exod. 24.) præterea cum is sit filius meus unigenitus, quamvis Israelitæ è medio sui eum expulerint, & indigni sint, quibus ex- hibeatur gratia, tamen propter electos, & ad salutem illorum filium meum ex Ægypto vocaturus sum, qui ovibus Israelis salutem afferat. Hæc Spanhemius è Junio repetit l. c. In notis Junio - Tremellianis hæc ita exhibentur ad hunc locum: Transit Pro- pheta ad enarrationem gratiosarum promissionum de reconciliatione Israëlitarum cum DEO, id est, san- ctarum reliquiarum secundum electionem gratiæ in Christo. Sensus igitur est, amorem DEI erga popu- lum ipsius æternum esse, quumque gratuiti illius amoris, & beneplaciti Dei fundamentum sit in Christo (quem exhibitum & natum in carne, neque Judæi neque Israëlitæ agnoverant) quamvis non fuisset futurum à justitia Dei alienum, ut eo in æternum privarentur (quod subductio illius in Ægy- ptum videbatur portendere) Deum tamen sibi in amore suo erga populum suum constare, & propter- ea Christum (quem ad sua venientem minime re- ceperant) ex Ægypto, quo fuerat subductus, in terram Israelis revocare. Est autem hæc Dei ar- gumentatio: Ego hunc diligo, ac proinde quos- cunque diligit, & pro quibus intercedit, eos di- lecturus sum: Diligit autem Israelem: nam puer est primogenitus Israelis, pro ipso apud me legitime intercedens: quapropter Israeli benefacturus sum in eo, quem diligo & ad hunc finem revoca- turus eundem ex Ægypto. Quam interpretatio- nem amplexus etiam est Joh. Piscator in notis ad Matth. 2. vers. 15. Observans nomen antecedens (filii) ex consuetudine Ebræorum postponi: regu- larem enim verborum collocationem hanc esse, quia Filius meus puer est, id est, minister Israelis, h. e. populi Israelitici, idcirco diligo eum, & pro- pter utramque causam vocavi eum ex Ægypto, ut scilicet in patriam reversus & Nazarethi educa- tus inde prodiret ad prædicandum Evangelium. Quam vero Spanhemius atutam potius & ingenio- sam, quam solidam esse judicat. Nec tamen ad- eo solida sunt, quæ illi opponit. Quod enim primo ait hyperbaticam eam nimis esse, & contor- tam in verbis, ei jam occurrit Piscator per illam E- bræorum consuetudinem. Quod deinde ἀνά- κλασιν in sensu & nexu ait, nec analysin inge- niosam Junii à transitu post comminationes ad correctionem, à correctione ad concessionem satisface- re, id expedient Patroni illius sententiæ simili mo- re scripturæ, cui talis transitus insolens non est. Ita habet apologia Junii in parallelis: Adjuncta vero ut repugnent huic interpretationi, videre non possu- mus: Contra enim maximam habent convenientiam cum hac interpretatione nostra; præcessit cap. 10. justissima Dei sententia de perdendis Israelitis. Huic sententiæ quædam veluti correctio subjicitur ad san- ctarum reliquiarum consolationem, cujus fundamen- tum est Christus, ut ante diximus. Ergo summa est cum rebus antecedentibus convenientia. Quid au- tem consequentibus fiet? Illis quoque optime convenit cum propositione ista. Est enim in verbis sequenti- bus concessio, & quædam velut contentio forensis, ac disceptatio: qua Israelitarum improbitatem vehe- mentissime Deus exaggerat, ut amplius deinde illu- stret suam misericordiam. Quidni evocassem ex Ægypto filium meum? inquit Dominus: Nam alioqui fuisset actum de tota hac Israelitarum gente: quæ, utut per Prophetas revocata fuerit; ad idola transfugit: utcunque meipsum operibus demonstra- verim, cæcutivit ultro neque ductu aut curatione mea, neque amantissimis officiis, liberationibus, alimentis, administratione, flagellis denique edomari hactenus potuit, nec dum oculos ad Deum supremum extulit. Quid ergo fuissem hic facturus aliud, quam ut filium meum peregre versantem reducerem? Nam quomodo te traditurus essem Ephraim? &c. Ita sententia de- mum de salute piorum fertur, ac si repente Dominus ex gravissimo istarum contentionum æstu emergeret. Non faciam, inquit, &c. tanquam si diceret; attamen puer meus es, mihi charus: damnabilis quidem propter peccata tua, at servandus propter natu- ram, veritatem, sanctitatem, & misericordiam meã in filio dilectionis meæ, quem vocavi ex Ægy- pto. Hanc genuinam esse loci intelligentiam ipsa orationis series attendentibus commonstrabit. Quæ pro acutis habet Rivetus judicio sine dubio valen- tior Spanhemio. At planior longe, Spanhemio judi- ce, analysis est minis propositis subjici commemoratio- nem & beneficiorum Dei & ingratitudinis populi. Admittimus. Num vero summum non est benefi- cium, quod Deus Israelitis filium suum ex Ægy- pto revocavit? Quod certe longe majus est illa Israelitarum ex Ægypto deductione. Quod tertio absurdum Spanhemio videtur, vocem נער hic ad primogenituram, vel ministerium Messiæ tantum referri sublato fundamento applica- tionis ad antitypum, id nec absurdum esse illi admit- tent, & petitione principii laborare, haud imme- rito dicent, quum id in quæstione sit; An hic ali- qua typi ratio locum habeat? Porro Quarto vocem ישׂראל non nisi violenter in generandi casu exponi, cum inde probat Spanhemius, quod certum & cla- rum sit ex inspectione textus, vocem בני hic literaliter esse prædicatum Israelis, in eo fallitur vehementer Spanhemius, nec nisi principium petit, quod ipsi perquam familiare est. Quod etiam in quinta ra- tione deprehenditur. Durum esse & crudum dicit, sensu plano & literali prorsus rejecto (nam de eo quæritur an ille sit sensus literalis?) subintelligere vocem בני filius meus, vel eam ex fine versus retra- here ad initium. At id Piscator ex Hebræorum con- suetudine deducit, præsertim quum ibi non בני occurrat, sed לבני cum præfixo. Qualia præfixa ni- hil obstare solent vocibus retrahendis ad anterio- ra: quia nomen solum respicitur, quod retrahen- dum est, ut Ebraice doctis notum est. Quod deni- que quærit Spanhemius, cur hic potius mentio fa- cta fuisset evocationis Filii Dei ex Ægypto, non desti- nationis vel missionis ejus in mundum? id levicu- lum nobis videtur. Siquidem nec præscribere fas sit Spiritui S. quænam allegare velit beneficia, & quum alias sæpe inculcatum illud beneficium sit destinationis Messiæ, commemorari alicubi etiam debuerit ista Filii in gratiam Judæorum facta ex Ægypto revocatio; quum cætera minutiora etiam de Messia non tacuerit vetus Scriptura; & hanc evocationem hic prædictam esset testat⁹ sit S. Mat- thæus. Adde quod missio in mundum commune sit beneficium, hæc vero evocatio in Judæorum gra- tiam facta proprium ipsis & peculiare donum sit: unde ad exprobrandum ipsis ingratitudieem ap- prime facit ejusdem commemoratio. Hæc ad- versus Spanhemium.

Scrupulum tamen illum de PUERO ISRAEL urget etiam Rivetus, idque pressius, ni fallor; id ta- men, inquit, coactum videtur, quod Junius Filium Dei Messiam appellari initio vult נער ישראל id est, ut interpretatur, primogenitum Israelis filium. Ad- duxit ad probationem locum ex cap. 24. Exod. v. 5. Ubi Moses dicitur misisse נערי naarei, id est, pueros filiorum Israel, qui fecerunt ascendere holocausta, quo loco primogenitos Israelitarum intelligi, eosque primogenitos duodecim principum Israelis, quia sa- cerdotium tunc erat annexum primogenituræ, verius existimat Lyranus, quam quod alii ad Nadab & Abiu futuros sacerdotes referunt; sed eum loci hujus interpretatio non sit certa, & possint intelligi per ju- venes Israelitarum ministri eorum qui pecus ad im- molandum aptum adduxerunt: nulla alioquin in- ter eos autoritate pollentes; ut 1. Sam. 2. vers. 13. puer sacerdotis dicitur, qui ministrabat ei, in gradu inferiore; non videtur posse aut debere hanc vocem de Christo intelligi. Hæc Rivetus. Nec immerito. Nam vocem נער idem esse quod filius primogenitus nunquam docebitur. Neque pro ministro, quod voluit Piscator, hic commode accipitur. Nam nec ille usus vocis demonstratus est, aut admitti debet hoc loco, quum non sit præter necessitatem à vocis proprio sensu ad improprium discedendum: neq; causa dilectionis paternæ Christi hæc est, quod mi- nister Israelis sit, nec temere discedendum à com- muni Interpretum consensu, qui vocem Israel casu nominandi hic accipiunt, non generandi: quem ta- men consensum a nota genitivi casus perperam hic probat Spanhemius. Denique vocem pueri re- ctius Israeli hic aptari in casu recto, collatio loci Luc. 1. v. 54. ἀνελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ su- scepit Israel puerum suum, confirmat.

Nona explicatio haec est, prius colon pertine- re ad Israelem: posterius vero, quod Matthaeus al- legavit, ad Messiam. Quae nobis probata semper fuit: quum facilis & expedita sit, atque interpre- tationi a Spiritu Sancto traditae consonet. Sensus ergo erit hic: Quamvis Israel נער est, & manet, h. e. puer, vel potius rudis, praecipitans in actionibus, excutiens (jugum) & transgressor: tamen dilexi eum, & ob amorem, quo eum complector, evocavi Filium meum ex Aegypto, ejus gratia, ut erudiat, in ordinem redigat & emendet ipsum. Nam id notat vox נער ex vi Etymi, & pro peccatore accipitur Esa. 65, 20. at cum voce חוטא peccator qui deflexit a via (qua insigne peccatum & delictum notatur Num. 15, 29. Psal. 4, 5. Psalm. 41, 5. Thren. 1, 8. Esa. 1, 4.) commutatur, נער puer filius centum annorum mo- rietur, & וְהַחוֹטֶא peccator filius centum annorum maledicetur. Rivetus ita reddit: quamvis sit puer Israel rudis & tenellus, tamen diligo eum, adducens LXX. Interpp. versionem διότι νήπιος Ἰσραὴλ: quia νηπιos non potest sibi ipsi relinqui sine periculo: id- circo ne omnino pereat sibi relictus, ex Aegypto vo- cavi Filium meum, qui illum susciperet & conser- varet in reliquiis suis, ne imprudentia & ruditate sua se prorsus praecipitaret. Alii eodem sensu vo- cem כִּי reddunt receptiori significatione QUIA, hoc modo: quia Israel puer, h. e. tenellus, rudis, curae indigus, tum ignorantia puerili laborans, tum imbecillitate, dilexi eum, & ob amorem, quo eum complector, ex Aegypto vocavi Filium meum, illi videlicet docendo, regendo, & ad officium revo- cando, ne defectu rectoris se praecipitem det in exitium. Sed quum Israelem redarguerit vehe- mentissime Propheta, non adeo convenire huic loco videtur illa explicatio, qua extenuantur vel- uti peccata Israelis, quasi ex ignorantia puerili, ac infirmitate profecta, quae elato brachio patrata; Ideo retento sensu adversativo vox נער non de ru- di, tenello & infirmo, sed de transgressore, jugumve ex- cutiente potius intelligenda, ut eo amplior sit di- vina gratia, quam huic praevaricatori Israeli ex- hibere dignatus est. Quam sententiam mihi probatam video etiam B. Tarnovium, dum eundem confero, fovisse, siquidem ita red- diderit: quamvis Israel sit puer, excutiens saepius jugum paternum.

Hoc ergo oraculum, quoad posterius colon, de Christo secundum Literam intelligendum esse, non de populo Israelitico, haec confirmant: Primo evidentia hujus interpretationis: Omnia enim ita sunt luculenta: nec quicquam duri, coacti, aut contorti est in illa interpretatione. Probabiliorem longe eam esse Juniana explicatione, ac constru- ctionem faciliorem & verborum & sensus, cum po- sterius colon tantum ad Christum refertur, agnoscit Spanhemius. Nec opus ita hyperbato, & verba omnia ex ordine fluunt, suumque nativum sensum retinent. Omnia & singula verba hunc sensum optime admittere Tarnovius docet p. 361. כִּי saepis- sime accipitur adversative pro quamvis, quod hic vertunt, quia vel quando; vid. exercit. Bibl. p. 63. & seqq. Nomen נער etsi significatione est generale, & vel aetate vel ministerio aliis inferiorem notat, ta- me ratione originis, quia est a נער i.e. excussit, & ad- junctae plerisque rebellionis, imo imperitiae ac mali- tiae cujusdam innatae, significat eum, qui crebro ju- gum parentis vel heri excutit, estque imperitus, fatuus, stolidus. Proverb. 1, 4. & 22, 15. Esa. 3, 3. Eccles. 10, 16. Jer. 1, 6. confer vocem νήπιος 1. Cor. 13, vers. 11. Eph. 4. vers. 11. &c. in Novo Testa- mento, ubi notetur Aben Esræ in h. l. & ad hoc no- men glossa. Respicit, inquit ad caput 10. v. 11. ubi עֶגְלָה מְלֻמָּדָה & sup. c. 4, 16. פָּרָה סֹרֵרָה; expende etiam ea, quæ de hoc puero dicuntur infra v. 3. & rectius hæc intelliges. Vau variis modis usurpatur, adeo ut Protheus à multis appelletur. Tamen notat Exod. 5, 16. stramen non datur servis tuis, lateres ta- men וּלְבֵנִים inquit nobis perficite, Job. 3, 26. וְלֹא tam advenit commotio Hos. 1, 10. וְהָיָה attamen erit numerus filiorum. Eccles. 9, 15. וְאָדָם לֹא זָכַר ta- men homo non recordatus est. Sic καὶ Luc. 7, 8. in Novo Testamento, Phil. 4, 10. sic paulo post idem Vau pro ideo, idcirco, quapropter, usurpatur in וּמִמִּצְרַיִם, videantur alia loca similia allegata in Commentar. Psal. 12. v. 10. pag. 59. ubi idem etiam de particula καὶ probatum. Hæc ille.

Deinde distinctio vocum בְּנִי & נַעַר. Quæ uti diversissimæ sunt significationis, ita juxta hanc in- terpretationem commodissime redduntur suoque subjecto assignantur rectissime. Nam nomen נַעַר Israeli ad ejus genium describendum, qualis fuerit, apprime convenire, nemo ambigit. Fuit enim sem- per aut rudis aut præceps, nec raro excutiens jugum, & transgressor pertinax: qualem etiam hunc po- pulum depinxit imprimis Hoseas. Id ergo nomen Israeli convenit, non Christo. Alterum vero no- men Filii mei simul cum illo, si contumacis pecca- toris & prævaricatoris significatio obtineat, quales omnino Israelitæ maximam partem erant, non ita commode jungitur, eidemque in una atque eadem oratione eo modo, quo hic, conjunctim non tri- buitur. Ideoque utrumque de Israele accipien- dum non est, sed potius prius solum de Israele, po- sterius vero de Christo explicandum.

Tertio vocis FILII MEI proprietas. Filii enim DEI nomen proprie acceptum non nisi Christo convenit. At propria vocis significatio retinenda, ubi non cogimur ad impropriam de- scendere, sanæ Theologiæ regula est, ajunt ipsimet Sociniani, nec esse recurrendum ad figuram, nisi cogat necessitas. Quum ergo hic nulla sit necessi- tas, imo omnia recte se habeant, ut filii Dei augu- stum nomen Messiæ proprium absolute ac simpli- citer positum pervicaci Israeli assignemus, quum Christum ipsum intelligere possimus, religio no- bis est, de alio, quam Christo id interpretari.

Quarto diversitas Israelis, quem dilexit DEUS etsi puerum, & Filii Dei, quem vocavit ex Ægy- pto, in Israelis gratiam. Nam si in eodem subjecto persisteret, ita potius loqueretur Propheta: Quam- vis Israel puer est, dilexi eum, & vocavi eum ex Æ- gypto. Quia vero hic aliud subjectum inferit, & vocavi FILIUM DEUM, haud obscure docet, in gratiam potius Israelis, & ob dilectionem ejus- dem vocatum dici Filium Dei, quam ipsum Israe- lem vocatum esse.

Quinto etiam interpretatio Sp. S. in N. T. quæ omni exceptione superior, longeque luculen- tissima est. Reddit enim Matthæus causam, cur Christus non in Ægypto manserit, sed revocatus fuerit ex Ægypto, ut nempe impleretur, quod di- ctum est per Prophetam dicentem: Ex Ægypto vo- cavi filium meum. Quod ergo de Filio Dei inter- pretatur Spiritus S. nostrum non est abripere ad Israelem, quod de vocatione Christi ex Ægypto Ev- angelista explicat, & in ea impletum esse dicit, id de eductione populi Israelitici ex Ægypto intelligi ne- potest, nec debet. Quod impletum demum est si- Novo Testamento, id factum non est olim Mosis tempore. Si dicas, sensu transumtivo vel accom- modativo tantum hæc à Matthæo ita explicari, sen- tentiam hanc non in Jansenio solum Episcopo Gandav. sed etiam in Bucero suo, ac Mercero refel- lit prolixe Spanhemius dubio LXIV. LXV. Loca à Jansenio citata ex Matth. 13, 14. 15. & c. 15. alius dicit esse generis, & vel de vitiis agere, vel de artibus communibus, ubi eadem ratio plurium ordinarie reperitur. Aliam esse rationem, ubi de Messia agi- tur, ad quem alludi tantum ejusmodi citatione & præter mentem quidem Sp. S. à ratione omni alie- num. Si vero eum Spanhemio obvertas, sensu my- stico hæc allegari à Matthæo, obstabunt pleraque Spanhemiana argumenta, quæ Jansenio opposita sunt: utpote quod citationes, quæ Messiam con- cernunt, studiose à Matthæo congestæ, non illustratio- nis tantum gratia, sed & probationis, hunc Jesum Na- zarenum esse verum Messiam, eo quod ab illo, in illo, & circa illum ea adimpleta legantur, quæ de Messia in Vetere Testamento prædicta fuere: quodq; parum conveniens sit sacro scriptori relicto vero loci Prophetici sensu, meram allusionem (sen- sum tantum mysticum) captare, imo quod stylus Evangelistarum alius longe sit à stylo Prophetarum; iste involutus, ille evolutus; in isto allegoriæ, figuræ, typi, in illo figurarum & typorum declaratio, non no- vanovarum allusionum seges. Et huc referri vult Spanhemius, quod apposite notat Junius, discipulos Christi non fuisse allegoristas, sed veros allegoriarum & typorum veterum ἀναγωγέας sive ἀναλυτάς, ad- eoque injuriam illis fieri, si typos & allegorias veteres, novis allegoriis dicantur obruere, & sacratissima Le- gis & Prophetarum verba in usum illum detorquere, qui sunt solidissimi omnium illorum interpretes. Ad- de quod hic ratio typi & mysticus ejusmodi sensus haud congruat, quod notatum etiam Riveto est: Nec valet consequentia, quam nectunt nonnulli: libera- tionem Ægyptiacam fuisse typum spiritualis liberatio- nis nemo pius dubitat: Merito igitur hæc evocatio ex Ægypto ad Christum spiritualis liberationis auto- rem refertur. Quid enim hoc ad reditum non spiri- tualem, sed temporalem & corporalem, ut ita loquar, Christi ex Ægypto? An quia ex Babylonica captivi- tate liberatio fuit figura spiritualis liberationis, de- buit propterea Christus in Babyloniam mitti, & postea evocari, ut typo responderet veritas? Hæc Ri- vetus p. 343. In quam rem plura habet Tarnovius in h. l. p. 356. Expendantur & hæc, 1. licet liberatio miraculosa ex Ægypto fuerit typus quidam liberatio- nis spiritualis per Christum ex inferno, ut ex Ægypto spirituali Apoc. 2, 8. tamen neque populus ille libera- tus typus fuit liberantis Christi (populus enim libe- rabatur, Christus liberabat: populus dura servitu- te in Ægypto premebatur, Christus in Ægypto tu- tus & securus à violentia Herodis degebat, quæ eum Judæa expulerat) neque liberatio illa Christi liberatoris. 2. Israel non evocabatur sola voce ex Ægypto, sed potenti manu educebatur, Christus sola voce Angeli Matth. 2, 19. 20. III. Quomodo possu- mus non Christo non tribuere ingratitudinem, si de illo utrumque membrum versus primi literaliter ex- ponamus velut de antitypo? IV. Quomodo unum verbum & præteritum tempus & futurum in uno lo- co significabit? Nec sibi constant satis, quæ pro sen- su mystico pugnant. Pareus certe modo literaliter de Israele tantum, mystice de Christo hæc intelligit, modo etiam in Christo literaliter impleta esse ait: Matthæus, inquit apud Tarnovium pag. 350. scribit oraculum hoc tunc fuisse impletum in Christo. Er- go non sola similitudo est causa. Concedendum est igitur ad literam de Judæorum adoptione & libera- tione ex Ægypto hæc nunc dici. Id enim scopus & o- mnes circumstantiæ exigunt. Ad Christum nihil- ominus duplicis typi nomine rectissime accom- modatur. Et paulo post: sicut nunc corpus Eccle- siæ ex Ægypto evocatum fuit, ita caput ipsum Christus inde revocari in Judæam debuit, ut quod in corpore gestum fuit, etiam in capite LITERALITER im- pleretur. Qualis hæc incertitudo, accommodatur & literaliter impletur? similitudinem refutat, & ipse eam instituit in hac explicatione. Piscator vero, etsi primum cum Hoseam explicaret, sensu literali hæc de Israele acceperit, & de Christo solum secun- dum sensum mysticum exposuerit, correxit tamen postea hac sententiam in Commentariis super Mat- thæum & secundum literam de solo CHRISTO hæc verba, de quibus nunc agimus, interpretatus est. Alia, quæ sensum illum mysticum excludant, antea indicata.

Sexto accedit, quod non temere Andreas Osian- der & Franc. Junius monuere (quod Argumentum movet Rivetum) quod Matthæus singulas ferme cir- cumstantias, quæ in Historia Christi obtigerunt, pro- bare voluerit, instituta prædictionum Vet. Testamenti cum eventu comparatione, ut ex complemento cir- cumstantiarum omnium Jesum esse Christum osten- deret. Ad talem autem probationem typus ejusmo- di, qualem hic locant, minime sufficere poterat. Ratio est, quia typi & allegoriæ tum demum firmas consequentias pariunt, cum in quæstione juris ver- santur, hoc est, si quando quæratur, utrum justum aut injustum aliquid dicatur esse. Quo de supra monuimus. Inde concludit Rivetus; Cum ergo videam, involvere se omnes, qui hæc verba à Matth. citata, vel allegorice, vel analogice, existimant, & primo referri putant ad liberationem populi Israelis ex Ægypto: nec satis facere huic rationi, quod ex tali typo, aut tali analogia, quam statuunt, nullum potest elici firmum argumentum: Matth. autem probare voluisse impletionem Prophetiæ levibus conjecturis, à tanti Apostoli prudentia alienum fuisse: non pos- sum in hac interpretatione ad Typum, aut analogiam confugere.

Septimo ita exaggeratur divina gratia & Israeli- tarum pervicacia, quod amor Dei erga Israelitas mere gratuitus sit, ideoque perseveret, etiamsi nihil habeant in se amore dignum, multa quæ odium mereantur; cujus gratuitæ dilectionis, quæ etiam alias deprædicatur Deut. 7, 7. cap. 9, 10. præcipuum documentum est in missione Filii, quum ad oves perditas, Israelis scil. præcipue missum esse testatus ipse est Matth. 15.

Ita octavo cohærent recte ea, quæ sequuntur. Hæc enim ratio est, cur Deus non rejicit prorsus Israelitas, etsi maxime refractarios, quia destinavit ipsis adhuc mittere Messiam, qui eos inviam revo- cet: unde non potuit jam universum Israelem de- lere. Nam etsi decreverat regnum Israelis everte- re, spes tamen supererat restitutionis sub Messia, qui ex Ægypto accersitus, Israelitas sparsos hinc in- de verbo prædicationis colligeret.
