But the Patriarch besought the wrestler of Jacob with weeping and tears of true peni- tent, and of ardent faith, and he sought a blessing from the same. Therefore, the wrestler of Jacob is not some created angel. Who then, if not that angel גֹּאֵל, from whom he also prayed for a blessing for his grandsons in Gen. 48. 16, that is, the Son of God? For what Grotius says, that Jacob performed for the Angel what the Israelites ought to perform for God in invocation, reeks of Popery. The worship of invocation is owed to God alone, and since Jacob performed it to the angel, he must be believed to have acknowledged the same as the true God. For it certainly was not angelolatry. Thirdly, I find in Bethel this one, with whom Jacob wrestled.

For whom did the Holy Patriarch find in Bethel? Perhaps a created angel? By no means, but the true GOD, to whom he built an altar and offered sacrifices; which are owed to no one but God alone, indeed, who testified with a resounding voice that he was the true God in Genesis 28, 13. 19. and called himself God in Bethel in chapter 30, 13. and chapter 35, 1. That same angel is also called [God] in Genesis 31, 11, from which comparison it is clearer than the sun that the angel who wrestled with Jacob, who appeared to the same in Bethel, is not a created angel, but an uncreated one, the Son of God. Moreover, this passage of Gen. 35 is especially looked back upon here, because this finding of the struggle with the Angel followed it, as if to say: See how much you owe to God, who not only once delivered your father from the hand of Esau, but also afterwards, when he had been brought into danger by the reckless deed of his sons, preserved him with his whole family, so that no one dared to hiss against him. Furthermore, God confirmed his blessings to him, which pertained to us, for he had looked forward to posterity; nevertheless, after so many and such great benefits, you have departed from God, as Rivetus rightly says on page 374. Fourthly, there is added the denomination of him who revealed himself to Jacob: to whom the Prophet attributes that most august name proper to the one GOD: AND THE LORD GOD OF HOSTS IS HIS MEMORIAL. What Grotius says is attributed to God, who revealed himself through an angel, but in the text there is no distinction between the God who revealed himself through an angel and the angel, if indeed that angel is declared to have been the God who wrestled with Jacob and whom Jacob invoked. And his name and memorial is said to be the Lord God Zebaoth, which name and memorial the same angel (the Son of God) claimed for himself as his own when he appeared to Moses in the burning bush, Exod. 3, 14. et seqq. Fifthly, the plural number is to be noted: AND THERE HE SPOKE WITH US. These words are of God, as Grotius wishes. Therefore, God speaks of himself in the plural. This is a testimony of several persons in God, namely that there are several divine persons with whom the Patriarch is said to have spoken, as if to say: The Holy Spirit spoke with the Angel the Son of God, with God the Father himself, and with me, he spoke WITH US with the divine persons: as Christ says: and we will come to him, John 14, 23. I see this is also observed by Cocceius, whose arguments for the uncreated angel I am pleased to submit here: Jacob, he says, had business with the Angel who tempted him, and Jacob acknowledged him, and with weeping and suppliant prayer extorted a blessing from him. For to weep and to supplicate is not the act of an angel striving to go forward, but of Jacob holding fast and seeking and soliciting a blessing. He who alone is set forth to Jacob as Mediator, (For the Angel is called the Son on account of his mediatorial office. See Exod. 23, 20. 21. Is. 63, 9. Malach. 3, 3. who was also called אלהים in verse 4. and Genesis 32, 28. because he is one with the Father, both in essence, and in power, and in grace, and in the authority of testifying, for the establishing of the covenant through faith) so that he might demand a blessing from him, he alone is also given to the Church of the New Testament as mediator for the obtaining of a blessing. And again: Jacob in Bethel spoke with God the Father and the Son. Therefore, the Son alone brings the faithful to God: nor is there need for other intercessors, neither Angels, nor men. This is a most noble passage showing several persons in the Godhead. For 1. there is here the plural pronoun, With us, that is, with me, and with the Angel. For from verse 10 it is clear that this is the speech of God, similar to Genesis 1, 25. 3, 22. 11, 7. Ezekiel 21, 15. or we will rejoice, namely I and my son. John 3, 11. we testify, I and the Spirit, John 14, 23. we will come to him, the Father and I. Which passage is clearly expressed from the present place. In a matter so evident, it is not necessary to refute those who ineptly and inconsistently, without any regard for the persons and the πρέποντος (propriety), so entangle this passage that it does not appear what and to what end the Prophet wished to speak. 2. There is mention of Jehovah and the Angel, who is Elohim; and indeed not ministerially (for he excludes ministerial gods in chapter 13, 4.) and אל God omnipotent, and God always to be expected, the God of Israel of the Old Testament, and Jehovah God of hosts, verse 6. Compare with these Genesis 32, 25. 29. 35, 9. 10, 11. 12. 13. Furthermore, this passage shows that the Son is the Mediator of the Patriarchs, and that they believed in him. Likewise, that the Patriarchs were brought to God through him alone without any other mediator or intercessor. Thus far Cocceius. Furthermore, the same man also subsequently pursues the argument from the property and truth of the name Jehovah. He who is the God of hosts, who is the Lord of all, and who has armies by which he manifests his goodness, and thus also the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of the nations who are partakers of the blessing in the seed of Abraham, he alone has this name Jehovah, and whatever that signifies, it belongs to him alone. And thus it is false that Jehovah does not do any of those things which are of Jehovah. Compare Is. 42, 8. Therefore, the Angel whom Jacob implored to bless him cannot be other than Jehovah, and a man who is not Jehovah cannot grant blessing, sanctification, and justification. These things it seemed good to add, because they illustrated our arguments and confirmed them more fully.

Sixthly, another plural locution may also be observed here, verse 1. 'But Judah is yet witness with God & with the HOLY ONES faithful,' which express the same thing, namely that 'with the HOLY ONES' is the same as 'with God,' as at Hos. 11:12. Grotius. He said the same thing twice, in the Hebrew manner. For the noun קדשים absolutely suits no one but God alone, and it is said of Him in Josh. 24:19. 'You will not be able to serve Jehovah, because He is Elohim Kedoschim.' Grotius refers that noun to the Prophets, others to the holy Patriarchs. But since the very same manner of speaking of a plural adjective with a singular, expressing the mystery of the Holy Trinity, occurs in the cited passage, it is entirely likely to our blessed Gesner that Hosea also wished to refer the plural adjective Kedoschim to the singular noun אל God. Which I see also confirmed by Cocceius: 'Holy' as a name of God is placed in Job 6:10, 1 John 2:20. An epithet of the name of God in the plural, Josh. 24:19, where those are joined in parallel: אל קנוא and אלהים קדשים. Nothing therefore prevents this Kedoschim from being placed in the plural, so that it can be taken as a name of God, which Kimchi also expressly asserts, as also Proverbs 9:10, 30:3. For דעת אלהים is דעת קדושים, Hos. 4:1, where דעת has a religious meaning.

Seventhly, the prophetic or divine inference especially deserves observation. The Chaldean, and most others, attribute those arguments to the Israelites, as if they... defending that they had placed the place of their worship in Bethel. This does not please Grotius, as far as it appears: Who attributes these things rather to God Himself, or to the Prophet, and wishes this inference to be now subjoined by the Prophet v. 6. THEREFORE do you also turn to God. So also the Blessed Luther in his Latin Commentary: The Prophet, he says, proposed the example of the Patriarch Jacob, whose name the idolatrous Israelites usurped, but did not imitate his faith. Now he subjoins an exhortation: Do you also the same, he says, and you will rightly be called Jacob. But how does that which is said, in the womb he took his brother by the heel, pertain to the faith of Jacob? The Blessed Luther explained this excellently: whose entire passage it is therefore helpful to subjoin: He called the kingdom of Israel by the customary name Jacob; But from this appellation he now takes the occasion for a most serious exhortation. For he proposes the faith and zeal for the promises of God, which was in the Patriarch Jacob, whose name the impious Israelites usurped, and he teaches that nothing similar is found in the Israelites. For they practiced impious worship and neglected the word entirely. This, in the judgment of this passage, is the simplest meaning, and it coheres rightly with the preceding and following verses. He commends, however, the faith of the Patriarch Jacob by the commemoration of two histories. The first is Gen. 25, that when Rebecca, who had been barren, was bringing forth twins at her first birth, Esau came out first, but Jacob in the womb took his brother by the heel, as if to hold him back, and envying him the prerogative of the birthright. A truly wonderful history, which he brings forward in this place of the Prophet for this reason, that we may conclude this was not done rashly. For why would he allege a rash act, and join with it that which is a matter of greatest admiration to us, that a man wrestled with God, yet could not be overcome? He shows, therefore, that in the embryo Jacob there was a huge desire and zeal for obtaining the promise made to the Fathers. And so, when the brother came out of the womb first, he tried to pull him back. For it is known what the right or privilege of the firstborn was. The promise concerning the seed that would crush the head of the serpent pertained to him. This Jacob strove to obtain even in his mother's womb, inasmuch as he tried to hinder Esau, so that he would not be born first. Whence, you will say, this sense in a fetus? From the Holy Spirit, of course, who so illuminated John, a six-month fetus, that he sensed the presence of the recently conceived Christ. For God is not only the God of adults, but also of infants, even of embryos, while they are still in the womb. And why is it a wonder that the Holy Spirit is effective in them in a way that we do not understand? Yet although they have life, flesh, and bones, they are not nourished in the womb in the way that we, who live in this light, are nourished. Thus the Blessed Luther. In the other history, Gen. 32, the faith of Jacob is clear and manifest to all. Now we must return to the conclusion. Since, therefore, the Israelites ought to turn to this God of theirs, whom Jacob found in Bethel, and with whom he wrestled, what is more certain than that that angel was God Himself? The Blessed Luther therefore noted this diligently: Observe here that the Jews (and Grotius, the Socinians, and the Papists) are strongly convinced in this place by the Prophet himself, because they falsely explain the word (Elohim) placed above as referring to Angels. For here the same name is repeated, and the Prophet commands that the Israelites turn themselves to that Angel, and that they always have hope in this Angel. Therefore this angel, to whom the Prophet commands his people to turn, and to hope in him, with whom Jacob wrestled, is not a created Angel, but the eternal Son of the eternal Father, our Lord Jesus Christ. The Prophet commands him to be acknowledged and received. Just as the Father also sounds forth with His own voice from heaven: This is my beloved Son, hear him. And the second Psalm commands: Kiss the Son. Here therefore see what a great dissimilarity there is. Jacob even in the womb fought with his brother about obtaining this promise, and in the struggle against the Angel he won by this very promise. But the people of Israel have absolutely no care for this promise. They retain idolatrous worship, instituted without God's command. By these they hope to merit thanks and the remission of sins. What more absurd thing can be imagined? And what is less suitable to the example of Jacob? Jacob wrestled with the Angel, and prayed to him weeping, that he might bless him. From this Angel Israel turns away, and the blessing, which this Angel offers of his own accord through his word, he rejects, and perishes in his idolatry. Rightly, therefore, the Prophet rebukes and exhorts the impious people, and says: Turn you also to your God. For here is the word (Elohim) with whom Jacob wrestled. Thus far again the Blessed Luther: whose analysis, not disapproved by Grotius, seems preferable to the resolution of others who hold the form of a disputation here in place of an exhortation. For these are the words of God, not of the Israelites, which is manifest from v. 1, 10, 11. Nor does any sign appear in the whole chapter that other speaking persons are introduced: therefore it is not for us to insert them. And these things concerning the Angel who wrestled with Jacob, about which one should also compare what we said on Gen. XXXII: and what Dr. Stephan Clotz in Angelolatria, and also Dr. Rivetus in his Commentary on this passage, set forth at length: where besides Andreas Masius, he also praises here the Jesuit Alphonsus Salmeron for our opinion in his Commentary on 1 Cor. X, Disp. 17, saying: It must also be believed that the Angel who went before the Israelites and was seen by Moses in Exod. 3 and 4, and is often called Jehovah, was Christ.

The second thing, which deserves to be noted here, concerns the bold alteration of the authentic text of Grotius, who with Cappel in this passage wants עִמּוֹ to be read as 'with us'—having changed, as he says, one vowel point—so that the sense emerges as 'with him.' Thus, therefore, it would have been read עִמּוֹ. But that is clearly foreign to Hebraism, in which עַמּוֹ is always 'with him,' and עִמּוֹ is never read. How great, therefore, is this boldness and license, not only to change the received reading, which all Hebrew codices and Chaldean translations exhibit and the Rabbis defend, but also to substitute an insolent and unheard-of word! Whence Cocceius also chastised Grotius here, and Buxtorf chastised Cappel in Vindic. p. 868.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ET DOMINVS DEVS EXERCITVVM, DO- MINVS MEMORIALE EJVS) Id est, nomen ejus, quo agnoscitur, Is Deus, qui per angelum se Jacobo patefe- cit, est longe potentissimus, nolite igitur potentiæ ejus dif- fidere: nulla mala tanta sunt, de quibus vos liberare non possit.

Notanda hic primum στρεβλότης illa, qua ad An- gelum creatum trahit, quæ de Filio Dei angelo in- creato accipienda sunt. Hunc enim fuisse Synago- nistam & colluctatorem Jacobi, varia non solum in Historia Mosaica Gen. 32. sed etiam in hoc Pro- phetico textu evincunt. Primo nomen אלהים, quod angelo huic tribuitur. Nullus enim angelus unus creatus nomine Elohim uspiam designatus est. Sed id nomen solum vel Deitatis personas πληθηντικῶς notat, vel uni è S. S. Trinitate perso- næ tribuitur, quod persona divina una non sit sine alia, ob περιχώρησιν essentialem, quæ ipsis interce- dit & ὁμουσίαν earum. Ideoque angelus, qui Elo- him vocatur, non est, nisi increatus angelus, Dei Filius. Nam quod Vulgata reddidit v.3. ET IN FORTITUDINE SUA DIRECTUS EST CUM ANGELO, & Grotius interpretatus est: Prævaluit Angelo, id in Ebræo est, prævaluit את אלהים ipsi Deo. Agnoscit Grotius in Ebræo eadem repeti verba, ad rei magnitudinem ostendendam v.3. & 4. Sed qui posteriori loco dicitur מלאך pri- ori vocatur אלהים, unde argumentum: Is quocum pugnavit & cui prævaluit ibi Jacob, est Elohim ve- rus Deus. AngelusDomini est is, quocum pugna- vit, & cui prævaluit ibi Jacob. Ergo Angelus ille Domini est Elohim verus Deus, adeoque non cre- atus est angelus, sed increatus. Porro idem con- firmat narratio angeli: Flevit & rogavit eum; is, quem cum fletu rogavit, & à quo benedictio- nem petiit Jacobus Patriarcha, certe non est creatus aliquis angelus. Ab hoc enim benedictio peti non de- bet. Et pœnitentiales ejusmodi lacrymæ non offeren- dæ angelis, sed uni Deo. At colluctatorem Jacobi ro- gavit Patriarcha cum fletu & lacrymis vera pæni- tentis, fideique ardentis, ac benedictionem ab eo- dem petiit. Colluctator ergo Jacobi non est crea- tus aliquis angelus. Quis ergo nisi angelus ille גֹּאֵל, à quo benedictionem etiam nepotibus suis precatus est Gen. 48. 16. hoc est, Filius Dei? Nam quod ait Grotius, id Jacobum Angelo præstitisse, quod Israëlitæ, in invocatione Deo præstare debent, Papismum redolet. Uni Deo debetur cultus in- vocationis, quem quum angelo præstiterit Jacob, eundem verum Deum agnovisse credendus est. Non enim certe fuit angelolatria. Tertio inven- tio in Bethel hujus, quicum luctatus est Jacob.

Quem enim invenit S. Patriarcha in Bethel? Num forte angelum creatum? Minime, sed verum DEUM, cui altare extruxit, & sacrificia obtulit; quæ non nisi uni Deo debentur, imo qui sonora voce testatus est se verum Deum Genes. 28, 13. 19. ac se Deum in Bethel vocavit cap. 30, 13. cap. 35, 1. Idem ille angelus etiam vocatur Genes. 31, 1. è qua collatione sole clarius est, angelum colluctatorem Jacobi, qui eidem apparuit in Bethel, non esse an- gelum creatum, sed increatum, Filium Dei. Respi- citur autem hic imprimis locus Gen. 35. quia hæc inventio luctæ cum Angelo succeslit, q. d. Videte, quantum debeatis Deo, qui non semel tantum pa- trem vestrum liberavit à manu Esavi, sed etiam postea, cum in periculum adductus fuisset, teme- rario filiorum suorum facinore, conservavit eum cum tota familia sua, ut nullus ausus sit contra eum hiscere. Deus præterea ipsi benedictiones suas confirmavit, quæ ad nos pertinebant, prospexe- rat enim posteritati; nihilominus post tot & tanta beneficia recessistis à Deo, ut recte Rivetus pag. 374. Quarto accedit denominatio illius, qui Jaco- bo se patefecit: cui tribuit Propheta nomen illud augustissimum uni DEO proprium: ET DO- MINUS DEUS EXERCITUUM MEMO- RIALE EJUS. Quod Grotius Deo, qui per an- gelum se patefecit, tributum esse ait, sed in textu nul- la est inter Deum, qui per angelum se patefecerit, & angelum distinctio, siquidem angelus ille Deus fuisse perhibeatur, qui cum Jacobo luctatus est, & quem Jacob invocavit. Et hujus nomen ac memo- riale dicitur, Dominus Deus Zebaoth, quale no- men ac memoriale idem angelus (FiliusDei)cum Mosi in rubo ardenti apparuit, sibi ceu proprium vendicavit Exod. 3, 14. seqq. Quinto notandus est numerus pluralis: ET IBI LOCUTUS EST NOBISCUM. Verba hæc sunt Dei, uti vult Grotius. Deus ergo de sese in plurali loquitur. Quod testi- monium est plurium personarum in Deo, plures nempe personas divinas esse, quibuscum loquu- tus Patriarcha dicitur, q.d. Spiritus Sanctus loquu- tus est cum Angelo Filio Dei, cum Deo Patre ipso, & mecum, loquutus est NOBISCUM cum perso- nis divinis: uti Christus ait: & nos veniemus ad eum Jeh. 14, 23. Video id observari etiam à Coc- cejo, cujus argumenta pro angelo increato hic subjicere placet: Jacobus, inquit, rem habuit cum Angelo, qui tentavit eum, & Jacobus eum agno- vit, & plorata ac supplici prece extorsit ei bene- dictionem. Nam flere & supplicare non est an- geli progredi nitentis, sed Jacobi retinentis & be- nedictionem petentis ac exambientis. Qui solus Ja- cobo propositus est Mediator, (Nam Angelus dici- tur Filius propter officium mediatorium. Vide Exod. 23, 20.21. Es.63, 9. Malach.3, 3. qui & אלהים dicebatur vers. 4. & Genes. 32, 28. propterea quia unum est cum Patre, tum essentia, tum potentia, tum gratia, tum testandi autoritate, ad fœdus fancien- dum per fidem) ut benedictionem ab ipso flagitaret, is solus etiam Ecclesiae Novi Testamenti datus est me- diator ad benedictionis impetrationem. Et rursus: Jacobus Bethele locutus est cum Deo Patre & Filio. Solus igitur Filius fideles ad Deum adducit: neque opus est aliis intercessoribus, neque Angelis, neque ho- minibus. Nobilissimus est hic locus ostendens plures personas in Deitate. Nam 1. est hic pronomen plu- rale, Nobiscum, hoc est, mecum, & cum Angelo. Nam ex vers. 10. patet, Dei hic sermonem esse, simile Genes. 1, 25. 3, 22. 11, 7. Ezech. 21, 15. vel hilarabi- mur, ego scil. & filius meus. Joh. 3, 11. testamur, ego & Spiritus, Joh. 14, 23. ad eum veniemus Pater & ego. Qui locus plane est ex praesenti loco expressus. In re tam evidenti non est necesse eos refutare, qui in- epte & desultorie, nulla habita ratione personarum & πρέποντος ita implicant hunc locum, ut quid & quo fine dicere voluerit Propheta non appareat. 2. Mentio sit Jehovae & Angeli, qui sit Elohim; & quidem non ministerialiter (nam Deos ministeriales excludit cap. 13, 4.) & אל Deus omnipotens, & Deus semper expectandus, Deus Israëlis Veteris Testamenti, & Jehova Deus exercituum, vers. 6. Confer his Genes. 32, 25. 29. 35, 9. 10, 11. 12. 13. Prae- terea ostendit hic locus, Filium esse Mediatorem Patriarcharum, & eos credidisse in ipsum. Item Pa- triarchas per eum solum adductos fuisse ad Deum absque alio mediatore, vel intercessore. Hactenus Coccejus. Porro exequitur idem etiam deinceps argumentum à proprietate & veritate nominis Je- hovah. Qui est Deus exercituum, qui est omnium Dominus, & qui exercitus habet, quibus manife- stet bonitatem suam, atque ita etiam Deus Abra- hami, Isaaci & Jacobi & gentium, qui sunt partici- pes benedictionis in semine Abraham, is solus ha- bet hoc nomen Jehovah, & quicquid illud signifi- cat, ipsi soli competit. Atque ita falsum est, quod Non Jehovah faciat quicquam illorum, quae sunt jehovae. Confer Es. 42, 8. Iccirco Angelus, quem imploravit Jacob, ut benediceret ipsi, non potest esse non Jehovah, & homo non Jehovah non potest bene- dictionem, sanctificationem, justificationem praestare. Quae adjicere visum fuit, quod argumenta nostra illustrarent, atque uberius confirmarent.

Sexto observari etiam alia pluralis locutio hic po- test vers. 1. Judas autem testis descendit cum Deo & Plurali lo- cum SANCTIS fidelis, quae idem exprimunt, ut cutione. nempe cum SANCTIS idem sit, quod cum Deo, uti ad Os. 11, 12. Grotius. Bis idem dixit, more He- breo. Nam nomen קדשים absolute nulli nisi soli DEO convenit, & de illo dicitur Joh. 24, 19. Non Nomen poteris Jehova servire, quia Elohim Kedoschim ipse. sancti plu- Ad Prophetas refert illud nomen Grotius, alii ad rale de Deo adhibitum sanctos Patriarchas. Sed cum eadem plane lo- mysteriis quendi ratio adjuncti pluralis ad singulare, expri- cousa. mendo S. Trinitatis mysterio loco laudato occur- rat, verisimile omnino est B. Gesnero nostro, Ho- seam quoque appositum plurale Kedoschim ad sin- gulare nomen אל Deus referre voluisse. Quod video etiam à Coccejo confirmari: Sanctus ut no- men Dei ponitur Job. 6, 10. 1. Joh. 2, 20. Epithetum nominis Dei in plurali Jos. 24, 19. ubi illa parallele con- junguntur אל קנוא & אלהים קדשים. Nihil igitur impedit, quo minus hoc loco Kedoschim plurative positum, ut nomen Dei accipi possit, quod & Kimchius diserte asserit, ut & Proverb. 9, 10. 30, 3. Nam דעת אלהים, est דעת קדושים Hos. 4, 1. ubi דעת religiosam significationem habet.

Septimo imprimis etiam observationem me- retur illatio prophetica vel divina. Argumenta illa Illatio Pro- Israëlitis Chaldaeus, & alii plerique tribuunt q. se phetica. defendentibus quod locum cultus sui Bethlehem posuissent. Non placet id Grotio, quantum ap- paret: Qui ea Deo ipsi potius tribuit, aut Prophe- tæ, & hanc illationem nunc à Propheta subjici vult v. 6. QVARE & tu ad Deum convertere. Sic etiam B. Lutherus in Latino Commentario: Propo- suit, inquit, Propheta exemplum Patriarchæ Jacob, cujus nomen Idololatræ Israelitæ usurpabant, sed non imitabantur fidem. Nunc subjicit exhortationem: Fac tu quoque eadem, inquit, & recte vocaberis Jacob. Quomodo autem illud ad fidem Jacobi fa- cit, quod dictum, in utero arripuit plantam fratris sui? id præclare exposuit B. Lutherus: cujus lo- cum integrum proinde juvat subjicere: Vocavit re- gnum Israel usitato nomine Jacob; At ex hac appella- tione jam sumit occasionem gravissimæ exhortationis. Proponit enim fidem, & studium promissionum Dei, quod fuit in Patriarcha Jacob, cujus nomen impii Is- raelitæ usurpabant, ac docet in Israelitis nihil inveniri simile. Nam exercebant impios cultus & verbum prorsus negligebant. Hanc judicio hujus loci el- te simplicissimam sententiam, ac recte cohæret cum præcedentibus & sequentibus. Commendat au- tem fidem Patriarcha Jacob, commemoratione dua- rum historiarum. Prima est Genes. 25. quod cum Rebecca, quæ sterilis fuerat, primo partu geminos eniteretur, exiit primus Esau, Jacob autem in utero arripuit plantam fratris, tanquam retenturus eum, & invidens ei primo genituræ prærogativam. Mi- rabilis profecto historia, quam hoc in loco Prophetæ i- deo adducit, ut statuamus non temere hoc esse factum. Cur enim allegaret temerarium factum, & cum eo conjungeret, quod maxime admirationi nobis est, quod homo cum Deo luctatus, tamen non potue- rit vinci? Ostendit igitur in embryone Jacob fuisse ingens desiderium, & studium consequendæ pro- missionis Patribus factæ. Itaque cum frater prior exiret ex utero, conatus est eum retrahere. No- tum enim est, quod fuerit primogeniti jus, seu privile- gium. Pertinebat ad eum promissio de semine con- trituro caput serpentis. Hunc Jacob etiam in utero matris studuit obtinere, siquidem conatus est impedire Esau, ne primus nasceretur. Unde, inquies, in fœtu hic sensus? Ex Spiritu sancto nimirum, qui Johan- nem sex mensium fœtum ita illuminavit, ut sentiret Christi recens concepti præsentiam. Est enim Deus non tantum adultorum Deus, sed etiam in- fantium, etiam embryonum, dum adhuc in utero sunt. Ac quid hoc mirum est, Spiritum sanctum in eis esse efficacem eo modo, quem nos non intelligimus? ta- men cum habeant vitam, carnem & ossa, non tamen aluntur in utero, eo modo, quo nos, qui in hac luce vi- vimus, alimur. Hæc B. Lutherus. In altera hi- storia Gen. 32. fides Jacobi luculenta est, & ma- nifesta omnibus. Jam ad συμπέρασμα redeundum. Quum ergo ad hunc Deum suum converti debe- ant Israelitæ, quem in Bethel invenit Jacob, & quo- cum luctatus, quid certius est, quam angelum il- lum fuisse ipsummet Deum? Notavit ergo sedulo hoc B. Lutherus: Hic observa Judæos (& Grotium, Socinianos ac Papistas) fortiter hoc in loco convinci ab ipso Propheta, quod falso vocabulum (Elohim) supra positum exponunt de Angelis. Nam hic idem nomen repetitur, & jubet Propheta, ut Israelitæ se convertant ad eum Angelum, & ut semper in hoc An- gelo spem habeant. Ergo angelus hic, ad quem Pro- pheta jubet converti populum suum, & sperare in eo, cum quo Jacobus luctatus est, non est Angelus creatus, sed æternus Filius æterni Patris, Dominus noster Jesus Christus. Hunc jubet Propheta agnosci, & accipi. Sicut Pater quoque sua voce de cælo sonat: Hic est Fi- lius meus dilectus, hunc audite. Et secundus Psal- mus mandat: Osculamini Filium. Hic igitur vide, quanta dissimilitudo sit. Jacob etiam in utero cum fratre depugnavit de consequenda hac promissione, & in lucta contra Angelum hac ipsa promissione vicit. Sed populus Israel prorsus nullam hujus promissio- nis curam habet. Retinet Idololatricos cultus, sine Dei mandato institutos. His sperat se mereri gra- tiam & remissionem peccatorum. Quid magis ab- surdum fingi potest? quodque minus conveniat ad Jacob exemplum? Luctatus est Jacob cum Angelo, & de- precatus est eum flens, ut benediceret. Ab hoc An- gelo avertit se Israel, ac benedictionem, quam ultro Angelus hic per verbum suum offert, abjicit, ac perit in idololatria sua. Recte igitur objurgat Prophe- ta, & hortatur impium populum, ac dicit: Converte- re tu quoque ad Deum tuum. Hic n. est vocabulum (Elohim) cum quo luctatus est Jacob. Hactenus ite- rum B. Lutherus: cujus ista analysis Grotio non im- probata, aliorum, qui disceptationis formam hic lo- co paraeneseos innehunt, ἐπιλύσει praeferenda vi- detur. Dei enim haec verba sunt, non Israelitarum, quod e v. 1. 10. 11. manifestum est. Neque ullum ap- paret signum in toto capite, quod aliae personae lo- quentes introducantur: Nostrum ergo non est il- las ingerere. Atque haec de Angelo colluctato- re Jacobi, de quo etiam conferenda, quae ad Genes. XXXII. diximus: & quae prolixe Dn. D. Stephanus Clotz in Angelolatria, nec non D. Rivetus Com- ment. in h. l. tradunt: ubi praeter Andr. Masium hic etiam Jesuitam Alphonsum Salmeronem pro nostra sententia laudat Comment. in 1. Cor. X. Disp. 17. dicentem: Credendum etiam Angelum, qui praeibat Israelitas & Mosi visum Exod. 3. & 4. & saepe vocatur Jehovah, fuisse Christum.

Alterum, quod hic notari meretur, concernit audacem mutationem textus authentici Grotii, qui cum Capello hoc loco עִמּוֹ nobiscum, uno, ut ait, mutato puncto, ita legendum esse vult, ut sensus pro- deat, cum eo. Sic ergo legendum fuerit עִמּוֹ. At id plane alienum est ab Ebraismo, in quo עַמּוֹ semper est cum eo, nunquam legitur עִמּוֹ. Quanta ergo haec audacia & licentia, non tantum receptam lectio- nem mutare, quam omnes Codices Ebraei & Chal- daicae translationes exhibent, ac Rabbini tuentur, sed etiam insolentem & inauditam vocem substi- tuere! unde castigavit hic etiam Grotium Coccejus, & Capellum Buxtorfius in Vindic. p. 868.

## 12:6
Verse 6.

AND THOU SHALT TURN TO THY GOD) Therefore turn thou also to thy God, by the example of Jacob.

KEEP MERCY AND JUDGMENT) Observe beneficence and innocence.

AND WAIT ON THY GOD CONTINUALLY) There is no reason why you should distrust Him, provided that you do your duty.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET TU AD DEUM TUUM CONVERTERIS) Quare & tu ad Deum tuum convertere, exemplo Iacobi.

MISERICORDIAM ET IUDICIUM CUSTODI) Beneficentiam & innocentiam serva.

ET SPERA IN DEO TVO SEMPER) Non est, quod ipsi diffidas, dummodo tu officium facias.

## 12:7
Verse 7.

CANAAN) Israel is like the Canaanite: of whom Homer says: 'Then there came a Phoenician man, knowing deceitful things, a swindler.' And Philostratus to the Phoenician: 'You have brought trade into disrepute, as being both money-loving and swindlers.'

THE BALANCES OF DECEIT ARE IN HIS HAND) He who promises more concerning a thing sold than he actually provides.

HE LOVED OPPRESSION) עָשַׁק here signifies every kind of πλεονέκτημα (covetousness/extortion), as the Chaldean interprets.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

CHANAAN) Israel Chananæo est similis: de quo Homerus: Δὴ τότε Φοῖνιξ ἦλθεν ἀνὴρ ἀπατήλια εἰδὼς Τρώκτης. Et Philostratus ad Phœnicem: τὰς ἐμπορίας διαβέβλησθε, ὡς φιλοχρήματοί τε καὶ τρῶκται.

IN MANU EIUS STATERA DOLOSA) Qui de re vendita plus pollicetur, quam revera exhibet.

CALUMNIAM DILEXIT) עָשַׁק hic significat omne πλεονέκτημα, ut interpretatur Chaldæus.

## 12:8
Verse 8.

AND EPHRAIM SAID) nevertheless Ephraim said.

I AM BECOME RICH) As if he were to say: No one will ask where you got it, but it is necessary to have it.

I HAVE FOUND AN IDOL FOR MYSELF) Better: I have acquired riches for myself. For that אוֹן, with the vowel which we have in the text, signifies this. Nor do the LXX and the Chaldean seem to have understood it otherwise.

ALL MY LABOURS SHALL NOT FIND FOR ME THE INIQUITY WHICH I HAVE COMMITTED) The Chaldean takes עון, for that which is mostly called עד נכן, which is an appointed time, and מצא for he shall pay, as in Gen. 31, 37. just as we have taken כפר in Dan. 9, 24. furthermore, both the Greeks and the Chaldean read יגיעו and לו. The sense according to the Chaldean here is: All wealth acquired by labour shall not remain to him in the time when he shall pay for his sins. The Greeks understand 'because' and derive עון from עוה: πάντες οἱ πόνοι αὐτῶ οὐχ ἑυρεθήσονται αὐτῷ, ἀδικίας ἃς ἥμαρτεν.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET DIXIT EPHRAIM) attamen dixit Ephraim.

DIVES EFFECTUS SUM) Quasi diceret: Vnde habeas quaeret nemo, sed oportet habere.

INVENI IDOLUM MIHI) Melius: acquisivi mihi divitias. Id enim אוֹן cum ista, quam nos in textu habe- mus, vocali significat. Nec aliter sumsisse videntur LXX. & Chaldæus.

OMNES LABORES MEI NON INVENIENT MIHI INIQVITATEM QVAM PECCAVI) Chaldæus עון sumfit, pro eo quod plerumque עד נכן dicitur, quod est tempus constitutum, & מצא pro luit, ut Genes. 31, 37. quomodo & כפר sumsimus Dan. 9, 24. præterea tam Græ- ci quam Chaldæus legerunt יגיעו & לו. Sensus secundum Chaldæum hic est: Omnes labore partæ opes non restabunt ei in tempore quo luet peccata sua. Græci propter subintelligunt, & עון à עוה derivant: πάντες οἱ πόνοι αὐτῶ οὐχ ἑυρεθήσονται αὐτῷ, ἀδικίας ἃς ἥμαρτεν.

## 12:9
Verse 9.

AND I THE LORD THY GOD FROM THE LAND OF EGYPT) Who brought thee out of the land of Egypt. SHALL I YET MAKE THEE TO DWELL) Should I make? And it is of one asking. After so many of thy crimes, should I suffer thee to live quietly at home? IN TABERNACLES) In your houses, which because of ancient custom are called tabernacles. AS IN THE DAYS OF THE FEAST) Joyfully and quietly: as on feast days.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ET EGO DOMINVS DEVS TVVS EX TER- RA ÆGYPTI) Qui te eduxi ex terra Ægypti. ADHVC SEDERE TE FACIAM) Facerem? & est interrogantis. Post tot flagitia tua patererne te domi tranquille vivere ? IN TABERNACLIS) In ædibus vestris, quæ ob veterem morem tabernacula vocantur. SICVT IN DIEBVS FESTIVITATIS) Læte & tranquille: ut in festis diebus.

## 12:10
Verse 10.

AND I HAVE SPOKEN BY THE PROPHETS) And I would speak (to Israel) by the Prophets. AND I HAVE MULTIPLIED VISION) I would multiply. I would send visions one after another to you. AND BY THE HAND OF THE PROPHETS HAVE I BEEN SIMILITUDINIZED) And by the Prophets would I use similitudes? Ezek. 20, 48. as if he were saying: I will no longer speak to you through Prophetic figures, but through the things themselves, which you shall feel.

Grotius takes these in the worse sense by way of a threat, as do not a few Interpreters, rendering these with Junius in the sense of questioning: Should I yet make thee to dwell? which others understood simply, and as they sound. Moreover, others have interpreted these two verses in the better sense, as Rivetus reports on page 385. They believe, namely, that it concerns the restoration of the true Israel under the kingdom of the Messiah, and that his spiritual redemption to be performed in Christ is promised, figured by the type of the old Church as in chapter 2, verses 14 and 15. And he shall sing there as in the days of his youth, and as in the day he came up from the land of Egypt. Thus the Genevans interpret it, I will yet redeem thee, that I may give thee true rest, promised to my faithful ones. So also Vatablus in his Notes, 'Yet,' he says, 'seems to pertain to the time of Christ.' The rest which follows concerning the Prophets, they take as concerning the future time, as a promise of that future liberation, of which in the preceding verse. is contained, illustrated by the excellent benefits then to be conferred upon the Church in Christ: And they believe that those words 'I will multiply vision' rightly agree with the kingdom of Christ and the preaching of the Gospel, proved from Joel 2, verse 28; I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, your sons shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions. For there is a much fuller and clearer knowledge of heavenly doctrine under Christ than there was under the legal shadows. Thus also the most learned Mercerus accepted that former part: Understand, he says, a spiritual reduction to be performed through Christ; which is often compared to the Egyptian [exodus] in the Scriptures, and was compared before at the beginning of the book. Furthermore, dwelling in tabernacles signifies deep peace and supreme security, and the tranquility of gifts through CHRIST. To which Rivetus adds his own vote: In such a variety of opinions and interpretations, it is not so ready to define what should be followed, especially since there are none among them that undermine the analogy of faith, or strike against it: none that do not have wholesome considerations. One must see, however, what more agrees with the scope of the Prophet, the argument of the discourse, and the acceptance of similar phrases used elsewhere, where there was no ambiguity. I, having diligently weighed everything, without prejudice to anyone, concede to the opinion which I last explained: namely, that GOD, who had recently exhorted the people to repentance through the Prophet, shows in these two verses, as above in chapter 2, verse 8, etc., that He does not wish to destroy Ephraim utterly, that He remembers His mercies, because, he said, I am GOD the mighty and not man. For it is an effective argument for repentance when the Lord testifies that He has not cast off the care of His people, nor is the matter entirely desperate. Nor does it stand in the way that two verses have been interjected, in which He exaggerated the perversity of the Israelites, and that others follow later, in which He will lash their idolatry as if brought to the extreme. For there is nothing absurd if threats and reproofs are occasionally mixed with promises, especially those which look to the Messiah, in whom alone the hope of restoration was established in desperate matters: if we remember that there was always a double class of men in the people, for whose diverse condition the Prophets sometimes seem to propose opposites. For sometimes they speak as if all things were desperate, and no hope of salvation remained: suddenly afterwards they pass to magnificent promises, as if they had forgotten both the extreme malice of the people and the inflamed divine wrath, the just heat of which they themselves had testified was aroused. Yet all things agree very well. For that severe and extreme [threat] is pronounced against the greater part, which consists of the impious and profane; the rest are added for the consolation of the pious, who, since they are subjected to other temporal punishments and inconveniences, might think they were invited to repentance in vain, unless another hope were proposed to them, namely, a saving restoration in Christ. This is he, who also calls the explanations of his own and of Calvin himself here under censure. The Belgian Paraphrasts also subscribe.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET LOCVTVS SVM SVPER PROPHETAS) Et ego loquerer (Israeli) per Prophetas. ET EGO VISIONEM MVLTIPLICAVI) Mul- tiplicarem. Alia super alia visa ad vos mitterem. ET IN MANV PROPHETARVM ASSIMVLATVS SVM) Et per Prophetas uterer similitudinibus? Ezech. 20, 48. quasi diceret: non ampliùs per figuras Propheticas vobis loquar, sed per res ipsas, quas sentietis.

In sequiorem partem per modum commina- tionis hæc accipit Grotius, ut non pauci Interpp. cum Junio hæc sensu interrogandi reddens: Adhuc sedere te facerem? quæ simpliciter, & ut sonant, alii intellexere. Cæterum in meliorem partem duos hosce versus alii interpretati sunt, uti refert Rivetus pag. 385. Censent nimirum agi de restau- ratione veri Israelis sub regno Messiæ, ejusque re- demtionem spiritualem in Christo præstandam promitti typo veteris Ecclesiæ figuratam ut cap. 2. vers. 14. & 15. Et canet ibi ut in diebus pueritiæ suæ, & quo die ascendit è terra Ægypti. Sic interpre- tantur Genevenses, adhuc redimam te, ut dem tibi veram quietem, fidelibus meis promissam. Ita etiam Vatablus in Notis, Adhuc, inquit, videtur pertinere ad tempus Christi. Reliqua quæ sequuntur de Prophetis, de futuro tempore accipiunt, ut futuræ illius liberationis promissio, de qua versu præced. contineatur, eximiis beneficiis, in Christo Ecclesiæ tum conferendis, illustrata: Et verba illa visionem multiplicabo, recte Christi regno & prædicationi Evangelii convenire, probari ex Joel 2. vers. 28. censent; Effundam Spiritum meum super omnem carnem, filii vestri prophetabunt, senes somniabunt somnia, juvenes visiones videbunt. Nam multo plenior & clarior doctrinæ cœlestis cognitio sub Christo, quam sub legalibus umbris erat. Sic etiam priorem illam partem accepit Doctiss. Mercerus: Spiritualem, inquit, reductionem intellige per Chri- stum præstandam; quæ sæpe Ægyptiacæ compara- tur, in Scripturis, & ante sub libri initium compa- rata est. Porro habitatio in tabernaculis, altam pa- cem & summam securitatem, munerumque tran- quillitatem per CHRISTUM significat. Quibus calculum suum adjicit Rivetus: In tanta sententia- rum & interpretationum varietate, quid sit sequen- dum, non est adeo definire paratum, cum præfer- tim ex illis nullæ sint, quæ fidei analogiam labefa- ctent, aut in eam impingant: nullæ quæ non habe- ant salutares considerationes. Videndum tamen quid magis conveniat scopo Prophetæ, concionis argumento, & similium phrasium, alibi usurpata- rum, ubi nulla erat ambiguitas, acceptioni. Ego o- mnibus diligenter expensis, sine alicujus præjudi- cio, in eam quam postremo explicavi sententiam concedo: ut nempe DEUS, qui nuper populum ad resipiscentiam hortatus erat per Prophetam, o- stendat his duobus versibus, ut supra cap. 2. verf. 8. &c. Se nolle prorsus perdere Ephraimum, meminisse misericordiarum suarum, quia, inquiebat, DEUS fortis sum & non vir. Est enim efficax argumen- tum ad resipiscentiam, cum testatur Dominus se non abjecisse curam populi sui, nec rem plane esse desperatam. Nec obstat, quod interjecti fuerint duo versus, quibus Israelitarum perversitatem exag- geravit, & sequantur postea alii, quibus ipsorum idololatriam ad extremum quasi perductam per- stringet. Nihil est enim absurdi, si minis & repre- hensionibus subinde misceantur promissiones, præsertim, quæ Messiam respiciant, in quo solo re- stitutionis spes in rebus desperatis constituebatur: si meminerimus semper in populo duplex fuisse hominum genus, pro cujus diversa conditione ali- quando videntur contraria proponere Prophetæ. Quandoque enim loquuntur, ac si omnia essent de- sperata, & nulla spes salutis reliqua esset: subito postea transeunt ad magnificas promissiones, quasi obliti essent & malitiæ extremæ populi, & iræ divi- næ inflammatæ, cujus ardorem justum concitatum ipsi testati erant. Omnia tamen optime conve- niunt. Nam severa illa & extrema pronunciatur adversus maximam partem, quæ ea impiis, & pro- fanis constat; reliqua adjiciuntur ad consolationem piorum, qui cum aliis temporalibus pœnis & in- commodis subjiciantur, putarent se frustra ad pœ- nitentiam invitari, nisi spes alia ipsis proponerê- tur, nempe salutaris restitutionis in Christo. Hæc ille, qui & suorum, & ipsius Calvini explicationes hic sub censuram vocat. Subscribunt quoque Paraphrastæ Belgici.

## 12:11
Verse 11.

IF GALAAD IS AN IDOL, THEREFORE THEY WERE IN VAIN) If there was an idol in Galaad, nevertheless they were in vain who worshipped that idol, because they could not be saved by the idol from the hand of Teglathphalasar, 2 Kings 15:29.

SACRIFICING WITH OXEN IN GALGAL) There is an ellipsis of the little word 'why'. The sense: why therefore do the two tribes still imitate that worship of the calves in Galgal? See above 4:11, 9:15.

FOR ALSO THEIR ALTARS) Of the Galaadites.

AS HEAPS) Namely, of stones.

UPON THE FURROWS OF THE FIELD) Which are gathered by farmers upon the furrows. Thus also those altars lie scattered.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

SI GALAAD IDOLUM, ERGO FRUSTRA ERANT) Si in Galaade idolum fuit, veruntamen frustra fu- erunt, qui illud idolum coluere, quia non potuere per ido- lum servari à manu Teglathphalasari, 2. Reg. 15, 29.

IN GALGAL BOBUS IMOLANTES) Est ἔλλειψις voculæ cur. Sensus: cur ergo adhuc duæ tribus cula tum illum vitulorum imitantur in Galgale? Vide supra 4, 11. 9, 15.

NAM ET ALTARIA EORUM) Galaadi- tarum.

QVASI ACERVI) Nempe lapidum.

SUPER SULCOS AGRI) Qui congeruntur ab agricolis super sulcos. Sic & altaria illa jacent disjecta.

## 12:12
Verse 12.

JACOB FLED INTO THE REGION OF SYRIA) He aggravates the indignity of the guilt from the contrary deeds of their ancestors in the same places. In the Hebrew it is: Jacob fled the field of Syria: that is, from the field of Syria into that land of Galaad, Gen. 31:21.

AND ISRAEL SERVED FOR A WIFE, AND FOR A WIFE HE KEPT) When Israel (that is, Jacob, the father of you all) had served for a wife, and for a wife had kept the flocks. By the way, GOD, on the occasion of the land of Galaad, sprinkles another reproach. Jacob served Laban for two wives, and fed his flocks for fourteen years. You, however, are unwilling to do anything for the sake of God.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

FUGIT JACOB IN REGIONEM STRIÆ) Indignitatem culpæ aggravat, ex contrariis factis majo- rum, in eisdem locis. In Hebræo est: Fugit Iacob agrum Syriæ: id est, ex agro Syriæ in illam Galaaditidem, Gen. 31, 21.

ET SERVIvit ISRAEL IN UXOREM, ET IN UVOREN SERVAVIT) Cum servisset Israel (id est, Ja- cob pater vestrum omnium) pro uxore, & pro uxore servasset pecudes. Obiter DEUS occasione Galaaditidis aliam ad- spergit exprobrationem. Jacob pro duabus uxoribus ser- vivit Labani, & greges ejus pavit per annos quatuordecim. Vos autem Dei causa nihil facere vultis.

## 12:13
Verse 13.

BUT BY A PROPHET THE LORD BROUGHT ISRAEL OUT OF EGYPT) When the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt by a Prophet (Moses).

AND BY A PROPHET HE WAS KEPT) Then by a Prophet (another, namely Joshua) Israel escaped from the desert, and arrived, namely, at Galgala, and there first kept the Passover. Joshua 5. From the very places in which they were sinning, he draws forth for them the histories of the ancients, to show how much they have degenerated from their ancestors.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

IN PROPHETA AUTEM EDUXIT DOMINUS ISRAEL DE ÆGYPTO) Cum Dominus per Prophetam (Mosen) Israelem eduxisset ex Ægypto.

ET IN PROPHETA SERVATUs EST) Tunc per Prophetam (alterum, Josuam scilicet) evasit Israel ex deserto, ac pervenit scilicet Galgala, ibique primum Pascha fecit. Josue V. Ex ipsis locis in quibus peccabatur, veteres illis depromit historias, ut ostendat quantum à majoribus degeneraverint.

## 12:14
Verse 14.

AD IRACVNDIAM ME PROVOCAVIT EPHRAIM IN AMARITVDINIBVS SVIS) That is, Ephraim acts differently than Jacob, or that people under Joshua. He calls impious deeds bitterness, the Greeks, ἐν τοῖς παραπι-

κρασμοῖς. Well; for כ is understood before תמרורים. It could also be translated as 'in heaps,' in the way this Hebrew word is taken in Jer. 31:21, so that by heaps of stones we may understand altars. HIS BLOOD SHALL COME UPON HIM.) In the Hebrew: God will bring his blood (poured out by him, that is, the punishment for the blood) upon him himself: for they had killed many pious men. See above 4:2. AND HIS REPROACH) The reproaches with which they afflicted the Prophets. Above 11:1, 2. HIS LORD WILL RESTORE TO HIM) He will repay him.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

AD IRACVNDIAM ME PROVOCAVIT EPHRAIM IN AMARITVDINIEBS SVIS) Id est, con- tra agit Ephraim quam Jacob, aut ille sub Josua populus. Amaritudines vocat facta impia, Græci, ἐν τοῖς παραπι-

κρασμοῖς. Bene; subauditur enim כ ante תמרורים. posset etiam verti in cumulis, quomodo vox hæc Hebræa sumitur Jer. 31, 21. ut per cumulos lapidum, altaria intelligamus. SANGVIS EJVS SVPER EVM VENIET.) In Hebræo: Sanguinem ejus (ab eo fusum, id est, pœnam san- guinis) in ipsam deferet Deus: nam multos pios occiderant. Vide supra 4, 2. ET OPPROBRIVM EJVS) Probra, quibus affece- runt Prophetas. Supra 11, 1. 2. RESTITVET EI DOMINVS SVVS) Reponet ei.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII.

He teaches that the salvation of Israel is from the Lord. The punishment for the idols of the calves and Baal, multiplied by other increased cults, with the addition of the immolation of children, is indicated; they are recalled to the worship of the one God the Savior, who, having cared for them in the desert and later having been sated with His benefits, provoked to anger, protests that He will encounter them like a bear and a lion, that their salvation is from Himself, but their destruction from their own fault, and that they cannot be helped by Kings, whom He gave in His anger and will take away again in His anger, and that they will experience the pains of women in labor: that this, however, remains, that they should trust in Christ who delivers us from death and hell, in whom Ephraim also will one day bear fruit among his Jewish brothers, even though now the Assyrian is about to dry them up and despoil them like a scorching wind. All other things harm; God alone delivers from the grave.

Ver. 1.

WHEN EPHRAIM SPOKE) Formerly, when the tribe of Ephraim spoke in public assemblies, whether under the judges or under King Saul, David, or Solomon, being powerful in men and resources. HONOR INVADED ISRAEL) The other tribes listened to them with great reverence and attributed much to their opinions. Compare Job 29:8, 9. AND HE OFFENDED IN BAAL) Even the calves are sometimes called בעלים by the Hebrews: because God alienates from Himself such images made for Him against His law, and does not value them more than those which are stirred up for false deities. AND HE DIED) Therefore he died: that is, he was consigned to destruction: a metonymy frequent enough.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII.

Salutem Israelis ex Domino esse docet. Pœna de idolis vitulorum & Baal multipliciter aliis cultibus auctis, accedentibus etiam li- berorum immolationibus, indicata, ad unius DEI salvatoris cultum revocantur, qui illis in deserto curatis, post beneficiis suis satura- tis, ad iram provocatus instar ursi & leonis occursurus, protestatur, salutem eorum ex se, perditionem autem ab ipsorummet culpa es- se, nec à Regibus ipsos juvari posse, quos in ira datos in ira iterum ablaturus est, quin par- turientium dolores experturi sint: id autem restare, ut Christo à morte & inferno nos li- beranti confidant, in quo Ephraim quoque inter fratres Judæos olim fructus feret, utut jam Assyrius instar urentis venti eos exsic- caturus & exspoliaturus sit. Cætera cuncta nocent, solus Deus eximit orco.

Vers. 1.

LOQVENTE EPHRAIM) Olim cum in communi- bus conventibus sive sub judicibus, sive sub rege Saule, Da- vide, Salomone loqueretur tribus Ephraim, viris & opi- bus pollens. HONOR INVASIT ISRAEL) Cæteræ tribus, cum magna reverentia eos audiebant, plurimumque tri- buebant illorum sententiis. Confer Jobum 29, 8. 9. ET DELIQVIT IN BAAL) Etiam vituli Hebræis vocantur interdum בעלים : quia Deus tales imagines contra legem suam sibi factas à se abalienat, neque pluris facit quam eas, quæ falsis numinibus excitantur. ET MORTUUS EST) Ideo mortuus est: id est, exitio addictus: μετωνυμία satis frequens.

## 13:2
Ver. 2.

AND NOW THEY HAVE ADDED TO SINNING) They proceed to the worse. AND THEY HAVE MADE FOR THEMSELVES A MOLTEN IMAGE FROM THEIR SILVER, AS THE LIKENESS OF IDOLS) It is certain that עצב is placed for idols, 1 Sam. 31:8, 1 Par. 10:8, 2 Paral. 24:18, Is. 10:11, 48:5, and several times in the Psalms, in which places the Greeks have placed εἴδωλον, elsewhere γλυπτόν. The sense is: not content with the calves, an old sin, they also made for themselves silver images, in imitation of those which the profane nations had, namely in human form, which the Chaldean adds here. IT IS THE WORK OF CRAFTSMEN ENTIRELY) There is nothing divine in it: nothing more than material and the price of labor, Isaiah 40:18, 20, 41:7, 44:12, 13, Jeremiah 10:13. OF THESE THEY THEMSELVES SAY: LET MEN SACRIFICE KISSING THE CALVES) There was a double reading here. Aquila reads ישקון: for he translates καταφιλῶντες, and that is a sign of showing veneration, which in Latin is usually called adoring. See Job 31:17. But since here the worship of images is openly distinguished from the worship of the calves, the reading of the LXX will perhaps be better, ישבות, that is, let the calves cease: we have sacrificed calves long enough: there is need of greater victims: for 'the calves have failed,' the LXX have, with a slightly different sense, but so that it appears they read ישבות.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ET NUNC ADDIDERUNT AD PECCAN- DUM) Procedunt in pejus. FECERUNTQVE SIBI CONFLATILE DE ARGEN- TO SUO, QUASI SIMILITUDINEM IDOLORUM) Certum est עצב poni pro idolis, 1. Sam. 31. 8. 1.Par. 10, 8. 2. Paral. 24, 18. Es. 10, 11. 48, 5. & Psalmis aliquoties, quibus in locis Græci posuere εἴδωλον, alibi γλυπτόν. Sensus est; non contenti vitulis, veteri peccato, fecere sibi etiam simulacra argentea, ad imitationem eorum, quæ habebant profanæ gentes, forma scilicet humana, quod hic addit Chaldæus. FACTURA ARTIFICUM TOTUM EST) Nihil est in eo divini: nihil amplius quam materia & manuprœti- um, Esaiæ 40, 18. 20. 41, 7. 44, 12. 13. Jerem. 10, 13. HIS IPSI DICUNT: IMMOLATE HOMINES VITULOS ADORANTES) Duplex hic fuit lectio. Aquila legit ישקון : vertit enim καταφιλῶντες, id autem est, vene- rationis signum exhibentes, quod Latine dici solet adoran- tes. Vide Jobi 31, 17. Verum cum hic imaginum cultus à cultu vitulorum aperte distinguatur, melior forte erit lectio LXX. ישבות id est, quiescant vituli: satis diu vitulos sa- crificavimus: majoribus victimis opus est: μόσχοι γὰρ ἐκλε- λοίπασι, habent LXX. sensu paulum diverso, sed ita ut eos legisse ישבות appareat.

## 13:3
Ver. 3.

THEREFORE THEY SHALL BE AS THE MORNING CLOUD, AND AS THE MORNING DEW THAT PASSES AWAY) They will not endure: as above. AS THE DUST DRIVEN BY A WHIRLWIND FROM THE THRESHING FLOOR) Psalm 1:4. AND AS SMOKE FROM THE CHIMNEY) ἀπὸ καπνοδόχης, as Theodotion translates: Symmachus, ἀπὸ καταῤῥάκτου: and Jerome says that a cataract is a hole made in a wall, through which smoke exits. The LXX translated it as 'from locusts,' deceived by the ambiguity of the word, because ארבה, which signifies a window or chimney, with changed vowels signifies a locust. From this version another reading flowed, corrupted by the proximity of letters, 'from tears,' which exists in many codices. Jerome mentions all these varieties.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

IDCIRCO ERUNT QVASI NUBES MATUTI- NA, ET SICUT ROS MATUTINUS PRÆTERIENS) Non durabunt: ut supra. SICUT PULVIS TURBINE RAPTUS EX AREA) Psalm. 1, 4. ET SICUT FUMUS DE FUMARIO) ἀπὸ καπνο- δόχης, quomodo vertit Theodotion: Symmachus, ἀπὸ κα- ταῤῥάκτου: esse autem cataracten ait Hieronymus, foramen in pariete fabricatum, per quod fumus egreditur. LXX. verterunt ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων, decepti vocis ambiguo, quia ארבה quod fenestram aut fumarium significat, mutatis vocalibus significat locustam. Ex hac versione lectio altera fluxit, vi- cinitate literarum corrupta, ἀπὸ δακρύων, quæ in multis ex- tat codicibus. Omnium harum varietatum meminit Hiero- nymus.

## 13:4
Ver. 4.

BUT I AM THE LORD THY GOD, FROM THE LAND OF EGYPT) It is again an ἔκθεσις, which is above 12:14, these words being cut from the beginning of the Decalogue. Before these words, certain things are placed in the edition of the LXX, which Jerome notes were not in the most ancient copies, so old are certain additions in those books.

AND YOU SHALL NOT KNOW A GOD BESIDE ME) You would not acknowledge a God besides me: that is, you ought not to acknowledge: as in 'But you, Alban, would remain by your words.'

AND THERE IS NO SAVIOR BESIDE ME) Because no one can save you (namely, from all evils) besides me.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

EGO AUTEM DOMINUS DEUS TUUS, EX TER- RA ÆGYPTI) Est iterum ἔκθεσις, quæ supra 12, 14. verba hæc curtata ex Decalogi initio. Ante hæc verba quædam sunt posita in editione LXX. quæ in antiquissimis exemplari- bus non fuisse notat Hieronymus, adeo veteres quædam in illis libris παραγραφαί.

ET DEUM ABSQUE ME NESCIES) Deum præ- ter me non agnosceres : id est, agnoscere non deberes : ut At tu dictis Albane maneres.

ET SALVATOR NON EST PRÆTER ME) Quia nemo potest vos servare (ab omnibus scilicet malis) præter me.

## 13:5
Ver. 5.

I KNEW YOU IN THE DESERT IN THE LAND OF SOLITUDE) To know is often to love: but both the LXX and the Chaldean read ידעתיך, I fed you: namely there, where all things were lacking, I gave you drinkable water, manna, birds.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

EGO COGNOVI TE IN DESERTO IN TER- RA SOLITUDINIS) Cognoscere sæpe est diligere : sed tam LXX, quam Chaldæus legerunt ידעתיך pavi te : ibi scilicet, ubi omnia deerant, dedi tibi aquam potabilem, manna, aves.

## 13:6
Ver. 6.

ACCORDING TO THEIR PASTURE THEY WERE FILLED AND THEY WERE SATIATED) In the Hebrew: According to their pasture and they were satiated, they were satiated: that is: where they were fully satiated, like sheep in pastures. See Deut. 8, 15.

AND THEY LIFTED UP THEIR HEART) The same sense as Deut. 32, 15.

AND THEY FORGOT ME) Contrary to what both reason suggested and God had warned in Deut. 6, 11, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

JUXTA PASCUA SUA ADIMPLETI SUNT ET SATURATI SUNT) In Hebræo : Iuxta pascua sua & satu- rati sunt, saturati sunt : id est : ubi plene saturati erant, velut oves in pascuis. Vide Deut. 8, 15.

ET LEVAVERUNT COR SUUM) Idem sensus qui Deut. 32, 15.

ET OBLITI SUNT MEI) Contra quam & ratio ferebat, & Deus monuerat Deut. 6, 11, 12.

## 13:7
Ver. 7.

AND I WILL BE AS A LIONESS) As a panther: for that is שחל both here and above 5, 14.

AS A LEOPARD) The leopard differs from the panther. Pliny 8, 17.

IN THE WAY OF THE ASSYRIANS) He followed the seventy elders, who have κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν Ἀσσυρίων. But the Chaldean and other interpreters do not wish אשור to be a proper noun, but a verb, so that the sense may be, I will lie in wait because of the way: which is the habit of the leopard in Jer. 5, 6. I will bring it about that they fall into ambushes on every side.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ET EGO ERO QVASI LEÆNA) Tanquam pan- thera : id enim שחל tum hic tum supra 5, 14.

SICUT PARDUS) Pardus à Panthera differt. Pli- nius 8, 17.

IN VIA ASSYRIORUM) Secutus est LXX. senes, qui habent κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν Ἀσσυρίων. At Chaldæus & alii in- terpretes non nomen volunt esse proprium אשור, sed ver- bum, ut sensus sit, propter viam insidiabor : qui mos pardo Je- rem. 5, 6. efficiam, ut undique in insidias incidant.

## 13:8
Verse 8.

I WILL MEET THEM AS A BEAR WHOSE CUPS HAVE BEEN SNATCHED AWAY) The sense is well expressed in the Hebrew: As a bear bereaved. Jerome on this passage: Those who have written about the natures of beasts say that among all wild animals there is nothing more savage than a bear when she has lost her cubs: Thus you have descriptions of lionesses and tigresses raging when their cubs have been snatched away in the poets.

AND I WILL TEAR OPEN THE INTERIORS OF THEIR LIVER) In the Hebrew: The enclosures of their heart: that is, the precordia. The sense is: I will scatter the people: for the people are as a body, individuals as members.

AND I WILL CONSUME THEM THERE, AS A LION) I will cause many to perish.

BEAST OF THE FIELD) The Assyrian, strong and ruthless.

HE SHALL TEAR THEM) He shall scatter the people.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

OCCURRAM EIS QVASI URSA RAPTIS CATU- LIS) Bene sensus expressus est in Hebræo : Quasi ursus orba- tus. Hieronymus ad hunc locum : Ajunt qui de bestiarum scripsere naturis, inter omnes feras nihil esse ursa sævius, cum perdiderit catulos : Sic & leænæ & tigridis descriptiones fu- rentium, ereptis catulis, habes apud Poetas.

ET DIRUMPAM INTERIORA JECORIS EO- RUM) In Hebræo : Claustra cordis eorum : id est, præcor- dia. Sensus est : dispergam populum : nam populus ut cor- pus, singuli ut membra.

ET CONSUMAM EOS IBI, QVASI LEO) Fa- ciam ut intereant multi.

BESTIA AGRI) Assyrius, fortis & immitis.

SCINDET EOS) Populum distrahet.

## 13:9
Verse 9. THY DESTRUCTION O ISRAEL: ONLY IN ME IS THY HELP) Thy depression: that is, it comes from thee that thou art handed over to foreigners. For if thou hadst hoped in me, I would have been a help to thee. This exposition best suits the Hebrew words, and connects the 'ki' which follows with these words. The Chaldean has the same sense.

Cocceius renders the same sense: whether 'shahat' is a noun, as 'shahat' in Deut. 32:35, or a verb. If the former, the sense is: Thy corruption it is, or thou hast corruption. If the latter, it is explained impersonally. The interpreters agree that the destruction of Israel is ascribed to Israel, his salvation solely to the Lord. How this maxim serves to refute the Stoic Calvinist dogma concerning the absolute reprobation of the greatest part of the human race may be seen in this place in the blessed Gefner. The sources of salvation and damnation are shown here, as the blessed Meisner rightly says in this place. Salvation is from God, destruction is from sin: God promises salvation on account of the merit of Christ; man incurs damnation on account of the merit of sin. Therefore, those who are saved are saved by the grace of God alone; those who perish, perish on account of their own sins, without fault of God. Thus Calvinism, by which absolute reprobation is established, and Pelagianism, by which the meritorious acquisition of salvation from our own works is asserted, are best avoided. Beautifully Augustine, book 3 against Julian, chapter 18: God is good, God is just; He can save without good merits, because He is good; He cannot damn without evil merits, because He is just.

Latin:

Vers. 9. PERDITIO TVA ISRAEL : TANTVMMO- DO IN ME AVXILIVM TVVM) Depressio tua : id est, à te venit, quod externis traderis. Nam si in me sperasses, auxi- lio tibi fuissem. Hæc expositio maxime convenit Hebræis vocibus, & כִּי, quod sequitur, cum his verbis connectit. Eundem sensum habet Chaldæus.

Eundem sensum reddit Coccejus: ut שׁחת vel nomen sit, uti שׁחת Deut. 32, 35. vel verbum. Si illud, sensus est : Corruptio tua est, vel corruptionem habes. Si hoc, impersonaliter explicatur. Consen- tiunt interpretes, perditionem Israelis Israeli, sa- lutem ejus unice Domino adscribi. Quæ gnome quomodo ad refellendum Stoicum dogma Calvi- nianum de absoluta reprobatione maximæ partis generis humani faciat, videri poterit in h. l. B. Gef- nerus. Monstrantur hic fontes salutis & damnatio- nis, ut recte B. Meisnerus in h. l. Salus ex Deo, per- ditio ex peccato est: Deus ob Christi meritum pro- mittit salutem; homo ob peccati meritum incur- rit damnationem. Qui ergo servantur, ex sola Dei gratia servantur, qui pereunt, ob propria peccata pereunt, sine culpa Dei. Sic evitatur optime Calvi- nismus, quo statuitur absoluta reprobatio, & Pela- gianismus, quo asseritur meritoria ex nostris operi- bus salutis acquisitio. Pulchre Augustinus lib. 3. contr. Jul. c. 18. Bonus est Deus, justus est Deus, potest sine bonis meritis salvare, quia bonus est; non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est.

## 13:10
Verse 10.

WHERE IS YOUR KING? MOSTLY NOW) In the Hebrew: Where is your king? You valued kings more than me. Where now are the forces for his kingdom?

LET HIM SAVE YOU IN ALL YOUR CITIES) Therefore let him save you, with all your cities, if he can: for you expected that from kings, 1 Sam. 8:20.

AND YOUR JUDGES!) That is, the prefects placed by the king.

OF WHOM YOU SAID: GIVE ME A KING AND PRINCES) When they sought a king, they simultaneously wanted royal prefects. For to appoint them is among the rights of a king, 1 Sam. 8:12.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

UBI EST REX TUUS? MAXIME NUNC) In Hebræo: Rex tuus ubi? Reges pluris fecisti quam me. Ubi nunc regi suæ vires?

SALVET TE IN OMNIBUS URBIBUS TUIS) Ergo servet te, cum omnibus urbibus tuis, si potest: nam id de regibus exspectasti 1. Sam. 8, 20.

ET JUDICES TU!) Id est, præfecti à rege positi.

DE QUIBUS DIXISTI: DA MIHI REGEM ET PRINCIPES) Cum regem petiverunt, simul voluere & præfectos regios. Nam eos constituere inter jura est regis, 1. Sam. 8, 12.

## 13:11
Verse 11.

I WILL GIVE YOU A KING IN MY FURY) I have given. Already quite often. That is, angered by your sins, I allowed you through seditions and slaughters to change kings at will. See 2 Kings 15.

AND I WILL TAKE AWAY IN MY INDIGNATION) Through the Assyrians. Thus evil deeds slip away worse.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

DABO TIBI REGEM IN FURORE MEO) Dedi. Jam sæpius. Id est, iratus peccatis vestris, sivi vos per sedi- tiones ac cædes, mutare reges pro lubitu. vide 2. Reg. 15.

ET AUFERAM IN INDIGNATIONE MEA) Per Assyrios. Ita mala facta pejus dilabuntur.

## 13:12
Verse 12.

THE INIQUITY OF EPHRAIM IS BOUND UP) All things cling to me at once, as those which are tied together in a bundle, so that nothing may fall out.

HIS SIN IS HIDDEN) Stored away: like that which must be repaid in its own time.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

COLLIGATA EST INIQUITAS EPHRAIM) Omnia simul mihi obhærent, ut quæ in fasciculum con- stringuntur, ne quid excidat.

ABSCONDITUM PECCATUM EJUS) Reposi- tum: ut id quod suo tempore reddi debet.

## 13:13
Verse 13.

THE PAINS OF A WOMAN IN LABOR SHALL COME UPON HIM) Most grievous torments, ὠδῖνες Matt. 24, 8.

HE IS NOT A WISE SON) As if a fetus not taking thought for itself, nor breaking forth from the womb. See Cant. 8, 14.

FOR NOW HE SHALL NOT STAND IN THE BREAKING FORTH OF CHILDREN) Otherwise he would not stand so long in the place from which children break forth. For that is מַשְׁבֵּר 4 Kings 19, 3. ἀναλογία: it signifies that Ephraim is not wise, in that he delays so long to repent, and thus to deliver himself from calamities.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

DOLORES PARTURIENTIS VENIENT EI) Gravissimi cruciatus, ὠδῖνες Matth. 24, 8.

IPSE FILIUS NON SAPIENS) Quasi fœtus sibi non consulens, neque ex utero erumpens. Vide Cant. 8, 14.

NUNC ENIM NON STABIT IN CONTRITI- ONE FILIORUM) Alioqui non tam diu staret in loco, unde erumpunt filii. Id enim מַשְׁבֵּר 4. Regum 19, 3. ἀναλογία: significat Ephraimum non sapere, quod tam diu differat pœ- nitentiam agere, ac sic semet eximere è calamitatibus.

## 13:14
Ver. 14.

I WILL DELIVER THEM FROM THE HAND OF DEATH) I would deliver them, if they would repent. The Hebrews, because they do not have a potential mood, are forced to misuse the future indicative. For death in the Hebrew is שְׁאוֹל, in Greek ᾅδης, from the hand of the grave, that is, from the dangers leading to the grave.

I WILL REDEEM THEM FROM DEATH) I would redeem them: that is, I would snatch them from destruction.

O DEATH, I WILL BE THY DEATH) I would be a plague to thee, O death; that is, I would extinguish all deadly things, as was done afterwards in the army of Sennacherib.

O GRAVE, I WILL BE THY DESTRUCTION) Destruction to thee, O grave. He understands the grave here as the pit into which whole peoples are cast, as happens in public disasters.

REPENTANCE IS HID FROM MINE EYES.) This is the opposite of the former. But now, since you are unwilling to repent though called for so long, there is nothing that can console me, that is, appease my wrath. Thus this word is used in Isa. 57, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

DE MANU MORTIS LIBERABO EOS) Libera- rem, si pœnitentiam agerent. Hebræi, quia potentialem mo- dum non habent, coguntur abuti futuro indicativi. Pro mortis in Hebræo est שְׁאוֹל, Græce ᾅδης, de manu sepulchri, id est, de periculis ad sepulcrum ducentibus.

DE MORTE REDIMAM EOS) Redimerem: id est, eriperem eos ab exitio.

ERO MORS TUA, O MORS) Essem pestis tibi, ô mors; id est, omnia mortifera exstinguerem, ut in Sennache- ribi exercitu factum est postea.

MORSUS TUUS ERO, INFERNE) Excidium tibi, ô sepulcrum. Sepulcrum hic intelligit fossam, in quam toti populi conjiciuntur, ut fit in publicis cladibus.

CONSOLATIO ABSCONDITA EST AB OCU- LIS MEIS.) Est oppositum prioribus. Nunc vero cum pœnitentiam agere tam diu vocati nolitis, nihil est, quod me consolari possit, id est, iram meam sedare. Sic vox hæc sumitur Esa. 57, 6.

## 13:15
Ver. 15.

FOR HE SHALL DIVIDE AMONG BRETHREN) For he shall multiply for his brethren, supply: sins. He has sinned more than Judah and Benjamin. So the Chaldean.

Grotius here again rashly perverts this excellent Evangelical sermon concerning the eternal liberation to come through the Messiah, as if the discourse were only about a corporal liberation. Furthermore, he here invents a potential mood, and in his gloss converts a simple promise into a hypothetical one; nay, he makes a mere threat out of a promise. For what else is this than to threaten and complain, when God protests that He will not liberate the people because they do not wish to repent, and that there is nothing that could appease His wrath? Which he has from R. David Kimchi, who likewise transformed the future into a potential mood. Nor could the Judaizing Calvin keep his hands off this distinguished oracle, although he was not unaware that interpreters with great consensus explain it concerning Christ. Whom he himself boldly pronounced to have erred in MANY WAYS, he being, forsooth, far wiser than them all. For, fascinated by Jewish glosses, he determined that it is not Christ who speaks these things, but God the Father; not concerning spiritual redemption, but corporal; not from the hand of eternal death and hell, but from the hand of temporal death and the straits of this life, in hope of a release from the ignominious Babylonian captivity. The same Calvin, as also the Tigurine version, even preceded our Grotius in this, in how the Prophet's saying can be explained conditionally, although he refers the conditional sense to perfect and eternal salvation. By which very thing Pareus wishes to excuse his Calvin, as if he were not at all siding with the Jews. But just as Calvin explains the Prophetic saying with the Jews concerning corporal liberation, so neither will the Jews deny what he himself affirms, that God is willing to redeem from every death if repentance is performed. He differs, therefore, in nothing from them in explaining this passage, which Rivetus has consequently joined here with Kimchi.

But that a promise concerning Christ is held here at all, we confirm with the following arguments. First, that the very letter of the text teaches that the discourse is not about liberation from some corporal destruction, not from dangers leading to the grave, as Grotius wishes, nor from temporal death alone, much less from civil death—as Zanchius in this place calls captivity—but rather from eternal death and from hell. For the word of death and hell does not denote any destruction whatsoever, or only some danger. Which signification is merely arbitrary, nor can examples of it be brought forth from the Scriptures. Nor would that be the proper sense, but the improper. For the customary and proper sense of DEATH and HELL, when they are joined in the Scriptures and when the matter is about liberation from them, implies true death, not just any destruction; true hell, not just a danger leading to the grave or hell. But one must not rashly depart from the literal sense to the figurative. Furthermore (2.), liberation from death and שאול is promised here absolutely. Whatever, therefore, is of death, and whatever the Israelites had to fear, or whatever we have to fear, whatever is of hell, or is expressed by שאול, liberation from all that is promised. For if one were to remain in any death, or in some τῷ שאול, it would not be this all-encompassing liberation. Those who are liberated from some destruction and temporal danger, but for whom eternal death and damnation awaits, are not so much liberated as they are left in death and hell. And what is the reason that I should restrict such a saying to temporal things, which is formed in general words and where no signs of a necessary restriction occur in the text? If you say that they would be fully liberated from death and hell conditionally, if they perform repentance, no trace of that condition appears here in the text. Nor can that promise be at once both absolute and conditional.

Thirdly, the discourse here is about redemption, which is made by the interposition of a λύτρον. God employs two words: the first, אֶפְדֵּם, ῥύσομαι, as the LXX and Vulgate render it, from פדה, which word denotes redemption made by the intervention of a certain price, Num. 28:15, "by redeeming you shall redeem the firstborn of man." Cf. Lev. 19:20, Exod. 21:8, 30, Num. 3:last verse, ch. 18:6, Ps. 49:8, in which places the LXX use λυτρώσαι, λύτρον, and ἀπολύτρον, which import the price of redemption. Which occur concerning the redemption of Christ in Isa. 35:last, and passim in the N.T. Then, אֶגְאָלֵם, the LXX translate λυτρώσομαι, from גאל, to redeem, to vindicate by right of kinship, Lev. 25:11. Which word, when it is used concerning a redeemer, does not denote just any redeemer indiscriminately, but him who by right of kinship, and by interposing a price he redeems and vindicates his kinsman. And therefore in this proper sense, it is proper to Christ, when it is a matter of the redemption of God, as one who has been made our kinsman through ἐνσάρκωσιν (incarnation), and by the right of kinship he redeemed us through the intervention of the λύτρε (ransom) of his blood, or of the ἀπολυτρώσεως (redemption) made by his blood,… Eph. 1, 7. 1 Pet. 1, 18. Therefore he is distinguished by the name גֹּאֵל (Goel), Redeemer, Gen. 48, 16. Isa. 63, 9. Since, therefore, it is a matter here of the redemption which is made by the Goel, by right of kinship and the intervention of the λύτρε (ransom), no other redemption and ἀπολύτρωσις (redemption) made by his death ought to be understood than that of Christ. To this pertains the promise made above, Hos. 1, 8. I, Jehovah, will have mercy on the House of Judah, says God the Father, and I will save them in Jehovah their God, in the Messiah and through the Messiah. Here, therefore, the testimony is now introduced, that and how he is about to save, namely, that he is about to deliver them from the hand of death and hell.

The other word מִמָּוֶת (mimmavet), from death, although it sometimes denotes the diseases, miseries, and hardships of this life, yet since it is viewed here as the wages of sin, from which we were to be delivered, from which Christ alone delivers us, Rom. 6, last, and liberation from death is promised ἁπλῶς (simply), it designates not only liberation from hardships or diseases, but primarily from eternal death, which is the death of glory, the fear of which is indeed most grave. Wherefore, so that the benefit of redemption might be plenary, we were to be delivered by Christ from everything that comes under the name of death, and to which we have been made subject through sin. Now, under the name of death come the hardships, agonies, diseases, and miseries of this life, by which we are daily worn away, and thus gradually die, Ex. 10, 18. 2 Kings 4, 40. 2 Cor. 1, 10. ch. 11, 23. and the guilt and corruption of sin, which is called the death of grace, and spiritual [death], Matt. 8, 22. John 5, 25. 1 Tim. 5, 6. and the dissolution of the soul from the body, which is called the death of nature, and temporal [death], Rom. 5, 12. 1 Cor. 1, 21. and the exclusion from heavenly life, and eternal damnation, which is called the death of glory, and the second or last [death], Rev. 2, 11. ch. 21, 14. From all these species of death Christ has redeemed us, by mitigating miseries, rendering them lighter, converting the death of nature into sleep, and clearly taking away the death of grace and glory from the faithful.

Fourthly, those to be redeemed are designated here in our text as the Israelites. But they were by no means delivered from destruction and the danger of destruction, nor were they redeemed from captivity, or released. For the Ephraimite kingdom was not restored, but only the tribe of Judah, and those who followed it, and were counted with it. Furthermore, through the person of the Israelites, all men are rightly understood, just as it is most customary for the benefits of the New Testament to be promised to all men under the person of the Israelites. For this benefit of redemption is not singular or special, but common, because we have all been bought with a price paid: and therefore, with respect to acquisition, the Redemption is universal, even if it becomes particular by reason of application.

Sixthly, the liberation is described even more magnificently, when the Lord through an apostrophe turns himself to death and hell, and as if provoking these living enemies (through prosopopoeia) to a contest, a certain destruction is sent into their very face, as they say: I will be thy death, דְבָרֶיךָ (debareicha), THY PESTILENCES, i.e., in many ways I will destroy thee, I will not pursue thee with one kind of pestilence. For this is the force in the plural number, THY PESTILENCES. I will be, O hell, קָטָבְךָ (kotbecha), thy excision, or thy destruction. Which apostrophe brings about nothing else than the plenary removal of death and infernal dominion, and the liberation of men from them. The blessed Luther deals diligently with the reading and meaning of these words in the place cited. Those two words (Deber) and (keteb) in the Scriptures are names of pestilences, as among the Latins those two, Pestis (plague) and lues (pestilence), and as lues is more atrocious than pestis, as they could not yet find a remedy for that disease which kills immediately, nay, rather a poison of nature than a disease, as Perottus says, so keteb is more atrocious in Hebrew than Deber. Whence some imagine them to be names of demons, about which it is permitted to see Lyra and Burgensis on Ps. 91. Since, therefore, Hosea joins keteb, a univocal, with deber, an equivocal, as if by a tautology, it is sufficiently clear that he restricted the equivocation to a univocation by this, and wished it to be read not dâbar, but deber. St. Paul translates it as thy keteb, thy victory; the LXX, thy sting, by which Paul rendered that (thy deber). Jerome, thy bite. Symmachus, thy encounter, as also in Ps. 91 the Latins have, from the encounter, that is, from keteb. The fifth edition, and Theodotion, thy plague. But if you read it from the noun (dabor diborecho), it signifies thy words, thy things, thy causes, in the plural. Thus Aquila and the Fifth edition read, Where are thy words? And the LXX, ποῦ ἡ δίκη σoυ; Where is thy cause, vengeance, punishment, thy right, and the like, about which [we speak] below. For to me that reading is held to be violent and forced. Thus, therefore, from the Hebrew, without prejudice, it seems to me that the words should be translated properly: Where are thy pestilences, O Death? Where is thy plague, O Hell? The Prophet does not speak, however, of pestilences literally or casually, about which it is for physicians to judge and dispute, just as he does not speak of casual death, but of natural pestilences and death innate to us, which rage and rave through every kind of man. Which pestilences even a young, healthy, robust, handsome person has. For all die. And we all die by the same pestilences. Just as in Psalm 51 he laments: Behold, I was conceived in iniquities. This

Fifthly, redemption is emphatically said to be made from the hand, that is, from the power of hell. Which word HAND certainly implies not danger, but power and dominion, because the strength of man is situated mostly in the hand and arm: by which name also the power and virtue of God is expressed, Jos. 4:24, Jud. 1:45, 1 Chron. 29:12, as also the power of men, Gen. 32:11, Exod. 2:19, Num. 10:9, which is therefore attributed to hell by prosopopoeia, so that its dominion over men may be denoted. For as the weak is held by the stronger hand, so hell as it were extended its hand, seized us all, and held us captive, and therefore from this hand and captivity we had to be redeemed through the higher hand and virtue of Christ. Cf. Exod. 14:8, Num. 33:3. Nor indeed is HAND OF HELL anywhere the same as danger leading to the grave. But by deliberation it is applied from the POWER OF HELL, made through Christ, Ps. 49:16. which power no one can escape, except through Christ, as David testifies, Psalm 89:49. The Hebrew name שְׁאוֹל, which the LXX render by ᾅδην, although it has various meanings, occurs for קֶבֶר, and the state of the damned, and the pains of hell, Num. 16:23, Isa. 28:15, 2 Sam. 22:5, Ps. 18:6, Luke 16:32.
