And here, where Jehovah speaks of such a notable deliverance, it is certainly not to be taken as only of danger leading to the grave, or of bodily misery, which by no means exhaust such an august and magnificent promise. And how were the Israelites immune from dangers leading to the grave? How were they free from destruction? Therefore others more correctly take it of the grave, that the Lord wishes to vindicate those consumed by death and the grave, or (which we prefer more) of hell. To which contributes what Blessed Luther notes in the addition to the present passage, T. IV. Jen. Lat. f. 557. notes that the word שְׁאוֹל in the Scriptures is so distinguished from קֶבֶר, that the latter (the grave) is assigned to the body, the former (hell) to the soul. The Papists' fiction concerning the deliverance from the Limbo of the Fathers is unworthy, for the refuting of which we should linger. For that Limbo is a mere old wives' tale.

These are the words of the blessed Luther. Therefore, the blessed Hunnius argues from this in his Anti-Pareus, p. 250, in this way: Where the Holy Scripture preaches liberation and victory against death and hell, there it undoubtedly preaches the benefit of the death and resurrection of Christ, and speaks about Christ. But in the present passage, the Holy Scripture preaches our liberation from death and hell. Therefore, it is discoursing about Christ and his benefits.

Seventh, the context does not contradict this interpretation, but rather confirms it. For after the Lord had completely taken away from the Israelites every hope of restoring a bodily kingdom, he now promises the restoration of the spiritual kingdom of Christ, as the blessed Gesner has it in this place. With whom Francis Junius agrees in Parall. 43. That Hosea, without controversy, looked toward that full restoration to be in Christ and through Christ, our blessed Luther explains the coherence of the text thus: After the Prophet threatened the idolaters with devastation, he now turns to the consolation of the pious, who were not only going to witness such horrible punishments, but also, as happens, were going to suffer them. For when public punishments rage, the pious also feel a part of them. But this consolation which he proposes to them is wonderful. For he does not say that it will come to pass that the Lord, when the Assyrian Monarch attacks, will deliver them from his hand. You too, he says, will be killed or led away captive among the Gentiles, nor will your condition be better than that of the idolaters, on account of whom such great wrath and calamity is raging. You will bear this punishment with an even mind and will hope for a far better liberation than if you were now to be delivered from the hand of the enemies. For I will deliver you from the hand of hell, that is, I will raise those who have already finished their life and are buried into a better and eternal life. Thus I will compensate for your sufferings and tribulations, which will produce an eternal weight of glory, etc. And before all, St. Cyril, Tom. III. Oper. p. 187. After he has spoken to the sinners out of wrath, and out of his own sorrow has foretold what would happen to them, he returns to the gentleness becoming to God, and indicates that he has not turned away from the entire human race, nor sent them into irrevocable and eternal exile, but that forgiveness would be given at some time, and a recall to the ancient state in Christ, adding that he would deliver them from the hand of hell, and redeem them from death, undoubtedly those who were from the beginning subject to the same on account of sins committed against the Creator and on account of the transgression of Adam. For such a promise was made later not only to Ephraim, or the progeny of Israel, but to all mortals. For, as the divine Paul writes: He is not the God of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles. For he justified the circumcision by faith, and the uncircumcision through faith. Nor could Rivetus deny that our interpretation fits the text perfectly (even though he would gladly have undertaken an apology for his Calvin), judging that this whole passage could and should be rendered paraphrastically thus: Although such is the condition of the mother and the children, that is, of the Republic of the Israelites, that they must perish on account of their folly: yet let those who will remain among them, who, touched by repentance, will have wished to return to a better way of life, not despair, as if no salvation or liberation from death remained for them: For I, the Messiah, will redeem them from the power of the grave, nor will there be any bond so strong that I will not break it, so as to restore them to life, and indeed to vindicate them from death itself. Where then are your plagues, O death, where is your destruction, O grave? You have lost your strength against those who receive themselves into my protection; whom I will not permit to perish with the crowd of the impious, nor will I utterly destroy Israel, but I myself will snatch him, saved in the remnant, for you and the grave, because I will never repent of my gift and calling, nor will the unbelief of men make the faith of GOD void.

Eighth, the sentence immediately subjoined also agrees. Which, if it be rendered, repentance (for the word נחם denotes both repentance and consolation) shall hide itself from my eyes: that is, I will not repent of this promise, it reports an immutable divine decree. Cf. Rom. 11:29. That is to say, what I have said, I will fulfill by the deed itself without any repentance. Therefore, this was not a hypothetical promise, but simple and categorical. Castalio retains the meaning of solace, and translates: My eyes shall lack solace, that is, I will not sleep until I have done this. The blessed Meisner judges that it can be explained thus: I will not console death and hell, no mercy for those enemies will touch me; but rather I will courageously destroy death and hell. Jerome and Ribera have these as the words not of Christ, but of the Prophet, that is to say: This consolation concerning the benefits of the Messiah is hidden from my eyes, I do not understand how it will come to pass, since hell divides between brothers, and snatches one after another away. But the first interpretation is the simplest, and is deservedly preferred. Which the blessed Gesner also approves; that the Lord testifies his promise is ἀμεταμέλητον, and that he will certainly perform this for the pious, and will never at any time change his promise; Repentance, he says, is hidden from my eyes, that is, I have promised the faithful liberation from death: I will not repent of this promise for all eternity. Nor will it be repugnant to our interpretation if, with Jerome, the LXX, and the blessed Luther, these words are taken concerning consolation, and attributed to the Church: namely, that the faithful under the storm of calamities complain of the weakness and blindness of the flesh, which is not affected and raised by the divine promise as it ought to be, but the consolation is hidden from carnal eyes. What is subjoined: Because he himself will divide between brothers, Grotius interprets as, because he himself multiplied for the brothers, i.e., sins. But what is this license to change the future into the past, and to add a new word which is not in the text? But he has that from the Chaldean; who rendered it thus: because they themselves were called sons, and multiplied corrupt works. The error of the Vulgate and LXX Interpreters concerning the division between brothers is because, for יפריא he will make fruitful, they read יפריד he will divide, whence Lyra and Vatablus explain it concerning a judicial division: he will divide between brothers; i.e., he will exercise judgment between the sheep and the goats. But in them there is nothing sound. Others indeed refer the pronoun to Ephraim, but concerning fruitfulness through an allusion to the name of Ephraim, and they explain the etymology: he will grow, or he will be fruitful among his brothers. This sense both agrees with the words and is more consistent with the preceding consolatory discourse, that Ephraim will also bear fruit among the Jews, as his brothers. Blessed Gesner refers these to Christ in this manner: Christ will bring forth among his brothers the most abundant fruits of evangelical doctrine and the Holy Spirit, namely, faith, new obedience, love of God and neighbor, that is, among the faithful, John 20:18. Which is also the paraphrase of Osiander, whence he likewise makes the former words about consolation hidden under the cross the words of the Church, so that the same discourse is continued here. Ludov. de Dieu interprets the final words also in a good sense: This verse, as regards the words, is easy enough, but as regards the sense, it is difficult, which we clarify thus: the Prophet says at the beginning of the verse: For he (Ephraim) will be fruitful among his brothers. It could be objected, what hope of fruitfulness is there, when he behaves like a true desert? The Prophet answers: An east wind will come, the wind of the Lord, ascending from the desert, and his spring will dry up, and his fountain will be parched, namely, of the desert. For deserts also have their own springs and fountains of water, from which they are nourished and rendered more uncultivated, otherwise they would perish if they were entirely destitute of waters. Therefore, God promises that He will dry up the fountains of the desert of His people with His wind. Then he (Ephraim) will plunder the treasures of all desirable vessels, that is, he will grow rich with the spoils of others. But the interpretation of those who understand it in a later sense seems simpler. Although such goods may fall to Ephraim; yet meanwhile the enemy will still come, like a most vehement wind, over everything, and will dry it up. Which B. Gesner and Meisner interpret as the total destruction of the Jewish Synagogue to come by the Romans, and others, as well as our Grotius, interpret it as the attack of the Assyrians: which opinion of his we do not disapprove of here. It is, however, pleasing to append here the Paschal Program publicly proposed in the year 1663 in the name of the Academic Rector, because it illustrates the sense of the oracle already expounded.

Just as there was never a sharper battle, no heavier conflict, than when the encounter with that strong armed man, the Great Dragon, the ancient Serpent, who had seduced the whole world, was CHRIST, that stronger one coming upon him, the true Michael, the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle: so no victory was ever obtained more glorious than by CHRIST, the King of glory, who overcame that strong armed man, took away from him all his armor in which he trusted, and distributed his spoils, and himself utterly trampled the head of the ancient serpent. But the more admirable this victory was, the more illustrious is the glory of our victor. And who does not stand amazed when he piously weighs the manner and method of the battle? Satan attacked CHRIST armed not only with anger and incredible fury, but equipped on all sides with arts and deceits far exceeding every human grasp. He attacked not alone, but with all the infernal forces, many thousands of legions, and not only with those, but having also attracted those who were the peculiar property and own people of the antagonist: Finally, he undertook that most bitter battle with such equipment that he seems to have risked all his strength, all his power, and wished to test whatever all the gates of hell were worth. On the other side, however, Christ was fighting, in whose mouth no deceit was found, and he alone and solitary, without any army, without any companion, fellow-soldier, or assistant. The winepress, he says, I have trodden alone, and of the nations there is no man with me. I looked around, and there was no helper, I sought, and there was no one to assist. Nor indeed did Christ enter the battle with such an enemy flashing with the rays and splendor of the majesty which he could have exerted while established in the form of GOD, by which he certainly would have been able to strike down all his power, however great it was, in an instant; but he appeared in a servile form, in a despised habit, and in a most abject state, and exposed, or rather subjected, himself to the fury of the enemy. For he emptied and humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, even the death of the cross. He had no beauty, nor comeliness: we saw him, and there was no appearance, and we desired him, the most despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity. And not only is the encounter of these antagonists worthy of admiration, but the manner of winning is also especially wonderful. For CHRIST conquered when he fell, he blotted out and took away sin when he transferred the sin of the world onto himself, he crushed the head of the ancient serpent when the serpent wounded his heel with a deadly bite, he triumphed over Satan when Satan's phalanx killed him on the cross; he destroyed the gates of hell when he underwent the pains of hell, he overcame death, the last enemy, when he met death. O how well you struck yourself with your own attack, O Devil! May it please us to address our enemy thus with Augustine, Sermon 122 de temp.: Your cruelty brought destruction to you, and advantage to us. While you spare no one, you finally destroy yourself; through the sin of one you captured all, through the justice of one you lost all nonetheless; if you attacked him who had consented to you, why did you kill him in whom you had found nothing, without cause? You have shed innocent blood, give back the condemned offspring. You are certainly that one who, puffed up, arrogated to yourself the likeness of divinity, now you are struck down and overcome by a divine man. And what wonder if divine virtue had overcome you, as being its own creature? But this is great and wonderful, that he should take from the dust that by which he might strike down and crush your wickedness? That you who were proudly exalted above the stars, are now overcome by flesh. That blood, therefore, which you shed, conquered you and redeemed me. Finally, I drink it, and saved, I no longer fear the destruction of your poison. You prevailed in Paradise, but you were conquered from the gallows. Why do you oppose to me the fiery sword placed around Paradise? Behold, the flowing wave of the exalted crucified one has quenched the turning flame. And thus the fruit of the victory of CHRIST also reveals itself to us as admirable. For the death of Christ, as St. Cyprian says in his sermon on the resurrection. of CHRIST, was a sacrifice for our sins, and the punishment of the cross met the excesses worthy of punishment, his labor lightened our burdens, his pain healed us, and his unmerited condemnation absolved us from eternal condemnation. You have asserted, says the same holy Martyr in his Sermon on the passion of CHRIST, you have ascended, O Lord, the palm, because that sign of your cross portended triumph over the Devil, and over the Principalities and powers and spiritual wickedness. I consider your works, and I admire you affixed to the cross among the condemned, now neither sad nor fearful, but the victor of punishments, with hands raised triumphing over Amalek, and as if sanctifying the people from on high, and raised on high and as if close to heaven, bringing the banner of the completed struggle to those above, and having erected a ladder for those below in the encounter with the Father. Hosea has encompassed the sum of such a mystery in his illustrious prophecy, chapter 13. I will deliver them from the hand of death, and I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite. For He promised redemption from death, and He received that He would redeem them from the hand of death in no other way than by death. By dying, He prophesied that He would be the death of death; He threatened that through infernal bites and pains He would be a bite to hell, with its greatest pain and the destruction of the infernal gates. St. Jerome interprets the hand of death thus: he calls it the works by which (death) kills, according to that which is written (Prov. XVIII) in the hand of the tongue are death and life. But the Lord delivered and redeemed all in the passion of the cross, and His flesh did not see corruption, and He spoke to death itself and to hell: O death, I will be thy death. For I have died for this reason, that you might die by my death. I will be thy bite, O hell, you who were devouring all with your jaws. For the prophecy is not to be understood as concerning the deliverance from the hand of Sennacherib by an Angel striking the Assyrians, with Ruffinus, or concerning the redemption and Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, with Theodoret and Ruffinus; much less concerning the Israelites being taken captive, and the hypothetical rescue of Ephraim, with Castrius, who rendered this sense very twisted, and peddled it as literal: I, says GOD, reserve to myself the iniquity of Ephraim, that I may punish it with captivity, in which he will suffer pains like a woman in labor. But he is so stupid that he does not care to repent; whereby he might beware, lest he remain for a long time in captivity, as it is ill for the fetus, which, when it does not emerge from the straits of the womb of the woman in labor, is crushed and broken: I indeed, if they had been wise, would have redeemed them from that dark hell, would have snatched them from that death, would have killed that death, would have destroyed that hell. But the stubborn wickedness of Ephraim offers me no reason for consolation. Because, therefore, it was he who made a divorce between the brothers, Judah and Israel, and sowed discord in religion, the Assyrian South wind will come and will snatch away the nation with its goods. Or also in this way: if some shall have been wise, even if they shall have been thrust into hell, I will redeem them; if they shall have been delivered to death, I will snatch them from its jaws: I will rush into death itself; and I will kill it; I will penetrate into hell itself, and I will destroy it with bites. But, woe is me, because the wicked Ephraim will affect me with no such pleasure, my eyes will be affected by no similar consolation offered by the stubborn Ephraim: because, therefore, he himself is the one who made a divorce between the brothers Judah and Israel, and sowed discord in the worship of GOD, he himself will suffer the punishment of captivity, of death, and of hell. For Assur will come, like a most violent wind, and will dry up all the veins of his wealth, the fields and their fertility: he will also dry up his fountain, the metropolis, Samaria, whence the veins flowed into other cities, and will plunder all his precious things. Than which double distortion of the Jesuit, none could be devised more stupid. Which, however, Hugo Grotius did not hesitate to choose over other interpretations, as he was very ingenious in interpolating any worst corruptions whatsoever. I WILL FREE THEM FROM THE HAND OF DEATH, I would free, if they were to repent. I WILL REDEEM THEM FROM DEATH, I would redeem, that is, I would snatch them from destruction. I WILL BE THY DEATH, O DEATH. I would be a plague to you, O death, that is, I would extinguish all deadly things, as was done afterwards in the army of Sennacherib. I WILL BE THY BITE, O HELL. Destruction to you, O grave. Understand the grave here as the pit into which whole peoples are cast, as happens in public disasters. Thus he, an artist of perverting Prophetic oracles, without compare. But that these things concern CHRIST literally, who by his passion and resurrection liberated us from hell and death, and is about to render all participants of this plenary liberation, in the resuscitation to eternal life, not only the Fathers and Doctors of the Church have taught with great consensus: Eusebius lib. IV. demonstr. Evangel. c. XII. St. Jerome in h. l. and in Epitaph. Nepot. St. Augustine serm. 137. de temp. Gregory the Great homil. 22. in Evang. and others, but it was also in confession among the older Hebrews, that these things are to be accepted concerning the liberation to be through the Messiah: whence R. Moses Hadarschan, witness Galatinus lib. 8. de arcanis Catholic. Verit c. 21. involving the mysteries of faith in the Rabbinic manner: The Messiah, son of David, went with me, until I arrived at the gates of Gehenna, and when the captives who were in Gehenna saw the light of the Messiah, they rejoiced to receive him, saying: This one will lead me out of these darknesses, just as it is said in Hosea 13: I will redeem them from the hand of the netherworld, I will liberate them from death. Which things are brought from R. Moses in Bereschith Rebba to Gen. 24, 67, by a collation of the place of Isaiah 35, 10: And the redeemed of the Lord shall return, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away: where Moses has fabulated that Kippod, the angel of death, measured hell, and that its depth is a journey of 300 years, but its length and breadth 500 years, as is to be read in

Pugio Fidei of Raimundus Martini part. 3. dist. 2. c. 8. §. 4. Nor did the Jesuit Christus find equal assent among his own, as he did with Grotius. For the Jesuits acknowledge that these things are to be understood concerning CHRIST, as to the letter, along with the praised Fathers, and Haymo, Hugo, Rupert, Lyranus, Vatablus, and Arias Montanus, Ribera, Menochius, Tirinus, Cornel. à Lapide, concerning which Theodoret also explains the prophecy, but in an allegorical sense. Not inelegantly Cornelius: It is a prosopopoeia: for death and hell are introduced here as if they were two persons and two Kings ruling widely, whom CHRIST despoiled of Kingdom and life by rising from death and hell, and triumphed over both: death indeed, because after the resurrection there will be no death: hell truly, because after the same it will be able to capture and devour no one further. The ancients celebrate the strength, victories, and triumphs of Achilles, Hercules, Alexander, Julius Caesar, and the like, whom no one in this life was able to resist: But all these were conquered by death and descended to the underworld. Christ alone is the tamer of death and hell. Whence he himself says Apoc. 1, 18. I have the keys of death and of hell. And we have an interpreter greater than any exception, the holy Apostle, who testifies with a sonorous voice that these things were predicted concerning CHRIST and are to be fulfilled plenarily in the universal resurrection, 1 Cor. 15, 54. But when this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is thy victory, O death? where is thy sting, O death? The sting of death, however, is sin: and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to GOD, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. What therefore is clearer, or more certain, than that these things were predicted concerning CHRIST, unless someone wishes to openly shout down the Apostle? This therefore is the epinikion of CHRIST triumphing over death and hell, nay, over sin and the law: This Epitaph is appropriate to death and hell: as Gregor. Nazianz. elegantly speaks in orat. 42: where is thy sting, O death? where is thy victory, O hell? The Cross prostrated you, the author of life brought death to you. You are lifeless, immobile, inert. We can now insult death with a joyful spirit, with Jerome in Epitaph. Nepot. ad Heliod., when it attacks us: He who once threatened you rigidly through Hosea, I will be thy death O death, I will be thy bite, O hell, by his death you are dead, by his death we live: you devoured, and you were devoured, and while you were soliciting the bait of the assumed body of CHRIST, and you thought it a prey for your dry jaws, your insides were pierced by a hooked tooth. We, your creatures, give thanks to you, CHRIST Savior, because while you were killing our so powerful adversary, you killed him. In this manner, Gerhard, brother of Bernard, received death with a most joyful heart; insulting it to the astonishment of those sitting by him: concerning which Bernard speaks excellently in sermon 26 on the Song of Songs. I have been summoned, he says, to that miracle, to see a man exulting in death, and insulting death: where is your victory, O death? where is your sting, O death? now it is not a sting, but a jubilation, now a man dies singing and sings while dying. You are usurped for joy, O mother of sorrow, you are usurped for glory, O enemy of glory, you are usurped for the entrance of the kingdom, O gate of the underworld, and pit of perdition for the finding of salvation, and that by a sinful man: justly indeed, because you unjustly usurped rash power over an innocent and just man, you are dead, O death, and pierced by the hook which you incautiously swallowed, whose voice is that in the Prophet: O death, I will be your death, O hell, I will be your bite. Pierced, I say, by that hook, you open a wide and joyful exit to life for the faithful passing through the midst of you. Wherefore to this victor, Redeemer our own, with the most devout Abbot in a sermon on the Passion of the Lord, let us turn ourselves: What, Lord JESUS, most valiant Zealot, what thanks shall I render, that I, a man, dust and a vile figment, may worthily render them? For what ought you to have done for my salvation, and did not do? From the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head, you immersed your whole self into the waters of the passions, that you might extract me entirely from them, and they entered even unto your soul. For you lost your soul in death, that you might restore my lost one to me. And behold, you have bound me with a double debt. For both for that which you gave your own, I am a debtor to you: and for my soul indeed, given to me by you twice, once in creation and once in redemption, I have nothing more just to render to you than itself. But for your precious soul so troubled, I find nothing that can be worthily repaid by man. For even if I could repay heaven and earth and all their adornment for it, certainly not even so could I in any way reach the measure of the debt. But that I may render that which I both owe and is possible for me: it is of your gift, Lord. You are to be loved, my Lord, with all my heart, with all my soul, with all my strength. And your footsteps are to be followed by me, who deigned to die for me. And how will that come to pass in me except through you? Let my soul cleave after you, because all its strength hangs from you. O how good, how sweet you are, Lord JESUS, redeemer of the lost, savior of the redeemed, hope of exiles, strength of the laboring, breadth to the anxiety of the spirit, both solace and sweet refreshment to the tearful soul running after you: crown of the triumphant, the unique reward and joy of all the heavenly citizens, most abundant fountain of all graces, renowned offspring of the highest GOD, and highest GOD, may all things that are in heaven above and that are on earth below bless you. Great are you and great is your name. Let us therefore do this, and let us wholly consecrate ourselves to CHRIST, who spent his whole self for us. He himself died for us, that we might live not for ourselves, but for him. He bore sins in his body upon the tree, that we, dead to sins, might live to righteousness. He rose from the dead, that we might rise from vices. Raised in soul, St. Augustine admonishes, let us live with righteousness through faith, that we may also rise in body to eternal joy. Let us depart from evil works, which mortify the soul, and while the body lives, that our soul may also attain to be in eternal goods, and the body. He lives with CHRIST, he reigns with CHRIST, who follows the innocence of the rising CHRIST, and imitates his life, according to Chrysologus, sermon CXIII. That this may be done, let us attend the Paschal assemblies assiduously, let us devoutly hear the Angels of the Lord, the heralds of the Resurrection, let us also deposit gifts at the altar for those who dispense spiritual and heavenly gifts to us. May our glorious Triumphator fill us all with the joys and fruits of the Paschal triumph, and convert our enemies, or crush them under our feet. On the eve of Easter, in the year 1663.

HE SHALL BRING A BURNING WIND) An eastern one, which is pestiferous in those places. At the same time, the location of Assyria is shown.

OF THE LORD) God sending it.

COMING UP FROM THE DESERT) Through the desert part of Syria, 1 Kings 19:15. For this was the route for the Assyrians into Samaria.

AND HE SHALL DRY UP ITS VEINS, AND SHALL MAKE ITS FOUNTAIN DESOLATE.) For the wind from the East was burning: whence it is called καύσων by the Greeks, and consequently also drying up, Ezekiel 17:10, 19:12. But what is signified by this allegory, the following words explain.

AND HE HIMSELF) The Assyrian, who is to be understood by that wind.

HE SHALL PLUNDER THE TREASURE OF EVERY DESIRABLE VESSEL) Of precious things. Thus these words are taken in 2 Chronicles 32:27, 36:10, Daniel 11:8, Nahum 2:9.

This interpretation, as I have said, can be admitted, provided the former parts are not taken for a communication, but the commination is said to be joined to the promise, which is very frequent among the Prophets. There are not wanting, however, those who explain it allegorically concerning the grace of the New Testament, so that by the bringing of the wind is noted the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, by the drying up of the fountain the obstruction of the vein of sins, by the plundering of the desirable vessels to be done by Ephraim or the Church, the victory to be reported by the Church over its enemies, which see in Meisner. Thus also Blessed Tarnovius explained these things through the promise made to Ephraim in this way: Because he (since it is so) will make it bear fruit among the brothers, and the redeemer himself will render his Ephraim or spiritual Israel fruitful; Christ will again add many others to his remaining brothers by the preaching of the Gospel, see Psalm 22 and 23, John 20:17. Hebrews 2:10, 11, 12, who may bear manifold fruit in the Church, John 15:2, 8, 16. The East wind will come, the wind of Jehovah (the greatest), the cruel and impetuous enemy the Assyrian rising from the desert, and his spring (of the afflicted people) will dry up; nevertheless that Ephraim will not only escape victor through Christ, but will also plunder the treasure of all desirable things. Thus Tarnovius.

Ninthly, the holy Apostle confirms this interpretation primarily in 1 Cor. 15, 54 ff., when from this oracle he proves that we shall rise incorruptible and immortal to eternal life. 'But when this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory (εἰς νῖκος into victory), O death, where is thy victory? O grave, where is thy sting?' In the Greek it is πῦ σγ, θάνατε, τὸ κέντρον, πῦ σγ, ᾅδη, τὸ νῖκος, 'O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?' The Apostle adds an explanation, what is the sting of death? v. 56. τὸ δὲ κέντρον ῾ῤ θανάτε ἡ ἁμαρτία, ἡ δὲ δύναμις τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ νόμος. 'The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law.' And a thanksgiving v. 57. 'But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.' Whence it shines forth clearer than the midday light that the Prophetic passage was understood by the Apostle not concerning the liberation of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity, nor concerning the restoration of the Israelites from the Assyrian dispersion, but concerning our liberation, accomplished through our Lord Jesus Christ; and that the liberation designated by the Prophet, according to the Apostolic interpretation, was not a liberation from bodily destruction, or from a danger leading to the grave, but a liberation from death, and the sting of death, sin, and the curse of the law, which is the strength of sin, as well as from hell, or eternal condemnation; the abolition of death, sin, the curse of the law, hell, or infernal power, which is called the hand of hell by the Prophet; and the victory granted against those spiritual enemies through Christ our Lord, who liberated us from the same through his death and resurrection by reason of merit, and as far as the acquisition of the victory is concerned, but who will fully liberate us on the last day by reason of efficacy for the plenary fruition of that victory, when the elect will rejoice that death has been utterly swallowed up in victory, and with this song of triumph will insult death and hell: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? For then not only will the elect be immune forever from the hand or power of hell, but the last enemy, death, will also be destroyed, which the Apostle calls such in verse 26, because we shall be raised from death, and we shall come forth not with a mortal body, but an immortal one, and this mortal shall put on immortality, nor will hell, condemnation, the curse, or the cursing law, or sin, the sting of death, have any power over us, but we shall obtain life, salvation, and eternal glory through Christ our Lord, and we shall enjoy his victory so fully for all eternity. Therefore, what the Holy Spirit himself interprets concerning the abolition of death and the glorious immortality acquired for us through Christ and his death and resurrection, and to be perfected in us in the blessed resurrection, that certainly does not speak of the mere liberation of Ephraim from the bodily destruction hanging over him at his own time. Yet the Holy Spirit interprets the emphatic sentence thus: I will redeem from death: I will be your plague, O death. Therefore, this sentence does not speak of the mere liberation of Ephraim from the bodily destruction hanging over him. What the Apostle interprets concerning the destruction of hell and eternal condemnation, and the reconciliation of life and eternal salvation, accomplished through Christ our Lord, that certainly does not deal with the liberation of the Israelites from the dangers leading to the grave. And thus the Apostle interprets the words of our Prophet: I will deliver them from the hand of hell: I will be your destruction, O hell. Therefore, those words do not deal with the liberation of the Israelites from the dangers leading to the grave.

Now if the other saying is compared, which the Apostle joined as a parallel in Isa. 25:8, He will swallow up death forever: it is again manifest that these things must be understood concerning the power and efficacy of the death and resurrection of Christ, as being that through which death is swallowed up in victory, through which the handwriting of the decree that was against us has been blotted out, and taken out of the way, and nailed to the cross, and principalities and powers have been despoiled, which he exposed confidently, triumphing over them openly in himself, as the same Apostle testifies in Col. 2:14. There is no doubt, therefore, that the redeemer who speaks here, I will deliver them from the hand of hell, I will redeem them from death, is Christ our Lord, in whom victory has been given to us: and that he is the same Lord who promises: I will be, O death, your plague: I will be, O hell, your destruction. Nor is there any further doubt that the victory obtained for us as to its merit was by the death and resurrection of Christ, when he was delivered for our sins and raised for our justification; but as to the full effect and fruit of that victory, it will be obtained in the glorious resuscitation from death and the concession of eternal life. For when this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass the word that is written, then it will come to pass (as to its full completion) that word which is written, both in Isaiah ch. 25:8 and in Hosea ch. 13:14. Which interpretation, as it is above all exception, so we judge that it can in no way be consistent with the gloss of Grotius or Calvin, being placed, as they say, on a single dish.

Calvin is inept, however, when he says that the Apostle neither alleges the words of Hosea, nor even alludes to them, but only adapts a proverb common among the Jews—that Jehovah is the Lord and victor of death—to his own purpose concerning the resuscitation of the dead to be done through Christ. For Paul does not speak of some Jewish proverb, but of a word written, and this is not a mere accommodation here, but he says that that written word will then be fulfilled. Whence Pareus himself says: I would not deny that it is an allegation. Wherefore we conclude with Jerome: That which the Apostle interpreted concerning the resurrection of the Lord, we can neither interpret otherwise, nor do we dare to.

Nor can that scruple concerning the variety of words move anyone who knows that the Apostles did not always strictly follow the very words of the text, but very often retained the received Greek versions when the sense came out the same, and sometimes even changed them a little to express the meaning of the original text, which was done here as well. For the LXX have it thus: Where is your judgment, O death, where is your sting, O hell? But the Apostle applies the sting to death, because it fits it more aptly, and the hand had been attributed to hell by the Prophet: I will deliver them from the hand of hell. Therefore, victory is more aptly attributed to hell, because the power of hell is not able to prevail against us, but has been overcome through Christ. And although some Greek copies of the LXX interpreters read judgment, others read victory, and some, like the Apostle, have victory. Nor do we think there is any need for us to investigate the individual words of the LXX interpreters from the Hebrew words, in which others labor in vain, as if they had read 'ayyeh, which is now 'ehi, and had rendered the word qeteb as sting, for the reason that among the Hebrews whatever penetrates suddenly by piercing and boring through, with most vehement force, as a sharp point is wont to do, is expressed by that name (derived from cutting off), (as Rivetus, along with certain others, wishes, but without the example of Scripture), and finally had derived your plagues from dabar, a word, as Aquila and the Fifth edition rendered it, where are your words? and had explained that word as judgment or cause. Drusius has yet a new discovery in his parallels, p. 116, as to why Paul turned your words into sting, namely that he read your goad, since a goad denotes a prick, or a sting fixed to a staff for goading a beast. But what will be the end of the changes to the text, if it is permitted to indulge in conjectures in this way? It is far simpler if the LXX interpreters are said to have expressed the sense, not to have rendered word for word, and that the Apostle followed them, but in such a way that the sentence might come out even more aptly, and the true sense of the Prophet might be more illuminated by Apostolic authority. For what the Prophet proposed categorically, the Apostle proposed by a figure of interrogation. In the former, the antecedent occurs, namely the very abolition of death; in the latter, he expressed the consequent, the epinikion or triumphal song, with which, after the abolition of death, they will triumph over death and hell. Thus, therefore, the elect insult death and glory against it: Hurrah! Christ has delivered us from death and the sting of death. Hurrah! Christ has been your plague, O death; where, therefore, now, O death, is your sting? You pierced us with your sting of sin, like a venomous beast, which by fixing its sting infuses deadly poison. But where now is that sting of yours, since Christ has been made your plague? You attempted to fix your sting in him, but by that very act you destroyed him, and with him lost, you yourself perished. For scorpions, wasps, and bees, once the sting is lost, must die. You unjustly and rashly usurped power over a just and innocent man. You are dead, O death, and pierced by the hook which you incautiously swallowed, as Bernard has it in Sermon 26 on the Song of Songs. By his death you are dead, by his death we live. You devoured, and were devoured, and while that enticement of the assumed body of Christ was soliciting you, and you thought it a prize for your greedy jaws, your insides were pierced by a hooked tooth (others say 'hook'). We give thanks to you, Christ the Savior, your creatures: because while he was killing, you killed our powerful adversary, as Saint Jerome elegantly says in the Epitaph of Nepotianus to Heliodorus. Thus the elect insult hell and boast against it: Hurrah! Christ has freed us from the hand of hell. Hurrah! Christ was your destruction, O hell; where then now, O hell, is your victory? You had brought us under your power and were triumphing over us. But where now is your power? Where now is your victory? You attempted to bring even Christ under your power: but he overcame you, despoiled you, and destroyed you, and powerfully freed us from your hand. Whence it is most manifest that there is a sweet agreement in meaning between the Prophetic saying and the Apostolic ἐπινικίε, and that they most elegantly explain one another. It is indeed A beautiful personification, says our B. Luther in the cited place p. 558, by which death and hell are imagined as enemies of human nature, terrible with their weapons, victors with their sting (Deber Keteb), triumphant, insulting forever in their victory, that is, sin and the disease of nature, which the Son of God by himself for us, like David Goliath, overthrew and took away forever, and into victory.

Tenth, from the authority of the Interpreters. No one is easily found who has treated this most illustrious saying as meagerly as Grotius. But the orthodox Fathers have accepted this concerning Christ with great consensus. Irenaeus, book 5 against heresies, ch. 13: 'Then these things will be justly said: where is, O death, thy sting? where is, O death, thy victory? when this mortal and corruptible flesh, about which death also is, and which is also pressed by a certain dominion of death, ascending into life shall have put on incorruption and immortality: For then truly will death be conquered, when that flesh, which is contained by it, shall have gone out from its dominion.' Tertullian, book 5 against Marcion, ch. 10, calls this word of the Prophet insulting concerning death, and triumphant. Athanasius, on the incarnation of the Word, Vol. I, p. m. 80. Thus, death now having been conquered and triumphed over by our Savior Jesus Christ on the cross, with its hands and feet bound, all who pass through it in Christ trample it underfoot, and the martyrs, offering themselves to Christ, harass it with jeers, mockeries, and insults, objecting also what was written above by the Apostle Paul: 'Death is swallowed up in victory: where, O death, is thy victory? where, O hell, is thy sting? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law.' Is that small moment concerning the weakness of death therefore something? Or is the demonstration of the victory of Jesus Christ reported over its death small? Eusebius, Demonstration of the Gospel, book 4, ch. 12, p. 166. The Savior of the universe himself, and our Lord, who is the Christ of God, and is called the bringer of victory, is introduced in the Prophetic prophecies rebuking death, and releasing the souls which were held bound there, where he pronounces the hymn of victory, saying these very things plainly: 'From the hand of hell I will snatch them, and from death I will free their souls: where, O death, is thy victory? where, O death, is thy sting?' Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on this place, thus explains this text, Vol. 3 of Works, page 187: 'He redeemed us (Christ) from the hand of hell, that is, from the tyranny of death. And the mode of redemption is understood as Christ's death. For he willingly endured slaughter for us on the tree, and triumphed over principalities and powers, the handwriting against us having been affixed to it. For then, then also all iniquity stopped its mouth, and the empire of death, sin having been removed, was destroyed. For it itself is the victory of death, and the sting of hell.' For if even the wise Paul has interpreted it for us. For he says: '(The sting of death is sin: and the strength of sin is the law.) Wherefore, the sin of all having been deleted, we also shall have rightly said: (Where is thy victory, O death? where is thy sting, O hell? For God, who justifies, who is he that condemns? Christ Jesus, who died for us.) Nay, who gave himself a redemption for all, one more worthy than all, through whom and in whom we have been made rich, that we may return to incorruption.' Jerome on this place: 'The Lord freed all, and redeemed them in the passion of the cross, and the shedding of his blood: when his soul descended into hell, and his flesh did not see corruption, and he spoke to death and hell itself: I will be thy death, O death. For I died for this reason, that you might die by my death. I will be thy bite, O hell, you who were devouring all with your jaws.' We also produced the same before from the Epitaph. of Nepotianus to Heliodorus. To which add Augustine, sermon 137 on the season: Gregory the Great, Homily 22 on the Gospels. Bernard, Sermon 26.

on the Song of Songs. Rupert, 6 on John. Peter Damian, book 2, Epistle 18. Haymo, Hugo, Lyranus, etc., who all understand it literally concerning Christ. What of the fact that both the Calvinists and the Jews likewise acknowledge the literal sense to pertain to Christ: especially Beza in Annotations on the New Testament, Junius in parallels, book 2, part 43. Polanus in Commentary, p. 278. Tremellius with Junius in the notes to this place. Paraeus himself, the champion of Calvin, on Hosea p. 561, concedes that these words are of Christ the SAVIOR, and are alleged by the Apostle, and principally treat of Christ and his spiritual redemption, even if he imagines a double sense, one in the type, the redemption of the Israelites from the sepulcher of captivity, the other more perfect in the antitype, the eternal redemption and vindication of the Church from death through Christ. Concerning the antitype, he says, it must be understood more perfectly, the kind of benefits promised here compels it, by no means only external or metaphorical, but eternal and proper: the authority of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament interpreting the oracle thus also compels it. But since that typical sense has no place here, nor is a duality of sense to be admitted in the same place, it remains that the Prophetic oracle must be interpreted solely concerning Christ. Which therefore Rivetus acknowledged in this place p. 410. That was fulfilled in Christ, when by his death he overcame death, and in the sepulcher triumphed over its power: the efficacy of which victory of his, those dead with him and buried rise again into a new life; and they live in the most certain hope of their future resurrection to eternal life, through him who died and rose again from the dead. It is therefore a simple and absolute promise pertaining to the elect, concerning future salvation and redemption to be made through Christ, yet so that in the liberation from death and the sepulcher we understand there to be a synecdoche, for liberation from all the enemies of the elect, of whom the one who is destroyed last is death, as Paul says, of whom therefore he also expressly mentions the sepulcher. It is clear that this sense serves best for proving the resurrection of bodies, as Paul intended, which is a part of the redemption through Christ, and that this promise had been most aptly subjected to grave threats, for the sake of the pious remnant, after the destruction of Israel was denounced, to raise them up and affect them with consolation, by this faith namely that the elect would one day be saved from death, even if the whole body in common is to perish. We therefore acquiesce in the opinion of those who judge these words to be Christ's, insulting death and the grave, which, even if it is not entirely manifest from the words of the Prophet, ought not to be called into doubt after the light of the Gospel. He does not say simply, I will free, but uses a word which signifies to free by a price or λύτρῳ of redemption given, Ephdem, whence pidion is taken among the Hebrews for the price by which one is redeemed. Furthermore, the other word Gaal, which signifies to redeem by right of kinship, whence Goël is a kinsman, to whom belonged the right of redeeming. Which words sufficiently intimate that Christ is speaking, who, by a price given and by the right of kinship entered into with us, redeemed his own from sin and death. Moreover, to be the plague of death and the destruction of the grave is to destroy death and the grave, as Paul explains in 1 Cor. 15:26: The last enemy, however, death, is abolished. Death, however, is not destroyed except through life, and the destruction of death is nothing other than the restoration of life, just as Paul teaches in the same place. This is Rivetus. Coccejus, I know not what Apocalyptic things he seemed to see here for himself, or rather he saw pots and gourds through bleary eyes: He calls death, he says, metonymically the False Prophet, the author of the second death, as in Apoc. 6:8. For he points to Baal, in whom Judah had been made guilty and had been dead, Hos. 13:1. Similarly, he calls hell the Kings committing adultery with the beast, and giving their power to it as in Apoc. 17:13, 17, who are also denoted by the name of Hell, Apocal. 6:8, because as the lower parts of the earth (which are properly called שׁאול hell, ᾴδης) are a prison for corpses and a place of corruption, and an impediment to life: so these kings by their edicts and tyranny cause, as much as possible, that men should persevere in the second death, in hatred of the truth which is demonstrated in Scripture, and in their errors. The manner of redeeming them from the hand of Death and Hell is this, that God delivered that whole nation, using evil counsels, into the hand of the Barbarian peoples, the Saracens and the Turks, under whom they could, if they wished, however much in distress, worship God according to their own conscience and the doctrine of Scripture. I will redeem them by the virtue of the price paid by me, and by great power and a strong hand I will snatch them from the hand of Death and Hell, that they may be free to serve me. I will vindicate them, as my own, as redeemed, as brothers, that the scepter of injustice may not be extended over them. Furthermore, the Prophet in the words of God mocks Death and Hell, and triumphs over the Plagues and the Virulence of both. קטב is untamed and conquering venom. The Apostle translates it νĩκē 1. Cor. 15, 55. The LXX δίκη, others νίκη. Symm. ἔσομαι ἡ πληγή σε. These things directly and immediately concern the Antichrist, and the tyrants who play the parasite to him, whom the Holy Spirit mocks as having been frustrated in their hope: since God has prepared a power by which, although in affliction, He may snatch a great part of the people from their power and yoke. St. Paul 1. Cor. 15, 55. 56. from this effects the Triumph of the Church over the death of the body as well: and truly, because unless death had been thoroughly conquered by Christ, the Prophet would not have so insulted this instrument of the Devil, prepared for inflicting the second death. These are the words of Cocceius: of which only the last, which refer to the sense of the Apostle, are true; the rest savor of the more than feverish dreams of a man. From the Jews, R. Moses Hadarschan (from R. Joshua Ben Levi) in Comment. Gen. 24, 6. 7. in Bereschit Rabba, brings these things forward: I went with Kippod the angel of death, and the Messiah son of David went with me until I arrived at the gates of Gehenna: but when the captives who are in Gehenna saw the light, or the radiance of the Messiah: they were rejoicing to receive him, saying: this one will lead us out of this darkness, just as it is said Hos. 13, 14. I will redeem them from the hand of hell. See Pug. Fid. Raim. Martini part. 3. Dist. 3. c. 17. p. 680.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

QUIA IPSE INTER FRATRES DIVIDET) Quia ipse pro fratribus multiplicabit, supple peccata. Plus pecca- vit quam Juda & Benjamin. Ita Chaldæus.

Hanc præclaram concionem Evangelicam de æterna liberatione per Messiam futura temere pervertit Grotius hic iterum ἰδαιάζων ac si de cor- porali solum liberatione sermo sit. Adhæc poten- tialem modum hic fingit, ac promissionem sim- plicem in hypotheticam glossa sua convertit, imo è promissione meram comminationem facit. Quid enim aliud hoc est, quam comminari, & conqueri, cum protestatur Deus, se non liberaturum popu- lum, quia pœnitentiam agere non vult, nec quic- quam esse, quod iram suam sedare posset? Quod à R. David Kimchio habet, qui itidem futurum in modum potentialem transformavit. Nec manus suas abstinere potuit ab hoc insigni oraculo Calvinus Judaizans, etsi non nesciret consensu magno inter- pretes de Christo id exponere. Quos ipse auda- cter MULTIS MODIS errasse, is sc. omnibus longe sapientior, pronunciavit. Judaicis namque glossis fascinatus statuit non Christum hæc loqui, sed Deum Patrem, non de redemtione spirituali, sed corporali, non ex manu mortis æternæ, & infer- ni, sed ex manu mortis temporalis & angustiis hu- jus vitæ, in spem de solutione ignominiosæ captivi- tatis Babylonicæ. Præivit etiam idem Calvinus, ut & Tigurina versio, Grotio nostro, in eo, quomodo conditionaliter exponi possit dictum Prophetæ, quamvis conditionalem sensum referat ad salutem perfectam & æternam. Quo ipso excusare Cal- vinum suum vult Pareus, ac si minime cum Judæis faciat. At quemadmodum cum Judæis de corpo- rali liberatione dictum Propheticum explicat Cal- vinus, ita nec id negaturi sunt Judæi, quod ipse affirmat, quod Deus ab omni morte redimere ve- lit, si agatur pœnitentia. Nihil ergo ab illis dif- fert, in hoc loco exponendo, quem proinde cum Kimchio hic conjunxit Rivetus.

Quod autem hic omnino promissio de Christo habeatur, sequentibus confirmamus argumentis. Primo, quod litera ipsa textus doceat, de libera- tione non ab exitio aliquo corporali, non de peri- culis ad sepulcrum ducentibus, ut Grotius vult, nec à morte solum tempoali, nedum à civili morte, quemadmodum Zanchius in h. l. vocat captivita- tem, sermonem esse, sed potius à morte æterna & ab inferno. Nam mortis & inferni vox non notat quodcunque exitium, aut solum aliquod periculum. Quæ significatio mere arbitraria est, nec è Scriptu- ris ejus exempla proferri possunt. Neque is sen- sus proprius foret, sed improprius. Nam sensus usitatus atque proprius MORTIS & INFERNI cum in Scripturis conjunguntur, & cum de libera- tione ex iisdem res est, infert veram mortem, non exitium quodcunq;, verum infernum, non tantum periculum ad sepulcrum aut infernum deducens. A literali autem sensu ad figuratum non est temere discedendum. Adhæc (2.) absolute hic promittitur liberatio à morte & שאול. Quicquid ergo mortis est, & quod metuere habebant Israelitæ, aut quod nobis metuendum, quicquid inferni est, vel per שאול exprimitur, ab illo omni liberatio promittitur. Nam si in aliqua morte manendum, aut in τῷ שאול quodam, non foret næc omnimoda li- beratio. Qui ab exitio & periculo temporali aliquo liberantur, sed expectat eos mors & da- mnatio æterna, illi non tam liberantur, quam relin- quuntur in morte & inferno. Et quæ causa est, ut ad temporalia restringam tale dictum, quod generalibus verbis formatum est & ubi nulla ne- cessariæ restrictionis signa in textu occurrunt? Si dicas, conditionaliter illos plene à morte & inferno liberatum iri, si agant pœnitentiam, ejus conditio- nis nullum hic in textu apparet vestigium. Nec potest illa promissio simul tum absoluta, tum conditionata esse.

Tertio sermo hic est de redemtione, quæ fit interposito λύτρῳ. Duo adhibet verba Deus, primum אפדם, ῥύσομαι, ut LXX. liberabo, ut Vulg. reddunt à פדה, quæ vox redemptionem interventu certi pretii factam notat Num. 28, 15. redimendo redimes primogenitum hominis. Conf. Lev. 19. v. 20. Exod. 21, 8. 30. Num. 3. v. ult. cap. 18, 6. Psal. 49, 8. in quibus locis LXX. λυτρώ- σαι, λύτρον & ἀπολύτρον, quæ pretium redem- tionis important, adhibent. Quæ de redem- tione Christi Esa. XXXV. ult. & passim in N.T. occurrunt. Deinde אגאלם LXX. vertunt λυ- τρώσομαι à גאל redimere, vindicare jure pro- pinquitatis Lev. 25, 11. Quæ vox cum de redem- ptore adhibetur, non promiscue quemvis re- demptorem notat, sed eum, qui jure cognationis, & interposito pretio redimit, ac vindicat propin- quum. Ideoque hoc sensu proprio, Christo pro- pria est, cum de redemtione Dei agitur, utpote qui noster propinquus factus est per ἐνσάρκωσιν, ac ju- re propinquitatis nos redemit per interventum λύτρε sanguinis, vel ἀπολυτρώσεως sanguine suo fa- ctam, Eph. 1, 7. 1. Pet. 1, 18. Ideo nomine גֹּאֵל Re- demtoris insignitur Gen. 48, 16. Esa. 63, 9. Quum ergo de redemtione, quæ à Goële fit, jure propin- quitatis, & interventu λύτρε, hic agatur, alia, quam Christi redemtio, & ἀπολύτρωσις morte ejus fa- cta, intelligi non debet. Quo pertinet promissio su- pra facta Hos. 1, 8. Ego Jehovah miserebor Domus Ju- da, inquit Deus Pater, & servabo eos in Jehovah Deo ipsorum, in Messia & per Messiam. Hic ergo jam in- troducitur testificatio, quod & quomodo servatu- rus, quod nempe ipsos à manu mortis, & inferni liberaturus sit.

Vox altera מִמָּוֶת à morte, etsi morbos, miserias & ærumnas hujus vitæ quandoque notet, tamen quum hic ut stipendium peccati, à quo liberandi e- ramus, à quo solus Christus nos liberat, Rom VI. ult. spectetur, & ἁπλῶς liberatio à morte promittatur, non solum ab ærumnis aut morbis liberationem de- signat, sed imprimis à morte æterna, quæ mors glo- riæ est, cujus metus utique gravissimus est. Quapro- pter ut plenarium sit redemptionis beneficium, ab omni illo, quod mortis nomine venit, & cui obno- xii facti sumus per peccatum, liberandi eramus per Christum. Mortis autem nomine veniunt ærumna, angores, morbi, & miseriæ hujus vitæ, quibus quo- tidie maceramur, & ita paulatim morimur Ex. 10, 18. 2. Reg. 4, 40. 2. Cor. 1, 10. c. 11, 23. & reatus ac cor- ruptio peccati, quæ dicitur mors gratiæ, & spiritualis Matth. 8, 22. Job. 5, 25. 1. Tim. 5, 6. & solutio animæ à corpore, quæ dicitur mors naturæ, & temporalis Rom. 5, 12. 1. Cor. 1, 21. & exclusio è vita cœlesti, ac damnatio æterna, quæ dicitur mors gloriæ, & secun- da vel novissima, Ap. 2, 11. c. 21, 14. Ab omnibus his mortis speciebus nos redemit Christus, miserias mitigando, leviores reddendo, mortem naturæ in somnum convertendo, mortem gratiæ & gloriæ à fidelibus plane auferendo.

Quarto redimendi hic in textu nostro designan- tur Israelitæ. At illi ab exitio & periculo exitii libe- rati minime sunt, neque etiam è captivitate redem- ti, aut dimissi. Non enim restitutum fuit regnum Ephraimiticum, sed tantum tribus Juda, &, qui il- lam sequuti, cum illa computati sunt. Cæterum per personam Israelitarum recte intelliguntur omnes homines, quemadmodum usitatissimum est, sub Is- raelitarum persona promitti beneficia N. T. omni- bus homnibus. Neque enim hoc beneficium re- demtionis singulare est aut speciale, sed commune, quia omnes pretio soluto emti sumus: ideoque ac- quisitionis respectu universalis est Redemtio, etsi particularis fiat ratione applicationis.

Sexto magnificentiùs adhuc liberatio describi- tur, cum Dominus per apostrophen se ad mortem & infernum convertit, & veluti vivos hostes istos (per prosopopœiam) ad certamen provocans, certum exi- tium iisdem in faciem, quod ajunt, mittatur: Ero mors דְבָרֶיךָ PESTES TUÆ, q. d. multis modis te perimam, non uno genere pestis te persequar. Hæc e- nim vis est in numero multitudinis PESTES TUAE. Ero ó inferne, קָטָבְךָ excisio tua, vel exitium tuum. Quæ apostrophe quid aliud infert, quam plenariam mortis & infernalis Dominii sublationem, & homi- num ab illis liberationem. De lectione & signifi- catione harum vocum sedulo agit B. Lutherus l. c. Ista duo vocabula (Deber) & (keteb) in Scripturis sunt nomina pestilentiarum, ut apud Latinos illa duo Pestis & lues, & ut lues, atrocius est, quam pestis, ut cui morbo statim necanti adhuc non potuerunt invenire remedium, imo venenum potius natu- ræ, quam morbus, sicut Perottus dicit, ita kateb atrocius in Ebræo est, quam Deber. Unde aliqui fingunt esse nomina Dæmonum, de quo videre li- cet Lyram & Burgensem Pf. 91. Cum ergo Hosea velut per tavtologiam conjungat keteb univocum cum deber æquivoco, satis patet, eum per hoc æqui- vocationem restrinxisse ad univocationem, & non dâbar, sed deber legi voluisse. S. Paulus vertit keteb tua, Victoria tua, LXX. Stimulus tuus, quo Paulus il- lud (deber tua) reddidit. Hieronymus, Morsus tuus. Symmachus, Occursus tuus, ut & Pf. 91. Latini habent, ab incursu, id est, à keteb. Quinta editio, & Theodotio, plaga tua. Si vero legas à nomine (dabor diborecho) significat verba tua, res tuæ, causæ tuæ, in plurali. Sic legit Aquila & Quinta editio, Ubi sunt sermones tui? Et LXX. πῦ ἡ δίκη σ४; Ubi est causa, vindicta, pœna, jus tuum & similia, de qui- bus infra. Nam mihi lectio ista habetur violenta & coacta. Sic ergo ex Ebræo, absque præjudicio, mi- hi vertenda videntur verba proprie, Ubi sunt pesti- lentiæ tuæ, Mors? Ubi est lues tua, Inferne? Non lo- quitur autem Propheta de pestibus ad literam seu casualibus, de quibus Medicorum est judicare & disputare, sicut nec de morte casuali, sed de na- turalibus pestibus & morte nobis congenitis, quæ per omne genus hominum sæviunt & furunt. Quas pestes habet etiam juvenis, sanus, robu- stus, formosus. Omnes enim moriuntur. Et eisdem pestibus morimur omnes. Sicut Pfalm. 51. plorat: Ecce in iniquitatibus conceptus sum. Hæc

Quinto redemtio facta emphatice dicitur ex ma- nu, h. e. de potestate inferni. Quæ vox MANUS cer- te non periculum, sed potestatem, & imperium infert, quia in manu & brachio robur hominis maxime si- tum est: quo nomine etiam potestas & virtus Dei exprimitur Jos. 4, 24. Jud. 1, 45. 1. Chron. 29, 12. ut & potestas hominum Gen. 32, 11. Exod. 2, 19. Num. 10, 9. quæ proinde inferno per prosopopœiam tri- buitur, ut denotetur ejus super homines imperium. Ut enim infirmus à robustiori manu tenetur, sic infernus manum quasi extendit, nos omnes arri- puit, & captivos tenuit, ideoque ex hac manu, & captivitate per excelsiorem Christi manum & vir- tutem redimendi fuimus. Conf. Exod. 14, 8.Num. 33, 3. Nec vero uspiam MANUS INFERNI idem est, quod periculum ad sepulcrum ducens. At deli- beratione ex POTESTATE INFERNI, per Chri- stum facta, adhibetur Pf. 49, 16. quam potestatem effugere nemo potest, nisi per Christum, teste Davide Psal. 89, 49. Nomen Ebræum שְׁאוֹל, quod per ᾅδην reddunt LXX. etsi varias habeat signifi- cationes, pro קֶבֶר, & statu damnatorum, & inferni doloribus occurrit Num. 16, 23. Esa. 28, 15. 2. Sam. 22, 5. Psal, 18, 6. Luc. 16, 32. Atque hic ubi de tam insigni liberatione Jehovah loquitur, non accipi- enda certe est de periculo solum ad sepulcrum ducen- te, aut de miseria corporali, quæ tam augustam & magnificam promissionem nequaquam exhauri- unt. Et quomodo Israelitæ à periculis ad sepulcrum ducentibus immunes fuere? Quomodo ab exitio fuere liberi? Ideoque alii rectius de sepulcro acci- piunt, quod à morte & à sepulcro absumtos vindi- care velit Dominus, vel (quod magis probamus) de inferno. Quo facit, quod B. Lutherus in additio- ne ad locum præsentem T. IV. Jen. Lat. f. 557. no- tat vocem שְׁאוֹל in Scripturis ita distingui à קֶבֶר, ut hoc (sepulcrum) corpori, illud v. (infernus) animæ deputetur. Papistarum commentum de liberatione è limbo Patrum indignum est, cui refutando inhæ- reamus. Limbus enim ille mera est anilis fabula.

Hæc B. Lutherus. Argumentatur ergo hinc B. Hunnius in Anti-Pareo suo p. 250. hoc modo: Ubi S. S. prædicat liberationem & victoriam contra mortem & infernum, ibidem absque dubitatione prædicat beneficium mortis & resurrectionis Chri- sti, & de Christo loquitur. At in præsente loco prædicat S. S. nostram ex morte & inferno libera- tionem. Ergo de Christo ejusque beneficiis con- cionatur.

Septimo non refragatur συνέχεια huic interpre- tationi, sed potius eandem confirmat. Postquam enim Dominus Israëlitis omnem spem corporalis regni restaurandi prorsus ademit, nunc spiritualis regni Christi instaurationem pollicetur, ut habet B. Gesnerus in h. l. Cui consonat Fr. Junius in Parall. 43. Hoseam citra controversiam ad plenam illam in- staurationem in Christo, & per Christum futuram re- spexisse B. Lutherus noster ita exponit textus cohæ- rentiam: Propheta postquam idololatris vastationem minatus est; Nunc vertitur ad consolationem piorum, qui non solum spectaturi tam horribiles pœnas erant, sed etiam, ut fit, eas passuri. Nam cum publicæ pœnæ grassantur, etiam pii partem earum sentiunt. Mi- rabilis autem hæc consolatio est, quam eis pro- ponit. Non enim dicit futurum, ut eos Domi- nus, cum ingruet Assyrius Monarcha, à manu ejus liberet. Occidemini, inquit, vos quoque, aut captivi abducemini in Gentes, nec erit melior vestra conditio, quam idololatrarum, propter quos tanta ira & calami- tas grassatur. Hanc pœnam sustinebitis æquo animo ac sperabitis longe meliorem liberationem, quam si nunc ex manu inimicorum liberaremini. Libe- rabo enim vos de manu inferni, hoc est, jam vita fun- ctos & sepultos excitabo in meliorem & æternam vi- tam. Sic pensabo passiones vestras, & tribulationes, quæ parient æternum pondus gloriæ &c. Et ante omnes S. Cyrillus Tom. III. Oper. p. 187. Postquam ex ira peccatoribus locutus est, & ex dolore suo illis e- ventura prænuntiavit, ad mansuetudinem Deo deco- ram revertitur, & se non universum genus humanum aversatum, neque in exilium irrevocabile sempi- ternumque misisse, sed datum iri aliquando ve- niam, & revocationem ad veterem statum in Christo, indicat, addens, liberaturum se de manu inferni, & de morte redempturum, haud dubie eidem pro- pter peccata in conditorem commissa, & propter trans- gressionem Adami à principio subjectos. Facta est enim postea talis promissio non solum Ephraim, seu pro- geniei Israel, sed mortalibus universis. Nam, ut scribit divinus Paulus: Non Judæorum Deus tan- tum, sed & gentium. Justificavit enim circum- cisionem ex fide, & præputium per fidem. Ne- que inficiari potuit Rivetus, apprime nostram in- terpretationem textui congruere, (etsi Calvini sui apologiam lubenter suscepisset) sic paraphrastice totum hunc locum reddi posse, & debere censens: Etsi talis sit conditio matris, & filiorum, id est, Reipubl. Israëlitarum, ut ipsis pereundum sit ob insipientiam suam: ne tamen desperent, qui inter eos reliqui erunt, qui tacti pœnitentia ad melio- rem frugem redire voluerint, quasi nulla ipsis su- peresset salus, aut liberatio à morte: Nam ego Mes- sias è potestate sepulchri redimam eos, nec erit aliquod tam forte vinculum, quod non solvam, ut eos vitæ re- stituam, atque adeo ab ipsa morte vindicem. Ubi ergo sunt pestes tuæ, ô mors, ubi exitium tuum, ô sepul- chrum? Vires tuas amisisti adversus eos, qui se in meam clientelam recipiunt; quos ego non permittam cum turba impiorum perire, nec penitus Israëlem de- lebo, sed in reliquiis servatum tibi & sepulchro ipse eripiam eum, quia nunquam me pœnitebit doni & vocationis meæ, nec hominum incredulitas fidem DEI faciet irritam.

Octavo congruit etiam immediate subjuncta sententia. Quæ si reddatur, pœnitentia (nam vox נחם & pœnitentiam & consolationem notat) abscon- det se ab oculis meis: id est, non pœnitebit me hujus promissionis, immutabile decretum divinum refert. Conf. Rom. 11, 29. Q. d. quod dixi, complebo ipso opere sine omni pœnitudine. Non ergo hypotheti- ca promissio hæc fuit, sed simplex & categorica. Castalio retinet significationem solatii, & vertit: So- latio carebunt oculi mei, id est, non dormiam, quin hoc fecero. B. Meisnerus sic explicari posse censet: Non consolabor mortem & infernum, nulla me illo- rum hostium tanget misericordia; sed potius animose destruam mortem & infernum. Hieronymus & Ribe- ra pro verbis non Christi, sed Prophetæ hæc habent, q. d. Consolatio hæc de beneficiis Messiæ abscon- dita est ab oculis meis, ego non intelligo, qui id fu- turum, quoniam infernus dividit inter fratres, u- num post alium abripit. Sed prima interpreta- tio simplicissima est, meritoque præfertur. Quam probat etiam B. Gesnerus; testari Dominum pro- missionem suam esse ἀμεταμέλητον, & se certo hoc piis præstiturum, nec promissionem suam ullo un- quam tempore mutaturum; Pœnitudo inquit, ab- scondita est ab oculis meis, id est, promisi fidelibus li- berationem à morte: hujus promissi me in omnem æternitatem non pœnitebit. Neque repugnabit nostræ interpretationi, si cum Hieronymo, LXX. & B. Luthero verba hæc de consolatione accipiantur, & Ecclesiæ tribuantur: quod nempe fideles sub tempe- state calamitatum conquerantur de carnis imbecilli- tate & cæcitate, quæ non ita, ut debebat, divina pro- missione efficitur, & erigitur, sed consolatio ab oculis carnalibus est abscondita. Quæ subjunguntur: Quia ipse inter fratres dividet, Grotius interpretatur, quia ipse pro fratribus multiplicavit, sc. peccata. Sed quæ hæc licentia futurum in præteritum commuta- re, novumque verbum addere, quod in textu non habetur? A Chaldæo autem id habet; qui ita reddi- dit: quia ipsi vocati sunt filii, & multiplicarunt opera corrupta. Vulgatæ & LXX. Interpr. error de divisione inter fratres, inde est, quod pro יפריא fructificavit, legerint יפריד divisit, unde Lyra, & Vatablus de di- visione judiciali exponunt: dividet inter fratres; h. e. judicum exercebit inter oves & hædos. Sed in illis ὀδὲν ὑγιὲς. Alii ad Ephraimum referunt quidem pronomen, sed de fructificatione per allusionem nominis Ephraimi, & etymon exponunt, crescet, vel fructificabit inter fratres. Hic sensus & verbis con- gruit, & sermoni præcedenti consolatorio magis consentaneus est, quod Ephraim etiam inter Judæos fructus laturus sit, ceu fratres suos. Ad Christum re- fert ea B. Gesnerus h. m. Christus inter fratres suos uberrimos fructus doctrinæ Evangelicæ & Sp. S. proferet, fidem sc. novam obedientiam, dilectio- nem Dei, & proximi, hoc est, inter fideles Joh. 20, 18. Quæ etiam est paraphrasis Osiandri, unde priora de consolatione sub cruce abscondita itidem facit Ec- clesiæ verba, ut hic ejusdem continuetur sermo. Lu- dov. de Dieu postrema quoque verba in partem bo- nam interpretatur: Versus hic, quoad verba, satis fa- cilis, quoad sensum difficilis, quem nos sic planamus, dicit Propheta initio versus: Nam ipse (Ephraim) inter fratres fructificabit. Objici poterat, quæ spes fru- ctificandi, cum instar veri deserti sese habeat? Respon- det Propheta: Veniet Eurus, ventus Domini, è de- serto adscendens, & exarescet scaturigo ejus, & sic- cabitur fons ejus, nempe deserti. Habent n. de- serta suas quoque aquarum scaturigines & fontes, unde nutriuntur, & magis inculta redduntur, alio- qui peritura, si aquis prorsus destituantur. Promit- tit ergo Deus se vento suo arefacturum fontes de- serti populi sui. Tunc ipse (Ephraim) diripit thesau- omnium vasorum desiderabilium, id est, ditescet alienis spoliis. Sed simplicior videtur eorum interpretatio, qui sensu sequiori intelligunt. Quanquam talia bona obtingant Ephraimo; ve- niet tamen interim adhuc hostis, instar venti vehementissimi, super omnia, & exsiccabit. Quod de totali excidio Synagogæ Judaicæ per Romanos futuro B. Gesnerus & Meisnerus, de Assyriorum vero impetu alii, & Grotius Noster in- terpretantur: quam ejus sententiam hic non im- probamus. Placet vero hic Programma Paschale Anno 1663. nomine Rectoris Academici publi- ce propositum, quia oraculi jam expositi sensum illustrat, subjungere.

Quemadmodum nulla unquam acrior pu- gna, nullus gravior conflictus fuit, quam cum congressus cum forti isto armato, Dracone Magno, Serpente antiquo, qui universum seduxerat orbem, CHRISTUS est, fortior ille superveniens, ve- rus Michael, Dominus fortis & potens, Dominus potens in prœlio: ita nulla obtenta unquam est victoria gloriosior, quam à CHRISTO, Re- ge gloriæ, qui fortem istum armatum superavit, universa arma ejus, in quibus confidebat, ipsi ab- stulit, & spolia ejus distribuit, ipsum que caput serpentis antiqui penitus conculcavit. Quan- to vero magis admiranda fuit hæc victoria, tan- to illustrior victoris Nostri est gloria. Ecquis autem non obstupescit, cum modum ac ratio- nem prælii pie expendit? adortus CHRISTUM est Satanas non ira tantum & furore incredibili armatus, sed artibus dolisque omnem humanum captum longe excedentibus, undiquaque instru- ctus. Aggressus est non solus, sed cum universis infernalibus copiis, multis legionum millibus, ne- que cum istis tantum, sed attractis etiam illis, qui peculium erant, & proprius populus anta- gonistæ: Tanto denique prælium illud acerri- mum suscepit apparatu, ut omnes vires suas, omne robur periclitatus videatur, & quicquid valebant universæ inferorum portæ, experiri voluerint. Ab altera v. parte Christus pugna- bat, in cujus ore dolus inventus non est, isque unus & solus, sine ullo exercitu, sine ullo socio, com- militone, aut parastata. Torcular, inquit, cal- cavi solus, & non est de gentibus vir mecum. Cir- cumspexi, & non erat auxiliator, quæsivi, & non fuit, qui adjuvaret. Neque vero Christus maje- statis, quam in forma DEI constitutus exerere poterat, radiis, & splendore coruscans, aut vir- tutis divinæ robore se ostentans prælium cum tanto hoste iniit, quo certe omnem ejus, quanta, quanta erat, potentiam, actutum prosternere va- luisset; sed in forma servili, habitu comtemto, statu- que abjectissimo comparuit, hostisque furori se objecit, vel potius subjecit. Nam exinanivit, & humiliavit semetipsum, obediens factus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Non erat spe- cies ei, neque decor: vidimus eum, & non erat aspectus, & desideravimus eum, despectissimum & novissimum virorum, virum dolorum, & scientem infirmitatem. Nec admiratione tantum dignus est horum antagonistarum congressus, sed impri- mis etiam mirabilis est vincendi modus. Nam vicit CHRISTUS, cum occubuit, peccatum de- levit, & sustulit, cum peccatum mundi in se transtulit, serpentis antiqui caput contrivit, cum serpens calcaneum ejus letifero morsu vulnera- vit, de Satana triumphum egit, cum in cruce Satanæ phalanx ipsum interfecit; inferni por- tas destruxit, cum inferni dolores subiit, mor- tem, hostem novissimum, superavit, cum mor- tem oppetiit. O quam bene te tuo impetu Dia- bole percussisti! lubeat sic hostem Nostrum cum Augustino serm. CXXII. de temp. compella- re: Crudelitas tua tibi exitium, nobis attulit com- modum. Dum nulli parcis, teipsum tandem inte- rimis, per unius delictum omnes captivasti, per unius justitiam omnes nihilo minus amisisti, si illum qui tibi consenserat, invasisti, istum in quo nihil inve- neras, cur indebite occidisti? Effudisti innoxium sanguinem, redde damnatam progeniem. Tu cer- te ille es, qui tibi divinitatis similitudinem arro- gabas elatus, nunc ab homine divino prosterneris superatus. Et quid mirum, si te, utpote creatu- ram suam, virtus divina vicisset? Sed hoc est ma- gnum atque mirificum, ut de pulvere assumeret, un- de nequitiam tuam prosterneret, atque contereret? Ut qui supra sidera superbus erigebaris, nunc à carne supereris. Ille igitur sanguis, quem effudi- sti, te vicit, me redemit. Denique illum bibo, & ve- neni tui perniciem salvatus ultra non timeo. Præ- valuisti in Paradiso, sed victus es de patibulo. Quid mihi circumjectam Paradiso igneam romphæam op- ponis? Ecce exaltati crucifixi profluens unda re- strinxit versatilem flammam. Atque ita admira- bilis etiam sese pandit nobis victoriæ CHRISTI fructus. Mors enim Christi, dicente S. Cypria- no serm. de resurr. CHRISTI, pro peccatis no- stris sacrificium fuit, & pœna crucis excessibus pœ- na dignis occurrit, labor ejus onera nostra depres- sit, dolor ejus nos sanavit, & damnatio indebita nos à damnatione æterna absolvit. Asseruisti, in- quit idem S. Martyr Serm. de passion. CHRI- STI, ascendisti Domine palmam, quia illud crucis tuæ signum portendebat triumphum de Diabolo, & de Principatibus & potestatibus & nequitiis spirituali- bus victoriam. Considero opera tua, & admiror te cruci inter damnatos affixum, jam nec tristem, nec pavidum, sed suppliciorum victorem, elevatis ma- nibus triumphantem de Amalech, & quasi sancti- ficantem de excelso plebem, & elevatum in sublimi & quasi cælo proximum, superioribus inferentem consummati agonis vexillum, & inferioribus ere- xisse scalam in Patris occursum. Summam tanti mysterii complexus Hoseas est vaticinio illustri c. XIII. De manu mortis liberabo eos, & de mor- te redimam eos: Ero mors tua, ô mors, morsus tuus, ero inferne. Nam & redemtionem à mor- te promisit, nec aliter quam morte se redem- turum de manu mortis recepit. Moriendo mor- tem mortis se fore vaticinatus est, per infer- nales morsus & dolores se inferno morsum, cum summo ejus dolore, protarumque infernalium destructione fore minatus est. Manum mortis, sic interpretatur S. Hieronymus, appellat ope- ra, quibus (mors) interfecit, juxta illud quod scriptum est (Prov. XIIX.) in manu linguæ mors & vita. Liberavit autem omnes Dominus & re- demit in passione crucis, & caro ejus non vidit cor- ruptionem, & ad ipsam mortem atque infernum locutus est; Ero mors tua ô mors. Idcirco e- nim mortuus sum, ut tu mea morte moriaris. Ero morsus tuus inferne, qui omnes faucibus tuis devo- rabas. Non enim de liberatione è manu Senna- cheribi per Angelum assyrios cædentem, cum Ruf- fino, vel de redemtione & captivitate Babylonica per Cyrum, cum Theodoreto, & Ruffino; nedum de Israëlitis captivandis, & hypothetica Ephraimi ere- ptione intelligendum vaticinium, cum Castrio, qui hunc sensum valde contortum reddidit, ac pro literali venditavit: Ego, ait DEUS, apud me reservo iniquitatem Ephraim, ut puniam ca- ptivitate, in qua dolores perferet similes parturien- tis. Sed adeo est stolidus, ut non curet resipiscere; quo caveat, ne longo tempore permaneat in captivita- te, ut male est fœtui, qui cum non egreditur ex uteri angustiis parturientis, conteritur ac confringitur: Ego sane, si sapuissent, è tenebroso illo inferno redemissem eos, ex illa morte eripuissem, mortem illam interemis- sem, illum infernum excidissem. Verum nullam con- solandi rationem offert mihi pertinax improbitas Ephraim. Quia igitur ipse fuit, qui divortium fe- cit inter fratres, Judam & Israelem, & discordiam sevit in religione, veniet quasi ventus Auster Assyrius & gentem cum bonis eripiet. Vel & hoc modo: aliqui si sapuerint etiamsi in infernum detrusi fuerint, ego re- dimam eos, si morti traditi, ex ejus faucibus eos eri- piam: In mortem ipsam irruam; & illam interimam; in ipsum infernum penetrabo, & morsibus excindam. Sed prob dolor, quia nulla ejusmodi voluptate afficiet me improbus Ephraim, nullam similem oculi mei affi- cient consolationem à pertinaci Ephraim oblatam: quia igitur ipse est, qui divortium fecit, inter fratres Judam & Israel, & discordiam in cultu DEI semina- vit, ipse perferet supplicium captivitatis, mortis & inferni. Nam veniet Assur, tanquam ventus vehe- mentissimus, & siccabit omnes opulentiæ illius venas, agros & ubertatem eorum: siccabit quoque fontem e- jus metropolim, Samariam, unde venæ emanabant in alias civitates, diripietque omnia pretiosa ejus. Qua gemina Jesuitæ detorsione nulla excogitari possit stolidior. Quam tamen non dubitavit præ alijs interpretationibus eligere Hugo Grotius, uti valde ingeniosus fuit in pessimis quibusvis corruptelis interpolandis.
