But chapter 3 exhibits mere promises; then of judgment against the enemies of his own people to be exercised for their liberation, then the roar of the word from Zion, in which holy mountain the Lord will dwell, and the mountains will flow with wine and the hills with milk, and a fountain of salvation will spring forth from the House of the Lord.

Latin:

PRÆLOQVI VM.

NOtat Hieronymus, qui in sua Versione Hebræum codicem sequitur, aliter hos Prophetas in Græcis codicibus digeri, nempe in hunc modum: Osee, Amos, Michæas, Joel, Abdias, Jonas, Nahum, Habacuc, Sophonias, Aggæus, Zacharias, Malachias. Sentit autem idem Hieronymus, quia Joelis liber tempus prænotatum non habet, & Osee subjungitur, fuisse eos συγχρόνους, quod & res in Joele contentæ evincunt. Sed sicut Oseæ dicta præcipue ad decem tribus, ita Joelis ad duas reliquas maxime pertinent.

Danaus statuit, in comment. ad c. 1. Prophetam sc. Joelem vaticinatum esse sub Josia, paulo antea quam fames illa gravissima, quæ à Jeremia quoque c. 14 prænunciata fuerat in Judæa, cui prophetabat, acciderat, illicque grassaretur. Recte autem duabus tribubus prædicasse Joel dicitur, quia decem tribuum non meminit, quæ tum jam abductæ erant; Domus autem Dei c.1, 9. 14. 16. & Sionis c. 2, 1. 15. 23. 32. c. 3, 16. 17. 21. mentionem facit, quæ Hierusolymis in tribu Benjaminis erat, & c. 3, 1. 6. promittit Deus, se multitudinem Judæ & Hierosolymorum reducturum.

JOel unde nomen habeat ambiguum videtur, quod ex interpretatione Hieronymi est ὁ ἀρχόμενος incipiens, B. Tarnovio vero conjectante idem, quod ἐρασμός desiderium à Rad. inusitata יָאַל, quæ in Hiphil significat voluit, desideravit. Filius fuit Pethuel, qui non Samuel est, ut Ebræi nonnulli credunt, hujus enim filii judices erant 1. Sam. 8, 1. & improbi v. 3. & 5. nec ratio temporis congruit; sed alterius cujusdam, quem de tribu Ruben fuisse dicunt, natumque Joelem in agro Bethoron ibique mortuum etiam ac sepultum ajunt Dorotheus in Synopsi, Isidorus de ortu & obitu Patrum, quæ nos suo loco relinquimus. De συνχρονισμῷ Grotiano Joelis & Hoseæ nulla certitudo. Referunt quidem nonnulli famem à Joele notatam ad Ezechiæ annum 14. antequam bellum Judæis inferretur à Sennacheribo cum Osiandro, sed Funccius, Montanus, Genebrardus, Castrio, ut & Drusius cum Autore Seder Olam Manassis temporibus Joelem vaticinatum esse malunt. B. Tarnovio vero maxime probabilis illorum videtur sententia, qui hæc sub Josia contigisse volunt, quum ejus tempore magna fames terrain occuparit, quæ Ier. 14, 1. 2. ferre eodem modo describitur. Conf. 2. Reg. 23, 6. Sic etiam Lambertus

Occasio Prophetiæ fuit immissio insectorum, gramina, flores, fructusque perdentium, ut populum ad sensum præsentis mali, & metum futuri per Chaldæos inducendi, moneret de seria pœnitentia, propositis resipiscentibus consolationibus insignibus partim temporariis istius seculi hominibus obventuris, partim perpetuis in Christo imprimis in N. T. implendis: in quo proinde summa & argumentum hujus vaticinii consistit. Partes sunt duæ, juxta duas prophetæ conciones. Prior cap. 1. absolvitur: posterior duobus reliquis capitibus. In prima quatuor morat, ac minatur præterea exercitus potentes & feroces vineas ac ficus vastaturos; atque hortatur Sacerdotes & populum ad pœnitentiam ob famem homines, & pecudes ac seras graviter affligturam. In posteriore c. 2. partim minatur bellicam calamitatem à Chaldæis inferendam, partim promittit pœnitentibus gratiam, cum corporalem qua satietatem frugum, & liberationem ab hostibus; tum spiritualem ipsummet Christum Doctorem Justitiæ & Spiritum S. super omnem carnem effundendum. Cap. vero 3. meras promissiones exhibet; tum judicii adversus hostes populi sui exercendi ad ejusdem liberationem, tum rugitus verbi è Zione, in quo mon- te sancto Dominus habitabit, montesque vino & colles lacte fluens, & fons salutaris è Domo Domi- ni scaturiet.

## 1:1 Argument
SERMON I. CHAPTER I. He excites to repentance on account of famine and war.

The canonization of Joel's proclamation having been premised, an unheard-of evil, memorable to posterity, from a fourfold kind of insects—caterpillar, locust, bruchus, and rust—devouring all things growing from the earth, is intimated; and an army of a huge and ferocious people, about to devastate the vineyards and fig trees, so that nothing remains for the sacrificial food and libation, is predicted, by which double calamity joy is to be turned into mourning. Then an exhortation is instituted to the priests, that they should mourn, and, a penitential fast having been proclaimed, they should invoke the Lord with a prescribed formula, by which the cry and roar of both men and beasts, in this scarcity of grain and fodder and drought of the land, is to be set before God.

Joel sings that the fields will be sad, and the temple sad. Vers. 2. HEAR THIS, YE OLD MEN.) You who remember many things. IF THIS HATH BEEN IN YOUR DAYS, OR IN THE DAYS OF YOUR FATHERS) Namely, something similar to so many evils as I now predict to you. Vers. 3. TELL YE YOUR CHILDREN OF IT.) Hand down these prophecies, so that they may be compared with the events later. Vers. 4. THAT WHICH THE CATERPILLAR HATH LEFT HATH THE LOCUST EATEN.) Will eat. A proverbial expression. The sense is: those whom Phul has left, Teglathphalasar will kill or carry away: for under the names of devastating animals are denoted armies, Jerem. 51, 14. 27. Nahum 3, 15. 16. AND THAT WHICH THE BRUCHUS HATH LEFT HATH THE RUST EATEN) Those whom Salmanasar has left, Sennacherib will kill or carry away. חסיל, which the LXX translate as ἐρυσίβην, that is, rust, the Chaldean more correctly (if I am not mistaken) considers to be a kind of animal, and translates it as שמרוט, that is, the attelabus. But there is something between the locust and the bruchus, with small wings, creeping rather than flying, and always leaping, and consuming everything even to destruction. Therefore חסיל is translated as βρου̃χος in 2 Paral. 4, 28, and elsewhere as ἀκρὶς in Isaiah 33, 4, and below in 2, 25. Vers. 5. AWAKE, YE DRUNKARDS.) Ye drunkards. AND HOWL.) Wail. The word corresponds to the Hebrew הילילו. YE THAT DRINK WINE IN SWEETNESS.) You who love to drink wine. FOR IT IS CUT OFF FROM YOUR MOUTH.) It has fled because the vineyards were cut down. Vers. 6. FOR A NATION IS COME UP UPON MY LAND.) Will come up. Take the following in the same way, and refer them to the devastation brought upon the lands by Phul and Salmanasar. Before those times, the ten tribes had lived in peace with the two, as appears in 2 Paralip. 28, v. 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Therefore, from the lands of the ten tribes, wine and food reached the two tribes, which ceased through that devastation, by which the land of the two tribes itself, on account of its proximity, could not be entirely immune.

Grotius assumes as certain that this chapter is to be understood concerning the warlike calamity brought by the Assyrian Kings, Phul, Teglathphalassar, Salmanassar, and Sennacherib. But this interpretation was not to be proposed as if it were indubitable, but was to be confirmed by reasons. For in the Scriptures we do not recognize that αὐτὸς ἔφα except of God alone. Some understand it of other wars, and especially those to which others have sometimes willingly lent their ears to Grotius. Others, as Jerome testifies, explain it concerning the four empires of the world, as if the caterpillar denotes the Babylonians and Assyrians, the locust the Medes and Persians, the bruchus the Macedonians and all the successors of Alexander the Great, and especially Antiochus Epiphanes, and the rust the Romans: because the land of the Jews was afflicted and devastated by all these four empires; which explanation, although it was approved by Remigius, Rupert, Haymo, Albert, Hugo, and Dionysius, as Christopher à Castro reports, nevertheless does not deserve approval, since it rests on no foundation. And future things are predicted here, not indeed is the discourse about past things. Nor do the caterpillar, locust, bruchus, and rust follow one another at such a long interval. Nor are the Assyrians read to have devastated the Jews, but only the land of Israel: the Medes and Persians did not harm them so much as they showed themselves benevolent to the Jews. The devastation of the Romans, however, followed only after the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. S. And therefore it could not be said here that it happened before the same. And how could they tell this devastation to their children and their children's children, or gather it from such an obscure prediction of it, and transmit the threat of the same to their posterity?

Furthermore, others with Theodoret explain it indeed concerning four enemies, but they refer this prophecy not, like Grotius, to the Jews or the two tribes only, but to the ten tribes at the same time. And by the caterpillar they understand Teglathphalasar, by the locust Salmanasar, by the bruchus Sennacherib, by the rust Nebuchadnezzar: the former of whom devastated the kingdom of Israel; the latter, the kingdom of Judah. Thirdly, others interpret those four evils concerning the enemies of the Jews, or those who overturned the Judean land, and especially Jerome: who in Ep. 113, or the preface to Joel, refers the prophecy of Joel to the Jews alone. Whence in Epist. ad Paulin. 3, oper. pag. 8, from which others gather that it is referred by him to the kingdom of Israel (to which Grotius also added himself), Albert thinks it is a σφάλμα, reading it thus: he describes the land of the two tribes, not the twelve; others, from the opinion of the Hebrews, judge that Jerome spoke only there. For in the cited preface his own opinion is clear: How, he says, in the prophecy of Hosea the prophecy is conferred upon the ten tribes under the name of Ephraim, which is often mentioned as either Samaria or Israel, so in all of Israel, it is to be believed that what is said pertains to the tribe of Judah and to Jerusalem, and that no mention at all of Israel, that is, the ten tribes, is made in this. However, Jerome seems to have taken the present passage only concerning the final arrival of the Chaldeans against Judea and Jerusalem. For indeed, regarding verse 5 of chapter 1, he wrote thus: It seems to us now that this is said more about the Babylonians and Chaldeans, whose cruelty and ferocity against the people of God is described, and if I am not mistaken, I seem to myself to have found something in this Prophet: The impiety of the enemies is narrated under the figure of locusts, and again it is said of the locusts themselves, as if they were compared to enemies, so that when you read of locusts, you think of enemies: when you have thought of enemies, you return to the locusts. Therefore, the nation of locusts, or the army of the Chaldeans, ascends over the land of God, strong and innumerable. For what is more innumerable and stronger than locusts, to which human industry cannot offer resistance? Its teeth, namely of the nation of locusts: but understand all things τοπικῶς; as the teeth of a lion, so that those who are equal to locusts in strength and multitude may be compared to lions in ferocity and cruelty. This nation, he says, has set my vine as a desert: which I brought over from Egypt, and planted, and it has stripped my fig tree, the people of the Jews, to whom the Savior came, that he might eat the fruits, and he did not find them: and he cursed it, and it withered forever: But let us recognize that all things are said under the metaphor of locusts: two to such an extent that they ravage everything, so that they gnaw off the barks of the trees and cast them aside: and having consumed all the greenery, they leave the high branches bare and dry. Thus Jerome. What the Prophet therefore says, that which the locust has left the caterpillar has eaten, etc., some understand as referring to different Kings and nations in the same army. What some left untouched, others devastateded.ed.

Fourthly, some understand this as referring to the various expeditions against the land of the Jews, and indeed to the four incursions of the Chaldeans, and they enumerate them with Eman. Saa in such a way that Nebuchadnezzar came like a caterpillar when he took Jehoiakim and led him to Babylon with Daniel; then like a locust when he took Jehoiachin; thirdly as a cankerworm when he occupied Jerusalem and led King Zedekiah to Babylon; fourthly when Nebuzaradan, like the palmerworm, burned the temple and the royal house and the houses of the princes, and destroyed the whole city.

Fifthly, Christ. à Castro thinks that Joel was one of the prophets who predicted the final destruction of the kingdom of Judah, on account of the abominations of Manasseh, 2 Kings 23:26, and although it was promised to Josiah that he would be gathered to his grave in peace, so that he would not see all the evil that the Lord was about to bring, 2 Chronicles 34:28. He thinks to himself, he says, that God left the completion of that threat to the time of the sons of Josiah, namely the four kings succeeding one another, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah, who by no means died in peace, but in captivity, or were killed by enemies. Wherefore, since they held the kingdom of Judah, and they themselves were four, consumed with no small depopulation of Judea up to the final slaughter: not undeservedly will they be said to have been devoured by the caterpillar, locust, cankerworm, and palmerworm: so that Necho, who took away Jehoahaz, is compared to the caterpillar, which lightly touched the land, having abducted King Jehoahaz; but King Jehoiakim, whom he appointed and left untouched, the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar, the brigands of the Chaldeans, Syria, Moab, and Ammon, invaded like locusts, killed, and buried with the burial of an ass. Thirdly, Nebuchadnezzar brought King Jehoiachin out of the land with many of the princes like a cankerworm, and led him captive to Babylon. Finally, the same man invaded Jerusalem with a huge army, and consumed the beauty of the city and temple like a palmerworm, and completely dissipated the Jewish Republic. Thus à Castro, p. 189. These three later explanations enjoy greater likelihood than the Grotian one, especially if we assume with Grotius that the Prophet's subject is the kingdom of Judah, not Israel: but if you explain it concerning all the tribes of Israel, Theodoret's interpretation will undoubtedly be preferable to it. For through the incursions made into the kingdom of Ephraim or the ten tribes, and their devastation, although the land of the Jews perhaps suffered some calamity, it was certainly not so devastated as the force and emphasis of the Prophet's words imply, and those disasters and their successive order and increases through Pul, Tiglath-Pileser, and Shalmaneser concern the land not of the Jews, but of the ten tribes, as is evident from 2 Kings 15 and 17.

people, because it does not feel its own plagues. The same is also the explanation of Tarnovius, p. 18. Because he asks about the past by the command of Moses, Deut. 32:7, he questions the elders, who, taught by long experience of affairs, if they see anything unusual, are accustomed to perceive that this is not from the ordinary course of nature, which they have observed for so many years. And since this present calamity from those insects was lasting longer than usual, and pressing more heavily, he warns them to return to the memory of former days, and to see whether such a thing had ever happened naturally before: but if no example is available, the Prophet's advice is that they should finally recognize that this is the hand of God from heaven. The end, however, is that they might be ashamed of their sloth; who do not notice this themselves, nor do they grow wise when struck so harshly, since this kind of vengeance can be considered in no other light than that of a prodigy. Now those things which follow in verse 6, follow, concerning another calamity and punishment of war, namely that already brought upon the Jews, Calvin interpreted in his Commentary on this passage, p. 4. That which others think, that a punishment is denounced here to the people which had not yet been inflicted, I repeat again, does not please me: but rather in my judgment the Prophet commemorates another vengeance of God, to show that God did not warn the Jews of their sins in only one way, so that he might finally recall them to a sound mind, but had tried everything to lead them back to the path, had they not been completely desperate. After he has therefore spoken of the sterility of the Jews, or of other calamities, he now adds that the Jews had also been afflicted by war. Certainly, famine should have touched them, especially when they noticed other troubles succeeding one another for several years beyond the accustomed course of nature, so that this could no longer be imputed to fortune. But when God, having already exhausted them with famine, pursued them again with war, was it not necessary for those who remained astonished at these vengeances of God and did not repent to be more than alienated from their mind? Tarnovius, however, although he acknowledges here the exaggeration of the present and past calamity, nevertheless understands by the strong and innumerable nation, not the enemies of the Jews, but the nation of caterpillars and locusts, noting from Kimchi on this passage that every congregation of living things is called גוי a nation or עם a people, see Prov. 30:25, 26. Which is also the opinion of Drusius and Cocceius, as well as the Belgian Paraphrasers. Furthermore, those who take the devastation of the land's produce literally, wish for that famine, which Elisha also foresaw would last for seven years, to be predicted here, and to be explained more explicitly here by Joel: Most understand the four preceding years succeeding one another, arising from the devastation of the earth through an abundance of caterpillars, locusts, and cankerworms, and through blight, as being in the future, which were followed by three other years in which they labored from a lack of rain, while Elisha was still living, which a Castro notes to have been the opinion of Ruffinus, Remigius, R. Solomon, Lyra, Vatablus, Robert, and Montanus, and of more recent Hebrews: such a punishment is also commemorated in Amos 4:9. However, Lyranus and Arias Montanus, although they acknowledge the matter was carried out as it has been reported, nevertheless believe that through it was shadowed forth and predicted by Elisha and Joel the devastation to be brought upon the Jews by the four empires, as if Joel had related that history which occurred under Elisha, in order to signify through it a hostile nation. Others, however, disagree about the time, and do not refer this to the age of Elisha, who flourished under King Joram, but to other times, even if the same are not designated in the history of the Kings.

Sixth, not a few love to speak of τὸ ῥητὸν and to retain the literal sense, so that the prophecy may be understood as concerning the devastation of fields, the destruction of crops, and a great scarcity of grain on account of drought and an abundance of harmful worms. This is the opinion of B. Gesner, Pappus, Tarnovius, and others. And of these, some establish this prophecy as one of future punishment, others wish for the calamity of former times to be set forth, so that they might be stirred to repentance. Thus Calvin: some think a punishment is denounced for a future time: but the context sufficiently shows that they err, and corrupt the genuine sense of the Prophet, for rather the Prophet here rebukes the hardness of the people. In this variety of interpretations, some sense was not to be assumed rashly, without reason, or newly devised, since Scripture is not ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, especially because τὸ ῥητὸν is left, from which one must not depart without grave cause. But they seem to have best attained the mind of the Prophet who interpret it as concerning the devastation of the earth's produce, and that not as future, but as even then continuing, if indeed the Prophet brings the drunken people and priests to the present matter, and speaks of the calamity not as something future, but as that which was pressing upon them at that time, λευκᾷ δι' Φωνῇ. Which the whole context of the speech, and those rhetorical amplifications which he employs, abundantly teach. Those things, however, which are introduced in verses 6 and 7, are to be understood rather of a hostile army and the slaughter of war, so that the devastation of the land's produce, of the crops, and of the vineyards may be attributed both to the abundance of insects and to a hostile hand. Which opinion I see is also approved by the Weimar Paraphrasts. Moreover, the very propriety of the letter confirms the same. We see no just cause why we should depart from it here. For the Prophet does not explain it otherwise, nor does he offer any proof of a figurative sense. Wherefore we understand the palmerworm, the locust, the cankerworm, and the caterpillar, as they sound, and we accept the nation ascending over the land of leonine ferocity and cruelty according to the letter concerning a hostile nation, so that by that army of locusts and other insects the produce of the land is devastated, and by this hostile force the vineyards and fig trees are indicated as having suffered damage, and by both the great desolation of the land of the Jews and the scarcity of provisions and the lack of wine are implied. Then the causes of such mourning are brought forward, which suit the drought and aridity of the times, not solely the devastation of wars: The wine is confounded, and the oil languishes. The farmers are confounded, the vinedressers have howled over the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished, the vine is confounded, and the fig tree has languished. The pomegranates and the palm and the apple, and all the trees of the field HAVE DRIED UP v. 10, 11, 12. And further v. 17. The beasts have rotted in their dung (others render more correctly from the Hebrew: the seeds have become moldy under their clods: Luther. The seed is rotted under the earth. Concerning which compare Tarnovius in this place. Grotius himself amends the Vulgate version: although he excuses it according to a preconceived opinion, as if it were born from a different reading: THE BEASTS HAVE ROTTED IN THEIR DUNG). The LXX and Jerome read פרות: we have פרדות, that signifies grains in Chaldean. גרפתים, which others have translated as dung, others translate as clods, others as mangers, others as heaps, from the verb גרף, which for the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Arabs is to sweep away. The sense is: the grains are corrupted by moisture in their heaps where they were gathered. The barns are demolished, the storehouses are dissipated, because the wheat is confounded.

Nor, thirdly, is the reason for the groaning of the animals in verse 18 any different. Why has the animal groaned, have the herds of cattle lowed? Because there is no pasture for them. But also the flocks of sheep have perished. Or fourthly, of the prayers of the Prophet himself in verse 19. To thee, O Lord, I will cry, because the fire has devoured the beautiful things of the desert, and the flame has set on fire all the trees of the region. All these things refer to the drought and excessive storm. Calvin: The fire has consumed the pastures or the habitations of the desert. Here again he prodigiously commemorates the judgments of God. We know that even if heat burns up all regions, yet pasture lands do not dry up so easily, especially mountainous ones. For here he speaks of those cold pastures. We know that however great the fertility of the mountains may be, yet cold dominates there, and in the greatest drought those mountain regions are always green. But the Prophet here recites as a prodigy that the habitations of the desert had been burned up; some translate נאות as pastures, others as habitations. But as far as the matter itself is concerned, it is the same whichever we read: because the Prophet here designates cold and humid regions, which moisture never deserts even in the highest heats. Others translate as beauties or the beautiful things of the desert, but wrongly. There is no doubt that he understands pastures or habitations, or folds. Therefore the fire has consumed the habitations or pastures of the desert. This is not accustomed to happen, nor does it fall into the common order of nature. Therefore it follows that it was a portent. This is the reason why the Prophet says that it is now time to cry to God, because it could not seem accidental that heat should burn up humid and watery regions. Thus far Calvin. Moreover, the Prophet explains himself clearly in the fifth place, when he expresses the thirst of the beasts of the field in verse 20: but also the beasts of the field, as a thirsty field, have looked up to thee for rain, because the fountains of waters are dried up, and the fire has devoured the beautiful things of the desert. Those in verse 20. AS A THIRSTY FIELD HAVE LOOKED UP TO ME FOR RAIN, Grotius does not explain it badly thus from the source: They have cried to me. ערג, which here is properly said of deer, and by catachresis of other wild beasts. That, as a thirsty field for rain, I do not know whence it crept in, for it is not in the Hebrew, nor in the Greek, nor in the Chaldean, nor does Jerome refer to these in his commentaries: perhaps it was written, as a thirsty hind for rain. Compare Psalm 42:1. To those words AND THE FIRE HAS DEVOURED THE BEAUTIFUL THINGS OF THE DESERT, he adds: Habitations, that is, folds and stables, whence wild beasts were accustomed to be fed. But the Hebrew word which is rendered as habitations denotes pastures, not in one place: 2 Sam. 7:8, Isa. 65:10, Jer. 33:3, Ezek. 34:14, Psalm 23:2. To take all these things rather of the fire of war than of excessive heat, drought, and the aridity of the times, whence comes the consumption of pastures and the burning of trees, foliage, and gardens, and the failure of herds and cattle from excessive thirst, and finally the drying up of fountains, rivers, and torrents, especially in mountainous places where there is an abundance of water, not a scarcity—what else is this than to vex the letter of the text? Calvin renders: The watercourses have dried up, with this commentary added: Again he inculcates what I said a moment ago, namely that that sterility proceeded from the clear judgment of God, and that it ought deservedly to strike horror into men, because it was, forsooth, a species of portent. While, therefore, the watercourses dry up in the very mountains, can this be called natural? אפיקים they call watercourses, or even valleys, through which waters run: nor is there any doubt that the Prophet here designates regions which always retained their fertility by an abundance of water. Since, therefore, the valleys themselves were parched, it was certainly necessary to acknowledge some miracle there: therefore he also attributes that cry to the beasts and brute animals, and not just any cry, but one by which they invoke God Himself. So he. To be compared especially is the passage Jer. 25, 2. et seqq. where there are similar complaints and lamentations concerning drought: and also Am. 4, 9. I struck you with a burning wind, and in the blight of your many gardens, and of your vineyards, the caterpillar ate your olive trees and your vineyards, and you did not return to me, says the Lord.

Sixthly, the promises of divine blessing made to the penitent in chapter 2, which the Prophet promises from divine kindness in place of those punishments, sufficiently teach that the present afflictions are to be understood not only of the calamity of war, but also of the scarcity of grain: Behold, says the Lord v. 19, I will send you grain, and wine and oil, and you shall be filled with them: And v. 22. Do not fear the animals of the field, for the beautiful things of the desert have sprouted: for the tree has brought forth its fruit, the fig tree and the vine have given their strength. Likewise v. 23. and 24. He will cause to descend to you the early and the latter rain, as in the beginning: and the threshing floors shall be filled with grain, and the wine presses shall overflow with wine and oil. And, lest anyone should have need to doubt whether these promises refer to the divine punishments designated in chapter 1, those things which are added in v. 25 remove every doubt. And I will restore to you the YEARS, which the locust, the cankerworm, and the mildew, and the caterpillar have eaten, my great army, which I sent among you. And you shall eat and be satisfied. Which promises look to the fruitful seasons that were to follow those barren years, and in place of this preternatural drought, they promise the early and the latter rain, that is, as Grotius himself explains, favorable weather at the time of sowing and harvest, Deut. 11. 14. Prov. 16, 16. Jer. 5, 24. Os. 6, 3. Since therefore, as Grotius admits, God in these words: AND I WILL RESTORE TO YOU THE YEARS, accepts that He will compensate for those bad years with good years, and that such compensation is made not through peaceful, but through fruitful seasons, it is certain that the bad years were designated in chapter 1 not only on account of wars and the ravages of enemies, but also on account of sterility and the scarcity of grain divinely sent: which, namely, the locusts, the bruchus, the rust, or the caterpillar (as Grotius prefers) and the cankerworm caused, not those which Phul, Tiglath-Pileser, Shalmaneser, and Sennacherib caused. Which according to some interpreters are also called the great army of God. Concerning which Blessed Luther in this place: It pleases me that Jerome refers these to the locusts, just as all the Greeks call armies δυνάμεις. And Jerome himself adds: the cankerworm is called the great power of the Lord, because in a slow and small worm the power of God and human frailty are demonstrated, as once in the Egyptian plagues through the small animals, the gnats, which are so small that they are scarcely seen by the eyes. Rightly also does the commentary of Calvin hold here: The Prophet confirms the previous doctrine and reasons from opposites, because, namely, it is no less easy for God to restore the abundant produce of the earth than it was previously easy to render the earth sterile by sending those corruptions. I will restore to you the years, (for the other years) he says, but so that the Jews might better understand that this whole matter is placed in the hand of God, he expressly pronounces that the cankerworms and the bruchi and the locusts were His soldiers, and indeed hired ones, whose labor He had used, just as it seemed good. The corruptions, therefore, which had consumed the entire produce of the earth, the Prophet says were as it were the satellites of God: The locusts, or cankerworms, or bruchi did not arise by chance, but God hired the labor of those soldiers; they were His forces and army to oppress them. But famine and starvation had finished off the whole people. Therefore, not in vain does the Prophet here commemorate that those little beasts were the army of God. Now we hold the argument from opposites, for if God consumed the entire substance of the earth through those armies: now it will not be difficult to restore abundance for those years. Now if anyone lays down arms, afterwards the lands will be cultivated, and will bring forth their accustomed fruit: thus also now the Lord shows that the land was sterile because He sent His armies, which would ravage all its produce. Now, He says, after I have returned to favor with you, there will be no soldiers who will devour your fruits. The earth, therefore, will feed you, because nothing will prevent you from receiving the accustomed produce. For unless this had been persuaded to the Jews, that the land had been sterile because the locusts and bruchi and cankerworms had been armed by the Lord, they could always fear for themselves from those corruptions: but the locusts will arise, the bruchi and cankerworms will arise, which will swallow all the crops. The Prophet shows that this was not fortuitous. Now therefore, after God has been appeased toward you, the earth itself will perform its duty: then nothing will prevent you from enjoying its abundance. That which he calls a great army shows that God has no need of strong forces to subdue men. For when He arms the locusts and little animals, which are of no moment, they snatch sustenance from the mouths of men, they leave them famished: even if no one draws a sword against them, they nevertheless waste away in their starvation.

Seventh, the Grotian explanation does not agree with the history of the times. For even if some devastation was brought upon the lands of Israel by Phul and Shalmaneser, it was not, however, upon the land of the Jews, which it is not consistent with sacred history, 2 Kings 15, to have suffered that desolation from them. Then, even if Grotius's conjecture is admitted to the greatest extent, and even if the land of the two tribes could not have been entirely immune from the damage of those incursions on account of its proximity: yet such great devastation did not happen to them from that source as the words of the Prophet imply, if they are to be understood truly of hostile desolation.

Therefore, as to that robust nation without number, which is said to have ascended, whose teeth are as the teeth of a lion, or (as Grotius prefers to interpret the word לביא from its usage and the Arabic translation) as the molars of a lioness, by which the vineyard of the Lord was placed into a desert, and the fig tree of the Lord was stripped of its bark: We certainly confess that these things are to be accepted concerning a hostile incursion and desolation, which is proposed to the people for the provocation of repentance alongside the devastation of the cankerworm and other living creatures; but just as all these things were brought upon the land of the two tribes, so that corruption seems to some to be explained concerning the army of Sennacherib, which was by far the most numerous and most ferocious, through which all the fortified cities were occupied, and the land of the Jews was greatly devastated, 2 Kings 18, 13. c. 19, 23. But it is more correctly understood concerning the devastation subsequently brought about by the Chaldeans, as will appear later. Which agree perfectly with the chronology according to the more accepted opinion, that Joel lived after the abduction of the ten tribes, which Blessed Luther also proved by his calculation in the Preface to this Prophet: At what time Joel preached is therefore doubted, because in the title he makes no mention of the Kings. And yet, to one considering the argument more diligently, not light conjectures offer themselves, following which we may establish that he lived after Isaiah, and that Isaiah was older. For first, he makes no mention of the kingdom of Israel, as Hosea and Isaiah do. And so we judge that it had already been devastated by the Assyrian, and the ten tribes abducted, when Joel began to preach. Then, he expressly shows that he is speaking about the devastation that would be through the Babylonians, and about the tribe of Judah. For he makes mention of the house of the Lord, which was only in Jerusalem, and says that the sacrifice and the libation had perished. Although therefore he names no Kings, yet we judge that he lived in the last times of Hezekiah, or under Manasseh. These are the words of Blessed Luther. Whence we recognize his second thoughts: inasmuch as in the German argument prefixed to the version of this Prophet, he had wished the abduction of the Israelites to be predicted here.

Eighthly, the authority of the interpreters, especially the Christians, favors our explanation. For although not a few have interpreted it allegorically, yet in their explanations nothing certain is held, nor is there any harmony among them: as must needs happen when one departs from the letter without reason. But those who take the words of the Prophet as they sound, easily agree among themselves: among whom B. Luther is especially to be mentioned here: after he had reviewed the allegorical interpretation of others, he adds this ἐπίκρισιν: If anyone wishes to embrace this opinion, I will not hinder him. A diligent interpreter, however, will everywhere follow that which is most proper to each passage. I am moved, therefore, first by the authority of Moses, to judge these things to be historical, not allegorical. For thus he threatens in Deut. 28. You shall sow much seed in the ground, and shall gather little, because the locusts shall devour all; you shall plant a vineyard and dig it, and shall not drink the wine, nor gather anything from it, because it shall be laid waste by worms. Therefore, the plague, or the punishment of sin defined, is a multitude of harmful worms, by which the harvest perishes. Furthermore, experience also agrees with Moses. For although this harmful multitude of worms is in itself a punishment for sin, yet we see it also exists with the signification of some more grievous punishment to follow. I therefore maintain that these things are not allegorical, but that in reality the impenitent people were punished, not for one year, by noxious worms, which, having devoured the fields and all the crops, brought about famine and pestilence. Most of our own follow B. Luther: Wigandus, Gesnerus, Winckelmannus, Pappus, Tarnovius, and others. From the Reformed, Calvin, Piscator, Coccejus, etc., understand the words of the Prophet concerning the devastation by those little animals which the Prophet commemorates, and the sterility in Judea. Which Cornelius à Lapide also acknowledges after Remigius, Ruffinus, Lyranus, Vatablus, Arias, R. Salomon, and others: nor does Mariana deny that both war and famine are designated here.

Verse of the same.

Latin:

CONCIO I. CAPUT I. Ob famem & bellum ad poeniten- tiam excitat.

Praemissa canonizatione praeconii Joëlis inau- ditum & posteris memorabile malum à qua- druplici genere insectorum, eruca, locusta, brucho, & rubigine omnia terrae nascentia demetente intimatur, & exercitus populi in- gentis & ferocis vineas & ficus vastaturus, ut nec sacrificiis cibariis & libationi aliquid supersit, praedicitur, qua utraque clade gau- dium in luctum convertendum. Tum exhor- tatio instituitur ad sacerdotes, ut lugeant, & jejunio poenitentiali indicto Dominum invo- cent formula praescripta, qua & hominum & jumentorum ac ferarum in ista frumenti & pabuli inopia, & terrae siccitate, clamor, ac rugitus prae fame ac siti, Deo sistendus.

Tristia rura canit Joel fore, tristeqne templum. Vers. 2. AUDITE HOC SENES.) Qui multa memi- nistis. SI FACTUM EST ISTUD IN DIEBUS VE- STRIS, AUT IN DIEBUS PATRUM VESTRO- RUM) Nempe simile quid tot malis, quanta jam vobis praedico, Vers. 3. SUPER HOC FILIIS VESTRIS NARRATE.) Per manus tradite haec vaticinia, ut cum eventis postea com- parentur. Vers. 4. RESIDUUM ERUCAE COMEDIT LO- CUSTA.) Comedet. Proverbialis locutio. Sensus est: quos reliquerit Phul, eos Teglathphalasar occidet, aut abducet: nam sub animalium vastantium nominibus denotantur ex- ercitus Jerem. 51, 14. 27. Nahum. 3, 15. 16. ET RESIDUUM BRUCHI COMEDIT RUBIGO) Quos reliquerit Salmanasar, eos occidet, vel avehet Sen- nacheribus. חסיל, quod LXX. ἐρυσίβην, id est, rubigi- nem vertunt, Chaldaeus rectius (ni fallor) censet animalis esse genus, vertitque שמרוט, id est, attelabum. Est au- tem quiddam inter locustam & bruchum, modicis pennis, reptans potius quam volans, semperque subsiliens, & usque ad interitum cuncta consumens. Itaque חסיל vertitur βρου̃χος 2. Paral. 4, 28. alibi ἀκρὶς Esaiae 33,4. & infra 2,25. Vers. 5. EXPERGISCEMINI EBRII.) Ebriosi. ET ULULATE.) Ejulate. Respondet vox He- braeo הילילו. QUI BIBITIS VINUM IN DULCEDINE. Qui amatis bibere vinum. QUONIAM PERIIT AB ORE VESTRO.) Fu- git excisis vineis. Vers. 6. GENS ENIM ASCENDIT SUPER TER- RAM MEAM.) Ascendet. Sic & sequentia sume, & refe: ad vastitatem illatam terris per Phulem & Salmanasarem Ante ea tempora in pace vixerant tribus decem cum dua bus, ut apparet 2. Paralip. 28. v. 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. Ita que ex terris decem tribuum vinum & esculenta pervenie bant ad duas tribus, quod cessavit per illam vastitatem, qua & ipsa terra duarum tribuum, ob vicinitatem, immu nis plane esse non potuit.

ASsumit tanquam certum Grotius, hoc caput d bellica clade â Regibus Assyriis, Phul, Teglath phalassar, Salmanassar & Sennacherib illata, intelli gendum esse. At haec interpretatio non ita tan quam indubitata proponenda, sed rationibus fir manda erat. In Scripturis enim non agnoscimus nisi de solo Deo illud αὐτὸς ἔφα. De aliis bellis in telligunt nonnulli, & imprimis iis, quib9 aures alic qui libenter praebuit Grotius. Alii, teste Hierony no, de quatuor mundi imperiis exponunt, quasi eru- ca Babylonios & Assyrios, locusta Medos & Persas, bruchus Macedones & omnes Alexandri M. suc- cessores, atque imprimis Antiochum Epiphanem, rubigo Romanos denotet : quia ab omnibus istis quatuor imperiis terra Judæorum afflicta, & deva- stata est : quæ explicatio, quanquam, Christophoro à Castro referente, Remigio, Ruperto, Haymoni, Al- berto, Hugoni, & Dionysio probata fuerit, non ta- men meretur calculum : siquidem nullo nitatur fundamento. Et futura hic prædicantur, non vero de præteritis sermo sit. Nec tam longo intervallo se subsequuntut eruca, locusta, bruchus, & rubigo. Neque Judæos, sed terram Israel solum vastasse le- guntur Assyrii: Medi ut Persæ non tam nocue- runt, quam benevolos se exhibuerunt Judæis. Ro- manorum autem vastatio sequuta demum est effu- sionem Sp. S. Adeoque ante eandem facta hic dici non potuit. Et quomodo vastationem hanc filiis & filiorum filiis narrare potuerunt, aut ex tam obscu- ra ejus prædictione eandem colligere, ac ad poste- ros suos ejusdem comminationem transmittere?

Porro alii cum Theodoreto exponunt quidem de quatuor hostibus, sed illi, non ut Grotius, ad Ju- dæos seu duas tribus solum, verum ad decem tribus simul hoc vaticinium referunt. Et per erucam Te- glathpalasarem, per locustam Salmanasarem, per bruchum Sennaheribum, per rubiginem Nabucho- donofarem intelligunt : quorum priores Israelis re- gnum devastarunt : posteriores regnum Juda. Ter- tio de hostibus Judæorum, vel qui terram Judæam e- verterunt quatuor illa mala alii interpretantur, & imprimis Hieronymus : Qui Ep. 113. seu præfatio- ne in Joelem ad Judæos solos Prophetiam Joelis refert. Unde in Epist. ad Paulin. 3. oper. pag. 8. è qua ad regnum Israelis eandem ab ipso referri alii colligunt (quibus etiam accessit Grotius) Alber- tus σφάλμα esse putat, ita legens, describit terram duarum tribuum, non duodecim; alii ex Ebræo- rum sententia illic solum loquutum esse censent Hieronymum. Nam in laudata præfatione senten- tia ejus propria luculenta est: Quomodo, inquit, in Hoseæ prophetia sub nomine Ephraim ad decem tri- bus confertur vaticinium, quæ vel Samaria vel Israel sæpe memoratur, sic in Israel omne, quod dicitur ad tribum Juda, & ad Ierusalem pertinere credendum est, & nullam omnino Israelis, id est, decem tribuum in hoc fieri mentionem. Videtur autem Hierony- mus locum præsentem de extremo solum Chaldæ- orum adventu contra Judæam & Jerusalem acce- pisse. Siquidem ad vers. 5. cap. 1. ita scripserit: Vide- tur nunc nobis magis hoc dici de Babyloniis atque Chal- dæis, quorum crudelitas in populum Dei feritasque de- scribitur, & ni fallor, videor mihi in hoc Propheta ali- quid reperisse : Narratur impietas hostium sub figura locustarum, & rursum sic de ipsis locustis dicitur, quasi hostibus comparentur, ut cum locustas legeris, hostes cogites : cum hostes cogitaveris, redeas ad locu- stas. Ascendit ergo gens locustarum de solitudine sive exercitus Chaldæorum super terram Dei, fortis & in- numerabilis. Quid enim locustis innumerabilius & fortius, quibus humana industria resistere non potest? Dentes ejus, gentis videlicet locustarum: omnia au- tem τοπικῶς intellige; quasi dentes leonis, ut qui in for- titudine & multitudine locustis coæquantur, in fero- citate & crudelitate leonibus comparentur. Hæc, in- quit, gens posuit vineam meam in desertum : quam de Ægypto transtuli, & plantavi, & ficum meam de- corticavit, populum Judæorum, ad quem venit Salva- tor, ut comederet fructus, & non invenit : maledi- xitque ei, & aruit in æternum: Omnia autem sub me- taphora locustarum dicta noscamus : duæ in tantum cuncta populantur, ut derodant arborum cortices ex- utasque projiciunt: & omni virore consumpto, altos ramos & aridos derelinquant. Hæc Hieronymus. Quod ergo dicit Propheta, residuum erucæ comedit locusta &c. nonnulli de diversis Regibus & natio- nibus in eodem exercitu intelligunt. Quod alii re- linquebant intactum, alii vastabant.

Quarto de diversis expeditionibus adversus ter- ram Judæorum, & quidem de quatuor Chaldæorum incursionibus nonnulli intelligunt, easque ita cum Eman. Saa enumerant, quod tanquam eruca Ne- bucadnezar venerit, cum cepit Jojakim, & Babylo- nem duxit cum Daniele, deinde tanquam locusta, cum cepit Jechoniam, tertio ut bruchus,cum occu- pavit Jerusalem & Sedeciam Regem duxit Babylo- nem: Quarto cum Nebuzaradan q. rubigo templum & domum regiam & domus principum combussit, totamque urbem delevit.

Quinto Christ. à Castro Joelem unum ex pro- phetis fuisse existimat,qui extremum prædixerunt regno Judæ exitium, ob flagitia Manassis 2. Reg. 23, 26. & quam Josiæ promissum fuerit,ipsum in pace collectum iri, ne videat omne malum, quod indu- cturus erat Dominus 2. Paral. 34, 28. Videtur sibi, ait,tempore filiorum Josiæ reliquisse Deum completio- nem illius comminationis, nempe quatuor regnum sibi invicem succedentium, Joachas, Joakim, Joachin, & Sedecià, qui nequaquam in pace mortui sunt, sed in captivitate, vel ab hostibus interfecti. Quapropter cum ipsi regnum Judæ continerent, & quatuor ipsi co- mesti sint cum non modica Judææ depopulatione usque ad ultimum stragem: non immerito ipsi dicentur de- vorati ab eruca, locusta, brucho & rubigine: ita ut Nechao, qui Joachaz abstulit,erucæ comparetur, quæ leviter tetigit terram, abducto rege Joachaz, Regem vero Joakim, quem ille constituit, & reliquit inta- ctum, Nabuchodonosaris milites, latrunculi Chaldæo- rum, Syriæ, Moab, & Amon, instar locustarum inva- serint, occiderint,& sepulturæ asini sepelierint. Ter- tio regem Joachin cum multis ex principibus Nabu- chodonosor, ut bruchus è terra eduxit, & captivum duxit Babylonem. Tandem idem ipse cum ingenti exercitu invasit Jerosolymam, & urbis,templique pul- chritudinem, ut rubigo consumpsit, & Judaicam Rempublicam omnino dissipavit. Hæc à Castro p. 189. Quæ tres posteriores explicationes majori gaudent verisimilitudine quam Grotiana, præfer- tim, si hoc assumamus cum Grotio quod Prophetæ res sit de regno Judæ, non Israelis: Si vero de omni- bus tribubus Israelis exponas, Theodoreti interpre- tatio fine dubio præferenda eidem erit. Nam per excursiones in regnum Ephraim vel decem tribu- um factas,earundemque vastationem,terra Judæo- rum etsi aliquid fortassis passa fuerit calamitatis, profecto ita vastata non fuit, ut vis & emphasis ver- borum Prophetæ importat,& clades illæ earumque successivus ordo atque incrementa per Phulem, Teglathphalassar, & Salmanassarem terram non Judæorum, sed decem tribuum concernunt, ut è 2. Reg. 15. & 17. constat.

puli, quod plagas suas non sentiat. Eadem etiam est Tarnovii explicatio, p. 18. Quia de præterito quærit ex mandato Mosis Deut. 32,7. interrogat seniores, qui longo rerum usu edocti, si quid vident insolitum, senti- re solent, non esse hoc ex ordinario naturæ cursu, quem jam tot annos observarunt. Et quoniam hæc præsens calamitas ab insectis illis præter morem durabat diu- tius, & premebat gravius, monet, ut regrediantur in memoriam dierum pristinorum, & videant, num an- tehac unquam tale naturaliter contigerit: quod si exemplum non suppetit, consilium Prophetæ est, ut tandem agnoscant, hanc esse Dei manum de cælo. Fi- nis vero ut eos pudeat suæ socordiæ; qui hoc ipfi non animadvertunt, nec tam duriter percussi sapiunt, cum hoc vindictæ genus nullo alio possit haberi loco, quam prodigii. Jam illa quæ v. 6. sequuntur, de alia cala- mitate & pœna belli, nempe Judæis jam illati, Calvi- nus interpretatus est in Comment. ad h. l. pag. 4. Quod alii putant,hic pœnam denunciari populo, quæ nondum inflicta erat,iterum repeto, mihi non placere: sed potius meo judicio commemorat Propheta aliam Dei vindictam, ut ostendat, Deum non uno tantum modo admonuisse Judæos, de suis peccatis, ut tandem revocaret ad sanam mentem, sed tentasse omnia, ut eos reduceret in viam,nisi fuissent prorsus desperati. Post- quam ergo de sterilitate Judæorum, vel de aliis cala- mitatibus locutus est, jam addit, etiam bello fuisse Judæos afflictos. Certe fames illos debuerat tangere, præsertim cum incommoda alia aliis succedentia ani- madverterent præter consuetum naturæ cursum plu- res annos occupare, ut jam non posset hoc imputari fortunæ. Sed ubi Deus fame jam confectos iterum bello persequutus est, nonne oportuit plusquam esse alienatos à mente, qui manerent in his Dei vindictis attoniti, & non resipiscerent? Tarnovius vero, etsi calamitatis præsentis & præteritæ exaggerationem hic agnoscat, per gentem tamen robustam & innu- meram, non hostes Judæorum, sed gentem eruca- rum & locustarum intelligit, notans è Kimchio ad h. l. quod omnis congregatio ex viventibus גוי gens appelletur vel עם populus, vid. Prov.30, 25. 26. Quæ etiam Drusii & Cocceji est sententia, ut & Paraphra- stærum Belgicorum. Porro qui proprie accipiunt va- stitatem terræ nascentium, famem illam, quam prævidit etiam Eliseus,septem annis duraturam hic prædici, eamq; explicatius hic à Joele tradi volunt: plerique de quatuor prioribus annis sibi succedenti- bus ex vastatione terræ nascentium per copiam erucæ, locustæ, bruchi & per rubiginem futura, intel- ligunt, quos alii tres sequuti anni, quibus pluviæ de- fectu laborarunt, vivente adhuc Eliseo,quam Ruffi- ni, Remigii, R. Salomonis, Lyræ, Vatabli, Roberti, & Montani, ac recentiorum Ebræorum sententiam fuisse notat à Castro: qualis pœna etiam Amos 4, 9. commemoratur. Cæterum Lyranus & Arias Mon- tanus, etsi agnoscant rem ita, ut relatum est, gestam, per illam tamen adumbratam censent, & prædictam ab Eliseo & Joele vastitatem Judæorum per quatuor imperia inferendam, quasi Joel historiam illam sub Eliseo gestam retulerit, ut per illam gentem hostilem significaret. Alii tamen de tempore discrepant, nec ad Elisei, qui sub Rege Joram floruit, ætatem hoc referunt, sed ad alia tempora, etsi eadem non de- signata sint in historia Regum.

Sexto non pauci amant τὸ ῥητὸν λέγειν & sen- sum literalem retinere, ut de vastitate agrorum,exi- tio frugum, & magna annonæ caritate, ob ficcitatem & vermium noxiorum copiam vaticinium intelli- gatur. Quæ B. Gesneri, Pappi, Tarnovii, & aliorum est sententia. Et ex his alii hoc vaticinium pœnæ futuræ constituunt, alii calamitatem priorum tem- porum proponi volunt, ut excitentur ad pœniten- tiam. Ita Calvinus: putant aliqui denunciari pœ- nam in futurum tempus: sed contextus satis oftendit eos errare, & corrumpere genuinum Prophetæ sen- sum, potius enim Propheta hic objurgat duritiem po- In hac varietate Interpretationum non erat te- mere, sine ratione assumendus, aut noviter excogi- tandus sensus aliquis, quum Scriptura non sit ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, imprimis quia relinquitur τὸ ῥητὸν,à quo sine gravi causa discedendum non est. Viden- tur autem optime mentem Prophetæ affequuti, qui de vastatione terræ nascentium, eaque non futura,sed etiamnum durante interpretantur, siquidem Pro- pheta ebriosos populum ac sacerdotes in rem præ- sentem deducat, & de calamitate non tanquam fu- tura, sed quæ ipsos tum premebat, λευκᾷ δι' Φωνῇ lo- quatur. Quod totus orationis contextus, & ampli- ficationes illæ Rhetoricæ, quas adhibet, abunde docent. Illa tamen quæ v. 6. & 7. inferuntur, de exercitu hostili, & clade bellica potius intelligen- da, ut vastatio terræ nascentium, frugum, & vinea- rum tum infectorum copia, tum hostili manu tribua- tur. Quam sententiam etiam Paraphrastis Vinari- ensibus probari video. Confirmat autem eandem primo ipsa literæ proprietas. A qua cur hic recedere debeamus, nullam justam causam videmus. Non enim secus explicat Propheta, aut figurati sensus ullum præbet documentum. Quapropter & eru- cam, locustam, bruchum, rubiginem, ut sonant, intelli- gimus, & gentem super terram ascendentem leoninæ ferociæ & crudelitatis, secundum literam de gente hostili accipimus, ut ab illo locustarum & aliorum insectorum exercitu terræ nascentia vastentur, ab hac v. hostili copia vineæ & ficus imprimis dam- num passæ indicentur, ab utrisque magna terræ Ju- dæorum vastitas & annonæ caritas, viniq; penuria innuatur. Deinde causæ ejusmodi luctus adferun- tur, quæ siccitati & ariditati temporum, non soli va- stationi bellorum conveniunt: Confusum est vinum, & elanguit oleum. Confusi sunt agricolæ, ululaverunt vinitores super frumento & hordeo, quia periit messis agri, vinea confusa est, & ficus elanguit. Mala grana- tum & palma & malum, & omnia ligna agri ARUE- RUNT v. 10. 11. 12. Et porro v. 17. Computruerunt jumenta in stercore suo (alii ex Ebræo reddunt re- ctius: mucida facta sunt sata sub glebis suis : Luther. Der Saame ist unter der Erden verfaulet. De quo conferatur Tarnov. in h. l. Grotius ipse e- mendat vulgatam versionem: quamvis eam juxta præconceptam opinionem q. ex diversa lectione nata sit, excuset: COMPUTRUERUNT JU- MENTA IN STERCORE SUO) Legerunt LXX. & Hieronymus פרות: nos habemus פרדות, id signi- ficat grana Chaldaice. גרפתים, quod alii stercora verterunt, alii glebas vertunt, alii præsepia, alii acer- vos, à verbo גרף, quod Hebræis, Chaldæis, & Ara- bibus est converrere. Sensus est: madore corrum- puntur grana, in acervis suis quo congesta sunt. De- molita sunt horrea, dissipatæ sunt apothecæ, quoniam confusum est triticum.

Nec tertio aliter se habet ratio gemitus anima- lium v. 18. Quid ingemuit animal, mugierunt gre- ges armenti? Quia non est pastua eis. Sed & gre- ges pecorum disperierunt. Aut quarto precum ipsius- met Prophetæ v. 19. Ad te Domine clamabo, quia ignis comedit speciosa deserti, & flamma succendit omnia ligna regionis. Hæc omnia ficcitatem, & tem- pestatem nimiam referunt. Calvinus: Ignis con- sumsit pascua vel habitacula deserti. Hic rursus pro- digiose Dei judicia commemorat. Scimus etiamsi æstus exurat omnes regiones, tamen loca pascua non tam facile exarescere, præsertim montosa. Hic enim loquitur de pascuis illis frigidis. Scimus quantalibet sit ubertas montium, tamen illic dominari frigus, & in maxima ficcitate semper virent illæ regiones mon- tanæ. Propheta autem hic prodigii loco recitat fuisse habitacula deserti exusta, נאות quidam vertunt pa- scua, alii Habitacula. Sed quantum ad rem ipsam spectat, perinde est utrumvis legamus: quia Pro- pheta hic designat frigidas regiones & humidas, quas nunquam humor etiam in summis caloribus destituit. Vertunt alii Pulchritudines vel speciosa deserti, sed male. Non dubium est, quin pascua vel habitacula, aut cautas intelligat. Ignis ergo con- sumpsit habitacula, vel pascua deserti. Hoc accide- re non solet, neque etiam cadit in communem or- dinem naturæ. Ergo sequitur fuisse portentum. Hæc ratio est, cur dicat Propheta, jam tempus esse clamandi ad Deum, quia non poterat fortuitum vi- deri, quod æstus exureret humidas & aquosas regi- ones. Hactenus Calvinus. Explicat autem sese quinto diserte Propheta, cum bestiarum agri sitim exprimit v. 20. sed & bestiæ agri, quasi area sitiens imbrem suspexerunt ad te, quoniam exiccati sunt fon- tes aquarum, & ignis deporavit speciosa deserti. Illa vers. 20. QUASI AREA SITIENS IMBREM SUSPEXERUNT AD ME, non male Grotius ita explicat e fonte: Clamarunt ad me. ערג, quod hic est proprie de cervis dicitur, & per καταχρησιν de feris aliis. Illud, quasi area sitiens imbrem, nescio unde ir- repserit, neque enim in Hebræo est, neque in Græ- co, neque in Chaldæo, neque in commentariis hæc refert Hieronymus: forte scriptum fuit, sicut cerva sitiens imbrem. Confer. Psal. 42, 1. Ad illa ET IGNIS DEVORAVIT SPECIOSA DESERTI, addit: Habitacula, id est caulas & stabula, unde feræ pasci so- lebant. Sed vox Ebræa quæ habitacula redditur, pa- scua notat, non uno loco 2. Sam. 7, 8. Esa. 65, 10. Jer. 33, 3. Ezech. 34, 14. Psal. 23, 2. Quæ omnia potius de belli incendio accipere, quam de æstu nimio, sicci- tate & ariditate temporum, unde est pascuorum consumtio & arborum, frondium & hortorum exu- stio & armentorum ac pecudum præ nimia siti de- fectio, ac denique fontium, fluminum ac torren- tium exsiccatio imprimis in montosis locis, ubi co- pia aquæ, non penuria, quid aliud est, quam lite- ram textus vexare? Calvinus reddit: Exaruerunt decursus aquarum, addito hoc Commentario: Ite- rum inculcat quod nuper dixi, nempe sterilitatem il- lam profectam esse ex claro Dei judicio, & quod hor- rorem merito incutere debeat hominibus, quia scilicet fuit species portenti. Dum ergo in ipsis montibus are- scunt decursus aquarum, an poterit hoc dici naturale? אפיקים vocant decursus aquarum, vel etiam valles, per quas decurrunt aquæ: nec dubium est, quin Propheta hic regiones designet, quæ semper copia aquarum ubertatem suam retinebant. Quum ergo valles ipsæ exustæ essent, certe oportuit agnoscere illic aliquod miraculum: ideo etiam tribuit clamo rem illum jumentis & brutis animalibus, nec quem libet clamorem, sed quo Deum ipsum invocent. Hæc ille. Conferendus imprimis est locus Ier. 25, 2. seqq. ubi similes querelæ & lamentationes de siccitate: nec non Am. 4, 9. Percussi vos in vento urente, & in aurigine multitudinem hortorum ve- strorum, & vinearum vestrarum, oliveta vestra, & vineta vestra comedit eruca, & non redistis ad me di- cit Dominus.

Sexto promissiones divinæ benedictionis pœ- nitentibus c. 2. factæ, quas loco istarum pœnarum a divina benignitate pollicetur Propheta, satis do- cent, non de belli tantum calamitate, sed de anno- næ etiam caritate supplicia præsentia intelligenda esse: Ecce, inquit Dominus v. 19. ego mittam vobis frumentum, & vinum & oleum, & replebimini eis: Et v. 22. Nolite timere animalia regionis, quia ger- minaverunt speciosa deserti: quia lignum attulit fructum suum, ficus & vinea dederunt virtutem suam. Item v. 23. & 24. Descendere faciet ad vos imbrem matutinum & serotinum, sicut in principio: & implebuntur areæ frumento, & redundabunt tor- cularia vino & oleo. Ac, ne ambigere quis opus haberet, anne hæ promissiones respiciant pœnas divinas cap. 1. designatas, omne dubium eximunt ea, quæ adduntur v. 25. Et reddam vobis ANNOS, quos comedit locusta, bruchus & rubigo, & eruca, fortitudo mea magna, quam misi in vos. Et comedetis vescentes, & saturabimini. Quæ promissiones tem- pora frugifera respiciunt successura annis illis ste- rilibus, loco que siccitatis istius præternaturalis pol- licentur imbrem matutinum & serotinum, h. e. uti explicat ipse Grotius, sementis & messis tempore commodas tempestates Deut. 11. 14. Prov. 16, 16. Jer. 5, 24. Os. 6, 3. Quum ergo, fatente Grotio, Deus verbis istis: ET REDDAM VOBIS ANNOS, compensaturum se bonis annis illos annos malos reci- piat, eaq; compensatio non per pacata, sed frugifera tempora fiat, certum est, annos malos, non ob bella solum & vastationes hostium, sed ob sterilitatem quoque & annonæ caritatem divinitus immissam capite 1. designatos fuisse: quos nempe locustæ, bru- chi, rubigo, vel attelabus (ut mavult Grotius) & eruca, non quos Phul, Teglathphalasarus, Salma- nassar, & Sennacherib fecerunt. Quæ secundum nonnullos Interpp. etiam dicuntur exercitus Dei magnus. De quo B. Lutheus in h. l. Mihi placet, quod Hieronymus hæc refert ad locustas, quemadmo- dum Græci omnes δυνάμεις vocant exercitus. Et Hie- ronymus ipse addit: eruca virtus Domini magna ap- pellatur, quia in tardo parvoque vermiculo Dei potentia & humana fragilitas demonstratur, ut quondam in Ægyptiis plagis per parva animalia Cyniphes, qui tam parvi sunt, ut vix cernantur o- culis. Recte etiam hic se habet Commentarius Cal- vini: Confirmat Propheta superiorem doctrinam & ratiocinatur à contrariis, quia scil. Deo non minus facile sit restituere uberem proventum terræ, quam prius facile fuit terram reddere sterilem, im- missis illis corruptelis. Reddam vobis annos, (pro aliis annis) inquit, sed quo melius intelligant Judæi, hoc totum in manu Dei esse positum, diserte pronun- cias, Erucas & bruchos & locustas fuisse suos milites, & quidem conductitios, quorum opera usus fuerit, quemadmodum visum est. Corruptelas ergo, quæ consumpserant totum terræ proventum, dicit Pro- pheta fuisse quasi satellites Dei: Non fortuito exor- tæ sunt locustæ, vel erucæ, vel bruchi, sed Deus con- duxit illorum militum operam, fuerunt ejus copiæ & exercitus ad ipsos opprimendos. Fames autem & inedia confecerat totum populum. Ergo non frustra hic Propheta commemorat fuisse exerci- tus Dei illas bestiolas. Jam tenemus argumentum à contrariis, si enim Deus consumpsit totam sub- stantiam terræ per illos exercitus: nunc non erit difficile restituere ubertatem pro illis annis. Jam si quis arma deponat, postea colentur terræ, & affe- rent solitum fructum: sic etiam nunc Dominus o- stendit terram fuisse sterilem, quia suos exercitus immisit, qui vastarent omnes ejus proventus. Nunc inquit, postquam rediero vobiscum in gratiam, nulli erunt milites, qui devorent fructus vestros. Terra igitur vos alet, quia nihil impediet, quo minus reci- piatis solitum proventum. Nisi enim hoc persva- sum fuisset Judæis terram fuisse sterilem, quoniam armatæ fuerant locustæ & bruchi & erucæ, à Domi- no, poterant sibi semper metuere ab illis corrupte- lis: atqui exorientur locustæ, exorientur bruchi & erucæ, quæ deglutient omnes fruges. Propheta ostendit hoc non fuisse fortuitum. Nunc ergo postquam placatus fuerit vobis Deus, terra ipsa of- ficium præstabit: deinde nihil impediet, quo mi- nus fruamini ejus abundantia. Quod vocat Exer- citum magnum, ostendit Deo non opus esse validis copiis, ut homines subigat. Nam ubi armat locustas & animalcula, quæ nullius sunt momenti, rapiunt victum ex hominum ore, relinquunt eos fameli- cos: etiamsi nullus exerat contra ipsos gladium, tabescunt tamen in sua inedia.

Septimo non convenit explicatio Grotiana cum historia temporum. Nam etsi aliqua vastitas il- lata terris Israelis per Phulem & Salmanassarem, non tamen terræ Judæorum, quam ab illis desolatio- nem passam esse, sacræ historiæ 2. Reg. 15. consen- taneum non est. Tum si maxime Grotii conjectu- ra admittatur, nec ipsam terram duarum tribuum ob vicinitatem immunem plane esse potuisse ab in- cursionum istarum damno: non tamen illi tanta vastitas inde accidit, quantam Prophetæ verba in- ferunt, si de hostili desolatione vera intelligenda.

Quod itaque ad gentem illam robustam & absque numero, quæ adscendisse dicitur, cujus dentes ut dentes leonis, vel (ut mavult Grotius vocem לביא ex usu ejusdem & Arabicæ translatione interpretari) ceu molares leænæ, à qua vinea Domini in desertum posi- ta, & ficus Domini decorticata: Fatemur sane hæc de hostili incursione & desolatione accipienda, quæ juxta cum vastatione erucæ, & aliorum animan- tium ad provocationem pœnitentiæ populo pro- ponitur; sed uti hæc omnia terræ duarum tribuum illata, ita corruptio illa de exercitu Sennacheribi longe numeratissimo, & ferocissimo quibusdam explicanda videtur, per quem civitates munitæ o- mnes occupatæ, ac terra Judæorum valde vastata fuit 2. Reg. 18, 13. c. 19, 23. Rectius vero de vasti- tate per Chaldæos deinceps inducta intelligitur, uti postea patebit. Quæ apprime consonant Chrono- logiæ juxta receptiorem sententiam, quod Joel vi- xerit post abductionem decem tribuum, quam etiam B. Lutherus calculo suo probavit Præfat. in hunc Prophetam: Quo tempore Joel concionatus sit, ideo dubitatur, quia in titulo nullam Regum mentionem facit. Et tamen consideranti diligentius argumen- tum, non leves conjecturæ se offerunt, quas secuti, sta- tuamus eum post Esaiam vixisse, ac Esaiam natu majorem fuisse. Primo enim non facit regni Israelis mentionem, sicut Oseas & Esaias. Itaque id ab Assyrio jam vastatum, & decem tribus abductas arbitra- mur, cum Joel cæpit concionari. Deinde diferte often- dit, se de vastitate per Babylonios futura, & de tribu Juda loqui. Facit enim mentionem domus Domi- ni, quæ tantum in Jerusalem fuit, ac dicit interiisse sacrificium & libationem. Etsi igitur Reges nul- los nominat, tamen in postremis Hiskiæ tempori- bus, aut sub Manasse vixisse eum judicamus. Hæc B. Lutherus. Unde Φροντίδες δευτέρας ejus agno- scimus: Siquidem in argumento Germanico ver- sioni hujus Prophetæ præmisso, hic abductionem Israelitarum prædici voluerit.

Octavo denique nostræ explicationi favet In- terpp. imprimis Christianorum autoritas. Quan- quam enim non pauci allegorice interpretati sint, in illorum tamen explicationibus nihil certi habe- tur, nec ulla est inter ipsos harmonia: quemadmo- dum fieri oportet, cum citra rationem à litera di- sceditur. At qui verba Prophetæ, uti sonant, acci- piunt, inter se facile consentiunt: è quibus B. Lu- therus hic maxime commemorandus: postquam is recensuisset allegoricam aliorum interpretatio- nem, hanc subjungit ἐπίκρισιν: Hanc sententiam, si quis amplecti volet, non impediam. Diligens tamen interpres hoc ubique sequetur, quod cujusque loci ma- xime proprium est. Moveor igitur primum autorita- te Mosis, ut historica hæc, non allegorica esse judicem. Sic enim minatur Deut. 28. Sementem multam ja- cies in terram, & modicum congregabis, quia lo- custæ devorabunt omnia, vineam plantabis & fo- dies, & non bibes vinum, nec colliges ex ea quip- piam, quoniam vastabitur à vermibus. Ergo plaga, seu peccati pœna definita est noxiorum vermium multitudo, qua annona perit. Deinde convenit cum Mose experientia quoque. Etsi enim hæc noxiorum vermium multitudo per se pœna est peccati, tamen videmus eam etiam cum significatione esse alicujus gravioris pœnæ secuturæ. Statuo igitur non allegori- ca hæc esse, sed revera impœnitentem populum puni- tum non uno anno noxiis vermibus, qui agros & fru- ges omnes depasti famem & pestem conciliarunt. Se- quuntur B. Lutherum plerique nostri Wigandus, Ges- nerus, Winckelmannus, Pappus, Tarnovius, alii. E Reformatis Calvinus, Piscator, Coccejus &c. de vastatione ab animalculis istis, quæ commemorat Propheta, & sterilitate in Judæa verba Prophetæ intelligunt. Quod etiam post Remigium, Ruffinum, Lyranum, Vatablum, Ariam, R. Salomonem & alios agnoscit Cornelius à Lapide: neque abnuit Maria- na, & bellum & famem hic designari.

Vers. eod.

## 1:6
HIS TEETH AS THE TEETH OF A LION.) Rapidity is signified. Daniel uses a similar image concerning the Medes, 7, 5.

AND HIS MOLARS AS THE WHELP OF A LION.) לביא, which is here in the Hebrew, seems to signify a lioness rather than a whelp of a lion, for the Arabs also take it thus, لبوة.

Latin:

DENTES EJVS VT DENTES LEONIS.) Ra- piditas significatur. Pari imagine de Medis utitur Da- niel. 7, 5.

ET MOLARES EJVS VT CATVLI LEONIS.) לביא quod hic in Hebræo est, leænam potius significare videtur, quam catulum leonis, nam & Arabes sic sumunt لبوة.

## 1:7
Verse 7. HE HATH LAID MY VINE IN A DESERT) Into a vast and unfruitful place.

AND MY FIG TREE)

HE HATH BARKED IT) The Chaldean also took it thus. The Hebrew word signifies foam, and thus the nails of trees, as Pliny calls them, seem to be named by similarity.

STRIPPING IT, HE HATH MADE IT BARE.) Of leaves, shoots, and fruits.

AND CAST IT AWAY.) He threw it down, its vigor having been consumed.

THE BRANCHES THEREOF ARE MADE WHITE.) The bark having been removed.

Latin:

Vers. 7. POSVIT VINEAM MEAM IN DESER- TVM) In locum vastum & infrugiferum.

ET FICVM MEAM) Arborem.

DECORTICAVIT) Sic & Chaldæus sumsit. He- bræa vox spumam significat, & sic videntur per similitudi- nem appellari clavi arborum, ut eos Plinius appellat.

NVDANS SPOLIAVIT EAM.) Foliis, surculis, fructibus.

ET PROJECT.) Dejecit, vigore absumto.

ALBI FACTI SVNT RAMI EJVS.) Detracto cortice.

## 1:8
Verse 8. GIRDED WITH SACKCLOTH.) In mourning attire.

FOR THE HUSBAND OF HER YOUTH.) Of her adolescence. For husbands are wont to be loved more by women to whom they were married while still young.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ACCINCTA SACCO.) Habitu lugubri.

SVPER VIRUM PVBERTATIS SUÆ.) Ado- lescentiæ suæ. Solent enim mariti à fœminis magis amari, quibus adolescentulis adhuc nuptæ sunt.

## 1:9
PERIIT SACRIFICIUM [THE SACRIFICE HAS PERISHED].) A hyperbolic expression, which signifies that there was a great scarcity of offerings. Moreover, מנחה is that offering which is made from fine flour, μανὰὰ to the interpreters: concerning which see the things said in Leviticus 2 and Mark 9:49.

ET LIBATIO [AND THE DRINK OFFERING]) On account of the lack of wine.

Latin:

Vers. 9. PERIIT SACRIFICIUM.) Locutio ὑπερβο- λικὴ, quæ significat magnam fuisse oblationum penuriam. Est autem מנחה oblatio illa quæ fit ex simila, μανὰὰ in- terpretibus: de quo vide dicta Levit. 2. & Marci 9, 49.

ET LIBATIO) Ob vini inopiam.

## 1:10
ELANGUIT OLEUM [THE OIL HAS LANGUISHED].) It is dissipated; in the way that שפך is taken in Lamentations 2:9. It flowed out, [says] the Chaldean in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ELANGUIT OLEUM.) Dissipatum est; quomodo שפך sumitur Thren. 2, 9. effluxit, Chaldæus hoc loco.

## 1:11
VLVLAVERUNT VINITORES [THE VINEDRESSERS HAVE HOWLED].) Howl. This is to be referred to that which follows after, the vine is confounded. The things which are in the middle pertain to the mourning of the farmer.

Latin:

Vers. 11. VLVLAVERUNT VINITORES.) Ejulate. Hoc referendum ad id, quod post sequitur, vinea confusa est, Quæ in medio sunt, ad agricolæ luctum pertinent.

## 1:12
Verse 12.

MALO GRANATVM [POMEGRANATE].) The Punic apple was also called a pomegranate in its own age, Pliny is the witness.

QVIA CONFVSVM EST GAVDIVM A FILIIS HOMINUM [BECAUSE JOY IS CONFOUNDED FROM THE SONS OF MEN]) Therefore joy has dried up from the sons of men. For gladness [comes] to men from food and wine. Psalm 4:8.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

MALO GRANATVM.) Malum punicum etiam granatum suo ævo dictum, testis est Plinius.

QVIA CONFVSVM EST GAVDIVM A FILIIS HOMINUM) Ideo exaruit gaudium à filiis hominum. Læ- titia enim hominibus ex victu & vino. Psal. 4, 8.

## 1:13
ACCINGITE VOS [GIRD YOURSELVES]) Namely, in mourning attire, as above [in verse] 8, and as now follows.

SACRIFICIVM ET LIBATIO [SACRIFICE AND DRINK OFFERING].) As above [in verse] 8.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ACCINGITE VOS) Nempe habitu luctuo- so, ut supra 8. & jam sequitur.

SACRIFICIVM ET LIBATIO.) Ut supra 8.

## 1:14
SANCTIFICATE JEJUNIVM [SANCTIFY A FAST].) Proclaimed.

CONGREGATE SENES [GATHER THE ELDERS].) Senators.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SANCTIFICATE JEJUNIVM.) Indictitium.

CONGREGATE SENES.) Senatores.

## 1:15
Verse 15.

FOR THE DAY OF THE LORD IS NEAR.) That is, the destruction of the Temple, which the priests had learned from Isaiah would follow after the deportation of the ten tribes.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

QVIA PROPE EST DIES DOMINI.) Id est, excidium Templi, quod secuturum post deportationem decem tribuum, didicerant sacerdotes ab Esaia.

## 1:16
Ver. 16.

BEFORE YOUR EYES.) Our eyes, in the Hebrew, so that the lamentation of the priests may be continued.

JOY AND GLADNESS.) Grain and wine, as above in 2.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

CORAM OCULIS VESTRIS.) Nostris, in He- bræo, ut continuetur sacerdotum planctus.

LÆTITIA ET EXVLTATIO.) Frumentum & vi- num, ut supra 2.

## 1:17
Ver. 17.

THE BEASTS HAVE ROTTED IN THEIR DUNG.) The LXX and Jerome read פרדות, we have פרדות. In Chaldean it signifies grains. גרפתים, which some have translated as dung, others as mangers, others as clods, and others as heaps, from the verb גרף, which for the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Arabs means to sweep together. The sense is: the grains are corrupted by moisture in their heaps where they were gathered; naturally because of the cause which follows.

THE BARNS ARE DEMOLISHED.) Burned by enemy fire.

THE STOREHOUSES ARE SCATTERED) The huts are demolished: that is, not only the barns, but also the villas, which Servius notes in the first book of the Aeneid are called not magalia but magaria by the Carthaginians. Villas, indeed, also in Judea: therefore the grain was corrupted by rains, because there was nothing in the fields in which they could be stored. The Chaldean refers these to corrupted wine jars, nor does it sufficiently appear how he read it.

FOR THE WHEAT IS CONFOUNDED.) Therefore the wheat has rotted. For יבש has a meaning close to באש, which is rendered as to stink and to cause a foul smell, and to בוש, which is translated as to be ashamed.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

COMPVTRVERVNT JVMENTA IN STER- CORE SVO.) Legerunt LXX. & Hieronymus פרדות, nos habemus פרדות. id significat grana Chaldaicé. גרפתים, quod alii stercora verterunt, alii præsepia, alii glebas vertunt, alii acervos, à verbo גרף, quod Hebræis, Chaldæis, & Arabibus est converrere. Sensus est: ma- dore corrumpuntur grana, in acervis suis quo congesta sunt; nimirum ob causam quæ sequitur.

DEMOLITA SVNT HORREA.) Incensa igne hostico.

DISSIPATÆ SVNT APOTHECÆ) Demolita sunt magaria: id est, non horrea tantum, sed & villæ, quas Pœ- nis dici non magalia, sed magaria notat ad primum Ænei- dos librum Servius. Villæ, nempe etiam in Judæa: ideo cor- rupta imbribus frumenta, quia nihil erat in agris quo condi possent. Chaldæus refert hæc ad corrupta vini dolia, nec satis apparet quomodo legerit.

QVONIAM CONFVSVM EST TRITICVM.) Ideo fœtuit triticum. Nam יבש vicinam habet fignificatio- nem cum באש, quod redditur προσόζειν & σαπρίζειν τὴν ὀσμὴν, & cum בוש, quod vertitur αἰσχύνεσθαι.

## 1:18
Ver. 18.

WHY HAS THE ANIMAL GROANED,) How greatly the beasts have groaned. For the word בהמה is accustomed among the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Arabs for the most part, when nothing else is added, to be taken for horses, mules, and donkeys.

THE HERDS OF CATTLE HAVE LOWED,) In Latin, horned cattle.

BECAUSE THERE IS NO PASTURE FOR THEM.) The land, that is. Therefore they groan and low, because they do not find where they may graze, all the herbs having been worn away by the army.

AND THE FLOCKS OF CATTLE HAVE PERISHED.) In the Hebrew: They are desolate: that is, reduced to a small number. צאן is said by the Hebrews, as pecus by the Latins, properly of the sheep and goat kind,

Latin:

Vers. 18.

QVID INGEMVIT ANIMAL,) Quantope- re ingemuerunt jumenta. Solet enim vox בהמה He- bræis, Chaldæis, & Arabibus plerumque, ubi nihil aliud additur, sumi pro equis, mulis, asinis.

MVGIERVNT GREGES ARMENTI,) Latine, ar- menta bucera.

QVIA NON EST PASCVA EIS.) Terra scilicet. Ideo gemunt & mugiunt, quia non inveniunt ubi pascan- tur, attritis ab exercitu herbis omnibus.

ET GREGES PECORVM DISPERIERVNT.) In Hebræo: Desolati sunt: id est, ad paucitatem redacti. צאן Hebræis, ut pecus Latinis, dicitur proprie de ovillo & caprugno genere,

## 1:19
Verse 19.

TO THEE O LORD I WILL CRY.) The words which the priests will say are continued, the lands being devastated round about.

BECAUSE FIRE HAS CONSUMED THE BEAUTIFUL PLACES OF THE DESERT.) The dwellings of the desert: as the Chaldean has it here. מדבר, that is, desert, is said by the Hebrews and Chaldeans of pasture places; therefore the dwellings here are the same as the folds a little before.

AND THE FLAME HAS KINDLED ALL THE TREES OF THE REGION.) All the trees, from whose fruits or barks the animals were living.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

AD TE DOMINE CLAMABO.) Continuantur verba, quæ sacerdotes dicent, terris circum vastatis.

QVIA IGNIS COMEDIT SPECIOSA DESER- TI.) Habitacula deserti: quomodo hic Chaldæus. מדבר, id est, desertum, Hebræis, & Chaldæis dicuntur loca pascua, habitacula ergo hic eadem, quæ paulo ante magaria.

ET FLAMMA SVCCENDIT OMNIA LIGNA REGIONIS.) Omnes arbores, de quarum fructibus, aut corticibus animalia vivebant.

## 1:20
Verse 20.

BUT ALSO THE BEASTS OF THE FIELD,) That is, wild animals: for the word שדה joined to the word בהמות requires this meaning.

AS A THIRSTY AREA LOOKED UP TO ME.) They cried to me. ערג, which is here, is said properly of deer, and by catachresis, of other wild animals. That, 'as a thirsty area [looks up to] the rain,' I do not know whence it crept in, for it is not in the Hebrew, nor in the Greek, nor in the Chaldean, nor does Jerome refer to this in his Commentaries: perhaps it was written, 'as a deer thirsty for the rain.' Compare Psalm 42, 1.

BECAUSE THE FOUNTAINS OF WATERS ARE DRIED UP.) The streams of waters. It is no wonder about the streams, if even the rivers have failed, not by being drunk up, as I think, but by the fountains being obstructed, by those immense forces under Xerxes.

AND FIRE HAS DEVOURED THE BEAUTIFUL PLACES OF THE DESERT.) Dwellings, as we just said: that is, the folds and stables, whence the wild animals were accustomed to be fed.

This is not the prayer of the priests, but a prediction of the prophet Joel, who prophesies that not only food and equipment, but also gladness and joy would be taken away from the House of the Lord by the Chaldeans. For he does not only seek an argument from the present calamity, from the devastation of the land of the Jews, brought about partly by the dryness of the seasons, partly by the corruption of war, so that he might exhort them to repentance as if by some signal: but also from the imminent day of the judgment of the Lord, which was to be executed by the Chaldeans. What is indicated here in a few words he pursues more fully in the following chapter. For the Prophet no longer speaks in the past, as in the former [passages], but says, THE DAY OF THE LORD IS NEAR. Nor is it likely that he himself prescribed to the priests a formula of complaint to be instituted in solemn fasts concerning the imminent day of the Lord, before he had prophesied in any word about that day of the Lord. For the preceding matters which are contained in verse 6, Grotius refers to the incursions of Phul and Salmanassar. Who, therefore, are the priests complaining about the destruction of the temple, concerning which he had hitherto given no indication? That the priests learned this from Isaiah does not contribute anything to the matter, because they ought to have taken the argument for instituting fasts from Joel, and they were here to be incited to that by his sermons: nor does it rest upon any certainty, nay, it is contrary to Grotius himself, inasmuch as he makes Isaiah not prior to Joel, but posterior, and judges that Joel spoke of Isaiah, when in chapter 2, 23, he prophesies concerning the Teacher of righteousness.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

SED ET BESTIÆ AGRI,) Id est, feræ: hanc enim significationem requirit vox שדה adjuncta voci בהמות.

QVASI AREA SITIENS IMBREM SVSPE- RVNT AD ME.) Clamarunt ad me. ערג, quod hic est, proprie de cervis dicitur, & per κατάχρησιν, de feris aliis. Il- lud, quasi area sitiens imbrem, nescio unde irrepserit, neque enim in Hebræo est, neque in Græco, neque ni Chaldæo, neque in Commentariis hæc refert Hieronymus: forte scri- ptum fuit, sicut cerva sitiens imbrem. Confer. Psalm. 42, 1.

QVONIAM EXSICCATI SVNT FONTES AQVARVM.) Rivi aquarum. Non mirum de rivis, si & flumina quandam defecere, non epotantibus, ut puto, sed fontes obstruentibus, immensis illi sub Xerxe copiis.

ET IGNIS DEVORAVIT SPECIOSA DESER- TI.) Habitacula, ut modo diximus: id est, caulas & stabula, unde feræ pasci solebant.

Non est hæc oratio sacerdotum, sed prædictio Joelis prophetæ, qui per Chaldæos non cibos tan- tum & apparatum, sed etiam lætitiam & gaudium à Domo Domini sublatum iri vaticinatur.
