Non enim tantum à præsenti calamitate, à terræ Judæo- rum vastitate, partim per siccitatem temporum, partim per corruptionem bellicam illata argumen- tum petit, ut eos veluti celevsmate quodam ad pœ- nitentiam exhortetur: sed etiam ab imminente die judicii Domini, quod per Chaldæos exequen- dum erat. Quod hic paucis indigitatum sequenti capite plenius persequitur. Nam non amplius in præterito loquitur Propheta, uti in prioribus, sed PROPE EST, inquit, dies Domini. Nec vero verosimile est, sacerdotibus ipsum præscripsisse formulam querelæ in jejuniis solemnibus de immi- nente die Domini instituendæ, priusquam ullo verbo de illo die Domini vaticinatus est. Superio- ra enim quæ versu 6. habentur, Grotius ad Phu- lis & Salmanassaris incursiones refert. Qui ergo conquerentur sacerdotes de excidio templi, de quo nullum hactenus indicium fecerat? Quod ab Esaia sacerdotes didicerint, nec quicquam ad rem facit, quia à Joele argumentum instituendi jejunia capere debebant, ejusque concionibus ad id ex- citandi hic erant: nec ulla certitudine nititur, imo Grotio ipsimet adversatur, utpote qui Esaiam Joele non priorem, sed posteriorem facit, & Joelem de Esaia loquutum esse censet, cum cap. 2, 23. de Do- ctore justitiæ vaticinatur.

## 2:1 Argument
SERMON II. CHAPTER II. Partly minatory, partly consolatory.

First, he commands the trumpet of war to be sounded in Zion, on account of the day of darkness of divine wrath, and the horrible attack of enemies devastating like a flame; then indeed, admonishing to repentance with the promise of grace and divine blessing, he wishes the trumpet of repentance and fasting to resound publicly, so that prayers may be poured out to God with tears, promising an abundance of food, the removal of enemies, and especially the sending of the Teacher of righteousness, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh, with notable prodigies on that truly great day as clear characters of the Savior, and of salvation to be provided through faith and the invocation of the name of the Lord to the Jews and the Gentiles on Mount Zion. Joined too closely to punishment, grace persuades to repent.

Ver. 1.

BLOW THE TRUMPET IN ZION.) Here is predicted the arrival of Sennacherib, and the siege of Jerusalem carried out by him. The trumpet was accustomed to sound the arrival of an enemy. Ezek. 33, 3. Hosea 5, 8.

HOWL.) Sound the taratantara.

LET THEM BE TROUBLED.) Let them tremble,

ALL THE INHABITANTS OF THE LAND.) Of Judea.

THE DAY OF THE LORD COMETH.) A day of the Lord indeed, but not yet that great one, of which below 3, 1.

Latin:

CONCIO II. CAPUT II. Partim comminatorium, partim consolatorium.

Tuba primum bellica in Zione clangi jubet, ob diem tenebrarum iræ divinæ, & hostium instar flammæ devastantium horribilem impetum; tum vero admonens ad pæniten- tiam cum promissione gratiæ & benedictio- nis divinæ tubam pœnitentiæ & jejunii pu- blice resonare vult, ut preces ad Deum cum lachrymis fundantur, promittens victus ab- undantiam, hostiumque remotionem, ac im- primis missionem Doctoris justitiæ, & Spiri- tus S. super omnem carnem effusionem, cum insignibus prodigiis in die illa vere magna ceu characteribus luculentis Salvatoris, & salvationis per fidem & invocationem no- minis Domini Judæis & gentibus in monte Zion præstandæ. Juncta nimis pœnæ, resipiscere gratia svadet.

Vers. 1.

CANITE TVBA IN SION.) Hic prædicitur ad- ventus Sennacheribi, & obsidium Hierosolymorum per eum factum. Clangi solerat hostis adventum. Ezech. 33, 3. Oseæ 5, 8.

VLVLATE.) Sonate taratantara.

CONTVRBENTVR.) Contremiscant,

OMNES HABITATORES TERRÆ.) Judææ.

VENIT DIES DOMINI.) Dies quidem Domini, sed nondum ille magnus, de quo infra 3, 1.

## 2:2
Ver. 2.

A DAY OF DARKNESS AND OF GLOOMINESS, A DAY OF CLOUDS AND OF THICK DARKNESS.) That is, a time of supreme calamities. Compare 8 and 29 of Isaiah.

AS THE MORNING SPREAD UPON THE MOUNTAINS A GREAT PEOPLE AND A STRONG.) As widely as the dawn spreads itself over the mountains, so widely shall the army of the Assyrians spread itself.

THERE HATH NOT BEEN EVER THE LIKE.) That army of the Assyrian was huge. See 2 Kings 19, 35.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

DIES TENEBRARVM ET CALIGINIS, DIES NVBIS ET TVRBINIS.) Id est, tempus summarum ca- lamitatum. Confer. 8. & 29. Esaiæ.

QVASI MANE EXPANSVM SVPER MONTES POPVLVS MVLTVS ET FORTIS.) Quam late au- rora se expandit super montes, tam late se expandet Assy- riorum exercitus.

SIMILIS ET NON FVIT A PRINCIPIO.) In- gens exercitus fuit ille Assyrii. Vide 2. Reg. 19, 35.

## 2:3
Verse 3.

BEFORE HIS FACE A CONSUMING FIRE: AND BEHIND HIM A BURNING FLAME.) That is, wherever he goes, all things will shine with conflagrations. Isaiah 9:18, 10:28.

AS A GARDEN OF PLEASURE THE LAND BEFORE HIM, AND BEHIND HIM A DESOLATION OF THE DESERT.) The land which before his arrival was like the garden of Eden, when he shall have come, will become most desolate,

NEITHER IS THERE ANY THAT SHALL ESCAPE HIM.) Thus all things will be held by his forces.

AS THE APPEARANCE OF HORSES, THE APPEARANCE OF THEM.) Often both Greeks and Latins compare a brave man to a noble horse, which dares to be the first to enter the way, and to attempt threatening rivers, and to commit itself to an unknown sea, nor does it dread empty noises.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ANTE FACIEM EJVS IGNIS VORANS: ET POST EVM EXVRENS FLAMMA.) Id est, quaqua ibit, omnia lucebunt incendiis. Esaiæ 9, 18. 10, 28.

QVASI HORTVS VOLVPTATIS TERRA CO- RAM EO, ET POST EVM SOLITVDO DESERTI.) Quæ terra ante ejus adventum erat ut hortus Hedenis, ubi ille venerit, fiet desertissima,

NEQVE EST QVI EFFVGIAT EVM.) Ita omnia tenebuntur ejus copiis.

QVASI ADSPECTVS EQVORVM, ADSPE- CTVS EORVM.) Sæpe & Græci & Latini, virum fortem, equo generoso comparant, qui Primus inire viam, & fluvios tentare minaces Audet, & ignoto sese committere ponto, Nec vanos horret strepitus.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

Vers. 4.

ET QVASI EQVITES SIC CVRRENT.) Pedi- tes ipsi erunt velocissimi.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

LIKE THE NOISE OF CHARIOTS UPON THE TOPS OF MOUNTAINS SHALL THEY LEAP,) They will come with a great noise.

AS THE NOISE OF A FLAME OF FIRE THAT DEVORETH THE STUBBLE.) By another simile he expresses the noise of the army.

AS A STRONG PEOPLE PREPARED FOR BATTLE,) Here is the כ, as the Hebrews say, כף אמונה. They will always march armed and prepared for battle.

Vers. 5.

SICVT SONITVS QVADRIGARVM SVPER CAPITA MONTIVM EXSILIENT,) Venient magno cum strepitu.

SICVT SONITVS FLAMMÆ IGNIS DEVO- RANTIS STIPVLAM.) Alia similitudine strepitum exer- citus exprimit.

VELVT POPVLVS FORTIS PRÆPARATVS AD PRÆLIVM,) Hic כ est, ut Hebræi loquuntur, כף אמונה. incedent semper armati, paratique prælio.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

AT HIS FACE THE PEOPLES SHALL BE TORMENTED.) The peoples shall grieve at his coming.

ALL FACES SHALL BE TURNED INTO A POT.) Into the soot of a pot. Thus the Greeks: that is, such as a pot is, as the Chaldean well explains. Faces grow black with fear, Isaiah 13, verse 8.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

A FACIE EJVS CRVCIABVNTVR POPVLI.) Dolebunt populi illo veniente.

OMNES VVLTVS REDIGENTVR IN OL- LAM.) In fuliginem ollæ. Ita Græci : id est, qualis est olla, ut Chaldæus bene explicat. Metu nigrescunt vultus, Esaias 13. vers. 8.

## 2:7
Verf. 7. AS MIGHTY MEN THEY SHALL RUN.) As those who fear nothing.

THEY SHALL CLIMB THE WALL.) The walls of many cities. 2 Chron. 32, 1. Isa. 36, 1.

MEN SHALL WALK IN THEIR WAYS.) They shall proceed where they wish.

AND THEY SHALL NOT TURN ASIDE FROM THEIR PATHS.) No one shall be able to turn them away.

Latin:

Verf. 7. SICVT FORTES CVRRENT.) Vt qui nihil timeant.

ADSENDENT MVRVM.) Muros urbium multa- rum. 2. Paralip. 32, 1. Esa. 36, 1.

VIRI IN VIIS SVIS GRADIENTVR.) Pergent quo voluerint.

ET NON DECLINABVNT A SEMITIS SVIS.) Nemo eos avertere poterit.

## 2:8
Vers. 8.

EVERY ONE SHALL NOT STRAITEN HIS BROTHER.) That is, one shall not hinder another on the journey: thus they shall march in well-constructed ranks.

EVERY ONE SHALL WALK IN HIS PATH.) In his own order.

BUT THEY SHALL ALSO FALL THROUGH THE WINDOWS, AND SHALL NOT BE DEMOLISHED.) Others translate well from the Hebrew: They shall rush upon swords, and shall not be wounded. For thus they shall be protected by arms. שלח sword, 2 Chron. 23, v. 10. chap. 32, 5. Nehem. 4, 23. according to the Greeks, who also here [have] ἐν τοῖς βέλεσιν. But בצע is translated sometimes as πλεονεκτεῖν, sometimes as διακόπτειν, ἐκτέμνειν. It is therefore here an active for a passive, as often in such verbs.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

VNVSQVISQVE FRATREM SVVM NON COARCTABIT.) Id est, alter alterum non impediet in itinere: ita bene structis ordinibus incedent.

SINGVLI IN CALLE SVO AMBVLABVNT.) In suo ordine.

SED ET PER FENESTRAS CADENT, ET NON DEMOLIENTVR.) Ex Hebræo bene vertunt alii: In gladios ruent, & non vulnerabuntur. Ita quippe armis muniti erunt. שלח gladius, 2. Paralip. 23. v. 10. cap. 32, 5. Nehem. 4, 23. secundum Græcos, qui & hic ἐν τοῖς βέλεσιν. בצע vero modo πλεονεκτεῖν vertitur, modo διακόπτειν, ἐκτέμνειν. Est ergo hic activum pro passivo, ut sæpe in talibus verbis.

## 2:9
Vers. 9.

THEY SHALL ENTER THE CITY, THEY SHALL RUN ON THE WALL) Into the city, i.e., against the city, they shall clash their arms, and shall run upon the walls, that they may strike them with engines.

THEY WILL CLIMB THE HOUSES) With a tortoise formation made, namely the houses situated at the edge of the cities.

THEY WILL ENTER THROUGH THE WINDOWS LIKE A THIEF) From an ambush: they will capture the towns in every way.

But how can these things be understood concerning the arrival of Sennacherib and the siege of Jerusalem, if Joel prophesied after the times of Isaiah, as Grotius recently indicated? And what is more evident than that the discourse is about that Day of the Lord, which brought destruction to the city? That insistence of the words concerning the calamity of that day, which was far more severe when the city was occupied by Nebuchadnezzar than in the time of Sennacherib, speaks of it; a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind; the pathetic address speaks of it, by which he commands the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem not to sound the trumpet at the arrival of the enemy or to sound the war-trumpet, but to play mournful songs on the trumpet, and to howl, groan, and weep. The scaling of the Jerusalem wall and the occupation of the city speak of it, which could not be done by Sennacherib, but was finally done by Nebuchadnezzar. THEY WILL CLIMB THE WALL. Which Grotius wrongly snatches away to other cities with this gloss of his, the walls of many cities 2. 2 Chronicles 32, 1. Isaiah 36, 1. For the Prophet's discourse here is not about other cities, but he addresses Zion, and commands her to sound the trumpet and howl, as the words of our Prophet are clear in verse 9. THEY WILL ENTER THE CITY, THEY WILL RUN ON THE WALL: THEY WILL CLIMB THE HOUSES, THEY WILL ENTER THROUGH THE WINDOWS LIKE A THIEF. Which do not fit Sennacherib. For concerning him the Lord says in 2 Kings 19, Isaiah 37, 33: He shall not enter this city, and he shall not shoot an arrow there, and a shield shall not occupy it, and he shall not cast a mound around it; by the way that he came, by it he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord.

But Grotius is in vain while he attempts to attach darkness to those words of our Prophet. For they are written with the very rays of the sun. Thus he perverts them: THEY WILL ENTER INTO THE CITY, that is, they will clash arms against the city. THEY WILL RUN ON THE WALL, and they will run against the walls, so that they may strike them with engines. Nor was that done by Sennacherib's army. For not only does the Lord deny that he himself will enter the city, but He also denies that he himself will shoot an arrow into it, He denies that he himself will erect a mound in its circuit. The Hebrew word ישקו does not imply the occupation of arms but a running about: THEY WILL RUN THROUGH THE CITY, i.e., it will not be enough for them to enter through the city and occupy it, but they will crawl through all its corners, they will search out all places most diligently. It can also be said that this is indicated: that they are about to invade the city with such alacrity, as if it were fortified by no walls and gates, but they were permitted to run through it themselves. Those words THEY SHALL CLIMB THE HOUSES are wrongly distorted to mean houses situated at the edge of cities to be climbed by forming a testudo, and those words perversely ENTER THROUGH THE WINDOWS LIKE A THIEF, are snatched away to mean towns to be captured in every way. For the Prophet speaks about the CITY, not about cities; he designates houses in the city of Jerusalem, not those situated at the edge of other cities, nor does he predict that towns will be occupied in every way, but that an irruption into houses will happen through the windows, so that they may look upon everything like thieves. But the gloss of the Belgian paraphrasts about locusts and caterpillars is altogether foreign and inappropriate here, even if Jerome was not foreign to it. The text is too clear about the judgment of the Lord through the Chaldeans against the city, in which most interpreters agree; even Jerome thinks the attack of the Chaldeans is described by the metaphor of locusts. And although he introduces locusts from time to time, here, however, dismissing that metaphor, he interprets those words about climbing houses as referring to the Chaldeans. He says, he keeps the narrative begun, so that he may say they enter the city, run about on the walls: and climb the houses, and enter through the windows like thieves: not that they have the fear of thieves, who are victors: but as thieves are accustomed to enter through windows, and secretly steal: so they, with doors closed, so that there may be no delay, will break in through the windows with total audacity.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

VRBEM INGREDIENTVR, IN MVRO CVR- RENT) In urbem, i. e. adversus urbem, arma concrepa- bunt, & in muros current, ut eos machinis verberent.

DOMOS CONSCENDENT) Testudine facta, do- mos scilicet in extremo urbium positas.

PER FENESTRAS INTRABVNT QVASI FVR) Ex insidiis: omni modo oppida capient.

QUomodo vero de adventu Sennacheribi & ob- sidione Hierosolymæ hæc accipi possunt, si post Esaiæ tempora Joel vaticinatus est, quod proxime indicavit Grotius? Et quid evendentius quam de illa Die Domini sermonem esse, quæ excidium attu- lit urbi? Id ἐπιμονὴ illa verborum de calamitate istius diei, quæ longe gravior fuit, cum urbs occu- paretur à Nebucadnezare, quam Sennacheribi tempore, loquitur, dies tenebrarum & caliginis, dies nubis & turbinis; id loquitur compellatio pathe- tica, qua urbis Hierosolymæ incolas non clange- re ad hostis adventum aut taratantara sonare ju- bet, sed carmina lugubria tuba canere, & ululare, gemere, ac plorare. Id loquitur ascensio muri Hie- rosolymitani & urbis occupatio, quæ à Sennache- ribo fieri non potuit, sed à Nebucadnezare facta demum est. ASCENDENT MURUM. Quod perperam Grotius ad alias urbes abripit hac glos- sa sua, muros urbium multarum 2. Paralip. 32, 1. Es. 36, 1. Non enim de aliis civitatibus hic Pro- phetæ sermo est, sed Sionem compellat, eamque tuba canere & ululare jubet, ut luculenta sunt ver- ba Prophetæ nostri vers. 9. URBEM INGRE- DIENTUR, IN MURO CURRENT: DO- MOS CONSCENDENT, PER FENESTRAS INTRABUNT QUASI FUR. Quæ Sennache- ribo non conveniunt. De hoc enim Dominus 2. Reg. 19. Es. 37, 53. Non intrabit civitatem hanc, & faciet ibi sagitam, & non occupabit eam clypeus, & non mittet in circuitu ejus aggerem, in via, qua venit, per eam revertetur, & civitatem hanc non in- gredietur, dicit Dominus.

Frustra autem est Grotius, dum illis verbis Prophetæ nostri caliginem affingere conatur. Ipsis enim solis radiis scripta sunt. Sic illa pervertit: INGREDIENTUR IN URBEM, id est, ad- versus urbem arma concrepabunt. IN MURO CURRENT, & in muros current, ut eos machi- nis verberent. Neque id à Sennacheribi factum exercitu. Nam non solum negat Dominus i- psum urbem ingressurum, sed negat etiam ipsum sagittam in eam jacturum, negat ipsum aggerem in ejus circuitu erecturum. Vox Ebræa ישקו non oc- cupationem armorum sed discursationem infert: CIVITATEM PERCURRENT, h. e. non satis fuerint eis per urbem ingredi, & occupare, sed omnes ejus perreptabunt angulos, omnia loca perquirent diligentissime. Dici etiam potest id indicari : quod tanta alacritate urbem invasuri sint, ac si nullis mu- ris ac portis esset munita, sed ipsis per eam liceret currere. Illa DOMOS CONSCENDENT perpe- ram detorquentur ad domos in extremo urbium positas testudine facta conscendendas, & per- verse illa : PER FENESTRAS INTRABUNT QUASI FUR, ad oppida omni modo capienda ab- ripiuntur. De URBE enim, non de urbibus lo- quitur Propheta, domos in urbe Hierosolyma de- signat, non in extremo aliarum urbium positas, nec oppida occupatum iri omni modo, sed per fenestras irruptionem in domos futuram prædi- cit, ut tanquam fures omnia suspiciant. Aliena autem prorsus & inconveniens hic est glossa Bel- garum paraphrastarum de locustis & erucis, etsi ab ea alienus non fuerit Hieronymus. Textus ni- mis luculentus est de judicio Domini per Chaldæos adversus urbem, in quo plerique Interpp. consen- tiunt; etiam Hieronymus per metaphoram locu- starum describi putat impetum Chaldæorum. Et quamvis subinde locustas ingerat, hic tamen illa de conscendendis domibus de Chaldæis, missa ista metaphora, interpretatur. Servat, inquit, cœptam narrationem, ut eos dicat urbem ingredi, in muris discurrere: domosque conscendere, & per fenestras intrare quasi fures: non quod furum timorem habe- ant, qui victores sunt: sed ut fures solent ingredi per fenestras, & occulte rapere: sic illi clausis januis, ne ulla sit mora, per fenestras tota irrumpent audacia.

## 2:10
Verse 10. THE EARTH TREMBLED BEFORE HIM) Under the weight of arms. THE SUN AND MOON HAVE BEEN DARKENED, AND THE STARS HAVE WITHDRAWN THEIR SPLENDOR) Smoke from the ruins of towns, and dust stirred up by such a great army, will take away the sight of all the stars. A similar thing, but from another cause, is at Ezek. 32:7.

Latin:

Vers. 10. A FACIE EJVS CONTREMVI T TERRA) Sub pondere armorum. SOL ET LUNA OBTENEBRATI SUNT, ET STELLÆ CONTRAXERVNT SPLENDOREM SUUM) Fumus ex ruinis oppidorum, & pulvis à tanto exercitu excitatus, omnium siderum conspectum adiment. Simile, sed ex causa alia, apud Ezech. 32, 7.

## 2:11
Verse 11. THE LORD HAS GIVEN HIS VOICE, BEFORE THE FACE OF HIS ARMY) Before his army: namely, Sennacherib's. He is about to execute his edicts through them, as his apparitors, as the following words explain. FOR HIS CAMP IS VERY GREAT) However huge his camp is. STRONG, AND DOING HIS WORD) However strong that army is, it will do what has been commanded by God. WHO SHALL SUSTAIN IT) How many will escape?

Latin:

Vers. 11. DOMINVS DEDIT VOCEM SVAM, ANTE FACIEM EXERCITVS SVI) Coram exercitu ipsius: nempe Sennacheribi. Edicta sua per eos, tanquam appari- tores suos, exsecuturus est, ut explicant sequentia. QVIA MVLTA SUNT NIMIS CASTRA EJVS) Vicunque ingentia sunt ejus castra. FORTIA, ET FACIENTIA VERBVM EJVS) Vicunque validus est ille exercitus, faciet quæ à Deo jussa. QVIS SVSTINEBIT EVM) Quotusquisque evadet ?

## 2:12
Verse 12. NOW THEREFORE SAYS THE LORD) Nevertheless says the Lord. He shows that there is still some hope of escaping. WITH ALL YOUR HEART) Seriously and in good faith. IN FASTING, AND IN WEEPING, AND IN MOURNING) To signify the grief conceived from sins.

Latin:

Vers. 12. NVNC ERGO DICIT DOMINVS) Attamen ait Dominus. Ostendit adhuc aliquam esse spem evadendi. IN TOTO CORDE VESTRO) Serio ac bo- na fide. IN JEJVNIO, ET IN FLETV, ET IN PLAN- CTV) Ad significandum dolorem ex peccatis conceptum.

## 2:13
Verse 13. AND REND YOUR HEARTS) Break off your vices from there. AND NOT YOUR GARMENTS) That is, not only your garments, which was accustomed to be done in mourning. A similar way of speaking is in Gen. 32:28 and elsewhere. FOR HE IS KIND AND MERCIFUL) Exod. 34:6. AND PRESTABLE OVER EVIL) In the Hebrew: repenting of the evil: which he has threatened, that is, and this, if man has changed his life for the better.

And who does not see that these things are forced, and do not fit the army of Sennacherib? For how did the earth tremble under the weight of arms? How are the sun and moon darkened by the ruins of towns? Others more correctly accept them with Jerome according to appearance (κατ' δόξαν), not that the earth or heaven is moved, but that to those suffering adversities, and especially to those feeling the flames of the wrath of GOD, these things seem to happen because of the magnitude of the terror: and that in this mourning all things will be most turbulent, which Luther wishes to hint at. Compare Isa. 13:10, Ezek. 32:20. Blessed Gesner refers these to the prodigies which preceded in the earth, clouds, heavens, and air. In the earth through an earthquake, a shaking (σεισμον) and concussion: in the clouds through thunders and lightnings: in the heaven through eclipses and horrible portents of the sun, moon, and stars. When those lights lose their splendor, they will put on a face either bloody or black, or pale, so that they may seem to weep for the calamity of the Israelite people. Finally, in the air, the Lord will give his voice with storms and whirlwinds of winds, and also with lightnings and thunder. Furthermore, how does the Grotian gloss fit the history of the expedition of Sennacherib: How many will escape? For the greatest part of the Jews and the whole metropolis escaped. Nor did Sennacherib do the word of the Lord then, but opposed himself to the Lord with an impious and blasphemous encounter, and his army was routed by the Angel of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ET SCINDITE CORDA VESTRA) Vitia inde abrumpite. ET NON VESTIMENTA VESTRA) Id est, non tantum vestimenta vestra, quod in luctu fieri solebat. Si- mile loquendi genus Gen. 32, 28. & alibi. QVIA BENIGNVS ET MISERICORS) Exod. 34, 6. ET PRÆSTABILIS SVPER MALITIA) In He- bræo: pænitens de malo: quod comminatus est scilicet, id- que, si homo vitam in melius mutaverit.

Et coacta hæc esse, & non convenire Sennache- ribi exercitui, quis non videt? Quomodo enim sub pondere armorum contremuit terra? quo- modo ex ruinis oppidorum sol & luna obtene- brantur? Rectius alii κατ' δόξαν cum Hieronymo ea accipiunt, non quod moveatur terra aut cælum, sed quod adversa patientibus, & præcipue iræ DEI sentientibus flammas, præ terroris magni- tudine hæc videantur fieri: quodque in hoc luctu omnia futura sint turbatissima, quod Lutherus in- nui vult. Confer. Es. 13, 10. Ezech. 32, 20. B. Gesne- rus ad prodigia hæc refert, quæ præcesserint in terra, nubibus, cælis & aëre. In terra per terræ mo- tum, σεισμον & concussionem: in nubibus per to- nitrua & fulmina: in cælo per ecclipses & horrenda solis, lunæ & stellarum portenta. Cum lumina ista splendorem suum amittent, faciem induent vel san- guineam vel atram, vel pallidam, ut calamitatem populiIsraelitici deflere videautur. In aëre denique Dominus ventorum procellis & turbinibus, nec non fulminibus & tonitru vocem suam edet. Por- ro, quomodo congruit historiæ de expeditione Sennacheribi glossa Grotiana: Quotusquisque evadet? Nam evasit maxima Judæorum & tota metropolis. Neque tum fecit verbum Domini Sennacherib, sed Domino se imprio ac blasphe- mo occursu opposuit, & fusus est exercitus ejus ab Angelo Domini.

## 2:14
Verse 14. WHO KNOWS?) The Prophet speaks, and mixes hope with fear, lest he either foster security or leave them in the mire through despair of pardon. See 2 Kings 19:4. IF HE MAY TURN AND FORGIVE) Whether, led by repentance, he may forgive. A similar expression is in Jer. 18:8. This phrase WHO KNOWS does not always introduce doubt, as if he mixes hope with fear: it often denotes an affirmation with a wish, as may be gathered from the similar phrase WHO WILL GIVE, which is translated by 'would that' by everyone, Num. 11:29, Job 6:8, 11:5, ch. 14:13, by which they express through a question what they wish to affirm most vehemently: and various examples teach this, in which these and similar particles are used not in a sense of doubting, but with certain faith. Num. 22:33, Jonah 3:5, 9, 10, Jer. 26:3, Amos 5:15, Lam. 3:29, whence Ambrose, book 2 on repentance, ch. 5: Certainly sometimes it is an assertive particle. Concerning which, let Tarnovius be consulted more fully here. The observation of Blessed Luther is beautiful: In our language this phrase sounds negative or rather dubitative: Who knows? But it is the most apt voice of a penitent. For it embraces both: the sense of sin, which makes us conclude that God is justly angry and punishing us, and the hope of liberation, if indeed God is by nature kind and placable. Thus when the leper in the Gospel says, if you will, you can cleanse me, first by this voice he casts himself at the feet of Christ, freely confessing that he deservedly sustains this punishment. Then he shows the hope of liberation through Christ shining forth in this sense of his sin. But this ought to be our perpetual form of praying, that first we humble ourselves because of sin. Then we raise ourselves into the hope of being heard because of the promises made in Christ. But this hope, as we said above, completes repentance and glorifies God. So also Calvin: For who knows? That is, God is placable, and one must not despair. The Prophet therefore proposes here the difficulty of obtaining pardon, not that he may leave men in suspense (for this would be contrary to the preceding doctrine) but that he may offer some taste of the grace of God, so that they may gradually gather their courage, and meanwhile not immediately rise to security, but come solicitously to God, and with much deliberation, when, that is, they have pondered their offenses. Nor should it be neglected in this place that the discourse is not about the remission of guilt, but about temporal affliction. Concerning the former, the faithful must by no means doubt, lest they derogate from the divine mercy celebrated even by this Prophet; however, the removal of corporal afflictions and the bestowal of corporal benefits are sought conditionally, if it pleases God, and does not hinder our salvation.

Verse of the same.

AND HE SHALL LEAVE BEHIND HIM A BLESSING) After that, namely the hostile army, may he give us that the earth may again bear fruits.

A SACRIFICE AND A DRINK OFFERING TO THE LORD YOUR GOD) That is, from which we may offer to God a μανὰν [gift/offering] and a drink offering. He refers to those things which were said above 1, 9. 13.

Vatablus, Drusius, Piscator, and Mariana also have 'he will leave behind him (the army)', but it is too remote, nor is the word 'army' repeated from verse 2 sufficiently appropriate in this place. Closer and more convenient is 'lamentation, mourning, and weeping', after him (the lamentation and weeping), as also 'the day of the Lord', so that the sense may be: after that day of the Lord, so that, if you cannot avert the judgment of the Lord entirely, the Lord may nevertheless leave behind after that judgment a blessing still: which not only refers to the fruit of the earth, but also to other benefits of God; both spiritual and corporal (since the word is general) for which they may rightly offer a drink offering and a sacrifice to God for the sake of gratitude; so that those words may not refer to the matter of the blessing to be left behind, but to the final cause, which is the celebration of the divine name. Rightly B. Luther: What he adds concerning the blessing is rightly understood as concerning a corporal blessing, that if the people do penance, the Lord is about to heap upon them every kind of blessing, and to deliver them from the Babylonian enemy. Yet it also includes the promise concerning Christ, which was exhibited in the last days. For then the Lord truly blessed his people, and restored the oblation and the drink offering, i.e., true worship, not feigned, faith, confession, invocation in dangers, the preaching of the mercy of God, etc. We are warned, however, in this place also, that God adorns us with his blessing for this reason, that we may confer it to the worship of God, not that we may abuse it for luxury. As, however, usually happens. The same calamity and scarcity of the same time is referred to in these and the preceding chapter verse 9. 13., nor does the opinion of Grotius itself admit that this is interpreted concerning the incursion of Sennacherib, and that concerning the incursion of Shalmaneser. Not badly Christ. à Castro, thus paraphrasing: Perhaps he will change his mind, and will not punish entirely but after a little (LXX. of years) space, he will leave us a blessing, so that, brought back into our land, we may renew from its fruits the former sacrifice with a drink offering to the Lord our God.

Latin:

Vers. 14. QVIS SCIT?) Propheta loquitur, & spem metu miscet, ne aut securitatem foveat, aut veniæ desperatione illos in luto relinquat. Vide 2. Reg. 19, 4. SI CONVERTATUR ET IGNOSCAT) An pœnitentia ductus ignoscat. Locutio similis apud Je- rem. 18, 8. Phrasis hæc מִי יוֹדֵעַ non semper dubitationem infert, quasi spem metu misceat: sæpe affirmatio- nem notat cum voto, ut è simili phrasi מִי יִתֵּן Quis dabit, quæ per utinam ab omnibus vertitur Num. 11,29. Job. 6, 8. 11, 5. cap. 14, 13. quâ quæ vehe- mentissime affirmare volunt, per interrogationem efferunt, colligere liceat: atque exempla varia do- cent, in quibus hæ & similes particulæ adhiben- tur non sensu dubitandi, sed fide certa. Num. 22, 33. Jon. 3, 5. 9. 10. Jerem. 26, 3. Am. 5, 15. Thr. 3, 29. unde Ambrosius lib. 2. de pœnitent. cap. 5. Certe quandoque particula assertiva est. De quo videatur fusius Tarnovius h. 1. Pulcra est obser- vatio B. Lutheri: In nostra lingua phrasis hæc ne- gative seu potius dubitative sonat: Quis scit? sed est aptissima pœnitentis vox. Utrumque enim comple- ctitur, & sensum peccati, qui facit, ut statuamus Deum juste irasci, ac nos plectere, & spem liberatio- nis, fiquidem Deus natura benignus & placabilis est. Sic cum leprosus in Evangelio dicit, si vis, po- tes me mundare, primum hac voce se abjicit ad pe- des Christi, libere confitens, se merito hanc pœnam sustinere. Deinde ostendit elucescentem in hoc sensu peccati sui spem liberationis per Christum. Debet autem perpetua hæc nostra orandi forma esse, ut pri- mum propter peccatum nos humiliemus. Deinde erigamus nos in spem exauditionis propter promissio- nes in Christo factas. Absolvit autem, ut supra diximus, hæc spes pœnitentiam, & glorificat Deum. Sic etiam Calvinus: Quis enim scit? Hoc est, Deus est placabilis, & non est desperandum. Propheta igitur hic difficultatem proponit impetrandæ veniæ, non ut relinquat suspensos homines (hoc enim con- trarium esset superiori doctrinæ) sed ut gustum ali- quem præbeat gratiæ DEI, ut paulatim colligant animos, & interea non statim assurgant ad securi- tatem, sed solicite veniant ad Deum, & cum mul- ta deliberatione, ubi scilicet reputaverint suas of- fensas. Neque negligendum hoc loco est, quod non de remissione culpæ, sed de afflictione tem- porali sermo sit. De illa nullo pacto dubitan- dum est fidelibus, ne misericordiæ divinæ ab hoc etiam Propheta celebratæ derogent; corpora- lium autem afflictionum ablatio, & beneficio- rum corporalium collatio sub conditione meriro petitur, si Deo placeat, nostræque saluti haud officiat.

Verf. eod.

ET RELINQVAT POST SE BENEDICTIO- NEM) Post illam, nempe exercitum hostilem, det nobis at rursum terra fruges ferar.

SACRIFICIVM ET LIBAMEN DOMINO DEO VESTRO) Id est, unde Deo μανὰν & libamen offeramus. Respicit ad ea quæ dicta sunt supra 1, 9. 13.

Illud relinquet post illum (exercitum) Vata- blus, Drusius, Piscator, Mariana etiam habent, sed nimis remota est, nec satis congrua hic loci vox exercitus repetita è vers. 2. Propinquior & convenientior est planctus, luctus & fletus, post illum (planctum & fletum) ut & dies Domini, ut sensus sit: post illum diem Domini, ut nem- pe, si judicium Domini non omnino averte- re possitis, relinquat tamen Dominus post il- lud judicium adhuc benedictionem: quæ non solum respicit terræ frugem, sed etiam alia bene- ficia Dei; cum spiritualia, tum corporalia (si- quidem vox generalis sit) ob quæ merito libent, & sacrificium Deo gratitudinis ergo offeratur; ut verba illa non materiam referant benedictionis re- linquendæ, sed causam finalem, quæ est celebratio nominis divini. Recte B. Lutherus: Quod de be- nedictione addit, recte hoc intelligitur de benedictione corporali, quod si agat populus pænitentiam, Domi- nus omni genere benedictionis eum sit cumulaturus, & liberaturus à Babylonico hoste. Includit tamen e- tiam promissionem de Christo, quæ in novissimis die- bus exhibita est. Tum enim vere benedixit Domi- nus populo suo, & restituit oblationem & libamen h. e. veros cultus, non simulatos, fidem, confessio- nem, invocationem in periculis, prædicationem misericordiæ Dei &c. Admonemur autem hoc in lo- co ejus quoque, quod benedictione sua Deus ideo nos ornat, ut eam conferamus ad cultum Dei, non ut ab- utamur ea ad luxum. Sicut tamen plerumque fit. Eandem calamitatem ac penuriam ejusdem tem- poris his & præcedente capite vers. 9. 13. respici, nec ipsa Grotii admittit sententia, qua hæc de Sennacheribi, illa de Salmanassaris interpreta- tur est incursione. Non male Christ. à Castro, ita παραφράζων: Fortasse mutabit sententiam, & non puniet omnino sed post paucum (LXX. an- norum) spatium, nobis relinquet benedictionem, ut reducti in terram nostram, ex fructibus illius reno- vemus sacrificium pristinum cum libatione Domino Deo nostro.

## 2:15
Verse 15.

BLOW THE TRUMPET IN ZION) For by a trumpet also the people were called together Num. 10, 7. SANCTIFY A FAST) What the Prophet advises here, Hezekiah followed at that time, concerning which it is treated here 2 Kings 19, 1. and following. CALL A CONGREGATION) As much as you can, which the following things explain more broadly.

Latin:

Verf. 15.

CANITE TVBA IN SION) Nam tuba etiam con- vocabatur populus Num. 10, 7. SANCTIFICATE JEJVNIVM) Quod hic monet Propheta, id secutus est Ezechias eo tempore, de quo hic agitur 2. Reg. 19, 1. & sequentibus. VOCATE COETVM) Quam maxime potestis, quod sequentia latius explicant.

## 2:16
Verse 16.

GATHER THE PEOPLE) The common folk. SANCTIFY THE CHURCH;) Let the Levites prepare themselves, who are the קהל [congregation] by excellence. ASSEMBLE THE ELDERS) Both that highest senate, and those who preside over individual cities. GATHER THE CHILDREN) Such was the custom of those nations Judith 6, 7. nor is it a wonder, since even the cattle were kept from fodder at such a time. Jonah 3, 7. in the cited place of Judith. AND THOSE THAT SUCK THE BREASTS) Even those that suck the breasts.

Why are the Levites the קהל [congregation] by excellence? And where is this word claimed for the Levites by way of eminence? Perhaps Grotius believed that the Levites in the Old [Testament], as in the N.T. under the Papacy, were considered the clergy by the Church by way of eminence?

Verse of the same.

LET THE BRIDEGROOM GO FORTH FROM HIS CHAMBER AND THE BRIDE FROM HER BRIDAL CHAMBER) The separation of the married couple has been a companion of fasting from antiquity, Exod. 19, 15. 1 Cor. 7, 5. B. Gesnerus thus: He commands even new bridegrooms and brides to come forth from the bridal chamber, and to convene in the public assembly of the Church, and to pour out prayers for the safety of the Republic. We do not, however, disapprove of the commentary of Grotius, if this be the sense: That the Prophet commands the Bridegroom and Bride to go out from their bridal chamber, i.e., not to enter the bridal chamber, and thus to cast aside all joy, to defer their nuptials to another opportune time, and now not to be free for delights, because, to wit, God appears armed against all, so that He may shake off security from all, where God is present with the signs of His wrath.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

CONGREGATE POPVLVM) Plebem. SANCTIFICATE ECCLESIAM;) Præparent se Levitæ, qui קהל per excellentiam. COADVNATE SENES) Tum illum summum se- natum, tum illos, qui urbibus singulis præsident. CONGREGATE PARVVLOS) Mos is erat illarum gentium Judith 6, 7. nec id mirum, cum & pecudes à pa- bulis tali tempore abstinerentur. Jonas 3,7. Judith dicto loco. ET SVGENTES VBERA) Etiam sugentes ubera.

Cur Levitæ קהל per excellentiam? Et ubi hæc vox Levitis ἐξοχικῶς vindicata? Num forte credi- dit Grotius Levitas in Veteri, ut in N. T. sub Papa- tu clericos habitos per Ecclesiam κατ' ἐξοχὴν?

Vers. eod.

EGREDIATVR SPONSVS DE CVBILI SVO ET SPONSA DE THALAMO SVO) Secubatio con jugum ab antiquo comes jejunii Exod. 19, 15. 1. Cor. 7, 5. B. Gesnerus ita: Jubet novos etiam conjuge sponsos & sponsas è thalamo prodire, inque publi- cum Ecclesiæ congressum convenire, & pro salu- te Reipublicæ preces fundere. Non tamen impro- bamus commentarium Grotianum, si hic sensus sit: Jubere Prophetam Sponsum & Sponsam exire è thalamo suo, h. e. non intrare thalamum, adeoque omnem abjicere lætitiam, differre suas nuptias in aliud tempus oportunum, & jam non vacare deli- tiis, quia sc. Deus apparet armatus contra omnes, ut excutiat omnibus securitatem, ubi Deus cum si- gnis iræ suæ adest.

## 2:17
Verse 17. BETWEEN THE VESTIBULE AND THE ALTAR THE PRIESTS, THE MINISTERS OF THE LORD, SHALL WEEP, AND SHALL SAY) Let them weep and say אולם, understand here the vestibule, that place from which one descended from the priestly basilica, from where the altar of burnt offerings was not far. It is fitting for the pious to testify to their grief over the sins of the people.

GIVE NOT THY HERITAGE TO REPROACH) Thy peculiar people.

THAT THE NATIONS SHOULD RULE OVER THEM) Those who make gods for themselves.

WHEREFORE DO THEY SAY AMONG THE PEOPLES) They would say.

WHERE IS THEIR GOD) Psal. 115, 2. Where is that God whom they boasted was known and worshipped by them alone?

Latin:

Vers. 17. INTER VESTIBVLVM ET ALTARE PLORABUNT SACERDOTES MINISTRI DOMINI, ET DICENT) Plorent & dicant אולם, vestibulum hic intellige, locum illum, quo descendebatur ex basilica sacerdotali, unde non longe erat altare holocaustorum. Convenit piis dolorem suum testari, super peccatis po- puli.

NE DES HEREDITATEM TVAM IN OPPRO- BRIVM) Populum tibi peculiarem.

VT DOMINENTVR EIS NATIONES) Illi qui sibi Deos faciunt.

QVARE DICVNT IN POPVLIS) Dicerent.

VBI EST DEVS EORVM) Psal. 115, 2. ubi ille Deus quem à se unis nosci & coli jactabant?

## 2:18
Verse 18.

THE LORD HAS BEEN JEALOUS FOR HIS LAND) That is, if you do these things, the Lord will no longer suffer the injury done to His people to go unpunished.

AND HAS SPARED HIS PEOPLE) He will spare the Jerusalemites, and those who shall flee to Jerusalem, so that through them the land may be cultivated again.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ZELATVS EST DOMINVS TERRAM SVAM) Id est, si hæc faciatis, jam non ultra inultam patietur Do- minus injuriam populo suo factam.

ET PEPERCIT POPVLO SVO) Parcet Hieroso- lymitanis, & iis qui Hierosolyma refugient, ut per eos rur- sum terra colatur.

## 2:19
Verse 19.

AND THE LORD ANSWERED) He will answer through Isaiah 2 Kings 19, 21. and the following. Isaiah 37, 21.

That the prediction of Joel does not agree with the chronology or history of Sennacherib has been shown before. Therefore, our interpreters understand the words: And the Lord answered, or is about to answer, according to the usage of Scripture, as concerning the hearing of prayers. For He is said to answer then, when He hears our prayers. B. Luther: And the Lord will answer: that is, He will not be silent to the prayers of His people. Being invoked, He will be present, He will hear, and He will say to His people, Behold, I send you grain.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ET RESPONDIT DOMINVS) Respondebit per Esaiam 2. Reg. 19, 21. & sequentibus. Esaias 37, 21.

Non convenire Chronologiæ, neque historiæ Sennacheribi prædictionem Joelis, antea osten- sum. Simplicius ergo nostri verba: Et respon- dit, vel responsurus est Dominus ex usu scripturæ in- telligunt de precum exauditione. Tum enim re- spondere dicitur, cum exaudit preces nostras. B. Lutherus: Et respondebit Dominus: h. e. Non ta- cebit ad populi sui preces. Invocatus aderit, exau- diet, & dicet populo suo, Ecce mitto vobis fru- mentum.

## 2:20
Vers. 20.

AND HIM WHO IS FROM THE NORTH I WILL REMOVE FAR FROM YOU) The Assyrian. Thus also the Chaldeans are called Northerners by the Hebrews. For צפון properly is the wind between the north and the east, and is translated also as ἀπηλιώτης, as we have said elsewhere. Assyria is more remote than Chaldea, but in the same region of the sky.

AND I WILL DRIVE HIM INTO A LAND UNPATHED AND DESERT) I will impel him (to ruin, that is) into that very land laid waste and desolate, by means of him.

AND THE FACE) Of those falling by that divinely-sent evil, concerning which see 2 Kings 19:35, Isaiah 37:36.

TOWARD THE EASTERN SEA) Toward the Asphaltite, I will turn them, that is, to show that they were no better than the inhabitants of Sodom.

AND HIS END TOWARD THE UTMOST SEA) They will lie with their backs turned to the Syrian sea, which is called האחרון by the Hebrews, Deut. 11:24, 34:2, namely so that their blood may flow out into it, and thus Judea may be purged.

AND HIS STENCH SHALL ASCEND, AND HIS ROT SHALL ASCEND) It will infect the sky for a long time. Isaiah 34:3.

BECAUSE HE HAS ACTED PROUDLY) Against God 2 Kings 19:22, Isaiah 37:22, Job 1:21, 1 Macc. 7:41.

These things cannot be understood of Sennacherib, to whom Grotius drags each point by the, as they say, twisted neck. He was not driven into a land unpathed and desert, but returned to his own land, which was then very flourishing and proud. Nor can the land of the Jews be understood by the unpathed and desert land, which was not reduced to such a standstill by Sennacherib that it deserved to be called unpathed and desert. Nor did he seek it in it. He was killed in the temple of Nisroch by his sons. Those words about the face of the falling ones, the evil διηλά- τω, do not appear in the text. And is that gloss not merely arbitrary, far-fetched, and frivolous, that God wishes to turn the face toward the eastern sea against the Asphaltite [Sea], to show that they were no better than the inhabitants of Sodom, and that they were about to turn their backs to the Syrian sea, so that their gore might flow out into it, and thus Judea be purged? For not even that is certain, that gore was poured out when the army was destroyed by the angel. Nor is there talk of the stench and putrefaction of the Assyrian army around Jerusalem, but of the enemy expelled into an impassable and desert land far from the land of the Jews: who is to be cast into the eastern sea and into the uttermost sea. Which, as they in no way fit Sennacherib, others apply to others: Ribera and Cornel. a Lapide to Holofernes, Judith ch. 2. Theodoret and Christopher a Castro say it was fulfilled when God

He overthrew Belshazzar with the city of Babylon and the whole kingdom through Cyrus, because the Chaldeans, who were then living in Judea and presiding over it (Jer. 40:10), having heard of this slaughter of their lord Belshazzar, fled in terror into impassable wildernesses, partly toward the Dead Sea, situated to the east of Judea, partly toward the Mediterranean Sea, situated to the west of the same, and many of them were killed by the Jews and Persians, so that the stench and putrefaction of the slain filled the air, and thus their pride and tyranny, by which they proudly oppressed the people of God, were punished. Blessed Luther thinks the promise was conditional, which was never fulfilled, since the condition was not fulfilled. Jerome, the Belgian Paraphrasts, and Tarnovius refer it to the army of locusts. But that seems forced. However, we do not think there is a need to apply these precisely to certain individuals. Indeed, God promises the Jewish people then an abundance of food; 'Behold I will send you grain, and wine, and oil,' by which terms all things necessary for sustenance are comprehended; then tranquility and security to be granted hereafter against the incursion of enemies, because He does not wish to give His people over to the reproach of enemies any longer, and to expose them to their petulance, but to bestow tranquility and peace upon His Church, which was fulfilled after the resolution of the Babylonian captivity; then the destruction of the enemies of the people, who were hostile to them from the North, namely the Chaldeans (of whom Joel treated), because He wishes to break their power and expel them far from His people, and cast them into an unpleasant, impassable, desert, and inhospitable land. Therefore, He threatens the Assyrian and Chaldean empire with the greatest destruction, while He says that its front part is to be dissipated to the Eastern ocean, and the rest to the Western. And He predicts not only exile, but also slaughter; that He wishes to kill their army, by sending in the greater power of some other, so that the bodies of the slain will lack the honor of burial, and be cast out and scattered here and there through the fields, and be trampled by feet, so that the stench rising from them might infect the air. The cause also of such a great slaughter is subjoined, because the Assyrian army acted proudly, namely ascribing the victory to its own power and wisdom, not bringing it as accepted from the Lord. Just as the same is signified at length in Isaiah 10:5, and is reproached to the Babylonian Tyrant. This was fulfilled in the Assyrians partly through the Persians and Medes, who took Babylon (Dan. 7:5), partly through Alexander the Great, who brought Assyria, Babylon, and Persia under his power (Dan. 8:20), as our Blessed Gesner explains these things. Similarly Blessed Wigandus: 'The stench shall ascend,' I will punish your enemies (the Babylonians), and he speaks figuratively, they will be stinking corpses. For God severely punishes the impious, after He has used their works in chastising His own.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ET EVM QVI AB AQVILONE EST PRO- CVL FACIAM A VOBIS) Assyrium. Sic & Chaldæi, A- quilonares Hebræis dicuntur. Nam צפון proprie est ventus inter septentrionem & ortum, vertiturque & ἀπηλιώτης, ut alibi diximus. Assyria Chaldæa remotior, sed in eadem cœli regione.

ET EXPELLAM EVM IN TERRAM INVIAM ET DESERTAM) Impellam eum (ad ruinam scilicet) in ipsa illa terra vastata atque desolata, per ipsum.

ET FACIEM) Cadentium illo malo θεηλάτῳ. de quo vide 2. Reg. 19, 35. Esaiæ 37, 36.

CONTRA MARE ORIENTALE) Versus Asphal- titen, convertam scilicet, ut ostendam, illos Sodomorum habitatoribus nihilo fuisse meliores.

ET EXTREMVM EJVS AD MARE NOVISSI- MVM) Jacebunt obversi terga mariSyriaco, quod האחרון dicitur Hebræis, Deut. 11, 24. 34, 2. nempe ut eo effluat eorum cruor, & sic Judæa purgetur.

ET ASCENDET FOETOR EJVS, ET ASCEN- DET PVTREDO EJVS) Inficiet diu cœlum. Esaias 34, 34.

QVIA SVPERBE EGIT) Adversus Deum 2. Reg. 19, 22. Esaias 37, 22. Job. 1, 21. 1. Macc. 7, 41.

De Sennacheribo hæc intelligi nequeunt, ad quem, obtorto, quod ajunt, collo singula abripit Grotius. Non expulsus is fuit in terram inviam, & desertam, sed in terram suam, tum valde floren- tem, ac superbam reversus. Nec per terram inviam & desertam Iudæorum terra intelligi potest, quæ per Sennacheribum ita ad incitas reducta non fuit, ut invia & deserta dici meruerit. Neque etiam in ea petiit Sennacherib. occisus in templo Nisroch à filiis. Illa de facie cadentium malo διηλά- τω in textu non comparent. Et annon mere arbi- traria, tricofa, atque frivola est illa glossa, quod fa- ciem contra mare orientale versus Asphaltitem con- vertere Deus velit, ut ostendat illos Sodomorum habi- tatoribus nihilo fuisse meliores, quodque terga obver- suri sint mari Syriaco, ut eo effluat eorum cruor, & sic Judæa purgetur. Nam ne id quidem certum est, cruorem effusum, cum ab angelo interemtus est ex- ercitus. Nec de fœtore ac putredine exercitus Assyria- ci circa Hierosolyma, sed hostis in terram inviam & desertam procul à Judæorum terra expulsi sermo est: qui ad mare orientale, & ad mare novissimum projiciendus. Quæ uti nullatenus Sennacheribo congruunt, alii ad alios applicant: Riebera & Cor- nel. à Lapide ad Holofernem Judith. c. 2. Theodoretus & Christophorus à Castro impletum dicunt, cum Deus

Balthasarem cum urbe Babylone totoque regno per Cy- rum evertit, quod Chaldæi, qui tum in Judæa dege- bant, illique præsidebant Jer. 40, 10. audita hac Bal- tasaris Domini sui clade, perterriti fugerint in in- vias solitudines, partim versus mare mortuum, si- tum ad Orientem Judææ, partim versus mare Medi- terraneum situm ad occidentem ejusdem, multi- que ex illis à Judæis & Persis cæsi sint, ita ut occiso- rum fœtor & putredo aërem compleret, sicque pu- nita sit eorum superbia & tyrannis, qua populum Dei superbe opprimebant. B. Lutherus conditiona- lem fuisse promissionem putat, quæ nunquam imple- ta sit, cum conditio impleta non fuerit. Ad exerci- tum locustarum referunt Hieronymus, Paraphrastæ Belgici, Tarnovius. Sed id coactum videtur. Non autem existimamus opus esse ad certa præcise indi- vidua hæc applicare. Nimirum promittit Deus po- pulo Judaico tum victus abundantiam; Ecce ego mittam vobis frumentum, & vinum & oleum, qui- bus appellationibus omnia ad victum necessaria comprehenduntur; tum ab hostium incursione tranquillitatem & securitatem olim præstandam, quod non velit deinceps amplius populum dare in opprobrium hostium, & petulantiæ ipsorum expo- nere, sed Ecclesiæ suæ tranquillitatem, & pacem largiri, quod impletum est post solutionem capti- vitatis Babylonicæ, tum hostium populi, qui ab A- quilone ipsis infesti erant, eversionem Chaldæo- rum nempe (de quibus egit Joel) quod eorum po- tentiam velit frangere, ipsosq; procul à populo suo expellere, atque in terram inamœnam, inviam, de- sertam, & inhospitam ejicere. Assyriaco proinde & Chaldaico imperio minatur maximam destructio- nem, dum ait, partem ejus anteriorem ad oceanum O- rientalem, & reliquam ad Occidentalem dissipatum iri. Neque exilium solummodo, sed etiam internecio- nem prædicit; quod exercitum ipsis velit intertice- re, immissa majore alterius cujuspiam potentia, ita ut interfectorum corpora sepulturæ honore ca- ritura sint, & hinc inde dispersa per campos abjici, ac pedibus proculcari debeant, ita ut fœtor ab illis ascendens aërem inficiat. Causa quoque tantæ cla- dis subjungitur, quia Assyriacus exercitus superbe egit, suæ scilicet potentiæ & sapientiæ victoriam adscribens, non Domino acceptam ferens. Sicut idem Es. 10, 5. prolixe significatur, & Tyranno Ba- bylonio exprobratur. Completum hoc est in Assy- riis partim per Persas & Medos, qui Babylonem ce- perunt Dan. 7, 5. partim per Alexandrum Magnum, qui Assyriam, Babylonem & Persidem in suam po- testatem redegit. Dan. 8, 20. ut hæc exponit B. Ge- snerus noster. Similiter B. Wigandus: Ascendet fœ- tor, puniam hostes vestros (Babylonios) ac loquitur figurate, erunt cadavera fœtentia. Nam Deus im- pij pios, postquam ipsorum opera in castigandis suis usus est, severe punit.

## 2:21
Verse 21. FEAR NOT, O LAND) O Jewish people, as above. He speaks as if he were present at those events, after the slaughter of Sennacherib, as the Prophets often do.

FOR THE LORD HATH DONE GREAT THINGS) He undertook great things to be done.

Latin:

Vers. 21. NOLITE TIMERE TERRA) Popule Ju- daice, ut supra. Loquitur, quasi rebus illis, post cladem Sennacheribi, interesset, ut sæpe Prophetæ.

QVONIAM MAGNIFICAVIT DOMINUS UT FACERET) Res magnas agendas suscepit.

## 2:22
Verse 22. FEAR NOT, YE BEASTS OF THE FIELD) Stags, does, and similar wild animals. See above 1:20.

GERMINAVERUNT) They sprout.

SPECIOSA) Pastures.

DESERTI) See above 1, 20.

QVIA LIGNUM ATTULIT FRUCTUM SUUM) Trees of every kind bear their fruits.

FICUS ET VINEA DEDERUNT VIRTUTEM SUAM.) Their riches.

Latin:

Vers. 22. NOLITE TIMERE ANIMALIA REGIO- NIS) Cervi, capreæ, & feræ similes. Vide supra 1, 20.

GERMINAVERUNT) Herbescunt.

SPECIOSA) Pascua.

DESERTI) Vide supra 1, 20.

QVIA LIGNUM ATTULIT FRUCTUM SUUM) Arbores omnis generis sua poma ferunt.

FICUS ET VINEA DEDERUNT VIRTUTEM SUAM.) Divitias suas.

## 2:23
Vers. 23. DEDIT VOBIS DOCTOREM JUSTITIÆ) Isaiah.

This is wrongly explained as referring to Isaiah. For Joel was later than Isaiah, and he has not prophesied about Sennacherib thus far, but about the army of the Chaldeans, which destroyed Jerusalem. And therefore the interpretation of some Jews, and of Ruffinus, who make this Teacher Hezekiah, who stirred up the people to piety and the worship of God (2 Chron. 30), is also rejected, as is that of others who understand King Josiah, who overturned the altars of the idols. Some more recent Rabbis, as also Lyranus, Hugo, and Dionysius, and others, interpret this as the Prophets of the Jews after the Babylonian captivity, Zechariah, Haggai, and Malachi, and they commonly render it 'Teachers of righteousness,' to which the translation of the blessed Luther seems to favor, rendering these in the plural number: 'Der Euch Lehrer zu Gerechtigkeit giebet' [He who gives you teachers of righteousness]: and the marginal gloss: 'He means to say/ until Christ comes/ there shall remain with you preaching and food/ spiritual and worldly government/ that is/ the teachers of righteousness/ and the fruits of the land/ as it happened at first/ and formerly.' Concerning Christ, however, our same blessed Luther understands it in the singular in his Commentary on this passage, which opinion the blessed Wigandus, the blessed Gefnerus, the blessed Winckelmannus, and others embrace. It seems to favor him: 1. because here the children of Zion are stirred up to joy in the Lord their God: which is accustomed to be done by the Prophets for the same reason when they prophesy about Christ (Is. 61, Zech. 2, ch. 9). Where the beautiful observation of the blessed Luther is not to be neglected: it is customary, says the Man of God, for the Church of the New Testament to come under the name of Zion: And that for this reason. On Mount Zion of Jerusalem was the royal citadel, built by David, as history teaches (2 Sam. 5). But because Christ was promised to David, Christ is also called the King of Zion, as the son and heir of David. Hence Mount Zion is called the holy mountain (Ps. 2). Because the holy seed is to reign there, just as Ps. 110 says, that this King would send forth his scepter from Zion. For this reason, therefore, the children of Zion are called the Church by their king, who was to dwell in Zion, and to inaugurate a new kingdom from there, through the preaching of the Gospel: the Church does not have its denomination from Mount Moriah. For although that mountain was dedicated to the worship of God, and therefore is also called holy by the Prophets, nevertheless, because these forms of worship were to be abrogated once Christ was exhibited, as a shadow and figure, the Church has its name rather from Zion.

2. That the Prophet speaks μοναδικῶς [uniquely] of one Teacher, and indeed with the He Hajediab, and also with the article הַ prefixed, which has the force of pointing out something singular and peculiar, so that there is designated that certain Teacher promised of old and well known to the faithful and vehemently desired, THAT TEACHER, whom the Holy Scripture calls thus κατ' ἀντονομασίαν [by antonomasia], that Prophet promised through Moses Deut. 18, 19. The Teacher and Evangelist of the nations Is. 55, 4. that unique Master and Rabbi Matt. 23, 8. (3) That he denotes him by his own proper name as the Teacher of righteousness, which Christ rightly claims for himself Is. 63, 1. I am the Teacher of righteousness. Concerning whom the blessed Luther, having instituted a comparison of Christ and Moses, elegantly says: The Prophet says that God will not only give a Teacher or master, but adds, for righteousness, that is, one who by his word and doctrine, which he will bring, will free men from sins and make them righteous. No one will say that Moses was such a Teacher. Moses teaches excellently concerning the will of God, what God demands of us, what must be done by us if we wish to do the will of God. On this subject Moses has no equal. But what does John the Baptist answer? This, namely: The Law was given through Moses, that is, Moses is only a Lawgiver, he only does this, that he shows what must be done by us. But meanwhile, hearts depraved by sin abhor this will of God, and prefer to follow their own desires. And if any do govern these vicious impulses in any way, this happens only from fear of punishment, and not indeed from a zeal for obedience or love of God, while the heart meanwhile hangs entirely in another direction. But because the law of God requires a pure heart, and we cannot even control our hands, tongue, and other members without often sinning against the law of God, hence it happens that, as Paul speaks, Moses is a minister of death, and the law increases sin, and kills. For if there were no law, there would be no sin. Now since the law has been placed, and our heart convicts us of a violated law, what else remains but that minds are troubled, that sin becomes exceedingly sinful, and the law exposes us to death? For just as a bond convicts you of a debt, so that you cannot deny it, so the Law is truly a handwriting against us, by which minds are convicted of sin, and consequently are subjected to the penalties established by the Law. The Jews boast of such a Teacher when they boast of the Law and Moses, who like a lictor and executioner seizes the thief and strangles him with a noose. And yet it is true that the doctrine of the Law is necessary, holy, and perfect. But all vice is in us. For through sin, with our will and intellect corrupted, we can neither see what is right, nor, if it is shown, perform it. Therefore, another doctrine is needed, another Teacher, who first heals this vice of the hearts. Then also he supplies the strength to perform those things which we are commanded by the law to do. Since Christ is such a Teacher, Joel attributes to him this excellent and sublime name, that he is the Teacher of righteousness, and not, like Moses, a Teacher of sin. For because he shows what we should do, but we cannot do it, he makes nothing else but sinners out of us, and burdens our consciences, disturbs our minds, and fills them with fear, nay, even with hatred of the judgment of God. For nature would prefer that God did not exist, rather than be subjected to eternal punishments. Not only does the law not heal this impiety, but it even kindles and increases it, not, as I said, by its own fault, for it is heavenly rain. But by our own, who, like a rock watered by heavy showers, yet remain perpetually barren. Christ, therefore, the King of Zion the holy mountain, is the Teacher of righteousness. For he changes hearts through the Holy Spirit, and what is vicious in us, this he forgives, just as the Baptist excellently says: The Law was given through Moses: but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Grace is the remission of sins, which is given to those who believe in Christ. Truth, however, is the gift of the Holy Spirit, who changes hearts and incites them to true obedience against sin, and excludes all hypocrisy. Such a Teacher the Prophet here promises to the Church, and bids it therefore to rejoice in the Lord. Thus Isaiah: My righteous servant by his knowledge will justify many, that is, the Son of God will reveal himself through the Gospel, and thus many will be justified. This is from the blessed Luther.

Some add (4) that by the early and latter rain a spiritual rain is designated: that namely, as Gesner explains on page 107, Christ is about to kindly refresh and irrigate the Church of the New Testament with the heavenly dew of his word and sacraments, immediately from the beginning of the sowing that has been done, and then also when it has grown into a mature crop, and the harvest of the last judgment has approached, concerning which below in chapter 3, 13. And certainly it was a most fruitful shower when Christ sent the Apostles into the whole world; and that Teacher of ours, when he had ascended to the heavens and sat down at the right hand of the eternal Father, gave to the Church pastors, teachers, evangelists, etc. Eph. 4, 11. Ps. 68, 19. This was that morning shower. But no less remarkable and fertile was the rain that occurred in these latter times, through the light of the reborn Gospel, to the minds and hearts of men, almost destroyed by the darkness of Papistic superstitions. And this is that evening shower, of which the Prophet speaks here. Thus Gesner. By which also those things which are added in verse 14, and the threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the wine presses will overflow with wine and oil, he interprets on page 108 as concerning spiritual produce. Since the bodily blessing of fields, vineyards, and gardens has been treated above copiously: here without doubt spiritual goods are understood, which are proper to the kingdom of Christ, which does not consist in food and drink, but in righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Rom. 14, 17. But the spiritual food and drink is Christ with all his benefits proposed to us in the Gospel and Sacraments. John 4, 14 and ch. 6, 48. Matt. 22, 2. Is. 25, 6. The rest, however, concerning the compensation of the years which the locust, the cankerworm, etc., ate, Gesner interprets as concerning bodily goods, that the Lord promises that he will add these to the spiritual ones. But B. Luther interpreted these also concerning spiritual benefits, likewise instituting an ἀντιθέσει of Moses and Christ: He signifies, he says, the Prophet the happy success of the Gospel, and the beautiful fruits, which will follow this doctrine of righteousness, not only in that brief corner, in which the Jews dwelt, but through the whole world. These are the barns full and the winepresses overflowing with must and oil. I will repay, or I will compensate you for the years, which the locusts have eaten, and eating you shall eat, that is, you shall eat eagerly and with singular pleasure, as the famished are wont to do. He looks back here also to the Law, it is rightly compared to food, which causes nausea. Not that the law is bad. For it is dew sent down divinely, as Moses calls it, that is, heavenly doctrine. But we have both a palate and a stomach that is vicious, such as that of the sick is wont to be, therefore we loathe wholesome food. Just as Paul says Rom. 8. The mind of the flesh is enmity against God, for it is not subject to the Law of God, for it cannot be. But those who live according to the flesh cannot please God. This is our disease, which vitiates the palate and stomach, so that heavenly food is loathed by us. For those things which please God, displease us. Conversely, those things which please us, displease God. But because the law threatens punishments to transgressors, therefore we abhor it, and we hate it. But the Gospel is that heavenly food, of which this Prophet preaches here, that we are to eat it eagerly and with the greatest pleasure. For it does not, like the law, teach what God demands of us, it does not threaten punishments, but it proposes God, as the Prophet said above, clement, merciful, slow to anger, beneficent, and relenting concerning evil. He shows that the Son of God therefore came into this flesh of ours, that He might destroy the works of the Devil, that is, that He might abolish sin, conquer death, reveal life, and overturn the tyranny of Satan. This is food grateful and sweet to the mind, which terrified souls at the sight of their sins, and from fear of the wrath and judgment of God, like a famished stomach, greedily seize. This is the first benefit of this Teacher, that he brings to us food, which eating we shall eat, that is, ea- eagerly & with singular pleasure. There is another thing, which he does not only say; You shall eat eagerly: But he even adds: & you shall be satisfied. Moreover, he here also looks obliquely to the Law. For although it has its own rites, although it shows what must be done, yet like food that does not satisfy hunger, but rather inflames and irritates the stomach; so the law leaves souls anxious and doubtful about salvation; minds cannot find rest in these. And this defect is in the nature of all studies and works which are undertaken to appease the wrath of God. For they leave souls more doubtful and anxious than they found them. On the contrary, the Gospel, which this Teacher of righteousness brings to us from the bosom of the Father, is solid food, which fills and satisfies the stomach and takes away hunger. For souls, looking upon the Son of God, made a victim for us, find rest in this sacrifice, are filled with joy, and have certain consolation even in death itself. It follows in the Prophet, And you shall praise the name of the Lord your God. This fruit always follows this satiety of heavenly food. You see here also a clear distinction between the Law and the Gospel. The Law works wrath. For souls are moved against God, they judge Him to be unjust and cruel because He burdened this weak nature with this huge mass of the law, which it is impossible to sustain. On the contrary, the Gospel, because it preaches about the mercy and eternal benefits of God the Father, who gave His Son for our sins, and of the Holy Spirit, who kindles in souls confidence toward God through Christ. Therefore, souls looking into these riches of the mercy and goodness of God, burst forth into the praise of God, they proclaim His goodness, they praise and adorn Him, and even cast away their lives rather than their confession. You shall praise, he says, the name of the Lord your God, because He has done wonderful things with you. For these wonderful things are not bodily blessing and abundance of crops, but that to us miserable sinners, who are by nature children of wrath, is given the Teacher of righteousness, the Son of God, who feeds us hungry ones, placed under the Law and the wrath of God, with His word, and in this way makes us just from sinners, pleasing to God from children of wrath, saved from the damned, immortal from mortals. These are truly wonderful things, which no one ever did, except this Teacher of righteousness, the Son of God. Thus B. Luther: Whom B. Winckelmann followed. Comm. in Minor. Prophet. page 210. AND THEY SHALL BE FILLED) The Prophet dwells on the allegory. But just as he compares the abundance of spiritual benefits and evangelical consolations with rain and fertility and the plenty of external things, so he compares the useless and weak [τὸ ἀνωφελὲς ϰαὶ ἀσθενὲς] nature of the law, not being able to bring a corrupt man to perfection, Heb. 7, with sterility, poverty, and defect. But the Gospel or the doctrine of righteousness provides that which is impossible for the law. AND YOU SHALL EAT EATING) that is, you shall eat eagerly. For men, recognizing sin and the wrath of God from the Law, are rightly compared to hungry people eating evangelical food greedily: which are, as the LXX have, foods for righteousness [τὰ βρώματα εἰς δικαιοσύνην]. For to them Christ, the bread of life, becomes sweet. YOU SHALL BE SATISFIED) that is, you shall find rest in God, who is merciful and propitious on account of the Messiah, as if satisfied with every good thing: AND YOU SHALL PRAISE THE NAME OF YOUR GOD) Opulence and satiety of external goods for the most part begets security and rebellion: as the Lord complains in Deut. 32. He grew fat, he kicked, he grew fat, he was covered. He forsook God his maker. But spiritual satiety begets doxology [δοξολογίαν]. WHO HAS DONE WONDERFUL THINGS) For truly the mission of the Son of God into this world, the redemption of the human race, and the mission of the Holy Spirit are wonderful works.

5. B. Luther urges especially also this, that it is promised here that it will not happen hereafter, forever, that the people should be put to shame. But how, he says, can this be said of the people of the law, who, even if they were restored from exile to their own seats, were nevertheless repeatedly harassed in various ways by the Syrians, Egyptians, and finally also by the Romans, and were all but oppressed. And afterwards f. 668. What he adds about not being put to shame forever, I said is a certain argument that these things are to be understood not of the reduction into the land of Canaan from Babel, but of the time of the Gospel, especially since Scripture is accustomed to use this very phrase in other places too, where it does not treat of bodily benefits, but of the remission of sins. Ps. 25 he says: All who waited for you shall not be put to shame, and Ps. 31. In you I hope, O Lord, I shall not be put to shame forever. But this particle also has a notable antithesis of the Gospel and the Law. Justified by faith, says Paul, we have peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access by faith to this grace, in which we stand. And Eph. 3. Through Christ we have freedom and access with confidence, which is through faith. And Heb. 4. Let us therefore approach with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace, that we may meet with help in time of need. For because the Gospel shows Christ, the Son of God, made a victim by the will of the Father, and that He has satisfied for sins, therefore souls do not doubt the benevolence of God, they do not fear, they do not flee from God, they have all their hope placed in the mercy of God. But what will the Law do? It indeed shows what the will of God is, as far as it pertains to our works, and what God demands of us, but because it does not provide the power to do it, nothing else follows the law than confusion. Similarly Winckelmann: AND THE PEOPLE SHALL NOT BE PUT TO SHAME. The Law, showing the turpitude of sin and the wrath of God, works confusion, because it is necessary for sinners to be put to shame before God: but the Gospel takes away confusion, and restores to us the lost glory. For he who believes in Christ shall not be put to shame, Rom. 10.

6. In the last verse of this chapter, B. Luther wishes Christ to be introduced speaking, who teaches that He is true man and true God. And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and I am the Lord your God, and none else. For it is not enough to know that He is in the midst of Israel, that is, that this Teacher is true man, but this must also be added, you shall know that I am the Lord your God and none else. Because, therefore, the Son of God assumed our flesh and dwelt in the midst of Israel, therefore my people shall not be confounded forever: For He came for this reason, that He might dissolve the works of the devil, so that, being freed from the law, sin, death, and Satan, we might be in eternal glory through His death and grace. Thus also Cyril of Alexandria in Comment. p. 226. Manifesting the manner of the economy of the incarnation, and promising that He would empty Himself, and would dwell with those of the earth, made like unto us, that is, made man. For then He was in the midst of Israel, and we escaped ignominy, and were exempted from confusion, death being surely prostrated, sin being killed, and the knowledge of the truth being introduced.

These things are not inappropriate, nor foreign to the Prophetic manner of speaking when they treat of the benefits of the New Testament, but since that compensation for the years of drought looks back to those things which the Prophet had said in the preceding chapter concerning the drought brought on by the locusts, the cankerworm, etc., there is no doubt that bodily benefits are insinuated by them, that the Lord is about to kindly compensate for the former scarcity of the fields and vineyards, which B. Gefner acknowledges here. Furthermore, it seems sufficiently manifest that that early rain, which to the Greeks is πρώϊμος ὑετός, falls then, when the sowing has been done, so that the seed cast into the field may be able to take root, and the latter rain, which ὄψιμος ὑετὸς falls then, when the crop has grown up into stalks and ears, so that the grains may swell, designates the rains customary among the Jews Deut. 11, 14. Jer. 5, 24. Zach. 10, 1. Jas. 5, 7. although text, even if it is not otherwise unknown that the doctrine is compared to rain Is. 50, 10. 11. (Cf. Job 29, 22. Is. 21, 1. 2. Am. 6, 26. Mic. 2, 6. c. 5, 2.) and that the early and latter rain are used allegorically Hos. 6, 3. c. 10, 12. Inasmuch as all those things so cohere, and mutually explain one another, which are promised concerning the early and latter rain, concerning the filling of barns and wine-presses, and concerning the compensation of sterile years, that they cannot be torn apart and accepted in such a disparate sense, as if they spoke of a spiritual blessing in one part and a bodily one in another. Nor does the person who promises a Teacher for righteousness seem to most to be different from the one who here promises his presence in Israel. And the marginal gloss of B. Luther appears simpler, to which we also adhere, as being more in agreement with the literal sense [τῷ ῥητῷ], along with B. Osiander, B. Pappus, and the Vinians, because along with the Teacher of righteousness, bodily goods are also promised, just as was also done by Isaiah c. 30. The Lord will give you the bread of tribulation, and the water of affliction, and your Teacher will no longer fly away from you, but your eyes will see your Teacher. And from Christ, to those seeking the kingdom of God and HIS RIGHTEOUSNESS, there is a promise of bodily benefits: The rest shall be added unto you. Matt. 6.

By that Teacher of righteousness, however, Christ can not inappropriately be understood in a unique sense [μοναδικῶς], whose advent is followed by the mission of the Holy Spirit, here promised according to the Petrine interpretation by Joel; unless perhaps someone might prefer that the Messiah himself is speaking here, since the Lord speaks of the Lord v. 26. For thus the Messiah himself promises that he wishes to be in the midst of Israel through his advent in the flesh, and that his people, that is, those who have believed in him, shall not be confounded forever, inasmuch as he then dwelt in the midst of Israel in a far closer way than he had dwelt before in his house John 1, 14. and the sum of the Gospel consists in this, that he who has believed in him shall not be confounded Rom. 10, 11. 1 Pet. 2, 6. which Joel thus expresses afterwards in this second chapter verse 23: whoever shall have called upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Although even after the Babylonian captivity they may have handed down Teachers of righteousness, yet by the very experience, and by a clearer knowledge, it was then finally given to learn and to know, when he dwelt in the midst of Israel, and when he poured out his spirit upon all flesh. Which interpretation may seem consistent with the Petrine sermon Acts 2 v. 33, inasmuch as he who poured out the Holy Spirit is Christ v. 33, from whom the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is promised here.

John Drusius, who wished to be singular here, although John Calvin and others had trodden the same path before him, and [who is] already noted by B. Gesner and Cornelius à Lapide, interpreted הַמּוֹרֶה as rain: which explanation was also seized upon by Junius and Tremellius, as well as Piscator in his translation, as also by D. John Tarnovius in his Commentary. The Drusian [notes] have it thus p. 458. Comment. on the Minor Prophets. TEACHER FOR RIGHTEOUSNESS. Thus the Chaldean, the Greeks, the Latins, the Vulgate, and the interpreters agree, so that they think Christ is signified, of whom [it is said] Hos. 10, 12. until he comes and teaches you righteousness; it may be so: yet to me, considering the series of the discourse, 'rain for righteousness' is not displeasing, just as neither is it in the cited passage of Hosea, if one, following the scholiast, translates it thus: until the rain of righteousness comes to you. The sense, however, is this: he gave you the rain of righteousness, that is, a generous, copious [rain], as the sun of righteousness Mal. 4, 2, which shines kindly when it warms: or 'he gave righteousness', that is, he bestows it: to which is similar: sow for righteousness, there in Hosea. Some render it 'according to righteousness', and by righteousness they understand justice and equity: as if he were saying: he gave you as much rain as is sufficient, and as equity demands. But John Coccejus refuted Drusius (and thus also his own Calvin, Piscator, and Junius), whose reasons we subjoin: By מורה [Teacher/Rain] must be understood 'Teacher'. 1. because it can be conveniently understood thus. 2. because it is distinguished from rain, which is called מרה. 3. because it is 'for righteousness'. But rain is not for the sake of righteousness, nor for righteousness. 4. because it is a reason for rejoicing in the Lord as their God, namely, alone. These are the words of Coccejus, who further proves thus that Christ alone is to be understood, and not some other Teacher, or that legislators are to be understood collectively: but that Teacher, ὁ διδάσκαλος [the Teacher], is not only a Teacher of righteousness, but also given for righteousness. And this is Christ 1. because this title 'Teacher and of righteousness' belongs to him alone; inasmuch as when he teaches that he is to be imitated, and teaches to believe in him, [he teaches] that by which we may be righteous, and bear the fruits of righteousness. 2. because he is promised. But the word 'he gave', and the article, look to the promise and the hope of the sons of Zion. 3. because he is given for righteousness, i.e., so that he might make purgation of sin in his blood, and take away the accusation of the Law, and consequently the servitude of the ceremonial Law. For righteousness is opposed to guilt and accusation, when the discourse is about a sinner. The המחוקקים [legislators] or elders urging the law are not understood collectively, 1. because he would rather have used this very word המחוקקים, from Gen. 49, 10. 2. because he would have spoken without the article. For the article indicates a certain one, and indeed that eminent one, and one opposed to all others designated by the same name. Thus הנביא [the prophet] ὁ προφήτης. 3. because the legislators did not teach righteousness, but accusation; and because of them the name of God was blasphemed Is. 52, 5. 4. because those are not given for righteousness who themselves were unworthy to be clothed with righteousness and salvation. Ps. 132. Not any other Prophet, because all these were not the light and righteousness of the people, but testified of it. But here the matter concerns the Master given for righteousness. Cf. Jer. 23, 5. 6. 33, 15. 16. Is. 53, 11. in the knowledge of himself my righteous servant shall justify many. Heb. 2, 4. The righteous shall live by his faith. Coccejus again adducing these same reasons, which B. Luther and B. Gesner have executed, from which the first three, with the fifth proposed above, easily obtain our assent, that we should understand this prophecy concerning the Messiah, which not only most interpreters have interpreted thus, Remigius, Rupertus, Haymo, Lutherus, Wigandus, Winckelmannus, Albertus, Arias, Vatablus, Riebera, à Castro, à Lapide, Coccejus; the Belgian Paraphrasts etc., but also some of the Jews, and among these the bitter enemy of Christ and Christians, Abarbanel.
