Rondeletius saw another on the Santonian shore, whose mouth and throat were of such vastness that it could have easily swallowed even a stout man. But because it is called a whale by Christ, and a Lamia or Carcharias is not properly a whale, it does not seem to have been a Lamia. And although Christoph. à Castro says that a whale has a narrower throat and stomach, so that it cannot swallow and contain a whole and unharmed man, that must be understood of small and common whales. For the larger ones are like mountains, which easily swallow men and whole oxen. Castrius himself reports several such from Pliny, Strabo, Diodorus Siculus, and others at this passage. Regarding the fable of Hercules, compare Cornelius from Theophylact and Salmeron.

IN THE BELLY OF THE FISH THREE DAYS.) Tzetzes, following Lycophron, also places the three days in that history, popularized under the name of Hercules. A clear figure of the resurrection of Christ.

It provided not only a clear figure of the resurrection of Christ, as Christ himself interprets in Matthew 12, but the fruits of the passion, death, and burial of Christ are also not obscurely adumbrated here. Regarding which Jerome says: The sea, which was raging while Jonah was absent, holding the desired one in its bowels, rejoices and cherishes him, and from the joy, tranquility returns. If we consider the errors of the world before the passion of Christ and the contrary winds of diverse dogmas, and the little ship and the whole human race—that is, the creature of the Lord—in danger; and after his passion, the tranquility of faith, and the peace of the world, and all things secure, and the conversion to God, we shall see how the sea ceased from its fervor after the casting of Jonah. Many miracles concur here, as Cornelius à Lapide notes: First, that the very hot belly of the fish did not consume Jonah and turn him into chyle. Second, that Jonah was able to live and breathe there and draw in cold air. Third, that the odor, which is most foul and intolerable in the belly of a whale, did not kill Jonah, but rather he bore it comfortably. Fourth, that in this most narrow and most uncomfortable prison, he was not only composed in soul but also in mind, and inspired by the spirit of God, he sang a distinguished and pious song to God.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

Ionas à ceto absorptus in ventre ejus per triduum hæsit, precando anxietatem cordis & fiduciam in Dominum exposuit, quem cetus vivum in terram evomuit.

Ad Dominum clamans, ex fauce repromitur orci.

Vers. 1.

PISCEM GRANDEM) Τρίτον κύνα, ut ait Lycophron, qui ab Hebræis acceptam historiam in Herculem transtulit, cui omnia grandia adscribi solebant, ut diximus libro primo de Veritate Religionis Christianæ.

Carchariam vel canem ab Italis & Nicandro Camiam vocatum fuisse Rondeletius l. 13. de Pisc. & Ulysses Aldrovandus l. 3. de Pisc. c. 32. Pineda l. 4. de reb. Salom. c. 12. Christoph. à Castro opinantur. Cornel. à Lapid. è Gellio refert Massilienses comprehendisse canem, in quo loricatum hominem invenissent. Rondeletius in Santonico littore alium vidit, cujus os & gula tanta fuere vastitate, ut hominem obesum etiam commode capere potuerit. Sed quia à Christo vocatur cetus, Lamia autem vel Charcharia proprie cetus non est, non videtur Lamia fuisse. Et quanquam Christoph. à Castro balænam arctiori gutture ac ventriculo esse dicat, ut hominem integrum & illæsum deglutire ac continere nequeat, id tamen de parvis & communibus balænis intelligendum. Nam majores sunt instar montium, quæ facile homines & boves integros glutiunt. Quales refert ipse Castrius plures è Plinio, Strabone, Diodoro Siculo, & aliis ad h. l. De fabula Herculis confer. è Theophyl. & Salmerone Cornelius.

IN VENTRE PISCIS TRIBUS DIEBUS.) Etiam triduum in historia illa, Herculis sub nomine vulgata, ponit ad Lycophronem Tzetzes. Figura resurrectionis Christi non obscura.

Non solum resurrectionis Christi figuram luculentam præbuit, interprete ipso Christo Matth. 12. sed fructus etiam passionis, mortis & sepulturæ Christi hic non obscure adumbratus. De quo Hieronym: Mare, quod absente Jona irascebatur, in visceribus suis desideratum tenens, gaudet & confovet, & ex gaudio tranquillitas redit. Si consideremus ante passionem Christi errores mundi & diversorum dogmatum flatus contrarios & naviculam totumque humanum genus, id est, creaturam Domini periclitantem: & post passionem ejus tranquillitatem fidei, & orbis pacem, & secura omnia & conversionem ad Deum, videbimus, quomodo post præcipitationem Jonæ fleterit mare à fervore suo. Multa hic miracula concurrunt, notante Cornelio à Lapide: Primum, quod venter piscis calidissimus Jonam non consumpserit, & in chylum converterit. Secundo, quod Jonas ibidem viveré, & respirare, aëremque frigidum attrahere potuerit. Tertium, quod odor, qui in ventre ceti est olidissimus, & intolerabilis, Jonam non exanimarit, quin potius ipse eum commode tulerit. Quartum, quod in hoc angustissimo & incommodissimo carcere non tantum animæ, sed & mentis compos fuerit, spirituque Dei afflatus, insigne & pium carmen Deo cecinerit.

## 2:1
Verse 2.

AND JONAH PRAYED TO THE LORD HIS GOD FROM THE BELLY OF THE FISH) Every place is instead of the Temple.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ET ORAVIT JONAS AD DOMINUM DEUM SUUM DE VENTRE PISCIS) Omnis locus pro Templo.

## 2:2
AND HE SAID) Jonah composed this poem afterwards, but it is appropriate to the exact time. See the third chapter of Lamentations.

Although we do not deny this, as Junius, Piscator, and the Dutch in their Annotations from the Reformed side say that Jonah composed it already delivered from the belly of the whale, which also seemed so to the blessed Bugenhagen and the blessed Walther, nevertheless nothing prevents us from concluding with Mercerus and Tarnovius that he thought such things in the belly of the fish, and we believe that he also uttered sighs and groans to the same effect at that time. The words of the text do not lead us to rise up with Oecolampadius and the Papist interpreters, who assert with the Rabbis that the same prayer was uttered in these words in the belly of the whale. For even if he is said to have prayed, and to have said these things, they do not prove that they were uttered by him in these very words (however it may be, whether by expressed voice or by sighs and groans). Something can be said either according to the letter or the literal sense, or according to the matter or the thought.

Verse 3.

AND HE HEARD ME) He will hear. For it is the mark of one hoping well, thus also you will hear immediately. See below 5.

FROM THE BELLY OF HELL) From the belly, which is to me in place of a sepulcher. Thus Ennius on the belly of a vulture: Alas, in what a cruel sepulcher he was burying his limbs.

Latin:

ET DIXIT) Hoc carmen postea composuit Ionas, sed conveniens exacto tempori. Vide caput tertium Thren.

Quamvis hoc non diffiteamur, uti è Reformatis Junius, Piscator & Belgæ in Annot. id composuisse Jonam ajunt jam liberatum ex ventre balænæ, quod etiam visum fuit B. Bugenhagio & B. Walthero, nihil tamen obstat, quo minus talia cogitasse in ventre piscis cum Mercero & Tarnovio statuamus, ac suspiria etiam in eandem sententiam ac gemitus ipsum tum edidisse credamus. Rabbinis eandem orationem hisce verbis in ventre balænæ prolatam asserentibus cum Oecolampadio & Pontificiis interpp. ut assurgamus verba textus non inducunt. Etiam si enim orasse dicatur, & dixisse hæc tamen totidem verbis ab ipso (quomodocunque seu voce expressa seu suspiriis & gemitibus) prolata esse non evincunt. Dici aliquid potest vel xτ γράμμα seu ῥητὸν, vel x'τ πρᾶγμα διάνοιαν.

Vers. 3.

ET EXAUDIVIT ME) Exaudiet. Est enim bene sperantis, Sic & statim exaudies. Vide infra 5.

DE VENTRE INFERI) De ventre, qui mihi est vice sepulchri. Sic de vulturis ventre Ennius: Heu quam crudeli condebat membra sepulchro.

## 2:7
Ver. 8.

WHEN MY SOUL FAINTED WITHIN ME) Although my soul fainted within me. Although I have my life on the outer lips.

TOWARD THINE HOLY TEMPLE) That is, even unto heaven, of which the Jerusalem Temple bore the image. See what was said at Matt. 27, 57. Add Ps. 115, v. 5. Micah 1, 2.

The temple of the Lord's holiness to which my prayer has arrived is heaven itself, and the throne of the Lord's glory, Ps. 11, 4. 2 Chron. 30, 27. It refers, however, without doubt to the promise made in 1 Kings 8, 38, which, so that those praying might recall it to their minds, they were accustomed of old to direct their face toward the Jerusalem temple, wherever they might be, Ps. 5, 8. Ps. 138, 2. Dan. 6, 11. Whence Snepfius rightly expresses the sense of this passage: I was heard no less truly while praying or groaning in the belly of the fish than if I had poured out prayers in the very temple of Solomon, at the ark of the covenant.

Templum sanctitatis Domini ad quod perveni oratio, cœlum ipsum est, & thronus gloriæ Domi- ni, Psal. 11, 4. 2. Chron. 30, 27. Respicit autem sine dubio promissionem 1. Reg. 8, 38. factam, quam ut in animum sibi revocarent orantes, consue- verunt olim faciem versus templum Hierosolymi- tanum dirigere, ubique existerent Psal. 5, 8. Psal 138. 2. Verse 10.

BUT I WITH THE VOICE OF PRAISE) תודה, in the same way that thanksgiving is spoken of, and the sacrifice itself, which accompanied the thanksgiving.

I WILL SACRIFICE TO THEE) Victims owed to such a cause according to the law, Lev. 7, 12. 13.

Too narrow a restriction both here and in ch. 1, 16, of vows to works of mercy. Vows should be understood more generally, and primarily referred to the first table. Cf. Psalm 116, 18. The name שלם denotes Eucharistic sacrifices, which were offered for peace and safety obtained, Am. 5, 22.

## 3:1 Argument
PART II. THE SECOND CALLING OF JONAH. CHAPTER III.

Jonah, commanded again by the Lord, predicts the subversion of the Ninevites, whom, however, having turned to God, the Lord spared.

Conversion saves trembling Nineveh by the voice of God.

Ver. 1. SECONDLY) In that place where he had been exposed.

Latin:

PARS II. ALTERA JONÆ VOCATIO. CAPUT III.

Ionas rursum jussus à Domino prædicit Nini- vitis subversionem, quibus vero ad Deum conversis pepercit Dominus.

Voce Dei trepidam Niniven conversio salvat.

Vers. 1. SECUNDO) Illo loco, quo expositus fuerat.

## 3:3
Ver. 3.

NINEVEH WAS A GREAT CITY.) The royal city of the Assyrians, in whose circuit the area was 400 stadia: the wall, however, abounding with 1500 towers, as we learn from Herodotus and Diodorus. After 'great' in the Hebrew follows לאלהים, which the Greeks translate τῷ θεῷ, the Chaldean 'before God': that is, God increasing it. Strabo, in book 16, says that the city of Nineveh was greater than Babylon.

A JOURNEY OF THREE DAYS.) If one were to walk around all those towers on foot.

Cocceius observes here that Diodorus is not correctly understood by Grotius: The sense, he says, of Diodorus is that Nineveh was in the shape of a parallelogram. And that it had two sides of length, each 150 stadia, and likewise sides of width of 90. Thus it was sixty stadia longer than it was wide. The area would have been 13,500 stadia, not, as Grotius wrongly followed Junius, 480. For that is the περίβολος or circuit. Herodotus attributes the same number of stadia to Babylon in a square figure: but Diodorus gives this one 360. A journey of three days makes 600 stadia, if we define a day's journey by 200 stadia according to Polybius and Herodotus: but a stadium makes 100 fathoms, as Herodotus wishes, which are 600 feet, 120 paces. The Romans measure a day's journey by 160 or at most 166 2/3 stadia. Then a journey of three days would be 480 stadia: which circuit Diodorus makes for Nineveh. See concerning these Casaubon on Strabo, book 1, p. 23. If we take these things concerning the circuit, Jonah, in the next verse, will be understood to have walked for a journey of one day in the city preaching, namely through the length of the city, 150 stadia, which number of stadia the length had according to Diodorus. That does not displease, if indeed this is to be maintained, that the Biblical account should agree with the Greek. Otherwise, it must be said that a day's journey was shorter for the Hebrews. Eight stadia are called a mile, i.e., making almost a thousand paces. Therefore 150 stadia would make eighteen miles and more. Aben Ezra takes it concerning the circuit. Abarbanel concerning the length, who also alleges from Bereshith Rabbah that Nineveh had a journey of forty days, namely with its suburbs and villages.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

NINIVE ERAT CIVITAS MAGNA.) Regia As- syriorum, cujus in ambitu area erat CCCC stadiorum : mu- rus autem cIɔ Iɔ turribus exuberans, ita ut ex Herodoto & Diodoro X, discimus. Post magna in Hebræo sequitur לאלהים, quod Græci vertunt τῷ θεῷ, Chaldæus co- ram Deo: id est, Deo eam augente. Ninum urbem ma- jorum fuisse Babylone, ait Strabo libro 16.

ITINERE TRIUM DIERUM.) Si quis omnes il- las turres pedibus circumiret.

Diodorum non recte intelligi à Grotio, Coc- cejus hic observat: Sensus, inquit, Diodori est, Niniven fuisse figura parallelogrammon. Et late- ra duo longitudinis habuisse singula 150. stadia, latera itidem latitudinis 90. Ita longiorem fuisse sexagin- ta stadiis, quam latiorem. Area fuerit 13500. sta- dia, non, ut post Junium Grotius male 480. Nam is περίβολός est sive ambitus. Herodotus Babyloni attribuit totidem stadia in figura quadrata: at huic Diodorus 360. dat. Tridui iter facit stadia sexcen- ta, si secundum Polybium & Herodotum iter diei stadiis ducentis definiamus: orgyas autem 100. facit stadium, ut vult Herodotus, qui sunt 600. pedes, pas- sus 120. Romani iter diei 160. aut summum 166 2/3. sta- diis metiuntur. Tum tridui iter esset 480. stadia: quem Diodorus ambitum Ninives facit. Vide de his Casaubonum ad Strabonem lib. 1. p. 23. Si nos hæc accipiamus de ambitu, Jonas, versu proximo, intelligetur iter diei unius in civitate ambulasse præconians, nimirum per longitudinem civitatis, stadia 150. quot stadia longitudo habebat secun- dum Diodorum. Id non displicet, si sane hoc cu- stodiendum est, ut ratio Biblica cum Græcanica consentiat. Alioqui dicendum, iter diei Hebræis fuiffe brevius. Stadia octo dicuntur milliare, h. e. mille propemodum passus conficere. Ergo sta- dia 150. facerent miliaria octodecim & amplius. Aben Efra de ambitu accipit. Abarbenel de lon- gitudine, qui & ex Bereschith Rabbah allegat, Ni- niven habuisse iter quadraginta dierum, nimirum cum suburbiis & pagis suis.

## 3:4
Ver. 4.

A JOURNEY OF ONE DAY.) Walking through the city as much as was permitted in one day.

Cocceius has it thus: That, according to the most probable reason, is to be taken in such a way that Jonah divided the spaces of his preaching so that, according to the width of the city, he would measure its length several times in different regions and streets of the city. Therefore, when he had once measured the length of the city, the humiliation of the Ninevites followed.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ITINERE DIEI UNIUS.) Perambulans urbem quantum uno die licebat

Coccejus ita habet: Id secundum probabilissi- mam rationem ita accipiendum est, quod Jonas suæ prædicationis spatia diviserit ita, ut secundum lati- tudinem urbis longitudinem ejus aliquoties eme- tiretur diversis urbis regionibus ac vicis. Igitur cum semel emensus esset urbis prolixitatem, secu- ta est Ninevitarum humiliatio.

## 3:4
YET FORTY DAYS, AND NINEVEH SHALL BE OVERTHROWN.) When Nineveh shall be overthrown. Concerning this number of forty days, we have spoken of matters not foreign to this at Matthew 4:2. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion have placed the same number here: but in the edition of the LXX there are τρεῖς ἡμέραι. Is it from ancient numerical notations, often differing much among themselves, which have now become obsolete? We have seemed to detect traces of this thing elsewhere as well. This threatening, however, is to be understood as applying while things remain as they are. Jeremiah 18:8 gives us this rule, which rule itself, however, has its own exception, unless it has been added, 'I will not hear them,' which God sometimes does after long-continued warnings and patience long eluded. See what [we wrote] at Luke 19:44.

Latin:

ADHUC QUADRAGINTA DIES, ET NINIVE SUBVERTETUR.) Cum Ninive subvertetur. De numero hoc dierum XL. diximus ab hac re non aliena ad Matth. 4, 2. Eundem numerum hic posuere Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion: at in editione LXX. sunt τρεῖς ἡμέραι. an ex notis numerum veteribus, & sæpe inter se pon multum distantibus, quæ nunc exoleverunt? visi sumus & alibi ejus rei deprehendisse vestigia. Intelligenda a. hæc com- minatio rebus sic manentibus. Regulam hanc nobis dat Jeremias 18, 8. quæ tamen regula suam & ipsa habet ex- ceptionem, nisi additum fuerit, non exaudiam eos, quod interdum Deus facit post diuturna monita, & elusam diu patientiam. Vide quæ ad Lucam 19, 44.

## 3:5
Ver. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

## 3:5
AND THE MEN OF NINEVEH BELIEVED IN GOD.) That is, in the words of God through Jonah, being conscious of their own grave crimes.

AND PROCLAIMED A FAST) The king and the nobles who were with him decreed it.

AND WERE CLOTHED WITH SACKCLOTH FROM THE GREATEST EVEN TO THE LEAST.) So that such a mournful habit itself might kindle their grief the more.

Latin:

ET CREDIDERUNT VIRI NINIVITÆ IN DE- UM.) Id est, verbis Dei per Jonam, conscii sibi gravium criminum.

ET PRÆDICAVERUNT JEJUNIUM) Indixerunt rex, & qui ei aderant proceres.

ET VESTITI SUNT SACCIS A MAJORE US- QUE AD MINOREM.) Ut ipse tam lugubris habitus do- lorem magis accenderet.

## 3:6
AND SAT IN ASHES.) ἐπὶ σποδῷ. See Matthew 11:21.

Verse 6.

THE WORD CAME UNTO THE KING OF NINEVEH, AND HE AROSE FROM HIS THRONE.) Because the word had arrived. He renders the cause of the proclaimed fast, and explains the manner.

AND HE CAST HIS GARMENT FROM HIM) He had cast off his garment, his royal one, of course, so that he might make himself equal to the others in mourning.

Latin:

ET SEDIT IN CINERE.) ἐπὶ σποδῷ. Vide Matth. 11, 21.

Vers. 6.

PERVENIT VERBUM AD REGEM NINIVE, ET SURREXIT DE SOLIO SVO.) Quia pervenerat ver- bum. Causam reddit indicti jejunii, modumque explicat.

ET ABJECIT VESTIMENTUM SUUM A SE) Abjecerat vestimentum, regale scilicet, ut se cæteris in luctu æquaret.

## 3:7
Verse 7.

AND HE CRIED, AND SAID IN NINEVEH.) In the Hebrew: he ordered it to be proclaimed, saying.

BY THE MOUTH OF THE KING AND HIS PRINCES.) See Esther 1:19, 21.

LET MAN AND BEAST, AND HERD, AND FLOCK TASTE ANYTHING, NOR FEED, NOR DRINK WATER.) That, 'let them not taste anything,' refers to men; the rest to the cattle; as in Virgil:

No one drove their fed oxen to the cold rivers in those days, Daphnis: no quadruped sipped the stream, nor touched a blade of grass.

This was done so that men might be moved even more to grief by the spectacle of the dumb animals.

Blessed Gerhard explained the reasons more fully at this passage: The brute animals are kept from pasture (1.) on account of the gravity of the matter, so that the lowing and clamor of the beasts of burden might serve the Ninevites as a form of exhortation, so that they might pray all the more fervently. (2.) On account of the enormity of the dangers. If Nineveh had perished, that πανολεθρία would have involved the brute animals as well.

(3) for a diversion from labor, as the Ninevites did, that they might spend the time which was to be devoted to the care of cattle in prayers and other exercises of piety. (4) for a notable utility; for Scripture testifies that beasts and the young of ravens call upon God, Ps. 147:9; such an invocation is not constituted like the prayers of men, but they call upon God in their own way, i. e., their condition and hunger seem, by a natural appetite for food, to demand and implore divine aid as it were.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ET CLAMAVIT, ET DIXIT IN NINIVE.) In Hebræo: proclamari jussit dicendo.

EX ORE REGIS ET PRINCIPUM EJUS.) Vide Ester. 1, 19. 21.

HOMINES ET JUMENTA, ET BOVES, ET PECORA NE GUSTENT QUICQUAM, NEC PA- SCANTUR, ET AQVAM NON BIBANT.) Illud, non gustent, quicquam, ad homines refertur cætera ad pecudes; ut apud Virg:

Non ulli pastos illis egere diebus Frigida, Daphni, boves ad flumina: nulla, neque amnem Libavit quadrupes, nec graminis attigit herbam.

Factum hoc ut etiam mutorum animantium spectaculo magis commoverentur homines ad dolorem.

Plenius causas exposuit B. Gerhardus ad hunc locum: Bruta à pastu arcentur (1.) ob rei gravi- tatem, ut boatus & clamor jumentorum Ninivitis essent loco cohortationis, ut tanto ardentius preca- rentur. (2.) ob periculorum immanitatem. Si Ninive interiiffet, πανολεθρία illa etiam bruta involvisset.

(3) ob avocamentum à labore, ut Ninivitæ tempus, quod curæ pecorum tribuendum erat, precibus & aliis pietatis exercitiis impenderent. (4) ob insignem utilitatem; testatur enim Scriptura, jumenta & pullos corvorum Deum invocare, Ps. 47, 9. talis invocatio non est ita comparata, sicut hominum preces, sed invocant Deum suo modo, i. e. eorum situs & fames naturali appetitu cibi divinam opem quasi exposcere & implorare videtur.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. AND FROM THE INIQUITY WHICH IS IN THEIR HANDS) That is, let him restore what was seized, without which there is no true repentance. See what we have said in De Jure Belli ac Pacis, book 3, chapter 10, § 3.

Thus the Chaldean. He urges not only the restitution of stolen goods, but the cessation of every kind of rapine and violence: let every courtier, who has hitherto been accustomed to be bribed by a gift, to administer justice in proportion to the money received, or to perform what he was bound to do by his office, abandon it; let the usurious merchant, and similar Ninevite vultures, abandon their rapine and their tricks for scraping together wealth by wicked means; and thus let everyone not feign, but truly perform repentance, as the blessed Tarnovius rightly says here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET AB INIQUITATE, QVÆ EST IN MANIBUS EORUM) Id est, rapta restituat, sine quo non est vera pœnitentia. Vide quæ diximus de jure Belli ac Pacis lib. 3. cap. 10. §. 3.

Ita Chaldæus. Non autem tantum raptorum restitutionem: sed cujusvis rapinæ & violentiæ intermissionem urget: Relinquat quisque aulicus, qui hactenus solitus est munere feriri, pro ratione nummorum jus dicere, vel quod ex officio debebat, exequi; relinquat mercator usurarius, & similes vultures Ninevitici rapinam suam, ac technas suas opes corradendi per nefas; atque ita non fingat, sed agat vere unusquisque pœnitentiam, uti recte hic B. Tarnovius.

## 3:8
Ver. 8. AND LET MEN AND BEASTS BE COVERED WITH SACKCLOTH.

These things pertain still to the King’s command, as is manifest from the Hebrew and Chaldean text; but not to the execution of the command, as the LXX rendered it and περιέθεντο σάκκᢵς οἱ ἄνθρωποι. Moreover, he commanded that even the beasts of burden be covered with sackcloth, so that by this means men might be the more admonished to serious repentance.

Verse of the same

AND THEY SHALL CRY UNTO THE LORD IN STRENGTH) With a loud voice. ἐκτενῶς, the Greeks.

AND LET THE MAN BE TURNED) Everyone.

FROM HIS EVIL WAY) Let him cast off the habit of sinning.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET OPERIANTUR SACCIS HOMINES ET JUMENTA.

Pertinent hæc adhuc ad mandatum Regis, ut ex Ebræo & Chaldæo textu manifestum est; non vero ad exquutionem mandati, uti LXX. reddidere & περιέθεντο σάκκᢵς οἱ ἄνθρωποι. Operiri autem sacco etiam jumenta præcepit, ut eo magis homines ad seriam pœnitentiam commonerentur.

Vers. eod.

ET CLAMENT AD DOMINUM IN FORTITUDINE) Alta voce. ἐκτενῶς, Græci.

ET CONVERTATUR VIR) Quisque.

A VIA SUA MALA) Exuat peccandi consuetudinem.

## 3:9
Verse 9.

WHO KNOWS IF HE MAY TURN) Whether he may change his mind. This is much in the Assyrian men, to show such great signs of repentance, under the hope of an uncertain pardon.

These words do not indicate the hope of an uncertain pardon, nor can that hope consist with true repentance, such as this of the Ninevites altogether was, because it is commended here by God Himself, is set forth by Christ as an example in Matth. 12, and obtained the condonation of punishment. For to repentance there is required not only the acknowledgment of sin, but also true faith and a certain confidence in divine grace, and consequently a firm hope of a certain pardon: namely, the pardon of the committed fault, which brings about the remission of sin, but not likewise of temporal punishment or affliction, since God sometimes sends temporal afflictions even upon truly faithful penitents who are certain of the gratuitous remission of sins and justified in the judgment of God, as David and Job are examples. And therefore, if Grotius understands an uncertain pardon concerning the pardon of temporal destruction and ruin, we do not gainsay it, because it is added here: AND WE SHALL NOT BE OVERTHROWN. If, however, one gathers from this, along with the Papists, an uncertain remission of guilt, that will by no means be approved. The Jesuits Sanctius and Castrius certainly accept this statement regarding the mitigation of afflictions or punishments, which God sends to His own even after reconciliation for the sake of amendment and testing, and the Jesuit Jacobus Tirinus, on a similar passage, Joel 2:14, annotates these things: 'Who knows if He may turn from His decree and His sentence concerning the temporal punishment to be inflicted upon you by the Chaldeans.' For although I am certain that God will remit to the penitent every offense regarding guilt and eternal punishment, I would not dare to assert the same as indubitable regarding temporal punishment, which for just causes He often does not remit entirely, as was evident in the penitent David, 2 Sam. 12:10, and so many others. Thus St. Jerome, Theodoret, Rufinus, and Rupertus: 'I hope, however, that He who is seriously converted will forgive even this temporal punishment.' So also in this place, Cornelius à Lapide. The Ninevites doubt not the remission of guilt, but of punishment, as if to say: 'Who knows if, through our repentance, God may be appeased and revoke the sentence concerning the overturning of Nineveh?' In a similar way, God pardoned David's adultery, but punished him with the death of the son born from it, 2 Sam. 12:19. Others, however, in the same author, wrongly extend this doubt to the remission of guilt in this sense: that although the promises of God are most certain, by which He promised pardon to the penitent, yet it is uncertain whether man fulfills the condition which the promise requires: for instance, that he be sufficiently disposed toward grace, namely, that he be truly contrite out of love for God, not merely attrite out of fear of punishments. Thus Gregor. de Valentia, 2.2, tract. de Gratia, disp. 8, q. 4, and Cardinal Bellarmine, lib. 3, de justif., c. 6; for these rely on a false hypothesis concerning the merits of repentance, as if we earned divine grace through our own dispositions. Add finally that that particle 'who knows' is perhaps not always that of one doubting, but sometimes assertive and affirmative and of one hoping well, as the Papists themselves admit: Salmeron, Tom. 1, Proleg. 16, p. 320; Cornelius à Lapide on Gen. 32, p. 218; Arias Montanus in this place. See John 14:12, 1 Sam. 14:6, 2 Sam. 12:22, c. 16:12 (Conf. 2 Sam. 7:10), Prov. 24:18, Ecc. 5:5, Job 8:19.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

QVIS SCIT SI CONVERTATUR) An sententiam mutet. Multum hoc in Assyriis hominibus, tanta edere pœnitentiæ signa, sub spe incertæ veniæ.

Hæ voces non indicant spem incertæ veniæ, nec ea cum vera pœnitentia, qualis omnino hæc Ninevitarum fuit, quia à Deo ipso hic commendatur, à Christo in exemplum sistitur Matth. 12. & condonationem pœnæ impetravit, consistere potest. Ad pœnitentiam enim non solum peccati agnitio, sed vera etiam fides, ac gratiæ divinæ certa fiducia, adeoque spes firma veniæ certæ requiritur: veniæ nempe commissæ culpæ, quæ remissionem peccati infert, non item temporalis pœnæ, vel afflictionis, quum etiam pœnitentibus vere fidelibus, & certis de gratuita peccatorum remissione ac justificatis in judicio Dei, afflictiones temporales Deus quandoque immittat, ut David & Hiob exemplo sunt. Ideoque si incertam veniam de venia temporalis excidionis, & interitus Grotius intelligit, non refragamur, quia additur hic: ET NON EVERTAMUR. Si vero cum Papicolis hinc incertam culpæ remissionem colligat, minime id probandum erit. Sanctius certe & Castrius Jesuitæ dictum hoc accipiunt de mitigatione afflictionum aut castigationum, quas Deus suis etiam post reconciliationem immittit ad emendationem & probationem, & Jacobus Tirinus Jesuita ad locum similem, Joel. 2, 14. hæc annotat: Quis scit, si convertatur à decreto & sententia sua de pœna temporali per Chaldæos vobis infligenda. Licet enim certus sim, Deum pœnitentibus remissurum omnem offensam quoad culpam, & pœnam æternam, non tamen ausim pro indubitato idem asserere, quoad pœnam temporalem, quam justas ob causas sæpe non omnem remittit, ut patuit in Davide pœnitente 2. Reg. 12, 10. & tot aliis. Ita S. Hieron. Theodoret. Ruffin. & Rupertus: Spero tamen, quod serio conversis ignoscat etiam hanc temporalem pœnam. Sic etiam h. l. Cornel. à Lap. Dubitant Ninivitæ de remissione non cul- pæ, sed pœnæ, q. d. Quis scit si per pœnitentiam no- stram Deus placetur, revocetq; sententiam de ever- tenda Ninive? Simili modo Deus condonavit adulte- rium Davidi, sed punivit eum morte filii ex eo geniti 2. Reg. 12, 19. Perperam vero alii apud eundem hanc dubitationen: extendunt ad remissionem culpæ hoc sensu, quod licet certissimæ sint promissiones Dei, quibus pœnitentibus promisit veniam; tamen in- certum est, an homo impleat conditionem, quam exigit promissio: puta, quod sit sufficienter dispo- situs ad gratiam, nimirum, quod sit vere contritus ex amore Dei, non attritus tantum ex timore pœ- narum. Ita Gregor. de Valentia 2. 2. tract. de Gratia disp. 8. q. 4. & Card. Bellarm. lib. 3. de justif. c. 6. hæc enim nituntur falsa hypothesi de meritis pœnitentiæ, quasi per dispositiones nostras gratiam divinam me- reamur. Adde denique, quod particula illa quis scit, forte non semper dubitantis sit, sed assertiva & affir- mativa quandoq; & bene sperantis, fatentibus ipsis- met Pontificiis Salmerone Tom. 1. Proleg. 16. p. 320. Cornel. à Lap. in Gen. 32. p. 218. Ariæmontani in h. l. Vid. Joh. 14, 12. 1. Sam. 14, 6. 2. Sam. 12, 22. c. 16, 12. (Conf. 2. Sam. 7, 10.) Prov. 24, 18. Ecc. 5, 5. Job. 8, 19.

## 3:10
Verse 10. AND GOD SAW THEIR WORKS) Signs of a healed mind.

AND GOD HAD COMPASSION UPON THE MALICE WHICH HE HAD SPOKEN THAT HE WOULD DO) Concerning the evil which He had said He would bring about. 'Malice' to this interpreter, as in Matt. 6:34, κακία, is any calamity or other sad thing.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET VIDIT DEUS OPERA EORUM) Sa- natæ mentis indicia.

ET MISERTUS EST DEUS SUPER MALITIAM, QVAM LOCUTUS FUERAT UT FACERET) De malo quod illaturum se dixerat. Malitia huic interpreti, ut Matth. 6, 34. κακία, est quævis calamitas, aut triste aliud.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

The Lord convinces Jonah, who was indignant because of the grace shown to the Ninevites, while he grieved over the withered ivy, that He spares the great city far more justly.

The Lord's compassion disapproves of the angry prophet.

Verse 1. AND JONAH WAS AFFLICTED WITH GREAT AFFLICTION) He grieved with great sorrow, thinking that his authority was in jeopardy. But it is not for an ambassador to ensure that a king does not change his sentence.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Jonam indignantem ob gratiam Ninivitis fa- ctam, quum de hedera arefacta doleret, con- vincit Dominus longe justius se magnæ ci- vitati parcere.

Improbat iratum Domini miseratio vatem.

Vers. 1. ET AFFLICTUS EST JONAS AFFLICTIONE MAGNA) Magno dolore indoluit, de autoritate sua se periclitari existimans. At non est legati præstare, ne rex sententiam mutet.

## 4:2
Verse 2. IS THIS NOT MY WORD) I had thought that this very thing would happen.

FOR I KNOW THAT YOU ARE A GRACIOUS AND MERCIFUL GOD, PATIENT AND OF GREAT COMPASSION AND RELENTING UPON MALICE) Repenting, that is, concerning the evil which You had threatened. Moses had learned this from examples, and from the pronouncement of God Himself. Exod. 34:6.

Latin:

Vers. 2. NUNQVID NON EST HOC VERBUM MEUM) Hoc ipsum fore cogitaveram.

SCIO ENIM, QVIA TU DEUS CLEMENS ET MISERICORS ES, PATIENS ET MULTÆ MI- SERATIONIS ET IGNOSCENS SUPER MALITIA) Pœnitens super malo, quod comminatus es, scilicet. Exemplis id didicerat Moses, & ipsius Dei pronunciato. Exod. 34, 6.

## 4:3
Verse 3. TAKE, I BESEECH YOU, MY SOUL FROM ME) My life. Great indignation, not for a just cause.

Latin:

Vers. 3. TOLLE, QVÆSO, ANIMAM MEAM A ME) Vitam. Magna indignatio, non justa ex causa.

## 4:4
Ver. 4. DO YOU THINK, ARE YOU RIGHTLY ANGRY?) Is your anger a good deed? Is this a just cause?

Latin:

Vers. 4. PUTASNE, BENE IRASCERIS TU?) An bonum factum est ira tua? estne hæc causa justa?

## 4:5
Ver. 5. AND HE SAT OPPOSITE THE EAST OF THE CITY) From where there was an excellent view into the city.

AND HE MADE HIMSELF A SHELTER THERE) A hut made of brushwood.

UNTIL HE MIGHT SEE WHAT WOULD HAPPEN TO THE CITY) Whether it might be punished by at least some evil.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET SEDIT CONTRA ORIENTEM CIVITA- TIS) Unde optimus erat in urbem despectus.

ET FECIT SIBIMET UMBRACULUM IBI) Tugurium ex virgulto.

DONEC VIDERET QVID ACCIDERET CI- VITATI) Annon aliquo saltem malo puniretur.

## 4:6
Ver. 6. AND THE LORD GOD PREPARED A GOURD) In Hebrew it is קיקיון, where ין is an addition. For the Egyptian name is κικι in Herodotus, Euterpe; Theophrastus, 1. 16; Pliny, 15, 7; Dioscorides, 1. 38; Galen, on simples. Herodotus calls it by another name, σιλλοκύπρια. Jerome, in his commentary on this passage, notes that it is called elkeron in the Syrian and Punic languages. It is a kind of shrub or small tree, having broad leaves like a vine leaf and very dense shade, supporting itself on its own trunk, which grows very frequently in Palestine, and especially in sandy places: and in a wonderful way, if you cast the seed into the ground, it quickly rises up into a tree, and within a few days, what you had seen as an herb, you look up at as a small tree. He shows, however, that 'ivy' was translated by him, not because it was the same thing, but because he could not find another name known to the Latins that approached this nature in any way.

Some have made a tumult in the Church, and Augustine rashly contends with Jerome because he translated 'gourd' as 'ivy'. But Cornelius and Asinius Pollio were unfair, who for that reason, as if accused of sacrilege. Calvin is also an unfair arbiter between both Fathers: he attributes superstition to Augustine, because he did not want the received version of the Old Testament changed due to a suspicion regarding the Jews, that they had attempted to corrupt the entire Law and the Prophets: but Augustine bore a far different testimony to the Jews in book 15 of The City of God, ch. 13, and ordered a return to the Hebrew text if the variety of translations brought about any doubt in his book on the days of Christ. He also argues against Jerome, because he deceived Augustine, since he knew the man did not know the Hebrew language, and thus mocked him like a boy because of his ignorance, and it seems he invented something new on the spot for his own convenience, namely the word Elkeca, because otherwise he admitted in his own age that that shrub was called Kikikajon in the Syriac language. As if there could not be a double name for a shrub among the Syrians. Coccejus also notes another name, עלוליבא. Such things were not to be presumed about the holy Father. And Coccejus observes from the Talmudic writings that in Syriac אלכרוע is the same as Kikajon. Jerome defends his translation thus: We, following Symmachus, Aquila, and Theodotion, translated it as ivy with a new name (lest if we had placed the Hebrew name Kikajon, the reader might imagine the beasts of India, or the mountains of Boeotia, or I know not what monster and prodigy) and that appropriately, because Kikajon creeps forth very quickly (and covers and overshadows, just as ivy does. Add from Theophrastus, book 3, ch. 18, and from Mattioli in Dioscorides, book 2, ch. 175, that there is one species of ivy with a larger leaf, which does not creep, but stands by itself, and grows into a tree, as the Kikajon does. For the same reason the LXX translated it as gourd, inventing a new name (which not only Luther, but as Cornelius à Lapide notes, the Syriac also, and both Arabic versions, and Pagninus followed) because it creeps forth and overshadows, and is healthy like a gourd, about which there is the proverb: It is healthier than a gourd.

But that which Grotius notes about Kiki, Cornelius à Lapide disapproves of in the Rabbis and those who follow the Rabbis. R. David, and from him Arias and the Rabbinizers, divine, or rather err, who think that Kikajon is that which the Greeks call Kiki, we call ricinus, or the palm or hand of Christ, because of the articulation of the leaves, which is broad-leaved and suited for shade. For ricinus is a poisonous herb, and consequently so is its shade. Who would believe that God prepared a poisonous herb for the shade of His prophet, when there were so many other health-giving ones at hand?

TO PROTECT HIM, (FOR HE HAD LABORED) In the Hebrew: to deliver him from evil: that is, from the heat.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET PRÆPARAVIT DOMINVS DEUS HE- DERAM) Hebræo est קיקיון, ubi ין est addititium. Nam nomen Ægyptium est κικι apud Herodotum Euterpe, Theo- phrastum 1. 16. Plinium 15, 7. Dioscoriden 1. 38. Galenum de simplicibus. Herodotus alio nomine σιλλοκύπρια vocat. Hieronymus in Commentario ad hunc locum lingua Syra & Punica elkeron dici notat. Esse autem genus virgulti vel arbusculæ, lata habens folia in modum pampini & um- bram densissimam, suo trunco se sustinens, quod in Palæsti- na creberrime nascitur, & maxime in arenosis locis: mirum- que in modum, si sementem in terram jeceris, cito consor- tam consurgere in arborem, & intra paucos dies, quam her- bam videras, arbusculam te suspicere. Ostendit autem à se hederam translatum, non quod idem esset, sed quod no- men Latinis notum, & ad hanc naturam aliquo modo acce- dens, aliud non reperiret.

TUmultuati sunt nonnulli in Ecclesia, & temere contendit cum Hieronymo Augustinus, quod pro cucubita hederam transtulerit. Iniqui autem fuere Cornelius & Asinius Pollio, qui eum ideo quasi facrilegii accufarunt. Calvinus etiam iniquus arbi- terest inter utrumque Patrem: Augustino supersti- tionem tribuit, quod nollet mutari receptam versi- onem V. Test. ob suspicionem de Judæis, quod co- nati essent totam legem & Prophetas corrumpere: sed longe aliud testimonium Judæis perhibuit Au- gustinus l. 15. de Civ. Dei c. 13. & ad Ebræum tex- tum recurrere jussit, si quam dubitationem attule- rit translationem varietas libr. de dieb. Christi. Hieronymum etiam arguit, quod fucum fecerit Au- gustino, quia sciverit hominem non tenere lin- guam Hebraicam, adeoque illuserit illi tanquam puero propter imperitiam, videaturque ex tem- pore pro suo commodo novi quid commentus, vo- cem nempe Elkeca, quia alias sua ætate lingua Sy- riaca fruticem illum Kikikajon dictum esse fassus est. Quasi non potuerit fruticis apud Syros geminum esse nomen. Notat Coccejus & aliud nomen עלוליבא. Non erant talia de S. Patre præsumenda. Et Syris אלכרוע idem esse quod Kikajon. è Talmu- dicis Coccejus observat. Hieronymus ita translatio- nem suam tuetur: Nos Symmach. Aquil. & Theo- dot. sequuti novo nomine vertimus hederam (ne se Hebreum nomen Kikajon posuissemus, lector bestias Indiæ, vel montes Bæotios, aut nescio quid monstri & portenti imaginaretur) idque congrue, quia Kikajon celerrime proserpit (atque obtegit, & obumbrat, uti he- dera. Adde ex Theophrasto lib. 3. c. 18. & ex Mat- thiolo in Dioscor. lib. 2. cap. 175. hederæ speciem u- nam esse majori folio, quæ non serpit, sed per se consistit, crescitque in arborem, ut facit Kikajon. Eadem de causa LXX. cucurbitam verterunt, no- vum nomen indentens (quos non Lutherus tantum, sed notante Cornel. à Lapid. Syrus etiam Arabicus uterque, & Pagninus sequuti) quia proserpit & ob- umbrat, & sana est ut cucurbita, de qua prover- bium: Sanior est cucurbita.

Illud vero quod de Kiki notat Grotius, in Rabbinis & Rabbinizantibus improbat Cornelius à Lapide. Divinant, vel potius errant R. David, & ex eo Arias & Rabbinizantes, qui Kikajon censent esse id, quod Græci Kiki vocant, nos ricinum, sive pal- mam vel manum Christi, ob foliorum articulationem, quæ foliis latis est, & ad umbram appositis. Ricinum enim est herba venenata, consequenter & umbra ejus. Quis credat Deum Prophetæ suo preparæsse ad umbrum herbam venenatam, cum ei ad manum ef- sent tot aliæ salutiferæ?

UT PROTEGERET EUM, (LABORAVERAT ENIM) In Hebræo: ad liberandum eum à malo: id est, ab æstu.

## 4:7
Verse 7.

AND GOD PREPARED A WORM.) God is said to do all things, even those which happen naturally, who both made and preserves nature, and uses it according to His will. There are many kinds of worms that infest trees, shrubs, and herbs.

That this worm was not an ordinary one is evident from the fact that it destroyed the ivy at dawn, so that it withered and fell before the sun could grow hot and strike Jonah's head: but a single natural and ordinary worm cannot do this so quickly. Thus Cornelius à Lapide. The same verb is used when, by the command of God, a fish was extraordinarily led to swallow Jonah unharmed, ch. 2, v. 1, and when God prepared the Kikajon, v. 6, i.e., He had extraordinarily caused it to spring up without seed very briskly in one night and to grow to such a size that it overshadowed the whole hut, and when an east wind is prepared to increase the heat.

Verse the same.

AT THE RISING OF THE DAWN ON THE NEXT DAY.) The day after, as the dawn was shining.

AND IT STRUCK THE IVY.) That Cici, with its root injured,

AND THEY ARE DRIED UP.) Destitute of the moisture of the earth.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ET PARAVIT DEUS VERMEM.) Omnia, etiam quæ naturaliter fiunt, Deus facere dicitur, qui na- turam & fecit & conservat, & ea pro arbitratu utitur. Vermium multa sunt genera arboribus, virgultis, herbis infesta.

Hunc vermem non fuisse ordinarium, patet ex eo, quod subito hederam eroferit in aurora, ita ut illa exaruerit, & deciderit, antequam Sol inca- lesceret & feriret caput Jonæ: hoc autem tam ci- to facere nequit vermis unus naturalis, & ordina- rius. Ita Cornelius à Lapide. Adhibetur idem verbum, cum jussu Dei piscis extraordinarie eo ductus est, ut Jonam deglutiat illæsum c. 2. v. 1. & cum Kikajon paravit Deus v. 6. h. e. extraordina- rie fecerat, ut sine semine oriretur valde alacriter una nocte & tanta magnitudine proveniret, ut to- tum tugurium obumbraret, & cum ventus orien- talis ad æstum augendum paratur.

Vers. eod.

ASCENSU DILUCULI IN CRASTINUM.) Po- stridie aurora illucescente.

ET PERCUSSIT HEDERAM.) Cici illud, radice læsa,

ET EXARUNT.) Humore terræ destitutum.

Verse 8.

AND WHEN THE SUN HAD RISEN) And had already advanced somewhat.

THE LORD COMMANDED A HOT AND SCORCHING WIND.) A silent east wind. Thus the Hebrew and Chaldean have it; a breeze without motion, without cold, which would assist the heat that had arisen in the sun.

AND HE WAS FAINTING.) In the Hebrew: He was losing heart, that is, nearly losing it.

IT IS BETTER FOR ME TO DIE THAN TO LIVE.) A description of an impatient temperament.

MELIUS EST MIHI MORI QVAM VIVERE.) Descriptio impatientis ingenii.

## 4:11
Verse 11.

WHO DO NOT KNOW WHAT IS BETWEEN THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT.) That is, of that age which does not yet know the distinctions between honorable and base, and to whom therefore it is fair to be spared. The right signifies those things which are straight, the left those which are contrary. Infancy is accustomed to be described by ignorance of right and base. See what we have brought forward at Deut. 1, 29.

AND MANY CATTLE.) If you have no pity for men:

What have the oxen done, an animal without deceit and guile?

The Pelagians concluded from this v. 11 that infants are devoid of sin, as is found in Jerome, book 3 against the Pelagians. I beg you, what have little infants sinned? Neither can the consciousness of a crime be imputed, nor ignorance, who according to the Prophet Jonah do not know their right hand and their left. But here original sin is not denied to infants, which Moses attributes to them in Gen. 6 and 8, Job ch. 14, 4, David in Ps. 51, 6, but actual sin, which is designated against knowledge and conscience, and these things are said comparatively by a comparison of the deeds of infants with adults. For the malice of the latter ascends to heaven; but the former were immune from such guilt. To the Papists, Calvinists, and especially the Anabaptists who deny faith to infants from this passage because there is no knowledge in them, it is answered otherwise: that faith is supernatural knowledge, kindled in a supernatural way by the Holy Spirit through the word, or the washing of water in the word: but here only the natural knowledge of worldly things, and that actual, is taken away from infants. For otherwise they also have the work of the law written in their hearts, Rom. 2, 14. The example of John proves that faith can be given to infants, Luke 1, 15. 41. Christ himself teaches that infants (τὰ βρέφη) believe, Matt. 18, Mark 9, 36, ch. 10, 13, 15, and he declares that the kingdom of heaven is theirs, which belongs only to the faithful, Luke 18, 16. Indeed, he commands us to be like them if we wish to enter into the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 18, 3, but these things are said paraphrastically. Blessed be the Lord, who is able to do all things superabundantly more than we ask or understand, according to the power by which he works in us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus, to all generations of the age of ages, Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

QVI NESCIUNT QVID SIT INTER DEX- TRAM ET SINISTRAM.) Id est, ejus ætatis quæ hone- sti ac turpis discrimina nondum novit, & cui propterea parci æquum est. Dextra significat ea, quæ recta sunt, sini- stra ea quæ contraria. Infans ætas describi solet ignorantia recti ac turpis. Vide quæ attulimus ad Deut. 1, 29.

ET JUMENTA MULTA.) Si hominum te non miseret:

Quid fecere boves animal sine fraude doloque?

Pelagiani ex hoc v. 11. concludebant, infantes peccati expertes esse, ut est apud Hieronym. l. 3. ad- vers. Pelag. Oro te, quid infantuli peccavêre? nec conscientia delicti imputari potest, nec ignorantia, qui juxta Jonam Prophetam manum dextram ne- sciunt & sinistram. Verum hic infantibus non derogatur peccatum originale, quod ipsis tribuit Moses Gen. 6. & 8. Job. cap. 14, 4. David. Ps. 51, 6. sed actuale, quod contra scientiam & conscientiam designatur, ac comparate hæc dicuntur συγκρίσει facta infantum cum adultis. Nam horum malitia in cœlum ascendit; Illi autem à tali culpa immu- nes erant. Pontificiis, Calvinianis & imprimis Ana- baptistis ex hoc loco fidem infantibus deroganti- bus, quia in illis notitia non est, alias respondetur: fidem esse notitiam supernaturalem, supernaturali modo à Sp. S. per verbum, vel lavacrum aquæ in verbo accensam: hic vero infantibus solum adimi notitiam rerum mundanarum naturalem, eamque actualem. Nam alioquin habent & illi opus legis in cordibus suis scriptum Rom. 2, 14. Posse fidem infantibus da- ri, exemplum Johannis probat Luc. 1, 15.41. credere τὰ βρέφη infantes Christus ipse docet Matth. 18. Marc. 9, 36. c. 10. 13. 15. eorumque esse regnum cælorum, quod nonnisi fidelium est, perhibet Luc. 18, 16. Imo nos iis similes esse jubet, si in regnum cælorum in- gredi velimus Matth. 18, 3. sed hæc παραφραδικῶς. Benedictus sit Dominus, qui potens est facere omnia superabundanter, quam petimus aut intelligimus, se- cundum virtutem, qua operatur in nobis, ipsi gloria in Ecclesia & in Christo Jesu, in omnes generatio- nes seculi seculorum, Amen.

# Micah

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
In the name of God. In the year of our Lord 1600. From the press.

The Prophet has the name מיכה from מי and the pronominal suffix י, 'Who is like unto thee?' Although others derive it from מך, 'he was poor,' because his fortune was very meager. He was almost contemporary with Isaiah, with whom he taught in the kingdom of Judah, while Hosea and Amos taught in the kingdom of Israel; as is gathered from the inscription: yet he threatened both kingdoms with destruction, Samaria by the Assyrians, Judah by the Chaldeans, but in such a way that he also promised a new spiritual kingdom to be instituted through Christ, and thus he preached the Law and the Gospel, which was the task of all the Prophets, so that he might stir up contrition and faith, which are required for true repentance, and lift up the faithful in the coming evils.

Three sermons seem to be established. The first is completed in chapters 1 and 2, and is for the most part legal, yet with an Evangelical promise subjoined at the end of chapter 2: For in chapter 1, a most grave threatening is held against Samaria and Jerusalem, on account of sins, and especially idolatry, concerning Samaria to be utterly destroyed together with its idols; and concerning Jerusalem to be carried away, and the damages of other cities. Then in chapter 2, on account of the unjust seizure of others' goods, he predicts the alienation of the land and denounces the punishment of the law of retaliation because of the long-suffering of God and impenitence; yet he promises the faithful a gathering, and the Lord as a breaker-through.

The second sermon is partly legal in chapter 3, where he indicates to the princes, on account of injustice and tyranny, the denial of being heard, and to the seducing prophets, darkness and confusion, and because both are rebuked for their security, he threatens the devastation of Jerusalem and the temple: it is partly Evangelical, which in chapter 4 promises the new exaltation of the house of the Lord, and tranquility to the faithful, even from the Gentiles, and prophesies the return of the daughter of Zion from Babylon, and furthermore in chapter 5, he predicts the coming forth of the Son of God from Bethlehem and His rule, the liberation of the people, the defeat of the enemies of the Church, and the extermination of idolatries.

The third sermon is penitential in chapters 6 and 7. There, having proposed the benefits of the leading out from Egypt and the liberation from Balak, requiring not sacrifices, but what the Lord demanded, he indicates famine and warlike devastation on account of injustice in commerce. Here, however, he complains of the scarcity of the upright, the bloodthirstiness of most, the injustice of the magistrate, and perfidy toward one's neighbor, even the most closely related. By his own example, however, he raises the pious to trust in the Salvation of the Lord and to patience, and promises the building up of spiritual Zion, the enlargement of the Lord's inheritance, the forgiveness of sins, and the fulfillment of the Patriarchal promises.

SERMON I. MOSTLY LEGAL.

Latin:

I. N. ANNO AD MIC PRÆLO

Propheta nomen מיכה habet à מי & affixio pronomine י Quis tibi? Quamvis alii id à מך tenuis fuit, deducant, quod fortunæ valde tenuis fuerit. Σύγχρονος fere fuit Esaia, quocum in regno Judæ docuit, cum Hoseas ac Amos in regno Israelis; ut ex inscri- ptione colligitur: utrique tamen regno excidium comminatus est, Samariæ per Assyrios, Judæ per Chaldæos, sed ita, ut promiserit etiam novum re- gnum spirituale per Christum instituendum, adeo- que Legem & Evangelium, quod omnium Propheta- rum fuit, prædicavit, ut contritionem & fidem, quæ ad veram pœnitentiam requiruntur, excitaret, & fideles in venturis malis erigeret.

Conciones videntur tres constituendæ. Prima cap. 1. & 2. absolvitur, estque maximam partem le- galis, subjuncta tamen sub Cap. 2. finem, promissio- ne Evangelica: Nam c. 1. comminatio adversus Sa- mariam & Jerusalem gravissima habetur, ob pecca- ta, & imprimis idololatriam, de Samaria funditus destruenda una cum idolis suis; deque Hierosolyma transportanda, & aliarum civitatum damnis. Tum Cap. 2. ob iniquum alienorum bonorum raptum do- minium terræ alienum prædicit & pœnam talionis securis propter longanimitatem Dei & impœni- tentiam denunciat: fidelibus tamen congregationem, & Dominum perruptorem promittit.

Secunda concio partim legalis est cap. 3. proceri- bus ob injustitiam & tyrannidem, exauditionis de- negationem, Prophetis seductoribus tenebras & con- fusionem indicit, & utrisque ob securitatem repre- hensis, Hierosolymæ & templi devastationem mina- tur: partim Evangelica, quæ Cap. 4. novam do- mus Domini exaltationem, & tranquillitatem fideli- bus, etiam è gentibus pollicetur, & filiæ Zionis redu- ctionem è Babylone vaticinatur, ac porro cap. 5. egressum Filii Dei è Bethlehem ejusque regimen, po- puli liberationem ac hostium Ecclesiæ devictionem & idololatriarum exterminationem prædicit.

Concio tertia pœnitentialis est c. 6. & 7. Illic pro- positis beneficii eductionis ex Ægypto & liberatio- nis à Balacko requirens non sacrificia, sed quæ Dominus postulavit, ob injustitiam in commer- ciis famem & bellicam devastationem indicit. Hic vero conqueritur de paucitate proborum, plero- rumque sanguinolentia, magistratus injustitia, per- fidia ergo proximum etiam conjunctissimum. Suo autem exemplo pios ad fiduciam in Salutem Domini ac patientiam erigit, & spiritualis Sionis ædificatio- nem, hæreditatis Domini ampliationem, pecca- torum condonationem & promissionum Patriar- chalium impletionem promittit.

CONCIO I. POTISSIMUM LEGALIS.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

The coming forth of the Lord to punish is terrible on account of the prevarications and especially the idolatry of the people, with the devastation of Samaria, and the desolation of idols, and the overthrow of Jerusalem and other cities.

Micah sings of the dangers about to come upon the idols.

Ver. 1.

TO MICAH THE MORASTHITE.) Jerome says that he is not the son of Imlah (1 Kings 22:8), but of Morasthi near Eleutheropolis.

OR Hebron in the tribe of Judah. But Epiphanius, Dorotheus, and Isidore refer Micah to the tribe of Ephraim. However, that this town is wrongly confused by some with מֹרֵשֶׁת, of which mention is made in v. 15 and Josh. 15:44, is apparent from the different form of the words themselves. Furthermore, that Jerome was mistaken in his letter to Paulinus in making this Micah one and the same with that one in 1 Kings 22:8 (although this was also done by Epiphanius and Dorotheus) is clear even from the fact that the latter was much earlier and lived in Israel, whereas this one of ours lived his life in Judah. From which it may also be gathered that this one of ours drew his family from the tribe of Judah: nor did the opinion of Epiphanius, that he was an Ephraimite, arise from any other source than the confusion of our prophet with that Israelite one.

IN THE DAYS OF JOTHAM, AHAZ, HEZEKIAH) It appears, therefore, that he began to be distinguished by prophecies a little later than those whom we have already had, who began to be known from the time of Uzziah, King of Judah, and likewise reached to the times of Hezekiah.

What is to be thought of him can be clear from those things which we prefaced to Joel.

WHICH HE SAW CONCERNING SAMARIA.) Whence evil flowed into the ten tribes.

AND JERUSALEM.) Whence the two tribes were corrupted.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

Egressus Domini ad puniendum terribilis ob prævaricationes & maxime idololatriam populi, cum vastatione Samariæ, ac de- solatione idolorum, & Hierosolymæ alia- rumque civitatum eversione.

Occinit idolis ventura pericula Michæas.

Vers. 1.

AD MICHÆAM MORASTHITEN.) Non illum filium Jemlæ 1. Reg. 22, 8. Hieronymus vinculum esse di- cit Marasthi juxta Eleutheropolim.

VEL Hebron in tribu Juda. Sed ad tribum Ephraim Micham referunt Epiphanius, Doro- theus, Isidorus. Perperam autem hoc oppidum cum מֹרֵשֶׁת cujus v. 15. & Jos. 15, 44. mentio fit, con- fundi à nonnullis ex ipsa vocum, diversa forma apparet. Cæterum falsum in eo fuisse Hieronymum, ad Paulin. quod hunc Micham cum illo 1. Reg. 22, 8. unum eundemque fecerit (quamvis hoc etiam ab Epiphanio, & Dorotheo factum sit) vel ex eo liquet, quod ille longe prior fuerit, & in Israel vixerit: quum hic noster in Juda vitam egerit. Unde etiam colligere liceat hunc nostrum è tribu Juda fami- liam traxisse: nec aliunde sententiam Epiphanii, quod Ephraimita fuerit, ortam, quam è confusione Prophetæ nostri, cum illo Israelitico.

IN DIEBUS JOATHAN, ACHAS, EZECHIÆ) Apparet ergo cœpisse eum. Prophetiis illustrari paulo serius, quam eos, quos jam ante habuimus, qui ab Oziæ Regis Judæi tempore cœpere cognosci, & pariter ad Eze- chiæ tempora pervenerunt.

Quid de eo habendum, ex iis quæ ad Joëlem præfati sumus, patere potest.

QVOD VIDIT SUPER SAMARIAM.) Unde malum fluxit in decem tribus.

ET JERUSALEM.) Unde corruptæ duæ tribus.

## 1:2
HEAR, ALL YE PEOPLES.) Sprung from Jacob.

Although the punishments predicted here concern the Israelites, yet all other peoples and the whole earth with all its fullness could be invited to observe the judgments of the Lord against a people most famous throughout the whole world, so that there is no need to understand and restrict to a particular sense those things which sound simply and universally, abandoning the letter.

AND LET THE EARTH ATTEND AND THE FULLNESS THEREOF.) That is, all you who dwell in the promised land.

LET THE LORD GOD BE A WITNESS AGAINST YOU.) The Chaldean interprets בכם as against you. If at any time the evils which I speak of come upon you, God will be a witness for me that I have subtracted nothing from those things which were commanded to me.

In the Hebrew, 'The Lord God [be] a witness among you': That 'AMONG YOU' can be understood of the presence of God among them: The Lord God, who is among you, be a witness. Thus God, present as a witness, is established as αὐτήκοος κᾀὐτόπτης [one who hears and sees for himself], and His gracious presence is set before them, lest, having disregarded it, they experience a visitation of wrath. To be 'for a witness' is a Hebraism, Gen. 2, 24. Exod. 2. v. 10. c. 4, 16. Ps. 31, 3.

THE LORD FROM HIS HOLY TEMPLE.) He who looks down upon all things from heaven, See above Jon, 2, 8.

Jerome, Theodoret, Haymo, and Lyra understand it thus, as if to say: I call God to witness that this prophecy of mine is not my own, but God's, in that I do not invent these things, but have heard them from God: But these things should rather be understood in such a way that the Prophet calls upon God to testify to his faithfulness in announcing the punishments: THE LORD, who resides in heaven, as if in his august temple, to be adored with all worship, and from there contemplates the earth and all the works of men, be witness for you and for me that I have announced these decrees of his to you. The Lord will be a witness to the announced danger and extreme misery, so that you may not complain afterwards as if you had not been forewarned by me. By the holy temple, Lyra indeed also understands heaven, in which God is said to be (Ps. 103:9, Matt. 6:9), not that he is included by heaven, but that he manifests himself there most of all: Theodoret and Luther, however, more correctly [understand it] of the temple of Jerusalem. understand it, in which he had the seat of his gracious presence as if it were his own (Ps. 24:3, Is. 31:9).

Latin:

AUDITE POPULI OMNES.) A Jacobo orti.

Etsi pœnæ hic prædictæ concernant Israelitas, poterant tamen ad observanda judicia Domini ad- versus populum toto orbe celeberrimum omnes alii populi, & terra tota cum omni plenitudine invi- tari, ut ita opus non sit ea, quæ ἁπλῶς universa- liter sonant, relicta litera, particulariter intellige- re, ac restringere.

ET ATTENDAT TERRA ET PLENITUDO EJUS.) Id est omnes, qui in terra promissa habitatis.

SIT DOMINUS DEUS VOBIS IN TESTEM.) Chaldæus בכם interpretatur contra vos. Si quando mala quæ dicam vobis evenient, Deus mihi testis erit, me nihil subtraxisse de eis, quæ mandata mihi erant.

In Ebr. Dominus Deus vobis in testem: Illud IN VOBIS, intelligi potest de præsentia Dei inter ipsos: Dominus Deus, qui est in vobis, sit in te- stem. Ita Deus præsens testis αὐτήκοος κᾀὐτόπτης constituitur, ejusque gratiosa præsentia ipsis sisti- tur, ne ea posthabita visitationem iræ experiantur. Esse in testem Ebraïsmus est Gen. 2, 24. Exod. 2. v. 10. c. 4, 16. Ps. 31, 3.

DOMINVS DE TEMPLO SANCTO SUO.) Qui ex cœlo omnia despectat, Vide supra Jon, 2, 8.

Hieronymus, Theodor. Haymo, & Lyr. ita acci- piunt, q. d. Testor Deum, hanc meam Prophetiam non esse meam, sed Dei, quod sc. ego hæc non sin- gam, sed à Deo audierim: Sed intelligenda potius ita hæc sunt, quod Propheta Deum advocet, ad te- standam fidelitatem in annunciandis pœnis: DO- MINUS, qui in cœlo, quasi in templo suo augu- stus, omnique cultu adorandus residet, atque inde terram contemplatur, & omnia hominum opera, sit vobis mihique testis, quod hæc ejus decreta vo- bis enunciaverim. Dominus in testem erit denun- ciati periculi, & extremæ miseriæ, ne postea con- queramini, quasi non fueritis à me præmoniti. Per templum sanctum intelligit quidem etiam Lyran. cœlum, in quo Deus esse dicitur Pf. CIII. 9. Matt. VI. 9. non quod cœlo includatur, sed quod ibi se maxime manifestet: Rectius tamen Theodore- tus, & Lutherus de templo Hierosol. accipiunt, in quo sedem gratiosæ præsentiæ velut propriam ha- buit Pf. XXIV. 3. Es. XXXI. 9.

## 1:3
Verse of the same. HE SHALL GO FORTH FROM HIS PLACE, AND SHALL DESCEND] God is said to go forth from heaven when he makes his benefits or judgments visible on earth.

AND HE SHALL TREAD UPON THE HIGH PLACES OF THE EARTH] He shall destroy the most fortified places. See Deuteronomy 32:13, 34:29.

Latin:

Vers. eod. EGREDIETUR DE LOCO SUO, ET DESCENDET] Deus exire de cœlo dicitur, cum in ter- ra beneficia sua aut judicia facit conspici.

ET CALCABIT SUPER EXCELSA TERRÆ] Destruet loca munitissima. Vide Deuteron. XXXII. 13. XXXIV. 29.

## 1:4
Verse 4. AND THE MOUNTAINS SHALL BE CONSUMED UNDER HIM] That is, the cities situated on the mountains, such as Jerusalem and Samaria, shall be burned.

AND THE VALLEYS SHALL BE CLEAVED] That is, the towns situated in the valleys shall be demolished.

AS WAX FROM THE FACE OF THE FIRE] This comparison refers to the first member.

AND AS WATERS THAT RUN DOWN A STEEP PLACE] This [refers] to the second.

To go forth from his place, that is, from heaven, and for God to descend, is said when he comes forth not by local motion, but by the manifestation of his presence; see Augustine, Book 1, On the City of God, ch. 5. By the high places of the earth and the mountains, others understand the nobles and the powerful of Israel, and by the valleys, the common people, meaning that both the powerful and the commoners are to perish. Thus Osiander, Cornelius a Lapide, and others. Blessed Luther, however, by the high places understands all that is sublime in Israel, Kings, Princes, Priests, and finally the worship and the temple itself, which he takes as mountains and hills of the whole region. It is a synecdoche, for he uses the container for the contained. For by the name of mountains and valleys he embraces the whole people, [meaning] that everything will be laid waste that is placed either on the mountains or in the valleys. For he alludes to the situation of the holy land, which is full of mountains and valleys, to signify extreme devastation, so that it might not be thought that anything at all would remain from which the enemy would withhold his hand. The similes which the Prophet uses tend to show that this wrath of the Lord cannot be restrained or hindered by any reason. For what is there that can save wax from the fire brought near it, so that it does not melt? What can restrain the rush of a river flowing down through steep places? The same reason, he says, will apply to the punishment, which will advance upon you with great force. The Lord is fire, you are softer than any wax; the Lord is a river rushing with great force. You are like shrubs barely clinging to a steep or sloping place: therefore, without difficulty, you will be swept away to punishment and will perish. Ps. 68:3, Ps. 97:3. Which things, however, are to be understood in such a way that an absolute decree is not invented, but that these judgments are announced to them based on the foreknowledge of their impenitence.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET CONSUMENTUR MONTES SUBTUS EUM] Id est, urbes in montibus sitæ, ut Jerusalem & Sa- maria, incendentur.

ET VALLES SCINDENTUR] Id est, oppida in vallibus sita diruentur.

SICUT CERA A FACIE IGNIS] Hæc compa- ratio respicit prius membrum.

ET SICUT AQUÆ QUÆ DECURRUNT IN PRÆCEPS] Hæc secundum.

Egredi è loco suo, id est è cœlo dicitur, & descen- dere Deus, cum prodit non motu locali, sed osten- sione præsentiæ suæ; vid. Aug. l. 1. de Civ. Dei c. 5. Per excelsa terræ & montes alii optimates & poten- tes Israel, per valles v. plebejos intelligunt, quod tam potentes quam plebeji perituri sint. Ita Osian- der, Cornelius a Lapide & alii. B. Lutherus tamen per excelsa, sublimia quæque in Israel, Reges, Principes, Sacerdotes, cultum denique & ipsum templum intelligit, qui montes & colles de tota re- gione accipit. Synecdoche est, usurpat enim conti- nens pro contento. Nam appellatione montium & vallium complectitur totum populum, quod omnia vastabuntur, quæ vel in montibus vel valli- bus sunt posita. Alludit enim ad situm terræ san- ctæ, quæ plena est montibus & vallibus, ut signi- ficet extremam vastitatem, ne quid usquam pute- tur reliquum fore, à quo hostis manum abstineat. Similitudines, quibus Propheta utitur, eo perti- nent, ut ostendat iram hanc Domini nulla ratione cohiberi, aut impediri posse. Quid enim est, quod ce- ram salvare possit adjuncto igni, ne liquefcat? Quid potest cohibere impetum fluminis, per præ- cipitia loca labentis? Eadem ratio, inquit, erit pœnæ, magno impetu grassantis in vos. Dominus est ignis, vos estis molliores quavis cera; Dominus est flumen magno impetu ruens. Vos estis ceu frutices ægre hærentes in præcipiti seu declivi lo- co: Sine negotio igitur abripiemini ad pœnam & peribitis. Pf. LXIIX. 3. Pf. XCVII. 3. Quæ vero ita accipienda, ne absolutum decretum fingatur, sed ex prævisione impœnitentiæ ipsorum hæc iis- dem denuncientur judicia.

## 1:5
Verse 5. FOR THE WICKEDNESS] Because of the wickedness, as the Chaldean translates. The Greeks [say] διὰ ἀσέβειαν.

WHAT IS THE WICKEDNESS OF JACOB?] That is, what is the origin of the wickedness in Jacob, or the ten tribes: metonymy.

IS NOT SAMARIA?] It is customary for an example to be spread more widely from primary cities.

AND WHAT ARE THE HIGH PLACES OF JUDAH?] What is the origin of the high places in Judah?

In the time of Ahaz the temple was closed, and in all the corners of Jerusalem altars were erected 2 Kings 16, 2 Chronicles 28.

Latin:

Vers. 5. IN SCELERE] Propter scelus, ut Chaldæus vertit. Græci διὰ ἀσέβειαν.

QUOD SCELUS IACOB?] Id est, quæ origo sce- leris Jacobo, sive decem tribubus: μετωνυμία.

NONNE SAMARIA?] Solet ab urbibus primariis latius fundi exemplum.

ET QUÆ EXCELSA JUDÆ] Quæ origo excel- sorum in Juda?

Tempore Achas templum claudebatur, & in omnibus angulis Hierosol. altaria erigebantur 2. Reg. XVI. 2. Chron. XXVIII.

## 1:6
I WILL MAKE SAMARIA AS A HEAP OF STONES] In the Hebrew: Into a mound of a field: that is, into a hill that may be plowed.

WHEN A VINEYARD IS PLANTED] Into a vineyard.

AND I WILL PULL DOWN HER STONES INTO THE VALLEY] I will cast down from the height into the places below.

AND I WILL DISCOVER THE FOUNDATIONS THEREOF] So that the foundations appear. These things and those which follow were fulfilled by Shalmaneser.

Latin:

PONAM SAMARIAM QUASI ACERVUM LAPIDUM] In Hebræo: In tumulum agri: id est, in collem qui aretur.

CUM PLANTATUR VINEA] In vinetum.

ET DETRAHAM IN VALLEM LAPIDES EJUS] Dejiciam ex edito in subjecta.

ET FUNDAMENTA EJUS REVELABO] Ita ut fundamenta appareant. Hæc & quæ sequuntur, impleta per Salmanasarem.

## 1:7
Verse 7. AND ALL THE GRAVEN IMAGES THEREOF SHALL BE BEATEN IN PIECES] See Amos 3:14.

AND ALL THE HIRES THEREOF SHALL BE BURNED WITH FIRE] The gifts of the Temple, sent to them by the Assyrians, whose worship they imitated.

FOR THEY ARE GATHERED OF THE HIRE OF AN HARLOT] They are the wages of idolatry.

AND THEY SHALL RETURN TO THE HIRE OF AN HARLOT] They shall go to Nineveh, which taught them idolatry; this shall be the δίδακτρον (tuition fee).

Others explain these things thus: He calls idolatry fornication; the wages or gain from harlotry are the fruits, riches, and comforts which the Samaritans and other idolaters boasted they received from their idols, or which they received from the commerce of the Chaldeans and other idolatrous nations. See Hosea 2:4, 12. Cornelius à Lapide attributes this opinion to St. Jerome, Remigius, Hugo, and Lyra, explaining it thus: Because Samaria is a harlot, that is, a worshiper of idols, and thinks that she has received her fruits and riches from them for this her worship, therefore I will cause that those things likewise be transferred and return to the harlots, that is, to the Assyrians, the worshipers of idols, as the Chaldean translates, who will lay waste Samaria, and who will attribute and consecrate them to their idols as the wages of idolatry. But it is better to understand the gifts, which were contributed partly by the inhabitants, partly by foreigners to the idols: because both the objects and the instruments of idolatry are commemorated, and their abolition is predicted; so that those things which had been collected from the hire of a harlot, might return as the hire of a harlot to be plundered by the Assyrians, whose metropolis Nineveh is called a beautiful harlot, Nah. III. 4. It is pleasing to append what the Blessed Luther has here on this passage, since the Calvinist iconoclasts are still making a tumult: This one passage is of the number of those which today has given the εἰκονομάχοις (iconoclasts) the occasion to cast all images without distinction out of the temple. Nor is this a new tumult in the Church. The second Nicene Synod, more than eleven hundred years ago, under Constantius and Irene his mother, was convened for this one reason, and a decree was made with great consensus against those who maintained that there was no use for images in temples. It would not, therefore, be absurd to show in a few words what can rightly be established concerning this matter. It is true that Moses and the Prophets everywhere prohibit and condemn images with great zeal, but it is foolish to understand that generally of all images. For the Jews also used images, even in the temple, as the building of Solomon shows. And who would doubt that there were not some painted tablets in the houses of Kings and Princes? For painting, because it represents things, has never been considered among the prohibited or illicit arts. Just as, therefore, the history of Solomon wisely judging between two harlots is recited without sin, so indeed the same history is painted without sin. Nor would I ever have judged the Jews to have been so barbaric that they did not have these monuments of things famously done painted even in public places, and not only within private walls. Just as they were extremely diligent in describing them. We would therefore judge not only barbarism, but also remarkable ignorance, because in many places even the images of Christ and the Apostles, without distinction, out of the temple have been cast out. For who does not see that, just as pious histories are recited without sin and even with profit to the hearers, in this same way, for the sake of the unlearned, such histories can also be painted and sculpted, not only in private houses but in public places? So that, just as in former times the decrees of republics were set forth in a public place, so the unlearned might everywhere be reminded of their salvation, of the benefits of God, of the punishments which have been inflicted upon sinners, and of whatever else is for edification.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET OMNIA SCULPTILIA EJUS CONCIDENTUR] Vide Am. III. 14.

ET OMNES MERCEDES EJUS COMBURENTUR IGNE] Donaria Templi, missa illis ab Assyriis, quorum cultum imitabantur.

QUIA DE MERCEDIBUS MERETRICIS CONGREGATA SUNT] Idololatriæ sunt mercedes.

ET USQUE AD MERCEDEM MERETRICIS REVERTENTUR] Ibunt Niniven, quæ ipsos idololatriam docuit, hoc erit δίδακτρον.

Alii hæc ita explicant: Idololatriam vocat fornicationem, merces seu quæstus ex meretricio sunt fruges, opes & commoda, quæ Samaritæ, aliique idololatræ se à suis idolis percipere jactabant, aut quæ ex commercio Chaldæorum, & aliarum gentium idololatrarum percipiebant. Vid. Hos. II. 4. 12. Hanc sententiam S. Hieronymo, Remigio, Hugoni, & Lyræ tribuit Cornel. à Lapide sic exponens: Quia Samaria meretrix, id est, cultrix idolorum, putat se ab iis pro hocce suo cultu recepisse suas fruges & opes, idcirco efficiam, ut illæ pariter ad meretrices, id est, ad Assyrios idolorum cultores, ut vertit Chaldæus, qui vastabunt Samariam, transferantur & redeant, qui eas ut idololatriæ mercedes, suis idolis acceptas referant & consecrent. Sed præstat donaria intelligere, quæ partim ab incolis, partim ab exteris idolis conferebantur: quia commemorantur tum objecta, tum instrumenta idololatriæ, eorumque abolitio prædicitur; ut quæ collecta erant ex meretricia mercede, redeant in mercedem meretricis diripienda ab Assyriis, quorum metropolis Ninive meretrix speciosa vocatur Nah. III. 4. Placet de hoc loco ea, quæ hic habet B. Lutherus, subjungere, siquidem adhuc Iconomachi Calviniani tumultuentur: Hic locus unus est ex eorum numero, qui hodie εἰκονομάχοις occasionem dedit, ut omnes imagines sine discrimine ex templi ejicerent. Neque hic novus in Ecclesia tumultus est. Nicena Synodus secunda annis retro plus mille & centum, sub Constantio, & Irene matre ejus, hanc ob unam causam coacta est, & decretum magno consensu est contra eos, qui statuebant nullum in templis imaginum usum esse. Non igitur absurdum fuerit paucis ostendere, quid de hoc negotio recte possit constitui. Verum est, quod Moses & Prophetæ magno studio ubique prohibent & damnant imagines, sed ineptum est, id in genere intelligere de omnibus imaginibus. Nam & Judæi imaginibus, etiam in templo sunt usi, sicut ostendit ædificium Salomonis. Et quis dubitet in Regum & Principum domibus non fuisse aliquas pictas tabulas? Pictura enim, quia res repræsentat, nunquam inter prohibitas, aut illicitas artes habita est. Sicut igitur sine peccato recitatur historia de Salomone, sapienter judicante inter duas meretrices. Ita profecto sine peccato eadem historia depingitur. Neque ego unquam tam barbaros fuisse Judæos judicaverim, quin etiam in publicis locis, & non tantum inter privatos parietes, hæc monumenta rerum præclare gestarum habuerint picta. Sicut in iis describendis perquam diligentes fuerunt. Non solum igitur barbariem, sed insignem quoq; inscitiam judicaverimus, quod in multis locis etiam Christi & Apostolorum imagines, sine discrimine ex templi ejectæ sunt. Quis enim non videt, quod sic- ut sine peccato piæ historiæ etiam cum fructu audito- rum recitantur, ad hunc modum propter rudes et- iam pingi tales historiæ & sculpi possint, non solum in privatis ædibus, sed in publicis locis. Ut sicut olim decreta rerum publicarum in publico loco propone- bantur, ita rudes ubiq; admoneantur salutis suæ, be- neficiorum Dei, pœnarum, quæ peccatoribus insti- ctæ sunt, & si quæ alia ad ædificationem.

## 1:8
Verse 8.

FOR THIS I WILL WAIL AND HOWL. The Prophet speaks and says that he will confirm with conspicuous signs of mourning how certain are the things he says. I WILL GO STRIPPED AND NAKED. Stripped of my outer garment. AND MOURNING LIKE THE OSTRICHES. As the young of the owl. Thus the Hebrew. Both similes are in Job 30:29, whence it appears to be proverbial.

It seems more correct to join the ostrich with the dragon, as the LXX and Pagninus render the word, as well as B. Luther, because elsewhere also in the description of desolation mention is made of the howling of ostriches and dragons (Isa. 13:21, ch. 34:14, Lam. 4:3). And just as the dragon emits great roars when it wishes to drink from the elephant—whose blood it seeks to quench its thirst—and is crushed by the falling beast, and terrifies men with its wailing so that it even kills them, according to Albertus Magnus, book 26, On Animals; so also Aelian, book 14, ch. 6, reports of the female ostrich that it groans greatly when it is pressed by thirst.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

SUPER HOC PLANGAM ET ULULABOJ Lo- quitur Propheta, & dicit, se etiam conspicuis luctus si- gnis confirmaturum, quam certa sint quæ dicat. VADAM SPOLIATUS ET NUDUS] Exutus ve- ste superiore. ET LUCTUM QUASI STRUTHIONUM] Qua- si pullorum ululæ. Sic Hebræum. Utraque similitudo est apud Jobum XXX. 29. unde apparet esse proverbiale.

Cum Dracone rectius conjungi videtur stru- thio, ut LXX. & Pagninus vocem reddunt, nec non B. Lutherus, quia etiam alibi in vastitate descri- benda mentio fit ululatus Struthionum & draco- num Es. XIII. 21. c. XXXIV. 14. Thr. IV. 3. Et ut Draco magnos rugitus edit, cum ab Elephante, cujus sanguinem sitis restinguendæ causa, bibere vult, corruente obruitur, & ejulatu suo homines terret, ut etiam ipsos interimat, apud Albert. M. l. XXVI. de anim. Sic etiam de Struthione fœ- mina refert Ælian. l. XIV. c. 6. quod maxime ge- mat, cum siti premitur

## 1:9
Verse 9.

HER WOUND IS DESPERATE. It will not be healed. FOR IT HAS COME EVEN TO JUDAH, IT HAS TOUCHED THE GATE OF MY PEOPLE EVEN TO JERUSALEM. After Samaria has been destroyed and the land of the ten tribes laid waste, the Assyrians will also lay waste the land of the two tribes, under the King of the Assyrians, Sennacherib, and will arrive even at the gates of Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

DESPERATA EST PLAGA EJUS] Non sanabi- tur. QUIA VENIT USQUE AD JUDAM, TETI- GIT PORTAM POPULI MEI USQUE AD JERU- SALEM] Assyrii post destructam Samariam, vastatam- que terram decem tribuum, etiam terram duarum tri- buum vastabunt, rege Assyriorum Sennacheribo, & ad portas usque Hierosolymorum pervenient,

## 1:10
Verse 10.

TELL IT NOT IN GATH. Would that the Philistines did not know these things, lest they mock us. Taken from 2 Sam. 1:20. WEEP NOT WITH TEARS. Do not weep by weeping: that is, do not wail excessively, lest those ancient enemies rejoice. IN THE HOUSE OF DUST SPRINKLE YOURSELVES WITH DUST. When you shall be sprinkled with dust in the house of dust. In the text it is התפלשתי, but in the margin התפלשי: it is the custom of this Prophet to use words of similar sound and common usage to obscurely denote proper names. עפרה is dust: but by that word Ephraim is signified, whose houses were to be reduced to dust.

But the Hebrews, Jerome in his Commentary, Arias, Clarius, Vatablus, and Mariana, as Cornelius notes, as well as Osiander, Höpfner, and others, take the word עפרה as the proper name of a city subject to Samaria, which was the city of the Gideonite in the tribe of Manasseh (Judg. 6:11) or in the tribe of Benjamin of the same name (Josh. 13:23), which, as being near to Jerusalem, is rather looked to here, rendering it in this way: 'because of the houses of Aphrah, roll yourself in the dust,' i.e., in Aphrah, that is, cast dust upon yourselves. Others, however, take it as an appellative, i.e., 'O Samaria, you shall no longer be called Samaria, or a watchtower, but Aphrah, that is, dust, because you will shortly be reduced to dust.' Mourn, therefore, and sprinkle yourself with dust. Behold, in the spirit I see you reduced to dust; therefore, among the ruins of the dust, sprinkle yourself with dust.
