But the former sense is to be preferred, in our judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

IN GETH NOLITE ANNUNCIARE] Utinam nesciant ista Palæstini, ne nos irrideant. Sumtum ex 2. Sam. I. 20. LACRYMIS NE PLORETIS] Ne flendo fleatis: id est, ne nimium edatis ploratum, ne illi veteres hostes gaudeant, IN DOMO PULVERIS PULVERE VOS CON- SPERGITE] Cum in domo pulveris pulvere conspergemini. In textu est התפלשתי, sed in margine התפלשי: mos est hujus Prophetæ voces vicini soni & communes sume- re, ad obscure notanda nomina propria עפרה est pulvis: sed per eam vocem significatur Ephraim; cujus domus e- sant in pulverem redigendæ.

Atqui Ebræi, Hier. in Comm. Arias, Clarius, Vatablus & Mariana, notante Cornelio, ut & Osian- der, Höpfnerus, & alii vocem עפרה habent pro nomine proprio urbis, Samariæ subjectæ, quæ ci- vitas Gideoniserat in tribu Manasse Jud. VI. 11. vel in tribu Benjamin ejusdem nominis Jos. XIII. 23. quæ ceu vicina Hierosolymæ hic potius respi- citur, hoc modo reddentes: propter domos Aphræ in pulvere volutate ipsam, q. d. in Aphra, id est, pulverem vobis injicite. Alii tamen ut appel- lativum accipiunt, q. d. ô Samaria, tu jam non Samaria, vel custodia vocaberis, sed Aphra, id est, pulvis, quia brevi in pulverem redigeris. Luge ergo, & pulvere te consperge. Ecce in spiritu video te in pulverem redactam, inter rui- nas ergo pulveris, pulvere te insperge. Sed prior sensus præferendus, nostro judicio.

## 1:11
Verse 11.

AND PASS ON, YOU FAIR HABITATION. And when your fair habitation shall perish. שפיר, which signifies fair, here hints at Samaria, by a related word, as we have said.

CONFUSED WITH SHAME. Naked in its private parts, that is, with walls thrown down, which are as the garments of cities: with foundations appearing, as was said above.

Jerome, Theodoret, Remigius, and Rupert also accept the word שפיר as an epithet of Samaria, which was very beautiful. Others, however, believe it to be the proper name of a city, along with Clarius, Pagninus, Vatablus, and Mariana, as if to say: 'You, O city of Saphir, boasted that you were beautiful and sapphire-like, and behold, you are all defiled and muddy.' Some wish this to be the Neo-Caesarea of Hegesippus and Jerome. Thus B. Höpfner, as if to say: 'Pass on, O Saphir, inhabitress and city, you who have lived here until now, now as one least decorous, pass on to another place, and consult your safety by flight.' B. Luther took it as an appellative and judged that Samaria was being indicated: 'You beautiful city must go away.' There is no allusion here, says B. Luther, in the word, but a beautiful antithesis in the thing itself (saphir) signifies that it is beautiful and decorous. This name, he says, you have had for Samaria until now, but where has your name gone? Where has your decor and beauty gone? For you lie devastated, as if you had never been, and you are all covered in confusion and ignominy. Just as if someone were to strip an elegant girl adorned in splendid clothing and expose her naked to be looked at by the eyes of men. Furthermore, there is a Hebraism here which can only be rendered in Latin by a circumlocution; for it sounds word for word thus: 'Pass on from you, O decorous city: (ibri lachem) that is, go away and flee to another place.' For that is the reality of the matter. That will profit you; consult your safety by flight, and there is also a figure in these vowels (Josebeth ibri). You have been Josebeth until now, you who lived securely, you are not accustomed to migrations, but now you will have to migrate (ibri, pass on). 'Up and away, there is no staying there anymore.'

Vers. eod. [Same verse] THE INHABITANT OF THE EXIT HAS NOT GONE FORTH] צאנן, which he translates here as 'from the exit,' from the root יצא, others perhaps more correctly interpret as 'the cattle-rich land' from the similarity of צאן to those which we have mentioned, it signifies Zion, in this sense: those who dwell in Zion have not even moved a foot to save the Ephraimites.

Some, along with the LXX, the Chaldean, Vatablus, Clarius, Pagninus, and Mariana, take the name צאנן likewise as the proper name of a city which was in the tribe of Judah, Sanaa (Josh. 15:37), or rather in the tribe of Naphtali, subject to Samaria, which was Scaanim (Josh. 19:33; Judg. 4:17). Others explain it differently. Rupert and Arias preceded Grotius, who rendered it thus: 'O Jerusalem, you who dwell in Sanaan, that is, so secure in the abundance and luxury of all things that, even having seen the disaster of neighboring Samaria, you have not gone forth either to relieve, or to lament, or to console it, but have remained at home, indulging and immersed in pleasures.' However, the former explanation is to be preferred with B. Luther. An allusion is likewise made to the name which descends from יצא, 'he went out,' as if to say: 'Zanaan will no longer be, it will not go out or spread itself, but because of the divinely inflicted plague, it will keep itself at home, as those who are mourning are accustomed to do.'

THE NEIGHBORING HOUSE WILL RECEIVE THE LAMENTATION FROM YOU WHO STOOD BY HERSELF] Bethaetzel will receive the lamentation from you (Zion), standing by herself; Bethaetzel signifies the house of separation, namely, from God. Bethel, once called the house of God, is indicated. The sense is: The city of Jerusalem will indeed hear the lamentation from Bethel, but it will go about its own affairs, and will not involve itself in the affairs of Bethel.

Some, along with Theodoret, Pagninus, Arias, Vatablus, and Mariana, take this word as the proper name of a particular city which was neighboring to the city of Sanaan. Osiander explains it thus: 'Hebrew: The inhabitress of Zaenan will not go forth because of the mourning of Bethazel: even when she transfers her station from you (that is, the city of Zaenan, which has its name from 'going out', as if she who might dare to break forth bravely against the enemy, will by no means sally forth against the enemy, but will timidly keep herself within the walls, terrified by the great slaughter which will befall the city of Beth-ezel from the Assyrian. Moreover, even when the Assyrian army shall move its camp from the city of Zaanan, yet the Zaanites will not dare to go out, fearing that they might be intercepted by the enemy lurking in ambush, and their city be occupied and burned. B. Höpfner: The fourth city is Beth-ezel. Ezel, however, is a proper name of a place, and is also found in Zech. XIV. 5. When, therefore, the Prophet says, The mourning of Beth-ezel, he (the enemy) will take his station from you, he means this: You rightly have your name from the neighborhood, O city of Beth-Ezel, because the station of the enemies will be very close to you, which will bring you cause for mourning. B. Luther, with Jerome, took it as an appellative. But by the neighboring house he understands Assur in Comment. T. IV. Jenens. f. 446, whose explanation we append: The city of Zaanan will not expatiate because of mourning: Zaanan is in the tribe of Judah, as is evident from Joshua. It has its name, however, from going out, as if you were to say 'the one that goes out.' But here again there is an allusion (Zaanan not Jazah), that is, she will not go out, she will keep herself in her own house, as those are accustomed to do who are placed in mourning. For these flee beyond the sight of men, so that they may be able to give themselves to tears. As the Prophet adds the cause: The neighboring house will take your substance from you. In this manner I understand this passage, because other interpretations which are brought forward by interpreters seem to be more forced. For even if you take Beth-Ezel properly, what will it be (Emdatho?) They explain it indeed as the station of the enemy, but it is a more forced interpretation to transfer it to that which this reward the enemy is about to receive for that delay which he spent there. Wherefore, since this opinion both approaches the matter more closely and is also not so contrary to grammar, I wished to retain it, because Beth Ezel, as an appellative for a neighboring house, namely Assur, will receive from the Zeenites their substance, that is to say, even those things which they themselves thought would be established and safe for them. Thus B. Luther. Verse 12. BECAUSE SHE THAT DWELLETH IN BITTERNESSES IS WEAKENED UNTO GOOD] Truly she that dwelleth (the people) in Maroth shall be grieved on account of the strong (that is, the strong who were slain, as the Chaldean has it here). מרות; because this signifies bitterness, by the transposition of letters it hints at רמות; there were many cities in the lot of the two tribes which had the name Rama: these are called in the plural רמות, compare Jer. XXXI. 15. It will profit the Jews nothing to have kept themselves quiet, when Samaria and the neighboring cities shall be destroyed. BECAUSE EVIL CAME DOWN FROM THE LORD UNTO THE GATE OF JERUSALEM] Sennacherib will come even to the gates. Osiander [explains] these things thus: Heb. she shall anxiously await good, (i. e. auxilium) the inhabitant of Maroth: for evil shall come down from the Lord even unto the gate of Jerusalem (i.e., the city of Maroth, when it hears that the surrender of the city of Jerusalem is also being demanded by the Assyrian, will be in the greatest straits, and yet will hope for a happier outcome in some way. There seems to be an allusion in the words Maroth and Jarad. Luther, with Jerome, took מדות as an appellative, rendering it: The troubled city cannot comfort itself. Those who take it as a proper name understand Maroth in the tribe of Judah, Jos. XV. 18, or Mara in the tribe of Manasseh. B. Luther, in his commentary, having brought forward various expositions, says: The simplest meaning is this, whether you take Maroth as a proper name or appellatively for a rebellious city, that it anxiously expects good. For men placed in dangers grieve and grow weak by that very fact, that they expect help, and expect it in vain. This affection the verb (halah) shows in this place. He renders therefore: Because the city of Maroth anxiously awaits good, but evil has descended from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET TRANSITE VOBIS HABITATIO PULCRA] Et cum peribit vobis habitatio pulchra. שפיר, quod pul- chram significat, hic Samariam innuit, affini, ut dixi- mus, voce.

CONFUSA IGNOMINIA] Nuda pudendis, id est, dejectis muris, quæ velut vestes sunt Urbium: fundamen- tis apparentibus, ut supra dictum.

Vocem שפיר ceu Epithetaon Samariæ, quæ valde pulchra fuit, etiam Hieronymus, Theodore- tus, Remigius, Rupertus accipiunt. Alii tamen credunt esse nomen proprium urbis cum Clario, Pagnino, Vatablo, & Mariana q. d. Iactabas ô urbs Sappir te pulcram & sapphirinam, & ecce tota conspurcata es, & lutea. Hanc Neo-Cæsariam Hegefippi & Hieronymi nonnulli volunt. Sic B. Höpfnerus q. d. Transi nobis Saphir babitatrix, & civitas, quæ hactenus habitasti, nunc tanquam minime decora, transi in alium locum, & fuga tibi consule. Pro appellativo habuit, & Samariam indigitari censuit B. Lutherus: Du schöne Stadt musst dahin. Non est hic allusio, inquit B. Lu- therus in vocabulo, sed pulchra in re antithesis (sa- phir) significat pulchrum & decorum esse. Hoc nomen, inquit, Samaria hactenus habuisti, sed quo abiit nomen tuum? Quo abiit decor & pul- chritudo tua? Jaces enim vastata, ac si nunquam fuisses, & es tota operta confusione & ignomi- nia. Perinde ac si quis elegantem puellam splen- dido vestitu ornatam exuat, & nudam objiciat spectandam oculis hominum. Porro hic Ebrai- smus est, qui Latine non nisi per circumlocutio- nem reddi potest; sic enim de verbo ad verbum sonat: Transi vobis civitas decora: (ibri lachem) hoc est, abi & fuge in alium locum. Id enim re tua est. Id tibi proderit, tibi fuga consule, & fi- gura etiam est in hisce vocalibus (Josebeth ibri) Fuisti hactenus Josebeth, quæ habitasti secura, non es affueta ad migrationes, sed nunc tibi migrandum erit (ibri, transi.) Auf und davon, da ist kein blei- bens mehr.

Vers. eod. NON EST EGRESSA QUÆ HABITAT IN EXITU] צאנן, quod hic vertit ab exitu, à radice יצא, alii forte rectius terram pecorosam interpretantur à צאן vicinitate simili iis, quas diximus, Sionem significat, hoc sensu: illi, qui in Sione habitant, ne pedem quidem moverunt ad servandos Ephraimitas.

Nomen צאנן itidem pro nomine proprio urbis quæ in tribu Juda Sanaa Jos. XV. 37. vel po- tius in tribu Napthtali Samariæ subjecta Scana- nim fuerit Jos. XIX. 33. Jud. IV. 17. nonnulli cum LXX. Chald. Vatablo, Clario, Pagnino, Mariana habent. Alii aliter explicant. Grotio præivit Rupertus & Arias, qui ita reddidere o Ierusalem, quæ habitas in Sanaan, id est, copia & luctu rerum omnium ita secura, ut etiam visa clade vicinæ Samariæ, ad eam vel levandam, vel plangendam, vel consolandam non exieris, sed domi voluptati- bus indulgens & immersa manseris. Præferenda autem prior explicatio cum B. Luthero Allusio i- tidem fit ad nomen quod à יצא exivit descendit q. d. non amplius erit Zanaan, non exibit aut exspatia- bitur, sed ob plagam divinitus afflictam, domi, ut lugentes solent, se continebit.

PLANCTUM DOMUS VICINA ACCIPIET EX VOBIS QUÆ STETIT SIBIMET] Planctum o Be- thaetzel accipiet à vobis (Sion) stans sibi Bethaetzel domum se- parationis significat, à Deo scilicet. Indicatur autem Bethel, domus Dei olim dicta. Sensus est: Urbs Hierosolyma plan- ctum quidem à Bethele audiet, sed res suas aget, neque se Be- thelis rebus miscebit.

Et hanc vocem pro nomine proprio peculia- ris civitatis, quæ vicina fuerit urbi Sanaan nonnul- li cum Theodoreto, Pagnino, Aria, Vatablo, & Maria- na habent. Osiander ita exponit: Hebr. Non egre- dietur habitatrix Zaenan propter luctum Bethazel: etiam cum à vobis stationem suam transferet (id est, urbs Zaenan quæ nomen ab egressu habet, quasi quæ fortiter in hostem erumpere audeat, nequa- quam in hostem excurret, sed timida sese inter mu- ros continebit, perterrita ingenti clade, quæ urbi Beth- azel ab Assyrio continget. Quin etiam cum As- fyriacus exercitus ab urbe Zænan castra sua amo- vebit: tamen Zænitæ egredi non audebunt: me- tuentes, ne ab hoste in insidiis latitante, interci- piantur, & urbs ipsorum occupetur atq́; incenda- tur. B. Höpfnerus: Quarta civitas est Beth-ezel. Ezel autem est nomen proprium loci, & habetur etiam Zach. XIV. 5. Cum ergo Propheta dicit, Luctus Beth-ezel, accipiet (hostis) à vobis stationem suam, hoc vult: Recte nomen habes à vicinia, ô ci- vitas Beth-Ezel, quia hostium statio tibi erit proxi- ma, Quæ tibi causam lugendi adferet. B. Lutherus cum Hieron. ut appellativum accepit. Per domum autem vicinam Assur intelligit in Comment. T. IV. Jenens. f. 446. cujus explicationem adscribimus: Non expatiabitur civitas Zaenan præ luctu: Zae- nan est in tribu Juda, sicut patet ex Josua. Habet autem nomen ab egrediendo, q. dicas expaciatri- cem. Est autem hic iterum allusio (Zaenan non Jazah,) hoc est, non egredietur, continebit se domi suæ, sicut solent, qui in luctu sunt positi. Hi enim ul- tra hominum conspectum fugiunt, ut possint va- care lachrymis. Sicut Propheta causam subjun- git: Domus vicina accipiet a vobis substantiam ve- stram. Ad hunc modum ego locum hunc intelligo, propterea, quod aliæ sententiæ quæ afferuntur ab interpretibus, videntur esse coactiores. Nam etiam- si BethEzel proprie accipias, quid erit (Emdatho?) Exponunt quidem, stationem hostis, sed coactior sententia est, id eo transferre, quod hoc præmium ho- stis accepturus sit pro ea mora, quam ibi traxit. Quare cum hæc sententia & propius ad rem acce- dat, & quoque Grammaticæ non ita adversetur, volui eam retinere, quod Beth Ezel appellative vicina do nus, nempe Assur, accipiet à Zeenitis sub- stantiam eorum, h. e. etiam illa, quæ ipsi putabant si- bi statuta, & tuta fore. Hæc B. Lutherus. Vers. 12. QUIA INFIRMATA EST IN BONUM QUÆ HABITAT IN AMARITUDINIBUS] Verum dolebit propter fortem (id est fortes occisos, ut hic habet Chaldæus) habitans (plebs) in Maroth. מרות; quod hic amaritudinem significat transpositis litteris innuit רמות; plures erant in duarum tribuum sorte urbes, quibus nomen Rama: eæ pluraliter dicuntur רמות confer Jer. XXXI. 15. Judæis nihil proderit quietos se continuisse, cum Sama- ria & vicinæ urbes destruentur. QUIA DESCENDIT MALUM A DOMINO IN PORTAM JERUSALEM] Ad portas usque veniet Sen- nacherib. Osiander hæc ita: Hebr. anxie exspectabit bonum, (i. e. auxilium) habitatrix Maroth: quia veniet malum a Domino etiam usque ad portam Ie- rosolymorum (i. e. civitas Maroth quando audiet etiam urbis Jerosolymitanæ deditionem ab Assy- rio postulari, in maximis versabitur angustiis, & tamen sperabit aliquo modo feliciorem eventum. Videtur autem allusio esse in vocabulis Maroth & Jarad. Lutherus cum Hieronymo מדות pro appel- lativohabuit, reddens: Die betruͤbte Stadt ver- mag sich nicht zu troͤsten. Qui pro nomine pro- prio habent Maroth in tribu Judæ Jos. XV. 18. vel Mara in tribu Manasse, intelligunt. B. Lutherus in commentar. allatis variis expositionibus simplicis- sima, inquit, sententia hæc est, sive Maroth pro pro- prio accipias, sive appellative pro rebelli civitate, quod anxie expectat bonum. Nam homines constituti in periculis, illo ipso dolent & infirmantur, quod exspectant auxilium, & frustra expectant. Hunc affe- ctum verbum (halah) hoc in loco ostendit. Reddit ergo: Quoniam anxie expectat bonum civitas Maroth, sed descendit malum a Domino ad portam Jerusalem.

## 1:13
THE TUMULT OF THE CHARIOT TO THE STUPOR OF THE INHABITANT OF LACHISH] In the Hebrew: Bind the chariot to the swift horses, inhabitant of Lachish. The chariot, namely, in which the envoys sent by Sennacherib to demand the surrender of Jerusalem might be carried. II Kings XVIII. 17.

THE BEGINNING OF SIN IS TO THE DAUGHTER OF ZION] To the daughter of Zion, that is, you were.

BECAUSE IN THEE WERE FOUND THE WICKEDNESSES OF ISRAEL] You transmitted to Jerusalem the idolatry received from Israel, that is, from the ten tribes.

Osiander expressed these things without doubt more correctly with B. Luther: Tumultus quadrigæ stuporis habitanti Lachis, Hebr. harness the chariot to the dromedary (singular for plural) You inhabitress of Lachis: i.e., you citizens in Lachis, prepare yourselves for flight, because your city will be captured by the Assyrians: Spane net an, und reisset aus, so lieb euch euer Leib und Leben ist. Moreover, this city will be punished by the Lord through the incursion of the enemy: For it is the beginning of sin to the Daughter of Zion: because in you, O Lachis, were found the crimes of the Kingdom of Israel, that is, this city was the first of all to receive idolatrous worship in imitation of the Kingdom of Israel: and from Lachis the Jerusalemites took the example, so that they contaminated themselves with similar impiety. Let it be noted here, because it is not found indicated elsewhere, that this city was the first in Judea to take up the idolatry of the Israelites. So also the Chaldean, Pagninus, Arias & Vatablus. It has its name from walking: But it is not for her to walk, but to flee quickly. Others render this meaning a little differently: the chariots of Sennacherib, tumultuating with their course, noise, and the collision of arms, wheels, hooves, and horses, will first invade the city of Lachish of Judea, and strike it with stupor, if indeed Lachish was the first in Judah to receive the worship of Baalim.

Latin:

TUMULTUS QUADRIGÆ STUPORI HABI- TANTI LACHIS] In Hebræo: Apta currum velocibus equis, habitatrix Lachis. Currum nempe quo vehantur mis- si à Sennacheribo feciales ad deposcendam deditionem Hierofolymorum. II. Regum XVIII. 17.

PRINCIPIUM PECCATI EST FILIÆ SION] Es filiæ Sion, id est, fuisti.

QUIA IN TE INVENTA SUNT SCELERA IS- RAEL] Tu idololatriam ab Israele, id est, decem tribu- bus acceptam, transmisisti Hierosolyma.

Rectius hæc sine hæc sine dubio cum B. Lu- thero expressit Osiander: Tumultus quadrigæ stuporis habitanti Lachis, Hebr. junge currum cum dromedario (singulare pro plurali) Tu habitatrix Lachis : i. e. vos cives in Lachis, parate vos ad fu- gam, quia urbs vestra ab Assyriis capietur: Spane net an, und reisset aus, so lieb euch euer Leib und Leben ist. Punietur autem hæc urbs a Domino per hostium incursionem: Principium enim pecca- ti ipsa est Filiæ Sion: quia in te, ô Lachis, inventa sunt scelera Regni Israel, id est, hæc urbs omnium primo recepit Idololatricos cultus ad imitationem Regni Israelis: & à Lachis exemplum sumsere Jerosolymitani, ut simili impietate sese contami- narent. Notetur hic, quia alibi non reperitur in- dicatum, quod hæc urbs prima in Judæa Israelita- rum idololatriam susceperit. Sic etiam Chaldæus, Pagninus, Arias & Vatablus. Ab ambulatione no- men habet: At non ambulandum ei, sed fugien- dum celeriter. Paulo aliter alii hunc sensum reddentes: quadrigæ Sennacherib suo cursu, stre- pitu, ac armorum, rotarum, ungularum & equo- rum collisione tumultuantes primo, invadent La- chis urbem Judææ, eique stuporem incutient, si- quidem Lachis prima in Juda cultum Baalim sus- ceperit.

## 1:14
Vers. 14.

THEREFORE HE WILL GIVE EMISSARIES OVER THE HERITAGE OF GATH] Moreover, he will give gifts to the heir of Gath. He calls the Assyrian the heir of Gath, who at that time held the cities of the Philistines.

THE HOUSE OF A LIE FOR A DECEPTION TO THE KINGS OF ISRAEL] In the Hebrew: The house of Achzib was for a deception to the kings of Israel. They hoped for help from there, but in vain. Achzib and Maresah, which follows, are towns of Judah, not far from Lachish. See Joshua 15:36, 42.

These things seem twisted: our Osiander has it thus: Heb. Therefore you shall give hostages (to the King of the Assyrians) over the inheritance of Gath (i.e., just as the Gittites gave hostages, so that they might be left in their territory: so also to you, O Lachish, it will have to be done. Thus B. Luther's version generally agrees: You will have to give captives as well as Gath. Other interpretations may be seen in Cornel. à Lapide. B. Luther rightly warned that the Prophet is difficult in this first chapter; in his commentary he explains this passage thus: Therefore send envoys to Moresheth-Gath, the house of Achzib, the kings of Israel will deceive) The word (Siluhim) is from Salach, he sent. Therefore it is optional whether you interpret it as a gift that is sent, or as envoys. The same meaning remains. For he exhorts through irony to seek help from neighbors, whom he nevertheless says are themselves struggling with the same dangers. Furthermore, the obscurity here lies in this, that some join this sentence with the previous one, so that Lachish may send gifts to Moresheth, the neighbors of the Gath of the Philistines. Others refer it to Achzib. But B. Luther refers it to the former; the great man B. Hoepfner follows him, and expresses the sum of the matter thus: Send envoys to Moresheth-Gath, which previously belonged to the kingdom of Gath, or of the Philistines, afterwards occupied by the Benjaminites 1 Chron. 8. The sense is, in vain will you enter into a treaty, and through envoys and gifts sent you will seek for help to be brought to you from the city of Maresah, since its own citizens are equally captives. Confer. v. 15. Now as to the prophecy concerning Achzib, B. Luther speaks of it thus: The Prophet here also uses a most beautiful allusion, the House of Achzib to Achzab for the kings of Israel. Now Achzab signifies a lie, from the word (Cazab) to lie, to deceive, to be in vain. Furthermore, in Joshua 15:44, it is named Achzib, as it is a city of Judah. This city, as the Prophet seems to show in this place, joined a league with the kingdom of Israel. But as almost always happens, the Prophet says, they are not helped in the league during the calamity that is to come through the Assyrian. Although the interpretation would not be inept if you take it passively: To a lie for the kings of Israel, that is, those whom the kings of Israel have deceived. Whom the kings of Israel have misled through idolatry.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

PROPTEREA DABIT EMISSARIOS SUPER HÆREDITATEM GETH] Quin etiam dabit dona hæ- redi Geth. Hæredem Geth vocat Assyrium, qui Phili- stinorum urbes tum tenebat.

DOMUS MENDACII IN DECEPTIONEM RE- GIBUS ISRAEL] In Hebræo: Domus Achzib in decep- tionem fuit regibus Israel. Speraverunt inde auxilium, sed frustra. Aczib & quæ sequitur Maresas oppida sunt Judæ, non longe à Lachiso. Vide Josuæ XV. 36. 42.

Contorta hæc videntur: Osiander noster ita habet: Hebr. Propterea dabis obsides (Regi Assy- riorum) super hæreditate Gath (i. e. sicut Gethæi dederunt obsides, ut relinquerentur in suo terri- torio: sic etiam tibi ô Lachis, erit faciendum. Ita fere consonat B. Lutheri versio: Du wirst muͤs- sen gefangene geben sowol als Gath. Aliæ in- terpretationes videantur apud Cornel. à Lapid. Recte monuit B. Lutherus difficilem esse Prophe- tam in hoc primo capite; in commentario ita hunc locum explicat: Propterea mitte Legatos ad Moreseth Gath, Domum Achzib, Reges israelfal- lent) Vocabulum (Siluhim) est à Salach, misit. Ita- que liberum est, sive donum quod mittitur, sive Legatos interpreteris. Manet eadem sententia. Hortatur enim per Ironiam ad quærenda auxilia à vicinis, quos tamen ipsos dicit cum iisdem pericu- lis conflictari. Porro in eo hic obscuritas est, quidam conjungunt hanc sententiam cum superiore, ut Lachis mittat munera Morasethis, vicinis Gath Palæstino- rum. Alii ad Achzib referunt. Sed ad priorem refert B. Lutherus; sequitur Megalandrum B. Hoͤpfnerus, & summam rei sic exprimit: Mitte legatos ad Mo- reseth Gath, quæ prius ad regnum Gath, seu Philisti- norum pertinebat, postea à Benjaminitis occupa- ta 1. Chron. IIX. sensus est, frustra fœdus inibis, & per legatos & dona missa tibi suppetias ferri petes à civitate Mareseth, quum ipsius cives æque sint ca- ptivi. Confer. v. 15. Jam quod ad vaticinium de Achzib, de eo ita B. Lutherus: Utitur hic Pro- pheta quoque bellissima allusione, Domus Achzib ad Achzab regibus Israel. Significat autem Achzab mendacium, a verbo (Cazeb) mentiri, fallere, fru- stra esse. Porro Josuæ XIV. 44. nominatur Achzib quod sit civitas Juda. Hæc sicut Propheta hoc in loco videtur ostendere, junxit fœdus cum regno Israel. Sed quod fere accidit, dicit Propheta, in fœdere non adjuvari eos in calamitate per Assyrium futura. Quanquam non inepta esset sententia, si passive ac- cipias: Ad mendacium regibus Israel, hoc est, quibus reges Israel mentiti sunt. Quos reges Israel deceperunt per idololatriam.

## 1:15
Ver. 15. I WILL YET BRING AN HEIR UNTO THEE THAT DWELLEST IN MARESHAH] An heir, that is, the Lord, and there is a παρονομασία between יורש, an heir, and מרשה, which signifies an inheritance. That enemy will possess not only the Philistine cities, but also the Judean ones.

THE GLORY OF ISRAEL SHALL COME EVEN UNTO ODOLLAM] That Assyrian, in whose alliance the Israelites once boasted (whence 2 Kings 15:18), shall come even unto Odollam; this town is also in the region of Judah, not far from Lachish, Joshua 15:33.

We do not deny the former member, which B. Luther also rendered in this sense: Ich will dir Maresa den rechten Erben bringen. Osiander: Maresa signifies inheritance. The Prophet therefore alludes to the word, and wishes to say: You citizens in Maresa, listen: the Lord is sending you an heir, the Assyrian King, who may take away all your possessions as if by hereditary right: Er wird euch erben, ehe ihr sterbet. (But let us ask the Lord not to send us such heirs, who take away our things (against our will and yet while we watch).) So also Corn. a Lapide ad h. l. and others. B. Luther in Comment. ad h. l. The Prophet covers a brief catalog of the cities of Judah, which King Sennacherib was about to devastate after the kingdom of Israel. There is, however, an elegant allusion here as well. Marescha adducam tibi Haresch, that is, an heir. Furthermore, the name Maresa signifies inheritance or possession. For it comes from the verb Jarasch. Q. d. Prophet, you have your name from inheritance, you Mareshah. Behold, I will cause you to become the inheritance of a powerful enemy, who will conquer and despoil you. In the final clause, the name "glory of Israel" does not seem to suit the Assyrian. Osiander has it thus concerning this: "The glory of Israel shall come even to Adullam." The cave of Adullam is well known in Scripture. The Prophet therefore wishes to signify: The kingdom of Israel, which now proudly boasts in glory, will shortly be reduced to caves, for its strongholds and cities will be overturned. Luther led the way in his Commentary, whose entire passage I am pleased to transcribe: "The cave of Adullam is well known from the history of David. I think, however, that this is as it were the conclusion of the threatened judgment." Q. d. Great is the glory of Israel, it relies on its own resources and power, and therefore it is secure in the greatest sins: but it will surely come to pass that all that glory, so many magnificent and wealthy cities, shall become like Adullam, an ignoble and desolate cave, because of the devastation which Sennacherib will bring. B. Luther adds, thus we have now emerged from these obscure passages, although in the matter itself there is no great labor, the grammar is a little more difficult. As sufficiently appears from the translation of Jerome, who often makes proper nouns out of common nouns, just as elsewhere he makes common nouns out of proper nouns. Moreover, this passage sufficiently shows how necessary the knowledge of the sacred language is for students of Theology. Cornelius a Lapide explains it in this way: The kingdom, dominion, and glory of Israel, as if driven and put to flight by the Assyrian, will arrive and come to a halt in the city of Adullam, once glorious, wherefore it will be as if extinguished by the same, and the glory of Israel will collapse. Which things have been done. B. Tarnovius explained it thus: Nay, this disaster about to befall these towns will reach even as far as Adullam (See Josh. xv. 35, 1 Sam. xxii. 1, 2 Sam. xxiii. 13, 1 Chron. xi. 15) and even to the holy city of Jerusalem (Compare v. 9), the glory and ornament of all Israel, Ps. xlviii. 2, 3, 12, 13, above v. 11. This is better than if you explain it with Mariana (who, like many other things, has this gloss from R. David Kimchi) as the glory of Israel, i.e., the enemy who possesses the glory of Israel. It is also better than Sa, who says the glory is, by irony, a calamity or ignominy. Thus far Tarnovius. But if his sense were to prevail, there would be need of a copulative, which is not found in the source, [to read] to Adullam AND to the city of Jerusalem. Nor does a noun of disaster or misery precede it. Others wish כבוד to denote not only glory, but also misery. It seems to us that the first member suggests the construction and sense: I will yet bring an heir unto thee, O inhabitant of Mareshah, even unto Adullam shall come (that heir), O glory of Israel, that is, O Samaria. For this was the glory of Israel. And the Prophet further addresses this one: and so he returns again now in this way to Israel, or to its metropolis, Samaria. Unless this is established, the following predicates will lack a subject: Make thee bald, pluck out thy hair. For it is in the Hebrew of the feminine gender, and so it looks to Samaria, not the masculine of Israel. Therefore the LXX, in order to make these things clearer, punctuated them thus: the glory of the daughter of Israel, make thee bald.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ADHUC HÆREDEM ADDUCAM TIBI QUÆ HABITAS IN MARESA] Hæredem, id est, Do- minum, & est παρονομασία יורש hæredem, & מרשה quod hæreditatem significat. Hostis ille non Philisthinas tantum urbes, sed & Judaicas possidebit.

USQUE AD ODOLLAM VENIT GLORIA ISRAEL] Assyrius ille, quo socio olim gloriati sunt Israe- litæ (unde 2. Reg. XV. 18.) perveniet ad Odollam, Est & hoc oppidum in parte Judæ a Lachiso non procul, Josuæ XV. 33.

De priori membro non abnuimus, quod etiam in hunc sensum B. Lutherus reddidit: Ich will dir Maresa den rechten Erben bringen. Osiander: Maresa hæreditatem significat. Alludit igitur Propheta ad vocabulum, & vult dicere: Vos cives in Maresa, auscultate: Dominus vobis hæredem mittit Regem Assyriacum: qui quasi hæreditario jure vestra omnia auferat: Er wird euch erben, ehe ihr sterbet. (Rogemus autem Dominum, ne tales nobis hæredes immittat, qui nostra (nobis invitis & tamen videntibus) auferant.) Sic etiam Corn. a Lapide ad h. l. & alii. B. Lutherus in Comment. ad h. l. Texit Propheta brevem catalogum civitatum Juda, quas Rex Sanherib erat post regnum Israel va- staturus. Est autem hic quoque elegans allusio. Marescha adducam tibi Haresch, hoc est, hæ- redem. Porro nomen Maresa significat hæredita- tem seu possessionem. Venit enim a verbo Jarasch. Q. d. Propheta, habes nomen ab hæreditate, tu Ma- resa. Ecce faciam, ut fias hæreditas potentis ho- stis, qui te expugnabit & spoliabit. In postremo membro haud videtur gloriæ Israelis nomen As- syrio convenire. Osiander de eo ita habet: us- que ad Odollam veniet gloria Israel. Nota est in scriptura spelunca Odollam. Vult igitur Pro- pheta significare: Regnum Israelis, quod nunc glo- riose superbit, brevi redigetur in speluncas, ever- tentur enim arces & urbes. Præivit Lutherus in Comment. cujus locum integrum adscribere pla- cer: Nota est spelunca Adullam ex historia Davidis. Puto autem hanc esse quasi conclusionem institutæ comminationis. Q. d. magna est gloria Israel, ni- titur opibus & potentia sua, atque ideo secura est in maximis peccatis: sed profecto fiet, ut ista omnis glo- ria, tot magnifica & locupletæ civitates, fiant sicut Adullam, ignobilis & vasta spelunca, propter vasti- tatem, quam Sanherib afferet. Addit B. Lutherus, sic emersimus jam ex istis obscuris locis, quanquam in re non magnus labor est, Grammatica paulo est im- peditior. Sicut satis apparet ex translatione Hie- ronymi, qui fere ex propriis facit appellativa, sicut alibi ex appellativis propria. Satis autem ostendit hic locus, quam necessaria Theologiæ studiosis sit co- gnitio sacræ linguæ. Cornelius a Lapide hoc pacto exponit: Regnum, Ditio & gloria Israel, quasi pro- pulsa & fugata ab Assyrio perveniet, sistetq; in Odo- llam urbe olim gloriosa, quare illa ab eodem cap- quasi extinguetur & corruet gloria Israel. Quæ acta sunt. B. Tarnovius sic exposuit: Quin et hæc clades hisce oppidis obventura ad Hadullamum tas co- iam usq́; perveniet. Vide Ios. XV. 35. 1. Sam. XXII. 1. 2. Sam. XXIII. 13. 1. Chron. XI. 15. & usque ad san- ctam urbem Hierosolymorum (Confer. v. 9.) gloriam & decus totius Israelis Ps. XLIIX. 2. 3. 12. 13. supra v. 11. Ita melius, quam si cum Mariana explices, (qui ut multa alia, ita & hanc glossam habet ex R. David Kimchii) gloria Israel i. e. hostis possessor gloriæ Is- rael. Etiam melius quam Sa gloria, inquit, est per ironiam calamitas seu ignominia. Hactenus Tarnovius. Sed si ejus sensus obtineret, opus esset copulativa, quæ non habetur in fonte, ad Adullam ET ad urbem Jerusalem. Nec præ- cedit nomen cladis vel miseriæ. Alii כבוד non tantum gloriam, sed etiam miseriam notare volunt. Nobis videtur constructionem & sensum suggere- re prius membrum: Adhuc hæredem adducam tibi ô habitatrix in Maresa, usq́; ad Odollam veniet (hæ- res ille) ô gloria Israel, id est, ô Samaria. Hæc enim erat Israelis gloria. Et hunc porro compellat Propheta: adeoque iterum nunc ita redit ad Is- raelem, vel metropolin, ejusdem Samariam. Quod nisi statuatur, sequentibus prædicatis subje- ctum deerit Decalvare, evelle tibi pilos. Est enim in Ebræo genus fæmininum, adeoque Samariam respicit, non masculinum Israelis. Ideo LXX. hæc (ut clariora redderent) ita dispunxere, gloria filiæ Israel, decalvare.

## 1:16
Vers. 16. DECALVARE] Pluck out your hair. Thus the Chaldean here; for to induce baldness upon oneself on account of the dead was indeed a custom among other nations, but it was not permitted to the Jews by the law of Deut. XIV. 1. The Prophet is here addressing the people of Judah, whose cities he had already named.

AND TO SHEAR] Cut off the curls and the delights of the hair.

ON THE SONS OF THY DELIGHTS] On account of most beloved sons, namely, those slain by the enemy.

ENLARGE THY BALDNESS AS THE EAGLE, BECAUSE THEY ARE GONE INTO CAPTIVITY FROM THEE] You whose children have not been killed, but carried away, testify your grief by bringing baldness upon your head, for the law did not forbid this, except in funeral mourning.

These things do not pertain to the Jews, but to the Israelites, as Osiander rightly says: Make yourself bald, O you unhappy kingdom of Israel, and shear yourself over the children of your delights: mourn over your delicate children, enlarge your baldness like the eagle, which at a certain time of the year casts off its feathers: The ancients in mourning either plucked out or sheared their hair, as Herodotus also testifies: because they are led captive from you: that is, your citizens, and most delicate men, most tenderly brought up, shall be led away into Assyrian captivity. Sennacherib, who is treated of here, could not take Jerusalem. Theodoret thinks the lamentation is woven concerning Jerusalem. But since this does not treat of its destruction brought about by the Chaldeans, by whom the Jews were led captive; but of the plundering by the Assyrians, namely Sennacherib, who took the fortified cities of Judah, and besieged Jerusalem, and did not take it, nor lead its citizens captive; it could not truly be said of it, 'because they are led captive from you.' Wherefore it seems more true, which also pleased Jerome himself, Remigius, Haymo, Rupert, and others, that the discourse is held with Samaria, or with the Israelite people: as if with the mother of the children about to be led into captivity; and for that reason he uses the Hebrew feminine imperative, when he says: 'Make yourself bald and shear,' etc. And it is proved from the text itself: for when Micah was amplifying the calamity of the devastation of Samaria, and of the region of Israel, which was also going to spread to Judah even to Jerusalem, and therefore enumerated some cities of Judah which sustained this evil, he then returns to the invective against Samaria, or the land of Israel, and predicts the captivity of its inhabitants, as Christoph. à Castro holds here. As therefore he began this chapter with Samaria, so also he concludes it with the same.

Latin:

Vers. 16. DECALVARE] Evelle tibi pilos. Ita hic Chaldæus; nam calvitium sibi ob mortuos inducere, mos quidem erat gentibus aliis, sed Judæis id non licebat per legem Deut. XIV. 1. Judæ populum hic alloquitur Prophe- ta, cujus urbes jam aliquas nominaverat.

ET TONDERE] Cincinnos & delicias comarum circumcide.

SUPER FILIOS DELICIARUM TUARUM] Pro- pter amatissimos filios, interfectos ab hoste scilicet.

DILATA CALVITIUM TUUM SICUT AQUI- LA, QUONIAM CAPTIVI DUCTI SUNT EX TE] Vos quorum liberi non interfecti, sed deportati sunt, in- ducto in caput calvitio dolorem testamini, lex enim id non vetabat, nisi in luctu funebri.

Non ad Judæos hæc pertinent, sed ad Israeli- tas, uti recte Osiander: Decalvare, ô tu infelix re- gnum Israeliticum & tondere super filios deliciarum tuarum: luge super delicatis filiis tuis, dilata calvi- tium tuum sicut aquila, quæ certo anni tempore plu- mas abjicit: Veteres in luctu aut evellebant aut tondebant crines, ut Herodotus etiam testatur: quoniam captivi ducti sunt ex te: id est cives tui, & delicatissimi homines, tenerrime educati, in capti- vitatem Assyriacam abducentur. Jerusalem cape- re non potuit Sennacherib, de quo hic agitur. Theo- doretus ad Ierusalem putat lamentationem texi. At hic cum non agatur de ejus eversione per Chaldæos facta, per quos Judæi ducti sunt capti- vi; sed de direptione Assyriorum, nempe Sennache- rib, qui cepit urbes Juda munitas, & obsedit Jeru- salem, & non cepit, neque ejus cives duxit capti- vos; non vere de ea diceretur, quoniam captivi du- cti sunt ex te. Quare verius videtur, quod placuit quoque ipsi Hieronymo, Remigio, Haymoni, Ruper- to, & aliis, cum Samaria, aut cum plebe Israelitica sermonem haberi: quasi cum matre filiorum in ca- ptivitatem ducendorum; & idcirco fœmineo im- perativo Hebraico utitur, cum ait: Decalvare & tondere &c. & probatur ex ipso textu: nam cum Michæas amplificaret calamitatem vastitatis Sama- riæ, & regionis Israelis, quod etiam pervasura erat Judam usque ad Ierusalem & ideo enumeravit ali- quas Judæ civitates, quæ hoc malum sustinuerunt, deinde redit ad invectivam Samariæ, vel terræ Is- rael, & prædicit incolarum ejus captivitatem, uti hic habet Christoph. à Castro. Sicut ergo ce- pit hoc caput in Samaria, ita & in eadem claudit.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

He denounces woe to the wicked, and to those who subject the land to foreign dominion and who, by the grace of GOD, lift themselves up in vain and unrepentant against the house of Jacob; he announces the deportation, the gathering of the remnant of Israel as if into a sheepfold, and the Lord as the breaker; he promises a King. He condemns the frauds of wealth and promises a sheepfold to the sheep.

Vers. 1. WOE TO YOU WHO DEVISE WHAT IS USELESS] This is another revelation, which came to the Prophet later, namely during the reign of Hezekiah, after the departure of Sennacherib, as is gathered from Jer. XXVI. 18. By this he knew that it would come to pass that Jerusalem would not only be besieged, but also captured, no less than Samaria, and this people no less than that would be deported, the causes of which evils he also explains: inhumanity toward their countrymen, and impiety toward God. אָוֶן, which is translated here as useless, often signifies injustice: and so the Chaldean takes it here. The passage in Jeremiah confirms that Micah had predicted the devastation of Judea in the time of Hezekiah. But the very words cited show that Jeremiah refers not to the present second chapter, but to the following chapter, Micah III. However, this chapter coheres with the preceding one, nor does it appear that a special revelation is had here, since the first and second chapters are connected immediately, without a special introduction, and just as the Prophet chastised the sins of the Israelites against the first table in chapter 1, so here he continues to rebuke their sins against the second table of the divine law. Theodoret indeed thought this prophecy concerned only the Jews: but others, more correctly, with Montanus, refer it to the Israelites, not excluding the two tribes: because it is similar to the former, and is deduced from it by a continuous thread. But did he there deal first against the ten tribes, and consequently or concomitantly against the Jews? Therefore in v. 12 he addresses Jacob and Israel: by which names all 12 tribes are included, see c. I. 5. Rupertus, Vatablus, and Christ. à Castro refer this prophecy only to the ten tribes.

Vers. Same. AND WORK EVIL UPON YOUR BEDS] To work is placed here for to plan, as μοιχεύειν in Matt. V. 28. They plan by night: they execute by day, as follows.

BECAUSE THEIR HAND IS AGAINST GOD] If only the matter is in their power. They will execute their thoughts, unless strength is lacking.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

Væ iniquis, & terræ sub dominium alienum subjectio- nem ac domui Iacob gratia DEI frustra sese erigen- tibus impænitentibus, deportationem, reliquiarum Israëlis congregationem velut in ovile, ac Domi- num perruptorem denunciat, Regem pollicetur. Damnat opum fraudes ovibus promittit ovile.

Vers. 1. VÆ QUI COGITASTIS INUTILE] Hæc est al- tera revelatio, quæ Prophetæ posterior contigit, regnante scilicet Ezechia, post discessum Sennacheribi, ut colligitur ex Jer. XXVI. 18. qua cognovit fore ut Hierosolyma non obsideretur tantum, sed etiam caperetur, non minus quam Samaria, & hic populus non minus quam ille de- portaretur, quorum malorum etiam causas explicat, in- humanitatem in populares, & impietatem in Deum. אָוֶן quod inutile hic vertitur, sæpe significat injustitiam: & ita hic sumit Chaldæus. Locus Jeremiæ confirmat prædixisse Mi- chæam devastationem Judææ, Ezechiæ tempore. Sed respicere Jeremiam non caput præsens secun- dum, verum sequens Mich. III. caput, verba ipsa adducta docent. Cohæret autem hoc caput cum præcedente, nec apparet peculiarem hic revela- tionem haberi, siquidem immediate connectatur primum & secundum caput, sine peculiari ingres- su, & uti peccata Israëlitarum contra primam ta- bulam castigavit Propheta cap. 1. ita hic pergit reprehendere peccata eorum, contra secundam le- gis divinæ Tabulam. Existimavit quidem Theodo- retus hoc vaticinium tantum Judæos concernere: At rectius alii, cum Montano, ad Israëlitas, non ex- clusis duabus tribubus referunt: quia simile prio- ri est, & ab eo continuo filo deducitur. Ibi au- tem primo egit contra decem tribus, consequenter vel concomitanter adversus Judæos? Ideo v. 12. al- loquitur Jacob & Israël: quibus nominibus inclu- duntur omnes 12. tribus, vid. c. I. 5. Rupertus, Va- tablus, Christ. à Castro ad decem tribus solum re- ferunt hoc vaticinium.

Vers. Eod. ET OPERAMINI MALUM IN CUBILI- BUS VESTRIS] Operari hic positum est pro constituere, ut μοιχεύειν Matth. V. 28. noctu constituunt: de die exse- quuntur, ut sequitur.

QUONIAM CONTRA DEUM EST MANUS EORUM] Si modo res sit in potestate eorum. Cogitata ex- sequentur, nisi vires desint.

## 2:2
Vers. 2. AND THEY COVETED FIELDS] They cast their eyes and mind upon the property of others.

AND VIOLENTLY TOOK AND SEIZED HOUSES] In the Hebrew: and they seized (namely fields) and houses (they coveted, taken from the common) and took. They made them their own, by force or by fraud.

AND THEY OPPRESSED] This interpreter is accustomed to translate עָשַׁק as to slander, which is more to oppress. See what is said at Luke III. 14.

A MAN AND HIS HOUSE] That is, an estate.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ET CONCUPIERUNT AGROS] Injiciunt oculos & animum rebus alienis.

ET VIOLENTER TULERUNT ET RAPUE- RUNT DOMOS] In Hebræo: & rapuerunt (nempe a- gros) & domos (concupierunt ἀπὸ κοινοῦ) & tulerunt. Fece- runt suas, vi aut dolo.

ET CALUMNIABANTUR] Solet hic interpres עָשַׁק vertere calumniari, quod magis est opprimere. Vide quæ ad Luc. III. 14.

VIRUM ET DOMUM EJUS] Id est, fundum.

## 2:3
Vers. 3. BEHOLD I AM DEVISING EVIL AGAINST THIS FAMILY] That is, against all the posterity of Jacob. They devised evils against their countrymen, I against them: they by injury, I by right.

FROM WHICH YOU SHALL NOT REMOVE YOUR NECKS] You shall not free your necks.

AND YOU SHALL NOT WALK PROUDLY] Erect. The yoke imposed will prevent you from walking erect.

BECAUSE THE TIME IS MOST EVIL] It will be most bitter. Namely, the time of deportation.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ECCE EGO COGITO SUPER FAMI- LIAM ISTAM MALUM] Id est, super omnem poste- ritatem Jacobi. Illi mala machinari sunt popularibus, e- go ipsis: illi injuria, ego jure.

UNDE NON AUFERETIS COLLA VESTRA] Non eximetis cervices vestras.

ET NON AMBULABITIS SUPERBI] Erecti. Jugum impositum impediet, ne erecti incedatis.

QUONIAM TEMPUS PESSIMUM EST] Acer- bissimum erit. Nempe tempus deportationis.

## 2:4
Ver. 4. A PARABLE SHALL BE TAKEN UP AGAINST YOU] A proverb shall be made about you.

AND A SONG SHALL BE SUNG WITH SWEETNESS] In the Hebrew: and he shall lament, supply: every foreigner in your person, a lament of a lament, a most sad lament.

THE PORTION OF MY PEOPLE HAS BEEN EXCHANGED] The land has changed its master.

HOW SHALL HE DEPART FROM ME] How he takes away from me. Namely, the fields, the Assyrian under Tiglath-Pileser.

WHEN HE RETURNS WHO DIVIDES OUR REGIONS] So that he even returns to divide our fields. The same people of the Assyrians under Shalmaneser.

Grotius understands this as referring to a different slaughter and incursion under Tiglath-Pileser and under Shalmaneser. But there is no trace of this in his text. B. Tarnovius seems to have rendered it more conveniently for us in this manner: We have been utterly devastated by the omnipotent God, and without any hope of restitution, because God is exchanging the portion of my people, by transferring it from the Israelites to the Assyrians, see 2 Kings ch. 15 and 17, and this very enemy distributes everything among his own, and gives it to his own inhabitants, ah, how he takes away from me what God had given to me, and by turning away he divides my fields, just as booty captured in war, which he may thereafter always retain. B. Osiander rendered it similarly word for word: we have been devastated by depopulation, the field of my people has been changed (it has obtained another master): (By) how it has been taken away from me. Will he (that tyrannical Assyrian possessor) ever return our fields to us, and divide them among us?

Latin:

Vers. 4. SUMETUR SUPER VOS PARABOLA] De vobis proverbium fiet.

ET CANTABITUR CANTICUM CUM SUA- VITATE] In Hebræo: & lamentabitur, supple quisque externus ex persona vestra, lamentum lamenti, tristissi- mum lamentum.

PARS POPULI MEI COMMUTATA EST] Terra mutavit dominum.

QUOMODO RECEDET A ME] Quomodo ad- emit mihi. Agros scilicet, Assyrius sub Teglathphalasa- ro.

CUM REVERTATUR QUI REGIONES NO- STRAS DIVIDAT] Ita, ut & revertatur ad agros nostros dividendos. Idem populus Assyriorum sub Salmana- sare.

De diversa clade & incursione sub Teglat- phalassaro, & sub Salmanasare intelligit Grotius. Sed in textu ejus non est vestigium. Quem com- modius reddidisse nobis videtur B. Tarnovius h. m. Ab omnipotente Deo prorsus vastati sumus, & sine ulla spe restitutionis, quoniam portionem populi mei commutat Deus, transferendo ab Israelitis ad Assyrios, vide 2. Reg. XV. & XVII. capp. & hic ipse hostis inter se distribuit omnia, suisque incolis donat, ah, quomodo adimit mihi, quæ mihi Deus dederat, & avertendo agros meos partitur, tan- quam prædam bello captam, quam deinceps sem- per retineat. Similiter reddidit B. Osiander κα- τὰ πόδα : depopulatione vastati sumus, ager populi mei mutatus (alium Dominum sortitus) est : (Ab) quo- modo ablatus est à me. Num aliquando (ille tyran- nicus possessor Assyrius) reddet nobis agros nostros, eosq́; inter nos dividet.

## 2:5
Ver. 5. THEREFORE] After that time. THERE SHALL BE NO ONE FOR YOU CASTING A CORD OF THE LOT IN THE ASSEMBLY OF THE LORD] Now, from the person expressed mimetically, that song of the foreigners turns itself to the Hebrews themselves, and says that it will not come to pass that they shall any longer divide among their fellows by lot the lands handed down to them by right of inheritance before the judges, whom the Hebrews themselves called קהל יהוה.

B. Luther renders the sense more correctly and simply: Here it appears again that the Lord is speaking of the final devastation, that the citizens of the kingdom of Israel will be led away in such a way that they will not return hereafter, nor will they have any part in the Church of the Lord, i.e., in the people of Israel. Similarly Osiander: it is not (O Israelite nation) for you to wait until the assembly of the people is gathered again before the Lord, so that lots may be cast there for distributing the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel: as was done in the time of Joshua, when he and Eleazar, the High Priest, divided the land by lot for the Israelite people. Josh. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PROPTER HOC] Post id tempus. NON ERIT TIBI MITTENS FUNICULUM SORTIS IN COETU DOMINI] Nunc à persona μι- μητικῶς expressa canticum illud externorum ad ipsos He- bræos se vertit, & ait non futurum, ut amplius illi coram judicibus, quos ipsi Hebræi vocabant קהל יהוה, terras hæreditatis jure sibi delatas inter consortes sorte divi- dant.

Rectius & simplicius sensum reddit B. Luthe- rus: Hic iterum apparet loqui Dominum de finali vastatione, quod sic abducentur cives regni Israel, ut posthac non redituri, neque partem aliquam in Ec- clesia Domini, h.e. in populo Israel habituri sint. Si- militer Osiander : non est (ô gens Israelitica) ut ex- pectes, dum aliquando rursus cætus populi coram Domino colligatur, ut ibi sortes mittantur, pro di- stribuenda terra Chanaan, inter tribus Israelis : si- cut factum est tempore Josuæ, cum ille & Eleasar, summus Sacerdos, populo Israelitico terram sor- te dividerent. Jos. XIV.

## 2:6
Ver. 6. DO NOT SPEAK] In the Hebrew: do not drip, that is: do not prophesy, for we have seen that this is signified by נטף in Ez. 22:2 and elsewhere. The Prophet imitates the words which the Hebrews used toward the Prophets, as can be seen in Isa. 30:10, Amos 7:12, 16. SPEAKING] In the Hebrew: they shall drip, that is: even if you do not wish it, nevertheless Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, and others, and I, shall perform the prophetic office. THEY SHALL NOT DRIP UPON THESE] In the Hebrew: They shall not drip to them, that is, but later a time will come when the Prophets will not speak to you, Ps. 14:9, Ezek. 7:26, Amos 8:11. Others think that by the former words DO NOT DRIP, it is said to our prophet and to others who were prophesying similar things, that they should not prophesy, for by the following word THEY SHALL DRIP, it is commanded that they be heard, or that the Pseudo-Prophets be permitted to drip, i.e., let those drip who preach pleasant and favorable things to us: finally THEY SHALL NOT DRIP, the reason for the prohibition is given: because Micah and those acting with him do not drip according to these, that is, the false Prophets, in their manner. Osiander provides another sense: Do not drip, say the Magistrates, that is, do not rebuke us and denounce punishments upon us) nay rather let them drip (says the Prophet of the Lord:) nay (say the Magistrates) let them not drip to these, for confusion shall not overtake us. CONFUSION SHALL NOT OVERTAKE] That is, it will come to pass that the Prophets will no longer be treated ignominiously by you, as has been done for a long time.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NE LOQUAMINI ] In Hebræo : ne stillete, id est : ne vaticinemini, nam id significari per נטף vidi- mus Ez. XXII. 2. & alibi imitatur Propheta verba, quibus Hebræi ad Prophetas utebantur, ut videre est Esa. XXX. 10. Amos. VII. 12. 16. LOQUENTES ] In Hebræo : stillabunt, id est, etiam- si vos nolitis, tamen Esaias, Osee, Joel, & alii, & ego munere prophetico fungemur. NON STILLABUNT SUPER ISTOS ] In He- bræo : Non stillabunt illis, id est, sed postea veniet tempus cum Prophetæ vobis non loquentur Ps. XIV. 9. Ezech. VII. 26. Amos. VIII. 11. Alii prioribus verbis NE STILLETIS inter dici prophetæ nostro, & aliis qui similia vaticina- bantur, ne vaticinarentur, verbo enim sequenti STILLA BUNT, juberi putant, ut audiantur, vel stillare permittantur Pseudo-Prophetæ, q. d. stillent isti, qui blanda nobis prædicunt, & fausta: postremo NON STILLANT, causam reddi inter- dicti : quia non stillant Michæas & cum ipso facien- tes secundum istos, id est, falsos Prophetas, eo- rum more. Alium sensum tradit Osiander : No- lite stillare, inquiunt Magistratus, id est arguere nos, & pœnas nobis denunciare) imo vero stillent (inquit Propheta domini :) imo (inquiunt Ma- gistratus ) non stillent istis, non comprehendet e- nim nos confusio. NON COMPREHENDIT CONFUSIO] Id est, ita fiet, ut Prophetæ non amplius à vobis ignominiose tractentur, sicut factum est diu.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. DICIT DOMUS JACOB ] In the Hebrew: These are the words to the house of Jacob. Refer this to what preceded a little before, do not drop. NUM QUID ABBREVIATUS EST SPIRITUS DOMINI] The Prophet refutes the malice of those who were unwilling to hear the prophets. The Spirit of the Lord here signifies mercy. Is it, he says, less now than it was before? AUT TALES SUNT COGITATIONES EJUS] Namely, that He should delight in your destruction, and in no way wish to regard those led by repentance? As if he were to say, the threats of the prophets are not to be understood in that way.

These words are not to be attributed to the Prophet, but rather to those who did not want the prophet to 'drip,' that is, to prophesy. For Grotius acknowledges that this is signified by 'to drip,' comparing Ez. XXII. 2, Isa. XXX. 10, Am. VII. 12, 16. The sense is, as Osiander interprets: Confusion will not overtake us. No dangers threaten us. The house of Jacob also says (the people of the Israelite Kingdom falsely console themselves in this manner): Is the Spirit of the Lord shortened? That is: granted, we may have sinned against the Lord (for we will not excuse all our words or deeds), but is it credible that the Lord, who is long-suffering by nature, has such a shortened Spirit, that is, is so prone and quick to anger: 'Ja solte darumb unser Herr und GOtt so kurz angebunden seyn' [Yes, should our Lord and God be so short-tempered for that reason], that He would cast us into exile on account of those few sins? or are such His thoughts? Namely, does God think about destroying us, whom He loves most tenderly, whom He cherishes in His bosom? Others not inappropriately establish two reasons here for why the people thought these prophecies of Micah were false: the first from the omnipotence of God, 'is the Spirit of the Lord shortened,' is the power of God restricted, so that He cannot provide us with a secure and intact government, as He promised: the second from the absurd: to destroy and wipe out His own people are not the actions of God. Thus, the blessed Luther, along with the Chaldean and LXX interpreters, attributes these words to the people; whence, in his response, the prophet, while conceding the omnipotence of God, limits His promises, which were given under the condition of obedience. God promised defense to the good and the penitent. But you are not such.

Verse same. ARE NOT MY WORDS GOOD WITH HIM WHO WALKS UPRIGHTLY] The Prophet now speaks in the person of God; understand 'words' here as counsels.

Latin:

Vers. 7. DICIT DOMUS JACOB ] In Hebræo : Hæc sunt dicta domui Iacobi. Refer ad illud quod paulo ante præcessit, ne stilletis. NUM QUID ABBREVIATUS EST SPIRITUS DOMINI] Refellit Propheta malitiam illorum, qui Prophe- tas audire nolebant. Spiritus Domini hic misericordiam significat. An ea, inquit, minor nunc est, quam ante fuit? AUT TALES SUNT COGITATIONES EJUS] Ut nempe exitio vestro delectetur, neque ullo modo pœ- nitentia ductos velit respicere ? quasi dicat, non ita in- telligendæ sunt comminationes Prophetarum.

Hæc verba non Prophetæ tribuenda, sed po- tius illis, qui stillare prophetam, h. e. vaticinari nolebant. Nam id significari per stillare agno- scit Grotius, conferens Ez. XXII. 2. Esa. XXX. 10. Am. VII. 12, 16. Sensus est, interprete Osiandro: Non comprehendet nos confusio. Nihil nobis pericu- lorum imminet. Dicit etiam domus Iacob (Populus Regni Israelitici ad hunc modum sese falso conso- latur) Nunquid abbreviatus est Spiritus Domini. Id est: sit sane, peccaverimus Domino (non enim o- mnia nostra dicta aut facta excusabimus) an vero credibile est, Dominum, qui longanimis est sua na- tura, adeo abbreviato esse Spiritu, id est, adeo pro- num & velocem ad iram: Ja solte darumb unser Herr und GOtt so kurz angebunden seyn, ut nos propter peccata illa aliqua in exilium ejiceret? aut tales sunt cogitationes ejus? scilicet Deus de nobis perdendis cogitat, quos tenerrime amat, quos in sinu fovet. Alii duas rationes non inconcinne hic statuunt, ob quas populus existimarit falsa esse hæc Michææ vaticinia: primam ab omnipotentia Dei, num abbreviatus est Spiritus Domini, num coar- ctata est potentia Dei, ut non possit nobis præsta- re politiam sartam tectam, uti promisit: alteram ab absurdo: perdere & delere populum suum non sunt actiones Dei. Sic verba hæc populo tribuit B. Lutherus cum Chald. & LXX. Interpp. unde in responsione propheta concessa Dei omnipotentia limitat ejus promissiones sub conditione obedien- tiæ datas, Bonis & pœnitentibus promisit Deus defen- sionem. Vos autem tales non estis.

Vers. eod. NONNE VERBA MEA BONA SUNT CUM EO, QUI RECTE GRADITUR] Ex Dei perso- na jam loquitur Propheta, Verba hic intellige consilia.

## 2:8
Verse 8. AND ON THE CONTRARY MY PEOPLE HAVE RISEN UP AS AN ADVERSARY] In the Hebrew: And yet he who yesterday was my people, (today) will rise up hostilely, namely against me. Yesterday, that is, a little while ago: as in Isa. XXX. 33.

FROM ABOVE THE TUNIC YOU HAVE TAKEN AWAY THE CLOAK] You have taken away the cloak over the tunic. From the poor, that is. A proverbial expression, as in Matt. V. 40.

AND THOSE WHO WERE PASSING BY SIMPLY, YOU HAVE TURNED INTO WAR] In the Hebrew: those passing by peacefully (are to you as if) returned from battle: that is, captured in war, against whom everything is permitted by the right of victory.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET E CONTRARIO POPULUS MEUS IN ADVERSARIUM CONSURREXIT] In Hebræo: At- qui qui heri erat populus meus, (hodie) hostiliter insurget, nem- pe in me. Heri, id est, paulo ante: ut Esa. XXX. 33.

DESUPER TUNICA PALLIUM SUSTULI- STIS] Super tunicam abstulistis & pallium. Pauperibus scilicet. Proverbialis locutio, ut Matth. V. 40.

ET EOS, QUI TRANSIBANT SIMPLICITER, CONVERTISTIS IN BELLUM] In Hebræo: trans- euntes pacifice (sunt vobis quasi) reversi à prælio: id est, bello capti, in quos omnia liceut victoriæ jure.

## 2:9
Verse 9. THE WOMEN OF MY PEOPLE YOU HAVE CAST OUT FROM THE HOUSE OF THEIR DELIGHTS] From their villages.

FROM THEIR LITTLE ONES YOU HAVE TAKEN AWAY MY PRAISE FOREVER] You have accustomed the little ones to idolatry, so that they would never think about worshipping me.

Latin:

Vers. 9. MULIERES POPULI MEI EJECISTIS DE DOMO DELICIARUM SUARUM] E villis.

A PARVULIS EARUM TULISTIS LAUDEM MEAM IN PERPETUUM] Assuefecistis idololatriæ parvulos, ne unquam de me colendo cogitarent.

## 2:10
Verse 10. ARISE AND GO] Depart, old settlers.

YOU HAVE NO REST HERE] This region will no longer be yours.

BECAUSE OF ITS UNCLEANNESS IT WILL BE CORRUPTED WITH A MOST GRIEVOUS ROT] It will corrupt (you) and indeed with a notable corruption. The sense is the same as in Lev. XVIII. 25; the noun however is נמרץ 1 Kings II. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 10. SURGITE ET ITE] Veteres migrate coloni.

NON HABETIS HIC REQUIEM] Hæc regio non ultra vestra erit.

PROPTER IMMUNDITIAM EJUS CORRUM- PETUR PVTREDINE PESSIMA] Corrumpet (vos) & quidem corruptione insigni. Sensus idem est qui Levit. XVIII. 25. nomen autem נמרץ 1. Reg. II. 8.

## 2:11
Verse 11. WOULD THAT I WERE NOT A MAN HAVING THE SPIRIT] The Prophet speaks: If there were, he says, someone walking in the wind. Pursuing empty things.

AND I WOULD RATHER SPEAK A LIE] And lying lies: saying, that is, what follows.

I WILL DRIP FOR YOU INTO WINE AND INTO DRUNKENNESS] I will drip for you instead of wine and strong drink: that is, I will prophesy.

AND HE SHALL BE UPON WHOM IT IS DRIPPED THIS PEOPLE] He would be the dripper, (that is, an excellent Prophet) to this people. He would be the one finally suited to their temperament. Such a one they want, such a one they seek.

Latin:

Vers. 11. VTINAM NON ESSEM VIR HABENS SPIRITVM] Propheta loquitur: Si esset, inquit, aliquis ambulans in vento. Inania persequens.

ET MENDACIVM POTIVS LOQVERER] Et mentiens mendacia: dicens scilicet quod sequitur.

STILLABO TIBI IN VINVM ET IN EBRIE- TATEM] Stillabo tibi pro vino & sicera: id est, vaticinabor.

ET ERIT SVPER QVEM STILLATVR PO- PVLVS ISTE] Is esset stillator, (id est, Propheta egregius) populo huic. Is demum accomodatus esset eorum inge- nio. Talem volunt, talem quærunt.

## 2:12
Ver. 12. I WILL SURELY GATHER JACOB ALL OF THEE] He imitates the words of the false prophets, but in another sense. I will gather, namely, so that they may be besieged within Samaria and Jerusalem, for a similar fate is predicted for both peoples. By Jacob understand the ten tribes. I will force you together to be deported, not in part, as by Tiglath-Pileser, but all, by Shalmaneser.

I WILL BRING TOGETHER INTO ONE THE REMNANT OF ISRAEL] The two remaining tribes, and that by Nebuchadnezzar.

I WILL LIKEWISE PLACE HIM AS A FLOCK

IN THE FOLD] Tityrus, gather the flock. In the Hebrew it is, as the flock of Bozrah: of the Moabites, in which Bozrah is, Jer. 48:24, it is a great pasture, 2 Kings 3:4, but the Chaldean and the Greeks read other points, and took the mem for a preposition: but Bozrah for straits, that is, a fold: which agrees better with the following words.

AS CATTLE IN THE MIDST OF THE PENS] In a crowd.

THEY SHALL BE IN A TUMULT BY REASON OF THE MULTITUDE OF MEN] They shall be disturbed: namely, when they see so many guards around them.

Latin:

Vers. 12. CONGREGATIONE CONGREGABO JACOB TOTVM TE] Imitatur verba Pseudoprophetarum, sed alio sensu. Congregabo, nempe, ut obsideantur intra Sa- mariam & Hierosolyma, nam pars fors utrique populo præ- dicitur. Per Jacobum intellige decem tribus. Cogam vos in unum deportandos, nec ex parte, ut per Theglath- phalasarum, sed omnes, per Salmanasarum.

IN VNVM CONDVCAM RELIQVIAS IS- RAEL] Duas tribus reliquas, idque per Nabuchodo- nosorum.

PARITER PONAM ILL VM QVASI GREGEM

IN OVILI] Tityre coge pecus. In Hebræo est, quasi gregem Bosra: Moabitis, in qua Bosra est, Jer. XLVII. 24. maxime pascua est 2. Reg. III. 4. at Chaldæus & Græci alia puncta legerunt, & מ fumfere pro præpositione: מצר autem pro angustiis, id est, ovili: quod cum verbis sequentibus melius convenit.

QVASI PECVS IN MEDIO CAVLARVM] Con- fertim.

TVMVLTVABVNTVR A MVLTITVDINE HOMINVM] Perturbabuntur: nempe cum tot custodes circum se videbunt.

## 2:13
Ver. 13.

FOR HE SHALL ASCEND OPENING A WAY BEFORE THEM] The breaker shall ascend before them, the soldier attacking those cities.

THEY SHALL DIVIDE AND PASS THROUGH THE GATE, AND SHALL ENTER BY IT] The Assyrians and Chaldeans shall break through the walls, and shall pass through the gate, through which the townspeople were accustomed to go out, 2 Kings 17:6, 25:4.

AND THEIR KING SHALL PASS BEFORE THEM] The captive shall be led away while the people look on. 2 Kings 17:6, 25:6.

AND THE LORD AT THEIR HEAD] Namely, of the Assyrians and Chaldeans. God will make all things prosper for them.

We have appended the entire depravation of the illustrious Evangelical prophecy, in which Grotius has again followed the Jews, especially Joseph Kimchi, having abandoned most Christian interpreters. For these understand the Prophetic prophecy concerning Christ. Calvin acknowledged this in this place. The greater part of interpreters inclines toward this, because God here promises some relief for Israel, after He had harshly rebuked them and had even threatened them with extremes. They therefore refer this passage to the kingdom of Christ, as if God were giving hope of a future restoration: but the same Calvin also departed from the greater part of interpreters. Grotius therefore had him as a predecessor, as well as Tremellius and Junius, the disciples of Calvin. But there is no reason at first to desert the consensus of most interpreters. For what Calvin urges, that the other things which precede are mere ἐπιτιμήσεις (rebukes), his own defender Dav. Pareus refutes more closely. The reason does not hinder me that all the preceding things are ἐπιτιμητικὰ (rebuking). For it is not infrequent for the Prophets to append consolations to threats abruptly, and to preach predictions of future devastation even concerning spiritual restoration and the kingdom of Christ. Examples are Hos. 3 and 6 and 13, Joel 2, Amos 5 and 9. And this consolation fits well with those things that precede: because among other things the Prophet had answered that the words of God are good to the good. After he had therefore announced their fate to the impenitent, he proceeds to lift up the spirits of the pious, to whom he testifies that in the midst of even public disasters, divine promises, especially spiritual ones, will be fulfilled. Concerning which also the blessed Luther in this place. This is the custom of the prophets, after they have chastised the impious sinning securely and have predicted future devastation, finally to preach also concerning the eternal kingdom of Christ, and that for the sake of the pious, not only so that they may console them in this way, but also so that they may increase their hope, lest they despair of the kingdom of CHRIST because of the fear of bodily inconveniences. Similarly, the blessed Höpfner in his unpublished commentary: as the Prophet previously preached to the impenitent, so now for the consolation of the pious and penitent, to whom he had said in verse 7 that the words of GOD are good, he promises that although they may be deprived of an earthly kingdom, they shall nevertheless be citizens of the spiritual kingdom of the Messiah, and he confirms this by a notable proof of the Church in the New Testament to be gathered in crowds from Jews and Gentiles. By gathering I will gather, that is, I will altogether or certainly gather. Then the words by gathering I will gather Jacob all of you, certainly a consolation, not a threat are, the words are sweet concerning the congregation of Jacob, and not sad. Which Coccejus acknowledges. A disciple of Calvin. Never is gathering the remnants placed outside the meaning of blessing and grace. Is. X. 20. 21. 22. Mich. IV. 6. c. V. 6. 7. Jes. XXIII. 3. It is called a leading into exile, and a casting out, not a gathering. ALL JACOB AND THE REMNANTS OF ISRAEL.

These things seem to conflict with one another. For if all Jacob is to be gathered, not only the remnants will be gathered! Therefore, the remnants distinguish between a calling which concerns all Jacob, and the outcome, because not all, but only the remnants of Israel, provide obedience to the calling God. Others say that all Jacob, namely the elect, is to be gathered. Their interpretation is more elegant, in the judgment of the blessed Höpfner, who, because of the accession of the Gentiles, think that all Jacob is called, both those who are so called according to the flesh, and those who according to the promise or the Spirit are children of Jacob, although they are sprung from the Gentiles. But the remnants of Israel are called the descendants of the Israelites who were converted to Christ in the New Testament, as below c. IV. 7. conf. Luke I. 33. The word אָסֹף which also occurs in c. IV. 6., is to gather, and in both places is rendered by συνάγειν, whence Christ's ἐπισυναγωγειν in Matthew XXIII. 37. and the word συναγωγῆς for the Church in James II. 2. & ἐπισυναγωγῆς Heb. X. 26. The word קָבֵץ is to gather the dispersed, and not individually but in troops, so that the number may seem to swell or grow, and the Piel is used to increase the abundance of this collection, as if to say, I will frequently gather. Thirdly, the likeness of a sheepfold fits the Church, which is the fold of the Lord. And to make them like sheep, and indeed like a flock in a pen, is not to restrain and shut up by siege, or to deport into captivity. Only a foreign desert is accustomed to be called a pen, not a fold, as Coccejus says again. Furthermore, the Prophet hints that Jews and Gentiles will be of equal right and dignity in the New Testament, where Christ made both (nations) one (ἕν i.e. one people), not indeed by converting the Gentile into the Jewish, as the Jews wanted in the time of Paul, nor the Jewish into the Gentile, but by changing both into another different one, i.e. a Christian people, Eph. II. 14, and thus he predicts an equal-honored calling of the Gentiles to the Catholic Church. בָּצְרָה is properly the metropolis of the Moabites (distinct from the Bozrah of the Edomites), famous for its pastures, whence the sheep of Bozrah, i.e., by no means common but most select, most delicate in the eyes of GOD, as being redeemed by the blood of the Son of God. The Chaldean and Latin render it in the fold, whom Luther follows, who translates it in einem festen Stall, to which translation the following words favor as an explanation of the former. For although Bozrah is the proper name of a city, which city nevertheless has its name from a fortification, and was famous for its select sheep, it can therefore be taken appellatively for a fortification and for a pen, in which sheep are confined and fortified, and the preposition ב can be understood in the LXX. to render it in affliction: which version, because Theodoret followed it, it is no wonder that he took this whole passage concerning punishment: but the Jesuit Ribera betrays his own ignorance, because he still tries to defend it, for whence is there a Hateph-kametz under the preposition ב? Junius saw these things, and Tarnovius thinks that Grotius, who made this comment of Aben-Ezra his own here, tried to meet it: that the Prophet is playing from the ambiguity in this verse, and mocking the words of the Pseudo-Prophets, who were promising great and many things, to whom God rightly says I will gather Judah and Israel, but with the intention that they might be led away into captivity in the greatest possible number, as if into a foreign fold. But that mimicry is fabricated, and not sufficiently consistent with the phraseology of Scripture.

For the Prophets were not accustomed to imitate the words of the Pseudo-Prophets in such a way that they would plainly neglect the phraseology of the Holy Spirit. But where is a foreign land called a fold, where is either confinement in a siege, or deportation into captivity, a gathering into a fold? Fourthly, the prophecy sounds concerning all Jacob and the remnants of Israel being gathered into one. But the twelve tribes have never been gathered into one corporally after the abduction into captivity; for by Jacob, Grotius understands the ten tribes, and by the remnants of Israel, the two remaining tribes. Now since the former were led away by Shalmaneser, and the latter by Nebuchadnezzar, how are they all gathered into ONE FOLD? Which the Prophet expresses so clearly here, that he not only says, in gathering I will gather all you Jacob, I will lead into ONE the remnants of Israel, but adds for the sake of declaration, I will place him equally as a flock in a fold, and again as cattle in the midst of pens, and finally they will be in a tumult from the multitude of men. Which multitude Grotius distorts to mean enemies, but against the text: for all those things speak of the gathering of the entire multitude of Israel, which the Prophet hints will be so great that it will as if produce a noise and sound. Es werde doͤs nen und wimmeln von Leuten. Rightly the blessed Luther here: Where there is a great frequency of men, there confused voices report a certain tumult. The blessed Höpfner indeed refers the former not to the multitude, but to the description of liberation. Yet in the latter he warns that a multitude is depicted. AS CATTLE IN THE MIDST OF PENS. It is not indicated that they are to be gathered so closely together, but primarily this likeness denotes liberation from destruction, which is prepared by gaping wolves and hellish lions for those who are not associated with the Church. The following words deal with the multitude. THEY WILL BE IN A TUMULT FROM THE MULTITUDE OF MEN. In the Hebrew, from man or from the multitude of men. He does not denote commotion and convulsion by the word of being in a tumult, but a very great multitude, and indeed such a one as would even bear the appearance of a public tumult among the impious. Which began to be fulfilled after the ascension of the Lord, so that from this the Apostles were often accused of being troublemakers, by whom they had disturbed the whole world. Acts XVII. 19. Therefore this particle pertains to the conversion of the Gentiles, and to the ministry of the word itself, which is therefore also compared to the voices of those in a tumult, because it disturbs the world and the world opposes itself to it. So that there may be no doubt that the discourse is about a gathering into one assembly. Since, therefore, such a bodily gathering into one assembly has nowhere and never taken place, it is manifest that these things must necessarily be understood as referring to a spiritual gathering. Nor were the two remaining tribes shut up in one city during the siege with the ten tribes, nor were the Israelites restored when the Jews returned after the release from the Babylonian captivity. This argument is urged especially by the blessed Luther. If you wish to connect this passage with the preceding ones and understand it as referring to the external or bodily restoration of the people, you will have wandered entirely from the path. For when was the kingdom of Israel restored? But if it was not restored, what does the Prophet mean by saying it is to be restored? The Jews, indeed, induced by these promises, stubbornly hope for a bodily liberation, but in vain. For the Prophet is not speaking of a bodily but of a spiritual liberation, which comes about through the Gospel of Christ proclaimed in the whole world. There all Jacob and the scattered remnants of Israel are, who through faith receive the Gospel and believe in the remission of sins and eternal life through Christ. This gathering, because the Jews they do not understand, it happens that when they expect and hope for a longer time, so much the less hope is left. But you will say, Why were these things not signified more clearly by the Prophets? I answer, The Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared them to us. For these things had to be wrapped up, so that the clarity of the Gospel might differ from the clarity of the Law, and might surpass it. The sermons of Christ and the Apostles interpret all these mysteries most clearly. Since the Jews are unwilling to acknowledge these, they are deservedly detained in that horrible blindness. Therefore, as far as the words of the Prophet are concerned, he says expressly: The whole of Jacob is to be gathered, and the remnants of Israel are to be collected. Just as also the promise to Abraham is universal: In thee shall all nations be blessed. These are the words of B. Luther, who also teaches excellently in the same place how these and similar universal promises obtain their truth. Here incautious readers stumble again, and refer universal promises to an event which is most particular. For neither do all believe, nor are all saved. A distinction must therefore be held. For it is one thing that all nations shall be blessed in thee. And another, that all nations shall receive this promise concerning the blessing. For the Gospel indeed offers to all the remission of sins and eternal life through Christ, but not all receive this promise of the Gospel. Thus in this place the Prophet says, I will gather the whole of thee, Jacob. And yet the event teaches that the greatest part of the people did not believe the Gospel, and therefore was rejected, as the same Prophet shows when he speaks of the remnants of Israel. Why then, you will say, are the sentences so universal? For this reason, clearly, that no one may exclude himself from the promise of the Gospel. For Christ is not the treasure of one people or time: but he is offered through the word to all; that not all receive Christ, however, is their own fault: because they do not believe, and indulge their own incredulity. Meanwhile, the sentence of God and the universal promise remains, that God wills all men to be saved. In this manner the Prophet indeed says that the whole of Jacob is to be collected. For God wills Christ to be the common treasure of all, just as Christ says: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. Behold the zeal for gathering, that he may gather all into one fold, to one grace through Christ, but the incredulous resist this will of God, when they are unwilling to obey the word and receive it. And so only the remnants of Israel are gathered and saved. These things we have thought fit to observe here for the sake of the Calvinists, the new Predestinarians, and also the Rintelenses who attribute a contrary sense to Megalandrus.
