A WICKED BALANCE, AND DECEITFUL WEIGHTS OF THE BAG] Lighter for selling, heavier for buying, as the Chaldean [paraphrast] says here. In the Hebrew, weights are called stones, for the Hebrews used such, and they stored them in a bag, as appears in Deut. XXV. 13. & Prov. XXI. 11.

Verf. 11.

Ver. 14.

THOU SHALT EAT AND SHALT NOT BE SATISFIED] When you are besieged, you will not find food that will benefit you.

AND THY HUMILIATION IN THE MIDST OF THEE] Thy depression in thy bowels. That is, thy bowels will collapse from hunger, so the Chaldean.

ET APPREHENDES] Apprehendet femina, id est, concipiet. Omnes ferme interpretes putant hic, ut alibi sæpe ס poni vice ש.

ET NON SALVABIS] Et non pariet. Ita מלט fumitur Job. XXI. 10. folent præ fame aut fœdis alimen- tis abortire mulieres.

ET QUOS SALVAVERIS] Quos pepererit fe- mina.

IN GLADIUM DABO] Tradam gladio hostili,

## 6:15
Verse 15.

YOU SHALL SOW AND SHALL NOT REAP] Shall the impious soldier possess these fields so cultivated? The barbarian these harvests. Lo, for whom we have tilled the fields! YOU SHALL TREAD THE OLIVE] You shall press. AND THE MUST] The grapes: The Chaldean.

Verf. 15.

TU SEMINABIS ET NON METES] Impius hæc tam culta novalia miles habebit? Barbarus has fegetes. En queis confevimus agros! TU CALCABIS OLIVAM] Premes. ET MUSTUM] Uvas: Chaldæus.

## 6:16
Verse 16.

AND YOU HAVE KEPT THE STATUTES OF OMRI] For the reason that the statutes (not of God, but) of Omri are observed (by you). Concerning whom 1 Kings XVI. 25. Evil examples flowed from Israel to Judah.

AND ALL THE WORK OF THE HOUSE OF AHAB] Who was the son of Omri, and surpassed both his father and all his progenitors in impiety. 1 Kings XVI. 30, 31, 32, 33. He rightly says the house of Ahab, because his posterity followed the same paths, for which reason it was cut off by Jehu.

AND YOU HAVE WALKED IN THEIR COUNSELS] You follow their institutions.

THAT I MIGHT GIVE YOU TO DESTRUCTION] It is למען for: so it shall come to pass, that I will give you to destruction.

AND THE INHABITANTS IN IT] The city, concerning which above 9.

FOR A HISSING] For a derision. See 1 Kings IX. 8. Lamentations II. 15.

AND YOU SHALL BEAR THE REPROACH OF MY PEOPLE] You bear it. All will say of you, O you rich (concerning whom it was treated above in 12), that you are the principal cause why the republic has been so utterly overturned.

Latin:

Verf. 16.

ET CUSTODISTI PRÆCEPTA AMRI] Ideo quod obfervantur (apud te) præcepta (non Dei, fed) Amri. De quo 1. Reg. XVI. 25. Ab Ifraele ad Judam mana- runt mala exempla.

ET OMNE OPUS DOMUS ACHAB] Qui Am- ri filius, & patrem & progenitores omnes impietate supe- ravit. 1. Reg. XVI. 30. 31. 32. 33. Domum autem A- chabi recte dicit, quia posteritas ejus easdem vias institit, ob id per Jehum excisa.

ET AMBULASTI IN VOLUNTATIBUS EO- RUM] Sectamini eorum instituta.

UT DAREM TE IN PERDITIONEM] Est למען pro: ita fiet, ut dem te exitio.

ET HABITANTES IN EA] Civitate, de qua fu- pra 9.

IN SIBILIUM] Irrifui. Vide 1. Reg. IX. 8. Thren. II. 15.

ET OPPROBRIUM POPULI MEI PORTABI- TIS] Portatis. Omnes dicent in vobis, ó divites, (de quibus actum est fupra 12.) præcipuam esse caufam cur respublica ita funditus everfa sit.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. Partly legal, partly Evangelical.

When in the vineyard of Judea vines are sought in vain and the righteous fail, the iniquity of the Magistrate prevails, and faith is utterly lacking even among those most closely related, the Prophet awaits the salvation of the Lord, restrains the Ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν (rejoicing in evil) of the enemies, in darkness, under the persona of the faithful, rejoices in the light of the Lord, and bearing the wrath of the Lord hopes for His mercy, with the contrition of the enemies, the repair of the walls of the Church, and the admiration and humiliation of all nations regarding the rule of His inheritance, and prays to GOD, because He graciously forgives sins and keeps the faith given to the Fathers.

The wicked is rebuked, consolations are given to the miserable.

Ver. 1.

WOE IS ME, FOR I AM BECOME AS ONE THAT GATHERETH IN THE AUTUMN THE GRAPES OF THE VINTAGE] That is, those remaining after a diligent vintage, which are wont to be very few. Here the Prophet describes what some pious person might rightly say during the reign of Manasseh, at which time good men were scarcely to be found: - - - as many as the gates of Thebes, or the mouths of the rich Nile.

IF it is permitted to thrust a persona upon the sacred text in this way, which is indicated by no word from the Prophets, what personas will not be able to be thrust upon it? For by that reasoning it would be enough for eliciting the sense, provided the prophecy could be applied to any time or person whatsoever by conjecture (ςοχασμὸν), even if the Prophets give no indication of that time or person. But what certainty of Scripture will finally be left by this method, if everyone, for the happiness of their conjectural (ςοχαςικῆς) faculty, devises subjects for themselves to which they know how to adapt the predicates by any means whatsoever? There is no indication here of the time of the reign of Manasseh, no indication of any pious person introduced by the Prophet. The Prophet himself speaks, and weaves this complaint. Therefore, no other persona is to be substituted. Micah deplores his own lot, that he has achieved almost nothing with so many exhortations: indeed, that this has happened to him which is wont to happen to one gathering ears of corn left by the reapers, and small clusters passed over by the vintagers. Coccejus makes Christ speak these things in the days of his flesh. Another would introduce others. That the Prophet speaks these things, not some pious person in the time of Manasseh, the Prophetic threatening in v. 4 teaches: The day of thy watchmen, thy visitation cometh, now shall be their perplexity.

THERE IS NO CLUSTER TO EAT] Jerome wrote, as appears from the Commentaries: there is no grape-cluster to eat. Using the Greek word, because the Latins do not have one that corresponds to it: for βότρυς is a coherence of grapes hanging from a cluster.

MY SOUL DESIRED THE FIRST-RIPE FIGS] This thing also is rare. Hosea IX, 10. it is understood as if.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. Partim legale, partim Evan- gelicum.

Quum in vinea Iudeæ frustra vites quærantur & justi deficiant, iniquitas Magistratus prævaleat, fi- des penitus desideretur etiam inter maxime cogna- tos, expectat salutare Domini Propheta Ἐπι- χαιρεκακίαν hostium compescit, in tenebris, sub persona fidelium, luce Domini lætatur, Domini- que iram portans misericordiam ejus sperat, cum hostium contritione, murorum Ecclesiæ reparatio- ne, & gentium omnium ob regimen hereditatis suæ admiratione, & humiliatione, ac DEUM, quod gratiose peccata condonet, & fidem Patribus da- tam servet, deprecatur.

Impius arguitur, misero solatia dantur.

Vers. 1.

VÆ MIHI, QUI FACTUS SUM SICUT QUI COLLIGIT IN AUTUMNO RACEMOS VINDE- MIÆ] Id est, restantes post vindemiam diligentem, qui perpauci esse solent. Describit hic Propheta, quæ pius aliquis jure dicturus sit regnante Manasse, quo tempore viri boni vix futuri erant: - - - totidem quot Thebarum portæ, vel divitis ostia Nili.

SI ita ingerere personam textui sacro licitum est, quæ nullo verbo indicatur à Prophetis, quæ non personæ ingeri poterunt? Nam ea ratione satis fuerit ad sensum eruendum, modo utcunque alicui tempori, aut personæ per ςοχασμὸν appli- cari possit vaticinium, utut Prophetæ temporis, aut personæ istius nullum indicium faciant. Quæ vero tandem hoc pacto relinquetur Scripturæ cer- titudo, si quisque pro facultatis ςοχαςικῆς felici- tate subjecta sibi excogitet, ad quæ prædicata qua- cunque ratione aptare noverit? Nullum hic indi- cium temporis regiminis Manasse, nullum pii ali- cujus à Propheta introducti. Loquitur Propheta ipse, & querelam hanc texit. Non ergo persona alia substituenda. Deplorat Michas suam sortem, quod tot exhortationibus nihil fere profecerit: quin id sibi acciderit, quod accidere solet colligenti spicas à messoribus relictas, & racemulos à vindemia- toribus prætermissos. Coccejus facit hæc Christum loquentem in diebus carnis. Alius alios intro- duceret. Prophetam hæc loqui, non pium ali- quem Manassis tempore, comminatio Prophetica v. 4. docet, Dies speculationis tuæ, visitatio tua venit, nunc erit vastitas eorum.

NON EST HORTUS AD COMEDENDUM] Scripsit Hieronymus, ut ex Commentariis apparet: non est botrus ad comedendum. Græcam vocem usurpans, quia Latinis non est una quæ ei respondeat: est enim βότρυς u- varum cohærentia à racemo dependens.

PRÆCOQUAS FICUS DESIDERAVIT ANI- MA MEA] Rem hanc quoque raram. Osee IX, 10. sub- auditur quasi.

## 7:2
Ver. 2.

THE HOLY MAN IS PERISHED FROM THE EARTH] חסיד (hasid) beneficent, whence ἀσίδαιοι (Hasideans), there is no one good, that is, scarcely anyone, as in Rom. III. 11. they express vehemently what they wish by superlatives (ὑπερβολαὶ).

THEY ALL LIE IN WAIT FOR BLOOD] Even unto blood.

VIR FRATREM SUUM] That is, a fellow citizen.

AD MORTEM VENATUR] In Hebrew: he hunts with a net.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

PERIIT SANCTUS DE TERRA] חסיד benefi- cus, unde ἀσίδαιοι nemo est bonus, id est, vix quisquam, ut Rom. III. 11. ὑπερβολαὶ vehementer quod volunt ex- primunt.

OMNES IN SANGUINE INSIDIANTUR] Ad sanguinem usque.

VIR FRATREM SUUM] Id est, popularem.

AD MORTEM VENATUR] In Hebræo: vena- tur sagena.

## 7:3
Vers. 3.

MALUM MANUUM SUARUM DICUNT BONUM: PRINCEPS POSTULAT, ET JUDEX IN REDDENDO EST] You might not wrongly connect this part with the preceding ones: To do evil with both hands (he hunts, as preceded,) for doing good the prince demands (something): & the Judge (supply: judges) for the sake of retribution. The Chaldean, for רריטיב, reads לא ח טיב, no one, that is, does good,

The placement of the accents rather favors the Vulgate. Upon the evil of the hands (they are,) to accomplish (that) good (or to adorn and paint it) as Cocceius interprets εὐπόδα: The prince demands, and the judge judges for compensation: τῶν ἀρχόντων δεήσις ἀνάγκη. Nor does the Judge refuse, since he expects a reward. For other interpretations of the passage, see, if you please, Ludov. de Dieu.

Vers. eod.

ET MAGNUS LOCUTUS EST DESIDERIUM ANIMÆ SUÆ] If some great man utters the depravity of his soul. הַוָּה depravity. Ps. V. 10. XXXVIII. 13. LVII. 2.

ET CONTURBAVERUNT EAM] Others (the lesser ones, that is) twist and double that very thing which he desired; three witnesses are like three twisted threads, which cannot be broken.

Thus, according to the Junian translation, Dievius also understands this: The great king is, he himself speaks the depravity of his heart, and others, flattering him, confirm that malice, and like a rope twist and double it. B. Luther rendered it almost similarly in his Commentary: The powerful man speaks according to the depravity of his soul, and they join their efforts (this I refer, he says, to all these three orders: Prince, Judge, powerful man). For it is a plural, which by joined efforts they overcome and break through to malice. For the verb (Abath) signifies to entangle, to condense, and by metalepsis, which is most common to this language, to strengthen, to make strong. As the proverb testifies: A threefold cord is not easily broken, hence from the connection they call (Aboth) a dense and strong rope. What Jerome translates as 'according to the desire of his soul,' he rendered the meaning rather than the words, although the meaning is less significant. For the word (Navah) signifies punishment and guilt. Just as when we say in German: Nach Unglück ringen, Unglück stiften. Thus in Ps. 91, where our translation has 'from the harmful pestilence,' or 'from an unhappy thing.' The meaning, therefore, is: Those who are powerful in works are full of depraved desires; they comply with these and indulge them freely. Megalander adds an ἐπανόρθωσιν (correction), which he would be blind who does not see to be far more necessary for our age. But see with what brief and yet wonderfully significant words you have the courts of almost all Princes described and depicted in their own colors. In what ages was it ever heard that such burdens were imposed upon subjects, just so that they might build sumptuously, dress splendidly, and feed a great crowd of courtiers fit and born to consume the fruits? For they do these things so that no ordinary revenues are enough for them. And so afterwards others also become masters of avarice, who ought to administer justice and manage the public offices necessary for the Republic. The plural can also be referred to the same subject taken distributively, i.e., each one speaks according to the depravity of his soul, nay, they thicken it, so that the plural verb corresponds in sense to the subject, even if it is expressed in the singular number, which sense the blessed Luther respects in his German translation: Die Gewaltigen rathen nach ihren Mutwillen Schaden zu thun, und drehens wie sie wollen. They thicken it, that is to say, like a rope. This is עֵץ עָבוֹת, thus עָבוֹת is a tree dense with branches and foliage. For their falsehoods have their consequences. Vara Vibiam sequitur. ἑνὸς δοθέντος ἀτόπꙋ ἕπεται πολλὰ; he who has placed one lie as a foundation through concupiscence, nay, through wickedness, must compose an entire system of lies, so that the lie might not limp in any part, or the rest might not conflict with a shred of truth. A lie is the rule of a lie, as Cocceius elegantly says here.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

MALUM MANUUM SUARUM DICUNT BO- NUM: PRINCEPS POSTULAT, ET JUDEX IN REDDENDO EST] Non male hanc partem connectas cum prioribus: Ad malefaciendum manu utraq (venatur ut præcessit, ) ad benefaciendum princeps (aliquid) postu- lat: & Judex (supple judicat) retributionis causa. Chal- dæus pro רריטיב, legit לא ח טיב, non facit bene, quisquam scilicet,

Accentuum positus Vulgatæ potius favet. Super malo manus (sunt,) ad (id) efficiendum bonum (sive ornandum & pingendum) ut Coccejus εὐ- πόδα interpretatur : Princeps postulat, & judex pro compensatione judicat : τῶν ἀρχόντων δεήσις ἀνάγκη. Nec abnuit Judex, quum retributio- nem expectet. Alias interpretationes loci vide sis apud Ludov. de Dieu.

Vers. eod.

ET MAGNUS LOCUTUS EST DESIDERIUM ANIMÆ SUÆ] Si magnus aliquis eloquatur pravitatem ani- mi sui. הַוָּה pravitas. Ps. V. 10. XXXVIII. 13. LVII. 2.

ET CONTURBAVERUNT EAM] Alii (minores scilicet) contorquent & duplicant idipsum, quod ille voluit testes tres sunt quasi tria fila contorta, quæ rumpi ne- queunt.

Sic juxta Iunianam translationem hæc etiam intelligit Dievius : Rex magnus est, loquitur ipsemet pravitatem cordis sui, & alii huic adulantes malitiam illam confirmant, & instar funis contorquent ac conduplicant. Similiter fere B. Lutherus reddidit in Commentario : Potens loquitur secundum pra- vitatem animæ suæ, & conjungunt studia (hoc refero, inquit, ad omnes istos tres ordines Prin- cipem, Judicem, potentem) Est enim plurale, quod conjunctis studiis ad malitiam vincunt & perrum- punt. Nam verbum (Abath) significat intricare, condensare, & per metalepsin, quæ huic linguæ communissima est, roborare, fortem facere. Sicut proverbium testatur : Funiculus triplex difficilius rumpitur, hinc à connexione vocant (Aboth) funem densum & fortem. Quod Hieronymus vertit se- cundum desiderium animæ suæ, sententiam ma- gis, quam verba reddidit, quanquam sententia mi- nus significans est. Nam vocabulum (Navah) si- gnificat pœnam & culpam. Sicut cum Germani- ce dicimus : Nach Unglück ringen, Unglück stif- ten. Sic in Ps. 91. ubi nostra translatio habet à peste noxia, seu à re infelici. Sententia igitur est. Qui operibus valent pleni sunt pravis cu- piditatibus, his obsequuntur & indulgent libere. Addit Megalander ἐπανόρθωσιν, quam nostræ æ- tati longe magis necessariam esse, cæcus sit, qui non videat. Vide autem quam brevibus & tamen mire significantibus verbis descriptas ac propriis co- loribus depictas habeas aulas omnium fere Principum. Quibus unquam seculis auditum est, tanta onera im- posita esse subditis, tantum ut sumptuose ædificare, splendide vestire, & magnam aulicorum turbam ad fruges consumendas aptam & natam possint alere. Hæc enim faciunt, ut nulli ordinarii reditus eis satis sint. Itaque postea alius etiam magistri avaritiæ fi- unt, qui jus administrare & publica officia Reipubl. necessaria administrare debebant. Potest etiam plurale ad idem subjectum distributive acceptum referri, h. m. potens (unusquisque) loquitur secun- dum pravitatem animæ suæ, imo condensant eam, ut plurale verbum respondeat quoad sensum sub- jecto, etsi singulari numero id expressum sit, quem sensum respicit B. Lutherus in translatione Germa- nica : Die Gewaltigen rathen nach ihren Mut- willen Schaden zu thun, und drehens wie sie wollen. Densant scilicet ut rudentem. Hoc est עֵץ עָבוֹת sic עָבוֹת arbor densa ramis, frondibus. Habent enim falsitates suas consequentias. Vara Vibiam sequitur. ἑνὸς δοθέντος ἀτόπꙋ ἕπεται πολλὰ qui unum mendacium per concupiscen- tiam, imo per nequitiam, posuerit pro fundamen- to, oportet integrum systema mendaciorum com- ponat, ut mendacium nulla ex parte claudiret, aut cum lacinia veritatis reliqua confligat. Menda- cium mendacii regula est, ut eleganter hic Cocce- jus.

Verse 4.

HE WHO IS BEST AMONG THEM IS LIKE A BRAMBLE] Retaining whatever he touches.

LIKE A THORN FROM A HEDGE] Pricking on all sides.

THE DAY OF YOUR WATCH] Of your watchings: that time predicted by the Prophets. For they call prophets watchmen. Ezek. 3:17, 33:2, 6, 7.

YOUR VISITATION SHALL COME] By which God is about to test you with most grievous trials, whether you are constant in piety.

NOW SHALL BE THEIR DESOLATION] Namely, of the prophets. All will be killed, or will flee.

Verf. 4.

QVI OPTIMVS IN EIS EST QVASI PALIU- RUS] Quicquid attigerit, retinens.

QUASI SPINA DE SEPE] Pungens undique.

DIES SPECULATIONIS TUÆ] Speculationum tuarum : id tempus à Prophetis prædictum. Prophetæ e- nim vocant speculatores. Ezech. III, 17. XXXIII. 2. 6. 7.

VISITATIO TVA VENIET] Qua Deus vos exploraturus est gravissimis tentamentis, an constantes si- tis in pietate.

NVNC ERIT VASTITAS EORUM] Nempe Prophetarum. Omnes interficientur, aut fugient.

## 7:5
Verse 5.

DO NOT TRUST A FRIEND] Where kings persecute piety with the most atrocious punishments, faith is nowhere safe then. See Matt. 10:35, Luke 12:53. Those who lacked an enemy were oppressed by friends, says Tacitus.

AND DO NOT TRUST IN A LEADER] Do not trust the head of your family: τῶ ἄρχοντι τῶ ὄικυ, as אלוף is explained in Job 22:14; those who were of the same family were accustomed to have refuge with them; the LXX also translated it as friend. Prov. 16:18, 17:9.

FROM HER WHO SLEEPS IN YOUR BOSOM] A description of a wife, Deut. 13:6, 28:54, 56. Lucretius: --- She often throws herself into his bosom, overcome by the eternal wound of love.

GUARD THE DOORS OF YOUR MOUTH] Beware of trusting anything secret to her, Ovid: The husband threatens the destruction of the wife, she that of the husband.

Latin:

Verf. 5.

NOLITE CREDERE AMICO] Ubi Reges pie- tatem pœnis atrocissimis persequuntur nusquam tunc fi- des tuta est. Vid. Matth. X. 35. Luc. XII, 53. Quibus deerat inimicus, per amicos oppressi, ait Tacitus.

ET NOLITE CONFIDERE IN DUCE] Noli fi- dere capiti familiæ vestræ : τῶ ἄρχοντι τῶ ὄικυ quomodo אלוף explicatur Job. XX II. 14. ad illos perfugium habe- re solebant qui ejusdem erant familiæ, LXX. etiam φίλον verterunt. Prov. XVI. 18. XVII. 9.

AB EA QUÆ DORMIT IN SINV TVO] De- scriptio uxoris Deut. XIII. 6. XXVIII. 54. 56. Lucre- tius: --- In gremium fæpe se Rejicit, æterno devictus vulnere amoris.

CVSTODI CLAVSTRA ORIS TVI] Cave quic- quam arcani ei credas, Ovidius: Imminet exitio vir conjugis, illa mariti.

## 7:6
Verse 6.

BECAUSE THE SON DOES AN INSULT TO THE FA- THER] He holds his father in contempt. It is the same as what Hesiod says. Αἶψα δὲ γηράσκοντας ἀτιμάσουσι τοκῆας.

DAUGHTER-IN-LAW AGAINST HER MOTHER-IN-LAW] See the cited passages of Matthew and Luke, Ovid: --- not guest is safe from host, nor father-in-law from son-in-law.

AND THE ENEMIES OF A MAN ARE HIS HOUSEHOLD] Even those of his household. Ovid: The affection of brothers also is rare.

Latin:

Verf. 6.

QVIA FILIVS CONTVMELIAM FACIT PA- TRI] Patrem vilipendit. Idem est, quod dicit Hesio- dus. Αἶψα δὲ γηράσκοντας ἀτιμάσουσι τοκῆας.

NVRVS ADVERSVS SOCRVM SVAM] Vide dicta loca Matthæi & Lucæ, Ovidius: --- non hospes ab hospite tutus, Non socer à genero.

ET INIMICI HOMINIS DOMESTICI EJVS] Etiam domestici. Ovidius: Fratrum quoque gratia rara est.

## 7:7
Verse 7.

BUT I WILL LOOK TO THE LORD] The words of some pious person who is to live in those times still continue.

The speech of the same person is continued: And when in the preceding part the Prophet has complained, here he raises himself and others by his example, as blessed Luther rightly observed in his Commentary on this passage. Since, therefore, he sees the impious world, with threats and salutary doctrine neglected, continuing in sins, he does two things which are most significant. First, he is not moved by the scandals of the impious multitude, but remains firm in his opinion, not intending to change it, even if all men are to be made enemies for that reason. This prophetic and heroic constancy is especially necessary in a faithful Teacher. But the second is greater, that since punishment and divine vengeance could not be far off given such morals, he nevertheless does not cast away all hope, but casts his eyes back to God, certain that even if a universal punishment is to rage like a flood, yet God knows how to rescue and save His own, just as Peter also says.

Latin:

Verf. 7.

EGO AVTEM AD DOMINVM ADSPICIAM] Durant adhuc verba pii alicujus victuri illis tempori- bus.

Continuatur ejusdem personæ sermo: Et quum in antecedente Propheta questus fuerit, hic erigit se & exemplo suo alios, ut recte observavit B. Lutherus in Comment. ad h. l. Cum itaq, videt impium mundum neglectis comminationibus & do- &trina salutari pergere in peccatis, duo facit quæ maxime sunt insignia. Primo non movetur scanda- lis impiæ multitudinis, sed manet firmus in sententia sua, non mutaturus eam, si capiendi ideo inimici sint omnes homines. Hæc Prophetica & Heroica con- stantia in fideli Doctore imprimis est necessaria. Sed alterum majus est, quod cum in talibus moribus non posset abesse longius pœna, & vindicta divina, non tamen spem omnem abjicit, sed oculos in Deum reji- cit certus, quod etiamsi universalis pœna tanquam diluvium grassatura sit, tamen Deus norit eripere & servare suos, Sicut Petrus quoq, dicit.

## 7:8
Verse 8.

DO NOT REJOICE, MY ENEMY, OVER ME] The speech is clearly new, in which the Jewish nation, having been deported, is introduced speaking: the enemy is the Chaldean nation.

I WILL ARISE WHEN I SIT IN DARKNESS] When I shall sit (for a long time) in darkness: that is, in misery.

THE LORD IS MY LIGHT] He will be the cause of my prosperity.

Latin:

Verf. 8.

NE LÆTERIS INIMICA MEA SUPER ME] Novus plane est sermo, in quo Judæa gens deportata lo- quens inducitur: inimica est gens Chaldæa,

CONSVRGAM CVM SEDERO IN TENEBRIS] Ubi sedero (diu) in tenebris: id est, in miseria.

DOMINVS LVX MEA EST] Erit causa meæ prosperitatis.

## 7:9
Verse 9.

I WILL BEAR THE WRATH OF THE LORD] I will patiently bear the punishment inflicted by God.

SINCE I HAVE SINNED AGAINST HIM] Against him: through idolatry, injustice, lack of mercy.

UNTIL HE JUDGES MY CAUSE, AND BRINGS FORTH MY JUDGMENT] Until he acknowledges my cause, and shall avenge my injuries: namely against the Babylonians, who mock and trample upon me, for the reason that, placed in such great evils, I persevere in serving one GOD.

HE WILL BRING ME FORTH INTO THE LIGHT] Into good circumstances.

I SHALL SEE HIS JUSTICE] goodness, which is often צדקה for the Hebrews.

Latin:

Verf. 9.

IRAM DOMINI PORTABO] Pœnam à Deo in- flictam patienter feram.

QVONIAM PECCAVI EI] In eum: per idolo- latriam, injustitiam, immisericordiam.

DONEC CAVSAM MEAM JVDICET, ET CIAT JVDICIVM MEVM] Donec causam meam cogno- scat, & injurias meas vindicaberit: nempe adversus Baby- lonios, qui me irrident atque proculcant, ideo quod in tantis malis posita uni DEO servire perseverem.

EDVCET ME IN LVCEM] In res bonas.

VIDEBO JVSTITIAM EJVS] bonitatem, quæ sæpe צדקה Hebræis.

## 7:10
Ver. 10.

AND MY ENEMY SHALL LOOK ON] The Chaldean nation, as we have said.

WHICH SAYS TO ME] Which said to me, when it held me captive.

WHERE IS THE LORD THY GOD?] That is: let him be present now, so that he may free you. See a similar passage in Matt. XXVII. 43. and what is said there.

MY EYES SHALL LOOK UPON HER] They shall look upon the Chaldean nation, under the yoke of the Persians.

NOW SHE SHALL BE FOR TRAMPLING AS THE MUD OF THE STREETS] She shall be trodden by the feet of the victor. See a similar passage in Ps. LX, 10. Is. XXVI. 6.

We admit that the discourse in v. 8 is entirely new and that the deported Jewish nation is introduced. However, regarding the enemy, others, with Theodoret, prefer to understand the Idumean; for Babylon was the enemy of all nations, but Idumea was the proper and known enemy of the Jews: whence almost all the Prophets threaten it with similar destruction on account of its Επιχαιρεκακίαν [malicious joy]. Conf. Ps. CXXXVII. 7. Obad. v. 12. Amos I. 11. Nevertheless, Jerome, Remigius, Vatablus, and others understand these things in our text concerning Babylon, and some even concerning Assyria. The Jews absurdly [understand them] concerning Rome.

Latin:

Verf. 10.

ET ADSPICIAT INIMICA MEA] Gens Chal- daica, ut diximus.

QVÆ DICIT AD ME] Quæ dixit ad me, cum captivam me teneret.

TBI EST DOMINVS DEVS TVVS? ] Id est: adsit nunc, ut te liberet. simile vid. Matth. XXVII. 23. & ibi dicta.

OCVLI MEI VIDEBVNT IN EAM] Adspicient gentem Chaldæam, sub jugo Persarum.

NVNC ERIT IN CONCVLCATIONEM VT LVTVM PLATEARVM ] Teretur pedibus victoris. Vide simile Pf. LX, 10. Es. XXVI. 6.

Admittimus, Novum plane sermonem esse v. 8. ac induci gentem Iudæam deportatam. Per inimi- cam vero alii cum Theodoreto malunt potius Idu- mæam intelligere, Babylon enim omnium gen- tium, sed Idumæa propria & nota fuit Judæorum inimica : Unde omnes fere Prophetæ ob Επιχαι- ρεκακίαν illi similę exitium comminantur. Conf. Pl. CXXXVII. 7. Obad. v. 12. Amos. I. 11. De Baby- lone tamen hæc in nostro textu intelligunt Hiero- nymus, Remigius, Vatablus, alii etiam de Assyria. Inepte Judæi de Roma.

## 7:11
Ver. 11.

THE DAY THAT THY WALLS SHALL BE BUILT] That is, the time will be long before thy ruins (that is, of thy cities) are repaired. He turns his words to the Chaldean nation.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

DIES VT ÆDIFICENTVR MACERIÆ TVÆ] Id est, longum erit tempus,antequam ruinæ tuæ (id est,ur- bium tuarum) reparentur. Vertit verba ad gentem Chal- dæam.

## 7:11
THE LAW SHALL BE FAR] The power of sending edicts to the nations shall be far from thee. A similar sense is found in Nahum concerning the Assyrians II. 13.

Latin:

LONGE FIET LEX] Longe à te aberit potestas edicta mittendi ad gentes. Par sensus apud Nahumum de Afsyriis II. 13.

## 7:12
Ver. 12.

IN THAT DAY] Of thy treading down, concerning which it began to be treated.

Latin:

Verf. 12.

IN DIE ILLA] Conculcationis tuæ, de qua agi cœpit.

## 7:12
IN THAT DAY AND EVEN TO THEE SHALL COME FROM ASSYRIA] Cyrus shall come to thee from Assyria. See above V. 6.

AND EVEN TO THE FORTIFIED CITIES] Babylon, Borsippa, and other most firm cities.

AND FROM THE FORTIFIED CITIES EVEN TO THE RIVER] When the river is placed simply, it is the Euphrates. The sense is: Cyrus will make the whole Euphrates subject to his own jurisdiction: the Euphrates will now flow softer with its waves.

AND TO THE SEA FROM SEA] From the Persian Sea, into which the Euphrates flows, he shall come to the Syrian Sea.

AND TO THE MOUNTAIN FROM MOUNTAIN] From Mount Taurus to Carmel of Syria.

These things are now twisted. For first, the persons are changed thus: the Prophet had spoken of those who were to be in the treading down in the third person; my eyes shall see HER. Here, however, there is an address to him to whom the speech is directed in the second person: The day that thy walls shall be built. Therefore, this building is not to be understood of Chaldea, even if the former things treated of Chaldea, which nevertheless sound rather of Edom. Then the Prophet says simply, the day that the walls shall be built; by what authority, therefore, does Grotius render these things thus: The time will be long before thy ruins are repaired? Which import almost the contrary meaning. Furthermore, the boundaries designated here are not obscurely for the Jews. Finally, these things do not refer to a threat, but to consolation. Wherefore Jerome, Remigius, Hugo, Isidore, Clarius, with the Chaldean, interpret these things concerning Jerusalem and its reparation, to whom Cornelius à Lapide, Christ. à Castro and others agree. The Chaldean renders it thus: In that time the congregation of Israel shall be built, which was dispersed in captivity; in that time the deserts of the peoples shall cease: in that time the captivities shall be gathered from Assyria, and from the cities of his strength, and from the great Armenia also, and from the fortified cities, and even to the Euphrates, and the western sea and the mountains of the mountain. Among our own people also, B. Luther and Chytræus admit that the former words concerning the restoration of Jerusalem—'The day in which thy walls shall be built'—are to be accepted, but so that the following words are accepted concerning the propagation of the Gospel into distant lands: 'IN THAT DAY THE DECREE SHALL BE PROPAGATED AFAR.' This, says our Luther, explains the building of which he spoke, that Jerusalem shall be so built that the decree may be propagated into distant lands. For there is here the word (Chok), which in the second Psalm is used in clearly the same meaning, where the Prophet preaches concerning the kingdom of Christ and says that Christ will preach the decree, namely this: 'The Lord said to me, Thou art my Son.' For this is the voice of the Gospel, that Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary, is the Son of God, in whom it pleased the Father that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. This decree of the Lord, or this doctrine, did indeed begin in Jerusalem and Mount Zion, as has also been said above, but it did not stop there. For it was published throughout the whole world, and this very publication was the true building of the city of Jerusalem, that is, of the kingdom of Christ. For thus a great and infinite kingdom was prepared for Christ through the word of the Gospel, just as the Prophet also explains this very thing more clearly now, so that there is no need to invent foreign and inept interpretations, but here also an antithesis must be observed. He does not speak of the law of Moses, that it is to be published among the nations, that the nations are to be circumcised and compelled to legal rites and other ceremonies. For that law remained only among the people of GOD, but this decree concerning hearing, adoring, and kissing the Son, this he says will be propagated afar, from sea to sea, from the river even to the ends of the earth. Just as Christ also for this very reason compares the Gospel to leaven, which is to pervade the whole world. Likewise to lightning, which is carried suddenly from the east to the west, and cannot be hindered by any human force. 'IN THAT DAY THEY SHALL COME EVEN TO THEE FROM ASSYRIA, AND FROM THE FORTIFIED CITIES, AND FROM THE FORTRESS EVEN TO THE RIVER, AND FROM SEA TO SEA, AND FROM MOUNTAIN TO MOUNTAIN.' I omit those trifles as to whether (Mazor), as the Seventy rendered it, are two words and Tyre is signified, or whether it is one word and signifies a fortress. For this Prophet retains the customary phrase which other Prophets have also used when they speak of the Kingdom of Christ, as in Psalm 72: 'He shall have dominion from sea even to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.' Who does not see that Micah wished to imitate this passage, just as Zechariah also in chapter 9: 'He shall speak peace to the nations, and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.' There is therefore no need here to dispute what are the rivers, what the mountains, what the fortified cities of which the Prophet speaks. For in general and simply he means this, that the word of the Gospel will be scattered throughout the whole world. Chytræus has summarized the matter thus: 'Concerning the restitution of the Church of Israel after the overthrow made by the Assyrians and Babylonians, and the beginning and propagation of the kingdom of Christ throughout the whole world, concerning the calling of the nations and Christ as the shepherd and King of the Church, it has been briefly said above in the third place of the second chapter, and in the three former places of the fourth chapter, and the third place of the fifth chapter.' From there, therefore, let those things be taken for the present prophecy of Micah. That the walls of Jerusalem, which had been trampled down, were to be restored through the propagation of the decree, of which it is said in Psalm 2: 'I will preach the decree: The Lord said to me: Thou art my Son.' 'Ask of me, and I will give thee the Nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession: Kiss the Son, blessed are all who trust in him,' or through the preaching of the Gospel of Christ scattered throughout the whole world, to which shepherd and king of his inheritance, the land and Jewish kingdom having been desolate and overthrown because of their sins, a great multitude of men will gather from the Assyrians and all places and nations of the world (Psalm 72, Zechariah 9: 'He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth'). Which will be abundantly fed and defended by the word of the Gospel in this desert of the world, and will be endowed with greater and more excellent goods than in the leading out from Egypt, with eternal liberation, life, and glory. The nations also, having cast away all trust in their own wisdom, strength, and worship, will no longer teach and preach their own religions and rites, nor will they listen to others teaching them, but they will acknowledge their sins and the curse of the wrath of God and eternal damnation imposed because of their sin: and therefore they will tremble with a true heart, and will cease to sin, and in the true fear of GOD, they will confirm all the counsels and actions of their life to the norm of the divine will and word. Similarly Winckelmann: 'The day that it may be built'—the Prophet prophesies for the consolation and exhilaration of the pious concerning the reduction of the people into the land from the Babylonian captivity, and thence the propagation of the Church to the nations. He compares the restitution of Israel into the land with the restoration of a collapsed house or city, just as Jerusalem, having collapsed, was in truth rebuilt. 'In that day the law shall be made afar'—a prophecy concerning the propagation of the law, that is, of heavenly doctrine among the Nations, and thus also the extension and amplification of the Church, as was said in the 4th chapter: 'The law shall go forth from Zion, and the decree of the Lord from Jerusalem.' 'It shall be made afar'—that is, from the earthly Jerusalem. 'And even to thee shall come Assyria?' Concerning the extension of the city of Jerusalem even into Assyria and other fortified cities of the nations, indeed even to the islands, mountains, and ends of the earth, so that access to it may be open to all nations. The blind Jews indeed understand these things concerning the rebuilding of the earthly Jerusalem. But just as the Prophet dealt with that in the preceding words: so now he passes to the spiritual Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, Galatians 4. To this, therefore, Assyria and other cities of the nations are referred. The prophecy of Zechariah 2 concerning Jerusalem being inhabited without walls, on account of the multitude of men and beasts, whose wall the Lord of hosts shall be, agrees with this passage. These are his words. By the borders of Judea are designated in the Prophetic manner the borders of the world from the fortified cities as far as the Euphrates, which is the border of Judea, which he further describes by its other borders also, from the western or great sea, from the eastern or dead sea, and from Mount Lebanon as far as Mount Sinai, that is, from the north to the south. See Joshua 1:4, Numbers 34. Tarnovius also acknowledges that these magnificent promises will be fulfilled for the most part only after this land has been in desolation, and thus under the New Testament.

Latin:

IN DIE ILLA ET VSQVE AD TE VENIET DE ASSVR] Ab Assyria ad te Cyrus veniet. Vide supra V. 6.

ET VSQVE AD CIVITATES MVNITAS] Ba- bylonem, Borsippa, & alias urbes firmissimas.

ET A CIVITATIBVS MVNITIS VSQVE AD FLVMEN] Flumen cum simpliciter ponitur est Euphra- tes. Sensus est: Cyrus totum Euphratem sui juris faciet: Euphrates ibit jam mollior undis.

ET AD MARE DE MARI] A mari Persico, in quod Euphrates illabitur, veniet ad mare Syriacum.

ET AD MONTEM DE MONTE] A Tauro mon- te ad Carmelum Syriæ.

Hæc jam contorta sunt. Nam primo Personæ ita mutantur: De illis,qui in conculcationem futuri erant, loquutus erat Prophetæ in tertia persona; oculi mei videbunt IN EAM. Hic vero compella- tio sit ejus, ad quem dirigitur oratio in secunda persona: Dies, ut ædificentur maceriæ tuæ. Non ergo hæc ædificatio de Chaldæa intelligenda, et- iamsi priora de Chaldæa egerent,quæ tamen potius de Edomæa sonant. Deinde simpliciter dicit Pro- pheta, dies ut ædificentur maceriæ; qua ergo pote- state Grotius hæc ita reddit : Longum erit tempus antequam ruinæ tuæ reparentur. Quæ fere con- trariam sententiam important. Porro haud ob- scure termini hic designati Judæis. Denique non comminationem hæc referunt, sed consolationem. Quapropter Hieronym. Remigius, Hugo, Isidor. Cla- rius cum Chaldæo, hæc de Jerusalem, ejusque re- paratione interpretantur,quibus Cornelius à Lapi- de, Christ. à Castro & alii accedunt. Chaldæus ita reddit: In tempore illo ædificabitur cœtus Israel, qui dispersus erat in captivitate; in tempore illo cessabunt deserta populorum : in tempore illo congregabuntur transmigrationes ab Assur, & à civitatibus fortitudi- nis ejus ab Armenia etiam grandi & à civitatibus mu- nitis & usq; ad Euphratem. & mare occidentale & montana montis. E nostris etiam B. Lutherus, & Chy- træus priora de restaurationeHierusalem : Dies in qua ædificabuntur maceriæ tuæ,accipi admittunt, sed ut sequentia de propagatione Evangelii in longinquas terras accipiantur: IN DIE ILLA LONGE PRO- PAGABITUR PRÆCEPTUM. Hoc exponit, in- quit Luth. noster, ædificationem de qua dixit, quod Jerusalem sic ædificabitur, ut propagetur in longin- quas terras præceptum. Est enim hic vocabulum (Chok) quod in secundo Psalmo, plane in eadem si- gnificatione usurpatur, ubi de regno Christi conciona- tur Propheta,& dicit. Quod Christus prædicabit præ- ceptum, nempe hoc, Dominus dixit ad me, Filius meus es tu. Hæc enim Evangelii vox est, quod Jesus ex Maria virgine natus, sit filius Dei, in quo pa- tri complacuit, ut omnis qui in eum credit, non pe- reat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Hoc præceptum Domini seu Doctrina hæc in Jerusalem & monte Zion incepit quidem, sicut supra quoque dictum est, Sed ibi non substitit. Invulgatum enim est in totum orbem terrarum, & hæc ipsa evulgatio fuit vera ædificatio civitatis Jerusalem, hoc est, regni Christi. Nam sic Christo magnum & infinitum regnum paratum est per verbum Evangelii, sicut Propheta etiam hoc ipsum clarius jam exponit, ut nihil opus sit peregrinas & ineptas sententias com- minisci, sed hic etiam antithesis observanda est. Non dicit de præcepto Mosi, quod id vulgandum sit in gentes, quod gentes circumcidendæ,ad sacra legalia & alios ritus adigendæ sint. Nam præce- ptum id mansit tantum in populo DEI, sed hoc præceptum de Filio audiendo, adorando, osculando, hoc dicit longe propagatum iri, à Mari ad mare, à flumine usq́; ad terminos terræ. Sicut etiam Christus hanc ipsam ob causam comparat Evange- lium fermento, quod totum mundum sit perva- surum. Item Fulmini, quod subito ab oriente in occidentem fertur,nec potest ulla humana vi im- pediri. IN DIE ILLA USQUE AD TE IBITUR AB ASSUR, ET CIVITATIBUS MUNITIS, ET A MUNITIONE USQUE AD FLUMEN, ET A MARI AD MARE, ET A MONTE AD MONTEM. Omitto nu- gas illas,an (Mazor) sicut septuaginta reddiderunt, sint duæ voces, & significetur Tyrus. An sit una vox, & significet munitionem! Retinet enim hic Pro- pheta usitatam phrasin, qua etiam alii Prophetæ usi sint, cum de Regno Christi loquuntur, sicut Ps. 72. Dominabitur à mari usq́; ad mare, & à flu- mine usq́; ad terminos terræ. Hunc locum quis non videt Micham voluisse imitari, sicut Zacha- riam quoque cap. 7. Loquetur pacem ad gentes, & dominium ejus à mari usq́; ad mare, & à flumine usq́; ad terminos terræ. Nihil igitur hic opus est disputare, quæ sint flumina, qui montes, quæ civi- tates munitæ, de quibus Propheta loquitur. Nam in genere & simpliciter hoc vult, quod verbum Ev- angelii spargetur in totum orbem terrarum. Sum- mam rei ita complexus est Chytræus: De resti- tutione Ecclesiæ Israel post eversionem ab Assyriis & Babyloniis factam, & inchoatione ac propagatione regni Christi per totum orbem terrarum, de vocatione gentium & Christo pastore ac Rege Ecclesiæ, supra in tertio loco secundi capitis, & in tribus prioribus locis quarti capitis, & tertio loco, quinti capitis bre- viter dictum est. Inde igitur ille ad præsens Mi- chææ vaticinium assumantur. Quod muros Jero- solymæ conculcatæ instauratum iri per propagationem præcepti, de quo Psalm. 2. dicitur, prædicabo præceptum : Dominus dixit ad me: Filius meus es tu. Postula à me, & dabo tibi Gentes hæreditatem tuam,& possessionem tuam terminos terræ: Oscula- ,,mini filium, beati omnes qui confidunt in eo, seu per ,,prædicationem Evangelii Christi toto orbe ter- ,,rarum sparsi, ad quem pastorem & regem hære- ,,ditatis suæ desolata & eversa terra & regno Judai- ,,co propter peccata sua, ex Assyriis & omnibus ,,locis ac gentibus orbis terrarum (Psal. LXXII. ,,Zach. IX. Dominabitur à mari ad mare, & à ,,flumine usœ ad terminos terræ) magna homi- ,,num multitudo conveniet. Quæ verbo Evan- ,,gelii in hoc mundi deserto copiose pascetur ac ,,defendetur, & majoribus ac præstantioribus bo- ,,nis, quam in eductione ex Ægypto, donabitur, ,,æterna liberatione, vita & gloria. Gentes et- ,,iam, abjecta omni suæ sapientiæ, fortitudinis & ,,cultuum fiducia, nec docebunt amplius ac præ- ,,dicabunt suas religiones & cultus, nec alios do- ,,centes audient, sed agnoscent peccata sua, & ma- ,,ledictionem iræ Dei & æternæ damnationis pro- ,,pter peccatum ipsius impositam: ideoque vero corde contremiscent, & peccare desinent, & vero timore DEI, omnia vitæ consilia & actiones ad normam voluntatis & verbi divini confirmabunt. Similiter Winckelmannus. Dies ut ædificetur) ad consolationem & exhilarationem piorum vatici- natur Propheta de reductione populi in terram ex captivitate Babylonica, atque inde Ecclesiæ ad gentes propagatione. Restitutionem Israelis in terram, confert cnm instauratione domus vel ci- vitatis collapsæ, sicut Hierusalem collapsa revera fuit reædificata. In die illa longe fiet lex) Vatici- nium de propagatione legis, hoc est, cœlestis do- ctrinæ inter Gentes, atque ita etiam Ecclesiæ dila- tatione & amplificatione, sicut 4. capite dictum est: Lex (Sion egredietur, & præceptum Domi- ni de Hierusalem. Longe fiet) id est, à terrena Hierusalem. Et usœ ad te veniet Assur? De ur- bis Jerusalem dilatatione usœ in Assyriam & alias civitates munitas gentium, imo usœ ad insulas, mon- tes & fines terræ, ut omnibus gentibus pateat ad eam accessus. Intelligunt quidem Judæi cæci hæc de terrenæ Hierusalem reædificatione. Sed sicut præcedentibus verbis Propheta de illa egit: ita jam transit ad spiritualem Hierusalem, quæ o- mnium nostrum mater est, Gal. 4. Ad hanc igi- tur Assur & aliæ civitates gentium referuntur. Convenit cum hoc loco vaticinium Zachariæ 2. de Jerusalem sine muris habitanda, præ multitudine, ho- minum & jumentorum, cujus murus igneus futurus sit Dominus exercituum. Hæc illi. Per terminos Judææ designantur more Prophetico termini mun- di à civitatibus munitis usœ ad Euphratem, qui est terminus Judææ, quam porro ab aliis quoque terminis suis describit à mari occidentali seu ma- gno, à mari trientali seu mortuo, & à monte Li- bano, usque ad montem Sina, id est à septen- trione ad meridiem. Vide Jos. I. 4. Num. IIX. Agnoscit etiam Tarnovius, promissiones has ma- gnificas maximam partem impletum iri demum, postquam terra hæc desolationi fuerit, adeoque sub N. Testamento.

## 7:13
Verse 13. AND THE LAND] Chaldaic. SHALL BE FOR A DESOLATION BECAUSE OF ITS INHABITANTS] With its inhabitants. The land shall be without cultivation, and the men without lands. It is a σύλληψις, for that word properly suits the land, and less properly suits the men. AND BECAUSE OF THE FRUIT OF THEIR THOUGHTS] In the Hebrew it is: and because of the fruit of their works: that is, because of the works which they previously brought forth, slaughters, rapines, impiety. Even if these things were said concerning the land of Chaldea, the former things are not therefore to be explained concerning the same: as is to be seen in Christoph. à Castro, and

Cornelius à Lapide, he paraphrases thus: And that land, which they (the Jews) have left, of the Chaldeans shall be desolate by the Medes and Persians, with its inhabitants, etc. Meanwhile, however, you, O Lord, shall feed your people. Osiander presents this connection: For their land shall be in desolation because of its wicked inhabitants, and because of the evil fruit of their thoughts, or their pursuits: that is, those nations shall not find a place at home where they may rest and be nourished, but because all things will be laid waste on account of their own sins, they shall flee to you, that they may be refreshed and preserved, lest they perish by famine.

Yet more to be approved is the exposition of Luther, which Winckelmann followed, because the destruction of the earthly Jerusalem and the devastation of Judea is predicted here, and that of Tarnovius: Meanwhile, lest the people hope for a worldly kingdom, he warns of the affliction that is to come, and lest they despair on account of it when it has already arrived. As above, ch. 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 5, 5, 6. For these magnificent promises will be fulfilled for the most part only after this land has been for a desolation, not because God pursues it with some absolute hatred, but because of its wicked inhabitants, and those especially given to idolatry, sup. 6, 16, because of the fruit of their actions, so that as they have sown, so they may reap, so that when they have brought forth bad fruits in the vineyard of the Lord, sub. v. 1, they may understand that they are justly cut off. These are the words of B. Luther: See the singular diligence of the Holy Spirit; he sees what the future wicked thoughts of the Synagogue will be, that it will hope for a bodily kingdom and will neglect the word of the Gospel. The Holy Spirit wishes to remedy in this place this error, which not only obscures the kingdom of Christ but simply removes it. Therefore, he adds concerning the land of the Jews that it shall be in desolation, that is, that the bodily kingdom together with the priesthood and the legal worship shall be entirely destroyed and laid waste. Therefore, what he said about the building of the walls is by no means to be referred to that bodily Jerusalem, but simply to the kingdom of Christ, which is spiritual and is built up through the word of the Gospel. Unless you follow this opinion, the Prophet will seem to contradict himself. For how is it consistent for Jerusalem to be built and the whole land to be laid waste? But these things do not conflict if you understand them concerning spiritual building.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ET TERRA] Chaldaica. ERIT IN DESOLATIONEM PROPTER HABI- TATORES SVOS] Cum habitatoribus suis. Terra erit si- ne cultu, & homines sine terris. Est σύλληψις nam ver- bum illud proprie terræ, minus proprie hominibus con- gruit. ET PROPTER FRVCTVM COGITATIONVM EORVM] In Hebræo est: & propter fructum operum eo- rum: id est, propter opera, quæ pridem ediderunt, cæ- des, rapinas, impietatem. Etiamsi hæc de terra Chaldæa dicerentur, prio- ra tamen de eadem idcirco non explicanda:quem- admodum videre est apud Christoph. à Castro, &

Cornel. à Lapide, ille ita παραφράζει: Et terra illa, quam reliquerunt (Iudæi) Chaldæorum desolabitur à Medis & Persis, cum ejus habitatoribus &c. Interim tamen tu ô Domine pasces populum tuum. Osiander hanc συνέχειαν exhibet: Etenim terra illorum erit in desolationem propter impios habitatores suos, & propter fructum malum cogitationum, seu studiorum eorum: id est, Non invenient illæ gentes domi locum, ubi acquiescant, & alantur, sed quia propter ipsorum peccata omnia erunt vastata, ad te confugient, ut recreèntur & conserventur, ne fame intereant.

Magis tamen probanda Lutheri ἔκθεσις: quam sequutus Winckelmannus, quod terrenæ Hierusalem excidium, & Judææ vastatio hic prædicatur, & Tarnovii: Interim ne populus speret regnum mundanum, afflictionem futuram, & ne propter eam, quando jam advenerit desperet, præmunit. ut supra c. 4. 8. 9. 10. 11. & 5, 5. 6. Nam maximam partem implebuntur demum hæ promissiones magnificæ, postquam fuerit hæc terra desolationi, non quod Deus absoluto quodam odio illam prosequatur, sed propter habitatores ipsius malos, & potissimum idololatriæ deditos sup. 6, 16. propter fructum actionum ipsorum, ut prout sementem fecerint, ita metant, ut cum in vinea Domini sub. v. 1. malos fructus protulerint, intelligant, se jure exscindi. B. Lutheri hæc sunt: Vide singularem diligentiam Spiritus Sancti, videt quæ sint futuræ cogitationes impiæ Synagogæ, quod speratura sit regnum corporale, & verbum Evangelii neglectura. Huic error, qui regnum Christi non solum obscurat, sed simpliciter tollit, vult Spiritus Sanctus hoc in loco mederi. Ideo addit de terra Iudæorum, quod erit in desolationem, hoc est, quod corporale regnum una cum sacerdotio & cultu legali totum destruetur ac vastabitur. Igitur quæ de ædificatione maceriarum dixit, neutiquam referenda sunt ad illam corporalem Jerusalem, sed simpliciter ad regnum Christi, quod est spirituale, & ædificatur per verbum Evangelii. Hanc sententiam nisi sequaris, Propheta sibi ipsi contradicere videbitur. Quomodo enim convenit ædificari Jerusalem, & totam terram vastari? Sic autem non pugnant hæc, si de ædificatione spirituali intelligas.

## 7:14
Verse 14.

FEED YOUR PEOPLE WITH YOUR ROD, THE FLOCK OF YOUR INHERITANCE] He returns to the prayers of the deported people, and by the rod he understands a shepherd's staff: for the comparison with the flock demands this. That staff signifies the special care of God for his people.

DWELLING ALONE IN THE FOREST IN THE MIDST OF CARMEL] Let (that people) dwell who had been solitary in the woods in the midst of the trees; the Hebrews call all fields Carmel: besides the fact that this name has especially adhered to a mountain in Syria, and to a place in Judea, where Nabal had lived.

THEY SHALL FEED IN BASHAN AND GILEAD ACCORDING TO THE DAYS OF OLD] After the fields, he comes to the pastures: and he says: let them feed in Bashan, etc.

Grotius thinks in a merely carnal way with the Jews, but here it was not fields, not pastures, not a shepherd's staff that were the concern of the Prophet, but spiritual pasture and governance, which is through the word, Ps. 23:4.

Although some, with Hugo, wish for God the Father and the Son to be speaking these things, they are more correctly held to be the prayer of the Church believing in the Gospel and seeing the ruin of the Synagogue, as Luther and Tarnovius do here. That not bodily but spiritual pasture is being looked to, a comparison with ch. 5:4 and other Prophets concerning the feeding of the Lord's people and concerning his one Shepherd, Is. 40, Ez. 34, etc., sufficiently teaches. Feed, he says, your people: therefore, the believers are looked to here, who are properly the people of the Lord, with the staff not of Moses, but yours, the word of your Gospel, and govern the flock of your possession (Ps. 2:8) because it dwells solitarily in the woods, in the midst of the trees, left by men, and moves among beasts and enemies, Mic. 5:8, so that they may securely feed in Bashan, which was a very fertile mountain, Am. 4, and Gilead, Obad. v. 19, Am. 1:3. Luther speaks beautifully about these. If you look for external appearance, the Synagogue had greater and more numerous testimonies than the Church of the New Testament. For here you do not see a temple, not circumcision, a sign impressed upon the body, not magnificent worship. Therefore, the Church of believers itself confesses in this place that it dwells alone in the field of the forest, where the Synagogue dwelt as if in a most cultivated city. For the things it has are without any appearance: The remission of sins and eternal life are proposed, but in the word only. The sign of this promise is Baptism, by which the skin is washed. Likewise the Supper of the Lord, spectacles truly ridiculous to the Gentiles and Jews, and indeed even to the Papists. Therefore, as far as this passage is concerned, the Church, which acknowledges itself to be the people and the flock of Christ's inheritance, prays that He would be willing to feed, and that with His rod. Here, first, another condition of this King is shown than that of the kings of the world. For these rule, they enjoy the labors of their subjects. But Christ, like a Shepherd, takes care of His subjects, He lays down His life for them. He does not flee from the Wolf, like hirelings, but He exposes Himself to the wolf, so that security may be provided for the sheep. He says expressly, Feed with your rod. For there is here the word (Schebet) which is in Ps. 23. Your rod and your staff they have comforted me. He does not, therefore, want the rod of Moses, which punishes wandering sheep. But that by which food is shown and Wolves are warded off. For the Church sees that it has need of the perpetual protection of the Word against Satan and his members. Nor is there any other remedy against spiritual wickedness and snares than the rod of the Shepherd, that is, the Word of the Gospel, which shows that the Prince of the world has been judged. The Prophet beautifully indicates this danger when he says that this flock dwells alone in the forest, where there is a great abundance of savage beasts, and therefore the danger to the Flock is greater. For it signifies that you, the Church, are surrounded on all sides by enemies, as Christ says: Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Yet in this danger, the consolations of the word are not lacking; therefore He says the forest is in Carmel, a fertile place. To this pertains what He adds: Let them feed in Bashan and Gilead. These were fertile pastures in the kingdom of Israel. But the Prophet also wished to show this rightly: that the remnants of Israel would also return to the kingdom of Christ. Prophets willingly use, when they speak of the kingdom of Christ, the likeness of the former kingdom, which was a type of the future one. Just as a little later Micah also uses the likeness of the exodus from Egypt. But these are not to be taken as referring to a bodily restoration, as Jerome, and after him Lyra, does. These are allegorical, and signify a great abundance of teachers and of the word: These are those joyful pastures of Bashan and Gilead in this kingdom, which the sheep of Christ desire and seek.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

PASCE POPULUM TUUM IN VIRGA TUA, GREGEM HÆREDITATIS TUÆ] Redit ad preces populi deportati, & per virgam, pedum pastorale intelligit: exigit enim id comparatio cum pecore. Id pedum curam Dei peculiarem pro populo suo significat.

HABITANTES SOLOS IN SALTU IN MEDIO CARMELI] Habitet (populus ille) qui solitarius in sylvis fuerat in medio arborum, arva omnia Hebræi כרמל vocant: præter quod eximie id nomen adhæsit monti in Syria, & loco in Judæa, ubi habitaverat Nabal.

PASCENTUR BASAN ET GALAAD JVXTA DIES ANTIQVOS] Post arva venit ad pascua: & ait: pascant in Basan, &c.

Mere carnalia cum Judæis sapit Grotius, at hic non arva, non pascua, non pedum pastorale curæ erant Prophetæ, sed pastura spiritualis, & gubernatio, quæ per verbum sit Ps. XXIII. 4.

Quamquam vero hæc Deum Patrem & Filium loqui nonnulli cum Hugone velint, rectius tamen habentur pro oratione Ecclesiæ credentis Evangelio, & videntis ruinam Synagogæ, ut hic Lutherus & Tarnovius. Non corporalem, sed spiritualem pasturam respici, collatio cum c. V. 4. & aliis Prophetis de pascendo populo Domini & de Pastore unico ejusdem Es. XL. Ez. XXXIV. &c. satis docet. Pasce, inquit, populum tuum: Spectantur ergo hic credentes, qui proprie populus Domini sunt, cum pedo non Mosis, sed tuo, tui Evangelii verbo, & guberna gregem possessionis tuæ (Ps. II. 8.) quia habitat solitarie in sylvis, in medio arvorum ab hominibus relictus, inter bestias & hostes versatur Mich. V. 8. factu, ut secure depascant Basan, qui erat mons val- de fertilis Am. IV. & Gilhad. Obad. v. 19. Am. I. 3. Pulchre de his Lutherus. Si externam speciem se- quaris, Synagoga majora testimonia & plura habuit, quam Ecclesia Novi Testamenti. Hic enim non tem- plum, non circumcisionem, signum corpori impressum, non magnificos cultus vides. Itaq; ipsa Ecclesia cre- dentium hoc loco fatetur, se habitare solam in campo sylvæ, ubi Synagoga ceu in cultissima urbe habitavit. Nam quæ habet, sine omni specie sunt: Remissio „peccatorum & vita æterna proponuntur, sed „in verbo tantum. Hujus promissionis signum „est Baptismus, quo cutis abluitur. Item Cœ- „na Domini, spectacula vere ridicula gentibus „& Judæis, imo etiam Papistis. Quod igitur ad „hunc locum attinet, Ecclesia, quæ se agnoscit „populum & gregem hæreditatis Christi esse, o- „rat ut velit pascere, idque in virga sua. Hic pri- „mum alia conditio hujus Regis ostenditur, „quam est Regum mundi. Hi enim dominan- „tur, fruuntur subditorum laboribus. At Chri- „stus, sicut Pastor, suorum subditorum curam ge- „rit, ponit animam suam pro eis. Non fugit Lu- „pum, ut Mercenarii, sed se objicit lupo, ut pa- „retur securitas ovibus. Diserte autem dicit, Pasce „in tua virga. Est enim hic vocabulum (Schebet) „quod est in Ps. 23. Virga tua & baculus tuus ipsa „me consolata sunt. Non igitur vult virgam Mo- „si, quæ aberrantes oves castigat. Sed qua mon- „stratur pabulum & arcentur Lupi. Videt e- „nim Ecclesia sibi perpetuo præsidio Verbi esse „opus contra Satanam, & ejus membra. Nec con- „tra spirituales nequitias & insidias aliud reme- „dium est, quam virga Pastoris, hoc est, Verbum „Evangelii, quod ostendit, Principem mundi es- „se judicatum. Hoc periculum pulchre indicat „Propheta, cum dicit, Hunc gregem solum habi- „tare in sylva, ubi magna immanium ferarum copia „est, & ideo majus Gregis periculum est. Signi- „ficat enim te Ecclesiam undique cinctam hosti- „bus, sicut Christus dicit: Ecce ego mitto vos, sicut „oves in medio luporum. Non tamen in hoc pe- „riculo desunt consolationes verbi, ideo dicit Syl- „vam esse in Carmelo, loco fertili. Huc pertinet, „quod addit: Pascantur in Basan & Gilead. „Fuerunt hæc fertilia pascua in regno Israel. Vo- „luit autem Propheta recte hoc etiam ostendere; „Redituras ad regnum Christi etiam reliquias Is- „rael. Libenter autem utuntur Prophetæ, cum „de regno Christi loquuntur, similitudine prioris „regni, quod typus fuit futuri. Sicut paulopost „Micha etiam utitur similitudine exitus ex Ægy- „pto. Sed non ideo hæc de corporali restitutio- „ne accipienda sunt, sicut Hieronymus, & post „eum Lyra facit. Allegorica hæc sunt, & signifi- „cant magnam copiam doctorum & verbi: Hæc „sunt illa læta pascua Basan & Gilead in hoc regno, „quæ oves Christi desiderant & petunt.

## 7:15
Vers. 15.

ACCORDING TO THE DAYS OF YOUR COMING OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT I WILL SHOW HIM MARVELOUS THINGS

These are, as are many things among the Prophets, ἀποτοθῆτα. For here God is introduced responding to the prayers of the people, I will show, He says, wonders against the Chaldeans, such as once against the Egyptians, when you were coming out of Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

SECVNDVM DIES EGRESSIONIS TUÆ DE TERRA ÆGYPTI OSTENDAM EI MIRABILIA]

Sunt hæc, ut multa apud Prophetas ἀποτοθῆτα. Hic enim Deus ad populi preces respondens inducitur, mira, inquit, in Chaldæos designabo, qualia olim in Ægyptios, cum de Ægypto exiretis.

## 7:16
Vers. 16.

THE GENTILES SHALL SEE AND BE CONFOUNDED OVER ALL THEIR MIGHT. The Gentiles (allies of the Chaldeans) shall be affected with shame because all their strength was so suddenly destroyed.

THEY SHALL LAY THEIR HAND UPON THEIR MOUTH] They will press their lip with a finger. THEIR EARS SHALL BE DEAF] They will become deaf; they will be so dismayed that they will not hear what is said.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

VIDEBVNT GENTES ET CONFVNDENTVR SVPER OMNI FORTITVDINE SVA] Pudore afficien- tur gentes (sociæ Chaldæorum) ob ita subito omne robur suum destructum.

PONENT MANUM SUPER OS] Digito com- pescent labellum. AURES EORUM SURDÆ ERUNT] Obsurde- scent; adeo erunt consternati, ut quæ dicentur, non ex- audiant.

## 7:17
Ver. 17. THEY SHALL LICK THE DUST LIKE SERPENTS, LIKE THE REPTILES OF THE EARTH] Here the Jews speak again. They shall lick the dust, that is, they will fall to the ground for fear. Regarding the matter, see Matt. XVII, 6; regarding the expression, Ps. LXXII. 9, Is. XLI. 23.

THEY SHALL BE TROUBLED IN THEIR HOUSES] They will be moved out of their strongholds. That is, they will be forced to go out of their fortified places and surrender them to the Persians.

THEY SHALL DREAD THE LORD OUR GOD, AND SHALL FEAR THEE] Namely, when they understand what was predicted by the Prophets and always believed by the Jews.

He does not explain what those great wonders are, such as were designated against the Egyptians or the Chaldeans. Nor indeed can any such things be shown after the return from Babylon. This argument is urged by the blessed Luther, along with other interpreters, against Lyra and the Jews, whom Grotius has followed here. Lyra refers these to the people brought back from captivity. Just as the Jews also do, but who does not see that the people of the law after the captivity saw none of those glories and miracles which the first Israel saw in Egypt? Therefore, Daniel does indeed promise that the walls of Jerusalem will be built, but in a time of distress, that is, not without great dangers and adversities. What the Lord says, therefore, 'I will show him wonders, as when he came out of Egypt,' certainly cannot be understood of the people of the law and a bodily kingdom; these things pertain to the kingdom of Christ, through whom a far more excellent and better liberation was made than that which was in Egypt. For Christ did not liberate his Church from the tyranny of men: He liberated it from death, sins, and the tyranny of the Devil. These are the spiritual and eternal enemies of the human race, nor can they be conquered by any human force. Therefore, it was necessary for the Son of God to become the enemy of these enemies. He alone takes away the sins of the world, as the Baptist speaks, and makes satisfaction for them, so that those who believe in him may have at once the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. Is this not an infinitely greater possession than that land of Canaan, granted to the people of the law? But why does he call (Niptaoth) wonders or marvelous things? Those were rather the wonders of the old people, when the sea divided itself, when the Jordan held back its course while the people crossed, when the Sun receded for some hours' space, etc. But just as the liberation in the New Testament was in many ways greater and more excellent than that from Egypt, so also the miracles are in infinitely many ways greater. For what can be called more wonderful than that the Son of God should put on the flesh of man and be born of a virgin? What is more stupendous than when the Son of God engages with death and Satan, allows himself to be conquered, exposes his own life to these enemies, and while he is conquered, conquers? Thus, it is the supreme miracle that Christ, a man dead on the cross, should rise again on the third day from death and the closed sepulcher, and with flesh henceforth immortal, ascend to heaven and sit at the right hand of God. What can be said, nay, even thought, similar to these miracles? But these are not the only ones in the kingdom of Christ, for the Prophet also commemorates others. 'The nations shall see and be confounded with all their strength, they shall lay their hand upon their mouth, and shall stop their ears: They shall lick the dust like a serpent, and like the worms of the earth they shall tremble in their hiding places, they shall dread before the Lord our God, and shall fear thee.' Lyra twists himself in various ways while he accommodates these things to the people restored from captivity, but to one looking at the New Testament and the preaching of the Gospel, all things are easy and straightforward. Christ miraculously liberates the remnant of the Jews. These miracles, when they are preached among

the nations, they themselves also approach the Church. This is also deservedly held in the place of the greatest miracle. For first they are confounded with all their strength, that is: They acknowledge that their religion, worship, and all the trust which they placed in idols is in vain. For this is properly to be confounded, to see that you have been deceived, and that you have placed your hope in things of naught, nay, that you have offended the true God most greatly when you thought that you were worshiping him most holily. This confusion is followed by the fact that they cover their mouths with their hands, that is, that they will no longer preach their idolatrous cults, but will rejoice that they have been removed from speech and memory. The third is that they even stop their ears, that is, that not only do they not teach idolatry themselves, but they cannot even endure to hear others teaching it any longer. The fourth is that they shall lick the dust like a serpent. By this figure the Prophet signifies not only external humiliation, but also the cause of humiliation, namely, the acknowledgment of sin and the sense of the curse on account of sin. Therefore, he also uses the similitude of the serpent because of the curse of man's sin in Genesis 3. Furthermore, a notable image of this sense is proposed in the adulterer David, when he is rebuked by the Prophet. What he adds about worms also pertains to these terrors of conscience. As the Prophet himself explains: 'They shall dread before the Lord our God, and shall fear thee.' This fear is truly the beginning of wisdom and salvation. For those who are terrified in this manner, and dread, they most greedily hear Christ teaching about the remission of sins and eternal life, and with violence they take the kingdom of God, Matt. XI. Thus far the blessed Luther, whom the blessed Chytreus, Winkelmannus, and Tarnovius follow.

The Papists set forth some things concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, but how jejunely, can be established by the example of Cornelius à Lapide, who explained them, saying as it were: Just as I miraculously led the Jews out of Egypt through so many plagues and portents brought forth by Moses, so likewise will I lead their descendants out of Babylon through many wonders, nay, miracles. For first, I will reconcile the idolaters Cyrus and Darius to them, so that they may free them from Babylon. Second, I will be present with them on the journey and the return, so that the little ones, women, old men, and the weak may complete that journey, though long and troublesome, without harm, happy and eager, just as their fathers completed it in the desert when they proceeded from Egypt into Canaan. Third, when they have arrived in Judea, I will curb the neighboring hostile and envious nations, so that they may not be able to harm them, nor hinder the building of Jerusalem and the temple. Thus He. But that the things which are predicted here are far more restricted, he would be a fool who does not understand.

Latin:

Vers. 17. LINGENT PULVEREM SICUT SERPEN- TES, VELUT REPTILIA TERRÆ] Hic iterum lo- quuntur Judæi. Lingent pulverem, id est, in terram conci- dent præ metu. De re vide Matth. XVII, 6. de locutio- ne Ps. LXXII. 9. Es. XLI. 23.

PERTURBABUNTUR IN ÆDIBUS SUIS] Com- movebuntur è claustris suis. Id est, cogentur exire de locis munitis & ea Persis, tradere.

DOMINUM DEUM NOSTRUM FORMIDA- BUNT, ET TIMEBUNT TE] Nempe cum intelligent à Prophetis prædicta, & à Judæis semper credita.

Non explicat, quænam illa mira tanta qua- lia, in Ægyptios, vel in Chaldæos designata sunt. Neque vero ulla talia ostendi possunt post redi- tum à Babylone. Quod argumentum urget B. Lutherus cum aliis Interpp. adversus Lyram, & Judæos, quos sequutus hic est Grotius. Lyra hæc refert ad populum reductum ex captivitate. Sicut Judæi quoq;, sed quis non videt populum legis post captivitatem nihil istarum gloriarum & miraculorum vidisse, quæ vidit primus Israel in Ægypto: itaq; pro- mittit quidem Daniel muros Jerusalem ædificandos, sed in angustia temporis, hoc est, non sine magnis pe- riculis & adversitatibus: Quod igitur Dominus di- cit ostendam ei mirabilia, sicut cum ex Ægypto egrederetur, profecto non potest intelligi de populo legis & corporali regno, ad Christi regnum hæc perti- nent, per quem liberatio longe præstantior & melior fa- cta est, quam illa, quæ in Ægypto fuit. Non enim liberavit Christus Ecclesiam suam à tyrannide homi- num: A morte, peccatis, tyrannide Diaboli liberavit. Hi spirituales & æterni hostes generis humani sunt, nec ulla humana vi possint vinci. Ideo DEI filium oportuit hostium fieri. Is solus mundi pec- cata, sicut Baptista loquitur, tollit, & pro iis satis- facit, ut credentes in eum, habeant simul remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum Sanctum, & vitam æternam. Hæc an non infinitis modis major possessio est, quam illa terra Canaan, populo legis concessa? Sed cur „vocat (Niptaoth) mirabilia seu miranda? illa po- „tius veteris populi fuerunt mirabilia, cum mare „se divisit, cum Jordanis cursu cohibuit, dum „transiret populus, cum Sol ad aliquot horarum „spatia recederet &c. Sed sicut liberatio in novo te- „stamento multis modis major fuit, & præstantior, „quam illa ex Ægypto, sic etiam miracula infinitis „modis sunt majora. Quid enim potest dici ad- „mirabilius, quam Dei Filium induere carnem ho- „minis, & ex virgine nasci? Quid magis stupen- „dum est, quam cum Filius Dei cum morte & Sa- „tana congreditur, se vinci sinit, suam vitam hosti- „bus his objicit, & dum vincitur vincit? Sic „summum miraculum est, Christum hominem „in cruce mortuum tertia die ex morte & se- „pulcro clauso resurgere, & cum carne posthac „immortali ascendere cælum & sedere ad dextram „Dei. Hisce miraculis quid simile dici, imo co- „gitari potest? sed hæc non sola sunt in regno „Christi. nam Propheta etiam alia commemo- „rat. Videbunt gentes & confundentur cum omni „fortitudine sua, ponent manum super os, & obtura- „bunt aures: Lingent pulverem sicut serpens, & si- „cut vermes terræ contremiscent in latibulis suis, co- „ram Domino Deo nostro pavebunt, & timebunt „te. Lyra varie se torquet, dum hæc ad populum „ex captivitate restitutum accommodat, sed re- „spicienti ad novum testamentum & Evangelii „prædicationem, omnia sunt facilia & expedita. „Christus liberat reliquias Judæorum miracu- „lose. Hæc miracula, cum per Apostolos inter

„gentes prædicantur, accedunt ipsæ quoque ad „Ecclesiam. Id quod etiam maximi miraculi lo- „co merito habetur. Primum enim confundun- „tur cum omni sua fortitudine, hoc est: Agnoscunt „religionem, cultus, & fiduciam suam omnem, „quam in idolis posuerunt, frustra esse. Hoc „enim proprie est confundi, videre quod dece- „ptus sis, & quod spem tuam posueris in res ni- „hili, imo quod verum Deum tuum offenderis „maxime, cum existimasti, te eum sanctissime co- „lere. Hanc confusionem sequitur, quod ora ve- „lant manibus, hoc est, quod non amplius prædi- „cabunt suos idololatricos cultus, sed gaudebunt „ex sermone & memoria omnium sublatos esse. „Tertium est, quod etiam aures obturant, hoc est, „quod non solum ipsi non doceant idololatriam, „sed ne alios quidem docentes amplius audire su- „stineant. Quartum est, quod pulverem lingent „sicut serpens. Hac figura significat Propheta „non solum externam humiliationem, sed etiam „humiliationis causam, nempe agnitionem pec- „cati, & sensum maledictionis propter pecca- „tum. Ideo etiam utitur similitudine serpentis „propter peccatum hominis maledictæ Genes. 3. „Porro hujus sensus insignis imago in adultero „Davide proposita est, cum à Propheta corripi- „tur. Quod de vermibus addit, etiam ad istos „conscientiæ terrores pertinet. Sicut Propheta „ipse se exponit: Pavebunt coram Domino Deo „nostro, & timebunt te. Hic timor vere est ini- „tium sapientiæ & salutis. Qui enim ad hunc „modum territi sunt, & pavent, hi Christum „docentem de remissione peccatorum, & vita æ- „terna avidissime audiunt, & cum violentia ra- „piunt regnum Dei Matth. XI. Hactenus B. Lu- therus, quem sequuntur B. Chytreus, Winkelman- nus, Tarnovius.

Pontificii de liberatione è captivitate Babylo- nica nonnulla exponunt, sed quam jejune, Cor- nelii à Lapide exemplo, qui ea explicuit, constare potest. q. d. Sicut Iudæos ex Ægypto per tot plagas & portenta à Mose edita miraculose eduxi, ita pariter eorum posteros ex Babylone per multa mira, imo mi- racula educam. Nam primo conciliabo eis Cyrum & Darium idololatras, ut eos Babylone liberent. Secundo in itinere & reditu eis adero, ut parvuli, fœ- minæ, senes, & debiles, sine noxa læti & alacres iter illud, licet longum & molestum conficiant, uti confecerunt patres eorum in deserto, cum ex Ægypto pergerent in Canaan. Tertio cum in Iudæam appu- lerint, gentes vicinas hostiles & invidas frænabo, ne eis nocere, neve fabricam Jerusalem & templi impe- dire queant. Hæc Ille. At longe angustiora esse, quæ hic prædicuntur, bardus sit, qui non intelligat.

## 7:18
Verse 18. WHO TAKEST AWAY INIQUITY] That is, the punishment, namely from those who convert, thou takest away at the time appointed by thee.

AND PASSEST OVER SIN] In the Hebrew: Thou passest over sin. That is, in Greek ὑπερβαίνων ἀσεβείας. By a similitude taken from a traveler, who passes by things he does not wish to look into.

OF THE REMNANT OF THINE HERITAGE] That is, of thy people, he blessed the remnant, as Virgil: The remnants of the Danaans and of cruel Achilles.

HE WILL NOT RETAIN HIS ANGER FOR EVER] In the Hebrew: He hath not retained his anger for ever, that is, he does not show himself implacable.

BECAUSE HE DELIGHTETH IN MERCY] For he loves to do good. Thus the Chaldean here: that is proper and natural to him; punishment and torments are extorted from him. And as often as he is forced to be cruel, he grieves.

To take away iniquity is not only to take away the punishment of iniquity, but primarily the guilt, which punishment follows as a companion: therefore the pardon of guilt and punishment is noted. But he loves to use the word of taking away

Sp. S. because it is completely taken away, so that guilt does not come into the sight of God: it is taken away, however, not so that it is not present, but so that it is not imputed, according to the well-worn rule of Augustine. Castrius acknowledges this. God, he says, by his mercy takes away guilt, so that once it is removed he simultaneously takes away the punishment. Regarding the Hebrew word, Winkelmannus is correct with B. Luther: In Hebrew Nose, taking away, lifting, the expression being taken from those who take a burden from others by which they were pressed, just as the Poet says: I will relieve you of this burden: And our iniquities are like a burden pressing upon us, nay, weighing us down into hell, unless it is taken from us. David uses the same verb in Ps. 32. Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven. But God takes our sins from us, and imputes them to the Son, who is the Lamb of God, taking away the sins of the world John 1. Theodoretus has it thus: This is certainly admirable, that he not only forgives, but also drives away sins from his memory, and delivers them into oblivion as if into the deep. For explaining this, the wonderful Micah said: He will submerge our sins: and all our sins will be cast into the depth of the sea: just as that which is cast into the depth of the sea does not exist at all: so, he says, oblivion will utterly overwhelm our sins because of the covenants made with our ancestors.

Latin:

Vers. 18. QUI AUFERS INIQUITATEM] Id est, pœnam, ab iis scilicet qui se convertunt, aufers tempore à te constituto.

ET TRANSIS PECCATUM] In Hebræo: Tran- sis super peccatum. Id est, Græce ὑπερβαίνων ἀσεβείας. Si- militudine à viatore sumta, qui quæ introspicere non vult, præterit.

RELIQUIARUM HEREDITATIS TUÆ] Id est, populi tui, benedixit reliquiarum, ut Virgilius. Relliquias Danaum atque immitis Achilli.

NON IMMITTET ULTRA FUROREM SUUM] In Hebræo: Non retinuit in perpetuum furorem suum id est, non ostendit se implacabilem.

QUONIAM VOLENS MISERICORDIAM EST] Amat enim benefacere. Ita hic Chaldæus: id ei proprium est ac naturale; pœna & supplicia ei extorquentur. Et quoties sævus cogitur esse dolet.

Auferre iniquitatem non tantum est pœnam iniquitatis auferre, sed imprimis culpam, quam pœna comes sequitur: condonatio igitur culpæ & pœnæ notatur. Sed ablationis voce uti amat

Sp. S. quia prorsus aufertur, ut non veniat culpa in conspectum Dei: aufertur autem non ut non insit, sed non imputetur, secundum regulam tritam Augustini. Agnoscit id Castrius. Deus, inquit, sua misericordia aufert culpam, ut ea remota simul auferat pœnam. De voce Ebræa recte cum B. Luthero Winkelmannus: In Hebr. Nose,tollens, levans, sumta locutione ab iis, qui onus ab aliis tollunt, quo premebantur, quemadmodum Poeta dicit: Ego hoc te fasce levabo: Atque iniquitates nostræ sunt instar oneris prementis nos, imo deprimentis in infernum, nisi tollatur a nobis. Eodem verbo utitur David Pf.32. Beati, quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates. Tollit autem Deus peccata nostra a nobis, & imputat ea filio, qui est agnus Dei, tollens peccata mundi Joh. 1. Theodoretus ita habet: Hoc certe admirabile, quod non solum ignoscit, sed etiam memoria sua pellit peccata, & tanquam in profundum in oblivionem tradit. Hoc enim explicans mirabilis Micheas dixit: Demerget peccata nostra: & projicientur in profundum maris omnia peccata nostra: quemadmodum id, quod in profundum maris abjicitur, penitus non extat: sic inquit, peccata nostra funditus oblivio obruet propter pactiones cum majoribus nostris factas.

## 7:19
Vers. 19. HE WILL RETURN, AND WILL HAVE MERCY ON US] That is, he will again have mercy on us: as often of old. A known Hebraism.

HE WILL LAY DOWN OUR INIQUITIES] In the Hebrew it is: He will subject, or, he will place under his feet: like those things which we do not wish to look upon.

AND WILL CAST ALL OUR SINS INTO THE DEPTH OF THE SEA] In the Hebrew: Of them, i.e., of each one of the people. Things for which no care is taken are said to be cast into the sea by both Greeks and Latins. Horace: - - - I will hand over sadness and fears to the wanton winds to carry into the Cretan sea.
