Also tröstet er nach seinem Namen (denn Nahum heist Consolator, auf deutsch ein Tröster) das Volk Gottes/ wie ihre Feinde die Assyrier, sollen widerum verstöret werden. Am Ende des 1. C. lautet er auch wie Es. 52, 7. von den guten Predigern die Fried und Heil verkündigen auf den Bergen/ und heist Juda frölich feyren. Und wiewol dasselbige verstanden mag werden von der Zeit Ezechia, nach Sennacherib/ da Juda errettet ward/ und für den König Sennache- rib blib: doch ist es eine gemeine Weissagung auch auf Christum/ daß in Juda bleiben solt die gute Botschafft/ und der fröliche Gottesdienst/ durch Gottes Wort ge- lehret und bekräfftiget/ daher er ja billich ein rechter Nahum heist. Sic B. Wigandus in h. l. p. 373. Ex- hortatio & Prophetia, ut Ecclesia ad gaudium ma- gnum se paret. Etsi autem gratissimum fuit nun- cium de Sennacherib trucidato à propriis liberis, ta- men ulterius Propheta prospicit, nempe quod ista Ju- dæ protectio & conservatio fiat potissimum propter exhibitionem Messiæ, & quod inde Evangelium, quod adfert pacem cordium, emanaturum sit in orbem ter- rarum universum. Ecce (congratulationem quan- dam hic continet, in re læta & ardua. Super montes, Ef. 52. eadem verba extant. Ideo consonant Pro phetæ in re omnium amplissima. Est autem Prophe- tia de Evangelio spargendo, per totum terrarum or- bem. Pacem (Effectus pro causa. Nam Evangelii effe- ctus est pax conscientiæ cum Deo. Celebra) Exhorta- tio. Ergo para te ad gaudium. Non inconcinne præsentem locum ad prædicationem Evangeli per Apostolos factam referri fatetur etiam B. Win- ckel. in h. l. Nec abnuunt Belgici Interp. convenire hæc spirituali redemtioni per Christum factæ.

NON ADJICIET ULTRA UT PERTRANSEAT IN TE BELIAL] Non ultra ad te perveniet ille nequam, Assyrius, qui Deum despexit.

Vers. eod. UNIVERSUS INTERIIT] Accisus est. Gloria Imperii ablata est.

Alii volunt non de Imperii gloria ablata, sed de excisione ipsius Assyrii, ejusdemque universi agi, si- quidem & exercitus ejus universus excisus, & ipse à filiis suis interfectus sit, ac posteritas etiam ejus excindenda, neque amplius ipse Judæam pertran- siturus sit. Ita prædicetur tum spiritualis felicitas Judæ, tum liberatio etiam ejusdem ab externo hoste. Quamvis enim Belialis nomen de Satana quoque intelligere liceat, quod is ultra non habeat potesta- tem in fideles, quia universus occisus est per Chri- stum: non repugnat tamen præcedentium expli- cationi de Evangelio pacis hæc de Assyrii interitu & excisione prædictio, ut nempe utrumque bene- ficium Judææ hic promittatur, & annunciationis Evangelicæ suo tempore sequuturæ, & liberationis à manu Assyrii, de cujus excisione antea actum e- rat. Tarnovius progredi vult Prophetam à terrenis ad cœlestia, à corporalibus ad spiritualia more Pro- phetarum: Si lætus de interitu hostis Sennacheribi est nuncius, quanto erit lætior Evangelii de CHRISTO nuncius, & de Diaboli reliquorumque infernalium & spiritualium inimicorum subjectione per Christum parta? Coccejus iterum hic novi quid commen- tus est; nimirum per Belialem intelligi Nebucadneza- rem de quo in textu nec vola est nec vestigium.

## 2:1 Argument
PART II. A fuller explanation of the Assyrian destruction. CHAP. II. A vivid description of the slaughter and destruction of the Ninevites and the Assyrian kingdom. He depicts the manner of the Prophet, how they are to be utterly cut off by Nebuchadnezzar, whose arming, the occupation of the city, the opening of the city gates by the waters, the captivity of the Queen and the virgins, the plundering of all precious things, and the destruction of the dwelling of the lions. By his own false strength, he shall be despoiled of his bronze.

Ver. 1. HE ASCENDS. WHO SCATTERS BEFORE THEE] Now he explains more pointedly the manner in which that change, of which he has treated, is about to happen. A scatterer ascends against thee, namely of thy walls, the Chaldean.

WHO GUARDS THE SIEGE] Besieged thy fortifications.

CONTEMPLATE THE WAY] The Chaldean interpreter took this also as an infinitive, to watch the ways. He comes to place watchmen on all the ways, so that no one may penetrate to him.

Ludov. de Dieu translates the first words thus: A Scatterer ascends against thy face, saying: let us besiege the fortification, and he notes moreover this paraphrase: The Scatterer has vanished before thee, the fortification is besieged, that is, the most fortified city of Nineveh (where the Assyrian scatterer held his seat) contemplate the way (namely, that which leads to Nineveh, you will easily perceive its distress, and thence) Strengthen the loins, fortify the strength greatly. But let his own observations be seen here. Coccejus understands Cyrus by the scatterer; but this prophecy was not directed against the Babylonians, whom Cyrus invaded, but against Nineveh, as witnessed by the ἄγγελος, & c. III. 8.

STRENGTHEN THE LOINS] That is, gird thyself with a sword, See II Sam. XX. 8. 2 Kings IV. 28.

STRENGTHEN THE MIGHT GREATLY] Increase the forces as much as possible; as if he were to say, all things are in vain. You have a similar passage in Is. VIII. 9. 10.

Latin:

PARS. II. Uberior excidii Assyriaci explicatio. CAP. II. Hypotyposis cladis & interitus Ninivitarum & regni Assyriorum. Depingit Prophetæ rationem qui funditus excindendi sint per Nebucadnezarem, cujus armatura, urbis occupatio, civitatis portis per aquas apertis Reginæ & virginum captivatio quorumvis pretiosorum de- prædatio, & habitaculi leonum destructio. Robore falsa suo, rapto spoliabitur ære.

Vers. 1. ASCENDIT. QUI DISPERGAT CORAM TE] Jam designatius modum eum, quo eventura est ea, de qua egit, mutatio explicat. Ascendit adversum te dissipator, murorum scilicet tuorum, Chaldæus.

QUI CUSTODIAT OBSIDIONEM] Obsessum munimenta tua.

CONTEMPLARE VIAM] Chaldæus interpres sumsit & hoc infinitive, speculatum vias. Venit ut in o- mnibus viis speculas ponat, nequis ad se penetret.

Ludov. de Dieu ita vertit prima verba: Ascendit Dissipator contra faciem tuam, dicens: obsideamus munitionem, notatque insuper hanc metaphrasin: Evanuit Dissipator coram te, obsessa est munitio, id est, munitissima civitas Ninive (ubi Assyrius dissipator sedem tenebat) speculare viam (nempe quæ ducit Ninivem, percipies facile ejus angustiam, atque in- de) Lumbos robora, fortifica robur valde. Sed videan- tur hic ipsæ ejus animadversiones. Coccejus per dissipatorem intelligit Cyrum; sed Prophetia hæc non contra Babylonios, quos Cyrus invasit, sed con- tra Niniven directa fuit teste ἄγγελος, & c. III. 8.

CONFORTA LUMBOS] Id est, accingere gladio, Vide II. Sam. XX. 8. 2. Reg. IV. 28.

ROBORA VIRTUTEM VALDE] Auge copias quamplu- rimum; quasi dicat, frustra omnia. Simile habes Es.IIX. 9. 10.

## 2:2
Ver. 2. BECAUSE THE LORD HAS RETURNED THE PRIDE OF JACOB, AS THE PRIDE OF ISRAEL] God returns to (the Assyrian) that pride which he himself exercised upon Jacob and Israel, by deporting the ten tribes and besieging Jerusalem.

BECAUSE THE WASTERS HAVE SCATTERED THEM] In the Hebrew: Because (the Assyrians) by emptying have emptied them: they have clearly snatched everything from the Judeans and Israelites,

So indeed the Chaldean, Jerome, and Hugo. Others, however, understand the wasters to be the enemies of the Assyrians, the Chaldeans, along with Theodoret, Theophylact, and B. Luther. Which opinion seems more convenient.

AND THEIR BRANCHES THEY HAVE CORRUPTED] Towns and villages. Thus the Chaldean interpreter.

B. Tarnovius interprets it thus: Jehovah will restore the excellence of Jacob, just as also the excellence of Israel, although the devastators or plunderers, the Assyrians, have emptied them with their rapine, and have corrupted their branches, that is, their towns and villages. His commentary deserves to be compared here. Nor are the Chaldean, Vatablus, Montanus, and B. Gesner far from that sense. We also add the translation and explanation of Lud. de Dieu: For the Lord is restoring the excellence of Jacob, as the excellence of Israel, that is, just as God himself is the 'excellence of Israel, so he cannot suffer that excellence to be perpetually exiled from Jacob or from Israel. 'Therefore he is even now restoring the excellence of Jacob.' Let the reader choose from these interpretations which he wishes.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QUIA REDDIDIT DOMINUS SUPERBIAM JACOB, SICUT SUPERBIAM ISRAEL] Reponit Deus, (Assyrio) illam superbiam, quam ipse in Jacobo & Israele exercuit, deportando decem tribus & obsidendo Hieroso- lyma.

QUIA VASTATORES DISSIPAVERUNT EOS] In Hebræo: Quia (Assyrii) vacuefaciendo vacuefecerunt eos: plane omnia eripuere Judæis & Israelitis,

Ita quidem Chald. Hieron. & Hugo. Alii ta- men vastatores hostes Assyriorum Chaldæos in- telligunt cum Theod. Theophyl. & B. Luther. Quæ sententia convenientio, videtur.

ET PROPAGINES EORUM CORRUPERUNT] Oppida & vicos. Ita Chaldæus interpres.

B. Tarnovius ita interpretatur: reducet Iehova excellentiam Iacobi, sicut & excellentiam Israelis, quamvis evacuaverint eos rapinis suis evacuatores seu populatores Assyrii, palmites eorum, h. e. oppida ac pagos corruperint. Cujus commentarius hic con- ferri meretur. Nec alieni ab eo sensu sunt Chal- dæus, Vatabl. Montanus, B. Gesnerus. Addimus etiam Lud. de Dieu translationem & explicatio- nem: Nam reducit Dominus excellentiam Iacobi, tan- quam excellentia Israelis, id est, sicut Deus ipse est „excellentia Israelis, ita non potest pati, ut excel- „lentia perpetuo à Jaçobo sive ab Israele exulet. „Itaque jamjam reducit excellentiam Jacobi. Eli- „gat lector ex his Interpretationibus quam velit.

## 2:3
Ver. 3. THE SHIELD OF HIS MIGHTY MEN IS MADE RED] It is red, namely from blood, he describes the Chaldeans.

THE MEN OF THE ARMY ARE IN SCARLET] Soldiers clothed in scarlet. We learn also from Herodotus that the peoples of the East made much use of such a cloak.

THE CHARIOTS ARE AS FLAMING TORCHES IN THE DAY OF HIS PREPARATION] Their chariots flash like fire from lamps at the time of the expedition, namely, being entirely sparkling.

AND THE CYPRESS SPEARS ARE BRANDISHED] The fir trees are poisoned. That is, weapons made of fir. He refers to the Scythians, who used to dip their arrows in viper's venom and human blood, by which, as Pliny relates in XI. 53, an irremediable crime, death is brought about instantly by a light touch.

Latin:

Vers. 3. CLTPEUS FORTIUM EJUS IGNITUS] Ru- bet, nempe à sanguine, Chaldæos describit.

VIRI EXERCITUS IN COCCINEIS] Milites coc- cinati. Tali sago multum usos orientis populos ex Hero- doto etiam discimus.

IGNEÆ HABENÆ CURRUS IN DIE PRÆPA- RATIONIS EJUS] Igne quasi lampadarum coruscant cur- rus eorum tempore expeditionis, nempe scintillantisbus totis.

ET AGITATORES CONSOPITI SUNT] Abietes venenatæ sunt. Id est, tela ex abiete. A Scythis ismos vene- rat, qui sagittas tingebant viperino semine, & humano sanguine, quo irremediabili scelere mortem illico adferri levi tactu tradit Plinius XI. 53.

## 2:4
Ver. 4. THEY ARE DISTURBED IN THE WAYS, THE CHARIOTS ARE DASHED AGAINST EACH OTHER IN THE STREETS] The chariots will roar in the ways, they will rattle through the streets, namely with arms, which the Chaldean interpreter wishes to be understood here.

THEIR APPEARANCE IS LIKE LAMPS] Burning eyes.

AS LIGHTNINGS RUNNING TO AND FRO] They shatter everything in their way like lightning. Thus Lucan and Plutarch compare Alexander to a thunderbolt.

Latin:

Vers. 4. IN ITINERIBUS CONTURBATI SUNT, QUADRIGÆ COLLISÆ SUNT IN PLATEIS] In viis perstrepent currus, concrepabunt per plateas, nempe armis, quod subaudiri hic vult Chaldæus interpres.

ADSPECTUS EORUM QUASI LAMPADES] Oculi ardentes.

QUASI FULGURA DISCURRENTIA] Quasi fulgura confringunt obvia omnia. Sic fulmini Alexandrum comparant Lucanus & Plutarchus.

## 2:5
Ver. 5. HE SHALL REMEMBER HIS MIGHTY MEN] The Babylonian king will choose every strongest man for the assault.

THEY SHALL STUMBLE IN THEIR WAYS] Each one will want to be first in the assault, so that in their haste they will overturn one another.

THEY SHALL HASTILY CLIMB ITS WALLS] While they hasten to the wall.

AND A SHIELD SHALL BE PREPARED] A tortoise, by which those covered undermine the walls.

Latin:

Vers. 5. RECORDABITUR FORTIUM SUORUM] rex Babylonius ad oppugnationem fortissimum quemque diliget.

RUENT IN ITINERIBUS SUIS] Quisque pri- mus esse volet in opugnatione, ita ut festinantes alter alte- rum evertant.

VELOCITER ASCENDENT MUROS EJUS] Dum properant ad murum.

ET PRÆPARABITUR UMBRACULUM] Testudo, qua tecti subruant mœnia.

## 2:6
Ver. 6. THE GATES OF THE RIVERS ARE OPENED] The bridges of the rivers are broken down. So the Chaldean Interpreter.

THE TEMPLE IS RAZED TO THE GROUND] The same Chaldean: The palace is liquefied, that is, those who were in the palace were terrified.

We prefer here the Tarnovian Commentary: The gates of the rivers i.e. of the Tigris, which on account of its magnitude and excellence, according to a custom familiar to the Hebrews, is called in the plural number. See Exercitat. Biblic. pag. 41. & 69. & 179. shall be opened, and the palace itself, whatever it be, as much of the idols as of the king, shall be dissolved, collapsed by the injury of the waters, so that the Prophet signifies (which the event also proved) that the enemies would enter the city through that part which the Tigris flows past. For historians relate that at that very time, when Nineveh was being besieged by the Chaldeans, the Tigris, swollen by frequent rains and filled with an unusual abundance of waters, threw down the walls of the city neighboring its bank for twenty stadia, which opportunity they seizing, took possession of the city. See at least Diodorus Siculus book 3 of the Bibliotheca, chapter 7.

Latin:

Vers. 6. PORTÆ FLUVIORUM APERTÆ SUNT] Pontes fluminum dissoluti sunt. Ita Chaldæus Interpres.

TEMPLUM AD SOLUM DIRUTUM] Idem Chaldæus: Palatium liquefactum, id est, perterriti qui in palatio erant.

Præferimus hic Tarnovianum Commenta- rium: Portæ fluminum i. e. Tygridis, qui propter magnitudinem & excellentiam, more Hebræis u- sitato in plurali appellatur numero. Vide Exerci- tat. Biblic. pag. 41. & 69. & 179. aperientur, & ipsum palatium, quodcunque tam idolorum, quam regis, dissolvetur aquarum injuria collapsum, ut significet Propheta (quod etiam eventus comprobavit) ho- stes ingressuros urbem per eam partem, quam Ty- gris præterlabitur. Narrant enim historici, quod eo ipso tempore, quo à Chaldæis obsidebatur Ni- nive, crebris imbribus auctus Tygris insolita aqua- rum repletus copia vicinos ripæ suæ urbis muros ad stadia viginti dejecerit, quam occasionem ca- ptantes illi, urbe potiti sunt. Vide saltem Dio- dor. Siculum libr. 3. Bibliothecæ cap. 7.

## 2:7
Ver. 7. AND THE SOLDIER IS TAKEN CAPTIVE] Nisibis is led away captive: it is ordered to ascend. Nisibis was written by the Assyrians נצב, as we learn from Stephanus, who interprets it as a heap. To this name is added here a demonstrative article, as if you were to say: That Nisibis, so much praised, is ordered to ascend, that is, the people led away toward Babylon.

AND HER MAIDSERVANTS WERE DRIVEN] Understand driven here as being led in the manner of cattle: for in this sense Jerome often uses that word: understand by maidservants the small towns and villages: but by them, those who had dwelt in them.

GROANING LIKE DOVES] The sense is well expressed in the Hebrew: according to the voice of the dove.

MURMURING IN THEIR HEARTS] Striking upon their hearts: i.e. beating their breasts with their palms.

Dievius translates these things thus: And it is decreed (and it is already ordered, or and it stands already) she shall be led into captivity, she shall be deported, and her maidservants shall lead her with a voice similar to doves, drumming upon their hearts: He took the word והצב not for a proper name, but for a verb, and it is decreed. The Chaldean paraphrast and other Masters of the Hebrews R. Solomon, R. Abraham Ezra, R. David Kimchi, Pagninus and Vatablus think it is the name of the Queen of Nineveh, Hutsab, i.e. CONSISTING, because she stood by the King, as it is said in Ps. XLV, the Queen stood at thy right hand: for so the Chaldean. And Hutsab the Queen, who was sitting in the inner seats of the palace, was held) she went out into captivity. And behold her maidservants led after her walked groaning. Others metaphorically understand by the Queen standing by, Nineveh the metropolis itself, and by the maidservants, the lesser cities. Jerome, Remigius, Haymo, Rupert, interpreted it as a stationary soldier. See more other explanations in Christ. a Castro and Cornel. a Lapide. To us the interpretation of the Hebrews seems not inconvenient: because mention is added of the maidservants, who look to the Queen herself, which also was approved by B. Tarnovius.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET MILES CAPTIVUS ABDUCTUS EST] Nisibis captiva abducitur: jubetur adscendere. Nisibis scri- bebatur Assyriis נצב, ut ex Stephano discimus, qui cu- mulum interpretatur. Huic nomini additur hic articulus demonstrativus, quasi dicas: Illa Nisibis adeo prædicata ju- betur adscendere, id est, Babylonem versus abducta plebs.

ET ANCILLÆ EJUS MINABANTUR] Mina- bantur hic intellige, agentur pecorum ritu: nam hoc sensu id verbum sæpe usurpat Hieronymus: ancillas intellige op- pidula & vicos: per ea autem ipsos, qui in iis habitaverant.

GEMENTES UT COLUMBÆ] Sensus bene ex- pressus in Hebræo: juxta vocem columbæ.

MURMURANTES IN CORDIBUS SUIS] Per- cutientes super corda sua : i. e. tundentes pectora palmis.

Dievius ita haec vertit : Et constitutum est (ende het is al bestelt, vel Ende het staet der al) abduce- tur in captivitatem, deportabitur, & ancillae ejus de- ducent eam voce simili columbarum, timpanisantes super corda sua : Vocem והצב non pro nomine proprio, sed pro verbo habuit, & constitutum est. Chaldaeus paraphrastes & alii Ebraeorum Magistri R. Salomo, R. Abraham Ezra, R. David Kimchi, Pagninus & Vatablus putant esse nomen Reginae Ni- nives Hutsab, q. CONSISTENS, quod adstaret Regi, uti Ps. XLV. dicitur, adstitit Regina a dextris tuis : sic enim Chaldaeus. Et Hutsab Regina, quae sedebat in penitioribus palatii sedibus contineba- tur) in captivitatem exibat. Et ecce ancillae ejus ab- ductae post eam incedebant gementes. Alii metapho- rice per Reginam adstantem Niniven ipsam me- tropolin, per ancillas minores urbes intelligunt. Hieronymus, Remigius, Haymo, Rupertus, militem stationarium interpretati sunt. Vid. plures aliae explicationes apud Christ. a Castro & Cornel. a La- pid. Nobis non incommoda videtur Ebraeorum interpretatio: quia mentio adjicitur ancillarum, quae respiciunt ipsam Reginam, quae etiam proba- ta est B. Tarnovio.

## 2:8
Ver. 8. NINEVEH IS LIKE A POOL OF WATERS, HER WATERS] The Chaldean interpreter: Nineveh was of old a pool of waters: that is, populous beyond measure; for waters, are peoples.

BUT THEY FLED] The waters themselves, that is, the peoples. מים is masculine for the Hebrews.

STAND, STAND, AND THERE IS NO ONE WHO TURNS BACK] ἔνευσις. Even if it is shouted to them, stand, stand, there is no one who looks back. For that is מפנה.

Latin:

Vers. 8. NINIVE QUASI PISCINA AQUARUM, AQUAE EJUS] Chaldaeus interpres : Ninive antiquitus fuit piscina aquarum : id est, supra modum populosa ; nam a- quae, populi.

IPSI VERO FUGERUNT] Ipsae aquae, id est, po- puli. מים Hebraeis Masculinum.

STATE, STATE, ET NON EST QUI REVER- TETUR] ἔνευσις. Etiamsi clametur eis, state, state, nemo est qui respiciat. Id enim מפנה.

## 2:9
Ver. 9, PLUNDER THE SILVER, PLUNDER THE GOLD] Now the Prophet addresses the Babylonians as if the matter were present. Similar to Isa. 26. 27.

AND THERE IS NO END OF THE RICHES] Of which (gold & silver) there is no end in weighing. Formerly coins were accustomed to be weighed, whence come impensae (expenditures) & expensae (expenses).

FROM ALL DESIRABLE VESSELS] In the Hebrew: magnificence (namely of the riches of Nineveh) above all precious vessels.

Latin:

Vers. 9, DIRIPITE ARGENTUM, DIRIPITE AU- RUM] Jam Babylonios quasi in re praesente alloquitur Propheta. Simile Esa. L. 26. 27.

ET NON EST FINIS DIVITIARUM] Quorum (auri & argenti) nullus est finis in ponderando. Olim num- mi pendi solebant, unde impensae & expensae.

EX OMNIBUS VASIS DESIDERABILIBUS ]In Hebraeo : magnificentia (nempe opum Ninives) supra o- mnia vasa pretiosa.

## 2:10
Ver. 10. IT IS DISSIPATED, IT IS TORN, AND RENT ASUNDER] Nineveh has been emptied, voided, lacerated, with the royal riches plundered.

AND A MELTING HEART] Because the heart has been liquefied: that is, there was no spirit in them, which is confirmed by the following signs.

AND THE DISSOLUTION OF THE KNEES] It befalls them, namely, Dan. V. 6.

AND FAINTNESS IN ALL LOINS] Isa. XLV. 1. Ezek. XXIX. 7.

THAT THE FACES OF ALL OF THEM ARE LIKE THE BLACKNESS OF A POT] Joel II. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DISSIPATA EST, EST SCISSA, ET DI- LACERATA] Vacuefacta, inanita, lacerata est Ninive, dire- ptis opibus regiis.

ET COR TABESCENS] Quia cor colliquatum est : id est, nihil ipsis fuit animi, quod sequentibus signis confirmatur.

ET DISSOLUTIO GENICULORUM] Obvenit scilicet illis Dan. V. 6.

ET DEFECTIO IN CUNCTIS RENIBUS] Esa. XLV. 1. Ezech. XXIX. 7.

UT FACIES OMNIUM EORUM SICUT NI- GREDO OLLAE] Joel. II. 6.

## 2:11
Ver. 11. WHERE IS THE HABITATION OF THE LIONS] Where now is that palace of the Assyrians, full of the spoils of so many nations, like a den of lions?

THE LION'S CUB, AND THERE IS NO ONE WHO FRIGHTENS] A Hebraism, for the lion's cub, whom no one frightens.

Latin:

Vers. 11. UBI EST HABITACULUM LEONUM] Ubi nunc regia illa Assyriorum, plena tot gentiumspoliis, ut leonum spelunca?

CATVLUS LEONIS, ET NON EST QUI EXTERREAT] Hebraismus, pro catulus leonis, quem ne- mo exterreat.

## 2:12
Ver. 12. THE LION TOOK SUFFICIENTLY FOR HIS CUBS] The lion who would take sufficient.

AND HE KILLED WITH HIS LIONS] That he might strangle (cattle for food) with his lions.

AND HE FILLED] That he might fill.

Latin:

Vers. 12. LEO CEPIT SUFFICIENTER CATV- LIS SVIS] Leo qui caperet sufficientia.

ET NECAVIT LAENIS SVIS] Ut strangularet (pecudes in cibum) leanis suis.

ET IMPLEVIT] Impleret.

## 2:13
V. 13. BEHOLD I AM AGAINST THEE] At last I have come against thee.

AND I WILL BURN UP THY CHARIOTS EVEN UNTO SMOKE] I will burn up thy chariots even unto smoke, that is to say, the royal ones.

---- Here were his arms, here was his chariot.

AND THE SWORD SHALL DEVOUR THY YOUNG LIONS] It devours: for he speaks as if the matter were present. Young lions, that is, soldiers in the surrounding fortresses.

AND I WILL CUT OFF THY PREY FROM THE EARTH] I will ensure that you no longer ravage any lands. The Chaldean Interpreter draws this to the trade which passed from Nineveh to Babylon.

AND THE VOICE OF THY MESSENGERS SHALL NO MORE BE HEARD] Of those bearing edicts. See Micah 7. 11.

Latin:

V. 13. ECCE EGO AD TE] Tandem ad te ego veni.

ET SVCCENDAM VSQVE AD FVMVM QVA- DRIGAS TVAS] Incendi ad fumum usque currus tuos, regios scilicet.

---- Hic illius arma Hic currus fuit.

ET LEVNCVLOS TVOS COMEDET GLA- DIVS] Comedit : nam loquitur ut in re praesente. Leuncu- los, id est, milites in castellis circumjectis.

ET EXTERMINABO DE TERRA PRAEDAM TVAM] Efficiam ne ullas terras populeris amplius. Chal- daeus Interpres ad commercia hoc trahit, quae a Ninive Babylonem transiere.

ET NON AVDIETVR VLTRA VOX NVN- TIORVM TVORVM] Edicta ferentium. Vid. Mich. 7. 11.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

A severe accusation of the Ninevites, interspersed with threats, and a solid refutation of vain confidence. Woe is intimated to Nineveh for lies and depredations, with the terrible arming of the enemy and the miserable slaughter of the city denounced; and because of abominable fornications and incantations, with the seduction of various nations, it is predicted that her nakedness is to be uncovered to the nations, and that she is to be visited with contempt and abomination, along with the exultation of her enemies; and the vanity of the confidence of her defenders and allies is taught by the example of conquered No-Ammon of the Egyptians; at the same time, confidence in the strength of soldiers, the firmness of walls, easy repair, the wealth of citizens, the care of nobles, and the protection of princes is confounded. The bloody, rapacious, and lying city shall perish by fire.

Ver. 1. WOE TO THE BLOODY CITY] Woe to the bloodthirsty city. Now God explains the causes for the empire taken away from the Assyrians. FULL OF ALL LIES AND ROBBERY] Totally full of lying and extortion. THE PREY DEPARTETH NOT] From which prey has not departed: that is, which has always lived from plunder. Ver. 2. THE NOISE OF A WHIP] The sound of a lash, namely, of one driving horses, comes upon you. AND THE NOISE OF THE RATTLING OF THE WHEELS] The sound of a wheel spinning around. AND OF THE PRANCING HORSES] Of the quadruped. For 'the hoof shakes the crumbling field with a quadrupedal sound.' AND OF THE JUMPING CHARIOTS] From the Greek ἀναβράσσοντος. The Chaldean expressed the Hebrew more correctly by 'leaping.' Ver. 3. THE HORSEMAN LIFTETH UP BOTH THE BRIGHT SWORD AND THE GLITTERING SPEAR] And the horseman lifting up both the edge of the sword and the lightning of the spear. Grotius's interpretation does not agree with the distinction of the accents, which Lud. de Dieu rightly observed here. I do not construe, he says, מעלה with the following words, which I see Pagninus and Junius have done, but just as it is distinguished by the Reviab accent, so I translate it distinctly: 'the horseman taking away, and the flame of the sword, and the flashing of the spear,' etc. Just as in the preceding verse he had threatened the sound of the whip, and the sound of the motion of the wheels, etc., so in this verse he threatens horsemen taking away, then the flaming sword and the flashing spear, etc. Moreover, a horseman taking away is one who carries off much booty, and makes it as it were ascend with him. For just as in Kal עלה (ascend) is often used for to go away, to depart, so in Hiphil העלה is often used for to take away, to remove, as Ps. 102:25, אל תעלני 'do not take me away in the midst of my days.' AND A MULTITUDE OF SLAIN] As is wont to happen in wars. AND A GREAT NUMBER OF CARCASSES] And a mass of corpses. AND THERE IS NONE END OF THEIR CORPSES] So that there is no end of the bodies laid low. AND THEY SHALL STUMBLE UPON THEIR CORPSES] But they shall stumble upon the bodies of their own people. Lucan: 'The first fell into the river, the highest upon the bodies.' Ver. 4. BECAUSE OF THE MULTITUDE OF THE WHOREDOMS OF THE WELL-FAVOURED HARLOT] He calls idolatrous cults whoredoms, especially those of kings like Ninus and Belus, concerning whom see Curtius. AND MISTRESS OF WITCHCRAFTS] Powerful in magical arts. Theocritus, Pharmaceutria: 'Such evil drugs I declare I keep, mistress, for the Assyrian, having learned them from a stranger.' THAT SELLETH NATIONS THROUGH HER WHOREDOMS] That enslaved nations by her fornications: that is, idolatries, because the most accepted method of transferring ownership is sale; therefore, whatever is enslaved to anything, even a thing, is said to be sold to it, as is evident in I Kings 21:25, Judith 7:14. For an example of what is said here, see II Kings 16:10. AND FAMILIES THROUGH HER WITCHCRAFTS] That is, she enslaved nations by her magical arts: she caused them to learn them, as appears from the passage of Theocritus already produced. Ver. 5. BEHOLD, I AM AGAINST THEE] Therefore I come to you, as above in 2:13. AND I WILL DISCOVER THY SKIRTS UPON THY FACE] I cast your hems (that is, the lower garment) over your face: as in Jer. 13:26, I treat you not as a matron, but as a harlot. See Isa. 47:2, 3; Ezek. 16:37.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Severa Ninivitarum inspersa commina- tione accusatio & solida fiduciæ vanæ confutatio. Væ intimatur Ninivi ob mendacia & deprædationes, denunciata armatura hostis terribili & strage urbis miserabili & ob fornicationes & incantationes a- bominabiles cum gentibus variarum seductione nuditatem ejus gentibus detegendam eamǫ con- temtu & abominatione, cum hostium tripudio, afficiendam esse prædicitur, ac vanitas fiduciæ pro- pugnatorum & confœderatorum exemplo devictæ No Ægyptiorum docetur; simul & fiducia in mi- litīs fortitudine, murorum firmitudine, facili reparatione, civium opulentia, optimatum cura, principum tutela confunditur. Sanguinolenta, rapax, & mendax igne peribit.

Vers. 1. VÆ CIVITAS SANGUINUM] Væ civitati sangui- nariæ. Jam causas Deus exponit adempti Assyriis imperii. UNIVERSA MENDACII DILACERATIONE PLENA] Toti plena mendacio & extorsione. NON RECEDET A TE RAPINA] A qua non recessit rapina: id est, quæ semper ex rapto vixit. Vers. 2. VOX FLAGELLI] Sonitus flagri, nempe e- quos agitantis, tibi supervenit. ET VOX IMPETUS ROTÆ] Sonitus circumvoli- tantis rotæ. ET EQUI FREMENTIS] Quadrupedantis. nam Quadrupedante putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum. ET QUADRIGÆ FERVENTIS] Ex Græco ἀνα- βράσσοντος. Chaldæus Hebræum rectius expressit per sub sultantis. Vers. 3. ET EQUITIS ASCENDENTIS, ET MI- CANTIS GLADII, ET FULGURANTIS HASTÆ] Et equitis attollentis, tum aciem gladii tum fulgur hastæ. NOn convenit Grotii interpretatio accen- tuum distinctioni, quam recte hīc observa- vit Lud. de Dieu. Non construo, inquit, מעלה cum sequentibus, quod Pagninum & Iunium fecisse video, sed sicut per accentum Reviab distinguitur, sic distin- cte verto, eques auferens & flamma gladii & corusca- tio hastæ &c. sicut vers. præcedenti minatus fuerat sonitum scuticæ, & sonitum motus rotarum &c. sic hoc versu minatur equites auferentes, deinde flam- mantem gladium & coruscantem hastam &c. Est autem eques auferens qui prædam multam subdu- cit, & quasi ascendere secum facit. Sicut enim in Kal עלה ascendit sæpe usurpatur pro abire, rece- dere, sic in Hiphil העלה sæpe pro auferre, tolle- re, ut Ps. 102, 25. אל תעלני ne aufer me in medio dierum meorum. ET MULTITUDINES INTERFECTÆ] Ut in bellis fieri solet. ET GRAVIS RUINÆ] Et molis cadaverum. NEC EST FINIS CADAVERUM] Ita ut finis non sit corporum stratorum. ET CORRUENT IN CORPORIBUS SUIS] Sed corruant in corpora suorum. Lucanus: In fluuium primi cecidere, in corpora summi. Vers. 4. PROPTER MULTITUDINEM FORNI- CATIONUM MERETRICIS SPECIOSÆ ET GRA- TÆ] Fornicationes vocat idololatricos cultus, regum maxime ut Nini & Beli, de quibus Curtium vide. ET HABENTIS MALEFICIA] Pollentis artibus magicis. Theocritus Pharmaceutria: Τοῖα οἷέν κίςα κακὰ φάρμακα Φαμὶ φυλάσσειν Ασσυρίω, δέσποινα, παρὰ ξείνοιο μαθοῖσα. QUÆ VENDIDIT GENTES IN FORNICA- TIONIBUS SUIS] Quæ mancipavit gentes scortationibus suis: Id est, idololatriis, quia receptissimus transferendæ proprietatis modus venditio; ideo quicquid alicui etiam rei mancipatur ei vendi dicitur, ut patet I. Reg. XXI. 25. Judith. VII. 14. Exemplum ejus quod hic dicitur vid. II. Reg. XVI. 10. ET FAMILIAS IN MALEFICIIS SUIS] Id est, mancipavit nationes artibus suis magicis: fecit ut eas ad- discerent, ut apparet ex producto jam Theocriti loco. Vers. 5. ECCE EGO AD TE] Ideo ad te venio ut supra II. 13. ET REVELABO PUDENDA TUA IN FACIE TUA] Fimbrias tuas, (id est, imam vestem) rejicio super faciem tuam : ut Jer. XIII. 26. tracto te non ut matronam, sed ut meretricem. Vide Esai XLVII. 2. 3. Ezech. XV. 37.

## 3:6
Ver. 6.

AND I WILL CAST ABOMINABLE FILTH UPON THEE] Dung. AND WILL MAKE THEE VILE] Into a spectacle, εἰς παράδειγμα, the Greeks: this is what others would say, 'I will make you a public show.'

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ET PROJICIAM SUPER TE ABOMINATIO- NES] Stercora. ET PONAM TE IN EXEMPLUM] In spectacu- lum, εἰς παράδειγμα, Graeci : hoc est, quod alii dicerent ἐκθεατρίσω σε.

## 3:7
Ver. 7. NINEVEH IS LAID WASTE] She is despoiled. WHO WILL BEMOAN HER?] In the Hebrew and Chaldean: will condole. That was wont to be signified by a bowed head. WHENCE SHALL I SEEK COMFORTERS FOR THEE?] As if he were to say, I shall find them nowhere: for you have offended all peoples in your prosperous affairs.

Latin:

Vers. 7. VASTATA EST NINIVE] Spoliata est. QUIS COMMOVEBIT SUPER TE CAPUT] In Hebraeo, & Chaldaeo : condolebit. Id autem significari dejecto capite solebat. UNDE QUAERAM CONSOLATOREM TIBI] Quasi dicat, nusquam inveniam : omnes enim populos offendisti in rebus tuis secundis.

## 3:8
Ver. 8. ART THOU BETTER] Why would you be better? Why would your condition be better? THAN POPULOUS NO] Not the nurse of peoples, which was in Pharos, near which Alexandria was later founded, whose name is placed here, as also in Jer. 46:25, by prolepsis. THAT WAS SITUATE AMONG THE RIVERS, THAT HAD THE WATERS ROUND ABOUT IT] Plutarch in the description of that place: 'For it is a strip of land having a breadth proportionate to the isthmus, separating a large lake and the sea, ending in a great harbor.' Homer: 'Then there is an island in the surging sea before Egypt, which they call Pharos.' WHOSE RAMPART WAS THE SEA] From goods brought by sea. AND HER WALL WAS FROM THE SEA] For cities situated in the sea and by great rivers are difficult to besiege.

Latin:

Vers. 8. NUNQUID MELIOR ES) Cur melior esses ? cur tua conditio esset melior ? ALEXANDRIA POPULORUM] Non nutrici po- pulorum, quae fuit in Pharo, apud quam postea condita Alexandria, cujus nomen hic, ut & Jerem. XLVI. 25. per πρόληψιν positum est. QUAE HABITAT IN FLUMINIBUS, AQUAE IN CIRCUITU EJUS] Plutarchus in ejus loci descriptio- ne : ταινία γάρ ἐστιν ἰσθμῷ πλάτος ἔχοντι σύμμετρον ἐπιεικῶς διέργουσα λίμνην τε πολλὴν καὶ θάλασσαν ἐν λιμένι μεγάλῳ τε- λευτῶσαν. Homerus : Νῆσος ἔπειτά τίς ἐστι πολυκλύστῳ ἐνὶ πόντῳ Αἰγύπτου προπάροιθε, Φάρον δέ ἑκικλήσκουσι. CUJUS DIVITIAE MARE] Ex mercibus mari advectis. AQUAE MURI EJUS] Difficiles enim oppugnatu urbes in mari & magnis amnibus sitae.

## 3:9
Ver. 9.

ETHIOPIA WAS HER STRENGTH] That is, her wealth, through goods carried by the Nile. AND EGYPT] From the head to the shore. AND IT WAS INFINITE] The commerce of that city had no end. PUT AND LUBIM WERE THY HELPERS] A poetic expression, for the speech turns from the third person to the second by apostrophe, then again to the third. What is Africa here is פוט in the Hebrew: that word signifies the Moors; but the Libyans are the Cyrenaicans and Marmaricans closer to Egypt. All these peoples had increased the wealth of that city.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

AETHIOPIA FORTITUDO EJUS] Id est, opu- lentia ejus, per merces Nilo ferente devectas. ET AEGYPTUS] A capite ad littus. ET NON EST FINIS] Non haestetere ejus urbis commercia. AFRICA ET LIBYES FUERUNT IN AUXILIO TUO] Locutio Poetica, nam a tertia persona ad secundam κατ᾽ ἀποστροφὴν, inde iterum ad tertiam sermo se vertit. Quod hic est Africa in Hebraeo est פוט. ea vox Mauros significat: Lybies vero sunt Cyrenaici & Marmarici Ae- gypto propiores. hi omnes populi auxerant urbis illius divitias.

## 3:10
Vers. 10. BUT SHE HERSELF ALSO WAS LED INTO TRANSMIGRATION INTO CAPTIVITY] Not only exiles, but also slaves were made of her citizens, namely by the Ethiopians, whose King Sabaco invaded Egypt and placed strong garrisons there, before the times of Psammetichus, as witnessed by Herodotus in Euterpe. AND UPON HER NOBLES THEY CAST LOTS] The Ethiopians did this concerning the Egyptian captives. We have noted that custom elsewhere. Let that of Euripides be added: Πολλοῖς δὲ κωκυτοῖσιν αἰχμαλωτίδων Βοᾷ Σκαμάνδρου δεσπότας κληρουμένων. AND ALL HER GREAT MEN WERE BOUND IN FETTERS]. They were bound with fetters.

Others wish for this to be held not as history, but as a prophecy concerning the subversion of No, that is to say: Do not trust, O Nineveh, in your strength and fortifications, by which you will not be delivered from the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, since even No, stronger than you and more fortified, will not deliver herself, for she too is to be destroyed. Thus Jerome, Theodoret, Remigius, Haymo, Albert the Great, Rupert, Hugh, Lyra, Dionysius, Castrius, Cornelius, Tarnovius, and others, also Cocceius, who indeed by the city of No, which he wishes to be called the city of Ammon because its idol was Amon, understands not Alexandria but Thebes, which he notes from Strabo to have been the metropolis of all Egypt, and observes that No among the LXX is explained as διόσπολιν, the city of Jupiter (which appellation is attributed to Thebes in Eustathius on Dionysius and Strabo, book 17). However, the explanation of Grotius does not seem to be disapproved, provided that the words of the Prophet sound not concerning the subversion of No or Alexandria (which finally happened under Nebuchadnezzar) but concerning the leading away into captivity, and the comparison with Nineveh does not seem to be extended further than that No, even though the approach to it was most difficult, and it was the most fortified and wealthiest, was nevertheless led away into captivity, and lots were cast upon her nobles, and all her nobles were bound with fetters. Nor are those things to be despised which follow here in Grotius, which I am pleased to subjoin.

Latin:

Vers. 10. SED ET IPSA IN TRANSMIGRATIONEM DUCTA EST IN CAPTIVITATEM] Non tantum ex- ules, sed & servi facti sunt cives ejus, nempe per Aethio- pas, quorum Rex Sabaco Aegyptum invasit & valida ibi praesidia posuit, ante Psammetichi tempora, teste Hero- doto in Euterpe. ET SUPER INCLYTOS EJUS MISERUNT SOR- TEM] Aethiopes hoc fecere de captivis Aegyptiis. Nota- vimus alibi eum morem. Accedat illud Euripidis : Πολλοῖς δὲ κωκυτοῖσιν αἰχμαλωτίδων Βοᾷ Σκαμάνδρου δεσπότας κληρουμένων. ET OMNES OPTIMATES EJUS CONFIXI SUNT IN COMPEDIBUS]. Constricti sunt compedibus.

Alii non historiam, sed prophetiam hic haberi volunt de subversione No, q. d. Ne fidas o Ninive virtute tua, & munitionibus, quibus non erueris de manibus Nabuchodonosoris, siquidem & No for- tior te, & magis munita non se eruet, nam & ea quo- que destruenda est. Ita Hieronym. Theodoret. Re- migius, Haymo, Albertus M. Rupertus, Hugo, Lyra, Dionysius, Castrius, Cornelius, Tarnovius, alii, etiam Coccejus, qui vero per urbem No, quam urbem Ammonis dici vult, quod idolum ejus fuerit Amon, non Alexandriam sed Thebas intelligit, quas totius Aegypti fuisse metropolin e Strabone notat, & Ez. XXX. 14. 15. No apud LXX. exponi διόσπολιν Iovis urbem, (quae appellatio Thebis tributa apud Eu- stathium ad Dionys. & Strabon. l. 17.) observat. Non videtur autem improbanda Grotii explicatio, si- quidem non de subversione No vel Alexandriae (quae demum sub Nebucadnezare facta) sed de traductione in captivitatem verba Prophetae sonent, neque ulterius videatur extendenda comparatio cum Ninive, quam quod No, etsi difficillimus ad eam accessus, eademque munitissima & ditis- sima fuerit, in captivitatem tamen abducta fuerit, & super inclutos ejus sors projecta, & omnes opti- mates ejus constricti fuerint compedibus. Nec contemnenda, quæ porro hic sequuntur apud Grotium, quæ subjicere placet.

## 3:11
Ver. 11. AND THOU THEREFORE SHALT BE DRUNKEN] Thou also, Nineveh, shalt be void of counsel, as drunkards are wont to be, Jer. 25, 16. 27.

AND THOU SHALT SEEK STRENGTH BECAUSE OF THE ENEMY] Thou shalt ask for safety from the enemy, namely by surrender.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET TU ERGO INEBRIABERIS] Tu quoque Ninive inops eris consilii ut esse solent ebrii, Jer. 25, 16.27.

ET TU QUÆRES AUXILIUM AB INIMICO] Salutem ab hoste posces, deditione scilicet.

## 3:12
Ver. 12. ALL THY STRONG HOLDS] The fortresses of Assyria.

LIKE THE FIG TREE WITH HER FIRST RIPE FIGS] With ripe figs. So the Chaldean here.

IF THEY BE SHAKEN THEY SHALL EVEN FALL INTO THE MOUTH OF THE EATER] So thou also shalt come into the power of the Chaldean without any difficulty.

Latin:

Vers. 12. OMNES MUNITIONES TUÆ] Castella Assyriæ.

SICUT FICUS CUM GROSSIS SUIS] Cum ficubus maturis. Ita hic Chaldæus.

SI CONCUSSÆ FUERINT CADENT IN OS COMEDENTIS] Ita & tu nullo negotio in potestatem Chaldæi venies.

## 3:13
Ver. 13. BEHOLD THY PEOPLE IN THE MIDST OF THEE ARE WOMEN] Ἀχαιΐδες, ὐκ ἔτ’ Ἀχαιοί. O truly Phrygian women, for you are no longer Phrygians.

THE GATES OF THY LAND SHALL BE SET WIDE OPEN UNTO THINE ENEMIES] By opening they shall be opened: that is, immediately, without delay.

THE FIRE SHALL DEVOUR THY BARS] The floodgates, which the enemy burns, so that they might not be of use.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ECCE POPULUS TUUS MVLIERES IN MEDIO TUI] Ἀχαιΐδες, ὐκ ἔτ’ Ἀχαιοί. O vere Phrygiæ, neque enim Phryges.

INIMICIS TUIS ADAPERTIONE PANDENTUR PORTÆ TUÆ] Aperiendo aperientur: id est, statim, sine mora.

DEVORABIT IGNIS VECTES TUOS] Portas cataractas, quas hostes uffit, ne essent usui.

## 3:14
Ver. 14.

DRAW THEE WATERS FOR THE SIEGE] Make cisterns for thyself, from which thou mayest have something to drink during the siege. Tacitus in his description of Jerusalem: A perennial fountain of water, mountains hollowed out beneath the earth, and pools and cisterns for preserving rain water. The founders had provided for all things, however much against a long siege, by the diversity of their customs. God says by way of mockery: prepare all things which are wont to be prepared against a long siege, those things will avail nothing, their minds being seized with fear. We had a similar manner of speaking above II, 1.

FORTIFY THY STRONG HOLDS] The bulwarks of the city.

ENTER INTO THE CLAY AND TREAD, PREPARING HOLD THE BRICK] In the Hebrew: Enter into the clay, and tread upon the clay, and hold (that is, defend) the brickwork. It often happens in great cities that, a part being captured, some part is defended by building interior fortifications. (see Jerem. XXXIII. 4. 5.) which fortifications were indeed made at that time mostly of brick, from which material the walls of Babylon also were; he says therefore: the gates having now been captured, retreat within the new fortifications of brick, ascend upon them, and defend them as much as you can. He signifies also that this effort will be of short duration and vain. We could interpret these and other things more distinctly if we had the Assyriaca of Abydenus, which I urge all students to seek with me; they say that book lies hidden in Florence.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

AQUAM PROPTER OBSIDIONEM HAURI TIBI] Cisternas tibi fac, unde habeas in obsidione quod bibas. Tacitus in descriptione Hierosolymorum: Fons perennis aquæ, cavati sub terra montes, & piscinæ, cisternæq, servandis imbribus. Providerant conditores ex diversitate morum crebrabella: inde cuncta, quamvis adversus longum obsidium. Per irrisum ait Deus: parate omnia quæ adversus longum obsidium parari solent, nihil illa proderunt, captis formidine animis. Simile loquendi genus supra habuimus II, 1.

EXSTRUE MUNITIONES TUAS] Propugnacula urbis.

INTRA IN LUTUM ET CALCA, SUBIGENS TENE LATEREM] In Hebræo: Intra in lutum, & calca super lutum, & tene (id est, defende) lateritium opus. Sæpe evenit in magnis urbibus, ut capta parte, pars aliqua defendatur, structis interioribus munimentis. (vide Jerem. XXXIII. 4. 5.) quæ quidem munimenta eo tempore maxime fiebant e latere, e qua materia & muri erant Babylonis: ait ergo: captis jam portis aliquibus recipe te intra nova munimenta a latere, ascende super illa, & illa defende quantum potes. Significat & hanc molitionem brevis temporis, & inanem fore. Hæc & alia distinctius possemus interpretari, si haberemus Abydeni Assyriaca, quæ ut mecum quærant studiosos omnes hortor sunt dicant delitescere illum librum Florentiæ.

## 3:15
Vers. 15.

THERE THE FIRE SHALL EAT YOU, YOU SHALL PERISH BY THE SWORD] There also torches and missiles thrown by the enemies will prevent you from standing; חרב signifies to the Hebrews every kind of weapon, and is translated both as σίδηρος and λόγχη.

IT SHALL DEVOUR YOU LIKE THE BRUCHUS] Better: like a bruchus; because of what follows. Locusts are food for the Syrians, and so are bruchi.

GATHERED LIKE THE BRUCHUS, MULTIPLIED LIKE THE LOCUST] Although the number of soldiers whom you have brought together may have been huge: for we said above on Joel I. 4 that soldiers are designated by the name of bruchi and locusts.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

IBI COMEDET TE IGNIS, PERIBIS GLADIO] Ibi quoque faces & tela ab hostibus jacta te vetabunt consistere, חרב Hebræis omne teli genus significat, vertiturque & σίδηρος & λόγχη.

DEVORABIT TE UT BRUCHUS] Melius ut bruchum: propter sequentia. Locustæ in cibo Syris, sic & bruchi.

CONGREGATE UT BRUCHUS, MULTIPLICATE UT LOCUSTA] Licet ingens fuerit numerus militum, quos confluxisti: nam milites bruchi & locustæ nomine designari diximus supra Joel. I. 4.

## 3:16
Vers. 16.

YOU HAVE MADE YOUR TRADINGS MORE THAN THE STARS OF HEAVEN ARE] And you have attracted more merchants than there are stars in the sky.

THE BRUCHUS HAS SPREAD OUT, AND FLOWN AWAY] It rushes in and flies away. He shows the habit of the bruchus, to which he will then more openly compare those mercenary soldiers and merchants.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

PLURES FECISTI NEGOTIATIONES TUAS QUAM STELLÆ SUNT COELI] Et plures attraxeris mercatores quam cæli sunt stellæ.

BRUCHUS EXPANSUS EST, ET AVOLAVIT] Irruit & avolat. Ostendit morem bruchi, cui deinde comparabit apertius mercenarios illos milites & mercatores.

## 3:17
Vers. 17.

YOUR GUARDS ARE LIKE LOCUSTS] מנזריך is an Assyrian name, and if we believe the Greeks, it signifies τῆς συμμίκτης, strangers from various nations. They are so called, it seems, because they wore a certain crown or plate, which the Chaldean has placed here, by which they were distinguished from the citizens.

AND YOUR LITTLE ONES ARE LIKE THE LOCUSTS OF LOCUSTS] טפסריך is another Assyrian name: which we noted approaches σατράπην at Jer. LI, 26. For locusts in the Hebrew it is not אבר, which preceded, but גוב גובי; in that גובי is a Syriac ending or a construct state, as the Grammarians say, for the absolute: just as in Isaiah XIX. 9. XX. 4. Jerem. XVII. 13. Ezech. XIII, 9. Hosea XI. 4. And the word גוב itself is Syriac or Chaldean, which in the ancient versions Exod. XIV. 19.

Levit. XI, 21. is placed for the Hebrew ארבה. There are, however, those who think it is a kind of insect similar indeed to the locust, but differing slightly, such as the attelabus. The doubling of the word denotes an extraordinary multitude.

WHICH FALL IN THE HEDGES, IN THE DAY OF COLD, THE SUN IS RISEN, AND THEY HAVE FLOWN AWAY] But when the sun is risen, they fly away. Jerome: For it is the nature of these locusts, that being torpid in the cold, they fly about through the heat. The apodosis is easily understood. Thus those mercenary leaders of yours, and merchants, have fled in the time of danger.

AND THE PLACE OF THEM IS NOT KNOWN WHERE THEY HAVE BEEN] No traces of them remain.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

CUSTODES TUI QUASI LOCUSTÆ] מנזריך Nomen est Assyriacum, & si Græcis credimus, τῆς συμμίκτης significat, extraneos ex variis gentibus. Sic dicti, ut videtur, quod coronam quandam aut laminam, quod hic posuit Chaldæus, gestarent, per quam a civibus dignoscebantur.

ET PARVULI TUI QUASI LOCUSTÆ LOCUSTARUM] טפסריך est alterum nomen Assyriacum: quod ad σατράπην accedere notavimus ad Jer. LI, 26. pro locustis in Hebræo est non אבר, quod præcessit, sed גוב גובי in isto גובי est terminatio Συριάχουσα aut regimen, ut loquuntur Grammatici, pro absoluto: quemadmodum Esaiæ XIX. 9. XX. 4. Jerem. XVII. 13. Ezech. XIII, 9. Oseæ XI. 4. Et ipsum גוב est Syriacum aut Chaldaicum, quod in versionibus antiquis Exod, XIV. 19.

Levit. XI, 21. ponitur pro Hebræo ארבה. Sunt tamen qui insecti genus per simile quidem locuste, sed paulum differens putant esse, quale est attelabus. Geminatio vocis multitudinem eximiam denotat.

QUÆ CONCIDUNT IN SEPIBUS, IN DIE FRIGORIS, SOL ORTUS EST, ET AVOLAVERUNT] Sole autem orto avolant. Hieronymus: Natum enim hæc locustarum est, ut in frigore torpentes, per calorem volitent. Facile intelligitur ἀπόδοσις. Sic illi tui duces mercenarii, & mercatores in periculo fugerunt.

ET NON EST COGNITUS LOCUS EARUM UBI FUERINT] Nulla eorum manent vestigia.

## 3:18
Vers. 18.

THY SHEPHERDS HAVE SLUMBERED, O KING OF ASSYRIA] They have slumbered: that is, thy shepherds, prefects, and leaders have behaved themselves negligently.

THY PRINCES SHALL BE BURIED] Thy princes have lain down, a metaphor from שכן similar to that which preceded.

THY PEOPLE HAVE HIDDEN THEMSELVES IN THE MOUNTAINS] Thy people are dispersed upon the mountains. By people here understand the common soldiers.

AND THERE IS NONE THAT GATHERETH] There is no one who might gather such dispersed ones back into a battle line.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

DORMITAVERUNT PASTORES TUI, REX ASSUR] Dormitarunt: id est, negligenter se gesserunt pastores tui, præfecti & duces.

SEPELIENTUR PRINCIPES TUI] Cubarunt principes tui, a שכן metaphora par ei quæ præcessit.

LATITAVIT POPULUS TUUS IN MONTIBUS] Dispersi sunt populus tuus super montes. Per populum hic gregarios milites intellige.

ET NON EST QUI CONGREGET] Nemo est, qui fic dispersos in agmen recolligat.

## 3:19
Vers. 19.

THY DESTRUCTION IS NOT OBSCURE] In the Hebrew: there is no binding for thy wound. Since Nineveh is surrendered, the soldiers dispersed, the leaders torpid, do you not see that your affairs have perished without remedy? The Greeks: there is no healing for thy destruction.

THY PLAGUE IS MOST GRIEVOUS] The Greeks: thy wound has become inflamed. Inflamed wounds are accustomed to bring about destruction.

FOR UPON WHOM HATH NOT THY MALICE PASSED ALWAYS?] To whom have thy injuries not reached at all times? To whom hast thou not been troublesome? The sense is the same as above in verse 7.

We add the explanation of B. Tarnovius. For just as in those merchants of yours there will be no abundance of counsel or aid for you, so neither will there be any protection in your own princes. For your crowned ones and the long-haired ones, who nourish their hair more studiously, just as the Nazarites of old refrained from shaving it by vow, are like the locust, both because of their slothful idleness, since they are born only to consume the fruits of the earth, and because of fear, because they are easily thrown into flight, just as locusts easily terrified fly away: and your younger princes who serve the king in the court, and have a peculiar name of dignity from their age and from their birth, Jer. LI. 27, so that they are called טפסרים, a compound word of טף, i.e., a little one, and סר or שר, that is, a prince, are like the locust of locusts, i.e., pregnant ones, like the greatest and most voracious locusts on account of their extreme luxury, so that גוב גובי is a Hebraism, similar to that King of Kings, Lord of Lords, concerning which see Buxt. Thef. p. 331. & גובי for גובים, as the same notes on page 82. They too will take to flight, like locusts which at night in the time of cold camp along the stone walls (I would translate it as stone walls rather than hedges, since גדרה, the plural of which appears in this passage, signifies a wall heaped up from rough stones, without lime or mortar) and because of their numbers have the appearance of a regular army, but in the morning when the sun has risen they wander off, flee away, and depart or fly off quickly (as ברח is understood in Cant. c. 8, 14. and φεύγε in Matth. 10, 23.), so that the place of each one of them or where they all were cannot be discerned; so too your younger princes will scatter when this evil of war rushes in, so that you will not know thereafter where they were. Thus he. We conclude with the consolatory ἐυλογία of Nahum: (c. I, 7.) The Lord is good, and a stronghold in the day of trouble, and he knows those who trust in him, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

NON EST OBSCURA CONTRITIO TUA] In Hebræo: non est ligamen vulneri tuo. Cum Ninos sit dedita, milites dispersi, duces torpidi, nonne vides perisse res tuas sine remedio. Græci: ἐκ ἔστι ἴασις τῇ συντριβῇ σου.

PESSIMA EST PLAGA TUA] Græci ἐφλέγμανεν ἡ πληγήσε. Inflammata vulnera solent exitium adferre.

QUIA SUPER QUEM NON TRANSIT MALITIA TUA SEMPER?] Ad quem non pervenerunt injuriæ tuæ omni tempore? Cui non molesta fuisti? sensus idem qui supra 7.

Addimus B. Tarnovii explicationem. Ut vero in illis negociatoribus tuis nulla tibi consilii vel auxilii copia, fic nec in tuis ipsius principibus erit quicquam præsidii. Nam diademati & comatuli tui, qui comam studiosius nutriunt, ut olim abradenda illa abstinebant Naziræi ex voto, sunt similes locustæ, tum propter otium ignavum, quandoquidem fruges tantum consumere nati, tum propter metum, quod facile in fugam conjiciuntur, ut locustæ facile territæ avolant: & principes tui juniores qui regi in aula ministrant, & peculiare dignitatis nomen ab ætate, ab ortu habent Jer. LI. 27. ut dicantur טפסרים composita voce טף, i.e. parvulus & סר sive שר id est, princeps sunt sicut locusta locustarum, i. e. prægnantes, velut locustæ maximæ & voracissimæ ob summum luxum, ut sit גוב גובי hebraismus, similis illi Rex Regum, Dominus Dominantium, de quo Buxt. Thef. p. 331. & גובי pro גובים, ut idem notat pag. 82. etiam illi fugam capessent, ut locustæ, quæ de nocte tempore frigoris castrametantur per macerias (potius verterim, quam per sepes, cum גדרה cujus plurale hoc loco extat, significet murum ex rudibus lapidibus congestum, sine calce ac camento) & ob copiam, justi exercitus speciem habet, sed mane sole exorto errant, aufugiunt, celeriter abeunt seu avolant (ut ברח Cant. c. 8, 14. & φεύγε, Matth. 10, 23. accipitur) ita ut non dignoscatur locus illius uniuscujusque vel ubi fuerint ipsi omnes, sic etiam tui juniores principes diffugient hoc malo belli irruente, ut non cognoscas deinceps, ubi fuerint. Hæc ille. Concludimus ἐυλογία Nahumi consolatoria: (c. I, 7.) Bonus Dominus, & confortans in die tribulationis, & sciens sperantes in se, cui gloria sit in secula seculorum Amen.

# Habakkuk

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
In the Name of Jesus. Annotations on Habakkuk.

Latin:

I. N. I. ANNOTATA AD HABACUC.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface
PREFACE.

Habakkuk, from the root חבק, that is, he embraced, designates a good embracer by the force of the name, not without an omen, because, as Luther says, he embraces, loves, and reclines his afflicted people in his arms, comforts and sustains them just as a sad, weeping little boy is taken up by his mother so that he may be silent. For although he threatens destruction to the Jews on account of their sins through the Chaldeans, nevertheless he not only predicts the mitigation of the punishment, but also, with the fulfillment of the promises of the Messiah and of Salvation through faith in Him confirmed, the punishment of the Chaldeans as enemies of the people on account of their pride, avarice, injustice, and tyranny; and he promises to the faithful a richer knowledge and the gracious presence of GOD, and at the same time leads them with a formula of prayer, by which, having exposed their calamity to the Lord, they rejoice in

GOD their Savior. He lived, however, not after the captivity, as seemed to Jerome, contrary to the express letter of chapter 1, verse 6 et seqq., but before it, under the reign of Josiah, as it appears, since he uses almost the same words and sentiments as Jeremiah, and indicates that the captivity is imminent.

There are two parts: 1. prophetic, consisting of prediction in chapters I and II; the other is supplicatory, consisting of prayer, in chapter III. The former part exhibits both a commination against the Jews in chapter I, and consolation partly from the fulfillment of the promise of the Messiah, through faith in whom life is obtained, and partly from the destruction of the enemies of the people, with a promise also interspersed concerning the knowledge of GOD that will fill the earth and concerning the presence of the Lord in His holy temple, in chapter II. In the latter part, divine mercy is sought through prayer, by the example of the liberation and manifold grace granted to the people, and joy is hoped for in the Lord JESUS, both on account of spiritual benefits and also for the liberation from the Babylonian captivity.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM.

Habbakuk à Rad. חבק, id est, amplexatus est, amplexatorem bonum vi nominis designat, non sine omine, quia populum suum afflictum, dicente Luthe- ro, amplexatur, amat, & in ul- nas reclinat, solatur & sustentat quemadmodum triste plorans puerulus à matre suscipitur, ut sileat. Quan- quam enim Judæis ob peccata exitium per Chal- dæos minetur, tamen non tantum prædicit mitiga- tionem pœnæ, sed etiam, confirmata impletione pro- missionum Messiæ & Salutis per fidem in ipsum, Chal- deorum ceu hostium populi ob superbiam, avari- tiam, injustitiam & tyrannidem pœnam; ac fidelibus cognitionem uberiorem & gratiosam DEI præsen- tiam promittit, simulque orationis formula præit iis- dem, qua, calamitate Domino exposita, lætatur in

DEO salutari suo. Vixit autem non post captivita- tem, ut Hieronymo visum est, contra expressam li- teram cap. 1. v. 6. seqq. sed ante eandem, sub regno Iosiæ, ut apparet, quum iisdem sere verbis & senten- tiis cum Jeremia utatur, & imminere captivitatem indicat.

Partes duæ sunt: 1. προφητική, prædictione cap. I. & II. altera est ἐνκτικὴ oratione constans, c. III. Pars prior tum comminationem exhibet adver- sus Judæos cap. I. tum consolationem partim à pro- missionis Messiæ, per cujus fidem vita obtinetur, com- plemento, partim ab hostium populi exitio, inspersa et. iam promissione de agnitione DEI terram repletura deque præsentia Domini, in templo suo sancto. c. II. In parte posteriori oratione expetitur divina miseri- cordia, exemplo liberationis & gratiæ multivariæ populo præstitæ, & speratur lætitia in Domino JE- SU, tum ob spiritualia beneficia, tum ob libera- tionem etiam è captivitate Babylonica.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. PROPHETIC. CHAPTER I. Comminatory and deprecatory for the Jews.

With the inscription of the Prophet premised, he expostulates with the Lord concerning the wickedness and perfidy of the Jews, and reporting the Lord's response concerning the siege and captivity of the Jews by the terrible and fierce Chaldean army, which mocks at any kings whatsoever, he intercedes with the Lord on behalf of the people for the mitigation of the punishment. With a mixed complaint and threats, Habakkuk hopes and prays.

The Hebrews think that he also wrote in the times of Manasseh, to which the place he holds from antiquity between Nahum, a contemporary of Manasseh, and Zephaniah, who flourished under Josiah, bears witness. But the argument itself also fits that time. For he deplores the laws and rights overturned, which never happened more than under Manasseh. He predicts the destruction of the nation by the Chaldeans, following in the footsteps of Isaiah, who had already predicted the same thing before Hezekiah: as we see in 2 Kings XX. 17, 18. At the same time, against the complaints into which the impatience of many was about to break out, he brings the justice of God into the open, and the punishments which He was later to inflict upon the Chaldeans, the victors of the Jews. The name of the Prophet is חבקוק, as this name is written in Hebrew and Chaldean books, but the Greeks read it חבקוס: they write—concerning the time of Habakkuk, authors vary. That he lived under Manasseh himself is also the opinion of Vatablus, Arias Montanus, Isidorus Clarius, à Castro, and others. To Cornelius à Lapide it seems that Habakkuk was one of the prophets whom God sent to Manasseh to rebuke him for his impieties, 2 Kings 21:20. There are not lacking, however, those to whom it seems more probable, because Habakkuk agrees with Jeremiah in matters and sentiments, and says that the captivity is imminent, into which Jeremiah fell, that he lived either in his time under the reign of Josiah, or did not long precede him. See Tarnov. in prolegomen. p. 5. That the prophet is called Αββακούμ in the Greek codices, whether it is a gloss of the interpreters or a mistake of the scribes, we do not dwell upon much. For such things are not rare among the Greeks.

Vers. 1. THE BURDEN WHICH HABAKKUK THE PROPHET SAW] Both against the Jews and against the Chaldeans.

HOW LONG, O LORD, SHALL I CRY, AND THOU WILT NOT HEAR?] That is, you will not hear me crying. I WILL CRY OUT TO THEE SUFFERING VIOLENCE] I will cry out to thee of rapine. That is, I will complain that violence is superior to law in Judea. See 2 Kings 21:16. AND THOU WILT NOT SAVE] With you not hindering.

Latin:

PARS I. PROPHETICA. CAPUT I. Comminatorium & deprecatorium pro Judæis.

Præmissa inscriptione Prophetæ de Judæorum impro- bitate ac perfidia cum Domino expostulat, & re- sponsionem Domini referens de Judæorum ab ex- ercitu Chaldaico terribili ac feroci Regibusq; qui- busvis illudente, obsidione, & captivatione, pro po- pulo apud Dominum pro mitigatione pœnæ inter- pellat. Mixta querela minis Habacuci sperat & orat.

Hunc quoque Manassis temporibus scripsisse sentiunt Hebæi, quibus adstipulatur ipse, quem ab antiquo ob- tinet, locus inter Nahumum, Manassi coævum, & Sopho- niam, qui sub Josia floruit. Sed & ipsum argumentum ei congruit tempori. Deplorat enim fas & jura eversa, quod nunquam magis, quam sub Manasse evenit. Prædi- cit excidium gentis per Chaldæos, Esaiæ premens vesti- gia, qui rem eandem jam ante Ezechia prædixerat: ut vi- demus 2. Reg. XX. 17. 18. simul adversus querelas, in quas e- ruptura erat multorum impatientia, justitiam Dei in aper- tum producit, & pœnas, quas postea victoribus Judæo- rum Chaldæis erat irrogaturus. Nomen Prophetæ est חבקוק quomodo hoc nomen scribitur in libris Hebrai- cis & Chaldaicis, at Græci legerunt חבקוס: scribunt- DE tempore Habacucis variant autores. Sub Manasse ipsum vixisse cum Ebræis etiam Va- tablus, Arias Montanus, Isidorus Clarius, à Castro & alii putant. Cornelio à Lapide videtur Haba- cuc unus fuisse è Prophetis, quos Deus ad Ma- nassen misit, ut eum de impietatibus arguerent 2. Reg. XXI. 20. Non desunt tamen, quibus pro- babilius videatur, quia rebus & sententiis cum Jeremia convenit Habacuc, & captivitatem insta- re dicit, in quam Jeremias incidit, quod vel tem- pore ejus sub regno Iosiæ vixerit, vel non longe eum antecesserit. Vide Tarnov. in prolegomen. p. 5. Quod Prophetæ Αββακούμ in Græcis Codici- bus vocetur sive παρεγκευα sit Interpp. sive σφάλμα descriptorum, parum moramur. Ta- lia enim non rara apud Græcos sunt.

Vers. 1. ONUS QUOD VIDIT HABACUC PROPHE- TA] Tum contra Judæos, tum contra Chaldæos.

USQUE QUO DOMINE CLAMABO, ET NON EXAUDIES? ] Id est, me clamantem non exaudies. VOCIFERABOR AD TE VIM PATIENS] Vo- ciferabo ad te rapinam. Id est, conquerar vim jure superio- rem esse in Judæa. Vid. 2. Reg. XXI, 16. ET NON SALVABIS] Te non impediente.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. WHY HAST THOU SHOWN ME] Thou hast made to appear

in my age. INIQUITY AND LABOR] That is, most iniquitous labor: hendiadys. So also the Chaldean understood it. TO SEE] Supply: thou makest me see. SPOIL AND INJUSTICE] Oppression and iniquity: that is, most iniquitous oppression. AGAINST ME] Before me, around me. AND JUDGMENT AND CONTRADICTION IS MORE POWERFUL] There is a lawsuit: that is, many a cause for complaining: and judgment has been taken away, the king, of course, whose name he suppresses.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QUARE OSTENDISTI MIHI] Apparere fecisti

mea ætate. INIQUITATEM ET LABOREM] Id est, labo- rem iniquissimum: ἐν διὰ δυοῖν. Ita & Chaldæus accepit. VIDERE] Supple facis. PRÆDAM ET INJUSTITIAM ] Oppressionem & iniquitatem: id est, iniquissimam oppressionem. CONTRA ME] Coram me, circum me. ET FACTUM EST JUDICIUM ET CON- TRADICTIO POTENTIOR] Est lis: id est, multa causa querendi: & judicium abstulit, rex scilicet, quod nomen subticet.

## 1:4
Vers. 4. THEREFORE THE LAW IS TORN ASUNDER] The divine law has lost its force.

AND JUDGMENT DOES NOT REACH UNTO THE END] Judgment never proceeds: the matter remains indefinite. BECAUSE THE WICKED PREVAILS AGAINST THE JUST] He surrounds him like a crown, that is, with a siege. THEREFORE PERVERSE JUDGMENT GOES FORTH] What is more, judgment proceeds, but it is perverse. Often there is no judgment: often, which is worse, it is judged clearly against the law.

Latin:

Vers. 4. PROPTER HOC LACERATA EST LEX] Vim

suam lex divina perdidit. ET NON PERVENIT USQUE AD FINEM JUDICIUM] Nunquam procedit judicium: res manet in- definita. QUIA IMPIUS PRÆVALET ADVERSUS JU- STUM] Circumbenit velut corona, id est, indagine. PROPTEREA EGREDITUR JUDICIUM PER- VERSUM] Quod amplius est, procedit judicium, sed per- versum. Sæpe non judicatur: sæpe, quod pejus est, pla- ne contra jus judicatur.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. BEHOLD AMONG THE NATIONS, AND SEE]

He looks at the needy. Namely, those whom I shall bring against you, the Chaldeans, as follows, and their allies. The Hebrews often append ב after verbs of perceiving, but the LXX and the anonymous interpreter, whom Jerome mentions here, read בגדי and translated them as 'despisers,' and this one as 'calumniators': in the vocative case, of course, both of them. This reading of the Greeks seems better to me. God addresses the Jews, the despisers of His divinity. And thus Luke cites it in Acts 13:41: 'Behold, ye despisers.' AND SEE: WONDER AND BE ASTONISHED] I.e., it will be that when you see, you will wonder and be astonished. The Greeks, for תמהו, seem to have read תמהו in the imperative Niphal from תמם, which is ἀφανίζεσθε. For they translate this passage thus: 'and look and wonder at wonders and perish.' To me, the reading which is in our Hebrew books, which both Jerome and the Chaldean follow, does not seem base.

The Hebrew fountains, which the divine providence of the Church has kept clear so that not one iota or tittle should perish, ought never to seem vile to us. Whatever, therefore, the LXX may have read here or there (if their version is intact in these places, it ought not to be a deception to the Hebrew truth, to which Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, the Chaldean, and the Vulgate Latin agree). But that the Holy Apostle retained the Greek version commonly received at that time, by that he did not approve or prefer it to the fountains; since where it made no difference in the underlying subject matter, the Holy Apostles willingly followed the common interpretation, saving the authority of the Hebrew truth, because it was commonly received and they saw that nothing was lost to the matter itself, and thus those speaking or writing in Greek retained the Greek translation. There is no need for us to say that the Greeks read בגדים for בגוים, when that καταφρονηταὶ can be considered to have been added by them for the sake of the sense. Look, you despisers, because this was highly appropriate for the Jews of his time, to whom a similar destruction was imminent from the nations, namely from the Roman people, such as Habakkuk had threatened them with from the Chaldeans; therefore the Apostle judged that the word καταφρονηταὶ should not be omitted. Thus the LXX neglected the word IN THE NATIONS because it was evident from the following verse: Behold I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter nation, etc. Cornelius a Lapide is inept here, [suggesting] that the Hebrew scripture was varied, one without vowels, another in the margin, signifying that it could be read in either way. To have narrated these things is to have refuted them; even if he pursues these trifles at greater length there, thinking that sometimes the Chaldeans, sometimes the Jews, are designated here by the name of nations, and having nothing certain to which he might hold. FOR A WORK HAS BEEN DONE IN YOUR DAYS] It will be done. Symmachus, as Jerome notes here. In the Hebrew it is, I am doing, and in the Greek and in Luke, ἐργάζομαι, for I will do. Luke, or rather Paul in Luke, adapts these words very well to the destruction that was about to happen through the Romans. WHICH NO ONE WILL BELIEVE WHEN IT IS TOLD] It will be so horrible, what I shall do, that no one will believe the narrator. In the Hebrew it is: which you will not believe: and in the Greek: ᾧ μὴ πιστεύσητε ἐάν τις ἐκδιηγῆται ὑμῖν. Jerome here put the second person for the indefinite: but in the Commentary more simply: A work which will be so great that if anyone were to predict now that it would happen, you would not easily give it credence.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ADSPICITE IN GENTIBUS, ET VIDETE]

Respicit egentes. Nempe quas contra vos adducam, Chal- dæos, ut sequitur, & eorum socios. Hebræi sæpe post vo- cabula sentiendi subjungunt ב, at LXX. & Interpres ἀ- νώνυμος, cujus hic meminit Hieronymus, legerunt בגדי verteruntque illi καταφρονηταὶ, hic calumniatores: in vo- cativo scilicet utrumque. Melior mihi videtur hæc lectio Græcorum. Alloquitur Deus Judæos sui numinis con- temptores. Et sic citat Lucas Act. XIII. 41. ἴδετε οἱ κα- ταφρονηταί. ET VIDETE: ADMIRAMINI ET OBSTUPESCI- TE] I. e. erit, quod ubi videritis admiremini & obstupesca- tis. Græci pro תמהו, legisse videntur תמהו in impera- tivo Niphal à תמם, quod est ἀφανίζεσθε. Vertunt enim sic hunc locum: κὶ ἐπιβλέψετε κὶ θαυμάσετε θαυμάσια καὶ ἀφανίσθητε. Mihi lectio, quæ in nostris est libris Hebræis, quam & Hieronymus & Chaldæus sequuntur, non sordet.

Nunquam sordere nobis debent Ebræi fon- tes, quos limpidos servavit Ecclesiæ divina provi- dentia, ne unum Jota vel apex periret. Quicquid ergo hic aut illic legerint LXX. (si eorum versio integra in his sit, fraudi esse non debet Ebraicæ ve- ritati, cui consentiunt Aquila, Symmachus, Theodo- tio, Chaldæus & Vulgatus Latinus. Quod autem S. Apostolus versionem Græcam vulgo tunc rece- ptam retinuerit, eo non approbavit aut prætulit eandem fontibus; siquidem ubi in materia sub- strata nihil referebat, lubenter S. Apostoli vulga- tam interpretationem, salva autoritate veritatis Ebraicæ, sequuti sint, quod eadem communiter recepta fuerit, ac rei ipsi nihil decedere viderint, adeoque Græce loquentes aut scribentes Græcam translationem retinuerint. Non opus est, ut dicamus Græcos, pro בגוים legisse בגדים, cum illud καταφρονηταὶ de suo, sensus causa addidisse censeri possint. Adspicite contemptores, quod quia apprime conveniebat Judæis sui temporis, quibus parile exitium cum gentibus imminebat, à populo nempe Romano, quale ipsis à Chaldæis minatus e- rat Habacuc; ideo vocem illam καταφρονηταὶ non prætermittendam judicabat Apostolus. Ita- que vocem IN GENTIBUS neglexêre LXX. quia eadem è versu sequenti constabat: Ecce ego susci- tabo Chaldæos gentem amaram &c. Ineptus hic est Cornelius Lapideus scripturam Ebræam fuisse variam unam sine vocalibus, ad marginem alte- ram, significans utrolibet modo legi posse. Quæ narrasse est refutasse; etsi istas nugas pluribus ibi exequatur, modo Chaldæos, modo Judæos gentium nomine hic designari existimans, nec certi quid habens, cui insistat. QUIA OPUS FACTUM EST IN DIEBUS VE- STRIS] Fiet. Symmachus, ut hic notat Hieronymus. In Hebræo est, facio, & in Græco ac in Luca, ἐργάζομαι, pro faciam. Lucas aut potius apud Lucam Paulus, optime hæc verba aptat ad excidium simile eventurum per Roma- nos. QUOD NEMO CREDET CUM NARRABI- TUR] Tam horribile futurum est, quod faciam, ut nar- ranti nemo fidem sit habiturus. In Hebræo est: quod non credetis: & in Græco: ᾧ μὴ πιστεύσητε ἐάν τις ἐκδιηγῆται ὑμῖν. Hieronymus hic secundam personam posuit pro indefini- ta: at in Commentario simplicius: Opus quod tam grande erit, ut si quis nunc futurum prædixerit, fidem non facile accom- modetis.

## 1:6
Ver. 6.

FOR BEHOLD I WILL RAISE UP THE CHALDEANS] It is deservedly a wonder, because the Chaldeans, who in the time of Hezekiah, Manasseh, and Josiah were allied with the Jews: if any evil was to be feared, it was thought to come from the Egyptians. This is a similar prediction to Isaiah, who signified that the most grievous evils would come from the Assyrians, in whom the Jews trusted most at that time, with the Jews thinking nothing less than this. Chap. VII. A BITTER NATION] Cruel. Jer. V. 16, 17. AND SWIFT] Isa. V. 26, 27. they were not ἀναβαλλόμενοι (delaying). WALKING UPON THE BREADTH OF THE EARTH] Ruling widely; See what we have brought forth concerning Nebuchadnezzar in the third book of the Truth of the Christian Religion. TO POSSESS TABERNACLES NOT THEIR OWN] The cities of the Jews.

Vers. 6.

QUIA ECCE EGO SUSCITABO CHALDÆOS] Merito mirum, quod Chaldæos, qui tempore Ezechiæ, Manassis, Josiæ fœderati erant Judæis: si quod autem ma- lum metuendum erat, id ab Ægyptiis venturum putaba- tur. Simile hoc prædictum Esaiæ qui ab Assyriis, quibus maxime tunc fidebant Judæi, gravissima mala ventura si- gnificavit, nihil minus quam hoc opinantibus Judæis. Cap. VII. GENTEM AMARAM] Crudelem. Jer. V. 16. 17. ET VELOCEM] Esa. V. 26. 27. non erant ἀνα- βαλλόμενοι. AMBULANTEM SUPER LATITUDINEM TER- RÆ] Late regnatricem; Vide quæ de Nabuchodonosoro protulimus ad III. librum de Veritate Religionis Chri- stianæ. UT POSSIDEAT TABERNACULA NON SUA] Judæorum urbes.

Ver. 7.

FROM ITSELF ITS JUDGMENT, AND ITS BURDEN SHALL GO FORTH] From that very (Chaldean people) its judgment and its decree will have effect. That is, it will decree whatever it wishes and gives effects. AND SWIFTER THAN EVENING WOLVES] Concerning which see Jeremiah in the same place. In the Hebrew: sharper: that is, fiercer. For evening wolves, the LXX translated Arabian wolves. ITS HORSEMEN SHALL SPREAD OUT] There will be many, who
