## 1:11
Vers. 11.

THEN THE SPIRIT SHALL CHANGE, AND HE SHALL PASS OVER] Among the Hebrews, the spirit is said to pass over or transgress, as often as it does not keep itself within the bounds of modesty: καὶ ὑπὲρκτ᾽ ἀνθρωπον φρονεῖ, as Sophocles speaks.

AND HE SHALL FALL] In the Hebrew: וְאָשֵׁם: that is, he shall sin gravely.

THIS IS HIS STRENGTH OF HIS GOD] There is an ellipsis of the participle saying: and of the little word that: so that the sense is, saying that these are his powers, as one who is for a GOD unto himself. See Dan. III. and compare what is below 16.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

TUNC MUTABITUR SPIRITUS, ET PER- TRANSIBIT] Hebræis Spiritus transire sive transgredi dicitur, quoties intra modestiæ fines se non tenet: καὶ ὑπὲρκτ᾽ ἀνθρωπον φρονεῖ, ut Sophocles loquitur.

ET CORRUET] In Hebræo: וְאָשֵׁם: id est, gra- viter peccabit.

HÆC EST FORTITUDO EJUS DEI SUI] Est ἔλλειψις participii dicens: & voculæ quod: ut sit sensus, di- cens has suas esse vires, ut qui sibimet ipsi sit pro DEO. Vide Dan. III. & confer quæ infra 16.

## 1:12
Vers. 12.

ART THOU NOT FROM THE BEGINNING O LORD MY GOD] That is, from eternity. Other gods sometimes had a beginning. The Hebrews do not have a proper word by which they explain eternity.

AND WE SHALL NOT DIE] לֹא נָמוּת as it is now read. Formerly it was לא תמות, which the Chaldean follows very well: thou shalt not die: as thou hast never begun, so thou shalt never end.

It is wrongly preferred here again that the Chaldean text is superior to the sources. Nor does it appear that the Chaldean read it otherwise, since he could have been looking at the sense, because when we call God holy, we acknowledge his word to be most truthful, and to remain for ages. As the Chaldean rendered it here, not so much as a Metaphrast, as a Paraphrast: Thou O God art a true judge, over all thy creatures, and holy in thy works, thy word remains for ages O Lord. The Hebrews however note that this passage is one of those eighteen which are called תקון סופרים in which they think it was written otherwise than we read today, but in such a way that the Canonical Scribes, Ezra with his colleagues, amended the old reading. Concerning which see Ioh. Buxtorf in Vind. Verit. Hebr. p. 750.

IN JUDGMENT THOU HAST SET HIM] Thou hast used Nebuchadnezzar, that thou mightest execute thy judgments.

THE STRONG, THAT THOU MIGHTEST CORRECT, THOU HAST FOUNDED] That thou mightest chastise, (namely the Jewish people) thou hast established him. In the Hebrew, for strong is, rock, that is, as an inexpugnable cliff.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

NUMQUID NON TU A PRINCIPIO DOMI- NE DEUS MEUS] Id est, ab æterno. Dii alii aliquando cœperunt. Hebræi non habent vocem propriam, qua æternitatem explicent.

ET NON MORIEMUR] לֹא נָמוּת ut nunc le- gitur. Olim fuit לא תמות, quod Chaldæus sequitur optime: non morieris tu: sicut nunquam cœpisti, ita nun- quam defines.

Perperam hic iterum præfertur Chaldæus textus fontibus. Neque tamen apparet, Chaldæum aliter legisse, cum sensum respicere potuerit, quia quum Deum sanctum appellamus, verbum ejus veracissimum esse, atq; in secula permanere agno- scimus. Uti hic reddidit Chaldæus, non tam Me- taphrastes, quam Paraphrastes: Tu Deus judex verus, super omnes creaturas tuas, & sanctus in o- peribus tuis, verbum tuum in secula permanet Domine. Ebræi tamen notant, hunc locum unum esse, ex octodecim illis, qui vocantur תקון סופרים in qui- bus putant aliter scriptum fuisse, quam hodie le- gimus, sed ita ut Scribæ Canonici, Esdra cum Col- legis, veterem lectionem emendarint. Quo de vid. Iob. Buxtorf. in Vind. Verit. Hebr. p. 750.

IN JUDICIUM POSUISTI EUM] Tu Nabucho- donosoro usus es, ut judicia tua exsequereris.

FORTEM, UT CORRIPERES, FUNDASTI EUM] Ut castigares, (nempe populum Judaicum) stabili- sti eum. In Hebræo, pro fortem est, petram, id est, quasi rupem inexpugnabilem.

## 1:13
PURE ARE THINE EYES, THAT THOU MAYEST NOT SEE EVIL] Thy eyes are purer, that is, thy judgments, than that thou shouldst see, that is, tolerate wickedness: namely so much, that the Chaldeans do all things according to the lust of their mind, and attribute their victories to idols.

AND THOU CANST NOT LOOK UPON INIQUITY] Thou canst not always bear deeds so cruel.

WHY DOST THOU LOOK UPON THOSE DOING INIQUITY] Why shouldst thou look upon them? For the Hebrews, because they do not have a potential mood, are forced to misuse the indicative, why shouldst thou bear men so wicked?

AND ART SILENT] Thou shouldst be silent, always of course. The Hebrews take to be silent for to dissemble.

WHEN THE WICKED DEVOURS ONE MORE JUST THAN HIMSELF] In the Hebrew: the just before himself. The Jews were involved in great crimes, but nevertheless they were much surpassed in that matter by the Chaldeans.

Latin:

MUNDI SUNT OCULI TUI, NE VIDEAS MALUM] Puriores sunt oculi tui, id est, judicia tua, quam ut videas, id est, perpetiaris malitiam: nempe tantam, ut Chaldæi omnia agant pro animi libidine, & i- dolis acceptas ferant victorias suas.

ET RESPICERE AD INIQUITATEM NON POTERIS] Ferre semper non potes facta tam crudelia.

QUARE RESPICIS SUPER INIQUA AGEN- TES] Quare respiceres? Nam Hebræi, quia potentialem modum non habent, indicativo abuti coguntur, quare fer- res homines tam sceleratos?

ET TACES] Taceres, semper scilicet. tacere He- bræi sumunt pro dissimulare.

DEVORANTE IMPIO JUSTIOREM SE] In He- bræo: justum præ se. Judæi magnis criminibus involu- ti erant, sed tamen multum in ea re à Chaldæis supera- bantur.

## 1:14
Verse 14.

AND THOU SHALT MAKE] Thou shouldst make, that is, thou shouldst have.

MEN AS THE FISHES OF THE SEA] Namely those whom thou placest outside that special care with which thou followest men. Thus Maimonides.

AND AS A REPTILE] The Hebrews call reptiles, רמשׂ remes, swimming things. Ps. CIV. 2. NOT HAVING A PRINCE] That is, a defender. HE SHALL LIFT UP ALL WITH A HOOK] You will suffer him to lift up all things as if with a hook; he pursues the comparison begun about fish through metaphors. HE HAS DRAWN] He may draw. HE HAS GATHERED] He may gather, Ver. 16. THEREFORE HE WILL SACRIFICE TO HIS NET AND OFFER TO HIS DRAGNET] That is, he will attribute all victories to his own strength: as above 11. BECAUSE IN THEM HIS PORTION IS MADE FAT, AND HIS FOOD IS CHOICE] As if through these things (that is, through his own strength) a fat portion had fallen to him, and delicate feasts. He calls the peoples consumed by the sword a portion and food, for אכל means to consume in Hebrew. THEREFORE FOR THIS] Since he attributes all things to himself, not to you. HE EXPANDS HIS NET] Interrogatively: And shall he expand? That is, shall he always be permitted to expand his net? AND SHALL HE NOT SPARE TO KILL THE NATIONS ALWAYS] He will never make an end of slaughters. Should your [God] bear this?

to compare time with the event, to show the providence of God. We have had a similar warning in Isa. VIII. 6. Jerem. XXII. 12. Dan. IIX. 26. AND IT SHALL APPEAR AT THE END] But at length it shall break forth: just as a state breaks forth. AND IT SHALL NOT LIE] This vision shall not deceive. IF IT MAKE DELAY WAIT FOR IT] That, you people of Judea. BECAUSE COMING IT SHALL COME] It shall certainly come to fulfillment. IT SHALL NOT TARRY] That is, it shall not be deferred forever.

We desire two things in this interpretation. First, that he understands this vision concerning the liberation that was to be through Cyrus, when the vision is rather designated concerning the coming of the Messiah. For this (1) is the proper and principal object of the Prophets, which they themselves most of all had to set before the eyes of all, since their primary office was situated in it, Acts X. 43. (2) If this were not proposed in this place by the Prophet Habakkuk, no prophecy concerning the coming of the Messiah would be held in this Prophet, to whom, however, St. Peter taught that all the prophets bear witness in the cited place. (3) This coming was AFAR OFF (if you translate it thus with Grotius) and this prophecy had to break forth לַקֵץ AT THE END, because these were the last days by the style of the Prophets, the days of the coming of the Messiah: if you translate the word לַמוֹעֵד AT THE APPOINTED TIME, the time primarily defined by God, and it is clear that the time of the coming of the Messiah was exactly constituted from the seventy weeks of Daniel. (4) The Jews were most of all to be confirmed concerning this coming, on account of the sadder fates which were impending, which seemed to render hope doubtful to many. And therefore the Prophet makes them more certain with such an apparatus of words: The vision or that Prophecy, sc. so called by way of excellence, which all the Prophets inculcated, which all the faithful most greedily desired, will fall AT THE APPOINTED time, certainly to happen, and it shall appear AT THE END, and it shall not lie, it shall not deceive, so often promised by GOD, predicted by the Prophets of God. (5) What other subject to be expected could be thought of, to whose faithful waiting the Prophet so greatly exhorts, than the promised Messiah, the Savior of the world? If it make delay, wait for HIM; he points out HIM, whom the faithful had in their mind and heart, whom they anxiously panted for and desired, whom they were expecting from the very first cradles of the world, q. d. if it should still make delay, wait for HIM, whom you desire most, wait still for the appointed time, that blessed seed, that Shiloh, that fruit of the womb, and branch of David, that holy of holies, the Messiah, and ruler in Israel. He did not express it, but tacitly hinted at the subject which they are ordered to expect, because the expectation itself reminded them of their own fates, who it was whom they were ordered to expect still. And therefore he adds for the sake of emphasis, coming it shall come, that is, it shall certainly come, it shall not tarry, q. d. he himself desires to come, and hastens to his own coming, and therefore he shall not tarry. (6) In those words COMING IT SHALL COME the name of this subject is contained by way of allusion, because this name was as it were proper to him, ὁ ἐρχόμενος. HE WHO IS TO COME, as the LXX rendered it here, ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἥξει. For thus was Christ once called, Matt. XI. 3. (7) Since the present passage is explained concerning saving faith, v. 4. the just shall live by his faith, Rom. I. 17. Galat. III. 11. Heb. X. 38. nothing is more convenient than that its proper object, which is Christ, is designated here, in whom we must believe, so that we may obtain eternal life. They are therefore ordered to expect Christ, and to place their trust in the same, so that they may live by this faith of theirs. (8) What if the Holy Spirit openly explains this place concerning Christ in the New Testament, namely that here concerning faith

tempore cum eventu comparari, ad monstrandum Dei providentiam. Simile monitum habuimus Esa. VIII. 6. Jerem. XXII. 12. Dan. IIX. 26. ET APPAREBIT IN FINEM] Sed tandem erum- pet: sicut status erumpit. ET NON MENTIETUR] Non fallet hoc visum. SI MORAM FECERIT EXSPECTA ILLUM] Illud, tu popule Judææ. QVIA VENIENS VENIET] Certo veniet imple- mentum. NON TARDABIT] Id est, non semper differetur.

Duo desideramus in hoc interpretamento. Pri- mo quod visionem hanc intelligat de liberatione per Cyrum futura, quum potius visio de adventu Mes- siæ designetur. Nam hæc (1) proprium ac præcipuum est objectum Prophetarum, quod vel maxime ipsi omnibus ob oculos ponere debebant, quum in eo primarium ipsorum officium situm fuerit Actor. X. 43. (2) Id si hoc loco a Propheta Habacuc non propositum, nullum de adventu Messiæ in Prophe- ta hocce habebitur vaticinium, cui tamen omnes Prophetas testimonium perhibere S. Petrus loco citato docuit. (3) Hic adventus erat PROCUL (si cum Grotio id ita vertas) & hoc vaticinium e- rumpere debebat לַקֵץ IN FINE, quia hi erant novissimi dies stylo Prophetarum dies adventus Messiæ: si vocem לַמוֹעֵד vertas IN STATU- TUM, tempus imprimis à Deo definitum, & ex- acte constitutum fuisse tempus adventus Messiæ è septuaginta Danielis septimanis liquet. (4)de hoc adventu maxime erant confirmandi Judæi, ob tri- stiora, quæ imminebant, fata, quæ multis dubiam spem reddere videbantur. Ideoque tanto ver- borum apparatu certiores eos reddit Propheta: Adhuc visio vel Prophetia illa, sc. ἐξοχικῶς ita dicta, quam omnes Prophetæ inculcabant, omnes fideles avidissime desiderabant, IN STATUTUM tem- pus incidet, certo eventura, & apparebit IN FI- NEM, & non mentietur, non fallet, toties à DEO promissa, à Prophetis Dei prædicta. (5) subjectum exspectandum quodnam aliud magis cogitari pote- rat, ad cujus præstolationem fiducialem tantopere exhortatur Propheta, quam promissus Messias Sal- vator mundi? Si moram fecerit, expecta EUM; ILLUM indigitat, quem in animo & corde habe- bant fideles, quem anxie anhelabant & desi- derabant, quem exspectabant inde à primis mun- di incunabulis q. d. si adhuc moram fecerit, ILLUM, quem desideratis maxime, expectate adhuc statutum tempus semen illud benedictum, Sehilo illum fructum ventris, & germen Davidis, sanctum illum sancto- rum Messiam, & dominatorem in Israel. Non ex- pressit, sed tacite innuit subjectum, quod expe- ctare jubentur, quia expectatio ipsa eorũ fatis ipsos commonefaciebat, quisnam sit, quem adhuc expe- ctare jubebantur. Ideoq; addit ἑτεαιώσεως gratia, veniens veniet, id est, certo veniet, non tardabit, q. d. ipse desiderat venire, & properat ad adventum suum, ideoq, non tardabit. (6) In verbis illis VENIENS VENIET subjecti hujus nomen continetur κατ' ἐπαίνιξιν quia hoc ipfi nomen velut proprium e- rat ὁ ἐρχόμενος. IS QUI VENTURUS EST, uti hic reddidere LXX. ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἥξει. Sic enim vocatus quondam Christus Matth. XI. 3. (7) Quum de fide salvifica explicetur præsens lo- cus v. 4. justus fide sua vivet, Rom. I. 17. Galat. III. 11. Ebr. X. 38. nihil convenientius est, quam objectum ejus proprium, quod est Christus, hic designari, in quod credendum, ut vitam æternam consequa- mur. Jubentur ergo exspectare Christum, & in eundem fiduciam collocare, ut hac fide sua vivant. (8) Quid quod de Christo palam hunc locum explicet Sp. S. in Nov. T. quod nempe hic de fide

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. Consolation of the faithful, with a commination against the Babylonian enemies.

To the Prophet anxiously awaiting the answer of the Lord, the description of the vision on a tablet is commanded, concerning the certainty of the fulfillment of the promise about the Messiah, to whom those who resist will be without rest, but those who trust will live by their faith; and the punishment of Babylon is predicted for its pride and insolence, as well as for its rapacity, avarice, and notable tyranny, both in general and in particular, that because of plunder they will be for plunder to the Medes and Persians, because of avarice, that it will result in loss; because of bloodthirstiness and injustice, that it is to be avenged by fire, for the recognition of the glory of the Lord throughout the whole earth: because of the fury delighting itself in the nakedness of a neighbor, that they are to be filled with ignominy: because of ferocity against the temple and the Jews, that they are to be made to drink the cup of the wrath of GOD, and that because of idolatry they are to be destroyed, having no salvation from idols, with the Lord sounding in his holy temple. By the faith of the prophecy, he shall come: by trust he shall live. Impious Babylon shall lose its wealth, and its proud things are at hand.

Ver. 1. I WILL STAND UPON MY WATCH, AND FIX MY STEP UPON THE FORTRESS, AND I WILL CONTEMPLATE] The Hebrews love an abundance of words: thus they express the same thing with many words. Prophets are compared to watchmen as we see in Ezekiel, III. and XXXIII. Hosea V. 1. just as watchmen hold themselves in their watchtower, and standing there remain, and have their eyes intent on all things that present themselves to view, so also the Prophets wait patiently for what God is about to reveal to them. The fortress here is the tower, the watchtower. THAT I MAY SEE WHAT IS SAID TO ME] That I may understand what God signifies to me. AND WHAT I SHALL ANSWER TO HIM WHO ARGUES WITH ME] To my argument: to that objection which I made concerning the greater sins of the Chaldeans, above II. 12. and following.

Latin:

CAPUT II. Consolatorium fidelium, cum commi- natione adversus hostes Babylonios.

Prophetæ anxie responsum Domini exspectanti man- datur visionis in tabula descriptio, de impletione promissionis de Messia certa, cui refragantes sine requie erunt, confidentes autem fide sua vivent; ac prædicitur Babylonis ob fastum & insolentiam nec non rapacitatem, avaritiam & tyrannidem insi- gnem pœna, tum in genere, tum in specie, quod ob rapinam Medis & Persis in rapinam futuri sint, ob avaritiam, quod damno ea cessura sit; ob san- guinolentiam & injustitiam, quod igne vindican- da sit, ad gloriæ Domini per universam terram agnitionem: ob furorem oblectantem se proximi nuditate, quod ignominia replendi sint: ob fero- ciam adversus templum & Judæos, quod calice iræ DEI potandi, & quod ob idololatriam perdendi, nullam ab idolis salutem habituri, Domino in templo suo sancto personante. Fide Prophetie, veniet: fiducia vivet. Impia perdet opes Babylon, adestq́; superbas.

Vers. 1. SUPER CUSTODIAM MEAM STABO, ET FIGAM GRADUM SUPER MUNITIONEM, ET CONTEMPLABOR] Amant Hebræi verborum copiam: ita que rem eandem multis verbis exprimunt. Prophetæ speculatoribus comparantur ut videmus Ezechiel, III. & XXXIII. Ose. V. 1. sicut speculatores in specula sua se te- nent, ibique stantes manent, & oculos intentos habent in omnia quæ in conspectum se dant, ita & Prophetæ exspe- ctant patienter, quid ipsis Deus sit revelaturus. Munitio hic est turris, specula. UT VIDEAM QUID DICATUR MIHI] Intel- ligam quid Deus mihi significet. ET QUID RESPONDEAM AD ARGUENTEM ME] Ad argumentum meum: ad objectionem illam quam feci de majoribus Chaldæorum peccatis, supra II. 12. & deinceps.

## 2:2
Vers. 2. WRITE THE VISION] That which I am about to tell you. For every perception is called a vision by the Hebrews. AND MAKE IT PLAIN UPON TABLES] באר is an infinitive used as an adverb, and is rightly translated here by the Greeks as σαφῶς, in which sense it is also found in Deut. XXVII. 8. For "it," put "that": that is, "that vision." The sense is, write, and indeed clearly. THAT HE MAY RUN THAT READETH IT] That is, that he who reads it may immediately grasp it, whence the Latins used to say "that it might be read plainly." Vers. 3. FOR THE VISION IS YET AFAR OFF] The fulfillment of that vision is far off from the time of Manasseh, to the times of Cyrus. Therefore he wishes the vision to be written out, so that it may be read well, and its own let the discourse be about Christ, Rom. I. 17, Gal. III. 11, and that he, ὁ ἐρχόμενος (the one who is coming), is Christ, Heb. X. 38, where Grotius wishes for fire to be understood in the common sense, and Christ in the more sublime sense. But that regarding fire is ἀλλότριον (foreign); (for where has mention of fire been made, and what is that fire? Unless it be a σφάλμα (error) and in place of fire, Cyrus ought to have been written) nor does a trace of a double sense appear there. (9) St. Jerome interpreted it thus in this place: 'But the vision itself, of which I spoke to you: write the vision and make it plain on a boxwood tablet, that he who reads may run: it is still for an appointed time, of which the Savior says: In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. And it will arise at the consummation of the world and in the last hour of the day, of which John also speaks: Little children, it is the last hour. And it will not come in vain, for it will save many, and with the remnants of the Israelite people it will gather a multitude of nations.' But if it withdraws itself a little, and if the vision, O reader, who are commanded to read on the boxwood tablet and on the tablets which the Prophet described, begins to come more slowly, wait for it, because coming it will come, and will not delay. But if your faith wavers and you think that what I promise will not come, you will have as a great punishment that you will be displeasing to my soul. But the just man who believes my words, and does not doubt these things which I promise, will have as a reward eternal life.' These are the words of Jerome, according to whom MANIFESTA (make plain), as his words have it, is a prophecy in these things concerning the advent of Christ. Calvin, although he explains it otherwise, nevertheless confesses that many refer these things to the advent of Christ. R. Abarbanel acknowledges that the ancient Rabbis in v. 3 understood it concerning the advent of the Messiah, from whom he indeed departs, but is chastised by Cocceius on this place, who, having deserted his Calvin, acknowledges that a promise concerning Christ is held here. And indeed by the former words, 'there will still be a vision,' it is promised that there will be a restoration of prophecy or of the Ecclesiastical ministry, and thus the reduction of the people into the land and the restoration of the temple and the city is co-signified. But by the following words, which he renders thus: 'AND THE HERALD WILL BE AT THE END, who will not lie,' the promise of the Messiah is exhibited. That herald or speaker is the Son of God, who will not be changed, that is, he is not about to come later, but at his own time, namely, at the end of that appointed term. Authors have accepted the place from the Hebrews concerning the Messiah in the tract Sanhedrin in the Talmud in the section Cheleck. R. Moses Maimonides in Jad Chazakah, tract. de Regib. c. 12. R. Solomon, who also explains the word פח concerning the Son of God, the λόγῳ (Word) and speech of God, comparing the place Ps. XXXIII. 6, where the Son of God is designated by the name of the Word. תפ therefore is a noun to Cocceius, not a verb: which also seemed so to Ludovicus de Dieu, who renders it SPEAKING, and R. David Kimchi in the Michlol and the Roots, who confesses it to be a תואר (noun). The Herald, says Cocceius, is opposed to the vision. The vision is of the future: The Herald, or, if you prefer with Mercerus, the Speaker, is he who does not announce future things, but publishes the thing and the truth. This is entirely an Εὐαγγελιστὴς (Evangelist), an ἀναγγελέυς (announcer). But who this herald or speaker is, can easily appear from the emphasis of the word, namely, he whose task it is to speak the words of God; to ἐξηγεῖσθαι (explain) the Father and His counsel: to say to Zion, Behold I am he who speaks, Isaiah LII. 6, whose task it is to announce the Gospel to the meek, Isa. LXI. 1, 2, finally, who is called ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ (the Word of God) John I, 1, Apoc. XIX. 13. The same is called by Moses a Prophet, Deut. XVIII. 15, by Isaiah a Counselor, Isa. IX. 5, and a witness of the nations, Isa. LV. 4, by John ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστὸς (the faithful witness) Apoc. III. 14.

beant: ἐὰν ὑποστείληται, οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή µου ἐν αὐτῷ (if he draws back, my soul has no pleasure in him): that which the divine writer follows in Hebrews X. 38, it appears they read עֻפְּלָה and נפשו in an excellent sense. If anyone shall fail, namely in waiting (for עפל is translated in Greek by ἐκλείπειν (to fail) and ὀλιγοψυχεῖν (to be faint-hearted)), he will not please me. These are the words of God. ὑποστολὴ (drawing back) is to do less than one ought, Acts XX. 20, 27, Gal. II. 12; hence ὑποστολὴ is opposed to τῇ πίστει (to faith) in the said chapter to the Hebrews X. 39.

Grotius again prefers the Greek text to the Hebrew, the streams to the fountain, which he undeservedly suspects to be corrupt. It is not certain by any sure proof that the LXX Interpreters read otherwise: whose version, as being received, since it did not differ in the sense from the original text, the holy Apostle followed, Heb. X. 39. Ludovicus de Dieu teaches that it responds excellently to the Hebrew text, from the Arabic usage of the word עפל, according to which it is to neglect, or rather to turn away and withdraw the mind, so that the sense may be, if this promise is neglected, and now the mind is turned away from it, his soul does not please itself in him. He reads עפל by a certain mode of interrogation: 'Is there a drawing back?' Which signification they also observe in Num. XII. 44, the LXX: ἐὰν ὑποστείληται (if he draws back), if a drawing back happens, or also, if anyone withdraws himself, his (the Messiah's) soul does not please itself in him: whence the antithesis is most conveniently situated: But the just man will live by his faith, who does not withdraw or turn his heart away from the promise concerning the Messiah, but apprehends him by faith, he will not only please Him, but by that faith of his he will live eternally. Others render the word עפלה as 'he is lifted up,' 'he is proud,' and they reconcile the Greek translation in this way: he who withdraws himself through unbelief, he also is proud, because, as to believe is of humility, so to believe no one is of a proud mind. Nor does Blessed Luther translate it inconveniently: 'was halsstarrig ist' (what is stiff-necked). He refers, namely, to those of whom the Prophet complains, that they argue against themselves, who, namely, refuse to apply faith to the promises, and stubbornly contradict them. Cocceius refers here the notion of the word ὑποστέλλεσθαι (to draw back) familiar to Polybius, by which it means to apply oneself to some fortification for security, as it is wont to happen in military service, if anyone has applied himself to another, namely, to a thing other than the Messiah as his fortification and protection, so that that which is contrary to faith may be noted, Ps. XVIII. 3. Prov. XVIII. 10. Ps. LII. 9. Moses Kimchi also explains it thus, citing his brother David Kimchi, he places the Hebrew עפלה on a slope and watchtower so that he may be exalted there from the face of the enemy, and he does not return to God and does not ask of Him to rescue him, but the Dievian explanation is simpler, and those things which Cocceius introduces here concerning the Empire and the Roman Anti-Christ are very foreign. It is the mark of a good interpreter to bring the sense out of the text, not to bring it into the text, which latter thing is indeed very familiar to Cocceius. He imagines here, besides the restoration of the Israelite Church in its entirety, and the coming of Christ, that seven times of the N.T. Church, which he calls, and boasts that he has demonstrated from Moses himself in the consideration of the last things of Moses, are proposed. Which no one saw before him, nor perhaps will anyone see after, whether in this Prophet, or in the last words of Moses. Jerome explains it thus: But thus he will displease, who, when I promise, shall doubt that what I pledge will come to pass: thus the just man who shall have believed my promise will live by his faith. Likewise, if your faith shall have doubted and you shall have thought that what I pledge will not come, you will have as a great punishment that you will displease my soul. But the just man who believes my words, and does not doubt concerning these things which I promise, will have as a reward eternal life.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SCRIBE VISUM] Id quod tibi dicturus sum. O- mnis enim perceptio visus Hebræis dicitur. ET EXPLANA EUM SUPER TABULAS] באר est infinitivus pro adverbio, & recte à Græcis hic vertitur σαφῶς, quo sensu invenitur & Deuteron. XXVII. 8. Pro eum, pone istud: id est, visum istud. Sensus est, scribe, & quidem dilucide. UT PERCURRAT QUI LEGERIT EVM] Id est, ut statim assequatur, qui illud legerit, unde de plano legi posset, dicebant Latini. Vers. 3. QVIA ADHVC VISVS PROCUL] Visi il- lius impletio longe abest à Manassis tempore, ad tempora Cyri. Ideo vult perscribi visum, ut bene legi possit, & suo in Christum sermo sit Rom. I. 17. Gal. III. 11. quod- que ille ὁ ἐρχόμενος sit Christus Ebr. X. 38. ubi Gro- tius ignem in sensu vulgari, in sensu sublimiore Chri- stum intelligi vult. Sed illud de igne ἀλλότριον est; (ubi enim ignis mentio facta, & quis ille ignis est? Nisi σφάλμα sit & ignis loco Cyrus scribi de- buerit) nec gemini sensus ibi vestigium apparet. (9) sic interpretatus est S. Hieronymus h. l. Ipsa autem visio, de qua tibi dixi: scribe visionem & manifesta in buxo, ut possit persequi qui legit: ad- huc in tempore constituto est, de quo salvator ait: Tempore acceptabili exaudivi te & in die salutis au- xiliatus sum tibi. Et orietur in consummatione mun- di & in extrema diei hora, de qua loquitur & Iohan- nes: Filioli, nunc hora novissima est. Et non fru- stra veniet, salvabit enim multos, & cum reliquiis Israelitici populi multitudinem gentium congregabit. Quod si paululum se subtraxerit, & votis tuis, ô lector, qui legere juberis in buxo & in tabulis, quas Propheta descripsit, venire tardius visio cœ- perit, exspecta eam, quia veniens veniet, & non tardabit. Si autem dubitaverit fides tua & puta- veris non venire, quod spondeo, habebis pro grandi pœna, quod meæ animæ displicebis. Justus autem qui credit verbis meis, & de his non ambi- git quæ polliceor habebit, præmium vitam sempi- ternam. Hæc Hieronymus, juxta quem MANI- FESTA, ut habent verba ejus, in his de adventu Christi Prophetia est. Calvinus, etsi aliter expli- cet, fatetur tamen, multos referre hæc ad Christi adventum. R. Abarbanel agnoscit veteres Rabbi- nos v. 3. de Messiæ adventu accepifse, à quibus ipse quidem abit, sed à Coccejo castigatur ad h. l. Qui Calvino suo deserto, agnoscit promissionem hic de Christo haberi. Et verbis quidem priori- bus, adhuc erit visio, promissam esse restitutio- nem prophetiæ seu ministerii Ecclesiastici adeo- que consignificatam reductionem populi in ter- ram & restitutionem templi & urbis. Verbis au- tem sequentibus, quæ ita reddit ET PRÆCO ERIT IN FINE, qui non mentietur, exhiberi pro- missionem Messiæ. Præconem illum sive eloquu- torem esse Filium Dei, qui non commutabitur, id est, serius non venturus est, sed suo tempore, ad finem sc. illius præstituti termini. Ex Ebræis de Messia locum accepere autores tr. Sanhedrim in Thalmude in dist. Cheleck. R. Moses Maimonid. in Jad Chazakah. tract. de Regib. c. 12. R. Salomo, qui vocem פח etiam de Filio Dei λόγῳ & sermone Dei explicat, conferens locum Ps. XXXIII. 6. ubi Filius Dei Verbi nomine designatur. תפ ergo no- men Coccejo est, non verbum: quod & Ludovico de Dieu visum, qui reddit id LOQUENS, & R. Da- vid Kimchio in Michlol & Radicibus, qui fatetur esse תואר nomen. Præco, inquit Coccejus, oppo- nitur visioni. Visio est futuri: Præco, sive, si ma- vis cum Mercero, Locutor est is, qui non futura de- nunciat, sed rem & veritatem publicat. Est hic omni- no Εὐαγγελιστὴς, ἀναγγελέυς. Quis vero sit is præ- co sive eloquutor, facile apparere potest ex emphasi vocis, nimirum is, cujus est verba Dei eloqui; Patrem & ipsius consilium ἐξηγεῖσθαι enarrare: dicere Zioni. Ecce ego is qui loquitur, Esaiæ LII. 6. cujus est Evangelium annunciare mansuetis Esa. LXI. 1. 2. denique qui vocatur ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ Joh. I, 1. Apoc. XIX. 13. Idem à Mose appellatur Propheta Deut. XIIX. 15. ab Esaia Consiliarius. Esa. IX. 5. & testis nationum Esa. LV. 4. à Johanne ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστὸς testis fidelis Apoc. III. 14.

beant: ἐὰν ὑποστείληται, οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή µου ἐν αὐτῷ: quod sequitur divinus scriptor ad Hebræos X. 38. apparet eos legisse עֻפְּלָה & נפשו sensu optimo. Si quis defece- rit, in exspectando scilicet (nam עפל vertitur Græce per ἐκλείπειν & ὀλιγοψυχεῖν) is mihi non placebit. Dei sunt ver- ba ὑποστολὴ est minus facere quam oportet Actor. XX. 20. 27. Gal. II. [12. hinc ὑποστολὴ opponitur τῇ πίστει dicto capite ad Hebræos X. 39.

Præfert iterum Grotius textum Græcum E- bræo, rivulos fonti, quem corruptum esse imme- rito suspicatur. Aliter legisse LXX. Interpp. cer- to documento haud constat: quorum versionem, ceu receptam, quum sensus ratione non discrepa- ret à textu originario, sequutus est S. Apostolus Ebr. X. 39. Ludov. de Dieu optime eam responde- re textui Ebræo, ex usu vocis עפל Arabico docet, juxta quem ea est negligere, vel potius animum a- vertere ac subducere, ut sensus sit, si negligatur hæc promissio, jam animus ab eo avertatur, non placet sibi anima ejus in eo. Legit autem עפל per modum quendam interrogationis: Subductio sit? Quam significationem etiam observant in Num. XII. 44. LXX. ἐὰν ὑποστείληται, si subductio fiat, vel etiam, si subtraxerit quis sese, non placet sibi anima ejus (Messiæ) in eo: unde commodissime se habet anti- thesis: Justus autem fide sua vivet, qui cor suum non subducit, vel avertit à promissione de Messia, sed fide illum apprehendit, non modo placebit ipsi, sed fide illa sua æternum vivet. Alii reddunt vocem עפלה elatus est, superbit, & conciliant ita conver- sionem Græcam, qui se subtrahit per incredulitatem, ille etiam superbit, quia, ut credere est humilitatis, i- ta nulli credere est animi elati. Nec incommo- de B. Lutherus, was halsstarrig ist. Respicit nempe hos de quibus Propheta conqueritur, quod sese arguant, qui sc. fidem promissionibus adhibe- re renuunt, iisque pertinaciter contradicunt. Coc- cejus huc refert verbi ὑποστέλλεσθαι notionem Po- lybio familiarem, qua valet, se applicare munimen- to alicui ad securitatem, ut in militia fieri amat, si quis applicavit sese alteri, sc. rei præter Messiam ceu munimento & præsidio suo, ut ita notetur id, quod fidei est contrarium Ps. XIIX. 3. Prov. XIIX. 10. Ps. LII. 9. Ita explicat quoque Moses Kimchitus citante fratre Dav. Kimchio Ebræum עפלה ponit se in clivo & specula ut ibi sublimetur à facie inimici, neque redit ad Deum & non petit ab ipso, ut eri- piat eum, sed explicatio Dieviana simplicior est, & valde aliena sunt, quæ Coccejus hic de Imperio & Anti-Christo Romano ingerit. Boni interpretis est efferre sensum è textu, non inferre textui, quod vero posterius Coccejo perquam familiare est. Fingit hic, præter restitutionem Ecclesiæ Israeliti- cæ in integro, & adventum Christi, septem tempo- ra Ecclesiæ N. T. quæ vocat, & ex Mose ipso in consideratione ultimorum Mosis se demonstrasse jactitat, proposita esse. Quæ nemo ante ipsum vidit, nec fortassis quisquam post visurus est, si- ve in hoc Propheta, sive in verbis Mosis novissi- mis. Hieronymus ita exponit: Sic autem displice- bit ille, qui me promittente dubitaverit venturum es- se quod spondeo: ita justus qui crediderit promif- siori meæ vivet in fide sua. Item si autem dubi- taverit fides tua & putaveris non venire, quod spondeo, habebis pro grandi pœna, quod meæ a- nimæ displicebis. Justus autem qui credit verbis meis, & de his non ambigit, quæ polliceor, ha- bebit præmium vitam sempiternam.

## 2:4
Verse of the same. BUT THE JUST MAN SHALL LIVE BY HIS FAITH] The

writer to the Hebrews simply [writes] ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται, in the same way we now read at Romans I, 17. But in the time of Jerome it was read there ἐκ πίστεώς µου, as the LXX have it. Jerome noted that in his Commentary on this passage; therefore the Greeks read אמונתי, my faith, that is, in me, for

Verse 4.

BEHOLD, HE WHO IS UNBELIEVING, HIS SOUL SHALL NOT BE UPRIGHT IN HIMSELF] In the Hebrew, which we have, he who is arrogant. But since the LXX have Such Hebrew suffixes, as also Greek and Latin genitives, signify now the subject matter, now the object matter. 'The just shall live by my faith,' that is, he who is good and upright shall remain constant in the expectation of those things which I have said. The Hebrews say that all the precepts of the law are contained in this saying, namely because there is no surer way to all that obedience which is owed to God than to have full faith in God's promises and threats. And this is what Paul inculcates so often, that men are made just through faith, that is, they attain to that probity to which they could not attain by their own reasoning and labor.

Everything in the golden aphorism is perverted by the man Grotius, both the subject 'just' and the predicate 'shall live,' and the reason for the compound predicate, which is contained in the word אמונתו, and the Apostolic interpretation itself of the whole prophetic aphorism. He interprets the subject JUST as 'he who is good and upright.' But what the Holy Spirit in the New Testament explained concerning him who is justified through faith in Christ, and taught that it must be understood concerning the justice revealed in the Gospel χώρις έργων νόμυ [apart from the works of the law], Rom. 1. 17: 'For the justice of God is revealed in it (the Gospel of Christ) from faith to faith, as it is written: the just shall live by faith,' concerning which justice Rom. III. 21, 22: 'But now the justice of GOD is manifested without the works of the law, being witnessed' [μαρτυρεμένη] confirmed by the testimony of the Law and the Prophets, namely that justice of God which is through faith in Jesus Christ unto all and upon all who believe. It is therefore manifest that the just man is called [just] by the justice of God and the justification which he has obtained through faith, since the Prophetic passage is applied to him, which was also done in Gal. III. 11: 'But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for the just shall live by faith,' not to mention that some codices, such as the Plantinian and others, punctuate it thus, if you attend to the reason of the accents: 'the just shall live in his faith.' Which reading Cocceius prefers, so that, to wit, three things are indicated: (1) that through faith a man is constituted just, (2) that this faith is in Christ, so that the pronoun is referred to Christ, as in Is. XXVIII. 17, c. LIII. 11, Ps. II. 12, (3) that to this justice is annexed the hope of life. Grotius thus perverts the predicate, SHALL LIVE, that is, 'he shall remain in the expectation of those things which I have said.' But it is noted that the predicate signifies not the virtue of the just man, but the fruit of justice and of faith, life. And no one is ignorant of what it is to live (concerning which see Lev. XVIII. 5, Neh. IX. 29, Ps. XXII. 27, Is. LVIII. 9, c. XXVI. 1, cap. XXXIII. 11), nor does the Apostle allow us to be ignorant of it, when he compares with one another the voice of the law, 'he who shall do these things shall live in them,' and the voice of the Gospel comprehended here, 'The just shall live by faith,' Gal. III. 11. For the Apostle discourses concerning the reason of justification and of obtaining life and eternal salvation, concerning which also those words of the law are understood, Luke X. 28. Finally, the Prophetic oracle is explained most expressly concerning the περιποιήσᾔ ψυχῆς [preservation of the soul] unto life and eternal salvation, Heb. X. 38, 39. To which is opposed ἀπώλεια [destruction], eternal perdition. But where 'TO LIVE' is the same as constancy of mind, Grotius has not yet taught, nor will he ever teach. Nor indeed is it lawful to change the pronoun in the word אמונתו, or to convert the Vav into a Chireck. Nor did Jerome indicate that the LXX had read otherwise in their codices, or that it had once been written differently, but rather he noted the carelessness and error of them, and observed the agreement of all the remaining interpreters with the sources of Hebrew truth, where the LXX placed: 'But the just shall live by my faith,' all others equally translated 'shall live by his faith.' Finally, Symmachus, interpreting more significantly, says: 'But the just shall live by his own proper faith': which in Greek is said δίκαιος τῇ ἑαυτᾶ πίςει ζήσε). באמונתו, inasmuch as it is interpreted 'in his faith': if it had a ' and not a ו letter at the end as the LXX thought, and it were read באמונתי, they would have correctly translated 'in my faith.' But now the similarity of the letters ו and י, which differ from each other only by a measure, was the cause of the error. And although Rom. I. 17 Jerome may have read in his codex ἐκ πίσεώς μꙋ [by my faith], yet the Hebrew text is not to be corrected from that, but with Jerome leading the way, a reconciliation is to be established with the Hebrew: so that the sense may be in safety. For the faith by which we live is both ours subjectively and Christ's objectively. But all Greek codices now read constantly without the pronoun. Furthermore, that the promise or truth of God is wrongly understood by Grotius through the word אמונה, when rather the faith which is placed in the promise or divine truth should be understood, is clear both from the proper signification of this word, concerning which Cocceius rightly [says]: properly אמונה is sustentation or carrying, as from the etymology it can scarcely signify anything prior: by which one sustains oneself in another: and from the opposition: which is to turn the mind and heart away from the Lord, not to incline with the heart in Him: and from the interpretation of the New Testament, because it is explained through πίσιν [faith], and indeed that which relies on the word of the Gospel, Rom. I. 17, is the ὑπόςασις [substance/assurance] of things hoped for, Heb. XI. 1, and is opposed to τῇ ὑποςολῇ [withdrawal], when someone, having faith in the promise, does not sustain himself, but withdraws himself from faith, or from Evangelical truth through incredulity, or ἀποςασίαν [apostasy], and turns his mind away from the promise, and does not adhere to it: Whence the Jews likewise interpret the Prophetic aphorism concerning the faith which is placed in the divine promise, Kimchi and Abarbanel, who puts the conjugate מאמין [believing].

Now, when he gathers the Apostle's opinion from the mind of the Hebrews, is he not to be thought to follow blind guides? For what do those understand about the reason for our Justification before God, who are ignorant of the imputation of the righteousness of Christ as the formal cause of justification, and strive to set up their own righteousness: which the Apostle already complained of regarding the Jews of his own time in Rom. IX. & X. Nor indeed does the Apostle act in this way, when he teaches that we are justified by faith, as to how we may become upright, or attain to uprightness, but how we may be absolved from sins before the judgment and tribunal of God, and be accepted into grace, which he teaches and demonstrates is done through faith in the blood and merit of Christ, so that the righteousness and obedience of Christ is imputed to those who believe in Christ; nay, the Apostle even maintains and defends this against those who required our works also for justification. But here Grotius wished to gratify the Papists, to whose side he leans not obscurely in this difficult article concerning justification, as those things teach which he annotated on Cassander's consultation on article IV of the Augustan Confession: concerning which it was treated in the Exegesis of the Augustan Confession.

Latin:

Vers. eod. JVSTVS AVTEM IN FIDE SVA VIVET] Scri-

ptor ad Hebræos simpliciterἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται, eodem mo- do nunc legimus ad Romanos I, 17. At tempore Hierony- mi ibi legebatur ἐκ πίστεώς µου, quomodo habent LXX. no- tavit id Hieronymus in Commentario ad hunc locum, le- gerunt ergo Græci אמונתי, fide mea, id est, in me, nam

Vers. 4.

ECCE QUI INCREDULUS EST NON ERIT RECTA ANIMA EJVS IN SEMETIPSO] In Hebræo, quod nos habemus, qui arrogans est, Sed cum LXX. ha- affixa talia Hebræa, ut & genitivi Græci & Latini, modo rem subjectam, modo objectam significant. Justus in fide mea vivet id est, qui bonus probusq; est, manebit constans in expectatione eorum quæ dixi. Ajunt Hebræi omnia le- gis præcepta in hoc dicto contineri, nimirum quia nulla est certior ad eam omnem, quæ Deo debetur, obedientiam via, quam Dei promissis minisque fidem plenam habere. Et hoc est quod toties inculcat Paulus, per fidem homines ju- stos fieri, id est, pertingere ad eam probitatem, ad quam suapte ratiocinatione ac labore pertingere non possent.

Omnia in aureo aphorismo pervertuntur à chum Gro- tio, & subjectum justus & prædicatum vivet, ac ratio copulati prædicati, quæ in voce אמונתו con- tinetur & interpretatio ipsa Apostolica totius a- phoristi prophetici. Subjectum JUSTUS inter- pretatur, qui bonus probusq́; est. Quod vero Sp. S. in N. T. de eo qui justificatur per fidem in Chri- stüm exposuit, & de justitia in Evangelio χώρις έργων νόμυ revelata intelligendum esse docuit Rom. 1. 17. δικαιοσύνη γὰρ θεᾶ ἐν ἀυτῷ (ἐυαγγε- λίῳ τῷ χριστᾶ) ἀποκαλύπτε) ἐκ πίςεως εἰς πίσιν καθὼς γέγραπ) ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίςεως ζήσε) de qua justitia Rom. III. 21. 22. Nunc vero sine o- peribus legis manifestatur justitia DEI μαρτυρεμένη testitnonio comprobata à lege & Prophetis, justitia nempe illa Dei, quæ per fidem Jesu Christi est in o- mnes & super omnes credentes. Manifestum ergo est justum dici justitia Dei & justificatione, quam per fidem consequutus est, quum eo adhibeatur locus Propheticus, quod etiam factum Gal. III. 11. ὅτι δὲ ἐν νόμῳ ἐδεὶς δικαιᾶται παρὰ τῷ θεῷ δῆ- λον : ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίςεως ζήσε), ut taceam, quod nonnulli codices, ut Plantinianus & alii sic interpungant, fi accentuum rationem attendas: ju- stus in fide illius vivet. Quam lectionem præfert Coccejus, ut sc. indigitentur tria (1) quod per fi- dem homo constituatur justus, (2) quod ea fides fit in Christum, ut pronomen ad Christum referatur, uti Es. XXIIX. 17. c. LIII. 11. Ps. II. 12. (3) quod ei justitiæ an- nexa sit spes vitæ. Prædicatum sic pervertit Grotius, VIVET, id est, manebit in expectatione eorum, quæ dixi. At notatur prædicato non virtus justi, sed fructus justitiæ, & fidei, vita. Et nemo ignorat, quid sit vivere, (de quo vid. Lev. XIIX. 5. Neh. IX. 29. Ps. XXII. 27. Es. XIIX. 9. c. XXVI. 1. cap. XXXIII. 11.) neque id patitur nos ignorare Apo- stolus, cum inter se componit vocem legis, qui fe- cerit ea, vivet in eis, & vocem Evangelii hic com- prehensam Justus fide vivet Gal. III. 11. De ra- tione enim justificationis & consequendi vitam & salutem æternam, disserit Apostolus, de qua etiam legis illa verba intelliguntur Luc. X. 28. Denique expreffissime de περιποιήσᾔ ψυχῆς conservatione animæ ad vitam & salutem æternam explicatur oraculum Propheticum Ebr. X. 38. 39. Cui oppo- nitur ἀπώλεια interitus sempiternus. Ubi vero VIVERE idem sit quod constantia mentis, nondum docuit Grotius, nec docebit unquam. Neque ve- ro fas est immutare pronomen in voce אמונתו, aut Vav in Chireck convertere. Nec Hieronymus in- dicavit, aliter legisse LXX. in Codicibus suis, aut secus quondam scriptum fuisse, sed notavit potius παρέργεια & errorem ipsorum, atque observavit consensum reliquorum interpp. omnium, cum fontibus Ebraicæ veritatis, ubi LXX. posuerunt: Justus autem ex fide mea vivet, omnes æqualiter transtulerunt ex fide sua vivet. Denique Symma- chus significantius interpretans ait: Justus autem per fidem propriam suam vivet: quod Græce dici- tur δίκαιος τῇ ἑαυτᾶ πίςει ζήσε). באמונתו,quip- pe quod interpretatur in fide sua: si ' & non ו lite- ram haberet in fine ut LXX. putaverunt, & lege- retur באמונתי recte transtulissent in fide mea. Nunc autem similitudo literæ ו & י, quæ mensura tantum inter se distant causa erroris fuit. Et licet Rom. I. 17. Hieronymus in Codice suo legerit ἐκ πίσεώς μꙋ, non tamen inde corrigendus est Hebræus textus, sed Hieronymo præeunte, conciliatio insti- tuenda cum Ebræo: ut sensus in tuto sit. Nam fi- des, qua vivimus & nostra est subjective & Christi ob- jective. Sed Græci Codices omnes constanter nunc legunt sine pronomine. Porro per vocem אמונה perperam promissionem vel veritatem Dei à Grotio intelligi, quum potius fides, quæ locatur in promif- sionem, vel veritatem divinam intelligenda sit, lu- culentum est tum è vocis hujus propria significa- tione, de qua recte Coccejus: proprie אמונה est sustentatio sive gestatio, ut ex etymo vix quicquam prius significare possit: qua quis se in alio retineat: tum ex oppositione: quod est avertere animum & cor à Domino, non inclinare corde in ipso: tum ex interpretatione N. T. quia per πίσιν fidem expo- nitur, & quidem eam, quæ nititur verbo Evan- gelii Rom. I. 17. est ὑπόςασις τ̃ ἐλπιζομβύων Ebr. XI. 1. atque opponitur τῇ ὑποςολῇ substractioni cum quis fide promissioni habita se non sustentat, sed subtrahit se fidei, vel Evangelicæ veritati per incredulitatem, vel ἀποςασίαν, animumque a- vertit à promissione, non adhærescit eidem: Unde Judæi itidem de fide, quæ in promissionem divinam collocatur, aphorismum Propheticum interpre- tantur, Kimchius & Abarbanael, qui conjugatum ponit מאמין credens.

Jam Apostoli sententiam, cum ex Ebræorum men- te colligit, annon cæcos ductores sequi putandus est. Quid enim intelligunt illi de ratione Justifi- cationis nostræ coram Deo, qui formale justificatio- nis imputationem justitiæ Christi ignorant, ac pro- priam justitiam erigere satagunt: quod de Judæis sui temporis jam questus est Apostolus Rom. IX. & X. Neque vero id agit Apostolus, cum per fidem nos justificari docet, quomodo probi evadamus, aut ad probitatem pertingamus, sed quomodo coram judi- cio ac tribunali Dei a peccatis absolvamur, & in gratiam acceptemur, quod per fidem in sanguinem & meritum Christi fieri, ita ut credentibus in Christum justitia & obedientia Christi imputetur, docet, ac demonstrat; imo etiam tuetur Apostolus, ac de- fendit adversus eos, qui opera etiam nostra ad ju- stificationem requirebant. Sed gratificari hic voluit Grotius Papistis, ad quorum partes non ob- scure in arduo hoc articulo de justificatione incli- nat, ut ea docent, quæ ad Cassandri consultatio- nem artic. IV. August. C. annotavit: de quo in Exegemate August. C. actum.

## 2:5
Vers. 5. AND AS WINE DECEIVES THE DRINKER, SO SHALL THE PROUD MAN BE] Such as the Chaldeans, drunk on sweet fortune.

AND HE SHALL NOT BE ADORNED] He shall not remain in his state: just as the drunkard does not remain, who is accustomed to fall.

WHO HAS ENLARGED HIS SOUL AS HELL, AND HE IS AS DEATH, AND IS NOT FILLED] The Chaldeans labor under a certain insatiable thirst for kingdoms: and they are best compared to death, or τῷ ᾅδῃ, Prov. XXVII. 20. Thus the Latins say: the insatiable kingdom of Dis.

AND SHALL GATHER UNTO HIM ALL NATIONS, AND SHALL HEAP UNTO HIM ALL PEOPLES] Even if he were to force all nations to himself, and draw all peoples to himself.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET QVOMODO VINVM POTANTEM DECIPIT, SIC ERIT SVPERBVS] Quales Chaldæi, dulci fortuna ebrii.

ET NON DECORABITVR] Non permanebit in suo statu: sicut nec ebrius manet, qui soit.

QVI DILATAVIT QVASI INFERNVS ANI- MAM SVAM, ET IPSE QVASI MORS, ET NON ADIMPLETUR] Chaldæi laborant insatiabili quadam regnorum siti: & in ea morti, sive τῷ ᾅδῃ, optime compa- rantur, Prov. XXVII. 20. Sic Latini dicunt: regnum in- satiabile Ditis.

ET CONGREGABIT AD SE OMNES GEN- TES, ET COACERVABIT AD SE OMNES POPVLOS] Etiamsi ad se cogeret omnes gentes, omnesque populos ad se contraheret.

## 2:6
Vers. 6. SHALL NOT ALL THESE TAKE UP A PARABLE AGAINST HIM?] Is it not fair that so many peoples badly treated by the Chaldeans should at some time sing of the turned tables with certain learned sayings? All sharp, or witty, or sententious sayings are משלים to the Hebrews.

AND THE SPEECH OF HIS RIDDLES] In the Hebrew: interpretation of riddles to him: that is, about him. He calls general maxims riddles, which the peoples will adapt to the Chaldeans.

AND IT SHALL BE SAID] By saying. A saying of Menander: WOE TO HIM WHO MULTIPLIES WHAT IS NOT HIS] A similar say- ing: pleonexia is the greatest evil for men. For those who wish to acquire more, while losing what they have, often fail, being overcome. And they add their own things to the things of others.

HOW LONG AND HE HEAPETH UP AGAINST HIMSELF THICK CLAY] To himself: עליו, how long shall he finish heaping up for himself such a force of clay, that is, of gold and silver: for as Naumachus says: χρυσὸς τοι κόνις ἐστὶ καὶ ἄργυρος. In Hebrew הכביד, is also to multiply.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NVMQVID NON OMNES ISTI, SVPER EVM PARABOLAM SVMENT?] Nonne æquum est, ut tot populi à Chaldæis male tractati aliquando versas vi- ces doctis quibusdam dictis decantent? omnia dicta a- cuta, aut lepida, aut sententiosa, sunt משלים Hebræis.

ET LOQVELAM ÆNIGMATVM EJVS] In Hebræo: interpretatione ænigmatum ei: id est, de eo. Ænig- mata vocat generales sententias, quas populi Chaldæis a- ptabunt.

ET DICETVR] Di endo. (ctum Menandri: VÆ EI QVI MVLTIPLICAT NON SVA] Simile di- Πλεονεξία μέγιστον ἀνθρώποις κακόν. Οἱ γὰρ θέλοντες προσλαβεῖν, τὰ δ᾽ ἀπόλλυας Ἀποτυγχάνουσι πολλάκις νικώμενοι. Τὰ δ᾽ ἴδια προστιθέασι τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις.

USQUEQUO ET AGGRAVAT CONTRA SE DENSUM LUTUM] Ad se: עליו, quousque ille sibi fi- neretur coacervare tantam vim luti, id est, auri & argen- ti: nam ut ait Naumachus: χρυσὸς τοι κόνις ἐστὶ καὶ ἄργυρος. Hebraeis הכביד, est etiam multiplicare.

## 2:7
Vers. 7.

SHALL THEY NOT RISE UP SUDDENLY THAT SHALL BITE THEE?] Was it not just that the Medes and Persians should rise up against thee, who might bite thee?

AND THEY SHALL BE RAISED UP THAT SHALL TEAR THEE AND THOU SHALT BE A SPOIL UNTO THEM] And that they should rise up against thee who would tear thee, and to whom thou wouldst be a prey?

Latin:

Vers. 7.

NUMQUID NON REPENTE CONSURGENT QUI MORDEANT TE?] Annon aequum fuit, ut con- surgerent adversus te Medi & Persae, qui te mordeant?

ET SUSCITABUNTUR LACERANTES TE ET ERIS IN RAPINAM EIS] Et ut surgerent contra te qui te lacerarent, ac quibus tu praeda esses?

## 2:8
Vers. 8.

BECAUSE THOU HAST SPOILED MANY NATIONS, ALL THAT SHALL BE LEFT OF THE PEOPLE SHALL SPOIL THEE] All other peoples. For very many nations, even Scythian ones, were in the army of Cyrus.

FOR THE BLOOD OF MAN] Very many slaughters.

AND THE INIQUITY OF THE LAND OF THE CITY, AND OF ALL THAT DWELL THEREIN] And the plundering of the land, (that is, of the lands) of the city, (that is, of the cities) and of all dwelling in it (that is, in those cities). You see that not all things which are said to be done according to the law of nations are held as lawful before God; but the cause and the manner are considered.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

QUIA TU SPOLIASTI GENTES MULTAS, SPOLIABUNT TE OMNES QUI RELIQUI FUE- RINT DE POPULIS] Omnes populi alii. Plurimae enim gentes etiam Scythicae fuere in Cyri exercitu.

PROPTER SANGUINEM HOMINIS] Caedes plurimas.

ET INIQUITATEM TERRAE CIVITATIS, ET OMNIUM HABITANTIUM IN EA] Et direptionem terrae, (id est, terrarum) civitatis, (idest, urbium) & omnium in ea (id est, in eis urbibus) habitantium. Vides non o- mnia quae ex gentium jure fieri dicuntur, apud Deum pro licitis haberi; sed spectari causam & modum.

## 2:9
Vers. 9.

WOE TO HIM THAT GATHERETH AN EVIL COVETOUSNESS TO HIS HOUSE] In the Hebrew: Woe to him who covets an evil covetousness for his house: that is, scraping together unjust wealth for his house, as the Chaldean interprets it. To the Hebrews, every unjust action which does not have its own name is called covetousness.

THAT HIS NEST MAY BE IN A HIGH PLACE, AND HE THINKS TO BE DELIVERED FROM THE HAND OF EVIL] That he may place his nest in high places. Birds are safe which nest in inaccessible cliffs. Thus the Chaldeans, who held very many places defended by their situation and works, thought themselves to be out of danger. The hand of evil here is the force of enemies.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

VAE QUI CONGREGAT AVARITIAM MA- LAM DOMUI SUAE] In Hebraeo: Vae concupiscenti con- cupiscentiam malam domui suae: id est, corradenti opes in- jurias domi suae, ut interpretatur Chaldaeus. Hebraeis o- mnis actio injusta, quae proprium nomen non habet, di- citur concupiscentia.

UT SIT IN EXCELSO NIDUS EJUS, ET LI- BERARI SE PUTAT DE MANU MALI] Ut ponat in locis celsis nidum suum. Aves tutae sunt, quae in rupibus in- accessis nidificant. Sic Chaldaei, qui plurima tenebant loca situ & operibus defensa, putabant se extra periculum esse. Manus mali hic est vis hostium.

## 2:10
Verse 10.

YOU HAVE DEVISED CONFUSION FOR YOUR HOUSE] That is, you have taken counsel for the downfall of your house, that is, of your fatherland, O Chaldean.

YOU HAVE CUT OFF [MANY] PEOPLES קצות to strip the bark. Therefore the Chaldean here translates, you have despoiled. The LXX: συνεπέρανας.

AND YOUR SOUL HAS SINNED] And your sinful soul: that is, sinning has turned into nature for you by habit.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

COGITASTI CONFUSIONEM DOMUI TUAE] Id est, consilia cepisti in domus tuae cafura pedecus, id est, patriae tuae, o Chaldaee.

CONCIDISTI POPULOS [MULTOS] קצות decorticare. Ideo Chaldaeus hic vertit, spoliasti. LXX. συνεπέρανας.

ET PECCAVIT ANIMA TUA] Et peccatrix ani- ma tua: id est, peccare tioi ex consuetudine in naturam vertit.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

FOR THE STONE SHALL CRY OUT FROM THE WALL, AND THE TIMBER THAT IS BETWEEN THE JOINTS OF THE BUILDINGS SHALL ANSWER] It shall bear witness. For because testimonies were rendered to an interrogation, therefore ענה is used for to testify, even in the Decalogue. It is asked what כפיס is. All the Greeks except the LXX translated it συνδεσμόν, and Jerome thinks that is what the Greeks commonly call ἱμάντωσιν, which word Suidas interprets as δέσιν ξύλων. The LXX here placed κάνθαρον, but the Chaldean [placed] segmentum: in which sense כפיס is also taken in other Chaldean books. Thus the sense will be: the testimony of your injustices is rendered by so many walls of demolished cities, so many fragments of buildings.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

QUIA LAPIS DE PARIETE CLAMABIT, ET LIGNUM QUOD INTER JUNCTURAS AEDIFI- CIORUM EST, RESPONDEBIT] Testabitur. Nam quia ad interrogationem reddebantur testimonia, ideo ענה ponitur pro testari, etiam in Decalogo. כפיס quid sit, quaeritur. Graeci omnes praeter LXX. transtulere συνδε- σμόν, idque Hieronymus putat esse, quod vulgo Graeci vo- cant ἱμάντωσιν, quam vocem Suidas interpretatur, δέσιν ξύλων. LXX. hic posuere κάνθαρον, Chaldaeus vero segmen tum: quo sensu etiam in aliis libris Chaldaicis sumitur כפיס. Ita sensus erit: tuae injustitiae restimonium red- dunt tot muri urbium dejecti, tot aedium fragmenta.

## 2:12
Verse 12. WOE TO HIM WHO BUILDS A CITY IN BLOOD, AND PREPARES A CITY IN INIQUITY] Woe to the Chaldeans, who increased Babylon from the ruins of other cities that had deserved no such thing.

Latin:

Vers. 12. VAE QUI AEDIFICAT CIVITATEM IN SANGUINIBUS, ET PRAEPARAT URBEM IN INI- QUITATE] Vae Chaldaeis, qui ex aliarum urbium, nihil tale commeritarum, ruinis Babylona auxerunt.

## 2:13
Verse 13.

ARE THESE NOT FROM THE LORD OF HOSTS] Shall this not be from the Lord of hosts? Namely, this which follows.

FOR THE PEOPLES SHALL LABOR IN MUCH FIRE] So that the peoples have labored in much fire. That is, so that the Chaldeans have prepared those works of Babylon for the flame.

AND THE NATIONS FOR NOTHING, AND THEY SHALL FAIL] And so that the nations have wearied themselves utterly in vain: so that they have built those things for no use of their own.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

NUMQUID NON HAEC SUNT A DOMINO EXERCITUUM] Annon hoc erit a Domino exercituum? nempe hoc quod sequitur.

LABORABUNT ENIM POPULI IN MULTO IGNE] Ut multo igne laboraverint populi. Id est, het ut Chaldaei ista Babylonis opera flammae paraverint.

ET GENTES IN VACUUM, ET DEFICIENT] Et ut gentes plane in vanum se laffaverint: ut nulli suo usui ista exstruxerint.

## 2:14
Verse 14.

[FOR THE EARTH SHALL BE FILLED, THAT THEY MAY KNOW THE GLORY OF THE LORD, AS THE WATERS COVER THE SEA] There is a transposition here, and an ἔλλειψις besides, which may be explained thus: For just as waters cover the bed of the sea, so the Babylonian land shall be filled with armies, so that the justice of GOD against the Chaldeans may appear to all nations.

That explanation of the ἐλλείψις is not approved; rather, as it appears from a similar place in Is. XI. 9, it should be explained thus: just as the waters of the sea cover the bed, so in Is. XI. 9 the earth shall be filled with the knowledge and cognition of the glory of the Lord. For after Cyrus conquered Babylon, the earth began to be filled with the glory of the Lord, when he promulgated an edict throughout the whole kingdom: 'The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem' (2 Chron. XXXVI. 23; Ezra I. 2). From there, furthermore, that diffusion of divine glory throughout the world can be extended to the times of Christ, concerning which Isaiah prophesied in the cited passage, which Calvin himself acknowledged here: (The Prophet) compares this fullness of knowledge to the waters of the sea, because, as we know, the sea is so deep that there is no measure of the waters: so Habakkuk signifies that the glory of God will be so illustrious that it will not only fill the earth, but in a way also overwhelm it; just as the waters of the sea cover the abysses with a huge multitude, so also the glory of God will fill heaven and earth, so that there is no end. Although if one wishes to extend this sentiment to the very coming of Christ, I do not object. For we know that the grace of redemption flowed in a perpetual course until Christ appeared to the world.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

QUIA REPLEBITUR TERRA, UT COGNO- SCANT GLORIAM DOMINI, QUASI AQUAE O- PERIENTES MARE] Est hic trajectio, & ἔλλειψις praete- rea, quam sic explicare liceat: Nam sicut aquae alveum maris operiunt, ita terra Babylonica implebitur exerciti bus, ut DEI justitia in Chaldaeos omnibus gentibus ap- pareat.

Non probatur ista ἐλλείψεως explicatio, imo An bic elli- è loco simili Es. XI. 9. apparet, ita potius eam ex-psis. plendam esse, sicut aquae maris alveum operiunt, ita Esa. XI. 9. terra implebitur scientia & cognitione gloria Domini: Postquam enim Babylonem expugnavit Cyrus, replevi cepit terra gloria Domini, ubi ille edictum per universum regnum promulgavit, omnia regna terrae dedit mihi Iehovah, Deus caeli & ipse praecepit mihi ut ei aedificem in Jerusalem 2. Par. XXXVI. 26. Esdr. I. 2. Inde porro ad tempora Christi exten- di potest illa gloriae divinae per orbem diffusio, de quibus Esaias loco laudato vaticinatus est, quod hic Calvinus ipse agnovit: Comparat (Propheta) hanc plenitudinem notitiae aquis maris, quia, sicuti scimus, mare tam profundum est, ut nulla sit aquarum mensura: ita significat Habacuc tam illustrem fore gloriam Dei, ut terram ipsam non modo impleat, sed quodammodo etiam obruat, quemadmodum a- quae maris ingenti multitudine operiunt abyssos, ita etiam gloria Dei calum & terram replebit, ut nul- lus sit finis. Quanquam si ad Christi usque adven- tum extendere sententiam hanc libeat, non reclamo. Scimus enim gratiam redemtionis perpetuo tenore fluxisse, donec Christus apparuit mundo.

## 2:15
Vers. 15.

[WOE TO HIM WHO GIVES DRINK TO HIS NEIGHBOR, POURING OUT HIS GALL, AND MAKING HIM DRUNK, THAT HE MAY LOOK ON HIS NAKEDNESS] The ancients vary here: because מספח and חמת are not taken in one way. This seems the best exposition: Woe to you who offer your hot wine to your closest friend, to make him drunk, then look upon his private parts. That is, that you may abuse him, which was frequent enough in the East in those times, but through this ἀναγωγία is understood the treachery of the Chaldeans, who enticed peoples with treaties, whom they then treated most ignominiously.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

VAE QUI POTUM DAT AMICO SUO, MIT- TENS FEL SUUM, ET INEBRIANS, UT ADSPI- CIAT NUDITATEM EJUS] Variant hic veteres: quia מספח & חמת non uno modo sumuntur. Optima ex- positio haec videtur: Vae tibi qui propinas amico conjunctissi- mo vinum tuum calidum, ut inebries eum, deinde adspicias ejus pudenda. Id est, ut cum percidas, quod illis tem- poribus satis frequens in Oriente, sed per hanc ἀναγωγίαν intelligitur perfidia Chaldaeorum, qui foederibus illiciebant, populos, quos deinde tractabant ignominiofissime.

## 2:16
Vers. 16. YOU ARE FILLED WITH SHAME FOR GLORY. These things the peoples say, rejoicing because the Chaldeans, the tamers of nations, have been tamed.

DRINK YOU ALSO] Of the cup of the wrath of God, as the following things explain. Jer. XXV. 17 and following.

AND BE UNCIRCUMCISED] He reads הרעל but our Codices have הערל. ערל is properly to remove the foreskin: metaphorically it is drawn to every uncovering. The sense is, you also are an uncoverer: as you uncovered others, that is, you are an uncoverer.

Grotius followed his Capellus here, but Buxtorf has already answered him in his Vindiciae, p. 266. He (the Vulgate) does not read it so in his codex, but accepted it by transposition as if here ערל meant the same as רעל, as has been observed in many others. And thus some Hebrews explain it, as Kimchi advises, whom see. Abarbenel also writes that הערל is from the meaning of הרעלה as if he were saying 'drink from the cup of stupor'.

[THE CUP OF THE LORD'S RIGHT HAND SHALL COME AROUND TO YOU] In the Hebrew: It shall turn itself upon you. Just as we say: the bottom of the wine-jar is turned. The sense is: you will drink the whole cup, so that when drained it can be turned.

AND SHAMEFUL VOMITING UPON YOUR GLORY] Filthy vomiting shall come upon your ornament. That is, you shall behave most shamefully in that calamity. Jer. XXV. 27.

Latin:

Vers. 16. REPLETUS ES IGNOMINIA PRO GLO- RIA] Haec dicunt gaudentes populi, ob domitos Chal- daeos gentium domitores.

BIBE TU QUOQUE] De calice irae Dei, ut se- quentia expi cant. Jer. XXV. 17. & fequentibus.

ET CONSOPJIRE] Legit הרעל at nostri Codices habent הערל. Est ערל proprie abducere praeputium: μεταφορικῶς ad omnem nudationem trahitur. Sensus est, nudator & tu: ut nudasti alios, id est, illuostor.

Sequutus hic Grotius est suum Capellum, sed respondit ei jam Buxtorfius in Vindiciis p. 266. Non ita legit (vulgatus) in suo codice, sed per transpo- sitionem accepit quasi hic ערל idem significaret, quod רעלut in pluribus aliis observatum. Et sic explicant quidam Hebraei, ut monet Kimchius, quem vide. A- barbenel etiam scribit הערל esse ex significatione הרעלה quasi diceret bibe ex calice soporis.

CIRCUMDABIT TE CALIX DEXTERAE DO- MINI] In Hebraeo: Vertet se super te. Sicut dicimus: vertitur Oenophoris fundus. Sensus est: totum calicem ebibes, ita ut ficcatus verti possit.

ET VOMITVS IGNOMINIAE SVPER GLO- RIAM TVAM] Vomitus foedus super ornatum tuum veniet. Id est, turpiffime te geras in illa calamitate Jer. XXV. 27.

## 2:17
Vers. 17.

FOR THE INIQUITY OF LIBANUS SHALL COVER THEE] The punishment of the destroyed temple, which is called Libanus, because it consisted for the greatest part of the cedars of Libanus. This appears in Ezech. XVII. 3. & Zach. XI. 1. nor did the Chaldean understand it otherwise here.

AND THE DEVASTATION OF ANIMALS SHALL TERRIFY THEM] The devastation of wild beasts (that is, such as wild beasts produce) shall crush those things: namely, those which the Chaldeans built, concerning which [see] above 12.

FOR THE BLOODS OF MEN] On account of human blood, as above 8. for he repeats what he had said there, but adapts it more specifically to the Jews, the land of Judea, and Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

QUIA INIQUITAS LIBANI OPERIET TE] Poenam seres destructi templi, quod Libanus vocatur, quia maximam partem ex cedris Libani constabat. Ap- paret id Ezech. XVII. 3. & Zach. XI. 1. nec aliter hic accepit Chaldaeus.

ET VASTITAS ANIMALIUM DETERREBIT EOS] Vastitas ferarum (id est, qualem edunt ferae) conte- ret illa: nempe quae struxerunt Chaldaei, de quibus supra 12.

DE SANGVINIBUS HOMINUM] Propter san- guinem humanum, ut supra 8. nam repetit quae ibi dixe- rat, sed specialius aptat ad Judaeos, terram Judaeam, & Hierosolyma.

## 2:18
Vers. 18.

WHAT PROFITETH THE GRAVEN THING] The Jews will say this: what have the images of gods profited the Chaldeans?

…FOR THE MAKER THEREOF HATH GRAVEN IT, A MOLTEN THING, AND A FALSE IMAGE] Which its craftsman made, a molten work, namely a document of falsehood. Rightly: because the true divinity was not in it, which nevertheless the deceived men thought was

BECAUSE HE HOPED IN THE FIGMENT OF HIS MAKER] Yet his maker placed his hope in the work. THAT HE MIGHT MAKE DUMB IDOLS] Although he had made dumb idols. Vers. 19. WOE TO HIM WHO SAYS TO WOOD, AWAKE: ARISE TO THE SILENT STONE] Deservedly it will be ill for such foolish men, who hope for an audience for their prayers from deaf things. WILL HE BE ABLE TO TEACH?] That very thing teaches you: namely, that it is deaf. BEHOLD THIS ONE IS COVERED WITH GOLD AND SILVER] It is indeed overlaid with gold or silver. Isa. XL. 18. Jerem. X, 4. AND EVERY SPIRIT IS NOT IN ITS BOWELS] But there is no life in them. Vers. 20. BUT THE LORD IS IN THY HOLY TEMPLE] But God (is not such, but) dwells in that most holy temple. That is, in heaven: from there He both looks down and governs all things. See Ps. CXV. 3. Jon. II, 8. Mich. I, 2. The temple which was at Jerusalem bore the figure of His temple. LET ALL THE EARTH KEEP SILENCE BEFORE HIS FACE] That is, let it fear Him, just as here the Greeks [Greek: εὐλαβείσθω ἀπὸ προσώπυ αὐτὲ πᾶσα ἡ γῆ]. It is a Hebrew locution, which you will find also in 1 Macc. 1, 3. Others explain it concerning the Messiah, whose promise was made in v. 4. A similar passage, Zach. II. 12, 13, favors them. Thus Blessed Wigandus: It is an antithesis and a consolation concerning Christ being sent, who was to teach in the second Jerusalem temple. Even if they plot the utter destruction of the Jews, yet that cannot be prevented. Let all the pious sustain themselves with this consolation. (Let it keep silence) Then there will be peace, there will be no movements, tumults, incursions. Thus when Christ was born of Mary in Bethlehem, a nourishing peace served Him as it were. For there was tranquility in almost the whole world, with Augustus governing the Roman empire.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

QUID PRODEST SCULPTILE] Hoc dicent Ju- daei: quid profuere Chaldaeis imagines deorum?

QUIA SCULPSIT ILLUD FICTOR SUUS, CONFLATILE, ET IMAGINEM FALSAM] Quod fecit faber suus, conflatile opus, nempe documentum menda- cii. Recte: quia verum numen non inerat, quod tamen pecepti homines putabant,

QUIA SPERAVIT IN FIGMENTO FICTOR EJUS] Attamen spem posuit in opere opifex suus. UT FACERET SIMULACHRA MUTA] Cum tamen fecisset simulachra muta. Vers. 19. VÆ QUI DICIT LIGNO, EXPERGISCERE: SURGE LAPIDI TACENTI] Merito male erit homini- bus tam stultis, qui precibus suis audientiam sperant a re- bus surdis. NUMQUID IPSE DOCERE POTERIT?] Ipsum illud te docet: nempe se esse surdum. ECCE ISTE COOPERTUS EST AURO AR- GENTO] Obductum quidem est auro vel argento. Esa. XL. 18. Jerem. X, 4. ET OMNIS SPIRITUS NON EST IN VISCE- RIBUS EJUS] Sed nulla vita est in ipsis. Vers. 20. DOMINUS AUTEM IN TEMPLO SAN- CTO TUO] At Deus (non est talis, sed) in templo illo san- ctissimo habitat. Id est, in cœlo: inde & despicit & guber- nat omnia. Vide Ps. CXV. 3. Jon. II, 8. Mich. I, 2. Ejus tem- pli figuram gerebat templum, quod erat Hierosolymis. SILEAT A FACIE EJUS OMNIS TERRA] Id est, timeat eum, quomodo hic Græci εὐλαβείσθω ἀπὸ προσώ- πυ αὐτὲ πᾶσα ἡ γῆ. Locutio est Hebraica, quam reperies & 1. Macc. 1, 3. Alii de Messia explicant, cujus promissio v. 4. facta. Quibus favet locus similis Zach. II. 12. 13. Ita B. Wigandus: Antithessi est & consolatio de Christo mittendo, qui in templo Hierosolymitano se- cundo sit docturus. Etsiamsi machinentur extremam internecionem Judæis, tamen id prohiberi non posse. Hac consolatione sustentent se omnes pii. (Sileat) Tum erit pax, non erunt motus, tumultus, in- cursiones. Sic Christo nato ex Maria in Bethlehem, alma pax ei quasi famulata est. Nam toto pene or- be tranquillitas extitit, Augusto imperium Roma moderante.

## 3:1 Argument
PART II. PRAYERFUL. CHAPTER III. A prayer for the pious and innocent. Terrified by the revelation of evils, he seeks the grace of GOD, lest He deal with the people by strict law, having brought forward the former benefits of GOD concerning the promulgation of the law, and the plagues of Egypt, in the waters of the Red Sea and those divided, as well as those granted to David, as also the most grave evils then imminent, and his declared confidence that in such great evils he may rejoice in the LORD JESUS, and hope for liberation. GOD, just in His wrath, is worshipped with praises and prayers.

Vers. 1. A PRAYER OF HABAKKUK THE PROPHET FOR IGNORANCES] A song of the prophet Habakkuk to the melodies of an ancient Canticle, which began with [Hebrew: שגיונות]. That it is a song is apparent from the word [Hebrew: סלה] below, which is found only in the Psalms.

This opinion concerning an ancient Canticle is not approved. For the Holy Spirit is not accustomed to adorn His songs to the melodies of any vulgar ditty. Simpler seems the opinion of those who interpret it according to erratic or mixed odes, from which class the inequality of the verses shows the song of Habakkuk to have been. Which Blessed Tarnovius followed in the title of Ps. VII, namely, that an erratic ode is denoted by that word (which also occurs in that title of the Psalm), which consists not of one or another certain kind of meter, but of variously intercurrent ones, whence those to whom that method of song was less known easily induced their minds to believe that there was an error in it, just as Horace said concerning the opinion of the vulgar about Pindar, that he was carried by numbers released from law, which for the same reason Ausonius called numberless numbers. See Commentary on some Psalms p. 143. Concerning the version of Blessed Luther for the innocent, he observes the same at this place. he observes that since in Hebrew it is not a concrete but an abstract, and the Hebrew word does not properly signify innocence (which is denoted by the word [Hebrew: נקיין] Ps. XXVI. 6.), by his own grave judgment he preferred to follow the Greek Interpreters here rather than the points of the Hebrew text, and thus wished to render it so that he might explain it better and more easily: and thus, with the sense of the argument expressed, he had no concern for that word: since this prayer for the pious and innocent was poured forth and written by the Prophet.

Latin:

PARS II. PRECATORIA. CAPUT III. Oratio pro piis atque innocentibus. Perterrefactus revelatione malorum gratiam DEI ex- petit, ne stricto jure cum populo agat, adductis pristinis DEI beneficiis circa legis promulgatio- nem, & plagas Ægypti, in aquis maris rubri & diffissis, nec non Davidi præstitis, ut & gravissi- mis tum imminentibus malis, & declarata fiducia sua, quod in tantis malis in DOMINO JESU gaudeat, ac liberationem speret. Laudibus & precibus colitur DEUS æquus in ira.

Vers. 1. ORATIO HABACUC PROPHETÆ PRO IGNORANTIIS] Carmen Habacuci prophetæ ad mo- dulos veteris Cantici, quod incipiebat שגיונות. Carmen esse, apparet ex voce סלה infra, quæ nonnisi in Psalmis invenitur.

Non probatur hæc sententia de veteri Cantico. Nam non solet Sp. S. ad modulos alicujus cantile- næ vulgaris adornare cantica sua. Simplicior eo- rum videtur opinio, qui interpretantur juxta Odas erraticas, seu mixtas, ex quarum genere fuisse car- men Habacuc inæqualitas versuum docet. Quam B. Tarnovius sequutus est in titulo Psal. VII. oden nempe erraticam illa voce (quæ in isto titulo Psal- mi etiam occurrit,) notari, quæ non uno tan- tum aut altero certo metrorum genere, sed ex varie intercurrentibus constat, unde quibus illa carminis ratio fuit minus cognita, in ea erratum fuisse, facile sibi in animum induxerunt, quemad- modum ex vulgi opinione de Pindaro dicebat Ho- ratius, illum numeris ferri lege solutis, quos eadem de causa numeros innumeros vocabat Ausonius. Vid. Commentar. in aliquot Psalmos p. 143. De B. Luther. versione für die Unschuldigen idem ad h. l. observat, quod quum in Ebræo non sit con- cretum sed abstractum, neque proprie vox Ebræa innocentiam (quæ denotatur voce נקיין Ps. XXVI. 6.) significet, suo consilio gravi Græcos Interpp. potius hic, quam apices textus Ebræi sequutus ita reddere voluerit, ut eum melius atque facilius ex- plicaret: atque ita sensu argumenti expresso, cura ei de verbo isto non fuerit: Siquidem oratio hæc pro piis atque innocentibus à Propheta fusa, atque scripta sit.

## 3:2
Vers. 2.

O LORD, I HAVE HEARD THY HEARING, AND I FEARED] Habakkuk responds to the revelation already received, and says: O Lord, I have heard Thy words, I have stood in awe: acknowledging Thy supreme justice, first against the Jews, then also against the Chaldeans.

O LORD, VIVIFY THY WORK IN THE MIDST OF THE YEARS] That [Hebrew: תחייהו] according to the Hebrew custom, when the prophet had known by divine revelation that the interval of time would be short between the devastation of Judea and the punishments to be inflicted upon the Chaldeans, he prays to God that in the middle time He may preserve His work, that is, the Jewish people. Indeed all men are the work of God, but the Jews peculiarly so, whom GOD, having led them out of Egypt, made a people and instructed with laws. The Greeks, for [Hebrew: שנים] read [Hebrew: חיים] in this place, for they translate it in the midst of two living creatures, which they seem to have understood concerning those celestial powers which are [Hebrew: חיות] in Ezekiel. For the various ways in which Christians have interpreted these things, see Jerome.

That the Jews are understood by the work of the Lord is without example. Although the Jews are peculiarly appropriated to God, yet the work of the Lord, as far as I know, never denotes the Jews. Osiander renders it: Exercise Thy proper work, which is to do good, toward us, and succor us in the midst of tribulation. More conveniently, the liberation of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity is understood by the work of the Lord, which the Prophet asks to be vivified and fulfilled. Since the Hebrews are accustomed to give life even to inanimate things, years, days, the air, fertility, liberation: when those things are and flourish, they are said by the Hebrews to be vivified and to live. R. Solomon explains it in a nearly similar way: Vivify Thy former work, by which Thou wast avenging us from our enemies, in the midst of the years of anguish in which we were dwelling, vivify, that is, resuscitate, and bring it back by postliminy. The words IN THE MIDST of the years of this calamity, Vatablus explains thus, when dangers shall rush in more violently, when with the waves of calamities flowing around on every side no hope of emerging shall shine forth: where the middle of the shadow of death Ps. XXIII. 4. others [explain it as] in the midst of the years, that is, within the preordained and destined years. B. Winckelmann explains in the midst of the years as in the greatest necessities, or even at the just and opportune time. That the LXX Interpreters read it otherwise is to be imputed not so much to the variety of the Codices as to their own ἀβλεψίᾳ [inattention], or excessive license (if they translated it so themselves). For Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, the Chaldean, and others agree with the Hebrew truth here and confirm it. What some relate here concerning the prophetic spirit of the seventy elders, or suspect concerning the distinction of Keri and Ketif in this place, deserves no credence. Those interpreters were subject to various lapses (which their translation proves too much), not the prophets: nor does any trace of that diverse textual and marginal reading appear in this text. From wherever those two animals finally crept in, the Hebrew truth is certainly not to be called into doubt. Indeed, the Vatican, Complutensian, Royal, and other Codices, along with Jerome, Cyril, and Theodoret, testify that the LXX Interpreters had שנים years in their Codices, because they added, when the years shall have approached, you shall be known, when the time shall have arrived, you shall be demonstrated.
