Christoph. à Castro notes the LXX. that the Vulgate, the Chaldean, the Tigurines, and Paghinus explain the Word as if it were a subject, and join it with the following verb, My Word & My Spirit will be in your midst, provided it is established that the article את is also joined to the nominative, as in 2 Kings VI, & the iron fell into the water. The gloss of the Jews, although Cornelius approves the same, is mere σρεβλότης: for they draw the imperative DO from the preceding parts to that את הדבר, i.e., do the word, i.e., the law, which I demand upon entering the covenant, I in turn will perform what I promised. Thus they tear apart the text, they snatch the word from elsewhere to this place, they insert a parenthesis: DO (since I am with you, says the Lord of hosts) THE WORD, which I have struck, and they confuse the promise with the precept, and finally transform an absolute promise into a hypothetical one. See Coccejus on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 6. VERBUM QUOD PEPIGI VOBISCUM CUM EGREDEREMINI DE TERRA ÆGYPTI] Præ- stabo vobis eadem, quæ majoribus vestris de Ægypto e- gredientibus promisi Exod. XV. 26. Jer. VII. 23.

ET SPIRITUS MEUS ERIT IN MEDIO VE- STRUM] Id est, habebitis Prophetas Aggæum, Zacha- riam, Malachiam. Ita Chaldæus recte.

De VERBO ὑποϛατικῶ & SPIRITUS SANCTO secunda & tertia divinitatis persona non ignobiles Interpp. accipiunt, ut habeatur hic S. S. Trinit. mysterium: Loquitur enim hic Deus Pater & promittit suam populo præsentiam, nec non verbi sui & Spiritus Sancti. Coccejus cla- rum hoc esse censet, magnum hic testimonium habe- ri de tribus Testibus. Et nisi reddantur verba: Ego vobiscum cum verbo, & Spiritus meus stat in medio vestri, contorta fore omnia & luxata. Red- dit autem CUM VERBO QUOD PROMISI VOBIS, cum exiretis ex Ægypto, ut indigitetur an- gelus fœderis, h. e. sponsor, interpres & applicator fœ- deris, & אֲשֶׁר sit quod vel de quo, uti Exod. XXXIII. de quo juravi Ps. XCV. 11. de quibus juravi &c. ac ver- bum כָּרַתּי sit promisi, uti 1. Sam. XXII. 8. 2. Chr. VII. 18. atque digitus intendatur in promissionem Ex. XXII. 20. 21. Mitto angelum ante te, quæ pro- missio deducatur ex antiquissima promissione de dando Filio Redemptore. Quæ non inerudita sunt, sed alia propinquior & magis conveniens rei promissio facta monstrari potest è collatione Ex. XX. 19. & Deut. XIIX. 16. 17. 18. 19. uti in explica- tione Deut. XIIX. observavimus. Quapropter pro astruendo testimonio S. S. Trinitatis hæc faciunt (1) quòd ῥητῶς exprimantur omnes personæ, Pa- ter loquens, verbum ejus, & Spiritus ejus. (2) Quod Filius Dei Verbum dicatur in V. T. uti è collatione 2. Sam. VII. 20. propter verbum tuum 1. Chr. XIIX. 19. propter servum tuum, colligitur: & impri- mis è Ps. XXXIII. 6. manifestum est. (3) Quod præsentia & assistentia Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. imprimis erigi potuerint & debuerint templi stru- ctores. Quæ enim lætior promissio, quæ major magnificentia esse potest in mundo, illa promis- sione & magnificentia Ecclesiæ, quod Deus Pater, in Filio Redemptore per Spiritum suum ipsi adesse ve- lit, & adsit? Ego pater, uti παραφραζει Cocce- jus, vobiscum sum qui vos olim abdicavi tanquam non populum meum & ero circa vos murus igneus. Me- cum Filius est Sponsor & Advocatus vester. Angelus fœderis est vobiscum, neque recedet à domo sua, ante- quam se victimam obtulerit: Spiritus meus est in me- dio vestri, neq; recedet à vobis, quin conservet legis- latores & doctores sedentes in cathedra Mosis donec secundum promissionem meam in filios vestros effun- datur. (4) Hic in memoriam revocatur ipsis promissio fœderalis, vel testamentaria VERBI vel MESSIÆ; cum verbo, quod promisi vobis. Hæc enim simplicissima est phraseos illius translatio. Quæ promissio fundamentum est omnis gratiæ & bene- dictionis. Qui reddunt, cum verbo IN QUO PE- PIGI, ellipsin præpositionis ב præter rem statu- unt, ne dicam cum Coccejo, quod insolens sit, ut legatur בַּאֲשֶׁר alii ellipsin ita supplent: verbum quod vobiscum pepigi scil. ratum faciam, sed ellipsin fingere opus non est, si nostra explicatio adhibea- tur. (5.) Consonabit ita Haggæus συγχρόνῳ & Collegæ suo Zachariæ, qui σκήνωσιν Dei aperte ali- quoties promittit in templo secundo, & angelum Dominum, qui hic vocatur verbum, clariffime de- scribit. Et cum Malachia, qui Angelum fœderis & Dominum templi λιγνάδι φωνῇ promittit cap. III. 2. (6) Promissi Verbi adventum hic spondet ver- su sequenti 6. Propheta noster, veniet desiderium omnium gentium. (7) Sic exposuit Hieronymus:

Ego sum vobiscum & Spiritus meus, & verbum, in quo posui Testamentum, agnoscens exhiberi hic my- sterium S. S. Trinitatis. Satis disertum testimonium de hoc mysterio hic ponit B. Tarnovius in h. l. Beat. Himmelius, etsi ad fœdus, quod Jehovah cum po- pulo pepigerat Exod. XX. referat, & orationem ellipticam statuat cum aliis, ex propria tamen sen- tentia adjicit: Imprimis sibi videri, respici ad promis- sionem populo factam de Propheta Magno Deuter. XIIX. de Christo, qui hic vocetur VERBUM. Cor- nelius à Lapide laudat etiam in hanc sententiam Athanasium, Epist. ad Serap. Gregor. Nyssen. l. testi- mon. contr. Jud. Cyrillum Hierosolymitan. Cat. XIX. Theodoretum, Remigium, Albertum, M. Haymonem, imo etiam Targum. Favet Chaldæus dum vertit, verbum meum erit vobis auxilio. Christoph. à Castro notat LXX. Vulgatum, Chaldæum, Tigurinos, & Pa- ghinum Verbum exponere, quasi sit suppositum, & cum sequenti verbo conjungere, Verbum & Spiri- tus meus erit in medio vestri, siquidem constet arti- culum את jungi quoque recto, ut 2. Reg. VI. & את ferrum cecidit in aquam. Glossa Judæorum, etsi Cor- nelius eandem approbet, mera σρεβλότης est: nam imperativum FACITE è superioribus trahunt ad illud אתהדבר h. m. facite verbum h. e. legem, quam inito pacto exigo, ego vicissim præstabo quod promisi. sic discerpunt textum, verbum aliunde huc ra- piunt, parenthesin interferunt: FACITE (quo- niam ego vobiscum sum, dicit Dominus exerci- tuum) VERBUM, quod pepigi, & promissionem cum præcepto confundunt, absolutam denique promissionem in hypotheticam transformant. vid. Coccejus in h. l.

## 2:6
Verse 7.

YET ONE LITTLE WHILE] A little time compared to that time from which the people of the Israelites existed. Otherwise, in itself, the space is not short, about five hundred years. But if you compare the times that intervened from the exodus out of Egypt to this structure, it will seem short.

I WILL SHAKE HEAVEN AND EARTH, THE SEA AND THE DRY LAND] Heaven and earth, that is, the sea and the dry ground: so that these two latter parts are an exposition of the word earth, which signifies that whole world composed of sea and ground. And it is a proverbial expression, by which a huge change of things is signified: but also the individual parts have something to do here. God had shaken heaven when lightnings were excited on Mount Sinai: He had shaken the earth, so that it might bring forth waters, He had shaken the sea, so that it might be divided. And in the time of Christ, God shook heaven, speaking from heaven: He shook the earth, so that it trembled: He shook the sea, commanding the sea and the winds.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ADHVC VNVM MODICUM EST] Modicum tempus præ eo tempore, ex quo fuit populus Israëlitarum. Alioqui per se spatium non est breve, annorum circiter quingentorum. Sed si tempora, quæ ab exitu ex Ægypto ad hanc structuram intercessere compares, breve videbitur.

EGO COMMOVEBO CŒLVM ET TERRAM, MARE ET ARIDAM] Cœlum & terram, id est, mare, & siccam humum: ut hæc duo posteriora sint expositio vo- cis terræ, quæ totum illum orbem ex mari humo que com- positum significat. Et autem proverbialis locutio, qua significatur ingens rerum mutatio: sed & singulæ partes habent hic quod agant. Commoverat Deus cœlum fulgu- ribus excitatis in monte Sinai: commoverat terram, ut aquas ederet, commoverat mare, ut scinderetur. Et Chri- sti tempore Deus cœlum commovit, locutus de cœlo: com- movit terram, ita ut tremeret: commovit mare, mari & ventis imperans.

## 2:7
Verse 8. AND THE DESIRED OF ALL NATIONS SHALL COME] When the desire of all nations shall have come, that is, he whom all nations ought to desire. He refers to the words of Jacob concerning Shiloh, which were in the mouths of the Jews and neighboring nations: as we said at Matthew II. The LXX here read in the plural חמות with Holem, the excellent τὰ ἐκλεκτά, less correctly.

AND I WILL FILL THIS HOUSE WITH GLORY] Great will be the glory of the second temple, because it will be seen in it. That King of all the pious, and in the temple itself, will perform miracles. See Matthew XXI. 12, 14. All the Jews who lived before the destruction believed that the Messiah would appear in the second temple. From that time they have concocted new, violent, and various interpretations for these most clear passages, δίκης χάριν σόφα φάρμακα, to which we can say: I know also some better myth than to understand it in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET VENIET DESIDERATIS CUNCTIS GENTIBUS] Vbi venerit desiderium gentium omnium, id est, quem desiderare omnes gentes debent. Respicit ad verba Jacobi de Siloh, quæ in ore erant Judæis & vicinis gentibus: ut diximus ad Matth. II. LXX. hic pluraliter le- gere חמות cum Holem, eximia τὰ ἐκλεκτὰ, minus recte.

ET IMPLEBO DOMUM ISTAM GLORIA] Magna erit secundi templi gloria, quod in eo conspicietur. Rex ille piorum omnium, & in ipso templo miracula e- det. Vide Matth. XXI. 12. 14. Messiam appariturum in templo secundo credidere Judæi omnes, qui ante excidium vixere. Ex eo tempore comminiscuntur interpretationes novas, violentas, varias, ad hæc loca clarissima, δίκης χάριν σόφα φάρμακα, quibus dicere possumus: Οἶδα δὲ καί τινα μῦϑον ἀμείνονα τῶ̃ δὲ νοῆσαι.

## 2:8
Verse 9. THE SILVER IS MINE, AND THE GOLD IS MINE, SAYS THE LORD OF HOSTS] That is, I do not need those things. A similar kind of speaking to that in Psalm L. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 9. MEVM EST ARGENTVM, ET MEVM EST AVRVM, DICIT DOMINUS EXERCITUUM] Id est, istis rebus non egeo. Simile loquendi genus illi in Ps. L. 10.

## 2:9
Verse 10. GREAT IS THE GLORY] Greater on account of those things which we have said.

OF THIS LATTER HOUSE] The Hebrew אחרון is also said of one of two: therefore in Latin you will correctly translate, of the latter.

It is a wonder that Grotius does not invent another literal sense here, but acknowledges that the Prophet prophesies concerning the Messiah according to the letter. For that has been customary for him up to this point: nor will he depart entirely from that custom in the remaining Prophets. Therefore, rightly from this passage to

Matthew 24:1 teaches that Christ ought to have come into the temple, and acknowledges that by חֶמְדַּת גּוֹיִם no one other than the Messiah is understood: which is easily confessed by all Christians. Calvin, however, preferred to Judaize here, and to take that word concerning the gold and silver of the nations, so that by that desire is designated, not Christ, but gold and silver to be consecrated to the Lord by the nations, following R. Kimchi who explains it thus: all the nations, which I will shake, shall come from their places, with the desire of all nations, i.e., they shall offer with their hands all desirable things which they shall find in their land from silver vessels, golden garments, precious stones. For he posits an ellipsis of the preposition ב in the word חמדת, which Rabbinic gloss Munster also embraced. Although indeed Calvin in his Commentaries in his Epistle to the Hebrews 11, explained that word concerning Christ, yet ten years later, when he was publishing his Commentary on the Minor Prophets, his opinion having changed not for the better, but for the worse, he expounded it concerning gold and silver and riches to be consecrated to the Lord. Whom therefore, as was fitting, the blessed Aegidius Hunnius chastised in his Calvin Judaizing, nor could Paraeus defend him, without feigning that Calvin had retained the sense concerning Christ, and that it is not rare for two or more senses of the same passage to be given, and BOTH RETAINED. But this is most absurd, that the word חֶמְדַּת should denote both Christ and gold and silver here at the same time; and who will admit that the word of coming is to be taken both concerning the advent of Christ into the world and concerning the consecration of wealth for the use and worship of the Lord? Absurdly, Paraeus also judges that Calvin's interpretation is not at all frivolous, as the blessed Hunnius demonstrated in his Anti-Pareus p. 287. For the scope of the Prophet (which is to raise the glory of the second house above the glory of the first house) does not permit these words (my silver and my gold) to be connected with the sense of Calvin otherwise than thus: however much this second house, now built after the captivity was ended, may not shine with gold and silver: yet it will be enriched at some time with gold and silver, when the converted Gentiles shall bring their riches, gold and silver, into it, and shall consecrate these their riches to the Lord. I appeal to all learned men, whether in this way (if indeed the scope of the Prophet ought to be attended to, as it certainly ought) the aforementioned words (mine is the silver, mine is the gold) ought to be connected with the interpretation of Calvin? But this connection, besides the fact that it reeks of Judaism, is also manifestly false in itself, since into that second temple, of which the Prophet speaks precisely and expressly, the riches of foreign nations were never brought: for piety does not allow us to interpret such a notable oracle concerning the impious King Herod, by whose riches the external structure of the temple was otherwise wonderfully adorned. Therefore, the aforementioned words, mine is the silver and mine is the gold, do not cohere with the preceding and following parts more correctly than that they have the force of a prolepsis or anticipation, by which, as I mentioned a little before, it is answered to those thinking of the Jewish people, that that external splendor of gold and silver has nothing to do with the matter, so that the former temple should be thought to be preferred to the latter: for the Lord does not care for these external things, since otherwise all the riches of the world are his. But that there is a glory and ornament incomparably more august, by which this second temple is to be illustrated before that former one, namely that in this last temple he is to show himself notable and admirable by doctrine and miracles, who is to be received by the applause of all nations as the true Messiah. These things the blessed Hunnius, by which we think Paraeus was sufficiently satisfied. The Jews themselves of the highest rank certainly acknowledged that these things look to the Messiah.

For Rabbi Akiba, who was the teacher of twenty-four thousand disciples, interpreted this prophecy concerning the Messiah in the tractate Sanhedrin, division Chelek, that this desire of the nations is King Messiah. Galatinus, in book IV, chapter IX, reports another Rabbinic exposition which rendered it thus: And afterwards the MESSIAH shall come. And indeed that illustrious name, DESIRE OF THE NATIONS, fits no one more correctly than the Messiah, who was not only the desire of the Jews, but since all nations ought to have adhered to him, and in him all nations were to be blessed, he was deservedly desirable to the nations: and in Canticles V. 16 he is called כֻּלּוֹ מַחֲמַדִּים, he is altogether desires, that is, most desirable. Whence his birth is intimated by the Angel in such a way that it caused joy to redound to all nations, Luke II. 10. If the desire of gold and silver were meant, that would be called the desire of the Jews more correctly than of the nations, as B. Luther. in his book On the Jews and Their Lies observed: The breath of the Jews stinks of the silver and gold of the Gentiles, for no people under the sun has been more greedy than they, etc. But there is no need for us to dispute at length with Castrio as to how the Messiah could have been desired by the nations who were ignorant of him! Let Cornel. à Lapide suffice in his Explanation of Hebrews XII; for although the nations, as long as they were nations and infidels, did not desire Christ, yet Christ in himself was desirable to them, as being their savior and redeemer, and all nations, as soon as they heard through the Apostles about the life and miracles of Christ, began to desire Christ, for which reason Christ is called by the Patriarch Jacob, Gen. 49, v. 10, and 16, the expectation of the nations, and the desire of the eternal hills, that is, the desire of the patriarchs and the prophets of old, and of the ancient ages, which stood out and excelled other men like hills on the earth in their wisdom and holiness. Add that the desire with which the nations received Christ is also regarded. See Acts XIII. 46, ch. XIV. 27. Nor indeed should the plural number בָאוּ move anyone, on account of which Junius and Tremellius explained this passage thus: And I will shake all nations, so that the desired of all nations may come, that is, whomever I shall choose from the nations. For among the Hebrews it is not rare for a verb to be added to two substantives, one of which governs the other, which corresponds to the latter, when it ought to agree with the former; see Gen. IV. 10, Job XV. 20, ch. XXXII. 7. Meanwhile, not inappropriately, Balt. Willius understands the preposition אֶל, they shall come TO the desire of the nations, as in Joel I. 14, that is, to Christ. From this passage, therefore, the Jews can be most solidly convinced of the coming of the Messiah. Since Grotius himself acknowledges this, we refrain from proving it laboriously. In brief, the prophecy is to be understood as concerning the Messiah, as confirmed by (1) The scope of the prophet, which was to confirm the faith of the people regarding every point of the promise, and to lift up, console, and strengthen the same in the building of the temple with the certainty of the fulfillment of the promise, which the faithful especially panted for and anxiously desired. (2) The preceding promise: THE WORD, which I promised you when you came out of the land of Egypt (that great Prophet, whom I promised you) shall be in your midst, which promise is now followed by a richer confirmation: Yet once more it is a little while, etc. (3) The shaking of heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land. No one doubts that this implies a significant change. And if that ever happened, it was in the time of the New Testament, when the old Ecclesiastical polity was changed into an entirely different form through the coming of Christ and after it, when the Lord shook heaven as well as earth: Which the holy Apostle observed and assumed as something lying outside of all controversy, when he wrote to the Hebrews, ch. XII, observing the weight of the words, that a far greater shaking is indicated here than that which occurred at the time of the giving of the law. For there the earth was shaken: but here it is predicted that not only the earth, but heaven itself is to be shaken. Whose voice shook the earth then, in the promulgation of the law: but now he promises again, saying: yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth, but also heaven. Which indeed happened at the coming of Christ: for he shook heaven by the testimony of angels and stars, the earth was shaken by a huge miracle, namely the very birth of the virgin, he shook the sea and the dry land when Christ was announced in the islands and in the whole world: as Augustine has it, book XVIII, On the City of God, ch. XXXV. But more such shakings that happened then are recounted: namely in heaven (1) That on the very day and moment that Christ was born, an Angel from heaven and a heavenly host appeared to the shepherds, Luke II. 14. (2) That an unusual star arose for the Magi in the east, and led them from there, Matthew II. 1. (3) That heaven was opened at the Baptism of Christ, God the Father proclaimed from heaven, and the HOLY SPIRIT descended from heaven upon him, Matthew III. (4) That Moses and Elijah appeared from heaven on the holy mountain when Christ was transfigured, Matthew XVII. (5) That a voice was heard from heaven, John XII. (6) That angels from heaven ministered to Christ in the temptation, in the passion, in the resurrection. (7) That the Sun in heaven suffered an eclipse in the whole world miraculously, whence Dionysius the Areopagite exclaimed: Either the God of nature is suffering, or the machinery of the world is being dissolved. (8) That he was gloriously assumed into heaven, and penetrated all the heavens: and that angels from heaven preached then about his visible return, Acts I. (9) That the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the Apostles not without a shaking of heaven, Acts II. (10) That Stephen saw heaven opened, Acts VI. (11) That Christ manifested himself from heaven to Paul with an illustrious epiphany, Acts IX, XXII. All of which are sufficiently constant from sacred history, and testify abundantly to the shaking of the heavens, so that we may be silent about some other things which foreign writers report happened from heaven at that time. Similarly, the earth was also moved, and not in one way; for from the whole world, by land and sea, men were flowing together to pay tribute: the easterners were moved when the Magi from the east, stirred by the star of the born Messiah, were moved, then Jerusalem and the land of the Jews were moved, Matt. II. The earth was also moved when the rocks were split and the tombs were opened at the passion of Christ: it was moved again when Christ rose again; finally, the whole earth, sea and dry land were moved in the preaching of the word throughout the whole world and by the various changing of things. To these are added various miracles done in heaven and on earth. Finally, I will move, says the Lord, all nations, which was done by the calling and conversion of all nations. From all of which it is clearer than light that that most notable commotion, which is predicted here, had its fulfillment at the coming of the Messiah.

Nor indeed is there need that the prophecy be restricted only to the very year or day of the birth of the Messiah, provided that regard is had not only to his coming, but also to the manifestation of his glory, and that whole reformation and change which those commotions were to reveal to the world, as the Apostolic demonstration instituted among the Hebrews proves that this was accepted by the Hebrews themselves: for he proves from this oracle the cessation of the old religion. But as to the fact that he says 'yet once more,' he declares the removal of those things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, so that those things which are unshakable may remain: by the things that are shaken he understands the tabernacle made by hands and other Levitical things, likewise the vessels and rites of the O.T. Which are called things that are shaken, because they were to be removed by Christ; the immovable things which are from Christ and in Christ are grace and truth, through which the abrogation of the old rites was made, as things made, figures, that is, which were truly fulfilled through the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, the Evangelical proclamation and the kingdom. But these things always remain, and are immovable. Therefore, that shaking is not to be restricted to the day and year of the coming of Christ, but is to be extended to the economy of the course of Christ, in the days of his flesh, passion, resurrection, ascension, and exaltation to the right hand, the mission of the Holy Spirit and the calling of the Gentiles through the ministry of the Apostles of Christ. Because he is promised here not only as the Messiah of the Jews, but as the desire of the nations. Rightly here Christ. à Castro p. 450. By the coming of Christ into the temple we must also understand his dispensation in the flesh, which the Greek Fathers call οἰκονομίαν. For the glory of that temple was rendered more illustrious, because in it Christ began his Church. For Christ used to meet at that place, with the whole Church, both to pray and to hear him speaking, as is evident from the Gospels and the Apostolic Acts. Whence in it, and from it, the whole Church scattered throughout the world draws its origin: because the law went forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

B. Luther fosters a peculiar explanation here concerning that shaking, understanding the movements to be excited throughout the whole world by the Devil against the seed of the woman, which were especially excited under the New Testament, whereas he raged before primarily in Judea against the blessed seed, concerning which let his praised book against the Jews be seen. But the gloss of the Jews, which R. Maimonides handed down in More Nebuch. p. II. c. XXIX., that Haggai speaks here of the destruction of the Persian kingdom, can in no way stand: since the scope of the Prophet was comforting: but what kind of consolation could redound to the Jews from the destruction of the Persian kingdom? Nor were all nations shaken then, which is predicted here: nor was peace thus reconciled to the Jews. Since Alexander the Great attacked Jerusalem with a great army, as Josephus testifies in book II. c. 8. And what will become of the desire of the nations? Shall we believe that Alexander the Great, the conqueror of the world, was the desire of the nations? What of the fact that the Prophet dealt with the movements and destruction of the Persian Kingdom in a special discourse, c. II. v. 20. He confirms our explanation (4) The glory of the second, and of the same most recent temple, which was to be reconciled to it through the presence and manifestation of the glory of the Messiah, so that the second temple turns out more glorious than the Solomonic one had been before. For the Prophet speaks of no other than the second temple. Some Jews invent a third temple, which they still expect, and wish the Prophet to be dealing with it. But the Prophet demonstrates the present temple through הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה Hajediah and the pronoun זֶה: This very house: which was then being erected: on account of which the Jews were somewhat sad, because it did not seem to attain the glory of the former temple: and he called it הָאַחֲרוֹן the most recent or last, just as that word is taken in Gen. XXXIII. 3. Dan. IV. 5. c. X. 11. For no other temple was ever promised to the Jews: for what Ezekiel describes is not a material temple, but clearly mystical, and with the destruction of that house the order of sacrifices, of priests, and the whole Levitical worship had to cease: whence when the repair of the temple was sometimes attempted, it was hindered from heaven. Wherefore Menasse Ben-Israel acknowledges in de term. vit. p. 155. that the prophecy of Haggai is to be understood of the second temple, and is so understood by R. Dav. Kimchi, R. Hazariah Ando, and a great part of the ancients p. 152. which R. Alschech also acknowledges in this place. Conf. Const.

L'Empereur in the preface to Codic. Middoth. The glory, therefore, which is promised here, is to be explained concerning the glory of the second temple. Which indeed not only yielded much to the Solomonic one regarding external splendor, but also regarding those things of primary importance which had previously rendered that temple especially glorious, but which were lacking in the latter: namely, the ark of the covenant, with the mercy seat, and the divine presence or σκηνώσει, the sacred fire, Urim and Thummim, and the Spirit of Prophecy: not to mention those ten singular things which are claimed for the former temple in the Talmud in Joma c. I. Since, therefore, besides the coming of the Messiah and his glorious manifestation, nothing can be named by which the other temple was rendered more illustrious and glorious, it must be confessed that that glory is designated here. For what the Jews chatter about, concerning the longer preservation of the second temple, that it stood for more than a decade, is very frivolous, whence they are deservedly laughed at by B. Luther: For age alone does not make a thing more glorious. Perhaps, says Megalander, the mule of David, upon which Solomon, as a king, rode, was older than Solomon, should it then for that reason have been more glorious than the king himself? Oh that they had had a good astronomer here, who had calculated it a little more accurately, he would perhaps have found that they would have been over it by the ten years, plus 3 months, 2 weeks, 5 days, 7 hours, 12 minutes and 10 half-minutes. If there were perhaps a shop that had shame-red for sale, I would dare to give the Jews a few guilders so that they would go there and buy a pound, and yet smear their foreheads, eyes, and cheeks with it, if they would not smear their shameless hearts and tongues with it. Equally inept is the exception concerning the adornment which Herod contributed. For neither was that as great as the Solomonic one 2. Chron. III. 5. 6. 7. nor was the chief glory of the former temple established in gold and silver, but in those five things which were lacking in the latter temple: And rightly B. Luther: Because Herod had no command from GOD to do such a thing, but as a godless enemy of GOD and of His people, out of vain glory and pride for his own honor did such building, so all his building and labor before GOD has not been as good as the smallest little stone which Zerubbabel laid upon the temple by the command of GOD. Finally, R. Lusitanus admits in the Middelburg Colloquy, fol. 119. 123. (contradicting in that part R. Isaac Ben Abraham Lib. I. c. 34. & R. Manasse Ben Israel l. c.) that the glory of the second house was not situated in gold and silver, but he imagines that the glory of the third house, situated also in far different things, is pointed out here. Which fiction concerning the third temple has already been exploded before: not to mention that R. Abraham in his Cabalistic book maintains that Herod's temple was the third. Since, therefore, it cannot be found what made the latest house more illustrious, besides the glorious presence of the Messiah, it remains that the Jews acknowledge that the Messiah has come, while the second temple was still standing. We, however, have the fulfillment in the New Testament when Christ was presented in the temple in infancy, when He sat among the Doctors in the temple in childhood, when He taught in the temple, purified the temple, and illustrated it with His glory, when according to Malachi c. III. the Lord came to the temple, and purified the sons of Levi: and openly demonstrated His glory, glory as it were of the only-begotten from the Father. see Luc. II. v. 27. & XIX. 47. Ioh. II. 4. c. VII. 4. which has now been desolate for almost 16 centuries. In Christ we have all those things, but in truth, which were lacking in the second temple: the true ark of the covenant, the true mercy seat, Rom. III. 24. The holy oil of gladness, & the holy fire of divine love, and also the Urim of knowledge or illumination of wisdom, and the Thummim of the perfection of justice 1. Cor. I. 29. finally שׁכנה the divine presence and habitation Joh. XIV. 11. Eph. III. 16. But not only is that glory regarded, which was brought about through the presence and preaching of Christ in this temple, but also through the fact that the Church of the New Testament was begun there, concerning which see Cornel. à Lapide page 148. Moreover, the exceptional glory of the second temple was that in it, through Christ, not only were the mysteries of the incarnate Word and of our redemption and salvation performed, but also the first believers and Apostles were adorned, and the first foundations of the Christian Church were laid, according to that passage in Is. ch. 2, 3. Out of Zion shall go forth the law. Christ therefore began his Church in this temple, built by Zerubbabel. Thus Rupert, Hugo, Burgenf., Clarius, Vatabl., and others.

There follows (5) The connection of the glory of the temple and the coming of the Messiah. And the desire of all nations shall come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. For from this it is by no means obscure that that glory was to be brought to the second temple by the coming of the Messiah, and that he himself would come to the second temple. For it has been shown before that by the desire of all nations the Messiah is understood: concerning whom Luther is to be heard here l. c. It shall come, Hemdath, the comfort of all nations, that is, the Messiah, the desire of all nations, which we have translated as comfort. For 'desire' is not understandable enough, because in German it means the inner desire and pleasure of the heart. But here it is used actively as 'desire,' the external passive that a heart desires. If one were to translate it into German thus: 'The joy and delight of all nations,' it would also not be wrong. In sum, it is the Messiah, in whom the unbelieving, hardened Jews were to have nothing but displeasure, disgust, and abomination, as Isaiah 53 ch. prophesies of them, but to the nations he was to be welcome, as the joy and delight of their heart, the desire and longing of all. For he brings them redemption from sins, death, the devil, hell, and every evil eternally. Yes, that is the desire, heart's delight, joy, and comfort of the nations. This agrees with the saying of Jacob Gen. 49, and to Shiloh or the Messiah the nations will obey, that is, they will receive him with joy, hear his word, and without the sword, unforced, become his people, as if he were saying: the unnoble, uncircumcised nations will do this, but my noble little fruits, my circumcised lost children will not do it, but will become raging and senseless against it. To this also agrees Isaiah 2, Micah 4. In the last days the mountain where the Lord's house is will be prepared, higher than all mountains, and will be raised above all hills, and all nations will run thither (without doubt unforced, out of desire and delight) and many peoples will hasten and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways, and we may walk in his paths. For out of Zion will go forth a law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and throughout the prophets speak of the Messiah's kingdom among the nations. And further fol. 85. God says: He wishes to give the nations the

Hemdath, and their obedience shall please him, as Jacob says in Gen. 49, and all the prophets, and he wishes to be so hard again against the hard head of the Jews, that he would rather cast them away and choose and accept the nations, regardless of whether they are still circumcised saints with the noble blood of the fathers. For thus says Hos. 2: I will call that which is not my people, my people, and it shall call me its God. But to the Jews he says: Lo-ammi, you are not my people, and I am not your God, which Moses sang to them long before in his song Deut. 32: They provoked me with that which is not God, and angered me with their useless deeds, so I will provoke them in turn with that which is not my people, and with a foolish nation I will anger them. This saying has now been strongly in effect for 1500 years, that we foolish nations, who were not God's people, are now God's. Thus Megalander. We add the paraphrase of B. Tarnovius v. 7. At this time in this way I, the God of heaven, am going to move not only inanimate things but especially men (since for their sake also all other things are done, miracles) and because it will be the time of the New Testament, that middle wall of partition will be broken down which hitherto distinguished between Jews and nations Eph. 2, 24. and I am going to bring to the Church all nations from the ends of the earth (just as we read that it happened in the histories of the New Testament concerning the Apostles Peter, Paul, and his companions, noted) then when that highest desire has already come (which the change of number and gender in the verb observed in the Hebrew text, and not used without cause, notes. See Buxtorff. th. p. 400. 401. 402. & 388.) of all nations, that Messiah, whom all nations deservedly ought to anxiously expect and seek, since every thing by the instinct of nature also most desires that which it most needs. Luther translates, 'then shall come the comfort of all nations,' and in the margin, 'that is, Christ, who shall comfort all the world through the forgiveness of sins.' And through this Messiah I will fill this house with glory, when that King of glory Ps. XXIV. 7. 8. who is greater than Solomon Matth. XII. 42. shall have taught in that temple and performed miracles, who is God and man, and whom the earlier shadows and histories of the Old Testament regard, when they narrate that the glory of God appeared at the ark of the mercy seat and at the sanctuary, as at other times in the tabernacle, so also at the dedication of Solomon's temple. Thus now the body itself will come, and with its glorious presence will adorn this place, which you are now preparing, with doctrine and miracles, says Jehovah the Lord of hosts, so that this may be the same promise which is repeated in Malachi ch. 3, and which brings great light to this place. It is thus: I will send my messenger, who shall prepare the way before me, and suddenly the Lord, whom you seek, shall come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight, that is, that most desired one, in which way we explain those words of our Prophet Haggai concerning Christ far better with other fathers and some others than with Junius and a few others, rather concerning the one choosing than the chosen, since he is called desire in the Hebrew phrase, when it is a thing most desired, as in Ps. 21:3, desire is put for a desirable thing, and otherwise the Hebrews by a certain peculiar idiom of the language name things or persons most desirable as things or men of desire or of desires Ezra 8:27, Gen. 27:15, Dan. 9:23, 2 Chron. 20:25, and 32:27, and 36:10, 19, Ps. 106:24, Jer. 3:19, and 12:10, and 25:34, Ez. 26:12, Dan. 10:3, 11, 19, and 11:8, 37, 43, Hos. 13:5, Am. 5:11, Nah. 2:10. Zachar. 7:14, and the abstract put for the concrete to imply a superlative has already been demonstrated several times above. See examples Gen. 3, 6. & 11, 34. & 27, 27. & 43, 11. Ps. 10, 15. & 67, 5. Dan. 10, 11. 19. Eccles. 10, 3. Ex. 12, 42. & 17, 12. Joel 2, 3. & 4, 17. Mark 13, 19. Amos 5, 11. Matt. 24, 15. 2 Cor. 5, 21. Eph. 5, 8. Col. 1, 13.

To this pertains (6) The gift of peace, which is to be amplified by the coming of the desire of the nations. And in that place, I will give peace, says the Lord of hosts, which cannot be understood as external worldly peace, for that never fell to the Jews in a solid way, as the wars, commotions, and persecutions of Antiochus 1 Macc. 1, 23 ff. in Josephus, Antiq. Book XI, ch. VII and Book I of the Jewish War, ch. 1, and of Pompey, Book I of the Jewish War, ch. V, and the fates of others testify. Therefore, this prophecy must be explained as referring to spiritual peace, which is to be brought about by the Messiah, and peace is promised in the times of the Messiah, Is. 53, 6. ch. 11, 6. 7. Zech. 9, 10. Which we do not have except in Christ, Luke 2, 14. John 14, 27. Rom. 5, 1. Eph. 2, 14. 15. This discourse is about that peace which ought to bring comfort to the nations no less than to the Jews, whence he is called the desire of all nations, whose coming is promised here, and in whose days peace was to be, concerning which peace and happiness one may also read in Is. 9, 6. Jer. 23, 6. Whence R. Isaac Ben-Abraham in Chissuk Emuna, Book I, 34, understands by peace in this place eternal peace, and R. Lusitanus in Coll. Mittelb. f. 22, acknowledges that the discourse here is about the temple, in which the Messiah was to appear, which the nations would seek, so that thus the Messiah might be established as that desire of all nations, f. 130. Cf. on these matters Mr. Dr. Muller, Judaism, Book 1, ch. IX.

(7) Designation of time. Yet a little while. Some explain מְעַט not as a smallness of time, but of dignity, that it is little and small, that you previously moved the earth, in respect to that commotion which is to be one day; Yet one time or once, a little, that is, I will move heaven and earth, thus Junius, that is a little, namely that which I had covenanted with you when coming out of Egypt, so that it is a comparison of the Law and the Gospel, to which Willius agrees, adding: that a comparison is also instituted by reason of the majesty of the promulgation: but those are forced, and foreign to the text: and Christians as well as Jews commonly explain these things as referring to a small amount of time. Ludov. de Dieu does not poorly elucidate the sense of the words: namely that אַחַת is to be translated "once," as the LXX rendered it, and the Apostle confirms, Heb. 12, 26. For it is understood as פַּעַם ONE "TIME, and it is so used in Exod. 30, 10. Joel 39. 35. just as with שְׁתַּיִם understand פְעָמוֹת, it is "two times, twice," 2 Kings 9. Furthermore, אַחַת as a substantive for time, and מְעַט as a substantive for time, include in themselves not only here, but also elsewhere in many places. Therefore, they are rightly constructed as two substantives in the genitive regimen, i.e., Yet one time (if it is to be expressed unusually, or one period) of a little time. And the sense is: since God has hitherto repeated the promise concerning the Messiah many times, and those of long periods, and has deferred the same as many times, namely from Adam to Abraham, thence to the Law given, hence to David, and the structure of Solomon's temple, from this to its restoration by Zerubbabel, now only one time (or period) yet remains, and that of a little time, namely from this second temple built to Christ: so he, not unlearnedly. But the Apostle urges that word ἔτι ἅπαξ, so that he may teach that not a fourth or fifth time (or period) is indicated by the Holy Spirit, but only a second time, and he refers the first time, to which he opposes this second one, to the promulgation of the Law, and from that concludes the translation of legal things: See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if they did not escape who refused him who spoke on earth, much more we, who turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven: whose voice moved the earth THEN: BUT NOW (behold the opposition between THEN and NOW, that former and this second time) he promises saying: Yet once more, and I will move NOT ONLY THE EARTH (as now) but also HEAVEN. But that he says YET ONCE (that is, a second time), he declares the translation of the noble things, as of things made, so that those things which are immovable may remain: For if such things as were immovable had been established by the first commotion (of the earth), there would be no need for another new and more solemn commotion (of heaven, for instance, and earth) which he promises. The sense is: Beware, lest you now refuse Christ speaking to you, lest you be punished, as those who refused him who spoke of old on Mount Sinai did not escape punishment. There he spoke on earth on the mountain. Here from heaven: because the Son of God not only descended from heaven, but when he was on earth, he was in heaven, John 3, 11. and his voice was also heard openly from heaven, Matt. 3, ch. 17, John 12, and the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven in a solemn and visible manner after Christ ascended into heaven, whose (Christ's) voice then, when he gave the Law, moved the earth: but when he promised through Haggai that he would yet once move the earth, and indeed not the earth only, but also heaven, which was certainly fulfilled by the coming from heaven to earth (where he moved heaven and earth in many ways), what else did that repeated commotion teach, than that those things which were not altogether immovable, having been established by the former commotion of the earth, and that a certain translation of these movable things, i.e., of legal things, should follow, and that a confirmation of immovable things should be made through that new inauguration of the commotion not only of the earth, but of heaven itself: Therefore the holy Apostle teaches that that YET ONCE declares and insinuates that the things of that old covenant, promulgated with the commotion of the earth, were to be abolished, which were made only to represent the true things of the new covenant, and therefore, upon the arrival or confirmation of the eternal and immovable goods in that new commotion of both heaven and earth, they necessarily had to yield. Wherefore the Apostle concludes divinely, that that YET ONCE MORE implies the abrogation of the old covenant and the establishment of the new, and compares the factitious and unstable things of the former with the eternal and perpetual things of the latter. Which receive light if they are compared with what is said in Heb. VIII and IX concerning the tabernacle made with hands. Whence it is very manifest that the Apostle is not here dealing with the most recent coming of Christ, or applying the Prophetic oracle to the same, as some wish, but is interpreting the Prophetic text concerning the first coming of Christ. Which is not only the opinion of Jerome on Hagg. II, but also of Augustine in book XVIII of The City of God, ch. XXXV, and book III, as also from the Greeks, Cyril in book V on Genesis. And in this most Prophetic interpreters agree on this passage: Rupert, Remigius, Haymo, Albert, Hugo, Lyranus, and of our own, Winckelmann, Himmelius, Tarnovius, and others.

Finally, there is no reason for the Jews to grumble that not a small amount of time, but five centuries, had flowed from this promise to the birth of Jesus: for the response is that it is called a little while with respect to the time elapsed, either from the promulgation of the law, when the earth was also shaken, or from the promulgation of the Proto-Evangelium, from which time the Messiah was expected, since chronologists count 3462 years (others 3434) from then until the second year of Darius Hystaspes, by the reckoning of which five hundred years are certainly considered a small amount of time. And these things are concerning that prophecy.

SERMON III.

Latin:

Vers. 10. MAGNA EST GLORIA] Major ob ea quæ diximus.

DOMUS ISTIVS NOVISSIMÆ] Hebræum אחרון etiam de uno ex duobus dicitur: itaque Latine recte verteris, posterioris.

Mirum, quod Grotius hic non fingat alium literalem sensum, sed κτ̓ τὸ ὑ̓ρητὸν de Messia vatici- nari Prophetam agnoscat. Id enim hactenus ipsi solenne fuit: nec ab eo more prorsus migrabit in residuis Prophetis. Recte itaque ex hoc loco ad- e

Matth. XXIV. 1. docet Christum in templum ad- venire debuisse, & agnoscit per חֶמְדַּת גּוֹיִם nul- lum alium, quam Messiam intelligi: Quod penes Christianos facile omnes in confesso est. Calvinus tamen hic ἰουδαΐζειν maluit, & de auro atque argento gentium vocem illam accipere, ut designetur per illud desiderium, non Christus, sed aurum & argen- tum Domino consecrandum à gentibus, sequutus R. Kimchium ita explicantem: omnes gentes, quas commovebo, è locis suis veniet, cum desiderio omnium gentium, q. d. offerent manibus suis omnes res de- siderabiles, quas invenient in terra sua ex vasis ar- genteis, aureis vestimentis, lapidibus pretiosis. Po- nit enim ellipsin præpositionis ב in voce חמדת, quam glossam Rabbinicam etiam amplexus est Mun- sterus. Quamvis vero Calvinus in Commentar. in Epist. ad Ebr. XI. vocem illam de Christo ex- plicarit, tamen decennio post, cum Commenta- rium in Prophetas minores ederet, sententia non in melius, sed in deterius mutata de auro & argento, & divitiis Domino consecrandis exposuit. Quem ideo, ut par erat, castigavit B. Ægidius Hunnius in Calvino Judaizante, nec defendere eum potuit Paræus, quin fingeret retinuisse Calvinum sensum de Christo, nec rarum esse, duos, vel plures sensus e- jusdem loci dari, & UTRUMQUE RETINE- RI. At hoc perabsurdum vocem חֶמְדַּת & Christum & aurum & argentum simul hic notare; ac verbum veniendi, & de adventu Christi in orbem & de consecratione opum in usum & cultum Domini accipi quis admittet? Absurde, etiam censet Pa- ræus, minime frivolam esse Calvini interpretatio- nem, uti demonstravit B. Hunnius Anti-Pareo p. 287. Scopus enim Prophetæ (qui est secundæ do- mus gloriam supra gloriam primæ domus attolle- re) non permittit hæc verba (meum argentum & meum aurum) cum sensu Calvini aliter connecti, quam sic: quantumvis hæc secunda domus modo post solutam captivitatem exstructa non fulgeat auro & argento: tamen ditabitur ea aliquando auro & ar- gento, quando conversi gentiles suas in eam divitias, aurum & argentum inferent, & has suas opes Domino consecrabunt. Appello omnes doctos, annon hoc pacto (si modo scopus Prophetæ attendi debeat, ut certe debet) prædicta verba (meum est argen- tum, meum est aurum) cum interpretatione Calvi- ni connecti oporteat? Hæc autem connexio, præterquam quod Iudaismum redolet, per se etiam manifeste falsa est, siquidem in secundum illud templum, de quo Propheta præcise, & ex professo loquitur, nunquam exterarum gentium opes illa- tæ sunt: Ut enim de impio Rege Herode, cujus alias opibus externa structura templi mirifice fuit exornata, interpretemur tam insigne oraculum, pietas non sinit. Proinde rectius præmemorata verba, meum est argentum & meum est aurum, cum antecedentibus & consequentibus non cohæ- rent, quam ut vim habeant προλήψεως occupatio- nis, qua, ut paulo ante memini, cogitantibus Judaici populi respondetur, nihil ad rem facere externum illum splendorem auri & argenti, ut prius templum posteriori putetur anteferendum: Dominum enim non curare externa hæc, cum alioquin sint ipsius o- mnes divitiæ mundi. Esse autem decus & ornamen- tum incomparabiliter augustius, quo Templum hoc secundum præ illo priori sit illustrandum, nempe quod in hoc postremo templo doctrina & miraculis sese insignem & admirabilem ostensurus sit is, qui omnium gentium plausu pro vero Mes- sia sit excipiendus. Hæc B. Hunnius, quibus ita satis- factum Pareo arbitramur. Iudæi certe ipsi præcipui commatis agnoverunt hæc ad Messiam spectare.

Nam R. Akiba, qui viginti quatuor millium difci- pulorum præceptor fuit, hanc Prophetiam de Messia interpretatus est in tractatu Sanhedrim dist. Chelek, quod desiderium illud gentium sit Rex Mes- sias. Refert & aliam expositionem Rabbinicam Galatinus lib. IV. c. IX. quæ ita reddidit: Et postea veniet MESSIAS. Et sane nomen illud illustre DESIDERII GENTIUM non alii rectius, quam Messia convenit, qui non Judæorum tantum desi- derium fuit, sed quum ei adhærere debuerint, in- que eo benedicendæ fuerint omnes gentes, meri- to gentibus desiderabilis fuit: & Cant. V. 16. vocatur כֻּלּוֹ מַחֲמַדִּים totus ipse desideria, hoc est, desidera- tissimus. Unde ab Angelo nativitas ejus ita intima- tur, quod ea redundarit gaudium in omnes gentes Luc. II. 10. Si desiderium auri & argenti notaretur, rectius id desiderium Judæorum, quam gentium vo- catur, ut B. Luther. Libr. von den Jüden und jüdi- schen Lügen observavit: Den Jüden stinckt der Odem nach der Heyden Silber und Gold, dann kein Volck unter der Sonnen geitziger, denn sie sind, gewesen ist &c. Non autem opus est, ut cum Castrio disputemus prolixe, quomodo Mes- sias à gentibus, quæ ipsum ignorarunt, desi- derari potuerit! sufficiat Cornel. à Lapide in Ebr. XII. Explicatio; Licet enim gentes, quamdiu gen- tes & infideles erant, Christum non desiderarint, ta- men Christus in se eis desiderabilis erat, utpote eo- rum salvator & redemtor, omnesque gentes, mox ut de Christi vita & miraculis per Apostolos inaudiverunt, Christum desiderare cœperunt, qua de causa Christus à Iacob Patriarcha Gen. 49. v. 10. & 16. vocatur ex- pectatio gentium, & desiderium collium æterno- rum, id est, desiderium patriarcharum & propheta- rum priorum, & antiquorum seculorum, quæ cæ- teris hominibus, quasi colles in terra eminuerunt, & præcelluerunt sua sapientia & sanctitate. Adde quod respiciatur desiderium, quo gentes Christum susceperunt. Vid. Act. XIII. 46. c. XIV. 27. Ne- que vero quenquam movere debet pluralis nu- merus בָאוּ propter quem Junius & Tremellius hunc locum sic exposuera: Et commoturus sum o- mnes gentes, ut veniant desiderati omnium gentium hoc est, quoscunque è gentibus elegero. Nam apud Ebræos rarum hoc non est, addi duobus substantivis, quorum unum regit alterum, ejusmodi verbum, quod respondeat posteriori, cum deberet convenire priori vid. Gen. IV. 10. Job. XV. 20. c. XXXII. 7. Interim non incommode Balt. Willius subintelligit præpo- sitionem אֶל venient AD desiderium gentium, ut Joel. I. 14. id est ad Christum. Ex hoc itaque loco con- vinci solidissime possunt Judæi de adventu Messiæ. Quod cum Grotius ipse agnoscat, operose proba- re supersedemus. Paucis, de Messia accipiendum esse vaticinium confirmat (1) Scopus prophetæ, qui erat, fidem confirmare populo de promissionis omnis apice, eundemque erigere, consolari, ro- borare in templi ædificatione certitudine com- plementi promissi, quod imprimis fideles anhela- bant & anxie desiderabant. (2) promissum antece- dens: VERBUM, quod promisi vobis, cum egredere- mini de terra Ægypti (Propheta ille magnus, quem promisi vobis) erit in medio vestrum, quam pro- missionem jam excipit uberior confirmatio: Ad- huc unum modicum est &c. (3) Commotio cæli & ter- ræ, maris & aridæ. Quæ insignem mutationem in- ferre nemo ambigit. Ea autem si unquam facta est, N.T. tempore, cum politia vetus Ecclesiastica in a- liam plane formam mutata est, per adventum Chri- sti & post eundem, ubi cælum pariter ac terram commovit Dominus: Quod observavit, & velut ἔ- ξω πάσης συῤῥάξεως κείμενον assumsit S. Aposto- lus, cum Ebræis scriberet c. XII. observatis verbo- rum ponderibus, quod longe major commotio hic indicata, quam tempore νομοθεσίας facta. Ibi enim commota fuit terra : hic vero non terram tantum, sed cœlum ipsum commotum iri prædici. Cujus vox movit terram tunc, in legis promulgatione : nunc autem re- promittit, dicens : adhuc semel, & ego movebo non so- lum terram, sed & cœlum. Quod sane factum sub ad- ventum Christi : nam cœlum movit angelorum, & si- derum testimonio, commota terra ingenti miraculo, ipso nempe virginis partu, movit mare & aridam, cum in insulis & orbe toto Christus annunciatur : ut habet August. lib. XIIX. de Civ. c. XXXV. sed recensentur plures ejusmodi commotiones tum factæ : utpote in cœlo (1) Quod eo ipso die & momento, quo na- tus est Christus, Angelus de cœlo & cœlestis ex- ercitus apparuerit pastoribus Luc. II. 14. (2) Quod stella insolita Magis in oriente exorta sit, at- que inde eos deduxerit Matth. II. 1. (3) Quod cœ- lum in Baptismo Christi apertum sit, Deus Pater de cœlo proclamarit, & SPIRITUS SANCTUS de cœlo descenderit super ipsum Matth. III. (4) Quod de cœlo apparuerint Moses & Elias in mon- te sancto, cum clarificaretur Christus Matth. XVII. (5) Quod vox de cœlo audita sit Joh. XII. (6) Quod angeli de cœlo in tentatione, in passione, in resur- rectione Christo ministraverint. (7) Quod Sol in cœlo ecclipsin in toto terrarum orbe passus sit mi- raculose, unde Dionysius Areopagita exclamavit : Aut Deus naturæ patitur, aut mundi machina dissol- vetur. (8) Quod in cœlum gloriose assumtus, o- mnesq; cœlos penetrarit : & quod angeli de cœ- lo de ipsius reditu visibili tum concionati sint Act. I. (9) Quod Sp. S. de cœlo non absque cœli com- motione super Apostolos descenderit Act. II. (10). Quod cœlum apertum viderit Stephanus Act. VI (11) Quod de cœlo Christus Paulo sese manifesta- rit illustri ἐπιφανείᾳ Act. IX. XXII. Quæ omnia ex historia sacra satis constant, & de commotione cælorum affatim testantur, ut alia nonnulla, quæ tum accidisse de cœlo exotici Scriptores referunt, ta- ceamus. Similiter commota etiam terra est non u- no modo; Nam ex universo orbe, terra mariq; con- fluebant homines, ad persolvendum tributum : commoti sunt orientales, cum Magi ex oriente stella nati Messiæ exciti sunt, commota tum Hiero- solyma & terra Judæorum Matth. II. mota etiam est terra, cum petræ scissæ, & monumenta aperta sunt, in Christi passione : commota iterum est, cum Chri- stus resurgeret, denique terra universa, mare & ari- da commota sunt, in verbi prædicatione per to- tum orbem, ac varia rerum mutatione. Quibus accedunt varia miracula in cælo & terra facta. De- nique movebo, inquit Dominus, omnes gentes, quod vocatione & conversione omnium gentium factum. E quibus omnibus luce clarius est, commotionem il- lam tam insignem, quæ hic prædicta est, comple- mentum habuisse sub adventum Messiæ.

Neque vero opus est, ut ad ipsum nativitatis Messiæ annum aut diem solum restringatur vatici- nium, siquidem respiciatur non solum adventus e- jus, sed etiam manifestatio gloriæ, atque tota illa re- formatio, & immutatio, quam orbi patefacere de- bebant illæ commotiones, uti id ab Ebræis ipsis ac- ceptum fuisse demonstratio Apostolica apud E- bræos instituta convincit : probat enim ex hoc o- raculo veteris religionis cessationem. Quod autem ad- huc semel dicit, declarat mobilium translationem, tanquam factorum, ut maneant ea, quæ sunt immobi- lia : per mobilia tabernaculum manufactum & alia Levitica intelligit, vasa item, & ritus V. T. Quæ mo- bilia dicuntur, quia amoveri debebant per Chri- stum; immobilia aquæ à Christo & in Christum sunt, gratia & veritas, per quam facta est rituum ve- terum abrogatio, tanquam factorum, figurarum pu- ta, quæ vere impletæ sunt per Christi sacrificium propitiatorium, Evangelicum præconium & re- gnum. Hæc autem semper manent, & immobi- lia sunt. Non ergo restringenda illa commotio ad diem & annum adventus Christi, sed exten- denda ad œconomiam curriculi Christi, diebus carnis, passionis, resurrectionis, ascensionis ejusdem, & exaltationis ad dextram, missionis Spir. S. & voca- tionis gentium per ministerium Apostolorum Chri- sti. Quia promittitur hic non solum ut Judæorum Messias, sed ut desiderium gentium. Recte hic Christ. à Castro p. 450. Per Christi adventum in tem- plum debemus etiam intelligere ejus in carne dis- pensationem, quam oἰκονομίαν vocant Græci Pa- tres. Nam illustrior reddita est gloria illius tem- pli, quod in eo Christus inchoavit suam Eccle- siam. Ad illud enim Christus conveniebat, cum Ec- clesia universa, tum ad orandum, tum ad eum lo- quentem audiendum, ut constat ex Evangeliis & Actis Apostolicis. Unde in illo, & ex illo uni- versa per orbem Ecclesia disseminata originem ducit: quia de Sion exivit lex, & verbum Domini de Jerusalem.

B. Lutherus peculiarem hic explicationem fovet de ista commotione, intelligens motus per u- niversum orbem à Diabolo excitandos adversus semen mulieris, qui maxime sub N. T. excitati, quum fureret antea potissimum in Judæa adversus semen benedictum, quo de videatur liber ejus- dem laudatus adversus Judæos. Nullo autem mo- do subsistere potest Judæorum glossa, quam R. Mai- monides in More Nebuch. p. II. c. XXIX. tradi- dit, quod Haggæus loquatur hic de interitu regni Persici: siquidem Prophetæ scopus paracleticus fue- rit: qualis vero consolatio ad Judæos ex interitu regni Persici redundare potuit? Nec tum motæ sunt omnes gentes, quod hic prædicatur: nec pax ita conciliata fuit Judæis. Siquidem Alexander M. cum magno exercitu adortus Hierosolymam sit, Josepho teste lib. II. c. 8. Et quid de desiderio gen- tium fiet? Num Alexandrum M. domitorem mun- di credemus fuisse gentium desiderium? Quid quod de Persici Regni motibus & interitu concione pecu- liari egerit Propheta, c. II. v. 20. Confirmat ex- plicationem nostram (4) Gloria secundi, ejusdem- que novissimi templi, quæ eidem per præsentiam & manifestationem gloriæ Messiæ concilianda erat, ita ut gloriosius evadat templum secundum, quam prius Salomoneum fuerat. Non enim de alio, quam secundo templo loquitur Propheta. Judæi nonnulli fingunt tertium templum, quod adhuc ex- pectant, & de eo Prophetam agere volunt. Sed Propheta per הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה Hajediah & pronomen זֶה demon- strat præsens templum: Hanc ipsam domum: quæ tum erigebatur: ob quam Judæi subtristes erant, quod non videretur assequi gloriam prioris tem- pli: eamque dicebat הָאַחֲרוֹן novissimam vel ulti- mam, uti vox ea accipitur Gen. XXXIII. 3. Dan. IV. 5. c. X. 11. Neque enim aliud templum Judæis un- quam promissum est: nam quod Ezechiel descri- bit, non materiale templum est, sed plane mysti- cum, & cum destructione domus istius cessare de- buit ordo sacrificiorum, sacerdotum, ac totus cultus Leviticus: unde cum reparatio templi aliquando tentate est, cœlitus eadem impedita fuit. Qua- propter agnoscit Menasse Ben-Israel de term. vit. p. 155. Prophetiam Haggæi intelligendam esse de se- cundo templo, atque ita intelligi à R. Dav. Kimchi, R. Hazariah Ando, & magna parte veterum p. 152. quod etiam agnoscit R. Alschech in h. l. Conf. Const.

L'Empereur præfat. sup. Codic. Middoth. Gloria ergo, quæ hic promittitur, de gloria templi secun- di explicanda est. Quod vero non solum quoad externum splendorem multum cedebat Salomo- neo, sed etiam quoad res illas præcipui momenti quæ prius istud templum imprimis gloriosum red- diderant, in posteriori autem desiderata sunt: ar- cam scil. fœderis, cum propitiatorio, & præsentia vel σκηνώσει divina, ignem sacrum, Urim & Thu- mim, & Spiritum Prophetiæ: ut taceamus decem illa singularia, quæ vindicantur priori templo in Talmud in Joma c. I. Quum itaque præter Mes- siæ adventum, & gloriosam manifestationem ni- hil denominari possit, quo illustrius & gloriosius redditum fuerit alterum templum, fatendum erit, eam gloriam hic designatam esse. Nam quod gar- riunt Judæi, de conservatione longiori templi secun- di, quod decennio amplius steterit, valde frivolum est, unde merito ridentur à B. Luthero: Ætas so- la enim rem non facit magis gloriosam. Viel- leicht, inquit Megalander, ist der Maulesel Da- vids, darauf Salomo, als ein König, einritt, älter gewesen, als Salomo, solte er dann dar- um herrlicher, als der König selber, gewesen seyn? Ach daß sie doch einen guten Astro- nomum hätten hier gehabt, der es ein we- nig genauer hätte abgerechnet, der würde viel- leicht gefunden haben, daß sie zu den zehen Jahren, noch 3. Monden, 2. Wochen, 5. Ta- ge, 7. Stunden, 12. Minuten und 10. hal- be Minuten wären darüber gewesen. Wo etwa ein Kram wäre, der Schamroth feil hätte, dörfte ich den Jüden ein paar Gülden schencken, daß sie hingiengen, und ein Pfund kauffeten, und doch die Stirne, Augen und Backen darmit bestrichen, wolten sie ihr unverschemtes Hertz und Zungen damit nicht bestreichen. Æque inepta est exceptio, de ornatu quem contulit Herodes. Nam neque tantus ille fuit, quantus Salomoneus 2. Chron. III. 5. 6. 7. nec in auro & argento gloria præci- pua prioris templi constituta fuit, sed in quinque illis rebus, quæ deficiebant in po- steriori templo: Et recte B. Lutherus: Weil Herodes keinen Befehl hatte von GOTT, solches zu thun, sondern als ein gottloser Feind GOTTES, und seines Volks aus eitelem Ruhm und Hochmuth zu seinen eigenen Eh- ren solchen Bau that, so ist all sein Bauen und Arbeit vor GOTT nit so gut gewesen, als das geringste Steinlein, das Zorobabel aus Befehl GOTTES an den Tempel ge- leget hat. Denique fatetur R. Lusitanus in Colloquio Mittelburg. fol. 119. 123. (contradi- cens ea parte R. Isaac Ben. Abraham Lib. I. c. 34. & R. Manasse Ben Israel l. c.) gloriam secun- dæ domus sitam non fuisse in auro & argento, fingens autem tertiæ domus gloriam etiam in longe aliis rebus sitam hic indigitari. Quod com- mentum de tertio templo jam ante explosum est: ut taceam, quod R. Abraham in libro Cabalistic. Herodis templum tertium fuisse statuit. Quum er- go non inveniri queat, quod illustriorem fecerit domum novissimam, præter gloriosam præsentiam Messiæ, restat, ut agnoscant Judæi, Messiam venisse, cum adhuc stetit templum secundum. Nos autem complementum habemus in Nov. Test. cum Chri- stus in templo repræsentatus in infantia, cum in templo inter Doctores sedit in pueritia, cum in templo docuit, templum repurgavit, illudque glo- ria sua illustravit, cum juxta Malachiam c. III. venit Dominus aut templum, & filios Levi purgavic: ac palam gloriam suam demonstravit, gloriam veluti- unigeniti à Patre. vid. Luc. II. v. 27. & XIX. 47. Ioh. II. 4. c. VII. 4. quod jam pene per XVI. secula desolatum fuit. In Christo habemus ea omnia, sed in veritate, quæ in templo secundo desiderabantur: veram arcam fœderis, verum propitiatorium, Rom. III. 24. Oleum sacrum lætitiæ, & ignem sacrum amo- ris divini, nec non Urim cognitionis vel illuminationis sapientiæ, & Thumim perfectionis justitiæ 1. Cor. I. 29. denique שׁכנה præsentiam & habitationem divinam Joh. XIV. 11. Eph. III. 16. Non autem so- lum gloria illa respicitur, quæ conciliata fuit per præsentiam & prædicationem Christi in hoc tem- plo, sed etiam per id, quod inchoata ibi Ecclesia Test. Nov. quo de Cornel. à Lapide pag. 148. In- super eximia gloria templi secundi fuit, quod in eo per Christum non tantum peracta sint mysteria Verbi in- carnati, nostræq́, redemptionis salutis, sed etiam pri- mi fideles & Apostoli adornati sint, jactaq́, prima Ecclesiæ Christianæ fundamenta, juxta illud Es. cap. 2, 3. De Sion exibit lex Christus ergo suam Eccle- siam inchoavit in templo hoc, à Zorobabele fa- bricato. Ita Rupert. Hugo, Burgenf. Clarius, Va- tabl. & alii.

Accedit (5) Connexio gloriæ templi & adven- tus Messiæ. Et veniet desideratis cunctis gentibus & implebo domum istam gloria, dicit Dominus exerci- tuum. Hinc enim minime obscurum est, gloriam il- lam templo secundo conciliatum iri ab adventu Messiæ, eundemque ad templum secundum ven- turum. Nam per desiderium omnium gentium Mes- siam intelligi, antea ostensum: De quo hic audien- dus Lutherus l. c. Es soll kommen Hemdath, aller Heyden Trost, das ist, Messias aller Heyden Be- gierde, welches wir Trost verdolmetschet haben. Dann Begierde ist nit verständlich genug, weil es im Teutschen heist die innerliche Begierde, und Lust des Hertzens. active aber hier heisset es Be- gierde, das eusserliche passive das ein Hertz begeh- ret. Wann mans auch verdeutschete also: Aller Heyden Freude und Wonne, wäre auch nit falsch. Summa es ist Messia, an dem die unglaubigen verstockten Jüden eitel Unlust, Eckel und Greuel solten haben, wie Esaias 53. C. von ihnen weissaget, aber den Heyden solte er willkommen heissen, als ihres Hertzens Freude und Lust, aller Wuntsch und Begierde. Dann er bringet ihnen Erlösung von Sünden, Todt, Teuffel, Höllen, und allem Ubel ewiglich. Ja das ist der Heyden Begierde, Hertzens-Lust, Freude und Trost. Solches stim- met mit dem Spruch Jacob Gen. 49. und dem Si- lo oder Messia werden die Völcker gehorchen, das ist, sie werden ihn mit Freuden annehmen, sein Wort hören, und ohne Schwert ungezwungen sein Volck werden, als solt er sagen, die unedlen unbeschnittenen Heyden werden solches thun, a- ber meine edle Früchtlein, meine beschnittene ver- lohrne Kinder werdens nit thun, sondern rasend und unsinnig darwider werden. Hiezu stimmet auch Esaias 2. Mich. 4. Es wird zur letzten Zeit der Berg, da des HErren Haus ist, zugerichtet werden, höher dann alle Berge, und über alle Hügel erhoben werden, und werden daselbst alle Heyden zulauffen (ohne Zweiffel ungezwungen, aus Begierde und Lust) und viel Völcker zueilen und sagen: Kommet, lasset uns auf den Berg des HErrn gehen, zum Hause des Gottes Ja- cob, daß er uns lehre seine Wege, und wir wan- deln auf seinen Stegen. Dann von Zion wird ein Gesetz ausgehen, und des HErren wort von Jerusalem, und durchaus reden die Prophe- ten von Messia Reich unter den Heyden. Et por- ro fol. 85. GOtt saget: Er wolle den Heyden den

Hemdath geben, und ihr Gehorsam soll ihm ges- fallen, wie Jacob Gen. 49. spricht, und alle Pro- pheten, und wolle wiederumb gegen der Jüden harten Kopf so hart seyn, daß er darüber ehe sie wolle verwerffen, und die Heyden erwehlen und annehmen, unangesehen, ob sie mit des edlen Blutes von den Vättern noch beschnittene Hei- ligen sind. Dann so spricht Hos. 2. Jch will das so nit mein Volck ist, mein Volck heissen, und es soll mich seinen GOtt heissen. Aber zu den Jüden spricht er: Lo ammi, ihr seyd nicht mein Volck, und ich bin nit euer GOtt, welches ih- nen Moses lang zuvor gesungen hat in seinem Lie- de Deut. 32. Sie erbitterten mich mit dem, das nit GOtt ist, und erzürneten mich mit ihrem un- nützen Thun, so will ich sie wiederum verbittern mit dem, das nit mein Volck ist, und mit ei- nem tollen Volck will ich sie erzürnen. Dieser Spruch ist nun starck gegangen bey 1500. Jah- ren, daß wir tolle Heyden, so nicht GOttes Volck gewesen, nun GOTTES sind. Hæc Megalander. Addimus B. Tarnovii paraphrasin v. 7. Atœ hoc modo Ego Deus cœli non tantum inani- mata sed maxime homines(quippe propter quos etiam reliqua omnia fiunt miracula) commoturus sum, & quia tempus erit Nov. Test. rumpetur paries ille in- tergerinus inter Iudæos & gentes hactenus distinguens Eph. 2, 24. & adducturus sum ad Ecclesiam gen- tes omnes ex finibus terræ (sicut & factum esse in historiis N. Test. de Apostolis Petro, Paulo item, ejus- que comitibus, annotatis legimus) tum quando jam venerit desiderium illud summum (id quod in tex- tu Ebræo enallage numeri & generis in verbo obser- vata, nec sine causa adhibita notat. Vide Buxtorff. th. p. 400. 401. 402. & 388.) omnium gentium, ille Messias, quem anxiè expectare merito & expetere de- bebant omnes gentes, quandoquidem unaquæœ res naturæ quoque instinctu maxime appetit id, quo ma- xime indiget. Luth. vertit, da soll dann kommen al- ler Heyden Trost, & in margine, das ist, Christus, der alle Welt trösten soll durch Vergebung der Sünden. Et per hunc Messiam impleturus sum domum hanc gloria, quando ille rex gloriæ Ps.XXIV. 7. 8. qui major est Salomone Matth. XII. 42. in eo templo docuerit & miracula ediderit, qui est Deus & homo, quemque priores V. T. umbræ & historiæ re- spiciunt, quando narrant, quod gloria Dei ad arcam propitiatorii & ad sanctuarium, cum alias in taber- naculo, tum in dedicatione templi Salomonici appa- ruerit. Ita nunc veniet corpus ipsum, & gloriosa sua præsentia doctrina & miraculis istum locum, quem vos jam paratis, ornabit, ait Jehova Dominus ex- ercituum, ut sit hæc eadem promissio, quæ apud Malachiam c. 31. repetitur, quæque magnam huic lo- co lucem affert. Sic autem habet: Missurus sum an- gelum meum, qui expediat viam ante me, & re- pente veniet in templum suum Dominus, quem vos quæritis, & angelus fœderis, quo vos delecta- mini, hoc est, desideratissimus ille, quomodo longe melius cum patribus aliisœ nonnullis, quam cum Iu- nio & paucis aliis explicamus illa verba nostri Prophe- tæ Haggæi de Christo, quam de Christianis, potius de eligente, quam de electis, siquidem vocatur desiderium phrasi Hebræa, cum sit res maxime desiderata, ut Ps. 21, 3. desiderium pro re desiderabili ponitur, & alias Hebræi peculiari quodam linguæ idiotismo res vel personas desiderabiles maxime, nominant res vel viros desiderii seu desideriorum Esdr. 8, 27. Genes. 27, 15. Dan. 9, 23. 2. Chron. 20, 25. & 32, 27. & 36, 10. 19. Ps. 106, 24. Jer. 3. 19. & 12, 10. & 25, 34. Ez. 26, 12. Dan. 10, 3. 11. 19. & 11, 8. 37. 43. Hos. 13, 5. Am. 5, 11. Nah. 2, 10. Zachar. 7, 14. & abstractum pro concreto positum superlativum innuere jam supra aliquoties demon- stratum est. Exempla vid. Gen. 3, 6. & 11, 34. & 27, 27. & 43, 11. Psal. 10, 15. & 67, 5. Dan. 10, 11. 19. Eccles. 10, 3. Ex. 12, 42. & 17, 12. Joel. 2, 3. & 4, 17. Marc. 13, 19. Amos. 5, 11. Matth. 24, 15. 2. Cor. 5, 21. Eph. 5, 8. Col. 1, 13.

Huc facit (6) Donum pacis, quod amplian- dum per adventum desiderii gentium. Et in loco i- sto dabo pacem, dicit Dominus exercituum, quod in- telligi nequit de externa mundana pace, ea enim nunquam obtigit Judæis solida, quod bella, motus & persequutiones Antiochi 1. Macc. I. 23. seqq. a- pud Joseph. L. XI. Antiqq. c. VII. & l. I. de Bell. Jud. cap. 1. Pompeji lib. I. de Bell. Jud. c. V. alio- rumque fatis testantur. Quapropter de spirituali pace hoc explicandum est vaticinium, quæ à Mes- sia concilianda, & temporibus Messiæ pax promif- sa est Es. LIII. 6. cap. XI. 6. 7. Zach. IX. 10. Quam non habemus nisi in Christo Luc. II. 14. Joh. XIV. 27. Rom. V. 1. Eph. II. 14. 15. De ea pace hic sermo est, quæ gentibus non minus quam Judæis solatium adferre debeat, unde desiderium gentium omnium vocatur, cujus adventus hic promittitur, & in cujus diebus pax futura erat, de qua pace ac felicitate etiam Es. IX. 6. Jer. XXIII. 6. legere est. Unde R. Isaac Ben-Abraham in Chissuk Emuna lib. I. 34. per pacem hoc loco intelligit æternam pacem, & R. Lusitanus in Coll. Mittelb. f. 22. agnoscit, sermo- nem hic esse de templo, in quo Messias compa- riturus sit, quod requisituræ sint gentes, ut ita Mes- sias desiderium illud gentium omnium statuatur f. 130. Conf. de his Dn. D. Muller. Judaism. l. 1. c. IX.

(7) Temporis designatio. Adhuc unum modicum. Nonnulli explicant מְעַט non de temporis exiguita- te, sed dignitatis, parum & exiguum esse, quod antea moveris terram, respectu illius commotionis, quæ futu- ra sit olim; Adhuc una vice vel semel, parum, id est, commovebo cœlum & terram, ita Junius, parum illud est, nempe quod pepigeram vobiscum exeuntibus ex Ægypto, ut sit collatio legis & Evangelii, cui an- nuit Willius, addens: comparationem etiam insti- tui ratione majestatis promulgationis: sed ea contor- ta sunt, atque aliena à textu: & communiter de tempore exiguo Christiani pariter atque Judæi hæc explicant. Sensum verborum non male enucleat Ludov. de Dieu: nimirum אַחַת Tò vertendum esse „semel, uti reddidere LXX. & confirmat Apostolus „Ebr. XII. 26. Subintelligitur enim פַּעַם UNA „VICE, atque ita usurpatur Exod. XXX. 10. Joël. „XXXIX. 35. sicut שְׁתַּיִם subintellige פְעָמוֹת est „duabus vicibus, bis 2. Reg. IX. Porro אַחַת substan- „tivum vicem מְעַט substantivum tempus in se in- „cludunt non hic tantum, sed & alibi passim. Itaq; „tanquam duo substantiva in regimine Genitivi re- „ďte construuntur h. m. Adhuc una vices (ut inusita- „te ita exprimatur, vel una periodus) exigui tempo- „ris est. Et sensus est: quum multis hactenus vi- „cibus, iisque longarum periodorum repetierit „DEUS promissionem de Messia, eandemque to- „tidem vicibus distulerit, nempe ab Adamo ad „Abrahamum, inde ad legem latam, hinc ad Davi- „dem, & templi Salomonici structuram, ab hac „ad ejusdem per Zorobabelem instaurationem, nunc una adhuc tantum vices (vel periodus) eaque pusilli temporis restat, nempe à structo hoc templo secundo ad Christum: ita ille non inerudite. Sed Apostolus vocem illam ἔτι ἅπαξ urget, ut non vi- cem (aut periodum) quartam vel quintam, sed vi- cem alteram tantum indigitatam à Spiritu S. doceat, ac primam vicem, cui hanc alteram opponit, ad legis promulgationem referat, atque ex eo legalium trans- fe- lationem concludit: Videte ne recusetis loquentem. Si enim illi non effugerunt recusantes eum, qui super terram loquebatur, multo magis nos, qui de cælis loquentem nobis avertimus: cujus vox movit terram TUNC: NUNC autem (ecce oppositionem inter TUNC & NUNC, illam priorem & hanc alteram vicem) repromittit dicens: Adhuc semel, & ego movebo NON SOLUM TERRAM (uti nunc) sed & COELUM. Quod autem adhuc SEMEL (id est, altera vice) dicit, declarat nobilium translationem, tanquam factorum, ut maneant ea, quæ sunt immobilia: Si enim prima commotione (terræ) sancita fuissent talia, quæ immobilia, non opus foret alia nova, & solenniori commotione (cœli puta & terræ) quam promittit. Sensus est: Cavete, ne recusetis modo Christum vobis loquentem, ne puniamini, ut recusantes loquentem olim in monte Sinai pœnam non effugerunt. Ibi loquutus est super terram in monte. Hic de cœlis: quia non tantum de cælis descendit Filius Dei, sed cum in terris ageret, in cælis fuit Joh. III. 11. & de cœlis etiam palam vox audita fuit Matth. III. c. XVII. Joh. XII. atque de cœlis missus est solemni ac visibili modo Spirit. S. postquam Christus in cælum ascendit, cujus (Christi) vox tunc, cum legem ferret, terram movit: at cum per Haggæum promiserit, adhuc semel se moturum terram, & quidem non terram solum, sed & cælum, quod utique impletum per adventum de cælo in terram, (ubi multis modis cœlum & terram movit) quid aliud docuit illa iterata commotione, quam quod ea, quæ priori terræ commotione sancita non fuerint omnino immobilia, quodque mobilium istorum, h. e. legalium translatio quædam succedere, rerumque immobilium confirmatio per novam illam inaugurationem commotionis non solum terræ, sed ipsius etiam cœli fieri debeat: Docet ergo S. Apostolus illud ADHUC SEMEL, declarare, atque insinuare, fœderis illius veteris cum commotione terræ promulgati res abolendas fuisse, quæ factæ tantum ad veras res novi fœderis repræsentandas, ac proinde advenientibus vel confirmatis in illa nova commotione, cum cæli, tum terræ, æternis & immobilibus bonis necessario cedere debuisse. Quapropter concludit Apostolus θεοπιςως, illud ADHUC SEMEL veteris fœderis abrogationem, & novi instaurationem inferre, & res illius factitias & instabiles, hujus vero æternas & perpetuas inter se conferre. Quæ lucem accipiunt, si conferantur, quæ Ebr. IIX. & IX. de tabernaculo manufacto dicta sunt. Unde manifestum oppido est, non hic Apostolum de novissimo adventu Christi agere, aut ad eundem Propheticum oraculum applicare, quod nonnulli volunt, sed de primo adventu Christi Propheticum textum interpretari. Quæ non solum Hieronymi in Hagg. II. sed etiam Augustini est sententia l. XIIX. de Civ. Dei c. XXXV. lib. III. ut & è Græcis Cyrilli lib. V. in Genes. Atque in eo consentiunt plerique Interpp. Prophetici h. l. Rupertus, Remigius, Haymo, Albert. Hugo, Lyranus, è nostris Winckelmannus, Himmelius, Tarnovius & alii.

Postremo non est, quod Judæi ogganniant, non exiguum tempus, sed quinq; secula fluxisse ab hac promissione ad nativitatem Jesu: Resp. enim modicum dici respectu temporis elapsi, vel inde à promulgatione legis, ubi terra etiam mota fuit, vel à promulgatione Prot-Evangelii, ex quo tempore expectatus fuit Messias, siquidem annos inde numerent Chronologi 3462. (alii 3434.) usque ad annum II. Darii Hystaspis, quorum ratione anni quingenti certe exiguum tempus censentur. Atque hæc de isto vaticinio.

CONCIO III.

## 2:10
Verse 11. IN THE TWENTY-FOURTH OF THE NINTH MONTH] Namely, at which time, after the wall was built up, the hand was again applied to the work, as appears below 16, 19.

Latin:

Verf. 11. IN VIGESIMA ET QVARTA NONI MENSIS] Quo scilicet tempore post maceriem congestam iterum manus admota operi est, ut apparet infra 16, 19.

## 2:11
Verse 12. ASK THE PRIESTS THE LAW] For it was their duty to answer concerning ceremonies, as they knew them best. Levit. X. 10. Ezech. XLIV. 23. Mal. II. 7.

Bellarmine collected from this passage, lib. III. de verbo Dei c. IV., that it is clearly not for private men to judge concerning the meaning of the law; but the Jesuit ought to have observed that the priests consulted by the Prophet are rebuked, are accused of negligence in their office, and were not to be a council, nor ought they to have invented interpretations from their own ingenuity, but were to be bound simply to the law or scripture, so that they might answer those consulting them about the law according to it in doubtful matters. But what kind of consequence is this? In doubtful matters in the Old Testament, especially ceremonial ones, the priests were to be consulted, who were compelled to give answers from the revealed word of God. Therefore, in the clearest sayings of scripture, for everyone always, even in the New Testament, will that only be their genuine sense which the Pope alone with a Council, besides and against Scripture, for the most part invents? Likewise, these priests are proven guilty of negligence in their office when this present question is proposed to them by the Prophet. Therefore, is the authority of the Roman Pope with a Council established here?
