Zorobabel ipse antiquus intelligitur, sed inclusa ejus posteritate, vel potius assumtio illa ita explicanda, ut se porrigat ad conservationem ejus, non tantum quoad vitam & regimen ejus, sed etiam quoad propagationem & benedictionem poste- ritatis. Assumam te Zorobabel, ita ut te conservem, ac tuear, & propagem genus tuum inter istas regno- rum turbas & eversiones. Ita Castrius: Inter hos tot casus, & tot discrimina rerum, & tam diversas re- gnorum mutationes ego sub mea cura te assumam cu- stodiendum ô Zorobabel, fili Salathielis, quod curave- ris cultum meum, domum mihi aedificando uti servus meus: & custodiam te, nempe tuam posteritatem, tanquam annulum signatorium in dextra manu mea ut sis totius Israelis ornamentum singulare. Te enim elegi ego Dominus exercituum, ut ex te suam ducat originem Christus, qui suum regnum eriget, & inter tot regnorum mutationes & ruinas, suum exeret caput. Est huic similis illa Danielis Prophetia capit. 2, 44.

(2) Dici etiam potest, assumtionem illam tribui fi- lio DEI, qui hic loquens introducatur, ut è vers. 7. collatione cum Ebr. XII. 26. colligitur, quod com- moturus ipse sit coelum pariter & terram, & subver- surus solium Regni. Atque ita assumpturus Zoroba- belem dicetur Filius Dei, ea ratione, ut ad specia- lem ἐπιλήψεως modum respiciat, quo non Ange- los, sed semen Abrahae dicitur ἐπιλαμβαίν ut Ebr. II. 16. & conferenda haec promissio erit cum illa, quae Abrahamo Gen. XII. 5. facta: In te benedicentur omnes gentes. Ut enim ibi Abrahamo quidem ipsi hoc promisit Deus, ejusque stemma ita nobilita- vit, atque ad hoc sublime axioma evexit, ut ex i- psius lumbis prodire debuerit fons & causa omnis benedictionis, non tamen in Abrahamo, sed in se- mine Abrahami benedictio eventura promittitur, interprete ipsomet Filio Dei Gen. XXII. 18. Ita hic promittitur ipsi Zorobabeli haec gratia, atq; digni- tas, quod assumendus sit à Filio DEI, quatenus ex ipso proditurum semen à Filio Dei assumendum. Quo referri potest expositio Cyrilli, Dorothei in vi- ta Haggaei in Synopsi Remigii, Lyrani, & Vata bli, cum censent, haec promitti non Zorobabeli, sed Christo secundum humanitatem, qua est semen Zo- robabelis. Coccejus in h. l. Accipiam te intelligit in sensu pleno & palpabilitate rei. Qui non male con- fert Ps. XLIX. 26. Et eodem res redit, sive dicatur Zorobabeli promissionem factam esse, non in se, sed in semine Christo secundum carnem, seu dicas, ipsi Christo, qua homini: congruentius tamen prius dicitur, quia Zorobabelem alloquitur Dominus, & de Zorobabele agit, eique hanc gratiam promit- tit, eo quod domum ipsi exstruxerit, interprete Ec- cles. XLIX. 13. (3) Notatu digna est observatio Ca- strii, quam hic tradidit: Erat olim celebre Deo, cum vellet suorum obsequia remunerari servorum, Chri- stum ex eorum progenie polliceri, quod in summo ipsi honore, & favore collocabant: atque hac sola spe seipsos felicissimos censebant. Hinc Gen. 12, 3. ut Abrahae remuneraret, quod egressus esset de terra sua, & cognatione sua, promisit illi Christum in posteris ejus futurum, cum dixit in te benedicen- tur omnes cognationes terrae. Et c. 32, 48. propter o- bedientiam filii sacrificati, dicitur illi: Benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terrae, quia obedisti voci meæ. Eademq; promissio facta est Jacob Gen. 28, 14. Davidi etiam ut vicem rependeret, quod jurasset Psal. 131, 5. Si introiero in tabernaculum domus meæ, si ascendero in lectum strati mei &c. Juravit Dominus David veritatem: de fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam. Propter hoc ipsum tam avide expectabant filios prisci Patres, ne tanto filio orbarentur, Christo. Atque ideo tam anxie deflebat se vita privari Ezechias Esa. 38, 12. cum dixit: Præcisa est velut à texente vita mea: dum adhuc ordirer, succidit me. Timet, ait Hieronymus, ne in telæ similitudinem in ipso lucis exordio præcidatur, & nequaquam de semine ejus Christus oriatur. Qua ergo ratione Davidi, quod procurasset ædificare domum Domino, tabernaculum Deo Jacob, promisit DEUS se illi ædificaturum domum, in qua Rex esset Christus, cujus regni non erit finis, Lucæ I. ita Zorobabeli, quod domum alteram DEO ædificare curaverit, pollicetur Deus, se illum illustraturum Christo Domino ex eo nascituro, & regno ejus in æternum permansuro. Et hæc est causa, cur soli Zorobabeli facta sit hujusmodi Prophetia, quod de ejus posteritate nasciturus esset Christus.

(4) In nomine itaque TE ponenda est figura, ut nomen Zorobabel sensum proprium retineat; Te assumam, id est, semen tuum, juxta analogiam similium Evangelicarum promissionum, utpote Genes. XII. 3. in TE, id est, in semine tuo benedicentur; cap. XIIX. 18. in ipso (Abrahamo) id est, in semine Abrahami. Sic etiam illud Te ponam ut sigillum exponit Cornelius à Lapide cum Castrio: Competunt hæc potius Zorobabeli in persona, non sua, sed Christi. De eo enim ad literam loquitur Aggæus, dicens: In die illa, scilicet tempore Christi q. d. inquit à Castro: Assumam tuam carnem ô Zorobabel, quam tanquam annulum signatorium aureum inseram dextræ meæ, nempe filio meo, qui est meum brachium, mea dextra, mea virtus & fortitudo Isaiæ 53, 1. ut tali filio ex te progenito colaris ab omnibus & glorificeris, imo super universos regis exalteris, ac quasi deificeris in natura humana, quam ex tua posteritate filius meus assumet, sibique uniet & deificabit, idque in æternum, ut ei semper in omnia secula adhæreat, sicut annulus digito. Ita ergo Christus hic signum, sive sigillum vocabitur Dei, qua homo, non qua Deus, qua humanitatem, non Deitatem, ex Zorobabelis carne & stirpe assumsit, tum per communicationem idiomatum, per quam ea, quæ sunt Dei, tribuuntur homini, quia enim Filius Dei & sigillum & imago Patris Ebr. I. χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως ἀυτῦ, ideo homo Christus etiam sigillum & imago dicitur Patris; tum quia filius DEI incarnatus est quasi sigillum expressum; in quo legimus, imo expressum videmus Dei amorem & voluntatem erga nos Joh. VI. 27. Filius DEI, qui in se est invisibilis vestivit & velavit se carne è Zorobabele assumpta, ut per eam ipse q. transpareret & translucereţ, sicut transparet gloria & majestas divina per stellas, quæ sunt quasi signacula divinæ potentiæ & gloriæ Job, IX. 7. Verbum enim caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis, & vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam veluti unigeniti à Patre Johan. I. 14. Sicut sigillum vel annulus signatorius imaginem expressam refert, præ omnibus rebus custoditur & charus habetur, ut semper veluti in oculis sit, & ornamenti instar est: Ita Christus est sigillum, & annulus signatorius, imaginem refert Dei, & custoditur, ac charus præ omnibus habetur, ceu unus homo in gratia, in quo est εὐδοκία Dei. De ornamento hujus sigilli Castrius ita habet: Sicut manus habentis pretiosum annulum, exornatur illo, ita carne ex tua assumpta posteritate, tanquam annulo exorna- bor & glorificabor. Nam si Filius Dei turba creden- tium coronatur, & martyres suis victoriis, quasi gemmarum varietate illi diadema imperii distin- guunt, juxta illud Isaiae LXII. 3. & eris corona gloriae in manu Domini & diadema regni in manu Dei tui, ut notat ibi Hieronymus. Unde & Paulus Philip. IV. 1. vocabat fideles gaudium & corona mea, cur non jure optimo Christi humanitas esset corona Filii Dei, diadema regni & summa gloria, & pretio- sus, quo exornetur, annulus, quamvis ab ipso suam omnem susceperit preciositatem? Porro sicut sigil- lum adhibetur ad obsignationem & imprimendam fi- guram vel characterem: ita per Christum, qui po- situs est signaculum, obsignantur fideles, sisque im- primitur figura & character divinus, ut habeant si- gnum Dei vivi Apoc. VII. 2. 1. Cor. IX. 2. uti cera non aliam figuram refert, quam sui sigilli, sic nos non aliam similitudinem referamus, quam Christi 1. Cor. XI. 1. & in eandem transformemur imagi- nem 2. Cor. III. 11. 1. Cor. XV. 49. Ut signaculum ad custodienda grata & pretiosa adhibetur: Ita Chri- stus dicitur signaculum ad custodiendos fideles, ut nemo eosdem rapiat: sicut olim circumcisione si- gnabantur Israelitae, quae signaculum fidei dicitur Rom. 4, 11. atque eo in coetu populi Dei custodie- bantur: ita modo charactere Baptismi, tanquam fidei signaculo, & Christi, fideles confignantur, & in- tra Ecclesiam custodiuntur: & quemadmodum o- lim Exod. 12, 13. sanguine agni oblitis postibus, & superlimmaribus filiorum Israel Angelus percu- tiens pertransibat eos, & Ezech. 9, 4. nullus in quo erat Tau, signum Dei vivi, Apoc. 7, 3. percutiebatur, quod, ut ait Origenes Homil. de Epiphan. Hieron. & Isid. esset crucis Dominicae figura, quo obsigna- bantur in fronte gementes, & dolentes: ita crucis divinissimo signaculo consignati, ac veri Dei agni sanguine obliti, custodiuntur, ne quis eos audeat at- tingere. Unde de illo Hebraeo, quem refert Gre- gorius cognomento Magnus lib. 3. Dialog. cap. 7. quod se cruce consignasset, dixit hostis crucis: vae vae, vas vacuum, sed signatum. Qua etiam ratione sponsi verba possunt intelligi: Pone me ut signacu- lum cor tuum. Hoc est, cura ut cor tuum, me tan- quam signaculo ita clausum custodias, & brachium tuum ita salvum conserves, ut nulli ad te ullum ac- cessum permittas; sed mihi te illaesam, intactam- que conserves. Quia adeo durus est amor, zelusq; ex eo profectus, ut mortis instar sit, atque inferni sinistrum aliquid in amore persentire; & bra- chium tuum contorquendum alteri, quam mihi permittere, aut cor tuum alteri, me despecto, re- serare, & tradere, ut iterum hic habet Castrius. De- nique (ut & hoc ex eodem Castrio adjiciamus) Christus recte dicitur signaculum ad conscribendos milites suos, ac distinguendos servos suos de ho- stibus triumphantem, a servis daemonis, qui sub ejus militant vexillo. Solebant Imperatores o- lim suis ducibus characterem militiae suae, nomine suo insculptum, tribuere, ut eum imprimerent mi- litibus, quos castris eorum congregabant, nomine imperatoris manui singulorum infigentes: quem regium, aut imperatoris characterem nuncupa- bant. Ut refert D. August. lib. 1. contra Cresconium Grammaticum cap. 30. & serm. super gestis cum Emerico Episcopo Donatista, & Tract. 6. in Joan. Ita Christi charactere confignantur, ac describun- tur ejus milites & diversi esse cognoscuntur ab a- liorum militibus ac servis. Erant quoque insignia quaedam e collo pendentia, qualis erat Roma- nis bulla, gestamen triumphantium, quam in trium- pho prae te gerebant, inclusis intra eam remediis, quæ crederent adversus invidiam valentissima, au- ctore Macrobio, lib. 1. Saturnal. cap. 6. & in scutis & peltis concedebantur brachiis adfixis, ut gens una, aut familia distingueretur ab alia: quæ vel suo Marte comparassent, vel amore alicujus præelegif- fent. Non dissimiliter Christianis conceditur Chri- ftus, qui tanquam monile è collo pendens pectori ad- hæreat, cordisque sedem exornet: scutumque fidei brachio affixum, in quo & ipse Christus, quasi effi- gies præstantissima, depingitur, ut tali stemmate divisi ab aliis, & amuleti cujusdam cœlestis instar ab omnibus hostium insidiis, ac fascinationibus præservati, eum tantum cogitemus, & militemus. Et hoc est, pone me ut signaculum super cor tuum, tan- quam monile è collo super pectus cordis sedem pendens: & tanquam signaculum in scuto brachii tui. Tu enim es signum sagittantium, ut quidam exciamat, ve- xillum pugnantium, brabium currentium, distinctio o- vium, custodia cordium, exemplar operantium, for- ma normaǵ; servorum, & sigillum ac character mi- litantium. Ut eo viso hostes fugiant, cæterisque omnes dicant: Ecce gens, cujus Dominus Deus ejus, populus, quem elegit Dominus in hæreditatem sibi. Hunc sensum tradidit Cyrillus: Non ad Zorobabe- lem revera; sed ad Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum potius, ut in Zorobabele per quam convenienter expres- sum, hæc verba fiunt: quoniam & ex tribu Iuda, & liberatorum è captivitate princeps, & domum Domi- ni ædificantium tanquam Præses erat. Te igitur, inquit, assumptum servum meum (hoc est, qui in forma servi apparuisti, cum natura liber sis) illo tempore, quo voluero dynastas seu potentes de throno dejicere, & à Principatibus removere, po- nam quasi signaculum. Filius enim Dei & Patris signaculum est, totam ejus & perfectam similitudi- nem continens, & in proprio decore genitoris na- tura coruscans. In ipso porro quoque ad simili- tudinem suam nos signat Deus: siquidem in Chri- stum transformati, velut imaginem Dei acquiri- mus. Signaculum igitur perfectum Dei & Pa- tris est Filius, & ipsum elegit, hoc est, eligibilem reddidit, & electum.

(5) Atque ita etiam tertium pronomen, quia elegi TE, intelligitur à Cyrillo de filio & semine Zorobabelis Christo: quia eligi TE, id est, filium & semen tuum. De quo etiam Esa. XLII. 1. 4. Electus meus &c. Ita quoque Coccejus: Ratio est divina electio & beneplacitum, quod includit æternam πρό- γνωσιν Christi, ut agni immaculati 1. Petr. I. 20. & quod Deo placuit omnem plenitudinem in ipso habi- tare Col. I. 19. & æternam prædestinationem nostri in filios in ipso Ephes. I. 5. 6. Chaldæus reddidit: quo- niam in te mihi complacuit: quæ vox Dei fuit de Christo Matth. III. 17. (6) Si non placeat illa μονό- τερης ASSUMTIONIS de hypostatica assumtio- ne significatio, atque sensus generalis protectionis & custodiæ præferatur, de Zorobabele, inclusa posteri- tate, hæc promissio intelligenda, de quo etiam illa ver- ba, ponam te quasi annulum signatorium, explicari po- terunt, quod ad ejus instar charum ipsum habere, eumque custodire, atque in oculis semper gerere velit Dominus: sed ut in postremis verbis rationis instar adjectis, QUIA ELEGI TE, respectus ha- beatur ad specialem illam electionem, qua Zorobabe- lem dignari voluit Dominus, ut nempe ex ipsius familia carnem suam assumeret, & è lumbis ejus prodiret desiderium omnium gentium, cujus causa cœlum & terram se commoturum iterum Zoroba- beli testatur. Quo abit paraphrasis Castrii p. 436. Subvertam Persicam monarchiam, & fortitudi- nem conteram regnorum gentium illi subjectarum.

Subvertam quoq́; regnum Græcorum in quatuor capi- ta dissectum, cum regibus eorum; & Romanorum equi cum equorum equitibus mutuis bellorum civilium gladiis corruent confossi. Atq́; eo tempore inter tot regnorum casus, te tuamq́; posteritatem sub patro- cinio meo protegendam assumam ô Zorobabel: quia ut servus meus fidelis procurasti cultum meum, do- mum mihi ædificando; & constituam te mihi conjun- ctissimum, ut signatorius annulus alicujus dexteræ solet adhærere: quod eligerim te, tuamq́; posteri- tatem, ut humanam carnem ex ea assumam, & spirituale regnum erigam perpetuo duraturum, ait Dominus exercituum, qui non potest mentiri. Ita relinquetur hoc epitheton juxta Syracydem cap. XLIX. 3. Zorobabeli, quod sit q. signum in dextera, & quemadmodum DEUS summum adversus Je- choniam fastidium testaturus Jerem. XXII. 24. ait: Etsi Iechonias esset sigillum in manu dextra mea, ta- men inde evellam te: ita ex adverso hic de Zoro- babele promittit: ponam te ut annulum signatorium, indicavit, quod ipse non modo charus Domino futurus sit, sed quod eum etiam ut rem pretio- sissimam digitis veluti circumgerere ac glorifica- re, & in confusione servare velit: Et nihilomi- nus designabitur illa dignitas, qua electus est Zoro- babel, ut genealogiæ Messiæ insereretur, & inter majores ejus censeretur.

(7) Ad hanc dignitatem Zorobabelis expri- mendam etiam non incommode Gualtherus ad- hibet simile de signaculo hom. VII. in Hagg. p. 266. In die illa, dicit Dominus exercituum, as- sumam te, ô Zorobabel, fili Salathielis, serve mi, dicit Dominus, & ponam te, quasi annulum &c. Habent singula verba emphasin. Diligenter enim & ipsius Zorobabelis meminit, & patris quoq́; Sealthielis nomen attingit, ut se omnia ejus novisse ostendat. Deinde servum suum vocat, nec sine magna amo- ris significatione ait, serve mi. Præterea, Assu- mam & te dicit, nimirum in meam fidem atque protectionem. Addit insuper: Et ponam te quasi annulum, id est, eris mihi loco annuli signatorii. Hoc alii de summo favore & diligentissima custo- dia exponunt. (Solent enim annuli signatorii in summo precio haberi, & ideo diligentius asservari, ne vel amittantur, vel in impostorum & fraudu- lentorum manum incidant.) Quorum sententiam ut non omnino rejicio, ita Deum majus quiddam & sublimius spectare puto: nimirum Messiæ promif- sionem, in quam omnes pios olim respexisse con- stat. Quia enim is ex Davidis stirpe expectabatur, Davidis posteri instar sigilli erant quo Deus suam promissionem quasi visibiliter obsignabat, cum inter tot motus atq́; pericula & horribiles illustrissimarum familiarum ruinas, eos incolumes servaret, ex qui- bus promissus ille Servator nasci debebat. Eodem sensu lucernæ etiam dicti sunt Davidis posteri, & ta- les fore Deus prædixerat in Psalmo 132. Ibi cornu Davidi propagabo & lucernam paravi uncto meo. Ut enim lucerna de lucerna accenditur, neque tenebris locus datur, ubi aliqua lucerna superest: Ita in Davidis posteritate perpetua fuit hæredum promissionis successio, quæ piorum fidem assi- due fovit, donec vera illa & æterna lux JESUS CHRISTUS, suo in mundum adventu tenebras omnes excussit, & humanis rebus deploratis salu- tem attulit. Pollicetur ergo DEUS, se Zoroba- belem pro germano Davidis filio agnoscere, nec un- quam defuturos ex ejus posteritate, qui promissio- nibus suis fidem faciant. Confirmant sensum i- stum genealogiæ Christi JESU, quas Matthæus & Lucas contexuerunt, in quibus perpetua illa posterorum Davidis successio usque ad CHRI- STUM ceu digito demonstratur. Quam expli- cationem suam fecit Balt. Willius, & è Zacharia il- lustravit pag. 77. Majus quid hac phrasi significari nullus dubito, eamq́; comparo cum simili, quo utitur Zacharias cap. III. 8. de Josua, ejusque sociis, docturus quod sint viva rerum futurarum, imprimis Messiæ summi Sacerdotis, testimonia : Audi nunc Io- sua, ait, sacerdos maxime, tu & socii tui, qui sedent coram te, quoniam ostento estis. Quemadmodum Jo- sua ibi dicitur ostentum, quia typum Messiæ vivum agebat, ut prolixius dicto loco explicavimus, ita etiam heic loci Zerubbabel vocatur annulus signa- torius cum suis posteris, quia hi in universum o- mnes sigilla erant divinam promissionem de Messia venturo ex semine Davidis confirmantia, & Israeli- tæ per ipsorum conspectum quotidie de divini pacti ve- ritate certiores reddebantur. Unde observat Wil- lius, præter Zerubabelem, posteros ejus, ipsumque Christum hic intelligi, qui ex lumbis ejus erat o- riturus, adeoque promissionem hanc Zorobabe- li ipsi promitti, pro sua persona inchoative, respectu vero posterorum continuative, & denique ipsius Christi finitive, ut sensus sit : temporibus posteris, tunc quando regna vicina subvertam, te Zerubabelem cum tuis posteris, imprimis vero Christum gratum & ac- ceptum habebo, accuriosissime vos in testimonium futuri Messiæ servabo. Quod etiam in illa ratione, quam subjunxit Dominus. Quia elegi TE, ob- servat. Cæterum subjicitur promissioni ratio & causa impulsiva, quam dicit DEUS electionem & beneplacitum suum, quo ipsi complacitum, Ze- rubabelem ceu Ducem & Principem populo ex familia Davidis eligere. Sic Psalm. LXXVII. 10. Elegit David servum suum. Hæc ratio æque late atque ipsa promissio patet. Ideo enim sigilla quo- que erunt & servabuntur Zerubabelis posteri, quia DEUS Davidis posteritatem elegit præ cæteris, ut ex ea Messias oriatur. Ideo quoque DEO in Christo complacebat, quia servus ejus electus est, qui gentibus & nationibus lucem vitæ & salutis præferre debet Esa. XLII. 1. Hæc Willius. Quæ ta- men per omnia probari nequeunt. Nam quomo- do signaculum hoc ad ipsum Christum refertur, si illa explicatio Waltheri accipiatur, Zorobabelem cum posteris instar sigilli fuisse, quo Deus suam promissionem de Messia quasi visibiliter designa- bat, num Messias sigillum promissionis de Messia, num in Christo testimonium futuri Messiæ? Quid ad Christum ea electio, qua Zorobabel dignus habi- tus est, ut in ea genealogia Christi, & inter ejus majores locaretur, num ad id Christus ipse ele- ctus cum Zorobabele ac nepotibus? Ideoque in- cluditur quidem huic vaticinio Christus, ut scopus præcipuus, sed non comprehenditur in subjecto, cui prædicata assumtionis, sigilli, & electionis conve- niant, juxta Gualtheri ἔκθεσιν.

(8) Atque ita etiam B. Winckelmannus noster es )

de Zorobabele cum successoribus exponit, ut B. VVinckel- Christum tamen haud negligat. ASSUMAM TE) Admodum consolatoria promissio pro Zorobabele, e- jusq́; successoribus, qua promittit se singularem ejus tanquam servi sui fidelis curam & custodiam susce- pturum, non secus ac si quis annulum signatorium non negligit, sed quam diligentissime custodit. Ostendit haec promissio Zorobabelem earum fuis- se DEO, etiam propter Christum ex ipso descensu- rum, qui instar gemmae pretiosissimae in hoc annulo lateat, quemadmodum Matthaeus Zorobabelem in genealogia Christi ponit. Quae à B. Himmelio quoque repetuntur & approbantur. Neque diffi- tentur Iudaei, Christum hoc vaticinio insinuatum esse: imo R. Abarbenel, notante Coccejo, hunc fa- cit sensum hujus pericopae: Deum quidem non da- turum Zorobabeli regnum sub domo secunda, & il- lam quoq́; non staturam, sed nihilominus olim in con- gregatione populi ex semine ipsius Messiam excitatum iri Regem, probatque ex veteribus Messiam hic de- signari. Quapropter cum & veteres Ecclesiae Dd. Dorotheus, Cyrillus, aliique, & è recentioribus In- terpp. Pontificii, Reformati, nostri pleriq́;, nec non è Iudaeorum Rabbinis nonnulli agnoscant, hanc promissionem Zorobabeli factam respicere caput omnium promissionum, de venturo Messia, (et- iamsi non eadem ratione omnes in eadem Chri- stum ostendant) non est, quod aliorum Judaeorum glossis, qui Christum ex hoc oraculo eliminant, & in Zorobabelis persona subsistunt, cum Grotio as- surgamus. Non enim solum hoc Principe tuta praestanda erat Judaea, sed usque ad adventum Messiae sceptrum & legislator conservari in ea de- buit: neque id unice aut praecipue in votis habe- bat ipse, ut à nemine suo tempore infestaretur Judaea, sed quam maxime cum aliis piis Regibus, Ducibus & Prophetis Messiam anhelabat, ac desi- derabat Zorobabel, cui nihil gratius, nihil hono- ratius annunciari atque promitti poterat, quam quod ipsum inter Majores Messiae Dominus accense- ri, & è stirpe ejus Messiam excitare velit. Et ἐξοχι- κῶς intelligendum illud, QUIA TE ELEGI, de praecipuo apice, ac fastigio dignitatis, & honoris, ad quos electus à Domino fuit Zorobabel. Sine dubio autem id praecipuum est, quod electus fue- rit, ut in catalogo majorum Messiae collocaretur: quo axiomate nihil prius, nihil antiquius habue- runt sancti Patriarchae, Reges & Duces sub Vete- ri Testamento. Atque haec etiam de isto oracu- lo. Suspiremus nunc cum Sponsa mystica (Cant. IIX. 6.) ad Christum animae nostrae Sponsum: Po- ne me ut signaculum super cor tuum, ut signaculum super brachium tuum. Respondeat desiderium omnium gentium animae fideli: Ponam te quasi si- gnaculum: quiate elegi.

Amen, Domine JESU, Amen. Tibi sit laus, honor & gloria in secula, Amen.

# Zechariah

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
In the name of Jesus. Annotations on Zechariah.

Latin:

I. N. I. ANNOTATA AD ZACHARIAM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface
Preface.

Zechariah from זכר (remembered) and יה (the Lord), is as it were μνησίθεος, remembering God, who not only was himself mindful of God, but also exhorted others to be so.

For when the people were rather slack in erecting the temple and divine worship, and a portion even, for fear of enemies after the Babylonian affliction, scarcely dared to undertake the restoration of divine worship, the Prophet was stirred up to urge the sluggish with exhortations and to support the faith of the weak with promises: therefore, notable visions are exhibited concerning future events both of the State and of the Church, and illustrious oracles are inspired concerning the coming, passion, death, kingdom, and benefits of Christ, so that the people might be recalled to repentance, the pious might be confirmed in the true faith, and all might be reminded of their duty:

There are three parts: the first, an exhortation entrusted to them for conversion with the promise of divine grace, is completed by various visions up to chapter VII. The second provides information concerning both ceremonial and certain moral matters in chapter VII. The third consists of Prophetic oracles concerning the preservation and expansion of the Church or the kingdom of Christ, and concerning Christ as King and Savior, and his office and benefits. The first part may be called Optical, the second Didactic, the third Prophetic. In the first part there are two sermons, the former summary, the latter more specific, in which eight visions are contained, with an illustration and confirmation, both symbolic and open, added at the end of them. These, however, are partly general, such as the two former in chapter I, concerning Christ as the Protector and Mediator of the people, seen among the myrtle trees, who helps the people and intercedes for them, and also concerning the four horns that scatter the people being crushed; partly special, which are both more open and more symbolic. The more open ones are found in chapters II, III, and IV, and they concern either the Church, such as the building of Jerusalem and its extension throughout the world, and its exhilaration through the coming and indwelling (ἐνοίκησιν) of the Messiah: chapter II; or the investiture and confirmation of the High Priest, which is established by the promise of the coming of the Branch (Zemach) and the cutting of the eye-stone, or the expiatory passion of Jesus in chapter III, or the structure of the temple to be completed by Zerubbabel: for which purpose in chapter 4 the golden lampstand and the two olive trees are exhibited. More symbolic are those which are presented in chapters V and VI: the former indeed concerning the flying scroll and the Ephah with the mass of lead, to designate the judgment of iniquity and the wickedness to be transported: the latter, however, concerning the four chariots seen from the midst of two bronze mountains, to figure the ministries of the Angels fighting for the Church, so that it may enjoy tranquility and not be scattered again before the exhibition of the Messiah. By the former the wicked are terrified, by the latter the pious are raised up. To illustrate and confirm which eight visions, a similar command is subjoined in the same chapter concerning the two crowns to be placed on Joshua and the promise concerning the Messiah as King and High Priest, shadowed forth by that figure, under which man, the Branch (Zemach), all things will grow, and the temple will be built for the Lord throughout the world. And all these things pertain to the second sermon, delivered on the 24th day of the eleventh month of the second year of Darius.

In the second part is the third sermon of the Prophet, instituted on the 4th day of the ninth month of the fourth year of Darius, consisting of the rejection of elective fasts and a serious exhortation to justice and works of charity, chapter VII.

The third part is completed by the four remaining sermons: The first is Paracletico-Paraenetica concerning the habitation and blessing of Jerusalem, for the sake of which, with fear dispelled, they ought to study truth and concord. The second is Consolatory concerning the turning of fasts into feasts and the gathering of the nations to the people of God, chapter VIII. The third sermon is presented in Chapters IX, X, XI, and is partly Consolatory in chapter IX, where, after the announced overthrow or conversion of enemies, the arrival of the King is intimated, who will release the captives from the infernal pit by his blood and will subject the nations to himself with his army, and in chapter X, strength, protection, and victory are promised under this Leader. It is partly comminatory concerning the overthrow of Jerusalem and the rejection of the Jewish people, who do not value Christ the true Shepherd, who is to be sold for a small price, but who adhere to seducers, chapter XI. The fourth sermon is purely Evangelical, chapters XII, XIII. and XIV is presented: and chapter XII indeed concerning the rescue of the true Israel, and strengthening against enemies, and concerning the outpouring of the Spirit of grace and the piercing of the Messiah, and the death that will bring about the most grievous lamentation, chapter XIII concerning the opening of the purifying fountain of Baptism, the excision of idols, the striking of Christ the Shepherd, the dispersion of the sheep, and the turning of the hand of the Lord to his own, chapter XIV concerning the battle of the Lord after the overthrow of Jerusalem against the nations, for which reason he is to ascend into heaven so that one King may rule everywhere and bless the entire spiritual Jerusalem, the Church, with tranquility, being about to afflict enemies with most grievous plagues, or to convert them to himself, to whom the rain of every kind of blessing, and the holiness and uniformity of spiritual sacrifices and divine worship are promised.

Which last and seventh, if all are counted, sermon can be divided by dichotomy in such a way that it deals partly with the true Israel, by rescuing, strengthening, and endowing it with the outpouring of the Spirit, which will follow the passion and death of the Messiah with penitential lamentation, chapter XII, and partly with the head of the same, namely the true Shepherd, who is to be struck for our sake in the time of the New Testament, whose characteristics are the institution of Baptism and the abolition of idols, as also the gathering of the sheep after their dispersion throughout the whole world, chapter XIII, and also the one King to be worshipped throughout the whole world, chapter XIV, namely after the overthrow of Jerusalem and the ascension into the heavens, and the subjugation and conversion of the nations to the people of the Lord: so that in every way the Lord may be worshipped, and sacrifices may be brought to him.

PART I. OPTIKE, consisting of visions through the first six chapters.

Latin:

PRÆLOQVI VM.

Zacharias à זכר recordatus est & יה Dominus, est q. μνησίθεος Dei recordans, qui non tantum ipfe memor Dei fuit, sed etiam alios, ut essent, hortatus est.

Quum enim populs remissior esset ad erigendum templum & cultum divinum, pars etiam præ metu hostium post afflictionem Babylonicam, restaurationem cultus divini vix ag- gredi auderet, exciatus est Propheta, qui segnes ex- hortationibus urgeret, infirmorum vero fidem pro- missionibus sublevaret: proinde insignes visiones ex- hibentur de futuris eventibus tum Politicæ, tum Ecclesiæ, oracula illustria, de Christi adventu, passione morte, regno & beneficiis inspirantur, ut populus ad pœnitentiam revocetur, pii in vera fide confir- mentur, universi de officio commoneantur:

Partes tres sunt: prima demandata exhortatio- ne ad conversionem cum promissione divinæ gra- tiæ, variis visionibus absolvitur usque ad cap. VII. Secunda informationem tum de ceremonialibus tum de moralibus quibusdam tradit cap. VII. Tertia va- ticiniis Propheticis constat, de conservatione & am- pliatione Ecclesiæ vel regni Christi, deque Christo Rege & Salvatore ac officio ac beneficiis ejusdem. Primam partem dicere licet Opticam, alteram di- dasticam, tertiam Propheticam. In prima parte duæ conciones, prior summaria, altera specialior, in qua octo visiones continentur, addita sub finem earum illustratione & confirmatione tum Symbolica tum aperta. Illæ autem sunt partim generales, utpote duæ priores cap. I. de populi Protectore & Mediatore Christo, inter myrtheta conspecto, qui populo suc- currit, & pro eodem intercedit, nec non de qua- tuor cornibus, populum dissipantibus contunden- dis; partim speciales, quæ tum apertiores sunt, tum magis Symbolicæ. Apertiores c. II. III. & IV. haben- tur, & vel Ecclesiam concernunt, utpote de Hieroso- lymæ exstructione, & per orbem extensione, ejusq; per adventum & ἐνοίκησιν Messiæ exhilaratione: cap. II. deque summi Pontificis investitura, & confirma- tione, quæ stabilitur promissione adventus Zemach & excisionis lapidis oculati, vel passione Iesu expia- toria cap. III. vel templi structuram per Zorobabe- lem absolvendam: quo fine cap. 4. exhibentur aureum candelabrum & oleæ duæ. Magis Symbolicæ sunt, quæ c. V. & VI. sistuntur: Illo quidem de Epistola volante, deque Epha cum massa plumbi ad designandum judicium iniquitatis & transportandæ impietatis: Hoc vero de quatuor quadrigis, de medio duorum montium æreorum visis, ad figu- randum ministeria Angelorum pro Ecclesia pu- gnantium, ut tranquillitate fruatur, nec iterum dis- sipetur ante Messiæ exhibitionem. Priori terren- tur impii, posteriori eriguntur pii. Quibus octo vi- sionibus illustrandis, & confirmandis simile subjun- gitur eodem capite mandatum de duabus coronis Josuæ imponendis & promissum de Messia Rege ac Sacerdote summo, ista figura adumbrato, sub quo viro Zemach omnia crescent, templumque Domi- no per orbem ædificabitur. Atque hæc omnia ad alteram concionem pertinent, d. 24. mensis undecimi anni secundi Darii habitam.

In secunda parte tertia concio Prophetæ habe- tur, instituta die 4. mensis noni, anni quarti Darii, jejuniorum electiciorum rejectione, seriaque ad justi- tiam & opera charitatis exhortatione constans c. VII.

Tertia pars quatuor concionibus reliquis absol- vitur: Prima est Paracletico - Parænetica de Hiero- solymæ inhabitatione ac benedictione, cujus gratia, ti- more pulso, veritati & concordiæ studere debeant. Altera Consolatoria de jejuniis in festa convertendis & gentibus populo Dei aggregandis cap. IIX. Concio tertia exhibetur Cap. IX. X. XI. estque partim Consolatoria cap. IX. ubi post denunciatam hostium aut eversionem, aut conversionem adventus Regis ca- ptivos è lacu infernali sanguine suo emissuri, & exer- citu suo gentes sibi subdituri intimatur, & cap. X. sub hoc Duce robur, tutela & victoria promittitur. Par- tim comminatoria de eversione Hierosolymæ & po- puli Iudaici, Christum verum Pastorem non æsti- mantis, pretio exiguo vendendum, seductoribus vero adhærentis, rejectione cap. XI. Quarta concio mere Evangelica c. XII. XIII. & XIV. sistitur: & c. XI. quidem de veri Israelis ereptione, & adversus hostes confortatione, deque Spiritus gratiæ effusione & Messiæ transfixione, ac morte planctum gravissimum conciliatura cap. XIII. de Baptismi fontis purifican- tis apertione, idolorum excisione, Christi Pastoris percussione ovium, dispersione, & manus Domini ad suos conversione cap. XIV. de Domini pugna post e- versam Hierosolymam adversus gentes, ideo cœ- lum ascensuri ut ubiq; Rex unus dominetur & univer- sam Hierosolymam spiritualem, Ecclesiam, tran- quillitate beet, inimicos plagis gravissimis affectu- rus, aut eosdem ad se conversurus, quibus pluvia omnigenæ benedictionis, & sacrificiorum spiritualium ac cultus divini sanctitas, & uniformitas promitti- tur.

Quæ ultima & septima, si omnes connume- rentur, concio per διχοτομίαν ita dispesci potest, quod partim de vero Israele agat, eripiendo, con- fortando & Spirit. effusione mactando, Messiæ pas- sionem & mortem planctu pœnitentiali prosequu- turo, cap. XII. partim de capite ejusdem, Pastore, nempe vero nostri causa percutiendo tempore Nov. Test. cujus characteres institutio Baptismi, & abolitios dolorum, designantur, ut & ovium post di- spersionem per mundum universum collectio cap. XXII. nec non Rege unico per totum orbem colendo cap. XIV. post eversionem scilicet Hierosoly- mæ & ascensionem in cælos, ac subjugationem & con- versionem gentium ad populum Domini: ut ita un- diquaque adoretur Dominus, eique adferantur sacrificia.

PARS I. ΟΠΤΙΚΗ visionibus constans per sex capita priora.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. Presenting the first summary sermon and the general visions from the second sermon.

At the time of the first sermon, in the eighth month of the second year of Darius, and with the command made to the people indicated, the sum of it, and of the whole Prophecy is set forth; turn to me and I will turn to you; the disobedience and punishment of the predecessors is illustrated: and the time of the second sermon is designated as the 24th day of the 11th month of the second year of Darius, and his two former visions are exhibited as general, the one concerning the horseman among the myrtle trees, Christ the defender of the people, and the same as the angel intercessor for the gracious conversion of God to Jerusalem; the other concerning the four scattering horns to be crushed by four smiths, or the enemies of the people to be overturned.

Returning to his homeland, Zechariah strengthens the Hebrews.

SERMON I. SUMMARY.

Ver. 1. IN THE EIGHTH MONTH] In the middle time between the sermons of Haggai, the first, and the other two.

SON OF BERECHIAH THE SON OF IDDO] Zechariah here is himself called the son of Iddo in Ezra 5:1, that is, grandson; for all those who are in descending degrees the Hebrews call sons.

That this Zechariah is the son of Berechiah, whom Isaiah joined to himself as a witness with Uriah the priest in Isaiah 8:2, Galatinus thinks in book VII of De Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis, chapter XVI, but that is a notable lapse in chronology. For Isaiah preceded Zechariah, a nearly most recent Prophet, by several centuries. Furthermore, Christ also commemorates Zechariah the son of Berechiah in Matthew 23:35. Whom Chrysostom in Luke on the nativity of John, Vatablus, Montanus, Sanctius, Ribera, Balduinus, Himmelius, and Gualtherus on Matthew 23 make the same as ours. But that our Prophet was killed between the temple and the altar is not certain: nor is it likely that the Jews at that time, when they returned from the Babylonian captivity as if tried by fire, were so wicked that they would kill a Prophet, which is the argument of Barradius in chapter III of the Concordance of the Gospels, book VIII, chapter 28, no. 50, with which Christ. à Castro and Jac. Salian. in the Annals of the Old Testament, year 3192, no. 17, agree. But concerning Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the High Priest, that is reported in 2 Chronicles 24:20; therefore St. Jerome, B. Luther, and Bede judge that Jehoiada was called by another name, Berechiah, and Grotius does not deny it on Matthew 23:36. Although he adds: that Christ so alludes to the ancient history that there is at the same time in his words a presage of the future. For the last of the good and notable men slaughtered by the Jerusalemites, and indeed in the temple itself, was also called Zechariah, and indeed the son of Baruch, which can be held to be the same as the name of Berechiah: whose siege followed immediately, as can be seen in Josephus. I would not easily say that Christ intended both to relate history and to make a presage, because the unity of the sense of Christ's words does not bear that. I would rather believe that Christ, even though he speaks in the past tense, looked to Zechariah the son of Baruch, or Berechiah, who was to be killed most recently, so that the past words used may be said to be in respect of the subsequent punishment: for this guilt also preceded the final destruction as a punishment, so that the words ὃν ἐφονεύσατε, whom you killed, are to be taken prophetically, that is, you are certainly going to kill: Because this was the last shedding of righteous blood in the second temple, but not that which is read in 2 Chronicles 24, which happened in the first, not the second temple. Which opinion I see now has also pleased Fr. Junius on Matthew 23 and Cocceius on this passage, as also Const. Lempereur in the treatise Middoth, p. 80. Compare Lud. de Dieu. Those who take Christ's words concerning Zechariah the father of the Baptist are Baronius, Toletus, Castrius, and others, even if they appeal to Origen, Basil, Cyril, Epiphanius, or whoever is the author of the book on the life of the Prophets, Euthymius and Theophylact. deserves no assent. And it is rejected not undeservedly by Grotius himself in the cited place. Jerome rightly refuted the story about the father of John the Baptist as groundless and for many reasons not at all likely. Compare B. Gerhard, Harmony, chapter 158, Dorscheus, Syn. Theol. Zachar. p. 2, and Glass. Phil. sacr. book 1, p. 190, who is industrious on behalf of the son of Jehoiada, whom most of our people favor. As also among the Calvinists, Ludov. Capellus in his Spicilegium is so addicted to this opinion that he did not fear to assert, with a most dangerous assertion and one injurious to the Holy Spirit himself, that for its sake either it was written by a very ancient copyist's slip 'Berechiah' instead of 'Jehoiada' or the Evangelist himself did not distinguish by a mnemonic error the Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom we have here at hand, from Zechariah the son of Jehoiada.

Latin:

CAPUT I. Concionem primam summariam & vi- siones generales è secunda concione exhibens.

Tempore concionis primæ, octavo mense secundi Da- rii, & mandato ad populum facto indicato, summa ejus, & totius Prophetiæ sistitur; convertimini ad me & convertar ad vos; illustrata antecessorum inobedientia & pœna: ac secundæ concionis tempus 24. dies mensis XI. secundi Darii designatur, ejusq́; visiones priores duæ generales exhibentur, altera de equite inter myrtheta, Christo populi defensore, eodemque angelo intercessore pro conversione Dei gratiosa ad Hierosolymam; altera de quatuor cornibus dissipatoriis à quatuor fabris contundendis, vel hostibus populi evertendis.

In patriam rediens Zacharias firmat Ebræos.

CONCIO I. SUMMARIA.

Vers. 1. IN MENSE OCTAVO] Medio tempore inter sermones Aggæi, primum, & duos alteros.

FILIUM BARACHIÆ FILII ADDO] Zacharias hic ipse Esdr. V. 1. filius Addo dicitur, id est, nepos; nam omnes qui in gradibus descendentibus sunt Hebræi filios vocant.

ZAchariam hunc Barachiæ filium esse, quem testem cum Uria sacerdote sibi adjunxit Esaias c. IIX. 2. Galatinus putat l. VII. de A. C. V. c. XVI. sed ille insignis est in Chronologia lapsus. Aliquot enim seculis antecessit Esaias Zachariam, Prophetam pene novissimum. Porro Zachariam filium Barachiæ etiam commemorat Christus Matth. XXIII. 25. Quem eundem cum nostro faciunt Chrysost. in Luca m de nativ. Joh. Vatablus, Montanus, Sanctius, Ribera, Balduinus, Himmelius, ac Gualtherus in Matth. 23. Sed Prophetam nostrum inter templum & altare occisum esse, non constat: nec verisimile est Judæos eo tempore, quo ex captivitate Babylonica velut igne probati redierunt, ita fuisse sceleratos, ut Prophetam interimerent, quod est Barradii argumentum c. III. Concord. Evang. l. IIX. c. 28. n. 50. cui consonat Christ. à Castro, & Jac. Salian. annal. V. T. ann. 3192. n. 17. De Zacharia vero Jojadæ Pontificis filio id refertur 2. Paral. XXIV. 2. proinde Jojadam alio nomine Barachiam dictum censent S. Hieronymus, B. Lutherus & Beda, neque abnuit Grotius ad Matth. XXIII. 36. Etsi addat: Christum ita alludere ad veterem historiam, ut simul insit ejus verbis futuri præsagium. Nam virorum bonorum atq́; insignium ultimus ab Hierosolymitis trucidatus, & quidem in ipso templo, dictus itidem est Zacharias, & quidem filius Baruchi, quod cum Barachiæ nomine idem haberi potest: cujus eadem statim secuta est obsidio, ut apud Josephum videre est. Non dixerim facile & historiam retulisse, & præsagium facere voluisse Christum, quia id non fert unitas sensus verborum Christi. Rectius crediderim, Christum, etsi in Præterito loquatur, Zacharium filium Baruchi, seu Barachiæ, qui occidendus novissime erat, respexisse, ut verba præterita adhibita dicantur respectu subsequuturæ pœnæ: nam antecessit & hæc culpa excidium finale, ceu pœnam, ut verba ὃν ἐφονεύσατε, quem occidistis, accipienda sint prophetice, id est, certi occisuri estis: Quia hæc postrema fuit justi sanguinis effusio in templo secundo, non vero illa, quæ 2. Par. XXIV. legitur, quæ in primo, non secundo templo contigit. Quam sententiam video nunc etiam Fr. Iunio, ad Matth. 23. & Coccejo in h. l. ut & Const. Lempereur in tr. Middoth. p. 80. placuisse. Conf. Lud. de Dieu. Qued de Zacharia Baptistæ patre verba Christi accipiunt Baronius, Toletus, Castrius, alii, etsi ad Origenem, Basilium, Cyrillum, Epiphanium, seu quisquis autor libri de vita Proph. Euthymium & Theophyl. provocent, assensum nullum meretur. Et à Grotio ipso rejicitur non immerito loco citato. De Iohannis Baptistæ patre ἀδέσποτον & multis de causis minime verisimilem fabulam recte refutavit Hieronymus. Conf. B. Gerhard. Harmon. c. 158. Dorscheus Syn. Theol. Zachar. p. 2. & Glass. Phil. sacr. l. 1. p. 190. qui pro filio Jojada operosus est, cui plerique nostratium favent. Ut & è Calvinia- nis Ludov. Capellis in spicilegio adeo huic opinio- ni addictus, ut ejus causa vel lapsu librarii antiquissi- mo scriptum fuisse Βαραχία pro Ιωάδα vel ipsum Evangelistam sphalmate μνημονικῷ non distinxisse Zachariam filium Barachiæ, quem hic præ manibus habemus, à Zacharia filio Jojadæ, asserere veritus non sit assertione maxime periculosa & in ipsum Spiritum S. injuriosa.

## 1:2
Ver. 2.

THE LORD WAS ANGRY WITH YOUR FATHERS WITH ANGER] The Lord was angry with the fathers with a severe anger.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

IRATUS EST DOMINUS SUPER PATRES VESTROS IRACUNDIA] Iratus fuit Dominus patribus seræigravi.

## 1:3
AND YOU SHALL SAY TO THEM] You shall say this further, Ver. 3.

TURN TO ME, SAYS THE LORD OF HOSTS, AND I WILL TURN TO YOU] Επί πλοκὴ. For the former 'to be turned' is to change one's life: the latter is to be rendered beneficent instead of angry. The sense is the same in Micah 7:19 & Jeremiah 3:12 & Ezekiel 18:30.

Gregory the Great excellently says in Psalm 7 of the penitential psalms: God, he says, who casts away the delinquent, turns to the penitent: he also calls the turned-away, grants sins to the converted, exhorts the sluggish, consoles the afflicted, teaches the studious, helps those fighting, confirms those laboring, hears those crying out from the heart. For he himself says through the Prophet: Turn to me, and I will turn to you. But because we cannot turn to him without him, let us cry out daily with the prophet: Do not turn your face away from me. Cocceius explains that 'I WILL TURN TO YOU' more fully: I will be among you and I will explain my benevolence and power in many ways in your midst (which Zechariah explains clearly in his prophecies), finally I will also visit you, and I will dwell among you in a more glorious way than I have ever dwelt before in the whole world, namely so that Jerusalem may become the seat of my glory, with my son walking through it, and performing my works in it, and pouring out the holy spirit upon his faithful disciples, and I will begin my kingdom, by which I will join the nations to my people as an inheritance, with him. All these things are distinctly proposed by Zechariah in their places, and are contained under the word 'I will return to you'. We add also this observation of his after B. Luther: In the words of the Prophet v. 3, it is held, 'Jehovah God of hosts said', which is not to be taken for βαττολογίἀ, it is once the word of the prophet, about to propose the word of God. It is twice in the words of God. God speaks in the name of God, i.e., one person in the name of two persons. For example, the Holy Spirit speaking in the Prophets in the name of the Father, commanding the Jews to return to him, and of the Son promising his coming.

Latin:

ET DICES AD EOS] Hoc amplius dices, Vers. 3.

CONVERTIMINI AD ME, AIT DOMINUS EXERCITUUM, ET CONVERTAR AD VOS] Επί πλοκὴ. nam prius illud converti est vitam mutare: alterum est pro irato beneficum reddi. Sensus est idem Mich. VII 19. & Jerem. III, 12. & Ezech. XVIII. 30.

Præclare Gregorius M. in Psal. VII. pœnitent. Deus, inquit, qui abjicit delinquentem, convertitur ad pœnitentem: vocat etiam aversos, donat peccata con- versis, hortatur pigros, consolatur afflictos, docet stu- diosos, adjuvat dimicantes, confirmat laborantes, ex- audit corde clamantes. Ipse namq́; per Prophetam dicit: Convertimini ad me, & ego convertar ad vos. Sed quia converti ad eum sine ipso non possumus, quo- tidie cum propheta clamemus: Ne avertas faciem tuam à me. Illud CONVERTAR AD VOS ple- nius explicat Coccejus: Ero inter vos & benevo- lentiam ac potentiam meam multis modis expli- cabo in medjo vestri (quod Zacharias in prophe- tiis suis luculenter explicat) deniq; etiam visitabo vos, & habitabo inter vos gloriosiori modo, quam unquam antea habitaverim in toto mundo, nimi- rum ut fiat Hierosolyma sedes gloriæ meæ, peram- bulante illam filio meo, & opera mea patrante in illo, & spiritum sanctum effundente in fideles suos discipulos, & regnum meum, quo gentes adjun- gam populo meo in hæreditatem, apud eum exor- diar. Hæc omnia à Zacharia suis locis distincte proponuntur, & sub vocabulo revertar ad vos con- tinentur. Addimus & hanc ejus post B. Luther. ob- servationem: In verbis Prophetæ v. 3. habetur, Di- xit Jehova Deus exercituum, quod non est accipiendum pro βαττολογίἀ, semel est verbum prophetæ, propo- situri verbum Dei. Bis est in Dei verbis. Deus in nomine Dei loquitur, h. e. una persona in nomine duarum personarum. Verbi causa Spiritus sanctus loquens in Prophetis in nomine Patris, jubentis Judæos ad se reverti, & Filii promittentis adventum suum.

## 1:4
Ver. 4. AND THEY DID NOT HEAR] II Chronicles 22, v. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET NON AUDIERUNT] II. Paralip. XXII, v. 16.

## 1:5
Ver. 5. YOUR FATHERS WHERE ARE THEY? AND THE PROPHETS SHALL THEY LIVE FOREVER] Did they live? They indeed went the common way: but my words do not die, but exert their power, although often at a much later time. Lamentations 2:17.

He understands the prophets according to Jerome, Albert, Hugo, and Lyra, as the fathers of the impious, for instance the false prophets, who falsely predicted happiness. Others more correctly, with Theodoret, Clarius, and Vatable, wish the true prophets to be indicated, i.e., as much the pious prophets as your fathers are dead. For the good die equally with the bad, but their prophecies and the threats which they leveled against your fathers, and against you when you imitate them, are not dead, but live and endure. That they are the same Prophets who are designated in the preceding and following parts, the Hebrew text here sufficiently indicates, and the continuity of the text requires.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PATRES VESTRI UBI SUNT? ET PRO- PHETÆ NUNQUID IN SEMPITERNUM VIVENT] Vixerunt? Illi quidem communem iverunt viam: at mea dicta non moriuntur, sed vim suam, quamvis sæpe multo post tempore, exserunt. Lam. II, 17.

Prophetas intelligit secundum Hieronymum, Albert. Hugon. & Lyran. patrum impiorum, puta Pseudoprophetas, qui falso felicitatem prædixere. Alii rectius cum Theodoreto, Clario, & Vatable ve- ros prophetas indigitari volunt, q. d. tam prophe- tæ pii, quam patres vestri mortui sunt. Boni enim æque ac mali moriuntur, sed prophetiæ eorum & minæ, quas Patribus vestris, vobisque, ubi eos imi- tamini, intentarunt, non sunt mortuæ, sed vivunt & perdurant. Eosdem esse Prophetas, qui in ante- cedentibus & consequentibus designantur HeHa- jediah h. l. satis indicat, & requirit συνέχεια textus.

## 1:6
Verse 6. AND MY STATUTES] Sanctions added to the law. HAVE THEY NOT OVERTAKEN YOUR FATHERS?] They came upon them, as the saying goes, πιχάνηται βραδὺς ὠκύν [the slow overtakes the swift]. AND THEY TURNED] They were finally led to repentance, being placed in those evils which had long before been predicted to them AS THE LORD OF HOSTS THOUGHT TO DO TO YOU] As He had decreed, and had signified the decree. ACCORDING TO OUR WAYS, AND ACCORDING TO OUR DEEDS] Jer. 4:18, 17:10, 23:2, 32:19, Ezek. 24:14, 36:31, Hos. 12:2. I have extorted this confession from your ancestors because of my punishments, says the Lord; see to it that you do not provoke me again by disobedience, so that I may produce in you examples of justice and judgment rather than of mercy and clemency.

SERMON II. OF THE PROPHET CONCERNING THE EIGHT VISIONS.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET LEGITIMA MEA] Sanctiones additæ legi. NUMQUID NON COMPREHENDERUNT PA- TRES VESTROS?] Supervenerunt ipsis, sicut dici solet πιχάνηται βραδὺς ὠκύν. ET CONVERSI SUNT] Pœnitentia tandem ducti sunt, in illis positi malis, quæ pridem ipsis prædicta fuerant SICUT COGITAVIT DOMINUS EXERCI- TUUM FACERE VOBIS] Sicut decreverat, & decre- tum significaverat. SECUNDUM VIAS NOSTRAS, ET SECUNDUM ADINVENTIONES NOSTRAS] Jer. IV. 18. XVII. 10. XXIII. 2. XXXII. 19. Ezech. XXIV. 14. XXXVI. 31. Os. XII. 2. Hanc Confessionem ex pœnis meis à majori- bus vestris extorsi, inquit Dominus, videte vos, ne inobedientia denuo me exacerbetis, ut in vos justitia & judicii potius, quam misericordia & cle- mentiæ exempla edam.

CONCIO II. PROPHETÆ DE OCTO VISIONIBUS.

## 1:7
Verse 7. ON THE TWENTY-FOURTH DAY OF THE ELEVENTH MONTH] This revelation from God to Zechariah happened three months later, which extends to the end of chapter 6. The discourse that preceded was only a certain introduction. What follows now was said when the people had already made much progress in the work of the temple, and needed to be stirred up to the new labor of fortifying the city. SEBAT] This is not a Hebrew name, but a Chaldean one. This month is named in the second paraphrase of Esther 3:7; it falls roughly in January. THE PROPHET SAYING] The prophet who said: that is, he thus recited the dream that had come to him divinely.

THE FIRST VISION OF THE HORSEMAN AMONG THE MYRTLES, THE PROTECTOR OF THE PEOPLE, THE MESSIAH, AND THE SAME AS THE INTERCESSOR FOR THE PEOPLE.

Latin:

Vers. 7. IN DIE VIGESIMA ET QUARTA UN- DECIMI MENSIS] Tribus mensibus serius hæc à Deo patefactio Zachariæ contigit, quæ extenditur ad finem ca- pitis VI. Is sermo qui præcessit εἰσαγωγὴ tantum quæ- dam fuit. Quæ nunc sequuntur dicta sunt cum jam po- pulus in opere templi multum profecisset, & ad novum laborem muniendæ urbis excitari deberet. SABATH] Nomen est non Hebraicum, sed Chal- daicum. Nominatur hic mensis in paraphrasi secunda Est- her. III. 7. incidit ferme in Januarium. PROPHETAM DICENS] Prophetam qui dixit: id est, sic recitavit quod sibi obvenerat divinitus somnium.

PRIMA VISIO EQUITIS INTER MYR- TOS, POPULI PROTECTORIS MESSIAE, EIUS- DEMQUE PRO POPULO INTER- CESSORIS.

## 1:8
Verse 8. AND BEHOLD A MAN RIDING UPON A RED HORSE, AND HE STOOD AMONG THE MYRTLE TREES, WHICH WERE IN THE DEEP] That this horseman is Michael, the guardian of the Jewish nation under God, the Hebrews do not poorly infer from Daniel and from these things which follow shortly in verse 12, as Jerome teaches us regarding this place. A red horse, or one of blood color, signifies slaughter, as can be seen in Revelation 6:4; but because the myrtle is a tree of pleasure, therefore this horse in the myrtle grove, and indeed kept in the deep so that he might not go out from there, signifies war repressed by deep peace, namely, that which the Persian empire extended over. This agrees with the beginnings of Darius.

Grotius follows the commentary of the Jews and the Papists concerning Michael the created angel, the guardian of the Jewish nation. But Scripture knows nothing of him, nor does the distribution of angelic guardians rest on any foundation. And what are the forces of the guardian of the Jewish nation to those which Grotius thinks were brought against Darius? The Papists (and with them Grotius) embraced the Jewish gloss all the more willingly because they saw that it makes for their dogma concerning angels praying for us and taking special care: See Bellarmine, Book 1, On the Beatitude of the Saints, ch. 12, 11. Fourth proposition. Bailius in Catech. q. 45. Whence Becanus concludes that angels are to be invoked, Vol. 5, Opusc. 1, On the Invocation of Saints, q. 7. Conf. Lyranus, Castrius, Cornel. à Lapide, and so also Fernand. on the Visions. Although the inference from the care and prayer of angels for us to the religious invocation of them is weak, or rather non-existent: unless they also wish for the saints on this earth who take care of the faithful and pray for them to be invoked. That opinion about Michael arose, without doubt, from the place in Dan. 10:13, misunderstood, as appears from Theodoret. Nor is there agreement among the Papists whether they ought to understand Michael or Gabriel here; since some, as Cornelius observes, think it was Gabriel, as a strong warrior for the people of God, Dan. 9:21. Some also establish a double sense, so that literally the created angel Michael is understood by the man among the myrtle trees, but mystically Christ, who in the flesh assumed from the myrtle, the Blessed Virgin, stands in the midst of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and saints of the Old and New Testaments, i.e., among the myrtle trees, as Cornelius holds. Arias Montanus, however, is clearly singular, understanding Alexander the Great by the man among the myrtles, because it was signified that he himself would transfer the empire from the Persians to the Greeks, which the Papists themselves acknowledge is clearly foreign to this place. We, with Cyril, Origen, Ambrose, Jerome—whose votes Ribera grants us—and other fathers, to whom the Reformed and most of our own theologians agree, assert that no one other than the Son of God appeared here to the Prophet in the form of a man on horseback, by undoubted marks: (1) from the tetragrammaton name, proper to God alone, which is attributed to this man-angel. I will show you, says this angel, v. 9. Concerning whom, however, the Prophet says, v. 10: Furthermore, JEHOVAH showed me. He, therefore, who shows these things, is not a created Angel here, but Jehovah. Which is especially confirmed from ch. 2:8, where this angel sent by the Lord is called Jehovah Zebaoth, and from ch. 3:2, Jehovah was speaking, says the Prophet, speaking of the angel before whom the high priest is said to have stood. He testifies with a resonant voice, therefore, that that angel was Jehovah. Who is none other than the Son of God. (2) From the description of the angel, who is presented here as the Lord of angels, having authority over them: which befits no created angel, but the Son of God, the angel of the face of the Lord, whom all the angels worship, Heb. 1:6. For the other horsemen, the angels, follow the man sitting on the red horse as their superior, verse 8, and are questioned by him as their guardian and prince as to what is happening in any of the kingdoms; they refer their answers to him as to a superior, v. 21, and are said to stand before him, that is, to minister to him, ch. 3:4; cf. Deut. 10:8, 1 Sam. 16:23, 1 Kings 10:5, ch. 17:1, Zech. 3:1. Just as angels are otherwise said to stand before the Lord, 1 Kings 22:19, Job 1:6, Isa. 6:2, Dan. 7:10, Zech. 6:5, Luke 1:19. (3) From the apparition of the angel, he was seen in the form of a man about to fight for the people, and as a Leader of the army, just as in Josh. 5:14 the Son of God was seen as the Leader of the heavenly army. He sat upon a red horse, and behind him followed a cavalry army, as in Rev. 19:13 he appeared. The horse denotes a happy success of the matter and a swift expedition. See Zech. 6:2, Rev. 6:2 ff., ch. 9:17, ch. 19:11. The red horse signifies the certainty and gravity of divine vengeance against his enemies: just as the red color is otherwise a sign of vengeance, Zech. 6:2, Isa. 63:2, Rev. 6:4, ch. 12:2, 3. But the fact that he is seen standing among the myrtles adumbrates his presence in the Church, the protection and defense of the same, just as the riding denotes the manner of that presence, and the extension to all the affairs of the Church. The myrtles figure the members of the Church, which are perpetually green, flourish, bring forth fruit, and are fragrant to Christ, but are hidden from the world as if in the deep. The myrtle is a beautiful tree, whence Esther is believed to have been called Hadassah (הדסה), myrtle-like, on account of her beauty, Esth. 2:7; it is also fragrant, even in Egypt, where, according to Pliny, although other things are without scent, lilies, violets, roses, yet the myrtle has the preeminent scent. It is festive and holy, used to adorn festive days, and accustomed to be used for triumphal crowns in former times, as Pliny again testifies, book 15, ch. 29. Cf. Lev. 23:40, Neh. 8:16. That tree was a sign of peace, and its flowers and leaves a symbol of victory. Venus formerly presided over the myrtle and over union, and thus this tree was a symbol of true union and sincere love, especially conjugal love. Thus Christ, that heavenly bridegroom, truly presides over the Church, which he has gathered in the unity of faith, and still preserves.

Dried myrtle leaves are remedies for ulcers: the leaves of the Church are examples of virtues, by which others living outside the Church are recalled to a sounder mind. From myrtle berries dried to aridity in the shade, wine was once made; from those not dried, oil; and another delicacy of noble name which is called myrtatum. Thus the faithful citizens of the Church, dried by the fire of the cross and of tribulations, pour forth prayers; and they exercise themselves in other kinds of virtues in hope and silence, Isa. ch. XXX. v. 15, all of which are before God most sweet nectar and ambrosia, concerning which matter David speaks in Ps. LXIX. 32, and the prayers of the saints are called incense, Apoc. V. v. 8; indeed, even the very death of the saints, by which they become completely drained of juice and bloodless, is precious in the sight of God, Ps. CXVI. 15; so also are all good works, which the elect do from faith unfeigned, I Tim. I. 5. (for these are berries not dried, but still flourishing) are pleasing to God; which He uses like wine and oil, esteeming all those things which have been bestowed upon one's neighbor as having happened to Himself; concerning which matter that heavenly bridegroom says in Cant. V. v. 1, I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk, that is, all your works proceeding from faith have wonderfully refreshed me like the sweetest honey or the most pleasant wine, as the blessed Bald. has it in Comment. p. 147. Cf. Cornel. à Lapid. in h. l. (4) From the interior impulse and inspiration of an Angel. That Angel was the one speaking IN ME, says Zachar. v. 9, 13, 14. The double He imports emphasis, and the word דבר with the letter ב indicates the instinct of the divine person speaking interiorly in the soul of man and dictating abstruse things. Num. XII. 2, 8. II. Sam. XXIII. 2. Hos. I. 2, as the blessed Tarnovius noted from Kimchi, and the Belgian interpreters agreed. But such an interior impulse and instinct is not attributed so much to a created angel as to the Son of God in the Holy Scriptures, whose Spirit dictated abstruse things to the Prophets, I Petr. I. 11. (5) From the intercession of this Angel. Since this angel prayed in such a way, and interceded for the people v. 12, O Lord of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem, and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast been angry? Such an intercession is nowhere attributed to a created angel, and is proper to the Son of God: whose office it is to intercede for the Church, Jer. XXX. 21. Rom. IIX. 32. I. Joh. I. 2. Heb. IX. 24. Ap. IIX. 3, 4. Whence Coccejus rightly calls this man in Zachar. verse 11 the Angel of the Lord. And because his intercession is submitted in verse 12, we understand that he is noted who is called מלאך פנים ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ἐμφανιζόμενος τῷ Θεῷ, Isa. LXIII. 9. The subject is known from its proper predicate. (6) From the exertion of divine vengeance against enemies. That angel and man seen among the myrtles on a red horse explains in Zach. II. 9 the vengeance which He had decreed to exercise against the enemies, not like a minister, but autocratically and divinely. I am about to move, He says, my hand against those nations, and they shall be a prey to their servants: thus you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me. What is this hand, if not the infinite power of God, Ps. CXXXIX. 7, 8, 9. Isa. XLIIX. 12, 13, or the grace of God in the subjection and conversion of the nations, of which later. (7) From that authoritative manner of speaking which is attributed to this Angel speaking in Zechariah ch. VI. 8: These who went out into the North country have quieted my spirit in the North country. Which words breathe the majesty of God speaking, however they may be explained: concerning which we shall see in ch. VI. 8. Other things both said and done, purely and truly divine, of this Angel will be evident from chapters II and III. From all of which it is manifest that the man seen among the myrtles, who is also called the Angel of the Lord v. 11, speaking in Zechariah v. 9, 13, 14, ch. II. 3, ch. IV. 1, 4, 5, and ch. V. 5, 10, ch. VI. 4, 8, is no other than the Son of God Himself: Cf. besides our interpreters and the Reformed

Mr. Dr. Steph. Klotz on Angel-worship, point XIV. I feel with the Christian interpreters that it was Christ, says this Willius, the head of the Church and Prince of the Angels, which the Prophet himself confirms when he calls him the angel of the Lord, v. 11, and the Lord v. 20. Calvin does not entirely deny it in his Commentary on the XII Minor Prophets, p. 602. If we accept that this Angel was Christ, the common usage of scripture does not object, for we know that Christ, as He is the head of the Angels, so He always rules them, so that they do nothing, when they obey God, except under his auspices. It can therefore happen that this one Angel held the primacy among the others, so that the Redeemer might come into the mind of the Prophet, who rules both the Angels and the whole Church. But Rud. Gualtherus asserts this with greater boldness, p. 270. He teaches that the Church, even if it seems plunged into a valley of miseries and destitute of all hope, is nevertheless under the care of God, and has at the same time a present help in the promised savior Christ, who is present to it, not as an idle spectator, but as an assertor and avenger: and thus like a leader of soldiers, who has already mounted a horse, and indeed a red horse, so that He may exact his cruel and bloody vengeance from the enemies of the Church by a just judgment. And at the same time, (so that the consolation may be more effective) his power and his propensity toward his own people is adumbrated: the former, while they return to Him, and the angels flow together, they render an account of their mission to Him, and finally follow Him as their Lord from behind: the latter, when He intercedes with such zeal and diligence before God for Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, and through another angel suggests arguments of consolation to the prophet, by which He may confirm the miserable and afflicted. The Belgian authors also in their annotations to the new version concerning the Son of God they explain these things. Similarly Danaeus, Commentary on the Minor Prophets, p. 827. That one, however, whom the other horsemen also address, and to whom alone they render an account of their duty below in verse 11, who sits among the myrtle trees on a horse, who guides, instructs, and teaches the prophet, is without doubt our Lord Jesus Christ, whom all creatures obey, as both God and head of the Church. He himself sits on a horse of a reddish color, that is, sad, obscure, and not yet bright. He keeps himself among the myrtle trees, which are shady places, because the state of the Church was still at that time, both on account of many not yet returned from Babylon, and also because of the storms still impending, that state was, I say, sad, mournful, obscure, not yet shining, joyful, with all the clouds of calamities wiped away. And so that Christ, the Horseman and head of the Church, assumed both the color and the place suitable for the sad matter which he is about to describe, sympathizing and grieving with his Church. Heb. IV. v. 15. From the ancients, St. Jerome: The man, he says, who was riding upon a red horse, is the Lord and Savior, who, assuming the dispensation of our flesh, hears in Isaiah, Why are your garments red? St. Cyril on this passage confesses that he saw the Lord in our form, etc.

The ancient Rabbis also acknowledged that one cannot understand a created angel, but that Jehovah himself appeared here to Zechariah in the book Sanhedrin, division Chelek. R. Jochanan said, what is that which is written in Zech. I. 8, Behold a man riding upon a red horse. There is no man in that place except the holy God, blessed be he, as it is said in Ex. XV. 3, The Lord is a man of war, etc. Among the myrtles: there are no myrtles except the righteous, as it is said in Esth. II. 7, And he was the foster-father of Hadassah, that is, the myrtle. She is Esther herself.

AND AFTER HIM WERE RED, SPECKLED, AND WHITE HORSES) Namely, together with their horsemen, as appears below in verse 10. These signify the fortunes of wars that would eventually happen under Darius, calamitous, happy, and various. The calamitous fortunes were against the Scythians and Greeks: the happy ones against Thrace and Macedonia, which were subdued by the Persians: the various ones against the Ionians and Egyptians. See Herodotus IV, VI, VII.

The mystical significance of the horseman among the myrtles was assigned less conveniently by Grotius, namely that a horse of blood-red color, kept in a myrtle grove and indeed a deep one, denoted war repressed by a profound peace. For the horseman was not kept there so that he might not exercise vengeance, even if he stood there; for to what end would he be seen on a red horse, unless he wished to exercise vengeance? And who could have restrained that horseman (if you understand only Michael)? Why also would the leader of the Judean people be restrained, so that he might not avenge his people? And why would he be seen surrounded by red, varied, and white horses, unless to help his own? Nor is that signification of the horses, which Grotius assigns, appropriate. For he separates the horses from that horseman Prince, as if the vision of the latter pertained to the beginnings of Darius, but the appearance of the former to subsequent times. Which in no way fits. Nor was this state of Darius to be outlined here, but courage was to be added to the faithful. Wherefore others more correctly establish that the Son of God appeared for the comfort of the faithful, about to fight against the enemies of the Church with a heavenly army. Although indeed some understand by the attendant horsemen the Doctors of the Church following Christ courageously, of whom some appear on red horses ready to pour out their lives, others on varied ones, serving the Church with their various gifts, others on white ones, honoring the doctrine with the integrity of their life and the candor of their morals: to whom also the Blessed Balduinus accedes in Comm. p. 146, with St. Jerome leading the way: it is better, however, to understand angels, not indeed evil angels, as Coccejus wishes, but good ones, who were placed on watch for the salvation of the Church after the Babylonian captivity, as also other interpreters acknowledge, and our Blessed Balduinus also explains in his Comment. p. 151. The red ones therefore denote the executors of the bloody judgments of God upon the enemies, the white ones bringing peace to the Church, the varied ones occupied in both kinds, as Willius has in this place. Similarly, Blessed Osiander: The red horses signify that the angels are ready to exercise vengeance upon those who disturb the Church of God: the purple and white horses denote that the ministry of the angels confers glory and joy upon the Church. The angels appearing among the myrtle groves with the horses signified that the Lord, through their work, prepares a shade for the Church, under which it may at times breathe from afflictions.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET ECCE VIR ADSCENDENS SUPER EQUUM RUFUM, ET IPSE STABAT INTER MYR- TETA, QUÆ ERANT IN PROFUNDO] Hunc equi- tem esse Michaelem Judææ gentis sub Deo præsidem, non male ex Daniele, & his, quæ mox sequuntur 12. colligunt Hebræi, ut ad hunc locum nos docet Hieronymus. Equus rufus, sive sanguinei coloris, cædes significat, ut videre est Apocalyp. VI. 4. sed quia Myrtus arbor est voluptatis, ideo equus hic in myrteto, & quidem profundo retentus, ne inde exiret, significat bellum alta pace repressum, nempe quam late patebat Persarum imperium. Id congruit ini- tiis Darii.

Sequitur Grotius commentum Judæorum & papicolarum de Michaele angelo creatogentis Iudai- cæ Præside. At de illo nihil novit scriptura, neque distributio præsidiorum angelicorum ullo nititur fundamento. Et quid ad illas, quas contra Darium productas putat Grotius, copi as præsesgentis Ju- daicæ? Eo autem libentius amplexi Judaicam glos- sam Papistæ sunt, (& cum illis Grotius) quod vide- rint eam facere pro dogmate suo de angelis pro no- bis orantibus, & curam gerentibus specialem: Vid. Bellarm. l. 1. de Beat. Sanct. c. XII. 11. Quarta pro- positio. Bailius in Catech. q. XLV. Unde conclu- dit Becanus, angelos invocandos esse Tom. V. Opusc. I. de Invocat. Sanct. q. VII. Conf. Lyranus, Castrius, Cornel. à Lapide, sic etiam Fernand. de Visionibus. Quamvis infirma, imo nulla sit illatio à cura & o- ratione angelorum pro nobis, ad invocationem eorum religiosam: nisi etiam sanctos in his terris curam fidelium gerentes, & pro iis orantes, invo- candos esse velint. Enata autem illa opinio de Mi- chaele, sine dubio, è loco Dan. 10, 13. male intelle- cto, ut ex Theodoreto apparet. Neque convenit in- ter Papistas, anne Michaelem, num vero Gabrielem hic intelligere debeant? siquidem nonnulli, ob- servante Cornelio, Gabrielem fuisse arbitrentur, ceu fortem præliatorem pro populo Dei Dan. IX. 21. Geminum etiam sensum nonnulli statuunt, ut literali quidem per virum inter myrteta Michael creatus angelus, mystice vero Christus intelligatur, qui in carne ex myrto, B. virgine, assumta in medio Patriarcharum, Prophetarum ac sancto- rum V. & N. T. q. inter myrteta consistit, uti ha- bet Cornelius. Arias Montanus vero plane singula- ris est, per virum inter myrtos Alexandrum M. in- telligens, quod significatum fuerit ipsum trans- laturum imperium, à Persis ad Græcos, quod vero plane hic ἀλλότριον esse, ipsi Papistæ agno- scunt. Nos cum Cyrillo, Origene, Ambro- sio, Hieronymo, quorum suffragia largitur nobis Ribera, aliisque patribus, quibus Reformati & No- strates Theologi plerique omnes astipulantur, nullum alium, quam Filium Dei, hic apparuisse Prophetæ, in forma viri equitis, indubitatis γνωρί- σμασι adferimus (1) à nomine teragrammato, soli Deo proprio, quod huic viro angelo tribuitur. E- go ostendam tibi, inquit hic angelus v. 9. De quo ve- ro Propheta v. 10. Ostendit, inquit præterea IEHO- VA. Is ergo, qui hæc ostendit, hic non Angelus creatus est, sed Jehovah. Quod cumprimis confir- mstur è cap. II. 8. ubi angelus hic à Domino missus dicitur Iehovah Zebaoth, & è c. III. 2. dicebat Ieho- vah, ait Propheta, loquens de angelo, coram quo sacerdos maximus stetisse dicitur. Angelum ergo illum Jehovam fuisse, sonora voce testatur. Qui alius nullus est, quam Filius Dei. (2) Ab angeli de- scriptione, qui hic sistitur ceu angelorum Dominus imperium in eosdem habens: quod nulli creato angelo convenit, sed Filio Dei, angelo faciei Domini, quem adorant omnes angeli Ebr. I. 6. Virum enim equo rufo insidentem cæteri equites angeli tan- quam superiorem pone sequuntur vers. 8. & ab eo ceu præside, & principe interrogantur, quid in re- gnis quibusvis agatur, ad eum, veluti superiorem, responsa sua referunt, v. 21. ac coram ipso stare, hoc est, ei ministrare dicuntur c. III. 4. conf. Deut. 10, 8. 1. Sam. XVI. 23. 1. Reg. X. 5. c. XVII. 1. Zach. III. 1. Quemadmodum angeli alias dicuntur stare coram Domino, 1. Reg. XXII. 19. Job. I. 6. Es. VI. 2. Dan. VII. 10. Zach. VI. 5. Luc. I. 19. (3) Ab angeli appa- ritione, visus est in forma viri pugnaturi pro popu- lo, ac Ducis exercitus, quemadmodum Jos. V. 14. ceu Dux cælestis exercitus conspectus est Filius Dei. Equo rufo insedit, ac pone ipsum sequutus exerci- tus equestris, uti Ap. XIX. 13. apparuit. Equus feli- cem rei successum, ac velocem expeditionem no- tat. Vid. Zach. VI. 2. Ap. VI. 2. seqq. c. IX. 17. c. XIX. 11. Equus rufus ultionis divinæ in hostes suos certitudinem & gravitatem significat: sicut alias rufus color vindictæ signum est Zach. VI. 2. Esa. LXIII. 2. Apoc. VI. 4. c. XII. 2. 3. Quod vero inter myrtos consistens videtur, adumbrat ejus in Eccle- sia præsentiam, tutelam ac defensionem ejusdem, uti equitatio modum illius præsentiæ, & extensio- nem ad omnes res Ecclesiæ. Myrti Ecclesiæ mem- bra figurant, quæ perpetuo virent, florent, fructum edunt, & odora Christo sunt, at pressum mundo ve- lut in profundo delitescunt. Myrtus arbor pulcra est, unde Esther ob pulcritudinem הדסה myrtea dicta creditur Esth. II. 7. est & odorifera etiam in Ægypto, ubi dicente Plinio, etsi cætera sine odore sint, lilia, violæ, rosæ, myrtis tamen præcipuus est o- dor. Est festiva, & sancta, festis diebus adornatum, ac triumphalibus olim coronis adhiberi solita, teste iterum Plinio l. XV. c. 29. Conf. Levit. XXIII. 40. Neh. IIX. 16. Arbor illa pacis fuit signum, & flores ac folia ejus victoriæ symbolum. Myrto & conjun- ctioni olim Venus præfuit, atque si hæc arbor veræ conjunctionis & finceri amoris, imprimis conju- galis fuit symbolum. Ita Christus sponsus ille cælestis, vere præest Ecclesiæ, quam in uni- tate fidei congregavit, & adhuc conservat.

Folia myrti siccata sunt ulcerum remedia: Ecclesiæ folia sunt exempla virtutum, quibus alii extra Ec- clesiam viventes ad saniorem mentem revocantur. Ex myrtorum baccis usque ad ariditatem siccatis in umbra vinum fiebat olim, ex non siccatis oleum, & aliud generosi nominis obsonium quod myrtatum vocatur. Ita fideles Ecclesiæ cives igne crucis atque tribulationum exsiccati preces fundunt; aliisque virtutum generibus in spe & silentio se exercent Esa. cap. XXX. v. 15. quæ omnia coram Deo suavif- simum sunt nectar & ambrosia, qua de re David loquitur Psal. LXIX. 32. & preces sanctorum odora- menta vocantur Apoc. V. v. 8. imo ipsa quoque mors sanctorum, qua exfucci prorsus fiunt & ex- sangues, pretiosa est in conspectu Dei Ps. CXVI. 15. sic & omnia bona opera, quæ electi ex fide non fi- cta faciunt I. Tim. I. 5. (hæ enim sunt baccæ non siccæ, sed adhuc floridæ) Deo placent; quibus in- star vini & olei utitur, æstimans ea omnia, quæ in proximum collata sunt, sibi accidisse; qua de re cœlestis ille sponsus Cant. V. v. 1. Comedi favum cum melle meo, bibi vinum meum cum lacte meo, hoc est, omnia vestra opera ex fide profecta instar dulcissimi mellis aut suavissimi vini mirifice me re- crearunt, ut habet B. Bald. in Comment. p. 147. Conf. Cornel. à Lapid. in h. l. (4) Ab interiori An- geli impulsu, atque inspiratione. Fuit ille Angelus ille loquens IN ME, ait Zachar. v. 9. 13. 14. Duplex He emphasin importat & דבר cum ב personæ di- vinæ interius in anima hominis loquentis, & res ab- strusas dictantis instinctum indicat. Num. XII. 2. 8. II. Sam. XXIII. 2. Os. I. 2. uti ex Kimchio notavit B. Tarnovius, annueruntq; Belgæ Interpp. Talis vero interior impulsus & instinctus non tam angelo creato tribuitur, quam Filio Dei in S. literis, cujus Spiritus Prophetis res abstrusas dictavit I. Petr. I. 11. (5) Ab Angeli hujus intercessione. Quandoqui- dem angelus hic ita precatus sit, atque intercesserit pro populo v. 12. Domine exercituum, usque quo tu non misereberis Jerusalem, & urbium Juda, quibus iratus es? Qualis intercessio nuspiam angelo creato tribuitur, & Filio Dei propria est: cujus officium est intercedere pro Ecclesia Jer. XXX. 21. Rom. IIX. 32. I. Joh. I. 2. Ebr. IX. 24. Ap. IIX. 3. 4. Unde recte Coccejus virum hunc Zachar. vers. 11. vocari An- gelum Domini. Et quia ejus intercessio subjicitur vers. 12. intelligimus notari eum, qui מלאך פנים ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ἐμφανιζόμενος τῷ Θεῷ vocatur Es. LXIII. 9. A prædicato proprio noscitur subjectum.
