(6) A vindicta divina in hostes exertione. Angelus ille ac vir inter myrtos visus in æquo rufo explicat Zach. II. 9. vindictam, quam exercere adversus ho- stes decreverat, non ministri instar, sed αὐτοκρατο- ρικῶς, & θεικῶς. Agitaturus sum, inquit, manum meam, contra illas gentes, & erunt præda servis: ita cognoscetis, Jehovam exercituum misisse me. Quæ hæc manus est, nisi potentia Dei infinita Ps. CXXXIX. 7. 8. 9. Es. XLIIX. 12. 13. vel gratia Dei in subjectio- ne & conversione gentium, de quo postea. (7) Ab autoritativa illa loquendi ratione, quæ Angelo isti loquenti in Zacharia c. VI. 8. tribuitur: Hi qui egressi sunt in terram Aquilonarem tranquillarunt spiri- tum meum in terra Aquilonari. Quæ verba majesta- tem Dei loquentis spirant, quomodocunque ea- dem explicentur: quo de c. VI. 8. visuri sumus. A- lia & dicta & facta mere ac vere divina hujus An- geli è cap. II. & III. constabunt. E quibus omnibus manifestum est, virum illum inter myrtos visum, qui & Angelus Domini v. 11. loquens in Zacharia. v. 9. 13. 14. c. II. 3. c. IV. 1. 4. 5. & c. V. 5. 10. c. VI. 4. 8. dicitur, nullum alium, quam ipsummet Filium Dei esse: Conf. præter Interpp. nostros & Reformatos

Dn. D. Steph. Klotz de Angelolatr. punct. XIV. Ego cum Christianis Interpp. Christum fuisse sentio, ait hic Willius, caput Ecclesiæ & Principem Angelorum, quod ipse Propheta confirmat, cum eum angelum Do- mini vocat, v. 11. & Dominum v. 20. Non abnuit omnino Calvinus in Comment. in XII. Proph. Minor. p. 602. Si recipimus hunc Angelum fuisse Christum, communis scripturæ usus non repugnat, sci- mus enim Christum, ut est Angelorum caput, ita semper eos regere, ut nihil agant, quum obsequuntur Deo, nisi sub ejus auspiciis. Potest igitur fieri, ut hic unus An- gelus primatum gesserit inter alios, ut Prophetæ in mentem veniret Redemptor, qui & Angelis & toti Ecclesiæ dominatur. Majori autem παῥῥησίᾳ asserit id Rud. Gualtherus p. 270. Docet Ecclesiam, etsi in vallem miseriarum demersa, & omni spe destituta videatur, esse tamen sub Dei cura, & habere simul præsens auxilium in promisso salvatore Christo, qui illi adsit, non otiosus spectator, sed assertor & vindex: adeoque instar ducis militum, qui jam equum con- scenderit, & rufum quidem equum, ut de hostibus Ec- clesiæ sua crudelem & sanguinariam vindictam justo judicio exigat. Simulque, (ut efficacior sit consolatio) ejus potentia & propensa ergo suum populum volun- tas adumbratur: Illa quidem, dum ad ipsum redeunt, & confluunt angeli, ipsi suæ legationis rationem red- dunt, ipsum denique ut Dominum suum à tergo se- quuntur: hæc vero cum pro Hierosolyma, & urbibus Juda tanto studio & diligentia apud Deum intercedit, & per angelum alterum consolationis argumenta pro- phetæ suggerit, quibus miseros & afflictos confirmet. Belgici quoque autores annot. ad novam versio- nem de Filio Dei hæc explicant. Similiter Danæus Comment. in Proph. Min. p. 827. Ille autem unus, quem & alii equites alloquuntur, cuique uni sui mu- neris infr. vers. 11. rationem reddunt, qui inter myrte- ta insidet equo, qui prophetam regit, instruit ac docet, est procul dubio Dominus noster Jesus Christus, cui omnes creaturæ, tanquam & Deo & capiti Ecclesiæ, parent. Ipse vero insidet equo ruffi coloris, id est, tri- stis, obscuræ, & nondum clari. Inter myrteta loca umbrosa nempe sese continet, quoniam status Ec- clesiæ erant adhuc tum propter multos è Babylo- nia nondum reversos, tum etiam imminentes ad- huc tempestates, erat, inquam, ille status tristis, mœstus, obscurus, nondum splendens, lætus, ab- stersis omnibus calamitatum nebulis. Itaque & co- lorem, & locum rei mœstæ, quam descripturus est aptum affumsit Christus ille Eques, & caput Ecclesiæ compatiens ac condolens cum Ecclesiæ sua. Heb. IV. v. 15. E veteribus S. Hieronymus: Vir, inquit, qui ascendebat super equum rufum, Do- minus, atque Salvator est, qui dispensationem nostræ carnis assumens audit in Esaia, Quare rubra sunt vestimenta tua. S. Cyrillus in h. l. Dominum se in forma nostra vidisse confitetur. &c.

Etiam Rabbini veteres agnovere, non posse in- telligit angelum creatum, sed ipsummet Jehovam hic apparuisse Zachariæ in libr. Sanhedrim di- stinct. chelek. Dixit R. Jochanan, quid est, quod scriptum est Zach. I. 8. Ecce vir equitans super equum rufum. Non est vir in isto loco, nisi Deus san- ctus benedictus, sicut dictum est Ex. XV. 3. Domi- nus vir pugnæ &c. inter myrtos: non sunt myrti nisi justi, sicut dictum est Esth. II. 7. Et erat nutritius Hadassa, id est myrti. Ipsa est Esther.

ET POST EUM EQUI RUFI VARII ET ALBI) Simul nempe cum suis equitibus, ut apparet infra 10. Hi significant casus bellorum aliquando sub Dario futuros, calamitosos, felices & varios. Calamitosi casus fuere con- tra Scythas & Græcos: felices contra Thraciam & Mace- doniam, qui subacti à Persis: varii contra Jonas & Ægy- ptios. Vide Herodotum IV. VI. VII.

Significatio mystica equitis inter myrtos minus commode assignata fuit à Grotio, quod nempe equus sanguinei coloris, in myrteto & quidem profundo retentus bellum alta pace repressum no- tarit. Siquidem non retentus ibi eques fuerit, ne vindictam exerceret, etsi illic constiterit, ad quid enim equo rufo conspiceretur, nisi quod vindi- ctam exercere velit? Et quis equitem illum (si Mi- chaelem solum intelligas) retinere potuisset? Cur etiam præses Judææ gentis retineretur, ne vindicet populum suum? Et cur stipatus conspiceretur equis rufis, variis, & albis, nisi suis opitulatorus? Neque conveniens est illa equorum significatio, quam assignat Grotius. Nam separat equos ab illo equite Principe, quasi hujus quidem visio ad initia Darij, istorum autem apparitio ad sequentia tempora pertineret. Quod nullatenus congruit. Neque Da- rii hic status adumbrandus, sed fidelibus animus addendus erat. Quapropter rectius alii statuunt, in solatium fidelium apparuisse Filium Dei, pugna- turum adversus hostes Ecclesiæ, cum cœlesti exer- citu. Quamvis vero nonnulli per equites stipatores Ecclesiæ Doctores Christum fortiter sequentes in- telligant, quorum alii equis rufis vitam profundere parati, alii variis coloribus, variis donis suis Ecclesiæ inservientes, alii albis integritate vitæ, & candore morum doctrinam cohonestantes compareant: quibus etiam B. Balduinus accedit in Comm. p. 146. præeunte S. Hieronymo : præstat tamen angelos in- telligere, non quidem angelos malos, uti Coccejus vult, sed bonos, qui in salutem Ecclesiæ, post capti- vitatem Babylonicam, q. in excubiis positi fuere, uti etiam cæteri Interpp. agnoscunt, & B. quoque Balduinus noster explicat in Comment. p. 151. Rufi igitur denotant executores judiciorum Dei cruen- torum in hostes, albi pacem Ecclesiæ adferentes, varii in utroque genere occupati, ut habet Willius in h. l. Similiter B. Osiander: Equi rufi significant, Angelos paratos esse ad exercendam vindictam in eos, qui Ecclesiam Dei perturbant: equi punicei, & albi denotant, Angelorum ministerium Eccle- siæ conferre gloriam & lætitiam. Inter myrteta cum equis apparentes angeli, significabant Domi- num ipsorum opera parare Ecclesiæ umbram, sub qua ab afflictionibus aliquando respiret.

## 1:9
Vers. 9.

AND I SAID WHAT ARE THESE MY LORD?) The angel said these things, as the following show. That it was the angel Gabriel, accustomed to being sent to the Prophets, is highly credible. See Dan. VIII. 16. and following: and IX. 21. Daniel addresses the angel with the same voice, my Lord. X. 16. THE ANGEL WHO WAS SPEAKING IN ME) To me. So also below 13. and thus in both places the Chaldean.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ET DIXI QVID SUNT ISTI DOMINE MI?) Hæc dixit Angelus, ut sequentia ostendunt. Eum Ange- lum fuisse Gabrielem, solitum mitti ad Prophetas, per- quam credibile est. Vide Dan. VIII. 16. & sequentibus: & IX. 21. eadem voce Domine mi, Angelum alloquitur Daniel. X. 16. ANGELUS QUI LOQVEBATUR IN ME) Mihi. Sic & infra 13. & ita utroque loco Chaldæus.

## 1:10
Vers. 10.

AND THE MAN WHO WAS STANDING AMONG THE MYRTLES ANSWERED) Gabriel is the greater: for he is among the princes: Gabriel among the legates. If the angel said these things, whom then did he call Lord except the Son of God? But it is too manifest that the angel did not say these things, but the Prophet: to whom the angel answered: as the words subjoined testify. The angel, who was speaking in me, Grotius perhaps wished to write (certainly he ought to have) He said these things to the Angel: He therefore invents another angel, with whom the Prophet spoke besides the Man among the myrtles, whom he believes to have been Gabriel. He introduces a different Angel here.

Gualterus, as also Cornel. à Lapide, but Coccejus makes this angel the Holy Spirit. But the H. S. is never called an angel in the Scriptures. This nomenclature is unheard of in the sacred writings. And since Coccejus acknowledges the interceding angel v. 12 to be the angel of the face of the Lord Is. LXIII. 9, the Son of God, and the same angel who interceded is called v. 13 the Angel speaking in the Prophet, and no other than that angel speaking in the Prophet is addressed in verse 9, nothing is more certain, nothing more open, than that the Angel whom this Prophet addressed, my Lord, is the interceding angel himself, and thus the angel of the face of the Lord, the Son of God. There is therefore no reason why another angel should be invented here as the interlocutor of the Prophet than that man who stood among the myrtles, who is openly called the angel of the Lord verse 11, which most other interpreters have observed and thus the Osiandrine paraphrase holds correctly here, with which the Vinarians and Belgians agree: And I spoke to the Captain of that cavalry (he was the son of God, who leads the heavenly army for the defense of his Church John 5. for below in this chapter this angel is called Jehovah) (But he is called an Angel, not because he is of angelic nature, but because he was sent by the Father to save the human race) And I said: who are those, my Lord? and that Angel of the Lord (sitting on a red horse) who was speaking in me said to me: I will show you what these are: more correctly, who these are. And the man (the Son of God in the figure of a man, who was speaking with me) answered, he himself, who was standing among the myrtles: (who sitting on a red horse remained in that place) and said, these are they whom the Lord has sent, that they may walk through the earth, that is, this is the equestrian army of God, which (with me being the supreme Captain) God sent into the world, so that they might repress the furies of the peoples, and effect peace, and not allow the nations to rage against the people of God. And those heavenly horsemen answered the Angel of the Lord, their Captain, who was standing among the myrtles (as above) and said: We have walked through the earth etc. The angel of the Lord therefore in v. 11 is that man who was standing among the myrtles, and not a person different from him. THESE ARE THEY WHOM THE LORD HAS SENT, THAT THEY MAY WALK THROUGH THE EARTH) These are the occurrences of wars, which God is accustomed to send into the lands. V. 11. WE HAVE WALKED THROUGH THE EARTH) We have sought the opportunity of giving effect to those things for which we were destined. AND BEHOLD ALL THE EARTH IS INHABITED AND IS AT REST) That is, it is inhabited in quiet, there are no seeds of wars. Therefore we find nothing to be done at this present time. The events of wars are not noted, but persons: namely the Angels, who are sent to perambulate the earth, as Willius rightly [notes] in this place; these are the couriers and angels of God, whom God uses as ministers of His providence, who, having surveyed all the affairs of the human race, report to Him what they have seen and heard. For just as kings and princes send out their couriers with horses stationed here and there, who inquire into the affairs and state of their subjects or neighbors, and report back concerning the same, so that they may thus arrange their counsels more rightly, and provide for themselves and their subjects: so God also, although all things are present to Him, uses the ministry of angels, and employs them as ministers of His providence, so that He may thus teach men more about His majesty and glory, and accommodate Himself to their weakness and diffidence regarding His providence, which is more easily overcome when they hear that infinite myriads of angels serve their salvation. The answer of the Angels: we have perambulated the earth, and behold all the earth is inhabited, and is at rest; some, along with Cornel. à Lapide, take this in the sense that there is full peace among the nations, especially those neighboring Judea, and that they will be peaceful toward the Jews, so that they will not provoke them with war, nor hinder the building of the city and the temple. But that explanation does not seem consistent with the mind of the Prophet: since the angels rather complain of the different lot of the enemies of the Church, who were enjoying tranquility, and of the Jewish people, who were not yet free from adversities, so much so that the interceding Angel still complains, how long will You not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah? He asks God, as Castrius rightly says, that if indeed all the nations are acting peacefully, he should not permit his people to still be in affliction and fear, but should bring them all back and command them to be of good courage, so that they may be able to restore the city and the temple. Since others, he says, live in peace, why do you delay to have mercy on Jerusalem? Thus Jerome, Theodoret, Haymo, Remigius, Albert, Hugo, Lyra, and Dionysius explain the peace desired for the people from a comparison with the nations.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET RESPONDIT VIR QUI STABAT INTER MYRTETA) Gabriele Major: nam hic inter principes est: Gabriel inter legatos. Si hæc dixit angelus, quem ergo vocavit Domi- num nisi Filium Dei? Sed nimis manifestum est, hæc non angelum dixisse, sed Prophetam: cui re- spondit angelus: ut verba subjuncta testantur. An- gelus, qui loquebatur in me, scribere fortassis voluit Grotius (certe debuit) Hæc dixit Angelo: Fingit ergo alium angelum, quo cum Propheta collocutus fuerit præter Virum inter myrteta, quem Gabrielem fuisse credit. Diversum Angelum hic introducit

Gualterus, ut & Cornel. à Lapide, Coccejus vero hunc angelum facit Spiritum Sanctum. At Spiritus S. nunquam in Scripturis angelus dicitur. Inaudita hæc est sacris literis nomenclatura. Et quum agno- scunt Coccejus angelum intercessorem v. 12. esse an- gelum faciei Domini Es. LXIII. 9. Filium Dei, atque idem angelus, qui intercessit, dicatur v. 13. Angelus loquens in Propheta, nec alius quam ille angelus lo- quens in Propheta compelletur vers. 9. nihil cer- tius, nihil apertius est, quam quod Angelus, quem compellavit hic Propheta, Domine mi, sit ipse an- gelus intercessor, adeoque angelus faciei Domi- ni, Filius Dei. Non ergo est, quod alius hic finga- tur angelus collocutor Prophetæ, quam vir ille, qui inter myrteta stetit, qui aperte vocatur angelus Do- mini vers. 11. quod observarunt cæteri plerique In- terpp. adeog; recte se hic habet paraphrasis Osian- drina, cui Vinarienses & Belgici consonant: Et allo- cutus sum Capitaneum illius equitatus (is fuit filius Dei, qui exercitum cœlestem pro Ecclesiæ suæ de- fensione ducit Joh. 5. infra enim in hoc capite hic angelus vocatur Jehovah) (Angelus autem appel- latur, non quod sit naturæ angelicæ, sed quod à Pa- tre mitteretur ad servandum genus humanum) Et dixi: qui sunt illi, Domine mi? & dixit ad me ille An- gelus Domini (equo rufo insidens) qui loquebatur in me: Ego ostendam tibi, quid sint hæc: rectius, qui- nam sint hi. Et respondit vir (Filius Dei in figura hominis, qui mecum loquebatur) ille ipse, qui sta- bat inter myrteta: (qui equo rufo insidens eo loco manebat) & dixit, isti sunt, quos misit Dominus, ut perambulent terram, id est, hic est equestris exer- citus Dei, quem (me supremo Capitaneo existen- te) emisit Deus in orbem, ut hi populorum furo- res reprimant, & pacem efficiant, neque gentes in populum Dei grassari sinant. Et responderunt illi cœlestes equites Angelo Domini, Capitaneo suo, qui stabat inter myrteta (ut supra) & dixerunt: Per- ambulavimus terram &c. Angelus ergo Domini vi p. 11. est vir ille, qui inter myrteta stabat, non ve- ro persona ab illo diversa. ISTI SVNT QVOS MISIT DOMINUS, UT PER- AMBULENT TERRAM) Isti sunt bellorum casus, quos Deus terris solet immittere. V. 11. PERAMBULAVIMUS TERRAM) Quæsivi- mus occasionem effecta dandi ea, quibus destinati sumus. ET ECCE OMNIS TERRA HABITATUR ET QVIESCIT) Id est, quiete habitatur, nulla sunt bellorum semina. Itaque nihil invenimus agendum hoc quidem tempore. Non bellorum casus notantur, sed personæ: An- geli nempe, qui mittuntur, ut terram perambulent, uti recte Willius h. l. isti sunt cursores & angeli Dei, quibus Deus ministris providentiæ suæ utitur, qui, omnibus humani generis rebus perlustratis, ad ipsum visa, audita perferunt. Quemadmodum enim reges & principes hinc inde dispositis equis cursores suos emittunt, qui in res & statum subditorum aut vicinorum inquirunt, & de iisdem referunt, ut sic consilia rectius disponere, sibique & subditis con- sulere possint: ita Deus quoque, licet ei omnia sint præsentia, angelorum ministerio utitur, eosque ceu ministros providentiæ suæ adhibet, quo sic ma- jestatem suam & gloriam magis homines doceat, ac imbecillitati ac diffidentiæ eorum circa provi- dentiam suam se accommodet, quæ facilius su- peratur, ubi infinitas angelorum myriades saluti suæ inservire audiunt. Responsum Angelorum: perambulavimus terram, & ecce omnis terra habi- tatur, & quiescit, hoc sensu accipiunt nonnulli, cum Cornel. à Lapide, plenam esse pacem inter gentes præ- sertim Judææ vicinas, illasque fore Judæis pacificas, ut eas bello non lacessant, nec impediant urbis templique fabricam. Sed ea explicatio non videtur menti Pro- phetæ consentanea: siquidem conqueruntur po- tius angeli diversam sortem hostium Ecclesiæ qui tranquillitate gaudebant, & populi Judaici, qui nondum immunis erat ab adverfitatibus, adeo ut adhuc queratur Angelus intercessor, quousque non misereberis Jerusalem & civitatum Iuda? Deum enim rogat, uti recte Castrius, ut siquidem gentes omnes pacate agunt, ne permittat suum populum adhuc in afflictione, ac timore esse, sed omnes eos reducat, & bono animo esse jubeat, ut possint ur- bem, templumque instaurare. Cum alii, inquit, in pace degant, cur tu differs misereri Jerusalem? Sic Hieronymus, Theodoretius, Haymo, Remigius, Alber- tus, Hugo, Lyra, & Dionysius, de optata populo pa- ce, ex collatione cum gentibus explicant.

## 1:12
Verse 12.

AND THE ANGEL OF THE LORD ANSWERED) Michael. HOW LONG WILL YOU NOT HAVE MERCY ON JERUSALEM, Which at that time was still lying without walls. AND ON THE CITIES OF JUDAH) Which themselves also were still lying in their ruins. WITH WHICH YOU HAVE BEEN ANGRY? THIS IS NOW THE SEVENTIETH YEAR) With which you have been angry for seventy years. That is, the whole time of the exile which we have endured: the whole time predicted by Jeremiah. And Michael prays that those edicts from Darius for the construction of the temple and the city and the towns be hastened, while there was deep peace throughout the Persian empire, and the peoples envying the Jews were easily kept in obedience, because when those wars were about to arise, as signified in Haggai at the end and in this chapter, it was credible that the king would not be free for lesser considerations, and if he were free, his edicts would not have the same authority.

Those seventy years are not the years of exile predicted by Jeremiah, but of the desolation of Jerusalem. For the years of exile or servitude had long since elapsed, the beginning of which we proved in the fourth year of Jehoiakim at Jer. XXIX must be imagined: Therefore they were finished in the 23rd year of the Persian Kingdom of Cyrus, who is the first of his Monarchy. And this distinction between the 70 years of servitude and the 70 years of the devastation of Jerusalem was observed by Theodoret here, although he did not correctly assign the term from which and to which of the former, sect. 1 to Ezek. from the 18th of Joshua to the first of Cyrus of the Persian Kingdom. It is, however, to be noted, he says at this place, that the time of the former captivity was completed in the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, or by the witness of the best and most merciful Lord, who in the dangers added to evils numbered the time of the prediction, which we showed more accurately in our Commentaries on Ezekiel. The seventy years of the devastation of Jerusalem were completed in the second year of the reign of Darius. This number must be started from the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah, under whom the city was captured. If anyone searches for the beginning of the counting, he will find that this time was completed in the second year of the Reign of Darius, son of Hystaspes. Concerning which Cornelius à Lapide also warned: The angel said these things in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, as is clear in verse 1. Therefore, in this second year these 70 years were fulfilled: whence it follows that they are different from the 70 years of the Babylonian captivity, about which Jeremiah speaks in chapter 25, 11 and chapter 29, 10. For those are finished in the first year of Cyrus, who dissolved the captivity and sent the Jews back from Babylon, which he had captured, to Jerusalem, as is clear in I Esdras 1:1. But these are begun from the city and temple cut down by the Chaldeans, which happened in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, which was the 18th of Nebuchadnezzar, and are finished in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, wherefore these of Zechariah are called the 70 years of the desolation, namely, of the city and temple; but the former of Jeremiah are called the 70 years of the captivity, namely, of the Jews: thus Eusebius in his Chronicle, Clement in book I of the Stromata, St. Jerome in the preface to Haggai, St. Augustine in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 26, Torniellus in his Chronology in the year of the world 3462 (who nevertheless starts these years of Zechariah from the last captivity of the Jews, by which, namely, after the destruction of Jerusalem, the fugitives into Egypt were led away from there by the Chaldeans into Babylon according to the oracle of Jeremiah, which happened in the 27th year of the transmigration of Jehoiachin or Jeconiah), Ribera, Sanchez, à Castro, and others here as also Fernandez in vision 19, sect. 1. Zechariah favors this in chapter VII, verse 5, where in the fourth year of Darius Hystaspes he says concerning these 70 years of desolation: When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month during these seventy years. Where note the pronoun 'these', which designates the present years, not those past before Cyrus. These are the words of Cornelius. With whom Castrius agrees entirely.

But those who did not see this so evident truth about the different 70 years are found to have tortured themselves in various ways here. Scaliger thinks the seventieth year is indicated from the edict of Xerxes against the Jews, which he admits was the fourth, not the second, year of Darius Nothus, nor could he prove by any testimony of Scripture that any epoch began from the edict of Xerxes, and that the years were counted, whence he did not even satisfy his own followers, who with him understand Darius Nothus, as can be seen from Willius and L. Danaeus at this place, not to mention others: who judge that he erred entirely, because he refers this history to the time of Darius Nothus, which belongs entirely to the Reign of Darius Hystaspes. Which we have already shown in the annotations to Jeremiah. Others take the words of the Prophet interrogatively. Are these the 70 years? or is this the seventieth year of our liberty predicted by Jeremiah in chapter XXV and Daniel c. IX. 2? but that interrogation would be very inappropriate if you institute the calculation from the first year of the captivity up to the second year of Darius Nothus, since the years of the captivity would have already been finished for over a century. Coccejus thinks the next years up to the second year of Darius Nothus are designated, but he could find nothing about them that would fit here either from sacred or exotic writers. Compare what we said about this place in our notes on Daniel concerning the 70 weeks, Daniel C. XII, § 36 and 37.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET RESPONDIT ANGELUS DOMINI) Michael. USQUE QUO TU NON MISEREBERIS JERU- SALEM, Quæ tunc adhuc jacebat sine mœnibus. ET URBIUM JUDÆ) Quæ & ipsæ adhuc in ruinis suis jacebant. QUIBUS IRATUS ES? ISTE JAM SEPTUAGE- SIMUS ANNUS EST) Quibus iratus fuisti per annos se- ptuaginta. Id est toto exilii tempore, quod pertulimus: toto tempore prædicto à Jeremia. Ideo autem orat Mi- chael deproperari edicta illa à Dario pro templi & urbis & oppidorum structura, dum alta per imperium Persicum pax erat, populique Judæis invidentes, facile in obsequio retinebantur, quod ubi exoritura essent illa bella apud Aggæum in fine, & hoc capite fignificata, credibile erat, neque regem vacaturum cogitationibus minoribus, & si vacaret, edictis ejus non idem auctoritatis fore.

Septuaginta illi anni non sunt anni exilii à Jere- mia prædicti, sed ἐρημώσεως Hierosolymæ. Nam jam pridem elapsi erant exilii vel servitutis anni, quorum initium fingendum esse in quarto Jojackimi ad Jer. XXIX. evicimus: Finiti ergo sunt XXIII. an- no Persici Regni Cyri, qui primus est Monarchiæ e- jus. Atque hanc distinctionem annorum servitu- tis LXX. & annorum LXX. Vastationis Hierosoly- mæ observavit hic Theodoretus, etsi priorum terminum à quo, & ad quem non recte assignarit sect. 1. ad Ezech. ab 18. Josuæ ad primum Cyri Re- gni Persici. Est autem inquit ad h. l. animadverten- dum, prioris captivitatis tempus completum fuisse an- no Cyri primo Persarum regis, vel teste Domino opti- mo & misericordissimo, qui in malorum a ditis pericu- lis tempus prædictionis annumeravit, quod accuratius in nostris Commentariis in Ezechielem oftendimus. Vastitatis Hierusalem septuaginta anni completi sunt secundo anno regni Darii. Hic numerus incipiendus est ab anno undecimo regni Sedechia, sub quo urbs capta fuit. Si quis numerandi exordium perscrute- tur, tempus hoc completum fuisse inveniet anno secun- do Regni Darii Hystaspis filii. De quo etiam monuit Cornelius à Lapide: Dixit hæc angelus anno secun- do Darii Hystaspis, ut patet vers. 1. Hoc ergo secun- do anno impleti sunt hi 70. anni: unde sequitur, eos diversos esse ab annis 70. captivitatis Babylo- nicæ, de quibus Jeremias cap. 25, 11. cap. 29, 10. Illi enim finiuntur anno primo Cyri, qui captivitatem solvit, & Judæos è Babylone à se capta remisit in Jerusalem, ut patet I. Esdræ I. 1. Hi vero inchoan- tur ab excisa à Chaldæis urbe & templo, quod con- tigit anno undecimo Sedeciæ, qui fuit 18. Nabucho- donosoris, ac finiuntur anno secundo Darii Hystaspis, quocirca hi Zachariæ vocantur anni 70. desolatio- nis scilicet urbis & templi; priores vero Jeremiæ vocantur anni 70. captivitatis, scilicet Judæorum: ita Euseb. in Chron. Clemens lib. I. Stromat. S. Hieron. procœmio in Aggæum, S. Augustinus lib. 18. de civ. cap. 26. Tornielius, in Chronol. anno mundi 3462. (qui tamen hosce Zachariæ annos inchoat ab ulti- ma captivitate Judæorum, qua scilicet post excisam Jerusalem profugi in Ægyptum, inde juxta oracu- lum Jeremiæ à Chaldæis abducti sunt in Babylo- nem, quod contigit anno 27. transmigrationis Joa- chin sive Jechoniæ) Ribera, Sanchez, à Castro, & alii hic ut & Fernandez visione 19. sect. 1. Favet Zacha- rias cap. VII. vers. 5. ubi anno quarto Darii Hystaspis de hisce 70. annis desolationis ait: Cum jejunare- tis & plangeretis in quinto & septimo per hos se- ptuaginta annos. Ubi nota pronomen hos, quod defignet annos præsentes, non præteritos ante Cy- rum. Hæc Cornelius. Cui ex asse consonat Castrius.

Qui autem hanc tam evidentem veritatem de diversis LXX. annis non viderunt, varie hic se tor- sisse deprehenduntur. Scaliger septuagesimum an- num ab edicto Xerxis contra Judæos indigitari pu- tat, quem vero fuisse quartum non secundum Da- rii Nothi annum fatetur, nec ullo scripturæ testi- monio probare potuit ab edicto Xerxis epocham ullam cepisse, annosque numeratos esse, unde ne suis quidem satisfecit, qui cum ipso Darium No- thum intelligunt, uti è Willio & L. Danæo ad h. l. videre est, nedum aliis: qui censent toto illum cœ- lo errasse, quod ad Darii Nothi tempus hanc hi- storiam referat, quæ omnino ad Regnum Darii Hystaspis pertinet. Quod in annotatis ad Jerem. jam ostendimus. Alii interrogative verba Prophe- tæ accipiunt. Istine sunt LXX. anni? vel istene est septuagesimus annus libertatis nostræ à Jeremia cap. XXV. & Daniele c. IX. 2. prædictus? sed illa inter- rogatio valde inconveniens fuerit, si à primo capti- vitatis anno usque ad secundum Darii Nothi cal- culum instituas, siquidem ultra seculum jam finiti fuerint captivitatis anni. Coccejus proximos annos usque ad secundum Darii Nothi designari putat, sed de illis nihil invenire potuit, quod huc quadra- ret vel è sacris vel exoticis scriptoribus. Confer. quæ ad Danielem de LXX. septimanis Daniel. C. XII. §. 36. & 37. de hoc loco diximus.

## 1:13
Verse 13.

THE LORD ANSWERED THE ANGEL) All things proceed in order. God speaks to the Angel, the Angel to the Prophet.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

RESPONDIT DOMINVS ANGELO) Omnia ordine eunt. Deus Angelo loquitur, Angelus Prophetæ.

## 1:14
I AM JEALOUS FOR JERUSALEM AND SION WITH GREAT JEALOUSY) I so love the Jews that I am unwilling to endure any longer the injuries inflicted upon them.

Latin:

ZELATVS SVM JERUSALEM ET SION ZELO MAGNO) Ita Judæos amo, ut injurias ipsis illatas diutius perpeti nolim.

## 1:15
Ver. 15.

AND I AM ANGRY WITH GREAT ANGER UPON THE WEALTHY NATIONS) In the Hebrew: at ease, those nations of the Persian Empire, which he had said above were living in quiet. God judges them unworthy of such profound peace.

FOR I WAS ANGRY A LITTLE) For some time, namely, with the Jews.

BUT THEY HELPED FOR EVIL) That is, they added something to the former evils, while they hindered that which Cyrus had permitted. See Ezra IV.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

ET IRA MAGNA EGO IRASCOR SVPER GEN- TES OPULENTAS) In hebræo: pacatas, gentes illas Im- perii Persici, quas supra dixerat quietem habitare. Judi- cat Deus illas indignas tam alta pace.

QVIA EGO IRATVS SVM PARVM) Ad tempus aliquod, Judæis scilicet.

IPSI VERO ADJUVERUNT IN MALVM) Id est aliquid adjecere ad mala priora, dum impediunt id, quod Cyrus permiserat. Vide Esdræ IV.

## 1:16
Ver. 16.

I WILL RETURN TO JERUSALEM IN MERCIES) That is, I will look upon those descendants of the Jerusalemites with a kindly eye.

MY HOUSE SHALL BE BUILT IN IT) The temple.

AND A PLUMBLINE SHALL BE STRETCHED OVER JERUSALEM) A rule, μέτρον here in the LXX, elsewhere σπαρτίον. The sense is: besides the temple, the city also shall be restored, which see fulfilled in Nehemiah II, III, and the following.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

REVERTAR AD JERVSALEM IN MISERICOR- DIIS) Id est, oculo benigno respiciam illos posteros Hie- rosolymitarum.

DOMVS MEA ÆDIFICABITVR IN EA) Tem- plum.

ET PERPENDICVLVM EXTENDETVR SVPER JERVSALEM) Regula, μέτρον hic LXX. alibi σπαρτίον. Sensus est: præter templum etiam urbs restituetur, quod impletum vide Nehem. II. III. & sequentibus.

## 1:17
Ver. 17.

MY CITIES SHALL YET FLOW WITH GOOD THINGS) Towns shall spread themselves here and there, on account of the goodness of the land, that is.

AND THE LORD SHALL YET COMFORT SION) He shall comfort Sion, by the punishments of its enemies, as follows.

AND SHALL YET CHOOSE JERUSALEM) He continues to love. That is, to do good, the cause for the effect, Haggai 2:24.

Others also explain the Hebrew text thus: B. Winckelmann. In the Hebrew it is: My cities shall yet be dispersed for goodness. For he indicates that there shall be many cities in the land of Judah and that they shall be wealthy, just as if they were scattered here and there, just as a farmer scatters seeds here and there in a field; at the same time he also promises an abundance of all necessary things. Similarly, Luther understood it concerning the dispersion of cities, that God wishes to scatter them as it were in every place, which some understand primarily of the heavenly Jerusalem, the Church of the New Testament, in which spiritual Jews, that is, Christians dispersed in all the ends of the earth abound in divine goodness, which God had already promised before, that He has its walls in His eyes, that its land will be too narrow for its inhabitants, that all peoples will bring their sons in their arms, and their daughters upon their shoulders, etc. Which can be admitted thus far, because the Lord is said to be about to choose Jerusalem still. For this election embraces not only the material restoration and corporal benefits, but primarily that distinguished ἀξίωμα, that from Jerusalem countless churches were to go forth to be disseminated here and there throughout the world: Thus these words were truly GOOD AND CONSOLATORY. Therefore Jerome, Lyra, Vatablus, Arias, Castrius, Cornelius à Lapide, Balduinus, Cocceius and others explained these things concerning the happy state under Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, so that the same should have been referred not to the times of the Maccabees, but better to the times of Christ. Which interpretation is confirmed primarily from those things which are predicted in chapter II concerning the great multitude of those inhabiting Jerusalem, and the calling of the Gentiles through Christ.

THE SECOND VISION OF THE IV. HORNS TO BE CRUSHED. Ver. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ADHUC AFFLVENT CIVITATES MEÆ BO- NIS) Spargent se oppida huc, illuc, ob bonitatem terræ sci- licet.

ET CONSOLABITVR ADHUC DOMINVS SION) Sionem consolabitur, pœnis inimicorum, ut sequitur.

ET ELIGET ADHUC JERVSALEM) Amare per- get. Id est, bene facere, causa pro effectu Agg. II. 24.

Ita Ebræum textum etiam explicant alii: B. Winckelmann. in Hebræo est: Adhuc dispergun- tur civitates meæ præ bonitate. Indicat enim mul- tas fore civitates in terra Judæ easque locuple- tes, perinde ac si hinc inde disseminatæ essent, sicut agricola semina hinc inde dispergit in a- grum, simul etiam promittit affluentiam omniũ rerum necessariarum. Similiter Lutherus intel- lexit de dispersione civitatum, quod Deus easdem q. in omni loco disseminare velit, quod imprimis de Hierosolyma cœlesti, Ecclesia N. T. intelligunt nonnulli, in qua Judæi spirituales, hoc est Chri- stiani in omnibus terræ finibus dispersi abundant bonitate divina, cui jam ante promiserat Deus, quod muros ejus in oculis suis habeat, quod terra ejus sit angustior futura præ habitatoribus, quod omnes populi filios sint allaturi in ulnis, & filias super humeris &c. Quod hactenus admitti potest, quia Jerusalem adhuc electurus dicitur Dominus. Nam hæc electio complectitur non tantum restaurationem materialem, & beneficia corporalia, sed imprimis insigne illud ἀξίωμα, quod ex Hierosolyma prodire debuerint innumeræ Ecclesiæ per orbem terrarum passim disseminandæ: Ita vere erant hæc verba BONA ET CONSOLATORIA. Ideo Hieronymus, Lyranus, Vatablus, Arias, Castrius, Cornelius à Lapide, Balduinus, Coccejos & alii hæc de felici statu sub Zorobabele ac Nehemia exposuere, ut ad tempora non Maccabæorum, sed melius ad tempora Christi eadem referenda fuerint. Quæ interpretatio confirmatur imprimis ex iis, quæ cap. II. de summa multitudine inhabitantium Hierosolymam, & per Christum vocatione gentium prædicuntur.

SECUNDA VISIO IV. CORNUUM CONTUNDENDORUM. Vers. 19.

## 1:19
THESE ARE THE HORNS, WHICH HAVE SCATTERED JUDAH AND ISRAEL, AND JERUSALEM) זרה, which is translated here as scatter, signifies to inconvenience in any way, and is translated by ἐλικμήσει in Prov. XX. 8. and by καθυβρίζειν in Jerem. LI. 2. also by to bind or surround by David Kimchi, Psalm CXXXIX. 3. by the Greeks in Prov. XV. 8. By Israel here understand the descendants of Benjamin and Levi: and if any from other tribes had joined themselves. The four horns, which especially hindered the Jerusalemites and other Jews, and the Israelites joined to them, from the work, are the Cuthites, Ammonites, Arabs, and Philistines. Nehem. IV. 7.

Latin:

HÆC SVNT CORNVA, QVÆ VENTILAVERUNT JUDAM ET ISRAEL, ET JERVSALEM) זרה, quod hic ventilare vertitur, quocunque modo incommodare significat, vertiturque per ἐλικμήσει Prov. XX. 8. & per καθυβρίζειν Jerem. LI. 2. etiam per ligare aut circumdare Davidi Kimchi, Psalm. CXXXIX. 3. Græcis Prov. XV. 8. Per Israelem hic intellige Benjaminis & Levi posteros: & si qui ex aliis tribubus se adjunxerant. Cornua quatuor, quæ præcipue Hierosolymitas & Judæos alios, eisque adjunctos Israelitas impedierunt ab opere, sunt Chutæi, Ammonitæ, Arabes, & Philistini. Nehem. IV. 7.

## 1:20
Ver. 20.

FOUR CARPENTERS) With adzes to hew down the horns, that is, the ferocity of those peoples. Those four carpenters, who took away that pride from the nations, are the Kings of Persia, Alexander, the Kings of Syria, the Kings of Egypt; for although these came into a share of the power of Alexander, the Prophets always place them separately from Alexander, because they did not have the principal seat of their empire at Pella, as Alexander did, but at Antioch and Alexandria.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

QVATUOR FABROS) Cum dolabris ad dedolanda cornua, id est, ferociam istorum populorum. Quatuor illi fabri, qui gentibus superbiam illam ademere, sunt Reges Persæ, Alexander, Reges Syriæ, Reges Ægypti; nam hos quanquam in partem venere potentiæ Alexandri, ab Alexandro semper seorsim ponunt Prophetæ, quod sedem præcipuam imperii non Pellæ habuerint, ut Alexander, sed Antiochiæ & Alexandriæ.

## 1:21
Ver. 21.

THESE ARE THE HORNS, WHICH HAVE SCATTERED JUDAH BY INDIVIDUAL MEN, AND NO ONE OF THEM LIFTED UP HIS HEAD) They so hindered them, that there was not anyone who dared to lift up his head.

AND THESE CAME) But these will come, the carpenters namely, that is, the kings, or the families of kings.

TO FRIGHTEN THEM) Those four nations.

TO CAST DOWN THE HORNS OF THE NATIONS) By cutting off their strength.

WHICH LIFTED UP A HORN) Ἐπαλλαγὴ, that is, horns.

UPON THE LAND OF ISRAEL) Against the land of Israel, that is, the nation.

THAT THEY MIGHT DISPERSE IT) That they might hinder it. For it is the same word which is twice above.

By the four horns are more correctly understood four kingdoms from all the corners of the world: For the Israelites had enemies from all the regions of the globe, the Philistines to the west, the Egyptians and Edomites to the south, the Ammonites and Moabites to the east, the Syrians, Assyrians, and Babylonians to the north. Thus Theodoret, Clarius, Riebera, Sanctius, Castrius, Cornelius, and most of our own. Most Hebrews understand the four Monarchies, but the Prophet is not dealing with the evils which the Jews were to endure under the Greeks or Romans, but with those which they had already sustained. Nor is the passage Neh. IV. 7, brought forward by Grotius, a parallel. For even those things which are narrated there are later than this vision, which adumbrates the persecutions and adversities of the people not as future, but as present, or even still enduring. These horns are not those which will scatter, but which HAVE SCATTERED Judah and Israel. Nor indeed are those alone looked upon who were to hinder the structure of the temple or were to hinder the city, but those who scattered Judah and Israel. Moreover, that by the name Israel only those who had joined themselves to the Jews are understood, will not be easily shown by parallel passages. Concerning these horns, B. Balduinus p. 175 rightly says: Because it makes express mention of four horns, it is signified that from the four parts of the world the nations had joined their forces, strength, and power against the people of God. From the east were the Moabites, Edomites, and Ammonites, against whose ferocity the Prophet Jeremiah, by the command of the Lord, sharpened his pen around that very time of the captivity, Jer. XLVIII. XLIX. From the west were the Philistines, against whom it is said in chapter XLVII of Jeremiah: From the south were the Egyptians and Ethiopians, whose cruelty toward the people of God Isaiah touches upon, and for that reason threatens them with devastation and destruction in chapters XVIII, XIX, XX, XXI of Isaiah. Finally, from the North were 1. The Syrians, whose King Benhadad besieged Samaria, the metropolis of the Israelites, in the time of Joram, King of Israel, II Kings VI. 24. 2. The Assyrians, by whom the ten tribes were led away and Samaria was captured, while Shalmaneser, King of the Assyrians, was besieging it, during the reign of Hoshea son of Elah over Israel, II Kings XVII. 9 seqq. 3. The Babylonians, by whom the remaining tribe of Judah was led away to Babylon, under the leadership of Nebuchadnezzar, in the times of Jehoahaz, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah, Kings of Judah, II Chron. XXXVI. By these four horns, that is, most powerful enemies collected from all parts of the world, the people of God were most grievously attacked; therefore the Prophet says, the horns scattered Judah and Israel; that is, they powerfully conquered and trampled them: for in this sense, the Royal Prophet uses this phrase against the enemies of God, Ps. XLIV. v. 6, With thee we will scatter our enemies with the horn. Moreover, the phrase is proper to bulls or other animals goring with the horn, which the Pseudo-Prophet Zedekiah dared to express by external gesture and visible likeness, who, having fashioned iron horns for himself and shaking his head, said to Ahab, King of Israel: With these you shall scatter Syria, until you destroy it, I Kings 22. v. 11. The Prophet, however, joined the three objects of the goring enemies, Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem, to show that nothing at all in the entire people of God was immune or exempt from that hostile incursion. For Judah and Israel were the two heads of the whole people, as is evident from I Kings XII. v. 16, 20, 21, and 2 Kings 17. v. 21. The metropolis of the Israelite tribes was Samaria; of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, Jerusalem, of which alone the Prophet makes mention in this place, because this whole vision was directed toward its restoration and the divine worship within it. Therefore he adds in verse 21, they scattered Judah by individual men, because, of course, each and every one had been led away into captivity.

Furthermore, Grotius does not correctly explain the craftsmen as the Kings of the Persians, Alexander, and the Kings of Syria and Egypt. These did not cast down the Hittites, Ammonites, Arabs, and Philistines, just as Grotius wishes the Prophet to threaten here. Others understand by the craftsmen those building without interruption, to whom Winckelmannus accedes; B. Luther and Osiander understand by these craftsmen as many Angels set over those kingdoms, whence the slaughter is to be feared by the Jews, as is read concerning the Angel of the Persians in Dan. X. 13. Tirinus, Castrius, and Cornel. à Lapide wish the angels of the provinces, the guardians of the Jews, who scatter the enemies, to be noted, and refer themselves to Jerome, Cyril, Theodoret, Remigius, and Haymo. Coccejus by the 4 horns understands Shalmaneser, Nebuchadnezzar, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes Longimanus. But he errs in chronology, while he makes all these prior to this vision. By the 4 smiths he wishes to indicate Nebuchadnezzar, Cyrus, the Greeks under Themistocles, who terrified Xerxes, and the Greeks under Cimon; but the former had already passed, and it is by no means likely that the latter are indicated. Rud. Gualtherus p. 272. By the horns are shadowed forth the nations or kingdoms which had hitherto been hostile to the Jews. In this vision, however, they appear to the Prophet so that they may understand again that nothing was done by these by chance, but by the certain counsel of God, who willed that His people be exercised. Four are indeed numbered, because hostile nations had come upon them from all the corners of the world. Willius observes here a diversity of figures: he had noted the enemies of the Jews by the likeness of harmful beasts, but he depicts the liberators in human form, because they treat the Church in a friendly and humane manner. He had represented the enemies by horns, the hard and ferocious instruments of animals, but he compares the liberators to smiths, who use iron instruments fit for breaking down anything hard. It was therefore signified that God would raise up from everywhere those who would promote the construction of the temple and the city, and who would cast down and disperse the power of the enemies. Others specifically understand the doctors of the Church by the smiths, as spiritual architects, who are raised up from all the regions of the world to resist the enemies of the Church and to take care of it. In which manner, in the Doctoral promotion in the year 1654 of the Candidates of Theology, Mr. Dr. JOH. MEISNER, Mr. Dr. MICH. WENDLER, Mr. Dr. JOH. ANDR. QUENSTEDT, and Mr. Dr. SIXT. BERTRAM, I called these four smiths into use when I, as Pro-Chancellor, granted the license to promote.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

HÆC SVNT CORNUA, QUÆ VENTILAVERUNT IUDAM PER SINGULOS VIROS, ET NEMO EORUM LEVAVIT CAPUT SUUM) Adeo eos impedierunt, ut non esset ullus qui caput suum auderet attollere.

ET VENERUNT ISTI) Sed venient isti, fabri scilicet, id est reges, aut regum familiæ.

DETERRERE EA) Illas gentes quatuor.

UT DEIICIANT CORNUA GENTIUM) Vires ipsis accidendo.

QVÆ LEVAVERUNT CORNU) Ἐπαλλαγὴ, id est, cornua.

SUPER TERRAM ISRAEL) Contra terram Israel, id est, gentem.

UT DISPERGERENT EAM) Ut impedirent eam. Est enim idem verbum, quod bis supra.

Per cornua quatuor rectius intelliguntur quatuor regna ab omnibus mundi cardinibus: Habuerunt enim Israelitæ hostes ab omnibus orbis plagis, ad occasum Philisthinos, ad meridiem Ægyptios & Idumæos, ad Orientem Ammonitas & Moabitas, ad Septentrionem Syros, Assyrios & Babylonios. Ita Theodoretus, Clarius, Riebera, Sanctius, Castrius, Cornelius & nostri plerique. Ebræi plerique quatuor Monarchias intelligunt, sed Propheta non de malis agit, quæ Judæi sub Græcis aut Romanis exantlaturi erant, sed de iis, quæ jam sustinuerant. Neque parallelus est locus Neh. IV. 7. à Grotio adductus. Nam & illa, quæ ibi narrantur, posteriora sunt hac visione, quæ persequationes, & adversitates populi non futuras, sed præsentes, aut etiamnum durantes adumbrat. Hæc cornua sunt, non quæ ventilabunt, sed quæ VENTILA- RUNT Judam & Israel. Neque vero solum illi re- spiciuntur, qui templi structuram impedire, aut urbis impedituri erunt, sed qui Judam & Israel ven- tilarunt. Nomine autem Israel solum illos, qui se Judæis adjunxerant, intelligi, locis parallelis haud facile ostendetur. De hisce cornibus recte B. Bal- duinus p. 175. Quod quatuor cornuum expressum facit mentionem, significatur, à quatuor partibus mundi gentes suas conjunxisse vires, robur ac po- tentiam, adversus Dei populum. Ab ortu erant Moabitæ, Idumæi, atque Ammonitæ, contra quo- rum ferociam circa illud ipsum tempus captivitatis ex mandato Domini stylum strinxit Propheta Jer. XLVIII. XLIX. Ab occasu erant Philistini, contra quos cap. XLVII. Jeremiæ dictum est: A meridie Ægyptii & Æthiopes, quorum crudelitatem er- ga Dei populum perstringit Esaias, eamque ob causam devastationem & interitum eis minatur Es. XVIII. XIX. XX. XXI. capitibus. A Septentrione denique erant 1. Syrii quorum Rex Benadad obse- dit Samariam, metropolin Israelitarum, tempore Jorami Regis Israelitici II. Reg. VI. 24. 2. Assyrii, à quibus decem tribus abductæ, & Samaria capta est, obsidente eam Salmanassare Assyriorum Re- ge, regnante super Israel Oseæ Filio Ela, II. Reg. XIIX. 9. seqq. 3. Babylonii, à quibus residua tribus Juda Babylonem abducta, duce Nebucadnezare, temporibus Joachazi, Jechoniæ, & Sedeciæ, Re- gum Juda II. Para. XXXVI. Ab his quatuor corni- bus, hoc est, hostibus potentissimus, ex omnibus mundi partibus collectis, gravissime impetebatur Dei populus; ideo dicit Propheta, ventilaverunt cornua Iudam & Israel; hoc est; potenter vicerunt & proculcaverunt: hoc enim sensu, hac phrasi Re- gius Propheta contra hostes Dei utitur Ps. XLIV. v. 6. In te inimicos nostros cornu ventilabimus. Est autem phrasis taurorum, aut aliorum animalium cornu petentium propria, quam externo gestu, & visibili similitudine exprimere audebat Pseudo- Propheta Sedecias, qui fabrefactis sibi ferreis cor- nubus, & agitato capite dicebat Achabo, Regi Israelis: His ventilabis Syriam, donec deleas eam, I. Reg. 22. v. 1. Conjunxit autem Propheta tria ho- stium cornupetentium objecta Judam, Israel & Jerusalem, ut ostenderet, nihil quidquam in uni- verso populo Dei ab incursione illa hostili fuisse immune, aut exemtum. Nam Juda & Israel duo e- rant capita totius populi, ut constat ex I. Reg. XII. v. 16. 20. 21. & 2. Reg. 17. v. 21. Metropolis Israeliti- carum tribuum erat Samaria; tribus Judæ & Ben- jamin Jerusalem, cujus solius hoc loco mentio- nem facit Propheta, quia ad instaurationem ejus, cultusque divini in ea hæc tota visio directa erat. Idcirco addit vers. 21. ventilaverunt Juda per singu- los viros, quia nimirum singuli & universi in captivi- tatem fuerant abducti.

Porro, nec fabros recte explicat Grotius de Re- gibus Persarum, Alexandro, Regibus Syriæ, & Æ- gypti. Non dejecerunt hi Hitzos, Ammonitas, A- rabes, & Philistinos, quemadmodum hic Prophe- tam minitari vult Grotius. Alii per fabros intelli- gunt ædificantes sine interturbatione, quibus ac- cedit Winckelmannus, B. Lutherus, & Osiander per hos fabros intelligunt totidem Angelos, regnis illis præpositos, unde clades Judæis metuenda, uti de Angelo Persarum legitur Dan. X. 13. Tirinus, Ca- strius, & Cornel. à Lapide, angelos provinciarum, Judæorum custodes, qui hostes ventilant, notari volunt, & ad Hieronym. Cyrill. Theodoret. Remigium, Haymonem sese referunt. Coccejus per 4. cornua Salmanassarem, Nabucadnezarem, Xerxem, & Ar- taxerxem Longimanum intelligit. Sed in Chronolo- gia errat, dum hos omnes hac visione priores facit. Per 4. fabros indigitari vult Nebucadnezarem, Cy- rum, Græcos sub Themistocle, qui Xerxem expa- vefecerunt, Græcos sub Cimone; verum priores jam transierant, posteriores indigitari minime ve- ro simile est. Rud. Gualtherus p. 272. Per cornua gentes sive regna adumbrantur, quæ Judæis hucus- que infesta fuerant. In visione autem ista Prophe- tæ apparent, ut rursus intelligant, nihil ab his for- tuito factum fuisse, sed certo Dei consilio, qui po- pulum suum exerceri voluerit. Quatuor vero nu- merantur, quia ab omnibus cardinibus mundi il- lis gentes inimicæ supervenerant. Willius figura- rum hic observat diversitatem: Hostes Judæorum notaverat similitudine bestiarum noxiarum, libera- tores vero humana specie pingit, quia amice & hu- maniter Ecclesiam tractant. Hostes per cornua re- præsentaverat, instrumenta animalium dura & fe- rocia, liberatores vero comparat fabris, qui instru- mentis ferreis ad dura quæque confringenda aptis utuntur. Significatum ergo fuit, excitaturum Deum undiquaque, qui templi & urbis exstructio- nem promoturi, hostiumque dejecturi & disper- furi sint potentiam. Alii specialiter doctores Ec- clesiæ per fabros intelligunt, ceu architectos spiri- tuales, qui ex omnibus mundi plagis excitantur, ut hostibus Ecclesiæ resistant, ejusque curam gerant. Quo pacto in promotione Doctorali An. ͻiɔ iɔc L- IV. Candidatorum Theolog. Dn. D. JOH. MEISNERI, Dn. D. MICH. WENDLERI, Dn. D. JOH. ANDR. QUENSTEDT & Dn. D. SIXT. BERTRAMI quatuor hosce fabros cum Pro-Cancellarius licentiam promovendi conce- derem in usum vocavi.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. Of the special visions, the first, in order the third.

A man is seen measuring Jerusalem, and a very frequent habitation of Jerusalem is announced, to whom the Lord will be for a wall, the dispersed are called together, assistance is promised against the enemies, Sion is excited to joy on account of the coming of the Lord and the gathering of the nations.

God wills to inhabit Jerusalem, increased by the nations.

Ver. 1.

AND I LIFTED UP MY EYES, AND SAW) In a daytime vision. AND BEHOLD A MAN) Nehemiah is here foreshadowed. AND IN HIS HAND A MEASURING LINE) For the purpose of making a designation of the city and its regions, as is accustomed to be done by architects. Nehem. II. 13, 14, 15, 20, III. and following. Compare Ezech. XL. Apocal. XI. 1.

Latin:

CAPUT II. E visionibus specialibus prima, ordine tertia.

Conspicitur vir mensurans Hierosolymam & denuntiatur Hierosolymæ frequentissima inhabitatio, cui Dominus pro muro erit, convocantur dispersi, promittitur assisten- tia adversus hostes, excitatur Sion ad gaudium ob adventum Domini, & aggre- gationem gentium.

Vult habitare Deus Solymas in gentibus auctas.

Vers. 1.

ET LEVAVI OCULOS MEOS, ET VIDI) In visu diurno. ET ECCE VIR) Nehemias hic præsignificatur. ET IN MANU EJUS FVNICVLVS MENSO- RVM) Ad designationem faciendam urbis regionumque ejus, ut ab architectis fieri solet. Nehem. II. 13. 14, 15. 20. III. & sequentibus. Confer. Ezech. XL. Apocal. XI. 1.

## 2:3
Ver. 3.

THE ANGEL WHO SPOKE IN ME) Who had spoken to me: concerning whom in the preceding chapter, verse 9, 14. WAS GOING FORTH) As if, the mandate having been performed, he was departing from me. AND ANOTHER ANGEL WAS GOING FORTH TO MEET HIM) Namely, bringing new mandates to Gabriel from the sanctuary.

The angel, or the man with the measuring line, is that same angel who is said to have spoken in Zechariah v. 3, where the emphatic ה is held. He is said, however, to have gone forth from the myrtle grove, as the Belgians note. Some suppose that that going forth signifies the going forth of Christ into the world, which he openly promises in v. 10. But the other angel, having gone forth to meet him, was not reporting, but receiving from him the mandate, which namely he ought to say to Zechariah, namely one of the created angels, who were following behind that man seen among the myrtles now with the measuring line, the angel speaking in Zechariah, the Son of God. Osiander's paraphrase is correct here, with which the Vinarians and the Belgians also agree: And I lifted up my eyes (says the Prophet) and I saw and behold a man, and in his hand was a measuring line, such as those who build are accustomed to use, so that they may measure the length and breadth of some place: for in olden times they used ropes more than reeds (but that man seen by the Prophet was the Son of God, appearing in the form of a man) And I said: Where are you going? And he said to me: I am going to measure Jerusalem, and to see how great its breadth is, and how great its length: i.e., I shall establish the boundaries of its length and breadth. (For the Lord knows and determines how far and wide the Church of God is to be propagated) And behold that angel, who was speaking in me, or more correctly with me, was going out (he was proceeding with his measuring line, with which he had begun:) and another Angel (a minister of this Son of God) was going out to meet him, awaiting his commands, so that he might execute them. And the Son of God said to him, run, hasten, speak, etc. Blessed Winckelman, Blessed Balduinus, Blessed Himmelius, and others also acknowledge that that man having the measuring line is the Son of God. Cornelius à Lapide also acknowledges that he is the same one who was seen among the myrtle trees, although he hallucinates in this, that he thinks the angel speaking in Zechariah is different from him. Indeed, he believes that three created angels met here: Michael the measurer, the angel who was the guardian of Zechariah, and Gabriel coming to meet him. For from a comparison of chapter I, it is clear that the angel speaking in Zechariah was the very man who stood among the myrtle trees, and is now seen going out from there with a measuring line. To meet him came an angel minister (whoever that may have been, for Scripture does not determine that it was Gabriel), and at his command he spoke to Zechariah.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ANGELVS QVI LOQVEBATVR IN ME) Qui mihi locutus fuerat: de quo in capite præcedente com- mate 9. 14. EGREDIEBATVR) Quasi peracto mandato à me abibat. ET ANGELVS ALIUS EGREDIEBATUR IN OCCURSUM EJUS) Nova scilicet mandata Gabrieli de adyto referens.

Angelus, vel vir cum funiculo mensorio idem ille angelus est, qui loquutus in Zacharia di- citur v. 3. ubi ה emphaticum habetur. Egressus au- tem dicitur è myrteto, ut Belgici notant. Egressum illum significare egressum Christi in mundum, quem aperte v. 10. pollicetur, nonnulli autumant. Alter vero angelus in occursum ejus egressus, non refere- bat, sed accipiebat ab ipso mandatum, quod nem- pe ad Zachariam dicere deberet, unus nempe è creatis angelis, qui pone sequebantur virum illum inter myrtos nunc cum funiculo mensorio visum, angelum in Zacharia loquentem, Filium Dei. Re- cte se hic habet Osiandri paraphrasis, cui etiam Vi- narienses & Belge consentiunt : Et levavi oculos meos (inquit Propheta)& vidi & ecce vir,& in ma- nu ejus erat funiculus mensorias, cujusmodi funicu- lis uti solent, qui ædificant, ut longitudinem & la- titudinem alicujus loci metiantur:olim enim funi- bus magis, quam arundinibus utebantur ( vir au- tem ille à Propheta conspectus, Filius Dei fuit, in forma viri apparens ) Et dixi : Quo tu vadis? Et di- xit ad me : vado ut metiar Jerusalem, & videam, quanta sit latitudo ejus,& quanta longitudo ejus: i. e. terminos longitudinis & latitudinis ejus constituam. (Dominus enim novit & decernit, quam longe la- teque Ecclesia Dei sit propaganda) Et ecce angelus ille, qui loquebatur in me, rectius mecum, egredie- batur ( pergebat cum suo funiculo mensorio, quo cœperat: ) & Angelus alius (hujus filii Dei mini- ster) egrediebatur in occursum ejus, exspectans ipsius jussa, ut ea exequeretur. Et dixit ad eum filius Dei, curre, festina, loquere &c. Virum illum habentem funiculum mensorium, Filium Dei esse agnoscunt etiam B. Winckelm. B. Balduinus, B. Himmelius, & alii. Eundem esse, qui inter myrtos visus, agno- scit etiam Cornel. à Lapide, etsi in eo hallucinatur, quod angelum in Zacharia loquentem diversum ab eo putet. imo tres angelos creatos hic convenisse credat, Michaelem mensorem, angelum Zachariæ custodem, & Gabrielem in ejus occursum venien- tem. E collatione enim cap. I. liquet angelum lo- quentem in Zacharia, ipsum virum fuisse, qui con- stitit inter myrtos, & nunc egressus inde cum fu- niculo mensorio conspicitur. Huic in occursum angelus minister ( quisquis ille fuerit, non enim determinat Scriptura Gabrielem fuisse,) venit, & ad ejus mandatum allocutus Zachariam est.

## 2:4
Vers. 4.

SPEAK TO THIS BOY) Young man. For thus נער is taken, and thus the Chaldean translates it in this place. Thus also the LXX, περὶ νεανίαν ἐκεῖνον, namely Zechariah, who as a young man began to be inspired by God.

This name is also accustomed to be of ministry Gen. XXIV. 52. Exod. XXXIII. 11. Num. XI. 27. I. Reg. XI. 28. II. Reg. IV. 12. c. XIX. 6. 11. Luc. I. 54. 60. Act. IV. For Zechariah was a minister not of an angel, as Cornelius wishes, but of God.

JERUSALEM SHALL BE INHABITED WITHOUT A WALL) It shall be inhabited like villages: that is, very many Jerusalemites, because they and their affairs cannot be contained by the circuit of the city, will disperse themselves through the nearby villages.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

LOQUERE AD PUERUM ISTUM ) Juvenem. Sic enim נער sumitur, atque sic vertit hoc loco Chal- dæus. Sic & LXX. περὶ νεανίαν ἐκεῖνον, nempe Zachariam, qui juvenis adhuc à Deo cœpit afflari.

Solet etiam hoc nomen esse ministerii Gen. XXIV. 52. Exod. XXXIII. 11. Num. XI. 27. I. Reg. XI. 28. II. Reg. IV. 12. c. XIX. 6. 11. Luc. I. 54. 60. Act. IV. Erat enim Zacharias minister non angeli, ut Corne- lius vult, sed Dei.

ABSQUE MURO HABITABITUR JERUSA- LEM) Vicatim habitabitur: id est, plurimi Hierosolymitæ, quod ipsi, resque eorum urbis ambitu teneri non possint, per proximos vicos se dispergent.

## 2:5
Vers. 5.

AND I WILL BE TO IT, SAYS THE LORD, A WALL OF FIRE ROUND ABOUT) To those living outside the city I will be an invincible protection. Compare II. Reg. VI. 17.

AND IN GLORY I WILL BE IN THE MIDST OF IT) That is, they will sing praises and thanks to me.

Without a wall, in Hebrew is פרזות villages, Jerusalem shall be inhabited, that is, it shall be inhabited like villages on account of the multitude of men and animals in its midst. Whence it is manifest that these things cannot be understood of the earthly Jerusalem, which was surrounded by a wall before it was devastated by the Romans, indeed it was most fortified, as Josephus testifies in book I against Apion. Nor indeed is the length and breadth of that city so great that it could not be surrounded by a wall, on account of the multitude of men, just as it is established that Babylon and Nineveh, most ample cities, were surrounded by walls. Wherefore it is necessary that we understand these things of the spiritual Jerusalem, of the Church, which was to be diffused into the whole world, and thus would be like very many villages, around which it would not be possible for a wall to be drawn. Furthermore, God promises that He will be a wall of fire, a wall around it: which was fulfilled not so much in the earthly Jerusalem as in the spiritual; for God allowed the former to be destroyed at length, and totally laid waste. Thirdly, He promises that He will demonstrate His glory in the midst of it, which was done in Jerusalem when they saw the glory of the only-begotten from the Father, John 1:14, and in the Church, because it was propagated from there throughout the Christian world, it is done through the glorious preservation of the faithful: because, sitting at the right hand of God, He is present to the Church all the days even to the consummation of the age, Matthew 28:20, and He rules, defends, and protects the same, and indeed miraculously, so that the majesty of the Son of God shines forth no less in governing and protecting the Church than if He were performing such miracles as He once performed in Judea and Jerusalem. Therefore, the observation of Blessed Luther, which he delivered in the preface to Habakkuk, has a place here: in Habakkuk: Whatever was done among the Jewish people after the Babylonian captivity was nothing other than an expedited and, as it were, extemporaneous preparation for the coming of Christ: the land was being restored in some way, the people previously dispersed were being gathered, so that there might be those among whom Christ would begin His kingdom by teaching. Whence it happened that the Prophets, especially the later ones, join that earthly and mystical Jerusalem, the Throne of David, and of Christ: to signify that Christ was about to come while the city and temple were still standing, and because the throne of David was already beginning to totter, therefore He whom the Lord had once promised to David as his eternal successor was at the door, 2 Samuel 7:12, Psalm 89:29. Thus our Zechariah, in the middle of the course of his discourse, changes as it were the manner of speaking, and when he was exhorting the people to the restoration of the city, he immediately transfers the type to the antitype, by sprinkling in the sweetest consolation concerning the restoration of the Church and the institution of the kingdom of Christ. For the Church of the New Testament is that which is inhabited without a wall; for the walls of the Church are the ends of the earth, according to that saying, in every place and in all creation which is under heaven, the Gospel concerning Christ is preached, Colossians 1:23, and Christ Himself rules from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth, Psalm 72:8. And in this Jerusalem, God Himself is a wall of fire, on account of that most ample defense which He provides for His Church on every side: He is also glorious, while He Himself is affected with honor and glory by His people, and while He renders His Church glorious, before all others on earth who do not call upon the name of the Lord, but are daily confounded by idolatry and the vanity of their own mind, as our Blessed Bald. rightly says here.

The argument of Grotius is too meager and jejune, even if Willius agrees with it, who renders it thus: the villages will inhabit Jerusalem, that is, they will inhabit the Jerusalemite villages, and having left the city, they will seek dwellings for themselves in them. The Belgian commentators are wiser, who, having recited that gloss of others, confess that the text must be understood concerning the kingdom of Christ and the propagation of the Church throughout the whole world, Isaiah 54:1, 2, 3, chapter 60:4, 11, Jeremiah 31:27. Nor indeed is there any reason why Grotius should conclude that this whole passage must be taken allegorically, contrary to the evidence of the text, because it speaks of the restoration of the old Jerusalem. For just as it is certain that the rebuilding was figured and promised here by the Prophet, so he did not persist in the same, but that he extends that restoration throughout the world is no less clear, because he promises an innumerable abundance of inhabitants, which could in no way be contained. Therefore Jerusalem had to stretch itself out and extend into the whole world, not by reason of external buildings, but of citizens who were to be gathered to it, such as not only Jews, but also Gentiles who were once alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, who, with the middle wall of partition broken down, had to become fellow citizens of the saints, Ephesians 2:12, 14, 19. For from Jerusalem went forth the Church, which was diffused throughout the world, and Jerusalem was extended and enlarged through the accession of the Gentiles. Cocceius acknowledges this sense here: By these things it is signified that they must be multiplied in the land of Israel, and diffused from it in innumerable colonies to every region of the world.

Nor indeed does God promise that He will be an invincible protection, or a wall of fire, only to those living outside the city, as Grotius perverts it, but to Jerusalem itself, which is to be inhabited without a wall, that it will have the Lord Himself as a wall: just as the Lord also promises that He will be the glory in the midst of it, which certainly must not be restricted only to those who live outside the city; nay, when He promises that He will be the glory in the MIDST OF THE CITY, it is manifest that villages outside the city are not indicated: but that the city will be like villages without a wall, fortified by the Lord, and that its glory will be illustrated. The sense is also too meager: I will be the glory in the midst of it, that is, they will sing praises and thanks to me. Cocceius explains it more fully: I will be glorified in it, and I will be its glory and sublimity, verse 3, we will make it glorious. And the Belgian Interpreters: I will affect and endow the citizens and inhabitants of this city with many and great benefits. Thus also Cyril, Theodoret, Haymo, Vatablus, Ribera, Sanctius, à Lapide, Tirinus, and others: I will glorify Jerusalem, and I will bring glory to it. Which very truly square with the Church of Christ, whose highest glory is Christ in the midst of it, as Tirinus says from Jerome, Haymo, Albert, and Remigius. To which also pertains the glory of miracles and of miraculous preservation, as we observed before. Although mention is made not only of men but also of beasts, that is nevertheless to be understood according to the prophetic style and custom. For the Prophets are accustomed to shadow forth the spiritual things of the New Testament by phrases taken from material things and bodily benefits to the ancient people. Such a phrase also occurs in Jer. XXXI. 27: There is therefore no need that, on account of the mention of beasts of burden, we should dismiss the sense concerning the Church: or that we should understand by beasts of burden men weak in faith, although this explanation of the blessed Luther and Winckelmann does not deserve to be censured by Willius; for nothing else is denoted by that phrase, Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls, for the multitude of men and beasts of burden in the midst of it, than that the magnitude of the Church and the multitude of inhabitants will be so great that it can neither be surrounded by walls, nor can any city surrounded by walls contain that multitude. Osiander rightly says: These things are to be understood concerning the Church of GOD, for it is spread much more widely in the world than to be able to be contained by any one city (even if that were much larger than Babylon). But if, someone will say, it is so widely scattered that it cannot be surrounded by a wall, how will it be safe from the assault of enemies? Hear: And I will be to it, says the Lord (Jehovah the Son of GOD), a wall of fire round about it, I will ward off enemies from it, and I will protect it, just as I protected the prophet Elisha in the town of Dothan: AND I WILL BE FOR GLORY IN THE MIDST OF IT

OF HIM, that is, I will demonstrate my glory and majesty in that city, says the Son of God. The Rabbis also explain this concerning the days of the Messiah: especially R. Rachmon on Jer. 31:27. The Chaldean version also sounds concerning the Messiah in v. 5, my word shall be to it, says the Lord, like a wall of fire surrounding it on every side.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ET EGO EI ERO, AIT DOMINUS, MURUS IGNIS IN CIRCUITV ) Illis extra urbem habitantibus ero præsidium invictum. Confer. II. Reg. VI. 17.

ET IN GLORIA ERO IN MEDIO EJUS) Id est, illi laudes mihi gratiasque decantabunt.

Absque muro, in Ebræo est פרזות villæ, habitabi- tur Jerusalem, id est, sicut villæ habitabitur præ mul- titudine hominum, & animalium in medio ejus. Un- de manifestum est, intelligi hæc non posse de Hie- rosolyma terrena, quæ muro cincta fuit, antequam vastata est à Romanis, imo munitissima erat, teste Josepho libr. I. contr. Appion. Neque vero illius urbis tanta est longitudo, & latitudo, ut muro cir- cumdari non possit, præ multitudine hominum, sicut constat Babylonem, & Ninivem amplissimas urbes mœnibus cinctas fuisse. Quapropter neces- sum est, de spirituali Hierosolyma hæc intelliga- mus, de Ecclesia, quæ in universum mundum erat diffundenda, adeoque futura instar plurimarum villarum, circa quas murum duci haut esset possi- bile. Porro promittit Deus, se futurum murum igneum, murum in circuitu ejus: quod non tam in terrena Hierosolyma, quam in spirituali im- pletum est; illam enim tandem Deus destrui, & totaliter desolari passus est. Tertio promittit se in medio ejus gloriam suam demonstraturum, quod in Hierosolyma factum, cum gloriam unigeniti à Patre viderunt Joh. I. 14. & in Ecclesia, quia in- de propagata est per orbem Christianum, sit per gloriosam fidelium conservationem: quia ad dextram Dei sedens adest Ecclesiae, omnibus die- bus usque ad consummationem seculi Matth. XXIX. 20. eandemque regit, defendit, ac tuetur, & quidem mirabiliter, ut non minus majestas Fi- lii Dei in gubernanda, & protegenda Ecclesia eluceat, quam si talia miracula, quae olim in Ju- daea, & Jerusalem, ederet. Locum ergo hic ha- bet B. Lutheri observatio, quam in prooem. in Habac. tradidit: Quicquid in populo Judaico post captivitatem Babylonicam factum est, nihil aliud fuit, quam expedita, & velut extemporanea quae- dam praeparatio ad Christi adventum: terra quali- tercunque restaurabatur, populus antea disper- sus congregabatur, ut essent, inter quos do- cendo regnum suum inchoaret Christus. Unde factum, quod Prophetae, posteriores imprimis, conjungunt terrenam illam & mysticam Hierusa- lem, Thronum Davidis, & Christi: ut signifi- carent Christum venturum, stante adhuc urbe & templo, & quia thronus Davidis jamjam nu- tare incipiat, ideo prae foribus esse eum, quem Dominus olim Davidis successorem aeternum promiserat II. Sam. VII. vers. 12. Psal. LXXXIX. vers. 29. Sic Zacharias noster in medio cursu ser- monis mutat quasi genus loquendi, & cum ad re- staurationem urbis populum cohortaretur, sta- tim transfert typum ad antitypum, inspergendo suavissimam consolationem de restitutione Ec- clesiae, & institutione regni Christi. Ecclesia e- nim Nov. Testamenti est, quae habitatur abs- que muro; muri enim Ecclesiae sunt fines orbis ter- rarum, juxta illud, in omni loco & in universa creatura quae sub caelo est, praedicatur Evangelium de Christo, Coloss. I. vers. 23. & ipse Christus dominatur à mari usque ad mare, & à flumine us- que ad terminos orbis terrarum Psalm. LXXII. vers. 8. Et in hac Hierosolyma Deus ipse igneus murus est, propter amplissimam illam defensionem, quam Ecclesiae suae undiquaque praestat: glorio- sus etiam est, dum ipse à populo suo honore, & gloria adficitur, & dum Ecclesiam suam glo- riosam reddit, prae cunctis aliis in terra, qui no- men Domini non invocant, sed idololatria atque vanitate mentis suae quotidie confunduntur, uti hic recte B. Bald. noster.

Nimis exile & jejunum est commentum Gro- tii, etsi eo accedat Willius, qui ita reddit, pa- gos habitabunt Hierosolyma, id est, Hierosolymita- nos pagos habitabunt, & relicta urbe, in eis domi- cilia sibi quaerent. Rectius sapiunt Belgici commen- tatores, qui, recitata ista aliorum glossa, faten- tur, intelligendum textum esse de regno Christi, & propagatione Ecclesiae, per totum orbem Esa. LIV. 1. 2. 3. cap. LX. 4. 11. Jerem. XXXI. 27. Neque vero est, quod statuat Grotius, ideo totum hunc locum allegorice accipiendum esse, contra evidentiam textus, quia de veteris Hierosolymae restauratione lo- quitur. Nam uti certum est, à Propheta reaedifi- cationem figuratam & promissam hic esse, ita non perstitit in eadem, sed extendere illum restaura- tionem per orbem, non minus luculentum, quia innumerabilem copiam habitatorum promittit, quæ nullo modo concludi possit. Porrigere er- go se debebat Hierosolyma, & extendere in uni- versum mundum, non ratione externorum ædifi- ciorum, sed civium, qui aggregandi ad eam e- rant, quales non solum Judæi, sed & gentiles o- lim ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς πολιτείας τᾶ Ἰσραὴλ e- rant, qui rupto τῷ μεσοτείχῳ τᾶ Φραγμᾶ συμπο- λῖται τῶν ἁγίων fieri debuere Ephes. II. 12. 14. 19. Nam è Jerusalem prodiit Ecclesia, quæ per orbem diffusa est, & Jerusalem extensa ampliata est per gentium accessum. Quem sensum agnoscit hic Coccejus : Hisce significatur, quod in terra Israel de- beant multiplicari, & ex illa diffundi innumerabili- bus coloniis in omnem plagam mundi.

Nec vero tantum extra urbem habitantibus Deus promittit, se fore præsidium invictum, vel mu- rum igneum, ut Grotius pervertit, sed ipsi Hie- rosolymæ, quæ absque muro habitanda, mu- rum habitura ipsum Dominum : quemadmodum etiam in medio ejus se gloriam fore Dominus pol- licetur, quod certe restringendum non est tan- tum ad eos, qui extra urbem habitant, imo cum in MEDIO URBIS gloriam se fore promittit, manifestum est, non indigitari vicos extra ur- bem : sed urbem instar vicorum sine muro futuram, à Domino munitam, gloriamque ejus illustratum iri. Nimis etiam exilis sensus est : In gloria ero in medio ejus, id est, illi laudes mihi, gratiasque can- tabunt. Plenius explicat Coccejus : Ego glorifica- bor in illa, & ero ipsius gloria & sublimitas, vers. 3. faciemus eam gloriosam. Et Belgici Interpp. Ego ci- ves & inhabitatores hujus urbis multis & magnis be- neficiis afficiam, & donabo. Sic & Cyrillus, Theo- doret. Haymo, Vatabl. Ribera, Sanctius, à Lapide, Tirinus, alij : glorificabo Jerusalem, & gloriam ei afferam. Quæ in Christi Ecclesiam verissime qua- drant, cujus gloria summa est Christus in medio ejus, ut ex Hieronym. Haym. Alberto, & Remi- gio Tirinus. Quo etiam pertinet gloria miraculo- rum, & miraculosæ conservationis, ut antea ob- servavimus. Quamvis vero non hominum tan- tum, sed & bestiarum mentio fiat, id tamen sty- lo & more intelligendum prophetico. Solent e- nim Prophetæ res spirituales Nov. Testamenti phrasibus desumtis à rebus materialibus, & be- neficiis corporalibus veteri populo adumbrare. Qualis phrasis etiam Jer. XXXI. 27. occurrit : Non ergo opus est, ut ob jumentorum mentionem sensum de Ecclesia dimittamus : aut per jumen- ta homines infirmos in fide intelligamus, quam- vis hæc explicatio B. Lutheri & Winckelman- ni non mereatur à Willio sugillari; nihil enim aliud ista phrasi, absque muro habitabitur Jeru- salem, præ multitudine hominum & jumentorum in medio ejus, notatur, quam quod tanta futu- ra sit Ecclesiæ magnitudo, & habitatorum multitudo, ut nec muris cingi possit, nec ul- la civitas muris cincta istam multitudinem cape- re queat. Recte Osiander : Hæc de Ecclesia DEI sunt accipienda, ea enim multo latius in orbe diffusa est, quam ut una aliqua ur- be (etsi illa multo major esset Babylone) com- prehendi possit. Si vero, inquiet aliquis, tam late sparsa est, ut muro cingi nequeat, quo- modo ab insultu hostium tuta erit? audi: Et ego ero ei ait Dominus (Jehovah Filius DEI) mu- rus igneus in circuitu ejus, ego arcebo ab ea ho- stes, eamque protegam, sicut protexi Pro- phetam Elisæum in oppido Dothan : ET IN GLORIAM EJUS ERO IN MEDIO

EJUS, id est gloriam & majestatem meam in ea urbe demonstrabo, inquit Filius Dei. De die- bus etiam Messiæ hæc explicant Rabbini : impri- mis R. Rachmon in Jer. XXXI. 27. De Messia quoque Chaldaica versio sonat v. 5. verbum meum erit ei, dicit Dominus, velut murus igneus illam per circuitum ambiens.

## 2:6
Ver. 6.

O, O FLEE FROM THE LAND OF THE NORTH) If any of you still remain in Babylon: for not all had yet betaken themselves to Judea.

It is evident from the books of Ezra and Nehemiah that many, even after receiving the power from Cyrus to return to their own lands, were unwilling to return, either because they did not entirely trust Cyrus, or because they were unwilling to abandon the family property which had been sufficiently increased during these eighty years and more; these, as being too incredulous regarding their own affairs and not sufficiently confident, he exhorts: Flee from the land of the North, that is, from Assyria and Babylon.

FOR I HAVE SPREAD YOU ABROAD TO THE FOUR WINDS OF HEAVEN) I will spread you out; That is, I will give you very wide lands to possess.

Latin:

Verf. 6.

O, ô FUGITE DE TERRA AQVILONIS ) Si qui adhuc restatis in Babylone : nondum enim omnes in Judæam se contulerant.

Constat id ex libris Esdræ & Nehemiæ, multos, etiam post acceptam à Cyro ad sua redeundi pote- statem, redire noluisse, vel quia Cyro non omni- no fidebant, vel quia rem familiarem per hos o- ctuaginta annos, & quod excurrebat, satis auctam deferere nolebant, quos, ut nimis incredulos re- bus suis, non satis confidentes hortatur : Fugite de terra Aquilonis, hoc est ex Assyria & Baby- lone.

QVONIAM IN QUATUOR VENTOS COELI DISPERSI VOS) Expandam vos; Id est, latissimas terras vobis dabo possidendas.

## 2:7
Ver. 7.

O SION) O you citizens of Sion.

Others explain it thus: because through the Babylonian captivity you now possess no proper seat of habitation, but being dispersed into all corners of the world you are truly exiles, exposed to infinite dangers. Grotius's exposition, however, is not unsuitable. For פרשׂ properly, as Willius notes, is to spread, to extend, to draw out by spreading, so that it may be implied that God had determined to extend them as widely as the four parts of the world reach, on account of the abundance of inhabitants, which was fulfilled especially in the time of the New Testament. Whence the promise concerning the calling of the Gentiles is subjoined afterwards in verse 8 and following.

Latin:

Verf. 7.

O SION) O vos cives Sionis.

Alii ita explicant: quoniam per captivitatem Babylonicam jam nullam rectam sedem habitatio- nis obtinetis, sed in omnes mundi angulos dispersi vere estis exules, infinitis expositi periculis. Gro- tii tamen ἔκθεσις non inconveniens est.
