Nam פרשׂ proprie, ut notat Willius, est expandere, extendere, diducere expandendo, ut innuatur, Deum consti- tuisse ipsos tam late, quam quatuor mundi partes patent, ob copiam habitatorum extendere, quod imprimis N. T. tempore impletum. Unde sub- jungitur postmodum promissio de vocatione gen tium vers. 8. seqq.

## 2:8
Ver. 8.

FOR THUS SAYS THE LORD OF HOSTS; AFTER THE GLORY HE HAS SENT ME TO THE NATIONS WHICH PLUNDERED YOU) Because God commanded this for the reflection of His glory. That is, to Michael, that he might speak to the Prophet. Michael is called אחר כבד, because he is a certain ἀπαύγασμα (effulgence) of God, Dan. 10:5, and compare with Ezekiel 1:27, 28 and 8:2. Thus David desires to be made אחר כבוד by God, Psalm 73:24, that is, a certain effulgence of divine light through gifts and mighty works. Michael, the procurator of the Jews, received a mandate from God to severely punish those nations neighboring and hostile to the Jews.

This new and unheard-of Commentary, that Michael is called the ἀπαύγασμα (radiance) of the glory of God, which is certain concerning the true Michael, the Son of God, Heb. I. 3, who also appeared gloriously to Ezekiel and Daniel, but is nowhere attributed to a created angel. Nor does David desire to become the ἀπαύγασμα of the glory of God, Ps. LXXIII. 24. But he says אחר כבוד תקחני, which Grotius interpreted thus: and with honor you have received me, you have made me King: with this observation added: אחר is translated by σὺν in Ps. XLIX. 18, with that meaning of the word retained, it will be more correctly rendered in the future, with glory you will take me. Others explain it: To glory you will take me. Not Michael the created angel is said here to be sent to the nations, but the Son of God, who alone could testify; Behold I lift up my hand over them, of which later. The Interpreters agree on this. to which the reasoning of the accents also seems to be favorable: That אחר כבוד is not to be drawn back to the words: thus says the Lord of hosts, but to pertain to the following, he sent me. Nor is אחר a noun, but a preposition. It is certainly nowhere taken as a noun. They vary, however, in its explanation: B. Luther [gives] these words in three ways

he says that אחר כבוד can be taken 1. concerning the glory of the kings of the Persians, as if he were saying, the kingdom of the Persians must be overturned first, before the Messiah comes, fully as Paul [says] concerning the Antichrist, the Antichrist does not come until the Roman empire is removed from the midst, II Thess. II. 4. 2. concerning the glory of the Jewish people, who boasted of their carnal lineage, that they were the sons of Abraham, the dignity of the priesthood, the majesty of the empire, the wealth of riches, and similar prerogatives, by which they excelled all foreigners. He hints that this external splendor will cease before the Messiah is born: for his kingdom is not of this world, and the glory of the king's daughter is from within, Ps. XLV. 14. 3. concerning the glory of the Jewish kingdom. For with the scepter removed from Judah, Shiloh was to be sent, according to the prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob, Gen. XLIX. 10. B. Balduinus judges all these interpretations to be sufficiently elegant and to agree with the sense of the Prophet, yet he acknowledges the third, with Luther, as the best, provided it agrees with the prophecy of Jacob, the promises made to David, and the very event of things. Others understand by the glory of the Messiah, miracles and glory, because, namely, with these manifested, he is to propagate the kingdom to the nations. Coccejus explains post gloriam as τελικῶς (finally), for the sake of obtaining glory or the tenor of justice and vengeance, and thus he wishes אחר to be taken in Job XXXIX. The Belgians [translate] thus: after glory [is to be shown] over you, or to you, that is, after he decided to glorify you, through liberation from captivity, he sent me to the nations. To which also the opinion of Calvin tends, as is added by Willius, and Junius. More correctly, says Willius, Calvin understands these things concerning the begun propagation of glory, so that the sense may be, after glory, that is, after the glory has been begun, and its first principles initiated through the glorious liberation, I have now been sent against the nations: how do these things contribute to the confidence and support of souls? Junius translates, after the glory has been declared, in this sense: God commanded me that I should declare the glory to you, and then that I should turn myself against the nations with the fire of judgments, which is also good. In this sense, however, he does not acquiesce, but submits another double one: but perhaps it is better to take post (after) for ad (to), by a Hebrew phrase, which also has a place in the German dialect. After glory, therefore, will be the same as, he sent me for glory to be sought and returned. He has sent me after the glory, that I may bring the same to pass. Thus the sense would be: the Lord sent me against the nations, that I might reclaim from them your glory, opulence, and splendor, of which they despoiled you. From this, therefore, the Jews could gather: for whose sake the angel of God was sent to the nations, that he might reclaim their glory from them: it will by no means be fitting for them to wallow in luxury and sloth among the nations, but to hasten to the predetermined place of glory. We are those for whose sake God sends out his legate to the nations for the sake of reclaiming our glory. Therefore it will be our duty, having abandoned the Gentile seats and all torpor, to hasten to the participation of glory. But the simplest of all is to take these things concerning the glory, about which [he spoke] above in verse 5, so that the sense may be: that he was sent after the glory promised and seen by him. So he. Osiander [says] sufficiently conveniently afterwards he will send me gloriously: Because אחר is absolutely afterwards, and כבוד can be taken with the preposition ב understood, in glory or he will send me gloriously. Ludov. de Dieu renders: Finally (there will be) glory: Finally at some time Zion will emerge from its ignominy, and will be restored in glory, or afterwards there will be glory: Comparing Gen. XXX. 7.

But a greater doubt seems to arise, if the Son of God says these things, introducing the Father as speaking: These things says the Lord of hosts; how can the Father say that he is sent to the nations, since the Father is sent by no one. Which was the cause, as appears to Grotius, of the new version: that God had commanded Michael this, that he should say to the Prophet: The Lord of hosts sent me to the nations: so that, indeed, Michael is understood to be the one sent. But Willius here posits a hyperbaton, let him be seen. But there is no need for that: For these are the words of the Angel, who had been ordered to run to the Prophet, and to indicate to him all those things which are read from verse 4 in this chapter. Now this Angel was a created one, who therefore introduces Jehovah Zebaoth speaking, that is to say, that divine person from whom he was sent to the Prophet, in order to report and explain His mind and words to him, that is, the Son of God. This Angel, therefore, introduced the Son of God speaking in v. 5. And I, says the Lord of hosts, the Son of God, will be a wall of fire, etc. Likewise v. 6. Flee from the North, says the Lord (the Son of God). For I have scattered you to the four winds of the heavens, says the Lord (the Son of God). For, says the Lord Zebaoth (the Son of God), after glory He sent me (he, namely, to whom alone the mission is appropriate, as Cocceius rightly says) to the nations. All those things are plain, if only this has been observed, that here, as we have said, it is not the Son of God speaking and introducing the Father, God Zebaoth, but an Angel created by the Son of God, ordered to go to the Prophet and to explain these things in his own name, introducing the very Son of God, Jehovah Zebaoth, speaking about his own mission to the nations, which was not observed by the interpreters. Whence that difficulty arose for Grotius, Willius, and others. Calvin himself also acknowledges that Christ is said here to be sent to the nations; nay, he says that this passage is violently twisted unless it is understood of Christ.

FOR HE WHO TOUCHED YOU, TOUCHES THE APPLE OF MY EYE) In the Hebrew עינו: that is, his eye, the Greeks τῆ ὀφθαλμῦ ἀυτῶ. For Michael speaks by God's command. See Deut. XXXII. 10. Ps. XVII. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

QVIA HÆC DICIT DOMINVS EXERCI- TVVM; POST GLORIAM MISIT ME AD GEN- TES QVÆ SPOLIAVERUNT VOS) Quia hoc præcepit Deus repercussioni gloriæ suæ. Id est, Michaeli, ut ille dice- ret Prophetæ. Michael vocatur אחר כבד, quia est ἀπαύγασμα quoddam Dei, Dan. X. 5. & confer cum E- zechiel I. 27. 28. & VIII. 2. Sic David optat à Deo fieri אחר כבוד Psal. LXXIII. 24. id est, effulgentia quædam lucis divinæ per dona ac virtutes. Michael Judæorum pro- curator mandatum à Deo accepit ad graviter puniendas illas gentes Judæis vicinas & infestas.

Novus hic & inauditus Commentarius, Mi- chaelem vocari ἀπαύγασμα gloriæ Dei, quod de vero Michaele Filio Dei certum est, Ebr. I. 3. qui etiam Ezechieli, ac Danieli visus est gloriose, nu- spiam autem angelo creato tribuitur. Neque Da- vid optat fieri ἀπαύγασμα gloriæ Dei Psal. LXXIII. 24. Sed אחר כבוד תקחני inquit, quod Grotius ita interpretatus est, & cum honore excepisti me, Feci- sti me Regem: addita hac observatione אחר per σὺν vertitur Pf. XLIX. 18. retenta ea fignificatione vocis, rectius in futuro reddetur, cum gloria affu- mes me. Alii exponunt: Ad gloriam affumet me. Non Michael angelus creatus ad gentes mittendus hic dicitur, sed Filius Dei, qui solus testari pote- rat ; Ecce ego levo manum meam super eos, de quo postea. Consentiunt in eo Interpp. quibus favere etiam videtur accentuū ratio: Illud אחר כבוד non retro trahendum ad verba: sic dicit Dominus exer- cituum, sed ad sequentia pertinere, misit me. Ne- que אחר esse nomen, sed præpositionem. Nuspiam certe id ut nomen accipitur. Variant autem in ejus explicatione: B. Lutherus tripliciter has voces

אחר כבוד accipi posse ait 1. de gloria regum Per- sarum, quasi dicat, evertendum prius est regnum Per- sarum, antequam veniat Messias, plene ut de Anti- Christo Paulus, non venit Antichristus, donec de medio fiat imperium Romanum II. Thessal. II. 4. 2. de gloria populi Judaici, qui superbiebat carnali prosapia, quod essent filii Abraham, dignitate sa- cerdotii, majestate imperii, divitiis opum, & si- milibus praerogativis, quibus exteros omnes ante- cellebant. Hunc externum splendorem desiturum innuit, antequam nascatur Messias : ejus enim re- gnum non est de hoc mundo, & gloria filiae regis ab intus Psal. XLV. 14. 3. de gloria regni Judaici. Sublato enim sceptro de Juda mittendus erat Siloh, juxta vaticinium Patriarchae Jacobi Gen. XLIX. 10. Omnes has interpretationes satis concinnas esse, & ad sensum Prophetae congruere censet B. Bal- duinus, tertiam tamen cum Luthero optimam a- gnoscit, siquidem cum vaticinio Jacobi, promis- sionibus Davidi factis & ipso rerum eventu con- gruat. Alii per gloriam Messiae miracula & gloriam intelligunt, quod nempe, ea manifestata, regnum ad gentes sit propagaturus. Coccejus post gloriam τελικῶς exponit, ad comparandam gloriam vel te- norem justitiae & ultionis, atque ita אחר accipi vult Job. XXXIX. Belgae ita: post gloriam super vos, vel vobis exhibendum) id est, postquam con- stituit vos glorificare, per liberationem e captivi- tate, misit me ad gentes. Quo etiam abit Calvini sententia, uti adjicitur a Willio, & Junii. Rectius, inquit Willius, Calvinus haec de cepta gloriae propa- gatione intelligit, ut sensus sit, post gloriam, id est, post inceptam gloriam, & prima ejus principia per gloriosam liberationem inita, missus jam sum con- tra gentes: quomodo haec ad fiduciam & sustenta- tionem animorum faciunt? Junius, post indictam gloriam, vertit, hoc sensu: Deus mihi imperavit, ut gloriam vobis indicem, & deinde me contra gentes igne judiciorum convertam, quod etiam bonum. In hoc tamen sensu non acquiefcit, sed alium geminum subjicit: sed forte melius est acci- pere post pro ad, phrasi Hebraea, quae & in Ger- manica locum habet dialecto. Post gloriam igi- tur idem erit, quod gloriam petendam & refe- rendam misit me. Er hat mich gesand nach der herrlichkeit, dass Ich dieselbe zu we- ge bringe. Ita sensus esset: misit me Dominus contra gentes, ut ab iis gloriam, opulentiam & splen- dorem vestrum repetam, quo vos spoliarunt. Hinc igitur colligere poterant Judaei: quorum causa an- gelus Dei missus ad gentes, ut eis inde gloriam ipsorum repetat : illos minime decebit inter gen- tes, luxuria & ignavia diffluere, sed ad praefini- tum gloriae locum properare. Nos illi sumus, quo- rum causa legatum suum ad gentes gloriae nostrae repetendae gratia Deus emittit. Ergo nostrum e- rit, missis sedibus gentilibus, & omni torpore, ad participationem gloriae festinare. Sed simpli- cissimum omnium est, accipere haec de gloria, de qua supra vers. 5. ut sensus sit: post gloriam promis- sam & sibi visam missum esse. Haec ille. Conve- nienter satis Osiander postea gloriose mittet me: Quia אחר absolute est postea, & כבוד accipi potest subintellecta praepositione ב in gloria vel gloriose mittet me. Ludov. de Dieu reddit: Tandem (erit) glo- ria: Tandem aliquando emerget Sion ex ignomi- nia sua, & in gloria restituetur, aut postea erit glo- ria: Conferens Gen. XXX. 7.

Dubium autem majus videtur, si haec Filius Dei dicat, Patrem introducens loquentem: Haec di cit Dominus exercituum; quomodo Pater inquiat, se missum esse ad gentes, cum Pater a nemine mitta- tur. Quæ causa fuit, ut apparet. Grotio, novæ ver- sionis: hoc præcepisse Michaeli Deum, ut ille di- ceret Prophetæ: Misit me Dominus ad gentes: ut nempe missus intelligatur Michael. Willius ve- ro hic ponit hyperbaton, qui videatur. Sed eo opus non est: Sunt enim hæc verba Angeli, qui jussus erat ad Prophetam currere, & illa omnia ipsi indicare, quæ à versu 4. hoc capite leguntur. An- gelus autem hic creatus erat, qui proinde loquen- tem introducit Jehovam Zebaoth, illam nempe per- sonam divinam,à qua mittebatur ad Prophetam, ut ejus mentem & verba ipsi referret, atque expone- ret, hoc est, Filium Dei. Hic ergo Angelus Filium Dei loquentem introduxit v. 5. Et ego, inquit Do- minus exercituum, Filius Dei, ero igneus murus &c. Item vers. 6. Fugite ab Aquilone, inquit Dominus (Filius Dei) Nam ego dispersi vos in quatuor ven- tos cæli, inquit Dominus (Filius Dei) Nam in- quit Dominus Zebaoth (Filius Dei) cum gloria misit me (ille sc. cui soli convenit missio, ut recte Coccejus) ad gentes. Illa omnia plana sunt, si tantum hoc observatum fuerit, quod hic, uti dixi- mus, loquatur non Filius Dei introducens Patrem Deum Zebaoth, sed Angelus creatus à Filio Dei ad Prophetam ire, atque hæc suo nomine expo- nere jussus, introducens ipsummet Filium Dei Je- hovam Zebaoth loquentem, de sua ad gentes mis- sione, quod ab inter pretibus non observa- tum. Unde Grotio, Willio, aliisque nata illa diffi- cultas. Christum hic missum dici ad gentes agnoscit etiam Calvinus ipse, imo violenter torqueri, ait, hunc locum, nisi de Christo intelligatur.

QVI ENIM TETIGIT VOS, TANGIT PVPIL- LAM OCULI MEI) In Hebræo עינו: id est, oculi ejus, Græci τῆ ὀφθαλμῦ ἀυτῶ. Nam Michael loquitur ex Dei præcepto. Vide Deut. XXXII. 10. Ps. XVII. 8.

## 2:9
Vers. 9.

BEHOLD I LIFT MY HAND OVER THEM) I will raise my hand against them, as those about to strike are accustomed to do. Job XXXI. 21.

AND THEY SHALL BE A SPOIL TO THOSE WHO SERVED THEM) That is, to the Jews, whom they had despised before them. This was fulfilled most of all through Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, I Macc. V. Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews XII. 11. 12. and through Hyrcanus. Jos. XIII. 17.

AND YOU SHALL KNOW THAT THE LORD OF HOSTS SENT ME) Michael.

Concerning the apple of their enemies' eyes, not a few interpreters explain it in this way: he who touches you, touches the apple of his own eye, i.e., he strikes and injures his own eyes; but it is more rightly referred to God the Father, to Him from whom the Son of God was sent to the nations, because Scripture is accustomed to describe things dear to God and under His protection in this way, Deut. XXXII. 11, Ps. XVII. 8; thus it also inculcates the religious keeping of the law, keep my teaching as the apple of your eyes, Prov. VII. 2, so that the sense may be: God sent me to the nations for your sake, because He bears the most studious care for you, and is tormented by your most exquisite evils, and he who labors to harm you does nothing else than presume to pierce God's eyes for himself.

But that that subject, by whom he professes himself to be sent, is not Michael or any other Angel, but Christ the Son of God, that indeed is most manifest from the words of the text. For he who testifies that he was sent is called Jehovah Zebaoth, the Lord of hosts, which can apply to no creature. Thus says Jehovah Zebaoth, after glory he sent me. We have, therefore, here Jehovah sent, we have Jehovah Zebaoth sending, v. 9, that you may know that Jehovah Zebaoth has sent me. Therefore, the Jehovah sent to the nations is none other than the Son of God, sent by God the Father, to whom the Father has given all judgment, John V. Then he confirms that truly divine work: For I, he said, will lift my hand against those nations, and they shall be a spoil to their servants. Which some interpret concerning the spiritual conversion of the nations, that the hand is to be shaken over them, not by exterior and corporal force, but by interior and spiritual, or by the grace of the word and Spirit, so that the nations shall be a spoil to their servants, i.e., to the Jews, whom they had pressed in miserable servitude, which they wish to have happened in that spiritual victory, where the nations from every nation which is under heaven were made a spoil by the preaching of the Gospel of the Jewish Apostles who were converting them. They observe that the sacrificial verb הניף is used, to shake, to lift, whence תנופה, elevation, Num. IIX. 13, for the cult of sacrifices of the N.T. also to be established among the nations. Nor can the words be understood of an external victory. Since it is nowhere read that the Jews were made masters of the Assyrians, or Chaldeans, or other Gentile enemies after the captivity was finished. And therefore it is to be accepted concerning spiritual spoil and victory, the fruit of conversion also being added: and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me, i.e., from such a wonderful increase of my kingdom, and the unhoped-for change of affairs, you will be able to conclude with certainty that I am he whom the eternal Father promised to you of old. Thus the blessed Balduinus. Similarly, Osiander almost: Behold I lift my hand over them, and they shall be a spoil to those who served them: i.e., you will receive the greatest benefits from those who previously dominated you, as if from your slaves. (This was fulfilled when the nations were converted to Christ in the greatest number, and helped the Church of Christ with their services and wealth. Of which matter many examples are found in the Acts of the Apostles and in Ecclesiastical history. For the nations, which had previously ruled proudly over the Jews, once the Jews were converted to Christ, offered all offices of charity and humanity (plainly as if they were their servants and prey) (And then you shall know, says Christ, that (because) the Lord of hosts has sent me: (For the admirable success of the preached Gospel teaches that Jesus of Nazareth is the eternal Son of God sent by God the Father into this world to liberate the human race. For how many myriades from the most powerful nations, by the mere preaching of the Gospel, have been subjected to Christ, the Son of God and man? Whom no human forces, no torments, however bitter, could turn away and recall from the faith of Christ.

Grotius does not understand this as a gracious lifting of the hand, but as the vengeance of God. Nor does this interpretation of the hand of grace please Mr. Willius; therefore, he wishes it to be about violent agitation and striking: and so he refers it to the times of the Maccabees, but since in those times the enemies did not yield to the Jews as prey, as is predicted here, Willius confesses that the full fulfillment cannot be found elsewhere than in the kingdom of Christ: and he says the truth was consummated in that, when the nations were converted to God with an easy and placid motion, and became like spiritual prey to the Gospel, and the Jews thus learned by experience and to their own detriment that God had spoken to them through the Son. Thus, therefore, he either establishes a double sense or, ἑκοντ᾽ ἀεκόντιγε θυμῷ, acknowledges that the discourse is only about spiritual prey. Lamb. Danæus, although he refers the fulfillment also to the kingdom of the Persians, the Antiochuses, and the Ptolemies, kings and enemies of the Church who were crushed, nevertheless confesses that it pertains most of all to the time when the Gospel of Christ was preached. Calvin approaches our explanation even more: He signifies that however many and robust enemies may spring forth to harm the Jews, they will nevertheless be safe, because they will be protected by the hand of GOD, and not only that, but whatever the enemies attempt will be in vain: because the Lord will ignominiously expose them as prey to the Jews themselves. For by servants he undoubtedly understands the Jews, who for a time had been burdened by the tyranny of their enemies. It is certain that this prophecy was by no means fulfilled at the time when the Jews thought they were flourishing and enjoying prosperous fortune: for then their condition was most miserable and shameful. not from the tribe of Judah. Furthermore, we know how tyrannically they ruled: moreover, that that kingdom was full of disgraces and tragic crimes. For they were almost all parricides, and whoever reads those histories will find now brothers cruelly oppressed by brothers, now parents themselves, and wickedly. Finally, to say nothing of the rest, nothing more detestable can be conceived than the house of Herod. We cannot, therefore, adapt this prophecy to the whole intermediate time which preceded the coming of Christ from the Babylonian exile. Therefore, under the kingdom of Christ, God finally brought it about that enemies yielded to the spiritual people as prey, namely, when they were subdued so that they might submit to the yoke of Christ. For, as we have said elsewhere, the sovereignty of the Church is in the head itself. Where, therefore, Christ is preeminent, then also the Church, which is his body, is said to obtain the Kingdom. For Christ wishes to have nothing separated from his members. Thus Danaeus. That is certainly beyond doubt, that that expression: I will shake my hand, whether you understand it to be done for the destruction or for the conversion of enemies, or the hand of punishing justice, 1 Kings 11:26, Job 31:21, or the hand of victorious grace, belongs not to an Angel, but to God alone, who can subject all things to himself αὐτοκρατορικῶς, Phil. 3:21.

Thirdly, that knowledge by which he says here that he will be known as sent by God is urged by Cocceius, because no one else is he than Christ. Since no Angel except Christ has been acknowledged. Willius himself acknowledged the force of the argument, explaining: The Jews will thus know that the Lord of hosts has sent him, namely Christ, that is, by experiencing it they will learn when they see these things, that in truth Christ the Θεάνθρωπος was the legate of the Father, and that he announced to them not his own opinions, but the truth and his commands.

Fourthly, especially to be observed here is the repetition in verse 8: Because the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. For the same words used there, which occur here, teach that it is the same person who predicts these things concerning his own knowledge and manifestation. But what other person is there who is said to be sent to Zion, to dwell in the midst of it, except the Son of God sent by the Father? Of a created Angel, this can certainly in no way be understood. Grotius renders it 'and I will dwell in the midst of you,' I will have my temple there. Which is not of an Angel, but of the one God. Christ, however, calls the temple his temple, Mal. 3:1. Finally, that it is the Messiah who is said to be sent here, Zech. 2:8, the Jews themselves acknowledge in Bereschith Rabba, Gen. 25:28.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ECCE EGO LEVO MANUM MEAM SUPER EOS) Attollam manum meam contra eos, ut solent ver- beraturi. Job. XXXI. 21.

ET ERUNT PRÆDÆ HIS, QVI SERVIEBANT SIBI) Id est, Judæis, quos illi præ se contempserant. Im- pletum hoc maxime per Judam Maccabæum & fratres e- jus, I. Macc. V. Josephus antiquæ historiæ XII. 11. 12. & per Hyrcanum. Jos. XIII. 17.

ET COGNOSCETIS, QVIA DOMINUS EXER- CITVVM MISIT ME) Michaelem.

De pupilla hostium ipsorum non pauci interpre- tantur hoc modo: qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam ocu- li sui, h.e. suos ipsius ferit & vitiat oculos, sed rectius ad Deum Patrem refertur, ad illum, à quo missus est ad gentes Filius Dei, quia ita solet Scriptura res Deo caras, ejusdemque custodiam describere Deut. XXXII. 11. Ps. XVII. 8. ita etiam religiosam legis custodiam inculcat, observa doctrinam meam ut pupillam oculorum tuorum, Prov. VII. 2. ut sensus sit, Deus misit me ad gentes vestri causa, quia studiosfissimam vestri curam geris, & exquisitissi- mis vestris malis cruciatur, nec aliud quid agit, qui vos lædere laborat, quam ut Dei oculos sibi con- figere præsumat.

Quod autem suppositum illud, quo se missum profitetur, non Michael, aut ullus alius Angelus sit, sed Christus Filius Dei, id vero longe manife- stissimum est è verbis textus. Nam is, qui se missum esse testatur, vocatur Jehovab Zebaoth, Dominus exercituum, quod nulli creaturæ convenire potest. Sic dicit Jehovah Zebaoth, post gloriam misit me. Habemus ergo hic Jehovam missum, habemus mit- tentem Jehovam Zebaoth v. 9. ut sciatis, quod me miserit Jehovah Zebaoth. Misus itaque Jehovah ad gentes nullus alius est, quam Filius Dei, à Deo Pa- tre missus, cui Pater dedit omne judicium Joh. V. Deinde confirmat id opus vère divinum: Nam ego, ajebat, levabo manum meum contra gentes illas, & erunt prædæ servis suis. Quod nonnulli interpre- tantur de spirituali gentium conversione, quod agi- tanda super eos manus sit, non vi exteriori & cor- porali, sed interiori & spirituali, vel verbi & Spiri- tus gratia, ita ut gentes præda sint futuræ servis suis, h. e. Judæis, quos miseranda servitute presserant, quod in spirituali illa victoria contigisse volunt, ubi gentes ex omni natione, quæ sub cœlo est, Ju- dæorum Apostolorum prædicatione Evangelii i- psas convertentium præda factæ sunt. Observant illi adhiberi verbum sacrificiale הניף agitare, leva- re, unde תנופה elevatio Num. IIX. 13. ad sacrificio- rum cultum N. T. etiam inter gentes instauran- dum. Neq; de externa victoria verba intelligi pos- se. Siquidem nuspiam legatur Judæos Assyriorum, aut Chaldæorum, aut aliorum hostium gentilium factos fuisse Dominos finita captivitate. Ideoque de spirituali præda atque victoria accipienda esse, fructum etiam subjici conversionis: & cognoscetis, quod Dominus exercituum misit me, h. e. ex tam mi- rabili incremento regni mei, & insperata rerum vicissitudine certo colligere poteritis, me esse eum, quem Pater æternus antiquitus vobis pro- misit. Ita B. Balduinus. Similiter fere Osiander: Ecce ego levo manum meam super eos, & erunt præda his, qui serviebant sibi: i. e. qui prius vobis dominaban- tur, ex illis, tanquam ex mancipiis vestris, maxima commoda percipietis. (Hoc impletum est, cum gentes ad Christum conversæ sunt maximo nume- ro, atque officiis ac opibus suis Ecclesiam Christi juverunt. Cujus rei in Actis Apostolicis, & in hi- storia Ecclesiastica multa exempla reperiuntur. Gentes enim, quæ prius superbe Judæis impera- verant, conversis ad Christum Judæis omnia cha- ritatis & humanitatis officia (plane quasi ipsorum servi & præda essent, exhibuerunt (Et tunc cogno- scetis, inquit Christus, quia (pro quod) Dominus exercituum miserit me: (Admirandus enim succes- sus prædicati Evangelii docet, Jesum Nazarenum esse Filium Dei æternum à Deo Patre in hunc mundum missum, ad liberandum genus huma- num. Quot enim myriades ex gentibus potissimis, sola prædicatione Evangelii, Christo Filio Dei & hominis subjectæ sunt? quas nullæ vires humanæ, nulla quantumvis acerbissima tormenta à fide Christi avertere & revocare potuerunt.

Grotius non de gratiosa elevatione manus, sed de ultione Dei intelligit. Nec placet ista de manu gratiæ in- terpretatio D. Willio, de violenta itaque agitatio- ne & percussione agi vult: Ideoque ad Maccabæo- rum tempora refert, sed quum illis temporibus ho- stes Judæis in prædam non cesserint, ut hic prædi- citur, plenum complementum alibi, quam in regno Christi reperiri non posse, fatetur Willius: in eoque consummatam veritatem dicit, quando facili & pla- cido motu gentes ad Deum conversæ, & Evangelio prædæ instar spiritualis factæ, Judæique sic experien- do suoque damno didicerunt, Deum per Filium ipsis loquutum. Sic ergo aut statuit geminum sensum aut ἑκοντ᾽ ἀεκόντιγε θυμῷ agnoscit de præda spi- rituali sermonem solum esse. Lamb. Danæus, etsi complementum etiam ad regnum Persarum, Antio- chos & Ptolomæos Reges, hostes Ecclesiæ, qui pes- fundati sunt, referat, maxime tamen ad tempus, quo Evangelium Christi prædicatum, pertinere fatetur. Magis adhuc nostræ explicationi ac- cedit Calvinus: Significat, quamlibet multi & robusti hostes prosiliant ad nocendum Judæis, tamen fore incolumes, quia protegentur manu DEI, neque id solum, sed quicquid tentent hostes, fo- re irritum: quia Dominus ignominiose eos in prædam exponet ipsis Judæis. Nam per servos intelli- git haud dubie Judæos, qui ad tempus gravati fue- rant tyrannide hostium suorum. Certum est, hoc vaticinium minime fuisse completum, quo tem- pore putarunt Judæi se florere, & uti prospera for- tuna: nam tunc miserrima fuit, & pudenda eorum conditio. Unde enim illis Reges? Certe non ex tribu Jehuda. Deinde scimus, quam tyrannice do- minati fuerint: adhæc fuisse regnum illud plenum probris & tragicis sceleribus. Fuerunt enim fere omnes Parricidæ, & quisquis leget historias illas, reperiet nunc fratres à fratribus, nunc parentes ipsos fuisse crudeliter oppressos & nefarie. Deni- que ut de cæteris taceam, Herodis domo nihil de- testabilius excogitari potest. Non possumus ergo aptare hoc vaticinium ad totum intermedium tempus, quod præcessit Christi adventum ab exi- lio Babylonico. Ergo sub regno Christi hoc demum præstitit Deus, quod spirituali populo cesserunt hostes in prædam, ubi scilicet subacti sunt, ut subirent ju- gum Christi. Nam, quemadmodum alibi diximus, principatus Ecclesiæ est in capite ipso. Ubi ergo emi- net Christus, tunc etiam dicitur Ecclesia, quæ cor- pus ejus est, Regnum obtinere. Christus enim ni- hil vult separatum habere à suis membris. Hæc Danæus. Id utique extra dubium est, vocem il- lam: Ego agitabo manum meam, sive ad deletionem id fieri, sive ad conversionem hostium seu manum punitricis justitiæ, I. Reg. XI. 26. Job. XXXI. 21. seu manum gratiæ victricis intelligas, non Angelo, sed Dei solius esse, qui αὐτοκρατορικῶς sibi subjicere potest omnia Phil. III. 21.

Tertio cognitio illa, qua hic à Deo missus se co- gnitum iri dicit, urgetur à Coccejo, quod alius nul- lus ipse sit, quam Christus. Siquidem nullus An- gelus nisi Christus agnitus sit. Quam argumenti vim Willius ipse agnovit exponens: Iudæi ita co- gnoscent Dominum exercituum misisse ipsum, nempe Christum, id est experiundo discent ubi isthæc vide- rint, revera Christum Θεάνθρωπον legatum patris fuisse, & non suas opiniones, sed veritatem ejus- que mandata ipsis renunciasse.

Quarto imprimis hic observanda repetitio vers. 8. Quia Dominus exercituum miserit me ad te. Eadem enim verba ibi adhibita, quæ hic occurrunt, do- cent eandem personam esse, quæ de sui cognitio ne, ac manifestatione hæc prædicit. Quæ autem alia persona est, quæ missa ad Zionem dicitur, ha- bitatura in medio ejus, nisi Filius Dei à Patre mis- sus? De Angelo certe creato hoc nullo modo intel- ligi potest. Grotius reddit & habitabo in medio tui, templum meum ibi habebo. Quod non est Ange- li, sed unius Dei. Christus autem templum vocat suum templum Mal. III. 1. Denique Messiam esse, qui hic missus dicitur Zach. II. 8. agnoscunt ipsimet Iudæi in Bereschith Rabba Gen. XXV. 28.

Verse 10.

AND I WILL DWELL IN THE MIDST OF YOU) I will have my temple there.

Vers. 10.

ET HABITABO IN MEDIO TVI) Templum meum ibi habebo.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

AND MANY NATIONS SHALL BE JOINED TO THE LORD IN THAT DAY) Many will come from various places, so that, having abandoned idolatry, they may serve the one true God, in the court of the Gentiles, 1 Kings 8:41, nor is that surprising, since both Cyrus and Darius wished for prayers to be offered for them in the Temple. So also the Lacedaemonians. Alexander offered victims to God in the temple: Ptolemy Philadelphus did the same, Augustus also and Tiberius: very many Kings, just as Sossius also sent gifts there.

Vers. 11.

ET APPLICABVNTVR GENTES MULTÆ AD DOMINUM IN DIE ILLA) Multi venient variis ex locis, ut relicta idololatria, uni veroque Deo serviant, in atrio gentium, I. Regum VIII. 41. nec id mirum, cum & Cyrus & Darius in Templo pro se orari voluerint. Sic & Lacedæmonii. Alexander Deo in templo victimas obtu- lit: idem fecere Ptolemæus Philadelphus, Augustus quo- que & Tiberius: Reges plurimi, ut & Sossius dona eo misere.

## 2:12
Verse 12.

AND THE LORD SHALL POSSESS JUDAH AS HIS PORTION) As his portion: as his peculiar treasure: he will wish to be worshipped by him.

AND HE SHALL YET CHOOSE JERUSALEM) He will love, as of old, above 1:17.

t

This dwelling in the midst of the people and the application of many nations to one cannot be restricted to the dwelling in the Temple, which was being built, and to those few assemblies of those who, having abandoned idolatry after the temple was built, served their God from among the Gentiles, or wished for sacrifices to be offered only for themselves, or sent gifts there. Far more illustrious are those things which the Lord promises. But first, one must observe his κέλευσμα, by which they are stirred to joy, which intimates not a small or brief joy, but a great and perennial one, and is similar to that which is held in chapter IX, which we know from the Evangelical interpretation of Matthew XXI pertains to the New Testament: Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Zion. Furthermore, that this matter of rejoicing is assigned primarily, namely his advent, as one which they desired so greatly: with the σκηνώσει and dwelling among them, not so much that shadowy and typical one in the material temple (although we do not deny that the advent to this temple is comprehended at the same time) as that true one, of which St. John says in chapter I, 14: The Word was made flesh, καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν, and dwelt among us. For the Lord came to that, and dwelt in the midst. This happened to the Church not only ἐνεργητικῶς and ἀοράτως, but was done conspicuously and σωματικῶς in Christ, as Danaeus rightly says in this place. Concerning which dwelling the Chaldean translation itself interprets the oracle: Rejoice and be glad, O Church of Zion, because behold I will be revealed, and I will place שכינתי my divinity in the midst of you; and the explicit Midrash of the Canticles on Canticles I. 4, where these things are held: R. Abin explained this, which is written in Psalm CXIIX, v. 24, etc. This is the day which the Lord has made; we will exult and rejoice in it. R. Abin said, They did not know in what they should rejoice, whether in the Day or in the Lord, until Solomon came and said, We will exult and rejoice in you: in you, in God, and in you, in your salvation. But this is similar to a certain matron whose King, her husband, went, and her sons and sons-in-law to a maritime city. They came and said to her: Your sons have come; she says, What is that to me? Let my daughters-in-law rejoice. Again they said, Your sons-in-law have come; she says, What is that to me? Let my daughters rejoice. But when they said to her, The King your husband has come; she says, Behold, this is perfect and sufficient joy for me! Thus it was to be, that the Prophets would be coming and saying to Jerusalem (Isaiah LX, v. 4), Your sons will come from afar, and she herself said to them, What is that to me? Let the sons of Judah exult. Ps. 97, v. 8. And your daughters will be nourished upon the side, Isaiah 60, v. 4. She said to them, What is that to me? Psalm 48, v. 12. Let Mount Zion rejoice. But when they said in Zechariah 9, v. 9, Behold your King comes, and he is just, and saved: and it was written in Zechariah 2, v. 10, Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, because behold I am coming and will dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord, and many nations will be gathered to the Lord in that day, and they will be to me for a people, and I will dwell in the midst of you, and you will know, or recognize, that the Lord of Hosts has sent me to you: In that hour she was saying (Isaiah 61, v. 10), I will rejoice with joy in the Lord, I will exult in my God; and this is we will exult, we will rejoice in you. See Pugio Fidei, p. 512.

Thirdly, therefore, one must observe the notable prediction of the calling of the Gentiles, and MANY NATIONS will be applied to the Lord in that day. He speaks not of a small, but of a notable number of Gentiles, to be gathered in that day of the σκηνώσεως or dwelling in the midst of the people, that is, in the time of the New Testament, after the ἐνσάρκωσιν of the Son of God. For this is that Day of the advent of the Lord, greatly celebrated and sung of in the Scriptures: as is most well-known from the prophecies of the Old Testament, and as we have already perceived from the confession of the Rabbis themselves. Fourthly, since here Jehovah speaks, sent by Jehovah, namely the Son of God, and testifies: AND THEY WILL BE TO ME (the nations) FOR A PEOPLE, it cannot be doubted that the times of the New Testament

to be regarded, and the coming of the Son of God into the world. For then the distinction between the nations and the Jews was taken away, and they began to be A PEOPLE, who before were NOT A PEOPLE Hos. II. and those who were strangers to the Jewish polity were added to the people of the Jews Eph. II. 14. seqq. Which furthermore is also designated (that we may observe this fifthly) when to them equally, to whom the Son of God was to come, and who were to be applied to the Lord, it is promised as to one people constituting one communion: AND I WILL DWELL IN THE MIDST OF THEE. For one communion, the middle wall of partition having been broken down, was made from Jews and Gentiles, and in the midst of this one communion the Lord dwells even until the consummation of the age, as He received Matth. XXVIII. 20. Therefore not without reason does He promise the dwelling twice. For first, through His coming into this world, He promises that He will dwell in the midst of the people of Zion, the Jewish people, which was fulfilled Joh. I. 14. But then also in the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles, when these shall be converted to the Lord, He promises that He wishes to dwell, which will be fulfilled until the consummation of the age, and the glorious coming of Christ. Sixthly, He also promises a more abundant knowledge to the Church: And thou shalt know, that the Lord hath sent me unto thee. Which indeed in that day, the time of the N. T., is that they are not only to receive the completion of the prophecies, but also to know more fully that mystery of the mission of the Son of God for the liberation of the human race, and the gathering of the Gentiles to the Church. Which work of the calling of the Gentiles is of such dignity, that from it also they are to have knowledge, that He is Christ, whom the Lord had promised to send to His people: for to Him the Gentiles were bound to adhere Gen. XLIX. 10. Who from two most diverse peoples and those burning with absolute deadly hatred among themselves, could and ought to make one Church. Seventhly, the possession of Judah in the sanctified land is to be noted. For by the promise of this are confirmed those who are recalled from Babylon ver. 11. Whence they had already returned, not that they were to be aggregated to the Gentiles, but which is the chief glory of the Jewish people, that the Gentiles were to be called to the Jewish people, as the peculiar treasure and possession of the Lord, and indeed in the sanctified land, from which the law was to go forth, and the scepter of the Messiah to be sent through the whole world. Therefore it is added, and Judah shall be the portion of the Lord, and the Lord hath yet chosen Jerusalem, that they might be rendered more certain of this axiom. For they were formerly the peculiar treasure and possession of the Lord Exod. XIX. 5. Deut. IV. 20. c. VII. 6. c. IX. 29. XXIX. 2. c. XXXII. 9. Psal. LXXXVII. 1. Psal. CXLVII. 20. and Jerusalem was chosen for a dwelling place. To this peculiar treasure of the Lord and to that chosen city of the Lord, He promises that the Gentiles are to be gathered, and that the Lord in that very sanctified land will possess Judah, or the faithful from the Jews, as His portion: so that with this portion the gathered Gentiles may coalesce into one people. Tit. II. 14. I. Petr. II. 8. 9. Coccejus rightly here recognizes that there is promised (1) the manifestation in the flesh, the incarnate visitation (2) the calling of the Gentiles, who are to be joined to Israel Is. XIV. 27. Eph. III. 6. so that there may be one people, one God, one King, one Faith, one Spirit, one word, one shoulder to serve God. (3) perpetual dwelling with illumination. But that he places the sequestration of Judah into the portion of the Lord, after the liberation from the Anti-Christ, is from his own interpretation.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET POSSIDEBIT DOMINVS IUDAM PARTEM SUAM) Ut partem suam: ut peculium suum: ab eo coli volet.

ET ELIGET ADHUC IERUSALEM) Amabit, ut olim, supra I. 17.

t

Hæc habitatio in medio populi & applicatio gentium multarum ad unum non potest restringi ad habitationem in Templo, quod extruebatur, & paucorum illorum cœtum, qui relicta idolatria post ædificatum templum è gentibus Deo suo servierunt, aut solum pro se victimas offerri voluere, vel dona eo misere. Longe illustriora sunt, quæ promittit Dominus. Primum autem observandum κέλευσμα ejus, quo excitantur ad lætitiam, quod non exiguum aut breve gaudium, sed magnum atque perenne intimat, & simile est illi, quod habetur c. IX. quod ad N. T. pertinere ex Evangelica interpretatione Matth. XXI. novimus: Lauda & lætare filia Sion. Porro gaudendi materiam hanc imprimis assignari, adventum nempe suum, utpote quem tantopere desiderarunt: cum σκηνώσει & inhabitatione inter ipsos, non tam umbratili illa & typica in templo materiali, (quamvis non negemus adventum ad hoc templum simul comprehendi) quam vera illa, de qua S. Johannes c. I. 14. Verbum caro factum est, καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν, & habitavit in nobis. Eo enim Dominus venit, & habitavit in medio. Hoc non tantum ἐνεργητικῶς & ἀοράτως evenit Ecclesiæ, sed conspicue & σωματικῶς in Christo factum est, ut recte h. l. Danæus. De qua habitatione ipsa Chaldaica translatio interpretatur oraculum: Gaude & lætare Ecclesia Sion, quia ecce revelabor, & ponam שכינתי divinitatem meam in medio tui; & expressus Midrasch Canticorum in Cant. I. 4. ubi hæc habentur: R. Abin exposuit hoc, quod scriptum est Psal. CXIIX. v. 24. &c. Hic est dies, quem fecit Dominus, exultabimus & gaudebimus in eo. Dixit R. Abin, Nesciebant, in quo esset lætandum, utrum in Die vel in Domino, donec venit Salomoh, & dixit, Exultabimus & lætabimur in te: in te, in Deo, & in te, in salute tua. Simile est autem hoc matronæ cuidam, cujus Rex, maritus ejus, ivit, & filii & generi ejus ad civitatem maritimam. Venerunt & dixerunt ei: Venerunt filii tui, ait, quid ad me? lætentur nurus meæ. Rursus dixerunt, venerunt generi tui, ait, quid ad me? lætentur filiæ meæ. Quando vero dixerunt ei, venit Rex maritus tuus; ait, Ecce hæc est mihi perfecta & sufficiens lætitia! Sic futurum fuit, ut Prophetæ essent venientes, & dicentes ad Jerusalem (Esaiæ LX. v. 4.) Filii tui de longe venient, & ipsa dixit eis, quid ad me? Exultent filii Judæ. Ps. 97. v. 8. Et filiæ tuæ super latus nutrientur Esa. 60. v. 4. Dixit ipsis, quid ad me? Psal. 48. v. 12. Lætetur mons Sion. Cum vero dixerunt Zachariæ 9. v. 9. Ecce Rex tuus venit & justus, & salvatus: & scriptum fuit Zachar. 2. v. 10. Canta & lætare filia Sion, quia ecce ego veniens habitabo in medio tui, ait Dominus, & congregabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illo, & erunt mihi ad populum, & habitabo in medio tui, & scies, vel cognosces, quod Dominus Sabbaot misit ad te: In illa hora fuit ipsa dicens (Esaiæ 61. v. 10.) Gaudens gaudebo in Domino, exultabo in Deo meo; & hoc est exultabimus, lætabimur in te. Videatur pugio fidei p. 512.

Tertio itaque observanda est vocationis gentium insignis prædictio, & applicabuntur GENTES MULTÆ ad Dominum in die illa. Non de exiguo, sed insigni gentium numero loquitur, in die illa σκηνώσεως vel habitationis in medio populi aggreganda, h. e. Novi Testamenti tempore, post ἐνσάρκωσιν Filii Dei. Hic enim est ille Dies adventus Domini in Scripturis maximopere celebris & decantatus: uti è vaticiniis V. T. notissimum, & ex ipsorum Rabbinorum confessione jam percepimus. Quarto, quũ hic loquatur Iehovah à Iehovah missus, Filius nempe Dei, ac testetur: ET ERUNT MIHI (gentes) IN POPULUM, dubitari nequit, tempora N. T.

respici, & adventus Filii Dei in mundum. Tum enim sublatum fuit inter gentes & Judæos discri- men, & IN POPULUM esse cœperunt, qui prius erant NON POPULUS Hos. II. atque ad Ju- dæorum populum illi,qui peregrini fuere à politia Judaica, adjecti sunt Eph. II. 14. seqq. Quod porro etiam designatur (ut id quinto observemus) cum illis pariter, ad quos venturus erat Filius Dei, & qui applicandi erant ad Dominum, promittitur ceu populo uni constituenti unam communio- nem: ET HABITABO IN MEDIO TUI. Una enim communio, rupto pariete intergerino facta est ex Judæis & gentibus & in hujus unius communionis medio habitat jam usque ad con- summationem seculi Dominus, uti recepit Matth. XXIIX. 20. Non ergo præter rem duabus vicibus habitationem pollicetur. Primo enim per adven- tum suum in hunc mundum in medio Sionis populi Judaici se habitaturum promittit, quod impletum Joh. I. 14. Tum vero etiam in Ecclesia collecta è Iu- dæis & gentibus, quando hæ convertentur ad Do- minum, se habitare velle spondet, quod implebitur usque ad consummationem seculi, & adventum Christi gloriosum. Sexto promittit etiam cognitio- nem uberiorem Ecclesiæ: Et scies, quia miserit me Dominus ad te. Quod nempe in die ista, tempore N. T. est, non modo complementum vaticiniorum percepturi sint, sed plenius etiam cognituri myste- rium illud missionis Filii Dei ad liberationem ge- neris humani, & congregationem gentium ad Ec- clesiam. Quod opus vocationis gentium tantæ di- gnitatis est, ut ex eo etiam cognoscere habeant, Christum esse, quem populo suo mittere promise- rat Dominus: huic enim adhærere debebant gen- tes Gen. XLIX. 10. Qui ex duobus diversissimis po- pulis & capitali prorsus odio inter se flagrantibus, unam facere potuit ac debuit Ecclesiam. Septimo notanda est possessio Judæ in terra sanctificata. Hujus enim promissione confirmantur, qui è Babylone revocantur vers. 11. Unde jam redierant, non se ad gentes aggregatum iri, sed quæ præcipua gloria est populi Judaici, gentes vocandas esse ad populum Iu- daicum, ceu peculium & possessionem Domini, & quidem in terra sanctificata, ex qua lex debuit exi- re, & sceptrum Messiæ emitti per totum orbem. Ideo additur, & Judam partem fore Domini, & Je- rusalem adhuc elegisse Dominum, ut de hoc axio- mate certiores redderentur. Erant enim olim pe- culium & possessio Domini Exod. XIX. 5. Deut. IV. 20. c. VII. 6. c. IX. 29. XXIX. 2. c. XXXII. 9. Psal. XXCVII. 1. Psal. CXLVII. 20. & Jerusalem electa in habitaculum. Ad hoc peculium Domini & ad illam electam civitatem Domini collectum iri gentes pro- mittit, Dominumque in ipsa terra sanctificata Ju- dam, vel fideles è Judæis possessurum ceu partem suam: ut cum hac portione gentes aggregatæ in u- num populum coalescant. Tit. II. 14. I. Petr. II. 8. 9. Coccejus recte hic agnoscit promitti (1) τὴν ἐπι- φάνειαν ἐν σαρκὶ τὴν ἔνσαρκον ἐπιδημίαν (2) voca- tionem gentium, quæ conjungendæ Israeli Es. XIV. 27. Eph. III. 6. ut unus sit populus, Deus unus, Rex unus, Fides una Spiritus unus, verbum unum, hu- merus unus ad serviendum Deo. (3) perpetuam habitationem cum illuminatione. Quod autem Judæ sequestrationem in partem Domini ponit, post liberationem ab Anti-Christo, ἐξ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως est.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. LET ALL FLESH BE SILENT BEFORE THE FACE OF THE LORD) Let them fear: for silence is wont to accompany fear. FOR HE HATH RISEN UP OUT OF HIS HOLY HABITATION) As if He will come forth from the temple, about to take vengeance upon the hostile nations.

It is not fear that is struck into the nations from divine vengeance, but silence is imposed upon the daughter of Zion on account of the coming of the Lord σωτήριον. The Angel herald had bidden her to exult, by the voice of the Lord which he was reporting, because the day of the advent was imminent. More correctly, therefore, do our people say: The Son of God girds Himself to come to liberate the human race and to gather the nations to the Jewish people. Let all flesh, therefore, be silent throughout the whole world, because the Savior of the whole world is coming. B. Balduinus notes here a peculiar benefit, the just repression of enemies. For if any shall have progressed to such a degree of audacity and madness, as to dare to kick against the pricks of so powerful a Lord, and either to impede the restoration of divine worship in Judea, or the return of the Jews to their fatherland, or even at length sometime the gathering of the Church from Jews and Gentiles alike, the Son of God Himself here imposes silence upon them, and exhorts that they desist from these attempts, and indeed on a double account: partly because they themselves are flesh, i.e., fragile, and weaker than any hay: for all flesh is hay Isa. XL. v. 6. But He to whom they resist is Jehovah, the Lord of hosts, from whose face the heaven trembles, and all the earth becomes silent: for all nations are as if they were not, so are they before God, and they are reputed by Him as nothing, and vanity Is. 40. 17. partly also, because now the time is imminent, that the Son of God Himself, who set His tabernacle in the Sun, should go forth as a bridegroom from His chamber, as Psal. XIX. 6. speaks, about to assume flesh, and to inaugurate the Church of the N. T., about to redeem it also with His blood Acts XX. And thus to show to His people, that not even all the gates of hell would prevail in the least against His Church. Others wish the preceding promises to be sealed by this epiphonema. Namely, lest the Jews think that those things are impossible, when they have so many enemies opposed to them, and so many impediments that occur, the Prophet shows that silence is to be imposed by God upon all these things Psal. II. 2. and VII. 2. and LXV. 1. That God is now awakened from his sanctuary, in which he seemed to have slept, as long as he allowed his own to be afflicted Ps. XLIV. 12. 23. Ps. LXXIV. 3. Ps. LXXIIX. 60. 65. Thus Lambert Daneau, referring the name of sanctuary to the temple, so that the Jews might understand that they have equal testimonies of God's favor, presence, and protection, which their fathers once had; for they used to say that God met them from the Sanctuary, that is, the Temple, Ps. XX. 1. 1 Kings VIII, when they signified that God was benevolent toward them. Willius similarly: Do not object to me the machinations of the enemies: they will not even dare to mutter, he implies that God, whereas he had previously lain hidden as if given to sleep, has now arisen, and from the temple, as if from his armory, is in readiness to terrify and restrain the enemies. The enemies will therefore be silent, because God is present in the temple, and will oppose them from the temple. But the Prophet, or the Angel speaking through the Prophet, wishes ALL FLESH to be silent, not just the enemies: Jews and Gentiles, whose mention has been made, to be silent, not only because of the certainty of the event, however much all things may seem arduous and difficult, and the certain confusion of the enemies, who will be reduced to silence, but especially because of the magnitude of the matter, and the religious veneration and admiration of the mystery. For it is confessedly a great mystery, that God was manifested in the flesh 1 Tim. III. 16. Which even the Angels are stunned by and admire 1 Pet. I. 11. Much more every man, who is nothing but flesh. For by the voice of all flesh all mortals are indicated. A parallel passage is Is. XL. 6. 9. The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and ALL FLESH shall see together (with admiration) that the mouth of the Lord has spoken, show yourself upon a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion: Say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God is present. Nor indeed are these things opposites, to be silent and to exult, as

Willius thinks that the allegorical interpretation concerning the giving of silence to the Gospel (he calls it so, but without reason. For why is this more allegorical than that concerning the enemies being reduced to silence) pleases him little, because where there is talk of the coming of Christ, it is customary for not silence, but joy, exultations, and jubilation to be commanded to Zion, Ps. 96, 97, 98, 99, 100. But these, I say, are subordinate or secondary, not contradictory or contrary: for it is necessary for the faithful both to venerate those mysteries with religious silence and to burst forth into proclamations of praise. The sublimity of the matter demands admiration and veneration, because we are obliged to restrain reason under the obedience of faith, to be as it were stunned at the magnitude of such a great mystery, and to venerate it with holy silence: yet joy and exultation are not inhibited on that account, but rather the faithful rejoice in the Lord with their heart, and with a joyful and exultant mouth celebrate such great grace, which they can never admire enough. Thus Ps. 65:1, 'Silence is praise to Thee, O God, in Zion,' because God himself seeks silence instead of all praise. Iob. de Reyroles in his Commentary on this passage also brings in here the custom of the Gentiles, about which Plutarch writes in the Life of Coriolanus: Numa seems to have instituted this for the Romans as the highest ornament of religion, so that when Princes and Priests perform a divine rite, a herald preceding with a huge voice cries: 'Hoc age' [Do this], commanding them, that is, to fix their minds on the sacrifice. By the Sanctuary, heaven is sometimes understood, or from 2. Chron. 8:21, as Willius himself admits, it is certain, and Willius did not doubt that this passage concerns the coming of the Lord, rendering this sense of the previous promises on p. 75: 'I myself, who was promised to the fathers and to you on that day, and at the appointed time of the New Testament, will present myself in the flesh; nay, then I will take not only you Jews, but the very Gentiles with you into the covenant, and by familiar conversation, works, and miracles I will demonstrate myself to be the true Messiah, and, with me thus as mediator, the Father will have a Church for himself from you and the Gentiles.' Finally, Cocceius admits that the words, 'Let all flesh be silent,' were spoken because of the preparation for the coming of the Lord, although he wishes them to be able to be understood also in the consideration of the last time. But that is foreign: because it is not the second coming of the Messiah that is treated here, but the first. Menochius rightly says: 'LET BE SILENT: Let him worship Him reverently and holily, and be subject to Him. ALL FLESH: The whole human race. HE HAS RISEN FROM HIS HOLY HABITATION.' Because, as if rising from heaven, His holy habitation, He brought us help, which is most true through the assumed flesh and through the work of our redemption, which He consummated on the cross. Furthermore, because the Prophetic command of verse 10 of this chapter was illustrated in the Birthday Program of the year 1658, it is pleasing to add these things to it: 'Praise and rejoice, O Daughter of Zion; for behold I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee, says the Lord.' Thus the Feast, which we now celebrate, He once intimated through Zechariah 2:10: Jehovah the Lord, as a feast of exultation and eternal joy, a feast of divine visitation and presence, a feast of the incarnation and hypostatic union. Thus that great Evangelist deigned both to exhibit the fruit of His coming and to present Himself as that COMING ONE, and to describe the manner of His coming; so that, namely, he might refresh the faithful of that age with the most joyful news of the coming, and excite them to solemn joy. Praise and rejoice, O Daughter of Zion! In the voice of jubilation and joy, the whole fruit of the Lord's nativity is comprehended. For what will eternal blessedness itself be, if not eternal joy, eternal celebration? All jubilation, all joy had been taken away from the whole human race: everything was squalid with mourning and eternal sadness. The sin that had been committed admitted no joy; it dragged eternal sadness with it. The infernal enemy had prevailed, and had dragged us to where there was weeping and gnashing of teeth. But now the turns of events are changed: Let sadness depart, let the daughter of Zion praise and rejoice with perennial joy. In the Lord's coming, every fear of the paternal transgression, which mortality, having been circumvented, incurred long ago by the Devil's frauds, is dissolved. For the judge of heaven and earth is present with us today, who, having torn up the handwriting of our offenses, has pitied and absolved our guilt. That Lord is present, who, loosening the yoke of ancient captivity from our necks, makes the sorrow of the world joyful with eternal liberty. That gentle king is present, who, walking through the spaces of the whole world with the steps of heavenly justice, crushes the pride of the raging enemy. And this is the joy that falls to the lot of the Daughter of Zion, which all the faithful enjoy joyfully through the Nativity of the Lord; nay, which the heavenly messenger proclaimed to all the people in this Birthday solemnity: 'Behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people; for a Savior is born to you today.' In this birthday, light has been added to the world, and immortality, which had perished through sin, has been restored to mortals. Let us therefore exult, with Leo the Great leading the way, in the Lord, and let us rejoice with spiritual gladness: because the day of new redemption, of ancient reparation, of eternal happiness has shone upon us. Exult, O daughter of Zion: shout for joy, O daughter of Jerusalem: Behold, your King comes to you, righteous and a Savior, warned Zechariah, the most sweet Prophet. Rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, rejoice; the Lord is near, exclaimed the leader of the Apostles. In dulci jubilo, nun singet und seid froh, the Church now sings in response, and the whole chorus of saints. Let Zion resound with praises, with joyful applause, together with the faithful: He has appeared, whom Mary bore. Today upon the earth the Angels sing, the Archangels rejoice, God Himself exults: Only the Devil and all the Demons with him tremble, because the human race is restored through the destruction of the Devil. The Lord Himself brings the cause of joy: because Behold, I come. The advent of the Son of God is the fountain and source of all our joy. He who speaks here is none other than the Son of God himself; Jehovah, who says he was sent by Jehovah, saying, that you may know that Jehovah Zebaoth has sent me to you: and the same is called by the Prophet the Angel of the Lord. But who is sent by the Lord, and is the Angel of the Lord, if not that angel of the covenant, the Angel of the great Counsel, the Angel of the face of the Lord, the Son of God? He promised that he would come, and under the name of THE ONE TO COME he was promised and celebrated everywhere. Nor is the speech which this person, who speaks here, uses more appropriate to any other than to the Son of God himself: Behold I come and I will dwell in the midst of you, and many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and they shall be to me for a people. He claims for himself those things which befit none but the one God: that he converts the nations and gathers them to himself as a people, that he has Judah as his hereditary portion, that he represses enemies, and that by his presence he brings joy to all. We have, therefore, a clear testimony that JEHOVAH himself, that one and true God, besides whom there is no other, has visited us. A Savior is born to you today, who is Christ the Lord, says the Angel. Christ is from the Fathers according to the flesh, and the same is God blessed forever over all things, the Apostle testifies. And this is that stupendous, and beyond controversy great, mystery of godliness, that God was manifested in the flesh: concerning which St. Augustine rightly exclaimed: O wonderful and unsearchable union, O new and unheard-of mixture! God, who is, and who was, is made a creature.

He who is immense is contained, He who makes rich is made poor, the incorporeal is clothed in flesh: The Word becomes coarse, the invisible is seen, the impalpable is touched, the incomprehensible is comprehended. He whom heaven and earth bless is placed in a narrow manger. He is numbered in the age, who is before the ages. This is the foundation and the fountain of our eternal blessedness, which no one could restore to us except the eternal God. For it was the office of no other, as Athanasius warns concerning the incarnation of the Word of God, to transmute the corruptible into incorruptibility, except the Savior himself, who in the beginning had created all things from nothing, nor was it the work of any other to restore to men the exemplar of the divine image, except of Him who was the image of the Father: nor of any other to raise the immortal from death, except of Him who is life itself. It became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain and author of their salvation perfect through sufferings, says the Apostle Heb. II. 10. Which words, by the interpretation of that same Great Athanasius, mean this: That it belonged to no other to receive men back from the corruption which had already settled upon them, except the Word of God, who had created them from the beginning. Which, finally, regarding the form and manner of the incarnation of the Son of God, is insinuated by the name of advent and inhabitation. For it is not an advent and inhabitation of sanctification or glorification, but an advent of appearance or manifestation in assumed flesh, and an inhabitation in the personal temple of the Lord's body, which the Ancients call ἐπιφάνειαν ἐν σαρκὶ καὶ ἔνσαρκον ἐπιδημίαν. Behold I come, says the Lord; by which voice the advent of the incarnation is accustomed to be expressed. Behold I come, in the volume of the book it is written of me, Ps. XL. 8. Behold, your God will come Is. XXXV. 4. Behold the Lord comes and his reward is with him. Is. XL. 10. Say to the Daughter of Zion, Behold your Salvation comes, Behold his reward is with him Is. LXII. 11. Behold your King comes to you, Zach. IX. 9. And the Lord, whom you seek, shall suddenly come to his temple Mal. III. 1. Therefore John asked through his Legates. Art thou he that is TO COME? Matth. XI. 3. What kind of advent this is, let St. Athanasius explain to us: That incorporeal and incorruptible λόγος of God approached our region, not indeed being far from it before, (for nothing is left empty of him in created things, since he has filled all things entirely, being present with his Father in all) but he approached in so far as, namely, he lowered himself to us by his Φιλανθρωπίᾳ and ἐπιφανείᾳ, and took to himself a body, and that not alien to our body. For he did not simply wish to consist in a body, or to exhibit a naked presence of himself, since it was in his power, if it had so pleased him, only to expose himself to the eyes, and through some other thing, which might be more excellent, to show his divine advent: But he assumed our body, which could die: so that it, having been made a participant of the Word which is above all, might suffice for a full satisfaction for all for death, and yet, because of the indwelling Word, might persevere incorruptible. Which the same Holy Father declares elsewhere, namely in his oration against the followers of Sabellius, in this way: Since therefore Majesty and magnificence is named in God as something super-celestial, and that which is contrary to this is called humble and earthly, and to be conversant on earth, you will very easily discover that the descent of the Word is an inclination from incorporeal majesty to the vileness of a body, since he gave himself, being incorporeal in nature, out of love for the human race and for the salutary providence of all, and therefore he will be found to have been sent, since by the ineffable will of the incorporeal Father he delivered himself to a body. Likewise the descent is the ἐπαμφία-

sis, a superinduction and investment, instituted according to the will of the Father. Nor does the name of inhabitation less fit the expression of the incarnation. The Chaldean rendered this: I will place my divinity, or my habitation, in the midst of you: The LXX Interpreters: κατασκηνώσω ἐν μέσῳ σꝫ. By which word St. John described the advent of the incarnation c. I. 14. ὁ λόγος σάρξ ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν. And the Word was made Flesh, and dwelt among us, just as Epiphanius interprets in book II. T. I. heresy LI. ἄνθρωπος γέγονε, he was made man: because he began to inhabit the same scene with us through the incarnation. For this κατασκήνωσις and inhabitation shows the human nature, in which the eternal Son of God also dwelt personally, as in his own temple with all his fullness, as the Apostle testifies Col. II. 9. and through which he conversed, and as it were fixed his tabernacle in the midst of his people. Which explanation also approved itself to Cyril in book I. on John. When he said that the Word of God was made flesh, lest anyone should most foolishly suspect that he had fallen out of his own nature, and had been truly transmuted into flesh, the Theologian rightly infers immediately, and dwelt among us, so that when you necessarily understand two things, both him who dwells, and that in which he is dwelt, you may not think that he was transmuted into flesh, but rather that he dwells in the flesh, as using his own body, the temple, which is from the holy virgin. Chrysostom agrees: This tabernacle always dwells. For he put on our flesh as if not about to lay it aside, but as if about to have it with him always. And thus also Ephraem the Patriarch of Theopolis explains it in Photius, Bibliotheca, Cod. CCXXIIX. p. 806. teaching that the union into one hypostasis and the unchangeableness of each nature is designated: Thus also he observes that Athanasius and Gregory the Theologian explain it with Cyril and Chrysostom. Nor does it seem doubtful that from this is derived that which Euthymius and Theophylact inculcate with Theodoret as ἀτρέπτῳ: that the tabernacle is one thing, and he who dwells in it is another. Nor is this ἐξήγησις alien from the phrase of Scripture or Greek writers: For the body is called σκῆνος by the Apostle 2. Cor. V. and Hesychius notes that σκῆνος is σῶμα, so that τὸ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν is nothing other than σκῆνος ἀνέλαβεν ἐν ἡμῖν, he assumed a body in us, or among us, or in us, in man and from man, as Heinsius has it at this place. Which will be clearer if the type of the body of Christ, the Mosaic tabernacle, is compared, of which the Apostle speaks in Heb. IX. Nor yet is the observation of Cyril to be despised, that by this phrase of speaking is expressed at once a notable fruit of the incarnation, the gracious indwelling of us. Moreover, he asserts that the Word has also dwelt in us usefully, revealing to us also that most high mystery. For we are all in Christ, and the person of common humanity revives in Him. In all, therefore, the Word dwelt through one, so that by the one Son of God being established in power according to the spirit of holiness, that dignity might redound into universal humanity, and thus through one of us might reach also unto us. And again: But the Word dwells in all, in one temple, to wit, which He assumed for our sake and from us, that having all in Himself, He might reconcile all in one body, as Paul says, to the Father. But to pursue these things, as was fitting, is not permitted. That the first faithful at the time of Christ are stirred up by the Prophet to rejoice and give thanks to God, because they see the Messiah, God incarnate, visibly moving in their midst, and there founding the Church, to which He is soon to gather all nations through the Apostles, is acknowledged by Corne- lius à Lapide, and he confesses that this is the sense of Jerome, Theodoret, Remigius, Lyranus, Vatablus, Arias, and others, although he says it is only mystical, contrary to the intention of those authors. Let Eusebius II. Dem. Evang. 18 be added, Albertus M., Haymo, Hugo, Dionysius, although some of these wish the assembly of the Jews returning from captivity to be addressed, so that they may rejoice in their fatherland, because they are finally to have the Son of God from themselves, clothed in flesh, and to dwell in their midst. Which are sounder than those things which Cornelius, Joh. de Rayroles, Christoph. à Castro, and other Papists hold. It remains that the prophetic κέλευσμα may also resound among us: Let all flesh be silent before the face of the Lord, because he has arisen from his holy habitation. Let all the tumults of the reprobate be silent and hushed: The prince of peace is present, about to defend the Church. Let all flesh be silent: because the judge of all flesh appears in the flesh. Therefore, a silence of attention is required, so that we may devoutly perceive the mysteries of the incarnation; a silence of faith and submission, so that we may reverently receive what is known, and not discuss it with the measuring rod of reason; a silence of piety and fear, so that we may live worthily, that is, piously, justly, and soberly, at the τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ of the Lord; a silence of patience and persevering expectation, so that we may act bravely in hope and silence. Let all anxiety cease, Christ has arrived as our true security. Let wars cease, let disputes end, today true peace descends from heaven. Let all bitterness cease, today the heavens have become honey-flowing through the whole world; let all impurity, all injustice, all envy cease; today the Holy of Holies, who is our justice and charity itself, has been brought into the light. Let our mind, our tongue, our life, as many of us as desire to be ἰσάγγελοι, sing with the angelic host: Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men. Therefore, let us not desert the sacred assemblies: but let us build one another up with mutual exhortations and holy examples: finally, let us frequently testify our thanksgiving to those who perform the embassy in the place of God to us, at the altar of the Lord. P. P. Wittenberg, on the eve of the Nativity of the Lord. In the year 1658.

THE LORD REBUKE THEE, O SATAN) ἐπιτιμήσαι κύριος ἐν σοι, LXX. here, for which ἐπιτιμήσει σοι, Jude. The sense is, may he restrain you, so that you may not harm this man further, who has suffered sufficiently harsh things.

IS NOT THIS A BRAND PLUCKED OUT OF THE FIRE?) Did not God save him from grave perils? The Jews invent fables that this Jesus was thrown into the fire by the Chaldeans, at the demand of the pseudo-prophets Ahab and Zedekiah, whose mention is in Jer. XXIX. 21, but that he himself was saved from the fire, with only his clothes burned.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SILEAT OMNIS CARO A FACIE DO- MINI) Timeant: nam timorem comitari solet silentium. QUIA CONSURREXIT DE HABITACVLO SAN- CTO SVO) Velut è templo prodibit, ultionem sumturus de gentibus inimicis.

Non timor ir cutitur gentibus, è vindicta divi- na, sed filiæ Sion silentium imponitur, ob adven- tum Domini σωτήριον. Quam exultare jusserat An- gelus præco, voce Domini, quam referebat, eo quod immineret dies adventûs. Rectius ergo no- stri: Filius Dei accingit se, ut veniat liberaturus ge- nus humanum, & collecturus ad Judaicum popu- lum gentes. SILEAT ergo omnis caro, per to- tum orbem: quia venit totius orbis Salvator. B. Balduinus notat hîc peculiare beneficium, hostium justam represssionem. Nam si qui eo audaciæ pari- ter & dementiæ progressi fuerint, ut contra stimu- lum tam potentis Domini calcitrare, & vel restau- rationem cultus divini in Judæa, vel reditum Ju- dæorum in patriam, vel etiam tandem aliquando collectionem Ecclesiæ ex Judæis pariter & genti- bus impedire ausint, his ipse Filius Dei hîc silen- tium imponit, & à conatibus istis desistant, horta- tur, & quidem duplici nomine: partim quia ipsi ca- ro sint, h. e. fragiles, & quovis fœno imbecillio- res: omnis enim caro fœnum Esa. XL. v. 6. Ille vero cui resistunt, Jehovah est, Dominus exercituum, à cujus facie cœlum tremiscit, & omnis terra conti- cescit: omnes enim gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram Deo, & quasi nihilum, & inane reputatæ sunt ei Es. 40. 17. partim etiam, quia jamjam tem- pus imminet, ut ipse Filius Dei, qui in Sole posuit tabernaculum, suum, progrediatur tanquam spon- sus è cubili suo, ut Psal. XIX. 6. loquitur, adsumtu- rus carnem, & auspicaturus Ecclesiam N. T. re- demturus etiam eam sanguine suo Actor. XX. At- que ita populo ostensurus, omnes etiam infero- rum portas Ecclesiæ suæ nihil quicquam prævali- turas esse. Alii epiphonemate hoc superiores pro- missiones obsignari volunt. Scilicet, ne putent Ju- dæi, ista esse ἀδύνατα, quum tot hostes habeant ob- jectos, tot sint impedimenta, quæ occurrant, o- stendere Prophetam, omnibus istis silentium à Deo iri impositum Psal. II. 2. & VII. 2. & LXV. 1. Quod jam Deus ex sanctuario suo sit excitatus, in quo dormiisse visus est, quam diu suos sivit affligi Ps. XLIV. 12. 23. Ps. LXXIV. 3. Ps. LXXIIX. 60. 65. Ita Lamb. Danæus sanctuarii nomen ad templum referens, ut Judæi intelligant, se habere paria Dei favoris præsentiæ, & tutelæ testimonia, quæ olim patres eorum habuerunt; nam illi ex Sanctuario, id est, Templo, Deum sibi occurrere dicebant Ps. XX. 1. Reg. IIX. cum Deum sibi benevolum significa- bant. Willius fere similiter: Noli mihi hostium ma- chinationes objicere: illi ne mutire quidem audebunt, innuit Deum, cum ante quasi somno deditus deli- tuerit, jam surrexisse, & ex templo, tanquam ar- mamentario suo in procinctu esse, ut hostes ter- reat, & compescat. Silebunt igitur hostes, quia Deus in templo præsens, & ex templo se ipsis op- ponet. Sed silere vult Propheta, vel Angelus lo- quens apud Prophetam OMNEM CARNEM, non hostes tantum: Judæos & gentes, quorum mentio facta silere, non tantum ob eventus certitudinem, utcunque omnia videantur ardua & difficilia, ho- stiumque certam confusionem, qui ad silentium re- digentur, sed cumprimis ob rei magnitudinem, & mysterii religiosam venerationem & admirationem. Nam ὁμολογυμένως μέγα μυσήριον est, quod Deus manifestatus est in carne I. Tim. III. 16. Quod stu- pent & mirantur etiam Angeli I. Petr. I. 11. Multo magis omnis homo, qui non nisi caro est. Nam vo- ce omnis carnis omnes mortales indigitantur. Pa- rallelus locus est Es. XL. 6. 9. Gloria Domini mani- festabitur, & OMNIS CARO pariter (cum ad- miratione) videbit, quod loquatur os Domini, su- per montem excelsum ostende tu, quæ evangelizas ô Sion: Dic civitatibus Judæ: Ecce Deus vester adest. Nec vero hæc opposita sunt silere & exultare, uti

Putat Willius, Allegoricam interpretationem de fi- lentio Evangelio dando (Sic vocat, at absque ratio- ne. Cur enim magis allegorica hæc, quam illa de hostibus ad silentium redigendis) parum sibi pla- cere, quia ubi de adventu Christi sermo est, Sioni non silentium, sed gaudium, exultationes & jubila impe- rare soleat Psal. XCVI. XCVII. XCVIII. XCIX. C. At ὑπάλληλα, inquam ego, vel subordinata hæc sunt, non ἐναντία aut contraria: nam & silentio reli- gioso mysteria illa venerari, & in laudum præconia erumpere oportet fideles. Sublimitas rei admiratio- nem, ac venerationem poscit, quia rationem sub obsequium fidei compescere, ad magnitudinem tanti mysterii veluti obstupescere, idque sancto si- lentio venerari necessum habemus: nec tamen ideo lætitia & exultatio inhibetur, quin fideles in Do- mino lætentur corde, atque ore læto, & exulta- bundo celebrent tantam gratiam, quam nunquam satis admirari possunt. Ita Ps. LXV. 1. Tibi silentium laus Deus in Sion, quod pro omni laude silentium quærat ipse Deus. Iob. de Reyroles Comment. ad h. l. adfert etiam hic morem gentilium, de quo Plu- tarchus in vit. Cariolani: Numa hoc Romanis ad summum religionis ornamentum instituisse vide- tur, ut, cum Principes ac Sacerdotes rem divinam faciunt, præco ingenti voce præcedens clamet: Hoc age, animos scil. sacrificio adhærere jubens. Per Sanctuarium aliquando cœlum intelligi vel è 2. Chron. IIX. 21. fatente ipsomet Willio, constat, neque de adventu Domini hic agi Willius dubita- vit, hunc sensum superiorum promissionum red- dens p. 75. Ego ipse, qui patribus & vobis promissus sum die illo, & tempore statuto Novi Testamenti in carne me sistam, imo tunc non modo vos Iudæos, verum ipsas gentes vobiscum assumam in fœdus, & familiari conversatione, operibus & miraculis me verum Mes- siam demonstrabo, atque, me ita intermedio, Pater sibi Ecclesiam ex vobis & gentibus habebit. Denique ver- ba, fileat omnis caro, dicta ob præparationem ad- ventus Domini, fatetur Coccejus, quamvis ea etiam intelligi posse in consideratione ultimi temporis velit. Quod vero alienum: quia non de secundo adventu Messiæ hic agitur, sed de primo. Recte Menochius: SILEAT: Reverenter & sancte eum colat, & illi subjecta sit. OMNIS CARO: Omne humanum genus. CONSURREXIT DE HABITACU- LO SANCTO SUO. Quia de cœlo habitaculo sancto suo quasi consurgens, opem nobis tulit, quod maxime verum est per assumptam carnem, & per o- pus redemptionis nostræ; quod in cruce consummavit. Cæterum quia illustratum κέλευσμα Propheticum capitis hujus v. 10. Programmate Genethliaco Ann. 1658. placet id his subjicere: Lauda & lætare Filia Sion; quia ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui, ait Dominus. Ita Festum, quod nunc celebramus, olim intimavit per Zacha- riam cap. II. 10. Jehovah Dominus, tanquam fe- stum exultationis & lætitiæ æternæ, festum vi- sitationis & præsentiæ divinæ, festum incarna- tionis & unionis hypostaticæ. Ita Evangelista il- le magnus & fructum adventus sui exhibere, & semetipsum ceu ἐρχόμενον VENTURUM illum sistere, & modum adventus sui describere digna- tus est; ut scil. lætissimo adventus nuncio fideles æ- tatis istius refocillaret, & ad gaudium solenne ex- citaret.
