Finally, it is manifest that the other members of this notable prophecy are very badly perverted by this Grotian comment, of which hereafter. Here we subjoin the Program proposed on the Feast of the Nativity of the Lord, in which we especially explained the name צמח, concerning which see verse 8. It is as follows:

That blessed night is imminent, which brought the true light to the world, more splendid than all days, the origin of light, of serenity, and of all happiness. When no light yet shone in the world, and the whole world immersed in darkness was nothing but Tohu vabohu, suddenly through the Word light shone forth, and illuminated the first night, than which none was ever darker. The whole world lay in spiritual darkness, which the Spirit of darkness had brought in, to be buried in the eternal gloom of darkness. But behold, on that night the saving light arose in the darkness, not through the Word of the Lord, but which is itself the Word of the Lord, illuminating the whole world. That first-born light was to be admired, which the wise can search into, but cannot examine and explain; truly it exceeds all, not said capacity, but admiration by a very long way, the first-born light begotten before every creature, light from light, the splendor of glory, and the sincere emanation of the clarity of the omnipotent God: whether you wish to search into that inaccessible light, how the true light proceeds from the true light, or the rising of the light in the hemisphere of the lower world, when the rising from on high deigned to visit us and shine upon us. For just as the sacrament of the divine generation transcends all intelligence, so that with Hilary you must needs profess concerning it, I am ignorant, I do not know, the archangels do not know, the angels have not heard, the Prophet has not perceived, I am in a fever, I am dull. Thus it is no less absurd to reason, and beyond controversy a great mystery of that piety, that the incorporeal light of divinity assumed a body of humanity, as Greg. M. l. XLIII. Moral. c. 3. and the Sun of divinity covered itself with the covering of human nature as with a certain shade, as Bede in his homily on the annunciation attempted to shadow forth that admirable ἐπισκιασμὸν of the power of the Most High. Concerning that night, in which the true light came forth into the light, it was once believed that, after the prayers of the B. Virgin, in the first watch a splendid light arose from heaven and covered the virgin alone, and a great company of angels descended from the first hierarchy, and sang sweetly beside the one giving birth: Let God go forth from his holy place, let him come that he may save his people. In the second watch of the night, with a greater light surrounding the whole house in which the Mother of God was, angels of the second hierarchy descended in greater numbers, and sang: Behold now comes the one desired by the nations. At the very middle of the night a light shone from heaven, illuminating not only the house and the city, but the whole world, with which angels of the third hierarchy in countless multitude mingled themselves, standing by the virgin in human but most radiant form, and singing: Let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior, whence the Blessed Virgin, as if absorbed into the abyss of Divine contemplation, with hands raised to heaven, brought forth the Savior with the greatest exultation of the angelic hosts. These things, perhaps conceived with a mind not impious to illustrate the splendor of that Night and the angelic joy; but the blessed Night, or the saving Nativity, the dispenser of true and eternal splendor, does not need these splendors. We know that those fiery flames, those shining Seraphim, those morning stars, far most splendid, illuminated the night when the great light was exposed to the light, and the Sun of righteousness proceeded from the bridal chamber of the virginal womb. But that was done to manifest this sun to the world, not to aid its rising or to pour any light upon it. What? The light and glory of our newborn Jesus, as the Lord of glory, surrounds the Angel, the herald of the Nativity, with its splendor; and all the angels glitter and shine with the glory and splendor of this little boy, who is the brightness of eternal light, and they yearn to παρακύψαι [stoop down] into the glory of the rising of that light. It is believed in the Papacy that when the Lord was born, three Suns appeared in Rome or in Spain, and gradually coalesced into one Solar Body; it is believed that at midnight a most shining splendor, to which the Sun can hardly be compared, arose and penetrated even to the abyss, the earth splitting open: it is believed that in the middle of the day a golden circle was seen around the Sun, and in the middle of it a virgin carrying a most beautiful boy in her bosom, which the Sibyl showed to the Emperor Augustus. But let that fictitious light of the excellent mythologists Bonaventure and the Jesuit Dauroultius delight the dark Papacy; for us, that true light will be uniquely delightful, which, having arisen on earth, uniquely restored to us the light of eternal life while we were sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. Which not only that excellent Psalmist of Israel, full of the Messiah of the God of Jacob, sang in his latest words, and the distinguished [prophet] of the O.T. the Evangelist exhibited as if to be looked upon, when that great light was shown to the people walking in darkness. A child, he exclaimed, is born to us, and a Son is given to us. Balaam the Prophet, not of good name, had also seen it from afar, but since he had to predict nothing but good and true things when God commanded, as he was a hearer of the word of God, and understood the knowledge of the Most High, and saw the visions of the Almighty with open eyes; A STAR, he says, SHALL ARISE out of Jacob, designating him who testifies of himself: I am the root and the offspring of David, the bright and morning star. The latest of the Prophets, Malachi, also saw him, sealing the books of the O.T. with this prophecy: THE SUN of Righteousness SHALL ARISE for you who fear my name. Which clause of his seems to have provided the material for the inaugural hymn, by which the first herald of the worthier sex and Evangelist of the coming of the Lord, Zacharias the priest, celebrated the completion of so many prophecies at the beginnings of the N.T.: When, he says, through the bowels of the mercy of our God, he has visited us, the ORIENT from on high. But he followed primarily in this appellation the prophet of the same name, a contemporary of Malachi, who gave a peculiar name to the Messiah, which is Zemach, ch. III. 8. Behold I bring my servant the ORIENT, ch. VI. 12. Behold the man whose name is ORIENT. For the LXX there rendered it ἀνατολὴ: whence, since Zacharias the Priest calls Christ by the same name, he seems to have taken it from the Prophet Zechariah. Nor indeed is the prophet's discourse about Zerubbabel, as some Jews, Theodoret, Eusebius, Remigius, Hugo, Hugo Grotius opine: But about the Messiah, which the Ancients teach with great consensus, Athanasius, Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, Chrysostom, and others, with the assent of the Chaldean paraphrase, which interprets it concerning the Messiah, R. Solomon Jarchi, R. David Kimchi, Joshua son of Levi, and others in the Pugio Fidei of Raymund Martin, and in Galatinus de Arcanis Catholicae Veritatis: For Jehovah calls that Zemach specifically his servant, which name, being used so absolutely κατ᾿ ἐξαίρετον λόγον [by a special reason], designates the Messiah: because he alone perfectly served God the Father, and performed his will entirely, by his obedience both active and passive, Isa. XLII. 1. ch. LII. 13. Ps. XL. 9. Phil. II. 9. The name Zemach itself is appropriated to the Messiah in a singular way, just as Zechariah says: His name shall be Zemach. For he is so called in Isa. IV. 1. Jerem. XXIII. 6. ch. XXXIII. 15. and from a cognate name in Isa. XI. 1. he was called a Nazarene, Matth. II. 23. Which passages Grotius impiously twists toward Zerubbabel, when they most openly treat of Christ, nor was Zerubbabel a King, much less could he have been called by the divine name Jehovah Zidkenu, and through the shoot from the Root of Jesse, Grotius elsewhere (at Isa. XI. 1.) understands Hezekiah. How then does he now form Zerubbabel from it? Which shoot St. Paul clearly teaches is Christ, Rom. XV. 12. Furthermore, whom Zechariah called Zemach, he designates by the stone upon which are seven eyes; which certainly is not Zerubbabel, nor a material stone placed for the foundation of the second temple, as Balt. Willius foolishly thinks; but that precious stone, the foundation of the Church, Christ, Ps. CXVIII. 12. Isa. XXIX. 16. Acts IV. 11. I Pet. II. 6. Distinguished by seven eyes, on account of the manifold gifts of the Holy Spirit, Rev. V. 6. Isa. XI. 1. which God himself engraved in the passion, so that the sins of the whole earth might be expiated on that great day of the passion, not otherwise than as on the day of Kippur the sins of the people were accustomed to be expiated. The Grotian gloss about a tin globule, about a plumb line hanging down, by which the divine power, seven eyes suddenly appeared, and about the removal of sterility, is frivolous, inept, and unworthy of refutation. Now why the reason for the name Zemach is given, because he shall germinate from under himself, as the Hebrew word has it, the Interpreters think it is hinted that this man is to be born without male seed, and is to establish a kingdom by his own power, or, as Blessed Luther says, that under him and his kingdom all things will germinate and flourish, as can be gathered from the name itself, that all the citizens of the kingdom will be in perpetual bloom, to whom can these things be vindicated, if not to the Messiah? Further, when he is said to be about to build a temple to the Lord according to the promise made to David II. Sam. VII. without doubt respect is had, and the Messiah is established as the architect of the spiritual temple of the Lord, of whom Matth. XVI. 16. Eph. II. 20. Nor did Zerubbabel wear a royal crown, much less did he perform the priesthood, both of which are predicted of this man, and were fulfilled in no other than the Messiah Ps. II. 6. CX. 4. Is. IX. 6. Luc. I. 32. Heb. VII. since under the O.T. priests and kings had to be distinct persons. Finally, he is said to be about to enter into a counsel of peace between both, both Jews and Gentiles: which suits not Zerubbabel, but Christ Eph. II. 13. seqq. since even those who are far off, that is, the Gentiles, are to be built into the spiritual temple Is. LVII. 19. There is no doubt, therefore, that the Messiah is designated here, which Grotius himself could not deny here, when he annotated these things to the words of ch. VI. 12. Behold the man: Pilate, with God directing, applied these to Christ, saying ἰδὲ ὁ ἄνθρωπος. And to ch. VII. 8. he observed that the Chaldean and other Jews interpret this passage of the Messiah, and by a Cabalistic ἰσόψηφον form from it the name מנחם, which signifies the Comforter, and is among the titles of the Messiah; nor did he doubt that in some mystical way this passage pertains to Christ, the author of eternal peace. But neither did the Jews explain it of the Messiah only in a mystical sense, as if in the literal sense it treats of Zerubbabel, nor is a double sense of this kind to be admitted in any text of Scripture, nor do these things in any way suit Zerubbabel according to the letter. Furthermore, as to that title of the Messiah, by which he is called Zemach, ἀνατολὴ properly signifies either the Orient region, or especially the rising of the sun among Plutarch and other Greeks, and most concede that it is accepted by Zacharias the priest in that notion, so that ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψους is the rising from on high, which the end and effect of this visitation of the ἀνατολὴ, subjoined, clearly confirms, namely the illumination of those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death:

Whence the Syrian rendered it by דנחא, a rising: It may therefore seem probable that by this name the rising of the Sun of righteousness is also signified by the Prophet, just as the Syrian translates: Behold the man, and his name is the rising, and he shall rise from beneath: and the Alexandrian Arabic: Behold the man his name is the rising: And it is so accepted by most of the Fathers: Chrysostom, Homily on the words of Zachariah, reads and explains it thus: Behold the man the Orient is his name, under his shadow the Sun shall rise, he himself shall come to save his people. What kind of name is Orient? Delightful, sweet, pleasant. Let us always desire this, that being turned from the West, intent upon the Orient, we may acknowledge God almighty. Under his shadow the Sun shall rise. And truly under his shadow the brightness of his divinity has risen, who placed his tabernacle in the Sun. Because the light came into the world, it radiated upon our dark minds, foul things were declared, hidden things were manifested, dark things were opened, that light might rise for us. St. Athanasius, on that passage, all things have been delivered to me by the Father: This is the day which the Lord has made: For God rises like the Sun, illuminating the mind of each one; when the Prophet had seen this, he spoke: Behold the man, the Orient is his surname. Gregory the Great, book XX of the Morals, ch. 18, because light rises from the east, he is rightly called the Orient, by the light of whose righteousness the night of our righteousness is illuminated. Rupert, no man, he says, besides him is rightly so named: because he alone is always in the rising and for him there is never any setting, when he shall be thought to set, he shall most of all rise. Nor is the most ancient of the Fathers, Justin Martyr, easily otherwise, Dial. ch. Trypho. The discourse of truth is more fervent, and illuminates more effectively than the power of the Sun, penetrating the innermost recesses of the mind and heart, and this is what Zachariah says: The Orient is his name. Finally, Philo himself, in his book on the Confusion of Tongues, explains it thus, and judges that the rising of the Son from the Father is indicated by this name, so that that incorporeal image referring to God may be understood. Thus therefore Zemach shall be called ἀνατολὴ or orient, or rising, the Messiah, because like light he rises from the Father through eternal generation, true light from true light: from the mother through temporal birth, when the incorporeal light assumed a body, and came into the world: and furthermore he rises in the faithful heart through spiritual conception, of which Peter, 2 Ep. 1:19, until the Phosphorus (Christ, Ap. 22:16) ἀνατείλῃ may rise in your hearts. Not a few interpreters, however, prefer to explain the word Zemach as SPROUT. Nor is there any doubt that it is so accepted in similar places, Is. 4:1, Jer. 23:5, ch. 33:15, and the Messiah is described elsewhere as a shoot and a sprout, Is. 11:1, 53:2, Ezek. 17:12. How then can it be rendered by ἀνατολὴν or rising, and be compared to the rising Sun? I would say that the word ἀνατολὴ generally designates a rising, whether of light or of a sprout. Just as the LXX interpreters also used ἀνατέλλειν in Gen. 2:5, ch. 3:10 regarding things born from the earth, and when in Jer. 23:5 they rendered the word Zemach as ἀνατολὴν, in the parallel passage ch. 33:15 they explained the same by βλαστὸς, a sprout: Therefore Jerome, on Zachariah 6, holds those as synonyms: Who is therefore called rising, that is, ἀνατολὴ, or ἀναφύιν or βλάστημα, that is, a sprout, because it suddenly grew up from itself, and sprouted from its root in the likeness of a sprout. And the LXX interpreters themselves used this word ἀνατολὴ for sprout in Ezek. 16:8. And thus also the Hebrew צמח, it sprouted, has a general meaning, so that it designates the rising of both a sprout and also of light, as appears among other things from Ps. 132:17. Wherefore the Messiah has his name from the rising, with a comparison established partly with the rising of a sprout, in Isaiah and Jeremiah, partly with the rising of light, in Zachariah, from which he is called by some a Solar sprout; and a germinating and rising Sun. But we cannot pursue these things at present. It will be your task, however, to adore this rising Sun, and to venerate his admirable rising with pious meditation; and above all to celebrate with a grateful mind that the orient from on high has deigned to visit us, that he might also shine upon us, and rise in our hearts. He himself warns most gravely: walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you: while you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light. John 12:35. He invites most sweetly: I am the light of the world, he who follows me, does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life. John 8:12. He does not enjoy this light, and the light of life, who does not believe in this light; he does not follow this light, he does not walk as a son of light. Behold, St. Athanasius acclaims to us in his tract on the Sabbath and Circumcision: The Man, the Orient is his surname: and again, to you who fear him the Sun of righteousness shall rise. For this day is not for all, but for those who are dead to sin and live to God. The Nativity night was turned into day, illuminated by the splendor of the Sun of righteousness. Let us not therefore turn the day, which the Lord has made, into night, by the works of darkness; rather let us cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light, let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires, etc.

Verse same. BEHOLD I WILL ENGRAVE THE ENGRAVING THEREOF, SAITH THE LORD OF HOSTS) I will engrave, that is, not any human hand, but my power caused those seven eyes to appear suddenly in that little globe, that is, that portent, to which the words above 8 refer.

AND I WILL TAKE AWAY THE INIQUITY OF THAT LAND IN ONE DAY) All punishment, that is, sterility. Concerning which Haggai ch. 1:6, 9, 10, 11.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

QUIA ECCE LAPIS) Per lapidem intelligit globulum stanneum, de perpendiculo dependentem, quo utens Zo- robabel, super illa jacta sub Cyro fundamenta primum la- pidem, ut Princeps gentis, erat positurus. IV. 7. 8. 9. 10. Hebraeis אבן generalius est, quam lapis apud Latinos, & omne ponderosum significat: ut Deuter. VIII, 9.

QUEM DEDI) Quem dari volui in manum Zoroba- belis. IV. 10.

SUPER LAPIDEM UNUM SEPTEM OCULI SVNT) Significantes Dei providentiam pervigilem adfu- turam isti operi. IV, 10.

Cohaerentia cum superioribus cogit per LAPI- DEM alium nullum intelligere, quam GER- MEN promissum, Messiam. Hic enim indigitatur nomine lapidis non raro Es. XXIIX. 16. Dan. II. 34. Ps. CXIIX. 27. Et coram Josua à Deo positus dici- tur, ut Josua sacerdos & praeceptor populi eum an te oculos habeat, ceu lapidem fundamenti & angu- li I. Cor. III, 11. Eph. II. 20. I. Petr. II. 4. Designat itaque coelestis Hierosolymae, Ecclesiae Dei, fun- damentum, quae nunc post insignem dissipationem restauranda erat super lapide fundamentali Chri- sto, idque ex occasione fundamenti & structurae templi: I. Cor. III. 11. utpote cui innitebantur omnia Sacerdotum Leviticorum sacra, & cui superstrui fideles debuere omnium temporum Ephes. II. 20. Qui etiam coram Josua datus, seu oculis ejus exposi- tus, quia Josua ipsum agnovit, & in ipsum credidit; ut Osiander exponit, ut & Danæus. Hic Lapis co- ram Josua & toto illo ordine Levitico, ac Ecclesia ipsa universa positus dicitur, ut omnes in eum in- cumbant, ac intueantur velut unicum suum funda- mentum. Nam quæ Josuæ, eadem Ecclesiæ ratio, & spectatur Josua, ut Sacerdos & Doctor Ecclesiæ. Paulo aliter B. Winckelmann. Coram Jesu: Id est, stante adhuc Sacerdotio Levitico, quod jam in Je- hosua instauratur. Alii lapidem hunc coram Josua positum fuisse in typo intelligunt, quia Deus, qui ipse Architectus fuit, templi lapidem fundamenta- lem ejus ponens in typo ita fundamentum Eccle- siæ se posuisse testatur: quod illa ædificatio templi adumbrasit Ecclesiam super unicum fundamen- tum, præter quod nemo aliud ponere potest, ex- truendam. Sic Paraphrastæ Vinarienses, ut & Bel- gici, qui verba Ebræa cum Ludov. de Dieu reddunt: Nam ecce, quod attinet lapidem, quem posui ante Jo- suam, super lapidem unum septem oculi sunt. Non- nulli hunc lapidem coram Josua positum dicunt, quod Deus ostenderit Josuæ per visionem Lapi- dem fundamentalem templi, eique revelarir, per il- lum Christum repræsentari. Sic Cornelius à Lapide cum Lyrano, Hugone, Vatablo, Clario, & aliis: Sensus nonTx incommode satis reddetur: Nam vide lapidem illum, quem posui coram facie Josua (qui & ipse si- gnum ac portentum est) super lapidem unum (illum nempe singularem & unicum lapidem, quem adum- bravi in ædificio templi prioris Ps. CXIIX. 22. atq; iterum adumbro in lapide fundameutali hujus templi) septem oculi ERUNT. Lapis ille non vul- garis erit, sed plane μονότροπον & admirandus. E- runt enim super illum septem oculi &c. Simplicior tamen prima est explicatio. Nam quamvis occasio- ne fundamenti templi secundi hæc dicta sint, de la- pide tamen agunt solum mystico. Christo funda- menti loco jam posito, cui superstruatur Ecclesia nunc denuo post calamitatem & dispersionem Ba- bylonicam restauranda. Quo etiam abit B. Luth. T. IV. Jen. Germ. f. 259. Hier giebt der Prophet selbst die Allegoria, oder Deutung des leiblichen Tempels, und redet von einem geistlichen Gebäu des lebendigen Tempels. In welchem gar viel ein ander Stein zum Grunde soll geleget werden, denn in jenem. Es soll ein einiger Stein seyn. Aber im leiblichem Tempel werden viel Steine geleget. Dieser Stein ist da Ef. 28. und Petrus I. Epist. II. von sagen: Und GOtt legete denselben Stein selber, nicht Josua, noch Serubabel, den Gott bauet diesen Tempel selber, wie Er hier spricht, den Stein, denn Ich für dem Angesicht Josua lege. Den GOTT fing schon an den geistlichen Tempel zu bauen, weil Er den leiblichen Tempel umb den geistlichen willen bauen lies: Und über das ist solch geistlich Gebäu für dem Angesicht Josua, das ist, für dem Angesicht des Priesterthumbs Josua. Den Christus Tempel und Reich gieng an, da Josua Stamm und Prie- sterthumb noch stund, damit angezeiget wird, daß Christus kommen solte, ehe denn Josua, und sein Stamm und Priesterthumb untergieng. Daß al- so bey Josuas Nachkommen, für ihren Augen die- ser Stein geleget ist, wiewohl sie es nicht sahen noch verstunden, ja Ihn auch darzu verworffen.

Septem oculos à lapide separatos, in lapidem illum respicientes dicunt Lyranus, Vatablus, Fernandes, Sanctius, Angelos esse in Christū intentos, ut volun- tatem ejus exequantur: Clarius vero & Arias putant Dei providentiam esse erga Christum; alii oculos omnium Angelorum & hominum, imprimis fide- lium in Christum directos, B. Balduinus Christia- norum oculos mentis illuminatos, qui vera & per- fecta fide intuentur, & agnoscunt Christum me- diatorem & servatorem mundi Eph. I. 18. Sic etiam Gualtherus, Coccejus, qui libenter apocalyptica mi- scet, oculos fidelium in septem periodis (quas A- pocalypsin finxit ex Prophetis V. T. distinguere) intelligit. At rectius oculi septem tribuuntur ipsi LAPIDI Christo, (1) ad denotandam ipsius omni- scientiam, & παντεποψίαν, quia numerus septe- narius est perfectionis, nihil enim coram oculis ejus absconditum est. (2) Ad designandam ejus provi- dentiam, qua cunctis prospicit in Ecclesia, quo de Lamb. Danaeus: Tribuuntur illi septem oculi, quibus omnibus ille Ecclesiae suae calamitatibus, ac rebus prospicit, ne eum lapidem caecum & inertem esse existimemus. (3) ad indicandam donorum Sp. S. septemplicem, h. e. multiplicem gratiam, q. d. in hunc lapidem effundam Spiritum meum absque mensura, ut septemplici Sp. S. gratia ornatus Ecclesiae suae opti- me, sapientissime, & felicissime, (quippe oculatis- simus) praesit. Ita Osiander, & Paraph. Belgici, qui hanc explicationem tradunt: In Christo septem ocu- li, intellige primum totam plenitudinem Deitatis, tum abundantiam donorum spiritualium, ac porro plenam curam & providentiam ejus pro Ecclesia. Vi- narienses & Tirinus conjungunt oculos, quibus lapis fundamenti ornatus, & oculos fidelium Chri- stum respicientes. Sed si oculi Christi, vel in Chri- sto intelliguntur, non possunt simul oculi Christia- norum super lapidem respicientes, vel in Christum directi intelligi. At Christi oculos indigitari e loco simili Ap. V. 6. liquet, ubi vidit S. Joh. agnum occisum habentem cornua septem, & oculos septem, qui sunt se- ptem Spiritus Dei missi in omnem terram: Ubi ut cor- nua, sic etiam oculi Christi ipsius intelliguntur, ejus nempe divina potentia, & vis per cornua, divina o- mniscientia, & universalis providentia per oculos de- signata, sunt dona illa multifaria Spiritus, quibus ille instructus, in regimine totius terrae utitur, ut- pote cui data est omnis potestas in caelo & in terra, ideo emitti dicuntur in omnem terram; Addunt alii locum hujus Prophetae similem c. IV. 10. Septem isti oculi sunt Domini, qui discurrunt per universam ter- ram. Qui non male, nostro judicio, quantum ad septem oculos cum hoc loco componitur. Quia ut hic spirituale templum Ecclesia vi oculatissimae Chri- sti providentiae conservandum & sustinendum in- sinuatur, ita c. IV. materialis etiam templi conser- vatio septem oculis Christi, h. e. παντεποψίᾳ & providentiae ejus committitur, cujus munere & ad fi- nem produci templi structura & adversus omnes insultus conservari idem debuit usq; ad finem Po- litiae Judaicae. Nonnulli conferunt hic etiam Che- rubinos Ezechielis c. I. 18. & Johannis Ap. IV. 8. ocu- lis plenos, ac rotas currus Cherubici Ez. I. 18. quibus re- praesentatur divinae providentiae actio, & exertio oculatissima & attentissima. De oculis etiam ipsius Christi hanc visionem interpretatur veteres, Hie- ronymus, Haymo, Remigius, Dionysius & alii, dona Sp. S. intelligentes, quae animam Christi oculatam reddunt. Gregor. M. l. XXIX. Moral. c. XVI. super lapidem unum septem oculi sunt. Huic enim lapidi (Christo) septem oculos habere, est simul omnem vir- tutem Spiritus septiformis gratiae in operatione retine- re. Alius namq; Prophetiam, alius scientiam, alius vir- tutes, alius genera linguarum, alius interpretationes sermonum juxta distributionem Sp. S. accipit: ad haben- da vero cuncta ejusdem Spiritus munera nemo pertin- git. At vero conditor noster infirma nostra suspiciens, quia per divinitatis suae potentia simul se habere omnes Sp. S. virtutes edocuit, micantes procul dubio Plejades junxit. E nostris B. Winckelmann. septem oculos de se- ptiformi munere Sp. S. explicat, quia Christus homo accipit Spiritum sine mensura (septem dona Spiri- tus, vel perfectionem omnium donorum, ) & ab ipso charismata Sp. in Ecclesiam redundant. B. Tar- novius ita commentatur p. 93. Ne quis putet, si Mef- sias est germen, regnum ejus erit fragile, ecce, (quæ Dei verba sunt de Christo) promissus Messias lapis ille est, super quo ædificata est Ecclesia lapis refu- gii piis, & lapis scandali suo vitio impiis Es. 8, 14. & 28, 16. Ps. 118, 22. I. Petr. 2, 7. quem ego firmiter po- no coram Jehosua, hoc est, in Ecclesia, ubi ille ty- pum gerit Christi, atq; ita pono, ut lapidi illi unico sint septem oculi, perfectissime ei adhibens absolu- tissimam providentiam, ut infra cap. IV. 10. siquidem Scripturæ stylo (cujus analogiam probare in pro- clivi est) oculi providentiam, septenarius numerus perfectionem denotat, & proinde non facile in eo- rum concessero sententiam, qui per oculos h. l. vel Ecclesiæ Doctores vel Angelos, vel piorum ac creden- tium fidem intelligunt, quandoquidem de oculis ipsius lapidis, non creaturæ ullius Propheta loqui- tur, nec Scripturæ analogia facile ostendi poterit. Corn. à Lapide agnoscit hic oculos Christi, per quos ipse circumspicit, lustrat, protegit, curat, promovet totam Ecclesiæ fabricam, intelligi, & tamen Ange- los primarios septem, per oculos septem indigitatos vult, addens insuper, pro more, alios plures sen- sus, tropologicum, allegoricum, symbolicum. Christoph à Castro illos jucundius, & elegantius explicare censet, qui lapidem ocellatum, aut oculis multiplicibus distinctu ajunt, sumta metaphora à vestibus pulcher- rime elaboratis, opere phrygionico, quasi quibusdam ocellis intextis, ac Christum lapidem ita elaboratum putat, & variis cælaturis distinctum, ut plenus esset oculis, eoque significari varietatem gratiarum, vir- tutum, & donorum illi inditorum, juxta id quod se- quitur, ego cælabo sculpturam ejus, aut certe de vi- bicibus & vulneribus id dici, quibus qs. quibusdam ocellis erat corpus Christi distinctum, & pulcher- rima varietate exornatum: quem sensum præfert in paraphrasi. Sed simplicior, & phrasi Scripturæ convenientior est, quem èPatribus dedimus, quem etiam Menochius adduxit: In uno lapide incisi septem oculi significant plenam & perfectam Christi provi- dentiam, & vigilantiam, circa templi, id est, Ecclesiæ suæ fabricam erigendam, augendam, promoven- dam, & conservandam: quamvis alii de septem Sp. S. donis intelligere malint, quæ animam illuminant & quodammo oculatam reddunt. Quam geminam explicationem pariter laudavit Castrius: Qui ocu- los lapidi ipsi insitos, quasi capiti, accipiunt, Hierony- mus, Haymo, Remigius, Lyra, Dionys. & Vatabl do- na Sp. S. exponunt, quæ animam oculatam, & illu- strem reddunt: ita Christi anima est illuminata, & oculata reddita. Alii existimant, esse Christi sum- mam providentiam, & protectionem, qua prospicit sponsæ suæ Ecclesiæ, ut è Par. 16, 9. dicitur: Oculi Domini contemplantur universam terram. Sed conjungi, ut antea monuimus, commode possunt: quia donis Sp. S. ita ornatus est Christus, ut oculatissime omnia intueatur, & Ecclesiæ imprimis suæ prospiciat. Ad id enim dona spiritus accepit εκ ἐκ μέτρε non ad mensuram Joh. III. 34. Si quis ta- men malit cum B. Balduino per oculos fideles Chri sto inædificatos, imprimis Doctores intelligere, quia Scriptura Doctores oculos vocat I. Cor. XII. 16. 17. habebit Luth. prævium Tom. IV. Jen. Germ. in h. l. Grotii glossa, quod stanneus globulus de perpendi- culo dependens, quem in manu sua habuerit Josua, intelligatur, oculis distinctus providentiam Dei designantibus, à Lyrano accepta, calculum nullum meretur. Quomodo enim de lapide perpendiculi stanneo sermonem esse probabitur? Locus Zach. IV. 10. plane alienus est. IBI LAPIS STANNI diserte exprimitur, adeoque περιφράσει tali desi- gnatur, qui est IN MANU ZOROBABEL. Hic vero nihil de lapide STANNI. Nec de Zorobabele sermo, sed de Josua, nec in manu ejus lapis ille esse dicitur, sed ante Josuam datus, vel positus. Porro de lapide singulari hic agitur, qui UNUS dicitur ante Josuam positus, in quo septem oculi. Non ergo ad vulgarem istum perpendiculi lapidem hæc ab- ripi possunt. Et quomodo lapis stanni, vel perpen- diculi oculatus fuit, aut quomodo oculi in illo desi- gnant providentiam Dei super illum, aut super fa- bricam templi? Nam si impressi oculi lapidi, aliquid in lapide, non vero oculos Domini lapidi intentos notabant. Deniq; manifestum est, cætera membra vaticinii hujus insignis pessime ita perverti com- mento isto Grotiano, de quibus deinceps. Hic sub- jicimus Programma in Festo Nativitatis Domini propositum, quo nomen צמח imprimis exposui- mus, de quo ad v. 8. Id vero ita habet:

Imminet beata illa nox, quæ veram lucem orbi attulit, diebus omnibus splendidior, lucis serenita- tis, felicitatis omnis origo. Quum nulla adhuc in orbe fulgeret lux, orbisque totus tenebris immer- sus nil nisi Tohu vabohu esset, subito per verbum lux emicuit, noctemq; primam, qua nulla unquam tenebrosior fuit, illustravit. Jacebat mundus uni- versus in spiritualibus tenebris, quas Spiritus tene- brarum invexerat, æterna sepeliendus tenebrarum caligine. Sed ecce nocte illa salutifera lux in tene- bris exorta est, non per verbum Domini, sed quæ ipsa verbum Domini, universum mundum illumi- nans. Admiranda erat lux ista πρωτότοκος, quam scrutari possunt sapientes, perscrutari & explicare non possunt; verum omnem, non dictam captum, sed admirationem longissime excedit lux πρωτό- τοκος genita ante omnem creaturam, lumen de lumine, splendor gloriæ, & emanatio sincera clari- tatis omnipotentis Dei: sive lucem illam inacces- sam scrutari velis, quomodo lumen verum de vero lumine prodeat, seu exortũ lucis in hemisphærio inferioris mundi, cum oriens ex alta nos visitare nobisque illucescere dignatus est. Nam sicut sacra- mentum divinæ generationis omnem intelligentiã transgreditur, ut cum Hilario profiteri de eo ne- cessum habeas, ignoro ego, nescio, archangeli nesciunt, angeli non audierunt, Propheta non sensit, æstuo, hebe- sco. Ita non minus quoque rationi absurdum, ac ci- tra controversiam magnum est pietatis illius my- sterium, quod lux incorporea divinitatis corpus as- sumsit humanitatis, ut Gregor. M. l. XLIII. Moral. c. 3. & Sol divinitatis se tegmine humanæ naturæ q. um- braculo quodam obtexit, ut Beda homil. de annun- ciat. admirandum illum ἐπισκιασμὸν virtutis altis- simi adumbrare conatus est. De nocte illa, qua lux vera in lucem prodiit, creditum quondam fuit, post preces B. Virginis prima vigilia lucem splendidam de cœlo exortam solam virginem cooperuisse, ma- gnumque angelorum cœtum è prima hierarchia descendisse, ac penes parturientem suaviter ceci- nisse: Egrediatur Deus de loco sancto suo, veniat ut salvet populum suum. In secunda noctis vigilia cum luce majori domum totam, in qua erat Deipara, cingente descendisse secundæ Hierarchiæ angelos, majori frequentia, & cantasse: Ecce jam venit desi- deratus gentibus. Sub ipsum noctis medium lucem cœlo fulsisse, non domum tantum & civitatem, sed totum mundum illuminantem, cui tertiæ hierar- chiæ innumera multitudine angeli se miscuerint, humana sed candidissima specie virgini adstantes, & cantantes; Aperiatur terra, & germinet Salvato- rem, unde Beata Virgo in abyssum Divinæ contem- plationis velut absorpta levatis in cœlum manibus Salvatorem cum maximo angelicarum turmarum- tripudio enixa fuerit. Quæ ad illustrandum Noctis illius splendorem, & angelicum gaudium animo fortassis non impio excogitata; Sed non eget istis splendoribus nox beata, aut Nativitas salutifera, veri & æterni splendoris proma conda. Novimus illuminasse noctem flammas illas igneas, fulgentes illos Seraphin, astra ista matutina longe splendidis- sima, cum magna lux luci exposita est, & Sol justi- tiæ de uteri virginalis thalamo processit. Sed id fa- ctum, ut orbi hunc solem manifestarent, non ut or- tum ejus juvarent, aut lucem aliquam ei affunde- rent. Quid? lux & gloria Jesuli nostri recens nati, ceu Domini gloriæ, Angelum Nativitatis præco- nem splendore suo circumcedit; omnesque angeli gloria & splendore hujus pueruli, qui æternæ lucis candor est, coruscant ac fulgent, & in gloriam or- tus lucis illius gestiunt παρακύψαι. Creditur in Pa- patu, nato Domino tres Soles Romæ, vel in Hispa- nia apparuisse, & paulatim in unum Corpus Solare coiisse; creditur, nocte modia fulgentissimũ splen- dorem, cui vix Sol comparari possit, exortum, in limbum usque, terra dehiscente, penetrasse: credi- tur, in media die visũ esse circa Solem aureum cir- culum, & in medio ejus virginem puerũ pulcher- rimum in sinu gestantem, quam Sybilla Imperatori Augusto ostenderit. Sed oblectet tenebrosum Pa- patum lux illa fictitia egregiorum mythologorum Bonaventuræ, & Dauroultij Jesuitæ; nobis volupe u- nice erit lux illa vera, quæ in terra exorta lucẽ æ- ternæ vitæ nobis in tenebris & umbra mortis seden- tibus unice reddidit. Quam non solum egregius il- le Psaltes Israel Messiæ Dei Jacob plenus in verbis suis novissimis cecinit, & insignis V. Test. Evangelista spectandam veluti exhibuit, cum luce illa magna populo in tenebris ambulanti monstrata. Parvulus, exclamavit, natus est nobis, & Filius datus est nobis. Viderat eam etiam eminus Bileam Propheta non boni nominis, sed cum Deo mandante non nisi bona & vera prædicere debuit, cum auditor esset sermonem Dei, & intelligeret doctrinam altissimi, & visiones omnipotentis oculis apertis videret; ORIE- TUR, inquit, Stella ex Iacob, eum designans, qui de se testatur: Ego sum radix & genus David stella splen- dida & matutina. Vidit eum quoque novissimus Prophetarum Malachias, hac Prophetia libros V. T. obsignans: ORIETUR vobis timentibus meum nomen SOL Iustitiæ. Quæ ejus clausula materiam videtur præbuisse auspicali hymno, quo primus dignioris sexus præco & Evangelista adventus Do- mini Zacharias sacerdos complementum tot vati- ciniorum sub N. Test. primordia celebravit: Cum per viscera misericordiæ Dei nostri, ait, nos visi- tasse ORIENTEM ex alto. Sed sequutus impri- mis hac appellatione est Prophetam cognominem, Malachiæ σύγχρονον, qui peculiare nomen Messiæ dedit, quod est Zemach, c. III. 8. Ecce ego adduco servum meum ORIENTEM, cap. VI. 12. Ecce vir ORIENS nomen ejus. Reddidere enim ibi LXX. ἀνατολὴ: unde quum eodem nomine Christum Za- charias Sacerdos vocet, à Zacharia Propheta id sumsisse videtur. Nec vero de Zorobabele sermo est Prophetæ, ut Judæi nonnulli, Theodoreto, Eusebius, Remigius, Hugo, Hugo Grotius opinantur: Sed de Messia, quod magno consensu Veteres docent A- thanas. Hieronym. Cyrill. Alexand. Chrysost. & alii, an- nuente Chaldaica paraphrasi, quæ de Messia inter- pretatur, R. Salomon Jarchi, R. David Kimchi, Iosua filio Levi, & aliis in Pugione fidei Raymundi Mar- tini, & apud Galatin. de Arcan. Cathol. verit: Nam Zemach illum vocat Jehovah peculiariter servum suum, quod nomen ita absolute adhibitũ κατ᾿ ἐξαί- ρετον λόγον Messiam designat: quia solus ipse perfe- cte serviit Deo Patri, ac voluntatẽ ejus ex asse præ- stitit, obedientia sua tum activa tum passiva tisa. XLII. 1. c. LII. 13. Ps. XL. 9. Phil. II. 9. Nomen ipsum Zemach Messia singulari ratione appropriatur, quemadmodum Zacharias ait: Nomen ejus fore Ze- mach. Nam ita appellatur Ef. IV. 1. Jerem. XXIII. 6. c. XXXIII. 15. & a cognato nomine Ef. XI. 1. Nazareus vocatus est Matth. II. 23. Quæ loca impie ad Zoro- babelem detorquet Grotius, quum apertissime de Christo agant, neq; Zorobabel Rex fuerit, nedum divino nomine Jehovah Zidkenu nuncupari potue- rit, & per surculum e Radice Iesse Grotius alibi (ad Ef. XI. 1. Ezechiam intelligat. Quomodo ergo jam Zorobabelem ex eo efformat? Quem v. surculum Christum esse S. Paulus luculenter docet Rom. XV. 12. Porro quem Zemach vocavit Zacharias, eum per lapidem super quem sunt septem oculi designat; qui certe non est Zorobabel, neque lapis materialis in fundamentum templi secundi positus, ut ineptit Balt. Willius; sed lapis ille pretiosus, fundamentu Ecclesiæ, Christus, Ps. CXIIX. 12. Ef. XXIX. 16. Act. IV. 11. I. Petr. II. 6. Septem oculis insignis, ob multifaria Sp. S. dona Ap. V. 6. Ef. XI. 1. que Deus ipse in passio- ne cælavit, ut peccata totius terræ magno illo pas- sionis die, expiarentur, non secus atque die Kippu- rim peccata populi expiari solebant. Grotiana glos- sa de globulo stanneo, de perpendiculo dependente f. per quo divina potentia, septem oculi subito apparuerint, & de ablatione sterilitatis, frivola, inepta, ac refuta- tione indigna est. Jam cu ratio redditur nominis Ze- mach, quia de sub se germinabit, ut vox Ebræa habet, innui censent Interpp. quod vir hic sine virili semine sit nasciturus, & regnum propria virtute constituturus, vel, ut B. Lutherus quod sub eo, ejusq; regno omnia ger- minabunt, & florebunt, ut ex ipso nomine colligi possit, omnes regni cives in perpetuo flore futu- ros, cuinam hæc vindicari possunt, nisi Messia? Ul- terius cum ædificaturus dicitur Domino templum ad promissionem Davidi factam II. Sam. VII. sine du- bio respectus habetur, ac Messias architectus tem- pli Domini Spiritualis constituitur, de quo Matth. XVI. 16. Eph. II. 20. Neque coronam regiam gestavit Zorobabel, nedum functus est Sacerdotio, quod u- trumq; de hoc viro prædicitur, neq; in ullo alio, nisi in Messia impletum est Ps. II. 6. CX. 4. Ef. IX. 6. Luc. I. 32. Ebr. VII. siquidem distinctæ personæ debue- rint esse sub V. T. Sacerdotes, & Reges. Denique con- silium pacis inter utrosq;, tum Judæos, tum gentes ini- turus dicitur: quod non Zorobabeli, sed Christo convenit Eph. II. 23. seqq. siquidem etiam login- qui, hoc est, gentiles in spirituali templo ædificaturi sint Ef. LVII. 19. Dubium ergo nullum est, Messiam hic designari, quod Grotius ipse hic diffiteri non potuit, cum ad verba c. VI. 12. Ecce vir, hæc annota- vit: Hæc Deo dirigente Pilatus ad Christum aptavit, dicens ἰδὲ ὁ ἄνθρωπος. Et ad c. VII. 8. observavit, Chaldæum & Judæos alios de Messia hunc locum inter- pretari, ac per Cabalam ἰσόψηφον nomen מנחם inde efformare, quod consolatorem significat, & inter indi- gitamenta est Messiæ; neq; dubitavit, quin mystico quo- dam modo hic locus ad Christum pacis æternæ autorem pertineat. Sed neq; Iudæi mystico sensu tantum de Messia eum exposuere, quasi literali sensu de Zoro- babele agat, neq; geminus ejusmodi sensus in ullo Script. textu admittendus est, neq; ullatenus quoad literam ista Zorobabeli conveniunt, Cæteru quod ad indigitamentum illud Messiæ, quo Zemach vo- catur, ἀνατολὴ proprie vel Orientem plagam, vel Ortu Solis potissimum significat apud Plutarchu & alios Græcos, eaq; notione à Zacharia Sacerdote eam ac- cipi pleriq; concedunt, ut ἀνατολὴ ἐξ ὕψες sit ortus ex alto, que sensu visitationis hujus ἀνατολῆς finis & effect9 subjunct9 luculenter confirmat, illuminatio nempe eoru qui in tenebris, & in umbra mortis sedet:

Unde Syrus per דנחא ortum reddidit : Probabile ergo videri possit, à Propheta etiam ortum Solis ju- stitiæ hoc nomine significatum esse, quemadmo- dum Syrus vertit: Ecce vir, & nomen ejus ortus, & desubter orietur : & Arabicus Alexandrinus: Ecce vir nomen ejus ortus: Et à plerisque Patribus ita ac- cipitur: Chrysost. Homil. in verb.Zach. ita legit & explicat: Ecce vir Oriens nomen ejus, sub umbra e- jus orietur Sol, ipse veniet ad salvandum populum suum. Quale nomen Oriens? delectabile, dulce, suave. Hoc semper appetamus, ut conversi ab Occidente, in- tenti ad Orientem agnoscamus Deum omnipotentem. Sub umbra ejus orietur Sol. Et vere sub umbra ejus orta est claritas divinitatis ejus, qui in Sole posuit ta- bernaculum suum. Quia lux venit in mundum, ra- diavit mentibus nostris obscuris, declarata sunt te- tra, manifestata sunt occulta, tenebrosa, aperta, ut lux oriretur nobis. S. Athanasius, in illud, omnia tradita sunt à Patre: Hæc est dies quam fecit Dominus: Solis enim instar Deus exoritur, illustrans uniuscujusque animum, hanc cum vidisset Propheta, locutus est: Ec- ce vir, Oriens illi cognomen. Gregorius M. lib. XX. Moral. c. XIIX. quia ab oriente lux surgit, recte Oriens dicitur, cujus justitiæ lumine nostræ justitiæ nox illu- minatur. Rupertus, nullus, inquit, virorum præter ipsum jure sic nominatur: quia solus hic semper est in ortu & nullus unquam illi est occasus, cum occidere putabitur, maxime orietur. Neque aliter Patrum facile antiquissimus Justinus Martyr Dial. c. Tryph. Fervidior est sermo veritatis, & illustrat efficacius, quam Solaris vis, intimos mentis cordisque sinus pene- trans, & hoc est, quod Zacharias dicit: Oriens no- men ejus. Denique Philo ipse lib. de Confus. lingu. sic explicat, & Filii à Patre ortum indigitari censet hoc nomine, ut incorporea illa Deum referens imago intelligatur. Ita ergo Zemach ἀνατολὴ vel oriens, aut ortus dicetur Messias, quia instar lucis oritur à Patre per æternam generationem, lumen verum de vero lumine: à matre per temporalem nativitatem, cum lux incorporea corpus assumsit, & in mundum venit: ac præterea oritur in fideli corde per Spiritua- lem conceptione, de quo Petrus II. Ep. I. 19. donec Pho- sphorus (Christus Ap. XXII. 16.) ἀνατείλῃ oriatur in cordibus vestris. Non pauci tamen Interpp. ma- lunt vocem Zemach per GERMEN exponere. Neque dubium est ita in locis similibus accipi Es. IV. 1. Jer. XXIII. 5. cap. XXXIII, 15. & describitur a- lias Messias tanquam virgultum & germen Es. XI. 1. LIII. 2. Ezech. XVII. 12. Quomodo ergo per ἀνα]ο- λὴν vel ortum reddi, & Soli oxorienti conferri po- test? Dixerim ego, vocem ἀνατολὴ generaliter or- tum sive lucis, sive germinis designare. Quemadmo- dum etiam LXX. Interpp. Gen. II. 5. c. III. 10. ἀνατέλ- λειν de terra nascentibus usurparunt, & quum Jerem. XXIII. 5. vocem Zemach ἀνα]ολὴν reddiderint, in loco parallelo c. XXXIII. 15. eandem per βλαστὸς germen exposuere : Ideo Hieronym. ad Zach. VI. illa pro Synonymis habet : Qui idcirco ortus, id est, ἀνα]ολὴ, vel ἀναφύιν sive βλάστημα nuncupatur, id est, germen, quia ex se repente succrevit, & ex radice sua in similitudinem germinis pullulavit. Et adhi- buere ipsimet LXX. Interpp. hanc vocem ἀνα]ολὴ pro germine Ezech. XVI. 8. Atque ita etiam Ebræum צמח pullulavit generalem significationem habet, ut ortum tum germinis, tum etiam lucis designet, ut in- ter alia è Ps. CXXXII. 17. apparet. Quapropter ab ortu nomen habet Messias, comparatione instituta partim cū germinis ortu, apud Esaiam & Jeremiam, partim cum ortu lucis, apud Zachariam utrumque unde à nonnullis dicitur germen Solare ; & Sol ger- minans & oriens. Sed hæc prosequi impræsentia- rum non possumus. Vestrum autem erit, Solem hunc orientem adorare, ortumque ejus admirabi- lem pia meditatione venerari; & grata cumprimis mente celebrare, quod oriens ex alto nos visitare di- gnatus est, ut nobis quoque illucesceret, & in cordi- bus nostris oriretur. Monet ipse gravissime: ambula- te dum lucem habetis, ut non vos tenebrae comprehen- dant: dum lucem habetis, credite in lucem, ut filii lu- cis sitis. Joh. XII. 35. invitat dulcissime: Ego sum lux mundi, qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitae Joh. IIX. 12. Non fruitur hac lu- ce, & vitae lumine, qui non credit in hanc lucem; non sequitur hanc lucem, non ambulat, ut lucis fi- lius. Ecce, acclamat nobis S. Athanasius tract. de Sabbath. & circumc. Vir, Oriens illi cognomen: ac rursum, vobis timentibus eum exorietur Sol justitiae. Non enim omnium haec dies est, sed eorum, qui mor- tui sunt peccato & vivunt Deo. Nox Genethliaca in diem vertebatur Solis justitiae splendore illu- strata. Ne ergo vertamus diem, quam fecit Domi- nus, in noctem, operibus tenebrarum; imo abji- ciamus opera tenebrarum, & induamur arma lucis, sicut in die, honeste ambulemus; non in commessatio- nibus & ebrietatibus, non in cubilibus, & impudici- tiis, non in contentione, & aemulatione, sed induamini Dominum Jesum Christum, & carnis curam ne fece- ritis in desideriis. &c.

Vers. Eod. ECCE EGO CÆLABO SCULPTURAM EJVS, AIT DOMINVS EXERCITVVM) Caelabi, id est, non humana ulla manus, sed mea potentia effecit, ut isti oculi septem in isto globulo subito apparerent, hoc est, portentum illud, quo respiciunt verba supra 8.

ET AVFERAM INIQVITATEM TERRÆ IL- LIVS IN DIE VNA) Poenam omnem, id est, sterilitatem. De qua Aggaeus c. I. 6. 9. 10. 11.

## 3:10
Verse 10. A MAN SHALL CALL HIS NEIGHBOR UNDER THE VINE AND UNDER THE FIG TREE) A sign likewise of abundance and tranquility. 1 Kings 4:25.

Thus, while Grotius wishes to look to the material building with the Jews, he has devised another gloss. They explain: Behold I will engrave its engraving: Behold I am finishing the building, and putting the final hand to it: because then the work is completed, pictures, flowers, and fruits are added to it, which are carved and painted on the outermost surface, or certainly because by the help of God the openings and apertures of the stones remained not only unpolished, but joined and distinguished with the greatest beauty, as Castrius explains their opinion. Grotius, however, has again devised a new and wonderful gloss: rendering what is said in the future in the past: Behold I will engrave, that is, I have engraved the sculpture, or the engraving of the eyes on a tin globule, as he imagines, suddenly seen. I have engraved, that is, not any human hand, but my power brought it about that those seven eyes suddenly appeared on that globule. Which miracle he invented from his own ingenuity. Again, he takes the removal of the iniquity of the land as the removal of the punishment of sterility, by the idea of επιλύσει: and establishes a merely corporal promise of the fertility and tranquility of the land. Not only departing from the common consensus of the interpreters, but even twisting the text of the Holy Spirit into a completely foreign meaning. For the ancients, and the new, more recent ones, have accepted these with great consensus as a spiritual promise. Arias explained it concerning the spiritual temple of the Church: Behold I will engrave, that is, I will complete it in all its parts, I will adorn it with all the virtues of gems and pearls. Most others understand it concerning Christ, as for instance (1) concerning the body of Christ, formed and engraved by divine power in the womb of the virgin, or concerning the human nature of Christ adorned with various gifts, so that Christ might be placed as a foundation in the temple of the Church, or even concerning the manifestation of this adornment, that it was engraved with virtues: so that the Hebrew word may be rendered: I will open, i.e., I will make manifest its opening engraved with various gifts: which manifestation shone forth in the passion. Thus

Irenaeus, book III, chapter 28. This stone consists of earth and of power and of the art of God. It signifies, however, its origin in the virgin earth, but artfully carved by the power of the Holy Spirit. Thus also Lyranus, Dionysius, and others. Concerning which Cornelius à Lapide, p. 186. He alludes to the first stone of a temple or structure, which architects place with solemnity and pomp in the foundations, and thus begin the structure. Whence that first stone is accustomed to be inscribed with the insignia of the Prince who is the author of the structure: thus God inscribed his own insignia and coats of arms upon Christ, as the first stone of the Church, first in his incarnation, in which the Holy Spirit fashioned the body and soul of Christ with such perfection that that humanity seemed most elegantly turned and carved by God. Moreover, he adorned and carved it with all wisdom, power, grace, and glory, like a certain divine heaven, carved and distinguished with the sun, moon, and most beautiful stars. Finally, through the grace of the hypostatic union, he so adapted it to the Word that the humanity seemed to be like a gem most polishedly carved and adapted to the golden ring of the divinity of the Word. (2) Concerning the passion of Christ, that God wishes to carve the openings of his hands, feet, and side, and the openings of the wounds for the cleansing of sins. Which meaning Jerome, Haymo, Remigius, Rupert, and the more recent ones for the most part hold. Cyril also explains the version of the LXX concerning the passion of Christ, even if this deviates from the sources. However, the phrase confirms this interpretation (1) Behold I will carve a carving, or I am about to carve his sculpture: because in the passion he was to be carved, lacerated, and pierced, which is ascribed to God in Isaiah 53:8. For the transgression of my people I struck him. And indeed the head of Christ, and the whole body lacerated, the hands and feet pierced with nails, the side pierced with a lance, was such that from here and there he could be seen as sculpted and carved. (2) The cause of that sculpture: which was necessary, both that it might satisfy divine justice and sins might be expiated, and that this stone might turn out suitable to be placed into the foundation of faith and salvation. Therefore it is added, and I will take away the iniquity of that land. Which words do not signify the removal of sterility, or of any other punishment whatsoever, but the expiation of sins, by a received phrase of Scripture. Moreover, it is called the iniquity of that land, and is named primarily the land of Judah, because in it Joshua was performing the priesthood, and the people were occupied there already long ago with various sacrifices, signifying this one propitiatory sacrifice. (3.) That one day, on which all iniquity was to be taken away, corresponds to those times in which all sacrifices were performed, i.e. Since you have need of a daily repetition of sacrifices, according to the Levitical ceremonies, in the fullness of time I am about to take away all iniquity IN ONE DAY. That repetition and accumulation of sacrifices is an argument of imperfection. But then on the one day of the passion and death of the Messiah, the remission of sins will be acquired for the land of Judah, nay, for the whole world, and all iniquity will be expiated. On which day of the passion, towards evening, all things were consummated, John 19:30, and by one oblation Christ perfected those who are sanctified forever, Hebrews 10:14. Whence Blessed Tarnovius in this place. Because there is no expiation and remission of sins except through the death of Christ, since that effect is here subjected, we conclude with most other interpreters, and Jerome rather than with Junius, that the cause also in the preceding similitude, through the sculpture of his stone, is shadowed forth, since just as other things are accustomed to be adorned through sculpture, so also it is denoted here that by the same work God the Father, when he will give seven eyes to that elect and precious stone, will also be about to deposit all ornaments in it, and will be about to hand over the Spirit of justice, sanctification, and life without measure, and through him will be about to communicate the remission of sins and all ornaments with the Church, a metaphor drawn from builders carving polished stones, but cutting the rough and unpolished ones, so that they may be fit for the building. Blessed Luther had preceded in Tom. IV. Jen. Germ. Although Calvin laughs at and attacks this explanation: That argument is futile, that God carved carvings where the side of Christ was pierced, where his hands and feet were transfixed; this is to play, not to interpret Scripture seriously, but the Prophet understands by the sculpture the precious and excellent appearance of this stone, i.e., the Stone will be distinguished by every excellence. For God will polish it with wonderful sculptures. And furthermore, by the word 'one day' he notes suddenly: Yet he could not obtain assent from his fellow believers and disciples: nay, he was expressly refuted by Rudolph Gualther, although his name was suppressed: By the name of sculpture, or opening, he understands the passion and wounds of Christ, by whose merit our sins have been expiated, and eternal salvation has been procured for us. And thus most of the ancients interpret this passage, among whom D. Jerome wrote thus: I will cause that stone to be wounded by the nails of the cross and the soldier's lance. Nor do I think this too subtle, or that those who feel this way are playing in the Scriptures. For why should we not interpret this passage concerning the death of Christ, which explains the fruit of that death in express words, namely the remission of sins? Or what else could be understood by the sculpture, if it is a sin to understand the wounds? Therefore God says the same thing here through Zechariah that was shadowed forth in the desert through the type of the Rock opened by the stroke of Moses, and which John testifies to have been fulfilled in reality, when blood and water flowed from the pierced side of Christ. But God does not use such a locution rashly, by which he attributes all this to himself, while he says that he carved those wounds and opened the side of Christ. For it looks to the eternal decree of His providence, and heals the scandal which could arise from the ignominious death of Christ: lest, namely, the death of Christ should offend anyone, which He endured by the decree of the Father, that He might provide for the salvation of men. A similar passage is found in Acts IV. 27, 28. Thus Gualtherus: whose sense the Belgian Paraphrasts also praised. Coccejus indeed explains the engraving otherwise, but refers that one day to the passion of Christ: I will engrave his engravings, that is, I will carve in him his name. Hagg. II. 23. ושמתך כחותם I will set thee as a seal. A seal has a Χαρακτῆρα, or is a Χαρακτὴρ. The sense: I will give to Him a name above every name. I will demonstrate Him to be my Son: I will manifest Him by all signs; so that all my promises in Him may become yea and amen. Is. IX. 5, 6. Apoc. XIX. 16. The fruit of His manifestation with His χαρακτῆρσιν is righteousness. And, when I shall have engraved His engravings, so that all the signs of the Messiah may be in Him, and thus ὅταν τελειωθῇ διὰ παθημάτων I will wipe away the sin of that land in one day, that is, by a single sacrifice ἅπαξ. (4) The internal peace of conscience, and the external concord of the faithful are the fruits of the expiation of sins made through the passion of Christ: Whence the Prophet subjoins so great a spiritual good, explaining it by a political phrase, by which indeed temporal happiness is accustomed to be signified, in a manner solemn to the Prophets. Compare Eph. II. 4. Mich. IV. 3. Under the vine and fig tree of the Gospel. Rupertus, under the shadow of Christ, who is the true vine, Jerome and Remigius indicate that the faithful will invite one another. More simply it is said that an allusion is made to the times of Solomon II. Reg. IV. 24. which under the heavenly Solomon IN THAT DAY, that is, in the time of the N. T. (as that phrase is often received) when through the sculpture of Christ health, through the death of Christ life, through the chastisement peace is to be established for the pious, who are to live tranquilly and enjoy an abundance of all things, which, however, B. Tarnovius rightly warns must all be understood spiritually concerning tranquility of mind and spiritual goods, just as Is. II. 4. 5. Hos. II. 15. 18. 21. 22. ch. XIV. 5. 6. 7. Joel III. 18. Am. IX. 13. 14. 15. Mich. IV. 3. 4. ch. V. 4. 5. and of the souls: yet here it is described by a metaphor of earthly things. Namely, under the description of that time, when everyone enjoys their own goods quietly, and securely and safely, disturbed by no one: and dares to invite others also to the enjoyment of the same goods, and can do so safely I. Reg. IV. v. 24. Mich. IV. v. 4.

The Belgian Paraphrasts also acknowledge this, interpreting it spiritually in the same manner. Indeed, even Calvin himself, although he joins temporal happiness to it: The sum is: where God has openly made it known that He is the guardian of His Church, the faithful will be free and released from all fear, and cheerful, so that they may dare to feast under the vine and under the fig tree, that is, under the sky and in the public way: because, namely, there will be no one who will terrify them: But because this promise is extended to the whole Kingdom of Christ, this ought to be referred to the spiritual peace which we enjoy, when we are certainly persuaded that God is at peace with us: because then we are also reconciled among ourselves, so that we no longer strive to harm one another. Nor do the Pontifical interpreters Castrius, Cornel. à Lapide, Menochius, etc., depart from this. Moreover, that formula of speaking is explained in two ways in that regard, either because, as we said before, spiritual tranquility is expressed by the phrase of temporal peace, or because a particle of similitude ought to be understood, as B. Tarnovius rendered it: On that day you shall act in peace, no otherwise than if you were each calling your friend under your fig tree; and under your vine. For to the pious, a tranquil mind is like a continual feast Prov. XV. 15. Cf. Is. XXV. 6. 7. 8. Matth. XXII. 4. Luc. XIV. 17. Cocceius: The fullest sense will be, you shall no longer call one another to the Chair of Moses, so that you may sit before the feet of those who sit in it: nor shall you Jews only call Jews to the fruit of friendship; but everywhere without servitude you shall call anyone to the communion of brotherhood and the common worship of God, under the shade of the true vine of Christ, in whom every living branch bears fruit, and of His true fig tree, which both protects and feeds; until at last everyone may be able to be gathered in peace under their own vine and fig tree. There is no doubt that an allusion is being made to the times and fruits of earthly peace. To which the observation of Cocceius on Ps. CXXVIII. v. 3 contributes. The ancients were accustomed to attach vines and fig trees to walls, as is done even now. Hence to sit under one's vine and fig tree, i.e., to live privately, comfortably, and tranquilly.

Balt. Willius is singular in this promise κατά πάντα: which one may also observe here and there in his commentaries. For common things do not please him, and therefore he has repeatedly devised new glosses, out of a mere desire for singularity. He acknowledges that these verses are explained by almost all interpreters concerning Christ, the cornerstone of the Church: yet he agitates against this common sense: nor does he spare the interpretation of his master Calvin: He says that these seven eyes are explained either through the delirium of the Scholastics concerning the sevenfold grace, or concerning the abundance of the Spirit in the person of the Messiah. But such a manner of speaking, in his own judgment, is clearly unused in Scripture, and the interpretation of those who take these eyes to refer to the multitude of the faithful looking toward Christ is equally inconsistent: and he says it is of the same flour as what Calvin explains concerning the eyes of the stone, i.e., that the stone would not only turn the eyes of others toward itself, but would illuminate others and emit a splendor which could, by its reflection, direct men to the sight of it. For he says it is abhorrent to the manner of speaking in Scripture, and has no probability from any parallel passage.

Furthermore, he easily judges with Calvin that most of the ancients and Jerome interpret the engraving of the stone as the wounds of Christ with futile subtlety. He himself, however, renders this sense of the whole passage: Your companions are a sign with you with their care and labor, for the cornerstone which they themselves placed, this I myself have placed, the care which they themselves apply in the structure and ornamentation of the temple, this is my care, by which I take the most accurate account of that building, and intend to adorn it, so that at the same time I may destroy all the contrary thoughts and machinations of enemies, and present you in quiet and deepest peace. But this gloss newly devised by Willius is truly futile and insipid. For (1.) there is nothing about the companions of Joshua in these words: nor, because of the precarious ἀναλυσιν of Willius, which he preconceived in his own mind, can they be inserted into this text (2) That the companions of Joshua are a sign with him, with their care and labor, or in the fact that God Himself placed the stone which they themselves had placed, cannot be carved out of the text. For although it may be granted that Joshua with his companions are men of a sign in this sense also, as far as the restoration of the temple and the Priesthood is concerned, this must nevertheless be held concerning them, not so much because the continuation of the building of the temple and the reparation of the Priesthood is signified in them, as that by this work they signified the restoration of the Church and the true priesthood of the New Testament, as Castrius observes, with his contemporaries and friends, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael and Daniel, men of a sign according to the common sense of Jerome, Haimo, Remigius, etc. called so because they foreshadowed future things under the New Testament by their persons and deeds. Although others provide other reasons for that designation. Certainly, they are not called men of portent here for the sole reason that God builds the temple through Joshua and his associates. (3) Nor are the seven eyes upon the single stone to be understood as the eyes of the Lord’s providence over a material stone in the structure of the temple. For the eyes are indicated IN the stone, and indeed in that ONE singular stone, not eyes directed at the stone; the eyes, I say, of the stone, not the eyes of divine providence. (4) Nor is the Lord said to be about to engrave the engraving of the stone in this sense, that He Himself is the ornament of the material temple. That sense is merely precarious, and is rejected by the almost common consensus of the interpreters. Even if a similar phrase seems to be used regarding the ornamentation of stones in Exod. XXVIII. vers. 11, 36, XXXIX. v. 6, II Chron. II. 13, it is nevertheless assumed without proof here that the discourse is about a material stone. And was only one stone in the structure of the temple adorned? What then do they mean here by the single stone? (5) The discourse is not about the destruction of the thoughts and machinations of enemies in hindering the structure of the temple, nor about quiet and temporal peace, but about the taking away of the iniquity of the land, and about the tranquility and spiritual peace which is the consequence of the removal of sin. (6) How was the iniquity of the land taken away IN ONE DAY, unless the day of the Lord’s passion and death is understood, as it is by most interpreters? (7) What of the fact that Willius himself acknowledges that the words in that day shall every man call his neighbor under the vine and under the fig tree denote the deep peace of the Gospel, which the peace of Solomon prefigured, and that this is evident from Micah IV. 4, nay, that the text expressly argues that there is a mystical meaning here, and he confesses that the phrase seems to be used of the day of the New Testament for the sake of revealing the mystery, why then does he disparage that sense? (8) There is no reason why Willius should find anything lacking in the sense or connection of the words, according to the common interpretation: What is that sense, he says, if you call Christ a stone: Behold Christ, whom I place before my providence, is adorned and cared for? What connection, or what explanation: I bring my servant the branch, because the stone, that is, that Christ is cared for by me before Joshua? Resp. The sense holds good, whether you call the stone Joshua as specifically signified, or typified, or placed before Joshua as a type, whether you understand it as following after Joshua, as others explain the phrase, or whether you take it as a material stone, as a sign of that UNIQUE stone, upon which there shall be seven eyes, namely Christ, and in the first place the material stone is called the unique and singular stone, truly μονότροπος (the thing signified), is to be understood. But that the providence of God is not to be understood by the seven eyes, but the multiform gifts of Christ, and that the ornamentation of the stone is not to be designated by the engraving, but the passion of Christ, has been previously noted. That this explanation coheres perfectly with the promise concerning the bringing of the branch, the righteous servant of God, everyone understands. For this foundational stone, having been marked, was to be furnished with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, to bear the care of the Church, and to be placed as the foundation of the Church, having been well engraved by the Lord in his passion, by which the sins of the whole world were to be expiated, so that we might enjoy solid peace and tranquility. Nor does the passage in Zech. IV. 10 help Willius. For there Willius assumed without foundation that the seven eyes are to be understood as the providence of God.

Latin:

Vers. 10. VOCABIT VIR AMICUM SVVM SUB- TER VITEM ET SVBTER FICUM) Signum pariter ubertatis & tranquillitatis. I. Regum IV. 25.

Ita cum Judaeis quidem materiale aedificium respi- ci vult Grotius, sed aliam glossam excogitavit. Illi exponunt: Ecce ego caelo caelaturam ejus: Ecce ego per- ficio aedificium, & ultimam ei manum impono: quia tunc absolvitur opus, ei adjiciuntur picturae, flo- res & poma, quae sculpuntur & pinguntur in extre- ma superficie, vel certe quia Dei ope orificia & a- perturae lapidum non solum impolita, sed maxima pulchritudine compacta, & distincta manserunt, ut eorum mentem exponit Castrius. Grotius vero novam iterum & mirabilem excogitavit glossam: quod in futuro dicitur, in praeterito reddens: Ecce ego caelabo, id est, caelavi sculpturam, vel caelatum de oculis in globulo stanneo, uti fingit, subito conspectis. Caelavi, id est, non humana ulla manus, sed mea po- tentia effecit, ut isti oculi septem in isto globulo subito apparerent. Quod miraculum de suo ingenio con- finxit. Rursus ablationem iniquitatis terrae, de abla- tione poenae sterilitatis, idia επιλύσει accipit: & me- re corporalem promissionem ubertatis & tranquil- litatis terrae statuit. Non tantum a communi In- terpp. consensu discedens, sed textumetiam Spiri- tus Sancti in alienam plane sententiam detorquens. Magno enim consensu haec accepere veteres, & novi recentiores ceu spiritualem promissionem. Arias de templo spirituali Ecclesiae exposuit: Ecce ego caelabo, hoc est, omnibus numeris absolvam, omnibus gemmarum unionumque virtutibus exornabo. Caete- ri plerique de Christo intelligunt, utpote (1) de cor- pore Christi, divina virtute in utero virginis forma- to ac caelato, vel de humana Christi natura dotibus variis exornata, ut Christus, ceu basis in templo Ecclesiae collocaretur, aut etiam de manifestatio- ne hujus ornatus, quod virtutibus caelata sit: ut ita verbum Ebraeum reddatur: Ego aperiam, i. e. manifestam faciam ejus aperturam caelatam variis donis: quae manifestatio enituerit in passione. Sic

Iren. l. III. c. 28. Hic lapis è terra & ex virtute, & arte constat Dei. Significat autem in terra virgine ortum, sed virtute Spiritus S. artificiose cælatum. Sic etiam Lyranus, Dionysius, alii. De quo Corne- lius à Lapide p. 186. Alludit ad primum templi vel fabricæ lapidem, quem architecti cum solemnitate & pompa in fundamentis ponunt, itaque fabricam inchoant. Unde lapis ille primus solet insignibus Principis, qui fabricæ est autor, insculpi: ita Chri- sto, quasi lapidi primo Ecclesiæ, Deus sua insignia & stemmata insculpsit, primo in ejus incarnatione, in qua Spiritus Sanctus Christi corpus, & animam tanta perfectione elaboravit, ut humanitas illa à Deo elegantissime tornata & cælata videretur. In- super eandem ornavit, & cælavit omni sapientia, virtute, gratia & gloria, quasi cœlum quoddam di- vinum, sole, luna & stellis pulcherrimis cælatum & distinctum. Denique per gratiam unionis hyposta- ticæ ita eam verbo adaptavit, ut videretur huma- nitas esse quasi gemma politissime cælata, & ada- ptata annulo aureo divinitatis verbi. (2) De passio- ne Christi, quod cælare velit Deus aperturas ma- nuum, pedum, & lateris ejus, & aperturas vulnera in emundationem peccatorum. Quem sensum Hieronymus, Haymo, Remigius, Rupertus, & recen- tiores maximam partem tenent. De passione Chri- sti etiam explicat Cyrillus versionem LXX. etsi hæc à fontibus declinet. Hanc autem interpretationem confirmat phrasis (1) Ecce ego cælabo cælaturam, vel sculpturus sum sculpturam ejus: quia in passione sculpendus, lacerandus, ac confodiendus fuit, quod Deo adscribitur Es. LIII. 8. Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum. Et sane caput Christi, ac corpus to- tum laceratum, manus ac pedes clavis pertusi, latus perfossum lancea ita fuit, ut hinc inde sculptus ac cælatus videri potuerit. (2) Causa istius sculpturæ: qua opus fuit, tum ut justitiæ divinæ satisfaceret, ac peccata expiarentur, tum ut lapis hic idoneus evaderet, ut in fundamentum fidei ac salutis pone- retur. Ideo additur, & auferam iniquitatem terræ illius. Quæ verba non ablationem sterilitatis, aut alius cujuscunque pœnæ, sed expiationem pecca- torum, phrasi Scripturæ recepta, important. Dici- tur autem iniquitas terræ istius, & nominatur im- primis terra Judæ, quia in illa Sacerdotio fungeba- tur Josua, & occupabatur populus ibi jam olim variis sacrificiis, hoc unicum sacrificium propitia- torium significantibus. (3.) Dies illa una, qua au- ferenda omnis iniquitas, respondet istis tempori- bus, quibus omnia sacrificia peragebantur, q. d. Quum opus habeatis repetitione sacrificiorum quotidiana, juxta Leviticas ceremonias, in tem- poris plenitudine UNA DIE omnem iniquita- tem ablaturus sum. Illa repetitio & cumulatio sa- crificiorum argumentum est imperfectionis. Tum autem in die una passionis & mortis Messiæ acqui- retur terræ Judæ, imo orbi toti remissio peccato- rum, & expiabitur omnis iniquitas. Qua die passio- nis sub vesperam omnia consummata sunt Joh. XIX. 30. & una oblatione consummavit Christus san- ctificatos in sempiternum Ebr. X. 14. Unde B. Tar- novius in h. l. Quia nulla expiatio, & remissio pecca- torum sit, nisi per mortem Christi, cum ille effectus hic subjicitur, etiam causam in præcedenti simili- tudine, per sculpturam lapidis ejus, adumbrari, cum plerisque aliis interpretibus, ac Hieronymo potius concludimus, quam cum Iunio, quod, quemadmo- dum per sculpturam alias res solet exornari, ita etiam hic denotetur, quod eadem opera Deus Pa- ter, quando septem oculos dabit illi electo ac pre- tioso lapidi, etiam omnia ornamenta in eo deposi- turus, ac sine mensura traditurus sit Spiritum justi- tiæ, sanctificationis ac vitæ, ac per eum remissio- nem peccatorum, ornamentaque omnia cum Ec- clesia communicaturus, metaphora ducta à stru- ctoribus Lapides politos sculptentibus, rudes vero ac impolitos cædentibus, ut sint apti ædificio. Præ- iverat B. Lutherus Tom. IV. Jen. Germ. Quam ex- plicationem etsi rideat Calvinus, atque exagitet: Argutia illa futilis est, quod Deus sculpsit sculptu- ras, ubi perfossum fuit latus Christi, ubi transfixæ fue- runt eius manus ac pedes, hoc est ludere, non serio in- terpretari Scripturam, sed Propheta per sculpturam intelligit pretiosam & eximiam speciem hujus lapi- dis, q. d. erit Lapis insignis omni præstantia. Deus enim mirabilibus sculpturis expoliet. Et porro die uno notatrepente: Non tamen à suis contribulibus & discipulis assensum impetrare potuit: imo à Rud. Gualthero diserte, suppresso licet nomine, refuta- tus fuit: Sculpturæ, vel apertionis nomine Christi passionem & vulnera intelligit, quorum merito pecca- ta nostra expiata sunt, & salus æterna nobis parta est. Et ita locum istum plerique veterum interpretan- tur, inter quos D. Hieronymus sic scripsit: Istum la- pidem clavis crucis & lancea militis faciam vulne- rari. Neque hoc argutum nimis puto, vel quod in Scripturis ludant, qui ita sentiunt. Cur enim non de morte Christi hunc locum interpretemur, qui mortis illius fructum verbis disertis explicat, pec- catorum scilicet remissionem? Vel quid aliud per sculpturam intelligi poterit, si vulnera intelligere nefas est? Idem ergo hic dicit per Zachariam Deus, quod in deserto per typum Petræ adictum Mosis a- pertæ fuit adumbratum, & quod reipsa impletum fuisse Johannes testatur, quando ex Christi latere perfosso sanguis & aqua manavit. Non temere au- tem tali locutione utitur Deus, qua hoc omne sibi tribuit, dum se vulnera illa sculpsisse, & Christi la- tus aperuisse ait. Respicit enim ad æternum suæ providentiæ decretum, & scandalo medetur, quod ex morte Christi ignominiosa oriri poterat : ne quem scilicet mors Christi offendat, quam ex Pa- tris decreto sustinuit, ut saluti hominum consule- ret. Similis locus habetur Act. IV. 27. 28. Hæc Gual- therus: quem sensum etiam laudarunt Paraphrastæ Belgici. Coccejus explicat quidem aliter cælaturam, at unum diem illum ad passionem Christi refert: Cæ- labo cælaturas ejus, hoc est, exarabo in ipso nomen ejus. Hagg. II. 23. ושמתך כחותם ponam te ut sigil- lum. Sigillum habet Χαρακτῆρα, vel est Χαρακτὴς. Sensus: Dabo ipsi nomen supra omne nomen. Demon- strabo eum esse Filium meum: omnibus signis eum ma- nifestabo; ita ut omnes promissiones meæ in ipso fiant ne & amen. Es. IX. 5. 6. Apoc. XIX. 16. Fructus pate- factionis ipsius cum suis χαρακτῆρσιν est justitia. Et, quum cælavero cælaturas ejus, ita ut omnia si- gna Messiæ in ipso sint, atque adeo ὅταν τελειωθῇ διὰ παθημάτων abstergam peccatum terræ illius uno die, id est, unico sacrificio ἅπαξ. (4) Pax interna conscientiæ, & concordia externa fidelium fructus sunt expiationis peccatorum per Christi passionem factæ : Unde subjungit Propheta tantum bonum spirituale, phrasi politica, exponens, qua nempe temporalis felicitas significari consuevit more Pro- phetis solemni. Confer. Ef. II. 4. Mich. IV. 3. Sub- ter vitem & ficum Evangelii. Rupertus, subter um- bram Christi, qui est vitis vera, Hieronymus & Re- migius sese mutuo invitaturos fideles indicant. Simplicius dicitur allusionem fieri ad tempora Salo- monis II. Reg. IV. 24. quod sub cœlesti Salomone IN DIE ILLA, id est, N. T. tempore (uti phra- sis illa sæpe accipitur) quando per Christi sculptu- ram sanitas, per Christi mortem vita, per castiga- tionem pax est piis instituenda, tranquille acturi, omniumque rerum abundantia perfruituri sint fi- deles, quæ tamen omnia spiritualiter de tranquilli- tate animi ac bonis spiritualibus accipienda esse recte monet B. Tarnovius, sicut Es. II. 4. 5. Hos. II. 15. 18. 21. 22. c. XIV. 5. 6. 7. Joel III. 18. Am. IX. 13. 14. 15. Mich. IV. 3. 4. c. V. 4. 5. Quod agnoscit Lamb. Danæus: Hæc vero pax licet vere spiritualis sit & animorum : tamen hic rerum terrenarum meta- phora describitur. Nempe sub illius temporis descri- ptione, quum quilibet suis bonis quiete, & secure & tuto fruitur, à nemine interturbatus : & ad eorundem bonorum fruitionem alios quoque invitare audet, & potest tuto I. Reg. IV. v. 24. Mich. IV. v. 4.

Agnoscunt quoque Paraphrastæ Belgici, ad eun- dem modum spiritualiter interpretantes. Imo etiã Calvinus ipse, etsi temporalem conjungat felicita- tem: Summa est : ubi Deus palam fecerit se custo- dem esse Ecclesiæ suæ, fideles omni metu vacuos & so- lutos hilares fore, ita ut epulari audeant sub vite & sub ficu, hoc est, sub cælo & in via publica : quoniam scilicet non erit, qui ipsos exterreat : Quia vero exten- ditur hæc promissio ad totum Christi Regnum, referri hoc debet ad pacem spiritualem, qua fruimur, ubi certo persuasi sumus Deum nobis esse pacatum : quia tunc etiam inter nos reconciliamur, ut alii aliis nocere amplius non studeant. Neque abeunt Interpp. Pon- tificii Castrius, Cornel. à Lapide, Menochius &c. Duobus autem modis ea ratione formula illa lo- quendi explicatur, vel quod phrasi, ut antea dixi- mus, temporalis pacis expressa sit spiritualis tran- quillitas, vel quod subintelligi debeat particula si- militudinis, uti reddidit B. Tarnovius : Die illo age- tis vos in pace, non secus ac si vocaretis quisque ami- cum suum sub ficum; & sub vitem vestram. Piis e- nim tranquillus animus est velut juge convivium Prov. XV. 15. Conf. Es. XXV. 6. 7. 8. Matth. XXII. 4. Luc. XIV. 17. Coccejos : Plenissimus sensus erit, non vocabitis amplius unus alterum ad Cathedram Mo- sis, ut coram pedibus illorum sedeatis, qui in illa se- dent: neq; tantum Iudæi Iudæos vocabitis ad fructum amicitiæ ; sed ubivis sine servitute quemvis ad com- munionem fraternitatis & communem cultum Dei vocabitis, sub umbraculo veræ vitis Christi, in quo o- mnis vivus palmes fructum fert, & veræ ficus ejus- dem, qui & protegit & cibat; donec tandem in pace sub vite & ficu quisque sua congregari possint. Allu- sionem fieri ad tempora & fructus pacis terrenæ nullũ est dubium. Quo facit observatio Coccei in Ps. CXXVIII. v. 3. Solebant veteres vites ficusq; adjun- gere parietibus, ut & nunc fit. Hinc sedere sub vite, & ficu sua h. e privatim commode & tranquille vivere.
