But the same person speaks thus of Jehovah in verse 7: 'And he also shall be a remnant for OUR GOD.'

But who is that Jehovah, who acknowledges Jehovah as his God, if not the Son of God, whose coming is predicted in verse 9? For he, according to the flesh, acknowledges God as his Lord, John XX. 17. Coccejus agrees, l. c. 'To our God.' Words of the first person precede and follow, which befit God alone. It is therefore fitting that the words of the divine person be understood here, who is sent by God the Father, and because of the command which he received from him to be carried out in human nature, he calls him, together with Israel, his God. Compare Micah VII. 17. For to posit a parenthesis, that these words are the Prophet's, seems too erratic. But in the following verse 9, God the Father is introduced as speaking, because he speaks of the coming King Christ, and he continues that discourse until the end of chapter X. For that the Son of God introduced this speaker, whom the Prophet previously called the Angel of the Lord speaking in him, and taught to be Jehovah, the clause in chapter X, verse 12, testifies: 'I WILL STRENGTHEN THEM IN JEHOVAH (the Son of God) and they shall walk in his name, says JEHOVAH, God the Father.' Therefore God the Father said all these things, whence from verse 9 of chapter IX he was introduced by the Son of God, having used this discourse, which the Prophet described from that place until the end of chapter X. But those words, 'now I have seen with my eyes,' the Son of God still speaks in his own person, and by them testifies that he has looked upon the miseries and pressures of the people, which they had sustained from their neighbors, and thus would henceforth undertake the defense of the same. Conf. Ex. II. 25, ch. III. 7. In this sense these words of the Lord were also understood by Theodoret, Lyranus, and others. Cocceius infers more from this passage on page 522. This passage of Zechariah testifies that God himself had to be born among the Jews, and be tempted by common afflictions, and by that very fact the people were to be free from servitude and distress, so that they might neither serve the elements of the world, nor dread exactions. Up to this point, however, the house of God was to be guarded by the Son of God with divine protection. All the following things are directed to the same end. All prophecies predict similar things. These, moreover, are truths of the greatest importance. For it is also evident from these things that Christ is the true God worshipped in the Temple by the Israelites, and the preserver of it, and that he was exhibited because he had to come while the temple was still guarded and he had to experience the sufferings of the people: and by that fact the people were made free: namely, as from the accusation of sin, so also from subjection to an earthly inheritance and the fear of death, and furthermore from the servitude of the elements of the world according to the ceremonial law, and the yoke of the elders, and dread in afflictions, so that they might even glory in them.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET CIRCUMDABO DOMUM MEAM EX HIS QVI MILITANT MIHI EUNTES ET RE- VERTENTES) Castra metabor circa domum meam contra exercitum, contra euntes & revertentes. Id est, dabo Ange- los qui custodiant Templum, ne aut ab hoste obsideri pos- sit, aut etiam incursibus infestari. Magna & minora peri- cula Templo avertam, nempe ad tempora usque An- tiochi.

ET NON TRANSIBIT SUPER EOS ULTRA EXACTOR) Id est, tyrannus, ut hic Chaldæus: nam mos est tyrannorum tributis populum opprimere.

Quia præcedentia de conversione gentium lo- quuntur, quæ tempore Nov. Test. futura erat, pro- missio hæc non restringenda præcise ad templum Zorobabelis, sed ad Ecclesiam Domini referenda, quæ domus Dei viventis I. Tim. III. 15. dicitur, cui pollicetur Deus ex illo tempore defensionem ad- versus vim hostium & præsidium S. angelorum Pf. XXXIV. 8. Alludere autem videtur ad templum in quo Levitæ & Sacerdotes excubias agebant. Vid. Pf. CXXXIV. adeoque se ipsum immediate & per angelos suos protecturum tunc & futuris tempo- ribus Ecclesiam suam promittit. Non ergo exclu- dimus hic tempora illa, quibus vicinæ gentes cla- des perpessuræ erant, Syri, Phœnices, Palæstini, sed includimus, quod nempe tum castra metaturus sit circa Ecclesiam suam Dominus, ne etiam populus suus cladibus istis involvatur, atque ita deinceps perpetuo protecturus sit Ecclesiam suam, ut op- primatur ab exactore. Chaldæus paraphrastes hæc ita illustrat: Et habitare faciam majestatem gloriæ meæ in domo sanctuarii mei, & fortitudo brachii po- tentiæ meæ erit, sicut murus ignis, in circuitu ejus, pro- pter transeuntes & redeuntes. Castra metatur Do- minus propter exercitum, propter transeuntes, & propter redeuntes,h.e. propter hostiles exercitus, & eorum excursiones, ET NON PERVADET EOS AMPLIUS EXACTOR, quod de libera- tione à maledictione legis, ac tyrannide Diaboli nonnulli intelligunt; sed uti cætera de defensione adversus vim hostium loquuntur, ita hic per נגש EXACTOR vel OPPRESSOR quilibet intelli- gitur. Conf. Ef. XIV. 2. 7. Zach. X. 4. Non am- plius Ecclesiam hostium violentiæ & direptioni- bus exponendam.

Vers. eod.

QUIA NUNC VIDI IN OCULIS MEIS) Quia nunc (id est, antehac) oculis meis vidi. Id est, apparet mihi multas vicinas esse gentes, quæ Templum invaderent ho- stiliter, aut prædonum more diriperent, nisi ego miris mo- dis obstarem.

Ebraismus est, pro vidi oculis meis. Nonnulli de Propheta exponunt. Sed verba sunt Filii Dei, quem hic loqui è collatione v. 6. 7. 8. constat. Nam qui vers. 6. dicit exscindam fastum Philistæorum, & v. 8. castra metabor ad domum meam, sine dubio Jeho- vah verus Deus est. Idem autem de Jehovah ita lo- quitur v. 7. Residuus autem fiet etiam ipse DEO

NOSTRO. Quis vero ille Jehovah, qui Jehovam Deum suum agnoscit, nisi Filius Dei, cujus adven- tus v. 9. prædicitur. Nam is secundum carnem a- gnoscit Deum Dominum suum Joh. XX. 17. Con- sonat Coccejus l. c. Deo nostro. Antecedunt & se- quuntur verba primæ personæ, quæ soli Deo conve- niunt. Conveniens igitur est, ut hic intelligantur ver- ba personæ divinæ, quæ mittitur à Deo Patre, & pro- pter mandatum, quod ab illo accepit peragendum in natura humana eum vocat una cum Israele Deum suum. Confer. Mich. VII. 17. Nam parenthesin statue- re, ut Prophetæ hæc verba sint, videtur nimis desulto- rum. Sequenti autem v. 9. loquens introducitur Deus Pater, quia loquitur de adventuro Rege Christo, & continuat illam orationem usque ad fi- nem cap. X. Nam quod hunc loquentem introdu- xerit Filius Dei, quem antea Angelum Domini lo- quentem in se nuncupavit, & Jehovam esse docuit Propheta, clausula c. X. v. 12. testatur, CONFOR- TABO EOS IN JEHOVAH (Filio Dei) & in nomine ejus ambulabunt, dicit JEHOVAH, Deus Pater. Hæc ergo omnia Deus Pater dixit, un- de à v. 9. c. IX. à Filio Dei introductus, hac usus o- ratione, quam Propheta ex illo loco ad finem us- que c. X. descripsit. Ista autem verba, nunc vidi ocu- lis meis ex persona propria adhuc loquitur Filius Dei, iisdemque testatur, se respexisse miserias, & pressuras populi, quas à vicinis sustinuerat, adeo- que deinceps defensionem ejusdem suscepturum Conf. Ex. II. 25. c. III. 7. Quo sensu hæc verba Do- mini etiam accepere Theodoreus, Lyranus & alii. Coccejus plura ex hoc loco infert pag. 522. Zacha- riæ hic locus testatur, Deum ipsum debuisse nasci in- ter Judæos, & tentari communibus afflictionibus, & eo ipso populum à servitute & angustia liberum futu- rum fuisse, ut nec serviant elementis mundi, neque exactiones exhorrescant. Huc usque autem divino præsidio domum Dei à Filio Dei custodiendam fuisse. Omnia sequentia eodem aurigantur. Omnes prophetiæ similia prædicant. Sunt autem eæ veri- tates maximi momenti. Nam & ex iis constat, Chri- stum esse verum Deum adoratum in Templo ab Israelitis, & conservatorem illius, & eum exhibi- tum esse, quia venire debuerit templo adhuc cu- stodito & eum debuisse experiri passiones populi: & ea re factum esse populum librum: nempe ut à peccati accusatione, ita & à subjectione in terre- nam hæreditatem & timorem mortis, & porro à servitute elementorum mundi secundum legem ceremonialem. & jugo seniorum, & pavore in af- flictionibus, ut in eis etiam gloriari possent.

## 9:9
Verse 9. REJOICE GREATLY) In the Hebrew: Exceedingly.

BEHOLD THY KING SHALL COME TO THEE JUST) It can be best translated, he comes: namely, when he was coming from Babylon. For the Hebrews very often express past events with future verbs, which are taken for present ones, and the passage pertains in its first and most obvious sense to Zerubbabel, who is called King also in Jer. XXIII. 5 and Ezek. XXXVII. 22, 24, naturally, because although he did not assume a royal name or royal pomp, lest he offend the King of the Persians, he was nevertheless so honored and observed by his own people, because of the descent he drew from David, as if he were King. Rabbi Solomon acknowledges, however, that these things are referred to the Messiah in a more sublime sense. But Aben Ezra says he doubts which of the two Messiahs this should be understood of: for when they saw a double state of the Messiah described, one despised, the other glorious, they made two Messiahs out of these, of whom they call the one the son of Joseph, the other the son of David, and most Jews refer these things indeed to the Messiah son of Joseph. But the most learned Rabbi Saadia Gaon says to Daniel that the same one is treated here who is denoted in Ps. LXXII and Dan. VII. 4. He, however, is the triumphant Messiah, as they themselves confess. Just, that is, equitable, a lover of his country, not a tyrant, of the kind just discussed.

AND SAVIOR) It is strange that not only the Latin but also the Greek and Chaldean versions have agreed in this, that the savior they might translate the matter: for in the Hebrew it is read נושׁע. Either therefore it was written נושׁיע in better Codices than those which the Masoretes used, or (which is strange) they all agreed in this, that they believed the passive was put for the active, just as נדברו is taken in Psalm CXIX. 23. Zorobabel was a savior of the people in his own way, and for a time, namely by a just government; Christ perfectly, and forever.

POOR) Without a retinue and royal pomp, for the reason which we have stated, the crown itself having been placed upon him for the sake of appearance, it did not remain in his possession, but was carried into the Temple.

AND RIDING UPON AN ASS, AND UPON A COLT THE FOAL OF AN ASS) And, for, that is: and in the Hebrew ועל־עיר is an ass, so that it can rightly be translated, riding on an ass, that is, a colt born of asses: not a mule, but an ass plainly, as much from the father as from the mother. That signified not only his modesty, but also his zeal for peace: for horses are armed for war. The ass is an animal of peace. The following things illustrate that.

The detestable interpretation of the most illustrious prophecy concerning Christ, which Grotius received from Theodore of Mopsuestia, who Judaized and Ebionized. For he also asserts that this king is Zorobabel, having been condemned on that account by Vigilius in the Roman Synod. The Jews explain it concerning Judas Maccabeus, so that they are not forced to acknowledge our Messiah predicted here. Grotius therefore brings aid to the perfidious Jews, while he denies that these things speak of Christ according to the letter. Which is also done by those who foolishly understand Alexander the Great coming honorably to Jerusalem and venerating the High Priest Jaddus. But that the Prophet speaks of no one else than the Messiah, according to the letter, these things confirm. First, since the scope of the Prophet was to exhort to the building of the temple, there is no doubt that this prediction concerning the coming of the Messiah, who was to enter the temple with solemn pomp in order to illuminate it with the reformation of doctrine and the glory of miracles, and thence to propagate his Church throughout the world, agrees with it primarily. Furthermore, since a promise was made concerning the excision of the people's enemies, the conversion of the nations, and the defense of the Church, now the prophecy is instituted concerning the coming of the Messiah, through whom the conversion of the nations is procured and the salvation and defense of the Church is provided, and lest they should think of worldly tranquility and earthly dominion, the Messiah is presented as a humble and unarmed king, and the condition of his kingdom is declared. Willius exhibits the summary thus, p. 304. Although you are not always to enjoy deep peace, but will often feel calamities, you ought not therefore to call into doubt the divine promise concerning the care and protection of you, nor to despond in your spirits from excessive grief, but rather to exult with joy and jubilate, on account of the coming of the Messiah the King, who will provide for you perfect salvation and liberation from all evils. For you are not to expect such a state or such a kingdom, in which the Messiah asserts you to eternal happiness and lifts you above the nations by an earthly arm and power, but a spiritual and humble kingdom, despised by the world, in which justice and eternal salvation are communicated to the meek in spirit and the peace of conscience, exhilarating the saints in my afflictions and calamities, is erected by the power of the Word and the Spirit, as much among the nations as among the Jews. Therefore, with respect to this salvation, it is fitting that you be perpetually cheerful, and that you oppose this condition of the kingdom and spiritual peace to all the afflictions that touch you. Calvin says: that the Prophet shows the manner of restoring the Church, because, namely, a King will again emerge from the tribe and family of David, who may restore all things to their original order. For since things were still collapsed among the Jews, he testifies that the Prophet did not speak in vain long ago concerning the coming of the Redeemer, but that one must hope well, until those prophecies are fulfilled in their own time.

Secondly, that huge exultation, concerning which the Prophet speaks, EXULT GREATLY, JUBILATE (by which words not a simple and vulgar but a singular joy is noted, to which the daughter of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem is excited, i.e., the citizens of the Jewish Church, all the faithful, who are accustomed to be designated by this name) had its fulfillment not in Zorobabel, but in Christ. Whence we conclude: The Prophet speaks of the coming of him whom the daughter of Zion accepted as he was coming with the greatest exultation and congratulation, and ought to have accepted, but he was not Zorobabel, concerning whom nothing of the sort is read, but Christ, concerning whom the Evangelists report.

Thirdly, that huge exultation demands a new and notable cause of joy, such as is not the entry of Zorobabel, or the coming of Alexander the Great or Judas Maccabeus. Zorobabel was certainly already present to them, he was already intent upon the work of building the temple, whence his coming could not be predicted as future, nor did they have need to be excited to receive him with joy. But to take the future for the past, neither does any necessity compel, nor is it agreeable to the text. For they could not be excited or invited to that which had passed, if indeed it had already passed. But here they are excited and invited to receive that King of theirs who is about to enter with joy. Wherefore these things are foolishly snatched away to Zorobabel. But when it is a matter of the Messiah and his benefits, such exhortations are solemn. See Ps. II. 11. Ps. XLVII. 2. 7. Ps. LVIII. 5. Ps. XCVI. Ps. XCVII. Ps. XCVIII. Ps. XCIX. Ps. 100. Is. 12. 4. ch. 49. 13. ch. 54. Coccejus is not bad here: The ἐγκελευστικὴ apostrophe has this simple notion, that God, upon the coming of Christ, will not only notify the Church of its duty, which is to rejoice, etc. But will also bring it about that He is received with joy and jubilation. It was done so, and indeed in such a circumstance as the Prophet describes here, Matt. 21. 8. 9. 11. 15. And Christ, from Ps. 8, instituted a defense for the children, showing that this is a divine efficacy in children. And Luke 19. 40, he asserts that this is so necessary to be done, that the stones would rather speak than that Christ should not have this jubilation. Yet this ought not to be taken only concerning that temporary reception of Christ, by which the omnipotence of Christ was signally demonstrated: but also concerning the faith, by which the Church was to receive Christ as King at all times. See John 10. 26. 27. and John 6. 37. This is Coccejus. Zorobabel was never a King, nor was he ever called by that name in the sacred writings. For as to those passages which Grotius cites, it is manifest that they are impiously twisted to Zorobabel as well, when they speak of no one other than the Messiah. Judas Maccabaeus was not a King, and Alexander, although he was a King, could not be called a King in Sion. Cornel. à Lapide thus compares and harmonizes the preceding: The Messiah or Christ will come, so that he may subject to himself the four chariots, that is, the Monarchies, of which he spoke in chapter 6, and consequently Tyre, Gaza, Azotus, and all of Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria, of which he treated in this chapter. For all kings and kingdoms end in the kingdom of Christ, as Daniel predicted in chapter 2. 44. and Zechariah here. Whence he adds: I will destroy the chariot, etc.

Fourthly, Coccejus not irrelevantly observes that Scripture uses the word WILL COME throughout concerning the ἐπιδημία (advent) of the Son of God, as for instance Hab. 2. 3. Ezek. 21. 27. Gen. 49. 10. Ps. 118. 26. Mal. 3. 3. And it corresponds to τὸ ἔρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν κόσμον (the coming into the world) John 1. 9. 11. Matt. 11. 3. John 4. 25. 6. 14. 9. 39. A synonym elsewhere is, to come from God, to come from above, to have descended from heaven.

Fifthly, that description of this King does not fit Zorobabel, but uniquely the Messiah: He is called first King in Sion and Jerusalem. That this is truly understood of the Messiah is clear from similar passages Ps. II. 6. Ps. LXXII. 1. seqq. Ps. CX. 2. Jer. IX. 6. Jer. XXIII. 6. Dan. VI. 14. 27. Mich. IV. 7. c. V. 3. but that this is to be understood of Zerubbabel, there is no testimony of Scripture. Secondly, the King who is to come is called JUST, which name, taken κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence), uniquely befits King Messiah, the just branch of David, which is said to work justice and judgment in the land Jer. XLIII. 6. Es. LIII. 11. Zach. II. 2. Who is just not only in himself, and as regards his own person, but also for Us! HE SHALL COME TO THEE JUST, to whom he gives his own justice I. Cor. I. 29. II. Cor. V. 21. But indeed, neither Zerubbabel nor any other ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (mere man) is called JUST so absolutely, that he is designated by that name as if it were his own and perpetual one. That gloss, that just is equitable, Φιλόπατρις (patriot), is colder than ice itself. Thirdly, that King is called נוֹשָׁע SAVED, which again is not to be understood in a common way, for thus there is no one who might not at some time be in need of salvation, or be said to have been saved from some danger. But since this name is singularly appropriated to this King, ἐξαιρέτως & μονοτρόπως (exceptionally and uniquely), it is not without reason understood of him who was saved before others and above others, in whom, and on account of whom, all others are deservedly said to be saved, i.e., of our Messiah, in whom alone is the salvation of all Act. IV. 12. For he, although he is our savior by reason of merit and efficacy, yet he himself first had to be saved from death and hell, so that he might deliver and save us from the death and hell into which he immersed himself for the sake of our salvation. For unless he himself had suffered death and undergone the infernal punishment for us, and had been saved from it, it would have been all over with the salvation of us all. Some render it ENDUED WITH SALVATION, and observe with Drusius: that participles of the passive voice, when they become nouns, denote an action, and that it is not unusual for Scripture to use passive forms actively, as Es. LXII. 11: Behold thy salvation comes, behold his reward is with him, where by salvation they understand the savior, and by reward the good things which he bestows upon others. Thus they have actively interpreted the Chaldean פָּרִיק Redeemer, savior, and the LXX σώζων saving. Which sense Villius prefers, because the Apostles also retained the active voice in the Evangelical history, in which, however, his memory deceived him. For in the Evangelical history, that word is not repeated by Matthew, ch. XXI, nor by John, ch. XII. Cornelius à Lapide wishes it not to be a participle, but a noun, signifying actively the same thing as Jesus, so that the letter Nun is Hæmantic, as in Naphthali, Nimrod, which is to be noted against Grotius, who pretends that the word was corrupted by the Jews, contrary to the Masora, as we have said elsewhere. But the passive meaning is more convenient for the text. For it is a question here of the state of emptying himself, and the entry into Jerusalem, of Christ about to undergo his passion. But Coccejus, p. 524, more correctly: In that being saved, τὸ נוֹשָׁע, the savior is contained. He is called saved, because he is snatched from his passions and death. But by this very fact we also are saved in him, as our head, and his perfect merit is manifested to us. Hebr. V. 7. 8. 9. Who in the days of his flesh, offering up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared, though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered; and being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him. Therefore, the word saved signifies 1. our passions and sins imposed upon him, from which he is saved: 2. his own snatching from death and servitude, and his translation from earth to heaven: 3. in him, as king, our salvation, who are his property and brothers. But that the Chaldean, the LXX, and the Latin rendered it in an active sense, is not from a different reading of better Codices, as was suspected beside the point by

Grotius (for the codices agree exactly here), but it is because they felt that the discourse was about the Messiah, to whom they believed the active name of savior was more fitting than the passive one of saved. But neither fits Zerubbabel, whom Grotius makes the Savior of his people ἄτερ γραφῆς (without scripture). Nor indeed is this letter to be taken concerning נושׁע who is such ONLY IN HIS OWN WAY, but to whom this now fits for a peculiar reason, so that it may be distinguished even by this criterion. But as he is said to come JUST not for himself, but for the daughter of Zion, so also SAVED not for his own sake, but for others: for whom indeed he himself underwent death, because he was delivered into death for our sins, but was raised again (and saved from death) for our justification Rom. IV. 24.

Fourthly comes that King עני, which word denotes one humiliated, afflicted, poor, so that in this way the state of the emptying or humiliation of the Messiah may be more expressed. It is therefore a question here of him, for whose humiliation the daughter of Zion is to rejoice: but she was not to rejoice for the affliction and humiliation of either Zerubbabel or Judah. Certainly not. Wherefore these things are ineptly drawn to them. But they treat clearly of Christ: whose humiliation and affliction is our exaltation and glorying Es. LII. 11. I. Cor. I. 29. seqq. II. Cor. V. 21. c. IIX. 10. Ebr. XI. 26. The LXX rendered it πραῢς (meek), which word among the Hellenists denotes not mild or gentle, but afflicted and humiliated Num. XII. 3. Ps. X. 17. Ps. XIIX. 36. Ps. XXXVII, 11. (Matth. V. 5. Ps. XXV. 8. 9. Ps. XXXIV. 3. Ps. XLV. 5. Ps. LXXVI. 10. Ps. CXLIX. 9. Prov. XV. 33. Zach. III. 2. And therefore there is no reason why we should believe with Willius that they read ענו instead of עני, since they wished to indicate not mild, but afflicted. Coccejus more correctly judges that a voluntary emptying is signified here, comparing Ps. XL. 18. The Latin interpretation PAUPER does not attain the force of the Hebrew word. For that denotes afflicted and humble. Concerning which B. Dorisch. Th. Zach p. 53. For עני is afflicted, humiliated, tyrannically oppressed, miserable, from ענה he was oppressed, by the yoke of servitude or tyranny. Gen. XV. 13. they shall afflict them for four hundred years. Zeph. III. 19. afflicting, pressing with servitude, slaughtering without mercy. For עני is he who is crushed in a hidden place. Abac. III. 13. who is crushed at the gate. Prov. XXII. 22. he is plundered Is. III. 14. he is oppressed Ezek. XVIII. 12. he is surrounded by snares for plundering Ps. X. 9. he has all days evil Prov. XV. 15. he is devastated Ps. XII. 6. whose face plots Is. III. 15. who kills Job XXIV. 14. Such affliction also applies to Christ. Whence Is. LIII. 4. he is said to be struck by God and afflicted, so that the manner of the affliction might shine forth more clearly, which is placed in the wounding and blood-letting of Jesus. But Grotius's commentary is inept, in that by this word is noted a poor entry, without a retinue and royal pomp. Which, however, when, where, or how Zerubbabel instituted, he did not have to say. Concerning the crown placed upon Zerubbabel for the sake of argument, Zechariah handed down nothing; he only commemorates the crown placed upon Joshua in Ch. VI. 11, whom he makes a type of Christ, as we said there.

Sixthly, the entry which Zechariah foretells, as a peculiar criterion of that KING about whom he prophesies, does not refer to Zerubbabel or Judas Maccabeus, much less Alexander the Great, but to Christ, who was to come ascending, or sitting upon a she-ass and the foal of a she-ass. Certainly Grotius could investigate nothing of the sort concerning Zerubbabel, and yet he drew that to Zerubbabel, that the Prophet wished by this to signify his entry (about which there is the deepest silence in history), and his modesty, and his zeal for peace. But Grotius ought rather to have been concerned about where and when Zerubbabel celebrated such an entry, than about what he signified by that entry.

An invincible argument, however, arises from this both against the Jews and against the Judaizing Grotius: Zechariah prophesies of Him here according to the letter, who instituted such an entry into Jerusalem upon a she-ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass, with a notable triumph of the citizens, and by this manner of entry, he wished to be recognized as by a certain criterion. But not Zerubbabel, but Christ instituted such an entry, and by that manner of entry wished to be recognized. Whence Chrysostom, Homily LXVII on Matthew: Let the Jews be asked which of the kings entered Jerusalem riding on an ass. They can surely name no one except Christ. The Jews indeed wish to strike down this weapon, in which Calvin presses his thumb, deservedly noted by our blessed Hunnius, contending in his Commentary on this passage that this is only figurative speech and metaphorical words, when it is said: the King will come riding upon an ass, and thus it is indicated that Christ would be as an obscure man, who does not exalt himself above the common manner of the vulgar. But one must not depart from the propriety of the letter to figures, unless necessity compels. But what necessity compels us here to abandon the letter? It concerns the Advent and entry into Jerusalem. Mention had already been made before of affliction and humiliation. Now the manner of entry is described, that he is about to enter riding upon an ass. What place is there here for figurative speech? Who does not see that these things are to be understood properly, namely, that he was not to enter riding on magnificent horses and carriages, but sitting upon an ass. Then if it had been the purpose of Zechariah by the word of the ass only to show the lowliness of the Messiah, the notation of the ass would have been sufficient to declare it, nor would there have been need for the mention of the colt to be added: whence the Evangelists themselves insist upon the letter, and openly show that this manner of entry was designated by the Prophet. But let blessed Aegidius Hunnius be read at greater length on this in the second Anti-Pareus, p. 457, who stopped the mouth of Pareus, who was defending the Judaizing Calvin in vain. Since Grotius acknowledges that the entry upon the ass is to be taken properly, we do not need to labor over it. But that he wishes the copulative particle Vav to be taken not in a copulative sense, but exegetically, and the ass to be explained as meaning a colt born of asses, i.e., not a mule, but an ass, that is frivolous and inept; for nowhere is an ass described as plainly such, as Grotius speaks, nor is there need for such an unusual periphrasis, since from the name of the ass this animal is sufficiently understood, and the more common meaning of the copulative particle is left aside without cause, indeed against the mind of the Holy Spirit through the Evangelist Matthew, and the very open fulfillment of the prophecy. For Matthew made mention of both animals, and Christ used both, so that this prophecy might be fulfilled, chapter XXI. 2: you will find an ass tied, AND A COLT WITH HER, and v. 5. But this WHOLE thing was done, that it might be fulfilled which was said by the Prophet, saying: Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold your King comes to you meek, sitting upon an ass, AND A COLT the foal of a beast of burden. And again v. 7: And they brought the ass AND THE COLT, and placed UPON THEM their garments. Therefore, exegesis is not to be admitted here; even though his own commentator also establishes it, explaining it thus: he sits upon the ass, and indeed upon the colt of the beast of burden of the ass, who however contradicts himself not a little: for he himself observes that Matthew mentions both the colt and the ass because he cites the present passage of Zechariah, and notes the command of Christ to bring both as the fulfillment of the prophecy. But the colt is called the son of asses, i.e., of one certain ass, such as plural modes of speaking are held for singulars, Jud. 12, 7; Matt. 26, 8; c. 27, 44. Which Grotius astutely recognized elsewhere, namely in his Annotations on Matthew XXI, v. 5. The Hebrew word, he says, is plural in sound, but singular in meaning because of an ellipsis. For בֶּן־אֲתֹנוֹת is correctly translated as the son of one of the asses. Thus also in the verse below, 7, ἐκάθισεν ἐπάνω αὐτῶν, the Syrian correctly translated it as upon him; that is, upon one of the beasts of burden, namely the colt, just as the Latin interpreter also accepted it. Similar are: he is buried in the cities of Gilead: he went down into the sides of the ship, and other things of that kind. In the codices of the LXX in the passage of Zechariah there is πῶλον νέον, but it must be rewritten from Justin as πῶλον ὄνε. Nor did he doubt that in that place the colt and the ass ought to be understood separately. Since ὄνꚙ, he says, is common in Greek, as is also the Hebrew חֲמוֹר, as can be seen in II Sam. XX. 26, where the LXX also had said τὴν ὄνον, the Latin interpreter correctly placed 'asinam' (she-ass) here. For the mother is best joined to the colt. But what the interpreters ask whether Christ was carried by the colt alone, and ought to have been carried, according to the prophecy of the Prophet, or rather by the ass at the same time, and how? It may seem that there is not much moment in that. That the Prophet indicated those two animals, and that Christ also used two for the sake of fulfillment, is certain: but whether he sat upon each by turns is doubtful, because the three Evangelists mentioned only the colt: but since the Prophet also says he was carried by an ass with the word חֲמוֹר, which denotes not only the male, but also the female, see II Kings XIX. 26. Whence the LXX interpreted it as 'of a beast of burden': by which word a colt not yet accustomed to the yoke could not be denoted: Matthew also openly testifies that Christ ordered both animals to be brought, and indeed for the reason that he had need of both, and that the disciples spread their garments upon both, which was done for the purpose that he might sit upon them, and that they made him sit UPON THEM (the animals) (some codices have ἐπ᾽ αὐτῆς upon her, the ass: because he first sat upon her, about to ascend the mountain), therefore it does not seem that one should depart from the clear letter, to which adhere Augustine, Book II de Consens. Evangel. c. LXVI, Theophylact, Rabanus, Albert the Great, Lyranus, Cajetan, Osiander, Hunnius, Gerhard, who has executed these things at greater length in Harmon. Evang. c. CXLIV. Thus also the present character of the Messianic entry is more evident, for the sake of which the Prophet also spoke of a foal of an ass, indicating that one was used which had hitherto still clung to its mother's teats, which circumstance Mark and Luke express in the fulfillment of the prophecy in such a way that no man had ever sat upon it, concerning which Blessed Gerhard, loc. cit. By the foal in this place is understood ὀνάριον, as John explains, a little ass or a foal of an ass, indeed one more adult and suitable for carrying a rider (as is gathered from the word עַיִר which Zechariah uses, for that is used for a foal fit for riding, Judg. 10:4, ch. 12:14), yet still tender, not yet separated from its mother for any use, consequently having suffered no rider hitherto, not yet accustomed to obey a bridle, but still raw and untamed, whence arose that allegory among the ancients concerning the untamed nations that would submit themselves to Christ, concerning which Chrysostom in Matthew. But you, marvel at the sudden taming of the foal, because while it was untamed and entirely devoid of a bridle, it did not recoil, nor did it struggle, but was carried quietly as if accustomed to it. For the obedience of the Gentiles was signified by this, and their sudden change to a better life. The mother ass, however, is called subjugalis, as the LXX Interpreters rendered בֶּן־אֲתֹנוֹת, υἱὸν ὑποζυγίꙋ, which Matthew repeats, in order to show that the prophecy was fulfilled in such an ass, which was not kept peculiarly for making journeys, as noble men and magnates are sometimes read to have been carried by she-asses and mules, Num. 22:21, Judg. 5:10, 1 Kings 1:33. But whose use was for carrying burdens, as the poor they were accustomed to be carried on the same beast of burden with which they plow their fields, which Gerhard noted in the cited place, p. 241. Thus all things exactly agree in the fulfillment of the prophecy.

Seventh, the kingdom of this King is designated of such a kind that it fits not Zerubbabel, nor Judas Maccabeus, but Christ alone. For not to mention that that kingdom is signified not to be of this world, which the King himself, afflicted and humble, and not as worldly Kings are accustomed to be with much pomp (Acts 25:23), but riding on an ass and the foal of an ass, had to enter, his kingdom is described primarily as peaceful and quiet: that chariots and horses, the movements of war, are to be cut off in his kingdom, and that that King is to preach and speak peace to the nations, not to extend the limits of his kingdom by wars, but by the proclamation of the Gospel, which is the word of peace, which was predicted concerning the Messiah in Isaiah 2:4, 11:13, Micah 4:4. Those boundaries also of this kingdom are established, which fit no worldly empire, let alone the rule of Zerubbabel, because his power is said to be about to be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth, that is, throughout the whole world. Which character is again of the kingdom of Christ, Ps. 2:8 and Ps. 72:8, Dan. 6:34, who alone rules throughout the entire world, and needs no vicars, but is most present to all the ends of his kingdom and to his subjects.

Eighth, there is speech concerning the coming of that King, with which is joined the sending forth of the prisoners from the pit, in which there is no water, through the blood of the covenant. But this sending forth was not done under Zerubbabel, but under the Messiah. Concerning which more fully later. These things, therefore, and what the exegesis will suggest in the following, confirm most solidly that the prophecy of Zechariah, according to the letter, can be understood of no one else than Christ. Which, finally, even the Rabbis of the Jews acknowledged. For these, not only in a more eminent sense, as Grotius perverts their mind,

but according to the proper and literal sense in the Commentary on Gen. 49, 'binding his foal to the vine': When the Messiah shall come into Jerusalem, he himself will be saddling his ass and will ride, and will come upon it into Jerusalem, that he may lead himself in poverty and humility, as it is written in Zech. 9, 'riding upon an ass.' Nor did R. Solomon, whom Grotius cites, interpret it only in a mystical sense concerning the Messiah: This prophecy, he says, cannot be explained except concerning the King Messiah. For it is said here, 'and his dominion from sea to sea,' and we do not find such a ruler for Israel in the second house. Likewise: 'And thou shalt be saved with him,' that is, the Messiah, just as he himself is righteous and saved, so also thou in the blood of thy covenant, which was poured out upon you on Mount Sinai. And those who have invented a twofold Messiah, one the son of Joseph, whose name they make Nehemiah son of Husiel, the other the son of David, the former to be killed in battle against Gog and Magog, the latter truly glorious, have accepted this place concerning the Messiah according to the letter, even if they understood the humble Messiah as the son of Joseph; who, however, are sufficiently convinced even from this very place that there is no other than the one Messiah, who is described both as an afflicted and humble, and as a glorious King about to rule in Zion even to the ends of the earth. Furthermore, R. Saadia Gaon, whom Grotius likewise praised here, interpreted the present place concerning the Messiah not only in a mystical sense, but in a literal one. Thus it is read in Sanhedrin, in the section Cheleck: R. Alexander said, it is written in Dan. 7 concerning the Messiah King: 'Behold with the clouds of heaven, as it were the son of man,' and it is written in Zech. 9. Humble, and riding upon an ass; if the Jews shall have merited it, he will come in the clouds of heaven; if they shall not have merited it, humble and riding upon an ass. In Midrash Koheleth on Eccl. 1:9, it is taught: The last redeemer will be the Messiah from this place, Zech. 9,

10. that R. Berachia said this in the name of R. Isaac. Concerning this last Redeemer, these things are held in Tanchuma, Lev. 17:3. R. Berachias the priest, son of Rabbi, said, see what is written in Zech. 9:9, 'Exult greatly, O daughter of Zion,' because 'behold thy King comes, righteous and savior,' it is not written here, but 'righteous and saved.' And thus he himself says in Is. 62:11, 'Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold thy Savior comes.' From which, since it is written in the law, it can be said, Israel will be saved, and it will be as if God himself is saved: and this is one of the harder scriptures, that the salvation of Israel is the salvation of God. R. Enjia said, Moses said to the congregation of Israel, Deut. 33:29, 'Blessed art thou, O Israel, who is like thee, a people saved in the Lord.' This will be similar to a certain man having a measure of the second tithe, what does he do? He gives the price and redeems it. Thus Israel, in or with whom will he be redeemed? Since it is written in the law, it can be said, 'A people saved in the Lord.' These things are in Bereschith Rabba on Gen. 49:8: on Gen. 14:18, it is held thus: Who is this? (a priest according to the order of Melchizedek:) this is the King righteous and savior, the King Messiah, of whom it was said in Zech. 9:9, 'Behold thy King comes to thee.' Finally, Grotius himself acknowledged in the annotations on Matt. 21 that the Rabbis understood these things according to the literal sense, and that they are to be understood in that way, praising the writer of Bereschith Rabba and Midrash Koheleth for that opinion.

Since these things are undoubted among the ancient Rabbis, it is all the less right for Christians to doubt, who know and believe that the holy Evangelists wrote ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερομένως, inasmuch as it is clearer than the sun from them that they understood the prophecy of Zechariah in this way, as far as the literal sense is concerned, since they taught that it was fulfilled when Christ ordered an ass and a colt to be brought, and riding upon them entered Jerusalem, Matt. 21, 4. But this WHOLE thing was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet saying: Tell the daughter of Sion: Behold thy King cometh unto thee meek, sitting upon an ass and a colt the foal of a beast of burden. And John 12, 14. And Jesus found a young ass, and sat thereon, as it is written, Fear not daughter of Sion, behold thy King coming upon the foal of an ass. St. John adds: These things his disciples understood not at the first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that THESE THINGS WERE WRITTEN OF HIM: where Grotius interprets: by remembering they understood the true sense of the Prophet. What audacity, therefore, what impiety, to wish to snatch away and distort to another sense according to the letter these things which the Evangelists testified were spoken solely of the Messiah and were fulfilled in him, and which the disciples, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, acknowledged were to be understood of no one else but Christ? We add finally the Grotian confession on Luke 19, 42, which may be seen in our annotations on the same passage.

Latin:

Vers. 9. EXULTA SATIS) In Hebræo: Valde.

ECCE REX TUUS VENIET TIBI JUSTUS) Optime verti potest, venit: nempe cum ex Babylone veni- ret. Nam præterita Hebræi sæpissime verbis futuris, quæ pro præsentibus sumuntur, exprimunt, pertinetque lo- cus primo & maxime obvio sensu ad Zorobabelem, qui Rex appellatur etiam Jer. XXIII. 5. & Ezech. XXXVII 22. 24. nimirum, quia quanquam nomen sibi regium, pompamque regiam non assumsit, ne id Persarum Re- gem offenderet, à suis tamen, ob ortum, quem trahebat à Davide, ita cultus observatusque fuit, quasi Rex esset. Ad Messiam autem sublimiore quodam sensu hæc referri, agnoscit Rabbi Salomo. Sed dubitare ait se Abenesdra de utro Messiarum hoc intelligendum sit: nam cum dupli- cem statum Messiæ describi viderent, contemtum alte- rum, alterum gloriosum, ex his duos Messias fecere, quo- rum illum vocant filium Josephi, hunc filium Davidis, & ad Josephi quidem filium Messiam hæc referunt Judæo- rum plerique. At doctissimus Rabbi Saadia Gaon ad Da- nielem ait de eodem hic agi, qui denotatur Ps. LXXII. & Dan. VII. 4. Is autem est triumphator Messias, ut ipsi fa- tentur. Justus, id est, æquus, Φιλόπατρις, non tyrannus, de quali modo actum.

ET SALVATOR) Mirum est non Latinum tantum sed & Græcos & Chaldæum in hoc consensisse, ut salvato- rem verterent: nam in Hebræo legitur נושׁע. Aut ergo in Codicibus melioribus quam quibus usi sunt Masoretici, scriptum fuit נושׁיע, aut (quod mirum est) omnes in eo convenerunt, ut passivum positum crederent pro activo, quomodo נדברו sumitur Psal. CXIX. 23. Zorobabel sal- vator populi suo modo, & ad tempus, justo scilicet regiini- ne; Christus perfecte, & in perpetuum.

PAUPER) Sine satellitio pompaque regia, ob eam, quam diximus, causam, ipsa corona ei dicis causa impo- sita, penes eum non mansit, sed in Templum perlata est.

ET ASCENDENS SUPER ASINAM, ET SU- PER PVLLVM FILIVM ASINÆ) Et, pro, id est: & in Hebræo ועל־עיר est asinus, ut recte verti possit, vectus asino, id est, pullo nato ex asinis: non mule, sed asino plane, tam ex patre quam ex matre. Id significabat non tantum mo- destiam ipsius, sed & pacis studium: nam Bello armantur equi. Asinus pacis animal. Illustrant id sequentia.

Detestanda πρεβλέτης illustrissimi de Christo va- ticinii, quam à Theodoro Mopsvestano Judaizante, & Ebionizante accepit Grotius. Nam & hic asse- ruit, regem hunc esse Zorobabelem, damnatus eo no- mine à Vigilio in Romana Synodo. Judæi de Juda Maccabæo explicant, ne Messiam nostrum hic præ- dictum agnoscere cogantur. Perfidis ergo Judæis hic suppetias fert Grotius, dum hæc de Christo se- cundum literam loqui negat. Quod ab illis etiam fit, qui Alex. M. inepte intelligunt honorifice Hierosolymam venientem, & Jaddo Pontificem venerantem. Quod autem de nullo alio, quam de Messia, secundum literam loquatur Propheta, hæc confirmant. Primo, quum scopus Prophetæ fuerit hortari ad structuram templi, nullum dubium est, quin apprime congruat eidem hæc prædictio de adventu Messiæ, solemni pompa templum ingres- suri, ut id doctrinæ reformatione ac miraculorum gloria illustret, & inde Ecclesiam suam per orbem propaget. Porro quum promissio facta sit de ho- stium populi excisione, gentium conversione, & Eccle- siæ defensione, nunc de Messiæ adventu, per quem gentium conversio procuratur, salus ac defensio Ecclesiæ præstatur, vaticinium instituitur, ac ne tranquillitatem mundanam, ac dominium terre- num cogitarent, Messias, ceu rex humilis & iner- mis sistitur, & regni ejus conditio declaratur. Sum- mam ita exhibet Willius, p. 304. Quamvis non sem- per alta pace sitis fruituri, sed sæpe calamitates sen- suri, non tamen propterea vel promissionem divi- nam de vestri cura & protectione in dubium voca- re, vel animos despondere, præ nimio mœrore de- betis, sed potius exultare præ lætitia & jubilare, propter Messiæ Regis adventum, qui perfectam vobis salutem & liberationem ab omnibus malis præstabit. Neque enim talis vobis status, aut tale regnum exspectandum, in quo terreno brachio & potentia Messias vos perpetuæ felicitati asserat, & supra gentes evehat, sed regnum spirituale & hu- mile ac mundo contemtum, in quo justitia & salus æterna mansuetis spiritu communicatur & pax conscientiæ in meis afflictionibus & calamitatibus sanctos exhilarans potentia verbi & Spiritus tam in gentibus, quam in Judæis erigitur. Hujus igi- tur salutis respectu perpetuo vos hilares esse con- venit, hancque regni conditionem & pacem spiri- tualem omnibus, quæ vos tangent, afflictionibus opponere. Calvinus dicit: Prophetam ostendere mo- dum restituendæ Ecclesiæ, quia sc. iterum emerget Rex ex tribu & familia Davidis, qui omnia in ordinem pristinum restituat. Quum enim adhuc res collapsæ fuerint inter Judæos, testari Prophetam, non fru- stra Deum olim loquutum esse de adventu Re- demtoris, sed bene sperandum esse, donec vatici- nia illa suo tempore impleantur.

Secundo exaltatio illa ingens, de qua Propheta, EXULTA מאד VALDE, JUBILA (quibus ver- bis non simplex & vulgaris sed singularis lætitia no- tatur, ad quam excitatur filia Sion, & filia Jerusa- lem, h. e. cives Ecclesiæ Judaicæ, fideles omnes, qui hoc nomine solent designari) complementum suum habuit non in Zorobabele, sed in Christo. Unde concludimus: De ejus adventu loquitur Propheta, quem summa cum exultatione & con- gratulatione acceptavit advenientem, & accepta- re debuit filia Sion, is autem non fuit Zorobabel, de quo nihil tale legitur, sed Christus, de quo Ev- angelistæ referunt.

Tertio exultatio illa ingens lætitiæ causam novam & insignem postulat, qualis non est ingressus Zo- robabelis, aut adventus Alexandri M. vel Judæ Maccabæi. Zorobabel certe jam aderat ipsis, jam incumbebat operi structuræ templi, unde ejusdem adventus, ut futurus prædici non poterat, nec ad excipiendum ipsum cum lætitia excitari ipsi opus habebant. Futurum autem pro præterito accipere, neque ulla cogit necessitas, neque textui consenta- neum est. Nam ad id quod præterierat, excitari non poterant, aut invitari, siquidem jam transie- rat. Hic autem excitantur & invitantur ad Regem illum suum ingressurum cum gaudio excipiendũ. Quapropter insulse hæc ad Zorobabelem abripiun- tur. De Messia autem ejusque beneficiis ubi agi- tur, solemnes sunt ejusmodi exhortationes. Vid. Ps. II. 11. Ps. XLVII. 2. 7. Ps. LVIII. 5. Ps. XCVI. Ps. XCVII. Ps. XCVIII. Ps. XCIX. Ps. C. Es. XII. 4. cap. XLIX. 13. c. LIV. Coccejus non male hic: Apostro- phe ἐγκελευστικὴ habet istam simplicem notionem, Deum, adveniente Christo, non tantum notificaturum Ecclesiæ officium suum, quod est gaudere, &c. Sed etiam effecturum, ut cum gaudio & jubilo recipiatur. Ita factum, & quidem in tali circumstantia, qualem hic Propheta describit Matth. XXI. 8. 9. 11. 15. Et Christus ex Psal. VIII. pro pueris ἀπολογίαν insti- tuit, ostendens, hanc esse in pueris divinam effica- ciam. Et Luc. XIX. 40. adeo hoc necessarium esse, ut fiat, asserit, ut potius lapides locuturi sint, quam ut non habeat hanc jubilationem Christus. Non tamen id tantum de illa πρόσκαιρῳ exceptione Christi debet accipi, qua insigniter fuit demon- strata Christi omnipotentia: sed etiam de fide, qua Ecclesia Christum, ut Regem, exceptura erat o- mni tempore. Vide Joh. X. 26. 27. & Joh. VI. 37. Hæc Coccejus. Zorobabel neque Rex fuit unquam, neque uspiam eo nomine appellatus est in sacris. Nam quod ad loca illa, quæ adducit Grotius, ma- nifestum est, ea impie ad Zorobabelem itidem de- torqueri, quum de alio nullo, quam de Messia lo- quantur. Judas Maccabæus Rex non fuit, Alexan- der vero, etsi Rex fuerit, non tamen Rex in Sion dici potuit. Cornel. à Lapid. ita hic superiora con- fert & concinnat: Messias sive Christus veniet, ut quatuor quadrigas, id est, Monarchias, de quibus ca- pite VI. ac consequenter Tyrum, Gazam, Azotum, to- tamque Palæstinam, Phœniciam & Syriam, de quibus egit hoc capite, sibi subigat. Nam in Christi regnum omnes reges & regna desinunt, uti prædixit Daniel cap. I. 44. & Zacharias hic. Unde subdit: Disper- dam quadrigam &c.

Quarto non præter rem observat Coccejus, quod Scriptura verbo VENIET utatur passim de ἐπι- δημίᾳ Filii Dei, utpote Habac. II. 33. Ezech. XXI. 27. Gen. XLIX. 10. Ps. CXVIII. 26. Mal. III. 3. Et re- spondet τὸ ἔρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν κόσμον Joh. I. 9. 11. Matth. XI. 3. Joh. IV. 25. VI. 14. IX. 39. Synonymum alibi est, venire à Deo, venire superne, descendisse de cœlo.

Quinto descriptio illa hujus Regis non conve- nit Zorobabeli, sed unice Messiæ: Dicitur primo Rex in Sion & Jerusalem. Quod vere de Messia ac- cipi è locis similibus liquet Psal. II. 6. Psal. LXXII. 1. seqq. Psal. CX. 2. Jer. IX. 6. Jer. XXIII. 6. Dan. VI. 14. 27. Mich. IV. 7. c. V. 3. de Zorobabele vero id intelligendum esse, nullo scripturæ testimonio constat. Dicitur secundo Rex venturus, JUSTUS, quod nomen κατ' ἐξοχὴν acceptum Regi Messiæ unice convenit, germini Davidi justo, quod justitiam & judicium operaturum dicitur in terra Jer. XLIII. 6. Es. LIII. 11. Zach. II. 2. Qui justus est non tantum per se, & quod ad suam personam, sed etiam Nobis! VENIET TIBI JUSTUS, qui- bus suam justitiam donat I. Cor. I. 29. II. Cor. V. 21. Ita vero absolute JUSTUS neque Zorobabel, ne- que ullus alius ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος vocatur, ut eo no- mine ceu sibi proprio, ac perpetuo designetur. Glossa illa, quod justus æquus sit, Φιλόπατρις, gla- cie ipsa frigidior est. Tertio vocatur Rex ille נוֹשָׁע SALVATUS, quod iterum non vulgari modo in- telligendum, ita enim nemo est, qui salutis non sit aliquando indigus, aut è periculo aliquo salvatus dici possit. Sed quum hoc nomen huic Regi singu- lariter approprietur, ἐξαιρέτως & μονοτρόπως, non immerito intelligitur de eo, qui præ aliis, & ante alios salvatus est, in quo, & ob quem alii omnes salvati merito dicuntur, h. e. de Messia nostro, in quo uno est salus omnium Act. IV. 12. Hic enim, etsi salvator noster sit ratione meriti & efficaciæ, sal- vari tamen primum ipse debuit è morte & inferno, ut nos è morte & inferno, cui se immersit nostræ salutis gratia, liberaret, atque salvaret. Nisi enim ipse mortem passus & pœnam infernalem pro no- bis subiisset, atque ex ea salvatus esset, de omnium nostrum salute actum fuisset. Nonnulli reddunt SALUTE PRÆDITUS, & observant cum Dru- sio: participia passivi generis, quando nominascunt, actionem denotare, nec insolens esse scripturæ passiva active usurpare, ut Es. LXII. 11: Ecce salus tua venit, ecce merces ejus cum eo, ubi per salutem salvatorem per mercedem bona quæ aliis elargitur, intelligunt. Sic active interpretati sunt Chaldæum פָּרִיק Redem- tor, salvator, LXX. σώζων salvans. Quem sensum præfert Villius, eo quod Apostoli etiam vocem activam in historia Evangelica retinuerint, in quo vero memoria ipsum sua fefellit. Nam in historia Evangelica, verbum illud nec à Matthæo, cap. XXI. nec à Johanne c. XII. repetitur. Cornelius à Lapide vult non participium esse, sed nomen, idem active significans, quod Jesus, ut litera Nun sit Hæmanti- ca, ut in Naphthali, Nimrod, quod adversus Gro- tium notandum, qui vocem à Judæis corruptam fingit, repugnante Masora, ut alias diximus. Sed passiva significatio textui convenientior. Agitur enim hic de statu exinanitionis, & ingressu in Hiero- solymam, Christi passionem subituri. Rectius autem Coccejus p. 524. In isto salvari τὸ נוֹשָׁע servator con- tinetur. Salvatus dicitur, quia eripitur ex passionibus suis & morte. At hoc ipso nos quoque servamur in ipso, ut capite nostro, & perfectum ejus meritum nobis ma- nifestatur. Hebr. V. 7. 8. 9. Qui in diebus carnis suæ petitiones & supplicationes ad eum, qui poterat ipsum salvare è morte, cum clamore valido & la- crymis offerens, & exauditus à timore, quamquam filius esset, didicit ab iis, quæ passus est, obedien- tiam, & consummatus factus est obedientibus sibi omnibus causa salutis æternæ. Ergo τὸ salvatus di- cit 1. passiones & peccata nostra ipsi imposita, à qui- bus salvetur: 2. ereptionem ipsius è morte & servi- tute, & translationem ex terra in cœlum: 3. in ipso, ut rege, nostram, qui ipsius peculium & fratres su- mus, salutem. Quod autem Chaldæus, LXX. & La- tinus activo sensu reddidere, non à diversa Codi- cum meliorum lectione, uti præter rem suspicatu

Grotius (consentiunt enim exacte hic codices) sed inde est, quod sentirent de Messia sermonem esse, cui credebant magis nomen activum salvato- ris, quam passivum salvati, convenire. Zorobabeli autem neutrum congruit, quem Salvatorem popu- li sui ἄτερ γραφῆς facit Grotius. Neque vero litera hæc de נושׁע qui talis SUO MODO solum sit, accipienda, sed cui peculiari ratione hoc nunc conveniat, ut ab hoc etiam κριτηρίῳ dignosci queat. Ut autem JUSTUS venire dicitur non sibi, sed fi- liæ Sioni, sic etiam SALVATUS non sui causa, sed aliis : pro quibus nempe ipse mortem subiit, quia traditus in mortem est propter peccata nostra, resusci- tatus autem (& salvatus est è morte) propter justi- tiam nostram Rom. IV. 24.

Quarto venit Rex ille עני, quæ vox humiliatum, afflictum, pauperem no- tat, ut ita magis status exinanitionis vel humiliatio- nis Messiæ exprimatur. De eo igitur hic agitur, ob cujus humiliationem filiæ Sion gaudendum est: at non gaudendum ei erat, ob afflictionem & humi- liationem vel Zorobabelis vel Judæ. Non utique. Quapropter inepte hæc trahuntur ad illos. Lucu- lenter autem agunt de Christo : cujus humiliatio & afflictio nostra est exaltatio & gloriatio Es. LII. 11. I. Cor. I. 29. seqq. II. Cor. V. 21. c. IIX. 10. Ebr. XI. 26. LXX. reddidere πραῢς, quæ vox apud Hellenistas non mitem aut clementem, sed afflictum & humi- liatum notat Num. XII. 3. Ps. X. 17. Ps. XIIX. 36. Ps. XXXVII, 11. (Matth. V. 5. Ps. XXV. 8. 9. Ps. XXXIV. 3. Ps. XLV. 5. Ps. LXXVI. 10. Ps. CXLIX. 9. Prov. XV. 33. Zach. III. 2. Ideoque non est, quod cum Willio cre- damus, illos legisse ענו pro עני, siquidem non mi- tem, sed afflictum indigitare voluerunt. Rectius Coccejus censet significari hic voluntariam exina- nitionem, conferens Ps. XL. 18. Non assequitur vim Ebrææ vocis Latina interpretatio PAUPER. Nam illa afflictum & humilem notat. De quo B. Dorisch. Th. Zach p. 53. Est enim עני afflictus, humi- liatus, oppressus tyrannice, miser, ab ענה oppressus fuit, jugo servitutis aut tyrannide. Gen. XV. 13. affli- gent eos quadringentis annis. Zeph. III. 19. affligen- tes, servitute prementes, sine misericordia jugulantes. עני enim est, qui editur in abdito. Abac. III. 13. qui in porta conteritur. Prov. XXII. 22. diripitur Es. III. 14. opprimitur Ezech. XIIX. 12. insidiis ad rapiendum circundatur Ps. X. 9. omnes dies habet malos Prov. XV. 15. devastatur Ps. XII. 6. cujus facies molitur Es. III. 15. qui interimiter Job. XXIV. 14. Christo talis afflictio etiam competit. Unde Es. LIII. 4. percus- sus à Deo & afflictus dicitur, ut modus afflictionis eo clarius elucescat, qui positus est in sauciatione & cruentatione Jesu. Ineptus autem est Commenta- rius Grotii, quod hac voce notetur ingressus pau- pertinus, sine satellitio pompâq; Regia. Quem tamen ubi, quando, aut quomodo instituerit Zorobabel, dicere non habuit. De corona Zorobabeli imposita dicis gratia, nihil Zacharias tradidit, solum Josuæ coronam impositam commemorat C. VI. 11. quem typum Christi facit, ut ibi diximus.

Sexto ingressus quem prænunciat Zacharias, ceu peculiare κριτήριον REGIS istius, de quo vaticina- tur, non Zorobabelem aut Judam Maccabæum, ne- dum Alexandrum M. refert, sed Christum, qui ve- nire debuit ascendens, vel sedens super asinam & pul- lum filium asinæ. Nihil certe tale de Zorobabele investigare potuit Grotius, & traxit id tamen ad Zorobabelem, quod hic ingressum ejus (de quo altissimum in historia silentium) & modestiam, & pacis studium significare voluerit Propheta. At solicitus debebat potius fuisse Grotius, ubinam, & quando ejusmodi ingressum celebrarrit Zorobabel, quam de eo, quidnam illo ingressu significarit. Ar-

gumentum autem hinc invictum tum contra Ju- dæos, tum contra Judaizantem Grotium nascitur : De illo hic vaticinatur secundum literam Zacha- rias, qui talem ingressum Hierosolymis instituit super Asinam, & super pullum filium Asinæ, cum insigni tripudio civium, atque hoc ingressus mo- do, ceu κριτηρίῳ certo dignosci voluit. At non Zo- robabel, sed Christus instituit talem ingressum, eo- que ingressus modo agnosci voluit. Unde Chrysost. hom. LXVII. in Matth. Interrogentur Judæi, quis- nam Regum asina vectus Hierosolymam intrarit. Ne- minem profecto præter Christum dicere possunt. Eli- dere quidem hoc Judæi telum volunt, quibus in eo pollicem premit Calvinus, à B. Hunnio nostro merito notatus, contendens in Commentario ad h. l. quod hic figuratus solum sit sermo, & verba me- taphorica, cum dicitur : veniet Rex super asinam e- quitans, adeoque id indigitetur, fore Christum quasi obscurum hominem, qui sese non extollit super com- munem vulgi modum. At à proprietate literæ non discedendum ad figuras, nisi cogente necessitate. Quæ vero hic cogit necessitas, ut literam desera- mus? Agitur de Adventu & ingressu in Hierosoly- mam. Afflictionis & humiliationis jam antea fa- cta erat mentio. Nunc modus ingressus describitur, quod ingressurus sit equitans super asinum. Quis hic locus figuratæ locutioni ? Quis non videt, proprie hæc intelligenda esse, quod nempe non magnificis caballis & rhedis vectus, sed sedens super asino in- gressurus sit. Tum si propositum fuisset Zachariæ asinæ voce tantum ostendere vilitatem Messiæ, sa- tis ad eam declarandam fuisset notatio asinæ, nec opus fuisset, quod pulli mentio adjiceretur: unde Evangelistæ ipsi literæ insistunt, atque hunc in- gressus modum à Propheta designatum fuisse pa- lam ostendunt. Sed de eo legatur pluribus B. Æ- gid. Hunnius in Anti-Pareo altero p. 457. qui Pa- reo nequicquam Calvinum Judaizantem defen- denti, os obturavit. Quum Grotius agnoscat in- gressum super asinam proprie accipiendum esse, la- borandum nobis de eo non est. Quod vero copu- lativam particulam Vav, non copulativo sensu, sed ἐξηγητικῶς accipi, & asinum explicari vult, quod intelligendus sit pullus natus ex asinis, h. e. non mu- lum, sed asinum, id frivolum est, atque ineptum, nuspiam enim ita describitur asinus plane talis, uti loquitur Grotius, nec opus tali περιφράσει insoli- ta, quum ex asini nomine satis intelligatur hoc ani- mal, & præter causam relinquitur usitatior signifi- catio particulæ copulativæ, imo contra mentem Spiritus Sancti per Evangelistam Matthæum, & complementum ipsum vaticinii apertum. Nam u- triusque animalis mentionem fecit Matthæus, & utrumque Christus adhibuit, ut impleretur hæc Pro- phetia cap. XXI. 2. invenietis asinam alligatam, ET PULLUM CUM EA, & v. 5. Hoc autem TO- TUM factum est, ut impleretur, quod dictum est per Prophetam, dicentem : Dicite filiæ Sion : Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus, sedens super asinam, ET PULLUM filium subjugalis. Et iterum v. 7. Et adduxerunt asinam ET PULLUM, & imposue- runt SUPER EOS vestimenta sua. Non ergo est hic exegesis admittenda ; etsi eam etiam statuit VV illius, ita explicans : insidet asinæ, & quidem pullo subjugis asinæ, qui vero non parum sibi contradicit: nam & pulli & asinæ Matthæum ideo meminisse observat ipse, quod præsentem Zachariæ locum ci- tet, & mandatum Christi, de adducendis utrisque, ceu complementum vaticinii notat. Dicitur autem pullus filius asinarum, h. e. unius alicujus asinæ, qua- les loquendi rationes plurales pro singularibus ha- bentur Jud, 12, 7. Matth. 26, 8. c. 27, 44. Quod a- stutè gnovit alibi Grotius, nempe in Annotat. ad Matth. XXI. v. 5. ὑποζυγίꙋ vox Hebræa, inquit, pluralis est sono, significatu autem singularis propter ἔλλειψιν. Nam בֶּן־אֲתֹנוֹת rectè vertitur filium unius asinarũ. Sic & commate infra 7. ἐκάθισεν ἐπάνω αὐτῶν rectè transtulit Syrus super eum; id est, super alterum ex jumentis, pullum videlicet, quomodo accepit & Lati- nus interpres. Similia sunt, sepultus est in urbibus Galaad: descendit in latera navis, & id genus alia. In codicibus LXX. in Zachariæ loco est πῶλον νέον, sed rescribendum ex Justino πῶλον ὄνε. Neque dubita- vit eo loco pullum & asinum seorsim intelligi debe- re. Cum ὄνꚙ, inquit, Græce sit ἐπίκοινον, quomodo & Hebræum חֲמוֹר, ut videre est II. Sam. XX. 26. ubi & LXX. τὴν ὄνον dixerant, rectè hic interpres Lati- nus asinam posuit. Nam pullo mater optime adjungi- tur. Quod autem quærunt Interpp. anne pullo solo vectus Christus sit, & vehi debuerit, juxta Prophetæ vaticinium, an vero simul asina & quomodo? in eo haud multum momenti esse, videri potest. Duo illa animantia indigitasse Prophetam, duo etiam com- plementi causa adhibuisse Christum, certum est: num vero utrique per vices insederit, dubium, quod tres Evangelistæ solum pulli mentionem fe- cerint: sed quum Propheta etiam asinâ vectum di- cat voce חֲמוֹר, quæ non solum marem, sed etiam fœminam notat, vid. II. Reg. XIX. 26. Unde LXX. ὑποζυγίου interpretati sunt: qua voce pullus non- dum jugo assuetus denotari haut potuit: Matthæus etiam aperte testatur, quod Christus utrumque a- nimal adduci jusserit, & quidem ea de causa, quod utroque opus habeat, & quod super utrumque vestes suas straverint discipuli, quod eo factum fine, ut il- lis insideret, quodque ἐπεκάθισαν ἐπάνω αὐτῶν SUPER ILLA (animantia) sedere fecerint (quidam Codices habent ἐπ᾽ αὐτῆς super eam asinam: quia primum illi insedit, montem adscensurus) ideo non videtur à clara litera discedendum, cui inhæ- rent August. l. II. de Consens. Evangel. c. LXVI. Theophylactus, Rabanus, Albertus M. Lyranus, Cajeta- nus, Osiander, Hunnius, Gerhardus, qui hæc pluribus exequtus est in Harmon. Evang. c. CXLIV. Sic etiam evidentior est character præsens ingressus Messiani, cujus gratia quoque Propheta pullum a- sinarum dixit, indigitans, eum adhibitum, qui ha- ctenus adhuc à matris uberibus hæserit, quam cir- cumstantiam in complemento vaticinii Marcus & Lucas ita exprimunt, quod nemo hominum unquam in ipso sederit, de quo B. Gerhard. l. c. Pullus hoc loco intelligitur ὀνάριον, ut Johannes explicat, asellus sive pullus asininus, adultior ille quidem & equitationi ferendæ idoneus (ut colligitur ex voce עַיִר qua Za- charias utitur, ea enim pro pullo equitationi apto u- surpatur Jud. X. 4. c. XII. 14.) adhuc tamen tener, nec dum à matre ad usum aliquem separatus, proinde nul- lum hactenus sessorem passus, nondum freno obedire assuetus, sed rudis adhuc atque indomitus, unde nata veteribus illa allegoria de gentibus indomitis Christo se submissuris, de quo Chrystost. in Matth. Tu vero subitam pulli domationem admirare, quod dum esset indomitus, & freni omnino expers, non resiliit, nec re- luctatus est, sed quiete quasi assuetus ferebatur. Gen- tium enim obedientia hinc significabatur & repentina in meliorem vitam mutatio. Asina autem mater vo- catur subjugalis, uti LXX. Interpp. בֶּן־אֲתֹנוֹת reddidere, υἱὸν ὑποζυγίꙋ, quod repetit Matthæus, ut ostendat Prophetiam in ejusmodi asina imple- tam, quæ non ad iter faciendum peculiariter ale- batur, sicut viri nobiles & magnates quandoque a- sinabus & mulabus vecti leguntur Num. XXII. v. 21. Judic. V. vers. 10. I. Regum I. vers. 33. Sed cu- jus usus erat ad onera gestanda, sicut pauperes eodem jumento, quo agros suos arant, vehi con- sveverunt, quod Gerhardus monuit l. c. p. 241. Ita o- mnia exacte consonant in vaticinii complemento.

Septimo regnum hujus Regis ejusmodi desi- gnatur, quod non Zorobabeli, nec Judæ Maccabæo, sed Christo unice convenit. Nam ne dicamus, quod regnum illud significetur non fore de hoc mun- do, quod Rex ipse afflictus & humilis, nec uti so- lent mundani Reges μετὰ πολλῆς Φαντασίας Act. XXV. 23. sed asino & pullo asinæ vectus ingredi debu- erit, describitur imprimis regnum ejus, tanquam pacificum & quietum: quod succidendi sint in regno ejus currus, & equi, motus bellici, & quod Rex ille pa- cem prædicaturus ac loquuturus sit gentibus, non Re- gni sui limites bellis ampliaturus, sed præconio Evan- gelii, quod est verbum pacis, quod de Messia præ- dictum est Es. 2, 4. c. 11, 13. Mich. 4, 4. Termini etiam illi constituuntur hujus regni, qui nulli mundano imperio nedum regimini Zorobabelis conveniunt, quia potestas ejus dicitur futura à mari usq́; ad mare, & à flumine usq́; ad fines terræ, h. e. per totum orbem. Qui character iterum est regni Christi Ps. 2, 8. & Ps. 72, 8. Dan. 6, 34, qui solus per universum mundum dominatur, nec vicariis indiget, sed omnibus sui re- gni finibus & subditis præsentissimus adest.

Octavo de illius Regis adventu sermo est, cum quo conjuncta est emissio vinctorum è lacu, in quo non est aqua, per sanguinem fœderis. At hæc emis- sio non facta sub Zorobabele, sed sub Messia. De qua postea uberius. Hæc ergo, & quæ in sequenti- bus suggeret ἐξήγησις, confirmant solidissime, va- ticinium Zachariæ quoad literam de nullo alio in- telligi posse, quam de Christo. Quod denique agno- verunt etiam Judæorum Rabbini. Hi enim non so- lum sensu eminentiori, uti pervertit eorum mentem

Grotius, sed secundum proprium & literalem sen- sum in Commentar. ad Gen. XLIX. ligans ad vi- tem pullum suum: Cum venerit Messias in Jerusa- lem, ipse erit cingens asinum suum & equitabit, & veniet super eum in Jerusalem, ut ducat seipsum in paupertate & humilitate, sicut scriptum est Zach. 10. equitans super asinam. Neq; R. Salomo, quem ad- ducit Grotius, solum sensu mystico de Messia inter- pretatus est: Hæc Prophetia, inquit, non potest ex plicari, nisi de Rege Messia. Dictum enim est hic, & dominatio ejus de mari ad mare, & non invenimus Israeli talem dominatorem in domo secunda. Item: Et tu salvaberis cum eo, id est, Messia, sicut ipse ju- stus & salvatus, ita etiam tu in sanguine pacti tui, qui effusus est super vos in monte Sinai. Et qui gemi- num Messiam, alium filium Joseph, cui nomen fa- ciunt Nehemias filius Husiel, alium filium Davidis, illum humilem in prælio contrà Gog & Magog oc- cidendum, hunc vero gloriosum commenti sunt, hunc locum de Messia secundum literam accepe- runt, etsi filium Josephi humilem Messiam intellexe- rint; qui vero vel ex hoc ipso loco satis convincun- tur, quod nonnisi unicus sit Messias, qui & ceu af- flictus atque humilis, & ceu gloriosus Rex in Sion dominaturus usque ad fines terræ describitur. Por- ro R. Saadia Gaon, quem itidem hic laudavit Gro- tius, non tantum sensu mystico, sed literali de Mes- sia præsentem locum interpretatus est. Sic legitur in Sanhedrim distinctione Cheleck: Dixit R. Ale- xander, scriptum est Dan. 7. de Messia Rege: Ecce cum nubibus cœli, quasi filius hominis, & scriptum est Zach. 9. Humilis, & equitans super asinam, si meruerint Judæi, veniet in nubibus cæli, si non me- ruerint, humilis & equitans super asinam. In Mi- drasch Koheleth super Eccl. 1, 9. docetur: Redem- torem ultimum fore Messiam ex hoc loco Zach. 9,

10. quod id dixerit R. Berachia in nomine R. Isaac. De hoc Redemtore ultimo hæc habentur in Tanchu- ma, Lev. 17, 3. Dixit R. Berachias sacerdos filius Rab- bi, vide quod scriptum est Zach. 9, 9. Exulta valde fi- lia Sion, quia ecce Rex tuus venit, justus & salvator, non est hic scriptum, sed justus & salvatus. Et sic ipse dicit Es. 62, 11. Dicite filiæ Sion: Ecce Salvator tuus venit. Ex quo in lege scriptum, dici potest, Israel salvabuntur, & erit ac si Deus ipse salvetur: & hæc est una de durioribus scripturis, quod salvatio Israel est salvatio Dei. Dixit R. Enjia, Moses dixit Eccle- siæ Israelis Deuter. 33, 29. Beatus tu Israel, quis sicut tu populus salvatus in Domino. Simile erit hoc homini cuidam habenti modium decimæ secundæ, quid facit ipse? dat pretiu & redimit illum. Sic Israel in vel cum quo redimetur? Ex quo in lege scri- ptum est, dici potest, Populus salvatus in Domi- no. Hæc in Bereschith Rabba ad Gen. 49, 8: ad Gen. 14, 18. ita habetur: Quis es iste? (sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech:) iste est Rex ju- stus & salvator Rex Messias, de quo dictum est Zach. 9, 9. Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi. Denique agnovit Grotius ipse in annot. ad Matth. 21. Rabbinos hæc secundum literalem sensum intellexisse, atque ita intelligenda esse, laudans in eam sententiam scri- ptorem Bereschith Rabba, & Midrasch Koheleth.

Quæ quum apud Rabbinos antiquos indubi- tata sint, eo minus fas est Christianos dubitare, qui norunt & credunt sanctos Evangelistas ὑπὸ πνεύ- ματος ἁγίε φερομένως scripsisse, utpote, è quibus sole clarius constat, quod Zachariæ Prophetiam ita intellexerint, quantum ad literalem sententiam, si- quidem impletam esse docuerint, cum Christus ad- duci jussit asinum & pullum, iisdemque vectus Hie- rosolymam ingressus est Matth. 21, 4. Hoc autem TOTUM factum est, ut adimpleretur, quod dictum est per Prophetam dicentem: Dicite filiæ Sion: Ecce Rex tuus venit tibi mansuetus, sedens super asinam & pullum filium subjugalis. Et Joh. 12, 14. Et invenit Jesus asellum, & sedit super eum, sicut scriptum est, Noli timere filia Sion, ecce Rex tuus veniens super pullum Asinæ. Addit S. Johannes: Hæc non agnove- runt discipuli ejus primum, sed quando glorificatus est Jesus, tunc recordati sunt, quia HÆC ERANT SCRIPTA DE EO: ubi Grotius interpretatur: reminiscendo verum intellexerunt sensum Prophetæ. Quæ ergo audacia, quæ impietas, hæc, quæ Evan- gelistæ de Messia unice loqui, & in eo impleta esse, testati sunt, quæ discipuli non de alio, quam Chri- sto intelligenda esse, illuminati à Spiritu Sancto, agnoverunt, ad alium sensum secundum literam abripere velle, ac detorquere? Addimus tandem confessionem Grotianam ad Luc. 19, 42. quæ in annot. nostris ibidem videatur.

## 9:10
Verse 10. AND I WILL CUT OFF THE CHARIOT FROM EPHRAIM) I will take away from the Jews and the Israelites who returned with them, every hostile chariot.

AND THE HORSE FROM JERUSALEM) The hostile cavalry,

AND THE BATTLE BOW SHALL BE CUT OFF) It shall be cut: that is, it will no more harm them than if the string were cut.

AND HE SHALL SPEAK PEACE UNTO THE HEATHEN,) Namely, the city of Jerusalem shall make treaties with Kings, with the Lacedaemonians, with the Romans.

AND HIS DOMINION FROM THE SEA.) The Red [Sea],

EVEN TO THE SEA.) The Syriac [version].

AND FROM THE RIVERS.) In the Hebrew: from the river, that is, from the Euphrates.

EVEN TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.) Namely, that which was promised to the Fathers: for Samaria, Galilee, the Gileadites, and other regions which had been separated since the times of Jeroboam came under the rule of Jerusalem. To understand these words, repeat the passage of Josephus which we just produced,

A new and significant distortion of the Prophetic text again. For (1) those things which were said of the Jews and Israelites are explained as being about enemies. Naturally, it is promised that among the Jews and Israelites there will be no chariots, nor horses, nor bows of war with which they themselves might fight, because the kingdom of this king is plainly peaceful and quiet, and does not need those things: just as is manifest from a similar passage in Micah 5:10. In that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will cut off the horses from the midst of you, and I will destroy your chariots. And from Hosea 1:7. I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God, and I will not save them by bow, or sword, or by war, by horses or by horsemen. Grotius, however, understands it of enemies: that there will no longer be hostile chariots, hostile cavalry, or the war-bow of enemies with which the Jews and Ephraim might be attacked. (2) This gloss is refuted by the event. For hostility against the Jews did not cease; indeed, they were exposed to various insults and evils in the time of Ptolemy Lagus Soter, who took Jerusalem and led a great number of Jews into Egypt, as Diodorus Siculus testifies in book XIX and Josephus in book XVIII, ch. 1; and likewise in the time of Ptolemy Philopator, when he was waging war with Antiochus the Great, as they were even reduced into the power of Antiochus, and were subject to various misfortunes, and especially in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, of whom one reads in the books of the Maccabees and in Josephus, book VII, ch. 7, etc. Whence it is manifest that these things cannot be understood of external quiet and tranquility under the second temple, and therefore must be explained of the spiritual peace and tranquility under the King Messiah, of whom the Prophet had treated before. For (3) the connection with the preceding passages demands this, which we know from the infallible interpretation of the New Testament and the very evidence of the text do not treat of Zerubbabel, but of the Messiah: the Prophet teaches that under him chariots, cavalry, and war-bows must be cut off, in order to explain more fully those things which he had said about the humble King Messiah, that his equipment would be meager, without any armor—not by chance or out of poverty, but because there will be no use for it—and to describe the quality of his kingdom. For the kingdom of the Messiah consists in the best constitution of the Church, which is promoted neither by chariots, nor by horses, nor by bows, or other instruments of war; whence it is no wonder that this king is alien to all external splendor and worldly pomp. And this is what was predicted concerning the Kingdom of the Messiah in Isaiah 2:4. They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more. And ch. 11:3. The envy of Ephraim shall depart, and the enemies of Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim. Beautifully here the blessed Gerhard, Harmony of the Gospels, ch. CXLIV, p. 244. Other kings usually bring war with them, especially if they are new kings and cannot possess their kingdom in peace without an adversary, but this King of ours is peaceful, who for the chariot of Ephraim, which he took from the midst, gave the chariot of the Evangelists; for the horses of Jerusalem he gave the Apostles, through whom, as if by spiritual chariots and horses, he was carried about in the whole world, speaking peace and thanks to all, Habakkuk 3:8; for the bow of war, he gave the bow of peace, that is, the word of God, which is the bow of salvation and a spiritual sword, Psalm 45:4, Gird yourself with your sword, v. 5, ride upon the word of truth. But lest the Anabaptists conclude from this that it is not permitted for Christians to wage wars, the blessed Balduinus rightly notes in his Commentary on this passage, p. 595, that it is treated here and in similar passages of the Kingdom of Christ, insofar as it is considered in itself, not insofar as it is gathered in the kingdoms of this world. In itself, therefore, and in its own nature, it does not need either the tumults of war or the strength of carnal arms, but is propagated by the sole power of the word and the grace of the Holy Spirit, in which respect the chariots are said to be dispersed, the horses and bows to be dissipated, and swords to be turned into plowshares and spears into pruning hooks, because the kingdom of Christ is not defended by external force and political arms. However, the Holy Spirit gives little hope of political peace to the citizens of the New Testament; indeed, the Son of God predicts the opposite, Matthew 10:34. But these things are by the way, and as it were in passing. (4) When the Prophet describes the Messiah as the Evangelist of peace among the nations, Grotius distorts it to the Jerusalemites who were about to enter into treaties with the nations, contrary to grammar, since the Prophet uses not the feminine gender, but the masculine; contrary to the connection of the text: for the Messiah is the subject of whom those predicates sound, not indeed Jerusalem: the power from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth belongs to the Messiah, not indeed to Jerusalem. Finally, contrary to the parallelism of other places of Scripture, in which that preaching of peace among the nations is attributed not to Jerusalem, but to the Messiah, Ephesians 2:14 ff., Isaiah 2:4, ch. 11:6, ch. 57:19, and dominion to the ends of the earth, Psalm 72:9, Daniel 7:27. Nor indeed, because parts were added which had been torn away from the Kingdom of Judah by Jeroboam, did the dominion of Zerubbabel or of Jerusalem extend as far as the borders of the promised land, Exodus 32:31. I will set your borders from the Red Sea even unto the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert unto the river, namely the Euphrates, such a district as King Solomon possessed, 1 Kings 4:21, but the Jews never again obtained such an ample dominion under the second temple. Wherefore the ecumenical power of Christ is described in this way, which extends itself from the east to the west, and from the north to the south, since the kingdom of Christ has its boundaries in the whole world, thence propagated from Jerusalem through the whole world, Luke 24:47, Acts 1:8. The blessed Dorschaeus observes in his Theology of Zechariah, ch. V, p. 49, that Scripture speaks differently when it explains the borders of the Israelite force, and differently when it sets forth the object of the Messianic dominion. For there the borders are named the desert, Lebanon, the sea, the Euphrates: within these is contained the possession destined for the seed of Abraham. But here the borders are sea and sea, the rivers and the ends of the earth. The manner of speaking is taken from the most wise coordination and joining together of creatures, by which one globe was made from water and earth, so that the seas, received into the bays of the earth, surround the orb of the earth like a belt.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET DISPERDAM QUADRIGAM EX EPHRAIM) Auferam è Judæis & Israelitis, qui cum eis rediere, omnem currum hostilem.

ET EQVUM DE JERUSALEM) Equitatum ho- stilem,

ET DISSIPABITUR ARCUS BELLI) Incidetur: id est, non magis ipsi nocebit, quam si incisus esset nervus.
