ET LOQVETUR PACEM GENTIBUS,) Nem- pe civitas Jerusalem fœdera faciet cum Regibus, cum La- cedæmoniis, cum Romanis.

ET POTESTAS EJUS A MARI.) Rubro,

USQUE AD MARE.) Syriacum.

ET A FLUMINIBUS.) In Hebræo: à flumine, id est, ab Euphrate.

USQUE AD FINES TERRÆ.) Nempe Patri- bus promissæ: nam sub imperium Hierosolymorum venit Samaria, Galilæa, Galaaditis & alia quæ à tempori- bus Jeroboami distracta fuerant. Ad hæc verba in- telligenda repete Josephi locum, quem modo produ- ximus,

Nova iterum textus Prophetici insignis depra- vatio. Nam (1) de hostibus explicantur, quæ de Judæis & Israelitis dicta sunt. Nimirum promitti- tur penes Judæos & Israelitas non fore currus, nec equos, nec arcus belli, quibus pugnent ipsi, quia re- gnum hujus regis plane pacificum, & quietum est, nec istis indiget: quemadmodum ex loco simili manifestum est Mich. 5, 10. Erit die illo, dicit Do- minus exercituum, exscindam equos è medio tui, & perdam currus tuos. Et ex Hos. 1, 7. Domus Judæ miserebor, servaboque eos per Dominum Deum ipso- rum, ac non servabo illos arcu, gladio, aut bello, e- quis aut equitibus. Grotius vero de hostibus in- telligit: non fore deinceps currus hostiles, equitatum hostilem, arcum bellicum hostium, quibus oppugnen- tur Judæi & Ephraim. (2) Glossa hæc ab eventu re- fellitur. Non enim desiit hostilitas adversus Judæ- os, imo variis illi insultibus & malis expositi fuere, tempore Ptolomæi Lagi Soteris, qui Hierosolyma cœpit, & Judæos magno numero in Ægyptum tra- duxit, teste Diodoro Siculo l. XIX. & Josepho l. XVIII. c. I. nec non Ptolomæi Philopatoris, cum bellum gereret cum Antiocho Magno, uti in Antio- chi potestatem etiam redacti sunt, variisque obno- xii fuere infortuniis, & imprimis tempore Antio- chi Epiphanis, de quo in libris Maccabæorum, & a- pud Josephum l. VII. c. 7. &c. Unde manifestum est, hæc non posse de quiete ac tranquillitate externa sub templo secundo intelligi, adeoque de pace ac tran- quillitate spirituali sub Messia Rege, de quo egerat antea Propheta, exponenda esse. Nam id postu- lat (3) συνέχεια cum superioribus, quæ non de Zo- robabele, sed de Messia agere, ex N. T. infallibli interpretatione, atque ipsa textus evidentia novi- mus: sub hoc exscindi debere currus, equitatus, & arcus bellicos, docet Propheta, ut ea, quæ de Messia Rege humili dixerat, uberius explicet, quod exiguus futurus sit ejus apparatus, absque ulla ar- matura, non casu, aut ex inopia, sed quia nullus ejus usus erit, & qualitatem regni ejus describat. Re- gnum enim Messiæ consistit in optima constitutio- ne Ecclesiæ, quæ neque quadrigis, neque equis, neque arcubus, aut aliis instrumentis bellicis pro- movetur; unde mirum non est, hunc regem ab omni splendore externo, atque pompa mundana alienum esse. Atq; hoc est, quod de Regno Messiæ prædictum est Es. 2, 4. Commutabunt gladios suos in ligones, & lanceas suas in falces, non levabit gens contra gentem gladium suum, & non discent ultra bellare. Et c. 11, 3. Recedet zelus Ephraim, & ho- stes Judæ excindentur, Ephraim non æmulabitur Ju- da, & Juda non angustiabit Ephraim. Pulcre hic B. Gerhardus Harmon. Evangel. C. CXLIV. p. 244. Alii Reges plerumque bellum fecum afferunt, præ- sertim si sint novi Reges, nec possint sine adversario regnum suum in pace possidere, sed hic Rex noster est pacificus, qui pro quadriga Ephraim, quam è me- dio tulit, dedit quadrigam Evangelistarum, pro e- quis Jerusalem dedit Apostolos, per quos velut currus & equos spirituales in toto orbe circumvectus est, gra- tiam & pacem omnibus loquens Hab. 3, 8. pro arcu belli, dedit arcum pacis, hoc est, verbum Dei, quod est arcus salutis & gladius spiritualis Psal. 45, 4. accinge te gladio tuo v. 5. equita super verbum ve- ritatis. Ne autem Anabaptistæ hinc concludant Christianis bella gerere non licere, recte notat B. Balduinus Comment. in h. l. p. 595. agi hic & in similibus locis de Regno Christi, quatenus in se spe- ctatur, non quatenus in regnis hujus mundi colli- gitur. In se igitur & sua natura non eget vel belli tumultibus, vel armorum carnaliu robore, sed pro- pagatur sola virtute verbi & gratia Spiritus Sancti, quo respectu quadrigae dispersae, equi & arcu: diffi- pati, gladii in vomeres, & lanceae in falces conver- sae dicuntur, quia vi externa & armis politicis re- gnum Christi non defenditur. Pacis autem poli- ticae spem exiguam facit Spiritus sanctus civibus Novi Testamenti, imo contrarium potius omina- tur Filius Dei, Matth. 10, 34. Sed haec obiter, & velut ἐν παρόδῳ. (4) Cum Propheta Messiam describit ceu Evangelistam pacis inter gentes, Grotius ad Hierosolymitanos foedera inituros cum gentibus detorquet, contra Grammaticam, siqui- dem non genus foemininum, sed masculinum adhi- beat Propheta; contra textus συνέχειαν: Nam Messias subjectum est, de quo illa praedicata sonant, non vero Hierosolyma: Messiae est potestas à mari ad mare & à flumine usque ad fines terrae, non vero Hierosolymae. Denique contra parallelismum alio- rum scripturae locorum, in quibus non Hierosoly- mae, sed Messiae tribuitur illa praedicatio pacis inter Gentes Eph. 2, 14. seqq. Es. 2, 4. c. 11, 6. c. 57, 19. & dominium usque ad terrae fines Psal. 72, 9. Dan. 7, 27. Nec vero ideo, quod partes accesserint, quae à Jeroboamo à Regno Judae avulsae fuere, domini- um Zorobabelis aut Hierosolymorum eousque se porrexit, quo fines terrae promissae, Ex. 32, 31. Po- nam terminos tuos à mari rubro, usque ad mare Philistaeorum, & à deserto usque ad flumen, puta Euphratis, qualem districtum Rex Salomo posse- dit 1. Reg. 4, 21. sed nunquam sub templo secundo tam amplum dominium Judaei consequuti iterum sunt. Quapropter describitur ita potestas oecu- menica Christi, quae se extendit ab oriente ad occi- dentem, & à septentrione ad meridiem, siquidem regnum Christi in universo mundo sua habeat po- moeria, inde ex Hierosolyma propagata per totum orbem Luc. 24, 47. Act. 1, 8. B. Dorschaeus obser- vat Theol. Zach. c. V. p. 49. aliter loqui scriptu- ram, quando Israeliticae fortis terminos explicat, aliter quando Messiani dominatus objectum expo- nit. Ibi namque termini nominantur desertum, Libanus, mare, Euphrates: intra hos continetur possessio semini Abrahae destinata. Hic vero ter- mini sunt mare & mare, flumina & fines terrae. Modus loquendi desumptus est ex ipsa sapientis- sima coordinatione & coagmentatione creatura- rum, qua ex aqua & terra unus factus est globus, ita ut maria in terrae sinus recepta, & cinguli instar ambiant orbem terrarum.

## 9:11
Verse 11.

YOU ALSO, BY THE BLOOD OF YOUR COVENANT, HAVE SENT FORTH YOUR PRISONERS FROM THE PIT, IN WHICH THERE WAS NO WATER: RETURN) From the Greek ἐξαπέστειλας, but in the Hebrew and Chaldean, I have sent forth; so that it is permissible to translate these words with the Chaldean as follows: You therefore (O posterity of Abraham: for אַתּ is feminine) whose prisoners, on account of the blood of your covenant (the promise sanctioned by the Paschal victim), I have sent forth (namely, from Egypt) and sent forth from the cistern in which there was no water (that is, from the most parched places of Arabia), return to me; mindful of the old benefits, and of the new, trust in me.

We must look here first at the genuine reading of the text, then at the meaning. Papists like Cornel. à Lapide here, Huntlaeus, Riebera on this passage, and others maintain that the text is corrupt, whether by the Jews or by the scribes, because feminine forms were substituted in place of masculine ones, and the verb of the first person שִׁלַּחְתִּי in place of the verb of the second person emisti שִׁלַּחְתְּ, since in this way the LXX, Jerome, and other ancients, as well as the Syrian and the Arab, read it. But the suspicion of corruption is vain, since the Hebrew codices agree entirely in this place, nor is it new for interpreters in translation not to press the words, but to express only the sense, which consists in the words, even if this apostrophe is directed not to Christ, but to Sion, or Jerusalem, by virtue of the feminine gender. Castrius himself refutes this opinion concerning the corrupt text: The Hebrew, he says, Even you, in the blood of your covenant I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit, in which there is no water, and the pronouns, both the primitive 'you', as well as the possessive 'your' and 'yours', are feminine, and the word is of the first person, 'I have sent forth'. And thus read the Chaldean, R. Salomon, Galat. lib. 8. cap. 20. and all the more recent ones: and thus Pagninus explains it. You also Jerusalem exult in the blood of your covenant. Or as others: You also daughter of Sion, or of the Church Jerusalem, have been saved, or shall be saved in the blood of your covenant, or in the blood of the author of your covenant, just as the Messiah was saved in his justice. Therefore these are the words of the Prophet addressing Sion, as above, exult greatly daughter of Sion, and rejoice daughter of Jerusalem, and saying: Even exult not only because your king will enter meek, sitting upon an ass and a colt, but also in the blood of the same, by which he confirmed the new covenant, which he entered into with you. Or as Salomon, Galat. Vat. Isid. Mont. and Rob. You also congregation of Sion shall be saved in the blood of Christ, by which he confirmed your covenant; just as Christ himself will come just and saved, and saving all. But more truly they are the words of God addressing Sion. You also Church of Sion exult, because you shall be saved in the blood of Christ, the author of your covenant. Whence he says the same: for I have sent forth, instead of I will send forth, your prisoners from the pit of limbo, in which there is no water, raising them up. They are therefore the words of God, as Hieronym. and Isidorus say, speaking to the Church of Sion. But the Septuagint. Vulgat. Hieronym. and all the Greek and Latin Fathers read: You also in the blood of your testament have sent forth your prisoners. And they are the words of either God, or the Prophet addressing Christ, as Origen Tract. 14. on Matthew, Hieronym. Theodor. Cyrill. Augustin. 18. de Civit. Dei c. 35. Remig. Rupert. Albert. Hugo, Lyra and Dionys. wish in this sense: And you O Christ, by the merit of the blood, by which you strengthened your new covenant, which you shed for men, you led out from limbo the just fathers, who were detained there, until you should free them. The diversity of the Hebrew reading is found almost only in the mutation of the points. Or at least the Vulgate has woven together more convenient words to explain the sense. For the Vulgate also brings forth the sense which the Hebrew words bring forth; as if God or Christ, or the Prophet are addressing the daughter of Sion: You also O Church of Sion, by the virtue of my blood, or of Christ, by which your testament or covenant was strengthened, which he entered into with her, you have sent forth, for you will send forth, your captive children from the limbo, in which they were held enclosed already for many years. This is, you shall see them free and shall possess them, Christ dismissing them. These are Castrius': He intersperses the limbo of the Fathers. But that will be destroyed subsequently.

Now as to the sense of the words, even if it does not seem to matter much for the investigation of the same, whether God the Father speaks those words, or indeed God the Son, yet that these are not of the Son of God, which the Blessed Dn. D. Dorsheus judged in Syn. Theol. Zach. c. III. v. 11. but of God the Father, is clear from the fact that he speaks in v. 10. of the Son as of another person: Behold your King will come to you. Meanwhile, we have previously observed that these words of God the Father introduce the Son of God. Grotius in rendering the sense has again followed the Jews, foolish Masters, and blind Doctors, who interpret it concerning the blood of victims, by which the covenant was sanctioned in Ex. 24, 8. and concerning the liberation from the captivity of Egypt once made. For thus the Chaldean explained it: You also with whom the pact was sanctioned in blood, I redeemed you from the subjection of the Egyptians, I gave you necessary things in the desert, which was desolate, like a pit in which there are no waters. Others, as Hugo notes, accept it concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, in whose footsteps it pleased Ion. Franc. Junius to insist in Bell. l. de purgat. c. 14. as also Calvin himself in l. II. Instit. c. XVI. and others. Willius in the explanation of Junius says that nothing is discordant, and that he himself had previously preferred the same, but in the commentary he refutes that with three reasons p. 307. First, he says, no convenient reason appears why God should have wished to repeat here a new repetition of a performed benefit. Then I do not see how they can be called prisoners of hope, who had already been freed a hundred years before. Thirdly, the exhortation concerning the repetition of the Jerusalemites would be in vain, where the greatest part of the Jews was already sticking. Nor is the business here for God with the rest in Babylon, but with the Church in Judea. Which arguments are solid enough, but he himself devised a new interpretation hitherto unheard of, concerning the liberation from the Egyptian captivity through Philadelphus, into which the Jews had been led by Ptolemy Lagus. The sense is, he says, p. 310. You, who are captive in Egypt, and uniquely seek liberation and redemption, and hope for it from your God, retrace your steps, and seek again Jerusalem, a place both fortified by itself, and which will be a fortification for you. But Willius was unmindful of his own admonition. For here the business for God is not with the rest among foreigners, but with the Church among the Jews. And that gloss is too jejune and frivolous: that Egypt is called a cistern, in which there is no water, because it almost never rains there. Furthermore, Willius accepts the blood of the covenant from the typical blood of sacrifices, which must be understood entirely concerning the blood of Christ humbled for us, afflicted, and saved from the infernal pit. Furthermore, there is added here a cause for the exultation of the daughter of Zion that is not less, but rather more ample and more illustrious, which Willius renders thus: Even you (exult) in the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners. For those words EVEN YOU have the force of amplification. You are to exult not only on account of the advent, but also and primarily on account of that redemption which you obtain in your Messiah and his blood. What if that command is applied particularly by the Holy Spirit as interpreter in the New Testament to the Jewish Church at the time of Christ's solemn entry into the city, by which he had to enter as one to be saved (for the past is put for the future, as is wont to happen in prophecies)? Therefore, the Prophet also addresses this Church, and intimates to it redemption from the pit in which there is no water. Therefore, that does not pertain to the times of the liberation by Philadelphus. Furthermore, the liberation from Egypt did not consist of blood. But here the discourse is about a liberation made by blood. Moreover, that fortress to which the prisoners of hope are commanded to turn is estimated too meagerly when it is understood as the city of Jerusalem. For who among the faithful could fix their hope upon that city and place their trust in it as a completely invincible fortification? And how would God himself command that? Nor is it entirely true that the Jews felt no refreshment in Egypt, as in a cistern in which there is no water of refreshment. Willius himself observed something else about the same on page 259. Ptolemy, called Soter, son of Lagus, having been liberated from a war threatened against him by Perdiccas, subjugates Syria and Phoenicia, and having routed Demetrius, he also captures Palestine itself and Jerusalem, and leads many from the mountainous tract of Judea and the vicinity of Jerusalem into Egypt. Diodorus Siculus, book XVIII, and Josephus, book XII, chapter 1. Yet they felt some refreshment from these calamities, while Seleucus Nicanor granted municipal rights to the Jews in the cities founded by him throughout Asia and lower Syria, and finally in the metropolis of Antioch itself. Josephus, book XII, chapter 3. Add that not all the captives in Egypt were redeemed and liberated by Philadelphus: but here concerning the prisoners of Zion indefinitely whosoever they may be, and it concerns the liberating of the prisoners of hope: and not only the redeeming of some from the cistern. Finally, how safe those were who were redeemed from Egypt by Philadelphus, and what kind of fortification for the prisoners of hope Willius leaves in the city of Jerusalem, let even his own historical recapitulation teach, p. 260. Ptolemy Philopator, son of Euergetes, and Ptolemy Epiphanes, son of Philopator, wage a bloody war with Antiochus the Great, during which time the Jews lived in continuous vexation, whether Antiochus was winning or losing, being badly treated, no differently than a ship attacked on both sides by waves, tossed between the prosperous and adverse fortune of Antiochus. At length, they yield to Antiochus the victor. Afterwards, they are again subjected by Scopas to Ptolemy Epiphanes, from whom they are again snatched away by Antiochus. The wars between Antiochus the Great and Ptolemy Epiphanes having ended, and friendship and affinity having been initiated, they are often harassed by the Samaritans. Josephus, book 12, chapter 3. But this regarding Willius: whose analysis, when he devotes effort to his own interpretation and new explanations, is indeed sometimes specious, but is never found to be solid. Cocceius more correctly recognizes the word 'evangelize,' by which God announces liberty to Israel, and he urges the emphasis on the word 'ALSO.' Not only did your King come, but I also sent forth your prisoners, which he thinks can also be rendered 'NEVERTHELESS,' i.e., although I cut off the chariot, yet I also sent forth the prisoners. To whom he wishes liberty to be announced, provided they are held in the servitude of the elements of the world for fear of death. Because they are no longer to be held by the external bonds of the law or of the inheritance of the people.

To return now to Grotius: we find these things lacking in him: First, that he makes the subject the posterity of Abraham, of which no mention was made in the preceding. Therefore, the same is inserted here without warrant. The Prophet had spoken of the daughter of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem, and indeed especially of that which was to be at the coming and entry of the Messiah into Jerusalem, whom he had provoked to exultation, though not excluding the faithful of his own age, for he wished all the faithful, since the Messiah was now about to come, to exult and to expect his coming with true faith, and to rejoice in him. Secondly, that he makes the predicate 'return to me.' It does not suit the subject 'YOU.' 'You, daughter of Zion, return to me.' And the word is wrongly pulled back to that subject 'YOU' in the following clause, since it has its own proper subject there: 'You prisoners of hope, return.' Thirdly, that he has the rest in this verse only as periphrases of the subject: 'You, posterity of Abraham, whose prisoners I have sent forth from the cistern because of the blood of your covenant.' For these do not pertain to the description of the subject, but constitute the predicate; if they were to be referred to the subject, the pronoun 'asher' (whose), which is not read here, would have been added. Fourthly, Grotius inserts a double sending forth at his own discretion, rendering it thus: 'whose prisoners I have sent forth because of the blood (promised, sanctioned by the paschal victim), namely from Egypt, and I have sent forth from the cistern in which there was no water (that is, from the most thirsty places of Arabia), return to me.' Only one terminus a quo of the sending forth is assigned here, so why does Grotius invent a double one, such as Egypt and the thirsty places of Arabia? If that cistern is the thirsty places of Arabia, how then is Egypt the terminus a quo of the sending forth? For the terminus a quo is that cistern. The Prophet handed down nothing about a double sending forth; he commemorates only one. Fifthly, the means of the sending forth is the blood of the covenant of the Church, or initiated with the Church. Grotius perverts this for the sake of his gloss: 'Because of the blood of your covenant,' that is, on account of the promise sanctioned by the paschal victim. If the promise of redemption through Christ, which had to be accomplished by his blood, were understood as adumbrated and sanctioned by the Sacrament of the paschal lamb, I would not object; but Grotius did not understand it so; he looks to the promised liberation from Egypt: and he explains it only of the typical blood of the paschal lamb, not of the blood of the Messiah: but in that he judaizes.

Most all Christian interpreters argue that the blood of Christ is understood here against the Jews. For (1) it concerns the time of the New Testament, namely the coming of the Messiah and his solemn entry into the city of Jerusalem for his passion, which he himself, as that righteous servant of God, afflicted and humbled for our sake, of whom Isaiah chapter 53 speaks, had to undergo, so that, having been rescued and saved from judgment, after he had laid down his soul as a sacrifice, he might save us, preach the Gospel of peace, and propagate his kingdom throughout the whole world. All of which are most clear from the text. Therefore, these things cannot be accepted regarding the blood of the paschal lamb or the victims of the Old Testament, but regarding the blood which was shed for the redemption of the human race, in the passion of Christ, who for its sake wished to present himself at Jerusalem as the true paschal lamb. For Christ entered for that reason, on that very day on which the paschal lamb was accustomed to be separated from the flock and introduced into the city with solemn ceremonies, so that he might show the type of the paschal lamb to be fulfilled in himself. Which was done on the tenth day of the month of Nisan, so that, namely, the paschal lamb might be sacrificed on the fourteenth of the same month, Ex. 12:3, 6, as Jacobus de Valentia also observes in Psalm 115, that the Jews brought it into the temple with solemn pomp, adorned with branches and flowers, and kept it there until the time of slaughter. If any traces of this rite exist among the Rabbis, a beautiful accommodation is found in the entry of Christ among green branches, as the antitype figured by the paschal lamb, John 1:29, 1 Cor. 5:7, 1 Pet. 1:19.

(2) The subject here is the Messiah SAVED for you, as the Prophet says: Behold your King comes to YOU SAVED. But how he was saved, we learn from his most ardent prayers in Ps. 69, 1. et seqq., Save me O God: for the waters have entered even unto my soul, I am stuck in the mire of the deep &c. v. 14. But as for me, my prayer is to you O Lord, in the time of your good pleasure, O GOD, in the multitude of your mercy hear me, in the truth of your salvation, deliver me from the mire &c. concerning the hearing of which prayers, Is. 49, 8. says this, The Lord says, in an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you, and I have given you for a covenant of the people. And Heb. 5, 7. Who in the days of his flesh, offering up prayers and supplications with a strong cry and tears to him who could save him from death, was heard for his reverence. And although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered, and being made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him. These passages illustrate our point, namely that Christ was immersed for our sake into the pit in which there is no water, and was saved from the same, so that we might be freed and sent forth from that pit. It is a most certain matter, says the blessed Dorscheus, Theol. Zach. part I. c. IIX. p. 158, that Jesus is a savior in this way, that he himself was also saved, not indeed meritoriously, but efficiently, by his own eternal power, whatever may be the case regarding the passage in Zech. 9, 9. But he who is saved, he has tasted something of the pit of damnation and curse. For he is saved from evil, from a burden, from injuries by which he was oppressed, or at least from the troubles by which he was affected. Salvation is opposed to evil, saving to a curse, and to that which arises from a curse. For where there is the evil of punishment, there it is necessary that the evil of guilt has preceded. And if there had not been the evil of guilt, the evil of punishment would not have been. Now both pertain to the pit, in which there is no water. He therefore who was saved from evils, was in evils, and was in the communion of the pit, in which there is no water. But Christ was saved from evils, and indeed the greatest, infinite, and most grievous of all, from which he could not be saved except by divine and infinite power. Therefore Christ was in evils, and indeed the greatest, infinite, and most grievous of all, etc. He was in the deepest communion of the ἀνύδρε pit.

(3) The subject is the MESSIAH JUST FOR US, who was made righteousness for us by God the Father, through his obedience even to the death of the cross, by which he himself bore the sins of many Is. 53, and was made sin for us, that we might be rendered the righteousness of God in him 2 Cor. 5:21. Which was done when he descended into the pit for us, that we might be released from there by his blood; therefore he is called עָנִי humbled, afflicted FOR US, or for our sake. For just as he was given and born for us Is. 9:6, so also he was afflicted and humbled for us, when he suffered for us, and shed his blood for us, for our ἀπολύτρωσιν: Behold thy King cometh unto THEE AFFLICTED & HUMBLED.

(4) The subject here is the Gospel of peace, or of our reconciliation with God, which was indeed foreshadowed by the blood of victims, but in order that captives might be released in reality, it had to be done by the blood of Jesus Christ Rom. 5:19, who is our peace, reconciling us to God through the cross, killing the enmities in himself, and coming he preached peace to those who were far off, i.e., among the Gentiles Eph. 2:16. Therefore, the discourse is about that blood of redemption, through which reconciliation and peace were obtained, which he was to preach among the Gentiles: which is the blood of Jesus Christ our savior. For he died for us, by his blood we are justified, and are saved from wrath, through his bloody death we have been reconciled to God, when we were his enemies Rom. 5:9, 10.

(5) The subject here is the kingdom of Christ, which was propagated through the Gospel of peace among the Gentiles and throughout the whole world, and therefore these things are to be understood concerning redemption through the blood of Christ, and not indeed concerning the liberation from Egypt through the blood of the paschal lamb. For the Prophet prophesies of that liberation which was to be proclaimed through the Gospel of peace among all nations, so that the kingdom of Christ might be erected and propagated throughout the whole world. But this is none other than the liberation which was accomplished through the death of Christ, concerning which Ps. 72:7 seqq. Righteousness and abundance of peace shall arise in his days, until the moon is taken away, and he shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth, all nations shall serve him. BECAUSE he shall deliver the poor from the mighty, and shall make the souls of the poor safe. Cf. Luke 24:46, 47.

(6) Here is held a prophecy concerning a future thing, and not a commemoration of a past thing, for the coming of the Messiah is predicted, the removal of cavalry and of weapons of war, the announcement of peace, the expansion of the Messianic empire throughout the world, and therefore the release of the bound also concerns a future benefit, and not the liberation once made from Egypt, the redemption of the blood of Christ, and not that by which the Israelites were liberated from the destroying Angel through the blood of the paschal lamb.

(7) The discourse here is of that blood of God, which is the blood of the New covenant, namely of reconciliation with God, and of peace, which is to be announced among the Gentiles. But this is the blood of Christ the Mediator, through whom the new covenant was established Heb. 9:12.

(8) In this place the benefit of the redemption of Christ is graphically described; for there is designated (1) the object of the redemption. THE BOUND of Zion, or of the daughter

Zion, I have sent forth thy bound. The feminine suffix pronoun refers to the preceding feminine noun, just as the feminine pronoun אַתְּ thou, ALSO thou daughter of Zion and daughter of Jerusalem. For the Lord addresses her, where most Interpreters posit an ἔκλειψιν. But some supply it in this manner: Also thou exult. But before, the daughter of Zion had already been excited to exultation. Others with R. Solomon in this manner: Also thou shalt be saved. Because it had been said concerning the Messiah King HE IS SAVED. For thus R. Solomon Jarchi. Also thou Church of Zion, and Jerusalem shalt be saved with the Messiah, just as he himself is righteous and saved. But although that sense may be suitable, that participle SAVED is nevertheless too remote. And therefore it is better to posit a Hebraism here, and to interpret these words: Also thou, in this way: Also as far as thou art concerned, namely on account of the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy bound. For Philologists, Mr. Dr. Varenius, and others observe that this manner of speaking is not unusual in Hebraism; by which method a special application to the Jews will be made, lest by chance they believe that this spiritual peace was to be announced only among the Gentiles, or that this promise pertains only to future times, when the kingdom of Christ was to be dilated throughout the whole world. For the liberation and salvation, which is obtained through blood, had to be done by virtue of the covenant entered into with the Jews, whence the Jews could the more especially apply the same to themselves. That גַּם אַתְּ ETIAM TU can also be referred to the immediately preceding words in this way: Even you, O Zion, or daughter of Zion, speak peace among the nations in the blood of your covenant, to which voice in Hebrew is added the accent Rebia Regius, having the force of making a greater incision, so that the Church is joined or subordinated to the Messiah in the announcement of peace, inasmuch as by its ministry peace was preached among the nations, concerning which Is. 40, 9: get you up into the high mountain, you that bring good tidings to Zion: &c. 11, 3: out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. But we can also understand the substantive verb, which is not rarely omitted, Job 3, 5. Is. 8, 10. 13. ch. 45, 9. 1 Cor. 3. 2 Cor. 11, 1. Eph. 1, 4. so that the sense may be: Even you shall be in the blood of your covenant. And thus the particle ETIAM is a mark of amplification, as if to say: not only do you have a cause for rejoicing on account of the coming of the Messiah, but also because in his blood, which is the blood of the covenant initiated with you, you are to be a sharer and participant in the benefits brought forth by his blood. Moreover, when the object of the sending forth from the pit, the bound or captives of Zion, are established in the Jewish Church, others are not excluded, nor is the universality of Christ's redemption denied. For the inclusion of one is not the exclusion of another. And that sending forth is understood either by reason of merit and acquisition, in which way it is common to all men 2 Cor. 5, 14. 1 Tim. 2, 5. 1 John 2, 2. or by reason of effect and actual enjoyment, and thus it is proper to the faithful John 10, 15. ch. XVII. 19. Add that the name of those bound is common to all men. For the whole human race is bound and captive after the fall. Our first parents were created in true liberty, neither captive by any bonds, nor pressed by any yoke of servitude, but through sin they cast themselves together with all their descendants into miserable servitude and captivity, having become servants of sin John 8, 34. Rom. 6, 40. 2 Pet. 2, 19. reduced under the power of darkness, or of the Devil himself Col. 1, 13. Luke 11, 21. The word אָסִיר denotes not only a captive, but one bound, because in that captivity we were constricted by the bonds of sins, by the snares of the Devil and of death, from which captivity we could not be freed by our own human or angelic powers Ps. 49, 21. but through the blood of the covenant initiated with the Church and the Patriarchs, through the blood of Christ, in which the covenant of grace is established Heb. IX. we were to be freed from that which the blood in circumcision, the paschal lamb, and the Levitical victims prefigured. Therefore the Word of the Gospel, by which that peace is announced and the reconciliation made through Christ is designated to the Church: when Zion is said to be about to speak peace in the blood of her covenant, because it is the word of the cross and of the blood of Christ, nor does it preach reconciliation except in the blood of Christ. Whence Paul wished to know nothing in his preaching, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified 1 Cor. II. 3. Thus therefore he addresses the Church, as interpreted by B. Dorscheus p. 80. But you flourish, grow, triumph, white, holy, saved, in the most precious and clearly divine blood of your covenant. He adds, indeed I have even sent forth your prisoners. The relative 'your' therefore also pertains to the Church. Whence the discourse in this place is about such prisoners, whom the Church especially regards. For those who are in the blood of the covenant, those prisoners are also hers. But the Church especially regards those who are spiritually bound, entangled by the burdens of sins, so that she may heal them, and liberty from those bonds may be bestowed by the divine hand. For she is that spiritual spouse, the physician of fornication, the heavenly queen, the tamer of disobedience, the priest of God, the destroyer of impiety, the city of God, the dwelling place of exiles, etc. She is the kingdom of restored grace and of subverted sin. Moreover, those prisoners are called prisoners of Zion and Jerusalem, that is, of the Church: both because the Church has true and solid knowledge of those bonds by which men are spiritually bound, and because the Church has the true and solid cure against those bonds by which men are spiritually bound. The Church is as it were a spiritual physician, who, as she suffices for knowing, so also she suffices for curing. Therefore the sick are hers, the prisoners are hers; as many as feel themselves to be bound hasten to the Church, that they may obtain liberation there; as many prisoners also as the Church knows of here and there, these she regards as her own to be liberated for herself, to be freed from bonds for herself. Those captives are also called captives of HOPE, because the hope of liberation was made for them in the Proto-Evangelium, and in other promises given to the Patriarchs and the people of the Lord, by which is insinuated the distinction between the captivity of the devils, who are bound by eternal and indissoluble bonds or chains 2 Pet. II. 4. Jude v. 6. without hope of liberation, and of men, who are bound by HOPE, on account of the hope of liberation made for them, and at the same time the medium is designated, through which the liberation provided by the Messiah is applied to us. Which is faith: since hope is often taken for faith, embracing the liberation of the Messiah, so that thus also a distinction is constituted between believers, as true members of the Church, who are bound by hope, expect, desire, and embrace the liberation made through Christ, and hope for and pant after full redemption Rom. VIII. 23. and unbelievers and Gentiles, who are not bound by hope, because they do not have the hope of liberation Eph. II. 12. 1 Thess. IV. 13.

(2) Here the price of redemption is designated, namely the blood of the covenant, not the blood which was shed in the circumcision of infants, as the Jews wish, nor the blood of victims, nor could redemption be made through human blood contaminated by the stain of sin, nor through the blood of brutes. But the blood of Christ, which alone is the ransom of the soul Matt. XX. 28. Mark X. 45. 1 Tim. II. 6. alone is the meritorious blood of divine grace and the remission of sins and of the covenant of grace, and therefore it is called the blood of the New covenant Matt. XXVI. 28. Indeed, God had entered into a legal covenant with the Israelite people, to the perfect observation of which He had bound them, with the addition of the promise of liberation from the infernal prison, which was the old covenant erected by the blood of bulls and goats, but because no one kept it, the New covenant was promised Jer. 31, 31. which was to be established through the blood of the Messiah concerning the remission of sins and the grace of God through faith in Christ, to whom all the Prophets bear witness. Acts 10, 43.

(3) The very sending forth of the prisoners is expressed, which God the Father, speaking here, indeed attributes to Himself, yet it is accomplished in the blood of the new covenant, in the blood of the only-begotten Son: the sending forth is common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but the price of the sending forth is proper to the Son. Therefore He Himself is also peculiarly called the Redeemer, because, namely, the λύτρον having been paid, He redeemed us, by which name He is said to lead forth אסירים the prisoners in chains Ps. 68, 7, to lead forth אסיר the prisoner from the prison (after he was given for a covenant of the people) from the prison house those sitting in darkness Is. 42, 6, c. 49, 8, and to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound c. 61, 2, which passages the Lord undoubtedly regarded here when He says: I will send forth thy prisoners. B. D. Dorscheus urges especially the comparison of the passage Jer. 31, 33, in this manner in Theol. Zachar. p. 83. Those bonds which are said to be loosed and broken asunder in the very passage concerning the covenant of the N. T. are also understood in Zechariah in the exposition of the fruit of the blood of the covenant: likewise, those prisoners to whom help and liberty are promised in the passage of the prophecy concerning the new covenant are the prisoners of that [covenant] which is in the blood of the covenant. For Zechariah points his finger entirely at the prophecy of St. Jeremiah and his illustrious promises concerning bonds and liberation. But in truth, it is spiritual bonds and the bonds of sins that are understood to be dissolved and broken asunder in that very passage concerning the covenant of the N. T. To those bound in sins, help and liberty are promised in the passage of the prophecy concerning the new covenant. For the most important part of liberty, or rather the entire loosing of bonds, is almost in the propitiation of iniquities and the oblivion of sins. Hence the Apostle Paul, Rom. 7, 23, complains that he, even though reborn, was still αἰχμαλωτισμένον. If, however, the αἰχμαλωτισμὸς of sin still clings to the regenerate and makes its torments as it were its own, how much greater and more atrocious is that αἰχμαλωτισμὸς which is in the unregenerate, namely in those who have not yet made the most happy transition to the covenant of grace. Furthermore, the Orthodox explain this release in more than one way: some say it was accomplished when it was procured by the merit of Christ, and thus the cause is rendered why the Church is in the blood of the covenant, because indeed it pleased God to release through the blood of the Messiah those bound by the chains of sins and the captivity of Satan, which release, accomplished by the death of Christ, he who embraces it with true faith flourishes and triumphs in the blood of the covenant of grace. Others interpret the sending forth as concerning the act of justification and the remission of sins, for then we are delivered from the pit wherein is no water, when we obtain the remission of sins, as regards both guilt and punishment, so that this may be the connection: Even Thou, O Sion, art in the blood of thy covenant, yea, I will also send forth thy prisoners, whosoever others there be who shall have turned themselves unto Thee, from that lake wherein is no water, that they likewise may be in the blood of thy covenant, and in the bosom of the grace of God in Christ Jesus. Which sense the blessed Dorscheus embraces on p. 97. The Lord prophesies that He will send forth the prisoners of the Church. I have sent forth thy prisoners. The prisoners, whom you can know intimately, in whose care you devote every effort, so that they may be able to be asserted from their bonds into liberty, who will approach you, and will wish to be yours, and will desire to be numbered among your own, who pertain to your inheritance, which is the Church to be increased from the whole world, which you are diffused into the whole world, which you are militant on earth, whom the Messiah will also visit on earth, as a righteous King, Savior, compassionate one, ruler. And page 95. You are the Church in the blood of your covenant, which you have newly established, you blossom and shine in that most holy sprinkling of incorruptible blood. And not you only, but furthermore I will send forth your prisoners from the pit, in which there is no water. Likewise page 92. You were, O Church, even in the pit, in which there is no water. Thus from Adam all flesh was born. no longer in the pit. You are in my bosom, in my covenant. But behold, there is an infinite crowd of men, which is still in the pit, which sticks in the miserable deep. That I will also take up. I will not suffer it to perish. If it shall come to you, if it shall profess itself to be bound, and shall receive itself into your bosom, it shall be sent forth from the pit just as you were received. And hence the blessed Dorscheus, page 155, reckons the words ἀποστρέφειν and ἐπιστρέφειν among the synonyms of SENDING FORTH from the pit. This indeed is from Acts 26:18, where Paul, a minister in the power of the federal blood of Jesus Christ, is said to be turning [them] back. The starting point is darkness and the power of Satan: what else than the Zacharian waterless pit? The destination is God, Light, forgiveness of sins, an inheritance among those who are sanctified; what else than the Zion covenant with God and its benefits? The instrument of apprehending that divine turning back is faith in Jesus. The price is the blood of Jesus. For by it they are made sanctified, Heb. 10:29. That indeed is used in Rom. 11:26: The Deliverer will come from Zion and will turn away ungodliness from Jacob. 27. And this is the covenant to them from me, when I shall take away their sins. The starting point is ungodliness and sin, in which, as in a waterless pit, they are held concluded under a curse, v. 32: God has concluded all in disobedience. The destination is: Israel shall be saved, v. 26. The form is the turning away of ungodliness and forgiveness of sins: The foundation is the covenant of God, the federal blood. This is our late lamented [scholar]. Which teach that the phrase of SENDING FORTH from the pit was referred by him to the act of justification: that others also are subsequently to be sent forth from that pit, and to be received into the bosom, just as Zion is in the bosom of grace and in the blood of the Messianic covenant: but not rarely he explained the same phrase in the prior sense concerning the sending forth which took place in the redemption of Christ, by which all men were sent forth by his blood, provided that his redemption is made universal, and he attributes the same sending forth also to Christ, and explains it through ἀγοράζειν, λυτρῶν, ἀπολυτρῶν, and other synonyms of the redemption of Christ. Such, he says on page 150, is the sending forth understood in this place, which arises from the sender's descent into the pit. The Zion King sends forth by descending into the pit, and receiving into himself whatever the waterless pit of damnation, tyranny, burden, and difficulty has, whether formally or virtually, and by way of an equivalent. Although it is indeed certain that this sending forth in this place is attributed to God the Father, not to Christ, yet even in the redemption made by the blood of Christ, God the Father is rightly said to have sent forth the prisoners entirely by reason of his divine authority, power of grace, and charity and jurisdiction, as well as the ordination, procurement, and acceptance of the satisfaction and redemption of the Son.

Wherefore neither explanation is unsuitable: yet we judge the former to be preferred here: namely, that the cause is rendered why Zion is in the blood of the covenant and the bosom of grace, because God was about to send forth, according to the economy of grace destined from eternity, the prisoners sticking in the captivity and bonds of sin and Satan through the blood of the covenant, which the Messiah the Son had to shed for the remission of sins, that ransom of redemption having been accepted, which sending forth, as the true citizens of Zion acknowledge and believe with undoubted faith, so through faith they are in the blood of the covenant and in the bosom of grace and in the covenant of grace, and they actually enjoy the covenant of grace. That sending forth is common to all men, but this existence in the covenant of blood is proper to the faithful. That was done in the redemption of Christ, of which the Apostle says in 2 Cor. 5:17: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sin to them. But this takes place in justification, when we are made actual participants through faith in the remission of sins obtained through Christ. There in Christ we were all sent forth, as our surety, sponsor, and Mediator. For just as by that one dying for all, we are all considered dead in the judgment of God, because God accepted the satisfaction of one for all, as if it had been performed by all, so by his being made alive, we have been made alive; by his being raised, we have all been raised, Hos. 6, Eph. 2:6. By his being sent forth from the pit in which there is no water, we have all been sent forth, because just as he himself was delivered up for our sins, so he was also raised for our justification, Rom. 4:24. Indeed, not only have we been sent forth in him from the infernal pit, but heaven itself is opened to all in him, so that now entrance into the holy of holies lies open to all through the veil of the flesh of Christ, Heb. 10:19, 20. Christ sent forth as regards the ransom through payment and merit; God the Father as regards the acceptance of the ransom paid and the good pleasure or acquiescence, or the ratification and favor, in that ransom or price of redemption, as an equivalent, and approved by himself for the sins of the whole human race,

(4) The term from which is expressed בּוֹר, a cistern, pit, or lake, in which there is no water. It refers without doubt to the history in Gen. 37:24 (which B. Gerhard preferred here), where it is said of Joseph that his brothers threw him into a cistern empty of water, in which he would have miserably perished had Judah not pulled him out. Thus we miserable humans were thrown into a pit of that kind, in which there was no water, that is, no refreshment, no comfort, Luke 16:24, in which consequently we would have had to perish eternally, had not the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Rev. 5:5—that is, Christ, sprung from the tribe of Judah, Heb. 7:14—liberated us from it and pulled us out. Therefore, by that cistern is understood neither Egypt nor even the desert of Arabia. For this lake is such a one in which there is no water. The Israelites were not destitute of water either in Egypt or in the desert of Arabia, whether you understand water properly, or improperly concerning the water of refreshment, nor did the release from the desert of Arabia consist of a price or blood. And therefore the Jews themselves acknowledged that by the lake in which there is no water, Gehenna is understood, in the Prologue to Echa Rabbathi: The Holy and Blessed God promised us that He would snatch us from Gehenna through the merit of circumcision. And where did He say this? In Zechariah, who says, 'As for you also, by the blood of your covenant I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water.' The Papists snatch these words to refer to the Limbo of the Fathers: Ribera and Cornel. à Lapide on this passage, as also the Tridentine Catechism in the article on the descent; but in the Limbo of the Fathers, which they form by circumscription, the water of consolation was not lacking, nor were the Patriarchs bound there, as Bellarmine admits in Book 1, On Purgatory, ch. 3, and Peter Thyræus of Neuss, the Jesuit, in the appendix to his work on the apparitions of spirits. 2. p. 91. Nay, the Patriarchs were immediately translated after death into the bosom of Abraham and Paradise, not into any limbo of hell, Luke 16:23, ch. 23. Others, with Bellarmine (loc. cit.) and Coster in his Enchiridion, p. 492, understand it of purgatory, but even in that, the water of consolation is not lacking, provided there is a certain hope of liberation there, as they describe their fictitious purgatory, nor can they call the souls there bound, whom they believe to travel from there to us in these lands. See Bellarmine, Book II, On Purgatory, ch. 8. Let the blessed D. Dorscheus, in his Theologia Zachariæ, part 1, ch. 7, p. 88, be compared here, where he shows at length that the Limbo of the Fathers or Purgatory is not meant. Wherefore the pious more correctly understand by the lake in which there is no water the ancients to be hell, in which there is not water, but sulphur as fire, in which there is no refreshment of consolation, no hope of salvation, Luke 16:24. From which, having been liberated through the blood of Christ, we are sent forth by God, on account of this ἀπολύτρωσιν (redemption), we who were held bound by God through the voice of the divine law under sin and condemnation, Rom. 11:32, Gal. 3, Deut. 27:26. Because Christ redeemed us from the hand of hell, Hos. 13:14. Therefore He is said to have the keys of death and of hell, Rev. 1:18. That pit is understood, in which men were before they were united to God through the divine covenant. For there is here an opposition between the most beneficent divine bosom, which is in the blood of the covenant of the Messiah, and the cursed diabolical pit, in which there is no water, as if to say: O Church, even in the pit in which there was no water, I saw you sticking, perishing, and defiled in that pit. I have had mercy on you, your King shall come to you, your righteous one, afflicted for you, saved for you, I make a covenant with you, with His blood I have clothed you in purple. Now you are no longer in the pit. You are in my bosom, in my covenant, in the blood of your covenant. That pit is understood, into which men of all times were immersed, and were subject to the danger of the soul. For it is a matter of the benefit of all times, of the King of all times, whose affliction and salvation were to be profitable for all times, whose righteousness was to be communicated to all men. That pit is understood, from which men are liberated by the virtue of the merit of Christ applied through faith. For this pit is opposed to the blood of the covenant of the Messiah, as the means and price of liberation. In the blood of the Messianic covenant men are sent forth from this pit: The blessed Lord Dr. Dorsheus, book 1, p. 117, thus proves that by the pit in which there is no water, the state of damnation is understood: (1) Because the state of damnation in a spiritual and metaphorical sense, which most truly has a place here, and is as it were in the highest degree, is a pit. For whatever danger, abominable, troublesome, or horrible thing a pit can have, which can be contrary to the happiness and salvation of man, all that is in the state of damnation in the highest degree.

(2) Because the word 'pit' elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures, most frequently in the Hagiographa and the later prophetic books, denotes the state of damnation and the miseries pertaining to it. Ps. 28:1, David asks that he may not become like those descending into the pit. Where he explains the consequence of divine desertion, the danger of all miseries, especially eternal damnation. Lorinus on this passage: it can also be taken for the place of the damned, where not even God hears anyone, because there is no redemption there. Bellarmine in his Commentary on this passage understands those who die and descend to the lower regions. John Bapt. Folengius, Commentary on this passage: the deepest abyss of despair. Basil and Eusebius agree: Apollinaris renders it πυθμένα χθόνιον (subterranean bottom), Ps. 30:4, those descending into the pit are those whose soul tends toward the state of damnation, from whose dangerous company God vindicated David. Apollinaris translates it πυθμένα γαίας (bottom of the earth). Lorinus and Bellarmine also apply to the state of the damned Ps. 40:35. Christ praises His Father because He brought him out of the pit of שׁאון (tumult/noise), the LXX render it λάκκον ταλαιπωρίας (pit of misery), commonly 'pit of misery': all those punishments are understood which Christ endured in our place and to expiate the whole human race, among which it is certain from Matt. 17:46, Ps. 22:2, Isa. 53:11, John 12:27, Gal. 3:13, and other foundations, that there were also the punishments of hell and the horrible stings of spiritual death, yet without despair, which is not the hellish punishment itself inflicted by God, as the Jesuits insipidly clamor against us and accuse us of teaching that Christ despaired, but it is a sin in unbelieving men resulting from the sense of the magnitude and eternity of the punishments. Lorinus on this passage understands the punishments of hell from antiquity.

Bellarmine [understands] the state of the impious, who lack the light of divine knowledge. Ps. 38:5, mention is made again of those descending into the pit, where by the pit Euthymius and Nicephorus understand the grave. Cassiodorus, the grave or hell. Jerome, hell; Basil, Augustine, and Theodoret, the inescapable spiritual calamities of this life and hell. Lorinus joins the opinions. In verse 7, mention is made of the lower pit, which is joined with the deepest and darkest places. By this lower pit is understood the taste of death owed to our sins, Heb. 2:9, which is the highest, horrible, hellish pain in the deepest emptying, Phil. 2:7, 8. Origen, Jerome, Placidus, Parmensis, Cajetan, Dionysius the Carthusian, and others expressly understand hellish miseries by the pit. Ps. 143:3, mention of those descending into the pit occurs again. Where Arnobius the Younger, Commentary on this passage, explains it concerning those to whom spiritual life is lacking, and who become like those damned by death. Pepinus transfers these things to Christ by allegory, as if Christ had asked His Father at the time of His passion not to turn away from His soul the communication of the vision of the divine essence, since thus He would be compared to those descending into the pit of hell. Isa. 14:15, God threatens the Babylonian King, not Satan, of whom there is no mention there, neither literally nor mystically, as indeed Cornelius à Lapide, Commentary on this passage, strives to deduce copiously against the immovable foundations. Caspar Sanctius on this passage and others, who could have been more correctly informed by Fr. Forerius, Commentary on this passage, [say] that Christ (whom Leo Castrius on this passage understands and thinks these are the words of demons mocking Christ in His passions, which the entire context contradicts) is not to be dragged to the side of the pit.

Because the terms explaining the state and place of the damned in Holy Scripture and elsewhere also agree perfectly with the name of a deep lake lacking water. The word Tophet agrees beautifully with a lake. Isa. 30:33, it is ordained from of old תפתה, a pit. The Targum גהנם, Gehenna, for the King himself; for the destruction of body and soul is denounced against the King of the Assyrians, see Avenarius in Lex. h. v. and Forster in dict. p. 340. Tophet is a pit, a place, and a lake in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, near Jerusalem, where children were burned to the idol Molech, so called from תוף, a drum, because drums and other musical instruments were played, so that the father might not hear the wailing of the boy who was being led through the fire, and demand him back from the hands of the priests, according to the Hebrews. The impious parents meanwhile danced to the drums, so that they would not hear the wailing, 2 Kings 23. Thus Schindler in his Lexicon p. 1985. Afterwards it is transferred to the place of the damned. To the Rabbis, indeed, תפת is Tartarus, the place of the lower regions. It was a place afterwards profaned by King Josiah and made abominable, 2 Kings 23:10, whence the word for a horrible state was adapted for extreme abomination. The word גהנם agrees, which is used in the Chaldean paraphrase of Isa. 30:33, and in the N.T. Matt. 5:22, 29, 30, and ch. 10:28, and ch. 23:15, 33, and Mark 9:43, 45, 47, Luke 12:5, James 3:6. גי־בן־הנם, the valley of the son of Hinnom, is written fully in Josh. 15:8, or contracted as גי־הנם, v. 8, and ch. 18:16, Nehem. 2:30, and in one word גיהנם, with the aspiration elided and the ם cast off by the Greeks, γέεννη and γεέννα. It was a valley near Jerusalem, highly contaminated by idolatry, and for that reason abominable. Tartarus, from which the word in 2 Pet. 2:4 comes, is according to Suidas κατώτερος τῷ ᾅδε τόπος, the lowest seat of the lower regions, παρὰ τὸ ἐκτετάραχθαι, καὶ συνκέχυσθαι τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ πάντα, as the Etymologicum Magnum says. Venetus. Hesychius in Etymolog. τάρταρος is ὁ ὑπὸ τὴν γῆν κατώτατος τόπος. To the Chaldeans it is אתר טרחא, a place of trouble. See Sanford, book 2, de desc. p. 128 and following. The name squares perfectly with the Zacharian lake, also the Abyss it touches the lake with great affinity. Luc. 8, 31. Rom. 10, 7. Apoc. 9, 1. c. 11, 7. c. 17, 8. c. 20, 1. & 3. Suidas βυσσὸς καὶ ἄβυσσος; & no one enters because of the depth, see Sanf. lib. 2. de desc. p. 118. & Parker lib. 3. p. 13. & seq. It is called a lake, in which there is no water, captivity, Ps. 68, 19. Eph. 4, 8. Φυλακὴ a prison, in which the last farthing must be paid Matth. 5, 26. Luc. 12, 58. 1. Petr. 3, 19. the court of Satan Luc. 11, 21. A furnace of fire, where there will be weeping & gnashing of teeth Matth. 13, 42. a place of torments Luc. 19, 28. a lake and winepress of wrath Apoc. 14, 19. a lake of fire burning in brimstone Apoc. 19, 20. a lake of fire and brimstone. Apoc. 20, 10. c. 21, 8. Pertaining to this are the ropes of darkness or chains of gloom, whence those bound in the lake 2. Petr. 2, 4. & outer darkness Matth. 22, 13. worms and fire Esa. 66, 24. Marc. 9, 44.

(4) Because no water, or the absence & lack of spiritual & mystical water, is properly referred to the state of damnation and that supreme misery. Zachar. 13, 1. mentions a cleansing fountain, which according to the blessed Dorscheus is the fountain of life Ps. 30, 10. the living fountain God Ps. 42, 3. the fountain of Israel Psal. 68, 27. the fountain of salvation Es. 12, 3. the fountain of living water Jerem. 2, 13. the fountain of water springing up into eternal life Joh. 4, 14. the fountain of the water of life Apoc. 21, 6. c. 3, 17. c. 8, 10. He also mentions living waters going out from Jerusalem Zach. 14, 8. Christ himself is the fountain opened to men in every age gushing forth the waters of divine grace & blessedness Joh. 4, 44. c. 7, 37. Esa. 16, 3. Apoc. 21, 6. cap. 22, 17. Which he both scatters in the kingdom of grace with most abundant streams, and pours out in the kingdom of glory with the whole channel. These waters are by no means with their fountain there, where the state of damnation and that supreme misery has its place. That lake is therefore understood in this place, where there is not even a drop of water refreshing. But in the state of damnation, and that supreme misery, there is not even a drop of water refreshing, Luc. 16. In whatever other state, however, there is at least some refreshing drop of water, even in those fictitious states of the Papists, as we heard above. Therefore the state of damnation and supreme misery is understood in the Zechariah prophecy. אין מים בו no water in it. A formula of speaking simply negating Gen: 16, 1. And Sarah was barren אין לה ילד no child to her. Job. 2. v. ult. ואין דובר & no one speaking a word to him, that is, there was no one who would speak. Exod. 5, 10. אינני נתן I am not giving you straw, &c. See Schindl. Lex. p. 69. & Buxtorff. in Grammat. p. 449. Compare, Prov. 8, 24.

(5) Because a lake placed and placing outside the divine covenant and communion with the blood of the Saviour Messiah cannot be anything other than a state of damnations. And yet it is established that this lake is opposed to the bosom of God the best and greatest, the bosom of Jesus Christ the Saviour, the most pleasant and beatific recesses of the wounds of the Messiah, the wings of the Holy Spirit, and in general the fountain of salvation. And likewise the fullness of the saving blood in the fountain of salvation is opposed to the emptiness of refreshing water in the lake. Whence the bound of the lake and those in covenant, purpled by the blood of Jesus, are also opposed. Whence this lake is outside the gracious and beneficent bosom of God the Best and Greatest: outside the bosom of Jesus Christ the Saviour: outside the beatific and most pleasant recesses of the wounds of the Messiah, outside the dove-like wings of the Holy Spirit, outside the entire fountain of salvation. And not only is the lake itself so constituted, but it also constitutes others in such a way. Now that which is outside the bosom of God the Best and Greatest, gracious and beneficent, is outside the bosom of Jesus Christ the Saviour, outside the beatific and most pleasant recesses of the wounds of the Messiah, outside the dove-like wings of the Holy Spirit, outside the entire fountain of salvation, that cannot be anything other than a state of damnation and supreme misery. And those who are placed in it are placed in a state of damnation and supreme misery.

And yet the lake, in which there is no water, which the Zechariah prophecy shows us, is outside all these things.

Thus far the blessed Dorscheus, who has very elegantly carried these things out at such length. Beautiful also are those things which the late lamented has on p. 140 concerning WATERS: From the Zechariah text it appears that this water is I. The object and cause of heavenly exultation, of shouting & spiritual joy, such as is given in the heavenly Jerusalem and mystical Zion verse 9. For this heavenly exultation, this shouting, this spiritual joy is not in the lake, in which there is no water, because there is no water there. For by that very fact the magnitude of the heavenly benefit conferred through the emission is indicated, because by reason of the term from which it was made from no waters: by reason of the term to which it leads to waters. II. A bringer of royal saving justice, of which there is talk in v. 9. For because in the lake, in which there is no water, because there is no water, there is not that royal justice & salvation, leading to the kingdom of grace, therefore by communicating those waters repugnant and adverse to the lake, the royal Messianic justice and salvation is communicated. For by that very fact the magnitude of the heavenly benefit conferred through the emission is indicated, that it was made from the marshes and pools of injustice, from the torrents of Belial, where there are no waters of divine blessing, to the fountains of salvation and justice, especially royal and Messianic. III. A bringer of peace. Peace, of which dissertation 2. c. 5. §. 49. page 30 was treated. IV. Flowing by the merit of the blood of the Messiah. For as the fruit of the blood of the Messiah is not in that lake, as something of the lake, but against the lake, for the destruction of the lake, so also the saving and beatific waters are not in it. Between water and blood there is the highest and closest connection. V. The water of the spiritual and mystical Church of Zion is its own proper good. But the Church is opposed to the pit. The Church seeks rescue from the pit. VI. The water of liberty. In which he who sails, well overcomes the remote and most foul chains of sin. VII. The water indicating the Holy Spirit as a fountain: of which John 4:14, ch. 7:37. Which Holy Spirit is the first principle of exultation, and of heavenly sounding, of communion with righteousness and Messianic salvation, of peace, of the enjoyment of the beatific blood, of the Church and of liberty. Which Holy Spirit is not in the pit by reason of a gracious presence, if you take the pit formally, but is against the pit, attempting to drain and empty the same for the bound, although with repugnance and reluctance, or malicious resistance, concerning which is the complaint of Jehovah in Gen. 6:3. Whence, unless the world receives the salutary waters, there follow avenging and sulphurous waters: indeed, even diluvian ones, as the outcome of the complaint taught.

(6) The authority of the Church, both ancient and modern, confirms this interpretation. In the ancient Latin Church, Jerome is to be heard first and foremost in his Commentary on this passage. After the speech of the Prophet, or rather God the Father Almighty himself, announced to Zion from Jerusalem that her King would come to them, meek, and riding upon a beast of burden, and a foal of an ass: and his power would be from sea even to sea, and from the rivers even to the ends of the earth: he makes an apostrophe to Christ himself, of whom the prophecy is, and speaks: You also, in the blood of your Testament or covenant, have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit, in which there is no water. Which is understood thus: In the blood of your passion, you, by your clemency, freed those who were held bound in the prison of hell, in which there is no mercy. Finally, after the Lord rose again, those who were held by the sins of Adam, or, as some wish, by the chains of ingrained error and death, rose with him and appeared in the holy city. Concerning this blood of the testament, he himself also, indicating his future passion, was speaking to the disciples: Take and drink, all of you, from this: for this is the chalice of the New Testament in my blood. In prefiguration of this, a pit which has no water, and Joseph was sent by his brothers into a pit: Daniel and Jeremiah by the Chaldeans and the people of the Jews: Benaiah also, in the time of snow and cold, went down into a pit, that he might kill a lion there. Jeremiah, however, is submerged not into the water of the pit, but into the mud and mire of the pit: which could suffocate more than refresh one who is thirsty. Whence it is written in the Psalm: I am stuck in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance. In this pit of hell dwelt that rich man formerly clothed in purple: whose boastful tongue was being burned by the fires of punishments: and he had so little refreshment of any waters, that he asked for a refreshment of the pauper's extreme finger dipped in water. Augustine. concerning this prophecy, book 18 of The City of God, chapter 35, has it thus: Zechariah concerning Christ and the Church: Exult, he says, greatly, O daughter of Zion, shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold thy king shall come to thee, just and a Savior: he himself poor and ascending upon a she-ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass: and his power shall be from sea even to sea, and from the rivers even to the ends of the earth. When this was done, that the Lord Christ used a beast of this kind on his journey, is read in the Gospel: where also this prophecy is commemorated in part, as much as seemed sufficient for that place. In another place, the prophecy speaking in the Spirit to Christ himself concerning the remission of sins through his blood: Thou also, he says, in the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit, in which there is no water. What he wishes to be understood by this pit, diverse things can be felt, even according to the right faith. To me, however, it seems that nothing better is signified by it than the dry and in some way sterile depth of human misery: where there are not the streams of justice, but the mud of iniquity. For concerning this pit it is also said in the Psalm: And he brought me out of the pit of misery, and from the mire of the clay. Where it appears that Augustine, by the sending forth from the pit, understands the very remission of sins: and by the dry and sterile depth of human misery, where there are not the streams of justice, understands the punishment which follows sins, the acme of which is the state of damnation. Agobard, Bishop of Lyon and Primate of the Aquitanian or Arlesian Kingdom in the eighth century, in his Tract on the Trinity and Christ, p. 338, handed down this concerning this waterless pit: This place of punishments is called (Gehenna) and a pit in which there is no water, just as it is said through Zechariah: Thou also in the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit, in which there is no water. And through King Hezekiah the just, Isaiah 38. They shall not wait, who go down into the pit, for thy truth. REMIGIUS in the 9th century, Vol. IX, part 1 of the Cologne Library of the Holy Fathers, p. 602, has it thus: Thou hast brought forth thy prisoners, that is, the saints, who were held bound, out of the pit in which there is no water: that is, thou hast freed them from hell, in which there is no mercy. From the Greeks, Cyril of Alexandria on this passage: The discourse now passes to the just and savior and also meek king himself, that is, Christ, and declares the illustrious and admirable works of his advent. (For he emptied himself) willingly, the only-begotten Word of God having become man (he endured the cross, despising the shame) and for the life of all he exchanged his own soul, he acquired the world for God and the Father in the blood of the eternal testament, of which the blood sprinkled by Moses the most wise upon the ancients was a type. For he says (Moses having taken the blood and the book itself, he sprinkled all the people, saying) this is the blood of the testament, which God has disposed to you, but those things were indeed a type and an image of the truth: the truth itself succeeded, Christ, who bought us all in the blood of the testament (For we have been redeemed not with corruptible gold or silver (as his disciple also says) but with the precious blood, as of the lamb immaculate and undefiled, Christ:) Thou therefore, he says, most just and most meek King, in the blood of the Testament thy prisoners,) that is, whom thou hast bound with the bonds of charity, and to whom thou hast persuaded, that they should submit the neck of their mind to thy yoke, and openly bind themselves) thou hast sent forth, that is, thou hast brought out, or led out, or dismissed (out of the pit not having water) By which words we say that either hell, where there is no life, is signified (for let us take water as a symbol of life) or certainly we shall most conveniently interpret hell as the fallacy of false gods. For it is truly a pit, into which if anyone has fallen deeply, he will lack future and everlasting life. That Christ dead emptied hell, and opened the gates of hell to the spirits held in custody, escapes no one. Which extreme things are to be understood concerning the moral and meritorious evacuation, and likewise the impetrative opening. For that the damned spirits were sent forth from the seat of damnation is absolutely a copy. Theodoret on this passage. Those whom thou hast redeemed with thy precious blood, and hast freed, these thou hast sent forth with the salutary tablets of thy Testament, that they might declare the liberty of the testament to all men: thou hast freed them from the pit not having water. But whether one wishes to understand this pit as either eternal death or the error of idols, he will not wander from the truth. Which interpretation Theophylact hands down in the same words in his Commentary on the XII Minor Prophets on this passage.

Of the more recent Doctors of the Church, almost all understand this sending forth as the liberation made through the blood of Christ from eternal condemnation. Concerning our Doctors, the matter is certain, if you perhaps except the Blessed John Tarnovius, who nevertheless, although he accepted those words, I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit in which there is no water, concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity (whom the Blessed Lord Dr. Dorscheus refuted in the cited place, p. 76), acknowledges that the preceding things treat of the redemption of Christ. In the words: But thou in the blood of thy covenant, the Prophet truly treats of our redemption, and of its precious ransom, see the blood of the Son of God, Acts 20:28, by which the new covenant was ratified with us, and that can be easily proved from there against the Calvinists, Pareus, and others, because it treats of the future, as is clear from the preceding, and through this blood we are made participants of the benefits hitherto commemorated. Our other Doctors readily agree with the blessed Luther that this must be understood concerning spiritual captivity and those bound in sins: which sense the blessed Dorscheus confirms in the cited place with these arguments. (1.) Because this name is most appropriate for those who are trampled and pressed by the burden and misery of sin, Is. 43, 5.6.7.8. ch. 49, 8.9.10. ch. 61, 1. Eph. 4, 8. Rom. 7, 23. (2) Because the Church looks especially to those captive by the captivity of sins, so that liberty from those bonds may be granted to them by the divine hand, to which this discourse is directed. (3) Because the discourse is about those bound in the bonds of sins in the seat of the New covenant, and the means of liberation are ordained for them there, namely Jerem. 31, 3. (4) Because mention is made most frequently of the snares of sins also in the consideration of the new covenant, and the coordination of men to it, Is. 8, 14. Psal. 19. 1. Tim. 6, 4. 2. Tim. 2, 24. 25. 26. Conf. 2. Sam. 22, 6. Job. 18, 8. 9. Ps. 25, 10. 11. 15. Psal. 119, 110. For of whatever snares Zacharias speaks in that explanation of the benefit of the N. T., he understands those bound in such a way.

From the Reformed, Johannes Piscator assents to this explanation in this place. The priestly office is declared in v. 11 from three arguments, namely from the manner of acting, from the end, and from the effect. The manner of acting was placed in the offering of his own blood: the end was the confirmation of the covenant between God and the elect: the effect was and is liberation from the bonds of sin and the power of the Devil. Similarly Johannes Cocceius: The medium of this liberty is the blood, which is considered as a price given: as captives are accustomed to be freed by a price given. The preposition ב notes this, as in Cant. 8, 7. 11. Gen. 29, 25. 27. It explains what kind of liberty that will be, and from where, which he was promising in v. 8. Compare Job 8, 36. That blood is called of the Testament, so that it may be understood 1. that this benefit of liberty, which also includes justice, depends on the divine promise by which God once declared his good pleasure to the fathers. 2. That the King promised to Zion was to shed blood according to the promise, for the attainment of the promised liberty. By which death is noted: from which he had indicated in v. 9 that they were to be saved. Balth. Willius, although he refers it to the Egyptian captivity under Ptolom. Lagus, nevertheless acknowledges that everything agrees with spiritual liberation.

From the Papists, Isidorus Clarius, Bishop of Fulginium, also confesses that it is signified in this place that all who were in the pit, destitute of saving water, and who, being bound, had hope that they would be freed by this blood, were redeemed by the blood of Christ. Antonius Braccioli in his Italian Commentary on this place, interpreted in Theol. Zachar. page 134. by B. Dorscheus: "Since hell is most truly also a cistern without water, i.e., of captivity, without consolation, and Christ frees the Fathers and us, since without him we had no consolation at all: since we were all bound by sin, and are freed, and led out by Christ from a most grievous prison." Georgius Ederus in Oeconom. Biblior. lib. II. Tab. 238. The Prophet returns to Christ, and describes his coming in four ways: That he would not be a warrior, nor would he enter upon a horse, but upon an ass, verse: behold thy King, that he would not have a bow or a chariot, verse: and I will destroy: but would acquire dominion by peace: verse: and he shall speak peace. Finally, that he would not liberate the people by arrow and bow, as the Jews falsely expect, but would redeem them by his own blood, verse: As for thee also, by the blood of the covenant, even to the end of chapter IX.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

TU QUOQUE IN SANGVINE TESTAMENTI TUI EMISISTI VINCTOS TUOS DE LACU, IN QUO NON ERAT AQVA: CONVERTIMINI) Ex Graeco ἐξαπέστειλας, at in Hebraeo & Chaldaeo emisi; ita ut cum Chaldaeo haec sic vertere liceat: Tu ergo (ô posteri- tas Abrahami: nam אַתּ foemininum est) cujus vinctos pro- pter sanguinem foederis tui (promissum sancitum Paschali vi- ctima) emisi (nempe ex Aegypto) & emisi de cisterna, in qua non erat aqua, (id est, ex siticulosissimis Arabiae locis) redite ad me; memores veterum beneficiorum, ac novo- rum, mihi confidite.

Videndum hic primum de germana textus le- ctione, tum de sensu. Textum corruptum esse sive à Judaeis, sive à librariis, volunt Papistae Cornel. à Lapide hic, Huntlaeus, Riebera in h. l. alii statuunt, quod foeminina substituta sint in lo- cum masculinorum, & verbum emisi primae per- sonae שִׁלַּחְתִּי in vicem verbi secundo personae emi- sisti שִׁלַּחְתְּ, siquidem hoc pacto LXX. Hiero- nymus, aliique veteres, Syrus item & Arabs legant. Sed vana est suspicio corruptelae, siqui- dem codices Ebraei ex asse consonent hoc in lo- co, neq; novum sit Interpp. in translatione, haut premere verba, sed sensum solum exprimere, qui verbis constat, etsi apostrophe hæc non ad Christum, sed ad Sion, vel Hierosolymam, vi generis fœmini- ni, directa sit. Refellit ipse Castrius hanc opi- nionem de corrupto textu: Hebræa, inquit, Etiam tu, in sanguine fœderis tui emisi vinctos tuos de la- cu, non aqua in eo, & pronomina tam primitivum tu, quam possessiva tui & tuos, & fœminea sunt את & ך & verbum primæ personæ est, שלחתי e- misi. Atque ita legunt Chaldæus, R. Salomon, Galat. lib. 8. cap. 20. & recentiores omnes : & ita explicat Pagnin. Tu etiam Jerusalem exulta in san- guine fœderis tui.
