FOR I HAVE REDEEMED THEM, AND I WILL MULTIPLY THEM, AS THEY HAD BEEN MULTIPLIED BEFORE, AND I WILL SOW THEM AMONG THE PEOPLES, AND THEY SHALL REMEMBER ME FROM AFAR, AND THEY SHALL LIVE WITH THEIR CHILDREN, AND THEY SHALL RETURN] I will deliver them, and I will multiply them to that number which they once were (in the times of David, as we have said), who, although I had dispersed them among the nations, yet in those distant places were mindful of me; therefore they shall survive with their children, and they shall return home. The conjunction ו here is taken as causative. The Chaldean wisely follows this sense.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

QUIA REDEMI EOS, ET MULTIPLICABO EOS, SICUT ANTEA FUERANT MULTIPLICA- TI, ET SEMINABO EOS IN POPVLIS, ET DE LONGE RECORDABVNTVR MEI, ET VIVENT CVM FILIIS SVIS, ET REVERTENTVR] Libe- rabo eos, & multiplicabo eos in eum numerum, quo olim fuere (Davidis ut diximus temporibus) qui cum dispersissem eos in- ter gentes, tamen in illis locis longinquis memores fuêre mei, id- eo superstites erunt cum filiis suis, & revertentur domum. Con- junctio ו hic sumitur pro causativa. Sensum hunc Chal- dæus prudenter sequitur.

## 10:10
Ver. 10.

AND I WILL BRING THEM BACK FROM THE LAND OF EGYPT] Through Ptolemy Philadelphus and others. AND FROM ASSYRIA I WILL GATHER THEM] Through Alexander, the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, and through both Demetriuses. See Josephus XIII, 4, 5, 7, 8. AND I WILL BRING THEM TO THE LAND OF GILEAD AND LEBANON] Concerning Gilead taken by the arms of the Maccabees, you have it in Josephus XII, 12. Concerning the cities of Syria taken by Hyrcanus and his successors XIII, 17, 23. AND PLACE SHALL NOT BE FOUND FOR THEM] So great shall be the multitude that the old borders will not contain them.

From these verses it is again clear that these things cannot be drawn to the times of the Maccabees. For the ten Israelite tribes, the house of Joseph, the Ephraimites, and the two remaining tribes were not then equally saved. And how were the Israelites in those times in such a flourishing state as was the case in David's time? For the fact that Grotius appeals to the Israelites who added themselves to the tribe of the Jews is nothing in comparison to so magnificent a promise. But when did they grow into that number which was in all Israel under David, and when were they so multiplied that the place could not contain them? Those whom Ptolemy Philadelphus redeemed certainly do not make up that number. The things which Zechariah proclaims here are far more sublime. Finally, who are the Israelites said to be gathered from the Assyrians, so that the land of Israel was no less filled with them than in David's time? Grotius says that these were gathered by Alexander, son of Antiochus Epiphanes, and by Demetrius, praising Josephus, book 13, chapters 4, 5, 6, but nothing of the sort is found there. Nor is there any evidence from elsewhere concerning the Israelite tribes having returned from Assyria. Although it cannot be denied that the Jews were greatly multiplied after their return from Babylon, yet they were never multiplied corporally as they were under David, who could bring into the field (if necessity demanded) thirteen hundred thousand armed men. Therefore, these things must be understood concerning the multiplication of Christians, as our people teach unanimously, and also the blessed Tarnovius on verse 6, page 270. Although all these things are said concerning Israel according to the flesh, yet because they were at that time the true Church, the fulfillment of those promises pertains most especially to this, and it still endures. For if we look to the Jews led back into the holy land from the Babylonian captivity, the traces of the promised grace appear at least slight, because they themselves often and suddenly turned away again from their God; therefore, these things pertain to the Israel of God, or those who are such through faith in Christ, and they are daily fulfilled by the Lord of heaven and earth, insofar as He restores those cast into exile with Adam and thrown out of paradise to their original seat, and always intercedes for them before the Father so that these good things may be their own, and thus the following things must be applied in the same way to this end. And on verse 8, he says, the Lord hissing to them with the softest voice, the sign having been given, since I can accomplish this matter without great labor, I will gather them, when I redeem them, and they shall be multiplied, just as they had been multiplied before, so that the vigor of the promise made to Abraham, Gen. 13:15, 16 and 17:2, may still appear, which, as interpreted by the Apostle, Gal. 3. and 4, also pertains to all the faithful in its own way, and was most especially fulfilled in the spiritual Israel when Christ Himself hissed with the voice of the Gospel, come to me, Matt. 11:28, if anyone thirsts, John 7:34, and the Apostles, by His command, propagated the same voice into the whole world, Mark 16:20, Col. 1:23. On verse 10. And thus (he refers to verse 8) I will bring them back from the land of Egypt, to which the Jews fled when the temple was destroyed, Jer. 44:1 and 43:2, and before that many from the ten tribes, when the Assyrian came, Hos. 8:13 and 9:3, 6, and from Assyria, to which the ten tribes were led away, 2 Kings 17, I will gather them, into the land of Gilead and Lebanon I will bring them: by which two boundaries, eastern and northern, the whole holy land is here circumscribed by synecdoche: see Num. 32:39, Deut. 3:12, John 1:4, and yet this whole land will not suffice for them: which things have truly been abundantly fulfilled in the New Testament, as predicted by Isaiah, chapter 49:20, and 54:1, Gal. 4:27. The blessed Balduinus, page 681, on verse 10, refutes the opinion of the Jews with these arguments: (1.) It cannot be taught when and on what occasion the Hebrews were led back from those places. 2. It is not likely that the ten Israelite tribes could have inhabited Gilead

and Lebanon, in which places previously the two tribes of Reuben and Gad with the half-tribe could barely have enough space. 3. By this reasoning, the former kingdom of the Israelites would be more excellent in dignity and extent than the restored kingdom, because that was contained by ten tribes, each of which had its own hereditary regions; here, however, ten tribes would barely be included in the hereditary region of two tribes. All of which things clearly prove that this passage is not explained sufficiently aptly according to the letter, but must be understood mystically, in this sense: I will bring back the sons of Israel, formerly captive in Assyria and Egypt, to the bosom of the Church, for he understands this by Gilead and Lebanon, which mountains, near the land of Canaan across the Jordan, sometimes denote the Church in Scripture. This is Balduinus. Thus, in the ancient Church, Cyril of Alexandria and Jerome explained it, who refers these things to the times of the New Testament: Then God, he says, says that He strengthens the house of Judah and the house of Joseph, so that those who were divided during the reign of Jeroboam may be associated while Christ reigns, and there may be one shepherd and one flock. And afterwards: They will have, he says, my hiss, so that I may gather them from my hiss, and teach them that I am the shepherd. For I have redeemed them and freed them from captivity with an outstretched arm: and I will multiply them, who had multiplied before: so that the dispersion among the peoples may not seem to be a division, but the operation of sowing, and with the crop of children and grandchildren multiplied, they may live with their sons, and return not only from the land of Egypt, but also from the Assyrians, and from both parts of the world they may return to Judea, and to the land of Gilead and Lebanon, which the ten tribes formerly possessed, which are called the house of Joseph and Ephraim, and the number of those brought back will be so great that the land will not contain the multitude. According to the anagoge, the Lord signifies and whistles to those who had previously been captive to sins, and speaks to them: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and you will find rest for your souls. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, for my yoke is sweet and my burden is light. What is more clement than this signification and whistling, by which the dispersed people is gathered? They are gathered, however, because the Lord redeemed them, not with corruptible silver and gold, from their vain conversation, but with the precious blood, as of an immaculate lamb, of the Lord Jesus. Whence he speaks in the Psalm: My exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me. And again: You have redeemed me, O Lord God of truth. And he will multiply them, just as they had been multiplied before, so that that which was promised to Abraham might be fulfilled. I will multiply him, and I will bless him, and he shall be blessed, so that he may become the father of many nations. However, we ought not to understand as children of Abraham those to whom the Lord speaks: If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of your father, but those to whom the Apostle says: As many as are of faith, they are children of Abraham. Isaiah also testifies concerning this multiplication in mystical speech, saying: He who is small shall be in thousands, and he who is little shall be a great nation. And to that, I WILL SOW THEM AMONG THE PEOPLES) Those were sown among the peoples who heard the word of the Lord: Going, teach all nations: And in another place: You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and have appointed you, that you should go, and should bring forth fruit, and your fruit should remain forever. And when the Apostles had been sown among the peoples, the nations and peoples placed far off will remember me: with that prophetic saying agreeing with this sentence: All the ends of the earth shall remember and be converted to the Lord. And all the families of the nations shall adore in his sight. For the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall have dominion over the nations. And that which is said: They shall remember me from afar: is similar to that: You who are far off, remember the Lord,

and let Jerusalem ascend upon your heart. The whole multitude of the nations was far off, yet it remembered God, because we are all generated from one parent. And with the Apostles sown among all nations, the nations placed far off remembered God: they shall live with their children, so that those who were previously dead in infidelity may begin to live by faith. These are the children whom Paul nourished in the Gospel, writing to the Corinthians: I gave you milk to drink. And Peter writes in the dispersion to the faithful who had been reborn: Not from corruptible seed, but incorruptible, through the word of the living and abiding God: just as infants recently generated: that they might desire the rational milk, and grow in it unto salvation. To these children the Evangelist John also wrote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Nor did Calvin doubt that this prophecy refers to the times of the N.T. in his Comment. p. 686. Now therefore Zechariah promises a common thing when he says that both peoples will be joined together, so that it coalesces again, just as it was before the defection, for the House of Joseph is worth as much as the house of Ephraim. We know, however, that by synecdoche the house of Ephraim is everywhere taken for the whole kingdom of Israel; now therefore we hold the counsel of the Prophet, namely that the state of the people will be more blessed than it had been since the ten tribes had been divided from the kingdom of Judah, or from the house of David, because clearly God will gather to Himself a Church from all the sons of Abraham. And at v. 8. The Prophet signifies that Christ will be the head of the Church in such a way that He will gather from all parts of the earth the Jews who had previously been dispersed: and thus the promised restitution shall be extended to all the tribes. At v. 9. Therefore, what God had so often threatened through Moses that He would disperse the Jews, He now says in another sense that He will sow them, namely so that they may produce fruit everywhere. And this was the admirable grace of God, that He so moderated His horrible judgment that the dissipation of the people was like a sowing, just as it has been said: for it happened here that some knowledge of heavenly doctrine shone everywhere: And finally, when the Gospel was promulgated, the approach to the nations was easier, since the Jews were dispersed through all the regions of the earth. The first lodgings of the Gospel were the Synagogues; we see how the Apostles, wherever they came, made a beginning from the Jews: when a few had been converted, the door was already open so that many more might approach. Then the Gentiles were also joined to the Jews. Therefore, the punishment of exile, which had been inflicted upon them, opened the door to the Gospel: and thus God dispersed His seed here and there, so that later the fruit might appear in its own time beyond the hope of all. He promises a return, however, not that they returned to their homeland, but because they were all joined together through the faith of the Gospel. Although therefore they did not change their place, nor did they lift a foot outside the lands in which they were wandering, yet that gathering which was made through the doctrine of the Gospel is called a return to the homeland, just as is sufficiently known from the common usage of all the Prophets. The Belgian Paraphrasts likewise refer this passage to the times of the N.T. Willius also acknowledges this, even if he would willingly refer those things to the times of the Maccabees, that the full complement pertains to the N.T. This promise, he says p. 350, was in part exhibited to the Israelites, when they experienced illustrious documents of divine grace in their homeland and outside their homeland, but especially when the preaching of evangelical grace was announced to them, and the people sitting in darkness saw a great light Matt. 4, 17. And Isa. 9, 12. And at verse 8. p. 353. These things, however, obtained their complement when many of the captive Israelites returned to their homeland, and there lived happily under the principate of Simon and Hyrcanus, yet the most full fulfillment looks to the kingdom of Christ, where by the whistle of the Gospel the Israelites were called to the Church for the sake of the redemption of Christ, and were imbued with spiritual blessing in it. Likewise at v. 9. These things, however, obtained their complement in the people of the Israelites, when they themselves, while the old Church still stood, were disseminated most widely through the nations, and everywhere in the world gained many proselytes, and brought them to the Church, and with them they aggregated themselves to the Church, but the more exact continuation of all things was made in the kingdom of Christ, where the citizens of the Church disseminated everywhere in the world increased the kingdom of the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET REDVCAM EOS DE TERRA ÆGYPTIJ Per Ptolemæum Philadelphum, & alios. ET DE ASSTRIIS CONGREGABO] Per Ale- xandrum Antiochi Epiphanis filium, & per Demetrium utrumque. Vide Josephum XIII, 4. 5. 7. 8. ET AD TERRAM GALAAD ET LIBANI ADDVCAM EOS] De Galaaditide capta Maccabæorum armis habes apud Iosephum XII. 12. De Syriæ urbibus captis ab Hyrcano & successoribus XIII. 17. 23. ET NON INVENIETVR EIS LOCVS] Tan- ta erit multitudo, ut veteres fines eos non capiant.

Ex his versibus iterum liquet, non posse hæc trahi ad Maccabæorum tempora. Non enim tun æque tribus decem Israeliticæ, domus Joseph, E phraitæ, ac duæ tribus reliquæ salvatæ sunt. E quomodo istis temporibus in tam florente statu fuere Israelitæ, qualis fuit Davidis tempore? Nam quod Grotius ad Israelitas provocat, qui se Judæi tri bui addiderunt, nihil est ad tam magnificam promif sionem. Quando vero in eum excreverunt nume- rum, qui sub Davide in Israele universo fuit, ec- quando ita multiplicati sunt, ut locus eos capere non potuerit? Illi, quos Ptolomæus Philadelphus re- demit, certe tantum non efficiunt numerum. Lon- ge sublimiora sunt, quæ hic prædicat Zacharias. Deniq; qui ab Assyriis congregati Israelitæ dicun- tur, ut non minus repleta fuerit iisdem terra Israe- lis, quam Davidis tempore? Quos per Alexandrum Antiochi Epiphanis filium & per Demetrium utrum- que congregatos dicit Grotius, laudans Joseph. 13. c. 4. 5. 6. sed ibi nihil tale reperitur. Nec aliunde de Israelitarum tribubus ex Assyria reversis quic- quam constat. Quamvis vero negari nequeat, Ju- dæos post reditum è Babylonia valde multiplica- tos esse, tamen nunquam ita multiplicati sunt corporaliter, sicut sub Davide, qui potuit in a- ciem producere (si necessitas postularet) tredecies centena millia virorum armatorum. Quapropter intelligenda hæc de multiplicatione Christiano- rum, ut Nostrates ὁμοθυμαδὸν docent, etiam B. Tar- novius ad v. 6. p. 270. Licet hæc omnia de Israele quoad carnem dicantur, tamen quia hi tum tem- poris erant veraEcclesia, ad hanc promissionem il- larum complementum potissimum spectat, & ad- huc durat. Si enim ad Judæos in terram sanctam re- ductos ex captivitate Babylonica respicimus, levia saltem apparent hic gratiæ promissæ vestigia, eo quod ipsi sæpe & subito denuo à Deo suo deflexe- rint; ad Israelem Dei itaq; seu eos, qui per fidem in Christum tales sunt, hæc pertinent, & quotidie im- plentur à Domino cœli & terræ, quatenus is cum Adamo in exilium ejectos, ac ex paradiso projectos in pristinam sedem restituit, & pro iis, ut bona hæc sint propria, apud Patrem semper intercedit, atq; ita sequentia eodem modo horsum applicari de- bent. Et ad v. 8. sibilans, inquit, Dominus ad eos lenis- sima voce tantum dato signo, cum sine magno labore hanc rem possim conficere, congregabo eos, quum re- dimam eos, & multiplicabuntur, sicut multiplicati antea fuerant, ut ita adhuc promissionis Abrahamo fa- ctæ Gen. 13. 15. 16. & 17, 2. vigor appareat, quæ inter- prete Apostolo Gal. 3. & 4. etiam ad omnes fideles suo modo pertinet, & tum in spirituali Israele maxime im- pleta est, cum & Christus ipse ita voce Evangelii sibi- laret, venite ad me Matth. 11, 28. si quis sitit Joh. 7, 34. & Apostoli, ejus jussu, in totum terrarum orbem eandem vocem propagarent Marc. 16, 20. Col. 1, 23. Ad v. 10. Atq; ita (respicit ad v. 8.) reducam eos è terra Ægypti, quo Judæi confugerunt everso tem- plo Jerem. 44, 1. & 43, 2. & antea è decem tribubus multi, veniente Assyrio Hos. 8, 13. & 9, 3. 6. & ab As- syria, quo decem tribus sunt abductæ 2. Reg. 17. congregabo eos, in terram Gilhadis, & Libani abdu- cam eos: quibus duobus terminis, orientali & se- ptentrionali tota terra sancta synecdochice hic cir- cumscribitur: vide Num. 32, 39. Deut. 3, 12. Johan. 1, 4. & tamen hæc tota terra non sufficiet eis: quæ revera abunde impleta sunt in Novo Testamento, ut prædictum ab Esaia cap. 49, 20. & 54, 1. Gal. 4, 27. B. Balduinus pag. 681. ad vers. 10. refellit Ju- dæorum sententiam his argumentis: (1.) doceri ne- quit, quando & qua occasione ex illis locis He- bræi reducti fuerint. 2. Non est verisimile, de- cem tribus Israeliticas habitare potuisse in Gilead

& Libanon, quibus in locis antehac vix duæ tribus Ruben & Gad cum dimidia fatis spatii habere po- tuerunt. 3. Hac ratione pristinum Israëlitarum regnum dignitate & amplitudine præstantius fo- ret regno instaurato, quià illud decem contineba- tur tribubus, quarum quælibet suas habebat regio- nes hæreditarias: hîc vero decem tribus vix dua- rum tribuum regione hæreditaria includerentur. Quæ omnia luculenter evincunt, locum hunc non satis apposite secundum literam exponi, sed mystice intelligendum esse, hoc sensu: reducam filios Israel in Assyria & Ægypto olim captivos ad gremium Ec- clesiæ, hanc enim intelligit per Gilead & Libanon, qui montes vicini terræ Chanaan trans Jordanem, Ecclesiam interdum notant in Scriptura. Hæc Balduin. Sic in antiqua Ecclesia exposuere Cy- rillus Alexandrinus & Hieronymus, qui ad tempo- ra Nov. Testam. hæc refert: Tunc Deus, inquit, domum Juda, & domum Joseph se confortare dicit, ut qui Jeroboam regnante, divisi sunt, Christo impe- rante socientur, & sit unus pastor & unus grex. Et postmodum: Meum, inquit, habebunt sibilum, ut ex sibilo meo illos congregem, & me doceam esse pasto- rem. Ego enim redemi eos & liberavi de captivitate extento brachio: & ego eos multiplicabo, qui ante multiplicaveram: ut dispersio in populis non videatur esse divisio, sed sementis operatio, & liberorum ac nepo- tum segete multiplicata, vivant cum filiis suis, & re- vertantur non solum de terra Ægypti, sed & de As- syriis, & ex utraq́; orbis parte redeant ad Judæam, & ad terram Galaad & Libani, quam prius decem possi- debant tribus, quæ appellantur domus Ioseph & E- phraim, & tantus erit numerus reductorum, ut mul- titudinem terra non capiat. Secundum ἀναγωγὴν significat Dominus & sibilat his, qui peccatis fuerant ante captivi, & loquitur ad eos: Venite ad me o- mnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & invenietis re- quiem animabus vestris. Tollite jugum meum super vos, & discite à me, quia mansuetus sum & humilis corde, jugum enim meum suave & onus meum leve est. Quid hac significatione sibiloq́; cle- mentius, quo dispersus populus congregatur? Congre- gantur autem, quia Dominus redemit eos, non corru- ptibilibus argento & auro, à vana sua conversatione, sed pretioso sanguine, quasi agni immaculati Domini Iesu. Unde loquitur in Psalmo: Exultatio mea erue me à circumdantibus me. Et iterum: Re- demisti me Domine Deus veritatis. Et multipli- cabit eos, sicut antea fuerant multiplicati, ut imple- retur illud, quod promissum est Abrahæ. Multiplica- bo eum, & benedicam illi, & benedictus erit, ut fiat pater multarum gentium. Filios autem Abraham non eos debemus accipere, quibus Dominus loquitur: Si filii essetis Abraham, opera patris vestri facere- tis, sed illos, quibus Apostolus ait: Quotquot ex fide sunt, filii sunt Abraham. De hac multiplicatione & E- saias mystico sermone testatur dicens: Qui modicus est, erit in millibus, & qui parvus erit in gentem magnam. Et ad illa, SEMINABO EOS IN PO- PULIS) Seminati sunt in populis, qui Domini audiere sermonem: Euntes docete omnes gentes: Et in a- lio loco: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos, & posui vos, & eatis, & fructum afferatis, & fructus vester maneat in æternum. Cumq́; Apostoli fuerint in populis seminati, gentes & populi longe positi recor- dabuntur mei: illo prophetico huic sententiæ congru- ente: Reminiscentur & convertentur ad domi- num universi fines terræ. Et adorabunt in con- spectu ejus universæ familiæ gentium. Quoniam Domini est regnum, & ipse dominabitur gentium. Quodq́; dicitur: De longo recordabuntur mei: illi simile est: Qui longe estis, recordamini Domini,

& Hierusalem ascendat super cor vestrum. Longe fuit omnis gentium multitudo, se recordata est Dei, quia ex uno omnes parente generamur. Cumque A- postolis in cunctis gentibus seminatis, gentes longe po- sitæ, Dei fuerint recordatæ: vivent cum filiis suis, ut qui prius infidelitate mortui erant, fide vivere inci- piant. Isti sunt filii,quos Paulus nutrivit in Evange- lio, scribens ad Corinthios: Lac vobis potum dedi. Et Petrus in dispersione scribit fidelibus, qui renati e- rant: Non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibi- li, per sermonem viventis Dei & permanentis: sicut modo generati parvuli: ut rationabile lac concu- piscerent, & in ipso crescerent in salutem. Ad hos fi- lios scribebat & Evangelista Johannes: Filioli custo- dite vos ab idolis. Neq; dubitavit Calvinus ad tem- pora N. T. hoc vaticinium spectare in Comment. p. 686. Jam ergo vulgare promittit Zacharias cum di- cit utrumque populum conjunctum fore, ita ut rursus coalescat, sicuti ante defectionem, nam Do- mus Joseph tantundem valet, ac domus Ephraim. Scimus autem per Synecdochen ubique sumi do- mum Ephraim pro toto regno Israelis, nunc ergo te- nemus consilium Prophetæ, nempe statum populi fore beatiorem, quam fuerit, ex quo divisæ fuerant decem tribus à regno Jehuda, vel à domo Davidis, quia scilicet Deus ex omnibus filiis Abrahæ colli- get sibi Ecclesiam. Et ad v. 8. Significat Propheta Christum sic fore caput Ecclesiæ, ut colligat ex omni- bus terræ partibus Judæos, qui prius dispersi fue- rant: atque ita extendatur restitutio promissa ad omnes tribus. Ad v. 9. Quam ergo toties minatus fuisset Deus per Mosen dispersurum se Judæos, nunc alio sensu dicit, se illos seminaturum, nempe ut fru- ctum ubique producant. Et hæc admirabilis fuit Dei gratia, quod horribili judicio suo sic est mode- ratus, ut dissipatio populi similis esset sationi, quem- admodum dictum est: quoniam hic contigit, ut ubique illuceret aliqua notitia cœlestis doctrinæ: Et tandem ubi promulgatum est Evangelium fuit aditus facilior ad gentes, quoniam per omnes ter- ræ plagas Judæi erant dispersi. Prima hospitia Ev- angelii fuerunt Synagogæ; videmus ut Apostoli quocunque venirent initium fecerint à Judæis: quum pauci essent conversi, jam aperta erat janua, ut complures accederent. Deinde Gentes etiam adjunctæ fuerunt Judæis. Pœna igitur exilii, quæ inflicta fuerat illis, januam aperuit Evangelio: atq; ita Deus semen suum dispersit huc & illuc, ut po- stea fructus suo tempore prodiret præter spem o- mnium. Promittit tamen reditum, non quod re- versi fuerint in patriam, sed quia conjuncti fuerint omnes per Evangelii fidem. Quamvis ergo lo- cum non mutaverint, neque pedem extulerint ex- tra terras in quibus peregrinabantur, tamen reditus in patriam vocatur illa collectio, quæ facta est per doctrinam Evangelii, quemadmodum satis ex com- muni omnium Prophetarum usu notum est. Para- phrastæ Belgici itidem locum hunc ad tempora N. T. referunt. Agnoscit id etiam Willius, etsi liben- ter ista ad tempora Maccabæorum referret, com- plementum plenum ad N. T. pertinere. Fuit hæc promissio, inquit p. 350. ex parte exhibita Israelitis, quando in patria & extra patriam illustria divinæ gratiæ documenta experti sunt, imprimis vero, quando concio gratiæ Evangelicæ ipsis annuncia- ta est, & populus in tenebris sedens vidit lucem ma- gnam Matth. 4, 17. Et Esa. 9, 12. Et ad vers. 8. p. 353. Hæc autem complementum suum nacta sunt, quando multi captivorum Israelitarum in patriam reversi, ibi feliciter sub Simonis & Hyrcani principatu ege- runt, plenissima tamen impletio ad regnum Christi spectat, ubi sibilo Evangelii Israelitæ ad Ecclesiam propter redemtionem Christi vocati, in ea spiri- tuali benedictione perfusi sunt. Item ad v. 9. Com- plementum autem hæc suum sortita sunt in Israelita- rum populo, quando ipsi latissime, stante adhuc ve- teri Ecclesia, per gentes disseminati, ubique terra- rum multos proselytos lucrifecerunt, & Ecclesiæ adduxerunt, ac cum iis Ecclesiæ se aggregarunt, exactius autem omnium continuatio facta in re- gno Christi, ubi cives Ecclesiæ ubique terrarum disseminati regnum Ecclesiæ auxerunt.

## 10:11
Ver. 11.

AND HE SHALL PASS THROUGH THE STRAIT OF THE SEA, AND SHALL STRIKE THE WAVES IN THE SEA, AND ALL THE DEPTHS OF THE RIVER SHALL BE CONFOUNDED] And as [that exiled people] passes [when Zechariah was saying these things] through the straits of the sea, He shall strike [God, that is ἐπιτιμήσει, as we have in Matt. 8, 26. He shall repress by His power] the waves, which shall be in that sea: then also all the channels of the river shall be dried up. When the river is called simply, the Euphrates is to be understood. From this passage is also taken that which is in the Apocalypse 16, 12. ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὐτẽ ἐπὶ τὸν ποταμὸν τὸν μέγαν εὐφράτην, καὶ ἐξηράνθη τὸ ὕδωρ ἀυτẽ. It is as if it were suppressed: For the sense is, the Euphrates shall be as passable to them as if it were entirely destitute of waters. See Isaiah 11, 15. The Hebrews, whom Jerome consulted, interpreted the jaws of the sea designated in this place as the Thracian Bosphorus between Byzantium and Chalcedon: not badly, if you consider that the empire of Nebuchadnezzar extended also to the right shore of the Pontus, that is to Dacia, of which thing Abydenus is a witness, whence we have also observed from the scholiast of Aristophanes that a part of the Hebrews was in Thrace. Therefore, to these whom either Nebuchadnezzar, or if the empire of the Assyrians came that far, Shalmaneser had deported to those places, God, when they were returning to their homeland, provided first the calm sea of the Bosphorus, then also the easy channels of the Euphrates, which are on the journey to Judea. From this passage flowed the fable which is in the book most full of fables, which is called the fourth of Ezra c. 13, 40.

AND THE PRIDE OF ASSYRIA SHALL BE HUMBLED] That is, of Antiochus Epiphanes, who among other things held Assyria: For we learn from Appian, Josephus, and others that the Seleucids reigned as far as Armenia: in a similar way this same Antiochus is called Gog, that is, Gygaean, by Ezekiel, because he held Lydia, as we said there.

AND THE SCEPTER OF EGYPT SHALL DEPART] Namely, from the Jews. The Jews had been under Ptolemy, the son of Lagus, and under certain other kings of Egypt, as can be learned from Josephus, 12.1 and following. After the times of the Maccabees, that did not happen anymore. This is clearly the same manner of speaking as in Gen. 49:10, from which it appears that the interpretations of that passage, which the Jews began to invent some centuries ago, are not only new, as the Chaldean Paraphrasts and Greek Interpreters show, but also at odds with the native manner of speaking.

Jerome has already rejected the opinion of the Jews, whom he followed here, as being like fables. The Egyptians did not have a scepter or rule over the Jews, except for those few who had retreated into Egypt. And it is absurd that Antiochus is understood by Assur: (He never appears under that name in the scriptures) just as it is equally absurd that the same Epiphanes should be understood by the Gog of Ezekiel, concerning whom we have spoken in the annotations to Ezekiel. The Hebrew text is to be rendered thus: And he shall pass through the sea in distress, and shall strike the waves in the sea, and all the deeps of the river shall be dried up: The sense is: the people will indeed not be multiplied without distress, but the distress will not be lasting; it will pass, and even the greatest ferocity of the enemies will be confounded (because waters and rivers are accustomed to denote peoples), two of whom he expresses particularly, the Assyrians and the Egyptians, inasmuch as the Israelites experienced their tyranny above all. Ludov. de Dieu refers this passage to God. and he shall pass through the sea to the enemy, צרה the enemy with the local ה צרתה towards the enemy. Others translate: he shall pass in the sea of distress. The Weimar Paraphrasts refer these predicates to Ephraim, named in v. 7: And he (Ephraim) will go through the sea of distress, and strike the waves in the sea, i.e., he will overcome the roaring of all enemies with prayers. This again admits a spiritual sense

B. Tarnovius: that from these regions also, Assyria and Egypt, many would subject themselves to the scepter of Christ. Which sense Calvin also seems to approve in his Commentary on this passage. Coccejus dreams that Egypt is called the papal kingdom, that by Assyria is understood the Turk or the Persian, or rather both, and that v. 10 indicates the reconciliation of Christians who are under Turkish rule with the Reformed Church, with liberty granted by the Assyrian, comparing to that opinion Mic. 4:6, Is. 11:11. But he professes that he does not know what is hinted at in v. 11, since those things are not yet illustrated by history, comparing the passage Is. 19:23 as a parallel prophecy, and Rev. 6:12, ch. 18:21.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET TRANSIBIT IN MARIS FRETO, ET PER- CUTIET IN MARI FLUCTUS, ET CONFUNDEN- TUR OMNIA PROFUNDA FLUMINIS] Et transeun- te [illo populo exsule, cum hæc loqueretur Zacharias] per maris angustias, percutiet [Deus, id est ἐπιτιμήσει, ut ha- bemus Matth. 8, 26. reprimet vi sua] fluctus, qui erunt in mari illo: deinde etiam siccabuntur omnes alvei fluminis. Flumen cum simpliciter appellatur, intelligendus Euphra- tes. Ex hoc loco desumitur & ille, qui est in Apocalypsi 16, 12. ἐξέχεε τὴν φιάλην αὐτẽ ἐπὶ τὸν ποταμὸν τὸν μέγαν εὐφράτην, καὶ ἐξηράνθη τὸ ὕδωρ ἀυτẽ. Subticetur quasi: Sensus enim est, Euphratem tam pervium ipsis fore, quam si totus ab aquis de- stitutus esset. Vide Esaiam 11, 15. Maris fauces hoc loco designatas Hebræi, quos Hieronymus consuluit, interpre- tabantur Bosphorum Thracium inter Byzantium & Chal- cedonem: non male, si consideres Nabuchodonosori im- perium pertinuisse etiam ad dextram Ponti oram, id est ad Daciam, cujus rei testis est Abydenus, unde & in Thra- cia partem fuisse Hebræorum ex Aristophanis scholiaste ob- servavimus. His ergo quos illa in loca aut Nabuchodo- nosor, aut si eo usque Assyriorum venit imperium, Salma- nasar deportaverat, Deus cum in patriam redirent, primum placidum mare Bosphori, deinde & faciles eos, qui in itine- re ad Judæam sunt, Euphratis alveos præstitit. Ex hoc lo- co fluxit fabula, quæ est in libro fabularum plenissimo, qui Esdræ quartus dicitur c. 13, 40.

ET HUMILIABITUR SUPERBIA ASSUR] Id est, Antiochi Epiphanis, qui inter cætera Assyriam tenebat: Nam ad Armeniam usque regnasse Seleucidas, ex Appia- no, Josepho, aliisque discimus: pari modo idem hic An- tiochus Gog, id est Gygæus dicitur Ezechieli, quia Lydiam tenebat, ut ibi diximus.

ET SCEPTRUM ÆGYPTI RECEDET] Nempe à Judæis. Fuerant Judæi sub Ptolemæo Lagi filio, & sub aliis quibusdam Ægypti regibus ut discere est Joseph. 12, 1. & sequentibus. Post Maccabæorum tempora id non eve- nit amplius. Est hic idem plane loquendi genus quod Gen. 49, 10. unde apparet, interpretationes ejus loci, quas Judæi ab aliquot jam seculis comminisci cœpere, non mo- do novas esse, quod ostendunt Chaldæi Paraphrastæ, & In- terpretes Græci, sed & à nativo loquendi genere dissenta- neas.

Judæorum sententiam, quos hic sequutus est, reprobavit jam ceu fabulis similem, Hieronymus. Sceptrum vel regimen super Judæos Ægyptii non habuere, nisi quod ad paucos illos, qui in Æ- gyptum se receperant. Et inepte Antiochus per Assurem intelligitur: (Nuspiam is eo nomine ve- nit in scripturis) æque uti ineptum eundem Epi- phanem per Gogum Ezechielis intelligendum esse, quo de annotat. ad Ezechiel. diximus. Ebræus textus ita reddendus: Et transibit in mari angustia, & percutiet in mari fluctus, & siccabuntur omnia profunda fluminis: Sensus est: non quidem sine an- gustia multiplicabitur populus, sed non erit diuturna angustia, transibit & confundetur etiam summa fe- rocia hostium, (quia aquæ & flumina notare solent populos) quorum duos peculiariter exprimit, As- syrios & Ægyptios, utpote quorum tyrannidem imprimis experti sint Israelitæ. Ludov. de Dieu ad Deum refert h. m. & transibit per mare ad hostem, צרה hostis cum ה locali צרתה hostem versus. Alii ver- tunt transibit in mari angustiæ. Vinarienses Para- phrastæ ad Ephraim v. 7. nominatum hæc prædi- cata referunt: Und er (Ephraim) wird durchs Meer der Angst gehen, und die Wellen im Meer schlagen, h. e. precibus superabit omnium hostium fremitum. Sensum spiritualem admittit hic iterum

B. Tarnovius: quod ex his etiam regionibus As- syria & Ægypto multi se sceptro Christi subjectu- ri sint. Quem sensum quoque approbare vide- tur Calvinus in Comment. ad h. l. Coccejus somniat Ægyptum appellari regnum papale, Assyriam in- telligi Turcam vel Persam, vel potius utrumque, & v. 10. indicari Christianorum, qui sunt in Turci- ca ditione, conciliationem cum Ecclesia Reformata, libertate concessa ab Assyrio, conferens in eam sententiam Mich. 4, 6. Es. 11, 11. Quid vero v. 11. innuatur se ignorare profitetur, siquidem ea non- dum illustrentur per historiam, conferens locum Es. 19, 23. ceu parallelam Prophetiam, & Ap. VI. 12. c. XVIII. 21.

## 10:12
Vers. 12. I WILL STRENGTHEN THEM IN THE LORD] That is, in myself. A noun for a pronoun, in the Hebrew manner, concerning which we have spoken elsewhere.

AND THEY SHALL WALK IN HIS NAME] They shall conduct their affairs under the protection of God: for הלך is often for the Hebrews to conduct affairs.

The Lord speaks here about the Lord, the Father about the Son, which we have shown elsewhere happens quite often in the scriptures. For in our Lord Christ is our strength, Is. 45:23, and in his name all things are to be done, Col. 3:17. For thus far he has introduced God the Father speaking, or the Son of God, or the Prophet, as the conclusion of this chapter teaches: SAYS JEHOVAH.

Latin:

Vers. 12. CONFORTABO EOS IN DOMINO] Id est in me ipso. Nomen pro pronomine, more Hebræo, de quo alibi egimus.

ET IN NOMINE EJUS AMBULABUNT] Sub præsidio Dei res suas agent: nam הלך sæpe est Hebræis res agere.

Loquitur hic Dominus de Domino, Pater de Filio, quod sæpius in scripturis fieri alias often- dimus. Nam in Domino nostro Christo fortitu- do nostra Es. 45, 23. & in nomine ejus res omnes a- gendæ sunt Col. 3, 17. Hactenus enim loquentem Deum Patrem introduxit, sive Filius Dei, sive Pro- pheta, uti conclusio hujus capitis docet DICIT JEHOVAH.

## 11:1 Argument
SECTION III. THREATENING. CHAPTER XI. The final destruction of the temple and the people, and the cause of the same, the rejection of Christ.

The burning of Jerusalem is denounced; for the nobles, the commoners, and also the Priests, a wailing; for the Magistrate, a roaring, because of their devastated magnificence: and because of the false doctrine of the shepherds, by which they were killing souls, and their insatiable avarice, who did not spare the sheep, the Lord threatens that he will not spare the inhabitants; especially because he himself was guarding the sheep as a shepherd, with the harmful ones cut off, but was rejected and sold for the cheap price of 30 shekels: Whence he cut off both pastoral staffs, in turn rejecting those same ones, and permitting the shepherds who were tearing and lacerating the sheep: to whom, however, punishment is also declared.

By fire shall Lebanon fall: Jehovah is sold for money.

Vers. 1. OPEN THY DOORS, O LEBANON] Lebanon is the Temple, as in Ezek. 27:3, Hab. 2:17. After the Prophet had predicted many prosperous things, he shows that evils will intervene, the causes of which evils he shows by a comparison of ancient things. The doors of the Temple, he says, will be open to outsiders. It is the same as what is said about Antiochus in 1 Macc. 1:23, 'And he entered into the sanctuary in pride.' And Is. 12:7.

AND LET THE FIRE DEVOUR THY CEDARS] That is, the cedar palaces around the Temple, as stated in 1 Macc. 1:23, 'And he fell upon the city suddenly, and struck it with a great blow, and destroyed much people of Israel, and took the spoils of the city, and burned it with fire, and pulled down its houses and its walls round about.'

Latin:

SECTIO III. COMMINATORIA. CAPUT XI. Excidium novissimum templi & populi, & causa ejusdem Christi rejectio.

Denunciatur Hierosolymæ incendium, pro- ceribus, plebejis, ut & Sacerdotibus ulula- tus, Magistratui rugitus, ob vastatam ma- gnificentiam eorum: & propter pastorum falsam doctrinam, qua occidebant ani- mas, & insatiabilem avaritiam, qui non parcebant ovibus, se incolis non parsurum minatur Dominus; imprimis quia ipse oves ut pastor, noxiis succisis, custodiebat, sed reprobatus, & pretio vili 30. siclorum ven- ditus: Unde utramq; virgam pastoralem præscidit, vicissim reprobatis iisdem, & permissis pastoribus oves discerpentibus & dilacerantibus: quibus tamen etiam pœna indicitur.

Igne cadet Libanon: venundatur ære Iehovah.

Vers. 1. APERI LIBANE PORTAS TUAS] Liba- nus est Templum, quomodo Ezech. 27, 3. Habac. 2, 17. Postquam res prosperas plurimas Propheta prædixerat, o- stendit interventura & mala, quorum malorum causas o- stendit comparatione rerum veterum. Portæ Templi, in- quit, patebunt externis. Idem est quod de Antiocho dicitur 1. Mac. 1, 23. Καὶ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ ἁγίασμα ἐν ὑπερη- φανίᾳ. Et Es. 12, 7.

ET COMEDAT IGNIS CEDROS TUAS] Id est, cedrina palatia circa Templum, dicto 1. Mac. 1, 23. Καὶ ἐπέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὴν πόλιν ἐξάπινα, κὴ ἐπάταξεν αὐτὴν πληγὴν με- γάλην, κὴ ἀπώλεσε λαὸν πολὺν ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ, κὴ ἔλαβε τὰ σκῦλα τῆς πόλεως, κὴ ἐνεπύρισεν αὐτὴν πυρὶ κὴ καθεῖλε τὰς οἴκας αὐ- τῆς κὴ τὰ τείχη αὐτῆς κύκλῳ.

## 11:2
Vers. 2. HOWL, O FIR TREE] You lesser towns, lament and fear.

BECAUSE THE CEDAR IS FALLEN] The city of Jerusalem, in great part burned. See 1 Macc. 1:33 and what is said there.

BECAUSE THE MAGNIFICENT ARE DEVASTATED] Those living magnificently have been stripped of their houses.

HOWL, O YE OAKS OF BASHAN] The same thing is signified as was just now by the fir tree.

FOR THE DEFENCED FOREST IS CUT DOWN] That city furnished with such great walls, which on account of the height of its buildings is compared to a forest.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ULULA ABIES] Oppida minora plangite & timete.

QUIA CECIDIT CEDRUS] Urbs Hierosolyma magna parte incensa. Vide 1. Macc. 1, 33. & ibi dicta.

QUONIAM MAGNIFICI VASTATI SUNT] Illi magnifice habitantes exuti sunt suis ædibus.

ULULATE QUERCUS BASAN] Idem significa- tur, quod modo per abietem.

QUONIAM SUCCISUS EST SALTUS MU- NITUS] Urbs illa tantis instructa mœnibus, quæ ob al- titudinem ædium sylvæ comparatur.

## 11:3
Ver. 3. A VOICE OF THE HOWLING OF THE SHEPHERDS] Princes: for we have said that these also are signified by the name of shepherds, together with kings, 10, 2.

FOR THEIR GLORY IS SPOILED] Their proud habitations.

A VOICE OF THE ROARING OF YOUNG LIONS] For they were called shepherds, but in reality they were lions, δημόβοροι (devourers of the people), which the following words explain.

FOR THE PRIDE OF JORDAN IS SPOILED] The glory of Judea. For rivers are accustomed to be named for regions, as Euphrates for Babylon.

There is no reason why we should disapprove of Grotius's paraphrase in these matters. It is accepted by common consent that by Lebanon the temple is noted, built from the timbers of Mount Lebanon, 1 Kings 5:5, or the city of Jerusalem, as the scholion of Blessed Luther has it: or the whole region of the Jews, which is the opinion of Cyril, although here Calvin thinks only for himself, and our Tarnovius also prefers to understand the mountain itself, which was the northern boundary of Judea, from which side the invading Romans first occupied everything. By the cedars, however, most understand the Magnificent Nobles, who, like cedars among other trees, stand out in height and excellence. But Tarnovius and some others also take Jordan literally, near which were the best pastures, and around whose adjacent wildernesses there were huge lions; so that Judea is described by the river, as its eastern boundary, as in verse 1. from the northern boundary, because in the other boundaries the Jews could have no refuge, since to the south Egypt, and to the west the great sea with the adjacent regions, had already obeyed the Romans. Finally, by Shepherds most understand those who preside in the Church, or only them, as by Lions they understand the Regents, or they include them together with the Princes. The following words absolutely demand this sense. Moreover, Grotius wrongly applies all these things to the times of the Maccabees. These things, by the common opinion of interpreters, deal with the destruction of Jerusalem. This the Jews themselves also acknowledged, whence R. Johanan son of Zaccai, forty years before the destruction of the temple, as P. Galatinus reports in book 4, de Arcan. Cath. Verit. c. 8, from the Talmud, when the temple had opened itself, which happened before the overthrow by Titus, as Josephus reports in book VII de Bell. Judaic. c. 12, is said to have exclaimed: Behold the prophecy of Zechariah, because he predicted that this temple was to be burned, and that its doors were to be opened first. Cyril provides this coherence with the preceding: When he had narrated what is sufficient, and most aptly, concerning the calling of the Gentiles to Christ through faith, he clearly predicts the future unbelief of the Israelites concerning Him at the time when He was a man among us: and for this reason the temple itself is to be burned, and also Jerusalem, and furthermore the cities of Israel themselves are to be subdued, and will perish with their inhabitants.

Latin:

Vers. 3. VOX ULULATUS PASTORUM] Princi- um: nam & hos pastorum nomine, simul cum regibus ignificari diximus 10, 2.

QUIA VASTATA EST MAGNIFICENTIA EORUM] Superba habitacula.

VOX RUGITUS LEONUM] Pastores enim di- cebantur, revera erant leones, δημόβοροι, quod explicant sequentia.

QUONIAM VASTATA EST SUPERBIA JOR- DANIS] Gloria Judææ. Solent enim amnes pro regio- nibus nominari, ut Euphrates pro Babylone.

Non est, quod improbemus in his paraphra- sin Grotii. Communi calculo receptum est, per Libanum templum notari, è lignis de monte Libani exstructum 1. Reg. 5, 5. aut urbem Hierosolymam, uti B. Lutheri scholion habet: vel totam Judæorum regionem, quæ Cyrilli est sententia, etsi hic sibi so- li sapiat Calvinus, & Tarnovius quoque noster malit ipsum montem intelligere, qui erat terminus Aquilonaris Judææ, à qua parte omnia primum occuparint invadentes Romani. Per cedros au- tem Proceres Magnificos, qui velut cedri inter re- liquas arbores altitudine & præstantia eminent, plerique intelligunt. Jordanem vero Tarnovius, & alii nonnulli, etiam proprie accipiunt, ad quem erant pascua optima, circa cujus adjacentes solitu- dines erant immanes leones; ut ita Judæa à fluvio, ceu termino orientali, describatur, uti vers. 1. à termino septentrionali, quia in reliquis terminis nullum habere poterant Judæi perfugium, cum à meridie Ægyptus, & ab occidente mare magnum cum adjacentibus regionibus jam paruerit Roma- nis. Denique per Pastores plerique eos, qui in Ecclesia præsunt, vel solos intelligunt, uti per Leo- nes Regentes, vel simul cum Principibus comple- ctuntur. Quem sensum sequentia omnino postu- lant. Cæterum hæc omnia perperam Grotius ad tempora Maccabæorum rapit. Quæ communi In- terpp. sententia de Excidio Hierosolymæ agunt. Quod agnovere etiam Judæi, unde R. Johanan fi- lius Zaccai quadraginta annis ante destructionem templi, perhibente P. Galatino l. 4. de Arcan. Cath. Verit. c. 8. ex Talmude, cum aperuisset sese templum, quod ante eversionem Titi factum, Jose- phus l. VII. de Bell. Judaic. c. 12. refert, exclamaf- se dicitur: En vaticinium Zachariæ, quia prædi- xit, templum hoc esse exurendum, & prius aperiendas esse ejus portas. Cohærentiam cum præcedentibus hanc tradit Cyrillus: Cum quod satis est, & aptis- sime narrasset de vocatione gentium in Christo per fi- dem, futuram super eo incredulitatem Israelitarum tempore, quo homo inter nos fuit videlicet, luculen- ter prænuntiat: & hac de causa incendendum tem- plum ipsum, atœ etiam Hierosolymam, & insuper subigendas ipsas urbes Israel, & cum ipsis incolis pe- rituras.

## 11:4
Ver. 4. THUS SAITH THE LORD MY GOD] Thus He said to me, namely to Zechariah.

FEED THE FLOCK OF THE SLAUGHTER] Instruct and comfort this people, whom, on account of their ambition, Jason, Menelaus, and Lysimachus will expose to slaughter and plunder. See Josephus 2, 6, and 2 Macc. 4, 13, and following.

Latin:

Vers. 4. HÆC DICIT DOMINUS DEUS MEUS] Hæc dixit mihi, nempe Zachariæ.

PASCE PECORA OCCISIONIS] Instrue & so- lare populum hunc, quem ob suam ambitionem Jason, Menelaus, Lysimachus, objicient cædibus & rapinis. Vide Josephum 2, 6. & 2. Macc. 4, 13. & sequentibus.

## 11:5
Ver. 5. THOSE WHO POSSESSED THEM KILLED] Those who receive them to be governed, these will be the cause of their slaughter. He is said to do a thing, who is the cause why anything is done.

AND THEY DID NOT GRIEVE] They were not moved by such great evils of the people, while they indulged their own inclination.

AND THEY SOLD THEM] They betrayed them, partly to be killed, partly to be plundered by outsiders.

SAYING: BLESSED BE THE LORD, WE HAVE BECOME RICH] Each one will say, praised be God, because I have become rich: as if he were to say: I care nothing for the common people, provided I make great profits from the priesthood. Thus also they abused the name of God for wicked desires. And how many there are today who give thanks to God for the success of their crimes.

AND THEIR SHEPHERDS DID NOT SPARE THEM] And so each one of their shepherds did not spare them.

This strange shepherd milks the sheep twice in a day.

These words were not spoken to Zechariah: 'Feed the flock of slaughter.' But He who speaks these things, and says that these things were spoken to Him, is the Son of God, that good shepherd whom Ezekiel also designated in chapters 34 and 37. For He testifies that these things were spoken to Him, and that the pasture was entrusted to Him, as seen in verses 7 and 8; intending to carry this out, He says: 'And I will feed the flock of slaughter, and I took unto me two staves, and I cut off three shepherds.' Now these things certainly do not fit Zechariah, as Grotius acknowledges, but solely the Son of God: wherefore these things cannot be explained as referring to the people exposed to slaughter and plunder by Jason, Menelaus, and Lysimachus, but they speak of the people at the coming of Christ, who had been sent to them as a good shepherd, destined for the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord God, my heavenly Father: He addressed me thus: 'Feed you the flock of slaughter, which those who possessed them were killing and did not grieve:' In Hebrew: 'And they did not reckon it for sin:' 'and they were selling those sheep (which they ought to have fed), saying, blessed and praised be the Lord, because all things are turning out for us according to our desire: we have become rich from the slaughtered and sold sheep.' And thus (says Christ) their shepherds acted with all those committed to them, and did not spare them: that is, the Pharisees, the Scribes, the priests, and the High Priests so institute divine worship and the exercises of Religion that they themselves become rich, meanwhile with false doctrine and in insincere Religion they slaughter the sheep and deliver them to Satan, as the paraphrase of Osiander has it here, with which the rest of our Commentators agree, indeed even most of the Reformed, here deserting their Calvin, who thinks that the Prophet speaks these things and takes upon himself the person of all the Shepherds. In no way, says Coccejus, is it fitting that the words of this chapter be attributed to the Prophet. He names his God from the covenant which he has with the Father concerning the salvation of the Church to be procured through his own obedience as a man. The command signifies nothing other than the will of the Father, by which the 'Epidemia' or visitation of the people by the Son through the 'ensarkosis' (incarnation) was brought about at the most opportune time. The command enjoins the feeding of the sheep. Which denotes nothing other than what is in Isaiah 40:9, 10, 11 and Ezekiel 34:11, 15, 22, 23, 24. The mission of the Son to the sheep is indicated, so that He may henceforth feed them by the power of His merit, through His word and His example and the Holy Spirit in liberty. Piscator likewise acknowledges with us without doubt that these words are Christ's. Fr. Junius provided this analysis of this chapter: This explanation of the judgments of God, poured out (as we said in verse 2), narrates first indeed the calling and institution of Christ for feeding the people up to verse 7, and finally the judgments up to the end of the chapter. In the calling, two kinds of Jews are established; to one of which Christ is entrusted to be fed, but the other is rejected on account of its impiety and inhumanity: 'FEED THE FLOCK OF SLAUGHTER,' that is, this poor people, who are exposed to the violence of their shepherds, and vindicate them from them. For Christ indeed came after those times to seek the lost sheep of Israel, during which times they had long been flayed by their shepherds, from the times of John Hyrcanus through Aristobulus the elder, Alexander, Hyrcanus, and Aristobulus the younger, Antipater, Herod, the Priests, the Pharisees, and the Sadducees, as ancient histories teach. This is Junius. Willius, although he wishes the Prophet to speak, and to act as a type of Christ (in which, however, he is mistaken, because nothing occurs here that exhibits a type, nor is there any trace of a figure), nevertheless institutes the analysis in such a way that, neglecting the Prophet, he presents only the Messiah here, and he teaches with Junius that his calling to the pastoral office is described in verses 5 and 6, and the outcome of the same in verse 7; from whom, however, he rightly departs concerning the object of the passion of Christ in that Junius restricts it to a peculiar kind of sheep distinct from the rest of the people: since Christ is said to have fed the same sheep which he afterwards rejected and took to himself to be fed, the flock of slaughter, that is, the whole people on account of the poor of the flock, that is, the remnant of the elect and the faithful. Now the sheep of slaughter are called Jews on account of the (1) cruelty of their shepherds: Their possessors (the Princes and Ecclesiastical and Political leaders, who have the people in their hand and possession) kill them, and are not held guilty. (2) Avarice. And they were selling them, saying: 'blessed be the Lord, we have become rich.' (3) Inclemency. And their shepherds did not spare, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QUÆ QUI POSSEDERANT OCCIDE- BANT] Qui eos regendos accipient, hi erunt causa occi- dionis ipsorum. Facere dicitur, qui causa est, cur quid fiat.

ET NON DOLEBANT] Non movebantur tan- tis populi malis, dum suo animo morem gererent.

ET VENDEBANT EA] Prodebant eos partim occidendos partim diripiendos externis.

DICENTES: BENEDICTUS DOMINUS, DI- VITES FACTI SUMUS] Dicent quisque, laudatus Deus, quod dives factus sum: quasi dicat: nihil plebem curo, dum ego ex sacerdotio magnos quæstus faciam. Ita etiam Dei nomine ad prava vota abutebantur. Et quam multi hodie sunt qui Deo gratias agunt de scelerum suorum successu.

ET PASTORES EORUM NON PASCEBANT EIS] Adeoque quisq́; eorum pastor non parcebat eis.

Hic alienus oves pastor bis mulget in born.

Hæc dicta non sunt Zachariæ: Pasce pecora occisionis. Sed is, qui hæc loquitur, & hæc sibi dicta ait, est Filius Dei, pastor ille bonus, quem Ezechiel etiam designavit c. 34, 37. Nam is hæc sibi dicta, & commendatam sibi pasturam testatur, qu. v. 7. 8. hoc exequuturus ait: Et ego pascam pecora illud occisionis, & assumsi mihi duas virgas, & succidi tres Pastores. Hæc autem utique non conveniunt Zachariæ, ut agnoscit Grotius, sed unice Filio Dei: quapropter explica ri ista non possunt de populo à Jasone, Menelao, Lysimacho cædibus & rapinis exposito, sed loquuntur de populo sub adventum Christi, qui ei missus erat ceu pastor bonus, ad oves perditas de domo Israelis destinatus. Hæc dicit Dominus Deus Pater meus cœlestis: Hic me alloquutus est: Pasce tu pecora occisionis, quæ qui possederant, occidebant & non dolebant: Hebraice: Et non pro peccato reputabant: & vendebant ea pecora: (quæ pascere debuerant) dicentes, benedictus & laudatus sit Dominus, quod omnia nobis ex animi sententia succedant: divites facti sumus ex ovibus mactatis & divenditis. Et sic (inquit Christus) egerunt pastores eorum cum omnibus sibi commissis, & non parcebant eis: id est Pharisæi, Legisperiti, sacerdotes, & Pontifices ita instituunt cultum divinum & exercitia Religionis, ut ipsi divites evadant, interim falsa doctrina, & in syncera Religione oves jugulant & Satanæ tradunt, ut hic habet paraphrasis Osiandri, cui consonant reliqui Commentatores Nostri, imo etiam è Reformatis plerique, hic deserentes Calvinum suum, qui putat Prophetam hæc loqui, & sumere in se personam omnium Pastorum. Nullo modo, inquit Coccejus, convenit, ut verba hujus capitis Prophetæ attribuantur. Deum suum nominat à pacto, quod cum Patre habet de salute Ecclesiæ per obedientiam suam, u hominis procuranda. Mandatum nihil aliud significat, quam voluntatem Patris, qua Filii Ἐπιδημία sive visitatio populi per ἐνσάρκωσιν in opportunissimum tempus collata est. Mandatum injungit pastionem ovium. Quod nihil aliud notat, quam quod est Jesaiæ 40, 9. 10. 11. & Ezech. 34, 11. 15. 22. 23. 24. Indigitatur missio Filii ad oves, ut pascat eas deinceps vi meriti sui, per verbum & exemplum suum & spiritum sanctum in libertate. Piscator verba hæc Christi esse itidem sine dubitatione nobiscum agnoscit. Fr. Junius hanc tradidit ἀνάλυσιν hujus capitis: Fusa hæc judiciorum Dei explicatio (ut diximus in versum 2.) enarrat primum quidem vocationem & institutionem Christi pascendo populo usque ad versum 7. ac postremo judicia ad finem usque capitis. In vocatione duo statuuntur Judæorum genera; quorum uni pascendi committuntur Christo, alteri vero propter impietatem & inhumanitatem suam abdicantur: PASCE OVES INTERFECTIONIS, id est, tenuem hunc populum, qui expositus est pastorum suorum violentiæ, eumque ab illis vindica. Christus enim revera post ea tempora quæsiturus oves Israelis amissas venit, quibus temporibus fuerant diu à suis pastoribus excarnificatæ, inde à Johannis Hyrcani temporibus per Aristobulum priorem, Alexandrum, Hyrcanum, & Aristobulum posteriorem, Antipatrum, Herodem, Sacerdotes, Pharisæos & Sadducæos, ut veteres historiæ docent. Hæc Junius. Willius, etsi Prophetam loqui velit, ac Christi typum agere, in quo tamen fallitur, quia hic nihil, quod typum exhibeat, occurrit, neque ullum figuræ est vestigium) analysin tamen ita instituit, ut neglecto Propheta, Mes- siam stiam solum hic sistat, ejusque vocationem ad offi- cium pastorale v. 5. 6. Pastorum v. 7. & exitum ejusdem describi cum Junio tradit, à quo vero re- cte circa objectum passionis Christi in eo abit, quod Junius id restringat ad peculiare ovium genus à reliquo populo distinctum: siquidem easdem oves Christus pavisse dicatur, quas postea abdicarit & assumpserit sibi pascendas oves interfectionis, id est, totum populum propter pauperes gregis, id est, reliquias electorum & fidelium. Vocantur autem oves interfectionis Judæi ob pastorum (1) crude- litatem: Possessores eorum (Principes & proceres Ecclesiastici & Politici, qui populum in manu & possessione sua habent) interficiunt, nec habentur rei. (2) Avaritiam. Et vendebant eos dicentes: be- nedictus Dominus, divites facti sumus. (3) incle- mentiam. Et pastores eorum non parcebant &c.

## 11:6
Ver. 6. AND I WILL NO LONGER SPARE THE INHABITANTS OF THE LAND] They do not spare the people: and I will not spare them, and those who will be approving of their deeds.

BEHOLD I WILL DELIVER MEN EVERY ONE INTO THE HAND OF HIS NEIGHBOR] They will rage against each other with mutual slaughters: for many Jews were following the side of Antiochus, 1 Macc. 1:55. Josephus in the cited book, Ezek. 39:26, Dan. 11:30, 32.

AND INTO THE HAND OF HIS KING] Into the hands of Antiochus.

AND THEY SHALL STRIKE THE LAND] That they may strike the land: namely, by falling.

AND I WILL NOT DELIVER OUT OF THEIR HAND] I will not deliver the approvers of such counsels out of the hand of either Antiochus or the Maccabees.

This is again from a preconceived opinion, as if they refer to the times of the Maccabees. Osiander is therefore more correct: and because I see, (says Christ) that impiety has prevailed as much among the shepherds as among the common people, I will no longer spare those dwelling upon the land of Canaan, says the Lord, but I will most severely punish the highest and the lowest. Behold, I will deliver men, every one into the hand of his neighbor: that they may be agitated by seditions, and the citizens themselves may mutually slaughter one another. (For horrible seditions arose among the Jerusalemites before the destruction of the city, concerning which seditions and robberies in the city itself Josephus writes much. And finally I will deliver them (says the Lord) into the hand of their King: that is, into the power of the Roman Caesar, for he is rightly called their King, because the Roman Emperors then ruled over Judea, and had their prefects in Jerusalem, with some garrison of soldiers, among whom was also Pontius Pilate, under whom Christ was crucified. And the Jews themselves, when Pilate asked whether he should crucify their King (Christ), said: We have no KING, but CAESAR. And they shall strike (that is, the Romans shall horribly devastate) the land of Judea: and I will not deliver the Jewish people out of their hand: but I will connive at all the miseries of the Jews, because they denied me as their God and King. Moreover, these evils are designated as punishments in place: namely, internal and domestic commotions: Behold, I will deliver men, every one into the hand of his neighbor: and the tyranny of the Roman enemies: and into the hand of their King, by whom some understand Herod, but others more correctly explain it as the Roman Caesar, John 19:15, since the Jews were so long vexed both by domestic seditions and by various agitations through the Roman governors, until they came into the hand of Vespasian and the Roman King. Furthermore, concerning the enemies the Prophet says: AND THEY SHALL STRIKE THE LAND, not that they must strike the land by falling, as Grotius absurdly says, but that the land of the Jews itself is to be crushed and ground down with its inhabitants, which the word כתת implies, 2 Chron. 34:7. Whence Is. 30:14, thus it perishes of the Jews is thus described: it shall be broken as a potter's vessel is broken with a very strong breaking, and there shall not be found among its fragments a shard in which a little fire may be carried from a burning, or a little water be drawn from a pit. Therefore it is added AND I WILL NOT SPARE FROM THEIR HAND, which is wrongly referred to the hand of Antiochus, or of the Maccabees. For these hands were mutually contrary and hostile to each other. But it is manifest that this designates the total excision and destruction of the people without liberation. And therefore these things by no means fit the times of the Maccabees. But Willius rightly recognizes in these two verses 5. and 6. that the history of Judea is contained, and of its evils, which it suffered before Herod, and under Herod, and his successors, and finally from domestic seditions, and the invasion of the Romans, even to the final destruction: and that this final destruction was the cause, among others, why God committed the people to be fed by the Messiah, if by chance he might yet snatch some from it.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET EGO NON PARCAM ULTRA SU- PER HABITANTES TERRAM] Illi populo non par- cunt: & ego ipsis non parcam, & iis, qui facta illorum e- runt approbaturi.

ECCE EGO TRADAM HOMINES UNUM- QUEMQUE IN MANU PROXIMI SUI] Inter se mu- tuis cædibus sævent: multi enim Judæi Antiochi partes sectabantur 1. Macc. 1, 55. Josephus dicto libro Ezech. 39, 26. Dan. 11, 30. 32.

ET IN MANU REGIS SUI] In manus Antiochi.

ET CONCIDENT TERRAM] Ut terram feriant : cadentes scilicet.

ET NON ERUAM DE MANU EORUM] Non eruam talium consiliorum approbatores de manu aut An- tiochi, aut Maccabæorum.

Hæc iterum è præconcepta opinione, quasi Maccabæorum tempora respiciant. Rectius ergo Osiander: & quia video, (inquit Christus) impieta- tem tam apud Pastores, quam apud plebem inva- luisse, Ego non parcam ultra supra habitantes terram Chanaan, dicit Dominus, sed gravissime puniam summos & infimos. Ecce ego tradam homines unum- quemque in manu proximi sui: ut seditionibus a- gitentur, & cives ipsi mutuo sese jugulent. (Ex- ortæ enim sunt horribiles seditiones inter Jeroso- lymitanos, ante urbis excidium, de quibus sedi- tionibus & latrociniis in ipsa urbe multa Josephus scribit. Et tandem tradam eos (inquit Dominus) in manu Regis sui: id est, in potestatem Romani Cæsaris, is enim recte ipsorum Rex dicitur, quia Romani Imperatores tum Judææ dominabantur, & præfectos suos Jerosolymis habebant, cum ali- quo militum præsidio, inter quos etiam fuit Pon- tius Pilatus, sub quo Christus est crucifixus. Et Ju- dæi ipsi, cum Pilatus quæreret, an deberet ipso- rum Regem (Christum) crucifigere, dixerunt: REGEM non habemus, nisi CÆSAREM. Et con- cident (id est, horribiliter vastabunt Romani) ter- ram Judæam: & non eruam populum Judaicum de manu eorum: sed connivebo ad omnes Judæorum miserias, quia me Deum & regem suum abnega- runt. Designantur autem pœnæ loco hæc mala: utpote motus intestini & domestici: Ecce ego tra- dam homines unumquemque in manu proximi sui: & Tyrannis hostium Romanorum: & in manu Re- gis sui, per quem nonnulli Herodem intelligunt, sed alii rectius de Romano Cæsare explicant Joh. 19, 15. siquidem & domesticis seditionibus, & va- riis exagitationibus per Romanos Præsides tam diu vexati sunt Judæi, donec in manum Vespasiani & Romani Regis venerint. De hostibus porro Pro- pheta: ET CONCIDENT TERRAM, non quod cadentes terram ferire debeant, uti inepte Grotius, sed quod ipsa Judæorum terra contun- denda sit, & conterenda cum incolis suis, quod vox כתת infert 2. Par. 34, 7. Unde Es. 30, 14. ita interi- tus Judæorum describitur, comminuetur sicut con- teritur lagena figuli contritione pervalida, & non invenietur de fragmentis ejus testa, in qua portatur igniculus de incendio, aut hauriatur parum aquæ de fovea. Ideo additur ET NON ERUAM DE MANU EORUM, quæ perperam ad manum tum Antiochi, tum Maccabæorum refert. Hæ e- nim manus erant sibi invicem contrariæ & hosti- les. Totalem autem excisionem, & interitum populi sine liberatione hæc designare manifestum est. Ideoque nequaquam temporibus Macca- bæorum hæc congruunt. Recte autem agnoscit Willius duobus hisce versibus 5. & 6. haberi histo- riam Judææ, & malorum ejus, quæ ante Herodem, & sub Herode, ejusque successoribus, ac denique ex domesticis seditionibus, & Romanorum invasione, ad ultimum usq; excidium perpessa est: atque hoc ultimum excidium causam fuisse inter alias, cur Deus Messiæ populum pascendum commiserit, si forte aliquos adhæc ex eo eripere posset.

## 11:7
V. 7. AND I WILL FEED THE FLOCK OF SLAUGHTER FOR THIS, O POOR OF THE FLOCK] For this, namely the meek of the flock. I will instruct the miserable people, exposed by their rulers to so many slaughters and evils, with an excellent document: which now follows, so that they may both understand the causes of their evils, and beware for themselves.

Grotius devised this gloss so that he might pave a way for himself to the depravation of what follows. It is not a matter of a document through which God the Father wishes to instruct the people, much less of a document from previous times which is then to be explained, but of the cause why the Messiah wishes to feed the flock of slaughter, namely for the sake of the poor of the flock. For now his pastoral office is described, why it had been committed in v. 4. AND I FED THE SHEEP OF SLAUGHTER FOR THE SAKE OF THE MISERABLE OF THE FLOCK, that is, I, having pity on the Israelites, because they were destitute of faithful shepherds, will teach them, for the sake of the elect, who have afflicted consciences, disturbed by the sense of the wrath of God. Some render the word לכן as FOR THE SAKE OF, Osiander, Willius: others, since it is an adverb, truly, indeed. R. David Kimchi, Pagninus for אכן or כן with a redundant Lamed, as Drusius teaches and Ludov. de Dieu, comparing for this meaning Ps. 63:24 and 117:2. The matter comes to the same thing. For these things also must be taken causally: if you render it, indeed they are the poor of the flock.

AND I TOOK TO ME TWO STAVES] Often among the Hebrews narratives begin with ו, as Jud. 1:1. This is what God says here: Already long ago I took to myself two staves, that is, two methods of governing the people happily, protection from external evils, and internal concord.

ONE I CALLED BEAUTY] Sweetness: for nothing is sweeter than to be liberated from evils.

AND THE OTHER I CALLED BANDS] So also the Greeks, σχοίνισμα: whence it appears that the word חבלים was read by them with vowels other than those which the Masoretes have added, for the same word read otherwise signifies either destroyers or ropes. But this latter reading clearly agrees with the sense, and signifies the care of God for keeping the people in concord, as appears below in 14. Just as we ought not to despise the diligence of the Masoretes, so neither ought we to bind ourselves too superstitiously and Judaically to their conjecture, where other better ones are available.

Concerning the two staves you will find as many meanings as there are heads. That there is an allusion to the staves of shepherds no one easily doubts. Jerome interprets the staff נעם concerning the calling of all nations, and חבלים as bands, as he renders it, concerning the Jews, the inheritance of God. The Hebrews wish this latter word to be taken for destroyers. Flacius does not disagree with them in his Clavis under the word Staff, judging that good and bad shepherds are denoted, but who will admit that the Messiah, when he fed the Jews, used destroyers? Some wish the law of nature to be denoted by the former word, and the law of Moses by the latter. But this is inept. Junius has it thus; The former staff, which is called beauty, figured the grace and good pleasure of God resting upon his people through the preaching of the word by Christ: but the latter, which is called the staff of those who bind, signifies the Church gathered together from Judah and the remnants of Israel; which was to precede before the calling of the Gentiles, as had been predicted by the Prophets, and Christ himself showed in Matt. 10:5 and 6. Which opinion Willius judges to be closest to the truth, that the staff of beauty is the Evangelical preaching, but the staff of those who bind is called the effort and zeal of Christ in combining and gathering the Jews. But the zeal and effort of Christ is not an instrument or medium in the pastoral office, such as it is agreed a staff is. And Willius himself devised another opinion, that חבלים are shipmasters from Jon. 1:6, or leaders and governors of a ship, Ezek. 27:28, 29. and that by the staff of beauty Christ himself and his office are signified: but by the staff of the conquered, the Apostles of Christ and their ministry. But Christ is distinguished here from the staff, as a shepherd from a crook. And as the staff is not the shepherd, or his office, but the instrument of the Shepherd: so Christ and his office are inconveniently understood by the staff. Nor can the ministers of the Shepherd be called his staff: and therefore neither are the Apostles of Christ his ministers designated here by his staff. Coccejus understands by the staff of clemency the Caesars and their governors, and by the sailors the presbytery. But these things are twisted. Calvin corrects the Hebrew text, which Grotius, as it appears, having followed with Capellus, also tries to render suspect, as if the word חבלים had once been read differently as far as the vowels are concerned, nor does he wish us to be bound to the points added to the Hebrew Codices, so that other better conjectures may be available, erring in this most gravely, with Calvin, as if the points added by the Masoretes were not coeval with the text: and that they added them by private conjectures. Which hypothesis being admitted, nothing certain will easily be had in the Scripture of the Old Testament, but his own conjecture will be free to everyone, if indeed it be a virtue, as Grotius judges, not to suffer oneself to be bound too superstitiously and Judaically to the points added to the Biblical codices. Calvin interprets the former staff as the elegance of order in divine government: the latter as unity or concord, because God gathered the dispersed Israelites again, so that they might be one body, after the return from Babylon. Grotius translates almost similarly, sweetness and cord: and by sweetness he understands perfection from external evils, by cord internal concord. But these explanations do not agree with the metaphorical expression: for how the elegance of order, and unity or perfection and concord can be compared with a pastoral staff, does not appear, and they are foreign to the text: since here the discourse is not about the government of God, but the pastorate of the God-man Messiah, not about the times of the Old Testament, but the New. Moreover, we have no reason to suspect any corruption here. For it cannot be taught that the word חבלים for cords is more convenient. The word חבלים fits perfectly, whether you render it with the meaning of destroying, which the blessed Luther respected, or with Junius, Tarnovius, and others, as binding or tying together. Ludov. de Dieu, from the Arabic, renders it as federated? But we do not see the reason why one should depart from the version of the blessed Luther; indeed, the opposition seems to demand it: for pleasantness and binding are not so much opposed to each other (unless you take it concerning the bonds of the law, which are adverse to sweetness and pleasantness) as the rod of pleasantness and the rod of those destroying, or those afflicting with deceit, which reason Buxtorf, among the Reformed, adduced here for the blessed Luther's interpretation: I called one Pleasant, the other I called Woe. He says in Vindic. Ebraic. Verit. p. 557, that in those two names the opposition of two rods seems to lie; so that one, namely, was נועם, that is, מקל נועם, the staff or rod of pleasantness, that is, of clemency and gentleness, the other מקל חובלים, the staff or rod of those destroying, or of those causing pain, that is, of wrath and severity, which He used to render void the brotherhood between Judah and Israel v. 14, that is, for the rejection of the entire Israelite people. Certainly God uses these two rods to feed, that is, to rule His people. But setting aside other expositions of these rods, B. Tarnovius also acknowledges as the most probable of all that of B. Luther, that by the staff of pleasantness the doctrine of the Gospel is designated, and by the staff of those binding (as he himself renders it) the moral law: which also most orthodox interpreters follow, to whom from antiquity we add Cyril of Alexandria. But after He became man like us, He took up two staves. For He feeds His worshippers, namely, those justified by faith and sanctified in the Spirit, not driving them to sacrifice oxen, nor teaching us to be zealous for offerings according to the law: but rather commanding that we celebrate worship in the Spirit as an unbloody sacrifice. But the things which Tarnovius brings forward against this received explanation are not of such moment that they can move us from it. He says the Prophet speaks of those staves which Christ alone, the Chief Shepherd, found before Him, and granted to no one after Him, since He broke both v. 10 and 14. Resp. Christ used those staves in feeding the flock of the Jewish people: but He is said to have broken them not absolutely, but with respect to that people who had rendered themselves unworthy of them. He says (2) that each staff had been cut off as something void. Resp. On the part of the Jewish people. He says (3) that by the staff of pleasantness being cut off, the covenant of God was made void. Resp. It was done not on the part of God, whose gifts are without repentance; but on the part of the Jewish people themselves. He says (4) if by the staff of pleasantness being cut off they finally acknowledged the word of God, the poor, or the few faithful, were saved without the Gospel. Resp. With respect to them the staff of pleasantness was not cut off, those who believed, but with respect to those who repudiated the kingdom of Christ from themselves. He says (5) that it would follow from that opinion that Christ deals with everyone first from the Gospel, then from the law, and that the Gospel flourished in the O.T. more and earlier than the law, that the staff of pleasantness flourished earlier and more in the O.T., or is used earlier among the sheep than the staff of the law. But he himself understands by the staff of pleasantness the prerogative of the Jews, by the staff of those who bind, as he calls it, the certain distinction of the tribes. But those are not the means or instruments of the Shepherd Christ, the prerogative of the Jews and the distinction of the Israelite tribes, in the way that a staff is some means or instrument of a shepherd of a flock. Therefore, the opinion of the blessed Luther is still to be preferred entirely. For the law and the Gospel are the means by which the Chief Shepherd, Christ, feeds the flock. The law is the staff of those who destroy, but the Gospel is the staff of pleasantness. But the Gospel is named first, not because this staff is prior in use, but because it is more worthy and excellent, and this rod of pleasantness is more proper to Christ, when the rod of destruction, which He does not use except so that there may be a place for the rod of pleasantness and sweetness, and so that He may be able to comfort us from it, as David sang of this Shepherd in Psalm 23:4: Thy rod and Thy staff, they have comforted me. Osiander: The two staves are two parts of heavenly doctrine. The doctrine of the Gospel is very pleasing to troubled consciences. The doctrine of the law excites pains in the conscience and yet it is also wholesome itself, if anyone uses it rightly. But Christ, although He principally taught the Gospel, yet He also explained the law of God: and purged it from the corruptions of the Pharisees.

V. same. AND I FED THE FLOCK] Happily through David. Verse 8. AND I CUT OFF THREE SHEPHERDS IN ONE MONTH] But I cut off. When the people had shown themselves most ungrateful toward God and David, in the wicked faction of Absalom, in one month He took away from him three excellent princes, David himself, Adonijah the king's son, and Joab the most valiant commander.

Latin:

V. 7. ET PASCAM PECUS OCCISIONIS PROPTER HOC, O PAUPERES GREGIS] Per hoc, nempe mites de grege. Instruam miseram plebem à rectoribus objectam tot cædibus ac malis egregio documento: quod jam se- quitur, ut scilicet & causas malorum intelligant, & sibi caveant.

Glossam hanc excogitavit Grotius, ut viam sibi ad sequentium depravationem sterneret. Non de documento, per quod instruere plebem velit Deus Pater, nedum de documento è superioribus temporibus, quod deinde exponatur, sermo est, sed de causa, cur pecus occisionis velit pascere Mes- sias, nempe propter pauperes gregis. Nam descri- bitur nunc officium pastoratus ejus, cur id v. 4. commissum erat. ET PAVI OVES INTER- FECTIONIS PROPTER MISEROS GREGIS, id est, ego misertus Israëlitarum, propterea, quod pastoribus fidelibus destituti erant, docebo eos, propter electos, qui afflictas, & sensu iræ Dei perturbatas conscientias habent. Verbum לכן nonnulli reddunt, PROPTER, Osiander, Wil- lius: alii, quum adverbium sit, profecto, vere. R. David Kimchius, Pagninus pro אכן sive כן Lamed redundante, ut Drusius docet & Ludov. de Dieu conferens pro hoc significatu Psal. 63, 24. & 117, 2. Res eodem recidit. Nam & ista αἰτιολογικῶς ac- cipienda: si reddas profecto pauperes gregis sunt.

ET ASSUMSI MIHI DUAS VIRGAS] Sæpea- pud Hebræos narrationes incipiunt per ו, ut Jud. 1, 1. Hoc est, quod hic dicit Deus: Jam olim duo mihi assumsi peda, id est, duas rationes populum feliciter gubernandi, pro- tectionem à malis externis, & internam concordiam.

UNAM VOCAVI DECOREM] Dulcedinem: ni- hil enim dulcius, quam à malis liberari.

ET ALTERAM VOCAVI FUNICULUM] Sic & Græci, σχοίνισμα: unde apparet vocem חבלים ab iis lectam cum vocalibus aliis, quam quas adscripsere Ma- soretici, nam eadem vox aliter lecta aut dissipantes signi- ficat, aut funes.
