Willius, however, takes it absolutely, understanding the beginning of the New Testament, where Christ first saved the tents of Judah when He began to kindle His light in Galilee and neighboring places for the people sitting in darkness, Matt. 4, 16. & and with the most abject of all he conferred dignities, inasmuch as he joined himself as a companion to publicans and sinners, and received them into the number of the children of God, and added angelic beauty to the house of David, when he himself presented himself to the world as that promised and great Angel of the covenant, and illustrated the abject and almost depressed family of David with his own splendor. For he rendered these things thus: The house of David is as Gods, (he wishes אלהים to denote angels as Ps. 8, 6.) as the Angel of the Lord before them, by whom he understands the Son of God, who preceded the Fathers Isa. 14, 19. c. 23, 22.23. Calvin had in part anticipated this: There is no doubt that here the Prophet compares the descendants of David to the Angel, who had been the leader to the people and the minister of redemption (The Son of God was not the MINISTER of redemption from Egypt, but with the Father and the Holy Spirit the principal cause. That expression, unworthy of the Son of God, is to be rejected) that Angel, because although God then destined many angels for His people, it was nevertheless Christ. The Prophet therefore here bids the Jews to hope for the perpetual help of God, since in the Royal house there will not only be Angels, but also that Leader of the Fathers, who had exercised the incredible power of God in redeeming the people. This is Calvin. But, how can the house of David be compared to Christ, so that it is, as the Son of God, the Angel of the covenant? For it is not said that the Angel will be in the house of David, but, just as he who will be sick (or infirm) is said to be like David, so the house of David is as the Angel of Jehovah before their face, as Calvin himself rendered it. Therefore, it does not appear here how the Son of God can be understood. Coccejus understands Christ by the house of David, but it is even more absurd to understand Christ by the house of David, and the gloss and reasoning which Coccejus has handed down here is twisted; let him who will read it.

But, to return to Willius, if these things had their fulfillment at the advent of Christ, how are the same things referred to the Philadelphian and Laodicean Church, i.e., the latest times, as he himself interprets? For he wishes the state of the Philadelphian Church to be described in v. 7, because in that Church God is about to save from the hour of temptation, and is about to inscribe His name on those sealed from all the tribes, Apoc. 3, 10. 12. c. 7, 3. The Laodicean, however, in v. 8, because it is about to hasten heavenly beauty for the pious, in which they will sit with Christ on His throne, Apoc. 3, 20. Those things which were fulfilled at the time of the first advent of Christ, when He received publicans and sinners, were not finally to be fulfilled at the time of the Philadelphian Church, when some are to be sealed, and the name of Christ is to be inscribed upon them. If beauty was given to the Davidic house as an angel, when the Messiah presented Himself to the world, according to this prediction, how will it finally be fulfilled in the latest advent of Christ, when the elect will sit on the throne of Christ? Who does not see that these so disparate meanings cannot possibly underlie the same words?

Joh. Cocceius rendered it: And Jehovah will save the tents of Judah FIRST, and he judged it to be taught that the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel had to take place outside Jerusalem, just as the Baptist preached at the Jordan in the desert, Isa. 40:3, and Christ in Galilee, Isa. 8:23, ch. 10:1. And Jehovah saved the tents of Judah. After they had endured and overcome that last affliction of Antiochus, and when they were already ruling in the whole land with no one hindering them, and indeed had filled very many cities as if with colonists, even in the cities of the Philistines, and Idumeans, and Arabs, and outside the land, at that time when the worship of God and the exercise of the ceremonial Law would flourish at Jerusalem, there the Lord will save a part of the people through illumination to the knowledge of the saving God. Whence Cocceius thinks the remaining words of v. 7 contain the reason for this order, and a twofold one: (1) that the earthly majesty, which the Davidic house had once held over Judah, and which had then lain low after the captivity, might not in any way be exalted over Judah again, i.e., that the Son of God, the seed of David according to the flesh, might not come in earthly and worldly majesty, such as David had, but עני, needy, as it is in Zech. 9:9, a worm and no man, the reproach of men and despised of the people, Ps. 22:7. (2) That the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, i.e., those whose ordinary residence, and one necessary on account of the state of the Republic, was at Jerusalem and at the Temple, might not be magnified over Judah. Because Christ ought not at all to come μετὰ παρατήρησεως and in ἀξιώματι σαρκικῷ, nor ought his ministers to have such a government as those sitting in Jerusalem had over Judah. But these things seem more subtle than solid. Nor do those things deserve approval which he brings from parallel passages concerning the same quality of the time of Christ's advent from Zech. 8:5, 6, 23, Jer. 3:16, 17, ch. 13, 14, 15, Isa. 9:2, Deut. 30:5, 6. For they do not treat of the expansion of the Judaic kingdom, which he wishes (though rashly) to be looked at here, but of the propagation of the Church of God, nor do they look to the antecedents of Christ's advent, but to the consequences. Nor is the proof firm that the inhabitants of Jerusalem must here be taken literally, because they are opposed to a certain part of Judah, both because glory over Judah is attributed to them, and because by both designations are understood those needing salvation or divine illumination. For with the ἀντιδιαστολή (distinction) of the tents of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem preserved, the interpretations of our people are correct: That the house or royal family of David may not magnificently boast against the citizens of the city of Jerusalem on account of the nobility of the family, and the glory of the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem may not proudly exalt itself against the whole region of Judah, on account of the fact that it itself is the metropolis of the kingdom, but that all may live together concordantly in true humility of mind and charity. In that day the Lord will protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that nothing may happen to the pious that might overturn their salvation. And he who has stumbled, Heb. he who has been weak among them, in that day, he shall be as David, that most valiant hero: and the house of David shall be as the house or family of God: that family shall be in great honor, as the Angel of the Lord in their sight, that is, even the weak (but nevertheless true Christians) shall be rendered so strong divinely through the Holy Spirit that they may conquer the Devil, just as David conquered Goliath the Philistine. By the house of David, however, he understands the spiritual Leaders, that is, the Apostles and others endowed with the Apostolic spirit: he says these will be in such authority as if they were clearly divine men and Angels of God. Thus Paul writes of the Galatians: As an ANGEL OF GOD you received ME, as CHRIST JESUS: oh how blessed you were then. For I will bear witness to you that, if it could have been done, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me, Gal. 4. Thus Osiander, with whom the Weimar theologians agree, as also the blessed Baldwin: i.e., the enemies of the Church having been defeated, there will be no reason why anyone should exalt himself above another, whether they be of the house of David or the royal lineage, or inhabit Jerusalem, or be of the priestly race, or even be inhabitants of Judah or men of plebeian condition: for all will be participants of one and the same salvation and divine benefit. Even the weak among my people (for these he calls those who stumble), armed by the power of the Holy Spirit and informed through the ecclesiastical ministry, will conquer the spiritual enemies of their souls, Satan, death, and hell. So also Jerome: They shall be so blessed, who have fought for the Church and have confessed the Lord in persecution: that he who is the least, and as a man has stumbled in some word or deed, shall be placed in the order of masters: And the masters, who have kept their rank, shall be as the house of God, and as the Angel of the Lord, because we labor with all zeal, placed on earth and sweating with various toil, that we may be transformed into angelic glory. Cyril says that it is beyond controversy that Jerusalem is understood in this place as the Church of Christ.

But those things are foreign which Grotius says about the fall, by the example of others against the law, which he says about such grave repentance as was David's on account of the sin against Uriah, which he says about the house of the descendants of David after the return to the city (from Babylon), so full of piety as if it were a temple and as if it always had a visible Angel with it. The latter things about the Angel in the text do not refer to the cause of the thing which is being handed down, but present a comparison with the Angel of God: The former things, however, not even Danaeus himself, from whom Grotius received the preceding and following glossed names, as far as appears, understands concerning the similarity of repentance, but concerning the strength being granted divinely: Admirable, he says, he promises to them, and that through a most illustrious gradation. The weak one then who will be in that city will nevertheless be as strenuous and strong as was once David, that most robust and military man, Ps. 18:34, 2 Sam. 17:8, ch. 18:3. Moreover, he who shall be of the royal lineage of David, inasmuch as he ought to be the Leader of others, shall be as an Angel, and indeed, such as went before them in the desert, and led them, that is, the most mighty Angel of God Exod. 32, 34. Thus he.

Latin:

Vers. 8. IN DIE ILLA PROTEGET DOMINUS HABITATORES JERUSALEM.) Post reditum in ur- bem.

ET ERIT, QUI OFFENDERIT EX EIS.) Qui imitatione aliorum lapsus fuerit contra legem.

QUASI DAVID.) Tam gravi pœnitentia tange- tur, quam David ob peccata in Uriam.

ET DOMUS DAVID QUASI DEI.) Domus posterum Davidis ita plena erit pietatis, quasi Templum esset.

SICUT ANGELUS DOMINI IN CONSPECTU EORUM.) Quasi Angelum aliquem Dei semper apud se conspicabilem haberent.

De restitutione urbis & oppidorum per Macca- bæos facta hæc agere, unde docebitur? Et quomodo ad eam tum aspirarunt Judæi vel tabernacula Judæ felicitate, quam habuere olim in principio? Quid? quod de Maccabæorum victoriis, & Hierosolymæ conservatione adversus Antiochum populosque vi- cinos superiora jam exposuerit Grotius vers. 2. 3. ac subsequutura tempora v. 4. designata velit. Qui ergo jam regreditur ad priora tempora? Unde non ummerito hic notavit Grotium (qui vero hic sedu- ctus à Lamb. Danæo, eodem modo hæc explicante) Coccejus: Grotius hic denuo suas anomalias sequitur: qui cap. 9, 9. Regem Zyonis primo scilicet & obvio sensus Zorobabelem intellexerat, quasi Zacharias sene jam Zorobabele, & quidem post victorias Judæorum prophetatas, proxime de Zorobabelis tanquam Regis adventu prophetare posset: is hoc loco, ubi rursus ora- culum de Christo Salvatore est, quum ipse vers. 5. & 6. animadvertat actum de victoriis Judæorum, tamen redit ad liberationem populi per Maccabæos ex ma- nu Antiochi. Apparet, istum virum data opera Pro- phetias plerasq́, de Christo & vera salute dissimulasse.

Illa IN PRINCIPIO alii accipiunt sensu com- parativo, alii absoluto. Prior explicatio commu- nior est. Et salvabit Dominus tabernacula Judæ, SICUT IN PRINCIPIO, hoc est, conservabit Ecclesias in orbe terrarum sparsas, quemadmodum ut fidelis Deus nunquam Ecclesiæ suæ curam abje- cit, ut Osiander, vel prout olim tabernacula Israeli- tarum in deserto conservavit, ut Vinarienses habent. Particulam similitudinis esse subaudiendam, agno- scit Calvinus, eamque refert ad habitationem Ju- dæorum in tabernaculis, cum redempti ex Ægypto terram ingressi essent, & ut plurimum in pagis de- gerent. Absolute autem accipit Willius, intelligens principium Novi Testamenti, ubi primum Christus servavit tentoria Judæ, quando in Galilæa & vicinis locis cepit lucem suam accendere populo sedenti in tenebris Matth. 4, 16. & cum abjectissimis qui- busvis dignitates contulit, utpote cum publicanis & peccatoribus socium se addidit, eosdemque in numerum filiorum Dei recepit, domui vero Davi- dis angelicum decus adjecit, quando ipse ceu pro- missus ille & magnus fœderis Angelus mundo se stitit, abjectamque ac fere depressam familiam Da- vidis splendore suo illustravit. Hæc enim ita red- didit: Est domus Davidis ut Dii, (אלהים notare an- gelos vult ut Ps. 8, 6.) ut Angelus Domini coram il- lis, per quem intelligit Filium Dei, qui Patres præ- cessit Esa. 14, 19. c. 23, 22.23. Cui ex parte præiverat Calvinus: Non dubium est, quin hic Propheta com- paret Davidis posteros Angelo, qui dux fuerat populo & minister redemtionis (Filius Dei non MINISTER erat redemtionis ex Ægypto, sed cum Patre & Sp. S. causa princeps. Reprobanda illa vox indigna Fi- lio Dei) Angelum illum, quia etsi plures Angelos Deus tunc populo suo destinavit, fuit tamen Christus. Propheta igitur hic sperare Judæos jubet de perpetuo Dei auxilio, quoniam in domo Regia non modo erunt Angeli, sed ille etiam Dux Patrum, qui exercuerat in- credibilem Dei potentiam in redimendo populo. Hæc Calvinus. Ast, quomodo domus Davidis com- parari potest Christo, ut sit, quemadmodum Filius Dei, Angelus fœderis? Non enim dicitur in domo Davidis futurus Angelus, sed, quemadmodum is, qui ægrotabit (vel infirmus) dicitur fore quasi Da- vid, ita domus Davidis sicut Angelus Jehovah coram facie illorum, ut reddidit ipse Calvinus. Non ergo hic apparet, quomodo Filius Dei intelligi possit. Coccejus per domum Davidis intelligit Christum è domo Davidis, sed hoc ineptius adhuc est per do- mum Davidis intelligere Christum, atque contorta est glossa & ratio, quam hic tradidit Coccejus, quam legat, qui volet.

Sed, ut ad VVillium revertamur, si hæc comple- mentum habuere sub adventum Christi, quomodo eadem referuntur ad Ecclesiam Philadelphensem & Laodicensem, h. e. tempora novissima, uti ipse inter- pretatur. Nam Philadelphensis Ecclesiæ statum v. 7. describi vult, quod in ea Deus Ecclesia ex hora tentationis servaturus, & signatis ex omnibus tri- bubus nomen suum insculpturus sit Apoc. 3, 10. 12. c. 7, 3. Laodicensis vero v. 8. quod ea piis decus cœ- leste acceleratura sit, in qua sedebunt cum Christo in throno ejus Apoc. 3, 20. Quæ impleta sunt tem- pore adventus Christi primi, cum publicanos & peccatores suscepit, ea non demum implenda e- rant tempore Ecclesiæ Philadelphensis, cum signan- di sunt nonnulli, iisque inscribendum est nomen Christi. Si Decus domui Davidicæ datum est an- gelicum, cum se stitit mundo Messias, juxta hanc prædictionem, quomodo ea demum implebitur in novissimo Christi adventu, cum sedebunt electi in throno Christi? Ecquis non videt hos tam dispara- tos sensus iisdem verbis haud subesse posse?

Joh. Coccejus reddidit: Et salvabit Jehovah ten- toria Judæ INITIO, atque doceri censuit, initium prædicationis Evangelii fieri debuisse extra Hiero- solymam, ut Baptista ad Jordanem in deserto præ- dicavit Esa. 40, 3. & Christus in Galilæa Es. 8, 23. cap. 10, 1. Et salvavit Jehovah tentoria Judæ. Post- quam ultimam illam afflictionem Antiochi sustinue- rint & pervicerint, & quum jam in tota terra impe- ritabunt nemine impediente, imo etiam in civitatibus Palæstinorum, & Idumæorum & Arabum & extra terram plurimas civitates quasi colonis impleverint eo tempore, quo Hierosolymæ cultus Dei & exercitium Legis ceremonialis vigebit, ibi partem populi salvabit Dominus per illuminationem ad cognitionem salutaris Dei. Unde reliqua verba v. 7. causam continere hujus ordinis putat Coccejus, eamque geminam (1) ne majestas terrena, quam domus Davidica olim habuerat supra Judam, & tunc post captivitatem jacuerat, ulla ratione super Judam extollatur iterum, h. e. ut filius Dei semen Davidis secundum car- nem, non in majestate terrena & mundana, qualem David habuit, veniret, sed עני inops, ut est Zachar. 9, 9. Vermis & non vir, opprobrium hominum & spre- tus populi Psal. 22, 7. (2) ne decus habitantium Hie- rosolymam, h. e. quorum ordinaria & propter statum Reipublicæ necessaria Hierosolymis, & apud Tem- plum habitatio erat, potestas magnificetur super Ju- dam. Quia omnino Christus non debeat venire μετὰ παρατήρησεως & in ἀξιώματι σαρκικῷ, neque mi- nistri ejus debebant habere tale regimen, quale sedentes Hierosolymæ habebant super Judam. Sed hæc arguta magis, quam solida videntur. Neque calculum merentur illa, quæ è parallelis locis ad- fert de eadem qualitate temporis adventus Christi è Zach. 8, 5 6. 23. Jer. 3, 16. 17. c. 13, 14. 15. Esa. 9, 2. Deuter. 30, 5. 6. Etenim non de dilatatione agunt regni Ju- daici, quam hic (licet temere) respici vult, sed de Ecclesiæ Dei propagatione, nec ad antecedentia ad- ventus Christi spectant, sed ad consequentia. Nec vero firma est probatio, quod habitantes Hieroso- ymam hic secundum literam accipi debeant, quia certæ parti Juda opponuntur, tum quia iis attribui- tur decus super Judam, tum quia per utrumque indigitamentum intelliguntur indigentes salvatio- ne sive illuminatione Dominica. Nam salva ἀντι- διαστολῇ tentoriorum Judæ & habitatorum Hiero- solymæ, recte se habent nostrorum interpretatio- nes: Ut non magnifice glorietur domus seu familia re- gia Davidis contra cives urbis Jerusalem propter fa- miliæ nobilitatem & gloria habitantium urbem Jerusa- lem non sese superbe efferat contra totam regionem Ju- dam, propter ea quod ipsa sit metropolis regni, sed omnes inter se in vera animi humilitate & charitate concorditer vivant. In die illa proteget Dominus ha- bitatores Jerusalem, ne quid piis accidat, quod ipso- rum salutem evertat. Et erit qui offenderit, Ebr. qui infirmus fuerit ex eis, in die illa, is erit quasi David heros iste fortissimus: & domus David erit quasi do- mus seu familia Dei: erit ista familia in magno hono- re, sicut Angelus Domini in conspectu eorum, id est etiam infirmi (sed veri tamen Christiani) tam for- tes reddentur divinitus per Spiritum Sanctum, ut Diabolum vincant, sicut David vicit Goliathern Philistinum. Per domum autem Davidis intelli- git spirituales Duces, hoc est, Apostolos, & alios spiri- tu Apostolico præditos: hos dicit in tanta autori- tate futuros, ac siessent homines plane divini, & An- geli Dei. Sic Paulus de Galatis scribit: Sicut AN- GELUM DEI excepiftis ME, sicut CHRISTUM JESUM: ô quam beati tum eratis. Testimonium en- nim perhibebo vobis, quod si fieri potuisset, ocu- os vestros eruiffetis, & dedissetis mihi, Gal. 4. Ita Osiander, cui consonaut Vinarienses, ut & B. Baldui- nus: q. d. devictis Ecclesiæ hostibus, non erit, cur quispiam se super alterum extollat, si sint de domo David seu stirpe regia, sive inhabitent Jerosoly- mam, seu sint de genere Sacerdotali, sive etiam sint incolæ Judæ, seu plebejæ conditionis homines: o- mnes enim unius ejusdemque salutis atque benefi- cii divini erunt participes. Etiam imbecilles in po- pulo meo (hos enim offendentes nominat) virtute Spiritus Sancti armati, & per ministerium Ecclesia- sticum informati vincent spirituales animarum ho- stes Satanam, mortem, infernum. Sic etiam Hie- ronymus: Tam beati erunt, qui pro Ecclesia milita- runt, & in persecutione Dominum sunt confessi: ut qui minimus fuerit, & quasi homo in aliquo peccato di- ctoq; offenderit, ponatur in ordine magistrorum: Et magistri, qui suum servaverint gradum, sint quasi domus Dei, & quasi Angelus Domini, quia hoc omni studio laboramus positi in terra, & vario labore su- dantes, ut transformemur in angelicam gloriam. Cyrillus extra controversiam esse dicit Hierosolymam boc loco intelligi Ecclesiam Christi.

Aliena autem sunt, quæ Grotius de lapsu, exemplo aliorum contra legem, quæ de tam gravi pœnitentia, qualis fuit Davidis ob peccatum in Uriam, quæ de domo posterum Davidis post reditum in urbem (è Babylone) ita plena pietatis, quasi templum esset & quasi semper Angelum conspicabilem apud se haberet. Posteriora de Angelo in textu, non causam rei quæ traditur, referunt, sed comparationem exhibent cum Angelo Dei: Priora autem, nec ipse Danæus, à quo præcedentia & sequentia nomina glosse- mata, quantum apparet, accepit Grotius, de pœni- tentiæ similitudine intelligit, sed de robore divinitus concedendo: Admirabile, inquit, eisdem pollicetur, idque per gradationem illustrissimam. Debilis tunc, qui erit in ea urbe erit tamen tam strenuus, & for- tis, quam fuit olim David vir ille robustissimus, ac militaris Pf. 18, 34. 2. Sam. 17, 8. c. 18, 3. Cæterum, qui erit è regia Davidis stirpe, utpote qui aliorum Dux esse debebat, erit velut Angelus, & quidem, qua- lis eos præcessit in deserto, eosque deduxit, id est, An- gelus Dei fortissimus Exod. 32, 34. Hæc ille.

## 12:9
Vers. 9.

I WILL SEEK TO DESTROY ALL THE NATIONS THAT COME AGAINST JERUSALEM.) That had come: that were in the army of Gorgias and Lysias.

It savors of nothing beyond Maccabean and carnal victories. Our scholars more correctly understand this as referring to the exterminating of the enemies of the Church of the New Testament. Cocceius and Willius also, as well as Rud. Gualtherus f. 317. But if you ask when these things were fulfilled, you will find nothing similar to this among the descendants of David who existed from that time, regarding the external splendor of the kingdom. Indeed, for three hundred and thirty-six years from this prophecy they did indeed reign among the Jews: But the difficulty of those times was so great that they could never emerge to their ancient glory and power. And finally, Jannaeus the second Hyrcanus, who was the last to reign from that family, was killed by Antiochus Epiphanes in the defense of a certain citadel: from which time the root of Jesse (as Isaiah had predicted) began to become a dead trunk, so that no one could hope for anything illustrious from it anymore. We are therefore compelled to refer these things to the times of Christ Jesus, who, having been made man from the virgin Mary, ennobled the house of David with heavenly and immortal glory. Thence he chose from the Jews the weak and clearly despised Apostles, whom he instructed with more than human powers, and through them he overcame whatever the world and its prince were plotting. Indeed Peter, who could seem weaker than the rest when he was shamefully denying his Lord, a little later preached Him with singular constancy and fortitude and brought very many to the obedience of faith. Similarly, Paul and Barnabas because of their singular power of speech and the wonderful the Lord once did, this same thing He has been accustomed to do perpetually. For He always protects all those who are citizens of that heavenly Jerusalem, nor do they allow themselves to be drawn away from His society. He daily instructs the same with new strengths, so that they can do all things in Him: and from time to time through those who seem to be of no value, He casts down the pride of the world, sophistry, superstitions, and idolatry. And it shall be in that day that I will seek to destroy, that is, I will be in this with great zeal, that I may destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. Therefore He remembers the enemies again, lest we, promising ourselves that all things are safe, become careless: but He promises His own zeal, by which He has determined not only to protect the Church, but to destroy its enemies. For we ought not to think that Satan is more vigilant in attacking the Church than Christ is in defending it, who delivered Himself to death for it. And it has emphasis, that He says He seeks the destruction of His enemies. He opposes this to the counsels and efforts of the impious enemies, as if He were saying: they indeed move every stone to destroy you. But I will be no less in this, that I may destroy them with worthy punishments. I will therefore bring forth all My strengths to this end, nor will I omit any of those things which can make for their destruction. Thus Gualther. Calvin himself approaches, who says, there is no doubt that this promise extends further than to the Jews; for he prophesies here concerning the kingdom of Christ: because if we consider the state of the people, in all that intermediate time which was from the return of the people until the coming of Christ, certainly this Prophet will seem to have made more of the hope than the thing itself bore, but he looked especially to Christ. Here therefore is promised the eternal defense of the Church. Which is to be opposed to Lamb. Danaeus, who restricts this to the times of the Maccabees.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

QUÆRAM CONTERERE OMNES GENTES, QUÆ VENIUNT CONTRA JERUSALEM.) Quæ ve- nerant: quæ erant in Gorgiæ Lysiæque exercitu.

Nil ultra Maccabaica & carnales victorias sapit. Rectius de exterminandis Ecclesiæ N. T. hostibus nostri intelligunt. Etiam Coccejus & Willius, nec non Rud. Gualtherus f. 317. Quod si autem quæ- ras, quando hæc impleta sint, nihil hujus simile re- peries inter Davidis posteros, qui ab eo tempore fuerunt, quoad externum regni splendorem. Quin per annos ab hoc vaticinio trecentos triginta sex regnarunt quidem illi inter Judæos: Sed tanta fuit temporum illorum difficultas, ut ad veterem glo- riam & potentiam nunquam potuerint emergere. Et tandem Janna secundus Hircanus, qui postre- mus ex illa familia regnavit, in defensione arcis cujusdam ab Antiocho Epiphane occisus est: à quo tempore radix Isai (sicut Esaias prædixerat) trun- cus emortuus fieri cœpit, ut nemo aliquid ex illa præclari amplius sperare possit. Cogimur ergo ad Christi Jesu tempora hæc referre, qui ex Maria virgi- ne homo factus Davidis domum gloria cœlesti & immortali nobilitavit. Inde ex Judæis infirmos & contemptos plane Apostolos delegit, quos viri- bus plus quam humanis instruxit, & per illos devi- cit, quæcunque adversus regnum ipsius mundus & princeps ejus moliebantur. Imo Petrus, qui reli- quis infirmior videri poterat, quando Dominum fuum turpiter abnegabat, paulo post singulari con- stantia & fortitudine illum prædicavit & quam plu- rimos ad fidei obedientiam adduxit. Similiter Pau- lum & Barnabam propter dicendi vim singularem & miraculorum virtutem Deorum loco habitos fuisse legimus Actor. 14. At quod olim fecit Domi- nus, hoc ipsum perpetuo facere consuevit. Prote- git enim semper omnes eos, qui cœlestis illius Hie- rosolymæ cives sunt, nec ab ejus societate sese ab- strahi patiuntur. Eosdem viribus quotidie novis instruit, ut in ipso possint omnia : & subinde per eos, qui nullius pretii esse videntur, mundi fastum, Sophisticen, superstitiones & idololatriam dejicit. Et erit in die illa quæram ad delendum, id est, magno studio in hoc ero, ut deleam omnes gentes, quæ ve- niunt contra Jerusalem. Rursum ergo hostium me- minit, ne nobis omnia tuta pollicentes fecuri red- damur: at suum studium promittit, quo non modo Ecclesiam tueri, sed illius hostes perdere statuerit. Nec enim putare debemus Satanam in oppugnan- da Ecclesia vigilantiorem esse, quam in illa defen- denda sit Christus, qui semetipsum in mortem pro illa tradidit. Et emphasin habet, quod se hostium suorum perditionem quærere dicit. Opponit hoc impiorum hostium consiliis atque conatibus, quasi diceret: movent quidem illi lapidem omnem, ut vos perdant. At ego non minus in hoc ero, ut illos dignis suppliciis perdam. Proferam ergo in hunc finem vires meas omnes, nec aliquid eorum intermittam, quæ ad perditionem illorum possunt facere. Hæc Gualtherus. Accedit Calvinus ipse, qui non dubium est, inquit, quin promissio hæc longius pateat quam ad Judæos; vaticinatur enim hic de regno Christi: quia si consideremus statum populi, toto illo intermedio tem- pore, quod à reditu populi usque ad Christi adventum fuit, certe videbitur hic Propheta longe fecisse spei, quam rei ferebat, sed respexit præcipue in Christum. Hic ergo promittitur æterna Ecclesiæ defensio. Quæ Lamb. Danæo opponenda, hæc ad tempora Mac- cabæorum restringenti.

## 12:10
Vers. 10.

AND I WILL POUR OUT UPON THE HOUSE OF DAVID] For many still remained from David, a part of whom you have named in Matthew and Luke.

AND UPON THE INHABITANTS OF JERUSALEM THE SPIRIT OF GRACE AND OF PRAYERS] I will give them a mind by which they may implore My grace with submissive prayers. A clean heart, a contrite and humbled heart Ps. 51, 11. 19.

The illustrious prophecy concerning the Holy Spirit's outpouring to be in the New Testament is very badly perverted, as if it were to be restricted to those few from the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the time of the Maccabees, when it treats of the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem understood in a spiritual sense, and looks to the times of the New Testament, to which also the following oracle related by St. John belongs. For it is established thus far that the preceding things treated of the spiritual house of David and Jerusalem. Therefore these do not look absolutely to the corporal house of David and the earthly Jerusalem: but the citizens of the Church are called by this name, partly because of the nature of the type, and partly because the firstfruits of the gifts of the Spirit were owed to the Jews, and were also paid to them, Acts 20, 2. Then, since it had been treated of the invincible and Evangelical strength of the faithful, both of those who were weaker and those endowed with stronger faith, who were understood by the house of David, such as were the Apostles and others adorned with excellent gifts of the Spirit, now the cause of such great strength is alleged, the most bountiful outpouring of the Holy Spirit, bestowing and sealing grace, and rendering the faithful certain and secure and invincible concerning the same; and the Spirit of prayers, because He teaches to pray, which are the weapons of Christians, by which they conquer their enemies and glory in the afflictions of the world; whence the paraphrase of Osiander rightly has: And in the meantime I will pour out (bountifully) upon the house of David (upon the Apostles and the remaining faithful ministers of the Church) and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem (upon the other Christians also) the Holy Spirit, who is the spirit of grace and of prayers. Thirdly, not a common, but a singular outpouring of the Holy Spirit in the Church is promised here, not only upon the Ministers of the Church, but also upon other believers. Not only upon the nobles of the people, but also upon men of lower condition in the spiritual Jerusalem, if indeed the Prophetic Scripture has been accustomed to use the word of pouring out concerning this mission of the Holy Spirit to be in the New Testament. See Is. 44, 3. Joel 2, 28. 29. the power of which Christ explains in John 7, 38. and St. Paul in Tit. 3, 6. Therefore a most bountiful and copious communication of spiritual gifts is signified, in which it does not trickle in a small amount, but diffuses itself like a river or an overflowing torrent, which is unusual and new, far greater than that which was exhibited in the old Church. Jerome observes that the word of outpouring implies a sense of bounty, who therefore interprets this prophecy likewise concerning the large donation of the Holy Spirit made in the New Testament. Fourthly, He who promises that He will pour out the Holy Spirit is the crucified Messiah. AND THEY SHALL LOOK UPON ME WHOM THEY HAVE PIERCED, which words cannot be understood otherwise than of the Messiah, by whose passion and crucifixion the outpouring of the Holy Spirit was also acquired, John 14, 16. ch. 16, 1. Eph. 4, 8. Therefore these things are not to be explained concerning the outpouring of the Spirit made before the incarnation of the Son of God. Fifthly, it is a discourse concerning that outpouring which had to happen around the time of the reprobation of the Jews and the assumption of the Gentiles, if indeed in the preceding parts it had been treated of that rejection of the Jews and the breaking of the covenant entered into with the Israelites, and the establishing of the same with all peoples. Sixthly, that outpouring of the Spirit is indicated which happened around the time of the opening of the fountain of the most holy Baptism, as the continuity with the following chapter teaches, when the Baptism of water and of the Spirit had to succeed one another in this way. Which happened in the time of the economy of grace, when the outpouring of the Holy Spirit followed immediately upon the institution of the Sacrament of Baptism, and by the very outpouring of the Spirit On the solemn day, three thousand souls are read to have received the Sacrament of Baptism, Acts 2. And since the baptism of the Spirit is joined with the baptism of the river, both regarding the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, Acts 10, and regarding the ordinary, Tit. 3, 5. Whence almost all interpreters refer these to the outpouring of the Holy Spirit made in the New Testament, from whose consensus to depart without grave reasons would be rash, nay, a crime, since it is confirmed by so many reasons.

The gloss of Calvin, who by the Spirit of grace understands not the Holy Spirit, but the bowels of God for pouring out mercy or grace itself, joined with the sense of faith, does not deserve to be heard. His own disciples acknowledge that the outpouring of the Spirit is promised here: we cite only Willet, who is opposed even in this merit to Calvin, because the latter prefers the Spirit of lamentations to be indicated, rather than of prayers. Pagninus, he says, and others (render it) of grace and mercies, that is, רחמים, just as the LXX and Targum also rendered it. But the Hebrew word is everywhere taken for prayers, and indeed of such a kind as are instituted for mercy and grace, which the notation of the word argues. We call these supplications Psalm XXVIII, verse 2. Hear the voice of my supplications. Where David himself explains what he calls תחנונים and what kind of prayers he understands in the following verse: Draw me not away with the wicked & to those working iniquity, namely the deprecations of evils. Compare Jerem. 31, 9. & Prov. 18, 23. The poor man utters deprecations, that is, prayers, supplications for grace & mercy. And thus the Spirit is called, because He is the author of grace & prayers. And His gifts are the senses of grace & deprecations.

Verse of the same.

AND THEY SHALL LOOK UPON ME WHOM THEY HAVE PIERCED] He reads אלי as we have it; other books have אליו. But it is the same. For the first person, especially with a relative following, is very often expressed by the third in these books, Whom they have pierced, אשר דקרו, εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν, as certain Greek Interpreters have had it, & John the Evangelist applying these things mystically to Christ XIX, 37. But the LXX, with letters changed that are very similar, read רקדו, ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ἐξωρχήσαντο. Our sense is the best: for they are said to pierce God who provoke Him with insults. For thus also נקב, which properly is to perforate, is put for βλασφημεῖν, Levit. 24, 11. The Rabbis commonly refer these things to David the son of Joseph, who they say will fall in battle against Gog. But Hadarsan in Gen. 28 understands it of the Messiah the Son of David.

AND THEY SHALL MOURN FOR HIM WITH A MOURNING AS FOR AN ONLY-BEGOTTEN] In the Hebrew: They shall mourn for him, namely because of the insults which they have brought upon God. Mourning for an only-begotten, is proverbial. Jerem. 6, 26. Amos 8, 10. where see the things said.

IN THE DEATH OF THE FIRSTBORN] Another proverbial way of speaking. For they are accustomed, where there are many children, for the firstborn to be loved more ardently, Jer. 31, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET EFFUNDAM SUPER DOMUM DAVID] Multi enim ex Davide adhuc restabant, quorum partem nominatam habes in Matthæo & Luca.

ET SUPER HABITATORES JERUSALEM SPI- RITUM GRATIÆ ET PRECUM] Animum illis da- bo, quo gratiam meam submissis precibus implorent. Cor mundum, cor contritum & humiliatum Pf. 51, 11. 19.

Illustre vaticinium de Sp. S. effusione in N. T. fu- tura pessime pervertitur, ac si ad paucos illos à domo Davidis & habitatores Jerusalem Maccabæorum tempore restringendum sit, cum de domo Davidis & habitatoribus Jerusalem sensu spirituali intellectis a- gat, & tempora N. Test. respiciat, ad quæ etiam se- quens oraculum à S. Johanne relatum est. Nam primum de domo Davidis & Hierusalem spirituali superiora egisse hactenus constat. Non ergo hæc ad domum Davidis corporalem & Hierusalem terre- strem ἀποτόμως spectant: sed vocantur hoc nomi- ne cives Ecclesiæ, partim ob typi rationem, partim ideo, quia primitiæ donorum Spiritus Judæis debe- bantur, atque etiam illis solutæ sint, Act. 20, 2. Dein- de quum de robore invicto & Evangelico fidelium cum infirmiorum, tum firmiore præditorum fide, qui per domum Davidis intelligebantur, cujusmodi fuere Apostoli & alii eximiis donis Spir. S. exor- nati, actum fuerit, nunc causa allegatur tanti robo- ris, effusio largissima Spir. S. gratiæ, largiens & obsi- gnans gratiam, atque de eadem certos atque secu- ros & invictos reddens fideles; &Spiritus precum, quia orare docet, quæ arma Christianorum sunt, quibus hostes suos vincunt, & gloriantur in mun- di afflictionibus; unde recte habet paraphrasis O- siandri: Et interea effundam (largiter) super domum David (super Apostolos & reliquos fideles Eccle- siæ ministros) & super habitatores Jerusalem (super cæteros etiam Christianos) Spiritum Sanctum, qui est spiritus gratiæ & precum. Tertio non vulgaris, sed singularis in Ecclesia effusio Spiritus S. non su- per Ministros tantum Ecclesiæ, sed etiam super a- lios credentes hic promittitur. Non tantum super proceres populi, sed etiam super inferioris conditionis homines in spirituali Hierosolyma, siquidem de hac missione Spiritus S. in N. T. futura, verbo ef- fundendi assueverit uti Scriptura Prophetica. Vid. Es. 44, 3. Joel. 2, 28. 29. cujus vim explicat Christus Joh. 7, 38. & S. Paulus Tit. 3, 6. Significatur ergo largissima & copiosissima donorum spiritualium communicatio, in qua non modica destillet, sed in- star fluminis sive torrentis exundantis se diffundat, quæ inusitata sit & nova, longe major illa, quæ in veteri Ecclesia fuit exhibita. Verbum effusionis sensum largitatis inferre observat Hieronymus, qui proinde de larga S. S. donatione in N. T. facta iti- dem hoc vaticinium interpretatur. Quarto is, qui Sp. S. effusurum se promittit, est Messias crucifixus. ET ADSPICIENT AD ME QUEM CONFI- XERUNT, quæ verba aliter intelligi nequeunt, quam de Messia, cujus passione & crucifixione ac- quisita etiam Sp. S. effusio Joh. 14, 16. c. 16, 1. Eph. 4, 8. Non ergo de effusione Spiritus ante ἐνσάρ- xωσιν Filii Dei facta hæc explicanda. Quinto, de illa effusione sermo est, quæ circa reprobationem Ju- dæorum & assamtionem gentium fieri debuit, siqui- dem in superioribus de illa Judæorum rejectione & rumpendo fœdere cum Israëlitis inito, eodem- que cum omnibus populis fanciendo actum fuerit. Sexto ea indigitatur Spiritus effusio, quæ circa tem- pus aperti fontis Baptismiatis Sacrosancti facta est, uti συνέχεια cum capite sequenti docet, quum ita Ba- ptismus fluminis & flaminis sese mutuo excipere debuerint. Quod factum tempore ὀικονομίας gra- tiæ, cum institutionem Sacramenti Baptismi sequu- ta sit proxime effusio Spiritus S. & ipso effusionis Sp. S. die solemni tria millia animarum Sacramen- tum Baptisn̄atos suscepisse legantur Act. 2. & cum fluminis βαπτισμῷ conjunctus sit βαπτισμὸς fla- minis, tum quoad extraordinaria dona Spir. S. Act. 10. tum quoad ordinaria Tit. 3, 5. Unde Interpp. plerique omnes hæc ad effusionem Spir. S. in No- vo Testamento factam referunt, à quorum con- sensu citra graves rationes discedere temerarium, imo nefas esset, quum is tot rationibus firmatus sit.

Glossa Calvini, qui per Spiritum gratiæ non Spir. S. intelligit, sed viscera Dei ad misericordiam effundendam vel gratiam ipsam, conjunctam cum sen- su fidei, non meretur audiri. Agnoscunt ipsimet ejus discipuli, Spiritus effusionem hic promitti: So- lum Willium adducimus, qui opponitur etiam me- rito in eo Calvino, quod hic malit Spiritum lamen- tationum indigitari, quam precum. Pagninus, inquit, & alii (reddunt) gratiæ & miserationum, id est, רחמים, quomodo etiam LXX. & Targum reddide- runt. Sed vox Hebræa ubique pro precibus sumi- tur, & quidem ejusmodi, quæ pro misericordia & gratia instituuntur, id quod vocis notatio arguit. Has deprecationes vocamus Psalm. XXVIII. vers. 2. Audi vocem deprecationum mearum. Ubi quid תחנונים vocet, & quales preces intelligat, ipse David explicat versu seq. Ne trahas me cum impiis & operantibus iniquitatem, nempe deprecationes malorum. Confer Jerem. 31, 9. & Prov. 18,23. De- precationes eloquitur pauper, id est, preces, supplica- tiones pro gratia & misericordia. Ita autem vo- catur Spiritus, quia gratiæ & precationum auctor est. Et dona ejus sensus gratiæ & deprecationes.

Vers. eod.

ET ADSPLICIENT AD ME QUEM CONFIXE- RUNT] Legit אלי ut nos habemus; alii libri habent אליו. Sed perinde est. Nam prima persona, sequente maxime relativo, sæpissime per tertiam in his libris exprimitur, Quem confixerunt, אשר דקרו, εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν, ut ha- buere Græci Interpretes quidam, & Johannes Evangelista ad Christum μυστικῶς hæc applicans XIX, 37. at LXX, com- mutatis literis perquam similibus, legerunt רקדו, ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ἐξωρχήσαντο. Noster sensus optimus est: nam configere Deum dicuntur, qui eum probris lacessunt. Nam sic & נקב, quod proprie est perforare, ponitur pro βλασφημεῖν, Levit. 24, 11. Referunt hæc vulgo Rabbini ad Davidem filium Josephi, quem occubiturum ajunt in prælio contra Gog. At Hadarsan in Gen. 28. de Messia Filio David intelligit.

ET PLANGENT EUM CUM PLANCTU QUA- SI SUPER UNIGENITUM] In Hebræo: Plangent de eo, nempe ob contumelias, quas Deo intulere. Planctus super unigenitum, proverbiale. Jerem. 6, 26. Amos 8, 10. ubi dicta vide.

IN MORTE PRIMOGENITI] Aliud loquendi genus proverbiale. Solent enim, ubi plures sunt liberi, primogeniti ardentius diligi, Jer. 31, 9.

## 12:11
Verse 11.

AS THE MOURNING OF HADADRIMMON IN THE PLAIN OF MEGIDDO] In the Hebrew it is: Haddarrimmon. Megiddo is known to be the plain in which King Josiah was killed with many of his men 2. Kings 23. concerning which we learn that the mourning was most grievous 2. Chron. 35, 24. of which history we have noted that Herodotus also makes mention in Book III of the Truth of the Christian Religion. Jerome teaches us, as he does about many of those places, that there was a city in that plain called Hadarrimmon, later called Maximianopolis, so that the same slaughter is indicated by a double name, just as that of Darius at Arbela from the Arbellitis region, & at Gaugamela, from a nearby town or village. The Chaldean, however, thought Hadarrimmon to be the name of the King of Syria who killed Ahab, of whom the history is 1. Kings 22, 31. 2. Chron. 18, 30. not improbably. For Rimmon was an idol of the Syrians, as appears 2. Kings 5, 18. Moreover, the Kings of Syria were accustomed to take names from Idols, as from Bel, Nabo, Merodach, Sach. And the name רמן joined, or placed separately, is frequent among the Syrians, which is accustomed to be confused in books with the other name רמן: nor is it a wonder, since not only are the letters related, but also the sense: for רון, from which by the custom of the Syrians the letter is repeated ררן, signifies glory, & רמן to the Syrians is to praise. The Chaldean therefore thought the mourning of Hadarrimmon to be called that which was issued because of the slaughter received from Hadarrimmon, in the way it is said 'Slow by the wound of Ulysses'. To me, the opinion of Jerome, to whom that place at Megiddo was better known than to the Chaldean, is more pleasing. The LXX read הדר ראון, they thought ῥοῶν & מגרן to be not a proper name, but a common one from גרד, which sometimes is to cut; for they translate, ἐν πεδίῳ ἐκκοπτομένε.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

SICUT PLANCTUS ADADREMMON IN CAMPO MAGEDDON] In Hebræo est: Haddarrim- mon. Mageddon constat esse campum, in quo occisus cum multis suorum rex Josias 2. Reg. 23. de quo gravissimum fuisse planctum discimus 2. Par. 35, 24. cujus historiæ & Herodotum meminisse annotavimus ad Librum III. pro veritate Religionis Christianæ. In eo campo fuisse urbem, dictam Hadarrimmon, postea dictam Maximianopolim, docet nos, ut multa illorum locorum, Hieronymus, ita ut eadem clades gemino indicetur nomine, sicut illa Darii ad Arbella ab Arbellitide regione, & ad Gaugamela, ex oppi- do aut vico propinquo. Chaldæus autem existimavit Ha- darrimmon esse nomen regis Syri, qui Achabum cecidit, de quo Historia est 1. Reg. 22, 31. 2. Par. 18, 30. non improbabiliter. Nam Rimmon erat idolum Syrorum, ut apparet 2. Reg. 5, 18. Solebant autem Reges Syri nomina ab Idolis sumere, ut à Bel, Nabo, Merodach, Sach. Et no- men רמן adjunctum, aut seorsim positum, frequens Syris, quod cum altero nomine רמן in libris confundi solet: ne- que mirum, cum non literæ tantum sint affines, sed & sen- sus: nam רון, unde Syrorum more repetita litera est ררן, gloriam significat, & רמן Syris est laudare. Existimavit ita que Chaldæus planctum Hadarrimmon dici eum, qui editus fuit ob cladem acceptam ab Hadarrimmon, quomodo dicitur Vulnere tardus Ulyffe. Mihi Hieronymi, cui locus ille ad Ma- geddonem notior fuit, quam Chaldæo, sententia magis placet. LXX. legerunt הדר ראון, ῥοῶν & מגרן puta- runt esse nomen non proprium, sed commune à גרד, quod interdum est incidere; vertunt enim, ἐν πεδίῳ ἐκκοπτομένε.

## 12:12
Verse 12.

AND THE LAND SHALL MOURN] The whole land shall be full of mourning. For there were few who had not been carried away by flatteries, or fear, or bad examples.

FAMILIES AND FAMILIES APART] Namely by the command of the Sanhedrin, with penalties indicted, to this family more severe, to that lighter, according as they had sinned more or less grievously: which analogy was best preserved by the example of the Jews by the Synod of Nicaea.

FAMILIES OF THE HOUSE OF DAVID APART] Not only had private individuals sinned, but also those who were of the royal house.

AND THEIR WIVES APART] For in a time of mourning or repentance, men used to sleep apart from women, and women from men. Joel 2:16, which, like all upright things that were among the Jews, Paul proposes for imitation in 1 Cor. 7:5.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET PLANGET TERRA] Tota terra plena erit planctu. Pauci enim erant, qui non blandimentis, aut metu, aut malis exemplis abrepti essent.

FAMILIÆ ET FAMILIÆ SEORSUM] Nempe ex præcepto Synedrii, indictis pœnis huic familiæ gravio- ribus, illi levioribus, prout gravius aut levius peccassent: quæ ἀναλογία exemplo Judæorum optime servata à Syno- do Nicæna.

FAMILIÆ DOMUS DAVID SEORSUM] Non privati tantum peccaverant, sed & illi, qui ex domo erant regia.

ET MULIERES EORUM SEORSUM] Nam in luctus aut pœnitentiæ tempore secubabant viri à mulieri- bus, mulieres à viris. Joel. 2, 16. quod, ut omnia proba, quæ apud Judæos erant, imitandum proponit Paulus 1. Cor. 7, 5.

## 12:13
Verse 13.

THE FAMILIES OF THE HOUSE OF NATHAN APART, AND THE WIVES APART] Doubtless the posterity of Zerubbabel, a man so pious, also sinned, and thus made itself unworthy of the kingdom, which it did not receive except in the Lord Jesus in a more sublime manner.

THE FAMILIES OF THE HOUSE OF LEVI APART, AND THEIR WIVES APART] Many priests also had sinned. The opposition in 1 Macc. 4:42 teaches this; see also 2 Macc. 4:13. And note, when Mattathias undertook to defend the cause of sacred things with arms (as those times then allowed), none of his colleagues stood with him.

THE FAMILIES OF SHIMEI APART, AND THEIR WIVES APART] Jerome testifies in this place that there were very many teachers from this family; and perhaps from them was Shemaiah, mentioned in later times by Josephus and by Jerome on Isaiah 8, but also often by the Talmudists and Rabbis.

FAMILIES AND FAMILIES APART AND THEIR WIVES APART] After he named the more illustrious families, he designates the rest by group, so that it may be understood that the number of those who had sinned was huge. Some had sacrificed to Greek gods; others had been drawn away; others had offered swine in the Temple; others had handed over the books of the law to those who were about to burn them.

One must look here partly at the genuine reading of verse 10, and partly at the true and genuine interpretation of it and the following verses. First, he thinks some read it differently than the authentic codex now has it. But if it is all the same as to the sense, whether the pronoun of the first person אלי is read, or of the third אליו, since the first person is very often expressed by the third when a relative follows, as Grotius observes, we have no cause to call the reading of our codices into doubt, even though no codex has yet been produced that has the latter reading, but the copies constantly retain the former, against which he opposes himself here entirely in vain, feigning a corruption of the Hebrew text in this word against the consensus not only of all codices, but also against the Greek, Vulgate, and other interpretations. Furthermore, as to the word דקרו, that the LXX interpreters read it differently in their codex is a less firm document because they rendered it differently. For the supreme consensus of the Hebrew codices stands in the way again, as well as that of the codices of certain Greek interpreters, whom Grotius praises, and especially the authority of St. John, concerning whom Jerome says in this place: John the Evangelist, who drew wisdom from the breast of the Lord, a Hebrew of Hebrews, whom the Savior loved very much, did not greatly care what the Greek letters contained, but interpreted word for word as he had read in the Hebrew, and said it was fulfilled at the time of the Lord's passion. But if anyone does not accept this, let him provide testimony from which place of the Holy Scriptures John brought these things forth, and when he has not found it, he will be forced against his will to accept the truth. Concerning the LXX interpreters, however, Cocceius says on page 556: That seems to be a hallucination of the interpreters who, when they did not know what a piercing was doing there, were able to think that there was a mistake in the writing, and by conjecture substituted רקדו. This is much more probable than that these letters רקדו were found in any codex. Let these things suffice here concerning the reading against Grotius.

One must labor more on the interpretation. According to the letter, Grotius explains these things as concerning God pierced with reproaches, perhaps following Calvin, who says that piercing is taken here metaphorically for continuous mockery, as if he were saying that the Jews by their stubbornness were as if girded for war, so that they might prick and pierce God with their malice, or with the darts of their rebellion, with which Lambert Daneau agrees here. But that these things are to be understood of the Son of God, not metaphorically pierced by the dart of calumnies or rebellion, but properly pierced in the assumed human nature in the great passion, the letter itself confirms first. For one must not descend from the proper sense to the metaphorical unless necessity itself compels it. Since, therefore, these words taken properly imply a piercing and a transfixing, why should we abandon that meaning and pursue a metaphorical one? Willius is correct here on page 456. דקר (daqar) to pierce, transfix, or run through with a sword, lance, or other deadly instrument. It is used of Phinehas running through the Israelite man with the Midianite harlot, Num. 25:8, and of the armor-bearer running through Abimelech, Jud. 9:54. In other places likewise, it is taken properly to mean violent piercing. Most correctly, therefore, it is explained here also as a piercing properly so called, and primarily it must be referred. What he says PRIMARILY, seems to admit another sense still, although a secondary one, which cannot be proven, since a double sense cannot be established for the same saying, one primary, another secondary.

Then, these words are not of God the Father, but of the Son of God, who in the preceding chapter is valued and sold for the price of XXX shekels v. 12, 15, and c. 9, 11, and is said to deliver with his blood the prisoners from the pit in which there is no water. Coccejus indeed thinks that God the Father is speaking here, yet he does not deny that the crucifixion of Christ is designated, but he interprets the words, and they shall look upon me with (him) whom they have pierced, in such a way that Christ is joined to God, as in Ps. 2, 2; John 17, 3. But in this way one departs from the common meaning of the particle את, which is the sign of the Accusative case, and a pronoun of the third person is thrust into the text, which is not contained in it, and from one person two are made. Thirdly, that the Son of God is he whom they are about to pierce, and for whom they will mourn, is hinted at by the mention of the only-begotten and the firstborn. For he is the only-begotten by reason of his divine nature, and the firstborn by reason of his human nature. And thus the particle כ can be accepted, as the כ of truth, as they call it, just as ὡς is accepted in John 1, 14. We saw his glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, i.e., which is truly the glory of the only-begotten. Whence Coccejus: the mourning is exaggerated by the estimation of the person. Who is the only-begotten Son of God John 1, 14 (for by reason of his humanity he would not be the only-begotten) and the firstborn of many brothers Rom. 8, 29, i.e., who is before all the sons of God, and without whom no one becomes a son of God (who in opposition to him, who is μονογενὴς and πρωτότοκος, are κτίσις and θετοὶ) and therefore in whom all the sons of God are sanctified. If the sense of similitude is retained, the comparison of mourning over the death of an only-begotten and firstborn is nevertheless more fitting to mourning over the death of the Son of God than over the reproaches and insults brought upon God the Father.

Fourthly, it is a question here of the aspect of him who was to be pierced. They shall see him whom they have pierced. He, therefore, who was to be pierced, was also to be looked upon with bodily eyes. But this does not befit God the Father, but the Son of God manifested in the flesh, whom the disciples saw with the eyes of the body in the days of his flesh Luke 10, 1; John 1; many pious people also saw him, and all, both believers and unbelievers, are one day to see him at his visible return. If the word ADSPICIENT is to be accepted here in an abstract sense, so that it can be understood of any looking, whether it happens by the eyes of the mind or of the body, the looking and intuition which happens by the eyes of the body is certainly not to be excluded. Because something peculiar is indicated here concerning this Lord and his being pierced or fixed, and his being looked upon in his transfixion.

Fifthly, this aspect is attributed to those who pierced the Lord, indefinitely to all, and thus to both believers and unbelievers, who will not be in the same condition. Some look upon him with true repentance and trust in him who was pierced, others without faith, without true repentance; Grotius takes it concerning the penitential intuition. Let it be that it is a question of the same thing here. But what is the object that the penitent and the faithful ought to look upon, so that they may obtain the remission of sins, if not the Messiah, suspended on the wood of the cross and pierced for us, whom looking upon through faith we are saved, just as those looking upon the bronze serpent suspended on the wood were saved John 3, 15. Nor, however, do only the penitent look upon the pierced one. Those who do not perform true repentance also look upon him, indeed all who pierced him look upon him. Whence sixthly we conclude thus: It is a question here of looking upon him who will be looked upon by all by whom he was pierced. But this is not God the Father, but the Messiah, who will be looked upon by all men on the last day, pierced by all, because we have wounded him with our sins, and we have all pierced him Isa. 53, 6; Rom. 4, 24, and he ought to be looked upon by all through faith, as having been pierced for all. Seventhly, therefore, the Spirit of grace and of supplications is given, so that we may be able to look upon him whom we have pierced, unto salvation; and by his passion and crucifixion the Messiah had merited for us this gift of the Spirit, so that, graciously illuminated by him, we might look with the eyes of faith upon this our Savior pierced and crucified for us.

Eighthly, the cause of the mourning is designated not only as the crucifixion of the Lord, but also his very death, and indeed the death of the only-begotten and firstborn. For, even if a proverbial expression were admitted, as in Jer. 6, 26; Amos 8, 10, such proverbial comparisons and expressions are usually employed which most aptly fit the subject matter, and in those places the killing of firstborns and only-begotten ones is not excluded, but is even primarily included among the causes of mourning, which in such public calamities is sufficient for a most grievous cause of mourning. And therefore, since the piercing of the Lord is the cause of mourning here, and that mourning is called as it were the mourning over the death of an only-begotten and firstborn, the Holy Spirit indicates not obscurely by this phrase that the cause of the mourning would be the death of the only-begotten and firstborn son, and that that piercing would be joined with the death of the pierced and transfixed one, just as the transfixion of Josiah was joined with his death 2. Chron. 35, 24, whose lamentation therefore most aptly fits this mourning over the piercing and death of the Lord, of whom a comparison of histories teaches that Josiah was also a notable type in several respects.

Ninthly, this lamentation can be taken either as the lamentation of conversion and penitence, or as the lamentation of confusion and ignominy. The former is truly that of the penitent and the faithful, which Grotius understands here and at Matthew 26:30. But the one proposed here, as a universal mourning of all the tribes, requires that one also assign a universal cause for such a universal lamentation, one suitable to all the faithful; yet this is not that injury against God. For certainly not all had provoked God with reproaches, not all had irritated Him and pierced Him with the darts of rebellion. But all, of whatever rank, condition, or tribe, who are truly faithful, have cause to lament on account of the piercing and death of Christ, inasmuch as He was pierced for our sins and delivered to death because of our sins. Who, therefore, of the faithful would not mourn, would not lament with true contrition of heart, that by his own sins he had pierced the very Son of God, and had driven the same to the cross and to death? But not only the lamentation of the converted is indicated: in general, the lamentation of those who pierced Him is noted, although we do not deny that the converted, truly faithful ones are primarily regarded. For that lamentation is also explained concerning those who have not performed penance, who do not grieve for their sins with salutary contrition, but gnash their teeth in sad desperation on account of the punishments for their sins. Lambertus Danaeus establishes the cause of this lamentation as the death of both Mattathias and Judas Maccabeus, 1 Maccabees 2:70, chapter 9:23, Josephus, Book XII, Antiquities, last chapter, and he refers the relative pronoun HIM in this sentence, 'and they shall mourn over him,' neither to God nor to Christ, but antonomastically to him and those through whom God at that time wrought the miraculous liberation of the people, namely to the first Maccabees. But how can the relative pronoun be referred to THEM, of whom no mention has been made in the text? How can this mourning concerning death be referred to the mourning concerning different deaths, both that of Mattathias and that of Judas, who died at such different times, when the discourse here is about a single subject, and the cause of the lamentation is assigned as the piercing, which Danaeus understands metaphorically as the irritation of God.

When Grotius saw this, he did not follow Danaeus in it, but the Hebrew words: 'they shall mourn for HIM,' he referred to that deed, namely the piercing, they shall mourn for the insults brought upon God. Indeed, that affixed pronoun of the third person can either be referred to the person, to HIM whom they had pierced, or to the act of piercing itself: both senses are convenient, and come to the same thing. Nor does it stand in the way of the former that a pronoun of the first person was used: 'THEY SHALL LOOK UPON ME'; for it is added: 'WHOM they have pierced,' i.e., they shall look upon me as upon HIM whom they have pierced, and over this one, whom they have pierced, they shall mourn. To this contributes the observation of Grotius himself, that the first person, when a relative follows, is very often expressed by the third in these books. Coccejus distinguishes the mourning in the prophetic text, and assigns one cause after another for it. He makes those who look upon God and Christ the first mourners, the faithful, because to look is the act of faith of one converting from vain hope to the true fortress of salvation, Zech. 9:12, and resting in it. Cf. Ps. 34:6, John 6:11, Isa. 45:22, provided that Christ's passion is exhibited here in the piercing. Cf. ch. 9:11, ch. 11:12, 13. He rightly acknowledges that the fulfillment of this mourning constitutes Acts 2:36, 37, yet that it is not of one article, just as the gift of the Spirit is not. The external effect, he says, is to mourn over the one pierced by them. Which mourning is exaggerated by the estimation of the Person. The mourning denotes the desperation of the sin that pierces Christ; we are all guilty of the pierced Christ, because for our sins he was pierced, Isa. 53. Furthermore, in the following verses 11, 12, 13, he thinks another mourning and other causes of mourning are introduced, namely because of the devastation of Jerusalem. It is a judgment, he says, upon those not mourning over the pierced one, that they should mourn for another cause; see the place of mourning in Jerusalem, the magnitude and estimation by comparison of the mourning which was the killing of Josiah in the war around Hadadrimmon. Individuals will have a private cause for mourning, just as they had had private desire. The house of David will mourn, having had the hope of the kingdom snatched from it: when they see the Republic perish. The house of Nathan the Prophet and his degenerate successors will weep for the destruction of their greatness, and will be angry at the Scriptures because the truth does not correspond to their own predictions. Thus the Priests because of the destruction of the Priesthood, the Shimeites, the family of the Levites, referring to that Shimei the Benjamite who cursed David, will mourn because of the abolition of their ministry. Thus the other families that will remain. (For many will be consumed, many will be snatched from that necessity through faith.) Each will lament for its own advantage through the destruction of the Republic. But the women will deplore their sons and the fruit of their womb. Compare Hos. 8:11, 12, 13, 14. These are the words of Coccejus. But here only a single cause of mourning is alleged: namely that most grievous guilt by which the Messiah himself was pierced: but no mention is made of mourning because of punishment and the judgment of God in the total destruction, and those things cohere, nor can they be torn apart, which are held in v. 10 and 11 and the following, nay, they serve to illustrate the same mourning, for the sake of which not only is mention made of mourning in the death of the only-begotten and first-born, but the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the death of Josiah is also compared. Meanwhile, we do not deny that an application can be made to those infidels who, having experienced the judgment of God, mourned in the Jerusalemite destruction, and, convicted in their conscience of the guilt of the pierced and killed Just One, had all the greater cause for mourning because they had brought such evil upon themselves by their own guilt and the provocation of divine vengeance, Matt. 27:25, which most grievous mourning Christ announced to them, Luke 23:28; but if one asks about the proper object of the mourning, about the proper cause for which that mourning is to be, which is hinted at by the Prophet in this place, they will mourn for themselves

HIM, it does not appear that the Jerusalemite destruction is indicated here, which is only dealt with in chapter 14, but rather the piercing of the Messiah, which all the faithful mourn, even if we do not understand Jerusalem and the families which are listed here precisely as the earthly city or the Israelite tribes, but the heavenly Jerusalem and believers of all orders, who are described by the words of the Old Testament received in the customary manner of Scripture: for otherwise no distinction of tribes has a place among the Israelites in the extreme confusion by which they were oppressed in the last time. And it is about that Jerusalem and the Davidic House that it is treated, to which is promised the outpouring of the Spirit of grace and supplications, as well as a fountain opened against sins and impurity. Which are promised not only to the Jerusalemites and the Davidic family, but to all in the Church in the time of the New Testament. For we understand and prove that these things are fulfilled daily among us (Christians) after the coming of Christ, says Jerome. The same Jerome explains the orders which are signified here thus: In David, the royal tribe is accepted, that is, Judah: In Nathan, the prophetic order is described: Levi is referred to the Priests, from whom the priesthood arose: In Shimei, the teachers are accepted: for from this tribe the hosts of masters have sprung. He was silent about the remaining tribes, which do not have any privilege of dignity. But in that he says, 'All the remaining tribes, tribe by tribe separately, and their wives separately,' he comprehends all without name. The similarity of the mourning for Josiah also favors our opinion: For the mourning there is not because of a public disaster, but because of the King killed, with whom is compared the mourning for the Messiah the King crucified and killed, of whom he was a type. And therefore the lamentation is not proclaimed on account of the destruction of Jerusalem, although in that destruction their conscience could suggest the cause to them, namely the piercing of their King, the Messiah. Which will also happen in the πανωλεθρίᾳ of the universe, where the unfaithful will mourn because they pierced the Messiah with sins, and especially with impenitence and final incredulity, because this will be the cause of their eternal destruction.

Regarding that comparison, Grotius, being doubtful, would render others doubtful, unless they knew that the express passage of the authentic text in 2 Kings 23:30 and 2 Chronicles 35:24 is to be preferred to the doubtful conjectures of the Chaldean regarding the name of the Syrian King Hadadrimmon, which has nothing to do with the present matter. Regarding the lamentation indeed, proclaimed by the order of the Sanhedrin with penalties decreed—heavier for this family, lighter for that one—on account of heavier and lighter sins, in the time of Antiochus and the Maccabees, Grotius puts forward mere dreams and deserves no credence. He indulges in a preconceived opinion. Which we also observe in Lambert Daneau at this place.

There is added, tenthly, a continuity with the following chapter, in which it is treated not only of the fountain opened against impurity in Holy Baptism, the destruction of idolatry, and of false prophets, but also of the striking of the only true Shepherd, the God-man, and the flight and conversion of his disciples. All of which pertain to the times of the New Testament. How, therefore, are these to be dragged to the Maccabean times?

Eleventhly, we have here the Rabbis themselves agreeing, who explain the prophecy concerning the Messiah, not in a mystical sense, but in a literal one, as is openly clear from R. Hadarsan in Genesis 28: He (the Messiah) will be the one giving grace and devotion to Israel, as it is said in Zechariah 12:10: 'And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the Spirit of grace, etc.' And in Massechet Sukkah, in the section Hachalil Camischa: 'And the land shall mourn, every family apart' (Zech. 12:12).

Why will this lamentation take place? The Rabbi said, R. Rosa and the Rabbanim, or Masters, are in disagreement about this; one said it is on account of the Messiah, or over the Messiah the son of Joseph, who will be killed, and one said it is over the evil impulse, or sensuality, or concupiscence, which will be killed; peace be to him who said it is over the Messiah the Son of Joseph, who will be killed; for this is what is already written (Zech. 12:10): And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced. Which passage R. Solomon Iarchi praises from the book Succa at this place.

Twelfth, the Holy Spirit himself interprets this passage concerning the Messiah, not in a mystical sense, but a literal one, and that in two places, first concerning the piercing of Christ done on the cross. For he testifies that it was fulfilled by what the Prophet predicted in this place, John 19:34 ff. They did not break his legs, but one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. And he who saw it has borne witness, and his testimony is true. And he knows that he says true things, so that you also may believe: for these things were done so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, you shall not break a bone of him. And again another Scripture says, they shall see whom they pierced. Grotius notes. to the N. T. at this place, he thinks the words ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν were brought in from some of the Greek versions, because that reading is found in many books, from Symmachus, Aquila, or Theodotion: but Jerome observed above that John did not care what the Greek letters contained, but that it was interpreted word for word, as they read in the Hebrew; he teaches, however, how the Greek word of the LXX Interpreters also agrees. The word κατωρχήσαντο among the Greeks is composed not from illusion, but from dancing: namely, that they danced against the Lord as if mocking, when they said, mocking and laughing: Vah, you who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself by coming down from the cross. These and other things they said while mocking and dancing in a certain frenzy of madness. That gloss, which Grotius has from Calvin, does not hold up at all: that what was said figuratively by God about himself being despised, happened to Jesus κατὰ πόδας. For if these things were said about God outside the economy of the incarnation in the time of the O. T. and were already fulfilled long ago, how can they contain a prophecy about God manifested in the flesh, to be fulfilled only at the time of his passion? If the words were said figuratively and are to be understood metaphorically, how are the same words to be taken in a proper and native sense? Is there both a proper and a figurative sense of the same saying at the same time in the same place? If they mean nothing else than that the Israelites sacrificed to Greek gods, or offered swine in the temple, or handed over the books of the law to be burned, and for other insults then brought upon God, how could St. John say that that Scripture was fulfilled when the Messiah was pierced on the cross? Whence Francis Junius, with Tremellius in his annotations at this place and in Parallel. LXXXV, book 1, as well as John Cocceius at this place, did not only depart from his Calvin here, but also refuted the same Balth. Willius: The most learned man judges less correctly that the words of the Prophet are not cited by the Evangelist with respect to repentance, but that his purpose is to show briefly that Christ is that God who had spoken from the beginning through the Prophets. For although the Evangelist does not treat of the repentance of the Jews, he nevertheless shows the object of true repentance. An argument for the divinity of Christ, however, can be sought from this, that that piercing, which the true God here attributes to himself, is said of Christ, and God and Christ are established as the subject of one and the same piercing. Moreover, this piercing is deservedly attributed to the Jews, although done by the spear of a Roman soldier, because they ordered and approved it. You have, however, in this way described, as I said, the object of repentance and the goal of faith, and at the same time the cause of conversion, which will be the consciousness of the sin committed in the crucifixion of Christ, and grief over that same evil. This is Willius.

But that lamentation had its fulfillment at the time of the passion of Christ in his disciples, and the pious women, and other believers, then especially after the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, just as in Acts 2 and following, several thousand Jews were converted, and without doubt with true repentance they deplored the sin of having pierced the Messiah: and at all times true believers grieve most of all that by their sins they were the cause of the only-begotten Son of God being pierced and delivered to death. But those who do not acknowledge this, nor grieve with true repentance of mind, are going to perish eternally, by the example of the Jews, who although they had affixed Christ to the cross with their own hands, and had killed the author of life, and had been constantly invited to repentance by his disciples, persisted in unbelief and impenitence, rather than acknowledge the most grievous sin and look upon the pierced and crucified Messiah, and for that reason were totally cut off and reprobated. Whence St. Cyril also applies this prophecy to them: Where he laid down his soul for us, and preached to the spirits in the underworld and revived, the monument being shaken by an earthquake, those who sat by in wonder said, (Truly this was the son of God) and many were seized with no small repentance. But after the Romans also pressed them with war, the region having been devastated, and cities burned, and houses emptied, and now Jerusalem itself besieged, and famine consuming the townspeople, hardly any acknowledged their wicked deeds against Christ, and finally they realized why they were suffering dire things, and that they were suffering those things because of what they had impiously committed against him. For with most profuse tears they always follow the death of a firstborn and beloved, nor do they sustain finding a way of lamenting and mourning, and the grief is clearly long-lasting, and as if perennial, macerating their minds by pricking them sharply and intolerably. But Christ predicted that the Jews would experience calamities of this kind, thus chastising the women weeping over him (Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and your children).

Concerning, therefore, the bodily vision of Christ the judge at his most recent coming and the lamentation of the infidels joined with eternal despair, the same St. John alleged the oracle Apoc. 1.7: Behold he comes with the clouds, and they shall see him, who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth shall wail because of him: as it is again manifest, that it is not brought forward only μυσικῶς, but that it is taught that he is that Christ, whom Zechariah designated according to the letter, and that the same shall be seen by the very eyes of the body by all, when indeed he shall arrive in the clouds, and even by those who pierced him. Wherefore this vision can not only be restricted in our oracle to the intuition of faith: but, as we have said, it also embraces bodily vision. Finally, that lamentation is attributed to the infidels, to all the tribes of the earth, who pierced him with their sins, and drove him to the cross, and did not look upon him with faith, but persevered in incredulity: and therefore that Zechariah cannot be understood only concerning penitential lamentation, but that the lamentation generally comprehends both that of the faithful, which is of true repentance and sorrow according to God, and that of the infidels, which brings eternal horror, the bite of conscience, and the worm that does not die. Both therefore lament, those when they grieve over sin and are converted, these when they pay the penalty of sin and perish eternally. Which sense Osiander rightly expressed: And they shall look upon me, whom they have pierced: they shall behold (says Christ) me, formerly the impious, on the last day, with the greatest horror, and they shall see, in how great majesty I am, whom they crucified; and whose side they pierced with a lance, so that blood and water flowed out.

But the Jews also, repenting, will understand that they crucified the Lord of glory. The disciples of Christ were most vehemently disturbed on account of his death. But the converted Jews also, without doubt, lamented with many tears that they had crucified the Leader of their salvation. (Now the only-begotten Son of God, and the firstborn of every creature, died on the cross, but that was done in the assumed humanity.) He explains the rest concerning the different tribes from the cross of the faithful of all orders, that it behooves all true Christians to suffer with Christ: Truly, because the cause of the mourning is rendered by the Prophet not as our cross, but as the piercing of Christ done for the sake of our guilt, it is better to acquiesce in the same, to which, however, the mourning can be reduced in our cross thus far, that the cause of the same is the same as that of the crucifixion of Christ, namely, our sins. In what manner the blessed Balduinus says of this lamentation, The pious, he says, lament the death of Christ, partly because, recognizing his innocence, they deplore the blindness of men who did not fear to cast bloody hands upon that Holy of Holies: partly because they consider the atrocity of the fall, which merited such great torments of body and soul for the Lamb of God bearing the sins of the world, and partly also because they know that they bear the στίγματα of Christ in their own body, and so, if not by an equal, yet by a similar persecution of enemies, are subject to the cross and afflictions: all of which meditations proceed from the Holy Spirit, who in this manner commands us to consider the passion of the Lord.
