(6.) Convenit oraculum capitis sequentis vers. 8. In die illa exibunt aquæ vivæ de Jerusalem, & medi- um earum fluet ad mare Orientale & medium earum ad mare novissimum, Zach. 14, 8. Quæ aqua recte hic confertur, etsi de Verbo Dei vel Sp. S. explice- tur à plerisque. Nam Sp. S. diffundit in Ecclesia dona sua non sine Sacramento Baptismatos, quod est fons gratiarum & donorum ejus; & lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis Sp. S. qui in eodem a- bunde effunditur Tit. 3, 5. nec non lavacrum aquæ in verbo Eph. 5, 26. Non ergo Baptismus excludi potest à fluxu aquarum vivarum ibi promisso, quem aquam vivam etiam appellat Theodoretes quæst. 26. in Genes. Baptismus dicitur aqua viva, non quod aqua Baptismatis naturam habeat diver- sam, sed quoniam per aquam illam divina gratia vitam donat æternam.

(7) Convenit analogia, quæ in novissimis Prophetis V. T. deprehenditur. Hi enim N. T. propiores ea γνωρίσματα adventus Christi desi- gnant, è quibus Christus prope esse, vel jam adesse agnosci debebat, qualis est illa insignis commotio cœ- li & terræ, & maris & aridæ Haggæi, & Prodromus Messiæ Johannes apud Malachiam, cujus rei gratia Zacharias etiam fontem hunc apertum sistere de- buit circa adventum Messiæ palam manifestan- dum, quem Protobaptista primum aperturus erat.

His addimus, quod (8) aliæ interpretatio- nes, si easdem contendamus cum hac nostra, meri- to ei cedant. (1) De fonte templi, quo abluebantur immundi & menstruatæ, tempore Maccabæorum restituto nonnulli explicant. Similiter Danæus de Sacrificiis tum restauratis interpretatur: Sed hoc frigidum & Judaicum. Nec in eo sibi constat Danæus, imo fatetur, vere hoc vaticinium tunc im- pletum fuisse, cum Johannes Baptista baptizavit in fluminibus omnes pœnitentes, qui ad se accedebant, & Baptismum Ecclesiæ (qui est omnium peccato- rum nostrorum ablutionis à Deo per Christi sangui- nem factæ testimonium) primus ex Dei jussis, & ex hac prophetia in Ecclesia usurpavit, adeoque conti- neri prophetiam ac promissionem instituendi ejus Baptismi, quem nos hodie in Ecclesia habemus, & qui à Johanne Baptista cœlitus fuisse à Deo præceptus dicitur, Mattb. 21, 25. Denique à Christo ipso pro- batus, sancitusque in sua ipsius persona Matth. 3. (2) de fonte misericordiæ divinæ interpretatur Hay- mo & Hugo. Sed fons misericordiæ divinæ semper apertus est fidelibus, hic vero aliquid peculiare, ac tempori N. T. proprium est promissum. (3) Re- migius per fontem doctrinam intelligit, uti Prov. 20. os justi vena vitæ dicitur, cui consonat Win- ckelsm. Fons ille patens est doctrina Evangelii, de gratia Dei & remissione peccatorum, per quam Spiritus Sanct. annunciat remissionem peccato- rum, ablutionem à peccato per fidem in sanguine Christi, & perterrefactas conscientias consolatur & vivificat; quo etiam abit Chaldaica versio, in tempo- re illo erit doctrina legis revelata, & scaturigo aqua- rum domui David. At doctrinæ scaturigine non de- stituta fuit domus Davidis, aut Hierosolyma Za- chariæ tempore; Et annon erat tum doctrina, quæ scaturiit ex ore Zachariæ, instar aperti fontis, si hic fons doctrinæ indigitetur? (4) Theodoretes, Gre- gor. M. Homil. IX. in Zach. Montanus, Castrius, Cornelius fontem hunc dicunt esse Deum incarna- tum, veram scaturiginem perenniter in homines quovis seculo aquam omnis gratiæ & doctrinæ scatu- rientem, qui fons & origo etiam est Spiritus S. quem in nos effundit, ut peccata expurget, & ani- mæ sitim restinguat. (5) Alii de Spiritu S. inter- pretantur, qui aqua viva à Christo vocatur Joh. 7, 34. (6) Nonnulli de latere Christi in cruce ada- perto, unde fluxit aqua & sanguis. (7) Coccejus fontem dicit notare ipsum sanguinem fœderis Zach. 9, 11. qui effusus per confossionem. Quo etiam bit explicatio Junii, ut & Piscator. Imo & Calvini b. l. Quæ sententia cæteris convenientior. Nam etsi Sp. S. fonti & aquæ vitæ comparetur, hic tamen character, quod ad ablutionem peccati & menstrua- tionis hic fons aperiatur, sanguini Christi proprius est. Cæterum, uti Christus θεάνθρωπος est causa efficiëns ablutionis nostræ, ita lateris Christi aper- tio, & sanguis Christi ad emundationem nostri fa- cjunt in genere causæ meritoriæ, hic vero communi- cationis & applicationis medium potius designatur, & fons aperitur domui David, & habitantibus Je- rusalem, ut eodem actu abluantur è sordibus pec- cati & menstruationis, quod fit quidem sanguine

Christi, sed qua in Baptismo dispensatur, utpote qui est lavacrum nostræ regenerationis Tit. 3, 5. in quo abluimur à peccatis, ut Act. 22, 15. Paulo dicebatur: Exurge, & baptizare, & ablue peccata tua invocato nomine Jesu.

Ideo ut (9) autoritates adducamus, Hieronymus, Cyrillus, Rupertus, Hugo, Lyranus, Raim. Martini, Dionysius Carthuf. Galatin. Isidorus Clarius, aliique fontem hunc esse Baptismum statuunt. Sic è nostris B. Balduinus: Promittitur tale lavacrum, quo & originale malum & actualia peccata eluuntur. B. Gerhard. LL. CC. de Baptism. §. 10. Apertus ille ac omnibus patens fons est, Baptismus peccata actualia & immunditiem originalem abluens Eph. 5, 26. Adde B. Wigandum, B. Pappum, B. Tarnovium, Dn. D. Müllerum in Judaitm. p. 785. Dn. D. Klotz. Disp. de Baptism. quibus plerique alii consentiunt. B. Lutherus, etsi contra Sacramentarios, non de Baptismo, sed de Sp. S. locum præsentem explicet, recte tamen de Baptismo eundem intelligi docet in Comment. Germanico T. IV. Jen. ad h. l. qui Commentarius adornatus fuit Anno 1528. Octennio vero post Megalander in explicatione Joel. anno 1536. tradita extra omnem dubitationem posuit hoc loco vaticinatum esse Prophetam de Baptismo, & cum præsenti oraculo contendit locum Ef. 12, 3. ut & Joel. 3, 18. & per omnes rivos Judæ ibunt aquæ, & fons de domo Domini egredietur, & irrigabit torrentem spinarum. Vid. Tom. IIX. Wittenb. Germ. f. 406. T. 6. Altenburg. p. 491. & T. IV. Lat. Jen. f. 481. Neque inficiantur recentiores Papistæ Baptismum hic prædictum. „Tirinus: Illa die, qua Christus (ut c. 12. præcessit) „è cruce suspensus aspicietur, patescet ex illo & illius vulneribus FONS uberrimus, non solum doctrinæ, ut vult Remigius, sed & Sacramentorum „& gratiarum omne genus, idque in ABLUTIONEM PECCATORIS cujuscunque, ET etiam „MENSTRUATÆ, id est, ad tollendam omnem „immunditiam, & sordes ex transgressione, seu „legis naturæ, seu legis Mosaicæ contractas. Alludit primo ad aquas expiationis, Num. 19, 11. deinde ad aquas Siloe Isaiæ 8, 6. & Joan. 9, 7. deniq; „ad aquas sub limine templi erumpentes, Ezech. „47, 1. Quæ omnes erant typi & figuræ vivi fontis „nostri Christi, ut etiam Hebræi à Galatino citati „agnoscunt. Patet autem perpetuo hic fons non „solum DOMINI, id est familiæ & posteris Davidis, id est, primatibus & nobilioribus personis, „sed promiscue omnibus HABITANTIBUS „JERUSALEM, etiam plebejis, etiam è gentilisino conversis. Nec ullius ponderis est ratio Castrii & Cornelii, quod fons hic dicatur aperiendus in ablutionem omnium peccatorum; peccata autem abluenda sint, non tantum ante, sed & post Baptismum commissa, quia Baptismi efficacia extendit se in futurum, fiquidem dona Dei sint ἀμεταμέλητα.

E Reformatis idem agnoscit Danæus, qui typice quidem de ablutionibus Leviticis per Maccabæos redintegrandis interpretatus, vere autem in Baptismo hoc vaticinium impletum esse professus est. Quanquam vero admittamus, per typicas ejusmodi ablutiones Baptismum etiam figuratum esse, literalem tamen sensum hujus vaticinii Maccabæorum tempora respicere, ac de Levitica ablutione agere negamus, neque vel hic, vel uspiam alias geminum ejusdem vaticinii sensum dari concedimus.

Denique agnovit & Grotius hic de Baptismo vaticinatum esse Prophetam Annot. Joh. 1, 25. ad Joh. 1, 25.

Singularis iterum hoc loco est Willius, atque, ut suam Smyrnensem periodum martyriis valentem ex hoc vaticinio exsculpat, comminiscitur, fontem „ intelligendum esse pro sanguinis vena & scate- „ bra, eumq; apertum iri respectuEcclesiæ quidem, „ martyres sacrificiorum instar se Deo offerant, & „ per effusionem sanguinis à gentilibus separent; „ respectu tyrannorum vero, ut pios piaculerum „ instar è genere humano tollant, & sacrificiorum „ loco pro peccatis offerant idolis suis, eosque tan- „ quam immundos & vitiis obsitos à se ejiciant. Ec- quis vero hunc sensum de vena sanguinis, & de causa illa fluxus, alia respectu Ecclesiæ, alia re- spectu tyrannorum, in iisdem verbis diversi- mode in eodem loco accipiendis in hoc oraculo vidisset præter hunc Bremensem Delium? Vox מקור absolute posita nuspiam venam sanguinis no- tat; Nam Lev. 20, 18. non occurrit absolute, sed indigitatur FONS MULIERIS, additurque insuper ἐξήγησις, fons sanguinis ejus. Nec ape- riendus dicitur fons, ut sacrificia offerantur, sed ut impuri à peccatis abluantur, tum si pii idolis pro peccatis gentilium ab ipsis offerendi dicuntur, quomodo iisdem verbis indigitatur pios semetipsos oblaturos uni vero Deo instar sacrificiorum benevo- lentium? Et ubi Martyrii causa separatio à gentili- bus vel activa vel passiva hoc loco constituitur? Deniq; annon ita impie Deo tribuitur, quod aper- turus sit fontem sanguinis, ut martyres sacrificiorum loco idolis gentilium offerantur?

## 13:2
Vers. 2. I WILL DESTROY THE NAMES OF THE IDOLS FROM THE EARTH.) Nothing is truer. For after that time there was no idolatry among the Jews. The Prophet sets this forth explicitly in many following words.

AND THE FALSE PROPHETS.) Such as many had been before. No one dared to arrogate the name of prophet to himself from this time until Christ. See 1 Macc. 4:46, 9:28, 14:41. Josephus: 'And from Artaxerxes until our own time, everything has been written, but it has not been deemed worthy of the same credit as those before them, because the exact succession of the prophets did not exist.'

AND I WILL REMOVE THE UNCLEAN SPIRIT FROM THE EARTH.) Thus are demons called in Matt. 10:1, 12:43, Mark 1:23, 26, 27, 3:11, 30, 5:2, 8, 13, 6:7, 7:25, 9:25, Luke 4:33, 36, 6:18, 8:29, 9:42, 11:24, Acts 5:16, 8:7. From these the false prophets often received what they uttered in the name of God. See 2 Sam. 22:20.

These things are wrongly snatched away to the times of the Maccabees. Nor is it true that from that time no idolatry, no false prophet, no demons and oracles flourished among the Jews. Idolatry is certainly most grave, because the Jews, not acknowledging that one true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, worship a God who is μονυπόςατος, of one person only, a Father who has no Son, nor a Spirit who is ὁμοόσιον, but is imagined to be without a coeternal Son, without a coeternal Holy Spirit, which is truly an idol, devised outside of and against the word of God. Concerning which idolatry we convict the Jews, against Calixtus, the patrons of the Jews, Father and Son, along with Grotius, in the Appendix to the Calixtine Syncretism. Whoever denies that various false prophets existed before, around, and after the advent of Christ, openly contradicts historical truth, and opposes the Evangelical and Apostolic History itself. But the unclean spirit and the demons at that time, when the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the Devil, exerted their power to the utmost, until they were restrained by His voice and Spirit, Acts 10. Nor did the oracles of the Gentiles cease, except towards the advent of the Messiah. What? That the Jews themselves constitute the extermination of idolatry as the character of the advent of the Messiah, as witnessed by R. Lusitanus in Colloq. Mittelb. f. 115. We confess that among the chief effects of the Messiah will be the calling of the Gentiles and the all-encompassing extermination of idolatry. Therefore, it was not already exterminated in the time of the Maccabees. Suidas reports in his life of Augustus that the Pythian oracle of Apollo still consulted him as to who would succeed him, to which it replied: 'A Hebrew boy, the king of the blessed gods, commands me to leave this house and return to the underworld again. Therefore, depart in silence from our altars.' A Hebrew boy, that King of the gods, commands me to leave this house and return to the Tartarean homes. Therefore, holding your mouth, leave our altars. Concerning a similar response, Porphyry reports in his book on the philosophy of oracles, in which Apollo ordered the tripods to lament, because he must depart on account of the heavenly light that had arisen. 'Woe is me, tripods, you shall lament, Apollo is gone, he is gone, you force me to flee, O heavenly light.' Sabellicus, Book I, Ennead 7, is the author that during the seven years that Christ spent in Egypt with Mary and Joseph, the oracles became mute and the idols fell of their own accord. In the time of Trajan, however, the remaining oracles ceased. Nor could Julian obtain a response from Apollo concerning his exit, because his temple was struck by lightning and consumed by heavenly fire. Whence Porphyry confessed in his book against Christ, 'Since Jesus is worshipped, we no longer obtain any benefit from the gods.' And Plutarch wrote a special work on the failure of oracles. To this point belong the things which Grotius has in Book IV of the Truth of the Christian Religion, ch. X. The spirits themselves, when questioned about the cause of their silence, were forced to say that they could do nothing when Christ was invoked. Tertullian, Apologeticus. See also Lucian. Whence Cyril in this place: 'After the only-begotten Word of God finally appeared to us, the foolish and childish trifles of idolatry vanished completely, and were extinguished, and with them was also removed the wicked and impious pursuit of the false prophets, who were full of a malignant and unclean spirit, and, infected with a genuine and similar error as the worshippers of idols, could most truly be convicted. For one was the leader of impiety for both, namely Satan.' Thus also Remigius, Haymo, Albert the Great, Hugo, and Dionysius.

Latin:

Vers. 2. DISPERDAM NOMINA IDOLORUM DE TERRA.) Nihil verius. Nam post id tempus nulla fuit inter Judæos idololatria. Hoc ipsum diserte multis se- quentibus verbis Propheta exsequitur.

ET PSEUDOPROPHETAS.) Quales multi an- tehac fuerant. Nullus Prophetæ nomen sibi arrogare au- sus est ab hoc tempore ad Christum. Vide 1. Macc. 4, 46. 9, 28. 14, 41. Josephus: ἀπὸ δὲ Ἀρταξέρξυ μέχρι τẽ μεθ' ἡ- μᾶς χρόνε, γέγραπται μὲν ἕκαστα, πίσεως δὲ οὐχ ὁμοίας ἠξίω- ται τοῖς πρὸ ἑαυτῶν, διὰ τὸ μὴ γενέθαι τὴν τῶν προφητῶν ἀ- κριβῆ διαδοχήν.

ET SPIRITUM IMMUNDUM AUFERAM DE TERRA.) Sic vocantur Dæmonia Matth. 10, 1. 12, 43. Marc. 1, 23. 26. 27. 3, 11. 30. 5, 2. 8. 13. 6, 7. 7, 25. 9, 25. Luc. 4, 33. 36. 6, 18. 8, 29. 9, 42. 11, 24. Act. 5, 16. 8, 7. Ab his accipiebant sæpe Pseudoprophetæ, quæ Dei nomine efferebant. Vide 2. Sam. 22, 20.

Male hæc abripiuntur ad Maccabæorum tem- pora. Neque verum est ex eo idololatriam nul- lam inter Judæos, nullum Pseudoprophetam, nul- la dæmonia, & oracula viguisse. Idololatria certe est gravissima, quod Judæi unum illum verumDe- um, Patrem, Filium & Sp. S. non agnoscentes, De- um colunt, qui μονυπόςατος est, unius tantum personæ, Patrem, qui non habet Filium, nec Spi- ritum ὁμοόσιον, sed sine coæterno Filio, sine coæ- ternoSpiritu S. esse fingitur, quod vere est idolum, extra & contra Dei verbum excogitatum. De qua idololatria convicimus Judæos adversus Calixtum Patrem & Filium cum Grotio Judæorum Patro- nos, in Appendice ad Syncretismum Calixtinum. Varios Pseudoprophetas ante, circa, & post ad- ventum Christi extitisse, qui negat, veritati histo- ricæ palam contradicit, ipsiq; Historiæ Evangelicæ & Apostolicæ refragatur. Spiritus autem immundus & Dæmonia illo tempore, cum apparuit Filius Dei, ut operaDiaboli destrueret, maxime vim suam ex- eruere, donec voce ac Spiritu ejus compesceren- tur Act. 10. Nec oracula defierunt gentilium, nisi sub adventum Messiæ. Quid? quod characterem ad- ventus Messiæ constituant ipsimet Judæi extermi- nationem idololatriæ, teste R. Lusitano in Colloq. Mittelb. f. 115. Fatemur inter præcipuos Messiæ effe- ctus futuram gentium vocationem & idololatriæ omnigenam exterminationem. Non ergo Macca- bæorum tempore ea jam exterminata. Oraculum Pythicum Apollinis adhuc consuluisse Augustum refert in vita ejus Suidas, quisnam ipsi successurus sit? quod respondit: Παῖς Ἑβραῖος κελεταί με θεὸς μακάρεσσιν ἀνάσσων, Τόν δε δόμον προλιπεῖν, καὶ ὁδὸν πάλιν αὖτις ἱκέσθαι Λοιπόν, ἄπιθι σιγῶν ἐκ βωμῶν ἡμετερᾴων. Me puer Hebræus jubet hinc, Rex ille Deorum Tartareas remeare domos, hac æde relicta. Post ergo ora tenens altaria nostra relinquas. De simili responso refert Porphyrius in libro περὶ εὐλογῶν Φιλοσόφ. quo jusserit Apollo tripo- des plangere, quia propter cælestem lucem obortam ipsi discedendum sit. Οἲ δὲ μοι, τρίποδες σοναχήσετε, ὄιχεθ’ Ἀπόλλων Οἴχεθ’ ἐπιφλύγυεν με βιάζετε ὀράνιον φῶς. Sabellicus L. I. Enn. 7. autor est, per illud se- ptennium, quod Christus in Ægypto cum Maria & Josepho exegit, oracula obmutuisse, & idola ul- tro corruisse. Tempore vero Trajani reliqua o- racula desiere. Neque responsum ab Apolline obtinere potuit de exitu suo Julianus, quia tem- plum ejus fulmine tactum & igne cœlesti absum- ptum fuit. Unde Porphyrius fassus est libr. advers. Christum, Ex quo Jesus colitur, nihil jam utilitatis à Diis consequimur. Et Plutarchus peculiare opus conscripsit de oraculorum defectu. Quo faciunt, quæ habet Grotius libr. IV. de Verit. Relig. Christ. c. X. Spiritus ipsi interrogati de silentii causa, dicere sunt coacti, nihil se posse, ubi Christus invocaretur. Tertullianus Apologet. Vide & Lucianum. Unde Cyrillus in h. l. Postquam aliquando unigenitum Dei verbum nobis apparuit, inepta & puerilia idolola- triæ ludicra prorsus evanuerunt, & extincta sunt, & sublatum cum ea nefarium quoque, & impium Pseudoprophetarum studium, qui maligno & im- mundo spiritu pleni erant, & cum idolorum cultor- ribus germano, ac simili errore infecti verissime co- argui potuissent. Unus quippe ambobus impietatis præses, nimirum Satanas. Sic etiam Remigius, Haymo, Albert. M. Hugo, & Dionysius.

## 13:3
Vers. 3. AND IT SHALL BE WHEN ANYONE SHALL PROPHESY ANY MORE.) He shows that the prophecy which is from God will cease.

HIS FATHER AND HIS MOTHER WHO BEGAT HIM SHALL SAY TO HIM) His parents themselves shall say this, if others do not say it: not parents by adoption, but by nature, whose affection is more tender. Compare the mention of equal fervor for the law, surpassing every other affection, Deut. 33, 9.

YOU SHALL NOT LIVE BECAUSE YOU HAVE SPOKEN A LIE IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.) You falsely say that you were sent by God: and therefore death is owed to you. Deut. 18, 20.

AND HIS FATHER AND HIS MOTHER SHALL PIERCE HIM THROUGH, WHEN HE SHALL PROPHESY.) If he persists in prophesying, his own father or his mother shall pierce him through. Namely, as Phinehas did Zimri, Num. 25, 14. Understand this concerning a false prophet, wishing to lead the people away to the worship of false gods. For the law armed any Jew whatsoever against such, Deut. 13, 8. 9. which law expressly adds that in such a crime one must not spare even a son. The Rabbis foolishly refer these and certain other things to the time after the resurrection.

These words do not speak of true prophecy coming to an end, but of false prophets to be condemned even by their closest kin. Because such will be the knowledge of God in the time of the New Testament that laymen also will be those who notice the frauds of false prophets, and will condemn them, even if they are their parents: not that false prophets are to be killed in the New Testament. But Zechariah speaks of New Testament matters in Old Testament phrases, in which false prophets were punished with death, Deut. 13, 5. 6. cf. Joel 2, 28. Zech. 6, 13. ch. 14, 16. seqq., whom in the New Testament it is necessary to slay with the sword of the Spirit, and in that matter one must not spare persons, or have regard for kinship, dignity, or the gifts which false teachers enjoy. Add that

Threatening words and severe rebukes are also said to pierce, Acts 2:37, 7:54, and are compared to nails, Eccl. 12:13. Nor does the word דקר always denote a deadly piercing; see Jer. 37:10. In vain, therefore, does Corn. a Lapide conclude from this passage that heretics are to be punished with death. We are commanded to beware, not to kill, Matt. 7:14; to bear, not to take away, ch. 13:3; to avoid, not to remove from the midst or slaughter heretics, Tit. 3:10; and thus to pierce the false prophet today is to slay impious doctrine with the sword of the divine word, so that it may be finished and unable to harm others, as Jerome says in the preface to book IV of his Commentary on Isaiah. Let us truncate the most arrogant heresy with the spiritual sword; and Augustine, book I against the letters of Petilian, ch. 29: Love the men, kill the errors without cruelty, fight for the truth. And book III against Crescentius. ch. 50. It has never pleased any good men in the Church that there should be cruelty toward anyone, even a heretic, even to the point of death. Regarding the meaning of this passage, Jerome says: "The names of idols having been removed from the earth, and the false prophets and the unclean spirit that spoke in them. If anyone wishes to tempt further, and to prophesy anything in the person of the Lord, his father and mother will immediately forget their parents, so that they may retain the service of God, and they will bring a sentence of death against their son: and the minds of all toward God will be so pious that a public judgment will not be awaited; but let those who are such perish by the sentence of their relatives."

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET ERIT CUM PROPHETAVERIT QUISPIAM ULTRA.) Ostendit cessaturam eam, quæ à Deo est prophetiam.

DICENT EI PATER EJUS ET MATER E- JUS QUI GENUERUNT EUM) Ipsi hoc dicent paren- tes, si alii non dixerint: nec per adoptionem parentes, sed per naturam, quorum tenerior est affectus. Confer men- tionem paris ardoris pro lege, omnem alium affectum su- perantis Deuter. 33, 9.

NON VIVES QUIA MENDACIUM LOCU- TUS ES IN NOMINE DOMINI.) Falso te à Deo missum dicis: ideoque mors tibi debetur. Devteron. 18, 20.

ET CONFIGENT EUM PATER EJUS, ET MATER EJUS, CUM PROPHETAVERIT.) Si persti- terit prophetare, transfodient eum pater ipse, vel mater ejus. Nempe ut Phinees Zambrin, Num. 25, 14. Hoc intel- lige de Pseudopropheta, populum volente abducere ad cultum falsorum Deorum. Nam in tales quemvis Judæ- um lex armabat, Deuteron. 13, 8. 9. quæ lex expresse ad- dit in tali crimine nec filio parcendum. Hæc & alia quædam stulte Rabbini referunt ad tempus post resurrectionem.

Non de Prophetia vera finem habitura, sed de Pseudoprophetis etiam à proximis agnatis da- mnandis hæc loquuntur. Quod ea futura sit Dei agnitio tempore N. T. ut Laici quoq; animadver- suri sint fraudes Pseudoprophetarum, eosque con- demnaturi, utut vel parentes eorum sint: non quod in N. T. interficiendi sint Pseudoprophetæ. Sed lo- quitur Zacharias de rebus N. T. phrasibus V. T. in quo Pseudoprophetæ morte multabantur Deut. 13, 5. 6. conf. Joel. 2, 28. Zach. 6, 13. c. 14, 16. seqq. quos in Novo Testamento gladio Spiritus oportet jugulare, nec ea in re personis parcendum, aut ra- tio habenda cognationis, dignitatis, aut donorum, quibus falsi Doctores gaudent. Adde, quod

Verba etiam comminatoria & graves reprehensio- nes dicantur transfigere Act. 2, 37. c. 7, 54. & clavis comparentur Eccl. 12, 13. Neque semper vox דקר transfossionem mortiferam notat; v. Jer. 37, 10. Fru- stra ergo ex hoc loco Corn. a Lapide colligit hære- ticos morte plectendos esse. Cavere, non interficere Matth. 7, 14. ferre, non auferre c. 13, 3. vitare, non e medio tollere, aut trucidare jubemur hæreticos Tit. 3, 10. adeoque configere Pseudoprophetam ho- die est gladio verbi divini impiam doctrinam jugu- lare, ut confecta habeatur, aliisque nocere non possit, uti Hieronym. in præfat. l. IV. Comment. in Es. ait. Superbissimam hæresin spirituali mucrone trunce- mus; & August. l. 1. contra liter. Petilian. c. 29. Diligite homines, interficite errores sine sævitate, pro veritate certate. Et l. III. contr. Crescent. c. L. Nullis bonis in Ecclesia unquam placuit, si usque ad mortem in quemquam, licet hæreticum, sæviatur. " De sensu loci hujus ita Hieronymus : Nomini- " bus idolorum de terra sublatis & Pseudoprophe- " tis atque immundo spiritu, qui loquebatur in " eis. Si quis ultra tentare voluerit, & quippiam " ex persona Domini prophetare, statim pater ejus " & mater obliviscentur parentum, ut Dei retine- " ant servitutem, & proferent contra filium mor- " tis sententiam : & tam piæ erunt omnium in " Deum mentes, ut non expectetur publicam ju- " dicium; Sed pereant, qui tales sunt, sententia " propinquorum.

## 13:4
V. 4. THE PROPHETS SHALL BE ASHAMED, EVERY ONE OF HIS VISION, WHEN HE HATH PROPHESIED.) They will not be able, for shame, to bear the mention of those prophecies which they rashly published before this general indulgence.

NEITHER SHALL THEY WEAR A ROUGH MANTLE TO DECEIVE.) A hairy mantle, which was the attire of the true prophets, 2 Kings 1:8, as it was also of those who imitated the true ones.

This was the attire of the prophets, says Jerome, that when they called the people to repentance, they were clothed in sackcloth. Whence it is also commanded to Isaiah: that he should take off the sackcloth from his loins, and walk naked: for it was by no means a time for repentance, but of imminent captivity. The conversion of certain false prophets is therefore predicted, who, when finally convicted and confounded, will renounce these deceits and will no longer pretend to be prophets.

Latin:

V. 4. CONFUNDENTUR PROPHETÆ UNUS- QUISQUE EX VISIONE SUA, CUM PROPHETA- VERIT.) Ferre non poterunt præ pudore mentionem fieri eorum vaticiniorum, quæ ante generalem hanc in- dulgentiam temere evulgarunt.

NEC OPERIENTUR PALLIO SACCINO UT MENTIANTUR.) Pallio hirto, qui habitus ut ve- rorum Prophetarum 2. Regum 1, 8. ita & veros imitan tium.

Hic erat habitus, inquit Hieronymus, Pro- phetarum, ut quando populum ad pœnitentiam pro vocabant, induerentur cilicio. Unde & Esaiæ præ cipitur : ut auferat saccum de lumbis suis, & nudu incedat: nequaquam enim tempus esse pœniten tiæ, sed imminentis captivitatis. Prædicitur ergo quorundam falsorum Prophetarum conversio, qu tandem convicti & confusi renunciabunt istis falla- ciis, nec amplius se mentientur esse Prophetas.

## 13:5
Vers. 5. I AM NO PROPHET,) A name which he was accustomed to affect, he will cast far from himself.

I AM A HUSBANDMAN.) Not by deceiving the people, but by my own labor I seek my living.

FOR MAN TAUGHT ME FROM MY YOUTH.) For some man taught me from my childhood: namely, agriculture, as the Chaldean explains here. Just as קנה is to learn, Prov. 4:5, 7; 17:16; 18:15, so הקנה is to teach.

Others render it: some man acquired me from my youth, i.e., I am more fit for the plow-tail and the plow than for the professor's chair, no differently than a SLAVE condemned from boyhood to the plow-tail. But Ribera foolishly says that Adam is the proper name here. How could Adam have instructed this man acting in the New Testament? Willius, more sharp-sighted than all other interpreters, saw here a period, as he calls it, the Pergamene; he saw Arius, Photinus, Macedonius, Priscillian, Nestorius, Eutyches; he saw the anathemas of the spiritual fathers in the seven Ecumenical Councils, and what not? He even drags Micah into it, and in him he imagines his own periods again. You have a similar sentiment in Micah 5:12. I will cut off thy graven images, and thy standing images out of the midst of thee; and thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands. And I will pluck up thy groves out of the midst of thee: so will I destroy thy cities. Where likewise Micah seems to describe this third period typically, just as also the remaining seven from chapter 4:1 to the very end of the whole prophecy, which we leave to more diligent consideration. But let those who please play the fool with Willius. To us, Scripture is too holy for us to think it should be profaned by any trifles whatsoever.

Latin:

Vers. 5. NON SUM PROPHE TA,) Nomen, quod affectari solebat, longe a se abjiciet.

HOMO AGRICOLA EGO SVM.) Non fucum plebi faciendo, sed meo labore victum mihi quæro.

QUONIAM ADAM EXEMPLUM MEUM AB ADOLESCENTIA MEA.) Nam homo aliquis docuit me a pueritia mea : nempe agriculturam, ut hic explicat Chal- dæus. Sicut קנה est discere, Prov. 4, 5. 7. 17, 16. 18, 15. ita הקנה est docere.

Alii reddunt: homo aliquis acquisivit me ab a- dolescentia mea, q. d. magis ad stivam & aratrum, quam ad Cathedram sum idoneus, non secus ac MANCIPIUM a pueris ad stivam condemnatum. Inepte vero Ribera אדם proprium hic esse dicit. Quomodo Adam hunc instituere potuit agentem in N. T.? Willius cæteris Interpp. universis ocu- latior vidit hic periodum, ut vocat, Pergamensem, vidit Arium, Photinum, Macedonium, Priscillia- num, Nestorium, Eutychem, vidit spiritualium Pa- trum in septem Oecumenicis Synodis anathemati- smos, & quid non? Trahit etiam eo Micheam, & in illo sibi fingit iterum suas periodos. Geminam sententiam habes Mich. 5, 12. Exscindam sculpti- lia tua, & statuas tuas e medio tui, & non incurva- bis te ultra operi manuum tuarum. Et evellam lucos tuos e medio tui & perdam adversarios. Ubi itidem Micheas typice hanc tertiam periodum vide- tur describere, quemadmodum etiam reliquas septem a cap. 4, 1. ad finem usque totius prophetiæ, quod dili- gentiori relinquimus considerationi. Sed ineptiant cum Willio, quibus placet. Nobis sanctior est Scriptura, quam ut affaniis quibusvis eam propha- nandam ducamus.

## 13:6
Vers. 6. WHAT ARE THESE WOUNDS IN THE MIDST OF THY HANDS.) That is, the stigmata branded on the hands, by which they were accustomed to enslave themselves to the gods of the nations, by having their wood, name, or number inscribed, Rev. 13:16, 17. Prudentius calls them seals and stigmata.

AND HE SAYS TO THESE, I WAS WOUNDED IN THE HOUSE OF THOSE WHO LOVED ME.) In the Hebrew it is 'house', not 'in the house'. That is, these stigmata do not pertain to any god, but to the honor of some powerful house, which loved me as its client, and to whose patronage I gave myself.

Others thus: but if then furthermore someone should say to him, what are these wounds in your hands, with which you have been wounded? do you still show yourself to them to be a False Prophet? (Compare 1 Kings 18:28.) he himself will say, not so, these are wounds, not which I brought upon myself voluntarily to deceive others, but with which I was struck against my will in the house of those loving me, and by those harsh remedies of theirs, when I was unwilling to obey milder ones before, calling me back from an evil practice to a good one. Thus Tarnovius. Which is the common explanation, from which he judges it to be evident that by 'pierce' in v. 3 is to be understood, not merely to rebuke, as most orthodox Interpreters hold (for from that no wounds are seen in the hands, which here nevertheless are expressly said to appear to others) nor entirely to kill, as all the Papists and some Calvinists, but to reprove with words first, and afterwards to chastise more harshly with lashes, when he had spurned earlier admonitions, in which way the zeal of men living at the beginning of the N.T. in preserving the purity of Sacred doctrine is denoted. For to parents themselves not only corrections of their own, but even blows and flagellations are granted Prov. 13:24, c. 23:13, 14, c. 29:15, 17, c. 22:15, Heb. 12:7. Cocceius's sense concerning Papal ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ in beating the breast and satisfactory flagellations is foreign. For here it is a matter of the conversion of a false Prophet and the acknowledgment of the sincere love of those by whose wounds he has been affected. Rupertus, Thomas, in Ps. 21. The Missal in the Mass of the Passion of Christ, R. Samuel in the Epistle on the coming of the Messiah c. 7, as also Galatinus l. 8, c. 17, and Ribera understand it of Christ, citing and approving Cornelius. B. Gerhardus in Harmon. Resurr. c. IX, p. m. 314, observes, and does not entirely disapprove, that some of the ancients place here a dialogue of Christ with the Angels and Patriarchs in his ascension. But the text teaches that it is about a False Prophet: in which Cyril, Theodoret, Jerome, Remigius and other Interpreters agree.

Latin:

Vers. 6. QVID SVNT PLAGÆ ISTÆ IN ME- DIO MANVUM TVARUM.) Id est, stigmata inusta manibus, per quæ solebant Diis gentium se mancipare, in- scripto eorum ligno, nomine, aut numero, Apocal. 13, 16. 17. Sphragitidas & stigmata vocat Prudentius.

ET DICIT HIS, PLAGATUS SUM IN DO- MO EORUM QVI DILIGEBANT ME.) In Hebræo est domus, non in domo. Id est, hæc stigmata non ad deum aliquem pertinent, sed ad honorem domus alicujus poten- tis, quæ me ut clientem suum dilexit, & cujus patrocinio me dedi.

Alii ita: quod si tum porro dixerit ei quispiam, quid plagæ istæ in manibus tuis, quibus vulneratus es? an adhuc te Pseudoprophetam esse iis ostentas? (Confer. 1. Reg. 18, 28.) dicet ipse, non ita, plagæ hæ sunt, non quas ego sponte mihi intuli ad fraudan- dum alios, sed quibus percussus fui invitus in domo amantium me, meą; istis duris remediis, cum mitio- ribus parere prius nollem, à malo instituto ad bonum revocantium. Sic Tarnovius. Quæ communis est explicatio, è qua patere arbitratur, quod per transfigere v. 3. intelligendum sit, non increpare tantum, ut plerique Interpretes orthodoxi habent (inde enim nullæ plagæ visuntur in manibus, quæ hic tamen expresse aliis apparere dicuntur) neque plane occidere, ut Pontificii omnes & Calviniani nonnulli, sed redarguere verbis primum, & postea durius castigare flagellis, cum admonitiones prio- res sprevit, quomodo hominum in N. T. initio viventium Zelus in puritate doctrinæ Sacræ con- servanda denotatur. Parentibus enim ipsis non cor- reptiones tantum suorum, sed etiam verbera & fla- gellationes concessæ sunt Prov. 13, 24. C. 23, 13. 14. c. 29, 15. 17. C. 22, 15. Ebr. 12, 7. Alienus est Cocceji sensus de ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ Papali in contundendo pe- ctore, & flagellationibus satisfactoriis. Hic enim de conversione falsi Prophetæ & agnitione sinceri amo- ris eorum, à quibus plagis affectus est, agitur. Ru- pertus, Thomas, in Pf. 21. Missale in Missa de Pass. Christi, R. Samuel in Epistol. de adventu Messiæ c. 7. ut & Galatinus l. 8. c, 17. & Ribera de Christo intelligunt, citante, & approbante Cornelio. Quos- dam è veteribus hic dialogismum ponere Christi cum Angelis & Patriarchis in sua ascensione observat, nec omnino improbat B. Gerhardus Harmon. Re- surr. c. IX. p. m. 314. Sed textus docet de Pseu- dopropheta agi: in quo consentiunt Cyrillus, Theo- doretus, Hieronymus, Remigius aliique Interpp.

## 13:7
V. 7. AWAKE, O SWORD, AGAINST MY SHEPHERD.) He continues to narrate future events. This Shepherd is Judas Maccabeus, who perished in battle with Bacchides, Jos. 12:19.

AND AGAINST THE MAN WHO IS JOINED TO ME, SAYS THE LORD OF HOSTS.) Against the man who is nearest to me: that is, whom I love most. As often as good men have perished by a violent death, so often has the faith of the resurrection grown among the pious, and this economy, differing from the legal one, was a preparation for the Gospel.

STRIKE THE SHEPHERD, AND THE SHEEP SHALL BE SCATTERED.) You, Bacchides, strike Judas, and his army will flee. See Josephus in the cited place.

AND I WILL TURN MY HAND TO THE LITTLE ONES.) I will make a few safe.

Latin:

V. 7. FRAMEA SUSCITATE SVPER PASTOREM MEUM.) Pergit narrare futura. Pastor hic est Judas Maccabæus, qui in prælio cum Bacchide interiit Jos. 12, 19.

ET SUPER VIRVM COHÆRENTEM MIHI, DICIT DOMINUS EXERCITVVM.) Super virum pro- ximum meum: id est, quem maxime amo. Quoties viri boni violenta morte perierunt, toties apud pios crevit fides resurrectionis, fuitque hæc ὀικονομία à legali differens, præ- paratio ad Evangelium.

PERCUTE PASTOREM, ET DISPERGEN- TVR OVES.) Tu Bacchide Judam percute, & fugiet e- jus exercitus. Vide Joseph. dicto loco.

ET CONVERTAM MANVM MEAM AD PAR- VULOS.) Paucos faciam sospites.

## 13:8
V. 8. AND IT SHALL BE IN ALL THE LAND, SAYS THE LORD, TWO PARTS IN IT SHALL BE SCATTERED AND SHALL PERISH.) For Bacchides had brought great slaughters upon the Jews not only in that battle, but also in others preceding it, as can be seen in Josephus chapter 18. Through them many perished, many fled.

Latin:

V. 8. ET ERVNT IN OMNI TERRA, DICIT DOMINVS, PARTES DUÆ IN EA DISPERGEN- TUR ET DEFICIENT.) Magnas enim clades Bacchides non isto tantum prælio, sed & aliis antecedentibus intu- lerat Judæis, ut Josephi cap. 18. videre est. Per eas multi interiere, multi fugere.

## 13:9
V. 9. AND I WILL BRING THE THIRD PART THROUGH THE FIRE AND WILL REFINE THEM AS SILVER IS REFINED, AND I WILL TEST THEM AS GOLD IS TESTED.) I.e., through many evils I will explore their constancy. Ps. 68:9. Namely, as tawny gold is viewed in the fires, so in hard times faith must be inspected.

HE SHALL CALL UPON MY NAME.) That people remaining from the slaughters.

A detestable depravation of a clear prophecy. For Grotius twists what is explicitly said about the passion of Christ to the persecution of Judas Maccabeus, so that he may leave us no prophecy about Christ, making nothing of the authentic interpretation of Christ himself, whose Spirit dictated these things to the Prophet 1 Pet. 1:11. L. Danaeus had preceded him, and especially the Judaizing Calvin: The sum is, before the Lord purges his Church and recalls it to perfect order, there will be most grievous intermediate slaughters: because a horrible dissipation will happen, when God shall have struck the shepherds themselves. Who did not hesitate to speak impiously even against Christ himself: Almost all of ours restrict this passage to the person of Christ, because that sentence is cited in Matt. 26, 'I will strike the Shepherd and the sheep will be scattered.' But the reasoning does not seem to be solid, because what is said about the Shepherd is more probably to be extended to the whole order itself, just as when God says, 'I will raise up a Prophet for you from your midst,' certainly there is no mention there of one Prophet only, but God includes all the Prophets. Thus he covers impiety with impiety, so that it may not leak. For the depravation of the Mosaic passage in Deut. 18 is no less impious than that of the Prophetic oracle which we have in hand. But B. Hunnius chastised Calvin as he deserved, whom the patron Paraeus could not defend in this perverse cause without giving up the fight: As far as I am concerned, I willingly accept the former opinion, for this reason especially, that God in the singular says his Shepherd and the man his fellow are to be struck; undoubtedly designating a certain Shepherd, and him not a common one, but the great one κατ’ ἐξοχὴν, who is Christ. Who nevertheless plays the trick that Calvin's opinion also must be retained at the same time, that the Prophet discourses not about Christ alone, but about the whole order of Shepherds. Whether this is not a most certain indication of abandoned shame and conscience, to prefer to state that contradictory things are true at the same time, rather than to give glory to God and confess that one has erred, B. Hunnius not undeservedly leaves to be judged by all who fear God. For he who approves this proposition: The Zechariah prophecy is to be understood of Christ ALONE, and not of others, nay, who even builds up with arguments that it pertains to Christ alone, with what mouth will he then say that a proposition diametrically opposed to this so approved one is not to be rejected? This is certainly to blow hot and cold from one mouth.

Willius, a Calvinian Doctor, devised another gloss, but an equally perverse one, because he drags what was said about one Christ, and according to Christ's own explanation, which is above all exception, is to be understood of the passion of Christ, in rendering the literal sense, to the persecution of the Church of Christ under the Papacy, understanding by the sword the Pontifical power, tyranny, wars, slaughters, burnings, and all the instruments of Pontifical persecution. Thus a blind impulse snatches men away to treat Holy Scripture at will, disregarding the evidence of the text and the clear interpretation of the Holy Spirit, and to drag it to any other things whatsoever. The Prophet treats of one Shepherd, and his striking, which is clearer than the sun. And it is dragged by Willius to the striking and affliction of innumerable members of the Church. The Prophet treats of the truly great Shepherd, called the Shepherd of the Lord κατ’ ἐξοχὴν, and it is twisted to a thousand others, I will not say Shepherds, but men of any sort: e.g., to the excommunication of the Emperor Leo the Isaurian by Pope Gregory II, and the persecution of Emperors and other Saints who resisted the Roman Pontiff. The Prophet prophesies about the great passion of Christ, which that good Shepherd underwent for us. Willius snatches that to the passions of the faithful under the Roman Pontiffs Gregory II and especially VII and those following. Moreover, this striking of this Shepherd and the man near to God was brought into effect by the Roman Anti-Christ, when he himself occupied his throne, and equating himself to God, arrogated to himself by universal right power over the Church and Political Princes, in Gregory VII, before called Hildebrand, and his successors, at which time the Sun of Justice Christ was struck in the third part by darkness, and together with him the Moon and stars, the Doctors of the Churches.

The Prophet predicts the dispersion of the Apostles of Christ at the time of his passion: Willius drags it by the neck to the dispersion and dissociation of the Western and Eastern Church, as also to the oppression and exile of particular members, and contends that this is the literal sense of the prophecy. The Prophet promises that the little ones who were dispersed will be collected in turn, with Christ himself as interpreter, when the dispersed Apostles will be gathered again. Willius on the contrary asserts that this is the proper and genuine meaning of the prophecy, that God will defend the faithful in the persecution of the woman Jezebel, and will console them with his grace, and he reports thus concerning its fulfillment: This conversion to the little ones happened when God, having saved certain remnants, snatched them from the tyranny of souls, and opposed them to Pontifical iniquity as witnesses of the truth, which the examples of Emperors and many pious men testify, among whom Leo the Isaurian, Constantine Copronymus, Leo the Armenian, Otto the Great, Henry III and IV, Frederick Barbarossa: among Princes, Bertram, Hincmar, Berengarius; Sigebert, Monk of Gembloux, Otto of Freising, the Waldensians, Thomas Bradwardine, John Wycliffe, Huss, Jerome of Prague, Laurentius Valla are eminent among the Doctors. Is this not to interpret Scripture egregiously?

Willius does not conceal that this testimony is cited in Matt. 26:31 by Christ himself as a prophecy concerning his passion and the subsequent dispersion of the Apostles, and that in place of that which says he will bring back or turn his hand to the little ones, it is promised to the Apostles by Christ, 'but after I have been raised, I will go before you into Galilee.' With what effrontery, therefore, does he contend that these words treat of the persecution of the faithful under the Roman Anti-Christ, contradicting Christ openly and to his face? Willius indeed objects that the passage of Zechariah is at least accommodated κατ' ἀναλογίαν to the passion of Christ in this sense, that the firstfruits of the truth predicted there manifested themselves in the death and passion of Christ and the dispersion of the Apostles. But this is to exercise a game of chance in interpreting not only Prophetic but also Evangelical sayings. For what is more certain than that Christ testifies that these words treat of the striking of himself in his great passion and the dispersion of the Apostles, and that they were fulfilled in himself and the Apostles, and were to be fulfilled further in the gathering of the Apostles? And what trace, I beseech you, either in the Prophet or in all the rest of Scripture, is there that these were to be fulfilled according to the literal and proper sense in the persecution under the Anti-Christ? From where will it be taught that the firstfruits of that truth were fulfilled only in Christ and the Apostles, but that they were truly fulfilled in the passion of the members of Christ and the dissociation of the Eastern and Western Church and the testimony of the witnesses of truth against the Roman Anti-Christ? Calvin, with Pareus, acts more prudently in this, that he acknowledges that in the passion of Christ, the Prince of Pastors, the words concerning the flight and conversion of the disciples were fulfilled not as to the firstfruits of the truth, but truly: although they contend that they speak generally about the order of Pastors: This, therefore, says Danaeus, is general, but κατ'

This is fulfilled in an eminent way in Christ, who was slaughtered by the Jews, Matt. 26, 30. For in that gloss, some respect is still observed between Christ the Prince of Shepherds and other subordinate shepherds under Christ, and likewise between the Shepherd to be struck and the flock to be scattered and, in turn, to be gathered: but in the distortion of William, that respect has no place. For he says that it is not the order of shepherds that is to be struck, as Calvin says, but any believers whatsoever: nor is the flock to be scattered under the order of the struck shepherds, but the Western Churches are to be dissociated from the Eastern: nor, finally, are those scattered ones to be gathered again; for the Eastern Church is never in turn coupled with the Western, but it will be found that they oppose the Roman Pontiff. Which are clearly inconsistent.

But to Grotius, who is sound only in this, that he acknowledges that the Prophet here continues to narrate future events: in the rest, there is nothing sound in his gloss. The shepherd for him in this place is Judas Maccabeus, who died in battle with Bacchides. Bacchides was ordered to strike the shepherd, the sheep scattered are the fugitive army of the Jews, the little ones to whom the hand of the Lord was turned are the few whom the Lord made safe: and whatever else are his trifles, more vain than Sicilian nonsense. Moreover, that the Prophet is not dealing here with Judas Maccabeus, but with Christ the Savior, can be taught by many things. First, from the circumstance of time. For it is not about the time of the Maccabees, but about the New Testament, in which the Spirit of grace and supplications was to be poured out most abundantly, Christ was to be pierced on the cross, the fountain of Baptism was to be openly opened, the idolatry and oracles of demons were to be destroyed everywhere, and many of the idolaters and false prophets were to be converted to God. For this striking of the Shepherd is referred to the same time, as Grotius does not deny. Next, from the context of the preceding passages, Theodoret says: After he said, 'They shall look upon me whom they have pierced,' lest they think that he suffered a saving passion against his will, he teaches how he came by his own will and emptied himself, becoming obedient even unto death, even the death of the cross; wherefore the prophetic discourse forms and delineates the divine concession, and shows the sword granted by the Father. As to what immediately precedes, after Zechariah had predicted either the overthrow or the conversion of the false prophets and shepherds, he now presents that great Prophet and Shepherd of the sheep to be struck by the divine sword, but with a far different outcome. For the sheep are not to perish with him, but however much they may be scattered in the passion, they are to be gathered in turn to him in his resurrection. After he had taught that some of the false teachers were to be converted, he now announces that the Apostles themselves would desert Christ, and would be gathered in turn to Christ, and he joins the example of the Apostles themselves, who were to be recalled from the desertion of Christ, to the converted false teachers. Regarding the reason for the coherence with the preceding, the blessed Lord Dr. Winckelmann has it thus: The Prophet seems to prophesy abruptly about the Passion and death of Christ, by which the faithful are confirmed, and are tested by the cross, just as gold is by fire. Yet he does not fall into this prophecy about the Passion of Christ entirely abruptly, but proposes Christ as an example to the faithful who have been converted from error, so that they may not be dejected in spirit because they are being corrected for their own merit, since Christ himself, the Son of God, was struck for our sake, innocent and without any merit of his own. Junius here, who is of the same mind as us (which we add for the sake of Calvin), connects it thus: The Prophet transitions to this place by way of anticipation in this manner: perhaps the whole promise of the aforementioned good things will seem to be vain, since my Shepherd Christ is to be oppressed by force and struck so grievously, just as if he were a false prophet: by which scandal the sheep themselves, that is, the flock of the disciples, will be so grievously affected that they will flee in a single moment, Matt. 26. But, says God, the pious ought at least to remember this, that that very scandal was predicted and ordained by me so many centuries ago, lest, when it happens, their minds be disturbed, as Christ himself warned in Matt. 26, 31, and John 14, 16, and 18. Then, indeed, this must be considered, that I cannot be restrained by any bonds from bringing my promises to pass in my elect.

Thirdly, from the simple denomination of the Shepherd of the Lord. He is designated simply as the Shepherd of the Lord. 'Awake, O sword, against MY SHEPHERD.' Who could think here of Judas Maccabeus, who was never called by this name and simply called Shepherd? But the Messiah is called Shepherd by antonomasia, and is famous by that name in the Scriptures, Ps. 23, 1; Ez. 34, 23; ch. 37, 24; John 10, 11; Heb. 13, 20; 1 Pet. 2, 25; ch. 5, 4. He says MY SHEPHERD, designating him whom he himself peculiarly chose, ordained, and constituted, not for some time or by reason of a certain people, but who is always the SHEPHERD OF JEHOVAH and the perpetual Shepherd of the Lord's flock, having no one before him, no one after him, to whom this office is proper and perpetual. Therefore he is simply called the Shepherd of the Lord. Just as the Lord never lacks his sheep, so he never ceases to preside over the feeding of the sheep; therefore he is also called the ONLY SHEPHERD, the Shepherd of the Lord, Ez. 34, 23; ch. 37, 24, who perpetually looks after all sheep everywhere, feeds, leads, defends, cherishes, and eternally saves them, nor does he allow them to be snatched from his hands; indeed, he lays down his life for them, John 10, 15, 28. Of whom St. Bernard says: Christ redeems the sheep preciously, feeds them sumptuously, leads them solicitously, and places them securely. For, says Cyril, 'Christ is our Prince Shepherd, and under him are all we who believe: yet not outside the hand of God and the Father. For he commands us in Christ, and through him and in him we are saved, and through him we have obtained access.' Therefore, the proper Shepherd and Son of God and the Father, not feeding a foreign flock, but rather his own and the Father's, while mercenary shepherds are understood not to be his own, who against all mercy slaughtered the sheep.

Fourth, from the comparison of this Shepherd with the former. The Lord calls this one His Shepherd, rejecting the former ones as false Prophets, v. 2. Since, therefore, the Lord's Shepherd is opposed to the False Prophets, it is manifest that by this Shepherd is not understood a Political Prince, Judas Maccabeus, but the Bishop of our souls, the Prince of Shepherds, Christ Jesus, 1 Pet. 2:25, ch. 5:4. God and Father, says Cyril, delivered His own Son for us, allowing by dispensation, although He was God and naturally begotten of Him in an inexplicable way, both to come in the form of a servant, and to become a man like us, and to endure the cross, that He might restore salvation to the world, and pluck out Satan's dominion over all, and overturn impure idolatry and divination, and abolish the False Prophecies and impostures proceeding from each one's own heart, and likewise take away the unclean spirit from the earth, and furthermore establish and form the world, transferring those who were led astray to the acknowledgment of the divinity, and impelling them to pious and honest ways of life, and to the forming of an opinion of all kinds of virtue concerning Him.

Fifth, from the mention of this Shepherd above. For Zechariah had already dealt in ch. 11:6 with the Shepherd, whom he had opposed to the faithless shepherds and who was to be sold for the price of thirty pieces of silver. Concerning whom, therefore, [he speaks] further here: Awake, O sword, against

My shepherd. For there is no reason for us to understand anyone other than the one whom the Prophet himself designated, or to summon the Lord's Shepherd from elsewhere, since that good Shepherd, who was to feed the poor of the flock and take up two staves for that purpose, even though he was to receive in return for his wages a wicked sale and betrayal, was introduced there by the Prophet himself. Just as these things had their fulfillment in the passion of Christ, so there is no doubt that the discourse here is likewise about the same Shepherd, Christ, being struck by the sword.

Sixth, from the description of this Shepherd. For God calls him THE MAN UNITED TO HIM, as the Vulgate has it: In the Hebrew it is: ועל־גבר עמיתי: upon the man my neighbor, by which phrase, as B. Glassius notes, another who is the same, the image of the invisible God, the character of the Father's substance, and the brightness of his glory is expressed, Heb. 1:3. And who, says the same author in Onomatolog. Mess. p. 282, is closer and more joined to the Father in heaven than the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father? The passage in Is. 44:24 pertains to this: I am the Lord who makes all things, stretching out the heavens alone, forming the earth מאתי from (him who is) with me, which Jonathan the Chaldean translated thus: I am God who makes all things, I stretched out the heavens BY MY WORD. Coccejus has this to say about it: As if he were saying, the man who is equal to me. "For the term עמת and לעמת signifies opposition in an equal position, disposition, form, magnitude, and right; as in the leading of the strong, as in 1 Chron. 25:8. Hence, when עמיתו, his neighbor, is joined to a man, it denotes אנוש כערכו (to imitate the phrase of Psalm 55:14), a man who is a participant of the same nature. Whatever the case, this word, 'My neighbor man,' uttered by the words of God, can signify nothing more lowly than he who is with me and cannot be torn away from me. But the term עמית among men is not significant of love or conjunction regarding place, but of communion of nature. Let him therefore be the neighbor man of God, who is one with the Father, with God, whom the Father loves, so that he may seek his glory, and for that reason, so that he may manifest his own glory, he gave all things into his hand, so that just as he willed and demanded from eternity, so he might also sanctify the people given to him by his blood and spirit, subject all things to God and to himself, and for that purpose finally, appearing ἶσα Θεῷ in the glory of the Father, he might make his own alive and condemn the world. My neighbor man, since it is first a denomination from human nature, according to which the sword also strikes him, and secondarily from the divine majesty, it is a communication of idioms, as the Son of man, who is in heaven, John 3:13. B. Tarnovius also notes this emphasis, referring the word גבר to human nature, Jer. 31:22, and the word עמתי to the Divine, which denotes strictly and properly not just any neighbor, who is called קרוב or חבר רע, but the most intimate one, who is always from the region in someone's sight or around him, with which word he compares the similar phrase used of intimate familiarity, which can exist between men, Gen. 2:18, כנגדו. Willius also had to admit this, and in doing so oppose himself to his Calvin, that Christ is denoted by this periphrasis. With what rashness, therefore, did he snatch away to the faithful of Christ and their afflictions what he could not deny was about the passion of Christ? Some, he says, give the reason for the name as that God associated Christ with himself to feed the sheep, and they explain these things in the same way regarding other Teachers, whom they wish God to distinguish with this name, who undertake the same office with him and represent his care. But I have no doubt that these things are more correctly applied to Christ himself because of the explicit testimony of the Evangelist Matthew, ch. 26:31. Christ is named thus, however, because in the divine essence he is equal to the Father in honor and dignity, and as an ἀντίπατρος opposite him in the sight of created things. Junius very beautifully: By this name God the Father honorably addresses Christ, because Christ is another who is the same, the image of the invisible God, the character of the Father's substance, and the brightness of his glory, shining opposite in the sight of all created things. The Hebrew word sounds like neighbor and friend, who stands from the region of another, etc. This is that person, and the Shepherd, against whom the sword is aroused. Our B. Gerhard also rightly notes in Harm. Pass. c. 1, p. 7, that the reason is expressed here at the same time why the striking of Christ, done by the heavenly Father, results in our redemption and plenary satisfaction for sins, namely, because he is a man near and equal to God, i.e., true God with the Father, because he admits no one into that society of heavenly majesty unless he is of the same essence with him, Is. 42:8. But this Shepherd, whom the heavenly Father strikes with the sword, is not only a man, that is, true man, but also the companion of the heavenly Father, and near to him; he is in the bosom of the Father, John 1:18, he is in the Father, John 14:10, nay, one with the Father, John 10:30; thence and for that reason, struck by the heavenly Father for our sins, he freed us from eternal blows. The word Shepherd also looks to the same thing, that is to say, that Christ is that true and supreme Shepherd of souls, who laid down his life for his sheep, and deigned to die for the flock, John 10:5.

Seventh, from the arousal of the sword. God does not arouse the sword of Bacchides to strike Judas. This is absurd. He does not arouse the sword of the Anti-Christ to strike the faithful, as Willius babbles. But by this arousal is taught the counsel of God in the redemption of the human race, for whose sake Jehovah willed to arouse the sword and strike the one near to him, just as in Acts 2:23 Christ is said to have been delivered by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, and in Is. 53 to have been struck by God with blows and humbled, and wounded for our transgressions. Jerome, in his book on the best kind of interpreting, to Pammachius, thinks these words of the Prophet are directed to the heavenly Father, who demands the passion of Christ, saying 'strike the Shepherd'; but it is clear from the context that the heavenly Father himself is addressing the sword, that it might arouse itself and strike the Shepherd. By which name of sword are metaphorically understood all the afflictions which Christ sustained both in body and soul, or all the instruments of divine judgment, as mention is made of the sword of the avenging God in Is. 27, 1. ch. 34, 5. Jer. 12, 52. Ez. 21, 8. and in Luke 2, 35 it is held: A sword shall pierce through your own soul: Cyril, arise against my Shepherd, and against the man his fellow (πολίτην αὐτοῦ, thus the LXX rendered it) Rhamphaea in this place, ὡς ἐν εἴδει, as in the form of, we say signifies the temptation of the sword, or the very torments themselves applied to Emmanuel from the madness of the Jews. He says therefore, O sword arise, that is, let the saving passion proceed henceforth, and let the time come, in which the good may show themselves. Nor has it been rashly observed by Gerhard in the place cited that the word sword refers us to the history of Gen. 22, 6. 10. for as Abraham in that place stretched out his sword against Isaac, so the heavenly Father, with sword as it were unsheathed, attacks in the passion his beloved Son on account of the sins of the world, which he had taken upon himself, to be sacrificed on the altar of the cross.

Eighthly, concerning the dispersion of the flock: Smite the Shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. As the Shepherd, so the sheep also are understood, not concerning a leader of war and an army, but concerning the Shepherd of souls and his sheep, nor is the discourse about a final dispersion of the sheep, in which they perish, or remain separated from their Shepherd, but about such a separation, from which they themselves are again to be gathered, and recalled to their Shepherd. The Shepherd alone is smitten, not the sheep. For these are only to be scattered, but not indeed to be smitten with the sword in this punishment, which may be applied to the dispersion of the disciples of Christ, where the Shepherd alone was struck by the sword, but the disciples themselves were kept unharmed, protected by the safe conduct of Christ, John 18:8. However, these things are ineptly drawn to the dispersion of the army of Judas. For neither was Judas alone struck, but many also of his army, nor were those who were dispersed gathered again to Judas, seeing that he perished in the war.

Ninth, from the turning of the hand of the Lord to the little ones. For by this are denoted none other than those who were dispersed when the Shepherd was struck: for whose consolation it is said that the Lord is willing to turn the hand of grace to them again, lest they perish in that dispersion. Therefore, those who remained after the slaughter of Judas, when others had fallen, cannot be understood by the little ones. The LXX Interpreters understand the Princes of the Jews; whence Cyril explains it concerning the turning of the avenging hand to them, not the hand of gathering grace. But the dispersed sheep are pointed out, who are to be gathered again: Therefore Jerome more correctly: After the good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, who spoke to the Father: Whom you have struck, they have persecuted, and they added to the pain of my wounds: He was struck by the will of the Father: and the man clinging to God, who says: I am in the Father and the Father in me: hung on the gibbet, and said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit: immediately the sheep were dispersed, the whole multitude of believers in Christ. And the Lord turned his hand, as we read in the LXX, to the Shepherds, whom many wrongly understand as the Princes of the Jews: But as it is written in the Hebrew, to the little ones, to whom the Lord had said in the Gospel: Fear not, little flock. And in Isaiah: Behold I and the children or little ones, whom God has given me. Wherefore the blessed Tarnovius well expressed the sense, rendering it thus: "Verily, indeed, when Christ the Shepherd is thus struck, and the sheep are dispersed, will it now be all over with the Church, and all the promises made hitherto void? Not so, but immediately a little after the resurrection I will bring back my hand, which I had withdrawn for a little while, leaving them to themselves, to the little ones, namely the Apostles and those like them, whom I will gather and, once gathered, will preserve, just as it is read to have happened in Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24, John 20 and 21, Acts 2." Which opinion of the Prophet, from the Reformed, Franc. Junius also acknowledged in book 1, Parall. XLVII. The end of this passage in the Prophet was clearly the same which we showed in Parall. VII. to have been proposed to Jeremiah (c. XXXI.), namely that by some certain, notable, and clear sign it might be publicly demonstrated that Jesus Christ is that Shepherd who, in the very struggle of his sufferings, cared for his dispersed sheep, whom he was afterwards to lead back into one fold by his own hand. And so the sum is, when it was near that Christ should suffer, he was struck by God the Father, and delivered into the hands of enemies: but his disciples and companions, each one offended by the gravity of that rod, went away here and there like wandering little sheep: but that they were both preserved by Christ our Savior during the time of that suffering, and then, after he had risen, were cared for and led back by his hand, just as the Prophet had predicted. Others interpret these things concerning the afflictions of the Apostles, as if to say, I will exercise them also with afflictions. But the former sense is more suitable. But Grotius clearly perverts these things: And I will turn my hand to the little ones: that is, I will make a few safe. For it is one thing to shelter some in a public slaughter while the rest perish, but another thing to turn the hand to those who are safe after the striking of one Shepherd.

Tenth, from the added promise concerning the Church of the New Testament. AND THERE SHALL BE, says the Lord, IN THE LAND

TWO PARTS, IN IT SHALL BE DISPERSED AND SHALL FAIL, AND THE THIRD PART SHALL BE LEFT IN IT. In the Hebrew it is, And it shall be in all the land. What is predicted does not concern a few now, nor only the Jewish land, but ALL THE LAND. Grotius very ineptly and perversely draws this to the slaughters which Bacchides had brought upon the Jews, not only in that battle in which Judas perished, but also in others preceding it. But the Prophet does not speak of those preceding, but of those following the striking of the Shepherd, and indeed throughout the whole earth. Namely, concerning the whole people of this Shepherd throughout the world after his passion and the reduction of the Apostles, because even if the whole earth is redeemed by his death, and the Apostles are to be sent into the whole earth, so that they may enjoy the redemption of this Shepherd and be fed with the food of the soul under him, two parts of the land are to be dispersed and to fail, and hardly a third part is to be left. Jerome understands those two parts as the Jews and Gentiles who persist in their error, and the third as the Christians turned to the Shepherd of souls; And two parts were made in all the land of the Jews and Gentiles, who likewise perished and failed, with the Jews and Gentiles perishing, a third part in the world, i.e., the third people of the Christians, suddenly grew up. Cyril explains it concerning the third part of the Jews saved while the rest perished, as does Fr. Junius: But the former explanation is more suitable: because it treats of the whole land, not only of the land of the Jews, and of an eternal, not a temporal, destruction. To which contributes that calculation of Edward Brerewood in his investigation of Languages and Religions. c. XIV. That the whole world, as far as it is known, being divided into 30 equal parts, Christians possess scarcely five portions, Mahometans obtaining six portions, pagan idolaters 19, while Jews are dispersed in many myriads throughout the whole world; if this modern state be compared with the ancient age of the Apostles, as being more fortunate, what wonder is it if scarcely a third part of the world has been a gathering of Christians, even though the Apostles announced Christ to every creature under heaven, where today not even a sixth portion of the known world shines with the beauty of the Christian name? B. Luther not inaptly understands two parts as those who fall away either by the cross and persecutions, or seduced by heretics and impostors: the third as the gathering of the faithful, who in the very cross hold fast the faith of Christ, and, like gold, are tested by fire. Which sense Winckelmann also embraces. Balt. Willius, I think through a feverish dream, saw here in the two parts to be cut off a most copious slaughter of martyrs in the time of the Waldensians and Hussites, and with the remaining part the restoration of the covenant at the beginning of the Sardian Church. But we dismiss those dreams. For the third part is opposed as the gathering of the faithful to the two as the infidels. Concerning that third part or gathering of the faithful, therefore, the Lord says: AND I WILL LEAD THE THIRD PART THROUGH THE FIRE, AND I WILL BURN THEM, AS SILVER IS BURNED, AND I WILL TEST THEM, AS GOLD IS TESTED. Which Grotius indeed correctly explains, through many evils I will test their constancy, but wrongly draws it to the remaining people concerning the slaughters of Bacchides. For they treat of the faithful of the N. T. to be tested by the fire of the cross 1. Pet. 1, 7. of whom this is the description: He (that people) shall call (invoke) my name; for this is proper to the people of the Lord, to be saved through the name of the Lord, and to invoke that in true faith, Joel 2. Rom. 9. & I will hear him Psalm 50, 15. Psalm 91, 15. Joh. 16. I will say, you are my people, and he shall say, the Lord my God, by which the highest communion of the faithful with God through faith, and the tenor of the covenant and spiritual betrothal is expressed Joh. 2, 19. conf. Joh. 20, 28. Rightly does Jerome say: The third part itself also, that it might not be delicate, and by secure confession, is proved as silver and gold through fire. When the little ones have been thus proved, over whom the Lord turns his hand, and through their calling the whole crowd of nations has believed, then the people of the believers will call Christ by his name: and upon his saying: You are my people; the people will answer: You are my Lord God.

To these is added an eleventh interpretation handed down in the New Testament, since Christ himself explains this prophecy (1) not of another Shepherd than himself, not of Judas Maccabeus, a warlike leader, but of himself, our redeemer. (2) Not of a slaughter in battle, but of a striking in the passion, which was then imminent for him. (3) Not of an army falling, but of the slaughter of one Shepherd. (4) Not of the slaughter and dissipation of warlike soldiers, or a military army, but of the dispersion of the sheep, the fearful disciples, and the scandal received from the passion of Christ. (5) Not of a final destruction or dissipation, but of such a dispersion from which the dispersed sheep are to be gathered again after Christ's resurrection. Then Jesus said to them (the disciples), says Matthew ch. 26, 31: All you will suffer scandal in me this night. For it is WRITTEN: I will strike the Shepherd and the sheep of the flock will be dispersed. But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee, that is, that I may gather you again. So also Mark has in chapter 14, 27: And Jesus says to them, all you will be scandalized in me this night, because it is written: I will strike the Shepherd and the sheep will be dispersed, but after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee. Let verses 50, 51, 52 be compared. Since, therefore, we have such a clear explanation of the entire prophecy, handed down by Christ himself, who would not wonder that Grotius and Calvin dared to take it in a completely different sense? Jerome certainly wonders about some who in his time attempted the same. I wonder that some wish to weaken this Prophecy, which the Evangelist Matthew referred to the Lord Savior, after the disciples fled in his passion, and then he says it was completed, by allegorical interpretations: and while they desire to seem to know more than the rest, they do not hold the rule of truth. For the Evangelist Matthew reports: Then Jesus says to them, all you will suffer scandal in me this night. For it is written: I will strike the Shepherd and the sheep of the flock will be dispersed. And again: But all this was done, that the Scriptures of the Prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples left him and fled. This is Jerome. But Grotius did not even make any mention of the explanation of Christ in this place, not because it could not have come into his mind, but because he treated it with indifference, which we have observed equally in most other prophecies thus far. He twisted everything to Judas Maccabeus, of whom there is not even a single iota in the whole prophecy.

Furthermore, since in his Annotations on Matthew he could not pass over this explanation of Christ, he progressed to such a point of rashness and impudence that he denied what, as far as is known, has been denied by no one, that Christ there looked to or cited the prophecy of Zechariah, and feigned that Christ merely used a certain proverb, and did not cite a Prophetic prophecy. Which, however, he did not dare to affirm for certain. IT SEEMS, he says, that Christ uses this saying in the manner of a proverb, so that the sense is: it happens, as is commonly said and as you remember is written somewhere: when the Shepherd is struck, the sheep are dispersed. But where such a proverb is written, the Polyhistor had nothing to say. And is it not sufficiently clear from the words of Christ that the Prophetic SCRIPTURE is pointed out, which it was necessary to FULFILL, because all things which were written concerning his passion had to be fulfilled in him, which Christ had so often professed, for whose sake also he himself, or his amanuenses the Evangelists, always appealed to Scripture, namely not any other, but Prophetic and Divine, so that they might teach that all things happened by the definite counsel of God and according to scripture. Nor, I believe, will anyone easily admit or bear with a calm mind this impious rashness, that Christ here looked not to a divine, but to some profane Scripture, in which perhaps such a proverb might be contained (although even the glutton of books, Grotius, could not find it). If Christ had not said, IT IS WRITTEN, but IT IS SAID, perhaps there would be some room for that fabrication; for that could perhaps have been snatched at for witticisms and proverbs. But, when Christ appeals to Scripture, and adds moreover that all this was done so that the Scriptures of the PROPHETS might be fulfilled, what room for doubt can remain that Divine and Prophetic Scripture was pointed out by him? But what conjectures, I ask, did Grotius have against this evidence of the matter for this proverbial diction? He says that Christ changed the imperative mood into the indicative, because it was more suitable for a proverbial expression. But the IMPERATIVE is held in Zechariah: STRIKE the Shepherd; if therefore Christ changed this imperative of Zechariah into the indicative I WILL STRIKE, certainly Christ had the passage of Zechariah in mind, not some other (I know not which, and Grotius did not know) Scripture. He adds: nor does that πατάξω designate a certain person, but the first person is put for any, and πατάξω τὸν ποιμένα is nothing other than πατάσσεται ὁ ποιμὴν. That indeed is false, that a certain person is not designated; for God the Father is looked to, who stirred up the sword, and with it struck the Shepherd. Which Grotius could have learned from Jerome, had not a comparison with the Prophet taught him the same, which is sufficiently clear: Nor is it to be thought that the testimony was assumed from another place: because in the Gospel God says the Shepherd was struck by him, and in the present place we read in the sword and the blade, it was commanded: Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be dispersed. This sword and this blade is the framea: of which in the twenty-first Psalm the Lord speaks to the Father: Deliver my soul from the framea, and my only one from the hand of the dog. That indeed, says B. Tarnovius, ought to disturb no one, that when in the Prophet it is in the imperative הַךְ strike, just as it was also formerly translated in Greek πάταξον, in direct speech to the sword, in the Evangelist it is the future πατάξω I will strike, also in the first person, as if God himself were striking. For since that sword strikes Christ only by the command of God, this is deservedly referred to him as the principal cause, and often elsewhere the imperative among the Hebrews is put for the future. Gen. 20, 7. Deut. 32, 50. Proverbs 3, 4. & 4, 4. & 20, 13. Psalm 37, 28. just as it is also evident from a comparison of the passage Isa. 6, 9. where the imperative is שִׁמְעוּ, and the citation of the same in Matt. 13, 14. Acts 28, 26. where it is the future ἀκούσετε: to which add what has been said at Amos 5, 25. 26. 27. concerning the general reconciliation of the sayings of Scripture, which seem to be cited in the N.T. otherwise than they exist. Franc. also acknowledged this. Junius, and for that reason openly contradicted his teacher Calvin here in Parallel. XLVII. There seems to be some change in the words, yet the matter is one and the same.

For instead of the fact that Zechariah addresses the sword with the words of God, saying, awake, O sword, strike, etc., Christ, omitting that figurative expression, states the matter in proper and simple words, strike the Shepherd, etc., namely with the sword, which had this office in the commands from God, as it is figured by Zechariah. Since these things are so, it is absolutely necessary that that passage be understood of Christ, just as Christ most holily interpreted it of himself, not by analogical accommodation, but by historical and necessary interpretation. Even Willius, however much he may have otherwise indulged here in his own speculations, which are most alien, confessed that the testimony of Matthew is EXPRESS, and that therefore he HAS NO DOUBT that this prophecy is applied to Christ.

But so that it may appear how he was agitated by a spirit of giddiness, not an interpreter, but a corrupter of Scripture (we point to Grotius), who explained this passage in our Prophet concerning Judas Maccabeus, a Pastor and Leader not evil, but distinguished by many merits, yet in his Annotations on Matthew he denied that it treats of the good Shepherd, and twisted it to the evil Shepherd, of whom the Prophet had treated in chapter 11, which passage is as far as heaven from our passage, as is most clear to one looking at it. But he says, it is so far from me to think that Christ is directly looked to by the words of Zechariah, that I much rather believe that it treats therein of some not good Shepherd, and indeed if I am not mistaken (in which indeed you were vehemently mistaken, Grotius, with all interpreters agreeing), of the same one of whom it had been treated at the end of chapter 11, where likewise he, whoever he is, is called my Shepherd (that is truly false, to call an idol shepherd or a god of nothing MY Shepherd) and the sword is said to threaten him. Who then, finally, is directly looked to by the Prophet, if Christ is not directly looked to? No one can be named. Not Judas Maccabeus; for Grotius would hardly have called him a not good shepherd, an idol shepherd and of nothing. Who then is that not good shepherd? And, how would God call a not good shepherd his shepherd, how would he call a man his neighbor?
