And what accuracy is there in the fact that he transforms a particular church, e.g., the Sardian, the Philadelphian, into a universal one, spread throughout the whole world, that he makes different periods out of different churches, and successive periods out of simultaneous ones, that he feigns that the Epistles concerning the present state, and directed to persons in the present, are prophecies about a future state in chapters 2 and 3 of the Apocalypse, and transfers them from the Apocalypse to the Prophet Zechariah, Willius? We leave that remarkable acuteness to him. Moreover, where it has been treated of Christ's passion, of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, of the total excision of Jerusalem, shall we deem it inconvenient that Christ's ascension from the Mount of Olives into heaven is also predicted? Is it not sufficiently consistent, since he has accurately predicted the remaining circumstances of Christ's course and the whole economy of his office? That the Spirit of Christ through the Prophets has also designated this remarkable circumstance, that he was about to ascend from the Mount of Olives, and thence was about to send the Apostles into the world? Why, therefore, when the words of the text agree, concerning the feet of the Lord standing on the Mount of Olives, so that he might thence ascend into heaven, and concerning the mountain splitting itself, and the division made spreading into all parts of the earth, when the Apostles were spread from the mountain into all the regions of the world, should it not be permitted to interpret these things? And indeed, since HIS FEET cannot be understood otherwise by the force of the context than as the feet of the Lord, who is said to be about to fight against the nations, it is necessary that we conceive of Christ the Lord, whose feet stood on the Mount of Olives, unless we wish to depart from the letter of the text at our own pleasure. For the antecedents and the consequents alike teach that he is the Lord who is indicated here: He is indeed understood, whose day is said to be coming in verse 1, and since the Lord God the Father speaks, who had spoken about his Shepherd and the man nearest to him in chapter 13, 7, about the Lord as another person in chapter 14, 3 and 9, who is to be King over the whole earth, whom all nations shall worship as their King in verse 16, it is by no means obscure that these things are to be accepted concerning Christ, Phil. 2, 9. But if, because of verse 5, you wish to say that these things are not God the Father, but the Prophet speaking in the last chapter, the comparison nevertheless with verses 1, 9, 16 teaches that by the Lord designated in verse 3, the Son of God is most correctly understood. Nor does the order of times contradict the prophecy, especially if you explain it with B. Tarnovius, so that it may be taught in this place, at what time that excision of the city is to be? After, to wit, his feet shall have stood at that time of the N. T. concerning which he prophesies, upon the mount of Olives, which is in the sight of Jerusalem, on the East, and is distant from that city only a Sabbath day's journey, Acts 1, 12, that is, two thousand lesser paces, or almost one German mile, as Tremellius teaches in this place, and after that mount, the Lord having been taken up from thence into heaven, was cleft in the midst, towards the East and the West into a very great valley, and one part of it withdrew now to the North, and the other part of it to the South: which happened after the day of Pentecost, when the Apostles, instructed with the miraculous gifts of the H. S., went forth into the whole world, Luke 24, 49, Acts 1, 2. For thus spiritually that mount of Olives, to which the Apostles had been gathered, was divided into all the regions of the world, when they betook themselves from thence into them, thus from a mount a valley was made, etc. For the particle Vav is used for after, from ch. Exod. 16, 20, Isa. 64, 4. Lev. 9, 22 teaches. If therefore the word be explained by the past tense, by Ribera's argument, that after the Prophet in v. 1, 2, 3 had spoken of the devastation of the city, he cannot now at last treat of Christ's ascension into Heaven, the nerve is cut, and all things cohere well. Although the same may also be conveniently taken in a causal sense, so that namely a reason is rendered why the Lord himself is to fight together with the nations against Jerusalem, because the Jews, although the Gospel had been preached to them first, which thence penetrated into the whole world, rejected the divine grace, which the nations throughout the world received with joy. Finally, if the most usual sense be retained, which is copulative, it will not be necessary that in the same order in which things follow one another in the event, they should also be predicted by the Prophets, but the Prophet could well treat first of the devastation of the city, and afterwards of the ascension of Christ into heaven, even if this preceded it in fulfillment or event. For those words IN THAT DAY are to be taken ὡς ἐν πλάτει, and in the Prophetic manner designate the whole time of the N. T., not precisely any point of time, and all these things look to the beginnings of the time of the N. T. And when concerning the wounding and striking or If it was done by the passion of Christ and the conversion of the nations that was to follow it, why could it not be fittingly argued concerning the devastation of the city, which was the punishment of the people for the Messiah being cut off and the Gospel rejected, and furthermore concerning the mode and manner of the propagation of the Gospel to the nations after the ascension of Christ into heaven? Why, therefore, should we seek a figurative sense in a letter that is clearly deserted, with Junius and Ribera, concerning the mountain trembling and fleeing from the majesty of God (Ps. 18, 8; Ps. 114, 5), when here a distinct and exact mention is made of all the regions of the world, into which we know the preaching Apostles arrived; but we do not read that the Mount of Olives was so split or scattered. It does not please Drusius that the mountain is said to be split into four parts: for he wishes it to be divided only into two: so that the splitting is understood to have been made towards the East and the West, in such a way that the middle part, because of the neighboring city to the North, and the other part, receded to the South: But it does not contradict the Hebrew text if you explain it with Osiander thus: that the whole mountain will first be split into two parts, so that one inclines to the East, the other to the West: But then indeed the Eastern part is also to be split, so that a part of it turns to the North, and some portion of it extends itself to the south, and a quite large valley is left in the middle of these mountains. Why should we say with Danaeus that the feet of God stood on the Mount of Olives, when the hostile forces of the Romans pitched their camps there, and that the mountain was split when it was dug through by them? Which explanation is too jejune. For neither are those armies the feet of God, nor did they dig through this mountain into all the corners of the world. Why should we admit with Willius that the Mount of Olives is understood improperly, so that it denotes the kingdom of Christ, when a description of the site is added, that it is in sight of Jerusalem to the East, which periphrasis sufficiently argues that the Mount of Olives is to be understood properly, of which Jerome says: The Mount of Olives to the East of Jerusalem with the torrent of Cedron flowing between, where the last footprints of the Lord impressed in the soil are shown to this day. But how is the kingdom of Christ in the sight of the Church, and looming over it from the East, as Willius drivels, when the kingdom of Christ is the Church itself? Why, when he accepts the splitting of the mountain in such a way that the kingdom of Christ will dilate itself through all parts of the world (which we know happened after the feet of Christ stood on the Mount of Olives, but we nowhere read that it will happen towards the end of the world, except in the commentaries of fanatics), does he not understand that station of the feet of the Lord on the Mount of Olives as the letter sounds? Doubtless Willius promises his followers a Calvinistic kingdom (which to him is the kingdom of Christ) that will first be extended to the East and West not without violence and labor (which is the figurative splitting), but afterwards, by the benefit of the valley made between the East and the West, will extend also to the North and South: Whence it remains: because it is only then to progress to that point, that in the Calvinistic kingdom, which is the kingdom of Christ, there is as yet no place in the East, nor in the West, nor to the North, nor to the South: which we readily grant. But while he imagines in it the fulfillment of the noble prophecy of Isaiah 60:3 ff., he is indeed vehemently mistaken. For that already began to be fulfilled when the Apostles were sent out through the world to all nations, by which sending and calling of the nations, if the Calvinists expect a more notable one, as long as they wish, we are certain that we are ignorant of a more notable one in Scripture, nor will they ever show it from the Scriptures. Nor do we value those inanities about fictitious periods so much that we should constitute the old Prophet Isaiah, in the place cited, as an interpreter of the new Prophet St. John (Apoc. 3:8, ch. 17:12), and believe that Isaiah, after the affliction of the twilight between the Sardian and Philadelphian churches, expressly denounces the amplification, and explains what the Apostle John called an open door, and furthermore ch. 59:20, 21 after. to begin the description of the Philadelphian Church (which, however, Willius p. 514 says is already described in ch. 25, as also in ch. 27:12, 13), which, if they are so express, so clear and illustrious, how did it happen that no one among the ancients, no one among the recent interpreters, and not even any of the Reformed themselves, could see these things either in the Johannine Apocalypse or in his commentary, if it pleases the Gods, on Isaiah? The sayings which he compiled here, following Alstedius's fanatical treatise on the thousand Apocalyptic years, hand down nothing concerning the conversion of the Jews towards the end of the world, so that I cannot sufficiently marvel at the man's rashness, when he says it is clearly asserted by many sayings of Scripture, and that the same will happen most certainly under the Philadelphian period (under which he also promises the brotherhood of the Lutheran Church and the Calvinist assembly) not long after those times in which he wrote these things (but he wrote them already 26 years ago). He dreams, forsooth, of a golden age in which all the saints are to be gathered into the Church, into one fold, in which the sheep of Christ's pasture will enjoy delights, and thus will adhere to God in mind, heart, and spirit, and the Jews, terrified by the most ample extension of the kingdom of Christ, are to be converted to the Messiah, for whose sake there will be a future presence and some singular indwelling of God, such as the Church has not experienced before, as he speaks on p. 516. Willius certainly could not approve his trifles to others in the Reformed Church; whence he complains on p. 520: I would not have wished any great man to have called them MERE QUIBBLES, with too precipitate and free a judgment.

Coccejus distinguishes the Mount of Olives from Jerusalem, and calls some part of the place of the Evangelical Church the Mount of Olives: which mountain he thinks is that of Megiddo, Rev. 16:16. By it he understands a great Empire, which has land connected to it from the West, in which the Church is gathered in the form of a city, which land to him is Belgium and Britain. He therefore wishes Germany to be noted, situated near Belgium and Britain; there the Lord will stand and will do battle, and from there the division of the mountain, i.e., of that empire, will arise, whose power had previously diminished the Church, comparing as parallels, in which nothing parallel is detected, Dan. 7:1, 25, Rev. 17:9, 10, which, as also all those things which are handed down here by Coccejus, taste of nothing but ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν, and are most alien to the context. For here the Prophet does not look to the end of the world, but to the destruction of Jerusalem; not to the conversion of the Jews, but to the end of the Jewish polity and the propagation of the kingdom of Christ. In this, however, we see Coccejus as sounder here than Willius, in that he indeed refers these prophecies to our own times, but does not dare to peddle that application as the fulfillment of the literal sense of the prophecy, but rather promises, if anyone prefers it so, that the affairs of our times are to be held only as homogeneous examples.

But we must return to the text. For the words of v. 5 are sufficiently difficult, along with the following v. 6 and 7. Osiander renders the Hebrew words thus: And you shall flee to that valley of the mountains, because that valley of the mountains will reach as far as Azel. He accepts, however, with not a few others, אצל as a proper name of a place, the mention of which is in 1 Sam. 20:19, where the stone האזל is designated, but from the writing of this name it appears that it is different by reason of the consonants as well as the vowels. Which also contradicts the conjecture and new version of Grotius, substituting the word אצל, denoting height or armpit: who also deserves no excuse, because he prefers the translation of the LXX and the Chaldean, 'it will be stopped, it will be closed,' to the authentic text: approaching the fables of R. David Kimchi and other Jews, that the parts of the mountains are to coalesce again, and feigning an awkward parenthesis beyond necessity. Willius takes it as the proper name of a place, which perhaps was situated on the borders of Judea or Galilee, so that it might thus be shown that the valley would pass through the whole region. Avenarius in his Lexicon likewise says it is the name of a higher place having the shape of an armpit. Jerome rendered it TO THE NEAREST: But that version neither agrees with the Hebrew source, nor produces a certain meaning. Most others take it as a verb, and render it: HE CHOSE, HE SEGREGATED, thus supplying the discourse to the mountain, which he chose, as Junius, Piscator, B. Tarnovius, B. Glassius in Philol. S. c. III. tract. II. c. 23. p. 203. so that the meaning is, then you will flee the valley of the mountains, you will betake yourselves toward the house of God astonished, when (God) reaches the valley of the mountains, to the mountain which he chose, struck with awe at the majesty of the approaching God.

Concerning the valley, it is most doubtful. To B. Luther, Osiander, Pappus, Winckelman, Balduinus, Tarnovius, Junius, Piscator, that valley of the mountains seems to be like a long and wide one, and horrible to behold, to be fled by the faithful, which, following these authors of our own who have been praised, we understand as the Jewish Synagogue, which arose among the kingdoms of Christians as if among mountains from the cleft Mount of Olives like a horrible valley, which all the pious flee, lest they perish eternally in it. This interpretation, however, in this sufficiently difficult passage seems to be preferred to the others, until a more suitable one is suggested, which, having considered the explanations of others, it has not yet been possible to find. Drusius and Tirinus explain the valley of the mountains as the valley of Mello, situated between the mountains of God, Zion and Moriah, because the LXX Interpreters read ὀρεῶν μ&, and Jerome to the valley of my mountains: But הרי is of the form חלוני of windows, שרי of fields, and the text teaches that the discourse is about the valley that was to intervene between the sections of the Mount of Olives, which Willius acknowledges, who by this valley understands the meek and humble Christian assembly, and thinks the accession of the Jews to the Church is noted; but if by the cleft Mount of Olives the kingdom of Christ divided into East and West is noted, which Willius does not deny, how will the same kingdom of Christ, or the Church and assembly of Christians, be the valley which the Prophet opposes to the divided mountains? Furthermore, he teaches that they would not betake themselves to that valley, but rather would accelerate their flight elsewhere at the sight of that valley, as Willius himself also admits. How then are we to understand that valley as the Church? The comparison certainly indicates a flight joined with horror and trembling: As you fled from the face of the earthquake, when you feared that the earth trembling under your feet would gape and swallow you up, in the days of Uzziah King of Judah, of which Amos also makes mention c. 1, 1. although in Biblical history this earthquake is nowhere mentioned. It must, however, have been horrible, because it gave occasion to a proverb, which they were accustomed to use in describing the flight of a most harmful thing. Wigandus only wishes for the speed in spreading the Gospel through the whole world to be depicted in this way. Although, however, the splitting of the mountain were to be understood according to the letter, yet these things should not be drawn to the times of the Maccabees, but would be explained more conveniently concerning the siege of Titus, thus Sanchiez explains it in three ways. First, he suspects that in the siege of the Romans, the Mount of Olives was actually divided by a huge earthquake, even if Josephus does not say so, nor any history: just as they do not mention the earthquake under Uzziah, which nevertheless Zechariah teaches here happened. Secondly, that the camps of the Romans on this mountain were so arranged by Titus that they lay open and extended from the east to the west, and left two parts on this side and that toward the North and South: but that the steep place is the great valley of Kidron, which the Romans also occupied: for a valley is nothing other than a cleft of mountains, i.e., the depth of Kidron will not fortify the Jews, will not hinder the Romans from invading and occupying the city, because they will fill everything with their soldiers. Thirdly, i.e. Titus will so fill and level the most profound abyss of Kidron, which lay between the city and his camps situated on the Mount of Olives, and fortified the city, with mounds brought together, that through it there may be an easy approach for the soldiers to invade the walls. For Josephus teaches that he did that in other valleys, book 6 of the war, chapter 4. And the same Josephus teaches that in the valley of Kidron itself there were mounds and walls built, book 6, c. 13. But it is better with Eusebius, book 6, demonstr. c. 18, to interpret allegorically that the mountain was split, when there, by Christ ascending into heaven, the Apostles were commanded to go into the whole world, and to preach the Gospel in all the regions of the world. But the anagogical meaning of the Papists concerning the fission of the Mount of Olives, when the Anti-Christ (whom they dream of) will want to ascend from it into heaven, and being cast down by Christ will fall, and who will be swallowed alive by the earth or the mountain gaping open, is merely fabulous, and unworthy of refutation. Of the same kind also is another of their meanings, concerning Christ the judge about to descend onto the Mount of Olives, from where by his majesty he is to shake it so, with a huge earthquake, that it itself, as if from horror and reverence for Christ the judge, trembles, and at the same time splits itself, and widens the valley of Jehoshaphat, for the purpose of taking all men to be judged there by Christ. On the day of judgment Christ will not appear on the Mount of Olives, but in the clouds of heaven, Matt. 26, 46. Some even from among the Papists themselves acknowledge that these things are to be taken allegorically, such as Stunica and Ribera and others, and that according to the literal sense, which Cornelius thus expresses from them, p. 295. When the Mount of Olives, that is, the Church of Christ, shall be scattered into the four corners of the world, then you, O unbelieving Jews, shall flee from the Gospel, Christ, and the Church, not indeed to idolatry and gentilism, but to the shady valley of my mountains, that is, to the worship, shadows, and ceremonies of the old law, which flourished on the mount of the temple, namely Moriah and Zion, which were once my mountains. Thus Eusebius, book 6 of the Demonstrations, chapter 18. What, he says, can be the valley of the mountains of God, if not that which was once celebrated according to the law of Moses in Jerusalem, the corporal and Jewish worship: Whence it follows, since the valley of the mountains shall be joined even to the next, that is to say, this valley, that is, this shady but obstinate religion of the Jews, will join itself the more tightly to the temple near to it and to the rites of the temple, the more it will see the Church of Christ being scattered and propagated. Otherwise Emanuel Sa, that is to say. This worship of the old law will be most tenaciously joined to the Jews, and will adhere closely wherever they may dwell. If anyone desires a simpler interpretation, with the Belgian Paraphrasts it may be said that by this figurative expression concerning the splitting of the mountain, only this is noted: that the Church of God, of which the nations had no knowledge before the coming of Christ, with all impediments removed which could have blocked access to them, will be opened to them, so that they will have an open path to it from all sides.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ET STABUNT PEDES EJUS.) Bacchidæ, qui gen- tibus illis præerit, Ita sæpe ex sensu subauditur persona. IN DIE ILLA SUPER MONTEM OLIVA- RUM,) Qui commodus ponendis castris.

Nimis temere ingeritur Bacchides. Si ita pro lubitu eas personas, quarum nulla in textu vesti- gia habentur, licet textui inserere, nihil certi re- linquetur in S. Literis. Sensus, ex quo illum du- cem subaudit, pariter nullo nititur fundamento. Consentiunt autem in eo omnes interpretes, Do- minum indigitari pronomine relativo, utpote cu- jus antea mentio facta. De Christo Domino in- terpretatur Cyrillus atque ita etiam alii.

ET SCINDETUR MONS OLIVARUM EX ME- DIA PARTE SUI AD ORIENTEM, ET AD OCCI- DENTEM, PRÆRUPTO GRANDI VALDE.) In He- bræo: grandi admodum convalle. Id est, multa humus egeretur, ita ut hiet mons magna sui parte,

ET SEPARABITUR MEDIUM MONTIS AD AQVILONEM, ET MEDIUM EJUS AD MERIDIEM.) Id est, ita humus egesta de monte feretur partim ad op- pugnanda Aquilonaria, partim ad oppugnanda Australiatempli. Vers. 5. ET FUGIETIS AD VALLEM MONTIUM EORUM, QUONIAM CONJUNGETUR VALLIS MONTIUM USQUE AD PROXIMUM.) Chaldæus אצל,quod hic proximum vertitur, sumsit pro nomine proprio:nec minus Græci. Iidem Græci, & Chaldæus hoc loco,Græci etiam in verbis sequentibus, נסתם, non sumuntin secunda plurali à נס, sed in tertia singulari à סתם,vertunt enim: καὶ ἐμφραγήσεται ἡ κοιλὰς τῶν ὀρέων καὶ συναφθήσεται ἡ φάραγξ τῶν ὀρέων ἕως Ἀσάηλ. Nomen proprium Azelposuere & Symmachus & Theodotion. Putant quidamLatinum interpretem scripsisse montium meorum, quia inHebræo est הרי: sed potest esse regimen pro absoluto,qualem permutationem & alibi notavimus. Maxime inhis scriptoribus, qui non raro συριάζουσι. Sensus mihi videtur hic esse: & (post discessum hostium) obstruetur vallismontium (quia egesta humus ex uno monte Oliveti velutduos fecerat) ita ut vallis illa montium adæquetur ad altitudinem: nempe montis. אציל altitudo etiam Ezechieli41, 8. ET FUGIETIS SICUT FUGISTIS.) Obstruetur,inquam, sicut obstructa fuit, nempe vallis olim eodemloco facta. A FACIE TERRÆMOTUS.) Id est, propterterræmotum, qui in eodem monte hiatum fecerat. IN DIEBUS OZIA REGIS JUDA.) Cujus terræmotus meminit Amos 1, 1. ubi dicta vide. Adde Esaiam1, 6. Hæc παρενθετικῶς dicta sunt, quia vallis ab hoste factæinciderat mentio, ne quis eam in perpetuam mansuramputaret.

Impletum hoc esse in die ascensionis Christi incælos Luc. ult. quo pedes ejus steterunt in monte Olivarum, & inde in cælum sublatus est, B. Lutherus, Osiander, Winckelmannus, Paraphrastæ Vinarienses, Tarnovius, & alii è nostris censent: (quemsensum neque Papistæ, neque è Reformatis Gwaltherus improbant; etsi alios sensus simul innui velint) quia Christus ibi stetit, ac simul mandata discipulis dedit de prædicando Evangelio in universoterrarum orbe. Non sapit hæc interpretatio palato Willii, cui nihil nisi τὰ ἴδια sapere videntur,utut eandem Paraphrastæ Belgici elegerint, ac sequuti sint. In ejusmodi interpretatione, inquit, nihilaccurati. Quid ergo ille accuratius promit? Philadelphensem periodum à vers. 3. comminiscitur, quonon solum assertionem Reformatæ Ecclesiæ ex manuhostium Anti-Christi, & ei addictorum Regum animo suo persuasit, verba huc trahens illa: post egredietur Dominus, & pugnabit contra gentes illas &c.cujus veritatem impleri cœptam, posthac impletum iri putat, ut ad plenam felicitatem (Philadelphenses Calviniani (syncretismi & pacis verbo Deihaud innixæ sectatores) pertingant. Sed etiamregni Calviniani (quod ipsi est regnum Christi) dilatationem amplissimam è v. 4. & 5. polliceri audet, acporro, nescio quod aureum seculum suæ Orthodoxæ h. e. Reformatæ Ecclesiæ promittit, de quoneque in hoc vaticinio, neque uspiam in scripturisquicquam habetur, quodque novissimorum temporum extremæ malitiæ, omnis fidei, omnis charitatis experti, seductorum & improbitatis longeplenissimæ minime congruit. Et quæ accuratio ineo, quod Ecclesiam particularem, v. c. Sardensem,Philadelphensem in universalem transformat, pertotum orbem diffusam, quod ex Ecclesiis diversisdiversas periodos, ex simultaneis periodis successivas facit, quod Epistolas de statu præsenti, & adpersonas in præsenti directas vaticinia esse de statufuturo in cap. 2. & 3. Apoc. fingit, easque ex Apocalypsi in Zachariam Prophetam traducit Willius?Præclarum illud acumen ipsi relinquimus. Cæterum illic, ubi de Christi passione, de Sp. S. effusione, de Hierosolymæ totali excisione actum, etiamChristi è monte Oliveti in cælum ascensionemprædici, num inconveniens censebimus? Nonne satis congruum, quum reliquas circumstantias.curriculi Christi & οἰκονομίας universæ officii e- jusdem accurate prædixerit. Spiritus Christi per Prophetas, hanc etiam insignem circumstantiam, quod è monte oliveti ascensuris, atque inde Apostolos in orbem emissurus sit, designarit? Quidni ergo cum verba textus congruant, de pedibus Domini in mon- te Oliveti stantibus, ut inde ascenderet in cælum, ac de monte sese dispescente, ac facta divisione in omnes terræ partes diffundente, cum Apostoli è monte in omnes mundi plagas diffunderentur, hæc inter- pretari liceat? Et sane quum PEDES ejus non in- telligi aliter possint vi contextus, quam de pedibus Domini, qui pugnaturus contra gentes dicitur, ne- cessum est, ut de Christo Domini, cujus pedes in monte Oliveti steterunt, nisi pro arbitrio à litera textus discedere velimus, concipiamus. Nam eum esse Dominum, qui hic indigitatur, antecedentia pariter & consequentia docent: Is nempe intelli- gitur, cujus dies vers. 1. venturus dicitur, & quum loquatur Dominus Deus Pater, qui de Pastore suo & viro sibi proximo c. 13, 7. loquutus erat, de Domino ceu persona alia c. 14, 3. & 9. qui Rex futurus est, su- per universam terram, quem adorabunt omnes gentes ceu Regem suum v. 16. de Christo hæc accipienda esse minime obscurum est, Phil. 2, 9. Quod si ob vers. 5. hæc non Deum Patrem, sed Prophetam lo- qui velis in postremo capite, collatio tamen cum v. 1. 9. 16. docet, per Dominum v. 3. designatum re- ctissime Filium Dei intelligi. Nec vero ordo tem- porum repugnat vaticinio, imprimis si id explices cum B. Tarnovio, ut doceatur hoc loco, quonam tempore illa urbis excisio futura sit? Postquam sc. steterint pedes ejus tempore illo N. T. de quo vatici- natur, super montem olivarum, qui est in conspectu Hierosolymæ, ab Oriente, & ab ea urbe tantum di- stat iterSabbati Act. 1, 12. h. e. bis mille passibus mi- noribus, vel uno fere miliari Germanico, docente h. l. Tremellio, & postquam mons ille, Domino inde in cælum sublato, scissus fuit medius, Orien- tem & Occidentem versus in vallem magnam valde, ejusque pars una recessit jam ad Aquilonem, & pars ejus altera ad Austrum: quod factum post diem Pen- tecostes, cum Apostoli Sp. S. donis miraculosis in- structi in omnem terrarum orbem egressi sunt Luc. 24, 49. Act. 1, 2. Ita enim spiritualiter mons ille Olivarum, ad quem congregati Apostoli fuerant, divisus fuit in omnes mundi plagas, cum illi inde se in eas contulere, ita ex monte facta fuit vallis &c. Particulam enim Vav pro postquam usurpari è c. Exod. 16, 20. Es. 64, 4. Lev. 9, 22. docet. Si ergo ver- bum per præteritum explicetur, Riberæ argumento, quod postquam Propheta v. 1. 2. 3. de vastatione urbis dixisset, non possit jam demum agere de Christi ascensione in Cælos, nervus inciditur, & omnia bene cohærent. Quanquam eadèm etiam sensu causali commode accipiatur, ut nempe ratio reddatur cur Dominus ipse pugnaturus sit una cum gentibus adversus Hierosolymam, quod Judæi utut ipsis prius Evangelium prædicatum fuerit, quod inde in totum terrarum orbem penetravit, gratiam divinam reprobarint, quam cum gaudio suscepe- runt passim gentes per orbem. Denique si sensus retineatur usitatissimus, qui est copulativus, non necessum erit, ut quo ordine quæque sese in even- tu consequuntur, eodem etiam illa prædicantur à Prophetis, quin de devastatione urbis primo agere probe potuerit Propheta, postmodum de ascen- sione Christi in cælum etsi hæc eam antecesserit in complemento vel eventu. Verba enim illa IN DIE ILLO ὡς ἐν πλάτει accipienda, & more Prophetico totum N. T. tempus, non præcise aliquem temporis articulum designant, atque hæc omnia ad primordia temporis N. T. spe- ctant. Et quum de vulneratione & percussione seu passione Christi eamque consequutura conversio- ne gentium actum fuerit, quidni de vastatione ur- bis, quæ pœna populi fuit ob excisum Messiam & re- jectum Evangelium, ac porro de modo & ratione pro- pagationis Evangelii ad gentes post ascensionem Chri- sti in cælum convenienter agi potuerit? Cur itaque litera plane deserta figuratum sensum quæramus cum Junio & Ribera de monte à majestate Dei tre- mente & fugiente Ps. 18, 8. Ps. 114, 5. quum hic distin- cta & exacta omnium plagarum mundi mentio fiat, in quas pervenisse scimus prædicantes Apostolos; montem autem olivarum ita dissectum aut disjectum esse, non legamus. Non placet Drusio, quod mons in quatuor partes fissus dicatur: vult enim eum tantum in duas divisum: ita ut scissio facta intelligatur ver- sus Orientem & Occidentem, hoc pacto, ut pars me- dia, propter vicinam urbem ad Aquilonem, pars al- tera ad Austrum recesserit: Sed non refragatur E- bræo textui, si cum Osiandro ita explices: totum montem primum in duas partes scissum iri, ita ut una ad Orientem, altera ad Occidentem inclinet: Dehinc vero Orientalem partem etiam findendam esse, ut pars ejus ad Aquilonem vergat, aliqua vero ejus portio ad meridiem sese extendat, & in medio horum montium vallis admodum magna relinquatur. Cur cum Da- næo dicamus pedes Dei in monte olivarum stetisse, cum ibi hostiles Romanorum copiæ castra posuerunt, & montem scissum esse, cum ab illis persossus est? Quæ explicatio nimis jejuna est. Neque enim exercitus illi sunt pedes Dei, neque in omnes mundi angulos hunc montem perfoderunt. Cur cum Willio ad- mittamus montem oliveti improprie intelligi, ut regnum Christi notet, quum addatur descriptio situs, quod in conspectu Hierosolymæ sit ad Orientem, quæ περίφρασις satis arguit proprie montem Oliveti intelligendum esse, de quo Hieronymus: Mons oliveti ad Orientem Hierosolymæ torrente Cedron in- terfluente, ubi ultima vestigia Domini humo impressa hodieque monstrantur. Quomodo vero regnum Chri- sti est in conspectu Ecclesiæ, & ab Oriente ei imminet, ut nugatur Willius, quum regnum Christi sit ipsa Ecclesia? Cur, quum scissionem montis ita accipiat, regnum Christi per omnes orbis terrarum partes se dilataturum (quod factum esse postquam pedes Christi in monte Olivarum stetere, novimus, futu- rum esse sub finem mundi nuspiam legimus, nisi in Commentis fanaticorum,) non intelligit statio- nem illam pedum Domini in monte Oliveti, uti sonat litera? Nimirum pollicetur suis Willius re- gnum Calvinisticum (quod ipsi est Christi regnum) prius non absque violentia ac labore (quæ scissione figurata) ad Orientales & Occidentales extentum iri, postea vero beneficio vallis inter Orientem & Occiden- tem factæ ad Aquilonem quoque & Austrum porre- cturum: Unde relinquitur: quia adhuc demum eo id progressurum, regno Calvinistico, quod sit re- gnum Christi, nec in Oriente, nec in Occidente, nec ad Aquilonem, nec ad Austrum adhuc dum lo- cum esse: quod facile, largimur. Dum autem in eo fingit complementum nobilis Prophetiæ Esa. 60, 3. seqq. næ vehementer fallitur. Illa enim jam im- pleri cœpit, emissis per orbem Apostolis, ad uni- versas gentes, qua emissione & vocatione gentium insigniorem exspectent Calviniani, quamdiu vo- lent, nos insigniorem ignorare scripturam certi su- mus, nec eam unquam è scripturis ostendent. Ne- que ineptias illas defictitiis periodis tanti facimus, ut Prophetam Veterem Esaiam l. c. cum Willio Prophetæ novi S. Johannis Apoc. 3, 8. cap. 17. 12. interpretem constituamus, & Esaiam post affli- ctionem crepusculi inter Sardicensem & Philadel- phensem Ecclesiarum amplificationem diserte denun- ciare, & quid Johannes Apostolus ostium apertum vo- caverit, explicare, ac porro c. 59, 20. 21. post. Sardensem Philadelphensis Ecclesiæ descriptionem inchoare (quam tamen Willius p. 514. jam cap. 25. ut & cap. 27, 12. 13. descriptam dicit) credamus, quæ si tam diserta, tam luculenta & illustria sunt, qui factum, quod ne- mo è veteribus, nemo è recentioribus Interpp. at- que nec ex ipsis quidem Reformatis ullus hæc vel in Apocalypsi Johannæa, vel in Commentario ejus- dem, si Diis placet, Esaiano videre potuerit? Quæ ille hic compilavit dicta, Alstedii fanaticum tracta- tum de mille annis Apocalypticis sequutus, nihil de Judæorum conversione sub finem mundi tradunt, ut mirari satis nequeam hominis temeritatem, quum pluribus Scripturæ dictis luculenter eam assertam dicat, eandemque certo certius sub Philadelphensi pe- riodo (sub qua etiam promittit fraternitatem Luthe- ranæ Ecclesiæ & Calviniani cœtus) non longe post illa tempora, quibus ista scripsit (Scripsit autem jam an- te 26. annos) eventuram, Scilicet aureum somniat seculum, in quo omnes sancti colligendi sint in Ec- clesia, in unum ovile, in quo oves pascui Christi de- licias agent, & sic animo, corde & spiritu Deo adhæ- rebunt, & Judæi amplissima regni Christi extensio- ne perterriti, ad Messiam convertendi sint, cujus causa futura sit præsentia, & inhabitatio Dei aliqua singularis, qualem antea Ecclesia non fuerit exper- ta, uti loquitur p. 516. Non probare certe potuit nænias suas Willius aliis in Ecclesia Reformata; unde queritur p. 520. Nollem virum aliquem ma- gnum MERAS ARGUTIAS dixisse, nimis præci- piti & libero judicio.

Coccejus montem oliveti distinguit ab Hierosolyma, & aliquam partem loci Ecclesiæ Evangelicæ mon- tem oliveti dicit : quem montem Magedontis esse putat Apoc. 16, 16. per illum intelligit Imperium ma- gnum, quod connexam habeat ab Occasu terram, in qua Ecclesia colligatur specie urbis, quæ terra ipsi Bel- gium est & Britannia. Germaniam itaque notari vult sitam ad Belgium & Britanniam; ibi staturum Dominum & præliaturum, atque inde divisionem montis, h. e. imperii illius orituram, cujus potentia antea imminuerit Ecclesiæ, conferens ceu paralle- la, in quibus nihil paralleli deprehenditur, Dan. 7, 1. 25. Apoc. 17, 9. 10. quæ uti etiam omnia illa, quæ hic à Coccejo traduntur, nil nisi ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν resi- piunt, & à contextu alienissima sunt. Hic enim non respicit Propheta finem mundi, sed excidium Hiero- solymæ; non conversionem Judæorum, sed finem politiæ Judaicæ, & regni Christi propagationem. In eo tamen Willio hic saniorem videmus Coccejum, quod hic ad nostra quidem tempora referat hæc vaticinia, sed non ausit venditare illam applicationem pro complemento sensus literalis vaticinii, quin promit- tat, si quis ita malit res nostrorum temporum pro ex- emplis tantum homogeneis haberi.

Sed redeundum nobis ad textum. Nam verba v. 5. satis difficilia sunt, cum sequentibus v. 6. & 7. Verba Ebræa ita reddit Osiander: Et fugietis vallem istam montium, quia pertinget vallis illa montium usque ad Azel. Accipit autem cum aliis non paucis אצל pro nomine proprio loci, cujus mentio 1. Sam. 20, 19. ubi designatur lapis האזל, sed ex scriptione hujus no- minis apparet, illud diversum esse ratione conso- nantium pariter & vocalium. Quæ repugnat quoq; conjecturæ & novæ versioni Grotii, substituentis vocem אצל, altitudinem notantem vel axillam: qui nullam etiam meretur excusationem, quod præfe- rat translationem LXX. & Chaldæi, obturabitur, con- cludetur, textui authentico: R. David Kimchii & alio- rum Judæorum fabellæ accedens, quod partes mon- tium iterum sint coalituræ, & παρένθεσιν incon- cinnam fingens præter necessitatem. Willius ut pro- prium nomen loci accipit, qui forte in finibus Ju- dææ aut Galilææ situs fuerit, ut ita monstretur val- lem totam regionem pertransituram. Avenarius in Lexic. itidem dicit esse nomen loci eminentioris ha- bentis formam axillæ. Hieronymus reddidit AD PROXIMUM: Sed ea versio neque fonti Ebræo convenit, neque certum gignit sensum. Plerique alii accipiunt pro verbo, & reddunt: SELEGIT, SEGREGAVIT, ita supplentes orationem ad montem, quem selegit, uti Junius, Piscator, B. Tarno- vius, B. Glassius Philol. S. c. III. tract. II. c. 23. p. 203. ut sensus sit, tum fugietis vos vallem montium, recipietis vos domum Dei versus attoniti, cum pertinget, (Deus) vallem montium, ad montem, quem selegit, obstupefa- cti majestate appropinquantis Dei.

De valle maxime dubium est. B. Luthero, Osian- dro, Pappo, Winckelm. Balduino, Tarnov. Junio, Pisca- tori videtur vallis illa montium ceu longa & lata, atque aspectu horrenda, fugienda fidelibus, quam lau- datis his Nostratibus autoribus præeuntibus de Sy- nagoga Judaica accipimus, quæ inter Christianorum regna velut inter montes ex dississo oliveti monte orta instar horribilis vallis, quam effugiunt omnes pii, ne æternum in illa pereant. Hæc v. interpretatio in hoc satis difficili loco cæteris præferenda videtur, do- nec suggeratur convenientior, quam considera- tis aliorum explicationibus nondum invenire licuit. Drusius & Tirinus vallem montium expo- nit de valle Mello, media inter montes Dei Sionem & Moria, quia LXX. Interpp. legerunt ὀρεῶν μ&, & Hieronymus ad vallem montium meorum: Sed הרי est formæ חלוני fenestræ שרי agri, & textus docet sermonem esse de valle inter sectiones montis oliveti intercessura, quod agnoscit Willius, qui per vallem hanc cætum Christianum mansuetum, & humilem intelligit, & Judæorum accessionem ad Ecclesiam no- tari putat; sed si per montem oliveti discissum re- gnum Christi in Orientem & Occidentem divisum no- tatur, quod Willius non diffitetur, quomodo idem regnum Christi, vel Ecclesia & cœtus Christiano- rum erit vallis, quam montibus divisis opponit Propheta? Adhæc non ad vallem illam se receptu- ros, sed potius conspectu vallis istius fugam alior- sum acceleraturos docet, fatente itidem Willio. Quomodo ergo vallem illam de Ecclesia intellige- mus? Fugam certe cum horrore & tremore conjun- ctam indicat similitudo: Sicut fugistis à facie terræ motus, cum metueretis, ne terra tremens sub pedi- bus vestris dehisceret, vosque deglutiret, in diebus Oziæ Regis Juda, cujus Amos quoque meminit c. 1, 1. etsi in historia Biblica nuspiam hic terræ motum commemoretur. Horribilem autem fuisse oportet, quia proverbio occasionem dedit, quo in descri- benda fuga rei nocentissimæ uti solebant. Wigandus tantum celeritatem in Evangelio diffundendo per totum orbem ita depingi vult. Etsiarnsi vero scissio mon- tis secundum literam intelligenda esset, non tamen hæc trahenda forent ad tempora Maccabæorum, sed exponerentur commodius de obsidione Titi, Sic tri- pliciter ea explicat Sanchiez. Primo suspicatur in ob- sidione Romanorum, montem Oliveti ingenti terræ motu revera fuisse divisum, etiamsi id non dicat Jose- phus, nec ulla historia: sicut nec meminerunt terræ motus sub Ozia, quem tamen contigisse hic docet Zacharias. Secundo castra Romanorum in monte hoc ita à Tito fuisse disposita, ut ab oriente in occi- dentem paterent, & porrigerentur, atque hinc inde ad Aquilonem & meridiem duas partes relinquerent: præruptum vero grandem esse vallem Cedron, quam etiam occuparunt Romani: vallis enim nihil aliud est quam montium scissura q. d. Cedronis profun- ditas non muniet Judæos, non impediet Romanos, quo minus urbem invadant & occupent, quia omnia suo milite complebunt. Tertio, q. d. Titus profundissimam voraginem Cedronis, quæ inter urbem & castra sua in monte oliveti sita interjacebat, urbemque muniebat, comportatis aggeribus ita implebit & complanabit, ut per eam facilis militibus ad muros invadendos sit accessus. Id enim eum fecisse in aliis vallibus docet Joseph. l. 6. belli cap. 4. Et in ipsa Cedronis valle esse aggeres exstructos & muros, docet idem Joseph. l. 6. c. 13. Sed præstat cum Euseb. l. 6. demonstr. c. 18. allegorice interpretari montem scissum esse, cum ibi à Christo ascendente in cœlum Apostoli jussi sunt in totum terrarum orbem ire, ac prædicare Evangelium in omnibus mundi plagis. Sensus autem Papistarum anagogicus de fissione montis Oliveti, cum Anti Christus (quem illi somniant) ex eo volet in cœlum con- scendere, & à Christo deturbatus corruet, quique à terra vel monte dehiscente vivus absorbebitur, mere fabulosus, & refutatione indignus est. Ejusdem generis etiam alter eorum sentus est, de Christo judice descensuro in montem oliveti, unde majestate sua ita eum concussurus sit, ingenti terræ motu, ut ipse quasi præ horrore & veneratione Christi judicis contremiscat, simulque se findat, ac vallem Josaphat ampliet, ad capiendos omnes homines ibidem à Christo judicandos. In die judicii Christus non in monte Oliveti apparebit, sed in nubibus cæli Matth. 26, 46. Agnofcunt ex ipsismet Pontificiis nonnulli, hæc allegorice accipienda esse, utpote Stunica & Ribera & alii, idque juxta literalem sensum, quem ita ex iisdem exprimit Cornelius p. 295. Cum mons Oliveti, id est, Ecclesia Christi spargetur in quatuor mundi plagas, tunc vos, ó Judæi increduli, ab Evangelio, Christo, & Ecclesia fugietis, non quidem ad idololatriam, & gentilismum, sed ad vallem umbrosam montium meorum, hoc est, ad cultum, umbras & ceremonias legis veteris, quæ viguit in monte templi, puta Moria & Sionis, qui olim fuerunt montes mei. Ita Euseb. l. 6. demonstr. cap. 18. Quæ, ait, potest esse vallis montium Dei, nisi quæ olim celebrabatur ex lege Mosis in Jerusalem corporalis & Judaica adoratio: Unde sequitur, quoniam conjungetur vallis montium usque ad proximum, q. d. hæc vallis, id est, hæc umbrosa, sed obstinata Judæorum religio, tanto arctius conjunget se vicino sibi templo templique ritibus, quanto mags videbit spargi & propagari Ecclesiam Christi. Aliter Emanuel Sa, q. d. Hic cultus legis veteris Judæis tenacissime conjungetur, & adhærebit proxime ubicunque degant. Si quis simpliciorem desideret interpretationem, cum Paraphrast. Belgicis dici poterit, hac figurata loquutione de scissione montis id solum notari, Ecclesiam Dei, cujus notitiam ante adventum Christi non habuere gentes, remotis omnibus impedimentis, quæ aditum ipsis præcludere poterant, iisdem patefactum iri, ut apertum aditum undique ad eam habituræ sint.

## 14:5
Verse of the same. AND THE LORD MY GOD SHALL COME, AND ALL THE SAINTS WITH HIM.) Namely, to bring help to the Temple, and to those besieged in the Temple. The saints are the angels, Dan. 8, 13.

Latin:

Vers. eod. ET VENIET DOMINUS DEUS MEUS, OMNESQVE SANCTI CUM EO.) Nempe ad opem ferendam Templo, & obsessis in Templo. Sancti sunt Angeli, Dan. 8, 13.

## 14:6
Verse 6. AND IT SHALL BE IN THAT DAY.) In that time of the siege: For the Hebrews call time a day. THERE SHALL BE NO LIGHT, BUT COLD, AND FROST,) There shall be no joy, but trembling and horror.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET ERIT IN DIE ILLA.) In tempore illo obsidionis: Nam Hebræi tempus diem vocant. NON ERIT LUX, SED FRIGUS, ET GELU,) Non erit gaudium, sed tremor & horror.

## 14:7
Verse 7. AND IT SHALL BE ONE DAY, WHICH IS KNOWN TO THE LORD, NEITHER DAY, NOR NIGHT) That time which is known to the Lord, that is, is predetermined (thus proegno is often also taken in the New Testament) shall have neither the joy of day, nor the rest of night.

AND IN THE TIME OF EVENING THERE SHALL BE LIGHT) When it is least expected, deliverance shall arrive, peace having been made.

The reason of the preceding context does not permit the coming of the Lord—as Grotius, along with some Papists, Castrio, Cornelius, and the Jews, wishes—to be understood as the coming to bring help to the Temple in the time of Judas Maccabeus. For the Prophet is prophesying about the time of the New Testament, as has been shown before.

Some, however, explain these things as the final coming of Christ, such as Junius, Piscator, the Belgian Paraphrasts, and among our own, Wigandus, because Christ himself joins the prophecy concerning the destruction of Jerusalem and his own future judgment at the end of the world. And indeed, since the discussion has been about the ascension of Christ from the Mount of Olives into heaven, it does not seem inappropriate for the return of Christ for judgment to be commemorated, just as the angels preached about it on the Mount of Olives, Acts 1:11: 'This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.' Jerome thinks it is manifest that these things are predicted concerning the second coming of the Savior, and he explains it thus: 'When the day of his coming has been fulfilled, there will not be law, but cold and frost; with the love of all grown cold, and because of the multitude of evils that are about to come, all will grow cold and lose the warmth of their former faith.' But after all sinners have contracted their cold and frost, there will be one perpetual day, with light and darkness, day and night, no longer succeeding one another; but the Lord himself will be the light of all. Concerning which Isaiah says more fully: 'The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the rising of the moon illuminate you by night, but the Lord shall be your eternal light, and your God your glory.' Finally, in the time of evening, that is, of the darkness and sadness of all sinners, there will be light for the saints, and one eternal day: which, if it is known to the Lord (for he cannot be ignorant of what he created), it must be considered how he says in the Gospel that neither the angels nor the Son knows that day, except the Father alone. Cyril, Remigius, Hugo, Lyranus, Ribera, Sanchez, and others here and there also interpret this as the coming to judgment, and they contend that this sense is literal, as Cornelius admits.

Others judge that a spiritual coming and the assistance of the Lord to the faithful are promised here. Namely, that Christ will be present with his own when the Gospel is preached throughout the world, and although persecutions are to be stirred up against them, there will not be light, but darkness (distresses) and cold and frost (the love of many will grow cold); yet at that time, which is known to the Lord, the persecutions will be gradually mitigated, so that it will be a kind of mixture of the darkness of tribulations and the light of peace and tranquility (it will be a day that will not be entirely day, nor yet mere night); and finally, the light of joy, peace, and tranquility will be restored (and in the time of evening there will be light again), just as Osiander explains, with whom B. Balduinus agrees on page 862. He says: 'It will be in that day, namely when the Gospel is preached, in the world there will not be light, but cold and frost.' In the Hebrew it is: 'there will not be light' יקרות יקפאון 'of precious things of density,' that is, it will not be a serene and tranquil day, such as are usually held in esteem, but harsh and unpleasant, and condensed by a kind of mist and gloom of persecutions; indeed, God has reserved for himself a certain time which will be neither day nor night: 'and in the time of evening there will be light,' that is, even if the persecutions remit somewhat, there will not yet be perpetual serenity, but it will be mixed with much storm, so that that time may seem more like twilight than day, until finally, toward the evening of the world, those darknesses are dispelled so that a serene light may shine forth. B. D. Cramer understands 'precious light' as Urim, and 'congealed snow,' as some render it, as Thummim, because those things will be lacking. But those things had already been lacking in the time of the Old Testament in the second temple, nor did they last until the New Testament, nor can they be conveniently expressed or understood by those words. Ludov. de Dieu posits a mistake in the vowels and reads יִקְפָאוּן 'they shall congeal,' i.e., 'there will not be precious light, they shall congeal,' that is, the Heaven, the Sun, the Moon. But it is not our place to admit a mistake in the authentic text and to correct it. And that sense is forced.

Joh. Coccejus renders it: 'there will not be light of brightness and coagulation,' gathering from the Hebrew distinction that first, in general, light is removed, then specifically, clear and thick light; by the other words, 'And it will be a day, not night,' he wishes to note the state of affairs in the Church, so that they can neither congratulate themselves on better things, and they are in great fear; yet again, they are without notable evil, with the enemies reduced to impotence.

As for the fulfillment, Osiander thinks it was accomplished when the light arose for Christians under Constantine the Great. B. Winckelmann, Papp., and the Vinarians refer it to our own times, and the rise of the Evangelical light from Papal darkness. B. Balduinus explains it generally regarding the matter of religion, which in truth had such a condition from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel down to these times, for the light was never always serene, but clouded by the ill-omened darkness of persecutions.

B. Tarnovius renders the words a little differently, and likewise accepts them in a general sense regarding the state of the Church in the time of the New Testament, but in comparison to the times of the Old Testament, to this effect: And it shall be on that day after the universal preaching of the Gospel, that a greater light shall shine upon the Church than has shone hitherto, and that the day of the knowledge of Jehovah shall not be variable and unstable, now serene, now cloudy, but shall run its course with a certain and steady tenor, as long as God wills. For then the light shall not be precious and dense, or clouded by darkness, such as is very often the case in the time of winter, when snow covers the lands. But it shall be one continuous and perfect day, which God will bring about, provide for, and preserve as long as it shall seem good to Him; and that day shall be known and approved by Jehovah, not variable, as before in the Old Testament, consisting of day and night, but shining with a wondrous light, Rom. 13:12, for it shall be as in the evening time, when it is wont to grow dark and night to approach, that there is light and sun, and the day of the Church shall not set, when all night and darkness shall then be banished. I see no reason why we should reject this sense. And Willius's version easily harmonizes with it; of which later.

Although those words concerning the coming of the Lord, and of ALL the saints with him (as they sound in the Vulgate), seem to imply the final coming of Christ, the continuity of the preceding and following context teaches that these refer to the state of the Church in this age rather than in the future. And those words from the Hebrew are to be rendered thus: And the Lord my God shall come: and all the saints with thee: which pronoun does not refer to God, but to the Church, or the assembly of the faithful, as B. Tarnovius correctly observed, who explains these as referring to the angels: And all his holy angels are with thee, O Church, they stand by thee, they provide ministries to thee by God's command, Ps. 91:11, Dan. 8:13, Heb. 1:14. Which can be understood no less conveniently of the saints and any of the faithful, to this effect: The Lord my God shall then be present with His own in gracious presence, and shall cherish, rule, and protect them: and all the saints shall be with thee, little flock, who shall escape that horrid valley of the Jewish Synagogue. And thus far Willius does not poorly [explain] the future consensus and universal union of the saints in the Church of Christ, [that there shall be] one shepherd and one fold.

But he is mistaken in this, that he restricts these to the final times, and that he promises for those times a singular presence of God, such as the Church has never before experienced.

For the rest, Willius is not poorly occupied in eliciting the sense of the words and phrases: It is said the light shall not be יְקָרוֹת יִקְפָאוּן. Jerome: And it shall be on that day there shall not be light, but cold and frost. So also the LXX and the Chaldean,

Junius, precious and dense light. Pagninus, precious light and congealed frost. Montanus expressed it word for word as light of preciousnesses and coagulations. יקר is preciousness, price, and the rarity that usually accompanies price, glory, splendor. Hence Drusius attempts to translate it as rare light, because rare and dense are opposed, and interpreters generally take these as distinct. But I think that these two words should be joined together and understood as one and the same light, in this sense: that the light will not be precious and dense, that is, not constituted of many things, not going to be common and exposed to all, so that there is no need to pay a price for it, nor will it be dense or obscure. As to the following words: But it shall be one day: The sense is, that day or time which the Lord is about to create will not consist of an interval of days and nights, but of a perpetual day, because even at evening there will be light. For with darkness and night removed, only day is left. This is the true meaning and explanation of the prophecy, which Jerome, Junius, and others also approve.

Cocceius tacitly criticizes that interpretation, both because it does not agree with the Hebrew distinction, according to which all light is taken away in v. 6, nor does 'precious' occur in the sense of rarity or dearness, and because in v. 7 it is not said: It shall be day, not day and night, but day or light. But it shall be day, not day and not night. But that distinction will be on shaky ground if you render the preceding words as Cocceius himself does: there shall not be light of brightnesses and coagulation, and you interpret it, there shall not be light partly of brightnesses or bright, partly of coagulation or nebulous (as Junius and Piscator) but it shall be one day. And since that Zakephkaton distinction does not always have force, nor is it unusual for 'precious' to be said for 'rare,' as the passage 1 Sam. 3:1 is an example, the remaining words explain each other. If it is one continuous day, it is not a successive day, nor an alternating night. Thus, therefore, the later words can be taken: And it shall be one (continuous) day, a day known to Jehovah, plainly singular; there shall not be (common) day, nor (common) night (following it), but there shall be at the time of evening (when night and darkness were bound to encroach) there shall be light. It shall therefore be pure day, see Isa. 60:16, Rev. 21:23. And therefore the interpretation of Tarnovius and Willius, which Junius and Piscator also handed down, correctly agrees with the Hebrew truth. Let the Belgian notes now be compared with these of ours, for I detect in them the same explanation of the Hebrew text that I have now provided. According to this interpretation, therefore, all those things bring in the same sense concerning the brightness of the light which is to be in the Church of the New Testament, and the later parts will be explanatory of the former.

If, however, anyone prefers that the former words designate a day covered in darkness and a time of tribulation for the Jews, with the evening bringing light, it will not be necessary to understand a time of peace and quiet under Jonathan, with Cornelius, Tirinus, and Menochius; rather, Castrius's explanation should be preferred entirely, concerning the calamities before the coming of Christ, during which, at the evening of the Jewish polity, the light of happiness and grace shone forth through the coming of Christ. More truly, he says, I think that the Prophet's discourse is about that whole time which preceded the coming of Christ, miserable and calamitous, in which both the worship and knowledge of God lay prostrate, for the priesthood was venal, and the scepter of the kingdom was in dispute and was being carried off to foreigners: whence there was no clear light, but it was concrete with darkness and the coldness of the knowledge of God and of charity; it was not a clear day, nor was it entirely night; indeed, there were some who were awaiting the redemption of Israel, but after these darknesses and night, there shone forth at evening the lucid day of Christ's advent and grace. For as Isaiah says, ch. 9:2, to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, a light has risen for them: which is called the eleventh hour by Christ himself in the parable of the vineyard: and John 12:35, Walk while you have the light, now is the light of the world, and at Rom. 13:12. The night has passed, but the day has approached: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light, as in the day let us walk honestly. There shall therefore be at evening, in the final hour of the world, the light of the Gospel so clear and perpetual that no night is to succeed it anymore, because it proceeds and grows until the perfect day: in which the fountains of waters will burst forth into the whole world, as the Prophet says immediately. And this seems a more convenient understanding. Whence almost all interpreters correctly understand those words, and it shall be one day, which is known to the Lord, not day nor night, and in the time of evening there shall be light: they understand it of that day which is not like ours, in which night succeeds day, and day night; for that will be a perpetual day without the succession of night, and therefore known to the Lord, not to men, who see the succession of days and nights. Thus Jerome explains it with his followers Lyra and Dionysius. Montanus, such as is certainly the day of Christ and of grace, Isa. 60:2. Behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples, but the Lord shall rise upon you, and his glory shall be seen upon you, and the nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the splendor of your rising, which shone upon us at the evening of the world. Calvin seems to look to the evening of calamities in general, when their end is present, the vicissitude of which is always in the Church, and he says that the whole of that time will be like a cloudy day, until Christ by his coming restores full light. Others explain it concerning the evening of the newest world, under which light is to rise. Lamb. Danaeus indeed refers that to extraordinary and miraculous effects, the coming of the Lord, but he thinks that it pertains to the times of the destruction of Jerusalem made by the Romans, not to the newest times, and he explains it concerning the coming of God in anger with his holy angels, with whom he shows himself to men full of majesty and terror, even if not in visible form, and he wishes the sad state of the Jews to be noted by those words 'there shall not be light,' etc., because at that time neither would light be pleasant or precious to them, nor would living itself be sweet and agreeable: yet Danaeus interprets the following words in such a way that he draws them also to the conversion of the Jews, which he thinks will happen toward the end of the world, etc. But to this day and state, so sad, there shall succeed, by the mercy of God, another day, not indeed at first entirely bright for them, but yet more joyful than the former, in the evening or end of which very second time and day, the true and full light shall shine for the Jews, since, as Paul says, the Jews shall then and towards the end of the world be converted, Rom. 11, 25. But there is no reason why we should restrict this day to the Jews, since the Prophet prophesies about the Church in general, and about the universal kingdom of Christ, as he explains himself in v. 9: And the Lord (Christ) shall be King over ALL the earth. Which cannot be restricted to the Jews. Nor do they agree with the calamity of the last times, which those men dream of, concerning mere light of joy, happiness, and tranquility towards the evening of the world. Whence those fabrications have already been refuted by the blessed Wigandus in the Jews and Chiliasts: the Jews and Chiliasts are insane, who dream that the whole world is to be converted to the Messiah before the last day, because Christ says: It shall be as in the days of Noah. Likewise: The Son of man shall scarcely find faith on earth.

Nor does Willius profit a whit, when he distinguishes between periods, namely the Philadelphian and the Laodicean, and under the Philadelphian indeed and penultimate he promises all things auspicious and joyful to the Church: but under the last, the Laodicean, he prophesies of a passive profanity about to reign everywhere, and the Church about to be oppressed: for that periodic distinction and an age of such great happiness and tranquility, which we would yet have to expect, Scripture knows nothing of; on the contrary, very many signs testify that our times, which we are now living in, are the very last, by which let those who will promise a certain universal conversion of the Jews and Gentiles with the fanatics, Chiliasts, and novel Prophets; we, in these extreme dregs of the world, repeat nothing else than that of the Spirit and the bride: Come Lord Jesus, come! But those of our own who refer these things to the evening of the world have no commerce with the fanatical opinion, but interpret them divinely as the rising of the light of the Gospel, rekindled in these last times through the ministry of Blessed Luther. Thus, therefore, the prophecy concerning the light of the New Testament, v. 6, 7, leaving aside those more alien interpretations, is explained by our people chiefly in two ways, either as intimating mere light in the Church in the time of the New Testament, so that the vicissitude of night and day or even evening may not be held; which is the exposition of Blessed Tarnovius: or so that distinct turns may be noted, first when there will not be the light of precious things and densities, which the Weimar Paraphrasts, along with Blessed Pappus, Winckelmann, and others, refer to the times of the Anti-Christ: then of the light of the Gospel about to rise toward the evening of the world, which they wish to look toward the times of the reformation of Blessed Luther: although others think that only in general those turns of the Church of the New Testament are designated here, but that no time in particular is looked to: Such three major vicissitudes are found in the ecclesiastical history of the New Testament. The first when there were shadows under the ten persecutions of the Tyrants, but toward the evening of those calamities, in the time of Constantine the Great, light arose. The second when shadows in turn encroached from the faction of the Arians and other heretics, which nevertheless were dispersed when light arose in the Church, until for the third time under the Anti-Christ shadows were made again: where, however, there was a day which was neither day nor night: because it had some light on account of some remaining knowledge of the parts of the Catechism and the light of the Gospel shining solidly through the confession of the witnesses of the truth: until toward the evening of the world a fuller light shone forth at the time of the Evangelical Reformation.

The Gloss of Grotius concerning all the angels bringing help to the Temple and those besieged in the temple, and concerning those words 'neither day nor night,' 'it will have neither the joy of day, nor the rest of night,' is clearly insipid. For that all angels concur with God for help of this kind is unwritten, and night and day are opposites. But joy and the lack of rest are by no means opposites. Then if light and day denote joy, which Grotius wishes, then night will surely indicate a sad state, not indeed rest. You may truly say of these Grotian commentaries: NOT LIGHT, BUT COLD AND FROST. For they are destitute of all light, and most are colder than cold and frost. Which the following will also testify.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET ERIT DIES UNA, QVÆ NOTA EST DOMINO, NEQVE DIES, NEQVE NOX) Tempus illud quod à Domino notum, id est, præfinitum est (sic πρόεγνω sæpe etiam in Novo Testamento sumitur) neque lætitiam diei habebit, neque noctis quietem.

ET IN TEMPORE VESPERI ERIT LUX) Cum minime sperabitur, adveniet liberatio, pace facta.

Adventum Domini, ut Grotius cum Papistis nonnullis Castrio, Cornelio, & Judæis vult, intelligendum esse de adventu ad ferendam Templo opem, tempore Judæ Maccabæi,non permittit antecedentium ratio. Vaticinatur enim Propheta de tempore N. T. quemadmodum antea ostensum.

Explicant autem hæc nonnulli de adventu Christi novissimo, utpote Junius, Piscator, Paraph. Belgici, & è nostris Wigandus, quia Christus ipse conjungit Prophetiam de interitu Hierosolymorum & de suo judicio futuro in fine mundi. Et sane cum de ascensione Christi è monte oliveti in cœlum actum fuerit, non videtur inconveniens reditum Christi ad judicium commemorari, quemadmodum Angeli in monte oliveti concionati de eo sunt Act. 1, 11. Hic Jesus, qui assumtus est à vobis in cœlum, sic veniet, quemadmodum vidistis eum euntem in cœlum. Hieronymus manifestum esse, censet, de secundo Salvatoris adventu hæc prædici, atque ita explicat: Cum dies adventus ejus fuerit impletus: non erit lex, sed frigus & gelu: refrigerata omnium charitate, & præ multitudine malorum, quæ superventura sunt, frigescentibus cunctis, & calorem pristinæ fidei perdentibus. Postquam autem omnes peccatores frigus suum geluque contraxerint: una dies erit atque perpetua, nequaquam sibi luce & tenebris, die & nocte succedentibus: sed ipse Dominus erit lux omnium. De quo Esaias plenius: Non erit,inquit, tibi sol in lucem diei, neque ortus lunæ illuminabit te per noctem, sed erit tibi Dominus lux æterna, & Deus tuus gloria tua. Denique in tempore vesperi, hoc est, tenebrarum & tristitiæ omnium peccatorum, sanctis lux erit, & una & æterna dies: quæ si nota erit Domino) neque enim ignorare poterit quam creavit) considerandum est quomodo dicat in Evangelio, quod diem illam nec angeli nec filius noverit, nisi solus Pater. De adventu ad judicium interpretatur etiam Cyrillus, Remigius, Hugo, Lyranus, Ribera, Sanchez & alii passim, qui contendunt hunc sensum esse literalem, fatente Cornelio.

Alii adventum spiritualem & assistentiam Domini fidelibus hic promitti censent. Christum nempe adfuturum fuis, cum Evangelium per orbem prædicabitur una cum angelis suis, & licet persequutio- nes adversus ipsos excitandæ sint non erit lux, sed tenebræ(angustiæ)& frigus & gelu (refrigescet charitas multorum) tempore tamen illo, quod Domino notum est,paulatim mitigatum iri persequutiones, ut sit q. mixtum quoddam ex tribulationum tenebris, & ex luce pacis atque tranquillitatis (erit dies, quæ non omnino dies erit, neque etiam mera nox) tandem vero restitutum iri lucem lætitiæ pacis & tranquillitatis (& in tempore vesperi erit iterum lux) quemadmodum explicat Osiander,cui consonat B. Balduinus p.862. Erit,inquit, in die illa, nempe cum prædicabitur Evangelium, in orbe terrarum non erit lux, sed frigus & gelu. In Hebræo est: non erit lux יקרות יקפאון pretiositatum densitatis, hoc est,non erit dies serenus & tranquillus,quales solent in pretio haberi,sed asper ac ingratus,ac persequutionum quadam quasi nebula caligineque condensatus:quin & Deus quoddam sibi reservavit tempus,quod neq; dies,neque nox erit: & in tempore vesperi erit lux,hoc est, etsi persecutiones nonnihil remittant, non tamen erit perpetua serenitas,sed multa tempestate mixta,ut tempus illud crepusculo similius videatur, quam dici,donec tandem sub vesperam mundi tenebræ illæ dispellantur, ut serena lux illucescat. B. D. Cramerus per lucem pretiosam Urim, per nivem coagulatam ut nonnulli reddunt, Thumim intelligit,quod ea defutura sint.Sed illa jam defuere tempore V.T. in templo secundo, nec durarunt usque ad N. T. neque commode per istas voces exprimi aut intelligi possunt. Ludov. de Dieu mendum ponit in vocalibus, & legit יִקְפָאוּן concrescant, h.m. non erit lux pretiosa, concrescent, id est, Cœlum, Sol, Luna. Sed nostrum non est mendum in textu au- thentico admittere, eumque emendare. Et sensus ille contortus est.

Joh. Coccejus reddit: non erit lux claritatum & coagulationis, ex Ebræa distincti- one colligens primo in genere tolli lucem, deinde in specie claram & crassam; verbis cæteris: Et erit dies, non nox, vult notari statum rerum in Ecclesia, ut nec possint sibi de rebus melioribus gratulari, & ver- sentur in magno metu: rursus sint absque notabili malo, hostibus ad impotentiam redactis.

Quantum vero ad complementum, impletum id censet Osiander, luce exorta Christianis sub Con- stantino M. B. Winckelmannus, Papp. & Vinarien- ses referunt ad nostra tempora, & ortum lucis Evan- gelicæ è tenebris Papalibus. B. Balduinus generali- ter de religionis negotio explicat, quod revera talem conditionem ab initio prædicati Evangelii ad hæc usque tempora habuit, nunquam enim semper fuit serena lux, sed infausta persequutionum caligine obnubilata.

B. Tarnovius verba paulo aliter red- dit, eademque itidem in genere accipit de statu Ec- clesiæ tempore N. T. sed in συγκρίσει ad Vet. Test. tempora, h. m. Et erit die illo post universalem Ev- angelii prædicationem, ut major lux Ecclesiæ affulge- at, quam hactenus splenduit, & ut dies agnitionis Je- hovæ non sit varius ac instabilis, modo serenus, mo- do nubilus, sed certo æquabilique tenore, quam- diu Deus volet, decurrat. Non enim erit tum lux pretiosa & densa, seu tenebris obnubilata, qualis esse solet sæpissime tempore hyemis, cum nix terras ob- ruit. Sed erit dies unus continuus ac perfectus, quem efficiet, curabit & conservabit Deus, quam- diu ipsi visum fuerit; & ille dies erit notus, atque probatus Iehovæ, non varius, ut antea in V. T. ex die & nocte constans, sed mira coruscans luce Rom. 13, 12. nam erit, ut tempore vespertino, quando solet adve- sperascere & nox adventare, sit lux & sol, Ecclesiæ- que dies non occidat, quando nox omnis & obscu- ritas tum exulabit. Quem sensum cur reprobare debeamus, nullam video causam. Et facile conso- nat Willii versio; de qua postea.

Quamvis vero verba illa de adventu Domini, & OMNIUM sanctorum cum eo, (ut in Vulgata sonant) videantur inferre adventum novissimum Christi, συνέχεια tamen antecedentium & consequentium hæc ad statum potius Ecclesiæ in hoc seculo, quam in futuro spectare, docet. Et verba illa ex Ebræo ita reddenda sunt: Et veniet Dominus Deus meus : & omnes sancti tecum: quod pronomen non Deum respicit, sed Ecclesiam, vel cætum fidelium, ut recte observavit B. Tarnovius, qui hæc de angelis explicat: Et omnes sancti angeli ejus tecum, ô Ecclesia, sunt, tibi adstant, tibi ministeria præbent ex Dei mandato Ps. 91, 11. Dan. 8, 13. Ebr. 1, 14. Quæ de sanctis & fideli- bus quibusvis non minnus commode intelligi po- terunt h. m. Aderit tum Dominus Deus meus gratio- so præsentia suis, eosque fovebit, reget ac tuebitur: & erunt tecum, parve grex, qui effugies horridam illam vallem Synagogæ Judaicæ, omnes sancti. At- que hactenus non male Willius sanctorum consen- sionem & unionem universalem in Ecclesia Christi fu- turam unum pastorem futurum, & unum, ovile.

Qui vero in eo fallitur, quod hæc restringat ad tempora novissima, quodque illis temporibus singularem pol- liceatur Dei præsentiam, qualem antea nunquam fuerit Ecclesia experta.

De cætero non male in sensu vocum & phrasium eruendo occupatur Willius: Dicitur lux non futura יְקָרוֹת יִקְפָאוּן. Hieron. Et erit in die illa non erit lux, sed frigus & gelu. Ita quoque LXX. & Chaldæus,

Junius, lux pretiosa & densa. Pagninus lux pretiosa & nix coagulata. Montanus ad verbum expressit lux pretiositatum & coagulationum. יקר est pretio- sitas, pretium, & quæ pretium comitari solet raritas Gloria, splendor. Hinc Drusius tentat vertere lu- cem raram, quia rarum & densum opponuntur, & plerumque hæc interpretes ut discreta accipiunt Sed ego censeo omnino duas hasce voces conjungendas ac de una & eadem luce accipiendas, hoc sensu, lucem non pretiosam & densam futuram, id est, non multi- constitutam, obviam futuram, & expositam omni- bus, ut pretium pro ea solvere opus non sit, non e- tiam futuram densam sive obscuram. Ad verba se- quentia: Sed erit dies unus: Sensus est, Diem sive tempus illud, quod Dominus creaturus, non constitu- rum ex intervallo dierum & noctium, sed die perpe- tua, quia sub vesperam etiam lux sit futura. Subla- tis enim tenebris & nocte, sola dies relinquitur. Hæc vera prophetiæ mens ac explicatio est, quam etiam Hieronymus, Junius aliique approbant.

Perstringit eam interpretationem tacite Cocce- jus, tum quod non congruat distinctioni Ebrææ, juxta quam omnis lux auferatur v. 6. neq; pretiosum in notione raritatis vel caritatis occurtat, tum quod v. 7. non dicatur; Erit dies, non dies, & nox, sed dies vel lux. Sed erit dies, non dies & non nox. Sed distin- ctio illa in vado erit, si ita priora verba reddas cum ipso Coccejo: non erit lux claritatum & coagulatio- nis, & interpreteris, non erit lux partim claritatum seu clara, partim coagulationis coagulata sive ne- bulosa (ut Junius & Piscator) sed erit dies unus. Et quum distinctio illa Zakephkaton non semper vim habeat, neque insolens sit pretiosum dici pro raro, ut exemplo est locus 1. Sam. 3, 1. verba reliqua se mu- tuo explicant. Si dies unus continue est, non est suc- cessive dies, nec nox alternans. Ita ergo accipi ver- ba posteriora poterunt: Et erit dies unus (continuus) dies notus Jehovæ plane singularis, non erit die (com- munis) neque nox (communis eam excipiens) sed e- rit tempore vesperæ, (quo nox, & tenebræ ingruere debebant) erit lux. Merus ergo erit dies, vid. Es. 60, 16. Apoc. 21, 23. Ideoque recte ita convenit Ebraicæ veritati Tarnovii & Willii interpretatio, quam etiam tradidit Junius & Piscator. Conferantur jam cum his nostris notæ Belgicæ, nam deprehendo in iis eandem, quam nunc tradidi, textus Ebræi explica- tionem. Juxta hanc itaque interpretationem o- mnia illa eundem sensum inferunt de claritate lu- cis, quæ futura sit in Ecclesia N. T. & posteriora erunt ἐξηγητικὰ priorum.

Si autem quis malit verbis prioribus designari diem tenebris obductam & tempus tribulationis Judæorum per vesperam lucem afferentem, non necessum erit intelligere tempus pacis & quietis sub Jonatha, cum Cornelio, Tirino & Menochio, quin præferenda o- mnino foret Castrii explicatio, de calamitatibus an- te adventum Christi, quibus ad vesperam politiæ Ju- daicæ illuxit lux felicitatis ac gratiæ per adventum Christi. Verius, inquit ille, existimo, sermonem esse Prophetæ de tempore illo toto, quod præcessit adventum Christi, misero, & calamitoso, in quo & Dei cultus, co- gnitioque jacebat, nam & sacerdotium venale erat, & sceptrum regni sub dissidio erat, & ad extraneos defe- rebatur: unde non erat lux clara, sed concreta tene- bris, & frigore scientiæ Dei, & charitatis, non erat dies clara, nec nox omnino; quin aliqui erant, qui expectabant redemptionem Israel, at post bas tenebras, & noctem illuxit ad vesperam dies lucida Christi ad- ventus & gratiæ. Nam ut ait Esaias cap. 9, 2. seden- tibus in tenebris & umbra mortis lux orta est eis: quæ vocatur undecima hora à Christo ipso in parabola vineæ: & Johan. 12, 35. Ambulate dum lucem ha- betis, nunc lux est mundi, & ad Rom. 13, 12. Nox præcessit, dies autem appropinquavit: abjiciamus ergo opera tenebrarum, & induamur arma lucis, sicut in die honeste ambulemus. Erit ergo sub ve- sperum, in extrema hora mundi, lux Evangelii adeo clara & perpetua, ut nulla amplius illi sit successura nox, quia procedit & crescit usque ad perfectam diem: in qua fontes aquarum erumpent in univer- sum mundum, ut statim ait Propheta. Atque hæc commodior videtur intelligentia. Unde recte fe- re omnes interpretes illa verba, & erit dies una, quæ nota est Domino, non dies neque nox, & in tempore ve- speri erit lux: de ea die intelligunt, quæ non est si- milis nostris, in quibus succedit diei nox, & nocti dies; illa enim perpetua dies erit absque successu noctis, & ideo nota Domino, non hominibus, qui successum dierum & noctium videmus. Ita expli- cant Hieron. cum sectatoribus Lyra, Dionys. Mont. qualis certe est dies Christi, & gratiæ Esa. 60, 2. Ec- ce tenebræ operient terram, & caligo populos, super te autem orietur Dominus, & gloria ejus in te videbi- tur, & ambulabunt gentes in lumine tuo, & reges in splendore ortus tui, qui sub Vesperam mundi illuxit nobis. Calvinus videtur vesperam calamitatum in genere respicere, cum finis earum adest, quarum vicissitudo semper est in Ecclesia, totumque tem- pus illud dicit simile fore diei turbido, usque dum Christus adventu suo plenam lucem restituat. Alii de vespera mundi novissimi explicant, sub qua lux oritura sit. Lamb. Danæus ad effecta extraordina- ria & mira refert quidem illam adventum Domi- ni, sed eundem ad tempora excidii Hierosolymitani per Romanos facti pertinere putat, non ad tempora novissima, & de adventu Dei irati cum suis angelis sanctis, cum quibus sese plenum majestatis & terro- ris, etsi non visibili forma, hominibus ostendit, ex- ponit, ac tristem Judæorum statum verbis istis non e- rit lux, &c. notari vult, quod eo tempore neque lux illis futura sit grata vel pretiosa, neque ipsum etiam vivere dulce & suave: sequentia tamen verba sic interpretatur Danæus, ut ea etiam ad conversionem Judæorum, quam sub finem mundi futuram putat, pertrahat, h.m. sed hunc tam tristi diei & statui succe- det, Dei misericordia, alius non quidem primum pla- ne illis lucidus: sed tamen superiore lætior dies, in cu- jus ipsius secundi temporis & diei vespertino seu extremo lumen verum & plenum lucebit Judæis, quoniam ad Christum, ut inquit Paulus, Judæi tunc & sub finam mundi convertentur Rom. 11, 25. Sed non est causa, cur hunc diem ad Judæos restringa- mus, quum de Ecclesia generatim vaticinetur Pro- pheta, ac de regno Christi universali, uti v. 9. sese ex- plicat: Et erit Dominus (Christus) Rex super O- MNEM terram. Quæ ad Judæos restringi neque- unt. Neque conveniunt calamitati novissimorum temporum, quæ illi homines de mera luce lætitiæ, felicitatis & tranquillitatis sub Vesperam mundi somniant. Unde ista commenta jam B.
