Wigandus in Judæis & Chiliastis profligavit: insaniunt Judæi & Chiliastæ, qui somniant totum orbem terrarum ad Messiam convertendum esse ante novissimum diem, quia Christus inquit: Erit sicut in diebus Noah. Item: Filius hominis vix reperturus est fidem in terris.

Nec hilum proficit Willius, cum inter periodos distinguit, Philadelphensem nempe & Laodicenam, ac sub Philadelphensi quidem ac penultima omnia fausta & læta pollicetur Ecclesiæ: sub ultima vero Laodicena vaticinatur de passiva profanitate ubique regnatura, & Ecclesia opprimenda: nam distinctio- nem illam periodicam & seculum, quod adhuc ex- pectare habeamus, tantæ felicitatis & tranquillitatis ignorat scriptura, imo nostra, quæ nunc agimus, tempora, novissima esse, signa testantur plurima, quibus universalem quandam Judæorum, & gen- tium conversionem cum fanaticis, Chiliastis, & no- vellis Prophetis polliceantur, qui velint, nos in hoc extrema mundi fæce, nihil aliud ingeminamus, quam illud Spiritus & sponsæ: Veni Domine Jesu, veni! Qui vero è nostris ad vesperam mundi hæc referunt, nihil commercii cum fanatica opinione habeant, sed de exortu lucis Evangelicæ extremis his temporibus per ministerium B. Lutheri iterum accensæ divinitus interpretantur. Ita ergo vatici- nium de luce Nov. Testam. v. 6. 7. relictis alienio- ribus istis interpretationibus bifariam potissimum explicatur à nostris, vel ut lucem meram intimet in Ecclesia tempore Nov. Testam. ut vicissitudo no- ctis & diei aut etiam vesperæ non habeatur; quæ B. Tarnovii ἔκθεσις est: vel ut distinctæ vices no- tentur, primum cum non erit lux pretiositatum & densitatum, quas tenebras ad tempora Anti-Christi referunt Vinarienses Paraphrastæ, cum B. Pappo, Winckelmanno, & aliis: deinde lucis Evangelicæ sub vesperam mundi orituræ, quæ ad tempora refor- mationis B. Lutheri spectare volunt: etsi alii solum in genere vices illas Ecclesiæ Nov. Testam. hic desi- gnari censeant, nullum vero in specie tempus re- spici: Quales vicissitudines trinæ potiores in hi- storia Ecclesiastica Nov. Testam. reperiuntur. Pri- ma cum tenebræ fuere sub decem perseqvutio- nibus Tyrannorum sub vesperam autem calami- tatum illarum tempore Constantini M. lux orta est. Altera cum tenebræ vicissim ingruerunt à factione Arianorum & aliorum hæreticorum, quæ tamen discussæ exorta luce in Ecclesia, us- que dum tertio sub Anti-Christo tenebræ factæ sint denuo: ubi tamen dies fuit, quæ neque dies neque nox: quia aliquid lucis habuit ob reli- ctam aliquam notitiam partium Catecheseos & so- lide emicantem per testium veritatis confessio- nem lucem Evangelicam: donec sub mundi ve- speram lux plenior effulserit tempore Reforma- tionis Evangelicæ.

Grotii Glossa de omnibus angelis ad opem feren- dam Templo & obsessis in templo, & ad illa verba neque dies neque nox, neque lætitiam diei habebit, neque noctis quietem, plane insipida est. Nam omnes angelos concurrere cum Deo ad auxilium ejus- modi ἄγραφον, & opposita sunt nox & dies. Lætitia autem & quietis defectus minime sunt opposita. Tum si lux & dies gaudium notat, quod vult Gro- tius, utique nox tristem statum indigitabit, non vero quietem. Vere dixeris de his commentis Grotia- nis: NON LUX, SED FRIGUS ET GE- LU. Sunt enim omni luce destituta, & frigore ac gelu frigidiora pleraque. Quod etiam sequen- tia testabuntur.

## 14:8
Verse 8.

AND IT SHALL BE IN THAT DAY.) After those calamitous times. LIVING WATERS SHALL GO OUT FROM JERUSALEM.) Excellent aqueducts will be made, as in deep peace. It is the same as what is said in Ezekiel 47 and Joel 3:18, where see the remarks. TO THE EASTERN SEA) The Asphaltite [Dead Sea]. TO THE HINDER SEA.) Thus the Syrian sea is called, Deut. 11:24 and 34, because the West is called the hinder part by the Hebrews. IN SUMMER AND IN WINTER THEY SHALL BE.) They shall be perennial waters, not like torrents, which fail in summer.

Grotius is concerned only with aqueducts, lest the waters fail the Jews to both the eastern and the hinder or western sea. But who would believe that God promised His faithful nothing more sublime with such magnificent promises? Waters not common are indicated, but living waters making for spiritual life, not to be diverted into Jerusalem, lest it be destitute of water, through aqueducts and channels, but about to have their exit and go out from Jerusalem: the matter is not about the fountains of Siloam, Dogel, the Dragon, or the torrent of Cedron, or the sheep pool, not about the fountain of Gihon, upper and lower, not about the aqueducts of Gibeon to be restored, as both the Jews and the Jesuits, Cornelius à Lapide and Tirinus, trifle: but it is about waters bubbling up in the city itself, and about to be led from it and go out toward the eastern and western sea, toward the east and the west, and toward all the regions of the world, which Tirinus himself acknowledges with Paulus à Palacio, and thus about to irrigate the whole orb of the earth. These waters are at no time failing: But who would say that those fountains never failed from that time? These living and perennial waters, with light that will never fail, will not refresh and recreate the faithful, the people of the Lord, with worldly happiness or external tranquility (which very often failed, and at length ceased entirely), but with spiritual and perennial blessedness and peace joined together: and will bring them perpetual joy and pleasure, Psalm 36:9. Those living waters will be most fruitful; for they will so drench and irrigate the whole earth, that the whole earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters of the sea, Isaiah 11:11, because the Lord God will be King, will be acknowledged as King, and will be worshipped throughout the whole earth. Those living waters, according to the interpretation of Christ, become in us a fountain of water springing up into eternal life, John 4:14. And therefore the Interpreters here acknowledge with great consensus that the spiritual waters of the Evangelical doctrine, or the spiritual benefits of the Holy Spirit and the streams of divine grace are noted. Eusebius, book VI, Evangelical Demonstration, ch. 18. Cyril of Alexandria, Jerome in this place and Ezekiel 47, Theodoret, Augustine in the book against the Fulgentian Donatists, ch. VI, Haymo, Remigius, Hugo, Vatablus, Montanus, Isidorus Clarius, and after Blessed Luther all of our people to a man, and also most of the Doctors of the Reformed party, which are about to irrigate the whole world, and are therefore said to go out to the eastern and western sea, and to flow perpetually, so that they never fail as long as winter and summer shall be. Which waters were to go out from Jerusalem, because the beginning of the Evangelical proclamation concerning the remission of sins, in the name of Jesus, at his command, had to be made there under the New Testament, but were to overflow into the whole world, because by the eastern sea and the hinder sea, which circles Palestine to the west, the eastern and western region is signified. The Jesuit Castrius also followed this sense, although he believed that in the preceding passages the discourse was about the time of the Maccabees. Which likewise one may observe in L. Danaeus, a Reformed [theologian]: as also in Gwalther. By waters he shadows forth the grace of God, for the reason that these both wash away sins and refresh sad souls. He calls them living, partly to denote the perpetual and inexhaustible flow of that grace, and partly on account of the effect, because they confer life and salvation. Furthermore, he establishes the widest boundaries of grace, namely the furthest seas to the East and West, by which he embraces the whole world. He adds that they do not fail in winter or summer, which pertains to the declaration of that which we said a little before concerning the perennial flow of grace. But if you compare these things according to the letter with the histories, you will find nothing similar to these things, unless all things are referred to Christ through anagoge. For with this [one] manifested in the flesh, the grace of God was diffused through the preaching of the Gospel from Jerusalem through the whole world to all nations, and many came from the rising and the setting [of the sun], that they might recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And it is full of consolation that the flow of this grace is neither dried up in summer nor constricted by winter frost: but in both favorable and adverse circumstances it suggests those things which serve our salvation. Some think that these things also refer to Baptism, through which the streams of grace also spread themselves. 'Living waters, MANY refer to Baptism,' says Jerome. The explanation of Theodoret contributes to this, joining the Sacraments to the Evangelical doctrine, which flowed from the side of Christ: By this is designated the saving proclamation, which has pervaded the whole world, and has enriched the East and the West with divine doctrine. At the same time, according to this history, one can discern the prophetic truth, which explains how on that day a fountain was opened from the holy side, from which flowed a double stream of mysteries, I mean water and blood, which he who saw it testified: one cleansing and purifying us from sins; the other nourishing, and watering, and causing to germinate. Danaeus does not deny this on p. 1005. By the name of waters, the spiritual graces of God are signified, Joel 3:18, Ezek. 36:35, John 7:38, of which our Baptism, instituted by God, is without doubt the type and sacrament. We also have Willius in agreement, even if he is mistaken in the application of the time to his Philadelphia: by both seas, the whole world and its regions, both eastern and western, can be understood. And the sense is that the grace of the Church will be derived most copiously to all parts of the world. Finally, the endurance and continuity of this flow is added: they will be in summer and in winter, that is, they will flow continuously and will endure. For the heat of summer is accustomed to dry up rivers, while the cold and frost of winter are accustomed to freeze them. Therefore, this flow will be perpetual and continuous, because they will neither be dried up in summer nor frozen in winter. Cocceius: 'Those to whom this grace is to come,' he says, 'are compared with the Dead Sea and the Great Sea.' So that Jerusalem is situated in the middle. We can understand the peoples who are to the east and west of the Church, so that in this way the whole world may be heard. Calvin, though otherwise willingly Judaizing, has no doubt that these things pertain to the times of the New Testament. 'There is no doubt,' he says, 'that this prophecy ought to be referred to the kingdom of Christ, which is sufficiently gathered from similar passages; therefore the Prophet has hitherto discussed the many afflictions which were impending, lest the Jews should either waver or fail entirely: but now he lifts up their spirits to the kingdom of Christ, from whence was to be hoped not only liberation from all evils, but a full restoration of the Church and, as it were, a recall of the world; there is also no doubt that there is a tacit antithesis underlying it between living waters and others, which easily dry up, therefore he says there will be a continuous flow in summer and winter.' We know that Judea labors under a scarcity of water, and it is known that there were no waters in the whole circuit of Jerusalem: there was only the fountain of Siloam: and from there a sufficiently good supply of water, and one which would suffice for all the uses of the citizens. But the Prophet promises living waters, which, namely, are not like torrents, but have a continuous flow, although he seems to look higher, so that by living waters he understands spiritual ones; thus he compares those waters to all earthly rivers, as if to say the fountain from which two rivers will arise will be inexhaustible, so that its abundance may never fail, but that it may send forth its rivers from one sea even to the other opposite sea and thus irrigate long tracts of land. Conf. and Annot. Belgicae. Cornelius also acknowledges this proposed sense, p. 298. Understand most especially the waters of the doctrine and grace of the Gospel: for Christ and the Apostles brought these forth from Jerusalem, as if from a matrix, and derived them through the whole East and West, etc. And the following words, written with the rays of the sun, confirm this explanation, which clearly describe the universal kingdom of Christ through the whole world, even though Grotius strives to obscure the same with unhappy inventions. Some refer these to the heavenly Jerusalem, such as Lyra, Dionysius, Piscator, who here compare Rev. 22:1. But the context proves that this is about the Church; just as Piscator himself interprets what follows concerning the Church in these lands. Junius explains the waters as irrigating the whole Church, which he says is adumbrated by the type of Judea, enclosed by the Mediterranean Sea and the Asphaltite Lake.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET ERIT IN DIE ILLA.) Post illa calamitosa tempora. EXIBVNT AQVÆ VIVÆ DE JERVSALEM.) Aquæductus fient egregii, ut in alta pace. Idem est quod dicitur Ezech. 47. & Joel. 3, 18. ubi dicta vide. AD MARE ORIENTALE) Asphaltiten. AD MARE NOVISSIMVM.) Sic dicitur mare Syriacum. Deut. 11, 24. & 34. quia Occidens Hebræis pars posterior appellatur. IN ÆSTATE ET IN HYEME ERVNT.) Erunt perennes aquæ, non ut torrentium, quæ æstate defi- ciunt.

De aquæductibus solum solicitus est Grotius, ne aquæ deficiant Judæis ad utrumque mare orienta- le, & novissimum vel occidentale. Quis vero cre- dat, Deum fidelibus suis tam magnificis promissis nihil sublimius pollicitum esse? Aquæ non vulga- res indigitantur, sed aquæ vivæ ad vitam spiritualem facientes, non in Hierosolymam, ne aqua destituatur, per aquæductus & canales derivandæ, sed Hiero- solyma exitum suum habituræ & egressuræ: non de fontibus Siloë, Dogel, Draconis, aut de torrente Cedron, vel probatica piscina, non de fonte Gihon, superi- ori & inferiori, non de aquæductu Gabaon instau- randis res est, uti nugantur & Judæi & Jesuitæ, Cor- nelius à Lapide ac Tirinus: de aquis in ipsa urbe sca- turientibus, & ex ea traducendis & exituris versus mare orientale, & occidentale, versus orientem & oc- cidentem, & versus omnes mundi plagas, quod cum Paulo à Palacio agnoscit Tirinus ipse, adeoque to- tum terrarum orbem irrigaturis agitur. Aquæ hæ sunt nullo unquam tempore deficientes: At frontes illos nunquam defecisse ex eo tempore, quis dixe- rit? Aquæ hæ vivæ ac perennes cum luce nunquam defitura, non mundanæ felicitatis, aut externæ tran- quillitatis (quæ sæpe sæpius defecit, ac tandem prorsus desiit) sed spiritualis & perennis beatitudinis & pacis conjunctæ simul, fideles, populum Domini reficient, ac recreabunt: & lætitiam ac voluptatem perpetuam ipsis afferent Psal. 36, 9. Aquæ illæ vivæ maxime fæcundæ erunt; nam ita perfundent & irri- gabunt omnem terram, ut terra omnis plena futu- ra sit cognitione Domini, sicut aquis maris Esa. 11, 11. quia Dominus Deus Rex erit, pro Rege agnoscetur, & coletur per universam terram. Aquæ illæ vivæ juxta interpretationem Christi, fiunt nobis in fon- tem aquæ in vitam æternam salientis, Johan. 4. v. 34. Ideoque agnoscunt hic magno consensu Interpp. aquas spirituales doctrinæ Evangelicæ, vel spiritualia beneficia Spiritus S. & gratiæ divinæ fluenta notari. Euseb. l. VI. Demonstr. Evangel. c. 18. Cyrill. A- lexandr. Hieronym. in h. l. & Ezech. 47. Theodore- tus, Augustinus libr. contr. Fulgent. Donatist. c. VI. Haymo, Remigius, Hugo, Vatablus, Montanus, Isido- rus Clarius, & post B. Lutherum nostrates ad unum omnes, nec non Reformatæ partis Doctores pleri- que, quæ universum orbem irrigaturæ sint, atque ideo ad orientale & occidentale mare exituræ dican- tur, & perpetuo manaturæ, ita ut nunquam deficiant, quamdiu hyems & æstas erit. Quæ aquæ ex Hieru- salem exituræ erant, quia ibi initium præconii Ev- angelici de remissione peccatorum, in nomine Je- su, ad ejus mandatum sub Nov. Testam. fieri de- buit, sed redundaturæ in totum orbem, quia per ori- entale mare, & mare novissimum, quod ad occasum circuit Palæstinam, plaga orientalis & occidentalis significatur. Quem sensum etiam sequutus est Jesuita Castrius, etsi in superioribus de Maccabæo- rum tempore sermonem esse crediderit. Quod iti- dem in L. Danæo, Reformato observare licet: ut & in Gvalthero. Per aquas Dei gratiam adumbrat, eo quod hæc & à peccatis abluit, & animos tristes recreat. Vivas vero dicit, partim ut perpetuum & inexhaustum illius gratiæ fluxum denotet, par- tim propter effectum, quia vitam & salutem con- ferunt. Terminos præterea gratiæ latissimos con- stituit, extrema nimirum maria ad Orientem & Oc- cidentem, quibus totum orbem terrarum comple- ctitur. Addit, quod nec hyeme, nec æstate deficiant, quod ad ejus declarationem pertinet, quod paulo ante de perenni gratiæ fluxu diximus. Quod si vero hæc juxta literam cum historiis conferas, ni- hil horum simile reperies, nisi per Anagogen omnia ad Christum referantur. Hoc enim in carne ma- nifestato, gratia Dei per Evangelii prædicationem ex Jerusalem per totum orbem in omnes gentes diffusa est, & multi venerunt ab ortu & occasu, ut in regno Dei discumbant cum Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Ja- cobo. Et consolationis plenum est, quod hujus gratiæ fluxus nec æstate siccatur, nec gelu hyberno constringitur: sed in secundis simul & adversis ea suggerit, quæ nostræ saluti inserviunt. Nonnulli hæc Baptismum quoq; respicere censent, per quem quoque se diffundant gratiæ fluenta. Aquas viventes, MULTI ad Baptismum referunt, inquit Hieronymus. Quo facit Theodoreti explicatio, conjungens doctrinæ Evangelicæ Sacramenta, quæ ex latere Christi profluxere: Per hoc designatur salutare præconium, quod per universum orbem pervasit, & Orientem atque Occidentem divina cumulavit doctrinâ. Simul juxta hanc historiam cernere est prophetic veritatem, quæ explicat, ut illa die ex sancto latere patuit fons, ex quo duplices mysteriorum latices, aquam, inquam & sanguinem, quæ qui vidit, testatus est unam purgantem, & nos à peccatis expiantem: alteram nutrientem, & rigantem & germinare facientem. Non abnuit Danæus p. 1005. Nomine aquarum spirituales Dei gratiæ significantur Joel. 3, 18. Ezech. 36, 35. Joh. 7. 38. quarum typus & sacramentum est procul dubio Baptismus noster à Deo institutus. Habemus etiam consentientem Willium, etsi in temporis applicatione ad suam Philadelphiam, fallatur: per mare utrumque mundus totus, ejusque plaga cùm orientalis tum occidentalis intelligi potest. Et sensus est, gratiam Ecclesiæ ad omnes orbis partes copiosissime derivatum iri. Additur denique duramentum & continuitas hujus fluxus: per æstatem & per hyemem futuræ sunt, id est, continuo decurrent, & durabunt. Solent enim ardores æstatis flumina exsiccare, frigora vero & gelu hyemis eadem congelare. Itaque perpetuus & continuus hic fluxus futurus est, quia nec æstate siccabuntur, nec hyeme congelascent. Coccejus: Hi ad quos hæc gratia perventura, comparantur, inquit, cum mari mortuo & mari magno. Ita ut Hierosolyma sit sita in medio. Possumus intelligere populos, qui sunt Ecclesiæ ad orientem & occasum, ut ita totus mundus exaudiatur. Calvinus, libenter alias Judaizans, nullus dubitat ad N. T. tempora hæc pertinere. Non dubium est, inquit, quin hôc vaticinium referri debeat ad regnum Christi, quod satis colligitur ex similibus locis, ergo Prophetâ hactenus disseruit de multis afflictionibus, quæ instabant, ne Judæi vel labascerent, vel prorsus deficerent: sed nunc attollit eorum animos ad regnum Christi, unde speranda erat non tantum liberatio, ab omnibus malis, sed plena restitutio Ecclesiæ & quasi revocatio mundi, non dubium etiam est, subesse tacitam antithesin inter aquas vivas & alias, quæ facile exarescunt, ideo dicit fore continuum fluxum æstate & hyeme. Scimus Judæam laborare penuria aquarum, & per totum circuitum Jerosolymitanum scitur nullas fuisse aquas: erat duntaxat fons Siloe: & inde satis bona copia aquarum & quæ sufficeret ad omnes civium usus. Propheta autem aquas promittit vivas, quæ scilicet non sint similes torrentibus, sed habeant continuum fluxum, quanquam videtur altius respicere, ut scilicet per aquas vivas intelligat spirituales; ita comparat aquas istas omnibus terrenis fluviis q. d. fontem ex quo orientur duo fluvii, fore inexhaustum, ita ut ejus ubertas nunquam deficiat, quin emittat fluvios suos, ab uno mari usque ad alterum mare oppositum & ita longos terrarum tractus irriget. Conf. & Annot. Belgicæ. Agnofcit etiam hunc sensum propositum Cornel. p. 298. Potissime intellige aquas doctrinæ & gratiæ Evangelicæ: has enim Christus & Apostoli ex Jerusalem, quasi ex matrice eructarunt & derivarunt per totum Orientem & Occidentem, &c. Atque hanc explicationem confirmant sequentia verba, Solis radiis scripta, quæ universale regnum Christi per totum orbem luculenter describunt, etsi eadem etiam obfuscare satagat Grotius infelicibus fuis commentis. Nonnulli ad cælestem Hierosoly- mam ea referunt, utpote Lyra, Dionysius, Piscator, qui hic conferunt Apoc. 22, 1. Sed contextus e- vincit de Ecclesia hic agi; quemadmodum etiam Piscator ipse ea, quæ sequuntur de Ecclesia in his terris interpretatur. Junius de aquis explicat Ec- clesiam totam irrigantibus, quam Judæa typo adum- brari ait, mari mediterraneo circumclusam & Aspal- tite lacu.

## 14:9
Ver. 9.

AND THE LORD SHALL BE KING OVER ALL THE EARTH.) The Jews, free from foreign empires, will worship God according to their own judgment. This happened because the neighboring kings, hostile to one another, vied in their zeal and favors toward the Jews. Which history is in Josephus XIII. 4. 5. IN THAT DAY THE LORD SHALL BE ONE AND HIS NAME ONE.) One God shall be worshipped, and shall be invoked by oath.

This is an overly violent distortion. For the Prophet is not dealing with Judea, or a particular kingdom, but with the whole earth; he says not that the Jews will be freed from external injuries, but that Christ will be King through the whole world, and that He will be celebrated by all, with the worship of idols abolished. AND JEHOVAH Jesus Christ SHALL BE KING OVER ALL THE EARTH, He will rule in the whole world. IN THAT DAY THE LORD SHALL BE UNIQUE, AND HIS NAME SHALL BE UNIQUE. No one but one God shall be worshipped, different gods shall not be acknowledged, as once among the Jews, Baal, Astaroth, Moloch, and among the nations Jupiter, Saturn, etc. But all Christians will worship one God, and His name shall be unique, His worship shall be unique. For the Gentiles worshipped idols in various ways, but God is to be followed only by the worship defined by Himself. So also Willius: The Lord alone shall be king of His people, and besides Him no one shall rule over the Church, nor shall any other be worshipped besides Him: or in other words, God shall be acknowledged by the pious, one and the same shall be worshipped, they shall not have a God besides the one, nor will they honor the same in any other than one way. Thus this member is opposed to idolatry and schisms. And it is frequent that the name of God is put for His worship. Thus the name of God is used in Micah 4: 'All peoples will walk each in the name of his god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever.' Even those who among the Papists snatched the former parts to the times of the Maccabees, and in that preceded Grotius with the Jews, were forced to confess that these things pertain to the times of the New Testament. Menochius, to whom Grotius attributes much: This, he says, scarcely fits the Maccabees and their time, but fits the Messiah and the Church aptly, for Christ, with the Gentile world converted to the faith, propagated His kingdom throughout the whole world. Tirinus also: THE LORD GOD SHALL BE KING, and shall be worshipped like a King OVER ALL THE EARTH, not of Judea only, but also of the whole world, namely through Christ who was soon to follow, and with idols driven away, ONE Lord everywhere, AND ONE NAME OF HIS, that is, of Christ, shall be celebrated in the whole world. Thus St. Jerome, Remigius, Rupertus, Haymo, Vatablus, Ribera, and à Lapide. So he. Castrius notes that all understand it to be about Christ being worshipped and invoked over all the earth alone, with idols abandoned, and that only Lyra and Dionysius explain it concerning the kingdom of Christ reigning in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Moreover, Jerome here noted the false interpretation of the Jews and Judaizing Christians: For to it the invention of certain fanatics today approaches with a certain rationale: The Jews and Judaizing Christians promise themselves for the end time the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem, and the waters going out from the midst of it, which flow down to both seas: when circumcision is to be practiced again, and victims are to be sacrificed:

and all the precepts of the law are to be kept: so that the Jews may not become Christians, but Christians may become Jews. In the day, they say, when Christ shall sit in a golden and gem-studded Jerusalem to reign, there will be no idols, nor any creature different from the divinity, but there will be one Lord: and all the land shall return even to the wilderness: that is, to its ancient state. Willius applies these things to his Philadelphians and imagines an age in which sects and schisms are to cease: But what kind of age will that be? For that saying of the Apostle is always true: There must be heresies, 1 Cor. 11. And therefore we leave to them those vain, sweet-sounding dreams from the Elysian fields of Φιλαδελφίας, of removing every schism and establishing a pure Φιλαδελφίας. Never have such times been in this world, never will they be. Nor are these to be hoped for except in heaven, where there is no place for the Devil, who in these lands never rests.

Nor is Coccejus to be heard here, because the accession of the Gentiles is described only in v. 16, and thus what is understood here is not the universal kingdom of the whole world, but the Reformed Church, and the abolition of the authority and jurisdiction which obscures the kingdom of God in the Church, which he wishes to be indicated by the abolition of the name of the great city Hamonah to cleanse the land, Ezek. 39:16, likewise by the falling of the stars from heaven, Apoc. 6, Matt. 24:2, and also the consensus of particular churches in the government instituted by God; so that God alone may be king without a partner. He wishes the same to be said in Is. 24:23, because the Lord has taken up the kingdom in Zion, and before his Elders is glory. As these things proceed from a preconceived false opinion, as if this passage were about the reformation of the kingdom of the Anti-Christ, and passages that are clearly ἀλλότρια are dragged in as if they were παράλληλα, they rest upon a very weak support. For although the conversion of the Gentiles is explained more fully in v. 16, it is nevertheless one continuous prophecy concerning the kingdom of Christ, who is proposed here as a catholic King over all the earth, the amplitude and tranquility of whose kingdom is exhibited under the type of Jerusalem in v. 20 et seqq., and the confusion or conversion of his enemies, and their gathering to it, is predicted. But Coccejus is greatly mistaken in that he promises that the restoration of Jerusalem will happen in the last times in v. 10, dragging in Jer. 31:38, 39, 40, and Luke 21:24. Nor could he satisfy himself with these inventions of his, if indeed it can be considered that it is too premature to assign the restoration of the earthly Jerusalem to that point in time, as also that of the Jewish nation, and that with too great a leap the application is skipped from the place of the Christian Church to the place of the converted Jewish Church, especially because afterwards in v. 14 Judah still comes in a mystical signification. Whence he imagines Jerusalem to be the Reformed Church, and Judah the Lutherans: And that Judea is indeed to be laid waste, but the city is to be inhabited securely. With such more-than-feverish dreams they amuse themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ET ERIT DOMINUS REX SUPER OMNEM TERRAM.) Judæi ab externis imperiis liberi Deum suo arbitratu colent. Id eo evenit, quia reges vicini inter se infensi studiis ac beneficiis in Judæos certabant. Quæ hi- storia est apud Josephum XIII. 4. 5. IN DIE ILLA ERIT DOMINUS UNUS ET NOMEN EJUS UNUM) Unus Deus coletur, & jurando advocabitur.

Nimis violenta hæc est detorsio. Non enim de Judæa agit Propheta, aut regno particulari, sed de universa terra, non Judæos liberatum iri ab exter- nis injuriis, sed Christum Regem futurum dicit per totum orbem, eumque ab omnibus celebratum iri, abolitis idolorum cultibus. ET ERIT JEHO- VAH Jesus Christus REX SUPER OMNEM TERRAM, dominabitur in universo terrarum or- be. IN DIE ILLA ERIT DOMINUS UNI- CUS, ET ERIT NOMEN EJUS UNICUM. Non coletur nisi unus Deus, non agnoscentur di- versi dii, ut olim inter Judæos, Baal, Astaroth, Mo- loch, & inter gentes Jupiter, Saturnus, &c. Sed Christiani omnes unum colent Deum, & nomen ejus erit unicum, cultus ejus erit unicus. Idola enim gentiles variis modis coluerunt, Deus autem non nisi abs se definito cultu prosequendus est. Ita quoque Willius: Dominus solus erit rex sui populi, & præter eum nullus Ecclesiæ dominabitur, nullus etiam præter ipsum coletur: vel h. m. Deus agnoscetur piis, unus idemque coletur, non habebunt De- um præter unum, nec alio, quam uno modo eun- dem honorabunt. Ita hoc membrum idololatriæ & schismatibus opponitur. Et frequens hoc, ut nomen Dei pro ejus cultu ponatur. Ita nomen Dei usurpat Mich. 4. omnes populi ambulabunt quis- que in nomine Dei sui, nos autem ambulabimus in nomine Domini Dei nostri in seculum, & in æter- num. Ad tempora N. T. hæc pertinere fateri co- acti sunt etiam illi, qui è Pontificiis priora ad Macca- bæorum tempora abripuere, atque in eo cum Judæis Grotio præivere. Menochius, cui multum Grotius tribuit: Vix hoc, inquit Maccabæis convenit, & eo- rum tempori, apte vero Messiæ & Ecclesiæ, nam Chri- stus conversa ad fidem gentilitate regnum suum per to- tum orbem propagavit. Etiam Tirinus: DOMI- NUS DEUS REX ERIT, & instar Regis coletur PER OMNEM TERRAM, non Judææ tantum, sed & totius orbis, nempe per Christum mox subsequu- turum, & abactis idolis UNUS ubique Dominus, ET UNUM NOMEN EJUS puta Christi, celebrabi- tur toto orbe. Ita S. Hieronymus, Remigius, Rupertus, Haymo, Vatablus, Ribera, & à Lapide. Hæc ille. Castrius notat, omnes intelligere, de Christo agi su- per omnem terram solo, relictis idolis, colendo, & invocando, Lyram solum, & Dionysium de regno Christi regnantis in cælesti Jerusalem exponere.

Cæterum Judæorum & Judaizantium Christia- norum ψευδερμηνείαν hic notavit Hieronymus: Ad eam enim fanaticorum quorundam hodie certa ra- tione accedit commentum: Extructionem urbis Hierusalem, & aquarum egressam de medio ejus, quæ ad utrumque defluant mare, Judæi & Christiani Iudai- zantes ultimo sibi tempore repromittunt: quum rur- sum exercenda circumcisio sit, & immolandæ victimæ:

& omnia legis præcepta servanda: ut non Judæi Chri- stiani, sed Christiani Judæi fiant. In die, inquiunt, il- quando Christus in Hierusalem aurea atque gemmata sederit regnaturus, non erunt idola, nec divinitatis cri- tura diversa, sed erit Dominus unus: & revertetur omnis terra usque ad solitudinem: id est, in anti- quum statum. Willius applicat hæc Philadelphi- fingitque seculum, quo sectæ & schismata cessatura sint: Sed quodnam illud erit? Semper enim verum illud Apostoli: Oportet hæreses esse, 1. Cor. 11. Ideo- que relinquimus illis Φιλαδελφίας vanæ parar- suavia è campo Elysio somnia, tollendi omnis schis- matis, & fanciendæ meræ Φιλαδελφίας. Nunquam fuere in hoc mundo talia tempora, nunquam erunt. Nec nisi in cœlo hæc speranda, ubi nullus Diaboli locus, qui in his terris nunquam quiescit.

Nec audiendus hic Coccejus, quod accessio gen- tium demum v. 16. describatur, adeoque hic intelligatur non universale regnum totius mundi, sed Ecclesiæ Refor- mata, & abolitio auctoritatis & jurisdictionis, quæ regnum Dei in Ecclesia obscurat, quam indigitari vult per abolitionem nominis urbis magnæ Hamonah ad purgandam terram Ezch. 39, 16. item per casum siderum de cælo Apoc. 6. Matth. 24, 2. nec non con- sensus Ecclesiarum particularium in regimen à Deo in- stitutum; ut ita Deus solus sit rex sine socio. Idem dici vult Es. 24, 23. quia regnum capessivit Dominus in Zion, & coram Senioribus ejus est gloria. Hæc uti è præconcepta falsa opinione procedunt, quasi aga- tur hoc loco de reformatione regni Anti-Christi, &amp; loca plane ἀλλότρια ceu παράλληλα eo abripiun- tur, ita valde infirmo nituntur tibicine. Nam etsi uberius vers. 16. explicetur gentium conversio, unum tamen & continuum est vaticinium de regno Chri- sti, qui hic ceu Rex catholicus super omnem terram proponitur, cujus regni amplitudo & tranquillitas sub typo Hierosolymæ v. 20. seqq. exhibetur, ho- stiumque vel confusio, vel conversio, & ad illud aggre- gatio prædicitur. Fallitur autem quam maxime Coccejus quod v. 10. restauratio Hierosolymæ ultimis temporibus futura promittatur, eo abripiens Jerem. 31, 38. 39. 40. & Luc. 21, 24. Neque hic commentis illis suis ipse sibi satisfacere potuit, si- quidem censeri possit, nimis maturum esse, ut in eum temporis articulum conferat Hierosolymæ terrestris re- stauratio nem, ut & gentis Judaicæ, saltuque nimis ma- gno applicationem transiliri à loco Ecclesiæ Christianæ ad locum Ecclesiæ Judaicæ conversæ, imprimis, quia adhuc postea v. 14. Juda in mystica significatione ve- nit. Unde fingit Hierosolymam esse Ecclesiam Re- formatam, & Judam Lutheranos: Et quod Judæa quidem vastanda sit, urbs autem secure habitanda. Talibus oblectant illi sese somniis plusquam fe- brilibus.

## 14:10
Verse 10.

AND ALL THE LAND SHALL RETURN EVEN TO THE DESERT.) In the Hebrew: The land shall be surrounded: That is, it shall be inhabited all around even to the desert, that is, even in places not inhabited before: namely, with Jews flocking to prosperous things from all over the world.

FROM THE HILL OF RIMMON.) In the Hebrew: From Geba to Rimmon, so also the Greeks and the Chaldean. Geba is at the end of Judea to the North, a town of Benjamin, 1 Sam. 13:2.

TO THE SOUTH OF JERUSALEM.) That is, which Rimmon is to the South for the Jews, as appears in Josh. 15:2, ch. 19:7.

AND IT SHALL BE EXALTED.) Supply, Jerusalem, with towers and walls.

AND IT SHALL DWELL IN ITS PLACE.) It shall be inhabited: where it was formerly.

FROM THE GATE OF BENJAMIN.) By which one goes into the field of Benjamin, Jer. 37:13. This was to the north of the city: the same as the gate of Ephraim, 2 Chron. 25:23.

AS FAR AS THE PLACE OF THE GATE. ) In Hebrew: the first: that is, the old, Nehem. 3, 6. that was to the West.

AND AS FAR AS THE CORNER GATE) 2 Chron. 25, 23. It is called the Corner Gate because of the towers built there. See Zeph. 1, verse 17. & ch. 3, 7. & mentioned there: that gate was to the East.

AND FROM THE TOWER OF HANANEEL.) Which was to the south, Nehem. 3, 1. The Chaldean calls it the tower of Pekos, the name having been changed by time. Compare the similar passage Jerem. 31, 6.

AS FAR AS THE KING'S WINEPRESSES.) Where the king's vineyards had been. See Cant. 8, 11. there also it shall be inhabited: that place was in the inner city near Zion.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET REVERTETVR OMNIS TERRA VSQVE AD DESERTVM.) In Hebræo: Circumdabitur terra: Id est, circumquaque habitabitur usque ad desertum, id est, in locis etiam non habitatis antehac: nempe affluentibus ad res prosperas ex omni orbe Judæis.

DE COLLE REMMON.) In Hebræo: A Gaba ad Remmon, Sic & Græci & Chaldæus. Gaba est in fine Judææ ad Septentrionein, oppidum Benjaminis, 1. Sam, 13. v. 2.

AD AVSTRVM JERVSALEM.) Id est, quæ Rimmon est ad Austrum Judæis, ut apparet Jos. 15. vers. 2. c. 19, 7.

ET EXALTABITVR.) Supple, Ierusalem, turribus & mœniis.

ET HABITABIT IN LOCO SVO.) Habitabitur: ubi olim.

A PORTA BENJAMIN.) Qua itur in agrum Ben- jaminis Jerem. 37, 13. Hæc erat urbi ad septentrionem: eadem porta Ephraim 2. Par. 25, 23.

VSQVE AD LOCVM PORTÆ PRIORIS. ) In Hebræo: primæ: id est veteris, Nehem. 3, 6. ea erat ad Occasum.

ET VSQVE AD PORTAM ANGVLORVM) 2. Paral. 25, 23. Porta angulorum dicitur ob turres ibi factas. Vide Sophon. I, vers. 17. & c. 3, 7. & ibi dictæ: ea porta erat ad Ortum.

ET A TVRRE HANANEEL.) Quæ erat ad me- ridiem, Nehem. 3, 1. Chaldæus turrem Pekos vocat, me- tato per ætatem nomine. Confer locum similem Jerem. 31, 6.

VSQVE AD TORCVLARIA REGIS.) Ubi vine- æ regnum fuerant. Vide Cant. 8, 11. ibi quoque habi- tabitur: is locus erat in urbe intima apud Sionem.

## 14:11
Ver. 11.

AND THEY SHALL DWELL IN IT.) Safely after the peace with Bacchides, and the treaties of the following kings.

AND THERE SHALL BE NO MORE ANATHEMA) חרם, that is, as the Chaldean translates, there shall be no more slaughter; the word חרם is used in Josh. 11, 11.

BUT JERUSALEM SHALL SIT SECURE) Jerusalem shall sit with confidence.

Concerning the borders of Judea, or Jerusalem, there is no reason for us to dispute. We admit that all these things are designated according to the Grotian explanation. That Judea is to be inhabited, even in places not previously inhabited, from Gaba at the North, and Rimnon, which are at the South for the Jews. That Jerusalem is to be inhabited from the northern Gate of Benjamin, to the place of the first or old gate to the west, and to the corner gate, or the tower to the east, and from the tower of Hananeel to the south as far as the King's winepresses, finally that a secure habitation with confidence is promised, and that the place shall not be for an anathema: but we deny that these things are to be understood of earthly Judea & Jerusalem, of worldly peace & security: we deny that they look to the times of the Maccabees. The Jesuits Cornelius, Tirinus, Menochius indeed thought so, in that these things are to be understood of the earthly Jerusalem, following the Jews, but since they acknowledged that in the preceding ninth verse it was treated of the recognition & worship of the Messiah under the New Testament, they wrongly snatch these things, which now follow in this tenth verse and those following, to the times preceding the advent of the Messiah. There is nothing here about the inhabitants of the land, who had fled for fear of Antiochus as far as the deserts, mountains, and caves, nothing about their return to the city, or into Judea, with peace restored by the Maccabees. Indeed, it had been treated before of the most recent occupation of Jerusalem, which brought upon it perpetual desolation, and therefore these things are not to be understood carnally with the Jews, but spiritually. For Zechariah brings forth heavenly things, in the prophetic manner, under the type and form of the words of earthly things. It is after he had prophesied concerning the streams of grace, and the Spirit irrigating the whole world, concerning the true recognition and worship of God throughout the whole world, under the reign of the Messiah, that he now exhibits the amplification of the Church to be gathered from the Gentiles through the ministry of the word, under the type of the old Jerusalem. And all the land shall be round about as that plain, which is from Gaba to Rimnon, towards the southern region of Jerusalem, as Osiander rightly rendered the Hebrew. The word יסוב is not 'it shall return,' but 'it shall be reduced round about,' nor is it necessary that we understand only the land around Jerusalem. For it is a matter of the whole land, as in the preceding verse, even if a comparison is made with the plain from Gaba to Rimnon from one extremity of Judea towards the north, where Gaba is situated in the borders of the kingdom Josh. 21, 17. 1 Kings 15, 12. Isa. 10, 2. to the other towards the south, where Rimnon was situated Josh. 15, 3. By which manner it is indicated that the whole land shall be flat, that all things in the Church shall be flat throughout the whole world, not otherwise than if the things which were mountainous around Jerusalem were rendered flat, or the whole of Judea from the North to the south were reduced into a mere plain. For the Gospel concerning Christ shows us a level and straight way into heaven, provided we walk in it, and it does not have anything perplexing, as human doctrines and opinions do: and by the benefit of the proclamation of the word, every valley was to be exalted, every mountain and hill was to be humbled, all crooked things were to be turned into straight, and rough things into plain ways. Isa. 40, 4. The matter comes to the same thing, as far as the sense is concerned, if by all the earth Judea is understood, because thus under the name and type of Judea the whole Church of Christ is depicted, just as it is likewise shadowed forth under the type of the city of Jerusalem. Balduin, he says, looks in these words to the site and parts of the city of Jerusalem. For the whole city was surrounded on all sides by mountains, to which site David alludes in Ps. 87 and 125. He says, therefore, that those mountains are to be reduced to a plain, for the true Church does not lead men around through winding paths or stony places, which the Synagogue of the malignant is accustomed to do, but shows a plain and straight way into heaven, as if one were to go from Gaba to Rimnon, with the mountains eradicated, in a continuous plain. And thus they explain it, in Castrius, p. 542, Remigius, Albertus, Vatablus, Montanus, and Isidorus: All the earth, which is in the circuit of Jerusalem, shall be leveled, with no mountain impeding its view, and it shall become so ample that it provides a pleasant and ample dwelling for all who flow into it, which is to be understood of the spiritual Jerusalem, which began in the earthly one: According to that of Isa. 2, 2. In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and all nations shall flow unto it, and Zachar. 2, 4. Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall. AND THE CITY OF JERUSALEM SHALL BE EXALTED, AND SHALL BE INHABITED IN ITS PLACE FROM THE GATE OF BENJAMIN EVEN UNTO THE PLACE OF THE FORMER GATE, more correctly first, and even unto the gate of the corners, and from the tower of Hananeel, which shall be the northern one, unto the winepresses of the King, which were situated in the Southern part, which are the names of the gates of Jerusalem, of which some mention is also made in the book of Nehemiah. It is signified, however, that the Church shall be famous and populous, frequent and abundant in number, and shall be extended from the East to the West, and from the North to the South. Which sense the following words also confirm. AND THEY SHALL DWELL IN IT, AND THERE SHALL BE NO MORE ANATHEMA, AND JERUSALEM SHALL SIT SECURE: Which cannot be taken of the earthly Jerusalem, for in it there was neither tranquility, nor constant security from anathema, inasmuch as histories testify that it was never not exposed to dangers. Some understand those things concerning the anathema thus: Gentiles shall no longer be excluded from the Church, as formerly in the old Jerusalem, but all shall dwell there secure, because they have obtained the peace announced through Christ in the Gospel. Others explain it thus: that there shall not be men in the Church worthy of anathema and excommunication. For although in the external congregation of the Church the evil are mixed with the good, yet in the true universal Church all are saints by the imputation of the justice of Christ, and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit. Most take it thus: There shall be no more anathema, that is, slaughter. The spiritual Jerusalem shall not be laid waste, as the earthly one was laid waste. Thus Danæus explains it: security is declared by these words: It shall be inhabited confidently, i.e., without any danger, whether internal or external: nor shall it suffer destruction any more. For Cherem here signifies destruction, which happened to that city very often. For it was destroyed both by Nebuchadnezzar and by the emperor Titus. But it was captured very often, as Josephus teaches, lib. VII. de Bell. Jud. c. 18. Therefore it shall neither be cut off afterwards, as before, nor when it is inhabited, shall it be dwelt in with fear, Psal. 121. and 144. v. 4. because God shall protect it under the shadow of His wings. This confidence and security, however, is to be understood spiritually rather than carnally, as Paul teaches, Rom. 8. Conf. Numer. 21, 1. seqq. Esa. 34, 2. Jer. 31, 40.

Moreover, in explaining this description of the city, Cocceius was primarily and diligently engaged. The entire circuit of Jerusalem is indicated by certain parts. Concerning the Gate of Benjamin, see Jer. 20, 2. c. 37, 13. unless the former passage seems to speak of a certain gate of the temple, which corresponded to the gate of Benjamin, and thence was called the upper gate of Benjamin. The gate of the corners, 2. Reg. 14, 13. where it is said that Joas tore down 400 cubits of the wall from the gate of Ephraim to the gate of the corner, and in Jerem. 31. verse 38. we read the gate of the corner. But 2. Chron. 25, 24. for the same is שער הפונה i.e. the gate looking out. What the first gate is, can hardly be said. Perhaps the gate of the corner is the same. The tower of Hananeel is mentioned also in Jerem. 31, 38. where this tower and the gate of the corner seem to be placed as the two extremes of the city. From Nehem. 15, 39. it is clear that the Tower of Hananeel and the tower of Meah were in the wall of that part of the city which are called by Josephus τὰ προςαρκτία τ̃ πόλεως and in Ps. 48. the sides of the North. Nehemiah divided the circuit of the city into two parts, to be walked around by two processions, so that one procession would turn to the right, the other to the left, and they would meet each other at the temple in the eastern part. To those who went to the right, there met them 1. The gate of the dung, namely from the western part of the city. 2. The gate of the fountain. 3. The ascent of the wall of the city of David. Now Mount Sion was situated at the southern side between the east, on which side it screened Mount Moriah, and the west. 4. The royal house of David. 5. The gate of the waters in the eastern part. 6. The temple. Those who went to the left, namely from the place in which they had been gathered, in the region of the city which was situated furthest from the temple, namely the gate of the valley, as is clear from a comparison of chapter 3, they encountered 1. the tower of the furnaces. 2. the broad wall. 3. The gate of Ephraim. 4. the old gate. 5. The gate of the fish. 6. the tower of Hananeel. 7. the tower of Meah. 8. the gate of the sheep. 9. the gate of the prison or of the guard and the temple. Hence it is understood that the procession from the temple to the right, or in the eastern part of the city towards the north, encounters 1. the gate of the sheep. 2. the tower of Meah. 3. the tower of Hananeel. Thus it is in Nehem. 3, 1. 4. the gate of the fish ibid. verse 3. 5. the old gate ibid. verse 6. 6. the broad wall v. 8. (the gate of Ephraim is passed over in silence, because Jerusalem had been left around it, i.e., the walls had not been destroyed) 7. the tower of the furnaces v. 11. consequently 8. that gate, where those dedicating the wall ascended together, namely the valley gate v. 13. through which Nehemiah had also gone out to inspect the wall c. 2, 13. it is for the length of a thousand cubits. 9. the dung gate ibid. &c. 2, 13. 10. the fountain gate v. 15. c. 2, 14. which is followed by the wall of the pool of השלח (perhaps of the conduit) to the king's garden. See Jerem. 52, 7. 11. the stairs that go down from the city of David the same verse. 12. the place situated opposite the sepulchres of David verse 16. then further the pool that was made: & the house of the mighty: next the place opposite עלות הנשק the ascent of the armoury, or to המקצוע, i.e., the corner v. 19. 20. Again another corner מקצוע likewise to פנה v. 24. there follows the upper royal house. Thence Ophel; where the Nethinim dwelt as far as 13. the water gate toward the east v. 26. Thence the wall of Ophel v. 27. the horse gate v. 28. Here begin the houses of the priests v. 28. there succeeds the gate המפקר, which is, as I think, the same as the gate מטרה, because there at the פקיד the guilty were deposited. It appears, however, from verse 25 that the house of the King and of the Priests, and the upper chamber of the corner, had been extended from there. Thus one returns to the sheep gate. If we compare these things with the passage in Jerem. XXXI. verses 38. 39. it will appear that the Tower of Hananeel marks the eastern side of the city.

But the gate of the corner is near to it on the northern side, up to which Joas had torn down the walls from the gate of Ephraim (which can be the fish gate) distinct from the eastern corner: and from there the line is to be led further towards the hill Gareb and towards Goam, through the valley (Tyropoeon) until it returns to the corner of the east, where the horse gate and the valley of Kidron are. In our place, therefore, unless something prevents it, I would like the gate of Benjamin to be the same as the gate of Ephraim, which Nehemiah mentions, and subjoins to them the first gate, or its place; the old gate mentioned by Nehemiah, which I see Junius also conjectures, who however is clearly mistaken, when he places the northern gate of Benjamin between the first western gate and the eastern gate of the corners and establishes the tower of Hananeel to the south. Which some follow ἀδοκιμάστως. Rather thus: Jerusalem shall be lifted up and inhabited from the gate of Benjamin or Ephraim along the northern side to the east, to the old and fish gate, or of the corners, and further to the tower of Hananeel situated on the eastern side, and further to the pools of the royal winepresses, which it is most likely were near the royal gardens to the south.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ET HABITABVNT IN EA.) Tuto post pacem cum Bacchide, & regum sequentium fœdera.

ET ANATHEMA NON ERIT AMPLIVS) חרם, id est, ut Chaldæus vertit, occisio non erit am- plius verbum חרם sumitur Jos. 11, 11.

SED SEDEBIT JERVSALEM SECVRA) Sede- bit Ierusalem cum fiducia.

De terminis Judææ, sive Hierosolymæ, non est quod disputemus. Admittimus designari hæc o- mnia juxta Grotianam explicationem. Habitatum iri Judæam, etiam in locis antea non habitatis, a Gaba fine ad Septentrionem, & Rimnon, quæ ad Austrum Judæis. Habitatum iri Hierosolymam à Porta Ben- jamin septentrionali, ad locum portæ primæ, vel veteris ad occasum, & ad portam angulorum, vel turrim ad ortum, & turre Mananeel ad meridiem usque ad tor- cularia Regis, denique habitationem promitti securam cum fiducia, nec locum fore anathemati: sed negamus hæc intelligenda esse de terrena Judæa & Hierosoly- ma, de mundana pace & securitate: negamus respi- cere tempora Maccabæorum. Censuere quidem ita Jesuitæ Cornelius, Tirinus, Menochius, in eo, quod de terrena Hierosolyma ista intelligenda sint, Judæos sequuti, sed quum agnoverint, versu præce- dente nono de Messiæ agnitione & cultu sub Nov. Test. actum esse, perperam hæc, quæ nunc sequuntur vers. hoc decimo & seqq. rapiunt ad tempora Messiæ adventum antegressa. Nihil hic de incolis terræ, qui metu Antiochi fugerant usque ad deserta, montes & ad speluncas, nihil de reditu eorum ad urbem, vel in Judæam, pace per Maccabæos restituta. Imo a- ctum erat antea de novissima Hierosolymæ occupatio- ne, quæ perennem vastitatem ei attulit, ideoque hæc non cum Judæis carnaliter, sed spiritualiter in- telligenda sunt. Profert enim Zacharias res cæle- stes, more Prophetico, sub typo, ac forma verborum rerum terrenarum. Est postquam de fluentis gratiæ, & Spiritus totum orbem irrigantibus, de vera Dei agni- tione & cultu per universum mundum, sub Messiæ regi- mine vaticinatus erat, jam amplificationem Ecclesiæ ex gentibus per ministerium verbi colligendæ, sub typo veteris Hierosolymæ exhibet. Et erit circumqua- que tota terra quasi planities illa, quæ est Gabaa ad Rimnon, versus meridionalem plagam Jerusalem, ut Ebræa recte reddidit Osiander. Verbum יסוב non est revertetur, sed circumcirca redigetur, nec neces- sum est, ut terram solum circa Hierusalem intelliga- mus. Agitur enim de universa terra, ut versu præcedenti, etsi comparatio fiat cum planitie à Ga- ba ad Rimnon ab una extremitate Judææ versus septen- trionem, ubi Gaba sita in finibus regni Jos. 21, 17. 1. Reg. 15, 12. Esa. 10, 2. ad alteram versus meridiem, ubi Rimnon sita erat Jos. 15, 3. Quo pacto indica- tur universam terram planam futuram, plana in Ecclesia fore omnia per totum orbem, non secus ac si circa Hierosolymam, quæ montosa erant, pla- na redderentur, vel universa Judæa à Septentrione ad meridiem in meram planitiem redigeretur. Evangelium enim de Christo monstrat nobis pla- nam & rectam viam in cœlum, modo in ea ambu- lemus, nec habet aliquid perplexi, ut doctrinæ & opiniones humanæ: & beneficio præconii verbi omnis vallis exaltanda, omnis mons, & collis humilian- dus erat, omnia prava in recta, & aspera in vias pla- nas convertenda erant. Esa. 40, 4. Res eodem, quan- tum ad sensum, redit, si per omnem terram Judæa intelligatur, quia ita sub nomine ac typo Judææ tota Ecclesia Christi depingitur, quemadmodum sub ty- po urbis Jerusalem itidem ea adumbratur. Respicit, inquit Balduin. his verbis ad situm & partes urbis Hierusalem. Tota enim civitas undiquaque montibus septa fuit, ad quem situm alludit David in Ps. 87. & 125. Illos igitur montes in planitiem redactos iri dicit, ve- ra enim Ecclesia non per anfractus, aut loca petrosa homines circumducit, quod facere solet Synagoga ma- lignantium, sed planam & rectam viam monstrat in cœlum, ac si à Gaba in Rimnon, eradicatis montibus, continua planitie iretur, Atque ita explicant, apud Castrium, p. 542. Remigius, Albertus, Vatablus, Mon- tanus & Isidorus: Omnis terra, quæ est in circuitu Ieru- salem, complanabitur, nullo monte visum ejus impedi- ente, & ita ampla fiet, ut omnibus ad eam confluentibus præstet Domicilium jucundum & amplum, quod de spirituali Jerusalem, quæ cœpit in terrena, est accipiendum: Juxta illud Es. 2, 2. Erit in novissi- mis diebus præparatus mons Domini in vertice mon- tium, & fluent ad eum omnes gentes, & Zachar. 2, 4. Absque muro habitabitur Jerusalem. ET URBS JERUSALEM EXALTABITUR, ET HABI- TABITUR IN LOCO SUO A PORTA BENJAMIN USQVE AD LOCUM POR- TÆ PRIORIS, rectius primæ, & usque ad portam angulorum, & à turre Hananael, quæ septentriona- lis erit, usque ad torcularia Regis, quæ sita erant in parte Meridionali, quæ nomina sunt portarum Je- rusalem, quarum aliqua etiam mentio facta in Ne- hemiæ libro. Significatur autem Ecclesiam fore celebrem & populosam, frequentem & numero abundantem, ac porrectam iri ab Oriente ad Occi- dentem, & à septentrione ad meridiem. Quem sen- sum etiam sequentia confirmant. ET HABI- TABUNT IN EA, ET ANATHEMA NON ERIT AMPLIUS, ET SEDEBIT JERUSA- LEM SECURA: Quod de terrena Hierosolyma non potest accipi, in ea enim nec tranquillitas, nec ab anathemate securitas constans fuit, utpote quam nunquam non periculis expositam fuisse, historiæ testantur. Illa de anathemate sic intelligunt non- nulli; non amplius excludentur ex Ecclesia gentiles, ut olim in veteri Hierosolyma, sed omnis habitabunt ibi securi, quia pacem per Christum in Evangelio annunciatam sint consequuti. Alii sic exponunt, in Ecclesia non fore homines anathemate, & excom- municatione dignos. Etsi enim in externa Eccle- siæ congregatione mali admixti sint bonis, tamen in veraEcclesia universali omnes sunt sancti impu- tatione justitiæ Christi, & sanctificatione SpiritusS. Plerique ita accipiunt: Non erit amplius anathema, id est, occisio. Non vastabitur Jerusalem spiritua- lis, sicut vastata est terrena. Sic exponit Danæus: securitas declaratur his verbis: Habitabitur con- fidenter i.e. absque periculo ullo, sive interno sive externo: neque excidium patietur amplius. Nam Cherem hic excidionem significat, quæ sæpius illi urbi contigit. Nam & à Nebucadnezare & à Tito imperatore excisa est. Sæpius autem capta, quem- admodum docet Joseph. lib. VII. de Bell. Jud. c. 18. Ergo neque exscindetur postea, ut antea, neque quum habitabitur, cum metu incoletur Psal. 121. & 144. v. 4. quia Deus proteget eam sub umbra ala- rum suarum. Hæc autem confidentia & securitas spiritualiter potius quam carnaliter est intelligen- da, ut docet Paul. Rom. 8. Conf. Numer. 21, 1. seqq. Esa. 34, 2. Jer. 31, 40.

Cæterum in explicanda hac urbis descriptione diligenter imprimis versatus fuit Coccejos. Hierofo- lymæ ambitus integer indicatur, per partes quasdam. De Porta Benjamin est Jer. 20, 2. c. 37, 13. nisi quod prior locus de quadam porta templi loqui videtur, quæ portæ Benjaminis responderit, atque inde por- ta Benjaminis superior appellata fuerit. Porta an- gulorum 2. Reg. 14, 13. ubi dicitur, quod Joas dirue- rit muri 400. cubita à porta Ephraim ad portam anguli, & Jerem. 31. vers. 38. legimus portam anguli. Sed 2. Chron. 25, 24. pro eodem est שער הפונה q. d. porta respiciens. Porta prima quæ sit, dici vix potest. Forte porta anguli eadem est. Turris Hana- neel memoratur & Jerem. 31, 38. ubi hæc turris & porta anguli duo extrema urbis videntur poni. Ex Nehem. 15, 39. liquet, Turrim Chananeelis, & tur- rim Meah fuisse in muro illius partis, urbis, quæ di- cuntur Josepho τὰ προςαρκτία τ̃ πόλεως & in Ps. 48. latera Aquilonis. Ambitum urbis Nehemias divisit in duas partes, duabus processionibus per- ambulandas, ita ut una processio flecteret ad de- xteram, altera ad sinistram, & sibi occurrerent, ad templum in parte orientali. Qui ad dexteram ive- runt, iis occurrit 1. Porta simeti scil. à parte urbis oc- cidentali. 2. Porta fontis. 3. ascensio muri urbis Da- vid. Erat autem mons Sion ad latus meridionale positus inter ortum, qua parte montem Morijah prætexebat & occasum. 4. regia domus Davidis. 5. porta aquarum in parte orientali. 6. templum. Qui ad sinistram, scil. à loco, in quo congregati fuerant, in regione urbis, quæ longissime à templo erat sita, nempe porta vallis, ut ex comparatione cap. 3. li- quet, ii inciderunt 1. in turrim fornacum. 2. mu- rum latum. 3. Portam Ephraim. 4. portam veterem. 5. Portam piscium. 6. turrim Chananeel. 7. turrim Meah. 8. portam ovium. 9. portam carceris sive custodiæ & templum. Hinc intelligitur proce- dentia à templo ad dextram, sive in parte orientali urbis versus boream, occurrere 1. portam ovium. 2. turrim Meah. 3. turrim Chananeel. Sic est Nehem. 3, 1. 4. portam piscium ibid. vers. 3. 5. portam vete- rem ibid. vers. 6. 6. murum latum v. 8. (tacita porta Ephraim propterea, quia circa illam relicta fuerat Hierosolyma, i. e. mœnia non erant destru- cta) 7. turrim fornacum v. 11. consequenter 8. eam portam, ubi ascenderunt dedicantes simul murum, nimirum portam vallis v. 13. per quam etiam exie- rat Nehemias speculaturus murum c. 2, 13. per lon- gitudinem mille cubitorum est. 9. porta simeti ib. &c. 2, 13. 10. porta fontis v. 15. c. 2, 14. quem sequitur murus piscinæ השלח (emissarii forte) ad hortum re- gis. Vide Jerem. 52, 7. 11. gradus descendentes ex ur- be Davidis vers. eodem. 12. locus positus ex adverso sepulchrorum Davidis vers. 16. tum porro Piscina facta: & Domus fortium: deinceps locus opposi- tus עלות הנשק ascensui armamentarii, sive ad המקצוע, i. e. angulum v. 19. 20. Rursus alius angu- lus מקצוע item ad פנה v. 24. sequitur domus Regia superior. Inde עפל Ophel; ubi sedebant Nathinæi usque ad 13. portam aquarum ad ortum v. 26. Inde murus Ophel v. 27. porta equorum v. 28. Incipiunt hic domus sacerdotum v. 28. succedit porta המפקר, quæ est, ut puto, eadem cum porta מטרה, quod ibi apud פקיד deponerentur rei. Apparet autem ex vers. 25. inde porrectam fuisse domum Regis & Sacerdotum, & cœnaculum anguli. Ita redi- tur ad portum ovium. Hæc si comparemus cum loco Jerem. XXXI. vers. 38. 39. apparebit Tur- rim Chananeelis insignire latus urbis Orientale.

Portam vero anguli ei proximam esse ad latus se- ptentrionale, usque ad quam à porta Ephraim diruerat mœniæ Joas (quæ potest esse porta pi- scium) distinctam ab angulo orientali: atque in- de lineam porro versum super collem Gareb & versus Goam esse circumducendam, per vallem (Tyropæon) donec redeat ad angulum orientis, ubi porta equorum est & vallis Kidron. In no- stro igitur loco, nisi quid impediat, velim por- tam Benjamin esse eandem cum porta Ephraim, quam memorat Nehemias, eisque subjungit por- tam primam, aut locum ejus; portam veterem dictam Nehemiæ, quod video & Junium conje- ctare, qui tamen plane fallitur, quum portam Ben- jamin septentrionalem ponit inter portam primam occidentalem, & portam angulorum orientalem & turrim Chananeel constituit ad meridiem. Quem ἀδοκιμάστως quidam sequuntur. Sic potius: super- efferetur & habitabitur Hierosolyma à porta Benja- minis sive Ephraim per septentrionale latus ad ori- entem, ad portam veterem & piscium, sive angulo- rum, & porro turrim Chananeelis sitam in latere o- rientali, & porro ad lacus torcularium regiorum, quæ fuisse prope hortos regios ad meridiem, veri- simillimum est.

## 14:12
Vers. 12.

AND THIS SHALL BE THE PLAGUE, WHEREWITH THE LORD WILL SMITE ALL THE NATIONS THAT HAVE FOUGHT AGAINST JERUSALEM: THE FLESH OF EVERY ONE STANDING UPON HIS FEET SHALL CONSUME AWAY, AND HIS EYES SHALL CONSUME AWAY IN THEIR HOLES, AND THEIR TONGUE SHALL CONSUME AWAY IN THEIR MOUTH.) That is, the Macedonians who will be in the citadel of Jerusalem will perish by famine, 1 Macc. 13, 49. Ovid in Metamorphoses VIII depicts famine with similar marks:

- - hollow eyes, paleness in the face, lips white with filth: teeth rough with rust, hard skin, through which the entrails can be seen. Bones stood out under the curved loins. There was a place for a belly instead of a belly: you would think the chest hung, and was held only by the crate of the spine.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ET HÆC ERIT PLAGA, QVA PERCVTIET DOMINVS OMNES GENTES, QVÆ PVGNAVE- RVNT ADVERSVS JERVSALEM: TABESCET CA- RO VNIVSCVJVSQVE STANTIS SVPER PEDES SVOS, ET OCVLI EJVS CONTABESCENT IN FO- RAMINIBVS SVIS, ET LINGVA EORVM CONTA- BESCET IN ORE SVO.) Id est, fame peribunt Mace- dones, qui erunt in arce Hierosolymitana 1. Macc. 13, 49. Ovidius metamorphoseos VIII. famem paribus notis depingit:

- - cava lumina, pallor in ore, Labra incana situ: scabri rubigine dentes, Dura cutis, per quam spectari viscera possunt. Ossa sub incurvis exstabant arida lumbis. Ventris erat pro ventre locus: pendere putares Pectus, & à spina tantummodo crate teneri.

## 14:13
Vers. 13.

IN THAT DAY THERE SHALL BE A GREAT TUMULT OF THE LORD AMONG THEM.) God will vehemently disturb those enemies of His people: and deservedly; which the following words explain.

AND A MAN SHALL LAY HOLD OF THE HAND OF HIS NEIGHBOR, AND HIS HAND SHALL BE CRUSHED UPON THE HAND OF HIS NEIGHBOR.) The sense is: alliances will be uncertain at that time. For he who joins his hand to another, he will be cut off through that hand (that is, society). To clap hands is a sign of society. Prov. 6, 1. But עלתה in this place is 'shall be plucked up': as the Chaldean translates. And what follows על is 'by'. Nothing could be said more congruously about that time, in which all things are full of treachery. See Joseph. XII, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

IN DIE ILLA ERIT TVMVLTVS DOMINI MAGNVS IN EIS.) Deus vehementer illos populi sui ho- stes perturbabit: & merito; quod explicant sequentia.

ET APPREHENDET VIR MANVM PROXI- MI SVI, ET CONTERETVR MANVS EJVS SVPER MANVM PROXIMI.) Sensus est: incerta erunt eo tem- pore fœdera. Nam qui manum alteri adjungit, is per eam manum (id est, societatem) exscindetur. Manum complodere est signum societatis. Prov. 6, 1. Est autem עלתה hoc loco evelletur: quomodo vertit Chaldæus. Et quod sequitur על est per. Nihil potuit de isto tem- pore congruentius dici, quo omnia plena perfidiæ. Vide Joseph. XII, 16.

## 14:14
Vers. 14.

BUT JUDAH ALSO SHALL FIGHT AGAINST JERUSALEM.) What had been said above about the times of Antiochus XII, 2, he repeats here, describing the times closest to Antiochus. You will translate it rightly as 'shall fight', so that you may understand how great the treachery will be. Many from the tribe of Judah, as once to Antiochus, so then will be present with Bacchides.

AND THE WEALTH OF ALL NATIONS ROUND ABOUT SHALL BE GATHERED, GOLD AND SILVER AND GARMENTS IN GREAT ABUNDANCE) There will be much wealth in the camp of Nicanor, Joseph. XII. 17. 2. Macc. 8, 30.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

SED ET JVDAS PVGNABIT ADVERSVS JE- RVSALEM.) Quod supra dictum fuerat de temporibus Antiochi XII, 2. idem hic tempora proxima Antiocho de- scribens repetit. Vertes autem recte bellabit, ut intelligas, quanta futura sit perfidia. Multi ex Judæ tribu, ut olim Antiocho, ita tunc Bachidæ aderunt.

ET CONGREGABVNTVR DIVITIÆ OMNI- VM GENTIVM IN CIRCVITV, AVRVM ET AR- GENTVM ET VESTES MVLTÆ SATIS) Multæ erunt divitiæ in Castris Nicanoris, Joseph. XII. 17. 2. Mac- cab. 8, 30.

## 14:15
AND SO SHALL BE THE RUIN OF THE HORSE, AND OF THE MULE AND OF THE CAMEL AND OF THE ASS, AND OF ALL THE BEASTS THAT SHALL BE IN THOSE CAMPS, AS THIS RUIN.) מגפה, which he translates here as ruin, signifies a plague. He says the slaughter of other living creatures will be no less than that of men, namely for the reasons already explained.

Regarding the punishments of the persecutors in general, these things are said: that is to say, they will appear as if they were certain living corpses; they will lose their flesh, that is, their power, their eyes or their prudence,

and their tongue or eloquence. For since he said that Jerusalem, as Cyril holds, which is the Church of the living God, would be inhabited confidently, and it was permitted to hope that this would be accomplished with the best right once the enemies were removed and those who had been accustomed to persecute it were overthrown, he necessarily narrates these things to us as well. For that common and natural death indeed causes the flesh of all to waste away and despoils them of their eyes and tongues, but it would not undeservedly be most bitter and most calamitous for the flesh of those still living and standing to waste away, and for their eyes to fall out, and for their tongues to be punished. And he says quite rightly that such things will happen to those who have pursued a life hateful and execrable to God. For punishments will be exacted not only for those things which they committed against the saints, but also for the pursuit of carnal things, with which they burned in this world: which likewise was the cause for them why they were unwilling to admit the faith, nor to cultivate piety, and to love the glory of life in Christ. For they turned aside, as I said, to absurd pleasures, and whatever they saw, they sought after with gaping mouth, as it were, and swallowed down. For they sharpened their tongues against Christ and impiously disparaged the sacred dogmas of the Church. Rightly, therefore, did they receive punishment in their flesh, and eyes, and tongues. But how these things were fulfilled, Jerome teaches thus: The present scripture testifies what the nations will suffer, which will fight against the city of the Lord. They will stand, he says, upon their feet, and their flesh will waste away and flow down, and their eyes will rot and fall from their sockets: the magniloquent tongue, which blasphemed the people of God, will be dissolved into pus and will rot within the wall of the teeth. That the Romans, who overthrew Jerusalem, did not suffer these things is clear to all; unless perhaps the Jews will assert that those nations will suffer them which are about to fight against the golden and jeweled Jerusalem. But we shall say that all persecutors who have afflicted the Church of the Lord, to say nothing of future torments, have received in the present age also what they did. Let us read the ecclesiastical histories: what Valerian, what Decius, what Diocletian, what Maximian, what the most savage of all, Maximinus, and recently Julian have suffered: and then we shall prove by the facts that the truth of the prophecy has been fulfilled even according to the letter: that their flesh has rotted, and their eyes have wasted away, and their tongue has been dissolved into filth and pus. Jerome interprets the rest tropologically. But it is manifest that the sense regarding the punishments of the persecutors is continued here. By the wasting away, Abarbenel understands the French disease, or some similar leprosy; others, the slow consumption and subsequent extinction of the enemies; others, the infernal punishment. Our Luther adapts these things to the Roman Empire itself and other kingdoms and nations opposing Christ and His Gospel: for the Roman Empire, although it was in its prime and had sharp eyes, that is, prudent and circumspect men, and tongues in its mouth, that is, eloquent men, nevertheless fell and wasted away in its prime. These things are from B. Luther. ON THAT DAY THERE WILL BE A TUMULT OF THE LORD, The enemies will also tumult against one another, and will stir up bloody wars, and each one will seize the hand of his neighbor, and they will rush into mutual conflicts, and will destroy one another. Judah will fight for or against Jerusalem. Furthermore, the riches of all the nations surrounding those attacking the Church will be plundered and looted, gold and silver and very many precious garments. And thus will be the plague of the horse and the mule, and the camel and the ass and all the beasts of burden that will be in those camps, like that plague which, to wit, happened to the persecutors, so that their flesh, eyes, and tongues waste away. But the helpers will pay similar punishments with those who will be the authors of the persecutions. Thus Cyril explained those things concerning Judah: Judah, that is, justified by faith in Christ, and Judah, whom we contemplate in our minds as circulating and rich in spiritual circumcision, will fight in Jerusalem, that is, will attack the enemies, and will prevail over the adversaries by virtue, and trampling them, like scorpions. Nor did Jerome disapprove of that sense: Judah, every confessor and faithful one, will not fight against Jerusalem, but will prepare himself in Jerusalem, so that he may fight against the adversaries. Others understand it of heretics and apostates, who are changed from children of the Church into enemies, that they will likewise fight against the Church. But the text seems to favor the former sense more, so that there is no need to establish a parenthesis as others do. That not only will Jehovah strike them with a horrible plague, and they, seized by a panic terror, will slaughter one another, but that Judah also, i.e., the pious and truly faithful, will fight for the Church with the greatest alacrity of spirit. Thus Lamb. Danaeus: & B. Tarnovius, rendering it in this manner: And you also, Judah, will fight in Jerusalem, you constant confessors in the Church will perform good work in converting the nations, thus it will come to pass that the Church will abound in the spoils of the enemies, just as once the tabernacle of Moses [was enriched] with Egyptian spoils, and the wealth of all nations which are round about will be received, gold and silver, and very many garments.

approved, who thinks Judah is among the enemies of Jerusalem, whom others truly make a defender of the same. Which opinion we have said is more convenient. Gualtherus, however, by these words, 'they will gather gold and silver,' thinks it is indicated that the enemies will be most well-equipped with all things that are necessary for waging war. But in that way there will be a need for a parenthesis. Simpler is the interpretation of those who refer these things to the punishment of the Church, because the enumeration of them is continued in the same way, just as the following words teach.

In the Grotian Commentary many things can be desired. First, he draws everything to the times of the Maccabees with Cornelius à Lapide: who, however, confesses that these things were TRULY completed in the persecutors of the Church of the New Testament. Next, he interprets too thinly the plague by which the Lord was about to strike the nations about to fight against Jerusalem; the Macedonians who will be in the Jerusalem citadel will perish by famine, 1 Macc. 13:19. Tirinus understands it of Lysias, Antiochus, the forces of Timotheus, and others, 2 Macc. 9:5, ch. 12:22, ch. 10:30. Others [understand it] of the enemies of the Maccabees struck with blindness and terrified by confusion, 1 Macc. 4, 2 Macc. 6. But those do not exhaust the force of the Prophet's words. Therefore Castrius rejects such interpretations, and with Jerome, Cyril, Remigius, Albert, Hugo, and others and more recent ones, explains it concerning the punishments of the enemies of the spiritual Jerusalem, inasmuch as they have experienced all their human power, wisdom, cunning, and eloquence, by which they thought they could prevail against Christian simplicity, broken, crushed, weakened, and lost. Thirdly, he twists the words of the text to treaties, rendering verse 13 thus: 'treaties will be uncertain at that time, for he who joins his hand to another, he will be cut off by that hand (that is, society).' That these things are foreign both to the words and to the context is plain. For it is a matter of the mutual conflicts of the enemies, who destroy themselves by the just judgment of God, in which almost all interpreters agree. Cf. Judg. 7:22. Fourthly, he understands the fight of Judah concerning the Jews who were about to join themselves to Bacchides in the battle against Jerusalem. It is more correctly explained concerning the fight of Judah for Jerusalem. And how do these things fit the history? For he had explained the preceding, v. 12, concerning the wasting away that would consume the enemies, concerning the time of the Jerusalem citadel besieged by Simon, Matt. 13:49; but now he slips back to Bacchides, nor does he find where to fix his foot. Tirinus, however, and Menochius, praised by Grotius, drag these back to the times of Antiochus, 2 Macc. 4 and 5. Fifthly, he explains the riches of ALL nations as the riches in the camps of Nicanor. But how were the riches of all nations there? Nor is it to be read of such great riches in 2 Macc. 8:30 as are designated here. We have already delivered the true sense concerning these.

Unjust and utterly unworthy of brotherly love (τῇ Φιλαδελφίᾳ), I add also twisted, is the explanation of Cocceius, by which he understands the Lutherans as Judah attacking Jerusalem, whom he confesses to have fellowship in the faith of the foundation with the Reformed (noted, as he wishes, by Jerusalem), attributing to them the unjust condemnation and persecution of brothers, and also the association of arms with professed enemies, and denouncing to them in place of a plague and punishment a wasting away, i.e., as he himself explains, envy, with an internal burning of heart and conscience, on account of hatred of the truth and the sense of an angry God, which state he calls the lake burning with sulfur and fire, Rev. 19:20, and points them out from Isaiah as corpses, whose worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished, ch. 66, and also the destruction of Judah itself, i.e., according to this Calvinist glossator, the Lutheran Church. Alas for brotherly affection in the Church and the Philadelphian period! For the same judgment is denounced against Judah as against the foreign nations, thinks the Socinian of Cocceius, Willius. Who, however, refers the wasting away to the subsequent extinction of the enemies throughout the whole Philadelphian period, who he says will not attack the Church with open force, because Satan is then bound: who is said to be bound for a thousand years in Rev. 20, which little agrees with the Willian opinion concerning Philadelphia being about to last for a very short time, p. 533, and interprets Judah not as the Lutherans, but as the profane citizens of the Reformed Church, because the citizens and members of the Church will fight against their own mother, partly while they will join themselves to open enemies, partly while they will move war against the Church by impiety. But let us leave those Cadmean brothers to themselves, who here also mix battles in their commentaries. Moreover, what we have set forth concerning the plagues of the enemies of the Church, concerning the Anti-Christ, and his army gathered from various nations, Lyranus also and Dionysius, and others, understand as signs of the last day, when men shall wither for fear and expectation of those things which shall come upon the world. But that Anti-Christ is fictitious, whom they trifle will arise toward the end of the world, nor are these things to be restricted to the last times, as we have previously taught. Indeed, the signs of the last day will strike terror not only into the enemies of the Church, but also into the faithful themselves. Here, however, the Prophet prophesies concerning the punishments of the enemies. Some understand the collection of gold, silver, and garments, not as a punishment, but interpret it as a means for attacking Jerusalem, which also Willius

Latin:

ET SIC ERIT RVINA EQVI, ET MVLI ET CAMELI ET ASINI, ET OMNIVM JVMENTO- RVM, QVÆ FVERINT IN CASTRIS ILLIS SI- CVT RVINA HÆC.) מגפה quod hic ruinam vertit, plagam significat. Dicit cladem non minorem fore ani- mantium aliorum, quam hominum, nempe ob causas jam explicatas.

De pœnis persequutorum in genere hæc dicta: q.d. Apparebunt quasi viva quædam cadavera, amittent carnes, id est, potentiam, oculos vel prudentiam,

& linguam vel eloquentiam. Quoniam enim Hie- rufalem, ut habet Cyrillus, quæ est Ecclesia Dei viven- tis, confidenter habitaturam dixit, licebatque hoc jure optimo confectum iri sperare sublatis hostibus, & ever- sis iis, qui eam persequi consueverant, necessario & hæc nobis narrat. Communis enim ista & naturalis mors omnium quidem carnes tabefacit, & oculos atque lin- guis spoliat, acerbissimum autem & calamitosissimum non immerito fuerit, viventium & stantium adhuc car- nes tabescere, & excidere oculos, & puniri linguas. Talia autem Deo exosam & execrandam vitam con- sectatis eventura admodum probe dicit. Reposcen- tur enim pœnæ non solum eorum, quæ in sanctos com- miserunt : sed etiam studii rerum carnalium, quo in hoc mundo flagrarunt : quæ item illis causa fuit, cur ne- que fidem admitterent, neque pietatem colere, & glo- riam vitæ in Christo diligere vellent. Declinaverunt enim, ut dixi, ad absurdas voluptates, & quæcunque vi- debant, ore hiante quodammodo appetebant, ac deglu- tiebant. Acuerunt enim linguas contra Christum & sacra Ecclesiæ dogmata impie carpserunt. Jure igitur in carne, & oculis & linguis pœnam suscepe- runt. Quomodo autem impleta hæc sint, ita docet Hieronymus : Quæ passuræ sint gentes, quo contra urbem Domini dimicabunt, præsens scriptura testa- tur. Stabunt, inquit, super pedes suos, & caro eorum tabescet, & defluet, & oculi eorum compu- trescent, & de suis foraminibus excident : lingua magniloqua, quæ Dei populum blasphemabat, sol- vetur in saniem, & intra vallum dentium compu- trescet. Hæc passos non esse Romanos, qui Hierusalem subverterunt, cunctis perspicuum est; nisi forte Judæi illas nationes asserent perpessuras, quæ contra auream & gemmatam dimicaturæ sunt Hierusalem. Nos autem dicemus, omnes persequutores, qui afflixerunt Ecclesiam Domini, ut taceamus de futuris cruciati- bus etiam in præsenti seculo recepisse, quæ fecerint.
