Le- gamus ecclesiasticas historias : quid Valerianus, quid Decius, quid Diocletianus, quid Maximinianus, quid sævissimus omnium Maximinus, & nuper Ju- lianus passi sint : & tunc rebus probabimus etiam ju- xta literam, prophetiæ veritatem esse completam: quod computruerint carnes eorum, & oculi contabuerint, & lingua in pedorem & saniem dissoluta sit. Cætera tropologice interpretatur Hieronymus. Sed sensum de pœnis persequutorum hic continuari, mani- festum est. Per tabem intelligit Abarbenel morbum Gallicum, aut similem aliquam lepram, alii lentam hostium consumptionem & succedaneam extinctio- nem, alii pœnam infernalem. Lutherus noster hæc ad ipsum Romanum imperium & alia regna ac gentes adversantes Christo & Evangelio ejus ac- commodat : Romanum enim imperium licet in flore esset, & haberet oculos perspicaces, id est, viros pru- dentes & circumspectos, linguas in ore, id est, viros di- sertos, tamen in suo flore concidit & contabuit. Hæc B. Lutherus. IN DIE ILLA ERIT TU- MULTUS DOMINI, Tumultuabuntur etiam in- ter se hostes, ac bella cruenta movebunt, & apprehen- det unusquisque manum proximi sui, & in mutuas rue ent concertationes, seque mutuo conficient. Pugnabit Juda pro vel adversus Jerusalem. Cæterum conva- sabuntur & diripientur divitiæ omnium gentium in circuitu Ecclesiam impugnantium, aurum & argen- tum & vestes pretiosæ multæ satis. Et sic erit plaga equi & muli, ac cameli & asini & omnium jumento- rum, quæ fuerint in castris illis sicut plaga illa, quæ sc. accidit persequutoribus, ut carnes, oculi, & linguæ eorum contabescant. Adjutores autem similes pœnas luent cum illis, qui persecutionum autores erunt. Ita illa de Juda exposuit Cyrillus: Judas, hoc est per fidem in Christum justificati, & Judæum, quem mente intuemur circumferentes & circumcisio- ne spirituali divites, pugnabunt in Hierusalem, hoc est, oppugnabunt hostes, & adversariis virtute prævale- bunt, & conculcantes, ut scorpiones. Nec improba- vit illum sensum Hieronymus: Judas omnis confi- tens & fidelis non adversum Hierusalem pugnabit, sed præparabit se in Jerusalem, ut contra adversarios di- micet. Alii de hæreticis & apostatis, qui ex Ecclesiæ filiis mutantur in hostes, intelligunt, adversus Ec- clesiam itidem pugnaturos. Sed priori sensui magis videtur textus favere, ne cum aliis opus sit paren- thesin statuere. Quod non tantum Jehovah ipsos percussurus sit plaga horribili, atque ipsi panico terrore correpti se mutuo trucidaturi, sed quod Ju- da etiam, h. e. pii & vere fideles summa animi ala- critate pro Ecclesiæ pugnaturi sint. Ita Lamb. Dana- us: & B. Tarnovius h, m. reddens: Et tu quoque Jehu- da pugnabis Jerosolymis, vos confessores constantes in Ecclesia bonam in gentibus convertendis nava- bitis operam, sic futurum est, ut hostium spoliis ab- unde ditescat Ecclesia, quemadmodum olim Mosis tabernaculum spoliis Ægyptiacis, & recipientur opes omnium gentium, quæ sunt circumquaque, aurum & argentum, vestesque multæ admodum.

probatum, qui Judam inter hostes putat Hierosoly- mæ, quem vero alii hyperaspisten ejusdem faciunt. Quem sententiam commodiorem esse diximus. Gualtherus vero istis verbis, congregabunt aurum & argentum, censet indicari, instructissimos fore ho- stes omnibus, quæ ad bellum gerendum necessaria sunt. Sed ita parenthesi opus erit. Simplicior est eo- rum interpretatio, qui hæc ad pœnam referunt Ec- clesiæ, quia continuatur iisdem earum enumeratio, quemadmodum verba sequentia edocent.

In Grotiano Commentario multa desiderari pos- sunt. Primo trahit omnia ad tempora Maccabæorum cum Cornelio à Lapide: qui vero fatetur, VERIUS hæc fuisse completa in persecutoribus Ecclesiæ N. T. Deinde plagam, qua percussurus erat Dominus gentes adversus Hierosolymam pugnaturas nimis exiliter interpretatur, fame peribunt Macedones, qui erunt in arce Hierosolymitana 1. Macc. 13, 19. Tirinus de Lysia, Antiocho, copiis Timothei & aliis 2. Macc. 9, 5. c. 12, 22. c. 10, 30. intelligit. Alii de Maccabæorum ho- stibus cæcitate percussis, & perturbatione perterri- tis 1. Macc. 4. 2. Macc. 6. Sed illa non exhauriunt vim verborum Prophetæ. Ideo reprobat ejusmodi interpretationes Castrius, & cum Hieronymo, Cyrillo, Remigio, Alberto, Hugone, aliisque & recentioribus, de suppliciis hostium spiritualis Hierosolymæ ex- plicat, siquidem omnem humanam suam poten- tiam, sapientiam, calliditatem & eloquentiam, qui- bus adversus Christianam simplicitatem valere se putabant, fractam, comminutam, debilitatam ac perditam experti sint. Tertio verba textus torquet ad fædera, versum 13. ita reddens: incerta erunt eo tempore fædera, nam qui manum alteri adjungit, is per eam manum (id est, societatem) excindetur. Quæ a- liena & à verbis esse, & à contextu palam est. Nam agitur de mutuis hostium conflictibus, qui semet- ipsos conscient justo Dei judicio, in quo consenti- unt omnes fere Interpp. Conf. Jud. 7, 22. Quarto Ju- dæ pugnam de Judæis sese Bacchidæ juncturis in præ- lio adversus Jerusalem intelligit. Rectius de pugna Judæ pro Jerusalem explicatur. Et quomodo hæc historiæ conveniunt? Superiora enim v. 12. de tabe hostes consumtura, de tempore obsessæ à Simone arcis Hierosolymitanæ exposuerat Matth. 13, 49. nunc ve- ro relabitur ad Bacchidem, nec invenit, ubi pedem figat. Tirinus vero & Menochius Grotio laudatus hæc ad Antiochi tempora retrahunt 2. Macc. 4. & 5. Quinto divitias OMNIUM gentium de divitiis in castris Nicanoris explicat. At quomodo ibi omnium gentium divitiæ erant? Neque de tantis divitiis le- gere est 2. Macc. 8, 30. quantæ hic designantur. Sen- tum verum de his antea tradidimus.

Iniqua & τῇ Φιλαδελφίᾳ prorsus indigna, addo & contorta est Cocceji explicatio, qua per Judam Hierosolymam oppugnantem Lutheranos intelligit, quos in fide fundamenti cum Reformatis (per Hie- rosolymam, uti vult, notatis) societatem habere fate- tus, tribuens illis injustam fratrum damnationem & persecutionem, nec non consociationem armorum cum professis hostibus, ac plagæ ac pœnæ loco denunci- ans iisdem tabem, h. e. ut ipse explicat, invidiam, cum ardore interno cordis & conscientiæ, ob odium verita- tis & sensum irati Dei, quem statum vocat lacum ar- dentem sulfure & igne Apoc. 19, 20. & ipsos ex Esaia indigitat cadavera, quorum vermis non moritur, & ignis non extinguetur, c. 66. nec non destructionem i- psius Judæ, h. e. secundum hunc Calvinianum glos- satorem, Ecclesiæ Lutheranæ. Proh fraternum affe- ctum in Ecclesia & periodo Philadelphica! Judici- um enim idem denunciari in Judam, quod in exte- ras gentes censet Sociennus Cocceji Willius. Qui tamen tabem ad hostium extinctionem succedaneam per totam periodum Philadelphensem refert, quos non grassaturos aperta vi in Ecclesiam, ob Satanam tum vinctum dicit: qui vero Apoc. 20. per mille an- nos ligandus dicitur, quod parum congruit Willia- næ sententiæ de Philadelphia brevi admodum tem- pore duratura p. 533. & Judam non de Lutheranis, sed de civibus Ecclesiæ Reformatæ prophanis interpre- tatur, quod pugnaturi sint cives Ecclesiæ & mem- bra in suam matrem, partim dum se apertis hosti- bus adjungent, partim dum impietate Ecclesiæ bel- lum movebunt. Sed committamus illos Cadmæos fratres inter se, qui hic quoque in commentis suis prælia miscent. Cæterum quæ de plagis hostium Ec- clesiæ exposuimus, de Anti-Christo, ejusque exercitu ex variis gentibus coacto Lyranus quoque & Diony- sius, alii de signis intelligunt extremæ diei, quando præ timore & expectatione eorum, quæ superve- nient orbi, arescent homines. Sed Anti-Christus ille fictitius est, quem sub finem mundi oriturum nugantur, nec ad tempora novissima hæc restrin- genda esse, antea docuimus. Signa vero extremæ diei non hostibus solum Ecclesiæ, sed ipsis quoque fidelibus terrorem incutient. Hic vero de pœnis hostium vaticinatur Propheta. Collectionem auri, argenti, & vestium nonnulli, non in pœnam in- telligunt, sed ceu medium ad oppugnandum Hie- rosolymam interpretantur, quod Willio etiam

## 14:16
Verse 16.

THEY SHALL GO UP FROM YEAR TO YEAR, TO WORSHIP THE KING THE LORD OF HOSTS, AND TO KEEP THE FEAST OF TABERNACLES) That is, many from the nations, having seen such great benefits of God toward the Jewish people, will become proselytes: and since, being placed further away, they cannot celebrate the annual feast days as the Jews do, they will certainly come once a year, at the time of Autumn, which is most convenient for journeys, to celebrate the memory of the people led through desert places and nourished in wondrous ways for 40 years, which time was a certain pledge and figure of all the benefits that followed afterward.

Tirinus understands this as concerning the Idumeans and others subdued by Hyrcanus. Menochius, however, although he explains it as concerning the proselytes who were converted to Judaism after the victories of the Maccabees, nevertheless admits that, because they were not many, what is said here applies more fully to Christians, which sense Cornelius also acknowledges here as the better one, even though he wishes those few converted after them to have been a type of them. But Stunica, Sanchez, and Castrius more correctly understand it as concerning those who are converted from the Gentiles, while the other enemies of the Church perish, they interpret it according to the literal sense. Thus Castrius, while refuting another opinion at the same time: Those who from the nations have submitted their yoke to the Church, having been converted to the faith, shall go up from year to year to the spiritual Jerusalem, that they may profess themselves strangers and pilgrims in this world, and to seek the future. Thus they refer these things to spiritual matters, taking the figure for the thing figured, Euseb. lib. 8. de Demonstrat. c. 4. Hieronym. Haymo, Remig. Albert. Hugo, Lyra, Dionys. Vatabl. Montan. & Isidorus. Theodorelus alone understands it of the nations which, after the victories of the Maccabees, went up to Jerusalem to celebrate the feast of tabernacles with them: but neither did the nations, if there were any, go up to this feast alone, but to worship the Lord in the temple, not being obligated as the Jews were, nor bound by any precept to go up from year to year. Wherefore, since it is certain that this did not happen in reality, we must have recourse to the thing signified and shadowed forth; for why would the Egyptians be punished? Why would the remaining nations not going up be punished, if they had not sinned? Wherefore we are compelled to explain it concerning those converted to the faith, who by that very fact are bound to obey the Church and to have recourse to it with many others. Let us hear Cyril: When he had said that the attackers of the churches, and those who proudly lifted their eyebrows against holy Jerusalem, would pay condign punishments, he announces the adoration of those left after them, namely that which is done through Christ into the faith. For he himself is the expectation of the nations according to the voice of the Patriarch. He is also placed as a light to the nations, and as a covenant of the race, that he may open the eyes of the blind, and free those bound from chains, and those sitting in darkness from the house of the prison. Therefore, having left behind the darkness of idolatry, and the chains of the devil and of stupidity having been broken, he declares that they will come from the nations to the light of truth, and will succeed under the yoke of the savior, saying that the rest of the punished attackers of the Church (and these are innumerable) will go up every year to worship the Lord almighty God, and to celebrate the feast of tabernacles. These things Cyril. Our own writers all agree to a man. That from all the nations which formerly opposed the Church, very many will be converted to Christ the King, and will serve him in the spiritual Jerusalem. For the Prophet describes the worship of Christians in the New Testament with the words of the Old Testament, and uses the phrases of his own age, both because he was speaking to Jews who knew only Jewish feasts, and because he wished to show that the Jewish feasts were figures of the true things under the New Testament. where Christians more truly keep the feast of tabernacles not once a year, but continuously, meditating not only on the departure from spiritual Egypt through Christ, which the departure of the Israelites had figured, but also on their state in this world, that it behooves us to wander in this desert as strangers 1 Pet. 2, 11. and to think perpetually of the heavenly inheritance Heb. 11, 9. and also because the Prophets speak prophetically, that is, parabolically, symbolically, enigmatically, not only because of the absence of future things, which they saw through shadows and figures, but also because of the elegance of prophecy: which method of proposing mysteries through hieroglyphics the Jews did not learn from the Egyptians, but rather these from those. For the Egyptians drew their wisdom from the Hebrews, as Eusebius lib. X. præpar. Clem. Alexandrin. lib. 1. Strom. Augustin. lib. XVIII. de Civ. Dei cap. 39 have proven. Rightly therefore Osiander: The Prophet uses the phrases of his own age. For the Jews used to set out to Jerusalem for the famous feasts. Now the feast of tabernacles was not only instituted to be a memorial that the Lord had nourished and preserved the Israelites in the desert for forty whole years: but by that feast they were also admonished to think that they were strangers in this world, and to meditate on the heavenly life, and to direct all their efforts toward it, so that they might one day be able to dwell in the eternal and heavenly tabernacles. The Prophet therefore wishes to say: The nations will be converted to Christ, and will worship him daily as a heavenly king, and the true and eternal God, the Lord of hosts, and will meditate on the heavenly life: they will prepare themselves with the greatest zeal for the other life. Therefore, while only the feast of tabernacles is named, not one feast alone is indicated, but under it all things are comprehended synecdochically.

The Jews therefore talk nonsense while they contend that the feast of tabernacles must be taken literally: whom Grotius has followed. Gualtherus, although he had dragged the preceding things to the times of the Maccabees, was finally forced to acknowledge here that these things pertain to the times of the New Testament: The sense is, at the coming of Christ, the nations also, which were previously enemies of the Church and alien to the worship of the true God, will come of their own accord to obedience, that they may join themselves to the Church, and having left behind superstitions, may truly worship God. But about to speak of the true and spiritual worship of God, he speaks in the common manner of the Prophets according to the reason of that age, when legal sacred rites, which God had instituted through Moses, were still in use. He also observes that the Jews had to go up to Jerusalem three times a year: because therefore he mentions only the feast of tabernacles, he teaches clearly enough that not Levitical sacred rites, but the mysteries of Christ are treated in this place. And he mentions the feast of tabernacles above others, because its mystery or signification was most suited to the present purpose. For it contained the memory of the liberation from Egypt, and of all the benefits which God had bestowed upon that nation for forty years, when they lived in the desert under tents and tabernacles. See Levit. 23. Furthermore, in a deeper sense, it shadowed forth the condition of life, that they might learn that they were strangers on earth, and having left all earthly things behind them, might strive for the heavenly fatherland. The Prophet therefore teaches that among those who have conceded to the Church of Christ, there will be a perpetual memory of the benefits of God and of the redemption made in Christ, and that they will take care to pass through the study of this life with constant faith and tireless zeal for innocence, and to obtain the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland with Christ their savior. These things Gualtherus. Concerning the feast of tabernacles, Cyril speaks thus: The law provided the reason for the feast, because Israel had dwelt in tents, freed from the dominion of the Egyptians. Which thing will be a certain type of the mystery in Christ. For we too have been snatched from the servitude of the devil, and called, as I have said, into liberty through Christ, and made subject to the King of all, and to life, having despised the cruelty of our former masters. We celebrate, however, the true feast of the scenopegia, that is, the day of the resurrection of Christ, when all bodies in him are as it were fixed and compacted, although dissolved by corruption and occupied by death. For he himself is the resurrection, he himself is life, as the firstfruits from the dead, (and the first of those who sleep) who fills us with fertility, which is known by understanding, and makes us accumulate the labors gathered as if from the fields into the heavenly barns.

Concerning the trifles of the Jews, Cocceius has it thus in this place: The Jews, as they are triflers, say that it will come to pass in the days of the Messiah that the nations will complain before God that the law was not given to them, as it was to Israel; otherwise they would have observed it equally. Then God will propose to them the commandment concerning the feast of tabernacles. There, however, God will so pierce the nations with solar rays that they will not be able to remain in the huts. Mere trifles, by which they mock, in their own fashion, the prophetic spirit: which asserts that the Gentiles will altogether perform this worship. But just as in the New Testament we keep the sabbath, and celebrate the new moon and the Passover (Heb. 4, 9. 11. 16. Ps. 81, 4. 1 Cor. 5, 7. 8.) so also we celebrate the scenopegia, namely, not in the letter, but in spirit and in truth.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

ADSCENDENT AB ANNO IN ANNUM, UT ADORENT REGEM DOMINUM EXERCITUVM, ET CELEBRENT FESTIVITATEM TABERNACU- LORUM) Id est, multi ex gentibus, conspectis tantis Dei beneficiis in populum Judaicum, fient proselyti: & cum longius positi, annuos dies festos celebrare non possint, ut Judæi, certe semel anno, Autumni tempore, quod ad itinera commodissimum, venient ad celebrandam memoriam, du- cti per loca deserta populi, nutritique miris modis per an- nos XL. quod tempus pignus quoddam & figura fuit o- mnium beneficiorum, quæ postea secuta sunt.

De Idumæis, & aliis ab Hircano subactis intelligit Tirinus. Menochius vero etsi de proselytis, qui post victorias Maccabæorum conversi sint ad Ju- daismum, explicet, fatetur tamen, quia illi non multi fuerunt, plenius, quæ hic dicuntur, Chri- stianis convenire, quem sensum potiorem hic a- gnoscit quoque Cornelius, etsi illos paucos post illos CONVERSOS eorum typum fuisse ve- lit. Rectius autem Stunica, Sanchez, & Ca- strius de illis, qui è gentilibus convertuntur, cæteris Ecclesiæ hostibus pereuntibus, secundum literalem sensum interpretantur. Ita Castrius alte- ram simul refellens sententiam: Qui ex gentibus jugum subjecerint Ecclesiæ, ad fidem conversi ascen- dent ab anno in annum Ierosolymam spiritualem, ut se profiteantur advenas & peregrinos in hoc mundo, & futurum inquirere. Sic ad spiritualia hæc referunt figuram pro re figurata accipientes, Euseb. lib. 8. de Demonstrat. c. 4. Hieronym. Haymo, Remig. Albert. Hugo, Lyra, Dionys. Vatabl. Montan. & Isidorus. So- lus Theodorelus intelligit de gentibus, quæ post victo- rias Maccabæorum ascendebant Jerusalem, ut cum eis celebrarent tabernaculorum festa: sed neq; ad hoc festum solum gentes, si quæ erant, ascendebant, sed ad adorandum Dominum in templo, non obli- gatæ, ut Judæi, neque ab anno in annum ascendere aliquo præcepto devinctæ. Quare cum hoc non accidisse constet reipsa, ad rem signatam & umbra- tam recurramus oportet, cur enim punirentur Æ- gyptii? cur reliquæ gentes non ascendentes, si non delinquissent? Quare de conversis ad fidem, qui eo ipso tenentur Ecclesiæ parere, & ad eam recurrere cum plurimis cogimur explicare. Cyrillum au- diamus: Ecclesiarum oppugnatores, & qui contra sanctam Hierusalem supercilium superbe sustulerunt, pœnas condignas luituros cum dixisset, post illos reli- ctorum adorationem prænunciat, illam scilicet, quæ fit per Christum in fidem. Ipse enim est exspectatio gentium juxta Patriarchæ vocem. Positus est quoque in lumen gentium, & in testamentum generis, ut ape- riat oculos nœcorum, & vinctos à vinculis, & à do- mo carceris sedentis in tenebris liberet. Idolola- træ igitur relicta caligine, diaboliq; & stoliditatis vin- culis diruptis de gentibus, ad veritatis lumen venturos, & sub salvatoris jugum successuros, declarat, dicens, reliquos de punitis Ecclesiæ oppugnatoribus (innume- rabiles autem isti) ascensuros in annos singulos ad ad- orandum Dominum omnipotentem Deum, & ad ce- lebrandum festum tabernaculorum. Hæc Cyrillus. Consonant Nostrates ad unum omnes. De uni- versis gentibus, quæ Ecclesiæ olim adversabantur, plurimos conversum iri ad Christum Regem, eiq; in spirituali Hierosolyma servituros. Describit e- nim Prophetα verbis Vet. Testam. cultum Chri- stianorum in N.T. utiturque sui seculi phrasibus, tum quia loquebatur Judæis, qui non nisi festa Judai- ca norant, tum quod ostendere voluerit, festa Iu- daica figuras fuisse rerum verarum sub N.T. ubi Chri- stiani verius agunt festum tabernaculorum non se- mel in anno, sed continuo meditantes non solum e- gressum ex Ægypto spirituali per Christum, quem egressus Israëlitarum figuraverat, sed & statum suum in hoc mundo, quod in hoc deserto peregrinari nos oporteat, tanquam advenas 1. Pet. 2, 11. & cœle- stem cogitare perpetuo hæreditatem Ebr. 11, 9. tum quia Prophetæ prophetice loquuntur, id est, paraboli- ce, symbolice, ænigmatice, non modo ob rerum futu- rarum absentiam, quas per umbras & figuras vide- bant, sed etiam ob prophetiæ elegantiam: quam rationem mysteria per hieroglyphica proponen- di non Judæi ab Ægyptiis, sed hi potius ab istis di- dicere. Hauserunt enim ab Ehræis Ægyptii sapien- tiam suam, ut evicere Eusebius lib. X. præpar. Clem. Alexandrin. lib. 1. Strom. Augustin. lib. XVIII. de Civ. Dei cap. 39. Recte ergo Osiander: Utitur Propheta sui seculi phrasibus. Judæi enim ad festa celebria Jerosolymam proficiscebantur. Festum autem tabernaculorum non tantum insti- tutum erat, ut esset memoriale, quod Dominus Is- raelitas, totos quadraginta annos, in deserto aluis- set & conservasset: sed eo festo etiam admoneban- tur, ut cogitarent se esse in hoc mundo peregrinos, & ut meditarentur cœlestem vitam, & eo omnes suos conatus dirigerent, ut aliquando habitare possent in æternis & cœlestibus tabernaculis. Vult igitur Propheta dicere: Gentes ad Christum con- vertentur, eumq́; ut regem cœlestem, & verum atq́; æ- ternum Deum, Dominum exercituum, quotidie colent, & meditabuntur vitam cœlestem: præparabunt se- se summo studio ad alteram vitam. Dum ergo nominatur solum festum tabernaculorum, non u- num solum festum indigitatur, sed sub illo Synec- dochice omnia comprehenduntur.

Ineptiunt itaq; Judæi, dum festum tabernaculo- rum proprie accipiendum esse, contendunt: quos sequutus est Grotius. Gualtherus, etsi superiora ad Maccabæorum tempora pertraxerit, agnoscere denique hic coactus fuit, hæc ad N. T. tempora per- tinere: Sensus est, sub Christi adventum, gentes e- tiam, quæ prius Ecclesiæ hostes, & à veri Dei cul- tu alienæ fuerint, sponte venturas ad obsequium, ut Ecclesiæ se conjungant, & relictis superstitio- nibus Deum vere colant. At de vero & spiritua- li Dei cultu dicturus, communi Prophetarum more pro illius seculi ratione loquitur, quando adhuc in usu erant sacra legalia, quæ Deus per Mo- sem instituerat. Observat etiam Judæos ter in an- no Hierosolymam ascendere debuisse: quia ergo solum festum tabernaculorum memorat, satis aperte doce- re, non Levitica sacra, sed Christi mysteria hoc loco tra- ctari. Et tabernaculorum festi præ aliis meminit, quia hujus mysterium seu fignificatio ad præsens institutum maxime faciebat. Continebat enim memoriam liberationis ex Ægypto, & omnium beneficiorum, quæ per annos quadraginta Deus in illam gentem contulerat, cum in deserto sub tentoriis & tabernaculis agerent. Vide Levit. 23. Altiori præterea sensu vitæ conditionem adum- brabat, ut se in terris peregrinos esse discerent, & relictis post se terrenis omnibus, ad cœlestem patriam contenderent. Docet ergo Propheta apud eos, qui ad Ecclesiam Christi concesserint, perpetuam fore beneficiorum Dei & redemtionis, in Christo factæ, memoriam, & eosdem curaturos, ut hujus vitæ studium constanti fide & indeffeso innocentiæ studio emetiantur, & cœlestis patriæ hæreditatem cum Christo salvatore suo obtineant. Hæc Gualtherus. De festo tabernaculorum ita Cyril- lus: Causam festi lex faciebat, quod Israel in ten- toriis habitasset, Ægyptiorum dominatu liberat9. Quæ res typus quidam erit mysterii in Christo. Erepti enim nos sumus quoq; è diaboli servitute, & vocati, ut dixi, in libertatem per Christum, & facti sub universorum rege, & vita, veterum Do- minorum immanitate contempta. Celebramus antem verum scenopegiæ festum, h.e. diem resur- rectionis Christi, quando omnia in ipso corpora quasi fixa & compacta sunt, quamvis corruptione dissoluta, & morte occupata. Ipse enim est resur- rectio, ipse vita, velut primitiæ ex mortuis, (& pri- mitiva dormientium) qui nos fertilitate, quæ intel- ligentia cognoscitur, replet, & quasi ex agris col- lectos labores in superna horrea accumulare facit."

De nugis Judæorum sic habet Coccejus in h. l. Judæi, ut sunt nugatores, ajunt fore in diebus Messiæ, ut gentes causentur coram Deo, sibi legem non da- tam, ut Israeli; alias æque observaturas se fuisse. Tum Deum ipsis propositurum præceptum de festo taberna- culorum. Ibi vero Deum gentes radiis solaribus ita puncturum, ut in tuguriis subsistere non possint. Nugæ meræ, quibus irrident, suo more, spiritum propheticum: qui asseverat, omnino Gentes hunc cultum obituras. Quemadmodum autem in N. T. σαββατιζόμενοι, & νεομηνίαν celebramus & Pascha (Hebr. 4, 9. 11. 16. Pf. 81, 4. 1. Cor. 5, 7. 8.) ita quoq; σκηνοπηγίαν scil. non in litera, sed in spiritu & veritate.

## 14:17
Verse 17.

AND IT SHALL BE, WHOEVER SHALL NOT ASCEND FROM THE FAMILIES OF THE EARTH] That is, from the Jews who were in those places from which Jerusalem could be reached once a year without too much inconvenience: for example, those who were in Syria, Cilicia, Cyprus, Crete, Arabia.

THERE SHALL NOT BE UPON THEM RAIN] What is said by way of comparison in Hosea 6:3 is here said by metaphor. That this is a shortened comparison is demonstrated: for by rain is understood divine favor, because rain is also accustomed to be called a blessing.

This gloss is again too arbitrary. For whence is it certain that what was said generally about the families of the EARTH must be restricted to the Jews? Whence will that determination about places nearer to Jerusalem be proven? And is it not sufficiently clear from the preceding words that the discourse is about the nations and families of any nations whatsoever throughout the whole earth? Therefore, Cyril, Jerome, Remigius, Albert, Hugo, and most others understand the whole world by the earth. Vatablus and Christ. à Castro indeed understand the Israelite land and the families of the tribes of Israel, but they explain it thus: If those tribes living in Judea or wherever in the world should not wish to ascend to the spiritual Jerusalem, they will be deprived of the rain of the word of God. Because the word with grace was to be offered to them first, then to the nations, which are designated by the Egyptians and the remaining nations. For the prophecy is not to be understood as concerning the earthly Jerusalem with the Jews, but the spiritual one, nor are these converts said to be going to approach Jerusalem with the steps of the body, but by the conjunction of the spirit. Those who are in the communion of saints are in the spiritual Jerusalem. How could that metropolis of Judea have contained all the nations of the earth? How is it possible for men from the whole world to come there every year? Therefore, those ascending, as Cyril says here, to worship God the Almighty and to perform the feast of Tabernacles, are those who have been justified by faith in Christ. Furthermore, he threatens destruction to those who do not ascend, and punishments equal to those which persecutors and the contumelious are to receive. For they will be led to the same place as the enemies who did not wish to love. And this, I think, is what Christ himself also said: He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters. Similarly St. Jerome. The Church of the Lord Jesus is called the heavenly Jerusalem, of which the Apostle writes: But the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all: And: You have approached Mount Sion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. And this Jerusalem is not situated in low places, but on a high mountain: of which the Savior speaks: A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden. Whence he who is about to worship the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem must ascend to the mountains. But he who is of the families and tribes of the earth, and therefore cannot worship the Lord, there shall not be upon him the early and the latter rain, nor shall his land be watered by the rains of heaven. Or as the Septuagint translated: whoever shall not ascend from all the tribes of the earth to Jerusalem, to worship the King, the Lord Almighty, that is, those who shall not have ascended from the families of the earth to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord Almighty, shall be reckoned with those who fought against Jerusalem, and whose flesh shall waste away and their eyes shall melt and their tongue shall rot. This punishment of drought is not to be understood as a lack of material rain, by which fields and lands are accustomed to be made fruitful, as Danaeus and Tirinus wish, but as a deprivation of spiritual rain, as the other Reformed acknowledge, which is, according to Cocceius, the understanding of the divine word, the consolation of the Holy Spirit, sanctification, and the gifts through which the Church is built. To those to whom rain is denied after sowing, there can be no hope of a crop to come: so those who do not have the consolation of the Spirit from the scriptures cannot have the hope of eternal life.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ET ERIT, QUI NON ASCENDERIT DE FAMILIIS TERRÆ] Id est, de Judæis, qui in illis locis e- rant, unde Hierosolyma semel anno veniri fine nimio in- commodo posset: puta qui erant in Syria, Cilicia, Cypro, Creta, Arabia.

NON ERIT SUPER EOS IMBER] Quod per comparationem dicitur Oseæ 6, 3. id hic per μεταφορὰν. Quæ curtata comparatio est, demonstratur: nam per im- brem intelligitur divinus favor: quia & imber vocari so- let ἐυλογὶα.

Glossa hæc iterum nimis arbitraria est. Unde enim constat, quæ de familiis TERRÆ generatim dicta, ad Iudæos restringenda esse? Unde illa deter- minatio probabitur de locis vicinioribus Hierosoly- mæ? Et annon satis liquet à verbis præcedentibus sermonem esse de gentibus & familiis nationum qua- rumvis per universam terram? ideo per terram u- niversum orbem intelligunt Cyrillus, Hieronym. Re- migius, Albertus, Hugo, & alii plerique. Vatablus & Christ. à Castro intelligunt quidem terram Israeliti- cam & familias tribuum Israelis, sed ita explicant: Si illæ tribus in Judæa habitantes aut ubicunq; terra- rum, noluerint ascendere in spiritualem Hierosolymam, imbre verbi Dei privabuntur. Quia illis primum offe- rendum erat verbum cum gratia, deinde gentibus: quæ per Ægyptios & reliquas gentes designantur. Neque enim de Hierosolyma terrena vaticinium accipiendum cum Judæis, sed de spirituali, neque hi conversi adituri dicuntur Hierosolymam passi- bus corporis, sed conjunctione spiritus. Qui in com- munione sanctorum sunt, in spirituali sunt Hiero- solyma. Quomodo metropolis illa Judææ capere potuisset omnes nationes terræ? Quomodo possi- bile quotannis homines ex toto orbe eo venire? Ergo ascendentes, ut hic Cyrillus, ad adorandum Deum omnipotentem & peragendum festum scenopegiæ sunt, qui per fidem in Christo justificati sunt. Minatur por- ro non ascendentibus perniciem, pœnasq; pares iis quas daturi sint persecutores, & contumeliosi. Eodem quippe loco ducentur, quo hostes, qui diligere nolue- rint. Et hoc, opinor, est, quod & ipse Christus dixit, Qui non est mecum, contra me est: & qui non col- ligit mecum, dispergit. Similiter S. Hieronym. Ec- clesia Domini Jesu appellatur cælestis Hierusalem: de qua Apostolus scribit: Quæ autem sursum est Hieru- salem, libera est, quæ est mater omnium nostro- rum: Et: Accessistis ad Sion montem & civitatem Dei viventis Hierusalem cælestem. Et hæc Hieru- salem non est in locis humilibus sita, sed in monte excel- so: de qua Salvator loquitur: Non potest civitas ab- scondi super montem posita. Unde qui adoraturus est Dominum exercituum in Hierusalem: debet ad montana conscendere. Qui autem de familiis ac tribu- bus terræ est: & idcirco Dominum non potest adora- re: non erit super eum imber temporaneus & seroti- nus: nec terra illius pluviis cali rigabitur. Sive ut ver- terunt Septuaginta ὅσοι ἐὰν μὴ ἀναβῶσιν ἐκ πασῶν τ̃ φυλῶν τ̃ γῆς εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, τ̃ προσκυνῆσαι τῷ βασιλεῖ κυρίῳ παντοκράτορι, id est, qui non ascenderint de familiis terræ ad Hierusalem: ut ado- rent regem dominum omnipotentem: cum illis repu- tabuntur, qui pugnaverunt adversum Hierusalem: & quorum tabescet caro & oculi defluent, & lingua pu- trescet. Pœna hæc ἀομβρία non intelligenda de pluviæ materialis, qua fundi & agri fœcundi reddi solent, defectu, uti vult Danæus & Tirinus, sed de pluviæ spiritualis privatione, ut agnoscunt cæteri Re- formati, quæ est, juxta Coccejum, intelligentia verbi divini, consolatio Sp. S. sanctificatio, & dona per quæ Ecclesia ædificatur. Quibus negatur pluvia post se- mentem, illis nulla segetis proventuræ spes esse po- test: ita qui non habent ex scripturis consolatio- nem Spiritus, ii non possunt habere spem vitæ æ- ternæ.

## 14:18
ALTHOUGH THE FAMILY OF EGYPT SHALL NOT ASCEND] Repeat from the above, the family of the earth, namely of Judea, which was in Egypt. He understands those who had gone into Egypt with Onias and had made a temple for themselves there: of whom Josephus writes in Antiquities of the Jews XIII. 6 and Jewish War VII. 37.

AND THERE SHALL NOT BE UPON THEM] Namely, the favor of God, by common usage: truly, as can be known from the cited places of Josephus; and the King of Egypt Ptolemy and Queen Cleopatra had foreseen this, who, if there were anything in the building of this temple contrary to the law of God or ungrateful to God, had wished to turn it not upon themselves, but upon Onias and his associates. This appears from the letter which Josephus brings forward. Demetrius in his Edict established that no one should have another temple to worship in Judea except only the one in Jerusalem.

BUT THERE SHALL BE RUIN] A plague, as above in 15; for it is the same noun in Hebrew.

FOR THE LORD SHALL STRIKE ALL THE NATIONS] Understand the Jews dispersed among the nations. Thus we have already shown several times that the tribes are called by the name of nations or peoples.

Latin:

QUOD ETSI FAMILIA ÆGYPTI NON ADSCENDERIT] Repete ex superiore, familia terræ, nempe Judææ, quæ in Ægypto. Intelligit eos, qui cum Onia in Ægyptum ierant, & ibi sibi Templum fecerant: de quibus Josephus Antiquæ historiæ XIII. 6. & Belli Judaici VII. 37.

NEC SUPER EOS ERIT] Nempe Dei favor, ἀπὸ κοινῦ: vere, ut ex dictis Josephi locis cognosci datur: & præviderant id Ægypti Rex Ptolemæus, & Regina Cleopatra, qui siquid in hujus templi exædificatione esset contra legem Dei, Deove ingratum, id non in se, sed in Oniam, ejusque socios vertere voluerant. Id ex epistola apparet, quam adfert Josephus. Demetrius in Edicto constituit, ἵνα μηδὲ εἰς Ἰοδαῖαν ἄλλο ἔχῃ ἱερὸν προσκυνεῖν ἢ μόνον τὸ ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις.

SED ERIT RUINA] Plaga, ut supra 15. est enim idem nomen in Hebræo.

QVIA PERCVTIET DOMINS OMNES GENTES] Intellîgc Judæos in gentibus dispersos. Sic & tribus vocari nomine gentium aut populorum oftendimus jam aliquoties.

## 14:19
Verse 19.

THIS SHALL BE THE SIN OF EGYPT] Of the Jews in Egypt.

AND THIS SHALL BE THE SIN OF ALL NATIONS] Of the dispersed Jews.

WHICH SHALL NOT GO UP TO CELEBRATE THE FEAST OF TABERNACLES] At least this one, if they cannot celebrate others: and understand this with the caution which we added above in 16.

Grotius repeats his glosses, in order to restrict a most clear text concerning the calling of the Gentiles to the kingdom of Christ to the legal worship of the Jews. But the family of EGYPT is one thing, the family of the LAND, namely Judea, which is in Egypt, is another. Nor is it right to understand by ALL NATIONS the Jews dispersed among the nations. And the Holy Spirit expressly points out both ALL who shall have remained FROM ALL THE NATIONS that came against Jerusalem, and the Egyptians, and ALL the remaining NATIONS, whence it has been undoubted among all interpreters that these things must be accepted concerning the conversion of the Gentiles, except for the Jesuits, from whom Grotius drew his gloss. For Cornelius, although he suggests the sense concerning the Jews who had erected an altar against an altar in Egypt, nevertheless acknowledges that by the Egyptians, who were neighbors to the Jews and hostile to them, and are specifically named here, any Gentiles whatsoever are noted synecdochically, as also are the enemies of the Church, so that it is indicated that even the most hostile enemies of the Church themselves will be converted to the Church, in which opinion he also praises Jerome, Theodoret, Remigius, Lyra, and Vatablus. Cornelius interprets that passage and those words, THIS SHALL BE THE SIN OF THE EGYPTIANS, concerning sin said antonomastically: This shall be the greatest sin of all sins, if indeed the nations are unwilling to depart from their gentilism and enter the Church of Christ, and in it celebrate the feast of tabernacles, as Theodoret, Jerome, Remigius, Hugo, Albert, Lyra, and Dionysius have explained: thus also the Jesuit Menochius: And if the family of Egypt, etc. And if the family of the nations that have afflicted the Church shall not wish to come, there shall be no rain upon them. Let us hear Jerome: He who is an Egyptian, and of the other nations: as long as he remains an Egyptian and a heathen, he shall not go up to Jerusalem: and because he cannot go up, nor raise a step to the heights, therefore there shall not be upon him the rain of the Lord's blessing. And this shall be the greatest sin for the Egyptian, the Assyrian, the Chaldean, the Syrian, the Moabite, and the Ammonite, if they shall wish to depart from their lands and go up to Jerusalem: that they may pass through the tabernacles into Jerusalem, and find an eternal home, and cease to be men of other nations, and be made Israelites, in whom there is no guile.

Others explain the word sin as punishment, as in Mal. 2:16, with the Chaldean, Pagninus, Montanus, and Isidore. But there is no reason why one should depart from the proper sense of the word, and the added σύνδεσις is proof that the discourse is about sin itself. Cocceius is correct here: This will be sin. Not that they will commit no other sin, or that they are not guilty without this; but because through this their guilt and their defection and their damnation will be manifested. For since forgiveness is promised in Christ to all who repent, he who spurns it judges himself unworthy of that grace and condemns himself. Compare John 3:19: This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light. Regarding which, Cyril also should be heard: Before the Savior's advent, perhaps the excuse of the Gentiles was still in part plausible, saying that they had been called by no one, for no one had preached to them. Wherefore also the Savior, showing this very thing to us in the Evangelical parables, says that the laborers called about the eleventh hour said: Because no one hired us. But after Christ shone forth, bound the strong man, took away those placed under his perversity, justified those approaching him by faith, and laid down his soul for the life of all, those who have not admitted such venerable grace will find no sufficient excuse henceforth. Therefore, Christ would rightly say even of the Gentiles: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin: but now they have no excuse for their sin.

Regarding the dreams of the Jews, St. Jerome holds this: Our Jews and Judaizers, or rather not ours, because the Judaizers hope for future things corporally. Promising themselves both circumcision and marriages in the empire of a thousand years, so that the curse which is written may not be fulfilled in them: Cursed is the barren one who does not make seed in Israel: And: Blessed is he who has seed in Sion, and domestics in Jerusalem. But if this is true, all the virgins whom the thousand-year kingdom finds will be subject to a curse and perpetual sterility, or at least they are to be married, so that they may escape the curse.

Willius imagines the Laodicean period from verse 16 onwards: in which passive profanity is to run rampant most freely. But in this, reason itself escapes him. For these things do not treat of passive profanity, but of the frequent confluence of the nations to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, Christ Jesus. For Willius himself understands the ascent toward Jerusalem as a continuous and constant access to the Church from year to year; indeed, he thinks the mention of the feast of tabernacles was made so that it might be taught that the Church will have the closest communion with God, that God will exhibit His most present grace to it, and that it will rejoice and luxuriate in it, no differently than if it had already been introduced into the heavenly habitation. Which sense he himself indeed wrongly elicits from Apoc. 21:3, because there the discourse is about heavenly glory, not about the state of the Church in these lands. But how does such and so great a happiness suit that period in which passive profanity runs rampant most freely? Nor does the Prophet designate only some particular multitude that is to separate itself from the profane, but he speaks of all the remnants from all the nations that have come against Jerusalem. Add that what is contained in the final verses contributes to the remarkable happiness and holiness of the Church, as Willius himself admits. How then will the reasons for the periods which he has invented hold together? For according to his opinion, such holiness or happiness certainly does not suit the Laodicean, the most recent period. Since he saw this clearly, he guarded himself with this invention, to append there

that the Prophet [is giving] a new description of Philadelphia, in a manner entirely twofold, just as John in the Apocalypse ch. 20, 10, 22 described the new Jerusalem as a type of Philadelphia. But this would be a mixing and confusion of different periods, from which finally nothing certain could be had about these periods, by which method periodic inventions must be wiped away like a sponge. And when he drags the Apocalypse here, what is this other than begging the question? Which fallacy Willius incurs in a twofold way, both because he assumes his periods observed in the Apocalypse gratuitously, and because he decides without proof that the Prophet must be explained from the Apocalypse. There is added the vice of false interpretation: since he explains the description of the heavenly Jerusalem, which St. John exhibited depicted with most elegant figures, falsely, or rather ineptly, as the state of the Church in this age in Philadelphia. Finally, since the judgment in verse 12 and following, described by our Prophet, seems to Willius to be about to follow the last day immediately, how could he still believe in the Laodicean period, and in it, passive profanity?

Latin:

Vers. 19.

HOC ERIT PECCATVM ÆGYPTI] Judæorum in Ægypto.

ET HOC PECCATVM OMNIVM GENTIVM] Judæorum dispersorum.

QVÆ NON ADSCENDERINT AD CELEBRANDAM FESTIVITATEM TABERNACVLORVM] Saltem hanc, si alias celebrare non possint: & intellige cum cautione, quam supra addidimus 16.

Repetit glossas suas Grotius, quo textum luculentissimum de vocatione gentium ad regnum Christi restringat ad Judæorum cultum legalem. At aliud est familia ÆGYPTI, aliud familia TERRÆ, nempe Judææ, quæ in Ægypto. Nec per OMNES GENTES Judæos in gentibus dispersos intelligere fas est. Et diserte Sp. S. tum OMNES, qui reliqui fuerint EX UNIVERSIS GENTIBUS, quæ venerunt contra Jerusalem, tum Ægyptios, & OMNES GENTES reliquas indigitat, unde penes Interpp. omnes indubitatum fuit de conversione gentium hæc accipienda esse, ne exceptis Jesuitis, à quibus glossam hausit Grotius. Nam Cornelius etsi suggerat sensum de Judæis, qui in Ægypto erexerant altare contra altare, agnoscit tamen, per Ægyptios, qui vicini Judæis, iisque infensi, peculiariter hic nominati sint, synecdochice quosvis gentiles, ut & hostes Ecclesiæ notari, ut ipsos etiam Ecclesiæ hostes infensissimos conversum iri ad Ecclesiam indicetur, in quam sententiam etiam laudat Hieronymum, Theodoretum, Remigium, Lyranum, & Vatablum. Locum, & verba illa, HOC ERIT PECCATUM Ægyptiorum, de peccato antonomastice dicto interpretatur Cornelius: Hoc erit peccatum peccatorum omnium maximum, si nimirum gentes nolint exire è suo gentilismo, & ingredi Christi Ecclesiam, & in ea festum tabernaculorum celebrare, uti exposuit Theodoretus, Hieronymus, Remigius, Hugo, Albertus, Lyra, Dionysius: sic etiam Jesuita Menochius: Et si familia Ægypti, &c. & si familia gentium, quæ afflixerunt Ecclesiam, noluerint venire, non erit super eas imber. Audiamus Hieronymum: Qui Ægyptius est, & gentium cæterarum: quamdiu Ægyptius & ethnicus permanet, non ascendet in Hierusalem: & quia ascendere non potest, nec gradum ad excelsa subrigere, ideo non erit super eum imber dominicæ benedictionis, Et hoc peccatum erit maximum Ægyptio, Assyrio, Chaldæo, Syro, Moabitæ & Ammonitæ, si voluerint egredi de terris suis, & ascendere Hierusalem: ut per tabernacula transeant in Hierusalem, & inveniant æternam domum, aliarumq́ gentium homines esse desistant, & efficiantur Israelitæ, in quibus dolus non est.

Alii de pœna explicant vocem peccati, ut Mal. 2, 16. cum Chaldæo, Pagnino, Montano & Isidoro. Sed non est, cur à proprio vocis sensu discedatur, & addita σύνδεσις documento est, de peccato "ipso sermonem esse. Recte hic Coccejus: Hoc "erit peccatum. Non quod nullum aliud pecca- "tum facient, aut non sine hoc sint rei; sed quia per "hoc reatus ipsorum & defectio ipsorum & da- "mnatio manifestabitur. Nam quum omnibus "pœnitentibus sit promissa venia in Christo, qui "eam spernit, is se non dignum illa gratia judicat "& se ipsum condemnat. Confer. Joh. 3, 19. Hoc "est judicium, quod venit lux in mundum, & ama- "verunt homines magis tenebras quam lucem. De "quo audiendus etiam Cyrillus: Ante Salvatoris "adventum forte adhuc ex parte speciosa erat gen- "tium excusatio dicentium, se à nemine vocatas, "nemo enim illis prædicarat. Quare & Salvator "in parabolis Evangelicis hoc ipsum nobis osten- "dens, operarios circa undecimam horam vocatos "dixisse ait: Quia nemo nos conduxit. Postquam "autem Christus illuxit, alligavit fortem, illius per- "versitati sub ipso positos ademit, fide ad ipsum "accedentes justificavit, animam suam pro o- "mnium vita posuit, nullam de cætero sufficien- "tem excusationem invenient, qui tam venerabi- "lem gratiam non admiserunt. Vera igitur Christus "etiam de gentibus diceret: Si non venissem & locutus eis fuissem, peccatum non haberent: nunc autem excusationem non habent de peccato suo.

De Judæorum somniis S. Hieronymus ita ha- bet: Judæi & Iudaizantes nostri, imo non nostri, quia Iudaizantes sperant futura corporaliter. Utique & circumcisionem sibi & conjugia in mille annorum imperio promittentes, ne impleatur in eis maledictio, quæ scripta est: Maledicta sterilis, quæ non facit se- men in Israel: Et: Beatus qui habet semen in Sion, & domesticos in Hierusalem. Quod si ve- rum est, omnes virgines, quas mille annorum regnum inveniet, maledictioni & sterilitati perpetuæ subja- cebunt, aut certe nupturæ sunt, ut maledictionem ef- fugiant.

Willius inde à vers. 16. Laodicensem periodum fingit: in qua passiva profanitas liberrime grassatura sit. At in eo ipsum ratio fugit. Non enim de passiva profanitate hæc agunt, sed de frequenti con- fluxu gentium ad adorandum Regem Dominum exer- cituum Christum Jesum. Nam per ascensum Hie- rosolymam versus de anno in annum accessum ju- gem & constantem ad Ecclesiam Willius ipse in- telligit, imo festi tabernaculorum ideo mentionem factam putat, ut doceatur, arctissimam communio- nem Ecclesiam cum Deo habituram, Deum suam i- psi gratiam præsentissimam exhibiturum, eandemque in ea gavisuram ac luxuriaturam, non aliter, ac si jam in cælestem habitationem esset intromissa. Quem sensum ipse quidem perperam ex Ap. 21, 3. elicit, quia ibi de cælesti gloria sermo est: non de statu Ecclesiæ in his terris. At quomodo talis & tanta felicitas convenit illi periodo, in qua liberrime grassatur passiva profanitas? Nec vero particulari- ter tantum aliquam multitudinem designat Pro- pheta, quæ à prophanis se separatura sit, sed de o- mnibus residuis ex universis gentibus, quæ venêre con- tra Hierosolymam loquitur. Adde, quod ad felicita- tem & sanctitatem insignem Ecclesiæ faciant, quæ po- stremis versibus habentur, fatente ipsomet Will. Quomodo ergo ipsi constabunt periodorum, quas commentus est, rationes? Laodicensi enim novissima periodo certe juxta ejus sententiam, non convenit tanta vel sanctitas vel felicitas. Quod quum viderit probe, hoc commento sibi cavit, subjungere ibi

Prophetam novam Philadelphiæ descriptionem, ge- mino prorsùs modo, ut Johannes in Apocalypsi c. 20, 10, 22. novam Hierosolymam ceu typum Phi- ladelphiæ descripsit. Sed hæc foret periodorum diversarum commixtio, & confusio, unde tandem nihil certi de periodis istis haberi possit, quo pa- cto commenta periodica in spongiam incumbere oportet. Et cum Apocalypsin huc trahit, quid alius hoc est, quam τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαμβάνειν; Quod sophisma duplici modo incurrit Willius, tum quod periodos suas in Apocalypsi observatas gratis af- sumit, tum quod ex Apocalypsi Prophetam expo- nendum esse, sine probatione decernit. Accedit vi- tium ψευδερμηνείας: siquidem falso, imo & inepte descriptionem cælestis Hierosolymæ, quam figuris e- legantissimis exhibuit depictam S. Johannes, ex- plicat de statu Ecclesiæ in hoc seculo in Philadelphiâ. Denique quum judicium vers. 12. & seqq. descri- ptum à Propheta nostro novissimum diem immedia- te sequuturum esse liquidum videatur Willio, quo- modo adhuc Laodicensem periodum, & in ea passi- vam profanitatem credere potuit?

## 14:20
Verse 20.

IN THAT DAY THERE SHALL BE THAT WHICH IS UPON THE BRIDLE OF THE HORSE HOLY TO THE LORD] The Hebrew word מְצִלּוֹת signifies bells, which are hung upon them: and עַל is with, that is, that which adheres to the bells of the horse shall be consecrated to God, namely the harness of the horses, which used to be of precious material and adorned with gems. See Claudian's Epigrams concerning such a harness. He says that those who return home will donate these to the Temple.

AND THE CALDRONS IN THE HOUSE OF THE LORD SHALL BE LIKE THE BOWLS BEFORE THE ALTAR] The number of bowls was huge, both for offering fine flour and oil, concerning which use we spoke above at IX. 15, and for pouring the blood of the victims around the altar, and for wine and incense. The caldrons were much fewer. Now he says there will be such a supply of victims that as many as there were bowls formerly, so many caldrons there will be. It is true: for almost all the kings and Princes of the East vied in liberality toward the Temple. Antiochus the Great alone sent 20,000 silver coins for the use of the victims of the Temple, oil, and incense, as Josephus testifies in XII. 3. Demetrius gave 150,000 of the same coins annually for victims, Jos. XIII. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

IN DIE ILLA ERIT QVOD SVPER FRENVM EQVI EST SANCTVM DOMINO] Vox Hebræa מְצִלּוֹת significat tintinnabula, quæ qui appenduntur: & עַל est cum, id est, quod cohæret equi tintinnabulis Deo sacrabitur, cinctus nempe equorum, qui solebat esse ex materia pretiosa, & ornatus gemmis. Vide Claudiani Epigrammata de cinctu tali. Hæc qui domum redibunt donaturos Templo dicit.

ET ERVNT LEBETES IN DOMO DOMINI QVA- SI PHIALÆ CORAM ALTARI] Ingens erat Phialarum numerus, tum ad offerendam similam & oleum, de quo usu diximus supra IX. 15. tum ad fundendum sanguinem victimarum circa altare, & ad vinum suffitusque. Le- betes multo pauciores. Nunc tantam dicit fore copiam victimarum, ut quot olim phialæ fuêre, tot futuri sint lebetes. Verum est: nam & reges & Principes Orientis fere omnes liberalitate in Templum certarunt. Antiochus Magnus solus XX. mille nummos argenteos misit in usum victimarum Templi, olei & thuris, teste Josepho XII. 3. Demetrius parium nummum ad victimas dedit CL. millia annua, Jos. XIII. 5.

## 14:21
Ver. 21.

AND EVERY CALDRON IN JERUSALEM AND IN JUDA SHALL BE HOLY TO THE LORD OF HOSTS, AND ALL THAT SACRIFICE SHALL COME, AND SHALL TAKE OF THEM, AND SHALL SEETHE IN THEM] Here the word 'like' is twice missing. For the sense is, 'like' holy, and 'like' those sacrificing: namely, because the liberality of the strangers was to be so great that, besides the victims, they would send other food cooked by themselves to the priests and Levites.

These commentaries are unworthy of a prolix refutation. For whom will Grotius persuade that the Holy Spirit was concerned about bells or the harness of horses? Shall we believe that He so curiously numbered such material gifts of horse trappings, and caldrons and bowls, and described them with such an apparatus of words, while spiritual adornment and worship were either neglected or only lightly insinuated? Furthermore, if every caldron in Jerusalem is holy to the Lord, what will the Israelites keep in their own homes to cook their food? But let us leave the bells, harnesses, bowls, and caldrons to Grotius. He received these commentaries from Cornelius à Lapide (or his epitomizers Tirinus and Menochius), who seems to have devised them in order to build up the chalices, patens, ciboria, reliquaries, censers, and other vessels of the Roman Church upon these Jewish instruments: or perhaps to persuade others that these things were predicted here parabolically, along with the bells, harness, and the equipment of the Roman Pope and Cardinals. But let Cornelius himself teach how much he attributed to this literal sense concerning such material gifts of the Jews: 'Corporally,' he says, 'in rigor' it is false that every pot in Jerusalem and Judah was sanctified to the Lord: for otherwise the Jerusalemites and Jews would have been obliged to bring all their pots to the Temple and dedicate them to God, nor could they have retained any at home for their own uses, which is clearly false. He concludes, therefore, that this must be understood spiritually: but he delivers this sense, that every pot is a priest and a believer consecrated to God in ordination and Baptism. Blessed Luther also understands Christians by these vessels, meaning that all Christians whatsoever would be fit to offer sacrifices to God and consecrate themselves entirely as a host pleasing to God, Rom. 12, 3.

Some, however, not inappropriately wish to note the consecration of things both political and domestic to divine uses, and of the former indeed, when it is said that holiness to Jehovah shall be inscribed upon the bridle of the horses, which used to be inscribed upon the priest's tiara, Ez. 28, 36. For the chief use of these is in wars and political administration. The LXX alone translated מצלר as χάλινον, that is, a bridle: whom we also, says Jerome, have followed in this place, so that we might not seem to bring something new into the common question. When I asked the Hebrew what it signified, he told me that we ought not to read מצולות, but מצילות, which signifies the trappings of horses and military ornament: and that except for this place, this word is found in no volume of the holy scriptures at all. Which, however, in Willius's opinion, seems best derived from צלל, to tinkle. But the pots refer to domestic things, of which it is said: And the pots in the house of the Lord shall be like the bowls before the altar, meaning that domestic things shall be consecrated to the Lord, so that pots may be held like bowls: whatever domestic things there are shall be consecrated to God: indeed, all things universally in the polity and family, or even those in civilian and military life, whose use is either in war or in peace, shall be dedicated to God. It does not look so much to the multitude, that there shall be as many bowls as there will be pots, or to the frequency of sacrifices, as to the promiscuous use: that the distinction between sacred and profane vessels shall cease, and every pot shall be holy to the Lord, and thus the Levitical worship of the O.T. slips away at the same time. Coccejus rightly: The pots of the house of the Lord are compared "with the sprinkling basins before the Altar. There were pots in which they cooked the Sin, the Guilt, and the Gift, Ezek. 46, 20. There were pots in which the blood was received for the making of the sprinkling. "The cooking of the flesh in the pot did not seem legitimate, so that it might be eaten by the priest, unless the sprinkling had first been done at the altar. When, therefore, the pots are equated to the sprinkling basins, it is signified that the blood has been shed once, and that those who devote effort so that the people may have communion of the body of Christ, which is the unique and true sacrifice, in faith, are equated to those who in the Old Testament devoted effort so that the sins of the people might be carnally expiated by the rite of the law, as it was commanded. Whence from this place Blessed Balduinus also not rashly concludes, p. 891. Since the Levitical sanctification, by which common utensils used to be consecrated to sacred use by certain ceremonies according to the command of the Lord, ought to cease in the "New Testament, it is a vain and hypocritical method "to consecrate altars, candles, candlesticks, and others by incense, oil, and other trifles, whose use "can be in temples, nay even weapons, with which they go out against the enemy, which is done in the Papacy, "where not only is such superstition indulged, but also by an altogether intolerable impiety, some peculiar virtue is assigned to such consecrated and exorcised things. Finally, so that a completely new consecration of all citizens may be indicated

of the Church in the New Testament, and thus the distinction of both Testaments is hinted at, it is added that all who sacrifice, or those who have dedicated sacred things to God, will come and will use those sacred instruments: And all who sacrifice shall come, and shall take of them, and shall cook from them, meaning that formerly only certain persons were destined for such sacred things, but then all the inhabitants of the city shall be holy to God, and fit for performing worship to God. The sum is that public and private things shall be consecrated to God, and men of whatever condition shall use them for the glory of God. Nor does Cyril rashly think that the time of peace under the N.T. is designated, so that with all war now lulled and the battle removed and enemies repressed and perpetual peace adorning the holy city, i.e., the Church, he says that military instruments, trappings, and the ornament of bridles will henceforth be idle. For what use, after all, of these for a horseman accustomed to fight bravely in battle, if there is no adversary at all? Wherefore, he says, the instruments and things devoted to God required for war shall be holy. For since He Himself is the arbiter of peace, the instruments of war, now superfluous and henceforth idle, will rightly be consecrated to Him. For as blessed Isaiah said of certain things: (they shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks, and nation shall not lift up sword against nation) and they shall no longer learn to wage war, the times of peace all but compelling them to forgo the necessities of war for rustic life, and as it were to run to other alliances, military studies being neglected. So also the divine Zechariah, as if with perennial peace henceforth granted by God, narrates that instruments fit for those warring will be transformed into a thing devoted to God. For warfare will cease entirely, nor will there be any care for horses, or bridles, or trappings, and minds will incline rather to studies in which one may excel in virtue and piety. Thus far S. Cyril.

Let the Jews therefore love (let Grotius love with them), let us say with Jerome, the bronze pots, who have loved the Egyptian pots and the meats and the melons, and the garlic and the onions and the cucumbers. Let us turn the Jewish pots, in which the meats of the victims were cooked, into the bowls of aromatics before the altar of the Lord, of which the bride says to the bridegroom: My kinsman has descended into my garden to the bowls of aromatics, to feed in the gardens and to gather lilies. The garden and paradise into which the bridegroom descends to the bride is the reading of the holy scriptures: from which he plucks lilies, violets, and roses, and various aromatics: so that he may fill the bowls of the souls of believers, and pour out offerings to the Lord from them. Such pots, when they have been turned into the vials of the Lord and have been able to say: We are the good odor of Christ, and instead of the virulence of the flesh have begun to bear the various flowers of virtues: then they shall be in Jerusalem and in Judah sanctified to the almighty Lord: of whom we have spoken more frequently, that Jerusalem expresses the vision of peace, and Judah the confessor. This is St. Jerome.

Verse of the same.

AND THERE SHALL BE NO MERCHANT ANY MORE IN THE HOUSE OF THE LORD] Namely, those who sell to the priests pots, vials, wine, oil, incense, and the like: for all these things, he says, will be given as a gift by strangers more than enough.

Thus Grotius had nothing in mind but pots, vials, wine, and oil, and things of this kind, being little or not at all concerned with spiritual worship in such illustrious prophecies. But the Hebrew source does not recognize that merchant who sells pots, vials, and wine, in which the word for Merchant is not found, even though Aquila, the Chaldean, and Vatablus have rendered it so along with the Vulgate. Whence Lyra, Dionysius, Arias, and Vatablus wish to intimate that simony is to be driven away from sacred things: which I wish were observed in the Papacy! others therefore remove the merchant, because in the New Testament there will be no need for merchants of oxen, sheep, and doves for sacred things. Whence those selling are cast out by Christ, Luke 19:45. Moreover, the word Cananæi is held, as the LXX render it. Pagninus & Tigur. and also a certain Theodoret apud Jerome, Hugo, Isidore, & other interpreters, by which name an impious person is denoted. Cyril explains it as ἀλλογενῆς κὶ εἰδωλολάτρης, an alien (not a Christian) and idolater. Menochius explains it, all will follow the same religion. Tirinus also admits a similar sense: that a wicked person will not be tolerated in the Church, which sense Albertus M. & Isidor. Clarius hand down. Rightly B. Bald. He looks to the state of the Hebrew Republic, where in the first entry into the promised land it was not possible for all the Canaanites to be expelled, but it was necessary to leave many among the people of God, for that reason which is noted in Exod. 23:29. & Deut. 7:22, whence seeds of manifold idolomania arose in the Hebrew nation: but he says that in the Church of Christ nothing such will be: infidel peoples will not be mixed, but they will either be converted to the true religion, or will be eliminated from the house of God in a legitimate manner and way, so that there may not be a mixture of religion, but that all may be able to serve the true God with one shoulder, just as it was also predicted in Zeph. 3:9. Conf. Joel 3:17. So also Theodoret; with whose wish & doxology it is pleasing to conclude this Prophet: There shall not be a Canaanite anymore in the house of the Lord Almighty, i.e., who follows the parts of the Canaanites: who lives impiously, namely, and is occupied in iniquity. May the Lord Almighty grant that this word be true at this time, so that no one among us may appear a Canaanite: but may we all live according to the Evangelical tradition, and await the blessed hope, and the appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ: to whom with the Father be glory, and with the Holy Spirit now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ET ERIT OMNIS LEBES IN IERVSALEM ET IN IVDA SANCTIFICATUS DOMINO EXER- CITUUM, ET VENIENT OMNES IMMOLANTES, ET SUMENT EX EIS, ET COQUENT IN EIS] Hic bis deest quasi. Sensus enim est, quasi sanctificatus, & quasi immolantes: nimirum quia tanta futura erat advena- rum liberalitas, ut præter victimas, alia edulia apud se cocta missuri essent ad sacerdotes & Levitas.

Indigna hæc commenta sunt prolixa confuta- tione. Cui enim persuadebit Grotius, Sp. S. de tin- tinnabulis, aut cinctu equorum solicitum fuisse? Num donaria ejusmodi materialia, de ornatu equorum, & lebetes ac phialas tam curiose ipsum numerasse, tantoque verborum apparatu descripsisse crede- mus, ornatu & cultu spirituali, vel neglecto, vel leviter solum insinuato? Porro si omnis lebes in Jerusalem sanctificatus Domino, quid domi suæ re- tinebunt Israelitæ, ut edulia sibi coquant? Sed re- linquamus Grotio tintinnabula, cinctus, phialas ac lebetes. Accepit hæc commenta à Cornelio à La- pide, (vel Epitomatoribus ejus Tirino ac Menochio) qui ea excogitasse videtur, ut calices, patinas, cibo- ria, hierothecas, thuribula, aliaq́, vasa Romanæ Ecclesiæ istis Judaicis instrumentis superstrueret: vel illa parabolice solum cum tintinnabulis, & cin- ctu, atque apparatu equorum Papæ fortassis Ro- mani, & Cardinalium hic prædicta persuaderet a- liis. Sed quantum huic sensui literali de donariis Judæorum ejusmodi materialibus tribuerit Corne- lius, ipse edoceat: Corporaliter, inquit, in rigore falsum est, quod omnis lebes in Jerusalem & Juda fuerit sanctificatus Domino: Alioqui enim Jerosolymitæ & Judæi debuissent omnes lebetes suos ad Templum deferre, & dicare Deo, nec ullos domi ad proprios usus retinere potuissent, quod liquet esse falsum. Spiritualiter ergo intelligendum hoc esse concludit: Sed hunc sensum tradit, quod lebes omnis sacerdos sit & fidelis in ordinatione & Baptismo Deo consecratus. B. Lutherus etiam per vasa ista intelligit Christianos, q. d. omnes omnino Christianos aptos fore qui offerant Deo victimas & se totos consecrent in hostiam Deo placentem Rom. 12, 3.

Non incommode tamen nonnulli consecrationem rerum tum politicarum tum domesticarum ad usus divinos notari volunt, & illarum quidem, cum dicitur, inscriptum fore freno equorum sanctitas Jehovah, quod tiaræ sacerdotis inscribi solebat Ez. 28, 36. Harum enim usus præcipuus in bellis & politica administratione. מצלר soli LXX. χάλινον id est frenum transtulerunt: quos & nos inquit Hieronymus, in hoc loco secuti sumus: ne novum aliquid in quæstione vulgata videremur afferre. Quod cum ab Hebræo quærerem: quid significaret, ait mihi non debere nos legere מצולות, sed מצילות quod significat phaleram equorum & ornatum bellicum: & excepto hoc loco in nullo penitus sanctarum scripturarum volumine hoc verbum reperiri. Quod tamen Willio censente optime à צלל tinnio deduci videtur. Ad res vero domesticas lebetes spectant, de quibus dicitur: Et erunt lebetes domo Domini quasi phialæ coram altari, q. d. res domesticæ Domino consecrabuntur, ut lebetes instar phialarum haberi possint: quicquid rerum domesticarum erit, Deo consecrabitur: imo omnia in universum in politia & familia, vel etiam togata & sagata, quorum vel in bello vel in pace usus est, Deo dicatum iri. Non respicitur tam ad multitudinem, quod tot phialæ, quot lebetes futuræ sint, aut ad frequentiam victimarum, quam ad promicuum usum: quod discrimen sacrorum & prophanorum vasorum cessaturum sit, omnisque lebes Domino sanctus futurus sit, labiturque ita simul cultus Leviticus V. T. Recte Coccejus: Comparantur ollæ domus Domini „cum pelvibus aspersoriis ante Altare. Erant ol„læ, in quibus coquebant, Peccatum, Reatum, & „Munus Ezech. 46, 20. Erant lebetes, quibus „excipiebatur sanguis ad aspersionem faciendam. „Non videbatur legitima coctio carnis in olla, ut „comederetur à sacerdote, nisi prius aspersio esset „facta ad altare. Quando igitur ollæ aspersoriis æ„quantur, significatur, sanguinem semel esse fusum, & eos, qui operam dant, ut populus communionem corporis Christi, quod unicum ac verum sacrificium est, habeat in fide, æquiparari iis, „qui in Veteri Testamento operam dabant, ut peccata populi ritu legis, uti præceptum erat, carnaliter expiarentur. Unde ex hoc loco etiam non temere colligit B. Balduinus p. 891. Quoniam sanctificatio Levitica, qua certis ceremoniis utensilia vulgaria ad usum sacrum consecrari solebant ex præcepto Domini, cessare deberet in „Novo Testamento, vana & hypocritica est ratio, „per suffitum, oleum & alias nugas consecrare altaria, candelas, candelabra, & alia, quorum usus „in templis esse potest, imo etiam arma, quibus adversus hostem egrediuntur, quod fit in Papatu, „ubi non tantum ejusmodi superstitionibus indulgetur, sed & per intolerabilem plane impietatem, „ejusmodi rebus consecratis & exorcisatis, peculiaris aliqua virtus adsignatur. Denique ut indicetur plane nova consecratio omnium civium

Ecclesiæ in Novo Testamento, adeoque ita discri- men utriusque Testamenti innuatur, additur, ven- turos omnes sacrificantes, vel eos qui res sacras Deo dedicarunt, & sacris istis instrumentis usuros: Et- venient omnes immolantes, & sument ex eis, & co- quentur ex eis, q. d. olim certæ tantum personæ ad talia sacra destinatæ erant, tum autem omnes inco- læ civitatis Deo sancti erunt, & ad cultum Deo præstandum idonei. Summa est, publica & privata Deo fore consecrata, iisque cujuscunque conditio- nis homines ad Dei gloriam usuros. Nec temere Cyrillus arbitratur tempus pacis sub N. T. designari, ut omni bello jam sopito & pugna sublata & hosti- bus repressis & perpetua pace sanctam civitatem, h. e. Ecclesiam decorante, otiosa deinceps fore ait instrumenta bellica, phaleras & frenorum ornatum. Quis enim tandem usus horum equiti in prælio fortiter dimicare sueto, si nullus omnino adversa- rius? Quamobrem, sancta erunt, inquit, instrumen- ta, & anathemata Deo ad bellum requisita. Quoniam enim ipse pacis est arbiter, ipsi quoque supervacanea jam, & de cætero otiosa belli instrumenta jure conse- crabuntur. Nam ut beatus Esaias de quibusdam di- xit: (concident gladios suos in aratra & lanceas suas in falces, & non tollet gens contra gentem gla- dium) & non discent amplius bellare temporibus pa- cis tantum non impellentibus eos ad bellica necessitati rusticationis condonanda, & veluti ad alia fœdera currendi, militaribus studiis posthabitis. Sic & di- vinus Zacharias, ut perenni deinceps pace donata a Deo, bellantibus idonea instrumenta in anathema Deo transformatum iri narrat. Penitus enim mi- litia desinet, nec equorum, nec frænorum, aut phalerarum cura geretur, & ad studia potius, qui- bus in virtute & pietate excellatur, inclinabunt ani- mi. Hactenus S. Cyrillus.

Ament ergo Iudæi (amet cum illis Grotius) dicamus cum Hieronymo, lebetes æneos, qui amave- runt ollas Ægyptias & carnes & pepones, & allia & cepe & cucumeres. Nos Iudaicos lebetes, in quibus coquebantur carnes victimarum, vertamus in phialas aromatum coram altari Domini, de quibus sponsa dicit ad sponsum: Fratruelis meus descendit in hortum meum ad phialas aromatum, pascere in hortis & colligere lilia. Hortus & paradisus in quem sponsus descendit ad sponsam, sanctarum lectio scripturarum est: de quibus lilia, violas & rosas, & varia decerpit aromata: ut impleat phialas anima- rum credentium, & Domino ex eis liba diffundat. Istiusmodi lebetes, cum versi fuerint in Phialas Domi- ni & dicere potuerint: Christi bonus odor sumus, & pro virulentia carnium varios cœperint flores gesta- re virtutum: tunc erunt in Hierusalem & in Ju- da sanctificati Domino omnipotenti: de quibus frequentius diximus, quod Hierusalem visionem pa- cis, & Judas exprimat confitentem. Hæc S. Hie- ronymus.

Vers. eod.

ET NON ERIT MERCATOR ULTRA IN DOMO DOMINI] Nempe qui vendant sacerdotibus le- betes, phialas, vinum, oleum, thus & similia: omnia e- nim ista, inquit, ab advenis dono dabuntur plusquam satis.

Ita nihil nisi lebetes, phialas, vinum & oleum, & quæ hujus generis sunt, in animo habuit Grotius, de cultu spirituali parum vel nihil in tam illustri- bus vaticiniis solicitus. Sed mercatorem illum, qui vendat lebetes, phialas, & vinum, non agnoscit fons Ebræus, in quo non habetur vox Mercatoris, etsi ita reddiderint Aquila, Chaldæus & Vatablus cum Vulgato. Unde Lyra, Dionysius, Arias, & Va- tablus Simoniam à rebus sacris propulsandam innuî volunt: quod utinam in Papatu observaretur! alii ideo mercatorem removent, quia in N. T. nihil o- pus erit mercatoribus boum, ovium, columbarum ad res sacras. Unde vendentes à Christo ejiciuntur Luc 19, 45. Habetur autem vox Cananæi, ut red- dunt LXX. Pagninus & Tigur. nec non Theodore- tus quidam apud Hieronymum, Hugo, Isidorus, & alii Interpp. quo nomine impius denotatur. Cyril- lus exponit ἀλλογενῆς κὶ εἰδωλολάτρης alienigena (non Christianus) & idololatra. Menochius expo- nit, omnes eandem sequentur religionem. Admit- tit etiam Tirinus sensum similem: Improbus non to- leratum iri in Ecclesia, quem sensum tradunt Al- bertus M. & Isidor. Clarius. Recte B. Bald. Re- spicit ad statum Reipubl. Hebrææ, ubi in primo ingressu in terram promissam non poterant o- mnes Chananæi expelli, sed multos relinque in po- pulo Dei necesse erat, ob causam illam, quæ anno- tatur Exod. 23, 29. & Deut. 7, 22. unde multiplicis idolomaniæ in gente Hebræa exorta sunt semina- ria: sed in Ecclesia Christi nihil tale futurum ait: non erunt permixti infideles populi, sed illi vel ad religionem veram convertentur, vel è domo Dei legitimo more modoque eliminabuntur, ne fiat re- ligionis mixtura, sed ut omnes possint vero Deo servire humero uno, quemadmodum etiam Soph. 3. v. 9. prædictum fuit. Conf. Joel. 3, 17. Sic etiam Theodoretus; cujus voto & δοξολογίᾳ hunc Pro- phetam concludere lubet: Non erit Cananæus ul- tra in domo Domini omnipotentis, h. e. qui partes Chananæorum sequatur: qui impie videlicet vivat, & in iniquitate versetur. Dominus omnipotens hanc vocem veram esse hoc tempore præstet, ut nemo in nobis Chananæus videatur: sed omnes secundum traditionem Evangelicam vivamus, & beatam spem expectemus, adventumque magni Dei Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi: cui cum Patre gloria, & cum Sancto Spiritu nunc & semper & in secula seculorum. Amen.

# Malachi

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON MALACHI.

The Grotian Preface.

This name in Hebrew sounds Angel, with the addition of a paragogic Jod, and the LXX, who took that name as a common noun, translate at the beginning of the book ἐν χειρὶ ἀγγέλε ἀυτẽ. And by this name of Angel, Clement of Alexandria and other Greeks, and sometimes Tertullian, are accustomed to cite this Prophet. But the Greek Interpreters, besides the LXX, named Malachi. And so Justin and almost all the Latins. Certain Hebrews think this writer to be Ezra, and that he is called Angel, because below he is called an angel of the Lord (such as Ezra was). But Ezra is called both priest and scribe, never however a Prophet. It is truer, therefore, that Malachi is the proper name of the Prophet, who was contemporary with Haggai and Zechariah, but began to be inspired by God after them. Which not only the order indicates, which he has held from antiquity last after all the Prophets, but also the subject matter. For he corrects many things which were being sinned in, now that the Temple was built.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD MALACHIAM.

Præfatio Grotiana.

NOmen hoc in Hebræo sonat Angelum, addito Jod pa- ragogico, & LXX. qui ut commune id nomen sumsere, in principio libri vertunt ἐν χειρὶ ἀγγέλε ἀυτẽ. Atque isto nomine Angeli citare solent hunc Prophetam Clemens Alexandrinus, Græcique alii, interdum & Tertullianus. At Græci Interpretes, præter LXX. nominarunt Mala- chiam. Atque ita Justinus & Latini ferme omnes. He- bræi quidam hunc scriptorem Esdram esse existimant, ac Angelum dici, quia infra sacerdos Domini (qualis Esdras fuit) vocetur Angelus. Sed Esdras & sacerdos & scriba appellatur, nusquam a. Propheta. Verius ergo Malachiam nomen proprium esse Prophetæ, qui σύγχρον Aggei & Zachariæ, sed post eos à Deo afflari cœperit. Quod non ordo tantum indicat, quem post omnes Prophetas postre- mum ab antiquo obtinet, sed & argumentum. Multa enim corrigit, quæ structo jam Templo peccabantur.

## 1:1 Introduction: Our Prolegomena
OUR PROLEGOMENA.

First, concerning the name, then concerning the author, thirdly concerning the order, and fourthly, finally, concerning the subject matter is treated here. Concerning the name there is no difficulty. Malachi is, however, by the reason of the name, My Angel. From this, however, Origen apud Jerome ignorantly concludes that Malachi was an angel who assumed a body to figure Christ. For the same person calls any priests whatsoever angels or messengers of God, ch. 2:7, and pre-eminently John the Baptist an angel, ch. 3:1. Concerning whom Cyril: "But the fiction of certain people concerning him is to be exploded, and not to be listened to, who believed and rashly fabled that he was an angel by nature, but that by the will of God he assumed the form and habit of a body, and performed the office of prophecy for the Israelites." For he was called an angel "in the first place, because his name, as I said, would have this notion: then because, since he announced heavenly discourses inspired by God to Israel, he could not ineptly be called an angel." There are also trifles when the Rabbis say that Malachi is called an angel because his oracles were delivered and confirmed by an angel from heaven. He obtained that name for the sake of a good omen, which was also fulfilled in him, both because he was a distinguished messenger of God, and because he was adorned with an angelic life.

But Malachi is not to be taken for Ezra, which the Hebrews, both the ancients and the more recent, R. Jonathan the paraphrast, David Kimchi, Aben Ezra, and others, likewise thought, not disapproved by Jerome, Remigius, Rupert, and the Jesuit Ribera: but that these men of God are to be distinguished, Grotius rightly maintains: in which most other ancients agree, Athanasius in the Synopsis, Theodoret here, Chrysostom Orat. II against the Jews, Augustine Book XVIII of the City of God ch. XXXVI, and of the more recent, Vatablus, Isid. Clarius, Montanus, Christoph. à Castro, Cornelius à Lapide, and all of ours to a man. Nowhere is Ezra called Malachi, or Malachi called Ezra. The former is everywhere called a scribe, the latter a Prophet; the former was older than Haggai and Zechariah, as being born before the Babylonian captivity, as is clear from a comparison of Ezra 7:1 and 2 Kings 25:18, 21.
