But the latter was younger in age than them. Some among the Jews believe Malachi to be Mordecai, others believe him to be Zechariah. But those opinions enjoy no probability at all.

Malachi is last in order, who censures the vices of the priests after the restoration of the temple, predicts the advent not only of the Messiah, but also of his precursor, as being imminent shortly, and at this boundary of the Old and New Testament concludes his prophecy and the entire prophetic system with John the Proto-baptist. Just as, in turn, Mark makes the beginning of his Gospel from this Prophet; so that the continuity of the prophetic conclusion of the Old and the beginning of the Evangelical New Testament might be more manifest. And just as the Old Testament ends with the announcement of the advent of the first Messiah: so the New Testament is terminated with the vow and desire for the second advent of the same, so that it may be taught that Christ is the end and scope of the entire canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testament.

Some conjecture, perhaps not without reason, that Malachi lived under the aged Nehemiah, since at that time the priests in the Church did not perform their duty as was fitting, in the Republic the people denied due obedience and the sustenance of the ministers of the temple, and in the economic state there was various confusion on account of illicit marriages and the treacherous license of divorces. Compare Ezra 10, Nehemiah 10 and 13, with Malachi 1 and 2. Certainly before John Hyrcanus and the unification of the Idumeans with the Israelites, having taken place under him, he prophesied, because c. 1, 3. 4. deals with the Idumeans, as not yet forgiven, as Cocceius rightly [notes] here.

The subject matter of the Prophet is both legal and corrective regarding the reprobate, whom he generally reproaches and rebukes for ingratitude toward God, and specifically the priests for the pollution of divine worship, and the people for various vices, not only against the second, but also the first table, marriages with foreigners, polygamy, profanity and atheism, and it is also Evangelical and consolatory, in that it encourages the pious among the people with promises concerning Christ and his forerunner; whence one may establish two parts of this prophecy, so that the former, chapters I and II, is a rebuke of the priests and the people, and the latter, chapters III and IV, is a prediction concerning the reformation of the temple and the introduction of the New Testament.

Latin:

PROLEGOMENA NOSTRA.

PRimum de nomine, tum de auto- re, tertio de ordine, quarto deni- que de argumento hic agitur. De nomine nulla difficultas. Est au- tem Malachias nominis ratione Angelus meus. Ex eo vero impe- rite Origenes apud Hieronymum concludit, Ma- lachiam fuisse angelum, qui corpus affumserit, ut Christum figuraret. Nam vocat idem & sacerdotes quosvis angelos seu legatos Dei c. 2, 7. & ἐξοχικῶς Johannem Baptistam angelum c. 3, 1. De quo Cy- „rillus: Explodendum est autem quorundam de „ipso, nec audiendum commentum, qui credide- „runt, temereque fabulati sunt, eum natura ange- „lum fuisse, sed voluntate Dei corporis formam „habitumque assumsisse, & Israëlitiserophetiæ of- „ficium præstitisse. Dictus est namque angelus „inprimis quidem, quod ejus nomen, ut dixi, „hanc notionem haberet: deinde quod cum cœ- „lestes, & à Deo inspiratos sermones Israeli nun- „tiarit, non inscite etiam angelus vocari possit. Nugæ etiam sunt cum Rabbini dicunt, Malachiam angelum vocari, quia oracula ejus ab angelo de cælo tradita & confirmata sint. Adeptus est id nomi- nis boni ominis causa, quod in ipso quoque imple- tum, tum quia insignis Dei legatus, tum quia vita an- gelica decorus fuit.

Non autem Malachiam pro Esdra haben- dum, quod itidem putarunt Ebræi, cum veteres, tum recentiores R. Jonathan paraphrastes, David Kimchi, Aben Esra, & alii, Hieronymo, Remigio, Ru- perto & Ribera Jesuitæ non improbatum: sed hos viros Dei distinguendos esse, recte statuit Gro- tius: in quo plerique alii veteres consentiunt, A- thanaf. in synopsi, Theodoret. hic, Chrysost. Orat. II. contr. Judæos, Augustinus L. XIIX. de Civ. Dei c. XXXVI. & è recentioribus Vatablus, Isid. Clarius, Montanus, Christoph. à Castro, Cornelius à Lapide, ac nostri ad unum omnes. Nuspiam Esdras Mala- chias, vel Malachias Esdras vocatur. Ille ubique scriba, hic Propheta dicitur, ille senior Haggæo & Zacharia fuit, utpote natus ante captivitatem Ba- bylonicam, ut è collatione Esdr. VII. 1. & 2. Reg. XXV. 18. 21. liquet. Hic autem ætate inferior ipsis fuit. Nonnulli è Judæis Malachiam Mardocheum, alii eundem Zachariam esse credunt. Sed illæ sen- tentiæ nulla plane verisimilitudine gaudent.

Ordine ultimus est Malachias, qui vitia sacer- dotum post restauratum templum taxat, adventum non Messiæ tantum, sed etiam præcursoris, ceu pro- pediem imminentem prædicat, & in hoc V. & N. T. limite Johanne Protobaptista vaticinium suum, totumq; propheticum Systema concludit. Quem- admodum vicissim Marcus Evangelii sui auspicium ab hoc Propheta facit; ut συνέχειæ manifestior es- set coronidis propheticæ Veteris, & initii Evange- lici N. T. Atque uti V. Testamentum prænuncia- tione adventus Messiæ primi finitur: ita N. Testa- mentum voto & desiderio adventus ejusdem se- cundi terminatur, ut Christum finem & scopum to- tius Scripturæ canonicæ V. & N. T. esse doceatur.

Vixisse autem Malachiam sub Nehemia sene, for- te non præter rem conjectant nonnulli, siquidem tum in Ecclesia Sacerdotes non functi sunt mune- re suo, uti par erat, in Rep. populus debita negaret obsequia, & ministrorum templi alimenta, & in statu œconomico varia fuerit confusio ob con- jugia illicita, & divortiorum perfidam licentiam. Conf. Esdr. X. Neh. X. & XIII. cum Mal. I. & II. Certe ante Johannem Hircanum & coadunationem Idumæorum cum Israëlitis, sub eo factam, pro- phetavit, quia c. 1, 3. 4. de Idumæis, ut nec dum condonatis, agit, ut recte hic Coccejus.

Argumentum Prophetæ tum legale est, & ἐπα- νορθωτικὸν quoad reprobos, quibus generatim in- gratitudinem adversus Deum, speciatim vero sacer- dotibus pollutionem cultus divini, populo vitia va- ria, non tantum adversus secundam, sed etiam pri- mam tabulam, conjugia cum exotericis, polygami- am, profanitatem & atheismum exprobrat, ac re- prehendit, tum Evangelicum & παρακλητικον, qua pios in populo promissionibus de Christo, ejus- demque prodromo erigit; unde duas partes consti- tuere licet hujus prophetiæ, ut prior cap. I. & II. sit Sacerdotum ac populi reprehensio, posterior c. III. & IV. de reformatione templi, & introductione N. T. prædictio.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. Chiefly CORRECTIVE. CHAPTER I. Contempt of sacred things among the Jews and the pure sacrifices of the Gentiles.

A divine protestation concerning love toward the Jewish people over the Esauites, and an expostulation concerning the ingratitude of the people, and especially of the priests in unclean and other illegitimate sacrifices, and an admonition concerning the deprecation of guilt, with the insertion of the offering of pure sacrifices of the Gentiles throughout the whole world, and the glorification of the divine name, and a rebuke of the Jews for the profanation of the same and for vicious and deformed sacrifices, and a curse upon the deceitful, because of the greatness and the fearful glory of the Lord.

By the word Priests, Malachi condemns the avaricious. Vers. 1. TO ISRAEL.) To those of all the tribes who had returned to their homeland: thus Zech. 12, 11.

That the Israelites returned to their homeland from all the tribes is not evident from the passage in Zechariah: which does not pertain to the times of the Old, but of the New Testament, nor can it be restricted to the Israelites according to the flesh. The Jews are indicated here, or the two tribes, along with those who were joined to them from the kingdom of Israel or the ten tribes themselves. For some of the sons of Ephraim and Manasseh had also dwelt in Jerusalem, 1 Chron. 10, 3, and by the decree of Cyrus, power was given to all, wherever they were in the lands under his Monarchy, to return, Ezra I, 3, such an indulgence as Artaxerxes also granted, c. VII, 13. Calvin is not wrong here: “Under the name of Israel he only designates those who had returned to their homeland, whether they were from the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, or from the tribe of Levi.” Although it is credible that some were also mixed in from other families: but almost only the Jews with their neighbors, that is, with the half-tribe of Benjamin, returned, I say besides the Levites, who were almost the leaders of the journey and encouraged the rest of the people: but they were indiscriminately called by the name of Israel, since pure religion flourished only among them. But those who lived dispersed among foreign and profane nations, although they had not entirely fallen away from the pure worship of God and piety, yet they had as it were lost their name. Therefore, those who were gathered again in the holy land, so that they might there enjoy the inheritance promised to them by God, were called Israelites by excellence.

Latin:

PARS I. Præcipue EPANORTHOTICA. CAPUT I. Contemtus Sacrorum penes Judæos & Sacrificia pura gentilium.

Protestatio divina de amore erga populum Ju- daicum præ Esavitis, & expostulatio de in- gratitudine populi, & imprimis Sacerdo- tum in sacrificiis immundis, aliisque illegi- timis, atque commonitio de culpæ depreca- tione, inserta sacrificiorum purorum genti- lium per orbem totum oblatione, nominis- que divini glorificatione, & increpatione Judæorum ob prophanationem ejusdem & sacrificia vitiosa, & deformia, ac maledi- ctione dolosorum, ob magnitudinem & glo- riam Domini tremendam.

Voce Sacerdotes Malachias damnat avaros. Vers. 1. AD ISRAEL.) Ad eos de omnibus tribubus, qui in patriam redierant: sic Zach. 12, 11.

De omnibus tribubus rediisse Israëlitas in pa- triam, è Zachariæ loco non constat: qui non perti- net ad tempora V. sed N. Test. nec ad Israëlitas se- cundum carnem restringi potest. Indigitantur hic Judæi, vel duæ tribus, cum illis, qui ex Israelis re- gno vel decem tribubus ipsis juncti fuere. Nam & Hierosolymis habitarant nonnulli è filiis Ephraim & Manasse 1. Chron. 10, 3. ac per diploma Cyri o- mnibus, ubicunque terrarum sub Monarchia ejus, potestas facta est redeundi Esdr. I, 3. qualem indul- gentiam concessit etiam Artaxerxes c. VII. 13. Non male hic Calvinus: “ Sub Israelis nomine tantum ,, eos designat, qui reversi erant in patriam, sive ,, essent ex tribu Jehudah & Benjamin, sive ex ,, tribu Levi. Quanquam credibile est, quosdam ,, etiam fuisse permixtos ex aliis familiis: sed ,, soli fere Judæi cum suis vicinis, hoc est, cum tri- ,, bu dimidia Benjamin reversi sunt, præter Levi- ,, tas dico, qui fere duces fuerunt itineris, & horta- ,, ti sunt reliquum populum: sed promiscue vocati ,, sunt nomine Israelis, quum tantum apud eos vi- ,, geret pura religio. Qui autem dispersi habita- ,, bant inter exteras gentes & profanas, etsi non ,, prorsus desciverant à puro Dei cultu & pietate, ,, tamen quasi suum nomen perdiderant. Ergo per ,, excellentiam vocati sunt Israëlitæ, qui iterum ,, collecti fuerunt in terra sancta, ut illic fruerentur ,, hæreditate sibi divinitus promissa.

## 1:2
Vers. 2. I HAVE LOVED YOU, SAYS THE LORD.) Namely, not only as men, but also above other men and above the other descendants of both Abraham and Isaac. Wherefore it was just (which is implied here) that an exceptional love should be repaid to me.

AND YOU HAVE SAID, IN WHAT HAVE YOU LOVED US.) That is, if you should say. Thus the Chaldean: In what have you loved us: that is, by what argument does that great love for us appear?

By this instance of the Jews against the testimony of God concerning His singular love for them, the Prophet notes their extreme ingratitude and contumacy, by which they did not acknowledge in word and deed the love of God toward them. The Vulgate therefore has it more correctly here: AND YOU HAVE SAID, IN WHAT HAVE I LOVED YOU, than the Grotian exposition, that if you should say. For that sense better suits the perversity of the Jews, which is often lashed in this Prophet by this formula, as Willius observes with Calvin.

V. On the same. WAS NOT ESAU JACOB'S BROTHER.) Here Esau and Jacob, as elsewhere Edom and Israel, signify the whole posterity sprung from Esau, who is also Edom, and from Israel, who is also Jacob. Thus David, that is, the posterity of David. Was not Esau Jacob's brother, supply, is: that is, do not you Idumeans also trace your origin from Abraham and Isaac? In the same sense the Idumean is called the brother of Israel, Deut. XXIII. 7.

The words of the Prophet are rightly explained concerning the whole nation and posterity of Jacob and Esau. Calvin and most of his school prefer to understand it of the person of Jacob and Esau, so that the following words, I have loved Jacob, but Esau I have hated, may be taken similarly. But even if it were granted that Jacob, the progenitor of the Israelites, is indicated with his brother, because they were begotten of the same parents, the Lord could nevertheless descend from them to their posterity, as if to say: Although Jacob and Esau were twin brothers, I did not follow their posterity with equal love, but I showed greater thanks to you Israelites than to the posterity of Esau, which sense of the prophet's words Willius acknowledges: by Esau, he says, both he himself and all his posterity are signified. The sense therefore is: Although Esau and Jacob were equals, yet I adopted Jacob and his posterity, and did good to them, while I left Esau and his posterity, and placed them after them. To the former, from the beginning of the nation, I was present with the greatest benefits, but to the latter not so; nay, I punished them with the most severe judgments according to their merits. And this sense is plain and easy, which the following words also confirm.

Latin:

Vers. 2. DILEXI VOS, DICIT DOMINUS.) Nempe non tantum ut homines, sed & præ cæteris hominibus præque aliis tum Abrahami, tum Isaaci posteris. Quare æquum erat (quod hic subintelligitur) eximium amorem mihi rependi.

ET DIXISTIS IN QVO DILEXISTI NOS.) Quod si dixeritis. Ita Chaldæus: In quo dilexisti nos: id est, quo argumento apparet amor ille tantus in nos?

Instantia hac Judæorum ad testificationem Dei de Dilectione sua adversus ipsos singulari, no- tat Propheta extremam ipsorum ingratitudinem & contumaciam, qua verbo & factis Dei in se amo- rem non agnoscebant. Rectius ergo Vulgata hic habet: ET DIXISTIS, IN QUO DILEXI VOS, quam expositio Grotiana, quod si dixeritis. Ille enim sensus magis Judæorum proterviæ con- venit, quæ sæpius hac formula in hoc Propheta perstringitur, ut cum Calvino observat Willius.

V. eod. NONNE FRATER ERAT ESAU JACOB.) Hic Esau & Jacob, ut alibi Edom & Israel, posteritatem to- tam significant ortam ab Esavo, qui & Edomus, & ab Israe- le, qui & Jacobus. Sic David, id est, posteritas Davidis. Non- ne frater Esau Iacobo, supple, est : id est, nonne Idumæi & vos ortum trahitis ex Abrahamo, & Isaaco? eodem sen- su Idumæus dicitur frater Israelis Deut. XXIII. 7.

Recte de tota gente & posteritate Jacobi & Esa- vi explicantur verba Prophetæ. Calvinus, & ple- rique de schola ejus malunt intelligere de persona Jacobi & Esavi, ut sequentia, dilexi Jacob, Esau au- tem odio habui, similiter accipiantur. Sed etiamsi datum fuerit, progenitorem Israelitarum Jacobum cum fratre suo indigitari, quod fuerint ex iisdem procreati parentibus, ab ipsis tamen ad posteros eorum descendere poterat Dominus, q. d. Etsi fra- tres fuerint gemelli Jacob & Esau, non tamen " parili amore prosequutus sum eorum posteros, " sed vobis Israelitis majorem exhibui gratiam, præ " Esavi posteritate, quem sensum esse verborum " prophetæ agnoscit Willius: per Esavum, inquit, & " ipse & omnis ejus posteritas significatur. Sensus " igitur est: Quamvis pares fuerint Esavus & Jaco-" bus, tamen Jacobum & ejus posteros adoptavi, " iisque benefeci, Esavum ejusque posteros reli- " qui, ac ipsis postposui. Illis ab initio gentis maxi- " mis beneficiis præsens fui, his vero non item, " imo gravissimis judiciis ipsos juxta merita ipso- " rum castigavi. Atque hic sensus planus & facilis est, quem etiam sequentia confirmant.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. AND I HAVE LOVED JACOB, BUT ESAU I HAVE HATED.) That is, I willed to do good to you, but not to them. Paul also uses this passage in chapter IX to the Romans, to show that God forgives sins to some, and does not forgive others, and when he confers certain excellent benefits upon these, he does not confer them upon those, doing injury to no one in that: nor is he to be called to account, although he is not without his own reasons, often hidden from us. The Jews had sinned grievously, no less than the Idumeans: God could by right have consigned both to slaughter, or left them in the greatest evils. He could likewise, by his supreme will, restore the Idumeans to a happy state, just as he restored the Jews. It pleased him to act otherwise on account of Jacob, and the promises made to him. There is reason for Jacob to give thanks, there is no reason for Esau to complain. Paul refers these things as types of future things to the Synagogue and the Church. The Synagogue was born first: the Church a long time after. The Hebrews had sinned grievously: the idolaters in the whole world, from whom the greatest part of the Church was gathered, had sinned more grievously. That spiritual righteousness, which has eternal promises, God conferred upon the Church through faith, and at the same time the gifts of healings, of prophecy, of tongues, and of casting out demons: and by these signs he showed that their sins, however grievous, were forgiven. He did not confer such righteousness upon the Synagogue through the law, he even took away the gifts, and thereby showed that their sins were retained. If anyone wishes to speak against these things, so clear and so manifest, the free right of God will be opposed to him, both in forgiving sins however grievous, and in conferring benefits, for the use of which right God is bound to render accounts to no one: ἐχ' ὑπευθυνῶ κρατῶ &c. yet he has reasons, not indeed why he must necessarily act so, but reasons which befit his own wisdom and goodness, and are most suitable for healing men more and more. But Paul also brings forward another thing, which does not pertain to this passage of Malachi: namely, the distinction made before the infants were born, so that the elder, that is, the people sprung from the elder would at some time be below the younger. Here too Paul observes the figure of the elder and younger. The synagogue, older by birth, is much below the Church. The Church possesses those gifts which the synagogue never had in such abundance, and what it did have, it lost. Whence this? From the decree of God before they were born: the former was called out of Egypt, the latter out of the world. The ancient Jews used this passage of Genesis for another purpose, namely, to show that certain seeds of virtues, ἀρετὰς φυσικὰς, as Aristotle speaks, are prepared for those not yet born, as Jeremiah acknowledges concerning himself. “God fashions some well even before their birth,” says Philo in his Allegories, and presently brings forward first the birth of Isaac, then what was said of Jacob: and in his books on Cain he says that in those two infants are signified δύο φύσεις ἀγαθῆ νὴ κακῆ, of which the latter precedes the former in dignity at this time: and he repeats the same in his book on the awakened Noah, adding the ignorance innate in us: but that the appetite for good is inserted later. It is of a good disposition, he says, to anticipate evil contagions, ϰὴ πτερνίζειν: which Jacob did: and not to fail in spirit because of boiling appetites, as Esau did, but to cook that pottage with Jacob: which are in the said book on Cain: also to withdraw from the wicked, lest they harm one by their snares: which the same Philo has in his book, that the worse lie in wait for the better: that rule is owed to the best: that it is for the good of others if they do not hold the liberty which they would use badly: which is in the book of the same Philo on piety: who also in his book on rewards and punishments says that there is an image of wildness in Esau, and of humanity in Jacob. These things, although not necessary for the understanding of Malachi, yet being connected to the argument to some extent, I thought should be brought forward here, so that by this specimen it might be understood what kind of ὑπόνοιαι (underlying meanings) the ancient Hebrews had in treating histories, which custom the Apostles follow, and especially Paul, but in such a way that they refer everything not to that imperfect goodness which is according to nature, or even according to the law, but to that divine goodness which is both commanded, and shown, and given in the Gospel.

Through Jacob and Esau, as we have said, Grotius rightly understands not the persons themselves of Jacob and Esau precisely, but their posterity. Calvin and his followers explain it concerning the persons themselves, and believe that the love of Jacob and the hatred of Esau look to the election of the former to eternal life and the reprobation of the latter to eternal death, and from there they attempt to carve out an absolute decree of election and reprobation, especially because the Apostle in Rom. IX. brings forward the words of the Prophet in this manner, verse 11: for when they had not yet been born, or had done anything good or evil, (that the purpose of God according to election might remain) it was said to her not from works, but from him who calls: Because the greater shall serve the lesser: as it is written: Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated. The Apostle joins the passage of Gen. XXV. 23. with this one of ours. But in the Mosaic oracle it is certain that the discourse is not about persons, but nations: Two nations are in your womb: The greater shall serve the lesser. Nor did Esau in his own person serve Jacob, but his descendants served the descendants of Jacob, when David subdued Edom. Cf. Gen. 27, 29. Add that the Prophet here speaks of the state of the posterity of Esau, in which it was at that time, and was to be thereafter. Furthermore, that the word of hatred is not to be taken absolutely here, but comparatively, Grotius likewise rightly observed, namely that Esau was not equally loved, or was postponed: just as to hate is sometimes the same as to postpone in love, or not to love so intensely. Cf. Gen. 29. verse 31. Prov. 13, 24. Matth. 6, 34. c. 10, 37. Luc. 14, 26. c. 16, 13. Which comparative sense Willius admits here.

For as far as the sense and scope of the Prophet's words are concerned, some of the Reformed maintain that our Prophet is not dealing here with common love or any benefits whatsoever, but with special love, such as is for the elect, and with the benefits of grace which are proper to them, and they draw these words to an absolute decree of election and reprobation, such as Junius in his notes on this passage, first

“a document of love, that God from the mere good pleasure of His will chose their parent long ago, but reprobated the others, when they had not yet been born, and had done nothing good or evil.” Compare also Parall. book II. part 11. Which is also the opinion of Piscator, and Pareus, and Coccejus does not seem to depart from it, who says: “this passage proves the special grace of election; to say nothing of others.” But it cannot be proven that the word “I have loved” is to be understood of such love, or “I have hated” is to be understood absolutely and explained of eternal reprobation; indeed, since the discourse is about the posterity of Jacob and Esau, who will say that the whole nation of the Esauites was reprobated and damned, and the whole posterity of Jacob was elected to eternal life, when even of the latter countless numbers perish eternally, and many of the former were called to the kingdom of God? Eph. 11, 14. Am. 9, 11. Mark 3, 7. If you restrict it to the person of Esau, it will be contrary to the Prophetic text, as we have said, nor will it be proven from the Scriptures that he was eternally reprobated; indeed, B. Luther in Gen. XXV. does not conjecture beside the point that Esau repented and was saved through faith in the Messiah. For he cultivated harmony with Jacob returning from Mesopotamia, Gen. XXXIII., by whom he was without doubt admonished to cultivate piety as a brother, especially concerning the burial of their parent, Gen. 35, 29. And if Esau had been eternally reprobated, with what eyes could Rebecca, who understood the answer of God well, have looked upon him as a slave of Satan: from which affection could Isaac have loved the infernal Tityus so much? To what end would they have conferred the Sacrament of circumcision upon him? That opinion does not deal with predestination, but with the temporal prerogative of the younger brother, and the postponement of the elder, as far as the right of primogeniture is concerned, if you look at the persons themselves, or rather as far as temporal benefits are concerned.

But as for the Apostle's application, he does not speak in those words of the absolute and unaccountable right of God, as Grotius wishes, nor does God use it in the pardoning or non-pardoning of sins: for what place would remain for repentance or faith, what place for exhortations to repentance and faith, if God were to pardon or not pardon sins by an absolute right? Nor does the Apostle teach that Esau and Jacob were a type of the Synagogue and the Church in this, that the Synagogue, although born first, and the idolaters from whom the Church was gathered had sinned more grievously, did not receive such righteousness and was even deprived of its own gifts. But that the Church gathered from idolatrous nations received spiritual righteousness, which has eternal promises, and at the same time the gifts of healings, prophecy, tongues, and casting out demons, and that sins were retained for the former, but sins, however grievous, were remitted for the latter, the Apostle has nothing at all to say about the absolute right of God in pardoning or not pardoning sins, as far as the Church and Synagogue are concerned: nay, he is rather occupied with the fact that God does not reject the Jews by absolute power, but because of unbelief, and there can be no doubt that just as God took care for that righteousness to be announced first to the Jews, so He also wished to confer the same upon them, Matt. 23:37, Acts 13:46.

Nor is it to be conceded to the Calvinists that the Apostle is discussing there an absolute decree of election and reprobation, which absolute election and reprobation is diametrically opposed to the perpetual consensus of Scripture. He rather teaches, according to the opinion of most interpreters, that carnal generation That it helps the Jews nothing, or their merits, nor on account of race, or birth, or on account of the regard for works, or merit, that either Jacob was preferred to Esau, or the Jacobites to the Esauites, but rather according to the free purpose of God. Nor indeed do they confirm that the discourse here is about rejection from glory, but only about preterition with respect to external grace, by an argument not obscure, since that rejection does not cut off all hope of obtaining salvation for them, inasmuch as the Apostle prays for their salvation, and considers that they can be restored, and like natural branches broken off through unbelief, can in turn be grafted into the olive tree: whence B. Menzer, Schroeder, as also B. Meisner, in the analysis of chapter 9 to the Romans, accept the purpose of God according to election not as concerning predestination to life, but as concerning election to peculiar grace, as that word is wont to be used concerning the temporal election of a people, see Deut. 4, 17. c. 7, 6. c. 26, 18. 1. Reg. 3, 82. Psal. 128, 67. Psal. 135, 4. Ezech. 20, 5. Jach. 2, 12.

Then, even if it were the case that election to glory were being treated here (which, however, we by no means concede), yet an absolute election or reprobation could not be constructed from the words of the Apostle. For there is nothing here about the exclusion of faith, nothing about the exclusion of unbelief in the foreknowledge (προγνώσει) of either those to be saved or those to be damned. Nor is that collection of any value which is sought from thence in this manner: Race, or birth, or works do nothing for election. Therefore, neither do the faithful belong to it. For I would conclude in the same way that faith does nothing for the justification of a man, because race, birth, and works do nothing for the same. The consequence is therefore inept, since faith is the correlate of the promise, and looks not to itself, nor to the men themselves, nor to anything in man, nor to the works of man, but to Christ alone, in whom alone both justification and election consist. Eph. 1, 3. And the present Apostolic dissertation also infers this: only the seed of Abraham is elected, or only true Israelites are elected; only the children of the promise, that is, those believing in Christ, are the seed of Abraham and true Israelites, v. 6, 7, 8. For where there is a promise, there faith is required, because faith and promise are correlates, Rom. 4, 16. Gal. 3, 7. But the promise is founded in Christ, Gen. 22, 18. c. 26, 4. c. 28, 14. Therefore, only the children of the promise, that is, those believing in Christ, are elected. It is permitted, therefore, to distinguish between the act and existence of faith and unbelief, and the intuition or eternal foresight; before Jacob and Esau were born, they could not indeed have faith or unbelief in act, but God could nevertheless attend to faith and unbelief in them, and from eternity look upon them, according to His indubitable and infallible foreknowledge (προγνώσει). If from the fact that, before they had done anything good or evil, they are said to have been loved or hated, it is valid to collect that the intuition of faith and unbelief and sins is to be simply excluded from predestination, or that they were elected before they were foreseen as either faithful or unbelieving; it will likewise have to be collected from the fact that, before those men were even born, it was said of them, that indeed in predestination the regard for the essence of man is also to be excluded, or that men were elected before they were foreseen to be men. Which is a contradiction. For what? Were men to be elected? Nay, according to most Calvinists, they come to be viewed in the divine foresight not only as men, but also as having already fallen into sin. Therefore, they were certainly foreseen as having already done something evil and having transgressed the law of God.

Most diligently, therefore, it is to be noted that by this expression, 'before they were born,' etc., every regard for condition is not excluded from the love of God in preferring Jacob to Esau, but only the dignity

and merit of both carnal birth and the holiness of works is excluded. If, therefore, this is applied to the business of election, even though there is no discourse here about the same, nothing can be inferred here other than that God does not elect men on account of the dignity and merit of their faith, but it is by no means to be collected from thence that election does not take place in faith, or that God does not regard faith in the man being elected, which Scripture teaches, Eph. 1, 4. 2. Thess. 2, 13. 1. Petr. 1, 2. Jac. 2, 5. However, therefore, works and faith are excluded from the decree of election by those words of the Apostle (before they had done anything good or evil), insofar as they are a meritorious cause, yet faith, which apprehends Christ, in whom election was made, is not to be excluded.

Moreover, one must beware in such an application to the decree of reprobation, lest the same be done beyond the scope of the Apostle and against the analogy of faith; for if the Adversaries wish to infer that the merit of sin and infidelity is not attended to in those being damned in the decree of reprobation, they will wander as far as heaven is from earth both from the scope of the Apostle and the truth of the faith. For they cannot show that Esau (reserving the superior analysis, upon which they themselves insist) is introduced either as a genuine example of reprobation or even as a type of the same, and that the scope of the Apostle is to establish absolute reprobation; and therefore Mr. Schröder aptly warns that Esau is brought forward only as an example that God is not bound by the prerogatives which He bestows, and is not constituted as a type of the rejection of the Jews from glory, but only of a temporal rejection from grace.

The matter, however, is evident, that there is no discourse here about election to eternal life, or reprobation, as Balthasar Willius, although a Reformed theologian, not only confessed this at length, but also, having instituted an analysis of the Apostolic treatment, openly demonstrates in his Commentary on Malachi 1, p. 100 seqq., that the scope for the Apostle was the same as that which our Menzer, Schröder, and others have stated, and which we have already produced according to their opinion. It is helpful here to bring forward the entire passage, so that a judgment may be instituted more correctly concerning the mind and opinion of the Apostle. That whole treatment and doctrine, he says, of chapters 9, 10, and 11 to the Romans arises from the final words of the preceding eighth chapter, by which the Apostle concludes and is persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any created thing can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus. With which words he makes Christ Jesus the foundation of divine love, in whom and on account of whom the Father loves us, and through whom we in turn love the Father, and are certain of his benevolence, according to Eph. 1, 6. John 14, 23. However, with Christ Jesus established as the foundation of divine love, it follows that all those who do not receive Jesus Christ by faith are alienated from divine love, and thus the Jews, that people of God once chosen and beloved, because they did not believe in Christ, have fallen away from divine love and salvation. As this matter was a source of grief to Paul, so it was a stumbling block to the believing Jews in particular, while it stirred up the indignation of the impenitent and provided an occasion for calumnies: Wherefore Paul, out of regard for all these, but especially for the sake of the weak believers, begins a new treatment concerning the right of adoption, in which he demonstrates that it pertains not to the children of the flesh but to the children of the promise, and that the unbelieving Jews, although they are endowed with distinguished privileges according to the flesh, are nevertheless alienated from God. Therefore, the scope of these chapters is to teach that the Jews, although they are endowed with very many privileges and carnal prerogatives, are nevertheless alienated from the grace of God and from his love and adoption as long as they persevere in unbelief.

To this end in all things the Apostle tends, to this he looks, when he shows that the word of God has not failed, that not all the sons of Abraham are the seed, and that there is no injustice and unfaithfulness with God, as can be easily manifest to anyone reading the words without prejudice of human authority, from demonstration and spiritual collation. The proposition therefore and the sole thesis here is that which is had in express words at the beginning of chapter IX. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. For that pathetic exordium of the Apostle is reduced to this statement: The Jews not believing in Christ have fallen from divine adoption and love, although they are instructed with many and those excellent carnal privileges. But this statement, as it is conceived distinctly by the Apostle, so in its confirmation it is resolved into its simple propositions, whence it was made, and because the privileges and prerogatives and promises seemed to derogate from the Apostolic sentence, in the first place he meets all those things which could apparently overturn the truth of his own enunciation, and shows that the truth and justice of God are by no means undermined by his doctrine, up to verse 30. In the second place he proceeds to the confirmation of the primary part, which had been in the proposition, and teaches the proper cause of the rejection to the end of the ninth chapter. But he assigns the cause of the rejection to the contempt of the righteousness of faith, of which he makes mention in such a way that by antithetical illustration he simultaneously adds the cause of the reception of the Gentiles, namely, the acceptance of the righteousness of faith. But because these principles of the Pauline sentence were not of undoubted truth on both sides, but stood in need of proof on the part of the Jews, therefore this aetiological antithesis, which was in c. IX. v. 30. 31. 32., is proved by parts in a hysteron proteron in chapter X., and two principal propositions of that chapter arise. The first of these is that Israel is destitute of the righteousness of God and the way to adoption, which is proposed and confirmed up to verse 14. The other is that the Gentiles have arrived at righteousness and adoption through faith, and that from a divine calling made to them freely, which is treated up to verse 18. In the third place he annexes a proleptic appendix, by which he anticipates all those things which could still be objected to him; among these the first is the ignorance of the mystery concerning the calling of the Gentiles, which he refutes from the Prophets to the end of the tenth chapter. The other is the total rejection of the Jews, which he denies by the limitation and exception of the elect in chapter XI. up to verse 33. Finally, the Apostle concludes with a notable exclamation, by which he proclaims the riches of the mercy and the most just judgments of God, to the very end. This is the economy of these three chapters. Furthermore, to come closer to our purpose, the chief thing which seemed to stand in the way of the rejection of the unbelieving Jews was the Word of the covenant and the promise made to Abraham and his seed, Genesis XVII. v. 7. The Jews proudly boasted that they were this seed, and therefore that it could not be that they should fall from the divine covenant, as long as God remained consistent with Himself in His promises and truth. The Apostle objects this argument to himself separately, at the beginning of verses 6 and 7, which words we have said in our Commentary are commonly translated poorly. But they must be rendered according to the flow of the source, and the apostolic sense, at the beginning of the sixth verse: Not indeed this, namely what I have said, is to be taken as meaning that the word of God has failed. But at the beginning of the seventh verse: Nor that because they are the seed of Abraham are all the sons of Abraham. If indeed you interpret these latter words as a reason for the proposition, which proves that the word of God has not failed, as has been done by everyone until now, manifest violence is brought upon the words of the Apostle, and his whole discourse is enervated, and those things which are opposed to one another are taken for one and the same. For there are opposed to the Apostle in this treatment the seed,

and the sons of Abraham, of whom the latter denotes carnal descendants, but the former denotes believers. Furthermore, as I have said, this is a single argument or a single objection against the truth of God, but divided on account of the parts of the preceding proposition, for because he had said that the Jews were rejected, it was easy to object: "If the Jews are rejected, as you say, it follows that the covenant and the promise of God are abolished, but if you say that these still endure, we are that seed." Both of these objections the Apostle objects to himself, and solves by a distinction between true Israelites and those such in name only, sons of Abraham and seed: The first with its solution is in the sixth verse. "Nor do I speak this because the word of God has failed. For not all who are of Israel are Israel." The sense is, not when I bring these things forward, will you think that I am accusing the promises of God of inconstancy, or as void, for there are two kinds of Israelites, others who are distinguished by an external name only, others who have the reality and nature of true Israelites; the promise looks to the latter, not likewise to the former, and so although these are passed over by God, yet His truth remains. The other with its solution follows again in verse 7. "Nor that because they are the seed of Abraham are all the sons," namely, it is to be thought, or I speak these things, "but in Isaac shall thy seed be called." The sense is: It is not to be thought that all the sons of Abraham are the seed of Abraham, because Isaac alone is as the seed, and in Isaac the seed was promised to him. Furthermore, what he means by seed and Israel, he explains when he adds. This is, not those who are the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted for the seed, that is: Not those who are born from the carnal posterity of Israel are counted as children of God, whose child Israel was, nor those who are born from the loins of Abraham are his seed, but the children who were born to him according to the promise, whom the promise as it were begat by embracing it, and who are still begotten to him through faith, as to the father of all believers, while they insist upon the footsteps of his faith. Finally, the foundation of the solution and distinction is sought from the examples of Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, both of which are recited, the former indeed more briefly, but the latter more prolixly, so that he says and proves that the former partly does the same, and partly leaves it. He says it makes for the same point as the preceding one, with these words of Isaac: Neither only Abraham but also Rebecca, when she had conceived by one, by Isaac our father, received a discourse of such a promise: he proves the same thing indeed from the time of the oracle pronounced before the boys were born, from the purpose, which was that the purpose of God, namely the purpose of calling sons according to election, His eternal decree, might remain not from works, but from Him who calls, might acquire its firmness not from their own good or evil works, but from the counsel of God who calls and makes sons. He recites the example itself or the word of the promise from Gen. XXV. 21. It was said to her: The greater shall serve the lesser; and he confirms its truth from the outcome, of which Malachi writes: Jacob I have loved: Esau I have hated. Here Ishmael and Isaac are not considered as any types of eternal election or reprobation, but as arguments of the most constant divine will, and of the administration in the Church, by which He reckons not the sons of the flesh, but of the promise in the seed, just as the most illustrious Junius judges most wisely concerning this passage in lib. II. Parall. 9. His words are: For thus the Apostle thinks, even if these words were said concerning one singular person, nevertheless they pertain analogically to the common or universal distinction and administration of the people of God, not only by example, which nevertheless obtains no mediocre momentum in divine matters, not only by type, when nevertheless the house of Abraham through that time was a type of our Church: not only the analogy taken from the part to the whole, which even in this argument cannot rightly be passed over, but most of all from the most constant nature of God, whose will and administration toward the Church is one and always constant to itself. A similar reasoning holds for the example of Jacob and Esau. Thus far Willius, whose analysis and explanation being admitted, no patronage is left for the opinion of those who wish the Apostle to be dealing with election to eternal glory, or reprobation from the same, in his application of it, let alone those who interpret our Prophet concerning the same.

Jacob Arminius meets this Calvinistic objection, as well as the others which are taken from the present chapter VIII of Romans, in another way, and he institutes a certain peculiar analysis of it, which is held in his works in the Appendix to the Examination of Perkinsian Predestination, and he reports that this is also the explanation of Gellius Snecanus. He teaches, therefore, that the scope of this chapter is one and the same as that of the whole Epistle: that the Gospel, not the law, is the power of God unto salvation, not to the worker, but to the believer: and that the Apostle defends this here against the objection of the Jews, so that he may establish it more and more. He assigns, however, this state of the question as accommodated to the present dispute: Whether the word of God becomes void if those of the Jews who seek righteousness not from faith, but from the law, are rejected by God; so that the Apostle may teach that the word of God includes only the children of the promise, with the children of the flesh excluded, and thus the word of God does not fail, even if the children of the flesh are rejected; and that the children of the flesh are those who pursue righteousness and salvation through the works of the law; the children of the promise are those who seek righteousness and salvation through faith in Christ? But that the word of promise includes only the children of the promise, with the children of the flesh excluded, the Apostle shows (according to Arminius) by a double type; one taken from the house of Abraham, the other from that of Isaac: so that Isaac and Jacob are types of all the children of the promise, and Ishmael and Esau of the children of the flesh. The prior proof, therefore, is that Isaac had to be reckoned in the seed, and Ishmael not reckoned: and thus, since Isaac is a type of the children of the promise, and Ishmael of the children of the flesh, the former had to be reckoned in the seed, and the latter had not to be, according to the word of the Lord. His other reason is that Jacob was loved, and Esau was hated, and indeed while they were not yet born, and before they could have done anything good or evil. Whence it is permitted to conclude that the purpose of God was made according to election, not from works, but from works, i.e., it does not concern the children of the flesh, who are from works, but the children of the promise, who are from faith, by which one obeys God calling. Whence the Apostolic proof according to Arminius stands thus: If the purpose according to election remains from the caller, and not from works, then it follows that those who are from the works of the law, and pursue righteousness and salvation through the law, are not contained in that purpose, but only those who obey God calling and promising through faith. But the former is true from the type of Esau and Jacob, by which both was signified, that the purpose of God is according to election, and then that it remains from the caller and not from works. The former because one is preferred to the other, which is a sign of a purpose according to election; the latter because the elder Esau is hated and subjected, but the younger Jacob is loved and preferred, which is a sign that this purpose is not firm from works, but from the caller, i.e., that God loves those who seek righteousness and salvation through faith in Christ, but hates those who pursue the same from the works of the law. But that God willed Ishmael and Esau to be types of the children

of the flesh, but Isaac and Jacob of the children of the promise, this reason is rendered by Arminius, that he taught this for the sake of the signification and convenience between the type and the antitype: With respect to the former type, that he who was born from the handmaid and by the power of the flesh was a type of the children of the flesh, and he who was born from the free woman and by the power of the promise, when the flesh was already spent, was a type of the children of the promise. But with respect to the latter type, that he who was born first bears the figure of the children of the flesh, and of the old or former covenant, or of the Jews who by zeal for the law sought righteousness and life through it, and he who was born later [bears the figure] of the children of the promise and of the later or new covenant, or of those who pursued righteousness and faith through faith in Christ. This is Arminius.

This mystical and allegorical sense does not please Willius, so that by the children of the flesh those who seek righteousness from the law, or legalistic Jews, are understood, and by the children of the promise believers are understood, and mystically by Isaac and Jacob the latter are designated, but by Ishmael and Esau the former, and especially that the example of Jacob is taken concerning the younger people of the new covenant, and that of Esau concerning the elder of the old covenant. 'But just as,' says Willius, 'they are not cited as types of reprobation or damnation and election, so neither are they cited as types of faith and works, and of the elder and younger people.' For although sometimes flesh denotes the same as works, and any carnal prerogative whatsoever, yet it cannot be proven from that that this is the genuine sense everywhere or in this place. And that interpretation of Scripture is too free, indeed frivolous, when we slip into allegories with the literal sense put aside. Nor is the patronage of this allegory situated in the place of the Apostle Gal. IV. 22. and following. Since the scope of that place is one thing, and the institution is another, beyond the boundaries of which an allegory must not be moved.

But whatever becomes of these Willian oppositions, and although that mystical and allegorical sense is also dismissed, which could not fully commend itself to us in every respect, nevertheless Arminius did not rashly designate the scope and argument of the Apostolic treatment; even if the children of the flesh by allegory are not the same as the justitiarii, who follow the righteousness of the law, yet materially they are here the same Jewish justitiarii, who are the only children of the flesh, and thus the only believers are the children. and therefore if in place of a type there is set an argument with Willius, or an example with B. Menzer and Schröder, and Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau are assumed not indeed as types, but as a similar example, or even as an argument of the divine will and administration always consistent with itself in the Church, which counts not the children of the flesh but of the promise in the seed, the scope and argument, as assigned by Arminius, will still be in shallow water, and without doubt the whole treatment of the Apostle will be more correctly consistent with itself, if it be said that it is not about election to eternal life and reprobation, as other Reformed wish, from whom Willius here departs, nor about rejection from grace and love, or adoption into the people, that is being treated directly and by design, but that the principal treatment is being continued, which he had hitherto pursued most of all through the whole Epistle, concerning our justification before God, which the Arminians especially show in their clear explanation, as they call it, of chapter IX to the Romans, in the Synodical writings p. 96. and following pages show. Concerning the true scope of the Apostle they confirm most fully that the holy Apostle is not treating of the giving of faith, how and to whom God wills to give faith, but of the giving of righteousness, how and whom He wills to justify and adopt: that he is treating of Justification in Romans IX, X, XI, and defending this thesis against the objections of the Jews: that it had been God's purpose from ancient times to justify not those who seek righteousness from the law, but those who believe in the promises of God revealed in the Gospel, to adopt, to bless, and that God, in this, is not unjust, [but has] the right and most free power of doing so; whence it is not difficult to gather that the controversy between the Apostle and the unbelievers was not properly about their rejection, but about the doctrine of the Apostle, from which it was necessary that it should follow, which was that righteousness and adoption are not from the works of the law, but from the faith of Christ.

This opinion, however, rests primarily upon the following foundations. I. That among the Jews it was indeed not a matter of doubt that not all who had descended carnally from Abraham were without distinction children of God and truly in covenant, and therefore the Apostle would have rashly undertaken to prove that which was established beyond the hazard of doubt. II. That in the time of the Apostle that scruple could not yet have arisen among the Jews, that the greater part of the Jews had been rejected, and so the promises of God would be altogether void, whether in respect of the converted, or in respect of those who were strangers to the faith of Christ; for these did not believe that this was a rejection of themselves, because they were strangers to Christ, but those could think that the promise of God was being fulfilled in themselves, and perhaps in the course of time would be fulfilled in many of their people. III. From the words: Not all children, who are the seed of Abraham, it is clear that this is not about the giving of faith, but about sonship, which presupposes faith, John 1:12; otherwise the Apostle would have said, Not all believers, who are the seed of Abraham. IV. As children of the promise are called in the scriptures those who are of the faith of Christ, Gal. 3:19, Rom. 4:11, so children of the flesh are to be understood by way of opposition as those who followed righteousness according to the flesh, i.e., from the law, Rom. 4:1-2, which in what sense it is to be admitted, we have said before. V. The purpose of God according to election is more correctly understood as the decree concerning the salvation of men, according to the Apostolic phrase, than as election into the peculiar people of God. But it can in no way be explained as the purpose of giving faith, or the grace necessary for faith; for thus those words would be in vain: Not from works. For who said that faith is given from works, so that this had to be denied? VI. The Apostle himself seems to explain this purpose thus, that it is firm not from works, but from the caller or grace, which two the Apostle perpetually opposes to each other in the article of salvation, and so those terms: From the caller, from grace, from a gift, through faith, according to the promise, etc., explain each other; whence also that opposition of children of the flesh and of the promise, and of our works and of the grace of the caller, declare themselves excellently. VII. The reasoning of the types (or rather examples, or arguments) corresponds neatly if it is said that the righteousness of works and of faith is represented. But if it is asserted that regard is had to the giving or negation of faith, the matter cannot be conveniently explained. For how will the younger be called, to whom faith is given, and the elder, to whom faith is denied, and furthermore how will serving signify not having faith? But the people of workers is rightly the elder, because it is prior to the people of believers, and the people of believers is the younger, as being posterior. Likewise, serving conveniently denotes not having the liberty of the children of God. Thus, therefore, the words concerning children not yet born, when they had done nothing good or evil, are brought forward for no other end than to teach that by this example and argument of divine economy (as the Apostle himself adds) the purpose of God according to election, or the decree of God concerning the salvation of men, is firm, not from works, but from the caller, and from faith, which embraces the divine calling: because, namely, without regard to works, before they had done anything good or evil, it was said, the elder shall serve the younger. We have, therefore, the most evident example and document of a divine promise made, even regarding external temporal prerogatives, without regard to works: whence much less will the promise of the grace of adoption and justification rest upon works, or our merits, but ought to be attributed solely to the grace of God. Which example is most suitable to the present discussion, because the Jews boasted of themselves as the progeny of Abraham. And yet Ishmael and Esau descended no less from Abraham than Isaac and Jacob, even though those prerogatives did not fall to them, because in Isaac the seed was called, not in Ishmael, that is, because the promise concerning the blessed seed was restricted to the family of Isaac, not of Ishmael, (which prerogative, even if external, was not the last among the prerogatives by which the Jews exalted themselves, namely, that from them the Messiah was to arise, v. 5) and because to Jacob, not to Esau, even though they were begotten not only from the same father, but also from the same mother, and before they had done anything good or evil, the preeminence was promised, even though Esau was the firstborn, just as the Jews were the earlier (certainly not by their own merits) than the Gentiles. It is manifest, therefore, from these examples, that whatever good befalls us is to be attributed not to our works or merits, but solely to divine grace, and that carnal lineage contributes nothing to it. Since the will of God toward us and His administration is always one and consistent with itself, as Junius before, and Willius from him. VIII. In this way, the comparison of our prophetic passage, which the Apostle institutes with the Mosaic oracle, fits perfectly, from which not only is the truth of that oracle proven, that a notable preeminence was granted to the younger over the elder, because the Lord loved Jacob over Esau or the Jacobites over the Esavites, as the fates of that time which had befallen them, and the prophecies which Malachi further foretold about them, testified: but it is also clearly perceived that whatever good redounds to us from God, let alone the gift of justification and salvation, is not to be ascribed to our merits, and thus far Grotius is not wrong: The Jews had sinned as grievously as the Edomites: He could by right have consigned both to destruction, or left them in the greatest evils. IX. The analysis of the whole of chapter 9 to the Romans is perfectly consistent with itself, once that theme and the state of the question concerning the justification of faith are admitted, which does not seem so plain if it be said that it treats primarily and per se of the rejection of the Jews, or even of the collation of faith or the negation of the same, as the comparison of both analyses can teach. This state of the question agrees as much as possible with the scope of the Apostolic treatment set forth in this Epistle; which the continuity with the previous chapters excellently illustrates. For as the Apostle had previously taught expressly that man is liberated solely through faith in Christ, both from the curse of sin, by which he is subjected to condemnation, and from the dominion of the same, by which he is enslaved to the service of sin, since the curse is not taken away except through gracious justification, which is only through Christ, and liberation from the dominion of sin must be effected through renewal, which is likewise a gift of God in Christ, flowing from being planted together with Him: Whence it follows that only Christians, who have true communion with Christ, are true children of God and heirs of eternal life, who do not call upon God as their father in lethal and servile fear, as under the law, but in undaunted filial boldness, and are able to serve Him. The Apostle now defends this saving doctrine against the Jews, as far as concerns the decree of God regarding the justifying and saving of men, not from the works of the flesh or the law, but through faith in Christ, demonstrating its truth by divine oracles from verse 6 to 13, and its equity from the most free right of God from verse 14 to 23, to the end of the chapter. To these is added 11. That verse 15 treats of the mercy of God, by which sins are remitted, but that necessarily presupposes faith; and therefore not of the faith- foundation, but concerning justification by faith these are to be understood. XII. That verse 16, justice, sonship, and inheritance are said to be not of the runner, or of him who pursues it through the works of the law, but of God showing mercy to the faithful and those believing in Christ. It is therefore a matter of the mercy of God in justifying the faithful. XIII. God is said to harden whom He wills, verse 18. But God does not harden except the unbeliever, and him who stubbornly rejects the offered grace, Is. VI. 9, ch. VIII. 12, Rom. IX. 33, ch. XI. 7, 1 Pet. II. 8, as even the example of Pharaoh testifies, who, being called so often through miracles and the word of God, rejecting the word of God, was hardened. Therefore, the words are not to be understood as concerning an absolute denial of faith, but concerning the hardening and reprobation of those who do not believe and who utterly reject the grace of God. Add XIV. that verse 21, a vessel for honor or dishonor, is not a vessel for faith or unbelief, or one to whom God wills to give or not give the grace to believe, but a vessel for honor is a vessel for inheritance, blessing, and glory, as is explained in verse 23 concerning the faithful, just as vessels for dishonor are the unbelievers themselves. XV. The prophecy of Hos. II. 23 is brought forward: I will call my people, who were not my people: But God does not call His people except through the intercession of faith, Ps. CX. 3, Heb. II. 6, which is hinted at from Hos. II. 19 and 20. Therefore, it is treated here also not concerning the absolute giving of faith or salvation, but concerning such a will of God, by which He wills to have the faithful as His people. XVI. From verse 26 it is clear that it is treated here concerning the seed or children of the promise, that is, concerning the faithful, and their sonship and adoption through faith is asserted, where the prophecy from Is. I. 9 is brought forward. XVII. This is seen more clearly from the execution of that decree, concerning which the Apostle treats, which is described in verse 30 and following. For from this it is most evident that it was not a matter of that decree by which God willed to save certain individual persons absolutely, or to endow them with faith, but by which He determined to justify the faithful and to exclude the unbelievers and workers from justice, because the Gentiles, who do not pursue justice, namely from works, are said to have apprehended justice, namely that which is from faith, as the Apostle himself explains. Israel, however, who pursued the law of justice, did not arrive at justice, because they sought it not from faith, but as if from works. XVIII. No less clearly does the whole Chapter X confirm this scope, where the Apostle treats the same matter, namely concerning the justice of faith, and thus teaches that the Jews, because they are ignorant of the justice consisting before God, and strive to demand their own justice, do not become participants in justification and adoption, which he proposes in verse 3 in express words, but in the following ones he draws it out, comparing the justice of faith with the justice of works, from Moses, Deut. ch. XXX, as also demonstrating the justice of faith from undoubted oracles, Is. XXIX. 10, He who believes in Him shall not be confounded, and Joel II. 32, He who calls upon the name of the Lord (which the Apostle teaches must be done by true faith in Christ) he shall be saved. XIX. Verse 12 of chapter X is to be compared primarily with Rom. III. 23, for as he teaches there that there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles, all being saved who through faith call upon one Lord: so he concluded there that there is no difference between them, all needing the glory of God, and being justified from grace through faith. XX.

Chapter XI also confirms the same scope, where the Apostle likewise meets the objection of the Jews, that from that doctrine it follows that the Jews would be rejected. He distinguishes, however, between the people whom God foreknew, namely by a special grace of acquisition, and whom He did not foreknow, verse 2, by which distinction, if only certain individual persons are designated without any regard for faith or unbelief, nothing is accomplished against the Jews; who indeed readily granted that not all Jews were to be saved. And therefore it is certain that they are said to be foreknown according to the foresight of faith, or those who are foreseen as going to believe in Christ, as is evident from Rom. VIII. 29, Eph. I. 6, 2 Tim. II. 19. XXI. Likewise, the election of grace in verse 5 is not spoken of concerning absolute grace, which Scripture does not know, but concerning the grace which Paul has inculcated throughout this whole Epistle, by which we are justified before God, which, as it is founded on the merit of Christ, so it is not opposed to the faith that apprehends the merit of Christ, but only to merits and any works whatsoever. XXII. Most clearly again, verse 6 confirms the same: If by grace, then no longer by works, where a comparison with Rom. IV. 4 sufficiently testifies that the same doctrine is treated there which was treated in the previous chapters 3, 4, and 5, concerning justification by faith, where the Apostle says, To him who does not work, but believes, faith is imputed for justice. XXIII. Finally, the argument is sought from the epiphonema of the Apostolic conclusion, ch. XI. 32. God has concluded all under unbelief, that He might have mercy on all, by which is comprehended the sum of the whole doctrine handed down by the Apostle concerning justification by faith, since it is completed by a twofold consideration. 1. Of the justice of God, by which all, as well Jews as Gentiles, on account of sin have been concluded under condemnation, so that no one can be justified before God through works. 2. Of the mercy of God, by which God has mercy on all those who have been concluded under unbelief, and thus on the whole human race, partly through the redemption of all men made by Christ, partly through the affection of grace, by which He seriously desires and procures the salvation of all men through the ordinary means of salvation, so that thus all may become participants of His mercy and salvation through faith in Christ, with no one excluded from it, unless he excludes himself, having spurned the mercy of God.

These are the stronger arguments (the force and strength of which, along with this interpretation of ours previously proposed in the Apostolic oracles, our blessed Lord Dr. Weller praised in his Annotations on the Epistle to the Romans, page 525) which show that the Apostle is dealing with the decree of justifying the faithful, the reprobate, and the unfaithful, not with the decree of granting faith or conferring salvation upon a few certain people out of an absolute good pleasure, with the rest entirely excluded from that grace, most of which are of such solidity that they could not be repelled by the Calvinists hitherto, or even now. Therefore, with that scope of the Apostolic treatment assumed, not only will the Calvinists have no support from it for their error, but they will also be solidly repelled from the whole treatment, since it is directed toward teaching that the decree concerning justifying and saving men is not absolute, nor made in view of works, but solely in view of faith persevering in Christ; although we are also certain that the Calvinists can obtain nothing at all to establish their inventions while the interpretation of others stands, who wish for the dissertation here to be instituted properly concerning the reprobation of the Jews from temporal grace. This was acknowledged especially by this Willius praised earlier (to say nothing of others now), who did not hesitate to oppose himself to his own companions in faith in this cause, convinced without doubt by the force and evidence of heavenly truth. Furthermore, he says, there are no traces of any absolute decree here either. For those words: when the children were not yet born, when they had done nothing good or evil, are brought forward for no other end than to prove that the word spoken to Rebecca is likewise a word of promise, because it was given to her before their birth. The following words also mean the same, by which the end of these words is said to be a demonstration of that which is the purpose of God calling children according to election, that it is and remains not from works or carnal prerogatives, but from the one calling, and his good pleasure and grace. Thus, therefore, that word of promise to Rebecca- that it was so, he teaches by two arguments: one from time, because it was uttered before the birth concerning future things, which are wont to fall under a promise; the other from the end, because by it God wished to teach that His purpose of saving and adopting some proceeds not from the works or merits of men, but from His own gratuitous mercy and good pleasure. So also, when he subjects the place of Malachi to the recounted formula of the promise, he does not inquire into the causes of election or reprobation, but shows that the truth of the oracle exhibited to Rebecca was proven by the event, because Malachi testifies that Jacob and his descendants were adopted by God and adorned with a singular blessing, but on the contrary, Esau and his descendants were passed over and agitated by divine judgments. And the site and evidence of the Apostle's words show that this is the sense of that allegation. These things being thus explained, there is now no difficulty in the sense or application of the words of Malachi. For that sense is the one we have stated, the literal one: that God adopted Jacob and the Jews as a people for Himself and enriched them with the gift of the promised land and infinite other proofs of benevolence, but on the contrary, exercised His judgments upon the Edomites, who were excluded from that adoption and inheritance. The application is likewise instituted according to the literal sense, and it is taught that by that very fact God justified His promise, by which He had declared that the greater would serve the lesser: These (adds Willius) are my sentiments concerning this passage of Malachi and Paul, which I would wish the fair reader to judge as well-weighed, and to think of it as opposed not so much out of prejudice or contradiction, but for the sake of aiding the understanding of the Scriptures. Nor indeed am I the first, but many before me have interpreted the passage of Malachi in this way, which can be seen in Jerome, Theodoret, and Oecolampadius. Nor is Calvin himself alien to this exposition, although he finally descends to the absolute decree of God. Thus Willius, who sets forth in his own words in what place that doctrine of the Reformers concerning absolute reprobation, proceeding from mere hatred of God, which some seek in this prophetic oracle and Apostolic application, ought to be held. Indeed, he continues in the cited passage, indeed all my senses vanish for me, and it is necessary that they vanish for others, because God Himself, the merciful Father of His creatures, vanishes when reprobation is attributed to such hatred or divine will without any consideration of sin. The whole Scripture vanishes, in which not even by the slightest title is such hatred of God taught, but the contrary is expressly affirmed. For if we are chosen in Christ, as Calvin rightly speaks, those who are reprobated are reprobated in Adam. Which, asserted simply, is false: for thus it would be necessary that all be reprobated: In Adam all merited reprobation, but after the expiation made through Christ, they are not reprobated unless they reject it through incredulity. How otherwise will that doctrine of Paul in Romans 5:13 and following stand, which teaches that guilt and condemnation flowed from one, but justification and life from the other? Nor does the justice of God, much less His goodness and mercy, suffer such hatred. Not mercy, because through it He loves even sinners and pities them. Not goodness, because through it God communicates Himself to creatures, and His favor, and He is alien to no one. Not justice, because He necessarily approves all these things which are good in creatures and from God, nor can He disapprove anything except that which departs from the goodness communicated to the creature. It is truly a wonder that learned men slip into such error; that they do not consider these things in God, and supinely, bewitched by the fascination of the human brain, neglect them. Indeed, the Fathers did not teach us these things, among whom the most celebrated in this very matter, Augustine, writes in the Enchiridion: He who said 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy' loved Jacob through gratuitous mercy, but hated Esau through due judgment. Likewise, Book I to Simplicianus, question 2: God does not hate Esau the man, but God hates Esau the sinner. And Epistle 105: If God were to damn anyone undeservedly, it is not believed that He would be unpunished for iniquity. And Epistle 106: Those to whom God does not impart mercy, they deserve not to have it imparted. Likewise, Book III against Julian, chapter 18: God is good, God is just. He can liberate some without good merits because He is good: He cannot damn anyone without evil merits because He is justice. Let us hear the same person, moreover, in the book which refutes some articles falsely imposed upon him, in which he responds to Article III, that God creates the greater part of the human race in such a way that He destroys it eternally, in this manner: God is indeed the creator of all men: but no one was created by Him in order to perish, because the cause of being born is one thing, the cause of perishing another. For that men are born is the benefit of the creator, but that they perish is the vice of the transgressor. For in Adam, in whom the nature of all men was formed, all have sinned, and are bound by the same sentence which he received, nor are they released from this bond, even if they lack their own sins, unless they are reborn in the Sacrament of the death and resurrection of Christ, through the Holy Spirit. Therefore, he is too impious and unlearned who does not distinguish the vice of nature from the Author of nature, from whom is absolutely alien whatever is to be condemned in each one. Blessed Fulgentius joins himself to Augustine in Book I to Monimus, where he contracts the sum of the true opinion concerning predestination in these words: It is fitting for the faithful to believe and confess: that God, being good and just, indeed foreknew that men would sin, because nothing of future things could be hidden from Him (for they would not even be future if they had not been in His foreknowledge), yet He did not predestine any man to sin. Because if God were to predestine a man to some sin, He would not punish the man for his sins. For by the predestination of God, either the pious remission of sins is prepared, or the just punishment of sins. Therefore, God could never have predestined men to that which He had disposed both to prohibit by commandment, and to wash away by mercy, and to punish by justice. Nor did Prosper of Aquitaine, Bishop of Riez, teach otherwise, in his responses to the chapters of the objections of the slandering Gauls, where he responds to the first objection: It is in no way right that those things which are done evilly by men be ascribed to predestination: who arrived at a proclivity for falling not from the condition of God, but from the transgression of the first father, from whose punishment no one is freed, except through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ prepared and predestined in the eternal counsel of God, before the foundation of the world. Likewise in the response to Objection VI. It is most ineptly said that the predestination of God works in men either for good or for evil, so that a certain necessity seems to impel men to both. Likewise in the opinion on Objection XIV. He who says that those who do not believe the evangelical preaching do not believe because of God's predestination, and that God has so defined it, that whoever does not believe, does not believe because of His predestination, is not a Catholic. For just as faith, which works through love, is a gift of God; so infidelity is not a constitution of God. The confessions of the orthodox Churches are illustrious, which I wished to cite for this reason, that I might teach that the absurdity of absolute reprobation was never approved by the public consensus of the Churches; but was condemned by them, and is the invention of particular persons. These things again Willius, appealing to the Gallican and Belgic Confession, about which it is not relevant to speak here; it has been spoken of the Calvinist opinion expressly in a writing published in the name of our Theological College; Thorough Proof that the Calvinist errors concern the foundation of the faith, and are detrimental to salvation p. 1490. Now we must return to Grotius. That opinion of the Jews, which he brings forward, who taught from this passage that certain seeds of certain mighty works are prepared for those not yet born, is neither gathered from this passage at all, nor can it consist with original sin, in which we are all conceived and born, of which since Aristotle was ignorant, it is no wonder that he posited natural virtues. To say that the Apostle follows such a manner of treating the sacred histories of the Old Testament is not sufficiently pious: whom we know to have written while borne by the Holy Spirit, and not to have followed the custom of the Hebrews.

and thus he teaches three things: First, the benefits of God about to come to Israel, then those illustrious benefits by which God might manifest his power, magnificence, and benevolence to the Jews; thirdly, that the Jews would acknowledge those benefits and celebrate them with public confession. Others render the preposition על as beyond; let the Lord be magnified beyond the border of Israel, i.e., the glory and magnificence of the Lord should not be constricted by the narrow borders of Israel, but should propagate and extend itself beyond them through the whole world. Which was begun under the Maccabees, and was fulfilled in the time of Christ and the Apostles.

Coccejus proves this sense from the versions, the force of the word, parallel passages, and the evidence of the matter: The LXX, above the borders, the Chaldean and I will extend the border of Israel. Drusius adds assertively, beyond the border. The matter cries out that it must be translated thus. It is true. For מעל signifies recession and distance. For its force is i.e., from near or from above: as the case requires. It is one thing to say ממעל as in Gen. XXII, 9, above the wood, which he imposed on those who translate it as above here.
