ET HABVIT FILIAM DEI ALIENI.) Id est, cultricem. Nam sicut dii à suis patres dicuntur, Jerem. 2, 27. ita qui eos colunt, filii: habuit, בעל, id est, in ma- trimonio habuit. Tangitur historia quæ est Esdræ 9, 10. Neh. 13, 23.

Novam hic tradidit Coccejus ἔκθεσιν, per fan- ctum Domini, quod diligit, à Juda profanatum in- „telligens Filium Dei: Qui Christum merum ho- „minem & nihilo minus regem in regno Dei & „dominum esse statuit, is profanat sanctum Do- „mini, & fornicatur cum idololatris, quia ex Chri- „sto facit Deum & Dominum novum, patribus in- „cognitum, aut saltem, in quem non speraverint „salutis & justitiæ causa patres. Sed quamvis hæc vera sint, textui tamen præsenti quomodo conve- niant, non apparet. Sanctitatem Domini, dicente Willio, vocat excellentiam populi Judaici præ o- mnibus aliis nationibus ipsis communicatam, & hanc dicit pollui, quod dilexit Juda & duxit uxorem filiam Dei alieni, id est, gentilem filiam, quæ Deos alienos colit. Sicuti enim veriDei cultores ejus fi- lii, ita falsorum quoque cultores ipsorum filii vo- „ cantur. Sensus est : Ideo perfide agere Judæos, „ & abominationem committere, quia alienas u- „ xores ducendo dignitatem & sanctitatem suam „ prostituant.

## 2:12
Ver. 12. THE LORD WILL CUT OFF THE MAN, THAT DOETH THIS.) Namely from the tabernacles of Jacob: that is, He will make him an exile. Ezra 10:8.

THE MASTER.) That is, the priests, who were leading others by such a bad example. Nehem. 13:28. In the Hebrew: the watcher: for it is the duty of masters to watch for their disciples.

AND THE SCHOLAR.) The common people. In the Hebrew: the one who answers: for the disciples used to answer the questions of the masters. Luke 3:27.

AND HIM THAT OFFERETH AN OFFERING UNTO THE LORD OF HOSTS.) That is, although he offers great gifts, this will profit him nothing.

Cocceius has again devised a new sense: drawing all these things to the times of the N.T.: that God, for the punishment of the faithless enemies of Christ, would abolish the whole polity (the faithful having been separated first and freed from the servitude of princes) and all the princes and leaders of the people together with the temple and the priesthood. But we have already said that Malachi was a reformer of the morals of his own time, and he dealt with that especially in these two chapters.

Latin:

Vers. 12. DISPERDET DOMINUS VIRUM, QVI FECERIT HOC.) Nempe de tabernaculis Jacob : id est, extorrem faciet. Esd. 10, 8.

MAGISTRUM.) Id est, sacerdotes, qui tam malo exemplo præibant aliis. Nehem. 13, 28. In Hebræo: vigilan- tem: nam Magistrorum est vigilare pro discipulis.

ET DISCIPULUM) Plebem. In Hebræo: Respon- dentem: nam ad interrogata magistrorum respondebant discipuli. Luc. 3, 27.

ET OFFERENTEM MUNUS DOMINO EX- ERCITUUM.) Id est, quamvis munera magna offerat, nihil hoc ei proderit.

Sensum iterum novum commentus est Cocce- jus: omnia ista trahens ad N. T. tempora: Deum in pœnam infidelium Christi hostium, totam politiam (separatis tamen prius fidelibus & liberatis à servi- tute principum) omnesque Principes & præstites populi cum templo & sacerdotio aboliturum. At jam diximus Malachiam Reformatorem fuisse morum sui temporis, idque in his imprimis duobus capi- tibus egit.

## 2:13
V. 13. AND THIS HAVE YE DONE AGAIN, COVERING THE ALTAR OF THE LORD WITH TEARS, WITH WEEPING, AND WITH CRYING OUT.) You do even more: for you fill the altar of the Lord with tears, and weeping and clamor: namely of the Jewish women, whom, for the sake of those foreign women, you treat as slaves, pressing them with hard labors, defrauding them of just food, clothing, and marital rights; who, being so badly treated, throw themselves upon the altar with weeping and wailing. See about this custom 1 Sam. 1:10.

Others explain this sin thus: that the Jews, besides their Israelite wives, had brought in foreign women against the express law of God, and had loved these more than them. Whence, when they brought both them and these into the temple for sacrifices, they offered the better parts of the sacrifices, which were consumed in feasts, to the foreign women, by which contempt the spirits of the Israelite women were gravely wounded, who groaned in the sight of the Lord, and complained of the injury of their husbands: for which reason they also sinned gravely against the law of God, Deut. 12, where the Lord had ordained that in those sacred feasts they themselves, their sons, daughters, menservants, maidservants, etc., should rejoice before Him. Hence it follows, what the Lord says: I will no longer look to the sacrifice: Jerome: “The abandoned Israelite wives, and beholding in the beds of their husbands the women of foreign nations, were fleeing to the help of God alone: day and night prostrate before the altar of the Lord, they were causing envy of His providence with tears, groaning, and wailing: because He was not looking at human affairs, and was not helping the miserable. Whence God says: that He cannot accept the sacrifice and victim from the hands of the priests who committed these things, hindered by the weeping and lamentations of the wives.

V. same verse. THAT I MAY NO LONGER LOOK TO THE SACRIFICE, NOR RECEIVE ANYTHING PLEASING FROM YOUR HAND.) In the Hebrew: That I may no longer look to minchah (these libations of flour, Levit. 11.) nor have I accepted the will (that is, the voluntary sacrifice, of which Lev. 7, 16.) from your hands: as if God were saying: these tears, these groanings so disturb me, that I cannot receive your gifts and victims with a joyful mind.

Latin:

V. 13. ET HOC RURSUM FECISTIS, OPERIE- BATIS LACRTMIS ALTARE DOMINI, FLETU ET MUGITU.) Amplius etiam facitis : nam altare Domini op- pletis lacrymis, fletuque & clamore : nempe fœminarum Ju- dæarum, quas, in gratiam illarum extranearum, tractatis quasi mancipia, duris operibus eas prementes, fraudantes justo victu, vestitu,concubitu; quæ tam male tractatæ cum ploratu ac planctu advolvuntur altari. Vide de hoc more 1. Sam. 1, 10.

Alii hoc peccatum ita declarant: Judæos præ- ter mulieresIsraeliticas superinduxisse contra legem Dei expressam alienigenas, & has præ illis dilexisse. Unde cum & illas & has in templum ad sacrificia adducerent, meliores sacrificiorum partes, quæ e- pulis insumebantur, præbebant alienigenis, quo contemptu graviter sauciabantur animi Israelitica- rum,quæ in conspectuDomini ingemiscebant, & de injuria maritorum conquerebantur: Qua ratione etiam graviter delinquebant contra legem Dei, Deuter.12. ubi Dominus sanciwerat,ut in illis sacris epulis gauderent coram ipso ipsi, filii, filiæ, famuli, famulæ &c. Hinc sequitur, quod Dominus ait: Non ultra respiciam ad sacrificium: Hieronymus : “ Derelictæ uxores Israeliticæ, & in thoris marito- “ rum alienarum gentium fœminas contemplan- “ tes,ad Dei solius auxilium confugiebant: diebus “ ac noctibus ante altare Domini provolutæ lacry- “ mis,gemitu, atque ejulatibus invidiam faciebant “ ejus providentiæ : quod non respiceret humana, “ & miseras non juvaret. Unde dicit Deus: sacrifi- “ cium & hostiam de manibus sacerdotum,qui ista “ commiserunt, se accipere non posse, uxorum “ fletu & planctibus impeditum.

V.eod. UT NON RESPICIAM ULTRA AD SACRI- FICIUM, NEC ACCIPIAM PLACABILE QUID DE MANU VESTRA.) In Hebræo: Vt jam ultra non respiciam minchah (liba ista è simila, Levit. 11.) neque acceptam ha- beam voluntatem (id est, voluntarium sacrificium, de quo Lev.7, 16.) de manibus vestris: quasi dicat Deus: istæ lacry- mæ, isti gemitus ita me turbant, ut læto animo vestra dona victimasque accipere nequeam.

## 2:14
Vers. 14. AND YOU HAVE SAID: FOR WHAT CAUSE?) If you shall say, for what cause can you not hold our gifts as pleasing?

BECAUSE THE LORD HAS TESTIFIED BETWEEN THEE AND THE WIFE OF THY YOUTH) You see what you do εἰς κουρίδιην ἄλοχον: you dismiss the girls: the flower of their age having been plucked, you trample them underfoot.

AND THIS YOUR PARTNER.) A partner in sacred things. AND THE WIFE OF YOUR COVENANT.) She is in the same covenant of God in which you are.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ET DIXISTIS: QUAM OB CAUSAM?) Si dixeritis, quam ob causam non potes grata habere dona nostra ?

QVIA DOMINUS TESTIFICATUS EST IN- TER TE ET UXOREM PUBERTATIS TUÆ) Vides quæ agatis εἰς κουρίδιην ἄλοχον: amœtis puellas: flore ætatis decerpto, eas proculcatis.

ET HÆC PARTICEPS TUA.) Particeps sa- crorum. ET UXOR FOEDERIS TUI.) In eodem Dei fœdere est, in quo tu.

## 2:15
Verse 15.

DID NOT ONE MAKE IT AND THE RESIDUE OF HIS SPIRIT IS IT.) Did that one (Abraham) act in such a way, of whose spirit we are the residue? The ל here is a sign of the genitive: we draw spirit from his spirit, according to the opinion, of course, of those who think that the soul is derived with the seed: which also pleased not a few of the ancient Christians. Abraham is called the one also in Isaiah 51:2, the beginning, of course, of the race. AND WHAT DOES THE ONE SEEK EXCEPT THE SEED OF GOD.) And what that one (did?) was seeking the seed of God. He was doing this solely, that he might have children who would worship God; but you prefer those mothers who lead their sons to idols: how far are you from Abraham? the seed of God, just as they are now called children of the gods.

The Osiandrian explanation holds this more correctly: "The Lord, who is present at betrothals and weddings, is a witness that He destined and joined to you your Israelite spouse (whom you, a youth, married as a youth) as a wife: and you have destroyed the faith to your spouse, and thus you both entered into the covenants of marriage. But you treat badly the companion of your life, whom the Lord gave to you, being weary of her, namely: because you have brought in another, a Gentile, whose form and manners please you more than those of your first and legitimate wife. The Lord detests this inconstancy and inhumanity of yours." "(But the Lord speaks of the Lord: The eternal Son of the eternal Father) This sense is also approved by Willius: that marriage was contracted with God as witness and intermediary, so that the sense is: God cares about that injury, because the matrimonial pact was initiated under his name, and confirmed by his authority, because he himself was invoked as a witness when they entered into mutual pacts. This explanation is consistent with the rites of the ancients, by which they invoked God as a witness in contracting marriage, and met under his auspices, and promised to each other a sacrosanct faith according to the law. You have certain traces of these ceremonies in Genesis 31:49, where Laban says to his son-in-law Jacob: "Let the Lord watch between me and you, when we shall be hidden one from the other, if you shall afflict my daughters, and if you shall take wives besides my daughters, no man is between us; let God see between me and you." "Thus in Tobit 7:13 the rite of copulation is described: Raguel taking her hand delivered her to Tobias as a wife, saying: Behold, according to the law of Moses take her, and lead her to your father, and he blessed them. But the law of Moses is found in Genesis 2:24: A man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be one flesh, which words our Savior repeats in Matthew 19:5, Mark 10:7. And such a rite still obtains today among Christians: Furthermore, God testifies between spouses first, while he himself as the author and patron of marriage is present at such a covenant, and leads the bride to the husband, and directs and inspects their affairs. Secondly, while he is invoked by them and over them as witness and protector. Finally, while the newlyweds bind themselves by his laws, and swear faith to each other in them."

This paraphrase does not fit the institution concerning polygamy. The Jews were seeking, as Winckelman rightly notes here, cloaks and excuses for their deed, and thus they were trying to defend themselves by the example of Abraham, who besides Sarah took the Egyptian handmaid Hagar, Genesis 16. But the Lord shows that there is a great dissimilarity of the deeds. That one, namely Abraham, did not do as you do, and the residue of the spirit was to him, that is, he was endowed with a signal gift of the Holy Spirit. What then did he seek by bringing in the handmaid Hagar? The seed of God. For because he had received the promise concerning the multiplication of his seed, he was seeking that most of all, when he was still the only one. And especially that blessed seed promised by God, namely Christ. The promise had been given to him then by God concerning the blessed seed, but not yet so declared, that he was to receive it from the body of Sarah: and therefore by the counsel and consent of Sarah, indeed Sarah herself desired to be built up from the handmaid. But actions are distinguished by their ends. Furthermore, there are many dissimilarities in the deed of Abraham and those Jews. For first, Abraham did not bring in Hagar by carnal desire, as the Jews did, but by the desire for seed. 2. He married her, not against the will of Sarah, but with her consent, indeed her counsel and command. 3. He married before the law concerning not marrying foreigners was enacted. 4. He did not marry an unbeliever, but a believer, educated in his house in the true knowledge of God. 5. He did not hold Sarah in hatred because of Hagar, but loved her most ardently as his mistress, and humbled the handmaid who was proud against her mistress, and finally even cast her out with her son, Genesis 21. He calls Abraham the one, as the Chaldean has it here, because all Israelites were propagated from him, as from a single stock. Cf. Isaiah 51:2.

Cocceius suggests another commentary: Did not one make it, understand one pair, one marriage of one with one, two one flesh, namely Adam and Eve. Did God do this out of impotence? Did his spirit fail him for working? For by his spirit he formed all the host of heaven and earth. Why did he not give Adam a thousand wives? What is that one? The one flesh of two? It indicates the end of marriage. He was seeking the seed of God, i.e., it did not befit God to propagate the human race from polygamy, which was instituted by him, because polygamy fights with conjugal love, and thus with the righteousness of spouses. Adultery is inherent in it. Therefore, the seed of God, i.e., endowed with the image of God, could not be propagated from polygamy any more than from adultery, and as from fallen man only impure things are born. But the former explanation is simpler and more common. Cocceius's opinion is twin to the explanation of Calvin, Junius, Danaeus, Drusius, Tarnovius, and Cornelius à Lapide. The Hebrews commonly hand down our view, as do many of our own, and also from the Reformed, Oecolampadius, Gualterus, and Willius, who brought forward these reasons for it: (1.) that it does not appear why the Prophet would have wished to speak so obscurely about the union of one spouse with a man. (2.) that the word unus is more aptly joined with some substantive than if it is taken so absolutely. (3) that in that construction the nominative and the subject of the predication are missing. (4) That nowhere does Scripture call children born from a legitimate marriage the seed of God, but the name of seed is used of the Messiah who was to arise from a woman and Abraham, Gen. III. 15, ch. XXII. 18. These things he opposes to his own.

Verse of the same. CUSTODITE ERGO SPIRITUM VESTRUM.) Restrain your anger: for spirit is θυμὸς, Job 15:13, Prov. 18:14, 29:11, Ezech. 39:29, Zach. 6:8, ὀργὴ Prov. 16:32, Esai. 59:19.

Willius renders it thus: Be therefore cautious in your spirit, and do not act treacherously against the wife of your youth. The meaning is: Take heed therefore to yourselves, lest you abuse the example of the best father, and guard your affections most diligently, lest you offend against your wives. Moreover, that which he says, 'Take heed to your spirit,' has emphasis: For thus he opposes the spirit of the Jews to the spirit of Abraham, and by this he seems to say as it were: Since Abraham himself, instructed with such an abundance of spirit, fell here, take heed to your own less-endowed spirit all the more diligently, and the less spiritual you are, the more you should guard your spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

NONNE UNUS FECIT ET RESIDUUM SPI- RITUS EJUS EST.) An unus ille (Abrahamus) ita egit, cujus de spiritu residuum nos sumus? ל hic nota est ge- nitivi: nos de spiritu illius spiritum trahimus, secundum sententiam scilicet eorum, qui cum semine animam deri- vari putant: quæ & veterum Christianorum non paucis placuit. Unus dicitur Abraham etiam Esaiz LI, 2. princi- pium scilicet generis. ET QUID UNUS QVÆRIT NISI SEMEN DEI.) Et quod ille unus (fecit?) erat quærens semen Dei. Hoc unice agebat, ut liberos haberet qui Deum colerent; vos autem eas præsertis matres, quæ filios ad idola de- ducant: quantum abestis ab Abrahamo? semen Dei, ut modo filiæ Deorum.

Rectius hic habet explicatio Osiandrina: Do- „ minus, qui sponsalibus & nuptiis adest, testis est „ quod tibi conjugem tuam Israeliticam (quam „ juvenis juvenem duxisti) in uxorem destinaverit „ atque adjunxerit: & tu conjugi tuæ fidem de- „ struxisti, atque ita in fœdera matrimonii ambo „ venistis. Tu vero vitæ sociam, quam tibi Do- „ minus dedit, male tractas, ejus videlicet pertæ- „ sus: quia superinduxisti aliam, Ethnicam, cujus „ forma & mores magis tibi, quam primæ & legi- „ timæ uxoris, placent. Hanc tuam inconstan- „ tiam & inhumanitatem Dominus detestatur. „ (Dominus autem de Domino loquitur: Filius „ æternus de Patre æterno) Probatur etiam hic sensus Willio: quod Deo teste & interveniente conjugium sit contractum, ut sit sensus: Deum cu- rare istam injuriam, quia pactum connubiale sit ejus sub nomine initum, & ejus auctoritate confirma- tum, quia ipse fuerit testis invocatus, cum mutua pacta inirent. Hæc explicatio veterum ritibus con- sentanea est, quibus Deum testem in conjugio contrahendo invocabant, & ejus auspiciis conve- niebant, ac sacrosanctam fidem sibi invicem con- juges ex lege pollicebantur. Vestigia quædam harum ceremoniarum habes Genes. XXXI. 39. „ ubi Laban ad Jacobum generum: Speculetur „ Dominus inter me & te, quando absconditi „ erimus alter ab altero, si afflixeris filias meas, „ & si assumseris mulieres præter filias meas, nemo „ homo inter nos; videat Deus inter me & te. „ Ita Tob. 7, 13. ritus copulationis describitur: Re- „ guel prehendens manum tradidit illam Tobiæ „ uxorem, dicens: Ecce secundum legem Mosis „ accipe illam, & abduc ad patrem tuum, & bene- „ dixit eis. Lex autem Mosis habetur Genes. II. „ 24. Relicturus est vir patrem suum & matrem „ suam, & adhærebit uxori suæ, eruntque in carnem „ unam, quæ verba repetit servator noster Matth. XIX. 5. Marc. X. 7. Et ejusmodi ritus adhuc hodie inter Christianos obtinet: Cæterum testificatur Deus inter conjuges primo, dum ipse ceu conjugii autor & fautor præsens ejusmodi fœderi est, ac nu- ptam viro adducit, eorumque res dirigit & inspicit. Deinde, dum ab ipsis & super ipsis testis & prote- ctor invocatur. Denique dum novi nuptie jus le- gibus se constringunt, ac in eas fidem sibi invicem jurant.

Non quadrat hæc paraphrasis instituto de Poly- gamia. Quærebant Judæi, ut hic recte Winckelm. facti sui palliamenta & excusationes, atque ita ex- emplo Abrahæ se tueri conabantur, qui præter Sa- ram duxit ancillam Ægyptiacam Hagarem, Ge- nes. XVI. Verum Dominus ostendit, magnum fa- ctorum esse dissimilitudinem. Unicus ille, scilicet Abraham, non ita fecit, ut vos facitis, & reliquus ei erat spiritus, id est, insigni Spiritus Sancti dono præditus erat. Quid ergo ille quæsivit superindu- cendo Agarem ancillam? Semen Dei. Quia enim acceperat promissionem de seminis sui multiplica- tione, maxime illam, cum unicus adhuc esset, quæ- rabat. Atque imprimis semen illud benedictum à Deo promissum, nimirum Christum. Data illi e- rat tum promissio à Deo de semine benedicto, sed nondum ita declarata, quod ex Saræ corpore illud suscepturus esset: atque ideo de consilio & consen- su Saræ, imo Sara ipsa ex ancilla ædificari cupiebat. Actiones autem distinguuntur finibus. Cæterum multæ sunt dissimilitudines in facto Abrahæ & Ju- dæorum illorum. Primum enim Abraham non vo- luntate carnali, ut Judæi, sed desiderio seminis su- perinducebat Agarem. 2. Ducebat eam, non con- tra voluntatem Saræ, sed cum ejus consensu, imo consilio & jussu. 3. Ante legem de non ducendis alie- nigenis latam ducebat. 4. Non ducebat infidelem, sed fidelem, domi suæ in vera Dei agnitione educa- tam. 5. Non propter Agarem odio habebat Saram, sed illam ut Dominam ardentissime amamabat, at- que ancillam superbientem adversus dominam hu- miliabat, tandem etiam cum filio suo ejiciebat Gen. XXI. Unicum dicit Abrahamum, ut hic Chaldæus habet, quia ab ipso omnes Israelitæ, tanquam ab unica stirpe propagati sunt. Conf. Es. LI. 2.

Alium Commentarium suggerit Coccejus, Nonne unum fecit, subintellige unum par, unum unius cum una conjugium, duos carnem unam, ni- mirum Adamum & Evam. Numquid hoc Deus per impotentiam fecit? spiritusne ipsi defecit ad operan- dum? Nam spiritu suo formavit omnem exercitum cœli & terræ. Quare non dedit Adamo mille con- juges? Quid unum illud? una caro duorum? Indi- cat finem conjugii. Quærebat semen Dei, h. e. Deum non decuit genus humanum propagare ex polyga- mia, quæ ab ipso esset instituta, quia polygamia pugnat cum amore conjugali, & sic rectitudine conjugum. Inest in ea machatio. Igitur ex polyga- mia æque non potuit propagari semen Dei, h. e. I- magine Dei præditum, atque ex adulterio & ut ab homine lapso non nisi impuri gignuntur. Sed prior explicatio simplicior & communior est. Cocceji sententia gemina est Calvini, Junii, Danæi, Drusii, Tarnovii, Cornelii à Lapide explicationi. Nostram vero Ebræi communiter tradunt, ut & è nostris plerique, nec non è Reformatis Oecolampadius, Gualterus, Willius, qui has adduxit ejus rationes, (1.) quod non appareat, cur ita obscure de conjugis unius copulatione cum viro loqui voluerit Pro- pheta. (2.) quod τὸ unus aptius cum substantivo aliquo jungatur, quam si ita absolute sumatur. (3) quod desit in illa constructione nominativus & sub- jectum prædicationis. (4) Quod nullibi scriptura liberos ex legitimo conjugio natos semen Dei vo- cet, sed nomen seminis de Messia ex muliere & Ab- rahamo orituro, usurpetur Gen. III. 15. c. XXII. 18. Hæc ille suis opponit.

Vers. eod. CUSTODITE ERGO SPIRITUM VE- STRUM.) Iram cohibete: nam spiritus est θυμὸς, Job. 15, 13. Prov. 18, 14. 29, 11. Ezech. 39, 29. Zach. 6, 8. ὀργὴ Prov. 16, 32. Esai. 59, 19.

Willius ita reddit: Estote igitur cauti in spiritu vestro, & in uxorem adolescentiæ tuæ perfide ne agatis. Sententia est: Cavete igitur vobis, ne exemplo patris optimi abutamini & custodite affectus ve- stros diligentissime, ne in uxores vestras delinqua- tis. Emphasin autem habet illud, quod dicit: Cave- te spiritui vestro: Ita enim spiritum Judæorum spi- ritui Abrahami opponit ac hoc quasi dicere vide- tur: Cum ipse Abrahamus tanta abundantia spiritus instructus, hic lapsus sit, cavete vos vestro spiritui minus dotato eo diligentius, & quo minus spiritua- les estis, eo magis spiritum vestrum custodite.

## 2:16
Ver. 16.

WHEN YOU HATE, DISMISS.) If you hate, dismiss rather than harass in such a way. The law permits this, Deut. 24:1; it prohibits cruelty, but Hebrew women could not depart from their husbands except by the permission of the husbands.

BUT INIQUITY SHALL COVER HIS GARMENT.) The Chaldean translates: and do not cover sin with your garment. He reads it, of course, with a question: shall (anyone doing this) cover iniquity with his garment? That is, is anyone still seeking veils for such open injustice? This is what the Latins call a pretext or a subterfuge, the Greeks πρόφασιν.

GUARD YOUR SPIRIT) He repeats, as being very necessary, what he had said in verse 15.

AND DO NOT DESPISE.) A wife joined by religion and covenant, as above.

Indeed, people commonly explain these things as if it were better to dismiss a wife than to treat her so harshly; but because God did not so much permit the dismissal of wives as tolerate it (Deut. 24:1; Matt. 19:8), nay, pollution is said to follow from it (Deut. 24:4), and the causal particle כי must not be neglected, the interpretation of B. Tarnovius is to be preferred: Because (God) hates from the heart that 'sending away' of yours, he covers violence as if with a cloak or his own garment, (he who dismisses); therefore you shall guard your spirit, so that you do not act perfidiously. Willius renders the words a little differently, but presents the same meaning: When he hates, let him dismiss, says the Lord God of Israel, (so that this may be the objection, but the response follows in this manner) but he shall cover violence with his garment. That is, he will indeed cloak the violence, nevertheless, because it is violence and cruelty, he will not accomplish it. And Castrius is not much removed from that sense: Otherwise, says the prophet, if you dismiss only because you hate, the punishment of iniquity shall cover your garment, that is, it shall occupy your whole body, for you will be most severely punished. Theodoreto also indicates this sense; when he says, unless you dissolve the marriage for just causes, and not from hate alone, your thoughts will be revealed by God as judge, and they will appear covered in iniquity, or the punishment of iniquity. He also notes that many Hebrews explain it this way. For to dismiss because of hate (or hatred) is no small iniquity. He himself provides this paraphrase: 'Indeed, you will inflict such a huge and grave injury upon her by dismissing her, that it cannot be covered by a garment, but rather it will overflow upon the garment.'

Latin:

Verf. 16.

CUM ODIO HABUERIS, DIMITTE.) Si oderis, dimitte potius, quam ita vexes. Hoc lex permittit Deut. XXIV. 1. sævitiam prohibet, non poterant autem mulieres Hebrææ à maritis discedere, nisi maritorum permissu.

OPERIET AUTEM INIQVITAS VESTIMENTUM EJUS.) Chaldæus vertit : & ne operias peccatum vestimento tuo. Legit nimirum cum interrogatione: operiatne (aliquis hoc faciens) iniquitatem vestimento suo? id est, adhuc ne tam apertæ injustitiæ velamenta aliquis quærat? hoc est, quod modo prætextum modo obtentum dicunt Latini, Græci πρόφασιν.

CUSTODITE SPIRITUM VESTRUM) Repetit, ut valde necessarium, quod dixerat v. 15.

ET NOLITE DESPICERE.) Uxorem conjunctam religione & fœdere, ut supra.

Explicant quidem hæc vulgo, quasi præstaret uxorem dimittere, quam ita acerbe tractare; sed quia Deus dimissionem uxorum non tam permisit, quam toleravit Deut. XXIV. 1. Matth. XIX. 8. imo pollutio inde sequi dicitur Deut. XXIV. 4. nec negligenda est particula כי causalis, præferenda B. Tarnovii interpretatio: Quia (Deus) odit ex animo illud vestrum שלח dimitte, operit violentiam velut pallio, aut veste sua, (qui dimittit) quare cavebitis spiritui vestro, ut non agatis perfide. Paulo aliter verba reddit, sed sensum eundem exhibet Willius: Quum oderit, dimittat, ait Dominus Deus Israelis, (ut hæc sit objectio, sequatur autem responsio h. m.) sed operiet violentiam veste sua. Id est, palliabit quidem violentiam, nihilo- minus quia violentia sit & crudelitas, non efficiet. Nec multum à sensu illo alienus est Castrius: Alioqui, ait propheta, si tantum quia odisti dimiseris, pœna iniquitatis operiet vestimentum tuum, id est, totum corpus tuum occupabit, nam gravissime punieris. Hunc quoque sensum indicat Theodoreto; cum ait, nisi justis de causis, & non ex odio solo dissolveritis matrimonium, Deo judice revelabuntur vestræ cogitationes, & operta eparebunt iniquitate, vel pœna iniquitatis. Qui notat etiam Ebræos multos ita exponere. Nam ad odisse (vel odium) dimittere, iniquitas non minima est. Ipse tradit „hanc paraphrasin : sane tam ingentem ac gravem ,,illi inferes injuriam dimittendo, ut obtegi non ,,possit vestimento, quin potius super vestimentum redundabit.

## 2:17
Ver. 17.

YOU HAVE MADE THE LORD LABOR IN YOUR WORDS.) The past tense for the future, in the Hebrew manner: you will cause trouble for God with your words: I foresee that it will happen in this way.

AND YOU HAVE SAID.) And if you say.

IN WHAT HAVE WE MADE HIM LABOR?) Why are we troublesome to him? Thus the Chaldean.

IN THAT YOU SAY: EVERYONE WHO DOES EVIL IS GOOD IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD, AND SUCH PLEASE HIM: OR CERTAINLY WHERE IS THE GOD OF JUDGMENT?) You will say, that is, you will think that God favors the wicked, when he permits wicked men to be promoted to leadership and priesthoods; as if they were saying, in what does God show himself at this time to be the judge and arbiter of men? Impious men were going to say this because for nearly five hundred years miracles and prophecies were to cease, as we said regarding Zechariah 13:2. That matter gave occasion not only to Sadduceeism, but also to the impiety which appeared most of all in the times of Antiochus, but it is not for us to know the times and occasions for doing such things, which God keeps in the treasuries of his wisdom. They had Moses, famous for so many miracles; they had the ancient Prophets; they should believe them until God should shine a new light.

Some, with Lyranus and Pagninus, begin the third chapter from this pericope, verse 17, because here begins a new expostulation against the atheism of the Jews, who deny God's providence and esteem every kind of life, whether perverse or good, as equal: but in the Hebrew text these things still pertain to the second chapter: and the third begins with the illustrious prophecy concerning Christ: Wherefore, a new ἐπανόρθωσις (correction) and accusation of the Jews is more rightly established here, whom he reproves on account of that extreme profanity into which they had gradually slipped from the habituation of the aforementioned vices, so that they even tore apart God's justice and truth with impious taunts. You have wearied the Lord with your words. For the impious and profane, and especially the blasphemous, weary, afflict, and exacerbate the Lord with such wickedness of theirs, which, however, though spoken ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (in human terms), must be understood θεοπρεπῶς (in a manner worthy of God). But there is no need for a refutation of that atheism: it was enough for the prophet that he should convict the Jews of that extreme profanity. And you have said: In what have we wearied him? In that you say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such please him: or certainly, where is the God of judgment? To have cited such atheisms is to have solidly refuted them. And therefore it did not pertain to dwell upon them; rather, God wished to set before them Him to whom all judgment was given, who was about to judge, cleanse, and purge them, and indeed was about to utterly abolish the Levitical priesthood. Therefore, these words are not to be taken προφητικῶς (prophetically) with Grotius; and rendered in the future: YOU WILL WEARY. For the Prophet was reproving the customs of his own time: even though it be true in the meantime that such atheisms are of all times, Psalm XIV. 1, 2 Peter III. 3, 4. Jerome reports the occasion, by which even the pious (of whom Psalm XXXVII and LXXIII speak) were affected with scandal, at the return from Babylon. Although by this speech the impious and extremely profane are rather noted. The people, he says, having returned from Babylon, and seeing all the nations in the circuit; and the Babylonians themselves serving idols, abounding in riches, flourishing in body: possessing all things which are thought to be good in the world: while they themselves, who have the knowledge of God, are covered in squalor, famine, and servitude: are scandalized and say: There is no providence in human affairs; all things are carried by uncertain chance: nor are they governed by the judgment of God: or rather, if God judges all things, where is his fair and just judgment?

Latin:

Vers. 17.

LABORARE FECISTIS DOMINUM IN SERMONIBUS VESTRIS.) Præteritum pro futuro, more Hebræo: molestiam exhibebitis Deo verbis vestris: prævideo, futurum ut id fiat ita.

ET DIXISTIS.) Et si dicatis.

IN QUO FECIMUS LABORARE.) Quare molesti ei sumus? Ita Chaldæus.

IN EO QUOD DICITIS: OMNIS QVI FACIT MALUM BONUS EST IN CONSPECTU DOMINI, ET TALES EI PLACENT: AUT CERTE UBI EST DEUS JUDICII?) Dicetis, id est, cogitabitis Deum malis favere, cum homines sceleratos permittit ad principatum ac sacerdotia provehi; quasi dicerent, in quo Deus oftendit se hoc tempore hominum esse judicem, & arbitrum? hoc ideo dicturi erant homines impii, quia per annos prope quingentos cessatura erant miracula & prophetiæ, ut diximus ad Zachariam 13, 2. Ea res non Sadducæismo tantum occasionem dedit, sed & impietati, quæ Antiochi temporibus maxime apparuit, sed non est nostrum nosse tempora & occasiones talia faciendi, quæ Deus in thesauris sapientiæ suæ custodit. Habebant Mosen tot miraculis clarum, habebant Prophetas veteres; iis crederent, donec novam lucem Deus alluceret.

Inchoant ab hac pericopa v. 17. nonnulli cum Lyrano & Pagnino caput tertium, quod hic incipiat nova expostulatio contra atheïsmum Judæorum, Dei providentiam negantium, ac quodcunque vitæ genus sive perversum sive bonum perinde æstimantium: sed in Ebræo textu pertinent ista adhuc ad secundum caput: ac tertium inchoatur ab illustri vaticinio de Christo: Quapropter rectius constituitur hic nova ἐπανόρθωσις & accusatio Judæorum, quos redarguit ob extremam istam prophanitatem in quam paulatim ex superiorum vitiorum allvefactione erant delapsi, ut etiam Dei justitiam & veritatem impiis dicteriis proscinderent. Laborare fecistis Dominum in sermonibus vestris. Nam impii & prophani, ac maxime blasphemi ejusmodi sua improbitate fatigant, affligunt, & exacerbent Dominum, quod tamen ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dictum θεοπρεπῶς intelligendum. Non opus autem illius atheïsmi confutatione: satis erat prophetæ, quod Judæos de ista extrema prophanitate convinceret. Et dixistis: in quo eum fecimus laborare? In eo, quod dicitis: Omnis qui facit malum, bonus est in conspectu Domini, & tales ei placent : aut certe, ubi est Deus judicii? Tales atheïsmos citasse est solide confutasse. Ideoque non attinebat illis immorari, sistere potius volebat ipsis Deus eum, cui omne judicium datum, qui eos judicaturus, emundaturus, & purgaturus, imo sacerdotium Leviticum prorfus sublaturus erat. Non ergo cum Grotio hæc verba προφητικῶς accipienda; & in futuro reddenda: LABORA RE FACIETIS. Nam redarguebat Propheta sui temporis mores: etsi verum interim sit, atheïsmos ejusmodi esse omnium temporum, Psalm. XIV. 1. 2. Petr. III. 3. 4. occasionem, de qua etiam pii (de quibus Psalm. XXXVII. & LXXIII.) scandalo affecti sint, sub reditum è Babylonia refert Hieronymus. Quanquam hac oratione impii, & extreme prophani potius notentur. Reversus, inquit, populus de Babylone, & videns cunctas in circuitu nationes; ipsosque Babylonios idolis servientes abundare divitiis, vigere corporibus: omnia quæ bona putantur, in seculo possidere: se vero, qui habeat notitiam Dei, squalore, inedia, servitute coopertum: scandalizatur & dicit: Non est in rebus humanis providentia; omnia casu feruntur incerto: nec Dei judicio gubernantur: quin potius mala ei placent, & bona displicent: aut certe si Deus cuncta dijudicat, ubi est illius æquum justumque judicium?

## 3:1 Argument
PART II. PROPHETIC & EVANGELICAL. CHAPTER III. The advent of the precursor Angel, and of the Lord as the Angel of the covenant.

The advent of Christ's forerunner, John, is predicted, and of the Lord who is soon to follow him, who is to come to his temple, like fire and fuller's soap to purge the people and the Levites, so that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the Lord, with a threat against sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, unjust oppressors, those devoid of the fear of GOD, and exhortation to repentance, that they may no longer mock God with the fraudulent offering of tithes and sacrifices, and a promise of divine blessing; and a rebuke of the Epicurean gibe concerning the uselessness of divine worship, but a commendation of the pious, who console themselves with the divine remembrance, who in the day of the Lord will be his peculiar treasure when the wicked are rejected.

Let the earth repent at the approaching advent of the Lord.

Ver. 1.

BEHOLD I SEND MY MESSENGER AND HE SHALL PREPARE THE WAY BEFORE MY FACE) This is what he says: I will test you again and again: nor will I give you any Prophet before him who will be the forerunner of the Messiah. He says before my face, because God lives in the Messiah, much more fully and perfectly than in any of the Prophets: Διὰ τὴν ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν, ἀχώριστον, ἀδιάλειπτον (On account of the hypostatic, inseparable, uninterrupted union).

AND IMMEDIATELY.) When he shall have come.

HE SHALL COME TO HIS TEMPLE.) Into this second Temple, which the Jews call the second Temple, בית שני, until it was destroyed by the arms of Vespasian. That the Messiah ought to have come into that Temple before the Lord Jesus was born, all the Jews held with firm faith, and Haggai 2:8 had already said the same thing most openly.

THE RULER WHOM YOU SEEK.) That promised Shiloh, who is to bring you the greatest goods, even in the public state, if you obey him, and will make even foreign nations (of whom it was spoken above 1:11) participants of your goods: the ruler from the stock of David, the mystical king of the people of God, who will show in reality that he is the king of kings and lord of lords.

AND THE MESSENGER OF THE COVENANT WHOM YOU DESIRE.) That great legate, who will not be sent for any trivial matter, but to strike a new covenant, better than the old, with the Jews and the Gentiles. Kimchi agreed that these things are to be understood of the Messiah.

Grotius therefore hands down this coherence of this prophecy—which is almost the only one remaining to us in the Prophets that treats of Christ according to the letter, with almost all others twisted to another person—that, as the Prophets were failing for some centuries, GOD promised that in his own time he would send a singular Prophet, the Baptist, and that the Messiah would immediately follow him. But since the Prophet mentions nothing about the failure of the Prophets, others more correctly assign other reasons for the connection. One is that remote and general one, that in the preceding he had refuted the vices of the priests of his own time, whence he wished to present Christ the High Priest as their corrector; so Rupert. And for almost the same reason also Cyril: These prophetic words passed very aptly to the mystery of Christ. For he has been made for us by God and the Father Emmanuel, righteousness and sanctification and redemption and the cleansing of all uncleanness, and the putting away of sins, and the casting off of dishonorable things, and a way to better and more decent things, and as a door and entrance to eternal life, and through him all things have been corrected, and the dominion of the devil overturned, and righteousness found. Another more special and immediate reason is that he answers the atheists, who were soliciting the judgment and truth of God, by the very fact as it were: They were saying, where is the God of judgment? Christ answers; for these are his words: Behold I am present: for I will send my messenger shortly, and he shall prepare the way before my face. Theodoret hints at this coherence: You said, in what have we provoked him? when you ought not to have been ignorant that God is the fountain of justice: whence it is that he detests those who embrace vices; although the reason of the divine dispensation is inexplicable, yet I teach you that the time of just retribution is coming: wishing to make this plain, he first predicts the advent of the Lord Christ, and shows the great John the Baptist as the forerunner of this advent.

I have said that these words are of Christ himself: Which can be established first from the preceding: for that speech and expostulation of the Lord in the second chapter cannot be understood of any other than that Lord, who also has a common father and Lord with us v. 10. Have we not all one father? Has not one God created us, and he declares that he does not wish to look upon the sacrifice any longer v. 13. Who is none other than Christ John XX. 17. whence Osiander acknowledges at v. 14. that the Lord speaks of the Lord, the eternal Son of the eternal Father. Then indeed the words themselves, which we are now treating, clearly indicate this: Behold I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face. For that person speaks here, for whom John the Baptist prepared the way, and of whom he was the forerunner and precursor: That person: before whose face he went, preparing the way for the same. But who is that, if not the Messiah? For John the Baptist was not the precursor, nor did he prepare the way before the Father and the Holy Spirit, but before the Son. For the Son alone came to you in the flesh. It is therefore certain that these are his words: And we have as a witness of this interpretation, one who is unexceptionable and most rich, St. Zechariah, saying to his son John Luke I. 76. You child shall be called the prophet of the highest, for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his way, namely of Christ, who through the bowels of the mercy of our God has visited us, the sunrise from on high; Nor does it hinder that soon there is speech about the Messiah in the third person: And the Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple, because in these words the Messiah now introduces his own father promising these things, as the words subjoined testify: Behold he comes, SAYS THE LORD OF HOSTS, my heavenly Father. He therefore testifies first that he will send his own precursor. But soon, for the sake of further certainty, he introduced God the Father promising the advent of the Messiah himself, as the Lord of the temple, and the desired angel of the covenant: Which I see St. Jerome also prudently distinguished: This therefore, which is said, Behold I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face: is said from the person of Christ: that he sent John into the desert of Judea, to preach the Baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. But what follows, And the Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant, whom you desire: he speaks of himself as if of another according to the custom of the scriptures: And there is no doubt for anyone, but that this Lord is the Savior: who is the creator of all: and is called the angel of the covenant, and the angel of the great counsel. And this is also the reason that Christ wished to attribute the former words to the Father himself as well Matthew 11. 10. inasmuch as in Malachi he not only spoke of sending a precursor of his advent, but also brought in God the Father in confirmation of his own next following advent, and introduced him promising it in his own words. Add that this mission of St. John pertains to the works ad extra, which are undivided for the Most Holy Trinity: Therefore just as the Son says here: Behold I send my messenger before my face: so he rightly makes the Father say the same

Matth. XI. 10. Behold I send my messenger before thy face, O Son, who shall prepare thy way before thee. Which is likewise observed in Mark c. I. 2. and in Luke c. VII. 29.

The argument by which the Jews are convinced from this passage, having compared the sayings of Is. XL. 1. Mal. IV. 5. 6., is thus set forth by Cocceius: He whom the Angel of GOD pointed out is in truth the King of Israel, that Lord and Angel of the Covenant. But the Angel of GOD pointed out Jesus of Nazareth. The matter returns to this, that it may be proved that John the Baptist is that Angel of GOD. It is proved thus: He who comes immediately after the last of the Prophets, Malachi, as the Doctor of repentance, recalling Israel to the faith of the fathers, and announcing the advent of Christ and his kingdom: He is in truth that Angel of GOD. But John the Baptist is that person. The reason for the consequence is, 1. because God was not going to permit a false forerunner to come. 2. Because it does not befit the same person to be truthful in the preaching of repentance and to be a deceiver in the announcement of the kingdom of God. 3. Because the announcement of the kingdom of GOD includes the abolition of the kingdom of men: which part is verified, whence it is necessary that the other part connected to this is also verified. 4. Because no one else came immediately after Malachi. But it is impossible, on account of the word of God, that no one has come thus far, just as it is that another has come, or that no one will ever come.

The Jews turn themselves into various forms here. R. Solomon understands the forerunner angel as the angel of death. Rab. Aben Ezra [understands] the Messiah son of Joseph, Abarbanel [understands] Malachi himself, R. Kimchi [understands] a celestial angel, comparing Ex. 23. The same Rab. David Kimchi interprets the Angel of the Covenant as Elijah, and distinguishes him from the Lord, who according to him is the son of David: but the Jews imagine Elijah to be called the angel of the Testament because he was zealous for the covenant of circumcision, therefore they still adorn the chair of Elijah at a circumcision, thinking him to be present and zealous for the law of the Lord. R. Aben Ezra explains both the Lord and the angel of the covenant as being about glory, Abarbanel, refuting the others, confesses that the Messiah is understood by the Lord and the angel of the covenant. Blessed Jerome convinces the Jews in a few words but solidly thus: The Jews understand this which is said: behold I send my messenger, as spoken of the prophet Elijah, and what follows: the Lord shall suddenly come to his temple, and whom you seek, and the angel of the testament whom you desire: they refer to ἠλειμμένον, that is, their Christ: whom they say is to come at the last time: but I marvel how the outcome of events does not teach them the truth. For what temple will the Lord find, which has been destroyed to the foundation? Or if it is to be built by another before Christ arrives: what more is their Christ to do, when all things have been restored by another? Our Lord in the Gospel, interpreting the prophet Elijah as John the Baptist, speaks: If you are willing to know, he is Elijah, who is to come: of whom also this same Prophet, whom we are now discussing, writes at the end: Behold I send you Elijah the Prophet, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. But how John is Elijah: he gave you a way of understanding: commemorating that he came in the power and spirit of Elijah. These are the words of Jerome.

We shall summarily comprehend most of the arguments which can be urged against the Jews from this oracle, and as far as it concerns the assertion of the Deity of Christ, can also be opposed to the Socinians and other enemies of the Deity of Christ. The first is from the time of the advent. Because it is hinted that after Malachi, who was the last of the Prophets, by the testimony of the Jews, no other angel and legate of God sent immediately by God is to be expected, until this angel, the forerunner of the Messiah, comes. And since the Lord testifies: Behold I send my messenger, and again God speaks of the Messiah as if present and about to be here shortly: Behold HE COMES, how did that befit the Messiah, or ἠλειμμένῳ, whom the Jews expect, at the time of Malachi, who was only to come after thousands of years? Behold, as the Tarnovian paraphrase has it, says the Savior in the Prophet, exciting attention, because he was about to say great things, you blasphemously ask: Where is the God of judgment? at the time divinely appointed I will most certainly show myself to be seen by you, I myself, who am about to announce judgment, nay rather about to bring forth judgment unto victory Matth. XII. 18. 20. shortly I am about to send (Benoni for that which is about to be shortly, as we have noted elsewhere) which is not without emphasis in this place, since he was miraculously conceived, born and educated, as is described at length in Luke I., my messenger, the chief herald and legate, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women, John the Baptist Matth. XI. 10. &c. Mark I. 2. Luke II. 17. and VII. 27. John I. 6. 33. who may clear, Hebr. וּפִנָּה, ו for the relative אֲשֶׁר as Psalm v. 12. which nevertheless at the same time turns the past into the future, and the word itself denotes, to remove from sight those things which were to be unpleasant to him who was about to walk the way before me, crying, prepare the way of the Lord, make straight his paths Matth. III. 3. every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made plain, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God Luke III. v. 5. 6. Mark I. 3. John I. 23. from Is. XL. 3. 4. 5.

Next, from the circumstance of the place, the Messiah had to come to his temple, as Abarbanel admits, and indeed to that temple in which those abuses of the despised altar of the Lord and of illegitimate offerings, which Malachi rebukes, had occurred. But that temple was razed to the ground almost sixteen centuries ago. Cyril, Theodoret, and Augustine, in book 18 of The City of God, chapter 35, understand the temple of the body of Christ (John 2:19), but the messenger of the covenant had to come to the temple after the mission of John to prepare the way, which took place when Christ was already thirty years old. Jerome, and likewise Cyril, explain it as referring to the Church, or to the faithful: but such an advent of grace was never lacking to the faithful at any time, and therefore Jerome himself, and most others, explain it more correctly as referring to the material temple, and the ancient Jews also understood it as the second temple, in which he had to show himself as in his own house, after the way had been prepared by the forerunner angel. Which, however, was reduced to ashes and embers so many centuries ago.

Thirdly, from the forerunner of the messenger of the covenant, who, as has been shown before, is John the Baptist. Nor can the Jews point to any other. For the mere recitation of their opinions shows how inept they are.

Fourthly, from the designation of the Messiah. For he is called THAT LORD demonstratively, so that he may be noted

The Lord, who is so celebrated in the Scriptures under the name of the Lord, is nevertheless a distinct person from God the Father, the Lord of hosts, inasmuch as He here speaks of that Lord as a distinct person. But who is He, if not the Messiah? Who is called Lord by antonomasia, whom David himself, having no superior on earth, acknowledged as his Lord, Ps. 110, 1, in whom as in a base (אדן) all things subsist, Col. 1, 17. Therefore R. David Kimchi confesses that the Lord the Son of David is understood here, and Abarbenel acknowledges that Christ is pointed out.

Fifth, from the appropriation of the temple. His arrival is designated, who is the Lord of the temple, and whose temple it is. For it is said that the Lord is about to come to HIS temple. But this cannot be understood of a mere man. To have a temple is a divine dignity. Every temple is the temple of God, says Basil, Epist. CXLI. see Exod. 34, 16. Ps. 26, 1. 1 Kings 13, 6. ch. 9. Hagg. ch. 1, 9. ch. 2, 8. 16. Zech. 3, 7. ch. 8, 9. Therefore the Messiah must be the true God.

Sixth, from the description of the Lord. He is called the Lord whom they were seeking. By which word, according to some, the desires of the pious are denoted, who were expecting and longing solely for the arrival of the Messiah and did not desire any other Lord. Conf. Luke 2, 25. ch. 10, 24. It can also be said that those words, whom you seek, refer to those things which are held at the end of ch. 2, 17: where is the God of judgment. For He is the King, the Son of the King, to whom the judgments of God are to be given, Ps. 72, 1. Add Is. 11, 3. 4. Thus Tarnovius, with Tremellius, takes the word בקש in a bad sense: because the antecedents in the question in v. 17 of ch. 2 and the consequents in this ch. 3, 2 deal with the wicked and the wrath of God toward them; then, because, as regards the matter itself, parallel passages confirm this explanation, since it is often evident from there that a good thing can be sought badly, and be desired curiously and with mockery, see Isa. 5, 19. Amos 5, 18. 2 Pet. 3, 3. Whence they conclude from the particular, who gather it thus: Wherever men seek or desire something divine, a good appetite for a good thing referring itself to the promises of God is understood. So he; but the former explanation is more accepted.

Seventh, from the name of the angel. For He is called the ANGEL simply. But only the Messiah could be sent on this mission: for the Church cannot be subjected to angels, Heb. 2, 5. And here a singular angel is referred to, famous in the scriptures, promised to the people, and often seen by the same: the angel whom the Patriarchs confessed, Gen. 48, 16, who called Moses, Exod. 3, was with Moses on the mountain, and gave the law to him, Acts 7, 34, whose voice shook the earth then, Ps. 58, 8. 9. 29. Heb. 12, 16, who led the Israelites, Exod. 14. ch. 23, 20. The angel of the face of the Lord, who saved them, Ps. 113, 9.

Eighth, from the peculiar naming of the angel. He is called the angel of the covenant, of whom, in whom, and through whom is the covenant. And by this title He is distinguished from Moses, and exalted above him. Indeed, Moses was not the interpreter of the covenant to Noah, Abraham, and the other Patriarchs, but only to the Israelites. But this one is the angel of the covenant simply; understand the covenant which God ever made with His own, in whom He commanded all to believe, to have a covenant with God, and thus of the New covenant, which Jeremiah ch. 31 promises: namely, concerning justification, the inscription on the heart, etc. Because He is the Angel of the covenant here, to Him

Heb. 3, 1. in part corresponds to the apostle of the confession, the legate of the stipulation, that is, who is sent by God so that He may propose to us the Testament of God, concerning the inheritance to be handed over to Him, and the Church to be justified in Him through faith, and through His word and His spirit may stipulate faith from us, so that we may rightly stipulate with Him through faith, and in it with a good conscience may seek again for indulgence and life, as Cocceius here.

Ninth, from the expectation of the angel of the covenant. Because there is talk here of the Gospel of the covenant, which the faithful desired greatly, and in which they had their sole pleasure, inasmuch as He had not only been promised in the covenant, Deut. 18, 15, but He alone could restore it when broken, and sanction a new one, Heb. 7, 22. ch. 8, 6. ch. 9, 15, in which therefore all the pious delighted. For that חפצים is to be taken in a good sense, as the previous מבקשים according to some is to be taken in a bad sense, as is evident from its constant usage, and there is no doubt that the discourse is about the faithful desiring from the heart the arrival of the angel of the covenant, not merely about the wicked mocking the same. The pronoun אתם again is to be taken partitively, as it indeed addresses the wicked first: the Lord WILL COME, about whom you wicked ones ask in your blasphemous question, where He is, and the angel of the covenant, in whom you faithful ones delight in your misery, as the Savior and deliverer who is to come. Cyril has it thus: The Lord will come, he says, whom you seek, saying out of faint-heartedness (where is the God of justice?) But He will come and will teach those things which are above the law and above the shadows and types. For He will be the angel of the testament, which was once announced by the voice of God and the Father. Thus Jerome: above we read of the question raised to the Lord by those who say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such please Him, or at least if He is displeased, where is the God of judgment, that is, where is the truth of justice? To which the word of the Lord responds to dissolve it: I will send my angel, who will prepare my way, and the ruler will come to his temple, whom you seek, who is the judge of truth, of whom it is said in the Psalm: Give your judgment to the king, O God, and your justice to the son of the king: For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, and He is the angel of the testament, whom you seek.

Tenth, from the office of the Messiah, which is as a refiner's fire and like fullers' soap, and eleventh, from the offering of sacrifices in the time of the New Testament, concerning which verse 4. For these likewise clearly demonstrate the Messiah. Twelfth, from the destruction of the city and temple, which follows the coming of the Lord, verse 5. Thirteenth, from the raising up of Elijah. Through whom again the πρωτοβαπτιςής is designated, chapters 4, 5, 6. All of which we shall then examine. Fourteenth, from the comparison of a parallel passage: Isaiah also predicted John the forerunner of the Messiah, chapter 40, 3, concerning whom we saw there. B. Tarnovius here also compares Psalm 132, 12, concerning the lamp prepared for the Lord's anointed (the Messiah). Which some of the ancients also understood concerning John, concerning which [see] at that place. Compare John 1, 7, chapter 7, 35. Fifteenth, from the New Testament explanation, Matthew 11, Mark 1, Luke 7.

To which, finally, let the confession of the Jews themselves be added. Grotius rightly observes: that all Jews before the birth of Christ held with firm faith that the Messiah ought to have come into the second temple: and that R. David Kimchi acknowledged that the present passage is to be understood concerning the Messiah. Which R. Abarbanel also acknowledged. benel, that Elijah is to be resurrected before the last day, and then the angel of the covenant, the Messiah, will come. But that is about Elijah being raised before the last day in a political sense, i.e., about John who came in the spirit of Elijah, Luke 1:17, Matthew 11:14, chapter 17:11, 12, as the forerunner of the Messiah. To this also pertains that of R. Moses Maimonides, in Jud. Chazakah, tractate on Kings, ch. XII. Some wise men say that before the coming of King Messiah, Elijah will come. Likewise: in the days of the Messiah, through the Holy Spirit who will rest upon him, the children of Israel will be genealogized by his mouth, as it is said (Malachi 3) Behold I send, etc. Likewise that of R. Saadia Gaon in the book Haemunoth, tractate 8, on the final Redemption; The precursor of the Messiah, son of David, will be, as it were, his legate, as it were preparing the people and clearing the way according to that: Behold I send my Angel, etc.

John is indeed called the Angel of Christ, not because he was an angel by nature clothed in a human body, as Origen, according to Bede in Mark 1, believed, for he was a true and mere man, John 1:7; not because of an angelic life, by which he seemed to surpass angelic purity, as pleased the Jesuit Costerus, part II, Concion. p. 69, who therefore asserts that St. John the Baptist did not suffer himself to be adored, as one looking up to the Apostolic and Angelic purity in him, shamefully and ignorantly confusing St. John the Apostle with St. John the Baptist. But because of his office, that he was a legate of the Son of God. Cornelius a Lapide here gives various reasons for the appellation, which are, however, for the most part frivolous, fabricated, and inept, such as that angels do not have infancy, and John had only six months of infancy; that the Baptist lived almost without food and drink like an angel; that he was most pure and always a virgin like an angel; that from a boy in the desert he was occupied with contemplation with God and conversed with angels; that he never lost the grace received, never sinned, at least deliberately and gravely, and other things of this kind. Only that one is true and fitting, that he is called an angel from his office. Concerning which we say with Cyril that the most holy Baptist was named an angel, not indeed because of his nature (for he was a man born of a woman, just as we are) but because the duty of preaching and announcing such things to us was imposed upon him. The name is therefore given from his office and does not signify the nature of angels.

Grotius rightly attributes the words BEFORE MY FACE to the Messiah, but that explanation, that God lives in the Messiah much more fully and perfectly than in any of the Prophets, could be accepted in that sense; as if the κατοίκησις of the Son of God in the assumed human nature differed only in degree from that indwelling by which He was present to the Prophets: which is Nestorian. The Orthodox Fathers observe that the same words are attributed to both the Father and the Son; I add the same face, because the Father and the Son are one by the unity of essence, even if they are distinguished by persons, John 10:30. But the reason why Christ cites these words differently in Matt. 11:10 seems to be that He wished to teach that God the Father, whom the Jews professed to be their God, did not pronounce those things about Himself or His own manifestation, but about the incarnation of the Son and His revelation, nay, that He is the same God of whom there is speech in that place, and who is speaking in the same place, as Willius rightly says here.

Furthermore, as to what Grotius interjects: that the Messiah would bring the greatest goods to the Jews even IN THE PUBLIC STATE, if they had obeyed him, whence he has that, and what goods of the Public State he understands, is not sufficiently clear, except that perhaps he himself drew that also from the traditions of the Jews, whom he followed in many things. We know from the divine oracles that the Messiah was promised not for the goods of the public state or temporal things, but for spiritual goods and those of the heavenly kingdom. For His kingdom was not of this world, nor was it to be. He came to His temple, not to the Republic, as the angel of the covenant of grace, not as a legate for the public state; He came as a ruler on Mount Zion or the Church, not as an earthly or political ruler.

BEHOLD HE COMES, SAYS THE LORD OF HOSTS.) He will come without doubt while this temple is standing: Wait for him.

Eusebius, book V, demonstr. Evang. ch. 28, Chrysostom, and Augustine, in the cited book, understand these as referring to the latter advent (even though they explain the preceding ones as referring to the former advent); Jerome, Haymo, and Hugo interpret them as referring to both advents. But Grotius rightly acknowledges that the discourse is still about the same advent of the angel of the covenant, of which the former things speak, and it is not to be doubted that the promise is repeated for the sake of certainty, and at the same time the nearness of the advent is indicated, just as a present participle is accustomed to be taken in that way. Which sense Theodoret also approved, and especially Cyril: For as if showing that He would be clearly present to them, nay, that He is already present, he pronounces in the clearest words that the time of His advent into this world would not be delayed for long. For He is said to be coming, so that He may cleanse the sons of Levi, so that they may offer sacrifices to the Lord in justice, which cannot be understood of the second advent and the last day.

Latin:

PARS II. PROPHETICA & EVANGELICA. CAPUT III. Adventus Angeli præcursoris, & Domini ceu Angeli fœderis.

Prædicitur adventus prodromi Christi Johannis eumque mox excepturi Domini ad templum suum venturi, instar ignis & smegmatis populum & Levitas purgaturi, ut Domino grata offerantur sacrificia, cum comminatione adversus incantatores, adulteros, perjuros, injustos oppressores, timoris DEI expertes, & ad- hortatione ad pœnitentiam, ne amplius Deo illudant decimarum & sacrificiorum fraudulenta oblatione, & promissione be- nedictionis divinæ; ac reprehensione Epi- curei dicterii de cultus divini inutilitate, commendatione vero piorum, divina re- cordatione sese solantium, qui in die Do- mini peculium ejus futuri improbis re- probatis.

Adventu Domini resipiscat terra propinquo.

Vers. 1.

ECCE EGO MITTO ANGELUM MEUM ET PRÆPARABIT VIAM ANTE FACIEM MEAM) Hoc est quod dicit: explorabo vos etiam atque etiam: neque ullum Prophetam vobis dabo, ante eum qui ante- ambulo erit Messiæ. Ante faciem meam dicit, quia in Messia vivit Deus, multo plenius ac perfectius quam in ullo Prophetarum: Διὰ τὴν ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν, ἀχώρι- στον, ἀδιάλειπτον.

ET STATIM.) Ubi ille venerit.

VENIET AD TEMPLUM SUUM.) In hoc Tem- plum secundum, quod ad excidium usque Vespafiani armis factum semper Templum secundum, בית שני Judæi vo- cant. In id Templum venire debuisse Messiam ante na- tum Dominum Jesum firma fide omnes Judæi tenuere & idem jam apertissime dixerat Aggæus 2, 8.

DOMINATOR QUEM VOS QUÆRITIS.) Ille promissus Siloh, qui vobis maxima bona, etiam in sta- tu publico, allaturus est, si ei pareatis, & vestrorum bo- norum etiam gentes exteras (de quibus dictum supra 1, 11.) faciet participes: dominator Davidis ex stirpe, rex mysti cus populi Dei, qui reipsa ostendet se regem regum, & dominum dominantium.

ET ANGELUS TESTAMENTI QUEM VOS VULTIS.) Legatus ille magnus, qui non quavis de re mittetur, sed ad pangendum foedus novum, melius ve- tere, cum Judæis & gentibus. De Messia hæc accipien da consensit Kimchi.

Cohærentiam itaque hujus vaticinii, quod fe- re unicum de Christo, quoad literam, agens in Prophetis reliquum nobis fecit, cæteris prope- modum omnibus in alienam personam detortis, hanc tradit Grotius, quod deficientibus per aliquot secula Prophetis, suo tempore DEUS singularem Prophetam Baptistam sese missurum promiserit, eumque statim sequuturus Messias sit. Verum quum de Prophetarum defectu nihil Propheta commemoretit, rectius alii alias assignant τῆς συν- εχείας rationes. Remotam quidem & generalem istam, quod in superioribus vitia sacerdotum sui temporis redarguerit, unde hic correctorem eorum sistere voluit Christum Pontificem; ita Ruper- tus. Atque eadem fere ratione etiam Cyrillus: Perapposite ad Christi mysterium verba ista prophe- tica transierunt. Factus est enim nobis a Deo & Patre Emmanuel justitia & sanctificatio & redem- tio & omnis immunditiæ emundatio, peccatorum- que depositio, & inhonestorum abjectio, & ad me- liora ac decentiora quædam via, & ad æternam vi- tam ceu janua & ingressus, & per ipsum correcta sunt omnia, & eversus diaboli dominatus, & in- venta justitia. Altera ratio specialior & immedia- ta est, quod atheis, Dei judicium & veritatem soli- citantibus ipso veluti facto respondeat: Dicebant illi, ubi est Deus judicii? Respondet Christus; nam hujus verba hæc sunt: Ecce adsum: nam mittam propediem angelum meum, & præparabit viam ante faciem meam. Hanc cohærentiam in- nuit Theodoretus: Dixisti, in quo provocavi- mus eum? cum vos non ignorare oporteret, Deum esse justitiæ fontem: unde sit ut vitia amplecten- tes detestetur; etsi dispensationis ratio divinæ sit " inexplicabilis, tamen vos doceo, quod venit tem- " pus justæ retributionis: id quod planum face- " re studens, prædicit primo priorum Domini " Christi adventum, & ostendit magnum Johannem " Baptistam hujus adventus præcursorem.

Verba hæc dixi esse ipsius Christi: Quod è superioribus primum constare potest: nam ora- tio & expostulatio illa Domini in capite secundo de alio intelligi nequit, quam de illo Domino, qui & communem nobiscum habet patrem & Dominum v. 10. Numquid non pater unus omnium nostrum? Numquid non Deus unus creavit nos, & se non vel- le ultra respicere ad sacrificium protestatur vers. 13. Qui alius non est quam Christus Joh. XX. 17. unde agnoscit Osiander ad v. 14. Dominum de Domi- no loqui, Filium æternum de æterno Patre. Tum vero verba ipsa, quæ jam tractamus, id luculenter indicant: Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, & præ- parabit viam ante faciem meam. Ea enim hic lo- quitur persona, cui viam præparavit Johannes Ba- ptista, & cujus prodromus & præcursor fuit: Ea: ante cujus faciem præivit, viam eidem præparans. At quæ illa, nisi Messias? Nam Johannes Baptista non fuit præcursor, nec præparavit viam ante Pa- trem & Sp. S. sed ante Filium. Solus enim Filius in carnem ad vos venit. Hujus itaque hæc verba es- se certum est: Et habemus hujus interpretationis testem ἀνυπεύθυνον locupletissimum S. Zachariam, Filio suo Johanni dicentem Luc. I. 76. Tu puer al- tissimi vocaberis, præibis enim ante faciem Domini parare viam ejus, Christi sc. qui per viscera mise- ricordiæ Dei nostri visitavit nos oriens ex alto; Neque officit, quod mox de Messia in tertia perso- na sermo fiat: Et statim veniet ad templum suum Dominator, quem vos quæritis, quia in his verbis jam Messias introducit ipsum patrem suum hæc pro- mittentem, ut verba subjuncta testantur: Ecce venit, DICIT DOMINUS EXERCITUUM, Pater meus cœlestis. Se ergo missurum prodro- mum suum primum testatur. Mox vero ulterioris certitudinis gratia Deum Patrem introduxit pro- mittentem adventum Messiæ ipsius, ceu Domini templi, & angeli testamenti desiderati: Quæ pru- denter discrevisse etiam S. Hieronym. video: Hoc er- go, quod dicitur, Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, & præparabit viam ante faciem meam: ex persone Christi dicitur: quod Johannem miserit in deserto Ju- dææ, prædicare Baptismum pœnitentiæ in remissio- nem peccatorum. Quod autem sequitur, Et statim veniet ad templum suum dominator, quem vos quæritis, & angelus testamenti, quem vos vultis: ita de se quasi de altero loquitur juxta consuetudinem scripturarum: Nullique dubium est, quin dominator iste salvatur sit: qui creator est omnium: & ange- lus testamenti, & magni consilii angelus appellatur. Atque hæc etiam causa est, quod Christus priora verba ipsi Patri quoque tribuere voluerit Matth. 11. 10. siquidem apud Malachiam non solum ipse lo- quutus fuerit de mittendo præcursore adventus sui, sed etiam in confirmationem proximi subse- quuturi adventus sui Deum Patrem adduxerit, & verbis suis id promittentem introduxerit. Adde, quod hæc missio S. Johannis ad opera ad extra per- tineat, quæ indivisa sunt S. S. Trinitati: Ideo uti Filius hic dicit: Ecce ego mitto angelum ante fa- ciem meam: ita patrem idem dicentem recte facit

Matth. XI. 10. Ecce ego mitto angelum meum an- te faciem tuam, ô Fili, qui preparabit viam tuam ante te. Quod pariter apud Marcum observatur c. I. 2. & apud Lucam c. VII. 29.

Argumentum, quo Judæi ex hoc loco con- vincuntur, collatis dictis Ef. XL. 1. Mal. IV. 5. 6. ita instruit Coccejus: Quem Angelus DEI mon- stravit, is est revera rex Israelis, dominus ille & Angelus Fœderis. Atqui Jesum Nazarenum An- gelus DEI monstravit. Redit huc res ut pro- betur Johannem Baptistam esse illum Angelum DEI. Id ita probatur: Qui venit proxime post ultimum Prophetarum Malachiam Doctor pœni- tentiæ, revocans Israelem ad fidem patrum, & de- nuntians adventum Christi & regni ejus: Is est re- vera Angelus is DEI. Atqui Johannes Baptista is est. Ratio consequentiæ est, 1. quia non erat Deus permissurus, ut veniret prodromus falsus. 2. Quia non convenit in eandem personam esse ve- racem in prædicatione pœnitentiæ, & esse fallacem in denuntiatione regni Dei. 3. Quia denunciatio regni DEI includit abolitionem regni hominum: quæ pars est virificata, unde necesse est & alteram partem huic connexam esse verificatam. 4. Quia proximus Malachiæ nullus alius venit. Impossi- bile autem est, propter verbum Dei, æque nul- lum venisse hactenus, atque alium venisse, aut nul- lum venire unquam.

In varias formas hic se convertunt Judæi. R. Salomo per angelum prodromum angelum mor- tis intelligit. Rab. Aben Ezra Messiam filium Jo- sephi, Abarbenel Malachiam ipsum, R. Kimchi Angelum cælestem, conferens Ex. 23. Angelum Fœderis interpretatur idem Rab. David Kimchi de Elia, eumque distinguit à Domino, qui secundum ipsum est Davidis filius: Eliam autem fingunt Ju- dæi angelum Testamenti dictum, quia zelatus fue- rit fœdus circumcisionis, ideo in circumcisione ad- huc adornant Eliæ sellam, putantes eum adesse, & zelari pro lege Domini. R. Aben Ezra de gloria & Dominum & angelum fœderis explicat, A- barbanel reliquos refellens, Messiam per Domi- num & angelum fœderis intelligi fatetur. B. Hie- ronymus paucis sed solide ita Judæos convincit: Judæi hoc quod dicitur: ecce ego mitto angelum meum, de Helia propheta dictum intelligunt, & quod sequitur: statim veniet ad templum suum domina- tor, & quem vos quæritis, & angelus testamenti quem vos vultis: referunt ad ἠλειμμένον, hoc est Christum suum: quem dicunt ultimo tempore esse venturum: sed miror, quomodo eos rerum exitus non doceat veritatem. Quod enim templum suum inveniet dominator, quod usque ad fundamentum de- structum est? aut si ab alio extruendum est, ante- quam Christus adveniat: quid Christus eorum am- plius facturus est, cum ab alio restituta sint omnia? Dominus noster in Evangelio Heliam Prophetam Jo- annem Baptistam interpretans loquitur: Si vultis scire, ipse est Helias, qui venturus est: de quo & hic idem Propheta, quem nunc disserimus, scribit in fine: Ecce ego mitto vobis Heliam Prophetam, an- tequam veniat dies Domini magnus & horribilis. Quomodo autem Helias Joannes sit: dedit vobis viam intelligentiæ: in virtute & spiritu Heliæ eum venisse commemorans. Hæc Hieronymus.

Nos summatim pleraque argumenta compre- hendemus, quæ adversus Judæos ex hoc oracu- lo urgeri, & quod assertionem Deitatis Christi atti- net, Socinianis etiam aliisque Deitatis Christi ho- stibus opponi possint. Primum à tempore adven- tus. Quia innuitur post Malachiam, qui Prophe- tarum ultimus fuit, testibus Judæis, non expe- ctandum alium angelum & legatum Dei immedia- te à Deo missum, donec veniat angelus hic Messiæ prodromus. Et quum Dominus testetur: Ecce ego mitto angelum, atque iterum Deus de Messia quasi præsente ac brevi adfuturo: Ecce VE- NIT, quomodo id Messiæ, vel ἠλειμμένῳ, quem expectant Judæi, conveniebat Malachiæ tempo- re, qui post millia annorum demum venturus erat? Ecce, ut habet paraphrasis Tarnoviana, inquit Salvator apud Prophetam, attentionem excitans, quia res magnas erat dicturus, vos blaspheme quæritis: Vbi est Deus judicii? tempore divi- nitus constituto certissime me videndum vobis præbebo, ego ipse, qui sum judicium annunciatu- rus, imo judicium ad victoriam prolaturus Matth. XII. 18. 20. paulo post missurus sum (Benoni pro paulo post futuro, ut alibi notavimus) quod non caret emphasi hoc loco, siquidem miraculose fuit conceptus, natus & educatus, sicut Luc. I. prolixe describitur, angelum meum, nuncium & legatum præcipuum, quo nemo major inter natos ex mulieribus extitit, Johannem baptistam Matth. XI. 10. &c. Marc. I. 2. Luc. II. 17. & VII. 27. Joh. I. 6. 33. qui expediat, Hebr. וּפִנָּה, ו pro relativo אֲשֶׁר ut Psalm. v. 12. quod tamen simul præteritum vertit in futurum, & verbum ipsum notat, removere ex conspectu ea quæ futura e- rant ingrata incessuro viam ante me, clamans, parate viam Domini, complanate semitas ejus Matth. III. 3. omnis vallis implebitur, & omnis mons & collis deprimetur, & quæ curva sunt, fient recta, & aspera viæ fient planæ, videbitque omnis caro sa- lutem Dei Luc. III. v. 5. 6. Marc. I. 3. Johann. I. 23. ex Jes. XL. 3. 4. 5.

Deinde à circumstantia loci, venire debuit Mes- sias ad templum suum, fatente Abarbenele, & qui- dem ad illud templum, in quo illi abusus erant despecti altaris Domini, & oblationum illegiti- marum, quos reprehendit Malachias. Id ve- ro templum jam ante sedecim fere secula solo æ- quatum est. Cyrillus, Theodoretes & Augusti- nus l. XIIX. de Civitate Dei cap. 35. intelligunt templum corporis Christi Johann. II. 19. sed ange- lus fœderis ad templum venire debuit post missio- nem Johannis ad præparandam viam, quæ facta est, cum Christus triginta annos jam haberet. Hieronymus, atque itidem Cyrillus de Ecclesia ex- plicant, vel de fidelibus: at talis adventus gratiæ ad fideles nullo defuit tempore, ideoque de materiali templo idem Hieronymus rectius expli- cat, & plerique alii, ac de templo secundo veteres etiam Judæi intellexere, in quo tanquam propria domo se ostendere debuit, post præparatam viam ab angelo prodromo. Quod vero ante tot secula in cineres & favillas redactum.

Tertio à prodromo angeli fœderis, quem Johan- nem Baptistam esse, antea ostensum. Nec alium monstrare possunt Judæi. Quam ineptæ enim eorum sint sententiæ, vel sola earum recitatio docent.

Quarto à Messiæ designatione. Vocatur enim DOMINUS ILLE δεικτικῶς, ut notetur ille

Dominus, qui adeo celebratur in Scripturis sub no- mine Domini, distincta tamen est persona a Deo Pa- tre Domino exercituum, utpote qui hic loquitur de illo Domino ceu distincta persona. Quis autem ille, nisi Messias? qui Dominus ἀντονομαςικῶς di- citur, quem David ipse, superiorem in terris non habens, pro Domino suo agnovit Pf. 110, 1. in quo tanquam in basi (אדן) omnia subsistunt Col. 1, 17. Ideo fatetur R. David. Kimchi per Dominum Fi- lium Davidis hic intelligi, & Abarbenel agnoscit Christum indigitari.

Quinto a templi appropriatione. Ejus adven- tus designatur, qui est Dominus templi, & cujus templum est. Dicitur enim Dominus venturus ad templum SUUM. At hoc de ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ intelligi nequit. Templum habere est ἀξίωμα divinum. Omne templum Dei templum est, ait Ba- sil. Epist. CXLI. vid. Exod. 34, 16. Pf. 26, 1. Reg. 13, 6. cap. 9. Hagg. c. 1, 9. cap. 2, 8. 16. Zach. 3, 7. c. 8, 9. Messiam ergo oportet esse verum Deum.

Sexto a Domini descriptione. Dicitur ille Dominus quem quærebant. Qua voce secundum nonnullos desideria piorum denotantur, qui ex- pectabant & anhelabant unice adventum Messiæ neque alium quendam Dominum desiderarunt. Conf. Luc. 2, 25. cap. 10, 24. Dici etiam potest quod verba illa, quem quæritis, respiciant ea, quæ sub finem cap. 2, 17. habentur: ubi est Deus judicii. Nam ipse est Rex Filius Regis, cui danda judicia Dei Pfal. 72, 1. Adde Es. 11, 3. 4. Sic verbum בקש in malam partem cum Tremell. accipit Tarnovius: quia antecedentia in quæstione v. 17. cap. 2. & con- sequentia hoc c. 3, 2. de malis, & ira Dei erga ipsos agunt, deinde, quia, quoad rem ipsam, loci paralleli hanc explicationem firmant, siquidem bonum ma- le quæri posse, & curiose ac cum ludibrio deside- rari sæpe inde constat, vide Esa. 5, 19. Amos 5, 18. 2. Petr. 3, 3. Unde a particulari concludunt, qui ita colligunt: Ubicunque homines aliquid divinum quærunt aut desiderant, bonus rei bonæ appetitus ad promissiones Dei se referens, intelligitur. Hæc ille; sed prior explicatio receptior est.

Septimo a nomine angeli. Vocatur enim AN- GELUS simpliciter. Solus autem Messias ad hanc legationem mitti potuit: nam angelis subjici non potest Ecclesia Ebr. 2, 5. Et respicitur hic angelus singularis, in scripturis celebris, populo promissus, atque sæpe eidem conspectus: angelus, quem Patriarchæ confessi sunt Genes. 48, 16. qui Mosen vocavit Exod. 3. cum Mose fuit in monte, eique legem dedit Actor. 7, 34. cujus vox concussit terram tunc Pf. 58, 8. 9. 29. Ebr. 12, 16. qui Israeli- tas deduxit Exod. 14. c. 23, 20. Angelus faciei Do- mini, qui eos salvavit Pf. 113, 9.

Octavo a peculiari angeli nuncupatione. Dici- tur angelus fœderis, de quo, in quo & per quem est fœdus. Et hoc elogio contradistinguitur Mo- si, & supra eum extollitur. Quippe Moses non fuit interpres fœderis ad Noachum, Abrahamum & cæ- teros Patriarchas, sed tantum ad Israelitas. Hic autem est angelus fœderis simpliciter; intellige fœ- deris, quod unquam fecit Deus cum suis, in quem jussit credere omnes, ad habendum fœdum cum Deo, atque adeo fœderis Novi, quod Jeremias cap. 31. promittit: nimirum de justificatione, inscriptio- ne in cor &c. Quod hic est Angelus fœderis, ei
